## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a Chronological Reprint of all the Monuments of Catholic Tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, diligently collated with one another and with certain manuscripts; most carefully corrected and continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating the subject matter contained below; expanded by works that are doubtful or apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be viewed at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual books of Scripture, and in which places of their works they did so.**

**The most accurate edition, and readily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection itself, which is unified, methodical, and chronological, bringing together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, collected from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

**FIRST SERIES. In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.**

## To the Works of

# Saint Augustine

## Bishop of Hippo

### Supplement

**Containing the celebrated investigations of the critics and defenders of the holy Doctor concerning his works, as well as the minor works of Saint Augustine, previously unpublished, brought to light by various collectors of unpublished texts, namely Amadutio, Mai, Mingarelli, and Fontani. Also included is the latest collection of variant readings in the sermons of the holy Father, whether genuine or spurious, which the most learned U. Caillau and B. Saint-Yves extracted from various manuscripts.**

**A single volume desirable—indeed necessary—for all students of Augustinian doctrine, whatever edition of his works, however commendable or extensive, they may possess: for no edition among the almost innumerable editions that have appeared since the invention of printing contains the rarest and most precious monuments which we have first undertaken to gather, lest the immortal edifice of the holy Father should for too long lack the crowning work desired by the hopes of scholars.**

# Supplement to the Works of St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo

[Col. 0009]

# Literary Notice on the Life, Writings, and Editions of the Works of St. Augustine

*(Schoenemann’s Library, Leipzig, 1794.)*

## Chapter One: The Life of St. Augustine

[Col. 0009A]

He was born at Tagaste, an obscure town of Africa in the interior of Numidia, situated not far from Madaura and Hippo Regius, on the Ides of November in the year 354—that is, in the three hundred and fifty-fourth year—to respectable parents belonging to the class of curiales, or those who administered public offices in the municipalities, as Possidius reports.

His father was Patricius, of modest means but generous and well-disposed toward everyone, though also irascible and fierce, as Augustine himself portrays him [Note: [Col. 0009C] *Confessions*, book IX, nos. 9 and 19.]; only toward the end of his life did he embrace the Christian faith. His mother was Monica, a name of the highest distinction among Christians. From the cradle she immediately imbued her children with an awareness and love of the Christian religion.

Concerning his infancy, his earliest education, and subsequently the training of his boyhood, Augustine himself related more in the *Confessions* than was necessary or useful for illuminating the later events of his life. His was evidently a lively, or rather ardent, intelligence as a boy and adolescent, partly inherited from his father’s blood and partly derived from the nature of the climate.

His father, as is clear from various recollections Augustine left of him, loved his children to the very marrow and rejoiced inwardly in whatever powers of mind or body they displayed. His pious mother, certainly no less prudent, nevertheless indulged her son’s inclination to a great extent; if he applied himself energetically to his studies, he seemed to her to be receiving a sufficiently good upbringing.

Thus, as he grew older, the seeds of immense vices matured along with him. Had they not utterly destroyed him, they nevertheless seemed likely to draw him away from the Christian faith and make him entirely estranged from it. After spending some time at Madaura chiefly on Latin literature and the elements of oratory—for at that time he was disgusted with Greek literature and afterward touched it only lightly—he was sent to Carthage [Col. 0010A] to cultivate his study of eloquence, the only path then open to men of moderate birth for attaining glory and wealth either in the courts or in the schools. For this purpose, as he himself relates, his father, eager for glory, supplied him with more money than the family’s resources could afford.

There he came to give himself, partly because he was enticed for a time by the examples of the city and his fellow students, partly because of his own natural inclination, and partly because he did not feel the limits of his means, to a more dissolute life. Before he was scarcely eighteen, he fathered by a concubine a son, Adeodatus, whom he praises more than once in his writings as a frugal and keen-minded boy, and whose premature death, in the very flower of adolescence, he mourned as a loss.

But before this boy was born, he lost his father. Nevertheless, he did not thereby suffer any great interruption in his studies [Col. 0010B], since his mother provided for his necessities by whatever means she could, and the generosity of a certain Romanian—whom for this reason he warmly praises—ensured that he lacked nothing, not merely for the necessities but also for the pleasures of life.

At about this time, when he was nineteen years old, he applied himself to the knowledge of wisdom, or philosophy, suddenly stimulated by Cicero’s book entitled *Hortensius*, which urged the embrace of wisdom. This thought so completely seized and held him for a time that, immediately setting aside his rhetorical exercises, he rejected and despised all hopes of advancement that did not seem capable of being joined with philosophy or of arising from it, although he still remained hesitant, as though caught among winding paths and rough places, uncertain which road he ought to enter upon [Col. 0010C].

On the one hand, he was drawn toward Christian teaching by a certain inward agitation of mind, touched and, as it were, breathed upon by some remnant of religious feeling left over from his earliest childhood. On the other hand, the various and manifold schools of the ancient Greek and Roman sages invited him [Col. 0011A].

But when he once began to read the Holy Scriptures, he was suddenly seized by such a distaste for their humble and, as it seemed to him, lowly style that, for one filled with Ciceronian dignity, it can be said that he avoided this path not merely by turning aside from it but by fleeing from it.

He therefore devoted himself to the other disciplines, though he did not entrust himself to the instruction of any teacher, but pursued them by his own study. He first seized upon Aristotle’s *Categories*, which he had heard his Carthaginian rhetorician and teacher praise extravagantly. He not only read them by himself but also understood them, as he discovered through conversations with those who had learned them at school, both orally and by means of figures drawn in the dust.

From that time onward he likewise read by himself all the books of the liberal arts, and understood all that he was able to read: everything concerning the art of speaking and reasoning, everything concerning the dimensions of figures, music, and numbers, without great difficulty and without anyone teaching him.

Through this very concern for attaining wisdom he fell in with the Manichaeans, whom, after he had come to know them thoroughly, he aptly calls “men deliriously proud, carnal, and talkative.” For while they promised their initiates some kind of hidden and abstruse wisdom, they sold trifles and empty subtleties; and, professing sobriety and chastity with their lips, they stained their lives with every kind of wickedness and depravity.

Although these things could not escape Augustine’s perceptive mind, they nevertheless could not prevent him from following them for nine full years, to his mother’s immense grief. What kept him in their company therefore seems to have been almost nothing other than the pleasing hope that, after passing through the stages of auditor and the other ranks of learners and teachers, he would at last penetrate to their mysteries.

Meanwhile he first taught grammar at Tagaste, where he had withdrawn for a time; after returning from there to Carthage, he taught rhetoric there. At that time also, in the twenty-sixth or twenty-seventh year of his age, he wrote his first books, *On the Fit and the Beautiful*, but these had already perished by the time he wrote the *Confessions*.

In the midst of these events, some of his friends who had decided to set out for Rome persuaded him to accompany them, promising both greater honor and more substantial profit in that city, where literary studies were nourished by very generous rewards, and where young men attending their teachers’ benches differed greatly from the ferocity of the Carthaginians in modesty of conduct and a certain orderliness of study [Col. 0011D].

Yet he scarcely managed, by a kind of stratagem, to tear himself from his mother’s embraces. When at last he arrived in Rome, he was afflicted by a serious illness that brought him close to death. As soon as he had recovered somewhat, he opened a school and found his pupils indeed far removed from Carthaginian license; but they had a very bad reputation because of the dishonest practice by which, as though conspiring against the teacher to whom they owed their fees, they would abandon him after attending his lectures for some time and transfer to another. He despised this conduct.

After the people of Milan had asked Symmachus, the prefect of the city [Col. 0012A], to provide them with a teacher of rhetoric, Augustine sought the position. Having been approved after delivering a speech, he was sent by Symmachus to Milan, about the year 384.

This, then, was the place from which the conversion and transformation of his entire life took its origin. At first he had attended the sermons of Ambrose, bishop of that city, which he customarily delivered to the people on appointed days, for no other reason than the charm of his eloquence. Gradually, however, the subjects themselves entered Augustine’s mind together with the words. First they shook the doctrines of the Manichaeans, which he had long wished to prove false; soon afterward, when he himself began to oppose them with all the powers of his intellect and spirit, they overthrew them completely.

It was shortly after this recent victory over his long-standing heresy [Col. 0012B] that his mother came to Milan. She had been unable to console herself from the time her son first crossed over to Italy, and she was overcome with extraordinary joy at the new state of affairs.

Although he had cast off that heresy and seemed to have returned to the Catholic faith, he was nevertheless uncertain what course of life and study he should pursue thereafter. He was harassed and tossed about by the goads of doubt and the rapid fluctuation of his plans. At one moment he devoted himself to one undertaking, at another to another; whatever he had just begun, he abandoned again halfway through, and, having scarcely entered upon a path elsewhere, stopped.

There was then no circumstance, whether in his own affairs or those of others, however accidental, that did not either torment his mind with some fresh anxiety or kindle it with some new purpose. The reading of the Platonists also greatly nourished and intensified this agitation of mind, through the frequent impulses of his senses and the violence of his emotions; he devoted a great deal of time to it.

To these he added the letters of Paul, whose obscure meaning, joined with its gravity, can readily be understood to have struck a mind suspended between fears and terrors and phantasms of every kind. There were also daily conversations with his intimate friends Alypius and Nebridius. The latter had come from Carthage to Milan for no other reason than to remain close to Augustine; the former discussed day and night plans for sharing their lives and establishing a permanent fellowship with one another.

Add to this his mother’s never-resting anxiety, sighs, and prayers, which she poured out tirelessly to God for the salvation of her son, both in the churches and at home [Col. 0012D]. These things could not possibly remain hidden from Augustine; indeed, they constituted a very large part of his intercourse with her. Add also the admonitions, exhortations, and friendly reproaches of Ambrose, and you will understand that there would have been few people whom such disturbances of mind would not have broken and wholly crushed.

Yet Augustine’s experience was otherwise, owing to the good fortune of his intellect and the fiery nature of his imagination. When he and Alypius heard a certain Pontitianus, an African serving in the palace of Valentinian at Milan, relate the life of St. Antony, the tumult and surging emotion of his heart so overcame all the perceptions and ideas of his mind that, every external impulse having been excluded, he seemed to seek heaven in thought and to compel the divine power itself, as it were, to intervene in this tumult.

For suddenly, as it seemed to him, a voice was heard by divine agency; and all this frenzy subsided, making room for calmer deliberations about shaping his manner of life.

Accordingly, he first decided—this occurred in 386—to bid farewell to all earthly concerns. He rejected the plan of marriage that had most recently settled in his mind; he came to despise the pursuit of glory through literature; and soon afterward, when the autumn vacation arrived, he resigned his teaching position.

Thus released from the gravest bonds of duties and desires, he withdrew to the countryside, to the estate at Cassiciacum, and in conversations with his mother and friends spent a holy leisure, wholly devoted to God, discussing useful and often subtle questions.

The various minor works that arose from his conversations with his friends during this period and were published by him can readily be identified from the date that each bears in the catalogue [Col. 0013B].

At length he returned from this retreat to Milan in order to receive holy baptism from Ambrose. This took place during the vigil of Easter, on the night before 25 April in the year 387.

Soon afterward, he and his friends Alypius and Evodius—the latter likewise from Tagaste—formed the plan of returning to Africa, serving God together and living in one community, and of seeking there a place suitable for their way of life. Monica cared for all of them as though she were the parent of each.

His brother Navigius and his son Adeodatus were with him. But when he reached Ostia on the Tiber, his excellent mother was suddenly seized by an illness and died—according to the calculations of the Benedictines, a few days [Col. 0013C] before the Ides of November in the year 387.

He expressed the grief caused by her death in the truest words, saying that his life, which had become one life formed from his own and hers, had been, as it were, torn apart [Note: [Col. 0013D] *Confessions*, book IX, chapter 12, no. 30.].

Now deprived of so sweet a companion on his journey, he postponed his return to Africa for a time and turned aside to Rome. Although he had previously lived on the most intimate terms with the Manichaeans, and they wished to restore the relationship interrupted by his departure, he refused them and seriously reproached them for their errors and depraved manner of life.

After various initial skirmishes, he finally launched into that open war against all of them individually and collectively which he waged with the utmost vigor, in speech and writing, without any relaxation of strength or spirit, until his death.

While established at Rome, therefore, he wrote without interruption books whose fame soon spread throughout all Africa: *On the Morals of the Catholic Church* and *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*. In these he sought to restrain their boastfulness concerning their false and deceptive continence.

There also he began the work *On Free Will*, against their arguments concerning the origin of evil. They derived evil from some immutable nature coeternal with God, whereas he derived it from the free choice of the will.

In these books—not yet, that is, in the first book, which alone he composed at Rome, while he added the other two when he was already a presbyter—he did not address the question of the grace of God, by which he had predestined his elect in such a way that, even in those who already made use of free will, he himself also prepared their wills. The only question at issue was the origin of evil, not how one might return to the original good or attain a greater good [Note: [Col. 0013D] *Retractations*, book I, chapter 9, § 2.].

Yet the Pelagians often afterward appealed to these same books, as though Augustine had defended their cause in them. In the books of the *Retractations*, he was therefore quite concerned to show the connection and, as it were, kinship between what he had argued at that time and his later opinions.

He left Rome in August or September of the year 388. At the end of winter he arrived in Africa and proceeded through Carthage to Tagaste, where he decided to live in the countryside—that is, on the ancestral lands that had fallen to him by hereditary right [Note: [Col. 0013D] Possidius, in the *Life of Augustine*, chapter 3, relates that as soon as Augustine had returned to Tagaste, he sold his lands and distributed the proceeds to the poor. If this report truly came from him [Col. 0014D], he must either have lived on lands that had been alienated or that belonged entirely to someone else, or at least have retained part of his own.].

He spent there almost three years, far from all worldly concerns, devoted to sacred meditations and exercises, differing scarcely at all from a monk.

He had adopted for the same way of life some friends, and he did not object when their number increased. He calls both this way of life and the place where they lived a monastery [Note: [Col. 0014D] *Sermon* 355, chapter 1, no. 2.].

Meanwhile, both the fame of his writings, which he issued from time to time in quite substantial volumes, and the reputation of this admirable life had spread so widely that his retreat was being talked about everywhere. He therefore took care not to visit places lacking a bishop, fearing that, if he were recognized, he might be forced against his will into the episcopate.

All the more unexpected, then, was what happened when, toward the end of 391, he went to Hippo Regius on behalf of a friend whom he hoped to win for God and have live with him in the monastery. He felt secure because the place already had a bishop. While he was attending the sermons of Valerius, Augustine was suddenly seized, amid the great tumult and acclamation of everyone, at Valerius’s suggestion that a presbyter needed to be ordained. No matter how much he resisted, he was made a presbyter.

It is reported that some people, seeing him shed tears, suspected that they were tears of regret that he had not immediately become a bishop. They attempted to console him by suggesting that the presbyterate was indeed beneath his dignity but nevertheless came immediately before the episcopate.

His tears, however, had another and more worthy cause, as he himself declared more than once in his writings. This entire responsibility of sacred office seemed to him far more exalted and serious than it did to the many who commonly sought it; and he feared that he did not possess within himself as much support as was necessary to discharge it properly [Col. 0014D].

For this reason, he asked that the period between his ordination and the feast of Easter in 392 be granted to him for preparation. When his request was granted, he withdrew into solitude.

The beginnings of his ministry may therefore rightly be reckoned from this time. His first concern was to establish a monastery at Hippo as well. Valerius assisted his wish by granting him the garden of the church of Hippo [Col. 0015A] for this purpose.

He next found, through the same Valerius, another splendid opportunity to benefit the Church and at the same time make his own name illustrious, because Valerius allowed him to preach in his presence. Previously this had been unusual for presbyters in the Latin churches; but once Valerius, a Greek by birth and slower in his use of the Latin language, had taken the lead, many bishops throughout Africa imitated the practice.

Amid these and the other interruptions of his office, Augustine did not cease, in writing, either to clarify and strengthen among his people the more important doctrines of the faith, or to establish and defend them against those who thought differently or incorrectly. He also maintained constant correspondence with very many friends, both those close to him geographically and those living at a great distance.

The esteem in which this presbyter was held by everyone, including the bishops of Africa [Col. 0015B], was so great and so free from envy that men of the highest rank among them, such as Aurelius, readily accepted his counsel. At the Council of Hippo in 393, they all went so far as to command him—without precedent—to deliver a discourse before them on the faith and the creed.

For all these reasons, Valerius, fearing with no empty apprehension that Augustine might suddenly be summoned to govern some church lacking a bishop, asked Aurelius, bishop of Carthage and primate of all Africa, for permission to make him his colleague and co-bishop.

When this had been granted, Valerius immediately announced it in the presence of his clergy and people and of several bishops. With the great agreement of everyone, he asked Megalius, bishop of Calama and primate of Numidia, whose responsibility this was, to ordain Augustine as bishop.

Megalius initially opposed his ordination, accusing him of some unspecified crime. But when, in the course of this very dispute, he learned that the accusation was false, he regretted his slander and no longer withheld his consent to the ordination.

Augustine himself also resisted, and he could be overcome only after several examples had been produced—not merely African but also overseas examples—showing that the practice of placing another bishop over a church while its existing bishop was still alive was not contrary to ecclesiastical custom.

The Benedictines aptly remarked at this point, in order to display the man’s character, concerning his refusal:

> His modesty and religious devotion were no less than those of the many illustrious men who, in that age, as he writes [Note: [Col. 0015D] His own words in *Letter to Donatus* 173, no. 3.], were held unwilling, led forward, shut in, guarded, and subjected to many things they did not want, until they became willing to undertake the good work.

His ordination took place toward the end of the year 395 or at the beginning of the following year.

Into this exceptionally eminent dignity he poured so much of his own honor and renown that the Latin Church has known no bishop more illustrious than he. For although, even before his elevation to the episcopate, the renown of the presbyter Augustine had been immense, and bishops themselves were not ashamed to carry out his counsels and wishes, his authority had not yet been confirmed by ecclesiastical laws, and his freedom of action remained circumscribed by the will of another.

But once he had been raised to govern the Church of Hippo, not only his co-bishop Valerius, but also Aurelius, bishop of Carthage and primate of all Africa, the entire African Church together with him, and indeed the churches overseas throughout the whole of the West, as well as very many churches in the regions of the East, came to depend upon his direction and administration.

Our present purpose, however, is not to compose a history of all his deeds and achievements, since these are so closely bound up with the entire sequence of those times and events that it could scarcely be done with proper coherence without a careful [Col. 0016B] narration of them; nor, if the subject were less foreign to our purpose, would they require our labor after the diligence of so many eminent men. What may be expected here is a portrait of the man as he was from this period onward, drawn from his writings and the memory of his deeds; and if I have not judged sharply enough what selection of colors ought to have been made, I shall not resent the criticism.

First, consideration of his private life belongs here. By nature he was impetuous and easily moved by his emotions, so that whatever was placed before him he would immediately embrace, and he often exceeded moderation in enjoyment. He therefore undertook daily exercises to remedy this illness and weakness of the soul—namely, contemplation of himself and investigation of his faults, together with constant prayer and the effort to increase God’s love within him. This last was especially his defense, which he was accustomed to employ against the assaults and snares of desire. In order either to restrain these swift movements and frequent tremors of the senses or at least to impede them, he needed to turn himself elsewhere through a kind of inward exertion and an elevation—or rather rapture—of the mind toward higher thoughts. It is well known that men of lively intelligence have been capable of this to a very great degree, at all times and in every kind of contemplation.

Nor was this effort a weakness of the brain, nor did it throw his mind out of its proper state. Even in such matters he employed a mode of reasoning peculiar to himself, and he seemed to be inflamed as though by perfect knowledge and a nearer vision. Hence he complained inwardly of his weariness, which prevented him from loving God as he wished. For he feared forming a bodily image of God, yet desired by sensation to embrace what belonged solely to the intellect. He praises God’s beauty and sweetness, says that his life runs toward God’s embrace, and conversed with him as with a friend and familiar, in gentle speech.

[Note: Confessions XIII.8.9: “Give me yourself, my God; restore yourself to me. For I love you, and if that is too little, let me love you more powerfully. I cannot measure, so as to know how much love is lacking in me for what would be enough, so that my life may run into your embraces and not turn away until it is hidden in the hiding-place of your face. This alone I know: it is evil apart from you, not only outside me, but also within me; and every abundance that is not God is poverty for me!” The same book, chapter 29 and following, at the end: “And I paid attention in order to discover whether you had seen seven or eight times, because your works are good when they please you; yet in your vision I did not find times by which I might understand that you had seen so many times the things you made. And I said, ‘O Lord, is not this your Scripture true, since you are truthful and Truth itself produced it? Why, then, do you tell me that there are no times in your vision, while your Scripture tells me day by day that the things you saw were good when you saw them? And when I counted them, I found how many times.’ To this you reply to me, since you are my God, and with a strong voice, breaking through my deafness into my inner ear, crying out: ‘O man, what my Scripture says, I say. Yet it speaks temporally, whereas no time affects my Word, because it remains with me in equal eternity. Thus I see the things you see through my Spirit, just as I say the things you say through my Spirit. And although you see them temporally, I do not see them temporally.’ And I heard, O Lord my God, and tasted a drop of sweetness from your truth.”]

Yet he never ceased correcting whatever faults he detected in himself; but he did so in such a way that he did not claim the credit for himself, believing rather that God himself was working within him, so that he in turn might embrace God with ever greater love from day to day. From this arose that view concerning God’s operation in human beings, or divine grace as the effective agent, which dominated much of his entire life.

Besides this, he was approachable and gentle, and wished well both to individuals and to his whole Church. The correction of morals was one of his foremost concerns; and, attributing nothing to artificial religion, he could clearly distinguish what arose from a proper intention of the soul and what proceeded from a momentary agitation or some frivolity. This is shown by so many of his counsels, admonitions, and exhortations communicated in letters, whether to friends or to others of every kind.

Nor did he enforce the discipline of the Church with severe laws, and he was exceedingly sparing in punishment. Likewise, he was not greedy in increasing the Church’s property, since he did not seek inheritances, and even refused and returned some that had been offered to him. For this reason some criticized him, saying that he took insufficient care of the Church’s goods.

Although he had previously been exceedingly eager for the solitary life, he could no longer pursue it because of the affairs of a bishop and the duties of hospitality imposed upon him by his new office. He therefore established a new monastery within the episcopal residence itself, from which he used periodically to advance younger students to ecclesiastical ministries. In Africa the administration of many different affairs was indeed joined to the office of a bishop in such a place. Yet in handling all of them he conducted himself so that people never thought the African Church had flourished more than when he presided over its affairs—not by the legal right of his office, but through the highest authority.

He preached not only without interruption on appointed days, but also very frequently on other occasions, and never without a great gathering and eager attention. He himself labored at this with the greatest ardor and intensity, even to exhaustion, so that his words might penetrate the minds of his hearers, strike them, move them, and set them on fire.

[Note: His words deserve to be read, as they often are by many and by the public at large, from On Catechizing the Uninstructed, chapter 2, §3: “Almost always my speech displeases me. For I am eager for something better, which I often enjoy inwardly before I begin to express it in sounding words. When I unfold it less adequately than it is known to me, I am distressed that my tongue has not [lacuna] been able to suffice for my heart. For I want all that I understand to be understood by the one who hears me; and I feel that I do not speak in such a way as to achieve this, especially because that understanding pours through the mind like a rapid flash of lightning, whereas speech is slow and extended and very unlike it. While speech is unfolding, the understanding has already withdrawn into its secret places; yet because it has impressed certain traces upon the memory in a wondrous manner, those traces remain along with the little delays of the syllables, and from those same traces we produce sounding signs. But we, usually burning intensely for the benefit of our hearer, wish to speak as we understand at the moment when, through the very intensity of our attention, we cannot speak. Since this does not succeed, we are distressed, and, as though we were laboring in vain, we wither from weariness. From this weariness the same speech becomes more languid and dull than it was when the weariness began. Yet the eagerness of those who wish to hear me often shows me that my eloquence is not as cold as it seems to me; and I recognize from their enjoyment that they derive some benefit from it. I therefore diligently urge myself not to fail in providing this service, in which I see that they gladly receive what is offered.”]

Moreover, every day he answered those who consulted him, whether they were present or questioned him about private matters, the affairs of the Church and the faith, morals, or—most frequently of all—passages of the Bible. I say nothing of those who, following a custom long established in the Churches, used to seek the bishop’s arbitration in contentious cases before bringing their dispute before the law; such appeals consumed no small amount of his time.

Those questions that, as we have said, were habitually brought to him generally arose from trivial circumstances and from the empty and frivolous diligence of the Africans. In this matter Erasmus truly said something that, if it had ever been said, would be worth quoting:

“His intellect would have yielded us richer fruits if it had happened to be born or to live in Italy or Gaul. Africa was uncultivated, eager for pleasures, hostile to learning, and desirous of curious matters. Hence they frequently wearied him with frivolous questions that contributed little to piety, and he was often forced to adapt his pen to the inclinations of his people. Yet such a thorny thicket required such a cultivator. Although he would have written works more worthy of reading if he had adapted himself either to the judgments of Romans or Greeks or had indulged less in the ignorance of simple people, Christian charity prefers to benefit the greatest possible number rather than to win the approval of the eminent; it thirsts more for the salvation of its brothers than for its own glory.”

Some people, especially little women, were also possessed by a kind of pious ambition, considering it a fine thing to obtain from a bishop some writing of any sort. Thus, while the devout man complied with everyone’s wishes, he sometimes satisfied the fastidious reader less well.

[Note: In the preface prefixed to the letters, which appears in volume II of the works, immediately on the reverse of the title page.]

This madness was not confined to Africa; in Italy and in other provinces of the West there were also people who thought that every question could be solved and explained by him as though by some oracle. He often had to answer them not merely in letters but in entire volumes, since, out of the utmost charity no less than from a desire for praise and honor—which he remained exceedingly eager for until the end of his life—he wished to satisfy everyone.

The public care of the Church then frequently summoned him to councils and synods. In these, discussion concerned either the general preservation, restoration, or moderation of Church discipline; particular customs; judgments regarding the life and conduct of individual clergy; or, finally, prudent measures for confirming and safeguarding doctrine. The teachings and practices of heretics and schismatics were condemned and attacked.

He therefore took part in the councils of which the following are known: the Carthaginian councils—the fourth in 398, the fifth in the same year, and the sixth and seventh, held in 419 concerning appeals; the third African council in 401 and the fourth in 407; the Conference against the Donatists in 411; the Council at Cirta against the same group in 412; and the Council at Milevis against the Pelagians in 418. Just as none of these synods produced clearer acts than those concerned with attacking heresies, so none of Augustine’s deeds, whether performed in them or on his own initiative, were more distinguished than those undertaken against the heretics of his age.

Here Schoenemann, indulging too much in the character of his own party, pursues St. Augustine’s most celebrated struggles against heresy with such hostility that he seems to be acting less as a historian than as a slanderer. We have therefore cut away whatever remained of his Notice and had been inserted into our columns with excessive confidence, and we supplement it from Possidius, applying a reparative sheet; preferring to repeat what has been said elsewhere rather than to publish heretical material. EDITOR.

“Possidius says: ‘He taught and preached, privately and publicly, at home and in church, the word of salvation with complete confidence against the African heresies, especially against the Donatists, Manichaeans, and pagans. He did so in completed books and in spontaneous sermons, to the unspeakable admiration and joy of Christians, who, wherever they could, did not keep silent about it but spread the news. Thus, with the Lord’s help, the Catholic Church in Africa began to lift its head. For a long time it had lain deceived and oppressed there while the heretics grew stronger, especially when the Donatist party, which rebaptized, had seduced the greater part of the Africans. Even the heretics themselves, coming together with the Catholics, listened with immense eagerness to these books or treatises of his, which by God’s wondrous grace proceeded and flowed forth, equipped with abundant reasoning and the authority of the holy Scriptures. Whoever wished and was able employed stenographers, and some even copied out what was said after it had been recorded.

“‘His statements and the things recorded from them, especially among the Donatists who lived in Hippo itself or in a neighboring town, they carried to their bishops. When the bishops had heard them and perhaps said something in reply, either their own people refuted them or the same answers were brought back to St. Augustine. When he had learned of these things, he worked patiently and gently—and, as it is written, with fear and trembling, for the salvation of all (Philippians 2:12)—showing how little they wished or were able to refute him, and how true and manifest was what the faith of the Church of God holds and teaches. These activities he carried on continually, by day and by night.

“‘He also sent private letters to each of the bishops of that same error and to prominent laymen, offering reasons and admonishing and exhorting them either to correct themselves of that perversity or at least to come to a disputation. But they, distrusting their cause, never wished to write back. Instead, in anger, they spoke furiously and proclaimed both privately and publicly that Augustine was a seducer and deceiver of souls. They said and maintained that, in defense of their flock, he ought to be killed like a wolf; and they declared that all sins could unquestionably be believed to be forgiven by God to those who were able to do and accomplish this, without fearing God or blushing before human beings.

“‘To make their distrust of their own cause known to everyone, he made every effort. When summoned by public proceedings, they did not dare to enter into discussion. These same Donatists also had, in nearly all their Churches, an unheard-of class of perverse and violent men who went about as though professing continence. They were called Circumcellions. They were present in great numbers and in mobs throughout almost every region of Africa. Instructed by evil teachers, with proud boldness and unlawful recklessness, they sometimes spared neither their own people nor others. In defiance of right and justice, they issued prohibitions against people in their disputes; and if the people did not obey, they inflicted the gravest injuries and killings upon them. Armed with various weapons, they raged through fields and estates and did not fear going so far as to shed blood.

“‘But while the word of God was diligently preached, and an effort for peace was made with those who hated peace, they fought against the one who spoke without cause. When the truth concerning their doctrine became known, those who wished and were able either freed themselves from it or withdrew from it, and joined themselves with their own people, as far as they could, to the peace and unity of the Church. Therefore, seeing the assemblies of their error diminish and envying the growth of the Church, they were inflamed and blazed up with the most violent anger. They organized intolerable persecutions against the unity of the Church and inflicted attacks by day and night and plunder of every kind upon Catholic priests and ministers. They weakened many servants of God by beatings. They even threw lime mixed with vinegar into the eyes of some and killed others. For this reason the same Donatists, the rebaptizers, came to be hated by their own people as well.

“‘Several times these same Circumcellions, armed, also beset the roads against God’s servant Augustine when he happened to be going, at someone’s request, to visit, instruct, and exhort Catholic communities—as he did very frequently. Once it happened that their ambush failed to secure its intended capture. Through God’s providence, but because of an error by the guide, the priest arrived with his companions by another road at the place to which he was going and, through this error, which he learned of only afterward, escaped their impious hands. After giving thanks in all things to God his deliverer, he himself, in his usual manner, spared neither laymen nor clergy, as the public records testify.

“‘Among these matters we must not be silent about what was undertaken and accomplished, to the praise of God, through the zeal of that outstanding man in the Church and his devotion to the house of God, against the aforesaid Donatist rebaptizers. One of those whom he had advanced from his monastery and clergy to be bishops of the Church happened to be visiting the diocese of the Church at Calama, which was entrusted to his care, and was preaching what he had learned for the peace of the Church against that heresy. It happened that in the middle of his journey he fell into their ambush, and they attacked him and all who accompanied him, taking their animals and possessions and inflicting the gravest insults and beating upon them.

“‘To prevent this matter from further obstructing the progress of the Church’s peace, the Church’s advocate did not remain silent amid the laws. Crispinus, who was bishop of the same Donatists in the city and region of Calama, was summoned and instructed that he was subject to the monetary penalty established by public laws against heretics. When he resisted the laws and was brought before the proconsul, denying that he was a heretic, it became necessary, after the Church’s advocate had withdrawn, for a Catholic bishop to oppose him and prove him to be what he had denied that he was. For if the Catholic bishop had overlooked the matter, perhaps those who were ignorant would have believed the Catholic bishop to be a heretic, since the other, while denying what he was, would thus have caused scandal among the weak.

“‘With the memorable bishop Augustine insisting in every way, both Calama bishops came to the dispute. They held a third contest with one another concerning that very difference of communion, while a great multitude of Christian people awaited the outcome of the case both at Carthage and throughout Africa. Crispinus was pronounced a heretic by a proconsular and written judgment. On his behalf the Catholic bishop interceded before the judge, so that the monetary penalty might not be exacted, and this favor was obtained for him.

“‘When he then appealed ungratefully to the most devout Emperor, the Emperor’s answer to the report was duly given and the required judgment followed: Donatist heretics were to have no place whatsoever, and everywhere they were to be subject to the force of all the laws enacted against heretics. Consequently, the judge, his office, and Crispinus himself were ordered to pay ten pounds of gold to the treasury, since the penalty had not been exacted. But the Catholic bishops, especially Augustine of holy memory, immediately took pains to have that condemnation by the emperor set aside through clemency; and, with the Lord’s help, this was accomplished.

“‘Through this diligence and holy zeal, with Christ’s help, the unity of peace grew and multiplied more and more from day to day, as did the brotherhood of the Church of God. This happened especially after the Conference held at Carthage by all the Catholic bishops with those same Donatist bishops, later conducted by order of the most glorious and devout Emperor Honorius. To bring it to completion, he had also sent to Africa from his own court Marcellinus, a tribune and notary, as judge.

“‘In that controversy the Donatists were refuted in every respect, convicted by the Catholics of their error, and marked by the judge’s sentence. After their appeal, they were justly condemned among the heretics by the answer of the most devout Emperor.

“‘Against the Pelagians as well, clever disputants who wrote with a subtler and more harmful art and who spoke publicly and in private houses wherever they could, he labored for nearly ten years, composing and publishing many books and very frequently disputing before the people in church concerning that error. Since those same perverse men, through their ambition, were trying to persuade the Apostolic See of the same perfidy, the holy bishops of the African councils also worked with the greatest urgency to persuade the holy pope of the City—first the venerable Innocent and afterward his successor, the holy Zosimus—that this sect was to be rejected and condemned by the Catholic faith.

“‘Those bishops of that great see, condemning the Pelagians at different times and cutting them off from the members of the Church, judged by letters sent both to the African and Western Churches and to the Churches of the East that they were to be anathematized and avoided by all Catholics. When the most devout Emperor Honorius also heard and followed this judgment pronounced by the Catholic Church of God, he decreed that they were condemned by his laws and were to be regarded as heretics. Consequently some of them returned to the bosom of holy Mother Church, from which they had recoiled, as the truth of the right faith became known and prevailed against that detestable error.

“‘That memorable man was a distinguished member of the Lord’s body and was always vigilant and concerned for the welfare of the universal Church. It was divinely granted to him that he should enjoy, even in this life, the fruit of his labors. First, in the Church and region of Hippo, over which he presided most directly, he saw unity and peace brought to perfection; then in other parts of Africa, either through himself or through others and through the priests whom he had appointed, he saw the Church of the Lord sprout and multiply. He rejoiced to see the Manichaeans, Donatists, Pelagians, and pagans, for the most part, fall away and be joined to the Church of God. He favored and celebrated every good person’s progress and zeal; he piously and devoutly tolerated the lack of discipline of his brothers, while groaning over the wickedness of evil people, whether those placed within the Church or outside it, always rejoicing, as I have said, in the Lord’s gains and mourning over its losses.

“‘His clothing, footwear, and bedding were of moderate and appropriate quality, neither excessively fine nor exceedingly poor. For people commonly use such things either to display themselves insolently or to abase themselves; in both cases they seek not the things of Jesus Christ but their own. He, as I have said, kept to the middle way, turning neither to the right nor to the left.

“‘He always had vegetables and legumes, and sometimes meat for guests or for weaker persons, but he always had wine, because he knew and taught, as the Apostle says, that every creature of God is good and that nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving, for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:4–5). And, as the holy Augustine himself wrote in his books of Confessions, he said: “I do not fear the uncleanness of food, but the uncleanness of desire. I know that Noah was permitted to eat every kind of flesh useful for food; that Elijah was restored with food consisting of meat; and that John, endowed with wondrous abstinence, was not polluted by animals—that is, locusts—being made into food. I know also that Esau was deceived by his desire for lentils; that David reproached himself because of his desire for water; and that our King was tempted not by meat but by bread. Therefore the people in the wilderness deserved blame, not because they desired meat, but because, through their desire for food, they murmured against God” (Confessions X.31.23).

“‘Regarding the consumption of wine, there is also the Apostle’s judgment in his letter to Timothy: “Do not continue drinking only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (1 Timothy 5:23).

“‘He used only silver spoons; the other vessels in which food was brought to the table were earthenware, wooden, or marble—not because of poverty or necessity, but by deliberate choice. He also always practiced hospitality. At table he preferred reading or discussion to eating and drinking. As a safeguard against the plague of human custom, he had the following written there:

> Whoever delights in gnawing at the lives of the absent  
> Must know that this table is forbidden to him.

“‘He therefore admonished every guest to abstain from superfluous and harmful conversation and from detraction. Once, when some of his most intimate fellow bishops had forgotten that inscription and were speaking against it, he rebuked them so sharply, in his agitation, that he said either the verses should be erased from the table or he would rise from the middle of the meal and withdraw to his room.

“‘He was always mindful of the poor and distributed to them from the same resources from which he provided for himself and for all who lived with him: either from the revenues of the Church’s estates or from the offerings of the faithful. When envy was aroused against the clergy on account of those estates, he addressed the people of God, saying that he would rather live from the contributions of the people of God than endure the administration or management of those estates; and that he was ready to surrender them to the clergy, so that all the servants and ministers of God might live in the manner in which they are said to have lived in the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 18:1), sharing in what belonged to the altar. But the laypeople never wished to accept this.’”

Thus Augustine, terrifying only to the enemies of the faith, showed himself in every respect holy, simple, and gentle. He perhaps earned no less glory through the integrity of his character than through the almost innumerable books that his intellect poured forth against heretics, schismatics, and pagans as though from an inexhaustible spring.

But before the catalogue of the works of that most glorious teacher is unfolded before the reader’s eyes, let us listen to Possidius as he tells us how Augustine departed this life. EDITOR.

“‘That holy man lived seventy-six years in this life, which had been divinely granted to him for the welfare and prosperity of the holy Catholic Church; he spent nearly forty years among the clergy or in the episcopate. In private conversations he was accustomed to tell us that, after receiving baptism, even Christians and priests who were praised by others ought not to depart from the body without worthy and appropriate penance.

“‘He himself did this during the final illness by which he died. He had ordered that the very few psalms of David concerning repentance be written out, and while lying in bed he kept looking at those pages, which had been placed against the wall, throughout the days of his illness. He read them and wept continually and abundantly. So that no one might interrupt his concentration, about ten days before he departed from the body he asked us, in the presence of others, not to allow anyone to enter to see him except at the hours when the physicians came in to examine him or when food was brought to him. This was observed and done, and throughout that entire time he devoted himself to prayer.

“‘He preached the word of God in the church without interruption, eagerly and courageously, with a sound mind and sound judgment, up to that very final illness. With all the members of his body sound, and with sight and hearing intact, while we stood by, watched, and prayed together with him, he fell asleep with his fathers, nourished in a good old age. In our presence, a sacrifice was offered to God for the commendation of his body, and he was buried.

“‘He made no will, because the poor man of God had nothing from which to make one. He always commanded that the Church’s library and all its books be carefully preserved for posterity. Whatever the Church possessed, whether in funds or ornaments, he left to the faithful priest who, under him, managed the affairs of the Church’s household.

“‘During his life and at his death he did not treat his relatives, whether they remained in the religious vocation or lived outside it, according to the custom of the world. While he was still alive, he distributed to them, if they needed it, what he distributed to others—not so that they might have riches, but so that they might suffer no want, or less want.

“‘He left the Church a very sufficient clergy and monasteries of men and women devoted to continence, filled with their superiors, together with libraries containing books and treatises by himself and by other saints. In these, by God’s gift, it may be known how great and eminent he was in the Church, and through these he is always found to live among the faithful.

“‘In accordance with this, one of the secular poets, ordering that a tomb be placed for him after his death on a public mound, composed the following as an epitaph:

> Traveler, would you know that the poet lives after death?  
> Behold, what you read I speak; your voice, indeed, is mine.

“‘In his writings, that priest beloved and dear to God is clearly shown, insofar as the truth shining upon us allows us to see, to have lived rightly and soundly in the Catholic Church’s faith, hope, and charity. Those who progress by reading him as he writes about divine matters acknowledge this. Yet I think that those who were able to hear and see him speaking in person in the church, and especially those who knew his conduct among people, could have gained still more from him.

“‘For he was not only a learned scribe instructed for the kingdom of heaven, bringing forth from his treasure things new and old, and one of the merchants who, having found a precious pearl, sold everything he had and bought it (Matthew 13:52, 45–46); he was also one of those to whom it is written, “So speak and so act” (James 2:12), and of whom the Savior says, “Whoever does and teaches these things will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:19).’”

## CHAPTER II. The Writings of St. Augustine

### § I. Augustine’s Genuine Writings, Following the Order of the *Retractations*, Which the Authors of the *Great Library of the Fathers* Likewise Followed

1. **Against the Academics**, three books. These were the first of all his works, written in 386, after the lost book *On the Beautiful and the Fitting*.

2. **On the Blessed Life**, one book consisting of three dialogues, written in the same year, 386—not after the books against the Academics, but between them.

3. **On Order**, two books and four dialogues, written at the same time as the preceding works.

4. **Soliloquies**, two books, written at the beginning of 387.

5. **On the Immortality of the Soul**, one book, written in 387.

6. **On Music**, six books, begun at Milan in 387 and completed in Africa in 389.

7. **On the Morals of the Catholic Church**

8. **On the Morals of the Manichaeans**

Two books, written at Rome around the beginning of 388.

9. **On the Quantity of the Soul**, a dialogue composed there at the same time.

10. **On Free Will**, three books. Augustine began the first at Rome in 388 and, after being ordained priest at Hippo, completed the other two in 395.

11. **On Genesis against the Manichaeans**, two books, written in retreat near Thagaste around 389.

12. **On the Teacher**, one book, written there and in the same year, 389.

13. **On True Religion**, written in the same year, 389 or 390.

These books, together with no. 35, are found in volume I of the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines.

14. **On the Usefulness of Believing**, one book, written at Hippo in 392. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume VI, and in the Benedictine edition, volume VIII.

15. **On Two Souls**, one book, completed in the same year, 392. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume VI, and in the Benedictine edition, volume VIII.

16. **Acts against a Certain Fortunatus, a Manichaean Priest**, with whom he disputed on August 28 and 29, 392. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume VI, and in the Benedictine edition, volume VIII.

17. **On Faith and the Creed**, one book originating from the sermon that, while still a priest, he delivered before the bishops at the Council of Hippo in 393. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume III, and in the Benedictine edition, volume VI.

18. **An Unfinished Literal Commentary on Genesis**, written around 393. It is found in volume III of the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines.

19. **On Christ’s Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 5–7**, two books, written around 393. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume IV, and in the Benedictine edition, volume III.

20. **A Psalm against the Donatists**, written in 393. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume VII, part 1, and in the Benedictine edition, volume IX.

[21.] To approximately the same year, 393, should be assigned the lost book **Against the Letter of Donatus, the Schismatic Bishop of Carthage**. For Augustine places it immediately after the *Psalm* in *Retractations* I.21.

22. **Against Adimantus**, one book, written in 394. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume VI, and in the Benedictine edition, volume VIII.

23. **Explanation of Certain Propositions from Paul’s Letter to the Romans**, delivered while he was still a priest at Carthage in 394. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume IV, and in the Benedictine edition, volume III.

24. **Explanation of the Letter to the Galatians**, written at approximately the same time. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume IV, and in the Benedictine edition, volume III.

25. **Explanation of the Letter to the Romans**, begun at approximately the same time. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume IV, and in the Benedictine edition, volume III.

26. **On Lying, to Consent(i)us**, one book, written in 395. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume IV, and in the Benedictine edition, volume VI.

27. **On Continence**, on Psalm 141:3–4, written around 395. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume IV, and in the Benedictine edition, volume VI.

28. **On Eighty-Three Different Questions**, or **Responses to Eighty-Three Questions**. Augustine dictated these in Africa around 390, when the brothers questioned him, without following any order. After becoming bishop, he ordered them to be collected and arranged them into a single book in 398. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume IV, and in the Benedictine edition, volume VI.

29. **On Seven Different Questions**, two books. These were the first works that Augustine wrote as bishop, addressed to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, who succeeded St. Ambrose in 397. They are found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume IV, and in the Benedictine edition, volume VI.

30. **Against the Letter of Manes, Entitled “The Foundation”**, one book, written around 397. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume VI, and in the Benedictine edition, volume VIII.

31. **On Christian Combat**, written in 396. It is found in the edition of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, volume III, and in the Benedictine edition, volume VI.

32. **On Christian Doctrine**, four books. He began these around 397; but he completed them through the third chapter of the third book and added the fourth book in 426. It is found in volume III of the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines.

[33.] The two books **Against the Party of Donatus**, mentioned in *Retractations* I.5, should likewise be assigned to 398. But they no longer exist.

34. **On Faith in Things Not Seen**. Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, following him, rejected this treatise as spurious and cobbled together from Augustine’s writings; the Benedictines, however, accepted it as genuine. It seems to belong to 399. It is found in volume IV of the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, and in the Appendix to volume VI of the Benedictine edition.

35. Thirteen books of the *Confessions*, written around 400. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. I.

36. Thirty-three disputations, or books, against Faustus the Manichaean. The work was completed around 400 and sent to Jerome in 404. It is extant in the editions of [Col. 0026D] Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VI, and the Benedictines, vol. VIII.

37. Two books on the proceedings with Felix the Manichaean: these are the records of the conference which Augustine held with him at Hippo in December 404. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VI, and the Benedictines, vol. VIII.

38. A book on the nature of the Good, against the Manichaeans, written after 404. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VI, and the Benedictines, vol. VIII.

39. A book against Secundinus the Manichaean, written around 405. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VI, and the Benedictines, vol. VIII.

[40.] Here should be included, if it still existed, the work which he testifies in the *Retractions*, book II, chapter 2, that he wrote against a certain Hilary, a lay Catholic and tribune [Col. 0027A].

41. Two books containing ninety-eight questions on the Gospels, which Augustine wrote with extreme haste after 400. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, and the Benedictines, vol. III.

42. Notes on Job, written around 400. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, and the Benedictines, vol. III.

43. A book on catechizing beginners, written after 400. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, and the Benedictines, vol. VI.

44. Fifteen books on the Trinity, begun in 400 and completed in 416. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. III, and the Benedictines, vol. VIII.

[Col. 0027B] 45. Four books on the Agreement of the Evangelists, written around 400, which he composed while writing the books on the Trinity. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, and the Benedictines, vol. III.

46. Against the Letter of Parmenian, Donatus’s successor in the see of Carthage, addressed to Tychonius, written around 400. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, and the Benedictines, vol. IX.

47. Seven books on Baptism, written at the same time against the Donatists. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, and the Benedictines, vol. IX.

[48.] In the series of the *Retractions*, book II, chapter 19, there follows immediately a book entitled *Against What Centurius Brought Forward from the Donatists*, which no longer exists.

49. Two books in response to the inquiries of Januarius, written around 400. [Col. 0027C] They are extant in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. II.

50. A book on the Work of Monks, written at the command of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, around 400. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. III, and the Benedictines, vol. VI.

51. A book on the Good of Marriage, against Jovinianus, written in 400. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. VI.

52. A book on Holy Virginity, written in 401. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. VI.

53. Twelve books on *Genesis Literally Interpreted*, begun in 401 and completed in 415. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. III.

54. Three books against the Letters of Petilian the Donatist, bishop of Cirta—or Constantina—in Numidia. [Col. 0027D] They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, and the Benedictines, vol. IX.

55. A Letter to the Catholics against the Donatists, commonly called *On the Unity of the Church*. Some consider it not to be Augustine’s, but Dupin asserts it to be his and assigns it to 402. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, and the Benedictines, vol. IX.

56. Four books against Cresconius the Grammarian, who had undertaken to defend Petilian’s case, written in 406. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, and the Benedictines, vol. IX.

The following three books should have been added here, if they still existed; Augustine mentions them in the *Retractions*, II, chapters 27, 28, and 29, namely:

[Col. 0028A] [57.] *The Book of Proofs and Testimonies against the Donatists.*

[58.] *Against Some Donatist or Other.*

[59.] *An Admonition to the Donatists concerning the Maximianists.*

60. A book on *The Divination of Demons*, written between 406 and 411. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. III, and the Benedictines, vol. VI.

61. A book addressed to Deogratias the presbyter, explaining six questions against the pagans; it seems to have been written around 408. Augustine mentions it in the *Retractions*, II, 31. It was published among the letters—formerly no. 49, now no. 102—in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. II.

[62.] The *Retractions*, book II, 32, next mentions an *Exposition of the Letter of Saint James*, which no longer exists.

63. Three books on the Merits and Remission of Sins and on the Baptism of Infants, addressed to Marcellinus and written in 412. [Col. 0028B] They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, part II, and the Benedictines, vol. X.

64. A book on the One Baptism, written at the same time. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, and the Benedictines, vol. IX.

[65.] After the work on the One Baptism, Augustine lists, in II, 35, a book on the Maximianists against the Donatists; it no longer survives.

66. A book on the Grace of the New Testament, addressed to Honoratus, written around 412. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. II.

67. A book on the Spirit and the Letter, addressed to Marcellinus, written in 412 or 413. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. III, and the Benedictines, vol. X.

68. A book on Faith and Works, written in 413. It is extant in the [Col. 0028C] editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, and the Benedictines, vol. VI.

69. A Short Account of the Conference against the Donatists, written toward the end of 411. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, and the Benedictines, vol. IX.

70. A book addressed to the Donatists after the aforementioned Conference, perhaps written at the beginning of 412. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, and the Benedictines, vol. IX.

71. A book on Seeing God, addressed to Paulina. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. II.

72. A book on Nature and Grace, against the Pelagians, written in 415. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, part II, and the Benedictines, vol. X.

73. A book, or letter, on the Perfection of Human Righteousness, addressed to Eutropius and Paulus, Gallic bishops, written in 415. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, [Col. 0028D] vol. VII, part II, and the Benedictines, vol. X.

74. Twenty-two books on the City of God, addressed to the count Marcellinus. Augustine began writing them in 413, after Rome had been captured by Alaric, king of the Goths; he finally completed them in 427 or 428. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. V, and the Benedictines, vol. VII.

75. A book—or letter—on the Good of Widowhood. He does not mention it in the *Retractions*, but Possidius included it in his catalogue. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, and the Benedictines, vol. VI.

76. A book against the Priscillianists and Origenists, written in 411 for Paulus Orosius the Spaniard. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VI, and the Benedictines, vol. VIII.

[Col. 0029A] 77. *On the Origin of the Soul*, addressed to Jerome. See below, no. 92.

[78.] The *Retractions*, book II, chapter 46, next mentions a book addressed to Emeritus, a Donatist bishop, which does not exist today. Compare nos. 85 and 86.

79. A book on the Proceedings of Pelagius against the Adversaries of the Grace of Our Lord Jesus Christ, written in 416 or 417 for Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. It is extant in Vignier’s *Supplement*, vol. I, pp. 413 ff., and in the Benedictines, vol. X.

80. A book on the Correction of the Donatists, addressed to Boniface, a tribune and eventually count in Africa, written around 417. It is extant among the letters—formerly no. 50, now no. 185—in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. II.

81. A book on the Presence of God, addressed to Dardanus, prefect in Gaul, written around the same time. It is extant among the [Col. 0029B] letters—formerly no. 57, now no. 187—in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. II.

82. One hundred and twenty-four treatises on the Gospel of John, preceded by a preface by an uncertain author. They are sermons delivered by Augustine to the congregation in 416 and 417. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IX, and the Benedictines, vol. III.

83. Ten treatises on the First Letter of Saint John to the Parthians, written around the same time. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IX, and the Benedictines, vol. III.

84. Two books on the Grace of Christ and Original Sin, against Pelagius and Coelestius, written around the middle of 408. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, and the Benedictines, vol. X.

85. A book on the proceedings with Emeritus, bishop of the Donatists at Caesarea in Mauretania, written in 413 or 418.

[Col. 0029C] 86. A sermon delivered in the presence of Emeritus to the people of the Church of Caesarea. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, and the Benedictines, vol. IX.

87. A book against a certain sermon of the Arians, without the author’s name, written in 418. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VI, and the Benedictines, vol. VIII.

88. A book—or rather, a sermon—on Patience, believed to have been written before 418. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, and the Benedictines, vol. VI.

89. Two books on Marriage and Concupiscence, addressed to the count Valerius. The first was written at the end of 418, the second in 420. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, part II, and the Benedictines, vol. X.

90. Seven books of *Expressions*, written around 419. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. III.

91. Seven books containing 665 questions on the Heptateuch, written in the same year, 419. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, and the Benedictines, vol. III.

92. Four books on the Soul and Its Origin, written in 419 and 420. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, part II, and the Benedictines, vol. X.

Moreover, in 415 Augustine wrote to Saint Jerome a book on the Origin of the Soul, which is extant among the letters as no. 166 in the Benedictine edition, formerly no. 28; and at the same time another on the saying of the apostle Saint James, 2:10, “Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all,” letter 167, formerly no. 29. [Col. 0030A] Augustine listed both of these as books in the *Retractions*, book II, chapter 45.

93. Two books on Adulterous Marriages, addressed to Pollentius, written in 419. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. VI.

94. Two books against the Adversary of the Law from the Prophets, written in 420. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VI, and the Benedictines, vol. VIII.

95. Two books against Gaudentius, bishop of Thamugadi among the Donatists, written in the same year, 420. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, and the Benedictines, vol. IX.

96. A book against Lying, addressed to Consentius, written in 420. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, and the Benedictines, vol. VI.

97. Four books against Two Letters of the Pelagians, addressed to Boniface I, bishop of Rome and successor of Zosimus, written in 420 or shortly afterward. They are extant in the [Col. 0030B] editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, part II, and the Benedictines, vol. X.

98. Six books against Julianus, written in 421. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, part I, and the Benedictines, vol. X.

99. The *Enchiridion*, or *Manual*, addressed to Laurentius, on Faith, Hope, and Charity, written in 421. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. III, and the Benedictines, vol. VI.

100. A book on Care for the Dead, written in 421. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, and the Benedictines, vol. VI.

101. A book on the Eight Questions of Dulcitius, written in 422. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, and the Benedictines, vol. VI.

102. The Rule for the servants of God, the last of three [Note: [Col. 0029D] For the others, see below, nos. 21 and 22, among the doubtful works], which Erasmus doubts, although he does not consider it unworthy of Augustine; the Benedictines, however, confidently affirm it to be his. It is extant in Letter 211, formerly no. 109, written by Augustine in 423 or 424 to the nuns. They say that it was drawn from this source and adapted for men. Editions: Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. I.

103. A book on Grace and Free Will, addressed to Valentinus, abbot, and the monks of Hadrumetum, written in 426 or 427. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VII, part II, and the Benedictines, vol. X.

104. A book on Correction and Grace, addressed likewise to the monks of Hadrumetum, written in 427.

105. Two books of *Retractions*, in which Augustine reviews ninety-four of his works, comprising 230 books, up to the year 427, when they were written. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. I.

106. A book on Heresies, completed between 428 and 430. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VI, and the Benedictines, vol. VIII.

[Col. 0030D] 107. A treatise, or book, on the Incarnation of the Lord against the Jews, placed by the Benedictines after the book on Heresies. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VI, and the Benedictines, vol. VIII.

108–109. A conference with Maximinus, an Arian bishop, and two books against the same man. The conference was held at Hippo in 428. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VI, and the Benedictines, vol. VIII.

110. A book on the Predestination of the Saints, addressed to Prosper and Hilary, written in 428 or 429. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VI, and the Benedictines, vol. X.

111. A second book on the Predestination of the Saints, commonly entitled *On the Gift of Perseverance*, addressed to the same persons and written in 428 or 429. [Col. 0031A] It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VI, and the Benedictines, vol. X.

112. *Against Julianus’s Second Reply*, an unfinished work comprising six books, written in 428 or 429. It is extant in Vignier’s *Supplement*, vol. II, and in the Benedictine edition, vol. X.

113. The *Speculum*, compiled from both Testaments under the year 427, and mentioned by Possidius in his *Catalogue* and in the *Life of Augustine*. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. III, Vignier’s *Supplement*, vol. I, and the Benedictines, vol. III.

114. Expositions of the 150 Psalms of David. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VIII, and the Benedictines, vol. IV.

115. Two hundred and seventy-one letters, arranged by the Benedictines in chronological order in four classes. [Col. 0031B] The first class contains those which Augustine wrote before becoming bishop, from 386 to 395.
