The second contains those which he wrote from that time until the Conference at Carthage with the Donatists and the discovery of the Pelagian heresy in Africa, that is, from 396 to 412. The third contains those which he wrote from that time until his death, namely, from 411 to 430. The fourth contains those whose date is less certain, although it is certain that all were written by Augustine after he had become bishop. A few hitherto unpublished letters have been added to Augustine’s previously published letters in the Benedictine edition. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. II. Many more are now read among the letters which Augustine listed as books in the *Retractions*; they will be found noted in their proper places.

[Col. 0031C] 116. Sermons. Various collections of these exist, of which the following five collections—apart from the *Sermons to the Brothers in the Hermitage*—were published in the Basel edition of Erasmus, 1529, vol. X.

1. *On the Words of the Lord*, or *On the Words of the Gospel*: sixty-four sermons. Of these, Sermon 14 is by Eradius the presbyter; Sermon 19 by Maximus of Turin; and Sermon 28 by Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan.

2. *On the Words of the Apostle*: thirty-five sermons. Of these, Sermon 25 is by Maximus; it is the ninth among the Ambrosian sermons.

3. Fifty homilies in which various passages of Scripture are explained and commonplaces are treated. The fourth of these was excerpted from the writings of Ambrose.

These three collections are ancient, having been made more than 800 years ago, though they are by no means contemporary with Augustine. The following two, however, were prepared with extreme carelessness by the editors of the Amerbach edition, namely:

4. *Sermons for the Liturgical Year*: 256 sermons, many of which present themselves as the work of other authors. Sermons 87, 215, and 255 are considered spurious. Phil. Labbe denies Sermon 191 to Augustine. Of these, Sermon 9 is by Bernard; 11 is attributed to Maximus; 15 is ascribed both to Severianus and to Fulgentius; 33 is by Saint Leo; 37 by Maximus; 48 is taken here and there from Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine; 63 is by Saint Leo; 68, 77, and 117 are by Saint Ambrose; 118 by Maximinus; 120 is attributed to Eusebius; 125 is almost the same as the Creed attributed to Damasus among the works of Saint Jerome; 128 is by Maximus; [Col. 0032A] 130 has Chrysostom as its author; 136, 138, 156, and 176 are counted among the Eusebian sermons; 177 is by Saint Gregory; 173 is taken from the latter’s writings; and 226, 228, 229, and 242 are from the writings of Ambrose.

5. *Sermons on the Saints*: fifty-one sermons. Of these, some attribute Sermons 1 and 18 to Fulgentius; Sermon 22 is excerpted from Peter of Ravenna; Sermon 26 is found among the Ambrosian sermons; 27 is by Maximus; 30 and 31 are spurious, the latter being counted among the Ambrosian sermons, as is Sermon 33; 35 is by Fulbert; 36 by Bishop Eusebius; 37 by the presbyter Alcuin, although it was compiled from various sources; and 47 is also attributed to Saint Leo.

6. Seventeen other sermons, of which six concern the liturgical year, the seventh the Words of the Apostle, and ten the saints, first published in the Paris edition of 1531. [Col. 0032B]

7. Four sermons, namely, on Jacob and Esau; for the feast of Saint Vincent; on Proverbs 13; on the Parable of the Sower; and on the passage in Matthew 16, “Whoever wishes to come after me,” etc. These were first published, together with a treatise on the Lord’s Prayer, in the Basel edition of 1556. Others were added in the edition of 1569.

8. Forty-three sermons *On Various Subjects*.

9. Twenty-seven fragments of sermons by Saint Augustine, taken from the *Thesaurus*, or collections, of Eugippius the abbot, addressed to the virgin Proba; from the commentaries of Florus, deacon of the Church of Lyons, on the letters of Paul; and from Augustine’s words printed under Bede’s name among his works and also separately.

10. One hundred and twenty-three sermons *On Various Subjects*, published by the Louvain scholars in 1571, vol. X, with the aforementioned forty-three sermons included in the count. The Louvain scholars themselves admit that many of these are spurious.

11. Eleven homilies published by the Parisians in 1614 from Carthusian manuscripts, and another thirteen from manuscripts of Pithou.

12. Forty sermons on various subjects, first published by the Jesuit Jacques Sirmond with notes, Paris, 1631, octavo. “Although,” says André Rivet, “I would not wish to deny that some of them have Augustine as their author, especially those numbered in Possidius’s *Catalogue*, the editor will nevertheless allow that others, which emerged from the monks’ crypts, should be regarded among us as of doubtful reliability until they are commended to us by more worthy evidence.” Among these forty sermons are those thirteen homilies mentioned above.

13. Six sermons first published at Rome in 1644 by Giovanni Battista Maro of Rome, canon of Sant’Angelo in Foro Piscium.

Vignier reprinted the four later collections of sermons in part I of his *Supplement*; in part II he added another forty-six, previously unpublished and drawn from various libraries.

Moreover, it should be noted concerning the sermons mentioned above that it frequently happens that the same sermon is numbered twice, or perhaps even more often, in different collections of sermons; and very many have been excerpted from other writings of Augustine. We have incidentally marked some of these sermons as spurious; but since the Benedictines carried this out much more accurately, we thought it useful to present in abridged form the *Censure of the Sermons* issued by them [Note: [Col. 0033D] We were conveniently given the opportunity here to turn to our own use the diligence of the authors of the *Great Ecclesiastical Library of Cologne*, who excerpted this material from the Benedictines after Cave and Oudinus.]. Accordingly, they arranged all the sermons with which volume V concludes—on this, see below under the notice of that edition—into four classes: sermons on the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, sermons for the liturgical year, sermons on the saints, and sermons on various subjects. A fifth order of doubtful sermons was added, since only those that were plainly spurious were rejected into the Appendix.

These five classes contain 394 sermons, apart from the fragments. Three hundred and seventeen sermons, regarded as certainly spurious, are rejected into the Appendix; they were selected here and there from the collections mentioned above, namely:

From the common collection of *Sermons on the Words of the Lord* (see above, no. 1): Sermons 3, 14, 19, 20, 22, 28, 34, 47, 52, 54, 56, 17, and 58.

From *Sermons on the Words of the Apostle* (no. 2): Sermons 21, 25, 26, 34, and 35.

From the fifty homilies (no. 3): Sermons 2, 3, 4, 6–10, 12, 15, 16, 21, 22, 26, 30, 31, 33, 35, 39, and 45–48.

From *Sermons for the Liturgical Year* (no. 4): Sermons 1, 2, and 3, and all the remaining ones except the fifth, 12, 16, 19, 20, 23, 25, 27, 28, 30, 31, 32, 34, 39, 42, 45, 49, 50, 52, 72, 74, 94, 96, 107, 109, 110, 113, 119, 135, 139, 140, 141, 143–149, 151, 155, 160, 164, 165, 170, 174, 186, 187, 196, 205, 212, 214, 220, 234–237, 245, 246, 254, and 256.

All the *Sermons on the Saints* (no. 5) are spurious except the fourth, 12, 17, 23, 24, 42, 45, 48, 50, and 51.

Among the seventeen sermons (see no. 6), the spurious ones are 1, 2—which forms part of Sermon 51 in the Benedictine collection—7—which forms part of Sermon 361—35, 36—which forms part of Sermon 279—38, 65, 96, 97, 98, 99, and 118—which forms part of Sermon 325.

Of the seventy-six sermons addressed to the brothers living in the Hermitage, etc., the Benedictines present only six in volume V and place the others in the following volume. Of these six, three are spurious: in the common collection of these sermons they occupy places 56, 70, and 72.

Of the sermons published by Jerome Vignier in part I of the *Supplement*, the spurious ones are 3, 4, 5, 13, 14, 15, 17, and 18. In part II, the spurious ones are 1, 2, 8, 10–14, 20, 23, 25, 26, 27, 29, 34, and 36–39.

Finally, the Benedictines rejected among the sermons in volume V several books which Erasmus and the Louvain scholars had placed among the treatises, namely:

117. A treatise on the Epicureans and Stoics in Acts 17. According to Erasmus’s judgment prefixed to it, it is not altogether bad, but contains little or nothing of Augustine. The Benedictines judge otherwise: they consider it entirely good and containing nothing except Augustine’s work. Possidius mentions it in his *Catalogue*, chapter 1. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. VI; in the Benedictine edition, vol. V, sermon 150, class 1.

118. On the passage of Exodus 3:14, “I am who I am,” namely, concerning the bush in which there was a flame, while the bush was not burned. In the Erasmian edition this treatise is prefaced as being by an uncertain author; but in the Ulimmer and Louvain editions it is attributed to Augustine. The Benedictines came very close to placing it among the doubtful works. It is found there, sermon 7.

119. A book, or sermon, on the Ten Strings, noted by Possidius in his catalogue, chapter 8, and cited by Eugippius and Florus. It is found there as sermon 9, and in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IX.

120. *On the Shepherds*, both sermons, on Ezekiel, chapter 34.

121. *On the Sheep*. In the same place, sermons 47 and 48, against the Donatists.

122. On the Correspondence between the Ten Plagues and the Ten Commandments. It is found there as sermon 8. Possidius also mentions it in his *Catalogue*, chapter 9, and Augustine himself in Psalm 77, no. 27. A fragment was found among Eugippius’s excerpts in a royal manuscript and in the manuscript of Victorinus.

## § II. Lost Writings

Besides those indicated in various places under nos. 21, 33, 40, [Col. 0034B] 48, 57, 58, 59, 62, and 78, William Cave carefully recorded the following:

1. Three books against the pagans, and an exhortation to the same.

2. On Spiritual Sacrifices, against the Manichaeans.

3. On the Evening Sacrifice. This treatise may perhaps be none other than the sermon of that title numbered 342 in the Benedictine edition, from the Sirmondian collection—formerly no. 8—in which the beginning of the Gospel of John is explained.

4. On the Day of the Lord according to the prophet Zephaniah, against the Manichaeans.

5. Various treatises against the Arians.

6. A memorandum addressed to Primianus, bishop of Carthage among the Donatists.

7. Three books on Tradition during Persecutions and on False Baptism, against the Donatists.

[Col. 0034C] 8. A book on Baptism, against the same people.

9. A work addressed to Mercator, a bishop, against the same people. In the Benedictine edition there first appeared, from a very old monastic manuscript of Saint Bertinus in Belgium, Augustine’s letter to Mercator—no. 193—in all probability written around 418 to a man whose first name was Marius. Possidius listed it in his *Catalogue*, chapter 4, and Augustine transferred its third part into the book on the Eight Questions of Dulcitius, mentioned above under no. 101.

10. Various treatises on Charity.

11. Foundations of Geometry, Arithmetic, and Philosophy.

12. Several letters, sermons, and treatises mentioned in Possidius’s *Catalogue*, by Bede, by Augustine himself, and elsewhere.

## § III. Doubtful, Pseudonymous, and Spurious Writings

1. Four books—or rather, sermons—on the Creed, or Rule of Faith, addressed to catechumens. They are extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IX, and the Benedictines, vol. VI, up to no. 8.

2. A sermon for Wednesday, or *The Cultivation of the Lord’s Field*.

3. On the Cataclysm, or Flood.

4. On the Barbarian Age, or on the Time of the Persecution by the Barbarians.

[Col. 0035A] 5. A sermon on the New Song, the Return to the Heavenly Homeland, and the Dangers of the Way, addressed to catechumens.

6. A sermon on Christian Discipline.

7. A sermon on the Usefulness of Fasting.

8. A sermon on the Destruction of the City.

The following works, through no. 15, are extant in the Appendix to vol. VI of the Benedictine edition, nos. 9, 10, and 11, and in vol. IX of the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars.

9. A sermon on Contempt for the World, by an uncertain author. Also a sermon on the Vanity of the Age, almost the whole of which is found in the treatise *On the Uprightness of Catholic Conduct*, mentioned below under no. 61.

10. A sermon on the Good of Discipline. Melchior Goldast of Haiminsfeld asserted it to be by Valerianus of Cemelium, bishop in the Maritime Alps in the fifth century; fragments of this little work found in an old Colbert manuscript also bear his name.

11. A sermon on Obedience and Humility.

12. A treatise on Charity, or on the words of the psalm, “The earth has given its fruit.”

13. A treatise on Prayer and Almsgiving—or rather, a fragment of a larger work—published by Jerome Vignier in volume II of the *Supplement*.

14. On the Universality of Almsgiving.

15. Miscellaneous Sentences. All these works are by an uncertain author and do not have the character of Augustine.

16. On the Creation of the First Man. This entire book has been inserted into the treatise *On the Spirit and the Soul*, no. 67. It is found among the works of Ambrose under the title *A Treatise on the Dignity of the First Man*, and among the works of Alcuin [Col. 0035C] under the title *Thoughts of Blessed Albinus the Levite on the Words of Genesis, “Let us make man in our image.”* It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IX, Appendix.

17. On the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus, the Louvain scholars, and the Benedictines, vol. IX, Appendix.

The following works, through no. 23, are extant in the Appendix to vol. I of the Benedictine edition.

18. A book on Grammar.

19. Foundations of Dialectic and Rhetoric. Three books.

20. Ten Categories excerpted from Aristotle. These four treatises, which had been attributed to Augustine in the earlier editions—Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. I—were rejected by the Benedictines into the Appendix and counted among the spurious works, vol. XI.

[Col. 0035D] 21. A fragment of the Rules given to Clerics.

22. A second Rule. (The third is genuine; see above, no. 102.) It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. I, Appendix.

23. A book on the Eremitic Life addressed to a sister, which Erasmus did not publish. It is extant in the Appendix to vol. I of the editions of the Louvain scholars and the Benedictines. According to Luke Holstenius, it is by Aelred of Rievaulx, who lived in the twelfth century. Approximately one-third of it is extant among the works of Anselm, namely, *Meditations* 15, 16, and 17.

The following works, through no. 26, are extant in the Appendix to vol. II of the editions of the Louvain scholars and the Benedictines.

24. Sixteen very brief reciprocal letters between Saint Augustine and Pope Boniface I. Erasmus admits that they are ancient, [Col. 0036A] but denies them to Augustine; Bellarmine and the Louvain scholars followed this judgment.

25. A letter to Demetrias. It is by Pelagius, as Pelagius himself admits in his letters to Pope Innocent.

26. Reciprocal letters between Saints Augustine and Cyril concerning the magnificent and admirable virtues and miracles of Saint Jerome. They are spurious.

27. A debate, or conference, between Saint Augustine and Pascentius the Arian, held at Hippo in the presence of Laurence, a distinguished man appointed judge by Pascentius. It is not by Augustine.

28. Three books on the Miracles of Sacred Scripture. They are by an uncertain author, who is said to have lived after 700. They are extant in Erasmus’s edition, vol. III, and in the editions of the Louvain scholars and the Benedictines in the Appendix there, where the following work is also found.

29. A short work on the Blessings of the Patriarch Jacob. It is excerpted from Jerome’s *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* and Gregory the Great’s *Moralia*, and has Alcuin as its author.

30. Questions on the Old and New Testaments, divided into three parts, to which the Louvain scholars added a fourth, containing twenty-five questions, but spurious, attributing them to Hilary the deacon. They are extant in the Appendix to vol. IV of the Louvain edition and vol. III of the Benedictine edition.

31. An Exposition, or eighteen Homilies, on the Apocalypse of Saint John. It may be by Tychonius the African, a Donatist. The notes are compiled from Victorinus, Primasius, and Bede. It is extant in Erasmus’s edition, vol. IX, in the Louvain edition in the Appendix there, and in the Benedictines, vol. III.

[Col. 0036C] The following works, through no. 65, are extant in the Appendix to vol. VI of the Benedictine edition, except for the *Sermons to the Brothers in the Hermitage* and the others mentioned above under nos. 9–15.

32. A Book of Twenty-One Sentences, or Questions, collected from Augustine and others by some extremely incompetent author without any order. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, Appendix, where the following work is also found.

33. A Dialogue of Sixty-Five Questions, compiled for the most part from various books of Augustine.

34. A book on Faith addressed to Peter the deacon, formerly printed among Augustine’s works but first denied to him by Erasmus. It is by Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. III, Appendix, where the following work is also found.

35. A book on the Spirit and the Soul. It contains sayings and collections excerpted from many different authors.

36. On Friendship. It is merely an epitome of Aelred of Rievaulx’s three books on the same subject. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, Appendix, where the following work is also found.

37. A book on the Substance of Affection and Love. Two books have been confused into one. The authors are unknown.

38. A book on Loving God, also entitled *Meditations*. It too has been compiled from various books by Hugh of Saint Victor, Bernard, and Anselm. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IX, Appendix, through no. 48.

39. A book entitled *The Soul’s Soliloquy with God*. It was compiled by an uncertain author not only from Augustine but also from other authors, such as Hugh of Saint Victor’s book *On the Soul’s Pledge*.

40. A book of *Meditations*. The Louvain scholars had left it among Augustine’s genuine offspring, and had pronounced nothing else about it beyond what Erasmus had earlier said, hesitantly and uncertainly: that its author was either Augustine or someone who had read his books with no little diligence. It was compiled chiefly from Anselm’s writings by a twelfth-century author, and also from the work of John, abbot of Fécamp.

41. A book on Contrition of Heart. A twelfth-century author pieced it together from the works of Anselm and Hugh of Saint Victor.

42. The *Manual*. A little work collected from various older writings and from writings of the eleventh century: from Augustine, Cyprian, Gregory, and Isidore, Anselm, Bernard, and others.

43. The *Speculum*, or *Manual*, as it is entitled in certain manuscripts; in the manuscript of the Bernardine Library at Paris it appears under the title *A Little Book of Catholic Faith*, and has another accompanying work. These two little works are no different from parts I and II of the *Confession of Faith*, which was published under Alcuin’s name through the care of Peter Francis Chifflet, Jesuit. Certainly its author is no earlier than the twelfth century.

44. *The Sinner’s Speculum*. It is by an uncertain author and does not exceed the twelfth century.

45. A book on the Threefold Dwelling. Its author is uncertain but not unlearned.

46. *The Ladder of Paradise*. It is by Guigo, or Guido, of the twelfth century.

47. On Knowledge of the True Life. It is thought to be by Honorius of Autun.

48. On the Christian Life. It is a book by Fastidius the Briton.

49. An exhortatory book, commonly entitled *On Saving Instructions*, addressed to a certain count. It is reasonably attributed to Paulinus of Aquileia, or of Friuli, who lived in the eighth century. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, Appendix.

50. On the Twelve Degrees of Abuse. It is falsely attributed both to Cyprian and to Augustine. The author is unknown. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IX, Appendix.

51. A treatise on the Seven Vices and the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit. It is by Hugh of Saint Victor. William Camerarius, a Scottish priest of the Congregation of the Oratory, Doctor of Theology of Paris, first published it among the *Monuments of the Holy Fathers*, Paris, 1634, saying that it was attributed to Augustine not by ancient manuscript codices but only by many learned men. Vignier thereafter included it in volume I of the *Supplement*. But since it commonly occurs among Hugh’s works, and since another related work, virtually a part of the same work, is found there under the title *On the Seven Mortal Sins, against Which the Seven Petitions of the Lord’s Prayer Are Effective*, the Benedictines omitted it.

52. On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues. It is by Ambrose Autpert, an eighth-century writer. This little work was attributed to four ancient doctors of the Church: [Col. 0038A] first to Augustine in all editions of his works; then to Pope Saint Leo in the Paris edition of 1511; afterward to Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, in the Roman edition of 1585, where it is addressed to Simplicianus; and finally to Saint Isidore of Seville in the Madrid edition of 1599 and the Paris edition of 1601. But Sigebert of Gembloux was greatly misled in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 55; he himself had been deceived by the false inscription of several old codices, which are said to bear the name of Isidore. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IX, Appendix, where the following work is also found.

53. On Sobriety and Chastity. It is by an unknown author, but is an ancient and elegant book, according to Dupin’s judgment.

54. On True and False Repentance, addressed to a devout woman of Christ. Almost the entire book was transferred, under Augustine’s name, into Gratian’s *Decrees* and Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*. Peter of Blois, Vincent of Beauvais, and Thomas Aquinas subsequently attributed it to him. Among more recent writers, the question of its author was debated beginning with Trithemius. The more probable opinion nevertheless prevailed: that its author was someone other than Augustine. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IV, Appendix.

55. On the Antichrist. It is generally attributed to Alcuin, among whose works it exists complete, whereas here and in Rabanus Maurus it is incomplete. It seems to belong to the ninth century. It is extant in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IX, Appendix.

56. A Psalter said to have been composed by Augustine for his mother. But in Royal Manuscript 4373 it is entitled: “A work of Blessed Pope John at Vienne.” This John is believed to be John XXII. It is extant in the [Col. 0038C] editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, vol. IX, Appendix, through no. 61.

57. An Exposition of the *Magnificat*. It is excerpted from Hugh of Saint Victor’s treatise on this hymn.

58. A book, or rather a sermon, on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Its author is believed to be Fulbert of Chartres, who died at the beginning of the eleventh century. Other manuscripts bear the name of Ambrose Autpert, who lived in the eighth century.

59. Two books on Visiting the Sick.

60. Two books, or sermons, on Consolation for the Dead, perhaps excerpted from John Chrysostom.

61. On the Uprightness of Catholic Conduct. It is found in book II of the *Life of Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon*, written by Saint Audoenus of Rouen. Others, however, wish it to have been compiled from Eligius himself—who lived in the eighth century—and Caesarius of Arles, who lived in the sixth.

62. A sermon on the Creed. It is collected in its entirety from the Creed of Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia; from the homilies of Saint Caesarius, pope; and from Ivo of Chartres, who lived in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. It also includes the entire Sermon 242, which is extant in the Appendix to volume V of the Benedictine edition, divided into pieces.

63. A sermon for the vigil of Easter on the eating of the lamb. It is also found among the spurious works of Saint Jerome.

64. A sermon on Psalm 41, addressed to the newly baptized, which is also falsely attributed to Jerome.

65. Three sermons on the Rites and Mystery of Baptism. Sirmond first published these in an Appendix after the forty sermons, but he considers them by no means to be Augustine’s.

[Col. 0039A] The following continues to no. 77 in the Appendix to vol. VIII of the Benedictine edition.

66. *Against Five Heresies*, or *Treatise against Five Kinds of Enemies*, namely, against Pagans, Jews, Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians. Erasmus had judged this work to be by an educated, clever, and eloquent man, though not by Augustine—unless, he said, Augustine had written it in his youth. Bellarmine, the Louvain editors, and others unhesitatingly deny it to Augustine, on the authority of Bede. It appears in the Erasmus and Louvain editions, vol. VI.

67. *Against Jews, Pagans, and Arians*. Another sermon, apparently different from the one listed in Possidius’s *Index*, which Bellarmine therefore rightly judges to be genuinely Augustine’s. For the author of this sermon seems to have copied St. Gregory both in its opening and in certain other passages of chapter 17. It appears in the Erasmus and Louvain editions, vol. VI.

68. *Dialogue on the Dispute between the Church and the Synagogue*. The author lived in the thirteenth or fourteenth century, for he claims to have been a contemporary of John Scotus. It appears in the Appendix to vol. VI of the Erasmus and Louvain editions.

69. *On the Faith, or Unity of the Trinity, against the Manichaeans*. On the authority of a very ancient Corbie manuscript, Jacob Sirmond asserted in his *History of Predestination*, chapter 1, that this work was by Evodius of Uzala, bishop in Africa. It appears in the Erasmus and Louvain editions, vol. VI.

70. *Admonition*—commonly circulated under the name of St. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church—concerning how one should deal with Manichaeans who are converted. It was published under Augustine’s name in the Appendix to vol. X of the Paris edition of 1586. It is a very ancient composition, which Dupin considers to be the enactment of some African council.

71. *Against Felicianus the Arian, on the Unity of the Trinity: a Book addressed to Optatus*. Erasmus formerly declared that it was not probable that this book was Augustine’s, since Augustine does not mention it in the *Retractions*. The Louvain editors, however, concealing Erasmus’s criticism, placed the work among Augustine’s genuine offspring, relying chiefly on the authority of Bede, Lanfranc, Alcuin, and Peter Lombard. It may perhaps be by Vigilius of Thapsus. It appears in the Erasmus and Louvain editions, vol. VI.

72. *Brief Questions on the Trinity and Genesis*, which have been copied from Alcuin. They appear in the Appendix to vol. III of the Erasmus and Louvain editions.

73. *Two Books on the Deity and Incarnation of the Word, addressed to Januarius*, compiled from Origen’s work *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*) according to the version of Rufinus of Aquileia, presbyter. They appear in the Appendix to vol. IV of the Erasmus and Louvain editions, through no. 76.

74. *A Book on the Trinity and Unity of God*. It was formerly divided into thirteen chapters. The nine later chapters contained almost the whole of St. Augustine’s book *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, though abridged and interpolated. The earlier chapters, however, present abbreviated and corrupted versions of several questions from the dialogue of Paulus Orosius, which appears in the Appendix to vol. VI.

75. *A Book on the Essence of the Divinity*. It has been attributed not only to Augustine but also to many others—to Ambrose, Jerome, Anselm, and Bonaventure. Its first and largest part is taken from the work of Eucherius of Lyon, bishop, *On Forms of Spiritual Understanding*.

76. *A Little Book, or Dialogue, on the Unity of the Holy Trinity*. By an unknown but very ancient author. It appears in the Appendix to the Paris edition of 1586.

77. *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, a book by Gennadius of Marseille, which Gerhard Elmenhorst also published separately under Gennadius’s name at Hamburg in 1614, in quarto. It appears in the Appendix to vol. III of the Erasmus and Louvain editions.

78. *Sermon on Rusticiano the Subdeacon*.

[Col. 0040B] 79. *Against Fulgentius the Donatist*. Not by Augustine, but nevertheless by a very ancient author, since he appears to have witnessed that Council of Carthage which proceeded against Caecilian. It appears in part I of the Appendix to vol. VII of the Erasmus and Louvain editions, and in the Appendix to vol. IX of the Benedictine edition.

80. *The Hypomnesticon against the Pelagians and Coelestians*, in six books, addressed to Sixtus III, Roman pontiff, in the year 432. The Jesuit Garnerius, along with others and with Sirmond, attributes it to Marius Mercator. It appears in part II of the Appendix to vol. VII of the Erasmus and Louvain editions, and in the Appendix to vol. X of the Benedictine edition, where the following two works also appear.

81. *A Book on Predestination and Grace*, believed by some to be by Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, but by others denied both to Augustine and to Fulgentius.

82. *A Little Book on God’s Predestination*, by an unknown author.

[Col. 0040C] 83. *Hymn: “We Praise You, O God”* (*Te Deum laudamus*), customarily attributed jointly to Ambrose and Augustine, though nothing certain can be established concerning its author.

# CHAPTER III

## The Various Editions of the Works of St. Augustine

### PREFACE

I do not think it necessary for students of literary and ecclesiastical history to investigate diligently the manner in which the many and extensive volumes comprising Augustine’s writings were transmitted from the author’s own hand and preserved until the salutary age of printing. For already during his lifetime, when copies of his works, together with his reputation, had spread through almost the whole world, and after his death, when their use by no means ceased, there were always people devoted to their preservation and continual multiplication.

[Note: [Col. 0039D] That the library at Hippo possessed a large—indeed, almost complete—collection of Augustine’s books, which survived even the flames and the plunder of the Vandals, is testified by many passages both in Augustine and in other authors. The final testimony is the fact that Possidius composed his catalogue of Augustine’s writings with that library before his eyes. Concerning all these matters, let those consult Engelbert Klüpfel’s dissertation, *Whether and How the Library of St. Augustine Was Preserved Intact in the Destruction of Hippo in 430*, inserted in the first volume, part I, of his *Ancient Ecclesiastical Library* (Freiburg im Breisgau, 1780, octavo), pp. 173 ff., if they attach sufficient importance to the question.]

Fabricius observes that, several centuries after Augustine’s death, those monuments were held in such high esteem that, when copies were lacking in Spain, Taio, bishop of Zaragoza, was sent to Rome around the year 650 for their sake.

[Note: [Col. 0040D] *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. II, book IV, chapter 3, Venetian edition, p. 353.]

In later times, when the light of good letters had quite thoroughly hidden its kindly radiance, the fact that Augustine’s books nevertheless did not disappear from the hands of monks is shown not only by the many surviving manuscript copies from the ninth, tenth, and immediately subsequent centuries, but also by those various Collections, or Florilegia of Sentences and notable passages, which were compiled and pieced together with modest effort from his works. A very few of these, by a fortunate turn, have been printed, but most remain buried under proper darkness in libraries.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] Below we have appended certain materials from Oudinus and from the Cologne *Ecclesiastical Library* concerning such Excerptors and Commentators, both ancient and recent.]

It is widely reported, on the testimony of Einhard, how highly Charlemagne valued the books *On the City of God*. But what few people know is that Charles V, king of France, compelled Radulphus de Preulles, by far the most eminent scholar among the learned men of his age, to undertake, for royal remuneration, the task of rendering that same work into French and illuminating it with learned commentaries.

[Note: [Col. 0042D] We have read somewhere in the Cologne Ecclesiastical Library that a Frenchman related the same story concerning the emperor Charles V in the *Journal des Savants*, 15 March 1666.]

When, in the fifteenth century, that remarkable art of multiplying books began, Augustine was immediately among the first authors whose works demanded the printer’s types, and no Latin author was afterward committed to the press more frequently than he.

The first of his works printed with tin type was his book *On the Art of Preaching*, or rather the final one of the four books *On Christian Doctrine*, produced around 1465 at Strasbourg by Johann Mentelin; Johann Fust reprinted it at Mainz in the same or the following year. Then, in 1467, his principal work, *The City of God*, emerged from the celebrated monastery at Subiaco, and in the immediately following year was reprinted at Rome by the same printers; it soon flew through nearly all the printing shops of Italy.

Thus it was printed at Venice in 1470, and twice there in 1475, by Nicolas Jenson and Gabriel Petrus of Treviso; at Rome in 1474, by Ulrich Gallus; at Naples in 1477; at Venice in 1486 and 1489; and at Toulouse in 1488. Germany, too, devoted no less attention to printing this work at roughly the same time, though sometimes later, once that first enthusiasm for printing books had somewhat abated in Italy. We know of only one earlier copy, printed at Mainz in 1473 by Peter Schoeffer. Then Michael Wenssler raised the standard at Basel in 1479, followed ten years later by the Amerbach impressions, Freiburg in 1499, Langendorf in 1515, and Lyon in 1520. A Louvain edition also exists from 1488.

The German editions generally appear with the commentaries of Thomas Valois and Nicholas Trevet, with which lovers of this somewhat obscure learning seem at that time to have been greatly pleased, until they were buried by Ludovicus Vives.

The books *On the Trinity* proceeded almost step by step with the Basel editions of *The City of God*. Their first printing seems to have been the Venetian edition, without a date, by Paganinus de Paganinis, or the Milanese edition by Leonhard Pachel in 1489. Germany may perhaps have possessed an earlier one in the edition which lacks any indication of place or year but bears signs of exceptional antiquity. In the same year named by the Milanese edition, Johann Amerbach committed it to the press, and again in 1490. This was followed by the Freiburg edition of 1494, the Basel edition of Langendorf in 1515, and the Lyon edition of 1520.

To these first German efforts devoted to Augustine’s books belongs also an edition of *On the Agreement of the Four Evangelists*, at Lavingen in 1473. Likewise, the books *On Faith and Works* appeared at Cologne in the same year, together with various smaller works printed there, all of which seem to belong to that same year.

A Confessions edition, perhaps approximately contemporary with these—if it is indeed German—is without indication of place and year. A very old printing of it was made at Milan in 1475, and soon afterward without place in 1482.

Sermons, too, frequently occupied the presses during this period. Among them were the oldest *Homilies*, printed at Augsburg by Anton Sorg in 1475. These were followed by the *Sermons to the Hermit Brothers*, at Modena in 1477; Milan in 1484; Brescia in 1486; Venice by Paganinus de Paganinis in 1487; and there by Vincent de Benaliis in 1492. Finally came the Amerbach Collection, including the newly assembled mass of *Sermons on the Seasons*, in 1494 and 1495; this was reprinted at Paris by Jodocus Badius in 1516 and at Hagenau in 1521.

The Epistles, besides an ancient edition without place or year, were printed by that same man whom we must praise so often, Johann Amerbach, in 1493 and 1494. He also allowed the *Expositions on the Psalms* to leave his workshop repeatedly, in 1489, 1493—an edition from which the Venetian printing is also commonly cited—1494, and 1497. He was followed by the Lyon printer in 1519.

Add to these the immense number of books which cannot be assigned to a definite year because they lack indications and notes. Among these are more than one edition of the books *On Christian Doctrine*, *On the Quantity of the Soul*, the *Soliloquies*, the *Sermons*, *On the Trinity*, the *Confessions*, the *Epistles*, *On the Agreement of the Four Evangelists*, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, *The City of God*, *On the Gospel of John*, the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, and others. We have carefully recorded all of them in their proper places and described them as far as our abilities allowed.

Meanwhile many of Augustine’s smaller works also began to be collected and formed into a single body, although in selecting the individual pieces the editors do not always seem to have followed any definite method or plan; rather, they appear to have yielded to chance, which had joined together various writings of his.

[Col. 0042D] First among these are the *Treatises*, jointly published at Venice in 1484 by Andrea de Bonetis of Pavia, in quarto—unless they had already been derived from the earlier Venetian edition by Octavianus Scotus in 1483, a point which I certainly cannot confirm—and the Strasbourg edition by Martin Flach in 1489, reprinted there in 1491. The later Venetian edition is considerably enlarged, although it agrees admirably with the other edition in more than half its contents, so closely that it is difficult to say whether it followed that edition’s footsteps or was prepared according to an entirely different plan.

[Col. 0043A] Both editions, however, contain works of such a kind that they do not occupy a large volume, and certainly are no longer than the books *On Christian Doctrine*. This is especially because some of those works were already available separately, such as *The City of God*, *On the Trinity*, and the books of the *Expositions on the Psalms*, while others each demanded special treatment, as we have also seen in the case of the Epistles and Sermons.

The same Venetian edition may perhaps have been reprinted there by Dionysius Berthold in 1491. The editions of Parma by Angelus Ugoletus and of Venice by Pelegrinus de Pasqualibus, both from 1491, differ from it. I believe that these served as the model for the edition of Jodocus Badius Ascensius, printed at Paris in 1520 by Johann Parvus and carefully used by the Maurist Fathers.

Nor should we pass over in silence the remarkable plan of Jodocus Badius and Augustine of Regensburg in collecting and publishing, with corrections, the various books of Augustine’s *Questions*. This work appeared at Lyon in 1497, printed by Johann Trechsel in folio, prepared with extraordinary industry and considerable judgment.

After all these preparations, Johann Amerbach—who had rendered outstanding service to all literary matters, especially to Latin ecclesiastical writers—undertook the plan of publishing Augustine’s complete works in parts. He did not do so merely to enjoy the diligence of others, since the matter was chiefly his own undertaking, but lest he fail to support the advances in learning that appeared ready to mature.

He therefore produced eleven volumes. In the first eight he arranged all Augustine’s writings in chronological order, according to the evidence of the *Retractions*, and added three further volumes containing works either omitted from the *Retractions* or composed later. At the same time, so that the bulk might not grow without limit, and because copies of certain works undoubtedly remained available, he took account of those which he had previously issued separately from his own workshop. He excluded the Epistles, Sermons, and *Expositions on the Psalms* from this edition.

This Amerbach edition appeared at Basel in 1506 and was received with great applause by all who valued these studies; it was also reprinted at Paris in 1515. This edition seems to have fully satisfied every desire. For until 1529, not only was nothing changed in Amerbach’s plan, but only a few smaller books of Augustine were published individually during the intervening period, chiefly at Cologne: in 1527, *On Christian Doctrine* and *On the Spirit and the Letter*; in 1528, *On Faith and Works*, *On Nature and Grace*, and others. Likewise, at Augsburg in 1523, *On Faith and Works* and the *Enchiridion to Laurentius* were published; and finally at Nuremberg, for example in 1524, *On Nature and Grace*. In all these cases Augustine’s text received no enlargement.

Fortune was much more generous to the books *The City of God*, accumulating in them everything that could be expected in that age from the intellect and diligence of learned men for the adornment of an old book. For Johann Ludovicus Vives, the defender and promoter of refined letters in Spain and Belgium, in the Basel edition printed by Frobenius not only supplied a revised text based on manuscript copies—bringing to their use a great command of Latin speech and ancient learning—but also illustrated it with a commentary whose richness and elegance no Italian had seen matched in any ancient writer. Such honor was paid to him by all lovers of learning in that age that Erasmus judged himself able to dispense with new labor on this work and incorporated the whole of it into his own edition.

The ERASMIAN recension, although, as customary, it encountered widely divergent judgments, nevertheless kindled an incredible degree of enthusiasm for this field of study. The plan was owed solely to Frobenius, who spared no expense and desired from the supreme deity only that his life might be prolonged long enough to see the project completed. But he did not obtain this wish: death carried him off when scarcely the first two volumes had been completed.

Erasmus had yielded to Frobenius’s pleas that, since no one wished to succeed him in bringing forward the work of which he had undertaken only a small part, he should finally assume the whole task. After Frobenius’s death, Erasmus considered himself obliged to render the same service to his sons.

Thus, in this edition, the scholar secured three considerable advantages for advancing his undertaking. First, he obtained elegance in the type and paper and a certain appropriate dignity in the work’s entire appearance and production. In the Amerbach impressions, as no one can be unaware, a more liberal elegance is rightly missed: in part, letters unpleasant to the eye were employed; in part, the paper is rather coarse; and finally every space on the page is so crammed that one might almost say Amerbach had presented himself in a shabby guise.

Second, the edition presented Augustine’s works in their entirety for the first time. Third, it offered a text corrected of innumerable faults, especially grammatical ones and those apparently arising from ignorance of antiquity and ancient learning; it also introduced a new division and judgments concerning works that were either wholly inauthentic or at least appeared doubtful.

This edition was repeatedly reissued and continually enlarged. Thus it was enriched with significant additions to the Sermons at Paris, by Chevallon, in 1531–32, and there by Charles Guillard in 1541, as well as in the successive Basel reprints: 1541–43, assisted by Martin Lypsius; 1556, edited by Johann Coster; and 1569, the last and most complete and beautiful of all the Frobenian editions. Into the latter also passed the Sermons which Johann Vlimmerius first brought out from manuscript copies and published at Louvain in 1564.

It was also reprinted at Lyon in 1561–63, in octavo, and at Paris in 1571, in folio. It suffered as well from the impure hands of Venetian booksellers in 1545, 1552, 1570, and 1584.

In general, all Augustine’s smaller works printed separately in different places after the Erasmus edition follow the Erasmian recension. Their number was by no means small, but Augustine’s reading gained nothing from them.

The *Confessions* in particular must have been frequently read: they were printed at Cologne in 1531 and 1569, at Louvain in 1563 and 1571, and at Antwerp in 1567 and 1568. Likewise, *On the Spirit and the Letter* was printed at Paris in 1538, Wittenberg in 1541, and Antwerp in 1568; *On Faith and Works* at Paris in 1534, Cologne in 1552, and Antwerp in 1568; *On the Agreement of the Four Evangelists* at Paris in 1538 and Cologne in 1539; *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead* at Paris in 1543; *On Free Choice* and *On Predestination and Grace* at Cologne in 1568; *On Nature and Grace* at Antwerp in 1568; *On Christian Doctrine* at Venice in 1534; and the *Enchiridion to Laurentius* at Cologne in 1532.

Lambertus Danaeus also published the *Enchiridion* at Geneva in 1575, with the commentary reprinted there in 1579, 1583, and 1597. The following year Danaeus added the book *On Heresies*, likewise reprinted in 1578, 1593, and 1595. Finally, *The City of God*, with the commentary of Johann Ludovicus Vives, was reprinted at Paris in 1544 and 1555, and at Basel in 1555 and 1570.

[Col. 0045B] But a new and sudden light arose for Augustine through the combined labors of the LOUVAIN THEOLOGIANS, in the edition of his works publicly issued at Antwerp by Christopher Plantin in 1577, in eleven folio volumes. In it there was not only more explicit criticism, but also this notable feature: the spurious and doubtful works were entirely separated from the rest and assigned to their respective volumes. I say nothing of the annotations and other conveniences which every later age has warmly approved in it.

It was reproduced competitively, usually with some additions: at Paris in 1586; Geneva in 1596; Paris in 1603, 1604, and 1613–14; Cologne in 1616; and Paris in 1626, 1635, and 1652.

Some additions were subsequently supplied from elsewhere. Thus in 1611 Marcus Welser had the first book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius* printed at Augsburg from a manuscript copy sent to him from Italy. Likewise, in 1617 Claudius Menardus of Angers first published at Paris the first two books *Against the Second Reply of Julian*. Michael Paludanus of Ghent subjected them anew to his recension at Louvain in 1642.

Jacob Sirmond published forty new Sermons at Paris in 1631, and Johann Marus published six Sermons together with several fragments at Rome in 1644. But the later reprints, though gradually enlarged, are far inferior to the first because of their frequent defects.

When Hieronymus Vignerius, a priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of Jesus at Paris, recognized that money had been spent on them with manifest loss, he sought to remedy the situation by publishing, in 1654 and 1655, a two-volume *Supplement to All the Works of Augustine Printed before 1614*. By acquiring this, scholars could retain either the earlier Erasmus or Louvain edition without loss, indeed with greater benefit. He also added the six books *Against the Second Reply of Julian*, the same work whose first two books Menardus had published, along with various Sermons and Treatises that had until then remained unpublished.

The writings of Augustine that were printed separately, or several together according to the affinity of their subject, from the end of the sixteenth century until the close of the seventeenth, followed the Louvain edition. These included the *Confessions*, at Würzburg in 1581 and Tours in 1588; *The City of God*, at Antwerp in 1600, Geneva and Lyon in 1610, Paris in 1613, 1636, and 1651, Frankfurt in 1624, and Hamburg in 1661; *On Christian Doctrine*, at Antwerp in 1601, Wittenberg in 1604, and Helmstedt in 1629 and 1655, edited by Georg Calixtus; *On the Unity of the Church*, at Mainz in 1602, with the notes of Justus Calvin, and at Helmstedt in 1657, edited by Georg Calixtus; likewise *On the Usefulness of Believing*, by the same editor, at the same place and in the same year, and later at Louvain in 1680; *On Heresies*, at Helmstedt in 1621 and Oxford in 1631, and at Helmstedt in 1678 with Danaeus’s commentary; *On Faith and Works*, at Frankfurt in 1652; the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, at Wittenberg in 1604 and Paris in 1665; and the Epistles, at Frankfurt in 1678, selected at Fleecia in 1638, and at Louvain in 1662.

Henri Sommalius, of the Society of Jesus, advertised a new recension of the *Confessions* based on several manuscripts. It is impossible to say how often it was printed and reprinted at Lyon, Cologne, Douai, Dillingen, and elsewhere.

[Col. 0046B] But critics assigned it little value. Nor are those various collections of works against the Pelagians of any significance, such as those published at Paris in 1644 and 1652, Louvain in 1647 and 1648, Rome in 1652, Brussels in 1654 and 1673, and Lyon in 1673.

Yet, surprisingly, certain benefit for establishing the text of this author resulted from several French translations that appeared frequently during this period, especially those of the Arnauld family.

Finally, a new and last series begins with the splendid work of the BENEDICTINES. A learned man of the Maurist Congregation, who had undertaken its direction, publicly announced an outline of this edition as early as 1671. Shortly afterward, however, he was expelled from the Congregation and was forced to surrender the undertaking to François Delfau.

[Col. 0046C] It was then entrusted to Thomas Blampin and Pierre Coustant, with several other members contributing their diligence as occasion allowed. Mabillon had no part in the undertaking, except that he is said to have composed the dedicatory epistle to King Louis XIV, under whose auspices the whole work was eagerly being carried forward.

The edition is the most complete in critical resources and in the editors’ diligence. Above all, its new examination of each author’s writings in relation to chronology, and its discrimination of spurious works from genuine ones, deserve the highest recommendation as exceedingly beneficial to the study of ecclesiastical history.

Johann Clericus had it reprinted at Antwerp—or, more accurately, Amsterdam—in 1700–1703, and enlarged it in a single volume with various dissertations on Augustine’s most important controversies and with observations of no ordinary merit. As a result, the use of this edition reached at least a larger number of Protestants.

The Italians seem not to have been equally pleased with it. For in 1706 Johann Baptist Clarellus, a Venetian printer, was preparing to commit the Benedictine Paris edition to the press again, making it identical in every respect with the original. He publicly announced this plan by sending scholars a *Protrepticus*, in which he spoke unfavorably of the Antwerp edition because of Clericus’s fidelity and intention. Yet this shameful device of a profiteering bookseller was not needed to stir Oudinus’s anger and induce him to undertake the defense of Clericus, toward whom he was by no means favorably disposed.

[Col. 0047A] [Note: [Col. 0047D] Clarellus’s letter is found in the *Acta Eruditorum* of Leipzig, February 1707, pp. 94–96. Compare Oudinus, *Commentaries*, vol. I, pp. 985 ff.]

For the rest, we do not know whether Clarellus’s plan succeeded, but it certainly differed little from the edition which Johann Baptist Albrizzi had printed there in 1729 and the following years.

The remaining works on Augustine produced separately since the Benedictine period do not merit lavish praise. Two Epistles to Optatus were recently recovered from a manuscript of the Abbey of Göttweig in Lower Austria: one *On the Nature and Origin of the Soul*, the other *On the Punishments of Children Who Die without Baptism*. They were printed at Vienna in 1732 and reprinted at Paris in 1734.

The edition by Johann Schilter, legal scholar, of the book *On Adulterous Marriages*, published at Jena in 1698, also seems worthy of mention. The rest—such as the edition at Troyes of the books *On Grace against Pelagius and Coelestius*, Mainz 1687; the *Book on Heresies*, Cambridge 1687 and Oxford 1721; the *Mirror of Augustine*, edited by Tommasi at Rome in 1679; the *Confessions*, published at Florence in 1757 with the very lengthy commentary of Francesco Arcangeli *On the Presentation*; and the little books which the Thuringian Teegius recently had printed at Leipzig in the manner of the Benedictines, in 1767, 1769, and 1770—are separated from them by long intervals.

In this great neglect of Augustine in more recent times, it would have been desirable that the institution begun by a certain Parisian, Ph. D. Pierres, whose excellent specimen was proposed in 1776 in a very elegant printing of the *Confessions*, had not been abandoned, or that others had imitated him under similar circumstances of critical support.

But let us finally proceed to the annals of Augustine’s editions, which we have described in such a way that they would present: I. the collected writings, from their earliest beginnings; II. the individual works according to the customary sequence adopted by us.

After all these have been completed, a separate section will be appended concerning Augustine’s Epitomators, Excerptors, and Commentators, both ancient and recent. We have judged that writings of this kind—works that serve not so much to explain or comment on particular books of Augustine as to treat Augustine’s doctrine as a whole or in its individual parts, whether for instruction, refutation, or rebuttal of other opinions—cannot suitably be gathered within the limits of this work.

## ARTICLE ONE

### Collections of Augustine’s Works and Smaller Works

[Col. 0047D]

## FIFTEENTH CENTURY

**1473. Cologne, large octavo. Augustine, *On Faith*.**

Beginning: “Here begins the book of Saint Augustine to Peter the Deacon on faith.”

End: “This book of Saint Augustine on the Catholic faith, addressed to Peter the Deacon, was printed at Cologne on the eve of Saint John the Baptist, in the year of the Lord 1473.”

The type of this volume is old, clear Gothic; the paper is thick, and the pages are printed in twenty-six broad lines. [Col. 0048A] There are no signatures for pages, leaves, or gatherings. For the distinctions that we call commas and points, the printer used a doubled stroke, which grammarians otherwise employ in compound words and call a *hyphen* (ὕφεν).

We have assigned this volume a place among the smaller works because of its similarity to those that follow. Even if they did not appear in the same year, they truly came from the same workshop, as we now judge from comparing them with one another, and they display an outstanding perfection of the art in a few gatherings.

The three volumes that follow are printed in the same type, but in a type so polished that scarcely anything more perfect in this genre can be imagined; the paper is much finer and glossy, and each page contains twenty-seven lines. Moreover, no printer’s marks at all are visible, nor is there any indication of place or year. They contain the following:

1. The book *On Christian Combat*, together with Augustine’s judgment on the same subject, taken from the books of the *Retractions*; and the book *On the Sermon Delivered by the Lord on the Mountain*. At the end, on the final page of the volume: “Here ends the first book of Blessed Augustine on the Mountain.”

2. The treatise *On Flight from Women*; the treatise *On Continence*; the book *On Contempt of the World*; the Epistle of Blessed Jerome to the presbyter Paulinus; and two sermons of Augustine on the common life of clerics, beginning “For which reason I wished …” and “and to your charity …”

3. Homilies of Blessed Augustine, first on what the Psalmist says: “Who is the man who desires life and longs to see good days?”; second on what is written: “Be reconciled with your adversary …,” and “He who hates his brother is a murderer”; third on what the Lord says: “Love your enemies”; fourth on what is written in Isaiah: “Cry out, do not cease”; fifth on what the Apostle says: “Covetousness is the root of all evils”; sixth on what is written: “Blessed is he who has not gone after gold”; seventh on what the Apostle says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”

The most recent Catalogue of Crevenna also mentions the smaller works listed under nos. 2 and 3, vol. I, pp. 106–107, and adds:

4. A book *On Christian Discipline*, entirely corresponding to those listed above, no. 470; and

5. A Sermon on the Lord’s Prayer, as well as the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*; no. 469. The editor holds that all the later treatises were printed by Ulrich Zel of Hanau around 1470, following in this the judgment of Debure in the Catalogue of the Duke de la Vallière’s Library, vol. I, pp. 172 ff. Under no. 478 Debure recorded these later treatises, adding that the first consists of nine leaves and the second of six. Under no. 473 they occur together with the books mentioned by us under no. 2, and indeed at the beginning.

6. St. Augustine’s book *On the Blessed Life*; the book *On the Modesty of Women*; and the little book *On the Uprightness of Life*.

[Col. 0049A]

**1483.**

Venice, under the care and at the expense of Octavianus Scotus, citizen of Modena, in quarto: *The Minor Ascetic Works of Blessed Augustine*. G. Pray records it in *The Rarer Books of the Buda Library*, vol. I.

**1484.**

Venice, by Andrea de Bonetis of Pavia, in quarto: *The Works of St. Augustine*. At the end:

“Here ends the book of Saint Augustine on true religion and on the life of clerics of Saint Augustine, as well as a most worthy treatise by a certain author on spirit and soul. All these are contained in this book and were printed at Venice with the greatest diligence by Master Andrea de Bonetis of Pavia, under the illustrious prince Giovanni Mocenigo, duke of Venice, on 22 July 1484.”

[Col. 0049B] It contains the same works that appear in the following Strasbourg edition, numbered 1–22. To these are added: 23. A letter of Eusebius Corradus, a Lateran canon regular, to Sixtus IV, Roman pontiff, concerning the removal from the Church of the error of those who write that St. Augustine was a hermit; 24. the Rule of St. Augustine; 25. the Life of St. Augustine written by St. Possidius, bishop of Calama; 26. Eusebius Corradus’s Annotation—or rather, a short treatise—addressed to Sixtus IV and the Cardinals, concerning the error of those who write that St. Augustine was a hermit; 27. St. Augustine’s book *On the Soul*.

The distinguished Seemiller carefully reviewed this edition, which had already been mentioned briefly by other bibliographers, in fascicle III, p. 7. Under his guidance we have found nothing more certain on this treacherous path. From him, therefore, we learn that all these smaller works were printed in the same type—namely, small Gothic—in two columns, on paper that was both bright and durable.

He further observes that the titles were printed above the leaves for the first twenty-two works, but not for the others. Initial letters, catchwords, and page numbers are lacking, although the leaves themselves are signed.

In the Catalogue of the Royal Library, vol. I, p. 376, it is cited under the first small work, the *Meditations*. It also frequently happens that individual books from this collection are recorded as having been printed separately, in this place or that and in this year or that, either through the carelessness of writers or because they sometimes occur detached from the rest of the body.

**1489.**

Strasbourg, by Martin Flach, in folio: *Many Smaller Works of Aurelius Augustine*. The first page bears nothing resembling a title except the following, printed in larger Gothic type. At the end:

“Here ends the very many smaller works, as well as the life of the most holy and most perspicacious Blessed Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo and doctor of the Church, printed with the utmost care at Strasbourg through the expense and labor of Martin Flach. Finished in the year from the birth of the Savior 1489, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April.”

Some delight in examining these with ingenious inquiry into truth.

Others are captivated by the charm of Dulichian words.

But others take pleasure in turning over varied little books.

There are those who like writings in which nothing pleases except what is sacred.

Whoever you are among these: for a few coins buy many books

Of Aurelius, and thereby relieve your thirst.

You will see them strong in the powers of their arguments, and

At the same time adorned with varied matters concerning the Godhead.

[Col. 0050A] Strasbourg has produced them free of errors, and Martin

Most skillful in his art, gave them to the press.

The type is Gothic. The pages are printed in two columns; the leaves, except for the first six, are numbered, and the individual chapters are very conveniently distinguished by their respective numbers and headings. They contain the following:

1. *Meditations*;  
2. *Soliloquies*;  
3. *Manual on the Word of God*;  
4. *Enchiridion for Laurence*;  
5. *The Book on the Threefold Dwelling*;  
6. *The Steps of Paradise*;  
7. *On the Twelve Degrees of Abuses*;  
8. *On the Blessed Life*;  
9. *On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary*;  
10. *On the Divination of Demons, against the Pagans*;  
11. *On the Modesty of Women*;  
12. *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead, to Paulinus, Bishop of Nola*;  
13. *On True and False Penance*;  
14. *On Contrition of Heart*;  
15. *On Contempt for the World, to Clerics*;  
16. *On the Correspondence between the Ten Commandments and the Ten Plagues of Egypt*;  
17. *On Knowledge of the True Life*;  
18. *Confessions*;  
19. *On Christian Doctrine*;  
20. *On Faith, to Peter the Deacon*;  
21. Two sermons on the life and conduct of clerics;  
22. *On True Religion, to Romanianus*;  
23. *On the Spirit and the Soul*;  
24. *On the Christian Life, to His Widowed Sister*;  
25. *On the Definitions of Orthodox Faith and Ecclesiastical Dogmas*;  
26. *On Christian Discipline*;  
27. *A Sermon on Charity*;  
28. *On the Ten Strings*;  
29. *A Sermon on Drunkenness*;  
30. *A Treatise on the Vanity of This World*;  
31. *On Obedience and Humility*;  
32. *On the Christian Contest*;  
33. *On the Good of Discipline*;  
34. *A Rule for the Common Life of Clerics*;  
35. Possidonius, *On the Life of Augustine*.

Besides the index of all the opuscula itself, several separate tables of contents for individual books precede the volume.

[Col. 0050C] I am surprised that the distinguished Seemiller, who listed this same edition in his *Commentaries*, fascicle III, p. 171, did not compare it with the Venetian edition of 1484. The distinguished Braun also mentions it in the same place, vol. II, p. 174.

### 1491

In the same place, by the same printer, in folio. The same edition, from the second printing. At the end: “M. CCCC. XCI, on the eleventh day of the month of August.” Gemeiner, in the same place, p. 203, noted a defective copy, whereas the distinguished Braun, in the same place, vol. II, p. 213, records one complete like ours.

At Parma, by Angelo Ugoletus, in folio. Various opuscula of Augustine, completed on the day before the Kalends of April. *Catalogue of the Smith Library*, p. 28, and *Crevenna’s Latest Catalogue*, vol. I, p. 110. They begin the series with the books *Against the Academics*, which is why Morellus, in the *Catalogue of the Pinelli Library*, lists them under this title.

At Venice, by Dionysius Bertoldus, in folio. “Very many opuscula of Aurelius Augustine, some not previously printed.” These words serve as the title on the first page of the first leaf. They begin with the *Meditations*, whose title is printed in red; the last item is his *Life*, written by Possidonius, at the end of which appears:

“Of the same Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo and most holy Doctor of the Church, and likewise of his life written by Possidonius: printed most carefully at Venice, at the expense and through the work of Dionysius Bertoldus of Bologna. The end, in the year from the birth of our Savior 1491, on 26 March.”

An epigram is appended to this. [Col. 0051A] The text occupies 339 leaves. At the beginning of the volume, in addition to the title, there are eight leaves containing a table of contents. At the end there remains a leaf bearing the register of the sheets and displaying the printer’s device. The type is Gothic. The description was made in two columns, with the numbers and signatures of the leaves displayed, though catchwords are lacking. We owe knowledge of this and the following edition to the distinguished Braun, *Literary Notices*, vol. II, p. 229. Would that this most diligent man had been willing either to enumerate the contents of the edition or at least to compare them with those of others.

At Venice, by Pelegrinus de Pasqualibus, small folio. “Very many opuscula of Saint Augustine.” This serves as the title. At the end: “The opuscula of Saint Augustine of Hippo are completed. They were printed at Venice by Pelegrinus de Pasqualibus of Bologna in the year from the birth of the Lord 1491, on 10 November.”

The volume consists of 131 leaves, printed in Gothic type and in two columns. It contains numbers and signatures, but no catchwords. It begins with the books *Against the Academics*, with this rubric printed in red:

“Of the divine Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *Against the Academics*, or *On the Academics*, which he composed while still a catechumen.”

A letter addressed to the reader by Severinus Chalci, provost of the Canons Regular of the Holy Cross of the Montanense Canonry, is prefixed; an index of the works and an epigram are appended to it.

### [1495]

At Basel, by Johann Amerbach, in folio, six volumes. *The Works of Saint Augustine*. Maett. vol. I, part II, p. 588, on the authority of de la Caille, p. 82. But we searched for it in vain among the catalogues of other learned men and in those of the best libraries. I therefore fear that, through some error unknown to me, such a notice has been introduced; this seems especially likely because the source reported two formats of the sheets, namely folio and quarto. Vignerius also mentions it in the preface to his *Supplement to the Works of Augustine*, but with no greater reliability. Indeed, I am almost certain that various editions of individual Augustinian writings—for example, the *Expositions on the Psalms*, the *Letters*, and the *Sermons*—repeatedly printed by Amerbach in the years 1493, 1494, 1495, and 1497, gave rise to this error.

### 1497

[Col. 0051D] At Lyon, by Joannes Trechsel, in folio. *The Book of Questions of the Divine Augustine, in which all the following are contained*:

The *Heptateuch*, a work of various questions concerning the seven books of the Bible, comprising an equal number—that is, seven—books.

Three books of *Questions on the New and Old Testament*.

Four books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*.

Three books of *Questions on the Gospels*.

One book of *Eighty-Three Questions*.

Sixty-five questions of Orosius, together with his *Dialogue*, which is one book.

One little book of eight questions by Dulcidius.

The *Enchiridion* to Laurence, on faith, hope, and charity.

Two books, *Inquiries to Januarius* and *On Ecclesiastical Customs*.

One book of questions to Honoratus, *On the Grace of the New Testament*.

One little book of five questions to Hilary.

One little book of six questions *Against the Pagans, to Deogratias*.

Also, indexes and *Retractations* of all these works, placed at the front.

These words appear at the beginning as the title, and beneath them are several verses in praise of Saint Augustine. At the end, in the first column of the final page:

“The end of the six questions of the divine Aurelius Augustine, bishop, against the pagans, to Deogratias, and consequently of the whole work. Thanks be to God.”

In the other column, after Badius’s peroration and the register of the sheets appended to it: [Col. 0052B]

“This work was printed at Lyon through the labor and expense of Master Johann Trechsel, a German, in the year of our salvation 1497, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May.”

The printer’s device is added on the final page. Jodocus Badius wrote the preface to Master Peter Gerard, professor of sacred theology and prior of the Augustinian Hermits of Paris [*Parchiensem*, sic] (Lyon, 7 days before the Kalends of May, 1497).

From this preface we learn that the work was collected and corrected by Augustinus of Regensburg, Bachelor of Sacred Theology, from writings of several scholastic doctors that had already been published; he deserved well of the undertaking. Nor was Badius’s own labor absent from the work, since he admits that, by seeking out as many treatises as possible that the former had been unable to obtain and by correcting them, he may claim for himself a considerable share of such diligence. For, he says:

“First, we wished the order that you see on the back to be observed: so that in the first place would stand the questions of the Old Testament alone; in the second, those of the New and Old Testament; in the third, those of the Gospels, which belong exclusively to the New Testament; and finally, the remainder. Moreover, if anyone should perhaps object that we have inserted *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* and the *Enchiridion* among the questions, he will not have properly observed how closely these works correspond to the questions.

“Next, wherever Augustine himself composed *Retractations*, we placed them before the work, and we marked them in the margins at the passages he treated. Then we wrote the Greek in its own characters and repeated it in Latin in the margin for those who do not know Greek, sometimes adding its meaning. Whenever in different manuscripts we encountered two readings, neither of which ought to be rejected, we included both, but placed one in the margin. Then we distinguished the books at the head of the sheets. We prefixed to each work indexes of everything contained in it, and sometimes placed them even before the individual chapters.

“In the first questions, however, which we restored to the form of questions, it did not seem necessary to repeat the work, lest the preliminary matter should become longer than the narrative itself. We have nevertheless carefully noted, along with the questions, the biblical passages from which they were taken.”

Nor should we entirely omit what is read in the final column: Badius’s statement concerning the completion of the work and, as they call it, the register, addressed to our master Peter Gerard, prior, and so forth. The peroration runs as follows:

“These are, most excellent Master Peter Gerard, the questions of the divine father Augustine, won after much labor, which we now publish, dedicated to your name. We ask all readers to receive them favorably and to grant pardon if we have omitted either fewer questions than the most holy doctor Augustine himself composed, or questions less well known. For we believe that only a few are missing, and those only which were written to Simplicianus, Bishop of Milan, which until now we have been unable to find. We have nevertheless left a place where they could be inserted: three gatherings, Mm, Nn, and Oo. If we have left this place unused, no one except an inhuman and malicious accuser will judge it blameworthy, since the individual works are already complete and can be issued separately.

“As for the errors that we fear, we believe them to be of such a kind that anyone can easily detect and correct them without our review or admonition. So that no one may be unaware of the order in which the sheets are to be turned, and therefore suppose that something is missing, the sequence is as follows: a–s, A–G, Aa–Ll, Pp. Of these, b, k, q, r, G, and Ll consist of three sheets each, the others of four, and so forth.”

This work is printed in small Gothic type, in two columns, with lines so closely set that each page contains fifty-five. It is, in fact, very attractively produced. Although the numbers of the leaves and pages, as well as catchwords, are lacking, it has the signatures of the sheets and a continuous heading at the top of the page, printed in larger type. The initial letters are indicated, though in small form; the first line of each chapter, however, is given a larger typeface, and each chapter has a heading and number prefixed to it, the number also being repeated in Roman numerals in the margin. [Col. 0053C]

A table of the questions precedes the work in seven leaves, together with Augustine’s own judgment on the questions from the books of the *Retractations*. In this table there remains one point worthy of observation: in a special note, the editor excuses and defends the reading “of the Holy Scriptures” (*scripturarum sanctarum*) against the alternative “the Holy Scriptures” (*scripturas sanctas*) on the authority of several manuscripts.

The distinguished Braun mentions this edition, vol. II, p. 295. It may perhaps be identical with the edition mentioned by Maettarius, under the title of the first volume of Augustine’s works, vol. I, p. 482, on the authority of de la Caille; in the latter, however, the year 1487 seems to have been written in error for 1497.

[Note: [Col. 0053D] I now see that Hamberger has likewise been informed of this, in volume III, p. 104.]

## THE SIXTEENTH CENTURY

[Col. 0053D]

### 1506

At Basel, in the workshop of Johann Amerbach, in folio, in nine volumes.

“Part I of the books of Saint Augustine, which he published while a catechumen. Part II: the books he wrote after baptism. Part III: the books he published as a presbyter. Parts IV–VIII: the books he published as bishop. Parts IX–XI: the books that he does not list in his *Retractations*.”

Copies of this first edition of Augustine’s works are so rare that, although I have examined many catalogues of different libraries, I have so far happened to find it mentioned in only two.

[Note: [Col. 0053D] Namely, in the catalogue of the Bodleian Library, which cites *Augustine’s Works in nine volumes*, by Amerbach, Basel, 1506; and in the *Catalogue of the Library of the Principal Church and Monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict at Saint Emmeram, Regensburg*, part I (1748, in octavo), where a fuller title is given on pp. 40ff. But since parts V, VI, VII, and X are omitted, it is shown to be an incomplete copy.]

Both give the same year that we have prominently displayed, the year also established by Maettarius.

[Note: [Col. 0053D] Vol. II, part I, p. 216.]

There is, to be sure, some discrepancy among the sources: some, such as the Cologne writers, give the year 1504, while others give 1501 and 1503.

[Note: [Col. 0053D] Relevant here is the passage also cited by the Cologne writers from Sweertius’s *Belgian Athens*, p. 148, where, concerning Dodo, he writes: “He was the first to collect and correct all the works of Saint Augustine, and he added headings and censures to the individual works; but the plague cut short his premature labor. The work was to have been sent to press in that very year, 1501, and it appeared after his death from the workshop of Amerbach in 1503.”]

From this one might perhaps reasonably conclude [Col. 0054B] that the entire edition was not completed in a single year, but begun in 1503 and finally brought to completion in 1506, with the individual volumes marked with that year because it was the date at which the complete work was finished.

[Note: [Col. 0054D] Oudinus agrees, saying in his *Commentaries*, vol. I, p. 934, that the work was begun around 1500 and completed in 1506. In that passage, the later date has been copied incorrectly as 1586 because of a printer’s error. The Cologne writers copied almost all of Oudinus, except that they added on their own authority that everything appeared in 1504.]

Nor do all sources give the same number of volumes. Some say that the entire work consists of nine, others of eleven—not through any scribal error, but stating the number expressly. What is more, Trithemius says that it was printed in fifteen volumes.

[Note: [Col. 0054D] In a letter addressed to Jacob Kymolanus, a Carmelite, written at Würzburg on 16 August 1507, in Maettarius, vol. II.]

Oudinus, however, has now spared us further investigation of these matters: after setting out the division of the whole, he makes it sufficiently clear that he himself inspected the edition. He states that it consists of eleven parts contained in nine volumes, divided as follows: the first eight contain those books of Augustine that he himself lists in his *Retractations*; the remaining parts contain the others, which are nowhere mentioned in that work. We learned that this is indeed the arrangement from the catalogue of the Emmeram Library, which shows the first three parts contained in a single volume.

He also notes that he did not wish to add to these eleven parts the many *Sermons*, the many *Letters*, or the *Expositions on the Psalms*, since he had already arranged for them to be printed in the years 1489, 1494, 1495, and 1497.

In preparing this edition, Johann Amerbach had made use of the services of a certain Augustinus Dodo, a Frisian canon of Saint Leonard’s at Basel, who, with Amerbach supplying the expense, had searched the libraries of Italy, France, and Germany. Had fate permitted him, Dodo himself would have undertaken the work after bringing together materials from everywhere.

### 1515

[Col. 0055A] At Paris . . . in folio, in nine volumes. *The Works of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, Copied after the Amerbach Edition.*

Maettarius does not record this edition. The Cologne writers mention it, and the catalogue of the Bodleian Library notes it. I think scarcely a single copy of it is to be found in Germany, nor in France either, unless it lies hidden in some obscure libraries. Certainly the catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris knows nothing of it.

### 1517

Without place of publication. In folio. *Index of the Works of Saint Augustine*, by the distinguished Johann Theuschlein of Frickenhausen, from Rottenburg on the Tauber. Thus it appears in the catalogue of the Emmeram Library, p. 41. I believe it belongs to the Amerbach edition.

[Col. 0051B]

### 1520

At Paris, by Johann Parvus.
