In quarto. *Three Books of the Divine Aurelius Augustine against the Academics, the Soliloquies, and Other Opuscula*: four works printed here for the first time—*On Visiting the Sick*, *On Adulterous Marriages*, *On the Good of Marriage*, and *On the Good of Virginity*. *Catalogue of the Royal Library*, vol. I, p. 376.

### 1528–1529

At Basel, from the Frobenian press, in folio, in ten volumes. *The Complete Works of Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Corrected by Desiderius Erasmus.*

We were not given a fuller title from which we might draw information. We suppose, however, that it does not differ greatly from the one displayed by the edition of 1543. But since we have now reached that edition which may be called not only the first complete and comprehensive one, but also the foundation of all those that followed, including the most recent, and which in a sense governs them all, it will be necessary first to communicate to readers everything that Erasmus himself brought forward concerning the principles of his undertaking.

The editors of the later editions either were content to send the Erasmian work to press after enriching it with various additions, or followed in his footsteps and, relying partly on manuscripts and partly on their own judgment, sought to produce a more corrected and reliable text, or else departed farther from him. None of all their studies and efforts can be assessed—or even examined—without an exact knowledge of Erasmus’s work.

Nor is it sufficient merely to know in general terms and in a few words that Erasmus corrected the text [Col. 0055D], separated genuine writings from spurious ones, and redistributed everything in a new order. Such information does little to help us understand either the author’s or the editor’s method. But since Erasmus was the first to undertake an explanation of the particular and distinctive excellence of Augustine, both in thought and in expression, and then transferred that conception—together with the critical skill he ordinarily applied to other ecclesiastical writers—to the investigation both of the genuineness of the writings as a whole and of the soundness of individual passages, and since from that point onward he led the way for every generation in restoring Augustine through some method of textual criticism, I do not think that anyone concerned with these studies will easily be able to dispense with this discussion by Erasmus without loss.

[Col. 0056A] Moreover, Erasmus was likewise the first to investigate the causes of corruption in Augustine’s text and the various kinds of corruptions. His description of them can in some sense provide the same service that one ordinarily expects from a well-explained knowledge of manuscripts.

I have prefaced the present discussion with these remarks so that we might not seem to some people to have inserted the following lengthy address carelessly or with insufficient respect. Let us now hear Erasmus himself. For this is how he speaks in the letter, dated at Freiburg im Breisgau in 1529, in which he dedicates the entire work to Alfonso Fonseca, prince and archbishop of Toledo and primate of all Spain, devoting half of it to the praises of Augustine:

“Where am I wandering? For I had not undertaken an encomium of Augustine; and if I had undertaken one, what small portion of his praises would this have been? I wished only to show how regrettable it was that so great a treasure of the Church had been brought forth into public view by printers so late—a treasure which it was especially important to have circulating in everyone’s hands. The printers were doubtless deterred by the magnitude of the expense.

The first to venture upon this outstanding undertaking was a man of singular piety, JOANNES AMERBACHIUS, who was sufficiently blessed in material circumstances, but far more blessed in the gifts of his mind. Neither immense expense, nor his persistence in collecting copies from every quarter, nor the tedium of collating them, nor the difficulty of the work, nor the risk of losing money, nor anything else deterred him from making the whole of Augustine common to everyone. The love of profit did not invite him to this task, but sincere piety, which breathes through all his prefaces, together with his desire to recall those ancient teachers of the Church whom he saw and regretted had become almost obsolete. I therefore do not doubt that all who have advanced in piety through Augustine’s books pray blessings upon his hands.

[Col. 0056B]

God summoned him to heaven while he was undertaking the whole of Jerome’s works with even greater zeal. Yet as he died he entrusted that task to his three sons, Bruno, Basil, and Boniface, whom he had taken care to have trained in the knowledge of the three languages. Through them what the excellent father desired was accomplished with no less zeal than fidelity. For he had educated them both in piety and in learning in such a way that, in a sense, he survived in them as a greater and better man—and survives even today. Only the eldest has now departed this life.

[Col. 0056C]

There are so many swarms of monks throughout the world whose leisure is sustained by great revenues. There are so many abbots with rich incomes, doing nothing but building, or feeding horses, or feasting. This was their proper labor, yet a layman undertook it of his own accord. In Augustine’s case, he devoted as much care, study, and vigilance as that age could then provide—an age still comparatively unrefined and possessing very few men trained in this kind of learning.

[Col. 0056D]

What is more astonishing is that, although Augustine’s writings had already been passing through the hands of the learned for so many years, no public complaint had arisen about them, whereas everyone complained about Jerome. Yet unless I had many witnesses who either supervised or assisted in printing the work, no one would believe me how many errors I encountered and removed, even in places where it was thought that nothing had been corrupted.

[Col. 0057A]

Augustine has a particular manner of expression: pointed, and involving many things in long, extended periods. It requires a reader who is familiar, sharp, attentive, and possessed of a good memory—in short, one [lacuna]-ientem in the face of tedium and labor, and such readers are not very numerous. Although he displays secular learning less openly than Jerome, he nevertheless frequently alludes to it in passing. These circumstances caused a reader, more audacious than intelligent, to alter whatever offended him.

Errors committed through the carelessness of copyists or the ignorance of readers have, at least, some appearance of justification, by which their fault may be, if not excused, at any rate diminished. Yet it ought to have been the public concern of princes, bishops, and abbots to ensure that copies of useful books, especially sacred volumes, carefully corrected by learned men, were preserved in public libraries.

[Col. 0057B]

But who could absolve from the charge of sacrilege those who, moved neither by error nor by necessity but by foolish caprice, deliberately altered this man’s writings—turning *que* into *et*, and *et* into *que*; *sed* into *at*, and *at* into *sed*; *dixit* into *ait*, and *ait* into *dixit*; a verb into a participle and a participle into a verb; and making countless other changes of the same sort, as though they had been playing with another person’s work?

We detected this outrage especially in the books *On the Trinity*. We detected it through comparison with a manuscript supplied to us by a monastery somewhere in Flanders, whose name does not presently come to mind: a very handsome and ancient copy, which one would have said was an exemplar of good faith and great authority.

[Col. 0057C]

Scarcely ever did two lines occur without something being butchered by a crosswise pen. This was not error or carelessness, but the impious game of an idle and ill-disposed man.

Elsewhere, someone had filled out sentences by adding several unnecessary words. For example, whenever blessed Augustine quoted from the canonical Scriptures, when what concerned the matter at hand was sufficiently stated, that person continued the scriptural testimony farther back and at greater length from the same passage, although nothing of it was necessary to the argument. We discovered that this had been done especially in the commentaries he wrote on the Epistle to the Romans and on the Epistle to the Galatians.

In many places we laughed at the remarkable delirium of scribes who transferred into the text what a foolish reader had noted in the margin of his manuscript.

[Col. 0057D]

I shall present two examples from many. One occurs in Letter 58, where Augustine’s words read as follows:

> “But these prophets, whom he placed after the apostles, I do not think are those who, in the order of time, preceded the apostles, but rather those to whom, already under the apostles, there was granted through grace either interpretation of the Scriptures and examination of minds, or prediction of the time to come.”

In the earlier edition we found the participle *secuturi* (“to come”), separated from its noun, *temporis* (“of the time”), by an extensive verbal digression. This was not only conspicuously unlearned and foolish, but did not contribute even the slightest thing to the matter. For there was no ambiguity there about who the apostles were or from where the word was derived; the question concerned the kind of prophets about whom the Apostle was speaking.

[Col. 0058A]

I shall not reproduce the lengthy nonsense here, lest I become tedious. I shall excerpt only a little, so that it may be easy to infer that the rest contains no sense. It begins in this fashion:

> “For if I myself should hope to make a distinction, so that you may know what I think about these matters…”

You recognize the elegance of the style. Soon afterward comes this:

> “For, to proceed to the force of the term, *apostles* is said in Greek to come from *apos*, which denotes an argument or pre-eminence, and *scolon*, which means sending, as though one were sent pre-eminently, namely for the increase of the catholic faith; or an apostle, as though *post-missus*—sent afterward, and so forth.”

What could be more extraordinary than this delirium? For among the Greeks *apos* means no more than *Kiskildrivium* among the Latins, while *scolon* in Greek means “stumbling-block.” Then, with the utmost foolishness, he imagines that in the word *apostolus* the element *apost* has been added in the sense of “afterward,” for which the Barbarians commonly say *depost*. Yet if *apostolus* is a Greek word, as he himself teaches, whence does the Latin preposition *post* come in it?

[Col. 0058B]

He continues:

> “But *prophet* comes from *pro*, that is, ‘far off,’ and *for, faris*…”

whereas among the Greeks *prophet* means nothing other than what “foreteller” means among the Latins.

I think it sufficient to have offered this taste of the whole piece of nonsense, which has been attached to the text as though someone had taught Paulinus in Augustine’s place, even though he had indicated that he was uncertain about him.

The other passage occurs in the second book *On the Sermon on the Mount*. Since Paul counts joy among the fruits of the Spirit, lest anyone suppose that he was speaking of just any kind of joy, Augustine explains the passage as follows:

[Col. 0058C]

> “It should certainly be understood that ‘joy’ is used here in its proper sense. For wicked men are properly said not to rejoice but to exult, just as above we said that ‘will’ was used in its proper sense, which the wicked do not possess, and so forth.”

These words of Augustine contain no obscurity; nevertheless, someone had attempted to explain the meaning more clearly, supposedly, in these words:

> “Nor is it the joy of virtue, as is the will; and these things rather belong to the saints, whereas for sinners exultation and desire are more properly assigned.”

This equally tasteless nonsense, transferred from the margin into the text, tormented us for some time.

We had to struggle repeatedly with such monstrosities. One man had constructed, as though it were a new work, a book under Augustine’s name from fragments snatched from every direction; another had mixed someone else’s material with Augustine’s writings; another had turned a question into a letter by sewing a few words onto the beginning.

[Col. 0058D]

Not to pursue every instance individually, the rashness of idle men has scarcely played as impiously with any other volumes as with those of this sacred teacher. I set aside for the moment the spurious works: some not without learning, some barely tolerable, and some utterly unlearned. Yet among everything falsely attributed to him, nothing is more tasteless or more shameless than the *Sermons to the Hermits*. In them there is nothing—neither words, nor sentences, nor spirit, nor anything at all—that is worthy of Augustine. Nevertheless, whoever fabricated this work, a pleasant fellow to himself, confidently promised that Augustine would be believed to be its author; and indeed he found lips suited to such lettuces.

We did not remove any of these works, except that when the same writings occurred twice or more among this man’s works, we were content to print them once, so as not to burden the bulk of the volumes with unnecessary baggage. We merely added critical judgments indicating what was spurious, what doubtful, and what composite.

[Col. 0059A]

It is therefore truly painful that such things should have been committed in the case of so exceptional a writer. It is equally astonishing that hitherto no complaint from scholars had been made about them. From this one may infer that formerly Saint Augustine was either not usually read by most theologians, or was read carelessly.

Even I could never have been persuaded that so many errors lay hidden in so celebrated a writer. I had, in fact, no intention whatever of undertaking this task. The immense bulk of the volumes and the difficulty of the work required youthful strength and a man of almost adamantine constitution, whereas both my age and my health were now wholly discouraging me from this kind of labor.

[Col. 0059B]

But the late JOANNES FROBENIUS, a man deserving the lasting love of all students because of his extraordinary favor toward learning, at last extracted from me by his entreaties a promise to correct a single gathering of the *Letters*, so that he could display a specimen of the work at the next fair. I promised, but on the condition that he expect nothing more. He agreed.

Yet when I perceived that he was firmly resolved to complete the volume of the *Letters*, and that no one was prepared either to undertake the task of correction or, at any rate, willing to do so, my determination was overcome both by the persistent will of my exceptional friend and, much more, by the piety of the undertaking itself.

[Col. 0059C]

I took the whole volume upon myself, while repeatedly testifying that, if he wished to continue, he should find another corrector and should not draw me away from better concerns—to his own loss as well as to the detriment of my studies.

What more need I say? Since no one appeared who wished to lift that burden onto his shoulders, and since Johannes Frobenius declared that he was resolved, if nothing else were provided, to print the whole of Augustine again just as it was, I—partly out of regard for my friend, to whom I could refuse nothing, but much more because I judged it an unforgivable sacrilege for so exceptional a doctor of the Church, covered with so many errors, to go forth again at such great expense into the theater of the world, marked by a greater deformity precisely because the elegance of its phrasing and the majesty of its volumes would attract everyone’s eyes to it—endured having the pack-saddle laid upon me, as though one were displaying splendid purple disfigured by foul stains.

[Col. 0059D]

At last, once I had entered so vast a sea and spread my sails to the winds, I discovered far more difficulty than I had expected, so that more than once I lost heart and considered abandoning the undertaking. The evident danger to my health invited—or, more accurately, compelled—me to do so. I was also frightened by the example of Johannes Frobenius, whom I saw consumed by this task, a man otherwise worthy both of a strong body and of a very long life.

Yet what at first glance had deterred me from the undertaking, when considered more closely, added spurs to it. The friendship of good men ought not to be bounded by the span of life, especially when the burden of this most difficult undertaking had fallen upon his sons, Jerome and Johannes Erasmus, and his other children, to whom it was even less fitting to fail, since they had been deprived of such a father.

[Col. 0060A]

Whatever affection I had felt for Frobenius, I transferred to them. Therefore, having strengthened my resolve and judging it better to spend my life upon so sacred a work than to leave incomplete what I had once undertaken, I overcame all weariness. The farther I advanced, the lighter the labor became through familiarity, while, as I believe, Augustine himself breathed upon our efforts from heaven with a favorable breeze of goodwill, until at last the harbor opened in the distance. Brought into it by the aid of a propitious divinity, we now sing our joyful song of arrival.

In arranging the volumes, we followed this order. In the First Volume we placed those works from which Augustine’s whole life, character, intellect, and affections can be understood. I judged that this would make him both more correctly understood and more eagerly read. Love of a teacher makes a pupil attentive and willing.

[Col. 0060B]

We added his preliminary exercises, in which, while still a child in Christ or a new recruit, he most auspiciously practiced for his later distinguished achievements.

We assigned the Letters to the Second Volume, partly because many of them were written when he was still young, and partly because his distinctive character is especially evident in them.

We devoted the Third and Fourth Volumes to the writings he prepared for instruction.

The Fifth contains *The City of God*, since this work, both teaching and refuting errors—especially pagan errors—was mixed in both respects.

In this section there is nothing belonging to our industry, for the exceptionally learned Joannes Ludovicus Vives, at my urging, had undertaken this task as his own.

[Col. 0060C]

In the Sixth and Seventh Volumes we arranged the struggles against various heresies.

The Eighth and Ninth contain the treatises—for that is what Augustine calls his explanations of Scripture delivered to the people—except that in the Ninth we added a kind of miscellany of little books which certain self-styled spiritual men seem to have prepared in order to inflame their affection for contemplation of heavenly things.

The Tenth Volume contains homilies on various subjects, among which there is much that is extraneous, as there is also in the Ninth.

In the individual volumes, so that there might be some order, we followed either the order of the sacred books that Augustine interprets or the origins of the heresies.

[Col. 0060D]

In the books of the *Retractations*, Augustine himself preferred to follow the order of his age and his progress in Christianity, reviewing what he had written as a catechumen, what after being reborn in the sacred washing, what as a priest, and what as a bishop. He seems to have intended to assign the letters and treatises their own place, but he did not complete this part of the task, as appears from several of his writings.

Indeed, he was already engaged in this work in his extreme old age, as though foreseeing that his final day was near, and he pursued it with such greater zeal because, since he could no longer benefit the Church for long through the office of his voice, he might remain for her in books, insofar as possible both corrected and intact. He almost achieved this.

For scarcely anything less has survived from the monuments of another writer; nothing at all could ever be safe from corrupters. We shall not exaggerate our own work here. Let anyone who has leisure compare it, and he will recognize what we have done. Yet I would not dare promise that nothing remains requiring a corrector.

[Col. 0061A]

In some places the ancient manuscripts failed us; sometimes, in so long a work, sleep crept upon us—which Horace thinks should be forgiven as part of human nature. If anything was committed through the carelessness of the printers, we could not have prevented it, since we have no dealings with the printing house. We can only warn those who supervise the shop—and we have done so diligently.

Whatever our modest ability could accomplish, it has performed in good faith.”

Here you have everything by which the new edition recommends itself. I consider it not superfluous but entirely necessary to append a list of the works contained in each individual volume. Although it had originally been decided not to enter into a continuous order of the books in the survey of editions, and I had easily persuaded myself that we could do without such a list—especially since the preceding survey carefully noted where each work could be found among the Erasmian, Louvain, and Benedictine editions—we have nevertheless learned by experience that no reliable understanding of the success of the labor devoted to the author can be formed unless one is permitted to inspect the number and sequence of the books in the principal editions.

[Col. 0061B]

The arrangement of this Erasmian edition is therefore as follows.

### Volume I

It contains:

- Book II of the *Retractations*, with a critical judgment;
- the thirteen books of the *Confessions*, with a critical judgment;
- one book *On Grammar*;
- *Principles of Dialectic*;
- the ten *Categories*;
- *Principles of Rhetoric*;
- the six books *On Music*;
- the three books *Against the Academics*;
- the two books *On Order*;
- *On the Happy Life*;
- the two books *Soliloquies*;
- *On the Teacher*;
- *On the Immortality of the Soul*;
- the three books *On Free Will*;
- *On True Religion*;
- the two books *On the Morals of the Catholic Church and on the Morals of the Manichaeans*, with a critical judgment;
- the two books *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, with a critical judgment;
- Augustine’s *Rule*, with a critical judgment;
- Possidius, *On the Life of Augustine*.

### Volume II

A miscellany of letters.

There are 242 letters—two hundred and forty-two—among which are several spurious ones, marked by Erasmus with an obelus but nevertheless not entirely removed from their place. This volume includes the letters commonly attributed to Augustine to Boniface and Boniface’s letters to Augustine. Of these Erasmus was willing to remove only one, exceedingly long and conspicuously unlearned, as he himself says. He also cut away a capping piece fabricated with extraordinary impudence under the names of Cyril, suddenly speaking Latin, and Augustine, a Greek writing bad Latin.

[Col. 0061C]

In addition to these letters, he added critical judgments both to individual letters, wherever the matter seemed to require it, and to the collection as a whole. He prefaced it with a letter to readers written at Basel in 1527, explaining partly matters concerning their external form: that, like popular speeches—homilies—they had never been arranged, either in the books of the *Retractations* or afterward, according to any principle of time, persons, or subject matter. Consequently, writings unworthy of Augustine were more easily mixed in with them or even fabricated. Nor had books and letters always been kept distinct from one another, since Augustine calls a work a “book” in one place and presents it as a “letter” elsewhere.

He also explains with remarkable clarity their character and force.

[Col. 0061D]

How extensive the use of these critical judgments is may be understood not only from the example we have given from the preface to the *Letters*, but much more clearly from those supplied by the Benedictine monks, which are far more fully developed.

A twofold index of contents has also been added after the preface, one arranged according to the sequence of the volumes and the other alphabetically, together with the order of the Amerbach edition, all with considerable convenience for the reader.

[Col. 0064C]

The index of contents in this edition, however, is not the one Oudinus advertises, but belongs to the latest Erasmian edition. Oudinus falsely claims that it contains Possidius’s list of Augustine’s writings together with the *Life*; that list was first published in 1564.

## 1528–1530

Cologne, at the press of Joannes Gymnicus; octavo.

From this workshop, within a very short period of time and under different titles—not infrequently combined in a single volume—various little works of Augustine appeared. They are distinguished by their respective titles as follows:

1. *The One Book of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on the Work of Monks, addressed to Aurelius, Bishop of Carthage.* In the year 1529, in August.

[Col. 0064D]

2. *The Enchiridion of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, addressed to Laurentius.* In the year 1528.

3. *One Book of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on Grace and Free Will, addressed to Valentinus and the Monks with him; and one book of the same author, on Rebuke and Grace, addressed to the same and to the monks with him.* Two letters of the Divine Augustine to Valentinus, against those who deny free will, precede these works. In the year 1530.

4. *One Book of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, On the Immortality of the Soul; and one book of the same author, On Christian Combat*, without indication of year or place.

## 1531–1532

Paris, from the press of Claudius Chevallonius; folio, in ten volumes.

*The Extant Works of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, corrected by Desiderius Erasmus.*

[Col. 0065A]

Oudinus praises this repetition of the Erasmian edition in his *Commentary*, pages 939 and following. He says that it was accompanied by a dedicatory letter from Jacobus Hemerius of Stuttgart to Gallus Millerus, theologian of the Church of Tübingen, which explains the entire arrangement of this edition at greater length.

He also notes that this edition first published seventeen sermons: six for the liturgical year, the seventh *On the Words of the Apostle*, and ten on the saints.

The *Catalogue of the Library of the British Museum* (London, 1789, folio), in mentioning this edition, gives the year 1532; for this reason I have thought fit to prefix both years.

## 1537

Augsburg, printed by Heinrich Steyner; folio.

[Col. 0065B]

*Little Works of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, Bishop*, namely:

- seven books *On the Books of Moses, Joshua, and Judges*;
- *Questions of the Old and New Testaments*;
- *Evangelical Questions According to Matthew*;
- one book *Questions Addressed to Orosius*;
- one book *Questions of Hilary*;
- one book *On the Eight Questions of Dulcitius*;
- the two books *On Various Questions to Saint Simplicianus*;
- the two books *Evangelical Questions*;
- one book *Eighty-Three Questions*;
- one book *On Six Questions against the Pagans*;
- two books *To Januarius on His Inquiries*;
- one book *On the Investigation of the Trinity*;
- one book *On Epicureans and Stoics*;
- one book *On Heresies, addressed to Quodvultdeus*;
- one book *On the Five Heresies*;
- one book *Against Jews, Pagans, and Arians*;
- one book *Against the Jews*;
- the two books *Retractations*.

[Col. 0065C]

This series of complete books constitutes the Third Volume of the *Epitome of Augustine’s Works* compiled by JOANNES PISCATORIUS. The texts were taken from the Lyon edition of 1497 and from the Amerbach edition, as the editor himself states in his preface.

## 1541

Paris, at the press of Charles Guillard; folio, in ten volumes.

*The Complete Works of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, corrected according to Desiderius Erasmus; a fuller and more complete edition, with a very full index, prepared through the care and scholarship of Florentius Bourgoin.*

Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

## 1543

Basel, in the Frobenian workshop, through Jerome Frobenius and Nicolaus Episcopius; folio, in eleven volumes.

[Col. 0065D]

*The First Volume of All the Works of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo—works which, on the authority of ancient copies and after all editions published down to the present day, have been cleansed anew with the utmost vigilance from countless errors, so that so great a doctor of the Church may rightly appear to have been born anew.*

“Examine it, reader, and you will admit that this is no empty promise. If you also wish to show gratitude, you will not allow so much labor and so much expense to have been undertaken in vain.”

At the end are appended two indexes, one of subjects and the other of passages of Scripture interpreted. We trust that these will provide the reader with no small assistance.

[Col. 0066A]

*(Here the title of the first volume and of the complete work bears the imprint-year 1543, but at the end of each volume stands the year in which that individual volume was completed.)*

The Second Volume of the Works of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, containing his *Letters*, corrected with considerable care by Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam. In the year 1541.

The Third Volume, containing *τὰ διδακτικά*—that is, works properly concerned with instruction. In the year 1541.

The Fourth Volume, containing the remainder of *τῶν διδακτικῶν*—the instructional works. In the year 1541.

The Fifth Volume, containing the twenty-two books *On the City of God*, carefully revised by the most learned Joannes Ludovicus Vives and illuminated by his commentaries, which the author himself revised anew. In the year 1542.

[Col. 0066B]

The Sixth Volume, containing *τὰ πολεμικά*—that is, disputations against heresies, especially those of the Jews, Manichaeans, Priscillianists, Origenists, Arians, and Jovinian. In the year 1542.

The Seventh Volume, containing the remaining part of *τῶν πολεμικῶν*—that is, the battles against the heresies of the Donatists and Pelagians. In the year 1542.

The Eighth Volume, containing expositions of the mystical Psalms. In the year 1542.

The Ninth Volume, containing his treatises—that is, expositions delivered to the people on the New Testament—together with other little works of various kinds, the list of which appears on the reverse side of this page. In the year 1542.

[Col. 0066C]

The Tenth Volume, containing the remaining treatises delivered to the people, the contents of which this page’s reverse side will indicate. In the year 1542.

Two indexes to all the writings of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, composed in such a way that you can neither miss anything worthy of annotation nor reject anything as superfluous. The first indicates the subjects treated throughout the works themselves; the second displays, according to the order of the biblical books, the interpretations of passages of sacred Scripture. In the year 1543. At the end: in September.

What new developments occurred in this second Frobenian edition of Augustine’s works, by whom it was supported, and by what resources, the booksellers explain in the preface printed on the reverse of the title page of the first volume.

[Col. 0066D]

Beginning with Amerbach’s merits, they observe that Erasmus would have acquired still greater gratitude for his labors among all readers if he alone had been free to undertake so immense a task, and had not been forced to divide a good part of it among his friends because other affairs intervened from the side.

They continue:

“But what he was hoped to provide intact and complete in a later edition was meanwhile undertaken by others. For when the Paris edition followed, several alumni of that most celebrated school applied themselves to the task: if anything had escaped Erasmus and his associates, they would repair it through their own efforts, not to be regretted by the Muses and by no means superfluous. At last, when fate was already pressing toward the final correcting hand, and, as it is reasonable to believe, the holy soul of Augustine himself was favoring so many splendid successes, there appeared a man worthy of the goodwill of all good men, and by nature formed and fashioned for this undertaking—formerly especially dear to Erasmus for this very reason, and, so to speak, assigned to assist him in this business—Martin Lypsius. [Col. 0067A]

This man had at his disposal time, leisure, an abundance of copies, freedom to choose collaborators for the work, suitable learning, and an industry equal to the undertaking; and in so great a task he possessed not merely diligence but conscientious devotion. In addition, he enjoyed the encouragement and exhortations of learned men, the attractions of rewards, and, finally, every kind of support that could be needed. For he had been an admirer of Augustine from his earliest years and, out of his particular devotion to that most holy man, had deliberately become a follower of his discipline. For more than twenty years he devoted himself almost exclusively to this one task, so that no error might remain hidden in Augustine’s writings. Indeed, even in our first edition he supplied Erasmus with more passages than any other of his friends. [Col. 0067B]

Then, beyond the domestic library of his fellow religious, he gathered ancient and uncorrupted copies from the neighboring monasteries round about; everyone readily contributed whatever was best suited to this purpose. He also enlisted several tireless assistants from his own community. Thus he left nothing undone, whether for others or for himself, in the highest degree of diligence: weighing great, middling, and minor matters in the same balance, and recording them.

You would scarcely believe, dear reader, that this is said without exaggeration unless you saw the margins of the copy he sent us, bearing witness to the man’s indefatigable study. By means of definite marks he produces three, four, or even more copies, and then indicates the extent to which they differ. [Col. 0067C] For, since he was no less modest than learned, he preferred to leave the task of judgment to others, though at times he added his own opinion; and we have always gladly accepted it.

The remaining judgments were entrusted to learned men who had long and thoroughly savored the flavor of Augustine’s style—something that would not have been easy for just anyone . . . . . It must not be concealed that, in a certain part of the tenth volume—not a very large part, if one considers only the genuine works—we were deprived of Lypsius’s assistance because, at that time, the Geldrians were ravaging Louvain and the surrounding region, where Lypsius was then living. The reader had to be informed of this, lest he should perhaps form a judgment about the rest from those few portions. In all other respects, let everyone trust his own eyes, which will run through everything without hindrance—provided, of course, that they are accustomed to Augustine’s style—rather than our testimony: he will find everything equally accurate, even the pseudepigraphical works not excepted. [Col. 0067D]

Moreover, in all this investigation and examination, only one little work, among the genuine works, was discovered and published for the first time: namely, the third book *Against Gaudentius*. From this it is clear that scarcely anything else that still exists was likely to be missing. For the sermons *On Time*, as they are called, and *On the Saints*, which certain men who served abundance more than selectivity have everywhere filled with extraordinary license, have no bearing on the present undertaking. It is evident to every learned person that some printed works, by their entire style, disown Augustine as their author, while others present themselves as the work of a Greek rather than a Latin author. [Col. 0068A]

It is therefore only fair that what candidates for Roman eloquence have received with great applause and open arms in the case of Cicero, Livy, Seneca, Pliny, and many others—where the later care of scholars has always added something to the earlier work—students of sacred literature should likewise not disdain in Augustine’s writings, if they wish to bring to their reading hearts such as the works deserve.”

The entire work was printed in two columns, in the type customary in the Frobenian workshop, though smaller and not especially clear, except in the preface, which was set in somewhat larger type.

## 1545

Venice, from the Erasmian workshop, apud Vincentium Valgrisium; in octavo, in three volumes.

*The first volume of the minor works of Aurelius Augustine, distinguished doctor of the Church, containing all matters relating to faith and works; the second volume, containing all matters relating to grace and free will; the third volume, containing all matters relating to election, calling, and glorification, explained from the books of the same author, excerpted by M. Augustinus Fregosus Sosteneus and enriched with scholia, summaries, and an index.* [Col. 0068B]

A very rare book, of which I do not remember having seen mention anywhere. No one should allow himself to be misled by the title, as though this were a miscellany of passages excerpted and torn from various places and now arranged according to different subject headings. He should know that complete books dealing with a single subject were collected in the following order:

The first volume: *The Four Books On Christian Doctrine*; *The Book On Christian Discipline*; *The Enchiridion to Laurentius*; *The Book On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*; *The Book On Heresies*; *The Discourse On Five Heresies*; *The Book On the Usefulness of Believing*; *The Book On Faith and the Creed*; *The Book On Faith to Peter the Deacon*; *The Book On Christian Combat*; *The Book On Faith and Works*; an exposition of Psalm 29; an exposition of Psalm 30; an exposition of Psalm 31. [Col. 0068C]

The second volume: *The Book of the Begun Exposition of the Epistle of the blessed Paul to the Romans*; *The Book of Expositions of Certain Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans*; *The Book of the Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians*; Hilary’s letter to Augustine; Augustine’s reply to Hilary; the letter of the Fathers of the Council of Carthage to Pope Innocent; Pope Innocent’s reply to the Fathers of the Council of Carthage; the letter of the Fathers of the Council of Milevis to Pope Innocent; Pope Innocent’s reply to the Fathers of the Council of Milevis; Augustine’s letter to Hilary; the letter of five bishops to Pope Innocent; Pope Innocent’s reply to the five bishops; *Three Books On Free Will*; Augustine’s first letter to Valentinus and the brothers with him; Augustine’s second letter to Valentinus and the brothers with him; Augustine’s first letter to the presbyter Sixtus; Augustine’s second letter to the presbyter Sixtus; the letter of Alypius and Augustine to Bishop Paulinus; *The Book On Grace and Free Will*, to Valentinus and the monks with him; *The Book On Nature and Grace*, to Timasius and James, against the Pelagians; the letter of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine *On Grace and Free Will* to Rufinus; *The Book On Grace and Free Will* by Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, in defense of the blessed Aurelius Augustine against the book of the presbyter Cassian; the letter of Saint Aurelius the bishop *On the Condemnation of Pelagius and Caelestius*; an excerpted letter from the synodal proceedings against the heretic Pelagius, whom the Palestinian synod compelled to condemn the accusations brought against him; thirteen canons; Pope Celestine’s letter on behalf of Prosper and Hilary concerning the grace of God against certain presbyters of Gaul, followers of Pelagius. [Col. 0068D]

The third volume: *Two Books of Retractations*; *Six Books of the Hypognosticon against the Pelagians and Caelestians*; *Four Books Against Two Pelagian Letters to Boniface*; *The Book On the Spirit and the Letter*, to Marcellinus; *The Book On Predestination and Grace*, entitled *On the Will of God*; Prosper of Aquitaine’s letter to Augustine *On the Remnants of the Pelagian Heresy*; Hilary of Arles’ letter to Augustine on the same subject; *The First Book On the Predestination of the Saints*; *The Second Book On the Gift of Perseverance*; Prosper’s replies to the excerpts sent from the city of Janua; *The Book On the Predestination of God*. [Col. 0069A]

Each volume is prefaced by a table explaining the subjects of the individual books and chapters. He entitled it: “Summaries of the subjects, concisely reduced to one whole by M. Augustinus Sosteneus Fregosus”; it also contains an alphabetical index of notable subjects. The editor dedicated his work to M. Hieronymus Suripandus, General of the entire Augustinian Order. The presentation is elegant, with clear, rounded type, white and soft paper, and very broad margins, extending well beyond the headings and biblical passages noted in the text itself. [Col. 0069B–C]

## 1552

Venice, at the sign of Hope; in quarto. In ten volumes.

*The first volume of all the works of the divine Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, carefully purged of innumerable errors on the authority of ancient copies, with the readings of the ancient copies marked by their own signs in the text and margin, so that with the greatest justice so great a doctor of the Church may seem to have been reborn. Examine it, reader, and you will admit that this is no empty promise; and if you are willing also to be grateful, you will not allow so much labor and expense to have been undertaken in vain. To it have been added several books, letters, sermons, and fragments never before printed. An index has also been added, much fuller than the Basel one.* 1552. [Col. 0069D]

The second volume of the remaining works, as in the Basel edition of 1543, now printed for the last time with greater accuracy than before. 1552.

The third volume, as in the Basel edition. 1552.

The fourth volume, containing the remainder of the *didactic works* (τὰ διδακτικά). Most of what had been thoroughly torn apart and dislocated was restored on the authority of ancient Victorine copies. 1551. [Col. 0070A]

The fifth volume, containing the twenty-two books *On the City of God*. To it were added the commentaries of Joannes Ludovicus Vives, revised by their author. 1551.

The sixth volume, as in the Basel edition. 1551.

The seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth volumes likewise. 1550.

*An index of everything notably said by the blessed Aurelius Augustine, newly made superior to the preceding editions and rendered much fuller and richer by F. Florentius Bourgoin of Paris, a Franciscan. Moreover, many things that were defective, mutilated, or merely begun, both in the index of the authorities of Sacred Scripture—that is, of the Old and New Testament—and in the reconciliation of several apparently conflicting passages of Sacred Scripture in Augustine, have been reformed, expanded, and purged. Read it through and judge.* 1552. [Col. 0070B]

This edition was seen outside Italy by very few people. We found it recorded in the catalogue of the Zurich library.[^c0007-1] Its copy had once been in Hanover, in the very rich collection of outstanding books belonging to Duvier; happily it fell into the hands of David Clément, who described it more carefully in his *Bibliothèque Historique Critique*, vol. II, pp. 269 ff.

He thereby performed two notable services for scholars. The first was that he was the first to bring to light this exceedingly rare book, which was in itself not unworthy of more accurate knowledge. The second, and even greater, was that by carefully collating it with the subsequent Venetian edition, he clearly demonstrated the whole structure and composition of this work and easily resolved the question disputed between Clericus and Richard Simon.

One must not suppose that it is merely a repetition of one of the preceding editions, but rather that it was formed from several, and almost all of the earlier ones.[^c0007-2] For it retained not all, but many, of Erasmus’s censures; it offers variant readings in the margin; and wherever something was admitted into the text, it indicates there from which edition it was derived. Not only was Erasmus’s preface to Alfonso Fonseca reprinted in volume I, but in the second volume as well there was reprinted the admonition to the reader by Jacobus Haemerus, whom we have seen above to have supervised the Paris edition of 1532. [Col. 0070C]

I do not know how true the promise made in the title concerning additions is. Clément reproaches another Venetian edition—which borrowed the same wording from this one and displayed it on its title page—for vanity and fraud, yet he neglected to raise the same objection against this edition. I, for my part, would have wished no less that he had examined the Victorine manuscripts which, they say, were available for the correction of the fourth volume. [Col. 0070D]

[^c0007-1]: Vol. I, p. 70. It reads: “Venice, quarto, ten volumes. The works of D. Aurelius Augustine, by F. Bourgoin.”

[^c0007-2]: “The editions of Basel, Paris, and Venice that preceded it formed the foundation on which the work was carried out.” I know of no earlier Venetian edition of the complete works than this one, and unless he wrote carelessly, I advise students of bibliography to pay attention to it.

## 1556

Basel, apud Hieronymum Frobenium and Nicolaus Episcopius; in folio, in ten volumes.

*The works of the blessed Aurelius Augustine, corrected by Erasmus of Rotterdam.* [Col. 0071A]

According to Oudinus, five sermons not previously printed were added in this edition, namely: *A Sermon to the People On Jacob and Esau*, col. 1487; *A Sermon On Chapter XIII of Solomon’s Proverbs*, col. 1505; *A Sermon On the Parable of the Sower*, col. 1517; *A Sermon On the Words of Matthew XVI: “Whoever wishes to come after me,” etc.*, col. 1519; and *A Treatise On the Lord’s Prayer*, col. 1523. We suspect that Joannes Costerus supervised this edition. It appears in the catalogues of the Bern and Thott libraries.

## 1561–1563

Lyons, apud Sebastianum Honoratum; at the end of volume II, printed by Jacobus Faure; in octavo, in ten volumes.

*The first volume of all the works of the blessed Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, containing the two books of the Retractations and various minor works of his, which the turned page will indicate. All of them, purged of innumerable errors by collation with ancient manuscripts and restored with the utmost fidelity to their former purity, now at last return to the light.* An extremely full index of selected subjects was also added. 1561. [Col. 0071B]

*The Letters of the blessed Aurelius Augustine, printed with greater care, fidelity, and conscientiousness than ever before, and freed from the defects with which they had formerly been contaminated through repeated printing. The second volume. With two indexes, one of the names of those to whom Augustine’s letters were sent, the other an exceedingly full index of everything contained in each letter.* 1561.

*The blessed Aurelius Augustine On the Trinity, together with his other books containing the didactic works* (τὰ διδακτικά), *the third volume. With a very full index of subjects and statements.* 1562. [Col. 0071C]

*The blessed Aurelius Augustine’s Questions on the Old and New Testament, together with the remainder of his volumes called the didactic works* (τὰ διδακτικά), *the first part of the fourth volume. With an index, etc.* The second part likewise. 1561.

*The blessed Aurelius Augustine’s twenty-two books On the City of God, etc., twelve of which are contained in the seventh volume of all his works*—incorrectly printed in this way for “the first part of the fifth volume,” as also shortly afterward the eighth volume, containing the remaining ten, is incorrectly given for “the second part of the fifth volume.” 1563. [Col. 0071D]

*The first part of the blessed Aurelius Augustine’s polemical works* (τῶν πολεμικῶν), *the sixth volume.* 1562. The second and third parts: the earlier and later portions of the seventh volume. 1562.

*The blessed Aurelius Augustine’s Expositions of the Mystical Psalms.* The first and second parts of the eighth volume. 1563. [Col. 0072A]

*The blessed Aurelius Augustine’s Expositions of the Gospel of John and the Apocalypse, together with various volumes of his, etc.* The ninth volume. 1562.

*The blessed Aurelius Augustine’s Sermons. Their series and number are as follows: On the Words of the Lord; On the Words of the Apostle; Fifty Homilies; Homilies On the Seasons; Homilies On the Saints to the Brothers in the Desert; Seventeen Sermons and several others.* The tenth volume. 1563.

An edition very rarely encountered, but arranged with considerable convenience, as may be seen from the extensive indexes of noteworthy subjects appended to each volume and even to each part of the volumes. The type is Roman, fairly attractive but somewhat small; in the margins biblical passages, less often headings, and also, though not frequently, variant readings are marked in italic type.

## 1569

Basel, by Ambrosius and Aurelius Frobenius, brothers; in folio, in eleven volumes. [Col. 0072B]

The first volume: *The distinguished Father, foremost among the greatest ornaments and lights of the Latin Church, the blessed Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, whose outstanding monuments of every kind that can in fact be found are all once again brought under examination against the best and most faithful copies, and, through a new revision by highly learned men, made much more correct than ever before, freed from innumerable errors, and finally enriched with several new censures and many additions not at all to be rejected. With a three-part index, appended at the end, fuller than all existing indexes and more convenient for students of theology. The entire plan and method of this new edition will become clearer from the following poem.*

The remaining volumes are entitled as in the edition of 1543, except that in volume III, which contains the *didactic works* (τὰ διδακτικά), the words “now corrected in many places with the greatest care against the evidence of ancient manuscripts, after Martin Lypsius” have been added.

Volume X bears this title:

*The tenth volume of the works of the blessed Aurelius Augustine, containing sermons to the people and clergy, now corrected anew in many places by collation with the most ancient copies. To the end we have added sermons On Various Subjects and certain fragments never before printed, brought out from darkness through the work and study of the most learned men Martin Lypsius, Joannes Vlimmerius, and others. The following page will give their catalogue.* [Col. 0072C]

The index was reproduced according to the earlier edition.

Sigismund Jacob Baumgarten once gave an accurate account of this edition.[^c0007-3] Whatever industry was devoted to it was directed exclusively to volumes IX and X: the former was supplied with a new collation of manuscripts, while in the case of the tenth they openly claim to have altered and reshaped the entire volume. Here are the verses from the preface, written in an unusual poetic form, which concern this matter:

[Col. 0072D]

> Much of the ninth volume we collated, so that it might  
> Conform to the ancient books; everyone will approve what was collated.  
>   
> But in the tenth part, which was wholly teeming with errors,  
> Innumerable always, as even an unfair judge must admit,  
> How much our industry has changed this part—  
>   
> In cleansing it, Lypsius also formerly accomplished much,  
> And Costerus followed him with equal diligence:  
> Great is their glory, and not a small one.  
>   
> Yet wishing to impose a better file,  
> We undertook a greater burden and greater enterprises.  
> Here Vlimmerius greatly assisted us  
> By his own keen diligence:  
> In watchful care and vigilant labor  
> He is far superior to all others.  
>   
> Leaving nothing incomplete, he restored many mutilated things  
> To wholeness and put ancient things back in their former place.  
> Add that from several ancient books he brought forth  
> Treatises and sacred sermons for the whole world,  
> Printed previously by no one and seen by no one:  
>   
> These we leave for you at the end of this part,  
> Fair-minded reader, so that you may see how great an addition has been made.  
>   
> You will also have, reader, not a few sermons  
> Joined to those printed earlier. But because a large part of them  
> Had been corrupted and was full of many faults,  
> If they had been supplemented in every respect,  
> The page would likewise have changed its former number and place,  
> And the benefit would have been small while the labor immense.  
>   
> The principle of the index had to be observed here, pious reader,  
> Since when the numbers were changed, it too would have to change.  
>   
> Yet lest you seem thereby to have been deprived of any hope:  
> Everything worthy of notice among the additions  
> Is contained in the old but much fuller index.  
>   
> The index of Possidius, long desired by many  
> But previously denied to many, which he who was a pupil  
> And disciple of the divine Author composed—  
> That same Vlimmerius makes us share in it  
> And presents it as an outstanding gift.  
>   
> And so that it might be suitable for our edition,  
> We undertook no small amount of work and labor,  
> So that a fair-minded reader might find nothing wanting in us.  
>   
> If a doubtful reading seemed to us to hang between differing statements,  
> Each reader will see it marked with signs  
> And will choose from it the meaning appropriate to himself.  
>   
> Moreover, many other volumes have been enlarged,  
> Which, attentive reader, will not lack their own praise. [Col. 0073A–B]

For Joannes Vlimmerius of Louvain, formerly a regular canon at Saint Martin’s and renowned in his homeland for editions of the writings of several Fathers,[^c0007-4] had published at Louvain in 1564 forty-three of Augustine’s *Sermons On Various Subjects* and twenty-seven fragments of sermons, excerpted from the *Treasury* of Eugippius the abbot and from the commentaries of Bede or Florus, deacon of the Church of Lyons. Together with these he published Possidius’s short index of Augustine’s writings, recently discovered by Vlimmerius in the library of the Abbey of Villers and furnished by him with marginal scholia. [Col. 0073C]

He dedicated those publications to Jacobus Pamelius, then a licentiate in sacred letters and a canon at Bruges, in a letter dated at Louvain, from his Martinian monastery, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, 1564. Just as these sermons, recently published by him, were appended to the end of volume X, so Possidius’s little book, together with Vlimmerius’s letter, opens the first volume.

That letter led Baumgarten to suppose that this edition had begun in 1564, since he was evidently unaware that Vlimmerius had previously inserted it in a separate edition. Vlimmerius also undertook the revision of the entire tenth volume, as is clear from this letter. [Col. 0073D]

The printing was carried out as in the earlier edition, in two columns, but on somewhat more elegant paper and with more attractive type. The first title was embellished with printed woodcut figures.

[^c0007-3]: *Nachrichten von merkwürdigen Büchern*, section LIII (vol. IX), Halle, 1756, pp. 400 ff.

[^c0007-4]: Compare Foppens, *Bibliotheca Belgica*, vol. II, p. 747.

## 1570

Basel, by the brothers Ambrosius and Aurelius Frobenius; in folio, in eleven volumes.

*The works of the blessed Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo.* [Col. 0074A]

It may perhaps seem strange to someone—and I confess that it happened to me—that when the same Frobenian brothers had issued a complete and definitive edition of Augustine’s works in the preceding year, they should now have brought the same work back under the press. I have learned with certainty that the complete edition was known to very few, and therefore thought I had good reason to doubt it had I received testimony from anyone other than the editor himself.

That editor was Hieremias Mylius of Picrobedia, apparently the corrector or administrator of the Frobenian brothers’ printing house. He prefaced the books *On the City of God* with a letter to the noble and well-born young man D. Stanislaus Starzechovius, a Pole, son of Joannes Starzechovius, Palatine of Podolia, dated at Basel on 16 February 1570. In it he makes the following statement about himself and his work:

“Since Ambrosius and Aurelius Frobenius had decided, because of the lack of copies, to put Augustine through the press for a fourth time, they begged me to devote my efforts anew to collating, purging, and illuminating it. At last, out of regard for the common good and overcome by the prayers of sacred doctors, they drew me into this exceedingly difficult and troublesome labor, moved especially by the example of so many great men and by the excellence of theological matters and of this author. [Col. 0074B]

After three full years, amid the other printing-house tasks with which I was overwhelmed, and after so many vigils, sweats, most intricate revisions, distinctions, and abrupt and varied reflections, all exhausted by tireless labor and even at the cost of my health, I hope that I have discharged this office in such a way that I may appear not to have wasted oil and effort, and may believe that I have gained no contemptible favor among students of theology and fair-minded judges.

But leaving these matters aside, I shall proceed to the work itself, which ought to be the principal subject of the preface to a new edition, and I shall enumerate what I have accomplished. First, besides typographical ornament, the index enlarged in many ways, and other useful additions, I distinguished Augustine’s works by collating the most carefully corrected copies, so that henceforth the reader will be much more at ease than before in understanding them.

Second, on the basis of the same collation, I inserted what had hitherto been omitted, corrected what was corrupt, and restored what had been displaced. Third, I noted in the margin the testimonies of Sacred Scripture and of other authors cited in these books—a great assistance indeed to those whose memory is not especially strong. [Col. 0074C]

Fourth, I added marginal summaries, with no small illumination of the whole work, so that those seeking a subject might find it more easily. The last two features, however, were added chiefly in the fifth and tenth volumes, on which I spent almost a year and a half. In the tenth volume especially I added a considerable number of treatises and sermons from the edition of Vlimmerius, a man devoted to venerable antiquity.

Fifth, I not only arranged all these things as many others commonly do, but also took pains to ensure that they were carried into execution with the greatest care, frequently standing beside the presses while the work was being done.

But perhaps,” he continues, “the envious Zoili and calumniators will confront me—men who, since they themselves do nothing or nothing better, always dislike the honorable efforts of others. They will mock me for acting, after so many great men, as though I were carrying out a work already completed, and will accuse me of arrogance.

I wish to answer them briefly as follows. I am not to be compared with Erasmus, the phoenix of Germany, or with Ludovicus Vives, a man of the greatest learning. Nevertheless, since they carried out their purgation chiefly through copies rather than by their own judgment, and since everything cannot be done at once, I, taught by the passage of days, with more men following their example and with the supply of copies increasing, have been able to remove errors that were not trivial, and certainly not insignificant.

Moreover, because they themselves were not present at the presses, the negligence of the workmen caused many things that had been correctly established to be corrupted or omitted. This has very often happened even to me, although I was sufficiently attentive to the task at hand. [Col. 0074D]

But why say more? A comparison of the editions themselves will abundantly testify to what has been accomplished for the diligent reader. Since this volume is more saleable than the others and more frequently found in the hands of learned men, I wished to preface it especially with an account of my labors on this distinguished Father.” [Col. 0075A]

I thought it worthwhile to excerpt this much from Mylius’s verbose letter, so that readers themselves might perceive what they would in no way infer merely from looking at the title of the volume to which the letter is attached: namely, that a complete edition of Augustine’s works had been produced anew in this year.

For, as we said earlier, the volume is before us and contains the books *On the City of God*. Below, when we come to the separate editions of those books, we shall give its title, which is entirely different from that of the 1569 edition. [Col. 0075B]

As for the letter itself, everyone can see how vainly and recklessly many things have been asserted in it; yet it will not be easy to understand the purpose of all this argument. To give only one example, the editor wants it to appear that for three years he had been rolling this stone uphill so that a more correct and better Augustine might emerge. In the meantime, are we to believe that the same men who had assigned him this task could have had the whole of Augustine printed without any expense or labor on his part?

Or is it credible that the Frobenians found buyers for so many editions, and especially for the latest one, so eager that they did not hesitate to entrust the correction of the works at the same time to several learned men, always ready to print whenever a sheet was ready for the press? [Col. 0075C]

The matter seems easier to understand if one persuades oneself that the booksellers wanted to deceive their buyers by selling as a new edition one to which nothing had been added except a new title and some prefatory material. Yet even so I do not sufficiently understand the stratagem of that letter.

## 1570

Venice, apud Vincentium Valgrisium, and also the Juntas and Dominicus Nicolinus; in quarto, in eleven volumes.

*The first volume of the works of the blessed Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo. To it have been added several books, letters, sermons, and fragments never before printed. In this volume, besides restoring many passages according to a collation of older copies, we have taken care to remove everything that might infect the minds of the faithful with heretical depravity or cause them to deviate from the Catholic and orthodox way. An index fuller and richer than all the others has been added. Newly printed, revised, and corrected. Venice, 1570.* [Col. 0075D]

The second volume, containing his letters sent to friends, together with several of their replies to him. In it, etc., as is found later in the individual titles. At the end of this volume one will easily find the list of those to whom Augustine wrote. Newly printed, etc. [Col. 0076A]

Volumes III–X are entitled as in the Basel edition of 1543, with the words just quoted added everywhere. Nevertheless, in the title of the fifth volume, mention of the commentaries of Joannes Ludovicus Vives has been omitted.

*An index of everything notably said by the blessed Aurelius Augustine, rendered much fuller and richer than before. Moreover, many things that were defective, mutilated, or merely begun, both in the index of the authorities of Sacred Scripture—that is, of the Old and New Testament—and in the reconciliation, in Augustine, of several apparently conflicting passages of Sacred Scripture, have been reformed, expanded, and purged.* Venice, 1570.

Audiffredus records this edition, though with an abbreviated title, in the *Catalogue of the Casanatense Library*, vol. I, p. 341. He states that the first volume appeared from Valgrisius, the remaining volumes through the eighth, together with the index, from the Juntas in the same place and year, and the ninth and tenth from Nicolinus. [Col. 0076B]

David Clément contradicts this testimony in the *Bibliotheca Historica Critica*, where, as we have already indicated, he gave an exact account of it.[^c0007-5] We borrowed from him the fuller title, which he himself had first excerpted from the catalogue of the Mager Library,[^c0007-6] and later, when he obtained the edition itself, confirmed by personal inspection.

He censures Fabricius for saying that Valgrisius printed it. Here, then, we have a pair of men, both learned and in their respective fields second to none in curiosity and diligence, contradicting each other in a minor matter in which error could scarcely be tolerated between eyewitnesses.

Someone may think it best to dismiss them both and await the testimony of a third person who happened to see the same edition. I do not object, yet I cannot refrain from adding my suspicions.

I find it difficult to believe that Audiffredus, a man more diligent than can be said in all matters concerning the description of a book he had inspected, could have erred in words so clear and distinct. Certainly there is no indication of the printer in the titles. Therefore it must be that the names were subscribed at the end of each volume.

But Clément had already transcribed the titles from elsewhere into his own library catalogue when a copy of this edition fell into his hands. What, then, do you think he did to investigate Fabricius’s reliability? Clearly he leafed through the individual volumes and examined the printers.

Yet he was not concerned only with this. He was then chiefly trying to establish the integrity of an edition which some had called into question and others had defended. While engaged in this task, however, he came upon the dedicatory letter of Dominicus Nicolinus, perhaps also the subscription of volumes IX and X; and when he had noticed, in addition, two errors committed by Fabricius in his account of the edition, he presumably thought there was no longer any reason to doubt the third. [Col. 0076C]

Perhaps what I have argued will be more readily believed if I quote the very words with which he attacks Fabricius; for this reason we have decided to place them here:

“Mr. Fabricius was mistaken when he said in his *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. III, p. 514: ‘Valgrisius printed Augustine’s works, contained in ten quarto volumes, in the year 1571.’ There are three errors here. First, the edition has eleven volumes, not ten; second, it is from the year 1570, not 1571; third, it was not produced by Valgrisius but by Dominicus Nicolinus, who enriched it with a dedication addressed to Joannes Antonius Fachinetus a Nuce, bishop of Novocastro and papal ambassador to the most serene Republic of Venice. It is dated at Venice, 15 October 1570.” [Col. 0076D–0077D]

[^c0007-5]: *The Curious, Historical, and Critical Library*, vol. II, pp. 265 ff.

[^c0007-6]: Published at Berlin, 1715, in octavo, p. 783.

[Col. 0077A] Having disposed of these matters, we proceed to what made this edition better—or rather famous. Its production was undertaken by the bookseller and Venetian printer Dominicus Nicolinus, either—as I would prefer to believe—with other booksellers taken into partnership, or by redeeming a project begun by others. His explicit confession, displayed on the very title page of the work, was that he had taken care to remove everything that might infect the minds of the faithful with heretical depravity or cause them to deviate from the Catholic and orthodox faith. Among the heterodox, this declaration did not meet with kindly judgments. Cave, in the *Prolegomena to the History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, section VII, and Jo. Clericus, in the preface to the third section of the *Art of Criticism*, § 9, attacked the edition on this account [Note: [Col. 0077D] Latest edition, Leiden, 1778, vol. I, p. 16.]. Before them, Franciscus Turretinus had inveighed against this undertaking with particular vehemence in his *Disputations on Our Necessary Separation from the Roman Church and the Impossibility of Syncretism with It* [Col. 0078D] [Note: Disputation V, § 26, p. 130. They were first published at Geneva by Samuel de Tournes, 1687, in quarto.].

Neither of these men, however, had seen the edition; nevertheless, relying on Nicolinus’s own confession, they judged it sufficiently convicted of malignity. Yet Cave and Clericus appear to have judged the matter more unfairly—or at least more hastily—than Richard Simon, who maintained that these alterations had been made not in the text itself, but only in the censures and scholia [Note: “Only in the summaries and scholia.” See the *Bibliothèque critique de Sainjore*, vol. I, p. 261 (Paris and Amsterdam, 1708, octavo), and *Selected Letters of M. Simon* (Amsterdam, 1730, duodecimo), vol. IV, p. 12.]. The statements drawn from P. de Vitry’s unpublished dissertation and cited in the *Mémoires de Trévoux* agree entirely with him [Note: *Mémoires de Trévoux*, September 1729, p. 1618.].

Clericus replied that he had no reason to regret his judgment. Simon, he said, had scarcely compared the text of this edition with another, while little credence ought to be given to the Italian correctors, who had declared their work in such vague terms [Note: See *Bibliothèque choisie*, vol. XVIII, p. 169.]. Thus the dispute remained unresolved for a long time, [Col. 0077C] until Clement finally undertook to arbitrate it. For, having had the rare good fortune in these matters to compare the Venetian editions of 1552 and 1570, he first observed what had remained entirely unknown until then: that the earlier edition had served, in a certain sense, as the foundation for this one, although the latter had not been copied from it in every respect. Rather, as seemed most advantageous for profit and most suited to the purpose declared by the bookseller, some things had been removed and others altered.

Thus he showed that the additions vaunted in the title were already promised in the same words in the earlier edition, and that the table of contents had plainly been taken from it, with only the title altered and the author’s name chiefly removed. On the other hand, he noticed that the present edition departed from it in many respects, omitting and inserting both individual words and entire booklets. He collected a considerable number of examples, and from all of them concluded that Simon had wrongly undertaken the defense of this edition.

Indeed, we do not see what Nicolinus had done to deserve Simon’s patronage, since we know of no caution anywhere offered by him in defense of his alterations. On the contrary, in his letter—whose opening we reproduce here from Clement—he openly confessed that he had allowed himself complete freedom and had spared the text in no way:

> “When I saw,” he says, “that the works of Saint Augustine were circulating to the great detriment of the Catholic faith, corrupted in many places by the cunning of heretics, I thought I should perform a worthwhile service if I printed them at this time after restoring them to their integrity. To accomplish this more easily, I took care above all that they should be examined by professors of sacred theology and compared with older manuscripts, so that they might be reduced to their genuine reading. I also took care that, during the printing, the attention and labor of the most excellent man Borgarutius a Borgarutiis, the most accurate and diligent corrector of type, should be added. How much he accomplished in correcting works of this kind will readily be apparent from a comparison with the other surviving copies.”

## 1571

At Lyon, by Morellius, and at Paris, by Nivellius. Fabricius reports that these were reissues of the Basel edition; how accurately, I would not dare affirm at once. But I remember finding an edition of Lyon from this year, in eight volumes, printed by Sebastianus Honoratus, in Hendrichius’s *Pandectae Brandenburgicae*, where the *Expositions on the Psalms* are praised in two octavo volumes; these unquestionably belong to a complete edition of the works.

## 1577

[Col. 0078C] Antwerp, from the workshop of Christopher Plantin; in folio, in eleven volumes.

*The Works of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo and Preeminent Doctor, Contained in Ten Volumes, Corrected with Much Labor from Manuscript Copies by the Louvain Theologians and Freed from Innumerable Errors; Further, Illustrated with Learned Censures and Enriched with Many Homilies and Several Letters of the Same Blessed Augustine, Previously Unpublished. With a Threefold Index.*

Although separate titles, taken almost entirely from the Erasmian titles, were added to the individual volumes, this general title is prefixed to the volume that one would rightly call the last, except that—as the title itself makes clear—it ought to be placed before all the others. It contains the indexes, the *Life of Possidius* together with the index of Augustine’s writings, and the preface explaining the plan of the entire undertaking.

Thomas Gozaeus Bellemontanus of Hainaut, professor of theology at the University of Louvain and apostolic and royal censor of books in Belgium, had first undertaken responsibility for this new and improved edition of Augustine’s works. He undertook it in such a way that the overall direction and authority of the entire work remained with him [Note: Molanus writes that he wished only difficulties and matters involving doubt to be referred to him.], while sharing the labor with several learned men joined to him by similar studies and devotion, and competing with one another in affection for Saint Augustine. He distributed the assignments among them, after gathering and dividing among his colleagues more than two hundred manuscript copies.

But after he was struck by apoplexy and exchanged life for sudden death on 8 March 1571, his successor in the censorial office, Joannes Molanus, allowed Plantin to impose this burden upon him as well. Having removed some readers and substituted others in their place [Note: Molanus calls “readers” those who, according to Gozaeus’s arrangement, devoted themselves to comparing Augustine’s books with manuscript copies, correcting them, and especially cleansing them of the censures of Erasmus and the commentaries of Vives. “After examining the readers’ work,” he says, “I found in many cases acute judgment joined with the greatest diligence; in others, although I did not find as much diligence, I thought that the zeal they possessed ought rather to be encouraged than censured. There were a few whom, because they seemed less suitable, I replaced with other men superior in learning and judgment. Following our instructions, these men carefully corrected both what had already been done and what remained, and referred to us only difficulties and doubtful passages.”], he finally saw the work brought to completion under what were virtually his own auspices.

[Col. 0079B] Administrators were not assigned only to the individual volumes; within each volume, several men worked according to the number of manuscripts involved. According to Molanus, the following supervised the work: the correction of the first volume was directed by Martinus Baccius of Tielt, later pastor of Aarschot; the letters, by Jacobus Baius of Meulun, president of the College of Savoy at Louvain. An addition to the letters was sent from Brussels by Joannes Gravius of the Society of Jesus.

Henricus Cuykius of Culemborg, then professor of ethics and later bishop of Roermond, labored on the third volume. The fourth was corrected by Embertus Everaerds of Arendonk, pastor of the Church of Saint James. Petrus Coretus of Ath, pastor and professor at Crispin, corrected the books *On the City of God*, which constitute the fifth volume. In the sixth volume Christophorus [Col. 0079C] Broide, summoned to the deanery of the church of Aire, did the work. The seventh volume, which is said to have teemed with errors, was reviewed by Henricus Gravius of Louvain, doctor of theology and royal professor, otherwise famous as well. Claudius Porta of Bapaume, bachelor of theology and later pastor and canon of Bindua, supervised the Psalms. Guilielmus Estius of Gorinchem contributed his labor and study to the correction of the ninth volume. All these men, except Henricus Gravius and Claudius Porta, had attained the rank of licentiate in theology.

Finally, the tenth volume was assigned to the Martinian Regulars, since Martinus Lipsius of Brussels and his pupils Joannes Costerius and Joannes Vlimmerius of Louvain had long before devoted great labor to it [Col. 0079D]. Joannes Vlimmerius also contributed to this edition various sermons of Augustine that he had discovered, and diligently transcribed many previously unpublished sermons from the manuscripts of Cambron. Molanus states that he himself had been assigned the task of prefacing each of Augustine’s books, as was customarily done in the manuscripts, with Augustine’s own *Retractations*, or, where these were lacking, with a brief judgment supported by the opinion of many theologians. Whatever was clearly found not to be Augustine’s, he decided to place in the appendix to his volume, after prefacing it with censures.

“In these censures,” he says, “Erasmus was several times useful to us, and even more so the index of Possidius, Bede’s citations, the manuscript judgment of the most learned theologian Joannes Hesselius concerning the nine volumes, and that of the revered Father Martinus Lipsius concerning the tenth volume. I introduced nothing without its having been approved by two professors of our college, Henricus Gravius and Laurentius Westerhovius, whom I certainly had as energetic colleagues and assistants in this part of the work.”

This is the judgment and declaration of a private man concerning what was virtually his own work. But it may also be useful to know the judgment that he issued with the authority of his public office, which is printed immediately on the reverse of the title page. Here it is:

> “The works of the most blessed Augustine, corrected by the Louvain theologians, ought to be preferred to all previous editions chiefly for three reasons. First, because innumerable and serious errors have been corrected throughout the individual volumes from the oldest manuscript copies, with the correction proper to each volume also appended at its end. Second, because whatever unlearned censures or annotations existed in these volumes—to say nothing more—are absent from this edition. Third, because each book is preceded by Augustine’s own *Retractation*, or, where that is lacking, by a brief judgment confirmed by the opinion of many theologians. Whatever has been certainly discovered not to be Augustine’s has been placed in the appendix to its respective volume, with censures prefixed that have been examined and approved by several Louvain theologians [Note: Signed at Louvain on the Kalends of September, 1571. “I, Joannes Molanus of Louvain, apostolic and royal inspector of books, have subscribed this in my own name and especially by mandate and authority of our venerable theological faculty.”].”

A few observations must now be made concerning these claims.
