It should first be noted that the division into volumes was retained from the Erasmian edition, but that the order of the books was altered in various places, especially those relegated to the appendices. They rightly claimed for themselves the correction of the text’s many serious errors on the basis of the manuscript copies of which they possessed an immense supply.

This is demonstrated by the corrections or reviews appended to the end of each volume, except the tenth. In these, the earlier reading is carefully, though briefly, compared with the reading of the collated manuscripts or with the reading newly adopted, with an index of the manuscripts used placed at the beginning throughout. A particularly abundant harvest of these corrections, or of passages requiring correction, grew in the seventh volume, which contains the controversies with the Donatists and Pelagians.

Many passages were so intricate or capable of being explained in either direction that Henricus Gravius, appointed editor of this volume, felt that his labor would achieve little unless he departed from the brevity observed in the other volumes. For, as he says, he was overcome

> “not so much by the infinite multitude of errors that most shamefully disfigured this volume as by the fact that it was frequently necessary to explain the reason for an altered reading, establish that the former reading was erroneous, and disclose the cause and occasions of the corruption; sometimes also to weigh various readings and decide between them by comparing other passages with one another, and at times even to maintain the common reading against the authority of the manuscript; on occasion, moreover, to propose a conjecture about how gaps might be filled, dislocated passages repaired, and corrupt readings restored.”

“Finally,” he says,

> “we also had to annotate passages that appeared suspect and to which we could not bring a remedy without manuscript support, so that diligent scholars might be given occasion to examine the old libraries of other regions, in case older or more reliable copies might be lying hidden somewhere, from which these passages could be corrected or amended.”

Once he had departed from the established plan, he ventured to proceed still further:

> “First, we briefly disclosed historical matters, many of which frequently occur here and are unknown; next, we elucidated obscure passages; then we explained doubtful and dangerous ones; thereafter we defended them against the attacks of others; moreover, we showed in what sense passages misunderstood by certain people ought to be taken; finally, if anything appeared to oppose the heresies of our own day, or was otherwise worthy of observation, we noted it briefly. Nor did it seem right to omit this: since we had been given a German copy to correct, while many people used a French edition that frequently contained errors different from those of the Frobenian edition, we also indicated those errors. We did this with reasonable diligence in several passages, but, pressed by the shortness of time, we could not complete the work.”

These discussions of Gravius constitute a singular volume, distinguished from the seventh volume itself by a separate title:

*Annotations on Volume VII of Blessed Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, in Which the Basis of the Corrections and the Variety of the Readings Are Indicated, Matters Worthy of Remembrance Are Observed, and More Obscure and Difficult Passages Are Explained and Illustrated.* Antwerp, 1577.

As for the other point that the official judgment counts among the merits of this edition, there is no need to discuss what displeased these theologians in Erasmus’s censures and in Vives’s commentary. The third point carries greater weight: spurious works were completely separated from genuine works and relegated to an appendix. In pursuing this task they showed considerably more learning than Erasmus, who was generally content merely to mark in his censures what he regarded as suspect, separating only a few items and entirely excluding certain others.

In the sermons, however, where it would have been difficult to pass particular judgment on each one, they professed to have followed the example of Martinus Lipsius. They gave Augustine’s name to those sermons that appeared certainly to be his and added supporting evidence from Bede or elsewhere, as it arose. Those that were certainly found not to be Augustine’s they relegated to the appendix. The remaining sermons—either insufficiently examined or regarded, on the judgment of certain learned men, as of doubtful authority—they left among the Augustinian works, without adding Augustine’s name.

So much for the studies of the Louvain theologians. As for the printer’s part, the works were printed in a clear enough round type, in two columns; the censures were in the same type, but smaller, while the arguments, as well as the marginal annotations, were in italic type. All the volumes except the one containing the indexes and bearing the title of the entire work, as well as the *Annotations on Volume VII*, bear the year 1576 on their title pages. Yet it is clear from the colophons that they were not all completed in that year: some give the year 1576, others 1577. Finally, we add that Plantin dedicated the edition to the cardinals Christophorus and Ludovicus Madrucius.

## 1584

Venice, by Joannes Baptista Sessa, under the sign of Felix; in quarto, in eleven volumes.

*The Complete Works of D. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Printed, Reviewed, and Corrected.* Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

This is a reissue of the earlier Venetian edition. At least Turretinus cites from this edition the words that we know offended him so greatly and that were quoted above. The scholars of Cologne confirm this, correcting Ancillon in the *Critical Miscellany*, vol. I, p. 243, who had incorrectly given the number 1548. Oudinus, however, vol. I, p. 952, reports that it is a description of the Plantinian edition, and Turrentinus himself has left me uncertain because he wishes the edition to have been printed by the Giunti, which is partly true of the earlier edition but is unclear to me in this case.

It could easily have happened that the printer correctly identified the edition intended, while confusing its year with that of the other Venetian edition. Clement, however, confirms us in the preceding judgment, adding other testimonies to those already cited in the *Bibliotheca Historico-Critica*, vol. II, p. 268.

## 1586

Paris, under the sign of the Great Ship; in folio, in eleven volumes.

*The Works of D. Aurelius Augustine, etc.*, as in the Antwerp edition. With several other homilies now published for the first time at Paris, which the second page of volume X will list [Col. 0082D], together with a threefold index.

The homilies newly added are thirteen, taken from a manuscript in the library of the Grande Chartreuse:

1. On the Birthday of the Martyrs.
2. On Susanna.
3. On the Gospel passage of John, “Until now you have asked nothing in my name.”
4. On the Birthday of Saints Castus and Aemilius, Martyrs.
5. A Treatise for the Vigil of Pentecost.
6. On the Reading from Exodus, concerning the Bush in which there was a Flame, and the Bush was not Consumed.
7. On Word and Voice, and on Fasting and Hungering.
8. On the Passage in John, “I am not going up to this Feast.”
9. On the Tree Which the Lord Cursed, and Which Withered Because He Found No Fruit on It.
10. On the Apostolic Saying, “We Brought Nothing into This World, and Certainly We Can Take Nothing Out of It.”
11. [Col. 0083A] On Paul’s Saying, “Whoever Boasts, Let Him Boast in the Lord.”
12. At the Night Vigil, concerning the Exodus passage: “When the lamb was sacrificed in Egypt.”
13. On Psalm XLI, for the Newly Baptized.

They note that the manuscript bears Augustine’s name and are convinced that no one will fail to acknowledge these works as his.

Besides the homilies, the following works by uncertain authors were also added, unquestionably taken from the same source:

- *A Warning to the Universal Church* [Note: The following is ascribed to it: “It seems to me rather to belong to Celestine, or Leo, or another pope, who by their own force drive out the gods.”];
- *A Form of a Letter Concerning a Certain Bishop of the Manichaean Sect*;
- *A Collation on the Trinity of Blessed Augustine from Himself to Himself*;
- *Miscellaneous Sentences Collected by Someone*;
- *A Treatise on the Twelve Stones Mentioned in the Apocalypse*.

In other respects, this edition surpasses the Plantinian edition in the clarity of its type and paper.

## 1596

[Col. 0083B] Geneva, printed by Jacobus Stoer; in octavo, in eleven volumes.

*The Works of D. Aurelius Augustine, Corrected by the Louvain Theologians.* Cited by the scholars of Cologne and by Ceillier.

I have been able to see only the fifth volume of this edition, containing the books *On the City of God*, with the following title:

*The Twenty-Two Books of D. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on the City of God. Now at Last Made Most Accurately Corrected by Collation with Ancient Copies and Illustrated with the Most Learned Commentaries of Ludovicus Vives. The First Twelve Books of Which Are Contained in the First Part of the Fifth Volume of All His Works. With an Index Made in This Latest Edition with the Greatest Accuracy and Fullness.*

The other volume is entitled:

*The Second Part of the Fifth Volume of the Works of D. A. A., Containing the Remaining Ten Books of the City of God*, etc.

It is not uncommon for the volumes of this edition and of the Lyon editions to appear separately. Indeed, their modest size and more convenient—and consequently more frequent—use made it easier for them to be separated and sold individually.

## The Seventeenth Century

## 1603

Paris, in folio, in eleven volumes. The works of D. Aurelius Augustine, from the same recension. Oudinus, and the scholars of Cologne following him.

## 1609

Paris . . . in folio, in eleven volumes. The works of D. Aurelius Augustine, reproduced according to the recension of the Louvain theologians. Vignerius cites it in the preface to the *Supplement*, and others follow him.

## 1613–1614

[Col. 0083D] Paris, under the sign of the Great Ship; in folio, in ten (eleven) volumes.

*The Works of D. Aurelius Augustine, Corrected and Enlarged from the Second Edition of the Louvain Theologians, Together with the Commentaries of Leonardus Coquaeus on the Books on the City of God.* Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris; add Oudinus.

Vignerius states in the preface to the *Supplement* that this edition, as well as the preceding one, was enriched with additions not to be regretted, but I do not know what they were. Nor do I sufficiently understand what the second edition of the Louvain theologians was, since the editors profess in the title to have followed it.

## 1616

[Col. 0084A] Cologne, at the expense of Antonius Hierat; in folio, in eleven volumes.

*The Works of D. Aurelius Augustine, from the Edition of the Louvain Theologians, Now Much Enlarged.*

Vignerius declares that this edition is more extensive than the preceding editions, but that it was printed on paper fit only for oil and pepper. I therefore have no doubt that it originated with the bookseller whom we have indicated, though with hesitation.

## 1626

Paris, in folio, in eleven volumes. *The Works of D. Aurelius Augustine, According to the Edition of the Louvain Theologians.* Vignerius.

## 1635

Paris, in folio, in eleven volumes. The same. Vignerius.

## 1644

[Col. 0084B] Paris, at the house of Antonius Vitray; in octavo, in two volumes.

*Augustine’s Works against the Pelagians.* Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris, vol. I, p. 377, no. 679.

## 1647–1648

Louvain, at the house of Bernardinus Masius; in quarto, in three volumes.

*The More Notable Works of Blessed Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, and of His Ancient Disciples, Against the Pelagians and Their Remnants, According to the Plantinian Edition.* Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

## 1651

Paris . . . in folio, in eleven volumes.

*The Works of Saint Aurelius Augustine from the Recension of the Louvain Theologians.*

The distinguished Rosler testifies that this description served him in volume V of his library. Unless, perhaps, this is one edition with the one cited immediately below from the following year, so that the earlier volumes, containing the *Retractations* and the letters, were printed in 1651, while the remaining volumes were printed in 1652.

## 1652

Rome, by Ignatius de Lazaris; in quarto.

*Some More Notable Works of Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Against the Pelagians and Their Remnants.* Catalogue of the Royal Library.

Paris, in folio, in eleven volumes.

*The Works of Saint Aurelius Augustine from the Recension of the Louvain Theologians.*

Vignerius reports that all these editions were indeed enlarged, but less carefully corrected.

## 1654

Brussels, in duodecimo.

*Some Selected Works of Saint Augustine.*

They contain: *On Grace and Free Will*, *On Rebuke and Grace*, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, together with three letters of Augustine:

1. To Paulinus, Bishop of Nola;
2. To Sixtus, a presbyter of the Roman Church, later pope;
3. To Vitalis of Carthage.

These were formerly numbered among the Augustinian letters 105, 106, and 107, and are now 194, 186, and 217. They are prefaced by two letters of Hilary and Prosper to Augustine. See M. *Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica*, col. 745–746. Whether the title is given there in its exact wording, I do not know.

## 1654–1655

Paris, at the expense of Simeon Piget, in the Rue Saint-Jacques, [Col. 0085A] under the sign of Prudence; in folio, in two volumes.

*Supplement to All the Works of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Published before the Year 1614 at Basel, Paris, Antwerp, Lyon, and Venice, Together with Six Books of the Second Reply of the Same Blessed Augustine against Julian the Heretical Pelagian, and Various Sermons and Treatises Hitherto Unpublished. Drawn from Manuscript Copies of the Best Reliability and Antiquity by Hieronymus Vignerius, Priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of Jesus.*

Volume I, second edition, 1655. At the end: 1654, from the printing house of François Le Cointe. Volume II, 1655.

Vignerius had noticed not only that, in the latest editions of Augustine’s works then available, many short works were missing that had recently been published and circulated separately, but also—and this was especially vexing for those intending to purchase an edition—that although all the recent editions were individually more extensive, none was complete, and in the purity and correction of its text each was far inferior to the much older editions.

He therefore resolved to prepare a supplement to the works of this holy doctor, not so much to recommend the newer editions by allowing them, with his work added, to be called entirely complete, but rather to oblige those who preferred to retain the older and more carefully corrected editions.

Volume I therefore contains:

1. Forty new sermons, edited by Sirmond at Paris in 1631 and thereafter received into later editions, together with an appendix of five sermons and Sirmond’s notes.
2. One hundred twenty-seven sermons *On Various Subjects*, divided into two parts and first published by the Louvain theologians in 1576.
3. Eleven homilies taken from a manuscript in the library of the Grande Chartreuse.
4. Six sermons published at Rome by Joannes Baptista Maro.

I do not know by what accident it happened that these six were brought together with the preceding items, so that not eleven sermons, as the title promises, but twelve sermons from the manuscript of the library of the Grande Chartreuse are presented. They are the same sermons first printed by the Parisians in 1586, except that the Paris set contained one additional sermon, which is lacking here; another, giving a brief explanation of the Creed, has taken its place. Vignerius notes that this sermon, as also the following three—*For the Kalends of January*, *On the Kalends of January*, and *Before the Altar, to the Infants, on the Sacrament*—was absent even from the latest Paris edition then available.

5. A *Treatise on the Seven Vices and the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit*, formerly published by Guilielmus Camerarius, a Scottish theologian, and likewise absent from the latest edition, that of 1652.
6. *The Book on the Proceedings of Pelagius*.
7. Letters that had been omitted from the older Basel, Paris, and Lyon editions.
8. *Augustine’s Mirror of Sacred Scripture*, previously unpublished, of which we shall speak below.

By far the most important part of this supplement, however, is contained in the second volume, where books hitherto unpublished are brought to light. Hence Vignerius says that, on account of this edition of the supplement, the whole Christian world applauds France, since the more important portion arises from the second volume rather than the first.

First, six books of Augustine against Julian come forth from the darkness in which they had until then been buried and almost extinguished. They had often been mentioned by Fulgentius, Bede, Servatus Lupus, and other later writers, but only a small portion of them had become known through the efforts of Claudius Menardus. Thus no one dared hope that more than two of the eight books survived, when, behold, fortune granted Vignerius the discovery of six complete books in a manuscript of the library of Clairvaux.

He exults in this good fortune so greatly that it might perhaps be said, not unjustly, that emotion took something away from his judgment and hurried his mind beyond calm consideration, since he wished it to appear that he had found not merely six books but all eight, as many as were said to have been written by Augustine. We shall discuss these works below, in the editions of the individual writings, no. 98.

The following works come next, as a second part of this second volume:

1. A single letter of Saint Augustine to Macrobius;
2. Forty unpublished sermons;
3. Two treatises, one *On Prayer*, from a manuscript at Dijon, the other entitled *On Prayer and Almsgiving*, from a manuscript of the Royal Library;
4. *Sentences against the Heretic Pelagian*.

Necessary indexes were added to both volumes. Vignerius dedicated the second volume to Claudius Largentier, Abbot of Clairvaux, and the first to Cardinal Gondi de Retz.

## 1673

Lyon, in duodecimo.

*Some Selected Works of Saint Augustine*, from the same collection that appeared at Brussels in 1654.

Brussels, in duodecimo. The same, from the fifth reprinting. The scholars of Cologne, in the same place.

## 1679–1700

Paris, at the house of François Muguet; in folio, in eleven volumes.

*The Works of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Corrected Again after the Recension of the Louvain Theologians, against French, Vatican, English, Belgian, and Other Manuscript Copies, as Well as against Older and More Carefully Corrected Editions. By the Labor and Study of the Monks of the Order of Saint Benedict of the Congregation of Saint Maur.*

Volumes I and II, 1679; III, 1680; IV, 1683; V, 1684; VI and VII, 1685; VIII and IX, 1688; X, 1690; XI, 1700. Volumes I and II were reprinted there in 1689.

The Maurist Fathers confess that, in preparing this new edition [in the general preface prefixed to volume XI], they had three objectives at heart: that it should be accurate, convenient, and properly illustrated [Col. 0086D]. They added a fourth, which in itself deserves not so much praise in an editor, where it is present, as blame where it is absent contrary to expectation; but here, for reasons known to everyone, it was much more serious and exceedingly difficult: namely, that the edition should be attached to the interests of no party.

First, they thought that maximum accuracy consisted in three conditions: that the genuine integrity of the text should be restored in accordance with the older and more reliable manuscripts; that works certainly genuine should be distinguished from doubtful and spurious works; and that the edition itself should be cleansed of typographical errors.

To make it especially convenient, they note that they had taken care of four things [Col. 0087A]: the order of the works, in establishing which they considered both the periods when the individual works were composed and their subject matter, so that works of the same kind—for example, exegetical or moral works—might be presented together while still being arranged according to chronological order; the divisions by which chapters were separated into more numerous and smaller sections for the considerable convenience of readers; summaries prefixed either to all the books and to most chapters, displaying their subject matter, or marginal headings, partly expressed in the words of the text itself and partly taken from the Louvain theologians; and finally indexes, not only for the individual volumes but also general and universal indexes, both of them extremely full.

The features intended to provide illustration include, in part, the prefaces prefixed to the individual volumes, in which historical matters rather than doctrinal matters are chiefly explained; in part, notices added to explain the subject matter of the individual works; and finally, notes in the lower margin, by which variant readings are indicated or obscure passages, especially through comparison with other passages, are explained.

As for the fourth objective, they affirm that it was deeply fixed in their minds and impressed upon them by their superiors that they should carefully avoid party interests in explaining Augustine’s doctrine. This was the reason they abstained from more extensive commentaries and observations, so as not to give anyone even the slightest offense or prejudice the opinion of any theologian.

Nevertheless, it is clear how many disturbances arose against them, and how many stratagems and snares were employed either to intercept the success of the work [Col. 0087C] or to bring the completed edition into disrepute. The Benedictines themselves, while composing the general preface to the eleventh volume and attempting to make their care and foresight publicly known, admit that it had been difficult to prevent something inadvertent from creeping into so vast a work, or to prevent hostile persons, ill-disposed toward their studies, from interpreting something otherwise than they had intended.

Yet they complain that they were dealing not with scrupulous but otherwise fair opponents, but with slanderers and enemies who shunned no kind of plot, however disgraceful, in attacking them without provocation. Since the king had imposed silence on both parties, they brought forward nothing else in the passage mentioned above for their defense except an effort to clear themselves, before pious and well-disposed men—some of whom might consequently have been troubled by certain scruples—from the most serious accusations laid against them.

But we do not concern ourselves with the history of these disputes and frivolous tactics. It is not even remotely relevant to our purpose, and there are more than enough commentaries by learned men for those who have happened to attend to the matter either from professional interest or personal inclination [Col. 0088A] [Note: Besides Dupin, *Bibliothèque nouvelle des auteurs ecclésiastiques*, vol. XVIII, under the article “New Edition of the Works of Saint Augustine,” and Bayle in the *Critical Dictionary*, see, among the more recent authors, the writers of the *Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica Coloniensis*, p. 464; Ceillier, vol. XII, pp. 680 ff.; and the writers of the *Literary History of the Congregation of Saint Maur* (Brussels, 1770, quarto). See Blampin, pp. 287 ff. What is more, a separate volume has even been written containing the history of this edition, by Antonius Vincentius Thuillier, formerly a member of the same congregation: *History of the New Edition of Saint Augustine Given by the Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur in France* (Paris, 1736, quarto). I have not seen it, but its own various fortunes are recounted in the same *History of the Congregation*, p. 528 ff.].

We proceed instead to review carefully the works contained in each volume and to explain the notable accomplishments of the learned Fathers here, while at the same time noting the order and distinctions of the Louvain theologians. The contents of each volume are as follows:

## Volume One

Works published while he was still a catechumen or not yet a presbyter, together with the *Retractations* and *Confessions*, in the following order: Book I–II of the *Retractations*; Book I–XIII of the *Confessions*; Book I–III *Against the Academics*; Book I *On the Blessed Life*; Book I–II *On Order*; Book I–II *Soliloquies*; Book I *On the Immortality of the Soul*; Book I *On the Quantity of the Soul*; Book I–VI *On Music*; Book I *On the Teacher*; Book I–III *On Free Choice of the Will*; Book I–II *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*; Book I–II *On the Morals of the Catholic Church and the Morals of the Manichaeans*; Book I *On True Religion*; *On the Rule for the Servants of God*.

In the appendix: *A Book on Grammar*; *Foundations of Dialectic*; *The Ten Categories*; *Foundations of Rhetoric*; a fragment of *The Rule Given to Clerics*; *The Second Rule*; *On the Eremitic Life*, addressed to his sister.

This volume contains everything that Erasmus and the Louvain editors had included in it. The only difference is that the Benedictines relegated to the appendix certain works which those editors had regarded as genuine writings of Augustine—namely, the little books *On Grammar*, *The Categories*, *Foundations of Dialectic*, and *Foundations of Rhetoric—and that they ordered certain other works to be moved to different places, so that, as far as possible, they might preserve the chronological sequence and order in which each work was produced by the author.

## Volume Two

Two hundred and seventy letters arranged according to chronological order and divided into four classes.

In the appendix: sixteen shorter letters attributed to Augustine addressed to Boniface and vice versa; Pelagius’ letter to Demetrias; a letter attributed to Augustine addressed to Cyril and vice versa, *On the Praises of Jerome*; and *The Dispute of Augustine with Pascentius*.

The most distinguished part of the work of these highly learned monks is contained in this volume—a part truly deserving that designation, in which one recognizes Coustant’s sagacity and sound learning. Although they list precisely the same number of letters as genuine as the Louvain editors, and although they relegated neither more nor fewer letters to the appendix of this volume, they nevertheless did not dare to proceed further and impose upon themselves the laborious and demanding task which all readers of Augustine had ardently desired: namely, to distinguish and finally disentangle the previously untouched sequence and interrelationship of letters of such diverse kinds and periods.

Everyone felt this desire all the more impatiently because, whereas almost all the other works could be known through Augustine’s own arrangement in the *Retractations*, according to the periods and occasions in which they had arisen, so that one could mentally accompany him, as it were, in his sacred studies and activities, the letters alone—although from them almost the fullest memory of the events and actions of that period was to be recovered—were deprived of this advantage.

The Benedictines, however, would have avoided this labor not so much from fear of the difficulties—which, though innumerable, they alone might have been permitted to disregard—as from fear that, by introducing a new arrangement, they would slow the reading of Augustine for those who had once become accustomed to the old one. Yet in the end Augustine’s love prevailed, together with the example of others, especially of their fellow members, in the case of other ecclesiastical writers. Let us now hear from their own words with what disposition they undertook this task.

> “In the earlier editions,” they say, “the order of Augustine’s letters was so confused that, as far as the history of the period is concerned, scarcely anyone could easily grasp the sequence of all the events without long and frequently repeated reading and reflection. For letters belonging to the same period and dealing with the same subject were scattered here and there throughout the entire body of the Collection; earlier letters were placed after later ones and relegated to an inferior position; and finally—an intolerable confusion—the replies of Augustine were sometimes located as far as possible from those who had asked the questions or sought the advice. Indeed, the replies were placed far before the letters of those who had consulted him, so that, for example, the letter of Evodius consulting him was followed only after many intervening letters by Augustine’s response. It was therefore desirable that Augustine’s letters should be arranged in proper order according to their dates. Augustine himself would undoubtedly have undertaken this, had he been able to complete the revision which he had begun. For in the preface to his *Retractations* he declares that he wishes his works to be read in the order in which they were written, and that he would devote himself to this end, so that readers might finally understand how he had progressed in writing.

> “But various considerations prevented us from attempting this: namely, the practice of earlier times; the order accepted for approximately one hundred and seventy years; and the customary citations, which it seemed wrong either to violate or ultimately to alter, lest this change cause the greatest inconvenience to students. In addition, there were no slight difficulties in establishing an order of the letters acceptable to everyone, since scholars dispute the date of some of them. This consideration especially held us back, since we had principally resolved not rashly to oppose or favor either side in this undertaking.

> “These, then, were the considerations that deterred us from changing the order of the letters, and it did not seem easy for us to undertake such a change against the earlier editions. On the other hand, however, other considerations urged us to do so: not only the various examples of learned men in the letters of Saint Cyprian, Saint Leo, and others, but also the authority of men distinguished no less by their judgment than by their dignity, who wished this new edition to serve posterity. Influenced altogether by these examples and authorities, we finally agreed to restore Augustine’s letters to a carefully determined sequence of years, insofar as this could be done.

> “And lest we seem to have established this sequence on slight foundations, we endeavored to investigate it not only through our own studies and counsels but also through those of others. Once the chronological order of the letters had been established, we divided them into four classes. The first presents those which Augustine wrote before he became bishop. In this we followed Augustine himself as our authority, since in the first book of his *Retractations* he reviewed only those works which he had published before becoming bishop.

> “The second class presents the letters which he issued from the beginning of his episcopate until the conference held at Carthage with the Donatists and the introduction of the Pelagian heresy into Africa. For these letters are concerned for the most part with exposing or purging these two errors, and they accurately describe their beginnings, development, and condemnation.

> “The third class of letters comprises those which the holy Doctor wrote from that time until the end of his life—those, namely, to which a definite period can be assigned. Finally, we placed in the fourth class the remaining letters of Augustine, which he certainly wrote as bishop but which bear no other indication of date or circumstance that would disclose a definite time.

> “This fourfold division of the classes will provide the advantage which we noted earlier: the diligent reader will be able to apprehend almost at a glance and in a continuous sequence whatever concerns the Donatist and Pelagian heresies.”

They further observe that they did not move certain treatises which had previously been incorporated into the order of the letters, although considerations of no small importance would have recommended doing so. But *The Dispute with Pascentius*, which had been numbered 178 among Augustine’s letters, they relegated to the appendix, as the Louvain editors had done long before.

They then state that they restored certain letters—not only those which Augustine sent to others in his own name, but also some of those which many people addressed to him. These included the letters of Timasius and James; of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius; of Quodvultdeus and Prosper; the letters to Pelagius and to Simplicianus concerning the work dedicated to him; the letters to Aurelius, Valerius, and Claudius; and the letters to Quodvultdeus concerning books dedicated in his name. These letters had previously been missing from the list of Augustine’s correspondence.

They therefore took care to insert all of them in their proper places, as well as the replies of the Catholic bishops to the tribune Marcellinus on the occasion of the Carthaginian conference, and the letter sent to Proculus and Cylinnius, Gallic bishops, on behalf of Leporius. “These writings,” they say, “must be regarded as no less true and genuine offspring of Augustine than those letters sent in the name of the Councils of Carthage and Milevis to Innocent, which everyone accepts, along with Augustine’s other letters, as having been dictated by the holy Doctor.”

In certain cases, however, they admit that they followed a usage long established. The treatise *On the Good of Widowhood* should, according to their own plan, have been restored, since it is genuinely a letter of Augustine and is not mentioned under that title in his book of the *Retractations*. But they did not wish to remove the title of a book that had long been attached to it.

The letter which Augustine wrote to the faithful entrusted to his pastoral care against Petilianus was in the same position. From Augustine’s own time, as he testifies in Book II, chapter 25, of the *Retractations*, it had occupied the place of the first book against that heretic’s letters. Nor did they dare to bring here the letter of Secundinus the Manichaean to Augustine; they left it in the sixth volume of the works, solely because it should be read in order to understand more fully what Augustine argues there against the errors of Secundinus.

Finally, they do not wish to appear merely to have restored previously published letters; they also brought several new ones to light for the first time. These include Letter 29, written by Augustine while still a presbyter to Alypius, bishop of Thagaste; two letters of Augustine, and letters of Augustine and Alypius to Paulinus of Nola, which complete the number of letters recorded in Possidius’ catalogue, numbers 42 and 45; and Augustine’s Letter 193 to Mercator, formerly presented only in part in the book addressed to Dulcitius, but now published for the first time in full.

Nevertheless, one is surprised how it happened that, although four letters were newly added and seventeen [Note: These are: 1. to Simplicianus, no. 37; 2. the conference of Silvanus and the other Catholic bishops with Marcellinus, no. 128; 3. the same bishops to Marcellinus, no. 129; 4. to Pelagius, no. 146; 5. of Timasius and James, no. 168; 6. to Aurelius, no. 174; 7. to Valerius the Count, no. 200; 8. of Honorius and Theodosius, no. 201; 9. to Claudius, no. 207; 10. of Aurelius Augustine and others to Proculus and Cylinnius, no. 219; 11. of Quodvultdeus, no. 221; 12. to Quodvultdeus, no. 222; 13. of Quodvultdeus, no. 223; 14. to Quodvultdeus, no. 224; 15. of Prosper, no. 225; 16. of Hilary the Gaul, no. 226; 17. of an anonymous author, no. 270.] were transferred here from other volumes of the earlier editions, the same total number should appear in the Louvain and Benedictine editions; nor is there any indication that they excluded any letters, apart from *The Dispute with Pascentius*.

As for the principles by which they were guided in determining the dates and places of the letters, they explained each matter individually and included it in a commentary divided according to the classes, entitled *The Chronological Order of the Letters Demonstrated by Arguments*. Nor did they allow any indexes required by practical use to be lacking. Particularly noteworthy is the index in which the letters are arranged according to their principal subjects, and in which theological, polemical, exegetical, ecclesiastical, moral, philosophical, historical, and miscellaneous letters are listed.

## Volume Three

Exegetical works, which had been distributed through Volumes III, IV, and IX of the Louvain edition, arranged according to the order of the Scriptures and divided into two parts, the Old and New Testaments. At the beginning are placed the books *On Christian Doctrine*, as a kind of key and method for the correct principles of interpretation which Augustine employed and which Catholic commentators after him followed.

### Part One

Book I–IV *On Christian Doctrine*; the unfinished book *On Genesis Literally*; Book I–XII *On Genesis Literally*; Book I–VII *Expressions* (Louvain, Vol. III); Book I–VII *Questions on the Heptateuch*; Book I *Annotations on Job* (Louvain, Vol. IV); *The Mirror* (Louvain, Vol. III).

### Part Two

Book I–IV *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*; Book I–II *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*; Book I–II *Evangelical Questions*; Book I *Questions according to Matthew* (Louvain, Vol. IV); 124 treatises *On the Gospel of John*; ten treatises *On the First Epistle of John to the Parthians* (Louvain, Vol. IX); Book I *An Exposition of Certain Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans*; Book I *An Inchoate Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans*; *An Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians* (Louvain, Vol. IV).

In the appendix: Book I–III *On the Miracles of Sacred Scripture*; *On the Blessings of the Patriarch Jacob*; *Questions of the Old and New Testaments*; *Questions of the Old and New Testaments Subsequently Published* (Louvain appendix, Vol. III). *An Exposition of the Apocalypse of Blessed John* (Louvain appendix, Vol. IX) is also included in the appendix.

In the preface they discuss Augustine’s outstanding gifts in expounding Scripture, with much praise of him, though not without justification. They strive not to defend his faults but to excuse them. Concerning the version which he used in expounding the Old Testament, they note that he himself accepted the Greek text of the Seventy (τῶν LXX), in the recension published by Nobilius. They add that most of the variant readings found in Augustine arose from defects in the editions, defects which they removed from their own edition with the aid of ancient manuscripts.

They explain, however, that in the books *Expressions* and *Questions on the Heptateuch*, which he composed in old age, and likewise in *The Mirror*, which he wrote near the end of his life, Augustine consulted a version derived more directly from Hebrew sources, corresponding to our common version and perhaps being Jerome’s. From this they infer that the same version, having been handed down among the people by Augustine through this book, compiled from various passages of Scripture, became the common and most widely received version.

As for their own work, they are especially careful that no one should attribute to negligence or rashness on their part the fact that one finds variation in some of Augustine’s biblical testimonies, or that one and the same sentence has not everywhere been restored in full and consistently, but only in certain places. Rather, they attribute this to the reverence and sincere fidelity with which they always followed the traces of the best manuscripts.

## Volume Four

The *Expositions on the Psalms* are contained here; these comprise the eighth volume of the Louvain editors.

In the preface they explain the varying method and character of these expositions according to the different occasions from which they arose. They also discuss the rules which Augustine observed in interpretation, rules which, as we learn from the book *On Christian Doctrine*, amount to a twofold concern: the literal sense and the spiritual sense.

Accordingly, they make many useful observations on both subjects. As one readily understands, the most important are those in which they discuss Augustine’s efforts to obtain a pure and complete text by comparing Latin and Greek copies and collecting and examining variant readings.

They insist that everything they say in commendation of this work is intended to defend Augustine’s method in general, not to force everyone to regard even his slightest allusions with the same veneration that they themselves show. They write that it is enough if fair-minded judges of these matters consider the works not unworthy of the subject treated.

They believe this judgment will be greatly assisted if readers bear in mind that Augustine had to serve the spirit of his age and accommodate himself to the understanding of the common people, following the example set by the Deity himself in the sacred writings. Moreover, they maintain that the merit of these commentaries should not be judged in comparison with the Hebrew text currently in use, nor even with Jerome’s text, since Augustine had resolved to follow the Seventy, who may have possessed a Hebrew exemplar equally or even more accurately corrected.

At this point there follows, extending almost to the end of the preface, a digression on the various versions of the Psalter derived from the Septuagint, which were in use during the age of Augustine and Jerome. In the course of this discussion they conceived an idea that would surely be welcome to many, including those who care less for Augustine: they would investigate what place Augustine’s Psalter should claim among the other Psalters; whether its various readings, in which it differs from our Vulgate, were supported by the testimony of others; and whether, finally, it agreed more or less with the Greek of the Seventy that exists in our own time.

To carry this out successfully, they compared different copies, both printed and written by hand, and displayed the most notable variations they discovered, together with the Augustinian readings, in a sort of table immediately after the preface. They added an index of the manuscript and printed copies.

## Volume Five

This volume comprises sermons to the people in two parts, divided into four classes: in the first part, (1) sermons on the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments and (2) sermons for the liturgical year; in the second part, (3) sermons on the saints and (4) sermons on various subjects. These are followed by (5) doubtful sermons. In the appendix are spurious sermons, likewise arranged in four classes.

They transferred the sermons of Augustine which had been read in the tenth volume of the Louvain edition into the fifth volume because most of them were regarded as dealing with Sacred Scripture and therefore ought to be closer to the treatises in Volumes III and IV, where the same Scriptures are expounded and which, they say, largely bear the form of homilies.

They also bound them together in a new order, different from the earlier one which we gave in the general survey of Augustine’s writings under no. 116, so that they might be arranged both according to their genuine sequence and separately from all the adulterine and spurious sermons.

There was much greater freedom in arranging these sermons because neither Augustine himself nor Possidius’ catalogue contains even the slightest instruction concerning their ordering. Nor has any record reached us of a distinct collection of Augustine’s treatises made during his lifetime or afterward from definite manuscripts.

For although the three oldest surviving collections—*On the Words of the Lord*, *On the Words of the Apostle*, and *Fifty Homilies*—are found in manuscripts eight hundred years old and more, they nevertheless do not reach back to Augustine’s own age, as some have attempted to persuade us. The Benedictine Fathers demonstrated this both from Possidius’ silence and from the fact that the collections contain spurious material. [Note: The Ballerini Fathers state in the preface to the sermons of Saint Leo that these collections were arranged from lectionaries, and that further sermons were subsequently copied from other lectionaries and added to the Augustinian sermons in editions that appeared later. *Works of Saint Leo*, Volume I, Part I, §64. They add there that other sermons of the same holy Doctor may still be derived from these sources, and that they themselves intend at some point to publish more than twenty of his genuine sermons in their *Miscellaneous Anecdotes*.]

Concerning the first class, *On the Words of the Lord*, the Benedictines observe that the sermons do not appear everywhere in the same order in the ancient copies. Many agree with the editions, but not all. The Louvain theologians had conjectured this from passages excerpted by Bede or Florus; they themselves discovered it with certainty in a Colbertine Library manuscript, approximately eight hundred years old, no. 2821. They confess that they drew from it a considerable number of sermons not previously published.

They also point out that the authentic title of this class, confirmed by the testimony both of Florus and of many manuscripts, did not read *On the Words of the Lord* but *On the Words of the Gospel*, since it comprised Augustine’s commentaries on every kind of passage taken from the four Gospels.

Their observation concerning the second class, *On the Words of the Apostle*, is that it is found nowhere except in conjunction with the first, although there are copies in which sermons *On the Words of the Lord* occur without those *On the Words of the Apostle*. From this they conclude that these two classes are nothing other than a single collection of sermons on the Scriptures of the New Testament.

They further say that the third class is always found separated from the others, but often contains more sermons than the printed editions. In some manuscripts there are sometimes two, sometimes four, or even more than fifty sermons. Yet in nearly all of them complete sermons are missing from among those which make up the total of fifty in the published books.

They judge, moreover, that this collection cannot be considered older than the time of Caesarius, because so many homilies written by Caesarius himself have been inserted into it, and because summaries of others, not unlike his style, were appended to most of them.

For the most part, Augustine’s sermons in this collection are truncated and interpolated with brief beginnings and endings adapted to audiences of every kind. This is approximately what the Benedictines think about the three oldest collections of Augustine’s sermons.

The collections that follow, except for the sermons *To the Brothers in the Desert*, which are contained in the next volume, are much less accurate, since they were extracted from far more numerous and mutually divergent manuscripts at a time when printing had already arisen. It is clear that the sermons subsequently added in various editions were not assigned to any definite category.

Since the arrangement of these classes was therefore largely arbitrary and brought with it so much confusion and disorder, anyone who gladly enjoys this nourishment of the holy Doctor will acknowledge, with due praise of the editors, that the old arrangement has been entirely abolished and replaced by a more accurate and orderly one. [Note: “Someone may observe,” say the Maurist Fathers, “that the sermons, which could more conveniently be reduced to four classes, had been scattered among twelve, some of which contained subjects properly belonging to others. He will recognize that the books called *On the Words of the Lord* and *On the Words of the Apostle* contain only part of the sermons belonging under those titles. He will understand that the sermons on feasts, although they ought to have been brought together in the classes *For the Liturgical Year* and *On the Saints*, had been dispersed among seven or eight others; and that of more than thirty sermons entitled as dealing with Easter festivals, to use this example, only ten are found in the series *For the Liturgical Year*. If someone wished to examine them all, he would have to search for the rest among the fifty homilies added by the Paris editors, in both classes of *Sermons on Various Subjects*, and in the later classes.”]

Another aim which they sought to achieve in the edition of the sermons was the separation of spurious sermons from genuine ones. In this task they admit that the following considerations principally guided their judgment:

1. **Style**, or color, or the distinctive character of the discourse, which is readily perceptible in Augustine’s reflections no less than in those of other eminent writers. They exercised caution, however, by recognizing that Augustine’s style must have varied somewhat according to his age, the difference between the subjects he treated as a young man and those he treated later in life, and his method of composition; some works were carefully and thoughtfully elaborated, while others were produced extemporaneously.

   > “For the proper execution of this kind of judgment,” they say, “besides requiring the style of a doubtful work to be measured against each individual work whose authenticity is certain, one must by no means neglect that force, or spirit, by which style is, as it were, animated. Augustine is everywhere recognized by a certain grave and serious kind of eloquence which subjugates the minds of his readers, not through the charm of polished and affected expression, but through a certain efficacy of judgment, prudence, piety, integrity, modesty, kindness, and other virtues. These qualities shine and flash forth so brightly throughout his discourse that no one can attain his style by imitation.

   > “This is the principal Lydian stone by which genuinely Augustinian sermons are tested. If anyone applies it to the appendix, he will recognize that almost the whole of it may be covered by the judgment pronounced concerning the *Hypognosticon*: ‘Both its meaning is judged inferior to his meaning, and the modesty and humility of his conduct and speech are not preserved there.’”

2. **The version** which each sermon uses in its citations from the Scriptures of the Old Testament. Since Augustine generally followed the ancient translation, whereas the new translation—that is, Jerome’s translation prepared from the Hebrew—was embraced from the fifth century onward by Salvian of Marseilles, Eucherius of Lyons, Leo of Rome, and others, it is easy to understand how broadly this criterion can be used and applied.

   Here we note that the Benedictines added certain new material, partly to supplement and partly to defend against the objections of some critics what they had discussed in the preface to Volume IV concerning the Vulgate translation of the Psalter.

3. **Doctrine**: they examined each sermon to determine whether it agreed with Augustine’s teaching, both in the doctrines of faith and morals and in his exposition and use of Scripture. They did not overlook cases in which Augustine was known to have changed either his opinion or his manner of expression.

4. **Consideration of periods, places, persons, affairs, events, errors, and other similar matters** discussed in the sermons. They affirm that they derived from these matters many arguments for establishing their critical judgments.

5. **Possidius’ catalogue**: not because they thought that all the sermons whose titles are found there should be attributed to Augustine, as though many preachers could not have treated the same subject, but so that they would not readily attribute to him sermons not designated there.

   To this catalogue they added the ancient calendar of the Church of Carthage, then recently published in the third volume of Mabillon’s *Analecta*. On the basis of these materials they marked with a censorial note certain sermons on solemnities—for example, the Litanies or Rogations, the Conversion of Saint Paul, the Chair of Saint Peter, the Annunciation of the Lord, the Assumption of Blessed Mary, and so forth—of which neither source contained any mention.

6. **The collections of Bede and Florus on Paul.** Here it must be understood that, by Bede’s collection, they mean some unpublished collection which unquestionably belongs to him and is inscribed with his name in manuscript copies. The collection commonly attributed to Bede among his published works they assign instead to Florus, a deacon of Lyons, and they supported this judgment with several arguments in the third volume of Mabillon’s *Analecta*.

7. **Manuscript codices**, an immense number of which they did not undertake to list. With their assistance, they affirm that they discovered, on the one hand, that certain passages which had moved some critics to deprive Augustine of possession of several genuinely Augustinian sermons were elegantly preserved in the printed editions; on the other hand, they uncovered the authors of some sermons that had been attributed to Augustine.

They further declare that they carefully read and compared the works of other Fathers, in order to determine from style and subject matter which sermons should be attributed to each author and to investigate the fragments from which adulterine treatises had been stitched together. They discovered that some of these sermons had been taken from Origen, Cyprian, Ambrose, Maximus, Faustus, Gregory the Great, Alcuin, Ivo of Chartres, and others. They demonstrate that a large portion of those in which they detected a false claim to Augustinian authorship belonged to Caesarius of Arles. More will be said about these works in the third volume of our *Library*.

Finally, they point out that the great majority of the sermons they rejected are among those which the Louvain theologians had called insufficiently examined or of doubtful authority. They also consulted the judgments of others on Augustine’s sermons, especially two: one by Simon Verlin, published in 1618, and the other by Bernard Winding, published in 1622. Although such exceptionally perceptive men were sometimes permitted to make mistakes, they hope that the same concession will be made to them if they occasionally err in judgment.

Finally, they affirm that they were most severe with sermons not previously published which were attributed to Augustine in manuscript codices. Of the very large number of these, they arranged for only eighteen, together with several fragments, to be added, since in them Augustine’s character, genius, and learning shone forth with the greatest clarity.

## Volume Six

Moral works are included here together with several books of questions, in the following order: Book I *Eighty-Three Different Questions*; Book I *Different Questions to Simplicianus*; Book I *Eight Questions of Dulcitius* (Louvain, Vol. IV); Book I *On Faith in Things Unseen* (Louvain appendix, Vol. III); Book I *On Faith and the Creed*; Book I *On Faith and Works* (Louvain, Vol. IV); Book I *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Charity*; Book I *On the Christian Contest* (Louvain, Vol. III); Book I *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*; Book I *On Continence* (Louvain, Vol. IV); Book I *On the Good of Marriage*; Book I *On Holy Virginity* (Louvain, Vol. VI); Book I *On the Good of Widowhood* (Louvain, Vol. IV); Book I–II *On Adulterous Marriages* (Louvain, Vol. VI); Book I *On Lying*; Book I *Against Lying* (Louvain, Vol. IV); Book I *On the Work of Monks*; Book I *On the Divination of Demons* (Louvain, Vol. III); Book I *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*; Book I *On Patience* (Louvain, Vol. IV); four treatises *On the Creed to the Catechumens*; one treatise *On Christian Discipline*; one treatise *On the New Song*; one treatise *On Wednesday*; one treatise *On the Deluge*; one treatise *On the Time of the Barbarians*; one treatise *On the Benefit of Fasting*; one treatise *On the Destruction of the City* (Louvain, Vol. IX).

In the appendix: *The Book of Twenty-One Sentences*; *A Dialogue of Sixty-Five Questions* (Louvain appendix, Vol. IV); *The Book on Faith to Peter*; *On the Spirit and the Soul* (Louvain appendix, Vol. III); *On Friendship*; *On the Substance of Love* (Louvain appendix, Vol. IV); *On Loving God*; *Soliloquies*; *Meditations*; *On Contrition of Heart*; *Manual*; *The Mirror*; *Another Mirror Called the Sinner’s*; *On the Threefold Dwelling*; *On the Ladder of Paradise*; *On Knowledge of the True Life*; *On the Christian Life* (Louvain appendix, Vol. IX); *On Saving Instructions* (Louvain appendix, Vol. IV); *On the Twelve Degrees of Abuse* (Louvain appendix, Vol. IX); *On the Seven Vices and Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit* (from Vignier’s supplement); *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*; *On Sobriety and Chastity* (Louvain appendix, Vol. IX); *On True and False Repentance* (Louvain appendix, Vol. IV); *On Antichrist*; *The Psalter Said to Have Been Composed by Augustine for His Mother*; *An Exposition of the Canticle Magnificat*; *A Treatise on the Assumption of Blessed Mary*; Book I–II *On Visiting the Sick*; *On the Uprightness of Catholic Conduct* (Louvain appendix, Vol. IX); *On the Creed* (Louvain appendix, Vol. X); *Sermons on the Eating of the Lamb to the Neophytes* (Paris edition, Vol. X appendix, edited by Jacques Sirmond); *On the Creation of the First Man*; *On the Vanity of the World*; *On Contempt for the World*; *On the Good of Discipline*; *On Obedience and Humility* (Louvain appendix, Vol. IX); other sermons to the people (from the appendix to Vol. X of the Paris edition, or from Vignier or Sirmond); *Sermons to the Brothers in the Desert* (Louvain appendix, Vol. X).

These works too, as is evident from the appended volume numbers, had been distributed by the Louvain editors among different volumes. Some were read among the exegetical books, some among the polemical books, and several after the treatises on John.

The foundation of the new arrangement is the similarity of genre and subject matter. By this means they hoped that the works, when read continuously and in order, would both be better understood and more deeply impressed upon the minds of students.

As for their critical work, they sometimes departed from the judgments of others, asserting the genuineness of certain works rejected by the Louvain editors and, conversely, eliminating works previously promoted as authentic. They devoted particular care to the appendix, especially to discovering and identifying the true authors of books attributed to Augustine.

## Volume Seven

Book I–XXII *The City of God against the Pagans*.

In the appendix are presented several writings concerning the discovery, translation, and miracles of the martyr Stephen: Avitus’ letter to Palchonius concerning the relics of Saint Stephen; Lucian’s letter, translated by him from Greek into Latin; Lucian’s letter to the universal Church concerning the revelation of the body of the martyr Stephen; Anastasius’ letter to Landuleus concerning the subsequent writing; a writing concerning another discovery and translation of Saint Stephen to the city of Byzantium, which Anastasius rendered into Latin; Severus’ letter to the whole Church concerning the miracles performed on the island of Minorca through the relics of Saint Stephen; and Book I–II *On the Miracles of Saint Stephen*, addressed to Evodius.

The Benedictines testify that they compared an exceptionally large number of manuscript copies, which this work required because of its diverse history and more recondite learning. They also retained the division into chapters together with their summaries, considering it to be either Augustine’s own work or something arranged at his command and added to the completed work. They say that this is confirmed by the testimony of manuscripts written more than nine hundred years ago.

From the fuller extant commentaries of learned men on these books, they excerpted very little—an arrangement which, as it seems to us, was not without good reason—and interspersed the excerpts with critical notes.

In the eighth volume are presented the polemical works against the Jews, Manichaeans, Priscillianists, and Arians, together with the book on heresies prefixed at the beginning and the books on the Trinity appended at the end: *On Heresies*, Book I, addressed to Quodvultdeus; *Treatise against the Jews*; *On the Usefulness of Believing*, Book I, addressed to Honoratus; *On the Two Souls against the Manichaeans*, Book I; *Acts, or Disputation, against Fortunatus the Manichaean*, Book I; *Against Adimantus, a Disciple of Mani*, Book I; *Against the Epistle of Mani, Which They Call the Foundation*, Book I; *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, Books XXXIII; *On the Proceedings with Felix the Manichaean*, Books II; *On the Nature of the Good against the Manichaeans*, Book I; *Against Secundinus the Manichaean*, Book I; *Against an Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, Books II; *To Orosius against the Priscillianists and Origenists*, Book I; *Sermon of the Arians*; *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, Book I; *Conference with Maximinus, Bishop of the Arians*; *Against the Same Maximinus the Arian*, Books II. (Louvain, vol. VI.) *On the Trinity*, Books XV. (Louvain, vol. III.)—In the Appendix: *Treatise against Five Heresies*; *Sermon against the Jews, Pagans, and Arians*. (Louvain, vol. VI.) *Dialogue on the Dispute between the Church and the Synagogue*. (Louvain, vol. VI, Appendix.) *A Book on Faith against the Manichaeans*, attributed to Evodius. (Louvain, vol. VI.) *Admonition* (commonly attributed to Augustine) on receiving converted Manichaeans. (Paris edition, vol. X, Appendix.) *Against Felicianus the Arian on the Faith of the Trinity*, a book restored to Vigilius, bishop of Tapsus. (Louvain, vol. VI, Appendix.) *Questions on the Trinity and Genesis*, transcribed from Alcuin. (Louvain, vol. III, Appendix.) *Two Books on the Incarnation of the Word, addressed to Januarius*, compiled from Origen. (Louvain, vol. IV, Appendix.) *Book on the Trinity and Unity of God*. (Louvain, vol. IV, Appendix.) *On the Essence of Divinity*. (Louvain, vol. IV.) *Dialogue on the Unity of the Holy Trinity*. (Paris edition, vol. X, Appendix.) *Book on Ecclesiastical Dogmas*. (Louvain, vol. III, Appendix.) [Col. 0099A–B]

In the ninth volume are the polemical works against the Donatists: *Psalm against the Party of Donatus*; *Against Parmenianus*, Books III; *On Baptism against the Donatists*, Books VII; *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, Books III; *Epistle to the Catholics against the Donatists*, commonly called *On the Unity of the Church*, Book I; *Against Cresconius the Donatist Grammarian*, Books IV; *On the One Baptism against Petilianus*; *Brief Account of the Conference with the Donatists*; *After the Conference, to the Donatists*, Book I; *Sermon Delivered to the People of the Church of Caesarea in the Presence of Emeritus*; *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*; *Against Gaudentius, Donatist Bishop*, Books II. (Louvain, vol. VII.) *Sermon on Rusticianus the Subdeacon, Rebaptized by the Donatists and Ordained Deacon*. (From Vignerius’s Supplement.)—In the Appendix: *Against Fulgentius the Donatist*, a book by an uncertain author; *Excerpts and Ancient Writings Relating to the History of the Donatists*. (Louvain, vol. VII, Appendix.) [Col. 0099C]

In the tenth volume are the polemical works against the Pelagians: *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins and on the Baptism of Infants*, addressed to Marcellinus, Books III; *On the Spirit and the Letter*, addressed to the same, Book I; *On Nature and Grace against Pelagius*, addressed to Timasius and James, Book I; *Epistle, or Book, on the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, addressed to Eutropius and Paul; *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, addressed to Aurelius, Book I; *On the Grace of Christ and Original Sin against Pelagius*, addressed to Albina, Pinianus, and Melania, Books II; *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, addressed to Valerius, Books II; *On the Soul and Its Origin against Vincentius Victor*, Books IV; *Against Two Epistles of the Pelagians*, addressed to Boniface, Books VI; *Against Julian, Defender of the Pelagian Heresy*, Books IV; *On Grace and Free Will*, addressed to Valentinus and the monks of Hadrumetum with him, Book I; *On Correction and Grace*, addressed to the same, Book I; *On the Predestination of the Saints*, addressed to Prosper and Hilary, Book I; *On the Gift of Perseverance*, addressed to the same, Book I. (Louvain, vol. VII.) *Against the Second Reply of Julian*, an unfinished work comprising six books. (From Vignerius’s Supplement.)—In the Appendix, Part One: *Hypomnesticon against the Pelagians and Coelestians*, commonly called the *Hypognosticon*; *Book by a Suspect Author on Predestination and Grace*; *Booklet by an Uncertain Author on the Predestination of God*. (Louvain, vol. VII, Appendix.) Part Two: Various writings and documents relating to Pelagian history. Part Three: Prosper of Aquitaine’s apologetic works on behalf of Augustine against the unjust critics of his teaching on grace and predestination, namely: *Epistle to Rufinus on Grace and Free Will*; *Book against the Collator*; *Replies to the Chapters of the Calumniating Gauls*; *Replies to the Chapters of the Vincentian Objections*. (Louvain, vol. VII, Appendix.) *Replies to the Excerpts Sent from the City of Genoa*. (Louvain, vol. V, Appendix.) A book of sentences by the same author, drawn from Augustine. (Louvain, vol. V, Appendix.) *Life of Augustine*, by Possidius; *Catalogue of Augustine’s Books, Treatises, and Letters*, edited by the care of Possidius. (Louvain, vol. I.) [Col. 0099D–0100B]

Since the sequence of the last three volumes agrees almost entirely with the Louvain order, less labor had to be expended on them. Accordingly, they applied themselves more vigorously to the origins and causes of the matters treated, and endeavored to explain carefully, at the beginning of each volume, the history of the Donatist and Pelagian controversies. To this diligence is also owed the fact that certain works of uncertain or alien authorship were included in the Appendix of the final volume, so that a fuller knowledge of these matters might be drawn from the documents assembled there. [Col. 0100C]

The eleventh volume contains, first, two general prefaces: one to the entire work, explaining its plan, occasion, aids, division of labor, success, obstacles, and patrons; the other, shorter, to the Appendices attached to the individual volumes, as well as to the contents of this eleventh volume itself. Closely connected with the latter is a catalogue of writings whose various booklets, wrongly attributed to Augustine, were again asserted to have other authors as their true writers. This is followed by the *Life of Saint Augustine*, largely translated from Tillemont’s notes, which the author had communicated to them while they were still unpublished. After this come the indexes of the books: the first gives the sequence of the books in each volume of the new edition; the second displays the Louvain order; the third is an alphabetical index of the individual works. Next come the subject indexes: the first, a universal index to the contents of all ten volumes, extremely full and extensive; the second, a general index of the Holy Scriptures; and finally an index of all the spurious works scattered through the appendices of the ten volumes. [Col. 0100D–0101A]

It remains for us to speak of the additions and embellishments that the Maurist edition derived from manuscript copies printed for the first time. The Louvain theologians had indeed assembled a considerable number of handwritten codices, yet almost all of them had been supplied by Belgium, apart from a few English manuscripts, which had reached them only later. A much richer harvest of variant readings could therefore be expected from the French libraries, especially those of monasteries, and the effort to collect them was further encouraged by a benefit both remarkable and unexpected.

For a hundred years had already passed when, under the auspices first of Sixtus and then of Clement VIII, Petrus Morinus, superintendent of the Vatican press, Abbot Adrianus, Obrius, a Parisian doctor, and other learned men undertook to construct a new edition of Augustine’s works upon the Vatican manuscripts. They relied both on the number of the manuscript copies and on their quality, since they asserted that these contained very many passages lacking in the Louvain edition, however accurate it might be. [Col. 0101A–B]

The Louvain books were therefore compared with the Vatican manuscripts with the utmost care, and variant readings were placed in the margin for the preparation of the edition over which the cardinal of Verona, dean of the Sacred College, presided. But when the undertaking failed to reach completion, all those variants were communicated, by order of Clement X, through Cardinal Bona to the Benedictines, so that they might use them in their new edition.

They then began to seek aids everywhere, both from their own libraries and from other libraries throughout France, and they required their fellow monks to collate manuscripts not only at Saint-Germain in Paris but also in other monasteries of their congregation in other provinces. The total number of these was truly immense. From them the text was genuinely corrected in very many places; in others, only preferable variant readings were recorded. [Col. 0101B–C]

The record of corrections, as well as of variants, is presented partly, as in the Louvain edition, in an index placed after the genuine books themselves, where the copies compared for each book are also identified by name; and partly immediately beneath the text itself. We have found neither the editors’ explanation for this division nor been able to discover it ourselves. The books relegated to the appendices, although not entirely excluded from this care, do not enjoy similar annotation. [Col. 0101C]

Finally, it would seem wrong to remain silent about the names of those who bore the principal burdens of so great a labor. At first, therefore, responsibility for the edition was entrusted by the superiors of that congregation to Father François Delfau, who is said to have published its prospectus in 1671. But when, after the publication in 1673 of a book entitled *L’Abbé Commendataire*, he incurred the penalty of exile, the task left by him was entrusted to Father Thomas Blampin, whom various members of the congregation assisted in different areas.

Pierre Coustant is responsible for the censures and indexes of all the spurious treatises, as well as for the revision of the sermons. Hugh Vaillant and Jacques du Frische, the editor of Ambrose, composed the *Life of Augustine*, or translated it from Tillemont’s commentaries with only slight alterations. Claude Guesnié prepared the general table and the indexes. Finally, Nicolas Goysot supervised the printing, undertook the most burdensome task of correcting the press sheets, and discharged it admirably. [Col. 0102A–B]

The celebrated Jean Mabillon contributed nothing to this edition except the dedicatory letter to Louis XIV. Hence Oudinus rightly, though with almost excessive insistence, criticized Cave, who had written in his *Literary History* that the edition had been completed under Mabillon as its leader and **ἐργοδιώκτης**—the one directing the work. [Col. 0102B]

**Note:** Oudin, *Commentaries*, vol. I, pp. 954 ff.; M. *Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica Coloniensis*, p. 761; *Literary History of the Congregation of Saint-Maur*, p. 292. [Col. 0101C]

We shall say nothing about the decoration and splendor of the work, worthy also on this account that it was offered to a king, adding only that an engraving of Augustine was issued together with volume XI. [Col. 0102B]

**Note:** Many detailed descriptions and shorter accounts of this edition exist, some of which we shall gladly mention. First should be named the learned journals that reviewed the volumes as soon as each appeared. These include the Paris *Journal des Savants*: for volume I, April 1679, p. 96; for volume II, the same year, p. 114; for volume III, August 1680, p. 272; for volume IV, November 1683, p. 325; for volume V, February 1684, p. 46; for volume VI, December 1685, p. 545; for volume VII, January 1686, p. 18; for volume VIII, September 1688, p. 415; and for volume IX, the same month and year, p. 422. Also the *Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensia*: volume II, 1683, January, pp. 1–5; volume VII, 1688, November, pp. 1618–23. [Col. 0101C–D]

The edition is also mentioned frequently in literary commentaries, for example by Cave in his *Literary History*, vol. I, first London edition, p. 242, and Oxford edition of 1740, pp. 292–98; by Johann Fabricius in *History of His Own Library*, vol. I (1717), pp. 203–29; † by Oudin in *Commentaries on the Saints of the Church*, vol. I, pp. 954–85; † in the *Great Library of the Church of Cologne*, vol. I (1734), pp. 761–65; in the *Sacred and Profane Critical Library* of Michael of Saint Joseph, vol. I (1741), pp. 419–23; in the *Catalogue of the Casanatense Library*, vol. I (1761), pp. 338–40; and in the *Augustinian Library* of Johann Felix Ossinger (1768), pp. 1–8. We have marked the more important and accurate of these with a cross. [Col. 0102C–D]

I could also mention Dupin, vol. III, pp. 160 ff., and Ceillier in the *General History of Ecclesiastical Authors*, vol. XI, p. 41, and vol. XII, p. 255 (1744). But these men were concerned less with the care of the edition than with composing a catalogue of Augustine’s writings according to it, explaining at length everywhere the subject and occasion of each work.

Those who happen to have one or another of these books, or all of them, at hand may compare ours with them if they wish, and, I hope, determine whether we have been content to profit from the labor of others or have ourselves examined each item. [Col. 0102D]

This work of the Benedictine Fathers, however, suffered a serious criticism from Richard Simon in *Critical Library*, vol. III, pp. 101–16, and again in the *Censure of Dupin’s Ecclesiastical Library*, vol. I, p. 147.

First, in general, he is angry with those who think that the defects or shortcomings of earlier editions of all ecclesiastical writers must always be remedied by new editions, since this could be done much more suitably and conveniently, and at less expense, if small, separate books were published, but books made far richer by their authors’ judgment, containing either a complete revision or supplements and a selection of variant readings. As examples he cites Arcudius’s *Isidorian Collations* and Combefis’s completely revised Basil; and, in the case of Augustine, we praised above Vignerius’s similar Supplement. [Col. 0102C–0103A]

We admit that the opinion of this learned and perceptive man is not displeasing to us, although we do not consider it entirely true and just. For in literary matters, as in ordinary life, something must be granted to the times and to the entertainments of refined or wealthy people.

Moreover, as time passes and older editions are used, copies become scarce; and if they must be transported to several regions, they are not easily obtained, even when they have often been reprinted. This is evident in the Louvain edition, of which copies of the Antwerp printing are extremely rare throughout Germany, while from the French printings only a few copies are usually shown, almost all from a single impression, namely the first, of 1586. I say nothing of Vignerius’s Supplement, which, I believe, one might seek in vain through many libraries, although it is acknowledged that without it all transcripts of the Louvain recension are incomplete. [Col. 0103A–B]

Simon is altogether wrong, however, when he maintains that no new edition of Augustine had a place after the Louvain edition; and he judges still more unfairly when he declares that the Louvain edition should be preferred to the Benedictine one for many reasons.

The same would be true if he wished to extend this judgment to the remaining Latin or Greek editions of the Benedictine Fathers: scarcely any of them—Hilary alone excepted by Simon himself—did not then require cultivation by learned minds and correction by the press.

But to come at last to those matters which he complains were done either wrongly or incompetently in the work of the Maurist Fathers: he first censures them for omitting the notes of the Louvain theologians, so useful to the cause of the Catholic Church—for this is what he means by *importantes à la religion*, “important to religion.” Nor does he accept the excuse by which they assert that they abstained entirely from theological notes.

He denies that this was wholly true of them, and condemns them in part for having left room for critical observations in theology as well as in grammar, the only field, he says, in which they had exercised themselves. [Col. 0103B–C]

But the greater reproach in all this—and one that would considerably raise the value of the edition, if he had adequately established it—is that the monks lacked all the abilities demanded by the work of criticism: competence, learning, judgment, and acumen.

He offers several examples in which one cannot deny that they handled matters with little skill. Yet almost all of them concern translations of passages from the Old or New Testament. If they expressed themselves somewhat timidly or even not sufficiently learnedly in such passages, who would endure this with so much irritation?

Besides, the examples are few. Although he indicates that he is presenting them as a sample of many, and although in the second of these censures he wrote that he had enough material concerning omissions and erroneous statements to compose a book of respectable size, nevertheless, since he never wrote such a book and nowhere increased the number of his examples, no one should too readily accept this judgment of the man. [Col. 0103C–D]

As for that branch of criticism which concerns the authenticity and integrity of books—a field in which the monks of this congregation have always been considered to have rendered outstanding service, and which in Augustine was certainly no minor labor—yet which Simon did not touch even in a word, what impartial judge, when sitting down to pronounce judgment on the work as a whole, would dare to pass it over? [Col. 0104A]

## 1700–1703

Antwerp, at the expense of the Society; folio, twelve volumes. *The Works of Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, volumes I–XI. Revised again after the recension of the Louvain theologians*, etc., as in the preceding edition. A new edition purged of many errors.

Volumes I–V appeared in 1700, volume VI in 1701, volumes VII–X in 1700, and volume XI in 1702.
