Finally, in 1703, at Antwerp, through Peter Mortier: *The Augustinian Appendix*, containing Saint Prosper’s poem *Against the Ungrateful*, with the notes of the Louvain theologian; the dissertations of John Garnerius, priest of the Society of Jesus, concerning Pelagian history; Pelagius the Briton’s commentaries on the Epistles of Saint Paul; and finally the prefaces, censures, notes, and observations of Desiderius Erasmus, Juan Luis Vives, Jacques Sirmond, Henry Noris, John Phereponus, and others on all the works of Saint Augustine. Volume XII, peculiar to this edition, was printed from the Paris edition alone, without alteration, while the preceding eleven volumes were reproduced. [Col. 0104A–B]

It is established that this edition was completed not at Antwerp but at Amsterdam by Peter Mortier, an Amsterdam bookseller. He not only put his own name on the title page of the Appendix, or twelfth volume, but also appended it to the end of volume XI.

By this deception the editors hoped to make it more saleable in lands that followed the Roman pontiff’s formula, if it appeared to have come from a city devoted to papal doctrine rather than if it bore the name of a heterodox city. It is equally well known that the editor was that celebrated man, though especially ill-regarded among Catholics, John Clericus, who wished to hide under the mask of John Phereponus. [Col. 0104B–C]

There are two kinds of writings that Clericus inserted into this appendix: books of certain ancient authors, and dissertations by more recent writers illuminating Augustine’s works. To these should be added the prefaces and censures of earlier editors, as well as Clericus’s own notes, recently written on the individual volumes of the works.

The first category includes Prosper’s poem and Pelagius’s commentaries; we shall have a more suitable opportunity to discuss these when we reach those authors themselves. It also includes Garnerius’s dissertations, which occupy a place between the works of Prosper and Pelagius and which we shall similarly mention under Marius Mercator.

Among the writings belonging to this category are the letters of Cardinal-Bishop Henry Noris, in which Garnerius’s errors in his *Sacred Geography of Africa* are pointed out and corrected. Garnerius had assigned bishops to the synods of the African and Numidian sees; Noris’s letters are placed among the observations appended to volume II. [Col. 0104C–D]

Regarding Pelagius, the editor observes that he would have added separately all of Pelagius’s surviving works, unless those works—apart from the *Epistle to Demetrias*—had already been collected in Garnerius’s dissertations. The *Epistle to Demetrias*, however, had found a place among Augustine’s letters in volume II of this Antwerp edition. [Col. 0105A]

As for the prefaces, the first is Erasmus’s dedication to Alfonso Fonseca, archbishop of Toledo; next comes John Vlimmerius’s preface, placed before the sermons he published in 1564 and repeated in the subsequent Basel edition; then the Basel preface of 1569 itself, composed in verse; and finally Erasmus’s censure of the books of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*.

I see no reason why this last should have been transcribed here separately from the other Erasmian censures, which he interspersed with his own observations. Nor do I better understand why he placed here one preface of Vlimmerius addressed to Pamelius, which properly concerns only the catalogue of Possidius published together with the sermons, while he assigned the other, addressed to Martin Rithovius, the first bishop of Ypres, and appended together with Sirmond’s preface to the *Forty Sermons* published at Paris in 1631, for reprinting before the observations on volume V. [Col. 0105A–B]

Certainly I seem to recognize in these matters a certain haste of the kind that often pressed Clericus when something had to be prepared for printing.

**Note:** He himself admits this in the admonition prefixed to the observations on volume X. An even greater confusion was caused by it. For the prefaces of the Louvain theologians, which he says in the preface to this appendix were inserted here, were omitted because, through inadvertence, he had designated for printing Vlimmerius’s letter to Pamelius. That letter is reproduced below among the observations on volume X, pp. 621 ff., a second time, but there in its proper place. [Col. 0105D–0106D]

But to come finally to his *Observations*: he declared generally that he had not undertaken to write a commentary or continuous notes on Saint Augustine, but only to annotate here and there various passages in his works.

Whenever he owed anything to others, he said that he had carefully given the authors’ names everywhere, so that each person might retain his own praise; other matters, which he left untouched or did not know whether anyone else had treated, he published under his own name. The material he presented was partly grammatical or critical and partly philosophical and theological, intermixed, because he had decided not merely to act as Augustine’s interpreter but also to assess his reasoning. [Col. 0105C]

> “We did not wish,” he says, “merely to explain certain obscure passages or to elucidate others, but also occasionally to honor with deserved praise what had been truly and correctly said, and to point out those matters in which he seemed to have been mistaken, lest they deceive others who are unwary or intimidated by the authority of the man. We knew that these books are not read in order to derive critical learning from them, but rather because of their reasoning and doctrines. Therefore we believed that these matters above all ought to be examined by us, so that our observations might serve as a kind of guide for those who cannot devote much time to reading them, but rightly think that the study of the ancients should cultivate and sharpen judgment more than memory.

> “Yet I seem to hear certain people loudly declaring that what I have said in various places is suited rather to corrupt than to cultivate judgment. I reply that, had I shared their opinion, I would have omitted those things; but since I thought otherwise, I could not allow myself to pass over what seemed to me best to say. They act in the same way themselves. For they too do not usually write what they think will be approved by me or by others, but what they themselves judge to be true. Everyone must plainly do what seems to him the best course. But there will later be a supreme Judge who will finally and certainly show which of us thought more rightly.

> “Indeed, our own age, not to mention posterity, will be able to pronounce judgment on this matter; and even if it cannot agree with my arguments, it will not at least be led astray by my authority, which is entirely negligible. I had reason to fear that I might be overwhelmed by the authority of Saint Augustine, even though I was superior in argument; but those who cannot fear anything from my authority unless I prove by the strongest arguments that what I defend is true will undoubtedly condemn me.” [Col. 0105C–0106A]

We said generally that Erasmus’s censures and admonitions were inserted among the observations, but his preface to the letters was also added to volume II. Clericus writes that Erasmus praised these letters so highly for the very reason that he wished not to violate established usage.

These observations also contain various matters concerning the Septuagint, the harassment of the Donatists and other heretics, and the condemnation of the Pelagians, which Clericus instructs the reader to assess free from prejudice.

The observations on volume III, which contains Augustine’s books on the interpretation of Holy Scripture, frequently display Augustine’s errors in interpretation arising from his lack of knowledge of Greek and Hebrew. We know that Clericus treated Jerome severely in the same manner of correction.

Volume IV contains Augustine’s sermons on the Psalms. We do not hesitate to reproduce Clericus’s own words, which express a judgment that is entirely true but at that time new and unheard of:

> “Erasmus greatly praises Augustine’s sermons on the Psalms, and, following their example, he himself also interpreted various Psalms in volume V of his works. But that method of interpreting Scripture has now rightly fallen out of use wherever the study of languages, especially Hebrew, has flourished for nearly two hundred years. Accordingly, we here subject Erasmus’s short preface to examination, and in the same work we show what use Augustine’s sermons may have, although they can contribute little or nothing to an accurate understanding of the Psalms.

> “Those who can read Hebrew and are not wholly unacquainted with sacred criticism will understand from reading only a few of these sermons that nothing could be truer. Others will also notice this if, led by a love of truth, they examine the analysis of Augustine’s interpretation of the first three Psalms. We had no time to examine more, nor was it necessary.” [Col. 0106B–D]

In the observations on volume V, Clericus inserted Sirmond’s notes in full, although the Benedictines had published only some of them, distinguishing them from his own by adding the author’s name.

The observations on volume VI consist for the most part of questions and objections. This volume contains theological works to which Clericus added various remarks that seemed scarcely capable of resolution from the principles set out in those books.

In particular, in the notes he made on the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, he attempted to demonstrate that Augustine’s view of free will is sometimes difficult to understand because Augustine gives the words “freedom” and “free will” a meaning different from their usual one. [Col. 0106D–0107A]

The observations on the books *On the City of God*, which constitute volume VII, are more extensive than the others but are also of different kinds. They are preceded by a preface of Juan Luis Vives.

Clericus had intended to add Coquaeus’s notes as well, but their length and the calamity of the war then spreading throughout Europe, which also disrupted the affairs of the book trade, deterred the booksellers.

Learn again from Clericus himself what kind of character the observations on volumes VIII and IX have:

> “Volume VIII is entirely against heretics, especially against the Manichaeans and Arians. We certainly do not wish them defended in any way, nor do we think that anyone should be farther removed from their madness than we are. But we would often have wished them attacked by another route and with other weapons, as will be especially clear from what we have written on the book *On the Usefulness of Believing* and on the books *On the Trinity*.

> “Otherwise, since we thought that Saint Augustine had attacked them well, we poured out praises upon him by the full measure, as elsewhere, and embraced his arguments with both arms, as in book XXXIII against Faustus the Manichaean.

> “Volume IX, in which Saint Augustine contends with the Donatists, did not greatly occupy us, because he repeats almost the same things there, while the Donatists, to the point of weariness, continually hurled the same objections and the same fallacies at their opponents. It is nevertheless remarkable that weariness or sleep did not overtake Saint Augustine as he said the same things so many times.

> “In the books against Parmenianus’s epistle we again dealt with the persecution of heretics, about which we had said enough in the observations on volume II; and we also dealt with the authority of councils in the books on baptism, although there we touched upon the matter only in summary.” [Col. 0107A–C]

Less attention was devoted to volume X. It contains only the following: the preface to the edition of the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, published at Augsburg in 1611; Henry Noris’s—then professor of ecclesiastical history at the University of Pisa, later cardinal—*Adventoria* to Francesco Macedonius, professor of ethics at the University of Padua, concerning the title of Saint Augustine’s book *On the Grace of Christ*, and concerning Albina, Pinianus, and Melania; a few observations on the book *On Correction and Grace*; the preface of Claudius Menard to the edition of the two books of the *Unfinished Work against Julian*; observations on the same work; Vlimmerius’s preface to the first edition of Possidius’s catalogue published by him, here printed for a second time; and an observation on the *Life of Augustine*. [Col. 0107C–D]

He explains that three things prevented him from adding more: the haste of the printers; the character of Augustine’s books against the Pelagians, in which innumerable repetitions occur, so that matters that could have been concluded in three words are expressed in thousands, with much additional extraneous material inserted; and finally his weariness of all these quarrels, which he says took hold of him so strongly that he could scarcely, or hardly at all, endure them.

Who, he exclaims, would not also feel nausea at so many and such lengthy—if I may use the expression of a later age—“rhetorical performances,” whether intended to evade the adversary’s blow, attack him, or arouse or escape odium?

> “For my part, they created such disgust in me while I was reading that I plainly need the refreshment of more agreeable and useful studies.” [Col. 0107D–0108A]

Thus Clericus serves his readers a full platter of what is cooked and uncooked alike. It must be admitted that, when writing under such influences, he was not always sufficiently reflective, and that his tongue often outran his judgment. This earned him serious, though not wholly unjust, criticism.

For Robert Jenkins, an Englishman, published a special critique of these observations at Cambridge in 1707.

**Note:** The full title of the book is *Defense of Saint Augustine against the Observations of John Phereponus on His Works*. Cambridge, printed at the University Press, at the expense of Richard Thurlbourne, Cambridge bookseller. It was offered for sale in London by Robert Knaplock, at the Angel in the churchyard of Saint Paul’s, 1707, octavo. It sometimes defends Augustine well, though it attacks the rest of Clericus’s opinions with less success. [Col. 0107D–0108D]

Ludovico Antonio Muratori also defended Augustine against the same writer in Book III of his work *On the Moderation of the Intellect in Religious Matters*, published in 1714 under the name Lamindi Pritanii.

The insults that Casimirus Oudinus directed against John Clericus in his account of this edition, and especially of the appendix, are entirely empty and utterly foolish. *Commentaries*, vol. I, pp. 986 ff.

The work is crowned by a very skillfully prepared index and by a notice to the bookseller, in which he promised that he would also sell this twelfth volume separately, both on smaller and on larger paper, so that it could be joined to the Paris edition. The *Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensia* reviewed the Augustinian Appendix in 1703, July, pp. 289–92. [Col. 0108B]

## 1729–32

Venice, printed by Giovanni Battista Albrizzi, son of Girolamo; folio. *The Works of Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, volumes I–V, revised again after the recension of the Louvain theologians and corrected against French, Vatican, and other manuscript codices*, etc. By the work and study of the monks of the Order of Saint Benedict of the Congregation of Saint-Maur.

This is merely a description of the Paris edition. The printer had declared as much from the beginning. See *Novelle della Repubblica delle Lettere*, March 1729, p. 94. In the same journal, June, p. 199, there is an indication that the first volume had appeared. The third volume is given with its full title there in June 1730, p. 193. The fifth appeared there in August 1731, p. 237. I confess that I do not know whether the remaining volumes appeared. [Col. 0108C–D]

## 1754

Rome, at the press of the Palearini Brothers; octavo, two volumes. *Selected Works of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on the Grace of God, Human Free Will, and the Predestination of the Saints.* A most carefully corrected edition, furnished with variant readings collected from every quarter, especially from the Vatican manuscript codices, prepared by P. F. F. (Pietro Francesco Foggini.)

These two volumes, which are sold separately, as the external title (*Selected Works of Saint Augustine*) indicates, also form part of a series with three other volumes by Prosper of Aquitaine and Fulgentius, presenting the principal works on the same subject. Together they are included under the single title *Selected Works of the Holy Fathers on the Grace of God and the Predestination of the Saints*. The edition is exceptionally neat and especially suitable for use in both format and presentation.

Of Augustine’s books on this subject, only those that he wrote, already a bishop, after the emergence of the Pelagian heresy have been included here. It was from that time, he himself admits, that he investigated these matters more carefully.

**Note:** *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapters 3 and 4. [Col. 0109A, D]

Accordingly, the first volume contains *The Book on the Grace of Christ against Pelagius and Coelestius*; the *Epistle to Sixtus*; two epistles to Abbot Valentinus and the monks of Hadrumetum with him; the epistle of Abbot Valentinus to Saint Augustine; *The Book on Correction and Grace*, addressed to Abbot Valentinus and the monks of Hadrumetum with him; and the *Epistle to Vitalis*.

The second volume contains Prosper’s epistle to Saint Augustine; Hilary’s epistle to the same; Saint Augustine’s book to Prosper and Hilary on *The Predestination of the Saints*; his book to the same on *The Gift of Perseverance*; and finally the *Enchiridion*, or book on *Faith, Hope, and Charity*, addressed to Laurentius. [Col. 0109A–B]

These two volumes were dedicated to Benedict XIV, then occupying the apostolic see. A substantial index common to both volumes was added to the second.

## APPENDIX TO THE FIRST ARTICLE

### I. VERSIONS
Several minor works of Augustine, collected for a definite purpose and translated together into another language—except into German [Col. 0109C]—I do not recall having found, nor do we know of any mention of them by others. For this reason, the mention of this German translation gives us all the greater pleasure. It consists of two volumes, bearing the following titles:

*Augustine, the holy bishop: Four Books on Christian Doctrine. Book I, On the Spirit and the Letter. Book I, On Faith and Works. Translated by Doctor Caspar Hedio. Never previously read in the German language; useful, however, to every Christian who desires to be instructed unto salvation. Strasbourg. In the year 1532.*

*Books of Augustine, the holy bishop: 1. On True Worship. 2. Enchiridion, that is, Handbook, on Faith, Hope, and Love. 3. On True Innocence. 4. On Nature and Grace. 5. On the Predestination of the Saints. 6. How Good a Thing Perseverance Is. All newly translated by Dr. Caspar Hedio, to advance truth and peace in our times. Strasbourg. In the year 1533.*

In the earlier volume, besides the works promised by the title, number IX is also added [Note: [Col. 0109D] The earlier volume is divided into nine numbers or parts. The five numbers I, II, III, IV, and V, as will shortly be stated, contain, in the manner of prolegomena, works not mentioned in the title. The following numbers, VI, VII, and VIII, constitute the main body and correspond to the title. Finally, as an appendix, there is number IX. EDIT.], *Ambrose, On Compassion toward the Poor, and When the Church Treasuries Are to Be Attacked*. Before the translated books there are also: no. I, *Preface of Dr. C. Hed. to the Reverend and Noble Lord Wilhelm, Count of Eysenberg*, etc.; no. II, *Explanation of Several Difficult Words in the Translated Books of Augustine*; no. III, *A Brief Outline of Augustine’s Life, without Any Danger*; no. IV, *Testimony of Saint Jerome Concerning Augustine*; no. V, *Clarification from the Books of the Retractations concerning the Books On Christian Doctrine, On the Spirit and the Letter, and On Faith and Works*.

The second volume contains, after the book *On Nature and Grace*, *Prosper’s Letter to Augustine* and *Hilary’s Letter to Augustine*. It is preceded by: no. I, *To the High-born Prince and Lord, Lord George, Count of Württemberg*, etc., *Preface of Dr. Caspar Hedio, in which a free Christian council is discussed, together with what the Christian and German nation should deliberate concerning it*, etc.; no. II, *A Brief Report to the Reader concerning Difficult Sentences and Words in Augustine*.

## II. Manuscripts

In examining the manuscript books of the Latin Fathers—so far as the writings relevant to our undertaking are concerned—which the editors have consulted, we have not hitherto followed a single method everywhere. For the most part we followed the editors themselves in this respect: if they had treated the manuscripts carefully, we considered ourselves no less obliged to provide an exact enumeration. For this diligence is of the greatest benefit not only for the history of the text of the individual works, which is its immediate purpose, but also for becoming acquainted with that immense abundance of writings which, because it lies hidden in chests and is enclosed behind barriers, almost habitually escapes the control of bibliographers [Col. 0110C]. For this reason, henceforth also, wherever the opportunity is given, we shall not grow weary in this part of our work, for the enlargement of literary history.

The situation was different when the books consulted were mentioned only briefly or generally, whether for an author’s works as a whole or for individual books. In that case we generally had to be content with a list of names, which we compiled with no little difficulty from scattered notices concerning individual books, provided that we were not forced to repeat the same names six hundred times in enumerating the manuscripts. Hilary, Ambrose, and Jerome are examples. The same situation now arises with Augustine, but it has cost us far more labor, although there were reasons that might have encouraged us to adopt the other method, which certainly involved less inconvenience.

For not only is the number of Augustine’s manuscript books enormous in almost every library, but the manuscripts themselves differ astonishingly according to the number of writings they contain. It was exceedingly difficult even for the editor to select all of them and reduce them to certain classes; and in fact neither the Louvain editors nor the Benedictines undertook anything of the kind. Erasmus, moreover—as we have often noted—made it his practice to place little value on describing manuscript books. Instead, at the end of each volume, in connection with the greater textual variants, they produced a long display of manuscript names to which the individual works had been compared [Col. 0110D]. Yet so far from any description having been added, those very names designate not individual manuscripts—distinguished by some indication of age, or by library numbers or other marks—but classes of several books belonging to one place. If anyone wished to discover which writings of Augustine belonged to each manuscript, much labor would have been spent in vain.

It might therefore not have been inappropriate for us to present that same enumeration of names for each of the holy Doctor’s writings. We could at least have hoped to achieve this much: that those who came upon the catalogues of libraries rich in manuscripts, and saw almost every page filled with Augustinian writings—or who visited the libraries themselves and learned that nearly all their shelves had been occupied by ecclesiastical writers—would admire these treasures more sparingly, having been warned that a sufficient number of excellent books had already been compared with this or that work.

But we also readily saw that the introduction of so many names would be pointless and empty unless a fuller explanation were added, showing the repositories from which those designations had been taken. At last the easier course seemed to be, although it involved much unpleasant labor, to arrange an alphabetical index of all those names and, under each as a kind of class and category, to note, as far as possible, how many manuscripts, and which ones, and of what character, had been used for the individual works. Thus, if not the individual manuscripts—which can scarcely ever be hoped for in Augustine and does not seem particularly desirable—at least the libraries in which they had been deposited would become known.

This work, however, pertains only to the Benedictine edition. For the Louvain edition we thought it sufficient to recite generally the names of the libraries to which the manuscripts belonged and the number of manuscripts, as reported by the editors themselves. The Benedictines, moreover, carefully cited the Belgian or Louvain manuscripts which they had again examined for individual books. The index now follows.

### A) Manuscripts examined by the Louvain theologians

**ALNENSES**, that is, the manuscripts of the library of the Cistercian abbey of Alne in the territory of Liège. There were twenty. Antonius Sanderus briefly lists the manuscripts of this library, including the Augustinian ones, in *Bibliotheca Belgica Manuscripta*, part II, pp. 234 [Col. 0111D] (241–43).

**S. AMANDI**, that is, of the Elnonensis monastery, commonly called Saint-Amand in Pabula. Thirty-two manuscripts had been sent by Maximilian Morillon, vicar general of the province of Mechelen. In *Bibliotheca Belgica Manuscripta*, part I, pp. 32 ff., one will find the Augustinian manuscripts of this monastery.

**CAMBRONENSES**, that is, of the library of the Cambron monastery of the Cistercian Order in Hainaut, not far from the city of Mons. Thirty were available. See *Bibliotheca Belgica Manuscripta*, part I, pp. 346 ff.

**FLOREFFIACENSES**, of some monastery at Floreffe, I do not know which. Eight.

**GEMBLACENSES**, that is, of the abbey of Gembloux. Thirty, all on parchment.

**LOVANIENSES.** Some of these had been received from the theological college, others from the college of the Society of Jesus, and others from the Carthusians, the Martinian Premonstratensians at Parc, and the Bethlehemites. They did not, however, indicate the number belonging to each group. In *Bibliotheca Belgica Manuscripta* there are listings of the manuscripts of the college of the Society of Jesus, part I, p. 326; of Parc Abbey, part II, p. 166; and of the Library of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine in Saint-Martin’s Valley, part II, pp. 210 ff.

**TORNACENSES**, that is, of the monastery of Saint Martin at Tournai, from which thirty-one had been brought. See *Bibliotheca Belgica Manuscripta*, part I, pp. 93 ff. [Col. 0112B].

### B) Manuscripts made available for the use of the Benedictines

#### a) Gallican manuscripts

[Note: [Col. 0111D] Some Belgian manuscripts are included among them, as are certain Corbie manuscripts which they consulted. We hesitated to separate these partly because the Benedictines themselves included them under the name “Gallican,” and partly because the manuscripts of the monastery of Corbie served the studies of the Maurist Fathers at all times so completely that they seem to have become, as it were, domestic manuscripts among them. [Col. 0112D]]

**ALBINENSES at Angers**, that is, the manuscripts of the Abbey of Saint-Albin at Angers. In many books of the first volume, including the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, they cite approximately one; likewise in volumes six and ten, and also in volume seven for the books *On the City of God* and in volume eight for the books *On the Trinity*. In volume six, for the book *On the Creed to the Catechumens*, they note that in an Albinian manuscript eight hundred years old the first of the four sermons comprising the work is found.

**ANTISSIODORENSES**, that is, the manuscripts of the Premonstratensian Abbey of Saint Marian at Auxerre. One of the four manuscripts with which they were equipped supplied the text for the books *Against the Second Response of Julian* [Col. 0112C].

A manuscript of the monastery of **SAINT ARNULF OF METZ**. I infer that there was one, since they invariably cite Arnulfianus in the singular. It is mentioned especially often in the first three volumes. They had readings from it, not the manuscript itself, as they note regarding the *Retractations*.

Manuscripts of the Abbey of **SAINT OUEN OF ROUEN**. From these Augustine’s *City*, sermons, and many other writings were corrected. They are especially often called Audoenenses in the first volume and more sparingly in the following volumes. We do not know whether they were all of the same age, but in the work *Expositions on the Psalms* they assign them an age of seven hundred years.

Manuscripts of the **Augustinian Fathers of the Greater Paris Convent**. Four were available for the books of the *Confessions*; one is mentioned more often.

Several manuscripts of the **BECC Abbey**, seven hundred years old, are cited for the *Work on the Psalms*; one for the *Retractations*, *City of God*, *Letters*, the book *On Heresies*, *On the Trinity*, and *Against the Donatists* (volumes eight and nine), and more often in volume ten; two for the books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* and *On the Sermon on the Mount*; several in the sermons.

They cite a **BECHERONENSE** exemplar in volume three, in the *Treatises on the Gospel of John*, and in volume eight, in the book *On Heresies*.

An extremely ancient exemplar of the **Church of Beauvais** was available for the *Treatises on the Letter of John*, with the following written at the end: “In the twelfth year of King Chlothar.” Another was also available for the later fifty Psalms in volumes three and four.

This differs from the **Beauvais manuscript of the Abbey of Saint-Quentin**, which was used for the same *Treatises on the Letter of John*.

**BENIGNIANI**, that is, the manuscripts of the Library of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon. In the books of the *Retractations* and *Confessions* they note one more than seven hundred years old. I do not know whether this is the same manuscript that was also available for the *Letters* and the *Treatises on John*, the book *On Various Questions against Lying*, *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, *On the Trinity*, and so forth. They report that the manuscript used for the book *On the Creed* was eight hundred years old. They had three or more for correcting the sermons.

One or two manuscript books of the **Bernardine College in Paris**. They were useful for the books *On the Work of Monks* in volume six, for the *Expositions on the Letter to the Romans and the Galatians* in volume three, and also for books VII *On Baptism* and books IV *Against Cresconius* in volume nine. They call the second one into use for the books *Against Maximinus* and the *Collation with Maximinus*. I think this is different from the book of the Fulian Fathers’ monastery of Saint Bernard in Paris, which they ordinarily call the Fulian exemplar.

One manuscript book of the **Bernardines, On the Mercy of God**, is cited in the book *On the Work of Monks*.

An extremely ancient manuscript of **Saint Bertin** in Belgium, from which Augustine’s *Letter to Mercator* was extracted; it first appeared in the Benedictine edition as no. 193.

**BIGOTIANUS**, that is, a manuscript from the library of Emeric Bigot of Rouen. From it the *Letters*, several books of volume six, *On the City of God* in volume seven, *On the Nature of the Good*, book XV *On the Trinity* in volume eight, and the six books *Against Julian* in volume ten were revised.

A manuscript book of the **Church of Carcassonne** is cited for the sermons in volume five and for the 124 *Treatises on the Gospel of John* in volume three.

**CARNOTENSIS**, that is, a manuscript of the Abbey of Saint Peter in the Chartres valley. One is mentioned for the book *Against Lying* in volume six, the books *Against Faustus* in volume eight, and the book *Against Secundinus*, which, having been sought in vain in the Belgian manuscripts, is said to have been cleansed of innumerable errors from this one manuscript alone; likewise for the books *On Nature and Grace* and *On the Perfection of Man* in volume ten.

Different from these is the book of the **Church of Chartres**, which is cited in the sermons.

**CASALENSIS or CASALINUS**, that is, a manuscript of the monastery of Casale Benedicti. From it—for they always cite it in the singular—the *Letters*, as well as several books of volume one and some books of volumes eight, nine, and ten, were corrected.

Manuscripts of the **Cistercian Abbey**, undoubtedly the Parisian one. From the Cistercian manuscript—if there was only one—nearly all the books of volumes one, three, six, and eight were corrected, as were the *Letters* in volume two. The Cistercian manuscript is also frequently named in the sermons. They cite two Cistercian manuscripts for *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* in volume three, *On the City of God* in volume seven, the book *On Various Questions* in volume six, and *On Grace and Free Will* in volume ten.

An old manuscript of the **Fathers of the Cistercian Abbey of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem at Rome**. The first edition of Letter 29, to Alypius, was made from it. They cite several such manuscripts in the sermons, and say that from them they learned the occasion of some sermons and also where Augustine had delivered them.

An exemplar of the six books **Against the Second Response of Julian** from the Abbey of Clairvaux. This is the very manuscript from which Vignerius had first drawn the books, and from which readings differing from the Vignerian edition were again excerpted for the use of the Benedictines.

Several manuscripts from the **Colbert Library** provided assistance. This library was exceedingly well supplied with ancient books, all of which later moved into the Royal Library. None were available in volume one, but the *Letters* were compared with them. Sometimes one, sometimes two, are also cited in volumes three and six; likewise, in volume four, the Colbert manuscripts of the *Expositions on the Psalms* are described as being of excellent quality [Note: [Col. 0113D] Among them was also one containing an epitome of Augustine’s commentaries on the Psalms. In this manuscript there was a gateway, painted in the form of a chamber enclosing an image of David, with the following words written on the arch: “Landulfus, rejoicing, ordered this little book to be made; you who read it, pour forth prayers and songs,” etc. At the feet of the image: “Pray for Anno, I beg this.” The verses below consist of fourteen couplets. They begin:

> Holding songs that celebrate Christ  
> with David’s plectrum,

> this flowering book contains them explained.

They end:

> And between the two Cherubim,  
> in a trembling voice,

> he thunders, and shines with the fire  
> of swift lightning.]; three for the work *On the City of God*. They are also mentioned throughout volume eight, and in the book *On Heresies* four are recorded; in volume ten, they are cited for nearly every book.

Among the several manuscripts from which the sermons in volume five were corrected, one in particular is mentioned, numbered 821. It contained sermons *On the Words of the Gospel*, arranged in the old order according to which they are generally cited in Bede’s or Florus’s collection, and included certain sermons of which nothing at all had previously been published, or only fragments had survived.

In volume six, in the book *On Lying*, a Colbert manuscript eight hundred years old is cited; in the same volume, in the book *On the Work of Monks*, another is called nearly nine hundred years old. From the Colbert Library they likewise obtained a manuscript of the incomplete work *Against the Second Response of Julian*, mutilated by one-third—the very manuscript from which Claudius Menard had first published the first two books in 1617.

By that time the Thuane manuscripts had already passed into the Colbert Library—though I do not know whether all of them had done so. Thus the Thuane manuscripts should sometimes be regarded as Colbert manuscripts, for example in the book *On Christian Combat* and *On the Good of Marriage* in volume six.

**COMPENDIENSES**, see **CORNELIENSES**.

**CORBEIENSES.** Extremely ancient and numerous. There is scarcely any book that was not corrected against them. At the very beginning, for the books of the *Retractations*, the book *On Order*, and the *Rule for the Servants of God*, a manuscript nearly nine hundred years old was available. For the *Confessions*, a Corbie manuscript written more than seven hundred years earlier is cited; and so, for nearly all the books of volume one, Corbie manuscripts of excellent quality are mentioned.

Most of those used for the *Letters* in volume two are said to have been written more than eight or nine hundred years earlier.

All the books of volume three, with one exception, were collated with Corbie manuscripts. One of these, for the books *On Questions of the Gospels*, is said to be nine hundred years old; another, for the books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, is said to be nine hundred or a thousand years old and written in an excellent hand.

For the books of the *Expositions on the Psalms* in volume four, two manuscripts were used throughout the work, and sometimes more for the same treatises; most were written more than eight hundred years earlier.

Likewise, in the sermons of volume five, Corbie manuscripts of excellent quality and great antiquity are noted. In nearly every book of volume six there are manuscripts eight or nine hundred years old, and for the books *On Various Questions to Simplicianus* one exceptionally fine manuscript written a thousand years earlier. Two were available for the books *On the City of God* in volume seven.

Nor is the mention of the extremely ancient and elegant books of the Abbey of Corbie any less frequent in the final three volumes. In the last volume, for the books *On Grace and Free Will* and *On Correction and Grace*, they judged one manuscript to be extremely old, written more than a thousand years earlier.

From the same library there was also a manuscript of Eugippius’s *Extracts* and a manuscript book written about five hundred years earlier, containing Florus’s or Bede’s published collection on the Apostle’s Letters.

**CORNELIENSES**, that is, the manuscript books of the Abbey of Saint Cornelius at Compiègne. One very ancient manuscript is mentioned for the book *On the Immortality of the Soul* in volume one. Several were used for the sermons in volume four.

Manuscripts of the **Abbey of Cultura near Le Mans**. One is cited for the *Letters* and also for the *Treatises on the Gospel of John* in volume three; likewise, in volume four, an extremely ancient manuscript containing the first fifty Psalms in the *Expositions*. It is also cited for the book *On the Soul and Its Origin* in volume ten.

The manuscript books of the **Dominican Fathers of the Greater Paris Convent on the Rue Saint-Jacques** were used for the books of the *Confessions* and *On Free Will* in volume one, for the books *On the Trinity* in volume eight, the book *On One Baptism* in volume nine, and the three books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* in volume ten.

**EBRULPHENSES**, that is, the manuscripts of Saint Ebrulf of Utica. One is cited for the books *On the Immortality of the Soul* and *On the Quantity of the Soul* in volume one, and for the books *On Christian Combat* and *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, as well as other books, in volume six.

The manuscript of **D. Anthony Faure**, doctor of theology in Paris, supplied the book *On Faith, Hope, and Charity* and the books *On the City of God*.

A manuscript of the **Abbey of Ferrières** contained twenty-six Psalms from the work *Expositions*, namely Psalms 63–98.

The **Fécamp** manuscript is noted for the book *On the Teacher* in volume one, the book *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* in volume three, the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed* in volume six, and *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets* in volume eight.

**FLORIACENSES.** The manuscripts of the Library of Fleury are cited extremely often, not only for entire volumes—for example, volume two, containing the *Letters*; volume four, containing the *Expositions on the Psalms*; and volume five, containing the sermons. Those cited for volume four are assigned an age of seven hundred years—but also for individual books in different volumes: for the *Retractations* and the book *On the Quantity of the Soul* in volume one; for nearly all of volume three; for the book *On the Eight Questions of Dulcitius* and *On Christian Combat*, in the latter case two manuscripts; for *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, *On the Work of Monks*, and *On Patience* in volume six; for the books *On Heresies*, *Against Faustus*, and *On the Trinity* in volume eight; for books VII *On Baptism*, *Against the Letters of Petilian*, *On the Unity of the Church*, and *On One Baptism* in volume nine; and finally for the six books *Against Julian* in volume ten.

The manuscripts of the Abbey of **Fossat** of Saint Maur: I do not know whether there was one or several, though the latter is more probable. They were used for the books of the *Confessions* in volume one, the *Letters* in volume two, and the books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* in volume three. An extremely ancient manuscript is cited for the Gradual Psalms in the *Expositions* in volume four. The sermons were also corrected from them; likewise, in volume six, book XXXVIII *On Various Questions* and *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*; in volume eight, the *Collation with Maximinus* and two books *Against Him*. For the *Treatises on the Gospel of John*, a Fossat manuscript is cited, written at the command of Abbot Ingilbert about the year 840.

A manuscript of the **Franciscan Fathers in Paris**. They supplied one manuscript for correcting the book *On the Morals of the Manichaeans* in volume one.

Two manuscript books of the **Fulians’ monastery of Saint Bernard in Paris** were used to correct the work *Expositions on the Psalms*. One contained sixteen Psalms, from 35 to 50; the other eighteen, from 101 to 118. The sermons were also collated with manuscripts of the same library, as were the book *On Continence*, four sermons *On the Creed to the Catechumens*, and the sermons *On the New Song*, *On Wednesday*, *On the Flood*, and *On the Time of the Barbarians* in volume six.

An exemplar of the **Fuxian College near Toulouse** was available for the *Letters*. It is also cited for the book *On Christian Combat* in volume six.

A manuscript of the **Church of Saint Gatianus at Tours**, of excellent quality, is cited for the *Expositions on the Psalms*, containing the first hundred Psalms; likewise for the books *On the Trinity* in volume eight.

The manuscript books of the **Abbey of Jumièges** are cited very often. From them the *Letters*, sermons, and *Expositions on the Psalms* were corrected, as was one copy of the work *On the City of God*. Moreover, in volume one: the books *On Free Will*, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, and *On True Religion*; in volume three: the books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, and the *Treatises on the Gospel of John*; in volume six: four sermons *On the Creed to the Catechumens*, together with the sermons that immediately follow them there, *On Christian Discipline*, *On the Time of the Barbarians*, *On the New Song*, and others.

**GENOFEVAEUS**, that is, a manuscript book of the library of the Abbey of Saint Geneviève in Paris, is cited in the book *On the Blessed Life* in volume one; in the books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* in volume three; in the book *On Eighty-Three Various Questions* and *On Questions to Simplicianus* in volume six; and in the book *On Nature and Grace* in volume ten.

**GEORGIANUS**, that is, the manuscript of Lord de Saint-Georges, canon of the chapter of Lyon, later bishop of Clermont, and, as the Maurist work was nearing completion, designated by the king as archbishop of Tours. It was used for the books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* in volume three; the book *On Eighty-Three Various Questions* in volume six; the books *On Baptism against Cresconius* and *On One Baptism* in volume nine; and the books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* and *On the Spirit and the Letter* in volume ten.

Very many ancient and elegant manuscripts from **Saint-Germain-des-Prés in the Paris suburbs** were collated for the entire volumes of the *Letters*, sermons, and *Expositions on the Psalms*; two for the work *On the City of God*; for the *Treatises on the Gospel*; and also for the *Treatises on the Letters of John* in volume three. One or two assisted with most of the books in volumes one, three, six, and eight. The manuscript collated for the book *On Lying* is estimated at eight hundred years old, and the one used for the book *On the Good of Widowhood* at a thousand years or more.

A highly notable Saint-Germain exemplar, which the Duke of Noailles had recently donated to the same library, was used for the book *On Christian Combat* in volume six.

A large and elegant manuscript of the **Gervasian College in Paris** is cited in the *Letters*.

The **Joly** exemplar belonged to Monsieur Joly. The *Letters* are said to have been corrected from it. It is also cited in the *Expositions on the Letters to the Romans and Galatians* in volume three. A Joly manuscript eight hundred years old is cited for the *Retractations*.

Manuscripts of the **Church of Laon** are cited for the *Letters* and sermons. In the former place they are called extremely ancient. They were used especially often for correcting many books of volume six, where the books of the Church of Laon are repeatedly mentioned. I do not think that, in terms of location, these differ from those called the books of the Greater Church of Laon in volume six for the book *On the Good of Widowhood* [Note: [Col. 0117] But the manuscript mentioned for the books of the *Retractations*, from the Laon Archives, belongs to the English collection.]. Under the latter title, a manuscript book is cited especially often in volume eight and once in volume nine.

A manuscript of the **Abbey of Saint Vincent at Laon** was used for the books *On the City of God* in volume seven and *On the Trinity* in volume eight.

Manuscripts of the **Abbey of Lyre** were collated for volume four, containing the *Expositions on the Psalms*, and volume five, containing the sermons. One was available for the books *On the City of God*, and also for the books of the *Confessions* in volume one; the books *On the Sermon on the Mount* in volume three; *On Christian Combat* in volume six; *On the Trinity* in volume eight; and the six books *Against Julian* in volume ten.

The exemplar of **Nicholas Manessier**, doctor of theology in Paris and member of the Sorbonne, was used to correct the book *On Grace and Free Will*, as well as the two books *On Correction and Grace to Prosper and Hilary*—that is, the books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*—in volume ten.

The book of **Monsieur Maran**, archdeacon of the Church of Toulouse, was used to correct the *Letters*, as well as the book *On the Usefulness of Believing*, *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, and the books of the *Collation with Maximinus* and *Against Him* in volume eight.

A **MARTINENSIS** manuscript is cited for the books *On Genesis against the Manichaeans* in volume one. Perhaps it is the same manuscript more frequently called Sagianus.

A **Médard** manuscript is cited for the *Rule for the Servants of God* in volume one.

**METENSES**, see **ARNULPHENSES**.

**MICHAELINI**, that is, the manuscripts of the monastery and Abbey of Saint Michael on the Mount in Peril of the Sea. They are cited extremely often throughout all ten volumes. This clearly indicates that there were several, although almost everywhere only one is mentioned; once, two are recorded for the books *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. The *Letters*, sermons, and *Expositions on the Psalms* were corrected from them, as were most, and almost all, of the books of volumes one, six, eight, nine, and ten; only a few of volume three.

Manuscripts of the **Navarre College or School in Paris**. They cite a very substantial exemplar of this collection for the *Letters*. They also used one from the same library in revising the sermons and the books *On the City of God*. Moreover, a Navarre manuscript is cited for the books *On the Soliloquies*, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, and *On True Religion* in volume one; two Navarre manuscripts for the book *On the Blessed Life* and the book *On the Teacher* in the same volume; the books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* in volume three were revised against one of them; likewise, the book *On Eighty-Three Various Questions* against two; and again, against one, the book *On Faith and the Creed*, *On Christian Combat*, and *On the Divination of Demons* in volume six.

**NOAILLES**, see under **GERMANENSES**.

Manuscripts of the **Church of Noyon**, at least six hundred years old, were used to correct the *Expositions on the Psalms*.

A parchment manuscript of the illustrious **Phimarcon family**, which the Benedictines suspect once belonged to the Church of Narbonne, was used for the sermons. From it two very brief letters, nos. 42 and 45, to Paulinus, previously unpublished, were extracted.

The **Charterhouse of Portes** in the Bugey region of Gaul supplied a manuscript exemplar of the books *Against the Second Response of Julian*.

**PRATELLENSES**, that is, the manuscript books of the Abbey of Saint Peter at Pratellis, copied more than six hundred years ago, are cited in the work *Expositions on the Psalms* [Col. 0119A]. The sermons were revised against them, as were individual books from the middle volumes—for example, the *Retractations*, *On Free Will*, and *On Genesis against the Manichaeans* in volume one; *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, *On the Sermon on the Mount*, and the *Treatises on the Gospel of John* in volume three; the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, *On Holy Virginity*, *On Adulterous Marriages*, *On Lying*, and *On Patience*; and, against two manuscripts, the book *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead* in volume six.

They are cited no less often in volume eight, for the books *Against Faustus*, *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, and *On the Trinity*; and in volume nine for the books *Against the Letter of Parmenianus*, *On Baptism*, and *Against the Letters of Petilian*; finally, in volume ten, for the books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, *On Nature and Grace*, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, *On the Soul and Its Origin*, the four books to Boniface *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, the six books *Against Julian*, *On Grace and Free Will*, *On Correction and Grace*, and finally the books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*.

A **PUXIAN** manuscript is cited for the book *On Continence*, with the addition that it was already to be found among the Colbert manuscripts.

**REMENSES.** This name refers to two kinds of manuscripts: those of the cathedral church of Reims and those of the Abbey of Saint Remigius at Reims. Usually, however, the bare designation refers to the books of the cathedral church. One of them was useful for the book *On the Teacher* in volume one; the *Letters*, the books *On Faith and Works*, *On the Good of Marriage*, *On Holy Virginity*, and *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead* in volume six; the books *On the City of God* in volume seven; the books *Against the Sermon of the Arians* and *On the Trinity* in volume eight; and finally the books *On Nature and Grace*, *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, *On Grace and Free Will*, and *On Correction and Grace* in volume ten.

**REMIGIENSES**, that is, the books of the Abbey of Saint Remigius at Reims. One was used for the book *On the Quantity of the Soul* in volume one and for the books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* and the *Treatises on the Gospel of John* in volume three.

Likewise, in volume four, several manuscripts were available for the same Psalms, some written more than five hundred years earlier and others more than eight hundred years earlier. Several were also consulted for the sermons. In volume six they were useful for the books *On Faith and the Creed*, *On Christian Combat*, *On the Work of Monks*, and *On the Divination of Demons*. One Remigian manuscript is also cited for the books *On the City of God*, and in volume eight for the books *Against Maximinus* and the *Collation with Him*; two are cited there for the books *On the Trinity*.

Finally, from one manuscript the books *On Baptism* in volume nine were corrected; and in volume ten, the books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, and *On the Soul and Its Origin*.

**ROYAL MANUSCRIPTS.** The Royal Library of Paris had already gathered a fairly large number of Augustine’s manuscript books; now, since the Colbert and Thuane manuscripts have moved into it, Augustine occupies nearly every page of its catalogues. It is therefore all the more useful to know which manuscripts were put to use, so that a more accurate judgment may be formed concerning the whole collection. Accordingly, nearly all the books of volume one were corrected against Royal manuscripts, with the exception of two or three. The same manuscripts were available for the *Letters*, but not for volumes three and nine.

For the *Expositions on the Psalms*, however, they were assisted by a Royal manuscript, which they described as follows:

> “It is a book of remarkable size, now divided into two volumes, which on the first blank page bears this inscription: ‘This immense work was given to me by the distinguished man, Lord Giovanni Boccaccio, poet of our time; it came to me from Florence to Milan on 10 April 1355.’ You will understand that it was written by the hand of Francesco Petrarch from the letter sent by him to Boccaccio, which is no. 24 in the Venetian edition and no. 22 in the Basel edition, beginning, ‘You have made me happy with a magnificent gift,’ etc. There he testifies that the entire immense work of Augustine on the Psalms, contained in a single volume, had been sent to him through Boccaccio’s kindness, writing from Milan on 11 May.”

The Benedictines arranged for this letter of Petrarch to be reprinted in the same volume, after the indices appended to the prefaces.

[Col. 0120C] At any rate, for the Sermons, in the fifth volume, besides other copies from the Royal Library, there was one remarkable volume, praised by Jacques Sirmond on the occasion of his edition of the Sermons. It contained the first two parts of the *Collectory of Augustinian Sermons*, compiled by Robert de Bardis, Chancellor of Paris.[^c0012-1]

[^c0012-1]: [Col. 0119D] Concerning this *Collectory*, the Benedictines themselves report the following in the preface to the fifth volume: “Robert de Bardis, Chancellor of Paris, had devised in his *Collectory*, as he calls it, of Augustine’s Sermons—never published—a more beautiful and ingenious arrangement of the Sermons than the commonly used one, which they had previously reviewed. He devised it about three hundred years ago, dividing the same Sermons into five parts. In the first part are collected Sermons concerning certain events and saints of the Old Testament. In the second, those concerning the solemnities and saints of the New Testament. In the third, those concerning sayings and writings of the Old Testament. In the fourth, those concerning sayings and writings of the New Testament. In the fifth, [Col. 0120D] those concerning the adornments and impediments of the Church, or of the faithful, and concerning the final rewards of the good and the wicked. One manuscript is preserved in the Royal Library containing the first two parts of this collection; and two in the Colbert Library, in which the index of the Sermons of all five parts is reproduced. Nevertheless, although Sirmond states in the preface to his forty Sermons that, in reviewing and approving Augustine’s works, ‘Robert’s judgment is by no means to be despised,’ they judge that he admitted almost innumerable spurious Sermons, so that, if he were to leave only the genuine ones in the first part of the *Collectory*, he would reduce it almost to nothing, etc.”

Moreover, not a few—indeed, almost all—the books of the sixth volume were corrected from the same sources; one of them, used for the book *Against Lying*, is thought to be nine hundred years old.

For reviewing the books *On the City of God*, two copies were available. Likewise, two were available for the book *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, in the seventh volume.

Finally, one was used in the tenth volume for the books *On Grace and Free Will*, *On Rebuke and [Col. 0120D] Grace*, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, and *On the Gift of Perseverance*.

**The Regiomontanus manuscript.** From this, with only a few exceptions, [Col. 0121A] all the books of the first volume were examined. It is also cited in the sixth volume for the book *On Lying*.

**The manuscript of the abbey of S. Martin at Sées.** Against it the books *On the Sermon on the Mount* were reviewed in the third volume; the book *Against Lying* and *On the Work of Monks* in the sixth; the books *Against Faustus* and *Against the Sermon of the Arians* in the eighth; and the books *On the Soul and Its Origin* in the tenth.

**The Sergianus**, that is, the book of S. Sergius of Angers, is cited in the first volume for the books *On the Quantity of the Soul* and *On Free Will*, for the unfinished exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians, and for the book *On Christian Combat*.

**The Sigiramnensis codex**, that is, the codex of the abbey of S. Cygiranus, or *Cygirannensis*. It is noted in the books *On the Good of Widowhood* and *Against Lying* in the sixth volume; for the books *On the [Col. 0121B] City of God* in the seventh; for the book addressed to Orosius *Against the Priscillianists* in the eighth; for the books *Against the Letters of Petilian*, *Against Cresconius*, and *On One Baptism* in the ninth; and likewise for the books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, *On Nature and Grace*, *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, *On the Grace of Christ* and *Original Sin*, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, and *On the Soul and Its Origin* in the tenth.

**The Silvamajorensis codex.** It is mentioned in connection with the books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* in the third volume.

A copy from the church of **Senlis** supplied the *Epistles* and the books *On the City of God*.

**The Sorbonici.** Sometimes one, sometimes two, and even three were repeatedly used for almost every book contained in the [Col. 0121C] first volume. The *Epistles* in the second volume, the books *On Questions of the Gospels* in the third, and the *Sermons* in the fifth were examined against the same copies; and in the sixth volume scarcely three or four books can be counted that were not corrected from them. In the eighth volume a Sorbonicus codex is praised for the book *Against Adimantus*, *Against the Epistle of the Manichaeans*, *On the Nature of the Good*, *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, the book addressed to Orosius *Against the Priscillianists*, *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, and *Against Maximinus*. The books *On the Trinity* were reviewed against five Sorbonici. Finally, in the tenth volume scarcely four books out of the whole number were not corrected from at least one Sorbonicus.

One book of the abbey of B. Mary at **Soissons** proved useful for reviewing the books *On the City of God*.

[Col. 0121D] **Codices of the Tellerian Library.** Approximately two are very frequently cited in the review of the *Epistles*.

**The Theodoricus books**, that is, those of the abbey of S. Thierry near Rheims. They cite one Theodoricus, formerly belonging to Hincmar of Rheims, for the *Retractations*. I do not know whether it is the same one that is also mentioned in the first volume for the books *Against the Academics*, *On Order*, *On Genesis Against the Manichaeans*, and *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*. It is repeatedly called of the highest quality and, for the books *On Order*, approximately nine hundred years old—a date that agrees with the age of Hincmar. The *Epistles* were reviewed against the same copies. A very old and excellent manuscript is cited for the *Treatises on the First Epistle of John* in the third volume; in the *Expositions on the Psalms*, however, they used books [Col. 0122A] of this library of somewhat more recent date. The Theodorici were also available for the *Sermons*; in the eighth volume, however, only the books *On the Trinity* received assistance from this source.

**Books of the Thuane Library.** The books of the *Confessions* were reviewed against a Thuaneus of seven or eight hundred years. It is perhaps the same one against which, in the same volume, the books *On the Blessed Life*, the *Soliloquies*, *On Free Will*, *On True Religion*, and the *Rule for the Servants of God* were collated. The books *On Order* had the benefit of two copies. In the third volume, a Thuaneus is cited for the *Exposition of Certain Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans*, and also in the unfinished *Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians*.

The **Valiensis** book is mentioned for the *Confessions*.

**The Vedastini**, that is, the books of the abbey of S. Vedastus at Arras. [Col. 0122B] A Vedastinus codex is praised in the first volume for the books *Retractations*, *Confessions*, *On the Blessed Life*, *On Order*, the *Soliloquies*, *On the Immortality of the Soul*, and *On Genesis Against the Manichaeans*; and likewise for the *Epistles* in the second volume.

**The Victorini**, or the codices of the abbey of S. Victor in Paris. Three were available for correcting the books *Retractations*, *Confessions*, *On Order*, *On the Teacher*, *On the Quantity of the Soul*, and *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*; two for the books *Against the Academics*, *On the Immortality of the Soul*, *On Genesis Against the Manichaeans*, and *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*; and one for the remainder of the first volume, with a few exceptions.

They also assisted in correcting the *Epistles* and *Sermons* in the second and fifth volumes, as well as the books *Questions on the Gospels* and *Seventeen Questions on [Col. 0122C] Matthew* in the third volume; likewise the books *On Various Questions to Simplicianus*, *On the Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, *On Faith and the Creed*, *On Christian Combat*, *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, *On the Good of Widowhood*, *On Lying*, *Against Lying*, *On the Work of Monks*, *On Care for the Dead*, and *On Patience*.

Similarly, in the eighth volume, the books *On Heresies*, *Against the Jews*, *On the Usefulness of Believing*, *On Two Souls*, *Against Fortunatus*, *Against Adimantus*, *Against the Epistle of the Manichaeans*, *Against Faustus*, the *Acts with Felix*, *On the Nature of the Good*, the book addressed to Orosius *Against the Priscillianists*, and one or two Victorini were examined; likewise the book *On One Baptism* in the ninth volume; and *On the Grace of Christ*, *On Original Sin*, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, and the six books *Against Julian* in the tenth.

[Col. 0122D] **Books of the abbey of Vendôme.** The books *Soliloquies*, *On the Immortality of the Soul*, and *On the Quantity of the Soul* in the first volume were corrected from one copy; likewise the *Epistles* in the second volume, the *Expositions on the Psalms* in the fourth, and the *Sermons* in the fifth. One was also used for the books *On the City of God* in the seventh volume. In the third volume, the books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* and *On the Sermon on the Mount* were collated with one copy; the *Treatises on the Epistle of John* with one; and the *Treatises on the Gospel of John* with two. In the sixth volume, the books *On Christian Combat* and *On Patience* were collated; in the eighth, the books *Against Faustus* and *On the Trinity*.

**Uticensis**, see **Ebrulphensis**.

### b) Italian codices

**The Vatican codices**, namely, the [Col. 0123A] variant readings formerly collected by selected scholars who, after the Louvain edition, had again undertaken the correction of St. Augustine’s works under the authority of Clement VIII, and which had been communicated to the Benedictines.

In general, the *Epistles* were reviewed against several of them; five were used for the books *On the City of God*, and one for the *Expositions on the Psalms*, covering the first forty-nine Psalms. Then, with one exception, all the books of the first volume were collated with some Vatican codex; the *Rule for the Servants of God* with two. Similarly, in the third volume scarcely three books are to be found that were not corrected against these codices; the books *On the Sermon on the Mount* against two; and the books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* against four.

In the sixth volume, likewise, sometimes two, usually three, and even four or five were [Col. 0123B] available. Similarly, in the eighth volume there are only two books to which no assistance came from these sources; other books were compared with two, four, five, or six, as in the books *Against Faustus*. They even record that eleven copies were used for the books *On the Trinity*.

They contributed less to the ninth volume: only two assisted with the books *Against the Epistle of Parmenianus* and the seven books *On Baptism*, while one was collated with the book *On One Baptism*. But in the tenth volume, if two are excluded, the individual books were not infrequently reviewed against four or five Vatican copies.

**The Christianeani codices**, as they are called—that is, the manuscripts of Christina, Queen of Sweden—should perhaps be counted among the Vatican codices. For if they did not yet belong to the Vatican Library at that time, they were certainly transferred there afterward. [Col. 0123C] But there is this further distinction between them and the others: the Vatican codices, as the Maurist Fathers call them, had been collated more than a hundred years earlier, whereas these were consulted only now and, as it seems to me, used directly by the Fathers themselves.

They cite one in the first volume for the book *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, which perhaps also contained part of the *Expositions on the Psalms*. For this work two copies were available: one containing seventeen of the earlier Psalms, namely XXXIV–L; the other containing the remaining thirty-two, from CXIX to CL.

The **Roman codex** of Augustine’s book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, whose variant readings Marcus Welser had noted in the margin of his own book.

The **Florentine codices**, that is, three manuscripts preserved in the Ducal [Col. 0123D] Library at Florence, whose variant readings they used in the same book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*.

### c) English codices

After the entire edition had been completed, variant readings from approximately eight codices in England were sent by E. Bernard, professor of astronomy at Oxford. From these, several corrections were transferred only into the second edition of the first volume, to which alone they pertain. Three were from the Bodleian Library, two from Merton College, one from the Laudian Archive, and two from Canterbury.[^c0012-2]

[^c0012-2]: [Col. 0123] Thus I interpret the abbreviation *Cant.* The first six were used for the books of the *Retractations*; four for the [Col. 0124A] *Confessions*, namely one Bodleian and Laudian copy and two Merton copies; five for the books of the *Soliloquies*, namely one Bodleian, two Merton, and two Canterbury copies.

This is what can be said about the codices from the indexes that the Benedictine Fathers appended at the end of the genuine writings in each volume, listing the variant readings of the individual books. There is no time to extract from them a few others that they occasionally cite in the notes appended to the text itself or amid the mass of variant readings.

It is nevertheless worthwhile to record also the older printed editions that they used in correcting the individual books, since these printed copies themselves should be regarded almost as manuscripts—manuscripts that the carelessness of those times held in little regard and considered unworthy of remembrance, provided only that the work had once been committed to print.

[Col. 0124B] In the first volume, therefore, the books of the *Retractations* were assisted by the Amerbach edition of 1505 and the first edition of Erasmus; the *Confessions*, besides those same editions, by the Badian edition—by which name are meant the small works that Jodocus Badius had printed through Jean Petit in 1520—and by the Arnaldine version, which appeared in 1649 after being reviewed against twelve manuscript codices.

Against the preceding three editions, the books *Against the Academics*, *On the Blessed Life*, *On Order*, *On the Immortality of the Soul*, and *On the Teacher* were additionally reviewed. Against the Badian and Erasmus editions alone, the books *Soliloquies*, *On the Quantity of the Soul*, and *On Free Will*; against the Badian, Erasmus, and later Arnaldine editions, the books *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, and *On True Religion*; against the Amerbach and Erasmus editions, the books *On Music*, *On Genesis Against the Manichaeans*, and the *Rule for the Servants [Col. 0124C] of God*.

In the second volume, the following editions of the *Epistles* are cited: the Amerbach edition of 1493, in folio; the Badian edition, Paris, 1515; and the Erasmus edition, Basel, Froben, 1528.

In the third volume, for the books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, they noted an edition of Jodocus Badius, which he had printed at Lyon in 1497 from the recension of Augustine of Regensburg, and the Erasmus edition of 1528. For the books *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, besides the Erasmus and Amerbach editions of 1506, they used the edition of Jacques Mareschal, Lyon, 1520. For the books *Questions on the Gospels* and *Seventeen Questions on Matthew*, they used the same Badian edition, as well as Erasmus and Amerbach; for the *Treatises on the Gospel of John*, Badius and Erasmus; for the *Treatises on the [Col. 0124D] Epistle of John*, Amerbach, Badius, and Erasmus; and for the *Exposition of Certain Propositions in the Epistles to the Romans and Galatians*, as well as the unfinished *Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans*—which was not found in the Gallican manuscripts and was corrected with the help of one Vatican copy—Amerbach and Erasmus.

In the fourth volume, for the *Expositions on the Psalms*, the Basel edition printed by Johann Amerbach in 1489 and the Erasmus edition of 1529 were available.

For correcting the *Sermons* in the fifth volume, they used the Amerbach editions of 1494 and 1495, the Erasmus edition of 1571, the Sirmond edition of 1631, and the second edition of the Vignier Supplement, 1655.

[Col. 0125A] In the sixth volume, for the book *On Eighty-Three Various Questions*, they consulted the Lyon edition printed under the care of Augustine of Regensburg by Johann Trechsel in 1497, and the Erasmus edition of 1528. For the books *On Various Questions*, *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, and *On Faith and Works*, they used Amerbach and Erasmus; for the book *On the Eight Questions of Dulcitius* and *On Faith and the Creed*, those same editions and the previously mentioned Lyon edition; for the *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Charity*, besides the Amerbach and Erasmus editions, those of Laubertus Danaeus and Antoine Arnauld; and finally, for the book *On Christian Combat*, besides Amerbach and Erasmus, the edition of Jean Petit, 1513.

The books *On the City of God* in the seventh volume were reviewed against the Venetian edition of Vindelinus of 1470, Amerbach’s edition of 1490, and Erasmus’s edition of 1529.

[Col. 0125B] Finally, the Amerbach and Erasmus editions were used throughout the eighth, ninth, and tenth volumes as well.

This list of printed books also shows that the Roman, Venetian, and other more important editions of Augustine’s individual works—editions which, had they wished to use them, they could not have lacked—were neglected by the Benedictine Fathers, except for one edition of *The City of God*.

## SECOND ARTICLE

### Annals of the editions of Augustine’s individual books

#### § I. Genuine books

##### (1) *Against the Academics* [Col. 0125C]

These books were never published separately. Nevertheless, they generally occupy the first place in several ancient collections of Augustine’s minor works, which will be mentioned below. They were translated into French according to the Benedictine edition by Villefort.

**1703.** Paris, chez Élie Josset; duodecimo. “The books of St. Augustine against the Academic philosophers, together with the treatise *On Grace and Free Will*, translated into French from the edition of the Benedictine Fathers by M. Villeford or Villefort.” *Catalogue of the Royal Library*. See also the *Journal des Savants*, 1703, p. 221.

##### II. (3) Two books *On Order*

They were never printed separately in Latin, but Villefort translated them into French together with the books *On Free Will* and *On Christian Doctrine*, each of which will be discussed in its proper place.

##### III. (4) Two books of the *Soliloquies*

[Col. 0125D] We have been able to find only one Latin edition of these books, and that the oldest. For most publications bearing this title concern spurious works and will be mentioned below. The edition in question is as follows.

**Without year, place, or printer; in folio.** *St. Augustine’s Two Books of the Soliloquies.*

The volume consists of twenty-three leaves, printed in broad type, thirty-five lines to a page. It begins with the words:

> Here begins, happily, the first book of the *Soliloquy* of Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo.

Similar words appear at the beginning of the second book on folio 11. At the end of the first book: “Aurelius, etc., ends.” But at the end of the second, which falls on the first page of folio 23, there is no formula whatsoever.

[Col. 0126A] The letters are Gothic, short and thick. Although many abbreviations of words and signs for letters are scattered throughout, they are nevertheless by no means unpleasant to the eye. It is usually attributed to Günther Zainer, an Augsburg printer who, from 1468 onward, devoted approximately ten years to printing books there.

Certainly, among numerous minor works both of Augustine and of other authors that closely resemble these books, and that are not infrequently contained in the same volume with them—works that plainly declare themselves to belong to one and the same family—there occurs [Col. 0126B] an edition of Thomas à Kempis’s *Imitation of Christ* bearing the colophon:

> Printed by Gintheus [sic] Zainer, born at Reutlingen, with borrowed type.

From this, men highly experienced in these matters draw a not implausible inference concerning the other books. See the works by Jerome that we cited on the occasion of certain similar minor writings, volume I, p. 488. Recently the distinguished Braun also revisited this edition in his *Historical and Literary Notices* (1788), p. 38.

##### IV. (7) *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*

There are two French versions of this work by the same translators who translated the book *On True Religion*. See that work.

##### V. (9) *On the Quantity of the Soul*

**Without year, place, or printer; in folio.** *St. Augustine’s book On the Quantity of the Soul.*

“We shall discuss more fully the type and every [Col. 0126C] aspect of the description of this volume in connection with the books of the *Soliloquies* issued from the same workshop. For the present we shall note only that it consists of [Col. 0126C] twenty-nine leaves and is usually found bound together with one or more printed books of the same kind, in which an unequal number of leaves is likewise found. From this it clearly follows that all these works were printed continuously and in one series.”

So Braun writes in his *Historical and Literary Notices*, p. 38. Bound in our copy are the two books of the *Soliloquies*, the *Mirror of the Sinner*, *On the Quantity of the Soul*, and the *Soliloquy on the Soul’s Earnest*.

It begins at the top of the page with the title:

> Here begins happily Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, *On the Quantity of the Soul*.

It ends at the bottom of the final leaf:

> Here ends Aurelius Augustine’s book *On the Quantity of the Soul*.

A learned Sicilian, at the end [Col. 0126D] of the last century, extensively explained the structure and entire character of this Augustinian book and composed almost a commentary upon it in the following work:

> *The Nature of the Human Soul Discovered by Augustine in the Books On the Quantity of the Soul, the Tenth Book On the Trinity, and On the Immortality of the Soul, explained by Michael Angelo Fardella of Trapani, Doctor of Sacred Theology and Professor of Astronomy and Meteorology at the Paduan Lyceum, and dedicated to the most eminent Henry Noris, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.* Venice, at the expense of Girolamo Albrizzi, 1698; in folio.

Its contents are described in *Acta Eruditorum*, Supplement III, pp. 302–307. A shorter account appears in the *Cologne Ecclesiastical Library*, [Col. 0127A] pp. 729 ff. The author himself again outlined the idea of his work in a letter inserted in the *Italian Journal*, *Giornale di Minerva*, volume III, part I, p. 29, Venice, at Albrizzi’s, 1700, in folio, under the following title:

> *Letter to the Most Illustrious and Most Learned Signor Antonio Magliabecchi, Librarian of His Most Serene Highness the Grand Duke of Tuscany, containing the subject and plan of his work recently printed under the title The Nature of the Human Soul Discovered by Augustine, etc.*

This is reported by Antonio Mongitore in the *Sicilian Library*, volume II, p. 71.[^c0012-3]

[^c0012-3]: [Col. 0127D] The author of the *Sicilian Library* was not examined carefully enough by the author of this article in the *Cologne Ecclesiastical Library*, when he imagined two editions of this letter, one separately in 1700 at Venice in folio and the other in the aforementioned *Journal*. Rather, in that same year and place, and in that format, a third volume of that *Journal* was published. [Col. 0128D]

##### VI. (10) Three books *On Free Will*

**1524.** Basel, octavo. *St. Augustine On Free Will, three books.* The scholars of Cologne cite it on the authority of the *Catalogue of the Utrecht Library*, part II, p. 59.
