[Col. 0127B] **1568.** Cologne, duodecimo. The same books reduced to the form of an *Enchiridion*. Also, his one book *On Predestination and Grace*. Cited by Possevinus, *Appendix*, p. 154, and Hendreich, *Brandenburg Pandects*, p. 341. See the book *On Grace*.

Villefort translated it into French together with the books *On Christian Doctrine*.

##### VII. (13) *On True Religion*

The scholars of Cologne cite a separate edition of this book, printed at Venice in 1484, in quarto; but they are mistaken. For the copy they saw was nothing more than the final portion of the *Minor Works* printed there. This could be conjectured from the colophon placed at the end.

**Translations.**

We have already briefly mentioned two French translations of this work. They appeared as follows:

[Col. 0127C] **1647.** Paris, chez Antoine Vitré; octavo.

> *The book of St. Augustine, On True Religion, translated into French, with the Latin following it, carefully revised; by Antoine Arnauld, Doctor of the Sorbonne.*

It was reprinted at Brussels in 1675. In the preface, Arnauld states that he corrected errors he had observed in the Louvain theologians with the help of older editions and several manuscript codices. See the *Great Cologne Library* and Antoine Arnauld. It appeared again in 1652 and 1657. I do not know, however, which book comes first in the volume and which second, for bibliographers report it in both arrangements.

**1690.** Paris, chez the widow of Jean-Baptiste Coignard; octavo.

> *The two books of St. Augustine, On True Religion and On the Morals of the Church, translated into French from the Latin edition of the Benedictine Fathers, with notes and new summaries of the chapters; by Philippe Goibaud du Bois.*

##### VIII. (14) *On the Usefulness of Believing*

[Col. 0127D] **1602.** Mainz. *St. Augustine’s book On the Usefulness of Believing, addressed to Honoratus, illustrated with arguments, notes, and analysis by Justus Calvinus.* It appears from p. 423 onward in his *Treatise on Prescriptions against Heretics*, published under the fictitious name Justus Baronius. I find the same book cited in the *Catalogue of the Bodleian Library* in 1605.

[Col. 0128A] **1680.** Leuven, printed by Hieronymus Nempaeus; duodecimo. *One book of St. Augustine addressed to Honoratus, On the Usefulness of Believing; and his little book On Catechizing the Uninstructed.* *Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.*

##### IX. (19) *On Christ’s Sermon on the Mount*

**1683.** Paris, chez André Pralard; duodecimo.

> *St. Augustine’s Commentaries on the Sermon of Our Lord on the Mountain, containing all the rules of Christian morality, translated into French by Pierre Lombert.*

Each chapter is supplied with an outline. See the *Journal des Savants*, 1683, no. XXIII, p. 273.

**1767.** Mantua, octavo.

> *The two books of St. Augustine explaining the Redeemer’s Discourse to His Disciples on the Mountain, etc., translated into Italian, with notes by Fr. Augustine Nicolo Bianchi.*

*Catalogue of the Firmian Library.*

[Col. 0128B] The scholars of Cologne refer to Richard Simon’s discussion of these books in his *Critical History of the New Testament Commentaries*, chapter 17. They do not, however, mention the observations made by Bayle on this book, which they cite from his *Dictionary* under the entry “Septimius Acindynus”; but that entry simply recounts the little story that Augustine says occurred at Antioch in the time of Constantius, under Acindynus as prefect, in chapter 50 of book I.

##### X. (23, 24, 25) Augustine on the Epistles of Paul

**1499.** Paris, printed by Ulrich Hering and Berthold Rembolt.

> [Col. 0128C] *A new and hitherto hidden interpretation by the divine Augustine of the sacred Epistles of Paul, collected with extraordinary diligence and the utmost labor by the venerable Bede from countless copies of Augustine’s works. Here one can hardly decide what ought first to be admired: the divine genius of the interpreter, or Bede’s singular skill alike in excerpting and polishing. However the matter may stand, you will find there an abyss of learning. Moreover, the printers arranged to add to the aforesaid interpretation seven golden homilies of Chrysostom, so that the diligent reader may readily recognize, with little labor but no small profit, the most illustrious praises, qualities, and proclamations of Paul.*

This is the title, together with a notable Rembolt device and an epigram printed in commendation of the work. At the end of the *Commentaries on the Epistle to the Hebrews*, after an epilogue again expressing the substance of the work in these words:

> The present work, for the glory of almighty God and the salutary instruction of the faithful, was printed through the labor and expense of Ulrich Hering and Master Berthold Rembolt, partners, in Paris, at the Golden Sun in the Sorbonne quarter, in the year [Col. 0128D] of the Lord’s Incarnation 1499, on 28 November.

It is preceded by a very extensive alphabetical index of subjects and words, beginning immediately on the verso of the title page, and by prefaces of Gaufridus Boussard, the least of the theologians, addressed to Peter Securabilis, interpreter of sacred Scripture and archdeacon of Rouen, and to all studious men and lovers of letters, concerning the following work of Bede and Augustine and Jerome’s work on all the Epistles of Paul.

[Col. 0129A] It seemed worthwhile to mention this old edition of the excerpts of Florus of Lyon, not only because we have learned that it was known to very few, but especially because the manuscript codices of this collection were not infrequently consulted with benefit by the Maurist Fathers.

The work praised by the scholars of Cologne concerns the Epistle to the Romans:

> *Augustine, the apostolic-Roman-Catholic interpreter of Paul to the Romans, or The Way of Truth and Life, demonstrated most recently and clearly through the genuine interpretation of St. Augustine on the Epistle to the Romans and through various theological-polemical deductions against atheists, pagans, Jews, Muslims, heretics, and all unbelievers, by Bartholomew Fibus of the Society of Jesus, Doctor of Sacred Theology.* Cologne, 1696, in folio.

##### XI. (27) *On Continence*

[Col. 0129B] A French version of this book is mentioned below under no. XVII.

##### XII. (29) Two books *On Various Questions*

They were published in the collection of Augustine’s *Questions*, Lyon, 1497, in folio; see it among his minor works.

##### XIII. (32) *On Christian Doctrine*

**Fifteenth century.** Without year or place, in folio. *St. Augustine, bishop, four books On Christian Doctrine.* Georg Pray records it in his *Index of Rare Books of the Buda Library*, calling it a very old type. He correctly inferred this from the absence of page numbers, signatures, and other marks. He adds that each sentence is separated by a single point, that the letter *i* everywhere appears with a tail, and so forth. He further notes that the initials in his copy were illuminated.

[Col. 0129C] The type of this volume is so crude that the scholar just mentioned stated that the letters resembled wooden letters more than letters cast in metal. What is much more worthy of mention is that he observed a notable divergence between this volume and the other editions of this book generally regarded as superior, and he supplied several specimens taken from the beginning and end of the books, which we too have thought should not be omitted.

Thus the beginning of book I runs as follows:

> I had divided this work of ours, entitled *On Christian Doctrine*, into two parts in my first arrangement. For, after the prologue in which I answered those who were going to criticize this work, there are, I say, two things upon which the whole treatment of Scripture rests: the method of discovering what is to be understood, and the method of presenting what has been understood. We shall discuss discovery first and presentation afterward. Since, therefore, we have already said much about discovery and, with the Lord’s help, have completed three volumes on this one part, we shall say a little about presentation, so that, if it can be done, we may close everything in one book and bring the whole work to an end in four volumes.

[Col. 0129D] The end of book IV is as follows:

> This book has become longer than I wished and than I had thought. … Nevertheless, I give thanks to our Lord Jesus Christ that in these four books I have discussed, with whatever small ability I possessed, not what I am like, lacking much, but what one who labors in sound doctrine ought to be like—one who strives to labor not only for himself but also for others. Here ends the fourth book of blessed Augustine, bishop, *On Christian Doctrine*.

[Col. 0130A] **Without year or place, large octavo.** *Blessed Augustine’s book On Christian Doctrine, divided into four parts.* It begins immediately with the prologue of the first book. At the end:

> The distinguished work of Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, on Christian doctrine, divided into four books, useful in every way for understanding the Scriptures and for presenting them in the order proper to a Catholic teacher, is finished. Thanks be to God.

The volume is printed in handsome Gothic type [Col. 0130B] on clean, heavy paper. The book number is marked in the upper margin and the sheet number in the lower; catchwords and folio numbers are absent.

**Without year or place [Strasbourg, at the workshop of Johann Mentelin]; in folio.** *Augustine’s book On the Art of Preaching*—which is the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine*.

An anonymous editor, judging that this book would be highly useful to preachers [Col. 0130B] and observing that, because of the size of the entire work, it was scarcely known to a few people, wished to benefit the studies of others by having it printed separately from the rest of the work. He also devoted substantial effort, if he is to be believed, to correcting and emending it from several copies. We consider his own words on the matter worthy of preservation. They run as follows:

> I therefore, with God as my witness, took great care over its correction, so that I carefully examined all the copies that I was able to find in the libraries of Heidelberg, Speyer, and Worms, and finally [Col. 0130C] also in Strasbourg. And when, in the course of this investigation, I learned by experience that Augustine’s same book is rarely found even in large and valuable libraries, and still more rarely can any copy from those libraries be obtained for rewriting; and, what is worse, that it can very rarely be found there corrected or emended, I was moved to work diligently at this, so that, according to my copy, this little book—corrected with as much zeal and labor as I was at least able to devote to it—might in a short time be multiplied in such a way that it could easily and quickly reach the use of many and every ecclesiastical benefit. Therefore, since I judged that this could be accomplished more expeditiously by no other means, I persuaded in every possible way the discreet man Johann Mentelin, a citizen of Strasbourg and master of the printing art, to undertake the burden and labor [Col. 0130D] of multiplying this little book by printing it, with my copy before his eyes, etc.

This preface bears the title:

> A canon for recommending this famous work, or following little book, *On the Art of Preaching* by St. Augustine.

The printed volume consists of twenty-one leaves, in small, blunt Gothic type unpleasant to the eye, with broad lines, thirty-nine to a page. All signatures and folio or page numbers of every kind are absent. The first and last pages were left blank, and a well-equipped index of notable subjects is added separately in two quires.

The index is arranged according to the letters by which the otherwise continuous text is divided into numerous sections in alphabetical order (A–LL). The letters are inserted within the lines at the beginning of each section. Hence the editor [Col. 0131A] says in his preface:

> Capital letters, both single and doubled, are interspersed throughout the work. They serve for the alphabetical table of the same little book, placed at the end. This table refers back to the same letters by means of individual points. Anyone who wishes may easily mark them with a pen in his own hand, even in the margins, in black or red ink, corresponding to the letters placed within the text. This will be quite useful, because the letters placed in the margin will appear more quickly to someone making a search. Thus, through the table’s references to those same letters, each of the contents of this little book can quickly be found whenever desired.

[Col. 0131B] This edition has been examined by the most learned bibliographers, the distinguished Morel in the *Pinelli Library*, volume I, pp. 87 ff., and Placidus Braun in the *Historical and Literary Notice of Books Printed from the Invention of the Art of Printing to the Year 1479 in the Monastery Library of S. Ulrich and S. Afra at Augsburg*, p. 3.

### [Mainz, by Jo. Fust.] Folio

The same book, faithfully reproduced from the preceding edition, so that in the printer’s prefatory notice only the name has been changed, and here one reads: “Having been persuaded in every way by the discreet Johann Fust, a native of Mainz and master of the printing art, etc.” In other respects, this volume consists of 22 leaves: the first two are occupied by the preface; thereafter the text extends to the middle of leaf 17; then follows the table of contents; and finally, on two leaves—the first printed on the verso, the second on the recto—two brief treatises close the volume: *On the Three Principal Works of the Preacher* and *On the Three Kinds of Speech Which a Preacher Ought to Use*. See more in Debure, [Col. 0131C] *Catalogue of the Library of the Duke de la Vallière*, vol. I, p. 174. The same edition is incidentally mentioned in the *Catalogue of the Bunau Library*. Compare the *Mémoires de Trévoux*, 1765, June, p. 1454, and the distinguished Steigenberger, in the place cited, p. 47.

As for the date of this and the preceding edition, Debure has already observed that the Fust edition must have been printed either in the year 1466 itself or earlier, since it is established that Johann Fust ceased practicing his craft after that year. Which of the two is older—this one or the Strasbourg edition—Morellus doubts; Gerhard Steigenberger is less hesitant to assign first place to the Strasbourg edition. He is led to this, first, by the argument of the two brief works by which the Mainz edition is richer than the Strasbourg one: he thinks that these were added anew to the former rather than omitted from the latter; and, secondly, because the preface [Col. 0131D] of the Mainz edition is four lines longer—a new observation of his. To these we add a third consideration: the letters by which the text is divided into sections are not, in the Mainz edition, scattered through the middle of the lines, but are visibly placed in the inner margin; from this I seem to discern some progress in the art. I should now like some learned man who has access to the Fust edition to examine the preface and attend particularly to whether the same words occur there as in the Strasbourg edition concerning the letters’ being drawn with a pen in the margin by private effort. If he should nevertheless discover that this was done, negligence must not have been so uncommon in editions of that period.

---

### [There], by the same printer; folio

The same work of the same edition, very similar to the preceding one, though not identical in every respect. Morellus testifies that he saw it at the house of a certain friend, in the place cited, p. 9; and the distinguished Gerhoh Steigenberger discovered it in the library of the Canons Regular at Rottenbuch, in his treatise *On the Two Oldest Printed German Bibles* (Munich, 1787, quarto), p. 48.

## Sixteenth Century

### 1527

Cologne, at the press of Heron Alopecius, at the expense of Godefridus Hittorpius, in July; octavo. *The four books of Aurelius Augustine, On Christian Doctrine*, exceedingly useful and necessary for all who wish either rightly to understand sacred Scripture or fruitfully to expound it to the people.

### 1534

Venice, by Joannes Patavinus and Venturinus de Ruffinellis; octavo. *The four books of Aurelius Augustine, On Christian Doctrine*, etc., as in the preceding edition.

### Without year

Cologne, octavo. *Saint Augustine, On Christian Doctrine*. Catalogue of the Library of Saint Augustine at the Nidum in Naples.

## Seventeenth Century

### 1601

Antwerp, octavo. The Cologne edition is praised.

### 1604

Wittenberg, from the Cratonian press; octavo. *Saint Aurelius Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, book IV*. Compare the preface of Salomon Gesner. Compare the *M. Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica Coloniensis* and the Catalogue of the Thott Library.

### 1629

Helmstedt, at the Julia Academy, but printed at the Calixtine press by Henningus Mullerus; octavo. *Of the holy Father and Doctor Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, the four books On Christian Doctrine; one book On Faith and the Creed; and the Commonitory of Vincent of Lérins*. Georgius Calixtus revised and edited them.

That highly renowned theologian, when an opportunity arose—which he could scarcely refuse—to purchase Greek and Latin type together with a press and the other tools necessary for practicing the printing art, had established a proper workshop in his home. From it, both for his own pleasure and as relaxation from more serious studies, and for the benefit of students whose means at home were limited, with the approval of the prince of Brunswick, he issued from that year onward a number of useful little books, among them these first volumes of Augustine and Vincent.

He explained the purpose of this undertaking more fully in the letter prefixed to these works and addressed to Petrus Tuckermannus, Doctor of Theology, chief ecclesiastical officer of the court and territory of Brunswick, and abbot of Riddagshausen. As for the plan behind publishing these books, he set it out in the following preface to the reader, in such a way that he both disclosed and commended their entire character and arrangement. [Col. 0132D] Nor could he protect himself from being disparaged by many religious people of that time because of Vincent’s commendation of the doctrine of ecclesiastical tradition. Since he saw that several leaves would remain unused at the end of the book, he decided to print upon them the third letter of Pacianus to his brother Sympronianus.

### 1643

Venice, quarto. *Saint Augustine, On Ecclesiastical Rhetoric* (that is, book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*). It appears in *Authors of Good Speaking*, vol. XII, final part, p. 57.

### 1655

Helmstedt, from the Calixtine press, produced by Henningus Mullerus, quarto. “Aurelius Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, four books, etc. Georgius Calixtus revised and edited it. The first edition appeared in the year 1629; now a second follows in the year 1655.” This second edition included, under the title *Admonition to the Reader*, Calixtus’s dissertation on the Symbols and Confessions of the ancient Christians; the injustice of the times lent it considerable importance.

## Eighteenth Century

### 1769

Leipzig, at the expense of Joannes Fridericus Langenhemius; octavo. *The four books of Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, On Christian Doctrine*, from the recension of the Benedictines of the Congregation of Saint Maur. It was illustrated with variant readings and brief notes, and published with a preface by S. R. Johann Friderich Burscher, Doctor of Theology and Ordinary Public Professor, etc., by Johann Christian Benjamin Teegius, of the Third College of Sangerhausen.

The elegance of this description is enhanced by the remarkable commendation deserved by the cleanliness of the paper and type, which makes one wish that more copies of the best Greek and Latin ecclesiastical Fathers’ writings, prepared with equal care and printed with equal brilliance, might be offered for sale. The Leipzig theologian, acting as interpreter of the task undertaken by the editor, relieved him of the need to write a preface. Teegius followed the Benedictine text as reproduced in Clericus’s Antwerp reprint, collated with the variants of the Amerbach edition and of the 1569 Erasmus edition, as well as with both Helmstedt editions. The divisions of these editions and of the Benedictine recension are conveniently marked by different numbers, and a not inconsiderable index has also been added.

## Versions

There are two French versions, one by Colletet and the other by Villefort, and one German version by Hedio, which we discussed above in the collections. [Col. 0133C]

### 1636

Paris, at the house of Jean Camusat, duodecimo. “The *Christian Doctrine of Saint Augustine*, divided into four books, with the manual addressed to Laurentius, all translated into French by Guillaume Colletet.”

### 1701

Paris, at the house of Jean-Baptiste Coignard, octavo, two volumes. “The books of Saint Augustine’s *Christian Doctrine* and the books *On Order* and *On Free Will*, by the same author. Translated into French from the new Latin edition of the Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur.”

The author is Monsieur de Villefort, who translated several of Augustine’s books into French with notable distinction. Concerning this translation, the authors of the *Journal des Savants* of Paris, 1702, p. 195, testify as follows:

> “The subjects treated by Saint Augustine in these three works, and especially in the book *On Order*, being abstract, were very difficult to translate in an intelligible and agreeable manner. Yet this is what Monsieur de Villefort has done. By rendering his author’s meaning exactly and adhering to purity of expression, he found a way to equal the beauty and freedom of the Original.”

It should further be noted that each of the two volumes of this translation may also be obtained separately, so that the four books *On Christian Doctrine*, as well as the remaining works, constitute separate volumes. Compare the Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris, vol. I, p. 379ff., nos. 724 and 727.

I do not know why this translation is there attributed to Philippe Goibaud du Bois. He was a member of the Paris Academy, who died in 1694, and was by no means without distinction. Nor am I unaware that his name was attached to another spurious translation, namely of the apocryphal book *Soliloquies*, so that the work might sell more readily under this borrowed sign. But the author of the present translation neither concealed nor wished to conceal himself; indeed, he devoted himself most earnestly to winning renown by translating several of Augustine’s books. I therefore now scarcely doubt that the compiler of the Royal Catalogue made an error.

Theodorus Bibliander, bishop of Cella and professor of theology at Zurich, published a *Compendium of Christian Doctrine* excerpted from Augustine’s books: Basel, 1550, octavo, in Lipenius and, from him, in the Cologne bibliographies. Following them, Balthasar Gibert, formerly professor of rhetoric at the Mazarin College, carefully examined the fourth book of this work, which chiefly treats sacred eloquence, and supported at length the proposition that its principles of Christian eloquence are no different from those of civic eloquence, in *Judgments of the Learned on Authors Who Have Treated Rhetoric*, vol. II, pp. 115–135, Paris, 1716. This book was noted in the *Acta Eruditorum* of Leipzig, 1721, p. 257.

# XIV. — (35) The Thirteen Books of Augustine’s *Confessions*

## Fifteenth Century

### 1475

Milan, quarto. *The thirteen books of the Confessions of Saint Aurelius Augustine*. On the recto of the final leaf are printed the following verses with a colophon:

> How joyful a fruit Augustine’s confession bears,  
> This printed page, brother, tells.  
> For good Johannes, supported by German money,  
> Printed this fruitful work at Milan.  
>   
> In the year of the Incarnation of Our Lord 1475,  
> On the twelfth day before the Kalends of August.

The type is round and elegant; there are 26 lines to a page. Numbers, signatures, and catchwords are lacking. Saxius attributes it to Johannes Wurster of Kempten. Compare the Catalogue of the Crevenna Library, latest edition. The Pinelli Library possessed two copies.

### 1482

Without place, octavo minor. *The thirteen books of the Confessions*. The description of the volume and the type are the same as those which we noted in the books *On Christian Doctrine*, printed in a similar format without place or year, except that the book number is absent from the upper margin. It begins with an annotation on certain obscure passages in these books of Augustine; this fills the first page of the leaf, while the first side has been left blank. At the end: “Here ends the thirteenth book of the Confessions of blessed Augustine. In the year of Our Lord 1482, on the eve of Saint Laurence.”

The Venetian edition of 1484, quarto, which the Cologne bibliographers praise, is not an edition of this book alone, but of several brief works; we have described it more fully in its proper place.

### Without year or place

Folio minor. *The books of the Confessions of Blessed Augustine, bishop*. The volume consists of 152 printed leaves. In other copies, as in the one examined by the distinguished Braun, one unprinted leaf precedes them; in our copy that leaf is missing. It begins with the passage “From the book of the Retractions of Saint Augustine, bishop.” The final formula is absent, having been left for the rubricator; the same was done in our copy both at the end of the whole work and at the end of each individual book. Nor are the beginnings of the books separated from the end of the preceding ones by large spaces: only a single line appears, “The book of Saint Augustine . . . begins.”

The type is medium Gothic, somewhat blunt. [Note: [Col. 0135D] Braun says that it is the same type with which the edition of the Letters of this holy Doctor was printed without statement of year or place, so that both must have come from the same workshop.] The pages contain 32 long lines, surrounded by broad margins. The punctuation consists of the point, colon, and question mark. Catchwords, signatures, numbers, and page titles are entirely absent. Debure mentions this most rare book in the Catalogue of the Library of the Duke de la Vallière, vol. I, p. 168; the distinguished Morellus in the *Bibliotheca Pinelliana*, vol. I, p. 90ff.; and recently Placidius Braun again described it in his *Historical and Literary Account* (1788), part II. Braun, moreover, to confirm its remarkable antiquity, observes that in the Tegernsee copy the year 1470 was written in by a calligrapher.

Audiffredus noted another edition of these books, in gatherings of four leaves, without any indication of place, year, printer, or editor, though he considers it Roman and certainly of the fifteenth century, in the Catalogue of the Casanatense Library. Add the Catalogue of the Pinelli Library.

## Sixteenth Century

### 1531

Cologne, octavo. *The thirteen books of Augustine’s Confessions*. Catalogue of the Bern Library, vol. I, p. 15.

### 1563

Louvain, duodecimo. *The thirteen books of the Confessions of Saint Augustine*. Catalogue of the Library of Saint Angelo at the Nidum in Naples.

### 1567

Antwerp, octavo. The same books. Possevinus, *Appendix*, vol. I, p. 154, and from him Hendreich in the *Brandenburg Pandects*, Lipenius, and the *M. Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica Coloniensis*.

### 1568

There, sextodecimo. The same books. Possevinus and, from him, the Cologne bibliographers.

### 1569

Cologne, duodecimo. The same books. Hendreich. I do not know, however, whether this is the same book which the Cologne bibliographers cite from Possevinus: “The thirteen books of the Confessions of Saint Augustine, reduced to an epitome by Johannes Schwayger, in folio; by Schwayger, scholasticus of the college of the Blessed Virgin at Frankfurt, Cologne, at the house of Cholinus.”

### 1573

Louvain, octavo. *The thirteen books of the Confessions of Saint Augustine*. Hendreich.

### 1578

Basel, octavo. *The Confessions of Hilary and Augustine*. The Cologne bibliographers.

### 1581

Würzburg, duodecimo. *The thirteen books of the Confessions of Saint Augustine*. Hendreich.

### 1588

Tours, at the house of Claudius Michaelus, [lacuna]. The same books. Possevinus, *Appendix*, vol. I, p. 154.

## Seventeenth Century

### 1604

Cologne, at the Birckmann press, duodecimo. *The thirteen books of the Confessions of the Lord Aurelius Augustine; his theological confession and concise exposition of the Roman Mass; all corrected from a manuscript codex by the work and study of the Louvain theologians*. Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

### 1606

Lyons, duodecimo. *The thirteen books of Saint Augustine’s Confessions according to the Louvain correction*. Hendreich.

### 1607

Douai, octavo. *The thirteen books of Saint Augustine’s Confessions*, edited by H. Sommalius. Catalogue of the Bodleian Library.

### 1608

Lyons, duodecimo. The same books, from the Louvain recension. Hendreich.

### 1610

There, duodecimo. The same books. Hendreich.

### 1619

Cologne, duodecimo. *The books of Augustine’s Confessions, thirteen*, by H. Sommalius. Catalogue of the British Museum.

### 1628

Douai, sextodecimo. The same books, from the recension of the same editor. Lipenius and the Cologne bibliographers.

### 1629

Cologne, at the house of Cornelius ab Egmond, twenty-fourmo, commonly called duodecimo. *The thirteen books of the Confessions of Aurelius Augustine, corrected against three manuscript copies by the work and study of Henricus Sommalius, S.J.*

### 1630

There, twenty-fourmo. The same books. Hendreich.

Dillingen, octavo. *The first ten books of Saint Augustine’s Confessions, with notes and summaries by Henricus Wagnereck, S.J.* The Cologne bibliographers cite it from Alegambe’s *Bibliotheca Scriptorum Societatis Jesu*.

### 1631

Cologne, octavo. *The thirteen books of Saint Augustine’s Confessions*, by Henricus Sommalius.

### 1632

There, sextodecimo. *The first ten books of Saint Augustine’s Confessions*, by Henricus Wagnereck. The same edition, with the same year and place, occurs in Hendreich. We have supplied the title of the book, since it is certain that Wagnereck published only ten books.

### 1637

Cologne, at the expense of Cornelius ab Egmond and his associates, duodecimo. *The thirteen books of the Confessions of Aurelius Augustine*. Sommalius’s edition.

### 1638

There, duodecimo. The same books. Hendreich.

### 1640

There, octavo. The same books. Hendreich.

### 1645

Lyons, at the house of Simon Rigaud, sextodecimo, commonly called duodecimo. The same Sommalian recension.

### 1646

Cologne, at the house of Jodocus Kalcovius and his associates, duodecimo. *The ten books of Aurelius Augustine’s Confessions, with notes by the Reverend Father Henricus Wagnereck, S.J.* A practical application is supplied after each chapter. This edition is in some sense connected with, and is bound together with, the copy in our hands, which bears the title: *The Simple and Humble Confession of the Penitent, with a Sermon on Saint Augustine*. The same place and printer.

### 1647

There, the same ten books, by the same editor. Hendreich.

### 1649

Cologne, at the expense of Egmond, sextodecimo or twenty-fourmo. *The thirteen books of the Confessions of Aurelius Augustine*, by Sommalius.

### 1650

Antwerp, from the Plantinian press of Balthasar Moretus, octavo. *The thirteen books of the Confessions of Aurelius Augustine*. Hendreich presents the Antwerp edition as a repetition of the Wagnereck edition. But this is incorrect, unless perhaps he saw an entirely different copy. Let the evidence be what the Cologne bibliographers report from a more careful inspection:

> “The printer states that, having heard that the copy revised by the Reverend Father Sommalius was praised above all others, he sought out various editions of it; by comparing them, he corrected many typographical errors, and afterward collated the copy with the edition of Augustine’s works printed by Christophorus Plantinus, observing that it differed in many respects. Nevertheless, he judged that in some places Sommalius’s recension, and in others the Plantinian edition, was preferable. Lest one accuse him of having done this rashly, he consulted a very ancient manuscript codex, written many centuries ago and preserved, together with many other manuscripts, in this Plantinian printing house. Having tested the extraordinary fidelity of this codex, he corrected the copy revised by Sommalius on its authority, and rejoices that learned men to whom he showed his corrections did not disapprove of them.”

### 1652

Douai, duodecimo. The same books, from Sommalius’s edition. Catalogue of the Thuane Library.

### 1661

Cologne, duodecimo. The same books. Hendreich.

### 1665

Lyons, twenty-fourmo. The same books. Catalogue of the Library of Nicolas Rossius.

### 1675

Leiden, at the house of Elzevir, duodecimo. *The books of Saint Augustine’s Confessions*. Debure records it in his *Bibliographie instructive*, vol. I, p. 249. Add the Catalogue of the Duke de la Vallière.

### 1679

Brussels, octavo. The same books, revised by the same Sommalius. [Col. 0137B]

### 1685

Augsburg, [details omitted]. *The eighth book of Saint Augustine’s Confessions*, from Sommalius’s recension. It appears in Theophilus Spizelius’s *Retreat of a Pious Man of Letters*, p. 42.

### 1687

Paris, at the house of Jean-Baptiste Coignard, duodecimo. *The thirteen books of the Confessions of Saint Aurelius Augustine, most carefully corrected and illustrated with notes, with new summaries for each chapter.*

### 1699

Antwerp, or Cologne, at the house of Cornelius ab Egmond, twenty-fourmo. The same books. This is exactly how the Cologne bibliographers describe it.

## Eighteenth Century

### 1740

Antwerp, at the house of Gotthard Johann Püttner, octavo. *The thirteen books of the Confessions of Aurelius Augustine*, prepared by Sommalius. The pages are printed in two columns.

### 1743

Antwerp, [details omitted], folio. *The Earlier Acts, or first part of the life, of Saint Augustine the Doctor, excerpted from the first nine books of the Confessions, from infancy to the age of thirty-three*. It appears in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. VI, p. 387ff.

### 1757

Florence, from the printing house of Pietro Cajetano Viviani, at the sign of Janus. *The thirteen books of the Confessions of Saint Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, illustrated with various kinds of commentary, and defended and cleared from the attacks of detractors and rivals—whether already made or yet to be made—in the form of insults, censures, or even quibbles; by the work and study of Brother Archangelus of the Presentation, professed priest of the Discalced Carmelites, lecturer in theology and sacred Scripture.*

### 1776

Paris, from the press of Philippe-Denis Pierres, Rue Saint-Jacques, sextodecimo. *The thirteen books of the Confessions of the divine Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo*. Various readings are added at the end. It is a very handsome, accurate, and carefully corrected edition, in which nothing relevant to typography and correction has been omitted. It was based not only on better printed copies but was also collated with the manuscript codices of the Royal and Sainte-Geneviève libraries. The numerous variants from all these copies, excerpted through the unsurpassed diligence of a certain learned man, L. St. Rondet—whose outstanding abilities in this field the printer duly praises in the preface—are printed at the end.

Some notes are also interspersed, and summaries of the books and chapters have been prepared with the greatest care; there is also, at the beginning, a *Augustinian Annals*, or *Abridged Life of Saint Augustine*, with chronological notes. The same printer had promised that, if readers approved this undertaking and specimen of his work, he would proceed to publish other minor writings of the Latin Fathers with similar brilliance and correction. I do not know whether his promise was fulfilled. We shall give below a list of the codices that served him here.

## Versions

There are Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, French, English, and German versions. No one will be surprised that the life of a man so eminent and, I might say, so greatly venerated—written by himself with such distinguished art and surpassing genius—has been read with pleasure by many. Indeed, even in times near our own it so pleased men of the highest rank that they thought it not unworthy of imitation. Petrarch, Huetius, and, most recently, Russavius, who even translated the title, each according to his own ability, sometimes more closely and sometimes from a distance, followed Augustine and produced comparable works. We shall therefore enumerate them in the order indicated.

### Italian

#### 1564

Venice, at the house of Bolognino Zaltieri, quarto. “The devout *Confessions* of the Divine Father Saint Augustine, translated [printed *tradote*] by the excellent physician Master Vincenzo Buondi.” Compare the latest Catalogue of the Crevenna Library.

#### 1595

Rome, at the Medicean printing house, at the house of Giacomo Luna, quarto. “The *Confession* of Saint Augustine, translated from Latin into Italian by Signor Giulio Mazzini, a nobleman of Brescia, and illustrated by him with annotations, both in the margins and at the end of the chapters, etc.” Catalogue of the Casanatense Library and the latest Catalogue of Crevenna.

#### 1620

Milan, by Giovanni Battista Bidelli, quarto. “The thirteen books, etc.,” in the same translation. Compare the *Biblioteca degli Autori volgari*, often cited by us.

#### 1760

Venice, at the house of Marzellino Piotto, quarto. “The thirteen books of the *Confessions* of Saint Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, illustrated with abundant commentaries and defended against the censures of his adversaries; translated into the vernacular by Father Giangiuseppe of Saint Anne, a Discalced Carmelite of the Venetian province.” An immense accumulation of notes drawn from the entire multitude of commentators. In particular, he carefully excerpted the Cologne translator Henricus Wagnereck.

Philippus Alegambe of the Society of Jesus, in the latest edition of the *Bibliotheca Scriptorum Societatis Jesu*, published at Rome in 1676 by Nathanael Solvello, p. 830, in listing books published by Jesuits while suppressing the authors’ names, also records an Italian translation of Augustine’s *Confessions* by Jacobo Fuligato. Hendreich in the *Brandenburg Pandects* and the Cologne bibliographers in the *Ecclesiastical Library* copied this. But neither of them saw it, nor have I anywhere found such a version mentioned, although it ought to have appeared between the years 1624 and 1653.

The Spanish translation of Augustine’s *Confessions*, *Meditations*, *Soliloquies*, and *Manual* was prepared by Petrus Ribadeneira of Toledo, of the Society of Jesus, and published at Madrid in 1598 in two volumes. It was reprinted in the works of the same author published at Madrid in 1604, folio, part III, p. 633ff. Hendreich, in the *Brandenburg Pandects*, mentions a Spanish version published at Brussels in 1674, twenty-fourmo. But repeated experience has taught me to place little weight on his authority.

Sebastian Toscano, or Tuscanus, an Augustinian hermit of Porto, translated it into Portuguese. Nicolas Antonio records two editions of this translation, Antwerp 1555 and Cologne 1556, in the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, vol. II, p. 186. Hendreich, in the place cited, incorrectly calls it Spanish.

### French

The Cologne bibliographers praise as the first a Paris edition of 1609, octavo, with notes by Hernequinus. This was followed by the translation of René de Ceriziers, of the Society of Jesus, which they report as having appeared at Lyons in 1649, duodecimo, and in 1650, twenty-fourmo. We shall mention a more recent one below. These were followed by Arnaldus d’Andilly in the same year, 1649, and most recently by Dubois, who, without the assistance of manuscript codices, relying solely on the acuity of his intellect, his learning, and his accurate knowledge of Augustine’s thought, is said to have corrected a great deal successfully. The works of both were very frequently printed; we shall now enumerate those editions that came before us in our investigations.

#### 1649

Paris, at the house of the widow of Jean Camusat, duodecimo. “The *Confessions of Saint Augustine*, translated into French by Robert Arnauld d’Andilly.” The same was reprinted by the same booksellers in 1651.

#### 1659

Paris, at the house of Pierre le Petit, octavo. “The *Confessions of Saint Augustine*, translated into French by Robert Arnaud d’Andilly; seventh edition, with the Latin alongside, revised and corrected against twelve ancient manuscripts, and with notes at the end explaining the principal corrections, by Antoine Arnauld, Doctor of the Sorbonne.” The same edition, printed by the same printer in 1656, duodecimo, is praised in the Catalogue of the Casanatense Library. Hendreich also records reprints in 1653, 1660, and 1665.

#### 1675

Paris, at the house of Pierre le Petit, octavo. “The *Confessions of Saint Augustine*, translated into French by Arnaud d’Andilly, new edition.” Hendreich, in the *Brandenburg Pandects*, mentions a translation made “by the gentlemen of Port-Royal” and printed that year at Brussels, duodecimo. The Cologne bibliographers testify that they also saw editions made in Paris in 1671, duodecimo, and at Brussels in 1691, octavo, p. 734, no. 68.

#### 1688

Paris, at the house of Jean-Baptiste Coignard, quarto. “The *Confessions of Saint Augustine*, a new translation from the Latin edition of the Benedictine Fathers, with notes and new chapter summaries by Philippe Goibaud du Bois.” It first appeared in 1686. The same booksellers reprinted it in 1700 and 1716.

#### 1690

Brussels, at the house of François Foppens, octavo. “The Conversion of Saint Augustine, described by himself” (books VIII and IX of the *Confessions*).

#### 1703

Paris, at the house of Charles Robustel, duodecimo. “The *Confessions of Saint Augustine* abridged, containing only what is most moving and accessible to everyone; a new translation by Simon Michel Treuvé.”

#### 1709

Paris, at the house of Nicolas le Gras, duodecimo. “The *Confessions of Saint Augustine*, translated into French by Father René de Ceriziers.”

#### 1719

Paris, at the house of Philippe-Nicolas Lottin, duodecimo. “The *Confessions of Saint Augustine* abridged, etc.” See the edition of 1703. But the translator’s name is absent. *Journal des Savants*, May 1719; Cologne Library.

#### 1722

Paris, at the house of Jean-Baptiste Coignard, duodecimo. A reprint of the preceding fourth edition of the Dubois translation.

#### 1740

Paris, octavo. The same books, by Arnaldus d’Andilly.

#### 1743

Paris, at the house of P. G. Le Mercier, octavo. “The *Confessions of Saint Augustine*, translated into French from the Latin edition of the Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur, with notes and new chapter summaries by Monsieur Du Bois, of the French Academy. New edition.”

### English

#### 1650

London, duodecimo. “Saint Augustine’s *Confessions*, translated and illustrated with some marginal notes, by William Wats”; or, *The Confessions of Saint Augustine, translated into English, with notes, by William Wats*. Catalogue of the Royal Library. The same translation had already been published in London in octavo form in 1631. Catalogue of the Bodleian Library.

### German

#### 1673

Cologne, at the house of Wilhelm Friessen, duodecimo. “The thirteen books of the holy and most enlightened Father Augustine, bishop of Hippo and distinguished teacher of the Church, of the Confessions.” We have shortened the title, which was excessively verbose, as far as possible.

## Codices Used in the Latest and Most Elegant Paris Edition of These Books

### Royal Codices

**I, no. 1807, Colbertinus.** Contains all thirteen books, but the last precedes the others. Assigned to the thirteenth century.

**II, no. 1911.** All thirteen books complete. Assigned to the ninth century.

**III, no. 1912.** All thirteen books complete. Assigned to the ninth century.

**IV, no. 1913, Colbertinus.** Contains all thirteen books, but leaves are missing from book VII, chapter 6, no. 4, through book VIII, chapter 5, no. 3. Assigned to the ninth century.

**V, no. 1913 A, Colbertinus.** All thirteen books complete. Assigned to the ninth century.

**VI, no. 1914, Colbertinus.** All thirteen books complete. Assigned to the eleventh century. Rondet testifies that he read this one in its entirety.

**VII, no. 1915, Colbertinus.** Thirteen books, but the opening leaves are missing through book I, chapter 16, no. 3. Assigned to the twelfth century.

**VIII, no. 1916, Colbertinus.** All thirteen books complete. Assigned to the thirteenth century.

**IX, no. 1917.** Thirteen books, but several leaves are missing in book IX, from chapter 4, no. 2, through chapter 9, no. 1. Assigned to the thirteenth century.

**X, no. 1918, Tellerianus.** All thirteen books complete. Assigned to the thirteenth century.

**XI, no. 1919, Colbertinus.** Under the title *Confessions* there is another work, having a closer affinity with the book *Meditations*, though likewise different from it. Since, however, certain fragments of the *Confessions* were found inserted in it, some distinctive readings could be drawn from them. Assigned to the fourteenth century.

**XII, no. 1948.** Thirteen books, mutilated at the end, in chapter 36 of the final book. Assigned to the fourteenth century.

**XIII, no. 2375.** All thirteen books complete. Assigned to the fourteenth century.

**XIV, no. 2694.** Thirteen books, but truncated at the beginning and end. Assigned to the thirteenth century.

**XV, no. 5296, Colbertinus.** A fragment of book I, from the beginning through chapter 11, no. 1. It appears to belong to the ninth century.

### Sainte-Geneviève Codex

**XVI, no. 34.** Thirteen books, but affected by lacunae in books X, XI, XII, and XV, and at the end. It should be assigned to the fourteenth century. Rondet also states that he read this one in its entirety.

*Little Flowers of Saint Augustine’s Confessions, with the thorns of difficult matters cut away and arranged in six little gardens.* Lyons, 1618, twenty-fourmo; and Cologne, 1620, duodecimo. Cologne bibliographers and Hendreich.

# XV. — (38) The Book *On the Nature of the Good*

Translated into French according to the Benedictine edition and inserted in the book entitled *The Distinction and Nature of Good and Evil*, etc. Paris, 1704, duodecimo. See the Cologne bibliographers, who refer readers concerning the same book to the following volume of their library, though that volume was never published.

# XVI. — (41) The Two Books of the Ninety-Eight Evangelical Questions

They are included in the work *Questions of Saint Augustine*, published at Lyons in 1497, discussed above. The Cologne bibliographers cite here Augustine *On the New Testament*, Paris 1619, as well as its French version in *Explanation by Saint Augustine and the Other Latin Fathers of the New Testament*, Paris 1675, octavo; and another—if I have correctly understood their meaning—a French version published at Lyons by Plaignard in 1694, octavo, four volumes.

# XVII. — (43) *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*

### 1678

Paris, at the house of André Pralard, duodecimo. “The books of Saint Augustine on how to teach the principles of the Christian religion to those who have not yet been instructed in them; on the virtue of continence and temperance; on patience; and against lying: translated into French.”

# XVIII. — (44) The Fifteen Books *On the Trinity*

### 1489

Milan, by Leon Pachel, folio. *The fifteen books of Saint Augustine On the Holy Trinity*. At the end: “Printed at Milan by Master Leonard Pachel, in the year from the birth of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1489, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June.”

These books were printed together with Hilary’s *On the Trinity*, and are often found bound in a single volume. Compare vol. I, p. 279. The verso of the final leaf of the volume containing Hilary provides a register of the sheets of both works. They are printed in small Gothic type, in two columns, on clean and sturdy paper. The initials are small. There are no page or leaf numbers. Braun describes it in the place cited, vol. II, p. 187.

### 1489

Basel, by Joannes Amerbach, folio. *Augustine, On the Trinity*. At the end of book XV: “The book of Aurelius Augustine *On the Trinity* is completed. In the year of the Lord 1489.” Immediately following is a table of the preceding books, at the end of which are ten couplets, beginning:

> If the Cyclops penetrates the waters, etc.

The last reads:

> By your holy power, O Father, protect Johannes,  
> Amerbach, who has printed this work for you.

It is printed in Gothic type in two columns, as are most of Amerbach’s books. It is usually found bound together with the books *On the City of God*, printed by the same printer in the same year.

### 1490

Basel, by Joannes Amerbach, folio. *Augustine, On the Trinity*. Everything agrees most exactly with the preceding edition. The type is clearer and more uniform. The same edition is mentioned by Denis in the *Garellian Library*, p. 135; by Gemeiner in the Regensburg Municipal Library, p. 197; and by Gesner in the Lübeck Municipal Library, p. 51. Masch described it more fully in *Contributions to the History of Remarkable Books*, vol. II, p. 73ff.

### 1494

Without place, folio. *Augustine, On the Trinity*. It follows the Amerbach edition, but the verses at the end of the table are absent. Unless my judgment at Freiburg deceives me, these books were printed by the same printers who also produced the work *On the City of God* that year.

### Without year or place

Folio. “Augustine, *On the Trinity*.” It begins immediately with *The Judgment of Blessed Augustine from the Book of the Retractions*. At the end: “The book of Aurelius Augustine, bishop, *On the Trinity*, ends happily.” The volume is printed in very large Gothic type, exceedingly elegant and clear, with broad lines that are nevertheless evenly spaced. The paper is white and dense; the leaves are of the largest format; there are two columns, [Col. 0142C] and broad margins. All signatures and numbers are absent.

Without year, place, or printer, in-folio, very large format. Saint Augustine’s book On the Trinity (fifteen books). At the end: “The book of Aurelius Augustine, bishop, On the Trinity, ends happily.” Of the descriptions of this most ancient and exceedingly rare book, which Denis first of all offered to lovers of these delights in the Garellian Library, p. 37, and after him Seemiller in Incunabula typographica Ingolstadiensia, Fascicle I, p. 34, we have seen that the desire for knowledge has been satisfied so fully that, however curious the comparison, we could scarcely discover what more might be added by us. The volume consists of 105 leaves of very large format, printed in pages divided into columns, with 47 lines, adorned by very broad margins and wide interlinear spaces. The paper is thick but somewhat coarse and not sufficiently white. The type is large Gothic and rather heavy. Page numbers, signatures, catchwords, and also the initial letters of the books and chapters are absent; our copy, however, has these letters painted in red. The chapters are nevertheless separated from one another by spaces of one or two lines, and their contents are indicated in summary before the beginning of each book. The whole begins with “The Statement of Blessed Augustine concerning the book of the Retractations” (sic), followed by “The Letter of Augustine Aurelius, bishop of Hippo, to Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage”; then, after the chapters have been set out, the beginning of the first book itself follows. In the copy described by the celebrated Denis, a contemporary hand had added the year 1471; the copy handled by Seemiller, however, bore the year 1478. Doctor Georgius Fingel, professor of theology at Ingolstadt, had purchased it for eight florins. Denis further indicated, and confirmed by several examples, that this edition contains numerous readings differing from the Benedictine and Antwerp editions; he also observed that the prefaces and the division of the chapters differ in the two editions. Since this has escaped all bibliographers until now, it should not be neglected. Cf. Braun, Historical-Literary Notices, p. 82.

Without year. Venice, printed by Paganinus de Paganinis, quarto. Saint Augustine’s fifteen books On the Trinity, with books by Hilary on the same subject. Cf. vol. I, p. 280.

## Sixteenth century

### 1515

Basel, printed by Johannes Adam de Langendorff, folio. “The fifteen books of the holy Doctor Augustine, bishop of Hippo, On the Supreme Trinity, which is God” (sic), addressed to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage: “a wholly divine work, before which every praise falls short, in which, by refuting with the most learned arguments the perverse doctrines of heretics, he disclosed with wondrous clarity of intellect the profound mysteries of the inaccessible divinity. To this are most suitably joined the theological truths of the illuminated Doctor Francis Maro.” Beneath the printer’s device: “In the year 1515.” Below: “Directory.” See the edition of the books On the City of God by the same printer; what is said there about that edition may be understood as said here also. The colophon gives the year 1514, on the Kalends of June. On the reverse of the title page there is a brief preface by Johannes Amerbach to the reader, but it deals only with praise of Augustine’s books.

### 1520

Lyons, at the expense of Johannes Koburger, but produced with the skill and care of Jacob Saccon, folio. Saint Augustine’s fifteen books On the Trinity, to which are joined the theological truths of the illuminated Doctor Francis Maro. They are usually circulated bound together with Augustine’s books On the City of God. Catalogue of the Casanatense Library, vol. I, p. 342.

## Translations

These books are said to have been translated into Greek by Maximus Planudes. Several chapters of his, which prove that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son, survive among the Golden Theological Opuscula of certain later Greeks, On the Procession of the Holy Spirit, collected by P. Arcudius and printed at Rome by the press of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, quarto, p. 187 onward. The same work had already been published there in 1630, and even much earlier, in 1578, at Basel in Greek and Latin, by Johannes Leunclavius, according to the Cologne scholars in their supplements to Wharton’s work on Cave. But I doubt whether Leunclavius’s work can be brought under this heading, since I remember from another source that it contains several chapters On the Trinity from the book On the Knowledge of True Life, which Arcudius likewise reproduced in the work mentioned above, p. 672.

As for the French translation mentioned by Crucius of Le Mans, the Cologne scholars correctly conclude that he confused the books On the Trinity with the books On the City of God, to which that translation actually belongs.

## XIX. — (45) Four Books On the Harmony of the Four Evangelists

Without year, place, or printer, folio. On the Harmony of the Four Evangelists. The volume is printed in very clear and even Gothic type, on white, thick paper, in two columns separated by a broad space; the library of our Royal Academy holds two copies, and its origin is doubtless to be assigned to Italy. It begins with Augustine’s own testimony concerning this work in the books of the Retractations, immediately followed by the beginning of the first book. The second, third, and fourth books are preceded by chapters, that is, summaries of each chapter. At the end: “Here ends happily the fourth book of Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, On the Harmony of the Holy Four Evangelists. Thanks be to God.” It has four-leaf gatherings numbered a–l. Other marks are absent. A completely blank space was left for the initial letters.

### 1473

Lauingen, without indication of the printer, folio. “The book of Blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, On the Harmony of the Evangelists in four books, begins happily.” Thus it reads on the very title page of the book. At the end: “The book of Blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, On the Harmony of the Evangelists, ends happily. In the city of Lauingen. Printed in the year of the saving birth of the Virgin, 1473, on the day before the Ides of April.” This edition consists of 105 leaves, printed in rounded, bright type, without catchwords, numbers, signatures, initial letters, or titles. The distinguished Braun described it in Historical-Literary Notices (1788), p. 154. Several bibliographers, whom Braun also cites, have testified that it is exceedingly rare.

### 1538

Paris, duodecimo. Saint Aurelius Augustine, On the Harmony of the Evangelists. British Museum.

### 1539

Cologne, from the workshop of Heron Alopecius, octavo. Saint Aurelius Augustine, four books On the Harmony of the Evangelists. Catalogue of Bunau.

## Translation

Jacques Le Long, in his Sacred Bibliography, p. 619, mentions a French translation of this work, Lyons 1526, octavo. The Cologne scholars.

## XX. — (52) On Holy Virginity

### 1562

Rome, at the press of Paulus Manutius. Saint Augustine’s book On Holy Virginity. It appears among the Opuscula of the holy doctors Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine On Virginity.

## Translations

### 1638

Paris, at the shop of Jean Camusat, octavo. “On Holy Virginity, a discourse translated from Saint Augustine, with remarks for clarity of doctrine, by Claude Seguenot” (under whose name they report that Jean du Vergier de Hauranne, abbot of Saint-Cyran, was concealed). The following belongs with this book: “The Censure of the Sacred Faculty of Theology of Paris, issued against the book entitled On Holy Virginity, etc.” Paris, at the shop of Adrian Tapuinort, 1638, quarto. Cf. Jansenist Bibliography, p. 198, 1722.

Also refer here:

### 1680

Paris, at the shop of Hélie Josset, duodecimo. “Moral Treatises of Saint Augustine, for all the states that compose the body of the Church, namely: 1. On Holy Virginity, for virgins; 2. On the Good of Widowhood; 3. On How Widows Ought to Pray to God; 4. On the Good of Marriage; 5. On Marriage and Concupiscence; translated into French by M. Jean Hamon.”

## XXI. — (55) On the Unity of the Church

### 1602

Mainz. Saint Augustine’s book, or Letter, On the Unity of the Church against the Letter of Petilianus the Donatist, illustrated with arguments, notes, and analysis, by the work of Justus Calvinus. It appears in his own Treatises of Prescriptions against Heretics, p. 249 onward. In the catalogue of the Bodleian Library the same book is praised with the year 1605 prefixed, as we have already once noted.

### 1657

Helmstedt, from the press of Calixtus, octavo. Treatises of Saints Cyprian and Augustine On the Unity of the Church. Added is a fragment of an Introduction to the reading of these books by Georgius Calixtus, Doctor of Sacred Theology and senior professor in the Julia Academy, edited by Friedrich Ulrich Calixtus, Georgius’s son.

### 1690

Utrecht, at the shop of the widow of Guilielmus Clerck, quarto. Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, book On the Unity of the Church against the Donatists. It appears with very extensive and useful commentaries in Melchior Leydecker’s Illustrated History of the African Church. Almost the whole of its second volume is constituted by the work entitled: “The Second Volume on Augustine’s Book On the Unity of the Church against the Donatists, dealing with the Principles of the African Church and its Faith in the Articles concerning Christ the Head and the Church, Unity and Schism, and many other points of the Christian religion.”

## Translation

Jacques Tigeou of Angers, Doctor of Theology and canon of the cathedral church of Metz, translated it into French and scattered notes throughout it to aid understanding of the more difficult passages. His translation appeared at Reims in 1567, octavo, under the title: “The Letter or Book of Saint Augustine On the Unity of the Church, against Petilianus, a Donatist bishop, with certain observations for understanding the more difficult passages; printed at Reims by Jean de Foigny.” Cf. Du Verdier, Juvigny edition, vol. IV, p. 314.

## XXII. — (67) One Book On the Spirit and the Letter

## Fifteenth century

Without year, place, or printer, quarto. Saint Augustine’s book On the Spirit and the Letter. Added is an anonymous Treatise On the Dangers that Occur Concerning the Sacrament of the Eucharist, to which is appended a resolution of the question: “Whether suffrages offered for many benefit each of them equally?” The distinguished Seemiller exhibits it in Fascicle I, p. 191. The entire volume consists of 38 leaves, copied in Gothic type, which another writer has described more precisely by comparison in the same place. There are 28 lines to a page. Numbers, signatures, catchwords, initial letters, and titles are absent, except that at the beginning one reads: “Here begins the prologue of Blessed Augustine, bishop, in the book” (sic) “On the Spirit and the Letter”; and at the end of the book, which falls on the first page of leaf 35: “Here ends the book of Blessed Augustine, bishop, On the Spirit and the Letter.”

## Sixteenth century

### 1524

Nuremberg. One book of Saint Aurelius Augustine On the Spirit and the Letter. Praised by the Cologne scholars.

### 1527

Cologne, at the shop of Heron Alopecius, octavo. One book of Saint Aurelius Augustine On the Spirit and the Letter. Ossinger records the same edition under the year 1528 in his Augustinian Bibliography.

### 1538

Paris, at the shop of Jean Roigny, sextodecimo. The same book. Ossinger.

Paris, at the shop of Antonius Augarellus, under the sign of Saint James, on the road to Saint James. Saint Aurelius Augustine’s one book On the Spirit and the Letter, together with his Letter to the priest Sixtus against the arguments of the Pelagians.

### 1542

Paris, octavo. The same book. The Cologne author testifies that he saw it.

### 1545

Wittenberg, printed by Joseph Klug, octavo. Augustine, bishop of Hippo (sic), book On the Spirit and the Letter. With a preface and a preliminary notice to the reader. I do not know whether Hendreich is mistaken in his Brandenburg Pandects, p. 341, where he praises a Wittenberg edition of 1548.

### 1568

Antwerp, sextodecimo. Saint Aurelius Augustine’s one book On the Spirit and the Letter to Marcellinus. Also his works On Nature and Grace and On Faith and Works. The Cologne scholars, from Lipenius and Bechmann’s Catalogue of the Frankfurt Library, p. 35, to which add Hendreich in the same place.

## Eighteenth century

### 1767

Leipzig, at the shop of Johann Friedrich Witzleben, octavo. One book of Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, On the Spirit and the Letter, addressed to Marcellinus, from the recension of the Benedictines of the Congregation of Saint Maur, illustrated with variant readings and brief notes by Johann Christian Benjamin Teegius, a student of sacred theology. The preface offers a few remarks on the occasion of this little book and on its editions and recensions; it also proceeds to mention other books edited separately. It was dedicated to Erdmann Rudolph Fischer, theologian of Coburg.

### 1770

Leipzig, at the shop of Johann Friedrich Langenheim, octavo. One book of Aurelius Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter to Marcellinus. Again edited by the Reverend Johann Christian Benjamin Teegius of the Sangerhausen School, Collegiate III. He declares this second edition to be more correct and further enlarged by an index of notable matters.

## Translations

### Italian

#### 1543

Venice, by Comin da Trino, octavo. “A very useful work of Blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, entitled On the Spirit and the Letter, addressed to Blessed Marcellinus, newly translated from Latin into the vernacular.”

### French

#### 1547

Lyons, by Jean Pitier, sextodecimo. “The Book of the Spirit and the Letter of Saint Augustine, translated by Jacques Le Conte.” Cf. Du Verdier, new edition, vol. IV, p. 274.

#### 1551

Paris, from the printing house of Michel Voscan, quarto. “A little work of Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo in Africa, On the Spirit and the Letter, translated by Valentin du Caunoy.” Maittaire, part II, vol. III, p. 598. Du Verdier, new edition, vol. IV, p. 439.

#### 1700

Paris, at the shop of Jean-Baptiste Coignard, duodecimo. “The Book of Saint Augustine On the Spirit and the Letter, translated into French from the edition of the Benedictine Fathers by Philippe Goibaud du Bois.”

## XXIII. — (68) One Book On Faith and Works

### 1473

Cologne, quarto. Blessed Augustine’s book On Faith and Works. Catalogue of the Boldeian Library.

### 1523

Strasbourg, from the literary workshop of the ingenious Johannes Grieninger, quarto. The golden little book of the divine Augustine On Faith and Works. It appears together with Isidore’s work On the Sects and Names of Heretics, and Jerome’s book On the Perpetual Virginity of Mary and his Letter against Vigilantius, published jointly by Jerome Gebwiler, schoolmaster of the Strasbourg cathedral school. Folios V–XXVI.

Augsburg, octavo. Saint Aurelius Augustine’s book On Faith and Works. Catalogue of the Main Library of the Church of Cologne, p. 737.

### 1528

Cologne. Printed by Eucharius Cervicornus, octavo. Saint Aurelius Augustine’s one book On Faith and Works. It is sometimes found bound together with his book On Nature and Grace from the same workshop.

### 1534

Paris, at the shop of Jean Roigny, sextodecimo. Saint Augustine’s book On Faith and Works. Maittaire, vol. II, part II, p. 799, second edition.

### 1539

Leipzig, octavo. Blessed Aurelius Augustine’s book On Faith and Works, with a preface by Georg Wicelius. Cf. Bechmann’s Catalogue of the Frankfurt Library, p. 35. From there it was already cited by Hendreich and the Cologne scholars.

### 1552

Cologne, at the shop of Peter Horst, octavo. The same book with his Enchiridion; see under its proper heading.

### 1568

Antwerp, octavo. The same book, cited by the Cologne scholars in the same place.

### 1652

Frankfurt am Main and Rinteln, octavo. Saint Aurelius Augustine’s book On Faith and Works, edited by Johann Hennichius. With a dissertation on the same subject by the same author. Hendreich, Brandenburg Pandects, p. 342.

## Translations

### 1545

Venice, by Comin da Trino, octavo. “The book of Blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, On Faith and Works, newly translated from Latin into the vernacular.”

## XXIV. — (72) On Nature and Grace

### 1524

Nuremberg, octavo. Saint Aurelius Augustine’s one book On Nature and Grace. Recorded by the Cologne scholars.

### 1528

Printed by Eucharius Cervicornus. At the end: “At Cologne, at the expense of the most distinguished citizen of Agrippina, Master Godfrey Hüttorp,” octavo. Saint Aurelius Augustine’s one book On Nature and Grace. Johannes Petreius supplied a brief preface.

### 1568

Antwerp, at the shop of Gymnicus, octavo. “Saint Aurelius Augustine’s book On Nature and Grace.” Main Library of the Church of Cologne, p. 737. If this report is accurate, the edition must be counted among the rarest, namely among the few books printed at Antwerp at the expense of Johannes Gymnicus, once a celebrated Cologne printer. I would prefer to conclude this rather than, with Maittaire, make Gymnicus himself migrate from Antwerp to Cologne, since the annals also establish that he was already operating a press at Cologne in 1535, and therefore could not have established his residence there only after 1540, the year of the Antwerp edition mentioned by Maittaire.

## Translation

### 1545

Venice, by Comin da Trino, octavo. “The book of Blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, On Nature and Grace, against the Pelagians, newly translated from Latin into the vernacular.”

## XXV. — (74) The Twenty-Two Books On the City of God

## Fifteenth century

### 1467

From the Subiaco Monastery, very large folio. Saint Aurelius Augustine’s twenty-two books On the City of God. At the end: “The twenty-second book of Aurelius Augustine, eminent Doctor and bishop of Hippo, On the City of God, against the pagans, here ends. In the year 1467 from the birth of the Lord; in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Paul II; in the third year of the reign of Frederick, Emperor of the Romans; in the fifteenth indiction, on the twelfth day of the month of June. Thanks be to God. GOD AL.” Conradus SW. and Arnoldus Pannartz printed it, doubtless with the assistance of some capable man whose name everyone so readily persuades himself is contained in the letters GOD AL, while expending his efforts in explaining their mysteries [Note: Lairius interprets “GOD AL” as “Gratias Omnipotenti Deo” (“Thanks to Almighty God”), derived from Laudenbach. But the words “Thanks be to God” seem wholly to stand in the way of this, as Audiffredus correctly observed. The opinion of Petrus Scriverius, who substitutes the name of Gottschalk or Godfrey the German, may seem more probable.]. The pages are printed in two columns of 44 lines, surrounded by broad margins. Twelve leaves of rubrics precede the text. Cf. Audiffredus, p. 6. It is also listed by Debure, Bibliographical Instructions, vol. I, p. 243. It was held in the library of the Duke de La Vallière.

### 1468

Rome, in the house of Peter de Maximo, very large folio. Saint Augustine’s twenty-two books On the City of God. At the end: “Here is Conrad’s work,” etc. “In the house of Peter de Maximo, 1468.” “In my judgment, the type of this edition is more elegant than that of the Lactantius of the same year. But the text is more corrupt and teems with the foulest errors. Fourteen leaves of rubrics precede it.” Cf. Debure, Bibliographical Instructions; Catalogue of the Smithian Library (Venice 1755, quarto), p. 27; and Catalogue of the Pinelli Library, vol. I, p. 86.

### 1470

Rome, at the same press, very large folio. Saint Augustine’s twenty-two books On the City of God. At the end: “You behold, illustrious one,” etc. Audiffredus, by a careful comparison of the three Roman editions, established beyond any doubt that they are distinct from one another and were separately reprinted. This one, the third, is also more correct than the preceding one and has removed most of its faults. It was held in the Pinelli Library.

Venice, printed by Johannes de Spira and his brother Vindelinus, folio. Augustine’s twenty-two books On the City of God. At the end:

> He who taught the Venetians that books could be copied, Johannes,
>
> Who in nearly three months had set one hundred volumes of Pliny,
>
> And just as many little books of great Cicero, Spira,
>
> Had begun the work of Aurelius, but, cut off by sudden death,
>
> Could not finish the volume he had begun for the Venetians.
>
> Vindelinus, his brother, is here, and in skill
>
> Is no less; he will remain in the Adriatic city.

1470. A table of rubrics in fourteen leaves precedes it. “Debure, Bibliographical Instructions; Smithian Library; Catalogue of Bunau. It is also praised by the Catalogue of the Royal Library and the Pinelli Library.”

### 1473

Mainz, printed by Peter Schoeffer of Gernsheim, folio, two volumes. Blessed Aurelius Augustine’s twenty-two books On the City of God, with the commentaries of Thomas Valois and Nicholas Trivet. At the end, in red letters: “Thus, therefore, the work of Aurelius Augustine,” etc. (Cf. the Hieronymian edition printed there in 1470 by the same printer.) “Completed by Peter Schoeffer of Gernsheim in the year of the Lord 1473, on the fifth day of September, while Sixtus III was presiding as Supreme Pontiff over the Catholic Church, Adolf II was the magnificent bishop of the Mainz see, and the most serene Emperor Frederick III, ever Augustus, held and governed the monarchy of Christendom.” It begins with a table of the chapters of the first book, which together with an excerpt from the books of the Retractations occupies one leaf. Then Augustine’s entire work follows, completed within this first volume; at the end one reads: “When the book is finished, let praise and glory be given to Christ.” Then, printed in red: “The text of Saint Augustine On the City of God, printed at Mainz, ends happily, in the year 1473.” The second volume contains the commentaries mentioned above, together with an alphabetical index. At the end of each volume, after the completed colophon, the printer’s device is seen printed in red in the customary manner. Debure, Bibliographical Instructions; Seemiller, Fascicle I, p. 49; Braun, Historical-Literary Notices (1788), p. 159.

The authors of these commentaries, which were printed here for the first time, were both Englishmen and both members of the Order of Preachers. Nicholas Treveth, or Trivet, also Traveth, was originally from Norwich, born around 1258 and deceased in 1328. He commented on all twenty-two books. Thomas Walleis, or Vallensis, also called Gualois or, corruptly, Valois, evidently because he came from the principality of Wales, was a Doctor of Theology at Oxford. He died in 1340 and wrote an exposition of the first ten books of the twenty-two of The City of God, ending at book X, chapter 29. The great esteem once accorded the work of both men is attested by the countless manuscripts, chiefly still preserved in the libraries of Paris; concerning these, see Echard, in the second volume of the *Scriptores Ordinis Praedicatorum*, pp. 561 and 597. It was once believed that Treveth and Thomas had composed these works through joint effort, but this is false. For this conjunction, just as it appears in this first edition, is due to the scribes and is customary in all the manuscript codices. Nicholas Treveth’s exposition of the first ten books was never published and may perhaps in this way have been lost to the light forever. Besides the already mentioned Echard, who is the fullest authority on these matters, cf. Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina medii et infimae aetatis*.

### 1474

Rome, at the press of Ulrich Gallus, very large folio. Saint Augustine’s twenty-two books On the City of God. At the end: “This distinguished work of Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, has been fashioned and diligently completed in the nourishing city of Rome, queen and most worthy empress of the whole world, which, just as it surpasses other cities in dignity, is likewise filled with ingenious men—not with a quill dipped in ink, nor with a bronze stylus, but by a certain ingenious invention, or the fashioning of letters—to the praise of God: by Ulrich Gallus the German and Simon Nicholas of Lucca. In the year of the Lord 1474, on the fourth day of February, in the third year of the pontificate of Sixtus IV, Pope by divine providence.” Thirteen leaves of rubrics precede it, together with two blank leaves. The type is not altogether as clear and large as that of the Roman editions, but is much more even.

### 1475

Venice, at the press of Nicholas Jenson, folio. Saint Augustine’s twenty-two books On the City of God. At the end: “The work of Aurelius Augustine On the City of God ends happily; completed at Venice by the excellent and diligent master Nicholas Jenson, under Pietro Mocenigo as doge, in the year from the birth of the Lord 1475, on the sixth day before the Nones of October.” It is printed in two columns and begins with a table of chapters occupying four leaves. Catalogue of the Library of the Duke de La Vallière, and also of the Smithian Library. It was formerly held in the Pinelli Library and likewise, together with the six preceding books, in the Crevenna Library. See the latest catalogue.

Venice, printed by Gabriel Peter of Treviso, folio. Augustine’s twenty-two books On the City of God. At the end: “The twenty-second and final book of Aurelius Augustine On the City of God ends happily. This work was printed by the diligent Master Gabriel Peter of Treviso in 1475, while Pietro Mocenigo was doge of Venice.” Catalogue of the Budé Library, vol. I, p. 89, where it is rightly counted among the rarest books. From the Catalogue of the Library of the Duke de La Vallière we learn that the volume was printed in two columns, preceded by a table of contents in fourteen leaves; the signatures run from a to D of the second alphabet. It is also mentioned in the recent edition of the Catalogue of the Bodleian Library, p. 88, and by Denis in the Garellian Library, vol. I, p. 135. Add the distinguished Reuss, in the Tübingen Library, 1780, p. 69.

### 1477

Naples, printed by Matthias Moravus, small folio. Saint Augustine’s twenty-two books On the City of God. At the end: “The twenty-second and final book of Aurelius Augustine On the City of God ends happily. This work was printed at Naples by the diligent Master Matthias Moravus in the year of Christ 1477.” Catalogue of the Library of the Duke de La Vallière.

### 1479

Basel, printed by Michael Wenssler, folio. The same books, with the commentaries of Thomas Valois and Nicholas Trivet. At the end, printed in red type:

> Thus the most distinguished work of Aurelius Augustine,
>
> the radiant star of the orthodox city, on the City of God,
>
> commented upon by two outstanding professors of Sacred Scripture,
>
> distinguished and separated by rubrics and a table,
>
> in the lofty city of Basel, in the German region,
>
> which is made famous not only by the mildness of its air
>
> and the fertility of its soil, but also by the skill of its printers,
>
> to the praise of the undivided Trinity, ruler of the City of God,
>
> by the skill and industry of Michael Wenssler.
>
> In the year of our salvation 1479,
>
> on the eighth day before the Kalends of April,
>
> it was laboriously completed.

Beneath this, the printer’s device likewise shines in red. It begins with Augustine’s statement from the books of the Retractations, immediately followed by the table of chapters of the first book; a similar table precedes each book. After the text one reads a subscription, likewise written in red type, with the printer’s device below: “The text of Saint Augustine On the City of God, printed at Basel, ends happily, in the year 1479.” Clear Gothic type was used: larger in the text and much smaller in the commentaries that follow. Two columns; numbers, signatures, catchwords, initial letters, and titles are entirely absent. Debure, in the Catalogue of the Library of the Duke de La Vallière; Seemiller, *Ingolstadt Incunabula*, Fascicle II, p. 36 onward.

### 1482

Rome. Folio. Augustine, On the City of God. Only a record of this edition survives in Labbe, *New Catalogue of Manuscripts*, p. 347, no. 689; from there Maittaire entered it in his files, vol. I, part II, p. 435. Laerius also cited p. 354, no. 1029, of the same book; but incorrectly, as Audiffredus long ago pointed out with his customary severity, p. 252.

### 1484

Louvain. Folio. Saint Augustine’s On the City of God with the Commentary of Thomas Valois. Maittaire, vol. I, part II, p. 455, adding Heida’s testimony from the catalogue, p. 6, no. 121, without fuller explanation. It is therefore uncertain whether he recognizes the same printer who committed it to the press in 1488, or another producer.

### 1486
