Venice, printed by Bonetus Locatellus, quarto. Blessed Augustine’s twenty-two books On the City of God. At the end: “The work On the City of God ends happily, completed at Venice by Bonetus Locatellus, at the expense and cost of Octavianus Scotus of Modena, in 1486, on the fifth day before the Ides of February.” Catalogue of Rarer Books of the Budé Library and the Pinelli Library.

### 1488

Toulouse, printed by Heinrich Mayer the German, on 12 October, small folio. The commentaries of Thomas Valois and Nicholas Trivet on Saint Augustine’s books On the City of God, together with the supplement of Brother Nicholas Cerseth. Cf. the latest Catalogue of the Crevenna Library.

Louvain, printed by Johannes Westfalensis, folio. Augustine’s twenty-two books On the City of God, with the commentaries of Thomas Valois and Nicholas Trivet. At the end: “Printed in the nourishing University of Louvain, which gives Brabant considerable distinction above other regions, through the skill and industry of Johannes Westfalensis, in the year 1488, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October.” Maittaire, vol. I, part II, p. 493. We find no mention of it, however, in other bibliographers, and it therefore rests solely on Maittaire’s authority; the Cologne scholars, Ossinger, and others cite the same edition on that basis.

### 1489

Venice, printed by Vincentus, at the press of Octavianus Scotus, folio. Augustine, On the City of God, with the commentaries of Thomas Valois, or Walleis, and Nicholas Trivet. Catalogue of the Casanatense Library; from it Maittaire, vol. I, part II, p. 510, may be supplemented.

Basel, at the press of Johannes Amerbach, folio. Augustine, On the City of God, with commentary. At the end:

> This work, completed by the divine art of Johannes
>
> Amerbach: reader, wherever you read,
>
> you find a marvel in the text—the glosses, that is, in the margin—
>
> by which the city of Basel rightly rejoices in its glory.
>
> In the year of the saving virgin birth,
>
> 1489, on the Ides of February.

The commentaries are by Thomas Valois and Nicholas Trivet, professors of Sacred Scripture of the Order of Preachers. The notes of the former end at chapter 29 of book X; the remainder was written by Nicholas Trivet. The table, or index, also came from Nicholas. The type is Gothic; there are two columns, but with the commentary placed on both sides, the page generally has four columns. On the inner title page an image of Augustine printed from a woodblock appears, together with another emblematic figure, an inscription, and verses. Braun described the same edition in Historical-Literary Notices, vol. II, p. 182.

### 1490

Basel, at the press of Johannes Amerbach, folio. A careful reprinting of the preceding year’s edition, completed on the Ides of February. Denis, Garellian Library, p. 134; Gemeiner, Regensburg Library, p. 197. It was also held in the Library of the Duke de La Vallière. Gessner, Lübeck Library, p. 51. Masch described it carefully, *Contributions to the History of Remarkable Books*, part II, p. 73 onward.

### 1494

Freiburg, folio. A repetition of the Amerbach edition. At the end: “This work was completed at Freiburg in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1494.” It also appears in the Catalogue of the Bodleian Library and the latest Catalogue of Crevenna.

Without year, place, or printer, folio. Saint Augustine’s twenty-two books On the City of God, with the commentaries of Thomas Valois and Nicholas Trivet.

The distinguished Morell, in the Pinelli Library, vol. I, p. 86, and Seemiller, Fascicle I, p. 120, supply information about this exceedingly rare and likewise very ancient edition; Placidius Braun described it again with no less diligence in Historical-Literary Notice, p. 9. Like the edition of 1473, it consists in a certain sense of two parts: the first presents the text in larger letters, while the second presents the commentary in smaller type, printed in two columns. The text has 47 lines per page, while the commentary has 57. Morell calls the letters German; Seemiller considers them entirely similar to those with which Augustine’s fourth book On Christian Doctrine was reprinted by Johannes Mentelin of Strasbourg, to whom he therefore unquestionably attributes it. Since Mentelin had already died in 1478, it must certainly have been printed before that date. But he considers it much older, and not far removed from the year 1470, so much so that it might perhaps be regarded as the first edition with the cited commentaries, an opinion which Morell had already embraced. It lacks all the marks which a later age gradually introduced through the progress of the art: the signs and numbers of leaves and pages, initial letters, and titles both at the front of the work and at the beginnings of the individual books and chapters. These are distinguished only by empty spaces, and not very large ones. Nevertheless, at the end of book XVIII there is a subscription, and from book XIX onward the titles of the books and chapters are found. Marginal notes frequently occur, set beside shortened lines of the text; I remember having observed the same feature in Basel editions of these books. Finally, at the end of the text one reads: “When the book is finished, let praise and glory be given to Christ.” After the commentaries, a table of contents occupying ten not entirely complete leaves ends with the words: “The Table ends.”

## Sixteenth century

### 1515

Basel, printed by Adam Petri of Langendorf, folio. “The twenty-two books of the divine Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, addressed to Marcellinus, On the City of God against the Pagans, a work most worthy, filled with the disciplines of human and divine letters with the greatest clarity. With the commentaries of Thomas Valois and Nicholas Trivet, as well as the additions of Jacob Passauantius and the theological truths of Francis Maro.” It was printed under the distinguished device of Adam Petri, with the year 1515 added. Below: “A directory of each book of the entire work, arranged in a reliable index.” On the reverse of the page are the same items found in the Amerbach edition. There follows a preface by Brother Conrad Leontorius of Maulbronn (sic), printed in Roman type, explaining the purpose and arrangement of Augustine’s work. At the end of the same Conrad Leontorius of Maulbronn (sic) there is an epilogue, in which he promises a substantial correction of the text, completed by comparison with many manuscripts, together with a colophon indicating that Johannes Koburger, a Nuremberg bookseller, bore the expense of printing the volume. This part too is in rounded type; the rest of the volume is printed in Gothic type, generally in four, and sometimes even five, columns, with frequent divisions. The result is hard on the eyes, both because of this arrangement and because different kinds of type appear on the same page. Caspar Barthius, *Adversaria* LIX, chapter 10, p. 2795, calls this edition much better than many manuscripts.

### 1520

Lyons, at the expense of Johannes Koburger and produced by the skill of Jacob Saccon, folio. Augustine, On the City of God, together with the books On the Trinity; see under that heading. It is an exact reproduction of the preceding Basel edition.

### 1522

Basel, at the press of Johannes Froben, folio. “The complete work of Saint Aurelius Augustine On the City of God, collated with ancient copies and illustrated with commentaries through the study and labor of Johannes Ludovicus Vives.” Catalogue of the Royal Library, the British Museum, and the Budé Library. This is the first edition with Vives’s commentaries. After the dedication to Henry VIII, king of England, dated at Louvain on the Nones of July 1522, there is a preface explaining the occasion of the Augustinian work, together with a separate dissertation on the ancient interpreters of this little book and on the Goths who captured Rome.

### 1554

Paris, folio. Saint Aurelius Augustine, On the City of God, edited by Ludovicus Vives. Catalogue of the Bern Library, vol. I, p. 16.

### 1555

Paris, at the shop of Charles Guillard, folio. The same books with the same commentary. Cited by the Cologne scholars, p. 739. If the preceding edition is correctly described, I have no doubt that it came from the same bookseller’s establishment as this one.
—Basel, printed by Hieronymus Froben and Nicolaus episcopus; folio. “The twenty-two books of the divine Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, On the City of God, once more collated against ancient and venerable exemplars and further illustrated and revised with the most learned commentaries throughout by Joannes Ludovicus Vives. A most fruitful index is appended.” On the reverse of the title page appears a letter from Henry, king of England, thanking Ludovicus Vives for the Augustine books presented to him; dated at Greenwich, 24 January 1523.

1570. Basel, printed by Ambrosius and Aurelius Froben, brothers; folio. “The twenty-two books of the divine Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, On the City of God, now once again collated with the ancient and venerable exemplars, after the work of the universally learned Joannes Ludovicus Vives, with the greatest care, and illustrated with his most learned commentaries. An Index, much fuller than before, is appended.”

See what we noted about this edition in the *Annals of the Collections*. In the entire volume there is nothing, apart from the preface, that concerns a complete edition of the works or could have prevented this volume from being sold separately.

1596. [Geneva,] printed by Jacobus Stoer; octavo, in two volumes. “The twenty-two books of the divine Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, On the City of God.” They constitute the fifth volume of the complete works printed here and there. See above in the *Annals of the Works*.

[Col. 0154A] **SEVENTEENTH CENTURY.**—1600. Antwerp, at the Plantin press; folio. The same books. *M. Bibl. Colon.*

1610. Geneva . . . octavo. The same books. Under the same auspices.

1613. Paris, under the city’s arms; folio. “The twenty-two books of Saint Augustine On the City of God, revised by the theologians of Leuven, with the commentaries of Leonardus Coquaeus and Joannes Ludovicus Vives.” *Cat. Bibl. Thott.*

1624. Frankfurt, printed by the Wechel press for Daniel and David Aubrius and Clemens Schleich; folio. Caspar Barthius’s *Commentaries on the City of God of the divine Aurelius Augustine*, book one, or book sixty of the *Adversaria*. It appears together with the *Adversaria*, from page 2816 onward. It is preceded by this notice of his:

“Behold for you, friendly reader, a specimen of our *Commentaries on Augustine’s Divine City*, long desired by many. The commentaries themselves will follow, if God grants me life: an immense work, and, one may venture to say, an eternal one. We have left matters as we wrote them, without removing what we transferred from the *Adversaria* into this commentary; and this by design, so that the nature of the work itself may more easily be discerned.”

We have transcribed Barthius’s words here all the more willingly because only recently we saw that the people of Cologne had placed such confidence in the authority of Lipenius—an often unreliable witness—that, despite the weightiest testimonies of Christian Daumius, once Barthius’s intimate associate, and of other writers of better repute whom they themselves produce, they nevertheless did not entirely abandon hope of a complete edition of this Barthian commentary, which Lipenius had reported as having appeared at Halle in Saxony in 1620, in folio. [Col. 0154C] They were also misled by the fact that Barthius himself had frequently mentioned this commentary on Augustine in his *Observations on Statius*. But the words which they quote from those works prove only that it had already been written, not, as they wish, that it had been published.

At that time, moreover, learned men had an immense desire for this commentary, especially because the author himself had spoken of it so magnificently, and because there were very few who did not admire that man’s exceptionally profound learning. Today, we believe that the learned world has suffered no greater loss through its absence than through the loss of the work which Salmasius was planning on Arnobius.

1636. Paris, under the sign of the Great Ship; folio. “The twenty-two books of Saint Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, *On the City of God*, purged of countless errors by the theologians of Leuven from the most ancient manuscript exemplars.” Their diligence is attested at the end of the volume by an account of the corrections and a record of variant readings, noted for the most part. With new and continuous commentaries by R. P. F. Leonardus Coquaeus, Augustinian Hermit, Doctor of Theology at Paris, and Joannes Ludovicus Vives.

Leonardus Coquaeus, confessor to Christina of Lorraine, Grand Duchess Mother of Tuscany, dedicated it to her. His notes display an equally abundant theological learning, while Ludovicus Vives’s commentary is distinguished by knowledge of every kind of antiquity. He too once more commented on the title, occasion, division, dignity, and usefulness of these books, matters which Vives had treated by no means superficially.

1651. Paris . . . folio. The same, with Coquaeus’s commentaries. Thus the Cologne cataloguers.

1661. Hamburg, at the expense of Zacharias Hertelius; quarto, in two volumes. “The twenty-two books of Saint Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, *On the City of God*, divided into two volumes, corrected from the most ancient manuscript exemplars, according to the latest Cologne edition. The learned and complete commentaries of Joannes Ludovicus Vives of Seville and Leonardus Coquaeus of Orléans are added. With two indexes, one of scriptural passages, the other, extremely full, of subjects and words.”

**EIGHTEENTH CENTURY.**—1748. Naples . . . quarto. “The twenty-two books of Saint Augustine *On the City of God*, with notes by the monks of Saint-Maur.” *Cat. Bibl. S. Aug. ad Nidum Neap.*

### Translations

The number of translations of this Augustinian work is also considerable. It was rendered into various languages, and more often than once into the same language, though into no language more frequently than French. Among the many Frenchmen who devoted their efforts to it, none failed to win praise among his countrymen; the endeavors of Raoul de Praelles, Gentian Hervet, de Ceriziers, Ludovicus Giry, and Petrus Lombert were received with particular enthusiasm and multiplied through the press. Let us briefly survey each of them.

### Italian

No place or date, folio. “The book of Saint Augustine, *The City of God*, divided into twenty-two books, translated into the vernacular.” *Cat. Bibl. Reg.* vol. I, p. 381, no. 786, with the lemma “an old edition.” In the *Smithian Library*, p. 28, one reads: “*The City of God*: translated (perhaps) by Jacopo Passavanti.” Debure judges it to have been printed about 1480 and writes that its type is small Roman, in two columns, with signatures A–H of the second alphabet and a table of contents prefixed at the beginning in eleven leaves. It was formerly in Crevenna’s possession, according to the latest catalogue of his library. Cf. *Biblioteca degli Autori volgarizzati* in *Raccolta d’Opuscoli scientifici e filologici*, vol. XXXII, p. 342.

The Italians themselves do not agree about the author of this translation. Some, including Fontanini in his work *On Italian Eloquence*, attributed it to Niccolò Piccolomini; Apostolo Zeno, however, refutes them in his *Annotations on Fontanini’s Book*. Others, such as Jacopo Corbinelli, identified Jacopo Passavanti as the author. Both positions were opposed by Pietro Bassaglia in the Venetian edition of 1742, who said that it had proceeded from an anonymous Florentine and had been prepared at Venice around 1480.

1734. Rome, printed by Antonio de Rossi; folio. “*The City of God*, the work of the great Father Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, translated into the Italian language by Father Don Cesare Benvenuti of Crema, general abbot of the Regular Canons of the Lateran Congregation.” Many features commend this work: the elegance of the translation, the ample index, the splendor of its production, and finally the very name of Pope Benedict XIV, to whom it is dedicated, as reported by the *Biblioteca degli Autori volgarizzati* in the *Raccolta d’Opuscoli scientifici e filologici*, vol. XXXII, p. 343.

1742. Venice, at the presses of Pietro Bassaglia and Francesco Hertzhauser; quarto. “*The City of God of Saint Aurelius Augustine*. Volume one, containing the first eleven books.” This is a new edition of that old translation whose author, as we have said, the editor Pietro Bassaglia discussed at length in the dedicatory epistle prefixed to this volume. The second volume had still not been completed in 1745, as the author of the *Biblioteca degli Autori volgarizzati* expressly observes. It must, however, have been added later, for Audiffredi cites two volumes in the *Catalogue of the Casanatense Library*. The Latin text is appended to the translation, and the *Life of Augustine* written by Possidius is also included in Latin.

### French

1486. Abbeville, at the shop of Jean du Pré and Pierre Gérard; folio, in two volumes. “The first ten books of Monseigneur Saint Augustine’s *City of God*, translated by Raoul de Preulles.” At the end of volume I: “Printed in the town of Abbeville by Jean du Pré and Pierre Gérard, merchant booksellers, completed on 28 November 1486.” Volume II: “The seven final books.” At the end: “Printed by the same men at Abbeville, 7 April 1486, after Easter.”

Maettarius commemorates this edition; so does Debure in *Bibliographie instructive*, vol. I, p. 248, and the elder Debure in the *Catalogue of the Library of the Duke de la Vallière*, vol. I, p. 167. It is also noted in the *Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris*. This is one of the few books printed at Abbeville. Yet the age of the translation itself is greater than that of the edition.

Its author, whose name is variously rendered—sometimes de Preulles, sometimes de Praelles, Praesles, Presles, and even de Praieres, while in Latin it appears as de Praellis, de Praieriis, or Preslaeus—flourished during the reign of Charles V, king of France, and held the office of master of petitions under him. He was born from the illicit union of Radulphus de Praellis, formerly a counselor of Philip the Fair in 1315, while his father was being held in harsh custody. But our Radulphus, already an old man, obtained the rights of a legitimate son through the favor of his king in 1376. He died in November 1382.

He had become famous for various writings, composed both in the vernacular and in Latin, when, late in life, he was compelled by a special royal command and stipend to prepare this translation of Augustine’s book. It is said that he began it on 1 November 1371 and completed it on 1 September 1375. [Note: The same author produced a French translation of the Bible, which P. le Long accurately described from a specimen in *Bibliotheca sacra*, p. 318; it too was owed to that king, who was inclined toward letters. Cf. Lancelot in *Mémoires de l’Académie des Inscriptions*, vol. XIII, p. 656.]

Thirty codices were available to him. Yet he followed them in such a way that he devoted less attention to the explanation of the words than to the meaning, and, obeying the king’s command, preferred to pursue the truth and clarity of the sense through circumlocutions of expression rather than endanger it by adhering too closely to the words. To make the work easier to read, he divided each book into several chapters, though I do not know whether this division agrees with that of the Latin text today.

Nor was he content merely to bring Augustine close to his countrymen through the eloquence of the French language. Wherever Augustine seemed to speak with greater learning, he also acted as his interpreter, appending to each chapter an exposition in which he discussed mythological, historical, philosophical, and other subjects of more recondite learning, insofar as the state of scholarship at that time permitted. He thereby showed that he was far superior to the learned men of his age.

The authors from whom he drew, with only a few exceptions, are no earlier than the seventh century. He frequently praises Isidore of Seville, Orosius, Paul the Deacon, Hugh, Papias, Fulgentius, the *Catholicon*, Nicholas Trevet, Vincent of Beauvais, Alanus in *The Complaint of Nature*, John of Salisbury, William of Paris, Peter Comestor, Helinandus, and others. He also occasionally cites Paul the Deacon’s *Marvels of the World*, Muhammad’s *Qur’an*, and John of Meun as the author of the French tale of the Rose.

He incorporated much material from both the history of his own time and the earlier history of France, as well as various traditions and popular superstitions scattered throughout the work. Lancelot, formerly a distinguished member of the Paris Academy of Inscriptions and Letters, presented some of these by way of specimen. Two of his essays on Radulphus Preslaeus and his writings are included in the memoirs of that Academy, vol. XIII, pp. 607–665.

Through the praiseworthy diligence of that scholar, everything concerning the author of this translation is now considered established according to the evidence of the best documents. At the same time, the darkness with which Crucius of Le Mans (La Croix du Maine) had enveloped the matter in *Bibliothèque française*, p. 427—and which the conjectures of the authors of the *Cologne Library* had done little to dispel (p. 740, no. 157)—has been illuminated by the clearest light.

Among all his writings, Lancelot carefully examined this book, which very few had seen and, so far as I know, no one had actually inspected, and he set forth its principal merits with sound judgment. On p. 654 he further lists several notable manuscript codices, all preserved in the Royal Library at Paris and identified by their respective numbers.

This first edition of the translation is exceedingly rare; another edition made long afterward is no less so.

1531. Paris, at the shop of Galiot du Pré, by Nicolas Savetier; folio, in two volumes. “*The City of God of Monseigneur Saint Augustine*, translated from Latin into French by Raoul de Praesles.” A splendid copy was formerly counted among the ornaments of the Library of the Duke de la Vallière. Cf. the catalogue, vol. I, p. 168, no. 458. The same edition is praised in the *Catalogue of the British Museum Library*.

It should be noted that Lancelot, like the Cologne cataloguers, also mentions this edition, but says that it appeared at the establishment of Galiot du Pré, whereas Debure, in the place cited, attributes it to Nicolas Savetier. We have therefore followed the conjecture and placed both names in the title, suspecting that one acted as bookseller and the other as printer.

1570. Paris, at the shop of Nicolas Chesneau; folio. “*The City of God of Saint Augustine*, translated into French by Gentian Hervet.” *Cat. Bibl. Mus. Britt.* Cf. *M. Bibl. Col.*

1585. Paris, at the shop of Michel Sonnius; folio. “*Saint Augustine’s City of God*, illustrated with the commentaries of Jean-Louis Vives, translated into French by Gentian Hervet, with the annotations and observations of François de Belleforest. Third edition, enlarged.” *Cat. Bibl. Reg.* The Cologne cataloguers report that it was reprinted in Paris in 1610, folio.

1655. Paris, at the shop of Pierre le Petit; folio. “*Saint Augustine, On the City of God*, translated into French by de Ceriziers, chaplain to the King.” *Cat. Bibl. Reg. et Casanat.*

1665 and 1667. Paris, at the shop of Pierre le Petit; octavo, in two volumes. “*Saint Augustine’s City of God*, translated into French by Louis Giry, volumes I and II, containing the first ten books.” *Cat. Bibl. Reg.*

1675. Paris, at the shop of André Pralard; octavo, in two volumes. “*Saint Augustine’s City of God*, translated into French and revised against several ancient manuscripts, with remarks and notes containing corrections of the text by Pierre Lombert.” *Cat. Bibl. Reg. et Ducis de la Valière.* The same edition was reprinted that year at Brussels and in 1693 at Paris, in two volumes. *Cat. Bibl. Thott.*

1701. Paris, at the shop of Nicolas Pepie; octavo, in two volumes. “*Saint Augustine’s City of God*, translated into French and revised against the edition of the Benedictine Fathers, with remarks, etc.”

1736. Amsterdam, at the shop of Pierre Mortier; octavo, in four volumes. “*Saint Augustine’s City of God*, translated into French and revised against several manuscripts, with remarks and notes containing numerous important corrections of the Latin text, and the Life of M. Lombert.”

The notes deal chiefly with the translation and excuse its freedom on the grounds that the translator owed a duty to elegance and meaning, and that the mutually divergent character of languages demands such freedom. Hence it seemed sufficient not to repeat the same observations everywhere, but to make them only concerning the first eleven books. He states that the corrections announced in the title were drawn from the readings of approximately ten or eleven French manuscripts and several Vatican manuscripts, which the Benedictine Fathers themselves had made available to him.

The same translation, in as many volumes in duodecimo, was printed in the same year at the same place by Jacques Rollin. Like the preceding edition, it bears the translator’s life on its title page; it is recorded in the *Catalogue of the Royal Library*, vol. I, p. 379. The same translation, printed in four duodecimo volumes at Paris in 1737, is praised in the *Catalogue of the Firmiana Library*.

### Spanish

1614. Madrid, folio. “Saint Augustine, *On the City of God*, twenty-two books, in Spanish, by Antonio de Roys y Rozas.” The Cologne cataloguers praise it.

1676. Antwerp, folio. The same books in the same translation. *Cat. Bibl. Thott.* They are said to have been reprinted there again in 1696, folio, in the *Library of the Church of Cologne*.

[Col. 0159A] The Cologne cataloguers report a Dutch translation printed at Leiden in 1621, citing the *Catalogue of the Utrecht Library*, vol. II, p. 3.

Possevinus, on the authority of Eisengrenius, mentions a German translation by Joannes Godofredus of Odernheim, who is said to have been pastor of the church at Oppenheim around 1495. Gemeiner, in *Regensburg Municipal Library*, p. 197, praises another, by Hans Nicolaus Sigmar of Schüsselberg, printed at Regensburg in 1666, quarto; he indicates, however, that it contains only the first book.

## XXVI.—(75) The Book *On the Good of Widowhood*

1517. Paris, at the shop of Jean Petit; quarto. “*On the State of Widowhood; On the Manner of Praying to God; The Life of Saint Monica; Minor Works of Saint Augustine*, translated by Adrian Gemelli (Jumel), priest, doctor of theology, and grand archdeacon of Laon in Picardy.” Du Verdier, recent edition, vol. I, p. 7. The treatise *On Praying to God* is counted among the letters as number 130.

## XXVII.—(79) The Book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*

1611. Augsburg, octavo. “The book of Augustine *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, now first published through the efforts of Marcus Welser.”

It had been found at Fiesole—a town in the Florentine territory, now called Fiesoli—in the library of the abbey of Saint Bartholomew belonging to the Lateran Canons Regular. From there its copy was sent from Rome to Marcus Welser, an Augsburg magistrate, by Cardinal Scipio Cobellutius, then secretary and confidential officer of the supreme pontiff.

Welser eagerly awaited for some time the editions said to be in preparation at Rome and Florence with the utmost care. But since the matter clearly indicated that this would be a lengthy undertaking, he judged that he would win the gratitude of pious and learned men who loved ancient learning—and that the Roman and Florentine editors themselves would not object—if he meanwhile offered Augustine’s bare words for use and enjoyment. He therefore had the copy sent from Rome faithfully reproduced, with the variant readings which had been compared in the margin likewise written in the outer margin, while other readings were placed at the foot of the page. The editor states that most of these were owed to Marcus Welser, then a canon of Freising, and says that they had been noted almost impromptu while reading; a few, he adds, were somewhat bolder and had been rejected by the author.

He emphatically declares that he himself admitted no readings into the text merely because they seemed persuasive, however plausible. Joannes Clericus reprinted this preface in the *Appendix Augustiniana*, vol. XII, Antwerp edition, p. 607.

Those long-awaited Roman and Florentine editions, however, never appeared. The work was soon afterward published at Paris together with the book *Against the Second Reply of Julian*, edited by Menardus; see no. 98. Nor do I doubt that it is among the works of Augustine and his disciples which we have brought forward above.

## XXVIII.—(80) The Book *On the Correction of the Donatists*

Nicolaus Bergius of Reval published this book separately at Stockholm in 1696, octavo, under the title: “The book of Saint Augustine *On the Moderate Coercion of Heretics*, addressed to Count Boniface.”

## XXIX.—(82, 83) Augustine on the Gospel of John and on His First Epistle, *To the Parthians*

No date, place, or printer; folio. *Augustine on John.*

[Col. 0160A]

These words, serving as the title, are printed in larger letters on the first leaf, which is otherwise blank. At the beginning of the text: “Here happily begins the first treatise of the divine Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, on the Gospel according to John: from what is written, ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word,’ up to what he says, ‘And the darkness did not comprehend it.’” At the end: “Here happily ends the exposition of the divine Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, on the Gospel according to John.”

It is preceded by an *Annotation*, or inventory of the principal sentences, as well as the titles or rubrics of the treatises, occupying ten leaves. The printing [Col. 0160B] is in small Gothic type, in two columns. The sheets are signed with letters, but the folio numbers and catchwords are lacking. At the top of the page not only the treatises but also the chapters are indicated. In the text itself, the words of the Gospel, or other biblical passages, and the beginnings of the commentaries are distinguished by medium and larger type respectively.

Marginal notes have been added, giving either parallel passages or variant readings of biblical passages cited by Augustine. In view of these features, everyone will recognize the remarkable similarity of this edition to the Amerbach editions, whose copies we have frequently listed above among the Augustinian books. I would nevertheless readily accept the view of the distinguished Braun, who states in volume II of the *Notes on Literary History*, p. 33, that it was printed at Nuremberg by Anton Koberger—provided that his judgment rests not merely on the similarity of the type, but on the description of the entire work. One further consideration is that Koberger issued many works without his name, whereas Amerbach issued either none or very few without his name.

### Translations

1670. Rome, printed by the press of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith; quarto. “Several chapters from different treatises on the Gospel of John, concerning the Holy Spirit, in Latin and Greek, translated by Maximus Planudes,” in the *Golden Minor Works* collected by P. Arcudius, p. 631 onward.

In the *Library of the Greater Church of Cologne* I find a book on the Holy Spirit collected from various Augustinian treatises on John, said to have appeared at Basel in 1578 in Greek and Latin. From this I seem to understand that the book indicated is none other than Leunclavius’s *Embassy of Manuel Comnenus to the Armenians*, into which several chapters on the Trinity translated from Augustine into Greek have been inserted.

But if this is the work which Lipenius intended as his authority in *Theological Library*, vol. II, p. 783, he is mistaken, for those words are not found there at all. I do not know, however, whether Augustine’s book *On the Holy Spirit*, Geneva 1540, octavo, which is listed in the *Catalogue of the Bernese Library*, vol. I, p. 15, may perhaps belong here.

1670. Paris, at the shop of Jean-Baptiste Coignard; duodecimo. “Homilies of Saint Augustine on the First Epistle of Saint John: a new translation.”

1700. Paris, at the shop of Jean-Baptiste Coignard; octavo, in four volumes. “The treatises of Saint Augustine on the Gospel of Saint John and his Epistle to the Parthians, translated into French from the edition of the Benedictine Fathers, with summaries in the margin, by Philippe Goisbaud du Bois.”

## XXX.—(84) *On the Grace of Christ and Original Sin*, against Pelagius and Coelestius

1687. Mainz, printed by Peter Hermans; octavo. “The book of the divine Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, *Against Pelagius and Coelestius, On the Grace of Christ*, illustrated with a brief continuous commentary by R. P. Carolus Josephus Tricassinus, of the Order of Friars Minor Capuchin of Saint Francis.” Cf. *Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensia*, supplement, vol. I, p. 134.

The editor’s book *Effective Grace Refuted from the Books of Saint Augustine*, printed by the same printer in that very year, concerns this book of Augustine. It is reviewed in the same volume of the *Acta Eruditorum*, pp. 128–133. They state that the author intended to show that the Pelagians were accused by Augustine of heresy because they admitted no grace of God whatsoever as necessary to the will, not because they held grace to be indifferent—that is, such that the human will might either obey or resist it.

Tricassinus had already taught nearly the same thing in his book *On the Nature of Original Sin according to the Mind of Saint Augustine*, etc., published at Paris in 1677, quarto. The Cologne author, however, believes that it was printed not at Mainz but at Troyes, Tricassinus’s native city.

### Translation

1738. Paris, at the shop of François Babuty; duodecimo. “The two books of Saint Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin*, translated into French from the edition of the Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur.”

## XXXI.—(93) Two Books *On Adulterous Marriages*

1698. Jena, printed by Johann Bielke; quarto. “The two books of the divine Aurelius Augustine *On Adulterous Marriages*, addressed to Pollentius, with notes by a most celebrated jurist, in which the Church’s doctrine concerning the dissolution of marriage is illustrated.”

The author of the notes is said to have been Johann Schilter, formerly a professor at Strasbourg, eminent among jurists both for talent and learning. The work was published and prefaced by Georg Schubart, then professor of humane letters at Jena.

They say that the occasion and cause of Schilter’s wish to remain concealed were provided by Ulrich Obrecht, a man distinguished at Strasbourg for elegant learning and many published writings. When, after the city of Strasbourg had been brought under the authority of Louis XIV, Obrecht was induced by the Jesuits’ enticements to enter the papal camp, and subsequently received as his reward the king’s appointment as president of the Strasbourg senate, he abolished the practice accepted in the courts of dissolving marriages on account of adultery—undoubtedly in obedience to the opinions of the fathers of that society—and is also said, for that reason, to have translated this book of Augustine into German. Cf. Morerius in the *Dictionary* (Amsterdam edition, supplement).

Although I would not dare assert this to posterity, I nevertheless believe that Augustine’s position was loudly invoked by the advocates in this case, and that this very circumstance moved Schilter—not to undertake the task of evading it, as one could not have expected from such a man, but to bring it once more before the court, examine it from every side, and present it after careful consideration. The circumstances of the time could easily have persuaded him to conceal his name in order to avoid hostility.

Let us now append a brief survey of his discussion, as it was outlined by Fridericus Benedictus Carpzov in his review of this book in the *Acta Eruditorum Lipsiensia* for 1698, p. 340:

“First,” he says, “Schilter observes that the controversy is twofold: one question concerns the right of divorce, which Augustine denied to be permitted except on account of adultery; the other concerns the right to marry again, which Augustine grants to no one while the other party is alive, not even on account of adultery—except that in chapter 6 he hints that Christian spouses alone are bound by this precept. From this one may infer that a second marriage was less strictly forbidden to one who separated from an adulterous non-Christian.

“The author of the notes teaches that Pollentius errs in the first question, carried away by the customs and laws of the Hebrews and Romans, among whom the liberty of divorce had become widespread. In this respect, therefore, Augustine’s eloquence and subtlety in argument triumph, although his arguments do not always establish what Augustine himself wishes to infer from them.

“Thus he observes that the Pauline passage, 1 Corinthians 7:10–11, is correctly understood and explained neither by Augustine nor by Pollentius. Augustine, because of a preconceived opinion, takes the woman who separates from her husband to mean one who divorces or is repudiated because of adultery, and thus, as the schools say, begs the question. Pollentius, on the other hand, accepts what the Apostle places under that condition as though it could lawfully happen, and thus wrongly understands statements of fact as statements of law.

“In the second part of the controversy, concerning the right to marry again after a divorce has taken place, Schilter notes that Augustine without cause departs from Christ’s plainly expressed words in Matthew 5:32 and does violence to them. Augustine wishes the matters removed from the rule by the exceptive particles to function not as exceptions but as examples, against common sense and the proper rules of interpretation, which refer them back to the principles of grammar, logic, and the subject matter itself.

“He demonstrates that Augustine’s remaining arguments are not so constituted as to compel us to seek refuge in a twisted interpretation of clear words, by exposing the paralogism in each argument. These are broadly the matters discussed and noted in the first book.

“In the second book the same controversy is examined, presented once more and more clearly by Pollentius and supported by new arguments. Augustine answers them, defending and refining his own position.

“The most learned Schilter follows Augustine here too κατὰ πόδα—‘step by step’—and examines with great judgment what is at issue, how much weight belongs to the arguments and replies advanced, and what points agree or disagree with one another. At the end, from book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 57, he observes that Augustine himself does not sufficiently trust or satisfy himself in this position.”

Thus far Carpzovius.

It remains for us to observe that this little work by Schilter is now extremely rare. Our own library lacks it, and we have searched in vain for any mention of it in the catalogues of the principal libraries, except in the catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.

## XXXII.—(98) *Against the Second Reply of Julian*, Six Books of the Unfinished Work

1617. Paris, at the shop of Sebastian Chappelet; octavo. “The two first books of the unfinished work of Saint Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, *Against the Second Reply of Julian*. Now first published from manuscript codices. Also added is Augustine’s book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, published a few years ago. Now first brought to light through the care of the distinguished Menardus, magistrate of Angers.”

The editor, not without distinction, sprinkled the work with a few but choice scholarly notes. He dedicated it to Dionysius de Marquemont, archbishop of Lyon, in a letter dated 4 August 1616. The same edition was printed in folio that year by the same printers. Cf. the *Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris*.

1642. Leuven, at the shop of Cornelius Coenestenius; quarto. “The first two books of Saint Aurelius Augustine’s *Against the Second Reply of Julian*, the unfinished work, restored by Brother Michael Paludanus of Ghent, Augustinian Hermit.” The same books are prefixed in the form in which they had been published at Paris in 1617. *Cat. Bibl. Casanat.*

—Leuven, at the shop of Jacob Gezers; quarto. “The first two books of Saint Aurelius Augustine’s *Unfinished Work Against the Second Reply of Julian*, according to the recension of Michael Paludanus.” *Cat. Bibl. Reg. Paris.* The Cologne cataloguers report, on Rivetus’s authority, that in this reprint the innumerable errors of the earlier edition were corrected solely by conjecture.

[Col. 0163C] 1654. Paris, at the expense of Simeon Piget; folio. “The six books of the Catholic bishop Saint Augustine *Against Julian the Pelagian Heretic*, the completed work.” In the supplement to Hieronymus Vignerius, vol. II, p. 1322.

Julian’s second reply consisted of eight books. Augustine undertook to refute it by opposing one book to each of Julian’s. But death overtook him before he could complete more than six books, and thus his reply remained unfinished, as Possidius also testifies.

For a long time only two of these books were available in print, published by Claudius Menardus at Paris in 1617. In 1654, however, Hieronymus Vignier, a member of the Society of Jesus, who had become well known that year through supplements to earlier Augustinian editions, not only recovered four more books from a manuscript of the abbey of Clairvaux, but also convinced himself—and attempted to convince others—that in these six books he was presenting Augustine’s complete work.

He based this claim, first, on the fact that none of the codices of Possidius which he had examined contained the word “unfinished”; second, on the fact that in the Clairvaux manuscript the little word *explicit* occurs only at the end of the sixth book and is not added to the others, from which he inferred that the end of the entire work was indicated there; and third—and this would have been by far the most important point, had it been proved—on the fact that the sixth book was longer than the others and that both Julian’s attacks and Augustine’s replies were more extended in it than in the rest.

He therefore concluded that it seemed probable that the three books of Julian had been collected together in this sixth book, and he attempted to establish this from Augustine’s final words, in which, he argues, everything agrees perfectly with the general conclusion drawn from the material.

The Benedictines, however, in volume X, part II, pronounce all these arguments invalid and demonstrate this clearly by contrary examples. The editor prefixed a discussion of Julian and his writings against Blessed Augustine, together with testimonies of ancient authors who mention these six books and brought passages from them into their own commentaries.

### Translation

1736. Paris, at the shop of François Babuty; duodecimo, in two volumes. “The six books of Saint Augustine against Julian, defender of the Pelagian heresy, translated into French from the edition of the Benedictine Fathers.”

## XXXIII.—(99) *Enchiridion to Laurentus*

[Col. 0164B] **FIFTEENTH CENTURY.**—No date or place, small folio. *Saint Augustine’s Enchiridion.* It consists of thirty-three leaves. It begins immediately with the prologue, in these words: “Here begins the book of the holy Augustine, the *Enchiridion*, on faith, hope, and charity.” At the end of the text, on the verso of leaf XXXI: “Thanks be to God.” Then, after the titles of the chapters, which begin on leaf XXXII, on the recto of leaf XXXIII: “Amen.”

The distinguished Seemiller describes this truly ancient edition in fascicle I, p. 156 onward, among those books whose printers he did not dare investigate even by conjecture. As for the date, he does not doubt that it was printed before 1477. He states that the letters in which it was produced appear, because of their irregularity, not to have been cast but engraved, although he forgot to identify their type. There is only one punctuation mark, namely the period, and that itself is used very rarely. There were no signs indicating pages or leaves, nor any initial letters; the chapters, however, were distinguished by Roman numerals. There were thirty-four lines to a page.

## Sixteenth Century

**1527. Augsburg or Cologne; octavo.** St. Aurelius Augustine’s *Enchiridion on Christian Doctrine*, addressed to Laurentius, first official secretary of the city of Rome, together with the same author’s little book *On the Essence of Divinity*. Hendreich cites it in *Pandectae Brandenburgicae*, p. 341, but indicates the place of printing so carelessly that I leave undecided whether he intended Augsburg or Cologne.

**1552. Cologne, at the press of Peter Horst; octavo.** “St. Aurelius Augustine’s *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Charity*, to which is added his book *On Faith and Works*.” Catalogue of the Thott Library.

**1575. [Geneva], at the press of Eustathius Vignon; octavo.** *The Enchiridion of the Lord Aurelius Augustine to Laurentius, first official secretary of the city of Rome, or a summary of the chief and principal points of the whole Christian religion. A most useful book for all who desire to possess, directly from Augustine himself—and indeed from Augustine already advanced in years—the briefest epitome of Augustinian doctrine; cleansed from the many errors and glosses with which it had previously abounded, on the basis of an old manuscript, and illustrated with commentaries. By Lambert Daneau. A threefold index is added to the work.*

In his dedicatory epistle to Edzard, prince of East Frisia, Lambert Daneau extols the plainly divine virtues of Augustine’s writings. He then proceeds to complain of the unjust fate that befell them shortly after their author’s death: some portions had been lost through the ravages of time, while others had been corrupted and interpolated through the malice of wicked men. From this he takes occasion to commend his own labor, boasting that by it he had not only healed the wounds in the wording but had also produced Augustine himself as his witness and interpreter.

He gives no further information about the manuscript he used to correct the text. Before the work itself there are, besides the epistle just mentioned, a discussion of the method of Augustine’s books and of the manner in which they should be studied, as well as *Prolegomena* to the book now published, in which he discusses its title, usefulness, date, and Laurentius, to whom it is addressed. In the commentaries, both Augustinian and Calvinist doctrines are explained at great length, and the views that this age had begun to cherish are vigorously defended against dissenters.

**1579. [Geneva], at the press of Eustathius Vignon; octavo.** The same book, a second edition enlarged and revised by the author himself.

**1583. Geneva, folio.** The same recension of this book, reprinted in Lambert Daneau’s *Theological Opuscula*, pp. 729–896.

**1597. There likewise, octavo.** The same recension, cited by Hendreich in *Pandectae Brandenburgicae*.

## Seventeenth Century

**1604. Wittenberg, at the expense of Paul Helwich, printed by the Cratonian press; octavo.** “The *Enchiridion* of the Lord Aurelius Augustine to Laurentius, first official secretary of the city of Rome, together with his little book *On the Essence of Divinity*, which appears among Augustine’s works in volume four. Published separately for the benefit of students of theology, with a preface and dedication by Solomon Gesner, theologian of Wittenberg, addressed to the illustrious and noble Barons Richard and John von Tschernemel, on the true reading of the Fathers and the usefulness of reading them.”

**1641. Leiden, duodecimo.** The same book. Hendreich records it in *Pandectae Brandenburgicae*.

**1656. Helmstedt, quarto.** The same book, according to Hendreich in *Pandectae Brandenburgicae*. But in all these notices this man’s work is so erratic that, although I have proceeded cautiously, I fear I may have misunderstood him. With regard to this edition, I fear that he is in error because he confuses different works of Augustine: the *Enchiridion of Christian Doctrine* with the four books *On Christian Doctrine*, which were published at Helmstedt in this form in 1655.

**1665. Paris, at the press of Étienne Loyson.** *Augustine’s Enchiridion to Laurentius, first official secretary of the city of Rome.* It appears in the *Spiritual Work*, beginning on p. 129.

## Eighteenth Century

**1705. Leipzig, at the expense of the widow of Johann Heinrich, printed by Johann Heinrich Richter; octavo.** The *Enchiridion of the Lord Aurelius Augustine to Laurentius, first official secretary of the city of Rome*, reprinted for the use of studious youth, with a preface on theological study by Dr. Adam Rechenberg.

### Translations

Demetrius Cydonius is said to have translated Augustine’s *Enchiridion* into Greek, says Possevinus, *Apparatus sacer*, vol. I, p. 153. But he does not say where he obtained this information. Certainly this translation has not been published; and if it ever existed, it must still be hidden in the Vatican Library.

> **Note:** Hendreich, in *Pandectae Brandenburgicae*, p. 342, cites a manuscript translation by Demetrius, referring to Hottinger’s *Bibliothecarius*, p. 372. Yet there is profound silence about it there.

Of the two French translations, we mentioned one by Colletet above, when we were cataloguing the editions of the books *On Christian Doctrine*. There remains the other, by Antoine Arnauld, which appeared as follows.

**1648. Paris, at the press of Antoine Vitré; octavo.** “St. Augustine’s book *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, translated into French by Antoine Arnauld, doctor of the Sorbonne, with the Latin text following, revised against six ancient manuscripts.” Hendreich adds that this translation was reprinted in 1652 and 1656.

**1681. Copenhagen, octavo.** The same book in Danish, “translated by Henrik Olafsen.” See the catalogue of the Thott Library.

A work especially related to this book of Augustine was published anonymously under the title *The Moral Theology of St. Augustine, in which the precept concerning the love of God is fully treated, etc.*, by E. B. S. M. R. D.; concerning it, see the *Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica Coloniensis*, p. 744.

# XXXIV. (100) The Book on Caring for the Dead

**1543. Paris, from the workshop of Jean Palier; octavo.** “The one book of the Lord Augustine *On Caring for the Dead*, addressed to Paulinus; also, in Latin, a homily of Chrysostom, explaining that one should not mourn for the dead but pray for them.” Maittaire, vol. III, part I, p. 345.

Lipenius, *Bibliotheca theologica*, vol. II, p. 329 and vol. I, p. 498, and, following him, the Cologne bibliographers, mention a German translation of this book by Vitus Miletus (Mainz, 1604 and 1634, duodecimo). In the latter catalogue one will also find some excellent observations on Augustine’s views concerning the dead and the cult of the saints, gathered from the writings of learned theologians.

# XXXV. (102) The Rule for the Servants of God, or, more correctly, the Rule Written for Nuns, formerly Epistle 211 or 109

Bernard Vinding and Prosper Stellart, both members of the Augustinian order, were the first to recognize that the *Rule for the Servants of God* had been extracted from the epistle just mentioned and adapted for men. It is unknown by whom or for whom this was done. It nevertheless appears to have happened very early.

The Benedictines observe that it forms the principal part of the very ancient Rule of Tarnat, that it is cited in the *Concordia regularum* by Benedict of Aniane, and that in the thousand-year-old Corbie manuscript it is presented in an adaptation for men and joined together with the work entitled the *Second Rule*.

It must be noted, however, that in this transformation the first part of the epistle, beginning with the words “Just as severity is prepared,” and continuing to “But rather the tears of Peter the shepherd,” was entirely discarded. In its place these few additional words are usually prefixed:

> “Above all, dearest brothers, let God be loved, then one’s neighbor, because these commandments have been given to us principally.”

In this form the work has often been printed separately from collections of Augustine’s works, so that it either forms a volume by itself, with commentaries by Hugh of Saint-Victor or Lairveltzius added, or is printed together with other constitutions of the Augustinian order.

Since this order is extremely extensive, however, and since so many different congregations are included under that name, whose constitutions—more or less connected with this rule—have often been printed, though by their nature they are handled by few and remain nearly hidden, it is easy to understand how difficult it is to compile an accurate or complete catalogue of editions of this rule.

I myself have seen very few of them, nor have I found the writers of catalogues of famous libraries sufficiently reliable in this matter to know whom I could follow when those editions failed me. Nevertheless, I have gathered what I could, and I seem at least to have achieved this: whatever is missing or incorrectly stated may, if others consider it worthwhile, be more easily supplied or corrected.

> **Note:** The editions marked with a cross are those that I found cited only in the catalogue of the Bodleian Library. That catalogue rightly ranks among the finest indexes of public libraries, but it is often adapted more to the needs of librarians than to general usefulness: books containing particular treatises are not identified by their titles, but by symbols indicating where they are found on the shelves. Moreover, I do not know whether all editions of the Constitutions of the Augustinian Order place this rule at the beginning. Their number could easily be increased from Lipenius, *Bibliotheca theologica*, vol. I, pp. 118 ff.; Hendreich, *Pandectae Brandenburgicae*, p. 343; and the catalogue of the Casanatense Library, under “Constitutiones.”

## Fifteenth Century

**1481. Rome, folio.** The Rule of St. Augustine with a commentary by Ambrose Coriolanus. Orlandi, pp. 284 and 316.

**1490. Strasbourg, printed by Martin Schott; folio.** *Canons of Aurelius Augustine, providing a way of life for every condition according to the threefold rule that he published.* The following titles appear in smaller type on the first page:

> Prelates are taught to obtain the authority to govern.  
> Here, subjects are taught to render the duty of obedience to their pastors.  
> All faithful Christians receive their moral instruction.

At the end:

> *The work of the canons of Aurelius Augustine, with a new and excellent interpretation by Ambrose Coriolanus, a most distinguished man and master general of the entire order of the Hermits of St. Augustine, was most carefully corrected and revised by the distinguished men Tilmann Limperger, a brother of the order of the Hermits of St. Augustine; Jacob Fedderer; and John Scherrer, professors of the liberal arts and formed bachelors of sacred theology. It was printed at Strasbourg by the skill and expense of the industrious Martin Schott, in the year of salvation 1490.*

To all this are appended six distichs addressed to the reader, signed with the letters F. D. L.

At the beginning appears a preface by Tilmann Limperger to Nicholas Friess, an Augustinian theologian and bishop of Tripoli. From the first folio through the eighth, there follows a life of Augustine by Coriolanus and a commendation of his rule. Then, beginning on folio IX, there are *Commentaries on the Rule of the divine Augustine*, published by Ambrose Coriolanus in dialogue form; they continue through the end of folio CXVIII.

After this, separately, from folio CXX through folio CXXXIII, there are printed Ambrose Coriolanus’s commentaries on the first rule of St. Augustine, together with three of his speeches in praise of, and on certain teachings of, this doctor.

The preface placed before this section on the reverse of folio CXIX is by Oliverius Servius of Tolentino, addressed to Guillaume de Estouteville, bishop of Ostia and cardinal. In it he says that he is publishing these materials for the first time; it seems, however, to refer to another edition that preceded this one.

The printers took great care not to allow blank pages. Accordingly, here and there—for example, on the reverse of folio VIII, on the same page as the title, and on the first page of folio CXIX—one sees a woodcut image of Augustine.

This work may also be compared with Braun, *Notitia historico-litteraria*, vol. II, p. 195.

**1500. Venice, at the expense of the Giunta press, printed by John of Speyer; quarto.** St. Augustine’s *Rule* together with his *Life*. It belongs among the four rules first approved, which will be discussed under Benedict; this edition will also be described more fully there.

## Sixteenth Century

**1516. Lyon, octavo.** St. Augustine’s *Rule*.

**[1517.] Without place or printer, octavo.** The *Rule of Blessed Augustine, bishop*. It appears in the *Constitutions of the Brothers Hermits of St. Augustine*, arranged according to the form of the apostolic privileges for the reform of Germany. It is preceded by an exhortation to all the convents of the order of the Brothers Hermits of St. Augustine throughout Germany, issued by John of Staupitz, prior general and at that time vicar for the business of the said reform, and dated 1517.

**1526. Paris.** *Hugh of Saint-Victor’s Exposition of the Rule of the Lord Augustine*, published in the first complete collection of his works made that year. I do not know whether the Rule itself was printed there as well. Hugh’s commentary was later reprinted in the Venetian edition (at the press of Giovanni Battista Somasco) of 1588, the Cologne edition of 1617, and the latest edition, which we shall list separately.

**1550. Venice, quarto.** *St. Augustine’s Rule for the Servants of God, or, more correctly, the Rule prescribed for nuns; preceded by a fragment of the Rule given to clerics together with the Second Rule*—the latter spurious. It appears toward the end of the four rules first approved, collected by Giovanni Francesco Brixiano of the Congregation of St. Justina of the Order of St. Benedict.

**1561. Venice, printed by Bernardino Fasiano at the expense of the Lateran Canons Regular; April; quarto.** St. Augustine’s *Rule*, with the exposition of Hugh of Saint-Victor in Latin and Italian. Catalogue of the Pinelli Library. See Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, edition of Mansi, vol. III, p. 301.

**1575. Cologne, octavo.** St. Augustine’s *Rule* and the Constitutions of the Brothers of the Order of Preachers. Catalogue of the Bodleian Library; add Hendreich, *Pandectae Brandenburgicae*.

**1581. Dillingen, quarto.** St. Augustine’s *Rule* with the commentary of Hugh of Saint-Victor. Lipenius, *Bibliotheca theologica*, vol. I, p. 119.

**1582. Venice.** St. Augustine’s *Rule*.

**1585. Mantua, quarto.** St. Augustine’s *Rule* and the Constitutions of the Hermits of the Lombard Congregation of Observance. Cited by Gregory Rivius Puritanus—that is, Georg Burchard Lauterbach—in *History of Western Monasticism*, vol. I, p. 45.

## Seventeenth Century

**1601. Venice.** St. Augustine’s *Rule*, with Hugh’s commentary. According to Lipenius.

**1605. Como, at the press of Jerome Froira; octavo.** The same, with Hugh of Saint-Victor’s exposition. Possevinus.

**1614. Cologne, octavo.** The same, with the commentary—or *Optics of the Regulars*—of Servatius de Lairvelt.

**1736. Ghent, octavo.** St. Augustine’s *Rule* and the Constitutions of the Brothers of the Order of Preachers. Hendreich.

**1618. Cologne, octavo.** The same, with Lairveltzius’s commentary, cited by Lipenius, vol. II, p. 647.

**1620. Barcelona, octavo.** St. Augustine’s *Rule* and the Constitutions of the Brothers of the Order of Preachers. Catalogue of the Library of St. Augustine at the Nest in Naples.

**1625. Paris, at the press of Sebastian Chappelet, Jacob’s Street, under the sign of the Rosary; octavo.** The *Rule of St. Augustine, bishop*, and the Constitutions of the Brothers and Sisters of the Order of Preachers, with declarations drawn from the acts of the General Chapters, etc., etc.

**Ingolstadt.** St. Augustine’s *Rule*.

**Rome.** St. Augustine’s *Rule* with the exposition of Hugh of Saint-Victor. Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*.

**1648. Rouen, folio.** Hugh of Saint-Victor’s *Exposition of the Rule of Augustine*, in his works, vol. II, p. 5.

**1660. Munich, duodecimo.** Augustine’s *Rule*. The Constitutions of the Canons Regular of the Gallican Congregation of the same St. Augustine were added. Dated 1638. Lipenius, vol. I, p. 118.

**1661. Rome, quarto.** The *Epistle 109 of Aurelius Augustine of Hippo*, containing the Rule prescribed for nuns. It appears in Holstenius’s *Code of Rules*, part III, containing the rules of the holy Fathers for virgins, beginning on p. 1.

**1663. Paris, at the press of Louis Billaine; quarto.** The same epistle, reprinted there in the same collection of rules.

## Eighteenth Century

**1759. Augsburg, folio.** The *Epistle 109 of Aurelius Augustine of Hippo*, containing the Rule written for nuns, in part III of Holstenius’s *Code of Rules*, newly edited by Father Mariano Broglio. Vol. I, pp. 347 ff.

### Translations

It seemed best to arrange the translations chronologically. English translations come first, followed immediately by Spanish and Italian translations; French translations occupy the final place.

### English

**1525. London, quarto.** “The Exposition of Saint Augustine’s Rule according to the great cleric and holy saint, Saint Hugh, called de Sancto Victore, by the wretch of Syon, Richard Whytford. Printed at London in Fleet Street by me, Wynkyn de Worde, 1525, on the twenty-eighth of November.” Maittaire.

### Spanish

**1600. Córdoba.** “The Rule of Saint Augustine Explained,” by Juan de Montoya, a Dominican of Madrid.

### Italian

**1613. Florence, at the press of Bartolomeo Sermartelli; quarto.** “The Rule of St. Augustine.” We noted another, older translation, with the Latin text, under the year 1561.

**1635. Viterbo, octavo.** “St. Augustine’s Constitutions of the Nuns of Penance.” Catalogue of the Library of St. Angelo at the Nest in Naples.

**1654. Venice, at the press of Giolito; quarto.** “The Rule of St. Augustine, bishop and doctor of the holy Catholic Church, contained in the book of the Epistles, in Epistle 109, faithfully translated from Latin into the vernacular by Bernardino Scardeone, canon of Padua, together with the exposition of Hugh of Saint-Victor.”

**1687. Brescia, at the press of Rizzardi; quarto.** “The Rule given by Father St. Augustine to nuns; here rendered into the vernacular and explained for their greater instruction and spiritual benefit by Father Master Brother Paolo Richiedei of the Order of Preachers.”

### French

**1691. Paris, at the press of Guillaume Desprez; duodecimo.** “The Rule of Saint Augustine Explained by the Venerable Doctor Hugh of Saint-Victor.” The author was Jean de la Grange, canon regular and subprior of the same abbey of Saint-Victor, to which that Hugh owed his name. He interpreted the Rule itself according to the Benedictine recension.

In the preface he discusses at greater length the few words that, as we noted above, were sewn onto the altered Augustinian rule and which, he shows, had not yet been read by Hugh. See the *Journal des Savants*, 1691 (Amsterdam, 1692, octavo), pp. 353 and 56.

Prosper Stellart, prior of the monastery of Tournai, died in 1626. His *Historical Digest of the Rule of St. Augustine* was published at Tournai by Guillaume of Tongres in 1618, octavo.

“Cloister Discourses on the Rule of the great Father St. Augustine, delivered to his religious by Father Prosper of Saint Joseph,” vicar general of the Discalced Augustinians. *Bibliotheca media Ecclesiae Coloniensis*.

# XXXVI. (103) On Grace and Free Will

**1563. Florence, at the request of Giorgio Maresotti, printed by Bartolomeo Sermartelli; duodecimo.** “The Book of St. Augustine, bishop of Hippo, on Grace and Free Will, addressed to Valentinus and the monks who were with him,” translated by Lodovico Domenichi. *Biblioteca degli Autori volgari*.

# XXXVII. (105) The Two Books of the Retractations

So far I have found only one edition of these books published separately: Lyon, at the press of the Frellon brothers, 1536, octavo. Maeltarius cites it from the *Pandects of Gesner*, vol. II, part II, p. 836.

Christoph Friedrich Roesler translated them into German and supplied the necessary annotations in volume V of the *Library of the Fathers of the Church* (Leipzig, 1785), pp. 237–416.

# XXXVIII. (106) On Heresies

**1576. Geneva, at the press of Eustathius Vignon; octavo.** “The book of the Lord Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus. Corrected and illustrated with commentaries by Lambert Daneau, who also added heresies from the creation of the world to the establishment of Papism and Mohammedanism, including those that Augustine had omitted. A fourfold index was added to the work, so that one might understand not only the chronological order of the heresies but also what benefit could be derived from them, and by whom error was committed in each commandment of the Decalogue, each article of the Apostles’ Creed, and the discussion of the sacraments. At the end of the work there is added a genealogical tree of heresies, from which it is clearly shown how some arose from and were propagated by others, and how one hydra often produced several heads. By the same Lambert Daneau. There is also added a treatise *On the Church*, showing by what gradual stages it finally fell into papal tyranny.”

Worthy of that age, and especially of the genius of this remarkable genealogist of heresies, is the letter he wrote to the Senate of Geneva. In it he congratulates himself on the lot divinely granted him, namely, that he had happened to live in a city that should be considered second to none in glory for rooting out the authors of heresies by fire and sword. He joyfully recounts the punishments inflicted on heretics at Geneva.

**1578. There likewise, at the same press; octavo.** Exactly the same edition. Catalogue of the Thott Library.

**1583. Geneva, folio.** The same book in Lambert Daneau’s *Theological Opuscula*, pp. 897–1048.

**1595. Geneva, octavo.** The same book with the same commentaries. Catalogue of the Bodleian Library.

**1621. Helmstedt, printed by the heirs of Jacob Levi; quarto.** “The book of the Lord Aurelius Augustine, *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus. Also the *Catalogue of Nearly All Heresies* by St. Philastrius, Augustine’s contemporary, known from the creation of the world to that age. A supplement to both writings and a genuine index were added: one chronological, the other alphabetical.”

**1631. Oxford, octavo.** St. Augustine’s book *On Heresies*. Catalogue of the Bodleian Library.

**1673. Helmstedt, at the press of Johann and Friedrich Luderwald; quarto.** The same book, with the commentaries and supplements of Lambert Daneau, edited by Gebhard Theodor Meier. See the Bunau catalogue.

**1687. Cambridge, duodecimo.** The same book with Vincent of Lérins’s commentary, pp. 169 and 269. Bunau catalogue. The Bodleian catalogue adds: “with the notes of Baluze.”

**1721. Oxford, from the Sheldon Theatre; octavo.** “The book of the Lord Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, together with the appendix of Gennadius of Marseilles. Edited and illustrated with notes by Edward Welchman, priest of the Church of England and formerly fellow of Merton College.” The notes are suitable, but were by no means written for learned readers.

“Historical-dogmatic commentaries on St. Augustine’s book *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus. Arranged and illustrated through the labor and study of Father Lorenzo Cozza of Saint Lawrence, of the Order of Friars Minor of the Observance, emeritus lecturer, writer of the same order, provincial minister in the Roman province, synodal examiner of the diocese of Viterbo, and consultant to the Sacred Congregation of the Index. Presented to the most eminent and reverend cardinals of the Roman Church, members of the same Sacred Congregation of the Index. A work filled with every kind of learning, useful to theologians, philosophers, writers, historians, preachers, confessors, those responsible for the care of souls, and students of human and divine letters and ecclesiastical affairs. Part One, containing twelve heresies, from Simon Magus to Marcion. At the end of each heresy is added a comparison of it with the more recent heresies of the Evangelicals. Rome, 1707, printed by Georgius Plachus at the expense of Val. Fregianti.”

Augustine’s words appear like rare swimmers in a vast whirlpool. The greater part of the volume is occupied by the comparison announced in the title. For the rest, I do not know whether the author’s zeal was more extinguished by death or whether the bookseller restrained the youthful impulse of the emeritus writer. See the *Mémoires de Trévoux*, June 1707, p. 1110, and the *Acta Eruditorum*, Leipzig, November 1708, p. 489.

# XXXIX. (110, 111) Two Books on the Predestination of the Saints, One of Which Is Usually Entitled *On the Gift of Perseverance*

See *On Grace and Free Will*, no. 103; also the *Selected Opuscula*.

**1711. Paris, at the press of Guillaume Desprez; folio.** Augustine’s books *On Predestination* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*. They appear in the works of St. Prosper beginning on p. 23.

### Translations

#### Italian

**1537. Brescia, at the press of Lodovico Britannico; quarto.** “On the Predestination of the Saints and on the Benefit of Perseverance,” without the translator’s name.

**1544. Venice, under the sign of the Well; sextodecimo.** “On the Benefit of Perseverance,” translated by Lodovico Domenichi.

**1547. Venice, at the press of Comin da Trino; octavo.** “The Book on the Benefit of Perseverance, composed by Blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, newly translated from Latin into the vernacular.” Despite what the title claims, this is the preceding translation; the same is true of the following.

**There likewise, octavo.** “The Book of Blessed Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on the Predestination of the Saints, newly translated from Latin into the vernacular.” These editions of the translations are cited in the *Biblioteca degli Autori volgari*. The translation is included in the *Collection of Scholarly and Philological Opuscula*, vol. XXXII, p. 349. Fontanini was chiefly responsible for it.

#### French

The Cologne bibliographers mention a French translation of both books, published at Lyon in 1616. Better known is the one published much later by Dubois, as reported in the *Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica Coloniensis*, p. 746. But the catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris identifies another under this title:

**1676. Paris, at the press of Guillaume Desprez; duodecimo.** “The two books of St. Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, together with letters 105, 106, and 107 of this holy doctor; all translated into French by Jean Segui.” The *Paris Ephemerides* (*Journal des Savants*) for this year, no. XIV, p. 92, says nothing at all about the author.

**1715. Paris, at the press of Jacques Estienne; duodecimo.** “The two books of St. Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, together with letters 105, 106, and 107 of the same saint; all translated into French.”

*Extracts from St. Augustine’s teaching on Predestination and Perseverance, with scholia by Georg Cassander of Belgium.* Paris, 1616. The same work in English by I. Scory, octavo. Lipenius, *Bibliotheca theologica*, vol. I, p. 525.

# XL. (113) The Mirror from Both Testaments

Several books have been published under this title, all of them claimed by their editors for Augustine. One, which has so far been printed in every edition of Augustine’s works and is included in the latest Benedictine reprint at Antwerp, vol. III, pp. 507–612, is arranged according to the sequence of the books of the Old and New Testaments.

Another was brought forth by Hieronymus Vignier in the supplement, vol. I, pp. 515–545, from an autograph manuscript of the Bible belonging to Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, who died around 820. In it, biblical statements are referred to under particular moral chapters, without a preface.

The Benedictines consider this work entirely spurious, since it agrees less with the words of Possidius and with the preface to Augustine’s copy published by them. Yet no one, as far as I know, has denied that this preface bears the mark of an Augustinian pen, except with regard to the biblical texts, which were copied not from the ancient version Augustine undoubtedly used, but from Jerome’s or the Vulgate version. Some very learned men, nevertheless opposed by the Benedictines, maintain with some probability that Augustine’s hand was tampered with by an ignorant monk.

> **Note:** See Cave, Dupin, and Richard Simon, *Critical History of Ecclesiastical Literature*, vol. I, p. 143.

**1679. Rome, at the press of Joseph Vanucci; octavo.** “The Mirror of the Lord Aurelius Augustine, first published in this smaller format, so that anyone may more easily recognize in it how obedient and disobedient he is to God. There is added the same doctor’s *Psalter*, which he composed for his mother.”

It was edited and prefaced, though under an assumed name, by Joseph Maria Tommasi—perhaps Tommasius—a cleric regular of Alicata in Sicily, the same man who later published *Selected Little Works of the Earlier Theological Fathers, Greek and Latin* (Rome, 1709–1712, three volumes, octavo).

> **Note:** He was given the purple by Clement XI in 1712 and died in 1713.

# XLI. (114) Expositions on the One Hundred and Fifty Psalms of David

**1489. Basel, printed by Johann Amerbach; folio.** *Aurelius Augustine’s First, Second, and Third Fifties.*

At the end of the third:

> “After this distinguished and excellent work of exposition of the Psalms had been completed through careful and painstaking correction, with God as author, it was finished. The work of Augustine, a holy and great doctor, truly shows itself to the readers to be worthy of greater commendation than can be expressed in any words, as may clearly be gathered both from the preface and from the prologue itself. Let those judge how carefully and accurately it has been corrected, amended, and arranged who have compared it with other similar works, whether written by hand or printed in bronze letters. It was completed at Basel by Master Johann Amerbach, in the year of our Lord 1489.”

It was printed in Gothic type, in two columns. Signatures, small initials, and running titles are present; catchwords and folio numbers are absent. On the first page of the first folio, in large Gothic type, appears: *Aurelius Augustine’s First Fifty*. It is preceded by an alphabetical index of subjects occupying fourteen folios.

Copies of this edition exist in the Bodleian Library and the University Library of Ingolstadt. See Seemiller, fascicle III, p. 164. Add Braun, vol. II, p. 181.

**1493. Venice, printed by Bernardino Benali; folio.** Augustine on the Psalms. Orlandi, p. 284.

**Basel, printed by Johann Amerbach; folio.** Augustine’s work on the Psalms. Maittaire, vol. I, part II, p. 563.

**1494. There likewise, folio.** Augustine on the Psalms. The same witness, vol. I.

**1495. There likewise, printed by the same; folio.** The same work.

**1497. Basel, printed by Johann Amerbach; folio.** The same work. Completed in the year of our Lord 1497. But instead of the brief index noted in the earlier edition, an annotation of the principal statements was added separately; this alone grew into a volume of moderate size. A copy is also recorded among the rarities of the Royal Library of Buda.

**1519. Lyon, folio.** Blessed Augustine on the Psalms. Cited by Hendreich in *Pandectae Brandenburgicae*, p. 342. It is preserved in the library of the monastery of the Order of the Hermits of St. Augustine at Munich, according to Ossinger, *Bibliotheca Augustiniana*, p. 11.

**1529. Basel, folio.** The same book, cited by Hendreich. It undoubtedly belongs to the first edition of the complete works from Erasmus’s recension. From Hendreich alone I find the following editions cited: 1543 and 1555, Paris; 1555, Lyon; 1556, Basel; and 1561, 1562, and 1563, Lyon—all with no greater reliability.

**1569. Basel, printed by Froben; folio.** Augustine on the Psalms. This is how it appears in Georg’s *General European Bookseller’s Lexicon*, supplement I, p. 21. But this is entirely wrong if it is meant as a separate edition; not so if one looks for it among the complete works. Hendreich records an edition of the same year at Geneva, but I fear he has erred in the year. There is an edition of Augustine’s works made at Geneva in 1596, not 1569, to which this may perhaps refer.

**1570. Venice, folio.** The same work. Hendreich. Anyone familiar with the Venetian edition of the complete works published this year will understand how much truth there is in the notice.

**1571. Lyon, at the press of Sebastian Honorat; octavo, two volumes.** Augustine’s *Expositions on the Psalms*. Cited by Hendreich and the Cologne bibliographers. See what we noted above under the annals of editions of the complete works for this year. The same applies to the Paris edition he records there.

**1576, 1577, and 1579. Antwerp.** Augustine’s *Expositions on the Psalms*, according to Hendreich. I do not know whether he intended to indicate several volumes published in different years or different editions of the entire work. I do know that this work exists not separately but together with the works edited at Leuven.

The same writer records the Venetian edition of 1584 and the Paris edition of 1586; the same comments apply to them. I shall not argue which Lyon edition of 1586 is meant.

**1653. Rouen, printed by David and Peter Geoffroy; octavo, three volumes.** Augustine’s *Expositions on the Psalms*, with a preface by some later writer, also included in the Benedictine edition.

**1662. Antwerp, folio.** The same work, with a preaching index. Hendreich, *Pandectae Brandenburgicae*. Cologne bibliographers.

**1680. Antwerp.** The same work, edited by Jacques Willemant, an Augustinian Hermit.

### Translations

**1521. Hagenau, at the press of Thomas Anselm; quarto.** “St. Augustine’s exposition of Psalm 126, translated into German by Georg Spalatin.”

Hendreich notes that the same Psalm exists in an Italian translation, but he is quite confused in recording the various translations of these commentaries.
