**1683. Paris, at the press of Pierre Le Petit; octavo, seven volumes.** “Sermons of St. Augustine on the Psalms, translated into French by Antoine Arnauld.” Volumes I–VII. Catalogue of Bunau and of the Royal Library of Paris.

*Collection of consolations and salutary instructions for the faithful soul, extracted from St. Augustine’s book on the Psalms*, by Jacques de Billy. Paris, at the press of Claude.

*Christian Instructions on the Psalms.* Brussels, 1662, octavo.

*Rules of St. Augustine for Understanding the Psalms.* Paris and Brussels, 1685, duodecimo.

# XLII. (115) Letters

Various letters of Augustine have often been published together with the works of other Fathers, such as Jerome, Paulinus, and Prosper of Aquitaine. I shall pass over these here, since I have undertaken to enumerate only collections of all or several letters, or cases in which individual letters were published separately. Their list follows.

## Fifteenth Century

**1493. Basel, printed by Johann Amerbach; folio.** *The Book of the Letters of Blessed Augustine, bishop of the Church of Hippo.*

At the end:

> “The book of the letters of the Lord Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, corrected and printed with vigilant and most careful labor, and briefly and clearly presented with a preliminary notice of new summaries, was completed through the work of Master Johann Amerbach, citizen of Basel, in the year of our Lord 1493. Happily it is finished.”

The type is Roman, except in the title, which, in Amerbach’s fashion, is printed in Gothic letters. It contains 206 letters. A brief annotation of the individual letters precedes it in seven folios, explaining their beginnings, subject matter, and order. After the colophon there follows a very full index of maxims and subjects.

Gemeiner also noted the same edition in the Regensburg Library, p. 213, and Gesner in the Lübeck Library, p. 56. The catalogue of the Bern Library, vol. I, p. 15, cites an Amerbach edition of the letters from the year 1483.

1494. Basel, at the press of Johann Amerbach; folio. The same work. It is held in the Lübeck Library. Compare Gesner, p. 58.

—Venice, by Bernardino Benalio; quarto. The same work. Catalogue of the Pinelli Library, vol. I, p. 92.

[Col. 0176B] Without year, place, or printer, large folio. The Letters of Saint Augustine, bishop. The first edition of Augustine’s Letters was first discovered and described by the learned Braun in *Historical and Literary Notices* (1788), p. 11. The volume consists of 263 leaves, printed in large type, in two columns, on clean and sturdy paper. Each column contains 50 lines; all page and leaf numbers or marks are absent, as are initial letters. Its punctuation consists of the period, colon, and question mark. It begins: “The Book of the Letters of Saint Augustine. It begins successfully”; but it ends, without any subscription, on the final page, in the first column, with the letter to Asellicus. The letters, some by Augustine himself and some by others to him, number 197; among them are also those of the African [Col. 0176C] bishops to Innocent I and his replies to them.

SIXTEENTH AND SEVENTEENTH CENTURIES.—1541. Bologna. Saint Augustine’s Tenth Letter to the Presbyter Xystus, on the Grace of God. Hendreich, in *Brandenburg Pandects*, p. 342.

1604.—Mainz, at the press of Balthasar Lippius; quarto. Saint Augustine’s Letter on the Holy Martyrs and on Loving Enemies, with notes by Gerard Vossius. Lipenius, in *Theological Library*, vol. II, p. 254, cites it as though it had been published separately. In fact, it is inserted in the works of Gregory Thaumaturgus, bishop of Neocaesarea, published by the same Vossius together with other brief works of the Fathers, at p. 228. That Vossius was provost of the Church of Tongeren; he issued several writings of this kind at that time and died in 1609. See Foppens, *Belgian Library*, vol. I, pp. 362–363.

[Col. 0176D] 1638.—La Flèche, quarto. Three Books of Selected Letters of Saint Aurelius Augustine. First edited, explained with fuller summaries, and illustrated with observations by Roland Phigerius, of the Society of Jesus, a Breton. The first book contains didactic letters, the second ethical and exhortatory letters, and the third mixed and familiar letters. The Cologne bibliographers record it. It also existed in the Thott Library.

1662. Louvain, duodecimo. Selected Letters of the Lord Augustine, with an appendix of spurious letters. Hendreich.

1678. Frankfurt, at the expense of Johann Cramer; quarto. Two hundred and seventy-eight Letters of Saint Aurelius Augustine and of certain others written to him or on his account, with an appendix of spurious letters, various readings, and other marginal notes and most useful indexes, published separately with the greatest accuracy under the care of Lucas Friedrich Reinhart of Nuremberg, professor of theology at the University of Altdorf.

Cyprian’s Letters, edited by the same learned man several years later, were mentioned in the first volume. He rendered no less service to Augustine and is especially to be praised because he was the first to present together several of Augustine’s letters which until then had not been collected with the others but, according to the subject matter, had customarily been scattered through the remaining volumes of his works. It was conveniently arranged that the letters of others to Augustine were printed in italic type, while round type was used for Augustine’s own letters. In the margin were noted both various readings [Col. 0177B] and citations from Holy Scripture, as well as passages from the Theodosian Code, Canon Law, Lombard, and Thomas Aquinas that could either be illustrated from Augustine or contained his words.

EIGHTEENTH CENTURY.—1721. Paris, folio. Two Letters of Saint Augustine: the first to Pope Boniface, the second to Celestine. They appear among the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs edited by Coustant, vol. I, pp. 1023 and 1051.

1732. Vienna, Austria, at the press of Johann Peter van Ghelen, large folio. The Second Letter of Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, to Optatus, bishop of Milevis, on the Nature and Origin of the Soul. There was added another letter of the same Saint Augustine, on the punishments of little children who die without baptism, written to Peter and Abraham. These now appear for the first time from the library of the free and exempt Benedictine abbey of Göttweig in Lower Austria. The same letters were printed there the following year by Johann Adam Schmid, bookseller of Nuremberg. [Col. 0177C] In the preface to the reader, Abbot Godefridus gives an erudite discussion of the occasion of both letters. The manuscript in which they were found—which, as the learned abbot seems rightly to have judged, is unique—is written on parchment, in folio format, and is assigned by him to at least the twelfth century. It was found in the abbey library under the shelfmark Lit. 6, no. 10. He dedicated these accidentally discovered treasures (*κειμήλια*) to Cardinal Passionei, then a great patron of learning in Italy and later chief prefect of the Vatican Library.

1734. Paris, at the press of the widow of Reymund Mazières; folio. Two letters of Saint Aurelius Augustine, recently discovered in Germany, illustrated with critical, historical, and chronological notes, through the work and study of Father Jacques Martin, priest of the Congregation of Saint-Maur. Catalogue of the Royal Library.

—Paris, at the press of the widow Mazières; octavo. “New Letters of Saint Augustine, translated into French, with the Latin opposite, and with critical, historical, and chronological notes, together with a treatise on the origin of the soul drawn from his writings, newly found in a manuscript of the Abbey of Göttweig, near the city of Vienna in Austria.”

## Translations

1573. Paris, at the press of Mathurin Prevost; octavo. “The forty-eighth letter of Saint Augustine, addressed to Vincent, bishop, concerning the Rogatian heresy, highly suitable both for restoring those separated and heretics to the unity of the Catholic Church and for maintaining and preserving those who have remained in it and returned to it, by Clément Vaillant” (a native of Beauvais, advocate in the supreme court of causes). The letter is numbered 93 in the Benedictine edition. Related to it, in a certain sense, is a *Theological Inquiry on the Question Whether Heretics and Schismatics May Be Compelled by Force to the Faith*, in which a great distinction is also shown between the case of the Donatists and that of the Protestants. By D. Elias Veiel, Ulm, 1689, quarto; written on the occasion of the persecution of the Reformers in France, whose supporters had also attempted to draw Augustine over to their side.

1574. Reims, by Jean de Foigny; octavo. “The form and manner of praying properly to God, which is the principal work of the good Christian; first written in Latin by Saint Augustine in his 101st letter to Proba, a widow, and translated into French by Nicolas Chesneau” (dean and canon of Saint Symphorianus at Reims). Du Verdier, revised by Juvigny, vol. V, p. 109.

1653–1659. Paris, at the press of Pierre le Petit; duodecimo, five volumes. “Selected Letters of Saint Augustine, translated into French by Louis Giry.” Volumes I and II were printed in 1653, III in 1656, IV in 1658, and V in 1659. Hendreich, in the *Brandenburg Pandects*, also lists another translation, by de la Cande, from 1653.

1684. Paris, at the press of Jean-Baptiste Coignard; folio, two volumes. “The Letters of Saint Augustine, translated into French from the new edition of the Benedictines of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, where they are arranged according to chronological order; revised and corrected from ancient manuscripts and augmented by several letters, with notes on points of history, chronology, and other matters that may require clarification, by Philippe Goibaud du Bois.” Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris. The same work is listed in six octavo volumes in the Catalogue of the Duke de La Vallière’s Library. See also the *Journal des savants*, Paris, 1685, no. II, and the *Nouvelles de la République des Lettres*, November 1684. He corrected several passages of the Benedictine edition from manuscript codices. They say that the notes are Tillemont’s. Compare the testimonies cited by the Cologne bibliographers.

1690. Lyon. “Letter XXXIX” (Louvain edition) “of Saint Augustine to a young man, Licentius, who had been his disciple and had entered secular life.” It appears in *Christian Solitude*, vol. I, p. 471.

1700. Cologne. “Letter of Saint Augustine to Count Boniface” (the second of three written to him), “translated by M. du Bois.” It appears in *The Instructed Christian Soldier*, etc., by Father Henri Godefroy.

1707. Lille, at the press of Jean-Baptiste Brovellio; duodecimo, six volumes. “The Letters of Saint Augustine, translated into French from the new edition of the Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, where they are arranged according to chronological order, revised and corrected from ancient manuscripts, and augmented by several letters that had not yet appeared, with notes, by M. du Bois. Third edition.” Catalogue of Bunau and of the Royal Library of Paris. This may perhaps be the same reprint that the Cologne bibliographers reported as having been made at Amsterdam in this year.

The Cologne bibliographers mention an English version of Letter XLVIII under the title: “Saint Augustine’s Judgment on the Penal Laws against Conventicles and on the Unity of Religion, proposed in Letter 48,” London, 1670, quarto, adding Lipenius’s testimony in the *Philosophical Library*, under “Conventicles.”

Finally, there appears to be a translation of the Letter on the punishments of little children who die without baptism, mentioned in the Catalogue of the Firmian Library under this title: “A Sermon of Saint Augustine, in which the punishment of children who die without baptism is discussed, translated with annotations by G. G., Pavia, 1778, octavo.”

[Col. 0179B] The learned Roesler inserted shorter or longer summaries of the more notable letters of Augustine in volume V of the *Library of the Church Fathers*, from p. 417 to the end.

## XLIII.—(116) Sermons and Homilies

FIFTEENTH CENTURY.—1475. Augsburg, by Anton Sorg; small folio. Saint Augustine’s work called *Fifty*, or Fifty Homilies. At the end: “In the year of our Lord 1475, around the Kalends of February, this book was printed in Augsburg by Anton Sorg, to the honor of God.” It begins with a register of the homilies, occupying the first leaf. The type is Gothic but elegant. There are no numbers or marks on the leaves or pages, according to the testimony of the learned Zapf in *Annals of Augsburg Typography*, p. 32, and Seemiller, fascicle I, p. 70. Add Braun, *Historical and Literary Notices* (1788), p. 179.

[Col. 0179C] 1477. Modena, by Balthasar de Struciis; quarto. Saint Augustine’s Sermons to the Brothers in the Desert. We have found it cited nowhere except in the Catalogue of the Pinelli Library, vol. I, p. 92.

1482. Speyer, produced by Peter Drach the Younger, on the vigil of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary; folio. Various Sermons of Blessed Augustine, in the present edition of the *Homiliary of Charlemagne*.

1484. Milan, by the Germans; quarto. Saint Augustine’s Sermons to the Brothers in the Desert. Catalogue of the Pinelli Library, vol. I, p. 92.

—Padua, by Matteo Cerdonis; quarto. Three Sermons of Blessed Augustine on the Life and Conduct of Clerics. The editor is Eusebius Corradus of Milan, a canon regular of the Lateran Congregation. The volume begins with his letter to Sixtus IV, supreme pontiff, [Col. 0179D] “for removing from the Church the error of those who write that Augustine was a hermit.” Besides the three sermons mentioned—of which the first begins, “To your charity,” etc.; the second, “For this reason I wished and asked,” etc.; and the third, “Before all things, brothers,” etc.—there is also the Life of Augustine written by Possidius (so the text has it), and, unless the table of contents is deceptive, immediately after the dedicatory letter there is a table of the contents. There is also Augustine’s Letter on Whether Clerics May Abandon the People and Flock Entrusted to Them in Time of Persecution. Yet I do not find it in the copy I have in hand, nor does the copy appear defective; instead, in its place there is a very brief note by the editor, addressed to Sixtus IV and to the patriarch of Aquileia, Cardinal and protector of Saint Mark, [Col. 0180A] and to the other cardinals, concerning the error of those who write that Saint Augustine was a hermit. Corradus says in the dedicatory letter that all these items are contained in the book, yet he makes no mention there of that letter, whereas the letter is not indicated in the table of contents mentioned above. At the end, however, one reads: “Here ends the three sermons of blessed Augustine on the life and conduct of clerics, together with the life of Saint Augustine and also a certain letter of his, ‘Whether clerics …,’ all of which were printed at Padua by Master Matteo Cerdonis. In the year of the Lord 1484.” Oda adds a colophon in praise of Augustine, beginning, “Out of the depths of darkness.” This edition consists of 36 leaves, printed with [an unspecified number of] lines per page. The type is clear Gothic. Apart from the signatures of the sheets, there are no marks of any kind on the leaves or pages. Initial letters are nevertheless present, printed from wooden blocks. Braun also mentions it in *Historical and Literary Notices*, vol. II, p. 111.

1486. Brescia, by Jacobus Britannicus of Brescia; octavo. Sermons of Saint Augustine, bishop, to the Hermit Brothers. At the end: “Printed at Brescia by Jacobus Britannicus of Brescia, in the year of our Lord 1486, on 5 January.”

The only notice of this edition, previously unknown to all bibliographers, is supplied by Braun, *Historical and Literary Notices*, vol. II, p. 130. He states that the volume consists of twenty-one gatherings, printed in Roman type of exceptional elegance, with all leaf and page marks lacking and small letters inserted in place of initials for the illuminator’s benefit. It contains all the same material, in the same order, including even the table of the sermons.

1487. Venice, by Paganino de’ Paganini; octavo. Sermons of Saint Augustine to the Hermits. It begins: “Here begin the sermons of Saint Augustine to the Hermits, some to his priests and some to others. First, on the establishment of the regular life …” [the printed text is corrupt]. At the end: “Printed at Venice by Paganino de’ Paganini of Brescia, in the year of the Lord 1487, on 26 May.”

Besides the fifty-nine sermons, the following are added: (1) Sermon LX on Saint Monica; (2) Callistus’s account of Saint Augustine’s conversion; (3) Sigebert’s account of the same, from his letter to Macedonius; (4) certain excerpts from Bede’s Chronicle; (5) other reports by uncertain authors; (6) a prayer on the Passion of the Lord, attributed by some to Saint Augustine, for the recitation of which on forty consecutive days Boniface VIII granted a plenary indulgence. The text is preceded by a table of the sermons occupying two incomplete leaves. It is printed in two columns in Gothic type. The printer sometimes added small initial letters and omitted them elsewhere. The sheets are signed a–r. Catchwords, numbers, and page headings are absent. Seemiller, fascicle III, p. 92.

1492. Venice, at the press of Vincent de Benaliis; octavo. Saint Augustine’s Sermons to the Hermits and to Others. It appears together with Saint Bernard’s *To His Sister on the Manner of Living Well*. Venice, 1493. So Audiffredi in the Catalogue of the Casanatense Library.

[Col. 0181A] 1493. Basel, produced by Nicolaus Kessler, on the day before the Kalends of October; folio. Various Sermons of Blessed Augustine, in the *Homiliary of the Doctors*, which appeared in this year and place under the care of Johann Ulrich Surgant, doctor of arts and of decrees, etc., as his prefatory letter to Nicolaus Kessler testifies.

1494. I. Basel, by Johann Amerbach; folio. “The Sermons of the divine Aurelius Augustine to his brothers dwelling in the desert and to certain others.” Although neither the place, nor the year, nor the printer is explicitly stated in this volume, we have nevertheless listed it without hesitation, since other writings of Augustine bound together with the present work, which bear all these particulars as though supplied by us, support our judgment through their similarity of type, description, and arrangement. The letters are Gothic, and the pages are printed in two columns. At the beginning [Note: [Col. 0181D] This is how it is usually seen. It should be borne in mind, however, that in more complete copies the following title is prefixed, written in Gothic letters: “Several and Various Works of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, namely:” (up to this point the type is larger; the rest is completed in smaller type.)

“To the Brothers Dwelling in the Desert: 76 Sermons. On the Words of the Lord: 64 Sermons. On the Words of the Apostle: 35 Sermons. On the First Canonical Letter of Blessed John: 10 Sermons. Homilies, that is, Popular Sermons: 50. On the Seasons: 256 Sermons. On the Saints: 51 Sermons.”

This shows at the same time that this collection of sermons originally comprised more material than most surviving copies now retain, and that copies such as ours, which are defective in the Homilies, should not be regarded as complete. On the reverse of the leaf there is a woodcut image of the bishop preaching, with the following verses beneath it: “Hail, jewel of confessors, Augustine, light of teachers.”

At the beginning there is a fairly lengthy elegiac poem by Sebastian Brant to the divine Aurelius Augustine, printed in Roman type. It is followed by a shorter account of his birth, character, learning, error, conversion, and sacred baptismal rebirth. Next comes the Ambrosian Hymn; a sermon by the same Blessed Ambrose on Augustine’s conversion; and three monastic rules of Augustine, together with the form according to which he gave a common sobriety to those who wished to join the fellowship of him and his brothers. Finally, after a table of contents, the seventy-six sermons themselves are presented, with an appendix of various accounts of Augustine by different authors, whose names are partly also given, such as Callistus, Sigebert, and Antoninus. At the end: “Here end certain selections from various sermons appended to the glory of blessed Augustine, addressed to the brothers in the desert: successfully completed.” Finally, a very extensive index of subjects and sentences, occupying ten leaves, closes the volume.

II. In the same place, by the same printer; folio. The Divine Aurelius Augustine on the Words of the Lord (sixty-four sermons). At the end: “The book of sermons has been completed … Basel, by Master Johann Amerbach, in the year 1494 of the life-giving virgin birth.” Everything agrees with the embellishment of the preceding work, including the tables of subjects and sentences and the index of sermons.

III. In the same place, by the same printer; folio. Sermons of the Divine Aurelius Augustine on the Words of the Apostle (thirty-five). At the end: “The book of sermons has been completed … of the Lord Aurelius Augustine, Basel, in the year of the Lord 1494.” It differs in nothing from the preceding volumes.

IV. In the same place, by the same printer; folio. Exposition by the Divine Aurelius Augustine on the Letter of Blessed John.

[Col. 0182A] V. In the same place, by the same printer; folio. The Work of Fifty Homilies of the Divine Aurelius Augustine. At the end: “Basel, 1494.”

1495. Basel, at the press of Johann Amerbach; folio. Sermons of Saint Augustine on the Seasons (256); the subscription has the same wording as in the sermons on the Words of the Lord from the preceding year. The table of the sermons contained in the volume has been prepared with the greatest care. But the index of subjects and sentences seems less extensive in proportion to the size of this volume when compared with the indexes of the preceding collections. In addition, the inner title page presents a woodcut emblematic image and Latin couplets prepared for this edition.

Without year, by Conrad of Homborch; folio. Various Sermons of Blessed Augustine for Sundays and feast days, in the present edition of Charlemagne’s *Homiliary*.

Without year or place, quarto. Sermons of Saint Augustine to the Hermits. These words are printed in large letters on the title. There are 159 sermons, with certain additions, printed in Gothic type in two columns, without any indication of place or year. I therefore do not know by what arguments the person who annotated our copy was led to state that it appeared around 1490. According to Gemeiner, at the Regensburg Library, loc. cit., p. 276, there is an edition of these sermons without place or year, printed four pages to a sheet, consisting of 108 leaves and containing fifty-nine sermons. Gemeiner briefly mentions a Venetian edition of 1490, loc. cit., p. 277; add Braun, *Historical and Literary Notices*, vol. II, p. 53.

Without year or place; quarto. Two Sermons—these words are printed in large Gothic letters; what follows is in larger Roman type—of Aurelius Augustine, bishop, on the Life and Conduct of Clerics. These are the first two of the three sermons published in the Paduan edition of 1484. There is also added, from the book of the *Retractions*, his remark on the book *On True Religion*. It is printed in very neat small Gothic type, in two columns. The subject of the volume is printed in Roman letters and runs along the upper margins of the individual pages.

SIXTEENTH CENTURY.—1513. Paris. Gemeiner, loc. cit., p. 277, briefly praises this edition of the Sermons to the Hermit Brothers. (I now conjecture that Clementius and Ossinger were its sponsors.)

1516. Lyon, by Johann Clemens Alemannus, on 7 August; folio. Various Sermons of Blessed Augustine, in the *Homiliary of the Doctors*, published, if we correctly infer from the prefixed letter, under the care of Johann Thiery of Langres, professor of both laws.

[Col. 0183A] —Paris, by Berthold Rembolt; large folio. “The most distinguished and invaluable works of the divine Aurelius Augustine’s sermons, in learning and usefulness, recently printed with the greatest care and diligence by Master Berthold Rembolt. At the printer’s own establishment under the Golden Sun in the Rue Saint-Jacques in Paris, and for sale in the workshops of Johann Coberger and Jodocus Badius, you will find what this volume contains in the following order, namely:

To the Brothers Dwelling in the Desert: 76 Sermons.

On the Words of the Lord: 64 Sermons.

On the Words of the Apostle: 35 Sermons.

On the First Canonical Letter of Blessed John: 10 Treatises.

Homilies, that is, Popular Sermons: 50.

[Col. 0183B] On the Gospel according to John: 124 Treatises.

On the Seasons: 266 Sermons.

On the Saints: 51 Sermons.

With very extensive tables and indexes.”

At the end: “Completed in Paris, in the workshop of Master Berthold Rembolt, in the year of the Lord …, on 19 December.”

The type is Gothic, the pages are printed in divided columns, and no other ornament is lacking.

1521. Hagenau, by Heinrich Grau; folio. The most distinguished works of Blessed Augustine’s sermons, recently revised and checked with the greatest care and corrected in many places. At the end: “This distinguished work was printed in the workshop of the industrious Heinrich Grau, citizen of the imperial town of Hagenau, at the cost and expense of the honorable Johann Rynman of Öhringen, chief bookseller, in October of the year 1521 after the birth of Christ.”

1525. Lyon, by Johann Crespin, on 10 January; folio. Various Sermons of Blessed Augustine for Sundays and feast days, among the Homilies of distinguished doctors on the Sunday Gospels, which Alcuin is said to have collected at the command of Charlemagne; printed here and in this year with a preface by Brother Lambertus Campester, theologian, addressed to Symphorianus Camperius, a patrician of Lyon.

1564. Louvain, at the press of Hieronymus Wellaeus; quarto. Sermons of the Lord Aurelius Augustine, together with the catalogue of the works of the Lord Augustine by Possidius, bishop of Calama, from the edition and with the marginal scholia of Johann Vlimmerius. Catalogue of the Royal Library. Compare what was given above concerning the Basel edition of the works in 1569.

[Col. 0183D] 1576. Cologne, folio. Various Homilies of Saint Augustine. They appear in the Collection of Brother Alcuin.

1588. Lyon, folio. Certain Homilies of Saint Augustine, in the *Homiliary* of Cumdius.

SEVENTEENTH CENTURY.—1631. Paris, at the press of Sébastien Cramoisy; octavo. Forty New Sermons of Saint Aurelius Augustine, together with five others collected from ancient copies, with notes, edited and prepared by Jacques Sirmond. Catalogue of the Royal Library and of the Casanatense Library.

1644. Rome, by Francesco Moneta; quarto. Several Sermons attributed to Saint Aurelius Augustine, excerpted from the Vatican and Barberini libraries, now published for the first time and illustrated with certain notes through the work and study of Giovanni Battista Mari. Catalogue of the Royal Library.

[Col. 0184A] 1647. Rome, at the press of Ludovico Grignani; quarto. Sermon of Saint Aurelius Augustine on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, now published for the first time, with observations by Giovanni Battista Mari. Catalogue of the Royal Library.

1648. Madrid, at the Royal Press; folio. Several Sermons of Saint Augustine on the Blessed Virgin. They appear in P. de Alva’s *Virgin Library*, vol. III, p. 448 onward. Audiffredi, in the Catalogue of the Casanatense Library.

1685. Paris, at the press of P. de Laulne; octavo. Three fragments of Augustine’s Sermons to the Hermits, preceded by a Summary of the Sermons to the Brothers in the Desert, of the Sermons to the Priests of Hippo, and of the Sermons to the People, from the autograph of Jordan of Saxony. They appear in the supplement to the works of Father Jacques Hommey, p. 644 onward.

## Translations

1493. Florence, by Master Antonio Miscomini, on 28 June; small quarto. “Vernacular Sermons of the Venerable Doctor Saint Aurelius Augustine, Father of the Hermit Rule, very devout and spiritual, for attaining the spiritual glory of Paradise.” Catalogue of Crevenna’s latest collection, vol. I, p. 107.

1546. Venice, at the press of Gabriel Giolito de’ Ferrari; quarto. “Various Sermons of Saint Augustine and of other Catholic and ancient Fathers, useful for the salvation of souls, collected and rendered into the vernacular by Monsignor Galeazzo, bishop of Sessa, with two tables, the first of the sermons and homilies, the second of the most notable matters.” *Library of Vernacular Authors*, in *Collection of Scientific and Philological Opuscula*, vol. XXXII, p. 345.

[Col. 0184C] 1553. Venice, at the press of the Giolito brothers. “Several Sermons of Saint Augustine on the Words of the Lord and of the Apostle, rendered into the vernacular by Monsignor Galeazzo Florimonte, bishop of Aquino.” It appears in *Various Sermons of Saint Augustine and Other Doctors, Rendered into the Vernacular by the Same*. Compare the Catalogue of the Casanatense Library. In the Catalogue of the Smith Library there is an edition from 1588, quarto.

1567. Venice, by the Giolito press; quarto. “Various Sermons, etc.”

1568. Venice, by the Sansovino press; quarto. “Various Sermons of Saint Augustine and of other Catholic and ancient doctors, in which various subjects are treated from various passages of Sacred Scripture of the Old and New Testament; containing material for the Christian who desires to live purely among other people and for the salvation of his soul, collected and rendered into the vernacular by Monsignor Galeazzo, bishop of Sessa, with two tables, one of the sermons and the other of notable matters.”

1572. Florence, by the Giunti press; quarto. “Book III of Various Sermons of Saint Augustine … collected and rendered into the vernacular by Raffaello Castruccio, monk of the abbey of Florence, in imitation of Monsignor Galeazzo, bishop of Sessa.” A fourth book was also published, but it contained nothing by Augustine. I find a second part printed in 1654 under this title:

1654. Venice, by Girolamo Scotto; quarto. “Second Part of the Sermons of Saint Augustine … translated into the vernacular by Monsignor Galeazzo Florimonzio, bishop of Sessa, with certain Homilies by the same.”

All this information was supplied to us by the *Library of Vernacular Authors*, loc. cit.

1694 and 1700. Paris, at the press of the widow of Jean-Baptiste Coignard; octavo, four volumes. “The Sermons of Saint Augustine on the New Testament, translated into French from the Latin edition of the Benedictine Fathers by Philippe Goibaud du Bois.”

1731. Florence, at the press of Domenico Maria Manni; quarto. “A Vernacular Rendering of the Forty Sermons Falsely Attributed to Saint Augustine, made by a Religious of the Order called that of Saint Augustine in the year 1300 and, as is believed, by Brother Augustine of Scarperia.” Catalogue of the Library of Saint Angelo at the Nest in Naples; Audiffredi, in the Catalogue of the Casanatense Library; likewise the Catalogue of the Smith Library.

## XLIV.—(119) Book on the Ten Strings

[Col. 0185B] The Cologne bibliographers, following Nicolás Antonio’s *Hispanic Library*, p. 425, mention a Spanish version of this work, by Gonzalo García de Santa María of Zaragoza, published in 1494, octavo, under the title *The Treatises on the Ten Strings of the Vanity of the World*.

# Continuation of the Second Article

## Annals of the Editions of the Individual Works of Augustine

### § II. Spurious Writings

## I.—(6) Six Books on Music

I do not know whether the item mentioned in the Catalogue of the Bodleian Library belongs here: a little book of Saint Augustine on Music, Basel, 1521, quarto.

## II.—(18) Book on Grammar

1605. Hanover, quarto. Augustine on Grammar. It appears among the *Ancient Authors on Latin Grammar* collected by Elias Putschius, p. 1975 onward.

## III.—(19) Two Books, Principles of Dialectic and Rhetoric

1479. Florence, at the press of Saint James of Ripoli; quarto. Augustine’s Logic. Catalogue of the Casanatense Library.

1599. Paris, quarto. Augustine’s Principles of Rhetoric. It appears among the *Ancient Rhetoricians*, p. 290 onward.

1643. Venice, at the Salicata press; quarto. “Saint Augustine on Rhetoric.” It appears in *Authors of Good Speaking*, vol. XXX, p. 21.

## IV.—(34) Book on Faith, addressed to Peter the Deacon

It was published separately without place or year, in folio. But see Fulgentius, volume III. Compare the material given above under the Minor Works for the year 1473, no. 1.

## V.—(35) On Spirit and Soul

[Col. 0185D] 1472. Without place or printer; quarto. Saint Augustine’s Book on Soul and Spirit; On Drunkenness; To Virgins on Chastity and Sobriety; On the Four Virtues of Charity; and On Contrition of Heart. At the end: “Here ends the book of blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, together with his other brief treatises. In the year 1472, on 9 November.” It is held in the Lübeck Library. Gesner, loc. cit., p. 26. From the similarity of the type and the paper-mark, a bull’s head, he seems with some justification to conclude that it was printed at Mainz by Peter Schoeffer, who printed books on the Christian life and the knowledge of the true life in the same format and without any indication of place or year. There, however, Schoeffer’s insignia are not absent, whereas they are absent from this volume.

## VI.—(36) On Friendship

1510. Leipzig, quarto. “The Book of the Lord Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, on Friendship, in which Cicero’s errors are corrected; useful and supremely necessary for all who love peace, concord, and true and perfect friendship.” The following couplets are immediately appended to this title:

> In this work Augustine, glory of the nations,  
> Tells what true friendship is.
>
> The great Aristotle, skilled in grasping nature’s  
> Mysteries with capacious genius, was ignorant of this.
>
> You too, divine teacher Plato, were ignorant of it,  
> Not knowing this virtue of the ancient world.

At the end: “Printed at Leipzig by Bachelor Wolfgang Monacensis. In the year 1510.” The type is Gothic. A preface to students and learned lovers of the liberal arts at the University of Leipzig was supplied by Magnus Hundt of Parthenopolis, as he calls himself, “the least among theologians,” in a letter given at the College of the Prince on the feast of Calixtus.

## VII.—(39) Soliloquies

1473. Without place; folio. Augustine’s *Soliloquy on the Soul’s Earnest*. It begins: “Here begins the soliloquy of the most blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo, on the soul’s earnest.” At the end: “Here ends this treatise of Augustine on the soul’s earnest, on Tuesday after the feast of Saint Dionysius, in the year of our Lord 1473” [the printed date is corrupt]. It belongs to the same edition as the genuine *Soliloquies*, without place or year, and the *Hieronymian* work on the divine essence, etc. Compare what was said concerning Augustine’s book *On the Quantity of the Soul*. Its extreme rarity may be inferred from the fact that it has hitherto been known to none of the bibliographers. Yet no one will readily deny that it is of the greatest importance for determining the date of those little works, if I say that it differs from them not even in the smallest detail. If, therefore, these works truly belong to Gunther Zainer, as some have believed—and I myself have no doubt of it—it follows that Hamberger’s opinion, that Zainer ceased using Gothic type after 1472, after first employing Roman type in November of that year for printing Isidore [Note: *Zuverlässige Nachrichten*, vol. IV, p. 806, where he discusses Zainer’s edition of Thomas à Kempis in particular], was mistaken. This is what commonly happens to those who like to confine the limits and dates of events or institutions within excessively exact formulas. And what plausible reason could be imagined for such a sudden distaste for Gothic type in that man?

[Col. 0186D] ## Translations

1489. Without place or printer. On 20 June [the printed form is corrupt]; small quarto. “The Soliloquies of the divine Father Saint Augustine.” The type is round. The editor of Crevenna’s latest catalogue, vol. I, p. 111, suspects that Florence was its place of origin.

1491. Florence. On 10 November; quarto. “The Soliloquies of Saint Augustine in the vernacular.” Catalogue of Crevenna’s latest collection, loc. cit.

1492. Milan … octavo. Denisius, in *Garell’s Library*, p. 235, mentions an Italian version of these books from this year, place, and format.

[Col. 0187A] 1663. Paris, at the press of Charles Savreux; duodecimo. “The Soliloquies, the Manual, and the Meditations of Saint Augustine, translated into French by D. L. C. C. F.”

1671. Lyon, octavo. “Saint Augustine: The Soliloquies, the Manual.” Catalogue of the Bern Library.

1684. Paris, at the press of Pierre le Petit; duodecimo. “The Soliloquies, the Meditations, and the Manual of Saint Augustine, translated into French by Father Nicolas Regnier.”

1691. Paris, at the press of Guillaume Desprez; duodecimo. The same works, “a new translation, revised against the Latin edition, augmented by *The Spirit* of the same saint, drawn from his *Confessions*.”

—Paris, at the press of Jean-Baptiste Coignard; duodecimo. “The Soliloquies, the Meditations, and the Manual of Saint Augustine, translated into French from the Latin edition of the Benedictine Fathers, with notes, by Philippe Goibaud du Bois.”

1696. Paris, at the press of Jean Couterot; octavo. “The Soliloquies of Saint Augustine, rendered into French verse, with the Latin and with a verse Meditation on the Last Judgment.”

1704. Paris, at the press of Nicolas Le Gras; duodecimo. “The Soliloquies and the Meditations of Saint Augustine, translated into French by Father René de Ceriziers.”

The author of this article supplied more information about various French versions of these books in the *Great Ecclesiastical Library of Cologne*, p. 729, no. 4. Since I have learned nothing about them from any other source, I shall not trouble myself over them.

## VIII.—(40) Meditations
Without year, place, or printer; in folio. Saint Augustine’s book *On Meditation*. From the very first page one reads:

[Col. 0187C] “Here begins the book of the speech of our most blessed father Augustine and of his contemplation” [*et ejus otemplatione*; the reading is evidently corrupt].

At the end: “The book on the meditation of our most blessed father Augustine is complete. Thanks be to God.”

The distinguished Seemiller praises this little work, fascicle I, p. 112, among those books which he persuaded himself had been printed without indication of place or year by Christoph Valdarser of Regensburg, who printed at Venice and Milan between 1471 and 1476, and of which he presented several—indeed all of them—as very similar to one another in type and in their remaining description. Concerning our book he reported that it was printed in slightly larger oblong type, comprised thirteen complete leaves and a few lines on the fourteenth, without folio or page numbers and likewise without initial letters.

[Col. 0187D] Without year or place; in quarto. *The Meditations of Blessed Augustine*. Catalogue of the Royal Library, vol. I, p. 376, where it is added: “An old edition, about the year 1500.”

Without year. Paris, by Antoine Cayllaut, in quarto. *The Meditations of Blessed Augustine*. Catalogue of the Library of the Duke de La Vallière, vol. I, p. 175.

SIXTEENTH AND SEVENTEENTH CENTURIES.—1516. Venice, … in octavo. “The Meditations of Saint Augustine. One book of the soul’s soliloquies addressed to God. The Manual. It appears in the *Booklet Full of Many Good Things*, from the beginning.” Thus Audiffred in the Catalogue of the Casanatense Library.

1608. Douai, by Balthasar Bellerus; in twenty-fourmo. *The Meditations, Soliloquies, and Manual of the Blessed Aurelius Augustine*, etc. See the complete title below.

[Col. 0188A] 1613. Douai, by Balthasar Bellerus; in twenty-fourmo. “The Meditations, Soliloquies, and Manual of the Blessed Aurelius Augustine. The Meditations of Saint Anselm, with a treatise on the redemption of the human race. The Meditations of Saint Bernard. The contemplations of the learned man Idiota on divine love. All corrected from manuscript exemplars and arranged in better order, through the work and care of the Reverend Father Henry Sommalius, theologian of the Society of Jesus.”

1614. Cologne, by Conrad Bulgenius. The same book, in the same edition.

1631. Lyons, in twenty-fourmo. *The Meditations of Saint Augustine*. Catalogue of the Library of Sant’Angelo a Nilo, Naples.

—Cologne, at the expense of Cornelius ab Egmond; in duodecimo. The same book from Henry Sommalius’s edition.

1637. In the same place, by the same printer; in duodecimo. The same edition.

[Col. 0188B] 1649. In the same place, in duodecimo. The same book, by the same printer.

1650. Paris, by Claude Cramoisy; in duodecimo. *The Meditations, Soliloquies, and Manual of the Blessed Aurelius Augustine: all corrected from manuscript exemplars, through the work and care of Henry Sommalius.*

1672. Rome, by Bartholomew Lupardus; in quarto. The same.

Without year. Dillingen, by Sebald Mayer; in octavo. *The Meditations, Soliloquies, and Manual of the Blessed Aurelius Augustine*. The Cologne authors, p. 729, n. 4, incidentally mention another Dillingen edition of these books in 1571.

EIGHTEENTH CENTURY.—1701. Antwerp, in octavo. *The Meditations, Soliloquies, and Manual of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, corrected from manuscript exemplars and arranged in better order, through the work and care of the Reverend Father Henry Sommalius* [Col. 0188C].

Translations.

Without year or place, in duodecimo. *The Soliloquies of Saint Augustine translated into vernacular Greek*. Catalogue of the Royal Library, vol. I, p. 377.

1671. Paris, by the widow of Charles Savreux; in duodecimo. The same, in French. “By Monsieur D. L. C. C. E.”

1679. Paris, by Guillaume Desprez; in octavo. “The Soliloquies, the Manual, and the Meditations of Saint Augustine. A new translation, very carefully revised against the Latin. A new edition to which have been added several devotional passages taken from the *Confessions* of this same saint, which will show what his spirit was like.” The last material was added under the title *The Spirit of Augustine Taken from His Confessions* [Col. 0188D].

1714. Brussels, in octavo. The same book in French, with notes. Catalogue of the Thott Library.

1604. Madrid, … The same, rendered into Spanish by Father Ribadeneira. It appears in vol. III of his works, pp. 633ff.

1600. Frankfurt on the Oder; in octavo. The same book in German, by Henry Raetell.

1717. Ghent, in octavo. The same book in Dutch, by Andrew van Loo. Catalogue of the Thott Library.

Audiffred notes in the Catalogue of the Casanatense Library that a poem by Saint Augustine, *On the Glory and Joys of Paradise*, composed in political verses, was excerpted from the *Meditations*. It appears among George Fabricius’s *Christian Poets* [Col. 0189A], Basel, 1564, in quarto, p. 815.

IX.—(42) *The Manual*.

1471. Treviso, by Gerard de Flanders, in small quarto. *Saint Augustine’s Book on Salvation, or on the Soul’s Aspiration to God*. At the end, printed in uncial letters, appears:

> An epigram in praise of the printer:
>
> Greatest glory is owed to Gerard Lisa,  
> Whom painted Flanders bore in her fields.  
> For he first began in the city of Treviso  
> To mark rare books in bronze through his craft.  
> And that the exalted powers of the king might favor him,  
> He now has given the sacred MANUAL of Aurelius.  
>
> TREVISO, 1471.

This little work, from which Morellus suspects that printing in Treviso began [Note: [Col. 0189D] In the Catalogue of the Pinelli Library], consists of twenty leaves [Col. 0189B], printed in elegant round type, with twenty-two lines per page. It contains only the first twenty-four chapters according to the arrangement of later editions. Audiffred, in the Catalogue of the Casanatense Library. Add Crevenna’s latest catalogue.

X.—(44) *The Mirror of the Sinner*.

Without year, place, or printer; in quarto. *The Mirror of Sinners of Blessed Augustine*. “An old edition, about the year 1500.” Thus the Catalogue of the Royal Library.

Without year, place, or printer; in folio. *The Mirror of the Sinner of Saint Augustine*. See what is noted concerning the book *On the Quantity of the Soul* from the same edition.

XI.—(47) *On Knowledge of the True Life*.

Without year. Mainz, by Peter Schoeffer—as is clear from his distinctive red-printed device at the end [Col. 0189C]—in quarto. It begins with a table of chapters occupying almost three pages, preceded by nine lines of verse beginning:

> Father Augustine, in the eagle-like manner of John,  
> You seek the lofty hidden things in heaven with the sails of genius, etc.

At the end: “The little book of Augustine on knowledge of the true life is complete.” The type is exactly the same as the forms of the preceding book. Debure suspects in the Catalogue of the Library of the Duke de La Vallière, vol. I, p. 176, that it was printed about the year 1470. It is also held in the Lübeck Library. See Gessner, p. 14, from whom Schelhorn, in his dissertation addressed to Quirinus (Lindau, 1761, in quarto), p. 37, and Schwindel, in *Historical-Critical Notes on Old and Rare Books*, book XXXVII, are cited.

1578. Basel, … “A fragment of Saint Augustine *On the Trinity*, from the book entitled *On Knowledge of the True Life* (whose author is Honorius of Autun), Greek and Latin, translated by Jerome Leunclavius.” It appears together with the *Embassy of the Emperor Manuel Comnenus to the Armenians*, etc.

1670. Rome, … The same, with some slight difference. It appears among the *Golden Theological Opuscula* of certain Greeks, collected by Father Arcudius, beginning at p. 672. Thus Audiffred in the Catalogue of the Casanatense Library.

XII.—(48) *On the Christian Life*.

Without year or place (Mainz, by Peter Schoeffer); in quarto. It begins: “The prologue of Blessed Augustine on the Christian life begins.” At the end: “The book of Blessed Augustine on the Christian life is complete. By doing these things, each person will obtain eternal life.” At the very end [Col. 0190A] one sees Schoeffer’s device printed in red, as usual. The type inclines from Gothic toward round, but is extremely thin and crude. Signatures and folio numbers are entirely absent. Compare the Catalogue of the Library of the Duke de La Vallière, vol. I, p. 174. It is also praised in the Catalogue of the Bunau Library and is held in the Lübeck Library.

Without year. Paris, by Jean Lambert; in octavo. *The Book of Blessed Augustine on the Christian Life*. This occupies the upper part of the page; the remainder is occupied, as was customary with Parisian printers at the end of the fifteenth and beginning of the sixteenth century, by the workshop device. At the end: “It is complete,” etc. “Printed in Paris by Jean Lambert, residing in the rue Saint-Jacques, for Dionysius Roce.” The letters are small Gothic type.

1467. By Ulrich Zel of Hanau; in quarto. *The Book of Blessed [Col. 0190B] Augustine on the Christian Life*. *His Book on the Singularity of Clerics*. At the end of the latter: “The book of Blessed Augustine, bishop, on the singularity of clerics is complete. By me, Ulrich Zel of Hanau, cleric of the diocese of Mainz. In the year 1467.” The first treatise comprises nineteen leaves, the second thirty-three, each page consisting of twenty-seven lines. Debure, in the Catalogue of the Duke de La Vallière, vol. I, p. 173. Above, under the minor works, you will find several treatises of Augustine very similar to this edition, printed by the same printer, doubtless, about the year 1470, as is believed.

XIII.—(50) *On the Twelve Degrees of the Abuses of the World*.

Without year and place; in folio. “The book of Aurelius Augustine, most worthy bishop of Hippo, on the twelve abuses of the age, begins happily.” At the end: “Praise to God.” Separately, on the final leaf [Col. 0190C], are printed *Augustine’s Most Excellent Authority on the Origin of the Soul* and *Augustine on the Divination of Demons*. At the end again: “Praise to God.” This explains why, in two copies of this edition held by Seemiller, fascicle I, p. 109, one contains only the little work mentioned first, while the other, in addition to the other two works contained on a single leaf, also includes two books of Blessed Anselm, *Why God Became Man*, printed in twenty-nine leaves.

There are four sheets. The Gothic types are rather crude and uneven, printed in broad lines; especially frequent is the contraction of the syllables *de*, *be*, *po*, *bo*, *vo*, *co*, *ho*, and *in* into a single character. There are also frequent syllabic abbreviations.

1514. Leipzig, in quarto. *The Book of the Blessed Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on the Twelve Degrees of the Abuses in the World: A Useful and Delightful Book* [Col. 0190D]. At the end, after repetition of the title: “Carefully printed at Leipzig by the bachelor Martin of Würzburg, in the year from the birth of Christ 1514.” The printer’s device follows at the very end.

1521. Augsburg, by Sigismund Grimm and Marx Wirsung; in quarto. “Augustine on the Twelve Steps of Abuse, from the New Song, showing how one may obtain the kingdom of heaven, translated into German by George Spalatin.”

XIV.—(55) *On the Antichrist*.

1522. Paris, … “A fragment of Saint Augustine from the treatise *On the Antichrist* (which is found among the works of Alcuin and Rabanus).” It appears in the *Miraculous Book* that demonstrates the Prophecies, etc. Audiffred, in the Catalogue of the Casanatense Library.

XV.—(75) *On the Essence of Divinity*.

1510. Leipzig, by Wolfgang Monacensis; in quarto. “The book of the Blessed Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on the essence of divinity, in which he chiefly refutes the errors of the Anthropomorphites and Vadians, arising from the false opinions of certain philosophers; explaining with the utmost clarity that bodily and human members are attributed to the divinity in the sacred Scriptures not carnally but spiritually. With certain annotations appended, collected extemporaneously by Doctor Magnus Hundt of Parchim, at the University of Leipzig, and highly useful to students of philosophy and lovers of sacred literature” [Col. 0191B].

The editor’s letter to Paul Schiller, professor of philosophy and sacred literature, is prefixed; it is dated at the Prince’s College, 17 October 1508. Augustine’s words and the annotations alternate with one another. The Cologne Library praises Hundt’s Leipzig edition of 1509, according to Becmann’s Catalogue of the Frankfurt Library, p. 35.

CONTINUATION OF THE SECOND ARTICLE. Annals of the editions of the individual books of Saint Augustine, § III. Works that are wholly doubtful.

I.—Commentary on Matthew.

Without year or place. *Saint Augustine’s Commentaries on Matthew*. George Pray reports in the Catalogue of the Buda Library, vol. I, p. 89, that it is in every respect similar to the edition of the books *On Christian Doctrine* printed without indication of place or year [Col. 0191C]. Both books were also contained in a single volume in that library, and Pray would have described this one more accurately had his copy not been mutilated. I do not know whether it is a portion of the *Evangelical Questions*, which are listed among the genuine works under no. 41.

II.—*On the Vanities of the Age*.

Without year, place, or printer; in quarto. “First, of Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, *On the Vanities of the Age*; second, *On the Christian Life*.”

The distinguished Seemiller preserved a record of this edition, like that of many others which are otherwise encountered only very rarely, fascicle II, p. 150. These two little works cannot be separated and together comprise twenty-three leaves, with twenty-five lines per page, printed in somewhat large, oblong, and handsome Gothic type [Col. 0191D], the same type used by Conrad Finer of Esslingen [Note: [Col. 0191D] For information about him, readers are referred to Gerhoch Steigenberger’s *Literary-Critical Dissertation on the Two Very Oldest Printed German Bibles*, etc., who had the same type engraved in copper, plate III, nos. 3 and 4.]. Catchwords, signatures, numbers, and page headings are absent. Nevertheless, the printer used two initial letters in woodcut forms for these works.

The beginning reads: “The book of Augustine on the vanities of the age begins.” At the bottom of the reverse side of the fifth leaf, in two lines: “The book of Saint Augustine on the vanities of the age is happily complete.” Then at the head of the sixth leaf: “The prologue of Blessed Augustine’s book on the Christian life begins happily”; and finally, on the last page, in three lines: “The book of Saint Augustine on the Christian [Col. 0192A] life is happily complete.”

For the rest, I confess that I do not know to which work I should assign the first treatise. I suspect, however, that it is the same as the sermon commonly entitled *On the Vanity of the Age*, listed among the doubtful works under no. 9.

III.—*Exposition of the Creed and of the Lord’s Prayer*.

Without year, place, or printer; in folio. “First, Saint Augustine’s Exposition of the Creed; second, his Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer.”

The distinguished Seemiller mentions these two little works, bound together with several works of Thomas Aquinas and Henry of Hesse dealing with nearly the same subject and printed in the same types, fascicle I, pp. 152ff. They are printed in somewhat large, oblong Gothic type. The punctuation marks, as the aforementioned scholar observed, are a point and a comma projecting above and below the line; sometimes a point is added beneath it in the form of an exclamation mark [Col. 0192B]. There are thirty lines to a full page. Numbers, signatures, catchwords, and initial letters are absent.

Without year, place, or printer; in small quarto. “First, Saint Augustine’s sermon on the Lord’s Prayer; second, his Exposition of the Creed; third, his Sermon on the Avoidance of Drunkenness.”

These three little works, whose record was preserved by the same learned man, fascicle I, p. 163, are contained in one volume of eight leaves and cannot be separated. According to the same witness, the types are small but very thick Gothic, not unlike those most often used by Ulrich Zel, though smaller. The mark of division is a loop in the following form: || ~ ||. The book lacks numbers, signatures, catchwords, and [Col. 0192C] initial letters. Each page contains approximately twenty-seven lines.

IV.—*On the Power of the Psalms*.

Without year, place, or printer; in quarto. At the beginning: “Augustine’s *On the Power of the Psalms* begins.” At the end: “Augustine’s *On the Power of the Psalms* is complete.” The distinguished Seemiller, fascicle II, p. 163. According to his testimony, the volume is printed in Gothic type of a distinctive form and proper size, on white, glossy paper, without catchwords, numbers, etc., except that the printer numbered the first five leaves.

Without year. Paris, by Dionysius Roce; in octavo. *Augustine on the Power of the Psalms*. The printer is recognizable from the device printed with the title. See the book *On the Christian Life* from the same workshop. The Catalogue of the Bodleian Library records an edition of this book in quires, without indication of place or year.

CHAPTER IV. The Principal Excerptors and Commentators on the Works of Saint Augustine.

Casimir Oudinus, in his *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 990, after completing his account of the life, writings, and editions of Saint Augustine, wrote a separate chapter on the principal excerptors or commentators on Augustine, both ancient and modern, and added it as the seventh and final chapter [Col. 0193A]. Following him, the authors of the *Ecclesiastical Library of Cologne* reproduced almost the whole of it, preserving even the heading, in their commentaries under the entry AUGUSTINE, no. VI, p. 767. They nevertheless omitted matters which they had more suitably treated elsewhere and also enlarged the account with a number of worthwhile additions.

It seemed to us that abandoning so excellent an arrangement could not be done without harm to readers. Yet we understood that what they had most recently assembled required some correction in only a few places, and that very little of it was unsuitable for our treatment. Nor could we hope to make it substantially fuller ourselves; indeed, we discovered that everything relating to this subject which we had arranged on our own cards had already been covered by them. Therefore [Col. 0193B] we did not hesitate in the least to transfer here, in their own words, whatever in the whole of Oudinus’s and the Cologne authors’ dissertation seemed sound to us, provided that we did not appear to diminish anyone else’s merit.

The first was Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, who about the year 450 composed a book of *Sentences Excerpted from Saint Augustine*, published several times separately through the care of John a Fuchte; we shall discuss it in its proper place. The Cologne authors, misled by an incomplete title, had inserted a notice of it after Lumnius’s *Thesaurus* as though it were the little work of the editor himself. The next in age was the man to whom Oudinus had given the first place in this series.

Eugyppius, an African abbot and presbyter of the sixth century, excerpted sentences, questions, and other material from the writings of Saint Augustine and collected them into a single body, which he named the *Thesaurus* [Col. 0193C]. Since he also belongs within the scope of our catalogue, you will find more about him in the following volume.

Among the manuscript codices of Cardinal Bessarion’s Venetian library there is, under the name of Peter, abbot of Tripolis, an *Exposition of the Epistles of Saint Paul from the Sermons of Saint Augustine*, on parchment. Baronius speaks of it under the year 562, after Cassiodorus’s *Divine Institutions*, chapter 8. But whether it is genuinely the work of Peter, abbot of Tripolis, must be examined cautiously, although James Philip Tomasini says so in his *Catalogue of the Public and Private Libraries of Venice*, which he arranged to be printed at Udine in 1650, in quarto. Oudinus.

The Venerable Bede, an Englishman by birth, a monk and presbyter by profession [Col. 0193D], flourished in and after the year 710. Among the works of the Venerable Bede are *Commentaries on All the Epistles of Saint Paul*, excerpted for the most part from Augustine’s works. Baronius, in his *Annals* under the year 562, raises a dispute over this work and considers that it should be attributed to Peter, abbot of Tripolis, whom Cassiodorus mentions in chapter 8 of the *Divine Institutions*.

John Mabillon, however, brilliantly resolves the dispute. In a special dissertation in volume I of the *Analecta*, p. 12, he demonstrates that the work belongs neither to Bede nor to Peter, but to Master Florus, a deacon of the Church of Lyons. In the meantime, Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, testifies in Letter 76 to Hincmar, p. 118, that he possessed Bede’s commentary—for Bede himself confirms in his catalogue of his works that he had explained Saint Paul’s Epistles—and also his *Collection on the Apostle*, excerpted from Augustine’s works, in a fairly large volume not yet printed [Col. 0194A]. It is, moreover, found in two manuscript copies belonging to John Mabillon, from the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, as he himself reports. See what Stephen Baluzius has in his notes to Lupus of Ferrières, p. 405. Oudinus.

Master Florus, deacon of the Church of Lyons, renowned about the year 850, wrote a *Commentary on All the Epistles of Saint Paul* composed from the writings of Saint Augustine. It is contained in volume VI of Bede’s works, falsely attributed to him. John Mabillon demonstrated from several manuscript codices that it belongs to this Florus, in a dissertation on the subject in volume I of the *Analecta*, pp. 12ff. [Col. 0194B]. He also showed that Bede’s genuine commentary differs from the published work and that he possessed the former, still unpublished, intending to bring it to light someday.

Elsewhere, however, he observes that in three manuscript codices of the Abbey of Saint Gall in Switzerland, dating from the eighth and seventh centuries, this very exposition of Bede is contained under the name of Florus the presbyter. See what he learnedly notes in volume IV of the *Analecta*, p. 630.

About the year 1180, Robert of Torigni, in Normandy, abbot of Saint Michael on the Mount in the diocese of Avranches, abridged Florus’s lengthy commentary on Paul’s Epistles. He believed it belonged to Peter of Tripolis, and Baronius adopted this opinion under the year 562 of Christ. A manuscript of the abridgment is held among the codices of the library of Saint Michael on the Mount [Col. 0194C]. There are also a letter and prologue to the *Abridgment of the Apostle’s Epistles According to Augustine* in the appendix to the works of Guibert, edited by Luc d’Achery, Paris, in folio, 1651, p. 715, which he brought forth from a manuscript codex. Thus Oudinus, who discusses the same matters more fully elsewhere, in his survey of the works of Bede and Florus of Lyons. Above we presented a separate and very ancient edition of these commentaries.

Bonizo, bishop of Sutri and Piacenza, about the year 1073 composed an Augustinian *Epitome*, or *Excerpt of the Sentences of the Miraculous Doctor Augustine*, divided into eight books. He dedicated it to Saint John Gualbert, founder and first abbot of Vallombrosa. It exists in manuscript in the Imperial Library at Vienna, among the manuscript codices brought there from the Ambrosian fortress, codex 85, as Peter Lambecius, its inspector and keeper, testifies in volume II, chapter 8, of the commentaries on that library, pp. 790ff. Oudinus.

William, abbot of Saint-Thierry near Reims in France, of the Order of Saint Benedict, later, after resigning the abbacy, became a monk of the Cistercian Order at Signy in the same diocese, in the twelfth century. Among his *Collections* there is a little work, *Sentences on Faith*, collected from the works of Saint Augustine. Oudinus testifies that he copied it from the author’s autograph manuscript in the Cistercian library at Signy and gave it to Thomas Blampin of the Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur, who promised to publish the collection under its author’s name in the appendix to the final volume of Saint Augustine’s works [Col. 0195A], but did not do so. The Cologne authors, following Oudinus.

Robert Kilwardby, of the Order of Preachers, an Englishman, archbishop of Canterbury and cardinal-bishop of Porto in the thirteenth century, divided nearly all the books of Saint Augustine, as well as those of several other doctors of the Church, into small chapters, briefly annotating the opinion of each. Various manuscript records of this labor survive in the Royal Library of Paris, listed by Echard in *Writers of the Order of Preachers* under the year 1279, p. 379, where he also mentions others from the English catalogue. The Cologne authors.

Bartholomew of Urbino, bishop about the middle of the fourteenth century and an Augustinian hermit, a constant reader of the works of Saint Augustine and Ambrose, excerpted the more noteworthy sentences of both and arranged them in alphabetical order, calling the work the *Milleloquium*. The *Milleloquium of Augustine’s Sentences*, begun by Augustine Triumphus of the same Order—commonly called “of Ancona”—his teacher, and completed by his disciple, was printed at Lyons in 1555. The *Milleloquium of Ambrose* was printed there in 1556, in folio. The Cologne authors, following Oudinus.

Antonio de Nomis of Florence—called Maciallensis by some—an Augustinian hermit who died in 1438, arranged chapters from Saint Augustine’s books containing nearly the whole treatment of sacred literature and entitled them *Flowers of the Doctor, Holy Father Augustine*. They are said to exist in the Library of the Holy Spirit at Florence. The Cologne authors.

John Frederick Lumnius’s [Note: [Col. 0195D] Incorrectly printed “Lunicius” in Lipenius, *Theological Library*, II, 916. The Cologne authors.] *Thesaurus of the Christian Man*, collected from the writings of Saint Augustine, Antwerp, 1588. The Cologne authors.

Labbe testifies [Note: [Col. 0195D] *Dissertation on Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the additions and corrections, p. 714, cited by Oudinus, col. 952. The Cologne authors.] that he had received from trustworthy men the three books of Saint Augustine’s *Dulciloquia*, first published from an old manuscript exemplar of the Romersdorf Library at Herborn in 1592, in duodecimo, although he says that he had not yet seen them. The Cologne authors. In the Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris, the book appears as published at Herborn in Nassau in 1614, in duodecimo, under the title: *The Three Books of Aurelius Augustine’s Dulciloquia, Now First Published from an Old Manuscript Exemplar of the Romersdorf Library, through the Care of William Rolichius*.

John Gastius of Breisach published *Commentaries on the Whole Bible Collected from Augustine’s Works*, Basel, by Hervagius, 1542, in two folio volumes. The Bodleian Library catalogue praises it. The Catalogue of the Thott Library records volume I of the same work, containing the Old Testament, in the Venetian edition from the Erasmus press, 1543.

Jerome Torres, or Torrensis, a Spaniard of the Society of Jesus, published *An Augustinian Confession*, divided into four books and arranged under particular headings of theological topics, collected with great care from all the works of Saint Augustine, Dillingen, 1568, and again, enlarged and corrected, 1569, in folio. [Note: [Col. 0195D] Alegambe gives 1569. Lipenius, however, in *Theological Library*, I, 117, gives 1596, as does Oudinus in his *Commentary*, col. 993. He says that Torres, having advanced to a very old age, corrected it, removing those passages he had attributed to Saint Augustine from the book *On Faith to Peter*, which is known to belong to Saint Fulgentius, and from the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, which belongs to Gennadius of Marseilles. The Cologne authors.]

He opposed it to the Augsburg Confession. In this work, says Alegambe in the *Bibliotheca of the Writers of the Society of Jesus*, p. 188, he does two things exceptionally well: first, he admirably proves and confirms Catholic doctrines and refutes the errors of heretics from Augustine; second, he restores exactly and interprets sincerely Augustine’s passages that had either been misunderstood or maliciously distorted and corrupted by heretics. Oudinus and the Cologne authors.

John Piscatorius of Leipzig composed an *Epitome of All the Works of Augustine* with diligence that was by no means contemptible. An edition printed at Augsburg by Heinrich Steyner in 1537, in folio, may be consulted here. Its title is:

*Epitome of All the Works of the Divine Aurelius Augustine, Bishop, Most Learned in Every Respect: What That Man Thought, Wrote, and Also Taught Concerning the Sacraments of the Church and the More Common and More Important Passages of Sacred Scripture, Collected in This Book Most Faithfully and with the Greatest Care, by a Certain Abbreviated Method, by John Piscatorius of Leipzig.*

The title also contains a brief admonition to the reader, in which he asserts that he has presented Augustine’s very words, precisely and without alteration, together with a ten-line poem by Stephen Vigilius of Pacimont in praise of the book. A preface by the same Vigilius is inserted before the author’s own preface. The work is divided into three volumes. The first presents Augustine’s sentences arranged according to the headings of Christian doctrine; the second offers miscellaneous and diverse material; the third provides complete books of Augustine, which we listed above in the annals of editions of his works.

John Pesselius laid rash hands upon Piscatorius’s work and repaid him with abuse instead of thanks. For there appeared:

*The Epitome of All the Works of Saint Augustine by John Pesselius, of the Order of Preachers, from Tiel in Gelderland: First Collected at Length and Maliciously by John Piscatorius the Heretic, and Revised by John Pesselius, Doubled in Size, and Restored to Catholic Meaning; To Which Is Added a Fourth Volume on the Seven Sacraments, Collected from the Same Augustine through His Labor.* Cologne, 1539, 1542, 1549, in folio. [Note: [Col. 0196D] From Echard, *Writers of the Order of Preachers*, under the year 1549, p. 135. The Cologne authors. But the edition dated 1535, recorded by the same authors, is false, since Piscatorius’s *Epitome* first appeared in 1537.]

Jacob Tribesci of Brescia, a Lateran canon regular, *Answers to a Thousand Questions on Nearly Every Discipline, Excerpted from All the Books of Saint Augustine*, Venice, 1583, in quarto. Elsewhere we found it recorded as Venice, by Bernhard Giunta, 1586, in quarto.

John Baptist Masculus, a Neapolitan of the Society of Jesus, *Homiletical Reflections on the Works of Saint Augustine*, Naples, 1652, in folio. [Note: [Col. 0196D] From Lipenius, *Theological Library*, I, 118.] Perhaps this is the same work that Toppi [Note: [Col. 0196D] *Neapolitan Library*, p. 137.] calls *Acroamatic Books of Learned Readings from Saint Augustine for Sermons, Condensed from Ten Volumes into One*, Naples, 1656, in folio. The Cologne authors.

[Col. 0197A] David Lenfant of Paris, of the Order of Preachers, *Augustinian Concordance, or a Collection of All the Sentences Found Scattered throughout All the Works of Saint Augustine, in the Manner of the Concordances of Sacred Scripture*, vol. I, Paris, 1656, in folio; vol. II, 1665.

His *Augustinian Bible*, or *Collection and Explanation of All the Passages of Sacred Scripture Found Scattered throughout All the Works of Saint Augustine, in Biblical Order*. Paris, 1661 and 1670, in two volumes.

Albert, Duke of Luynes, who died in Paris on 10 October 1690, aged sixty-nine, published *Sentences and Instructions Excerpted from Saint Augustine*. Paris, 1677. The Cologne authors, p. 214.

Thus far, let everything concerning Augustine be considered stated.

[Col. 0197]

VARIOUS AUTHORS [Note: [Col. 0197D] We wish to warn the reader concerning these authors that not all are commended equally for orthodoxy. For it is known to everyone that Erasmus of Rotterdam, as well as Phereponus—or rather John Le Clerc, concealed under this fictitious name—is regarded by Catholic writers as guilty of heterodoxy in many matters. Nevertheless, since many of their annotations on Saint Augustine are by no means without importance, we did not wish to suppress them on account of several passages that are not entirely free from criticism or even erroneous, from which every careful student will easily be able to guard himself. Moreover, who does not know that the works of certain heresiarchs and pagans were often deliberately collected, both so that anything good mixed among them might not be lost and so that whatever savored of error might furnish a new monument for ecclesiastical history? The scholiasts, commentators, and collectors of the preceding two centuries bear witness to this, especially the Benedictines, whom no one has ever blamed for having, in their editions, as it were, revived the errors of every kind of heterodox writer—for example, Celsus, Porphyry, Julian, Pelagius, and others. EDITOR.]

EXERCISES ON THE WORKS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE.

IN THE FIRST VOLUME.

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS’S CENSURE OF THE BOOKS OF THE *RETRACTIONS* AND THE *CONFESSIONS*.

[Col. 0197B]

Perhaps someone will wonder why we have given these two works the first place. Let him accept the reason: there are two things that greatly kindle one’s desire to read and contribute to understanding a book—the author’s life, once known, and the work’s subject, once it is no longer unfamiliar. For it matters greatly what opinion and what disposition one brings to reading; nor is it easy to say how much weight a preconceived opinion about a person carries in judgment. We frequently kiss with delight a saying uttered by someone we love and of whom we think highly, but would spit upon it if we believed it had come from someone else whom we hate.

The holy and prudent man Augustine provided us with both advantages in these two works. In the books of the *Retractations* he set out the subjects of all his works, and in the books of the *Confessions* he portrayed his entire life. He did both so carefully that someone less charitable might suspect that a human feeling akin to κενοδοξία (*kenodoxia*, vainglory) or φιλαυτία (*philautia*, self-love) had not been wholly absent. But the matter is far otherwise, if one considers the purpose of that excellent man.

In former times it was customary to celebrate the deeds of distinguished men in books and speeches. This practice passed from military life to scholarship, from Greeks to Latins and barbarians, and from generals and philosophers to bishops. Seeing, then, that histories of this kind frequently contain much falsehood—whether through excessive zeal, a writer’s error, or lack of trustworthiness combined with love of praise—he preferred to be his own historian. He knew, in the first place, how little he would flatter himself; and, in the second, he knew well that no mortal could be better known to him than he was to himself.

For, to say nothing of the hidden recesses of the soul, which everyone knows in himself, though no one fully knows in another, how small a portion of a person’s life is known even by those most closely joined to us? And how fickle and vain is reputation! How great, moreover, is the current of human memory! When two people report the same event or speech at which they were equally present, how great a difference there is in their accounts! What shall I say of those who shamelessly strive, through empty fables and fabricated miracles, to commend to the crowd the memory of those whom they favor, sometimes praising things which the person praised neither did nor approved?

I believe there have even been people who considered it pious, by such disguises, to kindle men’s minds toward religious devotion. I have always execrated this pestilential class of Christian babblers. They do not know how to sketch the true image of piety; and no one knows it except one who is truly pious. If they were such people, they would never deceive the disciples of him who is the truth with such falsehoods. By these devices they also bring it about that even those who tell the truth are not believed.

To prevent anything of this sort from happening, Augustine painted himself for us with his own brush. To do so with greater credibility, he concealed neither his faults nor the fact that he was speaking these things not to men but confessing them to God, to whom it is neither pious nor safe to lie.

When he considered how much imposture or misfortune there had been in the titles of books—how, through carelessness, many works of famous writers had perished; how, through ignorance or the fraudulent zeal of those who deprived authors of their works, they had been transferred by plagiarism under another person’s name; and how spurious little books by fools, not to mention heretics, were scattered among the public under the flattering title of pious men—he countered these evils in the books of the *Retractations* with such care that he recorded the titles, dates, subjects, occasions, and beginnings of each work. He omitted nothing, not even the works he had composed as a catechumen, those he had scarcely begun, those he did not acknowledge, or even a psalm written in popular meter against the Donatist party.

I will allow you to criticize this diligence only after you have calculated how many excellent books have been lost to us through the negligence of others, and how many nursery rhymes have been imposed upon the Christian world under false titles. Would that he had completed with equal diligence what he had begun! He reviewed everything that in any way deserved the name of a book. Letters and treatises remained; he himself testifies that others called the latter homilies. He divides the treatises into two classes: those dictated and those delivered to the people.

Some were spoken in such a way that, with the speaker’s consent, what was said was taken down by shorthand writers at the request of friends. The same sometimes happened before the people, as in solemn proceedings. Indeed, at that time the speed of the shorthand writers generally recorded whatever was said publicly before the multitude. Although it is troublesome to do this everywhere, it would have been extremely useful to do so in serious disputations or sermons.

Nowadays, before any crowd, however large, people say whatever comes into their heads. When pressed, they swear that they said nothing of the kind; while, conversely, some are brought into difficulty as though they had said what they did not say. If someone here calls the people as witness, the people are, as the poet says, “a many-headed beast”; a written record settles the dispute more securely. Works that have been reviewed have a certain parentage. Judgment concerning letters and treatises must be obtained elsewhere.

Yet whatever is not listed in the catalogue must not immediately be regarded as spurious, since a work may be neither a letter nor a homily. Although Augustine undertook this work in old age, it is certain that afterward he assigned certain works to be inserted into this order, such as the book *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus. Other evidence must therefore establish that some works are of uncertain parentage and others certainly false.

The books of the *Confessions* are useful here not only because we read more eagerly the writings of one whose most sincere piety toward God and most ardent love toward his neighbor we have come to know; they also have another, twofold usefulness. First, by knowing the persons involved, we understand his dialogues and letters more correctly. Second, those who have become familiar with the man’s character, thought, and style are not offended by many things that would gravely offend them if they did not know these facts. Everyday experience abundantly proves this to be true.

You might consider some people, naturally rather gloomy, unfriendly, unless you had come to understand their character. Others you might think flattering or mocking; still others, naturally inclined to jest by some hidden force of temperament, you might judge insufficiently serious unless you knew them more closely and domestically.

Nor do I doubt that this happens to many who newly approach the reading of Augustine’s works, as though entering into conversation with him.
