A certain appearance of loquacity offends them; his long-extended periods offend them; his language sometimes seems to degenerate into popular speech; the frequent repetition of the same things is irritating; and in some places one might say that there is something empty and that the author is excessively pleased with himself.

But once, through prolonged reading, one has become more familiar with him, the abundance of his speech and the repeated treatment of the same subjects are easily excused by his zeal for teaching and for fixing what he has taught deeply in people’s minds. His more extended circumlocutions, which are usually accompanied by obscurity, indicate an astonishing power of memory and, since an exceedingly fertile intellect continually offers him abundant material, a desire to compress much into few words.

The lowliness of his diction is excused by love—“which is not proud, but associates itself with the lowly” (*οὐχ ὑψηλοφρονοῦσα, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ταπεινοῖς συναπαγομένη*). We gladly use Paul’s words. And just as he was the most candid appreciator of others’ virtues, so he seems to have been remarkably φιλοστόργος (*philostorgos*, affectionate) toward relatives and friends; this itself is an indication of an exceptional humanity.

As for his own gifts, he neither failed to recognize them through stupidity nor hated them through disgust. Yet he did so in a way that in no respect compromised the man’s remarkable modesty. He loved and proclaimed God’s gifts in himself no differently than he would have loved and proclaimed them in others:

> “To be ignorant of your gifts is stupidity; not to proclaim the Lord’s kindness is ingratitude; not to devote to your neighbor’s benefit what you have received is impiety; not to rejoice in the brotherly fruit which the Lord has produced through you is at once impious and ungrateful envy. How can you put out your talent at interest if you do not recognize what has been entrusted to you? How could you become proud of it, once you understand that it is wholly the free gift of God’s kindness? Whenever divine goodness deigns to use you as an instrument to help others, you have no reason to become arrogant; but you have reason to rejoice with your brothers and to give thanks to God on behalf both of yourself and of them.”

Thus the most holy man loved and proclaimed his own gifts. Yet in the books he wrote as a catechumen, one may detect something of human glory—a feeling which we see implanted especially in the noblest minds, and not a bad one at all.

I will not attempt to excuse what he himself thought should be condemned. He said that the books he had written while still inexperienced and, as it were, an infant in Christian philosophy had served Christ in such a way that they still savored of the school of pride and breathed Plato’s doctrines more than the mysteries of Holy Scripture.

Africa has a certain characteristic temperament, and Augustine possessed something unmistakably belonging to his nation—unless Christ had transformed him into another man.

The books of the *Confessions*, which he seems to have written both at leisure and for those at leisure, possess a certain peculiar unpleasantness. First, he recalls many things about himself, some of them more trivial than a person of stricter judgment would have thought worth mentioning, and some approaching an appearance of self-glorification. What is more tiresome than the envy of the human intellect when someone speaks of himself, however modestly?

Moreover, when speaking of humbler, not to say more sordid, matters—of infancy, adolescence, the impulse of lust, and similar subjects—he endeavors to give what is said the dignity of elevated language. By covering the shamefulness of the subject with this veil, he sometimes becomes obscure.

But if you swallow these little annoyances, you will read what follows with greater profit and greater pleasure.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOKS OF THE *RETRACTATIONS*

[Note: In this collection of *Observations*, everything not marked with another name is to be attributed to Phereponus. —Ed.]

## Prologue, § 1. “Treatises.”

That is, speeches or sermons in which he interpreted Scripture for the people. In that period, *tractare* meant “to preach,” and *tractatores* were called interpreters of Scripture. Cyprian provides many examples of these words.

### “I will mark.”

That is, “I will brand with a serious mark of disapproval,” as it was the censor’s function to mark the conduct of bad men. This verb frequently occurs in this sense in Tertullian, as at the beginning of *On the Pallium*, where he speaks of marking a garment. See the index of Tertullian’s glosses.

## § 2. “Far be it from me to count verbosity,” etc.

Augustine expressed here the words of the comic poet Philemon, whom others also imitated:

> Consider him long-winded who says not even one of the things that ought to be said, even if he speaks two syllables.
>
> But do not consider him long-winded who speaks well, even if he says much and for a long time.
>
> Take Homer as a certain proof of this. He writes for us tens of thousands of verses, yet no one has called Homer long-winded.

A passage survives under title 36 of John Stobaeus’ *Florilegium*. See also Pliny, *Letters*, book I, letter 20.

# BOOK I

## Chapter 1, § 2. “The reason and cause of which are hidden.”

If these things were attributed only to chance and called accidental, these would merely be names by which we concealed our ignorance. But things properly called *contingent* in scholastic language may also rightly be called accidental—that is, things which may equally either happen or not happen. Such things depend upon the freedom of rational beings, who sometimes are led to act as they do without any necessity, and not even by reason or any impulse—or at least by no irresistible force.

Yet these matters too depend upon divine providence, without whose knowledge or consent nothing happens, and which can bring about any change in all things. Since, therefore, there is no necessary cause why we should desire certain things, they may for that reason be called accidental, but not merely because their cause and reason are hidden. This, however, is not the place to discuss the matter.

### Ibid., § 3. “Love of beauty.”

*Philocalia* (*φιλοκαλία*) has two meanings: in bodily matters, love of elegance and neatness; in matters relating to the soul, devotion to honorable things. Any lexicon will teach this. It is therefore less suitably translated “love of beauty,” since those words signify merely love of beautiful boys or beautiful women.

I admit that *philos* means “dear” and *kalos* means “beautiful,” as well as “elegant” or “honorable.” But words must be explained from usage, not etymology.

Augustine therefore rightly condemns his own *philocalia*, because he uses the word there for love of neatness. See book II of *Against the Academics*, chapter 2. If he had called *philocalia* love of honorable things, there would have been no reason to condemn the word as though it meant the same as philosophy. For every *philocalia* is not philosophy, if the word is interpreted according to established usage. Certainly Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus would not have called philosophy—except improperly—the excerpts from Origen to which they gave the title *Philocalia*.

### Ibid., § 4. “Praise itself also,” etc.

Augustine should therefore have retracted what he said about the Academics at the beginning of Letter 1, if he had reviewed his letters. He also touches on this incidentally in book IX of the *Confessions*, chapter 4, section 7.

## Chapter 3. “He will most readily hear those who live well.”

If Augustine had understood “those who live well” to mean people wholly free from every sin, and had said that only such people are heard by God, he would undoubtedly have been seriously mistaken. But if he meant those who strive to live according to the best moral principles—that is, those who fear God and endeavor each day to become better, although they sometimes sin through weakness rather than wickedness—I do not know why he retracted this passage.

For it is certain that the wicked, while remaining in their wickedness, are not heard by God. See the interpreters on John 9:31 and James 4:3.

## Chapter 7, § 6. “Almost no one doubts about beetles,” etc.

Many people rightly doubted this matter, which the most exact natural philosophers now deny altogether. See Francesco Redi, *On Insects*. It requires no less power and wisdom to create a gnat than a camel.

## Chapter 10, § 2. “What all people can do, if they wish.”

Augustine needed to explain this expression, because it is commonly understood as asserting that the people of whom we speak are able to wish. Who would not shudder on hearing someone say, “Christ the man can, if he wishes, fall away from his Father”? The expression ordinarily asserts that it is possible for the person under discussion to wish.

## Chapter 13, § 3. “The reality now called the Christian religion existed among the ancients.”

This must be understood in light of what is said in chapter 21, section 2. Otherwise it would be less true than the statements being retracted.

### Ibid., § 6. “He drove the sellers and buyers from the temple by flogging them.”

Yet this force cannot properly be said to have been force by which the merchants’ strength was overcome. They yielded rather to prophetic authority than to the physical force by which they were expelled.

Augustine was too severe a censor of himself when he believed that, because of this action of Christ, he had spoken less truly in saying that Christ did nothing by force but accomplished everything by persuasion and admonition.

These remarks were aimed, however, at supporting the opinion he later embraced concerning lawful persecution, as is clear from his letters to Boniface and Vincentius. In this matter, his δεύτεραι φροντίδες (“second thoughts”) were not σοφώτεραι (“wiser”).

## Chapter 17. “The competentes.”

That is, catechumens who jointly sought baptism, for which reason they were called *competentes*. See volume VI, *On Faith and Works*, chapters 6 and 11, section 9.

## Chapter 22, § 4. “It is in man’s power to change his will for the better.”

According to the position Augustine defends, he would have spoken more clearly if he had said: “It is in the power of the person whom God grants grace,” and so forth.

But in opposing the Manichaeans he had spoken incautiously. For the argument is valid only with this meaning: “Unless each person changes his will, he cannot do good”—something which he teaches elsewhere to be placed within our power, that is, within the power of everyone. Yet he later held that grace was not given to everyone.

# BOOK II

## Chapter 13. “From the pages of the codex.”

That is, from the margins of the book of Job, on which Augustine had placed these notes.

## Chapter 20. “To each person, according to his own will, it tasted in the mouth.”

Augustine was right to retract this statement, since the matter was extremely uncertain. Nevertheless, this was the common opinion of the Jews, as John Buxtorf demonstrates with many Jewish testimonies in his *Dissertation on Manna*.

## Chapter 32. “Porphyry the Sicilian.”

Porphyry was Tyrian, not Sicilian. Some nevertheless thought him Sicilian because he lived for a long time in Sicily, where he also published books against the Christian religion. See Lucas Holstenius’ life of Porphyry, appended to his work *On Abstinence from Animal Food*.

## Chapter 37. “Ceremonies, so called from abstaining.”

There are other, much more plausible opinions concerning the origin of this word, which may be read in G. J. Vossius’ *Etymological Dictionary*. Whatever its origin may be, it is astonishing that Augustine wanted to abstain from it because it is not used in Holy Scripture—that is, in the Latin interpretation of Scripture. How many other words are absent from Scripture but are nevertheless used everywhere by Christian writers?

How many words would Augustine himself have had to avoid in his controversies with the Arians and Pelagians if he had observed this rule? It was enough that the realities could genuinely be described in this way in Scripture. He therefore acted as too severe a censor of himself.

## Chapter 55, § 2. “Since he had to enter the holy of holies twice a day.”

Here Augustine disagrees with the most accurate interpreters of Moses, and with the truth itself, in two respects.

First, he believes that incense was offered twice every day in the most holy shrine, commonly called the holy of holies. But it was offered only in the sanctuary where the altar of incense stood, while the high priest ordinarily entered the holy of holies only once each year.

Second, he thinks that the daily incense was always offered by the high priest, whereas it could be offered by any priest, as is clear even from the example of Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist.

I admit that Exodus 30:7 assigns the offering of incense to Aaron. But there the name “Aaron” is used in place of the name of any priest. See the interpreters on that passage and on Leviticus, chapter 16.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOKS OF THE *CONFESSIONS*

# BOOK I

## Chapter 1. “And to praise.”

The word *et* (“and”) here has the force of *tamen* (“yet”), as the repetition of this clause that follows shows.

### Ibid. “To you.”

That is, “for your sake,” or “so that we might strive toward you,” as toward the sole and ultimate cause of supreme blessedness.

## Chapter 4. “Stable and incomprehensible.”

Some things are incomprehensible because of their extreme instability, such as shifting winds, whose cause therefore cannot be understood. But God, although he is always the same and without the least shadow of change, can no more be comprehended. Augustine therefore appropriately joins “stable” with “incomprehensible.”

## Chapter 5, § 5. “May I die, lest I die, so that I may see it.”

I know that an oxymoron (*ὀξύμωρον*) may be sought here, such as the saying of a soul thirsting for blessedness: “I die because I do not die.” Nevertheless, I would suspect that the passage should be punctuated as follows:

> “Do not hide your face from me. Shall I die? I shall die so that I may see it.”

Augustine is referring to the account in Exodus 33:17 and following, where Moses, desiring to see God’s glory or face, receives this answer: “You cannot see my face, for no human being shall see me and live.”

After asking God not to hide his face from him, Augustine immediately adds: “Shall I die?”—that is, “if I am to see it.” Reflecting on the matter and understanding that it was so great that he would lose his life because of it, he says: “I shall die,” if that is what must happen, “so that I may see it.”

## Chapter 7, § 11. “He recalls me.”

That is, “he brings me back to memory.” In this sense, the word is joined by Augustine with an accusative of the person; when it has the meaning “to relate,” however, it is constructed with a dative.

Thus the Greeks say *ἀναμιμνήσκω σέ τινος*—“I remind you of something,” that is, “I restore its memory to you.” Learned men have therefore rightly restored the accusative here from the manuscripts.

## Chapter 20, § 18. “The earth,” etc.

Augustine seems to call the corrupt human nature “earth,” since it breathes nothing but earthly things; and the “image” the image of God, renewed and restored through baptism. See the end of section 21.

## Chapter 16. “The river,” etc.

The comparison between a corrupted custom and a river is frequent among the best writers, including pagan authors. Hence “to direct one’s arms against the torrent” means the same as to oppose an evil custom.

Juvenal, *Satire* 4.89:

> He therefore never directed his arms against  
> the torrent.

## Chapter 16, § 26. “Above the school fees.”

That is, in addition to the *minerval*, the payment customarily made privately by each boy, teachers of grammar received publicly established salaries, or stipends paid from public funds.

Or perhaps *salarium* is distinguished from a monetary fee, so that the word refers to salt supplied publicly, meat, wine, oil, and so forth. Thus in the letter of Valerian preserved in Flavius Vopiscus’ *Life of Probus*, after the clothing and money which the praetorian prefect was ordered to give Probus have been mentioned, we read:

> Likewise, as a daily allowance: a pound of beef, six pounds of pork, ten pounds of goat meat, a chicken for two days, one sextarius of oil for two days, ten daily sextarii of old wine, with buffalo bacon; as much salt, vegetables, and wood as is sufficient.

See the interpreters on this passage and on the end of the *Life of Clodius Albinus*, where a stipend is also distinguished from a *salarium*. Likewise, in book X, title 52 of the Code, *On Professors and Physicians*, Constantine orders that fees and salaries be paid to them, so that they may educate many more readily in the liberal studies.

### Ibid., § 26. “The wine of error that was poured for us by drunken teachers.”

Although I am not unaware that Scripture mentions the wine of iniquity and of compunction, I believe that Augustine is here referring to the *Tablet of Cebes*, the famous Platonist. In it, Ἀπάτη (*Apatē*, Deception) is introduced as giving all children entering life to drink by her own power (*ποτίζουσα τῇ ἑαυτῆς δυνάμει*)—that is, *ποτηρίῳ πλάνης*, “with the cup of error.” See the beginning of that work.

## Chapter 18, § 29. “Written in the conscience.”

Augustine is referring to Romans 2:15, where the Gentiles are said to show that the work of the law is written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and so forth.

## Chapter 20, § 31. “Of the most secret unity,” etc.

That is, of God, whose will is like a most secret bond by which the unity of the universe is preserved whole and intact. See book IV of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 12, where he discusses the preservation of all things.

Moreover, the Platonists commonly call God *henad* and *monad* (*ἑνάδα* and *μονάδα*). Consult Proclus’ *Platonic Theology*.

# BOOK II

## Chapter 2. “I had become deaf.”

Those who published *obsordueram* thought that here *o* and *u* had been interchanged, as in *jocundus* for *jucundus*. Augustine seems to be referring to what is reported about the cataracts of the Nile, where the Nile, plunging downward with a roar, deprives the inhabitants of hearing, as Pliny says in *Natural History*, book VI, chapter 29.

## Chapter 6, § 14. “Could one freely do what was not permitted,” etc.

Ovid, that teacher of depravity, asserts—truthfully enough—in *Amores*, book II, elegy 19:

> What is permitted is distasteful; what is forbidden burns more fiercely;

And what follows:

> What pursues me I flee; what flees, I pursue continually.

And in book III, elegy 3:

> We always strive toward what is forbidden, and desire what is denied;  
> Thus the sick man longs for the prohibited waters.

To have no regard for the laws, but to conduct ourselves as though we were released from them, appears to human pride as something lofty and magnificent.

# BOOK III

## Chapter 3, § 6. “The overthrowers.”

This appears to have been the name given to more insolent young men who burst into the schools of rhetoricians—by whom they were not being taught—overturned everything there, and made sport of the teachers. Augustine recalls this wickedness again in *On True Religion*, chapter 40, section 75.

Concerning the insolence of the Carthaginian youth, see what is said below in book V, chapter 8, and compare it with chapter 12.

## Chapter 6, § 21. “The five caves of darkness,” etc.

Augustine explains and refutes these Manichaean ravings at greater length in *Against the Letter of Manichaeus*, chapter 15. That work is in volume VIII.

## Chapter 7, § 13. “Is justice variable and changeable?” etc.

Augustine examined this matter more carefully in his books against the Manichaeans. Anyone wishing to understand this answer properly should consult them. These books have been collected into one body in volume VIII.

# BOOK IV

## Chapter 3, § 5. “From the pages of some poet,” etc.

When people wished to consult the gods about the outcome of some undertaking, they would sometimes open a volume by a famous poet, such as Homer or Virgil, in one of the gods’ temples or privately, and take the first verse that appeared as the gods’ answer. See the interpreters on the *Life of Hadrian* by Spartianus, near the beginning.

Christians too abused Holy Scripture in a similar way, as we shall see in book VIII, chapter 12 of this work.

## Chapter 5. “Is weeping a bitter thing?” etc.

We take pleasure in sadness and mourning, as in all the other emotions to which we gladly give way and which we resist with difficulty, because overcoming them requires force to be imposed upon the disturbance of mind and body. Sadness also gradually diminishes when we freely pour it out in lamentation and tears.

These are the words of Euripides in the *Oenomaus*, quoted by Stobaeus in the *Florilegium*, title 123:

> For there is indeed pleasure even amid evils for mortals:  
> lamentations and streams of tears.  
>
> These relieve the sufferings of the mind  
> and release the heart from excessive pains.

Other passages with the same meaning occur there and elsewhere.

## Chapter 7. “To love people humanely.”

That is, with the kind of love that can be given to perishable things. The Greeks likewise used the word *anthropinōs* (*ἀνθρωπίνως*), as in a similar passage by Menander, quoted by Stobaeus in the *Florilegium*, title 125:

> Humanly one must bear misfortunes, stranger;  
> what is common must be endured in common.

## Chapter 12, § 18. “Behold where it is, where truth has taste.”

If you read it in this way, it seems that the punctuation should be: “Behold, where is it? Where truth has taste.” But perhaps it is better to read: “Behold where it is; there truth has taste”—that is, truth is sweet to the palate, so to speak, of the soul in which God is present.

## Chapter 14, § 21. “Hierius.”

Is this Flavius Hierius, who was consul with Flavius Ardaburius in the year 427? Certainly learned men were sometimes granted that dignity solely because of their learning, as happened to the poet Ausonius and others.

Nevertheless, I do not think so, given the other distinctions held by this man; see Jacob Gothofredus in his *Prosopography of the Theodosian Code*.

### Ibid., § 23. “Before the face of contemplation.”

If this is the correct reading, it means the same as “before the eyes of the mind.”

# BOOK V

## Chapter 9, § 16. “On the cross of a phantom.”

That is, on the cross from which the Manichaeans believed that a phantom, not Christ himself, had hung. See what Augustine says against this doctrine in volume VIII; or, if you want the matter described more briefly, consult his little book *On Heresies*, under the Manichaean heresy.

## Chapter 10, § 18. “Those whom they call the Elect.”

Among them these were people regarded as possessing primary virtue, or as being most devoted to the inventions of the sect. Those who were less perfect were called “hearers.” To use Augustine’s words from the work mentioned above, they wanted their Church to consist of these two classes, namely, the Elect and the Hearers.

### Ibid., § 20. “Unless they are mixed with the flesh.”

Those who first used *concerni* to mean “to be mixed” seem to have intended to express the Greek word *συγκιρνᾶσθαι*, which has the same meaning and does not differ greatly in sound from the Latin.

## Chapter 13. “He loved.”

I believe *direxit* should be read: “he assisted the foreign bishop with episcopal counsel.”

## Chapter 14, § 24. “When I took it literally, I was killed,” etc.

When Augustine was declaiming, he was accustomed to follow what was plausible rather than what had been investigated, and he allowed himself to be satisfied with similar reasoning in interpreting Scripture. Otherwise, it is clear that Ambrose was excessively devoted to allegories.

### Ibid., § 25. “As they are thought to be.”

See what Augustine conjectured concerning the true position of the Academics in book III of *Against the Academics*, chapter 17.

# BOOK VI

## Chapter 2. “By which he was now dividing not only the most watery but also the very warm water among those present with him in small sips.”

Learned men conjecture in the margin that the reading should be: “not only the most watery but also the very warm.” This passage can be corrected with less alteration, however, if we read *potaretur* (“was being drunk”), as the following words also suggest: for there he was seeking piety, not pleasure.

## Chapter 3, § 3. “Yet with whatever disposition,” etc.

If Augustine had been addressing people who wished to know how Ambrose had arranged his life, the preceding little narrative might perhaps have been acceptable. But I do not know how he thought it appropriate to relate such trivial details to God, details that occur everywhere. He was narrating these things more for the sake of human beings than of God; it would have been better to address a friend than God.

## Chapter 8. “The gladiatorial spectacle.”

These detestable games, condemned even by wise pagans, still seem to have been held for the benefit of the pagan populace. Yet it is astonishing that the bishops could not obtain from the emperors the abolition of that dreadful custom.

## Chapter 9, § 14. “The attendants of the court.”

*Aeditimus* is the same as *edituus*, namely, νεωκόρος (“temple attendant”). Here, however, it seems to mean the attendants who were present in the forum for purposes of guarding it, or those who maintained the curia.

## Chapter 10, § 16. “To the count of the Italian largesses.”

This was the usage of the period. See the Theodosian Code, book VI, title 19, the law *On Consular Governors and Presidents*.

## Chapter 13. “To distinguish, by a certain sense that she could not explain in words, the difference between you when revealing and her own soul when dreaming.”

Monnica therefore had to keep to herself the revelations which she believed were hers, although she could not explain how they differed from dreams. How easily the unlearned can go astray in such matters under the appearance of religion!

As for the outcome of dreams, one may say the same thing that Augustine said about the predictions of astrologers—sometimes not entirely vain—in book VII, section 8.

Yet it was flattering to Monnica’s son that his conversion had been foretold by God-sent dreams (*somniis θεοπέμπτοις*). Others, however, might have mentioned this more modestly.

## Chapter 16. “Turned and turned again onto my back, onto my sides, and onto my stomach—and everything is hard.”

The metaphor is taken from a sick person or one suffering from insomnia, who tosses about in bed and finds the mattress hard whichever way he turns. So the anxious mind, while seeking truth in which it may rest and failing to find it, grows dissatisfied with everything as though everything were harmful.

# BOOK VII

## Chapter 6, § 9. “Whiter roads.”

The paved roads were constructed as public works, laid with squared stone set in mortar. When they were repaired, fresh mortar was inserted into the cracks between the stones, and they appeared whiter. Hence roads that were more carefully maintained, and therefore more convenient, could commonly be called “whiter roads.” The metaphor seems to have been transferred from this usage.

If you have the opportunity, see Nicolas Bergier, *On the Public and Military Roads of the Roman Empire*, book II, chapter 18.

## Chapter 9, § 13. “There I read that in the beginning was the Word,” etc.

Deceived by the similarity of several words and statements, Augustine, like many Greek writers, mixed Platonism with Christian doctrine, although in this respect Platonism was pure Arianism. John Clericus demonstrates this in *Critical Letters* 7 and 8.

Perhaps Augustine is referring here to the works of Plotinus, whom he praises highly in book III of *Against the Academics*, section 41, and in book IX of *The City of God*, chapter 10.

### Ibid., § 15. “There I also read of the unchanging glory,” etc.

Although the Platonists had a more correct understanding of the nature of the supreme God than other philosophers, they mixed the vilest idolatry with those doctrines and were extremely hostile enemies of the Christians. This is clear even from Porphyry, Iamblichus, and others who flourished under Christian emperors.

# BOOK VIII

## Chapter 2, § 3. “Victorinus, once rhetorician of the city of Rome.”

Victorinus, says Jerome in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, was an African by birth and taught rhetoric at Rome under the emperor Constantine. In extreme old age, when he surrendered himself to the faith of Christ, he wrote against Arius books in the dialectical manner, extremely obscure and understood only by the learned, as well as commentaries on the Apostle.

In the preface to his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, Jerome calls him Marius Victorinus and says that he had been entirely ignorant of the Holy Scriptures.

But rhetorical minds, so to speak, because of their facility in speaking, think they know everything about which they can speak while the crowd applauds.

### Ibid. “Monsters of gods of every kind,” etc.

He is referring to a passage of Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.698, where the poet describes the Egyptian gods fighting for Antony and Cleopatra against Augustus at Actium:

> Monsters of gods of every kind, and the barking Anubis,  
>
> hold their weapons  
> against Neptune and Venus, and against Minerva.

I do not know whether such things may be said of God according to the laws of propriety, although they could rightly be spoken by someone fighting against the pagans.

### Ibid., § 5. “Which, expressed and retained in definite and carefully formulated words,” etc.

The creed called the Apostles’ Creed, or something similar.

### Chapter 3, § 6. “Father, you rejoice more.”

God is said to rejoice, and to rejoice more, only *anthropopathically* (ἀνθρωποπαθῶς), as Christ accommodates himself to human weakness. Nor can one press the matter or inquire why God rejoices more. But, to turn to grammar, I do not understand why learned men in the following words—and elsewhere as well—write *poenitentem* and *poenitentiam* with *ae*, since it is clear that the word comes from the noun *poena*, which derives from the Greek ποινή. I would not have remarked on this were it not that I see them taking care over such minutiae, since they regularly correct the orthography of earlier editions wherever they think it more correct. Thus they invariably write *jucundus* as *jocundus*, as though it came from *jocus* rather than *juvo*; but the ancient Latins frequently confused *o* and *u*. See Quintilian, *Institutio oratoria*, book I, chapter 4, and Vossius in his *Etymologicum*, under this word.

### Chapter 4. “When Paul, through his military service as proconsul, etc.”

Let others inquire whether it was fitting to tell God little stories, and indeed stories whose truth was by no means established—such as this account of the reason why Paul was called by that name, although in his native language he had been called Saul. Many highly learned men think the story false. Jerome candidly admits, in his commentary on the Epistle to Philemon, that it is a mere conjecture which no Scripture mentions.

### Ibid. “How much more gratefully, then, Victorinus’s heart was thought of.”

I would not mark the word *gratius* with an accent, as though it were an adverb, as the Parisian editor did. It is an adjective, with this meaning: “The more pleasing and acceptable Victorinus’s talent was thought likely to be to the Church, the more abundantly your children ought to rejoice.”

### Chapter 5, § 10. “From a perverse will lust arose; and while lust is served, habit arose; and while habit is not resisted, necessity arose.”

He most aptly describes the stages by which vice steals in and grows. But by the same stages it can gradually be diminished; for “necessity” here means something difficult to overcome, and before the habit of sinning there is no necessity to offend. See also the end of § 12.

### Ibid., § 11. “More combative.”

One should read *pugnacior*, as in the Basel edition, since it comes from *pugnare*; or *pugnantior*, if that is what the manuscript copies have.

### Chapter 6, § 15. “The *agentes in rebus*.”

These were the emperor’s messengers throughout the provinces, sent on official business. On them see Guido Pancirollus, in his notes on the *Notitia dignitatum Orientis*, chapter 65.

### Chapter 7, § 18. “They receive their wings upon freer shoulders.”

Augustine takes this from his Platonism. Plato teaches in the *Phaedrus*:

> ὅτι ψυχὴ τελέα μὲν οὖσα καὶ ἐπτερωμένη μετεωροπολεῖ τε καὶ ἅπαντα τὸν κόσμον διοικεῖ, ἠδὲ πτερορρυήσασα φέρεται ἕως ἂν στερεοῦ τινος ἀντιλάβηται

“That while the soul is perfect and winged, it flies aloft and governs the whole universe; but when its wings have fallen away, it is carried along until it grasps something solid.”

Not much later, on page 345 of Ficino’s Geneva edition, he adds:

> Εἰ τὸ γὰρ αὐτό, ὅθεν ἥκει ψυχὴ ἑκάστη, οὐ καθικνεῖται ἐτῶν μυρίων (οὐ γὰρ πτεροῦται πρὸ τοσούτου χρόνου) πλὴν ἡ τοῦ φιλοσοφήσαντος ἀδόλως, ἢ παιδεραστήσαντος μετὰ φιλοσοφίας, καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς

“For each soul does not return to the same place from which it came before ten thousand years—for it does not recover its wings before that length of time—except the soul of one who has philosophized without guile, or who has loved boys together with the pursuit of wisdom,” and so forth.

Thus his disciples later spoke commonly, and Christians, imitating them, called a return to one’s senses ἀναπτέρωσις, that is, the growth of new wings, as Augustine does here. Hence Chrysostom also used ἀναπτεροῦν to mean “to encourage” or “to impel.” See the *Thesaurus Ecclesiasticus* of Johann Caspar Suicer.

### Chapter 8, § 19. “Foot by foot.”

Following my footprints immediately behind me; in Greek κατὰ πόδα, as though one were to say, “with each foot placed in the preceding footprint.”

### Chapter 12, § 28. “Tomorrow and tomorrow.”

Augustine had in mind a passage from Persius, *Satires* 5.66, where the procrastinator who continually postpones his return to a better mind is described:

> “Tomorrow this will be done; the same tomorrow will do it. What great thing is it,  
> You ask, to grant a day? But when another light appears,  
> We have already consumed yesterday’s tomorrow; behold, another tomorrow  
> Has wasted these years, and it will always be a little farther off.”

### Ibid., § 29. “I hear a voice, etc.”

This strongly suggests the pagan superstition that draws omens from accidental words, something no moderately civilized person is unaware of. If someone thinks that this occurred by a special act of divine providence, so that a heavenly message was given to Augustine in his distress, he will have to show that such a miracle was necessary for Augustine to understand that he ought to read Scripture, so that from it he might learn what he should do. Since he heard this every day from Catholics, both in church and elsewhere, I do not see why one must have recourse to a miracle. But our rhetorician—said with due respect—exaggerates everything by which he could persuade us that this was not an ordinary man, but someone drawn to the Church by a special divine calling. Yet these things would have flowed more appropriately from another pen.

### Ibid. “Whether boys were accustomed, etc.”

As though it were necessary that only the customary songs of playing boys should have been heard! Could not someone playing have repeatedly uttered this over the discarded sheet of paper? One ought to have asked the neighbors who had produced the voice before judging that it had been sent by God.

### Ibid. “For I had heard about Antony.”

Athanasius, in his *Life of Antony*, § 2. For the sake of brevity I shall quote his words only from Evagrius’s translation:

> As he hurried, as was his custom, to the church, he recalled how the apostles, having abandoned everything, had followed the Savior; and how many, in the Acts of the Apostles, had sold their possessions and brought the proceeds to their feet, to be distributed to the needy; and what great hope was reserved for them in heaven. Turning these thoughts over in his mind, he entered the church, and it happened that the Gospel was then being read, in which the Lord says to the rich man: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven.”

> When he heard this, as though he had conceived the thought beforehand by divine prompting, and as though this Scripture had been recited for his sake, he took the Lord’s command personally. Immediately after leaving the church, he sold the possessions he had.

### Ibid. “I seized it, opened it, etc.”

This was not far removed from the Virgilian sortes, or from those practices by which people rashly sought the future by opening Scripture at random—a practice Augustine himself condemns in Epistle 55 to Januarius. Was it necessary, moreover, to open Scripture rashly in order to learn what even more respectable pagans did not ignore? On this matter see the learned Antonius van Dale, *De divinationibus idololatricis sub Veteri Testamento*, chapter 4.

## Book IX

### Chapter 2, § 3. “Lest we should sink to the lowest depths, etc.”

The learned men rightly preferred this reading to the alternative, *mergeremur*, “we should be submerged.” The verb *vergere*, as also *devergĕre*, is customarily used of things that are pressed downward by their own weight. Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*:

> “Since reason clearly demands that animals of a particular kind must also be understood to exist in the air, it remains for us to discuss what they are and of what sort. They are by no means earthly; for they sink downward under their weight.”

If necessary, see further examples in Nicolaus Heinsius’s notes on Valerius Flaccus, book I, line 289.

### Chapter 3, § 6. “Whatever that may be which is signified by that bosom.”

The expression is taken from Luke 16:22, where Abraham’s bosom signifies not so much the blessed seats as a distinguished place among them, as Hugo Grotius correctly observed in his notes on Luke. Augustine understood it as peaceful dwelling places of whatever kind, in which the souls of the pious await the resurrection of their bodies. In book XII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, § 63, he writes:

> “For neither Abraham nor that poor man was in pain in his bosom—that is, in the secret place of his rest.”

And in Sermon 14 to the people, on verse 14 of Psalm 9:

> “It happened,” he says, “that the poor man died and was carried away by angels. Where? Into Abraham’s bosom—that is, into the secret place where Abraham was.”

On this matter see the learned dissertation of Ludovicus Cappellus, entitled *Νεκρῶν Βίον*, among his works published at Amsterdam.

### Chapter 7, § 16. “You revealed in a vision to your bishop the place where the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius lay hidden, etc.”

If these and similar discoveries of saints’ bodies had not been connected with enormous profit and gain for those who dug them up, many who regard such things as the fabrications of clever men, devised to keep the common people obedient, would not so readily reject belief in them. This discovery, for example, greatly increased Ambrose’s reputation and authority. For, according to our author, it restrained the mind of Justina, the Arian empress: although it did not enlarge her understanding toward sound belief, it nevertheless curbed her fury in persecution.

Two further points may incidentally be observed here. First, Augustine says here, and also in *The City of God*, book XXII, chapter 8, that these bodies were revealed to Ambrose in a vision; Ambrose himself, however, says nothing at all about this in Epistle 22, class 1, where he narrates the discovery. Second, Ambrose describes the matter in such a way as to make the account suspicious. “We found,” he says, “two men of extraordinary size, as belonged to ancient times.” But what ancient times? The heroic age, after human beings had begun to diminish? For this race was already declining in Homer’s time. Or were people, during the three centuries from Christ’s birth to the time of Constantine, larger in stature than in the fourth or fifth century? Or were the martyrs taller than other people, or did their stature increase after death? No one, I think, will believe this.

But read the rest, where tormented demons, through the power of these martyrs, most opportunely condemn the Arians. You will no longer wonder that there are people who think this stratagem was devised by Ambrose to bind the common people to himself and terrify Justina and the Arians.

### Chapter 8, § 17. “Serving as an *agens in rebus*.”

See what was said above at book VIII, chapter 6, § 15.

### Ibid., § 18. “Through men placed over them.”

That is, those whom you set over yourself, so that you may hide, as it were, behind them and act secretly through them. Nothing, therefore, should be changed. Augustine here, as the saying goes, is raising a storm in a little cup.

### Chapter 10, § 25. “The images of the earth, etc.”

That is, the appearance of all earthly things which presents itself to our mind. See book III, chapter 6, § 10. Lucretius discusses these matters in book IV.

### Ibid. “The sound of a cloud.”

That is, a voice emitted from a cloud, such as Moses heard.

### Ibid., § 26. “May I see his servant.”

That is, that he has undertaken to lead a celibate life. Augustine often calls the ministers of the Church, by way of distinction, the servants of God, just as above he calls Monnica “the servant of the servants of God,” § 22.

### Chapter 12, § 32. “It also seemed to me that I should go and bathe, because I had heard that baths were given their name from the fact that the Greeks called them *balaneion*, since they drive anxiety from the mind.”

The Greeks really do say this, although the etymology is absurd. The author of the *Etymologicum Magnum* writes:

> Βαλανεῖον τὸ λουτρόν· τινὲς δὲ λέγουσι παρὰ τὸ ἀποβάλλειν τὰς ἀνίας· καὶ Ὅμηρος παρετυμολογεῖ λέγων·  
>   
> ἀρ’ ἐκ τρίποδος μεγάλοιο  
>   
> Ὄφρα μοι ἐκ κάματον θυμόφθορον εἵλετο γυίων.

“*Balanēion* means a bath. Some say that it comes from driving away anxieties; Homer also gives a false etymology, saying: ‘Then from the great tripod … until he removed from my limbs the soul-destroying weariness.’”

> Οὐ λέγουσι δὲ καλῶς, εἰ γὰρ ἦν ἐκ τούτου, ὤφειλε γράφεσθαι διὰ τῷ I. ἀλλ’ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν ὅτι ἀπὸ τῶν βαλάνων εἴρηται. οἱ γὰρ ἀρχαῖοι βαλάνους εἶχον ἔθος ὑποκαίειν. παρὰ τὸ τὰς βαλάνους αὔειν, τουτέστι τὰς δρῦς. οὕτω γὰρ καλοῦνται αἱ δρῦς, καὶ ἄλλο τι φυτόν. Ἐπαφρόδιτος δὲ παρὰ τὸ αὔω τὸ σημαῖνον τὸ καίω—ἵνα μήποθεν ἄλλοθεν αὔοι.

“But they do not speak correctly. For if it came from this, it ought to be written with *iota*. Rather, one may say that the word derives from *balanoi*, for the ancients had the custom of burning acorns. It comes from burning the *balanoi*, that is, the oaks; for the oaks are so called, as is another plant. Epaphroditus derives it from *auō*, meaning ‘I burn,’ so that he might not burn it from some other source.”

All this, however, is merely Greek trifling, to which Augustine would not have assented had he possessed a thorough knowledge of etymology. *Balanēion* derives from the Hebrew word *ballal*, meaning “to pour over” or “to drench” (Psalm 92:11), from which comes *ballahah*, “mist.” Among the Arabs as well it means “to be irrigated” or “to become wet.”

### Chapter 13, § 35. “Now I pray you for the sins of my mother, etc.”

There may perhaps be some appearance of piety here, but the practice rests neither on reason nor on revelation. See the book *On Care for the Dead*, volume VI.

## Book X

### Chapter 3. “What, then, have I to do with human beings, that they should hear my confessions, etc.?”

Augustine seems to have written this not merely after composing, but also after publishing, the preceding books of the *Confessions*. Those who knew him appear to have read them eagerly, and some of them wished Augustine to describe himself more precisely. Some suspect that, since his adversaries—of whom he had many—were bringing numerous accusations against him on account of his earlier life, he wrote these *Confessions* as a kind of indirect apology, in which he would confess before God what he could not deny, while omitting or softening the rest, and exaggerating whatever might contribute to his honor under the pretext of pursuing another subject.

Although these suspicions may perhaps be unfair, they arise from the unusual manner in which Augustine chats and argues with God, and from the rhetorical coloring with which these *Confessions* are painted. While he speaks at such length about himself before God—or rather before human beings—and narrates so many matters of very little importance, at least as far as others are concerned, everyone asks, “To what end?” Many are inclined to judge him maliciously and think that they see here an immense self-love, covered under the appearance of religion.

It is better, however, for us to be too indulgent than too severe, provided that we remember that the rule of life is to be sought in the Gospel and in its author, Christ, not in human beings. They themselves must be measured by that rule and never imitated except insofar as they are themselves imitators of Christ.

### Chapter 11, § 18. “They must be gathered again so that they may be known,” that is, collected as though from a kind of dispersion; hence the word *cogitare*.

*Cogo* is virtually *coago*, as Gerhard Johannes Vossius demonstrates in his *Etymologicum*, and *cogitatio* is virtually *coagitatio*. Festus writes:

> “*Cogitatio* is so called as though it were *coagitatio*, that is, the long agitation of the same matter during the same delay in unfolding a decision.”

See also Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book V. Augustine should add that it involves not merely agitation but also the bringing together of several things at once. This is the force of the preposition *cum*, from which arise the inseparable forms *con-* and *co-*.

### Chapter 31, § 47. “Drunkenness is far from me, but a hangover sometimes creeps upon your servant.”

He was not a drunkard, in the sense of being devoted to wine; nevertheless, he sometimes drank enough wine for a hangover to trouble him. For *crapula* in Latin is the same as κραιπάλη in Greek: the headache that remains from drinking the day before. Thomas Magister writes:

> κραιπάλη ἡ ἐκ τῆς χθὲς γενομένης οἰνοποσίας κάρωσις, μέθη δὲ ἡ ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς ἡμέρας.

“*Kraipalē* is the stupor resulting from yesterday’s wine-drinking; *methē* is that of the same day.”

### Chapter 35, § 57. “Our curiosity is tested every day, etc.”

No one would regard these as sins if only he did not neglect his other duties. Body and mind need a certain relaxation; the mind cannot always be occupied with serious matters and meditation, nor can the body always be engaged in labor. If anyone today counted such things among offenses, he would be thought, while making a display of humility, to be acting arrogantly and concealing greater faults. People would say that he was straining out gnats and swallowing camels. Yet it is considered impious to suspect this of Augustine.

### Chapter 38, § 64. “Those who are pleased with themselves, etc.”

I am surprised that it did not occur to this acute man that the Donatists, Manichaeans, and his other adversaries might say that he was not displeased with himself, since he spoke for so long not so much before God as before human beings about himself and his affairs; and while he either spoke ostentatiously of serious sins that could not be denied or of lesser ones, he by no means omitted his own praises.

I am also surprised that he did not fear that the same adversaries would here demand confessions of what followed his baptism and what is recorded in his life. Malicious men could easily say that it was not so surprising that he had bid farewell to the rhetorical art, which was to be taught among boys, for little profit and with slight honor, so that he might practice it in a much larger theater and with much greater advantage—in the Church, that is, equipped with sacred authority, where his eloquence could easily bring him great popular praise and substantial gifts from the wealthy, while he made a display of poverty.

They could say that it had been extremely convenient for an eloquent man, given the circumstances of the times, to be supported by the pious generosity of others without much labor; that it was no small pleasure, for one not entirely free from the desire to command, to govern the common people as though in God’s name, to expel opponents from ecclesiastical fellowship, to condemn and proscribe them; to act as leader of a faction because of his speaking ability and to stand far above his peers.

They could say that he had good reason to ask God’s forgiveness for undertaking to interpret what he did not understand, having been made a presbyter and bishop contrary to the canons of Nicaea, equipped only with the facility of speech and with a hasty reading of Scripture translated into Latin, without any knowledge of Hebrew or Greek, and for writing so many volumes on Scripture before acquiring the necessary resources for understanding it.

For whatever might be said—that he had been made presbyter and bishop against his will, that he was unaware of the Nicene canon forbidding a bishop to appoint a successor while still alive, that he had led a poor life, and so forth—malicious men would have said that some of these claims were mere pretense; that he was sufficiently wealthy to give to others and to take for himself as much as he wished; and, finally, that these methods had long been familiar, by which we now see humble men, supposedly despising the world, raised to such power.

As for me, just as I am not credulous toward accusations of this kind, so I admit that I would gladly have read Augustine’s defenses on these matters.

### Chapter 42, § 67. “Was I to approach the angels? With what prayer? With what sacraments? Many attempting to return to you, and unable to do so by themselves, have tried such things, as I hear, etc.”

He seems unmistakably to be referring to the theurgic rites of the Platonists, by which they thought that they could summon angels and archangels and unite themselves with God in a special manner. Iamblichus wrote extensively on this subject in his book *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, especially sections V and X. The Platonists of that age were astonishingly devoted to superstitious rites of this sort. See the *Life of Proclus*, written by Marinus and published in full at Hamburg in 1700 by the learned Johann Albert Fabricius.

## Book XI

### Chapter 2, § 3. “O Lord, perfect me and reveal these things to me.”

This is certainly a religious prayer worthy of a bishop, but it ought to have been joined with study of the languages in which Scripture was written and with the acquisition of all the other aids by which Scripture can finally be understood as it ought to be understood by one who is going to interpret it from the pulpit and in published writings.

God’s assistance does not consist in teaching us by an inward breath, without the use of our faculties, what we wish to know. Rather, it consists in supplying us with sufficient strength of mind and body to use those faculties, and in assisting us, if he so wills, in matters that human industry cannot accomplish.

Had Augustine understood this and put it into practice, his prayer would undoubtedly have been answered. But since he neglected these things, he understood in Scripture only what a man ignorant of languages and criticism could understand. In other matters he walks on air, and serves us Platonism in place of the teaching of the apostles, or thrusts empty subtleties upon us with a great display of words.

I am speaking, of course, of those matters that Augustine does not share with all interpreters of Scripture. For the common material he received, even as a catechumen, from those who instructed him; he did not reconstruct it by meditation. I say this not because I would detract from Augustine’s eloquence or acumen, especially in metaphysical matters, or because I am less willing to grant him his deserved praise, but because I see many abusing his authority and despising, on his account, men who cannot in any way be compared with him.

### Chapter 10, § 12. “What was God doing before he made heaven and earth, etc.?”

You could answer this question much more briefly by saying that you do not know, and that the human mind is swallowed up by the immensity of eternity; nor is faith in the creation of all things or religion thereby placed in any danger. Christians do not profess that they are ready to satisfy every question, but only that they can demonstrate what they affirm by the strongest arguments.

We can show that everything except God alone had a beginning, and that this earth of ours was created by him. That ought to be sufficient for us. As Socrates rightly said, the rest—those things above us—do not concern us.

What Augustine here argues about eternity and time, in the Platonic manner and at such length, has been examined much more clearly by later philosophers and theologians. Consult, for example, Jean Le Clerc’s *Pneumatology*. I shall not undertake to weigh the philosophical reflections of the bishop of Hippo on eternity and time; they are so tenuous that they vanish through their very tenuousness.

### Chapter 32, § 29. “The circuit of that little wooden wheel.”

That is, the wheel on which the sun, with the aid of a gnomon, marked the hours. Time is the duration itself of things, or their continued existence; but we measure that existence by the motion of the heavenly bodies, especially the sun and moon.

## Book XII, § 1. “Your promises are sure; and who should fear being deceived when Truth makes the promise?”

The words “Ask, and you shall receive,” etc. (Matthew 7:7), should not be understood as though God were obliged to grant the solution of every metaphysical question to whoever asks for it. They are to be understood only of things necessary for salvation, and with this condition as well: whoever wishes to understand such things must not merely have recourse to God in prayer, but must also do everything that reason advises him to do in order to attain what he seeks.

If someone asked God to grant him knowledge of Greek and Latin, would he therefore obtain it if he did nothing meanwhile to acquire it? Certainly such knowledge is not necessary for salvation, nor can it now be acquired without labor. The same could be said of other matters of this kind.

Nor would it be without danger if someone thought that he had received from God what he was thinking about some matter simply because he had first prayed that God would grant him knowledge of the truth. This would ultimately be sheer enthusiasm, by which every dream could be equated with divine revelation, even when right reason opposed it. See book XIII, chapter 25.

### Chapter 3, § 3. “For where would light be, if it were not above by rising high and illuminating?”

I would think that *emicando* should be read, for:

> “The fiery force of the vaulted and weightless heaven  
> Shone forth and chose for itself a place in the highest citadel,”

to use Ovid’s words.

### Chapter 17, § 24. “By the name ‘heaven and earth’ he first wished to signify the whole of this visible world universally and briefly, so that afterward, by enumerating the days, he might arrange in sections all the things which it pleased the Holy Spirit to state in this way.”

Whoever these contradictors may be, they understood Moses much better than Augustine, who, unless I am mistaken, was thinking here of the Platonic “supramundane place,” ὑπερκόσμιος τόπος, about which Plato speaks in the *Phaedrus*.

Meanwhile, it is worth noting that Augustine says in chapter 9 that this heaven, being created before time itself, is invisible and participates in eternity. But remarkable is the method of interpreting Scripture that he later proposes in chapter 18:

> “When each person tries to perceive in the holy Scriptures what the author perceived in them, what harm is there if he perceives what you, the light of all truthful minds, show to be true, even though the person whose writing he reads did not perceive it, since he too perceived the truth, although not this particular truth?”

The harm is that any truth can be extracted from any passage, and gradually no certain method of interpreting Scripture will remain, if no attention is paid to critical rules and the only question asked is whether what is said is true in itself. This may be convenient for declaimers, but it is plainly contrary to the proper study of sacred Scripture, whose aim is to make clear, insofar as possible, what each passage means.

When the meaning is ambiguous, however, and no method can establish what the sacred writer intended, then nothing should be affirmed. Things contrary to truth may be rejected, but there is no reason to prefer, among equally plausible alternatives, one that is not made more plausible by all the rules of critical art. To seek in a passage of Scripture something which no grammatical reasoning shows to be present is finally to interpret Scripture as children interpret the sound of bells.

## Book XIII

### Chapter 11, § 12. “Who understands the omnipotent Trinity? And who does not speak of it, if indeed he understands it? A rare soul is one who, when speaking of it, knows what he is saying. They contend and fight, and no one sees this vision in peace.”

Nothing truer could have been said. It would therefore be far better to speak sparingly about things we do not know and ought not to know, since they have not been clearly revealed by God, and to speak at length about all the duties of life whose performance God demands from us.

If we spoke only about what has been revealed to us, and, content with the expressions of Scripture, left unknown matters to God, there would not be so many disputes. I do not know whether these disputes illuminate the truth; I do see that they gravely injure Christian charity.

### Chapter 18, § 23. “At the beginning of the day.”

One should read *in principia*, “in the beginnings,” as the manuscript copies read a little later. Augustine is referring to Genesis 1:16, where the Septuagint says that God made the great luminary εἰς ἀρχὰς τῆς ἡμέρας, “for the beginnings of the day,” as the Latin version read in Augustine’s time. See, however, Flaminius Nobilius’s notes on the passage in Genesis.

### Chapter 21, § 29. “Let him eat a fish lifted from the deep.”

He refers to the word ἰχθύς, which, while meaning “fish,” contains the initial letters of the words Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς Θεοῦ Υἱὸς Σωτήρ, “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.” Hence Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 1:

> “But we little fishes, according to our ἰχθύς, Jesus Christ, are born in the water.”

### Chapter 24, § 36. “I confess to you, Lord, that I believe you did not speak in this way without purpose.”

The sacred writer would not have introduced God speaking in this way without purpose, although it could equally be said that God blessed the four-footed animals as well as the fish or birds. But in Scripture’s very simple style, many things are added or omitted, not to imply some hidden meaning, but because the character of that style permits additions and even omissions without any change in meaning.

Thus in Genesis 1:8 the Hebrew manuscripts do not contain the formula customary on the other days, “and God saw that it was good.” Yet it is no less applicable to what was created on the second day than to everything else. In the creation of the third day, from verse 9 to verse 13, the expression occurs twice; if it had been added only once, as on the other days, we would notice no deficiency.

Those who make subtleties out of such matters have not yet become sufficiently familiar with the style of Scripture. I do not think any learned person can now be found who approves allegorical fabrications of this kind.

### Chapter 25, § 38. “For I shall speak the truth, with you inspiring me.”

This follows from what we said above at book XII, chapter 1. Augustine here imposes upon us as divine revelation the allegorical interpretations which, although they contain true doctrine, cannot be deduced from Moses’ passage.

Paul, and the equity of the matter itself, ought to have taught him—without any revelation—that the necessities of pastors must be supplied by their flocks. But it was no more revealed to him that this doctrine was contained here than it was revealed to Philo and Origen when they extracted from Scripture, by the strings of allegory twisted into foreign meanings, the conclusions they drew.

### Chapter 19, § 44. “And so, while you see these things temporally, I do not see temporally.”

The conjunction *atque ita*, if there is no error here, must mean “but”; that is, it must have adversative force.

### Chapter 33, § 48. “Form and privation.”

Εἶδος καὶ στέρησιν, which in the language of the scholastics we now call “form and privation”; these are opposites.

### Chapter 36, § 51. “But the seventh day is without evening and has no setting.”

If we wish to argue over the point, the morning of the seventh day is no more mentioned than its evening. The morning mentioned in verse 31 belongs to the sixth day, since the Hebrews, following Moses, begin the *nychthēmeron* (νυχθήμερον), the night-day cycle, with evening, which is then followed by the day. Moses does not touch upon the parts of the seventh day because on that day God made nothing.

# Observations on the Books Against the Academics

## Book I

### Chapter 1, § 2. “If, when you were presenting bear combats and spectacles never before seen there by our citizens, the applause of the theater had always received you with the greatest success, etc.”

The reading *ursorum* is correct, for Augustine is discussing spectacles unknown in Africa, such as bear combats would have been. For, as Pliny states in book VIII, chapter 36, it is established that bears are not produced in Africa. He affirms the same in chapter 58.

### Ibid. “You would be proclaimed as fortunate, as you were.”

It is false that Romanianus could have been called fortunate, as Augustine shows in what follows. Therefore he could not have said *ut fuisti*, nor, for that matter, *ut suesti*, as some manuscript copies have. I would prefer *ut suevere isti*, that is, in the sense in which clients, citizens, and peoples proclaim someone blessed.

## Book II

### Chapter 2, § 5. “When, behold, certain books full of good Arabian things, as Celsinus says, breathed forth their fragrance upon us, etc.”

I do not understand how books can be called “full” unless it is added what they are full of. I therefore suspect that something is missing here, such as *wisdom* or something similar.

### Ibid., § 6. “Your adversary.”

The person with whom, apparently, Romanianus was involved in a lawsuit.

### Ibid. “Surely he would leave Baiae and the pleasant orchards.”

There are three errors here, of which the first and last were taken over from earlier editions, while the middle one is peculiar to this edition.

First, instead of *ne*, one should read *nae*, ναί, “indeed.” Augustine’s meaning is that if Romanianus could have presented his adversary with the appearance of philosophy, the man would certainly have abandoned his affairs and flown toward it. This error often occurs in manuscript copies because the two little words were pronounced alike.

Second, *Baias* should be written with a capital *B*, as in Erasmus’s edition, since it is the name of the most pleasant place on the Bay of Puteoli, around which the Romans had elegant villas. Horace often mentions it elsewhere, including *Epistles* I.1:

> “No place in the world outshines lovely Baiae.”

Finally, it is clear from the adjective *amoena* that one should read *pomaria*, not *pomeria*.

### Chapter 3, § 7. “This is commonly called Philocalia, etc.”

See the observations on the *Book of Retractations*, chapter 1, number 3.

### Ibid. “Without wings.”

Whose wings have fallen away. This comes from the teaching of the Platonists, as we noted in the *Confessions*, book VIII, chapter 7.

### Chapter 4, § 10. “Without meter.”

That is, ἄνευ μέτρου, “without measure.” Augustine plays on the ambiguity and does not miss the opportunity to produce a few Greek words that he knew.

### Chapter 6, § 14. “Archesilas.”

A shameful error. Everyone knows that this philosopher was called Ἀρκεσίλαος, not Ἀρχεσίλαος. This error, therefore, ought also to have been removed from the older editions, both here and in the following passages, where it occurs again and again. For although Augustine did not know Greek, he had the old manuscripts of Cicero, in which I do not think this error would have been left by more learned grammarians.

### Chapter 15, § 34. “But he was flat by chance, one of those whom the common people now call *Samardaci*.”

I would suppose this to be an African, or rather Punic, word, derived from the roots *schamar*, “to observe,” and *douck*, “to inspect.” It referred to deceitful men who hoped—or pretended—to foretell the future by observing the stars, omens, and prodigies, and by inspecting victims.

The old scholiast on Horace describes them in this way, at line 113 of Satire 6, book I:

> “He called him deceitful because of the *Sarmadaci*—write *Samardaci*—and the divining astrologers, who stood around the turning-posts as spectators and deceived the inexperienced with lots and trifles.”

A little later he also joins the *Samardaci* with the diviners and shows that they were fortune-tellers. Jacobus Cruquius, however, who published a more carefully corrected edition of this scholiast, suspects that the word is composed from *Sarmata* and *Dacus*, peoples who were once notoriously associated with such deceptions. Choose whichever explanation you prefer, and also consult Johann Meursius in his *Greek-Barbarian Lexicon*.

# Observations on the Book On the Happy Life

### § 3. “Which has nothing so full and solid within that, when the inflated ones walk over it, the fragile ground murmuring beneath them, it sinks and swallows them.”

I would read *inflato sibi*, “inflated within itself,” since he is describing to us a mountain swelling with wind. The *s* could easily have clung to the following word and become attached to the preceding one.

### § 4. “After reading a very few books of Plato.”

I would think that *Platonicis* should be read, for Augustine says in *Confessions* book VII, chapter 9, § 15, “certain books of the Platonists”—unless five manuscripts here have *Plotini*, which I believe to be the true reading.

Before I had examined this passage more closely, I had already suspected that those “Platonic” books in which Augustine believed he had found ideas similar to Christian theology were books of Plotinus. The manuscript reading strongly confirms me in this conjecture.

### § 5. “I was not frightened by your eloquence.”

There exists an elegant dissertation on the life of Flavius Mallius Theodorus, written by Albertus Rubenius and published at Utrecht in 1693. From it one may understand what Theodorus’s learning was and what offices he attained. We therefore refer the reader to it.

### § 7. “Since we all admit that a human being cannot exist either without a body or without a soul, why do we desire food because of either of these?”

Rather, should it read, “Do we desire?” It is Augustine’s question, to which Licentius answers, “Because of the body.” This was an error in the Basel edition, carried over into the present one.

[Col. 0220A] § 35. “This, then, is the soul’s complete satisfaction; this is the blessed life: to know piously and perfectly by whom you are led into truth, to enjoy that truth, and to be joined through whom to the highest manner of being.”] Although it is not difficult to understand what Augustine means, nevertheless there is reason to complain that throughout this entire discussion he has almost constantly abused metaphorical words and expressions, which he elsewhere defines by equally figurative terms. As a result, we have here nothing beyond clever quibbles extracted from ambiguity, and ideas that smell far too strongly of dialectic. I admit that he was speaking with children and a little woman; but when he published these things, I do not know how he could endure saying nothing through so many words. How easily he could have shown that blessedness, properly so called, is that state of mind in which, content with our lot, we neither desire nor fear anything! How readily he could have demonstrated that this state of mind cannot be attained in this life, in which there are always many things that we fear or desire! Having said this, he could have concluded that no blessed life can exist on this earth; that all human beings are wretched; but that those who, in accordance with the laws of the Gospel, can promise themselves blessedness after this mortal life are ultimately less wretched than the rest. But precise definitions of terms, simple language, and convenient arrangement were things almost unknown to the rhetoricians of that age.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOKS ON ORDER

### Book I

#### Chapter 1, § 2

“Who is so blind in mind that he would doubt assigning to divine power and governance whatever rationality there is in the movement of bodies that lies beyond human arrangement and will?”] Here the word *rationis* has been transposed; it ought to be placed immediately before *divinae*, so that the sequence is: “to the power and governance of Divine Reason” (*Rationis Divinae*), in Greek, δύναμι καὶ διοικήσει Λόγου Θείου—“the power and governance of the Divine Logos.” Augustine plainly borrowed “Divine Reason” from Platonic language; concerning this expression, see what Jean Le Clerc collected in his notes on John 1:1. The Benedictines say that they examined ten manuscripts in which this order was observed; but they have *rationi*, if indeed there is no error in the Benedictines’ note. Augustine later uses the same word in the same sense, in § 26, where he mentions the beauty of Reason—namely, divine Reason—which regulates and governs all things known and unknown, and draws its followers, who yearn for it, toward itself, wherever and in whatever place it commands them to be sought.

#### Chapter 3, § 6

“For he too, lying awake on his bed in the same room, was keeping watch, though we did not know it; for there was darkness, which in Italy is almost unavoidable even for the wealthy.”] He speaks thus for the benefit of his fellow Africans. If only he had also spoken for the benefit of posterity and added why, in Italy rather than elsewhere, they were lying in darkness. Was there in Africa an abundance of transparent stones that admitted the light of the moon and stars into rooms, while such stones were rarer in Italy? Did this cause rooms to be dark when their wooden shutters were closed? Let those more learned than I decide.

#### Chapter 11, § 31

“Theodorus, outstanding in intellect, eloquence, the very honors and offices bestowed by fortune, and—above all—in mind, whom you know well, is working so that neither now nor among posterity may any class of learned men rightly complain about the literature of our times.”] I wish there still existed Theodorus’ little work *On the Origin and Nature of the World*, which the distinguished Salmasius says lies hidden in libraries, in his preface to Ampelius. From it we could learn whether Augustine is flattering him here—which I strongly suspect, given the custom of his age, when, if ever at any other time, extravagant praise was common currency.

This Theodorus, after serving among the advocates of the praetorian prefecture in Italy, was prefect of part of Libya, then of part of Macedonia; afterward quaestor of the sacred palace, then *comes* of the sacred largesses, and finally praetorian prefect of Gaul in the year 380. After discharging these offices, he returned to private life, where he devoted himself to writing various short works. During this interval, around the year 386, Augustine was writing these words. He later attained still higher offices, as Albert Rubenius will show in the booklet mentioned above.

### Book II

#### Chapter 1, § 1

“Our mother was also with us. Her intellect—which I had previously come to know through long association and careful observation—appeared to me, in a certain discussion on a matter of no small importance, which I subsequently included in a little book, to be so great that nothing seemed more suited to true philosophy.”] If Augustine had said this to his mother in ordinary conversation, he could certainly not be blamed; indeed, he might perhaps have been praised on grounds of filial affection. But I do not know how he could bear to write and publish it for an educated man, especially since the book *On the Blessed Life*, in which Monica’s outstanding answers are recorded, was also to be published. Anyone who reads it will easily understand that, out of excessive love for his mother, the son found in the words of a good old woman an intellect that others would not readily perceive. What woman, if somewhat more liberally educated today, would not pour forth such remarks—and even better ones—while occupied with something else?

#### Chapter 2, § 4

“Define, then, if you please, what it is to be with God.” “I hate defining,” she replied.] Yet if one reads this book and the preceding one, one will find no definition that is even moderately precise, but only rhetorical descriptions, often more obscure than the thing described, or at least no less obscure. For example, “to be with God”—an improper and obscure expression—is defined as “to be governed by God,” or “to understand God,” and so forth. If such things were written and brought into the public eye today, they would certainly not receive the applause of the learned—nor would the countless empty quibbles with which these little works abound. But in that age words were valued far more highly than things themselves; and our own age still suffers from this fault more than one could wish.

#### Chapter 4, § 12

“What could be said that is dirtier, emptier of dignity, or fuller of shame than prostitutes, pimps, and the other pests of this kind? Remove prostitutes from human affairs, and you will throw everything into disorder through lust.”] Accordingly, if we follow Augustine’s judgment, legislators and rulers do rightly when they allow brothels to exist; for it is better that a few houses be polluted than that all things be thrown into disorder by lust. Hence, they say, such establishments are tolerated in the most distinguished city of all, lest men who are voluntarily celibate, but by no means therefore more chaste, should attack matrons and boys indiscriminately.

How much better it would have been to say that wicked women and lustful young men abuse the freedom granted by God, along with the other things now commonly said by the learned! If we wrote such things today, we could never impose penalties severe enough on those who admire them in ancient authors. I shall not discuss how vices contribute to order; too many words would be required merely to establish the question and arrange everything in due order. But I shall ask the reader to try to construct from what is found here in Augustine a clear and methodically arranged argument. If he succeeds, he will be a great Apollo to me.

#### Chapter 9, § 22

“The marvelous deception of aerial creatures, and so forth.”] The Platonists call *zōa* (ζῷα), or animals, all things endowed with a soul, such as those inferior gods whose dwelling they placed in the air. Augustine interpreted these as evil demons (*cacodaemones*). Apuleius discusses the view of the Platonists at considerable length in his books *On the World*, *On Natural Philosophy*, and *On the God of Socrates*.

#### Chapter 12, § 35

“Once these two things had been discovered—letters and numerical figures—there arose the profession of copyists and calculators, a kind of infancy of grammar, which Varro calls *litteratio*; but what it is called in Greek I do not sufficiently recall at present.”] It was called γραμματιστική (*grammatistikē*), and its teacher γραμματιστής (*grammatistēs*). Philo, in *On the Preliminary Studies*, says:

> “Writing and reading are the accomplishment of an incomplete grammar, which some, altering the term, call *grammatistics*.”

Martianus Capella, in Book III of *The Marriage of Mercury and Philology*, introduces Grammar speaking as follows:

> “In Greece I am called γραμματική (*grammatikē*), because γραμμή (*grammē*) means ‘line’ and γράμματα (*grammata*) means ‘letters’; and I have been assigned the task of tracing the forms of letters with their proper strokes. Hence Romulus gave me the name *litteratura*, although he wished to call me, in my infancy, *litteratio*, just as among the Greeks I was initially called γραμματιστική. He then appointed me a chief and gathered immature followers around me.”

Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book I, chapter 3:

> “The beginnings of the grammatical art are the ordinary letters, which copyists and calculators use; hence Varro also calls it *litteratio*.”

For further ancient testimony on this subject, see Jean Wower’s treatise *On Polymathy*, chapter 4, and Claude Saumaise’s notes toward the end of his notes on Tertullian’s *De Pallio*.

#### [Same passage, § 37: “History”]

This is not to be understood as the kind of history represented by the historians Thucydides, Polybius, and others of that sort, but as philology; its practitioners are called πολυΐστορες (*polyístores*), hence Alexander Polyhistor, Apion Polyhistor, and Gaius Julius Hyginus Polyhistor—as one might say, “knowing many things”—from πολύ (*poly*, “much”) and ἰσάσθαι (*isasthai*, “to know”). See the distinguished Salmasius on the title of Solinus’ *Polyhistor*. Augustine likewise uses the word “history” for any kind of knowledge in Book II of *On Music*, chapter 1, § 1.

## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS’ CENSURE OF THE BOOKS OF THE SOLILOQUIES

A work wonderfully suggestive of the infancy of a good man in Christ. For he makes Reason speak with Augustine as though Reason were not Augustine’s superior part. Seneca more tolerably imagines a dialogue between Reason and Sense. Moreover, as though two human beings were actually speaking, the conversation is split up into discussions and books so that they may not become fatigued; sometimes divine assistance is even invoked for sophistry and trivial quibbling. It requires a patient and fair-minded reader.

## J. PHEREPONUS’ OBSERVATIONS ON THE SAME BOOKS

### Book I

#### Chapter 1, § 1

“He suddenly said to me—or perhaps I myself did, or someone else within me or outside me; I do not know.”] This has the flavor of Platonism, according to which rational human beings are so called insofar as they participate in divine Reason. From that Reason they received not only their substance and the faculties of their minds, but also, whenever they reason correctly, secret admonition, as if from a teacher. See the book *On the Teacher*. Indeed, in Platonic fashion, Augustine also wants reason, considered abstractly, to be a substance; see *On the Immortality of the Soul*, § 11.
