For this reason he distinguished reason from his own mind and introduced it as conversing with that mind.

These points had to be noted because of Erasmus’ censure, lest Augustine should appear to have been more foolish than he really was. We could add other remarks concerning reason from what Photius quotes from Clement, codex 109. Otherwise, who would not be annoyed and wearied by the quibbles that Augustine attributes not to himself but to Reason itself?

#### § 2

“O God, who do not make evil, and make it exist so that it may not become worst.”] That is: “You do not voluntarily make evil, but only make it exist so that nothing worse may occur.” This statement, unless I am mistaken, deserved to be revised. For what is more alien to sound reason and to the sacred Scriptures than the claim that God makes evil exist? But see *On Order*, Book II, chapter 4, § 5.

In a certain sense one might say that God allows evils so that worse evils may not be committed by human beings, when he accommodates himself to the dispositions of free creatures—as when he tolerated divorce and other practices among the Jews. But he cannot be said to make these things. Nor is it surprising that someone who thrusts such notions upon God should obtain nothing from him; for in these two little books, in which he so often appeals for divine assistance, what is there, after all, that you can be glad to have read?

#### Chapter 12, § 21

“I am sometimes compelled to agree with Cornelius Celsus, who says that the highest good is wisdom, while the highest evil is bodily pain.”] He seems to be the author whose books on medicine we possess, since he also wrote on other arts, as Quintilian teaches in the *Institutes of Oratory*, Book XII, final chapter.

### Book II

#### Chapter 3, § 4

“It is more absurd to say that falsity cannot exist than to say that truth cannot exist.”] Erasmus was right to write in the margin here: “Sophistical induction.” Later, at the beginning of the following chapter, he added: “Here too he is sophisticating about the true and the false.” Certainly anyone who wrote such things today would be regarded not merely as a sophist but almost as a fool.

#### Chapter 6, § 12

“Thymian honey, from *thymian* honey.”] Erasmus has the following in his margin: “Virgil: ‘And the fragrant honeys smell of thyme.’ Elsewhere *Hymettine* and *Hymettine honey* occur, but the other reading is preferable.” Thus far Erasmus. I am surprised that the Parisian editors did not mention this variant. The honeys of Hymettus, named after a mountain of Attica, were famous, as were thyme honeys, that is, honey gathered from thyme. See Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XI, chapters 13 and following.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOK *ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL*

#### Chapter 1, § 1

“If knowledge exists anywhere, it can exist only in what lives and always exists; and nothing in which something always exists can fail always to exist. Therefore that in which knowledge exists always lives.”] As though the ideas of the sciences could not exist in the intellect of God even if no creatures existed! Indeed, they existed before creation.

Moreover, who does not know that one must distinguish the abstract idea and truth of a thing from an actual thought concerning such an idea or truth? Abstract ideas and truths may be called eternal because they are by their nature immutable; but who, apart from mere quibblers, would infer from this that minds thinking about them are eternal? By the same reasoning he could have concluded that human minds had no beginning. But we shall not linger over such toys of reasoning.

#### Chapter 7, § 12

“No division leads to nothing. For every part that remains is a body, and whatever is body occupies a place, however small the space.”] This is true and acute. From it he could have concluded that the substance of body cannot be utterly destroyed by human powers, but only changed. Likewise, it might be that something in the substance of mind could be changed by creatures, without its therefore being thought capable of destruction.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOK *ON THE QUANTITY OF THE SOUL*

#### Chapter 1, § 2

“Whence the soul comes.”] The meaning of this question was whether the soul was created by God, whether it was eternal, or whether it arose together with the body through generation. But Augustine resolves or evades it rhetorically, as though the question were what the soul’s homeland is. Who ever dreamed of that?

#### Same passage

“If you continued asking what the earth itself, or water, or air, or fire consists of, I would have nothing more to say.”] Yet everyone knew that these supposed elements of all things consisted of innumerable parts into which they could be resolved. If this could be said of the mind, its immortality would be finished. But comparisons made by those who philosophize less precisely should not be dissected to the quick. That this is not to be done here is clear from the fact that Augustine later denies that the mind is extended.

#### [Col. 0224D] Chapter 3, § 4

“And for the present this is sufficient.”] Evodius was certainly easy to satisfy, since he allowed himself to be satisfied by so few words concerning the nature of the soul. But you will find the same matter treated in the other discussion, *On the Quantity of the Soul*.

#### Same passage

“And therefore it is rightly commanded, even in the mysteries, that one despise everything corporeal and renounce this entire world.”] Erasmus correctly noted in the margin: “In baptism.” For it is well known that those who received baptism used to renounce the devil and the pomps of the world. The sponsors of infants did the same on their behalf, as Augustine testifies in *On Original Sin*, § 45, and in Book I of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 20, § 22.

#### Chapter 4, § 5

“Does it please you that we should believe justice itself to be nothing?”] It is indeed nothing if compared with substance; for justice in the abstract exists nowhere except in the mind of one who understands it. But the Platonists spoke of ideas as though they were substances.

#### Chapter 7, § 12

“To believe authority is a great shortcut and requires no labor, and so forth.”] Yet that authority must first be examined before we put faith in it, so that we may believe it in all things because we are convinced by indisputable arguments that it neither deceives nor is deceived. Otherwise it would be foolish to surrender one’s credulity to something that there is no rational basis for considering truthful. If this were not so, all barbarian peoples who rashly believe so many things told them by priests or elders would have to be said to act rightly. They too proceed by a shortcut, but one that leads them to every kind of error, from which they never extricate themselves.

Therefore all who care about the Christian religion must beware of giving it the same foundation on which the greatest and most shameful errors rest. Augustine speaks more accurately in *On True Religion*, § 45:

> “Authority demands faith and prepares a person for reason. Reason leads to understanding and knowledge. Yet reason does not wholly abandon authority, when one considers whom one ought to believe; and certainly the authority of truth already known and made clear is supreme.”

#### Chapter 30, § 39

“Sense is an affection of the body that is not hidden from the soul by itself.”] After so many words on the definition of sense, it is astonishing that no better definition was produced, especially since Augustine knew perfectly well that the mind senses, not the body.

“Sense” is used in two meanings. Sometimes it is the very faculty of sensing that resides in the mind; sometimes it is the affection by which that faculty is affected, which we barbarously call “sensation.” In the latter sense, sense is nothing other than the mind’s awareness arising on the occasion of a movement of its body; in the former, it is the faculty by which the mind is capable of such awareness. The whole matter could have been dispatched in a few words, whereas here it is tangled up in many.

I shall add nothing further, since these matters are familiar to everyone now that philosophy has fortunately been restored in our time and in that of our fathers, and since I have treated them sufficiently at length in my philosophical works. Nor did I undertake to write philosophical notes into Augustine; otherwise many things could be said by which his subsequent arguments might be refuted. In them he is as prodigal of words as he is sparing of substance.

#### [Col. 0225D] Chapter 33, § 76

“Vanity of those who make vain.”] In some Greek copies, the reading must once have been ματαιότης ματαιούντων—“vanity of those who make vain”—which the Latin translator used by Augustine rendered according to the corrupt reading. In ancient glosses we find ματαιοῦμαι, “I speak vainly”; its frequentative was *vanitor*.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOKS *ON MUSIC*

### Book I

#### Chapter 1, § 1

“It differs in that they have their accent in different places.”] He is speaking of the verb *pone* and the adverb *pone*, and by *acumen* he undoubtedly means accent. Presumably the verb had its accent on the first syllable and the adverb on the second, as a means of distinguishing them. From this one may understand how badly we all pronounce Latin today, and how incorrectly we read verses in particular: for who, while speaking, usually pronounces *ponè* and *pone* differently?

#### Chapter 10, § 17

“They are called sesquialterate when two numbers are related to one another in such a way that the greater contains as many parts of the lesser as the greater exceeds the lesser by a part of itself. I cannot easily explain the origin of this name, unless perhaps *sesque* is said as though from *se absque*, that is, ‘without itself,’ because five is greater than four by a fifth part of itself, which is what the lesser is.”] But the number is not five but six, if six is compared with four, that is, the number in a sesquialterate ratio. Julius Caesar Scaliger therefore rightly criticizes this etymology of Augustine in Book II of *On Poetic Composition*, chapter 26. He thinks that *sesqui* is used for *semis aequum*, “equal to a half,” which is the same as Greek ἡμιόλιον (*hēmiolion*). But Gerardus Joannes Vossius more successfully conjectured that *sesqui*—or *sesque*, as it is written here in Augustine—was the same as *semisque*, that is, “and a half,” with *-que* referring to the whole to which the half is added; hence the Greek ἡμιόλιον, “the whole and a half.”

### Book II

#### Chapter 1, § 1

“Know, if you please, that the entire science which is called grammar in Greek and *litteratura* in Latin professes to be the guardian of history, and so forth.”] Here “history” means knowledge of some matter that does not depend on reasoning but on human convention. A little later, when the grammarian teaches that a syllable is long or short, he is said to be the guardian of history—namely, of the usage of the Latin or Greek language concerning the quantity of syllables.

### Book III

#### Chapter 1, § 2

“Rhythm, that is, number.”] I know that what the Greeks call ῥυθμός (*rhythmos*) was called *numerus* by the Latins, but I fear that Augustine has confused ῥυθμός with ἀριθμός (*arithmos*). Greek is more fortunate here than Latin, for ῥυθμός is said to derive from ῥεῖν, “to flow”; it is what makes a verse easy to pronounce and more pleasing to the ear. The French call it *la cadence*, and they also call flowing verses *coulants*, verses in which there is nothing harsh or rough.

The modern word *rime* derives from *rhythmus*, but *rime* signifies the endings of verses with similar termination, ὁμοιοτελεύτων (*homoioteleutōn*), a meaning wholly foreign to the Greek word. This would not need to be noted except that a learned Frenchman, whom I shall not name, made this mistake.

### Book V

#### Chapter 3, § 4

“I do not think that a verse was given this name, as some suppose, because one returns from a fixed end to the beginning of the same number, so that the name was derived from those who turn as they retrace their path; for this appears to be common even to those meters that are not verses.”] For this reason not only the meters of poets are called verses, but also any lines of writing, as we now speak. Joannes Gerardus Vossius correctly observed this in his *Etymological Dictionary*, under the word *VERSUS*.

He also showed very well that there can be no doubt that individual lines of writing received the name *verse* because, just as a farmer turns the soil with a plow, so a writer turns the wax with a stylus; and just as the farmer, after completing one furrow in the earth, turns the plow and makes another, so the writer, turning the stylus to the left and moving it forward, traces a new furrow in the wax. Since, as he teaches, this occurs no less in prose than in poetry, it is clear that the word *verse* by its nature applies equally to unbound and bound discourse.

But because poets complete their verses with a fixed number of feet and therefore turn their stylus more frequently, it came about that they almost made the name *verse* their own. Add that *verse* really was called a furrow in agriculture, and that among the Greeks the word στίχος (*stichos*), by which they designate a written verse, was also borrowed from agriculture; Joannes Croyus has shown this learnedly in Part I of his *Observations on the New Testament*, chapter 9.

#### Same passage

“But perhaps the name was found in the opposite way: just as grammarians called a verb *deponent* when it does not lay aside the letter *r*, as in *lucror* and *conqueror*, so that which consists of two members, neither of which can be put in the place of the other while preserving the rule of numbers, may be called a *verse*, because it cannot be reversed.”] The former etymology is entirely false, as are nearly all etymologies invented by *antiphrasis*. For many deponent verbs once ended in both *o* and *or*, and Joannes Gerardus Vossius compiled their catalogue in Book V, chapter 7, of his *Aristarchus*. It is more credible that they were called deponent because they “laid aside” their passive signification, as he likewise suggests at the beginning of chapter 6; this was also the view of the great grammarian Francisco Sánchez.

But the author of the book *On Grammar*, which was once commonly attributed to Augustine, supplies us with another etymology. Speaking of verbs, he says:

> “The deponent verb remains, because it lays aside something from the quantity of the common verb. For although the common verb has four participles—present, as *criminans*; future, *criminaturus*; past, *criminatus*; and future passive, *criminandus*—the deponent verb does not have this one with passive signification. And therefore it is called deponent because it lays aside one future participle from the passive verb ending in the syllable *-dus*. Thus *opinor* and *miror* are deponent verbs.”

But Vossius’ etymology pleases me more.

What Augustine says about the verse is much more forced and also plainly false, for very many verses can be reversed in the manner in which he denies that they can be reversed. Quite a few pentameters, for example, can be reversed in this way—namely, all whose first part before the caesura consists of two dactyls. For we can say equally:

> *Semivirumque bovem, semibovemque virum*

Or:

> *Semibovemque virum, semivirumque bovem.*

You could likewise say:

> *Saepe tibi pater est, saepe legendus avus*

Or:

> *Saepe legendus avus, saepe tibi pater est.*

Anyone who turns the pages of an elegiac poet will encounter innumerable examples of this kind. Thus everything Augustine previously argued so verbosely about verses that cannot be reversed goes up in smoke.

Still, it is good that the modest man admits at the beginning of Book VI that he had lingered long enough—indeed, almost childishly—over the traces of numbers relating to the durations of time. Let us therefore forgive him these and other things, but let us not waste better time reading works in which one sees almost nothing except a tedious and unsuccessful display of ingenuity.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOK *ON THE TEACHER*

[Col. 0228A]

#### Chapter 5, § 16

“In his most distinguished speeches, which are called the Verrines, he called *coram* a noun, although in that place it may be an adverb.”] I do not have the leisure to read the Verrines carefully in order to locate the passage. This would have been a task for the diligence of the Benedictines, who have abundant leisure, and they should have added the location in the margin, as they have done elsewhere.

#### Chapter 9, § 28

“Persius places this above all the punishments that either the cruelty or the desire of tyrants has devised: that human beings are tormented when they are compelled to acknowledge the vices they cannot avoid.”] The passage is in Satire 3, line 35. We shall append its words, since elsewhere, in the notes on *Confessions*, Book XII, chapter 8, we observed that Augustine had Persius’ poem in view:

> Great father of the gods, would you wish to punish savage tyrants  
> By no other means, when dreadful lust, steeped in burning poison,  
> Has stirred their minds, than that they should see virtue  
> And waste away, having abandoned it?  
> Or did the mouths of the Sicilian bull groan more grievously?

#### Chapter 10, § 33

“Their *saraballae*.”] Since the Chaldean text of Daniel 3:27 has *Sarballehon*, it scarcely seems doubtful that one should write *Saraballa* or *Saraballae*, rather than *Sararbara*, as the Greek version has it. A corruption could very easily have entered a barbarous word in that version, especially since the liquids are readily confused by the ear. Written in this way, the word, through [an uncertain or missing form], is customary among the Talmudists and Arabs for a tunic, and the verb *sarbel* means “he covered.” It therefore seems to have been the name of a garment, as it still is among the Arabs.

#### [Col. 0228C] Chapter 14, § 46

“From the admonition of your words I learned that words do nothing more than admonish a person to learn, and that it is very little that appears through speech of the speaker’s thought.”] This is a summary of the whole book. It is astonishing how skilled Augustine was at expressing and obscuring a few clear philosophical or theological doctrines in many words. But this was the defect of the rhetoric of that age.

#### Same passage

“Whether what is said is true, he teaches only the person whom he has admonished, while speaking outwardly, that he dwells within; with his favor now assisting me, I shall love him more ardently the further I advance in learning.”] This is a Platonic doctrine, according to which the *Logos*—the name by which John called Christ—was established as the universal reason of all human beings. Thus Justin holds that Christ was known in part to Socrates:

> “For he was and is the Logos who exists in everything.”

Justin has similar remarks elsewhere, in what is called the *First Apology*, which I shall not transcribe. But these things must be carefully noted by those who wish to understand the Fathers; they will never attain that understanding unless they know what their philosophy was.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOKS *ON FREE WILL*

### Book I

#### Chapter 2, § 4

“Unless you believe, you will not understand.”] The passage is Isaiah 7:9. But in the Septuagint version, which does not agree with the Hebrew text, the Hebrew reads—as Jerome correctly translated it after Symmachus—“If you do not believe, you will not remain.” In that passage the prophet addresses the Jews and urges them to place confidence in divine assistance against the schemes of the Israelites and Syrians. If they do so, he promises that their affairs will remain firm.

Thus this passage contributes nothing to the matter Augustine is discussing here, and the good man praises, in support of his position, the invention of the Greek translators—if indeed they translated it in that way. But how did this happen? Simply because he wanted to believe before he understood. He believed that this was the meaning of Scripture before he knew whether one could trust the Septuagint translators in every matter, or whether it was established that they had translated this passage correctly. Elsewhere too he abuses this passage in the same way, as below in Book II, § 6.

#### Chapter 3, § 8

“Lust in adultery is evil.”] There is no doubt that lust in adultery is evil; but why is it evil? Because adultery itself is evil, since it completely disrupts human society. The foundation of human society is the union of husband and wife, which is the first of all unions and cannot remain intact without mutual affection between the two and their common care for children and household property. These things cannot coexist with adultery.

Moreover, the adultery of parents provides children with the most effective example of sexual misconduct; and if adultery were practiced indiscriminately, human society would also be finished. Such acts, then, are forbidden for the sake of human beings, whom they would gravely harm. Otherwise, lust—or desire for the opposite sex—has nothing evil in itself, provided it remains within the limits prescribed by God and indeed by Reason itself.

For this reason God constituted the bodies of all animals in such a way that, once they have matured, this desire is mechanically aroused in them, no differently from the desire to eat or drink. It follows from the nature of the body as created by God, as can be understood both from brute animals and from the very purpose of the propagation of species.

Evodius therefore spoke truly of adultery: “It is not evil because it is forbidden by the law; rather, it is forbidden by the law because it is evil.” But Augustine did not adequately indicate why it is evil. The same reasoning applies to murder and theft, which our author discusses later and which are evil because they are wholly contrary to human society; and therefore they are contrary to the purpose of God himself, who placed human beings on earth so that they might act amicably toward one another and punishes those who harm others, since he is the author and defender of that society.

#### Chapter 12, § 25

A. “I ask you whether there is any will in us.”  
E. “I do not know.”] It is astonishing that Evodius—who generally reasons quite acutely and answers the questioner prudently—is here represented as so stupid that he denies knowing whether human beings possess a will. Yet later, in Book III, § 3, the same Evodius can say that he cannot find anything that he may call his own if the will by which he wills and does not will is not his own. The detours of Platonic dialogues contain many things of this kind; I do not know what they are suited for except creating boredom in the reader.

### Book II

#### Chapter 2, § 5

“I would demonstrate what would be easiest for anyone: how much more reasonable it would be for him also to believe that God exists, on the basis of the books of such great men, who left written testimony that they had lived with the Son of God, and so forth.”] Yet it would first have to be shown that those books deserve belief; and this cannot be done more briefly than by demonstrating through natural reason that God exists.

#### Same passage, § 6

“The prophet would have spoken in vain: ‘Unless you believe, you will not understand.’”] We have already shown that the prophet said nothing of the kind, in the notes on Book I, chapter 2.

#### Same passage

“Our Lord himself also first urged those whom he called to salvation to believe, both by his words and by his deeds.”] He rightly says “by his deeds,” for through miracles Christ showed himself worthy of belief before demanding that faith be placed in him. But it is true that fuller knowledge follows upon faith, so that more general knowledge produces faith, while faith in turn generates more precise knowledge.

### Book III

#### Chapter 3, § 7

“We do not will by the will—who, even if delirious, would dare say so?”] Augustine wishes to show how God can have foreknowledge of free acts. But above all he ought to have defined freedom and not confused it with will; for these are not always joined together, as we shall later see.

Therefore, although God foreknows our future wills, it does not follow that we will something without willing it.] But two kinds of things that may be called voluntary must be distinguished. There are things that we do willingly but nevertheless not freely; for freedom is that faculty of the mind by which we can do something or not do it. There are also things that we will in such a way that we cannot refuse to will them.

When judging some doctrine while relying on obscure arguments that appear neither manifestly false nor manifestly true, we can reject or embrace that doctrine, and thus exercise our freedom. But if a mathematical axiom is proposed to us, or a proposition necessarily inferred from it, it is no longer within our power to refuse assent, provided we understand the words in which it is expressed. Here we assent willingly—for it cannot happen otherwise—but not freely, since we cannot refuse assent.

The question is not whether God foreknows these actions, for they are plainly necessary; nor are they worthy of praise or blame. There is also another kind of matter, apart from complete evidence, toward which we are indeed carried willingly but not freely; Augustine himself expresses it in the words that follow.

For when you said, concerning blessedness, that one is not made blessed by oneself, you spoke as though I had denied this; but I say that, when you are to be blessed, you will be so not unwillingly but willingly [Col. 0230D]. But here too there is no freedom: everyone necessarily desires supreme blessedness, and once they have attained it they cannot fail to rest content in it. Therefore this example has no bearing on the matter, since the discussion concerns what the Scholastics call volitions—not necessary volitions, but wholly free ones, such as those directed toward particular goods, whatever they may be.

Since, then, God foreknows your future blessedness, and nothing can happen otherwise than he has foreknown—for otherwise there would be no foreknowledge—we are nevertheless not thereby compelled to think what is utterly absurd and entirely contrary to truth: that you will become blessed without willing it. These matters are irrelevant to the question proposed. The question is how God can foreknow whether Evodius, for example, will assent to the Gospel, if Evodius is able to withhold that assent [Col. 0231A], not what his future will shall be when he attains blessedness.

Just as God’s foreknowledge—which even now is certain of your future blessedness—does not take away your will to be blessed once you have begun to be blessed, so too a culpable will, if one is going to exist in you, will not on that account cease to be a will because God foreknew that it would exist. God foresaw Evodius willingly becoming blessed, if he should attain blessedness, because this will is entirely necessary and therefore neither praiseworthy nor culpable. But this is not what is being asked. The question is how Evodius will freely believe and adhere to the Gospel, so that he could withdraw his faith from it and defect from it, and yet God could certainly foreknow this.

Suppose, on the contrary, that Evodius did not believe the [Col. 0231B] Gospel or rejected the message, and did so freely—that is, in such a way that he could have done the opposite—yet willingly did what he did. The question is how God could have foreseen an outcome which by its nature was not determined in either direction. I shall not undertake to treat the matter itself, which is certainly most difficult; but I will say that Augustine would not have believed that it could be resolved so cursorily had he understood the matter. As it is, we have seen that it entirely escaped his acumen—unless he employed rhetorical dissimulation here. This may perhaps also explain why he mixed together many matters unrelated to those which he had undertaken to discuss, lest he should seem to treat them too meagerly.

### Chapter 10, § 29

“For it was also appended, by the standard of equity, that man [Col. 0231C] should not be denied to the power of the devil himself, whom he had subjected to himself by evil persuasion. For it was unjust that he should not rule over one whom he had begun to possess.”

If someone were to say that it is equitable for a monarch to allow those to serve a rebel whom evil arts had withdrawn from his rule, he would surely be no more tolerated than someone who said that it was unjust for a thief to be deprived of what he had stolen from its rightful owners. Who, then, would tolerate the claim that it would have been unjust if the Creator—who commands his creatures by incomparably the best right—had taken away from the evil spirit, a rebellious creature, those whom that wicked spirit had fraudulently estranged from God? As for me, I could regard the Manichaeans, and all others who rave in similar fashion, as nothing but the most wretched rhetoricians, to speak as mildly as possible.

### Chapter 17, § 50

“Whatever this cause of the will is” [Col. 0231D] [namely, of the evil will], “if it cannot be resisted, one yields to it without sin; but if it can, one must not yield to it, and one will not sin.”

When Pelagius used this passage against Augustine to show that those who cannot resist native corruption cannot be condemned, Augustine replied in chapter 67 of *On Nature and Grace*, as the Benedictines observed, that this cause can be resisted with the help of him who cannot be deceived. But if he who cannot be deceived does not help except very few, and if his assistance is altogether necessary for resistance, as Augustine supposed, it follows that the cause of sin cannot be resisted by the others, and therefore that they yield to it without sin. For whoever does not do what he cannot do cannot be said to sin, or at any rate owes no punishment. I know what is usually said on this matter; but certainly the Augustinian rule which he lays down in this work *On Free Choice of the Will*, being founded upon immutable justice, cannot be obscured by such arguments [Col. 0232A].

### Chapter 19, § 53

“For it has not been offered to any human being to know that what is uselessly unknown is usefully sought.”

The Benedictines testify that this is the reading of most manuscripts. But the text should unquestionably read *ablatum* (“taken away”), not *oblatum* (“offered”). Augustine’s meaning is that no one has been deprived of the knowledge that those things whose ignorance is not demonstrably useful should be usefully sought. This is indeed how the word is read in the Basel edition, and perhaps this Paris edition is burdened by a typographical error. See § 57.

### Chapter 20, § 55

“That he might beget better offspring than he himself was, was neither [a matter] of equity…”

Nor would this have been unjust, had it seemed good to God; [Col. 0232B] nor would it have been equitable in such a way that, unless it happened, God could be accused of injustice. The order established by God in the propagation of all animals simply did not permit the bodies of children to be in a better condition than those of their parents. But was it equitable for the souls of Adam’s descendants to suffer punishment for a sin they had not themselves committed, and which they could in no way have prevented from being committed?

### § 56

“If one soul was made, from which the souls of all human beings who are born are derived, who can say that he did not sin when that first man sinned?”

Those who wished the soul to be transmitted from the parent did not rave so extravagantly as to suppose that the entire mass, so to speak, of all souls had existed in Adam, and was afterward torn apart piecemeal and distributed among his descendants. Rather, the soul is born as the body is born, and does not exist before it is born. The words that follow are exceedingly obscure, and I cannot persuade myself that even the author understood them. Therefore I shall not trouble myself to explain them [Col. 0232C].

### Chapter 22, § 63

“As we have long argued, sins are to be attributed only to the proper will of those [namely, of the souls], and no further cause of sins is to be sought.”

I myself do not doubt that this is entirely correct; but I do not understand how it agrees with what Augustine later taught concerning the punishments which Adam’s descendants, as he supposed, suffer because of Adam’s sin. I therefore marvel that he did not retract this passage, unless perhaps he preferred to conceal the matter, lest he gratify the Pelagians by admitting that he had held their position before attacking them. For from Augustine’s treatment of this book in the *Retractations* it appears that he wished it to seem that he had attacked the Pelagians before they arose, much less that he should frankly acknowledge having favored them [Col. 0232D].

### § 64

“But if ignorance and difficulty are natural, from that point the soul begins to advance and to be promoted toward knowledge and rest, until it is perfected in that blessed life, and so forth.”

These statements also disagree with what he later said against the Pelagians. For he regarded ignorance and difficulty as punishments of the first sin; without that sin, human beings would plainly have been born otherwise.

### Chapter 23, § 66

“For one need not fear that there could have been some intermediate life between right action and sin, while the judge’s sentence could not be intermediate between reward and punishment” [Col. 0233A].

These remarks concerning the condition of infants, as well as what follows, are in no way consistent with what he later taught concerning the punishments of original sin. Nearly the whole of the tenth volume, and especially the books against Julian, teach the exact opposite. These passages therefore ought to have been retracted. But see what was said at no. 63.

### Chapter 24, § 71

“Thus, just as an infant cannot be called foolish or wise, although he is already a human being—for it follows that human nature receives something intermediate which you could not properly call either foolishness or wisdom—so too, if someone were animated by such a disposition as those who through negligence lack wisdom, no one would properly call him foolish if he saw that the man was such not through fault but by nature.”

Here he describes Adam as first created in such a way that he could be called neither wise nor foolish, but capable of wisdom [Col. 0233B]. From this description he later easily shows how a human being could fall, passing from that intermediate condition into foolishness. Yet on account of this doctrine—which Augustine refused to retract, and for which he was never condemned—certain later theologians in the seventeenth century after Christ attacked some of their contemporaries with extraordinary insults. We have often observed that, through the sides of later men whom they hated, the reputation of the ancients was gravely wounded by ignorant people who professed to revere writers whose works they had not read, or had read carelessly.

## Remarks on the Books on Genesis

### Book I, chapter 2, § 3

[Col. 0233C]

“We answer that God made heaven and earth in the beginning—not in the beginning of time, but in Christ … For when the Jews asked our Lord Christ who he was, he answered: ‘The Beginning, who also speak to you.’”

The passage is John 8:25. But Augustine was mistaken, deceived by the Latin version. If he had then read the Greek, he would have seen Christ saying **τὴν ἀρχήν** (*tēn archēn*, “the beginning”) in the accusative case, and consequently this could not be taken as Christ’s name. Nevertheless, he attempts to defend this interpretation of his in *Tractate 38 on John*, perhaps lest it should appear that he had misunderstood the passage because of his ignorance of Greek. See Juan Maldonado’s commentary on this passage.

### Chapter 10, § 16

“Thus the remaining days are counted from morning to morning.”

He is mistaken. The **νυχθήμερα** (*nychthēmera*, “complete day-and-night periods”), following Hebrew usage, are consistently counted from evening to evening, so that evening always precedes the day [Col. 0233D]. This is now familiar to everyone, but at that time accurate interpretation of Scripture was almost unknown, as is clear even from reading these books; we shall not undertake to point out their **παρερμηνεῖαι** (*parer mēneiai*, “misinterpretations”).

### Chapter 15, § 24

“That Macedonian mountain called Olympus is said to be so high that on its summit neither wind is felt nor clouds gather, and so forth.”

Many have written this, but no one now doubts that it is a fable. Nor would anyone even moderately skilled in physics confuse vapors with air. We therefore pass over such matters.

### Book II, chapter 24, § 37

“This does not signify a change in God’s nature, but the assumption of an inferior person, that is, a human person.”

The Benedictine monks rightly, on the authority of the manuscripts, remove the word *nature*, which is enclosed in brackets [Col. 0234A]. It seems to have been added for no other reason than that it did not appear compatible with theology to say that the Word assumed a human person, since, according to established usage, the human nature is said to have been assumed by the divine nature into unity of person.

Augustine, however, uses the word *person* here not in that theological sense but in its ordinary Latin sense. By it he signifies not a **ὑφιστάμενον** (*hyphistamenon*, a subsisting individual), as the Greek theologians say, but a certain condition which we portray through our actions. It is therefore as though he had said that, before the incarnation, the Word bore the exalted person of God; but, having assumed human nature, he took on the role of a lower person. Everyone knows that Latins commonly spoke in this way.

Augustine himself says of Christ in Letter 140, § 18:

“These things Christ says in the person of his body, which is the Church. These things he says in the person of the weakness of the flesh of sin, which he transformed into the likeness of the flesh of sin that he assumed from the Virgin. The bridegroom speaks these things in the person of the bride, because in some manner he united her to himself” [Col. 0234B].

Accordingly, the meaning of these words of Augustine is the same as that contained in the words of the Apostle in Philippians 2:6–8.

### Chapter 29, § 43

“They say that the sins of others harm God’s nature; we deny this, but say that sins harm no nature except its own.”

To understand this, one should read the exposition of the Manichaean doctrine in the book *On Heresies*, concerning the origin of evil and the two souls. The Pelagians would certainly have abused this passage had they drawn it into support of their position. But the same does not apply to the passages in Book III of *On Free Choice of the Will*, which Augustine passed over without mentioning while explaining others that could be pressed much less severely [Col. 0234C]. Whether there was any deliberate strategy in this, let others judge. The *Retractations* display candor and modesty; but retractions ought to be made frankly, retracting whatever is thought false, not merely a few matters of little importance while leaving the more serious ones untouched, lest opponents perhaps object that they hold similar views. But God knew Augustine’s mind.

## Desiderius Erasmus’s Censure of the Books on the Customs of the Catholic Church and of the Manichaeans

The two short works that follow had been intended for another place: the first among the **πολεμικά** (*polemika*, “polemical works”), the second among the **διδακτικά** (*didaktika*, “instructional works”). But since in the first a most vigorous novice skirmisher has made his first assault upon the heretics, while in the second an admirable future teacher has made a preliminary exposition of the mystical Scriptures, treated according to their various senses, it seemed appropriate to add them as the conclusion of this volume [Col. 0234D].

As soon as he had pledged allegiance to the emperor Christ, in order to give his fellow soldiers the firmest assurance that he had sincerely defected from the Manichaeans, under whose standards he had served for nine years, he exposed their mysteries. He does so with an admirable elegance of language—if only he had been permitted to use it in his other labors. This work clearly shows that, if anything in his diction offended the learned, it was not due to ignorance but to charity, by which he lowered his style to the understanding of the uneducated.

For in those days both male and female weavers understood Latin prose woven in simple words and meanings, such as that of Saint Gregory, but would not have understood Hilary’s diction. Therefore, so that the usefulness of the reading might extend more broadly, he altered his style in the later work to suit the understanding of the common people; and he seems to have done the same in most of his works. In time, as commonly happens, habit became nature. Thus it has finally come about that today he is not adequately understood even by those with modest education, while the more polished read him with some tedium, unless devotion excludes weariness [Col. 0235A].

## Remarks on the Same Books

### Book I, chapter 2, § 3

“The order of nature is such that, when we learn something, authority precedes reason.”

That is, when we approach a teacher in order to learn. We ought to trust him for a time, until we ourselves are able to weigh matters independently. But in controversies there is no place for such an arrangement, since neither side in the dispute regards the other as its teacher. It is therefore strange that Augustine adds:

“But since we are dealing with people who both think and speak contrary to all order, and who say nothing more emphatically than that reason must first be given, I shall humor them; and I confess that in disputing I shall undertake something faulty.”

Yet it would have been absurd and unjust to act otherwise. Who would tolerate an argument from the authority of someone whose authority one does not at all acknowledge? See the notes on chapter 7 of the book *On the Quantity of the Soul* [Col. 0235B].

### Chapter 5, § 7

“Thus the supreme good of the body is neither its pleasure, nor *indoloria*, nor strength, and so forth.”

Since *indoloria* is not a Latin word, and since other editions read *indolentia*, this must be a typographical error. No manuscripts are reported to have this reading, nor, if they did, would they be trustworthy. It is well known that *indolentia* is a Ciceronian term [Col. 0235C].

### Chapter 31, § 67

“Who would not admire and praise those who, despising and abandoning the allurements of this world, have gathered together into a common and most chaste life and spend their years together? And so forth.”

He admirably describes the customs of monks living in communities, but as they ought to have been, not as they were. Too much is reported of their seditions in the history of the Eastern Churches for us to believe this panegyrist. Meanwhile, their best practice was the one he describes in these words:

“They work with their hands at things by which the body can be nourished and the mind cannot be hindered from God.”

Perhaps the text should read *et adeo* (“and so greatly”), for I scarcely think one would say that the mind is hindered by God, instead of being hindered from cleaving to God or diverted from God [Col. 0235D]. Modern beggars, as they are honorifically called, would do well to weigh these words carefully.

### Book II, chapter 13, § 28

“Catholic Christians can compare your abstinence from wine and meat with beasts of burden and with many sparrows, and finally even with countless kinds of worms.”

Are there, then, sparrows that eat meat and drink wine? None. Therefore, instead of *et multis*, read *et mulis*—“and with many mules.” Augustine is referring to what the Manichaeans objected to the nuns: that even a mule is a virgin; see the preceding passage. When *multis* had been written for *mulis*, the conjunction was later displaced. I wish the manuscripts had been carefully examined here [Col. 0236A].

### Ibid., § 29

“Let her drink mulsum, boiled wine, and raisin wine.”

A comma must be placed between *caroenum* and *passum*, for *caroenum* and *passum* are not the same thing. Augustine tells us below, § 47, that *caroenum* is nothing other than boiled wine. Palladius, in October, title 18, shows that *defrutum* and *caroenum* are made from must, and explains their difference as follows:

“*Defrutum*, so called from boiling down, is finished when it has been vigorously skimmed until it reaches thickness. *Caroenum* is made when, after one third has been lost, two parts remain.”

It was called **κάροινον** (*karoinon*) because it affects the **κάρα** (*kara*, “head”), like the dates of the palm, from which a wine was made that produced **καρηβαρία** (*karebaria*, “heaviness of the head”), as Pliny teaches in Book XIII, chapter 4. *Passum*, on the other hand, was wine flowing from dried grapes; Palladius discusses it in the following title [Col. 0236B].

### Chapter 15, § 39

“Why do you embrace in the violet the same color which you reject in sufferers from cholera, in the illness of jaundiced people, and finally in an infant’s stool?”

I scarcely think that in Africa people called jaundice *choleres*; I would prefer the reading *cholericis*, from *cholera*, a disease in which bile—or **χολή** (*cholē*, “bile”)—bursts out above and below, as Celsus teaches in *On Medicine*, Book IV, chapter 2.

### Chapter 19, § 69

“At the time when their assemblies were prohibited by law.”

He seems to refer to the year 372, when Valentinian and Valens decreed that wherever a Manichaean assembly or gathering of this kind was found, the teachers were to be punished with a severe penalty, and the houses and dwellings in which profane instruction was given were unquestionably to be confiscated for the treasury. These are the words of law 3, title 5, Book XVI of the Code.

## Remarks on the Book on True Religion

### Chapter 2, § 3

“Whether they did this out of fear of the severity of the times or from some knowledge of the times, it is not mine to judge.”

Since nine manuscript codices omit the word *severitatis*, I think it ought to be absent here, and that the passage should read: “whether they did this out of fear of the times or from some knowledge of the truth.” The meaning is sufficiently clear; and as for the fear of the times, Augustine himself shows that this was his expression in § 5, where he says of Plato: “So greatly did he fear the perverse opinion of these times” [Col. 0236C].

### Chapter 4, § 7

“If those men had been able to live this life again with us, they would certainly have seen by whose authority human beings could more easily be helped, and, with a few words and opinions changed, they would have become Christians—as many Platonists of our own times have done.”

But in the time of the Emperor Julian, the Platonists were most hostile to Christians and extremely superstitious. The same was true of Proclus’s teachers, and of Proclus himself, who was born at Byzantium toward the end of Augustine’s life. See the prolegomena of the most learned Johann Albert Fabricius to the life of Proclus written by Marinus of Naples. Augustine thought too favorably of the Platonists and judged the Christian religion to be closer to their doctrines than it really is [Col. 0236D].

### Chapter 14, § 27

“So voluntary is sin as an evil that it is in no way sin if it is not voluntary; and this is so evident that neither the small number of the learned nor the multitude of the unlearned disagrees.”

That is, if “voluntary” means free, so that the sin can be committed or not committed by the sinner himself. All human beings thought this before the Pelagian controversies arose; and Augustine himself would have thought no differently had those controversies arisen only after his death. Therefore the author of the *Retractations* vainly attempts to reconcile this passage with the position he later embraced, in Book I, chapter 13, § 5, as though “voluntary” meant merely what inheres in the will, even if it is not free [Col. 0237A].

### Chapter 55, § 3

“We honor them with love, not with servitude; nor do we build temples for them, for they do not wish to be honored by us in this way, and so forth.”

Let those who wish angels to be honored with the worship of **δουλεία** (*douleia*, “servitude”) consider this passage, and see how they can claim that they think and speak with Augustine. Nevertheless, even in his time certain practices had begun to be carried out among the people which, although condemned by wiser persons, were gradually admitted. Thus, in Book I of *On the Customs of the Catholic Church*, § 7, he says:

“I know that there are many worshipers of tombs and paintings, whom the Catholic Church does not wish the Manichaeans to reproach us with, and whose number eventually became very great” [Col. 0237B].

## Desiderius Erasmus’s Censure of the Rule of Saint Augustine

This rule closely resembles Augustine both in its sentiments and in its form of expression, and indeed presents its author as marked by pious courtesy and humanity. It is probable, however, that it was written not for clerics but for women who, gathered together under the direction of Augustine’s sister, lived in community [Col. 0237C]. He calls her their superior, but supreme authority belonged to the presbyter.

With certain alterations, they later adapted it for men—for example, where it commands women concerning modesty of dress:

“Let your clothing not be conspicuous, and do not seek to please by your garments but by your character. Do not wear head coverings so thin that hairnets appear beneath them.”

I think the text should read:

“Keep your hair covered on every side; let neither negligence scatter it outside nor artifice arrange it.”

They omitted what could not be adapted to men. In the next passage also, “In all your movements let nothing be done that might excite anyone’s lust” was altered to “that might offend anyone’s sight.” Again, the instructions not to look at women, to go out in pairs or threes [Col. 0237D], to wash one’s own clothes, to work for the common good, and many other matters fit poorly with the clerics of that period, whose freedom and dignity were then greater.

At the end, alluding to the care of appearance, to the mirror and perfumes in which the female sex takes particular delight, he says:

“May the Lord grant that you observe all these things as lovers of spiritual beauty, fragrant with the good odor of Christ through a good manner of life, and that you may look upon yourselves in this little book as in a mirror.”

These words are less suitable for men. There are other examples, but these are sufficient. Finally, although everything can be twisted to apply to clerics, there is certainly nothing here that clerics do not share with women [Col. 0238A]. Yet how much would have needed to be prescribed concerning the duties of presbyters, subdeacons, and deacons, if he had judged that a rule should be written for them?

Nevertheless, this rule is the foundation of many orders. If only the men would observe it as it was handed down to women. It is found in Letter 119.

It is foolish to dispute this man’s title; it is more relevant to determine, by emulating his piety and learning, that those who most closely reproduce Augustine’s virtues may rightly be called Augustinians. It is certain that the discourse mentioning the hood and belt was fabricated under Ambrose’s name. Augustine himself nowhere calls himself a monk, nor does he designate his clerics by that name, although little importance should be attached to the name.

[Col. 0238B]

He himself admits that he abandoned everything and encouraged many others to do the same. Then, in a speech before the people, he says that he would not wear the red cap called *pyrrhus*, which we corruptly call *byrrhus*. “It suits,” he says, “a bishop, but it does not suit Augustine”—though he should rather have said, “It does not suit a monk.”

In the books *On the Customs of the Catholic Church*, besides anchorites and coenobites, he describes a third kind: those who, because withdrawing into the desert was inconvenient, whether on account of parents, children, or other reasons, nevertheless lived no less quietly, with many dwelling in the same houses, governed by no authority but with everything regulated by free love. He calls these communities “lodgings,” of which he had seen many at Rome.

He seems to have imitated this model in Africa, so that they would not be conspicuous in dress, as monks were, and so that anyone could leave the association if it did not suit him. Possidius nevertheless calls these communities monasteries [Col. 0238C].

## Remarks on the Same Rule

### § 2

“What good is there in scattering one’s possessions by giving to the poor and becoming poor, when the miserable soul becomes more arrogant by despising riches than it had been by possessing them?”

I would not condemn those who, recognizing that they are unequal to the dangers threatening the virtuous in ordinary life, seek solitude and the seclusion of monasteries. But above all they must guard themselves not only against the grosser bodily vices, which offend everyone, but also against more hidden faults: pride, the desire to command, the vicious habit of judging rashly about people and things unknown, tyranny in ecclesiastical matters, factional character, laziness, anger, irreconcilable hostilities, and other faults of this kind. In monastic retreats these rule no less than in the most crowded gatherings and associations of other people [Col. 0238D].

Therefore prudent men, more experienced in human life—Desiderius Erasmus and others—have often spoken of the monastic way of life as a form of life no less dangerous to salvation than any other. Meanwhile, if they observed this Augustinian rule, there would certainly not be so many complaints about them as there have been.

# For the Second Volume

[Col. 0239]

## Desiderius Erasmus Sends Greetings to the Devout Reader

### [Col. 0239A]

From the conclusion of the second book of the *Retractations*, and from the letter prefixed to the catalogue of heresies addressed to Quodvultdeus, it is sufficiently clear that at that time Augustine had not arranged either his letters or his popular sermons. Nor was this later attended to by him; the fact that this volume appears to observe no order of times, persons, or subjects makes that clear.

It is even more clearly shown by the fact that certain works had been inserted which, at first taste, were recognized as not being Augustine’s. We have marked them with a censure: some were simply fabricated, such as the letters of Boniface to Augustine and of Augustine to Boniface. Nevertheless, we removed only one entirely from its place, and that one was extremely long and conspicuously unlearned; even this we would not have done had it not also appeared in the other volumes. Such was our caution that no one might complain of any interference on our part [Col. 0239B].

In addition, some works are interspersed which Augustine himself calls books in the *Retractations*. Although at times it is rather difficult to distinguish a letter from a book, Augustine sometimes speaks as though brevity or length gives or removes the name “letter” more truly than the form or subject of the discourse. This is especially notable because the apostles provided the example: they committed serious subjects to letters. Apart from the Gospels—a term by which we also include the Acts of the Apostles—they left nothing in writing except letters, and those letters concerned matters that were by no means merely private, which they wished everyone to read.

In one place he thinks that something should not be regarded as a letter unless it bears both the name of the writer and that of the person to whom it is written. There are indeed several writings which one could truly call letters, since they contain something familiar and resemble human conversation, though they are few. But on this matter let each person be free to judge for himself.

I venture to affirm that in no other work does the piety, charity, gentleness, humanity, courtesy, concern for the entrusted flock, love of concord, and zeal for the house of God of this most holy man shine more brightly. How he labors, contrives, and turns himself in every direction whenever some hope appears of drawing either a pagan to Christ or a heretic into communion with the Church! How he humbles himself and, in Paul’s manner, changes his voice, everywhere seeking an opportunity to kindle and spread piety wherever he senses a spark of good sense remaining!

To what little woman, commoner, courtier, pagan, or heretic does he not respond readily, gently, and graciously? With what anxious concern does he intercede for the most wicked circumcellions, who deserved more than a single death? Who ever pleaded more earnestly for his friends than he did for his enemies? With what effort does he bring everyone to birth for Christ; how he rejoices over those who repent; how carefully he watches over those in danger; how diligently he teaches those who are in error, striving to heal everyone and destroy no one [Col. 0240A]!

How painfully he burns at every obstacle that arises! You may truly see in him the anxious evangelical hen, concerned to gather and shelter her chicks beneath her wings.

In some letters one may also recognize the forensic style of speaking which the Greeks call **δικανικόν** (*dikanikon*, “forensic” or “legal”), especially when he acts against the Donatist faction. Nor is the subtlety of his arguments—peculiarly his own—lacking in **δείνωσις** (*deinōsis*, forceful or impassioned presentation).

Yet whether he teaches, reproves, or fights against despairing enemies, one never fails to sense the native sweetness of Christian charity. If the comparison is appropriate, he seems to me to reproduce a certain Micio from comedy, who remains gentle even when he reproves most severely.

In this one volume, as in a mirror, one may contemplate the bishop whom Paul portrays as **ἀνεπίληπτον, νηφάλιον, σώφρονα, κόσμιον, φιλόξενον, διδακτικὸν, μὴ πάροινον, μὴ πλήκτην, μὴ αἰχροκερδῆ, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπιεικῆ, ἄμαχον, ἀφιλάργυρον, μὴ αὐθάδη, μὴ ὀργίλον, φιλάγαθον, ἐγκρατῆ, ὅσιον, δίκαιον, ἀντεχόμενον τοῦ κατὰ τὴν διδαχὴν πιστοῦ λόγου, δυνατὸν καὶ παρακαλεῖν ἐν τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ, καὶ τοὺς ἀντιλέγοντας ἐλέγχειν μετὰ πάσης πρᾳότητος**:

“blameless, sober, self-controlled, orderly, hospitable, able to teach, not addicted to wine, not violent, not greedy for sordid gain, but gentle, peaceable, not loving money, not arrogant, not prone to anger, loving what is good, self-controlled, holy, just, holding fast the trustworthy word according to the teaching, able both to encourage through sound instruction and to refute those who contradict with complete gentleness.”

If bishops, and the theologians who occupy the chief function of bishops, were to contemplate themselves in this mirror, some of them, I think, would be ashamed of their arrogance joined with ignorance, and of their savagery joined with impure morals [Col. 0240B].

From Augustine’s other books one may see what he was like as an infant in Christ, from others what he was like as a young man and as an old man; but from this one volume you will come to know the whole Augustine at once.

That genius would have given us richer fruits had he happened to be born or to live in Italy or Gaul. Africa was uncultivated, eager for pleasures, hostile to learning, and fond of curious matters. Hence people frequently exercise him with rather frivolous questions, of little relevance to piety, and he is often compelled to adapt his pen to the inclinations of his people.

Yet such a cultivator was needed to till such a thorny field. Although he would have written works more worthy of reading had he accommodated himself either to the judgment of Romans or Greeks, or indulged less in the ignorance of ordinary people, Christian charity considers it more important to benefit the greatest number than to win the approval of the elite; it thirsts more for the salvation of brothers than for its own glory [Col. 0240C].

He had a certain pious ambition, especially toward some little women, who thought it a fine thing to obtain any written work whatsoever from a bishop. Thus, while the devout man complied with everyone’s wishes, he sometimes gave less satisfaction to the fastidious reader.

I scarcely think anyone will believe how much sweat I expended in removing errors and restoring order to the most confused divisions of the text. But the best alms are those bestowed upon someone who does not know that they are being given; more generous still are those bestowed upon someone who resists them. We lend these things to Christ, not to human beings, whose scarcely credible ingratitude we experience in far too many cases.

Nevertheless, their wickedness will never deter us from the practice of doing good, since we are dealing with a debtor of the utmost good faith [Col. 0241A].

To omit nothing: from the end of this volume we removed a most loquacious appendage under the names of Cyril, suddenly speaking Latin, and Augustine, a Greek badly writing Latin—a shameless fabrication. If anyone is nevertheless seized by a desire to read it, let him find it among the works appended to the volumes of Saint Jerome. There let whoever delights in such delicacies satisfy himself fully.

Dear reader, read these things attentively. You will not regret the time spent. Farewell.

Dated at Basel, in the year 1527.

## J. Phereponus’s Remarks on the Letters

### Letter 1, § 1

“I would never have dared to attack the Academics, not even in jest; for when would the authority of such great men not move me, unless I thought that they had held a view quite different from what is commonly believed?”

Here *quando* means “how”; or, if the negative question is changed into a simple assertion, the sense is as though he had said: “Their authority would always have moved me,” and so forth. The meaning is: I would have been moved by the authority of such great men and would not have dared to attack their opinion, unless I were certain that they had held another view, and therefore that, in attacking what they are said to have believed, I was in no way touching their true doctrines.

Certainly, in Book III, chapter 17, of his work against the Academics, Augustine shows that they concealed their own position and were no less dogmatic than the other philosophers. It should also be observed here that Augustine later regretted having exalted the Academics so highly. See *Retractations*, Book I, no. 4 [Col. 0241C].

### Ibid.

“It will be enough for me to have fitted the times, so that if anything genuine flowed from the Platonic fountain, it might be led among shady and thorny thickets to the pasture of a very few people, rather than, flowing through open spaces, be unable to remain clear and pure because herds rushed upon it from every side.”

Read *potionem* or *potationem* (“a drink”), for we drink liquid; we do not pasture on it.

Ibid. “Against such people, I think, I have usefully devised that art and method of the true God.”] I would suppose that Augustine had written *of concealing the truth* (*abscondendi veri*), and that, after the first three syllables had been worn away, when only “. . . di veri” remained, the monkish copyists made it read *Dei veri* (“of the true God”). Otherwise, if this reading is genuine, it must be said that Augustine is here referring to the parables which Christ used, lest he expose profound truth to the ridicule of the insufficiently religious multitude. On this matter see Matthew 13:11 and following verses, together with the commentators on that passage.

Ibid. “With a little garment for the body.”] That is, philosophers only as far as their cloak was concerned—men who possessed nothing philosophical apart from the little garment.

Epist. 3, § 1. “Whom Plato knew.”] He means the idea of the intelligible human being which Plato had formed in his mind. See *Against the Academics*, Book III, chapter 17.

Epist. 7, § 3. “The soul, before it uses the body to perceive bodies, can imagine those same bodies, etc.”] Here Augustine speaks according to Plato’s doctrine, who thought that human minds existed before they were joined to bodies. See *Retractions*, Book I, chapter 1, no. 3, and Book XII of *The City of God*, chapter 26. Origen and certain other Fathers had drawn this opinion from Plato. See also the most illustrious Father Daniel Huet, *Origenian Matters* (*Origenianorum*), Book II, Question 6.

Epist. 8, § 1. “By what art, by what devices, by what contrivances or instruments, or by what drugs?”] That is, by wondrous arts, such as those of illusionists. Hesychius: “Μάγγανα, φάρμακα, δίκτυα, γοητεύματα”—“devices, drugs, nets, enchantments.” It is also interpreted as μηχανεύματα, “contrivances.” Hence μαγγανεία signifies γοητεία, “sorcery,” as Suidas teaches from Procopius. All these words seem to have been derived from μάγος, “magician.” The old glossaries also have this word in Latin: Μάγγανον, *manganum*.

[Col. 0242B] Epist. 10, § 2. “For both of them it was permitted to become divine in leisure.”] That is, to become like God, which the Greek Fathers frequently call θεοῦσθαι, “to be deified.” In the same sense as Augustine here, Gregory of Nazianzus calls solitude θεοποιὸν, “deifying,” at the beginning of Oration 2. Elsewhere he often uses similar expressions, as does Dionysius, who is called the Areopagite.

Epist. 14, § 2. “Remove us and put Glaucia’s offspring in our place; you will have accomplished nothing. For even persons most alike are under so great a necessity to be moved in their own distinct ways as there was for each to be born separately.”] “Glaucia’s offspring” is a proverb derived from the twin sons of some Glaucia, I do not know whom, and omitted by the paroemiographers.

Ibid., § 3. “The stature of Naevius, taller by a foot than whoever is—or the tallest.”] The passage is corrupt. It should read: “than any of the tallest.” Columella, *On Agriculture*, Book III, chapter 8: “For Marcus Tullius Cicero too,” he says, “testifies that there was a Roman citizen, Naevius Pollio, a foot taller than anyone at all among the tallest.” Pliny also mentions him, *Natural History*, Book VII, chapter 16.

Ibid., § 4. “May contain reason.”] That is, in the language of the Stoics, a σπερματικὸς λόγος, “seminal reason.” See Diogenes Laertius, Book VII, §§ 135–136. The Platonists called the same thing an idea, or the intelligible exemplar according to which individual species were made. See *Retractions*, Book I, chapter 3, no. 2.

Ibid. “I have now surpassed Naevius.”] That is, I have written so long a letter that it surpasses the others by as much as Naevius surpassed other men. See the preceding note.

Epist. 16, § 2. “These tombs, if the matter is worth mentioning, are frequented by fools who neglect the spirits of their ancestors; so that the prophecy of that seer, who indignantly protested, stands out: ‘And Rome will swear by the shades in the temples of the gods.’”] Read *jurabit*, “will swear,” as in Lucan, Book V, line 454; for the grammarian of Madaura quotes this verse not as describing a past event, but as a prophecy of a future event. The corrupt pronunciation of those who confused *b* and *v* corrupted the passage.

Ibid., § 4. “Through whom.”] That is, in worshipping them we worship both them and their father, as though the worship of lesser divinities redounded to the glory of the one supreme God. By this reasoning the pagans of that time excused the multitude of their gods and their varied worship.

Epist. 17, § 2. “Eucaddires.”] Samuel Bochart, [Col. 0243A] *Canaan*, Book II, chapter 6, suspects that one should read *encaddir*, that is, *hhanouch-addir*, “initiate of the magnificent one,” namely, God.

Ibid. “Abaddires.”] *ab-addir* means “magnificent father.” I can scarcely believe that reference is made to the stone swallowed by Saturn, since the discussion concerns not Greek but Punic names.

Ibid. “For what else does Namphanio signify than ‘a man of good foot’?”] In Phoenician, *naham pahamo* signifies “his foot is beautiful,” according to Petit and Bochart. See the latter, in the passage cited above.

Epist. 23, § 4. On circumcision: “This sacrament restrained the river Jordan.”] Yet it is clear that the Hebrews crossed the Jordan while still uncircumcised, according to Joshua 5:2 and following verses. Augustine’s memory deceived him, for he thought that the Israelites crossed the Jordan only after circumcision had been received, and for this reason he supposed that the waters of the Jordan had stood still.

Ibid., § 6. “Let us remove from consideration the empty objections which the uninformed parties commonly hurl against one another, and do not bring up the times of Macarius.”] So called after Macarius, the envoy of the emperor Constans, who harassed the Donatists considerably in A.D. 348. On him see Baronius or Spondanus.

Ibid. “The Circumcellions.”] The seditious Donatists who wandered around the cells and encouraged the common people to take up arms against the prefects of the emperors. See the same authors on them under the year A.D. 321.

Ibid. “Let us believe words dictated by divinity.”] Just as the eloquence of this age was more inflated, so its ceremonious expressions of courtesy, which were commonly used, were excessively hyperbolical, as can be seen throughout the writers of this period. In this same age the imperial rescripts were called “heavenly,” the imperial court a “heavenly court,” and divinity and eternity were attributed to the emperors; Symmachus’s letters will teach this to those learned men who are ignorant of a matter so well known. Similar expressions also occur frequently in the Theodosian Code. Here we have a notable example of that elaborate and excessive courtesy in the hyperbolical praise of Augustine’s earliest writings. Although those works are by no means contemptible, they nevertheless bear the mark of a neophyte, as Augustine himself admits at the beginning of the *Retractions*. Unless the reader is aware of this custom of hyperbolically praising and blaming, he will often be misled in these writers. It will be enough to have given this warning once.

[Col. 0243D] Epist. 26, § 3. “Who gave the tones a number?”] Read *tonis*, “thunderclaps”—that is, “who assigned number to the thunderclaps,” as the following verse shows. He seems to be referring to Varro’s books *On Music*, for understanding which Licentius would have needed Augustine as an interpreter.

Epist. 28, § 2. “As for translating the canonical Holy Scriptures into Latin, I would not have you undertake the work except in the manner in which you interpreted Job, so that, by using signs, it might be apparent how your translation differs from that of the Seventy, whose authority is exceedingly weighty.”] It is astonishing that a modest man, as soon as he had become a presbyter, should have undertaken to advise a much more learned man about a matter of which he was wholly ignorant, since he knew no Hebrew at all and had scarcely tasted the Greek language. [Col. 0244A] For wishing to pass judgment on Jerome’s labors without diligent study of both those languages is like a man born blind undertaking to judge colors. It is fortunate, however, that Jerome rejected the advice; the whole Latin Church later followed his judgment.

Ibid. “I cannot sufficiently wonder if something is still found in the Hebrew copies which escaped all those interpreters who were so highly skilled in that language.”] He falsely thought those interpreters highly skilled in Hebrew. For when that language had long since become obsolete, by the time the Old Testament was translated into Greek, and when those interpreters had been assisted by scarcely any method at all, they left much to be corrected by the diligence of later scholars. This is why, for the past two hundred years, one biblical interpreter after another has arisen, each thinking—without any charge of arrogance or rashness—that he could translate the books more accurately than his predecessors. Thus, once the foundation on which Augustine’s entire argument rests has been undermined, whatever he has built upon it must necessarily collapse. Let us nevertheless hear what follows.

“For I pass over the Seventy, concerning whose greater agreement—whether of plan or of spirit—than if they had been one man, I do not dare to adopt any definite opinion, except that I consider their pre-eminent authority in this task to be unquestionably due to them.”] He refers to the offensive fable concerning the agreement of the Seventy translators, which Jerome rightly ridiculed and all learned men have now rejected. If you have the leisure, read it in Augustine himself, *The City of God*, Book XVIII, chapters 42–43. [Col. 0244C] There he also states that Jerome’s translation had been rejected in his own time, although the Jews admitted that it was accurate and contended that the translators of the Seventy had erred in many places. Someone might perhaps say that Aristæas, Philo, and Josephus, who were Jews, believed the story concerning the agreement of the Seventy translators to be true, and that the whole Christian Church, older than Jerome, had used that version. But, to answer in the manner of ὕστερον πρότερον—“the later first”—I will say that the apostles, when proclaiming the Gospel among Greek speakers, used that version because no other existed; and, so far as the general substance of Jewish history and religion is concerned, and insofar as it was useful for spreading the Christian religion, it was sufficiently reliable—not because they thought it free from every fault.

Certainly, neither from the apostles’ use of it nor from anything they said can one infer that they regarded that translation as complete in every respect. If later generations thought otherwise, it does not follow that the apostles thought so. As for the Jewish history concerning the agreement of the Seventy translators, it has been refuted by learned men so thoroughly that no one can defend it with even a semblance of truth. Finally, anyone who compares our Hebrew copy with that translation will discover that it teems with obvious errors, as the best interpreters have shown. I know that there have been men skilled in humane letters who judged otherwise; but either they had never carefully undertaken that comparison, or they did not understand both languages, or they suffered from obstinacy or weakness of judgment. Therefore the authority of the Seventy translators cannot be greater [Col. 0245A] than the facts themselves permit, whatever Augustine may argue to the contrary. As for the reason why those unlearned ages stubbornly used faulty translations and manuscripts, Jean Le Clerc candidly disclosed it in *Hieronymian Question* 9, § 18. Augustine nevertheless continues to argue about a matter he did not understand.

“Those interpreters,” he says, “move me more who, although they translated later and, as is reported, clung tenaciously to the way and rules of Hebrew words and expressions, not only agreed among themselves but also left many things remaining to be discovered and published long afterward.”] Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the other Greek interpreters, although learned, were not exempt from every danger of error. Nor were they so skilled in the Hebrew language—since it had long been dying out—that no room would remain after their harvest for gleaning. Moreover, many passages of the Old Testament are obscure either because the subjects themselves are unknown to us or because the manuscripts have been corrupted by age. We think that later scholars can interpret these passages, one better than another, by conjectures and arguments, which vary. There are also many features in the style of the earlier interpreters which please later readers less and seem to require correction. Aquila’s translations, for example, were more obscure because he attempted to translate everything word for word, so that they could not everywhere be understood by those skilled only in the Greek language.

Finally, their disagreement was not so great that they failed to agree on the general substance of the matter. But students of Holy Scripture, and those who interpret it publicly before the congregation, do not rest content with the general substance alone; they try, insofar as possible, to understand every detail. These things are easy to devise for those experienced in such matters, but they were obscure to Augustine, who spoke about those interpreters from hearsay and could not himself examine the matter directly. Thus here he is merely fighting shadows—σκιαμαχεῖ—even though he thought he was arguing acutely, especially in the words that follow.

“And they are either obscure or clear. For if they are obscure, it is believed that you too might have been mistaken in them; if they are clear, it is not believed that they could have been mistaken in them.”] There are many passages of both kinds in the Old Testament. In the clearest passages—those containing the substance of Jewish religion and history—the Greek interpreters agreed. In other passages, although they are clear to an attentive and skilled reader, much remained to be explained because the earlier interpreters had sometimes nodded off or failed to grasp certain things; all interpreters of later centuries rightly declare that they have experienced this. In obscure passages—that is, those which cannot be explained by a skilled person in such a way that he would dare to affirm that no other meaning could lie beneath the words—what prevents us from hearing several explanations? Is that not always what is done? Does Augustine himself not frequently offer various interpretations? No interpreter claims to be immune from error; he merely thinks that, in ambiguous matters, he can offer interpretations that are more probable, or at least equally probable. Augustine’s dilemma is therefore empty; Jerome also answered it differently in Letter 75 of this volume.

Moreover, Jerome deserved special gratitude from Augustine and the others who did not know Greek, because once Jerome had published his translation they could understand what was most probable in the Greek versions, from comparison with which he had chiefly prepared his own. In addition, comparison of Jerome’s version with the Greek translation of the Seventy, or with its Latin translations, would have shed considerable light for readers. Instead of thanking him for what they owed him, ignorant and stubborn men tried to discredit his labors. Why? Because those labors revealed that they had habitually interpreted innumerable passages badly, especially in the Old Testament. If the opinion had become widespread that all versions of Scripture should be compared with the originals, since they might contain errors, the learning of countless Latin rhetoricians who knew neither Greek nor Hebrew would have been finished.
