We have pursued this point somewhat more fully here, never to repeat it later, because we saw that the bishop of Hippo had stubbornly and undeservedly opposed a more learned man.

Nevertheless, since Augustine was not inferior to Jerome in matters depending on pure reasoning, he undoubtedly defended the better cause in that part of his scholarship which concerns Paul’s deed. We gladly note this here, lest we appear to favor Jerome beyond his deserts or to oppose Augustine too readily.

Epist. 31, § 2. “There was also something which no paper can contain: such joy in those who were telling the story that, through the very faces and eyes of the speakers, we read with ineffable delight that you were written in their hearts.”] [Col. 0246C] That is, “deeply impressed upon their memory.” On this expression see what Jean Le Clerc says in *The Art of Criticism*, Part II, section 1, chapter 4, § 8.

Ibid., § 4. “Unless it imposed upon me the greater burden of the episcopate.”] See the note on Epistle 213, § 4.

Epist. 33, § 1. “For I do not regard the error of schism as deserving any honor; but before everything else, I regard the fact that you are bound to us by the bond of human society.”] Rather, by the bond of the common Christian religion, for the Catholics counted the Donatists among the Christians, since they did not rebaptize them when they returned to the Catholic Church.

Epist. 35, § 1. “The public office, etc.”] See the note on Epistle 91, § 8.

Epist. 36, § 2. “For in those matters about which divine Scripture has established nothing certain, the custom of the people of God or the institutions of our ancestors are to be held as law.”] Correct—provided that such laws are not imposed as though they were necessary for salvation. If that is done, they are rightly opposed, because Christ alone possesses the right to close heaven so that no one may open it, and to open it so that no one may close it. If other rules are added to his laws as necessary, a new Gospel is fabricated, which Christ and the apostles wished all their disciples to reject. We have something similar in Epistle 54 to Januarius, § 5: “Whatever is not shown to be contrary either to the faith or to good morals is to be treated indifferently, and is to be observed for the sake of the society of those among whom one lives.”

Epist. 43, § 7. “He ought to have feared all the more that the peace of unity might be violated, the larger and more illustrious a city Carthage was … It was also near the regions beyond the sea, etc.”] Sicily, I think; for it is no nearer to the shores of Italy, Gaul, and Spain than are other maritime cities of Africa.

Epist. 44, where he recounts at length his conference with Fortunius, a Donatist bishop of Tibursicum, he says in § 11: “It was said that our people were still going to persecute them [the Donatists]; and he told us that he wished to see what sort of people we would show ourselves in that persecution, whether we would consent to such cruelty or lend it no support.”

Fortunius was not a bad prophet, as is clear from Epistle 89 to Festus, written eight years later, and Epistle 93 to Vincentius, written ten years later. From these it can be understood that a severe persecution was stirred up against the Donatists, with the Catholic bishops’ consent, while Augustine resisted his colleagues—forgetful of what he had said in this conference. “We were saying,” he continues in the immediately following words, “that God sees our hearts, which they could not see, and that they were still rashly fearing for themselves what, if it occurred, would come from evil people, whom they themselves regarded as worse; yet that we should not therefore separate ourselves from Catholic communion if something should happen against our will, or even, if we were able, despite our opposition, since we have learned peaceful forbearance, as the Apostle says: ‘bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.’”

If Augustine was truly disposed in this way at that time, he went over too easily to the opposite opinion, and the attitude of his colleagues was different, as Epistles 89 and 93 demonstrate. Nevertheless, there is reason to doubt whether Augustine was speaking from his genuine conviction or, as orators do, according to the demands of the case before him. For he could not have been unaware that the emperors—especially Theodosius and his sons, before the year 398, when this Epistle 44 was written—had enacted many laws ordering magistrates to persecute heretics by confiscating the places where they assembled, imposing fines of ten pounds of gold on each heretical priest, exile, beatings, and so forth. Augustine would not have dared seriously to call the authors or ministers of these laws wicked. It should also be noted incidentally that Pelagius held the Donatist opinion, as is clear from his commentary on chapter 4 of the Epistle to the Galatians, at the words: “The one who was born according to the flesh persecuted the one who was born according to the Spirit.”

Ibid., § 13. “The greater number of the Caelicolae.”] Jacobus Gothofredus discussed the Caelicolæ and this passage of Augustine at length in his note on Law 19, Title 8, Book XVI of the Theodosian Code; readers may consult it. Their hostile description, and their association now with the Jews and now with the Donatists, prevent us from understanding what they believed.

Epist. 53, § 2. “In the city he spread the name of the Montenses, or Cutzupitae.”] Since this is the reading of most manuscripts, both here and in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 3, and since it is sufficiently established that this surname is neither Greek nor Latin, it is credible that it was assigned to them by Africans. Therefore, before attempting to change anything here, we must investigate whether the word *Cutzupitae* has a meaning in the Phoenician or Punic language that bears some affinity to the name *Montenses*.

In Hebrew—which is demonstrably the same as Phoenician in many respects—*ketseb*, or, in the Syriac manner, *ketseph*, from the root *katsab*, “he cut off,” signifies “a cut-off cavern.” Thus Jonah says in the prayer found in chapter 2, verse 7, that he descended *l’kitsbe harim*, εἰς σχισμὰς ὀρέων, “into the clefts of the mountains,” as the translators of the Seventy render it. By these words the prophet means deep caves at the roots of the mountains. Accordingly, *Cutzupitae* could signify “people who resorted to a cavern,” which agrees remarkably with what Optatus says about the Donatists living at Rome, *On the Donatist Schism*, Book II: “Outside the city they enclosed a certain cave with hurdles, where at that very time they could hold their meeting; hence they were called Montenses.”

Jerome also observes in his *Chronicle*, under A.D. 356, that the Montenses were so called from the mountain to which they assembled. Near the end of his book *Against the Luciferians*, he calls them Montenses or Campates, or Campitae. Here I would read *Cutzupitae*, since “field” and “mountain” are plainly opposites.

For a similar reason, the Eunomians, according to Theodoret, *Haeretical Fables*, Book IV, were called Troglodytes or Troglitae, ὡς ἐν οἰκίαις λανθανούσαις τὰς συνόδους ποιούμενοι, “because they held their assemblies in concealed houses,” namely, ἀπὸ τῶν τρωγλῶν, “from the caves.” Therefore the *Scototopitae* invented by Jean-Baptiste Cotelier are mere “men of darkness,” whom we send back into the darkness from which they emerged. Nor should those be heeded who, on Jerome’s authority, would have us read *Campitae*. Yet the learned Louis Ellies du Pin, in his notes on Optatus’s passage, remarkably thinks this agrees with Optatus, who says that they enclosed a certain cave outside the city with hurdles; from this, he argues, they could equally have been called Campitae as Montenses.

In French, those who are outside cities are said to be *aux champs*; in Latin, *ruri* or *in agris*, “in the countryside” or “in the fields,” not *in campis*, since *campi* signify level ground, not the countryside. I see that our Frenchmen are sometimes deceived by the affinity of their language with Latin. Thus the ingenious Robert Arnauld d’Andilly also went wrong in this same word when he translated Josephus into French. Seeing the expression μέγα πεδίον, “a great plain,” applied to a region situated along the Jordan, and seeing that the Latin translators rendered it *magnum campum*, “a great field,” he translated it *le grand champ*, whereas he should have translated it *la grande campagne* or *la grande plaine*.

Epist. 71, § 4. “It will be a very difficult matter if your translation begins to be read more frequently throughout many churches, because the Latin churches will differ from the Greek churches, especially since a contradictor is easily refuted by producing a Greek book, that is, in the best-known language.”] It was not so important that all the churches use the same translation that they should therefore make permanent use of a faulty one. Nor would diversity have caused any difficulty, because, as we said in the note on Epistle 28, there would always have been agreement on the substance of the matter. Today we see Christians who use vernacular translations, although those translations differ, not quarrelling with one another on that account; for their disagreement arises not from the variety of translations but from differing interpretations of the same words.

Moreover, in Augustine’s time there was great variety among Latin manuscripts used by Latins and among Greek manuscripts used by Greeks, yet this presented no obstacle, since everyone knew that, owing to the passage of time and the ignorance or negligence of copyists, errors could scarcely have failed to enter the Greek manuscripts; while in the Latin manuscripts, in addition to such errors, variations had arisen from the differing judgments of those who had undertaken to translate the Greek. Augustine does not deny this in Epistle 71, § 6. Consequently, a somewhat more stubborn contradictor could not have been refuted as easily as Augustine here says by producing a Greek codex of the Seventy. Other Greek interpreters could also have been consulted; they could have been of great assistance not only for understanding the Hebrew but also for understanding the words of the Greek Seventy.

Ibid. “But whoever is disturbed by something unusual in what has been translated from Hebrew and brings an accusation of falsity will scarcely, or never, reach the Hebrew testimonies by which the charge can be defended.”] The fault lies with those who wished to appear outstanding interpreters of Scriptures they did not understand, since they depended entirely on a translation that was often obscure and faulty. Why did they not devote themselves to studying the Hebrew language, especially in Africa, where knowledge of Punic opened a path to Hebrew, which they rightly recognized as related to it, and which they would therefore have learned much more successfully than Jerome, if their judgment had not been perverse? Moreover, through comparison of the translations of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, Jerome’s version could easily have been defended by learned men; but the ignorant could accomplish nothing correctly in this matter.

Ibid. “But if one does reach them, who can tolerate the condemnation of so many Latin and Greek authorities?”] Hence, of course, those tears. For if one once admits that the translation of the Seventy cannot be trusted in every respect and contains errors, what will become of the reputation of so many Greek and Latin ecclesiastical orators who wrote so copiously about passages they had misunderstood? It will have to be said that they acted imprudently when they undertook to interpret what they could not properly understand, while neglecting to study the originals.

“But,” you will say, “the greatest lights of East and West will be obscured by a censor’s mark.” Let them indeed be obscured rather than let us undertake to defend falsehood for their sake. The issue is not the reputation of ecclesiastical men, but the discovery of truth, which must be preferred to the reputation of all mortals—indeed, which alone must be considered here. Because famous men defended something false, shall we therefore call it true? Shall we omit the investigation of truth lest someone’s reputation be diminished by its discovery? If all Jews had acted in this way, or all pagans to whom the apostles proclaimed the Gospel, no one would ever have believed the Gospel. If some corrupt custom had become established, it could never be corrected, for famous men who followed it are never lacking.

In the administration of the state, various things are done for present advantage, and even unjust and false things are proclaimed as true. But in matters pertaining to religion, truth alone must be sought, and only what is true is expedient. Indeed, for nearly two centuries Christians have discovered that it is far better to disregard the authority of ignorant interpreters—however great their reputation—and go directly to the sources, acquiring for that reason a knowledge of the Hebrew language. This has succeeded well for our fathers, and, I hope, will succeed no less well for this unhappy age.

Ibid. “Moreover, even consulted Hebrews may give another answer, so that you alone may appear necessary, since you could also refute them; but it would be astonishing if you could find a judge [to decide the matter].”] This is pure envy. Why did your Phoenicians, Augustine, not learn Hebrew, so that they would no longer need the Jews and would not have to resort to Jerome alone? But this was extremely difficult. No more difficult than it was in the memory of our fathers; indeed, much easier for African, Syrian, and Arab Christians, whose languages were related to Hebrew—especially since they had Origen’s *Hexapla*. Yet, to conceal nothing, it was much easier in those days to declaim this way before our unlearned populace.

Ibid. § 5. “For a certain brother of ours, a bishop, when he had begun having your translation read in the church over which he presides, introduced something in the prophet Jonah expressed quite differently by you from what had become fixed in everyone’s understanding and memory and had been sung through the succession of so many generations. Such a great tumult arose among the people, especially when the Greeks accused him and loudly denounced the charge of falsity, that the bishop was compelled—for it was that sort of city—to demand the testimony of the Jews.”] Yet there was no need for this. He should merely have consulted other Greek interpreters and compared them with Jerome’s version. Besides, what difference did it make to the general meaning of Jonah’s prophecy whether the word *kikajon* was translated as *cucurbita*, “gourd,” with the Seventy, or as *hedera*, “ivy,” with Jerome? Why could that little word not be translated in different ways, when so many other words of much greater importance were explained in more than one manner without offending the people? It was the bishop’s duty to mount the pulpit and teach his people this.

Ibid. “But whether they replied this because of ignorance or malice, they said that it was found in the Hebrew copies, just as the Greeks and Latins had it and asserted. What more is there to say? The man was compelled, as though correcting an error, to make the correction, wishing, after the great danger, not to remain without his people.”] As I said, he ought to have consulted other Greek interpreters, who had κισσός, that is, “ivy,” as Jerome explains in his note on Jonah, chapter 4, although he admits that the word is not suitable; for *kikajon* is another kind of plant for which there was no Latin name. Jerome therefore used a name that Latins could understand in its place.

The African populace would indeed have been bad if, for such a trifling reason, it had been ready to abandon its bishop. But, as Jerome rightly perceived, this seems to be a Punic fable by which the bishop of Hippo wished to frighten the man. Consult Jerome himself, Epistle 75 of this volume.

Epist. 78 Augustine relates that, when an accusation was obscure, he sent the accuser and the accused to Nola, to the tomb of Saint Felix, so that the truth might be discovered through the saint’s aid. He then adds: “For we ourselves know that at Milan, at the shrine of the saints, where demons miraculously and terrifyingly confess, a certain thief who had come to that place to deceive people by swearing falsely was compelled to confess his theft and return what he had taken. Surely Africa too is full of the bodies of holy martyrs? And yet we know of no such things happening anywhere here.”

Yet the things said to occur at Saint Stephen’s shrine in Calama and Hippo-Regius were no less remarkable, as is clear from the list of miracles found in Book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8. Why should thefts or other hidden crimes not also have been exposed there? Augustine replies: “For just as the Apostle says, ‘Not all the saints have gifts of healing, nor do all have the discernment of spirits,’ so he who distributes to each one individually as he wills did not wish these things to happen at every shrine of the saints.”

But who will believe that the same distribution remained in force after the saints’ deaths? Who will suppose that here evil demons were terrified by the relics of a martyr, while there they remained unmoved? To speak truthfully, the confidence I place in the miracles of Christ and the apostles—accompanied as they all are by every indication of truth—is matched by my distrust of more recent miracles, especially when they appear to have served superstition and profit far more than the spread of genuine virtue. Augustine himself does not deny, in *On True Religion*, § 47, that miracles had become rarer in his time. I know that he later retracted this, but I am surprised that he could previously have been mistaken in a matter so well known. I am not surprised that, in order to refute pagans, Donatists, and other heretics, miracles were proclaimed—miracles which, if they truly occurred, would have been far more numerous and remarkable than the miracles of Christ and the apostles, so that they could in no way have been said to occur less frequently than before. There are also other reasons for suspicion, which I will not set out in brief notes. See what we said on *Confessions*, Book VII, § 16.

Epist. 89, § 2, after saying that true martyrs are made not by punishment but by their cause, he adds: “And this indeed I would say against those whom only the darkness of heretical error envelops, for which sacrilege they would deserve to suffer the most fitting punishments, yet who would not dare to injure anyone through violent madness. But what shall I say against these people, whose most pernicious perversity is restrained by fear of losses or instructed by exile, and who prefer to attack rather than acknowledge how widely the Church has spread, as was foretold?”

Yet the crimes of the Circumcellions to which Augustine refers have nothing to do with the matter. They did not suffer punishments on account of those crimes, but on account of schism, as he himself admits and as is clear from the laws of Honorius against the Donatists, found in Book XVI of the Theodosian Code, where they are condemned as heretics, not as criminals.

What the “most fitting punishments,” or the “due punishment,” as Honorius calls it in Law 29, Title 5, Book XVI of the Theodosian Code, consisted of is explained by Augustine in his Letter to Boniface, which is Epistle 185. But the punishment is expressed more fully in Theodosius’s law against all heretics, Law 21, Title 5, Book XVI of the Theodosian Code. “In cases of heretical error,” says Theodosius in that law enacted in the year 392, “we decree that all who are found either to have ordained clerics or to have assumed clerical office shall, together with their sons, be fined ten pounds of gold apiece; and that the place where forbidden acts are attempted shall be added to the resources of our treasury if the owner’s connivance is evident. But if it is established that the owner was unaware of the matter, since it was conducted secretly, we order the tenant of that estate, if he is freeborn, to pay ten pounds of gold into our treasury; but if, descended from servile dregs, he despises the pecuniary penalty because of his poverty and low status, he shall be scourged with rods and condemned to deportation.”

## Letter 91, § 8

“On the following day, in order to instill fear into our ruined or desperate people [*perditis*; reading uncertain], public legal recourse was denied to those who seemed to wish to make a statement before the official records.”]

That is to say, in each city written records were kept of matters of somewhat greater importance that occurred there day by day; these were later sent to the proconsuls or emperors. Therefore, if anyone wished to have something officially attested, he went to the public office, so that his words might be recorded by it and thereby given evidentiary force. See Letter 35, § 1, and Letter 93, § 12.

## Letter 93, § 2

“If someone saw his enemy, rendered frenzied by dangerous fevers, running headlong toward destruction, would he not then do more harm in return for harm if he allowed him to run in that way than if he took care to seize and bind him?”]

In this letter the bishop of Hippo undertakes, at great length, to prove that persecution is lawful when used to bring those whom we think are living in error to a profession of the truth. Since many have abused—and even today continue to abuse—this opinion of his, it will not, as I think, be useless to show that Augustine seriously went wrong in this matter and moved away from the true position toward a worse one, although in other respects we by no means approve the schism and obstinacy of the Donatists.

Accordingly, we shall subject his principal arguments to examination, as they present themselves to us in order. As for the first, the comparison drawn from a frenzied person has no force. Frenzied people are, without any doubt, frenzied, and they plainly disturb civil society. Civil laws therefore permit and require them to be restrained until, once cured, they recover their former health.

But in religious controversies, in which one often sees opposing parties equally devoted to Christian virtues and equally obedient to the civil laws, the matter is neither so clear nor so evident that one party can regard the members of the other as frenzied; nor, amid passions as intense as those found here, can some persons serve as judges of others. Numbers or power, by which people usually arrogate to themselves the right of judging by force, have no bearing here, since God has nowhere promised that the truth would be found with the majority or with the most powerful. [Col. 0252B]

Indeed, assume the contrary and you will see that you have judged against yourself if circumstances change—as happened shortly afterward in Africa, where the Arian Vandals, and in Italy, where the Goths, adherents of the same heresy, were far more powerful. If Augustine had prolonged his life to those times and had seen the Catholic Africans mistreated by the Arian Vandals as impious and frenzied people, he would easily have realized that he had employed dangerous reasoning against the Donatists and would again have begun to defend the position that, under the influence of passion, he had retracted.

For it would have been futile for him to reply that the truth stood with his own party, as the Donatists did; the Arians would have denied this. And since they were judges in their own case, they would have acted toward him as toward a stubborn heretic and reproached him with all the vexations that the Arians had inflicted on the Catholics, just as Augustine here reproaches the Donatists with the outrages of the Circumcellions. [Col. 0252C]

O unhappy arguments, which shortly afterward became mere sophistries! O imprudent and deceitful lines of reasoning, which served error no less than truth! [Col. 0252D]

## Same passage

“Oh, if only I could show you from the Circumcellions themselves how many manifest Catholics we now have who condemn their former life,” etc.]

But who would believe that criminal men had suddenly been brought, not by arguments that they had always rejected before force was applied, but by punishments, to profess what they had condemned—and that they had thereby changed in mind, rather than merely gratifying the more powerful party with their lips? One would have to be exceedingly credulous to place such easy faith in words extorted by fear. [Col. 0253A]

The African persecutors were satisfied to have afflicted the Donatist party; they cared little whether they had truly healed their minds, provided only that they held their bodies subject to them. Moreover, the Arians could make similar boasts after they had mistreated the Catholics for some time, since they brought many of the weaker or more vicious among them, through fear of punishment, to abjure the Nicene Council.

Thus it happened that the very best people, who refused to act or speak against their conscience and were therefore deserving of praise, although otherwise they might have been in error, were punished most severely; while the most frivolous people and the cleverest dissemblers received praise from both Catholics and Arians.

## Same passage, § 3

“If they were frightened and not instructed, it would seem like an improper form of domination. Again, if they were instructed and not frightened, hardened by the antiquity of their custom, they would be moved more sluggishly to undertake the way of salvation,” etc.]

But terror joined to instruction makes the instruction highly suspect. People think that, unless it were supported by force and authority, it would collapse of its own accord, and that it makes use of the terror of laws only because it cannot win human minds for itself by the light of truth. Augustine would have brought these objections against the Arians, had he lived a little longer, when he saw them use the same arguments against the Catholics. [Col. 0253B]

## Same passage, § 4

“Who can love us more than God? Yet he does not cease not only to teach us gently but also to frighten us beneficially. Let us also love our enemies, because this is just and this God commands, so that we may be sons of our Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust. But just as we praise these gifts of his, so let us also consider his scourges upon those whom he loves.”]

Even without repeating that this too was an equivocal weapon that the Arians could equally have used against the Catholics, what human being would dare to claim for himself the same right over participants in his own nature that God possesses, unless he had forgotten that he was human? Who does not know that the Creator has one kind of right over creatures, and creatures another kind of right over one another, and that God’s disposition toward human beings differs from that of human beings toward one another?

God is supreme: by right of creation he is lord of the human race, and he is also the judge of every error, free from passion. Human beings, however, are fellow servants, subject to errors and evil passions. [Col. 0253C] Therefore Augustine had no reason to compare the persecutors’ love for their brothers with God’s love for the human race. [Col. 0253D]

## Same passage, § 5

“Do you think that no one ought to be compelled to justice, when you read that the master of the household said to his servants, ‘Compel all whom you find to enter’; when you also read that Saul himself, first, and afterward Paul, was compelled to know and hold the truth by the great violence of Christ compelling him,” etc.]

Before interpreting the compulsion mentioned in Luke 14:23 as force imposed through laws and punishments, Augustine ought to have considered the parable that Christ presents there. In it the servant, who had vainly summoned guests previously invited and who had most freely refused to come, is given this command. This part of the parable cannot be pressed against Augustine himself.

Augustine wanted everyone called to the Catholic Church to be compelled, whereas in the parable only the beggars, the lame, and the blind are compelled, while the others are passed over. Did Augustine think that this compulsion signified the imposition of punishments such as those we cited from the law of Theodosius in Letter 89? Is that how people are compelled to come to a banquet?

Who does not know that those are said to be compelled who are driven by entreaties? Thus Lot is said in Genesis 19:3 to have *καταβιάσασθαι*—“compelled”—the angels to spend the night with him. Likewise, in Matthew 14:22 and Mark 6:45, Jesus is said to have *ἀναγκάσαι*—“compelled”—the disciples to enter the boat. In Luke 24:29, the two disciples going to Emmaus are said to have *παραβιάσασθαι*—“compelled”—Jesus to dine with them. In Galatians 2:24 [as printed], Paul says that he reproached Peter because he was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize, using the verb *ἀναγκάζειν*. [Col. 0254A]

In all these cases no force was applied, but only entreaty, authority, or example, without any punishments; and this is how we ordinarily speak in almost every language.

As for Saul’s calling, that was a heavenly miracle. If Augustine had been able to employ similar methods to convert the Donatists, there would have been no reason for us to refute him here, and he would easily have overcome every obstinacy. But we cannot tolerate the comparison of force inflicted by soldiers, lictors, or magistrates with divine miracles; nor can we accept the inference that, because God sometimes used miracles to convince people, it is therefore lawful to use force. [Col. 0254B]

For what could be more unlike these things? If Augustine himself had lived into the period of the Vandal persecutions and had heard the Arians defend them in this way, he could scarcely have restrained himself from crying out that those who made such comparisons were blaspheming. [Col. 0254C]

## Same passage, § 6

“When we read that the slave woman and her son suffered severe afflictions from Sarah, the apostle Paul nevertheless says that Isaac suffered persecution from Ishmael: ‘But just as then the one who was according to the flesh persecuted the one who was according to the Spirit, so also now’; so that those who can may understand that the Catholic Church suffers persecution from the pride and impiety of carnal people, whom it strives to correct by temporal afflictions and terrors.”]

It is true that Hagar was badly treated by Sarah, but Paul is not referring to that here. Rather, he is referring to Ishmael’s action when he played insolently with Isaac, an action he calls persecution and compares with the persecution that Christians suffered from the Jews. That persecution did not consist in their seeing that the Jews were proud and obstinate—for no one but a Punic rhetorician would have called that persecution—but in their being subjected by the Jews to every kind of affliction and punishment.

It is absurd to compare the persecutions that Christians endured in Paul’s time with the state of mind of the African bishops and other clergy, who were distressed at being contradicted by the Donatists. Who would tolerate calling it persecution when a person suffers because he is unable to dominate others, and equating that with the misery of people who are stripped of all their possessions, sent into exile, beaten with clubs, and even killed—for this plainly happened, as is evident from Letter 100, in which Augustine intercedes that it should not happen any further? [Col. 0254D]

The Hipponensian rhetorician mocked these wretched people because he felt that everything could be said against them with impunity. But if the Arians had spoken in this way against the Catholics when they were in power, would the Catholics not have turned heaven and earth upside down?

Moreover, what ought first to have been stated Augustine here and everywhere assumes as established, although it was precisely what was in dispute: namely, that his own Church was the one Church of Christ, with the Donatists excluded. [Col. 0255A] I do not approve the Donatist schism, but in disputing with them it was absurd for him continually to assume what they stubbornly denied.

To understand how unjust this is, put Arians in Augustine’s place and imagine them saying similar things. You will then see that the Arians would be charged with precisely what the Donatists charged Augustine. [Col. 0255B]

What kind of law is this: “When my possessions are superior, judgment concerning the equity and truth of my case is to be assigned to me, although my adversaries protest; but if I am defeated by number and authority, I may not do to my adversaries what I have done”? What could be imagined more unjust? [Col. 0255C]

Yet almost all Augustine’s arguments tend in this direction, especially those that follow, which I shall not transcribe. [Col. 0255D]

## Same passage, § 7

“Consider also the times of the New Testament, when the very gentleness of charity had to be preserved not only in the heart but also displayed openly; when Christ recalls Peter’s sword into its sheath and shows that it ought not to have been drawn, not even for Christ.”]

If someone stopped reading here, he would easily believe that these were the words of a Donatist demonstrating that temporal punishments in matters pertaining to religion are unlawful, because they are wholly contrary to the character and spirit of evangelical teaching. But Augustine draws from this a completely different conclusion.

He wishes it to be inferred that, just as God the Father handed over his Son to the punishment of the cross and yet is no less merciful, so the African Church cannot be branded with cruelty because it handed the Donatists over to the lictors; for here, he says, one must consider the intention of those who handed them over, which was directed toward correcting those delivered up.

Thus, although the Catholics behaved no differently from persecutors, they were nevertheless not to be accused of unlawful persecution. “Let us learn,” he says, “brother, to distinguish the intentions of those who act by the similarity of their actions; let us not slander with closed eyes, nor accuse the benevolent as if they were harmful.”

But first, what similarity is there between God’s action in patiently allowing his willing Son to be killed by wicked people for the salvation of the human race, and the schemes of ecclesiastics who were inciting magistrates against the wretched Donatists? It is embarrassing to spend time refuting arguments of this kind, which would not be tolerated today even in beginners in logic.

But even if I grant that these things can be compared, was there any African so shameless that he dared to demand that the unhappy Donatists believe that the Catholics were as well disposed toward those whom they harassed as God was toward humanity when he handed over his Son to afflictions in order to save the human race?

God certainly gained nothing from our salvation. But the African bishops increased in authority, dignity, and wealth as their flocks grew larger; and this seems not to have been the least important cause of these vexations. [Col. 0256A]

Our rhetorician, however, has no regard not only for truth but not even for what is plausible; nor was there any need for such subtleties, since fines, prisons, exile, and death remained in store for those who would not yield in the least to these quibbles. [Col. 0256B]

## Same passage, § 8

“If it were always praiseworthy to suffer persecution, it would have been enough for the Lord to say, ‘Blessed are those who suffer persecution,’ without adding, ‘for righteousness’ sake.’”]

But the Donatists did not prefer their party to the Catholics merely because they were suffering persecution, but because, as they believed, this happened for the sake of righteousness—that is, for the sake of virtue. They refused to do what they believed was unlawful and displeasing to God.

Such a disposition of mind is certainly praiseworthy even in those who are in error. By contrast, those who extort from unwilling people, through fear of punishment, the performance of what they consider unlawful are to be blamed. For even if what unwilling people do were by its nature right, it could not fail to displease God, who does not wish to be worshiped merely with the mouth but above all in the mind, and who accepts nothing from unwilling persons. [Col. 0256C]

## Same passage

“Again, if it were always blameworthy to inflict persecution, it would not be written in the holy books: ‘The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted’; therefore sometimes the person who suffers persecution is unjust, and the one who inflicts it is just.”

But this is not a matter of persecution in every sense—that is, of punishments of every kind. It concerns only persecution carried out on account of doctrines, not on account of offenses that disturb civil society and for which punishments may be imposed under civil rather than religious laws.

In Psalm 100:5 the Septuagint version does indeed have *ἐδίωκον*—“I persecuted.” But even if we assume that they translated the word correctly, the passage is not speaking of a disputed doctrine but of slander—that is, of a sin whose perpetrator cannot deny that it is a sin.

King David promises God in that passage that he will take care to drive all slanderers from his presence: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor,” he says, “I will destroy; the one with haughty eyes and an inflated heart I will not tolerate.” [Col. 0256D]

What does this have to do with persecuting people who sincerely embrace some doctrine and whose morals are no worse than those of the rest of the citizens? Is this interpreting Scripture as one ought, or recklessly seizing upon a misunderstood word so that one may appear to say something while in reality saying nothing?

## Same passage

“The impious killed the prophets; the prophets also killed the impious.”

Augustine ought to have said whom the prophets killed on account of mere opinions. For if they killed people because of evil deeds punishable by death under the law of Moses itself, this has nothing to do with the Donatists or with others similarly in error. [Col. 0257A]

Moreover, it would have been necessary to show that everything the prophets did was lawful under the New Testament, since Christ expressly denies this in Luke 9:55–56; and Augustine’s authority cannot release anyone from the laws laid down by Christ.

“The Jews scourged Christ; Christ also scourged the Jews.” As though the scourging by which Christ drove livestock rather than human beings from the temple could be compared with the cruel scourging that Christ suffered at the hands of the Romans, who were gratifying the Jews!

Either Augustine held the Donatists’ intelligence in very low regard, hoping to stop their mouths with such arguments, or he had much greater confidence in the edicts of Honorius than in the weight of reason. [Col. 0257B]

He continues in the same way: “The apostles were handed over by human beings to human authority; the apostles also handed human beings over to the authority of Satan.”

You too would have handed the Donatists over to the authority of Satan if you had been able; but because you did not have Satan obedient to your command, you handed them over to lictors. There is a vast difference between these things. A wicked human being has often handed innocent people over to lictors, but never to Satan. Satan obeys no one except the person to whom God subjects him, and God subjects him to no one except a man of supreme virtue endowed with the power to perform miracles.

## Same passage, § 9

“The Donatists said: ‘No example is found in the evangelical and apostolic writings of anything being done by earthly kings on behalf of the Church against the enemies of the Church.’ Augustine replies: ‘Who denies that no such example is found? But that prophecy had not yet been fulfilled: “And now, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth,”’ etc.] [Col. 0257C]

Augustine evidently wishes to say that Christ and the apostles did not use the secular arm, as the phrase goes, to restrain and punish the enemies of the Church because there were no kings who favored them.

But surely this was not the natural character of Christ’s kingdom, which Christ himself testifies is not of this world, and for that reason was not defended by legions! Could Christ not, if he had wished, have summoned a vast number of Jews to arms to defend him against his enemies, and, if God had so willed, easily have supplied by divine miraculous power whatever was lacking in human strength? The same may be said of the apostles. [Col. 0257D]

## Same passage, § 11

Thus he addresses the Rogatists, who had separated in schism from the Donatists themselves:

“You seem to be gentler because you do not rage together with the savage herds of the Circumcellions. But no beast is called gentle merely because it does not wound anyone, if it lacks teeth and claws. You say that you do not wish to rage; I think that you are unable to,” etc.]

We do not know the Rogatists well enough, nor do we possess their books, to understand how they opposed persecution. But we easily understand that this reply is harsh and inhuman, and very far removed from the gentleness that Augustine ordinarily displayed.

For who knew their minds? Could it not have happened that they sincerely recoiled from all persecution? I readily persuade myself of this, since I cannot sufficiently marvel that Augustine could have been brought by such futile arguments to approve and praise persecution, and did not see that it could in no way coexist with Christian charity. [Col. 0258A]

He was blinded, I think, by passion.

## Same passage, § 17

“Accordingly, when these examples were presented by my colleagues, I yielded. For my original opinion had been that no one should be compelled to the unity of Christ; one should act by words, fight by debate, and conquer by reason, lest we have counterfeit Catholics whom we knew to be open heretics.”]

Just as Augustine knew from his rhetorical training how to say what circumstances required, so he also seems to have thought according to circumstances. For who doubts that, if the African churches had recoiled from persecution and had asked Honorius to repeal the laws against the Donatists, he would have argued the opposite case at great length? [Col. 0258B]

I certainly have no doubt that, if he had been required to plead the cause of the African churches persecuted by the Arians under the Vandals, he would have used arguments wholly contrary to these—arguments of the kind Christians formerly employed among the pagans when they were being mistreated by them.

Here Augustine does not consider whether the matter is in itself unjust, but only whether it seemed useful to the African Church. No such usefulness would have existed if Honorius had happened to favor the Donatists.

## Same passage

“But this opinion of mine—namely, that counterfeit Catholics are produced by persecution—was overcome not by the words of those who contradicted it but by the examples of those who demonstrated the contrary. For first my own city was set before me. Although it had been entirely on Donatus’s side, it was converted to Catholic unity through fear of the imperial laws; and now we see it detest the ruinous effects of your hostility so greatly that it is believed never to have been in your party.”]

It can easily happen that young men and girls change their opinion under harassment; but it is exceedingly difficult for older people and those of more discerning intelligence not to become much more alienated from a doctrine forced upon them.

Therefore, when such people say that they think differently because of fear of punishment, they are not worthy of belief.

“But,” you will say, “the later generation, which did not witness the schism and was raised in Catholic beliefs, embraces them just as it would have done if no schism had ever existed.”

I do not deny this, but I maintain that an end can be put to schism by harassment only unjustly and inhumanely; and that by such methods not only is a schism arising from obstinacy or ignorance removed, but all knowledge of the truth as well. [Col. 0258C]

This is clear even from the example of Africa itself, in which for many centuries not a single Christian has remained.

The fury of the Muslims extinguished the Christian religion there by methods similar to those by which the Donatist schism had once been torn out. Augustine therefore had no reason to boast about the outcome, since it is equivalent to all the vexations that had preceded it. [Col. 0258D]

## Same passage, § 18

“The terror of all these laws, by which kings serve the Lord in fear, benefited them so greatly that now some say: ‘This is what we wanted all along; but thanks be to God, who gave us the opportunity to do it immediately and cut short the delays,’” etc.]

Without repeating that those who spoke in this way were unworthy of belief, I shall say that such speeches are heard wherever some superior force has been brought to bear in a matter: they are the words of people seeking the favor of the victor and prepared to do and suffer anything so that they may enjoy their possessions in peace. [Col. 0259A]

Finally, I cannot understand how Augustine could have reasoned in this way, since he believed that people are converted to God and brought to eternal life solely by inward grace, which is granted only to the elect.

For what is more alien to divine grace than fines, exiles, and other punishments? Who could maintain—if he possessed even a little shame and had not stripped himself of all reverence for religion—that the preaching of the divine word is altogether ineffective and that divine grace is not joined to it unless persecution is added?

If divine grace does not in fact await persecution in order to soften human minds, what need is there for persecution when divine grace converts people without it?

“But,” you will say, “the Donatists did not listen to the arguments of the Catholics until they had been brought into the Catholic churches by fear.”

But were they not reading the New Testament? Was divine grace joined more closely to the sayings and writings of the Africans than to the word of God? [Col. 0259B]

Anyone who carefully weighs these matters will easily understand that far more was given here to personal passions than to the desire to bring others to a sounder mind, and that the African bishops wanted to see their churches filled with a larger populace, whatever the means.

Enough, and more than enough, has been said about persecution.

## Same passage, § 22

“You have discovered something great, learned historian.”]

Here “historian” is *πολυΐστωρ*, “one who knows many things.” See the note on *On Order*, Book II, chapter 12. [Col. 0259C]

## Same passage, § 35

“This kind of writing—the books of Hilary, Cyprian, and the other Fathers—must be distinguished from the authority of the canon. For they are not read as though testimony were being produced from them in such a way that it would be impermissible to think otherwise wherever they may have judged differently from what the truth requires.”]

These words ought to be written in letters of gold at the front of every individual work of the Fathers that is published, lest their authority be preferred to the truth. We have exercised the same right with respect to Augustine himself—a right which human beings must constantly exercise with regard to other human beings who are not inspired. Edmund Albertinus collected similar statements, both by Augustine himself and by others, in the preface to his book *On the Eucharist*.

## Letter 96, § 2

“That Paul, after he had become a bishop, was about to renounce all his possessions because of the immense accumulation of fiscal debts,” etc.] [Col. 0259D]

He had taken refuge in the bishopric as in an asylum, so that he would not be thrown into prison on account of his debts.

## Letter 97, § 2

“Let the enemies of the Church know that those laws concerning the destruction of idols and the correction of heretics which, while Stilicho was alive, were sent to Africa were established by the will of the most pious and faithful emperor.”]

That is to say, since Honorius was the weakest of mortals, the Catholics were extremely afraid that the pagans or Donatists might obtain some rescript that was more favorable to them.

For the history of these laws, see Book VI of the *Life of Augustine*, which appears in volume XI of this edition, and the notes of Jacobus Gothofredus on title 5 of Book XVI of the *Theodosian Code*.

## Letter 98, § 1

“For this reason he derived from Adam what was to be released by the grace of that sacrament, because the soul was not yet living separately—that is, another soul,” etc.] [Col. 0260A]

Augustine evidently thought that the souls of all human beings had in some way existed in Adam’s soul, because they had been propagated from it. See *On Free Choice of the Will*, Book III, chapter 20, § 56.

This is a remarkable opinion, as is also the method by which he resolves Boniface’s questions. Those who were satisfied with such answers must have been very easily persuaded.

## Same passage, § 9

“For if sacraments did not possess some likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. From this likeness they often also receive the names of the things themselves. Thus, in a certain manner, the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body, and the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood; so the sacrament of faith is faith.”]

As for the sacrament of the Eucharist, the matter is not difficult to understand. But who can understand the sponsor of an infant being baptized, when he answered “I believe” on behalf of the infant, as intending by this: “I receive baptism, or the sacrament of faith”? [Col. 0260B]

Who does not see that the original baptismal formula was devised for adults, who alone at first received baptism, and was later transferred to infants as well? It would have been better to establish a new formula for this purpose. If that had been done, Augustine would have had no need to resort to such strained and implausible arguments.

## Letter 100, § 1

“We wish them to be corrected, not killed; nor do we wish discipline concerning them to be neglected, nor that they be subjected to punishments of which they are worthy.”]

Under the law of Honorius issued on 24 November 408—law 44, title 5, *On Heretics*, Book XVI of the *Theodosian Code*, addressed to Donatus—punishment is ordered to be exacted from the Donatists. For, after mentioning them and the Jews, it says:

“Accordingly, we order that punishment by just correction be inflicted upon those who attempt anything contrary and opposed to the Catholic sect.”

For these words, see Jacobus Gothofredus. [Col. 0260C]

If Honorius, making a distinction, had ordered those who stirred up sedition to be punished by a just judgment under the Roman laws, while sparing those who had lived peacefully and were held only by a mistaken opinion, there would be no reason for us to criticize him. For he would have provided for public tranquility while taking into account, as was proper, humaneness and the weakness of the human mind.

But now he mixes the lowest with the highest and wishes similar punishments to be inflicted upon the mistaken and the seditious. Augustine likewise here mixes the mistaken with criminals, condemns them indiscriminately, and equally intercedes that they not be killed. [Col. 0260D]

At first sight there appears to be some mercy in this. But I fear that the Africans were more eager to acquire the reputation of mercy than to cultivate that virtue sincerely: first, because, as I have said, they treated all Donatists alike; and second, because, even apart from death, the laws of Theodosius and his sons were savage toward these wretched people.

Such, for example, is the fourth law of title 6, which among other things decrees that anyone subsequently discovered to have rebaptized another must be brought before the judge presiding over the province, so that, having been punished by the confiscation of all his property, he may suffer the penalty of poverty, to which he is to be subjected forever.

It further provides that those from the aforementioned group who do not fear repeating baptism, or who, by consenting to it, do not condemn this crime through the permission of their own association, are to know that they will be permanently denied not only the ability to make a will but also the ability to acquire anything under the guise of a gift or through the execution of contracts, unless an amendment directed by reverence for the true faith corrects the error of their depraved mind. [Col. 0261A]

Everyone can easily understand how great a calamity such laws would bring upon the Donatists if they were enforced, especially since other laws most carefully ordered their execution.

The African bishops therefore were not especially merciful merely because they did not want those people killed who were treated so badly that many preferred death to life. Who does not know whether they might not rather have wished to see wealthy Donatists paying taxes to them in their churches than lying in their graves, with their property assigned to the treasury?

Nothing is more unworthy of Christians than persecution; those who approve it can approve anything. [Col. 0261B]

## Letter 105, § 3, concerning a presbyter who had become a Catholic

“Why did your people persecute him and almost kill him, unless the hand of God, acting through the people who arrived, had restrained their violence?” etc.]

No one can doubt that the Donatists acted very wickedly and ought to have paid the penalty for such violence, but not for their opinions. Nevertheless, everything was forgiven them if only they returned to the Catholic Church, as is clear from law 41, title 5, Book XVI of the *Theodosian Code*.

## Same passage, § 6

“And yet what is better: to produce the true commands of the emperors on behalf of unity, or false concessions on behalf of perversity, as you did, filling all Africa suddenly with your lie?”]

The wretched people ought not to have been reproached for such a lie, if it was a lie. But Augustine was blinded by excessive passion and was mistaken. For, as the learned Benedictine observed in *The Life of Augustine*, Book VI, chapter 7, § 2, it is clear from the Council of Carthage held on 18 June 410 that at that time a law had been enacted forbidding anyone to embrace the worship of the Christian religion except by free choice. Consult that work. [Col. 0261C]

## Letter 120, § 3

“Far be it from us to believe that for this reason we should not receive or seek an explanation, since we could not even believe unless we possessed rational souls. Therefore, in certain matters pertaining to saving doctrine, which we are not yet able to grasp by reason but will one day be able to grasp, faith should precede reason, so that the heart may be cleansed and may receive and endure the light of great reason; and this itself is a matter of reason.”]

Nothing is truer, although I do not understand how this can be reconciled with what he says elsewhere concerning authority. See the note on volume I, *On the Greatness of the Soul*, § 12.

No one can fail to approve what appears in § 6: “Just as you should not avoid every speech because there is also false speech, so you should not avoid every argument because there is also false reasoning.” [Col. 0261D]

Something from the character of the Academics, whom he had admired greatly in his youth, seems to have adhered to Augustine. Whatever plausible considerations present themselves to his mind, he seizes upon them, heedless of all their consequences and of what he has said elsewhere. Cicero, in whom he had spent so much time reading, behaved in the same way. See John Clericus, *Hieronymian Questions*, question eight.

## Letter 126, § 7

“For I, according to the judgment of many—those who compare themselves with themselves, that is, apparently, those who judge the minds of others by their own minds—seem not to have abandoned riches but to have come into riches. For my paternal property can scarcely be reckoned a twentieth part in comparison with the estates of the Church, which I am now regarded as possessing as their master.”] [Col. 0262A]

I would not wish to judge harshly of anyone’s mind when it is unknown to me. But I cannot refrain from observing from this that it is wrong to infer from the change of a secular condition into an ecclesiastical one that ecclesiastics are better than laypeople.

For in that change, when someone prefers to become a cleric rather than marry and earn by his own labor a livelihood for himself, his wife, and the children born of her, there is often no small gain. It is not as valuable to have a wife with whom one may have intercourse as it is to become much richer and to lead a more peaceful and comfortable life—not to mention the dignity of those ecclesiastics who attained the episcopate. [Col. 0262B]

I admit that there may be, and have been, men who did not seek such wealth and dignities and who used them rightly. But it certainly cannot be said that their preference for these things over a private and obscure life arose from a mind that despised wealth and honors. Nor, for that reason, are they to be preferred to other human beings or praised because they wished to be happier and more honored than others.

Elsewhere, concerning Pinianus: “In any, and especially in any of the African churches, let this man of ours be, I say not a presbyter but a bishop: compared with his former wealth, he would be exceedingly poor, even if he needed it with a master's disposition. Thus Christian poverty is loved much more clearly and securely in one who cannot be thought to possess any desire for greater possessions.” But this was not the issue. Albina was not complaining that her son was being snatched away by the people of Hippo so that Pinianus might become richer; rather, because he was wealthy and generous, the people hoped that, if he served among them as presbyter, he would distribute his wealth to the poor—whether he retained the principal and shared its proceeds with them, or gave away the principal itself all at once. Paulinus of Nola had provided an example of such generosity; see chapter 8 of his Life in the Paris edition of 1685. If the people of Hippo, as Albina suspected, desired to have Pinianus as presbyter for this reason and demanded it seditiously, then this was seditious beggary and dangerous indeed, since it was robbing a wife of her husband so that the people might enjoy his spoils, rather than expressing love for Pinianus’s virtue. Augustine does not dare wholly to deny this, although he pretends not to understand why Albina should have suspected it; indeed, he almost admits it in these words: “And if among that multitude there were poor or beggarly persons who were shouting together and hoping to obtain from your venerable abundance a supplement to their need, even this desire, I think, is not disgraceful.” It is not disgraceful modestly to beg if one cannot otherwise sustain life; but it is disgraceful to issue threats in order to impose upon a man a way of life by which he will provide you with resources. Such beggary is not to be tolerated in the Church.

Elsewhere, § 8. “It remains, therefore,” he says, “that this most disgraceful desire for money is directed obliquely against the clergy, and especially against the bishop. For we are thought to rule over the Church’s possessions; we enjoy its wealth.” Augustine admits that this could plausibly have been said of the clergy of Hippo; yet he emphatically denies that it was true, and swears that he had not been corrupted by any desire for money. I believe him concerning himself, but I strongly suspect that some among the lower clergy had looked to the Church’s advantage, since it could not receive so wealthy a presbyter without profit; and this profit also flowed in some measure to the whole people of Hippo, since any of them might become the dependent of a bishop or presbyter. I do not understand why Augustine conceals this entirely, since the people were not accustomed to riot so that some poor foreigner might become a presbyter. Thus many matters were once concealed, in honor of the Church, which, if they were known, might prevent us from seeking examples of Christian life complete in every respect beyond the age of the apostles.

[Col. 0263B] Epistle 133, § 1. “I have been struck with the greatest anxiety, lest perhaps your Sublimity should judge that they ought to be punished with such severity of the laws that they should suffer what they have done.” He begs Marcellinus not to punish capitally the Donatist Circumcellions, whom he calls guilty of murder and other crimes. But why does he not intercede for those who were being ill-treated merely on account of their opinion, and who deserved to be treated more gently? Evidently, as I have already said elsewhere, he was seeking a reputation for mercy by securing the safety of notorious criminals. See also the following letter.

Epistle 138, § 19, concerning Apuleius of Madaura: “He was litigating over the erection of a statue for himself among the Coenses, from whose city he had taken a wife, against the opposition of certain citizens.” The Benedictines note that eleven manuscripts have *Ocenses*, five *Oeenses*, and two *Coenses*. But anyone who has read Apuleius’s *Apologia*, where he speaks at length of his marriage to the Oeensic widow Pudentilla, will have no doubt that the five manuscripts preserve the better reading. I therefore wonder that this reading was not admitted into the text.

Epistle 141, § 5. “The communion of the wicked does not stain anyone through participation in the sacraments, but through consent to their deeds.” Nothing is truer: so long as one is free publicly to disapprove of their deeds, one is in no way stained by them. But why should this not also be extended to doctrines? Nevertheless, on account of errors which it was permissible to condemn, and which were not even of great importance, people who were otherwise by no means wicked were very frequently expelled from ecclesiastical society.

Epistle 143, § 2. “I confess that I am trying to be among those who write in order to make progress, and make progress by writing. Therefore, if I have stated something incautiously or less learnedly, which deserves to be criticized not only by others who can see it, but also by myself—for I too ought at least to see it if I am making progress—this is neither surprising nor grievous. Rather, it ought to be forgiven and welcomed, not because an error was made, but because it was disapproved.” Augustine says this while explaining a passage in one of his books *On Free Choice of the Will*; certainly no one who is not wholly unjust could disapprove of these words. But I am surprised that he did not address other passages of the same work, which I pointed out in my observations on the third book of that work. I am also surprised that those who held similar views were condemned so harshly.

Elsewhere, § 7. “For if a reason is offered against the authority of the divine Scriptures, however acute it may be, it deceives by its plausibility and cannot be true. Again, if the authority of the holy Scriptures is set against a most manifest and certain reason, the person who does this does not understand that he is setting against the truth not the meaning of those Scriptures, which he was unable to penetrate, but rather his own meaning; nor is he opposing what he finds in them, but what he has found in himself as though it were on their behalf.” This is a golden rule. If no one departed from it, both the legitimate authority and proper meaning of Scripture, and the indubitable truth of reason, would remain secure. But because it is neglected, now the faith of Scripture and now the light of reason falters; or things that cannot disagree are shamefully set against one another. It would have been desirable for Augustine to have remembered this rule of his own in the Pelagian controversies. See the note on Epistle 120.

Epistle 149, § 3. “One [Greek manuscript] had what our Latin manuscripts also have: ‘Lord, destroying, scatter them from the earth’; another had, as you yourself have written: ‘from the few of the earth.’” This passage occurs in Psalm XVI, 14, according to the division of the Septuagint interpreters, and Augustine gives it in reply to Paulinus, who was asking about the meaning of these words. From this Augustine might have understood how necessary Jerome’s work was in translating the Scriptures of the Old Testament anew from the Hebrew sources. For since some Greek books had **ΑΠΟΛΛΥΩΝ** (*destroying*), while others had **ΑΠ ΟΛΙΓΩΝ** (*from the few*)—the former being found in the Vatican copy and the latter in the Alexandrian—and since the Latin manuscripts likewise varied, how could he choose between the readings without examining the archetypal text? If he had been able to read it, he would have seen that the word *mimthim* was translated “from mortals.” From this he would have concluded that the first Septuagint translators had read *methim*, “destroying,” which is a Hiphil participle; and thereafter he would have recognized that this translation is not correct, as I shall not demonstrate here. Jerome, nevertheless, also has here “those who are dead,” but without justification, as more recent translators have sufficiently shown.

Elsewhere, § 4. “As for what follows—‘They were filled with swine’—I have already explained what I thought of it. But what other manuscripts have, and are said to have more correctly, ‘They were filled with sons,’ because the more carefully prepared copies resolve, by means of an accentual mark, the ambiguity of the same Greek word according to Greek writing practice, is indeed more obscure, but seems better suited to the preferable meaning.” Some manuscripts, that is, had **ὑῶν**, “of swine” or “with swine,” while others had **υἱῶν**, “of sons” or “with sons.” Augustine thought, on the basis of his knowledge of Greek, that the difference was only one of accent, although the letter *iota* also differs. Some now have **ὑείων**, “of swine.” He partly perceived the correct reading, for the Hebrew is *banim*, “sons”; but he reached it by accident and through a faulty conjecture, since the sense is wholly alien to this passage. I shall add nothing about the subsequent interpretations, for it is sufficiently clear from more recent scholars how much value should be assigned to them. I have noted only a few matters, so that it might be clear that those who once wished to interpret the Old Testament without knowledge of the Hebrew language were walking in darkness. They would have acted much more correctly, as modesty required, by remaining silent; but those who had acquired some ability to invent and to speak thought that they could pronounce upon everything.

Epistle 157, § 2. “If you ask whether anyone in this life can progress so far in perfection of righteousness that he lives here entirely without any sin, consider what the apostle John said, whom the Lord especially loved among the disciples: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves,’ and so forth.” Augustine gives this answer to Hilary’s first question in the preceding letter, where Hilary says that certain Christians in Syracuse were teaching various things, and first of all that a human being can be without sin. The meaning of this doctrine is that living without sin ought not to be reckoned among impossibilities. This cannot be denied, since the matter is not impossible by its nature and, if it is not achieved by human beings, it could at least be achieved through divine grace. Furthermore, one must consider what is meant by the word “sin.” Perhaps Pelagius and his disciples understood by it not the lesser offenses of human weakness, which God certainly does not impute, but those which are incompatible with the established possession of all Christian virtues—virtues without which the apostles and other holy men appear to have lived, at least for a time. See what Joannes Garnerius cites from Pelagius’s *On Nature* in the appendix to Dissertation 6, and the fragments of Caelestius there as well. Augustine ought to have weighed these matters; instead, he immediately gives the Pelagian statement an invidious interpretation, as though Pelagius had simply said that there are people who do not sin, whereas he is concerned only with possibility, as the scholastics put it. To say that something can happen is plainly different from saying that it actually happens. Perhaps the Pelagians were not even speaking of every kind of sin.

[Col. 0265C] Elsewhere, § 4. “But these men,” he says, “are to be tolerated to some extent when they say that there is or has been here someone, apart from the one Holy of holies, who had no sin at all.” Yet, as we saw in the preceding question, this is not what they said. The bishop of Hippo continues: “But when they say that free will is sufficient for a human being to fulfill the Lord’s commandments, even if he is not assisted by God’s grace and the gift of the Holy Spirit for good works, this must be anathematized altogether and detested with every possible execration.” This is what he says concerning the doctrine that a human being can easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes. The claim signifies that a person who wishes to return to a sounder mind can reform his conduct and acquire habits of virtue opposed to his former ones; once this has been done, observance of God’s commandments will become easy—not in a single moment, as though someone long accustomed to wickedness could immediately pass to the highest degree of virtue, but gradually. As for the added phrase “without God’s grace,” without any distinction being made, Pelagius denied this. He acknowledged various forms of God’s grace, as Dionysius Petavius shows in *Dogmatic Theology*, volume III, *On the Pelagian Heresy*, chapter 2. But he did not wish to admit that inward grace by which, as though through some irresistible breath—or one which could not be resisted—a few elect persons were brought to faith. Augustine ought to have proved this from Scripture, and from passages that were not ambiguous, before he was inflamed with such zeal, which was not without bitterness. For that human beings need not only God’s commandments in order to live rightly, but also assistance not contained in the laws themselves, Pelagius by no means denied, as Petavius demonstrates at length in the work cited.

Elsewhere, § 11. “But when they say that an infant who dies before receiving baptism cannot perish because he is born without sin, the Apostle does not say this . . . . . For that teacher of the nations says: ‘Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and thus it passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned.’” But highly learned men demonstrated long ago that this passage of Paul concerns adults alone, who imitate Adam’s sin; and Augustine never proved that baptism was prescribed by Christ or the apostles for infants lest they perish. I shall say nothing else about what highly learned men have said on this matter, for I am not writing theological scholastic treatises, but brief observations. I shall say only this: Augustine speaks here with greater confidence precisely because he could not prove what he asserts. The passage in Paul, Romans 5, is too obscure to be explained by so ordinary an interpreter; this will become clear from the following observation.

[Col. 0266B] Epistle 164. “It is sufficiently established that the Lord, having been put to death in the flesh, came into hell. For one cannot contradict either the prophecy that said, ‘For you will not abandon my soul in hell,’ which Peter himself explains in the Acts of the Apostles, so that no one might dare to understand it otherwise; or those words of Peter himself in which he asserts that Christ loosed the pains of hell, in which it was impossible for him to be held. Who, then, unless he is an unbeliever, would deny that Christ was among the dead?” From this one may understand how dangerous it is to attempt to interpret Scripture when one is deprived of the necessary aids. First, something is found in it that is not there; then those who understand it better are bitterly condemned. Once someone rashly believes that something is plainly present in Scripture which is not there, he readily condemns those who think it is absent. Augustine conducted himself in this way here. In the speech of the Christians of that age who spoke Latin, *infernum* and *inferi* signified the place where the souls of condemned people suffer punishment. Because he found in Psalm 15:10, “You will not abandon my soul in hell,” a passage applied by Peter to Christ, he immediately concluded—though not alone, lest I conceal anything, but together with countless others—that Christ’s soul had descended into the place of punishment while his body lay in the tomb. Then he denounced as impious those who thought otherwise.

But above all, it must be established that Peter was not seeking in the psalm’s passage something that is in no way there. Peter must therefore be understood from the psalmist’s passage, just as the psalmist must be understood from Peter’s speech; and there is no disagreement between them, although they in no way agree with Augustine. There is no doubt that Peter recited the passage in Hebrew or Chaldean, the language he used. The words of the psalmist in the Hebrew text are as follows: “You will not leave my soul in the grave” (*lischol*), “nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption.” The words “my soul” mean the same as “I,” and have the same meaning as “your holy one” in the second member. The Hebrews commonly speak in this way, as everyone knows. The word [the Hebrew term is omitted in the supplied text], by the perpetual usage of the Hebrew language, signifies either a grave, or some place beneath the surface of the earth, or certainly the state and condition of the dead, whatever it may be; it never signifies a particular place assigned to the punishments of the wicked, as an examination of the passages in which it occurs will show.

The Greek interpreters called the Septuagint, however, who accommodated themselves to the Gentiles in more than one respect, always translated it **ᾅδης**, or **θάνατος**, and never **τάφος**, “grave,” although the latter was the proper meaning of the word. Thus here too they translated: **Οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψεις τὴν ψυχήν μου εἰς ᾅδην, οὐδὲ δώσεις τὸν ὅσιόν σου ἰδεῖν διαφθοράν**—“You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption.” This translation is awkward, for it is clear that the psalmist means, in a transferred sense, that God will not allow him to be killed. To leave someone in the grave, or to allow him to see corruption, is to permit someone who has been wounded or grievously afflicted to die. Nevertheless, in its proper sense these words fit Christ better, since God did not allow him to remain long in the grave or to corrupt there. Accordingly, in Acts 2:27 Peter shows that the passage concerns Christ’s resurrection from the grave.

Thus the Apostle speaks in verse 24: “Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of Hades (**τοῦ ᾅδου**), since it was impossible for him to be held by it.” This expression is taken from Psalm 18:5, where David says: “The pains of Hades”—which can be translated “the pains and cords of the grave”—“surrounded me; they overtook me.” Since Peter was speaking Chaldean at Jerusalem, a language understood by all Jews except the Hellenists, he uttered these same words and consequently understood them as bonds of death, which is undoubtedly how they should be understood. For although the word can also signify “pains,” the expressions “to loose” and “to be held” show that bonds are meant. This is also the psalmist’s meaning, as the following member shows. But Luke, accustomed to the Greek version and writing for the Greeks, employed the expression of the Septuagint translators. Peter therefore meant that God had loosed the bonds of death by which it was impossible for Christ to be held.

I know that Augustine says later: “It is easy to understand that the pains of hell were loosed in the same way as the snares of hunters can be loosed so that they do not hold, not because they held.” But first, it is completely false that *infernum* ever signifies the place of punishment; and the psalmist’s own words show that the bonds of death must be understood. Second, where is it said that God loosed the pains of hell so that Christ’s soul would not feel them? Nowhere. Peter is not speaking here of any such action of God preventing Christ from suffering the punishments of the damned, but solely of Christ’s resurrection: “Whom,” he says, “God raised,” **ἀνέστησε**, “having loosed,” and so forth.

He then continues: “For David says concerning him” (Psalm 16:8, according to the Hebrew division): “I foresaw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken . . . . . . For you will not abandon my soul,” and so forth. Then, in verse 31: “Foreseeing this, he spoke of the resurrection of Christ, that he was neither abandoned in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption. God raised up this Jesus,” and so forth.

It is therefore plainly clear that Augustine not only, through ignorance of the Hebrew language, drew from Scripture a doctrine that is in no way contained in it, but also paid too little attention to the sequence of Peter’s speech, from which he could have understood the meaning of his expression. I do not deny that other ecclesiastical writers commonly went astray in the same matter; one should consult the interpreters of the Apostles’ Creed concerning this, among whom Joannes Pearsonius stands out. But this interpretation, which the bishop of Hippo advances with such assurance to explain the obscure passage of 1 Peter 3:18, is no less false. Those who resorted to him as to an oracle whenever Scripture was being interpreted plainly did not know what it means to interpret Scripture.

Elsewhere, § 7. “I have nowhere been able to find the lower world (*inferi*) itself called good in Scripture.” But Hugo Grotius, a man considerably more learned and a better interpreter of Scripture, could find no passage where the word is taken in a bad sense—and neither can we. See Grotius on Matthew 16:18 and Luke 16:23.

Epistle 166, § 5. “I am also certain that the soul has fallen into sin through no fault of God, no necessity imposed by God or by itself, but by its own will, and so forth.” I do not know how this can be reconciled with original sin as theologians now explain it. For souls infected by that sin cannot be said to have been polluted by their own will, nor to have fallen into that sin under no necessity.
