If it is said that the passage concerns actual sin, it must be shown why, with respect to that sin, it is unjust to count as sin what is admitted not by one’s own will but under an imposed necessity, whereas the same does not apply to original sin.

Augustine, however, in order that human beings might be understood to have sinned by their own will and under no necessity, inclined toward the belief that all souls had been present in Adam’s soul and had been propagated from it, as I have observed elsewhere. He makes this sufficiently clear in § 10: “Tell me,” he says, “if souls are separately made for each person being born today, where do infants sin, so that they need remission of sin in the sacrament of Christ, sinning in Adam, from whom the flesh of sin was propagated? Or, if they do not sin, by what justice of the Creator are they bound by another’s sin, when, being propagated through mortal members, they are inserted into them so that condemnation overtakes them unless the Church comes to their aid, although it is not in their power to receive the assistance of baptism,” and so forth.

But if the souls of all human beings were in Adam’s soul, so that they sinned together with it, this is no easier to understand and is a most absurd invention. It would therefore have been much better to examine carefully the passages of Scripture from which such opinions were thought to have arisen, together with the purpose and nature of baptism. Had this been done more deeply, good men would have understood that, after seeking in Scripture what is not there, they had become entangled in inexplicable labyrinths of difficulties; and that articles of faith should not be extracted so readily from obscure passages and imposed upon Christians by threats of anathemas and every kind of punishment, as was done at that time by the African churches.

Elsewhere, § 10. “Since, therefore, we cannot say either that God compels souls to become sinful or that he punishes the innocent, and since we are not permitted to deny that those who have departed from their bodies without the sacrament of Christ—even infants—are dragged only to condemnation, I ask you: how is this opinion defended, according to which souls are believed not all to be made from that one soul of the first human being, but just as that one was made for one person, so each soul is made separately for each person?” It is absolutely certain that God neither compels souls to be sinful nor punishes the innocent; for God is undoubtedly both a lover of holiness and just. But Augustine ought to have produced some passage of Scripture from which it is plainly established that baptism is necessarily imposed upon infants, so that without it they are condemned. No such passage exists.

Even if I grant that baptism is necessarily imposed upon adult believers, as the public profession and token of Christianity, it does not follow that it is also imposed upon infants. For just as, although faith is required indiscriminately of all, those passages are understood to refer to people capable of faith, not to infants, who cannot believe before the use of reason; so, even if there were general commandments that everyone should receive baptism, they would always have to be understood with an exception for those in whose power it is to be baptized, not for those in whose power it is not.

Augustine, however, appeals in § 21 to the custom of the Church. He says that this is why people hurry and run to have infants baptized: because it is undoubtedly believed that they cannot otherwise be made alive in Christ at all. But why Christians believed this, we can find no certain explanation in the writings of the apostles. Nor is it permissible to derive a dogma of the Christian faith from custom or opinion, which might have arisen among the unlearned as readily as among the learned—especially when the doctrine is burdened with difficulties that cannot be resolved. Although infants are not improperly baptized, there is no indication, however slight, that the apostles did this, specifically so that unbaptized infants would not be condemned.

Elsewhere, § 21. “Whoever tells us that anyone can be made alive in the resurrection of the dead except in Christ must be detested as a common plague to the faith.” But what does “in Christ” mean? If “because of Christ” or “through Christ” is understood, it is true; but who has denied this? He continues: “Likewise, whoever says that even infants who depart this life without participating in his sacrament will be made alive in Christ plainly acts against the apostolic preaching and condemns the whole Church,” and so forth. Where did the apostles preach this concerning infants? Nowhere. We have already spoken of the custom of the Church. Therefore those who think otherwise should not so readily be regarded as common plagues to the faith. This is a cruel insult against people who cannot be refuted by Scripture.

Epistle 173, § 2. “But you do not think that this ought to have happened to you, because you believe that no one should be compelled to do good.” Correctly so; for what is done under compulsion cannot be good. God does not accept words or deeds in which the mind is not present. Someone who gives alms unwillingly is less pleasing to God than someone who obstinately refuses to give them.

Augustine, however, argues otherwise against a Donatist: “Consider what the Apostle said: ‘Whoever desires the office of bishop desires a good work.’ And yet so many are held against their will in order to undertake the episcopate; they are brought forward, confined, guarded, and made to suffer so much that they do not wish to suffer, until the willingness to undertake the good work comes to them.” But those who are compelled in this way—assuming that there really are people who are compelled to accept ecclesiastical dignities and wealth when previously they did not wish to accept them—also themselves think that the episcopate is a good work. They do not flee from it as though it were something evil, but only judge themselves unequal to bearing its burden properly.

The Donatists, however, thought that what they were compelled to do was evil in itself and displeasing to God, although they were mistaken in this; nor could they be brought by harassment to think otherwise. This example therefore has no relevance, and Augustine employs it only in the manner of those rhetoricians who require merely the faintest shadow of plausibility in order to imagine that they are reasoning correctly. Christian churches were filled with such men for many centuries, but especially in that age. It would be desirable for those who undertake the public cause of the churches to devote somewhat more diligent attention to stricter dialectic and rhetoric, lest they sell so many sophisms and empty ornaments to the common people.

# THE OBSERVATIONS OF HENRICUS DE NORIS ON EPISTLE 175

To the illustrious and most learned Antonio Magliabecchi of Florence: Brother Henricus de Noris, a Veronese Augustinian.

When I had decided to travel to Pisa and had already gathered my papers and writing materials, you suddenly delay my planned journey, most illustrious man, and at the same time impose upon me an extremely long expedition, ordering me to hasten to Africa and there labor to excavate the ruins of many cities which devouring time and the former fury of the barbarians have destroyed.

For you write that you recently received from Lyons the little books of Marius Mercator, furnished with extensive notes by Joannes Garnerius, and that you congratulate yourself on Mercator’s fortunate lot: after having lain hidden for twelve centuries, he has this year become known for the first time to the literary world, his little books having been published all at once in Paris, Brussels, and partly also at Padua. Do you see how posterity, though late, takes care of its most learned men—men whom long ages have never completely buried, but who emerge from the corners of libraries into the hands and mouths of human beings, as though restored from exile?

You add that you have read in Garnerius’s work the notes which he wrote in Dissertation 2 *On the Synods Held in the Matter of the Pelagians during the Life of Saint Augustine*, concerning both inscriptions of the letters of the synods of Carthage and Milevis held against the Pelagians in 416. There he attempted what I told you long ago in my letters that I could in no way accomplish; indeed, as he persuaded himself, he completed it entirely.

Since the synodical letter to Pope Saint Innocent has in its inscription only the names of the bishops, but not also their sees, as is clear from Epistles 90 and 92 among Augustine’s letters, Garnerius did not lose heart. Instead, by comparison with the Carthaginian conference convened five years earlier, namely in 411, he identified the cities of nearly all those bishops, over which they presided in ecclesiastical matters at that time.

I confess, most learned man, that I too once pursued this line of thought, as you know well, and applied my pen vigorously to the same task when I was composing the Pelagian history. But although I could infer the sees of many bishops from the celebrated conference, since very many cities remained entirely unknown to me, I withdrew my hand from the tablet when I realized that I was guessing rather than writing anything true.

Although I am occupied with more serious concerns, so that I cannot be drawn away from them by any contrivance, you nevertheless ask for my judgment on this matter. I have therefore written out my observations on Garnerius’s notes with a pen hastening toward other tasks. I cannot oppose your command, to whom I owe so much. This will be a new proof of my respect for you, since I willingly carry out what, if anyone else were commanding it, I would not merely do unwillingly but would not do at all.

And so that you may be spared the inconvenience of repeatedly taking up a large volume, I place Garnerius’s own words first, followed by my censorial remarks. For the rest, I thought it worthwhile to insert the inscription of the synodical letter of the Proconsular Fathers, copied from the title of Epistle 90 in Augustine.

To the most blessed and most honored holy brother, Pope Innocent: Aurelius, Mundius, Rusticanus, Fidentius, Eugarius, Antonius, Palatinus, Adeodatus, Vincentius, Publianus, Theasius, Tutus, Panthonius, Victor, Restitutus, Rusticus, Fortunatianus, another Restitutus, Ampelius, Animus, Felix, Donatianus, Adeodatus, Octavius, Serotinus, Majorinus, Posthumianus, Trispulus, Victor, another Victor, Leucius, Marianus, Fructuosus, Faustinianus, Quodvultdeus, Candorius, Maximus, Magarius, Rusticus, Rufianus, Proculianus, Thomas, Januarius, Octavianus, Praetextatus, Sixtus, Quodvultdeus, Penthadius, Quodvultdeus, Cyprianus, Servilius, Pelagius, Marcellus, Venantius, Didymus, Saturninus, Tiazacenus, Germanus, Germanianus, Juvenius, Majorinus, Inventius, Candidus, Cyprianus, Aemilianus, Romanus, Africanus, and Marcellinus, who were present at the council of the Church of Carthage.

Before Garnerius identifies the sees of the aforementioned Fathers of the province of Proconsularis, he introduces the matter as follows:

“It seemed, moreover, that it would be worthwhile, and that some favor might be gained from learned readers, if the names of the bishops who attended the synod were listed in such a way that—something no one has hitherto attempted—their respective Churches might be assigned to each of them, insofar as possible. These sees have indeed been collected, but not without care and labor, by comparing various ancient books with one another, and especially three: the first part of the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, the first part of the Carthaginian conference, and the *Notice of the Provinces of Africa* published by Father Sirmond.

“But how much favor he has won among learned men will be clear from what I shall set forth below. In fact, he expended care and labor to no purpose, and gained for himself only the praise of having fallen through attempting great things. He would deserve far greater commendation if he had undertaken a task which no one had previously attempted with greater diligence, or at least had left it untouched along with the rest. But let us come to the matter itself, for the brevity of the letter does not permit me to wander through empty digressions.”

AURELIUS OF CARTHAGE. He succeeded Genethlius, or Genedius, as is clear from Augustine’s Epistle 163, written in 412. In that letter, however, Genethlius is called “of blessed memory,” although Aurelius was still seated in office and, indeed, presided over the African synod thirteen years later, in 425. Baronius therefore cannot be followed when he substitutes Genethlius for Aurelius.

He would have done better not to follow Baronius at all in saying that the aforementioned Epistle 163 was written by Augustine in 412, when he was traveling to Cirta for a synod. It is certain that the letter was not written after 397, since Ambrose of Milan is mentioned in it as still living. After Augustine had prefaced the following words: “We encountered Fortunius, whom you have as bishop of Thubursicum, through that same city, although as hastily as possible, when we were traveling to the Church of Cirta,” he says:

“I asked him whether he thought Ambrose, bishop of the Church of Milan, was just and Christian. He was obviously forced to deny that the man was Christian and just; for if he admitted it, we would immediately object that he thought Ambrose ought to be rebaptized.”

Thus, if Augustine pressed upon Fortunius, the Donatist bishop, the claim that Ambrose ought to be rebaptized, Ambrose had not yet died in that year—or at least his death was not yet known to Augustine.

That Epistle 163 was given in 397 is plainly gathered from what Augustine writes toward its end: “But because the necessity of ordaining a bishop was already carrying us away from there”—that is, from Thubursicum—“immediately and without delay,” and so forth. He was therefore hurrying to Cirta to ordain Fortunatus there as bishop. I have shown at length in Book II of the *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 8, that Fortunatus was elected that year in the place of the deceased Profuturus. Since you can read those matters there, I have no time to transfer them here.

Moreover, Augustine testifies that he disputed with Fortunius, the Donatist of Thubursicum. But in 411, among the Donatists at the Conference, chapter 201, Januarius, bishop of Thubursicum in Numidia, is named; he had succeeded Fortunius, who had died some time earlier.

NUMIDIUS OF MAXULA. He must have governed the Church of Maxula for a long time, since he held second place as early as 403 and had not yet died in 419. The city of Maxula, now called Massa, is not far from ancient Carthage toward the east.

I praise Garnerius’s correction, who reads *Numidius* instead of *Mundius*. For the rest, I do not know how he learned that Numidius held second place from 403 onward. A synod was held in that year, during the consulship of Theodosius and Rurimundus, at Carthage. At its conclusion only Aurelius is named as having signed first, with the addition: “And likewise the other bishops signed.” The name of Numidius is nowhere heard in that synod; he may perhaps have been absent.

Garnerius could have proved the antiquity of Numidius’s episcopate much more effectively if he had cited the synod summoned by Genethlius in 390, in which we read: “Numidius of Maxula said,” and so forth; and the synod of Aquileia in 381, which Numidius attended as envoy of the Africans.

### RUSTICIANUS OF TABRACA

Tabraca was once a distinguished colony, situated between Hippo and Utica. I do not wish to accuse Charles of Saint-Paul and Holstenius of assigning Tabraca to Numidia; since it lies on the boundary between Numidia and Proconsular Africa, they could, on their own authority, have counted the same city among the churches of the Proconsular province. What cannot be tolerated is that, as you will see below, he says that another Rusticianus was bishop of Tabraca in this very year, 416, and at this very synod. Therefore either this Rusticianus or the other is incorrectly listed as bishop of Tabraca.

### FIDENTIUS OF CAEFALA

It is uncertain which city’s church he governed. In the Collation of the First Day, chapter 133, Fidentius, bishop of the church of Caefala, is praised. That this church belonged to the province of Proconsular Africa ought to have been demonstrated from the synodical letter of the fathers of that same province, inserted into the second session of the Lateran Council celebrated by Pope Saint Martin in the year 649, where Crescens, by the grace of God bishop of Caefala, is recorded as a signatory. Caefala, therefore, was a city of the Proconsular province.

### EVANGELUS OF ASSURIS

In the printed manuscripts Evagrius is read; but the presence of an error is established both because the name Evagrius was not common among Africans, whereas Evangelus was, and because Evangelus of Assuris is mentioned in the Collation. Garnerius had to prove both propositions: that the name Evagrius belonged to no African, and that Evangelus was customary and familiar among Africans. In the list of four hundred bishops in the *Notitia Africae*, not a single Evangelus is named; among the 286 bishops in the Carthaginian Collation, one Evangelus of Assuris is mentioned, just as one Evagrius appears in the heading of the synodical letter.

How, then, does he know that the name Evagrius was not common among Africans, while Evangelus was? Since no Evagrius was named in the Collation, and since he nevertheless wanted to assign a see to the bishop who was subscribed in fifth place, he turned Evagrius into Evangelus. But the corrector’s error is plainly exposed by the Carthaginian Synod of 401, in which, in canon 77 of the African Code, the legates to the city of Hippo Diarrhytus are named in this order: Reginus, Alypius, Augustine, Maternus, Theasius, Evodius, Placianus, Urbanus, Valerius, Ambivius, Fortunatus, Quodvultdeus, Honoratus, Januarius, Aptus, Honoratus, Ampelius, Victorianus, EVANGELUS, and Rogatianus.

Therefore, since Theasius and Ampelius are named after Evagrius in this heading, Evangelus cannot in any way be placed in the position of Evagrius, for Evangelus was later than both of the bishops just mentioned.

### ANTONIUS OF CARPIS

He is mentioned in the Collation of 411; he signed the letter that the African synod sent to Saint Celestine concerning the appeals and the case of Apiarius. Unless Antonius, having returned to life in 425, again assumed the see of Carpis, these statements are far from the truth. For in the Carthaginian Synod, in the case concerning appeals, Penthadius is named as a signatory, bishop of the Church of Carpis, or, as other manuscripts read, Penthadius of Carpis.

But since Antonius is named among the first signatories in the title of the letter to Celestine, why should this not be the same man who is read at the head of the synodical list in 416? Yet he could not have been of Carpis, since in 419 Penthadius occupied the see of Carpis. Another familiar error of this writer must be corrected: later in this Synod of 416 he declares Penthadius to have been bishop of Carpis. Thus either Antonius and Penthadius are placed as co-bishops at Carpis in the same see, or Garnerius was wrong in designating the see of one of them.

### PALATINUS OF BOSSETUM

Palatinus is mentioned in the letter of the African synod to Saint Celestine, and his see is called Bossetum in the Collation. In the heading of the letter to Saint Celestine we read: “Aurelius, Palatinus, Antonius, Tutus, etc.” In this heading, however, Antonius precedes Palatinus. Labbeus therefore correctly observes that Valentinus should be read: he was primate of Numidia in the time of Celestine.

His see is called Vosetum in chapter 202 and Bosetum in chapter 125. From this it is clear that the church belonged to the Proconsular province, although Charles of Saint-Paul and Holstenius assigned it to an uncertain province. Holstenius also erred on page 106 when he called it Visetum; for in 411 Palatinus the Catholic and Felix the Donatist were seated at the church of Bosetum, as chapter 125 of the Collation shows. At Visetum, however, there was Felix the Catholic, who in the same chapter 125 said: “I have no bishop opposed to me.”

### ADEODATUS OF BENCENNA

In the *Notitia* of the bishops expelled from the Proconsular province, mention is made of Gulosus of Beneventum—read Bencenna—who was deported to Corsica. After changing the bishop’s name, he also alters the city’s name, indeed merging two cities into one by transcribing Beneventum as Bencenna.

But that there was a city of Beneventum in Africa I infer, apart from the *Notitia episcoporum*, where Gulosus of Beneventum is read, from the First Synod of Arles, held in 314, which Anastasius of the city of Beneventum attended from Africa together with Caecilianus of Carthage.

Moreover, since Adeodatus of Simidicca from the Proconsular province was present at the same Collation, chapter 135, the assertion that the Adeodatus named sixth in the heading should be called Bencennensis rather than Simidiccensis rests solely on arbitrary judgment—especially since the Church of Bencenna is counted among those assigned to a wholly uncertain province.

### VINCENTIUS OF CULUSITANA

He must have been energetic in practical affairs and vigorous in defending the faith, etc. I know that in the Itinerary of Antoninus, where the coastal road from the mouths of the Ampsaga to Hippo is described, Paratiana, Culusitana, Tacatua, Sullucu, and Hippo are listed. The name Culusitana can mean nothing other than the two Colopes, or at least the smaller one.

Later: should the reading of the manuscripts be corrected, and should Curobitanus be restored in place of the bishop Culusitanus, or Colositanus, after the city of Curobis, situated near Neapolis in the Proconsular province? This controversy, which arises from the variation of a single letter, is immense—but entirely groundless.

For Antoninus does not write that Culusitana lies between Hippo and the mouths of the Ampsaga. On that supposition the city of Culusitana would properly belong to Numidia, since it would be nearer Sitifian Mauretania than the Carthaginian province. [Col. 0275A] Antoninus writes Culucitana, and the Peutinger Tables agree with him, placing Parantiana and Culucitana between Pusicada and Cirta.

Garnerius, however, reads Culusitana, and from this error argues, on Antoninus’s authority, that Culusitana must be located in Numidia. Thus Tacarata is a city of Numidia, and in the *Notitia* Crescentius of Tacarata is praised among the Numidians; Tagarata, however, is in the Proconsular province, where Honoratus of Tagarata is likewise named.

Therefore, although the Culucitani are assigned to Numidia, the Culusitani belong to the Proconsular province. Vincentius is called Culusitanus in chapter 133 of the Collation, and in the subscriptions of the Synod of 419 he is called both Culsitanus and Culusitanus. In the *Notitia* Aemilianus Culsitanus is listed among the Proconsular bishops; in the Synod of Boniface of Carthage in 525, Marcianus Culusitanus; and in the Carthaginian Synod under Gratus, canon 6, Nicasius Culusitanus. Nowhere is Culucitanus read.

Nor should the reading be changed so that the bishop Curobitanus is substituted for Culusitanus. Culusita and Curobis were distinct cities of the Proconsular province. For in the Carthaginian Synod under King Hilderic in 525, the subscriptions include Peregrinus, bishop of the church of Curobis, and Marcianus, bishop of the church of Culusita.

Do you see that Curobis was distinct from Culosita, or Culusita? The same is demonstrated by the Collation itself. In chapter 138 Vincentius of Culusitana said concerning his diocese: “It is Catholic.” But in chapter 198 Victor, bishop of Curobis, is listed among the Donatists. The matter is perfectly clear; only Garnerius could have doubted it.

### PUBLIANUS OF BAZARADIDACA

This is how he is read in the Collation. But since, so far as I know, no mention is made anywhere of such a city, someone might suspect an error and propose Mazaranacensis instead. There is indeed a city of Mazarana in the Proconsular province, between the river Bagradas and the source of the Catada, by which Carthage is watered.

In fact, we have the city of Bazaradidaca from chapter 125 of the Collation. Yet the name of the new city Mazarana occurs nowhere except in the new geography of Garnerius. In the Synod of Saint Cyprian cited by Augustine, *On Baptism*, book VII, chapter 10, Felix of Marazana is named, and in the tables of Charles of Saint-Paul it is written Marazana; Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage, praises the Synod of Marazana in canon 76.

Garnerius’s hallucination is evident here: he thinks that Marazana was situated in the Proconsular province, whereas it belonged to Byzacium. Hence in the *Notitia Africae* Vindicianus of Marazana is listed among the Byzacenians.

This is also proved by Antoninus, who writes that from Aquae Regiae to Marazania there were fifteen miles, and from Marazania to Sufes twenty-eight. Marazana therefore lay between Sufes and Aquae Regiae. That the former cities belonged to Byzacium is established by the aforementioned *Notitia*, in which Liberatus of Aquae Regiae and Eustrasius of Sufes are listed among the Byzacenians.

But the Carthaginian Collation removes all doubt. In chapter 127 Publianus is called bishop of the church of Bazaradidaca, while in chapter 133 Eunomius is called bishop of the church of Marazana. Only fools, therefore, could suspect that the same city is meant, when distinct bishops of the two towns are explicitly asserted in the same work.

From an error in Ortelius’s tables, where Mazarana is read instead of Marazana, he swallowed this mistake, despite so many incontrovertible testimonies against Mazarana.

### THEASIUS OF MEMBRESSA

There can be no doubt that Membressa was an episcopal city; Lucius of Membressa is mentioned in the Carthaginian Council concerning the rebaptizing of heretics, and Salvius of Membressa is mentioned by Augustine, etc.

He stumbled over the same stone again, confusing two cities into one. At the time of the Carthaginian Collation, Membressa, or Membresa, as Augustine and Antoninus write, was distinct from Memblosita. This is obvious from the aforementioned Collation, in which chapter 133 lists Gennadius, bishop of the church of Membressa, and likewise places Theasius, bishop of the church of Memblosita.

In the Synod of Cyprian cited by Augustine, *On Baptism*, book VII, chapter 26, Lucius of Membressa is named; Garnerius considered this city identical with Memblosita. He also argues there that Membressa belonged to the Proconsular province, because Antoninus establishes that the city lay between Mustitana and Sicilibba.

But Mustitana belonged to Numidia, according to the *Notitia Africae*, in which Antonianus of Mustitana is named among the Numidians. If Membressa had lain between two Proconsular cities, he might perhaps have proved what he intended. I am speaking here of the city Mustitana according to the common opinion.

He ought therefore to have demonstrated this from the synodical letter in the second session of the council of Pope Saint Martin, in which Victor of Membressa is praised among the Proconsular bishops, and from the Synod of Boniface of Carthage in 525, subscribed by Paschasius of Membressa.

### TUTUS OF MELDITA

In the Collation it is written Melzitanus, but I think this is erroneous. No one mentions a city of Melzita in the Proconsular province; everyone does mention Meldita, situated by the Hipponian marsh, whose location is described by Ptolemy.

Thus, according to Garnerius, Pliny and the 310 Donatist bishops are all worthless. Pliny, book V, chapter 4, praises in Africa the town of Melzita. The Donatist Synod of Bagai, among the twelve ordainers of Maximianus of Carthage, condemns Valerius of Melzita; see Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book III, chapters 19 and 53.

Therefore chapter 121 of the Collation correctly reads: “Tutus, bishop of the church of Melzita.” Ptolemy should not, however, be criticized for calling this same town Meldita. Among the ancients it was customary to use D for Z, as I have shown at length in book II of my *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 3.

Thus in the same province Antoninus praises Hippo Zarytus, and the Collation, chapter 139, names a bishop of Zarytus, although others call the same city Hippo Diarrhytus.

### PANTHONIUS OF PUPPUT

In the first part of the Collation Pannonius of Pupput is read, but with a double error, since the name Pannonius is unusual among Africans, Panthonius familiar, and the city whose see he held is called Pupput in the Itinerary of Antoninus.

Indeed, this criticism itself suffers from a double error. Since the text of the synodical heading ought to have been corrected from the Collation, he preferred to accuse the text of the Collation of error everywhere. In the manuscript of the most serene grand duke, which will be praised below, Pannonius—not Panthonius—is correctly read in the heading.

But who told him that the name Pannonius was unusual among Africans, while Panthonius was familiar? Besides Pannonius of Pupput, Pannonius of Bita is read among the Caesarean Moors in the *Notitia Africae*. Let him produce even one Panthonius from a corrupt heading, and another from unknown African books; then I shall affirm that Panthonius was a familiar African name, and he will be my great Apollo.

As for his claim that the name should be Pupputanus rather than Puppitanus because the city is called Pupput, Africans could scarcely hear it without indignation—as though this writer knew better than Africans themselves how the names of African cities should be declined.

In chapter 187 of the Collation, Victorianus of Pupput is named among the Donatists, a rival of Pannonius. The synodical letter of the Proconsular bishops, in the second session of the Lateran Council just mentioned, is subscribed by Gulosus of Pupput. In the Synod of Boniface of Carthage in 525, Fortunatus of Pupput is recorded.

Who, then, would say that these bishops did not know how to inflect the name of their own city in Latin?

### VICTOR OF VINA

His name is read in the first part of the Collation. Vina is a city near Pupput. He is merely guessing. Since the title of the letter that he adorns with such learned notes names three Victors, he extracts their sees from the Carthaginian Collation. He calls the first Vinensis, the second Uticensis, and the last Migirpensensis.

I raise no question with Garnerius about this arbitrary arrangement of their sees, although the first could have been Migirpensensis, the last Uticensis, and the middle one Vinensis.

But I would ask him why he omitted three other Victors who are listed in the Collation, and why he wished none of them to be named in the heading just mentioned. Chapter 116 lists Victor of Libertina. That this city belonged to the Proconsular province is clear from the synodical letter of the same province, in the second session of the Lateran Council, where Januarius, by the grace of God bishop of the holy church of Libertina, is named.

Again, in the same Collation, chapter 215, Victor of Abitina is recorded. That he too must be counted among the Proconsular bishops is established by the synodical letter just mentioned, in which Augustalis, by the grace of God bishop of the holy church of Abitina, is named; Cyprian also mentions Saturninus of Abitina.

Finally, a third Victor appears in chapter 133, where Quintus is said to have subscribed on behalf of Victor, bishop of the people of Tuburbo the Lesser. That Tuburbium was in the Proconsular province is shown by the *Notitia Africae*, in which Benenatus of Tuburbium is named; and the Peutinger Tables place both Tuburbia in the Proconsular province.

Why, then, did he exclude these three Victors, who attended the same Collation in 411 together with the three whom he mentions, from the Synod of 416? Why did he admit not even one of them into the synod, but only the bishop of Vina, the bishop of Utica, and the bishop of Migirpa? You see clearly, my Antonius, that Garnerius here acts as a pure and unmitigated guesser.

### RESTITUTUS OF MUZULA

In the Collation Muzucensis is read, but Augustine, *Against the Donatists*, book VII—read book VI—chapter 41, mentions a bishop of Muzula. From the frequently cited *Notitia* I infer that he belonged to the Proconsular province, since Felix of Muzula is listed among the bishops expelled from that province.

The geographer confuses the cities. In the Collation Restitutus is correctly called Muzucensis; his Donatist opponent in chapter 206 is called Idaxius of Muzuca. This city, moreover, was among the Byzacenians; hence Innocentius of Muzuca is listed among the Byzacene bishops in the *Notitia Africae*.

He also guesses in his customary fashion. In chapter 133 of the Collation Restitutus is written “bishop of the church of Simingita.” I infer that this bishop belonged to the Proconsular province from the Synod of Boniface, in which Cresconius is called bishop of the church of Simingita.

Garnerius is therefore wrong when, omitting Restitutus of Simingita from the Proconsular province, he transfers Restitutus of Muzuca from Byzacium to the Proconsular province and turns him into a bishop of Muzula.

### RUSTICUS, OR RATHER RUSTICIANUS OF TABRACA

This is how he is read in the Collation. Tabraca was a colony on the very boundary between the Proconsular province and Numidia, and this caused some authors to place it in Numidia and others in the Proconsular province.

He falls into error unfortunately. Since he found no Rusticus named in the Collation by which to designate this bishop’s see, he changed the same man from Rusticus into Rusticianus. But here he errs shamefully as well: above, he had called the bishop who is listed third after the primate Aurelius in the heading Rusticianus of Tabraca.

Thus, on Garnerius’s authority, in 416 two Catholic bishops named Rusticianus were seated at Tabraca, as though churches—and cities too—were governed by two magistrates at that time.

### FORTUNATIANUS OF NEAPOLIS OR OF SICCA

Two distinguished Fortunatiani existed at that time: one bishop of the Church of Neapolis, the other of the Church of Sicca, both in the Proconsular province, etc. Both undoubtedly attended the African Council of 418. It is uncertain which of them was chosen, together with legates from the other provinces, to settle the cases. Both likewise attended the Universal Council in 419. It is uncertain whose name is placed first in the letter of the Africans to Saint Celestine.

I praise the man’s learning in knowing two Fortunatiani and assigning them to different cities. I had feared that he would place two Fortunatiani in one city, just as he bestowed two Rusticiani on one city. But immediately he stumbles and plunges headlong.

For his statement that both Fortunatiani attended the universal African council in 419 cannot be admitted unless we imagine dead bishops casting votes and delivering judgments. In 419 Urbanus was seated at Sicca, having been substituted in place of the deceased Fortunatianus. The latter, after forbidding Apiarius fire and water the preceding year, and after Apiarius had appealed to Zosimus, was sharply rebuked by the pontiff. From this arose the longer controversies concerning appeals between the Africans and the Roman See.

In the letter of the African synod sent to Pope Boniface in 419 we read: “Our former fellow bishop Urbanus of Sicca, however, without any doubt corrected what had to be corrected in him, namely Apiarius.”

Therefore the one Fortunatianus who attended the African synods of 418 and 419 was Fortunatianus of Neapolis; the one Neapolitan was chosen to settle cases together with the legates of the other provinces; and the same man is placed at the head of the letter to Pope Saint Celestine.

Meanwhile, most illustrious sir, observe Garnerius’s confidence: he emphatically declares that the Fortunatianus of Sicca undoubtedly attended the synods just mentioned, although by that time he had undoubtedly died and Urbanus, a bishop from the clergy of Hippo, had succeeded him in the same see. Saint Augustine writes about the beginning of Urbanus’s episcopate in Letter 59 to Paulinus of Nola.

### RESTITUTUS OF CINCARI

In the Collation a bishop of this name and see is read; it is highly credible that he is the very man under discussion.

Here too he guesses. Restitutus, bishop of the church of Simingita, was also present at the Collation, chapter 133. In the Council of Boniface in 525, Cresconius, bishop of the church of Simingita, is praised among the Proconsular bishops.

Charles of Saint-Paul and Holstenius assign the Church of Cincari to an uncertain province, and Garnerius offers nothing in support of his position. I nevertheless think that this church belonged among the Proconsular churches. For in the synodical letter in the second session of the council of Pope Saint Martin, Quobulus of Ceciri is named among the bishops of that same province; this may perhaps be the same church as Cincari.

### AMPELIUS

His see is uncertain. For Ampelius, who is mentioned in canon 78 of the African Code, whose see in the Collation is said to have been Vaga, or rather Vada, and who is recorded as having spoken in chapter 176, seems to have been one of the Numidians, etc.

Accordingly, the text of the Collation should also be corrected further, in chapter 215, where two Catholic bishops are called bishops of Vaga: Ampelius and Primulus. It should be read Vadensis. He did not know that there were two Vagas in Africa, and so he insists that one city should be called Vada.

But Pliny, who knew the African cities better, in book V, chapter 4, names one Vaga among the fifteen towns of Roman citizens and another Vaga among the thirty free towns. He deliberately added “another” in order to distinguish the two Vagas. One had been granted Latin rights; the other was a free municipality.

From this he wrongly concludes that the Collation must be corrected, although it asserts that there were two Vagas. These towns, which are called Vaga in the Collation, are both called Vada in the *Notitia of Numidia*, where Rufinianus of Vada and Proficius of Vada are listed.

Indeed, a third Vaga is also placed in the same Collation. For when Privatus, bishop of Vaga, had been named in chapter 177, Rogatus the bishop said: “He is called Januarianus, not Privatus.” But Primianus, the primate of the Donatists of the Carthaginian province, replied in chapter 179: “There is Auzagga, where Januarianus was, who has now died; and another Auzagga, where Privatus is, who is now alive.”

It is clear that these Vagas were distinguished by the additional name Auzagga, so that they might be distinguished from the Vaga where Ampelius was seated.

Besides the two Vagas that Pliny places in Africa—that is, in the province of Zeugitana—Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 2, also places a Vaga among the inland cities of Caesarean Mauretania. Its location is shown by the ancient Peutinger Tables and by the more recent tables of Charles of Saint-Paul.

The Ampelius mentioned in canon 78 of the African Code is not the same as the Ampelius named here. The former was later than Ambivius of Pisitum, as is clear there; the latter preceded him, as I shall show immediately below.

### [Col. 0280A] ANIMUS

Unless the reading is corrupt—which someone might nevertheless reasonably suspect because of the unusualness of the word—the church of this bishop must be pronounced unknown.

If the reading is corrupt, someone might suspect that Timianus should be restored in place of Animus. As the Collation states, Timianus governed the Church of the city of Utina, which Ptolemy places below Carthage near the river Bagradas.

If he suspected a corrupt reading, why did he not consult an ancient manuscript? A letter of this Carthaginian synod survives in the manuscript of the library of the most serene grand duke, at Saint Laurence, shelf 12. There Animus is not read, but AMBIBIUS, who is called Ambivius in the rescript of Pope Innocent.

In chapter 133 of the Collation he is called, among the Catholic fathers, Ambibius, bishop of the church of Pisitum. Evodius of Uzalum, a disciple of Saint Augustine, mentions the city of Pisitum in book I of *The Miracles of Saint Stephen*, chapter 13.

Charles of Saint-Paul omitted the Church of Ambivius; Holstenius assigned it to an uncertain province and incorrectly distinguished it from Pisitum, although from this heading it can be inferred that it was in the Proconsular province.

Ambivius is mentioned in canon 78 of the African Code, where he is named before Evangelus, whom Garnerius substituted for Evagrius, as you have seen, but incorrectly. For in the aforementioned code Evagrius is named, and in place of Mundius, as the printed manuscripts corruptly have it, Nimidius is correctly read there.

Garnerius searched for the heading in no manuscripts. Yet, because of the booklets of Marius Mercator copied by someone else from the Vatican manuscripts—ah, what tragedies he raises at the end of his work, and into which ones!—

### FELIX OF UZITTA

In the Collation Vizicensis is read, but in the *Notitia* of the bishops of the Proconsular province mention is made of Caius of Uzitta, who is said to have died before reaching the place of exile; and the city of Uzitta is placed in the Ptolemaic Tables near Hadrumetum and Ruspinum.

Since these two cities were in Byzacium, Uzitta of Ptolemy must likewise be located in the same province. Aulus Hirtius clearly reports the location of the town of Uzitta in his book *On the Civil War in Africa*, where he says that Caesar pitched camp near Uzitta, six miles from the port of Leptis Minor.

Leptis was in Byzacium, above Hadrumetum toward Tripoli, eighteen miles away, according to Antoninus. From this it follows that the *Notitia* should read Caius of Ucita, not of Uzitta. The former church was in Byzacium; Ucita, however, was in the Proconsular province, in the synodical letter of whose bishops, in the second session of the Lateran Council, Tripolius of Ucita is praised—from the city of Uci, as I shall show below in the notes on FRUCTUOSUS.

Therefore he wrongly changes the Church of Visetum into that of Uzitta. In chapter 125 of the Collation it is written: “Felix, bishop of the church of Visetum.” I infer that this church belonged to the Proconsular province from the same synodical letter, where Valentinianus, bishop of the holy church of Usica, is counted among the Proconsular bishops.

This city was near Tabora, whose Donatist bishop Victor said to Felix of Visetum in the cited chapter 125: “I intervene on your behalf.” In chapter 201 the same Victor says: “I had indeed received the mandate; but because our most blessed father and primate Primianus has now received it, I must commit the matter to these acts.”

He was therefore a bishop in the Proconsular province, since he calls Primianus of Carthage his primate. In the dissertation *On Synod V*, chapter 10, I wrongly confused the Tabora of the Donatist Victor with another Tabora in Mauretania.

Tabora should therefore be added to the tables of the Proconsular bishops of Charles of Saint-Paul and Holstenius.

As for the see of this Felix, Garnerius is guessing. In chapter 127 of the Collation Felix, bishop of the church of Aptunga, is praised. Aptunga was in the Proconsular province, and another Felix of Aptunga had once consecrated Caecilianus of Carthage, as is found throughout Optatus, book I, Augustine’s Letters 68, 162, and 163, and his books against the Donatists.

Thus, omitting Felix of Aptunga, he arbitrarily brings Felix of Visetum into the Synod of 416.

### DONATIANUS OF ZEGGA OR ZELLA

In the Collation Donatianus of Zella is listed. In the *Notitia* of the Proconsular province mention is made of Vincentius of Zegga, expelled into exile.

He is stuck in the same mire, confusing Zigga with Zella. Zella was in Byzacium. For Strabo, listing the towns of this province in book XVII, says: “Nearby also were Zella and Achola, free cities.”

In the Peutinger Tables Achola is placed between the cities of Thapsus and Ruspa, in Byzacium; in the *Notitia* of that province Restitutus of Achola is listed. Ferrandus the deacon praises the Council of Zella; I have shown in book I of my *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 13, that it is wrongly called Telepte.

But Ziggera was a city in the Proconsular province, whose *Notitia* lists Vincentius of Zigga. Garnerius called him Zeggensis so that he could more easily turn him into one of Zella.

In the acts of Felix’s purification before the proconsul of Africa, at the end of Albaspinaeus’s edition of Optatus, Ingentius, decurion of the people of Ziga, is mentioned. As is clear there, this city was in the Proconsular province.

In the letters of the emperor Constantine, cited by Augustine in Letter 68 and in book III of *Against Cresconius*, chapter 70, the same man is called a decurion of the city of Ziga. Victor of Vita also mentions Mount Ziga in *On the Vandal Persecution*.

### ADEODATUS OF SIMITTU

He attended the Collation in 411 and in 419 was one of the ten legates of the Proconsular province who reviewed and subscribed the canons of the African Church together with legates from the other provinces.

Here again he confuses bishops and cities. Adeodatus, who reviewed the canons in 419, was bishop of Simittu, not of Simidicca. The subscriptions of the synod held at Carthage in 419 are preserved by Labbeus, where Adeodatus is called Simittuensis or Simitensis.

The town of Simittu is praised by Pliny, book V, chapter 3; Antoninus calls it Simittu. In chapter 135 of the Collation Benenatus is listed as bishop of the church of Simittu, and Adeodatus as bishop of the church of Simidicca.

Therefore Adeodatus, who reviewed the canons in 419, was not yet a bishop in 411, since Benenatus held the see of Simittu. The same is clearly shown by the subscription of the synod of 419, where we read: “Penthadius of Carpis, Adeodatus of Simittu.”

Adeodatus was therefore later in time as a bishop than Penthadius. For the Africans assigned names to synods and recorded them in the official registers according to the time at which the episcopate was conferred, as is clear from canon 53 of the African Code and Augustine’s Letter 217 to Victorianus.

Again, it is certain that Penthadius was not bishop of Carpis in 411, since in chapter 125 Antonius is listed as bishop of the church of Carpis.

From this we conclude that Adeodatus of Simittu was different from the Adeodatus of Simidicca who attended the Collation in 411, and that Simittu and Simidicca were different cities, since at the time of the Collation Adeodatus was exercising supreme ecclesiastical authority in one, while Benenatus was doing so in the other.

### OCTAVIUS OF UTHINA

He attended the Collation. Uthina is a city in the Proconsular province near the river Bagradas, according to the Ptolemaic Tables. In the Carthaginian Council, etc., Felix of Uthina delivered his opinion in twenty-seventh place, and Lampadius of Uthina subscribed to the Second Council of Arles.

He goes astray along the same line, confusing Utinuna with Uthina. In chapter 133 of the Carthaginian Collation, in the editions of Masson and Albaspinaeus, Octavius is read as “bishop of the church of Utinuna.”

I know that there were two Utinas in Africa. At the time of the Collation, chapter 125 reads: “Timianus, bishop of the church of Utina”; but chapter 133 has Isaac, “bishop of the church of Uthina.”

Therefore, if Octavius was likewise bishop of Utina, we must either posit a third Utina in Africa or place Octavius over Timianus or Isaac as their colleague. Isaac the Catholic bishop was opposed by Felicianus; Felix the Donatist bishop opposed Timianus.

But concerning Octavius I shall report the complete text from the Carthaginian Collation:

“Octavius, bishop of the church of Utinuna, before the distinguished man Marcellinus, tribune and notary, I previously gave and subscribed the mandate at Carthage.”

Therefore he said: “Bonifacius is opposed to me.” Thus, from three Catholic bishops and an equal number of Donatist adversaries, we find in Africa two Utinas and an Utinuna.

You should also note, most learned sir, that when he adds that Uthina was situated by the river Bagradas according to Ptolemy, Garnerius had said the same thing seventeen lines earlier about the other Utina, where Timianus was seated.

Ptolemy, in fact, places only one Utina. If our geographer places Octavius’s Uthina and Timianus’s other city by the Bagradas, he cannot in any way cite Ptolemy’s testimony for both.

Holstenius writes that one or the other Uthina should be written with aspiration, and indeed in Augustine, *On Baptism*, book VI, chapter 33, Felix of Uthina is recorded.

I omit the fact that he says there that Lampadius of Uthina subscribed to the Second Council of Arles. He meant the First Council, convened in the first year of Sylvester, 314.

Bonifacius, Octavius’s adversary, is called Utummensis in chapter 198; which of the two texts contains the error is uncertain.

### SEROTINUS OF THURUZITA

He attended the Collation. Ptolemy places Thursa near the colony of Vina, not far from Tunizza and therefore not very far from Carthage.

It is not written this way in the Collation. Chapter 133 lists Serotinus as “bishop of the church of Turuzita.” According to Garnerius alone, this inflection is derived from Ptolemy’s Thursa.

Certainly students who declined the adjective from Thursa as Thuruzitanus would be beaten; the adjective derives from Thuruzita. Ptolemy is therefore wrongly summoned as a witness.

Indeed, Thursa is nowhere read in Ptolemy, but only Thurza, which he places in Byzacium near Hadrumetum.

It is more correctly demonstrated from the Collation itself that Thuruzita was in the Proconsular province. When Serotinus the bishop said that he had no opposing bishop, Habetdeus, deacon of Primianus, the primate of Carthage, replied: “Cattus is presbyter there.”

This deacon frequently intervened when Proconsular bishops were under discussion, as is evident throughout that work, although I grant that once or twice he also spoke about others.

### MAJORINUS OF ZEMPTA

This is how he is read in the Collation; Zamensis would be better, since there was a city of Zama in the Proconsular province, if we believe Pliny, Ptolemy, and Strabo.

As many words, so many errors. In chapter 133 of the Collation Majorinus is praised as “bishop of the church of Zenta.” And correctly so: for in the synodical letter of the Proconsular bishops, in the second session of the Lateran Council, Florentius, by the grace of God bishop of the holy church of Zenta, is mentioned.

This excellent testimony proves that Zentensis is correctly written in the Collation, that Zemptensis is read incorrectly, and that Zenta was among the Proconsular cities.

Again, the fact that he changes Zenta into Zama can scarcely be endured. In chapter 121 of the Collation Dialogus is called bishop of Zama, and his adversary Montanus is listed as one of the seven Donatist collators.

Therefore it was not Majorinus but Dialogus who was bishop of Zama in 411.

### POSTUMIANUS OF TAGORA

Of an unknown see; for the man called Tagorensis in the *Collation* is different from this one. For the city Tagora, or Tagura, is in Numidia, not likewise in Proconsular Africa; and among the bishops from Numidia sent into exile, Timotheus Tagurensis is listed. He did not know that there were two Tagoras in Africa, although he could have understood this from the *Collation*, in which, among the Catholic prelates, Restitutus, bishop of Tagora, took part—he was keeper of the records, chapter 143—and Posthumianus, bishop of the church of Tagora, chapter 133. Therefore Posthumianus, who is listed in the heading, was bishop of Tagora in the province of Proconsular Africa.

I infer that Tagora existed in this province from the Peutinger Table, where the following is read: “Thacora 5, Gegetu [supply 15, from Antoninus, cited immediately below], Narragara 12, Sicca Veneria 30.” Antoninus writes the following in the itinerary from Musti to Cirta: “Sicca 32, Naraggara 30, Tagora 20, Tipasa 34.”

It is certain that Tipasa belonged to Numidia, for Rusticus Tipasensis is named in the register of that province. Carolus a Sancto Paulo and Holstenius assigned Naraggara, neighboring Tipasa, to Numidia, but wrongly; for Benenatus, bishop “by the grace of God of the holy Church of Narragara,” subscribed the synodical letter of the Proconsular bishops, act 2 of the Lateran council, and in the register Maximinus Maraggaritanus is listed among the Proconsular bishops, where *Naraggaritanus* must plainly be read. In the *Collation*, among the Donatists, chapter 207, Faustinus is also listed as bishop of Naraggara.

Beyond Naraggara, toward Numidia, lies Gegetu. Moreover, it is clear that this city too was within the diocese of the Proconsular bishops from Victor of Vita, who in book I of *The Vandal Persecution* names among the Proconsular bishops Vincentius Gigitanus. Thus Tagora, five miles distant from Gegetu, was the last city of the Carthaginian province, bordering on Tipasa; at the time of the *Collation* Posthumianus administered its church, and afterward, in the year 416, subscribed the sentence against the Pelagians. Tagora in Numidia was also called Tagura, as is clear from the *Notitia of Africa*.

### CRISPOLUS OF VOLITUM

In the commonly circulated manuscripts *Trispolus* is read, but the unusualness of the name itself reveals the error; therefore it must be corrected from the *Collation*. Here he rightly corrects the initial letter. In the manuscript of the Most Serene Grand Duke, *Crispolus* is read both in the heading of the synodical letter and in the rescript of Innocent.

### VICTOR OF UTICA

Certainly not the author of the books *On the Vandal Persecution*, initiated by Huneric against the Catholics in the year 484, but another man of the same name and see, who was at Carthage when the *Collation* was held.

Victor, who lived under Huneric and wrote the books *On the Vandal Persecution*, was not bishop of Utica but of Vita, as Chiffletius and Holstenius have admirably demonstrated from manuscripts. This is also proved by the list of bishops deported by Huneric into exile; among the Proconsular bishops Florentinus Uticensis is named, while among the Byzacene bishops appears Victor Vitensis, who wrote the books *On the Vandal Persecution*. You will read more on this matter in Chiffletius, whose volume, like many others, you have more than once lent me from that extremely extensive library of yours.

### VICTOR OF MIGIRPA

So it is read in the *Collation*, etc. Here, as with the preceding Victor, he returns to his customary conjectures. Three other Victors from the province of Proconsular Africa took part in the *Collation*: Libertinensis, Abitinensis, and Tuburbitanus. Does he suppose that these men died within five years, while the bishops of Migirpa and Utica survived, so that only these two—and none of the other three—could have attended the synod convened at Carthage in 416 against the Pelagians? But a man who found it easy to change, confuse, and invent cities at will considered it no matter at all to admit bishops to synods as he pleased and to exclude them as he pleased.

### LUCIUS OF TAGARATA

His name is listed in the *Collation*. The *Notitia of the bishops of the province of Proconsular Africa* mentions a bishop of Tagarata, for it reports that Honoratus Tagaratensis was driven into exile. I cannot but add my white counters [a mark of approval].

### MARIANUS OF UZIPPIRA

He is named in the *Collation*. The *Notitia of the bishops of the province of Proconsular Africa* mentions Augentius Uzipparitanus, expelled into exile. In most printed manuscripts *Macianus* is read, but the manuscript of the Laurentian Library supports Garnerius. In the Peutinger Table, Usippira is placed above Putput, in the interior toward the south. In the synod of Boniface Sementius is called Uzipparensis. Marianus was one of the Proconsular legates at the council of 419.

### FRUCTUOSUS OF ABZIRITA

So it is read in the *Collation*, although perhaps *Abderitensis* or *Abbiritensis* should be read. For Ptolemy mentions Abdera in Africa Proper, that is, in the province of Proconsular Africa, since he places it below Carthage; and the *Notitia of the province of Proconsular Africa* mentions Felix, bishop of Abarita.

This Fructuosus, however, cannot have survived for long; for in 419 Candidus Abbaritanus is listed among the legates of the province of Proconsular Africa. In the subscriptions he is nevertheless called “of Germanica,” but erroneously; for Germania, whether Old or New, belongs to Numidia, if any credence is to be given to the frequently cited *Notitia*, in which Felix, bishop of Abarita, is mentioned.

He has little knowledge of African geography, since he confuses the city of Abzirita with Abbirita. In chapter 128 of the *Collation*, Fructuosus is called bishop of the church of Abzirita. Pliny, book V, chapter 4, praises the town of Abzirita in Africa. In Ptolemy this city is called Abdera, for I have shown above that D is frequently substituted for Z. In the synod of Genethlius in 390, Victor Abziritanus and Abderitanus are read in different manuscripts.

Furthermore, two cities in Africa were still counted whose bishops were called Abbiritenses. For in chapter 215 of the aforementioned *Collation* Annibonius Abbiritensis is listed; but in chapter 133, Felix is called bishop of Abbirmajus. This city was so called in order to distinguish it from Abbirminus, where Annibonius sat; for the Africans used the terms *majus* and *minus* to distinguish two cities of the same name. Thus among them we find Leptiminus, that is, Lesser Leptis; and in the *Notitia*, among the Byzacene bishops, Fortunatianus Leptiminensis. Pliny likewise lists two towns called Ucita, Greater and Lesser; and chapter 133 of the *Collation* mentions Octavianus, bishop of the church of Ucimajus.

Therefore the same *Collation* of 411 included Fructuosus Abziritensis, Felix Abbirmajus, and Annibonius Abbirminus. In the synodical letter of the Proconsular bishops, act 2 of the Lateran council, the bishops Adeodatus Abbiritanus and Victorinus Abziritanus are named. It is not surprising that Garnerius confused their cities into one, since neither Carolus a Sancto Paulo nor Holstenius precisely distinguished them.

But further errors of Garnerius must also be corrected. It is false that Candidus succeeded Fructuosus; for Candidus was bishop of Abbiritensis, not Abziritensis. Thus it is read in the subscription of the synod convened at Carthage in 419: “Candidus, bishop of Abbiritensis Germanicianorum,” in Labbe, volume II of the *Councils*, page 1670. And rightly so; for Augustine, book VI *On Baptism*, chapter 23, names at the synod of Cyprian “Successus from Abbir Germaniciana.” If Garnerius had read *Germaniciae* instead of *Germaniae* in the better manuscripts, he would have corrected the text more accurately.

But nothing could be more obvious than the same author’s hallucination when he says that Fructuosus did not long survive the year 416 because Candidus was sitting in Fructuosus’s see in 419. When the discussion of Candidus arises below, I shall demonstrate the point; for he imagines both men present at this synod.

### QUODVULTDEUS OF VERES

He was one of the ten legates of the province of Proconsular Africa who, together with the legates of the other provinces, reviewed the canons in 419 in the name of the whole African synod.

That is not so. This Quodvultdeus was already a bishop before 411, for he is named before Thomas Cubdensis, who took part in the *Collation*. But Quodvultdeus Verensis obtained his bishopric after 411, since in the subscriptions of 419 he is placed after Penthadius Carpitana. I insert here the fragment that bears most directly on the matter:

> I, Penthadius, bishop of the church of Carpis, subscribed.  
> I, Ruffianus, bishop of the church of Maxa, subscribed.  
> I, Praetextatus, bishop of the church of Sicilibba, subscribed.  
> I, Quodvultdeus, bishop of the church of Veres, subscribed.  
> I, Candidus, bishop of the church of Abbiritensis Germanicianorum, subscribed.

In 411 Antonius was sitting at Carpis; Penthadius was substituted for him, according to chapter 125 of the repeatedly mentioned *Collation*. This same Quodvultdeus is also placed in the heading before Candorius Mullitensis, who took part in the *Collation*. Therefore he was plainly different from Quodvultdeus Verensis.

### CANDORIUS OF MULLITA

He is counted among the bishops who were at Carthage at the time of the *Collation*. Among the expelled Proconsular bishops, the *Notitia* has Liberatus Mullitanus. At last Garnerius, not without care and labor, has managed to discover something.

### MAXIMUS AND MEGARIUS

Their sees are unknown. But the sees of others were scarcely better known to him.

### RUFINUS OF DRUSILIANA

Although this is how it is read in the *Collation*, I think *Dinisianensis*, or rather *Dionisianensis*, should be read; for a bishop of this name is listed in the Carthaginian council of the rebaptizers, number 48. Is this not the see that is corruptly read in the *Notitia of the province of Proconsular Africa* as *Duassendelmai*?

These things cannot be heard without laughter. He wanders from the beginning of the book to its end. Read, my dear Antonius, the heading: you will see that not Rufinus but Rusticus is named. Thus, because two Rustici are written in the heading, Garnerius makes the first *Rusticianus* and changes the second into Rufinus. Since he cannot find Rusticus among the two hundred and eighty-six bishops who gave their names to the *Collation*, with a sufficiently urbane device he foists Rufinus upon us in place of Rusticus.

Moreover, in chapter 121 of the *Collation* Rufinus is called bishop of the church of Drusiliana. But eager for metamorphoses, he converts not only the bishop but also Drusiliana, his see, into another, saying: “I nevertheless think *Dinisianensis* should be read.” Do you think he wrote this seriously or jokingly? Where in the world—not merely in Africa, but anywhere—did a bishopric of Dinisiana appear?

But observe how he immediately overthrows, with another stroke of the pen, the same city of Dinisiana that he had suddenly raised up: “Or rather,” he says, “*Dionisianensis*.” Yet he wrongly confuses the church of Drusiliana with Dionysiana. The former belongs to the Proconsular province, as is clear from the Peutinger Table; the latter belongs to Byzacena, for among the sees of Byzacena that were without bishops in 484, Dionysiana is listed in the *Notitia of Africa*.

It is also plainly evident from the *Collation* that these were different cities. In chapter 187 Restitutus, bishop of Drusiliana, is listed among the Donatist bishops who took part in the *Collation*; and in chapter 198 Victor is listed as bishop of Dionysiana. Thus Drusiliana and Dionysiana were distinct cities in distinct provinces, over which distinct Donatist bishops presided. The new geographer, however, confuses them into one, transferring the latter from Byzacena into the Proconsular province without any machinery.

Nor was he satisfied with these changes. After turning Drusiliana into Dinisiana and then into Dionysiana, he finally builds a new city out of the ruins of all these demolished cities: “Is it not,” he says, “that see which is corruptly read in the *Notitia of the province of Proconsular Africa* as *Duassendelmai*?”

No: he himself reads it corruptly. For the cited *Notitia* does not say *Duassendelmai* but *Duassedemsai*. It names Mannucius Duassedemsai; and since his see is placed in the Proconsular province, it cannot be the same as Dionysiana, which the same *Notitia* locates in Byzacena.

Moreover, I think the church of Duassedemsai is the same one that is called Assenemsalensis in chapter 202 of the *Collation*. There Fortunatianus Assenemsalensis is listed among the Donatists; and in the synod of Boniface, Patronianus Senemsalensis is placed among the Proconsular bishops. Julianus, “by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of the two Senepsalitanae,” subscribed the synodical letter of the Proconsular bishops, act 2 of the Lateran synod.

You therefore have, in four lines, so many errors of this recent geographer—errors that he perhaps thought should be added to the *Reformed Geography* that someone—you know the man—has published.

### RUFIANUS OF MAXA

He is called Muzucensis in the *Collation*; he was one of the ten delegates from the province of Proconsular Africa in 419 appointed to review the canons, etc. He thought he was writing for the blind and the barbers when he inserted so many monstrous fictions into his pages.

He is mistaken when he writes that Rufianus is called Muzucensis in the *Collation*. He is called neither Rufianus nor Muzucensis, but in chapter 127 he is named Rufinianus Muzuensis. Muzu was in the Proconsular province, and among those expelled from that province into exile by Huneric Felix Muzuensis is listed. In the same *Collation*, chapter 133, Restitutus is called bishop of Muzucensis.

Finally, in the subscriptions cited above from the year 419, Penthadius—who was elected bishop of Carpis after 411—subscribes before Ruffianus Maxensis. Therefore this man was not yet a bishop in 411 and did not take part in the *Collation*, since in this heading he is placed before Penthadius and Thomas Cubdensis.

### PROCULIANUS

Either his see is unknown, or—and this is what I rather think—one should read “Proculus Ginesitensis of Salaria,” whose name is found in the *Collation*. For in the *Notitia of the bishops of the province of Proconsular Africa*, Carissimus Gisipensis is read, expelled into exile. I have no doubt that Ginesitensis is the same as Gisipensis.

I fear that so many metamorphoses may cause you nausea and weariness, most learned sir, and that I may become subject to no slight reproach for interrupting you in your more serious studies, to which you devote care day and night, in order to make you read these wholly fabulous matters. You know that Cato, after the most difficult deliberations of the senate, turned his mind to running and playing with boys. I, for my part, display from time to time the transformations of men, cities, and provinces, just as happens on the stage. In the meantime, refresh yourself and rest your eyes and ears, for new appearances of things are coming into view.

Here Proculianus is turned into Proculus, and Gisipa migrates into the city of Ginesita. A man’s name is usually changed through fraud or design, when by adoption people are transferred into other families; but Garnerius alone has attempted to insert cities into other cities.

How unsuccessfully—or, not to speak too mildly, how incompetently—may be gathered from chapter 133 of the *Collation*, in which Proculus is named bishop of the church of Ginesita of Salaria; and from chapter 135, where Januarianus is listed as bishop of the church of Gisipensis.

And yet, although the distinction between the two cities appears clearer than daylight, Garnerius confidently exclaims: “I have no doubt that Ginesitensis is the same as Gisipensis.” Add also that the name Proculianus was familiar among the Africans. For the bishop who remained in the Hipponian diocese, in the party of Donatus, against Augustine, was called Proculianus; a letter was addressed to him among Augustine’s letters, number 147, and he is also mentioned in letter 168. I admit, however, that the Laurentian manuscript reads *Proculus*. Yet in chapter 135 there is also a Proculus Serrensis.

### THOMAS

The silence concerning this name is everywhere remarkable, except that Leo the Great wrote to Thomas, an African bishop. But it is incredible that this Thomas of ours should have lived so long. If he had said this while present at the *Collation*, I would have declared him deaf; for in chapter 133 Thomas, bishop of the church of Cubda, is named in a loud voice by the Officer, and he also replied: “On the other side, we have no one [against him].”

Garnerius could have learned that this church belonged to the Proconsular province from the synodical letter, act 2 of the council of Saint Martin the pope, which Gentilis, “by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Cubda,” subscribed.

It may seem extraordinary to you that this writer did not see Thomas where he was actually present—in the *Collation*—but found this same man where he plainly was not, namely, in a letter of Saint Leo the Great. Leo the Great sent only one surviving letter to Africa: letter 87, addressed to the bishops of Caesarean Mauretania, in which no Thomas is named.

Meanwhile, I cannot but lament Garnerius’s utter, monstrous, and supine delusion. Not content with confusing African cities and bishops, he substitutes Leo the Great for Leo IX. Among the letters of Leo IX there is a third bearing this heading: “To Thomas, bishop of Africa”; yet he pretends that it was written by Leo the Great.

We therefore readily grant that it is incredible that the Thomas named in this heading should have lived so long. For from the time when the letters from the Apostolic See were written to Thomas, bishop of Africa, 633 years had elapsed; the first year of Leo IX was the year 1049 of our era. What if he had seen another Thomas, African bishop, in book II of Victor’s *On the Vandal Persecution*?

### JANUARIUS OF TIMIDA

In the *Collation* *Tunudensis* is read, but it plainly seems—note the confidence of the assertion—that *Timidensis* should be read throughout. For there was no city Tunuda in the Proconsular province, but Timida, which is sometimes called Regia.

He serves up the same stale dish again. Meanwhile, listen to what the same author writes in his notes on VINCENTIUS CULUSITANUS concerning the Proconsular cities: “For we scarcely know more than sixty-eight churches of that province, and not even those in known locations, although there were one hundred and sixty-four, if any credence is to be given to Victor of Vita.”

Why, then, was Tunuda not one of the nearly hundred that are unknown? It could nevertheless have belonged to another African province; for Tunuda is assigned by ecclesiastical geographers to an uncertain province.

In the Peutinger Table, within the Proconsular province, one reads: “Utica 20, Thunu 7, Maxula 21.” Perhaps the church of Thunudensis was named from Thunu. In the Ptolemaic Tables it is called Tunuba, where there is only a one-letter variation from the text of the *Collation*. Pliny, book IV, chapter 5, also praises the town of Tunudis in the Proconsular province.

From these sources Garnerius could have demonstrated the church in question more easily and plausibly than by converting it into Timidensis without evidence. Since no Timidensis is named among the Donatists, it follows with some clarity that this was a Catholic church—for Donatist bishops were rare in the Proconsular province, as Petilianus testifies in chapter 165 of the *Collation*—and that its bishop did not come to the synod. Unless it was one of the sixty-four Catholic churches that at the time of the *Collation* lacked bishops, no new bishops yet having been substituted for those who had died, as is stated in chapter 215 of the same *Collation*.

### OCTAVIANUS OF RESSA

So it is read in the *Collation*. By this extremely brief note he thinks he has made the matter plain to the eye. But he is mistaken when he counts the bishop of Ressanensis among the Proconsular bishops; he must be placed among the Numidian bishops, for in the *Notitia of Africa* Vigilius Ressanensis is listed among the Numidians.

This can also be gathered from the *Collation* itself, for in chapter 121 the following is written:

> Aspidius, bishop of the church of Tacarata.  
> The same man said: “I am present.”  
> Verissimus, the Donatist bishop, said: “I recognize him: there are four in my church—Datianus, Aspidius, Fortunatus, and Octavianus.”

Tacarata was in Numidia, and therefore Crescentius Tacaratensis is also listed there in the *Notitia*. Datianus was bishop of Leges, according to chapter 121; Octavianus was of Ressanensis. Those three dioceses were neighboring dioceses within Numidia. Octavianus Ressanensis, therefore, belongs to Numidia.

Garnerius nevertheless did not notice that in the same *Collation* there was another Octavianus, a Proconsular bishop: Octavianus, bishop of the church of Ucimajus, as chapter 133 records. The Pliny mentioned above listed two Ucitan towns, Greater and Lesser; and in the synodical letter of the Proconsular bishops, act 2 of the Lateran council, Tripolius, “by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Ucita,” is named. Therefore this man may have been Octavianus, bishop of Ucimajus.

### PRAETEXTATUS OF SICILIBBA

He was one of the ten legates of the province of Proconsular Africa who, together with the others from the other provinces, reviewed the canons in 419 in the name of the whole African synod.

Nor does he correctly conjecture this bishop’s see. Praetextatus was prelate of Sicilibra, or Sicilibba, and was later in rank than Penthadius Carpitana; for in the subscriptions of the synod cited by Garnerius he is placed after Penthadius, as is clear from the three subscriptions in Labbe, volume II of the *Councils*, pages 1168, 1669, and 1670, one example of which we gave above. But this Praetextatus is placed before Penthadius, since he is listed third in the heading by the same author.

I must reject here the opinion of Holstenius, who on page 36 writes that Cilibis was the same city as Sicilibba. For in the same *Collation*, among the Donatists, Quadratianus, bishop of Sicilibba, took part in chapter 198, and Tertullus, bishop of Ciliba, in chapter 206. In the synod of Boniface in 525, Restitutus Cilibiensis is named among the Proconsular bishops. Neither church appears in the *Notitia of Africa*. Carolus a Sancto Paulo, on page 114, assigned the bishopric of Cilibis to an uncertain province, although it belonged to the Carthaginian province.

### SEXTUS

His see is unknown. In the manuscript of the Laurentian Library *Sixtus* is read, but he is nowhere mentioned in the ancient records of Africa.

### QUODVULTDEUS OF GIVIRTA

Perhaps it should be read this way; for a bishop of the same name and see is mentioned in the *Collation*, yet the see of Givirta is not found elsewhere among the sees of the Proconsular province.

Certainly Garnerius did not read the subscriptions of the synod of Boniface of Carthage in Labbe, volume IV of the *Councils*, page 1640. For that synod was subscribed by Vincentius, bishop of the church of Gervita, legate of the province of Tripolitana. Therefore the see of Givirta lay outside the boundaries of the Proconsular province—indeed beyond Byzacena—and belonged to the Tripolitan province.

### PENTHADIUS OF CARPIS

He was one of the ten chosen from the province of Proconsular Africa to review the canons in 419. You see this writer imagining that two bishops of Carpis sat together and gave their names to the same synodical letter in 416. For above he had called Antonius, who is listed sixth in this heading, bishop of Carpis; now he makes Penthadius his colleague in that see.

### QUODVULTDEUS

His see is unknown. He should more correctly have called him Verensis, since he is read as subscribing after Penthadius in the synod of 419.

### CYPRIANUS OF TUBURBUS

So it is read in the *Collation*. Tuburbus, or Tuburbo, is a city in the province of Proconsular Africa; it was formerly a colony known to Pliny and Ptolemy. Antoninus mentions the same city in the itinerary from Hippo Regius to Carthage, placing it between Cluacaria and Cigisa.

He confuses two Tuburbitan cities into one. For chapter 133 of the *Collation* names Victor, bishop of Lesser Tuburbo; and chapter 135 names Cyprianus, bishop of the church of Greater Tuburbo. Victor, in the final book of *The Vandal Persecution*, mentions the city of Greater Tuburbo; and Antoninus, in his description of the itinerary mentioned above, writes: “Cluacaria 15, Lesser Tuburbo 28, Cigisa.”

The testimony of Antoninus is therefore wrongly adduced, because Cyprianus sat at Greater Tuburbo, which Antoninus does not mention. Nevertheless, the Peutinger Table describes the location of both Tuburbi. There Sicilibba is seen midway, facing both Tuburbi obliquely, and is twenty-eight miles distant from Greater Tuburbo.

He is also mistaken when he places Cyprianus after Penthadius Carpitana, for Cyprianus was already a bishop in 411, whereas Penthadius, as has been said, was not yet sitting at Carpis in that year.

### SERVILIUS

His see is unknown, as are those of Pelagius, Marcellus, Venantius, Didymus, Saturninus, Thiazacenus, Germanus, Germanianus, Juventius, Majorinus, and Juventius.

Here the Carthaginian *Collation* leaves the man without resources, and he could seek no assistance elsewhere; but no one can fail to see how unsuccessfully he has used that same *Collation*.

### CANDIDUS OF ABIRITA

He was one of the legates of the province of Proconsular Africa, etc. Hold back your laughter, my friend. Above, in the case of FRUCTUOSUS, whom he asserted to have been bishop of Abbiritensis, he had said precisely this:

“This Fructuosus cannot have survived for long, for in the year 419 Candidus Abbirita is listed among the legates of the province of Proconsular Africa.”

If Fructuosus and Candidus, both bishops of the same city of Abbiritensis, were present together at Carthage in the synod of 416 on the very same day, why could they not likewise be present together at the other Carthaginian synod in 419? So quickly did he forget himself that he made Candidus Fructuosus’s colleague in the episcopate, although shortly before he had declared him Fructuosus’s successor.

Do you think Garnerius can devise any answer to this, except at the Greek Kalends? Moreover, he also errs in making both bishops of the same city, since Fructuosus occupied the see of Abzirita, while Candidus was bishop of Abbiritensis Germanicianorum and succeeded Felix, who took part in the *Collation*, as I plainly demonstrated above when the discussion of Fructuosus arose.

### CYPRIANUS AND AEMILIANUS

Their sees are unknown. I neither know nor investigate them.

### ROMANUS OF MEGALOPOLIS

He is listed in the *Collation*. The *Notitia of the bishops of the province of Proconsular Africa* mentions Coronius Meglapolitanus, driven into exile. But in what part of the Proconsular province Megalopolis was situated is unknown to me.

Indeed, it was equally unknown to the Africans of that period. No Megalopolis ever existed in Africa; that name belonged to the famous city in the Peloponnese, the birthplace of the historian Polybius. There was, however, a Meglapolis in Africa.

Thus in chapter 133 of the *Collation* Romanus, bishop of the church of Meglapolis, is mentioned; and in the *Notitia* cited by Garnerius—but not correctly read—Coronius Meglapolitanus is named. Finally, in the synodical letter, act 2 of the synod of Saint Martin the pope, Reparatus, bishop of the holy Church of Meglapolis, is listed.

By removing a single letter, Garnerius drags these bishops from Africa into Europe.
