But whether the error originated with a copyist or a printer, Garnerius himself is responsible for the mistake of thinking that Romanus, who was a bishop before 411 and took part in the *Collation*, sat in the synod after Penthadius Carpitana and Candidus of Abbir Germaniciana, although both were raised to their sacred sees only after 411.

### AFRICANUS AND MARGELLINUS

Their sees are uncertain. In chapter 187 of the *Collation*, Marcus, a Donatist bishop, was questioned by our Alypius of Thagaste:

> “Where are you from? What is your city?”

He replied:

> “Secuta Prura Amidicca. Melimelimenia Nasuta Prura.”

Garnerius could have assigned Africanus to Secuta Prura Amidicca and Margellinus to Melimelimenia Nasuta Prura, exercising the same authority that he assumes in assigning episcopal sees according to his own will.

Thus far concerning Garnerius’s notes on the heading of the Proconsular Fathers. I now come to his notes on the title of another synodical letter, sent in the same year, 416, by the bishops of Numidia to Pope Innocent, likewise against the Pelagians.

### HIS NOTES ON LETTER 176

“To the most blessed, deservedly venerable, and in Christ honored Pope Innocent: Silvanus, Valentinus, Aurelius, Donatus, Restitutus, Lucianus, Alypius, Augustine, Placentius, Severus, Fortunatus, Possidius, Novatus, Secundus, Maurentius, Leo, Faustinianus, Cresconius, Malcus, Littorius, Fortunatus, Donatus, Ponticanus, Saturninus, Christonius, Honorius, Lucius, Adeodatus, Processus, Cresconius, Secundus, Felix, Asiaticus, Ruffinianus, Faustinus, Servus, Terentius, Cresconius, Sperantius, Quadratus, Lucillus, Sabinus, Faustinus, Cresconius, Victor, Gignantius, Posidonius, Antonius, Innocentius, Praesidius, Crescentius, Felix, Antonius, Victor, Honoratus, Donatus, Petrus, Praesidius, Cresconius, Lampadius, Delphinus, from the council of Milevis, greetings in the Lord.”

Under equally bad auspices, Garnerius also describes the sees of these bishops. I may perhaps seem to be wasting time by refuting his notes; but I regard this very matter as a gain, because by obliging you in this work I extend my devotion to you. There is no danger that it should be excessive when it ought to be at its greatest.

In the meantime, gather your strength and move from the Proconsular province into Numidia, summoned by Garnerius, so that you may hear concerning the bishops of the assembly of Milevis the same sorts of fictions that you heard concerning the Fathers of the Carthaginian council.

### SILVANUS OF SUMMA OR ZUMMA

The name of the see is written in both ways in the *Collation*. It was then the first see in the province of Numidia, etc. Where Summa or Zuma was situated is uncertain, unless perhaps it is said to have been Zama, which Pliny and Ptolemy place in Africa, or rather in Numidia.

Let no stranger to African history confuse Zama with Zumma. For on the Kalends of June in 411, Dialogus, bishop of Zama, took part in the Carthaginian *Collation*; against him stood Montanus, one of the seven Donatist collators, according to chapter 121. Silvanus, bishop of Zumma, appears in chapter 99; his opponent in the same diocese was the Donatist Felix, who in chapters 114, 201, and 202 is called Zummaensis.

This author had written the following in his notes on the heading of the Proconsular bishops:

“MAJORINUS OF ZEMPTA. So it is read in the *Collation*; better, of Zama, for there was a city Zama in the Proconsular province, if we believe Pliny, Ptolemy, and Strabo.”

He imposes the same inconsistency, with which he is everywhere afflicted, upon the learned men who designate the sees of these bishops. In listing the cities of those provinces, they do not provide the exact division of the two provinces as it was preserved by the ecclesiastical authorities, but divide them by rivers, as is obvious.

From the *Collation* we have Dialogus, bishop of Zama; Garnerius superimposes Majorinus and Silvanus upon him as colleagues, thereby establishing a triumvirate of bishops in the same city. Zama, first of Jugurtha and then of Juba in Numidia, called Regia, is celebrated by Sallust and Aulus Hirtius for the events that Metellus and Caesar conducted there. Zumma, by contrast, was a small town in the same province, known to ecclesiastical writers solely from the Carthaginian *Collation*.

### VALENTINUS OF VAJA

So it is read in the *Collation*. The see is uncertain; nevertheless, it was near Vegesela, for he is said to have subscribed in place of the bishop of Vegesela. In chapter 135 of the *Collation* the following is read:

> “I, Valentinus, bishop of Vaja, in place of my fellow priest Reginus of the church of Vegesela, who is detained here at Carthage because of illness, etc., have subscribed.”

His Donatist opponent is called Quintasius Vajensis in chapter 186. Vegesela was on the borders of Numidia toward Byzacena; for according to Antoninus it was thirty miles from the Byzacene city of Sufetula, on the route from Thenis to Theveste.

Vaja, or Baja, is mentioned more than once in the ecclesiastical records of Africa. Felix Bajanensis was present at the council of Gratus at Carthage; Bejanus Bejanensis was one of the twelve consecrators of Maximianus, condemned by the Donatists at Bagai, according to Augustine, book III against Cresconius, chapter 53.

Yet it is wrongly inferred from Valentinus’s subscription that he sat near Vegesela. In chapters 208 and 209 of the *Collation*, several Donatist bishops subscribed on behalf of colleagues who are said to have been detained on the journey by illness; nevertheless their dioceses were not neighboring. When Reginus was ill at Carthage, he could have asked Valentinus, who was visiting him, to authenticate the mandate in his name.

At the Council of Ephesus, Flavianus Philippensis subscribed for Rufus Thessalonicensis, although their sees were not near one another. The former was administering ecclesiastical affairs in Macedonia Secunda, the latter in Macedonia Prima.

### AURELIUS OF MACOMADA

Antoninus mentions the city of Macomada twice in his *Itinerary*: once when he describes the road leading from Carthage to Cirta, and again on the route from Assuras to Thenis. In the first place he sets it not far from Cirta, and in the second near Thenis. Therefore the lexicographers must be wrong when they think *Macomadem* should be read and place it near the Lesser Syrtis.

Afterward he writes:

“For there was a twin Macomada among the Numidians: one whose church Aurelius governed and whose opponent was the Donatist Sallustius; the other Resticiana, over which Proficentius presided on behalf of the party of Donatus.”

Indeed, Antoninus lists three Macomades. He places the first in Numidia, fifty-three miles from Cirta; the second in Byzacena, near Thenis, a city in Byzacena, whose *Notitia* names Pascasius Thenitanus. Again, on the same route, from Greater Leptis—which was the metropolitan city of the Tripolitan province—to Alexandria, he writes: “Macomades of the Syrtis.”

The Peutinger Table agrees with Antoninus, placing Lesser Macomades near Thenis in Byzacena. The lexicographers, whom he ridicules, will learn from Garnerius about a fourth Macomada among the Numidians.

Therefore the Donatist Proficentius sat at Macomades in Byzacena, for Antoninus calls this city a municipium. The Macomadian frontier is placed under the custody of the duke of Tripolitana in the *Notitia of the Western Empire*.

### DONATUS OF AMPORA

He is indeed called Auburensis in the *Collation*, but the *Notitia* mentions Cresconius Amporensis, who was expelled into exile with others. In chapter 121 of the *Collation* he is not called Auburensis but Anburensis; his opponent Servatus is called bishop of Amphorensis in chapter 198.

Donatus could have sat at Anbura, in the diocese of Amphora or Ampora, just as Delphinus, according to chapter 65 of the same *Collation*, resided in the diocese of Constantina; and there were four Catholics in the diocese of Adeodatus, the Donatist bishop of Milevis, as Petilianus complained in that same passage.

### RESTITUTUS OF NOVASIS

So it stands in the Collation. In the *List of Bishops of Numidia*, Candidus of Novasis is listed among those expelled. He took part in the Council of Carthage held before the Collation, in the year 411; then in the Council of Milevis in 416; and in the general African council of 418, in which he was third among the legates of the province of Numidia. These statements would be partly correct if one Restitutus of Novasis from Numidia were being referred to. But in the same Collation, chapter 143, Restitutus, bishop of Tagora, appears; Garnerius concedes that this church belonged to Numidia, because in the *List* of that province Timothy of Tagura is recorded. Again, at the synod of 418, the legates elected from the province of Numidia are said to have been Alypius, Augustine, and Restitutus. Therefore, since this Restitutus sat at the synod of 416 before Alypius and Augustine, it is erroneous to say that he was the same man who in 418 is named as legate of the Numidians, since the latter is mentioned there after Alypius and Augustine, as though he held the later episcopate.

### LUCIAN OF GUIRUM

He is listed among the bishops who held a synod at Carthage before the Collation, etc. Whether here and there the name of the church has been corrupted, and whether *Girbensis* ought to be restored in place of *Guirensis* or *Girensis*—the bishop of Girba gave his sentence in tenth place at the council of the rebaptizers—someone might perhaps doubt, and in my judgment not very rashly. I will not deny that, in the judgment of a geographer who repeatedly confuses cities, it would not be extremely rash to think so. But learned men would laugh at anyone who placed Girba in Numidia. Momillus of Garba, whom Garnerius places in the synod of the rebaptizers, belonged to the Tripolitans; for in the *List* of that province Faustinus of Girba is praised. No Girba is named in Numidia, but only Garbe. Hence, at the synod of Secundus of Tisigitanus at Cirta, Victor of Garbe was present, according to Optatus of Milevis, book I, and Augustine, book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 27.

### ALYPIUS OF THAGASTE

He is more distinguished not only by the writings of Augustine, Jerome, Paulinus, and others, but especially by the deeds and records of the Church, in which he is entered among the saints on 15 August, etc. Everything is excellent. But Alypius stands above all Garnerius’s praise.

### AUGUSTINE OF HIPPO

No note is needed here. Would that, just as this writer supplies no notes here concerning Augustine, no one had branded Augustine with notes either; for then the necessity of writing vindications would not have been imposed upon us. Hence the complaint of those who approve only themselves and their own views has broken out in more than one place.

### PLACENTIUS OF MADAURA

In the Collation he is indeed read as *Placentinus*, and likewise in the Latin codex of the African Church; but in the Greek text the form is *Placentius*, a name more common among the Africans. He took part in the African council of 418 and acted as legate of Numidia; he also spoke in the case of Maurentius of Tubursicum against the elders of New Germania. I accept the correction. Meanwhile, he himself should also correct the year of the synod in which Placentius took part against the elders of New Germania—for so it is read in chapter 67 of the African Code. The year must be given as 407, since at the synod convened under the consulship of Bassus and Philippus, in 408, no mention of Placentius is heard.

[Col. 0295A] ### SEVERUS OF MILEVIS

The Collation, as it has been published, passes over the church of Severus, although later it speaks of Severus, who arrived at Carthage with nineteen other Catholics, whose Catholic churches are named, etc. No note can be added to these notes. The passage is taken from chapter 215 of the Collation. Severus sat at Milevis before the year 397. Antoninus calls the place *Mileum*, and according to the Peutinger Tables it was a colony.

### FORTUNATUS OF CONSTANTINA

He was one of the seven Catholics who undertook the Collation against the Donatists. Whether the church of Constantina is the same as that of Cirta has been debated by learned men. After adducing arguments by which the same city appears to have been called by both names, he says: “Although reluctantly, the force of so many arguments compels me to agree with Gravius and Pamelius, whom he followed as his guide.”

[Col. 0295B] Yet the first argument he uses is altogether weak. For that Fortunatus of Cirta whom Augustine mentions in *On the One Baptism*, chapter 16, is certainly different from Fortunatus whom he calls of Constantina in book III *Against Petilian*, chapter 1, and book III, chapter 38. The former preceded Possidius in episcopal rank; the latter followed him. The bishop of Cirta succeeded Profuturus only a very few years before Augustine wrote *On the One Baptism*—he was writing it in 407—although Possidius was already a bishop before 394. The bishop of Constantina, however, preceded Possidius, as is clear from many subscriptions.

Aurelius Victor writes in his book *On the Caesars* that, after Constantine defeated Maxentius near the Milvian Bridge in the year 306, the Roman senate, having restored and adorned the town of Cirta, which had fallen under siege from Alexander, gave it the name Constantina.

[Col. 0295C] Hence Constans and Constantius, the sons of Constantine, issued a rescript to the council of the city of Constantina of the Cirtenses, in law 29 *On Decurions* of the Theodosian Code. Augustine says in book I *Against Petilian*, chapter 2: “In that same city of Constantina your ancestors ordained Silvanus bishop at the very beginning of their schism.” In book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 27, however, he calls Silvanus a bishop of Cirta. And in book III *Against Petilian* he says of Petilian, the Donatist bishop of Constantina: “I mentioned Silvanus of Cirta, whom, after an interval, he himself succeeded.” There he calls Petilian Silvanus’s fellow occupant of the episcopal seat. See also letter 165, and likewise the proceedings held before Zenophilus, consular governor of Numidia.

[Col. 0295D] Thus the same holy teacher sometimes calls Petilian and Fortunatus bishops of Cirta, and sometimes bishops of Constantina, as I have shown more fully in book II of my *History of the Pelagians*, chapter 8. These facts are clear. Yet Garnerius testifies that he comes to this opinion reluctantly; for he preferred to distinguish Constantina from Cirta, so that the man who had so often confused two cities into one might here dissect one city into two. But what he preferred to do with the cities, he did with the bishops, declaring Fortunatus of Cirta different from Fortunatus of Constantina.

Augustine writes in the aforementioned book *On the One Baptism*, chapter 16: “Therefore, if Profuturus died a very few years ago, and Fortunatus, who is still alive and succeeded him as bishop, etc.” Thus, in 407, when Augustine wrote these words, Fortunatus was alive as the successor of Profuturus in the see of Cirta. Moreover, Fortunatus of Constantina was also alive at the same time; for in book I *Against Petilian*, chapter 1, Augustine says: “When I was in the Church of Constantina, with Absentianus present, and with my colleague Fortunatus, its bishop.”

[Col. 0296A] But in book II, chapter 5, praising the Roman Church, he says: “In which Anastasius now sits.” From this one sees that the books against Petilian were written by the holy teacher while the holy Pope Anastasius was still alive. Since Anastasius died in 402, it follows that Fortunatus of Constantina had been bishop of Constantina before 402. Since he was present at the Collation in 411 and at the synod of Milevis in 419, according to Garnerius’s chronology he was sitting at Constantina in 407 together with another Fortunatus of Cirta, the successor of Profuturus. Thus, by making two Fortunati out of one, he once again plays out the story of the two Menæchmi quite neatly.

[Col. 0296B] ### POSSIDIUS OF CALAMA

He too was one of the collators, indeed almost inseparable from them, just as Alypius was Augustine’s associate in conducting the affairs of the Church, etc. Everything is in good order. But when, immediately above, in the notes on Fortunatus, he says that Possidius was a bishop before 494, the statement is riddled with anachronism.

Possidius of Calama himself writes in his *Life of Augustine*, chapter 8, that the holy teacher was consecrated at Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia and bishop of Calama. But according to the *Chronicle* of the blessed Prosper, a man of the same age as Augustine and his very close friend, Augustine was inaugurated as bishop in the consulship of Olybrius and Probinus, in the year 395. Therefore Megalius had not yet died in that year. Moreover, I have clearly shown in book II of my *Pelagian History*, chapter 8, that Fortunatus of Constantina and Possidius of Calama were ordained in 397.

### NOVATUS OF SINITUM

So it is read in the Collation. Augustine mentions the church of Sinitum in letter 128, addressed to Donatus; the *List of the Bishops of Numidia* likewise mentions it, recording that Stephen of Sinitum was driven into exile. What this city was, and where it was situated, is uncertain, except that it can be inferred from Augustine that it was not far from Hippo. Might it therefore be thought to have been Sinistu, a colony mentioned by Antoninus on the route from Hippo to Carthage, which is said to lie at a distance recorded as “III. M. LXXX. M. M.” from Hippo (reading uncertain)? He thoroughly turns everything upside down, transporting cities from one province to another and grievously corrupting the text of the Collation and of Antoninus.

In chapter 143 of the Collation we read: “Novatus, bishop of the Church of Sitifis”; and in chapter 204: “Novatus, bishop of the Catholic Church at Sitifis.” Sitifis was a celebrated city of Mauretania and, as Procopius says in book II *On the Vandalic War*, chapter 3, the capital of the region of Zabes, situated beyond Mount Auras. From it Mauretania Sitifensis, the fifth ecclesiastical province in Africa, took its name.

In chapter 127 of the African Code, Novatus of Sitifis is praised as legate of Mauretania Sitifensis. In order to list Novatus among the Numidians, Garnerius changed *Sitifensis* into *Sinitensis*. Sitifis was close to Numidia: according to Antoninus, it lay twenty-five miles from Guiculus, a Numidian city, with the river Ampsaga between them.

Antoninus nowhere mentions Sinistu on the route from Hippo Regius to Carthage. He writes: “Onellaba, 50 miles; Ad Aquas, 25 miles; Simittu, 5 miles; Bulla Regia, 7.” But he changes *Simittu* into *Sinistu*. Moreover, Simittu was in the proconsular province; for in the synodical proceedings, act 2.1, of the council of Saint Martin, Benenatus of Simittu is read among the proconsular Fathers; and in the synod of 419, Adeodatus of Simittu; while in chapter 125 of the Collation Benenatus of Simittu is named, who said: “I have neither another [bishop] nor heretics.” But in chapter 202 Cresconius, bishop of Sinitum, is named among the Donatists. Where this city was situated I shall say below, in its proper place, in the notes on LUCILLUS.

[Col. 0297A] ### SECUNDUS OF RUSPA

So it is read in the Collation. That Secundus, together with his church, belonged to the province of Numidia is established by canon 100 of the Code of the African Church, where he is said to have been chosen by Maurentius as one of the judges in his case before Xanthippus, primate of Numidia. For all the other bishops are Numidians, and the judgment was provincial.

There are so many errors in these few words that I do not know where to begin the criticism. I shall follow his footsteps, so as from time to time to raise him back onto his feet. Ruspa was a city of Byzacium, which Saint Fulgentius adorned both by the holiness of his life and by the excellence of his writings. In the *List of Byzacene Bishops*, Stephen of Ruspa is praised; and in the synodical proceedings of the same province, act 2 of the council of Saint Martin, Julian of Ruspa.

The Peutinger Tables place Ruspe and Ruspina in Byzacium. In Ptolemy’s Tables we read the following towns in Byzacium: Hadrumetum, Ruspina, Leptis Minor, Thapsus, Acholla, Ruspe, the promontory of Bracordes, etc. Pliny calls Ruspina a free town in book V, chapter 4. Therefore Secundus of Ruspa, who is named in the Collation, whether he sat at Ruspa or at Ruspina, is wrongly transferred to Numidia.

[Col. 0297C] The Secundus mentioned in canon 100 of the African Code was bishop of Megarmelita, as I shall show later. Finally, his statement that the bishops chosen in the case of Maurentius of Tubursicum were all Numidians is false. They were clearly Xanthippus of Tagos, primate; Augustine of Hippo; Florentius of Hippo Diarrhytus; Theasius of Memblosita; Samsucius of Turres; according to Augustine’s letter 168; Secundus of Megarmelita, according to chapter 125 of the Collation; and Possidius of Calama.

It is certain, however, that Memblosita and Hippo Diarrhytus were in the proconsular province. Garnerius said precisely this about Theasius in the notes on the preceding heading, although he did not know how to distinguish Membressa from Memblosita. In the synodical record at the council of Saint Martin, Donatus of Hippo Diarrhytus subscribes among the proconsular bishops. But these matters are perfectly clear, and I do not wish to detain you longer over them.

### MAURENTIUS OF TUBURSICUM

So it is read in the Collation, etc. He has struck the nail on the head; for this I congratulate him again and again. He raises himself from the ground—but alas, he immediately falls again.

### LEO OF THE MUNICIPIUM OF MOPTA

So it is read in the Collation. The *List of the Bishops of Numidia*, however, speaks of a *Municipium*, where Victor of Municipium is recorded among those sent into exile with others. Care must be taken not to confuse this Leo, because of the similarity of the names, with another bishop who governed the church of Mocta and attended the plenary council of 419. The church called Moptensis belonged to the province of Numidia; the one called Moctensis belonged to Mauretania Sitifensis.

He drags Mopta from the diocese of Sitifis into Numidia, where Garnerius alone places Mopta. In the Peutinger Tables, in Mauretania Sitifensis, we read: “Mopti, municipium.” But he forces this to mean a *municipium* as a town called *Municipium*, which was in Numidia, although Mopta was called a *municipium* because it was not a colony or a city granted Latin status, but lived under municipal law. The aforementioned Tables make it perfectly clear which towns were municipia and which were colonies.

As for Leo’s being called Moctensis at the synod of 419, this is written incorrectly. From the ancient Vatican manuscripts, Labbe restored *Moptensis* in volume II of the *Councils*, page 1670.

### FAUSTINIANUS OF THAMUGADI

So it stands in the Collation. Near the colony of Theveste in Numidia there is the city of Thamugadi, known to Augustine, Antoninus, Pliny, Ptolemy, and others.

It is by no means known from Antoninus that Thamugadi was near Theveste. He writes: “Theveste, 22 miles; Thimphadi, 20 miles; Vegesela, 18 miles; Mascula, 22 miles; Glaudi, 22 miles; Thamugadi.” Thus Thamugadi is not near Theveste according to Antoninus, since by the same testimony it was 104 miles distant from that city, with the episcopal cities of Mascula and Vegesela lying between them. At the time of the Collation Rheginus sat as bishop at the former, and Malchus at the latter.

Procopius praises the abundance of crops at Thamugadi in book II *On the Vandalic War*. In the same work, on page 97 of Grotius’s edition, he also states that Thamugadi was situated on plains to the east, opposite Mount Auras, which he says was three days’ journey from Carthage. In the same work, on page 120 of the cited edition, he calls Theveste a town six days’ journey from Carthage.

But that this Faustinianus was of Thamugadi is pure invention on Garnerius’s part. In chapter 215 of the Collation Faustinianus of Rusiccade is recited. Pliny places this city in Numidia in book V, chapter 3, writing that it was forty-eight miles from Cirta, the metropolis of Numidia. Antoninus places it sixty miles from Gullu of Numidia and fifty from Paratiana; these places were in Numidia, and Rusiccade lies between them.

Why, then, cannot Faustinianus of Rusiccade be affirmed to be the same man who took part in the synod of Milevis? In the cited chapter 215 he reads that Alypius said of Faustinianus of Rusiccade: “He is in this city, but he is seriously ill.” Thus he supposed that the same man died of illness at Carthage in 411; consequently, only a Faustinianus of Thamugadi remained in the Collation, whom he could assert without doubt had been present at the synod of Milevis. Do you wish to accept so plausible a conjecture?

### CRESCONIUS OF CUICULUM

So it stands in the Collation. It should perhaps be written *Culcuitanus*. Culcua is known not only to Antoninus but also to Ptolemy, a colony situated approximately midway between Cirta, the colony of Simittu, Lares, and Gansapha.

You may laugh at the marvels of the *New Geography*, if you wish. He places Cuiculum approximately midway on the route from Cirta eastward toward Carthage; and, more remarkably, he derives this from Antoninus, who nevertheless writes: “From Cirta to Mileum, 25 miles; to Idicra, 25 miles; to Cuiculi, 25 miles; to Sitifis, 25 miles.” You see that, according to Antoninus, Cuiculum lies on the route westward from Cirta toward the city of Sitifis. Since Sitifis was in Mauretania Sitifensis, it follows plainly that Cuiculum was the last city of Numidia toward Mauretania, although he places it approximately in the middle of Numidia.

Meanwhile, admire the ingenuity of the man who found in Antoninus a town called *Culcuitanum*, which nowhere appears in Antoninus’s Itinerary, but did not see *Cuiculitanum*, which is so plainly designated by the same author. Yet I can scarcely endure this commentator’s changing the church of Cuiculum into one of Culcuitum on the authority of Ptolemy—who nevertheless placed Calcu(a), not Culcua, as he corruptly reads it, among the new cities of Numidia—when no city is named more frequently in the ancient records of the African Church than Cuiculum.

In the synod of Gratus, Elpidophorus of Cuiculum is praised; in the synod of Saint Cyprian, Pudentianus of Cuiculum; in the *List of Africa*, Victor of Cuiculum; in the Collation, Cresconius, bishop of the people of Cuiculum; and in the fifth synod, Creses, bishop of the Church of the Cuiculitan province of Numidia.

I remember that at the beginning of his preface to his *Nestorian History*, Garnerius asserted that Christianus Lupus, a great restorer of ecclesiastical antiquity, was almost overwhelmed by the immense abundance of his learning. You see Garnerius far removed from that danger; for he has not yet been suffocated by that immense learning. As far as these notes are concerned, his entire literary equipment can be grasped in one fist.

### MALCHUS OF MASCULA

So it stands in the Collation. Antoninus, however, knows Mascula, sixty miles from Theveste, for travelers going toward the colony of Sitifis. Januarianus of Mascula is also listed among the bishops of Numidia, and Augustine mentions, in book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 27, Donatus of Mascula, who at the Donatist council of Cirta in 303, presided over by Secundus of Tisigitanus, primate of Numidia, confessed that he had been a traditor.

The statement about Malchus’s see is correct. In the synod of Boniface, Januarius of Mascula is likewise praised as legate of the province of Numidia. Nevertheless, in what he adds, he commits an anachronism of two years. For that synod, according to Optatus, book I, was convened at Cirta after the persecution. Augustine says in the cited book, chapter 26: “The council of Secundus of Tisigitanus, held with very few participants at Cirta after the persecution concerning the handing over of the books, survives, so that a bishop might be ordained there in place of the deceased.”

But from the municipal proceedings it appears that the persecution concerning the handing over of the books began at Cirta under the eighth consulship of Diocletian and the seventh of Maximian, in the year 303, on 19 May; according to the same chapter 29, Paul was then bishop of Cirta, and after his death in 305 Silvanus was appointed as his successor.

Augustine indicates the year and day of the council of Cirta in the brief account of the Collation, third day, chapter 18, where he also clarifies the period during which the persecution continued in Africa. “The proceedings,” he says, “of the martyrs, by which the time of the persecution was demonstrated, were held under the ninth consulship of Diocletian and the eighth of Maximian, on 12 February; but the episcopal proceedings of the decree of Cirta were held after that same consulship, on 5 March. Consequently, an interval of thirteen months is found between them.”

From Augustine you have it that the persecution raged even in 304, when the martyrs were killed; but that the council of Cirta was convened in 305, on 5 March, when the persecution had ceased in Africa after the abdication of Diocletian and Maximian, while Caesar Severus ruled in Italy and Africa. The most learned Henri Valois proves these matters at greater length in his notes on chapter 2 of book VIII of Eusebius of Caesarea.

You recently showed me the letter of Hadrian, the brother of Henri, which had been sent to you. Both men have deserved well of ecclesiastical and secular history and are therefore fully worthy of your friendship.

### LITTORIUS OF SUANUM

So it stands in the Collation, but perhaps *Sugunensis* should be read. Antoninus places Sugus in Numidia near Cirta, although the *List of the Bishops of Numidia* mentions Felix of Suaba, who was driven into exile. If he had read the *List* without merely skimming it, he would have known that Victor of Sugita is mentioned there. He would therefore have abandoned the idea that the church of Suaba or Suava—not, as he says, Suanum—should be changed into that of Sugita.

### FORTUNATUS OF CASENSI-CALANA

So it stands in the Collation. But since several men of this name are listed, it is doubtful whether our Fortunatus was bishop of this church. What scruples he now suffers, when elsewhere he admits certain bishops to this synod from the Collation while arbitrarily excluding others of precisely the same name!

Six Fortunati are listed among the Catholics in the Collation: of Rusuccurum, of Capsa, and of Constantina. The first belongs to the Mauretanians of Caesarea, the second to the Byzacenians, and the last to the Numidians; he is read before Possidius in the heading. Three others are listed: of Casensi-Calana, of Abbenza, and of Undesita. These two churches are commonly assigned to an uncertain province.

[Col. 0300C] In the *List of Numidia*, however, Optantius of Casensi-Calana is recorded. Garnerius therefore doubts whether Fortunatus was a Numidian bishop who sat at the church of Casensi-Calana—which certainly belonged to Numidia—or whether he was rather bishop of Undesita or Abbenza, towns whose province is entirely uncertain.

### DONATUS OF TIBILIS

Garnerius reads *Tigilitanus* in the Collation, but certainly wrongly; nowhere is any mention found of a city called Tigilis. I readily concede that his reading of Donatus as *Tigilitanus* is certainly erroneous—for no one but Garnerius reads it so. Anyone who knows his letters will read in chapter 121 of the Collation: “Donatus, bishop of Tisilis.” He also said: “I am present, but I do not have even a bishop against me.”

Yet Garnerius incorrectly called him *Tigilitanus* instead of *Tisilitensis*, as it is read in the three editions of Masson, Albaspinaeus, and Labbeus. Let this be blamed on a hasty reading. He commits another error as well: he places Donatus, a Catholic bishop, in the city of Tibilis in the year 411, although at that time Simplicius, a Donatist bishop, was sitting in the town of Tibilis. In chapter 197 of the Collation Simplicius said: “I have no adversary.”

Nevertheless, whether he wishes it or not, Garnerius joins Donatus the Catholic to this man as his adversary in the same city, although each testified in his own city that he had no opposing fellow bishop. Is this not an abuse of the patience of learned men?

### PONTICANUS, SATURNINUS, CHRISTONIUS, HONORIUS, LUCIUS

Their sees are uncertain. With a single word he frees us from the danger of criticism and from the trouble of discussing them.

[Col. 0301A] ### ADEODATUS OF BELLALIS

This is indeed how the church is called in the Collation; but in the *List of Numidia* it is read as *Bellalisensis*. Where such a city was situated in Numidia is unknown to me. But Garnerius will have to contend with another bishop of Numidian name, who in chapter 129 is called Adeodatus, bishop of the people of Bazarita. For the *List* of that same province shows that this city was in Numidia, in which Vitalianus of Vazarita is praised; and the place of Vazarita is mentioned in canon 54 of the African Code.

Thus he forces *Bellalisensis* upon us purely according to his own preference, excluding *Bazaritanus*. Therefore the city of this Adeodatus who is named in the synod is itself uncertain, and not merely the site of the city, as he asserted.

### PROCESSUS

His see is unknown. Let us proceed to the notes.

### CRESCONIUS OF CENTENARIUM

So it is read in the Collation. And indeed in the *List of the Bishops of Numidia*, Florentius of Centenarium is numbered among the bishops expelled from there. Since several Cresconii are listed in the Collation, I would not believe, without evidence, that this one, who is named thirtieth in the heading, sat at Centenarium—so this town is called in the Peutinger Tables—especially since Garnerius himself candidly admits that he cannot establish anything certain about the cities in Numidia associated with the Cresconii, as you will see below in its proper place.

### SECUNDUS OF MEGARMELITA, OR OF AQUAE

The Collation calls him of Megarmelita; Augustine additionally calls him of Aquae. Nowhere in Augustine’s works is the name of Secundus found either as “of Megarmelita” or “of Aquae.” Only in Leporius’s little book is the following subscription read: “I, Secundus, bishop of Aquae, or of Megarmitana, have subscribed to the little book presented to us by Leporius.” Here it is not Augustine—whose subscription appears there in the same form—but Secundus himself who called himself bishop of Aquae.

### FELIX OF VILLAREGIS

Although it is certain that, among two bishops of the same name in Numidia, one was of Villaregis and the other of Tubia, it is nevertheless doubtful which of them governed which church.

Later, canon 48 of the African Code contains the case of Cresconius of Villaregis. After he had violently seized the church of Tubia, abandoning that of Villaregis, and after he had repeatedly been admonished, he stubbornly refused to obey. But since the complaint was brought by Honoratus and Urbanus, legates of Mauretania Sitifensis, one might conjecture—and not rashly—that both of the aforementioned churches belonged to this Mauretania.

Yet since the author of the *List* holds the contrary opinion, I can scarcely approve the conjecture. For who could have known the location of the cities of Africa, and the churches governed by their respective associates, better than Victor of Utica? Therefore, until a greater light shines from elsewhere, I think we must adhere to the *List*. He stumbles on level ground and longs for greater light at midday.

He imagines that the testimony of the *List* contradicts the words of the African canon. In the *List of Numidia*, Donatus of Villaregis is recorded; but the church of Tubia is not listed there. Therefore Cresconius left the city of Villaregis in Numidia, went to Mauretania Sitifensis, and there seized the church of Tubia.

Hence the Sitifensian legates asked the synod for permission to proceed against Cresconius before the governor of the province. For Mauretania Sitifensis was a province governed by a president, as Sextus Rufus shows in his *Breviary*.

[Col. 0302A] From these facts it is plainly inferred that the church of Tubia must be assigned to this province, not to Numidia. Otherwise the legates of that province, rather than the Sitifensians, would have stood against Cresconius.

Charles of Saint Paul does not mention a bishopric of Tubia, and Holstenius, on pages 65 and 96 of his notes on the same work, incorrectly confuses it with Tubuna. Tubuna was in Numidia, as I shall say later.

Because Cresconius, after abandoning the town of Villaregis, occupied the see of Tubia, Garnerius asserted that both were cities of Numidia. We know from Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret that Euzoïus first sat at Germanicia in the province of Euphratesia, then invaded the Antiochene throne, and finally usurped the see of Constantinople. Eusebius, according to the Alexandrian synod cited in the Second Apology of Saint Athanasius, was first bishop at Berytus in Phoenicia Prima; thence he thrust himself into the see of Nicomedia in Bithynia, and finally, through the favor of the Emperor Constantius, seized Constantinople, ever defiling and gnawing at the cities of others, upon which he cast envious eyes.

According to the inference of Garnerius, these cities too would all be in the same province, although Constantinople was in Europe and the others in various Asian provinces far removed from one another. Perhaps, in order to spare this wandering Cresconius the inconvenience of a longer journey, he placed both the town of Villaregis and that of Tubia in the same province, so that Cresconius could easily leap from one to the other.

### ASIATICUS

His see is uncertain, as is that of RUFINIANUS. This is no place for a note of censorial severity. It is better for him to admit ignorance than to teach error.

### FAUSTINUS OF SILLITUM

So it stands in the Collation. In the *List of the Bishops of Numidia*, however, Maximus Sillitanus is mentioned. Wait a little, and you will hear of another Faustinus simultaneously occupying the see of Sillitium; indeed, on Garnerius’s authority, you will see a third fictitious Faustinus in this synod.

### SERVUSDEI OF BURA

So it stands in the Collation, except that *Tubursicensis Burae* is added. In the *List of the Bishops of Numidia*, however, he is simply called Leontius of Bura. This note suffers from more than one defect.

He imposes the agnomen of the city as though it were its name. Since there were two Tubursica in Africa, one was called Tubursicum Burae, the other Tubursicum of Numidia. This is clear from the Collation, in which chapter 121 Servusdei is praised as bishop of the people of Tubursicum Burae, against whom the heretic Donatus stood; in chapter 206 that Donatus is called Donatus of Tubursicum, without the addition “of Bura.” Hence it is clear that Servusdei should not be called “of Bura,” but “of Tubursicum.” He must be named from the city’s proper name, not from its agnomen; the latter merely indicates the distinction of this Tubursicum from the other city of the same name.

Thus we say “Utrecht of the Rhine” in order to distinguish this town from Utrecht on the Meuse, and it would be wrong to call the bishop of this city “of the Meuse.” The other Tubursicum was called Tubursicum of Numidia. Thus in the same Collation, chapter 201, Januarius of Tubursicum of Numidia is named among the Donatists; against him stood Maurentius the Catholic, according to chapter 143, where he is called bishop of the Church of Tubursicum.

[Col. 0303A] Holstenius confounded the two towns on page 55, and Charles of Saint Paul mentions only one of them. From this it also follows that Tubursicum, where Servusdei sat, is not correctly placed in Numidia. For, in order to distinguish the other Tubursicum from Tubursicum Burae, the former was called Tubursicum of Numidia.

Garnerius could have highly commended Servusdei from Augustine, book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 43, whose words should be quoted here and whose genuine reading restored. “A Catholic bishop,” Augustine says, “named Servus, from Thubursicum Burae, when he was reclaiming the place invaded by your people and the procurators of both parties were awaiting a proconsular hearing, suddenly, when your armed men burst upon him in the town mentioned, scarcely escaped alive.”

It is clear that *Thubursicum Burae* should be read. From the Collation Saint Augustine expressly calls Servus a bishop of Tubursicum, and in chapter 106 the heretic Donatus is called Tubursicensis, not Tubursicuburensis.

From Augustine’s words just quoted, it seems possible to infer that this Tubursicum Burae was in the proconsular province, because the case of that town was subject to proconsular judgment, while proconsuls governed the Carthaginian province and consular governors Numidia. But I see that this argument is weak and entirely slippery. For the proconsul heard the case of Possidius and Crispinus, bishops in Numidia, according to Augustine, book III, chapter 48, of the same work *Against Cresconius*. This is also established by letters 127 and 128 to Donatus, proconsul of Africa.

For proconsuls exercised the highest authority in all the African provinces except Mauretania Tingitana. Tubursicum of Numidia lay on the route from Hippo to Cirta, according to Augustine’s letter 163.

Finally, I ask you to note Garnerius’s stratagems—I do not wish to call them malice or cunning, for I know well that the man is far from such qualities. In order to drag Servus, or Servusdei, into Numidia without question together with that city of Bura which nowhere existed, he cited the *List of Africa*, writing that it simply says “Leontius of Bura,” although that is not how it is read there. For it simply says: “Leontius of Burca.” Thus from Burca he fabricated a new Numidian city called Bura. Burita was a city of Numidia, as will be clear below.

### TERENTIUS OF SELEUCIANA

So it stands in the Collation. In the *List of the Bishops of Numidia*, however, Proficius of Seleuciana is mentioned. Garnerius could have praised Terentius and Servusdei, whom he had just named, from the synodical letter of the African synod to Pope Coelestine, in whose heading Aurelius, Valentinus, Antonius, Tutus, Servusdei, Terentius, Fortunatus, and others are named.

Thus in both synods Servusdei and Terentius sat close together, as though consecrated at approximately the same time. From this heading, however, you will infer that the great heroes of our Augustinian community—Augustine, Alypius, Severus, and Possidius—were not present at that African council. For they would have been inscribed before Servusdei and Terentius, just as they are placed in the title of the letter so extensively annotated by Garnerius.

They understood that, at that council assembled from all Africa against Roman appeals, the most vigorous discussion and decision would have to be made. Since they themselves, being especially obedient toward the rights of the Roman Church, were far removed from that position, they therefore refused to attend that gathering of bishops.

### CRESCONIUS OF CASTELLUM TITULIANUM

He is read in the Collation as bishop of the people of Titulus; but the *Notitia* mentions Victorinus, bishop of Castellum Titulianum in Numidia.

Further on:

> It should also be noted now, since I remember it, that it is highly probable that the *Notitia of the Bishops*, which we have used so often (though how unsuccessfully!), was written by Victor of Utica himself, who composed three books *On the Vandal Persecution*, etc. From this anyone may easily see that the two works ought to be joined, whenever Victor’s history is published, as one work’s supplement and illumination.

He is repeatedly mistaken. In the Collation, chapter 125, Cresconius is written as bishop of the people of Titulus, against whom the Donatist Victor stood; yet in chapter 202 he is listed among the heretics as follows: “Victor, bishop of Titulus.” This Church, however, belonged to the Proconsular Province—a fact Garnerius could have learned plainly from the *Notitia of the Bishops*, which he claims so often to have used, but certainly did not use on this occasion. For there he would have read, among the proconsular bishops, Cresciturus of Titulus. Yet, in order to make Cresconius a bishop in Numidia, he orders the same man to fly, with the utmost haste, from the town of Titulus to Castellum Titulianum.

What he adds—that the *Notitia of the Bishops of Africa* should be inserted into Victor’s history *On the Vandal Persecution*, and that the two works should be joined whenever Victor’s history is published—you will scarcely read without laughter. For you have in your distinguished library Victor’s history edited by Pierre Chifflet, whom I habitually praise, after Petavius and Sirmond, among the most learned writers of the Society of Jesus; and in his fourth book the aforementioned *Notitia of Africa* is found. That truly most learned man not only anticipated Garnerius’s wish long ago but surpassed it: he did not attach the *Notitia* to Victor’s history as an appendix, which Garnerius says he would like, but inserted it in the very middle of the work.

That volume was published by Chifflet at Dijon in 1664. From this you may perhaps think that Garnerius, in the present year 1673, when he published Marius Mercator with notes, was entirely ignorant of Chifflet’s work—a work on everyone’s lips and handled by all scholars. But if you judge so, I shall come down only reluctantly to your opinion; for I do not wish to reproach so eminent a man with such utter ignorance of a celebrated volume.

I believe, however, that Garnerius had prepared these notes on both epigraphs nine years earlier. For he writes that he had undertaken an exceedingly difficult work, which no one before him had attempted, though not without care and labor. Indeed, in dissertation 5, page 319, he states that twenty-two years earlier he had been encouraged by Sirmond, who had shared with him very ancient materials, to illuminate the Pelagian History with commentaries.

For this reason I praise his judgment: following the poet’s injunction concerning the publication of a written work—“let it be held back until the ninth year”—he published, not very maturely, notes that had matured through a full nine-year interval since Chifflet’s edition of Victor. If you immediately reply from the same Horace:

> “Criticize what many days and much erasure have not restrained, and what, cut back ten times, has not been polished to the nail,”

I do not wish to prepare any answer on behalf of the man, lest, without realizing it, I suddenly become his advocate instead of his critic.

### SPERANTIUS, OR, AS HE APPEARS IN THE COLLATION, SPERATUS OF AMMAEDARA

I was uncertain whether the Church of Ammadaera should be reckoned in Numidia or in the Proconsular Province, although it is certain that it belonged to one or the other, even if it is found in the *Notitia* of neither. But since it lies close to the colony of Theveste, as we learn from Antoninus, and since Theveste, as is clear from the *Notitia of the Bishops of Numidia*, is a city of Numidia, Ammadaera likewise seems to have to be assigned to Numidia, however much the common maps—certainly none too exact—may resist this conclusion.

In the council of the rebaptizers, Eugenius of Ammadaera gave his judgment in the thirty-second place. Pamelius contributes nothing on this point in his otherwise learned notes that might bring the desired illumination. He does, however, cite the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, where the road leading from Carthage to Cirta is described as follows:

> Unuca, 22 miles; Sicilibba, 7 miles; Vallos, 15 miles; Coreva, 15 miles; Musti, 28 miles; the colony of Laribus, 30 miles; Attieuros, 16 miles; the colony of Ammadaera, 32 miles; the colony of Theveste, 25 miles, etc.

From this it is evident that Ammadaera must be assigned to Numidia, since it lies midway between Attieuros and Theveste, and both cities are in that province.

I ask you, most learned man, not to take it amiss that I linger for a while over these matters. For I shall report certain things hitherto unknown to ecclesiastical geographers, by which the boundaries of the African diocese may nevertheless be established more precisely.

Unuca is called Uluca by ecclesiastical writers. In chapter 127 of the Collation, Procericius of Ucula is mentioned; and in the synodical letter at the Lateran Council so often mentioned by us, Cresconius of Ucula is listed among the proconsular bishops.

Sicilibba was discussed in the preceding epigraph. Vallos also was an episcopal city, and in the synod of Boniface Restitutus is called bishop of the people of Vallis. The bishop of Coreva has nowhere appeared to me.

Here the learned ecclesiastical geographers Charles of Saint-Paul and Luca Holstenius mark the boundaries of the Proconsular Province. For they unquestionably judged from the *Notitia of Africa* that Musti, neighboring Coreva, belonged to Numidia; for there Antonianus of Musti is listed among the bishops of Numidia. But they were deceived in this because they failed to observe that Africa contained two cities of this name, one in Numidia and the other in the Proconsular Province.

This is clear from the Carthaginian Collation, in which, among the Donatists, chapter 206 names Cresconius, bishop of Musti. But earlier, in chapter 121, we read:

> Victorianus, bishop of the people of Musti.

The same man said:

> I am present. I have Felicianus of Musti and Donatus of Turres against me.

And immediately, in chapter 122, Alipius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:

> Concerning Felicianus: whether he is in Primianus’s communion.

From this you understand perfectly that at Musti in Numidia, when the Collation was held in 411, Cresconius the Donatist was seated, while at Musti in the Proconsular Province sat Felicianus, who is so often mentioned by Saint Augustine in his books against the Donatists.

I therefore maintain that Felicianus was a proconsular bishop and a man of great importance among the Donatist Maximianists. For Alipius asked whether Felicianus was in the communion of Primianus, the primate of the Proconsular Province, not of Januarius, the primate of Numidia; yet at the synod held at Bagai Felicianus was condemned by both primates on account of the ordination of Maximianus.

There is clear testimony for proconsular Musti in the synodical letter of act 2 of the council of Pope Saint Martin, in which Januarius, bishop of Musti, signs among the bishops of the Proconsular Province. Yet in the *Notitia of Numidia* Antonianus of Musti is also read.

The city of Turres in the Proconsular Province, whose church was governed by the Donatist Donatus—whom Victorianus of Musti called his neighbor—appears in the Peutinger Tables, where we find:

> Thurris, 6 miles; Sicilibba, 13; Inuca, etc.

The city of Turres was close to Sicilibba. I showed in the notes to the preceding epigraph that Sicilibba was proconsular, where I mentioned Praetextatus of Sicilibba among the legates of the Proconsular Province.

On this occasion I must also supplement the maps of the African Church published by the aforementioned geographers Charles of Saint-Paul and Holstenius. They omitted the Church of Inuca, thirteen miles distant from Sicilibba, although in chapter 187 of the Collation Valentinianus, bishop of Inuca, is named.

Hence you see that Philippe Labbe, whose death was mourned by sacred scholarship, and his distinguished colleague Cossart, incorrectly replaced *Inucensis* in the margin with *Juncensis*. The former Church was in the Proconsular Province, the latter in Byzacium. The synod held by Liberatus, primate of Byzacium, is praised in act 2 of the council of Boniface of Carthage; Ferrandus the Deacon also commends its canons.

The same geographers were mistaken in locating Laribus. For when they saw Lares placed near Vaga in Numidia in Ptolemy’s Tables, they assigned the same city to that province. But here too they stumbled on the same difficulty: there were two towns of this name. In chapter 207 of the Collation Restitutus of Laribus is listed, and in chapter 197 Honoratus of Lares; both were bishops on Donatus’s side.

But that Lares also belonged to the Proconsular Province is clear from the synod of Boniface, in which Vitulus, bishop of the people of Lares, signs with the Fathers of that province.

Moreover, the matter can be clarified from the Peutinger Tables, which you allowed me to inspect. They read as follows:

> Theveste, 11 miles; Ad Mercurium, 14; Admedera, 16; Mutia, 16; Orba, 7; Laribus, 12; Drusiliana, 7; Thacia, 7; Mubsi, 7; Aboia, 6; Tignica, 12; Tichilla, 16; Membressa, 8, etc.

In describing another route from Mutia, it says:

> Altuburos, 16 miles; Altesera, 10; Assures, etc.

Here *Mubsi* should be read as *Musti*.

From this it is evident that the sacred geographers were not sufficiently consistent when they placed Ammedera—written in this way by Augustine in book 7 of *On Baptism*, chapter 39, by the Collation in chapter 207, and by Antoninus—in the Proconsular Province, while assigning Lares, Drusiliana, and Musti to Numidia, although these cities, on the direct road from Theveste in Numidia above Ammedera, are closer to Carthage.

Sallust mentions the town of Lares in the *Jugurthine War*. Procopius, in book 2 of the *Vandalic War*, calls it Laribus; Victor of Vita, in book 2 of *On the Vandal Persecution*, writes *Laribus*, where he also calls the cities Sicca and Lares.

The same fragment of the Peutinger Tables reveals the location of Tignica in the Proconsular Province. The Collation mentions it in chapter 133, where Aufidius, bishop of the people of Tignica, is named. Charles of Saint-Paul assigns it to an uncertain province, while Holstenius omits it.

But what shall be said of Aboia? In the subscriptions of the fifth synod, Valerianus, bishop of Obba in the Proconsular Province, is listed. This city too is missing from Charles of Saint-Paul and Holstenius. Whether *Aobia* or *Obba* should be read in the Tables, I do not know.

Beyond Lares, at a distance of sixteen miles, Antoninus places Altieuros, or, as Surita reads it, Altituros. In both places the reading is corrupt; it should be *Altiburos*. This city was in the Proconsular Province. In the frequently mentioned synodical letter, Constantinus is called bishop of the Church of Altoburitana; and in the *Notitia* of the same province appears Vindemius of Altoburus.

Garnerius erroneously wrote *Attieuros*, although *Altieuros* appears in the *Itinerary*, whose words he quotes. He also incorrectly counts Altiburos, or Altoburos, among the cities of Numidia, contrary to the testimony of the ancient synods cited above.

Concerning Ammedera, I find nothing certain that would move me to assign it to the Proconsular Province rather than to Numidia. Since its bishop does not appear in the *Notitia of the Bishops of Numidia*, although 123 bishops are listed there, I believe that Ammedera was the last city of the proconsular diocese, while Theveste, twenty-five miles distant from it, belonged to Numidia.

Yet I do not thereby intend to quarrel with Garnerius because he placed it in Numidia. Rather, I thank him for providing the occasion to investigate the province in which Ammedera was situated. In the course of that investigation I have shown that there were two cities named Musti and two named Lares. From this the *Notitia of the African Church* is seen more accurately, and it becomes clear that the subscriptions of the synods do not disagree among themselves at all concerning the cities of the provinces. The maps of the African diocese can likewise be readily corrected and supplemented.

### QUADRATUS

His see is uncertain. The remaining notes would fit the truth more precisely if he had written them only in these words.

### LUCILLUS

His see is likewise uncertain, unless perhaps *Lucianus of Guira* should be read. For someone of this name is said to have signed the council that preceded the Collation.

There was indeed a bishop of Guira in the province of Numidia, since the *Notitia* mentions Martialis of Guira. He commits several errors. First, he expands and enlarges the diminutive name *Lucillus*, producing *Lucianus*. Again, he gives Guira, or Gira, in Numidia two co-bishops at once, since earlier he had likewise declared another Lucianus to be bishop of Gira. Finally, he thought Lucillus’s city unknown, although Augustine explicitly identifies it in book 22 of *The City of God*, chapter 8.

Speaking there of the miracles performed after Saint Stephen’s relics had been brought to Africa in 416, Augustine says:

> In the castellum of Siniti, which is near the colony of Hippo, Lucillus, bishop of that same place, etc.

In the printed editions the reading is *Synicensi*. But four manuscript codices in the library of the most serene Grand Duke plainly have:

> In the castellum of Siniti.

In his letter 128 to Donatus, proconsul of Africa, Augustine mentions colonists whom Donatus had in the territory of Siniti or Hippo. In the same place the holy Doctor identifies Lucillus’s predecessor, saying:

> My colleague at that time was Maximinus, bishop of the Church of Siniti.

The printed codices likewise read *Synicensis*. But the text should be emended on the basis of letter 163. There, writing to the Donatists, the holy Father says:

> Just now you sent a herald to shout at Siniti: “Whoever communicates with Maximinus, his house shall be burned.”

Maximinus had become Catholic from being a Donatist.

### SABINUS OF TUCCA

There are two cities named Tucca in Africa: one in Mauretania Sitifensis, on the river Serbet; the other nearly in the middle of Numidia, as the Ptolemaic Tables show. The Collation must be understood to concern the bishop of Numidia.

In the council of the rebaptizers, certainly, bishops of both Tuccas gave their judgments: one, Saturninus the Confessor, in the fifty-second place; the other, Honoratus, in the seventy-seventh.

The discussion proceeds through long errors, and under evil auspices he has undertaken a difficult work. First, four Tuccas are mentioned in Africa, and Sabinus was perhaps bishop not of Tucca but of Tunca.

Ptolemy mentions the first Tucca in Caesarian Mauretania. He places the second among the cities of New Numidia; the third between the river Bagradas and Thabraca; the fourth Antoninus locates in Byzacium, or the Proconsular Province. For on the route from Assures to Thenas he says:

> From Assures to Tucca Terebinthina, 15 miles; to Sufes, 25 miles.

Tucca Terebinthina was therefore midway between Assures, a proconsular city, and Byzacian Sufes. To which province it should be assigned is uncertain.

He, however, knows only two Tuccas, placing one on the river Serbet in Mauretania Sitifensis and the other in central Numidia.

Pliny gives the exact location of Tucca in Sitifensis in book 5, chapter 2:

> The town of Tucca, he says, was situated upon the sea and the river Ampsaga.

It was therefore on the borders of the province of Mauretania Sitifensis, which was separated from Numidia by the river Ampsaga. The Peutinger Tables agree, where we read:

> Tucca, boundary of Mauretania and Africa.

Dio Cassius, in book 48, mentions the city of Tucca under T. Sestius, prefect of Numidia, acting for the triumvir Antony.

The *Notitia of Sitifensis* mentions Uzulus of Tucca. Again, he incorrectly places Sabinus’s Tunca in the very middle of Numidia. For Petilianus, the Donatist bishop of Constantinople, said the following in chapter 65 of the Collation:

> For even in the plebs of my present most holy colleague and brother Adeodatus—the mule rubs against the mule—that is, in the city of Milevis, the matter was arranged in such a way that he has one adversary there and another in the city of Tunca, which belongs, of course, to this people from ancient times and appears to have been established two years ago.

This was Sabinus himself. For in chapter 130 of Labbe’s edition we find:

> Sabinus, bishop of Tucca.

The same man said:

> I am present.

Adeodatus, the bishop, said:

> He was ordained in my diocese.

Thus Tunca, or Tucca—I do not wish to draw out an argument with Garnerius over the name—was in the diocese of Milevis.

Milevis, which Antoninus calls Mileum, lay twenty-five miles from Cirta toward Ampsaga. In the Peutinger Tables it is written *Milev. colonia*, and is placed below Rusiccade, which according to Pliny was forty-eight miles from Cirta.

Cirta was not in central Numidia. It was ninety-four miles from Hippo Regius, while Numidia extended beyond Hippo to Thabraca, as far as the eastern boundary of the province, for sixty-four miles. From Milevis to Cuiculum, the westernmost city of Numidia, was a journey of fifty miles; to Thabraca, for those traveling toward the Proconsular Province, 183 miles. These facts are evident from the *Itinerary of Antoninus*.

Therefore Tunca, which was in the diocese of Milevis, was not in central Numidia but above Cirta, toward Sitifensis. The matter is plain to the eye in the Peutinger Tables.

From this I also conclude that Sabinus was bishop of neither of the Tuccas mentioned from the synod of Saint Cyprian. For those cities already had their own bishops before the year 258 of the Christian era, when Cyprian suffered martyrdom. Sabinus’s town, however, was first adorned with episcopal dignity two years before the Collation was held at Carthage—that is, in the year 409—although formerly it was counted within the diocese of the bishop of Milevis.

### FAUSTINUS OF SILLITUM

This is how he is read in the Collation. But in the *Notitia of Numidia* mention is made of Maximus of Sillitum, who died on the journey into exile.

On that same page he makes two bishops named Faustinus of Sillitum present at the synod of Milevis in 416. The error is monstrous, indicating not merely a failure of memory but almost of eyesight—if, indeed, he wrote it while awake.

Meanwhile, marvel that notes composed in exactly the same words are assigned to both Faustini. Certainly what is repeated concerning this Faustinus cannot have been written without care and labor—for what is easier than copying?

### THE OTHER FAUSTINUS

Either this man or the other was of Sillitum; one of the two had an unknown see. Neither this man nor the other was of Sillitum, unless the first Faustinus, whom he had placed in the see of Sillitum, is removed.

Besides, a third Faustinus now emerges in the synod of Milevis, known only to Garnerius and hitherto unknown to everyone else.

These three bishops are indeed listed in the epigraph, even by Garnerius himself: Sabinus, Faustinus, Cresconius. Yet with the same authority by which he founds new cities, places two bishops in one see, and mutilates, enlarges, and changes the names of cities and bishops—with that same authority, I say, he thrusts Faustinus, a bishop newly born in his own house, into the record without a synodical warrant, granting him the right to cast a vote in the Pelagian controversy.

I restrain my impulse, lest the letter turn into a satire. Yet I fear that you may be unable to restrain your laughter when you hear that these things were written by Garnerius not without care, although, lest any error creep into the counting of the bishops, he left the task of rereading the epigraphs for another time.

### CRESCONIUS OF TUBUNIUM

Since five men named Cresconius are inscribed in the synodical letter, we may know which Churches in Numidia were governed by them collectively, but we cannot determine which were governed by each individually.

A certain Cresconius is called of Tubunium in the Collation, while the *Notitia of Numidia* lists Reparatus of Tubunium. Everywhere it should be written *Tubuniensis*, as in the *Notitia*.

In the synod of the rebaptizers, Nemesianus of Tubuna is mentioned in Augustine, book 6 of *On Baptism*, chapter 12; likewise, in letter 70, he names Tubuna. But even this added precaution helps the man little.

Where does he get five Cresconii who attended the Collation in 411 and were still alive in 416, with not one of them dying in the intervening five years? Did the number of five Cresconii not decrease at all over a full five-year period, according to Garnerius, who, writing of Delphinus, announces—as I shall show—that eighteen bishops in one province died within the short span of two years?

Why did at least one of those Cresconii not remain at home? Or why did no bishop of the same name, consecrated within those five years, travel to Milevis?

I add that there was another Tubuna in Caesarian Mauretania, mentioned in the *Notitia*, and that Nemesianus, whom I identified from Cyprian’s synod, sat in one or the other of these cities.

### VICTOR, GIGNANTIUS, AND POSSIDONIUS

Their sees are uncertain.

What harm did Victor, bishop of Cullis, do to him? He is named in chapter 125 of the Collation. Cullu, or Colops, was a large town of Numidia, mentioned by Pliny, Ptolemy, Antoninus, and others in connection with Numidia; its location on the coastal road of that province is shown in the Peutinger Tables.

Solinus, discussing Numidia in chapter 27, says:

> It contains very many distinguished cities; but Cirta stands out, followed by Cullu, comparable in purple dye to the Tyrian fleeces.

So much for him.

### ANTONIUS, PERHAPS ANTONIANUS OF LAMFORTUM

He is mentioned in the Collation. That the Church of Lamfortum belonged to Numidia is proved by the *Notitia of the Bishops of Numidia*, since it lists Felix of Lamfortum among the confessors.

How shamefully he has transformed Antonius into Antonianus! Nowhere has he hallucinated more disastrously. For he has changed a Catholic bishop into a heretic.

In chapter 149 of the Collation, immediately after Januarius and Primianus, the Donatist primates, Antonianus, bishop of Lansortum, is listed. In chapter 163, when he is again named among the Donatist crowd, he said:

> I have no adversary there.

For he was a most wicked Donatist and held the whole diocese zealously for Donatus’s party.

And this chief standard-bearer of the Donatists, like Saul among the prophets, Garnerius places among the Catholic bishops of the synod of Milevis? Is this the immense abundance of scholarship under which Christianus Lupus is scarcely not crushed?

I pass over the fact that the Church of this heretic should not be called Lanfortensis but Lansortensis. That is how it is read in the Collation, whose testimony I just cited; in the *Notitia* Felix is called Lansortensis; and in the synod of Boniface in 525, Florentius is called Lansortensis.

When I hear Garnerius make Antonianus out of Antonius—that is, create a heretic out of a Catholic—I cannot refrain from repeating Jerome’s witty remark in his first apology against Rufinus. Rufinus had published a book by the Arian Eusebius under the title of the martyr Saint Pamphilus:

> Since you have such license, he says, in changing names that you have made Pamphilus out of Eusebius and a martyr out of a heretic, you are a man to be avoided, and especially to be shunned by me, lest, without my knowing it, you suddenly call me Sardanapalus instead of Jerome.

So much for him.

Garnerius could have told the Donatist Antonianus to go hang and read chapter 133 of the Collation, where among the Catholics appears Antonius, bishop of the people of Mutugenna.

Holstenius places this Church in Numidia. Augustine lists a farm called Mutugenna in the territory of Hippo in letter 204.

### INNOCENTIUS OF GERMANIUM

This is how he is read in the Collation. Germanium, however, is a city in Numidia, as is clear from the *Notitia*: among the confessors, it counts Crescentianus, bishop of Germanium.

If Innocentius of Germanium survived from 411 to 416, and no other bishop of this name existed among the 123 bishops of Numidia, he is speaking truthfully.

### PRAESIDIUS AND CRESCENTIUS

Their sees are uncertain. He nowhere takes such secure precautions for himself as when he speaks in this way.

### FELIX OF TUBIUM

This is how he is read in the Collation. But it can be inferred from canon 48 of the Code of the African Church that the Church of Tubium was situated not far from Villaregia and therefore should be placed in Numidia.

You have seen that the opposite conclusion is clearly derived from the same canon. I also said that, on pages 65 and 96, Holstenius confuses the Church of Tubium with that of Tubunium, although, according to chapter 121, Felix of Tubunium and, according to chapter 133, Felix of Tubium—both Catholic bishops—attended the same Collation.

### ANTONIUS OF FUSSALA

This is how it seems to me, although he is not mentioned in the Collation, perhaps because he had not yet been ordained.

By what right, then, did this Antonius, ordained after 411, sit in the synod of Milevis before Donatus, Lampadius, and Delphinus, whom Garnerius soon afterward writes had attended the same Collation? A younger bishop could not precede older bishops, according to canon 53 of the Code of the African Church.

### VICTOR

His see is likewise unknown, as is that of the other Victor mentioned shortly afterward. In writing this about both Victors, he wastes neither oil nor labor, just as he met the same unfortunate fate when assigning the sees of others.

### HONORATUS OF TABENNA

Why should I consider Honoratus, who attended this council of Milevis, to have been of Tabenna rather than of Moctar—or Matar—whose bishop is listed in the Collation, although that see also belonged to Numidia, just as Thabennensis did?

The reason is the sanctity and familiarity of Thabennensis with Augustine. The synod was convened at Augustine’s urging, and, since he regarded it as a matter undertaken for his own cause on account of his zeal for the faith, I think he did not omit his friends from the invitation.

Earlier he says:

> Ortelius suspects that Thabennum is the same as Thabba, which was known to Ptolemy. I do not think the suspicion a trivial one.

Since neither Pliny, Ptolemy, nor Strabo mentions Thabena; indeed, since its episcopal see was omitted by Charles of Saint-Paul and Holstenius, although from Saint Possidius, chapter 30 of the *Life of Saint Augustine*, Honoratus, bishop of Thabenna, is known, Garnerius, amid such silence among the writers, assigns Thabena to Numidia without a witness.

Aulus Hirtius alone gives an excellent account of the town of Thabena and its location in his book *On the African War*:

> The Thabennenses, he says, who had been accustomed to live under Juba’s rule and authority, were settled in the farthest coastal region of his kingdom. After killing the royal garrison, they sent envoys to Caesar. Caesar, approving their plan, sent Marcus Crispus, a tribune, with a cohort, archers, and several artillery pieces, as a garrison to Thebena.

At that time there were three kings in Africa. Juba, great-grandson of Massinissa, possessed the inland region of Numidia from Cirta to Zama, as well as Mauretania Sitifensis as far as the river Mulucha.

Bocchus governed Caesarian Mauretania. Dio, in book 49, says of him:

> He was king of Caesarian Mauretania.

Bogud held power last in Tingitanian Mauretania, as Dio states in book 48.

After Curio, commanding for Caesar in Africa, had been killed with his forces, Pompey and the Senate that followed him had declared Juba king. At that time Bocchus and Bogud were likewise honored by Caesar with royal status, events that occurred, according to Dio in book 41, near the beginning of the civil war.

Juba, however, had earlier held Getulia and Libya by hereditary right. For when Curio was tribune of the plebs, he had attempted, after expelling Juba, to reduce his kingdom to a Roman province, as Caesar testifies in book 2 of *The Civil War*.

According to Dio, book 40, Curio held the tribunate during the consulship of Marcellus and Rufus, two years before Juba killed him.

Pliny writes as follows in book 5, chapter 2, concerning Mauretania Tingitana and Caesariensis:

> For a long time the names of kings prevailed, so that the outermost region was called Bogudiana, and likewise Bocchus’s region, which is now Caesariensis. From it came the great harbor, named from its extent, and a town of Roman citizens; the river Mulucha was the boundary of Bocchus and the Massesylans.

But, as Rufus says, after the Jugurthine War Numidia came under the power of the Roman people. This must be understood of the coastal region of Numidia, which had been the domain of Adherbal, killed by Jugurtha, according to Sallustius, chapter 26 of the *Jugurthine War*. Caesar took Zama and Cirta, the royal cities in the interior of that province, from Juba. Hence that part of Numidia acquired the name of the New Province, according to Appian and Dio.

Therefore, if the Thabennenses lived under Juba’s authority in the farthest coastal region of his kingdom, they were certainly on the coastal shore of Mauretania Sitifensis, not far from the Mulucha, beyond which lay the Caesarian Mauretania of King Bocchus.

Indeed, it is clear from Aulus Hirtius that some part of Mauretania was subject to Juba. He writes that when the king had decided to march with his army into Byzacium to Scipio, he sent Sabura with other forces into Mauretania, lest King Bogud and Sitius, Caesar’s prefect, invade his kingdom from the opposite side.

Hence Florus, book 4, chapter 2, calls Juba “king of Mauretania.”

Hirtius adds near the end of his work:

> Meanwhile Publius Sitius, having routed the army of Sabura, Juba’s prefect, and killed Sabura himself, was traveling through Mauretania with a few men toward Caesar when he happened by chance upon Faustus and Afranius, etc.

At that time Caesar was at Utica in the Proconsular Province.

Thus that part of Mauretania which had formerly obeyed Micipsa and his son Hiempsal, and which afterward, following the division made by the Roman envoys, was handed over to Jugurtha, had come under the power of Juba, son of Hiempsal. Hirtius places the Thabennenses in the farthest coastal region of that kingdom.

You may say that I have pursued this matter with excessive curiosity. But the obscurity of the subject required it. The boundaries of those African kingdoms were often altered by the Romans, as you will know very well from Strabo, book 17, and Dio.

If Garnerius contends that Thabena was in some remote and personally known corner of Numidia on the Mediterranean, he ought at least to name a single witness capable of weakening the credibility of so many testimonies as I have produced.

From this you understand that the suspicion that Thabena should be identified with Ptolemy’s Thabba—a suspicion he considered far from trivial—is completely worthless. For Ptolemy places Thabba in the region situated between the rivers Bagradas and Triton. The former flows into the sea near Utica in the Proconsular Province; the latter near Tacape in Byzacium. During the civil war, no coastal town in that region was held by Juba. All those cities were occupied either by Caesarian forces or by the garrisons of Scipio and Cato, as is perfectly clear from the commentaries of Hirtius, Appian, and Dio.

### DONATUS OF BURITUM, OR OF BURCA

This is how he appears in the Collation. But where that city of Burca was situated, whose Church Donatus governed, is uncertain. The *Notitia of the Bishops of Numidia* mentions Leontius of Burca.

He completely turns everything upside down. In chapter 133 of the Collation we read:

> Donatus, bishop of the people of Buritanum.

But the outstanding craftsman in changing names turns *Buritanensis* into *Burcensis*, so that the man may be counted in Numidia, although the Church of Buritanum belongs to an uncertain province.

Again, earlier, in his notes on Servus Dei, he had said that this man had sat at Bura at the time of the Collation, and that in that city, later, in 484, as the *Notitia* records, there was a bishop whom he calls Leontius of Burensis.

Yet now he asserts that this same Leontius was the successor, after several intervening bishops, of Donatus of Buritanum, or Burca, who attended the same Collation.

I suspect that the Church of Buritanum belonged to the Proconsular Province. For in act 2 of the council of Saint Martin, among the bishops of that province, the synodical letter is signed by Cresciturus of Busitum, who perhaps should be called Buritanus. Or perhaps, conversely, Donatus should be called Busitanus. I leave the matter undecided.

### PETRUS, PRAESIDIUS, AND CRESCONIUS

Their sees are uncertain.

This sixth Cresconius came late to Garnerius. After assigning sees in Numidia to the five Cresconii previously named in the epigraph—having even transferred two cities, Titulus from the Proconsular Province and Tubium from Mauretania Sitifensis, into the census of Numidia—he had no city left in that province, or even in the neighboring provinces, to which he could send the sixth Cresconius as bishop.

I pity the fate of this prelate. After Garnerius distributed at will among the other Cresconii all the sacred governorships of the cities of Africa, he remains a bishop of uncertain see.

### LAMPADIUS OF TISEDIUM

This is indeed how he appears in the Collation, but he should rather be called *Tididitanus*. For the *Notitia of the Bishops of Numidia* mentions Abundius of Tididitum.

Indeed, the text of the *Notitia* may perhaps have to be corrected from the Collation. For in chapter 198 the Collation also mentions, among the Donatists, Donatus, bishop of Tisedium. His name should certainly be inserted in chapter 135, where Lampadius of Tisedium’s adversary is not read, a lacuna existing there.

Sallustius excellently identifies this city in chapter 62 of the *Jugurthine War*. He reports that, while Metellus, commander of the Roman army, was waging war in this very province against Jugurtha, king of Numidia, Jugurtha himself was summoned to Tisidium to negotiate peace.

Therefore Lampadius should be called bishop of Tisidium, or Tisiditum, not of Tididitum.

Charles of Saint-Paul omitted Lampadius’s city of Tisidium; Holstenius assigned it to an uncertain province. Yet it is clear from Sallustius, and from this epigraph in which Lampadius, bishop of the same town, is listed among the Numidian bishops, that it was in Numidia.

## DELPHINUS

He governed a church whose name is uncertain; nevertheless, it was near Constantina, as may be inferred from chapter 65 of the Collation, where the Donatist Petilianus said in reply: “In my people”—that is, in the city of Constantinensis—“I have Fortunatus as my adversary; [Col. 0314B] but in the midst of my diocese I now have one installed—or rather, they themselves have one—named Delphinus.” Augustine mentions this Delphinus in Letter 158, and elsewhere.

Here the sequence of episcopal entries comes to an end. In this matter I should certainly have wished to agree with Garnerius, so that, after having wrestled with him for a long time in the literary arena, I might leave the contest with friendly feelings toward him; and, just as dolphins indicate an approaching storm to sailors, so this Delphinus might, conversely, calm the geographical tempest thus far stirred up—one in which Garnerius came close to shipwreck—by introducing tranquility. Yet once again waves of difficulties rise up. The matter must be revisited from a deeper point, although briefly.
