In the year 411, Petilianus is said to have addressed the judge Marcellinus in the Collation, chapter 165, in these words, when several Catholic bishops [Col. 0314C] boasted that they did not have a Donatist bishop in their own cities:

“For it seems to be an advantage to those who have shown that they possess many against our people throughout this province, if in the province of Numidia we do not show that they possess none at all, or at least that they possess them only in rare places.”

Although these words were spoken emphatically by a former heretical advocate, it is nevertheless certain that the Donatist heresy—which, as Augustine says in Letter 134 to Pammachius, had arisen in the midst of consular Numidia—had so overrun the cities of that province that at that time many of them had only a Donatist bishop, without a Catholic rival or Catholic prelate.

The churches occupied especially by Donatist bishops alone are listed in the Collation: Lansortensis, chapter 143; Idassensis, chapter 182; Legensis, Lamiggensis, and Rotariensis, [Col. 0314D] chapter 187; Tibilitana, chapter 197; Rusticianensis, chapter 198; Lambiritensis, chapter 206; and many others, as may be clearly inferred from the frequent interventions of Aurelius, bishop of Macomadia in Numidia.

Again, at the time of the Collation, sixty-four Catholic sees were vacant throughout the six African provinces, chapter 215. At least ten of these were in Numidia, since only five bishops were counted in the province of Tripolitana. After the Collation had been completed, the defeated Donatist bishops, expelled from the cities by the emperor Honorius, were forced to change their residence, as is evident from the Theodosian Code, laws 54 and 55, *On Heretics*, issued under the consuls Constantius and Constans in the year 414.

At that time Catholic bishops were consecrated in all the cities of Africa where heretics had previously administered the sacred rites, [Col. 0315A] and new prelates were assigned to sees that had been left vacant. Thus in Numidia at least twenty bishops were inaugurated shortly after the year 411, all of whom Delphinus had already preceded as bishop from the year 411, before the Collation.

Therefore, if this is the same man who is listed last in the heading of the synod of Milevis, none of those twenty prelates ordained after 411 attended the synod of the year 416. This, at least, is what Garnerius alone has persuaded himself to believe.

Moreover, in the Collation, chapter 65, the same Petilianus said of Sabinus, bishop of Tunca: “He appears to have been appointed two years ago.” Therefore, in the year 409 Sabinus was the first bishop to sit at Tunca. In the same passage Petilianus testifies that Delphinus had now been installed as bishop in the diocese [Col. 0315B] of Constantinensis—that is, in 411, as I have just noted.

But since eighteen bishops are named in the heading between Sabinus and Delphinus, if this Delphinus is the one mentioned in chapter 65 of the Collation, Garnerius must affirm that within two years eighteen bishops died in the single province of Numidia, and that an equal number were substituted for them—those who are read in the middle between Sabinus and Delphinus. Without records, without a witness, I shall not believe this.

Indeed, the man who transported so many new cities into Africa may perhaps have imported some plague into Numidia, one that spread so widely within two years as to destroy so great a multitude of bishops. Nor do I believe that the Numidians would complain to Garnerius about so many bishops being removed in so short a time, since, with Mopta and the other Macomodia newly established in that province, and with the cities of Tituli, Tubiae, [Col. 0315C] Girba, Dionysiana, Zella, Ruspina, and others—previously assigned to neighboring provinces or to a province uncertain—transferred into his diocese, he has bound the Numidians so closely to himself that they may count it as gain that eighteen bishops were immediately removed by this “Polioctiste” of his, since by the addition of so many towns the boundaries of the province have been extended far and wide.

You have here, distinguished sir, my judgment concerning Garnerius’s notes on both the heading of the letters of the Council of Carthage and that of the Council of Milevis. In this criticism, as they say, with a light hand, I have weeded them over again.

Indeed, when you read that this writer has confused so many cities of Africa, been unaware of many, recently created some, transferred very many into the jurisdiction of another diocese, altered [Col. 0315D] at will the names of bishops and their cities, sometimes placed two Catholic prelates over one and the same town, represented bishops long dead as present at synods, and imposed Donatists upon us as orthodox Fathers—when, I say, you read these monstrosities, you will rightly declare that when Garnerius was sending to Africa the work which, he writes, no one had previously attempted, one might have applied to him the saying of Augustus, who, according to Macrobius, *Saturnalia* II, chapter 4, said to his rather forgetful nomenclator: “Take letters of introduction, because you know no one there.”

Our own Pliny of Verona writes in Book XV, chapter 18, that fresh figs were brought from the gardens of the Carthaginians to Rome in only a three-day voyage, and that Cato displayed them to the senators, thereby almost forcibly extracting from them a decree of the senate for the destruction of that rival city, always hostile to the Latin name, despite their reluctance. [Col. 0316A]

Accordingly, I now place before your eyes these fresh fruits of geography, which, at your command, I have plucked while spending a little time in Africa with a censor’s pen, so that you may decide that the many cities recently constructed throughout Africa by Garnerius should not merely be leveled to the ground, but, since they are entirely aerial, scattered by a single breath of the mouth.

Yet he himself testifies that he undertook with no small care and labor a work that no one had attempted until then. On these words of Garnerius I should like to play in this rough little poem:

> The MERCHANT’S work, enriched with wares so vast,  
> Was Garnerius’s care and labor unsurpassed.  
> He builds up cities, tears some from their seat,  
> And bids them race through Libya’s kingdoms fleet.  
> He rules the dead; when he sends them to the vote,  
> Whom black death long ago from life removed. [Col. 0316B]  
> Orpheus yields to him; Amphion’s fame is less:  
> What he once did, this man does oftener yet.

Here, however, I should like to warn you not to think that I mean by this to detract in any way from Garnerius’s more successful erudition in his other writings. I esteem him so highly that if his commentaries on Pelagian matters had preceded the history of that same heresy which I published this year at Padua, I would immediately—as I sincerely affirm and solemnly swear—have thrown my own writings entirely into a corner. For many things which I had originally thought I would be the first to publish on that subject, he has achieved so successfully that, beyond doubt, I would have been accused of plagiarism if, after Garnerius’s volume had appeared, I had dared to repeat the same things.

I admit that I disagree with him on certain points; and, to say nothing of other matters, I cannot approve his emendation [Col. 0316C] by which he corrects the text of the letters of the Pelagian bishops. For in Dissertation 5 he quotes from papers found by the great Sirmond in Verona, a city of Venetia, within the diocese of the patriarch of Aquileia, and communicated to him, a statement of faith of the Pelagians, which he says was sent by Julian of Eclanum to the apostolic see. Near its end we read:

“Furthermore, holy and venerable brother and father Augustine, we have thought it necessary to answer this also.”

Since it is certain, as he rightly proves, that they did not write these words to Saint Augustine of Hippo, he thought that an error had entered the ancient manuscript, and that Pope Zosimus ought to be substituted for Augustine. For Garnerius [Col. 0316D] clearly demonstrates that the Pelagian bishops were replying there to their own primate, by whom they had been ordered through letters to condemn that heresy.

Yet the learned man is mistaken. At that time Augustine of Aquileia was a celebrated primate of Venetia, Istria, both Noricums, and Raetia I. Hear Henry Palladius, than whom no one has written the affairs of the people of Aquileia more carefully or elegantly:

“After Chromatius, Augustine was elected patriarch, at the time when the other Augustine, bishop of Hippo, was burying the madness of the heretics in Africa beneath floods of eloquence and learning.”

In the patriarchal palace at Udine, epitaphs of all the primates of Aquileia are read, anciently inscribed in larger-than-uncial characters. Moreover, after Chromatius, this epigram is inscribed to Augustine:

[Col. 0317A]

> **AUGUSTINE, WHEN THE CITY OF ROME HAD BEEN LAID WASTE BY THE GOTHS, RAISED THE DISMAYED SPIRITS OF THE PEOPLE OF AQUILEIA BY FASTS AND SACRED SUPPLICATIONS, TO IMPLORE DIVINE HELP.**

Palladius writes there that Augustine obtained the see of Aquileia in the year 414 and left it with his life in 422, with Adelphus given to him as successor. You know that I noted Ughelli’s error in placing both primates in the wrong position in Book II of my *History of Pelagius*, chapter 12.

When Zosimus condemned the Pelagians in 418, he sent encyclical letters to the primates of Aquileia and Milan, so that they might publish them in their dioceses. Shortly before this, after the Origenists had been condemned at Rome by Pope Anastasius, Chromatius of Aquileia, Augustine’s predecessor, and Venerius of Milan had likewise, upon receiving letters from the apostolic see, arranged through their suffragan bishops for the Origenists to be proscribed in their respective [Col. 0317B] dioceses, as Jerome testifies in Book II of his *Apology against Rufinus*.

Thus Augustine, primate of Aquileia, sent the decree of the apostolic see against the Pelagians, together with letters, to the bishops of his provinces. Some of these, since they were held by Pelagian errors, gave the aforementioned statement of faith to Augustine the primate.

How deeply the Pelagian heresy had taken root in the diocese of the primate of Aquileia, especially among the clergy, is evident from the letters of Septimius of Altinum to Saint Leo the Great and from Leo’s replies to the primate of Aquileia. I have discussed these matters more fully in the same book on the Pelagian heresy.

I return to Garnerius. In publishing his notes, he hoped to win some favor with learned readers; [Col. 0317C] but he calculated so disastrously in this matter that it seems he should count it as gain if he can obtain from his readers pardon for so thick a mass of errors.

You must therefore admit that learned men sometimes, to use your expression, “play tragedy,” and lavish too much flattery upon their own writings, confidently and boldly putting into the eyes and hands of men things which it would be in their own interest to lock away in a chest and leave for the moths to gnaw.

And, speaking of myself—not because I would dare to count myself among the learned, but because, as the poet says, I am numbered among the crowd of the uneducated who write volumes everywhere—I believed that I had treated chronology in my *History of Pelagius* more carefully than others. But I immediately understood how greatly my opinion had deceived me: for right at the threshold I stumbled into a chronological [Col. 0317D] anticipation.

On the first page I wrote, with Baronius, that Saint Athanasius died in the year 372; indeed—and I say this with shame—while praising the paschal letter of Proterius of Alexandria to Leo the Great, although it is plainly deduced there from the era of Diocletian and the paschal cycle that his death ought to have been assigned to the following year.

Strict critics will find many errors in my books, and their procession awaits me. When they show me that I have been mistaken, I shall thank them most warmly, since through their care and labor—not, I will not say more learned, but less ignorant—I shall become. For I often repeat Seneca’s saying from chapter 18 of *On the Happy Life*: “When I reproach vices, I reproach my own above all.”

You, most distinguished sir, will escape this danger [Col. 0318A] safely. Like the great philosopher Socrates, you not only commit nothing to writing—I will not say that—but, as I have so often been accustomed to marvel in you, supported by an exceptionally retentive memory, once you have dismissed all the auxiliary supports of the same kind, you attach not even a single word to the pen. You devour volumes; like Aspendius’s dog, for yourself and the Muses, you avoid the hazard of public judgment, and are not tickled by any pathological urge to write.

For this reason I consider you most fortunate: far from the judgments of the envious, you have propagated your name to posterity with so much greater distinction by your exceptional services to men of letters, inasmuch as it is more worthy to extend one’s name through deeds rather than words.

Many volumes of considerable size, printed by French and Dutch presses and dedicated to you competitively as a mark of honor, as well as so many eulogies inscribed to you in their books by learned Italians everywhere, have been written that no future person devoted to the liberal arts will ever be able to remain unaware that Antonio Magliabecchi lived and deserved so well of the republic of letters that only the final day—which, by the worst fate of mortals, brings deep oblivion upon all books and letters—seems capable of putting an end to your name. [Col. 0318B]

For my part, I shall omit no service of gratitude by which I may in some small measure repay your kindness. For you not only approached me first with the most learned and humane letters; you also requested the assistance of the most illustrious senator and knight Ferrante Capponi—distinguished by the nobility of his lineage, his expertise in affairs, his knowledge of both laws, and his considerable favor with the prince—so that I might be summoned to Etruria as professor of sacred learning.

That man, generous beyond the power of even a prayer to imagine in granting favors, [Col. 0318C] consented. For he knew that the serene Cardinal Leopoldo—whose name the world reveres as a great increase to the glory of the Medici and as that of an incomparable cultivator and Maecenas of letters and men of letters—had nothing more at heart than that sacred history, which seemed to suffer exile among our people, should be honorably welcomed back into its homeland in Etruria.

Thus, through the efforts of the most eminent senator, it came about that the serene grand duke of Etruria, Cosimo, took Ecclesiastical History by the royal hand—history which, excluded from the public assemblies of the wise, had been lodging in Italy under a poor roof with certain reclusive men—and introduced it into the Pisan Athenaeum, that is, into his royal seat of all the sciences, and inaugurated an eminent chair for it.

Since that most wise and prudent [Col. 0318D] prince understood perfectly that history alone transmits the names of great kings to posterity with praise, he wished to win its favor by so noble a judgment and so generous a munificence that, when the final day—known only to distant descendants—shall bring him into heaven, he may live forever through the gift of history in the desires of the Etruscan people and in the minds of all peoples who know letters beyond barbarism.

Although his great reverence toward the divine, his rare love for his subjects, his exceptional cultivation of letters, and his careful and fortunate administration of government have already made him renowned throughout the world and set him up as a great example for those who rule scepters, nevertheless, through the grateful service of history he will be carried beyond the age on the lips of men, and will travel through the same expanses of time as the knowledge of his virtues and learning. [Col. 0319A]

Yet while everyone congratulates Ecclesiastical History on its fortunate destiny under so great a prince, I alone grieve over this: he appointed me, adorned with no equipment of sacred learning, as the first interpreter of that History in the Pisan Academy. For I fear that, although the majesty of history is sublime, it may appear diminished through the fault of its interpreter.

Nevertheless, you alone, most learned in every respect, lessen my immense distress, as you periodically send me books from your extremely rich library, which occupies the entrance hall, rooms, and every corner of your house, so that, strengthened by the resources of so great a learning, I may not lose heart.

Meanwhile, I beg you to commend me [Col. 0319B] to the serene lord who loves you and letters equally, so that, supported by the patronage of so great a prince, I may undertake the office entrusted to me under a happy and favorable auspice. Farewell, and love me as you are accustomed to do.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE SAME LETTER

### Letter 175

The inscriptions of this letter and the following one have been explained at length by the most eminent cardinal, against John Garnerius. But since he said nothing about the letters themselves, we shall offer a few observations concerning matters relevant to the teaching they contain.

Although—so that no one may accuse our candor—there are many things in the teaching of Pelagius and his followers that we reject, his opponents nevertheless did not conduct themselves or reason in such a way that we can approve everything on their side either. He was indeed condemned and attacked with reproaches [Col. 0319C] by everyone, including those to whom his doctrines were unknown, once he had been denounced by the African bishops. But no human condemnation can make what was true become false, and conversely no human praise can make truth arise from error.

Moreover, it is well known that in great assemblies important matters are judged under the influence of strong emotions. Nor was it easy for all those African bishops to distinguish truth from falsehood in such a difficult matter. Some of them are said not even to have been able to write, *Collation of Carthage* I, chapter 133; and, apart from their ability in speaking, I do not see what exceptional qualities they possessed, considering the standards of their age.

I would not say these things if I did not see them fighting by numbers and authority much more than by arguments.

### Ibid., § 2

“They”—Coelestius and Pelagius—[Col. 0319D] “attempt by their condemnable arguments to leave no room for the grace of God by not defending free choice, but rather exalting it in sacrilegious pride, although it is through that grace that we are Christians.”

I do not understand how they could have exalted free choice in pride, and indeed against God, when they confessed that he was the creator of human nature and of all its faculties, so that human beings owed him whatever good they possessed and depended upon him as upon the lord of all things.

They held that, although man was not by nature a sinner at all, he had fallen and continued to fall into sin through his own fault, not through God’s fault—as though God had denied him what was necessary to avoid sin. Nevertheless, they said that God wished to forgive his sins and grant him eternal life, although he deserved the opposite in every respect [Col. 0320A], provided that he obeyed the Gospel, since God had sent him, out of sheer grace, the Savior Jesus Christ, who would announce that grace of God to him and mercifully recall him to his duty.

And, lest man consider what Christ announced insufficiently credible, they said that Christ had added miracles by which he would establish faith in himself even among the obstinate; that he also supplied an inward assistance by which he enlightens human minds, although he does not necessarily lead them to believe; and that through baptism human beings are regenerated and become children of God.

Dionysius Petavius shows that Pelagius said this in many passages of his *History of Pelagian Dogmas*, which is volume III of his *Theological Dogmas*, Amsterdam edition.

Pelagius said only that it depended upon man whether he could use or abuse so many divine benefits properly. Although [Col. 0320B] those who abuse God’s benefits are certainly to be blamed to the highest degree, if we wish to be strict judges of our nature, those who use them properly are not greatly to be praised. For the fact that they can do this is wholly a divine gift, and it is not surprising that they should prefer to be happy forever rather than miserable.

It is indeed mad and impious, when God offers life and death, to choose death; but surely it does not require extraordinary wisdom and virtue to prefer life. Who would be proud of the wisdom and discernment by which he preferred living to dying?

Thus, according to Pelagius’s view, human beings have reason to give thanks to God, but not reason to take pleasure in themselves or applaud themselves. It was an exaggeration of African or Punic rhetoric to say that he exalted free choice into sacrilegious pride.

How easily Pelagius could have pressed the opposing [Col. 0320C] side with odious consequences: that God commands impossibilities, punishes human beings with eternal penalties because they failed to accomplish impossibilities, and other arguments of that kind, by which man is plainly excused and the entire blame is cast upon God.

They thought it a matter of Christian humility that God should be made the author of every good—and rightly so. But this ought not to be understood in such a way that, in the same act, he became an unjust judge, which is most insulting to God.

Indeed, moved by these considerations, later ages slipped into Pelagius’s opinion, which they also attributed to Augustine, assigning Pelagius’s own little works to him, because they could not persuade themselves that so great a man—as they believed him to have been by reputation—could have digested consequences of that kind.

Certainly, if those African Fathers had been what they wished to appear, after carefully weighing the serious [Col. 0320D] difficulties in the Augustinian position, they would have said that the matter was not clear to them rather than condemning, through condemnation after condemnation being sent in every direction, a doctrine they did not understand.

They continue with these words:

“By this grace our free choice truly becomes free, when it is liberated from the domination of carnal desires, as the Lord says: ‘If the Son sets you free, then you will be truly free.’ This assistance is obtained by faith, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

The Pelagians did not doubt that human beings would be freed from sins by divine grace, provided that they used it properly. But they thought that people could abuse it, and furthermore that no one was so enslaved to sin that this grace could not rouse him to flee that servitude. [Col. 0321A]

But what do the good African Fathers mean when they add that “this assistance is obtained by faith”? For the assistance obtained by faith is not the grace by which we become Christians, which precedes faith rather than following it. When we believe and obtain something from God through faith, we are already Christians.

Those words have the odor of semi-Pelagianism, or something similar. Therefore, either those good men did not yet understand Augustine’s teaching sufficiently, or this is an addition, since, as the Benedictines note, it is absent from two manuscript codices.

These men assert, as we have learned from brothers who read their books, that God’s grace is to be understood as consisting in the fact that he constituted and created human nature in such a way that, through its own will, it could fulfill God’s law [Col. 0321B], whether that law was naturally inscribed in the heart or given in writing.

They likewise say that the law itself belongs to God’s grace, because God gave it to human beings as an aid.

If we believe the author of the *Predestined*, at the first Council of Carthage, held five years earlier, Coelestius offered his books, in which he explained the Pelagian doctrines. If this were true, we could hardly fail to wonder that those books were not preserved at Carthage, so that it might be clear how justly he had been condemned and so that, when needed, they might be brought forward against him.

But this is scarcely credible, since here the Fathers of Carthage condemn Coelestius without having examined his books. It is also astonishing that grave bishops pronounced such harsh judgments against an absent man without reading his books and merely reciting the letters of his accusers. [Col. 0321C]

No one at all disposed toward fairness can defend such a method of judgment, especially since difficult questions were being discussed, in which it was extremely easy to misunderstand the opinion of someone who had not been heard.

The synod would therefore have acted more fairly and prudently if it had postponed its judgment until after the Pelagian writings had been read.

As for what is here taken from those writings, that creation and the law are gifts of God cannot be denied, since these are by far God’s greatest benefits. If God had not created us endowed with reason, we could not obey him or enjoy blessedness. And if he had not promulgated the evangelical law, our duty would have remained insufficiently known to us, and we would not possess the greatest incentives to believe or the most excellent rewards.

I truly do not understand why the African [Col. 0321D] Fathers speak contemptuously of these great graces of God, unless some kind of inspiration is added—one which cannot be resisted and which is granted only to a few.

The sacred writings are filled with references to the former benefits, and speak of them so clearly that those who believe Scripture cannot deny them without madness. But the African Fathers vainly strive to prove the latter, producing nothing except passages either wholly unrelated to what they are considering or, at most, ambiguous.

You may also justly regret this in their letter: they nowhere define their grace or discuss the ambiguity of the term, as though Scripture could be read only in the single sense they desired and as though it were sufficient to produce passages in which the word appeared in order to prove what they believed.

This is suitable, I admit, for arousing hostility, but it is by no means [Col. 0322A] candid or well adapted to proving what they wish among people who love truth alone.

### Ibid., § 3

“But they absolutely refuse to acknowledge that grace by which, as has been said, we are Christians, and of which the Apostle is the preacher when he says: ‘I delight in the law of God according to the inner man; but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord.’ They do not wish to acknowledge it at all, yet they do not even dare to oppose it openly.”

But in Paul’s words, what else is the grace of God than God’s mercy or God’s beneficence? No one will ever prove the contrary from the natural force or ordinary usage of the word.

Pelagius did not deny that human beings [Col. 0322B] were rescued from sin by God’s beneficence. But he denied that this happened through some inward inspiration which could not be resisted and without which all the other benefits of God would be useless.

The African prelates ought to have expressed their own position and Pelagius’s position clearly, so that, according to their judgment, it might plainly be evident what was to be accepted and what condemned.

But they would have stirred up the greater part of Christians against themselves if they had openly stated what they believed. For before that time, and before the definitions of the African councils, people had not thought differently about grace from Pelagius.

The Fathers of the Council of Carthage continue:

“But what else are they doing when they persist in persuading animal human beings, who do not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, to undertake and accomplish righteousness and fulfill God’s [Col. 0322C] commandments, while claiming that human nature alone is sufficient for them?”

But God’s commandments are not of such a kind that they are wholly devoid of power to move human minds. Their perfect agreement with right reason and with the very constitution of human nature, the splendid rewards attached to them, the miracles by which faith in them was established, the examples of holy men, and especially of Christ, who observed them, the miseries and calamities of this life—which show that the blessedness we desire so greatly is sought in it in vain—and other considerations of this kind are all exceedingly powerful in recalling people, gradually at least, to a better way of life.

“But the animal man,” you will say, “does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God,” as Paul teaches in 1 Corinthians 2:14, the passage to which the African prelates are referring.

Indeed, he does not admit them—*οὐ δέχεται*, that is, he does not [Col. 0322D] assent to them—while he remains animal and follows the impulse of brute creatures, seeking only present and tangible things.

But nothing prevents the animal man, once he has understood and considered the excellence of the Gospel, from eventually ceasing to be such.

Furthermore, I should like to ask the African Fathers whether God does not command animal human beings to cease obeying their animal desires; whether he does not punish those who neglect his commandments and therefore judge that they cannot be excused.

If this is so—and no Christian will deny it—then such people must either possess or be able to obtain whatever is necessary for obedience. Otherwise it would be unjust to command them to perform something for which they had been deprived of the necessary resources.

I shall add no more. For all who have touched upon these controversies [Col. 0323A] know what is usually said concerning this matter.

But let us hear the African bishops as they show that human nature alone is insufficient for obeying the Gospel, surrounded and supported by the circumstances mentioned earlier.

“They do not attend to what is written: ‘The Spirit helps our weakness’ (Romans 8:26); and: ‘It is not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy’ (Romans 9:16); and that we are all one in Christ, but individually members of one another, possessing different gifts according to the grace that has been given to us (Romans 12:5); and: ‘By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been empty, but I have labored more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God with me’ (1 Corinthians 15:10); and: ‘Thanks be to God, who has given us [Col. 0323B] the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ’ (ibid., 57); and: ‘Not that we are competent to think anything as from ourselves, but our competence is from God’ (2 Corinthians 3:5); and: ‘We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may be of God and not from us’ (2 Corinthians 4:7); and innumerable passages of the same kind. If we wished to gather them from all the Scriptures, time would not be sufficient.”

It must be remembered that all these passages are produced to prove the grace we have described: that is, an inward and necessary inspiration by which we believe in Christ. There is no doubt that the Fathers of the synod regarded these as the chief passages by which Pelagianism could be overthrown.

Yet not one of them proves what they wish. This was the manner of citing Scripture in those centuries, when the sounds of individual words were regarded much more seriously [Col. 0323C] than the meaning of passages considered within the whole sequence of the discourse.

As soon as the sound of the words did not appear wholly alien to the matter at hand, the case was considered settled and the disputed point proved. Clearly, declaiming and pouring out whatever came to one’s mouth before a populace which, should it happen to disagree with the declaimer, was to be excommunicated, was much easier than devoting oneself seriously to criticism.

The Spirit who helps our weakness, of whom Paul speaks, is the Spirit who is already in believers and helps them to offer their prayers properly before God.

“It is not of him who wills or runs, but of God who shows mercy,” refers to the sending of God’s word to some people in order to call them to knowledge of him. But what does this have to do with an inspiration given to individuals?

The grace according to which there are different gifts is not the grace by which individual believers are converted to God, but God’s varied beneficence, by which he had granted different gifts [Col. 0323D] to different people—or his ordinary providence, together with the extraordinary outpouring of spiritual gifts.

The grace of God by which Paul was what he was—that is, an apostle—is God’s mercy and generosity, by which he equipped him with the gifts necessary to sustain that office. No one has ever denied that God, through Jesus Christ, gave us victory over sin, or that we have reason to thank him for it. But Scripture nowhere teaches that this occurred through an inward and inescapable inspiration.

Certainly, the sufficiency of all Christians for thinking anything consistent with the Gospel comes from God. For who does not know that the Gospel is owed not to human ingenuity [Col. 0324A] but to God?

But the sufficiency of the apostles especially, for sustaining the office to which they had been called, was not human but divine.

Finally, the treasure in earthen vessels of which Paul speaks consists of apostolic gifts, as is clear from the context.

If one’s eyes are not cast upon the cited passages with complete carelessness, one will discover that everything we have said is most true and evident. From this it may be understood that those good African Fathers were poorly qualified interpreters of Scripture, and consequently that their mere authority ought to carry little weight.

### The Same, § 4

Let Your Holiness consider—and sympathize with us in our pastoral concern—how pestilential and destructive to Christ’s sheep is the necessary consequence of these men’s sacrilegious arguments: that we ought not to pray either that we “not enter into temptation,” which the Lord both warned the disciples about and included in the prayer He taught, or that our faith “not fail,” which He Himself testified that He had prayed for the Apostle Peter.

This does not necessarily follow. For that petition in the Lord’s Prayer, or Christ’s prayers for Peter, do not mean what the Fathers imply, as though they intended this: “O God, by an inward impulse which we cannot resist, cause us to overcome temptation.” Why, indeed, could God not prevent us from succumbing to temptation by diminishing and moderating the temptation itself, so that it does not exceed our strength? He knows how strong or weak we are better than we do, and He can remove those things to which we would scarcely be equal if they were present; once they have been removed, we remain steadfast in piety with ease.

“If these things,” the Africans nevertheless say, “are placed within the power of nature and the choice of the will, who does not see that they are vainly sought from God and deceitfully prayed for, when in prayer we ask for what is already obtainable by the sufficient powers of our nature as it has now been constituted?”

But even if Pelagius had perhaps conceded that no temptation so atrocious could befall a nature enlightened and corrected by the Gospel that it could not resist it, he nevertheless did not deny—and could not deny—that those placed in danger should flee to God’s help, even extraordinary help, for two reasons.

First, although by the powers once granted by God and confirmed by divine promises we can resist temptation, we can also fall into it. This happens less readily when we are aided by some unusual assistance from God—provided that it is not an irresistible impulse. Who, when in danger, would not wish for himself not only what is entirely necessary, but also the greatest possible strength, so that he might escape from it more easily and securely?

Second, among the very powers that God generously grants Christians as sufficient, nothing prevents unusual aids from being supplied according to the magnitude of the dangers. Therefore Pelagius could not rightly be accused as though his teaching had abolished the practice of prayer.

### The Same, § 5

Their contention also contradicts our benedictions, so that we seem to say in vain over the people whatever we ask from the Lord: that by living rightly and piously they may please Him; or what the Apostle prays for the faithful when he says:

“I bend my knees before God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ . . . that He may grant you, according to the riches of His glory, to be strengthened with power through His Spirit.”

If, then, in blessing the people we wish to say, “Grant them, Lord, to be strengthened with power through Your Spirit,” their argument contradicts us, asserting that free will is denied if we ask God for what lies within our power. “For if we wish to be strengthened with power,” they say, “we can do so by that capacity of nature which we do not now receive, but received when we were created.”

As though, apart from creation, there were not innumerable things that we can ask from God so that we may run the course of piety steadfastly—and yet which do not constitute an irresistible impulse! We must always devote ourselves to salvation with fear and trembling, because although God works in us both willing and accomplishing, we can misuse every aid. Nevertheless, we have less to fear when God removes from us many things that could weaken our virtue in this life.

Fear of this kind, and invocation of such divine aid, are entirely compatible with free will. Here, in Pelagius’ name, we could object to the Africans that, according to their view, nothing could have been requested from God, since He had determined from eternity to deny the reprobate what was necessary, but to grant the elect everything, even without their asking. Yet we must acknowledge that people do not always conduct themselves consistently with their doctrines; nor should they be accused except on account of what they actually do.

### The Same, § 6

They also deny that infants should be baptized on account of the salvation granted through Christ the Savior, and thus, by this deadly doctrine, they kill them eternally, while promising that even if they are not baptized, and so forth. Yet later they admit that Coelestius confessed that through Christ’s baptism infants are redeemed.

“But many,” they say, “who are reported to be, or to have been, their disciples do not cease to affirm these evils, by which they attempt to overturn the foundations of the Christian faith, in every way they can.”

I do not know what Pelagius judged concerning each of the questions that might be raised about baptism. But this I do know: it cannot in any way be proved from the New Testament that baptism is necessary for the salvation of infants, or that Christ commanded them to be baptized. Thus the Africans could call “foundations of the faith” only absurdly those matters about which the New Testament is profoundly silent.

Nevertheless, as I have already said elsewhere, I do not condemn infant baptism. If we wish, it may be understood not only as the parents’ profession of faith, but also as a symbol of the infants’ redemption—not from sin, of which they are free, but from the vanity to which they are subject along with the rest of creation, and from which Christ will free them in the final resurrection.

### Letter 176, § 2

Although the Lord taught us to say, “Forgive us our debts,” and so forth, these men say that a person can, in this life, once he has learned God’s commandments, attain such perfection of righteousness by free will alone, without the help of the Savior’s grace, that it is no longer necessary for him to say, “Forgive us,” and so forth.

Yet they did not say that anyone had lived entirely free from sins throughout his whole life, except Christ alone. It therefore followed, according to their view, that no one existed who ought not to say, “Forgive us,” and so forth. For until the end of life we all need to ask forgiveness for sins once committed.

This, then, is an odious accusation, as is the following: “But what follows—‘Do not lead us into temptation’—must not be understood as though we ought to ask for divine help so that, when tempted, we do not fall into sin; rather, this lies within our power.”

Although, according to Pelagius’ view, heavenly graces compel no one to perform his duty, they nevertheless help considerably in temptation, and without them people would succumb in severe temptations. Therefore, as he thought, those aids were to be requested from God.

Accordingly, the Numidian bishops add against him in vain, as though the Apostle had said in vain: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy”; and: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it.”

The Lord would likewise have said in vain to the Apostle Peter, “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail,” and to all His followers, “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation,” if the whole matter lay within human power.

We discussed the first passage, Romans 9, in connection with the preceding letter. The second, 1 Corinthians 10:13, is plainly contrary to Augustine’s opinion, since Paul teaches that God helps the faithful not so that, driven by an irresistible impulse, they may endure temptation, but so that they may be able to endure it—the only thing God promised. We have also dealt previously with the remaining passages.

### The Same

They wickedly presume that even young children and infants, although they receive none of the sacraments of Christian grace, will possess eternal life, thereby nullifying what the Apostle said:

“Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin, death; and thus it passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12);

and elsewhere:

“For as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

I had thought that in the passage from Romans 5 one should read, “death passed through,” since the word θάνατος (*thanatos*, “death”) appears in all the Greek manuscripts. Elsewhere, too, Augustine incorrectly cites this passage in this form, as in Book 4, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, no. 7. From this omission he also argues incorrectly.

The meaning of the passage, however, is: “Just as through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin, death, so also death passed to all human beings, because all sinned.” For οὕτως καὶ, “so also,” is equivalent to καὶ οὕτως, “and so,” as in Luke 17:24, 26 and James 2:26.

Furthermore, ἐφ’ ᾧ means “because” or “inasmuch as,” not “in whom,” as in 2 Corinthians 5:4 and Philippians 3:12. The most learned writers demonstrated this long ago, as well as the fact that this passage concerns actual sin, of which infants are incapable.

The other passage, 1 Corinthians 15, has nothing to do with the matter. Paul means that just as one Adam introduced death into the world, with all who imitate him dying, so Christ will also bring blessed resurrection to all who obey Him. There is no discussion here of the sin of infants, who die by the condition of nature because they were born as mortal human beings—not as though punishment were being exacted from them. This was demonstrated by the most learned theologians, whom we shall not name.

### Letter 177, § 2

“Having heard these words—that Pelagius professed to acknowledge the grace of God—the Catholic bishops, at the Council of Diospolis, could understand no other grace of God than that which they were accustomed to read in God’s books and preach to God’s peoples; namely, the grace of which the Apostle says: ‘I do not nullify the grace of God’ (Galatians 2:21). For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing—undoubtedly the grace by which we are justified from iniquity and saved from weakness, not the grace by which we were created with our own will.”

Yet Pelagius acknowledged not merely the benefits of creation, as we have often said, but also all the benefits of the Gospel. He did not, however, acknowledge that efficacious Augustinian grace, previously unknown, especially in the East. Accordingly, John of Jerusalem judged Pelagius to be orthodox, as is sufficiently clear from Paulus Orosius.

Paul’s passage does nothing against Pelagius, since “the grace of God” there means the Gospel, or the Gospel dispensation, by which God regards as righteous not those who are free from sin, but those who obey the Gospel—even though their previous life may have been stained by vices and they may not pass the rest of their lives without various falls.

Grace is always understood in this sense when it is opposed to the Law, which, according to the opinion of the Jews against whom Paul argues, demanded complete perfection. In this argument of the Epistle to the Galatians, as also in the similar argument in the Epistle to the Romans, grace is continually opposed to law and works—that is, mercy to strictness, and imperfect observance of God’s commandments to perfect holiness.

This is clearer than midday light, and none of the more recent interpreters failed to see it. Therefore grace is not understood here in the Augustinian sense, nor anywhere else in Scripture. Hence all the testimonies cited in § 8 are irrelevant.

Who could tolerate our being presented with men who read Scripture so carelessly and praised it so inattentively as models of outstanding interpreters? Who would allow dogmas to be imposed upon him as necessary for salvation, as they supposed, when they had been deduced from passages so badly understood?

### The Same, § 18

“But however this question may stand, since, although a person is not found in this life without sin, it is nevertheless said that this can be accomplished through the help of grace and the Spirit of God, and one must strive and ask for this to occur, anyone who errs in this matter errs tolerably; it is not diabolical impiety but human error.”

Here Augustine appears to distinguish degrees of error, as he does elsewhere. But he should also have distinguished everywhere degrees of necessity in doctrines, and should not have imposed as altogether necessary something which, even if true, is not necessarily required for us to believe by any passage of Scripture, nor connected by an unbroken bond with necessary doctrines.

### Letter 181, § 1

“You approved that the matter should be referred to our judgment, knowing what is owed to the Apostolic See, since we all desire to follow the Apostle, who was placed in this position, and so forth.”

A little later:

“Or rather, while preserving the institutions of the Fathers in our priestly office, you do not think that those things should be trampled upon which they decreed not by human but by divine judgment: namely, that whatever was being done, even in distant and remote provinces, should not be considered concluded before it had come to the knowledge of this See, so that by the authority of the whole See a just decision might be confirmed, and the other Churches might take their decisions from it,” and so forth.

It is worth observing how eagerly and cunningly Innocent claims for himself a certain right on the basis of the action of the African bishops. He interprets their conduct as though they had not dared to condemn Pelagian doctrines without consulting him, whereas they had condemned them entirely—and later condemned them even against the will of Zosimus, Innocent’s successor.

It is also well known that the African bishops, not only in Cyprian’s time but also in this period, were unwilling to depend in any way upon the judgments of the Roman bishops, as is clear from the controversy over appeals across the sea that arose at this very time.

This letter is a bombastic little declamation against those who had denied that God’s help was necessary for living piously. But neither the manner nor the kind of help is defined, which made it possible for Coelestius later to approve this letter readily.

### Letter 182, § 1

“For just as I consider it harsh to show indulgence toward sinners, so I judge it impious to deny something great to the converted.”

Here *magnum* is a typographical error for *manum*, as is clear from earlier editions. Erasmus’ edition has *conhibentiam* instead of *conniventiam*. This is also how the word is usually written in the Theodosian manuscript, as Jacob Gothofredus observed; see his *Glossarium Nomicum*. Those who wrote it that way thought that one should say *conhibeo*, not *conniveo*, but they were mistaken.

In this sentence of Innocent there also appears to be an inversion, so that perhaps it should read: “Just as I consider it impious to show indulgence toward sinners, so I judge it harsh to deny a hand to the converted.” Certainly the propriety of the language would require this.

### [The Same, § 5]

“But what your Fraternity asserts that they preach—that infants can be granted the rewards of eternal life even without the grace of baptism—is utterly foolish. For unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, they will not have life in themselves (John 6:54). Those who defend for them this life without regeneration seem to me to wish to abolish baptism itself, since they preach that these infants possess what, as is believed, can be conferred upon them only by baptism.”

Innocent did not think that Christ’s words in John 6 concerning eating His flesh referred to baptism, but to the Eucharist. If, however, you maintain that no one can be saved without the Eucharist—which he thought Christ taught in that passage—it follows that infants cannot obtain life without baptism, because the Eucharist was not customarily given to them until after they had been baptized.

Innocent plainly has this in view, and the force of his reasoning rests upon this custom. To defend life for infants without regeneration is to defend the doctrine that life is given to infants without baptism.

It is well known that in that age the Eucharist was given to infants, as though it were necessary for salvation no less than baptism; the ancients derived this practice from a mistaken interpretation of the passage in John.

Let us hear Augustine, *On the Merit of Sins*, Book 1, chapter 20:

“Let us hear the Lord—not speaking this about the sacrament of the bath, but about the sacrament of His holy table, to which no one properly comes unless baptized: ‘Unless you eat My flesh and drink My blood, you will not have life in yourselves.’ What more are we looking for? What can be answered to this?” and so forth.

“Will anyone even dare to say that this saying does not concern infants, and that they can have life in themselves without participating in this body and blood, because He did not say, ‘Whoever does not eat,’ as He said concerning baptism, ‘Whoever has not been reborn,’ but said, ‘Unless you eat,’ as though addressing those who could hear and understand—which infants obviously cannot do?”

All the most learned interpreters demonstrated long ago that these two passages in John were badly explained. It follows that baptism and the Supper are wrongly regarded as necessary for salvation. See also what Augustine says in Letter 117, chapter 5. But we shall not address these matters here.

We shall say only this: Innocent’s words make it clear, no less than Augustine’s passage, that they believed the Eucharist necessary for salvation. I know that some very learned men have thought otherwise; but certainly they did not seek the truth in this matter, but rather sought to reconcile Augustine with current opinions. See Cardinal Henricus Noris, *Augustinian Vindications*, chapter 4, § 4, where he discusses this passage of Innocent at length.

### Letter 185, § 12

Concerning the Donatists who inflicted death upon themselves:

“Those who do not know their custom think that they now kill themselves when, through the opportunity provided by these laws established for the sake of unity, so many people are freed from their utterly insane domination.”

These are plainly accusatory words. Augustine softens what was being done against the wretched Donatists when he says that the people were snatched away from them through the opportunity provided by the laws. He should have said, “through the terror of the laws and the gravest penalties,” as we demonstrated in connection with Letter 93.

Moreover, what he adds—that those who did not know them would think they had laid violent hands upon themselves because the people were being freed from their domination—is maliciously expressed. As though anyone would kill himself when he was permitted to live and quietly enjoy his possessions merely because he had been removed from ecclesiastical office!

The Donatist clergy did not dominate the people any more than the Catholics did. Nor could anyone suspect that these unfortunate people wished to die for so trivial a reason, especially since it is evident that they were then treated most harshly by the magistrates.

### The Same

“Those who know what they used to do even before the laws were enacted do not wonder at their deaths, but remember their customs. Especially when idolatry was still being practiced, enormous crowds came to the most celebrated pagan festivals, not to break the idols, but to be killed by the idol worshipers. For if they wished to do this after receiving lawful authority, they could have possessed at least some shadow of the name of martyrs; but they came solely so that, while the idols remained intact, they themselves might be killed. For each of the strongest young idol worshipers used to vow to the idols as many of them as he killed.”

I would indeed believe that some, through an ill-considered desire for martyrdom, mocked the pagan rites so that they might be killed by the pagans. But I would scarcely believe that this happened frequently, and in the presence of large groups of Christians, when the emperors were Christian. For the pagans were not permitted to kill Christians with impunity.

### The Same

“Some even thrust themselves upon armed travelers so that they might be slaughtered, threatening them terribly that they would strike them unless they killed them. Sometimes they even violently forced passing judges to have them struck by executioners, or by their own officials, and so forth. Moreover, killing themselves by throwing themselves down steep precipices, into water, or into flames became their daily amusement.”

It is not unbelievable that a few madmen rashly rushed to their deaths. But let others believe that this was done as a daily amusement, without any provocation. Certainly this could not be said of the period when the Donatists were being harassed with the utmost severity. Nor should an enemy ever be believed concerning his enemies. Even if he does not lie, he nevertheless disguises, diminishes, or magnifies many things according to what benefits the side he supports.

### The Same, § 19

“For when those who do not want just laws to be established against their impieties say that the Apostles did not request such things from the kings of the earth, they do not consider that the time was different then,” and so forth.

I refuted this already in connection with Letter 93, § 9. I also showed there how futile the other arguments are.

Yet I cannot help being astonished that a man who was not unintelligent could be so blinded by passion that, provided he triumphed over the Donatists, he had no concern whether he disgraced the entire Christian Church, which, before there were Christian emperors, had always protested gravely against persecutions as contrary to humanity.

For if we say that earlier Christians condemned harassment only because it was inflicted upon themselves and not upon the pagans; and that, if they had possessed supreme power favoring them and had been superior to the pagans, so that they could harass them without danger, they would immediately have contrived similar things against them as the pagans had done against Christians—then the earliest defenders of the Christian religion must be regarded as cunning dissemblers, serving only the interests of the moment when they condemned as impious and inhuman what they themselves would gladly have done if they had been able.

The earlier Christians did not condemn only the persecution they suffered, but every persecution whatsoever.

If the pagan magistrates had suspected that Christians complained merely because they themselves were not mistreating the pagans, they would have raged against them much more severely and with greater justification, treating them as seditious people who were merely waiting for an opportunity to overthrow the ancient religion by force and mistreat those devoted to it. Christians would then have had no legitimate grounds for complaint, except that their adversaries had forestalled them.

Christians could not say that they were champions of truth and that the pagans were champions of falsehood. Although this was true, that controversy was still pending, since the pagans held the contrary view. In the meantime, they were supplying the pagans with weapons against Christians: while the pagans believed themselves to stand for the truth, they ought, according to the Christian position, to harass those who thought otherwise.

If the pagans could have foreseen that a time would come when those who sacrificed to the gods would be put to death by Christian emperors, and not without the applause of bishops, even if the bishops had otherwise taken a different side, they would have branded the Christians as factious and evil men who did not say what they thought while loudly proclaiming that religion ought to be free.

Yet this is how Augustine addresses the Donatists in Letter 93, § 10:

“Who among us, who among you, does not praise the laws issued by the emperors against pagan sacrifices? And certainly a much severer punishment has been established there, for the penalty for that impiety is capital punishment.”

I do not doubt that the pagans who remained in the Roman Empire, and even neighboring idolaters such as the Persians, made such objections to the Christians. But far be it from us to approve these things!

### Letter 186, § 37

“Human nature, even if it remained in that integrity in which it was created, could in no way preserve itself without the help of its Creator.”

It should have been defined what kind of help of God is meant here, and this should have been proved from an unambiguous passage of Scripture. For who would deny that, if we speak generally, the creature always needs the help of the Creator in order to attain salvation?

### Letter 187, § 5

“But that this soul descended into hell, apostolic doctrine proclaims,” and so forth.

See what was said on this subject in connection with Letter 164, from which it is clear that Augustine is mistaken. It follows that here too he departed from the meaning of Christ’s words.

Christ is undoubtedly speaking of His own soul, with which the soul of the thief was in paradise. On the word “Paradise,” see Hugo Grotius’ comments on this passage.

### The Same, § 33

“That which was born in her . . .”

In the Greek text of Matthew, chapter 1:20, the reading is γεννηθέν (*gennēthen*), “generated” or “begotten.” Augustine should have mentioned this in passing. Perhaps, however, when composing this letter he had no one at hand who knew Greek. Otherwise, he sometimes answers questions reasonably well from the Greek language, as below in Letter 197, where he explains the difference between the words καιροί (*kairoi*) and χρόνοι (*chronoi*).

### Letter 213, § 1

“I wish the presbyter Heraclius to be my successor.”

These are Augustine’s words, by which he designated his successor in the presence of the people. It is astonishing that he did not know that this was plainly unlawful according to the ancient ecclesiastical constitutions—and that he who admits in § 4 that he himself was made bishop while his predecessor was still alive also chose a successor for himself contrary to those same laws.

Apostolic Canon 76 reads:

Οὐ χρὴ ἐπίσκοπον τῷ ἀδελφῷ, ἢ τῷ υἱῷ, ἢ τῷ ἑτέρῳ συγγενεῖ χαριζόμενον, εἰς τὸ ἀξίωμα τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς χειροτονεῖν ὃν βούλεται.

“It is not proper for a bishop, showing favor to a brother, a son, or another relative, to appoint as bishop whomever he wishes.”

The words are framed in such a way that if a bishop confers the episcopate upon his brother, son, or relative—or upon someone else for their benefit—he sins equally by acting arbitrarily.

It is astonishing if the Africans were not familiar with the very words of this canon. At the very least, the custom of the Easterners in this matter had not been adopted among the Africans, although it rests upon the gravest reasoning, expressed in the following words:

Κληρονόμους γὰρ τῆς ἐπισκοπῆς ποιεῖσθαι οὐ δίκαιον τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ χαριζόμενον πάθει ἀνθρωπίνῳ· οὐ γὰρ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ Ἐκκλησίαν ὑπὸ κληρονόμους ὀφείλει τιθέναι, εἰ δέ τις τοῦτο ποιήσοι, ἄκυρος μὲν ἔστω ἡ χειροτονία, αὐτὸς δὲ ἐπιτιμάσθω ἀφορισμῷ.

“For it is not right to make heirs of the episcopate, giving what belongs to God out of human affection. The Church of God ought not to be placed under heirs; and if anyone should do this, the ordination shall indeed be invalid, while he himself shall be punished with exclusion.”

Likewise, the Council of Antioch, held under Constantius, decrees in canon 23:

Ἐπισκόπῳ μὴ ἐξεῖναι ἀντ’ αὐτοῦ καθιστᾷν ἕτερον ἑαυτοῦ διάδοχον, κἂν περὶ τῇ τελευτῇ τοῦ βίου τυγχάνῃ.

“It is not permitted for a bishop to appoint another in his place as his successor, even if he happens to be near the end of his life.”

Balsamon and Zonaras observe that this confirms the aforementioned apostolic canon.

There is no need to show how serious are the disadvantages of acting contrary to this rule. Augustine nevertheless followed precisely that course, choosing a successor for himself by his authoritative declaration, “I wish”—as though even the consent of his fellow bishops had not been necessary, although the Council of Nicaea determined that it was.

I know that some will say that this was customary in Africa. Augustine himself says above that, through his efforts, the Church of Milevis received a bishop whom the predecessor, while still alive, had designated before the clergy.

They will add that, although wicked bishops might abuse this power, good bishops used it properly. But all of this is filled with suspicion. I would not suppose that the Africans were wiser than the Greeks, who considered it dangerous to leave such matters to the discretion of bishops.

See Theodoret’s judgment concerning such an election in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 5, chapter 23.

### The Same, § 4

“While my venerable father and bishop, the old Valerius, was still alive, I was ordained bishop and sat with him. I did not know that this had been prohibited by the Council of Nicaea, nor did he know it.”

This is canon 8 of the Council of Nicaea, where it is forbidden for there to be two bishops in one city. On this passage, see the notes of the most learned William Beveridge.

I do not understand how the Church’s own practice—which established that there ought to be one bishop in each city—did not warn the bishop of Hippo that this was unlawful. For if it was permissible for him to add one colleague to himself, why not several? What a great opening this gave Augustine’s adversaries to say that the man had often erred for his own advantage!

### Letter 217

This letter is against the Pelagian Vitalis, who maintained that God works through His word so that we may will.

#### § 2

“Tell me, then,” Augustine says, “in the clearest terms, that we ought not to pray for those to whom we preach the Gospel, that they may believe, but should merely preach to them,” and so forth.

Yet besides the bare preaching of the Gospel, there are many other means by which God commonly softens human minds. These must never be separated from the preaching of the Word, since, even when God employs other means, the Word remains the chief instrument He uses for this purpose.

These other means include, for example, the calamities of life; the good examples of religious people; punishments inflicted by Providence upon the wicked; the consequences of virtue and vice even in this life; the removal of temptations; the inward awakening of the mind to attention; the extinguishing or diminishing of impulses contrary to the Gospel; and other such things. All these are variously offered by God to human beings, according to His manifold wisdom, and are implanted in their minds.

For who knows how many ways God may approach the minds of human beings? Nor can anyone deny that God is able to act inwardly upon the human mind.

Such matters, whose choice is left to divine wisdom, are requested from God—but no irresistible impulse is requested. What is requested from God is what He ordinarily does and wills to do, not what He does not will and neither ordinarily does.

Those who interpret prayers otherwise press them contrary to the intention of those who utter them. Such prayers must establish that the commandments of the Gospel are legitimate and therefore can be observed by all to whom they are presented; otherwise they are insulting to God, whom they make unjust.

It is not permissible to interpret the Christian religion in such a way that, while defending one part of it as you understand it, you make that part contradict the rest.

Vitalis could have turned the argument against Augustine and said: “According to your opinion, you ought not to preach the Gospel, but to pray for people; for God does everything even without the Word.”

### The Same, § 16

Here Augustine summarizes his doctrine of grace in twelve chapters. We shall close with a brief examination of them, covering what we had to observe in this second volume.

#### I

“We know that those not yet born have done nothing good or evil in their own life, and that they do not enter the miseries of this life according to the merits of some prior life, since no individual could have had a prior life of his own.”

Pelagius would have granted this, and he would have added that individual human beings could not have had not only a prior personal life—as those who defended the pre-existence of souls, προΰπαρξις (*proüparxis*), such as Origen, believed—but not even a common prior life, as Augustine believed, who held that the souls of all human beings were in Adam.

Augustine adds:

“But nevertheless, those born carnally according to Adam contract the contagion of ancient death by their first birth.”

Pelagius would also have granted this, but not everything that follows in these words:

“And they are not freed from the punishment of eternal death, which, passing from one person to all, is a just condemnation, unless they are reborn through grace in Christ.”

He would have said, first, that it is false that condemnation passes from Adam to his descendants, but that each person who is condemned is condemned on account of his own fault; second, that being reborn in Christ—that is, properly speaking, being converted—applies only to those who were dead in sins, not to infants, who have not yet sinned.

#### II

“We know that God’s grace is given neither to infants nor to adults according to our merits.”

First, the word “grace” would have had to be carefully defined. Augustine appears to mean that impulse which, in his view, certainly converts the sinner.

Pelagius too could have admitted this according to his own position, since God bestows the preaching of the Gospel and the other means He employs to convert a person initially without being prompted by any merits whatsoever on the person’s part.

But if you understand this to refer to God’s subsequent benefits, which are given to those who already believe, even Augustine could not have denied that God grants them according to merits—that is, according to good deeds which God, in His mercy and beneficence, has determined to reward. For it is established that to the one who has, something is given, while to the one who does not have, it is not given, as Christ plainly teaches.

According to Pelagius’ view, nothing could be said to be given to infants according to merits, since infants are entirely incapable of virtue. Nor can they be punished on account of vices, which occur only in those who use reason.

#### III

“We know that grace is given to adults for individual acts.”

Pelagius would have denied that adults are so moved by an impulse that they cannot resist it, whether one considers conversion in general or individual acts. Nor could the contrary have been proved from Scripture against one who denied it.

#### IV

“We know that grace is not given to all human beings; and to those to whom it is given, it is given not only not according to the merits of their works, but not even according to the merits of their will—something that is especially apparent in infants.”

If grace, entirely necessary for believing and persevering in faith, is not given to all human beings, then those who do not believe or do not persevere cannot be blamed or punished with eternal penalties, because it was never within their power to obtain that grace which, according to Augustine’s view, God distributes at His discretion.

#### V

“We know that those to whom grace is given receive it as a free gift of God’s mercy.”

Pelagius would not have denied this if Augustine is speaking, as he appears to be, of the grace of initial conversion.

#### VI

“We know that those to whom grace is not given do not receive it by the just judgment of God.”

Pelagius would have agreed with this statement.

#### VII

“We know that we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each person may receive according to what he has done through the body, not according to what he would have done if he had lived longer, whether good or evil.”

Pelagius would not have denied agreement with this aphorism, unless perhaps he held the view that we shall discuss under the ninth rule.

VIII. We also know that infants will receive either good or evil according to what they have done through the body. Yet they have done nothing through the body, for they cannot do anything without the use of reason. Hear Augustine nevertheless:

> “They have done it, not through themselves, but through those who, acting as their representatives, are said to renounce the devil on their behalf [Col. 0334C] and to believe in God.”

Indeed, in the baptismal formula the sponsor said, “I believe, I renounce”; but that formula, as we said in the note on Letter 98, had originally been devised solely for the use of adults and was afterward inconveniently adapted to infants. No valid conclusion could be drawn from it, especially since it was burdened with great difficulties. Hence, says Augustine in what follows, “they too are counted among the faithful, belonging to the Lord’s sentence: ‘Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.’”

But in these words Christ speaks only of adults, who are capable of believing in him, since the Gospel is preached only to them. The Punic Aristotle, as one of his opponents called him, adds:

> “For this reason, what follows also happens to those who do not receive this sacrament: ‘But whoever does not [Col. 0334D] believe will be condemned.’”

Yet Christ is speaking of those who did not believe the Gospel after it had been preached to them, not of infants, to whom it is not preached. If someone could digest such interpretations of Scripture, what could he not find in it?

IX. We know that those who die in the Lord are blessed, and that whatever they would have done had they lived longer does not pertain to them. It was an invention of the Pelagians—who, like others, thought that children could not attain heavenly glory without baptism—to explain why some infants died unbaptized, while others were baptized before they perished. God, they supposed, had foreseen that the former would be wicked if they lived, whereas the latter would be good if they had a longer life. This is an absurd invention.

X. We know that those who believe in the Lord with their own hearts do so by their own will and free choice. Pelagius conceded this, but maintained that Augustine denied it, because Augustine’s irresistible impulse destroys freedom. Freedom exists only if one can omit what one does; that is, if one obeys the divine call in such a way that one can also disregard it.

XI. We know that, on behalf of those who do not wish to believe, we who already believe rightly and faithfully act when we pray to the Lord that they may wish to believe. Pelagius too offered such prayers; but he did not ask God irresistibly to bend human wills. He asked only that God do what we described above under § 2: soften the human heart. By such prayers he displayed the love with which he embraced his neighbor, while wishing that the neighbor would show himself obedient to the divine voice.

XII. We know that, on behalf of those among them who have believed, we rightly and truly ought, and are accustomed, to give thanks to God as for benefits. All the Pelagians acted in this way, or certainly ought to have done so; for, in their view, believers possessed nothing that they had not received from God. If God had not sent the Gospel to humanity and added many incentives to believing the Gospel, no one would have believed it.

What lover of wealth would not thank a man who had heaped riches upon him, even though he had not compelled him in the least to accept them? Who would not be grateful to someone who had offered sound advice on an important matter, even though the advice would have been fruitless unless it had been trusted? Who, reflecting upon his own faith or that of another, and upon the greatest benefits of God that follow from it, would not give thanks to God both for those benefits and for faith, whose chief author is God?

But this testimony of gratitude ought not to be of such a kind that, while we thank God for the faith of believers, we think of him as being no less the cause of the unbelief of the obstinate than of the faith of believers; nor should we say things from which it necessarily follows that such people cannot justly be punished by God. That is what those do who say that people were made sinners by Adam’s sin before they existed in the world, and are born as such, or that unbelievers lacked something necessary for faith.

But this is by the way, since highly learned men have written at length about these controversies, especially in the United Provinces, where they were once debated with great vehemence.

# INTO THE THIRD VOLUME

[Col. 0335]

## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS TO THE READER

[Col. 0335B]

[Col. 0335C] We have arranged these third and fourth volumes that follow as τὰ διδακτικά—that is, writings that are neither letters, nor addresses delivered to the people, nor works directed against heretics, but writings composed for the instruction of the reader. We have indicated the spurious works by adding censures, so that no one may err unknowingly.

# CRITICAL OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOKS ON CHRISTIAN DOCTRINE

## Prologue, § 1

> “I have undertaken to impart these things to those who wish and are able to learn, if God and our Lord do not withhold from me, as I write, those suggestions which he is accustomed to provide when I reflect upon this subject.”

Although we ought to refer all good thoughts to God, as the first cause of every good thing, we should not speak as though God breathed them into us and dictated whatever we believe to be good. First, we can often be mistaken and think something true that is not true—as frequently happened to Augustine—and therefore we must be careful not to attribute our errors to God. Second, everything that we say truly is not for that reason suggested by God, since we generally owe it to instruction and reading, without any intervention by God whatsoever. Finally, if another person, possessing an equal right, were to say that his thoughts had been suggested to him by God and were then to put forward contrary claims, who would reconcile us, men supposedly inspired? They would defame one another as false prophets and persecute one another in a war of extermination, while less religious people would laugh at religion itself when they observed it being mixed with dreams. There are other disadvantages that might arise from this, and I am surprised that they did not occur to Augustine. Indeed, today there is no learned person who would want published under his name [Col. 0336C] what the author had believed to be divine suggestions.

## Book I, chapter 30, § 31

> “Whether love also belongs among those two commandments—that is, love of God and of one’s neighbor—so as to include the love of angels, may reasonably be asked.”

Those who have read Scripture attentively know that “neighbor” signifies only a person of the same nation or family, or one who shares the same human nature. Nor did God command us to love angels, with whom we do not associate and whom no one can even hate.

## Chapter 36, § 41

On the interpreter of Scripture who seeks the true meaning in Scripture but in the wrong place:

> “Nevertheless, he must be corrected, and it must be shown how much better it is not to abandon the path, lest, through the habit of straying, he be compelled to go across it or along a perverse route,” etc.

These words should be compared with what we said concerning *Confessions*, Book XII, chapter 17, where God, if Augustine is to be believed about himself, was suggesting contrary things to him; for at the beginning of the book he indicates that what he says there had been suggested to him by God. But the second suggestion is much better than the first.

## Chapter 39, § 43

> “A person, therefore, supported by faith, hope, and charity, and holding to them firmly, has no need of the Scriptures except for instructing others. Thus many people live in solitude, without books, by means of these three.”

No one is so skilled in Scripture that he does not need books to consult and read from time to time. If someone cannot read, he ought rather to live where books are read than in solitude. If he can read, it is insolence and inexcusable negligence not to acquire books for himself. These statements reek of sheer enthusiasm.

[Col. 0337A]

## Book II, chapter 8, § 12

> “In the canonical Scriptures, however, they follow the authority of the many Catholic Churches, among which, certainly, are those that have been worthy to possess apostolic sees and to receive letters.”

Apostolic sees are those in which the apostles themselves appointed bishops. Since they were the oldest of all, they ought to have been the first of all to obtain the apostolic writings.
