It is astonishing that Augustine says nothing here about the opinion of those who, as far as the Old Testament is concerned, recognized no other canonical books than those written in Hebrew—an opinion he could have learned from Jerome’s writings.

## Ibid., § 13

> “Those two books, one entitled *Wisdom* and the other *Ecclesiasticus*, are said, by a certain resemblance, to be Solomon’s; and Jesus Sirach is most persistently declared to have composed them. Yet because they deserved to be received as authoritative, they are to be counted among the prophetic books.”

In *Retractions*, Book II, chapter 4, Augustine says that he later learned that the matter was not as certain as he had thought, and that it was more probable that Sirach was not the author of the Book of Wisdom. It is astonishing that a bishop of such renown remained for so long ignorant of such a small matter—one that catechumens ought to have been taught. He had never read the book carefully when he wrote this, for the author of the book does not say that he is Jesus son of Sirach, but the king of Israel, chapter IX, verses 7–8. If that is so, I do not understand how a little work whose author presents himself as having been a king, although he was not, could be counted among the prophetic books.

## Chapter 11, § 16

> “People who speak Latin, whom we have undertaken to instruct, need two other languages for knowledge of the divine Scriptures, namely Hebrew and Greek, so that they may return to the earlier exemplars if the endless variety of Latin translators should create any doubt.”

I am not surprised that Augustine commends the study of Greek, for he does so elsewhere as well; but I am greatly surprised that he adds Hebrew to Latin. Certainly, not only in Letter 21, which is thought to have been written around the year 395, but also in Letter 71, written in 403, Augustine plainly disapproves the study of translating Hebrew into Latin and rests content with an accurate version of the translation of the Septuagint interpreters. He speaks similarly below, in chapter 14 of this book, and in *The City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 43, he thinks that those same interpreters were divinely inspired and therefore preferable to Jerome, although the Jews preferred Jerome’s version to that of the Seventy. It is also astonishing that Augustine here commends the study of Hebrew, yet neither he nor anyone else in those centuries undertook anything to open a path for those who wished to enter upon that study. Nevertheless, later, in Book IV, chapter 7, he again says something about Jerome’s labor. To state my suspicion, I fear that something here has been interpolated by another hand, after Jerome’s version had acquired authority in the West. If not, these words must be attributed to Augustine’s academic temperament, which was insufficiently consistent with itself.

## Ibid.

> “Those who translated the Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek can be counted, but the Latin translators cannot. For whenever a Greek book came into anyone’s hands in the earliest times of the faith, and he appeared to himself to possess some ability in both languages, he ventured to translate it.”

I admit that some light can arise from comparing those various translations, as Augustine later shows; but a far greater benefit could have been obtained from reading a single more accurate Greek manuscript than from comparing twenty incompetent translators. It would therefore have been desirable for the Western Churches, instead of spending so much money on ignorant and idle monks, or on monks occupied with worthless labor, to have sent young men to Greece at public expense and by public decision, or to have summoned Greek teachers from the East, so that more people might understand Greek and hold a torch before others. It would likewise have been appropriate for Christians collectively to hire Hebrews from whom the Hebrew language could be taught, and to do everything that was done in Europe within the memory of our grandfathers to restore knowledge of that language for Christian use. What was done later could have been done earlier, and more easily too, if the people of that age had not shunned the labor.

## Chapter 16, § 25

To show that arithmetic is necessary for understanding Scripture, Augustine mentions the forty-day fasts of Moses, Elijah, and Christ, and then adds:

> “The figurative knot of this action cannot be untied unless one possesses knowledge and consideration of this number. For it contains the number ten four times, as the knowledge of things woven into times,” etc.

These things, with all due respect to Augustine, are Pythagorean and Platonic trifles, from which it would have been much better to abstain in so serious a matter. But somehow, at that time, the habit of displaying one’s cleverness in such matters had become so prevalent that people listened with applause to things deserving of laughter. Who today could endure being told that the five water jars at Cana, which held approximately three *metretae* each, signified the Holy Trinity, as Augustine says in his treatment of that passage in John 2? O happy people, who so easily acquired for themselves such a reputation for learning! But also, O blockheads, who once applauded such things, or still seriously favor them!

## Chapter 17, § 27

On those who say that there are nine Muses:

> “Varro refutes them; I do not know whether anyone among them could be more learned or more inquisitive about such matters. For he says that some city—I do not remember its name—commissioned three artists to make three statues of the Muses each, intending to place them as a gift in the temple of Apollo, so that whichever artist had produced the most beautiful ones, the city might buy those from him in preference. It therefore happened that the three artists displayed works equally beautiful, and the city liked all nine and bought them all, so that they might be dedicated in Apollo’s temple. Later, he says, the poet Hesiod assigned names to them,” etc.

If pagans were obliged to admit what Augustine said about numbers in interpreting Scripture, I do not see by what right they were not permitted to say that this story had been invented by Varro or someone else—especially since the matter concerns very ancient times, when histories were either not written at all or were rarely written—and then to philosophize Pythagoreanly about the number nine among the Muses. Why would they not have been permitted to say that the three Muses represented the three musical tones—low, middle, and high—and that they were called three times three because there were three choruses, corresponding to those three tones?

“But,” you will say, “you are inventing these interpretations at will.” I do not deny it. But were they not also inventing the mysteries of theological arithmetic at will? It must therefore not be allowed that we appear to illuminate the truth with the same freedom of invention by which one may interpret fables.

## Chapter 20, § 31

> “That was elegantly said by Cato. When someone consulted him because he said that mice had gnawed his shoes, Cato replied that this was not the portent; rather, it would truly have been a portent if mice had been gnawed by shoes.”

Ingenious. Menander has something similar in *The Superstitious Man*, which Grotius includes in his *Excerpts*, p. 714:

> **A.** May this turn out well for me, O highly honored gods,  
> for, while I was putting on my shoe, the strap  
> of the right sandal broke.  
> **B.** It happened deservedly, Clinia;  
> for it was worn out, and you are too stingy, unwilling  
> to buy a new one.

The Greek text reads:

> Α. Ἀγαθὸν γένοιτό μοι, ὦ πολυτίμητοι θεοί,  
> Ὑποδούμενος γὰρ, δεξιᾶς τῆς ἐμβάδος  
> Τὸν ἱμάντα διέῤῥηξ . Β. Εἲκότως γ`, ὥ Κλεινία,  
> Σαπρὸς γὰρ ἦν, σὺ δὲ σμικρολόγος οὐ θέλων  
> Καινὸν πρίασθαι .

That is, according to the translation of the eminent man:

> **A.** May this turn out well for me, O holy gods,  
> that, while putting on my right shoe,  
> its strap has broken.  
> **B.** It happened deservedly, Clinia,  
> for it was worn out, and you are excessively stingy,  
> since you would not buy a new one.

## Chapter 22, § 36

> “All arts of this kind, whether of frivolous or harmful superstition, arising from a pernicious association of human beings and demons and established as agreements of a faithless and deceitful friendship, must be utterly rejected and avoided.”

Most true; nevertheless, it is not useless to know theoretically what the pagans used to say and believe about those arts, so that we may explain the passages of Scripture that refer to them. In these last centuries highly learned men have successfully undertaken this task. Many things that are intrinsically empty must incidentally be learned because of such allusions.

# BOOK III, chapter 2, § 3

> “That heretical distinction—‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was’; so that the meaning is: ‘This Word was in the beginning with God’—does not wish to confess the Word to be God.”

From this passage and from the other things said on the subject, it is clear that no punctuation marks had been added in the manuscripts of Augustine’s time. On this matter, see what Jean Clericus wrote in *Ars Critica*, part 3, section 1, chapter 10.

## Chapter 3, § 9

> “At the outset, care must be taken not to take a figurative expression literally. To this belongs what the Apostle says: ‘The letter kills, but the spirit gives life’; for when something said figuratively is understood as though it had been said literally, the understanding is carnal.”

All allegorists misuse this passage of Paul, 2 Corinthians 3:6, in which nothing of the sort is signified. The Apostle’s meaning is that the Mosaic Law kills, whereas the Gospel gives life. For he often calls the Law γράμμα (*gramma*, “letter”), and the Gospel πνεῦμα (*pneuma*, “spirit”); because, as I think, the Law is merely a letter, which in itself does not disclose the legislator’s intention, whereas the Gospel reveals God’s very intention when he gave the Law. See what Jean Clericus noted on this subject in the additions to Henry Hammond’s *New Testament*.

## Chapter 10, § 14

> “Whatever in the divine discourse cannot properly be referred either to moral uprightness or to the truth of faith, recognize as figurative.”

This rule is expressed in terms that are too general and is therefore afterward interpreted by Augustine partly with reference to commandments; but even so it is not sufficiently satisfactory. For God’s command to Abraham to kill his son was not figurative, and yet it was contrary to moral uprightness. The command given to the prophet Hosea to marry a prostitute was also not figurative in itself, and yet it was indecorous. I would not wish rules to be laid down concerning figurative speech; the matter itself and the speaker’s intention sufficiently show what is literal and what is figurative. Moreover, Augustine mixes figurative action with typological narrative, although they differ as widely as heaven from earth.

## Chapter 12, § 18

> “Whatever appears disgraceful to the inexperienced, whether merely said or also done, either by God or by human beings whose holiness is commended to us, is wholly figurative.”

As far as God is concerned, whose holiness is perfect and unchanging, this is an entirely certain rule. But whatever holy men did under the Old Testament that was less than morally right is not for that reason typological or figurative. For example, polygamy, about which he says nothing typological or figurative in §§ 20 and 27, was neither praiseworthy nor figurative; it was tolerated in that age, as it was later among the Jews, just as divorce was. Praise and blame must always be understood in relation to times and persons. What Augustine says about the temperate use of several wives persuaded very few people, in my opinion.

## Chapter 16, § 24

> “If a preceptive expression forbids disgraceful or criminal conduct, or commands utility or beneficence, it is not figurative. But if it appears to command disgraceful or criminal conduct, or to forbid utility or beneficence, it is figurative. ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,’ he says, ‘you will not have life in yourselves.’ It appears to command a crime or disgraceful act; therefore it is a figure prescribing participation in the Lord’s passion and the sweet and beneficial retention in memory that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us.”

Augustine does not interpret Christ’s words badly, although elsewhere he wrongly thinks that they concern the reception of the Eucharist. But the rule itself is not sufficiently accurate, as we showed earlier. Let us nevertheless accept what is correct in it, and from this understand how Augustine believed that we could become participants in Christ’s body.

## Chapter 21, § 31

After recounting the parable by which Nathan drew from David’s own mouth a condemnation of the adultery he had committed, Augustine speaks as follows:

> “From this it is understood with what restraint he had many wives, since, concerning the one with whom he exceeded the proper measure, he was compelled to punish himself.”

Everyone can see that this conclusion is badly drawn. David was not punished because he had intercourse too immoderately with one woman, but because she was married to another man and he had committed adultery with her. The mention of one sheep in Nathan’s parable is made κατ’ ἀντίθεσιν (*kat’ antithesin*, “by way of contrast”) to David’s many wives. Yet, not content with those many wives, he had taken from the unfortunate Uriah the one wife he possessed; this circumstance increases the gravity of the crime. Hence, contrary to what Augustine did, one should conclude that David was a lustful man, who, although he had so many wives at home, was so easily inflamed by love for another man’s wife.

# BOOK IV, chapter 7, § 15

> “For when he says”—Paul, 2 Corinthians 11:6—“‘Although unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge,’ he seems to have spoken as though conceding the point to his detractors, not confessing it as something he recognized to be true.”

Yet the matter itself cries out that it is true. See the additions of Jean Clericus to Hammond’s *Annotations*. This does not make the divine Apostle any less worthy of esteem; we do not venerate him as an eloquent man, but as an apostle of Christ who discharged his office with the utmost faithfulness and courage.

## Ibid.

After saying that he would bring forward passages from Amos, Augustine adds:

> “Not according to the Septuagint interpreters, who, themselves also having interpreted under the divine Spirit, appear for this reason to have expressed certain things differently, so that the reader’s attention might be prompted to investigate the spiritual meaning,” etc.

“But as they have been translated from Hebrew into Latin speech by the presbyter Jerome, skilled in both languages…”

The words “themselves also interpreted by the divine Spirit” seem suspect to me. For who else in that age was believed to be moved by the divine Spirit? This claim about Jerome was made only in recent centuries. Perhaps, however, the word “also” refers not so much to another interpreter as to the sacred writers themselves, so that Augustine wished to say that not only the sacred writers but also the Greek translators themselves had been inspired by the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter 24, § 53

Speaking of the Caesareans, Augustine says that they acclaimed him:

> “Yet I did not think that I had accomplished anything when I heard them acclaiming; I thought so when I saw them weeping. For by their acclamations they indicated that they were instructed and delighted, but by their tears that they were moved.”

Such acclamations are often mentioned in ecclesiastical records. I do not know how much they affected sacred orators, but I do know that they were indecorous and remarkably suited to puffing them up. The crowd more often applauds nonsense, if it is delivered in a pleasant voice and with attractive gestures, than sound reasoning. When applause is given to foolishness and denied to better speech, the result is that things less pleasing to the crowd are neglected, while things contrary to right reason are honored. Such practices ought not to have been transferred from the forum and theater into the Church.

# CRITICAL OBSERVATIONS ON THE *IMPERFECT WORK ON THE LITERAL INTERPRETATION OF GENESIS*

## Chapter 1, § 3

> “Everything that God made is very good; evil, however, is not natural, but everything called evil is either sin or the punishment of sin. Nor is there sin except a perverse assent of the free will, when we incline toward things that justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain.”

This is a most accurate definition both of sin and of freedom, one approved by everyone and always destined to be approved, had the Pelagian controversies not arisen. Those controversies drew Augustine away from notions that may appropriately be called κοινὰς ἐννοίας (*koinas ennoias*, “common conceptions”), since they belong to the whole human race. Otherwise, the purpose of this work was not bad, for there is no correct interpretation that is not literal, from which moral and theological conclusions are afterward derived. But literal, or grammatical, interpretations were almost unknown in that age; neither at that time nor later was Augustine equipped with the necessary aids for this task.

## Chapter 4, § 17

> “It can also be understood in another way: that we should understand the spirit of God as a life-giving creature, by which this entire visible world and all corporeal things are contained and moved; to which almighty God granted a certain power of serving him, so that it might operate in the things that are generated.”

This was the opinion of Theophilus of Antioch, who speaks as follows in Book II *To Autolycus*:

> Πνεῦμα δὲ τὸ ἐπιφερόμενον ἐπὶ τοῦ ὕδατος ὃ ἔδωκεν ὁ Θεὸς ζωογόνησιν τῇ κτίσει καθάπερ ἀνθρώπῳ ψυχὴν, τῷ λεπτῷ τὸ λεπτὸν συγκεράσας· τὸ γάρ πνεῦμα λεπτὸν καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ λεπτὸν· ὅπως τὸ μὲν πνεῦμα τρέφῃ τὸ ὕδωρ, τὸ δὲ ὕδωρ σὺν τῷ πνεύματι τρέφῃ τὴν κτίσιν διϊκνούμενον πανταχόσε.

> “God gave the spirit that was borne over the waters to the creation, so that it might produce living things through its operation, just as he gave a soul to a human being, mingling the fine with the fine—for spirit is fine by nature, and water likewise—so that the spirit might nourish the water, and the water, together with the spirit, might nourish the whole creation, permeating everything.”

## Chapter 6, § 26

> “Every word serves for distinction. Hence even the word *name*, which denotes a thing, is so called as though it meant ‘that by which something is marked’ (*notamen*).”

Rather, *nomen* (“name”) derives from *nosco* (“I know”), because things are known through the agency of names. See Gerardus Joannes Vossius’s *Etymologicon* on this subject.

# CRITICAL OBSERVATIONS ON THE TWELVE BOOKS ON THE LITERAL INTERPRETATION OF GENESIS

## Book I, chapter 10, § 21

> “In the book called Ecclesiastes it is written: ‘The sun rises and the sun sets, and it is led to its place’—that is, to the place from which it rose. For he continues and says: ‘It itself, rising, goes toward the south and circles toward the north.’ When the southern region has the sun, it is day for us; but when, circling around, it reaches the northern region, it is night for us.”

Verse 5 of chapter I of Ecclesiastes does indeed concern the sun, but verse 6 seems to be understood as referring only to the wind, as more accurate interpreters will show. But this is not our present concern, for we are not writing a commentary on passages that Augustine explained poorly. Above all, one must note that there is an error in the word *illud* (“that”), and that *illic* (“there”) should be read instead. Thus Jerome quotes this passage from the ancient version: “and it itself rises there. It goes toward the south,” etc. Erasmus’s edition has *illuc* (“to there”), which comes closer to the true reading.

Next, one should ask from what astronomer Augustine learned that when the southern region has the sun, it is day for us, but when, circling around, it reaches the northern region, it is night for us. I suspect that he heard from someone that when the southern region—that is, the southern signs—are traversed by the sun, it is winter for us, whereas when it passes through the northern signs, it is summer; but because he was entirely unskilled in astronomy, he substituted day and night for summer and winter, his memory wavering. Jerome is much better at verse 6, if the subject there is indeed the sun:

> “From this,” he says, “we can judge that in winter the sun runs toward the southern region, and in summer is near the north.”

## Book II, chapter 5, § 9

After saying that astrologers regard Saturn’s star as cold, Augustine reasons against them as follows:

> “They are therefore asked why that star is cold, since it ought to be hotter in proportion as it is carried through a higher heaven. For clearly, when a rounded mass is driven in circular motion, its inner parts move more slowly and its outer parts more quickly, so that the larger distances may arrive at the same circuits together with the shorter ones; and whatever moves more quickly is necessarily hotter.”

Here one may see what it means to reason about a matter of which one has little knowledge. The astrologers whom Augustine refutes happened by chance to derive a true conclusion from absurd opinions; the bishop of Hippo, however, attacks the truth by correct reasoning. Both, in short, were flashing about in the darkness, yet they put forward their inventions no less confidently. The astrologers absurdly insisted that Saturn’s star was cold because poets represented Saturn as an old man, and indeed as castrated. See Servius on this line of Virgil, *Georgics* I.336:

> “Where the cold star of Saturn withdraws.”

Nevertheless, according to the true doctrines of modern astronomers, the planet called Saturn may be called cold because it is farthest from the sun, from which all the heat of our world comes. Augustine’s reasoning, by contrast, is indeed valid but badly applied, because he assumes that Saturn, along with all the other heavenly bodies, is carried around the earth within twenty-four hours—something everyone now knows to be false.

Therefore, he says:

> “That star ought consequently to have been hotter rather than colder. For although by its own motion, since it traverses a vast distance, it passes through its entire circuit in thirty years, nevertheless, because it is rotated in the opposite direction by the motion of the heavens, it must move more quickly, and therefore, as they say, since each revolution of the heavens produces a single day, it ought to have gathered greater heat from the more rapid heaven.”

He derived this from the common astronomy of his age, but he added to that astronomy another error, rashly joined to a misinterpretation of Genesis and to poetic fictions, as follows:

> “The proximity of the waters established above the heavens therefore makes it cold; and those who discuss the motion of the heaven and the stars, as I have briefly described it, do not wish to believe this.”

They rightly refused to believe it, because it was contrary to reason, whereas Scripture cannot conflict with reason, as Augustine himself teaches elsewhere.

## Ibid.

> “Some of our people employ conjectures against those who refuse to believe in waters above the heavens, and want that star to be cold which circles near the highest heaven, so that they may thereby be compelled to suppose that the nature of the waters is suspended there not in vaporous thinness but in icy solidity.”

Those were the vain conjectures of unlearned men attempting rashly to reconcile Scripture with poetic astronomy. The passage in Genesis concerning waters above the heavens should be understood as referring to clouds suspended in the lower air, as someone correctly conjectured long ago—for it cannot be identified otherwise—and as Augustine mentions above in chapter 4. It would have been better to follow that sound admonition than to dream of waters where there are none.

Thus he finally concludes the discussion:

> “However and whatever kind those waters may be, let us have no doubt that they are there; for the authority of this Scripture is greater than the capacity of every human intellect.”

He rightly said that Scripture should be believed rather than conjectures. But Scripture must first be properly understood, lest we thrust forward a fabricated meaning—that is, our own dreams—as its true sense, as the bishop of Hippo did here. See, besides the interpreters of Genesis, Dionysius Petavius, *Theological Dogmas*, vol. III, *On the Work of the Six Days*, Book I, chapter 11.

## Chapter 6, § 10

> “They say that the person of the Father is declared in what is written: ‘And God said, Let there be a firmament,’ etc.; and then, in order that it may be understood that the Son did what the Father said should be made, they suppose that the following words have been added: ‘And God made the firmament.’”

This λεπτολογία (*leptologia*, “subtle verbal analysis”), and other things of the same kind that Augustine has here, rest upon the faulty translation of the Latin interpreter. For in the Hebrew text, since it reads [Hebrew word absent in the supplied text], “let it be,” the Greeks translated it as γενηθήτω (*genēthētō*), which does not mean “let it be made,” but “let it be”; thus God’s command does not refer to another cause that makes what he commands, but signifies that by his sole will God caused things to exist.

# BOOK III, chapter 1, § 1

> “The heavens are spoken of in the plural, although they are one and the same thing, which is called one heaven.”

In Hebrew, *Schamajim*—the Hebrew term itself is absent in the supplied text—is always grammatically plural, although it is often understood in a singular sense. But the Greek translators used at times οὐρανόν (*ouranon*, “heaven”), according to Greek usage, and at times οὐρανούς (*ouranous*, “heavens”), following the Hebrew; the Latins imitated them, although they did not know why the number changed in this word.

## Chapter 21, § 33

> “How human beings were made immortal and received food along with the other animals—grass bearing seed, fruit-bearing wood, and green grass—is difficult to say.”

Yet from this passage, as from what follows, it is easy to understand that the human body was created mortal by its own nature. Nothing prevented God, if human beings had never sinned, from granting it immortality through extraordinary action. But because they sinned, God left it to be consumed according to its nature; in this way death became the wage of sin. Augustine himself clearly teaches this below, in Book VI, chapter 25, § 36.

# BOOK IV, § 2

> “We therefore find that the number six was the first perfect number, for it is completed by its own parts; that is, it consists of twice three.”

Whatever other number Augustine had selected, he would have found in it all the necessary perfections. Such were the inventions of Platonism, from which I am surprised that Augustine was not alienated, especially because they contained nothing fixed or certain.

## Chapter 35, § 56

> “Therefore, that day which God first made, if it is a spiritual and rational creature—that is, the supercelestial angels and powers—was presented to all the works of God in an order of presentation corresponding to an order of knowledge: by it he would know beforehand in the Word of God what was to be made, and would recognize it in the creature once made—not through delays of temporal intervals, but with a before and after in the connection of creatures, while, in the efficacy of the Creator, all things were simultaneous. For he makes things that will be, so that he does not make temporal things temporally, but the times run on after being made by him.”

Who would not be astonished that all these statements, in which he summarizes what he taught piecemeal in this book, are called literal interpretations? Who would not be stunned when reflecting that they were spoken seriously? Those to whom these feverish dreams of a delirious person appeared extraordinary must have been either extremely dull or extremely blinded by affection. What interpreter today would wish to write such things?

Ibid. And thus these seven days, which the revolving and returning light of the heavenly body unfolds and repeats, according to a certain shadowy symbolism, admonish us to seek those days in which created spiritual light could have been presented to all the works of God through the perfection of the number six, and from there to have the seventh rest of God with a morning and no evening, etc.] These notions could please those who thought highly of the mystical arithmetic of Plato or Pythagoras; but those who mocked it undoubtedly hissed all this off the stage as well—and deservedly so, as is now clear even from the agreement of more recent interpreters, to whom entirely different things have been pleasing. We can forgive these imaginings, but we cannot help wondering at men who so often require our indulgence.

**BOOK V, chap. 14, § 32.** “Nor must it be passed over that the more accurate manuscripts have [John 1:3–4]: ‘What was made in him was life,’ so that ‘was life’ is understood in the same way as: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. Therefore what was made was already life in him, and life was not of just any kind,’ etc.] Those more accurate manuscripts were undoubtedly suffering from faulty punctuation, as all modern editions and the matter itself demonstrate.

**BOOK VI, chap. 24 and following, § 36.** “The Apostle does not say, ‘the body indeed mortal because of sin,’ but ‘the body dead because of sin.’ For before sin it could be called both mortal in one respect and immortal in another—that is, mortal because it could die, etc.]” Augustine does not yet seem to have thought about this matter when he wrote Book III, chap. 21, as we briefly indicated at that passage.

**BOOK VII, chap. 2, § 3.** “It is a sacrilegious opinion to believe that it and God are of one substance.”] He is speaking of the opinion of the Manichaeans, who wished the human mind to be ὁμοούσιον, that is, consubstantial with God. See the book *On Heresies*, chap. 46.

**Chap. 22, § 32.** “It must be asked how it can be understood that the causal principle of it [the soul] was said to have existed in the works of God during the first six days; how God made man in his own image, which cannot rightly be understood except with reference to the soul.”] Augustine follows the terminology of the philosophers, who taught that there was a seminal principle—σπερματικὸς λόγος—in all things. By these words they seem to have understood something like a principle from which all combinations of prime matter were formed. See Justus Lipsius, *Physiologia Stoica*, Book II, dissertation 8. These same philosophers, and perhaps others as well, also seem to have spoken of an αἰτιατικὸς λόγος, “causal principle,” an expression Augustine often uses in these books.

**Ibid.** “But there is a danger that, when we say that God did not then create the very natures and substances that were destined to exist, while creating everything simultaneously, we may be thought to be saying something empty.”] No one now believes that God created everything simultaneously, but many believe that God created the matter of bodies before all else, on the basis of Genesis 1:1; nor can that opinion be considered absurd. But those who speak of a causal principle either of the body or of the mind are saying something empty, and Augustine does not show the contrary in what follows. I shall not refute the astonishing arguments he brings forward afterward, for there is no danger that anyone will assent to them. Augustine, accustomed to Platonic subtleties, often writes more than he understands and repeatedly accepts consequences as though they were valid; if these are denied, all the arguments immediately collapse, for none of them can in any way be proved.

**Ibid.** “And even if there was some hidden principle in the human body by which it was destined to be formed, there was also matter from which it would be formed—that is, earth—in which that principle could be seen to have lain hidden, as it were, in a seed.”] The Stoics taught, as Laërtius reports in Book VII, § 136, that in the beginning God, while existing within himself, transformed all substance through air into water. “And just as the seed is contained in the fetus, so also he left this seminal principle of the cosmos, being such, in the moist element, and so forth.” Augustine clearly imitated this Stoic expression.

**BOOK IX, chap. 10, § 16.** “Although it is more honorably and more reasonably believed that the animal bodies of those men, then established in paradise and not yet condemned under the law of death, were such that they did not have an appetite for carnal pleasure of the kind these bodies now have, etc.]” That appetite, as is clear even from animals, is as natural as the desire for food or drink, and the pleasure we experience when we eat while hungry or drink while thirsty. Surely no one will say that thirst or hunger, and the pleasure we experience in satisfying them, are effects of sin. The things said here and elsewhere are mere fictions. Augustine dealt with them at greater length in *The City of God*, Book XIV, chap. 16 and following.

**BOOK X, chap. 6.** “Let us now see, therefore, to which opinion the divine testimonies give greater support: whether to the opinion that God made one soul and gave it to the first man, from which he made the others, just as he made the other human bodies from his body; or to the opinion that he makes individual souls for individuals, just as he made that one, not from it.”] Augustine admits these two opinions as plausible, rejecting the others, and is rather more inclined toward the first because he thinks that from it can more easily be explained both why all are said to have sinned in Adam and how original sin is propagated from him. But I do not know how he could understand this opinion of his as compatible with what he thought about the incorporeal nature of the mind. See chap. 24. Thus he solved one difficulty by means of another—that is, he made the reader’s difficulty still greater by means of an impediment. Yet the good man was not frightened by difficulties, nor did he greatly care whether he understood what he was saying. For who can understand such propagation by transmission if one posits that the mind is wholly incorporeal?

**Chap. 19.** After bringing forward Hebrews 7:4 and following, concerning Levi being tithed in Abraham: “If this also applies to that distinction—how much the priesthood of Christ surpasses the Levitical priesthood—because Christ the priest was prefigured by the one who tithed Abraham, in whom Levi himself was also tithed, then certainly Christ was not tithed by him.”] The Apostle’s figurative expression, which he did not venture to use without first adding the mitigating phrase ὥς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, “so to speak,” should not be pressed so far as though it followed from it that absolutely all Abraham’s descendants, down to his most remote descendants, were tithed in him. For it would really follow from this that Christ himself paid tithes to Melchizedek, since no one can doubt that Christ, according to the flesh—that is, according to his humanity—was descended from Abraham. The author of Hebrews merely wished to show that it was not surprising if Christ’s priesthood were preferred to the Levitical priesthood, since there had been a priest in Palestine in the days of Abraham who had received tithes from Abraham, Levi’s great-grandfather, and had blessed him, and had therefore been superior to Abraham; this priest could be regarded as a foreshadowing of Christ. One must not proceed farther or rigorously deduce consequences from this as though from certain mathematical doctrines. The ancients were satisfied that their allegorical interpretations were true in some sense; they did not put them forward as geometrical axioms.

**Ibid.** “But if Levi was tithed because he was in Abraham’s loins, Christ was not tithed because he was not in Abraham’s loins. Moreover, if we understand Levi to have been in Abraham not according to the soul but only according to the flesh, Christ was also there, because Christ, according to the flesh, is from Abraham’s seed; and therefore he too was tithed.”] But when the Hebrews said that descendants came forth from the loins of their ancestors, or were in them, they did not understand this as though the bodies and souls of the descendants had literally been in the loins of their ancestors. The Hebrews did not philosophize so subtly; they meant only that descendants came from them by the order of propagation. Thus the author of Hebrews means that Levi, who originated from Abraham, can be considered to have paid tithes to Melchizedek, since his great-grandfather Abraham paid them.

**Ibid.** “What, then, is the point of bringing forward, as a great difference between Christ’s priesthood and Levi’s priesthood, the fact that Levi was tithed by Melchizedek while he was in Abraham’s loins, where Christ also was, and therefore they were tithed alike—unless we must understand that Christ was not there in some respect? But who can deny that he was there according to the flesh? Therefore he was not there according to the soul. Christ’s soul, then, is not descended by transmission from Adam’s transgression. Otherwise it too would have been there.”] But even if it were granted that souls are transmitted by descent—which I do not believe—it would not follow that the souls of descendants were in their ancestors. For why could minds not be generated, like bodies, so that they did not exist before generation? Furthermore, given the short interval of two generations between Abraham and Levi, one may say, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, “so to speak,” that Levi was tithed in Abraham; but to affirm the same of Christ after more than forty generations would be permissible only as an excessively bold figure of speech. Finally, if we wished to philosophize against Augustine on the basis of his own philosophical positions, we would deny that, according to his view that the mind is propagated by transmission, Christ originated from Abraham—unless Christ can be said to consist only of his body, with the soul excluded, which he would not have conceded. Nor could Christ’s example be set before us, because his mind would not be of the same kind as ours; nor would he be, as the same author of Hebrews teaches, like us in all things except sin. These and similar objections could be brought against his opinion, and they caused it later to be rejected by most theologians. But someone may perhaps say: Augustine was led to this view by the reasoning of the author of Hebrews. On the contrary, he sought there a support for his own opinion concerning the propagation of the mind, though no such support exists, as we showed earlier.

**BOOK XI, chap. 9, § 12.** “He [God] made them [the wicked] in such a way as to leave them the capacity to do something themselves, so that, whatever they might choose even culpably, they would find him working commendably in them. From themselves they have an evil will, but from him they have both a good nature and a just punishment.”] Everyone sees that Pelagius could have said this correctly, and indeed in the sense in which it must be understood in order to answer the question why God created those whom he foresaw would be wicked. For according to Pelagius’s opinion, the wicked have their evil will from themselves, but from God they have a good nature by which they can do something; and this certainly must be the answer to that question. But according to Augustine’s opinion, these statements cannot be made except very improperly, and in a sense that does not answer the question at all. Yet the Carthaginian Aristotle habitually resolves objections against Providence in this way, after the manner of Pelagius, while teaching everything contrary to what the objectors assert. We have already noted some such examples above, and many more will be noticed by anyone who carefully considers what he says about these matters.

**Chap. 16, § 22.** On the question whether the devil was blessed before his sin: “For how, he says, can he be believed to have led a blessed life among the blessed angels if he was not aware beforehand of his future sin and punishment—that is, of desertion and eternal fire? If he was not aware beforehand, it is rightly asked why he was not?”] The negative should be deleted in the words “he was not aware beforehand of eternal fire,” as is clear from what follows; nor can one who foresees that he will become miserable be blessed. In Erasmus’s edition there is a worse error, for after “eternal” there follows absurdly “if he was not aware beforehand,” with the preceding three words omitted. Augustine continues as follows: “For the holy angels are not uncertain of their eternal life and blessedness. For how could they be blessed if uncertain?” etc. He owed this argument, like many others, to his Cicero, who speaks as follows in *On Ends*, Book II, § 86: “If the blessed life can be lost, it cannot be blessed. For who trusts that what is fragile and transient will always remain stable and secure for him? But whoever distrusts the permanence of his blessings must necessarily fear that, once they have been lost, he will at some time be miserable.”

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOKS OF EXPRESSIONS

**BOOK I.** The title is framed as follows: *Expressions of Scripture that seem to arise from the peculiar usages—idiomata in Greek—of the Hebrew or Greek language.* Augustine therefore undertook here to note Hebraisms and Hellenisms, an excellent plan, because the Greek translation often follows the Hebrew word for word, while the old Latin translation had similarly rendered the Greek; hence great obscurity necessarily arose for those who knew only Latin. But this task would have been performed better by Jerome, who was skilled in both Hebrew and Greek, than by Augustine, who was entirely ignorant of Hebrew and possessed only the thinnest knowledge of Greek. Augustine calls anything unusual in Latin an “idiom” on conjecture, while leaving many genuine cases untouched. Nevertheless, the work is useful—not for the purpose Augustine had proposed, but certainly for confirming and recovering the true readings of the Septuagint interpreters and restoring, as far as possible, the old Latin translation, as is clear from Flaminius Nobilius’s notes on the Latin version of the Septuagint interpreters. We shall examine a few examples, since we are not undertaking to write a work on expressions ourselves.

**No. 1.** “And let them divide between the middle of the day and between the middle of the night.” The words occur at Genesis 1:14, but Augustine adds nothing about them. The subject is the lights of heaven, which God wishes to make divide day and night—that is, time—or divide all time into the alternations of night and day. The Greeks translated the particle *ben*, here and elsewhere, as ἀνὰ μέσον, which the Latin translator rendered *inter medium*, “between the middle,” although he should simply have rendered it *inter*, “between.” From this the obscurity arose.

**No. 2.** “Flying creatures flying over the earth, according to [κατά] the firmament of heaven.”] This is verse 20 of the same chapter, where the Hebrew has *hal pneh*, “toward the face,” excellently rendered by κατά, “according to,” that is, beside or along its extension. Augustine, however, asks how “according to the firmament” should be understood, and adds: “So also let us make man according to the image and according to the likeness,” although many Latin manuscripts have “in the image.” But these expressions have nothing in common: the first κατά, “according to,” indicates position; the second indicates likeness.

**No. 6.** Augustine observes that Genesis 2:9 has “the tree for knowing the knowable good and evil”—τοῦ εἰδέναι γνωστὸν καλοῦ καὶ πονηροῦ—which, he says, he does not know whether it is an idiom or rather conveys some definite meaning. It is merely a bad translation. The Hebrew simply has “the knowledge of good and evil,” which should not have been rendered—if the Septuagint interpreters in fact rendered it so—as “to know what can be known concerning good and evil.”

**BOOK II. No. 2.** “They made houses for themselves, because they feared God.”] Exodus 1:21, where the subject is the midwives. Augustine suspects that this refers to wealth, on the basis of Genesis 30:31; that interpretation is not altogether implausible, but I would rather understand it of children, so that Moses means that, because the midwives spared the lives of the Israelite infants, God granted them numerous offspring. If Augustine could have read the Hebrew or Aquila’s version, or had consulted Jerome’s, he would have observed that the Hebrew text says that God built houses for the midwives.

**No. 5.** “It is difficult to know what *thibin* [Exodus 2:3] is, because neither the Greek translator translated this name from the Hebrew nor the Latin translator from the Greek, but each transferred it as he found it.”] It is the Hebrew *tebah*, that is, “ark,” which the Septuagint interpreters called θίβιν, perhaps because the word was also in use in Egypt. If Augustine had had Jerome’s version at hand, he would have seen that it means a basket—that is, a small chest or wicker container.

**No. 31.** “If Pharaoh speaks to you, saying, ‘Give us a sign or portent,’ then you shall say to Aaron your brother, ‘Take the staff.’” Thus Moses has it at Exodus 7:9. Augustine asks what has been added there by the *et* before *dices*, “you shall say,” unless it is some peculiarity of Hebrew expression. It is true: in that language the conjunction *waw* is frequently redundant, something he could have understood from Jerome. See also Book III, nos. 23 and 30.

**No. 32.** “The Latins seem to me not to have translated Pharaoh’s σοφισταί [Exodus 7:11] suitably when they said ‘wise men’; for σοφοί means ‘wise men.’ The Latin translator could have said *sophistae*, since there is no way to say it in Latin, and therefore we now use this word as a Latin word, etc.]” But to Latin ears *sophista* meant something different from what σοφιστής signifies here, where it is used for an expert in magic. See what the learned Ludovicus Cresollius collected concerning this word in his *Theatre of the Rhetoricians Whom the Greeks Called Sophists*, at the beginning.

**BOOK III. No. 22.** “This is a very common and frequent expression in Scripture: ‘he spoke, saying.’ But the expression that follows [Leviticus 12:1] is variously found and restricts the poverty of Latin speech; for the Greek has καὶ ἐρεῖς πρὸς αὐτοὺς λέγων, which could be expressed in Latin as ‘and you shall say to them, saying.’ It is less objectionable if one says, ‘and you shall declare to them, saying’; and it is more like the Greek, because the Greek also did not say λέξεις πρὸς αὐτοὺς λέγων.”] But—to say nothing of the future form λέξω, which was not so customary—in the meaning itself there is not the slightest difference. It is astonishing that Augustine should quibble so finely, when he habitually omits so many idioms of the Hebrew language. We shall not pursue these trifles further.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE QUESTIONS ON THE HEPTATEUCH

**BOOK I, Question 3.** “It is asked how angels could have intercourse with the daughters of men, from which giants are said to have been born.”] He solves the question of angelic intercourse reasonably enough, a question on which many Greek Fathers had come to grief as on a reef; but he labors in vain to prove that there were giants. Above all, it should have been asked whether there was a Hebrew word signifying “giants” at Genesis 6:4. The words *nephilim* and *gibborim* certainly denote strong and warlike men, and the former may perhaps mean brigands; but no one has shown that they signify giants—that is, men of extraordinary stature. I admit that the Septuagint interpreters, whom Jerome himself followed, translated them in this way; but neither the native force of the words nor the circumstances of the passages favor them. Augustine stumbled over this word again in Question 18.

**Question 9.** “It should be noted,” he says, “that what is written [Genesis 7:15], ‘in which there is the breath of life,’ is said not only of human beings but also of cattle, because of what some wish to understand of the Holy Spirit where it is written [Genesis 2:7], ‘and God breathed into his face the spirit of life’; some manuscripts have ‘the breath of life’ more suitably.”] Latin speakers ordinarily used the word *spiritus* to signify something incorporeal and intelligent, not the word *flatus*, “breath.” Nevertheless, at the beginning of Book VII of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Augustine interprets Genesis 2:7 as referring to the immortal mind, not to the soul, which might be common to us and animals. I do not understand why he prefers to call it *breath* rather than *spirit*. In Genesis 2 the Greeks have πνοὴ ζωῆς, “breath of life,” but in chapter 8 they have πνεῦμα, “spirit.” As far as meaning is concerned, however, there is no difference between these words. Many questions are raised here that would not have been raised if Augustine had been learned in Hebrew, or at least in Greek; and many matters are solved differently from how they would have been solved.

**Question 11.** “Aquila said *obtained*; Symmachus, *prevailed* [Genesis 7:24], that is, the waters.”] Augustine had received this from someone else, but it is astonishing that he did not obtain these translations for himself and take care to translate them into Latin; for he could not have been unaware of how useful they might be. Who would not be astonished that, through his own experience of interpreting, he did not understand what aids he needed—or, if he understood, did not acquire them as far as he could—or finally, if he could not obtain them, did not refrain from proposing so many questions and composing so many books on the Old Testament, books so excessively wordy? I believe he was stirred up by flattery or by the foolish admiration of his fellow Africans, so that he did not stop dictating while he saw his dictations received so eagerly. Thus people think themselves great and learned, not because they are, but because others think them so; and from this they take a boldness that very often turns out badly for them.

**Question 105.** “What does Jacob mean when he says to his brother, ‘For this reason I have seen your face as when someone sees the face of God’? Did words spoken by a fearful and disturbed mind burst out into such flattery? Or can they be understood as having been spoken without sin in some sense? Perhaps, because the words ‘gods of the nations,’ which are demons, are also found, no prejudice should be drawn against the man of God from these words. For he does not say, ‘as if I were seeing the face of God,’ but ‘as when someone sees it.’”] Aquila’s version should have been consulted here, from which Augustine could have understood that he was wasting his ingenuity on the words “someone sees,” for there are no corresponding words in the Hebrew. Later he thinks that the gods of the nations may be intended, especially, he says, because the Greek expression lacks the article, by which the one true God is most clearly designated. For it does not say πρόσωπον τοῦ Θεοῦ, “the face of God,” but πρόσωπον Θεοῦ, “a face of God.” Those accustomed to hearing and understanding Greek eloquence readily perceive the distinction. This is indeed the practice of the New Testament, but Jacob spoke neither in the manner of the New Testament nor in Greek; he spoke in Hebrew, in which there is no article—or, as grammarians call it, no emphatic article—but simply *phne elohim*.

**BOOK VI, Question 4.** “And these stones shall be a memorial for you to the children of Israel, and forever.” These are the words of Joshua 4:7, concerning which Augustine reasons as follows: “How can it be ‘forever,’ when heaven and earth pass away? Or is it because these stones signify something eternal, although they themselves cannot be eternal?”] Why did he not remember the observation he himself brought forward more than once elsewhere, especially in a work written at the same time as these questions? In Expression 93 on Exodus, concerning the words of Exodus 21:6, “He shall serve him forever,” he says that the Greek has εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, “unto the age.” “See,” he says, “how Scripture in many places says, according to this Greek expression, ‘everlasting’ or ‘eternal.’ It does not mean that eternity according to which eternal things are promised to us … for this servant, who could not live forever, could not serve forever; rather, something is called eternal when its duration has no end.” He also notes in the Expressions on Leviticus 17 and 18 that something is sometimes called eternal which certainly will not be without end. He has similar remarks in Question 31 on Genesis. Nevertheless, he continues with these words: “Although what is in Greek, ἕως τοῦ αἰῶνος, can be rendered in Latin *usque in saeculum*, ‘unto the age,’ from which it does not follow that ‘eternal’ is intended.” Thus, while groping for the truth, he does not know whether he has found it and is ready to abandon his discovery as though it were an error. If he had devoted himself to the Hebrew language, he would have known that *olam* properly signifies a period whose end is hidden, from the root *alam*, “was hidden, lay concealed.” He would also have known that, when the Greeks translate this word as αἰών, they assign the same force to the word αἰών; and he would not have allowed academic fluctuations to distract his mind. In this matter, as in others, he could more properly be called a Carthaginian Carneades than an Aristotle.

**BOOK VII, Question 1.** “At the end of the Book of Joshua, the narrator briefly extended the history as far as the point at which the children of Israel turned aside to worship foreign gods.”] Although Augustine’s Latin is not sufficiently pure, I would prefer to read here *pertexit* or *pertexuit*, “continued” or “wove together”; for scarcely would even barbarians from central Africa say *porrigere historiam*, “to extend a history.”

**Question 16.** “And they served Baal and the Astartes.” Judges 2:13. “It is usually said,” Augustine remarks, “that Baal was the name among the peoples of those regions for Jupiter, while Astarte was that for Juno; the Punic language is also thought to show this. For the Punic people seem to call Baal ‘Lord’; hence *Baalsamin* is understood to mean ‘Lord of heaven,’ since they call heaven *samin*. Juno, moreover, is undoubtedly called Astarte by them.”] All this is excellent; would that many similar passages occurred in Augustine! We would prefer them to all allegorical interpretations and rhetorical subtleties. He indicated more than once that he understood the Punic and Hebrew languages to be related. Thus, above, in the Expression on Genesis 24: “What is written, ‘and he extended his hand, took her, and brought her in,’ etc., is,” he says, “an expression that I therefore think Hebrew because it is also very familiar in the Punic language, in which many things are found corresponding to Hebrew words; for ‘and he extended his hand’ would certainly be sufficient, even without the addition ‘his.’” Elsewhere too he has similar observations, which the eminent Samuel Bochart so strongly confirmed in his *Canaan* that no one can any longer doubt them. Since this is so, who would not be astonished at the negligence of the Punic Christians, who made no effort to bring the Hebrew language out of darkness? I think the greatest blame lay with the declaimers, who despised everything in favor of rhetorical display and were equal to no labor except that of speaking. John Selden dealt extensively with the matter at issue here in his work *On the Syrian Gods*.

**Ibid.** “This, that is, by the plural name ‘Junones,’ we know from the Greek according to the Septuagint, whereas in Latin it was singular.”] Although the ending *ashtaroth* is feminine plural, nothing prevents its meaning from being singular, as with *hhochmoth*, “wisdom,” and *bhemoth*, “hippopotamus,” etc.

**Ibid.** “In the copy that did not have the Septuagint interpretation but was from the Hebrew, we read *Astaroth*, and not *Baal* but *Baalim*.”] He seems to mean Aquila, although the present Hebrew text has *baal*, just as the Septuagint interpreters also read it.

**Question 25.** “And he struck down the foreigners—six hundred men—apart from the calves of oxen.” Judges 3:31. After Augustine has vainly asked what the words “apart from the calves of oxen” mean, he adds: “The translation from the Hebrew does not have ‘apart from the calves of oxen,’ as does this one according to the Septuagint, but—as the Hebrew one has—‘with an ox-goad he killed six hundred men,’ which this one does not have.”] In our Hebrew manuscripts we read *bmilmad habbakar*, that is, “with an ox-goad,” in place of which the Septuagint interpreters evidently read *milbad*, that is, ἐκτός, “apart from,” “excluding the oxen.” As is clear from this passage of Augustine, this is the true reading of the Septuagint interpreters, which was later interpolated by Aquila’s version, where he had rendered it ἀροτρόποδι, “with a plowshare.” Hence in the Alexandrian manuscript we see both readings joined together: ἀροτρόποδι ἐκτὸς μόσχων, “with a plowshare, apart from the calves.” Since this seemed less suitable, the Vatican manuscript has only ἀροτρόποδι τῶν βοῶν, “with a plowshare of oxen.” I shall not say that the Hebrew word is more correctly understood by those who translate it “ox-goad,” since that is not the issue here; but this passage of Augustine makes clear how corrupt the Septuagint version became, and how it was altered so that it might appear to have been translated in accordance with sound reasoning. Aquila, however, rendered it ἀροτρόποδι, because that part of the plow seemed more suitable for killing men than a goad, or a βουπλήξ, an ox-goad.

I shall add nothing more to this book, for I am not writing a commentary but only observations in which I chiefly wished to note the usefulness and abuse of Augustine’s works. I shall say nothing either about the *Annotations on Job*, which Augustine regarded as something like a miscarried fetus and did not consider worthy of correction. Job is indeed too difficult for Augustine to have been able to explain it.

## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS’S CENSURE OF THE *SPECULUM*

I would scarcely have attributed this work to Augustine if Posidonius—or, as some prefer, Possidius—had not expressly ascribed it to him in his *Life*, and the preface is not unlike his style. Cyprian was engaged in a similar undertaking, as were some of the Greeks, but with greater talent and care. Christian charity, however, is glad to serve even the lowliest.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE *SPECULUM*

There is indeed serious reason to doubt whether this work, in the form in which it has reached us, is Augustine’s, because throughout it praises not the old Latin translation used by the Western churches in that age, but Jerome’s. The learned men who prepared the Paris edition note, in the preface placed before this book, that when the Bishop of Hippo prepared the work for popular use, he employed a version not from the Greek of the Septuagint interpreters, which he ordinarily followed, but from the Hebrew, because he had only recently discovered that the Hebrew was clearer in many places. But this very consideration could have deterred Augustine from departing from the received version, since he was copying passages of Scripture for the benefit of the common people—passages worthy to be memorized and digested through continual meditation. The uneducated populace could not help being offended if it were presented with Scripture to be learned that differed from what was read in the churches; nor should a new version have been presented to them without at least a warning, of which none appears here. The learned editors add that Augustine occasionally praises Jerome’s version as clearer in the later books of the *Questions on the Heptateuch*, and especially in Book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*, chap. 7. But I do not know whether he always praises Jerome, or rather Aquila, when in the *Questions* he cites a translator who rendered from the Hebrew; nor is the passage from Book IV of *On Christian Doctrine* of such a kind as to exclude every suspicion of interpolation. But let us grant that toward the end of his life Augustine approved Jerome’s policy in books written for the benefit of the learned. Would a man like Augustine have presented a new translation to the common people in a book such as the *Speculum*, written for the use of the ordinary populace, especially without a warning? What then, you will say—do you therefore deny this work to Augustine? Not at all; but I suspect that the Scripture citations were once altered by some monk from Jerome’s version.

**On the Psalms, Psalm 2.** “Worship purely, lest he perhaps become angry.”] Who would believe that Augustine, who pursued spiritual meanings with the greatest eagerness even where none exist, cited this very notable passage from Jerome’s version, especially since it brought enormous odium upon Jerome? Even the Church of later centuries, after accepting Jerome’s version, did not wish to abolish the use of the old Latin translation in the Psalms, because they were commonly known by heart.

**On the Book of Wisdom**, before which these words are placed: “We have taken these passages from books that the Jews also hold to be canonical,” etc. This follows Jerome’s opinion, though I do not know whether it follows Augustine’s. See Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chap. 8.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOKS *ON THE AGREEMENT OF THE EVANGELISTS*

**BOOK I, chap. 2, § 4.** “Although each appears to have followed a certain order of narration of his own, none of them is found to have wished to write as though unaware of the preceding writer, or to omit things unknown to him that another is found to have written; but, as each was inspired, he added the non-superfluous contribution of his own labor.”] We can scarcely doubt that John had seen the other three Gospels. For when he reached extreme old age, he took care in his own Gospel not to repeat what had already been covered by the others, except for a few things, and those necessary. This is clear from the Gospel Harmonies, especially the one published by John Clericus. But I do not see how it can be asserted as certain that Mark knew that Matthew had written a Gospel, or that Luke knew this of both of them. If Mark had seen Matthew’s work, it is much more credible that he would have rested content with the work of Christ’s apostle—that is, of an eyewitness. Nor would Luke, who, as is clear from the beginning of his Gospel, had seen several accounts of Christ’s words and deeds, have failed to mention an apostle such as Matthew. Who could believe that he would bring forward a new genealogy of Christ without so much as mentioning the genealogy previously published by Matthew, especially when considerable difficulty would have arisen in harmonizing the two? Let no one deny that they were inspired; but they were not inspired in such a way that they ceased to use their reason, or that by their inspiration they would establish the historical credibility of their accounts among unbelievers, to whom that inspiration could not be proved. Those who think that the first three evangelists wrote their accounts independently, with neither aware of the others’ plans, seem to judge much more correctly; their testimony consequently carries greater weight. For when witnesses who have compared their accounts agree, they are more likely to be suspected; but witnesses who testify to the same thing separately, unaware of one another’s testimony, rightly appear to be telling the truth.

The same place. “Mark appears to have followed him, as though he were his attendant and abridger.”] I am astonished that Augustine should speak thus of an inspired writer; for no inspiration is needed for someone to be an attendant and abridger of another’s work. I would rather believe those who hold that Mark received the Gospel history from Peter; nor do I doubt that, when many had written accounts of Christ’s words and deeds—as Luke reports at the beginning of his Gospel—Mark and Luke, who had not been eyewitnesses of those events, gathered their own histories partly from some of those accounts that they saw to have been approved by the apostles and regarded as truthful. Indeed, nothing prevents Matthew himself from having used some account that he considered truthful. It could easily have happened that Mark encountered accounts very similar for the most part to those which Matthew had used. Nor does this prevent the Holy Spirit from presiding over their writing, so that they would write nothing false.

The same place. “But Luke appears to have been more occupied with the Lord’s priestly lineage and person.”] Why? For two reasons, if we believe Augustine. The first is that David himself, although he was plainly a king, nevertheless represented the person of a priest when he ate the bread of the Presence, which no one was permitted to eat except priests. But Luke, in ascending to David himself, did not follow the royal genealogy; rather, he proceeded through those who were not kings to Nathan, David’s son, who himself was not a king. Everyone can see that these are fabricated inferences; if anyone denies this, no one can prove them. But for such rhetoricians it was enough that something not be impossible, so that it might be put forward as probable. The second reason is no firmer, and runs as follows: “To this may be added that Luke alone records that Mary was declared by the angel to be related to Elizabeth, who was the wife of Zechariah the priest; concerning him he likewise wrote that he had taken her as a wife from the daughters of Aaron, that is, from the priestly tribe.” What then? Because Mary was related to a woman of priestly descent, was she herself therefore of priestly stock? Did the descendants of Aaron then contract no marriages with any other tribe? No such law was imposed upon them, nor was this observed as a custom. The conclusions therefore drawn from this concerning the different purposes of Matthew and Luke are empty. The statements made subsequently about John being concerned with the contemplative virtue, while the other evangelists were concerned with the active virtue, rest on no better foundation; nor do the claims about the animals assigned to the individual evangelists. I would not, however, have taken notice of these things if I had not seen such dreams applauded by certain people who vehemently oppose better judgments—as though a thousand years added weight to dreams, while mere novelty could diminish things demonstrated with the greatest accuracy.

## Chapter 15, § 23

“Certain philosophers among them, as Porphyry the Sicilian reported in his books, consulted their gods about what answer they should give concerning Christ; but those gods were compelled by their oracles to praise Christ.”] Porphyry was not Sicilian but Tyrian, as we have already observed in *The Retractions*, book II, chapter 32. See Porphyry’s words in Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, book III, chapter 6, and *The City of God*, book XIX, chapter 23.

## Chapter 22, § 30

“Others say that he is Saturn, I believe because of the sanctification of the Sabbath, since they assigned that day to Saturn.”] Others said that Bacchus was worshiped by them, because of I know not what similarities of rites, as is clear from Plutarch, *Table-Talk*, book IV, question 5. Tacitus denies this in *Histories*, book V, chapter 5—but for an absurd reason: “Liber,” he says, “established festive and cheerful rites; the custom of the Jews is absurd and filthy.” Rather, the custom of the Jews is wise and sober, whereas the rites are those of Bacchus, of drunken and frenzied men. Thus even serious and learned pagan men judged absurdly about divine matters; and, when they spoke of the gods of other nations on the basis of their own customs, they attributed their own opinions to foreigners. See what John Clericus noted on this subject in *The Art of Criticism*, part 2, section 1, chapter 13.

## Book II, chapter 4, § 8

“It was shrewdly observed that Matthew, who had intimated Christ’s royal person, named forty men in the sequence of the generations, Christ himself excepted.”] Matthew intended to name forty-two men, and he did name them, as is clear from verse 17, where he divides them all into three groups of fourteen. In the first group the fourteenth is David; in the second, Jeconiah, the son of Josiah; in the third, Joseph, the husband of Mary. But the first two generations are missing from the third group of fourteen, through the fault of copyists; for nothing more absurd can be imagined than to say that Matthew, while listing each person individually, counted only forty men, but, when totaling them, found forty-two. It would be as if someone, after listing ten fingers individually by their proper names, should afterwards say that he had eleven. Far be it from us to attribute such a thing to the evangelist! Augustine vainly sought a mystery in the copyists’ error in the words that follow.

The same place. “This number signifies the period during which, in this world and upon this earth, we must be ruled by Christ, according to the arduous discipline by which God chastises every son whom he receives, and so forth.”] If you ask Augustine why he interprets the number forty in this way, he answers: “Since, then, this number is the sacramental sign of this arduous period, it also declares that the fasting of forty days—that is, the humiliation of the soul—was consecrated; and the Law and the Prophets, through Moses and Elijah, who fasted for forty days; and the Gospel, through the Lord’s own fasting, during which forty days he was also tempted by the devil,” and so forth. But if someone says that this is the dream of a man who was awake, ready to dream anything about any other number, surely the opposite will never appear more probable than this assertion. I therefore marvel that Augustine, who labored on this work with great zeal in order to silence the pagans, should have endured the use of such arithmetical allegories. I would have the same said of the allegories that follow. Nothing can excuse these things except the good intention of those who indulged in allegories and failed to see that, instead of counsels of divine wisdom, they were presenting to a credulous crowd, for admiration, the mere inventions of ingenious ravers. Had they considered the matter seriously, they would have omitted all this; nor would they have ventured to speak unless they had possessed something better than silence.

We shall say nothing here about the order and reconciliation of the passages with one another, since we have so many harmonies from which such matters may be sought. See, for example, the *Evangelical Harmony* edited by John Clericus. In presenting the Harmonistic Canons on which his entire *Harmony* rests, he frequently uses Augustine’s words, taken from this work.

## Chapter 66, § 128

“It is evident that the translation called the Septuagint differs in certain places from what those who know Hebrew and have individually translated the same Hebrew books find in the Hebrew text. If the cause of this difference is sought—why the great authority of the Septuagint translation differs in many places from the truth found in the Hebrew manuscripts—I consider that nothing more probable can be offered than that those seventy translators translated by the same Spirit by whom the things they translated had been spoken; and this is confirmed by their remarkable agreement with one another, of which so much is said.”] Yet this agreement is a disgusting fable, which I regret was believed as readily as matters that establish their credibility by every argument by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. From it there arose the further falsehood that the Septuagint translators either translated correctly or, moved by the Spirit, said other things that the Spirit suggested to them. Those who have compared that version with the Hebrew text, and exposed the causes of its errors, know how false this is. But it was convenient for those who did not want to learn Hebrew to believe what Augustine says, lest they be accused of ignorance or arrogance because they had rashly interpreted the Scripture of the Old Testament throughout their lives from a corrupt translation. In the same way, many things were believed—or appeared to be believed—because it was in the interest of those who had undertaken to govern the populace that the populace should regard them as true. Meanwhile, this confirms what we conjectured concerning the *Speculum*: that a more recent monk substituted Jerome’s version for the old Italic version in that book.

# Book III

## Chapter 7, § 29

On Matthew 27:10. “If anyone is troubled because this testimony is not found in the Scripture of the prophet Jeremiah, and therefore thinks that something must be taken away from the evangelist’s credibility, let him first know that not all copies of the Gospels have ‘which was spoken through Jeremiah,’ but only ‘through the prophet.’ We could therefore say that greater credence should be given to those copies that do not contain the name Jeremiah. For this was spoken through a prophet—but Zechariah; and so the copies that contain the name Jeremiah are thought to be corrupt, because they ought either to have contained Zechariah or no name at all, as some do; or simply ‘through the prophet who said,’ by which Zechariah is of course understood.”] In fact, those who criticized Matthew on this account ought rather to have believed this than to suppose that a Jewish man, who continually heard the prophets read in the synagogues and also read them privately, and moved among others like himself, had erred in such a matter—especially since it made no difference to him whether Jeremiah or Zechariah was named.

“But,” Augustine says, “let whoever wishes use that defense. My reason for not approving it is that many copies contain the name Jeremiah, and those who examined the Gospel in the Greek manuscripts more carefully report that they found it so in the older Greek copies. There was no reason for the name to be added in order to create an error; but there was certainly a reason for it to be removed from some copies: bold ignorance did this when people were troubled by the question why this testimony could not be found in Jeremiah.” Here Augustine is plainly acting as a critic, and he defends the received reading with no lack of apparent reason. But whatever he may say, there is nothing to prevent us from believing that this was an error in some extremely ancient copy, from which it later passed into others, since the copyists did not dare to correct it, or perhaps did not know whether it was an error. We adopt this position because, after carefully weighing everything, we do not see how the words of Zechariah could be attributed to Jeremiah; nor does Augustine’s reasoning in what follows seem plausible.

“What, then, are we to understand,” he says, “except that this was done by the more hidden counsel of God’s providence, by which the minds of the evangelists were governed?” He later conjectures that, by this citation, it was intimated that all the holy prophets, speaking by one Spirit, agree with one another in a wonderful harmony; that this is much more than if all the things of all the prophets had been spoken by the mouth of one man; and that therefore everything the Holy Spirit said through them must be accepted without hesitation, each statement belonging to all of them and all of them to each statement. But on this principle what Zechariah said could be attributed to Moses, and what any other prophet wrote could be attributed to any other. Yet this has never happened and never will. If God had wished to teach us such a thing through the evangelist, he would have ensured that the evangelist stated it clearly, not in such a way that it had to be deduced from his words by a wavering and easily rejected conjecture. The same must be said of many other matters which Augustine and other ancients draw from Scripture as though with bowstrings, selling forced conjectures as the counsels of divine wisdom.

Only those things should finally be regarded as divine revelation which are read as explicitly revealed in Scripture, or which are their necessary consequences—just as laws in a state consist of commands or prohibitions explicitly laid down, or of consequences that necessarily follow once the laws are established. In a word, only those things should be received as divinely revealed which are inferred from knowledge of the language in which the revelation was composed and from common sense—by grammatical, so to speak, and dialectical necessity—so that they cannot be rejected without obstinacy. This should always be done both to satisfy ourselves and to satisfy unbelievers, who would otherwise rightly mock the license of conjecture; unless, perhaps, when we are dealing with obstinate people who cling stubbornly to preconceived opinions, we use an argument *ad hominem*, as the apostles did when they were dealing with Jews accustomed to listen to the doctrines of their teachers rather than to sound reasoning.

# The Same Author’s Remarks on the Books *On the Sermon on the Mount*

## Book I, chapter 2, § 9

On the words “Blessed are the peacemakers.” “There is perfection in peace,” he says, “where nothing resists; and therefore the peacemakers are sons of God, because nothing resists God. Those who are peacemakers within themselves are those who bring all the movements of their soul into order and subject them to reason—that is, to the mind and spirit—and, having subdued their carnal desires, become the kingdom of God,” and so forth.] Augustine rightly observed at the beginning of this book that these sermons of Christ contain all the precepts that pertain to the formation of life. But I marvel that he explained most of them allegorically, since, understood literally—as our author puts it—they contain a most beautiful and holy meaning. For example, who does not see that the word εἰρηνοποιούς (*eirenopoious*) means haters of war, quarrels, and every kind of dispute? On this subject many very beautiful and beneficial things could have been said, but they cannot be said if, by forcibly imposing a meaning upon the usage of the Greek language, one understands the word to refer to peace of the emotions. Yet our author continually pursues general allegories, which are always available not to the learned but to anyone who is talkative, without any reflection; while he omits the particular ethical precepts, which could not be explained in an orderly fashion without study and labor. In those ignorant ages it was commonly thought that it required greater ingenuity to hunt for uncertain allegories everywhere, in defiance of grammar and dialectic, than to interpret Scripture grammatically and dialectically.
