But, if we love truth, it required far less ingenuity to soar through the air on futile conjectures—ἀεροβατεῖν (*aerobatein*)—than to disclose the literal sense and reason from it in such a way that nothing could be denied except by the obstinate. I will not say that the latter required much greater judgment, since the former is nothing but frivolity in a serious matter. Compare with these Augustinian interpretations what Hugo Grotius has in his notes on Matthew chapters V, VI, and VII, or what Henry Hammond has in his *Practical Catechism*, and it will be clear that the difference between allegorical and true interpretations is as great as that between the reasoning of dreamers and that of people awake.

## Chapter 9, § 23

“But one obscure word is placed here, because *racha* is neither Greek nor Latin, whereas the other words are customary in our language.”] The words “judgment” and “council,” which occur here in Matthew 5:22, are indeed Latin words, but ones which good Augustine nevertheless did not understand. He did not even suspect that the passage referred to Jewish customs, as more recent critics have shown beautifully.

The same place. “Some have wished to derive an interpretation of this word from Greek, supposing that *racha* means ‘ragged,’ since a rag is called in Greek ῥάκος (*rhakos*); but when they are asked who—not what—is called ‘ragged’ in Greek, they do not answer ‘racha.’”] It should be written *raka*, and in Greek ῥακα (*raka*), with kappa, not chi; for in Syriac it is *raka* with qof, which corresponds in origin and sound to Greek kappa. Nor would those who proposed this false Greek etymology have referred it to ῥάκος, “rag,” but to ῥάχος, from which comes ῥαχίστης, “a wretched scoundrel.” Augustine was therefore right to resort to the Hebrew language.

“It is more probable,” he says, “that what I heard from a certain Hebrew is correct, when I asked him about it. For he said that it was a word signifying nothing, but expressing an emotion of an indignant mind.” Grammarians call such interjections particles of speech signifying an emotion of an agitated mind, as when a grieving person says “alas!” or an angry person “hem!” Such expressions belong to each language and are not easily transferred into another. This surely compelled both the Greek translator—for Matthew was believed to have written in Hebrew—and the Latin translator to preserve the word itself, since they could find no way of interpreting it.] I fear that Augustine did not adequately understand what that Jew meant. Certainly, if the Jew knew Hebrew and Syriac, he could not have said that *raka* was an interjection of indignation, for no such interjection exists in those languages. Rather, *reka*, as the Talmudists write and pronounce it, or *raka*, as the Syrians do, is an insult; and insults, like those of other languages, are not easily transferred into another tongue. I think this is what the Jew said to Augustine, who failed to grasp what he meant.

If we write *reka*, the word meant a man empty of wisdom and virtue, for its root is *herik*, “he emptied”; and there is no insulting Greek or Latin word that expresses this. But if we write *raka*, it comes from the Syriac root *raka*, “to spit,” and means a man worthy of being spat upon. This etymology is approved by Edmund Castellus in his *Polyglot Lexicon*. Theophylact also incidentally gives it in his comment on this passage: τινὲς δὲ τὸ Ῥάκα Συριστὶ κατάπτυστόν φασι σημαίνειν—“but some say that *Raka* in Syriac means ‘one to be spat upon.’” I do not think, however, that κατάπτυστον means the same thing as *Raka*; for the Greek word, by a transferred sense, means “abominable, to be shunned,” whereas the Hebrew word means “to be despised.” The former of the proposed etymologies is favored by the usage of the Talmudists, the latter by the pronunciation of the word itself. Whatever the case may be, *Raka* is not an interjection. Consult John Drusius and Hugo Grotius on Matthew.

## Chapter 11, § 31

On Matthew 5:25: “Be well disposed toward your adversary,” and so forth.] Augustine here perversely and ingeniously interprets the judge as Christ and the adversary as God—nothing more absurd could have been imagined. This surely deserved to be reconsidered, as did many other things found here, which are for the most part distorted and irrelevant. It would have been better for Augustine to remain silent longer than to bring immature studies into the public light. For he was only a presbyter when he published this work, and had not long been devoted to the study of Christian theology and Scripture.

## Chapter 16, § 50

“Acyndinus was prefect at that time, and had also been consul,” and so forth.] This is a remarkable history, by which the loss of time occasioned by reading the allegorical interpretations of this little work can to some extent be repaired.

# Book II

## Chapter 2, § 5

“When we stand for prayer, we turn toward the East, from which the sky rises,” and so forth.] I believe Christians did this in opposition to the Jewish custom. For the sanctuary in the Jerusalem temple faced west; consequently, the Jews prayed turned toward that part of the heavens. See John Clericus’s note on Exodus 26:33.

## Chapter 7, § 25

On daily bread in the Lord’s Prayer. “Daily bread either refers to everything that sustains the necessities of this life ... or to the sacrament of Christ’s body, which we receive daily.”] Yet, as he says in § 26, most people in the eastern regions do not receive communion at the Lord’s Supper every day. In Africa, from the time of Cyprian, the custom had already prevailed of receiving it daily, as is clear from his book on the Lord’s Prayer: “We receive the Eucharist daily as the food of salvation.” On this passage see John Fell, Bishop of Oxford.

# Remarks on the Books of *Questions on the Gospels*

## Book I, Question 2

“That the Lord’s disciples began to pluck ears of grain and eat them; and that they could not do this without rubbing them. Hence comes ‘Put to death your members that are upon the earth’; that is, because no one passes into the body of Christ unless he has been stripped of carnal garments.”] Most of the questions are of this kind, from which one may understand that Augustine’s purpose in these books was not an investigation of the true meaning, but the production of invented allegories, to which the evangelists were forcibly subjected. Happy brains, which found satisfaction in such trivial subtleties!

## Book II, Question 38, § 3

“Although whether that reception—into the eternal dwellings, Luke 16:19—takes place immediately after this life, or at the end of the age, in the resurrection of the dead and the final judgment of retribution, is no small question.”] On this subject a dissertation by the most learned Louis Cappel is well worth reading, entitled *The Life of the Dead*. It was published in his critical works, which appeared at Amsterdam in 1689.

## Question 51

“Not everything that we imagine is a lie, when, that is, we do not say that it is true. But when,” he says, “we imagine something that signifies nothing, then it is a lie.”] Rather, it is a lie when we say that what we imagine is true. If someone said that a parable should be regarded as a true history, he would be lying, whatever other meaning the parable might have. But just as not every simulation is to be condemned—as in Luke 24:28—so perhaps not every lie is to be condemned. Augustine wrote a whole work on this subject.

# Remarks on the Tractates on John

## Tractate 1, § 13

On John 1:3: “Without him nothing was made.” Augustine interprets this to mean: “Whatever has been made naturally, whatever exists among created things, absolutely everything that is fixed in heaven, that shines above, that flies beneath the sky, and that moves throughout the whole order of nature ... from an angel down to a little worm.”] Nothing is truer. Those who denied divine providence were also unwilling to admit that insects had been made by God. John Clericus discussed this matter at length in his notes on this passage and said things that can illuminate Augustine’s remarks. If only the bishop of Hippo, setting aside all his cold allegories and forced interpretations—which fill everything he elaborated on Scripture, had always offered interpretations of this kind! Instead of complaints and corrections, one would here read praise and thanksgiving.

He observes most truly in § 14 that, if we allow that flies were not made by God, we may gradually be led to deny that the elephant and human being are God’s work. To use his own progression: if a fly is an accidental product of heat, why not a locust? If a locust, why not a lizard? If a lizard, why not a bird? If a bird, why not a beast? If a beast, why not an ox? If an ox, why not an elephant? If an elephant, why not a human being? Yet I do not know how Augustine allows that worms—the source of flies—arise from putrefaction. I do not see what he could answer to the progression he himself proposed.

These Tractates, however, are popular addresses, as the title itself shows. In them he does not interpret John’s words or the matters themselves with precision, but says whatever came into his mind. One therefore looks in vain for anything refined here.

## Tractate 26, no. 11

“Eat the heavenly bread spiritually; bring innocence to the altar. Although sins are daily, let them not be mortal.”] Here *vel* may mean “at least,” or there may be an error, and perhaps we should read *at non sint mortifera*—“but let them not be mortal”—which was later changed to *aut*, and then to *vel*.

## Tractate 28, § 11

On John 8:25, where Christ says, “The beginning, because I also speak to you.” “Behold,” Augustine says, “what it means to be. The Beginning cannot be changed; the Beginning remains in itself and renews all things. The Beginning is the one to whom it was said: ‘But you are the same, and your years shall not fail.’”] These are the subtleties of a man ignorant of Greek, as the best interpreters long ago demonstrated. Augustine nevertheless took ἀρχήν (*archēn*) to be in the accusative; therefore he thinks Christ speaks as though the words “believe me” had preceded—namely, “the Beginning.” But those who know Greek understand that, according to the solemn usage of that language, κατά (*kata*) must be supplied. There is no need to demonstrate this at greater length; we are not writing a commentary on John, but merely show in passing that, without knowledge of languages, the ingenuity of Scripture interpreters is empty.

## Tractate 43, § 17

“He did not say, ‘Before Abraham was, I was,’ but ‘Before Abraham came to be’—and he could not have come to be except through me—‘I am.’”] Those who know Greek understand that the verb γενέσθαι (*genesthai*) is equivalent to εἶναι (*einai*), and therefore this subtlety, tolerable only to those who know Latin, would have been hissed off the stage by Greeks. The same is true of Faustus Socinus’s interpretation of this passage, which is rejected by everyone who knows the language: he wanted even the words “before Abraham came to be” to be translated in that way, although with an entirely different meaning.

## Tractate 47, § 4

“The Lord himself was there; there he chose his mother; there he wished to be conceived, there to be born, there to shed his blood. There are his footprints; now they are worshiped, where he last stood, from which he ascended into heaven.”] The Parisian editors observe that footprints impressed in the ground on the Mount of Olives are also mentioned in the book *On Hebrew Places*, among Jerome’s works. They rightly say that this work is among Jerome’s works, for it is not by Jerome himself, who is also praised in it. It appears in volume III of Jerome’s works in Erasmus’s edition; it follows the book *On Hebrew Places* and is entitled *On the Acts of the Apostles*.

To say what seems to me the case, I would believe that shortly before this period the story later celebrated with such a grand display of words—of the discovery of Christ’s cross by Helena, the mother of Constantine, and of these footprints of Christ as he departed—began to be fabricated, not in Judea itself or in the neighboring provinces, but somewhere far away. Otherwise Eusebius would not have omitted these matters in his *Life of Constantine*, in which he exalts Constantine and Helena to such a degree and discusses the churches that she built in Palestine; nor would Jerome have omitted them, since he was no insignificant celebrator of the notable places of Judea.

These fabrications were eagerly seized upon by people who thought that anything believed to contribute to the confirmation of the Christian faith should be readily admitted, without more careful consideration of whether it was true. From this arose innumerable tales and superstitions, by which the native beauty of the Christian religion has been greatly obscured. It would have been far better for people who had no doubt about the truth and divinity of Christian doctrine to recoil from every argument that was not only false but also trivial and uncertain. For proven truth cannot be joined to falsehood or to uncertain rumors without being obscured or even dishonored.

Who would not be indignant that an uncertain, or even false, report was admitted by religious people in the same manner as the very truth of the Gospel? Who, even without being suspicious by temperament, would not suspect that many Christians embraced Christianity not because they had been struck by an inward apprehension of the truth of its doctrine, but because it was advantageous once Christians had gained power—since they immediately assented to shameful fables, provided those fables were useful? Those who willingly accommodated their faith in Christianity to every fabrication dishonored the Christian religion. If they had believed that the revelation proclaimed by Christians contained the opposite of all these things, they would have embraced them no less readily.

## Tractate 120, on John 20:42, § 5

“When, because of the *parasceve*, which we more commonly call in Latin among us the ‘pure supper,’ the Jews were not permitted to do such a thing.”] Joseph Scaliger discussed the *parasceve* at length in *On the Correction of the Times*, book VI, p. 564 of the Roverian edition.

After quoting this passage of Augustine, he adds:

> “The old translator of John Chrysostom, in the sermon on the birthday of John the Baptist: ‘For on the same day on which the Lord was conceived, he also suffered. That very day was the pure supper, on which the fourteenth moon also occurred. You see that *parasceve* properly means the period interposed between evening and sunset ... Otherwise, either improperly or in ordinary usage—καταχρηστικῶς (*katachrēstikōs*) or ἰδιωτικῶς (*idiōtikōs*)—the whole of Friday is also called *parasceve*, at least from the sixth hour, as in John. Thus it is called *parasceve* before it has arrived, although properly it began ἀπὸ ἐνάτης ὥρας (*apo enatēs hōras*), “from the ninth hour,” which was called [a term missing in the source], that is, “offering.” Henceforth, from the ninth hour, it was not permitted to work on the days before festivals, as is explicitly found in the canons of the Hebrews: “Whoever works on the eve of Sabbaths and festival days from the evening offering onward shall never see a good sign of blessing.” From this you can understand why Augustine said that the time of the burial was hastened: so that those who had taken Christ down from the cross would not be overtaken by ἡ ἐνάτη (*hē enatē*), the ninth hour, or the time of the evening offering, from which it was impious to work.’”

This eminent man derived these claims from Jewish teaching, which is utterly false, as is clear from Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34; from these passages it is clear that Christ was buried only after the ninth hour. It is also a mere invention that the properly designated preparation consisted of the final four hours of Friday, since *parasceve* occurs only as a term for the whole of Friday.

In any case, the Jews had likewise persuaded Augustine that the *parasceve* was called the “pure supper.” The pagans called a supper “pure” when it was served to those who were observing chastity for the sake of some festival. The Greeks called this ἁγνεύειν (*hagneuein*) and προαγνεύειν (*proagneuein*), “to prepare oneself for the celebration of a festival.” Thus the Jews came to think that the pure supper and preparation for the festival were the same thing, and on this account they called Friday by that name. There was nothing similar on other days, as Isaac Casaubon correctly observed in *Exercises against Baronius*, XVI, no. 16; see that work. Consult also Festus under the word *penem*, and Fulvius Ursinus in the appendix to Peter Ciacconius’s *On the Dining Room*.

# Remarks on the Tractates on the First Epistle of John

## Tractate 5, § 1

“To profess that one is without sin is dangerous, and not only dangerous but also erroneous.”] That is, “full of falsehood,” as is sufficiently clear both from what follows and from the proper meaning of the word; for it derives from *mendum*, which sometimes means “false.” See what John Clericus noted in chapter 2 of the *Epistle of Barnabas*.

Augustine labors at length in this passage to reconcile John, who says in the First Epistle, chapter 1: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” with chapter 3:9, where he denies that one born of God sins. Finally, he decides that the latter words are to be understood of sin against love of neighbor. Those who deny that John means a person born of God habitually sins, but allow only a sudden temptation or weakness, interpreted him much better. So in nearly everything, whenever something a little more difficult arises, good Augustine stumbles—especially if his statements are compared with the labors of more recent writers.

# Remarks on the Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans

The presbyter Augustine composed this work around the year 394, when he interpreted Scripture according to common notions. Accordingly, it contains many things that are purely Pelagian, as can be understood even from the passage prefixed to *The Retractions*. It is astonishing that a man who had never been condemned by anyone as a heretic, but rather had been praised by everyone, later attacked the same doctrines as though they could not coexist with the Christian religion. Yet if the Pelagian disputes had never arisen, he would have died holding those opinions. Indeed, perhaps he would never have attacked them so violently if Pelagius had not criticized something in his writings.

In *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 20, no. 53, he recounts in these words the first occasion of his indignation against Pelagius:

> “What of my little works could have become known more frequently and more pleasantly than the books of my *Confessions*? I published them before the Pelagian heresy existed. In them I certainly said: ‘Give what you command, and command what you will.’ When these words of mine were recalled at Rome in the presence of Pelagius by a certain brother and fellow bishop of mine, he could not bear them; and, contradicting him with rather great agitation, he almost quarreled with the man who had recalled them.”

This was the first origin of the evil; for nothing is more irritable than writers who afterwards fight for their writings as though for their altars and hearths.

## Proposition 44

On Romans 7:19–20. “For now the human being is described as placed under the law before grace. Then he is overcome by sins while attempting to live justly by his own powers, without the aid of God’s liberating grace. But in free will he has the ability to believe in the liberator and receive grace, so that, once the one who gives that grace has liberated and assisted him, he may not sin,” and so forth.] This is at least Semi-Pelagianism. If that doctrine was not taught in the Church at that time, Augustine was extraordinarily rash to speak on so serious a matter against everyone’s judgment. If it was taught, I do not understand how those who taught it could have been condemned as innovators and destructive heretics, when they taught what had previously been taught everywhere and what Augustine himself had written with approval. Augustine later retracted this passage, as well as certain other statements favorable to Pelagius. As for this passage, however, all the best interpreters recognize here a μετασχηματισμός (*metaschēmatismos*), by which Paul transfers into his own person what pertains to an unregenerate human being; they have placed this beyond all doubt.

# Remarks on the Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians
§ 24. It is rendered as follows at verse 19 of chapter III of the Epistle to the Galatians: “Why then the law? It was put forward for the sake of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise was made, arranged through angels in the hand of a mediator.”] This is sheer corruption, both in punctuation and in the word *dispositum* (“arranged”). The Greek reads:

> Τὶ οὖν ὁ νόμος; τῶν παραβάσεων χάριν προσετέθη, ἄχρις οὗ ἔλθῃ τὸ σπέρμα ᾧ ἐπήγγελται, διαταγεὶς δι’ ἀγγέλων ἐν χειρὶ μεσίτου.

That is: “What then is the law? It was added for the sake of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise was made, having been ordained through angels in the hand of a mediator.”

The modern Vulgate reads: “What then is the law? It was established because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom he had promised it, ordained through angels in the hand of a mediator.” The matter itself shows that it ought to be read in this way, and Augustine would have acknowledged it had he compared better manuscripts. Pelagius reads it thus in his *Commentary on this Epistle*, provided his words have not been altered there. So too does that Ambrosiaster whose commentaries on Paul’s Epistles have been associated with Ambrose.

But to Augustine it made no difference how it was read, since he was ready to extract any meaning whatever from any source and took no care to unfold the sequence of the discourse. Often he explained the meaning no more successfully when he followed the correct reading than when he followed the false one. Yet he cannot be praised for undertaking, while still a novice—for he composed this exposition while he was still a presbyter—and, moreover, ignorant of Greek, to interpret the most difficult books of the New Testament, the Epistles to the Romans and to the Galatians, without even procuring corrected manuscripts for himself.

Someone may perhaps think that this should be forgiven as the product of his zeal and good intentions; and I do not object, provided that things deserving pardon are not praised, or better things condemned when compared with them—something that many nevertheless do, whether through ignorance, shall I say, or through partisan zeal.

§ 40. Hence John also says in his address to the Parthians: “I write to you, fathers,” etc.] The words occur in 1 John II, 13. The Benedictines correctly printed it thus, not “to the Fathers.” See the heading of the treatises on this very Epistle, and consult Hugo Grotius, easily the foremost of Scripture interpreters, on the First Epistle of John.

§ 64. “For I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus Christ.”] These are the Apostle’s words, Galatians VI, 17, which Augustine interprets as follows: “That is, I have other conflicts and struggles with my flesh, which fight together with me in the persecutions that I endure.”

After reading this, everyone would expect Augustine to speak about the brands of soldiers, since some interpret this passage in that way. But listen to what follows:

> “For brands are said to be certain marks of servile punishments: if, for example, a slave has been put in fetters because of some offense—that is, because of some fault—or has suffered something of this kind, he is said to bear brands; and for this reason, in the law of manumission, he belongs to the inferior class.”

Even if these statements are true, they contribute nothing to his interpretation. From this, however, he could have inferred that Paul means to say that he is Christ’s slave, which the marks, as though impressed upon him by Christ, signified.

Moreover, I would understand “marks” *by antithesis* to the superstitious marks of idolaters, about which H. Grotius and Henry Hammond may be consulted on Revelation XIII, 15. In any case, *stigmata* were not properly called welts, but inscribed dots with which runaway slaves were sometimes marked; hence they were called *stigmatiae*, as the Greek lexicographers will explain.

# INTO THE FOURTH VOLUME

[Col. 0367]

## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS TO THE READER

[Col. 0367B]

The expositions of sacred books delivered before the people, which the Greeks call *homilies*, Saint Augustine calls *treatises*; we may call them sermons. In these, stenographers generally used to take down what was said. Sometimes the speaker, either before speaking or afterward, arranged in a written outline what he was preparing to discuss or what he had said.

In this kind of discourse much allowance is made for the ears of an uneducated and indiscriminate crowd. In the first several psalms he is more restrained and precise. In the later ones he repeatedly wanders into long digressions, apparently because his intention has changed. Read attentively and you will find an incomparable treasure of secret doctrine. Farewell.

# NOTES ON THE EXPOSITIONS OF THE PSALMS

[Col. 0367C]

I suppose that by “secret doctrine” Erasmus means the allegorical meanings of the psalms; for I do not understand what else could here be called secret. For extracting the literal meaning, there is nothing in the *Expositions of the Psalms* that would not occur to anyone and everywhere. As for Christian theology and ethics, there is nothing here hidden or at all uncommon.

These are, plainly, expositions intended to instruct the uneducated common people, ready to drink in everything with attentive ears—not writings composed for the learned and for those devoted to the true meanings of Scripture.

Two things, it seems to me, may be required of an interpreter of the psalms. First, above all, he should show what the proper and grammatical meaning is, which is usually called the literal meaning. But this cannot be discovered unless the Hebrew is carefully consulted and, for easier understanding, interpreters are diligently compared with one another.

For it is plainly to grope in the dark to depend entirely upon a perhaps corrupt translation—or, worse still, upon a translation of that translation into another language—and yet to wish to interpret Scripture. We must therefore have recourse to the authoritative and original writings.

Augustine entirely neglected these, both because he could not consult the Hebrew text and its interpreters and because he did not wish to remain within the literal meaning. Consequently, he not only often failed to grasp the meaning of the psalmist himself, but did not even understand the Septuagint translators, whose frequently barbarous and obscure translation is much better understood from the Hebrew text than if it is read by itself.

Moreover, where the literal meaning is simple and clear, there was no need to desert it and wander into spiritual interpretations. Yet Augustine does this almost continually, and indeed in such a way that he applauds himself for it extraordinarily. Thus he does not make obscure things clearer through his labor, but makes what is clear as obscure as possible.

For example, the literal meaning of Psalm CXIX is scarcely anywhere clearer. The whole psalm concerns the excellence and observance of God’s law, and nothing could have been treated more appropriately by the prophet, both to strengthen himself in observing the law and to lead his countrymen toward holiness of conduct.

Yet Augustine, rejecting these matters as supposedly unworthy of the prophetic spirit, sought meanings of which no one would ever have thought who had properly understood the literal sense and its most beautiful consequences. “The clearer that psalm appears,” he says, “the deeper it usually seems to me, so that I cannot even demonstrate how deep it is. In the case of other psalms, which are difficult to understand, even if the meaning lies hidden in obscurity, the obscurity itself nevertheless appears. But in this one not even that does, because it presents such a surface that it seems to require a reader and hearer, not an expositor.”

Who does not see that the bishop of Hippo was here seeking a knot in a bulrush? In a simple interpretation he could not have displayed that *aperantologia*—his “boundless verbosity”—which Erasmus reproaches him with in Letter 67 of Book XX, as he did here. Ingenious and learned men used to say that those were the characteristics of the age: to speak at length about a subject that seemed to offer no material for eloquence.

A second thing that may be required of an interpreter of the psalms lies in extracting the spiritual meaning. In this matter the guiding star, so to speak, must be the apostles. Passages from the Psalms cited in the New Testament as prophecies should be explained in such a way that it is clear that the apostles did not praise them without reason.

For this purpose all the resources of sacred criticism must be employed—resources of which Augustine was almost entirely deprived, and therefore could not accomplish the task. But because the apostles understood and interpreted certain passages of the psalms in a spiritual sense, it does not follow that anyone, for any reason whatsoever, may twist everything at will into spiritual meanings. Yet Augustine did this continually, and with great praise from the uneducated ages and from those who imitated them.

In those apostolic citations, the apostles often seem to have had regard to Jewish traditions and opinions, from which they rightly reasoned against the Jews of their own time. Thus they are arguments that logicians call *ad hominem*, arguments which they would not have used as firm proofs before others. Often, too, the prophetic spirit with which the apostles were inspired disclosed to them things that would otherwise have escaped us, just as it had to the ancient prophets.

Thus everyone assents to their authority, and no one doubts that the passages were rightly cited by the apostles; yet no reasonable person today would tolerate anyone’s explaining the Old Testament in this manner. Why should we allow words to be thrust upon us with great pomp by men who are not inspired at all, and are even ignorant—words that cannot be proved in any way if they are denied? Why should everything that occurs to declaimers concerning any passage of Scripture be treated as sacred? What limit will there finally be to dreams, in a matter so serious, if we decide that such things must be admitted?

[Col. 0369C]

The usefulness of these Augustinian declamations for understanding the Psalms is therefore slight. Nevertheless, they were once not useless for instructing the common people and rousing them to virtue, because even things said beside the point and in an inappropriate place can be useful, provided only that they are true.

Let these works therefore be read as sermons and as various theological and moral meditations, not as interpretations of Scripture. Let what is rightly, sharply, and ingeniously said be excerpted from them and applied on suitable occasions, with the author duly praised. Augustine will be given whatever honor is owed him, and his works will not be deprived of their usefulness.

Anyone who opens the volume and reads several pages in it will discover that what we have said is entirely true and fair. Nevertheless, we shall illustrate the matter with several examples, for we are not undertaking to write notes on this enormous volume; nor would that labor bring any benefit commensurate with the effort it would require.

[Col. 0369D]

## ON PSALM I

He interprets verse 1 as follows: “It is to be understood of our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, of the Lord’s man.” Why so? Whoever observed the divine law was surely blessed both in fact and in hope. It is therefore absurd to apply by force to Christ what fits everyone perfectly.

The author of the *Exposition of the Psalms*, wrongly attributed to Jerome and published at the end of volume II of Jerome’s works, Paris, 1699, had this passage in mind. “Some,” says the writer of that *Exposition*, “report that the key of this psalm should be referred to the person of Christ our Lord, so that this blessed man may be Christ according to his humanity.” A good intention, certainly, but ignorance—though he himself is an interpreter of little worth.

In the same place, on the words “He did not sit in the seat of pestilence,” Augustine says:

> “He did not desire an earthly kingdom with pride. This is rightly understood as the seat of pestilence, because scarcely anyone is without a love of ruling or does not seek human glory. For pestilence is a disease widely spread and embracing everyone, or almost everyone.”

But although kings sit on a chair or throne, whenever the word “chair” occurs it does not therefore concern kingship, unless the circumstances of the passage lead the reader in that direction; here there are no such circumstances.

Although “of the pestilential” ought rather to have been translated than “of pestilence,” as I shall say shortly, even with the latter reading Augustine could easily have understood that the passage concerns the assembly of pestilential people, if he had been somewhat more skilled in critical method.

Psalm XXV, 4–5, makes this perfectly clear—I follow the Greek division—where the psalmist says, according to the ancient version:

> “I did not sit with the council of vanity,  
> and I will not enter with those who do evil.  
> I hated the assembly of the wicked,  
> and I will not sit with the ungodly.”

So also Psalm XLIX, 21, and Psalm CXVIII, 23.

Idle men commonly sit together in public places or in places where they customarily gather, and attack the reputations of others with slanderous speech. Hence Theophrastus, *Characters* 29, the chapter on slander, speaks of the slanderer as follows:

> Συγκαθήμενος δεινὸς περὶ τοῦ ἀναστάντος, εἰπεῖν

“Sitting among others, ready to speak about the one who has risen.”

We also have an example of “slanderers sitting in a physician’s office” in Aelian, *Various History*, Book III, chapter 7:

> καθεζομένων ἐν ἰατρείῳ ψογερῶν

Augustine would have understood this more easily if he had looked at the Greek version, which has *loimōn* (“of pestilential people”), a word that often signifies pestilent persons. If he had also compared Aquila’s version with it, he could have understood that the Hebrew word used here was one that the Jews commonly translated as *χλευασταί*, “mockers.”

He would also have learned that this is a plural noun, from which it was clear that the Latin translator had rendered it badly as *pestilentiae* (“of pestilence”); and since one could scarcely say “the seat of pestilences,” the word *loimoi* must signify pestilential people. He could have learned at least part of this from the Ambrosian exposition of this psalm, if he had consulted it.

[Col. 0370D]

In the same place, on verse 2—“But his will was in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night”—he reasons as follows:

> “The law is not laid down for the righteous, as the Apostle says; but it is one thing to be in the law and another to be under the law. He who is in the law acts according to the law; he who is under the law is acted upon according to the law. The former is free, the latter a slave.”

Because this seemed beautiful long ago to Numidians and other Africans who were not more learned, must we also consider it extraordinary? If such things came from us, would they be hissed off the stage or received with applause? I do not think the latter.

Therefore, with the permission of the Numidians and of all others who once found such things pleasing, we shall say: first, that Paul’s passage is entirely beside the point; second, that the psalm does not say that anyone is “in the law,” but that his will is in the law—that is, according to the constant usage of the Hebrew language, that he delights in the divine law and willingly obeys it; third, that the distinction between “under the law” and “in the law” is pointless, since no one says, “His will is under the law.”

Nevertheless, good Augustine continues to quibble in these words:

> “Next, one law is that which is written and imposed upon a servant; another is the law contemplated in the mind by one who does not need letters.”

But no other law is at issue here than the Mosaic law, which was committed to writing and imposed upon all Jews without exception. David is speaking here, a Hebrew man, and indeed about men of his own nation, who possessed the written law and observed it.

In the same place: “He will meditate day and night,” that is, it should be understood as “without interruption.” Excellent—if you delete the word “or.” But, carried away by Academic fluctuations, he adds even in a clear matter: “or by day, in joy; by night, in tribulations.”

I admit that daylight sometimes signifies prosperity and darkness adversity; but to do something by day and night has never signified doing it in prosperity and adversity. Because a word signifies something in a particular context, it does not follow that wherever it occurs it can be understood in the same way.

But let us hear his examples, for he offers two. “For it is said,” he writes, “John VIII, 56: ‘Abraham saw my day and rejoiced.’ And concerning tribulation it is said: ‘Moreover, even until night my reins corrected me,’ Psalm XV, 7.”

But in Christ’s words “day” does not signify joy, but the time when he was to be upon the earth. As for the psalmist’s passage, “even by night my reins instructed me,” it is too obscure to prove anything and can be understood more conveniently in another way, as any of the more recent interpreters will show.

In the same place, § 3. These are the words of verse 3: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water.”

Even children should understand that this is a simile, which can be explained only as a whole, and in such a way that the appropriateness of the entire comparison is shown—not by tearing it apart into separate pieces.

Nevertheless, after quoting these words, Augustine begins to interpret them as follows:

> “That is, either according to that very Wisdom which deigned to assume man for our salvation, so that the man himself may be the tree planted beside streams of water. For it may also be understood in the sense of what is said in another psalm, Psalm LXIV, 10: ‘The river of God is filled with water.’”

First, who does not know that in a simile the thing from which the comparison is drawn must be understood literally, as the phrase goes? Augustine himself did not fail to know this, but an excessive and untimely desire to quibble, together with African *aperantologia*, prevented him from using his own judgment.

Moreover, the passage in Psalm LXIV, 10, is neither similar nor does it mean what he wants. For the “river of God” there is the Jordan, as Ludovic Ferrandus correctly noted, I believe from Theodore of Mopsuestia.

Our author continues with the same acumen:

> “Or according to the Holy Spirit, according to whom it is said: ‘He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit,’ etc.”

No one will deny that the Holy Spirit is often compared with water; but in this simile he cannot be signified by “streams of water.”

A third interpretation is then offered, more absurd than the preceding ones:

> “Or according to the sins of the peoples, because the waters are also interpreted as peoples in the Apocalypse, and ‘streams’ may not absurdly be understood as falls, which pertains to sin.”

O what acumen! O Numidians endowed with patient ears—or eyes! Our countrymen today would not hear such things without laughter.

But listen to the rest:

> “That tree, therefore—that is, our Lord—draws them from the flowing waters, that is, from sinful peoples, along the way into the roots of his discipline.”

There is no need to point out how twisted this is. I shall say only that Augustine forgot that the blessed man of whom verse 1 speaks is compared with a tree planted beside water. Consequently, that tree cannot be Christ if the same blessed man is Christ, as he said. For the first and the latter parts of a simile cannot be the same thing.

“He will yield fruit”—that is, “he will establish churches”—“in his season”—that is, after he had been glorified by resurrection and ascension into heaven, etc.

Those who have worked most successfully in interpreting the parables of the New Testament observe that the individual parts of a simile should not be pressed too far, but that the simile as a whole should simply be applied to the whole subject under discussion. No parable rests upon a perfect correspondence between its individual parts, and it is uncertain whether Christ had those minor correspondences in mind.

Had Augustine reflected on this, he would have removed these and many other things from his *Expositions*.

In the same place, § 4, on verse 4: “Not so the ungodly, not so; but like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth,” he says:

> “Earth here must be understood as stability in God.”

To confirm this, he adduces passages of Scripture in which, as he thought, “earth” signifies that allegorically. But since all those allegorical fantasies can be refuted by a simple denial, this passage too rejects that interpretation, because in this part of the simile the word “earth” must be taken literally, as we demonstrated concerning the preceding simile.

Afterward he says: “From the face of whose earth the wind drives the ungodly—that is, pride, because it inflates.”

A fortunate discovery indeed! The ungodly is not said here to be driven from the face of the earth, but to be like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth. That is, his condition before God is utterly unstable and contemptible, as dust driven by the wind is among human beings. See the similar comparison in Psalm XVII, 42, Psalm XXXIV, 5, and elsewhere.

[Col. 0372D]

In the same place, § 5, on verse 5: “Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment.”

“Therefore,” he says, “because they are driven like dust from the face of the earth.” He rightly says that what the proud desire should be taken away from them—that is, the ability to judge—so that this very point may be understood more clearly in the following sentence: “nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous.”

But where does “to rise” or “to stand up in judgment” signify acting as judge? If he had consulted either the Hebrew text or a Jewish interpreter, he would have learned that the word David uses here signifies not so much “to rise” as “to stand.” From this he would have inferred that the psalmist means that the ungodly will not be able to stand in judgment—that is, that they will be defeated in their case. See Isaiah VII, 12; Malachi III, 2; Romans XIV, 4; and Hugo Grotius on this passage.

[Col. 0373A]

## ON PSALM II

§ 6, on the words of verse 6: “I have begotten you today.”

“Although,” he says, “that day may seem in prophecy to be the day on which Jesus Christ was born according to his humanity, nevertheless ‘today,’ because it signifies the present and in eternity there is neither anything past, as though it had ceased to exist, nor anything future, as though it did not yet exist, but only the present, because whatever is eternal always is—must be understood divinely according to the saying, ‘I have begotten you today.’ By this, the most sincere and Catholic faith proclaims the eternal generation of the power and wisdom of God, who is the only-begotten Son.”

Although this interpretation is not peculiar to Augustine, it should first of all be observed that this psalm ought to have been explained concerning David, who is speaking about himself; and then, in a higher sense, concerning Christ, since that is how the apostles understood this psalm.

[Col. 0373B]

As for David, he is said to have been begotten by God when he was appointed king, for kings are called sons of the Most High, Psalm LXXXI, 6. Indeed, it is plainly evident from what precedes and follows that his kingship is intended.

As for the spiritual meaning, if I deny that “today” is ever used in Scripture of eternity, I shall have no reason to fear that anyone will accuse me of error. Scripture should not be explained from philosophical doctrines and Platonic teachings without reason, as many Fathers did here and elsewhere.

Moreover, since the apostles taught us that this passage concerns Christ—something we would otherwise have been unaware of—we should also seek its genuine meaning from those same apostles. They do not refer it to eternal generation, but to the authority conferred upon Christ after his resurrection. Paul explains the passage of his resurrection in Acts XIII, 33; the writer to the Hebrews explains it of his priesthood, which he exercised especially in heaven, in chapter V, 5.

I would rather agree with them than with the Platonists. This also seemed right to Hilary, in his exposition of Psalm II, § 30, in the Benedictine edition:

> “Apostolic authority,” he says, “refers it neither to the birth from the virgin nor to the generation of baptism, but to the firstborn from the dead.”

In the same place, § 10. Augustine interprets “embrace discipline” as “understand and be instructed,” and indeed he could not have done otherwise. But if he had consulted the Hebrew, he would have found here a particular prophecy concerning Christ: “Kiss the son,” which more recent interpreters rightly understand as a kiss offered as a sign of honor, as though to a king. See Genesis XLI, 40; 1 Samuel X, 1.

## ON PSALM III

§ 1. Although the title of the psalm is “A Psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son,” Augustine begins his exposition as follows:

> “The fact that it was said, ‘I slept and took sleep, and I rose because the Lord will sustain me,’ persuades us that this psalm should be understood of Christ’s passion. For this sounds more appropriately of the Lord’s passion and resurrection than of that historical event in which David is written to have fled from the face of his son Absalom, who was waging war against him.”

I do not know how the twisted interpretations of allegorists could have been prevented, since even the clearest title of this psalm could not restrain us from indulging in allegorical dreams.

The passage he adduces fits the historical account of Christ’s death and resurrection in no way, but agrees perfectly with David’s circumstances. When many thought that the matter was lost because the overwhelming majority of the Israelites were following Absalom, the prophet says that he had fled to God’s help and that God had heard him. He immediately adds the quoted words, “I slept,” etc., which most appropriately signify the security and tranquillity of David’s mind after he had placed his trust in God. His security is described similarly in Psalm IV, 9.

Why, then, should another meaning have been sought, when this one was most beautiful and provided us with outstanding lessons not to despair but to place our confidence in God? The reason is that, disregarding what lay at their feet, they sought things that otherwise would never have occurred to anyone. This might be tolerated if the interpretation that first presented itself to the mind were not the best and most appropriate to the words; but the interpretation brought in from afar is forced and foreign to the words and the sequence of the discourse.

But let us hear Augustine, strangely abusing his ingenuity. “Some,” he says, “hold that Judas is signified by the name Absalom, and Christ by the person of David.” Then he adds:

> “Although historically it may be understood that he fled from his face when, after Absalom’s departure, he withdrew with the others to the mountain, yet spiritually, when the Son of God—the power and wisdom of God—deserted the mind of Judas . . . it is rightly understood that Christ fled from his face.”

Neither the historical nor the spiritual meaning can be tolerated except by those who see in Scripture whatever they wish, like children seeing shapes in the clouds.

[Col. 0374C]

Yet the meaning of the name Absalom greatly obstructed him. He speaks as follows:

> “Absalom, as some interpret it, is said in Latin to mean ‘peace of the father.’ This may seem surprising, whether in the history of the Kings, since Absalom waged war against his father, or in the history of the New Testament, since Judas was the Lord’s betrayer: how could ‘peace of the father’ be understood?”

If the name Absalom had been given only after his death, he would undoubtedly have acquired another name. But those who gave it to the infant had not foreseen that he would one day wage war against his father. Much less could they have known that there would one day be a Numidian rhetorician who would want the name Absalom to signify the betrayer of his Lord.

But who would not be astonished that, after fabricating an allegory, Augustine finds it astonishing that his invention does not fit the name Absalom? Why did he not rather abandon the invention? He later extricates himself by saying that David had been at peace with Absalom during that war because he wished to spare him, and that Christ had endured Judas among his followers with equanimity.

Thus conjecturers of this kind never lack a back door through which to escape if they cannot get out by another route. If the name of David’s son had happened to signify something warlike, with what applause these fictions would have been received! They did not even lack applause though the name sounds peaceful.

In the same place, § 3, on the words of verse 4, “But you, Lord, are my protector,” he writes:

> “According to his humanity, this is said to God, because the assumption of humanity is the Word made flesh.”

The entire force of this interpretation is drawn from the word “protector,” because the Word was said to have assumed human flesh. But the prophet was not speaking Latin. The Hebrew here has “you are a shield for me.” The Greeks, translating the sense rather than the precise wording, have *antilēptōr mou ei*, that is, “you are my helper”; for “protector” is a bad translation.

Thus Augustine extracted a great mystery from a bad translation. If we love truth, he ought either to have procured more resources for himself or to have refrained from interpreting when he lacked everything except Punic *aperantologia*.

In the same place: “You lift up my head.” “Here,” he says, “I think the human mind should be understood, since it may not absurdly be called the head of the soul.”

On the contrary, he invents an absurd expression, an expression of which no example has ever been heard in any language—especially since a most suitable interpretation is readily available. See Martin Geier and the other interpreters.

In the same place, § 4, on the words of verse 5, “With my voice I cried to the Lord,” he says:

> “That is, not with the voice of the body, which is produced with the noise of struck air,” etc.

Why not? Was it unbecoming for David to invoke God with a clear and loud voice when he was in such distress? I certainly would not think so.

Nevertheless, Augustine denies that “I cried to the Lord” can properly be said except when the soul alone speaks to the Lord, drawing nothing bodily and nothing of bodily intentions into its prayer, where God alone hears. Yet this too is called a cry because of the force of the intention itself.

I would not deny that, in a transferred sense, those who pray to the Lord without words and within the mind may be said to cry out to him. But I emphatically deny that those who genuinely cry out do not truly and properly cry out.

In the same place: “And he heard me from his holy mountain.” “We have,” he says, “the Lord himself spoken of as a mountain through the prophet, as it is written in Daniel II, 35.”

But even if we grant that Christ is described through the image of a mountain in Daniel, does it follow that whenever “the Lord’s mountain” is mentioned we should believe that Christ may be intended, even where the circumstances oppose it, as here? No one skilled in Scripture would say so; and it is clear that Mount Zion is meant here.

Augustine himself rejects this interpretation except through some contorted sense:

> “But this,” he says, “cannot be understood from his own person, unless perhaps he wished to say: ‘He heard me from myself, as from his holy mountain,’ when he dwelt in me, that is, in the mountain itself.”

Who has ever heard anything less plausible and more remote from all the usage of Holy Scripture? Nor did such things merely spill carelessly from Augustine while he was occupied with something else; this entire work, indeed all his works, teem with interpretations of this kind.

Listen also to what follows, which pleased him more:

> “It is clearer and more straightforward if we understand that God heard from his own righteousness: for, being righteous as one who was killed innocent and received evil in return for good, he raised him from the dead and assigned fitting punishment to his persecutors.”

The fact itself is completely true—who could deny it? But how it can be extracted from this passage of the psalmist, very few could guess.

“For we read,” he says, “‘Your righteousness is like the mountains of God,’ Psalm XXXV, 7. Does it therefore follow that the mountain of God signifies the righteousness of God?”

Who ever heard this expression—“to hear from righteousness”—before Augustine used it? There are recent heterodox writers who are accused of forced interpretations; but compared with this and similar interpretations, which fill every page in the ten volumes of Augustine that survive for us, everything in their works is clear and easy.

Nevertheless, the heterodox are assailed with insults, while Augustine is raised to heaven with praises.

In the same place, § 5: “I slept and took sleep.” He says:

> “It may appropriately be observed that the word ‘I’ is placed here to signify that he endured death by his own will, according to the saying: ‘Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life,’ etc., John X, 18.”

Who would ever have thought that the word “I” contained this emphasis unless instructed by Augustine? But if someone denied it, by what example could he prove it? By none. As for John’s passage, the little word “I” would not prove that Christ died voluntarily unless other words had been added that clearly signified this.

We have already seen that “sleep” here signifies David’s security amid dangers, relying on God’s help. Augustine therefore observed pointlessly that Scripture innumerably uses sleep for death. This applies to passages in which it is certain that someone’s death is being discussed, or at least in which there is nothing that rejects that meaning.

Everyone knows the enduring rule of interpretation: one must not flee to a metaphorical meaning while the literal meaning is possible. Here, however, the entire sequence of the discourse shows that the subject is either actual sleep or the security associated with sleep.

Nor should we ask, Augustine adds, why “I took sleep” was added when “I slept” had already been said. Scripture commonly has repetitions of this kind, as we demonstrated at length in the second psalm.

What he says about repetitions is true, but it has no bearing on this passage, in which the Hebrew words are [Hebrew expression unclear in the supplied text], that is, “I lay down and slept,” which are distinct actions. Augustine’s statements on this matter, both above and below, are therefore empty.

In the same place he says:

> “This should be observed even more carefully: how in one sentence he has placed a verb in the past tense and one in the future. For he said, ‘And I rose,’ which is past; and ‘he will sustain me,’ which is future, although he could not rise without that sustaining.”

There is nothing surprising in David’s using a future-tense verb—“he will support me” or “he will sustain me”—because when he wrote the psalm he had not yet been delivered from the danger created for him by Absalom. He composed it during the flight itself, as the title shows.

The additions concerning a future prophecy mingled with past events are therefore entirely beside the point.

In the same place, § 7. Verse 8 should not be punctuated as though this were one sentence: “Arise, Lord; save me, my God, because you have struck all those who oppose me without cause.”

For he does not save him because he struck his enemies; rather, after he had saved him, he struck them. Therefore the following words belong with the preceding clause, so that the meaning is:

> “Because you have struck all those who oppose me without cause, you have broken the teeth of sinners.”

That is, “you have broken the teeth of sinners because you have struck all those who oppose me.”

On the contrary, David is asking God to protect and save him because God had previously always exacted penalties from all his adversaries. He asks that former benefits be increased by new ones.

I shall not take up Augustine’s sophistry concerning the teeth, any more than the twofold interpretation by which he later explains this psalm as referring to the Church considered together with Christ its Head, or the tropological interpretation that follows afterward. The observations above have placed our judgment of this work in clear light; from them, moreover, a reader who has patience for tedium and abundant leisure may gather several points concerning [Col. 0377B] both the customs and doctrines of the Church of that age and Augustine’s own particular opinions. But these must be selected from the enormous heap of frigid allegories and twisted interpretations.

## ON PSALM LXXVII, § 3

Although the Jewish assembly is properly called the Synagogue, and the Christian assembly the Church—for [Col. 0378A] *congregatio* is ordinarily understood more as a gathering of animals, whereas *convocatio* more as a gathering of human beings—we nevertheless find that the former too is called “Church.”] Isaac Casaubon correctly observed, in *Exercitation* 16 against Baronius, no. 42, that the occasion for this quibble is the derivation of *congregare* from *grex*; but nothing similar can be sought in the Greek word συναγωγή (*synagōgē*). Moreover, in James 2:3 the Church is called a synagogue. See Casaubon himself. But who could tolerate the observation of such matters merely because of the name Asaph, attached to the title of the psalm and signifying “assembly”? Asaph, as is well known, is the author of twelve psalms; he was a Levite of the family of the Gershonites and was placed by David in charge of sacred music. See 1 Chronicles 6:31, 39.

## ON PSALM CVIII, § 1

Certain statements appear to concern the apostle Peter specifically, yet they have no [Col. 0378B] clear meaning unless they are referred to the Church, whose person he is acknowledged to have represented figuratively, because of the primacy which he held among the disciples, etc.] Isaac Casaubon has dealt at great length with Peter’s primacy on the basis of Augustine and the other Fathers, in *Exercise* 15 on the *Annals* of Caesar Baronius.

# ON THE FIFTH VOLUME

[Col. 0377]

## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS TO THE READER

[Note: [Col. 0377D] This brief preface had been prefixed to volume X, into which Erasmus had gathered all Augustine’s sermons; in the Paris edition, however, both the order of the volumes and that of the sermons was entirely changed. Nevertheless, we did not wish to [Col. 0378D] omit even this brief notice. The sermons *To the Brothers Living in the Desert*, of which this eminent man speaks, have been relegated to volume VI, where Erasmus’s brief censures will be presented. PHEREPONUS.]

[Col. 0377B]

We have placed first those works that are indisputably Augustine’s. We have relegated the most shameless fabrication, the *Sermons to the Brothers Living in the Desert*, to its own section; we shall say something about it in its proper place. [Col. 0377C] The remaining works also contain much that has little connection with Augustine’s style and learning, and we have marked some of it.

## DEDICATORY PREFACE OF JOHN ULIMMERIUS, REGULAR CANON OF THE MONASTERY OF ST MARTIN OF LOUVAIN, TO THE SERMONS OF ST AUGUSTINE AND OTHER SHORT WORKS EDITED BY HIM AT LOUVAIN, AT THE PRESS OF JEROME WELLAEUS, IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1564

To the most reverend father in Christ and lord, Lord Martin Rithovius, most worthy first bishop of the Church of Ypres, John Ulimmerius wishes perpetual happiness.

Since nothing in all nature is so firm, stable, and everlasting that it does not suffer some notable injury from age—which, as Varro writes, corrupts a few things but destroys many—most illustrious bishop, [Col. 0377D] those appear to me to render an outstanding service to the republic of letters who devote all their study, industry, and, finally, time to bringing ancient authors into the light as accurately as possible, authors whose works are either wholly corrupted or entirely lost. If anyone else has performed this service for blessed Augustine, the supreme pillar of the Catholic Church, with the greatest diligence, then certainly the most learned and painstaking man, Lord Martin Lypsius, appears to have done so above all.

[Col. 0378B] For he, who seems to have bound himself wholly to this task, was not content merely to rescue Augustine from the countless errors with which he had been defiled on every side. After examining, [Col. 0378C] with equal labor and diligence, various libraries that were celebrated for the abundance of their ancient volumes, he also took care to add to Augustine’s remaining writings whatever he found anywhere, hitherto unprinted, that seemed to reflect the Augustinian mind, majesty, and style. Nor did success altogether fail this pious undertaking. For, besides the third book *Against Gaudentius*, which the library of the canons of Parcens supplied to us, and besides the letters—more than twenty-two in number—he also collected, from various places, several sermons of those now published for the first time, which the ancients entitled *On Various Subjects*.

Indeed, he had resolved to have them printed together with his other sermons, had not that military upheaval which Martin Rossem had stirred up throughout our Belgium at that time [Col. 0378D] thrown everything into confusion. This certainly brought us much hardship and loss. To say nothing of the ravaged fields, the burning of houses, the driving away of cattle, the captivity of people of every age, and the incredible losses suffered by many as a result of so wicked an undertaking, the students of Augustine also suffered this disadvantage: that they were forced to remain deprived of so excellent a treasure, as though it had been dug out of underground veins rich in metals.

Thus, just as [Col. 0379A] Ausonius elegantly writes that labors are chained together and one undertaking gives rise to another, so it may be said that calamities are linked together in a kind of cycle of fetters, and that evil arises from evil. For when, as I have said, the noise of war was raging everywhere around us, and the roads did not seem sufficiently safe from the attacks of soldiers, while the tenth volume of Augustine’s works was laboring under the press and already anticipating the light of day, we waited in vain for someone to carry this little bundle into Germany. It was not conveyed there until the volume had, as they say, reached its final stages.

When a second edition was said to be in preparation at the Frobenian press, we tried to repair that unfavorable turn of events [Col. 0379B] through whatever labor we could provide, so that nothing might be lacking to our Augustine and so that Lypsius’s work might not in any way appear to have been lost. We therefore sent to Basel many of Augustine’s works, corrected far more carefully than before. Among them was the tenth volume, which until then had been more contaminated than the others: we had collated it with twenty or more ancient copies, and the sermons we are now publishing were, for the most part, included in that work.

But the bookseller, retaining everything and selecting only five sermons, suppressed the rest—I do not know for what reason—and sent nothing further back to us. Consequently, whatever labor our Lypsius had previously swallowed, we had to expend again, with the greatest nausea and weariness, both in seeking out what I had sent and in copying it. I could hardly say how much distress this caused me—not to mention the expense as well. [Col. 0379C] Yet one good thing came of it: what, after Lypsius and Coster, we had previously despaired of finding was discovered while we were occupied with another matter and happened, by good fortune, to be reading the life of that same blessed Augustine which had been appended here.

I mean the *Index* first promised by Bishop Possidius in his *Life* and composed later. Since the distinguished theologian Lord Jacob Pamelius, a canon of Bruges, repeatedly gave me no dull spur to undertake and complete these labors, I wished to dedicate and consecrate it to him. He searches out the works of ancient writers, especially theologians, with such ardor and such expense that I trust he will one day rescue from darkness, for the benefit of students, everything of Augustine’s that lies hidden anywhere in the world, [Col. 0379D] and will supply whatever is lacking from our marginal annotations.

Nevertheless, this did not alone ease the deep grief I had conceived over the suppression of Lord Augustine’s sermons. We also found many other sermons never before printed, and it seemed appropriate to dedicate them to Your Eminence after adding them to the Lypsian texts and correcting them through immense labor.

Many reasons moved me to think that these works should be offered especially to Your Lordship. I would enumerate them at greater length if I did not suppose that your singular modesty would find this burdensome, and fear that I might appear to flatter you rather than speak from the heart. Yet I cannot pass over this one point in silence: nothing seemed more fitting to me than that the memorials of a bishop should be dedicated to a bishop; all the more because your character, [Col. 0380A] learning, piety, and, in short, your entire manner of life seem to correspond with Augustine’s virtues.

How great was his care for his sheep! With what ardor did he instruct his subjects in a perfect and blessed manner of life! How gently and appropriately to the times did he stir the people, through various sermons, toward piety and holiness of life! But who does not admire all these qualities as eminent in Your Lordship? I pass over the fact that you are almost the only bishop who has a monastery of clerics with you—something our most holy Augustine also declares of himself in those two distinguished sermons that he delivered to the people of Hippo concerning the common life of his clerics.

Those sermons, omitted by Erasmus—I do not know whether through deliberate intention or some forgetfulness—and later mixed with spurious and eremitical sermons, I separated from them [Col. 0380B] and attached to the *Life*, since they make the fullest mention of that same saint. Receive, therefore, bishop from bishop: Augustine from one who is no less an admirer than an imitator of the Augustinian life. Do not disdain to commend these sermons to your own, so that henceforth, abstaining from colder and less worthy matters to read, they may prefer to devote their oil and labor to studies that are holier and more useful.

Moreover, I did not think it worthwhile to bring forward many arguments by which I might demonstrate, to any rash critics who may exist, that these works are true and genuine Augustine. First, because it would not be difficult to persuade you of this, since you have always been so attentive a reader of him that everywhere you recognize Augustine revealing himself, however deeply occupied with other matters, through a certain august piety. Second, because Possidius lists these works among his writings, and—[Col. 0380C] if the agreement of ancient manuscripts has any value—they are read under Augustine’s name in the oldest books.

But if anyone objects that constant and consistent attention must always be paid to style, let him know that this principle applies to those who either wrote or dictated books. I do not see how it can apply to one preaching before a mixed crowd, since speech must be adapted and accommodated to the habits of ordinary people. Indeed, the longer St Augustine served the ears of the common people by preaching, the more he relaxed the elegance of his language and the more he used a rustic—indeed, if I may say so, a more contemptible—style of speech.

Mystical subjects too have their own kind of diction, and Ciceronian perfume is not appropriate to things prepared for teaching. Add to this that he did not always preach in cathedral churches, where it is beyond dispute that [Col. 0380D] most of the people were more learned, but also in the other cities and small towns of his diocese.

Now, when Augustine was growing old, who does not know that Africa had become largely infected with barbarism because of the continual incursions of the Goths and Vandals? Or who could not learn this from the holy bishop Victor of Vita? In describing an exceedingly elegant eulogy of this bishop of ours, he says:

“When the city of Hippo Regius was under siege, and the blessed Augustine, a bishop worthy of every praise and author of many books, was governing it, the stream of eloquence that had flowed abundantly through all the fields of the Church was dried up by fear; and the sweetness of a pleasure offered with greater sweetness was turned [Col. 0381A] into the bitterness of wormwood, so that the words of David might be fulfilled: ‘When the sinner stood against me, I was struck dumb, humbled, and silenced from good things.’

“By that time he had already completed 232 books, apart from innumerable letters, his exposition of the entire Psalter and of the Gospels, and his popular treatises, which the Greeks call homilies; to reckon their number is virtually impossible.”

Thus far Victor. I could cite testimonies such as these, and similar ones from St Paulinus, Prosper, Leo, Fulgentius, Eugippius, Gregory, and others, showing how highly blessed Augustine was esteemed and honored by everyone. But I would feel it irreverent to detain you longer, since you constantly meditate upon Augustine’s divine virtues and measure your own character by their standard. [Col. 0381B] If anywhere, certainly in these sermons to the people, those virtues may be found in their greatest abundance.

In cleansing and purifying these sermons, if I did not accomplish what I wished, I certainly accomplished what I could. Nothing can be made so complete by the work of a single person that there is nothing left to desire in it. Our Lypsius learned this splendidly by experience; I have thoroughly investigated his incredible labors and his sleepless vigils, which cannot be valued highly enough, in correcting Augustine. I therefore think that very few people would believe me if, eager to say more about this matter, I were to describe what he accomplished, unless they themselves had tested with their own eyes, together with me, what he achieved.

It has now occurred to me that there are some who have begun to disparage everywhere his labors as fruitless and of little use. [Col. 0381C] I ask them only to take account of candor and human weakness, and not to judge everything immediately worthy of condemnation if somewhere a lapse or omission may have occurred. For the task of correcting books is especially harsh: it brings little pleasure and a great deal of trouble, particularly when one is often deprived of manuscript assistance and has only conjecture at one’s disposal.

By means of conjecture one may struggle, however imperfectly, out of labyrinths and darkness; but it will be difficult to persuade those who have never entered this arena of the difficulty. Their inclination to criticize is naturally greater precisely because they do not understand what they malign.

Add to this that, although every careful editor strains every nerve to bring an author into the light in the most corrected form possible, the negligence and carelessness of compositors [Col. 0381D] make it impossible for him to accomplish this fully. Indeed, it is sometimes discovered that more blemishes have crept in—whether without the editors’ knowledge or through the printers’ rash alteration of anything whatsoever—than have been eradicated at the root.

I believe this is why the earlier edition is sometimes preferred by most captious readers to the later one, even when the latter was produced with the greatest labor. Some complain loudly and angrily that this happened to Lypsius as well. I fear intensely that the same may happen to me, since, being frequently distracted by other matters, I have not been able to attend the press.

Take our attempt and whatever labor we have been able to provide in good part, most distinguished bishop. I thought I owed an account of my studies to you, since you have always encouraged me to embrace them. I thought this especially lest, when Your Lordship has been raised to [Col. 0382A] so high an honor and has returned from the holy ecumenical council, and when so many people applaud you with congratulatory voices, I alone should seem silent—though you have always appeared to pursue me with singular favor.

I pray Almighty God to preserve Your Reverence, and us, and His Church, safe for as long as possible. I commend myself to you again and again.

From our Martinian monastery at Louvain, in the year of salvation 1564, in the month of March.

## PREFACE OF JACQUES SIRMOND, PRIEST OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS, TO THE FORTY NEW SERMONS OF ST AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, COLLECTED FROM VARIOUS ANCIENT COPIES THROUGH THE STUDY AND LABOR OF THE SAME SIRMOND, AND PUBLISHED AT PARIS BY SEBASTIAN CRAMOISY, ON THE RUE SAINT-JACQUES, UNDER THE SIGN OF THE STORKS, 1631

### To the Reader

[Col. 0382B] No one who remembers that Augustine himself, Possidius, Victor of Vita, and others proclaimed the infinite multitude of his treatises and homilies will be surprised that new sermons of St Augustine, hidden until now, can still be found.

In the sermons we are publishing, the authority of a very ancient and highly approved manuscript written on parchment partly confirmed that the title “Augustine” was not false—a conclusion that was the nearest at hand. This was further supported by the testimony of Possidius, that same bishop, and of the priest Bede, who praise most of these sermons; their judgment carried the greatest weight in assessing and approving Augustine’s works, and there could be no doubt about it.

There was also the support of Robert de Bardis, formerly chancellor of Paris—not indeed an extremely ancient witness, but one by no means to be despised. With singular study and industry, three hundred years ago he compiled [Col. 0382C] a *Collection of the Sermons of St Augustine*, as he called it, and distributed them according to the various kinds of subject into five parts, as though into classes.

When, through the assistance of a friend, I obtained the first two parts of this work in the Royal Library, together with an index of all the individual sermons from the Paris chancery, I rejoiced to learn from the author that, with very few exceptions—perhaps works that had not come into his hands—all our sermons were unquestionably to be counted among Augustine’s.

You, reader, will immediately recognize Augustine’s spirit and eloquence here, so that there is no need for other judges. And since you are accustomed, rightly, to value highly everything belonging to that most gentle and holy teacher of the Church, I believe you will find a special pleasure in these sermons when you observe, in addition to their other benefits, [Col. 0382D] that they contain much that contributes to illuminating the memory and history of those times.

For the same reason we transferred into this little book, so that everyone might enjoy it, those sermons that we had printed in the latest Paris edition but that had been printed there against our wishes, together with the fragments of Nicolas Fabri. These fragments too had previously been incomplete and mutilated; now, with the help of other manuscripts, we have restored them to their former appearance and clarity.

Enjoy them happily, then, and farewell.

# NOTES ON THE SERMONS

## Sermon 1, Class 1, § 2

“For what will they say when I answer that [Col. 0383A] the very Beginning itself is the Son of God, in whom Genesis says that God made heaven and earth?” etc.] He later uses John 8:25 to prove this point. We refuted that argument in the notes on volume III, concerning explanations of Scripture. The same judgment must be made of the explanations of Scripture found in these sermons as of the interpretations of the Psalms. Otherwise, there are also various doctrinal, moral, and historical matters here that people with abundant leisure may extract and turn to their own use, not without benefit.

## Sermon 2: On Abraham’s Temptation, § 5

“Therefore, when Abraham’s obedience in devotion had been fulfilled, he heard God say: ‘Now I know that you fear God.’ This is understood as meaning that God caused what Abraham had done to become known to Abraham himself.”] Thus, according to Augustine’s interpretation, God would mean: “Now I have brought it about that you yourself should know that you fear God.”

[Col. 0383B] But this is plainly a twisted interpretation; and once it is admitted, I do not understand what other interpretation—being harsh and forced—could be rejected. Let us nevertheless hear Augustine producing, as he thinks, a similar example from Scripture.

“Just as,” he says, “when the prophet speaks, what do we say? We plainly say, ‘God said.’ We also say, ‘The prophet said,’ and both statements are rightly made,” etc.

But when we say, “God said,” we understand “through the prophet,” if something is brought forward from the books of the prophets. Likewise, when we speak of the same words and say, “The prophet said,” we understand that he spoke by God’s command or in God’s name, God speaking through him.

The same effect may indeed be attributed equally truly to the principal cause and to the instrumental cause, as metaphysicians call them, although not in precisely the same sense; this is the usage of all languages. [Col. 0383C] But here we cannot say that it makes no difference whether one says, “Abraham came to know that he feared God,” or “God came to know that He was feared by Abraham.” Abraham is not here an instrument God uses in order to know something.

It would therefore have been much better to acknowledge here an *anthropopathism* of God—ἀνθρωποπάθεια, that is, the attribution to God of human emotions or modes of expression—or an angel adapting himself in conduct and speech to human ways, rather than wrongly comparing things that are entirely unlike as though they were alike.

## Sermon 5: On Jacob’s Wrestling
