In the manuscript of St Victor the title is “On Jacob’s Wrestling”; in Possidius, “On Jacob’s Wrestling with the Angels.” I followed the heading of our old copy, which is also found in the manuscript of the Royal Library—the one that contains part of the *Collection* of the Paris chancellor mentioned in my preface—and which bears the prefixed number [Col. 0383D] CLXXXII. SIRMONDUS.

### § 5

“The Christian Roman emperor ordered that the Jews should not approach Jerusalem itself.”] Constantine the Great. For, as Chrysostom teaches in *Against the Jews*, Homily 3, because the Jews had attempted to restore their city contrary to the prohibition, he punished them severely by cutting off their ears and scattering them throughout various regions, so that they might be a terror to the others and prevent them from attempting the same thing in the future. SIRMONDUS.

—Correct, whatever the Benedictine may think, who added a note here; for no Christian emperor existed before Constantine. What Orosius and others claimed concerning Philip has now been rejected by everyone.

### The same passage

“And they were scattered throughout the world, [Col. 0384A] made like custodians of our books.”] Elsewhere he calls the Jews our *capsarii* and the book-bearers of the Christians. In the treatise on Psalm 40: “The elder shall serve the younger” has now been fulfilled; now, brothers, the Jews serve. They are like our book-carriers. While we study, they carry the codices. And on Psalm 56: “The Jew carries the book from which the Christian may believe. They have become our book-bearers. Just as servants customarily carry books after their masters, so that the latter grow weary from carrying while the former make progress by reading.” SIRMONDUS.

### § 7

“I have treated of this at some time.”] He refers to one of our sermons, no. 17—no. 244 in the Paris edition—which is *On the Words of the Gospel: Do Not Touch Me*. IDEM.

## Sermon 6, § 2

He shows that God appeared through angels, and in this matter he reasons much better than in the preceding explanation. Let us therefore hear him briefly:

[Col. 0384B] “Therefore, just as the Word of God—that is, the Son of God—assumed flesh in order to appear to the eyes, so God has always deigned, when appearing to human eyes, to appear in some visible creature. For you have the clearest statement in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 7:30), that an angel appeared to Moses in the bush. Is this Scripture true and that one (Exodus 3:2 and following) false? Or is that one true and this one false? But what then? If we are Christians, if we believe correctly, both are true.

“If both are true, how did God appear here, and how is an angel said to have appeared there, unless the Spirit who said in the Acts of the Apostles that an angel appeared explained this passage—namely, how God appeared? That explanation interprets this obscurity. So that you might not understand God to have appeared by Himself, it is explained there how God appeared [Col. 0384C] through a creature, an angel.

“Why, then, are you surprised that when an angel appears it is said, ‘God said,’ and ‘God called,’ etc.? Because attention is not directed to the angel as temple, but to the one dwelling in the angel. For the angel himself was the temple of God.”

Nothing could be truer. Augustine explained this opinion more fully in other places, as John Clericus observed in his notes on Genesis 18:1. See the same author, who discusses the matter at length in his notes on Genesis 16:13 and in the index to the Pentateuch under the word “Angels.”

## Sermon 19

### On the title: “In the Restored Basilica”

Which basilica was the larger one at Carthage, where the bishop’s see was located, as Victor of Vita relates in book I. In the Second Council of Carthage it is called by the double name Basilica Perpetua Restituta; in the subsequent councils recorded as having been held there, it is simply called Restituta, as here. SIRMONDUS.

[Col. 0384D] ### The same passage: “On the Day of the Shows”

An old copy has at the end of the sermon: “Here ends the sermon on the day of the shows.” It must therefore be understood as referring to a gladiatorial spectacle, which was properly called a *munus*. Hence the expression “gladiatorial show” in the Theodosian Code, *On Gladiators*, law 2, and in the Roman calendar of the Constantinian period, in the month of December, when gladiatorial combats were customarily held. There is frequent mention of the *munus*, beginning on the fourth day before the Nones of December, when the opening of the spectacle is recorded, and continuing until the ninth day before the Kalends of January, when these bloody and grim spectacles ended, as the emperor Julian also records at the end of his *Oration to the Sun*. IDEM.

That the word *munus* in that age frequently signified not only gladiatorial games but also hunts of wild beasts has been shown by [Col. 0385A] Francis Juretus in his notes on Symmachus, book VII, letter 4, and by Jacob Gothofredus in his notes on the Theodosian Code, book VI, title 4, law 4.

### § 1

“Because of my iniquity, etc.”] The manuscript of the Navarre College has the verse: “Turn Your face away from my sins.”

### § 4

“Christ came from the region of happiness, and here He did not find it, even for Himself. He was mocked, reproached, seized, scourged, bound, struck with the palms of their hands, subjected to the disgrace of spitting, crowned with thorns, hung upon the wood; finally, the death of the Lord.”

The final three words come from Psalm 77:21, but they have been completely twisted to an alien meaning. There the psalmist says that the ways out of death belong to God—that is, that death is in the Lord’s power. Here, however, Augustine takes the words [Col. 0385B] as though they signified that the Lord had died.

Nevertheless, in this passage the copyists added, as if in parentheses: “Here those who understood it applauded.” When such things were applauded that deserved hissing, what remained except for the best matters to be rejected with disgust or heard inattentively by the Africans? Concerning these acclamations, see the notes on *On Christian Doctrine*, book IV, chapter 24, in volume III.

### § 6

“Great earthquakes are reported from the East; some great cities have suddenly collapsed”—add “through disasters,” or “through ruin.”] Marcellinus Comes discusses these events in his *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta, in the year of Christ 419:

“Many cities and villages of Palestine collapsed in an earthquake. At that time many peoples of neighboring nations, of both sexes, terrified by what they saw and heard and inclined to believe, [Col. 0385C] were washed in the sacred font of Christ; and upon the tunics of all who had been baptized, the cross of Christ the Savior suddenly appeared and shone, by divine will.”

Our Idatius likewise writes in his *Chronicle*: “During the episcopate of the man mentioned above”—that is, John—“the holy places in Jerusalem were shaken by a most severe earthquake.” And in the *Fasti*, under the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta: “In that consulship St John sent throughout the churches of the world a letter that is preserved, concerning signs and terrors wrought by divine power.” SIRMONDUS.

### The same passage

In addition to the details given by Marcellinus and Idatius, Augustine adds a remarkable circumstance in the words that follow. He teaches that those whose tunics were seen to bear crosses after their baptism were Jews.

“Terrified,” he says, “the Jews, pagans, and catechumens who were in Jerusalem were all baptized. [Col. 0385D] Perhaps seven thousand people are said to have been baptized. The sign of Christ appeared upon the garments of the baptized Jews. These things are reported with the strongest possible assurance by faithful brethren.”

It would be much more credible if the report had been confirmed by unbelievers. Believers readily trusted priests, whose testimony could not always safely be challenged and who, already in those centuries, thought that the Christian religion’s reputation could rightly be advanced through pious frauds. Once a bishop had begun to circulate some report, the others considered it in the interest of the entire order, indeed of the Christian religion itself, that the story should appear true.

From the same source arose another circumstance reported by Marcellinus in the passage cited by Sirmond, and I do not know why the most learned Jesuit omitted it—unless he was reluctant to copy out a fable. [Col. 0386A] For Marcellinus’s words are as follows, after he has said that cities and villages collapsed in the earthquake:

“Our Lord Jesus Christ, always present everywhere, manifested Himself from a cloud upon the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem. Then many people of both sexes,” etc.

The reputation of such absurdities, spread abroad by priests, was easily disseminated among the ignorant and took deep root in their minds.

### The same passage

“The city of Sitifis too was shaken by a most severe earthquake.”] Sitifis, which gave its name to a province in Africa—that is, Mauretania Sitifensis. I do not know whether others have recorded the earthquake of that city. It is certain that Novatus was then bishop of Sitifis; he attended and signed the Council of Carthage in that same year, after the twelfth consulship of Honorius, and a few years earlier [Col. 0386B] had also taken part in the conference with the Donatists. SIRMONDUS.

### § 6

“You have gathered here in small numbers, but if you have listened well, you abound.”] They were few in the church because very many had gathered for the spectacle.

Chrysostom, in the opening of his sermon *On the Consubstantial*, concerning the circus spectacle:

“Again the horse races, and again the gathering of us has become smaller.”

Asterius the bishop, in his sermon *On the Feast of the Kalends*:

“Many, preferring the pleasures and diversions of vanity, were left behind from the assembly of the Church.”

SIRMONDUS.

## Sermon 20, § 1

“With a harmonious voice, with a concordant voice, praying to the Lord on behalf of our very heart, we said,” etc.] [Col. 0386C] In the *Collection of Sermons*, page 3, and in the manuscript of St Victor CC 16, there is appended to the sermon *On the Humility Required in Doing Penance and on Psalm 50, Have Mercy on Me, O God*, which is Homily 28 of the fifty.

Accordingly, its title in both copies is: “On the verse of the same psalm, ‘Create in me a clean heart, O God.’” As for everything that was missing from the copy written on parchment—which was mutilated and lacked its beginning—we supplied it all from the manuscript of St Victor. For we obtained only the index of Part 3 of the *Collection* and of the following parts. SIRMONDUS.

### After the sermon

A similar address to the people after the sermon is read at the end of Sermon 32 *On the Words of the Lord*: “And after the sermon, we bring to your attention what your Charity knows,” etc. IDEM.

### § 5

“We exhort Your Charity not to be reluctant to hear the word of God attentively [Col. 0386D] and vigilantly when it is ministered by priests.”] In former times only bishops preached the word of God in the Church, since this was properly their office. Later, priests too were permitted to preach, though not at the same time everywhere.

The Easterners began first, as is shown by the examples of Pierius, a priest among the Alexandrians, and Chrysostom, while he was still a priest among the Antiochenes, as well as by the examples of others elsewhere.

In Africa this was unusual before Augustine, to whom Valerius the bishop first granted such authority at Hippo. Possidius says in chapter 5 of his *Life*:

“To that same presbyter he granted the power to preach and expound the Gospel before him in the church, and very frequently to deliver sermons—contrary, indeed, to the custom and practice of the African churches.”

[Col. 0387A] Later others followed Valerius’s example, including Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. Augustine congratulated him on this in Letter 77, because he had begun to introduce the practice whereby priests would deliver sermons to the people in his presence.

Thus, as though the custom had already been accepted in Africa, Augustine joins priests with bishops in this matter in Sermon 49 *On the Words of the Lord*: “Has not either a priest or a bishop sometimes ascended and, from the higher place, said something other than that no one should seize another’s property?”

Among the Gauls the practice seems to have been adopted later. For the Second Synod of Vaison, held a hundred years after Augustine, grants priests the authority to preach. It is therefore conjectured that they did not possess this authority earlier; this is also confirmed by Cyprian the deacon in the *Life of Caesarius, Bishop of Arles*. SIRMONDUS.

### The same passage

[Col. 0387B] In the East, not only priests in the presence of bishops but also laymen preached long before the time of Pierius on occasion. This is clear from a notable passage in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 19, where he writes of Origen:

“After coming to Palestine, he settled at Caesarea, where the bishops of that region asked him to speak publicly in the Church’s assembly and expound the divine Scriptures, although he had not yet received ordination to the priesthood. This may likewise be made clear from what Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, and Theoctistus, bishop of Caesarea, wrote to Demetrius in defense of the matter, arguing as follows: ‘You added in your letter that it had never before been heard of, nor had it yet happened, that laymen should preach in the presence of bishops. In saying this, I do not know how you have so plainly spoken falsely. For wherever suitable persons are found who can benefit the brethren, the holy bishops invite them to address the people—as Euelpis at Laranda was invited by Neon, Paulinus at Iconium by Celsus, and Theodore at Synnada by Atticus, our blessed brethren.’”

That is, in the translation of Henry Valesius:

“He went to Palestine and established his residence at Caesarea, where the bishops of that region asked him to speak publicly in the church and expound the divine Scriptures, although he had not yet been ordained a priest. This is also clear from what Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, and Theoctistus, bishop of Caesarea, wrote to Demetrius in defense of this action, in the following terms:

“‘As for what you added in your letter—that it had never before been seen, nor had it yet happened, that laymen should preach in the presence of bishops—in this, I do not know how, [Col. 0387D] you have strayed very far from the truth. [Col. 0387C] For whenever people are found who can benefit the brethren, the holy bishops themselves urge them to preach to the people. Thus Euelpis at Laranda was asked by Neon, Paulinus at Iconium by Celsus, and Theodore at Synnada by Atticus, our most blessed brethren.’”

## Sermon 21, § 1

“The righteous man will rejoice in the Lord.”] Only fragments of the remainder of this sermon existed in the parchment manuscript. Later we encountered a complete copy in the manuscript of St Victor CC 16. It was also included in Part 3 of the Paris chancellor’s *Collection*, as we learned from the index. SIRMONDUS.

### § 6

“You lead your slave, whom you are about to manumit, into the church by the hand. Silence is made; your petition is read, [Col. 0388A] or your request is presented.”] The privilege of carrying out manumissions in the church before the bishop was granted by the favor of Constantine the Great, as we have observed elsewhere in our notes on Ennodius. Among his short works there is a petition, or written request, composed in the name of Agapetus, in which he asks the bishop to grant freedom to his slave Gerontius and explains the grounds of his request. These correspond wonderfully with Augustine’s words. IDEM.

It is found in column 1719 of volume I of Jacques Sirmond’s Paris edition of the complete works.

Ibid. “That you may free your slave, you break his tablets.”] At the manumission of slaves, the tablets containing the record of their purchase and servitude were broken. Augustine, Letter 51, concerning the Donatists: “The tablets of the worst slaves were broken so that they might depart as free men.” THE SAME.

[Col. 0388B] Whoever wishes to know more about this manumission should consult the most learned jurist Jacobus Gothofredus on Book IV of the Theodosian Code, title 7, law 1.

Sermon 24, § 1. “Thanks be to our Lord God, etc.”] We saw a single copy of this outstanding sermon, in the manuscript of Saint Victor CC 16. Nevertheless, Possidius records it in chapter 9 of his catalogue, and it was also in the Chancellor’s Collection, part 3. SIRMOND.

§ 2. “Would that dead stones might feel within themselves the mercy of living stones.”] He calls the pagans “dead stones,” on account of their dullness, and because their gods are like stones. At times the pagans themselves used a similar comparison. Juvenal, Satire 8.52:

> … But you  
> are nothing but a Cecropid, and very like  
> a headless Hermes.

[Col. 0388C] “For you surpass him in no other distinction than this:

> His head is marble, whereas your likeness lives.”

§ 6. “As Rome, so also Carthage. If the event took place in the capital of the nations, will the limbs not follow?”] From this it is evident that this sermon too was delivered at Carthage, and that the bishop mentioned shortly before is to be understood as the bishop of Carthage; likewise, that the judge below was the proconsul, to whom the Christians had petitioned for permission to mock Hercules. The Carthaginians had adopted the worship of Hercules from the Tyrians, whose colonists they were; for Tyre was devoted to Hercules. Nor was Hercules worshiped only at Carthage: it is clear that he was worshiped in other parts of Africa as well, for example among the Suffectans in the province of Byzacena. When Christians had smashed the statue of Hercules there, the populace suddenly attacked them, and sixty were killed. Rebuking this savage frenzy, Augustine also cleverly mocks Hercules as a god, as he does here, in Letter 267: “If you call him your Hercules,” he says, “we shall return him to you. There are metals; stones are not lacking,” etc. SIRMOND.

Sermon 35. In the title: “If you are wise, etc.”] The inscription of the Victorine manuscript DD 12 agrees with that found in Possidius and with the index of part 3 of the Collection. The passage from Proverbs is given according to the edition of the Septuagint interpreters, which is somewhat fuller and more explicit in these words than the Vulgate. In Chrysostom, however, in his Homily on Psalm 100 and elsewhere, when he quotes these words, the first clause does not read “if you are wise” (ἐὰν σοφὸς), but “if you are good,” as follows:

> Τέκνον, ἐὰν ἀγαθὸς ἦς, σεαυτῷ σοφὸς ἔσῃ, καὶ τοῖς πλησίον σου.

> “My child, if you are good, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbors.”

The rest does not differ. SIRMOND. — Augustine’s reading is better than Chrysostom’s, as is clear from the Hebrew text—if, indeed, this latter reading may be called a reading; it is no less an accurate quotation of the sort commonly made from memory.

Sermon 41, in the title: “Possess faith with your neighbor in his poverty.”] Even if everything else were lacking, the antiquity of the manuscript that contained most of it attests to this sermon. The remainder was supplied from the same manuscript of Saint Victor, DD 12—not indeed a manuscript of that early age, but one that had collected very many sermons of Saint Augustine of every kind. It was also included in part 3 of the Collection, as the index shows. SIRMOND.

§ 3. “The first part of this statement, according to the popular interpretation, pleases me; the latter, however, I confess, troubles me” (as does the phrase, “and that you may enjoy his goods,” Ecclesiasticus 23:18). “For if you remain with your friend in his poverty for this reason—that when he becomes rich you may enjoy his wealth—you do not yet love the friend, but something else in the friend.”] But the wise Hebrew does not speak as though he wished faith to be kept with a friend in his poverty for the sole reason that, if he should recover his wealth, we might derive some benefit from him. Rather, if we wish to enjoy our friend when he is prospering, we ought to keep faith with him in adversity.

Sermon 45. “Concerning what is written in Isaiah, chapter 57, etc.”] In Possidius, chapter 8, this title has been rashly divided into two, not through the author’s fault but the copyist’s, as though one sermon concerned the words of Isaiah and another the words of [Col. 0389C] the Apostle. SIRMOND.

§ 7. “If he had said, ‘That mountain grew and filled Africa,’ would they say to him anything except, ‘Because he is of the party of Donatus’?”] In the Tractate on Psalm 49: “He spoke and summoned the earth.” What earth? Perhaps Africa, on account of those who say, “The Church of Christ is the party of Donatus.” The Donatists, in their madness, imagined that the Church had been extinguished in every part of the world through communion with traditores and remained only among themselves in Africa. Augustine says the same in Letter 165 to Generosa: “You say that, because of the traditores—whom you do not identify—the Church of Christ has remained in Africa alone, belonging to the party of Donatus. This you recite not from the Law, not from the Prophets, not from the Psalm, not from the Apostle, not from the Gospel, but from your own heart and from the slanders of your ancestors.” Alluding to the same matter again in his commentary on Psalm 21: “In every place Paul says that all the faithful are a good fragrance; but the reply is made, ‘Africa alone smells sweet; the whole world stinks.’” SIRMOND.

Ibid. In § 8 Augustine addresses those who would indeed wish to sin if it could be done safely, but who do not dare to do so because of punishment and disgrace: “Lust burns; fear restrains. What do you fear? Being discovered and condemned, being discovered and publicly disgraced.”] That is, being dishonored and harassed with abuse—like the Greek word πομπεύεσθαι, “to be publicly paraded or disgraced.” See Henri Estienne in the Thesaurus of the Greek Language. Add also Harpocration under the words πομπείας and πομπεύειν.

Sermon 81. On the words of the Gospel of Matthew 18.] Delivered in the year of Christ 410, after the city had been captured by the Goths, when, upon the news of that disaster being brought to Africa, Rome was said to have been utterly destroyed and to have perished. We supplied the title from a very ancient manuscript; it is absent from Bede’s commonly circulated copies, where, at this point, the words are quoted without the sermon’s title. SIRMOND.

§ 9. “Rome falls, which Romulus founded.”] Sermon 29 on the Words of the Lord: “What God himself made will pass away; how much sooner what Romulus founded?” There Augustine discusses the capture of Rome and the whole subject in a similar manner, and again in Sermon 106 on Various Subjects and in Book III of The City of God, chapters 17 and 18. SIRMOND.

Sermon 90. “On the wedding feast of the King’s son.”] From the same Corbie volume from which we formerly copied the homilies of Valerian. It was mutilated, however, with its ending torn away. The missing supplement was therefore later sent to us from another manuscript of the same monastery. THE SAME.

“At Carthage, in the Restituta.”] We discussed the Basilica Restituta in connection with Sermon 19. The inscription indicates that Sermon 102 on Various Subjects was also delivered there. A third sermon on Various Subjects—the one on the words of the Psalm, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good”—and the Tractate on Psalm 55 are likewise said to have been delivered at Carthage in the Basilica Restituta: the former in the manuscript of Saint-Germain, the latter in ours. Nor were Augustine’s sermons delivered only in this basilica, which was the principal one; other Carthaginian basilicas are also mentioned: the Basilica of Faustus, Sermons 12 and 122 on Various Subjects; the Basilica of Leontiana, Sermon 11 on Various Subjects; the Basilica of Celerina, Sermon 195 on Time; the Basilica of the New Church, Sermon 110 on Time; the Basilica of Peter in the third region, Sermon 251 on Time; and the Basilica of Paul in the sixth region, Sermon 24 [Col. 0390C] on Time. THE SAME.

Sermon 113, § 2. “First, what is mammon? For it is a word that is not Latin. It is a Hebrew word related to the Punic language. These languages are connected by a certain closeness of meaning. What the Punic people call mammon is called lucrum, ‘profit,’ in Latin. What the Hebrews call mammona is called divitiae, ‘riches,’ in Latin.” See the note on Book VII of Questions on the Heptateuch, question 16, where Augustine has similar remarks about the Punic language. The more frequently we read such remarks, the more they stir our anger at the negligence of the Carthaginians, who allowed that language to perish unused while they copied so many cold and worthless Latin homilies.

Sermon 118. “On the same words of the Evangelist John 1, etc.”] We saw a single copy of this sermon as well, in the manuscript of Saint Victor DD 12. It seems, however, to be identified by Possidius in chapter 5 of his catalogue, where, among the works Augustine wrote against the Arians, he lists the tractate “In the Beginning was the Word.” There is also Sermon 14 on Various Subjects, on the same words of Genesis and John, against the Manichaeans; Possidius likewise mentions it in chapter 2. SIRMOND.

§ 1. “If you cannot understand, believe in order that you may understand. Faith comes first; understanding follows, because the prophet says: ‘Unless you believe, you will not understand.’”] With these same words he closes the sermon. See the notes on the work On Free Will, Book I, chapter 2.

Sermon 125. “On the five porticoes.”] The manuscript of Saint Vincent of Metz supplied this sermon to us. When Augustine says at the beginning of the sermon that he has already spoken on the same Gospel passage, I think he is referring to Sermon 42 on the Words of the Lord, entitled “On the sick man lying beside the pool.” Possidius, however, expressly mentions our sermon. SIRMOND.

§ 7. “In the number forty the completion of righteousness is symbolized.”] He explains the matter at greater length in § 9. He also discussed it in Book II of Christian Doctrine, § 25, although there he interprets the number not so much as the completion of righteousness as this troubled life. See what we said there.

Sermon 140. “Against a certain statement of Maximinus, an Arian bishop, who, together with Count Segisvult, was blaspheming in Africa.”] Prosper relates in his Chronicle that Count Segisvult was sent to Africa against Boniface in the consulship of Hierius and Ardabur, that is, in the year of Christ 427. Maximinus himself states that he came with him, at the beginning of the conference he held with Saint Augustine at Hippo: “I,” he says, “was sent to this city by Count Segisvult”—for this is how it should be read—“and I came in the interest of peace.” Besides the conference and the two books written against Maximinus after the conference, which are commonly attached to it but ought to be separated, Augustine also wrote a dogmatic letter to Maximinus. Only a mention of it survives in Possidius; it no longer exists. SIRMOND.

Sermon 167, § 4. “There is a well-known Punic proverb, which I shall give you in Latin, because not all of you know Punic. The ancient Punic proverb is: ‘Pestilence seeks a coin; give it two, and let it take itself away.’”] A truly wise proverb, and one that might arouse in us an intense longing for the Punic books. Would that we could buy them back with these treatises! In Hebrew one would say: [no Hebrew wording survives in the supplied text].

Sermon 118. “On a verse of Psalm 105.”] We ourselves added this part of the title, since in the ancient copy the inscription stood bare and without the author’s name: “On the Kalends of January.” The two parts agree, for the author is entirely occupied with criticizing the pagan rites of that day, and he elegantly adapts David’s words to this purpose. Concerning the same Kalends of January, which were polluted by various superstitions of the nations, there is a λόγος κατηγορικὸς τῆς ἑορτῆς τῶν καλανδῶν, “an invective discourse against the festival of the Kalends,” by Asterius, bishop of Amasea, whom I praised above. There are also Sermon 155 of Peter Chrysologus and Sermon 10 of Maximus of Turin. Our Augustine too, in Sermon 59 on Various Subjects, says: “The coming Kalends of January are at hand. You are all Christians; by God’s favor, the city is Christian. Let those things not be done which God hates. Iniquity through play, wickedness through jest. Let people not make themselves judges, lest they fall into the hands of the true Judge.” Judges—that is, magistrates—were represented among the other amusements of that day. Indeed, as Chrysologus teaches, they also represented their gods and disgraced them with mockery. SIRMOND.

§ 3. “Demons delight in songs of vanity; they delight in frivolous spectacles and in the various indecencies of the theaters, etc.”] Augustine treated this subject at great length in The City of God, Book II, chapter 8 and following.

[Col. 0392A] Sermon 244. “On the fifteenth day of Easter.”] It is found in part 2 of the Royal Collection and in Victorine DD 12.

§ 4. “Let the Arian come forward; let the Photinian come forward first. We answer the Photinian, etc.”] In Bede, when he quotes these words in his commentary on the Epistle to the Philippians, chapter 2, certain additional words are inserted as follows:

> “Let the Arian come forward; let the Photinian come forward first. Those heretics who know the Lord as nothing other than a man are called Homuncionists. These heretics are called Homuncionists because they know Christ as nothing other than a man. We shall answer the Photinian, etc.”

Since these words are absent from the manuscripts, they seemed best omitted. SIRMOND.

§ 2. On Christ’s words in John 20:17, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father,” after Augustine had proposed questions which he practically admits to be insoluble, he continues: “May the Lord help me so that it may be solved; may he who deigned to pose it deign to explain it. Pray with me for the result; lend your ears to me, your heart to him. What he deigns to suggest to me I shall communicate to you, etc.”] If Augustine had brought nothing prepared from home for this purpose, he rashly prayed to God, while standing before the congregation, to suggest to him extemporaneously the meaning of Christ’s words. God does not open to those who knock in this fashion—except to those endowed by him with the prophetic spirit; he teaches others nothing unless they join prayer to the labor and concentration of mind that ought to be applied to a serious and important matter. If, however, Augustine had already meditated upon what he says afterward, he performed a piece of theatrical display, if one may put it so, before the people of Hippo, speaking as though he had received the interpretation of this difficult passage through a sudden divine suggestion. But whichever of the two alternatives one prefers, the result is the same: Augustine was certainly not heard by God, since he interprets “to touch” here as “to believe,” and unfolds the meaning of the passage in § 3:

> “What, then, does ‘Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father’ mean? You see me as I am and think me to be only this: a man. I have not yet ascended to the Father. You see me as a man and think me a man; I am indeed a man, but do not let your faith stop here. Do not touch me in such a way that you believe me to be merely a man. For I have not yet ascended to my Father. I ascend to my Father, and touch me—that is, advance, understand that I am equal to the Father; then touch me, and you will be saved.”

Everyone can easily understand that so crude an interpretation, unworthy of a somewhat more competent man, was not suggested by God. Before producing it, Augustine himself confessed, in the words immediately following in § 2, what we quoted at the beginning: “Let whoever understands better teach me; I am a teacher in such a way that I am not incapable of learning.” You will say, “These are the words of a modest man.” I admit it. But it is not modest to say that God suggested to you something when you are prepared to learn better things. Elsewhere we have already noted traces of an ἐνθουσιασμός, “enthusiasm” or “divine inspiration,” which is not altogether consistent with his own position.

Sermon 256, § 2. “Turned toward the Lord.”] This was the solemn prayer with which Augustine customarily ended his sermons. In the old manuscript, as usual, only its opening words were given. The remainder was copied from Sermon 30 on the Words of the Lord. It is uncertain, however, whether he used this prayer in our sermon or another, shorter one, such as that in Sermon 121 on Various Subjects:

> “Turned toward the Lord himself, let us pray for ourselves and for all his people, who stand with us in the court of his house. May he deign to guard and protect them, through Jesus Christ his Son, our Lord, who lives and reigns with him for ever and ever. Amen.”

SIRMOND.

Sermon 159, § 2. “For the Lord will reign on earth with his saints, as the Scriptures say, and he will have here a Church into which no evil person will enter, separated and cleansed from every stain of wickedness. This is signified by those 153 fish of which, if I remember correctly, we have spoken at some time.”] Sermons 4 and 5 on Various Subjects, and Sermon 22—numbered 270 in this edition—among our own sermons. In other passages as well, both in his treatises and in his other books, Augustine frequently played upon this theme, claiming that the number of fish—153—caught after the resurrection at the Sea of Tiberias signified the number of the saints in eternal life.

The Greek Fathers sometimes played the same game, as did Gregory, bishop of Taormina. In Sermon 10 of those he entitled ἑωθινά, “morning sermons,” he teaches that Rebecca represented a type of the Church because the letters of Rebecca’s name, when converted into numerical values, produce the same number as the fish, 153:

> Ἡ γοῦν Ῥεβέκκα τὴν Ἐκκλησίαν εἰκόνιζε συναφθεῖσαν Χριστῷ διὰ βαπτίσματος. Τῶν γὰρ στοιχείων τῆς Ῥεβέκκας ὀνόματος εἰς ψήφους μεταλαμβανομένων, τρεῖς καὶ πεντήκοντα καὶ ἑκατὸν μονάδες συναχθήσονται, ὅσους καὶ τοὺς ἀγρευθέντας ἰχθῦς εὑρίσκομεν.

> “Rebecca, then, was an image of the Church joined to Christ through baptism; for when the letters of the name Rebecca are converted into numerical values, 153 units are obtained, as many as the fish we find to have been caught.”

For Ρ, the first letter of the name, is worth one hundred; Ε, five; Β, two; Κ, twenty; the second Κ, again twenty; and Α, one. Added together, these make 153. THE SAME.

Ibid. These were indeed games—games of those abusing their ingenuity—for they were invented according to the whims of dreamers. But one ought to have been more restrained in such games, and not present such inventions as though they were exceptional interpretations of Scripture.

§. “The days of rest have been completed; now the days of assemblies, exactions, and lawsuits will follow.”] Fifteen days, as he will say shortly: seven before Easter and an equal number after Easter, during which, by the law of Theodosius, all lawsuits and disputes ceased. Book II of the Theodosian Code, “On Holidays,” says: “We also number among the same observance of holidays the sacred days of Easter, which either precede or follow it by seven days.” SIRMOND.

Sermon 268. “On the day of Pentecost.”] We saw it not only in the Royal manuscript and Victorine DD 12, but also in other manuscripts. As for placing this first among the sermons on Pentecost, we followed Bede, who calls it Sermon 1 on Pentecost. THE SAME.

Sermon 270. “On the day of Pentecost.”] Bede also cites this sermon, as I noted, in his commentary on 2 Corinthians 3. In Bede’s commonly circulated copies, however, “from a sermon on Easter” has been written in place of “from a sermon on Pentecost.” It is found both in the Royal manuscript and in Victorine DD 12. THE SAME.

[Col. 0394A] § 3. “Forty days contain four times ten. In this number, so far as I think, the mystery is commended. For we speak as human beings to human beings, and we are rightly called interpreters of Scripture, not affirmers of our own opinions.”] Only the person who deals with a matter unquestionably found in Scripture is properly an interpreter of Scripture—not one who peddles every flimsy and worthless conjecture as a divine mystery, such as these arithmetical secrets. Whoever asserts them is certainly asserting his own opinions.

Augustine himself recognized this, as is clear from these Platonic words: “We speak as human beings to human beings”—that is, “We who are guided by probabilities speak to those for whom probability is sufficient when truth itself cannot be discovered.” Thus Timaeus says in Plato:

> Ἐὰν ἄρα μηδενὸς ἧττον παρεχώμεθα εἰκότας, ἀγαπᾷν χρὴ, μεμνημένον ὡς ὁ λέγων, ὑμεῖς τε οἱ κριταὶ φύσιν ἀνθρώπινον ἔχομεν· ὥστε περὶ τούτων τὸν εἰκότα μῦθον ἀποδεχομένους, πρέπει μηδὲν ἔτι πέρα ζητεῖν.

> “If, then, we offer accounts no less probable than anyone else’s, you ought to be content, remembering that both I who speak and you who are judges possess human nature. Therefore, if you accept a probable account of these matters, it is fitting that you seek nothing further.”

§ 7. “This number, 153, seems to grow like a tree from a certain seed; the seed of this great number is a certain smaller number, namely seventeen.”] He calls this the foundation in Sermon 4 on Various Subjects, where he explains more clearly how 153 arises from 17. “Now, then,” he says, “concerning the number 153 of the fish, why should I go over the same matter again? You know it. A growing number arises from seventeen. Begin with one and proceed to seventeen, adding them all: that is, add one to two and you get three; add three and you get six; add four and you get ten. Continue adding them all up to seventeen, and you will reach 153.” He pursues the same point at greater length and with greater clarity in the Tractate on Psalm 49. SIRMOND.

Sermon 279. “On Saint Paul the Apostle.”] In the Royal and Victorine manuscripts the title is: “On the Conversion of Saint Paul.” But we preferred to follow Bede, who consistently cites it as “From a sermon on the Apostle Paul.” He also cites another sermon, “On the Conversion of the Apostle,” namely Sermon 34 on Various Subjects. Moreover, from this single sermon of ours, divided into sections, two sermons in the commonly circulated copies have been composed: Sermon 14 on the Saints and Sermon 36 on Various Subjects. THE SAME.

§ 4. “Whatever it is that rages against you for the name of Christ: if it can be lived through, it is bearable; if it cannot be lived through, it makes you depart from here.”] That is: however savage the pain you suffer for the name of Christ may seem to you, endure it steadfastly. If it does not take your life, it can be borne; if it takes your life, it will be the beginning of your happiness. Nothing, therefore, should be changed here.

Augustine owes this statement to Epicurus, whose κυρία δόξα, “sovereign maxim,” that great pain is brief and prolonged pain slight, he had read in his Cicero. You will find it most beautifully illustrated in the notes of Pierre Gassendi on Book X of Diogenes Laertius.

Sermon 288. “On the birthday of Saint John the Baptist.”] The passages missing from the fragments of the most ancient book were supplied from the Royal manuscript and another manuscript of Saint Victor, DD 12. In both manuscripts, after this sermon there followed another on the same feast of Saint John, which Bede likewise cites in his commentary on Philippians 2. It is Sermon 23 on the Saints. SIRMOND.

Sermon 294. “On the birthday of the martyr Gudden.”] Although the Benedictines think that Gaudentius should be restored here, Theodoric Ruinart, a monk of the same order and a learned man, in the Authentic and Selected Acts of the Martyrs, note on the Life and Acts of Saint Cyprian, believes that the reading should be Gudennis, Gudenis, or Gundennis. She was a virgin who suffered at Carthage under the emperor Severus, during the consulship of Geta and Plantianus; the commonly circulated martyrologies commemorate her feast on July 18.

§ 3. After Matthew 25:33 had been read, he says: “By this he names the kingdom; by that, condemnation with the devil. No middle place has been left where you can put infants. The living and the dead will be judged; some will be on the right, others on the left. I know nothing else. You who introduce a middle place, get out of the middle; do not be offended by the one who seeks the right. I warn you yourself as well: get out of the middle, but do not go to the left, etc.”] I do not understand how this agrees with what the scholastics later wrote about limbo. Nor do I see how it can be reconciled with what he teaches elsewhere about purgatorial punishments, for example in The City of God, Book XXI, chapter 13.

§ 6. “You Pelagians say: ‘This unbaptized person will indeed have eternal life, but he will not have the kingdom of heaven.’ He replies: ‘On the contrary, he will have both life and the kingdom of heaven. Why do you snatch the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven from an innocent person?’ etc.”] Augustine argues correctly, and there was no reason to distinguish the kingdom of heaven from eternal life. But the Pelagians were forced to this position by John 3:5, which they understood as referring to infant baptism: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of God.” Yet it is sufficiently clear that in this passage Christ is speaking only of adults, as also in all the other passages in which heaven is promised under conditions that can be fulfilled only by adults.

§ 12. “What do you say to him so that he may believe? This is the response given by the person carrying the child. He is saved through another’s words who is wounded through another’s deed. Does he believe in Jesus Christ? The question is asked; the answer is given: ‘He believes.’”] Rather, “I believe,” in the first person, because the baptismal formula for adults had been transferred to infants without alteration. [Col. 0395D] See what was said in Volume II, Letter 98, § 9.

§ 17. “Tell me, I beg you: does Christ benefit baptized infants in any way, or not at all? He must say that he benefits them; he is pressed by the weight of Mother Church. Perhaps they would indeed wish to say this, for their arguments seem to compel them to it, but they are restrained by the authority of the Church, lest—not to say that they be overwhelmed by the spittle of men—they be swept away as by a river of the infants’ own tears.”] The latter is a rhetorical argument; the former is based on fear, not truth. For where did God promise that the greater part of Christians would never err in any matter of the highest importance? Nowhere. Where did he reveal that infants must necessarily be baptized, or that baptism benefits those who die in infancy? Nowhere either. Augustine therefore invokes the authority of the Church against the unfortunate Pelagians in vain. That authority would not have been highly regarded if imperial decrees had not come to the aid of their arguments’ failure—a more offensive procedure in the case of the Pelagians than in that of the Donatists.

§ 19. “If forgiveness of sins is granted even to the gravest sinners and to those who had long before sinned against the Lord, once they have afterward believed, and no one is prevented from baptism and grace, how much less ought an infant to be prevented—an infant who has just been born and has committed no sin, except that, born carnally according to Adam, he contracted the contagion of the ancient death through his first birth? He approaches more easily to receive forgiveness of sins precisely because what is forgiven him is not his own sins but another’s.”] These are Cyprian’s words, quoted by Augustine from Letter 64 to Fidus, to prove original sin by Cyprian’s authority. But why were the Pelagians not permitted to reject Cyprian’s authority in this matter, just as Augustine was permitted to do so concerning the baptism of heretics? Augustine certainly affirmed much more clearly, fully, and consistently that those coming from heretics to the Catholic Church should be baptized than the position maintained here by the bishop of Hippo.

Moreover, Cyprian does not say that any internal stain passes into infants by which their faculties are corrupted. He says only that they draw from Adam the contagion of death, because mortal children can be born only from a mortal father; this is far removed from Augustine’s position. Finally, he may have said rhetorically rather than didactically that another’s sins are forgiven. Strictly speaking, another’s sins can neither be imputed nor forgiven by a just judge. It is enough that many statements of ecclesiastical orators are true in a softened sense, since it is well established that they were not accustomed to speak with precision.

§ 20. “Let us therefore obtain from our brothers, if we can, that they not additionally call us heretics, since, if we wished, we might perhaps call them that as they argue such things—and yet we do not.”] Augustine wrote this in the year 413, near the beginning of the controversies, when minds had not yet been inflamed by opposing writings and hatred. Later he called them heretics openly and abused them with every kind of insult, as commonly happens.

“Let the mother sustain them with pious compassion, so that they may be healed; let her carry them while they are being taught, lest she mourn the dead. They are going too far; it is too much; it is scarcely tolerable; it is a great exercise of patience still to tolerate it,” etc.] These words are honeyed, but they were disgraced by the unbelievable bitterness of the times that followed. One might almost suspect that this gentleness was deliberately feigned in order to heap greater hatred upon the unfortunate men if they did not yield, and so that inexperienced people would afterward burn more fiercely against them. No one is unaware that sacred authorities have often employed such tactics; a striking example of this is seen in the condemnation of the Donatists.

Certainly, the rapid condemnation of Pelagian doctrines by at least twenty synods within a few years agrees very poorly with such beginnings. Once bishops had repeatedly been brought to condemn the Pelagians, no further opportunity could be found for hearing the parties so often condemned. For when synods have condemned someone, they think it part of their dignity that the person should appear to have been justly condemned, and they do not permit their decrees to be reconsidered. But read the edicts of Honorius and Constantius against the Pelagians, printed at the end of Volume X and often elsewhere, and it will be clear that the struggle against them was conducted with much greater vehemence than with arguments.

Sermon 305, in the title: “Delivered at the table of Saint Cyprian.”] At the altar of Saint Cyprian. They called the altar a table, just as the Greeks called it a ἱερὰ τράπεζα, “sacred table.” Concerning this table of Saint Cyprian at Carthage, Augustine says in Sermon 113 on Various Subjects:

> “As all of you who know Carthage know, in the very place where Cyprian’s blood was shed for the name of Christ, a table has been constructed for God. Yet it is called Cyprian’s table not because Cyprian ever feasted there, but because he was sacrificed there, and because by that very sacrifice he prepared this table—not one at which he might feed or be fed, but one upon which a sacrifice might be offered to God, to whom he himself was offered.”

Sermons 94 and 137 on Time and the Tractate on Psalm 38 were likewise delivered at the same table of Saint Cyprian at Carthage. SIRMOND.

Sermon 318, in the title: “On the martyr Stephen.”] We possess a sermon on the same subject, not yet published, by Faustus, bishop—perhaps of Riez—whose opening runs as follows:

> “From the reading just given we have learned of a vision celebrated by all the Churches. We have heard not dreams deceived by the error of the senses, but oracles confirmed by the effects of events. We rightly believe the revelation in the sermon, since we hold its fruit in the gift. Where are those who say that pious honors ought not to be paid to martyrs? Behold, this man, who has long enjoyed the blessed splendor of paradise, is now shown to the world so that he may be honored. Thus God, the dispenser of our benefits, clearly commanded him to be honored whom he enabled to be found. The sermon of the revelation therefore says, etc.”

Augustine himself relates in full, in Book XXII of The City of God, chapter 8, the discovery in Palestine, toward the end of the year 415, of Saint Stephen’s body; the bringing of his relics from there to Africa; and the shrines constructed in their honor at Uzalis by Bishop Evodius, at Calama by Possidius, and at Hippo by Augustine. THE SAME.

Ibid. For the discovery of Saint Stephen’s relics, see the account of Lucian, priest of Caphargamala, in Photius, codex 171. I am amazed that in these centuries, when, as that author says,

> “Even boys have the nose of a rhinoceros,”

such fabrications were believed—fabrications that plainly bear every mark of pious fraud. It appears from the facts themselves that many ecclesiastical leaders were then convinced that anything that was not intrinsically evil, and that could either bring pagans to the Christian faith, heal heretics, or at least strengthen the Catholic people in the faith, was permitted; and that one need not inquire too rigorously whether such things were true.

Add to this that whoever could once persuade the common people that miracles occurred more frequently among them through the relics of the saints attracted a vast crowd of people to his church and enriched himself through their gifts. Hence it came about that so many relics were fabricated at that time, and so many miracles reported—more than had ever previously been heard of.

“But,” you will say, “was there no one then for whom truth was more important than the interests of priests, and who would frankly expose those frauds?” I do not doubt that many recognized and mocked them at the time. But the power of those who employed such methods was so great, their favor among the common people so considerable, and the frenzy of the once-deceived populace so intense that it was unsafe to attempt or write anything openly against them. This is sufficiently clear from the examples of Vigilantius and Jovinian, whom Jerome and others treated so badly because they seemed to oppose the interests of the sacred order in such stories.

§ 1. “A few years ago, while we were present and residing at Milan, the bodies of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius appeared.”] In the Victorine manuscript: “while we were young.” Concerning the relics of Saints Gervasius and Protasius discovered at Milan by Saint Ambrose while Saint Augustine was staying in that city in the year of Christ 387, Augustine himself also writes in Book IX of the Confessions, chapter 7, and in the cited passage of The City of God: “I too,” he says, “was a witness to the great glory of the martyrs; when I was at Milan, I learned of the miracles that had occurred,” etc. SIRMOND.

Ibid. Nevertheless, the word “residing,” which follows, shows that “while we were present” cannot be read; unsound men added it in order to lend greater credibility to Ambrose’s scene. More correctly, as the Benedictines testify, several manuscripts read “while we were young.”

In Sermon 322 there can be read—and indeed ought to be read—a tale from which a reliable judgment may be formed about the entire theatrical performance of that age. On the first day of Easter, a certain Paul from Cappadocia is brought forward—I know not who he was—from that most prolific land of wicked men, if we believe the old reputation and Isidore of Pelusium, cured by Saint Stephen. But his little book, that is, the account of his illness and cure, is deferred, so that the populace may be inflamed all the more by the desire to know it.

This is the first act, contained in Sermon 320. “You who know,” Augustine says, “what you used to see in him” (read *used to*, for the sermon concerns a past event), “read with joy at the present what you see.” The second act is found in Sermon 321, where that marvelous little book of Paul is promised to the people, because he had disclosed certain things to Augustine which the people ought to know, for the greater admiration and glory of our Lord. The third is Sermon 322, in which Augustine first makes a preface and then orders the account of Paul, cured on Easter Day, to be read aloud. The fourth act is contained in Sermon 323, where, while Augustine is speaking to the people, Paul’s sister is suddenly cured, and the acclamation of the people follows. Finally, the fifth act is comprised in Sermon 324, where the devout bishop wisely turns everything to his own advantage and prudently reminds the people that, although God could have performed these very remarkable miracles elsewhere, where the relics of Saint Stephen were also present, Paul and his sister had nevertheless been directed to him. Unless I am mistaken, the whole tale was aimed at this.

Since this volume may perhaps fall into the hands of people who will not possess all the Works of Augustine, or even of those who would be too lazy to take up his fifth volume while reading these matters, I thought it appropriate to set out the entire comedy here. But I cannot conceal the grief that comes over me when I reflect that, while imprudent men try by such deceits to confer greater authority upon the Christian religion, they may indeed have gained for themselves no contemptible profit, but have greatly harmed religion among suspicious and hostile people. On account of recent miracles invented for the sake of utility, such people unjustly withdraw belief from apostolic miracles, although the latter possess as many indications of truth as there are reasons for not believing the more recent ones. But may God grant that at some time only truth be employed in defending the truth, and that by its own light alone he lead all minds to believe the most holy teaching of the Gospel and to express it in their conduct.

### Sermon 320

Where Augustine excuses himself for not having been able to preach a sermon; delivered on Easter Day.

“Concerning the miracles of God performed through the prayers of the most blessed martyr Stephen, we are accustomed to hear little books read. The little book’s appearance stands in place of writing, and a face is displayed in place of paper. You who know what you used to see in him with sorrow, read with joy at the present what you see, so that the Lord our God may be honored more abundantly, and so that what has been written in the little book may be written into your memory. Forgive me for not making the sermon lengthy; for you know my weariness. That yesterday, while fasting, I was able to accomplish so much and not fail, and that today I may speak with you as well, was granted by the prayers of Saint Stephen. Turned toward the Lord, etc.”

### Sermon 321

Where he preached on another day and promised the little book of the cured man; on Easter Monday.

“Yesterday, as your charity remembers, we said that the appearance of this man is itself his little book. Yet because he disclosed certain things to us which you ought to know, for the greater admiration and glory of our Lord, concerning the memorials of his saints, of whom it is said, ‘Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints,’ it is fitting also to provide a little book containing everything we learned from his mouth. But, if the Lord wills, it will be prepared today and read aloud to you tomorrow.”

### Sermon 322

Where he presented the promised little book of the cured man; on Easter Tuesday.

“Yesterday we promised your charity a little book in which you might hear about the man who was cured what you could not see. If, therefore, it pleases your charity—or rather, since what pleases me ought also to please you—let both brothers stand before you, so that those who had not seen the former may see in the latter what he suffered. Let both, then, stand: one to whom grace has been given, and the other for whom mercy must be sought.”

#### Copy of the little book given by Paul to Saint Augustine, bishop

“I ask you, most blessed lord Pope Augustine, to order this little book of mine, which I have presented at your command, to be read aloud to the holy people.”

“When we were still living in our homeland, Caesarea of Cappadocia, our eldest brother inflicted such grave and intolerable injuries upon our common mother that he did not hesitate even to lay hands upon her. We, all the children gathered together, endured this patiently, so that we did not say even a word to our brother on behalf of our mother, asking why he had done it. But she, driven by the goads of womanly grief, resolved to punish her injurious son by cursing him. As she hurried to the font of holy baptism, after the cockcrow, to invoke God’s anger upon the son mentioned above, some demon, apparently in the likeness of our uncle, met her and first asked her where she was going. She replied that she was going to curse her son because of the intolerable insult. Then that enemy, since he was easily able to find a place in the woman’s maddened heart, persuaded her to curse them all. Inflamed by his viperous counsels, she threw herself before the holy font and, with her hair disheveled and her breasts bared, asked this above all from God: that, exiled from our homeland and wandering through foreign lands, we might terrify the whole human race by our example.

“Immediately an effective vengeance followed the mother’s prayers, and such a great trembling of the limbs seized our same brother, older than I both in years and in guilt, as your holiness saw in me until three days ago. Then, preserving the order in which we had been born, the same punishment overtook all of us within one year. When our mother saw that her curses had attained such efficacy, she could no longer endure the consciousness of her wickedness and the reproach of others; but, tightening a noose around her throat, she ended her grievous life by a more dreadful death.

“Accordingly, all of us departed, unable to bear our disgrace, and, leaving our common homeland, were scattered here and there through different regions. Of all ten of us brothers, the one who in birth order comes first after the eldest obtained healing at the memorial of the glorious martyr Lawrence, which, as we heard, was recently established at Ravenna. But I, who am sixth in birth order among them, having learned that there were sacred places wherever in the world, wherever throughout the lands, God performed miracles, eagerly undertook the journey with my sister, who is younger than I. To say nothing of the other most celebrated holy places, I also reached Ancona, a city of Italy, where through the glorious martyr Stephen the Lord performs many miracles, traveling by the same circuitous route. But I could not be cured elsewhere because by divine predestination I had been reserved for this place.

“I did not omit the African city of Usalim, where blessed martyr Stephen is often said to perform great miracles. Nevertheless, three months ago—that is, on the first day of January—both my sister, who is here with me, and I, still afflicted by the same illness, were warned by a clear vision. For a certain man, distinguished in appearance and venerable with white hair, said to me that within the third month the healing I desired would come to me. In a vision your holiness appeared to my sister in the form in which we now see you present; by this it was signified to us that we ought to come to this place. Indeed, afterward I often saw your blessedness in other cities; on the journey by which we came, you appeared exactly as I now behold you.

“Thus warned by a clear divine authority, we came to this city about fifteen days ago. The witnesses to my illness are either your own eyes or my wretched sister, who offers an example of our common affliction for the instruction of all, so that those who see in her what I was may recognize in me how much the Lord has accomplished through his Holy Spirit.

“I prayed every day with many tears at the place where the memorial of the most glorious martyr Stephen is located. On Easter Sunday, as the others who were present had seen, while I was praying and holding the rail with great weeping, I suddenly fell. Deprived of consciousness, I do not know where I was. After a short time I rose and found that trembling no longer in my body. Therefore, not ungrateful for so great a benefit of God, I presented this little book, in which I have also displayed both what you did not know about our misfortunes and what you have learned about my recovery and health, so that you may deign to pray for my sister and to give thanks to God on my behalf.”

### Sermon 323

Augustine’s sermon delivered after the little book concerning Saint Stephen.

“Indeed, brothers, as we ought to believe, all these brothers, whom a single maternal blow of God’s wrath struck, will eventually attain the healing over which we rejoice. Nevertheless, let children learn obedience, and let parents fear to become angry. It is written: ‘A father’s blessing strengthens the house of his children; a mother’s curse uproots its foundations.’

“These men are now not in the foundations of their homeland but throughout the world; they provide a spectacle, they display their punishment; they expose their misery to the eyes of others and frighten the pride of others. Learn, children, what Scripture says: to render the honor due to parents. But you parents too, when you are offended, remember that you are parents. The mother prayed against her children and was heard, because God is truly just, because she had truly suffered an injury. One of them had both spoken insulting words and laid hands upon her, while the others patiently endured the injury done to their mother and did not answer their brother with a single word on her behalf. The just God, who heard the one praying, hears the one grieving.

“But what of that wretched woman? Was she not punished more severely in the very respect in which she was heard more quickly? Learn to ask this of God: that you may not fear being heard. As for us, brothers, let us earnestly give thanks to the Lord our God for the one who has been healed, and let us pour out prayers for the one who is still afflicted. Let us bless God because he has deemed us worthy to see this. For what are we, that I appeared to these people without knowing it? They saw me, while I did not know it; and they were warned to come to this city. Who am I? I am one man among many, not one of the great.

“And truly, let your charity hear me: I am greatly astonished and rejoice that this man was not cured at Ancona. Indeed, he could have been, but it was not done on our account, because it could very easily have happened. Many know how many miracles are performed in this city through the most blessed martyr Stephen. And hear something at which you will marvel. His memorial was ancient there, and it is still there. But perhaps you say: ‘His body had not yet appeared; how did he have a memorial there?’ The reason is hidden, but I will not conceal from your charity what report has brought to us.

“When Saint Stephen was being stoned, some innocent people, especially some who had already believed in Christ, were standing around. It is said that a stone struck him on the elbow and, being knocked away from there, came before a certain religious man. He picked it up and preserved it. He was one of those who sail; the lot of navigation brought him to the shore of Ancona, and it was revealed to him that the stone ought to be deposited there. He obeyed the revelation and did what had been commanded. From that time the memorial of Saint Stephen began to exist there, and there was a report that Saint Stephen’s arm was there, although people did not know what had happened.

“It is understood, however, that this was revealed for the following reason: that he should place there the stone knocked from the martyr’s elbow, because in Greek an elbow is called *aucon*, as printed. But let those who know what miracles occur there teach us. Those miracles did not begin to occur there until after the body of Saint Stephen had appeared.

“Behold, this young man was not cured there, so that he might be preserved for our eyes. At Usalim, where my brother Evodius is bishop, ask how many miracles occur there, and you will find out. Passing over the others, I will tell you of one that happened there, so that you may see how great the presence of divine majesty is there.

“A certain woman suddenly lost in her lap a sick son, a catechumen, whom she had not been able to help by hurrying to him. Crying out, she said: ‘My son, a catechumen, is dead.’”

As Augustine said this, the people began to cry out from the memorial of Saint Stephen: “Thanks be to God! Praise to Christ!” Amid this continuous outcry, the girl who had been cured was brought to the apse. When she was seen, the people, with joy and tears, prolonged the shouting for some time without any intervening words, but only with the intervening tumult. When silence had been made, Augustine the bishop said:

“It is written in the Psalm: ‘I said, I will speak out against myself my transgression to the Lord my God, and you forgave the impiety of my heart.’ ‘I said, I will speak out’: I had not yet spoken out. ‘I said, I will speak out,’ and you forgave. I commended this wretched woman—or rather, I commended her to your prayers as one who had been wretched. We resolved to pray, and we have been heard. Let our joy be an act of thanksgiving. Mother Church was heard more quickly than that mother whose curse brought destruction. Turned toward the Lord, etc.”

### Sermon 324

Augustine’s sermon completing the portion of the preceding sermon interrupted by the miracle.

“Yesterday’s sermon ought to be completed; it was interrupted by a greater joy. For I had decided, and had begun, to explain to your charity why these brothers seem to me to have been directed to this city by divine authority, so that here the healing they had long desired and awaited might be fulfilled.

“In wishing to say this, I had first begun to commend to your charity the holy places where they were not healed and from which they were directed to us. I spoke of Ancona, a city of Italy. I had begun to speak of the city of Usali, which is in Africa—it has as bishop my brother Evodius, whom you know—because the reputation of that same martyr and of his works had compelled them to come to that city as well. What could have been granted there was not granted, so that it might be granted here, where it ought to have been granted.

“But when I wished briefly to recall the works of God through the holy martyr, omitting the others I had decided to mention one: while I was telling it, the girl’s health was restored, and suddenly an uproar of joy arose, compelling us to end the sermon in another way.

“Thus we know that such a miracle occurred there, among many others, all of which certainly cannot be recounted. A certain woman lost in her lap a sick son, a catechumen, an infant still at the breast. When she saw him lost and irretrievably gone, she began to mourn him more as a believer than as a mother. For she did not desire the life of her son except in the age to come, and she mourned that this had been taken from her and lost.

“Filled with the emotion of faith, she took up the dead child, ran to the memorial of blessed martyr Stephen, and began to demand her son from him, saying: ‘Holy martyr, you see that no consolation remains to me. I cannot say that my son has gone before me, for you know that he has perished; you see why I mourn. Return my son to me, so that I may have him before the sight of your Crown-Giver.’

“As she prayed these and similar words with tears—not in a manner of asking, but, as I have said, of demanding—her son came back to life. And because she had said, ‘You know why I seek him,’ God also wished to display the truth of her intention. She immediately took him to the presbyters. He was baptized, sanctified, anointed, and hands were laid upon him. When all the sacraments had been completed, he was taken away. But she led him away with such an expression on her face as though she were not leading him to the repose of the grave, but to the bosom of the martyr Stephen. The faithful heart of the woman was proved.

“Since, then, God performed such a miracle there through his martyr, could he not have healed these people there? And yet they were directed here for our sake. Turned toward the Lord, etc.”

Thus far. We shall add nothing, except that the solemn conclusion has been omitted here; it could have been expressed in this or a similar manner: “May this turn out well for me and for you; spectators, applaud.”

### Sermon 330

The earlier part is identical with the earlier part of Sermon 118, *On Various Matters*. But what is appended in that sermon does not cohere with what precedes. Here, however, everything is suitable and connected through to the end. —Sirmondus.

#### Title: On Twenty Martyrs

Sermon 110, *On Various Matters*, was also delivered in honor of twenty martyrs. Augustine shows that their memorial was exceedingly famous at Hippo Regius by recalling a remarkable miracle that had occurred there, in Book XXII, chapter 8, of *The City of God*: “There was a certain old man,” etc. Since their names had until now been unknown, three are mentioned here: Fidentius the bishop, and Valeriana and Victoria, holy women. For this one reason alone, what we owe to this sermon is not insignificant—whether these martyrs are to be identified, as Cardinal Baronius thought, with the twenty martyrs who are said to have suffered at Tarsus in Cilicia under Diocletian, on the eighth day before the Ides of June; or whether, as I consider more probable, the Hipponenses discussed here were different from the people of Tarsus. —Sirmondus.

#### Sermon 330: On the Feast of Many Martyrs

Thus the Royal manuscript, together with Victorinus; but Bede cites it as “from the sermon *On the Words of the Gospel*.” —The same.

### Sermon 332

This sermon is found both in the Royal manuscript and in Victorinus. DD 12. —The same.

### § 4

“When Scripture had mentioned those who were not entering, it also named murderers—‘you were not terrified.’ It named fornicators—‘I heard that you beat your breasts.’”

From this it can be seen that they were accustomed to beat their breasts whenever they heard something that reminded them of the conscience of sin or of confession. They practiced this to such an extent that they sometimes used it inappropriately. Thus, in Sermon 8, *On the Words of the Lord*, when the people, according to custom, had beaten their breasts at the words “I confess to you, Father,” Augustine cleverly rebuked them:

“In this very thing that sounded—‘I confess’—you beat your breasts. But what is beating the breast except reproving what lies hidden in the breast and chastising the concealed sin by an evident blow? Why did you do this, unless because you heard, ‘I confess to you, Father’? You heard ‘I confess,’ but you did not attend to the one who confesses. Now pay attention. If Christ said ‘I confess,’ from whom all sin is far removed, it belongs not only to the sinner but also to the one who praises. We therefore confess either while praising God or while accusing ourselves.” —The same.

### Sermon 340

In the title: “On the Day of His Ordination.”

On the anniversary of his assumption of the episcopate. Bishops sometimes celebrated the birthday of their chair, or of their episcopate, just as emperors celebrated the birthdays of their reigns; this was called the bishop’s *birthday*. Three sermons of Saint Leo, pope, “on the day of his assumption,” provide evidence of this custom among the Romans. Among the Africans, besides Homilies 24 and 25 on the anniversary of Augustine’s episcopal ordination, to which this third sermon is added in the ancient manuscripts, further evidence is provided by the anniversary of Aurelius the bishop, concerning which there is Augustine’s address to the people that we have presented. It is not clear on what day Augustine was ordained; from Homily 25 we learn that he was ordained shortly before Christmas. —The same.

### Sermon 341

In the title: “On the Evening Sacrifice.”

Thus it is entitled in the manuscript of Saint Victor, CC 16, and Bede cites it in the same way, as “from the sermon *On the Evening Sacrifice*.” But in Part 3 of the *Collection of Sermons* it is called “A sermon on the verse of Psalm 140: ‘Let the lifting up of my hands be an evening sacrifice.’” —The same.

### Sermon 344

“On the Love of God and the Love of the World.”

We had a single copy, from the manuscript of Saint Victor, DD 12. It was nevertheless also in Part 5 of the *Collection of Sermons*, as the index shows. In both places it bears the title “On the Love of God and Neighbor.” But the title read by Bede, “On the Love of God and the Love of the World,” seemed more suitable and more consistent with Augustine’s words. —The same.

### Sermon 345

“On Contempt for the World.”

The old manuscript does not give the author’s name. Nevertheless, we did not doubt that it was Augustine’s, both because it was interwoven with other sermons of his and especially because it reflects Augustine’s style and character.

### § 5

“For however much you may have, when the fifth hour has come, before you approach the table you are hungry and faint because you are wretched.”

The fifth hour precedes the sixth, that is, noon, and is the customary hour for lunch. Our Sidonius, Book II, Letter 9, speaking of a messenger who summoned someone to lunch, approved his having arrived at the proper time while he himself was leaving at the fifth hour. In connection with this passage we have noted several matters concerning the ancient system of hours, to the same effect. —The same.

### § 6

“We celebrate the solemnity of the Tuburbitan women martyrs.”

Perpetua and Felicitas, whose bodies were buried at Carthage in the major basilica. Three sermons of Saint Augustine survive on their feast. Their anniversary is celebrated on the Nones of March. There were also other women, virgins—Maxima, Donatilla, and Secunda—who are said to have suffered at Tuburbum on the second day before the Kalends of August. There were two cities of that name, Tuburbum Maius and Tuburbum Minus; hence the Tuburbitani Maiores and Minores in the conference with the Donatists. —Sirmondus.

### Sermon 357

“On the Praise of Peace.”

From the manuscript of Saint Victor, DD 12. That it was also in Part 5 of the *Collection* is demonstrated by the index. Together with the two following sermons, it belongs to the period of the conference with the Donatists. From the opening of the Acts it is clear that the conference was held in the post-consulship of Varanius, in the year of Christ 412, and began on the Kalends of June. This date agrees with Augustine’s words: toward the end of the sermon he says that the Pentecost fast had been completed shortly before; in that year it ended on the fourth day before the Kalends of June. —The same.

### § 4

“From where am I your brother?”

The Donatists evidently did not want to be called brothers, and yet our people called them brothers. Optatus, Book I *Against Parmenianus*: “They do not want to be called our brothers. They are undoubtedly brothers, although not good ones. Therefore no one should wonder that I call them brothers, since they cannot fail to be brothers.” And in Book IV: “For you cannot fail to be brothers whom one mother, the Church, has generated from the same sacramental womb, whom God the Father has received in the same way as adopted sons.” Augustine says many things of the same kind in Book III of his work against Gaudentius and in Book III against Parmenianus, chapter 2. —The same.

#### Ibid.

“The Holy Spirit speaks through the prophet Isaiah: ‘Hear, you who fear the word of the Lord; say to those who hate you, “You are our brothers,”’ etc.”

Truly remarkable words, although they are found only among the LXX interpreters. Isaiah 66:5. But, alas, what followed did not at all correspond to these flatteries; for afterward that gentle and merciful Augustine maintained that it was permissible for these “brothers” of his to be persecuted with the utmost severity. His disposition was certainly not very brotherly. See Letter 93 and our notes on it.

### Sermon 358

“On Peace, etc.”

In the manuscript of Saint Victor and in the index of the *Collection*, this sermon is placed before the preceding one. What persuaded us to place it afterward is that toward its end, where he says that he had already warned them about joining fasting and almsgiving with prayer, he seems to allude to the preceding sermon. —Sirmondus.

### § 6

“Let none of you rush to the place of the conference, my brothers.”

To the Gargilian Baths. For the conference was held in their secretarial building at Carthage. In Book II of the *Ancient Epigrams* collected by Pithaeus there is an epigram on the Gargilian Baths, restored by King Thrasamund; the first and last letters of its verses indicate this in the words: “Thrasamund, making vows serene.”

—The same.

#### Ibid.

“You have read the edict of the illustrious man publicly posted.”

That of Marcellinus, tribune and notary, who presided as judge over the conference in the name of the emperor Honorius. His edict, contained in the acts of the first hearing, included the following provision concerning the people’s being admonished by the bishops:

“Therefore,” he says, “let no one, whether layman or bishop, attempt to approach that most peaceful place of the council beyond the number prescribed and contrary to the prohibition. Rather, let them also address their own congregations with a pious exhortation to quiet and modesty, discussing this beforehand in each church, so that the whole multitude may keep away from the day and place of the disputation, and so that the people, softened by the religious discipline of patience, may be prepared for Christian peace.”

The Catholic bishops professed that they would observe this edict in their formal declaration, which was read there, chapter 16. —The same.

#### Ibid.

“Support your prayers also with fasts and almsgiving, as we have already warned you. Add wings to them, by which they may fly to God.”

That is, almsgiving and fasting are called the two wings by which prayers are lifted to heaven. See Acts 10:4 and the commentators on that passage.

### Sermon 359

Delivered after the conference.

The first part was published as Sermon 91, *On Various Matters*; the latter part, which deals with the cause of the Donatists, was omitted by those who judged that they could do without it.
