We have reproduced it in full, as it was presented by a manuscript written on parchment, and we were not unaware that it had also been recognized by Bede. —Sirmondus.

### § 5

“We said that, for the sake of peace, brothers could be in agreement within one Church; for the concord of brothers is a beautiful thing.”

From the same formal declaration that the Catholic bishops presented to Marcellinus the judge, it is clear that they had agreed with the Donatists, confident in the truth, that if the Donatists won their case they would seek no honor among them; but if the Catholics themselves were victorious, they would nevertheless admit the Donatists into the fellowship of the episcopate.

The statements made here and the fuller explanation in that same declaration concern this fellowship, in these words:

“For each of us will be able, with a colleague joined to him in honor, to sit in turn in the more prominent place, just as a visiting bishop sits beside his colleague. When this is granted to both parties in alternate basilicas, each is anticipated by the other in mutual honor; for where the commandment of charity has enlarged hearts, the possession of peace does not become narrow. Thus, when one of them has died, thereafter a single successor may follow according to the former custom.”

But Optatus, Book I, shows that the Donatists had long been accustomed to reject this fellowship: “And because they do not want to share the episcopal college with us, let them not be colleagues if they do not wish to be; nevertheless, as we said above, they are brothers.” —The same.

#### Ibid.

“If the Catholics had afterward shown themselves humane toward the Donatists, there would be no one who would not praise this and judge it to have proceeded from a Christian spirit. But now, after they treated the Donatists—who were indeed obstinate and factious, who would deny it?—yet nevertheless Christian men, so badly, there are some who suspect that the Catholics carefully made their calculations and, comparing the number of Donatist bishops and the people attached to them with the number of Catholics, concluded that the union of the Churches would bring them profit, or at least no loss.

“Perhaps something else was concealed that we do not know. Certainly, if we believe many reports, these men were so eager for the golden rewards of the times—the honors and episcopal revenues—that, once they had acquired them, they would not easily give them up and would strive to break in upon them whenever an opportunity arose. It was therefore dangerous that, apart from the agreements, the man who was to be superior in authority might, according to African custom, designate his successor while still alive. Everyone knows the long-lasting schism of the Church of Antioch, which arose from a similar origin.

“As for the confidence in truth that is vaunted here, I fear that it ought to be changed into confidence in victory, conceived no less from the observed favor of the judge Marcellinus than from the merits of the case. Otherwise, it was dangerous, so to speak, to wish to make the case of so many bishops and Churches depend upon the judgment of one man who was attached to one of the parties.”

### § 6

“We undertook to examine the case of Caecilian, but as that of a brother, not as that of a father or mother. God is our father; the Church is our mother; Caecilian was a brother, etc.”

At the conference, on the third day, chapter 235, Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:

“Behold, I say it; whenever they wish, I say it: Caecilian is not my father, because I hear my Lord saying, ‘Do not call anyone your father on earth; one is your Father, God.’ I call Caecilian a brother—a good brother, if he is good; a bad brother, if he is bad—because, on account of our common sacraments, he is my brother.” —Sirmondus.

#### Ibid.

“Condemned once in his absence, acquitted three times in his presence.”

He had been condemned by the Donatists in a synod. He was first acquitted at Rome in the council under Melchiades; again at Arles, by a general council; and finally at Milan, by the emperor Constantine, to whom the opposing party had appealed. The entire accusation against him was that he had been ordained by Felix, bishop of Aptunga, who was said to have handed over the sacred books under Diocletian. Even if this had been true, it would not have been sufficient grounds for schism, because the cause of the Church is one thing and the cause of individuals another. Moreover, it was established by the public records that Felix the bishop had not been a traditor. —The same.

### § 8

“For new things have been reported to us: they cut out the tongue of one of our presbyters.”

Concerning another bishop whose tongue and hand the Donatists had cut off, Augustine writes in Letter 50 to Boniface:

“Bishops and clerics have endured terrible and harsh sufferings, which it would take too long to recount; for the eyes of some were extinguished, and the hand and tongue of a certain bishop were cut off.”

Letter 122 also relates that they poured lime and vinegar into the eyes of the clerics of Hippo, and other passages bear witness to other manifestations of the same fury. This also relates to Constitution 14 of the emperor Honorius, recently published in the appendix to the Theodosian Code. —The same.

#### Ibid.

“For these unspeakable crimes, whoever among them could be convicted ought to have paid severe penalties; but not every Donatist, even one of blameless conduct, should be harassed on account of his opinions, as we have already said in Volume II.”

### § 9

“You honored your bishop, so that you wished to call this basilica Florentia; but you yourselves are his Florentia.”

Just as the Basilica of Faustus and the Basilica of Leontius were named after their founders, Faustus and Leontius, so Florentia here means the basilica named after the bishop Florentius. It is uncertain to which see he belonged, unless it is preferred to understand Florentius as the bishop of Hippo Diarrhytus in the province of Proconsular Africa. He participated in the conference with the Donatists together with the others in this year, as the acts of the first hearing show, and several years later he subscribed, with Augustine and others, to the letter of the monk Leporius to the Gauls.

If this is correct, it would be appropriate to say that the sermon was delivered not at Carthage or Hippo Regius, but at Hippo Diarrhytus. —Sirmondus.

#### Ibid.

“This will be Florentia, truly Florentia.”

He speaks in this way of heavenly blessedness. Therefore, here and above, I interpret *Florentia* as a state of eternal flourishing, in which it is truly possible to glory. The Numidian Latin of that period invented many such expressions.

### Sermon 360

“A Donatist Returned to the Church.”

Since nothing could be asserted about the date of this sermon, we were led to place it after the preceding sermons because Augustine states that, after the conference, very many people returned from the Donatist schism to the Church—not only in the preceding sermon, but much more explicitly in Book I, chapter 29, against Gaudentius:

“How much consolation do you think we have,” he says, “that from that great madness of the party of Donatus, where not only the error of an unspeakable division but also a law of fury was established, many thousands, by far and incomparably more numerous, are being freed?” —Sirmondus.

#### Ibid.

“O vineyard beloved by my Lord, not only did my labor profit you nothing, but I was even serving your enemy against you, etc.”

The Parisian editors think that this sermon, read by a Donatist bishop, was dictated by Augustine; I do not disagree. But I do not think it should be passed over that this appears to be, so to speak, a kind of formula for a *palinode*, such as the Donatists ought to have sung. There is no doubt that this was no small part of the triumph of their opponents. But those who, through ignorance, had belonged to that party could not be received into the unity of the Church without great grief and amid such disgrace. Such was the humanity of the Africans.

### Sermon 363

In the title: “On the Song of Exodus.”

The Royal manuscript calls the sermon “On the Song of Exodus, after the crossing of the Red Sea.” But in the manuscript of Saint Victor it is called a treatise, and likewise by Possidius, who, among Augustine’s various treatises, mentions two: “On the Song of Isaiah” and “On the Song of Exodus.” —Sirmondus.

Or had the very learned man forgotten that treatises are commonly called sermons, such as those in Volume IV, *Treatises on John*? I do not know. But nothing is more frequent: in Augustinian usage, *to treat* and *to preach* are almost the same.

§ 1. The most manifest authority of the holy Scriptures themselves ought to govern our understanding in examining and interpreting those same Scriptures [Col. 0408D], so that from what is plainly stated we may be nourished, and what is stated more obscurely may be faithfully discussed for our exercise.]

This is certainly an excellent rule, and none is more reliable in the interpretation of Scripture. Therefore, once Holy Scripture has taught us certain things about God in such a way that no one can doubt their meaning unless he is insane, nothing should ever be extracted from obscure passages that contradicts them. For example, nothing is taught more clearly in Holy Scripture than that God is good and merciful, and observant of justice—that is, one who can indeed forgive the guilty and truly does forgive them according to definite laws, but who cannot punish the innocent. Whoever does not find these things in Scripture will understand nothing in it, for no doctrine is presented with greater clarity. But once this has been established, doctrines must not be gathered from certain obscure passages that plainly deprive God of all praise for goodness, mercy, and justice—such as those doctrines for whose confirmation, in our own times, the African synods have thrown heaven and earth into confusion.

Nor should you say here that there are certain profound matters in divine things that elude the acumen of the human mind. For those profundities must not be fabricated from obscure passages in such a way that they conflict with the clear doctrines of Scripture—as when one explains an obscure passage by making God cruel or unjust. Much more wisely do those act who, if they cannot find a suitable and consistent interpretation with the rest of Scripture, admit that they [Col. 0409B] do not understand those passages, than those who explain them in such a way that an open and violent conflict between scriptural passages and theological doctrines is introduced into Christian teaching. No rhetorical exclamations, no episcopal anathemas, no royal edicts will make what is wrong appear right to later good and prudent men. It may easily happen that we do not understand a passage of Scripture; but it cannot happen that Scripture contradicts itself and takes away from God what it attributes to him in the clearest words, with right reason also confirming it.

### Sermon 366. On Psalm XXII.

In the manuscript of Saint-Germain, from which it first came down to us, and in the two manuscripts of Saint-Victor, CC 6 and DD II, the title is: *Exposition of Saint Augustine on Psalm XXII*. In all these books it is inserted as though it belonged with various works of Saint [Col. 0409C] Augustine against the Pelagians. In part 3 of the *Collectory*: *Sermon, or exposition, on Psalm XXII*. It was delivered to those about to be baptized. —Sirmondus.

### Sermon 389.

The latter part is identical with the latter part of Sermon 50 *On Time*, except that there the entire story is omitted about the man who had distributed the price of a solidus among the poor. This is indeed an old confusion. For Sermon 50 in the manuscripts differs in no respect from the printed editions, while we have faithfully reproduced this present sermon from the Royal manuscript and another of Saint-Victor, DD 12. —The same.

### § 3. When he had sold the solidus, as usual.

He does not state for how much he sold the gold solidus; it may, however, be understood from Valentinian’s Novel 25 among the Theodosian legislation, by which it was provided that a solidus should never be sold for less than seven thousand coins. Cassiodorus states that it had formerly been sold for six thousand, in Book I of the *Variae*, Letter 10: “They determined that a solidus should be six thousand denarii.” —The same.

### Ibid. He ordered one hundred folles from the price of the solidus to be distributed among the poor.

He means bronze folles, not silver ones. For one hundred silver folles would not have been an insignificant part of a solidus. Thus, just as they called both silver and bronze coins *denarii*, so some folles were silver and others bronze. The value of the bronze folles was either the same as that of the coins, or denarii, six or seven thousand of which were reckoned as one solidus, or the difference between the two kinds was not great.

The value of the silver folles in Augustine’s age can be estimated from Law 3 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Swineherds*, which fixes the price of pork at six folles per pound, and from what is said about Florentius, the tailor of Hippo, in Book XXII, chapter 8, § 9 of *The City of God*. In both cases everything can correspond if *folles* is taken to mean *asses*, or solidi, of our French currency. For six solidi per pound would indeed have been a fair price for pork, and there is nothing absurd in selling a large fish for three hundred of our asses. Hence one may conjecture that the value of the folles and of our solidi was the same, or nearly so. These remarks, however, should be understood of the *follis* insofar as it signifies a definite kind of coin. For *follis* has other meanings in monetary matters that are irrelevant here. —The same.

# INTO VOLUME SIX

[Col. 0409]

## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS TO THE READER, ON THE EIGHTY-THREE QUESTIONS

[Col. 0409C]

Augustine does acknowledge this work, yet it seems to me to have been compiled by some diligent student from all his books, with whatever had been argued with particular subtlety collected into it. Favoring this project, Augustine revised it and removed certain passages. The conjecture that this is not entirely a fabrication is supported by the fact that Question 12 contains a fragment taken from the books of Fonteius. Chapter 31 also contains a passage copied from the second book of Cicero’s *De inventione*. There are also other passages that do not seem to me to possess Augustine’s diction in every respect. In addition, certain things were confused, either transferred here from the *Questions on the Gospels* or carried from here into that work. Finally, many passages have no appearance of being questions, except that whatever can be taught can also be asked. Thus as many questions would arise as there are propositions or statements. Nevertheless, the work itself is learned and worth reading.

## REMARKS ON THE SAME EIGHTY-THREE QUESTIONS

[Col. 0410C]

### Question 9. What does not remain cannot be perceived; for that is perceived which is grasped by knowledge. But what changes without interruption cannot be grasped. Therefore the truth’s purity is not to be expected from the bodily senses. [Col. 0410D]

Augustine resolves in this way the question whether truth can be perceived by the bodily senses. This is Platonic reasoning, whose use I do not understand—unless someone wishes thereby to call into doubt the testimony of the senses concerning bodily things, upon which Christian faith itself nevertheless rests. I know that, in a certain philosophical sense, one may say that the senses were not given to us by God so that by their means we might know the inner nature of things and their hidden truths; but such matters do not belong to theological questions. There is much here that smells of Platonism.

### Question 16. God is the cause of all things that exist. But whatever is the cause of all things is also the cause of his wisdom. [Col. 0411A]

Why does he not say that he is the cause of himself? Clearly because this conflicts with the most certain axioms of metaphysics. Yet he says the same thing in other words, since God’s wisdom is God himself. It should not be concealed that the Platonists were accustomed to speak in this way. Aristides, volume I, Oration 1, p. 5, *On God*: Ἐποίησε πρῶτος αὐτὸς ἑαυτόν—“He first made himself.” A little later: Ὅδε ἐστί, πρῶτός τε καὶ πρεσβύτατος καὶ ἀρχηγέτης τῶν πάντων, αὐτὸς ἐξ αὐτοῦ γενόμενος . . . αὐτοπάτωρ τε καὶ μείζων ἢ ἐξ ἄλλου γεγονέναι· καὶ ὥσπερ τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν ἄρα ἐκ τῆς κεφαλῆς ἔφυσε, καὶ γάμου οὐδὲν προσεδεήθη εἰς αὐτήν, οὕτως ἔτι πρότερον αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ ἐποίησε.

“This is the first and most ancient, and the ruler of all; he was made from himself . . . the father of himself, and greater than could be one made from another; and just as he produced Athena from his head and had no need of marriage for her, so still earlier he made himself from himself.”

Thus Augustine infers the eternity of the Son from the words cited: “Therefore the cause of his eternal wisdom is eternal, and it is not prior in time to his wisdom.” The same conclusion could be drawn, if the reasoning is correct, about all the other attributes of God. Yet nothing could be more absurd than to suppose that there are as many Sons of God as there are attributes. It would therefore have been better to abstain from such arguments, by which nothing can be proved, particularly in so serious a matter and one harassed by so many fierce controversies.

### Question 18. He proves the Trinity in this way: Everything that exists has one aspect by which it is constituted, another by which it is distinguished, and another by which it is harmonious. Therefore the whole creation, since it exists in some fashion, is very far removed from what is absolutely nothing, and is harmonious in its parts; it must also have a threefold cause: one by which it exists, one by which it is this particular thing, and one by which it is harmonious with itself. [Col. 0411C]

Apart from the fact that these distinctions exist only through an abstraction of the mind and therefore do not require different causes, can there not be one and the same utterly simple cause of various things? Unless this is admitted, as many divine persons will exist as there are properties distinguishable in created things. The heretics of that age must have been exceedingly obtuse if they were silenced by such arguments or did not mock their opponents. Yet the ears and eyes of the orthodox were also patient with every kind of speech and book, if they took pleasure in such reasoning.

To be candid, I am offended when I consider that such serious questions are solved by arguments so trifling, and that Christian theology is polluted by them and sometimes exposed to ridicule. Concerning matters known only by divine revelation and incapable of proof by reason, it would have been better to use only the authority of Scripture and its own words.

But let us hear what follows: “We call the cause of creation—that is, God—the author.” Quite true, but what follows from this? “There must therefore be a Trinity, than which perfect reason can find nothing more excellent, more intelligent, or happier.” That there is a Trinity, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the sacred Scriptures teach us; and we ought to believe them no less than our own reasonings. But this could not be inferred from what preceded, as we have already said. Otherwise, by the philosophy of that age, one might equally infer that there are five divine persons, because there are four elements and a fifth essence, from which the heavens and human minds are constituted. Innumerable such things could be imagined.

But let us also hear a rhetorical argument, lest the good bishop forget his art: “Therefore, even when truth is sought, there can be no more than three kinds of questions: whether something exists at all, whether it is this or something else, and whether it should be approved or rejected.” Why could someone else not similarly say that there are four persons because there are four parts of rhetoric—discovery, arrangement, expression, and delivery—or because there are four figures of syllogisms?

“But,” you will say, “Augustine did not put these forward as firm arguments, but rather poured forth certain philosophical and rhetorical illustrations of a truth discovered elsewhere; and indeed he was still a beginner, having only recently returned to Africa from Italy.” But, if we love truth, these are not illustrations but obscurations of the truth, which has no need of such futile subtleties and is dishonored by them. Moreover, as he himself testifies, when he was already a bishop he ordered this book to be compiled from old papers; for the greater part of it the Numidians could have done without, without the slightest loss. And there are many such passages in the books *On the Trinity*, which the bishop worked on with great diligence.

### Question 24. Sin is the merit of punishment, and a right action is the merit of reward. [Col. 0412B]

That is, sin is what incurs punishment, and a right action is what receives reward. He adds: “Neither sin nor a right action can justly be attributed to anyone who has done nothing by his own will.” Therefore both sin and right action lie within the freedom of the will.

In the *Retractions*, however, concerning this question he says: “That this is so is altogether most true; but in order that one may be free to do what is right, one must be set free by God’s grace.” This too is true. But in order to preserve Augustine’s earlier answer—that human actions, good and bad, can be attributed to their free will—not only those who are saved must be liberated by God’s grace, but those who are damned must also have been made slaves of sin in such a way that they did not sin necessarily and could remain in that slavery.

Moreover, how did infants who die unbaptized, and upon whom, according to Augustine’s view, punishments are inflicted, sin by their own will? Augustine revises his opinions in such a way that he wishes as little alteration as possible to appear in them. Hence he often excuses some points while omitting others that required no less a retraction. In this matter, however, the “second voyage” (δεύτερος πλοῦς) was not more successful.

## REMARKS ON THE VARIOUS QUESTIONS TO SIMPLICIAN

### Book I. Question 1. Romans 7:7 and following. It seems to me that the Apostle transformed into himself the man placed under the law, speaking in his own person through that man’s words.

This was the commonly accepted view at that time, and it was entirely correct; Augustine would never have abandoned it unless Pelagius had later arisen. See volume III, *Remarks on the Epistle to the Romans*.

### Question 2, § 2. I shall hold to Paul’s intention, which pervades the whole Epistle and which I shall consult. It is this: that no one should boast of the merits of works. The Israelites dared to boast of these, because they had served the law given to them and had received evangelical grace from it as something owed to their merits, since they served the law. Hence they did not want the same grace to be given to the Gentiles, as though they were unworthy, unless they accepted the Jewish sacraments.

If the first eleven chapters of the Epistle to the Romans are read with slightly greater attention, everyone will understand that Paul treats two chief questions in them. The first concerns the justification of a person before God. The Jews maintained that no one could be considered just—that is, good—by God unless he observed the Mosaic law, both its ceremonial and its moral precepts. Paul denies this and shows at length that people are justified, or regarded as just by God, without observance of the Mosaic law; [Col. 0413B] and therefore that justification is obtained not by works but by grace, that is, by God’s mercy. By this mercy the person who has never observed the law is regarded as good, provided only that he believes the Gospel and thereafter obeys it.

The second question is whether idolatrous Gentiles could be called by God to knowledge of the Gospel and be regarded as his people even while the Jews were neglected. The Jews denied this; Paul affirmed it. He shows that, in calling peoples to knowledge of himself, God takes no account of works or merits, but bestows his benefits on anyone, even though unworthy, while passing over those who were not less worthy than others of divine benefits.

These are the two principal points to which Paul’s entire argument must be referred, not what Augustine says here. Thus what follows in Augustine is irrelevant: “In many passages he repeatedly bears witness to this, placing the grace of faith above works—not to abolish works, but to show that works do not precede grace but follow it; so that no one may think he received grace because he acted well, but rather that he cannot act well unless he has received grace through faith. A person begins to receive grace when he begins to believe in God, moved to faith either by an inward or an outward admonition.”

I do not wish to examine these statements in detail, but I utterly deny that Paul had anything of this kind in mind when he argued against the Jews. They did not maintain that the grace of faith was owed to them or to anyone else, nor does the Apostle prove the contrary. Let the reader consult the best interpreters of Paul, but above all read Paul himself; he will understand that Augustine entirely failed to notice the Apostle’s purpose. Indeed, the Epistle to the Romans is too obscure to have been understood by a semi-Platonic rhetorician wholly untrained in criticism.

### Ibid., § 4. After citing Paul’s words, Romans 9:11–12: “From this,” he says, “the question arises in the mind why he said: ‘so that God’s purpose according to election might remain.’ For how is there a just election, or any election at all, where there is no difference? For if Jacob was chosen without merit, while not yet born and having done nothing, he could not have been chosen at all, since there was no difference by which he might be chosen. Likewise, if Esau was rejected without merit, because he too was not yet born and had done nothing, when it was said, ‘the elder shall serve the younger,’ how can his rejection be called just?” And so forth.

If Augustine had considered this very passage a little more carefully and, so to speak, more critically (κριτικώτερον), he would have shortened the lengthy discussion that follows concerning the election of individual persons, since it is plainly beside the point. For it is clear that Jacob and Esau are not considered here as individual men concerning whose conversion God is deliberating, but as the founders of two nations, one of which he would call to knowledge of himself and regard as his people, and not the other.

The whole sequence and occasion of the argument proclaim this; and the very words, “the elder shall serve the younger,” Genesis 25:23, plainly demonstrate it. For these words are spoken not of individual men but of peoples. God says to Rebecca, who was inquiring: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be separated from your body; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger.”

Indeed, the Idumeans, whose power became established sooner than that of the Israelites, later served them; but Esau himself was never subject to Jacob, whom he rather terrified, as John Clericus shows in his discussion of the passage in Genesis. Therefore the questions Augustine later raises—whether Jacob’s election arose from foreknowledge of faith, and Esau’s rejection from foreknowledge of disobedience, whether faith is to be numbered among the gifts of grace, and so forth—are ἀπροσδιόνυσα, irrelevant.

Yet while the Numidian oracle wanders so far beyond the olive trees, it discovers that faith is a gift of God—not from ecclesiastical tradition, nor from Paul, who says nothing here about the matter. In Augustine’s view, faith arises from an inward breath that cannot be resisted and that is granted only to a few elect people, although without it no one can maintain faith in the Gospel to the end of life.

The presbyter had not known this great mystery, nor had he known it when he first became a bishop; he discovered it while composing these answers to Simplician. Afterwards he bent Scripture to this doctrine of his, despite its resistance, paying no attention to the connection of the argument, the received meaning of the words, or the questions and controversies being debated between the apostles and the Jews.

He read Scripture as though individual periods or sentences were mathematical axioms, entirely unconnected with what preceded or followed, but capable of being explained separately and in themselves. If anything occurred that offered, or seemed to offer, an opportunity for an impressive little declamation, he eagerly seized it and spread the sails of Punic eloquence. No work displays more clearly that remarkable habit than this one. From it, however, there later flowed so many delusions that they might have been removed had force and authority not been brought against the remedies.

For this was evidently the character of the humble rhetoricians of that age: they readily ventured to speak about matters they did not understand, however little support they possessed; but they could be recalled only with the greatest difficulty from opinions once preconceived, which they defended with the utmost ferocity by anathemas and edicts whenever anyone dared to attack them.

### Book II. Question 4, § 2. On the question how Samuel could have been summoned by the woman who practiced divination, after saying that perhaps Samuel’s own soul could have been summoned, he adds: “Nevertheless, in this event there may be another, easier solution and more convenient interpretation: we should not believe that Samuel’s spirit was truly raised from its rest, but rather that some phantom and imaginary illusion was produced by the machinations of the devil. Scripture therefore calls it by the name of Samuel, because images of things are customarily called by the names of the things whose images they are.”

Why did he not rather say that Scripture there speaks from Saul’s point of view, since Saul truly believed that Samuel had been summoned? Why did nothing about the fraud of the diviner occur to this astute man, when she plainly seems to have raised a figure before the credulous and terrified Saul? Indeed, Saul himself is not even said to have seen this apparition; and in its name some wretched accomplice of the diviner could easily have spoken. On this matter see the acute and learned Antonius Van Dale, in his dissertation *On Idolatrous Divinations under the Old Testament*, chapter 9.

## REMARKS ON THE BOOK OF THE EIGHT QUESTIONS OF DULCITIUS

[Col. 0415B]

### Question 1, § 6. On the passage 1 Corinthians 3:11 and following, he decides that the foundation is faith in Christ, while gold, silver, and precious stones are certain outstanding good works; but wood, hay, and straw are those things in which something carnal has been admitted.

I am astonished that it did not occur to him that this passage concerns doctrine, and that he either proposed so many questions to a man who stumbled so badly over an entirely clear matter or allowed someone so superficially acquainted with Scripture to answer so many questions. O Africa, empty of students of Scripture! O stupid people, to whom such things were objects of admiration and who could endure reading such verbose disputations without learning anything!

### § 13. It is not incredible that something of this kind should occur after this life; and the question may be asked whether it is so, and may either be discovered or remain hidden: whether some of the faithful are saved through a certain purgatorial fire, more slowly or more quickly in proportion as they loved perishable goods more or less—so I read it, “more slowly or more quickly,” not “more slowly and more quickly”—yet not those of whom it was said, “They shall not possess the kingdom of God.”

He speaks about this matter with greater confidence in *The City of God*, Book XXI, chapter 13. See also what the Benedictines collected in their preface to Hilary, chapter 8. Certainly the custom, already established at that time, of praying for the dead led naturally to the affirmation that there is a purgatorial fire; Augustine discusses this in the following question. Hence the opinion concerning purgatorial punishments was eventually consecrated among most Christians by synodal decrees, lest the prayers of the Church appear useless to the dead, since they would release them from no punishments. We shall say something about these prayers in their proper place.

### Question 6, § 2. Likewise you ask, I say, whether the unclean spirit that was in the diviner could have acted so that Samuel might be seen by Saul, and so forth.

See the remarks on Book II of the *Various Questions to Simplician*, Question 4.

## DESIDERIUS ERASMUS’S CENSURE OF THE BOOK *ON FAITH*

This little book has been patched together from various letters of Augustine, especially as regards its statements. It is probable that it belongs to Hugh of Saint-Victor.

The Benedictines, however, rightly refuted Erasmus’s criticism. If anything here has been excerpted from Augustine’s letters, there is nothing to prevent Augustine himself from having done so; for he more than once copies himself in the preceding little book, in which he answers Dulcitius’s questions.

### Chapter 1, § 3. Certainly, if we ought not to believe things that have not been seen, then we should not believe the hearts of friends before they have been more certainly proved; and even when we have proved their good will toward us through our own misfortunes, we believe their goodwill toward us rather than see it.

The Parisian editors note in the margin that this passage is obscure and corrupt. But, unless I am mistaken, every difficulty will be removed if, instead of *quando* (“when”), we read *quomodo* (“how”), and place a question mark at the end of the sentence: “unless faith is so great”—the words cited immediately above follow—“that we may not unreasonably judge, with certain eyes of faith, that we see what we believe, when for that very reason we ought to believe because we cannot see?” Thus everything is clear to anyone who will not begrudge reading the entire sentence.

### Chapter 2, § 4. I shall omit saying how many things those who reproach us because we believe what we do not see nevertheless believe on the basis of report and history, or concerning places where they themselves have not been; yet they do not say, “We do not believe because we do not see.”

This was a magnificent argument by which he could easily have silenced his opponents, one that everyone could readily understand and that was highly appropriate to the matter under discussion, since, if we weigh the matter carefully, our faith rests above all on the truth of the evangelical history.

But I do not know how it happens that the ancients often almost entirely neglect, or at least touch only incidentally upon, the foundations of the Christian cause that are most secure, while laboriously explaining matters that could have had no force among unbelievers. Thus Augustine speaks at very great length about prophecies in what follows, and says things that could profitably be said among Christians but had no weight among unbelievers, since, when dealing with someone who denies the truth of the Jewish and Christian religions, we can scarcely ever prove from the force of the words and the connection of the argument that those prophecies refer to Christ.

Among unbelievers, therefore, these arguments should rather have been avoided, and historical evidence should have been used, against which they could offer no sound reply.

## REMARKS ON THE BOOK *ON FAITH AND THE CREED*

### Chapter 3, § 3. It is called the Father’s Word because through it the Father is made known. For just as, when we speak truthfully, we use our words to make our mind known to the listener, and whatever secret thing we hold in our heart is brought forth to another’s knowledge through signs of this kind, so that Wisdom which God the Father begot, because through it the most hidden Father is made known to worthy minds, is most appropriately called his Word.

I am astonished that matters so doubtful were set before catechumens as though they were articles of faith. For if someone had denied to Augustine that the word λόγος in John should be translated *Word*, and had argued that it meant “reason,” how could he have proved the contrary? Indeed, he could have been pressed by the authority of the Platonists, whom he greatly admired and whom he believed to agree with Christians on this matter.

Moreover, if someone had denied that it is the Son’s function to illuminate minds through himself in the way Augustine describes, how could he have proved what he asserts here, except perhaps from his Platonists, who believed that rational human beings participate in the Logos (τοῦ Λόγου)—though he would not have listened to them concerning the proper meaning of this word?

Many other things could have been said, which I omit and which may be read in the commentators on John, at chapter 1:1. But at that time, if we wish to speak truthfully, the question was not so much what was true and could be defended against any opponent by solid arguments, as what had been given even a slight appearance of probability and could be expressed impressively before ears ready to accept everything.

Let the following passages be read and weighed by a mind that loves truth. If I am judged not to have reached a true verdict, let these papers be cast away and left to be devoured by moths and cockroaches.

### Chapter 5, § 8. For by the gift of God, that is, by the Holy Spirit, such great humility of so great a God has been granted to us that he deigned to assume the whole human being.

I know that others have spoken in this way, but it is plainly contrary both to Holy Scripture and to right reason to attribute humility to the divine nature. Humility is a human virtue, called *modesty* by the Latins, but it cannot be attributed to God without something resembling blasphemy; yet I would not wish to accuse Augustine of this.

Hugo Grotius and John Clericus, in their additions to H. Hammond’s *Annotations on the New Testament*, have shown that the passage in Philippians 2:6, which might be brought against this view, should be understood of Christ’s human nature. What was accomplished by eternal reason when it became flesh was not, far from it, an example of humility, but of supreme goodness and generosity.

### Chapter 5, § 11. Therefore we believe in him who was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate. The name of the judge had to be added for the sake of identifying the time, and so forth.

At that time no mention having been made of the descent into hell, the following words are immediately added: “We also believe that on the third day he rose from the dead, the firstborn among the brothers who were to follow,” and so forth. Hence it is clear that at that time the article concerning the descent into hell was absent from the Creed of the African Church, as it was also from the Roman and other creeds, although it was later rashly joined to them. See what the most learned of all interpreters of the Creed, John Pearson, wrote on this matter in his English interpretation of the Creed.

## REMARKS ON THE BOOK *ON FAITH AND WORKS*

### Chapter 7, § 11. Whatever a person may seem to have done rightly, unless it is referred to piety toward God, ought not to be called right.

Whoever wishes to know how Augustine understood this and on what arguments he relied when he spoke in this way should consult Volume X, Book IV *Against Julian*, chapter 3, where he discusses the matter at length. The most eminent Cardinal Henri Noris should also be consulted, in the fourth section of his *Augustinian Vindications*.

Nevertheless, if we love truth, Augustine will persuade no one of this opinion who does not rest upon his bare authority but examines the arguments. For it is certain that whatever is done in accordance with the impulses of nature and right reason is good, even if revelation has not been added.

For example, honoring one’s parents and assisting them by every means, being moved by the sufferings of the afflicted and helping them, practicing chastity, raising one’s family decently, and six hundred similar things that right reason recommends and the happiness of human society demands are right and pleasing to God, who is no less the author of right reason and human society than of revelation.

Those who can be condemned without revelation for offenses committed against right reason must also be capable of being acquitted if they obey right reason. Paul teaches this too, in Romans 2:14–15. No one who has carefully considered the matter will persuade himself that God, through right reason, established the law of nature and confirmed it through the very constitution of human nature, yet condemns equally those who violate and those who observe it; nor that filial piety is less pleasing to God than parricide. Such notions are monstrosities born of the desire to argue and defend paradoxes.

### Chapter 15, § 24. Therefore one must carefully consider how that statement of the Apostle Paul, plainly difficult to understand, should be taken, where he says: “For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid,” and so forth, 1 Corinthians 3:11 and following.

He already dealt with this passage in the little book *On the Questions of Dulcitius*, yet even here he could not extricate himself from a difficulty that can be great only for someone who is inattentive. It is clear that Paul is speaking there not about morals but about doctrines, since the discussion concerns teachers, such as himself and Apollos, whose disciples the Corinthians claimed to be and for whose factions they therefore divided themselves.

## REMARKS ON THE *ENCHIRIDION TO LAURENTIUS*
Cap. 11, § 4. “What else is called evil than the privation of good?”] By the same right you could say to a Punic philosopher: “What else is called virtue than the privation of vice?” For surely virtue—for example, faith, hope, charity, and so forth—is no more a disposition of our soul acquired through repeated acts than are unbelief, despair, and hatred of one’s neighbor; nor are the effects of vices less significant than those of virtues. If you say that, when vice is removed, virtue is established, I shall similarly say that, when virtue is removed, vice is established. These things are indeed contrary, but they are not opposites in the manner of privation and disposition, or ignorance and knowledge.

Augustine, however, employs an analogy in this matter, by which someone might perhaps think that the case has been settled. I shall not say merely that an analogy illuminates a true and established matter, or fixes it more deeply in the memory, but cannot prove it if it is doubtful; rather, I shall examine the analogy itself. For he says:

“Just as, in the bodies of animals, to be afflicted by diseases and wounds is nothing other than to be deprived of health, so too whatever vices there are in souls are privations of natural goods; and when they are healed, those goods are not transferred elsewhere, but what was there will nowhere exist when it is no longer in that state of health.”

But diseases or wounds are not merely privations of health—unless someone should say that fever, for example, which has so many varieties and symptoms and which everyone knows consists for the most part in an extraordinary movement of the blood, is a mere privation; just as movement, however violent, would be a mere privation of rest. Who would tolerate reasoning in that way? Who would say that the severing of a muscle or nerve, the spilling of blood, the dislocation or fracture of a bone, are mere privations of what existed before? Let this philosophy be taught to goatsuckers and gravediggers, not to men refined by literary studies.

What he adds—that when vices are healed they are not transferred elsewhere but nowhere exist—proves as much that virtue is nothing as it demonstrates that vice is a mere privation. For the virtue that someone changes into the contrary vice is not transferred elsewhere, but nowhere exists. Who, if at all trained in metaphysics, does not know that accidents are not transferred when they change or perish, and yet are not thereby mere nothing? Everyone sees how evident this is, and nevertheless Augustine takes pleasure in so marvelous a subtlety. Between the two members of the analogy he inserts this parenthesis:

“For when treatment is applied, the purpose is not that these evils which were present—that is, diseases and wounds—should depart from here and exist elsewhere, but rather that they should not exist. For a wound or disease is not a substance, but a defect of bodily substance; and since flesh itself is a substance, it is certainly some good to which these evils attach themselves, that is, privations of the good called health.”

I could reason in the same way, against Augustine, to prove that health is merely the privation of disease. For when, for example, a poisoned drink is administered so that health may be undermined, the purpose is not that health should exist elsewhere, but that it should not exist at all. Who, moreover, would not be astonished at our philosopher, whom many consider so acute, speaking as though there were no distinction—philosophically speaking—between substance and non-being, and as though all accidents ought to be regarded as nothing? If this were true, health and virtue too would have to be regarded as names for mere nothing, since they are names of accidents. I do not know what the Manichaeans would have said in reply to this; but if they silently allowed themselves to be refuted in this way, they must have been exceedingly foolish.

I would not dwell on these matters at such length if I did not see both scholastics and other, more acute philosophers resting content with this notion received from the ancients, as though passing it from hand to hand. For that reason I do not linger over the philosophical subtleties that follow, although they have been placed in a rather unsuitable context: in the *Enchiridion*, after all, Laurentius wished to have not metaphysical speculations, but the Christian religion condensed into its principal points and briefly explained. But this is the nature of loquacious men: whatever presents itself to their minds, they pour forth at any time and in any place.

Cap. 21, § 7. “But in matters in which it makes no difference for attaining the kingdom of God whether they are believed or not, or whether they are true—or merely thought to be true—or false, in these matters to err, that is, to think one thing in place of another, ought not to be considered a sin; or, if it is one, it is the smallest and lightest.”]

If an error can be called a sin when it does not make us less fearful of God or less observant of his commandments, it is a sin, so to speak, in the philosophical sense—that is, an offense against the laws of logic, which, if we always observed them, would preserve us immune from error. But such sins, through which we do not form a less exalted judgment of God or consider ourselves less bound by the laws of the Gospel, are not those for which evangelical doctrine threatens punishment.

Thus Augustine is right in what follows, after mentioning certain harmless errors:

“In these and similar falsehoods we are deceived while the faith we have in God remains safe, and we go astray without abandoning the road that leads to him. Although these errors are not sins, they must nevertheless be counted among the evils of this life, which is so subject to vanity that here falsehoods are approved as truths, truths rejected as falsehoods, and uncertainties held as certainties.”

Some theologians ought to take these words to heart—men who, while wishing to appear to esteem Augustine highly, nevertheless contend that all errors are sins and that all sins, as the theologians of the schools put it, are mortal. Hence, as they suppose, it follows that no errors ought to be tolerated, since no deadly sins ought to be tolerated.

In the same place, after proving that every lie is a sin, Augustine says:

“It must not be denied that those who lie only for the sake of a person’s salvation have made very considerable progress toward the good; but in such progress of theirs, what rightly deserves praise, or even temporal reward, is benevolence, not deceit. For forgiveness is enough for deceit; it does not also deserve praise,” and so forth.]

Augustine appears to be speaking of eternal salvation, for the sake of which many people at that time lied in order to win certain persons, inventing innumerable miracles—so they said—with the sole aim of bringing unbelievers to the faith. Augustine does not praise them, but readily forgives them; and this, it seems, was a common evil among ecclesiastics of that age.

It is nevertheless worth observing, first, that those who lied for the sake of saving their neighbors very often derived no inconsiderable profit from that lie. For example, those who pretended that so many miracles were performed in their churches through the relics of Saint Stephen conducted themselves in such a way as to win unbelievers or doubters to the faith; but at the same time they received from them offerings that were by no means contemptible. For who, if able, would not have contributed something for the use of a church which blessed Stephen was deemed worthy to honor with so many and such great miracles? Thus, without excessive malice, one might say that they lied not less from hope of gain than from a desire to save their neighbors. Certainly those who lie in this way do not deserve to be considered better than we are.

Second, it is a very grave sin against God and the human race, when one possesses the most certain arguments by which unbelievers might, if possible, be led to believe, to resort to lies. For one plainly dishonors the truth that one upholds by a lie; and, moreover, one exposes it to grave danger, because if the lie should happen to be uncovered, the truth itself will be called into doubt. But Augustine was not so hostile to lying as he wished to appear.

Cap. 30. “Can this part of the human race, to which God has promised liberation and an eternal kingdom, be restored by the merits of its works? Far be it!”]

Who would not agree with Augustine? For there can be no merits belonging to the wicked, while they are wicked, that could be pleasing to God, so that he might consequently devise a plan for converting them to himself. He continues:

“For what good does the lost person accomplish, except insofar as he has been liberated from perdition? By the free choice of the will? Far be that too.”

All this is true, for no evil person does anything rightly insofar as he is evil. Nor can anyone who is not wholly evil be restored by the merits of his free will, for, strictly speaking, there are no merits where forgiveness is needed; and God owes salvation to no human being.

These doctrines are impressive and also entirely true, but it must be considered whether what follows accords with them. For Augustine says:

“By using free will badly, a human being both lost himself and free will itself.”

Adam, indeed, who was the first to make bad use of free will—or rather the only one, if we listen to Augustine—would have lost himself forever through that evil use unless divine mercy had forgiven him that offense. But he did not lose free will; for he did not, by that one action alone, become a sinner in such a way that he could do nothing good thereafter unless aided by the irresistible grace of God. This is established by no passage of Scripture and rests on no argument.

Nor did his descendants lose their freedom through the habit of sinning in such a way that, by acquiring a better habit, they could not gradually cast off the yoke of sin unless they were assisted by an inward impulse to which they could not resist. Otherwise God would impose laws upon them, confirmed by rewards and punishments, which he knew perfectly well they could not observe unless he continually inspired them—although he has by no means determined to do this toward everyone.

But this is not the place to refute his opinion. The one point that must carefully be committed to memory is that whenever Augustine acknowledges human freedom in the books written after the Pelagian controversies, this must be understood, according to his view, in a very improper sense, since here he teaches most explicitly that human beings have lost both themselves and free will.

Let us also hear the comparison that follows:

“For just as someone who kills himself certainly kills himself by living, but by killing himself does not live and cannot restore himself to life once he has killed himself, so, when sin was committed through free will, free will was lost when sin conquered. For by whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is made a slave” (II Peter 2:19).

To elude one comparison by means of another, I shall say that no one becomes a slave in war except unwillingly, and that, as soon as he can recover his freedom, he eagerly seizes the opportunity. Likewise, if someone teaches a person who recognizes that he has been conquered by sin and experiences the disadvantages of its servitude more effectively, that person will gladly bid farewell to sin.

But just as Adam could not lose all freedom through one sin, so no one can erase the habit of sinning through a single virtuous action. Sin did conquer, and human beings became its slaves, because they wished to obey it; but nothing prevents them from refusing to obey it except habit, which can gradually be overcome—as is clear from the fact that God calls all human beings to repentance.

One must not reason from a figurative expression such as “serving sin” as though, just as a captive loses bodily freedom and cannot recover it while bound, so one who is a slave of sin could never shake off its domination. No one urges a captive bound in chains and shut up in prison to break his chains and leave the prison, and becomes angry if he does not do so, because everyone knows that this is not within his power. But everyone is indignant with a wicked person when he has no reason to justify the exhortations of those who summon him back to a better way of life, because no one thinks that he is held by any necessity preventing him from bidding farewell to evil habits.

Augustine continues:

“This is certainly the statement of the apostle Peter. Since it is true, what freedom, I ask, can a slave possess, except when it pleases him to sin? For he serves freely who willingly does his master’s will; and consequently he is free to sin who is a slave of sin.”

But the more willingly people serve sin, the more completely they are bound and enslaved to it; nevertheless, they can gradually cast off that servitude. To serve one’s master willingly is one thing; to serve freely is another. The former can occur if a slave loves his master and is led willingly to obey by affection for him; the latter cannot, because someone is not free if he serves in such a way that he cannot shake off the yoke of servitude.

Accordingly, according to Augustine’s view, if we wish to speak precisely, it must be denied that a slave of sin is free in any sense. Yet Augustine often spoke improperly, because the ears of only a few could tolerate him speaking otherwise.

“Therefore,” he says, “he will not be free to do what is right unless, having been freed from sin, he begins to be a slave of righteousness. This is true freedom, because of the delight in right action—for I agree with the Benedictines in reading *libentiam*, ‘willingness’ or ‘delight,’ rather than *laetitiam* or *licentiam*, as other editions and books have it—and at the same time a pious servitude, because of obedience to the commandment.”

Here we see that the regenerate, who, according to Augustine’s view, are moved by an irresistible impulse, possess no properly so-called freedom either, if we believe him, but only a willingness to obey—which may rhetorically, but not truly, be called freedom.

The word *libentia* occurs in Aulus Gellius, book XV, chapter 2:

“Those to whom all the willingness and pleasure of banquets are unknown, and who are entirely unacquainted with them—if either inclination should lead them, chance bring them, or necessity compel them to share in pleasures of this kind—are usually enticed and captivated.”

Plato, moreover, says something similar in the Old *Onomasticon*: *lubentia*, εὐπάθεια (“pleasure” or “good feeling”). This meaning differs somewhat from Augustine’s, for he calls *libentia* the affection of the soul by which someone does something willingly, whereas Gellius and the *Onomasticon* use it for pleasure. Nevertheless, they show that *libentia* is not merely a word formed by analogy, but one that was also in customary use.

But whence will this freedom—or rather this willingness—to do good come to a person who is bound and sold, unless he redeems him whose word it is (John 8:36): “If the Son makes you free, then you will be truly free”? Before this begins to take place in a human being, how can anyone boast of free will in a good work, when he is not yet free to do good, unless he exalts himself, puffed up with empty pride?

The Apostle restrains this pride when he says: “By grace you have been saved through faith” (Ephesians 2:8). In truth, that willingness to do what is right does not arise in an evil person except through the liberation brought by the Son. Through the rewards and punishments set forth in the Gospel, with the light of heavenly truth shining forth, he rescues human beings from slavery to sin, but without any compulsion; just as he also keeps them in their duty without compulsion. Thus they adhere to good actions not merely willingly, but freely.

Nor can anyone boast of free will before using it rightly; and after using it rightly, he still cannot boast, as we have shown in volume II, letter 175, § 2.

Faith is certainly a gift of God, but it is not bestowed upon the unwilling. One may seize something from the unwilling, but one cannot give anything to the unwilling. God gives faith in that he is the author of the doctrine proposed for belief, in that he has sent to us human beings who would announce it, and in that he has done everything that God ought to do in order to persuade free creatures of the truth.

But enough, and more than enough, has been said about freedom. We shall not touch upon the rest of what Augustine says. It is nevertheless easy to understand that Laurentius, though a good man, cared far more about those disputed doctrines of his than about teaching the Christian religion.

Cap. 94, § 24. “For the Lord says most plainly: ‘Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes.’ And surely God did not unjustly refuse that they should be saved, when they could have been saved, IF THEY HAD WISHED.”]

The Benedictines testify that twenty-five ancient manuscripts read here *SI VELLET* (“if he had wished”), as Peter Lombard read it; the Louvain scholars and others judged that this should be the reading. The sentence itself, and what follows, strongly recommend that reading.

The meaning is: since they could have been saved if God had wished it, he justly refused to save them, although we do not know the reason for this if they are compared with others no better than they. Nevertheless, the printed editions and eleven manuscripts have *SI VELLENT* (“if they had wished”), evidently because copyists or critics paid more attention to the matter itself and to the opinion current in their own time than to Augustine’s meaning.

In later centuries, when almost the entire West had fallen into Pelagianism or Semi-Pelagianism—for why conceal the fact?—and had nevertheless not cast off that blind reverence with which earlier ages had honored Augustine, they wished to find their own view in him, lest they be forced to condemn one whom they had been taught to esteem highly.

In this particular passage, it could easily be persuaded to less acute minds that *vellent* (“they had wished”) ought to be read, because Augustine had mentioned justice; yet there is certainly no justice if the vast majority of human beings, through the fault of Adam, for whom God refused to provide the absolutely necessary remedy, were unable to wish to be saved. Augustine nevertheless wants justice to be present in this matter, though it is a justice that, he says, we shall understand only in the next life.

They fell into error all the more easily because Augustine, in order not to appear openly to affirm anything contrary to Scripture, sometimes says that people were not saved because they did not wish to be saved. Hear what he says in chapter 97:

“Therefore we must consider how it can be said of God (I Timothy 2:4) that he wishes all human beings to be saved. Since not all, but far more are not saved, it certainly appears that what God wishes to happen does not happen, human will hindering the will of God. For when the reason is asked why not all are saved, the customary answer is: because they themselves do not wish it.”

This was, in fact, the opinion of all Christians who used to speak in this way, and it rested on what both right reason and Scripture teach concerning the goodness and justice of God. There is no difficulty in the matter. When Paul says that God wishes all human beings to be saved, this must not be understood as though God wished to bestow eternal blessedness upon human beings, whether they wished it or not, without regard to their will.

God wishes all human beings to be saved because he has imposed upon all a common law of repentance, through the observance of which they can be saved, and which they really can observe if they wish; and because no one’s soul is so depraved that it cannot certainly be gradually corrected by the benefits that God scatters among all human beings.

If the law that God imposes upon human beings, on which salvation depends, could not be observed by them even if they wished; or if they were so disposed that the will to obey God could not arise in them unless God deigned to move them by an irresistible impulse—a favor he does not deign to grant to all—then indeed it would have to be denied that God wishes all human beings to be saved.

Augustine adds:

“This, however, cannot be said of infants, who do not yet possess the capacity to wish or refuse.”

But who taught him that infants are damned, when Christ expressly says that the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these?

“But more openly,” he says, “the Lord speaks in the Gospel, addressing the impious city: ‘How often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were unwilling?’—as though the will of God had been overcome by the will of human beings, and the most feeble, by their unwillingness, had prevented the Most Powerful from doing what he wished.”

But it is one thing to wish to reward the obedience of free natures, provided that they themselves do not refuse to obey; it is another thing to make creatures themselves happy. The latter God always does when he wishes; the former he does not, because he does not wish to bring about the result except with the consent of the creature, to which he refused to apply force.

Thus empty is the little exclamation that follows:

“And where is that omnipotence by which in heaven and on earth he has done whatever he wished, if he wished to gather the children of Jerusalem and did not do so?”

But who does not know that God, after establishing laws, does not use his omnipotence to ensure that they are observed, because he wishes them to be obeyed freely? Who is unaware that, if God wished to take no account of the freedom of creatures, he could extort anything from them?

Thus God does everything he wishes no less when he does not conquer by force the creatures to whom he has granted freedom, because he does not wish to do so.

“Or rather, Jerusalem itself did not wish its children to be gathered by him, but, even though it did not wish this, he gathered those of its children whom he wished? For in heaven and on earth he did not wish and do some things, and wish and do other things; rather, he did whatever he wished.”

But who does not see that Christ is lamenting that he had not bent the obstinacy of the inhabitants of Jerusalem by any exhortations or miracles? Otherwise, if he had merely determined to attract a few people by an irresistible impulse, and had accomplished this, there would have been nothing for him to lament.

God does everything that he himself wishes to do—who denies it? But he does not do what he wishes to be done freely by creatures, because he does not apply force to their freedom. Either this must be acknowledged, or, along with some others, it must be denied that God imposes any laws in the proper sense; rather, it must be said that laws are merely proposed to the elect, because God wishes to accomplish his will in them. As for the reprobate, God is said not to wish them to obey the laws, because he knows perfectly well that they will not and cannot obey, and wishes them to be condemned.

All these ideas conflict with the principles and institutions of Christ and the apostles.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOK *ON THE CHRISTIAN STRUGGLE*

[Col. 0425A]

Cap. 15, § 17. “Nor should we listen to those who become indignant and angry because we do not say that three gods are to be worshiped. For they do not know what one and the same substance is, and they are deceived by their own imaginings, because they are accustomed to see bodily either three animals or any three bodies separated in their respective places. Thus they think that the substance of God must be understood, and they are greatly mistaken,” and so forth.]

He seems to mean those who charged the Council of Nicaea with tritheism. Gregory Nazianzen also mentions them in Oration 37, p. 600, where he attempts to answer their objection. On this matter see Augustine himself, *On the Trinity*, book VII, chapter 4, and, if one wishes, the most learned Dionysius Petavius, *Dogmatic Theology*, volume II, book IV, chapter 2, in the Amsterdam edition; from his notes it will become clearer what Augustine thought.

Cap. 20, § 22. “The Word in the beginning, through whom all things were made, did not assume that human being as he assumed the other saints, but much more excellently and much more sublimely; for it was fitting that he alone should be assumed in whom Wisdom might appear to human beings, just as it was fitting that she should be displayed visibly.”]

Here Augustine speaks wisely and as becomes a theologian, concerning the ineffable conjunction of divine reason with the human being. But later, when Nestorian controversies arose and everything burned with hatred and contention, theologians, wishing boldly to explain what they did not understand and to mark everything with new names, became entangled in such labyrinths of difficulties that they could not extricate themselves and provoked laughter among those who held mistaken opinions.

Before those quarrels arose, whatever may commonly be said otherwise about this matter, people spoke better and more candidly about things that later became objects of controversy, because they were less impeded by passions and sought not victory but truth.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOK *ON INSTRUCTING BEGINNERS*

Cap. 5, § 9. “For if, while expecting some advantage from human beings, to whom he thinks he could not otherwise be pleasing, or while avoiding some disadvantage from human beings whose offense or hostility he fears, he wishes to become a Christian, he does not wish to become one but rather to pretend. For faith is not a matter of a body that salutes, but of a soul that believes.”]

The Parisian editors testify that the manuscripts of better quality read *salutantis corporis*, “of a body that salutes,” rather than *salvandi corporis*, “of a body that is to be saved.” They interpret it as referring to a body that signifies a greeting, or assent, by a gesture.

I would rather interpret *salutantis* here in the same sense in which the Latins used to say *salutare imperatorem*, “to salute the emperor,” that is, “to call” or “address.” The meaning is that faith is not a matter of a body saluting another in the name of a brother or Christian, but of a believing soul. In ancient glosses, *salutatio* is translated not only by ἀσπασμός (*aspasmós*, “greeting”), but also by προσηγορία (*prosēgoría*, “address” or “designation”).

Moreover, at that time pagans could easily be induced by hope or fear to become Christians. Honors at court were offered to Christians, and they obtained them more easily than those who clung stubbornly to paganism; ecclesiastical offices of no small importance were also available. On the other hand, pagans had much to fear, especially if, burning with devotion to their ancestral religion, they refused to abstain from sacrifices, which had been forbidden by the laws of Christian emperors.

Cap. 9, § 13. “Let them know”—the grammarians or orators who are being instructed in the faith and wish to become Christians—“that there is no voice for the ears of God except the disposition of the soul; thus they will not laugh if they happen to observe certain bishops and ministers of the Church either invoking God with barbarisms and solecisms, or failing to understand the very words they pronounce and distinguishing them confusedly.”]

They were certainly lazy and unworthy men to deliver public sermons to the people or offer prayers before them. Although they ought to have devoted themselves to a single language—Latin, and not even Ciceronian Latin, but the kind that the age allowed—they did not learn even that well enough to speak or read it without committing gross errors.

What a great and memorable difficulty it is to learn to speak the vernacular correctly when one is not devoted to any other studies! But what can one expect in those centuries when there were bishops who did not even know how to write, as is evident from the subscriptions to the councils?

In chapter 5 and the following chapters, Augustine extensively discusses the causes of the weariness experienced by catechists when they had to instruct the less educated. He proposes two forms of catechesis, one longer and the other shorter, on the model of which priests could shape their own instruction.

I shall not say that these are insufficiently precise descriptions of the Christian religion, and that they seem rather like impromptu little declamations than carefully composed accounts of Christianity. But it is astonishing that Augustine did not arrange for a learned priest to compose a little book for him, which he could provide to catechumens to read and about which he could later ask them questions—or which he himself could read aloud and explain, as is done today. This would have been much more convenient both for catechumens and for catechists than what he provides here.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS’S CRITIQUE OF THE BOOK *ON CONTINENCE*

A pious and not unlearned little book; its phrasing proves that it is not Augustine’s. It seems to me to be by Hugh of Saint Victor. (But see the Parisian editors in the admonition prefixed to this little book, where they refute Erasmus. PHEREP.)

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE SAME BOOK

Cap. 3, § 6. “But it is one thing to fight well, when one resists the contest with death; it is another to have no adversary, which will be the case when death, the last enemy, is destroyed.”]

The Benedictine monks correctly observed that Augustine was referring to I Corinthians 15:55, “Where is your contest, O death?” For Augustine cites this passage as though it were written, Ποῦ σου, ᾅδη, τὸ νεῖκος (“Where is your contest, O Hades?”), rather than νῖκος (“victory”), as it appears in our manuscripts. The similarity not only of the written forms but also of the pronunciations could have misled the interpreter. Nevertheless, Ambrose, in Letter 44 to Horontianus, gives the passage as follows: “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?”

Cap. 6, § 16. “It was not, however, beyond God’s power to make a human being who could not sin; but he preferred to make one for whom it would lie within his power to sin if he wished, and not to sin if he did not wish—prohibiting the one and commanding the other—so that first there would be the good merit of not sinning, and afterward the just reward of being unable to sin.”]

These words must be understood not only of Adam but also of human beings generally. Otherwise the objection of those who excused their sins on the grounds that the sins could not displease God—who would otherwise not have permitted them—would remain unanswered. The subject is not what Adam possessed, but what individual human beings possess in the condition in which they now exist.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOK *ON THE GOOD OF MARRIAGE*

Cap. 2, § 2. “Whether, therefore, without the embrace of intercourse or in some other way, they would have had children if they had not sinned,” and so forth.]

On this matter see what Augustine himself imagined in *The City of God*, book XIV, chapters 23 and 24.

Cap. 13, § 15. “In those times, however—that is, the times of the patriarchs—when the mystery of our salvation was still veiled under prophetic sacraments, even those who were continent before marriage entered into marriage for the duty of procreation, not overcome by lust but led by piety. If a choice such as was given after the New Testament had been revealed had been offered to them, when the Lord said, ‘Let the one who can receive it receive it,’ he does not doubt that they would have accepted it even with joy. This is clear to anyone who carefully considers how they made use of marriage, when one man was permitted to have several wives, whom he kept more chastely than any one of those men now keeps the single wife whom the Apostle permits them by way of concession.”]

Augustine took great pleasure in this argument, since he repeats and advances it confidently; for it served to restrain the Manichaeans, ignorant and foolish men who were accustomed to disparage the ancient patriarchs on account of polygamy. He says still more on this subject in what follows.

But those who read the Old Testament somewhat more carefully will easily observe that the age of the ancient patriarchs was like the infancy of true religion. In that period God tolerated many things that he would no longer tolerate under a mature religion, and he tested faith and the other virtues according to the measure of revelation and the understanding of that age.

The patriarchs, then, were like other men. They sought not only offspring but also the other things ordinarily sought in marriage; they did not think about the matters Augustine tells us about, of which there is neither trace nor vestige in the Old Testament. It is regrettable that he so often brought forward not what he had discovered to be true through careful examination, but what was convenient to say and could be handled more rhetorically among the ignorant populace.

Nevertheless, what he says in chapter 23, § 29, cannot fail to deserve praise:

“The good of obedience is greater than that of continence. For marriage is nowhere condemned by the authority of our Scriptures, whereas disobedience is nowhere acquitted.”

He rightly concludes from this that if a married woman obeys the precepts of the Gospel more faithfully than a virgin, she is the better person. But he considers that, all other things being equal, a virgin is superior to a married woman. This does not seem to be so. The use of marriage does not make people less pleasing to God, provided that in other respects they observe the commandments of the Gospel, any more than the use of well-prepared foods, or foods agreeable by nature, which our nature cannot do without, makes them less pleasing to God.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOK *ON HOLY VIRGINITY*

Cap. 4. Concerning the Virgin Mary:

“Her virginity too was therefore more pleasing and acceptable, because Christ, by his conception, did not snatch her virginity away in advance from a man who would violate it—the virginity he himself would preserve—but, before she conceived, he chose her, already dedicated to God, as the one from whom he would be born. This is indicated by the words Mary gave in reply to the angel announcing the child to her: ‘How will this happen,’ she says, ‘since I do not know a man?’ She certainly would not have said this unless she had previously vowed herself a virgin to God.”]

Yet from Mary’s words it is rather clear that the angel’s announcement, in verse 31, included the information that she would conceive immediately, before having intercourse with the man to whom she was betrothed. See Luke 1:27.

Thus what follows is empty:

“But because the customs of the Israelites still rejected this, she was betrothed to a righteous man, who would not violently take away what she had already vowed, but rather protect it against those who might use violence.”

### Chapter 12, § 12

“Let marriages possess their own good—not because they beget children, but because they beget them honorably, lawfully, chastely, and sociably; because they bring up the children they have begotten together, wholesomely, and diligently; because they preserve fidelity to one another in the marriage bed; because they do not violate the sacrament of marriage.”

No one will deny that all these things are of the greatest importance, since they contain the very foundations of human society, and none of them can rightly be accomplished without the highest virtue. For many dangers threaten married people, and many temptations press upon them, from which it is not always easy to extricate themselves, as Christians ought. They must often endure difficult dispositions; resist the perverse desires of their spouses; conceal and gently correct the faults either of spouses or of children. This requires no small degree of moderation, constancy, and prudence.

Most heads of households must labor to obtain the expenses with which they support wife and children. They must care for them, lest, left in excessive poverty, they succumb to temptations. To do this without injuring anyone, and to fulfill every honorable labor with an even temper, is certainly the mark of a good and prudent man. Amid all these things, to remain mindful of divine worship, to refer everything to God, and to be an example of religion to one’s own family, is the mark of a truly holy and religious man.

But those who lead a celibate life care for no one except themselves, nor do they need such great virtue to sustain themselves alone and tread the path of virtue, which is surrounded by far fewer dangers. “Yet,” you will say, “celibates disdain the pleasure of marriage, and in this great courage is needed.”

True enough—but if their bodily constitution is such that they cannot help desiring marriage, those who abstain from it do wrong; for it is better to marry than to burn.
