If, however, they are naturally colder and are not troubled by any such desire, there is certainly little virtue in abstaining from what one scarcely desires at all.

I know that Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 7:32 and following are brought forward here, where he teaches that married people are anxious about how they may please one another and about the affairs of this world, whereas celibates think about the things that belong to the Lord. But this does not prevent it from being easier—and therefore requiring less virtue—for a celibate person to think about the things of the Lord than for a married person, who is distracted by many necessary cares. To direct one’s mind to such cares while always thinking about the commandments of the Gospel, and without acquiring any habit of violating them, is no ordinary holiness.

Paul describes what ordinarily happens among married people, not what ought to happen; and conversely, what ought to happen among celibates, and what can easily happen, not what actually happens. Celibacy, moreover, is not in itself a condition more pleasing to God than marriage. Rather, in either state, the person most pleasing to God is the one who is more observant of his commandments.

There are, however, times when it is better to avoid marriage than to become entangled in it—for example, during periods of severe persecution, such as the apostolic age. Paul also has this in view in verse 26 of the same chapter, where he declares that he is speaking because of the present necessity. Anyone who has carefully considered these matters will not be greatly moved by the rhetorical arguments that follow later in this book.

## Desiderius Erasmus’s Censure of the Book *On the Good of Widowhood*

The remarkable ease and candor of the diction loudly proclaim that this is not Augustine’s work. It is probable that it belongs to Julian, whose letter to Demetrias on virginity is extant. The thread of the discourse agrees with it, and the author cites that little work twice. There are, however, certain passages on free will that seem to have been corrected by another hand. Add that the title is utterly foreign to Augustine’s customary usage. Someone attached it in order to claim an otherwise pious little work for a prestigious name. But on this censure, see the editors’ admonition prefixed to this book at Paris. (PHEREP.)

## Remarks on the Same Book

### Chapter 9, § 12

“In the marital bond, provided chastity is preserved, condemnation is not to be feared; but in widowhood and virgin continence, the excellence of a greater gift is sought. Once it has been sought, chosen, and offered as a debt owed by one’s vow, then not only is it damnable to contract a marriage, but even to wish to marry, though one does not do so, is damnable.”

First of all, it should have been shown that somewhere in the New Testament God signified that such vows are acceptable to him. This is certainly not established to my knowledge; indeed, I am quite certain that nothing of the kind is found anywhere.

Next, even grant that such vows are acceptable to God. Those vows alone will be acceptable that are made by women who are fully aware of their own self-control and promise what they are capable of fulfilling, not what they are unable to fulfill. Suppose, then, that some young widow, overcome by longing for her husband who has recently died and, through grief, not sufficiently in possession of herself, vows perpetual widowhood, but, once her mourning has subsided, understands that she can no longer maintain it. Will such a rash vow be pleasing to God? I do not think so.

It remains, therefore, that she should ask God’s forgiveness for her rash vow and enter a chaste marriage, rather than be forced to keep a rash vow, remain in perpetual danger, and burn inwardly until she finds a husband.

Augustine uses the authority of the Apostle for this point:

“For, to demonstrate this, the Apostle does not say, ‘When they have lived in pleasure, they marry in Christ,’ but, ‘They wish to marry’; and he says, ‘They have condemnation, because they have annulled their first faith.’ And even if they are condemned not for marrying but merely for wishing to marry, because marriages of this kind are themselves judged condemnable, nevertheless the fraud of their purpose is condemned, the faithfulness of their broken vow is condemned, and so forth.”

But above all it must be observed that Paul is not speaking of widows indiscriminately, but specifically of those whom the Greeks called deaconesses. They were employed in various ecclesiastical services and supported by the offerings of the Church. It was desirable for such women not to marry afterward for many reasons, especially because it was not convenient for the Church continually to make use of the service of different women. There was also reason to fear that, if they married pagans—as many such marriages were undoubtedly contracted at that time—this would harm Christians.

This seems to be precisely what the Apostle signifies by these words in 1 Timothy 5:11: ὅταν γὰρ καταστρηνιάσωσι τοῦ Χριστοῦ, γαμεῖν θέλουσι—that is, “for when they have behaved wantonly against Christ, they wish to marry.”

The meaning is that, if they have committed something unbecoming to Christian widows and are therefore disciplined, they wish to marry and bid farewell to the Church. What the Apostle adds belongs to the same matter: “having condemnation, because they have annulled their first faith.” These words are commonly understood as referring to the faith pledged to the Church, to which they had promised that thereafter they would undertake the duties entrusted to them. But I do not know whether they should not instead be understood of the Christian faith itself, which they would annul by marrying pagans whose religion they followed. Certainly, no sound argument can demonstrate that this is not what is meant.

I know that Augustine punctuates this passage differently, as follows: “For when they have lived in pleasure, they wish to marry in Christ.” But no one somewhat better educated now doubts whether it should be punctuated as we have done above; for the structure of the Greek phrase necessarily requires this.

## Remarks on the Books *On Adulterous Marriages*

### Book I, Chapter 1, § 1

“The first question is [lacuna] what the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 7:10–11): ‘To those who are married I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband; but if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband; and let the husband not dismiss his wife.’ Is this to be understood as meaning that he forbade remarriage to a woman who had departed from her husband without the cause of fornication—for this is what you think—or, as I have thought, [lacuna] that he commanded those women to remain unmarried who had separated from their husbands for the one cause that is permitted, namely, fornication?”

Although Paul is referring to Christ’s words, by which he forbids married people to separate except in the case of adultery, and uses them to prevent the dissolutions of marriage that were taking place among the Greeks, who lived under their own laws and separated for every conceivable reason, it does not follow that what Augustine wants is true—namely, that those who have been separated from their spouses by public judgment on account of adultery are not permitted to contract new marriages.

For although Christ’s laws did not permit a person to dismiss a spouse for any reason other than adultery, it does not follow that Greeks recently brought to the Christian religion did not sometimes continue to misuse their former customs. Paul indicates this clearly when he says, “but if she departs, let her remain unmarried,” for from this it is evident that such a separation was not approved by the Apostle.

But the more recent interpreters of Paul and of the other New Testament passages that Augustine cites on this subject should be consulted; it would be too long to examine all his παρερμηνείαι—that is, his misinterpretations.

### Book II, Chapter 6, § 5

“Some people of little faith—or rather, I believe, enemies of the true faith—fearing that impunity in sin would be granted to their wives, removed from their copies what the Lord did concerning the pardon of the adulteress, as though he had granted permission to sin when he said, ‘From now on, do not sin,’ or as though that sin ought not to have been healed by the physician God through the remission of the sin, lest the insane should be offended.”

Augustine seems to indicate that only the particular passage he mentions had been erased from the copies. It is strange that Augustine did not know that the entire story was absent from most Greek copies. Indeed, Theodor Beza and Hugo Grotius have shown that there are serious reasons for doubting the whole story. See also what John Clericus noted in the additions to Hammond II.

## Remarks on the Book *On Lying*

### Chapter 5, § 7

“Concerning the examples of those who are said to have lied in the Old Testament: We must believe,” he says, “that those people who are mentioned as having possessed authority in prophetic times performed and said everything that is written about them prophetically; and that whatever happened to them happened no less prophetically, so that they judged it should be committed to memory and writing by the same prophetic Spirit.”

I do not know whom Augustine wants us to believe this about, for certainly the sacred writers nowhere demanded such belief. The history of the best people who lived in prophetic times is history, not prophecy. It does not conceal the faults and offenses of the patriarchs and of the prophets themselves, such as David—not because those faults or offenses contain anything prophetic, but because the truth of the history and the benefit of the readers require this.

From this we understand how diligently we must guard against sin, since even men otherwise worthy of praise fell into it; and, if through ignorance or weakness we should happen to fall into it, that we must not despair of divine mercy.

Moreover, if we compare the laws of the Old Testament with those of the New, we will easily understand that ancient times were, as it were, the infancy of religion, when many things were tolerated that would now be tolerated not at all. We will then have reason to give thanks to God for having bestowed upon us greater light and for having recalled us from sin by greater—or at least clearer—promises.

These and other matters that are self-evident and necessarily arise from the facts themselves ought to be stated, rather than our inventing anything whatsoever in order to interpret the simplest histories allegorically.

Augustine adds:

“Concerning the midwives (of whom Exodus 1:19 speaks), since they cannot say that, in order to signify future truth by the prophetic Spirit, they reported one thing to Pharaoh in place of another—even if what was done through them signified something of which they themselves were unaware—they say that, according to their degree, they were approved and rewarded by God. For whoever is accustomed to lie in order to cause harm, if he now lies in order to help someone, has made considerable progress.”

But when Augustine, speaking in the name of those whose opinion he reports, says that something was signified by the midwives’ action, what is this except a dream? If weight is assigned to such claims, which lack every appearance of probability, what will ever be considered trivial?

There are many things that are both said and repeated merely because they were once uttered by a celebrated writer, from whom they derive their authority. Yet when someone who will not allow himself to be persuaded by the mere authority of deceitful people denies them without arguments, they vanish into thin air.

Moreover, who does not see that the midwives’ lie—which was uttered without an intention of deceiving that would cause harm, and which in fact could harm no one, especially since there was no other way of preserving the infants’ lives—was an outstanding act of humanity? Certainly no one would fail to act in that way, and everyone would think that he ought to do so, if such an occasion arose.

Only three conditions need to be posited, as we have said. First, there must be no intention of causing harm through the lie. Second, the lie must be of such a kind that it truly cannot cause harm. Third, there must be no other way by which the impending evil can be avoided.

Under these circumstances it ought certainly to be lawful to lie, if it is not unlawful to lie in jest, which Augustine permits. See chapter 11.

Nor should you suppose that those who repeatedly claimed to abhor useful and necessary lying were such rigid defenders of truth that they never lied for the sake of advantage. The contrary is suggested by the many fabricated miracles devised to win popular veneration for certain churches and basilicas, and by the many rhetorical fictions in disputes with heretics, which occupy whole pages in numerous writers.

But, if we may say what we suspect, many attacked lawful lies of the sort we have described so fiercely for no other reason than that they might afterward lie more profitably for their own interests. Simple people did not suspect that they were being deceived by those who professed such hostility to lying.

For so many centuries we have seen the same story acted out, with only the persons changed; and people of every age are so much alike in so many matters that by now we ought either to be more prudent or deserve to be made a laughingstock and deceived even by Cappadocians.

## Remarks on the Book *Against Lying, to Consentium*

### Chapter 7, § 17

“If therefore lies are just—not merely ordinary lies, but blasphemous ones—because they are made with the intention of exposing hidden heretics, then adulteries may in the same way be chaste, if they are committed with the same intention.”

Augustine rightly attacks those who wickedly pretended to be Priscillianists in order to expose people whom they suspected of concealing Priscillianist heresy in their hearts. This was done with the intention of harming the unfortunate Priscillianists, so that proceedings might be brought against them under the laws enacted against heretics.

Under the law of Arcadius enacted in 395, people were to be regarded as heretics if they were discovered, even on slight evidence, to have deviated from the judgment and path of the Catholic religion. This is the twenty-eighth law of title 5, book 16, of the Theodosian Code.

Moreover, it was impious for those who thought Priscillian’s opinions wicked to pretend to be Priscillianists—if indeed those opinions were what ecclesiastical writers report them to have been. It was harmful to truth and contrary to the divine commandments not to profess the truth in a serious matter. Therefore such lies could not even be considered harmless on that account.

### Chapter 18, § 37

After asking whether one should tell a sick father that his son is dead, lest the father die of grief, Augustine adds:

“Here another consideration must be added, where we must lament more grievously: if we grant that, for the sick man’s recovery, it was permissible to lie about his son’s life, this evil gradually and little by little increases and, by short advances, slowly insinuating itself into so great a heap of criminal lies, reaches such a point that it can never be discovered where resistance might be made to so great a plague, growing immeasurably through the smallest additions.”

But this progression of lies is easily halted by what we noted concerning the preceding book: namely, if we never lie unless the lie benefits someone in such a way that it can never harm anyone in any respect, and unless necessity drives us to it.

Indeed, pious people who have occasionally made use of a useful and necessary lie would nevertheless have been unwilling to perjure themselves, blaspheme, or do anything else forbidden by divine law. I think many people even today are disposed in the same way.

Once this is granted, the tragic exaggerations of the Numidian orator collapse: if it is conceded that it is sometimes permissible to use a lie, it does not follow that one will proceed to perjury, blasphemy, or even sexual immorality whenever these things benefit those for whose sake they are committed.

We maintain that such acts are always evil and can never be beneficial, whatever case may be imagined. Nor is a lie concerning matters that are morally indifferent of the same nature as one that bears upon virtue or truth considered generally.

“But Scripture,” you will say, “condemns sexual violation, and likewise lying.”

Certainly—but it condemns harmful lying, the kind performed with the intention of causing harm; for this is always contrary to the laws of human society, just as sexual immorality is.

For example, consider the psalmist’s words in Psalm 5:6–7: “You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak lies; the Lord abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man.” Who could doubt that this refers to fraudulent lying devised to the injury and destruction of others?

But this is more than enough.

## Remarks on the Book *On the Work of Monks*

It is well known that throughout the East and Africa, when vast numbers of monks first began to exist, they initially worked with their own hands in their solitudes, so that they might provide themselves with at least a meager subsistence.

But when they began to invade the cities, they preferred to abandon that work of the saddle-maker and live on the offerings of religious people. From these offerings, as we see, they eventually amassed enormous wealth, especially the older orders.

It was against such men that Augustine wrote this little work, at the request of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. The Benedictine monks have summarized its subject very well. “First,” they say, “he demonstrates that the Apostle gave God’s servants both a command and an example to perform bodily work, by which they might provide themselves with food and clothing. He then shows that those evangelical commandments by which those monks supported not only their idleness but also their arrogance are not contrary to the apostolic command.”

Certainly, those who, remembering Augustine’s instructions, devoted themselves to much more honorable labor of mind and body deserve praise. I mean the editions of the Fathers that they prepared with such great diligence.

For although by that labor they did not obtain their livelihood, since they draw sufficiently ample revenues from estates and large landed properties to support themselves, nevertheless they seemed worthy of enjoying those revenues, whoever they were who benefited the republic of letters in this way—especially those who, mindful of monastic modesty, did not bite any upright person while wishing to appear deserving of everyone’s good opinion.

But what should be done with all those deceivers and beggars of whom Erasmus speaks in his dedication to Cardinal Fonseca? Let them read and reread this work of Augustine, so that, if they cannot provide themselves with necessities by learned labor, or are not worthy of having others provide for them, they may use the work of their hands for this purpose.

## Remarks on the Book *On the Care for the Dead*

### Chapter 1, § 2

After citing 2 Corinthians 5:10, where the Apostle says, “For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil,” from which it is entirely clear that each person’s condition after death depends upon the character of his previous life—and from which it would follow that prayers for the dead are useless—Augustine replies:

“This question is resolved in this way: by a certain kind of life, while one lives in this body, one acquires the possibility that these things may help the dead; and thus, according to what they did through the body, they are helped by the pious acts performed for them after the body.”

But a passage of Scripture or a certain revelation ought to have been produced for this claim. For how did Augustine know that God wanted the prayers of the Church to benefit certain people after death, when there is profound silence on the subject and the dead person’s fate after death is everywhere referred to his previous conduct?

It is not enough that this could happen. How many things does God not will, although he could have willed them?

“For there are some,” he says, “whom these things do not help at all”—that is, the prayers of the Church for the dead—“whether they are offered for those whose merits are so evil that they are not worthy of being helped even by such means, or for those whose merits are so good that they do not need such assistance.”

Nothing is truer. Those whom the laws of the Gospel openly condemn cannot be saved by the prayers of the survivors; and those whom the Gospel openly wishes to save will be saved no less if the survivors remain silent than if they pray.

But in Augustine’s judgment there are certain people of an intermediate kind whom the prayers of the Church benefit. He had to prove this. For to ask God to forgive those concerning whom he has made no promise is to waste words, and perhaps even to offend him who wishes to be worshiped not according to human opinion but according to his own command.

Later, however, the bishop of Hippo cites the passage from 2 Maccabees 12:43: “In the books of the Maccabees,” he says, “we read that a sacrifice was offered for the dead.”

But where did the Law command such sacrifices, or where did God promise that he would be favorable to rites devised by human beings? Nowhere.

“But,” he says, “even if it were nowhere at all in the Old Scriptures”—add, “or in the New”—“the authority of the universal Church, which shines forth in this practice, is not insignificant; in the prayers of the priest poured out to the Lord God at his altar, a place is also given to the commending of the dead.”

But who had taught Augustine that, from the time of the Apostles onward, corrupt opinions and practices could never gradually creep in? No promise of God is found concerning this matter. The situation of people who join together into an ecclesiastical commonwealth is the same as that of those who join together into a civil one; bad customs can gradually creep into the former no less than into the latter.

This happened all the more easily because great and certain profit for ecclesiastics was connected with certain practices. Such is the prayer for the dead, which is now purchased throughout the whole of the West for a great sum of money.

On the origin of prayers for the dead, see John Fell on the First Letter of Cyprian.

## Desiderius Erasmus’s Censure of the Book *On Patience*

The diction shows that this is not Augustine’s work, since it agrees with that of the preceding little books. But concerning this censure, see the admonition prefixed to this book by the editors at Paris. (PHEREP.)

## Remarks on the Same Book

### Chapter 15, § 12

“But true patience, which is worthy of the name of this virtue, must be sought by asking whence it is obtained. For there are people who attribute it to the powers of the human will—not the powers it possesses from divine assistance, but those it possesses from free will.”

Ever since Augustine began to fight with the Donatists and Pelagians, he attacks and pursues them εὐκαίρως, ἀκαίρως—that is, at every suitable and unsuitable opportunity—even where one would expect nothing of the kind, just as Cicero pursued the remnants of the Catilinarian faction.

And it was certainly easy to do so, for the same things were always repeated, and the same odium was heaped upon the unfortunate men.

Here he distinguishes God’s assistance from free will as though free will were not itself also a gift of God, who does not permit a human being to fall into altogether incurable vices, since, by means of the faculties received from God, a person can always overcome them, if not suddenly, then gradually.

Thus he defames the Pelagians as though they denied that divine assistance should be implored, although they professed to implore it and, according to their own doctrine, ought altogether to have done so.

But we have already touched upon these matters elsewhere, and perhaps we shall pursue them more fully in a more suitable place. For now, it is enough to have indicated Augustine’s habitual practice, so that no one may doubt whether this little book is his.

## Desiderius Erasmus’s Censure of the Sermons *To the Brothers in the Desert*

A discourse pieced together from Augustine’s Rule, but otherwise containing nothing of Augustine. The craftsman who fabricated it did so in order to commend to the world the order called Augustinian. Accordingly, we have marked all works of this kind with a θ prefixed.

[Note: Since the Benedictines slaughtered all these sermons—most of which Erasmus had marked with a prefixed θ, except two—with a critical obelus, there is no need to identify those which the great man had condemned. PHEREP.]

## Into the Whole of the Seventh [Book]

### Joannes Ludovicus Vives to the Illustrious Prince Henry VIII, King of England, Lord of Ireland, etc.

Human nature is so constituted, most illustrious king, that we truly and wholeheartedly admire only those whom we see excelling in the art that pleases and satisfies us most of all. Different people devote themselves to different studies and exercises. Such is the nature of things that the world is beautiful and marvelous through this very variety; and yet, as that man says, “To each his own is beautiful.”

In former times, when you possessed wealth and an empire extending so widely—not acquired by arms and bloodshed, but handed down from your ancestors—and when you possessed strength of mind and body and military virtue, you were both dear to everyone and worthy of admiration.

But now, after you have also given proof of how much you are capable of through the powers of your intellect and your devotion to wisdom, you have become greater and more admirable to all educated people—not that they had previously esteemed you lightly, especially since you joined to a kingdom, whose power and majesty on earth are second only to God and greatest of all, the gentleness and integrity of your character, by which you became a truer and more distinct image of the nature of a prince: one who, as he is greatest, is also best—and is better before he is greatest.

Those devoted to study do not esteem wealth or power in the same way. They embraced in you the fact that you were good and pursued you with immense affection; but they did not consider it so remarkable that you were a king, since wicked men have often been kings, and have also been distinguished by bodily gifts.

When your defense of the sacraments appeared—something that could be neither more elegant, nor purer, nor holier, nor, to use one word, more Christian—the good opinion of your character was strengthened, if that was possible. For it had already been fixed in everyone’s mind, as though fastened by nails, through many examples, and admiration had already arisen everywhere.

This was true both among those who think that nothing is greater or more august than royal power, and among those who place wealth above all things; among those who attach the greatest value to the gifts of the body—beauty, muscular strength, and agility—and among those who are devoted to the arts of war as though these made them all-powerful and masters of the world.

Hence all princes vie with one another in seeking your friendship by whatever means and paths they can, all desiring to be joined to you either by treaty or, what is more desirable, by blood.

Nor are you lacking the devotion of private persons, which you yourself inspire by the splendor of your virtues: attracting some by generosity, or rather magnificence; others by humanity and sweetness of character; and everyone by prudence and justice, which are indeed two royal virtues.

Since you are such a man, I confess the audacity with which I have often desired to make myself known to you. For this is my opinion: it is no ordinary praise for me even to be known to you.

Since an opportunity had always been lacking, one now presented itself spontaneously. I had prepared commentaries on Augustine’s books *On the City of God*, and while considering to whom I might dedicate them—so that I might both obtain from you some not wholly contemptible gratitude for my labor and ensure that the person to whom they were dedicated would not regard the offering of letters, books, and burdensome bundles of boxes as equivalent to straw; and so that I might send them, as it were, to the most severe of judges, whose single approval would make them seem approved and commended by the votes of all—you came before me for many reasons.

First, you possess such virtue and learning that I would have dedicated them to you even if you had been a private citizen. Second, I saw in this the most convenient path by which I might easily fulfill a desire conceived and vowed long ago.

In addition, as those who have experienced it report, you are accessible and open to gifts of this kind, and scarcely any gifts can be more agreeable to you. Anyone who offers you gold, silver, gems, garments, horses, or arms is plainly, as the saying goes, carrying water to the sea or wood to the forest.

And, as in all other matters, so also in this you act most prudently, since you consider that a glory worthy of your virtue and merits should be prepared for you among posterity by the books of learned men. If not by my books or those of people like me, then certainly by making yourself accessible and most courteous to the learned, you will encounter someone whose pen, like a highly accomplished brush, will portray and shape the image of that most excellent and noble character and commend it to immortality.

It will not be covered by the dust of oblivion or corrupted by the injury of age, and a posterity incorruptible as a witness to your virtues will not remain silent about what deserves to be remembered. This will be partly for the glory of you, who will long ago have been restored to heaven—though that is a slight and negligible consideration—and above all as an example for those who will then be living.

Besides all these considerations, this work suits both your intellect and your studies. In it Augustine deposited, as though in treasuries, the best part of what he had read in ancient authors, intending to debate with all the keenest minds, those endowed with the greatest eloquence and learning.

Thus, while engaged in another task, he preserved more of the remains of the best things, after the dwellings and almost the very seats in which they had previously been sought had been overthrown.

Accordingly, in works on the commonwealth, great men of the later age—Hermolaus, Politianus, Blondus, and Beroaldus—were aided by these writings of Augustine in place of Varro, Sallust, Livy, and Cicero. You will not read all this as something new and unheard of, but as something ancient that you are recognizing again.

Add that Augustine’s and your own purposes in writing seem to have been almost the same. For just as you wrote against Babylon in favor of that better Rome, so Augustine defended Christian and holier Rome against that ancient Babylonian Rome.

The work also accords with your greatness—not my work, but Augustine’s, beneath whose name I myself lie concealed, whether one considers the author or the subject matter.

The author is Augustine—good heavens, how holy and learned a man, what an example and pillar of the Christian commonwealth! On him alone it rests through many rites, statutes, customs, and pious and venerable ceremonies—and not unjustly.

For that man possessed an extraordinarily abundant application to study, an exact knowledge of the sacred Scriptures, a sharp and polished judgment, and an intellect astonishingly acute. He was himself the most diligent defender of sincere piety, gentle in character and shaped and molded according to evangelical charity, distinguished by the integrity and holiness of his life, and worthy of reverence.

It would be impossible to pursue all these qualities even in a proper volume, much less in a letter. It is fortunate that we are dealing with a writer known to everyone and familiar to you as well.

There is no need now to speak of the children of Niobe, as the saying goes, or of the gates of Thebes; nor of mending clothes, preparing pleasures, or cultivating fields—subjects that might otherwise be more suitable for dedication to kings—but of the two cities, the city of the world and the city of God, in which all angels, demons, and human beings are contained: how they were born, how they were raised, how they grew, toward what they tend, and what they will do once they have run to the finish.

In explaining these matters, Augustine omitted neither profane nor sacred learning that he did not touch upon and expound. He discusses the deeds, gods, rites, and ceremonies of the Romans; the doctrines of the philosophers; the origins of heaven and earth, and of angels, demons, and human beings.

He then explains by what beginnings the people of God grew and how it was led down to Christ the Lord. The two cities—the city of God and the city of the world—are compared, and the Assyrian, Sicyonian, Argive, Athenian, Latin, and Persian kingdoms are introduced.

After this comes what prophets, pagans, and Jews foretold concerning Christ. Then, when he is about to speak of true happiness, he refutes and rejects the opinions of the ancient philosophers concerning it.

Next, Christ is proclaimed as destined to come as judge of the living and the dead, to pass judgment on good and evil. He also discusses the punishments of the wicked, and finally the joys of the righteous and eternal happiness.

All these subjects he treats with marvelous intelligence, the greatest acuteness, highly cultivated learning, and a polished and refined style, as befitted an author practiced and experienced in every branch of learning and writing, and as befitted both those great and outstanding matters and the people with whom he was debating.

Read it, therefore, most illustrious and excellent king, during those hours that you steal from the immense business and occupations of your kingdom in order to devote them to letters and the cultivation of your intellect. At the same time, you will sample our commentaries, concerning which I may say what Ovid said of his books of the *Fasti* when he sent them to Germanicus Caesar:

> The page now moves to face the judgment of the learned prince,  
> like one sent to the god of Claros to be read.

If I learn that they have not displeased you, I will have no fear that they will be insufficiently approved by others. Who would be so shameless as not to blush to disagree with such exact judgment? And if anyone should dare to do so, your authority, even if silent, will nevertheless defend me.

Farewell, excellent king, and count Vives, wholly devoted to you, in whatever place you please, provided only that you count me among your own.

Written at Louvain, on the Nones of July, 1522.

## Joannes Ludovicus Vives of Valencia, in His Commentaries on the Books *On the City of God*

### [Col. 0439A]

When we have said as much as seemed appropriate about Augustine and his work, I should now like to discuss these Commentaries of mine somewhat more familiarly with the reader himself.

Erasmus of Rotterdam is a man so highly praised by so many that my commendation of him could add nothing, or scarcely anything, to the sum of his glory. When, after revising Jerome and Cyprian, he had resolved to purge Augustine also in the same manner, and could not devote himself to so great a number of books, being occupied with other great and distinguished matters, he brought others into association with him, whether as fellow workers or assistants. Among these he enrolled me as well. To the others, whose learning was broader, whose talent more fortunate, and whose diligence more capable, he entrusted the more serious and greater tasks; to me he assigned the twenty-two books of *The City of God*. [Col. 0439B]

That work was largely taken up both with narratives of historical events and myths, and with philosophical discussions—matters to which we seemed to have devoted a good part of our life, with great effort and desire, though, would that the result had been equal. Although it contained much theology, it perhaps did not contain it as abundantly as his other books, even though we were never alien to that most sacred discipline, insofar as our age and our study of the other arts, which wonderfully captivated us, permitted.

Nor was I chosen for this task as though I were expected to execute it exceptionally well, but so that there should not be absolutely no one to undertake it, since Erasmus’s other friends were occupied with other matters. And, to tell the truth, I seized the work offered by Erasmus with the greatest eagerness, promising that I would put the final hand to the Commentaries within two or three months. For I remembered having once read several volumes of the work, which did not seem to me especially corrupt and were sufficiently easy; they seemed the sort of books into which I could pour no small part of my knowledge of antiquity, acquired through continual reading. Thus, with the same labor, I might at once exercise my style and intellect, bring some fruit of my studies to others, and win some measure of credit for my talent and learning. [Col. 0439C]

That was indeed a youthful thought, and the work proceeded very differently in practice from the way I had reasoned with myself. For, besides being exceedingly long, it contains an extraordinary variety of subjects: history, mythology, natural science, rhetoric, mathematics, geography, ethics, and theology; and scarcely any of these is treated superficially or moderately.

Moreover, the books were more corrupt than can be expressed in words; through faulty writing they turned Augustine’s entire meaning in another direction. Here there was no small labor in correcting the text from ancient books, and also in conjecturing: for very often it was necessary to conjecture and to restore the true reading by conjecture.

Nevertheless, I began writing around the Kalends of January of the preceding year—that is, 1521—and, having completed the first book by the end of the month, news was brought of the death of Cardinal Guilielmus Croij, my patron, who had died at Worms. [Col. 0439D]

Everyone can easily understand how that event shook the peace of my studies, since the man who alone made as much leisure available to me as I desired had been taken away. Then, since no calamity ever comes alone, I fell into a serious illness. I was therefore compelled, in order to care for my health, to go to Bruges to my Spanish friends, among whom I could be treated more comfortably, in accordance with my condition and habits. [Col. 0440A]

I recovered in June. And since it was being said that Caesar Charles and the English cardinal would be coming there at the same time, that circumstance kept me there for several months, so that I might meet Erasmus and More, and see Tonstall and Montjoy, as well as many other learned men and most of my friends, who were also said to be coming there.

I could not write in that place, because I did not possess the library I wanted, from which the materials for writing could be supplied. I merely compared several books with ancient exemplars. One of these had been given to me by Marcus Lautinus, dean of Saint Donatian’s in Bruges; another belonged to the Carmelite friars of Bruges; a third had been sent to Erasmus at Cologne, and was said to have been written in the hand of Saint Ludger, bishop. [Col. 0440B]

The variety among the manuscripts is astonishing: each copyist seems to have thought that he was permitted to place the words as he pleased, provided that the sense remained intact—as though the work were a translation rather than a transcription. Thus in one book you read *I think*, in another *I suppose*; in one *signified*, in another *figured*; here *the present one*, elsewhere *that one*; here *therefore*, elsewhere *accordingly*; here *eternal*, elsewhere *immortal*; here *to have bent*, elsewhere *to have turned aside*, and elsewhere *to have bent inward*.

These differences might perhaps be tolerated. But what of words omitted, added, or transposed? How often errors arose when they tried to twist the version of the Seventy Interpreters, which Augustine cites everywhere, into our own version, and to make one text out of two that fitted together badly! Nothing was equally troublesome to me as weighing, examining, and sifting the variant reading in each chapter, often more than once. [Col. 0440C]

The more difficult matters I noted in the Commentaries; the clearer and more straightforward ones I placed in the margin. I did this more carefully in passages from Holy Scripture, because of their mystery. In most places I indicated the more accurate reading and disclosed my own view. In the remaining cases I was content to add what others had read, prejudging nothing for the reader and leaving him a free and unimpaired judgment. Through me, let each reader enjoy the exercise either of his own talent or of his own judgment.

After Caesar and the cardinal had departed, I returned to Leuven toward the end of September. There, after putting my affairs in order and arranging my library, I began to devote myself entirely to writing. Thus during that winter I progressed as far as the fifteenth book. [Col. 0440D]

At the end of spring, because friends were preparing to depart for Spain with Caesar and had to be visited, I interrupted the work. Erasmus repeatedly urged and pressed me to finish it and send it to him. I returned to Leuven and, with as much diligence as I could manage, completed the four final books in a single month, together with a large part of the eighteenth.

I came to write these prefaces so exhausted, and so broken by labor both great and varied, that my mind turned away from all books and letters—I scarcely know how—as a raw and overloaded stomach rejects all food. I longed miserably to be freed from that burden, desiring with every wish and prayer that, when I reached the end, I would consider neither money, nor the favor of scholars, nor anything else an equal reward for the labor, compared with being at last released and liberated from work so winding and for the most part so unpleasant. [Col. 0441A]

My task had required myths and histories to be recounted; regions and cities to be described; nearly all the Platonists and the remaining schools of philosophers to be consulted; and theological matters to be treated. In these matters I was more sparing than in secular subjects, for several reasons.

First, it was not fitting for a layman, especially one advanced in age, rashly either to define or to dispute about the most sacred matters. Second, the history of Holy Scripture is usually more familiar to those who will read Augustine and authors of this kind than to require me to repeat it. At the places indicated, it can be learned from the sacred books more fully and clearly than it seemed necessary for me to explain it here at length. [Col. 0441B]

Some passages from the hidden writings of our religion, cited by Augustine, I have explained; others I have passed over because I saw that this was not the place to explain them. I introduced frequent secular authors as witnesses to confirm Augustine’s statements, because the authority of his assertions rested with them, especially in secular matters, which Augustine borrowed from them. For in matters belonging to our piety, pagans have no part; and I used our own writers less freely, lest Augustine’s authority should seem insufficiently firm unless supported by them like musicians accompanying a singer.

It seemed sufficient simply to have said, “Augustine.” I called upon Jerome more frequently, especially when the meanings or interpretations of languages were at issue, because in knowledge both of Greek and Hebrew and of Holy Scripture he far surpasses all the writers of our religion. [Col. 0441C]

Nor did I think it appropriate for an interpreter to stir up those controversies that our theologians debate with great passion in the schools, although in our earliest years we were imbued with doctrines that differ greatly from Augustine’s purpose, mind, and reasoning. He would have scorned them and been indignant that they were mixed into his work like darnel among wheat, wherever that pure and most holy spirit looks down upon human affairs from its place in heaven.

Therefore I did not think that I should dispute either with this class of men or with the ancients, whoever among them differed from Augustine’s view. That would no longer be the task of an interpreter, but of a defender and advocate; yet Augustine needs neither my defense nor anyone else’s protection. [Col. 0441D]

I therefore did what Jerome says in the preface to his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians* that he did: for the most part, I merely reported the opinions of others. In the same way, content to explain to our readers what others had said and thought, we restrained our own judgment, following the ancient custom of the Academy.

I did this both because I considered it more appropriate to an expositor of another’s work, and because I thought it more fitting, especially before one’s gray hairs, to hesitate, not disclose one’s own opinion, and pursue and display the statements of others rather than one’s own. Such restraint is fitting for those whose censures and judgments acquire no little authority from age—and not undeservedly.

Many things now seem true, certain, and established to me which, if I live longer, may appear not merely doubtful on account of age but perhaps utterly false. [Col. 0442A] For that reason, in most places I preferred to delight the reader rather than to teach him. And if I did teach anything, I wished to persuade not by issuing stern commands but by gentle requests and admonitions.

Sometimes we were led to this course because Augustine is generally expansive and is himself his own interpreter. Once the burden of teaching had been removed, I enjoyed playing a little and leading the reader for a while into excursions that were not wholly unpleasant. At the same time, I could occasionally lighten part of my own labor—not by laying down the burden, certainly, but by sprinkling it with cold water, leading along a somewhat better-protected road, and making the journey more pleasant amid fields and cultivated land, pleasant to look upon. [Col. 0442B]

For all the things I have mentioned, although they possess their own restorations and refreshments for the mind, nevertheless have their rough places and steep little hills, over which one cannot carry the burden without sweating. They also have their descents, where one cannot travel without danger of slipping, lest, weighed down by the load, one be carried headlong.

There you find no road laid out at all, nothing to refresh the eyes, nothing by which you may turn aside even for a moment, not even a place where you may sit when exhausted. One must compare dates; point out differences, indeed contradictions, between authors; often remove them; search out and turn over the evidence; and conjecture where the passage is that Augustine cites from some author.

Finding the passage, after much and prolonged searching, is more often a matter of chance than of learning. The most ignorant person may frequently stumble upon what a learned man could not discover despite long investigation.

This was all the more difficult for me and consumed more time because I approached the work unprepared. Previously I had read only four or five volumes of it, and I had made no indexes from my reading, either for this purpose or for any similar one. Those who possess such indexes are, indeed, fortunate in their studies, since a considerable part of the labor is removed from them. [Col. 0442C]

To these difficulties was added the scarcity of Greek books, which is extraordinary in this region. For although one frequently encounters learned men, if you ask to borrow Aristotle in Greek, or Demosthenes, or the Old Testament, or Pausanias, or Isocrates, or Julius Pollux, or Eustathius, they deny that they possess them; nor can you find them for sale among the booksellers.

When Erasmus was present, I was assisted by his library. Even while engaged in other work there, I had extracted several passages for myself, as though my mind foresaw that they would someday be useful to me. I incorporated them into these Commentaries. [Col. 0442D]

I had Plato in Greek when writing the eighth, ninth, and tenth books; Strabo for the most part; Pausanias occasionally, but especially when commenting on the eighteenth book; and several others, of which I had less need than of these.

This was not because Augustine required a large supply of Greek authors for his exposition, since he followed only Latin authors, whom alone he had almost always read, or authors translated from Greek. But certainly, if I had been assisted by a greater abundance of Greek materials, the work could have emerged somewhat more polished and richer.

Thus some things have been omitted by us: some could not be obtained from any surviving author; others had to be extracted from the more hidden Greek literature. If at another time we obtain a larger library of Greek manuscripts, we shall, when opportunity permits, repair these omissions for the reader. [Col. 0443A]

Nevertheless, above all else we carefully watched and took pains to ensure that there should not be many things in this work that diligent and thoughtful scholars could miss. To have supplied all this would have been easy for others, whether because of their broader knowledge, greater talent, or more fortunate memory.

No one should really believe how tedious and full of disgust this work has been for me. Hence that original ease of completion which first spurred me toward the task has entirely vanished.

How great its usefulness will be is not for me to declare, since no one is either an impartial or unsuspected judge of his own work. No one can announce that the outcome of a work lies in the hands and power of Fortune, nor can I make any promise about it.

The work will live, be read, please, and be useful if its genius is favorable; but if that genius is adverse, it will collapse and perish. Many things are pleasing and useful only because Fortune has so willed it. [Col. 0443B]

I can pray only that, if anything is gained by wishing, readers may find the work as useful as it was burdensome and troublesome for me to write.

We have already lost the first of these things; the second is uncertain; and the third—favor, from which a writer’s name and glory return to him—is certainly no more assured.

I am well aware how much fame and admiration even the best work loses when it is written about another author: that is, when it is built upon another’s surface, and its subject matter is supplied by someone else—unless perhaps one is commenting on Holy Scripture, because of its sacred majesty, or on Aristotle, because of the authority he enjoys in all the schools. [Col. 0443C]

To this is added the fact that many people, for whom everything they neglect or fail to understand is turned into grammar, will call this book “grammar,” although we have treated sacred, philosophical, and obscure subjects in it. They will do so chiefly because we have narrated histories and myths. They would say the same about Augustine’s own work, if shame and reverence for a name so sacred and admirable to everyone did not prevent them.

Others will reject and condemn the whole work without having seen or judged it, whatever name it may be given. Recently, for example, a certain licentiate in theology, when he heard that I was writing on the books of *The City of God*, scorned my work with great disdain as entirely useless and vain.

“What need,” he said, “is there for an interpreter of books that are already sufficiently clear and intelligible in themselves?”

O fortunate man, whoever you are, to whom these books of *The City of God* are so open and easy! [Col. 0443D]

Those who heard this were astonished either at the man’s talent, his learning, or at least his shamelessness. For he spoke with extreme ignorance and was entirely inexperienced and uneducated in every matter of antiquity.

One of those who had heard him asked why he held this opinion, since there were so many histories, so many myths, so much philosophy, geography, and mathematics.

“What have those things to do with a theologian?” he replied. “Then let them be *a* or *b*; I am not concerned.”

This is the sort of person who thinks that Cicero, Virgil, Pliny, and other similar authors require no interpreter, since it makes no difference to him who Scipio, Caesar, Pompey, or Cato was; what or where Carthage or Babylonia was; whether a plant or a stone, mallow or beet (*beata*); whether a stone or wood, magnet or diamond; whether an animal or a metal, tiger or kite; whether the mountain that burns is Etna or the Alps; whether it burns with kindled sulfur or sand. [Col. 0444A]

He cares nothing what Plato said or thought, what Democritus’ atoms produce, what Anaxagoras’ similar or dissimilar parts are, or what Pythagoras’ transmigration of souls means.

To all such matters these men are a “white line,” as the saying goes, on a white stone. They think only those questions worth considering and weighing: whether God can *supposit* this pen with which I write; whether he can command hatred of himself; whether the pope can dispense someone from a vow to travel to Rome or Jerusalem; or whether a priest may buy back a benefice pension with money, and whether that is simony.

But let these men judge the work as they please. I do not write for them, nor do I care whether they read me. I attach no value to their judgment or criticism, and I do not strive to please them. I shall think that I have written more learnedly if I have displeased them.

But this is greatly to be lamented: that the destructive poison of envy so often takes hold of the minds of learned but not equally good men, through which they attack and tear apart good works, or try to destroy what might prove beneficial, or obscure what might bring light. [Col. 0444B]

From this come hatred; from hatred, rabid abuse; from an uncontrolled spirit, insults, quarrels, disputes, and slanders. From this, too, often comes the despair and withdrawal of better minds, when, disgusted with so bitter and unattractive a business, they turn away from every form of writing and of helping posterity, and often from study itself.

This is so far from causing envious minds sorrow that they regard it as a singular benefit and the reward of their own labor. Their aim is achieved if everyone stops and no one does good work. Terence wisely portrayed this aspect of human behavior, as he did so many others, when he says that a malicious and envious poet used all his strength to deter another from writing and drive him into idleness. [Col. 0444C]

Nor do I say this because I resent being admonished or even criticized—God grant me a better mind! On the contrary, I shall openly acknowledge that I owe much to anyone who offers better suggestions and criticizes me learnedly.

I shall not be reluctant to change my opinion if study or advancing age teaches me something better. But it is extremely troublesome and intolerable for someone to pronounce judgment on an entire work at once and condemn it as ignorant or worthless when he has neither read it nor, perhaps, if he had read it, found so many things to attack; or when, if he attempted to produce as much himself, he would either be unable to do so or would sweat sufficiently in the effort.

Nor is it right to reject and despise an entire work so great and varied because one has found one error, or at most two—just as though, in Horace’s words, one were to condemn an excellent body because it contained a few moles. [Col. 0444D]

In short, since I do not control people’s tongues, and since free tongues are fitting in free studies, I do not ask anyone to refrain from thinking and speaking about the work as he wishes.

If the work is bad, I ought not to become angry at the truth. But if it is good, those who have spoken maliciously will be consumed by their own envy like poison. In this one matter envy is entirely just; in all other matters it is unjust.

This alone I ask and earnestly entreat: if anyone disagrees with me and wishes to testify to that disagreement in writing, let him remember moderation and teach me, without insults or harsh bites, what I have failed to understand. [Col. 0445A]

For although a book may deserve insults and perhaps severe criticism, my purpose and the effort of my mind do not deserve them. In this way, I too shall receive the fruit of his learning, recognize the great benefit he has conferred, and be eternally grateful. And that better teacher will understand that he has helped me, while securing for his learning the highest praise, uncorrupted and undefiled by any immodesty—which is worse than ignorance.

Let humanity not be absent from the studies of humanity, and let that tranquility of spirit be preserved in which the Muses rejoice above all other things. Let us begin to abolish the custom that unfaithful Furies have introduced into distinguished studies: attacking and tearing apart the person whom fellowship in study and cultivation of the same Muses ought to have made our closest and dearest companion—to say nothing of baptism and the charity of Christ. [Col. 0445B]

Those have long been empty names to deaf ears and insubstantial shadows without bodies to diseased eyes. Let us cultivate letters so that they may delight and help us, not so that they may plunge us into bitter conflict or provide weapons of learning or style with which, gratifying our corrupt passions, we may strike and wound an enemy.

But there will be a time to speak about these matters, when I find a more suitable place. For now, to return to what I had begun, all my hope rests in those who approach the reading of these books with an open and upright heart, whether they are learned or unlearned. [Col. 0445C]

Finally, I console myself in this way: if no gratitude returns to us from human beings, there will still be considerations which, having led and impelled me to undertake this work, will ensure that I never regret it.

For it gives me as much pleasure to have obeyed my Erasmus as it would have been wicked to refuse a burden imposed by one who, because of both the close friendship that binds him to me and his status as a teacher who has deserved the greatest gratitude, possesses a right and authority over me.

Meanwhile, while I have been reflecting on these matters, I have occupied myself with a most honorable exercise and filled my mind and spirit with frequent thoughts full of honor and holiness—thoughts that make me readier and more capable of living well and as a Christian.

Even if everything else were lacking, this alone would be an ample and magnificent reward. Finally, even if I consider nothing else but that I wished to consecrate some part of my studies to Augustine and therefore to Christ, I must consider myself to have been very well treated. [Col. 0445D]

For Christ has promised that he will not leave unrewarded even a cup of cold water offered for his sake and his name. He will likewise show gratitude for this intention of mine, which alone he values—especially since I wish all my labors to be valid for me only if they are approved by Christ and by his most chaste and blameless bride, the Church.

## On the Earlier Interpreters of This Work

A friend of mine told me today that, while conversing with several brothers of the Dominican order and institution, he had happened to speak about these Commentaries of mine. They replied that I was wasting useless labor and effort, and that I could have saved myself the time, since certain Preaching Friars had written on Augustine’s books *The City of God* with miraculous learning, skill, accuracy, and success—nothing more was needed. [Col. 0446A]

If this is really so, I was exceedingly presumptuous to hope that I could surpass writings so astonishing with my meager talent and learning; insane to believe that my little lamp could obscure so great a light; foolish not to use their work instead, as one uses the commentaries of Valerius Probus, Servius, or Donatus; and badly employed, to have voluntarily wasted so much time doing what they call doing the same thing twice.

Erasmus himself was imprudent to commission new Commentaries when such old ones existed. And every learned man who favored the wishes of this work of ours was supremely foolish—so these brothers believe—in supporting something superfluous.

I would dare swear that these brothers have not read even a single word of those Commentaries, but have merely seen their titles; or, if they have read and approve them, they are plainly like the commentators themselves.

Since I never intended to refute such obvious ignorance and such foolish and witless expositions, I did not collect a number of especially ridiculous and ignorant passages from which those who had not read the whole work could form a judgment. [Col. 0446B]

Nor was this necessary. For in this age, already cultivated by so many letters and disciplines, very few people who read any passage in those Commentaries cannot immediately judge from even the smallest example what the entire mass is like.

Thus I have been spared the great and disagreeable burden of exposing those absurdities to learned men. Nothing is heavier or more unpleasant than refuting foolishness intelligently. If you merely point it out, it will be dismissed as foolish; but if you spend effort revealing its nature, you make it not so much contemptible as less foolish in the eyes of certain people.

There are also men of the same order who might think—and certainly do think—how base and despicable those writings are: unworthy not only of Augustine but even of Theodulus, *Facetus*, or *Floretus*. [Col. 0446C]

Yet because this is not believed only by those who condemned my entire labor as empty, but also by many others, merely because those men are called Preaching Friars, I wish to justify to them the rationale of my work—if only they permit it to be justified, or understand the justification.

I believe that some of them are such that they see no difference between the diction of Cicero and that of the *Catholicon*, or between the history of Livy and that of Vincent; between Pliny’s knowledge of things and that of Bartholomew of England; or between Jerome and Hugh of Carensis.

How could they distinguish these things, when they know no Latin and have never touched any good authors, but have always been nourished by and immersed up to both ears in the *Sermonaries*, *Discipuli*, or *Dormisecure*? [Col. 0446D]

If I make no progress with them—not through any fault of mine, but through theirs—I shall make progress with others who possess sounder judgment and better learning. Their order contains some men of this kind, including several who are very dear friends of mine. Through the benefit of better letters, they recognize and regret the common error of their fellows and, insofar as they can, avoid it.

I shall therefore do unwillingly what I had not originally intended: recall dead men, now beyond all envy, to judgment and criticism. I do this especially because, in my opinion, those men were honest and did what they could, although their work was as ignorant and inept as they themselves generally were in that age. [Col. 0447A]

They therefore profess to have written on this work: Thomas Valois, Nicholas Trivet, and James of Passavant. Francis de Maronis, a Minorite, also gathers the truths, so that the Preaching Friars may not possess the kingdom alone.

First, I suppose Thomas Valois judged the work immense and too great for one man’s strength. He did not dare undertake the whole of it alone, but took a companion, as a substitute partner, Nicholas Trivet, as like himself as one egg is like another. To him, as the saying goes, he would hand over the torch when tired—I do not know in which volume, for although I read it, I did not make notes. [Col. 0447B]

Nor did they undertake to explain anything other than myths and histories. I suppose they thought it sacrilegious to touch sacred matters. In this respect, at least, I praise their moderation to no small degree: they thought it sufficient to contaminate secular matters and abstained from sacred ones.

Thus they wrote almost nothing from the eleventh through the eighteenth books, or from the nineteenth through the twenty-second. Anyone can readily see this, since the books are at hand.

But in the eighth, ninth, and tenth books, where Augustine disputes against the Platonists, what could those poor men have said? They had seen not only no Plato or Platonist, but not even the shadow of a philosopher.

Thus, lest they should lack something to do, they devote themselves entirely to dividing and distributing the text: [Col. 0447C]

“Here Augustine treats this or that, and he does two things. The first is that he rejects Plato, at this point; the second is that he says this or that, at that point—and he says so.”

Then, what Augustine had expressed purely and in good Latin, they drag into their own filth and obscenity merely to fill pages, as though later generations could not understand it in any other way.

Now, in five books and part of the eighteenth, myths and histories are treated. Here they think they are in their own arena, and they roam about and strut like a horse, as they say, in an open field.

I shall pass over the filth and foulness of their language and their foolish, tasteless narratives—although they sometimes took them from the most eloquent authors. No stomach can be so hardy that it could swallow one or two of them, except perhaps the stomachs for which harmful things are healthy.

But let me come to the subjects themselves. [Col. 0447D] These Commentaries are certainly useful to those who do not wish to know anything truly and correctly—such as certain minds that cannot even hear history narrated truthfully, as the event actually occurred, believing, I suppose, that it is sacrilege for anything genuine and uncorrupted to remain.

They are therefore mistaken in countless places, and mislead anyone who follows them, both because their knowledge of what they write is confused and uncertain and because, through ignorance of Latin, they repeatedly stumble even in the matters themselves.

In addition, they introduce many inventions that no author ever dreamed of, some drawn from moralized accounts of Roman deeds, others from things they had heard told orally while drinking in the communal refectory.

I shall gather a few examples that first come to hand. [Col. 0448A]

In Book I, chapter 5, when Caesar in Sallust describes what usually happens in wars—virgins are carried off and boys torn from their parents’ embraces—the commentator says that Caesar means these things had already been done by Catiline: a true commentator, indeed, as though he were inventing rather than commenting.

Then, in chapter 24, he says that Portius Latro, the declaimer, was Cato. There he argues brilliantly about whether this is the same man who composed *Catunculus* for boys.

In Book II, chapter 4, he says that Atys was offered to his mother, the goddess, in her temple so that he might vow chastity. I suppose he learned this from some Gaul devoted to the Mother of the Gods.

A little later he says:

“*Symphoniaci* are those who sing with trumpets or produce a great sound in some other way. From sweet harmony he makes great sounds and trumpets.”

And a few words later:

“Here Augustine calls *symphoniaci* those who performed certain indecent acts in honor of the goddess Pudicitia. He could not have spoken better if he had lived in that age.”

A few words farther on, he says that Pallas is washed with the Mother of the Gods in the river Almo. One might think Varro had said this—merely because Augustine mentions the heavenly virgin there, as though there were no other virgin goddess than Pallas.

And soon afterward:

“Properly speaking, the *scaena* was a little house in the middle of the theater, like the little houses of shopkeepers or merchants at fairs, according to Huguitio.”

O miserable stages of Scaurus, Curio, and Pompey—stages so broad and adorned with gold and silver! How have you been reduced to the little houses of merchants at fairs?

But this is more tolerable. He adds:

“In the *scaena* there was a platform, which those who recited the plays climbed; and however many verses there were, they considered that they had set out an equal number of dishes.”

This is the most ingenious interpretation of *ferculum*. [Col. 0448B]

He continues:

“Below, masked actors and mimes were also hiding. Suddenly emerging before the people, they expressed through bodily movements the histories or myths that had been recited; and these were properly called *scenici*. The *scaena* is also sometimes used for the whole theater itself, sometimes for a play, and sometimes for the recitation of a play.”

Who could deny that all this is astonishing, since no one had ever heard it before? Who ever called a theater a *scaena*, or a play, or the recitation of a play?

Then he adds that Valerius Maximus says that, before the image of the Mother of the Gods had been transferred from Pessinus, Roman commanders often went to Pessinus to fulfill their vows. [Col. 0448C]

Where did Valerius ever dream that up? It is not enough for you to invent things unless you also attribute your lies to others.

Valerius does indeed recount in Book I that Roman commanders went there, but not before the Mother of the Gods had been transferred; at that time no Roman had ever gone there.

He adds that Domitian built the Pantheon as a temple for the Great Mother of the Gods, although Agrippa had built the Pantheon before Domitian, first for Jupiter the Victor and then for the other gods.

All this appears in the same truly golden and copious chapter 4 of Book II—which you may call a cornucopia. [Col. 0448D]

In chapter 6, however, there are verses of Persius, which he explains with extraordinary wit:

> Learn, O wretched ones, and understand the causes of things:  
> What we are, and for what we are born to live, the order …

[The supplied source ends here, mid-quotation.]

Who was given? [Col. 0449A] “Thus,” he says, “human nature was ordered in such a way that it is superior to brute animals.” I thought it meant inferior. Or what about the turn at *meta*—how smooth is it? “*Meta*,” he says, “that is, death.” Yet from death there is no turning. “What useful thing does a rough coin possess?” Since he did not know why a coin was called *asper* (“rough”), moralizing was not lacking. “*Asper*,” he says, “that is, how much roughness it contains, because of the great anxieties it causes; and for this reason riches are also compared with thorns.” Persius did not understand his own words so sharply, nor so piously.

And in chapter eight there is an annotation on poets worthy of being learned by heart. “There are,” he says, “two kinds of poets, ancient and modern. The ancient poets turned everything they sang into laughter; hence they dealt with prostitutes, sexual offenses, and whatever could provoke laughter, as Plautus and Terence did. The modern poets, however, reproved the vices of men by name; and thus they attacked men, picking out their vices, whether true or invented; and they were depicted naked because they stripped vices bare. Such poets are called comic satirists, such as Horace, Persius, Juvenal, and the like.” And shortly afterward:

“Tragic poets, like comic poets, can also be divided into two parts. The first are pure tragedians; the second are elegists, treating of elegy, that is, misery.”

So he speaks, I believe, from Aristotle—or from whoever else wrote more learnedly about poets. Yet anyone who has never heard anything about these kinds of poets will not understand how frivolous and ignorant these statements are, to say nothing of their being foolish and ridiculous. If he has heard of them, these statements will seem to him just as absurd as if someone were to say, “The craft of architects is to sew shoes, while that of cobblers is to build houses”; or, when he calls modern comic poets satirists, as if someone were to say that tailors are weavers; or, when he calls comic poets elegiac, as if someone were to call mule-drivers sailors, or barbers charcoal-burners. And when he explains *elegy* as “misery,” it is no different from interpreting “bookcase” as “book.”

And in chapter 109, when he was discussing Plautus, he wrote: “This man, he says, wrote the comedy called *The Pot of Gold*,” as though he had written no other. He also wished to philosophize in book VII. For after Augustine had said that the goddess Mena, who presides over menstruation, contributes menstrual flows to the growth of what has been conceived, he—unaware that *menstrual flow* also means the woman’s blood which would flow during the month unless it were retained by a fetus or some other cause—begins to distinguish menstrual blood. In one sense, he says, it is understood as the cleansing of nature, which is expelled each month. In another sense, it is understood as the blood that is cleansed through expulsion; and after the menstrual flow, it contributes to the growth of the fetus only accidentally, namely, through its absence. For it contributes in this respect: when it is expelled, the blood from which the fetus grows becomes cleaner and better suited to its growth. But blessed Augustine, speaking broadly, calls that blood which is purified “menstrual flow.” So he says.

First, who has ever called the blood that remains purer in a woman’s body after the menstrual discharge “menstrual flow”? Second, how do fetuses grow through this process? If that menstrual fluid flows away, they become weaker; and if it flows more abundantly, or as it is accustomed to flow at another time, the fetus departs with it and can neither grow nor be nourished.

But would you like to hear explanations of words? Augustine exclaims in book II: “O genuinely Roman spirits!” “*Germane*,” he says, “means deeply or monstrously, for the Germans have monstrous and lofty bodies.” And in the same work Augustine, speaking of the linen or little woolen band of the flamines with which they bound the head, which they called the *apex*, as though it meant “summit,” says: “*Apex* is the name of a certain historiographer. Thus it should no longer be surprising that God made human beings from clay, since this man makes them from linen.”

And when, in book IV, Augustine had listed among prodigies women, hens, and men changed into the male sex, he says: “I believe the wording is corrupt, although many books have it. The wording ought to be: ‘into men and the male sex.’ For he means that women were changed into men—that is, into males—and hens into the male sex.”

O pitiable darkness of that age! Yet their eyes had become so accustomed to it that they could not bear to look upon the light already introduced. Close all those windows and cracks, lest any light be able to enter, and let them freely enjoy their night; indeed, light a lamp at midday itself, however dim and feeble, in the darkened room.

In the same interpreter I also marvel at this: although he had the weightiest authorities, from whom he was accustomed to draw some material, and could have brought forward other things from those same sources, he preferred to seek them from Isidore—or from men worse than Isidore, Huguccio and Vincent the Historian. This makes me suspect either that he used someone else’s work when citing authorities, or that he found the cited authorities in some *vade mecum*, or in a *rapiamus totum* (“let us seize the whole”), or that he had heard of them from someone.

For the definition of God which Augustine cites from Cicero’s first *Tusculan Disputation*, he says can be gathered from the matters Cicero treats sporadically in book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*. And concerning the consolation on the death of a daughter, he says he does not know whether it is in book XII of the *Orations*, although Cicero himself, as well as Lactantius and Pliny, mentions it in the *Academica* and the *Tusculan Disputations*. He says he does not recall having read anything about Valerius Soranus, although he is mentioned by Pliny, Solinus, Lactantius, Plutarch, Servius, and Macrobius.

Again, joining and soldering together one Diogenes out of many Diogeneses, one Aeschines out of many Aeschineses, and the same Socrates and Isocrates, against their will and in a badly fitting combination, is not uncommon—nor are many other things. If I tried to pursue all these matters individually, I would extend the discussion indefinitely.

The examples I have produced are merely specimens, which certainly came before me as soon as I began turning the book’s pages. They are so frequent and dense that there is no danger they will remain hidden if they are not pointed out: they stand forth, present themselves, and even thrust themselves upon the eyes of everyone willing to look—although I have not pursued them all within the work itself. I refrained partly lest I weary the reader with such prolixity, and partly because they are too inept to deserve the expenditure of effort required to refute them.

Whoever does not trust me should read the work himself, and either judge it, if he is learned, or seek the opinion of more learned men and agree with them. But if anyone perhaps embraces and loves these things exclusively and earnestly, he possesses not only these commentaries but also Huguccio, Papias, the *Graecista*, John of Garland, and the *Catholicon*. Let him amuse himself with all of them; may that be good and prosperous for him, and may he remain attached to their embrace.

As for Thomas of Wales and Nicholas Trevet, James Passavanti appeared as a kind of substitute, whose very name indicates that he was some amusing jester who entertained the entire brotherhood. I believe that the other brothers gave him the name *Passavant* as a joke and in play.

“When Tertullian is to be discussed, nothing occurs to me; let it be reserved with the others. Concerning Valerius Soranus, nothing occurs to me at present; let it be reserved with the others. Concerning Xenophanes and Anaxagoras, and concerning Lactantius, let it be reserved with the others.”

What on earth are these “others”? Where do you reserve them? For what use? What of the fact that he had not even read the very interpreters to whom he says he adds his own material? Thus, in book III, chapter 12, he writes:

“In this chapter 12 Augustine mentions the goddess Fever, about whom the expositor says that she was the mother of Aesculapius, that she is a goddess of the underworld, and that King Numa consecrated the month of February to the goddess Fever.”

Yet the expositor never wrote this—unless perhaps such a foolish statement was erased from the manuscripts by other brothers who had discovered it. Apparently, however, some brother had told Passavanti over supper that the expositor said this.
