But let us hear how he refutes it:

“This does not seem to have been well said,” he writes, “with due respect to him. For, as will be said below, Aesculapius is thought to have been the son of Phoebus and Coronis, as Ovid wishes in the second book of the *Metamorphoses*. It is never read that Phoebus consorted with Fever or fathered a son by her.”

Then he begins to philosophize and search for conjectures:

“Nor is Aesculapius appropriately imagined as the son of Fever, since he was afterward regarded as the god of medicine, which is meant to drive out fever.”

And, lest there be no opportunity for others to answer on his behalf, he adds:

“Unless one should say that he was such a cruel son that he pursued his mother everywhere and drove her from every dwelling.”

These additions are jocular, prepared to provoke laughter among the brothers.

Along with all these comes Francis of Maro, no ordinary doctor but an “illuminated” one; and he collects truths as though everything else were false. Yet he is no more relevant to this work than to Augustine’s other works. From all of these, he seems to have selected and set aside truths as Virgil selected gems from Ennius’ dung.

If people foreign to our religion take Augustine’s works into their hands, illuminated, that is, by the truths of this “illuminated” man, what will they think of such truths? What will they suspect or believe? Surely they will suppose that the rest are either not very true or suspect to the Church, and that only those truths are held and asserted by us as firm and indisputable which the illuminated doctor has pointed out—although among them he will find much that is contentious, other things ambiguous, and many things false.

For if everything in Augustine is equally true, what have I to do with your “truths,” most of which add nothing to Augustine’s statements? And when you do add something, you sophisticate the matter. You do not follow Augustine’s truth; rather, you force him, with his neck twisted, wherever you yourself wish—namely, toward the Scottish faction—so that he may appear to have spoken against Thomas. And you try to make him seem to say things that no one of his age ever even thought.

You collect truths from history and fables no less than from theological matters. What coldness there is in this! When Augustine says that Ninus was the first ruler of the Assyrians, you immediately rush forward as a molder of truths, with your formulas for manufacturing a truth from this—as though the truth could not exist otherwise.

“Truth,” you say: “Ninus was the first king of the Assyrians.” Why is what is read a little earlier not also true? Why not what follows a little later? I have offered one example in place of many thousands.

And how is it for you to be a potter of truths while mixing in with them things uncertain and, above all, controversial? This is especially the case when you dispute against the Thomists, an activity you undertake neither more willingly nor more frequently. You even mix in matters uncertain to yourself—for example, when you say that Holofernes in the book of Judith was Cyrus, the son of Ahasuerus and Esther, and later express doubts about some of these “truths.” Or you mix in things false even to children, as in this very matter when you say that Darius was the son of Ahasuerus and Esther; and when you say that Augustine did not remember the Third Book of Ezra, although he cites from it that question concerning the thing that surpassed all others in strength.

Even in the same chapter in which you say this, in book XVIII, you do not seem to fashion your truths from one simple truth, but partly from true things, partly from uncertain things, partly from contentious things, and partly from false things—like the statue which Nebuchadnezzar saw in a dream, formed from gold, silver, steel, iron, and clay.

But let these be truths, as much as others may desire; I do not object, and let them be read by those who enjoy such things. As for me, I consider whatever he reports verbatim from Augustine to belong to Augustine. The rest, which he adds from his own resources, belongs to Augustine no more particularly than the nearly infinite things written on similar subjects by authors of elementary summaries or compilations.

This little that I have said about the interpreters of this work must suffice for me, weary and hurrying on to other matters. I have said it merely to warn good minds, so that I may not have labored altogether in vain on these books. 

# Who the Goths Were, and How They Captured Rome

Since Augustine took the occasion of Rome’s captivity to write *The City of God*, in order to answer those who attributed that disaster to the Christian religion, it will be worthwhile to explain more fully, beginning the narrative further back, who the Goths were, how they came into Italy, and how they captured the City.

First of all, I see that it is almost universally agreed that what a later age called Goths, an earlier age called Getae—so long as that small remnant of ancient terminology was not corrupted. Thus the poets Rutilius and Claudian, whenever they speak of the Goths, always call them Getae.

Orosius likewise says in his *History*:

“The Getae, who are now the Goths, whom Alexander declared should be avoided, whom Pyrrhus dreaded, and whom Caesar avoided, after their settlements had been abandoned and laid waste, entered the Roman provinces with all their forces, relying on their own strength.”

Jerome testifies in his commentary on Genesis that the Goths were called Getae by learned men of antiquity.

The Getae, however, are those who dwell around the river Ister, as Strabo, Mela, Pliny, and others report. They possess a broad region, largely uncultivated and harsh because of its severe climate. They occupy the lands beyond the Ister toward Scythia, and those nearer the river toward Thrace, where Tomis—famous for the exile of the poet Ovid—is situated. Ovid repeatedly writes in the *Tristia* and the *Letters from Pontus* that he lived among the Getae.

They also occupy the inland regions toward Germany and the source of the Ister. Strabo says in book VII that these peoples were called Daci, and formerly Davi, while those nearer the Black Sea were called Getae by the Greeks; he also says that both peoples spoke the same language. Although Pliny seems to indicate no other distinction between these peoples than that those whom the Greeks call Getae are called Daci by the Romans, we shall follow Strabo here.

The Getae are a barbarous and savage people, possessing immense strength and courage, and contemptuous of death because they are convinced that souls return, as Mela writes; or, if they do not return, that they are nevertheless not extinguished but migrate to better dwelling places; and if neither occurs, that death is certainly preferable to life.

It is reported that in later times the Getae were called Ostrogoths, while the Daci were called Visigoths by their native names, because the latter looked more toward the West and the former toward the East. Yet these designations are often confused by writers, not only by more recent writers but also by ancient ones.

They say that this people, when Roman power was flourishing most vigorously, once made an incursion into a province of the Roman people during the Mithridatic War. Lucullus, who was conducting military operations in Asia as commander with a large army, drove them out of Mysia after inflicting a defeat upon them.

Later, under their leader Boerebista, after he had accustomed them to toil and military discipline, they left their own region, subdued many peoples, crossed the Ister with an enormous force, devastated Thrace, Macedonia, and Illyricum far and wide, and caused immense terror among the Romans.

Meanwhile, while Roman arms were being prepared against them, Boerebista died. Augustus sent nearly ten legions against them and weakened their power to such an extent that he reduced their forces from two hundred thousand soldiers to forty thousand, and came very close to subjecting the entire nation to Roman rule.

Some years later they entered Roman territory and killed Oppius Sabinus, a consular man, together with his army. They were finally subdued by Cornelius Fuscus under the emperor Domitian after various battles. The emperor Trajan waged a long and highly glorious war against them. Antoninus Caracalla severely afflicted them on an occasion when they suspected no such thing.

In the time of the Gordians they poured into Roman territory with great frequency; the younger Gordian compelled them to withdraw from the province with little difficulty. They were a fierce and restless people, dissatisfied with their own settlements, and continually seeking opportunities to invade the lands of others.

Accordingly, under Philip of Bostra, the emperor who was the first of the Roman rulers to profess Christian piety, they invaded nearby Thrace and Mysia in a force of nearly three hundred thousand men, after inflicting many massacres and devastations. Decius was sent to drive them out, but he too left unfinished a campaign that had generally been attempted with little success; Philip’s successor concealed the failure when he assumed the principate.

Gallus, the father, and Volusianus, the son, made peace with them under conditions unfavorable to themselves. The Goths did not maintain it for very long, relying on the negligence and indolence of the emperor Gallienus. They no longer attacked Thrace and Mysia but began to test Asia Minor itself. They harassed and plundered Bithynia, then returned to Europe and ravaged Thrace and Macedonia.

When they came into Achaea, Macrinus opposed them, defeated and pursued them, until he forced them back within their own borders. Yet they did not remain there for long. Although they came out against a most energetic emperor—a man no less fortunate than virtuous, if only a longer life had been granted him in the principate—he was Claudius, who destroyed or captured three hundred thousand of them.

This nation must have possessed an immense population. For not many years later, while Aurelian held the empire, they returned to arms and were defeated in their first battle on the Danube. Flavius Constantine inflicted such slaughter upon them that he finally compelled them to remain quiet for many years.

They fought in such a way that when they won, it was at great cost to their enemies; when they were defeated, it was at no lesser cost to themselves.

These, then, were the deeds of the Goths for as long as they possessed fixed settlements of their own.

Under the emperor Valens, the Huns—who are themselves Scythians, but more savage and less refined in human intercourse—dwelling nearer to the Riphaean Mountains, and confined between the Tanais and the Massagetae, violently expelled the Goths from the region they inhabited. Although that region, because of its severe climate, was scarcely suitable for human use, the Huns considered it the healthiest and most pleasant of all regions, being people born and raised beyond the paths and courses of the sun.

The Goths, now deprived of their settlements, homes, household gods, and ancestral hearths—although they had formerly been accustomed to invade the borders of others—were compelled either to meet death bravely or to cling to possession of foreign soil when they no longer possessed any of their own.

Some report that it was not the Getae whom we have called Ostrogoths who came into the territory of the Roman people, but that the Visigoths, terrified by the misfortune of their allies, deliberated about changing their settlements, fearing that they would suffer the same fate as the Ostrogoths, while the Hunnic armies spread like a rising sea and destroyed the neighboring regions.

This circumstance moved the Visigoths to decide to send ambassadors to Valens, the Roman emperor, requesting in the name of their people that Mysia on this side of the Danube be assigned to them for habitation. They promised that, in the name of the entire people, they would all accept Christian piety, become good and faithful soldiers in Roman pay, and diligently defend those territories of the Roman people against the incursions of the remaining Scythians with their arms and resources.

Moved by these conditions, Valens sent Lupicinus and Maximus, as though they were duumvirs for the distribution of lands, to assign settlements to the Visigoths.

These men treated the people greedily and cruelly. At first the Goths endured this and concealed the injury, lest they immediately initiate a revolt upon entering a foreign region, thinking that once the leaders had satisfied themselves with their resources, they would cease their cruelty and plundering.

But while those men maliciously distributed and controlled the provisions, they created an intolerable famine, which proved fatal both to the leaders themselves and to the Roman emperor.

For when the Goths saw that, driven by hunger, they were being attacked like wild beasts, they seized their weapons in tumultuous fashion, cruelly slaughtered the Roman leaders and their garrisons, and, thus armed, overran all Mysia. They crossed into neighboring Thrace and made it tributary to themselves.

Valens encountered them there. A fierce battle was fought; the Romans were routed and put to flight, and great slaughter was inflicted upon them. The wounded emperor fell alive into the power of the enemy. After so much blood had been shed, the Goths, in their savagery, burned him alive. Then they marched directly toward Byzantium and, encountering no armed resistance, surrounded the city with a ring of troops.

For some time the city endured the siege through the resources and planning of Dominica, the wife of Valens, who strengthened the citizens’ loyalty to the emperor through her great generosity. After the siege was lifted through the courage of Valentinian, the brother of Valens, the Goths withdrew.

Valentinian adopted Theodosius, a Spaniard summoned from Spain, and made him his partner in the empire. Theodosius defeated and crushed the Goths in many battles and compelled them to ask humbly for peace. After he had granted it, their king Athalaric came to Byzantium to visit the ailing Theodosius; the king himself fell ill and died some months later.

Throughout the entire reign of Theodosius, the Goths served under the Roman emperor. They had no other king and no commander except one whom the Roman emperor had appointed.

Meanwhile, Theodosius died at Milan. He had been, without dispute, the best ruler in both war and peace. The consuls were Bassus and Philippus. He left behind his sons Arcadius and Honorius and his daughter Placidia.

He assigned the Eastern Empire and Byzantium to Arcadius, and the Western Empire and the city of Rome to Honorius. Since they were still very young, he appointed guardians and tutors for them in his will: Ruffinus for Arcadius and Stilicho for Honorius. Both were crafty and wicked men, the sort of characters who most easily insinuate themselves into the innermost courts.

Taking advantage of the emperors’ youth and vulnerability, each sought to increase his own wealth and acquire great and immoderate power. They no longer thought about some private position of greatness but directed their criminal ambitions toward the very summit of imperial power. Ruffinus aspired to the empire for himself; Stilicho aspired to it for his son.

While both were devising these plans, war was necessary to accomplish them. In times of disturbance, their desires would be less easily detected and more easily fulfilled, since the emperors, shaken by the terrors of war, would grant everything to the men closest to them and to those who controlled all affairs.

For they knew that in peacetime, as under a clear and tranquil sky, the emperors could both recognize the darkness of their minds and punish their schemes at leisure.

Accordingly, each of them tempted the Goths—an exceedingly suitable people for stirring up revolts and military disturbances—with the hope of enormous booty, urging them to make war against his own emperor.

The Goths, thinking that an opportunity had arisen either to accomplish some successful undertaking or, at any rate, to return home with considerable booty after launching a war, put on their armor. They chose as their king Alaric, a man from their own body and from the illustrious family of the Balti, and marched beyond their borders, greatly terrifying their neighbors.

Not long afterward Rhadagaisus joined him with two hundred thousand Goths. Since no single land could adequately feed such a multitude, the leaders divided the army into camps. Setting out by different routes through Pannonia, Illyricum, and Noricum, they burned and ravaged everything they encountered and came into Italy.

Ruffinus, because he was carrying out his plans too imprudently, was killed by soldiers at Thessalonica. Stilicho concealed his designs more cunningly. Rhadagaisus was marching through Etruria toward Rome with his army, displaying flight and terror far and wide wherever he went.

The frightened Roman state opposed him with mercenary commanders. Rhadagaisus, imprudently arranging his army and camp, threw himself into unfavorable terrain. Deprived of supplies, he exhausted his forces through hunger. Finally, recognizing the hopelessness of his situation, he attempted to flee secretly with a few companions; Roman soldiers intercepted and killed him, while the Gothic multitude was sold for the most trifling prices.

After this defeat of the Goths, Alaric came into Italy, throwing everything into even greater terror than Rhadagaisus had done. When Stilicho heard the news—he was at Byzantium—he sent ahead a portion of his forces to harass the rear of the Goths and deter the enemy from any great slaughter or devastation of the countryside. He himself came upon the enemy along the coast of the Upper Sea with his infantry and cavalry.

The two armies brought their camps near Ravenna. The Goths held the road to Pollentia. They were superior in number but in no way comparable with the Roman army in skill and military discipline.

Stilicho generally overcame the Goths through military cunning and forced them into a narrow place where, had he wished, he could have completed the war while they were trapped. But he had decided to remain with the army until his fellow Vandals arrived in Gaul. For he regarded their arrival as a certain opportunity to secure the empire for his son Eucherius.

Thus, by provoking the enemy with several minor engagements, he prolonged the matter. When Alaric discovered this through secret channels, he reported it to Honorius. Thinking that through this service he would gain a more favorable Honorius, Alaric, through the same ambassadors whom he had sent to reveal Stilicho’s crime to Honorius, requested a part of Gaul for his people. He promised that they would live under Roman laws, would be of considerable use to the empire and to Roman wars, and would yield to no provincial people in loyalty or obedience toward the Romans.

The emperor, shaken by a double danger, preferred to admit the Goths into part of his dominions rather than prepare destruction for himself and his people through Stilicho’s treachery. Alaric was not the first to report to Honorius the crime Stilicho was plotting. Yet Stilicho did not consider it safe to remove at any time a man who, through two marriages, was his father-in-law and who possessed power and wealth beyond a private station.

Accordingly, together with the Gothic ambassadors, he sent a letter to Stilicho ordering him to allow the Goths to go to Gaul at the earliest opportunity.

This message was harsh and unwelcome to Stilicho. He saw that he was being cheated of so great a hope and suspected that his plans had been exposed. His fierce and violent mind hesitated for some time; finally, following the safer course, he replied that he would obey the orders of his emperor.

But lest the whole matter slip from his hands, he secretly prepared a certain Saul, who, following closely upon the Goths, was to kill several thousand of them at an opportune moment and drive the irritable people to break the treaty.

Saul attacked them on the Lord’s Day, the day on which, according to the ancient custom of our religion, we abstain from work. The Goths were wholly devoted to sacred observances. In the first confusion he struck down several of them.

The Goths, suddenly terrified, deliberated, as far as was possible amid the panic, whether they should take up arms. For it seemed religiously wrong to handle weapons, shed human blood, and kill human beings on the feast day of the Savior.

But when the Jews did not cease killing and slaughtering, each man made his own decision, without waiting for a common resolution, and took up arms for his own defense. When a considerable number had gathered under arms, Alaric quickly formed a battle line and easily halted the unmilitary mass of men.

Then, pressing forward somewhat, the Goths routed and put the Jews to flight. They complained that they had been forced by violators of human law to profane and contaminate divine law. Invoking Christ himself, by whose sworn divinity the treaty had been established on both sides, and whose feast they had stained against their will with blood, slaughter, and carnage, they were inflamed with anger and marched through the middle of Italy toward Rome.

Stilicho had dismissed some soldiers as useless in the absence of war. He was forced to request them back from the emperor, together with reinforcements, so that the Goths’ efforts might be met with the greatest possible forces.

Honorius, having discovered Stilicho’s plans, sent a large force of soldiers against him, secretly instructing the commanders to seize a suitable opportunity and kill Stilicho and his son.

After consulting together and setting a day on which they would vigorously carry out the emperor’s orders, they attacked Stilicho and his son separately and killed both of them, along with several of their associates who were preparing resistance, in the Forum of Peace at Rome.

Yet the imprudent and cowardly emperor, after removing his commander, appointed no one in his place. I suppose he feared that someone who acquired equal power might plot similar things.

Thus the army, left without any principal commander, was miserably defeated by the Goths, and through many disasters acquired an immense terror of the Gothic name.

The victorious Goths marched with hostile standards against the city of Rome. After pressing it for a long time under siege, they captured and plundered it, with greater tumult and destruction of property than with massacres, sexual violations, or the other horrible and shameful crimes that soldiers’ insolence usually perpetrates in conquered cities.

For before entering the city, Alaric had posted two orders in the camp. The first commanded the Goths to abstain from slaughter and violation of persons, since he would be displeased by such acts. The second declared that anyone who harmed a person seeking refuge in the temples of the apostles, or who violated the temples themselves, would be punished by death.

Rome was captured by the Goths 1,164 years after its foundation, on the Kalends of April, during the consulship of Flavius and Varro.

The historians of these events explain the manner of its capture only poorly. Baptista Egnatius says that he derives his account from the Greek Procopius, and he wonders whether the translator knowingly and prudently passed over that passage, or, if he happened upon a mutilated manuscript, failed to notice adequately what was missing.

I have not yet seen the Greek Procopius. The responsibility for accuracy will rest with Egnatius, a diligent and well-educated man, as far as I can judge from his writings.

He therefore writes:

“Alaric had besieged Rome for two years, and Honorius, who was idling at Ravenna, could neither provide assistance nor dare to do so. Since he was concerned about nothing less than the safety of the City, after Stilicho had been killed he had appointed no commander over the army to conduct the war against the Goths. Hence the Goths conceived the idea of besieging the City, while the Roman soldiers had either dispersed or were conducting the campaign sluggishly.

“Yet when they were unable to capture it by force, although they had besieged it in vain, the barbarian enemy turned to deceit. He pretended that he was departing for his homeland and selected three hundred young men distinguished in body and spirit, whom he presented as a gift to the Roman leaders. He first instructed them to strive to win the favor of their masters through every form of obedience and, on a fixed day, around midday, when the Roman leaders were occupied with sleep or leisure, to hurry to the Asinarian Gate. There they were to kill the guards by a surprise attack and open the gate for their comrades, who would be waiting nearby.

“Meanwhile, while the Goths repeatedly postponed their return by pretending that one thing after another was lacking, the three hundred young men made excellent use of the opportunity. In broad daylight they opened the gate for their people, and once the Goths had been admitted, they plundered the entire city, causing greater disgrace than material loss.”

Some think that the gate was opened to the Goths through the agency of Proba, a distinguished and exceedingly wealthy woman, who pitied the Roman populace as it fell everywhere from hunger and disease like cattle.

There are two matters not unworthy of notice. First, Alaric issued an order that no violence should be inflicted upon anyone who fled to the temples of the gods, especially those of Peter and Paul; and this order was observed with complete fidelity.

Second, when it was reported to Honorius at Ravenna that Rome had been lost, he believed that the report referred to a fighting cock named Rome. He was greatly astonished that it had perished so suddenly, since he had been playing most cheerfully with it shortly before.

This is Egnatius’ account.

That most accursed and impious people attributed all these disasters to the Christian religion, denying that Rome would ever have been captured if they had maintained the religious practices of the gods cultivated by their ancestors and handed down to their descendants.

As though, for the very same reason—because human law had been violated—the Gauls had not once captured and destroyed the City when, as they say, those most impious insanities were at their height! As though many Christian emperors had not administered affairs exceptionally well! As though the decline of the empire and its evident fall toward ruin had not begun under pagan emperors! And as though Honorius had not lost Rome through the same negligence and cowardice by which Gallienus lost Egypt, Asia, and Gaul—concerning the reports of whose losses he had amused himself with witty remarks!

Against these men, then, who were enemies and hostile to the holy religion even if no disaster had occurred, Augustine wrote twenty-two books, *The City of God*—that is, defending the Christian religion against their furious and impious complaints.

# Observations on the Books of *The City of God*

## Book I

### Chapter 1

“Are not those Romans also hostile to the name of Christ for whom the barbarians spared people because of Christ? The places of the martyrs and the basilicas of the apostles testify to this: during that devastation of the City they received within themselves those who fled to them, both their own people and strangers.”

Yet it should not have been concealed that these barbarians were Christians, although they followed the sect of Arius. See Paul Orosius, book VII, chapter 6, at the end. But then the heretics would have had to be praised, and the remarkable nature of the event diminished—something a simpler writer might have done, but not a crafty rhetorician.

### Chapter 3

“See to what sort of gods the Romans joyfully entrusted the preservation of their city. O most lamentable error!” and so forth.

He is mocking, naturally, the gods who could preserve neither their temples nor their statues. Lactantius does the same in book II, chapter 4, of the *Divine Institutes*, and elsewhere. Other ancient Christians did so as well. But, unless I am mistaken, they acted imprudently, since similar objections could in some measure be directed against the Jews, who nevertheless worshiped the true God.

In other instances too, less prudent Christians did the same: they hurled at the pagans objections that the pagans had hurled at them, as learned men have observed. If they had been more prudent, they ought to have used, in defense of the Christian religion, weapons that had never been and could never have been useful to the pagans, since truth has nothing in common with falsehood.

But rhetoricians, excessively eager to seize upon what seems plausible, paid no attention at all to such counsels.

## Chapter 5

“Caesar also does not fail to mention this custom in his own speech, which he delivered concerning the conspirators in the Senate, just as Sallustius writes—Sallustius, that historian distinguished for the nobility of his truthfulness.”]

When I first read this, I immediately thought that *nobilitatus* should be read here. But after consulting Erasmus’s edition, I saw that this was a typographical error, and that *nobilitate* should be read—that is, “with distinguished truthfulness.” The Benedictines observe, however, that in all the manuscripts the reading is not *Caesar* but *Cato*; yet because the words Augustine later quotes occur in Caesar’s speech, not Cato’s, the name was altered by the critics. They themselves suspect that Augustine may have suffered a lapse of memory. We are all the more willing to agree with them because Augustine, while occupied with another matter and seeing that these words suited the purpose of Cato’s speech better than Caesar’s, may for that reason have attributed them to Cato. When the mind is seriously fixed upon some subject, memory is often less reliable.

## Chapter 9

“While taking thought for their reputation and safety, as they feared the plots and attacks of evil men.”]

Joannes Fridericus Gronovius long ago observed, in his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 17, that the word *consulentes* is absent from the manuscripts and should therefore be deleted. Augustine often speaks in this way, as below in chapter 30: “Fearing this calamity for you”; and in chapter 32: “That overthrow of virtue and honor which that Scipio feared for you.” The Parisian editors confirmed this observation by their judgment.

## Chapter 17

“And consequently, as for those women who killed themselves, lest they suffer anything of this sort—lest they, consecrated women, be violated by soldiers—what human feeling would not wish them forgiven?”]

He discusses this matter at length in what follows, where he rightly and firmly attacks *αὐτοχειρίαν* (*autocheiria*, self-killing). Yet it is one thing to wish forgiveness for those who acted similarly in an extreme situation, with their minds overwhelmed by the terror of danger; it is another to approve the act itself. I nevertheless wish that our Augustine had been more equitable toward Lucretia and Cato, since pagan declaimers might have cast similar accusations against Christian virgins and more fervent martyrs. But after the Pelagian controversies he was more hostile to them than all the pagans had been, because he maintained that nothing was good without grace—that is, without an unusual divine inspiration—and he did not wish that grace to be attributed to pagans.

## Chapter 26

“Certain holy women, during the persecution, threw themselves into a river that would carry them away and kill them, in order to escape their persecutors and avoid the violation of their chastity; and in this way they died. Their martyrdoms are celebrated with the greatest veneration throughout the Catholic Church.”]

Such were the daughters of Domnina, Bernice and Prosdoce, whose feast the Greeks celebrate on 4 October and concerning whom there is an elegant homily by John Chrysostom in volume 1, homily 51. Theod. Ruinart inserted it in Latin into his *Sincere and Selected Acts of the Martyrs*, where, in the prefatory notice, he also presents certain other material on this subject that is not unworthy of reading.

### Ibid.

“Concerning these women I venture to judge nothing rashly. For whether divine authority persuaded the Church, through certain trustworthy testimonies, to honor their memory in this way, I do not know.”]

It is much more credible that neighboring churches first enrolled these virgins among the martyrs, judging that whatever sin there had been was sufficiently expiated by the disposition in which they had fallen into it—that is, by their love of undefiled chastity and of the Christian religion. Certainly many things are praised in which such courage did not shine forth as brightly as it did in acts that require apology. Accordingly, Chrysostom did not hesitate to praise their deed and to call it a new and unprecedented baptism. Things established in the Church often creep into it gradually and without any mature deliberation. Indeed, even in councils, where everything was decided by votes, it was not the more learned—who were few—but the majority, that is, the unlearned or at least those superior in authority and eloquence, who were listened to, as everyone knows; nor was Augustine himself unaware of this.

# Book II

## Chapter 3

“But remember that, in mentioning these matters, I am still arguing against the ignorant, whose ignorance also gave rise to that common proverb: ‘There is no rain because of the Christians.’ For there are some who, trained in liberal studies, take pleasure in history and therefore know these matters very easily; but, in order to make the mobs of the uneducated violently hostile to us, they pretend not to know them, and so on.”]

They knew, namely, what Augustine had said earlier: that droughts and other calamities of this kind had occurred no less before the Christian era than afterward. No one has developed and refuted this objection more fully, with a greater abundance of examples, than Arnobius in book I *Against the Pagans*. Among the learned men Augustine mentions, that Symmachus who was prefect of the City must also be counted. He makes such statements in the report submitted to Valentinian in the year 384, which Ambrose refuted. See section 14 in the Ambrosian edition. At Augustine’s request, Paul Orosius undertook to write a history in order to refute that slander, as he himself testifies in the preface addressed to Augustine.

## Chapter 7

After reproaching the pagan gods for supplying their worshipers with no precepts of virtue, he continues:

“Will they perhaps remind us of the schools and disputations of the philosophers? … These are not precepts of the gods, but inventions of human beings, who, endowed with exceptionally keen intellects, nevertheless made some effort, by reasoning, to investigate what lay hidden in the nature of things, what ought to be desired in conduct, what ought to be avoided, and so forth.”]

The religion that the pagans called religion was, of course, a kind of superstitious discipline concerning the rites of worship by which they thought the gods could be appeased. This was to be learned from priests and pontiffs, not from philosophers. But anyone who wished to know what should be thought about the divine power and how one’s conduct should be ordered had to turn to the philosophers.

Let us hear on this subject the most eloquent of the Latin Fathers, Lactantius, in book IV, chapter 3, of the *Divine Institutes*, where he discusses true wisdom:

“The worship of the gods,” he says, “does not possess wisdom—not only because it subjects the divine creature, the human being, to earthly and fragile things, but also because nothing is discussed there that contributes to the cultivation of morals and the shaping of life, nor does it contain any inquiry into truth, but only a rite of worship, which consists not in the service of the mind but in the ministry of the body. Therefore it must not be judged a true religion, since it instructs in no precepts of justice or virtue and does not make people better. Philosophy, then, because it does not possess true religion—that is, supreme piety—is not true wisdom.”

“Since, therefore, as I have said, philosophy and the religion of the gods are separate and widely divided—since some are teachers of wisdom, through whom one certainly does not approach the gods, while others are ministers of religion, through whom one does not learn wisdom—it is evident that neither the former is true wisdom nor the latter true religion,” and so forth.

In my judgment, this objection should be regarded as one of the greatest and strongest by which pagan superstition could have been shaken and utterly destroyed, and by which the Christian religion could have been illuminated and confirmed, whenever Christians had to deal with pagans who were somewhat better educated.

## Chapter 17

“Or is it perhaps because, as Sallustius says, the Roman people had no laws established by the divine powers, since among them right and justice prevailed no more through laws than through nature? I suppose that the Sabine women were carried off by this right and justice. For what could be more just and better than that the daughters of others, lured by the deception of a spectacle, should not be received from their parents but seized by force, each man taking whichever he could?”]

Augustine rightly mocks here, and in what follows, the boasts that the Romans made about the virtue of the founders of their republic and of the generations immediately following them. For, as he shows from Sallustius—and likewise from Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus—it is clear that those ancient Romans were harassed at home by perpetual seditions born of the intolerable injustice of the nobility, while abroad they afflicted all their neighbors with wars that were not conducted without the greatest injustice, inhumanity, and cruelty, although historians conceal these things beneath impressive names such as love of empire, patriotism, and courage.

If Roman history were written without embellishment, employing not the rhetorical colors by which vice is sold as virtue, nor rashly preconceived opinions, but the light of right reason and true virtue, it would become clear that those highly praised ancient Romans were mere brigands: enemies to one another at home, and never united except to harass their neighbors with brigandage. If they had not yet been weakened by luxury, because they were still poor, they were not thereby better than when they began to sin more expensively and luxuriously.

Who, indeed, would value the barbarous harshness of the Scythians—whom we now call Muscovites or Tartars—more highly than the softer wickedness of the southern peoples? I admit that their poor barbarism is better for war and for repelling enemies; but is it better with respect to morals—that is, more just, more temperate, or more prudent? I do not think so. In both cases there is barbarism and savagery, whether joined with luxury or with a poorer manner of life and diet.

But people wearied and impatient of the vices of their own age habitually prefer past times to the present. Had they lived in those earlier periods, they would have poured out similar complaints and sought greater virtue and happiness in still more ancient ages. If more recent Romans had seriously recalled these things to mind, no one would have said with Juvenal, *Satire* 3:

> Happy were the forefathers of our great-grandfathers, and happy those ages  
> which once, under kings and tribunes, saw Rome content with a single prison!

## Chapter 25

“Many people had already been moved by the story of a certain soldier who, while stripping the spoils from a slain man, recognized his brother after the corpse had been stripped; and, cursing the civil wars, killed himself there and joined himself to his brother’s body.”]

In the *Catalecta of the Ancient Poets*, edited by Joseph Scaliger, there are two exceedingly elegant epigrams on Maevius, who unknowingly killed his brother. But this pitiable deed is assigned to the Actian War, which Augustus waged against Antony, whereas the event narrated here belongs to the beginning of Sulla’s war and occurred in the battle fought by Gnaeus Pompeius against Lucius Cornelius Cinna, concerning which Livy writes in book 79. The same thing may have happened twice, or the poet may have referred to another war in which a similar event occurred.

> The poets’ fertile license extends without limit  
> and does not bind its words to historical truth.

## Chapter 27

“The serious man and would-be philosopher Tullius, soon to be an aedile, was shouting, and so forth.”]

Although Augustine rightly despised pagan philosophy when compared with Christian wisdom, he always held Cicero in the highest esteem and spoke of him everywhere with honor. Perhaps he owed Cicero much of what he knew about philosophy, since, as is well known, he never went to the Greek sources. I therefore cannot persuade myself that Cicero was treated by Augustine with such contempt that he called him a “would-be philosopher.”

Most manuscripts read *philosophus Tertullius*. Others have *Tertullius*. One Corbie manuscript has *philosophaster Tullius*, the reading Ludovicus Vives conjectured. I believe that the ancient codices originally read *PHILOSOPHUS M. TULLIUS*. Then, because a hurried scribe read or wrote *III* in place of *M*, the sign was subsequently reproduced three times. Hence arose *philosophus Tertullius*, or “three-times Tullius,” or finally *philosophaster Tullius*—unless I am mistaken, against Augustine’s intention. Augustine believed that philosophy had been begun and perfected by Cicero in the Latin language, *Against the Academics*, book I, section 8.

Indeed, in this very passage the word *gravis* (“serious,” “weighty”) shows that Augustine wished to speak of him honorably; nor do the words *gravis* and *philosophaster* agree with one another.

# Book III

## Chapter 4

“The very learned Varro of their number almost admits, though not boldly or confidently, that these things are false. Yet he says that it is useful for states that brave men should believe themselves born from the gods, even if this is false, so that in this way the human spirit, bearing as it were the confidence of divine descent, may more boldly undertake great deeds, and so forth.”]

No one even moderately skilled in philosophy believed that the eternal divine power could be captivated by love for women. More sensible thinkers therefore had to seek the reasons why ancient tradition proclaimed so many sons of the gods. Varro reported one such explanation in one of the many books he wrote, most of which have perished.

Nevertheless, I would judge that those sons of the gods were, for the most part, the products of the deceptions of priests and little women—whether deceived themselves or voluntarily unchaste. When lustful priests had violated a virgin in the temple or sacred grove of some divine power, and it was not in their interest to marry her in order to preserve her honor, they would say that the child had been born from that divinity. The girl and her relatives did not deny the matter, since this fraud served to protect the honor of the violated woman. In the earliest times, uncultivated people, refined by no studies, foolishly allowed themselves to be persuaded of such things. Joannes Clericus discussed this matter at greater length in his notes on Hesiod’s *Theogony*.

## Chapter 10

“Or do they reply that, unless the Roman empire had been enlarged by wars that were constant and followed one another without interruption, it could not have grown so far and wide or been celebrated with such great glory?”]

J. Fridericus Gronovius rightly observed here that *diffamari* is equivalent to *celebrari* (“to be celebrated”) and that the word can be taken in either sense; he proves this from Nonius Marcellus. He adds that the manuscript parchment copies do not contain *succedentibus* and thinks that *assiduis sibique continuis bellis* should be read instead. *Observations*, book III, chapter 16. I am surprised that the Benedictines did not mention this variant reading.

As for the word *diffamare*, Augustine not infrequently uses it in a favorable sense, as in chapter 31 of this book: “The reception and spread of the Christian religion among the Romans would have been much less tolerable to them if it had been followed by either that invasion of the Gauls, or that devastation by the Tiber’s flooding and by fires, or—what precedes every evil—civil wars.”

## Chapter 18

“Those sacred objects connected with destiny, which had already weighed upon the three cities in which they had been kept … the pontiff Metellus, having in a certain sense forgotten his own safety, rushed in and carried them away, half-burned.”]

Justus Lipsius shows that Troy, Lanuvium, and Alba are correctly understood here, in his *Syntagma on Vesta and the Vestal Virgins*, chapter 2, where he explains this passage of Augustine at length.

## Chapter 31

“When earth rained, when clay rained, when stones rained—not stones in the sense in which hail is usually called by that name, but stones in the literal sense—these things could certainly have caused serious harm.”

When they said that it had rained stones, I believe that they meant exceptionally large hail, especially since Augustine observes that hail is so called when it is larger than usual. The author of *The African War*, chapter 47, writes: “During the second watch of the night, a huge storm arose with a STONY HAIL.”

### Ibid.

“They recorded in writing that the multitude of locusts in Africa was like a portent, when Africa had already become a province of the Roman people.”]

Anyone who wishes to see this matter illustrated by a great number of examples should consult Samuel Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, part 2, book IV, chapters 1–6, and Joannes Clericus’s dissertation on the salt statue appended to his commentary on Genesis.

### Ibid.

“Then at Utica they affirm that, out of thirty thousand young men who were there, ten remained.”]

The Benedictines rightly observed that *juniores* here means soldiers of the garrison. You will find this confirmed by numerous examples in Justus Lipsius, *Epistolical Questions*, book I, letter 1.

# Book IV

## Chapter 4

“When justice is removed, what are kingdoms except great robberies? For what are robberies themselves except little kingdoms?”]

The sentence would flow more smoothly if, with the mark of interrogation placed before it, we read *quin* instead of *quia*. Lactantius, book V of the *Divine Institutes*, has much that is elegant and true on the subject itself.

## Chapter 8

“For in this work, so illustrious and so full of dignity, by which the boundaries of the Roman empire were extended, they do not dare to assign any part to the goddess Cloacina, or to Volupia, or to Vaticanus, who presides over the cries of infants, or to Cunina, who takes care of their cradles.”]

The Parisian editors testify that not only several editions but also the manuscripts read not *Vaticano* but *Vagitano*. I do not understand why they did not adopt this reading in the text, since the other divine names show that this name too ought to have been derived from *vagitus* (“a cry”). See also chapter 21.

I know that Varro’s passage is quoted by Aulus Gellius in book XVI, chapter 17, and that he seems to favor the reading *Vaticanus*. But since that etymology is absurd, I think that the deity was commonly called *Vagitanus*.

## Chapter 9

“Varro believes that this Jupiter is also worshiped by those who worship one God alone, without an image, but call him by another name.”]

On this opinion of Varro, see what Joannes Clericus observed in part 2, section 1, chapter 13, of his *Art of Criticism*.

## Chapter 10

“For who could tolerate the fact that, although they attributed so much honor and something like chastity to fire, they were sometimes not ashamed even to call Vesta Venus?”]

Justus Lipsius rightly observed in his *Syntagma on Vesta and the Vestal Virgins*, chapter 2, that examples of Vesta being called Venus are scarcely to be found, and that there is no sufficiently clear explanation of the matter unless perhaps the heat of love is compared with fire. Consult him if you have the opportunity.

## Chapter 13

“But if they maintain that only rational animals, such as human beings, are parts of God, I do not see—if the whole universe is God—how they separate animals from his parts.”]

He means the Stoics, who said that the universe is God. See Justus Lipsius, *Physiology of the Stoics*, book I, dissertation 8.

## Chapter 16

“They called … the goddess Murcia, who moved and made a person, as Pomponius says, *murcidus*—that is, excessively sluggish and inactive.”]

Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chapter 8, writes:

“They wish Murcia to be the goddess of slackness (*marcor*), to whom they vowed a temple in that place.”

Thus it should be read, not *marmoris* or *amoris*, as some have emended it. The ancients nowhere reported that Murcia was the goddess of love, but rather of slackness and idleness; for *murcus* meant the same among the ancients as “sluggish.” Hence, in the later period of Latin, men who had cut off their thumbs so as not to be enrolled for military service were jokingly called *murci*. Ammianus Marcellinus writes:

“Nor did any one of them, as in Italy, fearing military service, ever cut off his own thumb; such men are jokingly called *murci*.”

They used the term for the idle, sluggish, and unwarlike. *Murcus*, *murcidus*, just as *flaccus*, *flaccidus*. Festus writes: “*Murcidum*: sluggish, foolish.” Plautus has: “Sluggish man, coward, good-for-nothing.” The printed editions wrongly have *murricide*, which Scaliger explained as *μυοκτόνον* (*myoktonon*), that is, “mouse-killer.” Arnobius writes: “Murcia, goddess of the sluggish.” Claudius Salmasius discusses these and other matters in his edition of Solinus, page 636, Utrecht edition.

## Chapter 19

“They attribute so much to this power, as to a divinity, whom they call Fortune, that they have even committed to memory that her image, which had been dedicated by the matrons, spoke, and that it said—not once but twice—that the matrons had dedicated it properly.”]

Valerius Maximus, book I, chapter 4 of the *Memorable Deeds and Sayings of the Romans*, according to Justus Lipsius’s emendation, has:

“It is established that the image spoke not once but twice, first with these words: ‘MATRONS, YOU HAVE LOOKED UPON ME PROPERLY’; then: ‘YOU HAVE DEDICATED ME PROPERLY.’”

This is the true reading, and it appears to have been before Augustine’s eyes.

## Chapter 21

“Goddess Fructesea.”]

The manuscript copies of Augustine, in the words of Claudius Salmasius on Solinus, page 50 of the Utrecht edition, which we once saw in Germany, had: “and especially to the goddess Frutes Seia”; in others it was *Frutisseia*. I think Augustine wrote: “To the goddess of produce, Seia” (*Divae frugis, Seiae*). He calls Seia, or Sea, the goddess of produce, to whom farmers chiefly prayed that she might promote the abundance of their crops. The same Augustine, in book IV, chapter 8, says from Varro that she was set over the crops while they were still beneath the earth. Pliny states that Seia was so called from *serere*, “to sow,” book XVIII, chapter 2.

## Chapter 31

“The same exceptionally acute and learned author, Varro, says that those alone seem to him to have understood what God is who believed him to be the spirit governing the universe by movement and reason.”]

“The word *motu*,” says Justus Lipsius, *Physiology of the Stoics*, book II, dissertation 10, “is not entirely inappropriate, I admit; nevertheless, I would more truly believe that *mente* should be read.”

Cicero, *First Academica*, concerning the Stoics, writes:

“They say that the universe is held together by a sentient nature in which perfect reason resides, which is likewise eternal. They call that power the spirit of the universe, and they say that it is the same as the perfect mind and wisdom which they call God.”

I, however, do not think that anything should be changed in the common reading. Manilius speaks almost in this way, not far from the beginning of book II, where he says that he has determined to sing of God, who governs all things:

> and that the whole universe lives in alternating harmony  
> and is moved by the MOTION OF REASON, while one spirit  
> dwells throughout its interconnected parts, and so forth.

# Book V

## Chapter 1

“Human kingdoms are established wholly by divine providence. If anyone attributes them to fate because he calls the will or power of God itself by the name ‘fate,’ let him retain his opinion but correct his language. Why does he not say at the outset what he will say later, when someone asks him what he meant by fate?”]

This is an exceedingly beautiful statement, worthy of being inscribed in golden letters in the lecture halls of philosophers and theologians, so that they may learn to speak clearly at once. This would save time by removing so many empty words that require lengthy explanations; once these have been heard, we learn nothing new concerning the matters themselves, but merely understand the use of scholastic language.

Anyone who reads dissertations 12 and following in book I of Justus Lipsius’s *Physiology of the Stoics* will understand why this warning concerning fate was necessary. There Lipsius maintains that fate is the effect of divine providence, and he shows that many of the ancients also held this belief.

## Chapter 10

After presenting in chapter 9 Cicero’s argument, by which he tried to prove that, if anything lay within our power, God could not have foreknown it with certainty, since it might fail to occur—or that, if everything were foreknown by God with certainty, nothing would lie within our power, since everything would happen necessarily—Augustine replies in chapter 10, but in such a way that he seems either not to have perceived the force of the objection or, if he perceived it, to have concealed it.

“Therefore,” he says, “it is not the case that nothing is in our will because God foreknew what would occur in our will.”

But Cicero had said “in our power,” meaning what we were able either to refuse or to will, so that the will would not necessarily be bent toward one or the other—as it is naturally disposed to assent to manifest truth and to desire happiness.

Here, as elsewhere, Augustine confuses what is voluntary with what is free, although these are distinct in ordinary human speech. We assent to an evident proposition voluntarily, but not freely; similarly, we desire happiness voluntarily, but not freely. For we cannot refuse to assent to what is evident, refuse to be happy, or deliberate about these matters.

He adds: “For the one who foreknew this did not foreknow nothing.” But Cicero did not deny that God foreknows something; he denied only that God foreknows free acts. Augustine continues:

“If he foreknew what would occur in our will, then he certainly foreknew not nothing but something; and, while he foreknows it, something exists in our will.”

This is true, but Cicero would have denied that what God foreknows will occur in our will is within our power. Such things include desiring happiness and assenting to what is clear. These do indeed belong to our will—we assent and desire willingly—but they are not within our power, since we cannot move in the opposite direction.

“Therefore,” says the Carthaginian philosopher, “we are in no way compelled either to abolish freedom of the will while retaining God’s foreknowledge—or, while retaining freedom of the will, to deny God, which would be impious, the foreknowledge of future events.”

He should have added “free” after “will,” that is, free to incline in either direction. “But we embrace both; we faithfully and truthfully confess both: the one so that we may believe rightly, the other so that we may live rightly. We live badly if we do not believe rightly concerning God.”

I gladly accept these final statements. But if Cicero had risen from the underworld, or if some Ciceronian philosopher had replied to Augustine, he would have denied that Augustine retained free will. Augustine himself does not deny this when he speaks outside the heat of controversy. See the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 30, in volume VI.

He continues:

“Therefore laws, reproaches, exhortations, praises, and censures are not without purpose, because he foreknew that these too would occur, and they are effective to the extent that he foreknew they would be effective. Prayers are effective for obtaining the things that he foreknew he would grant to those who pray; and rewards for good deeds and punishments for sins have justly been established.”

Both would be unjust if we were no more able to abstain from good deeds and sins than from assenting to an evident proposition or desiring happiness. The other things likewise are not without purpose because human beings are free—that is, they do not sin merely willingly, for the human mind acts only by willing, but also freely, so that they could refuse what they willed and will what they refused.

The ground of the laws that God imposes upon free creatures is not foreknowledge, but the holiness of God and the freedom of creatures.

“For a human being does not sin because God foreknew that he would sin.”

The better manuscripts, as the Benedictines testify, read here: “For a human being does not therefore *not* sin.” But this double negation does not seem to have greater force than a single one. On this matter see Gerardus Joannes Vossius, *On the Art of Grammar*, book VII, chapter 61. Alternatively, the second negation should be placed in the following clause: “because God foreknew that he would not sin.”

This is certainly true, but a Ciceronian would have replied that, according to Augustine’s position, a person sins because he could not refrain from sinning, and that for the same reason God foreknew this. Otherwise God would not have foreknown it if the act were free.

Nor would Augustine escape the force of Cicero’s argument in the following words:

“Indeed, it is for this reason that there is no doubt that a person sins when he sins: the one whose foreknowledge cannot be deceived foreknew that he himself would sin—not fate, not fortune, nor anything else.”

But it is not true that we believe human beings sin because God foreknew that they would sin. We believe it because we see them violating the divine laws, and we are conscious that they could have refrained from violating them, since they share the same freedom that we do.

“But if he does not wish to sin,” our Carneades finally says, “he certainly does not sin.”

“Yet if he had not wished to sin, God also foreknew this.”

Certainly, if a person does not wish to sin, he does not sin. But he must be able to will and not will in order to be capable of sin; and Augustine should have shown, against Cicero, that God can foreknow as future an act that the person who will perform it will be able not to will.

From this one can see how great the difference is between rhetorical cleverness and philosophical reasoning.

## Chapter 15

“Concerning the Romans: Since God was not going to give them eternal life … if he did not grant them this earthly glory of an exceptionally great empire, the reward for their good qualities—that is, the virtues by which they strove to attain such glory—would not be paid to them.”]

Yet earlier Augustine showed that these virtues were mere vices. For, as he says in chapter 13, in pursuit of honor, praise, and glory they served their country, in which they sought glory itself, and did not hesitate to place its safety before their own. For this one vice—that is, the love of praise—they suppressed their desire for money and many other vices.

But for that reason God did not owe them a reward. It would have been better to say that God permitted them, or even for certain reasons known only to himself wished them, to possess power over the world rather than another people.

Two further considerations should be added. First, the ancient Romans were not what their descendants sometimes portray them as being, as Augustine himself demonstrated in book II, where we also said something about the matter. Second, the neighboring peoples of Italy and even of Greece, as well as others whom there is no need to name, were in no way inferior to the ancient Romans in their morals, and therefore were not less pleasing to God.

## Chapter 17

“Are there not many senators in other lands who do not even know Rome by sight?”]

This was not new in Augustine’s time. It had already occurred under Claudius, when the inhabitants of Gallia Comata demanded that honors be granted to them at Rome. The Italians commonly asked: “Was it not enough that the Veneti and Insubres burst into the Senate House, unless a gathering of foreigners were to be introduced like a captivity?” Tacitus, *Annals*, book XI, chapter 23.

# Book VI

## Chapter 1, § 2

“Or will those exceptionally skilled and acute men, who boast that they have taught matters committed to writing as a great benefit—Varro, whom he discussed in book IV, chapter 22—so that it might be known why one should pray to each god and what should be requested from each, be able to advise someone praying to the immortal gods that, after he has asked wine from the Water-Nymphs and they have replied, ‘We have water; ask Liber for that,’ he may rightly say: ‘If you do not have wine, at least give me eternal life’?”]

The printed books had *Nymphis*, but the manuscripts consistently have *Lymphis*, as the Benedictines observe. Learned men Nicolaus Heinsius, in his notes on the *Letter of Oenone to Paris*, line 31, and Janus Broukhusius, on Propertius, book III, elegy 14, line 4, have noted that these words are often confused in ancient books.

Nevertheless, I think that Augustine actually wrote *Lymphas*. Although *Nymphae* can also refer to Oreads and Hamadryads, *Lymphae* seems to have denoted only those nymphs who presided over waters, even though the word is derived from *Nymphae* through the change of *N* into *L*.

Festus writes:

“*Lymphae* are so called from *Nymphae*. It is commonly recorded that whoever saw some sort of apparition from a spring—that is, an image of a nymph—did not cease to rage; the Greeks call such people *νυμφόληπτοι* (*nympholēptoi*, nymph-possessed), while the Latins call them *lymphati*.”

See *Aeneid* VII, 377.

## Chapter 9, § 1

“They wish Liber to have been named from *liberamentum*, because males, in sexual intercourse, are freed through his benefit when their seed is emitted.”]

Seneca refers to this in *On Benefits*, book IV, chapter 8:

“Our people think that Liber Pater, Hercules, and Mercury are this one god. Liber Pater, because he is the father of all things, since the power of seed was first discovered by him, destined to provide for posterity through pleasure.”

I do not know what could have been invented that is more absurd, both in matter and in etymology. Yet Varro’s etymologies are better than his theology.

## Chapter 10, § 2

“There are women who arrange the hair of Juno and Minerva; standing far from the temple, and not merely from the image, they move their fingers in the manner of women dressing hair.”]

Seneca says similar things in letter 95. Tertullian, in *On Fasting*, chapter 16, shows that this service was called “performing a toilette”:

“Those who are said to perform a toilette in adorning idols and decorating altars, and in greeting them at every hour.”

### Ibid.

“Certain women sit on the Capitol who think that they are loved by Jupiter; nor are they frightened by Juno—even if you choose to believe the poets—although she is exceedingly wrathful.”]

Thus Seneca spoke in his splendid book *On Superstition*, which I would prefer to have been copied out by the monks and carefully transmitted to us rather than so many cold homilies. Perhaps immodest little women, captivated by love for the temple custodians, sat on the Capitol so that, if they happened to become pregnant, they could persuade fools that they had given birth to a child by Jupiter. The story of Mundus and Paulina, in Josephus, is well known. See also what Joannes Clericus noted concerning the sons of the gods in his commentary on Hesiod’s *Theogony*.

## Chapter 11

“To such an extent did the custom of that most wicked nation prevail that it has now been adopted throughout all lands; the conquered gave laws to their conquerors.”]

These are certainly ill-considered words of Seneca concerning the Jews. Rutilius Namatianus seems to have referred to them in his *Itinerary*, line 395:

> Would that Judaea had never been subdued  
> by the wars and empire of Pompey and Titus!  
> The contagion of the destroyed pest spreads farther;  
> the conquered nation oppresses its conquerors.

# Book VII

## Chapter 1

“On this matter I will not mention what Tertullian perhaps says more wittily than truly: ‘If gods are selected like onions, then surely the rest are judged rejected.’”]

The Benedictines noted in the margin that something similar occurs in the *Apologeticus*, chapter 13. But the actual words are found in the work *Against the Nations*, book II, chapter 9, where the exceptionally learned Nicolaus Rigaltius observes that Augustine has unfairly ridiculed this statement of Tertullian.

Indeed, in what is called God there can be no selection, just as there can be among human beings, from whom Augustine improperly takes his examples. All the gods ought to be able to do all things, as Rigaltius likewise observes.

## Chapter 2

“There is Liber, who frees the male through the emission of seed. There is Libera, whom they also wish to be Venus, who grants this same benefit to the female, so that she too is freed when her seed has been emitted.”]

Augustine said these things in chapter 9 of the preceding book. I am surprised that a bishop—and a serious and elderly one, although in his youth he had led a sufficiently lustful life—should so often speak *περὶ τοῦ σπέρματος* (“about semen”) in a work also intended to be read by women and adolescents.

I know that these were the obscenities of the pagans, but it would have been better to touch upon them in more general terms than to repeat them in a way offensive to chaste ears. See also what he says in the same chapter about Subigo, Prema, and Pertunda. Elsewhere we shall note other matters no more decent, in a more serious context.

## Chapter 14

“If Mercury himself is speech, as even they themselves admit, then he is not God.”]

I am surprised that Augustine was not afraid that someone would object to him on the basis of what he repeatedly says about the Word. For a similar objection could have been raised, and Augustine’s response could likewise have been evaded.

### Chapter 21

“At the crossroads of Italy certain rites of Liber were celebrated, with such license in obscenity that in his honor male genitals were worshiped, etc.” Similar things were done in the rites of Osiris, as Diodorus Siculus teaches in Book I of his *Bibliotheca*, where he supposes that these practices were transmitted by the Egyptians to the Greeks.

### Chapter 26

“As for the effeminate men consecrated to the same Great Mother, against all the modesty of men and women—men who until yesterday, with their hair wet, their faces whitened, their limbs flowing loosely, and their gait feminine, demanded contributions from the crowds in the streets and alleys of Carthage, by which they might live disgracefully—Varro did not wish to say anything, nor do I remember ever having read anything about them.” I am surprised, since innumerable writers have spoken of them; Gérard will indicate several of their passages. See Joannes Vossius, *De Origine et Progressu Idololatriae*, Book III, chapter 53. Consult also Catullus’ poem entitled *Attis*, together with its commentators, who will abundantly supply what Augustine lacks here. Those priests were called *Metragyrtae* (Μητραγύρται); Menander wrote a comedy with that title—if only it still existed!

### Chapter 27

“Euhemerus sets forth the whole history of this matter, which Ennius translated into Latin; and since many writers who before us wrote against errors of this kind, either in Greek or in Latin, have treated it extensively, I have not wished to linger over it.” He seems chiefly to mean Lactantius, who in Book I of the *Divine Institutions* preserved for us fairly extensive fragments of Euhemerus. Some pagan writers judge him unfavorably for having utterly disgraced their religion, although, for the rest, I would not wish to endorse everything he held. I am surprised that Christians did not preserve this material in Greek or Latin.

### Chapter 34

“A certain Terentius owned an estate near the Janiculum. His herdsman, while passing by the tomb of Numa Pompilius and turning up the soil with his plow, unearthed books of Numa’s in which the reasons for the establishment of the rites had been written. He brought them into the city to the praetor. But when the praetor had examined the beginnings of the work, he reported the matter only to the senate. When the leading senators had read some of the reasons why each rite had been instituted, after Numa’s death, the senate agreed, and the enrolled fathers decreed that the praetor should burn the books as religious documents.”

Pliny, Book XIII, chapter 13, also calls the owner of the field in which the books were dug up Gnaeus Terentius, as does Festus under the entry *Numa*. But Livy, Book XL, chapter 29, and Valerius Maximus, Book I, chapter 1, call him Lucius Petillius. Who can say which account is correct? It is not, in truth, of much importance. But it is credible that Numa’s commentaries treated with contempt the superstition of the Roman and Italian populace, whose religious tastes he had been compelled to accommodate. Nothing prevents him from having thought about God in the manner of the philosophers, like Mucius Scaevola and Marcus Terentius Varro, concerning whom see Book IV, chapter 27, and Book VI, chapter 5, while at the same time adapting himself, along with them, to the unreflective multitude.

Augustine, however, says on Varro’s authority that the senate agreed after Numa’s death that, since Numa had arranged for the books to be buried with him so that they might not become known to the people, the senate therefore decreed that they should be burned for the same reason.

## BOOK VIII

### Chapter 9

“Other nations too are found to have had men regarded as wise men or philosophers: Atlanteans, Libyans, Egyptians, Indians, Persians, Chaldaeans, Scythians, Gauls, Spaniards, and others, etc.” Justus Lipsius, in Book I, dissertation 5, of his *Manuductio ad Stoicam Philosophiam*, greatly elucidates this passage and understands the Atlanteans to mean the sages of Mauretania, led there by that Atlas. By the Libyans, or Libyans proper, I would understand either the inhabitants of inner Libya or those of the region neighboring Egypt.

### Chapter 19

“Finally, was Apuleius himself ever accused before Christian judges of magical practices?” From this it was evident that Christians could not be reproached for accusing the Platonists of magic, since Apuleius, a celebrated Platonist, had been accused before Maximus Claudius, a pagan judge.

### Chapter 22

“It remains, then, that we must in no way believe what Apuleius endeavors to persuade us of—and what all other philosophers who hold the same opinion maintain—namely, that demons are intermediaries between gods and human beings, acting as messengers and interpreters: carrying our petitions from here and bringing back the gods’ assistance from there.”

If this is understood of evil demons, it is true that they are not, and cannot be, intermediaries between God and human beings. But I do not see that Augustine proved the contrary concerning good demons, although he treats this matter at intolerable length. Indeed, a considerable number of Christians today hold something of this sort concerning angels. The bishop of Hippo sometimes engages in mere verbal disputation with the Platonists, just as he does with other opponents.

[Col. 0471C] ### Chapter 23

“That Egyptian Hermes, whom they call Trismegistus, thought and wrote differently about them.” Isaac Casaubon demonstrates at length in Dissertation 1 of his *Apparatus to the Annals of Cardinal Baronius* that this Hermes was fabricated by some Christian who wished, through his authority, to confirm the doctrines of the Christian religion—an act of deliberate fraud, unworthy of a lover of truth and of such a man. The matter is so obvious that it is astonishing that the Fathers dared to make use of such nonsense. Perhaps they themselves did not understand the fraud, although it is sufficiently plain; but it is remarkable that they were not hissed off the stage by more sharp-witted pagans.

Certainly those deserved to be mocked with bared teeth who, if they believed the books attributed to those whose names they bore, so eagerly seized upon frauds so badly sewn together. But if they did understand the fraud—which I would not deny—they were doing great injury to the truth, which they attempted to support with disgraceful lies, and they prevented the remnants of paganism from placing faith in the Gospel. In short, we cannot now judge them otherwise than as either very poor critics or men who did not sufficiently understand the force of truth, which certainly has no need of such frauds; nor can we regard them as quite so hostile to falsehood as their published books pretended.

### Chapter 27

“Yet we do not establish temples, priesthoods, rites, and sacrifices for these same martyrs, because it is not they but their God who is our God. Certainly we honor their memories as those of holy men of God, who fought for the truth even to the death of their bodies, etc. But who has ever heard a priest standing at the altar of the faithful—even at an altar built for the honor and worship of God over the sacred body of a martyr—say in his prayers, ‘I offer sacrifice to you, Peter, or Paul, or Cyprian, etc.’?”

Yet the pomp with which their relics were carried, the honor paid to them by kneeling, and the invocations of the saints, as though they heard prayers—an example of which we encountered earlier, in volume V, page 152, column 2—persuaded pagans that the martyrs were worshiped as a kind of lesser gods. Nor, if at last we may speak without concealment, were they far from the truth, since some Christians too were offended by such worship. This is clear from Jerome’s tract, in which that vehement man attacks Vigilantius with abuse because such practices had deeply offended him.

[Col. 0472B] Thus our author answers in the manner of rhetoricians: he conceals the matters raised by the pagans, passes over the worship that was in fact offered to the martyrs’ relics, and which rightly offended the pagans.

## BOOK IX

### Chapter 15

“Yet he is not Mediator on this account, because he is the Word—especially since the immortal and supremely blessed Word is far removed from mortal miseries (not ‘miserable things’), but he is Mediator through whom the human being …”

Indeed. So far as God is concerned, he himself does not need a Mediator whose agency would enable him to act with us; but we can scarcely rise to such majesty without a mediator, and specifically one of our own kind.

### Chapter 22

“Concerning angels. For this reason they know temporal and mutable things even more certainly, because they behold their principal causes in the Word of God, through which the world was made; by these causes some things are approved and others rejected.”

Above all, I would like to know whether those who make such assertions about angels and the Word understand sufficiently what they mean. As far as I am concerned, I confess that I do not understand how angels can see the notions and thoughts of eternal Reason, so that, by contemplating its nature, they know what it wishes or does not wish to happen. To speak frankly, I do not think that anyone can understand how a creature may grasp the mind of the Creator—which he has not revealed—merely by contemplating him.

Next I would like to know where theologians obtained this doctrine: from philosophical reasoning or from Scripture. As for Scripture, I would dare affirm that there is no clear passage from which this can plausibly be deduced. How such things could be inferred from philosophical reasoning, I understand even less. Nevertheless Augustine repeatedly asserts this, as though it were a dogma of Christian theology, and states it with such confidence as though the matter had been established; and the scholastic theologians eagerly adopted it with broad agreement. See what Dionysius Petavius collected on this subject in volume I, Book IV, chapter 2, and volume III, *On Angels*, Book I, chapter 4.

### Chapter 23, §1

“But where God is called ‘God of gods,’ he cannot be understood as ‘God of demons’; and where he is called ‘the great King above all gods,’ heaven forbid that he should be called King above all demons.”

Among the Hebrews, as learned men demonstrated long ago, the word *elohim* signifies whatever is worshiped, σέβασμα (*sebasma*), whether it is in heaven or on earth. Thus, when the true God is called “God of gods,” it is equivalent to calling him the most exalted of all those whom we worship, just as the *Song of Songs* is so called because it is preeminent in its category.

“Although there are those who are called gods,” Paul says in 1 Corinthians 8:5, “whether in heaven or on earth—for indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, etc.” Likewise Psalm 94:3: “The great God is Lord, and the great King above all gods,” equivalent to “King of kings” or “Lord of lords.”

### Same passage

“But Scripture also calls human beings in the people of God gods. ‘I said,’ he says, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’ The God of these gods, therefore, can be understood as the one called ‘God of gods,’ and as the great King over these gods.”

Nothing is truer than this latter observation of Augustine. But when he says that human beings among the people of God are called gods, he has not expressed himself with sufficient precision. For not just any human beings from the people of God are called gods in Psalm 81:6, but only kings and judges—that is, magistrates. Accordingly, the heading of this chapter is also badly conceived. It reads: “The name of gods is falsely attributed to the gods of the nations, although, on the authority of the divine Scriptures, it is shared by holy angels and righteous human beings.”

For nowhere in Scripture is this the name of righteous human beings as such, but only of those elevated to public offices, whatever their character may otherwise be. Their virtue is not being considered, but their dignity.

### Same passage, §2

“Nevertheless, when it is asked of us why human beings are called gods because they belong to the people of God, whom God addresses through angels or through human beings, what shall we answer except that immortal beings who enjoy the blessedness to which human beings desire to attain by worshiping God are even more worthy of this name?
