What shall we answer except that in the Holy Scriptures human beings are expressly called gods rather than those immortal and blessed beings to whom we are promised that we shall be equal in the resurrection? This was so that, on account of their excellence, unbelieving human weakness might not dare to make one of them its god. It is easy to avoid this error in the case of a human being.”

We, however, who have drawn these waters not from muddy streams but from the fountain itself, shall answer differently: namely, that angels are most explicitly called gods in Psalm 8:6, where the Hebrew has, concerning humanity, “[text not supplied], and you made him a little lower than gods”; the Septuagint translators have, Ἠλάττωσας αὐτὸν βραχύ τι παρ’ ἀγγέλους, “You made him a little lower than the angels.”

The Chaldaean likewise has, in place of the omitted reading, *mimmalachajo*, “than the angels.” So too the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 2, verse 7. Similarly, Psalm 96:7, according to the Greek division, reads in the Septuagint, προσκυνήσατε αὐτῷ πάντες ἄγγελοι αὐτοῦ, “Worship him, all his angels,” and in the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 1, verse 6, where the Hebrew words read: “Worship him, all gods, [text not supplied].”

We shall not add other passages, but we shall observe that it is dangerous to invent explanations of the usage of the sacred language before that usage has been fully investigated. It is easy to be misled by theories and to indulge in them, as Augustine does here, unless we read the Greek and Hebrew carefully. We could confirm this power of the word *God* with many more passages, but consult Joan. Clericus, *Ars Critica*, Part I, section 2, chapter 3.

[Col. 0474A] ## BOOK X

### Chapter 1, §2

“For this is the worship owed to the Divinity—or, if it must be expressed more precisely, to the Godhead—for which, since no sufficiently suitable Latin word occurs to me as a single-word designation, I indicate in Greek, wherever necessary, what I mean. Our translators have rendered *latreia* (λατρεία), wherever it occurs in the Holy Scriptures, as ‘service.’ But the service owed to human beings, according to which the Apostle commands slaves to be subject to their masters, is usually called by another Greek name.”

He means the word *douleia* (δουλεία). Although *latreia*, according to the proper meaning of the word, does not signify among the Greeks the worship of God more than the worship of human beings, as Joan. Lud. Vives correctly observes in commenting on this passage, nevertheless, from the usage of the Septuagint translators and the New Testament, *latreia*, as Augustine says below, denotes divine worship; whereas *douleia* is used indiscriminately for both kinds, as the concordances will show. Therefore, even if *latreia* in the sacred books signifies a superior form of worship, it does not immediately follow that *douleia* signifies a less exalted form. This should be carefully noted.

### Chapter 11, §1

“There he censures all human beings, whom he says draw up a moist vapor through their imprudence and therefore exist not in the ether but in the air beneath the moon, and even within the sphere of the moon itself.”

From this philosophy Lucan, at the beginning of Book IX, speaks as follows concerning the soul of Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus:

> Yet Pompey’s spirit did not lie in Pharian ash,  
> nor did a little dust restrain so great a shade;  
> it sprang forth from the tomb, leaving its half-burned limbs behind,  
> and, abandoning the ignoble pyre, followed the vault of the Thunderer.  
> Where the dark air is joined to the star-bearing axes,  
> and where it lies open between earth and the moon’s pathways,  
> the spirits of demigods dwell—spirits whom fiery virtue  
> made harmless inhabitants of the lower ether  
> and gathered their souls into eternal spheres.

But Apuleius the Platonist treated this matter at length in his little book *On the God of Socrates*.

### Chapter 16, §1

“Let the theurgists—or rather the *periurgists*, for this is the more appropriate name for those arts—answer.”

Augustine seems to have heard from someone acquainted with Greek that those magical arts were called περιέργοι, that is, “improperly curious.” When he saw that their practitioners were called *theurgists*, he said, with an uncertain memory, that they ought to be called *periurgists*. That word, however, is not in ordinary use. For although θεουργός is formed from θεός and ἔργον, just as κακουργός, πανοῦργος, χειρουργός, and similar words are formed, it does not therefore follow that περιουργός is formed from περί and ἔργον, as those acquainted with usage and analogy know.

Concerning *periergon* (περίεργον), taken in a bad sense, see Hugo Grotius on Acts 19:19. The ancient glosses have: περίεργος, “curious, insane.” Hesychius has: Περίεργον—so the sequence of letters shows that it should be read, not περιερόν—“extravagant or distorted.” *Periergia* (περιεργία), not περιερεία, means καθαρσία, or rather κάθαρσις, or τὰ καθάρσια—that is, “superstitious purification,” of the kind with which the rites of the theurgists were filled. Iamblichus treated these rites chiefly in his book *On the Egyptian Mysteries*. See also Augustine below in this book, chapters 22 and 27.

Accordingly, the very learned Joan. Lud. Vives is mistaken when he asks whether *periurgists* are so called from *perurgere*, “to urge intensely,” or whether *perurgi* comes from *perurere*, “to burn thoroughly.” Nor, however, would I agree with Leonardus Coquaeus, who conjectured that *periergi* should be read. That reading destroys the elegance of the allusion, and it is not necessary to suppose that Augustine had retained the Greek word accurately.

### Chapter 23

“Concerning Porphyry: For he speaks of God the Father and God the Son, whom he calls in Greek the paternal intellect or paternal mind (πατρικὸς νοῦς, ‘the paternal intellect,’ from the Chaldaean Oracles); but concerning the Holy Spirit he says either nothing or nothing clearly. Yet I do not understand whom else he can call the intermediary between these. For if, like Plotinus when he discusses the three principal substances, he also wished the nature of the soul to be understood as the third, he certainly would not have called it the intermediary between them—that is, between the Father and the Son.”

Augustine did not possess all of Porphyry’s works translated into Latin. Otherwise, the Tyrian philosopher had spoken very explicitly about the three principles in his *Philosophical History*. Cyril of Alexandria quotes the following from that work in Book VIII *Against Julian*:

> Porphyry writes, then, in Book IV of his *Philosophical History*: “For Plato said that the divine essence proceeds as far as three hypostases; the supreme God is the Good, after him comes the second, the Creator, and third is the Soul of the world. For divinity proceeds as far as the Soul; thereafter, what is without divinity begins with corporeal differentiation.”

Thus Porphyry writes in Book IV of his *Philosophical History*: “Plato said that the divine essence proceeds as far as three hypostases; the supreme God is the Good, after him comes the second, the Creator, and third is the Soul of the world. For divinity proceeds as far as the Soul; the remainder, deprived of divinity, begins with corporeal differentiation.” This is plainly what Augustine wanted. Cyril has passages from Plato and Plotinus relevant to the matter in the same place.

### Same passage

“And, clearly, he said this as best he could—or as he wished—in order to express what we say: that the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone or of the Son alone, but of both. Philosophers speak freely, and in matters exceedingly difficult to understand they do not fear offending religious ears. But we are permitted to speak according to a fixed rule, lest freedom in our words generate an impious opinion concerning the things signified by them.”

This deserved to be noted, lest the unlearned be deceived by the similarity: those philosophers may seem in their words to agree with sacred Scripture, but in reality they depart from it completely. The Platonists maintained that there were three substances and that they were unequal. Anyone who reads Plotinus attentively, especially Book III, Ennead 9, will easily understand this; Cyril correctly observed it in the passage previously cited from Book VIII *Against Julian*. Joan. Clericus also treated the matter at greater length in volume III, letter 7, of his *Ars Critica*.

Nevertheless, Augustine was not without reason in saying that the philosophers used freer language. They openly said that the three principal substances were three gods. Others, who thought them entirely equal, were accustomed to deny this—not so much because, according to their own view, it was false if one wished to speak precisely, as because they feared offending religious ears, which could not bear to hear that there were several gods, contrary to the perpetual language of all Scripture.

### Chapter 27

“But you learned this not from Plato but from the Chaldaean teachers, so that you might raise human vices to the ethereal or empyrean heights of the world and the heavenly firmaments, enabling your gods to pronounce divine things to the theurgists.”

The Chaldaeans evidently thought that the gods could be compelled, by means of threats and terrors, to say what the theurgists wished to know. See above, chapters 9 and 11. Yet, not to conceal anything, Iamblichus denies in Book VI, chapter 7, of *On the Mysteries* that the Chaldaeans used such threats:

> Among the Chaldaeans, among whom pure speech directed solely to the gods is distinguished, no mention of threats is ever made. But the Egyptians, who mix with the divine symbols those things that pertain to demons, sometimes also make use of threats.

But who could bring into harmony that wisdom of superstitious and lying men, raging in delusion?

## BOOK XI

### Chapter 5

“If they imagine infinite stretches of time before the world, during which it does not seem to them possible that God could have ceased from his work, let them similarly imagine infinite stretches of place outside the world. If someone says that the Almighty could not be idle in those regions, will it not follow that they must, with Epicurus, dream of innumerable worlds? etc.”

But if someone granted that throughout the infinite extent of the world there are everywhere various habitations of various and innumerable creatures—such as our earth, and the larger planets that revolve with us around our sun—there would be no reason for him to fear the philosophers’ arguments greatly. As for the theologians, since revelation is silent, they have nothing to assert confidently on this subject.

Such a person might contend that those who placed inhabitants only on this tiny clod of earth, and those inhabitants sufficiently miserable, while creating nothing else possessing reason throughout the immense spaces of the world except angels, had too narrow a conception of God. Conversely, he might claim that those speak worthily of God who say that the works of the infinite Maker are infinite in number.

He might also appeal to what the very learned and ingenious Christian mathematician and physicist Christiaan Huygens says in his *Cosmotheoros* about the inhabitants of the neighboring planets. Concerning duration, he might say that this earth was not the first habitation created by God for intelligent natures, and that nothing prevents us—if we began to survey the whole universe of things—from never reaching the last of the divine works. Likewise, if we could contemplate in our minds the past duration, which had no beginning, and know what God accomplished within it, no creature would ever meet us as we moved backward through bygone ages that could be called the first of all divine works.

It is not surprising that difficulties arise here, since the subject is the infinite. But it is better to think about the duties God has imposed upon us than about those things which, according to our faltering judgment, God—if it is permissible to speak in this way—ought to have done.

### Chapter 8

“Therefore, most appropriately, when prophetic authority tells us that God rested, the rest of those who rest in him is signified, and of those whom he himself causes to rest.”

Nothing more forced could have been invented to explain the rest of the seventh day. That rest cannot be understood otherwise than as the cessation of creation, so that thereafter God created no new kinds of things, as is evident both from the matter itself and from the agreement of the best interpreters. Augustine arrived at this interpretation in order to answer the objection of pagan philosophers, who repeatedly declared that it was unseemly for God to rest, as though he were exhausted. Rutilius Namatianus, *Itinerary*, verse 391:

> Each seventh day, condemned to shameful slumber,  
> as though it were the image of a weary, enervated God.

But to cease from doing a work once it has been completed is an indication of wisdom, not of exhaustion; for the same thing ought not always to be done.

### Chapter 11

“Although not everything eternal is immediately blessed—for penal fire too is called eternal—nevertheless, if a truly and perfectly blessed life is eternal and nothing else, the life of those people, which would at some time come to an end, was not such a life and therefore was not eternal, whether they knew this or, in ignorance, thought otherwise.”

I do not know why Augustine pursues this empty question. But, as all who read his works will notice, he gladly repeats his own arguments. See volume III, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book XI, chapter 16, and what we noted there.

### Chapter 15

“That the devil sins from the beginning should not be understood to mean from the beginning at which he was created; rather, it means from the beginning of sin, which began with his pride.”

Why not understand this as referring to the beginning of the world, as Christ seems to suggest in John 8:44, and as one may reasonably believe the same apostle John also intended in his First Epistle, chapter 3, verse 8? The word “beginning” is used in this sense more than once in John. See the Gospel, chapter 1, verse 1.

### Chapter 19

“It does not seem to me an absurd—or perhaps incongruous—opinion concerning the works of God if, when that first light was made, the angels are understood to have been created, and a distinction was made between the holy angels and the unclean, when it was said: ‘And God divided the light from the darkness; and God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night.’”

Nothing seems more foreign to me than this interpretation of the mind and words of Moses. Nor, if it is denied, can it be proved by any argument. The literal sense of Moses is excellent and most beautiful: God divided all time into light and darkness. Joan. Clericus treated this subject in his *Philological Commentary on Genesis 1:4*. Once this meaning has been found, the meaning that presents itself spontaneously to the minds of readers, it would be madness to seek another.

[Col. 0477D] ### Chapter 24

“Whether, then, because the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the good Father and the good Son and is common to both, it can rightly be called the goodness of both, I do not dare rashly to pronounce. Nevertheless, I shall more readily dare to call him the holiness of both—not as though he were a quality of both, but as himself also a substance and the third person in the Trinity.”

I do not understand why Augustine wished such inconvenient expressions to be introduced into theology, since he himself admits that they are ambiguous and unknown to Scripture. It is plainly an abuse of language when, without necessity, ambiguous expressions are employed in a matter difficult in itself.

I admit that these expressions were fashioned on the model of the one by which the Son of God is said to be called his wisdom in Proverbs 8. But the most learned interpreters have shown that the passage is not really about any actual person, but, by personification (*κατὰ προσωποποιίαν*), about wisdom, which is an attribute of the divine essence. Nevertheless, many Fathers abused that ambiguity. See Dionysius Petavius, *Dogmatic Theology*, volume II, Book VI, chapter 9.

It should be noted, however, that Augustine says that the Holy Spirit himself is also a substance. From this it is clear that he believed the other individual persons to be distinct substances, although equal and most closely united.

### Chapter 29

“For those holy angels do not learn about God through sounding words.”

I could readily concede this, but I do not know the means by which they receive God’s commands. Augustine, however, knew, for he continues: “but through the very presence of immutable truth, that is, his only-begotten Word.” These are indeed words and expressions, but what power the writer would submit to them, I think he himself could scarcely have said. See the notes on Book IX, chapter 22.

### Same passage

“They know that the Trinity is inseparable, and that each person in it is one substance, yet that all together are not three gods but one; and they know this more fully than we ourselves know it.”

If each person is one substance, there are as many substances as there are persons; Augustine did not deny this. See the note on chapter 24 and Dionysius Petavius, *Dogmatic Theology*, volume II, Book IV, chapter 4. Nevertheless, he often says that there is one substance when he is speaking of unity in species, as the scholastics call it, not of numerical unity. Augustine himself speaks more clearly about this in his books *On the Trinity*.

## BOOK XII

### Chapter 7

“Let no one, therefore, seek an efficient cause of an evil will. It is not efficient but deficient, because it is not an effecting but a defect.”

I mean the cause of an evil volition. To avoid ambiguity, I shall speak here with the scholastics: the efficient cause is the will, or the free mind, which can sin through ignorance, imprudence, or passion. For sins are not nothing, but genuine acts of the mind, which every mind can perform through the faculty it has received from God. The overly subtle arguments of certain philosophers are empty; they would persuade us that what we ourselves experience within us does not exist. See the notes in volume VI, on the *Enchiridion to Laurence*, chapter 11.

### Chapter 10, §2

“They are deceived by certain thoroughly false writings, which they claim contain many thousands of years in their history of time, whereas from the sacred writings we calculate not yet six thousand years from the creation of humanity.”

Augustine seems chiefly to have in mind the Egyptian writings. Joannes Marsham showed acutely and ingeniously, in the *Prolegomena to the Canonical Chronicle* (προκατασκευὴ Χρονικοῦ Κανόνος), that these writings contain not a chronological calculation but an astronomical period, although previously he had been wrongly persuaded that the period contained genuinely elapsed times.

### Chapter 12

Against those who complained that the world was too recent:

“If the brevity of the period offends them, because the number of years since humanity was created, as our authorities relate, seems so small to them, let them consider that nothing is long-lasting if it has an end, and that all spans of the ages, when compared with boundless eternity, must be understood not as small but as nothing.”

This is acute and learned indeed. We praise a person just as readily as we withdraw from someone who thinks less correctly. Thus a period is called long or short in relation to human life, whereas in comparison with eternity all periods are nothing.

But let us hear what follows:

> And therefore, even if not five or six thousand years but sixty thousand, or six hundred thousand, or sixty million, or six hundred million years were said to have passed since God made humanity; or if this total were multiplied again and again by as many times as one might wish, until we had no name left for the number—one could equally ask why God had not made humanity earlier.

Everything here is excellent, so that nothing better could have been said on this subject. I have sometimes been moved to wonder at an otherwise learned writer, endowed with exceptional judgment, who answered the question Augustine raises here by suggesting that the world might be older than is commonly believed today, because the chronology of the Septuagint is longer than that of the Hebrew text. He would never have said this if he had reflected on Augustine’s answer.

Yet, although it is entirely true, this does not in the least diminish the proposed difficulty: it will always follow that God’s infinite goodness gave no indication of itself throughout the eternity of past time. Since it is certain that philosophers ought to be restrained by philosophical arguments, let us say to them, if they wish, that God created not merely our earth and a few neighboring bodies, but innumerable others, long before this planet of ours existed. Thus, if they could distinguish which of those divine works were created earlier and which later, they could move backward from our earth through the past expanses of time, through age after age, and never arrive at the most ancient of God’s works.

I do not see how they could prove the contrary, nor could they say anything here that could not also be said against the infinity of space and of the parts of any body—an infinity that is nevertheless supported by mathematical demonstrations. In this way the proud minds of philosophers could be checked and brought to more modest reflections. We have already said something about this matter, which we wish experts in philosophy would consider.

### Chapter 16

The Apostle also speaks of eternal times—not future times, but, what is more astonishing, past times. For he says (Titus 1:2–3):

> In hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before eternal times; but in his own times he manifested his Word.

Behold, he said that there had been times in the past which nevertheless had not been co-eternal. Before proceeding further, I shall briefly state the true meaning of the passage. The *χρόνοι αἰώνιοι* (*chronoi aiōnioi*, “eternal times”), as Hugo Grotius will show, are ancient times—Hebrew [the Hebrew terms are missing in the supplied text]—by which a long, not eternal, period is signified. See the Chaldean paraphrase of Jonathan on Micah 5:2. Thus the Apostle means that eternal life, formerly promised and later to be revealed through the Messiah, had been promised long ago. See Romans 16:25; 2 Timothy 1:9.

This cannot be obscure to anyone who knows Hebrew and reads those passages or others like them. But to someone ignorant of Hebrew, interpreting the writer not from an examined knowledge of the style of the sacred language but from certain philosophical opinions—I scarcely know what sort—they are all obscure. Hence our author dreams here of eternal times which nevertheless were not co-eternal with God—as though one thing could be more eternal than another eternal thing!

“For,” he says, “before eternal times he not only existed, but also promised eternal life, which he manifested in his own times, that is, at suitable times; what else could this be but his Word? For this is eternal life.” I shall not say that nothing can exist before eternity, but that Augustine supplied the Arians with a means of evading many passages of the Fathers before the Council of Nicaea concerning the eternity of the Son. They could say that the Son was described as eternal in precisely the sense in which Augustine speaks here, while denying that he was co-eternal with the Father.

But the statement that God is said to have promised eternal life before those times which were called eternal ought surely to have warned Augustine that only more ancient times of the Old Testament were meant. Yet he did not notice even this.

“How, then,” he asks, “did he promise what he certainly promised to human beings who did not yet exist before eternal times, unless it was already fixed by predestination in his own eternity and in his own Word, co-eternal with him, that what was to happen in its own time would come to pass?”

This might in some fashion be tolerated if it had said “from eternity.” But to promise before eternal times, in the sense of having eternally determined within himself to give something, is without precedent.

What is remarkable is that Augustine himself, around the same time as he wrote this, partly understood the true sense of this expression. Thus, against the Priscillianists, chapter 6:

> The Apostle called the earlier times eternal and ancient, as it is read in Greek: *πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων* (“before eternal times”). For when he writes to Titus, etc.

So far, excellent. But listen to his strange explanation of the expression:

> Since, looking backward, the times from the creation of the world seem to have a beginning, how are they eternal, unless he called those things eternal which have no time before them?

On this reasoning, the world could be called eternal, because, according to Augustine’s teaching, it had no time before it, since only eternity preceded its creation. Yet who among Christians would tolerate someone saying that the world is eternal?

Since this is so, I am astonished that the Parisian editors could have been satisfied with this interpretation when they could have consulted Hugo Grotius, among others.

But this same passage had troubled Jerome, who was much more learned than Augustine, as is clear from the following note of his on chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus. After mentioning the creation of the world and of time, he continues:

> Before these times of the world, therefore, we must believe that there was a certain eternity of ages, in which the Father was always with the Son and the Holy Spirit; and, to put it so, all eternity is one time of God—or rather, there are countless times, since he himself is infinite, who existed before times and surpasses every time. Six thousand years have not yet been completed for our world; how many prior eternities, how many times, how many beginnings of ages must we suppose there were, in which angels, thrones, dominions, and the other powers served God and, at his command, continued to exist without the changes and measures of time?

Thus “before eternal times” would mean before vast stretches of time that had elapsed before the world was created. But this too is without precedent, and it supplies the Arians with a notion of a new eternity which they could attribute to the Son while retaining their entire position concerning his creation.

I shall say no more on this matter, except that Jerome did not here employ the expertise in Hebrew which he had acquired—though it was not as great as many commonly believe, as Joannes Clericus has demonstrated at length in his *Hieronymian Questions*.

### Chapter 19

Concerning the expression “ages of ages,” after proposing two opinions plainly foreign to its true force, he adds:

> Which of these two alternatives is correct—or whether something else can be understood by “ages of ages” besides these two—is a question of the greatest depth.

But who now does not know that this is an idiom of the Hebrew and Chaldean languages, signifying a time either without end or, at any rate, a long time? For just as in the Old Testament we read *dor dorim* (“generation of generations”), or “age of ages,” in the sense we have described—for example, Psalm 102:25 and Isaiah 51:8—so in the speech of the Jews in apostolic times they said in Syriac *lhalam halmin*, meaning “for all eternity.”

This expression seems to have arisen because, in speaking of such a matter, everyone could say that individual ages, or successive generations, would extend into the ages to come. But whatever its origin, its meaning is perfectly familiar from the constant usage of the New Testament, from which it is clear that *εἰς αἰῶνα* (“unto the age”) and *εἰς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων* (“unto the ages of ages”) amount to the same thing.

Yet Jerome was similarly perplexed in this matter, in his commentary on Galatians, chapter 5.

## Book XIII

### Chapter 12

After explaining what the first and second deaths are, Augustine writes:

> When God therefore first said to that man whom he had placed in paradise, concerning the forbidden food, “On whatever day you [plural] eat from it, you shall die,” that threat included not merely the earlier part of the first death, in which the soul is deprived of God, nor merely the later part, in which the body is deprived of the soul, nor merely the whole of the first death itself, in which the soul is punished after being separated both from God and from the body, but everything that belongs to death, even up to the final death, which is called the second death, after which there is no other.

Two things must be observed here. First, Augustine asserts these things imperiously, without proving them. Nowhere in any law is there a passage in which “you shall die the death” signifies anything other than simply dying. Nor is there any mention anywhere in the entire Old Testament of deaths other than that in which the body is dissolved, if one may use that expression. Therefore, if it is denied that anything here is meant beyond simple death, or the dissolution of the body, there will be no fear that the contrary can be made even plausible.

Second, it is entirely false that God imposed upon anyone the necessity of sinning as a punishment for sin. For God would then undoubtedly be both the author and the avenger of sin—a thought horrifying to conceive or utter.

### Chapter 13

Concerning the first parents, who after their sin began to be ashamed of their nakedness:

> They therefore experienced a new movement of disobedience in their flesh, as a reciprocal punishment for their disobedience.

He elaborates on this at greater length in what follows and repeats it frequently, especially in Book XIV, from which it is clear that this invention greatly pleased its author.

Yet, to say nothing else here, he should not have said “they experienced,” but “Adam experienced,” for either there was no such movement in Eve, or it was certainly not conspicuous and could not have strengthened her. On the nakedness of the first parents, see, among other interpreters, especially Joannes Clericus on Genesis.

### Chapter 19

> Although there can be no legitimate doubt that the souls of the righteous and devout dead live in repose, it would nevertheless be so much better for them to live again with their sound bodies that even those who consider existence without a body to be supremely blessed refute this opinion of theirs by their own contrary judgment.

Here he is referring to the Platonists, who could nevertheless easily defend themselves against him. That, however, is not the issue here. We shall merely observe that it is indeed better for the souls of the dead to be reunited with bodies raised from the grave, so that they may enjoy complete happiness with them, since Scripture postpones this to the resurrection of the body. But there is no doubt that it would be worse for them if they were living here on earth with us in their sound bodies. They have been freed from all the miseries of life and, most importantly, from the danger of falling from divine grace.

Augustine nevertheless argues here against the Platonists in a very confused manner, although defending them would not be particularly difficult.

## Book XIV

### Chapter 5

> For, according to them, that dreadful desire—as the noble speaker says—is so far from arising from the body that it compels the soul, purified from every bodily pollution and established outside every body, to be in a body.

He is referring to Virgil, quoted earlier, specifically *Aeneid* 6.321:

> [What is] that dreadful desire for light  
> for the wretched?

But I can scarcely persuade myself that Virgil should be called “the speaker.” Ludovicus Vives notes elsewhere that Cicero is so called by him, though I do not remember the passage. In both places I would prefer “author” to “speaker.”

### Chapter 17

> What disobedient desire therefore moved those members against the condemned will on account of the guilt of disobedience, shame modestly covered.

He already said this in Book XIII, chapter 13, where we noted that it could have been said of Adam but not equally of Eve. Augustine apparently thinks, with most others, that the first parents made themselves only girdles, not clothing. Recent interpreters, however, have offered arguments on this matter that deserve examination.

**The same passage:**

> And all nations, since they were descended from that stock, have so deeply implanted in them the practice of covering their private parts that certain barbarians do not even have those parts naked in the baths, but bathe with their coverings. Even through the shadowy wildernesses of India, although certain men philosophize naked—whence they are called Gymnosophists—they nevertheless apply coverings to their genitals, though they lack coverings for the rest of their limbs.

Recent voyages, both through our hemisphere and among our antipodes, have taught us that there are peoples in Africa and America who are completely naked. As for the Brahmans, eyewitnesses plainly testify that they are entirely naked, among them Franciscus Bernier, a man of candid intellect and cultivated in philosophical studies who lived for a long time in India.

Nor do I think they were more fully clothed in ancient times, whatever that most mendacious and disgusting writer Philostratus may say in his *Apollonius*.

For the rest, shame at nakedness seems to have arisen partly from the cause Augustine gives, but many other causes were added. When Adam and Eve had children, they had to be clothed lest the children handle their uncovered parts and learn too early to misuse their own. Women also ought to be clothed from puberty onward, lest something offensive appear to the eyes each month. Married couples too ought to be clothed, lest desire aroused through the eyes violate the best and most useful laws of marriage and adulteries be widely committed—something that could not happen without the ruin of human society.

Thus shame at nakedness gradually arose and was carefully implanted by parents in the minds of their children, not without the gravest reasons. But we shall not discuss these matters at greater length, lest we ourselves offend against modesty.

### Chapter 18

> For who does not know what husbands and wives do with one another so that children may be born? After all, wives are married with such ceremony precisely so that this may be done; and yet, when the act from which children are born is performed, not even the children themselves, if any have already been born from it, are permitted to be witnesses.

This is not because the act, considered in itself, is shameful, but because it would be dangerous if children, through untimely imitation, imitated their parents under circumstances in which the act would be unlawful and gravely harmful to human society. For this reason children must be imbued with that sense of shame from childhood, so that they will not dare to do what would be harmful.

Nevertheless, this shame increases or diminishes according to the customs of times and peoples, as is clear from the unrestrained lust not only of the ancient pagans of Europe and Asia but also of the modern barbarians of Africa and America.

### Chapter 20

> Hence I think that Diogenes—the man who wished to have intercourse publicly with a prostitute—or those who are reported to have done so, rather displayed to the eyes of people who did not know what was taking place beneath the cloak the movements of persons having intercourse than that they could have carried out that pleasure under the pressure of human observation.

I would have preferred him not to touch upon this rather than to philosophize so expertly about so shameful a matter, especially at the age Augustine had reached. Yet he seems not unwilling to speak about such things, as we have already seen and shall see again later.

It is useful to note such matters carefully, lest certain people continue with impunity to abuse the authority of a great man to such an extent that they consecrate his errors no less than his genuine statements.

### Chapter 23, § 3

Concerning the manner in which the human race would have been propagated without Adam’s sin:

> The members, he says, would have served the will like all the others. Thus the genital field, as a vessel created for this work, would have sown its seed, just as the hand now sows the earth—that is, without any desire for pleasure, for Augustine wishes that desire to be sin.

By the same reasoning he ought to have said that the appetite for pleasant food is sin, and that the first parents, when they ate lawful and enjoyable fruits, were not stimulated by any pleasure or induced to choose some rather than others, but ate merely to sustain the body.

He ought also to have added that brute animals, whose organs are not unlike ours, seek no pleasure in their natural actions, since they certainly did not sin, but carry them out spontaneously by the force of nature, entirely without desire. These propositions are just as consistent with reason as Augustine’s conjectures.

After describing God as entirely different from what he is and from the picture Scripture gives us, Augustine also does violence to the whole of nature in order to defend perverse interpretations of certain obscure passages of Scripture. It would have been far better to acknowledge that those interpretations were false because they contradicted the nature of things, with which Scripture cannot conflict.

### Chapter 24, § 1

> The man would therefore sow his offspring, and the woman would receive it with her genital members, which would be moved as much as necessary by the will and not excited by desire. For we move at will not only those members whose joints are articulated by compact bones, such as the feet, hands, and fingers, but also those which are relaxed in soft sinews. When we wish, we move them by agitating and extending them; by twisting we bend them, and by contracting we make them firm. Such are the parts which the will moves, as far as it can, in the mouth and face.

Augustine prefaced this with a futile appeal to the dignity of his readers’ ears. Such material can scarcely be tolerated in the mouth of an old man and bishop addressing everyone indiscriminately: obscenities amassed so laboriously and repeated so deliberately to illustrate—as mildly as possible—an empty conjecture.

Whom, after all, did this disgusting material teach? Girls, I suppose; for African boys, born and raised beneath a burning sky, knew such things soon enough.

A little earlier he did say that a modest and religious reader could easily forgive him so long as he was refuting unbelief—not arguing from faith about things never experienced, but from the experience of things known. Yet there will be modest and religious people who are ashamed of an invention that could be defended only by such obscene conjectures. They will not tolerate being called unbelievers because they reject faith in such dreams; rather, they will contend that those who impose such opinions upon the people in the name of the divine word are extremely audacious—to use no harsher expression.

But our orator uses the Apostle’s example to defend himself:

> For he reads these things without offense who does not recoil from the Apostle’s denunciation of the dreadful enormities of women who exchanged the natural use for that which is against nature.

The Apostle, however, thunders against the perpetrators of such crimes with the utmost and most justified indignation. Augustine, by contrast, serves up shameful conjectures merely to explain an event that neither occurred nor ever will occur: namely, the generation of children in a state of innocence, if the first parents had remained in it.

He does this because he declares sinful what belongs to the nature of all animals and is nowhere condemned, provided it is kept within lawful bounds—namely, the desire for sexual union after reaching puberty.

His own obscene discourse therefore compares poorly with Paul’s righteous indignation. I shall not even mention that Paul refers to the vices of the pagans once and briefly, whereas Augustine repeatedly returns to this subject and embellishes everything with rhetorical coloring, as is sufficiently clear from the words quoted.

## Book XV

### Chapter 9

To prove that giants existed on the basis of Genesis 6:4, “There were giants upon the earth in those days,” Augustine reasons as follows:

> Their most distinguished poet, Virgil, says of a huge stone which a mighty man of those times—namely, the heroic age—had torn from a field boundary while fighting, carried, whirled, and hurled:
>
> *Scarcely could twelve men, twice six, lift it upon their necks,*  
> *Such as the earth now produces in the bodies of men.*
>
> This indicates that the earth then used to produce larger bodies. How much more, therefore, in the more recent times of the world, before that famous and widely reported flood? Etc.

The learned Theodorus Ryckius treated this subject most fully and learnedly in the discourse he appended to Lucas Holstenius’s notes on Stephanus of Byzantium. He showed that there had indeed been giants here and there, that is, people of unusually large stature, but that human beings in ancient times were not generally taller than people today. Readers who wish to examine this question should consult him.

We shall observe only two things here. First, before asking whether giants existed, Augustine should have consulted the Greek interpreters of the Old Testament, Symmachus and Aquila. From them he would have learned that there is no Hebrew word here meaning “giants,” and consequently that this passage provides no basis for asking whether giants existed.

Second, Virgil’s authority—lying after Homer—was too slight among serious people to be useful in defending sacred history against the pagans. The answer was ready: Virgil was a poet, and therefore permitted to invent; in this matter he was an imitator of Homer, whom no one was obliged to believe.

**The same passage:**

> Pliny the Elder, a very learned man, testifies that the more the course of the ages advances, the smaller bodies nature produces.

Pliny does indeed say this in Book VII, chapter 16, of his *Natural History*. But everyone knows that it is false, as the aforementioned Theodorus Ryckius has shown at length.

### Chapter 13

After a long and anxious discussion of the difference between Hebrew and Greek chronology in the years assigned to the antediluvian patriarchs, Augustine finally closes his reasoning as follows:

> But however one may wish to understand the matter—whether one believes that it happened in this way or does not believe it, whether it was so or was not so—I would never doubt that the proper course is this: whenever something different is found in the two codices, since both cannot be true with respect to the factual truth of what happened, preference should be given to the language from which the translation into the other language was made by interpreters.

Nothing could be truer. Yet this appears to have been forced from Augustine by the passage in the version of the Septuagint concerning Methuselah’s years, according to which, on their reckoning, he would have survived the Flood—something entirely contrary to Scripture.

In the meantime, let us embrace what he gives us and thank him for having brought forth the truth, although he acted in no way consistently with this confession, since he made no effort to learn Hebrew.

He adds:

> For in certain Greek codices—three of them—and in one Latin codex, as well as in one Syriac codex, all agreeing among themselves, Methuselah was found to have perished six years before the Flood.

I would suppose that by the Syriac interpretation he means a translation from the Hebrew codex; by the Latin, Jerome’s version; and by the other translations, those of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion. It is no wonder that these agreed with the Hebrew source, since they were derived from it.

### Chapter 17

> Moreover, Seth is interpreted as “resurrection,” and Enosh, his son, is interpreted as “man.”

The latter interpretation is correct, for in Hebrew *enosh* truly means “man.” But *Seth* does not mean “resurrection”; rather, it means “placed” or “set,” from the verb “he set.” This is clear from Genesis 4:25, where the etymology of the name is given:

> And she called his name Seth, because God has set (*shath*) another offspring for me in place of Abel.

The Septuagint rendered this:

> Καὶ ἐπωνόμασε τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Σὴθ, λέγουσα, ἐξανέστησε γάρ μοι ὁ Θεὸς σπέρμα ἕτερον ἀντὶ Ἄβελ.  
> “And she called his name Seth, saying, ‘For God has raised up another seed for me in place of Abel.’”

Hence the author of the little book *Hebrew Names* rashly concluded that the word Seth signifies *ἀνάστασις* (“resurrection”), although the Septuagint translators expressed the sense rather than the proper force of the Hebrew word.

It is dangerous to rely on others in a matter one does not understand at all, when one does not know whether they themselves are competent in it.

**The same passage:**

> Enosh, his son, is interpreted as “man,” not like Adam—for that name too is interpreted as “man”—but it is said to be a common term in that language, namely Hebrew, for male and female. For it is written of him: “He made them male and female, and blessed them, and called their name Adam.” Hence there is no doubt that the woman was called Eve by her proper name, while Adam, which is interpreted as “man,” was the name of both.

Augustine is correct concerning the name Adam, but wrong concerning the name Enosh, as he explains more fully later:

> Enosh is interpreted as “man” in such a way that those skilled in that language affirm that a woman cannot be called by it, just as “sons of the resurrection” will neither marry nor be given in marriage. For there will be no generation there, since regeneration will have brought them there.

If Augustine had said this from the pulpit, who would doubt that he received astonishing applause from the ignorant Numidian crowd? Nor do I doubt that the dull Punic minds, and others no more learned, admired the acumen of the orator of Hippo.

Yet just as it is false that the word Seth signifies “resurrection,” as we have seen, so it is also false that the word signifies only “male,” especially in the singular, where among the Hebrews it is the same as *Adam*, and among the Greeks *ἄνθρωπος* (“human being”), consistently embracing both sexes. In the plural it often means “men,” or *ἄνδρες*, but not invariably, as Hebrew concordances and ordinary lexicons will show.

Instead of applause, therefore, this good man deserved the sharpest whistles of the shepherd’s pipe. He should not have spoken about such a matter on the authority of others.

But listen also to what follows:

> For this reason I think it should not be noted without purpose that in those generations which are descended from the one called Seth, although sons and daughters are said to have been begotten, no female born into them is expressly named. In the generations descended from Cain, however, at the very end, as far as they extend, the last female born is named.

Since this subtle argument rests upon the foundation already destroyed—the meaning of the word Enosh—it must collapse entirely, and this African mystery must be regarded as a dream.

### Chapter 23, § 3

Concerning the passage in Genesis 6:2, “When the angels of God saw the daughters of men,” etc.

Augustine rightly observes that those angels of God were human beings, and then adds:

> The Septuagint translators indeed called these both “angels of God” and “sons of God,” although not all codices contain this reading; for some have only “sons of God.” Aquila, however, whom the Jews prefer to the other translators, rendered it not “angels of God” nor “sons of God,” but “sons of gods.”

There were therefore codices that had *ἄγγελοι Θεοῦ καὶ υἱοὶ Θεοῦ* (“angels of God and sons of God”), and others that undoubtedly had a corrupt reading. Since the Hebrew codex contains *bĕnê ’ĕlōhîm* only once, it could be translated in only one of the two ways.

Someone had undoubtedly written *υἱοὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ* (“sons of God”) opposite the words *ἄγγελοι τοῦ Θεοῦ* (“angels of God”) to indicate either that it should be read that way or that the Septuagint translators would have rendered it better in that form. This was later rashly inserted into the text, as many such additions occur in that version.

Our author’s statement that certain codices had nothing except “sons of God” is shown to be true by the very ancient Vatican Codex, in which this is the only reading. But in the equally ancient Alexandrian Codex only *ἄγγελοι Θεοῦ* (“angels of God”) is read. This appears to be the reading followed by many very ancient Greek and Latin Fathers, who consequently concluded with great unanimity that angels had been captivated by love for mortal women. See Denis Petau, *Theological Dogmas*, volume III, and his work *On Angels*, Book III, chapter 2.

As for Aquila, it is not surprising that he translated “sons of gods,” since the Hebrew expression is plural. It is well known that he translated *κατὰ πόδας* (“literally,” or “word for word”), especially in that version which was *κατ’ ἀκρίβειαν* (“according to exactness”).

Augustine continues:

> Both are true. For they were also sons of God, under which father their own fathers’ brothers were, together with whom they themselves were also gods, according to the saying of the Psalm: “I said, You are gods,” etc.

But this passage from the Psalm does not apply to everyone, and the passage in Genesis must be understood of the entire lineage of Seth, as the most learned interpreters have shown in their comments on it.

Augustine finally closes this reasoning with these words:

> For the Septuagint translators are rightly believed to have received the prophetic Spirit, so that if they changed anything by his authority and said what they were translating differently from the original, no one would doubt that this too had been spoken divinely.

This opinion rested chiefly upon three supports.

The first was the absurd fable of the pseudo-Aristeas concerning the manner in which these translators, though separated in individual cells, translated the Old Testament in exactly the same way. Jerome long ago mocked this fable, and all more sensible people now laugh at it in the same manner. Those who think otherwise either do not know Hebrew or hold—or wish to appear to hold—their view with foolish obstinacy.

The second was the ignorance of Hebrew among certain Jews and Christians who had never compared that version with the Hebrew codex. Had they made the comparison, they would have discovered that these translators had committed obvious errors in innumerable places, arising from a less accurate knowledge of Hebrew.

The third, finally, was a very weighty consideration if one looks to worldly prudence, but entirely without weight if one considers truth alone: namely, that once Jerome’s opinion was admitted concerning the faults of the Septuagint version and the necessity of resorting to the Hebrew codex, the books and reputation of innumerable Greek and Latin preachers and interpreters of Scripture would be ruined. Most of their works would have had to be destroyed, and they would have been obliged to maintain a shameful silence concerning matters about which they had habitually spoken from the pulpit with such confidence and rhetorical display.

Go now, severe reader, and wonder why such men rightly believed this, when it was so greatly in their interest that it should appear true.

Yet Augustine, who maintains that if the Septuagint translators changed anything, it was changed by prophetic inspiration, did not dare to assert this concerning the years of the antediluvian patriarchs in chapter 10 and the following chapters of this book.

### Chapter 27

> They seem to reckon only three hundred cubits in length and fifty in width, without considering that there would be the same amount above, and again the same amount above that, so that, when those cubits are taken three times, they become nine hundred in length and one hundred and fifty in width.

In printed copies, after “in width,” the words “thirty in height” are added. In what follows, so that the later statements agree with the earlier ones, we read:

> The cubits would amount to nine hundred in length, one hundred and fifty in width, and ninety in height.

But the Benedictines corrected this on the basis of manuscript codices. They say that the cubits of height are rightly absent, since, for resolving the difficulty in question, they cannot be multiplied in the same way as the cubits of length and width without violating the truth of Scripture.

I confess that I do not fully understand what these words mean. No cubits may be multiplied in a way permitted by the truth of Scripture. Scripture teaches us that the ark’s length was only three hundred cubits and its width fifty cubits. These cannot be multiplied threefold so as to produce an ark nine hundred cubits long and one hundred and fifty wide, for that would plainly contradict Scripture.

Indeed, this is entirely contrary to Augustine himself, who understood the words of Scripture as though Genesis 6:15 gave the dimensions not merely of the ark itself but of each of the stories composing it, so that each was fifty cubits wide and three hundred cubits long, and the ark was therefore three times larger than it was commonly believed to be.

This is clear from Augustine’s words. But to calculate correctly, the height of each story also had to be determined, and Scripture assigns the ark a height of thirty cubits. Alternatively, if one wishes to increase only the length and width, one must deny that the ark had three stories, contrary to the express words of Scripture in Genesis 6:16:

> *κατάγαια, διόροφα καὶ τριόροφα ποιήσεις αὐτήν*—  
> “You shall make it with lower, second, and third stories.”

The Hebrew codex and the authoritative interpreters of both East and West have this reading.

Therefore, if we follow the Benedictine reading and suppose that Augustine did not describe the ark as higher than it was commonly believed to be—namely, thirty cubits—but only as wider and longer, he will contradict the express words of Scripture. If we follow the earlier editions, his only error will be that he understood as referring to each of the ark’s stories what was said of the ark as a whole.

Whichever alternative is chosen, it must be admitted that Augustine was mistaken. I would rather, however, have the manuscript codices examined more carefully in the passages that follow, where the word *epiros* occurs and where Coquaeus, following Meursius, suspected that it should be emended to *ἐπιούρους*, or *epiuros*. See the Benedictines at the end of the volume.

## Book XVI

### Chapter 3

> What is said about that land—that is, the land of Shinar, which belonged to the kingdom of Nimrod—that Assur went out from it and built Nineveh and the other cities he lists happened much later. He mentioned it on this occasion because of the renown of the Assyrian kingdom, etc.

See what Joannes Clericus noted on this matter in his *Philological Commentary on Genesis* 10:11. Without it, Augustine’s statement here can scarcely be understood.

**The same passage, § 2:**

For it is read:

> And Shem was born also to him, the father of all the sons of Eber, the brother of Japheth the elder.

The order of the words is:

> And Eber was also born to Shem; that is, Eber was born to Shem, who is the father of all his sons.

The proper names, left undeclined according to Greek or Latin usage, hindered the good Augustine. He therefore departed entirely from the meaning of the passage, which should be translated:

> Shem also had offspring; indeed, he was the father of all who dwell beyond the river, together with Japheth, his elder brother.

See the interpreter mentioned earlier on Genesis 10:21.

### Chapter 5

> If God had already descended—for example, in Genesis 11:7—what does “Come, and let us descend and confuse their language there” mean, if it is understood as spoken to the angels, except that he descended through the angels, who descended while he was present in the angels?

The same interpreter followed and explained this interpretation in his notes on Genesis 11:7.

**The same passage, § 2:**

> The statement, “Nothing that they have undertaken to do will fail among them” (Genesis 11:6), was not spoken as a confirmation, but as though in the form of a question, as threatening speakers commonly express themselves.

This is an elliptical expression, by which God signifies that this would happen unless he intervened. See the interpreters on that passage.

### Chapter 8, § 1

> It is also asked whether we should believe that certain monstrous races of human beings mentioned in the histories of nations were propagated from the sons of Noah, or rather from that one man from whom they themselves arose—for example, certain people are said to have had one eye in the middle of their forehead, etc.

All these stories can be read in Pliny’s *Natural History*, Book II, chapter 8, to which Augustine appears to have been referring. Pomponius Mela, Book I, chapters 4 and following, may be joined with Pliny; similar falsehoods are narrated there, though more modestly.

Augustine closes his discussion of these falsehoods as follows:

> Therefore, to conclude this question gradually and cautiously: either those things which are reported about certain nations do not exist at all; or, if they exist, the beings are not human; or, if they are human, they are descended from Adam.

Before entering upon the question itself, he ought first to have stated the first of these alternatives: namely, that it is unnecessary to seek an explanation for things that perhaps exist nowhere. The question would be raised soon enough once the facts were established. In this way many of Plutarch’s *Table-Talk* questions could also have been avoided, since before seeking the explanation of a thing, we must establish the thing itself.

**The same passage, § 2:**

> A few years ago, certainly within our own memory, a twofold human being was born in the East: his upper limbs were double, but his lower limbs were single. For he had two heads, two chests, one belly, and two feet, like one man; and he lived long enough for rumor to draw many people to see him.

Augustine owed this story to Jerome, who writes in his letter to the presbyter Vitalis:

> Just because in our own time a double man was born at Lydda, with two heads, four hands, one belly, and two feet, must all human beings therefore be born in that way?

### Chapter 9. On the Antipodes

They do not claim to have learned this through any historical knowledge either, but conjecture it as though by reasoning: since the earth is suspended within the vault of heaven, and the universe has the same place both as its lowest point and its center, they suppose that the other part of the earth, which lies below, cannot be without human habitation.

[Col. 0490B] Joan. Lud. Vives rightly observed that the southern hemisphere was not known through mere conjectures, but through the voyages of those who set out through the Strait of Hercules and returned by way of the Arabian Sea—which had already been known since the time of Herodotus, as is clear from Book IV, chapter 42. See also Pliny, *Natural History*, Book II, and the commentators on him.

Moreover, Augustine himself denied the existence of the antipodes only because he did not think that a passage through the torrid zone from our hemisphere—that is, the northern one—into the southern could be made by human beings. Yet this had already been discovered to be false by geographers of earlier centuries, who had mentioned peoples living beyond the Tropic of Cancer and even beyond the equator. Once this was admitted, there was no reason to deny that people could have proceeded farther south, since it was well known even to those not altogether unacquainted with astronomy that, for travelers heading south, [Col. 0490C] another temperate zone had to be encountered.

It is truly remarkable that men who were otherwise by no means dull did not see this. But Augustine here opposes to us the authority of Scripture:

> “Since,” he says, “the Scripture in question cannot in any way lie, for it confirms the things it recounts as past by the fulfillment of its predictions, it is excessively absurd to say that some people could have sailed from one region to the other, crossing the immensity of the Ocean, and arrived there, so that even there the human race might be established from that one first man.”

But it is excessively absurd here to invoke the immensity of the Ocean. First, because this was by no means established, and it could have happened that Carthaginian ships, carried by favorable winds, were brought to a place where they did not wish to go. Indeed, [Col. 0490D] it is now clear to us that if any ship, sailing southward, passes beyond the thirtieth degree of northern latitude, it can scarcely avoid being carried on a direct course to southern America, which was thus easily discovered.

Since these things could have been so, and no contrary evidence was brought against them, they ought not to have been rejected as absurd. In the second place, it was not at all necessary to cross the Ocean in order to reach the hemisphere opposite ours: Africans could have reached it on foot, and in fact did reach it. They could also have gone there by ship while following the coast of Africa.

Hanno the Carthaginian had reported that he could not sail beyond the western promontory—namely, the one now called Cape Verde—not because of any difficulty in navigation, but solely because of a shortage of provisions:

> Οὐ γὰρ ἔτι ἐπλεύσαμεν προσωτέρω, τῶν σίτων ἡμᾶς ἐπιλιπόντων·

> “For we sailed no farther, because [Col. 0491A] our provisions had run out.”

Thus the authority of Scripture contributed nothing to this matter. Scripture does not teach that only the northern hemisphere is inhabited, but merely that the first human beings were created in it; from this it does not follow that they could not have gone over into the opposite hemisphere.

Go now and trust a man who gathers so many conclusions about God’s will and the future world from obscure passages of Scripture, when he could not even reason correctly about the earth he trod underfoot, or agree with those who reasoned correctly. Yet the things we shall see there will be far more marvelous than those discovered by our ancestors in this other world. Concerning him one might aptly say what someone said about Thales:

> “He does not see what lies before his feet,  
> yet he searches out the regions of heaven!”

### Chapter 11

Even when everyone had one language, the sons of pestilence were not [Col. 0491B] lacking. Before the Flood also there had been one language, yet all except the one righteous household of Noah deserved to be destroyed by the Flood. Likewise, when the nations were punished and divided through the diversity of their languages, as a deserved consequence of more exalted impiety, and the city of the wicked received the name of confusion—that is, was called Babylon—the household of Heber did not fail to exist, in which the language that had previously belonged to everyone remained.

Joan Clericus, in his dissertation *On the Hebrew Language*, demonstrates at length that this is a mere invention and contrary to Scripture itself. Nor could Augustine properly judge this matter, since he did not know the Hebrew language. Yet, by some strange fate, he undertook everywhere to judge matters unknown to him, and did not hesitate repeatedly to assume as established facts things he could never have proved.

Nevertheless, the scholastics—though not more skilled in languages—[Col. 0491C]and others descended from those scholastics followed him as the blind follow a blind guide—or, more remarkably, as sighted men follow one while voluntarily closing their eyes.

### Chapter 17

The kingdom of the Assyrians was far more powerful and exalted. For that king Ninus, son of Belus, had subjected the peoples of all Asia except India.

The same recent interpreter of Moses demonstrates that this too conflicts with Sacred Scripture, in his notes on Genesis 10:10.

### Chapter 29

Likewise, God appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre in the form of three men, who must unquestionably have been angels.

Excellent—as the interpreter just mentioned also shows. He follows Augustine equally readily when he thinks Augustine is leading along the right path, and departs from him when he thinks Augustine is wandering. Would that he—or some other interpreter of Scripture—always present himself as a reliable [Col. 0491D] guide!

He would greatly relieve the burden of those of us who must weigh everything, since, because nearly everyone has at some time been deceived, it is permissible to trust none of them without examination—ἀβασανίστως, that is, without testing.

## Book XVII

### Chapter 4

In explaining Hannah’s song, after interpreting the earlier words concerning Christ, Augustine finally comes to these words: “He shall exalt the horn of his Christ” (1 Samuel 2:10):

> “How,” he asks, “will Christ exalt the horn of his Christ? For concerning whom was it said above, ‘The Lord ascended into heaven’? And the Lord Christ was understood. He himself, as it is said here, will exalt the horn of his Christ. Who, then, is the Christ of his Christ? Or will he exalt the horn of each one of his faithful, just as she herself says at the beginning of this hymn: ‘My horn has been exalted in my [Col. 0492A] God’?” For we may rightly call all those anointed with his chrism ‘christs’; yet all of this, together with its head, is one Christ.”

But where is the Church called “the Christ of Christ”? Where is anyone called “christ” except a king or priest? We ought to interpret Scripture not according to some merely possible style—as I may put it—which we ourselves devise, but according to the style consecrated by established usage.

Thus, since he nowhere found any Christian called “christ” in the singular, and moreover saw that the passage concerned a king, he ought rather to have inferred that the preceding words had been misunderstood. Indeed, if he had consulted Aquila, Theodotion, or Symmachus, he would have understood that the preceding words had been translated incorrectly: “The Lord ascended into heaven and thundered.” They should be translated, as Jerome’s version has them: “He will thunder over [Col. 0492B] them” or “against them” in heaven. From those words he would not have inferred that Christ was being discussed, on the ground that Christ alone ascended into heaven.

### Chapter 7, § 4

The story recorded in 1 Samuel 7:12 is related:

> “He took one stone and set it between the new Mizpah and the old, and called its name Ebenezer, which in Latin means ‘stone of help’; and he said, ‘Thus far the Lord has helped us.’ Mizpah is interpreted as ‘intention.’ That stone of help is a figure of the Savior, through whom one must pass from the old Mizpah to the new—that is, from the intention by which false, carnal blessedness was expected in a carnal kingdom, to the intention by which, through the New Testament, the truest spiritual blessedness is expected in the kingdom of heaven.”

The Septuagint interpreters did not have “between the new Mizpah and the old,” but:

> ἀναμέσον Μασσηφὰθ καὶ ἀναμέσον τῆς παλαιᾶς

[Col. 0492C] These words correspond to the Hebrew: “between Mitspha and Schen.” They incorrectly translated the latter word, which is a proper name, with the common noun παλαιά, “old,” reading *jaschan* instead of *hasschen*. Hence the ancient Latin translator believed that “new” had been omitted, and translated: “between the new and old Masphat.”

Augustine’s entire argument rests on this false translation. It is truly astonishing that a man sufficiently acute did not reflect that he could not speak with adequate confidence about Sacred Scripture day and night unless he knew precisely what the text meant—which he could not always understand from an unreliable translation.

Similarly, what he derives from the meaning of the word *Mizpah* is absurd, because he did not understand what [Col. 0492D] “intention” meant in this passage. It is the intention of the eyes. For *mitsphah* may be derived from *tsaphah*, “he looked out,” “he watched,” and hence “he directed his eyes.” Indeed, in the Greek lexicon of names it is rendered ἀποσκόπευσις, “looking away” or “watching,” and in the book of Hebrew Names corrected by Jerome, *speculatio* or *contemplatio*, “observation” or “contemplation.”

But whatever the word means, Joan Clericus demonstrates in his *Hieronymian Questions* that nothing is emptier than allegorical interpretations derived from the meanings of names.

### Chapter 11

> “Remember what my substance is. Nothing is better understood here than Jesus himself, the substance of his people, from whom his flesh has its nature. For you did not establish all the sons of men in vain, he says. Unless there were one Son of Man as the substance of Israel, through [Col. 0493A] whom many sons of men would be delivered, all the sons of men would indeed have been established in vain.”

Beginning with chapter 9, Augustine undertook to interpret Psalm 88 according to the Greek division. We shall examine only this portion of his interpretation, namely verse 47.

The Hebrew text has: “Remember: I am of what age”—that is, “how short my life is.” The Septuagint interpreters translated it:

> μνήσθητι τίς μου ἡ ὑπόστασις

That is, “Remember what my”—to speak barbarously—“subsistence” is, or how long I shall continue to subsist here.

But the Latin translator rendered it incorrectly as “substance.” Augustine could not compare the Greek translation with the Hebrew text, with which it must be compared if the passage is to be understood; and so he seized upon the twisted interpretation we have quoted. See also [Col. 0493B] his interpretation of this psalm.

That man could carve almost any meaning out of any passage. Yet I am astonished that he did not perceive that this entire method of interpretation was fabricated, and that he had ventured to present inventions devised at will with such security and confidence.

### Chapter 14

> “It seems more credible to me that those who attribute all one hundred and fifty psalms to David’s work are right, and that he prefixed some of them with the names of others, and so forth.”

This opinion is truly astonishing. If David could prefix certain psalms with the names of others, who taught Augustine that those bearing David’s name might not have been prefixed by someone else? As for his claim that David prefixed them with names symbolically relevant to the subject, who does not see that this is a mere [Col. 0493C] invention?

Moreover, no one could attribute to David psalms in which the Babylonian captivity is mentioned as a past event, such as Psalm 136.

## Book XVIII

### Chapter 3

Concerning the time of Isaac’s birth:

> “At that time,” he says, “Aralius was the fifth king of the Assyrians”—that is, after Belus, whose son Ninus is said to have been.

If he is following Eusebius here, as he appears to be, he ought to have said: “Arius was the fourth king,” as is clear from Scaliger’s edition. Indeed, the Benedictines testify that *Arrium* is read in several manuscripts, and that *quartus* (“fourth”) ought also to be read.

In any case, many think that this succession of Assyrian kings was fabricated. See Joan Clericus on Genesis 10:10. In Abraham’s time, it was not the king of the Babylonians—who is here called the king of the Assyrians—but the most powerful [Col. 0493D] of the kings beyond the Euphrates, the king of the Elamites. See Genesis 14:4.

### Ibid.

Io is said to have been the daughter of Inachus and later to have been called Isis, worshiped in Egypt as a great goddess. Others, however, write that she came from Ethiopia to Egypt as queen, and that, because she ruled widely and justly and instituted many benefits and the use of letters for the Egyptians, divine honor was paid to her after her death—indeed, such honor that anyone who said she had been a human being was liable to capital punishment.

The Greeks rashly confused their own Io with the most ancient queen of Egypt, wishing to appear older than the Egyptians, relying only on the slight similarity of the names and on the fact that Isis was worshiped in the image of a [Col. 0494A] cow, into which the Argive Io was said to have been transformed.

These are not sufficiently firm indications of identity—ταυτότητος. Nor will anyone readily believe that, in those most ancient times, the Egyptians received a queen and goddess from the Greeks.

Herodotus, Book I, chapter 1, does indeed report that the peoples of the East said that Io went to Egypt, but that she had been carried off by Phoenicians and apparently sold there.

Let us therefore say, with Diodorus Siculus in Book I of the *Bibliotheca*, that the Egyptian Isis was indeed the most ancient queen of Egypt—for even her name signifies this. The same author testifies that:

> Ἴσιν μεθερμηνευομένην εἶναι παλαιάν

> “Isis, when translated, means ‘ancient’”—

and in the Hebrew language, which was related to the Egyptian, *jaschisch* means “old.”

Nevertheless, Augustine could rightly argue against the Greeks in the manner he does, although he could not persuade the Egyptians in this way, since they considered themselves, not without reason, much older [Col. 0494B] than the Greeks.

### Chapter 5

> “At this time”—namely, in the time of Jacob—“Apis, king of the Argives, was transported by ship to Egypt. After he died there, he became Serapis, the greatest of all the Egyptian gods. Varro gave the easiest explanation of why he was called Serapis rather than Apis even after death. Since the chest in which a dead person is placed is called in Greek σορὸς—what everyone now calls a σαρκοφάγος—and since they had begun to worship him there after his burial, before his temple had been built, he was called as though ‘soros-Apis.’”

As though Egypt lacked people whom it could elevate to the rank of gods, so that it would immediately give divine honors to newcomers from the Peloponnese! Or as though the Egyptians spoke Greek!

Accordingly, learned men rightly rejected Varro’s etymology and considered Serapis [Col. 0494C] to be one of the most ancient Egyptian divinities, existing several centuries before the Argive Apis. See Joseph Scaliger, *Annotations on Eusebius*, under the year 1730, and Gerhard Johannes Vossius, *On the Idolatry of the Gentiles*, Book I, chapter 29—although we do not approve the latter’s opinion, according to which he wishes the patriarch Joseph to have been called Serapis.

### Chapter 8

> “Minerva, however, was much older than these”—Hercules and Mercury. “For in the time of Ogyges she is said to have appeared at the lake called Tritonis in the form of a maiden; hence she was also called Tritonia,” and so forth.

Joan Clericus, in his notes on Hesiod’s *Theogony*, line 895, supplied a more plausible etymology of the name Tritonia and an explanation of why she was said to have been born from Jupiter’s head.

### Chapter 12

> “At this time Hercules was held in renown in Syria”—the manuscripts [Col. 0494D] read “in Syria,” not “in Tyre,” as the printed editions have it—“but plainly another Hercules, not the one of whom we spoke above. For, according to a more secret history, there are said to have been several Liber Pater figures and several Hercules figures.”

It is certain that Hercules was a Phoenician divinity, to whom the city of Tyre was consecrated. Indeed, some maintain that there were several Tyrian Hercules figures, as Gerhard Johannes Vossius observes in *On the Idolatry of the Gentiles*, Book I, chapters 22 and 34.

I would believe that the Theban or Argive Hercules himself originated from that same source, whether the figures were one or several. See what Joan Clericus says incidentally on this subject in his notes on section 3 of John Selden’s dissertation *On Tithes*. There is no time, nor is it necessary, to discuss the matter here at greater length.

But it is clear from this that “in Syria” is correctly read here and should not be emended [Col. 0495A] to “in Tiryns,” as Joan Lud. Vives thought.

### Chapter 14

> “During the same period there arose poets—Orpheus, Musaeus, and Linus, in the time of the judges of Israel—who were also called theologians because they composed songs about the gods. Yet these gods were either great men, though still human beings; or the elements of this world, which the true God made; or beings appointed in principalities and powers according to the Creator’s will and according to their own merits.”

This is clear from Hesiod’s *Theogony*, in which the most ancient divinities are Chaos, Heaven, and Earth; then certain spirits, I do not know what sort, whom he places over various parts of nature; and finally the souls of human beings who have fulfilled their fate.

I have no doubt that the earlier theological poets imitated him in this respect, although some of the ancients make him the first author of the *Theogony*. [Col. 0495B] See Joan Clericus on the title of Hesiod’s *Theogony*, and the preface of Diogenes Laërtius, where he discusses the *Theogony* of Linus.

### Chapter 18

> “For if we say that such things are not to be believed, even today there are people who insist that they have either heard with complete certainty or even experienced things of this kind themselves. When we were in Italy, we too heard such stories about a certain region in those parts, where they said that female innkeepers, skilled in these evil arts, used to give cheese to whichever travelers they wished or were able to give it to, whereupon the travelers were immediately changed into beasts of burden and carried whatever was necessary; once their task had been completed, they returned to themselves,” and so forth.

I am astonished that Augustine presents these matters as though they might be true and that they could scarcely be denied, when he later says that such things were either false or so unusual that they rightly [Col. 0495C] ought not to be believed. He thinks instead that the imagination of people who, in their madness, believed themselves to be beasts of burden had been disturbed by demons.

Later he also recounts that something of this kind happened in a dream to the father of a certain Praestantius after he had eaten such cheese. But if this occurred through the agency of demons, what need did they have for medicated food? Or if such food brought it about, what need was there for demons?

Moreover, if human imagination depended so completely on the will of demons that people could neither resist their power after eating the food nor overcome the images produced by their disturbed imagination, this would itself have been no small miracle.

It would therefore have been better to deny openly the inventions of those little women than to seek explanations for such events.

### Chapter 22
