> “For after that great and universal [Col. 0495D] Flood, when only eight human beings escaped in Noah’s ark, not much more than a thousand years had passed when Ninus subjected all Asia except India.”

In fact, according to the reckoning of the Septuagint interpreters, no more than 1,132 years had elapsed by the year of Abraham’s birth, as Isaac Vossius demonstrates in his book *On the Age of the World*, chapter 6.

But from the time of Peleg, when the human race departed into various colonies, to the time of Ninus—according to the same reckoning by which Eusebius determines that Ninus conquered Asia shortly before Abraham was born—not much more than 500 years had elapsed. Asia therefore possessed almost nothing but deserts, since within that period the human population could not have increased enough to fill such vast stretches of land.

Accordingly, those who [Col. 0496A] maintain that Ninus reigned later are more correct. See chapter 2 of this book.

### Chapter 23

> “At the same time some report that the Erythraean Sibyl prophesied. Varro, however, stated that there were several Sibyls, not one. This Erythraean Sibyl certainly wrote certain unmistakable things about Christ, which we too had previously read in Latin, in badly formed and metrically defective Latin verses, through the incompetence of some translator, as we later discovered,” and so forth.

He later says that Flaccianus showed him a Greek copy, and he produces an acrostic translated into verses which, as he puts it, were metrically sound. Their initial letters are:

> ΙΗΣΟΥΣ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΣ ΘΕΟΥ ΥΙΟΣ ΣΩΤΗΡ

> “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.”

This must be understood of the Greek verses, since those letters could not appear in Latin. I am therefore astonished that the translator is accused of incompetence. [Col. 0496B], since he certainly could not reproduce this in Latin verse.

But I am even more astonished that Augustine—who rightly defended the γνησιότης, “genuineness,” of the sacred books against the Manichaeans—did not notice that this was an obvious forgery.

I know that many other Christian writers followed him in this matter, and I shall not repeat the observations made against them both by others and by David Blondel in his French work on the Sibyls.

There is certainly reason to suspect that many of them easily detected the forged nature of this production, but, because the uneducated populace was captivated by arguments so slight rather than by serious ones, they seized upon this argument—as they did many others—not because it seemed true to them, but because it served their cause.

Otherwise, if their judgment had been so blunted that they noticed no forgery here, they would have been unable to distinguish any forged productions from genuine ones.

Historical credibility does [Col. 0496C] not permit us to doubt that there were certain prophetic women who foretold various things, especially concerning the Roman Empire. But this has nothing to do with the Christian religion.

To offer my own conjecture as well, I would believe that those fanatical women brought their name from the East, together with the art of deception, and that the Greeks called such women “Sibyls” because the Phoenicians called this kind of woman *schebola*—that is, “one who grows old.” For these prophetesses were old women, and their old age was celebrated no less than their prophecies.

Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book XIV, lines 132 and following, introduces the Sibyl speaking as follows:

> “An eternal light, one without end, was offered to me,  
> if my virginity had yielded to Phoebus in love.
>
> While he hoped for this, while he wished to corrupt me with gifts,  
> he said: ‘Choose, maiden of Cumae, what you wish;  
> you shall obtain what you wish.’
>
> I, pointing out a heap of dust I had gathered, [Col. 0496D]  
> and showing how many bodies of dust it contained,  
> foolishly asked that as many birthdays be granted to me.
>
> I forgot to ask also for the years of youth at once.  
> He would have given me those as well, and eternal youth,  
> if I had accepted Venus.
>
> I remain unmarried, having rejected Phoebus’ gift,  
> but the happier age has now turned its back on me,  
> and sick old age comes with trembling step,  
> which I must endure for a long time.
>
> For you see that seven centuries have already passed for me;  
> what remains is for me to equal the number of grains of dust:  
> to see three hundred harvests and three hundred vintages.”

These are poetic inventions arising from the claim that the Sibyl was extremely old.

### Ibid., § 11

Lactantius also inserts into his work certain prophecies of a Sibyl concerning Christ, although he does not specify which Sibyl.

He was referring to a passage in Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book I, chapter 6, where, after mentioning various Sibyls, he says:

> “The verses of all these Sibyls are both circulated [Col. 0497A] and preserved, except those of the Cumaean Sibyl, whose books are kept concealed by the Romans; nor is it permitted for anyone to inspect them except the fifteen men. There are separate books belonging to each of them. Because they are inscribed with the name ‘Sibyl,’ they are thought to belong to one person, and they have become confused.”

Up to this point, there is nothing inconsistent with Augustine’s passage. But what follows contradicts it. The elegant writer continues:

> “They cannot be distinguished or assigned to their respective authors, except in the case of the Erythraean Sibyl, who inserted her true name into the poem and foretold that she would be called Erythraean, although she was born in Babylon. Nevertheless, we too shall speak generally of ‘the Sibyl’ wherever it is necessary to make use of their testimonies.”

Later, too, he expressly presents verses of the Erythraean Sibyl in Book IV, chapter 15, and in *On Anger*, chapter 22. The facts themselves [Col. 0497B] cry out that all these things were fabricated by Christians unworthy of that name.

### Chapter 37

> “In the time of our prophets, whose writings had by then come to the knowledge of nearly all nations, there were not yet philosophers among the gentiles who were called by this name. The term began with Pythagoras of Samos, who began to excel and become known at the time when the captivity of the Jews was brought to an end.”

Nothing is truer than this, and it is an excellent argument for showing how recent Greek philosophy is.

The Parisian editors also illuminated this chronology, but some errors in their annotation arose either from the typesetters or from a hurried pen. I shall correct them here so that they may be removed from any editions that may be produced later.

First, they say that Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*, places Pythagoras in the sixty-third Olympiad. But it is the sixty-fifth Olympiad under which one reads in the Eusebian [Col. 0497C] *Chronicle*: “Pythagoras, the distinguished natural philosopher, is held in honor.”

The Benedictines add that Eusebius himself, in Book X of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 3, writes that Pythagoras flourished in the sixty-second Olympiad. Yet in that chapter Eusebius says nothing about Pythagoras’ age, but only in the following chapter, where he says merely that Pythagoras lived long after the Seven Sages.

They further add, concerning that period: “Servius Sulpitius was reigning among the Romans.” The learned men meant to say Servius Tullius, since Servius Sulpicius was a jurist contemporary with Cicero.

Finally, in speaking of the year of Pythagoras’ death, they write:

> “Pythagoras died in the seventieth Olympiad, in its fourth or fifth year, according to Eusebius’ *Chronicle*.”

It should read “the third or fourth,” and I think that is what the learned men wrote, since even children know that each Olympiad contains only [Col. 0497D] four years.

I mention this not in order to attack them—far from it! I least of all despise their labor—but so that other malicious people may learn from such examples that good and learned men should not therefore be mocked, especially when they show themselves accommodating toward others in such matters.

### Ibid.

Isis, moreover, is reported to have been the daughter of Inachus, who first began to reign among the Argives.

That is, if we believe the story of Io—which we previously demonstrated to be rather implausible in Book XVIII, chapter 3.

### Chapter 39

Moses appointed people among the nation to supervise the teaching of letters before they knew any letters of the divine law. Scripture calls them γραμματοεισαγωγεῖς, which may be rendered in Latin as “introducers of letters” or “those who lead into letters,” [Col. 0498A] because they introduce them, so to speak, into the hearts of learners—or rather into the learners themselves whom they teach.

The person who interpreted the Greek word for Augustine misled him. The Septuagint interpreters use the word to translate the Hebrew *schoter*, which does not mean a grammarian at all, but an officer or attendant of magistrates. See what Joan Clericus noted concerning this word in his comments on Exodus 5:6.

### Chapter 43

After mentioning the translations of Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Fifth Version, Augustine says:

> “Yet this translation, the Septuagint, the Church accepts as though it alone existed, and the Christian Greek peoples use it, most of whom know nothing of any other.”

That is, women, artisans, and the rest of the common people, resembling wandering Numidians. For the others, who had at least been lightly touched by sacred learning, had read or heard something [Col. 0498B] about Origen’s Tetrapla or Hexapla.

He continues:

> “From this Septuagint translation, what the Latin Churches possess was also translated into the Latin language.”

Thus learned and prudent men were reading a translation of a translation, neither of which most of the clergy could examine. Two people, or perhaps no one, as Augustine puts it, were able to compare the Greek with the Hebrew text; more could compare the Latin with the Greek, but few compared with those who knew no Greek—including Augustine.

Go now and praise in such men either their acumen in interpreting Scripture, their diligence in sacred studies, or their prudence in resting content with translations whose quality—whether good or bad—they did not know.

> “Nevertheless,” he says, “in our own time there was [Col. 0498C] the presbyter Jerome, a most learned man and skilled in all three languages, who translated these same Scriptures into Latin not from the Greek but from the Hebrew.”

Joan Clericus demonstrates rather clearly in his *Hieronymian Questions* the extent of Jerome’s learning in both languages, Greek and Hebrew. Yet, compared with others, the presbyter of Stridon was certainly very learned.

Augustine continues:

> “Although the Jews admit that his labor was learned and truthful, while the Septuagint interpreters are said by them to have erred in many places, nevertheless the Church of Christ judges no one preferable to the authority of so many men, chosen for this work by Eleazar, then the high priest. For even if one divine spirit had not appeared in them, but the learned Septuagint interpreters [Col. 0498D] had compared the words of their translation among themselves in the human manner, so that what pleased everyone might remain, no single interpreter ought to be preferred to them.”

Even if there were nothing to say in reply to this argument, it could not prevail against the facts themselves, so that a man learned in Hebrew would begin to believe that the obvious errors found in the Septuagint translation were not errors. Arguments derived from what appears to be fitting cannot be set against the facts themselves, because what ought not to have happened has often happened, and what ought to have happened has not happened.

Moreover, the entire story of the Septuagint interpreters is a mere fable, fabricated by a Hellenistic Jew, perhaps to accommodate the laziness of the Hellenists, so that they would not have to learn Hebrew when they believed they possessed a θεόπνευστον, [Col. 0499A] “God-inspired,” translation.

I confess that I am distressed to find so many and such great examples among the ancients not of circumspect faith founded upon sound reasoning, but of heedless credulity that seizes upon everything rashly—unless one would rather call this what we now call political cleverness.

Whichever explanation one accepts, we must conclude that, apart from Christ and the apostles who faithfully adhered to his teaching, we should not seek teachers in whose authority we may rest. Christ himself explicitly warned us about this in Matthew 23:8.

Moreover, it could easily have happened that not seventy, but several hundred men, were less skilled than one man. Indeed, how often have entire assemblies gone astray? And what is more familiar to lovers of truth than that votes are to be evaluated not by number but by [Col. 0499B] weight?

Almost no truth—not even the Christian religion itself—can be defended if numerical majority is treated as the mark and proof of truth.

Finally, as I have already said, the story of Aristaeus concerning the Septuagint interpreters is a ridiculous little tale. See what we have already noted on this subject in Volume II, Letter 28.

It is therefore worthy of laughter that the following is expressed in such weighty words:

> “But when so great a sign of divinity appeared in them, surely whoever else translates those Scriptures from Hebrew into any other language is truthful either if he agrees with those Septuagint interpreters, or, if he does not appear to agree, the prophetic profundity must be judged to be present there.”

Either something has dropped out here, or the following clause must be mentally supplied after “if he does not appear to agree”: “and yet agrees with the Hebrew text.” For [Col. 0499C] this is plainly what Augustine intends, as the following words show.

These are truly astonishing and unheard-of claims, and they ought not to be asserted rashly or without serious reasons. Who could persuade himself that the prophetic Spirit dictated one definite meaning to the Hebrew prophets who first committed the divine oracles to writing, and then breathed into the Greek translators of those same prophets a different or contrary meaning?

Let no one readily persuade himself of such things. Here no reason for belief presents itself except that senile fable of Aristaeus, which contains every sign of a badly contrived falsehood and which the facts themselves contradict.

For when one compares the translation with the Hebrew context, it is clear that very many errors were committed by the Septuagint interpreters—or by whoever it was who composed that translation: they read the Hebrew words incorrectly in their [Col. 0499D] exemplar; they confused letters that resembled one another; they did not know the meanings of rare words; they failed to understand obscure passages; and sometimes they did not sufficiently understand even clear ones.

These are the marks of a human and hallucinating spirit, not of a divine one.

Augustine himself could not have known these things from personal knowledge. But he ought rather to have kept silent about a matter he plainly did not understand than to pour forth so many empty arguments.

If we love truth, we must admit that such absurd opinions did not displease men who were by no means dull, because those opinions served the interests of their laziness and their reputation, as we have already indicated elsewhere.

## Chapter 44

“But,” someone may say, “how shall I know what the prophet Jonah said to the Ninevites: whether, ‘Three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown,’ or, ‘Forty days’? For who does not see that both could not then have been said by the prophet who had been sent to terrify the city with the threat of impending destruction? [Col. 0500A] … If, therefore, I am asked which of these Jonah said, I think it was rather what is read in the Hebrew: ‘Forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.’”

Very well. From this it ought to have been concluded either that the translators of the Septuagint had seriously erred, or that their manuscripts were corrupt. Augustine was unwilling to admit the former; therefore one would have had to resort to the latter, unless he had foreseen certain difficulties arising from it—namely, that the populace would say that their bishops had been very lazy, ill-advised, or unlearned, since they had continued to have the Latin version, derived from faulty Greek manuscripts, read aloud to them. For if they had erred through ignorance, this would have been a mark of great ignorance; and if they had been unwilling to inquire into the truth and correct the defects of the version, it would have shown no less laziness or imprudence. This was much worse, and exposed them to more dangerous consequences, than Jerome’s new translation of the Hebrew word *kikajon* in the same prophet—a matter concerning which Augustine had poured forth such complaints to be carried away by the winds. See his Epistle 71 and our notes upon it.

The Carthaginian orator therefore turned to another σοφὸν φάρμακον (“wise remedy”). “The Septuagint,” he says, “who translated much later, could have said something else which nevertheless pertained to the matter and converged upon one and the same meaning, although under another signification; and this would admonish the reader, without rejecting either authority, to rise from the history to seek those things for the signification of which the history itself was written.”

These things can indeed be counted among those which are not by their nature contradictory and therefore impossible; otherwise, however, they are touched by not even the slightest plausibility. The translators of the Septuagint, precisely because they profess to be translators, promise that they will say in Greek what has been written in Hebrew. If they fail to do this, they cannot escape the charge either of incompetence, negligence, or bad faith. This is always true in the interpretation of histories, if one may speak in that way; indeed, it is truer still: whoever introduces into a translation someone saying what is not in the original that he is translating is lying.

“But,” you will say, “one may alter the words somewhat if the meaning remains the same.” I do not deny it; but this can be done only when the genius of the language used by the translator requires it, not when there is no necessity. Moreover, it is false that, as regards the meaning, “forty days still” and “three days still” are the same.

But let us hear Augustine violently applying allegorical contrivances in order to defend the Greek translators:

“If by that city the Church of the Gentiles, prophetically prefigured, is rightly understood—overthrown, that is, through repentance, so that it would no longer be what it had been—then, because this was accomplished through Christ in the Church of the Gentiles, of which Nineveh bore the figure, whether by forty days or by three days, the same Christ is signified: by forty, because he spent that many days with his disciples after the resurrection and ascended into heaven; by three days, because he rose again on the third day.”

All this is fabricated. First, if I deny that Nineveh in Jonah is a figure of the Church of the Gentiles, no one will prove the contrary from Scripture. [Col. 0501A] In the second place, I shall say that it is absurd to call the overthrow intended for Nineveh on account of its sins, unless it should repent, a figure of the change of conduct that takes place through repentance. Surely, if sins and destruction on account of sins are a figure of repentance and of the alteration of former institutions through repentance, then everything can be a figure of everything, and no resemblance between figures and the things figured will any longer be sought. Round things may be regarded as archetypes of square things, and square things as antitypes of round things. Darkness will be an image of light, and light of darkness. Finally, the forty or three days granted for repentance cannot be figures of the days of Christ’s fasting and death, since they have nothing in common except a similarity of number.

Indeed, even if so many violent interpretations were admitted, it still would not have been permissible for the translators of the Septuagint to alter the prophet’s number. And what Augustine says here about their prophetic spirit is plainly empty and fit only to be thrown as a stumbling-block before readers. For who would not immediately say that, if the translators of the Septuagint had been endowed with a prophetic spirit, they would by its aid have poured forth new prophecies rather than corrupting old ones through ignorance?

Thus Jerome rightly writes in his Commentary on Jonah:

“The number three, which is given by the Septuagint, does not suit repentance, and I am sufficiently astonished that it was translated in this way, since in the Hebrew there is no likeness of letters, syllables, accents, or word between the two. For ‘three’ is said *shalosh*, and ‘forty’ *arbaim*. Otherwise, the prophet, sent from Judaea on so long a journey to the Assyrians, demanded a repentance worthy of his preaching, so that ancient and festering wounds might be healed by an ointment applied for a long time. Moreover, the number forty is appropriate to sinners, fasting, prayer, sackcloth, tears, and perseverance in supplication; for this reason Moses also fasted for forty days on Mount Sinai,” and so forth.

Accordingly, learned men have conjectured that there is an error in the Septuagint: either they used a faulty manuscript in which, instead of an unreadable word meaning “forty,” there stood an unreadable word meaning “three”; or else a defect entered the Greek manuscript and Γ was written instead of Μ. The frequent errors found in numbers among ancient writers led outstanding critics to believe that numbers were once marked not by complete words but by letters. See John Drusius and Hugo Grotius on Jonah.

Nothing, however, prevents us here also from hearing Isaac Vossius, who believed that this task had been assigned to him so that he might defend the translators of the Septuagint:

“In this age,” he says, “the Greek version is unanimously rejected at this passage, and not without reason. Augustine, in Book XVIII, chapter 44, of *The City of God*, attempts to reconcile this discrepancy, but in my judgment achieves nothing. Theodoret does better, attributing the error of the Greek copies not to the translators but to the scribes. Jerome is astonished at this variation, since there is no similarity of either words or numbers between three and forty. But Justin Martyr resolves the question: in his dialogue with Trypho, reproducing the very words of the translators, he counts forty-three days. He repeats the same number twice, so that no one might suppose that a fault was present.

“If, therefore, we follow this reading of the Septuagint, we shall now have an evident explanation of the discrepancy. The smaller number, namely, has dropped out of the Hebrew manuscripts, while the larger is absent from the Greek copies now extant; but it was formerly present in them, not—as is commonly printed—‘three more days,’ but clearly, as can be inferred from Justin, ‘three and forty days.’ This number, moreover, is entirely consistent with the circumstances. Three days were absolutely required for preaching and traversing the city. After completing one day’s journey, he foretold that the city would perish after forty-three days. On the second day, having advanced farther, he indicated forty-two days. Thus, when the third day had elapsed and the city had already been traversed, only forty days remained.”

This is from Vossius, *On the Translation of the Septuagint*, chapter 23. It is ingenious; but it seems to me much more plausible—since the other Fathers and manuscripts agree in the common reading—that Justin possessed a manuscript in whose text *treis* (“three”) was written, but on whose margin someone had added *tessarakonta* (“forty”) from a Hebrew manuscript; Justin, thinking that the marginal addition had been omitted from the text, said “forty-three.” [Col. 0502B]

## Chapter 52

After mentioning the ten persecutions:

“For the plagues of the Egyptians,” he says, “since there were ten of them before the people of God began to depart from there, are thought to refer to this interpretation … But I do not think that those persecutions were prophetically signified by what happened in Egypt, although to those who hold this view the individual plagues seem to have been elaborately and ingeniously compared with the individual persecutions; not by the prophetic spirit, but by the conjecture of the human mind, which sometimes reaches the truth and sometimes is mistaken.” [Col. 0502C]

Who would not exclaim here: καλῶς, σοφῶς—“Well said! Wisely!” Nothing could be better. We too pass the same judgment on the many mystical interpretations of Augustine, by which he twisted almost the whole Old Testament into foreign meanings.

For the ten persecutions, see also Sulpicius Severus, Book II of *Sacred History*.

## Book XIX

### Chapter 1, § 3

“Finally, there were some who, although they pursued different final goods—some virtue, others pleasure—nevertheless maintained the same manner and custom, from which they were called Cynics.”

For this reason Apollinaris Sidonius writes in Poem 2, verse 167:

> Whatever the Cynic crowd in the Erichthian gymnasia  
> turns over in mind, imitating, Epicurus, your companions.

Jacques Sirmond cites this passage to illuminate the subject.

### Chapter 7

“Care was taken that the imperious city should impose upon the conquered nations not only its yoke but also its language through the peace of alliance, by which there would be no lack—indeed, there would be an abundance—of interpreters.”

The very learned Justus Lipsius discussed this matter extensively in chapter 4 of *On the Correct Pronunciation of the Latin Language*. He rightly observes there that one should read here not *pacem societatis* (“the peace of alliance”), but *speciem societatis* (“the appearance of alliance”), or *per pacem sociatis* (“through those joined by peace”). I wish that the Benedictines had brought forward the reading of the manuscript copies.

### Chapter 24

After showing that there is no people without love of God and neighbor, Augustine begins the chapter as follows:

“But if a people is defined not in this way but in another, for example, if it is said that a people is an assembly of a rational multitude united in harmonious fellowship concerning the things it loves, then clearly, in order to see what sort of people each one is, we must look at what it loves. Whatever it may love, if it is an assembly of a multitude—not of animals but of rational creatures—and is united by harmonious fellowship in the things it loves, it is not improperly called a people; all the better, then, the better the things in which it agrees; and all the worse, the worse the things in which its agreement lies.”

Then he adds:

“According to this definition of ours, the Roman people is a people,” and so forth.

I am surprised that Augustine did not recall the passage of Deuteronomy 32:21:

> They provoked me with that which was not God,  
> and angered me with their vanities;  
> and I will provoke them with that which is not a people,  
> and anger them with a foolish nation.

There God is looking toward the calling of the nations, as Paul teaches in Romans 10:19. Certainly those described by Lucilius were scarcely worthy of the name “people”:

> But now from morning until night, on holiday and working day alike,  
> all day long, people and senators together,  
> they all boast in the forum and never depart,  
> all devoting themselves to one and the same pursuit and craft:  
> to deceive with words cunningly, to fight deceitfully,  
> to compete in flattering, to pretend to be a good man,  
> to lay ambushes, as though all were enemies to all.

Lactantius preserved these elegant verses for us in *The Divine Institutes*, Book V, chapter 9.

## Book XX

### Chapter 7

Concerning Revelation 20:1 and following:

“Now the thousand years,” he says, “can, as far as occurs to me, be understood in two ways: either because this event takes place during the last thousand years—that is, in the sixth millennium of years, as on the sixth day, whose latter portions are now passing—followed then by the Sabbath that has no evening, namely, the rest of the saints, which has no end,” and so forth. [Col. 0503C]

These are the fruits of allegorical arithmetic, from which many of the ancients inferred that the duration of this world would be six thousand years, that the seventh millennium would bring it to an end, and that then there would be an eternal Sabbath for the godly. Thus Saint Barnabas, *Epistle*, chapter 15. See there the notes of the very learned Jean-Baptiste Cotelier, who supplies the names and passages of others who agree with him.

### Chapter 15

Concerning this passage from Revelation 20:13:

“And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, and death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them.”

Augustine reasons as follows:

“But who are the dead whom the sea gave up, who were in it? For surely those who die in the sea are not in hell, nor are their bodies preserved in the sea; or, what is even more absurd, did the sea have good dead people and hell bad ones? Who would think this? But certainly some appropriately understand the sea in this passage as signifying this present age.”

Augustine was repeatedly misled by the Latin word *infernus* (“hell”), because he did not know that ᾅδης (*Hades*), in Hebrew [the Hebrew term is omitted in the supplied text], means “the grave.” See what we noted concerning Volume II, Epistle 64.

The dead whom the sea will give up are the corpses of those who perished in it; death and the grave are the remaining dead, who fell on land, whether unburied or buried. For “death” and ᾅδης (*Hades*) are often placed in parallel, as in 1 Corinthians 15:54 and Revelation 20:14. See the commentators on those passages.

### Chapter 19

Concerning 2 Thessalonians 2:1 and following, § 3:

“Some think that this was said about the Roman Empire, and that for this reason the Apostle Paul did not wish to write it openly, lest he incur the charge of wishing evil upon the Roman Empire, which was expected to be eternal; so that when he said, ‘For the mystery of iniquity is already at work,’ he intended Nero to be understood, whose deeds already seemed like those of Antichrist.”

[Col. 0504A] It seems to me much more probable that Paul was speaking here about the rebellion of the Jews against the Romans, about which he spoke more obscurely so as not to harm his countrymen. See on this subject the commentary of Henry Hammond, in the additions that he incorporated into that writer’s notes. But I consider this observation of Augustine excellent as an explanation of the obscurity of the Apocalypse, in which the destruction of pagan Rome was foretold under the name Babylon.

### Chapter 29

“Through this great and wondrous prophet Elijah, after the law had been expounded to him, it is a very celebrated belief in the speech and hearts of the faithful that, at the end of time, before the judgment, the Jews will believe in the true Christ, that is, in our Christ.”

It is remarkable that in those times this opinion had taken such deep root in people’s minds and had been received with such general agreement, when Christ had most explicitly taught in Matthew 17:12, and in the other evangelists, that John the Baptist was to be understood under the name Elijah. It was easy to understand that “the great and terrible day of the Lord” was the day or period when God allowed Jerusalem and Judaea to be plundered by the Romans and devastated by sword and fire. But no interpreter placed this in clearer light than Henry Hammond, in his notes on Matthew 24 and elsewhere.

It has often happened that many people who were by no means dull have agreed in an error because they preferred to follow their predecessors rather than examine their opinions. See Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 35.

## Book XXI

### Chapter 3, § 1

Against the eternity of the punishments of the wicked, Augustine proposes this objection:

“There is no body,” they say, “that can suffer pain and yet cannot die.”

He refutes this objection at great length, introducing various incredible and false stories from Pliny, yet he does not satisfy the matter. What could have been easier to say than that at that time the laws governing bodies and spirits would be different from those that govern them now, and that God could bring it about that, through a certain movement of the body—one not so great as to injure the body—an immense pain would be excited in the minds of the wicked? See Denis Petau, *Theological Dogmas*, Volume III, *On Angels*, Book III, chapter 5.

### Chapter 24

“That God may soften and turn his sentence toward the better.”

Jean-Frédéric Gronovius rightly reads *in mollius* (“toward the gentler”) here, in *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 6.

Thus Hegesippus, *On the Destruction of Jerusalem*, Book I, chapter 12:

“They prevailed upon Aristobulus to turn his mother from carrying out the harsher command toward gentler measures.”

So the manuscripts read, whereas the printed books have *meliora* (“better things”). This wording was drawn from writers of a better age. Tacitus, *Annals* I: “The offence was sufficiently and more than sufficiently compensated by dismissal, money, and gentle counsels.” Hegesippus again, chapter 16: “And with words humbly turned toward gentler measures, he softened the consul’s indignation.”

### Chapter 26

In introducing Paul’s passage in 1 Corinthians 3:11 concerning the foundation upon which some build gold, silver, and other precious materials, while others build wood, hay, and stubble, [Col. 0505A] Augustine introduces people who believed that baptism and communion with the Catholic Church were sufficient to avoid eternal condemnation. He then hesitates greatly over the passage, as though it concerned conduct, whereas Paul is speaking about doctrine. He was similarly agitated elsewhere in interpreting it. See the notes on Volume VI, *On Faith and Works*, chapter 15.

From this arose another hesitation, revealed in these words:

“After the death of this body, until one reaches that final day of condemnation and reward which will come after the resurrection of bodies, if it is said that the spirits of the dead undergo a fire of such a kind that those who in the life of this body did not possess such conduct and loves that their wood, hay, and stubble should be consumed do not feel it, while others do feel it, namely those who carried such buildings with them—whether only there, or both here and there; or whether for this reason they find here, so that they may not find it there, a fire of transitory tribulation that burns up worldly things, although pardonable as regards condemnation—I do not refute it, because perhaps it is true.”

Thus this passage of Paul was like a reef upon which Augustine struck more than once. Yet many hold him out to us as a great interpreter of Scripture—though those who will ultimately believe such advocates are people with no study of the sacred books, or those who have never read Augustine’s works attentively.

## Book XXII

### Chapter 7

“Since Romulus lived approximately six hundred years before Cicero,” and so forth.

J. Ludovicus Vives published *before Scipio*—namely, Aemilianus, whom Cicero introduced speaking in the books *On the Republic*—because Cicero was not born until the 648th year after the founding of the City. But the Benedictines rightly retained the reading cited, which is found in all the manuscript copies, since it is by no means necessary to suppose that Augustine, speaking from memory, calculated more precisely; nor is the error so great that he could not have fallen into it.

### Chapter 8, § 1

“Why,” they ask, “are those miracles that you proclaim to have happened not happening now?”

This is an objection of the pagans. To resolve it more conveniently, innumerable fabricated miracles of relics were produced, especially in the fourth century, miracles unheard of before that time. When the Christians of this period spoke more incautiously and therefore more truthfully, they admitted that miracles no longer occurred. This happened to Augustine in *On True Religion*, chapter 25, where he denies that those miracles—such as those of the apostles—had been permitted to continue into his own time. But later he retracted these words on account of the new miracles, the usefulness of which he began to recognize only afterward.

Here too he recounts many things, all of which he concludes with that admirable narrative about which we have written in Volume V. But concerning all these matters, and especially the fabricated miracles of the fourth century, see Henry Dodwell, *Irenaean Dissertation* 2.

### Chapter 24, § 3

“What he has contrived to be seen by spectators in the theatres as marvelous, to be heard as incredible, and to be exhibited—namely, by human craftsmanship.”

As Justus Lipsius thinks, he means *pegmata*, or theatrical machines, whose forms and movements provided marvelous spectacles. The very learned author demonstrates this at length in *On the Amphitheatre*, chapter 22; it will not be regretted that one has read it.

# Into the Eighth Volume

[Col. 0505]

## Desiderius Erasmus to the Reader

[Col. 0505C]

Just as in battles the valor and ardor of soldiers and commanders usually shine forth most brilliantly, so the divine Augustine—although he is everywhere worthy of admiration for many reasons—nowhere else displayed so clearly the force of his intellectual penetration, the subtlety of his judgment, and the vigor, abundance, and range of his argumentation as in these books. In them he fights against heresies for the tranquility of the house of God, which he loved above all else. And although he pursued these heresies with the greater hatred because he loved Christ’s bride, the Church, more intensely, he nevertheless labors everywhere with singular charity, seeking to heal people rather than destroy them.

Read prosperously, and farewell.

# Notes on the Book *On Heresies*

[Col. 0505D]

## Preface

“Our Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, recently removed from human affairs, also wrote six books concerning eighty heresies, recounting everything in historical narrative and engaging in no disputation on behalf of the truth against falsehood.”

The Benedictines note concerning these words that Augustine had seen only Epiphanius’s *Anacephalaeosis*. Yet he did not even see this work in its entirety, for at its beginning and in several passages the author indicates that he is writing an epitome of a larger work. [Col. 0506C] It is credible that Augustine possessed only excerpts from it, made by someone who knew Greek.

### Heresy 1: The Heresy of the Simonians

“He wished to be believed to be Jupiter, and a certain prostitute named Helen to be Minerva; he had made her his partner in crimes. He also supplied his disciples with images of himself and of the prostitute for worship; and he had publicly established them at Rome as statues of the gods.”

Thus fables gradually grow as they are narrated by more people—like a stream which, as more and more waters join it, eventually becomes a river. The author of the *Clementine Recognitions*, Book II, § 9, and Justin Martyr, *Apology* 1, do indeed mention a statue of Simon set up at Rome; but they say nothing about a statue of Selena or Helena, his concubine. This, therefore, must be an addition by Augustine, writing this from memory.

It is remarkable that the story of a statue so disgraceful and so obvious, supposedly erected by the Romans and therefore rightly mocked by the pagans, pleased the ancients to such an extent that they affirmed it with one voice. See Jean-Baptiste Cotelier’s notes on the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book VI, chapter 9, and on the *Recognitions*, Book II, chapter 9.

But the very learned author is mistaken when he implies that Augustine denied the story told about Simon’s death in Epistle 36 to Casulanus. Augustine merely says that the Romans denied that Peter had fasted on the Sabbath, since he was going to fight Simon Magus on the following Sunday.

The learned now almost unanimously agree that Justin, or another author of this story, was deceived by a statue erected to Hercules on the Tiber Island, whose base still survives today with the inscription:

> SEMONI SANCO DEO

“to the god Semo Sancus.”

See Desiderius Heraldus on Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 13; Henri Valois on Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 13; and others in many places.

This makes clear how much weight should be given to the agreement of many people who, without examination, affirm the same thing one after another. A similar example may be observed in *The City of God*, Book XX, chapter 29, concerning the coming of Elijah before the final judgment.

If we wish to avoid error in matters commonly established by the testimony of several people, we must first of all examine how far the matter could have been known to those who agree, and separate them from one another. For those who merely repeat what they have received from others—things into which they themselves made no investigation—do not deserve to be counted as witnesses. And if even the first assertors of the matter reported something they did not know well, that splendid cloud of witnesses is very easily dispersed.

This can be observed in the history of the statue of Simon Magus; and I do not know whether the same may not be said of the whole sect of the Simonians. For although it is established from the Acts of the Apostles that Simon was a wicked man, many things were invented about him, as is clear from Clement’s *Recognitions*.

### Heresy 50

“Epiphanius calls them Vadians and wishes them to be regarded as schismatics, not heretics; others call them Anthropomorphites.”

Since Augustine praises Epiphanius as his authority here, I am entirely convinced that we should read *Audians*. The bishop of Constantia calls them heretics after Audius, their founder. I would not linger over scribal errors here, just as Sirmond did not in the *Work of the Predestined*, although the manuscript read *Valdiani*. Names that are less familiar are always most easily corrupted by scribes. Thus in Facundus of Hermiane, Book VIII, in Sirmond’s edition of 1696, column 671, the same heretics are called *Basiani*, a word derived from *Vadiani*.

### Heresy 88: The Heresy of the Pelagians

“They are enemies of the grace of God, through which we have been predestined for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ and through which we are rescued from the power of darkness, to such an extent that they believe a person can fulfill all the divine commandments without it,” and so forth. [Col. 0507D]

Anathema upon all who are enemies of divine grace! Nor do I think that Pelagius, if he were to return to life, would deliberate about whether he could answer “Amen”; he would immediately reply to it in a loud voice.

But Augustine accuses of hostility to God’s grace those who rejected the inward inspiration necessary for each individual act, an inspiration that is irresistible and given only to the elect until the end of life. That is, they rejected Augustine’s grace, not God’s; for he never demonstrated from Scripture that this inspiration is called either “grace” or “the grace of God.”

Moreover, when God gives someone commandments, that person is undoubtedly able to observe them. For God, who is just, neither commands impossibilities nor inflicts punishments upon those who have not done the impossible. And if, beyond the bare command, some other divine assistance is necessary—which Pelagius did not deny—God does not withhold it from anyone to whom he gives a command.

But here, as elsewhere in Augustine, everything has been arranged to provoke hatred. On this matter, one should consult Denis Petau’s *On the Pelagian and Semi-Pelagian Heresy*, which appears in Volume III of his *Theological Dogmas*. We shall not touch upon the remaining matters, concerning which we said enough in our notes on Augustine’s letters. But from this we shall observe that, when the position of opponents is under discussion, one should not readily believe their adversaries.

# Notes on the Treatise *Against the Jews*

## Chapter 3, § 4

“What, then, can be meant by the fact that certain psalms are prefaced in this way—psalms which they themselves also read and possess among the authoritative sacred writings—so that their titles say, ‘For those things that will be changed,’ while the text of those same psalms proclaims Christ, unless it is because their change was foretold as destined to take place through him by whom it is seen to have been fulfilled?”

Augustine is referring to the titles of the psalms in the Greek division: Psalms 44, 68, and 79. If we do not wish to conceal the truth, we must admit that Augustine was extremely well equipped to blunt the obstinacy of the Donatists or the foolish impiety of the Manichaeans. But he ought not to have entered the arena against the Jews, since he lacked weapons absolutely necessary for that battle—namely, knowledge of the Hebrew language and a literal understanding of the Old Testament.

The whole treatise makes this clear, but especially the following argument, which he pursues at greater length. [Col. 0508C] The Jews could have replied, and with good reason, that the Septuagint had mistranslated the Hebrew words found here, *al shoshanim*, as ὑπὲρ τῶν ἀλλοιωθησομένων (“for those who will be changed”), as though the Hebrew had to be read *sheshonim*, meaning “those who change” or “those who are different.” They could have said that the passage should be translated, with Aquila, “upon lilies,” since *shoshan* means “lily,” and the word here signifies either a musical instrument or the beginning of a song. How could Augustine have proved the contrary?

Furthermore, if they had conceded that the passage should be translated as the Septuagint translated it, they would have denied that it followed from this that the law ought to be changed by the Messiah. They would have said only that, whenever he came, the wretched condition of their nation would be changed into a happier one. Augustine would therefore have labored in vain to silence those who used such arguments or arguments like them.

In fact, there are only two ways of debating with the Jews that can produce any useful result. The first is to use not only the Scriptures of the Old Testament, which they know how to evade, but also their own opinions and writers against them. Augustine could not do this, since those arsenals were unknown to him. The other is to demonstrate that the history and miracles of Jesus of Nazareth truly occurred. Augustine could have done this if, abandoning allegories and frigid sophistries, he had turned to precise reasoning such as that found in Books II and III of the work *On the Truth of the Christian Religion* composed by Hugo Grotius. These arguments are also set out more fully in other works of recent authors.

But in those centuries, however much the ignorant or partisan might boast of it, the precise method of reasoning and proof was little known. [Col. 0509A]

# Notes on the Book *On the Usefulness of Believing*

## Chapter 3, § 5

“All Scripture called the Old Testament is presented in four ways to those who desire to know it carefully: according to history, according to etiology, according to analogy, and according to allegory.”

All these must be referred to one matter—namely, what is signified by the words of Scripture, which must be explained according to all the rules of grammarians and critics. Etiology, analogy, and allegory, when they do not rest upon the foundation of literal interpretation, are mere trappings for the populace, as learned men demonstrated long ago.

But let us see how Augustine understands these categories:

“According to history,” he says, “it is presented when one is taught what was written or what was done; and what was not done but merely written as though it had been done.”

On this account everything would be historical, because things are either written or done. Nor is anything written as though it had been done when it had not been, except parables. Augustine nevertheless adduces as an example of true history the incident commended by Christ in Matthew 12:3–4.

“According to etiology,” he says, “it is presented when one is taught for what reason something was done or said.”

An example of this is Christ’s statement concerning the reason why Moses permitted divorce in Matthew 19:8. But in investigating causes of this kind, one must either possess the prior authority of Christ and the apostles, or have extremely certain history and indisputable reasons. Otherwise, any reasons whatever may be assigned for anything whatever—reasons which account for both sides among the ancients.

“Third, according to analogy,” he says, “it is presented when it is demonstrated that the two Testaments, the Old and the New, do not contradict one another.”

This is entirely true if God’s intention and the difference between the two economies are properly observed. For the law contained στοιχεῖα (*stoicheia*), as Paul calls them—elements of religion by which the Jews were gradually led toward Christian perfection, as by a pedagogue. Thus many things were permitted under the law that are no longer permitted under the Gospel, although in both cases God’s intention was the same. He used, however, different economies according to the capacity of peoples and times.

If these matters are confused and the Old Testament is twisted by violent allegories so that it appears to teach exactly the same things as the Gospel in every respect, then no analogy will be preserved.

Finally, “according to allegory,” he says, “it is presented when one is taught that certain things written are not to be taken literally but understood figuratively.”

I know what the defenders of allegories are accustomed to say. But only those things should ultimately be understood allegorically that clearly present the appearance of an allegory, such as Ecclesiastes 12:4 and following. Everything else should be understood literally. But on this subject, another time.

### Chapter 9

“True religion cannot properly be undertaken in any way unless those things are believed which each person will later, if he has conducted himself well and proved worthy, attain and apprehend; nor can it be undertaken at all without a certain weighty compulsion of authority.”

These words are directed against the Manichaeans, who chiefly accused the Catholic Church on the ground that it commanded those who came to her to believe, whereas they themselves promised to demonstrate everything by reason. In this matter they were certainly intolerable, since they produced nothing but monstrosities, and things wholly devoid of even the appearance of probability, much less supported by reason, as Augustine correctly shows in many places.

Here, however, he answers them otherwise than I would wish and than the case required. By what argument could he prove that certain things must first be believed without reason—for this is what must be understood—which would later be apprehended? What purveyor of lies and fables could not demand something similar and then say, if anyone rejected his inventions, that he had been unworthy to attain them? Could not Jews and pagans have replied the same to Christians who reasoned against them: that one must believe rather than reason? Christians, therefore, if they wished to act with equal justice, ought to have endured this being used against them which they had used against pagans and Jews. Nor was there any reason for them to fear on that account, since the Christian religion would prove far superior in reason, as Hugo Grotius and others sufficiently demonstrated when they began, with a most commendable purpose and the happiest success, to defend it by reason.

But three things in Augustine’s time caused faith to be demanded without reason. First, they were not sufficiently trained in philosophy and criticism to defend Scripture adequately against the objections of the Manichaeans and others. This is clear even from the account of creation, which so tormented Augustine that neither in the *Confessions* nor in his books *On Genesis Literally* did he satisfy either himself or anyone else. The creation divided into seven days, and God’s rest on the seventh day, were reefs against which he struck whenever he ventured to navigate this part of the sacred ocean. He rejects the literal sense as contrary to reason, but embraces an allegorical sense plainly at variance with the words.

Second, they were genuinely conscious that they were saying not a few things plainly contrary to sound reason—such as the many propositions concerning grace and predestination, and other doctrines connected with them, which Augustine proposed as articles of faith to be believed.

Finally, this was the language of a party already conscious of its strength and relying upon its numbers. Augustine often boasts of this here, while despising the small number of those who thought otherwise. Parties and minds of this kind cannot tolerate being contradicted by a minority; they want faith to be immediately granted to those who speak.

### Chapter 10

After attempting by many arguments to prove that a priest ought to believe a person who desires to have the Christian religion proved to him, provided that the person is acting with a mind eager for truth, Augustine concludes from this that such a person in turn ought to believe the priest when he affirms something concerning religion. “In religion,” he says, “what could be more unjust than for the ministers of God to believe us when we promise them an honest intention, while we refuse to believe them when they give us commands?”

I am amazed that our rhetorician was willing to pursue such a feeble argument at such length. First, a Jewish or pagan priest could have said similar things to Christians, since Jews and pagans were superior in power and numbers within the Roman Empire. It would therefore have been better for a Christian to refrain from such a reply.

Second, who taught Augustine that the Christian religion ought to be explained only to those believed to be devoted to truth? Do not the sacred writers disclose everything to the unworthy as well, since in books destined to fall into anyone’s hands they set forth the Christian religion no less than the Jewish? I admit that sometimes, to avoid danger or useless disputation, it is better to keep silent than to proclaim among wicked people what they will despise or receive with indignation. But apart from such circumstances, religion ought to be demonstrated with the greatest care to everyone, especially in books. Indeed, Augustine himself acted in this way, as did all Christian teachers.

Third, everyone must be regarded as good until it is established that he is wicked. But who knows the mind of one who asks that religion be explained to him, unless his conduct has previously revealed it? The case of doctrine, however, is entirely different: no one ought to assent to it before its truth has been established. One ought not condemn it before hearing the arguments, but no law commands one to embrace it.

Fourth and finally, if someone commands me imperiously to believe something which by its nature is no better known to him than to me, and gives no reason, I can believe him only foolishly; for each person’s mind is best known to that person himself.

But why continue? If Augustine had lived among pagans, such as the Persians and other Eastern peoples still were in his time, and had approached a priest or magian and asked him for the reasons why the Persians worshipped fire, intending to believe him only after discovering that the reasons were sound, and if that priest had replied with the same arguments concerning the usefulness of belief that Augustine here reports to the Manichaean, Augustine would undoubtedly have felt that such tyranny was intolerable, and would have said so if he had dared. Let us not, then, regard as sound reasoning in Christian Africa what would have been a paralogism at the source of the Euphrates.

### Chapter 12

“I ask, then: if what is unknown ought not to be believed, how do children obey their parents and love them with mutual affection, when they do not believe that those persons are their parents? For this cannot in any way be known by reason; rather, with the mother’s authority intervening, the father is believed, while concerning the mother herself belief is often placed not even in the mother, but in midwives, nurses, servants, and so forth.”

But these cases are entirely dissimilar. Parents and others can know—and in fact do know—which children are theirs and which are the children of particular people; nor are they usually led by any advantage to substitute other people’s children for their own. Priests, however, who want to be believed concerning religion, are no more conscious of its truth than other people are if they lack arguments; and usually they increased their flock not without considerable benefit to themselves.

### Chapter 14

“If the heretic commands me to believe nothing, I do not believe that any true religion exists at all among human affairs. Since I do not believe that one exists, I do not seek it. But he, I suppose, will point it out to one who seeks it … I would not come, therefore, to the one who forbids me to believe unless I already believed something. Is there any greater madness than that I should offend him through the very faith which alone, unsupported by knowledge, led me to him?”

But whoever believes that some religion is true, or that God wishes to be worshipped by human beings, without any reason whatsoever, is either insane or so dull that he is not far removed from the insane. Whoever has trusted you without reason will also, when it seems appropriate, withdraw his trust from you without reason; and he will assent just as readily to the Arians if they gain power, or even, which is worse, to the Muslims—as the Africans in fact did after Augustine’s time. Whoever believes that some religion is true and seeks where he may find it is not so foolish as to fail to demand that some reason be given him.

### Same passage, § 21

“What of the fact that all heretics urge us to believe in Christ?” etc.

That is true. But was there ever a heretic so shameless or so dull as to say that there were no sound reasons for believing in Christ? I do not think so. Was there ever a priest so ignorant or so stupid that he could not produce some of those reasons? Certainly, if there was, he was unworthy of the priestly order and had been improperly admitted to it.

There is no one who would refuse to believe what he has not seen, provided only that it is established to him that those who teach what he has not seen were able to discover the truth and did not wish to deceive him, or that they themselves were not deceived. This becomes clear to us in the case of Christ and the apostles both from the nature of the things they taught and especially from the miracles.

“But how do you know,” you will say, “that such miracles occurred, and that the events narrated in the writings of the apostles really happened?” I know it in the same way in which I know all the other established events of ancient history—indeed, supported by stronger arguments—not because I believe the authority of someone from whom I do not know whether I am being deceived.

### Same passage, § 32

“We see Christ himself, insofar as the history—which they too believe—teaches us, wishing nothing earlier or more insistently than that people believe in him, although those with whom he had to deal were not yet fit to apprehend divine mysteries.”

Christ proclaimed the Gospel among the Jews. Yet there was no Jew who could not easily perceive that he was in no way urging idolatry and that he was giving outstanding moral precepts, even though they did not understand everything he said. Nor was there any among them who could not easily see that he performed miracles—both in number and in kind unlike those performed by the ancient prophets.

These two facts were sufficiently weighty reasons for belief. Christ cannot, with Augustine’s indulgence, be compared with those who wish to be believed without reason. In the Gospel according to John he repeatedly insists that his doctrine was received from his Father; but he does not demand belief in himself unless he confirms his words by miracles. Indeed, he speaks to his disciples in chapter 15:24:

> “If I had not done among them the works which no other has done, they would not have sin.”

Christ therefore by no means demanded that people believe in him without reason. Nor did he demand faith from those whom he healed, who had been brought to him for healing, until after he had already performed many miracles.

Yet, to conceal nothing, Augustine understood this point, as the following words show:

> “For what else do so many and such great miracles accomplish,” he says, “since he himself also says that they were performed for no other reason than that people might believe in him?”

Nothing is truer. But the miracles themselves were the strongest reason why they could safely believe him and understand that they were able to believe him. They knew that “God does not hear sinners”—that is, to perform miracles by which they might win belief for their frauds—“but if anyone is a worshipper of God and does his will, he hears him” (John 9:31).

Augustine therefore could not use Christ’s example to prove that the Catholic Church rightly demands to be believed without reason. Thus Christ, bringing a remedy that was to heal the most corrupt morals, secured authority for himself by miracles and, by authority, earned faith. These are Augustine’s words, with which we entirely agree. But we do not agree with what follows:

> “By faith he gathered a multitude; by the multitude he obtained antiquity; by antiquity he strengthened the religion.”

Although he founded and increased his Church after faith in him had been produced among the multitude, he did not aim thereby eventually to strengthen the religion through antiquity, as though antiquity would at some point become an argument for its truth. We do not follow Christ’s doctrines because their faith is ancient, but because it agrees with heavenly truth, to which Christ gave confirmation through his miracles.

Augustine found it convenient to use such arguments against heretics and schismatics, whom he repeatedly reproaches for novelty and small numbers—charges which pagans had once brought against Christians.

### Chapter 18

“When, therefore, we see so much divine assistance, so much progress and fruit, shall we hesitate to establish ourselves in the bosom of that Church which, until the confession of the human race, has obtained the summit of authority from the apostolic see, through the succession of bishops, while the heretics bark around her in vain and are condemned partly by the judgment of the people themselves, partly by the weight of councils, and partly also by the majesty of miracles?”

I do not know whether the words “until the confession of the human race” are sound. If they are, the meaning will be “while the human race confesses it.” But the words “from the apostolic see” seem much more suspect to me, since in the West the Roman see was commonly called by that name. Monks who copied ecclesiastical books attempted by every means to magnify its authority.

If Augustine understood this of the Church spread throughout all lands, it is false that it obtained the summit of authority from the apostolic see. Everyone knows that the Eastern Churches were earlier in time and did not wish to derive any authority from any Western church. If the apostolic see possessed any authority, it flowed from the communion which it had with the other Christian Churches, all of which together owed their entire power to Christ their head.

Nor did the African Churches, in the time of Cyprian and Augustine himself, wish to owe their authority to the Roman Church, as is sufficiently clear from the dispute with Stephen and from the other controversy concerning appeals overseas, although they may perhaps have acknowledged it as a mother.

Therefore, to disclose what I suspect, I would believe that the reading should be *ab apostolica fide*—“from the apostolic faith.” The first authority of the Christian Church was derived from the apostolic faith, that is, from agreement with the apostles. Tertullian reasons in this way in *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapters 20 and 21, and mentions several apostolic sees, not one alone:

> “The apostles founded Churches in each city, from which the other Churches subsequently borrowed, and daily continue to borrow, the root of faith and the seeds of doctrine, so that they might become Churches. Through this, they too are counted as apostolic, as offspring of the apostolic Churches.”

A little later:

> “From this, then, we establish our prescription: if the Lord Jesus Christ sent the apostles to preach, no others are to be received as preachers than those whom Christ appointed; for no one knows the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son has revealed him, nor does the Son appear to have revealed him to others than the apostles whom he sent to preach everywhere what he had revealed to them. But what they revealed—that is, what Christ revealed to them—I shall here also prescribe as something that ought to be proved in no other way than through the very Churches which the apostles themselves founded, preaching to them both with what they call the living voice and afterward through letters.”

If these things are so, it follows that every doctrine which agrees with those apostolic Churches, the mothers and original sources of the faith, must unquestionably be regarded as true, since it holds what the Churches received from the apostles, the apostles from Christ, and Christ from God.

These words show that *apostolic faith* can be read in Augustine with an excellent meaning, from which the apostolic sees themselves derived all their authority. They were believed for this reason: they professed to agree with the apostolic writings, which writings many of the most ancient heretics rejected.

But if Augustine actually wrote “the apostolic see,” he intended to bring the African Manichaeans to the African Catholic Church, which agreed with the Roman see. That argument, however, is weaker. For who had promised that the apostolic Churches would never depart from Christ’s doctrine? No one.

The same applies to what he derives from the agreement of the people and councils, which can favor false things no less than true ones; and from heretics condemned by the majesty of miracles, which in that age were ecclesiastical stratagems by which the common people were deceived. See *Against the Letter of the Fundamental*, chapter 4.

### Chapter 18

“It is not a report about smoke, nor some Persian little tale, for which it is enough to lend an ear and possess a mind not subtle but thoroughly childish.”

He calls the absurd doctrines of Mani a Persian tale, since Mani was Persian or Babylonian. See also Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 46, and later the book *Against the Letter of Mani*.

## Observations on the Book *Against the Letter of Mani*

### Chapter 1

“Our task, therefore, was to choose and desire better things, so that we might gain access to your correction—not through contention, rivalry, and persecutions, but by gently consoling, kindly exhorting, and mildly disputing, as it is written: ‘The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting in meekness those who think differently.’ It was therefore our task to wish to undertake these functions; it belongs to God to grant what is good to those who wish and ask for it.”

Who would not praise Augustine’s gentleness in this matter? Who would not applaud a bishop so timely mindful of Paul’s admonitions? Certainly I cannot sufficiently kiss these words. I shall also gladly transcribe the following, worthy of being preserved like cedar:

> “Let those rage against you who do not know with what labor truth is found and how difficult it is to avoid errors. Let those rage against you who do not know how rare and arduous it is to overcome carnal phantasms with the serenity of a devout mind. Let those rage against you who do not know with what difficulty the eye of the inner person is healed, so that it may be able to behold its sun, etc. Let those rage against you who do not know with what sighs and groans it comes about that God can be understood, even in however small a part.”

Nothing is truer than that those finally rage against others in order, as they think, to bring them to the right faith who do not know how easy it is to err and how difficult it is to heal judgments once formed.

I regret that Augustine did not persist in this pious view until his death. For he wrote this book around the year 397; but by the year 412 he had completely changed his mind, as is clear from his letter to Vincentius. At that point he finally understood that it was exceedingly easy and perfectly just to bring people to the Catholic Church by punishments, terror, and military force—and, what is astonishing, at the very time when he began attributing all good human actions to the irresistible inspiration of grace.

I also regret that, in Augustine’s pious words, one reads a condemnation of the emperors who enacted so many bloody laws against the Manichaeans, laws which are still read in the Theodosian Code. I know that their *elect* were accused of disgraceful sexual crimes, as Augustine tells us in *On Heresies*; but he also tells us that those who were merely hearers were ignorant of those impious mysteries. If, therefore, the Manichaeans were to be punished, penalties ought to have been imposed upon them with distinctions; yet this was not done.

By law 7, title 5, book XVI of the Theodosian Code, the Manichaeans of every kind are deprived of the right to make a will or to succeed, by will, to the property of their father or anyone else. Theodosius did not intend that constitution to apply only in the future but, contrary to all custom, also to the past. See also law 19 in the same title, and the commentary of Jacobus Gothofredus.

## Observations on the Books *Against Faustus the Manichaean*

In book XIV, *Against Moses*, Faustus had argued as follows:

> “He says (Deuteronomy 21:23) that everyone who hangs upon a tree is accursed. Do you therefore want me to accept him and believe him, when, if he was divine, it is clear that he knowingly and willingly cursed Christ; but if he cursed him unwillingly and unknowingly, it is clear that he was not divine?”

It is astonishing that Augustine could not refute so easy an objection. For he wants death and the curse to be one and the same thing, and cannot extricate himself in any way. Then, concerning the added words “accursed by God,” he interprets them thus:

> “For if God did not hate sin and our death, he would not send his Son to undergo and abolish it. What wonder, then, if that which God hates is accursed by God?”

But Moses makes no mention of sin or of any particular death, but only of a corpse hanging from a tree; and Moses teaches that this is an exceedingly polluted thing. See Johann Clericus on that passage.

## Book XVI, Chapter 22

“Here too is the passage whose ambiguity deceives Faustus: ‘You shall see your life hanging before you, and you shall not believe in your life.’ Someone may say that these words can be understood in another way; but that they cannot be understood of Christ Faustus neither dared to say, nor will anyone at all dare to say, unless he denies either that Christ is life, or that he was seen hanging by the Jews, or that they did not believe in him. Since he himself also says, ‘I am life,’ and it is established that he hung before the eyes of the unbelieving Jews, I do not see why we should doubt that the one of whom Christ says, ‘For he wrote about me,’ wrote this also concerning Christ.”

We, indeed, acknowledge no less than Augustine that Christ is the life of human beings, that he hung before unbelieving Jews, and that we are perhaps more distant from the doctrines of the Manichaeans than he was. Nevertheless, we absolutely deny that the passage in Deuteronomy concerns Christ.

It is Deuteronomy 28:66, where Moses describes the anxiety of the Jews carried away into captivity:

> “Among those nations also,” he says, “you shall find no rest, nor shall the sole of your foot have repose. For there the Lord will give you a trembling heart, failing eyes, and a soul consumed with grief. Your life shall hang before you. You shall fear night and day, and you shall not believe in your life. In the morning you shall say, ‘Would that it were evening!’ and in the evening, ‘Would that it were morning!’ because of the fear of your heart,” etc.

Everyone sees that the passage concerns a life uncertain and precarious which, in a metaphor familiar even to the Latins, is said to “hang.” The preceding and following context plainly demonstrates that this is the meaning. “Not believing in one’s life” unquestionably means not being secure about one’s life.

But if one may trample upon the proper meaning of words and forms of speech—by which an excellent sense most appropriate to the circumstances of the passage arises—and flee to a figurative meaning, while paying no attention to what precedes or follows, then first it will be possible to derive everything from every passage of Scripture; and next, nothing in the interpretation of Scripture will be certain, and any invention whatsoever may be proved from it.

I know that Athanasius and other Greek and Latin Fathers explained this passage in the same way. But even if many more were produced, their authority would not make all the laws of sound interpretation invalid. It is evident—for what compels us here to lie or conceal the truth?—that almost all of them were ignorant of sacred criticism and unfortunate interpreters of Scripture, whatever those may say who have read neither them nor Scripture with sufficient care.

## Book XVII, Chapter 1

Faustus reasons foolishly concerning the words of Matthew 5:17, “I did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it”:

> “Who testifies that Jesus said this? Matthew. Where did he say it? On the mountain. Who was present? Peter, Andrew, James, and John—only these four, for he had not yet chosen the others, nor Matthew himself,” etc.

Faustus reasoned in this way because he believed that Matthew had observed chronological order in his narrative. Johann Clericus shows in his *Evangelical Harmony* that Matthew did not do this. From that work it is clear that not only Matthew but all the other apostles had already been chosen at that time and had heard the sermon delivered on the mountain.

Consult that work, if the matter is worth the trouble. I am surprised that Augustine did not make this reply, since otherwise he refutes Faustus’s frivolous arguments reasonably well. This observation escaped not only Faustus but many others as well, and led some of them into errors.

## Book XXII, Chapter 35

“Since Abraham was living at that time in human affairs when the custom—which no law or authority prohibited—still joined in marriage the children of brothers and other blood relatives of a more distant degree, whereas it was no longer permitted for brothers born of both, or of one or the other, parent to be joined in marriage, what wonder is it that he had his sister, that is, one born from his father’s blood, as his wife? For when the king returned her to him, he himself said that she was his sister by his father, not by his mother.”

But he does not merely call her “sister,” which could have been ambiguous; he calls her his father’s daughter, though not his mother’s, in Genesis 20:12, from which it is clear that this must be understood literally.

In fact, there is no history which teaches us that among the Chaldaeans at that time the marriages of brothers and sisters were illicit, although Augustine asserts this. Epiphanius held the same opinion, as he testifies in *Heresy* 39, section 7, and Jerome in his book *Against Helvidius*. But neither offers any certain argument for the matter, which could not have been better known to them than to us. Augustine appears to have followed Jerome rashly.

## Book XXXIII, Chapter 6

“But what shall I do with you”—he addresses the Manichaeans, who entirely rejected the Scriptures of the Old Testament and maintained that those of the New Testament had been falsified—“you whose iniquity has made you so deaf to the testimonies of Scripture that, whatever is brought from it against you, you dare to say was not spoken by the Apostle but was written under his name by some unknown falsifier?”

Nothing more unjust or absurd could have been devised than what the Manichaeans did. Relying on no critical argument, but blinded only by prejudices—and extremely absurd ones at that—they declared falsified whatever in the writings of the apostles was contrary to their own opinions.

Augustine rightly brings this reasoning against them in book XXIV:

> “In the apostles’ letters, whatever we want is true; whatever we do not want is false.”

Nothing more shameless or foolish could have been invented. I suspect that, if they had dared, such people would have rejected all Scripture, both of the New and of the Old Testament. But because they wanted to be counted among Christians, they fell into absurd conjectures.

### Same passage

“Concerning which book it will be certain whose it is, if the letters which the Church says and maintains were propagated by the apostles themselves and made known throughout all nations with such eminence are uncertain as to whether they are apostolic; and if what the heretics opposed to this Church bring forward under the names of their authors—authors who lived long after the apostles—will be certain to have been written by the apostles?”

Excellent indeed. Since we see almost all Christians, from those who immediately succeeded the apostolic age onward, affirming with one voice—with few exceptions—that these writings are apostolic, there is no reason for anyone to doubt their testimony, provided only that there is nothing in those books which sound reason demonstrates to be unworthy of the divine Spirit.

No one who is not foolish or perversely disposed will read them without judging them entirely worthy of the authors to whom they are attributed and of men sent by God. A certain divine simplicity and sincerity also shines in them, wholly unlike the inventions and embellishments of later centuries. It is therefore easy to understand that they are more ancient and proceeded from the hands of men like whom, as we see, none existed afterward.

Since there is not even the slightest indication of forgery in the writings themselves, the testimony of Christians cannot be more suspect than that of pagan writers, who unanimously testify that the *Aeneid* was the work of a poet contemporary with Augustus, and whose testimony is given enormous weight by the style and excellence of the poem.
