Those, therefore, are not to be heeded who, without any critical arguments, began long after the time of the apostles to call their books into question merely because they were contrary to their own inventions.

### Same passage

“As though there were not also, in secular literature—this should rather be read *fuerint* than *fuerunt*—very certain authors under whose names many works were later brought forward and therefore rejected, either because they did not at all correspond to what was known to be theirs, or because, at the time when they wrote, they had in no way become known and did not deserve to be transmitted and commended to posterity by them or by their closest associates.”

Nothing could be more critical (*κριτικώτερον*) than this. We have an example in Augustine himself. In the barbarous centuries many spurious works were mixed with his genuine writings. Erasmus’s diligence removed some of them, but the Louvain scholars and especially the Benedictines were rightly moved to do so on a much larger scale, assisted by the catalogue of the works of the bishop of Hippo compiled by Possidius of Calama, his friend and disciple, which Johann Vlimmerius was the first to publish.

Consequently, many works praised as Augustine’s in earlier centuries were rightly rejected afterward, and will henceforth rightly be rejected on the authority of the Benedictine scholars. Since this is so, a critical obelus ought to be placed beside many passages drawn from those little works and adduced by writers on theological controversies in earlier centuries.

Lovers of truth ought therefore to thank the Benedictines; here we gladly offer them our own thanks.

### Same passage

“Need I mention others, when certain books brought forward under the name of Hippocrates, the most celebrated physician, were not accepted as authoritative by physicians? Nor did some similarity of subject and wording help them, once they were judged inferior when compared with those works which were truly known to be Hippocrates’, and because they did not become known at the time when his other writings too became known to be genuinely his.”

For criticism of the works of Hippocrates and the various judgments made concerning them, one should consult the learned physician Daniel Clericus, in his *History of Medicine*, written in French and published at Amsterdam in the year 1701, part 1, book 3, chapter 30.

The dissimilarity of the writings caused countless little books to be removed from Augustine’s works; they can now be seen at the end of the individual volumes. The same process has also begun to be carried out with the other Greek and Latin Fathers.

### Same passage

“But concerning those books by comparison with which works brought forward from elsewhere are rejected, how do we know that they are Hippocrates’—so that, if anyone denies this, he is not even refuted but laughed at—unless the continuous succession of testimony has commended them in this way, from Hippocrates’ own time down to the present and onward, so that it would be madness to doubt them?”

These and the other matters which Johann Clericus illustrated with many examples and testimonies of the ancients concerning the recognition of genuine authors are treated in part 3, section 2 of his *Art of Criticism*, where he discusses the indications of forgery. Indeed, the most excellent of critics could scarcely produce better arguments for this purpose.

### Same passage

“Whence do people know that the books of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, Varro, and other authors of this kind are theirs, except from the same continuous succession of testimony passed from one generation to the next?”

Add also that those who made such statements had no proposed reward or advantage for lying.

All this can be said most truly of those sacred books which have always been regarded as belonging to the people whose names they bear. In the writings themselves there is nothing that is not entirely worthy of men inspired by God. They have always been regarded as the genuine offspring of those men by all who professed to be their disciples, and there was no reason for them to lie.

For once Christians admitted those books as divine, they gained no advantage whatsoever in this life. On the contrary, from almost the beginning their morals and customs, and even many of their opinions—especially in later ages—could be reproved from those books. If they had been fabricated, they would have been written in such a way as to promote the advantage and reputation of those who used them. They would not have condemned those people so openly, as they do, nor have branded them as degenerate Christians and shown them to have been the founders of new doctrines and rites.

### Same passage

“Many have written many things about ecclesiastical literature, not indeed with canonical authority, but with some desire either to help or to learn. How is it established what belongs to whom, unless because, in the periods when each person wrote, he made known and published what he could, and from there the information, transmitted continuously and increasingly confirmed from one person to another, reached later generations and even our own time, so that, when asked whose a particular book is, we do not hesitate what we ought to answer?”

This is most true of the more distinguished books, which had circulated in everyone’s hands from the very age of the writers to whom they are attributed. Otherwise, even in that period, many works had been forged, as has been shown to many in the section of the *Art of Criticism* already mentioned.

From this Augustine could also have understood that books attributed to the Sibyls and to Hermes Trismegistus had been forged, although only a few centuries earlier they had been completely unknown. But from the fact that many books are forged it does not follow that all can be dragged under suspicion of forgery; nor, because many are genuine, can all be regarded as legitimate offspring of those to whom they are attributed.

This should be noted against those who, through ignorance of criticism or excessive partiality, have fallen into one or the other of these extremes.

### Same passage

“But why should I proceed into the distant past? Look at these writings which we have in our hands: if, after some time has passed from our present life, someone should deny either that those are Faustus’s or that these are mine, how is he refuted except because those who now know these things transmit their knowledge through an unbroken succession of descendants to those who will live far in the future?”

We can experience such things daily in writings produced in the age of our forefathers. Many of them were so celebrated that they were in everyone’s hands from the beginning and will remain so afterward.

For example, we have the works of Desiderius Erasmus, published both separately and collectively during his lifetime. They have been transmitted to us, and we too will transmit them to posterity. No one except a madman could doubt them—unless, perhaps, some letter lying concealed somewhere were later produced as though it were Erasmus’s and then called into question by others.

Nevertheless, to conceal nothing, the art of printing has made the matter much more certain and easier. From manuscript codices many spurious works could be brought forward which, because copies were rare, could not easily be refuted. Indeed, the most brilliant light of criticism was required to separate Augustine’s genuine works from the spurious ones.

Finally, he concludes this excellent discussion as follows:

> “Since this is so, who, unless overthrown by consenting to the wickedness and deceit of lying demons, is blinded by such madness as to say that the Church of the apostles could not have merited (that is, attained, as elsewhere) this: such a faithful and so numerous a concord among the brethren that they would transmit their writings faithfully—when they have preserved their sees in an unbroken succession down to the present bishops, and when the same thing occurs with the writings of any sort of people, whether outside the Church or within the Church, with such ease?” [Col. 0520B]

These points should be carefully weighed by those who deny that the apostolic writings were known to everyone from the apostles’ own age, circulated throughout the churches, and read publicly, and who instead maintain that they were only brought to light by men of the second century. Augustine seems to have had in mind this passage of Tertullian’s *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 36:

> “Come now, if you wish to exercise your curiosity more profitably in the matter of your salvation, visit the apostolic churches, in which the very chairs of the apostles still preside in their own places, in which their authentic letters are recited, sounding the voice and displaying the face of each one. Are you near Achaia? You have Corinth. If you are not far from Macedonia, you have Philippi; you have the Thessalonians. If you can travel into Asia, you have Ephesus. And if you are near Italy, you have Rome, from which authority is available to us as well.” [Col. 0520C]

Therefore, since their authentic letters had been recited from apostolic times in the churches they had founded, they were rejected by heretics arising in later generations only with the utmost impudence.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOKS ON THE TRINITY

## BOOK I

### Chapter 1, § 1

“There is also another class of people, those who strive to transcend the whole of creation—which is certainly mutable—in order to raise their understanding toward the immutable substance, which is God, etc.”

He means the Platonists, or those devoted to the study of the Platonists; for, more than all others, they maintained that the supreme Godhead is incorporeal. He refers to the same people in these words, with which the paragraph concludes:

> “But whoever thinks that God possesses such power that he generated himself is all the more mistaken because not only is God not such, but neither is any spiritual or corporeal creature; for there is absolutely nothing that generates itself in order to exist.”

Thus the Platonists commonly spoke, calling God the parent of himself. We have demonstrated this with a notable example in volume VI, *On the Eighty-Three Questions*, question 16.

### Chapter 4, § 7

“He teaches that Catholic writers teach that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, by the inseparable equality of one and the same substance, indicate the unity of the Godhead; and therefore that they are not three Gods but one God, etc.”

For these and similar statements to be understood correctly, the word “equality” must be carefully examined. From it, it is clear that the ancients, although they speak of one and the same substance, did not understand what we today mean by one substance in number—a substance that is not ordinarily said to be equal to itself—but one in species, whose three individuals are rightly said to be equal to one another. See Dionysius Petavius, *Dogmatic Theology*, volume II, *On the Trinity*, books IV, chapters 9 and 11, and the notes appended in the Amsterdam edition.

Today we often use expressions on this subject that are awkward, borrowed from the ancients; because they were devised by people whose views we mistakenly suppose to have been the same as ours, and because they were sufficiently apt for expressing their opinions, they can no longer conveniently express ours. Unless the reader of these books keeps this in mind, he will repeatedly encounter obscurity in them and stumble from time to time.

### Chapter 6, § 13

“The Holy Spirit is certainly not a creature, to whom all the saints offer such service—not *δουλεία* [*douleia*], but *λατρεία* [*latreia]—as the Apostle says: ‘For we are the circumcision, who serve the Spirit of God’ (*Nos enim sumus circumcisio, Spiritui Dei servientes*, Philippians 3:3), which in Greek is *λατρεύοντες*. For many copies, including Latin ones, read in this way: ‘who serve the Spirit of God’; and all, or almost all, the Greek copies do so. In some Latin copies, however, we find not ‘who serve the Spirit of God,’ but ‘who serve God in spirit’ (*spiritu Deo servimus*).”

Yet in volume V, sermon 169, the Bishop of Hippo says:

> “I know,” he says, “that most copies—Latin copies, for he speaks of the Greek ones afterward—have ‘who serve God in spirit’; but, as far as we have been able to examine, more Greek copies have ‘who serve the Spirit of God.’”

See what Jean Le Clerc says about this passage in *The Art of Criticism*, part 3, section 1, chapter 14, § 15.

Although we believe that those who wished to make the Holy Spirit a creature were mistaken, we would nevertheless not wish to use this passage against them, since most Latin books, supported by many Greek ones, correctly read “serving God in spirit,” as most now judge. The variation in Augustine should be noted: here he says that the majority of Latin copies read *Dei* (“of God”), whereas in the sermon he says that most read *Deo* (“God”). Again, in volume X, book III, *To Boniface*, chapter 7, he says that some copies read *Spiritu Deo*, others *Spiritui Deo*, and others *Spiritui Dei*. The first two readings are rather variant interpretations of the words *πνεύματι Θεῷ*.

### Chapter 12, § 23

Mark 13:32:

> “But concerning that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, except the Father.”

To this the Bishop of Hippo responds:

> “For he does not know what he makes others not know; that is, he did not know it in such a way as then to disclose it to the disciples. It is like what was said to Abraham: ‘Now I know that you fear God’; that is, ‘Now I have caused you to know,’ because he himself also became known to himself as tested in that trial.”

We have shown in volume V, sermon 2, that this interpretation of Genesis 22:12 is violent, if ever there was one. The interpretation of the passage in Mark is no more satisfactory, and I cannot understand how people hoped by such an answer to silence the Arians. See, nevertheless, what Dionysius Petavius has collected on this subject in *Dogmatic Theology*, volume V, book XI, chapter 1. It would have been much better to say that Christ is speaking here as a human being, and that omniscience cannot enter the human mind, than to twist Christ’s words violently so as to make them agree with a hypothesis adopted arbitrarily. The Arians were thereby made more obstinate, since they could not doubt that their opponents’ interpretation was tortured, although they themselves were gravely mistaken in attributing that ignorance to Christ’s divinity.

## BOOK II

### Chapter 11, § 20

Concerning the angels who appeared to Abraham, Genesis 18:2:

> “When three men were seen, and none of them was said to be greater than the others in form, age, or power, why should we not understand that the equality of the Trinity was visibly signified through a visible creature? Etc.”

Augustine interpreted this apparition more clearly in *The City of God*, book XVI, chapter 29. See, nevertheless, below, book III, chapter 11, where he also demonstrates that they were angels.

## BOOK III

### Chapter 11, § 23

After saying that divine apparitions were made through the ministry of angels, he writes:

> “But someone may say: ‘Why, then, is it written, “The Lord said to Moses,” rather than, “The angel said to Moses”?’ Because when a herald proclaims the words of a judge, the record does not say, ‘The herald said,’ but ‘The judge said.’”

See the preceding note and the interpreters on Exodus 3 and 20.

## BOOK IV

After saying that our Savior expended his single death for our double death—of soul and body—he proceeds in chapter 4 to an allegorical arithmetic:

> “This relation,” he says, “of the single to the double has its origin in the number three, for one and two make three; but the whole matter I have mentioned reaches the number six, for one, two, and three make six. This number is therefore called perfect because it is completed by its parts. It has three such parts: a sixth, a third, and a half; and no other part can be found in it that can be described as being such-and-such a fraction of it.”

These are the Platonic and Pythagorean inanities found in Philo, among other places, in his book *On the Creation of the World*. There is no one now who does not laugh at such things—not only with a wanton, spleenful guffaw, but even by those who are otherwise said not to laugh. No one would wish to have his name attached to such inventions. They are all the less tolerable because Augustine is engaged here in a serious matter, if ever there was one, and wanders away from the subject of his work for reasons I cannot understand. Yet few of Augustine’s books are without such digressions, which frustrate the reader who is left gaping.

## BOOK V

### Chapter 5, § 6

> “Although it is one thing for the Father to be and another thing for the Son to be, the substance is not different; for these are not said according to substance but according to relation, which relation nevertheless is not an accident, since it is not mutable.”

The word “different” (*diversa*) should be noted, for Augustine frequently uses it in this matter. It does not mean distinct but of another kind. Thus, to speak scholastically, he means that paternity and filiation do not make the substances belong to two genera, but that they belong to the same genus and are distinguished solely by the relation of the Father to the Son and of the Son to the Father. Dionysius Petavius has much to say on this subject, though it is sufficiently intricate, in *Dogmatic Theology*, volume II, book IV, chapter 11, *On the Trinity*.

### Chapter 8, §§ 9–10

> “I call ‘essence’ what is called *οὐσία* in Greek, which we more commonly call ‘substance.’ They too use the term *hypostasis*, but I do not know what distinction they intend between *ousia* and *hypostasis*. Thus most of our writers who treat these matters in Greek have been accustomed to say *μίαν οὐσίαν, τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις*, which in Latin is ‘one essence, three substances.’”

That is, an essence of one genus, but three distinct substances, though not different; or one essence in three substances, which differ only in their various modes of subsistence—that is, by their relations.

### Chapter 9

> “But because our customary way of speaking has now established that when we say ‘essence’ this is understood in the same way as when we say ‘substance,’ we do not dare to say ‘one essence, three substances,’ but ‘one essence, or substance, and three persons’; just as many Latins who treated these matters, and who were worthy of authority, said when they could find no more suitable way of expressing in words what they understood without words.”

We find similar statements in book VII, chapter 4, § 7. I am surprised that “essence” and “substance” were confused, since the words have different meanings. Since the Latin language already possessed the word “substance,” the word “essence” was invented and was not rejected by learned men as useless. Quintilian writes in *The Orator’s Education*, book III, chapter 8:

> “Many new words have been formed from Greek, and very many by Sergius Flavius; some of them seem exceedingly harsh, such as *ens* and *essentia*. I see no reason why we should be so disdainful of them, unless it is that we are unfair judges against ourselves and therefore suffer from poverty of speech.”

Certainly neither the metaphysicians of earlier centuries nor the philosophers and theologians of our own time could have done without this word, nor could they, without great ambiguity, have confused it with “substance.” When the ancients spoke of one essence or substance in the divine persons, they understood a unity in species; when they spoke of three persons, they understood three substances that were not different but distinct. On the unity, see below, book VI, chapter 3, § 4.

For Augustine adds:

> “In reality, since the Father is not the Son, and the Son is not the Father, and that Holy Spirit, who is also called the gift of God, is neither the Father nor the Son, there are certainly three. Therefore it was said in the plural: ‘I and the Father are one.’ For he did not say, ‘The one is,’ as the Sabellians say, but ‘We are one.’”

It should be observed that Augustine and all the other ancients do not say—speaking scholastically—that paternity, filiation, and spirituality are three things, or three relations in one substance numerically, as we now speak. Rather, they say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three persons—that is, according to Boethius’ definition, individual substances of a rational nature. Thus a person is something absolute, although personality is something relative. Because Dionysius Petavius did not sufficiently notice this, he did not understand Augustine, as is clear from volume II of *Dogmatic Theology*, book IV, chapter 11, *On the Trinity*. Or, if he did understand him, he did not dare to bring the matter more clearly to light.

Many nevertheless did not wish to admit that there are three substances, lest they appear to contradict themselves and lest anyone imagine three different natures, after the manner of the Arians. Hence Augustine writes:

> “Yet when it is asked, ‘Why three?’ human speech is afflicted by utter poverty. Nevertheless, the expression ‘three persons’ was used—not so that this should be said, but so that nothing should remain unsaid.”

That is, it was not said in order to assert that there are three persons such as three human beings, who, although they belong to the same species, nevertheless differ greatly from one another, are separated, and act independently—qualities that the ancients rightly denied could exist in the divine persons. See book VII, chapter 4, §§ 7–9.

## BOOK VI

### Chapter 1, § 1

“Among the disputes our people had with those Arians who said, ‘There was a time when the Son was not,’ some also introduced this reasoning: ‘If the Son of God is the power and wisdom of God, and God was never without wisdom and power, the Son is coeternal with God the Father.’ The Apostle calls Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God, and it is the statement of a madman that God at some time did not possess power or wisdom; therefore there was no time when the Son was not.”

Everyone can see that this is a paralogism, and Augustine rightly rejects it in the following book, as well as in the last one. For the Father’s wisdom is his property in a way that the Son is not; Paul calls Christ the power and wisdom of God the Father in 1 Corinthians 1:24 merely because God’s power and wisdom shine forth especially in him. Nevertheless, many of the ancients reasoned in this way, as Dionysius Petavius demonstrates in *On the Trinity*, book VI, chapter 9. Such reasoning is also found before the Arian period, when people called God rational because he possessed reason within himself. See Athenagoras’ *Apology for the Christians* and Tertullian *Against Praxeas*, chapter 5.

Clearly, those good men were pleased not only by arguments rigorously conformed to the laws of logic, but also by arguments that were firm only in appearance. I am surprised that Augustine poured out so many words on this subject, since it could have been resolved in a few. He seems to have wished to appear to write much rather than to write what was relevant.

## BOOK VII

### Chapter 1, § 2

Against those who spoke of the Son as though he were a property of the Father’s essence:

> “How, then, is the Son of the same essence as the Father, since, with respect to himself, he is neither essence nor anything at all with respect to himself, but even his being is with respect to the Son? Yet all the more are they of one and the same essence, because the Father and the Son are one and the same essence; since the Father’s very being is not with respect to himself but with respect to the Son, the essence which he generated and by which he is whatever he is—namely, the Son.”

See Petavius on this subject in chapter 10 of the work mentioned above, although he attempts to obscure everything. It is certainly not commendable in the ancients, in a matter difficult in itself, to seek ambiguity of terms; nor was it appropriate for later writers to increase it by attributing to the ancients what they did not think. The same words expressed the matter, but very inconveniently. The whole question could have been treated with far fewer words and much greater clarity.

### Chapter 4, § 7

> “Therefore, for the sake of speaking about ineffable things, so that we might in some way say what we cannot say at all, the Greek writers among us said, ‘one essence, three substances’; the Latins, however, said, ‘one substance or essence, three persons.’”

We have already explained these matters in book V, chapters 8 and 9. Here we shall only urge those who wish to know what the ancients thought about the unity of God and the plurality of persons to read carefully what follows in this book, all the way to the end. They understood that there are three distinct substances, equally perfect in every respect and alike, not separated or set apart like three bodies, but most closely united, while nevertheless distinguished from one another by their relations.

Augustine admits in § 8 that three Gods could have been said, had Scripture not contradicted it, and that three essences could have been said, had their closest union and complete equality in all respects not prevented it. Finally, from his entire discussion it is clear that the ancients spoke about these matters very ambiguously. “What, then,” he asks in § 9, “remains except that we acknowledge that these terms arose from the necessity of speaking, when an extensive argument was required against the snares or errors of heretics?”

But surely the terms ought not to have been ambiguous, lest the common people meanwhile be deceived, or lest later generations think that the ancients had asserted the opposite of what they believed—as happened, especially since they thought that the very foundation and summit of the Christian religion, from the time of Nicaea onward, lay in their explanation of the Trinity.

For when human poverty attempted through speech to present to human understanding what it grasps, according to its capacity, in the inner chamber of the mind concerning the Lord God, its creator—whether through pious faith or through whatever understanding—it feared to say “three essences,” lest any diversity be understood within that supreme equality. Yet it could not say that they were not three in some respect, because Sabellius fell into heresy by saying this.

What, then, shall we conclude from these things? That we too ought to believe there are three essences, distinct only in number, but otherwise so closely united that one God may be said to exist? Certainly not! The churches of later centuries, while rightly maintaining that no one in this matter was permitted to depart from Sacred Scripture, and therefore that the doctrine of Scripture had been transmitted by earlier generations—which they did not suspect of having departed from that rule—interpreted the earlier generations’ opinion according to Scripture. They attributed to the ancients not what they had believed, but what they ought to have believed.

Let us, then, speak and think from Scripture also concerning the unity of God and concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Let us not suppose that we can clearly explain what has not been clearly revealed, or express in our own words more adequately what we do not grasp than it was expressed in the words of Christ and the apostles—especially since so many and such great disputes have arisen from new expressions.

If we forgive the ancients for teaching that the divine nature in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit has unity in species, let us not be merciless toward those who perhaps think differently from us today on this matter, provided that they hold Sacred Scripture as the rule of their faith, observe the precepts of the Gospel, and, together with us, await the return from heaven of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead.

Both the difficulty of the matter and the weakness of the human intellect necessarily demand this fairness from us—unless we wish, with extraordinary injustice, to make the condition of later people worse than that of the ancients, whom, when they were mistaken, we customarily grant not merely pardon but the highest praise.

# IN THE NINTH VOLUME

[Col. 0525]

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOKS AGAINST THE LETTER OF PARMENIAN

## BOOK I

### Chapter 8, § 13

> “Parmenian even dares to complain that Constantine ordered those men to be led to the field—that is, to execution—who, having been defeated before ecclesiastical judges, were unable to prove before Constantine himself what they alleged, and who were still being carried along in the sacrilegious madness of separation from the holy Church.”

Yet they ought not therefore to have been killed because they had been unable to prove that Caecilian of Carthage had been a traditor, or had been ordained by traditors; nor because they had seceded, however unjustly, from the other Christian churches—provided that in other respects they obeyed the civil laws. These offenses and wounds ought to have been treated with gentler remedies.

### Chapter 9, § 15

> “Against these heretics, by the hidden command of God expressed through the manifest authority of human beings, many provisions were established by which they might be restrained with the utmost severity—not only against heretics, however they may have been whitened with the Christian name, but also against the pagans themselves. For they too are impious through a false religion, and their images were ordered by recent laws to be overthrown and shattered, while sacrifices were also prohibited under threat of capital punishment.”

Augustine spoke more correctly than he realized when he said that God’s command concerning the persecution of heretics was hidden. For it is so deeply concealed in the writings of the apostles that neither he nor anyone else has yet been able to bring it forth. But because it is hidden, Christian emperors who, imitating the pagans, treated mere opinions as crimes and inflicted severe punishments on them cannot be excused.

A matter of such importance, and with such dreadful consequences, ought never to have been attempted by Christians—not only because God was silent, but also because he expressly forbade it by so many repeated and unequivocal commands concerning love for the entire human race. Let book XVI of the Theodosian Code be read and compared with the laws of pagan rulers against Christians. It will immediately be possible to understand that, in roughly the same span of time, the pagans enacted fewer laws against Christians than Christians enacted against heretics. This is certainly a stain upon the Christian name, which rulers and magistrates will never erase except by adopting contrary policies. We have said enough about this in the letter to Vincent, note to volume II.

As for the pagans, when Augustine speaks of their being punished by capital punishment if they sacrificed to their gods, he seems to have in mind laws 15, 16, and 18 of title 10, book XVI of the Theodosian Code, which were enacted in the year 399. In any case, capital punishment was not first threatened only at that time against those who sacrificed to idols. Law 4 of the same title, enacted by Constantius in 353, reads as follows:

> “It has been decreed that temples should immediately be closed in all places and throughout every city, and that access to them should be forbidden to everyone, so that permission to commit offenses may be denied to those who have abandoned themselves to wrongdoing. For we wish all people to abstain from sacrifices. If anyone should happen to perpetrate anything of this sort, let him be struck down by the avenging sword. We also decree that the property of the condemned person be confiscated for the treasury, and that provincial governors be punished in the same way if they neglect to avenge such crimes.”

This was a cruel law, utterly unworthy of Christian gentleness. If anyone denies that it was enforced everywhere at that time, he will nevertheless do little to preserve Constantius’ honor; for it was not through any failure on his part that the law was not enforced, and he gave later rulers an example of acting in this way.

Augustine praises this savagery not only here but also in letter 93, § 10:

> “Who among us,” he says, “who among you does not praise the laws enacted by the emperors against pagan sacrifices? And certainly a much more severe penalty was established there: capital punishment was imposed for that impiety.”

If these things could be praised, then everything said by Christians during the first three centuries against persecution on religious grounds would have to be regarded as foolish or insincere. It would have been foolish to attack what one considered entirely just; for they could not have opposed persecution itself as something inherently evil, but only persecution directed against those who thought correctly.

While they were still pagans, Christians wished pagans to abandon every impulse to persecute—that is, they wished not to be harassed by them, even though the pagans believed that Christians were in error. This could be demonstrated in many passages. But if Christians did not disapprove of persecution, provided that it was exercised by those who thought correctly against those in error, then, had they wished to reveal their true intentions, they ought to have addressed the pagans as follows:

> “At present, while we are the weaker party, O pagans, we wish to be treated kindly by you, though we dissent from you. But if we should ever gain possession of affairs, do not be deceived: we do not intend to show you the same kindness. We shall overthrow all your altars, temples, and images, and we shall prohibit your sacrifices so thoroughly that offering sacrifices to your gods will become a capital offense. Meanwhile, we ask you to treat us kindly while you are superior, although, if we should ever be able to have Christian emperors, we intend to kill you as impious people if you wish to defend the worship of your religion.”

This is how Christians ought to have spoken if they had wished to tell the truth. Or at least nothing prevented the pagans from interpreting their words in this way, if they believed what Augustine believed in these later times. Let all those who have not stripped themselves of every trace of candor and integrity now judge whether people whose minds were disposed in this manner should be considered good. Yet these are the necessary consequences of Augustine’s position.

There is, moreover, another point that must be carefully noted—one that we failed to observe in connection with letter 44. In the year 398, Fortunatus the Donatist reproached Augustine, saying that the Catholic bishops were so disposed that, if power were granted them, they would fiercely persecute the Donatists, although they concealed this intention. See letter 44, § 11. Augustine denied this in the words we excerpted in volume II, and called God as witness of their hearts. But two years later, in 400—that is, the year in which this book was written—he held and expressed the opposite view.

### Chapter 10, § 16

> “Or perhaps they will say that, even if they are convicted of sacrilegious dissent [lacuna], nevertheless such matters ought not to belong to the authority of emperors to restrain or punish? On this point I ask what they will say. Is it because such authorities should take no concern for a faulty or false religion? But we have also said much about the pagans and about the demons themselves, namely, that they suffer persecution from emperors. Does this too displease them?”

These statements were highly inflammatory and involved great danger. If the Donatists had openly said that such responsibility did not belong to emperors, they would have been regarded as seditious. Nor could they admit this without danger in the sense Augustine understood, for if the matter lay within the emperors’ discretion, then they had to be obeyed.

The ambiguity of the whole matter therefore had to be examined. It is universally agreed that among all peoples the supreme authorities have been entrusted by the populace—either through written laws or at least through tacit consent—with the protection of the civil laws and public tranquility. In order to preserve these intact, the authorities must be guided by justice; that is, they must judge everyone according to the laws and equity.

Yet there is no society that has entrusted these same authorities with the care of opinions, especially theoretical opinions, so that they may sanction whatever opinions please them, proscribe all others, and, by their authority and arms if necessary, eliminate them from the commonwealth. No one is so insane as to think that he must follow the opinions of the supreme authority, whom he otherwise willingly obeys in matters pertaining to the facts of life and civil society.

Otherwise the Jews first, and then the Christians, would have had to accept the religious convictions of pagan magistrates and embrace idolatry; for pagans exercised no less legitimate rule than Christian emperors later did. Similarly, everyone living in Muslim kingdoms or in lands still devoted to idolatry would have to renounce the Christian religion.

If you say that erring authorities may not do what authorities who think correctly may do, you will plunge yourself into an inextricable labyrinth. For who, finally, will judge here concerning error? Pagans believe, Muslims believe, and heretical rulers believe that you are in error even though you think yourself correct; therefore they ought to harass you—unless perhaps you wish everyone to believe you while you believe no one, which would be madness.

It is established that each person ought to follow and do what, in his own judgment, appears to him most true and best—not what he believes to be false and harmful, whatever other people may think about it. Should a pagan, Muslim, or heretical ruler favor the religion or sect that he believes to be false, while harassing those who seem to him to think correctly? All authorities, whatever their opinions, must therefore be subjected to a common law, lest, while we wish to favor lovers of truth in some kingdom or commonwealth, we inadvertently place weapons in the hands of devotees of falsehood that we could never take away by any means.

“But,” you will say, “should rulers take no care for religion?” They should take the greatest care, and chiefly in this respect: that no one should harass or mistreat another on account of religion if that person otherwise obeys the civil laws; and that no one should incite sedition or take up arms in order to kill or expel fellow citizens who think differently.

Truth requires no other protection than that it be permitted to turn people’s eyes toward itself, shining by its own light, and to attract their minds by sound arguments. No attack upon error is more certain than to refute it clearly and freely expose its delusions. Thus magistrates should favor truth and oppose error. Wherever both are permitted, truth will soon triumph over error.

If human ignorance, stupidity, or emotion delays truth’s triumph to some extent, the delay will not be long, and some allowance must certainly be made for human weakness. The most reliable and effective remedies by which bodily illnesses are cured also require some time in which to exert their force and efficacy. Can it then seem surprising or unjust to allow the illnesses of the mind some time in which to be cured? Certainly not to anyone except one who does not understand himself.

“But,” you will say, “it has often happened that errors resisted brilliant truth for a very long time. This is evident from the example of paganism, which survived in the Roman Empire for at least a hundred years after Constantine’s time, and perhaps would never have died out if it had not been conquered by the force of laws.”

I, however, think that those very laws were partly responsible for the longevity of the error, since people customarily cling more stubbornly to opinions that are attacked by force. Moreover, it was not the unalloyed light of the Gospel that was being opposed to the darkness of paganism, nor was it mere sound reason that was attacking error. By that time many things in the doctrines, rites, and morals of Christians were giving pagans legitimate offense—for what now, especially, prevents us from admitting the truth?

Christian teachers, too, who sufficiently overthrew pagan errors often defended the Christian religion badly and incompetently. Thus the eyes of the pagans, already clouded, were dazzled on one side by the light of truth, while on the other they were impeded by the mists of faulty and false reasoning; they mixed the firmest arguments with paralogisms.

They also saw a certain class of people, by whom they were chiefly attacked, wishing them to embrace the Christian religion not only from benevolent feeling toward them, but also because, as the number of Christians increased, the boundaries of a certain new kind of kingdom possessed by those people were being extended, and their wealth and authority were increasing.

These and similar obstacles were placed before the pagans, preventing them from embracing the Christian religion as quickly as they might have done—not because edicts against them had failed to be sufficiently harsh and cruel, or because divine truth, when it shines alone, has little power, since no force can prevent it from shining. But enough, and more than enough, has been said on this subject.

Likewise. I ask this: since the Apostle plainly lists the works of the flesh—“which are,” he says, “fornications, uncleannesses, quarrels, rivalries, hostilities, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkennesses, revelries, and things of this kind”—what do they think, that they suppose the crime of idolatry ought rightly to be punished by the emperors; or, if they do not wish this, why do they acknowledge that the force of the laws is justly exercised against poisoners, but refuse to acknowledge it against heretics and impious dissensions, when, by apostolic authority, they are counted among the same fruits of iniquity?] If the Donatists were stuck on this point, they were certainly worthy of Augustine’s contempt. For who does not know that whatever is condemned by the laws of the Gospel—and especially what Paul censures in the passage cited by Augustine—usually is not, and cannot be, punished by civil laws? For example, rivalries, hostilities, dissensions, envy, avarice, pride, ambition, and love of the things of this life are never punished by human beings, provided that the laws of the state are not violated on their account; yet they are no less hateful to God for that reason, nor do they exclude people any less from the heavenly kingdom.

We could easily show why such things cannot be punished by human beings, if that were the issue. It will be enough to say that civil laws are adapted to the human condition and do not demand from people an extraordinary holiness, but only that virtue without which civil society cannot remain secure. Opinions likewise are not subject to the penalties of civil laws, because all more equitable legislators punish only those things that daily experience establishes as evil and that everyone regards as such—at least everyone who is in possession of his faculties—such as murder, theft, adultery, and the like. If these were neglected, human society could not stand.

Therefore Augustine’s reasoning has no force. If the Donatists approved the punishments inflicted on pagans, they were certainly worthy of being harassed themselves; for what they did not wish to be done to them, they could not justly wish to be done to others. There is no similarity between poisoners and heretics. Convicted poisoners admit that they administered poisons contrary to law and right, and the matter involves no obscurity. But when the subject is opinions, which those who follow them believe to be true, and on account of which they violate no civil law, the punishments are utterly unjust, for the reasons given above.

“Or perhaps,” Augustine adds, “these human authorities are not permitted to take care of such matters? Why, then, does he carry the sword who is called God’s minister, an avenger for wrath against those who do evil?” If such matters are handled by human authorities through force and arms, they are undoubtedly abusing their power contrary to right and law; for such matters are not to be dealt with by force and arms. “Religion must be defended,” Lactantius says, *Divine Institutes*, book V, chapter 19, “not by killing, but by dying; not by savagery, but by patience; not by crime, but by faith. For the former belong to the wicked, the latter to the good,” etc. “Nothing is so voluntary as religion; and if the mind of the one sacrificing is unwilling, religion is already abolished, already nonexistent.”

The sword was given to rulers only against those whom, under the civil laws, they are commanded to punish with the sword on account of crimes by which civil society is violated—not against those who, otherwise harmless, deviate from sound opinions and must be recalled to the right path by persuasion and gentleness.

Suppose the opposite were true. What would you say to pagan magistrates who refused to hear your arguments? What answer would Augustine have given to Constantius the Arian, when he was persecuting the followers of the Nicene synod? What would he have said to the Vandals, who, not much later than Augustine’s lifetime, expelled from Africa the bishops who adhered more firmly to the Nicene decrees, and harshly treated the populace who shared their opinion? Clearly, he would have had to resort to his own methods and sing a recantation of his harsh judgment that persecution was lawful, so that he might return to his former gentleness.

Let us, however, hold such an opinion of divine and human law that we may never be ashamed or regret that we have held it.

## BOOK II, chapter 13, § 29

“Although some layman, compelled by necessity, has given to one who was dying”—baptism and the Eucharist, for these were joined together; see the note to volume II, letter 172, § 5—“what he had learned how to give when he himself received it, I do not know whether anyone could piously say that it ought to be repeated. For if it is done without necessity compelling it, it is an usurpation of another’s office; but if necessity presses, it is either no fault or a venial fault.”]

If you suppose these sacraments to be necessary for salvation, as people generally believed in Augustine’s time, it is surely better that they be administered by laymen and considered valid than that, as those who hold similar opinions would have it, people should rather be allowed to perish. Yet neither side can demonstrate that these things are necessary for salvation. See Hugo Grotius’s dissertation *On the Administration of the Eucharist Where There Are No Pastors*, together with the observations on it by Dionysius Petavius and Henry Dodwell.

## Likewise

“And in no way will the imperial standard be violated by a devoted soldier, through what has been usurped by private persons.”]

Dionysius Petavius illustrated these words in *Observations on Epiphanius*, p. 78, under heresy 42. From there we shall extract what is relevant here. καθοσιῶσαι (*kathosiōsai*) is the same as “to consecrate” or “to dedicate.” Hence καθοσίωσις (*kathosiōsis*) means “devotion,” and καθωσιωμένος (*kathōsiōmenos*) “devoted,” “fellow-consecrated.” Therefore those who devoted themselves to a ruler and consecrated themselves by some religious rite were called καθωσιωμένοι (*kathōsiōmenoi*), as soldiers were.

Capitolinus, in *Maximinus*, says: “consecrated comrades,” or rather “fellow-consecrated comrades.” Such were the ancient Gallic devotees, whom they called *soldurii*, says Caesar in book I of the *Commentaries*—that is, καθωσιωμένοι (*kathōsiōmenoi*). This seems to me more suitable than the rendering of the Greek translator, συνωμόται (*synōmotai*, “sworn confederates”), although the meaning is nearly the same, since they were accustomed to be compelled by oath.

Dio, book LIII, gives an outstanding example of τῆς καθωσιώσεως (*tēs kathōsiōseōs*, “devotion” or “consecration”) in the year 725 from the founding of the City. He relates that a certain Sextus Pacuvius, or Apadius, tribune of the plebs, devoted himself to Augustus in the Senate and urged the other senators to do the same:

ἐν τῷ γὰρ συνεδρίῳ τε ἑαυτὸν οἱ τὸν τῶν Ἰβήρων τρόπον καθωσίωσε, καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις συνεβούλευε τοῦτο ποιῆσαι.

“For in the assembly he devoted himself to him according to the manner of the Iberians, and advised the others to do this as well.”

But when Augustus objected, the tribune of the plebs rushed out to the people and compelled everyone he encountered, and afterward the other citizens, to καθιερῶσαι ἀφῶς [F. ἄφνως] τῷ Αὐγούστῳ—“to consecrate themselves suddenly [F. *unexpectedly*] to Augustus.”

ἀφ’ οὗπερ καὶ νῦν, προτρεπόμενοι τὸν κρατοῦντα, λέγειν εἰώθαμεν ὅτι τοι καθωσιώμεθα.

“From that time, even now, when encouraging the ruler, we have been accustomed to say, ‘May we be devoted to you.’”

Hence the designation καθωσιωμένων (*kathōsiōmenōn*) was applied adjectivally, according to a formula attached to most imperial offices and attendants, especially, as has been said, to military personnel. On this subject he cites this passage of Augustine and adds other material, which I shall not transcribe. I shall merely point out that the passage he cites from Capitolinus does not occur in the *Life of Maximinus*, but in the *Lives of the Three Gordians*, where Maximinus’ speech is found. See also the *Glossary of Legal Terms* of Jacob Gothofredus, on the Theodosian Code.

## Likewise

“If someone, whether a deserter or one who has never served at all, marks some private person with a military brand, is not that marked person, once he has been detected, punished as a deserter—and all the more severely insofar as it can be proved that he had never served at all—with the most audacious marker punished at the same time if he has betrayed him, etc.]”

He alludes to military brands; on these, see Hugo Grotius on Galatians VI, 7. Law 4, book X, title 21, in the Theodosian Code, reads: “Brands—that is, a public mark—shall be inflicted on the arms of factory workers, in imitation of recruits,” etc. On this passage, read the commentary of Jacob Gothofredus.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOKS ON BAPTISM AGAINST THE DONATISTS

## Book II, chapter 3, § 4

“Who, then, does not know that the canonical Holy Scripture, both of the Old and of the New Testament, is contained within its own fixed limits, and that it is placed above all later letters of bishops in such a way that there can be absolutely no doubt or dispute as to whether anything established to have been written in it is true or right?””]

Nothing is truer, and no Christian could call it into question. But what follows is also golden and worthy of being constantly sung to those who abuse Augustine’s authority to such an extent that they would have us believe him rather than sound reason:

“But the letters of bishops,” he says, “which were written or are written after the canon was confirmed, may be criticized if, perhaps, something in them has deviated from the truth, whether through the more learned speech of someone more skilled in that matter, or through the more weighty authority and more informed judgment of other bishops; and likewise the councils held in particular regions or provinces may yield without equivocation to the authority of plenary councils held from the entire Christian world; and the earlier plenary councils themselves may often be corrected by later ones, when some experience of events reveals what had been hidden and makes known what had escaped notice—with no insolence of sacrilegious pride, no inflated neck of arrogance, no contentiousness of spiteful envy, but with holy humility, Catholic peace, and Christian charity?”

Here ends the period, which has been extended beyond all measure. From the final words it is clear that, in Augustine’s view, neither provincial nor plenary councils were free from the danger of error, since he held that earlier councils could be corrected by later ones.

But two further points must be observed here. The first concerns the investigation of truth: especially in an obscure matter, whatever the source of its obscurity, numbers accomplish nothing; only the expertise and integrity of those who assemble matter. If, for example, you had gathered all the bishops of Africa to give judgment on the meaning of a passage of the Old or New Testament, none of whom knew Hebrew and only very few of whom knew Greek, that enormous multitude of ignorant men would have been less fit to judge correctly than one man skilled in both languages—for example, Jerome of Stridon alone, although his expertise was not as great as is commonly supposed.

Who would doubt that even in the preceding seventeenth century one Hugo Grotius, or one John Drusius, could have interpreted the Scripture of the Old and New Testament more correctly than all the bishops of Italy and Spain putting their heads together? Therefore, whether councils are plenary or less than plenary makes no difference to me as far as the hope of discovering truth is concerned. I shall not place greater trust in an ignorant multitude that defines something imperiously and threatens anathemas, while offering no reasons—or only bad reasons—for its definition, than in a few people or even one person.

Indeed, I shall immediately assent to one learned man who offers sound arguments once I understand them, and I shall never count his opponents. Number contributes nothing to truth; indeed, often the more people are gathered to define it, the more ignorant and factious people are assembled—people who neither know what is true nor seek it, but only what is advantageous, or appears advantageous, to themselves.

Those ecclesiastical assemblies were formed according to the model of civil assemblies; and because the more people gather in them, the greater their authority is thought to be, a similar judgment is made concerning ecclesiastical bodies. But civil assemblies deal only with matters belonging to this life, matters well known to human beings and subject to many changes; human beings are also masters of these matters, and therefore the multitude undoubtedly has a greater right concerning them than a few people do. For that reason the leading citizens are rightly summoned in large numbers to govern and arrange such matters, and the greater number of votes prevails over the smaller.

But when heavenly truth is at issue—truth that no one knows except through study and attention, that is subject to no change, of which no one is master, and concerning whose definition more people have received no greater authority from God than fewer people have—votes must not be counted; rather, the reasons for each vote must be weighed. The matter is clear, but we cannot discuss it here in proportion to its usefulness and importance. Therefore we shall not refute the objections that could be raised against what we have said.

The second point we wished to note here was this: since councils are subject to error, their decrees must not be believed ἀβασανίστως (*abasanistōs*, “without examination”). Consequently—and not to repeat other reasons that I have often touched upon in these *Observations*—those who think that what councils have defined is not true should by no means be persecuted, provided that, in civil matters, they fulfill all the duties of good citizens.

Pelagius, Coelestius, and their disciples were therefore treated unjustly and cruelly when an edict was issued against them by which they were driven into exile and stripped of all their property. Indeed, wherever they were brought before a judge, without regard to the identity of the accuser, their goods were to be confiscated and they were to suffer irrevocable exile.

This controversy was more difficult than Honorius—a stupid man, always dependent on the counsels of others—and his courtiers, who cared about anything rather than acquiring knowledge of such matters, understood. Nor could the lictors of the African councils act as executioners without displaying the greatest imprudence. And certainly, both at that time and afterward, throughout the East and West, more people spoke and thought with Pelagius than with Augustine. They revered Augustine because of his reputation, even though they disagreed with him.

## Chapter 4, § 5

“This is what the health of peace accomplishes: when more obscure matters are investigated for a longer time and, because of the difficulty of discovering the truth, produce divergent opinions in fraternal debate, the bond of unity remains until the truth is made clear, so that an incurable wound of error does not remain in a severed part.”]

This was certainly an excellent admonition and duty, which he rightly demanded of the Donatists. But he himself ought not to have withdrawn from it in the Pelagian controversy, in which nothing was sought more earnestly than that irrevocable anathemas should not be pronounced on the basis of the hasty judgments of many synods, without ever properly hearing the brethren. John Garnerius will demonstrate this in his enumeration of the councils assembled against the Pelagians. Nevertheless, it must be admitted that this was a matter capable of troubling not merely ordinary minds but even the most outstanding intellects.

## Chapter 7, § 12

“Therefore the holy Cyprian says that this most salutary custom, through his predecessor Agrippinus, began, as it were, to be corrected.”]

Cyprian himself, in Letter 73 to Jubaianus, teaches that Agrippinus was not his immediate predecessor. “Among us,” he says, “it is not a new or sudden matter that we should judge those who come to the Church from the heretics to be baptized, since many years and a long age have passed from the time when, under Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, many bishops assembled together and decreed this; and from that time to the present day, so many thousands of heretics in our provinces have been converted to the Church and have not disdained,” etc.

# OBSERVATIONS ON THE BOOKS AGAINST THE LETTERS OF PETILIAN

## Book I, chapter 9, § 19

“When he hears, ‘The washing of one who is baptized by a dead man does not profit him’ (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV, 30), he will answer: ‘Christ lives; he no longer dies, and death shall no longer rule over him,’ etc.”]

The Donatists abused that passage of Ecclesiasticus to demonstrate that baptism conferred by an evil priest—or by one who was dead in sins—was of no benefit. I do not know how many ways Augustine twists himself in order to show that nothing can be extracted from the passage, when he ought to have ridiculed the Donatists for seeking Christian baptism here, since the author of Ecclesiasticus plainly had an entirely different meaning.

This is the author’s complete statement:

Βαπτιζόμενος ἀπὸ νεκροῦ, καὶ πάλιν ἁπτόμενος αὐτοῦ, τί ὠφέλησεν ἐν τῷ λουτρῷ αὐτοῦ

“That is: One who is washed after touching a corpse, and again touches it, what benefit does he receive from his washing?”

It is clear that the reference is to the legal washings that had to be performed after touching a corpse, by command of the law, Numbers XIX, 11, and that these have absolutely nothing to do with Christian baptism.

But if you read what follows, you will see that this is the first part of a comparison; for these words follow, containing the other part:

Οὕτως ἄνθρωπος νηστεύων ἐπὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτοῦ, καὶ πάλιν πορευόμενος καὶ τὰ αὐτὰ ποιῶν, τῆς προσευχῆς αὐτοῦ τίς εἰσακούσεται; καὶ τί ὠφέλησεν ἐν τῷ ταπεινωθῆναι αὐτόν;

“Thus, in the case of a man who fasts on account of his sins, and then falls again and does the same things, who will listen to his prayer? And what benefit will he receive from humbling himself?”

None of this has anything to do with baptism, although Cyprian too applies this passage to baptism, and cites it in truncated form in Letter 71. But, as Nicolaus Rigaltius correctly observed in his note on that passage, Cyprian, like other Fathers, very often seizes upon whatever in Scripture appears, even by the mere sound of the words, to serve his purpose, although it ought to be understood in a very different sense.

This is so common in Cyprian, Augustine, and others that there is no need, along with that most learned man, to seek an excuse for them in citing this passage, since many other similar examples cannot be excused. Scarcely anyone can say how much harm popular orators, ignorant of all criticism and dialectic, have done to the true understanding of Scripture and to the peace of the Church. Since they paid no attention to the rules of either of those disciplines, they sought every possible meaning everywhere and believed that they could prove anything by similarity of sound. From this arose innumerable quarrels.

In former times, however, such men, because of their eloquence, were either elevated to the principal sees or acquired a kind of sovereignty in synods. I shall say no more, for these matters are known to those skilled in ecclesiastical history and who have exercised judgment in reading it. I do not concern myself with the others, who are always ready to disguise, lie, and attack those who love the truth.

## Book III, chapter 25, § 30

“When I came to Milan before the consulship of Bauton, and on the Kalends of January recited a panegyric to that consul, in accordance with my rhetorical profession at that time.”]

The consular panegyrics, delivered in both languages, in verse as well as in prose, by Mamertinus, Libanius, Themistius, Claudian, and Sidonius, bear witness to the custom of publicly praising the consuls on the Kalends of January, when they entered office. Jacob Sirmondus noted this, later adducing this passage of Augustine in his note on Sidonius, book VIII, letter 6, where Sidonius mentions this custom.

# INTO THE TENTH VOLUME

[Col. 0535]

## JOHN PHEREPONUS TO THE READER

[Col. 0535B]

We could easily have added many notes to this final volume of Augustine, but two or three considerations prevented us from doing so, and it is somewhat important for you, reader, to know them.

The first is the haste of the printers, to whom, once the whole of Augustine had already been published together with its index, it seemed burdensome to wait any longer for our observations, which other occupations did not permit us to prepare so quickly.

The second is that there was no need for us to say or elaborate anything here, because in these arguments of the Bishop of Hippo against the Pelagians there are innumerable repetitions, and, as far as the substance of the matters is concerned, nothing new occurs beyond what had already been said about this subject in the letters, to which we have already added whatever notes seemed appropriate. For the whole controversy, if it is properly examined, turns on the interpretation of certain passages of Scripture, about which we had already spoken.

Added to this was the fact that we too had finally become so weary of these quarrels that we could scarcely endure them at all; nor, surely, would anyone occupied with better things tolerate reading or saying the same thing a thousand times—especially when what could have been settled in three words is expressed in several thousand, and many irrelevant matters are stuffed in, as has happened here.

Who, moreover, would not be nauseated by so many and such lengthy—if I may use the expression of a later age—“rhetorical performances,” whether intended to evade the adversary’s blow, attack him, or finally to arouse or avoid ill will? For my part, they created such disgust in me while I was reading that I plainly need the refreshment of more agreeable and useful studies.

Therefore, reader, make the best of what follows; or take up the pen yourself, so that you may supply what is lacking in my work. But remember above all to take account only of truth, to which alone I have tried to offer sacrifice. Farewell.

# PREFACE TO THE BOOK ON THE PROCEEDINGS OF PELAGIUS, FIRST PUBLISHED AT AUGSBURG IN 1611

Saint Augustine, *Retractations*, book II, chapter 47: “At the same time in the East, that is, in Syria, etc.,” up to the words: “Here begins the book: After it had come into our hands.”

In these words Saint Augustine explains the reason for writing and the subject of the book. Until now, all those who had searched out the works of Augustine—men outstanding in learning and diligence—had failed to find it. It has only now been discovered at Fiesole, in the library of the abbey of Saint Bartholomew of the Lateran regular canons.

When Scipio Cobellutius, secretary and confidential officer of the Supreme Pontiff, had sent its copy from Rome to the distinguished Marcus Velser at Augsburg, it seemed that so beautiful a jewel ought not to be denied the light of public day. For what benefit is there in hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure?

It was being reported that extremely accurate editions, illuminated with commentaries, were being prepared at Rome and Florence, and we remembered that one ought not to put the sickle into another’s harvest. But since the work, as circumstances made clear, would take a long time—and a matter of such importance should certainly not be rushed—if in the meantime we should offer Augustine’s bare words for use and enjoyment, we hoped that we would win the favor of pious and learned men who love ancient learning, without displeasing the Roman and Florentine editors themselves, whose industry would not thereby be hindered, especially since we had not even plucked the flower of dedication.

We faithfully reproduced the copy sent from Rome, and the variant readings written in the margin come from that copy. But of the readings that Antonius Velserus, a canon of Freising, noted at the bottom of most pages as he read, by spontaneous conjecture, he does not acknowledge a few that are somewhat bolder. We admitted none of them into the text, however much they might flatter us with an appearance of probability.

Augustine also mentions this book in book II of *On Original Sin*, chapter 14: “But what you know,” etc. . . . I have written to Aurelius.

Possidius, in his catalogue, chapter 4: “One book against the proceedings of Pelagius.”

[Col. 0537B]

Photius too, in the *Bibliotheca*, translated by Andreas Schottus, no. 54: “Pelagius at that synod,” etc. . . . Thus Augustine reports in what he wrote to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage.

We shall not transcribe the remaining material concerning the synod and the whole affair, which Cardinal Baronius—who believed Augustine’s book had perished—carefully and extensively collected from Augustine himself, Jerome, and Prosper under the years 415 and following, and which Severinus Binius collected in the first volume of the councils, lest we repeat what has already been done.

We remark in passing that what Augustine writes at the end of the book about the incredible audacity of the Pelagians—“that the servants and maidservants of God who belonged to the care of the presbyter Jerome were subjected to the most atrocious slaughter,” etc.—is undoubtedly the very event that Pope Innocent mentions in Letter 24, or 32, to John, bishop of Jerusalem:

“Robberies, murders, fires, every crime of the utmost madness—the most noble holy virgins, Eustochium and Paula, lamented that the devil had perpetrated in the places belonging to your Church.”

And in Letter 25, or 33, to Jerome:

“Your grief and groaning shake our very vitals, so that there is no possibility of considering or devising a course of action.”

# A SUPPLEMENT TO MY MOST FRIENDLY AND LEARNED P. FRANCISCO MACEDO, PROFESSOR OF ETHICS AT THE UNIVERSITY OF PADUA; IN WHICH THE INSCRIPTION OF SAINT AUGUSTINE’S BOOK *ON THE GRACE OF CHRIST*, TO ALBINUS, PINIANUS, AND MELANIA, IS DISCUSSED BY HENRY NORIS OF VERONA, AN AUGUSTINIAN AND PROFESSOR OF ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY AT THE UNIVERSITY OF PISA

Most reverend and most learned Father,

[Col. 0537D]

I had received a letter from a friend in which he informed me that you had departed from Venice toward Bologna, but that he did not know to what city you had directed this unexpected journey of yours. He also sent me the little book that you recently published at Verona against my opinion concerning the doctrine of certain ancient inhabitants of Lérins.

I myself read that volume eagerly, examined it carefully, and marked it accurately. For I hoped that, once you had crossed the Apennine heights, you would soon come to Florence, and that on that occasion I could sincerely and amicably make clear to you what in your little book I thought deserved to be marked with white pebbles and what with a black theta.

But when you had approached Florence, you wished to conceal your arrival from me so carefully that I almost fear you have, by this silence of yours, sent a dismissal to our ancient friendship—especially since you did not arrange for even a single copy of your little book to be brought to me.

Nevertheless, lest I too should seem to fail in the duties that, by right of our old familiarity, I expected from you, I shall carry out by letter what I had hoped to do in person. And indeed, my Macedo, I am not so dull or stupid that I do not understand perfectly that no mortal, however dear through friendship, should be preferred in love to the gods. I know the old proverb: “A friend even to the altars.” Therefore I should be judged foolish if I wished so much to receive from a friend that he love me more than the gods.

Would that you had carried out with suitable merit the defense you undertook of the teaching of Saints Hilary of Arles and Vincent of Lérins, and had successfully completed the matter from ancient records and the witnesses of the earlier Church! I would certainly have thanked you greatly, and would have owed you still more, since you would have shown that two most famous Fathers, contemporaries of Augustine, were opposed to that holy Doctor in no doctrine but agreed with him in everything. For I desire nothing more than to see Augustine’s doctrine confirmed by the common testimony of the Fathers.

But when I see you everywhere indulging in rhetoric, neglecting the records of antiquity, yielding to your own imaginings, and presenting, in place of history, entities of reason and “second intentions,” as you call them—or certain empty idols of your own mind—I cannot help lamenting your position, since you have not provided a good cause with an equally good advocate.

Within six or eight days I shall bring the refutation of your latest apology to completion, and shall make it plain that you follow, support, and exaggerate the opinions of Dallaeus, Blondellus, and the other Protestants; that you merely boast verbally of defending Baronius, while opposing him even when you promise, with great gaping, to act as his advocate; and that, having neglected the volumes of the ancient writers, you everywhere put forward new histories—that is, pure fables.

Yet lest I seem to be speaking empty embellishments to the crowd, I shall present a specimen of your entire work in one or two pages of chapter seven of this letter: partly so that you may not deceive those who have not even lightly engaged in ecclesiastical history, and partly so that, in place of a letter of welcome, it may meet you in Rome, lest I, who yield to no one in affection for you, outdo in such offices your friends, whom you count by the hundreds in Rome.

For no duties among friends are more praiseworthy than those in which they lay their complaints before their friends without an intermediary, reveal the secrets of their hearts, and wish to keep nothing concealed that concerns their interests; and if at any time they depart from benevolence, humanity, and truth, they restore them to their proper courses and recall them to their duty.

I shall perform these tasks in a complete volume, which I shall soon send to you, printed outside Italy in the finest type—for the Florentine printers are occupied with printing various books and pamphlets—although, as you passed through Florence, you did not wish to give me any opportunity to read your little book, even though it was very much in my interest to learn from you what errors I should avoid and to see the truth that I should pursue.

In chapter seven of your earlier treatise, most ingeniously composed in defense of the people of Lérins, on page 51, fearing that the reading of a shorter work might draw near to tedium, you descend from the citadel of the argument to certain remote and playful matters, intending to expose me to the ridicule of everyone by raising for me an amusing question about Albinus.

“But behold,” you say, “as I season this troublesome work with some wit and flavor, I come upon a passage of Noris in which I miss grammar.” And because you considered this very matter one of the principal points that readers ought to observe in your work, you wrote in the index: “Noris is convicted of grammatical ignorance.”

Indeed, after you had sent me from the sacred theological academies to the chronologists on the very next page, you immediately thrust me down to the benches of the grammarians, to be chastised by Orbilius, as you put it.

Surely readers who turn over writings seasoned by you with such wit and flavor will repeat, with Terence:

“Witty, charming, elegant—nothing beyond this. O most delightful chapter.” *Eunuchus* III, 1, 3.

But I, for my part, thrust upon you the verses of the equally most learned and most holy bishop of Nola addressed to Ausonius, a man of rank:

“Let many things be open to jokes; let it also be permitted to play with inventions.

But while your tongue caresses, let it strike a grave tooth,

To play with burning flatteries, and to ferment

Jokes that are falsely sweet in the vinegar of biting satire.

Such things often become poets; they never suit parents.”

You do not season your writings with wit, my father, but you drench my skin—as though it were elephantine—with so much salt that, although you call me your very dear friend in the same place, you are undoubtedly regarded as

“the informer of a great friend.” Juvenal, *Satire* I, 33.

But you order me to meet you on unequal ground when you appeal to grammar, which is your kingdom, in which you applaud yourself and triumph. For while I had not yet learned to say “mamma” and “tata,” you were publicly teaching rhetoric at Madrid as a master of eloquence, to which from your earliest fingernails you had devoted strenuous and tireless effort, just like the man

“whom his father, bleary-eyed from the soot of the glowing mass,

from the coal, the tongs, and the anvil preparing swords,

and from tawny Vulcan, sent to the rhetorician.”

Juvenal, *Satire* X, 30.

Certainly I would never have feared so much danger to my back from a most intimate friend, such as you have declared yourself to be, that the whips of Orbilius should be drawn against me by that same friend,

“and the grim ferules, the scepters of schoolmasters.” Martial, book X, 62.

“Am I, from my Macedo, whom I have so often exalted in published volumes with the highest praises,

ordered to weep among the chairs of schoolboys?” Horace, *Satires* I, 10.

Let me offer you Augustine’s opinion as the place of a solid apology, in book II *Against Cresconius*, chapter 1:

“For if,” he says, “Demosthenes, the most illustrious of orators, who took as much care with words as with subject matter, although Aeschines had charged him with some unusualness of speech, denied that the fortunes of Greece depended on whether he had used this word or that, or whether he had extended his hand this way or that—how much less ought we to labor over the rules for deriving nouns, when, whether we say this or that, what we say is understood without ambiguity, since our chief concern is not the polishing of speech but the demonstration of truth?”

In the meantime, do not fear me, since you see that grammar is necessary. But lest you think I am evading the issue, I enter the school of the grammarians, to be chastised by Orbilius, as you threaten.

When, in book I of the *Pelagian History*, chapter 15, I examined the inscription of Saint Augustine’s books *On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin*, namely, “To the most sincere brothers, beloved by God, Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania,” I did not accept Baronius’s correction, by which he thought that *Albina* should be restored in place of *Albinus* in the year 409—unless, he adds in the same place, there was there an Albinus son in addition to Albina the mother.

For in that age the names of women were not always expressed with feminine endings. Paula’s daughter had a surname with a neuter ending, namely *Eustochium*. Indeed, I asserted that women’s names were at that time customarily expressed by the holy Fathers with masculine endings. Thus I indicated that the mother of the younger Melania, Albina, was commonly called *Albinus* in the nominative case.

Apart from the inscription of the book *On the Grace of Christ*, Augustine gave this title to Letter 227: “To Albinus, Pinianus, and Melianus.” Here it is certain that *Melaniae* must be read. Jerome, Letter 79, says: “Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania greet you.” Possidius of Calama, in his catalogue of the books of the holy Doctor of Hippo, writes that the books *On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin* were sent to Pinianus, Albinus, and Melania. Saint Paulinus, in Letter 44, which is Letter 249 among Augustine’s letters, wrote *Melanius* in place of *Melania*. Thus the Fathers who flourished around the year 400 wrote the name of the most noble woman Albina.

“An extraordinary argument,” you say (p. 52), “certainly, for explaining matters—a method unknown to the ancient Priscianists and Donatists, and to the recent Despauteriuses and Nebrissenses, one that no age has ever tolerated, namely, that the inflection of nouns should be free, and that masculine and feminine forms should be declined indiscriminately; and consequently that *Albina* should be used for *Albinus*, and *Melanius* for *Melania*.”

You would have spoken more correctly had you written that *Albinus* was put for *Albina*, and *Melanius* for *Melania*. But, setting this aside, I appeal to the tribunal of Donatus, whom you invoked. He writes in Book V *On Gender*:

“There are also other words masculine in sound but feminine in meaning, such as *Eunuchus*, a comedy; *Orestes*, a tragedy; *Centaurus*, a ship. Others are neuter in sound but feminine in meaning, such as *Phronesium*, *Glycerium*, and *Sophronium*, which are women.” [Col. 0540D]

Therefore, according to Donatus as judge, a name ending in *-us*, otherwise of masculine termination, if imposed upon a female person, acquires feminine signification while retaining its masculine termination.
