Thus *Eunuchus* is a name masculine both in termination and meaning when it denotes a castrated man; but if it is given to one of Terence’s comedies, its termination remaining unchanged while its meaning changes, it becomes feminine in gender, and we say “Terence’s charming *Eunuchus*.” *Aegyptus* is a name of feminine signification; but if that name is imposed upon some man, it becomes masculine in gender. The reason is that the termination in *-us* is merely the matter and substrate of the name; its signification alone, under Donatus as teacher, receives the character of form.

I call as a witness beyond all exception Vossius, who in Book III of his *Grammar*, Book I *On Analogy*, chapter 24, after quoting the testimony of Quintilian cited above, says:

“Fabius therefore wished the same rule to apply in *Muraena* and *Glycerium*: just as *Muraena* is masculine on account of its signification, although its termination may seem to require something else, so *Glycerium* is feminine, although its termination is neuter.”

Thus, although this cognomen *Albinus* has a masculine termination, simply because it was imposed upon a woman—as in fact it was imposed by so many Fathers—it assumes feminine signification, which is entirely compatible with a masculine termination.

Indeed, my sweetest Macedonian, Heribert Rosweyd was not troubled by these scruples of yours when, in the preface to Book VIII of the *Lives of the Fathers*, no. 6, he noted:

“Baronius’s conjecture is sound; but it is not necessary to restore *Albinam* in place of *Albino*. For it is established that in that age women’s names were sometimes expressed with masculine terminations. Thus, in ancient authors, a woman is found called now *Melanius*, now *Melanium*.”

He later confirmed this very point in his notes on Saint Paulinus’s Epistle 44, where he says:

“*Melanio*: he means Melania herself, who is variously called *Melania*, *Melanius*, and *Melanium*.”

Augustine’s Epistle 227 should accordingly be understood in this way:

“To our dearest brothers, Albinus, Pinianus, and Melanius.”

I read *Melanio* in place of *Meliano*. He means Albina and Melania, when they were staying with Alypius, bishop of Tagaste in Africa.

Do you see how entirely Rosweyd is on my side? I certainly had him before my eyes when I wrote those words and refused to admit Baronius’s correction. Yet you say (p. 35):

“He dissents from the grammarians, and must be chastised by Orbilius; nor need Baronius fear him, for he wished merely to prick him incidentally, while I vindicate him.”

What, my friend, will you do with Rosweyd? Remember that he is the man whom, on p. 150, you called “a most learned and elegant author”; in your index you write: “Rosweyd, a most elegant author.” Or perhaps, so that you may not spare me your blows, you will say that, together with me, Rosweyd too must be chastised by Orbilius? Beware of the many rods which the learned companions of Rosweyd wield in the schools. Either erase the title “most elegant,” if you demand grammar in him just as you demand it in me; or, if you judge that course close to rashness, release me also—who spoke in Rosweyd’s words—from Orbilius’s rods. For the present, know this: I have resolved that I would rather be beaten along with Rosweyd than learn the grammatical rules of the Macedonian.

Yet you are mistaken if you think that I oppose to you only this one Heribert. I have many other writers, both ancient and recent, both Greek and Latin, who speak on my behalf, and before whom you would not even dare to open your mouth; you would merely wonder, and perhaps grieve. For:

> This is a quarrel in which you strike and I merely take the blows.  
> —Juvenal, *Satire* 3.228

“You object,” you say (p. 53), “that the example of *Eustochium* is irrelevant, since *Eustochium* was the proper name of Paula’s daughter, who could not be called *Eustochia*, because it ought to be *Eustochium*—just as Terence’s *Glycerium* could not be called *Glyceria*. For there were certain names ending in *-um* that were proper to both men and women: for example, *Dynacium* and *Pegnium* for men, *Eustochium* and *Glycerium* for women. That declension therefore was neither free nor promiscuous, but a necessary construction of grammar.”

Remember that you are dealing with a school of grammarians, by whom pupils would be beaten if they called *Eustochium* the proper name of the virgin. It was, in fact, the cognomen of the daughter of Toxotius and Paula; her actual name was Julia. Jerome writes of Saint Paula in Epistle 27:

“She was married to Toxotius, who derived the noblest blood of Aeneas and the Julii; hence his virgin daughter was also called Eustochium Julia.”

From this I correct Glandorp, who in his *Onomasticon* counted the Toxotii among the Junii. The same is also clear from Capitolinus, in his *Life of the Younger Maximinus*. He says:

“Julia Fadilla, great-granddaughter of Antoninus, was betrothed to him; afterward Toxotius, a senator of the same family, married her.”

Gruter, however, is mistaken in reading “Junia Fadilla.” But more on this elsewhere. I shall not subject you—who have made the virgin’s name into a cognomen—to the rod of Orbilius; I am not so harsh a critic of grammar toward a friend as you profess to be toward me.

Chifflet notes on p. 45 of his annotations on the letters of Paulinus of Nola that, in the printed volumes, at the end of the letter to Pammachius, one reads *Eustochium*, whereas, as he says, *Eustochia* is written in the Putean and Viennese manuscripts. He calls the Putean codex, on p. 8, “extremely ancient and of the highest quality.”

I pass to Terence’s *Glycerium*. For I see that you have little familiarity with ancient monuments, and especially with Priscian, whom you call a second judge—or witness—against me. Priscian notes that women’s names ending in *-um* are expressed figuratively in this way, not properly. I give his own words from Book VI:

“Nevertheless, among comic poets many such Greek names are found, to which they customarily prefix articles of the feminine gender because of their signification: ἡ Δόρκιον, *this Dorcium*; ἡ Γλυκέριον, *this Glycerium*. This is usually done as a term of endearment, or to indicate youth.”

In Book V he likewise writes that women’s names end figuratively in *-um*, as in “my *Glycerium*, *Dorcium*, and *Philotium*.”

Therefore, if *Glyceria* could be called *Glycerium* by Latins merely in imitation of the Greeks, then, properly and correctly—in Latin usage—it ought to have been called *Glyceria*, not *Glycerium*. What, then, do you mean by saying, “Nor could Terence’s *Glycerium* be called *Glyceria*”? On the contrary, I see that among Latin writers the woman bearing that name was commonly called *Glycera*.

Martial, Book II, Epigram 41, says:

> “Glycera replied that her teeth hurt.”

Horace, Book I, Ode 19:

> “Glycera’s radiance burns me,  
> More pure than marble shining from Paros.”

Ode 30:

> “O Venus, queen of Cnidus and Paphos,  
> Reject beloved Cyprus, and transfer  
> To your temple the beauty of Glycera,  
> Who calls upon you with abundant incense.”

The same is evident from several inscriptions. I shall append one or two. At Rome, near Saint Clement’s:

> FLAVIA DOMITILLA, DAUGHTER OF FLAVIA DOMITILLA, GRANDDAUGHTER OF THE EMPEROR CAESAR . . . . ANI, MADE THIS FOR GLYCERA, [POSSIBLY HER FREEDWOMAN], AND FOR HER FREEDMEN, FREEDWOMEN, AND THEIR DESCENDANTS.

Another is found in Gruter, p. MVIII, no. 6:

> TO THE DIVINE MANES OF FLAVIUS SEVERUS, HIS DEAREST SON, WHO LIVED SIX YEARS, FIVE MONTHS. FLAVIUS VITALIS, VETERAN, AND GLYCERA, HIS MOST UNHAPPY PARENTS, [DEDICATED THIS].

From these examples you understand that the name *Glycera* was familiar to the Latins. Thus, in the calendars of the Roman Church, under 13 May, you will read: “At Heraclea, Saint Glyceria, martyr.”

Indeed, we read *Glyceria* or *Glycera* not only among the Latins but also among the Greeks. Simocatta, in Books I and VIII *On the Affairs of the Emperor Maurice*, praises the cult of “Glyceria the martyr” (Γλυκερίας τῆς μάρτυρος). Athenaeus, Book XIII, lists among famous women “Glycera” (τὴν Γλυκέραν), whom he says Harpalus summoned to Athens. Lucian, in *The Rhetoricians’ Precepts*, names Glycera (Γλυκέραν) together with Thais and Malthace.

The aforementioned Priscian notes in Book VI that the woman Glycera was expressed, as a kind of endearment—or, as I would say, playfulness—with the neuter termination of the name. Thus Athenaeus, in the same passage, quotes the following verses from the poet Machon:

> Glycerium, which she had received from  
> Her Corinthian lover, immediately  
> Handed over to the fuller as a summer garment.

Lucian likewise calls her *Glycerium* (Γλυκέριον) in the *Dialogues of the Courtesans*. Courtesans are also expressed by Plautus with Greek terminations. Thus *Silenium* and *Gymnasium* are named in the *Cistellaria*; *Philocomasium* and *Acroteleutium* in the *Miles Gloriosus*; *Phoenicium* in the *Pseudolus*, and so forth. Aristaenetus likewise gives the names of prostitutes in Book I, Letters 14 and 24, and Book II, Letter 13. See, my Macedonian, what sort of books your censorship forces me, a professor of ecclesiastical history, to consult!

But, since you possess a sharp and subtle intellect, you will reply that the woman called *Glycerium* by Terence could never have been called *Glycera*, just as one who was called *Glycera* could not have been called *Glycerium* in the nominative case. Yet this escape helps you little. Reread Lucian’s dialogues just mentioned. You will see that one of them is given by the author the title “Glycera and Thais” (ΓΛΥΚΕΡΑ ΚΑΙ ΘΑΙΣ), while in the dialogue itself she is called *Glycerium* (Γλυκέριον). This is how it is read in the printed editions and in two manuscripts of His Serene Highness the Grand Duke, in bookcase 57.

The most learned men, Jacobus Micyllus and Joannes Benedictus, interpret it precisely in this way: in the title they render it “Glycera and Thais,” but in the text they translate *Glycerium*. Cardinal Baronius, in his notes on 13 May, letter C, writes “Glyceria, or Glycerium.” In his *Annals*, under the year 175, he praises Glyceria the martyr, who in the index of the same volume is called *Glycerium*.

I return to Terence’s *Glycerium*. You know that Terence’s *Andria* is a comedy of Menander, which he declares in the prologue that he transferred into Latin:

> Menander composed the *Andria* and the *Perinthia*.

But Athenaeus, Book XIII, testifies that Menander loved the courtesan Glycera: “Everyone knows that Glycera was loved by Menander.” In Greek you read Γλυκέραν. Menander therefore inserted his beloved into the play, just as our Maro sang of his Alexis in the second eclogue. Although Menander’s comedies have perished through the unfortunate fate of Greek poetry, it is evident from Terence’s adaptation that the woman was called *Glycerium* in the Greek play whom Athenaeus called *Glycera*.

What, then, do you mean by writing, “Nor could Terence’s *Glycerium* in the *Andria* be called *Glyceria*”?

Let Gentianus Hervetus, thoroughly skilled in both languages, bring up the rear. You may read his learned translations at your leisure in Possevinus. He was the first to make the *Lausiac History* of Palladius, bishop of Helenopolis, accessible to Latin ears. He writes in chapter 86:

“There Evagrius is received by the blessed Melania.”

Later:

“The blessed Melanium says to him.”

Again, in chapter 97:

“To her, at one time, the younger Melanium, granddaughter of the elder Melania, about whom I shall speak later, sent five hundred coins.”

Finally, in chapter 118:

“But when,” he says, “his own granddaughter Melanium, and so forth.”

What you say may not be used, Hervetus used not merely once, but a second and a third time, calling the same woman indifferently *Melanium* and *Melaniam*, although in Palladius’s Greek text *Melanium* is never found, but the same woman’s name is always expressed with a feminine termination.

Yet you, more learned than Hervetus, write: “That declension was neither free nor promiscuous, but a necessary construction of grammar.” Will you dare to break wind at such writers? Will you declare Martial, Horace, Lucian, Athenaeus, and the translators Micyllus, Benedictus, Hervetus, Rosweyd—and, if it please the gods above, the great Baronius—to be chastised by Orbilius and accused of grammatical ignorance?

Erase rather that hasty judgment of yours. If you had examined the writings of the ancients more carefully, I do not doubt that you would have refrained from it, lest you be regarded as a foolish corrector of another man’s grammar. If, however, you ask why the Fathers whom I praised at the beginning put *Albinum* and *Melanium* in place of *Albina* and *Melania*, Rosweyd will teach you in his notes on Saint Paulinus’s Epistle 44. I do not quote his words because I want you to drink from the source.

Now you see and feel, my friend, that your judgment—which, as an outstanding specimen of your work, you wrote in your index in these words, “Noris is accused of grammatical ignorance and lies crushed beneath the weight of so many testimonies”—has been overthrown. Yet, lest I be thought inhuman, I place a gravestone upon it, adding an epitaph in which its deserved suppression may be expressed in capital letters. I take it from the heaps of Gruter’s inscriptions:

> SATURNINUS, SON OF SEVERUS, HAD THIS MADE FOR HIMSELF AND FOR RAMA URSULA, HIS DEAREST WIFE, AND FOR THEIR SON, WHO LIVED EIGHT YEARS, AND THEIR SON, WHO LIVED THIRTEEN YEARS.

Later readers, following Joseph Scaliger, chapter 19 of Gruter’s index, will read: “Ramus Ursula.”

But if you remain harder than stone in your once-formed conjecture, throw down your pen, take up the engraver’s chisel and mallet, and cut *Ramae* in place of *Ramo*, so that even the silent spirits of the dead may speak from the tombstone of your excellence in grammar, and so that it may never appear anywhere in the world that a woman’s name was expressed with a masculine termination.

I feel, however, that you are summoning me into the arena once again. “But let us dismiss,” you say (p. 5), “these trifles, though not to be despised, lest we seem to linger over a mere trifle.”

Would that you had omitted what you dismiss as trifling! You would certainly have consulted more securely the encyclopedia of yours, of which you hint in the preface that you have more than once produced a specimen. You call trifling things which you could not have called more correctly. At least I rejoice; would that I could congratulate you also that an end has finally been placed to this war of words.

You continue:

“Let us examine the persons to whom Augustine dedicated that work of his, and let us discover which of us has the better judgment. The inscription is: ‘Albine, Piniane, and Melania.’”

Thus you appeal from grammar to history. Take care, however, lest, where you were not a good corrector in grammar, you be judged a bad writer of history. For my part, I would rather contend with you in the field of history than within the barriers of grammar. When you pursue an ornate abundance of expression and periods clattering with Ciceronian eloquence, fighting with a drum rather than a sword, I, devoted to facts, serve the evidence and search out knowledge of events buried beneath the ruins of an earlier age, so that, if I do not take the greatest care with language, I may at least take the greatest care with truth.

Come, then: explain what you think concerning the persons to whom the holy doctor dedicated his book *On the Grace of Christ*.

“For my part,” you say (p. 52), “at first I did not approve of the name *Albine* being understood as referring to Pinianus’s son, lest a son be placed before his parents.”

[Col. 0545C]

If you had read Palladius’s history, you would never have thought of a son of Pinianus. For in the same chapter 119 he writes:

“When Melania had borne two sons, and both had died, she came to such a hatred of marriage for Christ’s sake that she said this to her husband Pinianus, the son of the former prefect Severus, and so forth.”

Pinianus had therefore lost his sons before he left Italy and adopted, together with his wife Melania, a purpose of chastity. The author of Saint Melania’s life, in Surius under 31 December, reports that Melania first gave birth to a girl and afterward to a boy. He says:

“What was born was indeed male; but as soon as he was born and regenerated through holy baptism, he departed from this world and was sent to the One who is there.”

You proceed (ibid.):

“It seemed preferable either to change the name *Albine* to *Albina*, as Baronius wishes, so that Albina would be the mother-in-law, or to retain *Albinum* for the father-in-law or grandfather of one of the two, Pinianus and Melania; and this latter view pleased me more.”

That last view pleased you more, although it is ridiculous. To make you understand this more clearly, and to strip you, under my instruction, of these fantasies, know that the son of the elder Melania married Albina, a woman of the highest nobility, by whom he had the younger Melania, who afterward became Pinianus’s wife. This is related by Palladius, a friend of the elder Melania, in chapter 10 of the *Lausiac History*. Palladius had also been the guest of Melania and Pinianus in Italy when he came to Rome as an envoy in the case of Saint John Chrysostom, as he himself testifies in chapter 121.

The aforementioned writer says in chapter 118:

“But when the elder Melania had also instructed her granddaughter Melanium”—thus Hervetus translates it; do not revive your defeated quarrel over the name—“together with her husband Pinianus, and had instructed Albina, her daughter-in-law, the wife of her son, in the catechesis, and had persuaded all of them to sell what they possessed, she led them out of Rome.”

Thus the grandfather of the younger Melania was the husband of the elder Melania. But it is certain that the husband of the elder Melania was not alive in the year 373. Hear Jerome in Epistle 24:

“Saint Melania, while her husband’s body was still warm and not yet buried, lost two sons at once.”

Later:

“Indeed, how completely she despised them in spirit she demonstrated afterward in her only son, to whom, after granting all the property she possessed, she sailed to Jerusalem as winter was already approaching.”

Jerome likewise writes in his *Chronicle*, under the tenth year of the emperor Valens:

“Melania, the noblest of Roman women, daughter of the former consul Marcellinus, leaving behind her only son, then urban praetor, sailed to Jerusalem.”

In the year 373 of the Christian era, the tenth year of Valens was already passing after 28 March, according to Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVI, p. 315 in the edition of Valesius, a man of consular rank.

But you, my Macedonian, make the husband of the elder Melania—and consequently the grandfather of the other Melania—still alive in the year 418, when Saint Augustine wrote the book *On the Grace of Christ*. For you imagine that Albinus was the grandfather of the younger Melania, to whom the holy doctor dedicated the volume in question.

Palladius says in chapter 117:

“Among them was also the most blessed Melania of Rome, who was indeed the daughter of Marcellus the consul, and the wife of a certain man who held great authority, whose name I do not properly remember.”

It is surely closer to a miracle that Palladius, the closest friend of both Melanias and a client of a most noble family, should have forgotten the name of Melania’s husband, whereas you, after twelve or more centuries, should produce it as Albinus. Nor can it properly be asserted that Albinus was Pinianus’s grandfather. For, as I shall show, around the year 400 Pinianus and Melania adopted a purpose of chastity, distributing a large portion of their paternal property among the poor.

When Severus, Pinianus’s brother, learned this and grieved that the family of Pinianus had been deprived of its very wealthy inheritance through his piety, he was, as the author of Saint Melania’s life says, “inspired by the insane prompting of the demon.” He began to harass his brother, seizing his fields, carrying off his produce, insulting him in every way, and using violence against him. He also persuaded Pinianus’s wicked slaves to say not only that they themselves belonged to Severus, but that the fields in which they lived belonged to him as well, and to call them Severus’s property.

From this it is clear that at that time not only was Pinianus’s grandfather no longer living, but even his father was not alive, since Severus was attempting to seize by force the property of Pinianus his brother, while Pinianus was disposing of his lands and slaves before sailing to Africa. Or will you thrust upon me some military property known only to yourself?

Your belief that Albinus was at least the father-in-law of one of the two is refuted with equal ease. For Melania’s father-in-law was called Severus. You would have read this explicitly in the aforementioned book of Palladius, bishop of Helenopolis, chapter 119, where he says:

“When Melania had borne two sons, and both had died, she came to such a hatred of marriage for Christ’s sake that she said this to her husband Pinianus, the son of Severus, the former prefect.”

Do you hear that Severus was Melania’s father-in-law, not your Albinus? Nor can Albinus be called Pinianus’s father-in-law, for the father of the younger Melania was called Publicola. You could have learned this from the notes of the most learned Peter Francis Chifflet on Paul’s letters, part 1, chapter 24, and again part 2, chapters 26 and 34.

It is amusing to wonder where you acquired such power—using Jerome’s words—of changing names, so that you impose the name Albinus upon Severus and Publicola. “This,” you say, “pleased me more.” I complained of you because, in chapter 2, p. 64, of your apology, you called me Pyrgopolynices; but in future I shall restrain my complaints, when I see that you are so learned a name-giver. I have not yet earned that nickname, for you know that, according to Plautus, Pyrgopolynices is said to have killed sixty Macedonians in a single day. When I have refuted your entire volume and cast down one Macedonian, then call me Pyrgopolynices as much as you please.

You add (p. 53):

“Baronius changes *Albine* to *Albina* and considers it an error; yet he does not reject *Albine* for the son of Albina, so that the sense may be ‘Albine, man.’ Noris says that *Albine* should be retained, and that by this name a woman is meant, in accordance with the license of that age and for the reason just given. I, on the contrary, think that *Albine* must absolutely be read as masculine.”

Where, where, my friend, is the defense of Baronius that you promised in the title of the chapter (p. 47)? “Baronius is vindicated from Noris’s criticism.” May I perish if you have afforded Baronius the defense you promised him so many times anywhere in this work! You are as far from him as one doorway is from another, although you publicly declare yourself his follower.

I demonstrate this plainly in the apology I am forging. Baronius writes that an error has entered the word *Albine*, since Albina must be understood as Melania’s mother. As far as the person is concerned, I agree with Baronius; I deny, however, that an error has entered the text, since Albina could have assumed either termination of the name. But you insist on reading *Albine*, and you think this is a man who was either Pinianus’s uncle, father, father-in-law, or paternal uncle. Is this how you vindicate Baronius from Noris’s criticism?

My only dispute with Baronius concerns a single letter: namely, that Albina, Melania’s mother, was called *Albine* in the vocative case in accordance with the license of that age. You change the sex entirely. You make male the person whom Baronius correctly called a woman; indeed, where he conjectures that the person was Albina’s son, you imagine Albinus—not, with Baronius, a relative of Pinianus, but his grandfather, father, or uncle.

Go now and advertise yourself as Baronius’s advocate, while opposing him as completely as possible. What were you thinking when you committed this splendid defense of Baronius to writing?

You continue (p. 54):

“I infer this from Augustine’s words. For he says: ‘Most sincere brothers, beloved by God, Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania.’ The word *brothers* signifies that the greater part are male, and the epithets confirm it: ‘most sincere,’ ‘beloved.’”

I fear that you will also turn Therasia, Saint Paulinus’s wife, into a man. For in the title of Saint Augustine’s Epistle 34 these words are written:

“To our most beloved and most sincere lords, truly most blessed brothers, rich in the abundant grace of God, Paulinus and Therasia.”

In the body of the letter:

“Holy brothers and beloved by God.”

At the end:

“To our most beloved, most sincere, truly gracious and most distinguished brothers, rich in the abundant grace of the Lord.”

Here you see that the title addresses both spouses, although the gender of the nouns is taken from the more distinguished person. Thus one Pinianus governs those epithets as far as grammatical gender is concerned, although a mother-in-law and a wife are designated together.

You add (ibid.):

“But who that Albinus was remains hidden. Here is Rhodes, here the leap; here is the work, here the labor, O Macedonian.”

You had written in the title of this, your seventh chapter: “Who Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania were is explained.” Of Pinianus and Melania you say only that they were married, and nothing more. The name of Albinus fills both pages. Come, then: explain who he was. You answer: “It remains hidden.”

I summon you, willingly or unwillingly, to the jurisdiction of your title. Fulfill the faith you pledged, lest, as Horace says, you be called a promise-maker who leaves great gaps. Remember that you said: “Who Albinus was is explained.” If he remains hidden, then, in your own judgment, he is not explained. Does your encyclopedia—which you boast about in the preface—suggest nothing to you? Let me reply from Plautus’s *Trinummus*:

> See, man, that you recognize a man!

“Yet I,” you say, “think that he was either Pinianus’s father, father-in-law, paternal uncle, or maternal uncle, so that he would be older and, by virtue of his age, would claim the first place.”

Thus, by repeating *either* four times, you thought you had explained your Albinus, that man of yours. For you used that disjunction as an Ariadne’s thread and escaped from the tangled labyrinth of Albinian genealogy.

Alas, in how many errors you are entangled, my friend! Albinus was not Pinianus’s father, for, according to the *Lausiac History*, whose words I gave above from chapter 119, Pinianus’s father was called Severus, the former prefect. There survive rescripts of three Augusti addressed to Severus, prefect of the City, in the Theodosian Code: the sole law *On Beggars* and law 2 *On the Profits of Offices*, issued under the consulship of Antonius and Syagrius, namely in the year 382.

Pinianus, the son of Severus, was joined to the younger Melania in the year 397, when Melania, the grandmother of Pinianus’s wife, came from Palestine to Rome with Jerome during the pontificate of Siricius, as Jerome relates in the second book of his apology against Rufinus; Palladius likewise bears witness in chapter 118.

Nor, as I clearly demonstrate, was he Pinianus’s father-in-law. Saint Augustine writes in Book II of his *Retractions*, chapter 50:

“After the Pelagian heresy, together with its authors, had first been refuted and condemned by the bishops of the Roman Church, Innocent and afterward Zosimus, with the cooperation of the letters of the African councils, I wrote two books against them, one *On the Grace of Christ*, the other *On Original Sin*.”

Augustine dedicated these books to Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania, as is immediately apparent from the first chapter. Innocent condemned Pelagius’s heresy in the year 416, as is clear from his letter sent to the Fathers of the Council of Milevis on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus and Constantius, men of consular rank. In the year 418 Zosimus proscribed the same heretics by a repeated judgment. Therefore the two books that the holy doctor inscribed to Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania were published in that same year, 418.

But the son of the elder Melania, Pinianus’s father-in-law, had died twenty years earlier. I know that Baronius, under the year 409, and Chifflet, part 2, notes on Paulinus’s letters, chapters 34 and 35, assign his death to the year 416. But I clearly refute the chronological errors of both.

The author of Saint Melania’s life relates that she was joined to Pinianus in marriage in the fourteenth year of her age, and that after bearing and losing two sons she seriously considered the celibate life, but was prevented by her father from carrying out that pious purpose. He then says:

“Her father departed this life. When he had died, Melania, together with Pinianus, released from the bond of the marriage bed, carried out the purpose of chaste living which she had long conceived.”

Let the aforementioned author be heard:

“When the one who had prevented them had been removed, when it was pleasing to God and the time was calling them, they immediately departed from the great city, bidding farewell to urban crowds and disturbances. At that time Pinianus was twenty-four years old, while Melania was twenty.”

Palladius likewise writes of her in chapter 119:

“Accordingly, in the twentieth year of her age, she renounced the world.”

Therefore Pinianus lived with his wife Melania for only six years while his father-in-law was still alive.

But Palladius, writing of the elder Melania in chapter 118, says:

“Many years later, when she had learned about the condition of her granddaughter, that she had married and wished to renounce the world, the old woman, fearing that they might be drawn into some doctrine, heresy, or evil way of life, boarded a ship at the age of sixty and sailed from Caesarea to Rome in twenty days.”

Saint Paulinus, in Epistle 10 to Severus, gives a fuller account of her arrival in Italy together with Rufinus and of her journey to Rome; she was his guest in Campania.

Since Melania and Rufinus arrived at Rome while Siricius was still alive, as Jerome testifies both in his second apology and in Epistle 16, entitled the *Epitaph of Marcella*, it is evident that in the year 397, the last year of Siricius’s pontificate, Pinianus had already been joined to the younger Melania. It is consequently impossible to extend the death of her father—and Pinianus’s father-in-law—either to the year 409 with Baronius or to the year 416 with Chifflet, since Pinianus lived with his wife for only six years while his father-in-law survived.

There exists an important letter concerning the death of this father-in-law, Saint Paulinus’s Epistle 44 to Saint Augustine, which is also numbered 249 among Augustine’s letters. The holy doctor replied to it in the following letter, no. 250. From this letter I clearly deduce the year of death of the son of the elder Melania, who was Pinianus’s father-in-law.

The following words are found there:

“Accordingly, when you hear from our brother Possidius, who is with you, what sorrowful cause compelled him, you will learn most truly from him, and so forth.”

The sorrowful cause that compelled Possidius, bishop, to sail to Italy is related by Augustine in Epistle 202 to Nectarius. The pagans of Calama in Numidia, whose religious rites Possidius supervised, had caused a riot and afterward attempted to destroy the Christians’ church with stones and torches; they had sought the bishop Possidius himself in order to kill him.

Augustine writes that this crime was committed in defiance of the most recent laws against the pagans, enacted by the emperors Arcadius and Honorius in Africa on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Manlius Theodorus, namely in the year 399. He says the same in Book XVIII of *The City of God*, chapter 54. In the same letter he says that the pagans rioted on the Kalends of June, while they were celebrating the Floralia.

The date of Possidius’s voyage may be gathered from another of Augustine’s letters to Nectarius, Epistle 254, where he says:

“For I had written back when the holy brother and my fellow bishop Possidius was still with us and had not yet sailed. I received the letters that you graciously returned to him on my account on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, nearly eight months after I had written.”

Thus, at the beginning of August in the year 399, Possidius had not yet departed for Italy; nevertheless, before the sixth day before the Kalends of April in the year 400 he had returned to Africa, since before that date Nectarius of Calama had delivered Saint Augustine’s letters to him.

Indeed, if you wish to investigate the matter more precisely, note, I beg you, that Paulinus in the aforementioned Epistle 44—where he speaks with praise of the death of Pinianus’s father-in-law and of Melania’s mother’s steadfastness—writes that he received Augustine’s letter from the deacon Victor around the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul. Victor had previously stayed for some time in Rome but had not taken care to send the letter to him sooner in Campania.

Now pay attention to what Augustine wrote in that letter. He says:

“You have taught me, in the spirit of truth, to greet that moderation of mind among mortals in the West, by which you saw that blessed mother and grandmother Melania mourn the bodily death of their only son—with silent weeping, indeed, but not with a grief dry of maternal tears.”

From this you may infer that Pinianus’s father-in-law, the son of the elder Melania and father of the younger, died before May of the year 399, since Paulinus learned of the mother’s steadfastness at her son’s death from Augustine’s letter around the feast of the Apostles, as he testifies in Epistle 44. Augustine replied to that letter with Epistle 250 while Possidius was staying in Italy; after July of that same year, according to Epistle 254, Possidius had sailed from Africa to the imperial court.

I have explained these matters at greater length, not because it was so important to refute your fantasies about Albinus as Pinianus’s father-in-law, but so that the chronology of the letters of Saints Paulinus and Augustine might become known, since Baronius and Chifflet cite them at entirely inappropriate dates.

See how highly I value that utterly cold admonition of yours, on p. 287, at the end of your work against Lupus:

“Let Noris know that, when he departs from the prince of ecclesiastical history, he departs from the truth.”

I both revere Baronius and turn over his *Annals*, worthy of the cedar, with day-and-night diligence; yet I am not so devoted to the man that I consider him preferable to truth. But you shall hear more about these matters in the apology.

Would that you, who neglected to investigate the ancient sources from which you could have drawn knowledge of so many matters relating to Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania, had at least approached the streams flowing from Baronius, which were derived from those sources! You would certainly have learned that Pinianus’s father-in-law died in 409, or that the great annalist recorded his death in that very year, and you would not have imagined him still alive in 418.

You have therefore been convicted of a double error: you thought Albinus was Pinianus’s father or father-in-law. You add “paternal uncle.” Here the monuments of antiquity fail me. Meanwhile, accept a reply from Plautus’s *Trinummus*:

> I neither know nor know for certain whether he was born or not.

Finally, you conclude: “or maternal uncle.” Earlier you had written (p. 52) that *Albinum* could be retained for the father-in-law or grandfather of one of the two, Pinianus and Melania, and that this view pleased you more. Hold back your laughter, my friend, when you now think Albinus not Pinianus’s grandfather but his maternal uncle.

You seem determined to include all of Pinianus’s kinship and affinity when you write that Albinus was his father, father-in-law, paternal uncle, or maternal uncle. Tell me, please, why did you omit grandfather, when you had just been thinking of him? Why did grandfather so quickly migrate into maternal uncle? I am ashamed to spend good hours refuting these fantasies of yours.

You give an account of all these matters. He may have been the elder, and on account of his age may have claimed the first place. You do not understand the matter. For that reason Augustine named Albinus first in the inscription mentioned above—not because that man was older than the other two, but because, when those three wrote together from Palestine, where they were staying with Pelagius, to Augustine in Africa, Pinianus, out of deference to Albina’s age and because she loved him as a son—hence the holy Doctor calls him Albina’s son in Epistle 225—assigned the first place in the subscription of the letter as a mark of honor and respect. Accordingly, in replying to them, St. Augustine wished the order preserved in the inscription to be the same as the order he had observed in their inscription.

Thus, as St. Possidius testifies in the index of the holy Father’s letters, he places this inscription among the others: “To Albina, Pinianus, and Melania,” where the mother-in-law is named before the son-in-law. Hence you may observe that Augustine and his contemporary Fathers, Possidius and Prosper, whenever it was necessary to cite the books in question, either omitted the names of the women Albina and Melania, or placed Pinianus before the women. Hear our holy Doctor, in whom you boast that you dwell on page 287, *Against Julian*, book IV, chapter 8:

> At the end of the first book of mine to St. Pinianus, whose title is *On the Grace of God against Pelagius*.

St. Possidius, bishop of Calama, says in his catalogue of Augustine’s books:

> Two books to Pinianus, Albinus, and Melania, against Pelagius and Coelestius, on the grace of Christ and original sin.

Do you see that here Pinianus is placed before the woman Albina, not because of any privilege of age, but because of the dignity of his sex? Augustine calls her “Albinus,” not “Albina,” so that you may now understand, fully and beyond all doubt, that you have stirred up so much grammatical dust against a man who is most friendly to you without any justification whatever. St. Prosper, at the end of his work against the *Collator*, when reviewing most of Augustine’s books, names among them two addressed to St. Pinianus. Admit that in that inscription it was not the man Albinus whom you imagine, but Albina, the mother-in-law, who, because of the privilege of age, took the first place; otherwise, on account of the dignity of sex, either Pinianus alone, or at least Pinianus first, as the son-in-law, would have been placed there.

You add, you say (p. 54), that Augustine writes in Epistle 227, “To Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania,” who seem to be the same persons whom we have named, unless there is an error in “Melanius” and “Melania” ought to be read. And so you are almost persuaded that “Albinus” must be retained as designating a man.

If you had read Possidius’s index, you would have abandoned this opinion of yours concerning a male Albinus. He thus gives the title of that letter there: “To Albina, Pinianus, and Melania.” Augustine calls the same woman “Albinus”; his colleague Possidius names her “Albina.” If you had listened to the author of the life of St. Melania, you would never have placed a male Albinus as her mother-in-law in Africa. “And when,” he says, “it seemed good to Melania, the sea received her, while her mother—namely Albina—and Pinianus were present together.”

In the year 410 Albina, the mother-in-law, was in Sicily with her daughter and son-in-law, at the time when Alaric was ravaging Calabria. Rufinus, in the preface to Origen’s *Homilies on Numbers*—a work restored to its author by Emericus Bigotius, a man superior to all praise, and communicated to the distinguished Henry Valesius—says:

> Although our most beloved son Pinianus, whose religious company we accompany as fugitives for the love of chastity, imposes other duties as well …

In the same place he testifies that, from the Sicilian shore, he saw the torches that had been thrown into the town of Rhegium across the very narrow strait. Shortly afterward Rufinus died, and Albina, Pinianus, and Melania went to Alypius at Tagaste. When Augustine learned of their arrival, he wrote to them that he could not leave Hippo, pleading the severity of winter. After they had spent seven years in Africa, they crossed into Palestine, as is clear from the acts of St. Melania. From there, in the year 418, they wrote to Augustine in support of Pelagius, and the most holy Father replied with two extremely learned books.

I had cited St. Paulinus’s letter numbered 249 among Augustine’s letters, in which “Melanius” is written instead of “Melania.” Its words are:

> But I shall cease recounting further things concerning a man so dear to me and so devoted to Christ, since I shall repeat that in my earlier letters I related no small number of things about him, and since I could not praise anything concerning the blessed mother of this son, and the father—the root of holy branches—better or more holily than your holiness has deigned to speak and argue concerning her.

You write that these words are not sufficiently understood by me. “He was misled,” you say, “because he thought that the name ‘Melanius’ ought to be attributed to Melania, and that only one person was signified here.” Later you write:

> But two persons are named here, mother and son: Melania and Melanius. “Of the blessed mother”—there is one; and “the father, the root of holy branches”—there is the other, namely Melanius.

If you had read the notes of the most learned and elegant Rosweyde on the letter in question, you would have noted the textual error that misled you. That distinguished man writes on page 887:

> The preceding and following context show that we should read, “Melania, likewise the root of holy branches”; for nowhere else is there any mention of Melanius as her father.

But Paulinus had already spoken of Melania, and immediately adds the words in question. We must consider whether “Melanius” may perhaps have been written in the manner of “Glycerius.” And rightly so. For if he had placed Melania the mother and Melanius the father immediately next to one another, he would have said not “to her” (*in eam*), but “to them” (*in eos*). Add that Melania’s son was called not Melanius but Publicola, as Chiffletius can show you in more than one place in his notes on the same letters of Paulinus.

But you refused to listen to these two most celebrated writers of the Society of Jesus. Why did you not at least listen to yourself? Did you not say that Pinianus’s father-in-law was named Albinus? By what right do you add Melanius as his brother? Or will you perhaps say that Melania had two sons, one Melanius, whose death Paulinus mourned, and the other Albinus, the father of the younger Melania and Pinianus’s father-in-law?

What a man you are! From the year 373 Melania had remained a widow, the mother of an only son. Palladius writes in chapter 118:

> She was not drawn away from her love of her son; desire for her only-begotten son did not separate her from the love of Christ.

Jerome writes in Epistle 24:

> Indeed, how contemptuously she regarded them—namely, her dead husband and her two sons—she demonstrated afterward in the case of her only son.

Paulinus writes in Epistle 44 that Melania mourned the bodily death of her only son.

Yet, contrary to the statements of eyewitnesses, you thrust upon us two sons of Melania, Albinus and Melanius, although her only son was Publicola. If you had seen these words of Jerome in Epistle 41 to Rufinus:

> Hilas, the servant of the holy Melanius, was also with us,

you would surely have sung a triumph for yourself over Melanius the man. But the textual error must be corrected from the best manuscript of the library of His Serene Highness the Grand Duke, shelf 19, where “of the holy Melania” is read. Perhaps “of the holy Melanius” had been written by Jerome, and copyists, failing to understand it, either corrupted the text by making it “of the holy man,” or emended it without necessity by writing “of Melania.”

Baronius’s annotator must also be corrected. In the year 409, where the most learned Cardinal cites Paulinus’s letter to Augustine, he writes in the margin: “Melanius, Melania’s father.” For Palladius writes of Melania in chapter 117:

> She was indeed the daughter of Marcellus, a consular.

I know that in the Chronicle of St. Jerome, under the tenth year of Valens, Melania is called the daughter of the consul Marcellinus. But Rufinus, when reporting the words of Jerome’s Chronicle in book II of his *Invectives against Jerome*, writes: “the granddaughter of the consul Marcellinus.” Flavius Marcellinus held the consulship with Probinus as his colleague in the year 341.

You thought, my friend, that you were illuminating the genealogy of your Albinus with those repeated alternatives—“or this, or that”—as with torches. But you have not merely enveloped it in the densest darkness; you have also plainly revealed how great a loss of light you suffer in ecclesiastical history.

I beg you not to take it ill or angrily that a friend admonishes you in Augustine’s words:

> If, then, you are not thoroughly instructed, why do you not remain entirely silent, or speak in such a way as to show that you desire to be instructed?

*Against Cresconius*, book I, chapter 3.

When you had framed your challenge in these precise words:

> Let us examine the persons to whom Augustine dedicated that work of his, and let us discover which of us has the better judgment,

you ought to have consulted the volumes of the ancient writers, so that from them you might obtain knowledge of the persons concerning whom you had begun a dispute with me.

Those three persons and their relatives are praised by Augustine, Jerome, Paulinus, Palladius, Rufinus, and Possidius—men who not only lived with them, but also knew them personally and had been their hosts, clients, or panegyrists.

You say in chapter 3, page 25:

> My familiar Noris knows that I am a man who reads authors with the utmost care and concentration, immerses myself in them, enters deeply into them, and diligently investigates their meaning.

Certainly, if I were summoned to court, I would not dare give such testimony on your behalf. For I suspect that, when you wrote those words, you had not even once seen the authors just mentioned, much less immersed yourself wholly in them and entered deeply into them.

In the preface to your work against the professors of ecclesiastical history, giving free rein to your eloquence and declaiming with a great clamor of words, you say:

> They busy themselves among ruins and wreckage: so long as they display themselves as antiquarians, they satisfy themselves; they are literary men and rubble-men. Like stonecutters, they hew the quarries of ancient monuments, bring forth stones, and build heaps.

I wish you to know that those very vigorous “porters” sometimes act as diligent stonecutters as well. They turn and turn over stones with the same hand with which they handle volumes, since inscribed stones are for them the most certain witnesses of antiquity.

Attend now to what can be brought forward by stonecutters, so that Albina—concerning whom I see you raising so much dust from your own ingenuity—may be understood to have had both a father and a brother, and even a family.

In the little book on the life of St. Melania, printed by Surius on December 31 and by Lippomanus on January 31, the following is related of her when she arrived at Byzantium:

> She also found her uncle Volusianus overcome by a serious illness.

The same little book exists in Greek in the library of His Serene Highness the Grand Duke, among the minor works of St. Gregory Nazianzenus, shelf 7, no. 6, where the quoted words read:

> εὑρίσκει δὲ καὶ τὸν θεῖον αὐτῆς Βολουσιανὸν χαλεπῇ νόσῳ κεκρατημένον.
>
> “She also finds her uncle Volusianus overcome by a grievous illness.”

Yet it is false that Volusianus was St. Melania’s paternal uncle. For Melania’s father had no brother, since Melania the elder had an only son, as Jerome, Paulinus, and Palladius—whose words I quoted above—most explicitly attest.

Therefore, since Volusianus was not the brother of the father of Melania the younger, he cannot be described as her paternal uncle. The common error arose from the translators’ fault. Photius mentions Volusianus in codex 52, and there he too is called:

> θεῖος τῆς ἁγίας Μελίανιας

“the uncle of the holy Melania.”

Among the Greeks, however, the word *theios* (θεῖος) indiscriminately signifies the brother of either the father or the mother—that is, a paternal uncle or a maternal uncle—just as among the Italians the word *zio*, and among the Spaniards *tío*. I am certain that these words were borrowed from the Greeks, and perhaps the distinguished Octavius Ferrarius, a great pillar and protector of the liberal arts in Italy, will also demonstrate this in his work *On the Origin of the Italian Language*, which he will soon publish.

The translators, among them Schottus, being ignorant of Melania’s genealogy, rendered the word *theion* (τεῖον) into Latin as “paternal uncle,” when they ought to have written “maternal uncle.” Baronius, in the year 420, correctly called Volusianus St. Melania’s maternal uncle.

Thus Volusianus was Albina’s brother and St. Melania’s maternal uncle. From these facts it becomes clear that Albina’s father, brother, and family—none of whom has hitherto been investigated by the writers—were as follows. She was the daughter of Rufius Ceionius Albinus and the sister of Rufius Ceionius Volusianus, as I shall demonstrate later.

That the Albini belonged to the Ceionian family is evident from the letter of Ceionius to Aelius Bassianus, preserved by Capitolinus in the life of Albinus, chapter 4. There Clodius Albinus, the son of Ceionius, who was Caesar together with Septimius Severus, is praised by Capitolinus as deriving his origin from Roman families, namely the Postumii and the Ceionian Albini:

> This family, he says, is still today most noble, O Constantine, and has been increased and is to be increased through you; it grew greatly through the Gordians and Gallienus.

Which member of this family attained the highest honors under Constantine is gathered from the following mutilated inscription, preserved by Gruterus on page 377, no. 5:

> **RELIGIOSISSIMOQUE. C. CEIONIO. RVFO. VOLVSIANO. V. C. CORR. ITALIAE. PER ANNOS OCTO. PROCONSVLI AFRICAE. COMITI. DOMINI. NOSTRI. CONSTANTINI. INVICTI. ET PERPET VI. SEMPER AVGVTIS. PRAEFECTO. VERBI. IVDICI. SACRARVM. COGNITIONVM. CONSVLI.**
>
> And to the most religious Gaius Ceionius Rufius Volusianus, of clarissimus rank, corrector of Italy for eight years, proconsul of Africa, companion of our lord Constantine, unconquered and perpetual Augustus, prefect of the judicial tribunal, consul.

But before Albinus, the colleague of Severus, the Ceionian family had governed the Roman world. For L. Ceionius, transferred by adoption into the family of Aelius and Antoninus, was Augustus with the philosopher Antoninus and was called L. Ceionius Aelius Commodus Verus Antoninus, as Capitolinus relates at the beginning of his life.

His father, Ceionius Commodus, had been designated Caesar by Hadrian but died shortly afterward by an unexpected death. It is also established that the Ceionian Albini bore the cognomen Volusianus from the following inscription, preserved by my Panvinius in the year of the City 1297:

> **S. P. Q. CEIONIVM. RVFVM. ALBINVM. V. C. PHILOSOPHVM. RVFI. VOLVSIANI. IVD. ORD. CONS. FILIVM. SENAT. CONSVLTO SVOQ . . . EIVS. LIBERIS. POST. CAESARIANA. TEMPORA. I. POST. ANNOS. CCCLXXX. ET. I. AVCTORITATE. DECREVIT. FL. MAGNVS. IANVARIVS. V. C. VII. STATVARVM.**
>
> The Senate and People [honoured] Ceionius Rufus Albinus, of clarissimus rank, philosopher, son of Rufius Volusianus, ordinary judge and consul. By decree of the Senate and at his own [lacuna], [he honoured] his children after the Caesarian times, one [lacuna] after 381 years; Flavius Magnus Januarius, of clarissimus rank, overseer of statues, decreed this by authority. [The damaged inscription is materially uncertain.]

Since they reckoned among their ancestors Volusus, the leader of the Rutulians, Rutilius Namatianus writes in book I of his *Itinerary*, verse 167, that the Albini consequently assumed the cognomen Volusianus:

> Now, while others are returning to Rome, Rufius remains with the traveler,
>
> The living glory of his father Albinus;
>
> He derives his name from the ancient lineage of Volusus,
>
> And, as Maro testifies, traces his descent from the Rutulian kings.

That Rufius Volusianus, the son of Ceionius Albinus, brother of our Albina, and maternal uncle of St. Melania, was the man who later, when prefect of the City for a second time, published an edict against the Pelagians, is stated by the most learned men, Cardinal Baronius under the year 412 and Jacobus Sirmondus in his notes on letter 16 of book IX of Sidonius. Rutilius’s commentator, Caspar Barthius, agrees with them in note 169.

Thus Ceionia Albina was Melania’s mother and Pinianus’s mother-in-law; she was the sister of Ceionius Venerius Rufus Albinus Volusianus, who held the prefecture of the City several times and, while living in Africa with his mother, wrote to Augustine as a pagan, as is clear from Epistle 2 in volume II of St. Augustine’s works.

Rutilius, his predecessor in the urban prefecture, dedicated his *Itinerary* to this Volusianus; from this the names of the latter are brought together.

Since I am writing these things in Etruria, to which His Serene Highness Grand Duke Cosimo III, an outstanding patron and most munificent protector of the liberal arts, has summoned me, I may observe that the Albini Volusiani originated in Etruria and from there moved to Rome. Capitolinus testifies to this in *The Emperor Verus*, chapter 2.

The same Rutilius affirms that Albinus Volusianus, the brother of our Albina, had a villa in the territory of Volaterrae. For he writes that, as he was passing by ship through the Volaterran shallows, he was overtaken by a sudden storm, went ashore, and made for the villa of Albinus Volusianus. He says this in verse 463:

> There the swift Corus forced me to come to a halt,
>
> Such as he is accustomed to break through the forest glades.
>
> Scarcely protected by the houses, we endured the savage rains;
>
> Nearby, the villa of my Albinus stood open.
>
> For he is mine, whom Rome joined to my honour,
>
> Through whom the rights of my official robe continue.

That this honor was the prefecture of the City he asserts somewhat earlier, in verse 415:

> Here we recognize that the prefecture of the sacred City
>
> Was conferred because of your merits, dear friend.
>
> I would wish to include your true name in verse,
>
> But the harsh rule of meter avoids certain feet.
>
> Your cognomen, Venerius, most dear Rufus,
>
> Our page has long since sung to you by that name.
>
> May the festive day, which formerly deigned to visit my household,
>
> Now celebrate your vows crowned with a second offering.

Rufius Volusianus held the prefecture of the City in the year 417 of the Christian era. For Rutilius writes, addressing Rome, in verse 135:

> Although sixteen tens and a thousand years have been completed,
>
> And now your ninth year besides is passing.

The 1169th year of the City, beginning at the Parilia—that is, April 21—coincides with the Dionysian year 417. In that year Rutilius departed from Rome and found Volusianus designated prefect of the City.

For a long time after Constantine’s reign, the Ceionii continued to follow pagan superstition. This is established by the following inscription preserved by Gruterus on page 28, no. 5:

> **CEIONIVS. RVFIVS. VOLVSI ANVS. V. C. ET INLVSTRIS. EX. VICARIO. ASIAE. ET CEIO NI. RVFI. VOLVSIANI. V. C. ET. INLVSTRIS. EX. PREFECTO. PRE TORIO. ET. EX. PREFECTO. URBIS. ET. CECINE. LOLLIANE. CLARISSI ME. ET. INLVSTRIS. FEMINE. DEE. ISIDIS. SACERDOTIS. FILIVS. ITERATO. EX. VIGINTI. ANNIS. EX. PERCEP TIS. TAVROBOLIIS. VI. ARAM CONSTITVIT. ET. CONSECRAVIT. VI. KAL. IVN. D. N. VALEN TINIANO. AVG. ET. NEOTERICO CONSS.**
>
> Ceionius Rufius Volusianus, of clarissimus and illustrious rank, formerly vicar of Asia, son of Ceionius Rufius Volusianus, of clarissimus and illustrious rank, formerly praetorian prefect and prefect of the City, and of Cecina Lolliana, a woman of clarissimus and illustrious rank, priestess of the goddess Isis, on a second occasion, after twenty years and after receiving six taurobolia, set up and consecrated an altar on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [May 27], in the consulship of our lord Valentinian Augustus and Neoterius.

Thus, in the year 390, they had turned away from the Christian religion. That Volusianus was likewise devoted to this superstition is evident from his own letter and also from the letters of Augustine and Marcellinus, at the very beginning of the second volume of the holy Doctor’s works.

Melania brought her maternal uncle to the true doctrine at Byzantium shortly before his death. One might also infer from Palladius, in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 118, that Albina, too, had been in the same error: he says that both the pagan Apronianus and Albina were instructed in catechesis by Melania the elder. You will read more about Albina in the acts of her daughter Melania.

Meanwhile, see how benevolently disposed I am toward you. When, confidently challenging me to a contest, you exclaimed:

> Let us examine the persons to whom Augustine dedicated his work, and let us discover which of us has the better judgment,

I appoint and summon you yourself as judge against your own adversary.

You pronounced concerning Albinus:

> But who that Albinus was remains hidden.

I have shown that the person was not a man but a woman; that her father was Albinus; her brother Rufius Volusianus; her family the Ceionian family; her mother-in-law Melania; her husband Publicola; her daughter Melania the younger; her ancestors’ homeland Etruria; her villas at the Volaterran shallows—whose name still survives in the town between Populonium and Liburnum—and, finally, her friends and panegyrists Augustine, Jerome, Palladius, and Rufinus.

I have shown all these things about Albina, so that you may now discover, sufficiently and beyond all doubt, which of us has the better judgment.

Call me a porter, antiquarian, rubble-man, or stonecutter, as you please—as long as you admit that, concerning the persons to whom Augustine addressed the books mentioned above, I have produced, from the writings of eyewitnesses themselves, from the most ancient records of the holy Fathers, and from the inscriptions of ancient stones, evidence far more certain than what you have brought forth concerning the same persons from your own ingenuity, without any support whatever from books—a thing I am ashamed to say.

And if you declare that you are the most ingenious of authors because you proceed from ingenuity, while I am merely a vigorous porter working from my back, I shall accept your judgment and appeal to no other judge.

Let these words serve as a specimen of the just apology that I am now preparing against your latest book.

Since I understand that some people criticize me there because I said that the saints Hilary, bishop of Arles, and Vincent of Lérins adhered to the party of Cassian against St. Augustine’s doctrine of predestination—as though I were either the only person or the first to assert this—and since you also write in chapter 16, page 119:

> Give me, I ask you, Father Noris, some good or bad writer who calls Hilary of Arles a Semipelagian. So far I have been unable to find one; I have decided to cite certain distinguished writers.

Let St. Prosper lead the procession. In his letter to Augustine, after reporting the opinions and objections of the followers of Cassian—whom later scholastics called Semipelagians—he writes:

> We believe and hope that not only will our weakness be strengthened by the support of your discussions, but that even those who are distinguished by merits and honors, yet whom the darkness of this opinion obscures, will receive the purest light of grace. For one of them, a man of outstanding authority and spiritual devotion, the holy Hilary, bishop of Arles, is, as your Blessedness should know, an admirer and follower of your teaching in all other respects; and concerning this matter, which he brings forward as a complaint, he has long wished to communicate his opinion to your holiness by letter.

Hence Augustine, in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 21, does not hesitate, though suppressing his name, to count Hilary among those who denied that the beginning of faith is a gift of God.

You will soon understand how violently you twist those words. You ask for some good writer, or bad one. Hear Ussher in *On the Antiquity of the British Church*, chapter 11, page 346:

> Finally, Prosper numbers that Hilary of Arles among those who disagree with Augustine in the doctrine of predestination.

Perhaps you will reply that Ussher was a Calvinist. But you yourself were asking for some bad writer. Nevertheless, Father Riccioli calls Ussher in book I, chapter 20, of his *Reformed Chronology* “a man most learned in ecclesiastical antiquity.”

This does little to help your case against yourself, since you demanded a good writer or a bad one. Attend to good, better, and best writers, whom you would scarcely dare to oppose.

Father Theophilus Raynaud, in chapter 4 of his *Apology for Valerian of Cimiez*, writes:

> Hilary, bishop of Arles, was one of those who raised complaints against the holy Augustine.

Hear Prosper at the end of his letter to Augustine. After the words I have just quoted, he weighs the phrases “one of them”—that is, one of those acting against Augustine, of whom the discussion was concerned—and “in all other respects”:

> As regards the matter that Prosper discusses throughout the letter, and therefore as regards the Semipelagian error, he was not an admirer of Augustine’s doctrine; rather, he brought it forward as a complaint.

Prosper plainly testifies that he regarded him with suspicion, since he was uncertain with what purpose Hilary was going to conduct his correspondence with Augustine.

Let a fourth witness after Prosper be added: Father Gabriel de Henao, in volume [section] 28, number 184, of his work on middle knowledge. He says:

> The distinction concerning Hilary is also clear. He sent a letter to St. Augustine together with St. Prosper. That Hilary was not obscured by the darkness of an opinion opposed to St. Augustine, nor did he bring Augustine’s doctrine into dispute concerning the matter of grace; rather, that was the other Hilary, the bishop of Arles.

These are two distinguished writers of the Society of Jesus. But I have a third witness from that same most learned family: Jacobus Sirmondus, a great promoter of sacred and secular learning. In his notes on Pope Coelestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul, he writes that the letter—which is entirely in defense of St. Augustine—cannot be reconciled with Hilary of Arles, who, as Prosper testifies in his letter, while he admired Augustine’s teaching in other matters, **did not approve** it in this matter.

In Labbe and Cossart, volume II of the *Councils*, page 1818, I glory and triumph in the testimony of so great a man.

Do you want other witnesses, after asking for someone either bad or good? Here is a pair of witnesses, speaking with one voice. They are the most learned Sammarthani in volume I of *Gallia Christiana*, page 36:

> It is established that Hilary, who wrote to St. Augustine and on whose account Augustine sent the books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, was distinct from Hilary, bishop of Arles. First, because Hilary, in his letter to Augustine, indicates that he was a layman. But Prosper, writing to Augustine at the same time and on the same day, says that Hilary of Arles was then a bishop and opposed to his doctrine, in these words: “We believe that those whom the darkness of this opinion obscures, though distinguished by merits and honors, will receive the purest light of grace—of Semipelagianism” [the Sammarthani insert this word; I do not]. “For one of them, a man of outstanding authority and spiritual devotion, the holy Hilary of Arles,” and so forth.

They quote Prosper’s words.

Do you ask for another witness, the seventh to close the procession of the others? There is one from the same Gaul: the most learned Gilbert Mauguin, adviser to the Most Christian King, who died a few days ago. He writes in part II, chapter 11, page 650, of his *Refutation of the Predestination Fable*:

> According to Prosper’s testimony in his letter to Augustine, Hilary, bishop of Arles, and many other men no less distinguished for authority than for piety, rejected St. Augustine’s doctrine of God’s gratuitous predestination no less than they rejected heresy.

And on page 475 he testifies, again from Prosper, that Hilary was infected with the remnants of Pelagian depravity.

When you say, “So far I have been unable to find anyone who has written that St. Hilary of Arles opposed St. Augustine’s doctrine,” may I never think that you have lied. I know the candor, sincerity, and simplicity of your spirit. Therefore you read none of the writers I have cited.

It is often harmful, my Macedonian friend, to bring everything from one’s own ingenuity. Learn at last what advantage there is in acting as porters rather than as authors—in having study in one’s back rather than in one’s brain. For in these precise words you insulted the professors of ecclesiastical history in your preface.

That most confident address of yours—“Give me, Father Noris, some good writer or bad one”—comes from your own ingenuity. But your friend Noris’s weighty and square answer comes from his back.

I think nothing more need be added about Vincent of Lérins. For you write that I have other supporters of my statement; recently the distinguished Louvain doctor Christian Lupus joined them, in part 4 of his notes on the synods, page 757.

I beg you, my sweetest Macedonian, to take these matters in good part, and not to sing a triumph through Italy all the way to Rome before victory has been won.

And since, at the age of seventy-seven, after all the vigils you have endured in publishing more than forty volumes, with your aged body worn down, you fear to commit yourself to the vast sea of ecclesiastical learning, afraid that life may fail you in mid-course, allow me—whom you once saw as a beardless young man in Rome and whom you know to be more devoted than all others to the study of your name—allow me, I say, to spread my sails; and, secure in the harbor, wish me a prosperous voyage in Horace’s verse:

> The ship in which you have entrusted
>
> Your Historian to be carried across the straits,
>
> Bring Noris back, I beg you,
>
> And preserve half of my soul.
>
> Book I, Ode 3.

Farewell, most beloved and most ingenious Father. Commend me there to your friends, and make your patrons kindly disposed toward me, or at least less angry.

# Observations on the Book *On Rebuke and Grace*

## Chapter 1, § 2

> “Therefore we must confess that we possess free choice both for doing evil and for doing good; but in doing evil each person is free from righteousness and a slave of sin; in doing good, however, no one can be free unless he has been freed,” and so forth.

Here Augustine understands by the words “free choice” the will, not what everyone ordinarily used to understand by that expression—namely, that faculty of the mind by which a person can do or omit something, whether good or evil.

According to him, human beings are born and always remain, before regeneration, free from righteousness and slaves of sin. That is, they can do nothing but evil and can do no good; but they do evil willingly and omit good unwillingly, although, without the divine miracle that takes place in regeneration, the will cannot be changed.

It is sufficiently clear that, if all other mortals had thought in this way, they would have denied that human beings possess free choice. And Augustine himself did indeed deny it when he was speaking outside the heat of controversy, as is clear from the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 30. See the note on volume VI.

**Chapter 2, § 5.** He presents the objection to his doctrine of grace—by which, as he himself explains, people not only know what must be done, but also, through grace [lacuna] enabling them, do with love what they know—in this way:

> “Then,” they say, “let those who preside over us merely command us what we ought to do, and let them pray for us that we may do it; but let them not correct and rebuke us if we do not do it.”

For, plainly, if someone has not obeyed the divine commandments, then, according to Augustine’s view, this is certain evidence that efficacious grace was not present to him. When that grace assists, it is impossible that he should not obey; when it is absent, no one can obey.

What does Augustine reply to this? “Rather,” he says, “let everything be done; for the teachers of the churches—the apostles—did everything: they both commanded what was to be done, rebuked people if it was not done, and prayed that it might be done.” He demonstrates this with examples.

Yet those who brought forward these objections did not concede that the apostles held Augustine’s view. Indeed, Augustine himself could have inferred that they thought otherwise from the fact that divinely inspired men would not have done what could not stand with their position. He later says:

> “O man, in the command learn what you ought to have; in the correction learn that you have it through your own fault; in prayer learn from where you may receive what you wish to have.”

It is sufficiently clear that help is to be requested from God for the future, but not for past matters, since past offenses cannot be made not to have happened. Yet past offenses are what is at issue here, for correction concerns the past. Augustine therefore rhetorically evades the objection; he does not answer it.

Moreover, even prayers for the future cannot, according to his doctrine, truly be offered with effect. For God’s decrees concerning the elect will be carried out whether you pray or remain silent; and concerning the reprobate, nothing will be accomplished by your prayers. Therefore:

> Cease hoping to bend the decrees of God by praying.

Correction plainly shows that each person has sinned through his own fault; otherwise it would be unjust. But for a fault to be called ours, it must have been incurred by our own guilt, and it must be possible to overcome it if we are commanded to overcome it. For there is no guilt in one who does what he can neither do now nor ever could have done before.

If no one could have prevented himself from being stained by that fault—as Augustine maintains—then he ought not to be corrected for it. Nor should he be corrected if, once stained by it, he could in no way overcome it, because he lacked the assistance without which the fault could not be overcome.

Accordingly, Augustine could not, consistently with his own position, say: “Through your own fault you do not have what is necessary for observing the divine commandments.” Nor, on his doctrine, can one learn from the commandment what a person ought to have. For he ought not to have what he was no more able to have, without God’s willing it, than to halt the course of the stars.

The Bishop of Hippo is continually trying to blunt objections with words that clash violently with his own position. If he had been obliged to speak consistently with that position in every respect, the language of Scripture—and indeed of the whole human race—would have had to be condemned and altered; and, by the same operation, the firmest foundations of human society would have had to be torn down.

**Chapter 6, § 9.** “We have not received this grace,” say the Pelagians, speaking in the person of sinners. “Why, then, are we corrected as though we could give it to ourselves but were unwilling to do so?”

Nothing could be clearer. I do not understand how Augustine, faced with consequences so necessary and evident, failed to notice that he had not properly understood what Scripture says on these matters.

He is not lacking in words—words that somewhat more practiced rhetoricians can always supply—but from those words one can easily understand that the man ought to have been reduced to silence, unless his reputation, his published books, the authority of the councils, and everything undertaken with such zeal against the Pelagians had needed to be defended.

Hear Augustine himself:

> “They do not consider that, if they have not yet been regenerated, the first reason why they ought to be displeased with themselves when reproved for being disobedient to God is this…”

But this is a mere begging of the question, as the logicians say. These people denied that they ought—that is, that they were bound by any law—to do what they could not do. Such a thing would be to be displeased with themselves on account of their sins, although they had received no divine grace necessary for that purpose.

Augustine, however, as though he were about to solve this difficulty, adds:

> “Because God made man upright at the beginning of human creation, and there is no iniquity with God.”

Which man did he make upright? Adam alone, not those who did not yet exist—unless, by an absurd fiction, one says, as Augustine at one time approved, that the minds of all human beings who now exist, who have existed, and who will exist in later ages were in Adam’s mind, and consequently sinned before they came into their own bodies.

See the note to volume I, book III, *On Free Will*, chapter 20, and to volume II, Letter 98. I will not attack this fiction, since no one now defends or can defend it.

Therefore, unless there is iniquity with God—which Augustine removes from Him verbally—He cannot demand of Adam’s descendants that they be upright, since they were never upright and could not have been so, if we believe Augustine; for they could not avoid the transmission of original sin.

Thus it is sheer deception when he adds:

> “And therefore the first depravity by which God is disobeyed comes from man, because, falling by his own evil will from the uprightness in which God originally made him, he became depraved.”

He may say this of Adam; but it cannot be said of his descendants, who alone are being discussed here. Accordingly, it has no bearing on the matter and does not touch the objection of those who, many centuries after Adam, were born and conceived in original sin in such a way that, if we believe the African theologian, they could not escape its power.

But here another evasion follows, by which he tries to turn the mind away from the question:

> “Is this depravity not to be corrected in a human being because it is not peculiar to the person being corrected, but common to everyone? On the contrary, let it be corrected in each individual, because it belongs to all. For it does not cease to belong to anyone merely because no one is free from it.”

The Pelagians did not insist on the commonality of depravity in order to excuse it. Rather, they denied that Gaius, for example, or Titius could be corrected for offenses if it had never been within their power to avoid sin—first original sin, and then all actual sins—because Gaius and Titius (not “man” in general, which was not their subject) had never possessed the grace of God necessary for that purpose.

Let Adam have possessed it, if he needed it; but if Gaius and Titius never possessed it, they certainly could not be corrected without injustice.

“Those original sins,” the Punic Carneades next says, “are called alien because individuals draw them from their parents; but they are also called ours, not without reason, because in that one man all sinned, as the Apostle says.”

But in this controversy sins are called ours not in a transferred sense, but properly. The subject is sins on account of which we may justly suffer not metaphorical but properly understood punishments, by divine—that is, perfect—justice, because we could have abstained from them and succumbed to them only through our own properly understood guilt.

In any event, the sins of parents cannot be called ours in such a way that we may rightly be corrected and punished on their account. Nor does the Apostle say that we sinned in Adam, as Augustine, who was so often ignorant of the Greek language, repeatedly asserts.

Thus Paul says in Romans 5:12:

> Ὥσπερ δι᾽ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἡ ἁμαρτία εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθε, καὶ διὰ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὁ θάνατος· καὶ οὕτως εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους ὁ θάνατος διῆλθεν, ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον.

> “Just as through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, so death passed to all human beings, because all sinned.”

With Desiderius Erasmus, we translate ἐφ᾽ ᾧ as “because,” not “in whom,” since otherwise the sentence is disjointed and harsh.

But even if this were not clear, the translation followed by Augustine is certainly not so secure that the passage can be pressed as though it were unambiguous—especially since the doctrine is inferred almost entirely, or at least chiefly, from this passage, although it is burdened with so many difficulties that I scarcely think any greater ones can be found in another theological doctrine. We have seen examples of these difficulties above, and Augustine was wholly unable to satisfy them.

He adds:

> “Let the condemnable origin therefore be corrected, so that from the pain of correction the will to regeneration may arise.”

But by what right can anyone be corrected for having been born stained by original sin, when he could no more have avoided this than he can prevent the sun from rising and setting? Where is an example of such correction to be found in the whole of Scripture?

Augustine wishes original sin to be the punishment for Adam’s sin, inflicted by God, as he teaches in book XIII, chapter 12, of *The City of God*. But what creature can avoid the punishments inflicted by the Creator? And how can anyone be corrected for not having avoided them? No one has ever solved these knots, nor will anyone solve them.

These are Augustine’s claims concerning the corruption of the unregenerate. Concerning the correction of the regenerate, he reasons as follows:

> “But if someone, already regenerated and justified, falls back into an evil life by his own will, certainly he cannot say: ‘I did not receive it,’ because by his free will he has lost the grace of God which he received.”

Augustine believed that some people who were not predestined to salvation were justified, and therefore had not received from God the gift of perseverance; he also believed that they fell away, as he teaches in many passages that follow.
