Since this is so, his answer would be correct in Pelagius’s mouth, but in his own mouth it is entirely meaningless. For if the subject is a person not predestined, he cannot be corrected, because God has not determined to give him perseverance, without which he cannot remain steadfast to the end.

“But perhaps,” you will say, “the subject here is one of the elect.” Yet even such a person cannot be corrected, according to Augustine’s hypothesis, by which he maintains that grace is absolutely necessary for each individual good act, that it is never present without the effect following, and that it is never absent without the person’s falling.

Whatever good people do in life, they do solely through the force of inspiration. When inspiration ceases, they necessarily sin; and they do not lose the subsequent inspiration except because God had withdrawn the preceding one.

Human beings have no role whatever in this matter. They are like bellows: when expanded, they take in wind; when compressed, they let it out; and they cannot hold or expel more than is supplied by the hand that expands or compresses them.

I will make no further annotations on this little book. The few points I have brought forward sufficiently, indeed abundantly, show into what straits Augustine was driven when he was pressed by the necessary consequences of his doctrine.

I will add only that I have written these and other observations solely under the guidance of love for the truth, so that the holiness of the Gospel and the justice of God might be displayed in a brighter light, and so that those who read these things might be led more effectively to obey the commandments of Jesus Christ.

God is my witness that this is my intention. I pray that He may either calm the most bitter controversies arising from the definitions of the African councils, or at least, by the coming of His Son Jesus Christ, finally bring an end to all our sins.

## CLAUDIUS MENARD’S PREFACE TO THE TWO EARLIER BOOKS OF THE *IMPERFECT WORK*

To the most illustrious and reverend Lord Dionysius de Marquemont, Archbishop and Count of Lyon, etc.

What happens to those, most illustrious Primate, who gather the pearls of foreign shores as the supreme glory of luxury—that they plunge bodies emaciated by hunger into the deep sea and, having long explored the bottom and tracked their quarry amid reefs impoverished by a thousand perils of death, return to land with a tenacious and prolonged breath, to lavish abroad the marvels and delights of nature—I feel happens to us, stirred by a fated but fortunate passion in this constant, shared diving among ancient manuscripts from every quarter.

After strength has been worn away by frantic labour, we immerse ourselves in the deep recesses of libraries, creep here and there, and, through the varying fortunes of research and the deadly disappointments, nevertheless swim forth to display to the public world of letters the hidden treasures of minds and ages.

If I do not admit that I am among these men, I am vain. For several years, driven onward by an inner impulse, I desired nothing more earnestly than that my native land, my rejoicing parent, and my beloved foster-city should rise up in the glory of letters, weave together its vine-leaves, and offer literary laurels.

And, by God’s will, this came to pass. When my cares had been almost wholly consumed by that thought, this pearl of heaven and earth unexpectedly shone forth from the filthy dust of moths and books. Having been deceived for several years by ignorance of its possession, while entirely occupied with other matters, I at last realized that I had become happy through a scarcely attainable treasure.

How much joy grew within us from this happiness, let the work itself declare. And if a comparable light has shone upon anyone who desires such things, it now shines more fully because this eagle, higher and more divine than all the Fathers of the Church Militant, soars among them; and more purely because this book, not swollen with the prerogatives of age and eloquence, but invigorated by the testimony of its final breath, shows its author both dying and fighting.

Fighting rightly: as many moments as his life contained, so many battle-lines; as many words, so many laurels.

I should therefore be impious, and a profane weakling of the blessed name with which Mother Church has marked me, if, as a new diver, I were to hold back the catalogue that has been submerged in the waves of so many years and offered to our desires.

Whom should I more fittingly call the patron of its restoration, now for the first time, to the light? Public interest itself points to you. For through close association with you the African bishop, once the guiding spirit of so many synods, ought to be cherished; you who are acclaimed as legate both of our region and of the Gauls, with the genuine mysteries of the pallium and lawful rites.

The annals of Spanish affairs relate that around the year 685, under the Gothic ruler Chindaswinth, thirty bishops were assembled at Toledo (the Seventh Council of Toledo). Since the book of the *Morals*, which the great and most holy Gregory had once composed at the urging of Leander of Seville, was no longer extant, the bishops chose, with their approval, Tajon of Zaragoza, distinguished in religion and learning, to consult the Roman archives and restore to the Spaniards the books lost through the negligence of their custodians.

While he was undertaking this work, during the pontificate of Martin I, the books were found and copied after an angel indicated their location, since, amid the multitude of manuscripts, they could neither be sought out nor guessed at even in the sacred archives.

The wily teaching of Rufinus and Pelagius had first breathed out its deadly poison among the crags of Sicily. When the presbyter Hilary—later bishop of Arles [Note: This is an error: he was another man than the bishop of Arles.]—pointed it out, the divine spirit of that most holy old man, having undertaken the defence of the faith, destroyed the misshapen monster in a long war lasting ten years.

What was therefore undertaken for the Gauls at the urging of their bishop, and what was brought to completion by great spirits under his defense, under whose auspices and companionship could it have grown after so many years, except under those of the man who, after long displaying the resources of his rich intellect in the very citadel of the City and the world, has been adorned through his perpetual legation to Gaul?

He was not among famous Numidians distinguished by brigandage, nor among uncultivated Moors, disputing in the theater of the most expansive Gaul—that is, of every kind of refinement—but either thundering for the restoration of the Catholic name or anxiously pleading for the cultivation of stricter discipline.

Such was the applause of the vast crowd that hung upon him in wonder that, seated on the loftiest throne of honour, he seems to have been placed there not by piety, but to exercise authority amid the purple robes—or amid something greater still, had Gallic fortune possessed it.

Continue, most illustrious Count, in your virtues. Though they burden you more truly than they honor you with the summit of so great an office, they ought nevertheless, in a sky fertile in vices, to be regarded as a specimen rather than a reward: religion, faith, constancy, and piety. You recall and subdue these virtues, wandering about in rags, so thoroughly that henceforth the admiration of such great virtues may boast that you were not produced by them, but that they were born from you and taught by you.

There is also a private reason that makes me obligated to so great a work. If I could neglect it with closed and consenting eyes, my guilty conscience would accuse me of a great crime.

You bathe your dearest brother—immersed in the private delights of repose and thoughts of a sterner calling, scarcely known and not expecting it—in the solemn radiance of your kindness; and you so overtake him, almost despite his resistance, that in the rays of so great a sun he entrusts both his whole life and whatever remains of his fortune.

Let this sacred and solemn anathema therefore stand at the entrance of this august work, which the whole household, willingly and deservedly devoted to your love and benefactions, hangs here with private feeling and public devotion.

This sacred tablet, which will never die, shall perpetually attest it as yours. At Juliomagus of the Andegavians. On the day before the Nones of August, 1616.

Devoted to Your Most Illustrious Lordship,

**Claudius Menard, Procurator of the City of Angers**

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE *IMPERFECT WORK AGAINST JULIAN*

### Book I, § 3

Julian, concerning Augustine:

> “By this very fact it becomes clear how ignorant and profane an interpreter he is of divine law: anyone who thinks that his sanction defends what justice cannot vindicate.”

Augustine replies:

> “Rather, what you say cannot be defended by any consideration of justice; for, if there is no original sin, the misery of the human race—from which we see no human being exempt from birth to death—does not belong to the judgment of the Almighty.”

Yet he ought to have said this only of infants or young children, since adults commit enough actual sins to be deserving of the miseries of this life.

But let us suppose that he spoke, as he ought to have done, only of infants or young children. Original sin, as Augustine explains it, supplies no satisfactory reason for defending divine justice, since it is wholly incompatible with that justice, as Augustine’s opponents believed; and he nowhere properly refuted them.

“But,” you will say, “although I do not understand how the imputation of Adam’s sin to his descendants and the necessary transmission of vice to them can be reconciled with divine holiness and justice, infants and children must nevertheless be sinners, since they are miserable and God is just.”

It would be far better for you to say that you do not know why the innocent are miserable than to invent, in order to make them guilty, a hypothesis burdened with so many difficulties.

But what are these very brief miseries of infants and children when compared with the eternal blessedness with which God compensates them? They are absolutely nothing—or, if anything could be less than nothing, less than that. Therefore it cannot seem surprising that God does not remove them from these miseries during this life.

### § 8

Julian says that Augustine wrote things which, out of reverence for decency, ought to be driven into oblivion.

See the notes to volume VII, *The City of God*, book XIV, chapters 18 and following.

### § 10

Julian:

> “He also praises the powerful man Valerius—Augustine, book I of *On Marriage*, chapter 2—because, when our petitions demanded nothing else than that judges be appointed for so serious a matter, so that proceedings known to have been conducted through underhanded means might be corrected rather than punished by judicial inquiry, Valerius, by the weight of his dignity, stood in the way and would not allow time or opportunity for a hearing to be obtained.”

Augustine really does praise Valerius, in the passage indicated, because Valerius had effectively resisted by his authority those whom Augustine himself resisted in debate, by pursuing and pressing the matter.

This certainly was not worthy of praise. In a serious and difficult matter, in which Augustine knew perfectly well that there were such great difficulties that he was not equal to resolving them, it would have been better to hear his opponents repeatedly and then judge the case than to condemn people unheard at once, to stigmatize them with one anathema after another from the synods so that no return to milder counsels might remain open, and to persecute them with the emperor’s edict in the harshest manner.

If Augustine had possessed any confidence in the truth, it ought to have led him and the others to postpone the final judgment on the controversy and to hear the Pelagians more often than was necessary, lest they go wrong in condemning them—either because they did not sufficiently understand the matter itself, which was certainly arduous and difficult, or because they failed to grasp the mind of their opponents.

A matter that had confounded so many minds distinguished by learning and acuity, and had provoked so many controversies throughout the ages, ought not immediately to have been entrusted to the judgment of a few Numidians and Africans. Later, unable to yield, they would defend this judgment of theirs by every possible means, as in fact happened.

Even a true doctrine, but one full of difficulties, ought not to have been imposed as though it were a necessary article of faith, without any authority from Christ or the apostles establishing its necessity.

Finally, the Pelagians ought not to have been given the most just cause for complaint: that they had been condemned unheard.

But let us hear Augustine’s reply:

> “Far be it from the Christian authorities of the earthly commonwealth to doubt the ancient Catholic faith and, on that account, grant its attackers a time and place for examination; rather, being certain and firmly grounded in it, let them impose the discipline of coercion upon enemies such as you are.”

These are the words of a victor, but of one who relied more upon earthly authority than upon arguments.

Are Christian magistrates, then, without any examination, to harass those whom a few bishops have condemned unheard, because the ancient faith is to be accepted ἀβασανίστως—that is, without examination—when it has been approved in provincial synods by a numerical majority of votes?

Are magistrates therefore the lictors of ecclesiastical assemblies, whom people must obey rather than answer? If the Arians had said such things when they were in power, they would surely have been accused, with good reason, of intolerable tyranny.

But I have long since had enough of such matters. So—enough.

## JOHN ULIMMER’S PREFACE TO JACOB PAMELIUS, LICENTIATE IN SACRED LETTERS AND CANON OF BRUGES, ON POSSIDIUS’S CATALOGUE

How great, most gracious sir, has been the rashness of certain men in judging—men who loudly proclaim that anything whatever is Augustine’s and protest according to the dictates of their own minds—no one would easily believe unless he examined more closely the truth of the matter as transmitted by earlier generations and, as they say, cut it back to the living tissue.

In this kind of controversy, no one ought to be regarded as a better disputant for us than Saint Possidius, since he was Augustine’s disciple. For blessed Augustine published, dictated, and vigorously debated so many things in the Church; he received and corrected so many writings composed either against heretics or as expositions of the canonical books, that scarcely any student could be equal to knowing and reading them all.

No one should therefore find it surprising that some things have been mixed into his writings that are barely worthy of some learned and pious man, much less of Saint Augustine, a man of supreme learning and piety. Conversely, certain conjectures—if I may not call them precipitate judgments and reckless daring—have removed some passages which, even if everyone else were silent, the very phrasing and the astonishing piety of Augustine proclaimed to be his.

Therefore, lest Possidius seem to defraud in any way those most eager for truth and for the word of God—Possidius, who by God’s kindness and gift lived familiarly and sweetly with this our bishop for nearly forty years, without any bitter disagreement, as I gladly express it in his own words—he composed and presented the catalogue of the books, treatises, and letters of that same man which had been promised to all students.

Until this day, however, all who cannot help favoring Augustine have desired it with ardent wishes and the greatest expectation, so that henceforth, as you most rightly write, they might not waver uncertainly amid the rash judgments of certain critics.

I found it while I was extremely occupied in examining the venerable and extraordinarily well-equipped library of the abbey of Villers, in its manuscripts of great antiquity, although I had thought I had found it nowhere and that it existed nowhere else. Like you, I was eager for it.

You encouraged me more than once, in letters sent to me, in which you most generously offered both your labor and a large part of the expenses, to publish it at last in the light of day, to which it had never before been accustomed, lest learned men—whom I believe to have desired nothing more eagerly—should be frustrated any longer in their expectation.

Thus far, however, I thought it best to delay its publication, although it had been so greatly requested, so that, illuminated by our marginal notes—which demonstrate, through Augustine himself and through the ancient Fathers who do not hesitate to cite his writings everywhere, that these works belong to Augustine—and rearranged into a more convenient and somewhat more orderly form, it might appear under the auspices of your name. I was certain that nothing else could be more agreeable to you.

For although I had previously learned how much you delight in these same studies from your kinsman Ludovicus Carrio, a young man of no small learning, in whose mouth you seemed to me plainly to dwell—so frequently and with such great delight he praises your devotion, generosity, and favor toward him—your venerable Bede, recently reborn in the Hervagian press and enlarged by the addition of many books at immense expense and effort, testified to it even more strongly.

I am therefore led to the greatest hope that you will eventually bring into the open those works which, through the injury of time, still lie in darkness and somewhere wage war with cockroaches and moths. Such is your indefatigable diligence in seeking out ancient materials; and I am confident that you will add whatever is lacking from our own imperfect labors.

For I too have discovered, after completing this edition of ours, that a careful reader might wish for some things to be transmitted more exactly and more fully in their proper order.

In the margins of our books, however, so that you may also understand the reason for this policy of mine, we were content to note the volumes and books, omitting the page numbers, since these differ greatly in different copies and cannot correspond equally to all of them.

When I recalled that this little work and whatever industry we had undertaken under your patronage, I could not refrain from humbly dedicating it to your distinguished Lordship. Accept it, therefore, in the spirit in which we offer it, and, in accordance with your customary kindness, defend our efforts against the attacks of slanderers.

Farewell, most esteemed lord, and continue to love us, who are devoted to you, with equal affection.

From our Martinian monastery at Leuven, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, 1564.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

### Preface, concerning those who had written the lives of ecclesiastical men

> “Inspired by the divine Spirit, in their own speech and style, they brought before the notice of students, by speaking and writing similar things for the benefit of those who wished to know through their ears and eyes, what kind and how great men, by the common grace of the Lord, deserved both to live in human affairs and to persevere until the end of death.”

He calls those who wrote the lives of earlier men “inspired by the divine Spirit,” because they acted with good counsel and intention, since he thought that all good things proceeded from divine inspiration.

Yet no one should deny that certain human actions are rightly performed and are owed to God as the author of human nature, if we ascend to the supreme cause; but it is inappropriate to say that they are performed only through His inspiration, because they contain too many imperfections of human intelligence.

He and others therefore wrote, as they thought, with good intentions, the lives of earlier bishops. Their intention, I believe, arose from their knowledge of their office and, consequently, is also attributable to God, who exacts the duties of that office, at least in this sense.

But they were certainly not inspired by God to conceal almost all the faults and offenses of those whose lives they were writing, to exaggerate their modest virtues and gifts beyond all measure, and to describe things deserving pardon as though they were objects of wonder.

Such encomiums, apart from other objections, have the effect not so much of encouraging careless readers to imitate their virtues and follow true principles as of presenting concealed vices as though they were lawful and honorable, and errors as though they were truths to be defended.

For readers think that, if these things had been to be avoided, the writers of these lives would have concealed them; nor do they believe that they themselves can sin while imitating men praised to such an extent.

We wished to prevent this harm in our observations. Just as we have candidly and willingly praised what deserved praise, so we have not concealed what deserved blame—although we are far from having touched upon everything, since that would have been an immense task and could not have been accomplished in a single volume.

But whatever I have attempted, He knows from whom the secrets of hearts are open, that it flowed from love of God and neighbor. I pray Him again and again to dispel, by the light of the coming of His Son, the darkness of our opinions and the frustrations of our affections.

Amen.

# AUGUSTINIAN VINDICATIONS, BY WHICH THE WRITINGS OF THE HOLY DOCTOR AGAINST THE PELAGIANS AND SEMI-PELAGIANS ARE DEFENDED AGAINST THE CENSURES OF RECENT CRITICS

By Father Henry de Noris, Veronese Augustinian

> … His companions follow with a great shout,  
> while the father, protected by the shield of his son, departs.  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* X, 799–800

## Epigram

A certain learned speaker, they say,  
has attacked the books of the aged Augustine  
and composed a work against him.

Could his excellent intellect and rich eloquence  
display their art in no other way?

Unless he stirred up wars  
in new battle-lines already overthrown,  
and gave impious weapons to enemies already destroyed?

This battle, instigator, is your death;  
that style destroys you,  
and you perish by your own words.

While you teach how powerful the free mind is,  
you show that your own will is sufficient  
to bring about your ruin.

Turn back; flee destruction;  
see everywhere the rebels laid low  
by the thunderbolt of the Apostolic mouth.

Nor think that you can defend yourself  
by changing the name,  
if you wish to wound the shepherd of the sheep:  
you are a wolf.

—Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, *Against a Slanderer*

## Another Epigram

A certain writer, they say, has begun to creep against Augustine,  
one whom consuming envy burned long ago.

He has compelled the wretched serpent,  
whose head was somehow woven into dark caverns,  
to lift itself from the ground.

Perhaps the Britons of the sea fed this creature  
with its native grain;  
perhaps its heart swells  
with Campanian grass.

Let it bring forth what it has conceived,  
let it produce what it has labored to bear,  
whether it is armed with an old doctrine or a new one.

However it twists the coils of its spirals  
through whatever recesses,  
and however it tortures its deceitful head  
with much skill,

the viper will not be able to make the old man  
swerve from his course over worn-out asps and basilisks.

—Saint Prosper, same work

## Preface
I consider that no one can fail to wonder at the animosity of certain recent writers—if I may put it as mildly as possible—who have dared, in published books, to attack Augustine, that great teacher of the Catholic world, so that the necessity of defending him has been imposed upon those who hold him in especially high regard.

Indeed, from the very beginnings of the evil, our predecessors, who by the institution of their life most reverently honored Augustine as a father, attempted to restrain the erupting audacity of the new censors. Ludovicus ab Angelis, an eminent interpreter of the sacred mysteries among the people of Lisbon, vindicated the authority of the holy Doctor from the calumnies of many (*The Life of Augustine*, book V, chapters 14–15), and with singular diligence collected the praises bestowed upon him by the holy Fathers for his overthrow of the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians; later, the others borrowed the same material from him.

But as the evil grew daily, and in the scholastic disputations of certain recent writers Augustine’s doctrine was everywhere misrepresented, especially in those questions that he had taken up against the enemies of divine grace, matters reached the point where the supreme Doctor of the Church seemed soon destined to be reduced to the ranks. Basil Pontius of León, a great theologian among the scholars of Salamanca, drew not only his own Augustinians, but also the most learned Fathers of the Dominican Order and the University of Salamanca itself into Augustine’s cause (*Defense of the Salamanca Oath*), so that the authority of the holy Doctor might be fortified by this reserve support against the assaults of recent writers.

Accordingly, through Pontius’s initiative, that famous compact was concluded at Salamanca in 1627, chiefly on the condition that those who were to be awarded the theological degree should first bind themselves by an oath to defend Augustinian doctrine. By this action of the most illustrious University, Augustine’s authority seemed sufficiently safeguarded, especially [Col. 0573] since the sacred faculty of theology at Louvain had long before sworn allegiance to Augustine’s teaching.

Nevertheless, when the Jansenist disputes arose, most men did not hesitate to speak and write far more harshly against Augustine. Yet there were not lacking men from our own family who defended the cause of our great father with the utmost vigor. Among them Father Charles Moreau, a Frenchman, stood out; in the first volume of his *Annotations on Tertullian* he inserted a sufficiently extensive defense of Augustine, just as the distinguished Belgian Johannes Rivius had earlier done in the fourth book of his *Life of Augustine*.

But we have learned by experience that these writers of ours washed bricks and sang to deaf ears. For from abandoning their undertaking they were so far removed that they advanced against Augustine with much greater preparation and more hostile weapons, writing the following against the Doctor of Hippo:

“Augustine’s doctrine is obscure, difficult, extremely intricate, self-contradictory, and exposed to numerous errors. He was placed beneath a cloud of darkness. In attacking the Pelagians, he was carried beyond the limits of truth by the heat of disputation. It is not permissible to admit him—not merely as a judge, but not even as an honorary arbitrator—in controversies concerning divine grace. His weapons are neither impregnable nor sufficiently suitable for overcoming the Calvinists. He by no means satisfied the arguments of the heretics, nor did he establish the theses he had proposed with convincing arguments. Scholastic theology must not be buried so that Augustine alone may reign; Augustine himself must instead be tested by the scholastic standard. The ridiculous worshipers of Augustine heap nauseatingly hyperbolic praises upon him. Anyone wishing to attack Augustine’s opinions will have God as his helper.”

They added these and almost countless other statements, which we shall report at the end of this *Apology*.

It is related that the son of King Croesus, mute from childhood (Herodotus, book I), when he saw an enemy attacking his father’s throat with a drawn sword, suddenly burst the bonds of perpetual silence through an impulse of compassionate nature and cried out: “Man, do not kill Croesus!” But shall we, who possess the full use of speech, permit Augustine—our excellent and most learned father—to be torn apart with impunity by the writings of the new censors? Shall we allow them to heap a thousand wagonloads of insults upon the holy Doctor while we receive the same insults with ears fully open, preserving a contrived peace as though none of this concerned us?

We should rightly be judged degenerate and illegitimate—or rather utterly insane or made of stone—if, in such grave danger to our father, we spared our pen, since we wish both to be and to be regarded as Augustinians. The father’s honor is attacked; piety requires us to vindicate him from the words of his adversaries. The doctrine of the teacher of the Church is assailed; faith requires us to defend it against every attack. The reputation of a saint is diminished; religion requires us to preserve it intact.

How many crimes, then, would we incur if, restrained perhaps by the common estimation of our adversaries, or by the authority of those who have sold their allegiance to them, we were to let such unjust censures against Augustine pass by with deaf ears? For a long time we remained silent, and tried to give vent to our immense inward grief through private complaints, praying that these men might adopt a better attitude toward Augustine. But our patience achieved nothing except that graver insults were inflicted upon us, as though we were easily able to endure them. Thus, hearing worse things day after day, we have at last been compelled to lend Augustine whatever small assistance our advocacy can provide.

I do not think that anyone will be so devoid of piety and religion as to regard this *Apology* with a hostile eye and mark it with a black theta. For, as Lactantius once wrote to the Emperor Constantine (Institutes, book V, chapter 1):

“If power of defending themselves is granted to sacrilegious men, traitors, and poisoners, and no one may be condemned beforehand without his case being known, we seem not to be asking unjustly…”

—to Augustine, who, according to Pope Saint Celestine, “was everywhere both loved and honored by all,” some opportunity for defense should be granted.

For the condition of our times would be most deplorable if both ears were given to Augustine’s censors, and their excessively insulting books against Augustine were circulated through the mouths and hands of men, while the defenders of the holy Doctor were not only excluded from judgment without being heard, but were also subjected to a general decree of silence.

It would be an example of monstrous and utterly barbarous savagery if our age were to imitate Rhadamistus, the most savage of tyrants, who slaughtered the sons of Mithridates, king of Armenia, because they “had wept over the slaughter of their parents” (Tacitus, *Annals*, book XII). You would certainly be an unjust judge if, while our Father was assailed with a thousand insults, you did not permit even “a groan and tears to be freely given to grief,” to use Jerome’s words (*Apology II against Rufinus*).

We read that, under Nero, when every virtue was regarded as a crime, it was “a capital offense” for Arulenus Rusticus and Herennius Senecio to have praised the most innocent and wisest citizens; and that violence was directed not only against the authors themselves but also against their children (Tacitus, preface to the *Life of Agricola*). But far be it from us that such a crime should be characteristic or an example of our age. We must not suppose that men have so far withdrawn from their ancestral reverence toward the saints that they would listen with indignation to Augustine’s praises and, with angry hand, tear apart this book of ours published on his behalf.

Seneca, the great teacher of the Stoic sect, rightly curses the impious words of Praexaspes, the Persian satrap (On Anger, book III, chapter 14). When Praexaspes had seen his son pierced through before his eyes by King Cambyses without uttering a groan, and when the tyrant asked him whether he had aimed accurately at the target after dining [reading uncertain], he praised the tyrant’s right hand, stained and still smoking with his son’s blood through detestable flattery, and said that in shooting it was equal to Apollo’s.

Are we therefore to fill with praises—or even kisses—the hands of the new censors who, following the example of slaves in body and, still more, in soul, have raised against Augustine pens armed for attack? Are we to accept this most unjust law imposed upon us by men who love men more than saints? We know ourselves to be free from it, since the decrees of the Apostolic See impel us to undertake Augustine’s defense, and to resist them would be impious.

When those ancient Pelagians, the “Augustine-whippers,” had published certain letters in which the holy Doctor was most viciously misrepresented, Pope Boniface, indignant that the name of so learned a man should be assailed by any insult, arranged for those heretical letters to be carried to Augustine through Alypius, so that he might defend himself from the calumnies of impostors [Col. 0575].

Writing from there to his most loving father Boniface, Augustine says (Book I to Boniface, chapter 1):

“I give thanks for your most sincere goodwill toward us, because you did not wish to conceal from me the letters of the enemies of God’s grace, in which you found my name maliciously and plainly displayed. But I hope in the Lord our God that they do not tear me with a slanderous tooth without receiving a reward in heaven.”

Boniface’s successor, Celestine, likewise wished to provide most carefully for the honor of the same most holy Doctor. For scarcely had Augustine been numbered among the blessed when certain men who, according to Saint Prosper (*Preface against the Collator*), “seemed neither contemptible in their standing in the Church nor in their abilities,” dared impudently to speak against him in Gaul and to examine his books with censorial authority. Although, according to the same Prosper, they were “men of good reputation, displaying in their zeal the appearance of piety,” they would have brought the reputation and doctrine of the Doctor of Hippo into serious danger had Celestine not confronted the growing evil with an immediate remedy.

When he learned of the adversaries’ machinations from Prosper and Hilary, he sent a letter to the bishops of Gaul. Indignant that they were permitting Augustine to be attacked with impunity, he wrote:

“I fear that to connive is to remain silent; I fear that those who permit such speech are themselves speaking more loudly. In such cases silence does not escape suspicion, because truth would intervene if falsehood were displeasing. The matter rightly concerns us if, through silence, we favor error. Therefore let such men be corrected; let them not be free to speak as they please.”

Then, overflowing with praise for Saint Augustine, who had long been his friend while still alive, he continued:

“We have always held Augustine, a man of holy memory, in our communion, on account of his life and merits; never did even a rumor of sinister suspicion touch him. We remember that he was once a man of such great learning that he was always counted by my predecessors among the best teachers. All therefore judged rightly of him in common, since he was everywhere both loved and honored by all. Therefore we must resist such men, whom we see growing in evil.”

The Apostolic See therefore commands that Augustine’s censors be “corrected” and that “they not be free to speak as they please”; by a formal decree it also establishes that “such men must be resisted.”

The leading figures of the ancient Augustinian school—Prosper, Fulgentius, Caesarius, Prudentius, and Remigius—famous alike for learning and holiness, carried this out with great courage, defending Augustine’s writings against the attacks of the Semi-Pelagians and others. Many more recent writers performed the same service with the highest praise. All of them, however, were surpassed by the outstanding Father Macedo, who published so many books in defense of the doctrine of the same Father.

Accordingly, obeying the pontifical commands, and following—though at a great distance—the examples of so many Fathers, I have resolved to summon certain recent censors of Augustinian doctrine before the bar of judgment. I shall pursue this judgment with as much modesty as I can. Petulance has never improved a good cause, but it has often made a bad one worse.

They are my friends—but only up to the altar, and only up to my Augustine. I shall pass over everything that seems harsher to say, considering not only what they deserve to hear but also what it is fitting for me to say. If something bitter should happen to escape me, let them attribute it to their own excessive provocations, by which they have forced us into such a necessity that at times we can scarcely defend Augustine according to his dignity without more serious criticism of their censures.

This book, meanwhile, to use Tacitus’s words about Agricola, is dedicated to the honor of Augustine, Our Father; through its profession of piety, it will either be praised or excused.

# AUGUSTINIAN VINDICATIONS

[Col. 0575]

## CHAPTER ONE

Arguments are refuted by which certain men contend that the doctrine of Saint Augustine concerning predestination and grace is difficult and obscure. The most holy judgment of Clement X, supreme pontiff, in favor of the holy Doctor.

[Col. 0575A]

Before I report and refute individually the many insults that certain recent writers have heaped upon the holy Doctor, I thought it worthwhile first to review what they universally set against Augustine concerning the doctrine that he handed down against the Pelagians on divine grace and predestination. For they say that this doctrine is extremely difficult, obscure, intricate, inconsistent, changeable, and that it runs beyond the boundaries of truth.

Since they attempt to persuade us of this accusation by numerous arguments [Col. 0575B], those arguments must be answered by us, lest Augustinian doctrine suffer any harm among the uninstructed and excessively credulous.

Joannes Adamus constructed these objections against Augustine [Col. 0576A]. I judge the deed of this author worthy of a double hatred: first, because he attempted to suppress a doctrine that the wisest men have exalted to the stars; and especially because, while professing to fight against Calvin with Augustinian weapons, he disgraces those very weapons with a thousand insults, leaving it uncertain whether Augustine or Calvin is to be regarded as his more hostile enemy.

Adamus gave the following title to a book written in the vernacular:

*Calvin Defeated by Himself and by the Weapons of Saint Augustine, Which He Had Unjustly Usurped in Matters of Grace, Freedom, and Predestination.*

That is, “Calvin destroyed by his own weapons and by the weapons of Saint Augustine, which he unjustly usurped in matters concerning grace, freedom, and predestination.” The name “Augustine” was printed in larger characters [Col. 0576B], extending across the page from side to side.

The volume is divided into three parts. In the first and second, nothing is discussed concerning grace and predestination, and Augustine’s name is heard only rarely in them. He reserved discussion of those mysteries for the final part. No one is unaware of his purpose in doing this: he wrote at the very time when the Jansenist disturbances were boiling over in France.

In the final part of the volume, however, he devotes more effort to attacking Augustine than to attacking Calvin. In the first ten chapters he launches a broad assault against Augustine and fights him with all his strength. In the five chapters that follow, as though exhausted by persecuting Augustine, he turns his pen against Calvin. But in the sixteenth chapter, with which he places a noble conclusion upon the whole volume, he gathers his strength and once again rushes upon Augustine, so that anyone who could read such insulting words against so holy a Doctor without—not merely indignation, but even abhorrence—would surely have to be judged hard-hearted [Col. 0577B].

Is this, Adamus, to destroy Calvin—or Augustine? You promised that you would enter combat with Calvin using the weapons of Saint Augustine. But how highly, on your own testimony, do you value those victorious weapons? You cry out: “Augustine’s weapons are not impregnable” (chapter 4, p. 581). Do you therefore brandish leaden daggers with which to attack your adversary’s throat, as Augustine wittily says in *The Unfinished Work against Julian*, book III, chapter 7?

Under Augustine’s auspices you advance against the enemy, and you load this commander of yours with a thousand insults? You promise that Augustine will be rescued by you from the Calvinists, and yet you betray him to his enemies?

You say this on page 640, chapter 8: “If I confined myself within the limits of Saint Augustine’s words, I would be a Calvinist.” You add in chapter 16, page 760: “It is known throughout the world that, among all the Fathers, Augustine confused the mystery of the Eucharist more than anyone else” [Col. 0577C].

What of your statement on page 596, chapter 4, that Augustine’s words are not suitable for disarming the Calvinists? Furthermore, you say that Augustine held the rejection of impious men to derive from original sin, and that this is its sole cause (page 584); yet in chapter 10, page 667, you write that you are permitted to shudder at this opinion, because it is the mother of the opinion that Calvin, with such impiety and fury against the Church, inculcates.

And on page 624, chapter 7, you testify that Augustine said that manna and the Eucharist are “equally a figure of Jesus Christ.” This is the first heresy of the Calvinists.

Do you suppose that Calvin’s followers and the school of Geneva did not receive these statements of yours with full ears and enormous applause, when, in your judgment, they see Augustine almost belonging to them—although you had promised to demonstrate that he stood against them?

But let us pass over these matters, for which the Calvinists owe you thanks. Let us at least hear what accusation you bring against the holy Doctor.

Accordingly, Adamus, whom I understand to be counted by his associates among the celebrated authors, gave chapter 4 the following title (Dialogue VI on Probable Opinion):

“The doctrine of Saint Augustine concerning the mysteries of grace, freedom, predestination, and the Eucharist is extremely difficult to understand, and this obscurity produced great divisions both during Augustine’s life and after his death.”

He gives chapter 6 the following title:

“New arguments for proving that Saint Augustine’s doctrine concerning the mysteries of grace and predestination is obscure and difficult to understand.”

On page 610, after pronouncing many things in that chapter that are both false and calumnious [Col. 0578A], he concludes with this most remarkable censure:

“But what covered the books of this holy and wise Doctor with darkness and clouds, and what was noted by the most celebrated theologians, is that he does not always, except after profound meditation, distinguish between what he teaches as doubtful and what he hands down as certain; nor does he distinguish between what he says while attacking his adversaries and what he teaches while defending his own position. He often turns against his adversaries the objections they have brought against him, driving them into remarkable absurdities. He answers an objection with another objection. He refutes an incongruity by means of a difficulty far greater. Furthermore, he does not clearly explain whether he proposes objections in order to attack his enemies or whether he agrees with them in those matters, and so forth.

“These things, added to the perplexity of his expression in this subject, together with the distinction between the books written before his episcopate and those written during his episcopate, and also the disagreements among scholars concerning the true understanding of his doctrine, permit me to conclude that he either did not wish to explain his opinions clearly or was not sufficiently successful in explaining them, so that no room for doubt concerning his mind would remain. Therefore they are wrong to wish to make him the oracle of grace and the interpreter of the Council of Trent.”

I do not see what could be said more arrogantly, more absurdly, or more indecently against Augustine. But the purpose with which he spewed forth these statements is sufficiently clear: he wished to display the alleged necessity imposed upon him of abandoning Augustine. For who would prefer to follow Augustine above others if what Adamus brings against him were true?

Hence, in chapter 16, page 760 [Col. 0578C], he cries out:

“These shadows of Augustine compel me to seek light elsewhere; and I find it in the councils and the books of other Doctors.”

We have the man’s confession.

Victorinus, once the most celebrated rhetorician at Rome and known throughout the world through the praise of Jerome and Augustine, used to say that the obscurity of books arises from three causes, as Saint Jerome testifies in the preface to book XIII of his commentary on Ezekiel:

“Either from the greatness of the subject, or from the incompetence of the teacher, or from the dullness of the listener.”

He could have added a fourth: the malice of the teacher, which is charged against Aristotle, who concealed his meaning beneath obscure verbal coverings.

We willingly grant that Saint Augustine’s doctrine concerning grace, free choice, and predestination is obscure and difficult because of the greatness of the subject, the depth of the divine counsels, and the profundity of this most secret mystery [Col. 0578D]. For who does not know how much difficulty the harmony of the freedom of the human will with divine foreknowledge and predestination has caused the wise of every age?

The errors of the ancient philosophers bear witness to this. The Stoics, introducing fate, suffocated free choice. Others, with Cicero, removed from God knowledge of contingent events. From the same source arose the long-standing and perpetual disagreements among scholastic theologians.

Even the recent writers who boast that they proceed along a clearer path acknowledge the difficulty of the matter in the many disputes they wage among themselves concerning divine predeterminations—namely, concerning the object of middle knowledge, congruous grace, and other matters [Col. 0579A]. Their civil war confesses the difficulty of the subject.

Molina, in the *Concordia*, question 14, article 13, disputation 53, member 2, section “They Make Light of It,” admits that he labored stubbornly for twenty years to reconcile human freedom with the mysteries of grace and predestination. Yet, in the judgment of the Thomists, he expended his labor in vain. But leaving that dispute aside, his attempt certainly shows that he undertook an exceedingly difficult task.

Suárez, the most weighty of all the recent writers, makes the same candid admission in volume II of *On Grace*, book V, in the preliminary discussion of efficacious grace.

Hence Augustine, in letter 47 to Valentinus, calls this question “extremely difficult and intelligible to few,” and in chapter 47 of *On the Grace of Christ* calls it difficult to discern.

In sermon 5 *On the Words of the Apostle*, when he was about to speak to the people about divine grace, he said that, because of the obscurity of the matters, he had a difficult discourse to deliver.

Nevertheless, that most wise man brought as much light to obscure matters and as much ease to difficult ones as he could. He spared no labor so that he might speak with the greatest possible clarity and simplicity. He also repeatedly begged God in prayer to grant him the ability to discuss grace according to the understanding of the people.

Let us hear him in the preface to sermon 13 *On the Words of the Apostle*, after he had discoursed at length in earlier sermons on law and grace:

“The height of the word of God exercises the intellect; it does not deny understanding. If everything were closed, there would be nothing from which obscure things could be revealed. Again, if everything were covered, there would be nothing from which the soul could receive nourishment and gain strength with which to knock at what is closed.

“In the preceding apostolic readings, which, insofar as the Lord has deigned to help, we have expounded for your Charity, we have suffered much labor and anxiety. We sympathized with you and were concerned both for ourselves and for you. But, as I think, the Lord helped both us and you, and he deigned through us to unravel those matters that seemed altogether difficult, so that no question remained to disturb the pious mind. For an impious mind hates understanding itself,” and so forth [Col. 0579C].

Likewise, in book III of *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, chapter 2, he stopped the mouths of future adversaries who would object to him that he spoke obscurely:

“Since they still do not understand what I consider to have been stated clearly in accordance with the nature of the questions, let them not accuse me of negligence or of lack of ability; rather, let them pray to God to receive understanding.”

These books were among the first of the more than thirty works that he composed in defense of divine grace against its enemies.

Therefore, if Augustine said that he had spoken clearly at the very beginning of a controversy that had only recently arisen and was sufficiently obscure and difficult, how much more must he be judged to have scattered the rays of a most lucid doctrine over a matter examined and explained for so many years, in so many public and private encounters, and finally in so many volumes and letters?

When Julian had charged the holy Doctor with obscurity, Augustine gave him this answer:

“Because they expose your darkness, clear things do not seem clear to you; and whatever troubles you through its own radiant light, against those things you close your heart, lest the night of error be driven away.”

*The Unfinished Work*, book III, chapter 61.

And when the same heretic objected that the holy Doctor’s opinion was difficult to understand, Augustine replied:

“I am understood perfectly, whether you wish it or not. But since you intend to say nothing against these things, you wish what I have said most truly and firmly not to be understood.”

*The Unfinished Work*, book IV, chapter 140. Read more on these matters in the *Antitheses*.

Adamus, however, reheating the stale cabbage once cooked by the Pelagians, brands Augustinian doctrine with the fault of obscurity. He attributes this obscurity not to the greatness of the mysteries or to the weakness of the readers’ understanding, but to Augustine’s malice, since Augustine either did not wish or at least was unable to express his opinions clearly, as Adamus writes on page 615.

Do you judge that great African genius—by which name Augustine was praised by Prosper in chapter 2 *Against the Ungrateful*—to have been so dull or envious that, after almost twenty years of effort, he still could not explain his own opinion? Or that he refused to do so, merely to appear wise alone, at such great cost to the whole Church?

But let us see by what arguments this recent writer attempts, in chapters 4, 5, and 6, to prove that Saint Augustine’s doctrine concerning grace and free choice, as well as predestination, is obscure and difficult.

At the very beginning of chapter 4, on page 590, he argues that the monk Florus of Hadrumetum was the first person to dogmatize against free choice after being misled by the obscurity of Augustinian doctrine. Since he did not understand Augustine’s letter to Sixtus, he thought that it spoke against human freedom. But when the other monks defended the opposite position, the matter was brought by Florus and others before Augustine [Col. 0580C]. To instruct them, the holy Doctor sent two letters to Abbot Valentinus, adding one book *On Grace and Free Choice* and another *On Rebuke and Grace*, in which he explained more clearly what he had said more obscurely in the letter to Sixtus.

Before I show, however, that Florus’s mistaken understanding of that letter arose not from Augustine’s obscurity but from the dullness of the readers, to use Victorinus’s expression, Adamus’s careless reading of Augustine must be corrected. He falsely accuses the monk Florus of having failed to grasp the correct meaning of that letter, although Augustine plainly testifies that Florus had understood it correctly and that the others had not understood Florus.

Thus Augustine writes to those monks in chapter 1 of *On Rebuke and Grace*:

“I rejoice that I have found in our brother Florus this faith, which is undoubtedly the true prophetic and apostolic faith. Therefore it is rather those who did not understand him who must be corrected; by God’s favor, I now believe that they have been corrected.”

Certain monks, then, did not understand the holy Doctor’s letter, although Florus had grasped its meaning perfectly and suffered no obscurity at all from Augustine’s words. Their mistaken understanding must therefore be attributed not to any defect in Augustine—who either did not wish or was unable to speak clearly—but to the weak capacity of the monks, who not only failed at first to understand the Augustinian letter but also failed to understand Florus when he explained it at greater length.

We have discussed these matters more fully in book I of the *Pelagian History*, chapter 23, and book II, chapter 15.

[Col. 0581A] Adamus adds on page 591:

“These first disturbances in Africa, which arose from the obscurity of Augustinian doctrine, were followed by the Gallic disturbances. Men distinguished both for piety and learning at Massilia and in the neighboring islands were distressed that Augustine, whose standing in the Church was great, had taught certain things which, because of their obscurity, seemed at that time to lend support to the Predestinarian heresy spreading through Gaul. When these matters were more widely circulated, Prosper and Hilary informed Augustine of them by letter, so that he might disclose his mind more clearly.”

This writer weaves together attractive fictions. Those about whom Prosper and Hilary wrote to Augustine were by no means Predestinarians who had fallen into error because of the obscurity of Augustine’s doctrine. They were Semi-Pelagians: Cassian, Hilary, Vincentius, Faustus, and others, as has been demonstrated at greater length in book II of the *Pelagian History* [Col. 0581B]. They denied that faith and perseverance were gifts of God, repeatedly asserting that these proceeded from ourselves.

That there were no Predestinarians at that time is perfectly clear from the letters of Prosper and Hilary. They do not say that Predestinarians took Augustine’s own doctrine as the foundation of their erroneous dogmas; rather, they say that many attacked that doctrine as novel and absurd.

I shall give the beginning of Saint Prosper’s letter. From it the obscurity attributed to Augustine, from which the adversary pretends that disturbances arose in Gaul, will disappear:

“Many, then, of the servants of Christ who reside in the city of Massilia think that whatever you discussed in your writings against the heretical Pelagians concerning the calling of the elect according to God’s purpose is contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and to ecclesiastical understanding.

“For some time they preferred to blame their own slowness rather than criticize what they did not understand, and some of them wished to request from Your Beatitude a clearer and more explicit explanation on this subject. It happened, through the arrangement of God’s mercy, that when similar concerns had stirred certain people in Africa, you published the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, full of divine authority.

“When it reached our knowledge at an unexpected and most opportune moment, we all thought that the complaints of those who resisted would be silenced, because all the questions on which Your Holiness was to be consulted had there been answered so fully and completely, as though you had made it your special purpose to settle the matters that were disturbed among us.

“After this book of Your Beatitude had been read, those who had previously followed the holy and apostolic authority of your teaching became much more intelligent and better instructed. But those who were obstructed by the obscurity of their own conviction withdrew even more opposed than before.”

This is what he says.

Do you hear that the men of Massilia did not charge Augustine with obscurity, but preferred to blame their own slowness rather than criticize what they had not understood? He says that some requested a clearer explanation, not because the things Augustine had established were obscure, but because they greatly desired those same things to be explained more clearly according to their own capacity; nevertheless, they were sufficiently evident to men of sharper intellect.

Again, he says that afterward those same men, obstructed by the obscurity of their own opinion [Col. 0582A], openly and properly understood Augustine’s doctrine and attacked it, while Augustine’s followers became much more intelligent and better instructed from those same books of the holy Doctor.

This does not concern rumors arising in Gaul because Augustine’s meaning was misunderstood through obscurity, as Adamus invents. Rather, disputes arose concerning the universally known truth of the doctrine itself, with Prosper, Hilary, and others defending Augustine, while Cassian and his associates attacked him.

Adamus writes on page 594 that Prosper and Hilary, seeing that certain Predestinarian priests were bolstering their own errors with Augustine’s name, were moved by the disgrace of the matter and went to Pope Celestine. The Pope immediately sent a letter to the bishops of Gaul, by which, in Adamus’s words on page 595, he “stopped the mouths of all those priests who concealed their errors beneath the obscurity of Saint Augustine’s words.”

If the statements of Prosper, the accuser, and the formal judgment of Celestine, the judge, issued in defense of Augustine, had perished, Adamus might perhaps have invented something of this sort in order to persuade us that Augustinian obscurity was the source of those disturbances.

But he is convicted of manifest falsehood by the writings of Prosper and Celestine. Those against whom Prosper and his colleague Hilary went to Rome were not some unknown Predestinarian priests selling their errors under Augustine’s name. They were plainly the Semi-Pelagians of Massilia, who were tearing apart the books and doctrine of Saint Augustine.

We have proved this at greater length in book II of the *Pelagian History*, chapter 15, and there is no opportunity to repeat it here.

[Col. 0582C] Adamus continues his undertaking, striving by new arguments to prove the obscurity of Augustine’s doctrine. He objects that there is enormous controversy among theologians concerning Augustine’s position on predestination; on page 596 he adds that it is so difficult that it has stirred up serious disturbances in the Church. He also reports that some of Augustine’s followers abandoned him in the matter of grace, or did not dare publicly to defend Augustine’s teachings (p. 610, at the beginning of chapter 10). He says, too, that Augustine changed his position on this question three times (p. 597), and on page 611 adds that Augustine often confessed that the difficulties proposed either by himself or by his opponents against the mysteries of grace and predestination were not removed by the solutions he supplied, and that his mind was more agitated by the objections than calmed by the answers. He further states that Augustine, when weighed down by some supposedly insuperable difficulty, took refuge in those words of Scripture: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” etc. (Rom. 11). Moreover, he reports in the same place that Augustine began a Commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, where the Apostle treats the mystery of predestination, but, deterred by the profundity of the subject, left the work unfinished. Finally, on page 614 he proves the difficulty of attaining Augustine’s true and genuine position from the fact that Augustine’s opinion was not one and consistently uniform, but diverse and conflicting.

I shall touch upon the reply briefly; for the adversary’s objections cause us no difficulty. Those Gallican disturbances did not arise because Augustine’s doctrine was considered obscure or difficult to understand, but because most people, although they properly understood that doctrine, thought it contrary to the definitions of the ancient Fathers, as Prosper testifies in his letter to Augustine. Two things must here be distinguished: either Augustine’s doctrine is called difficult because it can be understood only with difficulty, or because, although correctly perceived, it appears harsh to the human intellect and does not readily obtain its assent.

The first assertion is certainly false. For the Massilians understood Augustine’s doctrine perfectly well concerning the grace of Adam both standing and restored, concerning the predestination of the elect, concerning their definite number, and concerning the gift of perseverance, as is clear from the letters of Prosper and Hilary, who, together with others, likewise held the true meaning of Augustine. If some were unable to grasp it, this should be attributed to the weakness of their intellect; for it cannot be counted as a fault belonging only to him that a mole does not see it.

In the second sense, Augustine did not himself deny that the holy Doctor’s doctrine of predestination might appear difficult. It is indeed a most secret matter, which nevertheless he made as accessible as he could in so many books. I shall not deny that Saint Augustine’s teaching on predestination before foreseen merits disturbed many people in Gaul, from which very serious disputes arose, with learned men divided into opposing camps. The unlearned did not perceive how absolute predestination could be reconciled with human freedom, and even learned men found it difficult to grasp the same point.

Nevertheless, once Augustine had learned of those disagreements, he both consistently maintained and most solidly confirmed the same doctrine of predestination in his books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*. Indeed, in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 20, responding to the Massilians, who said, “There was no need for the hearts of so many less intelligent people to be disturbed by the uncertainty of such a disputation; for the Catholic faith was defended no less usefully for so many years without this definition of predestination,” he shows that long ago, before the Pelagians arose, he had taught the same things which he was afterward compelled to demonstrate against them with greater labor and care:

> “Predestination,” he says, “must be preached, so that the true grace of God—that is, grace which is not given according to our merits—may be defended with an impregnable fortification.” (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 21.)

The holy Doctor indeed made the gift of faith and the first grace depend upon God’s absolute decree, so that divine grace would precede every merit altogether. Hence the Semi-Pelagians, becoming Augustine’s enemies, troubled Gaul with various disputes for nearly a hundred years, until at the Second Council of Orange those long controversies among learned men were brought to an end by answers drawn from Augustine’s books.

Augustine certainly should not be charged with any fault on this account; rather, he deserves the highest praise. Neither the wisdom nor the authority of the Semi-Pelagians deterred him from demonstrating at length the doctrine once handed down concerning divine grace and predestination, at least with respect to the beginning of faith—a point acknowledged by everyone. Nor was it in any way due to him that, by sending to Gaul his two distinguished books, *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, he did not quell the disturbances that had arisen there.

Since Augustine taught concerning the beginning of faith and the gift of perseverance what is entirely true, and since the same teaching afterward passed into the canons of the councils, Cassian, Faustus, Hilary of Arles, and the others deserve criticism: by contradicting Augustine and defending erroneous doctrine, they produced the gravest disturbances in Gaul. From this it is clear that Adamus judged those Gallican controversies perversely.

Accordingly, under Saint Remigius, the most holy and learned bishop of Gaul, the Church of Lyons rightly pronounced on this matter eight hundred years ago:

> “Augustine could not be broken or recalled from the purpose of his most truthful and faithful teaching by so great a disturbance and agitation of the faithful. Rather, through his writings, insofar as he could, he admonished and instructed them, and faithfully assisted them by pouring forth prayers before God, so that they might understand and recognize how necessarily and beneficially, for the commendation of divine grace, the truth of that predestination must be wholly both believed and preached.”  
> (*On Three Letters*, chapter 35.)

Thus Ludovicus Molina spoke falsely against Saint Augustine in his *Concordia*, when he wrote:

> “Augustine’s doctrine of predestination greatly disturbed many of the faithful, especially those who lived in Gaul—not only the unlearned but also the learned—to an astonishing degree, not to say that on its account their salvation was endangered. For, lest they adhere to such a doctrine, they thought that they ought rather to assent in part to the Pelagian heresy.”

Medicines should not be rejected merely because, when first swallowed, they usually upset a delicate stomach. The salvation of those people was not endangered who, concerning a question not yet decided by the Apostolic See, were not immediately ready to accept Augustine’s position. For we know that Cassian, Faustus, and Hilary, bishop of Arles—the leaders of the Semi-Pelagians—are venerated as saints in Gaul, as we described in *Pelagian History*, book II, chapter 12.

Who, however, would not be displeased that more recent writers represent Augustine’s doctrine as the cause of the Gallican quarrels, when that very doctrine alone both calmed and removed those controversies altogether? For the canons of Orange, which gave peace to Gaul, are Augustine’s teachings copied word for word. This peace would indeed have been achieved at the outset if the Semi-Pelagians had preferred to accept the holy Doctor’s teachings rather than, by contradicting them, entangle the province in dissensions.

From this, as we inferred earlier, the origin of those disturbances must be attributed not to Augustine but to his enemies. Moreover, it is false that Adamus writes on page 610 that, in the matter of grace and predestination, some of Saint Augustine’s followers abandoned him or did not dare publicly to defend him in Gaul at that time.

Prosper and Hilary testify to the contrary in letters sent to Augustine on that subject:

> “When this book of Your Beatitude had been read,” Prosper says, “those who had previously followed the holy and apostolic authority of your teaching became much more intelligent and better instructed; while those who had been hindered by the obscurity of their own persuasion withdrew more alienated than they had been.”

Thus Augustine’s followers, receiving new books from the holy Doctor from time to time, supported his cause with greater courage. Hilary, for his part, speaks as follows:

> “There are among them persons of such standing”—namely, the Semi-Pelagians—“that ecclesiastical custom requires the laity to show them the highest reverence. With God’s help, we have taken care to observe this, while nevertheless, when necessary, we did not remain silent concerning what the weakness of our powers suggested in support of this question.”

I know that Prosper admits in the same letter that some did not dare publicly to defend Augustine’s pronouncements. But this was not because they regarded them as difficult or paradoxical to believe, as the adversary contends. Rather, as Prosper himself testifies, the dignity and respect commanded by Hilary, bishop of Arles, and by other very learned enemies of Augustine inspired them with fear.

The matters which he invents on page 611 to persuade readers of the difficulty of Augustinian doctrines must now be examined. There he says: “Augustine often confessed that difficulties proposed either by himself or by his adversaries in this matter exceeded the solutions he supplied, and that he was more disturbed by objections than calmed by answers.” He adds: “When, however, he was pressed by some insuperable difficulty, he took refuge in those words of Scripture: ‘O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!’ etc. (Rom. 11).”

May I perish if Augustine ever affirmed the things Adamus attributes to him. In so grave a matter he ought to have cited some text of the holy Doctor. But it is not so, Adamus. For I hear Augustine, speaking against Julian, the keenest and fiercest of all adversaries, say at the end of book VI: “I think you see, Julian, if you are not obstinate, that I have answered all your arguments and refuted them all, etc.” At the end of book I: “I shall break your glassy subtleties and your fragile arguments, by which you seem to yourself exceedingly keen and brilliant.” And in book III, chapter 3: “I shall leave none of your seemingly acute arguments unsolved and unbroken.” Hence Saint Prosper sings in chapter 2 of *Against the Ungrateful* that no Pelagian argument was left unanswered:

> And learned faith left no argument at all that it did not dissolve.

Saint Prudentius likewise writes in his letter to Hincmar and Pardulus that the arguments of those same heretics were answered by Saint Augustine with the fullest sufficiency and adequacy. See what was said in chapter 1 of the appendix to the dissertation on the Fifth Synod.

Yet the question Augustine regarded as insuperable was why God predestined this person rather than that one. He treats it learnedly in Sermon 11 *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 14; Letter 105 to Sixtus; and book IV to Boniface, chapter 6, where he says: “This is the very question which pertains to that depth, which the Apostle himself, wishing to behold, was in some fashion terrified by and exclaimed: ‘O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!’ etc.” Thus Augustine submitted the powers of his supreme intellect to the hidden counsels of divine providence—a point which even modern writers are compelled to admit if asked why God gives congruous grace to this man but denies it to another.

What Adamus adds—that Augustine left unfinished the exposition on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans which he had begun, in which the mysteries of grace are discussed, as though he had succumbed to the subject’s difficulty—does not prove Augustine’s doctrine difficult, which was what Adamus had proposed to prove in that chapter. The holy Doctor gives this reason for discontinuing the commentary in book I of the *Retractations*, chapter 25: “Deterred by the magnitude and labor of the work itself, I turned aside to other, easier tasks”; not because he did not know what, in accordance with the Apostle’s teaching, ought to be held concerning predestination and grace. For he deduced this so often from the same Epistle of Paul to the Romans in books, letters, and sermons that Bede, Florus, Victor of Tripoli, and others, from Augustine’s interpretations of that Pauline Epistle scattered through his works alone, stitched together complete commentaries as a cento and expounded virtually the entire Epistle in Augustinian words.

Finally, it is false that Adamus writes on page 612 that Augustine said his doctrine of predestination ought not to be preached to the people. And, what is supremely false, he purports to prove this from chapter 15 of *On the Gift of Perseverance*. For there, over several chapters, Augustine insists both that the doctrine of gratuitous predestination must be preached and assigns the manner in which it may be preached without disturbing the unlearned. Hear the holy Doctor as he begins chapter 14 of *On the Gift of Perseverance*: “But they say that the definition of predestination is contrary to the usefulness of preaching.” Do you hear, Adamus, that this was the view of the Semi-Pelagians, whom the holy Father refutes there, yet which you, to speak mildly, rather carelessly fasten upon him? Meanwhile receive Augustine’s answer: “As though it were opposed to the Apostle in his preaching! Did not that Teacher of the Gentiles commend predestination so often in faith and truth, and yet not cease to preach the word of God?”

While we were writing these things, our Holy Father Clement X opportunely pronounced in Augustine’s favor a judgment that should be inscribed in golden characters on the depths of our hearts. In a rare and singular diploma, issued on 18 December 1671, by which he grants a plenary indulgence to all Christ’s faithful who visit the churches of our order on the feast-day of Saint Augustine and pray devoutly there, he says: “Therefore, gratefully and devoutly recalling in our hearts the glories of Saint Augustine, bishop and confessor, most excellent Doctor of the Church, whose outstanding renown surpasses every human praise, who, filled with the Spirit of God, scattered the darkness of heresies and errors by writings of the most profound learning, yet brighter than the sun, like a most brilliant radiance of Christian instruction, and kindled human hearts with that fire of charity with which he himself burned most ardently,” etc.

By this most honorable, weighty, and holy judgment of the Apostolic See, all clouds cast over Augustinian books by any adversaries whatsoever are wholly put to flight and dispersed. This diploma, drawn up in the form of a Brief, as they call it, was written by the most illustrious John Gualterius Slusius, a prelate of acknowledged learning, renowned throughout the city and the world, secretary of briefs to Clement X, supreme pontiff. Printed by the Apostolic Camera, it was brought to that same supreme pontiff by the most illustrious Joseph Eusanius, prefect of the Apostolic Sacristy and an ornament of the Augustinian order. As he once adorned that order in the pulpit and the academic chair, so he now adorns it with almost continuous benefactions. He brought, I say, the praised Brief on the twenty-fourth day of that same month, at the fourteenth hour, after the supreme pontiff had celebrated the most holy mysteries.

I wished to forewarn readers of these matters, lest anyone later invent that the diploma had neither been seen nor read by the pontiff, as a certain modern writer publicly declared under oath concerning another diploma issued by Alexander VII to the Louvain theologians, in which Saint Augustine and his doctrine are highly commended. We shall rebuke that man’s words below in chapter 6. These letters of Clement X will indeed be displayed annually, as is customary, at Augustine’s solemnities wherever throughout the world the Augustinian commonwealth has established colonies. The great Doctor’s writings will appear brighter than the sun by the judgment issuing from the apostolic mouth, and henceforth everyone will recognize as false and utterly empty the words of that modern writer who dared to babble that Saint Augustine’s books are covered with darkness and clouds, when, by the oracle of the Apostolic See, they shine forth brighter than the sun.

[Col. 0587C] I intentionally omit further testimonies of the holy Fathers by which Augustine is vindicated from the charge of obscurity; for I shall produce them, and indeed the most distinguished of them, at the end of this work. Yet it is pleasing here to repeat Saint Prosper’s words in the preface to the excerpts of the Genoese. At its beginning he says: “In the books of Augustine, bishop of blessed memory, etc., if any obscurity delayed you, you ought to have hastened to the Father of lights, from whom descends every good gift and every perfect donation, and from whom the spirit of wisdom and understanding is given.” He said this not because he thought Augustine’s words obscure, but because they appeared obscure to those to whom he wrote owing to their limited understanding; for he concludes that work in these very words: “In these there is no obscurity, if, concerning the faith of predestination and the grace of God, from which arises the origin of all good things and the perseverance of merits, one holds what truth contains.”

Augustine himself earnestly urged this upon readers at the end of *On Grace and Free Will*: “Read this book repeatedly; and if you understand it, give thanks to God; but where you do not understand, pray that you may understand, for the Lord will give you understanding.” Speaking of the same volume at the beginning of *On Rebuke and Grace*, he says: “Do not suppose that, having read it once, it could by any means have become sufficiently known to you. Therefore, if you wish it to be most fruitful, do not be reluctant to make it most familiar by rereading it.”

I wish to adduce alongside Prosper a most learned bishop of Gaul, who by his weighty judgment strikes down the perverse judgment of Adamus, a Gallican writer, concerning Augustine’s writings, so that it may be evident that learned men make nothing of the arguments brought forward by the adversary. The most illustrious Joseph Maria Suaresius, bishop of Vaison, says in the first dissertation on the chronology of Saint Augustine’s works: “But what Saint Peter, prince of the Apostles, thought of the Epistles of his fellow Apostle Saint Paul, I dare to apply to the works of Saint Augustine: namely, that in them the holy Father speaks of matters in which there are certain things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction. This happens through no fault whatever of the author, but through the fault of readers, who, either insufficiently discerning or previously imbued with wandering errors, and especially ignorant of the order of the books and disputations, could not grasp the most acute mind and the most sound judgments of the most learned Father; blinded by self-love (*philautia*), they cast clouds before themselves and invent empty monstrosities.” He wrote this three years ago; and the judgment of so great a bishop will fittingly conclude this first chapter.

## CHAPTER II. Modern writers accuse the same doctrine of Saint Augustine of contradictions. They are refuted.

The same writers inflict a second and more serious injury on Augustine. They say that the same holy Doctor is burdened with so many and such great contradictions that they could compile a sizeable volume out of them. I shall recite the accusation in their own words. Adamus, chapter 6, page 614, shamelessly belches forth: “I may add that, if I wished to collect Saint Augustine’s various opinions in this matter, I should construct a certain body composed of the most diverse parts.
