In one place he says that our salvation is determined by an absolute decree; elsewhere he nevertheless affirms that it depends on our will. He says that foreknowledge is later than the decree of reprobation, and also earlier; that grace is fulfilled by our freedom, and freedom is brought into use by grace; that grace is victorious, but that our freedom also resists it; that original sin alone casts many into eternal condemnation, and that people are condemned only for their own offenses and the rebellion of free will. Here he took up arms against grace, and there he exalted it. From this I conclude that, if I may not say that Saint Augustine contradicted himself in various passages of his books, at least I may believe that his doctrine is most intricate, since none more intricate can be found than one that seems to conflict with itself.” Thus speaks this modern defender of Saint Augustine.

These assertions aim to strip the supreme teacher of the Church of all authority whatever. For how many are there who would believe a man who does not even believe himself? Will those things be certain to me which seemed most uncertain to their very author? Where division and diversity of opinions exist, truth dwells far away; since truth is one, it cannot be divided into parts. He who teaches opposites teaches nothing, but rather pulls down and builds up. Error alone neither coheres with nor agrees with itself. If what the adversary objects to Augustine is true, Augustine will be an impostor and a liar; and, leaping from one thing to another forgetful of what he had said, he breaks both his pipe and his neck. If Augustine so abounds in contradictions that one would sooner understand any enigma than discover his true and genuine opinion; if he is to be believed to have entangled in obscure wrappings of words the truth which he had undertaken to explain, by what right or title did Clement VIII, in those great disputes concerning the aids of divine grace, order that Augustine alone be consulted, in order that the secrets of truth might be sought from him? It would surely have been a most wretched plan to seek light amid obscurities and a way of settling disagreements among Augustine’s mutually conflicting opinions.

The Pelagians of old, and afterward the Semi-Pelagians, cast the same calumnies upon Augustine. Their words have been given elsewhere. Saint Prosper severely rebukes them in chapter 41 of *Against the Collator*, so that Adamus proposes nothing against the holy Doctor that did not come from the mouths of his ancient enemies. Yet Augustine refuted them all by this brief saying: “This is why you think—or wish others to think—that my opinions are contrary to one another: as though I disapproved what I had previously approved, or embraced what I had previously rejected. Hear, therefore, my plain opinion, and understand it yourself, or allow others to understand it, without casting the darkness of misty disputation over the serenity of most sincere truth.” Book V, *Against Julian*, chapter 9.

Indeed, what happened to Augustine is common to the rest who, elevated above others by an exceptional intellect and an abundance of learning, became masters of schools. For followers, while eagerly striving to devote more careful study to reading the patron of their school, nevertheless indulging their own intellects too much, bring their teachers under suspicion of contradiction by teaching diverse things. This happened to Aristotle, to Plato, and later to Saint Thomas and Scotus, princes of the most distinguished schools, as disciples so often fought fiercely among themselves about their teacher’s meaning. Yet none of their followers charges those great men with contradiction; rather, they attempt to explain by fitting interpretations what their adversaries adduce. Therefore, since Augustine has left all others far behind in the number of his books, the subtlety of his learning, and, above all, his treatment of almost contrary arguments, he too came near this danger: that he should be thought to have taught contradictory things, while writers who are opposed and mutually hostile compete in publishing that he favors them. Yet it belongs to a malicious and wholly irreligious reader to affirm that so great a Doctor taught contradictory things.

But Adamus, untroubled by such scruples, cries out on page 590 that “Augustine divided the schools of theologians into parties and the Doctors into factions.” You are mistaken: on the contrary, the various factions of schools and Doctors tore Augustine’s doctrine into opposing parts. For when they approach Augustine’s writings with preoccupied minds and wish to use him not as a teacher but as an advocate, they boldly fasten their little opinions upon the greatest Doctor of the Church. For which modern writer opens the holy Doctor’s volumes with the intention of renouncing even his own opinion and resolving to adhere to Augustine’s judgment alone? Yet, willing or unwilling, Augustine must be drawn into parties and machines, and the teacher of the Church—if heaven so pleases—proclaimed their disciple.

Continuing this same accusation, the adversary says in chapter 6, page 611: “We have also shown that Saint Augustine changed his position three times in this matter.” In the margin he cites chapter 3 of *On the Predestination of the Saints*. Yet the holy Doctor writes there that he changed his position only once. He had formerly thought that the beginning of faith came from us, not from God; later, having come to know the matter more accurately from the Apostle, he rejected that error. This change of position should be attributed to him not as a fault but as praise, since he turned from error to truth. Indeed, he writes in chapter 4 that God revealed to him that he had abandoned his former opinion:

> “Behold,” he says, “why I said above that, chiefly through this apostolic testimony, I myself had been convicted, since I had previously held a different view concerning this matter from that which God revealed to me when, as I said, I was writing to Bishop Simplicianus in order to resolve this question.”

Thus a wise man, warned by God’s revelation, contradicted himself when he was in error. Correcting his earlier error by his later position, he intended—and indeed achieved—a single, entirely coherent doctrine concerning grace and predestination.

We know that theologians dispute among themselves concerning Augustine’s position. Yet those same theologians eagerly produce passages of Sacred Scripture in their own favor, and they contend no less vigorously about the meaning of Scripture than about Augustine’s meaning. Who, however, would be driven by such madness as to dare say that the statements of the sacred text are most intricate, that they have given rise to disturbances in the Church, that they have divided learned men into factions, or anything similar to what Adamus has written about Augustine?

There were, nevertheless, scoundrels hostile to the Christian religion who accused the Sacred Scriptures of contradiction. Among others, Saint Augustine refutes them in his book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*.

But the arguments which the adversary adduces to support Augustine’s supposed contradictions are entirely frivolous and scarcely bear repeating without disgust. First, he objects that Augustine taught that our salvation was determined by God’s absolute decree, while elsewhere he taught that it nevertheless depended upon our will.

This is precisely the position of Saint Thomas, to which not only his followers but also theologians of better reputation subscribe. They say that glory was fixed for the predestined in God’s intention by an absolute decree, but that in its execution it depends upon their merits. Augustine discusses this matter in *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 18, where he asks how eternal life can be given to our merits as a reward and at the same time be given by grace without presupposing any merits.

The second contradiction he raises is that Augustine taught that foreknowledge was posterior to the decree of reprobation and also that it was prior to it. But this recent writer should have indicated the books and chapters in which he had noted these Augustinian contradictions. We do not consider him a man of such authority that we ought to believe him when he asserts something without offering any proof, especially in a matter of the greatest importance, where he calls the teaching and authority of the saints into question.

For the present, we say that it is falsely asserted that Saint Augustine placed reprobation before the foreknowledge of demerits. His oft-repeated statement is well known:

> “God is good; God is just. He can free without good merits, because he is good; he cannot condemn without evil merits, because he is just.”

Accordingly, against the Pelagians he proves that God would be unjust if he excluded from glory infants who were guilty of no sin. He makes this point almost everywhere in his later work against Julian, and also in the earlier work, book III, chapters 4 and 12; in Sermon 14 on the Words of the Apostle; and in Letter 106. The adversary will find no passage in which Augustine teaches that anyone is rejected by God whose demerit God had not foreseen.

Third, he says that Augustine taught that “grace is completed by our freedom, and that freedom is brought into operation by grace.” But these statements are entirely compatible. Grace alone does not produce a good act in us; rather, it does so together with the free will, which grace moves beforehand and brings into action. Thus grace and free will together constitute the complete principle of good acts, though freedom remains subject to grace.

Indeed, since nothing can be done without grace in the manner required for salvation, human freedom can be moved to a good and meritorious use only by grace. I shall not cite Augustine’s texts, because this matter is evident in every school, although the manner in which these motions occur is debated.

The first point may be read in Augustine, *Sermon 13 on the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 11, under the section “Recognize what you ask,” and elsewhere, where he writes, among other things:

> “If you were not an agent, he would not be a co-agent.”

See also book II of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 5, and elsewhere. The second point, however, is affirmed on every page of Augustine’s books against the Pelagians, where he constantly insists upon the Catholic doctrine that nothing good and meritorious can be done without grace.

A fourth contradiction is then brought forward against Augustine:

> “Grace is victorious, yet our freedom resists it.”

But Augustine never imagined this of the same grace in one and the same individual: namely, that grace should at once conquer freedom and subject it to itself, while nevertheless being rejected by that freedom. For if it is rejected, it is no longer victorious; rather, it is repelled in defeat.

If Augustine said this of different and distinct kinds of grace, every shadow of contradiction is far removed from his words. Indeed, recent theologians openly affirm that congruent grace is always victorious, while non-congruent grace is resisted by free will. Their opponents likewise teach this concerning determining grace and merely sufficient grace. If these positions involve a contradiction, Adamus deserves public thanks for having freed all the scholastics from an entrenched error.

Thus, when Augustine writes in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 8:

> “This grace, therefore, which is secretly bestowed upon human hearts by divine generosity, is rejected by no hard heart”;

and when he says that it moves “indeflectibly, irresistibly, and most invincibly” in chapter 12 of *On Rebuke and Grace*; that it acts “with the most effective powers” in *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 16; and with “most hidden and effective power” in book I to Boniface, chapter 20—when, I say, the holy Doctor expresses the power of victorious grace through these and other epithets, he must be understood as speaking of congruent and efficacious grace.

But when he teaches that our freedom resists a certain weak grace, as is evident from book I, question 2, to Simplicianus, and from chapter 9 of *On the Predestination of the Saints*, where he says:

> “Why one of two impious men, already advanced in age, is called so that he follows the one calling, while the other is either not called or is not called in such a way that he follows the one calling—these are the inscrutable judgments of God”;

it is clear that some resist God when he calls them. The same follows from chapter 11 of *On Rebuke and Grace*, where he writes that the assistance given to angels before their fall is also supplied to some in the state of fallen nature, while it is not given to others as punishment for sin.

When, I say, he teaches these things, he is speaking of another kind of grace: weak, incongruent, and remotely sufficient. Thus no suspicion of contradiction touches Augustine here.

The fifth contradiction is this: Augustine is said to teach that “many are condemned solely because of original sin,” while also teaching that “people are not condemned except on account of personal sins and rebellion of their own free will.”

That is not so, Adamus. Augustine teaches that infants who die without baptism are condemned solely on account of original sin, whereas adults are condemned both on account of original sin and on account of other sins which their own wickedness has added. There is no shadow of contradiction here.

Let the holy Doctor be heard in *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 13:

> “Those, therefore, who do not belong to this most certain and blessed number are judged with the greatest justice according to their merits. For either they lie under the sin which they originally drew from their generation and depart from this life with that inherited debt, which has not been remitted through regeneration; or through free will they have added further sins—free, I say, but not liberated: free with respect to righteousness, but enslaved to sin—by which they are carried through various harmful desires, some more, others less, but all evil, and according to this difference are to be judged with different punishments.”

Again, how those whose original sin was remitted in baptism can be said to have been left in the mass of perdition on account of original sin, the holy Doctor explains in chapter 7. We shall discuss this below, when we address the errors attributed to Augustine. Certainly, such people cannot in any way be condemned on account of the guilt of original sin; it is of them that Augustine speaks when he says that no one is condemned except on account of his own crimes.

The sixth contradiction he formulates as follows: “Here Augustine took up arms against grace, and elsewhere he exalted it.” But we do not so readily grant assent to anyone who produces no word of Augustine. Where did Augustine take up arms against divine grace? Where was he injurious to it? By what word did he harm it even in the slightest? Certainly, in the books written against the Manichaeans on the freedom of the human will, before the Pelagians had arisen, he mentioned divine grace and declared its necessity for living justly and piously in a memorable statement, as though he had foreseen the future enemies of that same grace. [Col. 0593A] Therefore, in *Book I of the Retractations*, chapter 9, after citing several passages from the books *On Free Will* in favor of grace, he concludes: “Behold how long before the Pelagian heresy existed we argued in this way, as though we were already arguing against them.”

Thus, although in the first book addressed to Simplicianus he had said much in favor of free will, he nevertheless subjected it to grace; he did not exalt it above grace. Hence, in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 4, he says: “In resolving this question, work was indeed undertaken on behalf of the free choice of the human will, but God’s grace prevailed.” Therefore, if Augustine, even when he was wielding decisive weapons in defense of free will, granted victory to grace, where did he draw his sword against it?

The more recent writer places these contradictions of Augustine’s views before us. Yet, not daring to attribute so great an error to Augustine, and since doing so would trouble his religious conscience, he added: “Hence I conclude that, if I am not permitted to say that Saint Augustine contradicted himself in various passages of his books, at least I am permitted to believe that his doctrine is exceedingly complicated,” and so forth. He does not say, “Hence I conclude, since I am not permitted to say,” and so on, but speaks as though doubting whether he may accuse Augustine of contradiction: “If I am not permitted,” he says. Yet neither are you permitted to say the first thing, nor is the second belief lawful for you—namely, that the doctrine of Saint Augustine is exceedingly complicated. For you thus affix an extraordinary mark of disgrace to the books of the Church’s most illustrious teacher, a mark that you would by no means tolerate being inflicted upon your Suarez or Vasquez by anyone. Believe me, [Col. 0593C] you are not permitted to think so basely of Augustine. For what could be more irreligious than to introduce Augustine as a many-formed Proteus in his thinking, now affirming, now denying, now white, now black, continually changing his buskins so many times in the same scene? Augustine, therefore, is not contradictory to himself; rather, Adamus fights against himself. For although he gave his book the title *Calvin Destroyed by the Arms of Saint Augustine*, he nevertheless asserts, with remarkable consistency, in chapter 4, page 596, that the writings of Saint Augustine are not sufficiently suitable for disarming the Calvinists.

Let us close this chapter with the graceful statement of the great Doctor, in *Book V Against Julian*, chapter 5: “My words, therefore, are not contradictory to one another, although they allow you to make them so, either by not understanding them or by preventing others from understanding.” He adds: “You, then, who have marked out and attacked in me opinions supposedly fighting against one another, explain how you yourself are consistent with yourself and do not resist yourself.”

## CHAPTER III. More recent writers accuse Saint Augustine’s doctrine against the Pelagians of excess.

Some recent writers who have published books on theology, now at last sensing that they are too heavily burdened by Saint Augustine’s authority, and fearing openly to reject it lest they appear to yield in that field to opponents who invoke Augustine’s name everywhere, try to escape from him by fastening upon the holy Doctor a new charge. For they say that Augustine, “carried away by the heat of controversy, went beyond the limits of necessary truth, so that there is a certain excessive severity and unjust harshness which commands one to cross that middle ground where truth resides, if Augustine leads the way.” These are the words of Annatus, in Book VIII of his *Augustine*, chapter 2, page 862. Adamus gave this title to his seventh chapter: “That Saint Augustine allowed himself to be carried away too far by the heat of controversy against the Pelagians, and went farther than he intended.” The famous statement of Saint Bonaventure on this matter is explained on page 616. Moraines, Decamps, and the other recent writers reproduce these words in full.

Nor do they think that this happened to Augustine only once or twice, but in almost all his controversies against the Pelagians. They adopted this very easy way of escape so that they would not have to wear out their intellects any longer in interpreting Augustine. Yet these modern critics of Augustine produce nothing that the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians did not already bring against the holy Doctor twelve centuries ago.

Julian, the most insolent of the Pelagians, charging Augustine with this fault, used to say: “If anyone says either that human beings possess free will or that God is the creator of those who are born, he is called a Coelestian and a Pelagian. Therefore, lest they be called heretics, they become Manichaeans; and while they fear a false disgrace, they incur a true crime, like wild beasts surrounded by wings so that they may be driven into nets.” This is found in Augustine, *Book II On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 3, where the holy Doctor skillfully refuted that slander against himself and the other Catholics.

The Semi-Pelagians likewise published this charge in order to undermine the same authority. These are Cassian’s words, *Conference* 13, chapter 11: “For many, believing each of these things and asserting them more strongly than is just, have become entangled in various errors opposed to one another.” Faustus says the same in Book I, chapters 1, 6, and 17.

These men, as utterly shameless detractors, are sharply rebuked in the letter that the more recent writers with whom we are disputing attribute to Pope Celestine: “Because some who glory in the Catholic name, yet remain in the condemned opinions of heretics, whether through perversity or ignorance, presume to oppose the most devout disputants, and although they do not hesitate to anathematize Pelagius and Coelestius, nevertheless speak against our teachers as though they had exceeded the necessary measure.”

Thus we see the excessive boldness of these recent writers, who once again spew forth with full mouth condemned insults against Augustine. Indeed, when Augustine corrected with censorious severity all the volumes he had written, and candidly admitted in *Book I of the Retractations*, chapter 1, that he had exceeded the proper measure in praising the Platonists, he did not notice so many excesses of his own in attacking the Pelagians. Perhaps he left that censorship to the modern writers, so that they might append it as an addition to the books of the *Retractations*.

Calvin certainly protects himself with this shield against the testimonies of the Fathers. His words appear in Taperus, article 7, *On Free Will*: “The Greeks, and above all, and among them especially Chrysostom, exceeded the proper measure in extolling the power of the human will.” Although he sometimes took it badly that Pighius also charged Augustine with this excess, he nevertheless contrived, with the same audacity, to make Augustine suffer from the same fault, writing that “not even Augustine’s opinion is to be accepted in every respect.” By this he plainly indicated that, in his judgment, the holy Doctor had sometimes said more than was consonant with truth.

Indeed, if these excesses—which, according to the opponents, are sufficiently frequent in Augustine—are admitted, and if other Fathers are likewise subjected to the same fault, heretics could scarcely be convicted by any testimony of the saints. Whenever they felt themselves pressed by some opinion of the Fathers, they would cry out that the Fathers had exceeded the proper measure. By this reasoning the authority of all antiquity is weakened, and every path to convicting the heterodox is closed.

### § I. What the more recent writers understand by “excess” is investigated. The testimonies of Saints Thomas and Bonaventure do not support them. Excess is wrongly charged against Augustine.

[Col. 0595B]

If we ask the more recent writers what they understand by the term “Augustinian excesses,” Adamus replies, on page 626, that Augustine, inflamed by the excessive heat of controversy and seemingly favoring the heretics, ran beyond the limits of truth. Annatus adds, on page 862: “So that there is a certain excessive severity and unjust harshness which commands one to cross that middle ground where truth resides, if Augustine leads the way.”

They nevertheless admit that Augustine did not lie on this account. Rather, as Moraines excellently explains, he spoke “unwittingly,” speaking as he felt, but, through the heat of controversy and the vehemence of his spirit, occasionally inclined toward the opposite extreme “in understanding as well as in words.” This, he says, is not to lie, but “to be mistaken and to say what is false without lying.” *Anti-Jansenian Disputation* 40, section 6, number 65.

Thus Augustine is convicted before the tribunal of the modern writers as guilty not of lying, but nevertheless of manifest falsity. To persuade themselves that they have judged Augustine justly in this way, they summon as witnesses several theologians of no mean standing who said that the holy Doctor exceeded the proper measure when disputing against the Pelagians. We shall examine their words expressly in chapter 5. Here we make a few observations concerning Saints Thomas and Bonaventure—for these are the men they set against Augustine.

When the book of Saint Fulgentius, *On Faith to Peter*, was read by the earlier scholastics under Augustine’s name, and in chapter 27 it asserted that children who died with original sin alone were punished with the penalty of eternal fire, Saint Thomas said that the words “fire” and “punishment,” and so forth, were to be understood broadly, in *Question 5 On Evil*, article 2, so that a species might be put for a genus. He added: “The saints used this manner of speaking in order to make the error of the Pelagians detestable, since they asserted that there was no sin in little children and that no punishment was due to them.”

Saint Bonaventure, likewise explaining the same testimony—which he thought Augustinian—said that Augustine had stated it “saying more, while intending less to be understood.” In these words the opponents claim a triumph for themselves. Adamus calls it an “eminent statement” in the title of chapter 7. Annatus expressed the same words in larger type in Book VIII, chapter 2, so that they might immediately fill the eyes of the readers. Hence Adamus cries out: “What will our opponents reply to the two illustrious Doctors of the Church, Saint Thomas and Saint Bonaventure, who have confessed these excesses in the books of Saint Augustine?” Page 629.

Let Adamus raise both ears and hear what we reply. You declare that Augustine fell into excesses, that is, that he went beyond the limits of truth, in understanding as well as in words—which is not to lie, but to be mistaken, as Moraines admits. But the Seraphic Doctor attributed that excess not to Augustine’s understanding, but only to his words. “Saying more,” he says, “while intending less to be understood.” This means that Saint Augustine used a more emphatic expression not in his mind but only verbally—not in reality, but apparently and without any falsity—namely, the word “fire” to explain the punishment of infants, although, according to the Seraphic Doctor’s opinion, he did not hold that meaning in his mind. [Col. 0596B] The opponents, however, contend that Augustine held what was false “in understanding as well as in words.”

I plainly do not see how Bonaventure’s testimony helps them, since the Seraphic Doctor removes far from Augustine’s mind the falsity that they themselves introduce into it. There is therefore no reason for you to boast of the support of that most celebrated Doctor; for, insofar as Augustine’s excesses are concerned, he agrees with you in no way.

Nor does Saint Thomas’s statement support you. For when he says that Augustine spoke broadly, he indicates that Augustine merely used a more emphatic word, not that he crossed the limits of truth. He affirms that the word must be taken broadly, and in this way he believed Augustine understood it.

For if Augustine is said to have gone beyond the truth—as Adamus explains his excess on page 626—he would have had to take the term “punishment,” and likewise “Gehenna,” “torment,” and so forth, strictly, narrowly, and with complete rigor. Otherwise, if he understood it broadly, he restrained himself within the bounds of truth.

Those holy Doctors, therefore, stand so plainly against the opinions of the modern writers that it is astonishing that they should be brought against Augustine so inconsiderately and confidently, and that Adamus should arouse such commotion throughout his seventh chapter on the basis of their words.

Yet this must by no means be omitted: they assert only once, and with respect to a single expression, that the holy Doctor spoke more emphatically. But what charge will confront the writer of more than two hundred volumes if he used a word not entirely properly only once? Let us ask the opponents whether Augustine taught by means of only a single word that predestination is prior to foreseen merits; that lust (*libido*) is evil; that the Old Law makes people guilty without the grace of the Redeemer; that there are no true virtues among unbelievers without grace; and that he exceeded the proper measure in these and many other matters, as they proclaim.

I certainly do not believe that they will affirm this, since the holy Doctor not only tried to establish these opinions with many arguments, but also exerted all the powers of his great intellect to persuade others of them; indeed, he maintained that some of them were to be regarded as Catholic. This, good men, is not “saying more while intending less to be understood.” This is not using a broad expression only once, and only in a single word. Rather, I think you now see what it is, since you are convicted of lacking the support of Saints Thomas and Bonaventure. [Col. 0597A]

I am genuinely amused by the witty examples offered by recent writers to explain—or perhaps excuse—Augustine’s excesses. “Just as gardeners,” Adamus says, chapter 8, page 111, “when they wish to straighten a crooked plant, bend it toward the opposite side—not because they want it to remain in that position, but so that it may more easily be raised into straightness—so likewise Augustine,” says Moraines, *Disputation* 19, number 35, “when disputing against the Pelagians, who excessively exalted the natural powers of free will and asserted that they were sufficient without grace not only for every kind of natural virtue but also for salvation, seems sometimes to have been carried away by the heat of controversy toward the opposite extreme, in order to lead them away from that error.”

Agreeing with this, Adamus writes in chapter 7, page 631: “Augustine cast his enemies into dangerous extremes, not in order to leave them there, but to bring them back to moderation, from which heresy had dragged them.”

But who does not know that, on this account, Augustine would have been a completely foolish and imprudent disputant if he had defended against the Pelagians a position utterly opposed to the truth, in order to bring them back from error? For since they granted everything to free will, leaving no place for grace, they would have obstinately refused to accept Augustine’s diametrically opposed position, by which he seemed, through excess, to grant nothing to free will but to place everything under the right of grace.

Augustine would have done much better if he had granted some things to free will and some things to grace as well, in order to remove them from error. For everyone is more easily driven from one extreme to the middle than to the opposite extreme. Hence Saint Thomas said above that Augustine spoke broadly, not in order by that expression to draw the heretics over to his own opinion, but to make the heretics’ error more detestable to Catholics.

Thus, if the modern writers were forced to abandon their old opinion concerning the divine aids, they would more easily descend to the opinion that morally predetermines the will than to the one that asserts physical predetermination; for they detest the latter too greatly.

The causes assigned by the opponents for driving Augustine into those excesses are also laughable. Adamus says on page 624: “The temperament of his body, his disposition, his eloquence, his familiar manner of treating the truths of faith, his great love for the Platonists, whose inventions are generally loftier, and his hatred of all enemies of the truth cast Augustine into propositions so apparently insolent.”

We know that Africans are of a more impetuous nature beneath a hotter sky, but let Adamus alone affirm, without evidence, that Augustine had a hot temperament. I myself do not fail to know that the holy Doctor was less able to endure cold, as appears from Letter 227; but it is certain that he attacked the heretics with a calm mind and composed style, as I shall soon demonstrate.

Meanwhile, it is permissible to wonder how Augustine’s disposition could have become so precisely known to a man living twelve centuries after his death. Nor can eloquence be called the source of those excesses. For if Augustine had declaimed against the Pelagians from the public platform, insulting them more by an abundance of words than by the force of arguments, he might perhaps have used some hyperbole—that is, an expression exceeding the truth of the matter in its wording—and added certain things by way of exaggeration, as is permitted to orators.

But since he confirmed the doctrines that the opponents say slipped from Augustine through excess with so many arguments, and established them with such great effort through testimonies drawn from sacred mysteries, writing more than six hundred lines on more than one occasion to persuade others of them, he cannot be said to have pursued the empty pomp of an orator through hyperbole. Rather, he must be said to have weighed the very periods, indeed the very words, with sufficient deliberation, as the importance of the matter and the gravity and wisdom of so great a Doctor required.

Moreover, it is ridiculous to derive Augustine’s fall into those excesses from his love of the Platonists. Augustine certainly held the Platonists in high esteem and engaged with their writings with the greatest praise, as is understood from the books he wrote against the Academics. But how he could have overflowed beyond the lines of necessary truth in discussions of divine grace through reading them, we cannot even suspect. Indeed, although Adamus boldly asserts it, I do not think he himself knew this.

For what understanding of grace is found in the books of the Platonists? Unless he prefers to derive from the Platonic school that impulse to dispute which, he says, was familiar to Augustine. Since neither Plotinus, Philo, nor Ficino transmitted such a thing in their books, Adamus himself must prove it by examining the books of the Old Academy.

Nor did those excesses originate in the hatred with which Augustine pursued the enemies of the truth. For when the holy Father wrote against the heretics, he protested that he was far removed from every cause for hatred.

No enemy rose up against Augustine who was more hostile or more bitter than Julian, so that it seems that the entire poison of the Pelagians was poured forth against Augustine through the mouth of that one Julian. Yet Augustine not only wielded his pen against him without hatred; he also wrote the following words expressing love for his enemy, and indeed the greatest love, in *Book I Against Julian*, chapter 7: “For my part, because of the love I have for you—may God in his mercy prevent you from uprooting it from the marrow of my heart by any insult whatsoever—I would rather, my son Julian,” and so forth.

Since, therefore, the holy Doctor was far removed from all the causes of excess that Adamus investigated in Augustine, he must likewise be placed far from those excesses.

Adamus presses the matter in chapter 16, page 760: “When Augustine defends liberty against the Manichaeans, he seems to destroy the necessity of grace; but when he contends for grace against the Pelagians, he overturns liberty.” At the end of chapter 7, page 632, he wonders that some “have never known that Saint Augustine himself confessed this impulse of his spirit in several passages of his books.”

Here we may exclaim with Augustine: “Who would expect wisdom from one who knows the faith of a liar?” *Book IV Against Julian*, chapter 8.

For what was more frequently brought against Augustine by the Pelagians than the charge that, out of hatred for Pelagianism, he inclined toward Manichaeism? Yet the most holy teacher very often stripped this slander from himself. Let *Book II On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapters 3 and 23, and *Book II to Boniface*, chapters 1 and 2, be read. There, after recounting at length the extreme errors of the Pelagians and Manichaeans, he concludes with the position of the Catholic Church midway between them:

“For two errors may be opposed to one another, but both are detestable, because both are opposed to the truth. For if the Pelagians are to be loved because they hate the Manichaeans, then the Manichaeans are also to be loved because they hate the Pelagians. But far be it from the Catholic mother, because of the hatred of one group, to choose to love the other, since, with the Lord warning and helping, she ought to avoid both and desires to heal both!”

Again, he begins *Book IV*, chapter 3, as follows: “Whoever, with a Catholic mind, recoils from these impious and damnable doctrines in this threefold division, let him avoid the hiding places and snares of that fivefold division, and let him be so cautious between the two that he avoids the Manichaean without inclining toward the Pelagian, and again separates himself from the Pelagians without joining himself to the Manichaeans; or, if he is already held by either group, let him not so protect himself from one of the others as to rush into the other.”

O excellent teacher, and most tenacious guardian of his principles! For, if Adamus is to be believed, Augustine became so heated in his disputations against the Pelagians and Manichaeans that he inclined toward the error opposed to the one he had undertaken to attack, page 632.

But these are pure fabrications of the anti-Augustinians. No mortal understood the errors of the Pelagians and Manichaeans so precisely as Augustine. He not only maintained the middle path between them, but also taught it everywhere in the books addressed to Boniface. There he recounted the five principal errors of the Pelagians and Manichaeans, diametrically opposed them to that middle path handed down by the Church, and did so in a way that makes it astonishing that the opponents should so confidently sell these stories about the holy Doctor.

As for what they add—that Augustine himself recognized these impulses of his mind, and that he acknowledged this in several places—that is false, indeed utterly false. Adamus cites the beginning of the book *On Grace and Free Will*. But there Augustine writes only this:

“There are some who defend the grace of God in such a way that they deny human free will; or, when grace is defended, they think that free will is being denied,” and so forth.

I want you, Adamus, to be the judge here: does Augustine confess there the heat, impulses, and excesses of his own disputation? You will be able to say only that he recounted extreme errors there.

He also produces *Book IV Against Julian*, chapter 8. But there Augustine reproves Julian as a public slanderer. Julian had written that Augustine said free will was denied if grace were commended, and that grace was denied if free will were defended. The holy Father replies:

“I did not say that grace was denied, but that it might appear to be denied. I did not say that free will was denied or taken away, but I said that it might be thought to be taken away.”

There is not even a word about a vehemence or excess inherent in Augustine’s manner of disputing. [Col. 0600A] He said that grace might appear to be denied when free will was commended because, given the difficulty of the question, this might appear so to those who understood less well.

He also appeals to *Book V Against Julian*, chapter 9, and to *Book I On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 15. But in the former passage he discusses only concupiscence; in the latter, the origin of the soul. In neither place does he say anything about an impulse, zeal, fervor, or excess of his own mind.

Moreover, everyone can see how much danger Augustine’s doctrine faces from these alleged excesses. For if Augustine depressed the powers of free will more than was just and elevated the powers of grace too highly in those excesses, then Calvin will be said to have agreed with Augustine, since he founded his own doctrine upon those excesses.

We know that Calvin was accustomed to boast falsely as well as arrogantly that Augustine belonged entirely to him. Adamus himself represents him as shouting this on page 561: “All of Augustine is ours.”

Our writers reply that Augustine’s doctrine slightly exceeds the limits of truth and, in this respect, favors Calvin; that his doctrine is not to be accepted unless those excesses are shorn away, into which he plunged headlong through the native fury of his spirit.

Hence Adamus writes in chapter 8, page 640: “Provided that I do not fall into the errors of the Pelagians, whom Augustine attacks, I may refuse to follow the force of the words he uses to overthrow them. Thus I stand midway between Pelagius and Calvin. For if, by softening Augustine’s words, I lowered myself too much, I would be a Pelagian. But if I wished to retain their elevation, I would be a Calvinist. Therefore I hold the middle position with the Church.”

Indeed, you seem to imitate that cruel woman who, as the story is told in the *Arcana*, rejoiced when, before Solomon, the wisest of kings, the child was divided in two and given partly to her and partly to her adversary. You judge that Augustine must be divided into parts, so that the part in which he is raised into the height of excesses may be surrendered to Calvin, while the part in which he is more humble may belong to you—or rather, to the Church.

But what else is this than to betray Augustine to Calvin, whom you claimed to be rescuing from Calvin? Yet the authorities above forbid Augustine to be divided into parts. He must be granted whole to those who demand the whole of him; and those who say that they are content with a part of Augustine possess not even the smallest fragment of him.

Calvin, however, invented the claim that Augustine belonged entirely to him by a wholly empty assertion. For compelled by the truth, he himself admitted that he rejected part of Augustine in *Book III of the Institutes*, chapter 11, saying: “Not even Augustine’s opinion is to be accepted in every respect.”

Thus, in Calvin’s judgment, Augustine’s opinion is partly to be accepted and partly rejected; and our Adamus agrees with him very neatly. But this injury is so damaging that, whether they wish it or not, it overturns Augustine’s entire authority. For by what protection will we finally be able to discern when Augustine stands at the boundary of truth and when he runs beyond it? Let them consider whether they are making the Church’s greatest Doctor suspect of excess everywhere.

Here I must examine whether these insults fall upon Augustine alone, or whether they also disfigure the Church’s most beautiful and immaculate face. We know that when Hormisdas was asked by Possessor, an African bishop, what should be held concerning questions of grace and free will, he replied: “What the Roman—that is, the Catholic—Church follows and asserts concerning the grace of God and free will may be known from the various books of Blessed Augustine,” and so forth.

We know that Boniface, although highly learned, nevertheless awaited Augustine’s answers in opposition to the Pelagians. We know that Clement VIII ordered the grave controversy concerning the divine aids to be evaluated according to the mind of Augustine alone.

What care would the Roman bishops have shown in nourishing the faithful flock with wholesome pastures if they had led it to Augustine’s meadows, where so many deadly weeds of contradictions, excesses, and errors flourished? But if the Roman pontiffs followed Augustine in their discussions of grace and clung to his side and footsteps, I do not know with what face Adamus can assert that they trod some middle path between Pelagius and Augustine, crying out: “Therefore I hold the middle position with the Church.”

Know that in these matters the Church followed Augustine immediately after the sacred Scriptures, so that the middle path which you pretend she followed may plainly be removed from consideration altogether.

### § II. Whether Saint Augustine exceeded the proper measure when he wrote that concupiscence is contrary to reason and evil, and that it is a defect of human nature arising from original sin, but not at all its natural good.

We shall examine the statements of Antoninus Moraines alone, who frequently accuses the holy Doctor of excess in his *Anti-Jansenian*. The author of that book is Joannes Martinonus, as Father Macedo testified to me. I associate here at Padua most familiarly with this exceedingly learned man, and he in turn embraces me with singular goodwill. He also encouraged me to publish both my *Pelagian History* and these *Vindications*. For I had resolved, like Aspendius, to sing privately within myself to the Muses and not to risk public judgment.

The same praised writer made it known that Moraines was Martinonus in his golden work *Saint Augustine*, chapter 13; this is also evident from an anagram of the fictitious name.

It is not my intention here to undertake a more elaborate defense of Augustine. I shall deal with the cause of the holy Father briefly, when I show that the very doctrines in which Augustine is said to have exceeded were approved by the Roman pontiffs and by synods of the Fathers.

Augustine asserts that concupiscence is evil in itself and a vice of human nature derived from the first sin, and that it is not a natural passion of human beings. He demonstrates this by various arguments in the last four books of his first work against Julian.

Nevertheless, the holy Doctor did not think that concupiscence was sin itself, but that it was like a vicious habit inclining toward evil. The Pelagians, on the contrary, contended that concupiscence was a perfection and a natural good implanted in the first parent for the propagation of the human race. Hence, by way of ridicule, concupiscence was called by Augustine, in *Book IV Against Julian*, chapter 11, “the Pelagians’ adopted child,” and in *Book V*, chapter 5, “their most beautiful servant.”

The more recent writers reject the opinion of Saint Augustine. With Moraines, *Disputation* 13, number 87, they object that he exceeded the proper measure through the heat of controversy and, out of hatred for the heresy he was attacking, sometimes inclined toward extremes.

But Moraines is mistaken, and he abuses the ignorance of the less informed when he maintains that Augustine sometimes inclined toward extremes in a matter which he inculcates everywhere and repeatedly with the greatest solidity and constancy.

The question concerning concupiscence was one of the five principal questions that Saint Augustine disputed with the Pelagians. Thus, when Julian said: “He who observes the proper measure of natural concupiscence uses a good thing well; he who does not observe the proper measure uses a good thing badly; but he who, out of love for holy virginity, has even despised the proper measure does not use a good thing better,” Augustine replies in opposition, in *Book III Against Julian*, chapter 21:

“I, for my part, reply to these statements of yours as follows: He who observes the proper measure of carnal concupiscence uses an evil thing well; he who does not observe the proper measure uses an evil thing badly; but he who, out of love for holy virginity, has even despised the proper measure does not use an evil thing better.”

Then, as though the signal for battle had been given, he cries out: “In this controversy, the whole issue between us concerns whether this thing is used well as a good thing or as an evil thing.”

Julian fought so fiercely for concupiscence as a natural perfection that, as Augustine states in the same place, he pursued the matter throughout the entire book.

They object that the holy Doctor exceeded the proper measure in this opinion. But we contend that this view did not slip from him while he was occupied with something else. Rather, he defended it seriously and deliberately with all his strength against the heretics.

If Augustine exceeded the proper measure, then the ancient Church also suffered from the same fault. For before Augustine and together with Augustine, she followed the opinion just recited. The opponents must be taught this by us, since they either do not know it or at least conceal it.

Augustine, at the end of *Book V Against Julian*, chapter 12, proposes five questions concerning concupiscence that he disputed with the Pelagians. The third is this: “Whether that is not evil to which one must not consent when resisting it, lest it proceed to its own excess.”

After adding two other questions, he says: “This is what is debated between us. In these questions, your impious novelty is suffocated by the Catholic truth handed down from ancient times.”

What rebuke would Augustine deserve if he had published false opinions—and opinions into which he had been driven headlong by the fury of controversy—as Catholic truth?

Let Suarez be heard, *Prolegomena* 6 *On Grace*, chapter 6: “Furthermore,” he says, “we add that whatever Augustine affirms as certain in this matter and as pertaining to the doctrines of faith must be held and defended by every prudent and learned theologian, even if it is not certainly established that it has been defined by the Church. This is so because the Church has deferred so much to Augustine in this matter that, since she followed his doctrine in condemning errors opposed to the grace of God, it would be a great act of rashness for a private Doctor to dare contradict Augustine when he teaches something orthodox concerning the grace of God—especially since he labored for the defense and explanation of divine grace for so many years, with such wisdom, such intellect, such diligence and perseverance, and, above all, with so many gifts and aids.”

Cardinal Bellarmine agrees with Suarez, *Book II On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 11: “Augustine could not be defended from enormous rashness if he had not only fought so fiercely for a falsehood, but had also dared to present it as Catholic faith.”

Such are their words.

The disciples of this holy Father followed the same opinion concerning concupiscence. Saint Fulgentius writes in his *Letter on the Good of Marriage*, chapter 3:

> “Among those goods, namely, which God made, there is found the chaste union of wife and husband. In these works of God, lust cannot be found; nor does it ever accord with justice, since it came upon human beings not as a gift of their creation, but as a defect of the first transgression.”

Saint [Col. 0603B] Prosper, or Pomerius, writes in book III of *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 2:

> “Concupiscence itself, vicious—not natural, but imposed and implanted in our nature as a punishment—resists our pious efforts. It was brought about by sin and, if it prevails, makes sin.”

The Council of Trent favors Augustine’s opinion in its decree on original sin, where it teaches that concupiscence is called “sin” by the Apostle because it is from sin and inclines toward sin. To incline toward evil, however, is proper to a vicious habit, which continually drives a person toward depraved acts.

Nor were there lacking many scholastics who vigorously defended the opinion of Augustine just cited. Peter Aureolus, a man of exceptionally acute intellect, writes in book II, distinction 30, article 2:

> “The habitual rebellion of the sensitive appetite is not in us simply by the nature of the sensitive appetite [Col. 0603C] alone. I say this because of the opinion of certain people who say that the appetite, even if left in its pure natural state, would still possess that habitual rebellion. I say that in itself it is indifferent to obeying or not obeying reason; but through something added—for example, through a morbid quality—it becomes disobedient to reason. This conclusion could be proved by authorities and arguments, for it is the express opinion of Augustine.”

Our own Gregory of Rimini vigorously defends the same opinion of the holy doctor, in book II, distinction 30, question 1, article 2, where he says:

> “The Master followed this opinion of Augustine, as is evident in this distinction 30 and those that follow, where he treats this subject; and many ancient and modern doctors likewise follow it.”

Thus, according to Aureolus, only certain people held the opinion contrary to Augustine, whereas, according to Gregory, many ancient and modern writers of that period adhered to the holy doctor.

This led the most distinguished scholastics of the Nominalist school, from ancient times and in accordance with Augustine’s positions, to defend that famous “morbid quality.” Of the more recent writers, let Father Macedo alone stand for all. In book IV of *The Keys of Saint Peter*, chapter 10, part 2, he fortifies the holy doctor’s opinion as solidly as he does everything else.

Indeed, distinguished writers even from the Society have taught that concupiscence is evil and is in no way to be numbered among the works of God. Bellarmine, a great ornament not only of the Society but also of the Catholic Church, entitles chapter 14 of book VI of *On the Loss of Grace* as follows: “It Is Shown against the Pelagians That Concupiscence Is Evil.” He then demonstrates this by several arguments drawn from Augustine.

I shall repeat his eighth argument:

> “It is evil,” he says, “for lower things to resist higher things, for that is contrary to equity and right reason. But on account of concupiscence the lower part of the soul resists the higher part—that is, reason—does not obey the law of the mind, and opposes the spirit. Who, then, could doubt that it must be called evil?”

This is Augustine’s argument in book V against Julian, chapter 3.

John Bagocius, in book V of *Demonstrations of Christian Doctrine*, disputation 8, chapter 1, section 3, proves Saint Augustine’s opinion by several arguments and concludes:

> “Far be it from any Catholic to believe that God is the author of something so foul and so perversely inciting to evil, since, if He had created a human being with that stimulus of sin without any preceding sin, He would have to be regarded as the author both of that stimulus of sin and of human nature and of all its natural qualities and powers!” [Col. 0604B]

The most learned Father Elisalda agrees with Augustine in this same opinion. While presiding over the theological chair at the Roman College, he dictated the same doctrine. Hence, in the public theses defended by the Fathers of the Society during the summer of 1658, according to custom, the Augustinian opinion was formulated in precisely these words:

> “This concupiscence, under which name many things are included that can be reduced to one, is by its nature either a part of sin or an effect of sin. In human nature it is a vice, indeed a corruption and infirmity, and in no way its natural constitution and [Col. 0604C] composition. It consists in a certain depraved and corrupted habit, which is called a languor of the soul; and in the same way it is to be reduced, or not reduced, to the category of quality and of bodily infirmity, whose mode it imitates. A component of this habit is the disordered relation of the powers of the soul among themselves, and the non-subjection of the lower part to the higher.”

The holy doctor also amassed many arguments against Julian, who defended concupiscence, and at times he stings and ridicules the heretic with sharp wit. The same heretic, as Augustine testifies in book II *Against Julian*, chapter 7, labors throughout book II and the first part of book III against the first book of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, which Augustine had sent to Valerius in support of the cause he had undertaken. The holy Father refutes him in books IV and V [Col. 0604D] of that earlier work.

I shall present one or two of his arguments on this matter. In book IV, chapter 13, he presses the point as follows:

> “For two goods that come from God the Father cannot fight against each other; but continence and concupiscence do fight against each other. Answer which of these you would rather have come from the Father. I see what distress you are suffering: you favor concupiscence, but you are ashamed of continence.”

This is confirmed first from book V, chapter 7:

> “There is no conflict without evil. For whenever there is a conflict, either good fights against evil, or evil against evil; or, if two goods fight against each other, the conflict itself is a great evil.”

Since continence fights against concupiscence, Augustine there deduces that concupiscence is evil. Hence he says:

> “You are still not awake enough to understand that it is not our nature but a vice against which we fight by virtue.” [Col. 0605A]

It is confirmed secondly in the same place:

> “For when lust conquers, the devil also conquers; when lust is conquered, the devil also is conquered. The one whom lust conquers, and by whom it is conquered, is its enemy. But the one with whom it conquers and is conquered is its author.”

The force of these arguments consists in this: God’s gifts support and perfect one another. They are multiplied, not so that earlier gifts may be destroyed by later ones, but so that they may be increased by a new accumulation through those later gifts. Thus hope strengthens faith, and charity strengthens both. For later gifts are given as a reward for good works, and through them the subject is made better.

Since continence is a gift of God, as Augustine proves from the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 7, in book I of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 3, it follows that concupiscence cannot be a natural gift of God, but must be merely a vice and defect.

Another argument that the holy doctor presses against Julian is this: no work of God is a matter of shame; but concupiscence is a matter of shame; therefore it is not a work of God and consequently is not a natural perfection.

The major premise is certain. For God saw everything that He had made, and it was very good (Genesis 1:31). What is good, however, is not a matter of shame but of glory and praise.

Let Augustine be heard in book II of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 9:

> “For what could God have made that its herald would be ashamed to mention? And, what is more serious, that a human being should be ashamed of some work which not a human being but God made in the human being, when all craftsmen work with as much labor and skill as they can so as not to be ashamed of their works.” [Col. 0605C]

Now that concupiscence is a matter of embarrassment and shame is more certain and more evident than anything that could be established by another argument. The holy doctor writes in the same work, chapter 5:

> “Even those who first covered their shameful parts were ashamed of this concupiscence. Those parts had not previously been shameful, but were to be proclaimed and gloried in as works of God. They covered them, then, when they became ashamed; and they became ashamed when, after their disobedience, they felt their disobedient members.”

Augustine also treats this very subject repeatedly in the *Unfinished Work*.

Indeed, he subtly and sharply attacks Julian, who praised concupiscence while at the same time fighting against it—pretending by his praise that it was good, but testifying by his struggle that it was evil. Since Augustine’s arguments are armed on every side with barbs, by which the heretic is not merely pricked but struck, I shall append some of them here.

Thus, at the beginning of book IV, he writes:

> “By praising this evil against me, you appear to be my adversary; but by fighting it within yourself, you are my witness. If, however, you do not fight it, you are your own enemy.”

The statement in book III, chapter 21, is longer, but it is wholly sprinkled with wit:

> “Perhaps, then, you pretend to praise it because you do not pretend to fight it. For how you can faithfully do these two things at once, I do not see: praise it as a friend and attack it as an enemy. We believe one of these things, but choose which one we are to believe. If you fight wholeheartedly, you do not praise wholeheartedly; but if you act sincerely in your praise, you are merely playing in battle.” [Col. 0606A]

And afterward:

> “I would rather you deceitfully praise concupiscence than deceitfully attack it. For it is more tolerable that your tongue should lie than your life; more tolerable that you should pretend in your opinion than in your continence. You fabricate praise by which you are an adversary of my opinion, if you do not fabricate the chastity by which you are an adversary of your own concupiscence.”

Again, in the final chapter of the same book, he presses Julian in this way:

> “Why do you praise those against whom you fight? How am I to believe that you conquer your enemies by virtue when you do not dare to tear them apart in words? If both of us conquer concupiscence, why do we not both condemn it? Since you boast that you conquer it by continence, why do you not wish to condemn it in your judgment?” [Col. 0606B]

Because the Pelagians especially professed continence, by which they waged war against concupiscence, Augustine cleverly brings their continence itself under suspicion of hypocrisy, adding in the same place:

> “Your war is hidden; your friendship is visible. From what is visible, you make what is hidden suspect. For what do you want us to believe about the war you wage secretly, when we see your friendship openly? How do you want us to think that you are fighting against the sting of lust when you fill your books with praise of lust? But behold, I overcome my suspicion: I believe that you attack what you praise, but I grieve that you praise what you attack.”

Furthermore, in book III, chapter 21:

> “You wish to conquer concupiscence by attacking it, whereas I wish to conquer it by praising it. But I answer: Let the one who fights judge the one who praises, so that the latter may be conquered. If it is evil, why does he praise it? If it is good, why does he attack it? But if it is neither good nor evil, why does he praise it, and why does he attack it? Therefore, as long as you are the attacker of lust, you will be the judge on my behalf against yourself. Or perhaps you will not fight against lust, lest you be defeated in this conflict that you have with me, saying to yourself: ‘It is better not to fight than to show by fighting that what I praise is evil.’ Do not do this, I beg you. For who am I, whom you desire to conquer as though it were a great achievement? Let truth conquer you instead, so that you may conquer lust,” and so forth.

Therefore, as though his adversary had been struck down, Augustine taunts him:

> “My victory over you is secure, since that evil is fighting with you.”

Book IV, chapter 2.

The holy doctor also attacked the Pelagians’ opinion on the grounds that they praised continence, even though it was the enemy of concupiscence. He often presses this point against Julian no less elegantly than wittily:

> “For two goods that come from God the Father cannot fight against each other; but continence and concupiscence do fight against each other. Answer which of these you would rather have come from the Father. I see what distress you are suffering: you favor concupiscence, but you are ashamed of continence. Let your shame prevail, and by it let your error be conquered.”

Book IV, chapter 13.

He wittily reinforces the same point in chapter 14:

> “As timid in war, you try to praise both of the combatants who are waging war against each other, as though you feared to have one as your enemy because it might conquer the other.”

Since Julian professed himself a devotee of continence—for he was a bishop—Augustine ridiculed him for acting as a praiser of lust:

> “A most courageous man—not indeed an administrator, but certainly an encourager and preacher—of nocturnal wars.”

Book V, chapter 7. Yet Augustine urged him to abandon that perverse opinion:

> “I ask you: if this lust, as we believe, causes you only the trouble of resisting and offers no pleasure at all, why do you think that so great a reward of praise should be paid to it, even if the praise is false?”

Book III of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 76. He adds in chapter 87:

> “Will it love you more for that reason? You are completely mistaken. It does not love the human being; rather, it plainly goads him to love what he ought not to love.”

I see two responses given to each of the holy Augustine’s arguments.

First, Julian said that two things must be distinguished in concupiscence: the natural power and inclination by which the species is propagated through generation, and the excess of that same power, by which human beings are also driven toward dishonorable and illicit things. The former, he said, is good, a gift of God, and praiseworthy, and is not a source of shame; the latter is something vicious and blameworthy.

Moraines followed this response of Julian. Other more recent writers, ashamed to speak in Julian’s words, try to escape by another route. They say that concupiscence is a gift of God, but a gift accompanied by some imperfection, since everything created is defective. Chastity, they say, fights against and resists the imperfections of concupiscence, and is ashamed of and troubled by those imperfections. From this they maintain that it does not follow that the thing to which those imperfections are attached is evil—just as the will is capable of sin because of its imperfection, since it comes from nothing, and yet we are not ashamed of it, nor do we say that it is itself evil or a natural vice.

But neither response is sufficient to weaken the force of Augustine’s arguments.

The holy doctor often refutes Julian’s and Moraines’s first response. In book V against Julian, chapter 7, he says:

> “What does it help you that you appear to criticize the excess of that whose movement you approve? For it exceeds the permitted limit when one yields to its movements, because resistance is made to evil, lest the good of chastity perish if one does not resist this evil.”

The point is acute: concupiscence is evil precisely because it drives toward evil. For this is the property of a vicious habit—to incline toward an evil act.

Hence Father Macedo, with excellent justification, uses the example of a vicious habit which Suarez, in *Metaphysics*, disputation 44, section 13, number 26, denies can be produced by God in a human being, because God would thereby incline that person toward evil. Macedo presses the same doctor while conceding that concupiscence could be produced by God in a human being in the state of pure nature.

Moreover, Augustine says in book IV, chapter 14:

> “To prevent the evil of excess, one must resist the evil of desiring. Therefore there are two evils: one that we possess, and another that we commit if we do not resist the evil that we possess.”

Likewise, in book III, chapter 20, he says:

> “Then you begin to argue about the excess of concupiscence, which you call blameworthy, as though, when a married person uses it well, the very horse itself—which is evil—were to be praised, rather than its driver.”

Hence the same Father writes in book I of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 70:

> “If you consent to it, recognize the evil by sinning; if you resist it, recognize the evil by fighting.”

Furthermore, in book IV of the same work, chapter 41:

> “Behold, then, you say that God established a measure for lust in the human being. Why does it not remain within the measure in which it was divinely established, but exceed it unless restrained? How, then, can that be called good which urges and compels a human being to do evil?”

And he concludes:

> “Therefore the excess of lust is in sin, but its impulse also is in crime”—that is, in a vice functioning as a habit.

Nor can the second response be accepted. For imperfection consists in the privation and absence of perfection and actuality, whereas the impulsive power of concupiscence toward evil explains a stronger causality. It therefore cannot be constituted in mere privation, which can efficiently cause nothing, but only as a pure terminus *a quo*, as the Aristotelians teach.

Thus, just as a vicious habit, insofar as it moves more efficaciously toward depraved acts, signifies a greater intensity of its being, so concupiscence, insofar as it more powerfully excites a person toward every kind of dishonorable act, displays a greater intensity of its actuality.

Furthermore, the same response is refuted because every natural virtue or passion has some good movements; for natural goodness is known posteriorly from this fact. But concupiscence has no good acts, as Augustine proves in book IV against Julian, chapter 2. For in the continent saints concupiscence produces no good acts:

> “What, then, does it do there, where whatever it does is evil, as soon as one consents to it and it carries the matter through? What does this concupiscence do there, where nothing good is desired through it? What does lust do there, where nothing good will be desired through it?”

Read more there. [Col. 0608C]

You may say that continent saints voluntarily deprive themselves of the more perfect good acts of concupiscence, which they could licitly perform if they married. Augustine destroys this response in that same second chapter, saying:

> “Conjugal chastity restrains concupiscence when it longs to experience pleasure either from what is illicit or from what is licit: it restrains it from the illicit and permits it with respect to the licit. This is good, but it is not the good of concupiscence; it is the good of the person who uses it well. But for concupiscence itself to burn indifferently toward what is licit or illicit is evil. Conjugal chastity therefore uses this evil well.”

Indeed, Augustine consistently taught everywhere that married people make good use of an evil. He proved this again from the fact that concupiscence in married persons drives toward evil, excites pregnant women, and rises up toward every lustful act.

> “It should not improperly be said,” he writes in the same place, “that it exists in married persons. For if they occupy the highest summit of conjugal chastity, they do something good through it, although they do nothing because of it.”

Certainly, the holy doctor nowhere called concupiscence good, but everywhere called it evil. Thus it becomes entirely evident that it is evil according to its proper essence, not merely according to an accompanying imperfection, as those more recent writers contend.

Indeed, he often presses against Julian the point that, once concupiscence is admitted as having been inserted into human beings from their first creation, the heresy of the Manichaeans is promoted. For when they see that concupiscence is evil and that a good God cannot be established as the author of evil, they immediately introduce an evil god as the creator of evil concupiscence.

This is Augustine’s line of argument in book I against Julian, chapter 8 and following; book V, chapter 16; and in the *Unfinished Work*, book III, chapters 178, 208, and 213; book V, chapter 30; and book VI, chapters 5 and 36.

I shall give one testimony from the same book VI, chapter 6:

> “But you, who do not know what you are saying, charge me with saying that God creates sin. Resist the Manichaean who says that, in the conflict between flesh and spirit, contrary natures—one evil and one good—appear in opposition to each other. This is the one answer we give, so that this plague may be overcome: namely, that the discord of the first human being was turned into our nature. By denying this, you attempt to make those contrary natures prevail, and you plainly reveal yourself to be a pretended opponent and a genuine helper of the Manichaeans.”

In chapter 14 he also develops the same point at length and learnedly.

The example that these same writers offer from the will—namely, that it is liable to sin because of its nothingness, from which it originates—is irrelevant. For the will elicits many good acts, which are good and praiseworthy in their natural order; hence it is known to be good itself.

Concupiscence, however, has no good acts. It does not produce acts directed only toward a licit end, but boils over toward every illicit object; the will, by contrast, fixes the goal of its act upon an honorable end, so that it does not break out toward forbidden things.

They object that Augustine said in book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 9:

> “Even if ignorance and difficulty”—he is speaking of the difficulty arising from concupiscence—“were the natural beginnings of the human being, God would still not be blamed but praised.”

“Therefore,” they say, “according to Augustine, God would have to be praised even if He had created the human being without perfect subjection of concupiscence.”

They sing a victory song over this one testimony of Augustine, which they claim is so clear, although the holy doctor asserts the contrary in innumerable passages and did not teach their opinion there, as they mistakenly suppose.

For in that passage the holy doctor was disputing against the Manichaeans, who said that concupiscence was evil and that it was impossible for a human being to be produced without it. Since it could not be created by a good God, they devised some evil nature that produced all evils.

To refute them, Augustine admitted both hypotheses for the sake of argument: namely, that a human being was created with concupiscence, and that it could in no way be created without it. He pressed the heretics by arguing that even then God would have to be praised, since God would bear no fault for doing what could not be done.

That the Manichaeans thought it impossible for a human being to be created without the evil of concupiscence is attested by the holy doctor in book I against Julian, chapter 5, and book III, chapter 12.

Therefore, in that hypothesis, God would still have to be praised, as Augustine proves in book III of *On Free Choice of the Will*.

Hence he writes in book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 9:

> “This discussion is directed against the Manichaeans, who do not accept the holy Scriptures of the Old Testament, in which original sin is related.”

He continues:

> “Against the Pelagians, however, what both Scriptures commend must be defended, since they profess to accept them.”

That is, the evil of concupiscence was not inserted into the human being by God at the first creation, because God made the human being upright (Ecclesiastes 7). He repeatedly insists upon this testimony against the Pelagians: in book XIV of *The City of God*, chapter 11; book XIII, chapter 14; *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 6; Letter 105 to Sixtus; book IV of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 44; and elsewhere.

Concupiscence, however, removed the human being’s uprightness and made him inclined—indeed, precipitate—toward illicit things.

In addition to this testimony, Augustine also employed another celebrated passage from chapter 40 of Ecclesiasticus: “A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb,” and so forth. He repeats this in almost every page of the *Unfinished Work*, proving that God would have to be accused of injustice if, without any preceding fault, He had burdened a human being with the yoke of conquering concupiscence. For this is the greatest misery, and the human being experiences it as a severe punishment. But every punishment is inflicted unjustly if no fault has merited it.

Thus, the hypothesis that Augustine admitted in disputing with the Manichaeans for the sake of argument, far from proving it in his books against the Pelagians, he actually demolished it with the strongest arguments.

Julian amassed many arguments to prove that concupiscence is a natural perfection of the human being, that it is good, and that only its excess is blameworthy.

In book IV of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 56, he uses the argument that concupiscence is a natural perfection of animals and a good thing that serves the propagation of their species. Hence, he says, it ought likewise to be called a perfection of the human being insofar as the human being agrees with brute animals in the sensory level.

Again, in book I of the same *Unfinished Work*, chapter 70, he argues that concupiscence existed before sin. For Adam sinned because his sensitive appetite desired the forbidden fruit.

Furthermore, if concupiscence is the punishment of sin, then it must be praised; it is good and honorable, since it is good and honorable for a sinner to be punished. Thus he argues in Augustine, book V of the earlier work, chapter 4.

Finally, he proves by the example of food that its excess is blameworthy. For just as food is good while its use can be evil, so concupiscence is good even though its abuse is evil. This argument appears in the holy Father, book III, chapter 20, and book I of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 19.

Augustine responds to the first point that concupiscence is a perfection in animals because it conforms to their nature and does not conflict with the spirit in brute creatures.

In his book *On Original Sin*, chapter 40, he says:

> “For the human being is of such great excellence in comparison with the animal that what is a vice in the human being is the nature of the animal.”

And in book IV of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 56:

> “Thus, if you do not have the soul of an ass, recognize in lust both the nature of the animal and the punishment of the human being.”

There he also notes that concupiscence in brute animals does not lust after pregnant females or after acts contrary to nature, as it does in the human being. Therefore lust is far worse in the human being than in brute animals.

To the second point he responds in the same place by denying that, in the earthly paradise, an act of concupiscence preceded the act of the will by which Adam desired to eat the forbidden fruit. I give his words:

> “An evil will preceded it—the will by which he believed the deceitful serpent—and an evil concupiscence followed, by which he desired the illicit food. Thus, although both were already evil, desire led the will, not the will desire; desire neither preceded the will nor resisted the will.” [Col. 0611A]

To the third point he denies the inference. Concupiscence, insofar as it is a punishment, is justly imposed by God; but it is evil with respect to the human being upon whom it is inflicted. Thus death is evil for the human being but good with respect to God, who decrees it as punishment for sin.

He adds the example of blindness of heart, by which God, as judge, punishes offenders for their past crimes, although that blindness is their greatest evil. He concludes:

> “Therefore, everything you have said in support of your blind and thoughtless opinion—that because we say carnal concupiscence is the punishment of sin, you have thought it should not only not be blamed but even praised—has certainly vanished, however lengthy a discussion you have devoted to it.”

To the fourth point Augustine responds in book III against Julian, chapter 20:
