> “You do not understand what you are saying to such an extent that you do not see that the creature of bread and wine does not desire against the spirit, but is itself rather desired dishonorably by those who use it badly, and enters our body from outside.”

Hence no one is ashamed to eat openly in public, as was once the Roman custom; yet married people are ashamed to use concupiscence openly even licitly. This clearly shows that concupiscence is evil, since even its licit use causes shame.

See the holy Father, book I to Boniface, chapter 16. [Col. 0611C]

More recent writers object against this same opinion of the holy doctor.

The movements of concupiscence precede reason because they occur before every choice. Therefore, they say, concupiscence is not wholly subject to reason, since it has movements prior to every act of reason.

Again, they argue that the human being is carried toward honorable things by the rational appetite, but toward pleasant things by the sensitive appetite, or concupiscence. Therefore the latter longs for pleasant things with a more vehement impulse than the former desires honorable things, since honorable objects are represented through alien species and consequently move less strongly, whereas pleasant things attract the senses immediately through their proper species.

Finally, they insist: nothing that belongs to nature by right is lost through sin; but the subjection of the lower part to the rational appetite has been lost; therefore that subjection is not a perfection owed to nature. [Col. 0611D]

These objections, however, were refuted long ago by Augustine.

To the first he responds that the movements of concupiscence precede the deliberation of the rational appetite only as a punishment for sin. If the human being had not sinned, the movements of the sensitive appetite would indeed have preceded the acts of the will, but they would not have imposed force upon the will, seized reason with a more violent impulse, or overwhelmed it, as in fact happens. Rather, they would have attracted it gently, as also occurred in paradise, where “desire did not lead the will, nor precede the will, nor resist the will,” book I of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 70.

To the second, the consequence is denied. For right order requires that the lower be moved by the higher, not the higher by the lower. Hence the best constitution of the human being requires that the higher part have full authority over the lower, not that the lower subject and overthrow the higher.

It belongs to the punishment and misery of the human being that, like an animal, he is drawn more powerfully by what is pleasant than by what is honorable. This arises from ignorance, which is another vice derived from original sin into the human race. For if the honorable were perfectly represented to the will, the will would not abandon it for what is pleasant.

Thus, in that disproportion and greater force by which, in the state of fallen nature, the pleasant draws more strongly than the honorable, the rebellion of the sensitive appetite against the rational appetite consists.

Augustine writes as follows in book V against Julian, chapter 3:

> “If you understood this wisely, you would surely see that there is an injustice by which the lower part of the human being resists the higher and better part.”

The third argument is worthless. For according to Augustine’s opinion, it is false that natural things remained intact after the first sin. Through sin, the human being was stripped of gratuitous gifts and was also wounded in his natural faculties. This is suggested by the parable of the traveler to Jericho in Luke 10, which Archbishop Florentius Conrius expounds through almost an entire volume.

Father Macedo indicates Augustine’s testimonies on this matter in his *Curtain*, thesis 34, and in book IV of *The Keys of Peter*, in the discussion of original sin, chapter 12, where he vigorously contends in support of the holy doctor’s opinion.

One objection seems to stand in the way, and the more recent theologians press it with great force. For this proposition of Baius was condemned [Col. 0612C], proposition 55: “God could not have created such a man at the beginning as is now born.” Therefore God could have created man in a state of pure nature, subject to concupiscence such as that in which he is now born.

Theologians differ in their interpretation of these propositions of Baius. Father Vasquez, a man of great repute among the more recent theologians, in *1–2*, disp. 190, chap. 18, sets out the words of the bull, which are as follows:

> “Having weighed these propositions, strictly examined before us, although some of them might in some manner be maintained, nevertheless, in the strict and proper sense of the words intended by their authors, we condemn them, respectively, as heretical, erroneous, suspect, rash, scandalous, and offensive to pious ears; and whatever has been issued concerning them, whether orally or in writing, we condemn by the authority of these present letters.”

Concerning this censure he judges as follows:

> “Many of them contain a harsh judgment by which that doctor [Baius] accused the opinions of others. They were condemned merely as exposed to scandal and offense, and were prohibited only on that account. For boldness and excessive arrogance in maliciously picking at and tearing apart the opinions of others are accustomed to cause no little scandal, from which learned and prudent theologians ought to abstain in their writings.”

This is confirmed by the most weighty testimony of Cardinal Francisco Toledo, who was delegated by the Apostolic See to Louvain in the case of Baius. Since Baius accused of Pelagian heresy those who asserted that a man such as is now born could have been created by God, his proposition was subjected to censure on account of the mark of infamy that he stamped upon the authors of the opposing opinion.

This is evident from the censures of the same man that are reported in the same bull. For example, concerning proposition 37 he says:

> “He who acknowledges something naturally good—that is, something arising from the powers of nature alone—has a view consonant with Pelagius.”

Vasquez defends this interpretation in *1–2*, disp. 190, chap. 18, where he testifies that it was Baius’s censure, not the proposition itself, that was condemned by the Apostolic See, since canon 22 of the Council of Orange says: “No one has anything of his own except falsehood and sin.”

Furthermore, proposition 13 is written as follows:

> “It is the opinion of Pelagius that a good work performed without the grace of adoption is not meritorious of the kingdom of heaven.”

Since the Louvain author, in his customary manner, accused the opposing opinion concerning the creation of man with concupiscence implanted by the Author of nature of being unmistakably Pelagian, his proposition was rightly proscribed as scandalous on account of that censure.

Again, in the bull of Baius the propositions are said to be condemned “respectively,” that is, in the proper sense of the words intended by their authors. That proposition 55 is condemned with reference to proposition 27, which reads:

> “The original integrity of creation was not an undue exaltation of human nature, but its natural condition.”

The implication is that subjection to concupiscence did not come from the Creator’s gift, but from the natural exigency of the human substance, as though it were its proper passion. This is false. For two things must be distinguished: whether subjection to concupiscence was given to the first man by the exigency of a created thing, or merely from what may be called propriety or fittingness. The first we deny; the second we assert. This is clear from Augustine, who writes in *Against Julian*, book III, chapter 11:

> “In human nature before sin there ought to have been peace, not war.”

I know that the same author writes the following concerning our first parents in *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book II, chapter 22:

> “Although they bore an animal body, they felt nothing disobedient moving within it against themselves. For the order of justice brought this about: since their soul had received a servant-body from the Lord, just as the soul itself obeyed its Lord, so the body obeyed and offered to it a service suited to life, without any resistance.”

By the term “justice” he did not mean a strict obligation founded in human nature, but something deriving from the mere fittingness established by the Creator.

It should further be known that some ambiguous propositions are at one time rejected by the Church and at another time approved. We demonstrated this in book II of the *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 20, concerning the proposition, “One of the Trinity suffered.” Hormisdas rejected it, whereas John II, Vigilius, and the Fifth Council defined it as Catholic. It was condemned in the Eutychian sense, as though the Word had suffered in the divine nature. Although some added “in the flesh,” nevertheless, because of its affinity with the heresy of Eutyches, it was suspect, and holy Hormisdas rightly refused to approve it.

Baius is said to have taught the following in proposition 74:

> “Concupiscence in the regenerate who have fallen back into mortal sin, in whom it now reigns, is sin.”

This is utterly false, for concupiscence itself is never sin, as is clear from the Council of Trent. Therefore that proposition of Baius [Col. 0614A] was condemned not only on account of the censure, but also because it agreed with the error of recent heretics condemned by the Tridentine Fathers. For they stubbornly maintain that concupiscence is sin, as is evident in Bellarmine, *On the Loss of Grace*, book V, chapter 5.

Proposition 55 of Baius is founded on this error insofar as it concerns concupiscence, yet we are very far removed from its condemned meaning. We do not say that God could not have created man with rebellious concupiscence because concupiscence is formally sin; rather, although it is not itself sin, it inclines toward sin, and indeed more vehemently than any other vicious habit contracted by man.

Certainly, Baius’s thesis—that man could not have been produced by God in the condition in which he is now born—is true according to his fuller expression. For who would say that God could create man with original sin, with which he is now born? This was precisely the absurdity that the Pelagians pressed against the orthodox: that God would be the author of sin if man were born infected by it.

Martin de Esparza, an eminent theologian of our age, writes as follows in question 10 of *On Grace*:

> “After sin, concupiscence has been so released that it reigns in the flesh of sin—that is, it obtains predominance against reason, its inclination toward evil, destruction, and the condemnation of man outweighing the inclination of the higher reason toward honest good, salvation, and the final happiness of that same man. Such and so great an evil of the lower part’s seizure of kingship against the higher part would by no means have existed in a state of pure nature.”

Therefore, according to this author, man could not have been created by God in a state of pure nature with concupiscence predominating over reason and exercising legislative power over it, as he says there in the sixth argument, although in fact man is born subject to such concupiscence.

Thus far concerning the meaning of Baius’s proposition 55.

It may be asked whether the holy Doctor admitted as possible a concupiscence subject to reason, so that he denied that it could have been implanted in the first man according to his condition, not in itself, but only in its predominance over reason.

I answer that Augustine regarded concupiscence in itself as a vice, and not merely as something corrupted. Thus he pronounced it a vice that is not from God in *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book I, chapter 23. He says the same in book II, chapter 34, and frequently in his works against the Pelagians.

Nevertheless, he said that this would have been sufficient for him if the heretics had at least conceded that it was corrupted, since the wound of original sin would immediately have appeared from that concession. The holy Doctor writes in the last chapter of book II of *Against Julian*, cited above:

> “And if he does not wish to concede that lust is a vice, let him at least say that, through the disobedience of those men, that very vice too is the concupiscence of the flesh, so that what once moved obediently and in an orderly manner now moves disobediently and disorderly,” etc.

And in *Against Julian*, book V, chapter 5, he says:

> “But when you say that even the genital organs serve the command of the mind, you are speaking of a certain new lust—or perhaps one exceedingly ancient, such as might also have existed in paradise if no one had sinned.”

And in *The Unfinished Work*, book II, chapter 122, he writes concerning concupiscence:

> “Either there was none there, or it neither preceded nor exceeded the will of the mind.”

He repeats the same in book IV, chapter 56, and in book IV of the earlier work, chapters 5 and 14.

Nevertheless, the holy Doctor consistently held that there was no concupiscence in the first man before sin—not merely no concupiscence according to that tyrannical power over reason, but none at all, even if subject to reason. This is proved from *Against Julian*, book IV, chapter 11, where he says:

> “For who denies that there would have been intercourse even if sin had not preceded it? But it would have occurred with the genital organs moved by the will, just as the other members, not aroused by lust; or certainly even with lust itself—so that we do not become excessively distressed about it—not such as it is now, but serving at the command of the will.”

See chapter 14.

And in book V, chapter 7, he taunts his adversaries with these words:

> “But behold, we are not contending with you concerning the presence or absence of lust, nor do we offend the affection that we see you ought to have for it—provided only that in that place of happiness you subject it to the command of the will.”

The holy Doctor treats this same matter in book I of *To Boniface*, chapter 17, where he assigns four ways in which the fruitfulness of marriage could have been accomplished. The last two are:

> “Either then lust would have arisen at the command of the will, whenever chaste modesty perceived that intercourse was necessary; or, with no lust existing there at all, the genital organs too, like the other members, each for its own function, would have served without any difficulty the commands of those who willed.”

Afterward, concerning these two alternatives, he says:

> “Whichever of the remaining two you choose, there is no need to labor in any dispute against you. For even if you do not wish to choose the fourth, in which all the members obey, with complete tranquility and without any lust—since the force of your disputes has already made you hostile to it—you will at least approve what we placed third.”

The entire chapter should be read. For from it it is evident that the holy Doctor thought there had been no concupiscence in the earthly paradise, and admitted concupiscence subject to the will only for the sake of argument, so as not to distress his adversaries too much concerning it, as we have just quoted from the same passage. [Col. 0615D]

Augustine wrote these things about concupiscence, proving them from 1 John, chapter II, verse 16: “The concupiscence of the flesh is not from the Father.” The Pelagians interpreted this text as referring to forbidden acts of concupiscence.

How absurd the holy Father regarded their opinion may be gathered from what he writes in *The Unfinished Work*, book IV, chapter 69:

> “Therefore,” he says, “evil works are not avoided unless evil concupiscence is restrained—which you, with HORRIBLE SHAMELESSNESS, or rather MADNESS, call good. You are neither ashamed nor horrified that you have reached SUCH DISGRACE, so that no one is freed from your evil unless he does not consent to your good. Therefore the concupiscence of the flesh, by which forbidden things are desired, is not from the Father. In vain you think—or rather wish it to be thought—that when the Apostle John said this, he placed the concupiscence of the flesh for lust. Certainly, if lust is not from the Father, neither is that from which lust is conceived and brought forth when one consents to it. For whatever it tries to obtain by its movements, I ask, is it not trying to arrive at lust? How, then, is that good which tries to arrive at evil? How is that our good which compels us toward evil?”

Read more in the same place.

## § III. Whether Saint Augustine Went Too Far in Deriving the Guilt of Original Sin from the Countless Miseries of Human Life. An Outstanding Testimony of Thomas Aquinas in Favor of the Augustinian Position

I proceed to the second alleged excess of Saint Augustine. In order to refute the Pelagians, he not only sought testimony from the sacred mysteries, but, being a man of subtle and ready intellect, also employed arguments evident by the natural light of reason.

Among his other arguments, the great Doctor found a particularly famous one by which to establish original sin: he inferred it from the countless miseries of human life. Thus, appealing to the saying of Ecclesiasticus, chapter XL, at the beginning—“A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb”—he argued that, in order to preserve God’s justice, some crime must be affirmed in those who are born, lest innocent persons be thought to be punished with so many miseries.

This argument occurs everywhere in Augustine—not merely in his books, but on nearly every page of his books. In *The Unfinished Work*, book VI, chapter 36, he heaps together the following statements:

> “But what is every punishment of man except the punishment of the image of God? If it is inflicted unjustly, then surely the one by whom it is inflicted is unjust. Who, moreover, would doubt that punishment is unjustly inflicted upon the image of God, unless guilt had deserved it?”

And in chapter 27:

> “God is just, as you continually say against yourself and do not understand. God is just, I say, and therefore he would neither make nor permit those being born to become wretched unless he knew them to be guilty.”

Again:

> “They, as you suppose, carry no sin with them; yet, if this is so, they undoubtedly endure punishments undeservedly. Where is the justice of God? If you considered it, you would never believe that those being born could be so wretched without any merit of original sin.”

Moraines responds in disp. 13, no. 106, that Augustine, in proving original sin from the miseries of human life, “went too far, carried away by the fervor of disputation, and, out of hatred for the Pelagian heresy, inclined toward the opposite extreme; nor did the Church approve his teaching in this respect.”

It is agreeable that he did not say that Augustine sometimes inclined toward the extreme, for he would have to be said to have inclined toward it everywhere, since he calls this argument one that had been made so often and would have to be made still more often, in chapter 23 of the sixth book mentioned above.

Therefore Augustine used this argument knowingly, deliberately, and willingly—not driven by the heat and fury of disputation, as his adversaries claim. Indeed, the Pelagians exerted all their strength to escape the same argument, as is clear from Julian’s work, book VI, chapter 25, where, mocking the Augustinian reasoning, he says:

> “But why should we think that we must follow only the reasoning of such a stunned truth, when the phalanx of our enemies relies upon the very dangers of events and rises up against us with the support of miseries? For he wishes to prove by the shame of intercourse, the pain of childbirth, and the sweat of labor that guilt and punishments are transmitted into the seeds, so that by these signs—the difficulty of childbirth, the sweat of farmers, and the breaking up of new fields—the natural crime may be believed, on account of which the human race is exercised through so many hardships.”

There was therefore a deliberate controversy over this argument between the Pelagians and Augustine, especially since Augustine refuted everything Julian opposed in order to weaken it, as is evident from book VI of the work mentioned above.

As for what they write—that the Church did not approve Augustine’s teaching on this matter—their learning is exposed by the fact that they fail to notice that the same teaching was consecrated by decrees of both the Roman Pontiff and the councils.

Pope Saint Gelasius, in letter 7 to the bishops throughout Picenum, employs the same Augustinian argument against a certain Pelagian named Seneca in order to prove original sin:

> “Therefore,” he says, “he was excluded from the splendor of his happiness and, by a heavenly utterance, condemned to thorns, thistles, and manifold miseries. Such a punishment, certainly, would by no means have been inflicted upon one persevering in the good by a just judgment, and it would be proved to have been imposed only when it was FITTINGLY INFLICTED FOR EVIL.”

Behold the words of Augustine faithfully echoed by the Apostolic See.

The same thing is taught by the Council of the African Fathers exiled in Sardinia, in *On the Incarnation and Grace*, chapter 14:

> “If, then,” they say, “there are some who strive to assert that only death, and not sin as well, passed from the first man into the human race, it is astonishing if they do not understand by what snares they bind themselves through their own position. First, because they call God unjust in causing infants to die, whom they themselves do not wish to be polluted by any contagion of original sin.”

Again:

> “By what justice, then, does the just God inflict punishment upon infants born without sin, in whom he finds no cause of punishment?” etc.

Furthermore, the Second Council of Orange says in canon 2:

> “If anyone asserts that Adam’s transgression harmed only himself and not his descendants, or certainly testifies that only bodily death, which is the punishment of sin, and not also sin, which is the death of the soul, passed through one man into the entire human race, he attributes injustice to God.”

Therefore, whoever says that the greatest of miseries—namely, death—befalls man without sin makes God unjust. This is Saint Augustine’s argument.

Some people, seeing this text of Orange, respond that death could not have been inflicted upon man under the aspect of punishment without guilt, without injustice on God’s part; but that God could have created the human race, without injustice, in a state of pure nature, without the gift of immortality and subject to natural death.

But this response is worthless. For the Pelagians said that death was natural to man from his bodily composition and was not inflicted upon him as a punishment. Against them, the Council of Orange, following Augustine, concludes that if bodily death passed without sin into Adam’s descendants, God is made unjust by the Pelagians.

For the fact that death is an evil under the aspect of punishment was a consequence drawn against the heretics. As punishment, it necessarily presupposes sin, from which it is called penal by an extrinsic denomination. But the Fathers insisted that death itself, from its very gravity, and the other miseries preceding it, was an extremely serious evil, in order to infer that it could justly have been inflicted only as a punishment. Otherwise they would have presupposed in their premise what the Pelagians absolutely denied.

Other Fathers subscribe to the same argument.

Saint Prosper, *Against the Collations*, chapter 20:

> “For it is exceedingly impious to think this concerning God’s justice: that he wished those who were free from transgression to be condemned together with the guilty. Guilt is therefore evident where punishment is not hidden, and participation in punishment proves participation in sin, so that what belongs to human misery comes not from the Creator’s institution but from the Judge’s retribution.”

Anselm, *On the Virgin’s Conception and Original Sin*, chapter 13:

> “By the very reasoning,” he says, “by which the rational mind clearly recognizes that God ought not to have made Adam except as just and burdened by no debt or disadvantage, it likewise recognizes that the one whom he produced by his own will and power ought not to be subjected to any evil. For it is exceedingly unfitting to the goodness of the omnipotent and wise God to make a rational creature subject, solely by his own will, to such an evil from matter in which there is no sin.”

Again, in *Why God Became Man*, book II, chapter 2, he says:

> “It is contrary to wisdom and justice to compel one to suffer death without guilt whom he had made just for eternal blessedness.”

Moreover, the very ancient author of the *Hypognosticon*, at the beginning of book II, reasons in the same way:

> “Human nature itself, spread throughout the whole world, bears witness that we are bound by this sentence of punishment, since, in accordance with the testimony of the holy law, it sees itself laboring beneath the torments of its fathers. But by what justice do we suffer this, if we are not heirs of our parents’ sin?”

Read more there.

Again, in book V he says, among other things:

> “According to your error, God, who made nature such that the soul is tormented by penal sufferings, is cruel, or certainly unjust, if he permits holy innocence, entirely free from any fault, to be oppressed by such great dangers and sometimes even deprived of life amid them.”

Augustine, in *Against Julian*, book IV, chapter 12, reporting the opinions of those who, ignorant of original sin, accused God’s equity on account of human misery, says that they saw the matter but did not know its cause. Others said that souls had sinned in an earlier life and were therefore compelled to be born again in order to undergo miseries as punishment. He discusses these views learnedly at the end of the same book.

From these things it is clear that most philosophers, by the light of nature, recognized that an innocent man would be unjustly afflicted with such great miseries.

Therefore Augustine’s argument for establishing original sin was not only approved by the Church, but also by the pagans themselves, at least insofar as concerned the guilt of sin. So evident and exceedingly clear is it even by the natural light alone.

Thus the great Bellarmine, after adducing several arguments for the opposing opinion in book VI of *On the Loss of Grace*, chapter 15, wrote at the end with great learning and sincerity:

> “For it is altogether probable that the supremely good God, who loves our race most dearly, would not have created man as wretched as he now is unless the magnitude of our sin had deserved such punishment.”

He confirms this by the opinion of the pagans cited from Augustine.

Therefore what Bellarmine taught God would never have done out of his love for human beings and his own goodness, Augustine, together with so many Fathers, affirmed that God could not do on account of his justice.

If recent theologians attempt, by means of some interpretation, to explain away the testimonies of Gelasius and the other authorities of the ancient Church, we ask them to do the same with Augustine, whose words alone those authorities echoed. But if they declare that the others too, carried away by the heat of disputation, exceeded the boundary of truth, we shall pass over their words with deaf ears, while so many learned and holy witnesses support Augustine.

Nor should they insist upon the condemnation of Baius’s proposition:

> “God could not have created man at the beginning as he is now born.”

We reply with Gregory of Rimini, *1*, dist. 42, question 1, article 2, response to the second contrary argument of the conclusion:

> “God cannot do something according to justice that he can do according to power.”

Thus there is no impossibility in Judas’s being drawn into heaven, but it would be contrary to God’s justice. Therefore, although it is possible according to power, it is not possible according to justice to create such a man as is now born. The person who denies this understands the proposition only in the former sense, and in that sense agrees with the condemned proposition of Baius.

Certainly, as we said above, God could not at the beginning have created man with original sin, with which he is now born. The condemned proposition must therefore have another meaning, concerning which several things were said in the preceding section and cannot now be repeated.

The Apostolic See, so many Fathers, and especially both councils—the Council of Sardinia and the Council of Orange—used this argument of Saint Augustine. The ignorance or rashness of Moraines should therefore now be sufficiently apparent: either he was ignorant of this, or he involved Augustine and so many great Fathers in the charge of excess.

But let us engage in combat with this scholastic by the testimony of the prince of all scholastics. He is the great disciple of Augustine and the foremost teacher of the most noble school, Saint Thomas, who writes that Augustine derived original sin from the miseries of human life “quite probably.”

Thus the Angelic Teacher, at the beginning of *Against the Gentiles*, book IV, chapter 52, teaches that the miseries of human nature are certain probable signs of original sin, and adds:

> “Someone might nevertheless say that such defects, both bodily and spiritual, are not penal but natural defects resulting necessarily from matter. For the human body, since it is composed of contraries, must be corruptible, and the sensory appetite must be moved toward those things that are pleasurable to the senses, which are sometimes contrary to reason,” etc.

This is precisely the response that recent theologians apply to Saint Augustine’s argument. But the Angelic Doctor immediately refutes it in these words:

> “Nevertheless, if one considers the matter rightly, he will be able to judge QUITE PROBABLY, once divine providence is presupposed—for divine providence has joined things capable of perfection to the perfections suited to each—that God united the higher nature to the lower so that the higher might rule it. If any impediment to this dominion should arise from a defect of nature, it would be removed by God’s special and supernatural gift. Thus, since the rational soul is of a higher nature than the body, it may be believed to have been joined to the body under such a condition that nothing in the body could be contrary to the soul, by which the body lives.”

After saying several other things to the same effect, he concludes:

> “Thus, although such defects may seem natural to man when human nature is considered absolutely, from the standpoint of what is lower in it, nevertheless, when divine providence and the dignity of the higher part of human nature are considered, it may be proved QUITE PROBABLY that such defects are penal, and thus it may be inferred that the human race is infected with some sin.”

This is what Saint Thomas says. Since so many exceedingly wise and subtle Doctors follow him, you can now see what and how many adherents that inference of Augustine’s has: the inference that original sin is posited quite probably from the miseries of human life.

Nor were there lacking writers from our Society who offered Augustine their support in this opinion. Let us hear one of them, John Bagocius. In book V of the *Demonstration of Christian Dogma*, disputation 8, chapter 5, section 2, he asks in the title:

> “Would God be unjust if he compelled a man to die without the guilt of sin?”

He answers:

> “Saint Augustine and his other disciples, as well as the very Fathers of the canons of the Council of Orange, say that God could not subject a man to the necessity of dying unless he were guilty of sin, and they maintain that, if God did this, he would be unjust, because he would inflict punishment upon one who had not deserved it.”

And in chapter 7, section 3, he says:

> “I also confess that God, according to his power ordered by goodness and wisdom, could not have willed to make man subject to death and create him with the depravity of carnal concupiscence, without permitting any sin.”

This author, a man of no small reputation among the more recent theologians, afterward wrote against Jansenism under the distinguished names of Thomas and Augustine.

## § IV. Whether Saint Augustine Went Too Far When Arguing about the Virtues of Unbelievers

The same Moraines, considering the holy Doctor’s opinion concerning the virtues of unbelievers too rigorous, writes in disputation 19, no. 35:

> “In arguing against the Pelagians, who, by excessively extolling the natural powers of free will, asserted that these powers were sufficient without grace not only for every kind of natural virtue but also for salvation, Augustine, in order to draw them away from that error, sometimes seems to have been carried toward the opposite extreme by the heat of disputation.”

But here too this critic stumbles over the same stone. For the holy Doctor did not discuss the virtues of unbelievers under the impulse of the heat of disputation, but, challenged by his adversaries to enter that arena, descended into it willingly and courageously.

For the Pelagians, in order to prove that man could act well without grace, produced examples of unbelievers whom they asserted had flourished in many virtues without God’s grace.

Let us hear the holy Father in *Against Julian*, book IV, chapter 3:

> “For you are accustomed, while denying that the virtues by which one lives rightly are gifts of God, and attributing them to human nature and will rather than to God’s grace, to use this as an argument: that unbelievers sometimes possess them,” etc.

But Augustine there proves through more than seven hundred lines that the virtues of unbelievers possessed only civic goodness and were praiseworthy among men merely in outward appearance. In particular, he employs the testimony of Romans 14: “Whatever is not from faith is sin.”

Since Augustine disputed the works of unbelievers with the Pelagians with such labor and care, and there closed every avenue against his adversaries by the most subtle arguments, he did not advance this position in the heat of disputation, but only after long reflection upon a most difficult matter and serious consideration of the entire question.

The holy Doctor asserted two things. First, no virtues are found in unbelievers from the powers of free will alone. Second, if there were any virtues in them, these should in no way be attributed to their will, but to divine grace.

I know that, concerning the first point, most scholastic theologians departed from Augustine’s opinion. They discussed virtues according to Aristotle’s *Ethics*, although the philosophers were unaware of the weakness of human nature deriving from the original stain and strayed farther from the truth in their knowledge of the highest good.

Augustine, however, derived his own opinion from the sacred writings and from a higher and more subtle theology.

The central point of the Augustinian position is that virtues are distinguished from vices not by their function but by their end. Let us hear Augustine in the book of *Against Julian* cited above:

> “Know, therefore,” he says, “that virtues must be distinguished from vices not by their functions but by their ends. A function is what ought to be done; an end is that for the sake of which it ought to be done. Therefore, when a man does something in which he does not seem to sin, if he does not do it for the sake of that for which he ought to do it, he is proved to be sinning.”

He proves this there by the example of misers, who pretend to pursue moral virtues, but whose pursuits nevertheless end in vices because they serve avarice.

Therefore one must not attend only to the substance of an act that appears good by reason of its object; one must also consider the end for which the same act is elicited.

After Augustine had proved these points at length in the same place, he attempted to establish that there were no true virtues in unbelievers, because they subjected them to human praise and glory, and thus turned them into vices, since they served pride.

He writes the following in *Against Julian*, book IV, chapter 3:

> “Or perhaps even those who displayed a Babylonian love for their earthly homeland, and who served demons or human glory by civic virtue—not true virtue, but something resembling it—” etc.

Earlier he had said:

> “It is good to help a man in danger, especially an innocent man. But if the one who does this does it by loving human glory more than God, he does not do a good deed well, because he does not act well who does what he does without a good will.”

Thus, when Julian had objected in the same place:

> “If a Gentile clothes a naked man, is it sin simply because it is not from faith?”

Augustine responds:

> “Certainly, insofar as it is not from faith, it is sin—not because the act itself, namely clothing the naked, is sin, but because only an impious person denies that it is sin not to glory in the Lord concerning such a work.”

He brings together many further points on this matter there, with subtlety and acumen.

These points are indeed certain, for no Catholic writer can call into question that moral acts serving human glory, although otherwise good in their object, are nevertheless corrupted by a depraved intention—just as the acts of the Epicureans, outwardly resembling good, degenerated from the virtues because, as Augustine says in the same place, the master of that sect “introduces the virtues as handmaids of pleasure.” Yet the proponents of the contrary view object that an unbeliever can perform acts of virtue solely because of the intrinsic honesty of the act itself, without desiring to obtain any praise from others. For since moral goodness belongs within the object of the will, it can be desired by the will precisely for its own sake.

Augustine, however, with remarkable acuteness of intellect, demolished this response in Book IV, chapter 3, Against Julian, writing as follows:

> Nothing exists among creatures which, insofar as it concerns the merits of the natures established by God, is superior to the rational mind. It follows that a good mind takes greater pleasure in itself and delights more in itself than in any other creature. But how dangerously—indeed, how destructively—it takes pleasure in itself when, through this, it swells with arrogance and is lifted up by the disease of self-inflation, so long as it does not see—as it will see at the end—that supreme and unchangeable good, in comparison with which it despises itself and becomes contemptible to itself through love of that good.

He gives a similar teaching in Book XIX, chapter 25, On the City of God:

> Therefore, he says, the virtues which the human mind seems to possess for itself, by which it rules the body and the vices in order to obtain or retain anything, unless it refers them to God, are themselves vices rather than virtues. For although some then consider them true and honorable virtues when they are referred to themselves and are desired for no other reason, even then they are inflated and proud; and therefore they must be judged not virtues but vices.

Thus, when virtue is desired merely for its own honesty, it causes the person who pursues and attains it to take pleasure in himself through his work and to suffer from the vice of self-love (*philautia*). Therefore, just as someone who acts honorably in order to please others and be praised by them sins through the sin of vainglory, so likewise one who acts honorably while taking pleasure in himself and glorifying himself is guilty of self-love.

Hence the Apostle said: “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. VIII). For by the very fact that a person recognizes himself as endowed with virtue, he takes pleasure in himself, places himself above others, and glories in himself rather than in the Lord. The first step toward pride is to think more highly of oneself than of others and to attribute virtue to oneself rather than to God.

Augustine’s pronouncement—that virtue, when desired for its own intrinsic honesty, is proud and corrupted by self-love—is established at length by the same holy teacher in Sermon 13, On the Words of the Apostle, through the example of the Stoics. They pursued virtue for its own sake, yet their virtues served pride. There he introduces Paul speaking at Athens with the Stoics and Epicureans—for Acts XVII says: “But certain Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debated with him”—and among other things he writes:

> The Epicurean said: “Blessed is the one whose pleasure of the flesh is his reward.” The Stoic said: “Rather, blessed is the one whose spiritual virtue is his reward.” The Apostle said: “Blessed is the one whose hope is the name of the Lord.” The Epicurean is mistaken; for it is false that a person is blessed whose reward is the pleasure of his flesh. The Stoic is also mistaken; for it is false, and altogether most erroneous, that a person is blessed whose reward is the virtue of his spirit.

Indeed, whether virtue pursued solely for its own intrinsic honesty inflates the person who possesses it and causes self-love is manifest from this very clear example. Therefore, whatever may be the case with the matter considered speculatively, in practice Augustine’s opinion is true.

Moreover, the pride of the Stoics was so great that, in their folly, they denied that we need divine assistance in order to acquire virtue. We quoted their words in Book I of the History of Pelagianism, chapter 1, where we also proved that the pride of the Pelagians, by which they denied the necessity of divine grace, derived from the doctrine of the Stoics. The holy teacher said admirably against the Pelagians in the same Sermon 13:

> Do you wish to act by yourself? Do you wish to be moved by yourself toward the mortification of the acts of the flesh? What does it profit you that you will not be an Epicurean but will be a Stoic?

The same great teacher, in Book V, chapter 20, On the City of God, after saying that certain philosophers, in order to display the shamefulness of Epicurus, skillfully painted pleasure on a panel seated like a queen on a royal throne, while the virtues stood before her as attendants and awaited her command so that they might promptly carry out whatever she ordered, adds:

> They say that nothing is more shameful or deformed than this picture.

He then ridicules the Stoics:

> But I do not think the picture possesses the decorum it ought to have if it is also imagined as one in which the human virtues serve human glory. For although this glory is not a delicate woman, it is nevertheless inflated and possesses a great deal of emptiness.

Anticipating the response of more recent writers, he adds:

> Nor can those who despise the judgments of others, as though they were despisers of glory, defend themselves from this disgrace when they seem wise to themselves and take pleasure in themselves. For their virtue, if indeed they have any, is subject to human praise in another manner; for the person who takes pleasure in himself is nevertheless a human being.

The same points are confirmed by the example of the fallen angels and of our first parents, whose fall arose from self-love. Saint Prosper writes to Demetrias:

> This pride took its beginning from the devil, who, because he took pleasure in himself in the power and dignity which he had received from the Creator, was cast down from heavenly exaltation.

And concerning man Augustine says in Book X, chapter 13, On the City of God:

> The devil would not have captured man unless man had already begun to take pleasure in himself.

Hence he writes with equal acuteness in Book XIV, chapter 28, of the same work:

> Thus two cities were created by two loves: the earthly city by love of self even to contempt of God, and the heavenly city by love of God even to contempt of self. Finally, the one glories in itself, while the other glories in the Lord.

Therefore pride takes its beginning from love of self, and pride is the poison of all the virtues, to be expelled only by the antidote of divine grace.

These considerations strongly prove that virtue pursued even for its own sake inflates the person who pursues it. The reason is that everyone loves himself by a natural love, and the more good things he observes in himself, the more he takes pleasure in himself. Hence he esteems himself above others, swells with self-love, and, like Narcissus, is captivated by his own beauty.

The proponents of the contrary view could offer one objection which, if the person performing honorable acts consequently swelled with empty self-satisfaction, would conclude everything said above very well: it may happen that someone acts honorably—for example, gives alms to a poor person—and immediately afterward turns his mind to something else. In that case he would not glorify himself before himself through a reflex act.

I admit that, if the mind is immediately drawn elsewhere by a new object, it can happen that no glory or boastfulness whatsoever is stirred within the person. But this occurs accidentally. [Col. 0624B] For a moral agent must consider whether he has acted rightly and whether, through that action, he has comported himself properly toward his end. In considering these things, he loves his work and glorifies himself.

Nevertheless, I maintain that these good works were not performed by unbelievers left to their own powers, but with the assistance of special divine graces supplied beforehand. Through these, it may sometimes have happened that, after acting rightly, they did not glorify themselves at all in their good work because their minds had been occupied by a new object. For since the fall from an act of virtue into self-love is so easy—indeed, since it is irreparable—it was the work of divine grace whenever unbelievers did not become swollen with pride because of a good work.

I see this doctrine expressly taught by Ripalda, a celebrated theologian among more recent writers. In disputation 20, section 6, number 25, he says:

> It is rightly said that a will deprived of the assistance of grace in this order of Providence, and left to its own powers, can do nothing but pride and sin.

In the same place he develops this at greater length, especially praising the following judgment of the holy teacher:

> Free will abandoned by divine assistance, however excellent it may be in its knowledge of the law, possesses no solidity of justice, but only the inflation of impious pride.

Therefore, wherever no pride arises in the soul from a good work, the assistance of divine grace is present.

That unbelievers sometimes acted well through a special assistance of grace is proved from Book I to Boniface, chapter 20, where Augustine attributes the sudden gentleness that arose in the heart of King Ahasuerus to grace:

> God, he says, before the king had heard the woman’s request, turned his heart by a most hidden and efficacious power and transferred it from indignation to gentleness—that is, from a will to harm to a will to favor.

He repeats the same point in On the Grace of Christ, chapter 24. Furthermore, in Letter 130 he says that the continence of the philosopher Polemo ought to be attributed to divine grace:

> Yet I would not attribute even that which was better in him to human achievement, but to God.

Nevertheless, the following must be observed from Augustine: the good acts of unbelievers that derive from divine grace are, for the most part, corrupted and lose the goodness that they possessed, as gifts from God, in their own production, because of the subsequent evil circumstances surrounding the acts. I infer this from Augustine, Book IV, chapter 3, Against Julian, where he writes:

> From this it follows that even the good works which unbelievers perform do not belong to them but to the one who makes good use of evil things; whereas the sins belong to them, by which they do good things badly, because they perform them not with a believing but with an unbelieving—that is, foolish and harmful—will. Such a will, no Christian doubting it, is a bad tree, which can produce only bad fruits, that is, sins alone. For everything that is not from faith, whether you wish it or not, is sin.

Augustine means that only faith directs the will to perform a work with the proper circumstance of reference to God as the ultimate end. Hence he had said earlier in the same place:

> When God’s gifts are not referred to their author, those who use them become evil and unjust by that very fact. If they possess any virtues, they do not possess true ones; and consequently continence or chastity is not a true virtue among the impious.

In this chapter the holy teacher defends against Julian’s objections what he had written in Book I, chapter 3, On Marriage and Concupiscence. After saying that continence is a gift of God, he asks:

> What, then, shall we say when conjugal chastity is found even among certain impious people? Are they to be said to sin because they misuse God’s gift, not referring it to the worship of him from whom they received it? Or perhaps these should not be considered gifts of God when unbelievers perform them, according to the Apostle’s statement: “Everything that is not from faith is sin”?

He chooses the latter alternative in the same place, saying:

> Who would dare to say that a gift of God is sin?

After having stated that the natural goods of soul and body with which unbelievers are born are gifts of God, he adds:

> But concerning the things they do, it has been said: “Everything that is not from faith is sin.” Therefore, when people without faith perform these acts which seem to pertain to conjugal chastity—whether seeking to please human beings, themselves or others; or avoiding human annoyances in matters which they viciously desire; or serving demons—they do not restrain sins but overcome some sins by means of other sins. Therefore, far be it from us to call someone truly chaste who does not, for the sake of the true God, render the fidelity of marriage to his wife.

In the aforementioned chapter 3, Against Julian, he defends this opinion of his at the greatest length against the many arguments that the heretic presses against it. Consistently with himself, he denies that true chastity existed among the Gentiles.

I know that some maintain that Augustine said that those acts are sins which are not positively referred to God as their ultimate end, but not those which fail to refer to him negatively. For example, a person who is continent in order to please himself or others, seeking glory before himself or others, sins because he positively assigns vainglory to himself as the end of that chastity; and thus the work positively deviates from God as its ultimate end. But if someone undertakes continence because of the honesty of the act alone, without glorifying himself or others in it, then the act fails negatively to regard God as its ultimate end, yet it appears vicious in no respect.

This doctrine may be admitted, especially because the holy teacher taught that the virtues of the Gentiles were corrupted because they sought glory from them, either before themselves or before others. These statements should be understood of acts of virtue that are not corrupted accidentally, as we said occurs immediately upon their first production. For if someone frequently performs the same act of virtue and devotes himself to it with particular intensity—for example, to conjugal chastity—he cannot, without special divine assistance, refrain from self-love or from empty glory before others.

Therefore the holy teacher rightly said, for this reason, that unbelievers cannot possess true virtues, moved especially by the Apostle’s statement: “Everything that is not from faith is sin.” Moraines writes that these words of Paul were wrongly understood by Augustine; but I shall show below, in chapter 4, § 5, that the holy Father’s interpretation was approved by the Apostolic See and by the Catholic Church.

Hence Augustine, in On the Predestination of the Saints, chapter 7, teaches that the good works of Cornelius in Acts X proceeded from faith in God:

> His alms, he says, were accepted and his prayers heard before he had believed in Christ; yet he neither gave nor prayed without some faith. For how could he call upon one in whom he had not believed?

From this it is clear that, in order to refer good works to God, faith in Christ is not required; faith in God is sufficient. Indeed, it can be gathered from Book On Patience, chapters 26 and 27, that even acquired faith alone suffices, where he writes that the patience of schismatics is both good and deserving of praise. We shall quote his words shortly afterward.

I see, however, that the holy teacher concedes one good act to unbelievers and to other human beings without grace: namely, the act by which a person desires the supreme good. In the Enchiridion, chapter 25, he says:

> Yet this nature, amid its evils, could not lose the desire for blessedness.

He says the same in chapter 125 and in Book IV, chapter 3, Against Julian:

> For we would not all wish, by natural instinct, to be immortal and blessed unless it were possible for us to be so.

But because of the ignorance contracted through original sin, a person left to his own powers does not know in what true blessedness and happiness consist. Hence so many philosophical opinions concerning the supreme good have arisen. Faith alone has revealed that the God who is clearly seen is the supreme good of man, and that a person becomes blessed through possession of him alone.

This was Augustine’s opinion concerning the works of unbelievers, and the Fathers and most distinguished teachers followed it.

Saint Leo the Great says in Sermon II, On the Fast of Pentecost:

> Among the pagans themselves there are certain vain fasts. For reason acts one way under truth, and deception under falsehood acts another way. Among us faith sanctifies even the one who eats; among them unbelief pollutes the one who fasts. Therefore, since outside the Catholic Church nothing is whole and nothing is pure, as the Apostle says: “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV).

Boniface II asserts the same in his letter to Saint Caesarius of Arles, as does Saint Fulgentius together with the synod of the Byzacene Fathers exiled in Sardinia. We shall quote their words below, in chapter 4, § 5.

Saint Prosper writes in his letter to Rufinus:

> “Everything that is not from faith is sin,” so that he may understand that the justice of unbelievers is not justice, because nature without grace is sullied.

And in his poem Against the Ungrateful, chapter 16, he sings:

> For every work of uprightness, unless it arises  
> From the seed of true faith, is sin, and is turned  
> Into guilt; and sterile glory heaps punishment  
> Upon itself.

Julian Pomerius, the teacher of Saint Caesarius of Arles, whose books Saint Isidore praises—as we said in Book II of the History of Pelagianism, chapter 14—transcribes Augustine’s opinion in full in Book III, chapter 1, On the Contemplative Life:

> Although these things can be discerned by human ingenuity, nevertheless, without the gift of God, as I see it, neither virtues can be desired or possessed, nor can their likenesses—which are vices imitating virtues—be avoided to such an extent that we should believe that they have profited unbelievers, even if they have performed certain virtuous acts through the body. For they will have believed neither that they received these things from their God nor wished to refer them to him who is the end of all good things. And what do I mean by saying that they have not profited? Rather, they have harmed them, according to the Apostle’s statement: “Everything that is not from faith is sin.” Let the entire chapter be read, where he explains the same doctrine more fully.

Cassiodorus, and generally the other writers as well, attribute these books to Saint Prosper; we have discussed the matter at greater length in the History of Pelagianism.

Bede held the same opinion in the preface to the Song of Songs, where he attacks Pelagius’s opinion concerning the virtues of philosophers, saying:

> As for what he says—that many philosophers possess patience, chastity, moderation, and other virtues from the good of nature—it is clear that, since whichever philosophers did not know Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, they could not possess any true wisdom. But insofar as they possessed some taste of any wisdom or an image of virtue, they received all of it from above, not only through the gift of the first creation but also through his daily grace.

Saint Remigius, together with his Church of Lyons, agrees with Augustine in Book On Holding to the Truth of Sacred Scripture, chapter 11, writing:

> But human nature can sometimes desire and perform such human goods, which it can desire through human affection. When they are desired for temporal goods, they are unquestionably desires; when they are desired for the sole honesty of life, they are unquestionably inflated and elevated. Nevertheless, nature can discern them, can desire them, and can possess them, insofar as it is assisted by natural goodness and human nature is permitted to do so by God’s arrangement.

Many other learned points are asserted there.

I deliberately omit the testimonies of Cyprian, Book I, On Patience, section “The Philosophers Profess That They Follow This”; of Tertullian, On the Adornment of Women, at the beginning of the section “By the Women of the Nations”; and of Gregory the Great, Book II of the Moralia, chapter 15, section “If Not First.” For the statements of these writers can be explained by our opponents as referring to meritorious good works, which are never found in those who lack faith.

Indeed, almost all the scholastic writers who do not speak of the works of unbelievers in the same way as Augustine, so as not to seem opposed to the holy teacher, say that Augustine denied that the works of unbelievers are good—that is, meritorious—as the Pelagians maintained. But these writers plainly read Augustine’s books superficially. For neither Julian nor the other Pelagians ever admitted meritorious works—that is, works conferring a right to glory—without sanctifying grace.

I shall reproduce Julian’s words from Book IV, chapter 3, of Saint Augustine’s work Against Julian:

> The origin of all virtues, he says, is situated in the rational soul, and all the dispositions by which we are either fruitfully or fruitlessly good are located in our mind: prudence, justice, temperance, and fortitude. Although the power of these dispositions is naturally present in everyone, it does not hasten toward one end in everyone; rather, according to the judgment of the will, whose command they obey, they are directed either toward eternal things or toward temporal things. When this occurs, they differ not in what they are, nor in what they do—the scholastics call this the substance of the work—but solely in what they merit.

And afterward:

> I called those people fruitlessly good who, because they do not do the good things they do for God, do not receive eternal life from him.

Thus Julian called the virtues acquired by unbelievers through the powers of nature true virtues according to their substance, while denying that they were meritorious of eternal glory.

Augustine, on the contrary, concluded that fruitless works cannot be called good but only evil, both because they lack reference to God and because of the self-love that follows from this, as we explained above.

> Your liking for virtues without faith, says the holy teacher, is such that you declare them true and call people good because of them; and yet, as though you had repented of praising them, you do not hesitate to pronounce them fruitless.

Again:

> Or certainly, since at least you concede that the works of unbelievers which seem good to you nevertheless do not lead them to eternal salvation and the kingdom.

The Pelagians asserted this because they believed that, by sanctifying grace alone, Catholics become adopted children of God with a right to glory, while they denied that this right could be possessed through the powers of nature.

Their testimonies may be read in Augustine’s Book On Original Sin, chapter 5; Book VI, Against Julian, chapter 17; and most clearly in Book III of the Unfinished Work, chapters 108 and 117, and Book V, chapter 9. From these passages it is sufficiently evident that the Pelagians did not admit in unbelievers meritorious works of the heavenly kingdom and glory, but disputed with Augustine only over the goodness of those works according to their substance.

Two distinguished Augustinian theologians have argued admirably on this question according to the mind of the holy Father: Gregory of Rimini, in Book II, distinction 26, question 1, and Gaspar Casalius Lusitanus, bishop of Leiria, in Book I, On Fourfold Justice, in several chapters.

Basilius Pontius of León, in the first part of his Relections on Grace, chapter 75, in his response to the second objection, writes that he will discuss the works of unbelievers in the second part according to the mind of Saint Augustine. I was never able to find that book.

Among foreigners, Father Macedo defends Augustine’s opinion with great learning in The Curtain of Saint Augustine, question 2, On the Necessity of Grace. These theologians also resolve the arguments commonly advanced against the holy Father’s opinion. Therefore, so as not to repeat what has already been done, we do not reproduce them here. Let Gregory of Rimini be read, for he meets all the objections extremely well; nor have more recent writers produced new arguments with which to attack the Augustinian position.

I know that they object to the proposition of Baius that was condemned: “All the works of unbelievers are sins,” and so forth. But this condemnation in no way affects the holy Father’s opinion. For here he openly concedes that unbelievers perform certain good works, at least in the first production of those works, although these are given through grace.

Moreover, even without grace, according to Augustine’s opinion, man loves the supreme good through an innate desire; for there is no one who does not wish to be blessed.

This is enough on that matter.

But since Augustine is criticized by Maldonado precisely because of this opinion concerning the works of unbelievers, let us refute the man’s statements briefly. In his commentary on Matthew VI, verse 18, he writes:

> Nor should that opinion be followed which the Council of Trent recently and rightly condemned: that all works of sinners, or even of unbelievers, are sins, although it may seem that its principal author, Saint Augustine, held it in Book IV, chapter 3, Against Julian; in Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, chapter 5; and in Prosper, sentence 106.

The holy Father nowhere taught that all the works of sinners are vicious. That is the error of recent heretics, condemned at the Council of Trent, session 6, canon 7. On the contrary, Augustine often teaches the opposite. For in chapter 7 of On the Predestination of the Saints he says that all the good works of Cornelius, before he believed, ought to be attributed as acceptable to God, as we have just shown.

Likewise, in On Patience, chapter 26, he teaches that a schismatic who, tortured by fear of eternal punishments, endures suffering rather than deny Christ acts well, though without merit of eternal life:

> These things are in no way to be blamed, he says; indeed, this patience is also to be praised.

And in chapter 27 he says:

> For surely it is a good thing for a person to believe that he will be punished with eternal torment if he denies Christ, so that for this faith he may endure whatever punishment and despise human punishment. Therefore, just as it must not be denied that this too is a gift of God, so it must be understood that there are other gifts of God belonging to the children of that Jerusalem which is above and is our free mother. These are, in a certain sense, hereditary gifts, in which we are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ. There are other gifts, however, which even the children of concubines can receive; the carnal Jews, schismatics, and heretics are compared with them.

Cornelius before baptism, and likewise Jews and heretics, are counted among sinners; yet Augustine concedes that some of their works are worthy of praise, as gifts of God.

But what Maldonado dares to assert cannot be tolerated at all: that the Council of Trent condemned Augustine’s opinion concerning the works of unbelievers. Where, I ask you, does the synod speak of the works of unbelievers? In canon 7 it condemns the person who says:

> All works performed before justification, however they may have been performed, are truly sins or merit the hatred of God.

That anathema strikes down the error of the innovators who said that all works performed by a person outside charity and in a state of sin are sins, because they are corrupted by the guilt of conscience. This opinion is both false and was formerly condemned, as we saw, by Augustine.

So far were the Fathers of Trent from condemning the holy teacher’s opinion that, on the contrary, there was among them a man distinguished by both learning and status who afterward defended Augustine’s opinion even in a stricter sense. This was the most learned Gaspar Casalius, a member of the Augustinian order and bishop of Leiria in Portugal. In 1562 he composed at Trent a large volume entitled On Fourfold Justice and dedicated it to the legates of the Holy See. In Book I, beginning with chapter 22, he defends Saint Augustine’s opinion at great length, confirming it by the authority and arguments both of the Fathers and of theologians.

But the session on justification had been celebrated in 1547. Are we to say that this man possessed so much audacity that he defended again, with such determination, an opinion condemned by the synod?

Let us hear Casalius:

> What, then, he says, is to be said about that other point which Augustine always seems to teach: that outside faith and outside knowledge of the true God no true virtue is found which is not a vice? What is to be said, I ask, according to his opinion and that of the other holy teachers? As for Augustine himself, we say this: he did indeed teach it, and because he was truthful and spoke from the heart, he believed it. Others now say otherwise, but they do not thereby show themselves wiser than Augustine.

Nevertheless, the holy teacher did not speak so rigorously about the works of unbelievers, for he openly conceded that they sometimes performed certain acts of virtue, as is sufficiently clear from what has been said.

## § V. Whether Saint Augustine, in asserting that infants are punished by the mildest punishment of sense in the underworld, spoke excessively

I know of no matter in which Augustine’s critics appear to accuse him of excess on stronger grounds than when he disputed with the Pelagians concerning the punishments of children who die without baptism. Even the ancient scholastics published this very judgment concerning the holy teacher. Scotus, Richard, Major, Capreolus, and others handed it down by unanimous agreement.

Saint Bonaventure wrote of this opinion of Augustine:

> He said more, while intending that less be understood.

Annatus transcribed this statement in larger characters and repeatedly thrust it forward in order to magnify Augustine’s authority.

Nor were there lacking writers who explained the matter by what seemed to them a rather polished comparison, as Hauzer reports in volume II of The Augustinian Anatomy, column 765:

> Hence, just as armed horsemen, when they charge against the enemy, commonly trample under the same impulse even upon unarmed children who meet them, so Blessed Augustine, while pursuing the Pelagians, seems to some, because of the fervor of battle, to have spared those little ones even less.

Some did not even refrain from mockery. Soto asserts that those who defend the stated opinion of Saint Augustine are called, as an insult, “torturers of children.” Our Puteanus, in Book I–II, question 83, article 4, doubt 4, testifies that Gregory of Rimini, because he taught things similar to Augustine’s, was called a torturer of children.

Thus Adamus, chapter 6, page 666, writes that Augustine, in assigning punishment to infants, was “drawn by an excess of zeal beyond the question he was discussing with the Pelagians, and spoke beyond his intention.” He also adds that all the Fathers who wrote on this question handed down the contrary opinion.

Moraines says the same in disputation 40, number 60. As for the fact that Gregory the Great and Fulgentius of Ruspe agreed with Saint Augustine in this doctrine, he writes:

> They asserted it not according to the mind of the Church, as its witnesses, but from their own opinion.

I believe that I shall do something pleasing to the Augustinian school if I free the holy Father in this matter from every suspicion of excess and at the same time show that he taught a dogma approved by the Catholic Church, a common teaching of the ancient Fathers, and an opinion worthy of himself. Conversely, I shall show that most of the scholastics descended into certain opinions concerning the punishments of infants which plainly contradict the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, synods, and Fathers.

I shall set out the matter briefly as follows.

The opinion of Saint Augustine concerning the sensible punishments of infants who die without baptism, handed down against the Pelagians. The first argument in its favor from Sacred Scripture. The responses of the opponents refuted.

Although the Pelagians asserted that children are born without original sin, they nevertheless denied that children who died unpurified by the sacred waters entered the kingdom of heaven, out of reverence for the Lord’s statement:

> Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven (John III, 3).

Augustine writes in Sermon 14, On the Words of the Apostle:

> Therefore I cannot promise the kingdom of God to an unbaptized infant, contrary to the Lord’s clear statement.

But since they declared children free from every crime, they denied that they were cast into a place of punishment. They said that a second kind of happiness had been established for them, in a certain intermediate place between the glory of the heavenly kingdom and the punishments of hell.

Where this intermediate place might be, Pelagius himself candidly admitted that he did not know, in that celebrated statement quoted by Augustine in On Original Sin, chapter 21:

> I know where infants who die without baptism do not go; where they go, I do not know.

Nor did his disciples teach anything more definite. They asserted only that children go to a place of a second happiness, as I noted above.

Augustine, however, not only ridiculed this happiness promised by the Pelagians to children but also proved by solid arguments that infants who die without baptism are sent into the fiery Gehenna.

For this reason the heretics rejected Augustine’s opinion as cruel, as is clear from these words of Julian in Book III of the Unfinished Work, chapter 199:

> But you object. Let us hear, then, what you produce, Aristotle of the Punic people. “So great,” you say, “is the evil in him that he is possessed by the devil and deserves eternal fire.”

So Julian spoke. Augustine replied:

> But if the infant is not rescued from the power of darkness and remains there, why do you wonder that he will be with the devil in eternal fire, since he is not permitted to enter the kingdom of God? Or because the Pelagians prepare some place of rest and eternal life for unbaptized infants outside the kingdom of God, will Christ’s statement therefore be false: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned”?

The holy Father first drew an argument for the punishments of infants from chapter 25 of Matthew, which he set forth in Sermon 14 on the Words of the Apostle as follows:

> “The Lord will come and judge the living and the dead, as the Gospel says; he will make two divisions, the right and the left. To those on the left he will say: ‘Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels’; to those on the right he will say: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.’ He names this the kingdom, and that the condemnation with the devil. THERE IS NO INTERMEDIATE PLACE LEFT where you might put infants. The living and the dead will be judged; some will be on the right, others on the left. I know nothing else. YOU WHO POINT TO A MIDDLE PLACE, DEPART FROM THE MIDDLE. Let him not offend you who seeks the right and admonishes you yourself. Depart from the middle, but do not go to the left. If, then, there will be a right and a left, and we know from the Gospel of no intermediate place, behold, on the right is the kingdom of heaven: ‘Receive the kingdom,’ he says. Whoever is not there is on the left. What will be on the left? ‘Go into the eternal fire.’ On the right, certainly, is the eternal kingdom; on the left, the eternal fire. Whoever is not on the right is undoubtedly on the left. THEREFORE WHOEVER IS NOT IN THE KINGDOM IS UNDOUBTEDLY IN THE ETERNAL FIRE.”

Here, looking down upon those who held a contrary opinion as though they were the dregs of the populace, he says: “Here you seek a middle place, man from the middle [i.e. the common rabble].”

Augustine publicly recited these words in a sermon at Carthage, in the principal basilica, before Aurelius, Primate of all Africa, at whose command he delivered that address, as we have related more fully in book I of the *History of the Pelagians*, chapter 5. Toward the end he says:

> “I read only one thing: it is Saint Cyprian, whom I have taken into my hands, the ancient bishop of this see.”

Thus, at that time, the opinion concerning the sensible punishment of infants was publicly proposed for orthodox Christians to hold. The holy Father asserted it with such certainty that he declared infants would undoubtedly go into the eternal fire. Accordingly, he should not be thought to have been the first to teach this, but to have followed the faith of the whole Church of that age.

Augustine also employs another testimony, which I shall indicate here because it is related to the one just quoted. In book I of *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, chapter 28, he says:

> “There is no intermediate place for anyone, so that he can be anywhere except with the devil who is not with Christ. Therefore the Lord himself, wishing to remove from the hearts of those who believe wrongly THIS SORT OF MIDDLE CONDITION, which certain people try to assign to unbaptized infants—so that, as though on account of their innocence, they might be in eternal life, but because they are not baptized they might not be with Christ in his kingdom—uttered a definitive sentence to close their mouths, when he said: ‘Whoever is not with me is against me,’ etc. (Matthew 12).”

The most ancient author of the *Hypognosticon* turns to this same argument in book V, chapter 5, where he says:

> “Behold, the unbaptized person, deprived even of the life-giving food and drink, is separated from the kingdom of heaven, where Christ, the fountain of the living, remains. Give me, apart from this, another place where there can be perpetual rest in life. For the Catholic faith, on divine authority, has believed the first place to be the kingdom of heaven; from it, as I have said, the unbaptized person is excluded. The second is Gehenna, where every apostate or person alienated from the faith of Christ will suffer eternal punishments. We entirely ignore a third place; indeed, we do not find that one exists in the Holy Scriptures. Imagine, Pelagian, a place devised in the workshop of your perverse doctrine, where infants alienated from Christ’s grace might possess a life of rest and glory. The right hand is the kingdom of the just Judge seated in judgment, and the left is Gehenna; life and death, the just and the unjust. On the right, therefore, are the just; on the left, the workers of iniquity. In the kingdom is the rest of the baptized; in Gehenna, the punishment of unbelievers. Life leads to the joy of glory; death to weeping and the gnashing of teeth. The just are in the kingdom of the Father with Christ; the unjust in the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. In saying this I have not supplied many divisions of places, but only two, because all these things refer to two destinations, namely the kingdom and Gehenna, even if more expressions are used, etc. Whoever, therefore, has not been baptized cannot be found among the things belonging to the kingdom of heaven. And if he is not there, do you suppose, Pelagian, that you now know where he is—or at least say where he is?”

[Col. 0633B] Scholastic writers commonly offer various responses to this argument, but all of them are easily rejected. Catharinus, in his little work *On the State of Infants*, after saying that this argument is the Achilles of the opposing position, denies that infants ought to appear at the judgment. Moraines, *Disputation* 40 *On Grace*, no. 11, replies first that the opponent wrongly assumes it to be a dogma of faith that, at the general judgment of which Christ speaks in Matthew 25, infants will appear and there be placed either on the right or on the left. For Durandus and Albertus affirm the contrary without error against the faith. In no. 12 he replies secondly that it is not even certain by divine faith that, although infants will appear at the general judgment, they will be among those judged. He cites Tostatus, the Carthusian, and Saint Thomas, book IV, distinction 47, question [unclear], article 3, response to objection 3, where Thomas affirms that children who die before reaching maturity will appear at the judgment, not to be judged but to see the glory of the Judge. Suarez, according to the same Moraines, considers this probable. In no. 13 he responds further that it is not sufficiently established that they will be placed on the left rather than in some intermediate place.

None of these responses, however, can be admitted. For it was plainly defined in the African council, as I shall show shortly, that infants will be on the left, in these words:

> “For whoever lacks the right will undoubtedly incur the left-hand portion.”

And Pope Gelasius, in his letter to the bishops throughout Picenum, says against the Pelagians concerning these same infants:

> “And because we read of no other than the right and the left, let them not cause them, without baptism, to remain in the region on the left; rather, let them permit the baptized to be transferred to the saving right hand through holy regeneration.”

Moraines read this letter of Gelasius and calls it learned in *Disputation* 2, no. 31. But let us set aside the African canon and the letter of Gelasius—for the older scholastics did not read them. Did Augustine not hand down this opinion as an orthodox dogma?
