The holy Doctor established twelve rules in his letter 107 to Vitalis. The seventh and eighth are set down in these words:

> “We know that we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each person may receive according to what he has done through the body, not according to what he would have done had he lived longer, whether good or evil. We also know that infants will receive either good or evil according to what they have done through the body. They have done this not by themselves but through those who answer on their behalf; through their hearts and mouths the infants themselves are said to renounce the devil and believe in God, and hence are numbered among the faithful, belonging to the sentence of the Lord who says: ‘Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved’ (Mark 16). Therefore what follows also applies to those who do not receive this sacrament: ‘Whoever does not believe will be condemned’ (ibid.). Accordingly, they too, as I have said, if they die in that early age, are judged according to what they have done through the body—that is, during the time when they were in the body, when through the hearts and mouths of those carrying them they believed or did not believe, when they were baptized or not baptized, when they ate the flesh of the Lord or did not eat it, when they drank his blood or did not drink it. According, therefore, to what they have done through the body, and not according to what they would have done had they lived long here, they are judged.”

Moreover, in the same place the holy Father taught that these two sentences, together with the other ten, pertain to the Catholic faith, in these words:

> “Indeed, it is clear from those twelve sentences, which you are not permitted to deny belong to the Catholic faith,” etc.

Here I shall repeat Bellarmine’s words from book II of *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 11, although he uttered them on another occasion:

> “For if Augustine’s opinion concerning predestination”—I shall say, concerning the punishments of infants who are to be judged—“were false, Augustine could not be defended from enormous rashness, since he not only fought so fiercely for a falsehood, but also dared to market it as the Catholic faith.”

Later he taught the same thing in book V of his final work against Julian.

Bede, too, who flourished long after Augustine, affirms that according to the Catholic faith infants are to be judged. For in the preliminary material to the sacred book of the *Canticles*, against Julian, he says:

> “What Julian says—that some judge others and others are judged for no reason except that within the same nature there is a differing will, and that, although all of us are capable of the same things, we do different things—contradicts the Catholic faith, which also confesses THAT INFANTS ARE TO BE JUDGED: namely, those who, placed in the same nature, were taken away without baptism before they could do or will anything good or evil, or even at least know anything.”

[Col. 0634D] **The second argument from Scripture. Children are born under the power of the demons, from which their sensible punishment is plainly demonstrated. How unsuccessfully opponents answer this argument. Eight punishments imposed upon infants, briefly enumerated.**

The second argument is drawn from all those passages of Holy Scripture in which the captivity of the human race under the prince of the demon is indicated. John 12:31: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out.” Mark 3:27: “No one can enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man; then he will plunder his house.” The Lord himself likewise testifies in Matthew 12:29: “How can anyone enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man?” In Luke 11 the Lord compares the demon to a strong, armed man guarding his courtyard.

From these passages the holy Doctor infers that infants are to be burned with the prince of the demons in eternal fire. Hear the complete discussion of this great man in book III of the *Imperfect Work against Julian*, chapter 199, of which I supplied a fragment above:

> “But you,” he says, “who deny that it”—namely, the image of God—“is possessed by the devil, undoubtedly deny that it is rescued from the power of darkness when, through regeneration, it is transferred into the kingdom of Christ; and you accuse the whole Catholic Church of a grave crime against majesty. For under the laws of this world, no one who blows upon the emperor’s image, even if it is not alive, is held guilty. Yet infants are exsufflated in the exorcism before they are baptized. Therefore living images are exsufflated—not of some king, but of God. Indeed, it is the devil who is exsufflated, for through the contagion of sin he undoubtedly holds the infant guilty, so that, once the devil has been sent out, the infant may be transferred to Christ. Let Julian’s madness, then, be exsufflated, lest the Church be declared guilty of treason in the cleansing and exsufflation of infants. But if the infant is not rescued from the power of darkness and remains there, why are you surprised that he will be IN THE ETERNAL FIRE WITH THE DEVIL, since he is not permitted to enter the kingdom of God? Or because the Pelagians prepare, apart from the kingdom of God, some unknown place of rest and eternal life for unbaptized infants, will Christ’s sentence therefore be false: ‘Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned’ (Mark 16)?”

Again, in book V of the same work, chapter 6:

> “Or perhaps,” he says, “are human beings not among those who are rescued from the power of darkness, over which the devil holds dominion? Or are you so foolish as to assert that the devil does not claim for himself those whom he possesses and keeps subject to his power? But, to say nothing of those whom you can claim to be possessed by the devil through their own evil will, what will you say about the one whose father, when questioned by the Lord, replied that from infancy he had been tormented by an unclean spirit? Did not the devil claim as his own, in order to afflict them, his limbs and senses—all of which were established by God as author and are common gifts of the impious and the pious? Etc.”

This argument greatly troubles the opponents, who attempt, as I believe unsuccessfully, to evade its force by offering various solutions.

A certain otherwise very celebrated theologian replies first:

> “This punishment does not appear to be due to original sin. Just as the punishment of sense is not due to it, neither is the simultaneous handing-over into the power of a most powerful and hostile enemy, who would bring a person into the moral necessity of incurring such a punishment, together with the prohibition of helpers from bringing assistance. For this would be a punishment more severe than the punishment of sense; it is more tolerable merely to be tormented than to be placed under a moral necessity of a new crime that deserves such torment.”

This response is inconsistent with the Church’s decrees, from which it is plainly gathered that through original sin we are captives of the demon. Saint Celestine, as is commonly thought, defines the matter in his letter to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 12:

> “Let us also not contemplate with idle attention what the holy Church uniformly performs throughout the world concerning those who are to be baptized. Whether infants or young people come to the sacrament of regeneration, they do not first approach the fountain of life until, through the exorcisms and exsufflations of the clergy, the unclean spirit has been driven away from them. Thus it truly becomes apparent how ‘the prince of this world is cast out’ (John 12), and how the strong man is first bound and afterward his goods are plundered and transferred into the possession of the victor, who ‘leads captivity captive’ (Psalm 117) and ‘gives gifts to men’ (Ephesians 4). Therefore, etc.”

The whole Church later handed down this doctrine, as is evident from the chapter *Sacerdotes*, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, and the chapters *Parvuli*, *Sicut nostis*, *Dehinc*, etc. The Council of Trent explicitly defined in session 5, *On Original Sin*, that Adam

> “fell, together with death, into captivity under the power of him who thereafter held dominion over death, that is, the devil.”

Hence Saint Augustine, in book VI of the *Imperfect Work against Julian*, chapter 20, rebukes Julian for being distressed that the devil is imposed as lord and possessor upon the image of God. He writes:

> “Jesus says—he who, in accordance with his name, saves his people from their sins—‘No one enters the house of a strong man unless he first binds the strong man.’ Yet you do not admit that infants belong to this people of Christ, whom he saves from their sins; you wish them to be bound neither by their own sins nor by original sins, and by your deceitful speech you diminish the strength of him whom Truth called strong.”

He adds:

> “Nor should it seem unworthy to you that the image of God is subject to the devil. This would not happen except by the judgment of God, nor is this condemnation removed except by the grace of God, etc.”

Catharinus, in his customary manner—that is, boldly—says in the work cited:

> “Nor will they remain perpetually under the devil’s power, because on the last day the devil will be cast out for their sake also, so that he will have no further right over them.”

This response, however, as Bellarmine rightly observed, cannot at all be defended by a Catholic. I ask why infants are now captives of the demon. The Church’s dogmas are clear: because of the stain of original sin. Catharinus must again be asked whether this stain will remain after the day of judgment or not. If he says no, he falls into error; for that guilt is destroyed by baptism alone:

> “Do not say this,” Augustine says, “if you wish to be Catholic” (book III of *On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 9).

If he says yes, then the devil’s full right over the children will remain even after the day of judgment, since they will still be subject to original sin.

Let him hear Augustine, whether he wishes to or not. In this question, as in many others, he often attacks Augustine in book I of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 23:

> “This wound inflicted upon the human race by the devil compels whatever is born through it to be under the devil, as though he were lawfully plucking fruit from his own tree—not because human nature is from him, for it is from God alone, but because the defect is not from God. Human nature, which is praiseworthy because it is God’s work, is not condemned on its own account, but on account of the condemnable defect by which it has been corrupted. And because of that for which it is condemned, it is also subjected to the condemnable devil, because the devil himself is an unclean spirit.”

Saint Fulgentius asserted the same in book I of *On the Truth of Predestination*, chapter 14:

> “The cause of adults and children who complete the course of this present life in unbelief without baptism is one and the same, insofar as the fellowship of original sin is concerned. Because of it, both will go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels, since in them the Savior’s grace has not erased the bond by which the malice of the deceiver subjected them to himself.”

Arriaga replies, volume I, *On the First and Second Parts of the Summa*, disputation 52, that saying children are under the devil’s power means nothing more than that they are sinners. Others, however, think that children are under the devil’s power through original sin because, from that sin, the demon acquired the power to tempt the human race and consequently to destroy it in Gehenna.

But it is one thing to be a sinner and another to be captive to the devil. Captivity is the effect of sin, just as if a prince were to thrust a subject, on account of some crime, into the power of a tyrant. Moreover, just as mortal sin transfers a person into the family subject to the devil, so too does original sin. Hence the holy Doctor says at the beginning of book I of *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, chapter 34:

> “What shall I say about the very form of the sacrament? I wish that one of those who hold contrary opinions would bring me an infant to be baptized. What is my exorcism doing in him if he is not held in the devil’s family?”

As for what others say—that the human race is under the demon’s power because he acquired from that sin the power and right to tempt human beings—it is wholly foolish. First, because he cannot tempt children, who are incapable of willing anything; second, because he was able to tempt Adam, who nevertheless was not yet under the demon’s power; and third, because being able to be tempted is not the same as being captive, but only as being capable of becoming captive.

Children, however, are actually born captives of the demon. Hence Pope Zosimus says in letter 157, according to Saint Augustine:

> “No one becomes free except one who is a slave of sin; nor can anyone be called redeemed unless he was truly captive beforehand through sin.”

Saint Gregory likewise clearly distinguishes captivity from the power to tempt in book XXVI of the *Moralia*, chapter 20:

> “‘Now the prince of this world will be cast out.’ Hence he now possesses holy people not by holding them, but by persecuting them through temptation. Because he does not reign inwardly in them, he fights against them outwardly; and because he has lost dominion within, he wages war outside.”

Furthermore, it is false that children are under the demon’s power through original sin in the same way as through any actual sin, as Moraines teaches, no. 13. For in infants and in other unbaptized persons the demon has a right as over his own slave. As Pope Celestine defined above, exorcisms and the exsufflations of the clergy are used so that the unclean spirit may be driven away from them. Therefore they are truly possessed by the demon through indwelling, since the unclean spirit cannot be driven away, nor the prince cast out, unless he is within the infant.

We do not, however, use these exorcisms and exsufflations to absolve a sinner, even the worst of sinners, but only in healing those possessed, who are held within by the devil through indwelling. This was noted by that distinguished Carmelite, John Bacon, who, whereas the other ancient scholastics say scarcely a few words about this captivity from which the punishments of infants are sufficiently clearly inferred, alone adhered to the Augustinian-Catholic opinion in book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 39, question 1. Concerning the demon’s dominion he says:

> “I say that he dwells within—not as a form informing the subject, nor through some form that he creates in the sinful soul, as God creates it—but he dwells through dominion in the sinner, or, in other words, by right of dominion and power.”

There, in response to the second objection, he defines original sin as

> “the compliance of our will with the devil and, consequently, also the indwelling of the devil.”

The demon therefore dwells in the bodies of the unbaptized, both children and adults—not so that they are truly possessed persons, but as a prince dwelling by right of dominion in his kingdom. Such is the power that the prince of darkness exercises over them. All this is gathered from the exsufflations and exorcisms, since when an infant is baptized the priest says:

> “Come out, unclean spirit, and give place to the Holy Spirit.”

Faithful sinners, however, belong to the body of the Church, whose head is Christ. The holy Doctor discusses the demon’s power over unbelievers at length in letter 107 to Vitalis.

Moraines replies finally:

> “The third argument,” he says in no. 17, “does not touch us at all, since we do not deny that those infants will remain eternally hated by God on account of original sin, and in a certain manner under the captivity and servitude of the devil, as in this life—namely, deprived of that special protection of God by which they would be made immune from his invasions and attacks.”

What is especially displeasing in this response is the phrase “in a certain manner,” which limits the demon’s power over his captives. Augustine says admirably in book VI against Julian, chapter 20:

> “By your deceitful speech you diminish the strength of him whom Truth called strong.”

Why is a restriction added which neither councils nor popes appended? What is especially pleasing in the same response, however, is that he admits children will not be immune from the demon’s invasions and attacks. This is precisely what we intend to establish: they will be subject to sensible punishments because they will be under the power of the most cruel tyrant. Unless he says that infants will suffer no harm from such invasions and attacks—which would be more foolish than anything one could say—for they are tormented not by cold or heat but by the demon, who possesses a thousand arts of harming.

A similar argument is drawn from the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 9:

> “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make his power known, endured with much patience vessels of wrath made for destruction.”

The Apostle there also calls these vessels of wrath “vessels of dishonor.” Since infants, therefore, are vessels of dishonor, to what place, I ask, will God assign them?

> “God,” says Fulgentius, “will assign the vessels of dishonor to an eternal fire in which they will always burn.”

The African Fathers say in the synodal letter, chapter 13:

> “They are vessels of dishonor, to whom it is said: ‘Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.’”

This had earlier been taught by the teacher of the African Church in book I of the *Imperfect Work against Julian*, at the end:

> “We indeed proclaim God as the maker of infants, but from the same mass we do not grant an intermediate place for vessels in which they are made neither for honor nor for dishonor—a place the Apostle did not give.”

Let the opponents therefore consider that the demon has such power over his vessels that, as Christ says, the demon’s conqueror had first to bind him before the vessels could be snatched from his house. Let them not diminish, as the holy Doctor says, through deceitful speech the strength of him whom Truth called strong.

It is therefore certain that unbaptized infants are vessels of dishonor in the demon’s house, from which they have not been rescued through Christ, and that they are held captive there by the strong, armed man guarding his courtyard. The older scholastics called this dark house limbo, in which infants are detained. So did Saints Thomas and Bonaventure, as well as Scotus, Aegidius, Durandus, Richard, and others generally, according to Bellarmine, chapter 2 above.

From this doctrine, whether they wish it or not, the punishment of sense is proved. For this purpose it should be noted that the holy Doctor teaches in book XXI of *The City of God*, chapter 11:

> “There are eight kinds of punishments in the laws: loss, bonds, blows, retaliation, disgrace, exile, death, and servitude.”

Therefore, since infants, besides the punishment of exile—which the scholastics call the punishment of loss—suffer servitude under the demon and imprisonment, they certainly suffer another punishment in addition to the punishment of loss.

We have heard above from a very celebrated theologian what kind of punishment this servitude under the prince of darkness and the strong, armed man is. He said:

> “For this would be a punishment more severe than the punishment of sense.”

Most truly. Suppose, for example, that a prince were not only to punish the children of one of his subjects with exile and deprive them of their paternal inheritance, but also to sell them as slaves to some tyrant. Surely this last punishment of captivity would not be insignificant. But there is no captivity worse, harsher, or more atrocious than being under the demon—a Phalaris, Dionysius, or Maxentius more cruel, the most savage of all tyrants.

Nor should the punishment of imprisonment be considered light, especially under a strong, armed man guarding his courtyard. This too another writer of the Society, the modern Arriaga, does not deny. He says in *On the First and Second Parts*, disputation 52, no. 5, that the punishment of that prison would be extremely severe, where, like logs (*stipites*), they could neither see, smell, nor taste anything; indeed, this would be a sensible punishment.

For this reason, several of the same recent scholastics, unwilling to afflict children with the punishment of imprisonment, invent some unknown third place for deceiving infants, as the Pelagians once did, according to Pope Gelasius—whose words were quoted just above—and as Saint Augustine very often affirmed and ridiculed.

But what will the opponents say if we prove that infants endure those eight kinds of punishment? They themselves concede the punishment of loss and exile, while from Holy Scripture we have clearly derived the punishments of captivity and imprisonment. We prove the same concerning the remaining four.

It is certain that they suffer bonds, since they are captives, and those bonds cannot be loosed unless the strong, armed guardian of the courtyard himself is first bound. They also suffer the punishment of disgrace, for according to the Apostle they are vessels of dishonor (Romans 9). Hence the holy Doctor says in book I against Julian of the *Imperfect Work*, chapter 138:

> “Although you admit that from that mass some are adopted into the kingdom of God—whom you undoubtedly concede to have been made vessels for honor—you shamelessly deny, unless you agree intelligently, that others are not adopted for this purpose and have been made vessels for dishonor. For even if, as you wish, it is not the punishment of condemnation, will it not at least be a dishonor to the image of God to be separated from the kingdom of God?”

Moreover, they suffer blows, for, as Moraines says in no. 17, they lack that special protection of God by which they would be made immune from his—that is, the demon’s—invasions and attacks. Nor should this tyrant be thought so mild that he never strikes his slaves, even once. It is enough that infants are vessels in his house, as Christ says, and that they are held captive in the devil’s family, as the holy Father teaches in the cited book *On the Merits of Sins*, chapter 34.

Add to these the punishment of retaliation. For those who did not wish to be under God with their first parent became slaves under the devil. Hold fast to the golden words of the holy Doctor in book XIV of *The City of God*, chapter 15:

> “A just condemnation followed, a condemnation such that he who, by guarding the commandment, had been spiritual even in the flesh became carnal even in mind. And because he had pleased himself through his pride, by God’s justice he was abandoned to himself. He was not, as he desired, in complete power over himself; rather, disagreeing even with himself, he performed under the one to whom he consented by sin a harsh and miserable servitude in place of the freedom he had desired. He died willingly in spirit and was destined to die unwillingly in body; having deserted eternal life, he was condemned also to eternal death unless grace should set him free.”

As for death, the last of the punishments, it is certain that the entire posterity of Adam incurred through sin not only bodily but also spiritual death. The holy Doctor repeatedly teaches that infants are punished with the penalty of the second death on account of original sin. In book I to Boniface, chapter 22, he says:

> “Or if the words of the Gospel compel you to confess that infants leaving the body cannot have life and salvation unless they have been baptized, ask why those who have not been baptized are compelled to undergo the punishment of the second death.”

The second death is understood from chapter 20 of the Apocalypse, where we read:

> “And whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.”

And afterward:

> “Hell and death were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.”

Since children dying without baptism are not written in the book of life, they are undoubtedly assigned to the second death—that is, to the fire. The archbishop of Tuam presses this argument at length and learnedly from Augustine in his little work on this question, chapters 11 and 12.

I know that Moraines replies in no. 69 that the second death is deprivation of the vision of God. But Augustine rejects this response in chapter 92 of the *Enchiridion*, and in book XIII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, and book XIX, chapter 28. Saint Fulgentius likewise rejects it in book I to Monimus, chapter 6, where, on the basis of Holy Scripture, they declare that the first death occurs when the soul is separated from the body, while the second occurs when the same soul is punished eternally with the body.

The same opinion of the holy Doctor is proved from the African councils and the letters of Pope Innocent. The assertion concerning the punishments of infants was included among the dogmas of faith by the African Church, according to Saint Fulgentius. An especially notable testimony for the same matter is provided by Pope Gelasius.

The scholastics who departed from Augustine’s opinion in determining the punishments of infants have published that his opinion has only Augustine as its patron, as Catharinus says, and that very few follow it, as Moraines says. Indeed, Catharinus, setting Augustine alone against himself, writes:

> “But, they say, Augustine’s authority is great—certainly great, but the authority of the truth, which is now manifest, is far greater; far greater too is the authority of the popes, of the Church teaching from the chair, and of the common opinion of the Doctors.”

By these words that author plainly showed himself a stranger to the writings of the ancient Fathers. For we shall confirm the holy Father’s opinion by the testimonies of councils and popes, and by testimonies so evident that I have no doubt that, if the scholastics had encountered them, they would not have departed from the Augustinian opinion by so much as a finger’s breadth.

Scotus rightly said in book II, distinction 33, single question, that the position of the Parisian masters stood against Augustine. Against them, however, we shall set the more ancient bishops of all Africa.

Indeed, the teachers of the older Parisian school, having devoted their exceptionally gifted minds to the subtleties of scholasticism, were insufficiently versed in reading the synods and the Fathers [Col. 0641C]. Hence, through lack of learning, they introduced certain opinions from which the teachers of the ancient Church stood at a considerable distance. This will become clear in the present controversy, in which the scholastics, through their incomplete knowledge of the Pelagian heresy, not only departed from the opinion received from antiquity but also, for the most part, agreed with the Pelagians on certain points. This was likewise noted, with an introductory commendation, by the cardinal Bellarmine, whose words I shall quote near the end of this controversy.

First of all, the African Fathers struck down the errors of the Pelagians with an anathema in both synods of the province of Carthage, likewise in the other synod of Milevis, and afterward in plenary councils, as we have described more fully in the first book of the *History of the Pelagian Heresy*. In these sacred assemblies, I demonstrate that sensible punishments were decreed for children dying without baptism [Col. 0641D].

The Fathers of the Council of Carthage, in their letter to Innocent, preserved in Augustine’s Epistle 90, write the following about the Pelagians:

> “They also deny that little children are to be baptized for the sake of the salvation given through Christ the Savior, and thus, by this deadly doctrine, they kill them eternally, promising that, even if they are not baptized, they will possess eternal life.”

The Fathers of the province of Numidia, in their letter to the same Innocent, which is Augustine’s Epistle 92, write the following about those same heretics:

> “They wickedly insist that little children too, if they are not renewed by any sacraments of Christian grace, will possess eternal life.”

Pope Innocent, having received these letters, struck down the falsehood of the new heresy in a grave rescript:

> “But that which your fraternity says they preach—namely, that little children can be granted the rewards of eternal life even without the grace of baptism—is utterly foolish.”

*Epistle* 95, in Augustine.

Thus both the synods and the pope denied to children who died in original sin that eternal life which the Pelagians granted to those same children. Eternal life means the perpetual possession of God, which blesses the soul in the kingdom of heaven, and consequently the exclusion of every misery. Opposed to this life is eternal death, which consists in the perpetual loss of the highest good and in enduring affliction and torments in hell.

Yet the Pelagians nowhere dared to say that children without baptism would enter the kingdom of heaven, as we explained above from the sermon cited earlier, *On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 14. Augustine writes concerning the same people in book I, chapter 18, of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*:

> “They say that little children, newly brought forth from their mothers’ wombs into this life, receive baptism not for the remission of sin, but so that, since they have not had spiritual birth, they may be created in Christ and become participants in his kingdom, and in this way become children and heirs of God, and co-heirs of Christ.”

Hence the same holy teacher says against the Pelagians in book II, chapter 113, of the *Unfinished Work*:

> “Answer what you are, you who separate so many images of God from the kingdom of God without any merit of that sin, and make two eternal felicities: one which is in the kingdom of God, and another which is outside the kingdom of God.”

And in book I, chapter 132, of the same work, he reports that, according to the Pelagians, little children would be

> “in some place of a second felicity, which,” he says, “your heresy has constructed for such persons.”

From this it follows that the eternal life which those heretics promised children was situated in a certain second felicity—that is, one inferior to that enjoyed by the blessed in the kingdom of heaven. For since the children in that place would suffer no torments throughout all eternity, they were said by the Pelagians to live eternally happy.

Saint Fulgentius writes in book I, chapter 6, *To Monimus*, that God threatened the soul dead through sin with a twofold death:

> “The first, in the separation of soul and body; the second, in the eternal torment of soul and body. Accordingly, the first occurs when, as the soul departs, the flesh alone dies; the second, when the soul returns to the flesh and is tormented in that flesh and together with that flesh in which it sinned.”

Temporal life is opposed to the first death, while eternal life is opposed to the second, when the soul will enjoy perpetual happiness. On this matter, see Augustine, book XX, chapter 6, *City of God*. Thus the eternal life of infants, according to the opinion of the Pelagians, is that which is opposed to the second death. For this reason Augustine, in book XVIII, chapter 28, of the same work, says that it is called “the second death”:

> “because neither can the soul there be said to live, since it will be alienated from the life of God, nor the body, since it will be subject to eternal pains.”

Therefore, when the African synods and Saint Innocent condemned those who said that children who died without baptism possessed eternal life, they rejected that second felicity which the Pelagians promised infants outside the kingdom of God; and consequently they decreed that those same children would also undergo the second death [Col. 0643A], which is opposed to blessed life.

Moreover, that eternally blessed life which the Pelagians assigned to children had already been rejected before the African synods at the Council of Diospolis in 415. There, when Pelagius was accused of having taught, through his disciple Caelestius, that “infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life,” he denied having said this. Hence Augustine pressed Pelagius, in Epistle 106 to Paulinus of Nola, with the claim that children without the grace of regeneration in Christ “do not have life in themselves and therefore are liable to eternal punishment.”

Conrius and Moraines thought that the eternal life which the Pelagians promised little children consisted in the clear vision of God, although outside the kingdom of heaven. To them one might reply, on the basis of what we have established thus far, that the synods decreed that children could not enjoy eternal life without baptism [Col. 0643B]—that is, the clear vision of God—yet that it does not immediately follow that they were to be punished by the second death in its full extent, since this term may signify merely deprivation of the vision of God and not also the torments and eternal punishments of soul and body.

But this opinion cannot be admitted for any reason if we consider what the Pelagians understood by the name “kingdom of heaven.” And although Moraines, no. 55, says that they did not express this sufficiently clearly, their opinion can nevertheless be gathered from Julian, book VI, chapter 37, of the *Unfinished Work*, where he says:

> “Most especially, the entire glorified assembly of the saints will not cease to be subject to God, but the whole body worthy of the kingdom of heaven, which is built under Christ its head, will cling to the divine will with perfect affection, so that, with every desire for sin extinguished, God may both hold all people and make them complete.”

From this it follows that the Pelagians did not promise children the beatific vision. For one who sees God clings to the divine will with perfect affection, so that, with every desire for sin extinguished, God both contains and fills that person. Therefore, if the children enjoyed the clear vision of God, they would in reality be in the kingdom of God, which the Pelagians denied.

Again, Saint Augustine everywhere presses the Pelagians, who denied original sin, with the objection that it would be undeserved and unjust for children excluded from the kingdom of heaven to be tormented by such great misery. In book II, chapter 113, of the *Unfinished Work*, he says:

> “At last you admit that unregenerate little children will be unhappy outside the kingdom of God. Tell us, then, what is the merit of this unhappiness, you verbose and contentious men who deny original sin.”

And in book IV, chapter 99, he says:

> “You love him in such a way that you do not believe that not being there, or at least suffering a light punishment there, is the condition of a human being, but rather no punishment at all.”

But if the Pelagians granted little children the vision of God outside the kingdom of God, Augustine would not have appropriately inferred against them that the children would be unhappy and subject to punishment. For one who sees God possesses the highest good and cannot in any way be unhappy or subject to any punishment.

Moreover, in book II, chapter 113, of the *Unfinished Work*, the holy Father presses Julian and his associates with these words:

> “Tell me, I beg you, in that felicity which will be outside the kingdom of God, will anyone reign, or no one? If no one, that felicity will doubtless be freer, without any king; but if someone will reign in it, who will be the king of the images of God if he is not God?”

But in that second felicity the children would enjoy the vision of God, and God would certainly reign in them; Augustine would not have struck his opponents with that dilemma. For when God is clearly seen, he alone reigns in the soul of the one who sees him and governs and directs all that person’s acts.

Thus the Pelagians assigned children a natural beatitude. For just as they asserted that children were naturally innocent, so they introduced for them a felicity of the same order. Yet on this doctrine they never made known to us what they actually thought; hence Augustine and the other Fathers admitted that they could not clearly grasp their opinion. In his book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 13, Augustine relates that the Pelagians promised children “a place of I know not what felicity,” and in *On Heresies*, chapter 88, he speaks of “a certain eternal and blessed life” of theirs. The same is found in book I, *On the Origin of the Soul*, whose words I shall quote shortly [Col. 0644B]. Pelagius himself used to say, “I do not know where they go,” as was stated above from Augustine.

I return to the African synods. At the Council held at Carthage in 418 against the Pelagians, the following canon is found in the ancient codices:

> “It was likewise decreed that if anyone says that the Lord’s statement, ‘In my Father’s house are many mansions’ (John XIV), was spoken so that it might be understood that in the kingdom of heaven there will be some middle place, or any place anywhere, where the little children who have departed this life without baptism may live blessedly—for without baptism they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, which is eternal life—let him be anathema. For when the Lord says, ‘Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven,’ what Catholic would doubt that the one who has not deserved to be a co-heir of Christ will be a participant of the devil? For whoever lacks the right hand will undoubtedly incur the left-hand portion.”

In book I, chapter 13, of the *History of the Pelagian Heresy*, I quoted this canon, where, on the authority of Photius, I showed that it had been written in the ancient codices. Binius likewise testifies to this, although some have omitted it. I do not wish to engage in a contentious dispute with anyone about the matter. In the meantime, I shall confirm this very point by the testimony of Saint Augustine, who writes in book II, chapter 12, *On the Origin of the Soul*:

> “The authority of the Catholic councils and of the apostolic see most justly condemned the recent Pelagian heretics, because they dared to grant unbaptized little children a place of rest and salvation even apart from the kingdom of heaven.”

Hence it is sufficiently probable that the cited canon was in fact drafted by the African synods.

It should be observed, however, that the Fathers denied the existence of another place anywhere because the sacred Scriptures name only two places—namely, the right and left hand of the Judge. Hence they assert that the children will be on the left and consequently will be participants of the devil.

In the same book, *On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 9, the holy Father writes:

> “Let no one promise unbaptized little children, between damnation and the kingdom of heaven, a place of rest or any kind of felicity, anywhere whatsoever, as though it were a middle place. For the Pelagian heresy promised them this as well.”

Therefore, since Augustine counted that opinion concerning a quasi-middle place—namely, one between the punishments of hell and the joys of the heavenly kingdom—among the errors of the Pelagian heresy, it is clear that it was also condemned by the African Fathers, who watched most diligently against that heresy [Col. 0645A], as will most clearly appear from what follows.

I shall add the opinion of the synod of the Byzacene Fathers, exiled to Sardinia by Thrasamund, the Arian king of the Vandals. When serious disputes concerning divine grace were being waged at Constantinople, certain monks went to Rome to settle them. Having heard of the African bishops exiled in Sardinia, they sent a delegation to them and also sent a book on the Lord’s Incarnation and divine grace, composed by themselves, asking the bishops to pass judgment on it.

After the Byzacene Fathers had deliberated in common council about what should be written in reply to the monks, they commissioned Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, to put the Fathers’ decrees into writing. He immediately composed a book entitled *On the Incarnation and Grace* [Col. 0645B].

In it Augustine’s opinion concerning the punishments of children is set forth with the utmost clarity. For in chapter 14 they say:

> “What justice is there in this: that the image of God, which could not sin by itself, should not be permitted to enter the kingdom of God unless it is redeemed by the blood of the Son of God? Whoever does not enter there will certainly be tormented by the interminable punishments of eternal fire. By what justice, then, does the just God inflict punishment upon infants born without sin, in whom he finds no cause for punishment?”

Likewise, chapter 30 reads:

> “How does he grant eternal salvation to infants who are baptized and die in that same infancy, whose good will he neither awaits nor finds? Again, how does he condemn others who have died without baptism to eternal torments, when he finds in them no fault of an evil will? Does not their perversity compel these enemies of God’s grace—who are neither defenders but deceivers of human free choice—to suppose that God is unjust in the death of all little children, when, without any goodness or wickedness of will intervening, they see some obtain the kingdom and others assigned to unending fire?”

This book is included among the works of Saint Fulgentius, because it was dictated by him. Yet it is clear that it was approved by the synod and sent to the monks at Rome from its very opening, where the Byzacene bishops are named:

> “To our most beloved and greatly cherished holy brothers, Peter the deacon, John, Leontius, and another John, and to the rest of the brothers, etc., Dacianus, Fortunatus, Boethus, Victor, Scholasticus, Orontius, Vindicianus, Victor, Januarius, Victorianus, Photinus, Quodvultdeus, Fulgentius, Felix, and Januarius send greetings in the Lord.”

Thus fifteen most learned and holy bishops adopted Augustine’s opinion without reservation. Nor does it matter that the cited volume was written by Fulgentius’s own hand, since he vigorously defended the opinion of Augustine the Father. In all synods, it is customary to entrust the task of committing the public decrees of the Fathers to writing to some one person distinguished for learning and eloquence.

Fulgentius’s disciple writes in chapter 20 of the *Life of Fulgentius*:

> “After the longest delays of deliberation, whatever the common decision had found was entrusted to blessed Fulgentius to be eloquently presented to the understanding of the others.”

And afterward:

> “Therefore, whenever they wrote in reply to those who consulted them, the names of all the bishops were stated in the heading, but only the speech of Blessed Fulgentius was preserved in the written style.”

Accordingly, this was the opinion of all the Fathers of Byzacena, whose primate at that time was Dacianus.

We also possess their synodal letter, in which Fulgentius is not named among the bishops. Sirmond published it, and it is included among the works of Fulgentius in volume VI of the Cologne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, published in 1618. The same opinion is set forth in chapter 8 of that letter. I shall quote the words below.

Here I wish to demonstrate clearly that in antiquity, in the African Church, which numbered four hundred and sixty-six bishops, it was so firmly established that children who died without baptism were punished in the underworld with sensible punishment that the doctrine was reckoned among the dogmas of the faith.

When Peter the deacon, a very learned man—as is clear from his book *On the Incarnation and Grace*—was about to travel to the East, he asked Saint Fulgentius by letter to send him a brief summary of the Catholic faith, to which he could conform. For he understood that many heresies were spreading throughout the East.

Fulgentius sent him a book entitled *On the Faith to Peter*, concerning which I spoke in book II, chapter 19, of the *History of the Pelagian Heresy*. In that volume he enumerates forty dogmas belonging to the Catholic faith and arranges them into separate chapters, which begin as follows: “Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt.” The first dogma is set forth in chapter 4.

After he had placed in chapter 26 the twenty-third dogma, concerning original sin, he writes in the following chapter, 27:

> “Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that not only human beings who already exercise reason, but also little children who, whether still in their mothers’ wombs or having been born from their mothers, depart from this world without the sacrament of holy baptism, which is given in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, are to be punished with the everlasting punishment of eternal fire; for although they have committed no sin through their own action, they have nevertheless drawn the condemnation of original sin through carnal conception and birth.”

He proposed this as the twenty-fourth dogma—or, as he calls it, chapter—to be believed by Peter concerning the faith. Afterward, having recited the remaining chapters, he says in chapter 44:

> “In the meantime, faithfully believe, firmly hold, and truthfully and patiently defend these forty chapters, which most firmly belong to the rule of true faith. If you discover anyone dogmatizing contrary to them, flee from him as from a plague and reject him as a heretic. For the doctrines we have set forth agree so closely with the Catholic faith that if anyone wishes to oppose not only all of them but even individual ones, and does not hesitate to teach things contrary to them, he will appear to be a heretic and an enemy of the Christian faith and, on this account, must be anathematized by all Catholics.”

Thus Fulgentius testifies that little children dying with original sin alone are to be punished with the everlasting punishment of eternal fire, that this belongs to the rule of true faith, and that anyone who wishes to contradict it is to be rejected as a heretic. These words require no interpreter, only a reader.

Who, then, could fail to understand from this that the African Church counted Augustine’s opinion concerning the punishments of infants among the dogmas of the faith [Col. 0647A]? For it cannot be said that the most learned of all the African bishops was deceived in this matter, or that he wished to deceive others by selling his own little opinions as the Church’s unshaken dogmas.

What sort of man Fulgentius was, and how great, is clear from his life. It is enough here to quote what is said in chapter 20 of the *Life of Fulgentius*:

> “For sixty or more bishops were then bound by the chain of exile, and blessed Bishop Fulgentius was their tongue and intellect.”

The many books of his that have been published abundantly reveal his outstanding learning. See what I have said about him in book II, chapters 21 and 24, of the *History of the Pelagian Heresy*.

The same conclusion is drawn from Augustine. In book I, chapter 28, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, he calls those who assert that children will exist in some middle place “wrong believers.” Likewise, in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 12, he says:

> “When infants die, either through the merit of regeneration they pass from evil to good, or through the merit of their origin they pass from evil to evil. The Catholic faith knows this.”

Moreover, in book V, chapter 64, against Julian in the *Unfinished Work*, he says:

> “Among the reprobate there are certainly very many who, if they were snatched from this life as infants, would, according to your false heresy, be removed entirely from all condemnation, but according to the Catholic faith would be removed from the gravest condemnation.”

It is certain that the Catholic faith asserts in little children the punishment which the Pelagians denied. Yet they readily conceded the punishment of loss—that is, exclusion from the kingdom of heaven. Hence Augustine said in sermon 14, *On the Words of the Apostle*:

> “You may seem merciful to yourself because you do not take life away from him; yet you condemn the one whom you separate from the kingdom of heaven. You condemn him; you do not strike him, but you send him into exile.”

Thus the Pelagians did not strike children—that is, they did not subject them to punishment of sense—but imposed only the punishment of loss, by sending them into exile. Therefore, according to Augustine’s testimony, the Catholic faith teaches that little children are struck, and are not merely sent into exile, which the Pelagians readily admitted.

Again, in tractate 67 on John, he says:

> “Accordingly, those people must be rejected from a Christian heart who think that ‘there are many mansions’ was said because outside the kingdom of heaven there will be some place where the blessed innocents who departed this life without baptism may remain, since without baptism they could not enter the kingdom of heaven. This is not faith, because it is not the true and Catholic faith.”

And yet we see many scholastics promising little children a most perfect natural beatitude, without pain or sadness, outside the kingdom of God. Their opinion is less tolerable than that of the Pelagians, because the Pelagians maintained that infants were innocent and stained by no fault, so that it did not seem so great an absurdity to prepare some felicity for them. The scholastics, however—men who are not without distinction—assert with the Catholic Church that children are infected with original corruption and are under the power of the devil, children of wrath, yet afterward do not hesitate to promise them a certain blessed life.

But Saint Gelasius, raised from that same Africa to the Roman apostolic see, confirmed Augustine’s opinion so openly that nothing more solid can be brought forward in this dispute [Col. 0648A]. In a letter sent to the bishops throughout Picenum against Seneca, that delirious old Pelagian, he writes:

> “As for what he asserts concerning little children—namely, that they cannot be condemned for original sin alone without baptism—it is a sufficiently impious, sufficiently profane proposition.”

The Pelagians, however, never promised children the kingdom of heaven without baptism, but rather some third place between heaven and hell. Let the aforementioned Gelasius be heard:

> “There is therefore no reason for them to say that unregenerate infants are unable to enter the kingdom of heaven only, but are not punished by perpetual condemnation.”

Since the pope declares that, in addition to exclusion from the heavenly kingdom, which is the punishment of loss, children are punished by perpetual condemnation, it is evident that he approved Augustine’s opinion. He concludes:

> “Let them therefore say how those established in perpetual death are not to be considered condemned. Let them therefore remove from the midst that I-know-not-what third place which they create for deceiving little children.”

Thus the pope argues: the children are condemned; therefore let them remove the third place which they create for deceiving little children.

From this it is clear that in the antecedent Gelasius is speaking of condemnation in hell, by which the children endure the punishments of perpetual—that is, the second—death. Hence he rightly infers that the third place must be removed. But why does he call it “third” unless to declare that there are only two places: heaven, the abode of the blessed, and hell, the prison of the condemned?

The defenders of Augustine’s opinion are called by the scholastics “torturers of children,” but Gelasius struck them with a far graver censure when, in the language of the apostolic mouth, he pronounced them deceivers of little children, since by an empty assertion they promised them a place of second felicity.

Indeed, in the same passage he rejects that third place, moved by the same testimony of sacred Scripture which we quoted at the beginning from Augustine. For the pope writes:

> “Let them therefore remove from the midst that I-know-not-what third place which they create for deceiving little children. And because we read only of the right side and the left, let them not make those who are without baptism remain in the left region, but let them allow those who have been baptized to be transferred by sacred regeneration to the saving right hand.”

Therefore Pope Gelasius approved not only the holy teacher’s opinion but also his reasoning.

Moreover, that judgment is definitive:

> “Let them therefore remove from the midst that I-know-not-what third place which they create for deceiving little children.”

By saying “I-know-not-what,” he declares that he neither knows nor investigates what or where the second felicity promised to children by the Pelagians might be. He condemns their dogma for the reason that they create a third place between the kingdom of heaven—which is given to those who will be on the right—and the punishments of hell, which are assigned to those who will be on the left.

For this reason Gelasius is rightly called by Gabriel Vasquez, part I, disputation 91, no. 75, “Augustinian in every respect.” Indeed, as we have noted elsewhere, in that same letter he condensed the more powerful essence of Augustine’s entire doctrine against the Pelagians.

Accordingly, when, through a grant from Pope Clement, the Augustinian family had obtained permission to commemorate annually the memory of that same holy pontiff, it inserted among the offices of prayer a summary of his life, notable for Gelasius’s devotion to the doctrine of Saint Augustine.

Dionysius Exiguus recounts Gelasius’s praises in a letter to the presbyter Julian, in which he highly commends the doctrine and piety of that pontiff, as well as the labors he endured for the orthodox faith. You will read this letter at the end of the first part of Luca Holstenius’s Roman collection.

That this was at that time the common opinion in the Church—namely, that children dying without baptism were thrust into hell—is clear from the book of faith which the Pelagian bishops composed. For in it they exaggerate the sensible punishments of children as though they were a monstrous absurdity.

The same assertion of Augustine is confirmed by the authority of the Fathers and of many more recent theologians.

[Col. 0649B]

As is fitting, Jerome will lead the procession of the Fathers. He contended more closely with Pelagius in Palestine, as though foot had been set against foot. He published *Dialogues Against the Same Arch-Heretic*, in which he introduced Pelagius speaking under the name Critobolus and a Catholic man under the name Atticus.

Thus, at the end of the third book, Critobolus objects:

> “I ask you, what sin have little infants committed? Neither can the awareness of guilt be charged to them, nor ignorance, since, according to the prophet Jonah, they do not know their right hand from their left. They cannot sin, and yet they can perish; their knees are weak, they cannot articulate words by crying, their babbling tongue is laughed at, and the torments of eternal misery are prepared for the wretched.”

There Pelagius reproaches the Catholics as though it were absurd that children should suffer torments in another’s life [Col. 0649C]. What does Jerome reply to this? Perhaps those words of Annatus: “We deny the harsh consequence”? Book 8 of his Augustine, chapter 1, p. 858.

Certainly not. Rather, he proves original sin from the Apostle Paul, so that it may not appear that torments are inflicted upon children unjustly.

The same sensible punishment of infants is asserted by Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, who flourished in Gaul around the year 500. For in a poem to his sister Fuscina he wrote elegantly:

> “Yet this is graver for all, if envious death  
> hurls the tender child, deprived of the washing  
> of the divine font, into Gehenna,  
> born to a harsh destiny;  
> as soon as he ceases to be his mother’s son,  
> he will belong to perdition. Then those whom they have borne  
> reject their sad offspring—  
> mothers who have produced their pledges only for the flames.”

Alcimus Avitus was a most learned bishop and presided over the Council of Epaon and others [Col. 0649D].

To him I shall join Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, who lived at the same time as Avitus. In book *On the Faith to Peter the Deacon*, chapter 27, he taught the same opinion as something to be held as a matter of faith; I quoted his words above.

Likewise, in book I, chapter 12, *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, he says:

> “There is therefore no difference of cause among infants that would cause one to be chosen and another rejected. But if the will of the parents is considered, those who are Christians earnestly desired and diligently worked for their child to be baptized; nevertheless, when their child was overtaken by death before being baptized, he was assigned to eternal fires.”

He also writes in chapter 14:

> “The cause of adults and children who complete the course of the present life in unbelief without baptism is one and the same insofar as participation in original sin is concerned. From this both will go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels, because the Savior’s grace has not erased in them the bond by which the malice of the deceiver subjected them to himself.”

And immediately afterward:

> “He will repay each according to his works, so that they may burn in eternal fires not only on account of original sin—for little children too who die without baptism, having done nothing good or evil, are destined to burn in them—but also on account of their evil will, suffering so much more severely as they add more of their own iniquity.”

These books of Fulgentius are highly commended by the African Fathers exiled in Sardinia for the orthodox faith, in their synodal letter, chapter 18 [Col. 0650B].

At the end of that same century, Saint Gregory the Great, and at the beginning of the following century Saint Isidore of Seville, approved Augustine’s opinion, since it was then commonly held in the Church.

Gregory, book IX of the *Moralia*, chapter 12, commenting on Job’s words, “He multiplies my wounds even without cause,” writes:

> “For some are taken away from the light of the present life before they reach the point of producing the merits of good or evil in active life. Since the sacraments of salvation do not free them from the guilt of their origin, and since here they have done nothing of their own, they nevertheless arrive there at torments. For them one wound is to be born corruptibly, another to die carnally. But because eternal death also follows after death, by a hidden and just judgment wounds are multiplied for them even without cause; for they receive perpetual torments, although they have sinned nothing through their own will.”

And afterward:

> “How severely the strict Judge punishes those whom the guilt of their own actions condemns, if he also strikes eternally those whom liability to blame through free choice does not condemn?”

These statements are so clear that Moraines says Gregory asserted them not from the Church’s teaching but from his own opinion.

Saint Isidore likewise teaches the same thing in book II, *Differences of the Spirit*, no. 26:

> “This, however, must be held: the souls of little children are bound by the chain of original sin. Unless they receive the sacrament of baptism, they cannot be participants in the kingdom of heaven; but together with the flesh they will share the same sin and, by an equal judgment, will be condemned into eternal fire.”

And in book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 22, he says:

> “For original guilt alone, newly born infants pay punishments in hell.”

Thus that assertion concerning the punishments of children was certain in the Latin Church. Augustine, Fulgentius, and the synods taught it in Africa; Gelasius and Gregory, most holy pontiffs, transmitted it in Italy; Saint Avitus asserted it in Gaul, and Saint Isidore in Spain, without any doubt.

I believe that the same opinion continued for a long time, down to the age of the scholastics.

Saint Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, who flourished in the year 850, says in his book *On Predestination*, chapter 16:

> “This punishment is divided in two ways: first, in the separation of the soul from its body, which corresponds to the merit of that first transgression, since it was transmitted and implanted from the very root into the whole race of its posterity; and afterward in Gehenna, which has been acquired through the multiplicity of this and other crimes contracted by wanton perversity.”

And below, concerning little children, he writes:

> “Those who die outside the grace of baptism are condemned to everlasting punishment—not for their own sin, but for the sin of the first parent.”

Let Anselm come from England. In his book *On the Conception of the Virgin and Original Sin*, chapter 22, he taught:

> “But since no one doubts that equal punishment will not follow unequal sins, the condemnation of personal sin and of original sin is nevertheless similar in this respect: no one is admitted to the kingdom of God, for which human beings were made, except through the death of Christ, without which what is owed on account of Adam’s sin is not restored, although not all deserve to be tormented equally in hell. For after the day of judgment there will be no angel or human being except either in the kingdom of God or in hell.”

He rejects that third place of second felicity which many promise to little children.

Finally, let Saint Aelredus, a contemporary of Saint Bernard, be added, in book I, chapter 15, of the *Mirror of Charity*. He had posed this objection to himself:

> “What reason consigns little children to damnation, whom neither creation made evil nor their own will made unjust?”

He replies:

> “What then? Do you consider it unjust that useless and fruitless wood should be consumed by fire? Consider, I beg you, the whole human race as dry wood, fruitless wood, wood corrupted at its very root, infected as it is by the poison of the ancient serpent, most justly assigned to the flames, destined and adjudged to damnation. What then? Do you show yourself ungrateful, useless wood, because certain little branches are rescued from the fire after being cut off from your already dead root, so that, grafted onto a fruitful trunk, they may be restored to their former freedom?”

Read the rule of this holy man in Holstenius, p. 187, part II of the *Roman Collection*.

From all this it is evident how falsely Adamus said that all the Fathers stood against Augustine. Certainly neither Father Suarez nor Father Vasquez agree with Augustine in this matter. Rather, all the Latin Fathers who touched upon the controversy in any way followed the holy teacher, whereas Adamus was completely unfamiliar with their writings.

Thus this was the position of the ancient Church and of the holy Fathers concerning the punishments of infants, until, after the year 1200 of the Christian [Col. 0651D] era, new opinions were devised by the scholastics. If they had devoted as much study and labor to the volumes of the Fathers as they expended in explaining Aristotle, they certainly would not have obscured the position of Saint Augustine, nor would most of them have so deeply fixed in people’s minds the Pelagian opinion concerning that natural blessedness of children. Yet the force of truth was so great, and Augustine’s authority carried such weight, that most of the scholastics too followed Augustine’s position.

The first was Gregory of Rimini, the most subtle doctor of the ancient Parisian school, who most vigorously defended sensible punishments for infants in *Sentences* II, distinction 30, question 3. None of the ancient scholastics surpassed Gregory in his interpretation of Augustine [Col. 0652A]. More recent writers readily grant him this distinction. Vasquez says, *1–2*, disputation 185, number 13, that he was thoroughly versed in Augustine’s doctrine. Vandero calls him a most learned man, and, if anyone was, deeply devoted to Augustinian teaching, disputation 1 *On the Freedom of God*, number 23. Fasolus adds, part 1, question 23, article 1, doubt 3, number 34, that his books abound everywhere in Augustine’s authorities and opinions. Raynaud likewise calls him a man most thoroughly versed in Augustine’s teaching, *Censure against the Unoffending* [*For Valerius of Ceme­lium*], censure, number 2. Finally, Decamps writes:

“Gregory of Rimini, whom all who have even briefly touched his books know to have been Augustine not only in the discipline of his life but also in doctrine.”

Book III *On the Jansenist Heresy*, disputation 3, chapter 20. I have deliberately inserted these remarks here [Col. 0652B] so that it may be clear how much authority ought to be granted to Rimini when Augustine’s mind is under discussion. For I see this distinguished doctor defending as genuinely Augustinian many opinions which more recent writers reject as monstrosities and wholly anti-Augustinian paradoxes. This most subtle man therefore placed Augustine’s authority above the common opinion of the scholastics of his age.

Albert the Great too, in the *Summa*, tractate 18, acknowledges Augustine’s position as probable, as does Polman, doctor of Douai, at the end of the *Theological Breviary*, number 469. Sonnius agrees, tractates *On the Last Judgment*, chapters 6 and 7; so does Driedo, book I *On Grace and Free Will*, tractate 3, chapter 2, part I.

Apart from Gregory, the same position is defended at length by members of the Augustinian family: Augustine Musaeus, in his *Apology to Paul III*; Alipius Reylof of Belgium, book VIII *On the Soul according to the Mind of Saint Augustine*, chapter 2, section 13; and Michael Paludanus, the distinguished doctor of Louvain, in a letter to Conrius, archbishop of Tuam, which is read at the beginning of the same Conrius’s book, to be praised shortly.

Finally, Charles Moreau, a Frenchman, in volume I, part II, pages 89 and following, of his *Tertullian*, says:

“Let those also who admit in them only the punishment of loss consider that they are very far removed from the ancient sense of the Church and the Fathers.”

There he cites several testimonies of the Fathers. Yet opponents will easily say that these are to be understood as referring generically to damnation; for he did not produce the authorities of Gelasius, Avitus, Isidore, Prudentius, and others, which we cited above.

Nevertheless, I acknowledge that the Augustinians owe very much here to the most learned Fathers of the Seraphic family, for I see as many of them standing for the Augustinian position as there are from our own side. Alphonsus de Castro, a distinguished theologian, says in his book *Against Heresies*, under “Baptism,” that children infected with original sin are subject to hell. Matthias Hauzer teaches the same in volume II of the *Augustinian Anatomy*, page 764. The same is taught by John Poncius the Irishman, disputation 18 of the *Theological Course*, throughout question 6, and in his *Commentary on Scotus’s Second Book of the Sentences*, distinction 33; by Father Macedo, book IV *On the Keys*, chapter 18, controversy *On Original Sin*, section 3. The labors of all these were surpassed by Florentius Conrius, archbishop of Tuam, in a whole volume published in support of Saint Augustine’s assertion, in which he demonstrated at great length from Sacred Scripture and [Col. 0653A] Augustine that infants suffer sensible punishments.

He omitted the testimonies of the Fathers, for Augustine alone was equivalent to them all. Yet when, in chapter 2, he had reported that many held the opinion that Augustine had fallen into excesses—a view that is the refrain of recent writers—he could not restrain himself from exclaiming:

“O statement filled not only with extraordinary vehemence, but perhaps also completely full of insult against Augustine, his holy fellow teachers, and the very Apostolic See!”

I see this most learned prelate called by Morainus the forerunner of the new dogmatists, although he defended the most ancient opinion of the Fathers. But because he placed Augustine’s name at the beginning of his book and described a foreign Jericho­nite in another volume, in which he admirably explained the condition of human nature according to Augustine’s mind, Conrius was for this reason given the title of precursor of the “dogmatists” whom he mentions. All that it cost Conrius was that he defended Augustine.

These professors of the most subtle school, although otherwise most devoted to Scotus, understood that in the present controversy their master agreed less with Augustine, and therefore considered it a matter of conscience not to prefer Scotus to Augustine. Indeed, by doing so they followed Scotus himself—not necessarily his doctrine, but at least his example. For that most subtle of doctors showed such deference to Augustine that the Friars Minor, in a petition presented to the Castilian senate in 1628, when they denounced as an insult to the subtle doctor the oath of the University of Salamanca in defense of the teaching of Saint Thomas—who was a most diligent disciple of Augustine—wrote the following:

“Scotus was so devoted to Augustinian doctrine that, in his theological commentaries alone, he brought forward Saint Augustine as a witness to his assertions eight hundred and fifteen times,” and so forth.

You may read these and other matters in the first volume of the Spanish *History of Augustine* written by Peter de Campo, book III, chapter 30, and in Luke Wadding’s *Life of Scotus*, volume I of the latter’s works, chapter 15, number 69.

The thesis concerning sensible punishment of infants in the underworld is supported by arguments. On this occasion it is shown that the Roman Church recites the same opinion of the holy doctor among the offices of prayer. Augustine calls that punishment the mildest. It is established that, through the punishment of loss, children suffer deep sadness.

Nor are sufficiently strong arguments lacking to show Saint Augustine’s opinion to be not merely probable but much more probable [Col. 0653D]. For, as concerns the synods and the Fathers, his opinion is true.

The first argument is this: original sin introduced the sensible miseries of children’s present life; therefore it will also extend those same miseries throughout eternity. The consequence is proved as follows: the sensible punishments of this life are not sufficient to satisfy, by suffering satisfaction, for the stain of original sin; and however great they are, the human race justly suffers them. Therefore, so long as the same stain of sin remains throughout eternity, children infected with original guilt will justly suffer the same things forever.

The scholastics commonly respond that these miseries are punishments of original sin accidentally; for original justice exempted human beings from the miseries they would have endured in a state of pure nature. Therefore, since original sin in itself removed original justice, it introduced miseries accidentally.

We refuted this response above, section 2. Here we refute it again with an excellent testimony of Augustine, book VI of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 37:

“It remains that this which now exists”—namely, bodily death—“should itself finally, that is, at the end, be destroyed, when the resurrection of the flesh takes place, so that it may no longer be an enemy, as it would be if it were natural in such a way that it were not penal. But under a just and omnipotent God and judge, it could in no way be penal unless it had occurred because of the merits of sin.”

When death is called penal, it is not called so because of the relation it bears to guilt, of which it is the punishment; rather, Augustine calls it penal because it brings torment and pain. Hence one punishment is just and another unjust. Unjust is that which a tyrant inflicts upon an innocent person without prior demerit.

But death cannot be natural without also being penal. The soul cannot be separated from the body except through preceding illnesses and pains, whether these are long or brief; for what is brief is severe. Therefore, according to the holy doctor, death cannot be natural under a just and omnipotent God: as just, He would not inflict the evil of punishment without guilt; as omnipotent, He would not allow it to be inflicted by another upon an entirely innocent nature.

Hence he cries out in the same book VI, chapter 20:

“No one can be miserable under a just God unless he deserves it.”

The holy doctor explains admirably in the same work, chapter 39, how Adam, although composed of the elements and of an animal body, would not have died. But leaving this aside, I attack the response directly.

Even if a human being in a state of pure nature would have been subject to those miseries which arise from the combination of the elements of which he consists and in which he lives, there are many other extremely serious miseries which a human being does not suffer from his nature. Children are often attacked by demons and tormented even unto death; that punishment does not arise from the condition of matter.

Augustine presses this argument in book VI *Against Julian*, chapter 6:

“Assert, if you can, how he does not obscurely but openly claim for himself the infants whom unclean spirits torment. If you say that they have been handed over to him, we both see the punishment; you say that there is merit. We both see the penalty; you, who say that no evil merits are derived from parents, although we both acknowledge God to be just, demonstrate, if you can, the guilt in infants deserving this punishment. Or do you not recognize that this too belongs to that heavy yoke which is upon the sons of Adam from the day of their departure from their mother’s womb (Ecclesiasticus 40), and so forth?”

Demons are permitted to torment children with such sufferings precisely because they are disfigured by sin. Therefore, so long as the same guilt remains, the demon will justly be able to afflict them.

The same response is rejected again. If miseries follow accidentally upon the deprivation of original justice in the state of the present life, why in the other state should those same miseries not likewise follow, at least accidentally, upon the deprivation of original innocence? Certainly, since sin remains in children in the present life just as in the future life, I do not know from where they derive the conclusion that divine justice will be more lenient toward infants in the next age, when it punishes sinners more severely in the life of another.

Indeed, if God had not destined Adam to death after his sin, and if he had lived eternally amid miseries together with his descendants, no one could have blamed God’s judgment for subjecting an enemy race, polluted by filth, to punishments. Therefore, on that hypothesis, children would justly suffer punishments eternally for original sin alone.

The second proof is this: God hates children polluted by original guilt; He is angry with them and their enemy. Therefore, He can justly exercise acts of retributive justice against them, insofar as this justice inflicts sensible punishment.

The antecedent is gathered from John 3:36:

“But whoever is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.”

The holy doctor applies this statement to unbelieving infants in book I *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 20.

The Apostle also writes, Ephesians 2:3:

“We were by nature children of wrath,” namely because of original sin. Since this sin is transmitted with nature to offspring, the result is that a newly born child is turned away from God and consequently becomes His enemy.

Augustine draws the consequence sharply in tractate 44 on John:

“The Apostle, born among the people of the prophets, says: ‘We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest.’ If children of wrath, then children of vengeance, children of punishment, children of hell. How by nature, unless, when the first man sinned, vice grew in place of nature?”

These inferences are excellent. If God is angry with children, He can therefore exercise an act of retributive justice against them; He can therefore also afflict them with punishment, for the object of retributive justice is the punishment of the guilty; He can therefore assign them to hell, that is, to the flames of the underworld, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 22:13).

It is no answer to say that God’s wrath and the vengeance of His justice appear in the punishment of loss by which children are punished, and that it is not necessary for the same justice to chastise them with sensible punishment. For children are guilty of precisely the same sin that Adam committed, so that the crime which was actual in Adam became original in his descendants. Hence the Apostle says, Romans 5: “In whom all sinned.”

Therefore, just as Adam’s actual sin was punished by the infliction of sensible punishment, so in his descendants they too may be chastised by the same penalty. A plague harms not only the person in whose body it first arises, but also another who is infected by contact with it. Thus Augustine said that children die through the contagion of their father’s sin, book VI *Against Julian*, chapter 4.

Here also belongs what Saint Thomas teaches, *1–2*, question 81, article 2, reply to objection 1:

“Children are sometimes punished with bodily punishment by divine or human judgment on account of their parents, insofar as a son is something of his father according to the body.”

God removed David’s son from life in order to punish the father’s adultery, although the little boy was not guilty of his father’s crime. Hence Exodus 20:5 says that God visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation.

With how much stronger a right, then, can God punish with sensible punishment children who in fact contract the stain of their first parents?

But even if Augustine’s inferences from the Apostle’s words—“we too were once by nature children of wrath”—could somehow be evaded, it is enough for us meanwhile that they are recited by the Roman Church among the offices of prayer on Wednesday of the Fourth Sunday of Lent, in the earlier reading of the exposition of the Gospel. For just as it is certain that Augustine there spoke according to his own position concerning the sensible punishment of children in hell, so his doctrine, inserted by the Church into its prayers, is supported by enormous authority. At the very least, it is freed from all censure; and that alone is what we intend here against recent critics who charge Augustine with excess.

The third proof is this: predestined children will have, through the merits of Christ, bodily goods in the other life—gifts which theologians call *endowments*; therefore rejected children will suffer bodily evils in the other life through Adam’s demerits.

Augustine presents a similar argument in book VI *Against Julian*, chapter 10, where he calls those who deny the parity unreasonable. I give his words:
