“See, then, how unreasonably you refuse to let a little child bring away evil from another’s sin, while you want him to bring away good from another’s righteous deed—not just any good, but the kingdom of God. For it is another’s work when he believes through another, just as it was another’s work when he sinned in another.”

They respond by denying the parity. Although divine goodness may give bodily goods to those who did nothing good with the same body as an instrument for acquiring them, nevertheless it is contrary to equity for the body of one who never sinned with that body to suffer—especially since the punishment of sense is proportionate to the sinful pleasures perceived through the body.

But the contrary follows, because just as in the other life there is no new merit or demerit—for souls are at their final state—so God afterward treats them according to the condition in which they departed. Since children who die without baptism are counted among the devil’s household, just as, conversely, those who die after receiving the sacrament are counted among Christ’s household, it is equitable that, just as the latter receive bodily goods under Christ, so the former should experience bodily evils under the demon.

For if in this life they are under the demon’s power, so that he torments them in the body, as was shown above, why in the other life, where there is no redemption, should they be removed from his power over their bodies, which he previously possessed?

The holy doctor just cited writes:

“Give yourselves an account, then, and do not think it unworthy that those who are not admitted into the kingdom of God should be under him who fell from the kingdom of God, and that those who do not have life should be under him who lost life.”

Nor does it help to say that children did not sin in the body and therefore do not seem liable to bodily punishment. The sin of the will alone, when that will is proud, is justly punished by punishment of sense; demons too did not sin in the body, yet they are afflicted with sensible punishment.

Indeed, since the whole sin which was actual in Adam is original in children, and they fully undergo its guilt, and since Adam’s sin included the pleasure of sense in eating the fruit, his unhappy posterity also pays the penalty of that pleasure, whose guilt was likewise transmitted to them through generation.

Here one must note, however, that Augustine asserts that the punishment infants undergo in the underworld is the mildest. He calls that damnation the lightest of all in book V *Against Julian*, chapter 11—which is chapter 8 in the Basel edition—and certainly the mildest of all punishments in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 93, and book I *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 16.

Fire warms, and, if its heat is intense, it also burns. Since according to Augustine that punishment is the lightest and mildest, children will be warmed by a heating fire with some discomfort, but will not be burned by it. Thus, just as rejected adults will burn more intensely the more crimes they have committed, so children, who are guilty only of hereditary crime, will be afflicted by heat intense enough to cause discomfort and pain.

I see that Fulgentius, cited above, writes that children will burn; by that word, however, he signified heat acting upon the body with pain, which can nevertheless exist without combustion.

This is confirmed by the book V *Against Julian* just mentioned, where Augustine says that children “will be in the lightest of all damnations. What sort, of what nature, and how great it will be, I cannot define; nevertheless I do not dare to say that it would be more advantageous for them not to exist than to exist there.”

If they were burned by fire, it would certainly be better for them never to have existed. Yet Augustine does not refuse there to define the kind of punishment or its species—namely, whether they are in fire, and whether there they are merely warmed or burned—but only the degree or intensity of the heat by which those children are tormented.

The scholastics commonly ask whether the punishment of loss causes sadness in children. The leaders of the schools answer that children are affected by no sadness [Col. 0657C]. Most recent writers, however, among whom Bellarmine is prominent, book VI *On the Loss of Grace*, and so forth, chapter 6, admit sadness in infants because they see themselves excluded from eternal glory.

I am ashamed to cite certain passages from Augustine, for it will become evident from them how far those doctors have departed from Augustine’s position who declare that no sadness arises in children from exclusion from glory, and how much closer they have come to the paradoxes of the Pelagians.

The holy doctor mocked, indeed cursed, the Pelagians who held this view, as though they were despisers of the heavenly kingdom. He writes in book III of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 99:

“You think it is no insult that the image of God does not enter the kingdom of God; you love the kingdom itself so much that you do not believe it to be even a light punishment for a human being not to be there, but NO punishment at all.”

He also gravely accuses the Pelagians in book III *Against Julian*, chapter 3:

“But you, excellent lovers of that life which is to be eternal with Christ, think that it is NO PUNISHMENT for the image of God to be exiled from the kingdom of God. For if you said that it was a small punishment, this would not be the voice of a blessed lover of that kingdom, but of a WRETCHED DESPISER.”

Again, in book V, chapter 1, speaking of ordinary Christians, he says:

“If one of them, carrying his little son, should call out—not without an envious shout, and in a place where no one would hear—and say: ‘With the mind, understanding, and reason in which I was made in the image of God, I love the kingdom of God so much that I judge it a GREAT PUNISHMENT for a human being never to be able to enter it’—then would you, not a man from the crowd of the unlearned, but one among the few most prudent lovers of that kingdom, all the more ardent because the most fervent fellowship of the few inflames you toward it, while the colder multitude does not make you grow sluggish—would you answer the man and say: ‘It is NOT ONLY NOT GREAT, but there is NO PUNISHMENT AT ALL in the image of God’s never being able to enter the kingdom of God’? I think you would not dare say this even to one man whose power and testimony you would not fear. Then, whether you answered anything or, as Christian—or at least human—modesty would more strongly require of you, kept silent, he would bring his little child before your eyes,” and so forth.

I shall show below that punishment here is understood as inflicting pain, not merely as something evil in itself.

I do not believe that the ancients read that passage; for they would not have publicly taught a position which Augustine thought could not even be secretly instilled by the most insolent of the Pelagians, Julian, into one individual—not a learned man, but someone from the lowest dregs of the common people—without any witness.

Do you suppose Mastrius was concerned with what Augustine thought on this matter? For he cites Augustine in *Sentences* II, disputation 4, *On Man*, question 6, number 163, as saying, “Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 27, asserting that infants in limbo are not sad and suffer no pain.”

Augustine wrote three books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, which Mastrius does not distinguish; at the same time he saddles him with the opinion which Augustine detested as a paradox. Let no one therefore blame us if we desire greater diligence from the scholastics in reading Augustine.

Morainus, together with others, responds that children will have that small sadness because of exclusion from glory. But this was the response of the other Pelagians, as Augustine testifies in book III *Against Julian*, chapter 3:

“Moreover, if you at least admit that the punishment is SMALL which is sufficient for this cause—although it is a great thing that the image of God is not permitted to enter the kingdom of God,” and so forth.

In sermon 14 *On the Words of the Apostle*, he argues against the Pelagians in the same way:

“If one loves his homeland, the punishment is great; but if one does not love his homeland, the punishment of the heart is worse. Is it a small evil in a human heart not to seek the fellowship of the saints, not to desire the kingdom of heaven? If he does not desire it, the punishment arises from perversity; but if he desires it, the punishment arises from charity being defrauded. But if, as you wish, the punishment is small, even that small punishment is great if there is no guilt.”

So much for Augustine.

Nor does it help to reply that this sadness is either nonexistent—because the loss is of a supernatural good which was not naturally owed to them—or at least slight—because they see that they were expelled from eternal glory not by their own fault but by that of their first parent.

Human nature was ordered toward glory, which grace had been decreed for all Adam’s descendants. When they see that they have fallen from it because of his offense, a powerful cause of grief presents itself. Thus, if someone lost, because of the crime of treason, goods previously bestowed on him by a prince, would not his children be seized with great sadness whenever they compared their present poverty with the abundance of goods they had lost? The fact that they had fallen into that condition through another’s fault would lessen shame, but not grief; indeed, it would increase the latter.

In children, moreover, not only is punishment inflicted, but guilt is also present, and they are truly sinners. Thus, along with sadness, shame is found in them as well.

Others respond that children will have no knowledge of eternal glory, because it is supernatural and cannot be reached by the natural cognition of children.

This response was rejected above, where we proved that children will be on the left hand. They will see the elect on the opposite side and see them called to eternal glory.

Meanwhile, what would Augustine reply to those who thought it absurd that children, as images of God, should not love the kingdom of God? He writes in book VI *Against Julian*, chapter 4:

“If this will not be an evil for them, then those wholly innocent images of God will not love the kingdom of God. But if they will love it, and will love it as much as the innocent ought to love the kingdom of Him in whose image they are created, how will they suffer any evil from this very separation?”

What, I ask, would he reply to them if he heard in the schools that children not only do not love the kingdom of God, but do not even know it? The noble scholastics have departed very far from Augustine’s paths.

Let us nevertheless grant them this; I prove the sadness of children from another source. They are not only turned away from God as the supernatural author, but also as the author of nature. For Adam, by sin, abandoned the immutable good and clung to created good. Since children draw this sin from their origin, they are made turned away from God and turned toward the creature.

This is confirmed as follows. Either children have some natural end whose possession satisfies them, or they cannot possess any such end. If the first is granted, I ask whether this end will be God or a creature. If a creature, then they will be sinners and turned away from God as the author of nature. But if God will be the ultimate end, insofar as He is known abstractly, then they will love God and will also be loved by God. How, then, does the wrath of God remain upon them (John 3:36)? Are they not truly enemies of God through sin? How, then, will they love Him?

If the second alternative is asserted—namely, that children will have no ultimate end—then they will be miserable forever, excluded as they are from possession of the highest good.

Indeed, I think it scarcely possible to explain how children could be affected by no sadness when they see that the wrath of God remains upon them, when they see themselves infected with the stain of sin. Does it grieve them that they are in sin? Who could deny this? Their perversity would then be great, and they would deserve to be assigned to more severe punishments, if they did not grieve over sin.

But if the state of sin causes pain, then they are also saddened. Sadness is pain over things which happen against our will. I consider it certain that children do not wish to be in the state of sin, although, against their will, it will remain with them forever.

Certainly, I think that those who deny that infants are saddened do not even think about the stain of sin, although children are truly sinners. The Pelagians, who thought children innocent, spoke more consistently when they said that they suffered either little sadness or none.

Scotus, in fact, proves from this that children are not saddened: such a thing could not occur unless they were unwilling to lack blessedness or to be held captive in prison, and these punishments would happen against their will. But then they would sin, because they would have a will contrary to the divine will.

From this argument it is clear that the most subtle doctor did not even consider the sadness arising from sin. Nor does the argument which our Aegidius produced before Scotus prove anything. For since children are sinners, they have a will contrary to the divine will; they are turned away from God and turned toward the creature; they are vessels of wrath and dishonor; they belong to the number of the rejected. They have not been reconciled to God, but are counted among His enemies. Hence the wrath of God remains upon them.

They therefore have, from their origin, a will contrary to the divine will. But if they justly see themselves being tormented, do they therefore endure their torments patiently?

Poncius responds, number 34:

“It is not inconsistent that little ones in hell should sin by an act. For since they possess the use of free choice and are punished eternally by God, both by deprivation of blessedness and by punishment of sense, it would certainly be the greatest virtue in them to conform themselves to the divine will.”

But if martyrs needed the most intense grace in order not to fail amid torments but to fight for religion, it scarcely seems possible that children, by the powers of nature alone, could patiently endure such great and such prolonged sufferings. Nor, on the other hand, does it seem consonant with divine justice that He should bestow such a great force of divine grace upon His enemies, who belong to the devil’s household.

Arguments for the contrary opinions are resolved.

[Col. 0660C] I believe that the John Poncius praised above judged very well when he said, number 10, that the arguments for the opposing position were of little weight. This will briefly appear from the following refutation of them.

They object, first, that Augustine doubted about the punishments of infants and, to use Goneti’s words, disputation 7 *On Original Sin*, article 7, number 190, was doubtful and anxious in this matter. For in book III *On Free Choice*, chapter 23, he says:

“For it is not to be feared that there could have been some intermediate life between right action and sin, while there could not be an intermediate judgment between reward and punishment.”

There he is speaking about infants.

Bellar­mine adds: “Augustine never retracted that, so far as I know.”

Leaving aside Father Macedo’s response—not because it is false, but because the following one of ours seems better—I say that the Semi-Pelagians formerly abused this same testimony in order to take a step toward weakening the argument which Augustine drew from infants, so that they might reject grace as arising from merits.

Hilary writes this to Augustine:

“They do not allow the case of infants to be brought forward by analogy with that of adults. They say that Your Holiness touched on it to the extent of wishing it to be UNCERTAIN, and preferring to DOUBT concerning their punishments. You remember that you placed it this way in the third book *On Free Choice*, so that you could provide them with this opportunity.”

The holy doctor responds to this objection of the Massilians in his book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 12, saying that, while still a priest, he completed in Africa the books *On Free Choice* which he had begun as a layman at Rome, namely before the year 359.

Therefore, even if he had then doubted concerning the punishments of infants, “no one,” he says, “I think, would be so unjust and envious as to prevent me from making progress, and to judge that I ought to remain in this doubt.”

He adds that one should not believe that he had doubted about this matter. Rather, the point was that the Manichaeans had to be rejected whatever one might think concerning the punishments of infants, lest anyone believe in a mixture of two natures, namely evil and good.

He concludes:

“Far be it from us to leave the case of infants in such a way that we say it is uncertain to us whether infants, if they die after being regenerated in Christ, pass into eternal salvation, while those not regenerated pass into the second death,” and so forth.

Thus the holy doctor did not retract what he had once taught concerning the punishments of infants, because he had not doubted about them.

Indeed, in letter 28 to Jerome, written in the year 414, when Orosius was traveling to Asia, the holy Father writes concerning the same book III *On Free Choice*:

“Nevertheless, I did not then think that anything should be said concerning the damnation of those infants who depart from this life without Him”—that is, without baptism—“because what is now under discussion was not then under discussion.”

For Augustine there discusses only the punishments which infants suffer in this life.

This is why Jerome agreed with Augustine. For in the same letter he explicitly writes that the souls of infants are damned, saying:

“That they are damned if they depart from the body in this condition, both Holy Scripture and the holy Church bear witness.”

Orosius, together with this letter, brought to Asia to Jerome three books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, in the first of which, chapter 28, Augustine rejects the intermediate state of children. Therefore, after reading these books and praising them at the end of his *Dialogues*, Jerome adhered to Augustine’s position, as was shown above.

They object, secondly, that the holy Fathers held the opposite view. For Nazianzen, in his Oration on Holy Baptism, says that children are affected by neither heavenly glory nor punishments from the just Judge. Gregory of Nyssa, in Oration 1, writes that children who die without baptism are neither in pains nor in sorrow. They add Ambrose, in his commentary on Romans 5, where he says: “There is also another death, which is called the second death; we do not suffer it because of Adam’s sin, but acquire it through our own sins on its occasion.” Finally, Innocent III, in Book III of the Decretals, title “On Baptism,” chapter *Majores* [Col. 0661D], writes: “The punishment of original sin is deprivation of the vision of God; the actual punishment of sin, however, is the torment of everlasting Gehenna.”

I reply in nearly the same manner by which the holy Father, in chapter 14 of *On the Predestination of the Saints*, answers the Massilians, who objected that the earlier Fathers had held a different view from Augustine concerning the predestination of human beings:

“What need, then,” he says, “is there for us to scrutinize the short works of those who, before this heresy arose, had no necessity to engage with this difficult question requiring solution—something they would undoubtedly have done had they been compelled to answer such people? Hence it happened that, concerning the grace of God (I shall speak of the punishments of infants), they briefly and only in passing touched upon what they thought in certain places of their writings, while they lingered over those matters which they were discussing against the other enemies of the Church.”

I reply again that Gregory Nazianzen, in that passage, enumerates three classes of people who die without baptism: one consisting of those who despised baptism; another of those who omitted it through negligence; and a final class of those who died without it neither through contempt nor through negligence. He compares the punishments of these groups: he says that the first suffer severe punishments, the second lesser ones, and the last are neither granted heavenly glory nor subjected to the punishments inflicted upon those who omitted baptism either contemptuously or negligently. This is entirely true, for the former committed actual sin by despising or omitting baptism; since children are not guilty of that offense, they cannot be tormented by the same punishments [Col. 0662B].

Gregory of Nyssa, however, speaks hesitantly, for in the same place he calls this question concerning children dying without baptism difficult and perplexing. He adds that he does not know whether each soul will see the Judge, or whether it will stand with the others before the tribunal, and so forth. Yet all these matters were later defined; for, as Bede testifies in the preface to the *Canticles*, whoever denies that children are to be judged contradicts the Catholic faith. Gelasius, too, defined that children without baptism remain in the region on the left.

To the testimony of Ambrose I reply that Cardinal Bellarmine rightly observed that those commentaries on the Epistles of Paul are wrongly attributed to Ambrose. For they are everywhere sprinkled with Pelagian opinions, as Conrius proves fully and learnedly in chapter 8. Indeed, in chapter 5, on the Apostle’s words, “For if by one man’s offense,” and so forth [Col. 0662C], he says: “More receive grace than died through Adam’s offense.” Moreover, in chapter 8 he says: “To call is to assist one who is thinking about faith.” Likewise, in chapter 9, on the words, “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills,” and so forth, he writes: “He speaks in the person of the one objecting.” He also consistently teaches that those people sinned in Adam’s likeness who, following his example, despised God—all of which was asserted by the Pelagians.

Nor does it matter that Gonet objects that this writer lived under Damasus, when the Pelagian heresy had not yet broken out. For Saint Augustine writes that Pelagius lived in Rome for a very long time. On this matter, see what we have said in Book I of the *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 3.

Finally, what is brought forward from Pope Innocent’s decretal was answered three hundred years ago by Gregory of Rimini [Col. 0662D]. Moreover, Poncius, no. 28, says that the pontiff intended to show that baptism cannot be given to an adult who is asleep or does not consent, because in that case original sin would be removed but not actual sin; consequently, if that person died, he would not lack the vision of God, since he would not have original sin, and yet he would be in hell because he would be in actual sin.

This argument is worthless, for deprivation of the vision of God is also due on account of actual sin. Hence the Gloss calls that argument superficial; nor does it appear to have been asserted by the pontiff himself, but rather added by some insufficiently learned secretary. So much for that.

But, leaving this response aside, I can easily say that just as he says the punishment of actual guilt is the torment of Gehenna in hell—and yet the punishment of loss is not thereby excluded, because he does not insert a restrictive or exclusive particle such as “only” or “alone”—so the punishment of original sin is rightly established as deprivation of the vision of God, but not as deprivation alone.

They object, secondly: sensible punishment is not proportionate to original sin; therefore children are not tormented by fire in hell on account of it. They prove the antecedent by arguing that the punishment of sense consists in the suffering of a particular person, whereas original sin was not committed through the act of the will of any particular person but is contracted through the infection of nature.

I reply by denying the antecedent together with its proof. For all human beings sinned in Adam, and that sin was imputed to each of those propagated from him, so that what was actual sin in him was original sin in his descendants. Let us hear Augustine, Book I of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 10 [Col. 0663B]:

“For if you understand the sin which entered the world through one man, in whom all sinned (Romans 9), it is certain and evident that the sins proper to each person are one thing—sins in which only those whose sins they are commit sin—and that other sin, the one sin in which all sinned, when all were that one man.”

Therefore the sin of one man was also the sin of all who were the same in that one man. For this reason, the punishment of sense is equally assigned to all and each who were the same in Adam, and is due to the whole of nature, except insofar as it is withdrawn from that nature by the grace of baptism.

Accordingly, just as the laws of princes bind the wills of minors to the will of their guardians, so that what the guardians will is ratified for the minors, in the same way God bound the wills of all Adam’s descendants to Adam’s will, so that what he did would be imputed to all human beings [Col. 0663C]. Thus, just as minors sometimes suffer losses through the failure of a wicked guardian, so through Adam’s sin the human race fell into misery.

Indeed, the punishment of sense appears more proportionate to original sin than the punishment of loss. For the punishment of loss is in the soul, while the punishment of sense is in the body; and Adam’s descendants receive the soul from God the Creator, whereas the body is derived from Adam by generation. Therefore, since children can be punished for the sins of their parents insofar as, according to the body, they are something belonging to their parents, as we have explained from Saint Thomas, the human race—which, according to the body, is something of Adam, derived from him by seminal power—can with even greater justice be punished according to the body for his sin, which also became its own, than according to the soul [Col. 0663D].

Hence, if a soul created by God were infused into a body that had not been transmitted from Adam through seminal power, that soul would in no way contract original sin. Therefore sin is transmitted insofar as the soul is placed in a body propagated from Adam through carnal concupiscence. These considerations confirm our position: if flesh begotten through concupiscence is the cause why the soul is infected with sin and consequently suffers punishment, then that very flesh, which was as it were the vehicle of sin, should by no means be exempt from every punishment.

They object, thirdly: original sin does not abolish the natural order but the supernatural order—namely, conversion toward God through the gift of habitual grace. Therefore it ought to be punished only by deprivation of the good to which it is opposed, and not by punishment of nature, which it does not injure in anything due to it.

I reply, first, by denying the consequence. For actual sin likewise does not injure the natural goods of a human being, but only deprives the person of sanctifying grace; nevertheless, it is punished by the punishment of sense. Indeed, according to those who say that sin formally consists in the privation of grace, that privation cannot itself be punishment, since punishment is imposed by the will of a judge and, with respect to the person upon whom it is inflicted, is contrary to that person’s will and produces pain.

I reply, secondly, by denying the antecedent: first, because original sin removes conformity to right reason, just as every actual and habitual sin does, whereas that order is natural; and secondly, because, as stated in section 2, concupiscence arose from original sin [Col. 0664B], and this injured human nature.

Hence Augustine writes in *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 3:

“All the good things which nature possesses in formation, life, the senses, and the mind, it has from God Most High, its Creator and Craftsman. But the defect which darkens and weakens these natural goods, so that it needs illumination and healing, was not contracted from a blameless Craftsman; rather, it arose from original sin, which was committed by free will. Consequently, a penal nature belongs to a most just vengeance.”

Furthermore, through original sin a human being is born subject to the devil and belonging to his household, as we showed above from the exorcisms performed in baptism. This captivity certainly both afflicts and disfigures human nature. After Driedo, our great Salamancan theologian Basil Poncius treats this captivity learnedly in Part I of his *Relectio on Grace*, chapter 16.

Finally, grace is a gift freely given by God to a human being. But when a person gravely offends another—for example, a king through the crime of lèse-majesté—it is not a sufficient punishment merely to deprive the rebel of a benefit once freely bestowed upon him; another punishment is also required. In Adam, however, all his descendants rebelled against God. Hence they are born enemies of God, and through the grace of baptism they become his friends. Without that grace they are not only unworthy of grace freely bestowed but worthy of punishments justly imposed.

They object, fourthly, with Vasquez, Part I–II, disputation 124, no. 8; Gonetus, disputation 7, cited no. 178; Morainus; and others: No one ought to be punished for something for which he cannot even be blamed or reproached. But no one can be blamed for original sin; therefore no one can be punished for it.

The major premise is clear, because sensible punishments possess a certain power of reprimand. The minor is proved from Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* III, chapter 6, where he says that no one is worthy of blame and reproach unless he does what he could have refrained from doing. But children cannot refrain from contracting original sin; therefore they are worthy of no reproach on account of it.

The reply is that the minor is to be denied. Nor does the philosopher’s statement delay us, since he knew only actual and personal offenses; Aristotle’s statement does not apply to original sin. Indeed, the Pelagians attempted to abolish original sin on the basis of Aristotle’s teaching. Hence Augustine writes in Book VI against Julian, chapter 20:

“For your heresy has been reduced to this: that your followers lament that dialectical judges cannot be found in the Church from the schools of the Peripatetics or Stoics, by whom you might be acquitted.”

Julian complained that the Catholic bishops by whom he had been condemned did not know how to judge doctrines according to Aristotle’s categories. Certainly, if Aristotelian principles are to be followed, original sin must be denied. For one who is born, like a blank tablet, cannot carry the stains of an ancient crime according to Aristotle, since generation is the work of nature, not of the will, which possesses the capacity to sin.

It is certain from the faith that God is angry with children when they are born on account of original guilt. For, according to the Apostle, we are born by nature children of wrath; and through sin we are turned away from God. God hates children insofar as they are sinners—this being a Catholic dogma. Therefore God reproves the vice which he himself did not produce in the human being.

Add that infants are vessels of dishonor and consequently worthy of dishonor and reproach. I am amazed at Vasquez, a man so deeply versed in Augustine’s teaching that the scholars of Complutense called him “another Augustine,” or at least “Augustine’s mind and tongue.” I am amazed, I say, that he should have proposed as solid an argument which Augustine had nevertheless explicitly overturned.

Let us hear the holy Doctor in *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 6:

“Is this depravity, then, not to be rebuked in a human being because it is not proper to the person who is rebuked but common to all? On the contrary, let that which belongs to all be rebuked in each individual. For it does not follow that something belongs to no one because no one is immune from it. These sins are called original sins because each individual draws them from his parents; but they are also called ours, and not without reason, because in that one man all sinned, as the Apostle says. Let the condemnable origin therefore be rebuked, so that from the pain of the rebuke the will to regeneration may arise,” and so forth.

From this it is clear that a person can be rebuked on account of original sin.

Morainus insists, no. 41, that not only Aristotle and pagan philosophers say that no one is worthy of blame or reproach for something he did not freely do or omit; this is also the common voice of all believers and unbelievers, as Saint Augustine confirms in *On Two Souls*, chapter 11. Since no one freely committed original sin, but contracts it through the infection of nature, no one can be blamed or reproached for it [Col. 0665D].

I reply that the testimony of the holy Doctor just cited was repeatedly and insistently brought against Augustine himself by Julian, in Book I of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 45; Book V, chapters 43 and 45; and elsewhere. The holy Father answers him in Book I of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 48:

“It is Adam himself,” he says, “whom that definition of ours which pleased you had in view when I said: ‘Sin is the will to retain or obtain what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain’ (*On Two Souls*, chapter 11). For when Adam sinned, he had absolutely nothing evil in himself by which he might be unwillingly driven to do evil, and on account of which he might say: ‘I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do’ (Romans 7:19). Therefore, by sinning he did what justice forbade and from which it had been free for him to abstain. For one who says, ‘The evil that I do not wish, that I do,’ it is not free to abstain from it.

“Accordingly, distinguish these three things and understand that one thing is sin, another the punishment of sin, and a third both together—that is, sin in such a way that it is itself also the punishment of sin. You understand which of these three belongs to that definition in which it says: ‘The will to do what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain.’ Sin is defined in this way; it is not the punishment of sin, nor both together.”

And afterward:

“Original sin, however, belongs to that third kind, in which it is sin in such a way that it is itself also the punishment of sin.”

It is therefore certain that original sin can truly and properly be sin, even if it is not free to abstain from it. The teaching which the holy Doctor transmitted in *On Two Souls*, chapter 11, and which Morainus, following Julian, brings forward, must not be applied to original sin, about which the holy Father was not speaking there.

Hence what Morainus adds afterward is false:

“If original sin and its punishment are to be judged according to the mind of Saint Augustine—or rather according to the sense of the whole Church and the agreement of the human race—it must be said that no one, on account of something he did not himself commit but necessarily contracted by origin, is worthy of reproach and blame, and consequently neither of positive and natural punishment.”

These statements, I say, are false. For according to the mind of the holy Doctor the opposite must be said. He teaches that even one who sins in that third manner is to be reproved. For he says in the same place [Col. 0666C]:

“The third kind, in which sin itself is also the punishment of sin, can be understood in the case of one who says: ‘The evil that I do not wish, that I do.’ To this also belong all those things which are done through ignorance: they are not thought to be evil, or are even thought to be good. For blindness of heart, if it were not sin, would be unjustly reproved; but it is justly reproved when it is said: ‘Blind Pharisee,’ and in many other passages of the divine utterances.”

Indeed, that necessity destroys blame was Julian’s very objection when he said in Book V of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 52:

“His blame does not apply to what is necessary, because whatever reaches necessity strikes the author himself”—namely, God.

The holy Father answers him:

“Does this evil of the human being, when he says, ‘The evil that I do not wish, that I do,’ strike the author of the human being himself? And yet it is sufficiently clear that the one who acts in this way has reached necessity; for he acts by necessity in what he does not do by his will.”

They object, fifthly, that it seems harsh and wholly inconsistent with divine goodness that infants should be punished by the fire of eternity, although they did not sin by their own will, but only through another’s will and through the force and misery of their origin, by which they are infected with original sin.

Augustine responds in Book V of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 13:

“If you consider it cruel that infants should be condemned, although you do not think that they contract original sin, then it should seem cruel to you that infants are not snatched from this life who, according to you, have absolutely no sin, even though God knows that they will die amid many great sins without any change for the better. For according to human reasonings, it seems more cruel not to deliver, when he can, one stained by neither small nor great sins, than to condemn the offspring of a sinner. Yet when you loudly proclaim with one voice that the former is just, with what face do you contend that the latter is unjust?”

Indeed, if we speak according to human reasonings, it also seems harsh that a person should be condemned eternally on account of a single wicked desire which vanished in an instant; yet we believe this by faith. For there was no sensible delight in that act, and nevertheless the person will be tormented eternally by the punishment of sense.

Therefore it should not seem harsh that children are punished according to sense, although they did not sin by sense, except insofar as they were the same as Adam.

Moreover, since the first parent, had he persevered in goodness, would have transmitted original righteousness and every good of both soul and body to his descendants, as the holy Father teaches in Book III of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 199, why should it seem harsh if, having transgressed, he made miseries and punishments hereditary for his descendants?

They object, sixthly: on account of original sin, those who are to be baptized are not assigned any penance, nor are they commanded to feel any sorrow for it. Therefore no punishment of sense corresponds to it, as such punishment corresponds to actual sins.

I reply, first, that most of the opponents who press this argument concede that children suffer sadness on account of the deprivation of the vision of God which they undergo. Therefore an interior pain is due to original sin, even if the Church does not prescribe any interior sorrow for original sin.

I reply, secondly, granting the first part of the antecedent, by denying the consequence. Since the miseries of this life are effects of original sin, why should a new punishment be imposed, when we must undergo innumerable punishments for the same sin? It is enough to tell catechumens that all human beings sinned in Adam and were consequently expelled from the earthly paradise and subjected to so many and such great punishments, which, with the help of divine grace, we can endure courageously.

I reply, thirdly, by denying the second part of the antecedent—namely, that catechumens are not commanded to feel any sorrow on account of original sin. Augustine explicitly teaches the opposite; indeed, in the chapter of *On Rebuke and Grace* cited above, he commands it, saying [Col. 0667C]:

“Let the condemned origin therefore be rebuked, so that from the pain of the rebuke the will to regeneration may arise. If, however, the person is rebuked, he is a son of promise, so that while the sound of rebuke resounds outwardly and scourges him, God may work inwardly in him by a hidden inspiration the willing.”

Must not a catechumen first be taught that he has been in sin from birth, is an enemy of God, under the power of the devil, a member of his household, and belonging to his family? When he hears these things, he is immediately seized by sorrow that he was born under the devil’s power and lived under it for so long.

Let us hear Saint Augustine, Book I of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 19:

“Someone may say: ‘How, then, are they themselves also called to repentance? Can such a tiny child repent of anything?’ The answer is: If they are not to be called repentant because they do not yet possess the sense of repentance, neither should they be called believers, since likewise they do not yet possess the sense of believing. But if they are rightly called believers because they somehow profess faith through the words of those carrying them, why should they not also be regarded first as repentant, since through the words of those carrying them they are shown to renounce the devil and this world?”

Therefore, if the holy Doctor asserts repentance in children in this manner, will adults approaching baptism not possess the same repentance? They then feel sorrow for original sin when, according to Augustine, they say that they renounce the devil.

Before I close this discussion, I wish to recite an objection by William of Rubione, who in Book II, distinction 32, question 2, article 2, attacks the punishment of children with this argument:

“One who is equally innocent when another sins as when that other does not sin ought not to be afflicted; nor can he justly be afflicted more after another’s sin than if that person had never sinned. But because of the sin of the first parents, their children, who never sinned, are no more culpable than they would have been if their parents themselves had not sinned. Indeed, after their parents’ sin they are equally innocent as they would have been had their parents never sinned. Although they are now guilty, therefore,” and so forth [Col. 0668B].

This writer denies that there is a true and proper stain in children before baptism, and in this he speaks with little conformity to the canons of the Church. For he thinks that descendants are called sinners by an extrinsic denomination derived from Adam’s guilt, as is clear from what he says in distinction 30, question 2, section “And therefore.” Thus, according to him, guilt was in Adam alone, while liability—or obligation to punishment, which, as he says in the same place, is the effect of guilt and something consequent upon it—was in the descendants.

But the Council of Trent, in its decree on original sin, defined that anyone is anathema who says that Adam, “through the sin of disobedience, transmitted death and bodily punishments alone to the whole human race, but not also sin, which is the death of the soul.” And in session 6, chapter 1, the Fathers declare:

“All human beings lost innocence in Adam’s transgression, were made unclean, and, as the Apostle says, by nature children of wrath,” and so forth.

That Nominalist, however, says that children are equally innocent after the sin of their progenitors as they would have been if their progenitors had never sinned. Since Rubione therefore attributes so much innocence to children, it is no wonder that he denies their punishments after death.

These, then, are the arguments they bring against the Augustinian position. They are easily resolved [Col. 0668D], and they cannot make the opposing opinion more probable than the Augustinian one, as Estius notes in distinction 33, section 8; to him the assertion of the holy Father appeared probable. Nor should Duvallius be heeded, in his treatise *On Sin*, question 4, article 3, where he says that the opinion opposed to Augustine approaches the faith and possesses reasons that are evidently conclusive.

At this point the opinions concerning the punishments of children—namely, those of Saint Augustine, the Pelagians, and the scholastics—should be compared. But since this can easily be inferred from what has been said so far, and since attempting it might perhaps bring envy upon me, I willingly omit the perilous comparison.

I am certain of this: in establishing the punishments of infants [Col. 0669A], Augustine did not go too far; rather, those scholastics went too far who write that children are to be granted natural blessedness and promise them a most happy region. This was the judgment of Cardinal Bellarmine, that most vigorous defender of the Catholic religion, who in volume III, Book VI, chapter 3, makes the following censure:

“Augustine, therefore, should not be judged to have undergone anything human or to have gone too far in this dogma. Rather, those undergo something human and go too far who place children in the higher part of the earth, as though in an earthly paradise, and call them blessed and happy.”

I shall add the judgment concerning the same matter of the most reverend Father Laurentius Brancatus of Lauria, prefect of the Vatican library and an outstanding theologian of our age. In his most learned volume *On the Last Things*, disputation 27, article 7, no. 152, he says [Col. 0669B]:

“What our modern writers say, I consider empty, novel, and ridiculous: namely, their claims about a station, dwelling, and wandering upon the earth. Where did they get this? Who revealed it to them?”

I cannot sufficiently wonder when I see the ancient scholastics—Saint Thomas, Saint Bonaventure, Giles, Scotus, and others—deny that children grieve over the loss of glory, although Augustine asserted the opposite so openly, so explicitly, and so emphatically, and sharply rebuked the Pelagians for thinking otherwise.

I know that they do not affirm that the punishment of loss is light or nonexistent in itself. For insofar as it is the privation of possession of the highest good in the heavenly homeland, they call it the greatest evil, since its gravity is measured by the excellence of the good of which it deprives. Thus we may seem to have spoken somewhat imprecisely when, above, we intensified the testimonies of the holy Doctor in which he teaches that not being in the heavenly homeland is a great punishment, since the scholastics readily concede this.

But the holy Doctor was certainly not disputing with the Pelagians about punishment understood in this way. Since they were extremely acute, they by no means denied that exclusion from the kingdom of heaven, insofar as it denotes the mere privation of possession of God in the heavenly homeland, is in itself a great evil. Rather, they said that for children it was a light or nonexistent punishment because it inflicted no pain, or only slight pain, upon them.

For the loss which a person suffers in the loss of a good inflicts punishment upon him insofar as it is felt. If it is not felt, it is no punishment for him, as is clear in the case of children whose goods are squandered: they suffer an evil but do not feel it, because through their lack of knowledge they do not perceive it.

Punishment, especially when intended by a judge, does not signify an evil understood as the bare privation of good, without any consideration of the subject. Rather, it signifies what is evil for another insofar as it causes that person pain, either by imposing or removing something which the guilty person would not wish.

That Augustine understood punishment in this way is certain. For in Book VI against Julian, chapter 10, he says:

“If this will not be evil for them, then those innocent images of God will not love the kingdom of God so greatly.”

Having set aside as absurd this supposition—which Julian would never have admitted—he continues:

“But if they will love it, and will love it as greatly as the innocent ought to love the kingdom of the one in whose image they are created, will they suffer no evil from this very separation?”

The evil felt through the loss of a good that is loved has the character of punishment afflicting the subject who is deprived of the good loved by that subject.

Moreover, when Augustine, in Sermon 14 on the Words of the Apostle, had said that the Pelagians do not strike children—that is, do not inflict upon them the punishment of sense—but merely send them into exile by denying them the kingdom of heaven, he proves that they suffer and are tormented by exclusion from that kingdom:

“If the homeland is loved, it is a great punishment; but if the homeland is not loved, it is a worse punishment of the heart. Is it a small evil in the human heart not to seek the fellowship of the saints, not to desire the kingdom of heaven? If he does not desire it, there is punishment because of perversity; but if he does desire it, there is punishment because of frustrated charity.”

From this it is perfectly clear that Augustine wants children to be tormented by exclusion from the heavenly homeland because they love and desire it. If they did not love it, they would be perverse and evil, since they would not seek the fellowship of the saints.

But the evil felt through the loss of a good that is loved causes pain and sorrow, for we grieve and are saddened whenever we are deprived of a beloved good.

Now, if the support of the Fathers who favor Augustine is counted, there will be twenty-four elders. For there were fifteen Byzacene bishops who subscribed to Saint Augustine’s opinion. Among the Fathers was Pope Gelasius, who in a decretal epistle decreed that the third position invented by the Pelagians was to be removed.

There is also support from the scholastics. Albert the Great, Estius, Driedo, and Polman defend Augustine’s opinion as probable. Five from the Order of Friars Minor stand united in favor of the same position, as do an equal number of our Augustinian theologians.

Indeed, I hope that in the future, when this discussion of ours is read—if posterity will have any concern for the writings of these authors—more people will adopt the side of Saint Augustine, or at least refrain from censures and not accuse the holy Doctor of excess in handing down an opinion which popes, councils, and Fathers taught with unanimous agreement, as has been clearly demonstrated up to this point.

§ VI. Whether Augustine, in arguing against the Pelagians concerning the Old Law, went too far.

The Pelagians, so that they might not incur the indignation of orthodox believers by denying grace altogether (for they saw that this same grace was present in the sacred writings and especially commended by Paul), said that the law by which God commands human beings what must be done or avoided is grace—inasmuch as God mercifully set it before Adam’s descendants, who were afflicted by profound ignorance of what ought to be done and whose natural light had been almost extinguished by long habituation to vice. Indeed, they most shamelessly set up the law against grace. For they argued from the law that no other grace of God was necessary. This is Caelestius’s sixth argument, reported by the holy doctor in chapter 3 of *On Perfection in Righteousness*:

> “It must be asked whether it was commanded that a human being be without sin. For either he cannot, and it was not commanded; or, because it was commanded, he can.”

And in book *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 16, Augustine writes:

> “The Pelagians think they know something important when they say: ‘God would not command what he knew could not be done by a human being.’ Who does not know this?”

Hence the heretics, lavish in their praises of the law, believed themselves safe under it, as though it were the stronghold of their cause. Let us hear the great teacher of the Church, book IV, *To Pope Boniface*, chapter 5, exposing the enemies’ deceitful efforts:

> “Nowhere,” he says, “do these enemies of grace contrive more hidden snares for attacking that same grace with greater force than where they praise the law, which undoubtedly ought to be praised. For throughout all their disputations they wish the law to be understood as grace, by means of various modes of expression and a diversity of words, etc.”

Augustine, in order to overthrow the Pelagian heresy from its foundations, demonstrates from the sacred writings and from the force of the most subtle arguments that the law is not grace assisting human beings to attain good works; rather, by commanding, terrifying, and punishing, without assisting, it merely makes them guilty. The books of the holy Father are full of expressions of this kind, especially the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, which is entirely concerned with this argument. P. Macedo Cortina indicates many passages in thesis 48. I shall produce one testimony from chapter 8 of the book *On the Grace of Christ*:

> “Accordingly,” he says, “law and grace are so different that the law not only does no good, but does very great harm, unless grace assists; and this is the usefulness of the law: that it makes those whom it renders guilty of transgression flee to grace, so that they may be liberated and helped to overcome evil desires. For it commands more than it helps; it teaches that there is a disease but does not heal it. Indeed, it rather increases the disease, because it is not healed, so that the medicine of grace may be sought more attentively and earnestly.”

But when Moraines examines Augustine’s statements about the old law, he gives the following judgment concerning them in *Anti-Jansenius*, disputation 24, number 44:

> “Augustine speaks more harshly about the old law in several places; but, as he himself says in book III of *Christian Doctrine*, chapter 10, when the words of Scripture seem to present something incongruous, they should be interpreted in a benign and advantageous sense. Why should the words of Augustine himself not also be interpreted in this way whenever, carried away either by the natural impulse of his mind or by the heat of disputation, he seems to incline toward extremes?”

What, then, did Augustine say more harshly about the old law? It will not be difficult to investigate, since we know very well in what doctrine of the holy Father Moraines accuses him of fury and excess in disputation. Augustine said, with the Apostle in Galatians 3, that the law was given because of transgression; he discusses this at greater length in sermon 11, *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapters 8 and 9. With the same Apostle in 2 Corinthians 3, he said that “the letter kills,” and he explains those words in an entire volume. With Paul in Romans 3, he said: “The law entered in so that transgression might abound.” He explains this statement in sermon 13, *On the Words of the Apostle*, and in letter 89, question 3. With the same Apostle in Galatians 3, he called the law a most burdensome “pedagogue,” and he approved the comparison in the same sermon and in letter 144, where he also calls the law not an aid to justification but a bond of guilt.

What drew Augustine into suspicion of excess, and what appears to have been asserted more harshly, is his statement that the law was so far from helping human beings that, without grace, it instead made them guilty by commanding and not assisting. In chapter 1 of *On Rebuke and Grace* he writes that to turn away from evil and do good:

> “No one can do this without the Spirit of grace; and if grace is absent, the law is present for the purpose of making people guilty and killing them.”

In sermon 6, *On the Words of the Apostle*, he says:

> “For the law commanded but did not fulfill, because the flesh, where grace was absent, etc. How, then, would the law help me by commanding through the letter and not giving grace?”

In the aforementioned sermon 13 he said:

> “The law gave fear.”

But where grace does not infuse love, observance of the law, proceeding from pure servile fear, makes a transgressor. He treats this matter admirably in letter 144, *To Anastasius*.

Augustine therefore seems to have held that human beings are compelled by the law to act rightly, while assisting grace is nevertheless not always present. From this it appears to follow that at such times God’s commandments are impossible to observe, since they cannot be fulfilled without grace, while Augustine also teaches that people may lack it. For this reason Julian reproached Augustine in book III of his *Unfinished Work*, chapter 119:

> “For the moment I say nothing of the fury with which you rage against the whole law, which you believe commanded these things to mortals who, in your view, had no ability to perform them.”

He sings this refrain repeatedly.

Two matters here may create difficulty: first, whether the law can at some time command and, as they say, bind under sin, if assisting grace for fulfilling the law is absent, as Augustine seems to maintain; and second, whether in the old law only servile fear reigned without grace, which some likewise think he held. These two points perhaps appear especially harsh to Moraines, who believes that Augustine leapt beyond the bounds of truth in them.

To resolve the first difficulty, I must take the matter up from a deeper point. First of all, a distinction must be established between observance of the law in the state of innocent nature and in the state of corrupted nature. Adam possessed an aid immediately sufficient for observing every commandment on every occasion and at every moment. Augustine explains this assistance learnedly in chapters 11 and 12 of *On Rebuke and Grace*. He calls it an assistance “without which,” not “by which” (*sine quo*, not *quo*); for once Adam had received that assistance, he did not immediately act, but, whenever he wished, he could always act while it was present.

> “Such,” he says in chapter 11, “was the assistance that he would abandon whenever he wished and in which he would remain if he wished—not assistance by which he would be made to wish. This is the first grace, which was given to the first Adam; but the second Adam possesses a more powerful grace. The first is that by which a human being is made able to possess righteousness if he wishes, etc.”

He adds that in this first assistance the power of free choice was displayed. For, as he had previously stated, God left that assistance within Adam’s free choice; and, as he says in book III of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 112, Adam “had a governor whom God left to his free choice.” Therefore that assistance was always available to Adam; Augustine writes that Adam would abandon it “whenever he wished.”

A little later in the same chapter 11 he states:

> “But if this assistance had been lacking to an angel or a human being when they were first made—since their nature had not been made in such a way that they could remain upright without divine assistance if they wished—they would certainly not have fallen through their own fault. The assistance without which they could not remain upright would have been lacking. But now, for those from whom such assistance is absent, it is already the punishment of sin; while to those to whom it is given, it is given according to grace.”

From this I infer, first, that in the state of fallen nature this assistance is not given to everyone and is not always present; otherwise prayer would be superfluous. For, as Augustine says in the book *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 18, “What could be more foolish than to pray that you may do what lies within your power?” And in letter 95: “Prayer itself, therefore, is the clearest testimony of grace.” We do not ask God to give us what we possess, but what we most need; for, according to letter 105, if something lay within our power, it would certainly not be requested.

Therefore, since whenever a commandment presses upon him a human being can pray that God grant grace for fulfilling that commandment, this is a sign that the grace is not always present in everyone and on every occasion. Hence it happened that, since Adam possessed that grace abiding within him for every moment and occasion, he did not need prayer in order to observe any commandment.

I know that recent writers do not approve this last point, considering it a novel paradox; nevertheless, it is plainly Augustine’s most explicit teaching in book VI of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 15:

> “The Lord’s Prayer bears witness to this, in which we say not only, ‘Forgive us our debts,’ because of the evils we have committed, but also, ‘Do not lead us into temptation,’ precisely so that we may not do evil. Hence the Apostle also says: ‘We pray to the Lord that you do nothing evil.’ But if this lay within our power—as it did before sin, before human nature was corrupted—it would certainly not be requested in prayer; rather, it would be maintained by action.”

Therefore, since Adam, by reason of the divine assistance abiding within him and continually present, could have fulfilled the law at every moment, it would have been pointless for him to pray that God supply him with strength to perform the commandments.

The most acute theologian of our age, Basil Poncius, understood this point. In *Relections on Grace*, part I, final chapter, page 213, he writes:

> “This is the assistance which Augustine often says Adam possessed but which we do not possess in our present state, because we do not have persevering thoughts and affections directed toward the good for every individual occasion, as is evident. Hence Adam did not need prayer in order to obtain that assistance, because by God’s gift it was already innate in him along with his very nature; he needed rather to give thanks for so great a benefit, which he had received from God at the beginning of his existence.”

Nor would it rightly be said that Adam could have asked for a more intense grace in order to fulfill the law more easily. It would have been vain to request new strength when it was so easy not to sin, as the holy Father says in chapter 12. Adam could, however, have prayed that God keep the tempter far away, lest he be enticed toward evil or come near the danger of falling. But once temptation had been placed before him, he could not have asked God for strength to resist it except vainly.

In the state of fallen nature, however, that assistance, immediately sufficient for every moment and occasion, is not always present to human beings. Thus the necessity of prayer becomes clear: we ask God to enable us to fulfill his commandments. Hence Augustine writes in the same work:

> “For this reason God wanted us in this struggle to contend more by prayers than by strength, because he himself supplies to those who struggle the strength—even whatever measure of strength it is fitting for us to have here—for which we ask him. If, then, those whose spirit lusts against the flesh need God’s grace for individual acts, so that they may not be overcome, what freedom of will can those possess who have not yet been snatched from the power of darkness, who, with iniquity ruling them, have not even begun to struggle—or who, if they have wished to struggle, are overcome by the bondage of a will not yet liberated?”

Here he affirms that grace is given for each individual act of virtue, while nevertheless not being supplied to everyone. He states the same more briefly in letter 107, *To Vitalis*:

> “We know that grace is given to the greater ones for each individual act. We know that it is not given to all human beings.”

And in book IV of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 128, he writes:

> “Accordingly, commandments for living are given to human beings who by nature are children of wrath, because grace also is given, so that the one who commands may also help, and thus not only the evils added by the will but also those that are innate may be overcome. For what is impossible for human beings is easy for God. But those to whom grace is not given—on account of which it was said, ‘Who distinguishes you? And what do you have that you did not receive?’ (1 Corinthians 4)—become transgressors when the law is added, not righteous. Yet if they live in some way for the benefit of the children of mercy, so that, seeing them and understanding that what is given to them is given not by merit but by grace, they may not become proud, but ‘whoever boasts may boast in the Lord.’”

Statements of this kind occur throughout Augustine.

That the law, in order to bind, need not presuppose in the person acting an immediate power to perform the work commanded is a constant doctrine of the same holy Father against the Pelagians. As we have seen, they proclaimed from the imposition of commandments the power of the human will to perform them, while excluding every kind of divine assistance. Augustine and his African colleagues answer them in letter 93, *To Pope Innocent*:

> “Law and grace must be distinguished. The law knows how to command; grace, how to help. Nor would the law command unless there were a will, nor would grace help if the will were sufficient.”

After reinforcing the point with sacred testimonies in which the law and prayer are asserted, he concludes:

> “Just as, then, we recognize the will when these things are commanded, so let him also recognize grace when they are requested.”

Therefore, since whenever a commandment of the law is pressing upon him a human being ought to pray to God—not mockingly but sincerely—that grace be granted to him for performing the commandment, this is a sign that the divine grace necessary for carrying out the commanded work is not present at every moment and on every occasion. For, as the great doctor cries out everywhere:

> “If the possibility is present, why do they pray?”

Book *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 53.

This doctrine, which is plainly most true, is confirmed by the Council of Trent, session 6, *On Justification*, chapter 11, where it says:

> “God does not command the impossible, but by commanding he both admonishes you to do what you can and to ask for what you cannot, and he assists you so that you can.”

This statement is copied from Augustine’s book *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 43. Although the final words, “and he assists you so that you can,” are not explicitly asserted by Augustine, they are implied; for if you ask him to enable you, this is a sign that he is the one who assists you so that you can.

But I shall present the same statement in full from *Tractate 53 on John*:

> “Let us hear,” he says, “the Lord both commanding and assisting: commanding what we ought to do, and helping us so that we may be able to fulfill it.”

I emphasize those words of the holy council drawn from Augustine: “and to ask for what you cannot.” Therefore, while you are asking—or even before you ask—you stand under a commanding law, and you do not yet possess assisting grace; for at that point you cannot do what the law commands.

Thus the Pelagians were mistaken, believing from the fact that the law binds here and now that a human being could carry out what was commanded by his own powers. This also refutes several theologians who think that the law cannot bind here and now unless assisting grace is present; otherwise, they say, a person would be excused from observing the law on account of inability. For if the law, in order to bind, always entails the presence of sufficient grace, it would follow that sufficient grace necessary for observing the law was not lost through Adam’s sin. Although many concede this, I consider it utterly false.

The consequence is proved as follows. By his sin Adam did not exempt human beings from the natural law; for this law binds equally whether Adam sins or does not sin. Therefore, if, in order for the law to bind, it has connected with it the assistance of sufficient grace, then this sufficient grace was connected with the law as binding whether Adam remained upright or fell. Consequently, it was not lost through the sin of our first parent.

I prove that this sufficient grace was lost by the same argument Paul used in Galatians 2 to crush the pride of those who said that the law could justify. He argues briefly but most firmly:

> “If righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.”

The entire force of this argument consists in the following: if the law alone were sufficient to enable human beings, by observing its commandments, to preserve themselves innocent, Christ would be said to have suffered for nothing. For why did he come into the world and endure so many torments if human beings could preserve themselves righteous through the teaching of the law?

The Apostle’s reasoning has the same force against sufficient grace: if a human being could fulfill the whole law through the law and sufficient grace, then Christ died for nothing.

They will answer that Christ came so that human nature might be strengthened by more abundant grace. We press the point: then Christ died so that we might more easily fulfill the law through the gifts of his grace, although we could have fulfilled it—with greater difficulty, to be sure—through sufficient grace even without the death of the Redeemer.

The Pelagians fled to the word “more easily” as to a sacred anchor in a storm. Augustine curses them for this in book II of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 198. After repeating Paul’s words, he says:

> “That is the Apostle’s voice, not mine. Come out into the open, enemies of the cross of Christ. What are you afraid of—the great people of Christ? Do you not fear the great judgment of Christ? Say openly: ‘We can be justified by nature; we can be justified by the law; Christ died for nothing.’ But, fearing the Christian multitude, you insert a Pelagian statement. When people ask you why Christ died, if nature or the law makes people righteous, you answer: ‘So that this might happen more easily,’ as though it could happen, though with greater difficulty, either through nature or through the law. You may add, ‘or through sufficient grace necessarily connected with the binding law.’ Christ, answer, conquer and refute them; cry out: ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15:5), so that those who cry, ‘Although with greater difficulty, nevertheless we can do it without you,’ may be silent—or, if they cannot be silent, may withdraw into some hiding places lest they lead others astray.”

Basil Poncius learnedly defends our position in part I of *Relections on Grace*, chapter 14, where he resolves the arguments of Suárez and Vásquez. Vásquez frankly admits in *Prima Secundae*, disputation 139, chapter 4, number 36, that Augustine held precisely the position I have expounded.

According to Augustine, therefore, the law was given to human beings not so that, with sufficient grace necessarily connected to it, it might assist them—already equipped with knowledge of what must be done—in fulfilling the commanded works. Rather, it was given so that a person, attempting to do what was commanded and seeing that he could not carry it out by himself, might implore the assistance of grace.

Augustine writes this to Anastasius in letter 144:

> “Thus, by teaching and commanding what cannot be fulfilled without grace, the law demonstrates to a human being his weakness, so that the weakness that has been demonstrated may seek the Savior, by whom the will may be healed and thus be able to do what, in its weakness, it could not do.”

The disciples of Augustine teach the same. Fulgentius writes in book II of *On the Truth of Predestination*, chapter 4:

> “When, therefore, we are commanded to will, what we ought to possess is shown to us. But because we cannot possess it from ourselves, we are admonished to ask assistance from the one by whom the commandment is given to us.”

And Prosper writes in his letter to Demetrias:

> “A commandment is never given for any other reason than that the assistance of the one who commands may be sought.”

The law, therefore, does not confer upon the will an immediate power to do what is commanded and consequently does not have annexed to it sufficient grace immediately enabling the commanded work.

Following the Apostle in Galatians 3, Augustine calls the law a pedagogue because the law leads to grace. Let sermon 13, *On the Words of the Apostle*, be read. He speaks admirably in the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 19:

> “The law, then, was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the law might be fulfilled. For the law was not unfulfilled through any fault of its own, but through the fault of the wisdom of the flesh. That fault had to be demonstrated by the law and healed by grace.”

The holy doctor proceeds further, writing that the law commands what must be done, while faith obtains assistance for carrying out what is commanded. Hence his celebrated statement became well known:

> “Faith obtains what the law commands.”

This appears in letter 89, question 2; in the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 29; and elsewhere. We should hear chapter 13 of the same work, cited immediately above:

> “Accordingly, by the law of works God says: ‘Do what I command.’ By the law of faith it is said to God: ‘Give what you command.’ For the law commands in order to admonish faith what it should do: namely, so that the one who is commanded, if he cannot yet do it, may know what he should ask for; but if he can do it immediately and does so obediently, he should also know by whose gift he does it.”

From this it is clear that immediate sufficient assistance is sometimes present; for he says, “but if he can do it immediately.” Yet this is certain from Augustine: faith itself cannot move a human being to ask for divine assistance so that he may be able to fulfill the commandments unless God infuses actual grace by which the person is moved to pray.

The Semi-Pelagians’ error was that a human being could, by his own powers, ask for and desire grace. The Council of Orange condemned this error on the basis of Augustine, in canon 6. For even if someone is a believer, he does not have, at every moment, the immediate sufficient divine assistance necessary for prayer. This is found repeatedly in Augustine.

In the book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 23, he says of the Semi-Pelagians:

> “They are unwilling to understand that even this is a divine gift: that we pray—that is, ask, seek, and knock. For we receive the Spirit of adoption in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’ (Romans 8), etc.”

He says the same in letter 105, in *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 1, and in letter 121, chapter 15.

In book I of the *Questions to Simplicianus*, question 2, he proves from this that fervent prayer, by which we obtain what we ask, comes from God:

> “Is not our very prayer sometimes so tepid—or rather, so cold and almost nothing, indeed sometimes so entirely nothing—that we do not even notice this in ourselves with grief? For if we grieve even over this, we are already praying.”

From these passages it can be gathered how unbelievers sin by failing to observe the law: without faith they remain only under a commanding law, not under grace immediately assisting them. Hence the works they perform are always sins, except when God sometimes works certain good acts in their wills without their knowledge.

Augustine writes in letter 144:

> “The law, therefore, leads to faith; faith obtains a fuller Spirit; the Spirit spreads love; love fulfills the law. For this reason the law is called a pedagogue. Under its most threatening severity, whoever calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved. But how will they call upon him in whom they have not believed (Romans 10)?”

Since unbelievers do not believe in Christ, they do not ask for God’s grace to fulfill the natural law. Hence they do not observe it; and if they appear to perform some good works, they do not perform them well, as was proved in § 4.

Augustine explains why they are nevertheless not excused in the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 33, and in letter 105, *To Sixtus*. Although they lack immediately sufficient assistance, they nevertheless possess certain remote aids. Consequently, they do not suffer from an antecedent necessity of sinning. Although the human race incurred such necessity through the sin of its first parent, it was removed through the benefit of Christ the Redeemer, as our Poncius proves acutely in part I of *Relections on Grace*, chapter 15.

Augustine, therefore, did not assert anything harsher about the law under the impulse of his mind or in the heat of disputation, as Moraines contended. I shall show that he likewise pronounced nothing harsher about the old law.

First, if one considers only the words as they sound outwardly, it would certainly be Paul, not Augustine, who should be judged to have spoken more harshly about the old Mosaic law. He said in Romans 5:

> “The law entered in so that transgression might abound,”

although the law is promulgated precisely so that transgressions may be removed and cease.

He said in 2 Corinthians 3:

> “The letter kills,”

although the law restrains those subject to it from crimes.

He said in 1 Corinthians 15:

> “The power of sin is the law,”

although the law forbids sins.

Augustine explained these forms of speech in the passages praised above and showed that they contain nothing absurd.

The holy doctor is criticized, however, because he seemed to assert that the old law made human beings guilty by commanding and not assisting, or because he said that works performed under the old law were sins, since the Jews performed them out of fear of punishment rather than love of righteousness.

The Jews, possessing the law, fell into such pride that they thought the law alone was sufficient to justify a human being and that God’s grace was unnecessary, with only free choice being required. This error was so deeply rooted in their minds that many of those who were converted from Judaism to the faith persisted even more obstinately in the old error. Hence the Apostle rebukes them in the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 2, with the argument cited above:

> “If righteousness comes from the law, then Christ died for nothing.”

Augustine testifies that the Apostle repeatedly impressed this very point upon them in order to crush their pride:

> “The Apostle leads to this conclusion and commends this teaching,” he says in sermon 13, *On the Words of the Apostle*, “because of the Jews, who gloried in the law and thought that their free choice was sufficient for the law. And because they thought that their free choice was sufficient for the law, they were ignorant of God’s righteousness—that is, the righteousness given by the Lord through faith—and, wishing to establish their own righteousness, as though it were fulfilled by their own powers and obtained not through faith but through themselves, they were not subject to the righteousness of God, as he says.”

And in the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 29, he says:

> “Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain to the law of righteousness. Why? Because it was not from faith, but as though from works—that is, as though they themselves were working it out by themselves, rather than believing that God was working in them.”
