When the Pelagians later absorbed this error, asserting that the grace of God in the Old Testament was nothing other than the law delivered by Moses, while the grace of the New Testament was the Gospel and the example of Christ, Augustine, in order to refute their error, demonstrated incisively that the law separated from grace makes human beings guilty by commanding and not assisting, as the testimonies already cited establish.

Nor did he do an injustice to the law. It was not imposed so that human beings might make themselves righteous by the law alone, but so that it might show what had to be done; and when a person recognized that he was unequal to fulfilling the commandments, he might flee to the assistance of grace. We have proved this from the holy doctor and his disciples, showing that one does not speak more harshly by asserting that, on the hypothesis that the law alone commands and immediately sufficient grace is absent, the law nevertheless binds and the transgressor is guilty of sin.

Just as the Hebrews did not perform good works out of love of righteousness, so they avoided evil works merely from fear of punishment. Hence Augustine said that the works of the Jews under the old law were sins and that the law was a servile law, because those who fulfilled it were serving fear.

The holy doctor writes in book IV, *To Boniface*, chapter 5:

> “The testimony from the law cited by the Apostle is understood as referring to temporal life. Because of fear of losing that life, people performed the works of the law, not from faith—which same law commanded transgressors to be killed by the people.”

Likewise, in the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 32, he proves his position from the Apostle’s words in Romans 8:15:

> “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’”

The old law was therefore a law of fear, because that carnal people, loving only themselves and their own interests, performed whatever good they did according to the commandments of the law out of self-love: desiring benefits for themselves and fearing evils.

The law therefore instills fear as it does in servants; grace, which is obtained through faith in Christ, inspires love. Hence the holy Father says in the same book, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 29:

> “From the law we fear God; from faith we hope in God. But for those who fear punishment, grace remains hidden.”

Why grace is hidden from those who fulfill the law from pure servile fear, he explains in the same work, chapter 19; in sermon 13, *On the Words of the Apostle*; and in letter 144, where he says:

> “Who is found innocent before God if, when what is forbidden is removed from view, he wishes to do what is forbidden? Accordingly, he is guilty in his very will: he wishes to do what may not be done, but does not do it only because it cannot be done with impunity. For, insofar as it depends on him, he would prefer that there were no righteousness forbidding and punishing sins. And if he would prefer that there were no righteousness, who would doubt that, if he could, he would abolish it? How, then, is he righteous who is such an enemy of righteousness that, if power were given him, he would abolish it as it commands, lest he endure it as it threatens and judges?”

More may be read there.

Fear, however, if it ceases to be purely servile and begins, through some love of God, to become chaste fear, is good and does not corrupt the works that proceed from it. On this subject two distinguished doctors of the University of Louvain, the Augustinians Christian Lupus and Franciscus Fervacques, have argued both extensively and learnedly, publishing books and apologies on the same subject every year for the past six years.

Nevertheless, many of the Fathers of the Old Testament were not merely under the law but also under assisting grace, because, conscious of their own weakness, they implored the help of divine assistance in pursuing works of virtue.

For my part, I think I can gather from Augustine that at least remote assistance is present to all human beings. In the book *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 67, he cites and approves, from book III of *On Free Choice*, chapter 10, the following statement against those who attributed every crime to Adam’s sin and asserted their own innocence:

> “They might perhaps rightly inquire into this if no human being were found to conquer error and desire. But since the one who calls back the estranged is everywhere present, who, through many means and through the creature serving its Lord, calls the estranged, teaches the believer, consoles the one who hopes, exhorts the one who loves, assists the one who strives, and hears the one who prays, you are not held guilty for what you unwillingly fail to know, but for neglecting to believe what you do not know. Nor are you held guilty for failing to bind up wounded members, but for scorning the one who wishes to heal.”

In what these remote aids consist, however, is not so easily explained. For Augustine himself most truly affirms in book I, *To Boniface*, chapter 19, that God moves human wills toward good by marvelous means. It is better to venerate these means in humble silence than to investigate them through curious disputation.

I believe the same holy doctor speaks of these remote aids in the book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 9, where he says:

> “Why one of two impious men, both already advanced in age, is called in such a way that he follows the one calling him, while the other is either not called so that he follows the one calling him, or is not called in such a way that he follows the one calling him—these are the inscrutable judgments of God.”

The calling of the one who does not follow is through weak and remote assistance. By it the intellect briefly elicits certain good thoughts, but they are so weak that they do not draw the will toward good; they merely rouse it lightly, and the intellect quickly flies elsewhere, while the will, hardened by long habituation to crimes, is carried toward evil.

## § VII. Whether the opinion of Saint Augustine concerning predestination to glory before the foreknowledge of any merits was stated excessively

[Col. 0680B]

Joannes Adamus and Antoninus Moraines, in the question of predestination as well—indeed, the principal question—bring a serious charge of excess against Augustine.

Adamus writes the following about him in book III of his *Calvin Destroyed*, chapter 8, page 639:

> “Certainly, since it is established that he spoke excessively in the matter of grace and predestination, and that his words must be softened lest, because of their sharpness, I be driven into the opposite error, I must be permitted to seek some Catholic moderation.”

One is reminded of Augustine’s statement in book III of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 57:

> “Say what you are going to say, excellent corrector.”

Moraines, having said that Didacus Ruiz teaches gratuitous predestination from Saint Augustine, says:

> “Ruiz assumes something false; and if Augustine did this, it was not doctrinal affinity or connection—for there is none—but the heat of disputation that impelled him to it.”

This appears in disputation 9, number 50.

But the opinion that predestination to glory is gratuitous and precedes foreseen merits was taught by Saint Prosper, Saint Fulgentius, the African Fathers in their synodal letter, and others with such certainty that Saint Fulgentius said the following—or rather, together with Fulgentius, the Fathers of the Council of Sardica, at the end of the book *On the Incarnation and Grace*:

> “For God, who created the human being, himself prepared by his predestination the gift of illumination for believing, the gift of perseverance for progressing and remaining steadfast, and the gift of glorification for reigning—for those to whom he willed to give them. He completes his work in no other way than he has arranged in his eternal and unchangeable will.
>
> “The Apostle testifies that by this truth of predestination we were predestined in Christ before the foundation of the world. If anyone refuses to receive this truth with the believing acceptance of his heart or to confess it with his mouth, and if, before the final day of his present life, he does not cast off the obstinacy of his impiety by which he rebels against the living and true God, it is manifest that he does not belong to the number of those whom God, before the foundation of the world, freely chose and predestined in Christ for the kingdom.”

The Semi-Pelagians had long since said that, without that doctrine [Col. 0681A] of predestination, the cause of the Church had been defended against the Pelagians for many years, as Hilary reports in his letter to Augustine. Responding to them, the holy Doctor says in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 20:

> “This is the manifest and certain predestination of the saints, which necessity compelled us later to defend more carefully and earnestly, when we were already disputing against the Pelagians. For we learned that each heresy had introduced its own questions into the Church, against which divine Scripture would be defended more diligently than if no such necessity compelled us.”

Whom, then, should we trust more: Augustine, who testifies that necessity compelled him to affirm that dogma concerning predestination, in order to refute the Pelagians more carefully from the Scriptures; or Morainius, who invents the claim that Augustine undertook this with no affinity or connection whatsoever to his doctrine? But since Annatus too denies this connection, I shall prove it against them in chapter 8.

The great writer of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, Baronius, rightly censures the excesses of certain recent authors who, while fleeing Calvin’s heresy, turn aside in the opposite direction, departing from the doctrine of Saint Augustine—especially in this matter of predestination:

> “Since, therefore, the opinion of Faustus was everywhere contradicted by the Church, let certain recent authors consider how great a danger they incur when, rising up against the innovators in order to refute them, they depart from Saint Augustine’s opinion concerning predestination, although otherwise weapons are not lacking by which the adversaries may be defeated.”

Year 490, p. 449.

[Col. 0681C] But I hear Petavius loudly proclaiming:

> “For a long time the question of predestination began to be disputed in the schools on both sides, and Augustine’s authority was not thought to carry any prejudicial force in this controversy.”

Volume I of *Dogmatic Theology*, book X, chapter 1.

I shall silence this recent author’s words by a most weighty testimony—one moreover arising from within his own camp. In the year 1584, Claudius Aquaviva, that great and incomparable superior of the whole Society, after a preliminary examination by six very learned theologians of the same order, selected certain propositions that all its members were to defend, lest they be carried about by every wind of doctrine. On page 37, where the selection of opinions is discussed, we read:

> “It has likewise been defined that, on our part, predestination has neither a reason nor a condition. Someone may say that this contributes little to piety; yet this doctrine of Augustine has not only been commonly received by the theological schools, but also by the Fathers of the Church for approximately twelve hundred years. They insist that it is proved from the Scriptures and from the responses of the Roman pontiffs—namely, Zosimus, Sixtus, Coelestine, Leo, and Gelasius—among whom the Massilians, Cassian, Faustus, and the other opponents of this predestination have always had a bad reputation.”

This proposition, together with the others, was examined by the Spaniard Juan Azor, the Portuguese Gaspar Gonzalez, the Frenchman Jacobus Tirius, the Austrian Peter Bufa[e]us, Antonio Guisano of Upper Germany, and Stefano Tuccio, who was residing in Rome, as is asserted in the preface to that book. Noble names of theologians.

These men defended Saint Augustine’s opinion concerning gracious predestination to glory prior to the foreknowledge of merits, before the so-called Augustinian excesses were invented. Saint Thomas, his most distinguished school, the better part of the Scotists, and many very eminent and learned writers from the Society likewise uphold this same position. Against the censures of recent authors, I appeal to their judgments.

## § VIII. Whether Saint Augustine erred in teaching that marital intercourse undertaken solely for pleasure is a venial sin

Augustine taught that intercourse with one’s wife, without the intention of generating offspring and undertaken solely for pleasure, is a venial sin. Morainius does not approve this statement of Augustine. Rather, in disputation 17, no. 22, he says that Augustine sometimes went astray, carried away by the heat of debate, and, out of hatred for the heresy he was attacking, turned aside to the opposite extreme. Lest the charge of this fault attributed to Augustine offend the eyes of his readers, he softens the harshness of the accusation with the adverb “sometimes,” although, as I was saying, he makes Augustine rush headlong into these excesses everywhere and on every occasion.

In any case, the opinion of the holy Doctor is entirely true, in accordance with the common judgment of the holy Fathers and the ancient scholastics. Augustine says in volume VI, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 6:

> “Marital intercourse undertaken for the sake of begetting has no fault; but intercourse for the satisfaction of lust, although with one’s spouse and on account of the fidelity of the marriage bed, has venial fault.”

Clement of Rome had taught this proposition in book VI of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, as they say in chapter 7:

> “For pleasure alone, if anyone makes use of it even in marriage, is contrary to the laws, unjust, and alien to reason.”

Saint Anselm holds the same opinion in his commentary on 1 Corinthians 7, on the words “But this I say by way of concession,” where he says:

> “Husband and wife are free from fault in intercourse only when they unite not to satisfy lust but to receive offspring. Nevertheless, the other intercourse which takes place solely for pleasure has received pardon on account of the marriage.”

Saint Fulgentius writes in his letter *On the Conjugal Duty*, chapter 3:

> “Therefore, if a married person commits fornication, he sins damnably. But if he does not abandon fidelity to the marriage bed, and in his wife alone exceeds somewhat through natural use, being somewhat intemperate—not seeking generation alone, but at times obeying the lust of the flesh—he certainly does not do this without fault.”

And in chapter 4:

> “Therefore, when fidelity to the marriage bed is retained, it removes the stain contracted through the weakness of the flesh, provided that a man does not unite with another woman, whoever unites with his wife not for generation alone but also because of the weakness of his flesh.”

But this is proved most beautifully from Pope Saint Gregory. When the monk Augustine, whom Saint Gregory had sent to Britain to convert the English to the faith, had proposed certain questions to him—including whether a man who had united with his wife could enter a church or approach Holy Communion before washing himself—Saint Gregory responds in book XII of his *Letters*, chapter 10, in answer to Augustine’s questions:

> “Nevertheless, it has always been the practice of the Romans, from ancient times, after intercourse with one’s own wife, to seek purification by washing and reverently to abstain for a short time from entering the church. In saying this, we do not consider marriage itself to be a fault; but because lawful intercourse between husband and wife cannot take place without carnal pleasure, one ought to abstain from entering the sacred place, since pleasure itself can in no way be without fault.”

And afterward:

> “If, therefore, someone uses his wife not seized by desire for pleasure but solely for the sake of begetting children, he should certainly be left to his own judgment concerning entering the church or receiving the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood. He ought not to be prohibited by us from receiving it, since he is placed in the fire without knowing how to burn. But when it is not love of begetting offspring but pleasure that dominates the act of intercourse, married persons have something to mourn even in their intercourse.”

Likewise, after quoting Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 7, “But this I say by way of concession,” he says:

> “For what is lawful and just is not granted by way of concession. In saying that it is granted by way of concession, he showed that it is a fault.”

Here, then, Augustine’s opinion is not only affirmed by Gregory the Great speaking from the apostolic See for the instruction of the faithful; it is also confirmed from the Apostle and from the ancient rite of the Roman Church. What will you answer to this, Morainius? Will you say that Gregory, Fulgentius, Anselm, and Clement likewise turned aside to extremes? Yet these men spoke without being carried away by any heat of debate. Consequently, they must be said to have erred more seriously, since Augustine can be excused by his zeal for overcoming his opponents.

[Col. 0683C] But I wish to show that the leaders of scholastic theology agree with Augustine in the same opinion. Let the first be the Master of the Sentences, whom everyone followed. In book IV, distinction 31, he writes:

> “To prevent this from conflicting with what was said above, it must be understood of those who do not unite for the sake of offspring, whose pleasure is not without sin.”

He is speaking of married persons.

Let Albert the Great be added, volume XVI, *Commentary on the Sentences*, book IV, distinction 31, article 21, under “Response,” where he says:

> “But when lust alone moves a person, and so forth, it either burns within the bounds of honesty and the permission of marriage; in that case it must be called venial, as is clear from the words of Augustine set down in the text.”

Alexander of Hales may be placed alongside him, part II of the *Summa*, question 147, member 2:

> “For if that pleasure is subject to God, it is a venial sin; it is excused on account of the sacrament of marriage. Hence Augustine, in *On the Good of Marriage*, and so forth.”

Thus these two lights of the theological school hand down this opinion, following Augustine’s authority.

The Angelic Master, Saint Thomas, does not disagree. In the cited distinction 31, question 2, article 3, he asks whether a man sins mortally when he knows his wife while intending pleasure alone. At the end of the body of the question he responds:

> “But if the pleasure is sought within the limits of marriage—that is, if such pleasure is sought in no one other than one’s spouse—then it is a venial sin.”

Let the Seraphic Doctor, Bonaventure, be joined to the Angelic Doctor. In the same distinction, question 3, at the end, he judges as follows:

> “But if he wishes to take pleasure in her because she is his wife, and would in no way have intercourse with her if she were not his wife, then there is not complete disorder; it is therefore a venial sin, and it is excused by the good of marriage, so that it is not mortal.”

I could add innumerable doctors who unanimously approve Augustine’s opinion. I appeal to Sánchez, the most learned of the more recent authors, who in volume III, *On Marriage*, book IX, disputation 11, no. 4, proposes this thesis:

> “Second conclusion: A conjugal act undertaken solely for pleasure, while not transgressing the ends of marriage, is a venial fault.”

He strengthens this assertion with the testimonies of fifty doctors, both ancient and recent. Our own Father Alipius Reylof, a Belgian, recently defended this opinion of Saint Augustine in book IV, *On the Soul*, chapter 2, section 4.

Go now, Morainius, and charge Augustine with excessive fury and excessive impetuosity in debate. It is true that he turned aside from the royal road toward extremes; but he dragged the Fathers and all the leaders of theology along with him. With so many wise men leading the way, anyone may now travel that path without stumbling, even if Morainius proceeds by another route. Had he perhaps noticed the footprints of so many great men, he too would have followed them—though at a long distance—and would have better looked after his own interests.

These statements concerning the excesses attributed by Morainius alone to Augustinian doctrine should suffice. If the recent authors themselves considered them more attentively, they would doubtless admit that it was not Augustine but themselves who turned aside into dangerous excesses. For when they heard from Jansenius, Bishop of Ypres, that Augustine alone was praised everywhere, that the opinions of Augustine alone were produced as though they were oracular responses, and that Augustine was exalted above the other Fathers of the Church in the theological arena, they were carried away by the heat of debate to such an extent—precisely insofar as they wished to distance themselves from Jansenius—that they almost sent Augustine away, crying out with Morainius in the preface to the *Anti-Jansenist*:

> “Those who formerly demanded Augustine as judge in everything now think it permissible not to admit him there even as an honorary arbiter in other matters.””

Indeed, to encourage the others more easily to examine Augustine’s statements, they promised that divine assistance would be available to them for so holy a task, using the words of Annatus in book VIII of his *Augustine Vindicated*, chapter 5, p. 897:

> “Nor is this plan so perverse that it cannot have God as its helper.”

At the beginning of his book *On Grace and Free Will*, Augustine wrote to the monks of Hadrumetum that, in order to understand his own writings, they should implore divine aid: “Pray to the Lord that you may understand.” Annatus, however, promised God as a ready helper for censuring those same writings of the holy Doctor, even without being asked, when he ought rather to have feared the avenger of rashness.

Adamus, p. 632, at the end of chapter 7, called Augustine’s excesses an innocent passion against the Pelagians; but by this clever expression he did not mitigate the harshness of the accusation. Whether the excesses of recent authors in criticizing Augustine can be called an innocent passion against Augustine, I leave to their own consciences. For my part, I certainly judge it so.

# CHAPTER IV. Recent authors wrongly attribute several errors to Saint Augustine

[Col. 0685A]

Reluctantly I am dragged by recent authors into this arena, since, against Augustine’s wishes, I undertake to defend Augustine’s cause. I fear that I may be blamed for resisting the command of a Father. For when the distinguished man Saint Marcellinus, delegated by Honorius to Africa with supreme authority against the Donatists, learned that some error—I do not know which—was being attributed to Augustine, he informed that most friendly bishop by letter so that he might counter the slanders of his detractors. Augustine, however, replied:

> “But you, who love me greatly, if you assert me against those whose malice, ignorance, or understanding leads them to criticize me in such a way that you say I have nowhere erred in my writings, are laboring in vain and undertaking a bad cause. With me as judge, you are easily defeated in it.”

Letter 7.

Nevertheless, I hope that I shall readily obtain pardon from the great Father if I imitate his conduct. When he learned from Marcellinus’s letter that the error of which he had been accused was far removed from his writings, he refuted the false opinion formed about his teaching, showing that the accusation was attributable not to the understanding of his correctors but to their malice and ignorance.

Therefore, since Augustine is also accused by recent authors of being guilty of several errors—not indeed because of their malice, but, to speak more mildly, because of their ignorance—it is our task to vindicate our innocent Father from the objections of his adversaries.

The holy Doctors who fought against the remnants of Pelagianism on behalf of the Church and Augustine’s doctrine likewise undertook this task of defense. For some went so far in their audacity that they were not ashamed to compile an index of Saint Augustine’s errors—to use the words of Saint Prosper—

> “so that the things they boasted of having found condemnable in the books of the aforesaid man might be published in brief lists of chapters, and by such a device they might both secure detestation of the man whom they attacked and turn the frightened reader’s attention away from the things they had branded.”

Preface to the *Chapters of the Gauls*.

Following in their footsteps, certain recent writers have published an index of several of Augustine’s errors, so that the fame and authority of the holy Doctor might be reduced to order. More than one person has published such catalogues. Adamus, however, in part III, chapter 3, p. 584, and Moraines, in disputation 12 of the *Anti-Jansenist*, from no. 32 onward, devoted more diligent work to this matter than the others.

Against these censors of Augustinian doctrine, the most learned Father Charles Moreau, an Augustinian, sharpened his pen with great distinction in an entire volume entitled *Peaceful Vindications*, which he appended to the first volume of his *Tertullian*. There he demonstrates at great length that the errors attributed to Augustine are far removed from the doctrine of so great a Father. We shall refute only those arranged by Adamus and Morainius, which they attribute as capital errors in order to diminish—or at least to undermine—Augustine’s reputation. In doing so, I shall proceed in such a way that I will supply here only what learned readers might find lacking in Moreau, while for the present I do not wish to borrow anything from that author.

[Col. 0686A] Among the countless volumes that Augustine bequeathed to the memory of posterity, his books of *Retractions* and *Confessions* are praised first. In the former, they say, he exposed to the whole world the errors of his intellect; in the latter, the errors of his will—errors that others usually conceal with such art and effort. It is uncertain in which of the two he is more deserving of praise.

Indeed, so that he might examine with the greatest care the volumes he had published, he obtained Heraclius as his successor in the episcopate while he himself was still alive. Thus withdrawn from the great tumult of affairs, he devoted himself day and night to the work he had undertaken and subjected everything he had said to critical authority, so that no judge could have been more severe than Augustine in examining Augustine’s books.

Yet that diligence and such rigorous criticism did not satisfy recent authors. Wishing to mark the sun of Hippo with new blemishes, they summoned Augustine’s books once again for judgment, loudly proclaiming that they had detected new flaws and stains in the Augustinian books, so that they might be regarded as more clear-sighted than Augustine. But let us now hear these new censors.

## § I. Whether Saint Augustine erred in thinking that rational souls and angels are corporeal

Adamus first alleges that Augustine taught that souls and angels are corporeal and that only God is immaterial, p. 585. Moraines writes: “He also holds that angels and demons are corporeal.”

Adamus must first be refuted, since he imposes the error of the Semi-Pelagians upon their own opponent, Augustine. Cassian taught in *Conference* 7, chapter 13, that God alone is spiritual, while human souls are corporeal. Faustus, in his letter to Paulinus, and Gennadius, in *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapter 11, followed him in this opinion, just as they followed him in the matter of grace.

But Saint Augustine asserted not only that the rational soul is spiritual, without any admixture of corporeal matter; he also demonstrated this solidly. In letter 28 to Jerome he says:

> “Although it may be difficult to persuade those who are slow of understanding that the soul is incorporeal, I nevertheless confess that I am persuaded of it.”

He supported this by the excellent argument that the soul could not be wholly present simultaneously in all and in each of the body’s parts if it were diffused through them in the manner in which we see “bodies diffused through spatial regions occupy smaller spaces with their smaller parts and larger spaces with their larger parts.” He says that he holds this opinion most firmly concerning the soul.

And in book XII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 33, he says:

> “I dare to profess not merely that I think the soul is not corporeal, but that I know it plainly.”

In the book *On the Quantity of the Soul* he says:

> “It has been argued with the greatest care and subtlety in order to show, if we could, that it does not possess corporeal quantity.”

*Retractions*, book I, chapter 8.

Moreover, in book IV of *On the Origin of the Soul*, from chapter 12 through chapter 22, he proves by evident arguments that the soul is incorporeal. What could Augustine ever have said more clearly? And yet Adamus fastens this absurdity upon the holy Doctor.

He writes in book X of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 24:

> “Nothing is more nearly related—or perhaps nothing follows more consistently—than that, once it is believed that the soul is a body, God too should be believed to be a body.”

He adds in chapter 25, citing letter 157 to Optatus, that this happened to Tertullian:

> “Those who assert that souls are propagated from the one soul that God gave to the first man, and who therefore say that they are drawn from their parents, if they follow Tertullian’s opinion, certainly maintain that souls are not spirits but bodies, and that they arise from corporeal seeds. What could be said more perversely than this? Nor is it surprising that Tertullian dreamed this, since he also thinks that God the Creator himself is nothing other than a body. Once this madness has been rejected, and so forth.”

Did Augustine, then, teach that the soul is corporeal, when he declared this opinion a dream and madness, and asserted that nothing more perverse could be said? Adamus attributes that heresy to Augustine without even identifying a single passage in Augustine where he thought the soul corporeal—as though this opinion of Augustine had been so famous that it needed no citation of any text.

Meanwhile, let Claudianus Mamercus be heard. He lived in the same century, somewhat after Augustine, and speaks of the holy Doctor as follows:

> “Aurelius Augustine, in acuteness of intellect, in the multitude of his subjects, and in the magnitude of his work, was like a certain Chrysippus in argumentative power, a Zeno in subtlety of sense, or our Varro in the vastness of his volumes. He was surely of such a nature, through attention and learning, that not without reason he dissented from the corporeal Epicureans or Cynics of our age as a spiritual sophist. In his book to Jerome, *On the Origin of the Soul*, he declares: ‘Although it may be difficult to persuade those who are slow of understanding that the soul is incorporeal, I nevertheless confess that I am persuaded of it.’ And when he proves this by great reasons and an unanswerable argument, and so forth.”

Book II of *On the State of the Soul*, chapter 9.

Do you think, reader, that Adamus ever read one of these reasons or arguments?

But now that this writer has been convicted of the most evident falsehood, let us see what Augustine thought concerning the bodies of angels.

It was a celebrated opinion among the Platonists that angels were composed of spirit and some exceedingly subtle elemental body, far more noble than any ordinary body. Augustine reports this at length from Apuleius in book VIII of *The City of God*, chapters 8 and 16. Among the Fathers, Origen, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Justin Martyr, and Lactantius followed this opinion. Athanasius, Basil, and Methodius are also cited in its support by John, Bishop of Antioch, whose words are likewise found in the Second Council of Nicaea, session 5:

> “God alone is incorporeal and without form. But intelligible creatures are by no means entirely incorporeal, and are representable in an image.””

Cassian, Faustus, Gennadius, and others adhered to the same opinion.

Yet many of the wisest Fathers held the opposite view, removing all corporeality from angels. Augustine, because he did not wish to address the question expressly and saw that both sides were supported by the authority of many, suspended judgment on this difficult and doubtful matter. He writes in book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 23, that the matter is ambiguous.

But in book XXI, chapter 10, where he asks whether corporeal fire can torment demons, he says:

> “Demons too have certain bodies of their own, as has seemed to learned men,”

and so forth.

Later he says:

> “But if someone asserts that demons have no bodies at all, there is no need to labor over an arduous investigation or fight a contentious dispute about this matter. Why should we not say that, although by wondrous yet true means, incorporeal spirits can also be afflicted by the punishment of corporeal fire, since the spirits of human beings themselves are certainly incorporeal and yet have been able to be enclosed in corporeal members? And so, if demons have no bodies, their spirits—or rather, the demons as spirits—will cling to corporeal fires and be tormented by them, although they are incorporeal.”

From this he indicates that he was uncertain about the corporeality of angels, but not about the soul, which he expressly declared incorporeal. Thus Adamus is again refuted by this very testimony, as is Morainius’s hallucination when he says that Augustine asserted as certain an opinion that was always doubtful for him, although Augustine sometimes presupposes that angels are corporeal so that a newly introduced question will not divert him from his argument.

There were nevertheless those who followed Augustine in his uncertainty. One among a thousand is Saint Bernard, who says in book V of *On Consideration*, chapter 4:

> “Although concerning the bodies of these beings—namely, angels—not only their origin but even whether they exist in any sense is a matter on which the opinion of some is uncertain, if anyone thinks that this should be placed among matters of opinion, I do not object.”

And in sermon 5 on the *Song of Songs*:

> “Furthermore, whether angelic bodies are natural to the spirits themselves, as human bodies are to human beings, and whether angels are animals like human beings, and so forth, the Fathers seem to have held different opinions about such matters. Nor is it clear to me from what basis I should teach one position or the other, and I confess that I do not know. I also think that knowledge of these things contributes little to your progress.”

Thus spoke this most holy and most learned Father.

## § II. Whether the holy Doctor asserted that the sun and stars are animate

Morainius again objects against the holy Father:

> “He likewise doubted whether the sun and moon, and the other stars that we see with our eyes, are animate.”

At the same place.

Here too the adversary’s learning is either lacking or misapplied. Among the ancients, not only philosophers but also the Fathers disputed whether the heavens were animate.

The Platonists and Stoics held that the heavens were animate. Cicero, in book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, and Pliny, in book II of the *Natural History*, chapter 9, adopted this opinion. Many of the Peripatetics likewise held it, as is clear from Raguseo, volume I of *Philosophy*, disputation 14, and Alexander Achillinus, book III of *On the Orbs*, chapter 1. The latter also argues at considerable length that the same opinion can be derived from Aristotle.

The more common Peripatetic opinion, however, grants that intelligences attend the heavens, but does not grant that they inform them.

The Fathers likewise did not hold one uniform opinion concerning the soul of the heavens. Thus, since the holy Doctor did not wish to become involved in such disputes, he suspended judgment—namely, whether angels truly informed the celestial spheres or merely propelled them in their rotation.

Accordingly, at the end of book II of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, he says:

> “It is also usually asked whether these visible heavenly lights are merely bodies, or whether they have certain spirits as their rulers; and, if they have them, whether they are also given vital animation by those spirits, just as flesh is animated by the souls of animals, or whether those bodies are present alone without any admixture.”

Leaving these questions unresolved, he says that they cannot easily be understood.

For this reason Saint Thomas, in part I, question 70, article 3, where he asks whether the heavenly lights are animate, says:

> “Likewise, there was diversity of opinion among the teachers of the faith concerning this matter. Origen held that the heavenly bodies were animate; Jerome also seems to have held the same view, and so forth. Basil, however, and Damascene assert that the heavenly bodies are not animate. Augustine left the matter doubtful, inclining to neither side.”

The same Angelic Doctor openly testifies in *Against the Gentiles*, book II, chapter 70, that the Church has defined nothing concerning the soul of the heavens:

> “We have not stated this concerning the animation of the heavens as though we were asserting it according to the teaching of the faith, to which it makes no difference whether one says it is so or otherwise.”

Scotus, however, in book II, distinction 14, question 1, at the end, writes:

> “If the heavens are not animate, this is believed more than it is proved by reason.”

If, then, neither by the authority of the Church, as the Angelic Doctor says, nor by an effective argument, as the Subtle Doctor adds, has anything certain been established concerning the soul of the heavens, could not our great Doctor rightly have doubted about this matter?

When he had reported Plato’s opinion in book XIII of *The City of God*, chapter 16, he says:

> “Whether Plato speaks truly about the stars is another question. For it must not immediately be granted that those globes of light—or little spheres shining over the earth with bodily light by day or by night—live by certain souls of their own, intellectual and blessed, and so forth.”

From this it is clear that Augustine was not greatly pleased by the opinion concerning souls of the heavens. Nevertheless, because of the authority of the Platonists and especially of the Fathers, he left the matter open.

In any case, he taught more than once, on his own authority, that the heavens should be regarded as without a soul. In the later book of the *Retractions*, chapter 7, where he corrects his books against Faustus, he says:

> “In the fourteenth book, statements were made concerning the sun and moon as though they perceived, and therefore tolerated their vain worshipers.” Although the words there can be understood as transferred from an animate thing to an inanimate one, according to a manner of speech called in Greek *metaphora* [metaphor].”

Do you see that the holy Father retracts the opinion by which he had seemed to give souls to the stars, and openly declares that this must be understood only metaphorically?

In these books he effectively rendered a definitive judgment, making known what he himself thought concerning the souls of the stars, so that even if he had said the opposite elsewhere, the later assertion would correct it. He says the same in tractate 1 on John, on the words “What was made in him was life.”

The learned Father Alipius Reylof, an Augustinian, may be consulted, book I *On the Soul*, chapter 4, where he discusses Saint Augustine’s opinion with great learning.

The opinion concerning the soul of the heavens is finally read as condemned in the letter written by the emperor Justinian to Menas, patriarch of Constantinople. Among the other anathemas appears this one:

> “If anyone says that heaven, the sun, the moon, the stars, and the waters that are above the heavens are animate and material powers, let him be anathema.”

Thus that principal error of Origen was proscribed.

Moreover, Pope Vigilius, together with the whole Catholic Church, approved Justinian’s letter, as testified by Liberatus, the distinguished Carthaginian deacon of that time, in chapter 23 of his *Breviary*. We have discussed this matter at greater length in the dissertation *On the Fifth Council*.

Nicephorus writes in book XVII, chapter 27, that this canon was approved in the same Fifth Ecumenical Council, celebrated in the year 553. Father Lupus accordingly illustrates it, as is his custom, with learned notes and scholia as a decree of that council.

Whether the soul of the heavens can now be defended after that opinion of Origen was condemned, I do not wish to debate. Someone might reply that only the opinion understood according to Origen’s conception was condemned. Saint Jerome writes the following about this in letter 61, against John of Jerusalem:

> “Origen teaches that the sun itself, the moon, and the entire host of the stars are the souls of certain rational and formerly incorporeal creatures. These creatures, now subjected to vanity—that is, to fiery bodies, which we ignorant and uneducated people call the lights of the world—will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the children of God.”

Concerning Origen’s opinion, Saint Augustine transmits the following in volume VI, in his book *Against the Errors of the Priscillianists*, chapter 8:

> “Concerning the sun and moon and the other stars, we see that they are heavenly bodies; that they are animate, we do not see. Let this be read in the divine books, and we believe it.”

Thus far Augustine.

Fromondus, in book I of *On the Soul*, chapter 1, article 8, admits that someone who granted a vegetative soul, or even a sensitive soul, to the stars would not sin against the Fifth Council, which excluded only intellectual souls from the heavenly bodies.

Peter Aureolus, the outstanding glory of the Parisian school and the singular ornament of the Order of Friars Minor—whom Basil Poncius testifies that he never read without admiration in his *Quodlibets*, question 8, chapter 3—was, considering either the abundance or the force of his arguments, second to none among the scholastics, given his intellectual acuity and the many new assertions that he generally supported with arguments of his own invention.

This Aureolus, then, after investigating at length in book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 14, question 2, article 2, whether the intelligence that moves the heavens is united to them as a mover or rather as a form, and after adducing probable reasons in support of the soul of the heavens and resolving the arguments commonly advanced by theologians against that opinion, concludes as follows:

> “But, setting aside philosophers and others, it must be understood in this matter which of the two aforementioned paths is more probable, since both appear sufficiently probable. I answer: Augustine says”—after citing one testimony and then another—“‘But I am not certain whether the sun, moon, and all the stars belong to the same society, although to some they appear to be luminous bodies without sensation or intelligence.’ This is Augustine. Therefore, if so great a Doctor doubted in this matter, I define nothing on this point.”

Morainius is thus ridiculous for counting Augustine’s doubt among his errors, when the most subtle of the scholastics, moved solely by the authority and example of the holy Doctor, followed him—namely, Aureolus, “whose footsteps the entire school of the Neutrals is not ashamed to follow, abandoning the principles of Saint Thomas and Scotus.” These are the words of the most learned Father Mastrius of Meldula in the preface to volume I of his *Metaphysics*.

## § III. Augustine is wrongly accused of error for doubting the origin of the soul. The adherence of the holy Fathers to Augustine in this doubt for many centuries is demonstrated.

The third, manifest and capital error of Saint Augustine must be examined. Morainius cries out: “He also doubted the origin of souls, whether they are newly created—which is absolutely certain—or propagated from Adam.” But in turning this doubt into an error of Augustine, this more recent writer reveals the abysmal ignorance from which he suffers regarding the whole of antiquity. In ancient times there was not one single opinion among the Fathers concerning the origin of the soul, as may be seen in Augustine’s Letter 157 to Bishop Optatus and in Jerome’s letter to Marcellinus, which is numbered 27 among Augustine’s letters. Yet, with the others rejected, two opinions became more celebrated in the Church. Some said that souls are created by God at the conception of each individual human being; but very many maintained that the soul is not created by God, but transmitted from the soul of the parent.

Augustine brought all the powers of his exceptionally great intellect to bear upon this question, leaving nothing at all unexamined by which he might attain the truth of the matter. But when he perceived that neither side of the question could be proved to him by an effective authority or a demonstrative argument, he adhered to neither one [Col. 0691C]. Nevertheless, he discussed the matter at length in Book X of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 6 and following; in the four books *On the Origin of the Soul*; in Letter 28 to Jerome; and in three letters to Optatus, which Saint Fulgentius praises in Book III of *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, chapter 18.

Afterward, however, when the Pelagians arose, denying original sin and especially proclaiming the argument that souls are created by God and cannot be produced by God with sin, the opinion defending the propagation of souls began to appear more probable to the holy doctor. Let Augustine be heard in the cited Book X of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 23, where, after a very long discussion, he concludes:

“Having therefore treated these matters as far as we have been able at the present time, I would declare the considerations on both sides of the arguments and testimonies to be equal or nearly equal [Col. 0691D], unless the opinion of those who think that souls are created from parents outweighed them because of the baptism of infants.”

Thus Augustine persevered in that doubt until the end of his life. Moreover, Augustine’s example had such force that the wisest Fathers, following him, continued for many centuries to doubt with Augustine concerning the origin of souls, until, when the opinion of the scholastics prevailed and the doctrine of the transmission of souls had fallen into disuse, their creation became the common teaching in the Church.

This must be demonstrated with particular care, because Bellarmine, in Book IV of *On the Loss of Grace*, chapter 11, argues from ecclesiastical tradition that the opinion concerning the creation of souls is certain. Yet it will appear just as false as it is true that, in ancient times, Augustine’s doubt was received on the basis of ecclesiastical tradition.

Indeed, before Augustine, Rufinus doubted the origin of the soul in his letter to Saint Anastasius. After recounting three opinions concerning the soul’s origin, he says:

“But I, having read each of these things, declare before God that, up to the present, I hold nothing certain or defined concerning this question; rather, I leave it to God to know what is true, and whether He will deign to reveal it to anyone.”

Since Rufinus had put forward a third opinion about souls—“that, having been made long ago, that is, at the time when God created all things from nothing, they are now assigned by His judgment to bodies”—which he adds was Origen’s view, he is rightly scourged by Jerome in the *Apology* and in his letter to Marcellinus. Augustine, however, never doubted whether this opinion of Origen was false, as he admits in Letter 28 to Jerome, explaining why he had argued from that supposition in his books *On Free Choice of the Will*.

Rufinus nevertheless testifies that in his own time, namely under Anastasius, the supreme pontiff, the question of the soul had begun to be agitated in great disputes; and Jerome, in the letter just mentioned, calls it the greatest ecclesiastical question. But in the time of Saint Augustine, after the Pelagians had arisen, the disputes concerning this matter broke out again. Hence Orosius undertook journeys to Africa to Augustine, and from there to Asia to Jerome; hence Augustine’s letters to Jerome and Optatus’s letters to Augustine; hence one volume by Optatus, four by Augustine, and two by a certain Vincentius concerning the origin of the soul [Col. 0692C]. Yet the matter remained doubtful, and nothing was accomplished by so many labors.

Jerome was more inclined to believe the opinion asserting that individual souls are created for individual human beings, although he wrote that the Western Church was accustomed to hold the transmission of souls, as Augustine reports in Letter 157. But he did not hold the creation of souls in such a way that he failed candidly to acknowledge the matter’s uncertainty. When Augustine consulted him about it, he replied: “Let each person abound in his own judgment.”

Therefore Saint Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, commenting on Genesis 3, at the words “And the Lord God built,” says:

“Whether, just as the flesh of those being born comes from flesh, souls likewise are produced from souls, or whether new souls are always created by God from nothing—this question is difficult to define, because nothing has been stated more clearly concerning it either by holy men or by the authority of Scripture.”

Pomerius, an exceptionally learned African living near Massilia, also wrote eight books *On the Soul*. In the fourth he discussed:

“Whether the soul that is to be infused into the body about to be born is newly made without sin, or whether, produced from the substance of the soul of the first man as a shoot from a root, it also draws original sin along with it from the first soul.”

Gennadius mentions this in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 98. Although we do not know what Pomerius thought about the question, he nevertheless clearly indicates that in his own time the matter was uncertain. He flourished around the year 480.

The sixth century follows, in which both the Fathers and synods doubted the origin of the soul together with Augustine. When disputes about the origin of the soul arose at Constantinople, the African bishops were consulted on the same subject. In a synodal letter sent to Byzantium from Sardinia, where they were living in exile, they replied:

“As for the question of souls, we ought either to leave it unspoken or to discuss it without contention, because whether they come by propagation or are newly made for each body, since the authority of the sacred Scriptures does not clearly pronounce upon this, it must be investigated with caution—especially since the faithful may remain ignorant of it without harm to the faith.”

Chapter 10.

Saint Fulgentius likewise shared this doubt. In Book III of *The Truth of Predestination and Grace*, beginning with chapter 18, after praising Augustine with extraordinary commendation because he doubted concerning this matter, he concludes in chapter 20:

“How much better, then, that we should refrain from disputing this question, in which we recognize that we labor fruitlessly—especially since we see that what was not at all defined by the holy men who preceded us must be sought by us with so much greater caution and restraint, the more clearly we perceive that those illustrious men did not reach its solution.”

Fulgentius’s contemporary Cassiodorus, in Book *On the Soul*, chapter 14, is far from censuring Augustine’s doubt; rather, he praises him on that account:

“Father Augustine, who must be praised for his most religious devotion, says that nothing should be rashly affirmed, but that such matters remain in God’s secret, as do many other things that our limited understanding cannot know.”

Immediately afterward he adds:

“For in matters so hidden, it is better to confess ignorance than perhaps to assume a dangerous boldness.”

Thus, in the second century after Augustine, doubt concerning the origin of the soul had become deeply fixed in the minds of the wisest Fathers [Col. 0693C].

Around the seventh century, however, the Augustinian doubt became much more celebrated and authoritative. The apostolic see approved it by its own judgment and made it its own, while the most learned Fathers included it among matters of faith.

Saint Gregory the Great writes in Book VII, Letter 53, to Secundinus:

“But concerning this matter, let your most loving Charity know that among the holy Fathers there has been no small inquiry concerning the origin of the soul. Yet whether it descended from Adam or is certainly given to each individual, the matter remained uncertain, and they confessed that the question was insoluble in this life; for it is a grave question and cannot be grasped by human beings.”

Thus wrote this most learned and holy pontiff [Col. 0693D]. From these words Bellarmine’s supposed ecclesiastical tradition, from which he derives the creation of the soul, completely disappears. For, according to Gregory, the holy Fathers confessed that the origin of the soul was an insoluble question.

You see, then, that Morainius accuses not only Augustine of error, but also Gregory, the apostolic see, and the council of the Fathers, by whom Augustine’s doubt was approved.

But something still more important must be added. Since doubt concerning the origin of the soul was widespread, that doubt gained such authority in the Church that Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, did not hesitate to place it among the rules of faith, as something to be believed by all Catholics.

For in Book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 23, which begins, “This, then, is the most certain faith after the Apostles’ Creed, which our teachers have handed down,” among the other propositions concerning faith that he presents for acceptance, he inserts this one:

“That the origin of the soul is uncertain.”

O the extraordinary learning of recent writers, who turn into an error Augustine’s doubt—a doubt to which the apostolic see, synods, and the Fathers subscribed with full agreement, and which one of those distinguished for doctrine and piety proposed to the faithful as an article of faith!

Yet neither in the eighth nor in the ninth century was the matter defined. The wisest Fathers still doubted with Augustine, indeed with the apostolic see. Saint Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, is a witness. Saussay praises him in the *Gallican Martyrology* under April 6 [Col. 0694B]. In Book *On Predestination*, against John Scotus Eriugena, chapter 16, Prudentius says:

“For flesh is born from flesh, but whether the soul likewise is born from the soul is a great question, one long and extensively discussed by the Fathers, but left without a certain definition.”

Thus, up to the year 850, when Saint Prudentius lived, the opinion concerning the origin of the soul remained doubtful according to ecclesiastical tradition.

Nor, after the year 1000, was the opinion concerning creation so certain that many did not still doubt it. Saint Anselm, bishop of Canterbury, was near death when a certain close companion said to him: “You are leaving the world and going to the court of your Lord Paschal.” He replied:

“Indeed, if that is his will, I do not oppose his will. But if he would prefer me to remain among you a little longer—at least until I could resolve the question concerning the origin of the soul that I turn over in my mind—I would gladly receive that favor, since I do not know whether anyone will resolve it after I am dead.”

This occurred in the year 1109, according to his disciple in Book II of *His Life*, chapter 59, in Surius under April 21.

Hugh of Saint-Victor, in Book I of *On the Sacraments*, part VII, chapter 30, proves that the soul is not transmitted but created. Yet he says:

“It is more probable that souls are not transmitted.”

And later:

“By these and similar arguments it has become probable that souls are not transmitted, but are newly created from nothing and made for new bodies each day from paternal seed, and, once formed in the womb, are again infused for the giving of life. Yet in all these matters no argument or authority has ever prevailed so greatly as to remove the doubt from the question, except only that the Catholic faith has chosen to believe that the souls joined each day to bodies in order to give them life are made from nothing, rather than propagated from the transmission of the body and according to the nature of human flesh.”

From this it is clear that, up to the year 1130, when Hugh flourished, the doubt concerning the origin of the soul had been removed neither by reason nor by authority. It was merely the opinion concerning the creation of souls that was then more commonly defended in the Church.

Hence Peter Lombard, in Book II, distinction 19, said that the Catholic Church teaches that souls are not transmitted. Once this opinion had been received by the scholastics, the creation of souls was asserted [Col. 0695A], although, as Bellarmine reports in Book IV of *On the Loss of Grace and the State of Sin*, chapter 10, at the end, there are still some who think that one should remain with Saint Augustine in his doubt.

Estius, a distinguished theologian, writes in his commentary on Book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 17, section 14, that nothing concerning the origin of the soul has been defined by the Church, and that those who doubted about it would not thereby become guilty of injury to the faith.

Let those who would still wish the matter to remain doubtful look to that. For me, it is enough to have shown that Augustine rightly doubted the origin of the soul and that this doubt pleased the holy Fathers for many centuries.

Certainly he must be called most prudent who suspended judgment in an exceedingly difficult question, knowing that nothing certain had been defined by the Church:

“For when an obscure matter is being disputed, without the clear and certain testimony of the divine Scriptures to assist, human presumption ought to restrain itself and do nothing by inclining toward either side.”

In this way he defends his perplexity in Book II of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 36.

Since the Pelagians, by exaggerating the creation of souls, derived from it the conclusion that souls could not possess original sin—for otherwise the fault would return upon God as creator—Saint Augustine demonstrated, in Book III to Boniface, at the end, and from the letters of Zosimus, a fragment of which he cites in Letter 157, that original sin could be reconciled with either opinion: both the opinion of those affirming the transmission of souls and that of those denying it. He attempted to explain the matter as certain in the Church under either view, lest original sin should appear incredible to anyone.

[Col. 0695C] Bellarmine concedes that Augustine doubted the origin of the soul. He nevertheless adds that, in writings composed after the books *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Augustine most clearly refuted the opinion concerning the transmission of souls, since in Letter 157 to Optatus he writes:

“Therefore those who defend the propagation of souls with inconsiderate rashness—”

And earlier, speaking of Tertullian’s opinion, which posited the transmission of souls, he says:

“What could be said more perversely than this?”

I do not agree. In that letter Augustine still confesses that he is in doubt. For, after recounting both opinions, concerning the creation and the transmission of souls, he says at the very beginning of the letter:

“But consideration of these things and causes moves me in such a way that my assent does not incline toward either assertion, but I am STILL disputing between the two.”

And in Book I of *On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 16, he says concerning the transmission of souls:

“I neither defend nor refute it.”

The holy doctor composed these books after the letter that he sent from Caesarea to Optatus, as we showed in Book I of *The History of Pelagianism*, chapter 15. In those books he defended his doubt at great length against the criticisms of Vincentius Victor.

There, as usual, he answered the arguments for both opinions. This does not amount to refuting the opinion concerning transmission, but to demonstrating its uncertainty. Thus he accuses its defenders of inconsiderate rashness—not because he thought they were asserting something false, but because he censured their ready boldness in contentiously defending as true an opinion not established by certain arguments. For, as he says in the letter just mentioned:

“When a matter naturally obscure surpasses our small capacity and divine Scripture does not clearly come to our aid, human conjecture rashly presumes to define something here.”

Accordingly, among Augustine’s opponents there were also some who, with inconsiderate rashness, stubbornly upheld the contrary opinion concerning the creation of souls.

Nor should what Augustine said about Tertullian’s opinion be understood as a refutation of the transmission of souls in the sense explained by Augustine, namely, as though he were answering the arguments of the opposing opinion. Tertullian is criticized by Augustine not because he posited the transmission of souls, but because he did not assert it correctly: he thought that the soul was corporeal and therefore transmitted through the corporeal seed of the one generating it.

“For those also,” Augustine writes, “who assert that souls are propagated from the one soul that God gave to the first man, and thus say that they are drawn from parents, if they follow Tertullian’s opinion, certainly contend that they are not spirits but bodies, and that they arise from corporeal seeds. What could be said more perversely than this?” [Col. 0696B]

In this sense Saint Thomas, in Part I, question 118, article 2, says that it is heretical to say that the soul is transmitted with the seed—that is, with corporeal seed—as he proves in the same place. It is also in this sense that the scholastics commonly reject the opinion of the transmission of souls in Book II, distinctions 17 and 18.

But the holy doctor never doubted this particular form of Tertullian’s doctrine concerning the transmission of the soul. He rejected it both in that letter and in Book X of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 25, and declared it an incredible doctrine.

Augustine did doubt “whether an INCORPOREAL seed, by some hidden and invisible means belonging to the soul, runs separately from the father into the mother when conception takes place in the woman.” Letter 157.

Of those who defended transmission with less difficulty, he writes in Book X of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 20:

“For they wish the soul’s seed also to be transmitted through the seed of the father who has intercourse.”

Only those who thought that the rational soul had been made from corporeal matter said that it was a body, according to Augustine in Book VII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 9. Against them he argues most sharply in that book.

Thus Augustine’s censure touches only those who asserted that the soul, being corporeal, derives its origin from corporeal seeds, in accordance with Tertullian’s error.

But let us hear how Augustine presented himself with respect to both opinions. In Book X of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 21, he writes:

“I am still uncertain between the two, and at one time I am moved in this direction, at another in that.”

And in chapter 23:

“I admonish those whom this opinion has preoccupied, so that they believe souls are propagated from parents, to consider themselves as much as they can, and meanwhile to understand that bodies are not their souls.”

From this Adamus is refuted once again when he writes that Augustine believed the soul to be corporeal—a mistake that the holy doctor pursues throughout that entire book.

Bellarmine, in order to prove from ecclesiastical tradition that souls are created by God, brings forward certain Fathers. Even if they could be explained in some way, they ought to present no obstacle to us, since among the Greeks, in the Eastern Church, the creation of souls was commonly held. Among the Westerners, however, according to Jerome’s testimony, the opinion of transmission prevailed.

At first, this same Father ridiculed the latter opinion in the final chapter of Ecclesiasticus, commenting on the words, “And the spirit returns to God who gave it,” verse 7. But Augustine gives this testimony an excellent interpretation in Book X of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 9. After showing in Letter 28 to Jerome that the passage favors those who think that all souls derive from one, he no longer ridiculed the opinion of transmission. Rather, after praising Augustine’s diligence in explaining the testimonies of sacred Scripture, he replied in Letter 30, preserved among Augustine’s letters:

“Let each person abound in his own judgment.”

He also declared that he found nothing to criticize in Augustine’s writings, in which Augustine had discussed the origin of the soul at great length.

Jerome, moved by those words, at first ridiculed this latter opinion in the final chapter of Ecclesiastes. He wrote his commentaries on Ecclesiastes about ten years before writing to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem, namely in the year 483; for that letter was written in 493, as Baronius learnedly proves in section 2 under that year.

Since Augustine’s books were eagerly read throughout the Church, all the wiser men began to doubt with Augustine, inclining toward neither side. This brought great glory to Augustine, since the Fathers who followed him held his authority in such high esteem that they wished to follow him not only when he taught but even when he doubted, as though despairing of attaining a truth that Augustine’s intellect had been unable to reach.

Thus the holy doctor explained with such care and diligence all the passages of Scripture brought forward for either side that he made the matter sufficiently doubtful for later generations and persuaded them to share his uncertainty.

Bellarmine proves that ecclesiastical tradition from Jerome in the following way:

“In the letter to Pammachius concerning the errors of John of Jerusalem, after recounting opinions of the heretics Origen, Tertullian, and Apollinaris concerning the soul, Jerome says that it is an ecclesiastical doctrine that God fashions souls every day. Since he opposes an ecclesiastical doctrine to the opinions of heretics, he seems certainly to have held that it must be maintained by Catholic faith that souls are not transmitted from parents but created.”

Thus Bellarmine.

But it is better to hear Jerome’s own words in his letter to Pammachius:

“Or perhaps”—which is ecclesiastical according to the sayings of the Savior: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17); and according to that passage of Isaiah: “Who forms the spirit of man within him” (Isaiah 42); and in the Psalms: “He who fashions their hearts one by one” (Psalm 32)—“God fashions souls every day,” and so forth [Col. 0697D].

Bellarmine adds the word “doctrine” and omits the phrase “according to the sayings of the Savior,” although Jerome called the assertion ecclesiastical not because it was a doctrine defined by the Catholic Church and to be held as a matter of faith—for Jerome wrote that Western ecclesiastics commonly defended transmission, as Bellarmine himself admits in that same chapter 11, section “The Fourth Opinion”—but because it accorded with the authority of Scripture, which appears to suggest creation.

Yet Augustine, whom we cited above, explains those passages. Bellarmine himself says:

“Therefore, as Saint Augustine argues in Letter 28 to Jerome, perhaps no passage of Scripture will be found in which it is clearly taught that souls are not made by propagation but are created.”

Accordingly, the assertion concerning the creation of souls is not clearly established “according to the sayings of the Savior.” Thus Bellarmine departs from Jerome, whom he had brought forward on his own behalf. Nor will the assertion any longer be an “ecclesiastical” assertion, since Jerome gives it that designation only because it accords with the sayings of the Savior, according to the interpretation of the authors of that opinion.

The same author brings forward Leo the Great, who, in his letter to Turibius, chapter 10, is said to write:

“Catholic faith steadfastly and truthfully proclaims that human souls did not exist before they were breathed into their own bodies, nor are they incorporated by anyone except God the creator, who is the creator both of them and of bodies.”

But there the pontiff refutes Origen’s opinion concerning the ancient and simultaneous creation of all souls, as is clear from that letter, chapter 10, at the beginning. Nor does the passage say any less that God is the creator of bodies and souls. Therefore, just as it cannot be inferred from that manner of speaking that the body is not transmitted, so in no way can it be inferred that the soul itself is not produced by transmission.

Leo also adds that, in Letter 11 to Julian, he speaks of Christ’s soul as follows:

“Nor was a soul infused into him at a different beginning from that of other human beings, one that would excel not by diversity of kind but by sublimity of virtue.”

But Christ’s soul was produced from nothing, not propagated by transmission, according to Augustine in Book X of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 19 and 20. Therefore, according to Leo’s decree, the souls of other human beings must also be believed to have been created by God.

But Leo is there condemning the opinion of Eutyches, who agreed with Origen. For he says:

“For I think that one who speaks in this way is persuaded that the soul which the Savior assumed had dwelt previously in heaven, before He was born from the Virgin Mary and the Word united it to Himself in the womb.”

From this it is clear that the words “Nor was a soul infused into him at a different beginning from that of other human beings” do not signify a beginning that is the productive cause of the soul—for that was not at issue between Leo and the heretic—but a beginning understood as the commencement of duration. This was the same in Christ as in us: namely, the beginning of life in the body, not in heaven before the formation of the body.

Hear the pontiff’s words concerning the Word:

“For He did not assume either a soul that had existed previously or flesh that did not belong to a mother’s body.”

But how could those defending transmission prove with subtle arguments that Christ’s soul was created by God, while the souls of other human beings were not? Read Augustine in Book X of the cited work, chapter 20.

For us, it is enough to have shown that Leo established nothing against transmission. Thus the ecclesiastical tradition concerning the creation of souls asserted by Bellarmine appears to rest on no foundations. Rather, the doubt concerning the origin of the soul, strengthened by Augustinian reflection, prevailed among the Fathers for many centuries, as has been sufficiently demonstrated thus far.

[Col. 0699A] Moraines, who placed the holy Father’s doubt in his catalogue of errors, not only ignored everything that had been said in antiquity, but also plainly failed to understand what more recent writers boldly proclaimed.

When he was still young and playing with his pen, the most learned Christian Lupus wrote in his *Defense of the Apology on the Soul of the Egg*, chapter 15, that the doctors of the University of Marburg defended this thesis:

“The rational soul is infused by transmission; it is not created.”

Vossius, in Book II of *The History of Pelagianism*, part I, first thesis, and Alipius Reylof, in Book VI of *On the Soul according to the Mind of Saint Augustine*, chapter 2, section 3, also testify that others held this opinion. Reylof names Timothy Bright of Cambridge, George Sohnius, and Daniel Sennert, who, although he deservedly ranks among the most celebrated physicians of our age because of his outstanding learning, must be heard, though not approved.

Sennert therefore says in *Hypomnemata* 4, chapter 14:

“The rational soul was indeed founded by God Almighty in the first creation and implanted in the human body; yet through the command ‘Increase and multiply’ (Genesis 1) it received the power of propagating and multiplying itself, and indeed together with the seed. For the rational soul is not a complete essence in itself, like the angels, subsisting by itself alone; rather, it is the other part of the human being, informing the human body. Therefore, just as association with the body detracts nothing from its nobility, so neither does propagation with the seed.”

In the same place he adds:

“What Fienus considers false, absurd, and foreign to the Catholic religion—namely, that the soul is transmitted—is most true and consonant with the sacred writings.”

He also brings forward certain testimonies from sacred Scripture, although Augustine long ago explained them learnedly so that no prejudice against the opposing opinion might be drawn from the sacred mysteries.

I report these things, I repeat, but I do not approve them.

It must nevertheless be observed that, as we indicated above from Letter 157 to Optatus, Augustine doubted whether the soul was transmitted through an INCORPOREAL seed. In this opinion no evident contradiction need be supposed, since many scholastics admit that spiritual matter is not impossible.

Thus Saint Bonaventure, in Book II, distinction 3, in Part I, article 1, question 2; Alexander of Hales, in Part II, question 20, member 2, section 1; and Aureolus, in Book II, distinction 3, question 1, article 3, compose angels from spiritual matter.

Among more recent writers, Bubalus, in question 50 of Saint Thomas *On Angels*, article 2, question 2, difficulty 2, section 1; Arriaga, *Disputation 1 on the Soul*, section 5; and Compton, *Disputation 9 on the Soul*, section 8, teach that such matter is possible.

Father Matthew Vegliensis, moderator of the theological chair of Scotus in this celebrated University of Padua, a man of rare intellect and greater than our praise, defended this opinion of spiritual matter from which the soul might be composed at considerable length. In the first volume of his work *On Angels*, question 27, he proves that angels are composed of spiritual matter, and in the following question argues that the same must be said of the soul, citing in chapter 1, number 3, certain Scotists who adopted the same opinion.

Once this spiritual matter of souls is admitted—a matter defended by so many scholastics—it will not be difficult to maintain the derivation of souls according to form from that same spiritual matter [Col. 0700A].

Our Alipius Reylof, mentioned above, defends the possibility of the transmission of souls on the ground that the soul, as God’s instrument, can create another soul—a power that eminent scholastics have judged capable of being communicated to a creature.

But the former method pleases me more.

I have wished to suggest these things here in order to refute the foolish censures of certain people who criticize Augustine for asserting the transmission of souls as probable, although it is evidently clear that souls cannot be drawn from the potentiality of corporeal matter, since otherwise they would be mortal.

For the holy doctor nowhere thought that souls could be drawn from corporeal matter, but only from spiritual matter, which so many of the doctors mentioned above concede to be possible. Once that is granted, I do not see why the derivation of a spiritual form from spiritual matter should appear so evidently impossible that Augustine ought to be turned into an offender for having judged that derivation probable.

I admit that spiritual matter from which the soul might be made appeared difficult to Augustine, as is clear from Book VII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 6 and following. Thus in chapter 7 he says:

“But that spiritual matter—if there was any from which the soul was made, or if there is any from which souls are made—what is it itself? What is its name? What form does it have? What function does it hold among created things? Is it alive or not? And so forth.”

There he examines spiritual matter at length in the manner of one conducting an inquiry.

The same holy Father, in Letter 157 to Optatus, sets out the difficulties that arise once that spiritual seed from which the soul is made is posited. From this it is sufficiently clear how much effort he devoted to resolving that doubt [Col. 0700C]. But when he saw himself pressed by great difficulties on both sides, he suspended his assent.

Nor can I approve these words of Bellarmine in Book IV of *On the Loss of Grace*, chapter 11:

“Certainly, if Saint Augustine were now living among human beings, he would not merely favor but would also give thanks to those who defended our opinion”—that is, the opinion of creation.

But why would Augustine owe such thanks to recent writers? Because they had demonstrated the opinion of the creation of souls from Scripture? Augustine examined and tested all the testimonies of sacred Scripture.

Or would he follow the authority of the scholastics? On the contrary, with the Fathers whom I have cited, he would still persist in his ancient doubt.

Would he be convinced by their arguments against transmission? Apart from the fact that those arguments can easily be answered by those who affirm spiritual matter, they would prove only that Augustine should refrain from assenting to transmission—which he always did—not that they would draw him into the opinion concerning the creation of individual souls. In that opinion he perceived himself to be pressed by no fewer difficulties, especially because, once that opinion is granted—the same opinion that the Pelagians vigorously urged—the difficulty of transmitting original sin immediately arises.

The scholastics are so burdened by this difficulty that, when assigning the manner in which that stain is transmitted through generation, they are hardly in agreement with one another. Rather, they fiercely attack one another.

Augustine, then, would even now suspend his assent, and would give thanks only when they proposed a certain method by which, once the creation of souls was granted, the propagation of original sin would be established by such evident reasoning that no one could reject it [Col. 0701A].

From what has been said thus far it is sufficiently clear how undeservedly you, Morainius, brand Augustine with error because he doubted the origin of the soul. He is acquitted by the full agreement of the holy Fathers; and, against your will, the great ornament of the African Church, Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, recites a panegyric in his honor, expressed in these very words:
