“Seeing the profundity of the question concerning the origin of the soul to be unfathomable to him, Blessed Augustine did not wish to put forward any defined opinion concerning the matter. He considered it wholly inappropriate to wish to affirm without hesitation something that another person could overturn by a contrary answer.

“In this matter, his discussion shines forth as no less extensive than profound: both in Book X of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, and in the books concerning the origin of the soul addressed to Vincentius Victor, and also in the first of the two books that he wrote to Saint Jerome, as well as in the three letters that he composed to Bishop Optatus concerning this question.

“His discussion is all the more praiseworthy because it is governed by a fitting moderation. Whatever he saw should be investigated and examined through acuteness of intellect, orderly reasoning, and the weight of authority, he investigated with singular care and examined thoroughly. Yet he withheld his assent from both definitions, lest he undertake the labor of so great a disputation in vain, when a rash definition of either opinion would nullify it.”

Book III of *The Truth of Predestination and Grace*, chapter 18.

§ IV. Whether it was the opinion of Saint Augustine that baptized children cannot be saved without actually receiving the Eucharist?

[Col. 0701C]

Let us now pass to the remaining errors that more recent writers publish concerning Augustine. Adamus, p. 584, charges that Augustine taught that infants, even after receiving baptism, cannot be saved without actually receiving the most holy Eucharist. After quoting the words of Saint Augustine, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book I, chapter 20, under the heading “Let the doubt now be removed,” Moraines says:

> “These words are so clear that they scarcely admit the kindly interpretation by which most theologians try to excuse Augustine from error; for this is an error noted and condemned under an anathema by the Council of Trent.”

Here too Augustine’s case is secure, with the Roman Church giving its patronage to the holy Doctor, [Col. 0701D] for the pontiffs of the Apostolic See used precisely these words of Augustine against the Pelagians. When the heretics, compelled by those words of the Lord in John 3:5—“Unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God”—admitted that children who died without baptism would not enter the kingdom of heaven, while wishing them to be without original sin, they denied that those same children should be cast into eternal fire. Instead, they said that they would possess some sort of eternal, blessed, and happy life, as Augustine reports in Sermon 14, *On the Words of the Apostle*, book IV, *On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 13, Letter 106, and elsewhere.

Therefore, in order to close off this escape route for the Pelagians, he opposed to them the words of John 6:54: “Unless you eat [Col. 0702A] the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” He inferred that children dying without baptism, since they had not eaten the flesh of the Son of Man or drunk his blood, would not possess blessed life and consequently would be damned.

Regarding this argument drawn by Augustine from Sacred Scripture, Moraines writes in the same place:

> “Likewise, in book I of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 20; in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 13; and in book II of the *Unfinished Work against Julian*, chapter 29, he seems to teach that the sacrament of the Eucharist is no less necessary for little children unto salvation than baptism, and that the words of John 6:54—‘Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not [Col. 0702B] have life in yourselves’—apply to them no less than those of John 3:5—‘Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God,’ and so forth.”

But after Augustine, the Roman pontiffs who condemned the Pelagians likewise used precisely this testimony from John 6 in order to eliminate that life which the Pelagians promised to children without baptism.

Saint Innocent, in his letter to the Fathers of the Council of Milevis, writes:

> “But what your Fraternity says they preach—namely, that little children can be granted the rewards of eternal life even without the grace of baptism—is utterly foolish. For unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, they will not have life in themselves. Those who defend for them this life without regeneration seem to me to wish to abolish baptism [Col. 0702C] itself, since they proclaim that they possess what is believed to be conferred upon them only by baptism.”

Maldonatus thinks that the text is corrupt, saying that Innocent’s words can scarcely have any coherent meaning:

> “Where it says *defendunt* [‘they defend’], I think one ought to read *deferunt* [‘they attribute’]; and where it says *nisi baptismate* [‘unless by baptism’], I think one ought to read *sine baptismate* [‘without baptism’].”

Vasquez, part III, disputation 279, chapter 4, no. 55, having noted Maldonatus’s observations, reads *in eis defendunt*—“they defend in them.” But those words have an excellent sense, for even Cicero himself used those particles, *non nisi*, in *On Friendship*: “This is my first conviction: that friendship cannot exist except among the good.” Likewise, in the Council of Carthage in 397, canon 29, we read: “So that the sacraments of the altar may be celebrated only by fasting men.”

Horace joins the verb [Col. 0702D] *defendo* with a dative in book I of the *Odes*, ode 17: “He protects summer for the little goats”; and Virgil does so in Eclogue 4: “Protect the solstice for the flock.” Nor should one say that a prefect protects a city *for himself*, but rather *for the prince*. Therefore Saint Innocent’s text does not need to be restored by any novel grammatical correction. It is enough to have indicated these minor points.

Saint Pope Gelasius likewise pursued the Pelagians with precisely the same testimony in his letter to the bishops throughout Picenum:

> “So that the providence of God might cut off all the wickedness of the Pelagians,” he says, “it was said not only, ‘Whoever has not been born again of water and the Holy Spirit will not enter the kingdom of heaven’ (John 3:5), but it was also said in the same way, ‘Whoever does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his [Col. 0703A] blood will not have life in himself’ (John 6:54). No one doubts that this was said concerning eternal life, since many who do not eat this sacrament nevertheless appear to possess present life.”

You hear, Moraines, that the words of John 6—“Unless you eat,” and so forth—apply to little children no less than those of John 3—“Unless someone is born again,” and so forth. Innocent believed this; Gelasius established it—yet you reproached it in Augustine as a fundamental error.

Maldonatus, in his *Commentary on John* 6:54, says:

> “I set aside the opinion of Augustine and Innocent I, which prevailed in the Church for approximately six hundred years: namely, that the Eucharist was also necessary for infants.”

Again, in the same place he asserts that Augustine and Innocent “were led by that testimony of John 6 to believe that even baptized infants [Col. 0703B] could not be saved unless they received the Eucharist.” Thus they attribute Innocent as Augustine’s companion in error; and if they had read Gelasius, they would have added him as well.

Here we must do two things: correct Maldonatus and defend Augustine, together with the Apostolic See, from error and censures. First, it is certain that the ancient Fathers customarily administered the sacred Eucharist to children immediately after baptism, as Cyprian reports in *On the Lapsed*; Gennadius in *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapter 52; Augustine in Letter 107; and the Second Council of Toledo, chapter 11.

But Maldonatus’s claim that they did this because they thought the Eucharist necessary even for infants cannot be conceded in any way. It contradicts the decree of Trent, session 21, [Col. 0703C] chapter 4, which, speaking of the same ancient practice of giving the Eucharist to little children, says:

> “For just as those most holy Fathers had a probable reason for their practice in accordance with the circumstances of that time, so certainly it must be believed without controversy that they did not do this because of any necessity for salvation.”

Maldonatus’s further claim—that Saints Innocent and Augustine said that even baptized infants, unless they received the Eucharist, could not be saved—and Adamus’s claim that Augustine taught that infants, even after receiving baptism, could not be saved without actually receiving the most holy Eucharist, are utterly false.

They did indeed say that infants could not be saved without the sacrament of the Eucharist; but they never asserted this of baptized children, since at that time the Eucharist was given immediately after baptism to everyone, including infants. [Col. 0703D]

For this reason, both the Roman pontiffs and Augustine made excellent use of that testimony from John 6 against the Pelagians. For when the Pelagians granted eternal life outside the kingdom of God to little children dying without baptism, the holy Fathers argued as follows: No one without baptism can receive the Eucharist, through which, according to the Lord’s words in John 6, eternal life is given; therefore children dying without the sacraments of baptism and the Eucharist cannot participate in eternal life.

But they never said that infants who had received baptism alone did not possess grace and a right to eternal life before receiving the Eucharist. The Pelagians were very properly refuted by this argument, because they had no basis from which to promise eternal life to little children.

Marius Mercator, Augustine’s friend and defender, [Col. 0704A] uses this very argument in his short work against Julian, and in precisely the sense in which we have explained it. I give his statement from the Vatican manuscript of the Palatine Library, no. 234, p. 8, col. 2:

> “The voice of the Savior says: ‘Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves.’ Certainly, without any evasion, no one without baptism claims this for himself, nor does he become a participant in that sacrament.”

Eusebius, a Gallican bishop, whose homilies circulate under the name of Eusebius of Emesa—although he was later than, and superior to, the Emesene—testifies that this argument is exceedingly strong. In Homily 5, *On Easter*, he says:

> “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. This [Col. 0704B] testimony is MOST CLEAR and MOST POWERFUL against the blasphemies of Pelagius, who, having seized upon impiety, presumes to assert that baptism is conferred upon little children not for life but for the kingdom of heaven. For under these words of God, by which the Evangelist declares, ‘You will not have life in yourselves,’ it must plainly be understood that every soul deprived of the gift of baptism lacks not only glory but also life.”

Volume V of the *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*, part I, p. 560, Cologne edition.

That Saint Augustine used this authority of Sacred Scripture in this way is clear from his Letter 106 to Paulinus, where he says:

> “But if they yield to the Apostolic See—or rather, to that Teacher and Lord of the Apostles who says that they will not have life in themselves unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, which, of course, the UNBAPTIZED [Col. 0704C] cannot do—then at last they will admit that the UNBAPTIZED cannot have life.”

Nor does Saint Innocent write that eternal life is conferred upon even baptized children only through the Eucharist, as Maldonatus imposes upon him. Rather, he says that it is believed to be conferred upon them *only through baptism*, thereby signifying that eternal life is conferred not by the Eucharist but by baptism.

Thus Augustine, in the letter to Paulinus mentioned above, observes that the Apostolic See employed that evangelical testimony so that it would not be believed that UNBAPTIZED children could possess life. He does not say that it was employed so that it would not be believed that even baptized children could possess life without receiving the Eucharist. This is a serious delusion on the part of his opponents.

But since at that time both sacraments—namely, baptism and the Eucharist—were given to everyone [Col. 0704D], we do not often read what Augustine thought about the case in which baptism alone was conferred without the Eucharist. Nevertheless, I find him treating that case once, in book I of *On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 9, and book III, chapter 9.

When Vincent Victor proved by the example of the good thief that children could be saved without baptism, the holy Doctor replied that it could have happened that the thief had been baptized and had received remission of sins in baptism before he went to prison; or, as many believed, that he had been baptized on the cross itself by the water flowing from Christ’s side. In book II of the *Retractations*, chapter 18, he says that it is uncertain whether the thief was baptized; this matter will be discussed again in chapter 5, § 11.

But it is certain [Col. 0705A] that the thief did not receive the Eucharist, which the Lord had instituted at the supper on the day before his death. Therefore, according to Augustine, a man who has received only baptism, without actually receiving the Eucharist, can receive remission of sins and eternal salvation.

This also follows from his consistent teaching that faith and conversion of heart, which occurs through actual charity, can make a person saved if an unforeseen necessity prevents him from receiving baptism. He writes this repeatedly in his books against the Donatists, especially book IV of *On Baptism*, chapter 22.

But a baptized child, even if he does not receive the Eucharist, possesses faith and charity infused by God in the sacrament of regeneration in a far more perfect manner. Therefore, according to the teaching of Saint Augustine, he will truly be saved.

When [Col. 0705B] the holy Fathers teach that no one can attain eternal life without participation in the body and blood of the Lord, they are to be understood as speaking of spiritual participation: through infused faith they become participants in Christ’s body when they become members of Christ, into whom they are incorporated by faith. Likewise, those who receive the Eucharist are said to become members of Christ when they remain in him and Christ in them.

Hence Augustine, in Tractate 27 on John, says much about this, including:

> “But that we may be his members, unity binds us together; and what produces the unity that binds us together except charity?”

And in Tractate 26:

> “To eat that food and drink that drink, then, is to remain in Christ and to have him remaining in us.”

The holy Father explains himself in the same way in those books against [Col. 0705C] the Pelagians. In book III of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 4, after saying, “Unless human beings eat his flesh—that is, become participants in his body—they will not have life,” he had shortly before assigned the manner in which children participate in Christ’s body:

> “From this it follows,” he says, “that since nothing else is accomplished when little children are baptized except that they are incorporated into the Church—that is, into the body of Christ—and joined to his members.”

Saint Fulgentius testifies that this was Augustine’s very mind in his *Response to Two Questions of the Deacon Ferrandus*. Ferrandus had written that a young Ethiopian, having been baptized while near death, had died immediately before receiving the Eucharist, and he asked whether he could be saved in that condition.

Fulgentius replied that through baptism a person becomes a participant in the body of Christ, or is incorporated into Christ, even if he does not actually receive the sacrament of the Eucharist. After adducing many testimonies from Sacred Scripture in support of this, he finally brought forward a sermon of Saint Augustine addressed to infants before the altar, where the holy Doctor says, among other things:

> “Understand and rejoice: unity, piety, truth, charity; one bread, one body—we are many. Recall, for bread is not made from one grain but from many. Therefore, when you were being exorcised, you were, as it were, ground; when you were baptized, you were, as it were, mixed; when you received the sanctification of the Spirit, you were, as it were, baked. Be what you see, and receive what you are.”

Therefore, according to Augustine, infants become members of the body [Col. 0705D] of Christ through the sanctifying grace of baptism.

Moreover, after these words [Col. 0706A] of Augustine, Fulgentius concludes:

> “I believe, holy brother, that our discussion has been confirmed by the sermon of the illustrious Doctor Augustine, and that there can be no doubt whatever that each of the faithful becomes a participant in the Lord’s body and blood when, in baptism, he is made a member of Christ’s body. Nor is he separated from participation in the bread and cup, even if, before eating that bread and drinking the cup, he departs from this world established in the unity of Christ’s body.”

In the *Response to the Questions of the Deacon Ferrandus*.

Bede, in volume VI of his *Commentary on chapter 10 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians*, which was compiled from excerpts of Augustine, cites those earlier words of Saint Augustine in such a way that he also attributes to him the following words, which we have quoted from Fulgentius, [Col. 0706B] omitting the preceding line, “I believe, holy brother,” and so forth. The compiler of the canons likewise stumbled over this stone in the chapter *Nulli*, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, attributing Fulgentius’s words to Augustine.

From all this, the error attributed by more recent writers to Augustine—that infants require, in addition to baptism, the actual reception of the Eucharist—vanishes into smoke. Since the Roman pontiffs used Augustine’s words to refute those same enemies [Col. 0706C] of divine grace, he cannot be accused of this as his sole error; rather, the Apostolic See must be accused together with Augustine, especially since the holy Doctor repeatedly presented that testimony from John 6 as having been employed by the Apostolic See, as we showed from Letter 106.

If more recent writers regard it as too irreverent to think so perversely about the Roman pontiffs, who expressed their judgments against the Pelagians in accordance with the common sense of the Church, let them also adopt more charitable attitudes toward Augustine. In precisely the same case, let them receive both the Roman prelates and the bishop of Hippo with charitable interpretations—not inventing such interpretations from their own minds under the pretext of honor, but hearing them from Augustine himself together with Fulgentius.

For Augustine alone is the key to understanding Augustine, and he is the clear and sincere interpreter of his own meanings.

## § V. That the holy Doctor did not err in explaining the Apostle’s statement in Romans 14:23, “Whatever is not from faith is sin.” The Catholic Church, the Roman pontiffs, and the holy Fathers approve Saint Augustine’s interpretation.

But Moraines again cries out against Augustine: [Col. 0706D]

> “He also wrongly explains what the Apostle says in Romans 14:23: ‘Whatever is not from faith is sin,’ as though the Apostle wished to say that all the works of unbelievers are sins and that no good work can be performed without true faith. Yet the passage concerns what is not done according to the dictate of a conscience that judges in good faith that the act being performed is lawful, as is clear from the text itself; and the common interpretation of the Doctors contradicts Augustine. In several places, as we have noted elsewhere, he also seems to restrict his assertion to a good work useful for attaining eternal life, and so forth. Both interpretations, however, are plainly foreign to the Apostle’s true meaning in the cited passage.”

So he writes.

In the preceding chapter, § 4, we indicated what the holy Doctor’s mind was concerning the works of unbelievers. [Col. 0707A] Now Moraines’s ignorance must be corrected, since he did not hesitate to call entirely foreign to the true meaning of the Apostle the interpretation followed by the Church amid its sacred ceremonies.

For according to an ancient rite of the Church, the bishop addresses those about to be ordained subdeacons as follows:

> “Be such men, therefore, that you may be able to serve worthily in the divine sacrifices and in the Church of God—that is, in the body of Christ—founded upon the true and catholic faith, since, as the Apostle says, ‘Whatever is not from faith is sin’; it is schismatic and outside the unity of the Church.”

In the *Roman Pontifical*.

Behold the Augustinian interpretation, consecrated by the approval of the Catholic Church and recited by bishops throughout the orthodox world during the sacred ceremonies. Therefore the Church [Col. 0707B] and Augustine have one and the same judgment concerning those words of the Apostle: they are to be understood of the true Christian faith.

I seem to see the new censors, as the saying goes, stuck in the shallows. If they say that the Catholic Church has explained the Apostle’s text wrongly, they now see what a grave offense they incur. But if they consider it irreverent to reject the Church’s words, let them at last, compelled by ecclesiastical authority, yield to Augustine as well.

Nor is it surprising that the Catholic Church understood the Apostle’s words in this way, for the pontiffs of the Apostolic See interpreted them in precisely this manner from ancient times.

Saint Leo the Great, discussing the virtues of unbelievers and Christians in Sermon 2, *On the Fast of Pentecost*, explains the Apostle’s judgment as follows:

> “Reason acts in one way under truth, deception under falsehood. Among us, faith justifies [Col. 0707C] even the one who eats; among them, unbelief pollutes the one who fasts. Therefore, since outside the Catholic Church nothing is whole and nothing is pure, as the Apostle says, ‘Whatever is not from faith is sin,’ and so forth.”

The same Pope says in Sermon 8, *On Lent*:

> “He prepares himself with true and reasonable purification whose heart is polluted by no unbelief, as the Apostle says: ‘Whatever is not from faith is sin.’ The fasts of those whom the father of lies deceives with his illusions will be useless and vain, and the true flesh of Christ does not nourish them.”

Perhaps you will say that this was Leo’s private interpretation, since in this matter he agreed with Augustine; that Leo taught these things while preaching publicly, but did not define anything from the chair against heresies.

But this argument helps you very little, since Catholics heard the praised explanation from the Apostolic [Col. 0707D] mouth; and you can say only rashly that Leo, although not defining it from the chair but teaching it, spoke wrongly.

We also have Pope Boniface II, who, seventy years after Leo’s death, pronounced judgment from the chair against the Semi-Pelagians and approved the Augustinian interpretation. For in his letter to Saint Caesarius of Arles, speaking about the Christian faith, he says:

> “Apart from it [the faith], there is nothing good that anyone can perform according to God, just as the blessed Apostle says: ‘Whatever is not from faith is sin.’ Since this is so, either they will attribute no good to grace if they attempt to remove faith from it, or, if they say that something is good by grace, then faith itself must necessarily be attributed to grace.”

But if two Roman pontiffs do not add sufficient authority [Col. 0708A] to Augustine’s interpretation, I shall produce the testimony of fifteen most learned and most holy Fathers. King Thrasamund, an Arian, deported them from Africa into exile in Sardinia. In their book *On the Incarnation and Grace*, approved by the subscription of them all, as is clear from its title, they write in chapter 25:

> “Who would dare to understand by ‘the nations’ in this passage those whom it is evident have not been justified by faith, when the Apostle himself testifies that ‘Whatever is not from faith is sin,’ and that ‘Without faith it is impossible to please God’ (Hebrews 11)? And since it is clear that Abraham was justified by faith, and so forth.”

This was the Byzacene synod.

These statements certainly make it possible for our Father’s explanation to be subjected to censure only rashly. Other Fathers and ancient writers likewise cast their white stones in favor of the same interpretation: Saint Prosper, in his letter to Rufinus; [Col. 0708B] Saint Fulgentius, book II of *On the Remission of Sins*, chapter 1; Saint Isidore, book of *The Highest Good*, chapter 2; Saint Bernard, Sermons 30 and 51 on the *Song of Songs*; Julianus Pomerius, book III of *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 1; Facundus of Hermiane, book I of *On the Three Chapters* addressed to the Emperor Justinian, at the end of chapter 1; and others.

Thus, if the testimonies of the Fathers are counted, more than twenty agree with Augustine in this understanding of the Apostle’s text, whereas far fewer are named by recent writers in support of the other interpretation—unless those writers likewise count among their supporters men from whom they are separated by so great an interval.

And yet Moraines boldly insists that “the common interpretation of the Doctors [Col. 0708C] contradicts Augustine,” as though the Fathers we have cited were not Doctors but common rabble from the dregs of the Subura.

I do, however, see that Bernard also admits the other interpretation: namely, that “what is not from conscience is sin,” in his book *On Precepts and Dispensations*, chapters 18 and 20.

Vossius, a man sufficiently renowned under his own name, attempts in book III of his *History of Pelagianism*, part III, thesis 12, to reconcile Augustine’s interpretation with the other interpretation concerning conscience in a single phrase:

> “Namely, that the Apostle’s meaning is: Whatever does not proceed from Christian faith applied through conscience to an action is considered sin.”

But Augustine needs no such interpretations. He disputed with Julian about the true meaning of Paul’s statement.

When the holy Doctor, at the beginning of book I of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 3, [Col. 0708D] where he begins his dispute against Julian, had inferred from the Apostle’s words, “Whatever is not from faith is sin,” that without faith chastity is not a true virtue, Julian opposed four books to that single Augustinian book. Rejecting the holy Father’s interpretation, he unquestionably assumed the other interpretation concerning conscience in order to blunt the force of the argument.

But Augustine immediately wrote another book, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, against those four books of Julian; then he composed six additional volumes with much greater labor. In the fourth of these, chapter 3, he rejects Julian’s explanation and consistently defends the one he had given in chapter 3 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, in these exact words:

> “You accepted and explained that testimony which I quoted from the Apostle—‘Whatever is not from faith [Col. 0709A] is sin’—as it seemed to you—not according to its meaning, but according to your own understanding. The Apostle was speaking about foods. For after saying, ‘But whoever doubts and eats is condemned, because it is not from faith’ (Romans 14:23), he wished to prove this particular kind of sin, of which he was speaking, by a general statement, immediately adding: ‘For whatever is not from faith is sin.’”

These are Augustine’s words. From them it follows that the dictate of conscience must be directed by faith, by which alone, as he proves in the same place, an action is referred to its ultimate end; and he always requires this condition for the moral goodness of an action that is perfect in every circumstance.

For the practical judgment that dictates abstention from foods forbidden by law is directed by faith, through which one believes that those precepts must be observed in relation to the ultimate end. Therefore, “whoever doubts and eats is condemned,” because he does not act from faith [Col. 0709B] directing the practical judgment, or conscience. Proving this by a general statement, the Apostle says: “Whatever is not from faith”—the only principle by which a good work can at least virtually be referred to God—“is sin.”

Nor should we heed Cornelius à Lapide’s forced interpretation of this Pauline text, where he says:

> “Augustine and his followers take the *τὸ* ‘what is not from faith’ by *meiosis* [rhetorical understatement], as though the Apostle were saying: what proceeds from unbelief, or what is against faith, or what is done for the worship of an idol, is sin; and because Saint Augustine thought that most works are performed by unbelievers for this purpose—namely, to worship an idol—he consequently thought that most works were sins.”

For the holy [Col. 0709C] Father considered reference to the ultimate end so necessary to true virtue that he affirmed that even virtues could not be sought without fault merely on account of their inherent moral beauty, as we proved more fully in chapter 3, § 4. For they lack at least a proximate virtual reference to the ultimate end, because they are elicited by a person deprived of knowledge of the true God and are corrupted by the vice of self-love—a position that remained constant in Augustine.

You will say: Therefore, if everything that is not from faith is sin—namely, if every action that does not presuppose faith in the person acting, by which it may be directed to the ultimate end, is sin—and if this is the genuine meaning of the Apostle’s words, as established by the interpretation of the Fathers, the popes, and the entire Catholic Church, it follows that all the works of unbelievers are sins. Yet this is proposition 26 of Baius, repeatedly condemned by the Apostolic See.

I reply that we already indicated above, in chapter 3, § 4, that Augustine’s position is far removed from the condemned proposition of Baius. But lest we seem to set the more recent popes, who repeatedly proscribed the aforementioned thesis, against their ancient predecessors—or even against the Catholic Church itself, which teaches from the Apostle that everything not from faith is sin—I shall add a few further observations here.

First, Baius’s proposition 26 is quoted by most authors [Possevinus, under the entry “Michael Baius”], but especially by Suárez, in this form:

> “The following opinion must be rejected as Pelagian: ‘All the works of unbelievers are sins, and the virtues of philosophers are vices.’”

Turrianus, however, writes in his treatise *On the Errors of Baius*, appended to the volume *On Grace*, chapter 5, § 1, no. 4:

> “That is how several bulls printed at Rome, and several manuscripts that I myself saw, have it.”

It is certain, however, that the thesis has been incorrectly represented in this form. For the Pelagians were so far from saying that all the works of unbelievers are sins that, on the contrary, they rather asserted that unbelievers perform many virtuous works, thinking that by this reasoning they could eliminate divine grace from Augustine, book 4 *Against Julian*, chapter 3.

Suárez, *Prolegomena* 6 *On Grace*, chapter 2, no. 7, says:

> “Hence I suspect that in that hypothetical proposition some negation or negative verb is missing, namely: ‘The following opinion must be rejected as Pelagian: Not all the works of unbelievers are sins, and the virtues of philosophers are not vices.’”

Vázquez, however, *1–2*, disputation 191, chapter 2, quotes the proposition as follows: “All the works of unbelievers are sins,” and so forth. Moreover, in the same bull, issued more than once at Rome against Jansenius, the words “as Pelagian,” and so forth, are omitted.

In the first place, that proposition was condemned because of the censure by which it accused of Pelagianism those who denied that all the works of unbelievers are sins. That this censure originally appeared in the bulls is evident from those issued at Rome in earlier times, which Turrianus, a distinguished writer of the Society, also testifies that he had read. Who would dare say that the Roman printers added those words on their own authority?

This is confirmed by proposition 23 of the same Baius, namely:

> “To agree with Pelagius is to understand the Apostle’s text, Romans 2: ‘The Gentiles who do not have the law naturally do the things of the law,’ as referring to Gentiles who do not possess the grace of faith.”

This proposition may indeed be understood according to the historical account—that is, as saying that those who hold this view assert what Pelagius likewise asserted. In this sense the proposition is true and cannot in any way be condemned, for Pelagius explains those words of the Apostle in this way in his *Letter to Demetrias*, chapter 4. The Fathers of Byzacena, in their book *On the Incarnation and Grace*, chapter 5, after quoting that statement of Paul, write:

> “Those who contradict grace attempt to assign this passage of the Apostle to unbelieving Gentiles.”

Augustine likewise conveys this in book 4 *Against Julian*, chapter 3, under “Hence they too.”

Alternatively, the assertion may be understood as censuring those who interpret the cited text as referring to unbelievers, as though by doing so they were teaching the Pelagian heresy. In that case, the same proposition is rightly condemned as scandalous because of its shameless censure.

Thus proposition 26 was also proscribed because of its censure, since it contains the same doctrine as proposition 23. For the opposite of thesis 26 is usually proved by everyone from the Apostle’s cited text, Romans 2.

I reply, secondly, that these propositions were condemned respectively and in the sense intended by their proponents, as is stated at the end of the bull. Proposition 26 was condemned in relation to proposition 35, which reads:

> “Everything that a sinner, or a slave of sin, does is sin.”

From this it necessarily follows that all the works of unbelievers are sins and that the virtues of philosophers are vices, since unbelievers are sinners. It was therefore rightly condemned as derived from the heretical doctrine rejected by the Council of Trent, session 6, canon 7, and by Augustine, as we showed against Maldonado in chapter 3, § 4.

I reply, thirdly, that some unbelievers perform good acts, to which they are moved beforehand by God; and these certainly cannot be sins. The holy Doctor expressly teaches this in chapter 24 *On the Grace of Christ*. After quoting the testimony of Holy Scripture concerning Ahasuerus’s change, Esther 15:11, “God changed and turned his indignation into gentleness,” and having first stated that Ahasuerus was at that time an unbeliever and a sinner, he concludes:

> “God works inward and hidden wonders, by an ineffable power, in the hearts of human beings—not only true revelations, but also GOOD WILL.”

Baius, however, maintained that unbelievers perform no good acts from God’s grace, because he admitted only the grace of the Holy Spirit inhabiting the soul. Since the Holy Spirit does not inhabit an unbeliever, he therefore supposed that no assistance of divine grace could be found in such a person.

I call Gabriel Vázquez as a witness to this, *1–2*, disputation 190, chapter 18, no. 184, where, concerning Baius’s opinion in *On the Justice and Virtues of the Wicked*, chapters 4 and 5, he writes:

> “He did not admit the distinction between the grace of the Holy Spirit not yet inhabiting the soul, such as we grant before the remission of sins, and the grace of the Spirit inhabiting it, which we say exists after remission.”

This doctrine is contrary to the Council of Trent, which, in session 14, chapter 4, admits the impulse of the Holy Spirit—not yet indeed inhabiting the soul, but merely moving it.

From this it is clear that our Gregory of Rimini in no way agrees with Michael Baius on this thesis. For although, in *Sentences* 2, distinction 26, question 1, article 1, he says that all the works of unbelievers are sins, nevertheless, in article 3, in response to Augustine’s testimonies, he says:

> “If, however, some act of this kind—namely, performed with the proper end and the other proper circumstances—is found to have been done by unbelievers, it must be said that they did it not without God’s special assistance.”

In his response to the eighth objection, he grants that this occurred in the case of the Egyptian midwives who concealed the Hebrew children—namely, with God’s special assistance. There too he proves the point by the testimony of the holy Doctor, book 4 *Against Julian*, chapter 3, where Augustine grants that some good works arise in unbelievers from God’s special grace, and further admits the assistance of God, or of the Holy Spirit not yet inhabiting the soul. Baius asserted neither of these.

Basilius Poncius, part 1, *Relectio on Grace*, final chapter, p. 204, says:

> “Let us suppose what a PROBABLE OPINION maintains, as I shall say in the second part: that all the works of unbelievers are sins,”

and so forth.

Who could think that a man of such renown among the theologians of Salamanca regarded Baius’s opinion as probable, especially since he deals with Baius’s propositions in chapter 15? Indeed, learned men rightly count Poncius among the leading theologians of this age.

The learned Carmelite Fathers of Salamanca, the Discalced, erected this epitaph to him as a mark of honor in treatise 3 *On the Knowledge of God*, disputation 10, doubt 8, no. 130:

> “Although we cannot fail to mention that great man who, while we were laboring on this work, was recently taken from the living, to the greatest grief of all and to the loss of this entire university—or rather of the whole world—namely, Master Basilius Poncius of León, the distinguished offspring of the most august Augustinian family, and the most deserving head of the principal chair of sacred theology in this academy.”

Since, therefore, the proposition “All the works of unbelievers are sins” was defended even after the bull against Baius had been issued by the most eminent theologians, it is evident that it can be understood in an orthodox sense, far removed from Baius’s meaning. Accordingly, that same thesis was rightly proscribed by the Apostolic See.

I have pursued this matter at greater length not only to show that the supreme pontiffs and so many Fathers—and indeed the Catholic Church itself—when they explain the words of the Apostle, Romans 14, “Everything that is not from faith is sin,” as referring to Christian faith, in no way support Baius’s condemned proposition, but also to refute the rather troublesome insistence of certain recent writers, who wish to condemn that crude proposition without distinguishing the several senses in which, as I have shown, it can be understood.

## § VI. Saint Augustine never held that lingering thoughts are merely venial sin, as recent writers falsely attribute to him

Moraines nevertheless renews the accusation and charges Augustine with another error in these words:

> “Furthermore, in book 2 *Against Julian*, chapter 10, he teaches that lingering thoughts, or voluntary pleasures concerning sexual matters, are merely venial sin, provided that consent to the act, or an evil desire, or the danger of such, is absent. This doctrine has long since been rejected by all Catholics and could not be advanced by anyone without scandal.”

We reply that Augustine must be understood as speaking of pleasure that occurs without full awareness of its malice or danger. In that case, it is the common opinion of theologians that the pleasure is not mortal sin, as is testified by Salas, *1–2*, title 13, disputation 6, section 6, and Vázquez, *1–2*, disputation 97, chapter 3 (Saint Thomas, *Question 15 on Evil*, article 2, response to objection 16).

That the holy Doctor was speaking of pleasure arising in this way is clearly understood from his own words:

> “When,” he says, “they linger over such thoughts with SOME pleasure—not indeed deciding upon a shameful act, but failing to turn the mind away from them as it ought, lest it fall into them, or, if it has fallen into them, failing to tear it away.”

Cited chapter 10.

If the mind falls into such thoughts, it must immediately turn away from them. If this does not happen because of a lack of full awareness—which often occurs, since it is not in our power to control what enters our mind, and shameful thoughts sometimes creep in and touch the spirit with sudden pleasure—the matter is by no means judged to be mortal sin.

For this reason Augustine deliberately added “with some pleasure,” to show that its gravity and force were not sufficient to cause mortal sin.

Moreover, that Augustine considered lingering thoughts, or lingering pleasures, to be mortal sin is clear from book 12 *On the Trinity*, chapter 12. There he plainly teaches that such deliberate pleasures are sufficient sin to bring a person into eternal damnation unless the guilt is remitted through sacramental grace:

> “Thus it may be said,” he writes, “that in one human being, if thought willingly feeds only upon illicit pleasures from which it ought immediately to turn away, and if evil acts are not decided upon but are merely held pleasantly in remembrance, it is like saying that a woman can be condemned without a man—far be it from us to believe this. For this is one person, one human being, and the whole person will be condemned unless, through the grace of the Mediator, those things are remitted which, without the will to perform the act but with the will to delight the mind in such things, are nevertheless perceived as sins of thought alone.”

Here we have the holy Doctor’s clear and explicit judgment. If elsewhere he spoke in a way that could be drawn either toward a bad or toward a good sense, why does Moraines not accept him as the interpreter of his own words? Instead, because he has once formed an opinion against him, he twists Augustine’s words into an erroneous sense in order to create a more plausible basis for accusing him.

We ought to treat the writings of others as we wish readers to treat our own writings: candidly, fairly, without hatred or envy, explaining by suitable interpretations whatever may perhaps have slipped out ambiguously.

Moreover, how greatly that most holy Doctor of the Church feared and dreaded these pleasures stealthily entering the mind can be understood abundantly from the prayers that he poured forth to God at the end of his excellent work *On the Trinity*:

> “Many are my thoughts,” he says, “such as you know, the thoughts of human beings, for they are vain. Grant me not to consent to them; and if at any time they delight me, grant that I may nevertheless disapprove of them and not linger over them as though drowsing. Let them not have such power over me that anything proceeds from them into my actions; but at least let my judgment and conscience be safe from them, while you protect me.”

What does it mean to linger over pleasures as though drowsing, except to linger through incomplete awareness, just as one who is drowsy does not fully notice what is happening?

## § VII. Whether Saint Augustine thought that baptism administered without intention is valid

The adversary again entangles Augustine in another error:

> “Likewise,” he says, “he doubted whether baptism administered without intention, in jest and mockery, is valid, book 7 *On Baptism*, chapter 53, and he holds that a revelation must be awaited before such a person is rebaptized.”

So Moraines writes in the same place.

I admit that theologians do not all agree in explaining Augustine, lest he seem to have removed the necessity of intention from baptism, although both the Council of Florence and the Council of Trent decreed that intention is necessarily required.

The Master of the Sentences, book 4, distinction 6, concedes that Augustine was in doubt. Saint Thomas, however, in the same place, at the end of the distinction, explaining the text, teaches that someone may baptize mockingly in two ways.

He may do so merely for the pleasure he derives from the external action, without intending meanwhile to do what the Church does or to confer the reality of the sacrament, namely grace. In this case, Thomas says, there is no baptism.

Or someone may baptize another playfully while indeed intending to do what the Church does, but not to confer the reality of the sacrament, which he himself judges false and nonexistent. In this latter sense, he says, the baptism is valid.

Since we do not know which of these two kinds of intention was present when the person playfully baptized another, Saint Thomas says that divine revelation must be awaited, as Augustine teaches.

P. Macedo, book 4 *On the Keys*, first part, chapter 8, adopts this explanation, praising Augustine’s prudence. Augustine judged that the testimony of God alone, who searches the hearts, was necessary in order to uncover the hidden thought of the person who baptized playfully.

Macedo adds in the same place that recent writers behave insolently when they criticize Augustine for this, as did Antonius Moraines in his *Anti-Jansenian*:

> “He is a most unjust author concerning Augustine,” Moraines says, “but I am not surprised, since in that book, when he assumed the role of an author, he laid aside his dignity. He ought to have imitated Bellarmine, who was much more learned and better than he, and who understood and defended Augustine.”

But Moraines, who says that Augustine doubted the necessity of the minister’s intention, is himself imitating Bellarmine. For Bellarmine, book 1, chapter 28, solution 3 to Chemnitz’s argument, writes that Augustine doubted the necessity of intention, adding:

> “But now the matter has been defined in the two general councils, Florence and Trent.”

This explanation, however, cannot in any way satisfy me. For in a case of doubt, baptism must be repeated, as the common opinion of the Doctors teaches from the Council of Carthage, held after the consulship of Flavius Stilicho in the year 401. There, in the case of doubt whether a barbarian child who had been sold had been baptized, it was decreed that the child should be baptized.

It is better to expose the sacrament to the danger of invalidity than to expose a person to the danger of damnation. Yet the Fathers do not say that divine revelation should be invoked in that doubt.

Moreover, that decree was known to Augustine. In his presence it was repeated, together with the other canons of the African synods held at Carthage under Aurelius, in the plenary African Council of 419.

Therefore, when the intention of the person baptizing playfully is not apparent, baptism must be repeated.

Thus, if a Jew were baptized among his own people in a sacred theatrical performance mocking us, but later wished to approach the faith, the Church would baptize him and would not await a revelation making known the intention of the Jew who had previously baptized him in the performance.

When Augustine says in chapter 53:

> “Whether the baptism administered in this way should be approved, I would judge that divine judgment ought to be sought through the oracle of some revelation,”

he does not mean a doubt of fact, but a doubt of law. For a person baptized in this way would have to be baptized again.

He says that revelation must be awaited concerning whether this manner of baptizing is sufficient and valid, so that it might be established as a certain doctrine of the Church. He does not mean a revelation given to some private person by a new miracle, but one given to the Fathers of a synod through the customary illuminations of the Holy Spirit. Hence he immediately adds:

> “Thus, I would humbly await those who were to state their opinions after me, lest they bring forward anything already examined and known.”

Among the more recent writers who discuss the meaning of this Augustinian chapter 53, the leading places are held by Vázquez, part 3, disputation 138, chapter 4, and Cardinal Lugo, disputation 8 *On the Sacraments in General*, section 3.

I shall form my judgment by beginning again from the start.

On the occasion of the question raised by the Donatists concerning the rebaptization of those who had been baptized by heretics and had then become Catholics, certain doubts about baptism had arisen among the Catholics themselves. Saint Augustine postponed these questions to the end of the seventh and final book *On Baptism*. He does not recount them there in order to solve them, but rather to propose them for solution by posterity.

Thus he begins chapter 53:

> “It is also customary to ask whether the baptism received from one who has not received it himself should be approved,”

and so forth.

He proposes three principal questions.

The first is whether someone who deceitfully and falsely administers baptism truly baptizes—someone, that is, who deceives within the Church or within what is thought to be the Church.

The second question is whether someone who deceitfully and falsely receives baptism in the Church is truly and validly baptized.

The final question is whether both the person administering baptism and the person receiving it, when outside the Church and performing the washing mimically and playfully, truly bring about the sacrament of baptism.

In these doubts Augustine does not dare to define anything. Rather, he says:

> “It is safe for us not to advance in this matter with any rash judgment, since it has been initiated in no Catholic regional council and concluded in no plenary council.”

He then suggests that, if he were sitting in the synod in which those doubts were to be resolved, he would prefer to follow the judgments of others. If he were then in the state of mind he possessed when dictating those words, he would answer as follows.

To the first question:

> “Those have baptism who, wherever and from whomever they received it, accepted it with the evangelical words by which it is consecrated, without their own deception and with some faith.”

To the second question:

> “In accordance with the statutes of our predecessors, I do not doubt that those also have baptism who, although they receive it deceitfully, nevertheless receive it in the Church, or in what is thought to be the Church, from those in whose fellowship it is received.”

Thus, according to Augustine’s judgment, it is sufficient for the validity of baptism that true faith be present in only one of the two parties, even though one of them may be guilty of deceit and dissimulation.

It is not certain, however, whether he is speaking about the intention necessary for baptism. Vázquez thinks that through the expressions *simulated mind*, deceit, and dissimulation (*simulatus animus, fallacia, simulatio*), true intention is excluded from either the minister or the recipient of baptism.

Accordingly, when Augustine speaks of those who deceitfully receive baptism, he means the same as receiving it without intention. Vázquez concludes that Augustine thought intention was not necessary in both the minister and the recipient, but that it was sufficient for it to be present in one or the other. This opinion, however, is no longer safe because of the decrees of the councils.

This explanation encounters a difficulty. Augustine plainly writes:

> “In accordance with the statutes of our predecessors, I do not doubt that those also have baptism who, although they receive it deceitfully, nevertheless receive it in the Church.”

If, therefore, to receive baptism deceitfully means to receive baptism without intention, then the statutes of the predecessors had decreed that a recipient without intention was truly baptized. This is what Augustine testifies when, on the basis of those statutes of his predecessors, he does not doubt that someone who receives baptism with such deceit and dissimulation is validly baptized.

Earlier, speaking of the minister and recipient acting deceitfully, he says:

> “Are those who are truthful, among whom the matter is performed, more effective for confirming the sacrament than those who are deceitful, by whom and among whom it is performed, are effective for nullifying it? And yet, if the deception is later exposed, NO ONE REPEATS IT; rather, the dissimulation is punished by excommunication or healed by repentance.”

By “those who are deceitful, by whom the matter is performed,” the ministers of baptism are understood; by “among whom it is performed,” the recipients of baptism are understood.

But if deceit and dissimulation signify a lack of intention, who does not see that the common opinion once held in the ancient Church was condemned by the Council of Trent—namely, the opinion that intention is not required for the validity of a sacrament?

For Augustine calls “the statutes of our predecessors” those by which it had been decreed that a person who deceitfully—that is, without intention, as Vázquez explains—received baptism nevertheless possessed true baptism.

He also testifies that those baptized with such deceit, if their dissimulation were exposed, were excommunicated rather than rebaptized. This is what he means by the words “no one repeats it,” namely, baptism. The Church now teaches the opposite: since it defines baptism conferred without intention as invalid, it orders that baptism to be repeated.

Therefore, Vázquez’s explanation of Augustine’s words cannot stand in any way, unless we say either that the ancient Fathers were mistaken and that, by not rebaptizing those who had performed baptism with dissimulation, they caused their damnation, or else that the Fathers of Florence and Trent decreed against the judgment of the more ancient Church that intention is necessary for the validity of a sacrament. Both alternatives are false and absurd.

The fictitious Moraines, in the theological disputations that he published under his real name, namely Joannes Martinonius, part 3, disputation 22, section 3, no. 33, accusing Augustine of an incoherent doctrine, says:

> “Since Saint Augustine rightly judged in the same place that one does not receive baptism who approaches it falsely and without the intention of receiving it, the same reasoning should have led him not to doubt that one who baptizes without seriousness and without intention does not truly baptize.”

But the holy Doctor wrote precisely the opposite. His words quoted above are clear:

> “I do not doubt that those also have baptism who, although they receive it deceitfully”—that is, without intention, as Martinonius interprets him together with Vázquez—“nevertheless receive it in the Church.”

Augustine was therefore not the author of an incoherent opinion, as Martinonius thinks. Rather, he said that baptism is valid both in the case of the deceitful recipient and in the case of the deceitful minister.

It must therefore be explained what Augustine understands by the terms deceit and dissimulation, since it cannot be said that he meant the absence of the intention that the Council of Trent later declared necessary for the validity of baptism.

Deceit and dissimulation can be understood in two senses: either insofar as they exclude the intention of doing what the Church does in conferring the sacrament, or insofar as they exclude faith, belief, or an estimation concerning the reality and effect of the sacrament, which is the sanctification of the soul through the infusion of grace.

These two things are very different. If a Gentile wishes to be baptized because he hopes to receive some benefit from a Christian prince, he receives baptism with a deceitful and simulated mind. Yet the deceit and dissimulation do not exclude the intention necessary for the validity of the sacrament—the intention by which he intends to do what the Church does. Rather, they exclude belief in the reality and effect of the sacrament, namely sanctifying grace.

Since, therefore, from what has been said against Vázquez, Augustine cannot be understood as speaking of deceit and dissimulation that exclude the intention of doing what the Church does—an intention that later synods declared necessary for the validity of the sacrament—he must be understood as speaking of deceit and dissimulation that exclude intention, belief, or estimation concerning the reality and effect of the sacrament.

Hence Augustine requires, for the validity of the sacrament, that those who receive it deceitfully nevertheless receive it in the Church, and so forth. Earlier he says:

> “Whether one who deceives, as in the Church or in what is thought to be the Church.”

For someone who asks for baptism in the Church certainly wishes that what the Church does should be externally performed in him, even if he believes nothing about the effect of grace.

The same Augustine, book 1 *On Baptism*, chapter 12, after saying that sins had been forgiven Simon Magus in baptism, asks:

> “What if he approached baptism itself deceitfully?”

That is, what if he did not possess faith or an intention concerning the effect of baptism, but approached with a simulated and deceitful mind?

He adds:

> “I ask whether, if he afterward confessed his deception with a shaken heart and true sorrow, he should be judged to require baptism again. To say this would be the height of madness,”

and so forth.

From this it is clear that by that deception the intention concerning the reality and effect of baptism is excluded, not the intention of doing what the Church does. For if it were to be understood in the latter sense, how would it be the height of madness to say that he should be baptized again, since the Church now teaches from the Council of Trent that such a person should be baptized again?

Moreover, in that passage Augustine contrasts the person who deceives in the Church with someone joking in a theatrical performance while receiving baptism. He asks whether baptism performed with dissimulation is valid—whether it is the baptism of one who deceives, as in the Church or in what is thought to be the Church, or of someone joking, as in a theatrical performance.

The person who deceives in the Church and the person joking in a theatrical performance agree in this: neither possesses faith concerning the effect of baptism, and therefore neither has an intention concerning the sanctification of the soul.

They differ, however, in this: the person who deceives in the Church seriously intends to perform what belongs to the external action, namely what the Church does, so that he too may be considered a Christian. The person joking in a theatrical performance merely wishes, by play, to represent what the Church does. He does not seriously wish to do what the Church does, but rather wishes, through play, to mock what the Church does.

But what did Augustine answer concerning that third difficulty?

> “But where there was neither any fellowship of people believing in this way, nor did the person receiving it there believe in this way, but the whole matter was conducted playfully, mimically, and jokingly, should the baptism administered in this way be approved?”

He replies that the matter is sufficiently doubtful, and that, for a certain definition to be established in a synod, divine assistance must be sought from the Fathers.

It must indeed be said that the holy Father doubted something that is now placed beyond doubt. When he says that baptism was conferred mimically and playfully, he either understood “mimically and playfully” in such a way that not only the intention concerning the effect of the sacrament was absent, but also the intention of doing what the Church does; or he understood it in such a way that this second intention was not excluded.

If he doubted in the second sense, it is now established that the intention of doing what the Church does is sufficient for the validity of baptism. If he was doubtful in the first sense, it is likewise now certain among Catholics that baptism from which every intention is excluded is invalid.

Indeed, Augustine’s words clearly show that every kind of intention was then excluded. He says:

> “But the whole matter was conducted playfully, mimically, and jokingly.”

For if the serious intention of doing what the Church does had been present, then the whole matter—that is, in every respect—would not have been conducted jokingly and playfully.

Who, except Moraines—a writer insufficiently fair toward Augustine—would turn this doubt into a fault, when he attributes to the holy Doctor opinions whose opposites Augustine undoubtedly declares himself to hold?

Augustine rightly suspended judgment, especially at a time when, because of the Donatist rebaptizations, any assertion that baptism administered playfully required repetition could have drawn less knowledgeable and simple-minded believers into error through the long route of schismatics who rebaptized them. Augustine prudently guarded against this danger.

As for Augustine’s wish that the matter be defined in a plenary synod, it has now been defined at the Council of Florence, in the decree on the faith after the final session, and at the Council of Trent, session 7, canon 11, where the minister’s intention is declared to be required for the validity of the sacraments.

Augustine had concluded that chapter 53 as follows:

> “How much more, then, should what I have said now be accepted without prejudice to a more careful inquiry or greater authority!”

By suspending his judgment in this way, he wished to prejudice neither the more careful inquiry into the necessity of intention, which the wisest Fathers undertook with the greatest diligence at both ecumenical councils, nor the greater authority of the two councils, which defined beyond doubt that intention is necessary for the validity of the sacrament.

Nor should the heterodox, whose leader is Chemnitz, congratulate themselves by falsely claiming Augustine as their own while denying the necessity of intention. Augustine is plainly opposed to them.

He doubted whether baptism without intention is valid; they boldly and without any doubt declare that it is valid.

Augustine said that he did not wish to advance “with any rash judgment” in a matter that had been initiated in no Catholic regional council and concluded in no plenary council. But once the truth—hidden in Augustine’s time—had later been brought to light in one council and then another, his doubt gives them no assistance.

Where Augustine said that he would humbly await those who would state their judgments, so that he might not bring forward anything already examined and known, they ought to follow the judgment pronounced by the two councils, rather than ignoring Augustine’s words.

Let later writers admire Augustine’s intellect, since he doubted the necessity of intention because he saw that it could be supported by some argument. But because it had not been decreed by the authority of any council, they should praise his modesty: he refused to issue a certain judgment concerning uncertain matters.

Thus, from the very doubt for which Moraines accuses Augustine, he emerges as especially worthy of our praise.

## § VIII. Whether Augustine said that the earth is not round and that there are no antipodes

Up to this point we have driven back from the books of the holy Father the errors that Moraines attributed to Augustine. We must now refute Adamus, who, although inferior in learning to the other recent writers, has easily surpassed them all in issuing censures against Augustine.

He publishes certain errors concerning Augustine that Moraines also advanced, although we have shown that the holy Doctor was far removed from them. But Adamus adds that Augustine also said that the earth is not round and that there are no antipodes, p. 585, chapter 3.

With the same brazenness with which he fabricated the claim that Augustine denied the soul’s spirituality, he now invents the story that the holy Doctor was ignorant of the earth’s roundness.

For someone who thought himself permitted to assert whatever he pleased about Augustine, without citing any text of Augustine, it was easy enough to attribute such monstrosities to the Bishop of Hippo.

Augustine plainly acknowledges that the earth is round in book 1 *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 12:

> “For when,” he says, “water still covered the whole earth, nothing prevented the watery and GLOBULAR mass from producing day on one side through the presence of light and night on the other through the absence of light.”

And in book 16 *The City of God*, chapter 9, where he discusses the antipodes, he says:

> “They do not consider that, even if the world is believed to be globular and round in shape, or is demonstrated to be so by some argument, it does not nevertheless follow that on the other side of it the land must also be bare of the mass of waters.”

No error concerning the earth’s roundness is therefore found in Augustine. Adamus’s objections are empty.

I will not deny that Augustine denied the existence of the antipodes, but he followed the common opinion of mankind. Pliny testifies that there had been a great dispute about the antipodes between men of letters and the common people. Augustine, however, was led to that opinion by an argument far from commonplace—namely, that there was a danger that those who pressed their feet opposite to ours might fall upward into the sky. Yet he considered arguments drawn both from sacred and from profane history, [Col. 0719D] arguments that had brought even the wisest men to that conclusion. That Ligurian Argonaut, the discoverer of the New World, was regarded by more than one prince as a mere charlatan when he promised to lead a fleet to the antipodes; nor, as I think, did the king of Aragon place complete trust in that great promiser. Rather, such is the insatiable human desire for gain: he counted it as profit to expose a few ships to the hazards of shipwreck in the hope of a world.

Macrobius, in book II of *The Dream of Scipio*, chapter 9, said that the antipodes were believed to exist on the opposite side of the world only by conjecture: “because, on account of a similar climate, it is inhabited in a similar manner, but by peoples whom it has never been permitted, nor ever will be permitted, for us to know.” Aristotle, Pliny, Ptolemy, and the other ancient historians, cosmographers, and philosophers, to whose view the Parisian scholastics [Col. 0720A] adhered, held that the earth was not habitable everywhere, but only beneath the temperate zones, although it is certain that the earth is inhabited even beneath the torrid zone and beneath both frigid zones. Moreover, Pope Zachary, in his tenth letter to Boniface, written in the year 748, calls it a perverse and wicked doctrine to assert that another world and other human beings exist beneath the earth. He, indeed, followed the common opinion. We have learned these matters from the voyages of our own time.

But just as those earlier wise men, to whom we owe all our learning, are not blamed for having written that the greater part of the earth was uninhabitable, so Augustine should not be reproached if he denied that the same earth was inhabited on the opposite side. It seemed difficult to him that human beings descended from one Adam could have crossed the immense expanse of the Ocean and once reached [Col. 0720B] the opposite part of the earth, and then, after the Flood, have been transported there again, without any mention of so remarkable an event being found either in sacred or in profane writings. Certainly, to this day it is unknown how human beings reached that place twice from Europe.

Therefore, since those who posited the antipodes were moved to say so only by conjecture—a conjecture that produces entirely slight and weak certainty—and since Augustine denied the antipodes, supported by the testimony of all historians and by the most ancient tradition of the Fathers, he removed the antipodes with better grounds than others adduced for establishing them. Yet the opinion denying the antipodes did not cling so firmly to Augustine that he never admitted them. For in his book *On the Ten Categories*, chapter 10, he says: “The earth which is seen is everywhere beneath us in the middle, and our antipodes, who are said to plant their feet opposite [Col. 0720C] to ours, have the sky above them.”

Father Macedo, a man thoroughly versed in Augustine’s writings, appears in his volume entitled *Euchological Harmony*, in his commentaries on the prayer for the feast of Saint Mark, to suggest that America was known to Augustine, since he asserts in more than one place that the earth has four parts: “It is marvelous,” he says, “that Augustine names the four parts of the world so clearly, as though America had already been discovered in his own time.”

The holy Doctor, in book XVI of *The City of God*, chapter 9, rejected as absurd the opinion affirming the antipodes: “It is exceedingly absurd,” he says, “to say that some human beings could have sailed from this part to that part, crossing the immense expanse of the Ocean, and reached it, so that there too [Col. 0720D] the human race might be established from that one first man.”

Augustine spoke of four parts, namely east, west, south, and north. Thus he says in *Tractate 118 on John*: “For this reason he says elsewhere (Matthew XXIV) that he will send his angels to gather his elect from the four winds. What is this but from the four parts of the world: east, west, north, and south?” These parts, however, were properly understood as belonging to the Old World, even if America was unknown.

§ IX. Whether Saint Augustine’s opinion concerning the simultaneous creation of things is erroneous

Here too the complaints—indeed, the censures—of recent writers, by which they assail the eminent interpretation of the holy Doctor in chapter I [Col. 0721A] of Genesis, must be refuted. That extraordinary marvel of intellect, if anywhere else he displayed admirable subtlety in explaining the Hexaemeron, acquired among the ancients as much praise as he has drawn reproach from more recent writers, or perhaps even more. Augustine saw that the six first days during which Moses writes that the world was created by God, if taken literally, were subject to the gravest difficulties, which he himself proposes in his books *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*. He therefore devised an exceedingly subtle opinion worthy of himself: those days were to be understood mystically, according to the angels’ knowledge of things in God and in their own proper kind; and he designated, in the mountain of the angels, the order of things created simultaneously by God, as well as the order of the days.

Saint Thomas briefly reports this explanation of the holy [Col. 0721B] Father concerning the simultaneous creation of things, mystically divided among those six days, in Part I, question 74, article 2. Yet such was Augustine’s modesty that he taught this interpretation devised by himself in such a way that he expressly declared that he did not wish to prejudice a better explanation:

“Whoever, therefore, seeks in the enumeration of those days not the interpretation which, according to the measure of our ability, we have been able either to investigate or to suppose, but another view which can be understood more appropriately and more truly in the condition of these creatures—not figuratively in prophecy, but properly in the creation of things—let him seek it, and, with divine assistance, find it. For it may happen that I too may perhaps find another explanation more consonant with these words of divine Scripture. I do not confirm this one in such a way as to maintain that another, which ought to be preferred, cannot be [Col. 0721C] found.”

With this statement he wished to fortify himself against the censures of hostile readers, in book IV of *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, chapter 28. These words of Augustine alone ought to be regarded as a solid apology, and nothing further would need to be added in defense of his interpretation.

For the rest, among our own writers, Master Emmanuel Cerda, the Portuguese public professor of theology at the University of Coimbra, vigorously defends the opinion of the great Father against the attack of recent authors in his *Theological Quodlibets*. He demonstrates both their audacity in censuring and their weakness in opposing him. Charles Moreau, our fellow countryman from Bourges, did the same in his *Peaceful Vindications*. I intend to compare the accusations of recent writers [Col. 0721D] with the judgments of the ancient theologians, especially the leading ones; whoever desires an exact defense of Augustine’s opinion should read Cerda.

Ludovicus Molina, then, in his treatise *On the Work of the Six Days*, disputation 1, judges Augustine’s explanation in these terms: “To expound the Scriptures in that sense is certainly to weaken their authority and perhaps to expose it to ridicule before unbelievers.”

But Saint Thomas, that great doctor of theology, indeed of the Church, did not think so contemptuously of Augustine’s interpretation. In book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 12, question 1, article 2, he says: “Of these interpretations, then, the first—that of Augustine—is more subtle and better defends the Scriptures against the mockery of unbelievers.”

I shall soon cite another passage from that same Angelic teacher in which he writes the exact opposite of what that recent writer asserted about Augustine. Cornelius a Lapide, [Col. 0722A] assuming the role of censor against Augustine, says: “All the other Fathers teach the contrary, and the simple and historical narrative of Moses entirely prevails; therefore it is now erroneous to say that everything was created in one day.”

Albert, however, agrees with Augustine. Because of his extensive and remarkable learning, he was distinguished by the title “the Great,” and he writes in precisely these words: “Without prejudice to a better opinion, Augustine’s view seems to deserve assent,” Part I of the *Summa*, question 12, *On the Four Coeval Things*. Saint Thomas, whom I have just cited, adds: “This opinion [that of Augustine] pleases me more.”

So, Cornelius, has that opinion—which Albert the Great [Col. 0722B] and Saint Thomas, the lights and pillars of the scholastics, approve and follow—become erroneous in our age? Which synod proscribed it? Which Roman prelates? Which academies of learned men? Or is it to be judged erroneous because it displeases you and your associates?

Know, however, that it is approved by more recent Augustinian theologians: by Cerda, Moreau, and Ludovicus ab Angelis, the theologian of Coimbra, in book V of *The Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 9. There he brings forward other Fathers who agreed with Augustine on this matter and attacks Molina for having censured the Father.

The third accuser of Augustine, Arriaga, cries out: “This explanation is considered improbable by everyone, nor do I doubt that, if it did not have Augustine as its patron, it would plainly have been condemned as heretical,” volume II, on Part I, disputation 28, number 40.

But two eminent theologians of the Parisian school, Saint Bonaventure and Giles of Rome: [Col. 0722C] silence the words of this recent writer. The former writes in book II, distinction 13, article 1, question 1: “Although this position is probable and reasonable, nevertheless the Catholic writers who followed Augustine approved another way more.” The latter writes in Part I of his *Hexaemeron*, chapter 28: “We do not say these things in order to disapprove Augustine’s opinion, which is exceedingly subtle and authoritative.”

But let us hear at last what that censor of Augustine, Moraines, has to say. In reciting a catalogue of errors attributed to the holy Father, he placed this first: “He held that the world was created in an instant, etc., which does not agree with what Moses wrote in chapter I of Genesis, as the more exact theologians demonstrate, especially Suárez, Molina, MARTINON”—for he thus counts himself among the more exact theologians—“and which is commonly rejected by [Col. 0722D] Catholic doctors,” disputation 12 of the *Anti-Jansenists*, number 32.

But Dionysius Carthusian did not judge the matter in this way. In his commentary on chapter I of Genesis, article 5, he wrote: “Augustine devised a certain subtle interpretation by which he defends Scripture against such mockery and nevertheless preserves the truth of Scripture and faith.” Before him, Saint Thomas, after reporting Augustine’s explanation and that of the other Fathers, said: “The circumstances of the text permit both interpretations,” in the cited passage from book II of the *Sentences*.

Are Saint Thomas, Albert the Great, Saint Bonaventure, and Giles of Rome therefore [Col. 0723A] not to be counted among the more exact theologians? Are they to belong to the lowest rabble of theologians, while Suárez, Molina, and Martinon are senators? On the contrary, those former men are the noblest of all, before whom even Suárez and Molina should rise, while Martinon should not be mentioned on the same day as they.

Such was the judgment of the leading theologians concerning Saint Augustine’s interpretation, although others before Augustine had opened the way for it. Philo, the Plato of the Hebrews, not only rejected the common opinion concerning the work of the six days but even mocked it, saying in book I of the *Allegories*: “It is the mark of rustic simplicity to think that the world was created in six days, or at least within a definite period of time.”

Among the Greeks, Clement of Alexandria, in book VI of the *Stromata*, followed the same interpretation, which among the Latins our Augustine illuminated most fully. All the scholastic doctors also esteemed it so highly that they labored with great care to explain Augustine’s opinion concerning the morning and evening knowledge of things—namely, in the divine nature and in things themselves.

Thus the leading teachers of the schools dispute among themselves, and not lightly, concerning Augustine’s true meaning [Col. 0723B]: Albert the Great, Part I of the *Summa*, questions 12, articles 6 and 7; Saint Thomas, Part I, questions 58, articles 6 and 7; Bonaventure, book II, distinction 4, article 3, question 1; Scotus, book II, distinction 3, question 9; Giles, Part I of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 29; and others generally. The leaders of the Jesuit school followed them with praise in investigating the same mind of Augustine: Suárez, book I of *The Work of the Six Days*, chapter 10; and Vásquez, Part I, disputation 51, chapter 2.

I pass over here what our Portuguese theologians Cerda and Ludovicus ab Angelis bring forward from Cassiodorus, Isidore, Junilius, and others in commendation of Augustine’s interpretation. Father Macedo, in the second theological volume of his *Conferences on the Angels*, defends the holy Father’s interpretation with great learning, Conference 6, distinction 2, where he praises several more recent writers who embraced Augustine’s opinion.
