In the meantime, Augustine himself must certainly be read [Col. 0723C] in book XII of the *Confessions*, where, from chapter 14 through chapter 32, with which the book ends, he prepared a proper defense of himself and solidly refuted those who mocked his interpretations of Moses.

§ X. Saint Augustine did not err in asserting that original sin is the cause of reprobation

Attend, reader, for Adam attributes an utterly monstrous error to Augustine [Col. 0723D] when he writes in chapter 3, page 584, and chapter 6, page 614, that Augustine held original sin alone to be the cause of the reprobation of the damned. Later, in chapter 10, page 667, he attacks this same opinion of Augustine with the following censure:

“But if this doctor”—namely Augustine—“were to add that original sin is the sole cause of reprobation, and that it is by this that God is moved to separate the saved from the damned, I would not only be unwilling to face death in defense of this opinion, but I believe myself permitted to abhor it, because it is the mother of that opinion which Calvin presses against the Church with such impiety and fury.”

What error is the offspring of Augustine’s opinion he left unstated. It was enough for him to associate the assertion of the holy Doctor with Calvinism and thereby render it not merely suspect but hateful. I should like to ask Adam whether that Calvinist opinion which Calvin derives from Saint Augustine’s thesis that reprobation arises from original sin alone truly follows from it or only apparently does so.

If he says that it truly follows, he will make Augustine [Col. 0724A], a doctor of the Church, the teacher of a Calvinist error—which it is impious even to imagine. If, however, he maintains that it follows only apparently, he will see that Saint Augustine’s opinion is not only in reality not the mother of the Calvinist heresy, as he wrongly thinks, but not even akin to it, and that it can be very well reconciled with the refutation of Calvinist error.

Where, then, Adam, did you invent such a monster? Is it because the Calvinists think so? But if you follow their prejudices, you might as well abhor Augustine’s entire doctrine—or even the sacred books themselves—in summary fashion. For Calvinists, who foster every monstrous heresy, attempt by every artifice to wrap them all in scraps, as it were, of sacred Scripture and Augustine’s robe, lest they appear stripped of the patronage of antiquity.

Would that you had brought forward this saying of Calvin deduced from Augustine’s opinion! [Col. 0724B] We would have had no difficulty refuting it, since we know that darkness is not brought in but driven away by the presence of the sun. But since you cited no such dogma, your silence clearly indicated that it was not the offspring of Augustine’s opinion, but a fiction born from your own brain—if, indeed, you wrote those things while awake.

Come, then, let us see how far Saint Augustine’s opinion—that reprobation arises from original sin alone—stands from Calvin’s error. Saint Augustine held with certainty that reprobation necessarily presupposes at least original sin. Therefore, when discussing Paul’s words in Romans IX, 11, 13—“when they had not yet been born, nor had done anything good or evil,” and “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated”—in which the reprobation of Esau is designated, he taught that it presupposes original sin.

In letter 105 he says: “What did he hate in Esau [Col. 0724C] before he had done anything evil, except original sin?” And in book I to Simplicianus, question 2, he writes: “God therefore does not hate Esau as a man, but Esau as a sinner.” He proves in the same place that this sin was not made by God, who is the author only of good things, concluding: “For he hates in them the impiety which he himself does not make.”

Accordingly, he asserts that God could not be just if he reprobated human beings without any sin existing in them: “But how could he hate Esau except on account of the merit of injustice? It is unjust,” in the same place. And in letter 106 to Paulinus: “If this mass were so neutral that, just as it deserved no good, it also deserved no evil, it would not seem unjust without cause that vessels should be made from it for dishonor.”

He says the same in letter 157 [Col. 0724D] to Optatus: “It would rightly seem unjust that vessels of wrath should be made for destruction if the entire mass had not been condemned in Adam. That they are made vessels of wrath by being born from it belongs to the punishment that is due.”

For this reason, against the Pelagians he insists that God would be unjust if he condemned children dying without original sin, even if they had not been baptized, saying: “God is good; God is just. He can free some without good merits, because he is good; he cannot condemn anyone without merits, because he is just,” book III against Julian, chapter 18.

There are many [Col. 0725A] other testimonies of the holy Father, scattered throughout his writings, proving this same point. Thus Augustine’s fixed and constant opinion was that no one is reprobated by God before the foreknowledge of at least original sin.

Calvin, however, went in an entirely contrary direction, saying that by his decree God not only reprobates human beings before foreseeing their sin, but that human sins arise from the divine reprobation itself. He teaches this at length in book III of the *Institutes*, chapters 22 and 23. I shall offer several testimonies.

In chapter 23, section 4, he writes: “I freely confess that all the children of Adam have fallen by God’s will into the misery of the condition in which they are now bound; and this is what I said at the beginning, that one must always return at last to the sole determination of the divine will.”

And in section 7: “They explicitly deny [Col. 0725B] that it stands forth that it was decreed by God that Adam should perish by his defection.” Later he says: “I confess that this is a horrible decree, yet no one can deny that God foresaw what the end of man would be before he created him, and that he foresaw it because he had ordained it by his decree.”

Likewise, in section 1: “It is by no means fitting to transfer the preparation for destruction elsewhere than to the hidden counsel of God.” And in chapter 22, section 11: “If we cannot assign any reason why he deigns to show mercy to his own except that it pleases him to do so, then neither in reprobating others will we have anything other than his will.”

Moreover, in chapter 23, section 9: “The reprobate wish [Col. 0725C] to be regarded as excusable in sinning because they cannot escape the necessity of sinning, especially since this necessity is imposed upon them by God’s ordinance. We, however, deny that they are thereby rightly excused, since the equity of God’s ordinance—which they complain has destined them to destruction—is indeed unknown to us but most certain to him.”

He repeats this same position at greater length in his book *On the Eternal Predestination of God*, page 917 of the Geneva edition of 1552:

“But how it was established by God’s foreknowledge and decree what would happen to man, and yet God is not drawn into participation in the guilt, as though he were either the author or approver of transgression—since it is plainly a secret far above the insight of the human mind—so that one need not be ashamed to confess ignorance.”

Hence Zanchius says in book V of *The Nature of God*, chapter 2: “This was the first thing that God ordained concerning the reprobate from eternity: namely, the predestination of certain human beings to eternal destruction; and their sins were ordained for this purpose.”

Calvin’s opinion, then, is that God by his immutable decree drives human beings into sins; [Col. 0725D] hence God’s reprobation precedes the foreknowledge of sins, which, as they say, are effects of reprobation itself. But why should I say more, as though Calvin’s opinion were not known to everyone, when Adam himself openly admits it in chapter 14, page 725, writing that Calvin says “God withdraws the light and grace necessary for salvation from all those whose condemnation he decreed either before or after the foreknowledge of original sin”?

Now, if the opinions of Saint Augustine and Calvin are set in contradiction to one another, how could we depart farther from Calvin’s error—whatever error you imagine—than by approaching the opinion of the holy Doctor, which directly conflicts with Calvin’s error concerning the reprobation of the wicked before the foreknowledge of sin?

And yet, if heaven permits it, Adam dared [Col. 0726A] to publish Augustine’s opinion as not merely close to the Calvinist heresy but extremely close to it, even asserting that it was the mother of the heresy, although in fact it presses hard upon and suffocates the Calvinists. This Calvinist decree, compelling the reprobate into sins, is the mother of all the errors Calvin accumulated concerning predestination, grace, and free will. For by it human freedom is overthrown, a necessity of sinning is imposed, the fatal decree of the Stoics is introduced, God is proclaimed the author of crimes, and a thousand such monstrous errors are born. None of these follows from the opinion of the holy Father just mentioned.

[Col. 0726B] Saint Augustine’s opinion is therefore celebrated, as John of Saint Thomas says: original sin was the cause of the reprobation of all the damned. The holy Father often taught this—in letter 105 to Sixtus, letter 106 to Paulinus, letter 157 to Optatus, in the *Enchiridion*, chapters 98 and 99, and in book II to Boniface, chapter 7. Father Macedo indicates many other passages in thesis 20.

Augustine’s school followed him: Fulgentius, book I of *The Truth of Predestination and Grace*, immediately after the beginning; Prosper, in the seventh objection of the Gauls; the African Fathers exiled in Sardinia, in their synodal letter, chapter 6; and Saint Thomas, question 6 of *Truth*, article 2, response to objection 9.

Accordingly, in accordance with the mind of the Angelic Teacher, eminent Dominican theologians defend the same position: Thomas de Lemos, the most illustrious Godoy, and John Baptist Gonet, volume IV of the *Thomistic Shield*, disputation 5, article 3, who cites those earlier doctors from within his own order.

From the Society of Jesus, Suárez agrees with Augustine [Col. 0726C] in Part I, book V, *On Reprobation*, chapter 5; and Vásquez, disputation 95, chapter 4, number 17, and chapter 9, number 60. They differ among themselves, however, concerning the manner in which original sin is the cause of reprobation. The former says that original sin is the cause insofar as it exists in the first parent, through whom the denial of sufficient grace was merited for his descendants; the latter thinks that the demeritorious force belongs to original sin itself, insofar as it infects each individual.

Didacus Ruiz, the most learned of the more recent writers, explains and extensively defends the same position more successfully in disputation 14 on predestination, section 4 and following.

But, in order to repel Adam’s objection, I shall cite the decree by which the theologians of the Society were ordered by Claudius Aquaviva, prefect of the entire order, to defend Augustine’s opinion that reprobation arises from original sin.

As we said earlier, in chapter 3, section 7, a book entitled [Col. 0726D] *On the Plan of Studies of the Society* was printed at Rome in the year 1586 and presented to all as a rule both for learning and for teaching, following an annual disputation by six eminent doctors of the Society and a very lengthy examination.

There, in the section on the selection of opinions, rule 6, page 14, the following proposition 12 is proposed, selected, and determined to be taught throughout all the schools of the Society:

“On our part there was not only no reason or condition of predestination, but it must not even be said absolutely that it lies within our power to be predestined; nor will anyone be saved unless predestined.”

And proposition 13:

“The cause of reprobation, [Col. 0727A] by which the rest of humanity is permitted to fall away from its ultimate end, was original sin.”

There it is. Do you now see, Adam? Do you now understand what reverence your most learned ancient theologians had for Augustine’s opinion that reprobation derives primarily from original sin alone—an opinion which, in your singular piety, learning, and zeal, you nevertheless say you abhor as the mother of Calvinist error?

Many theologians have devised various ways of explaining and defending this doctrine of the holy Fathers. Dominicus Bañez, Part I, question 23, article 5, reports five explanations, none of which he approves. Gonet also lists five ways, in the cited section 6, leaving each of them at the level of probability.

I shall propose a solution to this most difficult mystery according to the teaching of Saint Augustine; for it is not easy to search out the secrets of the divine will: “For who has been his counselor?”

It is a certain dogma that, through the sin of the first parent, humanity became a mass of perdition, [Col. 0727B] so that, apart from the grace of the Redeemer, it could never rise again by its own powers. This was established long ago by Innocent I and by the African councils against the Pelagians.

All human beings therefore became in Adam by nature children of wrath, subject to the power of the devil, enemies of God, and unworthy of any grace; they became objects of divine hatred and vengeance. The supreme justice of God could have punished the human race, infected with original sin, with everlasting damnation by denying it any grace, even the least grace.

Augustine taught this very frequently. In the *Enchiridion*, chapter 99, he says:

“The whole human race was condemned by such a just divine judgment [Col. 0727C] in its apostate root that, even if no one were liberated from it, no one could rightly reproach God’s justice; and those who are liberated had to be liberated in such a way that, from the many who are not liberated and are most justly left in condemnation, it might be shown what the entire mass deserved, and to what the just judgment of God would lead even these, unless his undeserved mercy came to their aid.”

He says similar things in *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 10; *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 8, at the beginning; and *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 8.

He confirms this by the example of the wicked angels in chapter 27 of the *Enchiridion*: “And if he had wished there to be no restoration whatsoever of human beings to a better state, just as there is none of the wicked angels, this would not have happened unjustly.”

Humanity therefore became, in that mass of perdition, unworthy of the entire order of graces. Among these, the first are sanctifying grace, by which a person approaches God, and the grace of final perseverance, by which a person can no longer depart from God.

Through original sin, then, human beings fell into deprivation of sanctifying grace [Col. 0727D] and deprivation of the power immediately fitted for persevering in sanctifying grace once received. Since these privations concern different forms, they are also distinct from one another, and God can grant one without the other. This is certain from the case of the faithful who are damned: God gave them sanctifying grace, yet denied them the grace of final perseverance.

Hence the Council of Trent, session 6, canon 22, taught [Col. 0728A] that perseverance comes from a special assistance of God; so too had the Second Council of Orange, canon 10, under the guidance of Saint Augustine, who most solidly defended Catholic truth against the Semi-Pelagians in his entire volume entitled *On the Gift of Perseverance*.

The difference between the two privations is this: deprivation of sanctifying grace is either the formal essence of sin itself or necessarily connected with sin. The other deprivation—namely, deprivation of the power immediately fitted for persevering—can coexist with sanctifying grace. The saints pray that God grant them perseverance; therefore they do not possess it, as Augustine proves throughout chapter 23. Otherwise it would not be a special benefit of God distinct from the grace of justification. Thus sanctifying grace does not remove the privation of the power immediately fitted for persevering.

This privation is a punishment for the first sin, [Col. 0728B] just as is the privation of the subjection of concupiscence to reason. Although in baptism “there is no condemnation for those who have truly been buried with Christ through baptism into death,” as Trent says in its decree on original sin—and as Augustine had earlier said in book I to Boniface, chapter 10: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus”—this is not understood as referring to punishments, as the theologians put it, but to guilt, none of which remains after baptism. Those punishments, however, remain even after baptism.

That this privation remains as a punishment for the first sin is so well known in Saint Augustine’s teaching that even the Semi-Pelagians used to assume it from Augustine and argue against him on that basis. For when they wished to prove that Adam had fallen without fault because he had not received the gift of perseverance, they sought to block Augustine’s customary and familiar response and pressed him in these terms, as Hilary reports in his letter to Augustine:

“For it cannot be said that he did not receive it because he was not separated by the generosity of grace from the mass of perdition; for that mass of perdition did not yet exist in the human race before he sinned, from which the corrupted origin was derived.”

They therefore assume, according to the mind of the holy Doctor, [Col. 0728C] that deprivation of the power immediately fitted for persevering is a punishment of the mass infected with original sin. To answer this argument, the holy Doctor composed those three golden chapters of *On Rebuke and Grace*, namely chapters 10, 11, and 12.

In chapter 11 he openly concedes that the assistance for persevering is lacking as a punishment for sin, although it could not have been lacking to the angels or to Adam:

“But if this assistance had been lacking to either an angel or a human being [Col. 0728D] when they were first made—since such a nature had not been made that it could remain, if it wished, without divine assistance—they would not have fallen through their own fault; for the assistance without which they could not remain would have been lacking. But now, for those to whom such assistance is lacking, it is already a punishment for sin; while to those to whom it is given, it is given according to grace.”

Augustine cannot mean anything other than that the gift of perseverance is denied as a punishment for original sin. [Col. 0729A] For the baptized person, when he first commits a mortal sin, lacks the gift of perseverance in the good once received; therefore it was denied by God as a punishment for original sin.

He teaches the same thing at length in chapter 8 of *On the Gift of Perseverance*. When asked why God did not give certain people, who had worshiped him in good faith, the ability to persevere to the end, he replies that perseverance is not owed to nature but is a grace that can be denied. Why it is denied, he explains at the beginning of the chapter:

“For from one origin all were judged to go into condemnation—not an unjust condemnation, but a just one. Therefore, let the one who is liberated love grace; let the one who is not liberated acknowledge what is owed.”

He calls perseverance so great a benefit in *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 8, at the end. He expressly proves in chapters 8 and 9 of that work, and again in chapters 8 and 9 of *On the Gift of Perseverance*, that by this alone the elect are distinguished from the mass of perdition.

Hence he says in chapter 7 of *On Rebuke and Grace*:

“But by this fact, both those who have not heard the Gospel and those who, after hearing it and being changed for the better, have not received perseverance, etc., have not been separated from that mass which is clearly condemned, since all go from one origin into condemnation.”

Immediately afterward he says: [Col. 0729B]

“We must understand that no one can be separated from that mass of perdition which came into being through the first Adam, except that whoever possesses this gift possesses what he received from the grace of the Savior.”

According to Augustine, then, through Adam’s sin we fell into deprivation of the gift of perseverance, which is given gratuitously and only to the predestined by the Savior.

The deprivation of this great benefit is a cause leading to damnation, [Col. 0729C] for whoever lacks the gift of perseverance will be damned. Hence it plainly follows that original sin is the cause of reprobation.

I conclude in one sentence: the lack of the gift of perseverance is the cause of damnation; but original sin is the cause of the lack of the gift of perseverance; therefore original sin is the cause of damnation.

The minor premise is Augustine’s, and it has also been proved above, because through original sin human beings are unworthy of the entire order of graces. Even if a person has been baptized, he still has the deprivation of the gift of perseverance, which is a special benefit of God.

The major premise, however, must not be understood as though this lack were the per se cause of damnation, but only as a cause that does not remove an obstacle. For a justified person, if he is assailed by a grave temptation and remains under the deprivation of the power immediately fitted for persevering, will infallibly succumb unless God grants him, through a special assistance, the power to persevere. Since that assistance is not owed to a human being on account of original sin, God can justly deny it. See what I said above, chapter 3, section 6.

This view of reprobation arising from original sin is also deduced from the synodical letter of the African Fathers exiled in Sardinia, where, in chapter 6, they say:

“You have therefore said that, although Esau and Jacob had not yet been born, Jacob was chosen through gratuitous mercy, while Esau, held under original sin, was hated by God’s just judgment. They, on the contrary, say that Esau represents the Jewish people, to be condemned on account of future evil works, whereas Jacob represents the Gentile people, to be saved on account of future good works. It is good that you join these two propositions, each of which you put forward, in Catholic agreement.”

Thus, according to these very Fathers, it is Catholic to say that Esau, held under original sin, was hated by God’s just judgment. But in chapter 7 they write:

“In Esau, however, he displayed the judgment of just severity. Although Esau had received the sacrament of circumcision on the eighth day, according to the tenor of the divine ordinance, and had thereby been freed from the guilt of original sin, he nevertheless remained, through the wickedness of his heart, in the ancient condition of the earthly man, abandoned there by the judgment of him who freely saves and justly condemns.”

But Esau was not held under original sin with respect to guilt; therefore he was held under something caused by original sin. For he was abandoned to God’s judgment, which is to lack the gift of perseverance. For, as I argued above, the permission of actual first sin results from God’s just judgment in denying the gift of perseverance in the good of justice received through baptism. But, according to Augustine, that gift is denied as punishment for a sin that is not actual—for I am speaking of the first actual sin. Therefore it is denied as punishment for original sin. Saint Gregory the pope proceeds in the same way in his commentary on Psalm 101, at the verse, “For I ate ashes like bread,” where he says:

“And since, according to the Apostle’s judgment, it is ‘not of him that wills, nor of him that runs, but of God who shows mercy,’ he mercifully raises up some who had fallen, while he justly permits others who seemed to be standing to fall. For from the sin of our first parent we received the condition that we cannot remain stable even in that very justice.”

This is the same as what I was saying: we have undergone the loss of the power immediately equipped for perseverance, which is not removed except through God’s special assistance. Read Saint Prosper, *Response to the Seven Chapters of the Gauls*.

Therefore the principal punishments left by original sin are concupiscence and the deprivation of the power immediately equipped for perseverance. That concupiscence was left behind for the struggle is a dogma of faith, according to the Council of Trent’s decree on Original Sin. On this subject Augustine writes elegantly in Book II *Against Julian*, chapter 4:

“Against it the regenerate person, if he is already using reason, struggles as in an arena, with that one watching over him and assisting him; for virtue is perfected in weakness, while that in us which falls short of justice is opposed by that in us which advances toward justice, so that, when progress conquers, the whole person may rise toward better things, and, when deficiency conquers, the whole person may decline toward worse.”

This penal struggle was left to us by God’s judgment so that, recognizing his own weakness, a person might suppress that pride by which he once arrogantly rebelled against the Lord in paradise, and might humbly implore divine assistance. Hear Augustine in Book IV *Against Julian*, chapter 2:

“But because, in this human misery, pride—the worse enemy—must be guarded against, that concupiscence is not entirely extinguished in the flesh of continent saints, so that, when they struggle against it, the mind may be warned of its dangers and not become presumptuously puffed up, until human frailty reaches such perfection of health that no corruption of wantonness and no swelling of pride need be feared.”

The same must likewise be said of the deprivation of this power immediately equipped for perseverance: it was left to us for the struggle and for the crushing of human pride. Thus concupiscence and this deprivation, like confederate enemies, lie in wait for a person and assist one another. For from concupiscence, which inclines toward sin, there is fostered the inability and weakness [Col. 0731A] to stand firm in the good intention of justice.

The author of Book II *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 28, teaches this elegantly:

“But among other human beings, so long as the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, and so long as the spirit is indeed ready but the flesh is weak, an unchangeable strength of mind cannot be found, because truly perfect and secure happiness belongs not to this life but to the other. In the uncertainty of the present struggle, where the whole of life is temptation and not even victory itself is safe from ambushing pride, one is not free from the danger of change. And although divine protection grants countless saints of his the power to persevere to the end, it nevertheless removes from none of them that which resists them from within themselves, so that in all their pursuits and efforts their unwillingness and willingness may always contend with one another.”

The holy Father had taught this same thing in his book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 8. Answering someone who asked why God denies the gift of perseverance to a believer, he says:

“God, however, judged it better to mingle with the certain number of his saints some who would not persevere, so that those for whom security in the temptation of this life is not beneficial might not be secure. For he restrains many from a destructive exaltation by what the Apostle says: ‘Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall’ (1 Cor. 10:12). He who falls falls by his own will, and he who stands stands by God’s will,” and so forth.

Hence whatever objections are usually raised against this deprivation are to be resolved in precisely the same way as those which the Pelagians formerly brought against Augustine concerning the penal character of concupiscence.

[Col. 0731C] A difficulty must be addressed here; its treatment will greatly illuminate the explanation of the Augustinian position. “The absence of the gift of perseverance,” they say, “was present in Adam. For Augustine says in *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 11, that if Adam had possessed the gift of perseverance, he would have persevered. Therefore the deprivation of the gift of perseverance is not a punishment for sin, since it was present in a human being before sin.”

The Semi-Pelagians formerly raised this objection against Augustine in the same work, chapter 10, where they say of Adam:

“Therefore he did not have perseverance in that good; and if he did not have it, he certainly did not receive it. For how could he both have received perseverance and not have persevered? Moreover, if he did not have it because he did not receive it, how did he sin by not persevering, when he had not received perseverance? For it cannot be said that he did not receive it because he had not been separated by the generosity of grace from the mass of perdition; for that mass of perdition did not yet exist in the human race before he sinned, from which the corrupted origin was derived.”

No argument has ever been resolved by Augustine with greater subtlety or labor than this one. He seems to have devoted all the powers of his great intellect to dissolving it. Indeed, he devoted three chapters of *On Rebuke and Grace* to a complete response. The substance of his answer is that Adam possessed God’s assistance, through which he could immediately and readily persevere, but in such a way that actual perseverance was placed in the free use of that assistance, a use proceeding from Adam’s own will, which the assistance helped as a kind of habit.

To explain this, he wrote those two chapters, 11 and 12. I shall give one or two passages rather than transfer the whole work here:

“Therefore, so that the first man might not receive this gift of God—that is, perseverance in the good—but might be left to his own choice whether to persevere or not, his will possessed such powers, since it had been established without any sin and nothing in it resisted from itself in the manner of concupiscence, that the choice of persevering could rightly be entrusted to such great goodness and such facility in living well”; chapter 12.

And in chapter 11 he writes:

“Then God had given man a good will, for he had made him upright, in whom he had made him. He had also given him assistance, without which he could not remain in that good if he wished; but whether he would wish it, he left to his free choice.”

Thus Adam did not need the gift of actual perseverance, because he possessed assistance through which, as a habit, he had within him the power immediately equipped for perseverance. Hence Augustine says at the end of chapter 12:

“Although the will of the first man, strong and sound in the greater good, did not persevere, though it possessed the power of free choice and though God’s assistance would not have been lacking, without which he could not have persevered if he had wished, that assistance was nevertheless not of such a kind that God would work in him to make him will. For God left him very strong and permitted him to do what he wished.”

Therefore, nothing was lacking on God’s part for Adam to be able to persevere; what was lacking was his own will. For if he had wished, he would have persevered with the greatest ease.

Augustine adds that if God had denied this assistance, Adam and the angels likewise would have fallen without their own fault, assigning this reason:

“For the assistance would have been lacking, without which they could not remain. But now, for those to whom such assistance is lacking, it is already the punishment of sin; while to those to whom it is given, it is given according to grace, not according to debt.”

Therefore the gift that supplied the power immediately equipped for perseverance was given to Adam in such a way that the absence of actual perseverance could not have been imputed to him as guilt if he had lacked that assistance. Nevertheless, through sin he deprived both himself and us of this assistance, which constitutes the power immediately equipped for perseverance. Therefore the deprivation of this power is in us a punishment for the first sin, since it is given according to grace and not according to debt.

Through Adam’s sin, however, such an inability to persevere immediately and readily was contracted that, even if the very same assistance that had been given to Adam for perseverance were granted to us in the state of fallen nature, it would not suffice to remove that inability to persevere. Saint Augustine teaches this near the end of chapter 12, where he says:

“If, in the great weakness of this life—a weakness in which virtue nevertheless had to be perfected in order to restrain pride—their own will were left to them, so that they might remain, if they wished, in God’s assistance, without which they could not persevere, and God did not work in them to make them will, then amid so many and such great temptations their will, through its weakness, would itself succumb. Therefore they could not persevere, because, weakened by frailty, they would not will, or through the weakness of their will would not will in such a way that they could.”

From this the solution to the proposed argument is clear. Its antecedent must be denied if it is understood as referring to the deprivation of the power immediately equipped for perseverance. Adam did not suffer this deprivation, since he possessed assistance fully sufficient for perseverance; only his willing was lacking. But he inflicted upon himself and upon the entire human race that followed him the deprivation of such power, through which so many crimes are committed. I explained this doctrine more fully above, chapter 3. Gregory of Rimini likewise teaches the same from Augustine in Book II, distinction 26, questions 1 and 2.

Many object that, although they concede original sin to be a sufficient motive for reprobation in those from whom it has not been remitted, they believe that this cannot in any way be said of the baptized. For remitted sin cannot be the cause of a person’s damnation: it would not have been remitted if the person were punished with everlasting death because of it. But original sin is remitted to the baptized, and no one is subject to punishment because of it; nor can the will to remit sin be reconciled with the will to condemn and punish it eternally.

Certainly the Council of Trent, in its decree on Original Sin, declares that there is nothing condemnable in the baptized. But there would be much that was condemnable if anything deserving eternal punishment remained in them.

The Semi-Pelagians likewise brought this objection against Saint Augustine. When he asserted that original sin was the reason why human beings in general had been reprobated—those whom divine predestination had not made its own—they inferred from Augustine’s position the absurdity that the grace of baptism does not remove original sin from those who are not predestined to life. This was the second objection of the Gauls, by which, according to Prosper, they mocked the doctrine of the holy Father.

I reply that original sin inflicted punishments proper to nature itself, and that these are not remitted through baptism. The principal ones are concupiscence and the deprivation of the power immediately equipped for perseverance in the justice received. Thus nothing condemnable remains in the baptized insofar as condemnation signifies guilt, though not insofar as it signifies punishment. For in the same place the holy synod teaches that concupiscence remains, which is from sin and inclines toward sin.

It is in no way conceded that a baptized person is condemned formally because of original sin, or that he is reprobated on account of it as his proximate cause. Rather, we say that original sin is radically the cause of the reprobation of the faithful who are damned, insofar as from it arose the deprivation of the power immediately equipped for perseverance. Without the special assistance of God, under this deprivation a person does not attain salvation but falls into sins, on account of which God condemns him proximately and formally.

Nor do we deny that God reprobates someone on account of actual sins. Nor do we say that God first reprobates a person because of original sin and then also because of actual sins, as John of Saint Thomas objects in *On Reprobation*, disputation 10, article 2, number 30. Rather, we assert that God immediately condemns a person to eternal punishment on account of the actual sins into which he falls because of his inability to persevere—that is, because of the deprivation of the power immediately equipped for perseverance. This deprivation is a punishment left to human nature for the struggle on account of Adam’s sin.

In baptism, however, the guilt and the punishment due to the person who sinned are remitted, but not the punishment inflicted upon nature itself because of the first sin. The example of concupiscence makes this clear. Therefore Saint Augustine concedes that people are condemned on account of actual sins in chapter 13 of *On Rebuke and Grace*, at the end, where, speaking of the reprobate, he says:

“For either they lie under the sin that they originally brought with them from their generation, and they depart from this life with that hereditary debt, which was not remitted through regeneration; or through free choice they have added other sins besides, some more, others less, but all evil, and on account of this difference they are to be judged with different punishments; or they receive God’s grace, but are temporary and do not persevere; they abandon it, and are abandoned. For they were handed over to free choice, without receiving the gift of perseverance, by God’s just and hidden judgment.”

Read chapter 93 of the *Enchiridion*. From these passages I conclude that the measure of punishment depends upon the actual sins into which a person falls because he abandons God. He abandons God because he has been handed over to free choice without receiving the gift of perseverance, by God’s just judgment—that is, as punishment for original sin.

Nevertheless, although a baptized person has this deprivation of the gift of perseverance and is not worthy to possess it, since it is not given according to debt, he should not be called unworthy of it in the sense that he has a debt not to possess it, as sinners do. Rather, he simply lacks the debt of possessing it. Adam had that debt. Therefore the absence of this power immediately equipped for perseverance cannot be called mere negation, but is a true deprivation, because it is the absence of a gift otherwise owed to nature insofar as nature has been elevated to a supernatural end.

So much may be said to explain the position of Saint Augustine. The same position is explained and defended at greater length by the most learned theologians Ruiz and Gonet, whom I have cited. Hence I do not know what sudden panic struck Adamus, causing him to recoil from that position and accuse it of being the mother of Calvinist heresy.

On closer consideration, I believe that he understood a sufficiently familiar error: namely, that in the baptized the sin of origin truly remains. For if, after baptism, a believer can still be reprobated on account of original sin, then it has not been erased and remitted, since something remains in the regenerate on account of which they are eternally condemned.

But this was the old slander by which the Semi-Pelagians, as we showed from Prosper, attacked the Augustinian position. We have shown that the position is entirely free from it.

The holy Doctor is also very far from the Calvinists’ position. They think that concupiscence itself is formally original sin. Since it remains after baptism, they say that sin has not been erased but merely covered and not imputed. The holy Doctor, however, does not place the essence of original sin in concupiscence itself, but in the guilt and stain, which are wholly erased in baptism.

Thus, speaking of concupiscence in Book II *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 28, he says:

“It does not remain in the members of those who have been reborn from water and the Spirit as though forgiveness had not been granted for it; rather, there forgiveness of sins is entirely full and perfect, with all the enmities by which we were separated from God destroyed.”

Read Bellarmine, volume IV, Book V, *On the Loss of Grace*, chapter 8, where he proves this learnedly from Augustine. Father Macedo explains the same matter better and more fully in Book IV *On the Keys of Peter*, chapters 5 and 7.

There is therefore no reason for Adamus to accuse the celebrated position of the holy Father of Calvinism, since Calvin, in this matter, departed farther from Augustine than anyone else. But let us pass on to other matters, and leave the reasons for his procedure to our opponent.

§ XI. Whether Augustine Was Mistaken in Teaching That It Is Not Permitted to Kill an Assailant Who Threatens One’s Life

We now examine the final error that they attribute to the holy Father. They say that he taught that it is not lawful to kill an assailant who wishes to take one’s life. This is Adamus’s accusation against Augustine in chapter 3, page 585.

Augustine discusses in Book I *On Free Choice of the Will*, chapter 5, whether it is possible to kill without guilt an enemy who attacks, or a murderous ambusher, whether for the sake of one’s life, liberty, or chastity. After saying that Roman law permits assailants to be killed with impunity while they are attempting to take another’s life with a drawn sword, he says:

“I do not criticize the law that permits such men to be killed, but I cannot find how to defend those who kill them.”

From these words of Augustine, the most serious writers have gone in various directions. Many thought that Augustine denied that it was lawful to kill an aggressor even with the moderation of blameless self-defense. Some of them, moved by the authority of so great a Doctor, subscribed to the same view or at least considered it probable.

Augustine Triumphus of Ancona, an eminent Augustinian theologian, sets out and proves this conclusion in his book *On Ecclesiastical Power*, question 52, article 3:

“I think that it is a fault to kill a person so that one may not oneself be killed, however unavoidable the necessity under which this occurs. In support of this,” he adds, “there is Augustine’s authority in several places; first in *On Free Choice of the Will*, where he says,” and so forth.

Tostatus, that prodigy of intellect, after reporting Triumphus’s position and the opposing, more common view in his commentary on Matthew 5:9, page 109, says:

“Each of these positions appears in some way reasonable, especially since the second seems in some measure to be Augustine’s intention.”

Vazquez, in chapter 2 *On Restitution*, doubt 6, number 18, asserts that Augustine followed this position, which, he says, some canonists embrace. Molina, in the cited disputation 3, number 3, says: “There is strong suspicion that Augustine held this position.” Gerson is reported in favor of the same view in his treatise *On the Eucharist*. Certainly, in Part II of the *Compendium of Theology*, in his exposition of the fifth commandment, he says:

“Some say that it is never lawful to kill, even in self-defense, especially for a perfect man; and this seems to be Anselm’s opinion.”

There he also reports the contrary opinion, but rejects neither. Accursius and the Gloss likewise follow it in *Lex Vim vi*, in the *Digest* title *On Justice and Law*. Richard of Saint-Victor and Almain are also cited by our Salonius.

Augustine therefore was not alone in holding this position; he had both theologians and jurists as followers, among whom the authority of Augustine alone carried more weight than the common opinion of others.

Before explaining the holy Doctor’s position, however, I note that some writers did not need to search with such care for testimonies from both bodies of law by which the killing of an aggressor with the moderation of blameless self-defense is permitted. The holy Doctor answered them long ago in the cited chapter 5 with a single statement:

“I see clearly enough that the law is well defended against an accusation of this kind. In the people whom it governs, it granted permission for lesser crimes so that greater ones would not be committed. For it is much milder that one who lies in wait for another’s life should be killed than that one who defends his own should be killed.”

There he asks whether people whom civil laws permit to kill an aggressor are nevertheless bound by some more powerful and most secret law not to kill such persons.

Saint Thomas, in the *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, question 64, article 7, unwilling to depart either from Saint Augustine’s position or from the common opinion, distinguishes two ways in which someone defending himself can kill an aggressor.

A person may intend only to defend himself, even though the death of the aggressor follows accidentally from this; or he may intend the killing of the aggressor either as a means or as an end, as Cajetan explains there.

This can be clarified by a suitable example. A physician orders a sick person’s vein to be cut so that the patient may be cured by the discharge of blood, even though he knows that the patient will faint from the bloodletting—something he would not want if the patient could be cured by another means. In this case the physician wills the patient’s health as the end and the discharge of blood as the means; he does not in any way intend the fainting, except as something that follows accidentally and beyond his intention, to which he consents only materially.

In this second manner, therefore, the person under attack may kill the aggressor, but he may in no way intend the death of the attacking assailant, either as a means or as an end.

Salonius rightly shows at the end of article 7 that this is the mind of the holy Doctor, and Tostatus, already cited, explains it in the same way. Thus Saint Thomas writes in his response to the first objection that Augustine must be understood as speaking of the intention to kill the aggressor, but not of the case in which one directly intends to preserve one’s own life. Such an act, he says, does not have the character of an illicit act, since it is natural to everyone to preserve himself in being as far as he can.

I omit the fact that this position can scarcely be put into practice. For who, when anger rises and the mind is suddenly aroused to defend itself, can possess that intention? Salonius, Molina, and others have noted this.

Certainly that explanation does not accord with Augustine’s mind. Molina nevertheless says in volume IV, disputation 3, number 3:

“Perhaps Augustine’s testimonies moved Saint Thomas to assert that the person under attack cannot intend the death of the aggressor. For Augustine proves that the killing of the aggressor is evil on the ground that it arises from the desire to preserve life, which ought not to be loved but despised.”

Augustine says:

“How, in the presence of that divine providence, are those persons free from sin who have polluted themselves with human slaughter for the sake of things that ought to be despised?”

And earlier:

“For it does not compel them to kill, but leaves it in their power. It is therefore free for them to kill no one for the sake of things which they can lose against their will and which, for that reason, they ought not to love.”

Saint Thomas, however, wishes each person to love his own life, by the instinct of nature, as much as he can. From this love follows the defense by which it is preserved, even with the death of the person lying in wait.

Augustine, on the other hand, places life among the things that ought to be despised. He does so by using the dilemma concerning the life of the soul when the body is destroyed: if life can be taken away, it is to be despised; if it cannot, there is nothing to fear.

The Angelic Doctor thinks that this intention is infected with evil when it arises from anger against the enemy. Augustine, however, thought that the killing was corrupted by excessive concupiscence and immoderate self-love.

[Col. 0737B] But we must now see how Augustine arrived at this position. In investigating the origin of evil against the Manichaeans, he had determined that it arose from lust or perverse desire. He says that all wrongdoing is evil for no other reason than that it is done through lust, that is, through reprehensible desire. In chapter 4 he then asks in chapter 5 whether an attacking enemy or a murderous ambusher can be killed without any lust, whether for the sake of life, liberty, or chastity.

He replies that those who kill attackers are not free from this perverse desire:

“How can I regard as free from lust those who fight for things which they can lose against their will?” and so forth.

He immediately objects to himself that Roman laws permit an aggressor to be killed with impunity, whereas what is permitted by law cannot in any way be a sin.

He replies that such persons are indeed not held guilty under the temporal law of rulers, but are held by some more powerful and most secret law:

“For how, in the presence of that law, are those persons free from sin who have polluted themselves with human slaughter for the sake of things that ought to be despised?”

Once these points were established, the whole difficulty was to explain why, under the civil laws, the killer of an aggressor was not guilty of homicide, but was guilty under the eternal and immutable law.

To prove this, the holy Doctor devoted the remainder of that book. Its substance is that the eternal law wills all things to be ordered in the highest degree, chapter 6. It follows that a human being must be perfectly ordered within himself, chapter 7.

Human beings have many impulses in common with beasts: to seek bodily pleasures and to avoid pains is the action of every animal life, chapter 8.

“When reason rules these movements of the soul, a person is to be called ordered. For there is no right order, nor can it be called order at all, where inferior things are subjected to superior things. Therefore, when reason, or mind, or spirit governs the irrational movements of the soul, that governs in a human being which, by the law we have discovered to be eternal, is owed dominion. When a human being is constituted and ordered in this way, does he not seem wise to you?” chapter 8.

“For I call those wise whom truth commands to be called wise—that is, those in whom the kingdom of the mind has subjected every lust of sin,” chapter 9.

“Do you think that lust is more powerful than that mind to which we recognize that eternal law has granted dominion over lust? I certainly do not think so. For it would not be perfectly ordered if weaker things ruled stronger things. Therefore I consider it necessary that the mind should be more powerful than desire, precisely because it rightly and justly rules over desire,” chapter 10.

From these premises Augustine draws his conclusion. When someone kills an aggressor, he is ruled not by reason but by desire:

“How can I regard as free from lust those who fight for things which they can lose against their will? Or, if they cannot lose them, what need is there to go so far as the killing of a human being for their sake?”

For the act of killing is governed not by reason but by desire, since reason teaches that life is not the true good of human beings, because they can lose it against their will.

The claim that self-preservation and the defense of one’s own good are implanted in us by nature does not help. Bodily life is not a human being’s proper good, but the lowest part of the human being, chapter 16.

Wild animals rightly preserve their lives by natural instinct, even by killing an aggressor, because life is their one and highest good. They do this out of a desire to preserve themselves, so as not to lose their existence.

But if a human being kills an attacker in self-defense, he is moved by the same desire that impels beasts in such circumstances. He considers bodily life so great a good that he thinks it necessary to proceed as far as killing a human being in order to preserve it, chapter 5.

For it is characteristic of beasts to seek bodily pleasures and avoid pains, chapter 8. Therefore, at that moment, desire moves human beings to kill, and they are no better than beasts. Nor does reason then govern the irrational movements of the soul, in the same place. Therefore the human being does not act in an orderly way and, consequently, acts against the eternal law, which, as Augustine had already stated, wills all things to be perfectly ordered.

You may object: “Then will we be unable to love bodily life without fault?”

The holy Doctor replies in chapter 15 that we may love life and the other goods of the body by using them, not by enjoying them. He explains this excellently as follows:

“Since, therefore, one person uses the same things badly and another well, the one who uses them badly clings to and becomes entangled in them through love, being subjected to things that ought to have been subjected to him, and establishing as his goods things which he himself ought to be good in ordering and managing well. But the person who uses them rightly shows that they are good, but not good for him. For they do not make him good or better; rather, they are made such by him. Therefore he should not be glued to them by love, nor make them, as it were, members of his soul—which happens through loving them—lest, when they begin to be cut away, they defile him with torment and corruption. Rather, he should rise entirely above them and be ready to possess and govern them when necessary, and even more ready to lose them or not possess them.”

Therefore, the person who kills an aggressor does not rise entirely above him, nor govern the good of bodily life. Rather, he clings to it through love and makes it a member of his soul, grieving with torment when it is cut away from him. He is not more ready not to possess it, but struggles with all his strength to have it, thinking that it is his good, for the preservation of which he fights.

Yet bodily life contributes nothing to blessed life. For to live blessedly is to rejoice in true and certain goods, chapter 13. Bodily life is not numbered among these goods, since it is continually disturbed by so many different emotions, which the holy Doctor gathers together learnedly in chapter 11.

Finally, in chapter 15, after a lengthy discussion, Augustine assigns the difference explaining why the civil law of rulers permits the aggressor against one’s life, honor, or possessions to be killed, while the eternal law forbids it in another respect.

The civil law of the temporal commonwealth “commands nothing other than that these things, which may be called ours for a time, should, when people cling to them through desire, be possessed under that law by which human peace and society are preserved, insofar as such peace can be preserved in these matters.”

Later he says:

“Therefore it bends and redirects the wretched minds of human beings toward what it wills, since it has been adapted to govern them. For while they fear losing these things, they observe in their use a certain measure suited to the bond of citizenship, such as can be established among people of this kind. But it does not avenge sin when these things are loved; it avenges sin when they are wickedly taken from others.”

But in order that we may attain the final end, the eternal law forbids loving those things that are not means toward attaining it, namely things that people “can fail to obtain even when they wish to, and can lose against their will,” chapter 15.

“Therefore the eternal law commands us to turn love away from temporal things and, once purified, direct it toward eternal things,” in the same place.

What a doctrine worthy of Augustine! The civil law of rulers does not avenge sin when bodily life is loved, but when it is wickedly taken from others; and it pays little attention to that harmful desire, since it establishes no rule concerning inward matters. But the eternal law condemns this desire when it dominates a person and governs reason—when someone judges bodily life to be such a great good that he proceeds as far as killing a human being in order to defend it, although bodily life is in no way his true good.

For bodily life does not make him better; that belongs exclusively to the goods of the soul, which no one can lose against his will, and which a person possesses if he wishes. Augustine treats this matter at length from chapter 12 onward.

Who does not see by what right Augustine called the distinction drawn between the two laws “a distinction aiming at certain sublime things,” as he says at the end of chapter 5?

Moved by this argument, the holy Father adopted the position in which, when presenting and confirming it, he did not employ a single testimony from Sacred Scripture; rather, since his dispute was with the Manichaeans, he philosophized by relying solely on reason. Yet these ideas ought not to seem novel to anyone, for the Stoics and many other ancient philosophers [Col. 0739D] pursued this line of argument with the highest praise. In order to persuade people of that celebrated doctrine of *apatheia*, and to place every human good in the citadel of the mind, they argued at length that nothing outside virtue should be counted among goods.

Seneca proved this in his splendid work entitled *That Injury Cannot Befall the Wise Man*. Philo pursued the same aim in his little work entitled *That Every Good Man Is Free*. Lactantius likewise established it in the third book of the *Institutes*; but among the other Fathers, John Chrysostom treated it more subtly and elegantly in the homily to which he gave this title: *No One Is Harmed Except by Himself*. Others later illustrated the same position in extensive commentaries.

Accordingly, our Augustine, in that first book *On Free Choice of the Will*, himself acting as a philosopher, raised the human mind above all bodily things toward knowledge of its true good, and vindicated reason’s own dominion after subduing the movements of depraved desire [Col. 0740A]. He certainly taught that all such temporal goods ought to be regarded as nothing—goods which wretched mortals pursue with a thousand wishes, even to the point of madness—for they do not clear a path toward the attainment of the supreme good but obstruct it. If this is true, he said that the desire of the person who draws his sword to defend a bubble (for so the wise called the bodily life of man), and thereby stains himself with human blood, ought to be blamed.

Augustine of Ancona, who expressly defended this position of the holy Doctor, confirmed it by another and wholly different argument, namely, because “I am more bound to love the soul of my neighbor than my own body, which I can lose against my will.” It is clear, however, that the soul of one’s neighbor is lost from the moment he is killed by me in an act of unjust aggression. Cardinal Lugo yields to this argument in volume I of *On Justice and Law*, disputation 10, section 6, no. 143, if it is restricted to a drunken man who is attacking and to someone defending himself who probably believes that he is in a state of grace; Tostatus discusses this matter at greater length. Our task, however, is only to explain Augustine’s position, which rests on philosophical reason.

Moreover, although Augustine, in accordance with the principles of subtler philosophy, denied that it is lawful to kill an aggressor, did he perhaps think that such a killing was also contrary to the law of God? Would it follow that a man attacked by a robber, when there is no other way for him to escape, must be judged guilty of homicide if he kills the aggressor? That is so certainly contrary to the common opinion of theologians that Salon, in the cited conclusion 2, says: “The contrary opinion is perhaps rash, since it conflicts with so many texts and with the common judgment of nearly all the doctors.”

I judge, however, that Augustine later taught the opposite position on the basis of Sacred Scripture, since, when writing the first book *On Free Choice of the Will*, he attests that he was not yet well versed in Scripture. God gave the Hebrews this law in Exodus 22: “If a thief breaking into a house, or digging through it, is found, and, having been struck, dies, the one who struck him shall not be liable for bloodshed. But if he did this after sunrise, he has committed homicide, and he himself shall die.” From this it is plainly inferred that killing an aggressor is not contrary to the law of God, since God himself permitted it and denied that the killer was guilty of homicide.

But the holy Doctor, volume IV, question 84 on Exodus, assigns a distinction explaining why a thief may be killed at night without homicide, but not during the day. He says as follows (see the *Letter to Macedonius*):

“It is therefore understood that it does not pertain to homicide if a thief is killed at night; but if he is killed during the day, it does pertain to homicide, and so forth. For it could be discerned that he had come to steal, not to kill, and therefore ought not to be killed. This is also found in the ancient secular laws (*Digest*, *On the Aquilian Law*, law 4), although that law is older than these provisions: a nocturnal thief may be killed in any manner, but a thief by day may be killed if he defends himself with a weapon, for by then he is more than a thief.”

Therefore, if it is doubtful whether a thief intends to kill me, I may, according to the divine law and Augustine’s interpretation, kill him without the sin of homicide. With even stronger justification, then, I may lawfully kill that same man if he threatens me with certain death while brandishing a sword. For it is not permissible to say that God permitted a sin and, as though by promulgating a law, did not condemn it. Although that law was given to establish the civil commonwealth of the Hebrews, it nevertheless made clear that the divine will permitted homicide, just as worldly legislators have permitted it. And just as one who kills an aggressor does not act contrary to the will of the civil legislator, so he must not be said to act contrary to the will of God, the legislator.

It is not necessary, however, to say that the holy Doctor retracted his earlier position. After writing the first book *On Free Choice of the Will*, more than thirty years later, he wrote the books of the *Retractions*; since he did not erase that earlier position, he must be considered to have approved it again. Thus the two statements must be reconciled by means of a saying of the same holy Father in book I of *On Free Choice of the Will*, chapter 5, where he says:

“One may therefore obey without lust that law which, for the sake of protecting citizens, commands hostile force to be repelled by the same force.”

For Augustine, in order that the killing of an enemy might be lawful, requires only that the act of killing proceed from something other than that harmful desire. Thus, if someone defending himself acts not from the desire by which even brute animals are driven to defend themselves, but under the calm command of reason—namely, for the good of the commonwealth or of his family, or so that he may die with a greater probability of salvation, a consideration especially becoming to a Christian, or for any other more worthy purpose far removed from the impulse of irrational desire—a person who undertakes the defense may lawfully kill the aggressor without guilt [Col. 0741C]. This consideration, although it may not seem readily available in such straits, is defended with the same probability with which Saint Thomas distinguished the intention of killing an enemy as either an end or a means, in order to show that one may lawfully kill an aggressor, as will be evident to anyone who considers the matter for himself.

There is also another, easier way of explaining Augustine’s position: we may say that when Augustine called the killing of an aggressor a sin, he understood this as a moral defect in the action of someone who, abandoning a far more perfect act, chooses an imperfect one; hence he is said to act out of foolishness. But the person who allows himself to be killed, and does not care, when he can prevent it, to redeem his life by the death of the enemy, shows that he possesses a soul superior to every misfortune. He does not count as a good the life which he is prepared to lose, and is even more prepared not to possess. Thus he deserves the highest praise—just as Anaxarchus, Stilpo, and other ancients earned the acclamation of posterity.

The person who acts otherwise, however, shows himself to be of a mean spirit: possession of the most worthless good fills him, and he values life so highly that he thinks he must fight with all his strength to preserve it. Therefore, according to true wisdom, he will be judged to act foolishly, and, as a mean-spirited man, he will suffer the penalty of being deprived of that vast accumulation of praise which is owed to one who despises bodily life.

Furthermore, greater courage is displayed by the person who nobly endures evils than by the person who inflicts them. Saint Thomas proves this after Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* III, chapter 9, in *Summa theologiae* II-II, question 123, article 6. Hence the holy Father says in the cited chapter 13:

“What is courage? Is it not that disposition of the soul by which we despise all the hardships and losses of things not placed in our power?”

Moreover, it is certain that an act of outstanding charity would be performed by someone who willingly underwent death rather than, by killing an attacking enemy, become the cause of that enemy’s eternal damnation. This is taught by Aragon, Salon, Cajetan, and others in their commentaries on the cited question 64 of Saint Thomas.

This explanation may be gathered from what Augustine himself writes in that first book *On Free Choice of the Will*. After saying that the killing of an aggressor is punished by no civil law, he says in chapter 5:

“Those faults, however, have punishments appropriate to them, from which wisdom alone seems to me able to deliver a person.”

But one does not act according to the rules of wisdom who, in order to preserve the most worthless thing in man, deprives himself of great praise. Therefore, according to those same rules of wisdom, he acts defectively—and to act defectively is to sin.

Yet I admit that the holy Doctor intended something more. For in that same chapter 5 he says:

“How, then, are those who have stained themselves with human blood for the sake of things that ought to be despised free from sin in the sight of that providence? It therefore seems to me that this law, which is written for governing the people, rightly permits such acts, and that they are avenged by divine providence.”

These words plainly make the killer of an aggressor guilty of something more than the aforementioned moral defect, and guilty in a way that involves sin. Therefore the holy Doctor’s position, deduced from the principles of subtler philosophy, and worthy of a more generous and self-respecting spirit, can be censured only unjustly, since the wisest men among the Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins defended it before Augustine. They rejected life as belonging among contemptible goods; hence our Father’s assertion derives from them, as we have clearly demonstrated from his own words.

I had written these things. When a most learned man in Rome read them after they had been printed, he immediately came to see me, almost indignant that I had defended so anxiously a position familiar to the ancient Fathers of the Church. At the same time, he pointed out numerous testimonies of the Fathers in order to free me from my groundless fear.

In the first place, Augustine, who was himself a bishop, consistently held the same position and even persuaded military commanders of it. Publicola, an eminent man responsible for the frontier in the region of Arzugis, sent the holy Doctor several questions by letter for resolution. The twelfth was formulated in precisely these words:

“If a Christian sees that he is about to be killed by a barbarian or a Roman, ought the Christian himself to kill them so that he will not be killed by them?”

The holy Doctor responds to this difficulty in his Letter 154 to the same man:

“As for killing people so that one may not be killed by them, I do not approve such advice—unless perhaps the person is a soldier or holds a public office, so that he does this not for himself but for others or for the state in which he himself also lives, having received legitimate authority, if this is appropriate to his person.”

Augustine had plainly received this doctrine from the African Fathers. Tertullian had said in the *Apologeticus*:

“According to this discipline—that is, the Christian discipline—it is more permissible to be killed than to kill.”

Certainly Christ, by disarming Peter, taught every Christian not to repel force with force. Cyprian agrees with Tertullian in Letter 56, where he cries out:

“It is not permitted to kill, but it is necessary to be killed.”

And in the following Letter 57, to Cornelianus:

“It is not permitted for the innocent to kill even one who is guilty.”

Lactantius adds the same teaching in book VI of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 20. After saying, “He also warns that those things should not be done which are regarded among men as permissible,” he adds:

“Therefore, under this commandment of God, no one at all ought to be exempt from the rule that killing a human being is always unlawful.”

Indeed, Augustine had learned this very doctrine from his teacher Ambrose of Milan, who writes in book III of *On Duties*, chapter 4:

“Nevertheless, it does not seem that a Christian, a just and wise man, ought to seek his own life through another’s death. Thus, even if he encounters an armed robber who is striking him, he cannot strike back, lest, while defending his safety, he stain his piety.”

Who does not see how much authority is added to this position by Ambrose, Cyprian, and Augustine? Does not that most holy and learned triad of Fathers outweigh an entire century of casuists, whom Guimenius, Pirotus, and other leading Probabilists recite in a long procession in order to support those opinions—if not by the authority, at least by the number, of witnesses—which the older teachers of the Church prescribed as bloodthirsty?

Indeed, the teachers of the new theology, who taught, not without scandalizing the good, that it is lawful to kill someone who detracts from our reputation, derive from this a monstrous and cruel assertion: honor must be valued more highly than life; and since it is lawful to kill an ambusher or aggressor in defense of life, then with even stronger justification the person who, defending his honor, kills a slanderer when there is no other way of escape will not be guilty of a crime.

That learned man brought forward these and many other arguments; he also testified that he had conveyed them to another person, who later had them printed as well. Let the fear of the new casuists therefore depart. Let us leave their Tamburinis and Bannii to them; we shall listen to Ambrose and Augustine. With them, it will be a source of glory not merely to think rightly, but even to err in the company of casuist judges.

## § XII. Saint Augustine, in the books of the *Retractions*, expunged nothing that he had asserted concerning divine grace in the books written against the Pelagians.

Adam and Moraines bring these errors against Augustine, but with wholly futile results. For by that wrongful labor they have not diminished the reputation or authority of the Bishop of Hippo; rather, they have advanced it as much as possible.

Who, at the beginning of this controversy, would not have feared that Augustine—among the more than two hundred books he published, the many letters he issued, the innumerable sermons he delivered to the people, and the many commentaries and questions in which he explained Sacred Scripture—might be held guilty of some error by these severe censors, since even good Homer is said occasionally to nod in his maxims?

It was not possible for him to weigh every statement. At times he wrote with his mind distracted and his pen hurrying toward other matters. Add to this the immense forest of heresies against which Augustine alone brought both axe and torch, to cut it down and burn it. At one time the Manichaeans had to be refuted, at another the Arians; then he had to write against the Donatists and immediately proceed against the Pelagians; often all of them had to be condemned at once. Nor could this conveniently be done because of the countless consultations requested of him, both orally and in writing, and subsequently answered.

He was not allowed to keep his volumes under pressure for nine years, but was compelled to issue them rough and unfinished. He was so pressed by lack of time that he could not even read through books he had dictated once, as he himself testifies in his letter to Marcellinus. Therefore, if anything less consonant with the truth had slipped from him, he would rightly and deservedly have been excused.

But this point above all deserves notice: when Augustine reviewed with censorial severity all the books he had labored over, and often applied the sponge, he said that only two things needed correction when reviewing the volumes written against the Pelagians. One was that in book V *Against Julian* he had given, as though it were certain, the name of a particular physician, although he later discovered that the man was completely unknown. The other was that in the book *On Nature and Grace* he had attributed a certain book to Pope Sixtus, following the testimony of Pelagius, although it had in fact been published by the philosopher Sextus.

Apart from this, in those books against the Pelagians he recanted no dogma that he had asserted; he corrected no proposition—not to mention erasing a single word as unsuitable. Instead, he approved the whole and every part with the authority of old age. From this alone it may be believed that divine grace, which he had defended with such ferocity in more than thirty books against the attacks of the Pelagians, was present with him, repaying so great a labor with a work worthy of it, so that he might write those volumes, worthy to be preserved like cedar, far removed from every error, however slight.

And yet these recent Aristarchuses boast that they have detected in those books so many excesses, so many contradictions, and so many errors!

Augustine, a man of the most modest disposition, wishes to admonish these censors in the conclusion of *On the Gift of Perseverance*:

“Those who think that I am in error should consider again and again what has been said, lest perhaps they themselves be in error. But when, through those who read my labors, I become not only more learned but also more corrected, I recognize that God is gracious to me; and this above all I expect from the teachers of the Church, if what I write comes into their hands and they deign to know it.”

When the supreme historian of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, and the immortal glory of the Vatican senate, Caesar Baronius, read these words, he burst forth into the following praises of Augustine’s genius:

“This very thing is worthy of the holy Augustine’s modesty and of the admirable submissiveness and reverence of his mind. Thus, unless from elsewhere, at least from these words you may understand that he wrote them under the inspiration of the divine Spirit, since God testified through the prophet that the divine presence rests upon no one except the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at the word of God.”

But so far were the teachers of the Church from correcting Augustine’s doctrine of divine grace by even a single stroke of the pen that, venerating it as something given from a more sacred curtain, they defended it against the Semi-Pelagians, and the Roman Church itself proposed it for the faithful to follow.

If, rejecting the approval of so many past centuries, more recent writers call themselves the teachers of the Church to whom Augustine entrusted the examination of his writings, one would have to congratulate this age—nourisher of such great men—if they could nevertheless persuade us of Augustine’s errors more successfully than they have so far.

But I pray the powers above to grant them a better mind and a better disposition toward my Augustine, so that “the preaching of the supreme man in the Church” (these are Prosper’s words concerning the ancient detractors of Augustine, in a letter to Rufinus) may be strengthened even by those who at present are trying to tear it down.

# CHAPTER V. More recent writers produce the testimonies of thirty-five doctors—namely, pontiffs, cardinals, bishops, and others—against Saint Augustine; their reliability is examined.

[Col. 0745B]

Some recent writers, lest they should incur the indignation of all good people by abandoning the authority of Saint Augustine anywhere, adopted the strategy of examining the notes of every writer and bringing into public view anything asserted in them that was less than respectful toward Augustine. For once they had shown that they followed in the footsteps of others, they thought they would escape all odium for what they had done.

John Adam and Francis Annatus carried this out with great zeal and immense labor: the former in part III of *Calvin Destroyed*, chapter 7, p. 631; the latter in the place where he ought to have shown greater reverence toward Augustine.

For in order to restrain the boastfulness of the Jansenists, who claimed Augustine entirely for themselves, Annatus produced a substantial volume in which he attempted to demonstrate that Augustine stood against Jansenism. He speaks against his adversary solely in Augustine’s words; and just as veins are spread throughout the entire body, so those words wander and resound throughout the whole work.

To show himself Augustine’s defender and champion, he gave the book this title: *Augustine Vindicated from the Baians*. He called the Jansenists “Baians” as a term of disgrace, because they were said to defend the condemned theses of Michael Baius, which had been proscribed by the Apostolic See.

How faithfully he accomplished this in the first seven books may be judged by those against whom he contends; I stand far removed from their cause. The eighth book of the same volume is entirely against Augustine, and plainly seems to demand a second and completely opposite title, since in that final book Annatus brings forward, with great industry and labor, every disparaging remark against Saint Augustine that he has collected here and there.

You call Augustine judge, Annatus; you dispute with the Jansenists before his tribunal; you say that you stand by his judgment.
