Yet, though we had no fear for your good faith, you pronounce Augustine not merely a judge of suspect reliability—which might somehow be tolerated—but make him the defendant and produce more than thirty witnesses against him. You loudly proclaim that you are naming the chief princes and most celebrated shepherds of the Church, the most learned doctors of ecclesiastical meanings, and men entirely free from suspicion, book VIII, at the beginning.

And lest this conspiracy of a few against Augustine be thought insignificant, you protest in chapter 3 that you have summoned witnesses from Gaul, Italy, Spain, and Germany. I wonder why you did not also summon some from Japan!

When you promise to show us Augustine vindicated from the Baians, you present him miserably torn to pieces. We had hoped to see that great Hipponian commander, defended by your valor, triumphing in the Capitol, so that we might weave a laurel for him and a civic crown for you. But suddenly we find that you have summoned an enemy in place of a defender: you turn the battle line from Jansenius against Augustine, and, dragging countless men along with you, attack him yourself.

I should like to know what reason, Annatus—if there can be any reason in this matter—drove you to write this longer and harsher censure. You reply in chapter 4, p. 877:

“I thought these points ought to be proposed so that we might understand that those who perhaps do not readily accept everything that someone may think was proposed by Augustine are not excessively shameless.”

You add on p. 874:

“Many people seem not to have paid sufficient attention to this while exaggerating Molina’s audacity in indicating that Augustine lacked some light in reconciling the efficacy of the divine decrees and aids with created freedom.”

So, in order to excuse Molina’s audacity, which they exaggerate, was that outstanding Doctor of the Church, Augustine, to be accused before the Catholic world of so many errors, with a vast crowd of witnesses assembled?

Annatus even produces several testimonies against Augustine to which he himself says that he does not give complete credence. Hence those pious words of his at the beginning of chapter 3, p. 864:

“I merely report them; I do not approve them.”

He repeats the same in chapter 4, p. 876:

“I report these things, but I do not approve them.”

Indeed, in one place, while bringing forward men who speak most offensively against Augustine, as though grieving over the treatment of the holy Doctor, he publicly declares at the beginning of chapter 3:

“I wish this and certain other things that I shall add had been expressed more mildly.”

And on p. 876, chapter 4, while reciting the insults of Pighius against Augustine, he says:

“I omit, out of respect, what he adds about Augustine.”

On the following page he says:

“I shall not report what he said in book VI, and so forth, since what he said seems to me to have been expressed more harshly against the holy Doctor than I would wish.”

It is astonishing that Annatus should have felt such scruples! I had resolved to let this writer’s words pass by on deaf ears. For who could be so irreligious toward the powers above as to lend an ear to someone who says he intends to give testimony against Augustine, rather than curse the man’s audacious plan and order him to go far away?

Nevertheless, lest Augustine appear to succumb to the testimonies of men of every sort, let us repeat those testimonies. For to weaken or reject the testimony of adversaries is the work of a good advocate and a good cause, especially when he produces so many witnesses against Augustine who have always been deeply devoted to Augustine’s name.

At the beginning, however, Annatus names as witnesses men before whom even the judges themselves should rise: Pope Celestine, [who, in his letter to the bishops of Gaul, did not approve Augustine’s entire doctrine, as Annatus thinks, but only certain specific propositions about which there is no controversy at all. We shall examine this matter more fully below, in its proper place, chapter 8.] He then adds the purple-clad Fathers of the Vatican senate, namely Baronius, Sadoletus, Bonaventure, Cajetan, Perronius, and Valerius; each of them must be judged separately.

## § I. The testimonies of Baronius and Sadoletus examined. The statements of Ludovicus Donius on behalf of Sadoletus against Saint Augustine are refuted.

Accordingly, Annatus, book VIII, chapter 2, says that Baronius, after reporting in volume V, under the year 431, these words of Celestine at the end of his letter to the bishops of Gaul—“But the deeper matters, etc.”—says:

“By these words, I say, he professes that those deeper questions concerning the predestination of the saints were by no means defined by the Apostolic See, and that only those matters were established which seemed sufficient for the condemnation of the errors.”

After quoting this, Annatus adds:

“Here, then, I ask what those questions of the authors concerning predestination are, regarding which Celestine, as Baronius interprets him, grants freedom to affirm or deny.”

I think this recent writer was deceived, since he publishes about Baronius something that Baronius nowhere asserted. For that most learned writer did not at all attribute the chapters appended to Celestine’s letter to Celestine himself; rather, he said that they were Prosper’s. He says there:

“Those chapters are thought to be Prosper’s, who, as he seems to acknowledge, collected them from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs and from the African councils. The same author has the following at the end: ‘But the deeper and more difficult matters, etc.’”

And yet Annatus dares to claim that Baronius interpreted Celestine’s words in this way, although Baronius attributed them to Prosper. Indeed, Baronius did not even dare to assert beyond doubt that Prosper was the author of that chapter; he merely said that Prosper was thought to be its author.

Let Prosper and Baronius themselves teach us whether they affirmed, without fear of criticism, that the question of predestination to glory without the foreknowledge of merits could be resolved against Saint Augustine.

Saint Prosper, in response to doubt 10 of the Genoese, says that Augustine:

“By a pious and steadfast doctrine abundantly proved that the Church must preach predestination, in which there is the preparation of grace; grace, in which there is the effect of predestination; and the foreknowledge of God, by which, before the ages, he foreknew to whom he would grant his gifts. Whoever attacks this preaching is a most manifest helper of Pelagian presumption.”

Baronius, however, in volume VI, under the year 490, after saying that all the Fathers had united against the writings of Faustus, adds:

“Since, then, the Church everywhere contradicted Faustus’s opinion, let those more recent writers consider at what peril they depart from Saint Augustine’s position on predestination while rising up against the innovators in order to refute them, when otherwise weapons are not lacking with which to defeat the adversaries.”

Yet concerning the holy Doctor’s position on predestination to glory, Annatus writes:

“Although Augustine inclines toward the contrary position, the determination of this question must nevertheless be left to the free choice of disputants; Cardinal Baronius also held this view,” chapter 1, p. 857.

If we had no use of our eyes and believed only what that recent writer publishes about Baronius, Augustine might perhaps lose his case. But since the cardinal clearly and explicitly declares the opposite, without evasions, Annatus’s reliability must be called into question. Augustine’s cause is secure; his adversary has been convicted of falsehood at the very beginning of the case. Annatus stumbled at the threshold—an inauspicious omen.

Another purple-clad witness is produced: James Sadoletus. In book II of his commentary on the Letter to the Romans, interpreting Paul’s words, “Those whom he foreknew, etc.,” he says the following, as Annatus reports on p. 860:

“On the other hand, although the greatest Doctor of all—and likewise a most serious and holy man—stands on that side, nevertheless it seems exceedingly harsh to me, and something that cannot easily enter our minds, that, if absolutely nothing in us is effective for obtaining grace when all are in an equal condition, some should be chosen in such a way that the others are left in misery and ruin,” and so forth.

But whereas we saw Annatus to be false in reporting Baronius’s testimony, here we may call him, if not malicious, at least negligent. He diminishes the praises that Sadoletus bestowed upon Augustine by repeating the witness’s own words inaccurately.

Sadoletus writes:

“But on the other hand, although the GREATEST DOCTOR OF ALL, and likewise a most serious and holy man, stands on that side, and so forth.”

Do you see the force of the word “OF ALL,” by which Sadoletus places Augustine above the other Doctors of the Church? Yet that word stuck to Annatus’s pen. I would grant that this happened by accident, not design, if the adversary’s disposition toward Augustine did not draw me toward another conclusion.

Indeed, if you called Suárez the greatest Doctor, and likewise a most serious one, people would gladly hear it. But if you added that he was the greatest and most serious of all, you would heap enormous envy upon him, as though you were making him superior to Aquinas, Scotus, Albert, and the other leading Scholastics.

But let us return to Sadoletus.

This writer speaks not only against Augustine but also against Annatus himself. Annatus, in chapters 1 and 2, teaches that human beings are predestined to grace without merits, and, he says on page 860, “let us say that human beings are predestined to grace before foreseen merits, but after the foreseen good use of grace they are predestined to glory,” etc. But Sadoletus requires some merit for obtaining grace; for he admits that it seems hard to him if there is absolutely nothing in us that is capable of obtaining GRACE. Do you hear? He said grace, not glory—which was in fact the condemned opinion of the Semi-Pelagians—in which Sadoletus imprudently became entangled. But since, after Annatus’s book had been published, Sadoletus found an eloquent advocate in Ludovicus Donius, volume III of *History of the Cardinals*, p. 206, who not only defends Sadoletus but also, in no. 110, censures Saint Augustine because he “while fighting with all the force of his spirit and words in defense of divine grace against the Pelagians, who exalt free will to the injury of divine grace, seems to slip into something like the opposite pit, and sometimes to attribute less than is fitting to human free will.” Donius copied this censure word for word from Sixtus Senensis, in the preface to book V of the *Bibliotheca Sancta*—indeed, from Julian, that most bitter enemy of Augustine, as quoted by the holy Doctor in book II of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 3. Therefore, in order to expose the error of this witness hired by Annatus and defended by Donius, we must show his opinion concerning the beginnings of faith and the other virtues. For if we demonstrate that on this point he approached the Semi-Pelagians, who will not immediately understand that no credibility can be attached to his testimony, seeing that he conspired with Augustine’s enemies?

Jacobus Sadoletus wrote commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans. There, wishing to depart from Augustine’s position on predestination, he miserably inclined toward the Semi-Pelagians. On the Apostle’s words in chapter VIII, verse 29, “For those whom he foreknew and predestined,” etc., he writes:

> “Thus I add this: that even in this very act we cannot understand his wisdom if, without any cause or reason making a distinction, he rejects and casts some away to destruction, while receiving others to salvation and his grace; for to act and work in this manner would seem to belong more to chance than to deliberation.”

Thus he wishes something good, on the part of free will, to precede, so that grace may be given to one rather than to another. Cassian plainly held this same view. His words concerning God are found in *Collation* 13, chapter 12:

> “Lest he should seem to confer his gifts upon one wholly asleep or dissolved in inactive leisure, seeking, as it were, opportunities by which, after shaking off the body of human sluggishness, the generosity of his munificence might not appear irrational, while he bestows it under the guise of a certain desire and labor.”

Nevertheless, Sadoletus there affirms that these beginnings of good will, which we establish by ourselves, are certain imperfect goods; for he concedes that virtue, according to its perfection, cannot be possessed without grace.

> “For nothing,” he says, “can be perfect in us. But the beginnings of both thinking and willing are OURS. And they are ours in such a way that God also occupies a large part in them. For necessarily we have him himself as the object set before us, when we desire and think of him, so that he himself may first be the stimulus of our thoughts and wishes. When we have inclined toward him—which Paul calls a good purpose—it is then more PERFECT for us, through that good purpose, to will and work by God, since by his help and support we are both upheld and moved forward to act rightly and to will steadfastly.”

The Semi-Pelagians taught this very thing: they attributed the beginnings of good, and only the beginning of imperfect good, to the powers of free will. Let Cassian himself be heard, in book XII of *The Institutes of the Monks*, chapter 14:

> “But most firmly I define—not by my own judgment, but by that of the elders—that PERFECTION absolutely cannot be attained without these things, yet that no one can complete it by these things alone without the grace of God. For just as we say that our efforts cannot attain it by themselves without God’s assistance, so we declare that God’s mercy and grace are conferred only upon those who labor and toil.”

This the holy Father refutes in chapter 23 of *On the Gift of Perseverance*.

The same Sadoletus, commenting on chapter IX, verse 22, “But if God, wishing to show his wrath,” etc., writes:

> “Some beginnings of good will proceed from us, so that we may be prepared and made fit for mercy.”

He does not differ from Cassian, book VI of *The Institutes of the Monks*, chapter 18, where he says:

> “The same grace of the Holy Spirit is not granted to everyone, but to the degree to which each person has rendered himself worthy and fit by his own zeal or industry.”

Furthermore, Sadoletus writes the following on the aforementioned chapter IX:

> “For since we were born under the bondage of sin, and cannot by our own help and strength emerge from it or cast ourselves out of it, we indeed will and strive FROM OURSELVES; nevertheless, to rise up we need God’s help. He assists by his mercy those who STRETCH OUT THEIR ARMS toward him and move their bodies, so as to free themselves, but he leaves the sluggish and idle, who do nothing for which they ought to be helped, stuck in the very mud and lost.”

In this he agrees admirably with Faustus, the leading figure of the Semi-Pelagians, book I of *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 17:

> “And thus,” he says, “these two things are joined together: the power of the one who draws and the affection of the one who obeys—just as when a sick person attempts to rise, but his strength does not follow his will, and for that reason begs that a right hand be extended to him.”

He adds:

> “The servant EXTENDS to the Lord, who stands by and calls, the HAND of faith by which he may be drawn,” etc.

But lest Sadoletus seem, by positing the beginnings of good will as arising from the powers of nature apart from God’s assistance, to conclude that grace for more perfect virtue is given on the basis of merits, he adds:

> “Thus our simple and inchoate believing, by which we begin to incline toward obedience to God, does not immediately constitute merit; but we merit only when, strengthened in good will by God himself, etc.”

The Semi-Pelagians taught this same thing. Their leader says in *Collation* 13, chapter 13:

> “While he bestows it [grace] under the guise of a certain desire and labor, and nevertheless God’s grace remains GRATUITOUS, since by certain small and insignificant efforts he bestows, with immeasurable generosity, such great glory of immortality and such great gifts of everlasting blessedness.”

Augustine mocked this evasion in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 2:

> “Who,” he says, “would say that one who has already begun to believe merits nothing from him in whom he has believed? Hence it follows that other things are added to one who already merits, by divine recompense, and thus that God’s grace is given according to our merits.”

See also the same author, book IV to Boniface, chapter 6.

From these things it is clear that Sadoletus, while imprudently deviating from Augustine’s position, adhered to the Semi-Pelagians, who asserted that certain beginnings of faith and good will arise in us from ourselves. The Second Council of Orange condemned them in canon 5:

> “If anyone says that, just as the increase of faith, so also the BEGINNING of faith itself, and the very AFFECTION OF BELIEVING by which we believe in him who justifies the ungodly and come to the regeneration of baptism, is naturally in us, and not through the gift of grace—that is, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit correcting our will from unbelief to faith and from impiety to piety—he is shown to be opposed to the apostolic teachings,” etc.

Here, however, we must deal with Donius, who writes in no. 106:

> “But who would believe that so great and so orthodox a man was entangled in the snares of Semi-Pelagianism, whether willingly or through imprudence?”

I am amazed that this writer read Sadoletus’s letters so superficially that he did not understand from them that Sadoletus was reprimanded in letters by the most learned and wisest Cardinal Gaspare Contarini because of the position on the beginnings of the virtues that he had inserted into his commentaries on Paul. For Sadoletus replies in book IX, letter 9:

> “As for the fact that I was more sparing than I ought to have been in explaining God’s prevenient grace, I acknowledge that error, since that is how it appears to you.”

Yet in the same place he again says:

> “I do not think it is Pelagian if we retain something at the beginnings that is ours.”

Contarini had complained in a friendly manner that Sadoletus had not spoken with sufficient dignity of Augustine’s position in those same interpretations. For Contarini saw that this opinion concerning the beginnings of the virtues, as arising from the powers of free will alone, had been most solidly refuted by Augustine in the remnants of Pelagianism.

But in a letter written the following year, letter 10, Sadoletus replied to him as follows:

> “When I wrote to Paul that in a certain matter I differed slightly from you, and he told me that you wished to know where and concerning what the disagreement was, I first inform you that in that position concerning free will I do not entirely agree with Augustine, who CLEARLY TAKES AWAY the freedom of our will; and while he wishes especially to embrace God’s glory, it seems to me that he detracts from it rather than attributes to it what he appears to attribute. If we were together and had the books in hand, I would confidently expect easily to prove this to you.”

Had Annatus read this, without doubt he would have listed it among the more notable testimonies against the holy Doctor. But Donius too did not read Sadoletus’s commentaries; for if he had even glanced at them, he would certainly have understood that he was wasting his labor in trying to vindicate Sadoletus from error, as though Sadoletus had intended only this: “that in the beginnings, produced through the spirit of operative grace, something of ours should be found, because the soul or its powers physically influence supernatural vital acts.”

But Sadoletus speaks too harshly for his words to be softened in this way. For in the passage cited above from Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, chapter VIII, in order to remove the whole question and free himself from any suspicion of error on account of the beginnings of the virtues being naturally established, he writes that “since God is the cause of good things in two ways, either as maker and the agent himself, or as the end and the thing desired,” in the former way God moves us to the nobler and more perfect acts of the virtues of faith, love of God, religion, and so forth. He then adds:

> “But insofar as God is the final cause of things, and our minds are moved toward him as toward the highest good, our will, thought, and those first and inchoate plans of our actions are also from God.”

He gives this reason:

> “For then he is not himself the author and universal principle of our will as one who moves and impels, but as one who is desired and longed for—nevertheless bringing great influence even then toward inclining and attracting us.”

Therefore, according to Sadoletus, those first good movements toward God do not arise from the spirit of operative grace, as Donius maintained. For at that time God does not move as maker and the agent himself, in which capacity he always moves through the spirit of operative grace. Hence the words of canon 9 of the Council of Orange:

> “Whenever we do good, God works in us and with us, so that we may work.”

Nor did the Semi-Pelagians deny that God moves toward those beginnings of good works in the role of the end. For God was the object apprehended under the aspect of truth and goodness; they believed in him initially, desired him, and sought him. But they were condemned because it is not enough for God to move merely as an object; he must move as an agent, so that we may believe and will through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, according to canon 6 of the same Council of Orange and canon 5, where it is established that the beginning of faith itself, and the affection of believing, occurs in us through the gift of grace—that is, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

Donius could also have understood Sadoletus’s error from what he himself writes about Augustine:

> “He clearly takes away the freedom of our will.”

These are the foul expressions of both the ancient and the modern Semi-Pelagians. Concerning the former, Saint Prosper writes to Rufinus:

> “They disgrace his writings”—namely, Augustine’s—“in which the error of the Pelagians is attacked, saying that he completely removes free will.”

The Arminians, a new offspring of the Semi-Pelagians, likewise blew the same trumpets against Augustine. One of them, Hugo Grotius, says in book XVII of his *History of the Netherlands*:

> “Augustine was the first of all, once the struggle with Pelagius and his followers had begun—for before that he himself had thought differently—to leave so little room for the language of freedom in his vigorous disputation that he placed certain decrees of God before it, which seemed to destroy freedom’s very power.”

Who, then, will henceforth deny that Sadoletus conspired with the Semi-Pelagians in that error, though incautiously and unknowingly, when he hurls their abuse against Augustine?

Donius, in no. 108, says that the words “But the deeper matters,” etc., which he thinks are read at the end of the letter of Celestine, deserve the greatest attention. Yet he ought also to have paid the greatest attention to what is asserted in chapter 3, where, concerning the Semi-Pelagians writing against Augustine, the following is quoted:

> “Although they do not hesitate to anathematize Pelagius and Celestius, nevertheless they attack our teachers, as though they had exceeded the NECESSARY LIMIT.”

If he had paid close attention to this, he would certainly not have pronounced, in no. 110, that “Augustine seems to slip into something like the opposite pit, and sometimes to attribute less than is fitting to human free will.”

From what has thus far been established at greater length, it is evident that Jacobus Sadoletus thought incautiously with the Semi-Pelagians against Augustine and that, in the heat of disputation rather than through considered and calm reasoning, he actually transferred himself to the extreme and most remote position. He deservedly ought to hear these words, which he himself unjustly employed in that same letter 10 to the illustrious Contarini against the holy Doctor.

Meanwhile, let Annatus consider what sort of witness he has called against Augustine: a writer who, concerning the beginnings of the virtues, conspired with the Semi-Pelagians against him. Yet at the beginning of book VIII he had immediately promised to bring forward in judgment witnesses who were entirely free from suspicion.

[Col. 0753A]

Thus much concerning Sadoletus. I would more willingly have kept silent about his error, but the accusation brought against the holy Father by Annatus and Donius on the basis of Sadoletus’s words has, against my deepest will and resistance, compelled the foregoing remarks.

## § II. The Statements of Saint Bonaventure and Cajetan Examined

As a third witness he brings forward Saint Bonaventure, in book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 33, question 2, article 3, who says:

> “To the first objection made against this, based on Augustine’s words, it must be said that in those words Augustine does not intend to say that infants are tormented perceptibly, but intends to make their punishment clear with regard to the deprivation of the vision of God, and also with regard to the suitability of the place; and he expresses this very abundantly, saying more while wishing less to be understood.”

But Bonaventure’s testimony against Augustine causes us no difficulty, for in that passage he is speaking of the book *On the Faith to Peter the Deacon*, chapter 27, where we read that children dying without baptism are punished with the eternal punishment of everlasting fire. That book belongs to Fulgentius, not Augustine.

Therefore, if the Seraphic Doctor, led by the common opinion of his age, thought those words belonged to Augustine, since they belong to another, we do not rely upon his testimony. For his statement has no weight before judges when, through deception, it affirms something about someone that is known to have been asserted not by him but by another. Here the modesty of the holy Doctor shines forth: he did not attack Augustine’s position, as he understood it, with a harsher censure, but softened it through a lenient interpretation.

But Annatus, with grave solemnity, thunders in the same vein in book VIII, chapter 1:

> “We deny the cruel consequence.”

Again, he used Bonaventure’s statement that Augustine “said more while wishing less to be understood,” once, and in a context that had been handed down incidentally against the Pelagian heresy. But Annatus, on page 893, abuses Saint Bonaventure’s moderation in order to soften Augustine’s positions in the question of the efficacy of divine grace. For he writes:

> “And if anyone insists that Augustine expresses this in other passages, who does not see that, if this were so, nothing else would follow than what Saint Bonaventure says: that in those passages Augustine says more, while in those cited by us he wishes less to be understood?”

But whether Augustine held that position concerning the punishments of infants has nothing to do with the present issue. For Bonaventure was speaking of the book *On the Faith to Peter*, and we have already shown abundantly, in chapter 3, section 1, how little his words help the adversaries.

Let us hear the fourth cardinal, Cajetan, who speaks as follows in part I, question 70, article 3:

> “The words, however, support this gloss, because when the discussion was against Averroes, it was permissible to incline toward the opposite position, as Augustine does against the Pelagians.”

“This,” says Annatus on page 862, “is to exceed the line of necessary truth: it is a certain excessive severity and unjust harassment, which commands one to cross that middle point where truth sits, if Augustine leads the way.”

But Augustine loudly claims to keep to the middle, and he was the first among mortals to teach this, in book IV of *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 3, addressed to Pope Boniface. He writes:

> “Whoever, with a Catholic mind, shudders at these wicked and condemnable teachings in this threefold division should avoid the hiding places and snares of that fivefold one, and should be so cautious between the two that he avoids Manichaeism without inclining toward Pelagianism, and again separates himself from the Pelagians without joining himself to the Manichaeans; or, if he is already held by either side, he should not preserve himself from some opponents in such a way that he rushes upon the others.”

Who, then, would believe Cajetan in this matter rather than Augustine, who made this protest before the apostolic see?

But perhaps you will say that, in the force of disputation, Augustine ran beyond the limits he himself had established, that is, beyond the line of necessary truth, as the procurer of these witnesses puts it. I am amazed at Annatus, who thinks the headings appended to Celestine’s letter belong to Celestine himself—and, indeed, such are his diligence and learning that he did not even hesitate to cook this same cabbage a second time.

That was an old calumny directed against Augustine by the Semi-Pelagians. Hence the pontiff rejected them as falsifiers and detractors, as we said in the preceding section. Since they repeat the accusation, we must repeat his words in our defense as well. For he writes:

> “Because some who glory in the Catholic name nevertheless remain in the condemned opinions or depravity of heretics, whether through perversity or ignorance, presume to oppose the most devout disputants; and although they do not hesitate to anathematize Pelagius and Celestius, they nevertheless attack our teachers as though they had exceeded the necessary limit.”

But Annatus, who had before his eyes only the appendix of the letter, “But the deeper matters,” etc., was unable to read these words on the preceding page—or reading them and neglecting them amounted to the same thing.

Therefore, according to Celestine’s judgment—or, if you deny that, at least according to his testimony—Augustine did not exceed the line of necessary truth. Who, then, would place the testimony of one Cajetan above the declaration of Saint Celestine the pope?

## § III. Cardinal Perron, Cardinal Valerius, and Saint Charles Borromeo Improperly Cited against Saint Augustine

Next comes the fifth witness summoned from Gaul, Cardinal Perron, famous both for his purple and for the trophies he erected through his continual warfare against heretics. Annatus says that Perron’s words are these:

> “I sufficiently warned in the fourth of my observations that we must carefully distinguish Saint Augustine’s own opinions, when he speaks as a private doctor, from his narratives, in which he speaks as a witness to the common usage of the Church, or from statements in which he conforms to the common consensus of the doctors of his age. From the former we argue only probabilistically; from the latter, demonstratively.”

He certainly thought well and worthily of Augustine. For who would include Augustine’s private opinions within the bounds of faith in an explanation, for example, of Sacred Scripture?

But the question here is what Perron thinks of Augustine’s authority in the matter of predestination and grace. For in the very title of book VIII you promised that you would produce testimonies concerning Augustine’s authority in matters relating to divine providence toward human beings. Permit me to turn Augustine’s words here:

> “Enter, Perron, enter and sit with your brothers, from whom no reasoning and no temptation has separated you. Your opinion is needed, and especially yours.”

These words are found in book I of *Against Julian*, chapter 6.

Listen, Annatus. Perron gives his testimony concerning Augustine:

> “Augustine, the greatest doctor of predestination after the Apostles, indeed the MOUTH and TONGUE OF THE ANCIENT CHURCH with regard to that doctrine of grace.”

This is in book I of *Responses to the King of England*, chapter 12.

“What, then,” Augustine adds, “did it help you that you inserted Perron’s testimony as though it supported you?”

Would you like to know whether Augustine taught his own position on predestination as a private doctor or as a witness to the common usage of the Church? Hear him say this himself, in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 23, at the end:

> “And thus the faith of this predestination, which is now defended with fresh concern against new heretics, has never been absent from the Church of Christ.”

Therefore, in this matter Augustine did not speak as a private doctor but, as Perron teaches, as the mouth and tongue of the ancient Church. Who, then, would not be indignant at Annatus, who names as witnesses against Augustine men who raise the holy Doctor’s opinions to the heavens with their praises?

Will our Verona now produce as the sixth witness against Augustine, as you say, the more recent Cardinal Valerius of Venice? In book III of *Ecclesiastical Rhetoric*, chapter 42, he warns the clergy as follows:

> “Clerics should read the writings of Blessed Augustine with the greatest caution. For he excelled in sharpness of intellect and argued so subtly concerning difficult matters that men of no ordinary intellect, when reading his books, have sometimes fallen into errors.”

Annatus attaches this fine scholium on page 863:

> “And what else is this than precisely what we heard Bonaventure warning: that Augustine sometimes says more while wishing less to be understood?”

O splendid invention of our commentator! Cardinal Valerius writes that some readers of Augustine’s books fell into errors because they failed to grasp Augustine’s most subtle meaning. Annatus infers from Valerius that they fell because Augustine, while arguing, sometimes went too far in his wording—though Valerius says not that Augustine argued about difficult matters so subtly, but that, as the interpreter contends, he argued so carelessly.

O gentle spirits of heaven! That great bishop of my homeland praises the sharpness of Augustine’s intellect and his subtlety in disputation, which many men, although endowed with noble intelligence, could not grasp. Annatus constructs from this an accusation of excess against Augustine and pretends to set up as a witness against the holy Doctor one who is an outstanding praiser of that same Augustine.

As for those of whom Valerius speaks, is it Augustine’s fault that they fell into error, or the fault of those who did not understand Augustine? Who does not know that many have rushed into heresy because they failed to grasp the profound meanings of certain words of Sacred Scripture? Shall we transfer the blame to the Holy Spirit, the author of sacred speech, or rather to the rashness of those who tried to raise themselves beyond the powers of their intellect?

Hence the learned Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, who wrote under Justinian in defense of the Three Chapters, says in his book *Against Mocianus*:

> “What, then,” he says, “should we marvel at in this? For Augustine could not have spoken better than the prophets, the Apostles, and the Evangelists, whose meanings, when similarly misunderstood and improperly applied, so many people try to use in defense of their errors.”

Annatus also notes in the same place that Saint Charles Borromeo encouraged Valerius to write that work and approved it once completed. Hence Annatus imagines that, just as Valerius, so Saint Charles too stood against Augustine:

> “So that this one testimony may appear, and ought to appear, to belong to two cardinals eminent in virtue and holiness.”

Thus he makes Saint Charles contrary to the holy Doctor, although Charles never even dreamed of such a thing. But since Valerius speaks in defense of Augustine, Borromeo must be added to him as his equal.

Let us therefore produce Saint Charles’s own testimony concerning Augustine. In a letter to the city of Milan he says:

> “No one is unaware how much benefit and fruit that great Doctor Augustine brought to the Church of God. He extinguished the Manichaeans in Africa, drove out the Donatists, reduced the Pelagian heretics to nothing, refuted Fortunatus the arch-heretic, and, to sum everything up briefly, removed all the poisons vomited by the demon against the purity of orthodox religion. Hence it came about that from his teaching, from the Fathers who followed him, and from synods, theologians, and Catholic academies, so many doctrines of the Church received support and strength.”

Such, then, was the opinion of the most holy bishop of Milan concerning Saint Augustine.

## § IV. Those Who Slander Saint Augustine as Sometimes Too Unjust toward Free Will Are Mistaken

After the purple-clad witnesses, they bring forward against Saint Augustine a vast crowd of other writers. There is no time to repeat them individually, but I shall arrange them into certain classes whenever several have joined in the same opinion concerning Augustine.

First, Annatus in book VIII, Adamus in part III of *The Destruction of the Calendar*, chapter 7, and Decampsius in book III of *The Jansenist Heresies*, disputation 1, chapter 3, oppose to Augustine Bishop Genebrardus of Aix, in the letter prefixed to Origen’s works; Albertus Pighius, book III of *On Free Will*; and Sixtus Senensis, in the preface to book V of the *Bibliotheca*, saying that Augustine was sometimes too unjust toward free will.

This is indeed an old and rancid calumny of the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians. Julian, in book I of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 54, writes against Augustine:

> “Free will persists in human nature. Just as you deny it with the Manichaeans, so we confess it with the Apostles and all Catholics.”

As for the Semi-Pelagians, this is clear from Prosper’s letter to Rufinus, whose words were given in section 1.

How truthfully Augustine repelled this calumny, I believe only those can fail to know who have not even greeted the holy Doctor’s books from afar. The entire book *On Grace and Free Will* contends for human freedom. At the very beginning he writes:

> “Since there are some who defend God’s grace in such a way as to deny human free will, or who think that, when grace is defended, free will is denied, I have taken care, compelled by mutual charity, to write something to your Charity, brother Valentinus, and to the others who serve God together with you.”

Genebrardus says: Augustine was sometimes too unjust toward free will. Sixtus Senensis, on page 875, testifies that the holy Doctor sometimes attributed less than is fitting to human free will. These men affirm that the holy Doctor was SOMETIMES less fair to free will.

But Decampsius, mentioned immediately above, writes of the same men:

> “They affirm that Saint Augustine was VERY OFTEN less fair to free will.”

Nor do they present the witnesses’ statements faithfully. Indeed, Augustine would not even be offended by Sixtus Senensis, who explicitly says in *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 47:

> “But this question, in which free choice of the will and God’s grace are discussed, is so difficult to distinguish that when free will is defended, God’s grace seems to be denied, while when God’s grace is asserted, free will is thought to be taken away.”

When Julian had objected to Augustine that, by commending God’s grace, he said free will was denied, Augustine replied in book IV against that same Julian, chapter 8:

> “I did not say that free choice was denied or taken away, but I said that it was thought to be taken away.”

Albertus Pighius is the most inept censor of the holy Doctor. For in book III of *On Free Will* he did not hesitate to blurt out the following against Saint Augustine:

> “In some places he seems too unjust toward free will; he attributes to it even less than he can. He either diminishes, disguises, or evades its power; certainly he casts it down with all his strength.”

But who would believe the testimony of such an impudent man, when Pope Saint Hormisdas writes in his letter to Possessor:

> “As for free choice and the grace of God, what the Roman—that is, the Catholic—Church follows and preserves can be known abundantly from the various books of Blessed Augustine, and especially from those addressed to Prosper and Hilary,” etc.

Thus Augustine’s teaching concerning free will is the teaching of the Church. Augustine, therefore, is not unjust toward free will; he does not destroy it, diminish it, or suffocate it. Otherwise the Church would be following the worst of teachers.

Who, moreover, would not despise Pighius’s foolish advice, by which he recommends that, in order to grasp the true doctrine of free will, one should read the books of the holy Doctor addressed to Catholics rather than those written against the Pelagians? Foolishly—as though he had followed different paths in the two groups of works.

Saint Prosper mocked this escape of the Massilians, who refused to accept all the holy Doctor’s books, at the end of his book *Against the Collator*:

> “Let this condition remain—yes, let it plainly remain—that the novelty of these books should be rejected if the antiquity of the same man disagrees on the same issue, and that what is found to differ from the works he composed against the Pelagians should be judged useless or inappropriate.”

If, moreover, we ask what moved these same writers to burden Augustine with so great a calumny, the cited Decampsius answers that Augustine said free will was lost and destroyed through Adam’s sin. He expressed this in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 30:

> “By using free will badly, the human being both destroyed himself and destroyed it.”

But with the same rod the synods and popes will also be beaten, since they defined the holy Master’s meaning in the same words.

Pope Saint Gelasius says in his letter to the bishops throughout Picenum:

> “They say that human beings become blessed through free will—which they corrupted, defiled, and LOST—with the assistance of good nature.”

The Council of Orange likewise defines in canon 13:

> “The choice of the will, weakened in the first human being, cannot be restored except through the grace of baptism; what was LOST cannot be restored except by him from whom it was able to be given.”

For who would deny that Adam lost, through the sin committed, the power to act well and meritoriously? Certainly this is the definition of Saint Innocent in his letter to the Carthaginian Fathers:

> “For free will,” he says, “having suffered this, while using its goods too thoughtlessly, fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression, and found no way by which it could rise thereafter. It would have lain crushed beneath this ruin, deceived in its freedom forever, unless Christ’s coming had raised it up afterward through his grace.”

Meanwhile, let Augustine himself be heard as his own interpreter, explaining his statements before the apostolic see:

> “We do not say that through Adam’s sin free will perished from human nature, but that, in human beings subject to the devil, it is effective for sinning, yet not effective for living well and piously unless the human will itself has been liberated by God’s grace and assisted toward every good action, word, and thought.”

(*On the Letter to Boniface*, book II, chapter 5, and book I, chapter 2.)

## § V. Those Who Say That Saint Augustine Inclined toward Sabellius against Arius and toward Arius against Sabellius Are Likewise Mistaken

[Col. 0758C]

Annatus unwillingly drags forward two other witnesses against Augustine: Cornelius Mussus, bishop of Bitonto, on page 865, and the great theologian John Scotus, on page 872.

The former says in chapter 5 of his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans:

> “Therefore, let Augustine move you not at all. For this is peculiar to him: when he attacks some error, he exaggerates it with such vehemence that he seems to provide grounds for the opposing error. Thus, when he attacks Arius, he seems to favor Sabellius; when he attacks Sabellius, Arius; when he attacks Pelagius, the Manichaeans; and when he attacks the Manichaeans, Pelagius.”

The latter, in book II, distinction 33, question 2, response to the first objection, writes:

> “And thus great weight must be given to the heretics against whom the saints were speaking, just as Augustine, against Arius, seems somehow to incline toward Sabellius, and conversely; similarly, against Pelagius he seems to incline toward Arius.”

Annatus correctly suggests that perhaps “Manichaean” should be read there. So much for him.

But Mussus speaks modestly: he says that Augustine, when disputing against Arius, seems to favor Sabellius. Scotus expressed the same point more mildly, for he added “as it were, he seems.” They said this not because of an inept method on Augustine’s part, but because of the difficulty of the mystery and the less perceptive intellect of certain readers—something Augustine willingly concedes, as we have noted.

Yet Annatus says on the same page, 872:

> “Thus it came about, as we previously reported from others, that Augustine inclined toward the opposite.”

Nevertheless, the others write that he appeared, or seemed as if, to incline in that direction.

But for modern writers to try to prove from this that Saint Augustine, when disputing against Arius, inclined toward Sabellius is an obvious calumny. For when disputing against Arius and asserting the unity of essence, he never seemed to confuse the persons into one, so that he should be said to favor Sabellius.

Let them produce even one statement of Augustine’s, and we shall concede the entire case to them. Indeed, no mortal ever held the middle path between Arius and Sabellius so precisely as Augustine, who walked along the very central line of that path.

I shall produce one or two testimonies by which the adversaries may be utterly convicted of falsehood.

The holy Doctor, in Treatise 37 on John, addressed his people of Hippo as follows [Col. 0759B]:

> “In the error of the Sabellians, there is only one, the Father himself who is the Son. In the error of the Arians, the Father is indeed one and the Son another, but the Son himself is not only another person but also another thing. What then are you, IN THE MIDDLE? You have excluded the Sabellian; exclude the Arian as well. The Father is Father, the Son is Son: another person, not another thing, because he says, ‘I and the Father are one,’ just as yesterday also, insofar as I was able, I emphasized. When they hear ‘we are,’ let the confused Sabellian withdraw; when they hear ‘one,’ let the confused Arian withdraw. Let the Catholic guide his vessel of faith BETWEEN THE TWO, because shipwreck must be avoided on both sides.”

What could have been said more learnedly, more subtly, or more truly? He impressed this upon the people everywhere, so that the royal road between Sabellius and Arius might be followed. Augustine must certainly be heard again, in Treatise 71 on John, where he refutes the heretics most elegantly in these words [Col. 0759C]:

> “You speak contrary things, but not in the same way as falsehood is contrary to truth; rather, you speak as two false things are contrary to each other. By going astray, you proceed in opposite directions; THE WAY IN THE MIDDLE is the way that you abandon. You are separated from one another by a greater distance than either of you is from the way itself, whose deserters you are. You come from this side, and you from that side, toward this place; do not cross over from one to the other, but, by coming from both sides to us, meet one another in us. Sabellians, recognize the one whom you pass over; Arians, make equal the one whom you subordinate, and you will walk with us on the true way. For each of you certainly ought to be admonished by the other. Hear, Sabellian: the Son is so far from being the Father himself, but is another, that the Arian asserts him to be unequal to the Father. Hear, Arian: the Son is so far equal to the Father that the Sabellian says he is the same as the Father. You, add what you remove; you, complete what you diminish; and both of you will stand with us, because neither do you remove nor do you diminish the one who is both another than the Father, so as to refute the Sabellian, and equal to the Father, so as to refute the Arian. For to both he cries: ‘I and the Father are one.’ Let the Arians hear what he says, ‘one’; let the Sabellians hear what he says, ‘we are’; and let neither be vain: the former by denying that he is equal, the latter by denying that he is another.”

Is this, if heaven allows it, the man who not only always walked along the royal road, but who showed that same road to posterity—not, I will not say, with his finger, but by making it with his feet—now to be said to have run outside its course and declined to extremes? I would sooner believe that Phaethon, driving the sun’s chariot, had actually been hurled headlong outside the ecliptic [Col. 0760A] than give credence to such claims about Augustine’s deviations.

## VI. The testimony of those who accuse Saint Augustine of innovation is examined

These are the three prelates whose authority and teaching Annatus greatly magnifies: namely, Claudius Xaintes in his book *On Atheism*, under the title “On Predestination”; Ambrosius Catharinus, likewise in a treatise on predestination; and Hieronymus Osorius, book IX *On Justice*. They accuse Saint Augustine’s teaching concerning predestination and reprobation of novelty, as though he had held an opinion contrary to all the Fathers who preceded him.

This is plainly the old refrain of the Semi-Pelagians against Saint Augustine, as is evident from the letters of Prosper. To him the holy Doctor replies in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 14:

> “Why, then, is it necessary for us to examine the little works of those who, before this heresy arose, had no need to engage with this difficult question, which they would undoubtedly have done if they had been compelled to answer such people?”

But more has been said elsewhere on this subject. Certainly Clement VIII, in the Molinaist controversies concerning grace, measured the question against the standard of Augustine’s doctrine of predestination; and Faustus, bishop of Riez, was rejected chiefly because he attacked the holy Doctor’s position on predestination. The Fathers who followed Augustine—Prosper, Fulgentius, Caesarius, and the African bishops exiled in Sardinia, as well as the Scythian monks, Remigius, Prudentius, and others—defended that position. Saint Thomas, together with the better part of the scholastics, agreed with them [Col. 0760B].

It should nevertheless be noted that more recent writers themselves do not approve exactly the testimony of these three bishops against Augustine. Moraines, *Disputation* 9, no. 57, after quoting these rather disrespectful words of Claudius Xaintes concerning the holy Doctor—

> “For the resolution of my faith, which I submit to the judgment of the Catholic Church, I hold that Doctor Augustine, inflamed by excessive zeal against the Pelagians, too precipitately disregarded the opinion and consensus of his predecessors”—

disapproving this very judgment, says:

> “Thus far the bishop of Évreux, who, as I think—and I say this with due respect to him—would have acted more prudently, and more suitably to the authority of so great a Doctor, if he had always and consistently interpreted whatever Augustine said in that favorable sense, rather than attributing to him such inconsistency in his opinions” [Col. 0760C].

Xaintes had said that Augustine was inconsistent in this matter.

Ambrosius Catharinus, in his book *On Foreknowledge and Predestination*, is so insolent against Saint Augustine that he provoked even Vasquez’s indignation. Thus Vasquez rebukes Catharinus in part I, disputation 90, no. 11:

> “Catharinus speaks with little modesty against Augustine, and is carried with abusive insolence against Augustine’s teaching, interpreted in his own fashion, and so forth. But Catharinus certainly fell most disgracefully in this matter: first, because, failing to understand Augustine’s mind, he shamelessly attacks and rejects him; and second, because Augustine himself is honorably defended against the Massilians and others by Celestine I in his first letter to the bishops of Gaul.”

After quoting Celestine’s eulogy, Vasquez adds:

> “This testimony of Celestine is sufficient to close Catharinus’s mouth.”

Let two most distinguished Doctors of the Dominican Order from Spain also be brought forward, who chastise this man’s license in attacking Augustine. Dominicus Soto, in chapter IX of his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, says of Catharinus:

> “This reverend Father could not, without the stigma of rashness, despise not only Augustine but all the saints by his novel and unheard-of commentary.”

And Bañez, part I, question 23, article 7, near the beginning, speaks of Catharinus in this way:

> “He published three little books on predestination, in which there is no erudition, but a great deal of error.”

But who, and what sort of man, this critic of Saint Augustine was, and from where he emerged, Soto relates in his *Apology for the Certainty of Grace*. At the beginning he addresses Catharinus himself:

> “Already advanced in age, you suddenly emerged from being a jurist as a theologian—you had reached your thirtieth year when at Florence you joined the Dominican Order—and at the same time began both to be heard in the schools and to write against the outstanding Doctors of the schools” [Col. 0761B].

Such is Catharinus’s authority among his own people!

For the rest, I cannot refrain from expressing indignation at Annatus, who appends this gloss to Catharinus’s testimony on page 866:

> “Ambrosius Catharinus’s judgment would rightly be suspect if he alone claimed the liberty which he sometimes professes of departing from Augustine. But the great agreement of the other Doctors sufficiently shows that in this matter Catharinus held this opinion not as Catharinus, who often indulged his own ingenuity too much, but as the archbishop and Doctor of the Catholic Church,” and so forth.

You are mistaken, Annatus; you are mistaken. Catharinus wrote those books on predestination before he became a bishop, for they were published at Paris in 1541. He, however, was appointed bishop of Minori in the Picentine region on 27 August 1546, according to Ughelli’s seventh volume of *Italia Sacra*; and archbishop of Conza on 3 June 1552. He therefore did not speak as an archbishop of the Catholic Church, but, as Soto testifies, as a theologian recently emerged from the profession of law, in books in which, according to Bañez, there is no erudition but a great deal of error. Hence Catharinus the jurist frequently praised legal codes and the *Digest* in those books, in order to persuade theologians of his opinions concerning predestination [Col. 0761C].

Osorius remains. Of him Gabriel Vasquez says in part I, disputation 89, chapter 8, no. 62:

> “The second point on which these authors—namely, Catharinus, Camerarius, and Osorius—were deceived is that they thought the Greek Fathers taught things contrary to Augustine, as though Augustine had asserted that men were chosen for glory without merits,” and so forth.

Thus, according to Vasquez, Osorius was deceived. In the first book of his *Augustine*, from chapter 2 through chapter 9, Annatus attempts at length to prove that Augustine did not hold an opinion contrary to the ancient Fathers, especially in chapter 6, where he introduces Faustus speaking against Augustine. By what reasoning, then, does he attack Augustine with these testimonies? If he says that he is merely reporting what those men thought, not what they ought to have thought about Augustine, that is enough for us: these witnesses were not fully approved by the more recent writers themselves, since, by their own admission, the first spoke less prudently, the second was shameless, immodest, and insolent, indeed did not understand Augustine’s mind, and the last is said to have been deceived.

Annatus, are these your witnesses against Augustine? But let us now hear others.

## VII. The testimonies produced against Saint Augustine from Driedo, Taper, Medina, and Vallosillo are falsified and not faithfully reported

The more recent writers, as though they were writing for the nearsighted—or rather the blind—dared to summon as witnesses against Saint Augustine men who most vigorously defend the holy Doctor’s authority. Annatus could accomplish this only by employing various tricks. For he cites men who, in plain words and without any contrary interpretation, prove themselves not merely Augustinian but most Augustinian; novel expressions are necessary to chastise the unusual assertions of the recent writers. Yet, in order to lend credibility to his witnesses, he conceals some of their words, truncates others, and alters still others, inflicting a serious injury upon so many Doctors [Col. 0762B].

First he appeals to Driedo, reporting on page 878 that he wrote:

> “Nor does he think contrary to divine grace, nor, if he is deceived, is he perniciously deceived, who, although Augustine thinks otherwise, recognizes a general goodness toward all human beings when they first attain the use of reason, so that God may assist them with particular aids.”

Driedo, in that place—namely, book *On the Captivity and Redemption of the Human Race*, treatise 4, section 2, part 8—immediately before the words cited by the opponent, says:

> “Although anyone who, with the venerable Father Augustine, humbles himself beneath the mighty hand of God and frees himself from the inquisitive questions of men through divine mercy and justice, rather than through sufficient aids proposed equally to all adults, lives SAFER.”

He then shows that the opinion concerning common aids which he suggests there does not apply to infants, an insoluble argument by which Saint Augustine had always opposed it. But he says that anyone who thinks otherwise is not perniciously deceived, if he is deceived, nor does he think contrary to divine grace. For he thinks contrary to justice rather than to grace, and is deceived tolerably, not perniciously.

But you, Annatus—to use Augustine’s words at the end of book VI *Against Julian*, whether you wish it or not—I must tell you: you are pitiably deceived, or even detestably deceived, when you pretend that Driedo bears witness against Augustine, although he expressly declares the holy Doctor’s SAFER opinion [Col. 0762D].

Again he cites the same Driedo, book I *On Free Choice*, chapter 2, part 5, where he says:

> “From the sacred Scriptures cited by Augustine, it cannot be expressly and effectively concluded in this matter that infants dying without baptism are to be tormented by the punishment of eternal fire.”

Annatus adds this notable scholion:

> “Behold how he admits that the proofs cited by Augustine from sacred Scripture are ineffective, and how he leaves it to the choice of students whether they should follow or abandon him.”

Driedo means that the scriptural testimonies brought forward by Augustine do not effectively—that is, demonstratively—prove the punishment of sense for children in the afterlife. For immediately before this he had said concerning both opinions:

> “Neither appears to be effectively demonstrable from sacred Scripture. Nor do we claim that this opinion has been demonstrated; otherwise no one could defend the opposite.”

Nor does he offer us the choice of either following or abandoning Augustine. On the contrary, he taught by his example that we should remain attached to Augustine even in this opinion, asserting:

> “Therefore, to present what appears to us MORE PROBABLE and more consonant with the sacred Scriptures, we judge that such infants are tortured by some sensible discomfort or affliction from fire and in fire.”

Do you hear, Annatus, that the opinion which you condemn as cruel on page 858 is asserted by Driedo to be more probable and more consonant with sacred Scripture? That learned man therefore serves Augustine’s cause, and no artifice can carry him over into the camp of the recent writers; you merely invent his empty name to deceive the unwary [Col. 0763B].

They next produce, as a teacher equal to Driedo, Ruardus Taperus, also a Doctor from the University of Louvain. Annatus reports on page 879 that he wrote against Augustine:

> “Nevertheless, another opinion is more consonant with Augustine, namely, that God does not grant such assistance to everyone,” and so forth.

And afterward:

> “Nevertheless, the former of these opinions appears to commend divine goodness more,” and so forth.

But here we have cause to complain about Annatus, since he omitted words of Taperus that greatly favor the Augustinian opinion. For Taperus writes at article 7, page 222:

> “Nevertheless, another opinion is more consonant with Augustine AND WITH THE COUNCILS OF THE FATHERS, namely, that God does not grant such assistance to everyone.”

Those two words pierced the mind of the recent writer. For who would not see from them how much weight, according to Taperus, is added to the Augustinian opinion? He therefore omitted them deliberately. Hence, with Augustine in book IV *Against Julian*, chapter 8, we may rightly exclaim:

> “So that it may be clear by what frauds you argue concerning so great a matter.”

Annatus adds that Taperus indicates this to be the opinion of Adrian VI, *Sentences* IV, question 1, on penance. Hence he mocks on page 886:

> “Adrian VI, too, according to what we previously reported from Ruardus Taperus, will have to be added to the list.”

But you will certainly perform no tricks upon us. What did Adrian write at the cited folio 3, in the section ‘Doubt’? We now set it forth:

> “God grants to those on the wayfarer’s journey, as I hold probably, that mercy by which he sufficiently assists them and offers them his grace, so that, by striving at least to the utmost of their strength, they might merit the forgiveness of sins; in this respect those still on the way differ from those who have passed beyond the boundary. If, however, he does the opposite—that is, if he does not grant them forgiveness of sins when they strive to the extent of their powers, which is doubtful and uncertain among the Doctors—he could in no way be accused of injustice.”

You see, first, that he says he holds this only probably. You see, second, that according to Adrian the principle “God does not deny grace to one who does what lies within him,” which the recent writers regard as absolutely certain, is doubtful and uncertain. You see, third, that God cannot be blamed if he still denies grace to those who strive to the extent of their powers. These statements of Adrian do not agree with the theology of those men.

In the same place he says:

> “In all these matters we must exclaim with Augustine: ‘O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!’”

Yet the recent writers not only fail to imitate this exclamation of Saint Augustine, but ridicule it, as was made clear above from John Adam.

In the third place comes Bartholomew Medina, a great theologian of the Dominican Order. Annatus reports his words on page 875:

> “Without doubt, it is Augustine’s opinion that a human being in pure nature possesses a natural power of acting which he does not possess in fallen nature. Nevertheless, it does not please the Doctors.”

O copyist of unimpeachable fidelity!

In that place, after presenting the opinion of certain people who asserted that the power of acting differs in a human being standing and fallen, Medina says:

> “This undoubtedly appears to be the opinion of Saint Augustine.”

Annatus reports this as:

> “Without doubt, it is Augustine’s opinion.”

You are mistaken, good man! Medina does not write that way. He says that it appears to be, not that it really is, Augustine’s opinion. But you scrape away the word “appears,” so that from Medina’s words you may insult Augustine more aggressively.

Nor does he say, “It does not please the Doctors.” Read again, and you will see that it is written:

> “Nevertheless, it does not please the learned men”—*viris doctoribus*—

by which he indicates that the opinion pleased some men, perhaps less learned, as he himself thought. He had indicated those men shortly before without naming them.

But another objection must again be heard. After reporting Medina’s opinion, the recent writer exclaims on page 876:

> “And in this way this author admits that Augustine’s doctrine on this point is both indisputable and contrary to the Doctors, and that it is contrary to HIMSELF, without any scruple about violating faith or despising antiquity.”

Annatus invents this beautifully for himself. After reporting his own opinion, Medina openly protests that he does not have Augustine as an adversary. These are his words:

> “Nor does Saint Augustine in any way oppose our opinion.”

And you dare affirm before judges that Medina admits Augustine’s doctrine to be opposed to himself? Augustine says admirably in book IV *Against Julian*, chapter 8:

> “Who would not expect wisdom from one who is arguing, if he has recognized the faith of one who is lying?”

With the same fidelity and spirit, Annatus on page 870 drags Ferdinand Vallosillo before the tribunal against Augustine, willingly or unwillingly. He says that Vallosillo indicates in many places that one is free occasionally to depart from Augustine. He then produces several testimonies of Vallosillo. Yet Vallosillo professes himself so consistently to stand with Augustine that, considering the matter with me, I am led to think that Annatus read these passages with someone else’s eyes. It is shameful and distressing to suspect such gross blunders—not frauds, for I will not call them that—in a man of such great reputation among recent writers.

But let us examine the objections themselves.

> “In many places,” he says, “he sufficiently indicates that one is free occasionally to depart from Augustine, as in question 13 on Chrysostom, volume II, when he asks about the cause of predestination and reprobation.”

But why do you not produce Vallosillo’s words against Augustine, as you did when reporting the testimonies of the others? Surely because there are none. I should say rather that they are contrary: for he adheres so stubbornly to the Augustinian opinion of gratuitous predestination that he says in the same place:

> “The contrary opinion is not probable, although it is not heretical, and no one ought to assert it in the schools or elsewhere.”

And you say that this man, in a disputation on predestination, grants freedom to depart from Augustine?

Again, in the same place—that is, in question 13—after explaining Chrysostom’s testimonies, he adds:

> “Augustine needs no advocate. For although he had previously adhered steadfastly to this dogma, after examining the matter more carefully he retracted, in countless places, the opinion that God predestines human beings on the basis of foreseen merits of natural faith.”

The opponent adds:

> “And in question 18, volume III of Saint Augustine, where he disputes whether other virtues can exist without faith, he speaks as follows, and so forth. For Saint Thomas does not agree with Gregory of Rimini, nor with Blessed Augustine, that all acts of unbelievers are sins.”

We reply that Vallosillo said this while writing from the opinion of others and hurrying on to other matters. For in question 22 on Saint Ambrose, where he treats the issue explicitly—and to which he refers in volume VII of Augustine, questions 18 and 19, and in volume VIII, question 3, and elsewhere—he plainly states, in the section “Against Gregory’s arguments,” in the response to the fourth argument, that Saint Augustine did not hold the same opinion as Gregory of Rimini concerning the works of unbelievers.

And in volume III, question 18, he writes that Saint Augustine agreed with Saint Thomas concerning the virtues of unbelievers. In volume VIII, question 3, asking whether all the works of unbelievers are sins, he says of the same holy Doctor:

> “And thus in the matter itself he agrees with the common sense of the Church and with the teaching of the scholastic Doctors.”

This, then, is Vallosillo’s opinion concerning Augustine [Col. 0765C].

Annatus continues:

> “And in question 25, volume III of Augustine, where he concludes that servile fear is both good and meritorious, although Augustine appears to have thought otherwise; in this Vallosillo may perhaps have been deceived.”

I appeal to the eyes of the readers, for he says nothing there about Augustine, as Annatus pretends. At the end of that question, however, he interprets a statement of the holy Doctor; nowhere does he write that Augustine appears to have asserted that servile fear is not good. Thus the recent writer is not only injurious to Saint Augustine, but also to Vallosillo himself, whom he calls deceived while attributing to him statements about Augustine that Vallosillo never even dreamed of making [Col. 0765D].

He adds, fourth:

> “And in question 10, volume X, where he says that Augustine’s opinion concerning the cause of reprobation displeased most of the ancient Fathers.”

Very well; but immediately he indicates who those Fathers were: the Massilians and Faustus of Riez. Annatus kept this silent, for he saw that those Fathers were the teachers of the Semi-Pelagians—that is, men of no authority whatever.

Moreover, in the same place Vallosillo refutes Catharinus, who criticized Saint Augustine’s opinion, and concludes:

> “There is therefore no reason why Catharinus should have said in the preface to his little book that he had reached the point of predestination by a true method—a point that had always been hidden from Augustine and the other earlier Fathers.”

Finally, he concludes as follows:

> “And in question 30, volume IV, where he responds to the authority of Augustine, which is opposed to him in that question of whether a wife may fornicate with her husband’s consent, he begins his response in this way: ‘On behalf of Blessed Augustine, we reply that we have determined what must be held according to the truth.’”

Annatus reports Vallosillo’s testimony in such truncated form that Augustine’s authority appears to have been held in little regard. For that writer immediately adds:

> “And Augustine himself merely proposed the question whether, in that case, a wife could licitly fornicate with the consent of her husband—a sense in which the scholastic Doctors do not dispute the question.”

Afterward he appends another explanation:

> “Second, we say that Blessed Augustine did not define the case, as is clear from his words. For after proposing the case, he concluded by asserting: ‘I do not argue here for either side; let each person think what he wishes,’ and so forth. From this text it is clear that when he says, ‘Let each person think what he wishes,’ he asserted nothing definitively, but left the matter to the opinion and judgment of others.”

This is what that most learned bishop says. With the utmost diligence and immense labor he explained every doubt that might arise throughout the volumes of Saint Augustine, and he especially set himself to demonstrate that Augustine had nowhere asserted anything false.

Who, therefore, would not resent, and resent bitterly, the fact that this vigorous defender of the holy Doctor is dragged by recent writers before the tribunal against that same Doctor, and is made, by their own mouths, to say things that he not only did not say, but which he most solidly demonstrated to be far removed from Augustine’s meaning? [Col. 0766C]

## VIII. The testimonies of Viguerius, Soto, Faber, and Horantius examined

Although the recent writers have been convicted in the preceding repetition of their witnesses, they nevertheless do not blush to look upon the faces of the judges, much less to open their mouths again against Augustine. Indeed, they produce new witnesses against the holy Doctor, so that, if the contest were to be decided by the number of witnesses, one might fear that Augustine would be overwhelmed by their multitude. But, having been encouraged by the success that has thus far attended us, we proceed to examine the remaining witnesses.

John Viguerius is named on page 872 because he wrote the following in section 6, *On Original Sin*:

> “Furthermore, Saint Augustine is not held in this matter. Hence Gennadius, speaking of the same Augustine in *On Illustrious Men*, says: ‘Although he caused the less capable to doubt concerning aborted infants, nevertheless his error, as I said above, being contracted through much discussion and magnified by the struggle of his opponents, had not yet raised the question of heresy.’ By these words he indicates that Saint Augustine erred in this opinion, but was not himself a heretic, because he was not pertinacious; indeed, he retracted it in his letter to Julian . . . Furthermore, the decretal *Majores*, on baptism, in which it was determined that they do not suffer the punishment of sense, had not yet been published in Saint Augustine’s time. For the same Augustine, who revered the Church beyond measure, would not have asserted the opposite if it had been published.”

But this witness deserves no credibility before the judges, because he reveals himself to be completely ignorant of what he says. First, Gennadius, in chapter 38, is not speaking of Saint Augustine’s opinion concerning the punishments of children who die without baptism, but of the resurrection of children who die in their mothers’ wombs.

For after Gennadius had said that Augustine had erred through excessive discursiveness, he adds:

> “He proceeded with similar integrity also concerning the resurrection of the dead, although he caused the less capable to doubt concerning aborted infants. Nevertheless, he remained Catholic, and his error, contracted through much discussion, as I said, and magnified by the struggle of his opponents, had not yet raised the question of heresy.”

For the holy Doctor, in book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 13, raises the question whether aborted births will rise on the day of judgment.

Viguerius therefore neither understood Gennadius’s words nor reported them faithfully, for he omitted the following:

> “Nevertheless, he remained Catholic.”

Those words change the sense of the period. For Gennadius does not charge the error concerning aborted infants, but the error concerning predestination by an absolute decree of God, as has been said elsewhere.

Nor was Augustine’s opinion concerning the punishments of children magnified by the struggle of his opponents. The Semi-Pelagians merely said that Augustine had doubts about them, as is clear from Hilary’s letter to Augustine.

Furthermore, it is false that the holy Doctor retracted that opinion in a letter to Julian, for Augustine wrote no letter to Julian. Indeed, in the *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book III, chapter 200, composed in his final years, he remained constant in the same opinion:

> “But if the child is not rescued from the power of darkness and remains there, why should you be surprised that he will be with the devil in eternal fire, since he is not permitted to enter the kingdom of God?”

Nor was this assertion of the holy Doctor condemned by Innocent III in that decretal, as Gregory rightly notes in *Sentences* II, distinction 33, question 3; and we have already demonstrated this at length [Col. 0767C].

The number of witnesses is increased by Dominicus Soto’s criticism, in which he attacks Saint Augustine’s opinion concerning the punishments of children. In book I *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 14, as Annatus reports on page 874, Soto says:

> “Augustine appears to torment children more than is just; hence those who subscribe to his opinion are very few and are called tormentors of children.”

Annatus likewise had brought John Faber, bishop of Vienna, forward on page 871, in homily 9 *On Original Sin*, as agreeing with Soto’s opinion, since Faber said that Augustine, holding this view, had spoken excessively.

But Augustine nowhere treated the question of the punishments of children explicitly. He stated his opinion because of the occasion provided by the Pelagians; in Sermon 14 *On the Words of the Apostle* he spoke about it at greater length than elsewhere.

Nor are those who adhere to him very few. The pontiffs Gelasius and Gregory, Avitus, Fulgentius, Isidore, the Sardinian synod of African Fathers, Prudentius, Bede, Aelred, and other holy Fathers followed the Augustinian opinion concerning the punishments of children. Likewise among theologians there were Gregory, Driedo, Musaeus, Moreau, Macedo, Polman, Paludanus, Poncius, Conrius, and the Doctors of Louvain generally. We listed the testimonies of all of them in chapter 3, section 5 [Col. 0768A].

How much respect Soto showed to Augustine in the controversies concerning grace may be gathered from chapter 2 of the same book, where he says:

> “Augustine himself recognized this, as he recognized most of the other things that can be devised in support of this work. It is therefore no wonder if we repeatedly summon him here as ALMOST THE SOLE LEADER, ABOVE THE OTHER FATHERS.”

So much for him.

Francis Horantius is also cited against Augustine—a genuinely learned man who took part in the Council of Trent. After saying that Cyprian and Jerome had erred in certain matters, he adds the following concerning Augustine in book IV, chapter 3, *On Theological Topics*:

> “The same thing happened to the most learned Augustine. But where am I being carried? To whom has it not happened?”

Anyone who refused to say that Augustine had ever erred would deprive him of extraordinary praise by eliminating the two books of the *Retractions*. But Annatus had to prove that Horantius had criticized Augustine in his books against the Pelagians; for he had promised that he would establish this by the testimony of writers.

In the meantime, hear that writer’s judgment concerning Augustine. In book I, chapter 51, where he discusses grace and free choice, he appends this noble eulogy of Augustine:

> “Augustine is by far the foremost of all in examining the mysteries of our faith. We receive this teaching as though it had fallen from heaven; we venerate it as holy; we embrace it as conforming to the rule of our faith; and we retain it as fully consistent with the ancient tradition of the Fathers and in every way agreeing and corresponding with the truth” [Col. 0768C].

In chapter 46 he calls Saint Augustine “the most learned and holiest of all”; in chapter 48 he says: “Let the mind of the great Augustine be weighed.”

This, then, is Horantius’s judgment concerning the holy Doctor, so that the recent writers cannot justly name him against Augustine.

## IX. The testimonies of John of Bologna, Arboreus, Aragon, Pennot, Estius, Vega, and Tostatus examined

The recent writers rifled through the catalogs of all the libraries, searching for statements by Doctors, even those who were not especially celebrated, by which Augustine’s authority might be diminished. In fact, they happened upon a small book by some John of Bologna.
