Annatus reports on page 878 that, refusing to accept Augustine’s interpretations of the Apostle’s words, “God wills all human beings to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4), he said:

> “This manner of speaking does not appear sufficient.”

Likewise:

> “It is not probable that the Apostle meant this.”

First, this writer, in his tacit resolution of the objections on page 365 of the Louvain edition of 1555, followed Augustine’s other interpretation but did not wish to name the holy Doctor, in order to pass over the name more modestly. He considered it a matter of religious scruple to depart openly from so sacred a name, and instead said:

> “Finally, I am not unaware that a certain outstanding interpreter of sacred Scripture explains this passage in this way.”

Later he says:

> “The same outstanding Doctor proposes another meaning.”

But the recent writers not only reject these interpretations when Augustine is named; they also burden them with insults. Molina calls them, even at first sight, foreign and forced in the *Concordia*, question 19, article 6, disputation 1; Petavius says they appear more suitable for evasion than straight and solid reasoning, volume I of *Theological Dogmas*, book X, chapter 3 [Col. 0769A].

Yet the same writer, in the principal question concerning predestination, says:

> “We shall next set forth our opinion, and establish it by statements of Blessed Fulgentius taken from Blessed Augustine.”

Throughout that work he repeatedly impresses the testimonies of Saint Augustine upon the reader.

He opposes [this] on p. 880, citing Johannes Arboreus on the words of the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 3: “Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith.” There he calls Saint Augustine’s interpretation barren and to be rejected. I am surprised that the other [writer] escaped Annatus’s supreme diligence; for he says: “It is a ridiculous interpretation and to be rejected.” But rather [Col. 0769B] let Arboreus be the ridiculous witness, since he presumes to teach Augustine Latin grammar.

The holy Doctor, in book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 10, adduces those words of the Apostle to prove that people are not justified by the law, but by faith obtaining the help of grace, adding the following:

> “Whether he meant ‘boasting’ in the praiseworthy sense—that which is in the Lord—and said that it had been excluded, that is, not driven away so that it would disappear, but brought forth so that it might stand out (whence certain craftsmen who work in silver are also called *exclusores*, ‘formers’ or ‘expressers’); or whether he wished to mention the blameworthy boasting that arises from pride, namely, that of those who seem to themselves to live justly and boast as though they had not received what he says is excluded—not by the law of works, but by the law of faith—that is, expelled and cast away, because through the law of faith each person recognizes that, if he lives well in any respect, [Col. 0769C] he possesses this by the grace of God.”

Thus the holy Doctor, having indicated the first interpretation, which might perhaps occur to someone, proceeds to the second, to which he consistently adheres in his books against the Pelagians. Arboreus, however, plays the ridiculous grammarian, accusing Augustine of barbarism and saying:

> “Neither are eminent painters, nor the makers or delineators of the most elegant paintings, customarily called *exclusores*, but rather sculptors or image-makers.”

As though Augustine could have been ignorant of the vernacular name used in his day by certain craftsmen of the silversmith’s art. The same holy Father writes on Psalm 67, concerning the words “that these may bring forth [the form],” and says:

> “In the art of silverworking, those are called *exclusores* who know how to bring forth the form of a vessel from a shapeless mass.”

Hence it is clear that those silversmiths whom we call in Latin *fusores*, “casters,” were called by the common people *exclusores* in Augustine’s [Col. 0769D] time. Certainly, just as in 2 Kings 24 the silversmiths who enclosed gems in gold or silver are called *clusores*, so those who cast vessels from gold or silver were called *exclusores*. There is no need to investigate the etymology of this word more carefully, since names are also assigned arbitrarily and that word was in ordinary use. Arboreus, however, wrongly applies the term to painters and painting, whereas Augustine understands it of silversmiths who emboss or strike out (*excusores*), that is, of those who produce statues or anything else by stamping or engraving.

Arboreus therefore cast his vote ineptly in this matter. Annatus, however, adds this noble scholion on p. 881:

> “And yet that book was written by Augustine against the Pelagians, and Paul’s passage there is pressed against the same [Col. 0770A] people.”

What of it? The holy Doctor writes that two interpretations can be devised for the celebrated saying of Paul, and that Pelagian heresy is strangled by either of them. If one interpretation is displeasing, the other may be accepted; this was sufficient for Augustine. Nor is someone who does not accept the first interpretation immediately to be judged an enemy of Augustine. Augustine does not require this when he says, “whether he meant praiseworthy boasting,” and so forth, “or blameworthy boasting.” By these words he indicates that he does not wish to linger over the precise explanation of the terms: the Pelagians are convicted by either interpretation, and one may follow whichever interpretation one prefers.

In any case, those matters may have escaped Arboreus, provided that in questions concerning predestination and grace he professes himself Augustinian. In book 10 of the *Theosophy*, chapter 9, he says: “Augustine was the most devoted champion of free will.” In book 14, [Col. 0770B] chapter 7:

> “If you possess any judgment at all, you will easily recognize, from Augustine’s sound and lucid doctrine, that God did not love Jacob because he had foreseen his future merits.”

Throughout that volume, in the questions concerning grace, he says: “This is the Augustinian assertion.” And at the beginning of the book, wishing to show from the outset how devoted he is to the holy Doctor, he writes:

> “We shall establish separately those aspects of this assertion that bear the character of Augustinian doctrine.”

Thus the recent writers cannot conceal their own judgment concerning Augustine, insofar as the doctrines of predestination and grace are concerned, beneath either the leaves or the shadow of this tree.

Yet, in order to batter Augustine’s authority more closely, they call Peter of Aragon and Gabriel Pennoto, Augustinians, to their aid. Aragon, in *2–2*, [Col. 0770C] question 10, article 6, after having proved that a person can perform a morally good act without the grace of God, adds:

> “From what has been said, therefore, it follows that Saint Augustine’s position was that people can perform no morally good work without the grace of God; Gregory affirmed the same.”

Hence Annatus says on p. 882:

> “And thus Peter of Aragon openly professes that he departs from Augustine.”

Pennoto, however, in book 5 of the *Defence*, chapter 6, says that one must by no means believe that

> “every argument of Augustine is an exact demonstration, every answer a dogma of faith, and every interpretation of passages of Sacred Scripture a certain and infallible rule for interpreting the divine Scriptures themselves,”

and so forth. After quoting these words, Annatus mocks him:

> “See, reader, with what moderation in commending the doctrine of Saint [Col. 0770D] Augustine even those who, by profession, are his worshipers, imitators, and disciples in both orders—the canons and the hermits—conduct themselves. Thus one may perceive how superstitious is the religion of the modern Baians, who, under the specious pretext of opposing errors, pretend to have only Augustine on their lips, before their eyes, and in their hearts.”

I cannot deny that Aragon held that opinion. Nevertheless, in the same place, conclusion 2, he admits that a person without grace can rarely, infrequently, and only with great difficulty perform a good work, so that he seems to depart very little from the Augustinian doctrine. Further, in the section beginning “Nevertheless,” despite this, he proves that Saint Augustine’s opinion contains no error and can therefore be maintained.

Yet lest this domestic witness move you even [Col. 0771A] slightly, we set against him three celebrated doctors from our own eremitical family, who cling tenaciously to the opinion of Saint Augustine: Gregory of Rimini, *2*, distinction 29, question 1, article 2; Basil Pontius, the great theologian of Salamanca, in the *Relections on the Aids of Divine Grace*; and Gaspar Casalius, the Portuguese bishop, in book 1 of *The Fourfold Justice*. They explain Augustine’s doctrine, fortify it with the strongest arguments, and defend it against the darts of its adversaries.

Indeed, the most subtle of the more recent writers, Vasquez, argues for the same doctrine at great length in *1–2*, disputation 190. He is followed, from the same family, by Turrianus, *Treatise on Grace*, disputation 4; Maeratius, volume 2, the same treatise, section 8; Ripalda, volume 1, *On the Supernatural Being*, disputation 20, section 6; and others.

[Col. 0771B] Pennoto, however, is not opposed to Augustine. Augustine used even probable arguments in confirmation of his opinions; if those arguments were demonstrative, we would call the recent writers foolish for devising answers to them. We maintain only that the principal positions of Saint Augustine against the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians cannot be attacked without incurring the mark of rashness.

How little Pennoto favors the cause of the recent writers, everyone can see from these words of his:

> “If Celestine, pontiff of the Roman Church, calls the slanderers of the doctrine of Saint Augustine concerning predestination ‘plants growing badly’ and ‘wicked men’ upon whom perpetual silence ought to be imposed, and calls them followers of perverse and condemned doctrines, then, by [Col. 0771C] contrast, he approves Augustine’s doctrine of predestination as sound, pious, catholic, and a matter of faith, a doctrine which Catholics cannot contradict.”

Book 5 of the *Defence*, chapter 16, number 2.

Annatus nevertheless says, in book 8, chapter 2, p. 860:

> “Let us posit the position that favors free will more strongly, and let us say that, before foreseen merits, people are predestined to grace, but after the good use of grace has been foreseen, they are predestined to glory. What follows from this against the rules laid down by Celestine? Absolutely nothing. This, therefore, is one of the questions which Celestine does not wish to have asserted, if we believe Baronius.”

You now perceive, you now see, how beautifully Pennoto sings in harmony with you. As for what you add concerning Baronius, we demonstrated in section 1, from Baronius himself, that it is false.

[Col. 0771D] William Estius is also brought forward. In book 1 of the *Sentences*, distinction 44, section 14, he says:

> “But if someone nevertheless insists that Augustine’s words, which have been brought forward, cannot be bent to this meaning, and thinks that he really held another opinion, then we shall reply that those things which he disputed concerning the aid given to the first man and to the angels—things expressed obscurely and, as it seems, outside the authority of Scripture—were presented so that, by comparison with our restoration through Christ, the grace of that restoration might shine forth more clearly. They ought not, therefore, to prejudice the doctrine which, among other Fathers and in Saint Thomas himself, who is a most exact teacher in matters of this kind, is found expressed more clearly.”

To demonstrate his reverence for the holy Doctor, Estius expended much [Col. 0772A] effort in the same distinction 44, sections 13 and 14, to draw Augustine over to his own position. But because he saw that the matters just quoted could scarcely be made convincing, he added them—not so that we should judge Augustine to be held in low esteem, but so that he might perhaps evade an inconvenient objection from an adversary.

What displeased Estius, however, Hilary of Arles writes had formerly displeased the Semi-Pelagians as well, in his letter to Augustine, in the section beginning “Furthermore, they are troubled”:

> “Furthermore, they are troubled that grace is divided in this way—grace which was given either then to the first man or is now given to all,”

and so forth.

Yet that writer says in book 2, distinction 24, section 10:

> “Let Augustine be the first of these, since it is certain that he defended the cause of the catholic faith against the Pelagians more sharply and more fully than the other ecclesiastical writers.”

And in book 1, distinction 41, section 6:

> “Celestine, the pontiff, approved Saint Augustine’s doctrine concerning the grace of Christ, which for the most [Col. 0772B] part consists in asserting gratuitous predestination, in his letter to the bishops of Gaul.”

I omit the many other passages that Estius repeatedly quotes in praise of the holy Doctor; for the Louvain and Douai theologians have always been accustomed to be wholly devoted to Augustine.

Alphonsus Tostatus disagrees with Augustine on certain matters relating to the interpretation of Sacred Scripture. Yet Annatus says on p. 867:

> “See, reader … whether he thinks that no one should be granted the freedom to contradict any of the things that Augustine wrote against the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians.”

We maintain that Saint Augustine’s doctrine against the Pelagians, on account of the Church’s extensive approval, must be placed in a higher degree of authority than the doctrine of those who, as Tostatus [Col. 0772C] says according to Annatus, wrote solely by human ingenuity.

For the rest, read Tostatus’s distinguished encomium of Augustine in Macedo’s *Euchological Harmony*, p. 431, where he says of Tostatus:

> “Although he sometimes disagrees with Augustine on certain minor questions, in the matter of predestination and grace he is wholly in agreement with Augustine.”

Adam, in part 3 of his *Calvin Destroyed*, chapter 6, adds Andrew Vega, who said that he regretted that Augustine had not clearly answered the objections of his adversaries against grace, in book 12 on the Council of Trent, chapter 22, concerning justification.

Nevertheless, in the same place, after saying that the Pelagians had brought sixteen arguments against divine grace, Vega writes:

> “And to all of these Augustine replied copiously and learnedly, in accordance with his outstanding doctrine.”

He nevertheless adds [Col. 0772D] there certain things that cannot please even Augustine’s adversaries. For he gives preachers the following rule for preaching the mystery of predestination and of the necessary grace required for believing, loving God, repenting, and so forth:

> “I would wish this to be taught clearly and distinctly: that all exercises of the virtues for which we believe special grace from God to be necessary are just as much within our power as if God’s general concurrence alone were sufficient, indeed as if nothing were required for all of them except our own will alone.”

After several similar remarks, he adds:

> “I have often wished that Augustine had replied openly and plainly to those who objected to him that preaching predestination and grace before the people ought to be abandoned.”

But who does not [Col. 0773A] see from Vega’s rule that prayer ought never to be urged upon hearers? Prayer is a testimony to divine grace, since no one asks another for help in doing something that he can perform just as easily by himself. By this argument the Pelagians were convicted by the Fathers.

If the faithful are to be exhorted to implore divine assistance, as the Church does in the sacred mysteries, the will must not be commended as though it alone were sufficient for undertaking the virtues and avoiding temptations. Yet I am astonished, when I hear Vega insert this opinion in the same place, that we are nevertheless required to implore God’s help with continual and importunate groans.

Moreover, if this is what the people are to be taught, how is the power of the human will alone to be asserted? Rather, its supreme weakness is shown, since to assist it the grace of God is not merely awaited but [Col. 0773B] implored with continual and importunate groans.

Augustine treats these matters so solidly in his book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, from chapter 14 onward, that no one could desire anything either clearer or more effective. Accordingly, even Vega’s adversaries themselves ought not to approve his testimony, since he asserts things that they themselves would reject, if they possess sound judgment.

## X. The testimony of Dominic Bañez against Augustine is examined more closely and shown to have been exaggerated.

The testimony of this Spanish theologian, whom the recent writers have always found hostile, they magnify against the holy Doctor with great confidence. Since they proceed in this matter in bad faith, we must examine it more carefully.

Adam, in part 3 of his *Calvin Destroyed*, chapter 9, p. 667, writes that he is [Col. 0773C] permitted to shudder at Saint Augustine’s opinion that reprobation arises from original sin alone, because that opinion is the mother of the doctrine which Calvin, with such impiety and fury, inculcates against the Church. He then invokes Bañez’s support or testimony, since Bañez writes of the same Augustinian opinion in part 1, question 23, article 5:

> “This opinion is not probable. It contains no small difficulty. It seems impossible and altogether incredible that God should have reprobated a person on account of original guilt. No believer will dare to say this. If Saint Augustine had wished to attend to the flaw in this consequence, he would never have asserted that original sin alone is the cause of the reprobation of all reprobate human beings.”

Annatus, in the cited book 8, chapter 4, p. 874, omitting the preceding words, printed the words “If Saint Augustine…” and the rest in much [Col. 0773D] larger characters, so that they would immediately catch and fill the reader’s eyes. After quoting them, he exclaims:

> “These are Bañez’s words—words which most people seem not to have sufficiently noticed while exaggerating Molina’s audacity in alleging that Augustine lacked some light for reconciling the efficacy of the divine decrees and aids with created freedom.”

Thus they brandish the support of an eminent theologian against Augustine.

Adam comments on the words spoken by Bañez against Augustine, although that writer asserted the opposite. For after recounting Saint Augustine’s opinion concerning predestination, Bañez admits that it contains no small difficulty, and immediately, to demonstrate this, proposes six arguments against it. At the end of the [Col. 0774A] third he writes:

> “Therefore Augustine’s opinion is not probable.”

At the end of the second:

> “It seems impossible and altogether incredible,”

and so forth.

But he did not put these words forward as his own opinion; rather, he introduced them in the person of someone arguing against Augustine, as is clear from what he teaches afterward. In the same place he reports three opinions: first, Saint Augustine’s; second, that of certain Thomists; and third, Saint Thomas’s.

Concerning the second, in the section beginning “Furthermore, it is manifest,” he judges as follows:

> “And thus the second opinion can easily be maintained; nor do I think that it differs from Saint Thomas’s opinion except in name alone.”

Then, in the section beginning “The third opinion is Saint Thomas’s,” after comparing Augustine’s opinion with that second opinion, he says:

> “Therefore, as we shall say later, the second opinion is no less probable—or perhaps even more probable—than the first, that of Saint Augustine.”

Therefore, according to [Col. 0774B] Bañez, Saint Augustine’s opinion is probable; indeed, he is uncertain whether the second opinion is more probable—he says “perhaps”—than that of Saint Augustine. And this second opinion, he thinks, differs from Saint Thomas’s opinion only in name.

Adam is therefore proved false when he declares that the words “Therefore Augustine’s opinion is not probable,” which that theologian uttered for the sake of argument, were his own judgment concerning Augustine’s opinion.

The same must again be said concerning Bañez’s other statement. In the second argument he says:

> “It seems impossible and altogether incredible that God should have determined from eternity mercifully and truly to remit original guilt and nevertheless to have reprobated a person because of that guilt.”

And in the third argument he concludes:

> “Therefore original sin, already remitted, is the cause and reason of eternal [Col. 0774C] condemnation, which no believer will dare to say.”

Adam, however, having erased the words “already remitted,” and so forth, hastily lumped the remainder together into a single proposition, so as to make the censure more severe.

But Bañez shows that he spoke those words in the person of his adversaries, when shortly afterward he writes:

> “But it will be worthwhile first to note certain things concerning Augustine’s opinion, which must be avoided by those who wish to defend it.”

And immediately afterward:

> “Above all, one must be careful not to concede that anyone is condemned to the punishment of loss on account of original sin, already remitted, as though on account of a demeriting cause,”

and so forth.

From these words it is clear that the proposition which he infers in the arguments—“Original sin, already remitted, is the cause and reason of eternal condemnation”—is to be utterly [Col. 0774D] denied by those who wish to defend the opinion of the holy Doctor.

Therefore, if he thinks that proposition must be removed from Augustine’s assertion as absurd, how can he himself impose it upon Augustine? Indeed, Augustine nowhere said that remitted original sin was the sole cause and reason why many are reprobated, at least not in the formal sense. We have discussed this more fully in chapter 4, section 10.

Let these remarks suffice against the man who hired the witness. We must now deal with Bañez himself. The words of Bañez, as Annatus cites them, are as follows:

> “Finally, this is our judgment concerning the matter, if our judgment has any weight. For I would believe that Augustine was so concerned to destroy the error of the Pelagians, who asserted that foreseen [Col. 0775A] merits were the cause of divine predestination and election, that, since it was considered that the foreknowledge of Esau’s evil works was the cause of his reprobation, it immediately seemed to Augustine to follow that Jacob’s future good works were likewise the cause of his predestination. For this reason he always denied that the foreknowledge of Esau’s evil works was the cause of his reprobation.”

He then gives the reason why that inference is not legitimate: good merits themselves are effects of predestination, whereas sins are not effects of reprobation. Hence sins can indeed be the reason and cause of [Col. 0775B] reprobation.

Finally, he adds the censure which Annatus printed in larger characters:

> “Therefore it is manifest that the reason for predestination and reprobation is not the same, so that, if a cause of reprobation is granted on our part, a cause of predestination must likewise be granted. If, therefore, Saint Augustine had wished to attend to the flaw in this consequence, he would never have asserted that original sin alone, universally, is the cause of reprobation,”

and so forth.

I have reproduced nearly the whole opinion which this writer brought forward against Augustine. Once I have refuted it, it will be clear that Bañez’s censure provides Augustine with no prejudice.

First, Bañez was mistaken in believing that, in book 1 to Simplician, question 2—where the holy Doctor discusses this matter at greater length—Augustine had been concerned to refute the error of the Pelagians. That book was written at the beginning of Augustine’s episcopate, as is clear from book 2 of the *Retractations*, chapter 1, and from the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 4. The beginning of the holy Father’s episcopate, however, fell in the year 395, whereas the Pelagians did not begin to appear in the [Col. 0775C] world until the year 411.

Therefore, in that work addressed to Simplician, Augustine was not at all refuting the error of the Pelagians. Rather, at the request of that bishop of Milan, he explained at length the seventh chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, from verse 10 through verse 30; for this is what Simplician had requested, as is clear from the beginning of the second question.

He discusses more extensively Paul’s words beginning at verse 11:

> “For when they had not yet been born, nor had done anything good or evil, so that the purpose of God according to election might remain, not from works but from him who calls, it was said to him: ‘The elder shall serve the younger,’ as it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.’”

After demonstrating that Jacob was not elected on account of foreseen good works, Augustine inferred that the same must be said, by parity of reasoning, of Esau—namely, that Esau too was not hated on account of foreseen [Col. 0775D] evil works.

Let the holy Doctor be heard:

> “Or perhaps,” he says, “just as that statement concerning Jacob was made without any merits of good action, so Esau was hateful without any merits of evil action? For if, because God foreknew his future evil works, he predestined him to serve the younger, then for that same reason he predestined Jacob so that the elder should serve him, because he foreknew Jacob’s future good works; and then what he says—‘not from works’—is false. But if it is true that it was not from works, and he proves this because it was said concerning those not yet born and who had not yet done anything, then, since faith likewise did not yet exist in those not yet born, by what merit would Esau be hated before he was born?”

From that word “perhaps” [Col. 0776A] I infer that the holy Father is speaking in the manner of someone conducting an argument. This is also evident from what he says shortly afterward:

> “But how could he hate Esau, unless it is unjust to hate someone without the merit of injustice? If we concede this, Jacob begins to be loved for the merit of justice. But if that is true, then what he says—‘not from works’—is false.”

See also the section “Why, then, was Esau rejected?”

Augustine therefore introduced that consequence while arguing, not because he considered it true, as we shall explain. The whole force of the inference lies in the words of the Apostle, who plainly excludes both good works as the reason Jacob was loved and evil works as the reason Esau was hated. For he says: “before they had done anything good or evil”—that is, before they had performed any evil or good works—“not from works,” namely, good or evil works, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

Hence it is false what Bañez [Col. 0776B] says in the section beginning “Therefore it is manifest”: that when Paul says “not from works,” he is speaking only of Jacob’s good works. For, as Augustine says:

> “‘Not from works,’ and he proves this because it was said concerning those not yet born and who had not yet done anything.”

For if Paul had wished to exclude only Jacob’s good works, he would have said: “When he had not yet been born or done anything good … it was said—not from works but from him who calls: ‘The elder shall serve the younger.’”

It is therefore certain that the Apostle is speaking there of the works of both. This is also confirmed by what he adds in the same place:

> “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated. What, then, shall we say? Is there injustice with God?”

Neither of them had done anything good or evil, yet God loved one and hated the other. By what justice, then, did God do this? But if God had foreseen Esau’s future evil works, there would be no room for such an accusation.

From these words the force of the parity becomes clear which the holy Doctor introduces in the manner of one conducting an argument. His reasoning is as follows:

> “For if, because God foreknew his future [Col. 0776C] evil works, he predestined him to serve the younger, then he also predestined Jacob so that the elder should serve him, because he foreknew Jacob’s future good works.”

This inference is established because the Apostle equally excludes the good works on account of which Jacob was elected and the evil works on account of which Esau was reprobated. Therefore the same reasoning applies to the works of both with respect to love and hatred. Augustine thus argues while, for the moment, suspending judgment.

Bañez, however, [Col. 0776D] writes:

> “Therefore it is manifest that the reason for predestination and reprobation is not the same, so that, if a cause of reprobation is granted on our part, a cause of predestination must likewise be granted. If, therefore, Saint Augustine had wished to attend to the flaw in this consequence,”

and so forth.

These words plainly show that the writer lacked diligence in reading Augustine’s books. Augustine not only attended to the flaw in the consequence but also solidly refuted it—and, what is astonishing, in precisely the passage where Bañez thought him less attentive.

For Augustine always denied this parity:

> “God reprobates on the basis of foreseen demerit or sin; therefore, conversely, he predestines on the basis of foreseen good work.”

Here is the entire argument, derived from that parity, which the Pelagians advance in letter 106 to Paulinus:

> “How is Esau not [Col. 0777A] condemned undeservedly, if it was said, ‘not from works but from him who calls: the elder shall serve the younger’? For just as no good works had preceded in Jacob, so that he might belong to grace, so neither had evil works preceded in Esau, so that he ought to belong to punishment.”

The holy Doctor replies:

> “There were plainly no works, either good or evil, in either of them; but each was subject to that one in whom all sinned, and so forth. Yet both, who had not yet performed their own works, whether good or evil, were born guilty by their origin. Let the one who is delivered praise mercy; let no one who is punished blame judgment.”

You see that Augustine denies the parity. Esau was reprobated on account of the stain contracted from Adam, whereas Jacob was delivered solely by mercy.

Hence Augustine’s celebrated maxim, as it were, is:

> “God is good; God is [Col. 0777B] just. He can deliver some without good merits, because he is good; he cannot condemn anyone without merits, because he is just.”

Book 3 against Julian, chapter 18.

Hear the reason for the difference, and acknowledge that Augustine clearly saw that the reason for predestination and reprobation is not the same, so that, if a cause of reprobation is granted on our part, a cause of predestination must likewise be granted.

For the act of reprobation is an act of punitive justice condemning a person. But Augustine cries out:

> “He cannot condemn anyone without merits, because he is just.”

Predestination, however, is an act of God’s pure mercy and goodness. It presupposes no good works of ours, but produces them. Hence Augustine says:

> “He can deliver some without good merits, because he is good.”

Therefore:

> “Let the one who is delivered praise mercy; let no one who is punished blame judgment.”

Let Bañez now [Col. 0777C] come forward and add that Augustine did not wish to attend to the flaw in the consequence, and let Annatus transcribe these very words in the largest possible characters.

But in the same second question to Simplician, where Augustine, arguing, pressed the parity—“How could he hate Esau, unless it is unjust to hate someone without the merit of injustice? If we concede this, Jacob begins to be loved for the merit of justice”—he responds and ultimately dissolves the question, which he had entangled with numerous arguments on both sides.

There he proves at greater length that no good works preceded Jacob’s election—not even faith, in view of which Jacob might have been elected—and he concludes:

> “Therefore grace precedes every merit.”

Afterward he establishes learnedly and with many arguments that God could not have hated Esau before he saw sin in [Col. 0777D] him, because:

> “Every creature of God is good, and every human being, insofar as he is human, is a creature, not insofar as he is a sinner. God is therefore the creator both of the human body and of the human soul. Neither of these is evil, and God hates neither of them, and so forth; nor does he hate anything in a human being except sin.”

From these words he concludes:

> “God therefore did not hate Esau the human being; God hated Esau the sinner.”

Thus, after confirming the proposition:

> “But how could he hate Esau, unless it is unjust to hate someone without the merit of injustice?”

he denies the inference:

> “Therefore Jacob begins to be loved for the merit of justice.”

For, once the earlier statement has been granted, he proves false what they deduce afterward—namely, that Jacob too was loved on account of good merits:

> “Why, then,” he adds, “did he love Jacob? Was he perhaps a sinner? But in him he loved not the guilt that he was removing, but the grace that he was [Col. 0778A] bestowing.”

According to Augustine, therefore, there is a great difference between reprobation and predestination. Reprobation presupposes an evil merit, which it hates; predestination, however, presupposes no good merit, but causes it.

Bañez was deceived because, without reading Augustine resolving the question, he supposed that the holy Doctor had affirmed what he had proposed before explaining his own opinion, in order to increase the difficulty of the question with all his strength.

Saint Augustine, therefore, did not refuse to attend to the flaw in the consequence. Rather, Bañez refused to attend to Augustine attending to that flaw and refuting it most solidly.

Again, we should note what Bañez wrote in the same place [Col. 0778B] in order to demonstrate the malignity of that Augustinian inference. For, he says, “It could easily have been denied by those who follow the contrary opinion, and a distinction could have been assigned between predestination and reprobation: predestination is the cause not only of attaining the final end, but also of the merits directed toward the final end. Reprobation, however, although it is the cause of what will be assigned in the future—namely, eternal punishment—is nevertheless not the cause of what exists in the present—namely, sin, on account of which the entire effect of reprobation can fall upon the reprobate as on account of demerit.”

Yet Augustine certainly saw this distinction; and, without sending Bañez to other books of the holy Doctor, he saw it in that very passage where Bañez says that Augustine had by no means observed it. For, while demonstrating at length there that predestination [Col. 0778C] is the cause of merits, Augustine says:

> “Grace, then, belongs to the One who calls ‘according to purpose’; good works consequently belong to the one who receives grace—not works that produce grace, but works produced by grace. Fire does not make something hot in order that it may burn, but because it burns; nor does a wheel run in order to be round, but because it is round. Thus no one does good works in order to receive grace, but because he has received grace.”

See chapter 10 of *On the Predestination of the Saints*. Afterwards he gives the distinction between reprobation and predestination: reprobation does not cause the sin on account of which a person is reprobated, although it causes the punishment due to the crime. Thus he speaks of God as the Reprobator:

> “For he hates in them the impiety which he himself did not make. Just as a judge hates theft in a person, but does not hate what is sent to the mines—for the former is made by the thief, the latter by the judge—so God does not hate what he makes from the mixture of the impious, making vessels of perdition; that is, he does not hate the work of his ordering in the punishment due to those who perish.” [Col. 0778D]

Augustine therefore knew the broad difference between predestination and reprobation: predestination is the cause, on God’s part as the One who calls, of good works, whereas reprobation is not the cause of evil works. Indeed, the holy Father asserted this disparity so consistently that from it alone he inferred original sin, and he defeated the Pelagians three lustres before they emerged.

For once he had established that divine election presupposes no merits in a human being, while on the other hand he understood that demerits are required for just reprobation, he asked about the reprobation of Esau. If Esau was rejected without any merit, he requested an explanation of how his rejection could be called just. Since it is clear from the Apostle that he was not reprobated on account of his own works, while it was also absolutely certain that, if God were to hate Esau without the merit of injustice, this would itself be unjust, Augustine concludes that there had been formed one mass of all humanity, coming from the transmission of sin—namely, because “carnal concupiscence, already reigning as the punishment of sin, had confused the entire human race, as one whole and single lump, under original guilt, which remained in all.”

Earlier he had written:

> “For there is one mass of sinners from Adam, in which both Jews and Gentiles, apart from the grace of God, belong to one and the same lump.”

How, from this mass, some vessels are chosen for honor through election and others for dishonor through reprobation, he explains at greater length in the same place. Hence it was rightly said by him [Col. 0779B]: “Behold, he hates Esau—the vessel he himself made for dishonor.”

Who would not marvel at Augustine’s vast intellect, which in that work discussed the efficacy of grace, the predestination of the saints, reprobation, and original sin so extensively, as though he were already contending with the Pelagians in open combat, although they did not arise until three lustres later? From this one may see that the Pelagians had in Augustine a single implacable enemy, by whom they saw that their most depraved heresy had been strangled before it was born.

All those engaged in controversies against Pelagius concerning divine grace owe him the first place, for no one wrote either better or more extensively than Augustine. Indeed, he left the other Fathers so far behind him in this argument that, even if everything asserted by the earlier Fathers concerning grace and original sin were collected, this one question addressed to Simplicianus would nevertheless, whether one considers the weight of its arguments, the acuity of its doctrine, or its explanation of matters of the greatest difficulty, unquestionably seem to surpass them. Yet this question, as we have said, was written before the Pelagians were heard.

Thus, from this fact alone, the tiresome voices of recent writers calling upon the other Fathers may be effectively silenced. For what the holy Father writes to Simplicianus clearly demonstrates that, in questions concerning divine grace, the other Fathers are useful, but Augustine is necessary. This was so certain that Vasquez, the most acute of the recent authors whose objections we are answering, bestowed this praise upon Augustine’s authority:

> “In the matter of grace and predestination, Augustine shines among the other Fathers of the Church no otherwise than the sun shines among the lesser stars,”

part I, disputation 89, chapter 1, number 8.

I wish to point out one matter here, by which Bañez’s censure of Augustine may be rejected in such a way that Bañez himself may be struck by the same charge. I therefore say that the distinction between predestination and reprobation—that the latter presupposes evil merits which it punishes, whereas the former does not presuppose good merits which it rewards—was asserted and defended by Augustine much more consistently and rigorously than by Bañez himself.

For if this argument were brought against the latter writer: “Divine providence assumes a person to eternal glory without foreknowledge of merits; therefore the same providence can exclude a person from glory without foreknowledge of demerits,” he notes no malignity in the inference [Col. 0780A]. He does not repeat here the distinction which Bañez, as it were, suggests to Augustine—namely, that predestination causes merits, whereas reprobation does not cause demerits but presupposes them. Rather, he concedes the whole point. For in his response to argument 2 he says:

> “Before foreknown sin, God can be understood to hate certain persons—that is, not to love them unto eternal life.”

There, along with others, he freely concedes what is commonly called negative reprobation, by which God denies glory not as punishment for sin but as a purely gratuitous and undue gift, without presupposing foreknowledge of demerits.

But Saint Augustine upholds the stated disparity between reprobation and predestination so tenaciously that he everywhere excluded this reprobation without foreknowledge of demerits—even when it was negative—and always condemned it in the Pelagians. [Col. 0780B] For the Pelagians maintained that children are born without any original sin, yet they denied that they could be admitted to the eternal life of the heavenly kingdom unless they were adopted through the grace of baptism. Since glory is freely bestowed by God, they said that God had decreed to confer it only upon the baptized.

Their very words, as Augustine records them in book *On Original Sin*, chapter 5, are these:

> “Because the Lord has decreed that the kingdom of heaven can be bestowed only upon the baptized, and because they do not possess the powers of nature for this, it is necessary that it be bestowed through the freedom of grace.”

Hence their celebrated axiom, found in the author of book II of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 24:

> “Grace has what may adopt; water has nothing with which it may wash away.”

Thus children dying without baptism were excluded from the kingdom of heaven, not as punishment for original sin [Col. 0780C]—which the Pelagians denied—but because possession of the kingdom of heaven was not owed to them. For, they said, they did not possess the powers of nature by which they could acquire it.

Accordingly, in Augustine’s *Against Julian*, book III, chapter 3, and book IV of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 99, they asserted that the exclusion of such children from the kingdom of heaven was no punishment; and in book V, chapter 11, he says that, according to the Pelagian position, children who died without baptism were free from every condemnation.

They were therefore excluded by purely negative reprobation—that is, they were not admitted into the kingdom of heaven—while no punishment was inflicted upon them. Indeed, the exclusion itself, or their non-admission to the kingdom of heaven, was said to be no punishment for them.

But Saint Augustine everywhere contended against the Pelagians that children dying without baptism, if they were tainted by no fault of origin, would be unjustly excluded from the kingdom of God by negative reprobation. [Col. 0780D] He presses this point against the heretics in hundreds of passages.

In book I of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 30:

> “They never explain how, by justice, an image of God having no sin is separated from the kingdom of God.”

And in book V of *Against Julian*, chapter 11:

> “But you also, who insist that they are free from every condemnation, refuse to consider by what condemnation you punish them when you alienate from the life of God and from the kingdom of God so many images of God, and so forth. Yet they suffer these things unjustly if they have absolutely no sin; or, if they suffer them justly, then they have original sin.”

And in book II of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 325:

> “You will never say that it is just for little children who have died without baptism, through no fault of their own and often through no fault even of their parents, to be separated from believing parents [Col. 0781A] and relatives and not admitted to the kingdom of God.”

In book V of *Against Julian*, chapter 9, he writes:

> “Therefore those born from Adam must be transferred to Christ by being born anew, lest the images of God perish from the kingdom of God. Whoever says that this can happen without evil possesses neither love nor fear of God.”

And in letter 106 he writes that this is “utterly alien to the justice of God.”

In book VI, chapter 4:

> “If they had deserved no evil, they would never have been deprived, in the common condition, of the deprivation of so great a good.”

See sermon 14, *On the Words of the Apostle*, where he cries out:

> “Why do you take away the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven from an innocent? Whoever does not acquire the kingdom of heaven is certainly defrauded of a great good. What sort of justice is this?” and so forth.

The holy Pope Gelasius taught the same thing in his letter to the bishops throughout Picenum against the Pelagians:

> “Why, then,” he says, “is the infant confined by this lot—that is, not admitted to the kingdom of heaven—if he has absolutely no sin? Indeed, God would seem—God forbid—to be unjust if punishment were inflicted where there is no guilt.” [Col. 0781B]

The synod of the Fathers of Byzacena agrees, in *On the Incarnation and Grace*, chapter 14, where they say:

> “Since there is no iniquity with God, who made man in his own image, what justice is it that the image of God—which could itself commit no offense, unless it is redeemed by the blood of the Son of God—is not permitted to enter the kingdom of God?”

I have deliberately added these two testimonies because some consider the aforementioned opinion of the holy Doctor to be false.

It was therefore altogether fixed and certain in Augustine, and in the holy Fathers who followed his teaching, that no one can be reprobated without guilt, purely negatively, from the kingdom of heaven as from an undue benefit. It was equally certain for him that, in the state of fallen nature, no one is predestined on the foreknowledge of any good work.

He therefore said that the necessary distinction between predestination and reprobation is this: God could not, without injustice, exclude guiltless infants from the kingdom of heaven, even if he did not do so as a punishment.

Augustine therefore does not need to be taught this distinction, or the malignity of the inference, by Bañez. He knew it better than Bañez himself and defended it far more rigorously.

Recent writers—Alarcón, Herice, and others—cast the soot of Calvinism upon that negative reprobation prior to foreknown demerits. Hence the Thomists raise great complaints against them, as may be seen in John of Saint Thomas, part I, disputation 10, *On Reprobation*, number 19, and Gonetti, disputation 5, volume IV, article 2, section 3.

Certainly Calvin asserted positive reprobation prior to the foreknowledge of sins; indeed, he said that sins were caused by it and that human beings were impelled to commit them. The Thomists, together with the other Catholics, deny this.

But far be it from us to impose Pelagianism upon these most learned men, our comrades and allies in defending Augustine under the Salmantician oath. We have said only what was necessary to refute Bañez’s censure more fully.

Nevertheless, there is no reason for our opponents to produce this theologian’s testimony against Augustine. In the same place—namely, in that fifth article—while refuting Javelli’s opinion, he says:

> “Augustine is an outstanding witness and preacher of the grace of God.”

And in the section beginning, “These opinions, therefore,” he adds:

> “The true opinion must be established according to the mind of Augustine and of Saint Thomas.”

Thus, if he said anything about Augustine through error, we certainly consider him deserving of excuse; but he should not be treated as possessing such authority that his testimony against the holy Doctor, expressed by his opponents in conspicuous lettering, ought to be exaggerated.

## § XI. Saint Bernard improperly produced against Augustine by Annat.

The recent writers, in order to close the enormous procession of witnesses by which they attempted not merely to dislodge Saint Augustine from his position but to overwhelm him entirely, affirm that the testimony of the most noble Father, Saint Bernard, gives support against Augustine. They shout with Annat, page 884:

> “Let Saint Bernard, then, come after the last; he ought to have been named before the first.”

But he will never descend against Augustine, not even if you bring all your engines to bear.

They reply:

> “Therefore Saint Bernard, so devout a worshiper of Saint Augustine, so diligent a reader, so suitable an arbiter in ecclesiastical and necessary doctrine, nevertheless rejects, in his letter to the canons of Lyons, a particular opinion of Augustine—namely, that Saint John the Baptist did not receive the fullness of sanctifying grace in his mother’s womb—and opposes to the principle on which Augustine relied, namely, that no one can be called reborn before being born, the contrary claim that someone can be holy before being born.”

Although they know that Bernard sometimes called Augustine “the most powerful hammer of the heretics” and “the pillar of the Catholic religion,” they conclude, almost mockingly:

> “It is therefore clear, from the example of Saint Bernard, that those two columns of which he spoke can be such that one need not necessarily fear if someone is so torn away from Augustine that he nevertheless relies upon Ambrose, even in those matters which Augustine disputed against the Pelagians; nor need it seem impossible that the most powerful hammer of the heretics might at some time suffer an uncertain blow.”

Such is their argument.

We admit that the holy Doctor held a particular opinion when disputing against the Pelagians concerning original sin: Jeremiah and John the Baptist had not been completely freed from original sin in their mothers’ wombs through sanctifying grace. He taught this in letter 57 to Dardanus and in book IV of *Against Julian*, the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 133, where he says:

> “For both Jeremiah and John, although sanctified in their mothers’ wombs, nevertheless carried original sin. For by what other merit would their souls perish from their people unless they were circumcised on the eighth day, unless they came to the grace of Christ, and so forth? They were therefore by nature children of wrath from their mothers’ wombs, and by grace children of mercy from their mothers’ wombs, because they did not yet possess that holiness which would dissolve the bond of the liable succession—which had to be dissolved in its own time—yet they did possess that holiness which designated the herald of Christ from his mother’s womb.”

Two matters must be considered here. John the Baptist was filled, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, with the gift of prophecy; afterwards, he was freed from original guilt in the womb.

Saint Augustine concedes the first, but denies the second, as his words clearly show. Saint Bernard also concedes the first without hesitation; concerning the second, however, he says that he does not dare to define anything.

Let the sweet words of the Honey-flowing Doctor be heard, lest Annat’s bitter speech against Augustine disgust us:

> “Most certainly,” he says, “the Holy Spirit, with whom he was filled, sanctified him. But to what extent this very sanctification availed against original sin, whether in the case of this prophet or that one, or of anyone else who may have been preceded by a similar grace, I WOULD NOT SPEAK RASHLY.”

Then, considering Saint Augustine’s opinion, he adds:

> “Yet who would say that one filled with the Holy Spirit nevertheless remains a son of wrath, and that, if he happened to die in the womb, he would suffer the punishments of condemnation with this fullness of the Spirit? [Col. 0783B] It is a hard question; NEVERTHELESS, I DARE NOT AT ALL DEFINE ANYTHING ON THIS MATTER ACCORDING TO MY OWN JUDGMENT. But whatever may be the case, and so forth.”

You see, Annat, that Bernard defines nothing in this matter. He was restrained, as I rightly believe, by the authority of Augustine alone—whom, as you say, he had present to his mind when he wrote these words.

Augustine’s opinion seemed harsh to him, but he confessed that it would be harsher still to depart from Augustine:

> “Nevertheless,” he says, “I dare not at all define anything on this matter according to my own judgment.”

Is this, Annat, as you jest, to be torn away from Augustine? Is this to suppose that the most powerful hammer of the heretics might at some time suffer an uncertain blow?

On the contrary, it is to deceive readers and to treat Bernard with excessive injustice, by making him recite about Augustine what he never even imagined. Such, then, is the opinion of the Honey-flowing Doctor in letter 174 to the canons of Lyons.

[Col. 0783C] But Annat chatters about something else and contends that Bernard held a different—even an opposing—view, by departing from Augustine in that very place where he professes that, with Augustine, he is either in error or in the right: namely, letter 77 to Hugh.

I give Annat’s words:

> “To say nothing of the fact that, although he relates that opinion according to which Augustine held that an inward conversion of the heart to God could supply for the outward reception of baptism, this man, who was by no means boastful, dares to deny that Augustine ever retracted it, even though he did retract the example he had proposed of the good thief, on the grounds that it was uncertain whether the thief had been baptized.”

I do not know what purpose Annat serves here by his *paraleipsis*—his passing over the point. Come now, explain why you think it a religious duty to accuse Augustine on Bernard’s authority.

It is so: Bernard, a man by no means boastful, dares to deny that Augustine ever retracted his opinion that inward conversion of the heart to God can supply for baptism. Do you perhaps think that Augustine ought to have retracted this opinion?

Saint Cyprian had taught it before Saint Augustine; the holy Doctor praises him in book IV of *On Baptism*, chapter 22, where he says that, if baptism is absent through necessity, faith and conversion of heart can supply for it, because the sacrament is then invisibly fulfilled when the mystery of baptism is excluded not by contempt for religion but by the circumstance of necessity.

Saint Ambrose also taught this very thing concerning the Emperor Valentinian, as is clear from his oration in which he recites the praises of the deceased Valentinian.

Saint Bernard follows both Ambrose and Augustine [Col. 0784A] in letter 77, praising their testimonies. He writes:

> “From these two columns—by which I mean Augustine and Ambrose—believe me, I am with difficulty torn away. With them, I say, I confess that I am either in error or in the right; believing also that a person can be saved by faith alone, together with the desire to receive the sacrament, provided that death, coming beforehand, or some other irresistible force, prevents the fulfillment of that pious desire.”

You hear Bernard, a man by no means boastful, agreeing with Augustine and believing that a person can be saved by faith alone together with the desire to receive the sacrament.

Why, then, would he say that Augustine had ever retracted this opinion, into which he followed him wholeheartedly?

Moreover, the Apostolic See approved the same opinion on Augustine’s authority. Innocent III, in his letter to the bishop of Cremona, preserved in Gregory IX, book III, title 43, chapter 2, writes:

> “Concerning the man whom you reported to have closed his final day without the water of baptism, because he persevered in the faith of holy Mother Church and in the name of Christ, we unhesitatingly assert that he was freed from original sin and attained the joys of the heavenly homeland. Read Augustine’s eighth book *On the City of God*, where, among other things, one reads: ‘Baptism is administered invisibly when it is excluded not by contempt for religion but by the limit of necessity.’”

An error has nevertheless crept in, for those words are found not in book VIII of *The City of God* but in book IV of *On Baptism*, as we have quoted them; the same words were also cited by Bernard, whom he praised, from that fourth book.

Hence theologians teach that baptism of the Spirit justifies; and the Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 4, decrees that baptism in desire justifies. [Col. 0784C]

What, then, came into your mind, Annat, when you listed as deserving of retraction that opinion of the holy Doctor which had been approved by the Church, and which he himself maintained consistently after the Pelagians arose, until the end of his life? Read book I of *On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 9, and book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 18.

Anyone wishing to know more about this matter should consult Christian Lupus, a sufficiently well-known author, in his book *On Attrition and Contrition*, chapter 8.

Or are you perhaps mocking what Augustine suggested concerning the baptism of the good thief?

The holy Doctor admitted that the matter he regarded as certain—namely, that conversion of heart could take the place of baptism—could not be demonstrated with sufficient force by that example. In book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 18, he affirmed that some people not implausibly say that the thief was washed in that water which flowed from Christ’s side, as though by a most sacred baptism, as he had written in the first book cited above.

Nevertheless, the same Father did not think that the thief had been baptized before the crucifixion. He says plainly in the same place:

> “That thief was not a follower before the Lord’s cross, but a confessor upon the cross, and so forth. Then, too, his faith blossomed from the wood, when that of the disciples withered.”

He adduces these considerations concerning the thief’s baptism in order to refute the error of Vincent Victor, who argued from the example of the thief that children dying without baptism could attain the forgiveness of original sins. This is clear from book III of *On the Origin of the Soul*, addressed to Vincent, where he discusses the thief’s baptism throughout chapter 9.

Yet he adduced these considerations in such a way as to remove every opportunity for error from the example of that thief. Hence, after reviewing in book I, chapter 9, the various ways in which the thief was said, or could be said, to have been baptized, he concluded:

> “Let each person accept these matters as he wishes, provided that the example of this thief is not used to prescribe anything concerning baptism against the command of the Savior.” [Col. 0785A]

Bernard himself agrees that it is uncertain whether the thief had been baptized, saying:

> “Since it is plainly uncertain whether he had been baptized.”

Hence Father Lupus, who read the holy Fathers with the highest distinction, says in the work cited above, *On Contrition and Attrition*, chapter 9:

> “The thief’s baptism is uncertain. Not only Augustine but all the Fathers generally vary on the matter.”

I have added these points because, from that letter 77 of Saint Bernard to Hugh, I cannot see at all how Augustine’s statement can rightly be exposed by an opponent to criticism through silence; nor do I think that Annat himself saw it.

## § XII. They produce Saint Augustine against Augustine.

They persuade themselves that they have completed the case and overthrown Augustine entirely, aided, as they boast, by the testimony “of three supreme pontiffs, six cardinals from the entire number of the most learned and almost holiest men, and so many bishops and doctors of every school, order, and nation.”

These are the words of Annat, singing of his own victory and triumph, chapter 4, page 887.

But in order to block every possible avenue of escape for Augustine, they appeal to Augustine’s own confession. They claim that, convicted by the voices of so many witnesses superior to all exception, he will himself concede the entire dispute to them.

Let Annat be heard, chapter 5, page 888. So secure is he in his victory that he enters the arena without hesitation, prepared to fight Augustine himself, as judge, in the final battle:

> “When we dispute on the condition that we stand by Augustine’s judgment, this too must be investigated: did Augustine judge that all his opinions, including those which he expounded while attacking the Pelagians, must necessarily be embraced?”

They first contend that Augustine established only three doctrines as doctrines to be held against the Pelagians in accordance with the Catholic faith, as Sadoletus once said when teaching the recent writers in his letter to Contarenus, as we related in section 1.

Again, they produce several testimonies of the holy Father in which he says that he does not wish to impose this rule upon his readers: that they must assent to every assertion put forward by him, with all freedom to contradict entirely removed. I shall give one, since the sense of the others is the same, expressed only in different words.

In his letter to Fortunatianus he writes:

> “For we ought not to regard the disputations of just anyone, even of Catholic and praiseworthy men, as we regard the canonical Scriptures, so that it would not be permitted us—while preserving the honor due to those men—to disapprove and reject something in their writings if we should find that they have thought differently from what the truth requires, whether the truth has been understood by divine assistance by others or by us. Such as I am in the writings of others, such I wish readers to be with respect to mine.”

From this and other passages cited to the same effect they exclaim:

> “It is therefore permissible to evaluate Augustine’s doctrine from Augustine according to the judgment of other writers; it is also permissible to do so according to one’s own judgment, and this while preserving due honor. Nor is this plan so perverse that it cannot have God as its helper.”

Thus Annat speaks, page 897.

Yet these critics contribute nothing new. They merely repeat in full the words of the Pelagians and Lutherans against Augustine.

When the Pelagians were attacked by Augustine with testimonies from the Fathers, they insolently replied, on the basis of Augustine’s own books, that they had no necessity of adhering to the Fathers. Let Julian be heard, book IV of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 111:

> “But it is well that you have relieved us of the burden of such persons. For in the book which you composed against free choice for Timasius, when Saint Pelagius had recalled the venerable men Ambrose and Cyprian, both of whom had commended free choice in their books, you replied that you were not burdened by the authority of such men, saying that, if they had thought wrongly, they had expiated it through the progress of a better life. Let what you have reported concerning yourself serve this purpose, so that you may be ashamed to arouse ill will merely by mentioning names.”

But that this is a familiar evasion not only of the ancient heretics but also of recent dogmatists, used to elude the authority of the holy Fathers, and especially of Augustine, is attested by the most learned man Stapleton, volume I, controversy 3, book VII, chapter 15:

> “Others,” he says, speaking of Protestants, “argue that no more should be attributed to them—that is, to the Fathers—than the Fathers themselves demand should be attributed to them. In this place they produce various statements of Augustine in which he asks that his writings be believed only insofar as he has confirmed his opinion from sacred Scripture or evident reason.” [Col. 0786C]

He adds that they rejoice exceedingly in Augustine’s words from book XI of *Against Faustus*, chapter 5, the passage in which Annat takes pride on page 897.

This most learned and likewise most holy Father added modesty to the other virtues with which, by divine gift, he was adorned even to the point of astonishment. He never wished so much to be attributed to him as was attributed to Pythagoras by his disciples, so that the formula “He himself said” (*Αὐτός ἔφα*) might serve as an unanswerable argument.

This is the sole request Augustine makes throughout his seventh letter to Marcellinus.

Yet, when disputing against the Pelagians, he repeatedly professes that he is defending fundamental doctrines as Catholic opinions. Thus in book V of *Against Julian*, chapter 12, he discusses five questions concerning concupiscence, where he says:

> “In these questions, your impious novelty is suffocated by the Catholic truth handed down from ancient times.”

In letter 107 to Vitalis he lays down twelve theses concerning grace, asserting that they “belong to the right and Catholic faith.”

He teaches the same concerning predestination in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 23, at the end.

Above all, we must again recall that, although the holy Doctor corrected several opinions in the books of his *Retractions*, he removed no thesis established or defended against the Pelagians. It is therefore plain that Augustine judged everything, individually and collectively, that he had taught against them in his books to be consistent with the truth. He may perhaps have left to recent writers the new labor and more exact diligence of examining once again, as Annat says on page 897, the same writings of the Bishop of Hippo with a stricter judgment, under God’s inspiration, and demonstrating that they contain errors. [Col. 0787A]

When the Semi-Pelagians once accused Augustine of error in the books he had forged against the Pelagians, that most modest man replied at the end of *On the Gift of Perseverance*:

> “But those who think that I am in error should consider carefully, again and again, what has been said, lest perhaps they themselves be in error.”

In the same work, chapter 21, he says:

> “Although I do not wish anyone to embrace everything of mine in such a way as to follow me, except in those matters in which he has seen that I am not in error—for this reason I am now composing books in which I have undertaken to retract my shorter works, so that I may demonstrate that I have not followed even myself in everything,”

and so forth.

When the great writer of ecclesiastical annals, Cardinal Baronius, considered these words with a more attentive cast of mind, he wrote the following in praise of Augustine, volume V, under the year 426, page 498. Although they have been quoted above, it will be pleasing to repeat them here:

> “These words,” he says, “are worthy of Saint Augustine’s modesty and of the admirable submissive reverence of his spirit. Thus, unless from elsewhere you can discern that he wrote these things inspired by the divine Spirit, you may at least discern it from these words, since God testified through the prophet that the divine presence rests upon none but the humble, quiet, and trembling at God’s word; as James likewise taught when he said: ‘The wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peaceful, modest, persuasive, and consenting to what is good.’”

So far Baronius.

And yet Annat went so far as not to fear asserting, chapter V, page 897, that the opponent of Augustine would have God as his helper!

And this man wishes to be numbered among the defenders of the holy Doctor by vindicating Augustine against the Baians? This is not, Annat, to defend Augustine’s cause, but to betray it.

Yet although Augustine, out of the modesty of his spirit, thought so humbly of himself, his doctrine concerning divine grace was approved by the judgment of the Catholic Church so fully that even the recent writers who later wrote against Jansenism, after Annat, were compelled by the evidence of the matter to grant this to Augustine’s authority—not, I will not say, praise or testimony, but a confession, together with Decamps:

> “The sanctions of the councils and the edicts of the Roman pontiffs by which the Pelagian heresy was strangled and overthrown were taken from the books of Saint Augustine; they contain the doctrine of Saint Augustine and are expressed in the words of Saint Augustine. Augustine was, in a certain way, the precentor of the Church, for he preceded the Roman pontiffs and councils in voice when they pronounced judgment on that most proud heresy. He was the tongue of the Church when decrees were formulated in his words, and when the words that had previously been Augustine’s began to be the oracles of the Holy Spirit. He was the leader and intellect of the councils when he supplied them with the reasons and arguments by which they broke Pelagius and his associates,”

book III of *The Jansenist Heresy*, disputation 1, chapter 6.

I see Annat raising a thick cloud of dust here in order to obscure the great light of the Roman Church, Augustine, which shines in every direction. What clouds does he not gather throughout the whole of chapter 6, in order to darken the praises bestowed upon Augustine by the Roman prelates? Yet we shall restrain his futile efforts in the following chapter, where we shall assert the authority of the holy Doctor—so often fortified by the judgment of the Apostolic See—against the objections and perverse interpretations of this defender of the holy Father, as he boasts himself to be. [Col. 0788A]

Nevertheless, even if none of the ancient Fathers stood for Augustine, and all the oracles of the Vatican were entirely silent, Augustine’s cause should not be regarded as so utterly hopeless that, with Annat opposing him, it could find no favorable judge anywhere in the world. This is especially so since it is evident that he falsified several testimonies, invented others entirely, and called as witnesses certain men infected with Semi-Pelagian error, unskilled in grammar, recent theologians drawn from the jurists, or men who spoke impudently and with insufficient deliberation, and who were completely ignorant of Augustine’s books. [Col. 0788B]

But since the doctrine of Saint Augustine has been adorned, fortified, and defended by the praises of so many Roman prelates, the decrees of so many councils, and the encomia of all the Fathers of the ancient Church, who could suspect that, having recently been summoned to judgment by the recent writers, it could be condemned even in the smallest part?

On Augustine’s side stands antiquity; on the side of the recent writers, novelty. On the one side, holiness; on the other, audacity. On the one side, the ancient Fathers; on the other, new authors. On the one side, the consensus of so many centuries; on the other, a small portion of the scholastics of our own age.

When I consider these matters more attentively, I sometimes reflect to myself that I do not know whether, through this work, I have won or incurred praise or hatred among upright men. Indeed, I think there will be some who will say that I have undertaken a futile labor by defending Augustine in judgment against the accusations of recent writers, as though the rashness of these men were not immediately apparent from the beginning of the case: they have dared to fight against the supreme teacher of the Church by bringing hired witnesses before the orthodox world.

But I ask pardon if I have seemed to fear any harm to Augustine from the witnesses of the recent writers. I undertook to defend his cause so that, among the ignorant and excessively credulous, the names of such great witnesses—which his opponents proudly paraded in a long procession against Augustine—might neither gain credence nor at least plant suspicion.

## CHAPTER VI. The praises bestowed by the supreme pontiffs upon Augustine’s doctrine against the Pelagians are vindicated from the sinister interpretations of recent writers.

[Col. 0788D]

It is certainly no small mark of ill will that the recent writers have shown in the matter on which we are here embarking. The Roman pontiffs consecrated Saint Augustine’s teaching on divine grace with wondrous praises. Hence such veneration was bestowed upon him by everyone throughout all the intervening centuries that, after the testimonies of those same pontiffs, the orthodox heard only one Augustine—or rather, Augustine’s doctrines passed into the decrees of the pontiffs and the canons of the synods, as we demonstrated in the *Pelagian History*. This indeed stung the recent writers’ minds more deeply; and so they have boldly, though not equally successfully, attempted partly to cut short and partly to evade, by false interpretations, the praises of Augustine’s doctrine delivered by the Roman pontiffs. [Col. 0789A]

The first of the pontiffs brought forward as having commended Saint Augustine is Innocent, who, after receiving from Augustine a letter signed by four other colleagues, in which the errors of Pelagius were reported to him, replied in Letter 96 among the Augustinian letters:

> “Since the whole tenor and structure of these letters consists in consideration of God’s daily grace and in the correction of those who think otherwise, it is wholly sound, so that it can both remove every error from them and provide, in the example supplied by our law, a suitable teacher worthy to be followed by anyone.”

Let what we said in Book I of the *Pelagian History*, chapter 11, be read. The recent writers contend that Innocent did not approve Saint Augustine’s entire doctrine against the Pelagians, but only that part in which he contended against the two errors of Pelagius condemned there by the pontiff. I quote the words of Moraines, *Disputation 12 against Jansenius*, no. 49:

> “From this approval of letters speaking about only one or another error, to wish to infer that the whole of Doctor Augustine’s doctrine of grace was specially approved by Innocent is maliciously to deceive the simple and intolerably to abuse the patience of the learned.”

But because Saint Augustine, in order to show Innocent the face of the Pelagian heresy painted in its own colors more clearly, had sent him the heresiarch’s book issued in praise of nature, together with the volume he himself had composed against it, *On Nature and Grace*, Moraines adds in the same place:

> “Innocent, replying in the following Letter 96, makes no mention of Pelagius’s other errors, nor of Doctor Augustine’s book *On Nature and Grace*, but merely praises the preceding letter written to him by them.”

He says that only two errors were condemned there: namely, that original sin does not exist and that God’s grace is not necessary for living rightly and piously.

Let us hear what Saint Innocent decided concerning Pelagius’s book:

> “As for the book,” he says, “which was said to be his and which your charity sent to us, we read through it. In it there is MUCH blasphemy, nothing that pleased us, NOTHING that did not utterly displease us—something to be condemned and trampled upon by anyone, and which no one except the author of such things could have admitted into his mind or held as his opinion.”

What then? To say that nothing in Pelagius’s book pleased Innocent, that nothing was written in it which did not displease him—is this to condemn one or another error only, or rather to judge the book full of errors? In the meantime, correct one little disjunctive particle, Moraines. You said that Innocent’s letter spoke of one or another error; replace the conjunction, making the sentence speak of one *and* another, lest someone more ill-disposed toward you say that you left it doubtful whether those letters proscribed two errors of Pelagius or only one.

But I return to my Augustine. When he sent Pelagius’s book to Innocent together with his own refutation, he marked with asterisks the passages in which Pelagius had held an incorrect view of divine grace. Who could doubt that these passages displeased Innocent, to whom nothing in that little book had given pleasure? That Augustine’s book was approved and praised—and indeed that it argued that human beings are made guilty by the law without grace, a doctrine which Moraines, in *Disputation 24*, no. 44, pretends that Augustine, in rage against the heretics, let slip as a falsehood—is gathered from these words of Innocent:

> “For we did not think it necessary at this point to discuss the law more extensively, as though Pelagius were present and resisting, since we are conversing with you, who know EVERYTHING and rejoice in an agreement equal to ours.”

Do you hear? Augustine knew everything and was in every respect fully in agreement with Innocent in what he had just argued concerning the law making human beings guilty without sufficiently effective grace?

Innocent was succeeded by Zosimus, and then by Boniface; both held Saint Augustine in extraordinary honor, and his doctrine was approved by them. Annatus, Book VIII, chapter 6, page 908, writes:

> “Therefore instruction for conceiving the condemnation of the contrary error could be sought from such a teacher, as Zosimus, as Boniface, and as Felix IV of that name are said to have sought it from Augustine.”

This is correctly stated, but it would be more correct to say that the matter was asserted with certainty, not merely reported by common rumor. We use that phrase when we know a matter less securely; for who, at high noon, would say that the sun is *said* to shine? We know Annatus’s attitude toward Augustine, and therefore we allow room for suspicion. Zosimus did not issue his definitive sentence in the case of Coelestius and Pelagius until he had received letters from the African synods—whose spirit, according to Prosper, was Augustine—as we stated in Book I, chapter 13, of the *Pelagian History*. Boniface likewise sent Augustine Julian’s letters for refutation, as we also related there, chapter 21. Concerning Pope Felix we spoke in Book II, chapter 23. So as not to repeat what has already been done, we do not recount these matters again. Thus those pontiffs really did seek instruction from Augustine against the Pelagians; this is manifest not merely from popular report, but from Augustine’s own books and from the Fathers of that same age. [Col. 0790B]

Boniface was succeeded by Coelestine, who not only praised Saint Augustine’s doctrine but also struck his calumniators through letters sent to the bishops of Gaul. He appended this encomium, like a sepulchral inscription placed shortly before on the dead Augustine:

> “We have always held Augustine, a man of holy memory, in our communion because of his life and merits, and never did even a rumor of sinister suspicion stain him, whom we remember to have once possessed SUCH GREAT KNOWLEDGE that he was always regarded, even by my predecessors, among the best teachers. ALL, therefore, COMMONLY HELD THE SAME OPINION ABOUT HIM, since EVERYWHERE HE WAS BOTH LOVED AND HONORED BY ALL. Hence resistance must be made to such men, whom we see growing in wickedness.”
