Coelestine reports—and indeed commands—that resistance be made to those who diminish Augustine’s reputation. When Saint Prosper had quoted this outstanding praise of Augustine from Coelestine at the end of his book *Against the Collator*, he exclaimed:

> “Against this trumpet of the clearest praise, against the dignity of this most sacred testimony, does anyone dare to utter a murmur of MALICIOUS INTERPRETATION and cast a cloud of crooked ambiguity over a clear and most sincere [Col. 0791A] judgment?”

Precisely so, O Prosper: this is what the recent writers attempt and dare! Indeed, just as that praise is rightly and deservedly placed first among the commendations granted to Augustine by the Apostolic See, so they labor with all the powers of their intellect to cast a cloud of crooked ambiguity over the splendor of such praises, lest so much light should thereby flow toward Augustine.

Annatus, in Book I of his *Augustine*, chapter 8, after hearing Coelestine’s encomium, says:

> “He does not say that Augustine is the Father of Fathers, the teacher of teachers, the first angel among the other bishops, the most outstanding of all, truly irrefragable and ineffably wondrous. He says that he was regarded by his predecessors Innocent, Zosimus, and Boniface as one of the best teachers. And thus, surely, other holy Fathers were also thought to be excellent teachers. If Augustine had disagreed with them, what do we suppose Coelestine would have commanded us—to prefer the best to the best, and one man to many? By what right or on what grounds?”

But when Coelestine later, as they think, in chapter 3, rebukes the Semi-Pelagians who presume to oppose the most pious disputants, Annatus adds:

> “Coelestine therefore says that these men opposed not Augustine alone, but the most pious disputants and teachers; and there is no doubt that Jerome too was included in these words.”

With every artifice they strive almost to reduce Augustine to the ranks, so that in the Pelagian war he may be regarded not as supreme commander, but as one possessing authority equal to that of many, as though he were merely one of the prefects. They contrive this for the following purpose: since they have finally begun to feel that Augustine’s name weighs heavily upon them, they may boast the support of other Fathers who, as Augustine says in chapter 14 of *On the Predestination of the Saints*, touched briefly and in passing, in certain passages of their writings, on what they thought about grace. For since those Fathers did not discuss the mysteries of divine predestination and grace so openly and clearly—when, as Augustine writes in Book I *Against Julian*, chapter 6, they spoke more securely because they were not yet disputing with the Pelagians—the recent writers seize upon certain statements of theirs as apparently favorable to themselves, while setting aside Augustine’s clearest, most open, and most evident judgments. They give this reason for placing Augustine below the other Fathers, together with Adam, *Destruction of Calvinism*, part III, chapter 16, page 760:

> “These shadows [of Augustine] compel me to seek light elsewhere, which I find in the synods and in the books of other teachers.” [Col. 0791D]

They teach astonishing things. Certainly, I will not say that the other Fathers spoke obscurely, but they must be said not to have spoken so clearly, since they touched only briefly and in passing upon certain matters concerning grace; Augustine, however, who discussed that same grace most fully and extensively in more than thirty books, is different. From brevity comes obscurity; from abundance of discourse comes clarity.

But the Fathers of the older Church handed down that Augustine must be preferred to the others when the aids of divine grace are under discussion, as the supreme leader of the Catholic army. Saint Prosper sings this in *Against the Ungrateful*, chapter 3:

> **AMONG ALL THOSE WHO DROVE THE MAD BEASTS**  
> **FROM THE HOLY FLOCK, HIS ZEAL WAS GREATER.**  
> **A GREATER WORK, MORE EXCELLENT THAN ALL,**  
> **PERMEATED THE WHOLE WORLD.**

Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, says in Book II of *The Truth of Predestination and Grace*, chapter 17:

> “Thus this doctrine, handed down in the Church through the apostolic instructions of the Catholic Fathers, remains there without doubt—a doctrine which the Greek and Latin pontiffs, strengthened by the infusion of the Holy Spirit, have always held with one and indivisible agreement. In this matter blessed Augustine, clothed with power from on high, labored more abundantly than all of them; yet it was not he, but the grace of God with him. Through his ministry the Lord provided his faithful with richer instruction concerning this matter,” and so forth.

Let that great Prosper, whom we have just praised, be heard once more. In the preface to *Against the Collator* he says:

> “For more than twenty years the Catholic line has fought and conquered against the enemies of God’s grace under the leadership of THIS MAN.”

Perhaps Annatus will reply, together with his Vasquez, part I, disputation 97, chapter 3, no. 20:

> “I freely admit that the testimonies of Prosper and Fulgentius are suspect to me, because they were Augustine’s most diligent and exact disciples.”

Let him therefore hear Vasquez’s own confession, since the testimonies of both those Fathers are suspect. Vasquez writes in part I, disputation 90, chapter 6, no. 37:

> “Even if there were none among the Fathers mentioned whom the scholastic teachers could cite in support of this opinion concerning the necessity of grace for individual good moral works, they would gladly place the support of their position in Augustine alone and in his school, and would rightly regard him as sufficient for themselves, because he is the ONE MAN who, when the necessity of grace is under discussion, shines like the sun among the rest.”

But we do not learn these things from Vasquez; we learn them from the pontiffs of the Roman Church. When Julian had written against divine grace, Saint Pope Boniface requested a response from Augustine alone. When the East was divided into factions because of the books of Faustus of Riez, Saint Hormisdas wrote that one should learn from Augustine what the Roman Church followed and preserved. When Gaul had been battered for nearly a hundred years by the same disputes, Felix IV brought peace by extracting his judgments from Augustine’s books alone. In our own age, when all Europe was torn into factions by disputes concerning the aids of divine grace, Clement VIII ordered those controversies to be argued before Augustine’s tribunal alone. By these actions the Roman pontiffs clearly indicated that, in controversies concerning divine grace, we must cling to the footsteps of Augustine alone.

Yet Augustine is nowhere alone: he draws with him a vast host of Fathers who followed him—Prosper, Fulgentius, Caesarius, Peter the Deacon, the Byzacene Fathers exiled in Sardinia, Remigius, Prudentius, Anselm, Bernard, and others who follow the footsteps of the holy teacher in these controversies. This consideration demolishes that enormous apparatus which Annatus constructs throughout several chapters of his first book, as though Augustine could be solitary in some doctrine concerning grace.

Indeed, Prosper and Fulgentius, who triumphed over the Semi-Pelagians, are always with Augustine. Thus, even if Augustine and only these two stood on one side, while far more Fathers were counted on the opposite side, who would not rather cling to that triad of Fathers which triumphed over the Pelagian heresy and cannot be accused of error without recklessness?

Let those complaints of Moraines, in the preface addressed to the orthodox, also depart far from here:

> “For what if heretics could prove by their arguments that they had not been openly condemned by Augustine? Would the cause of the Church have to be abandoned, and would the consensus of all the other Fathers in defense of the truth be insufficient, because Augustine is necessary? The condition of the Church would certainly be unjust, since God promised her not one teacher but teachers, so that we might not be carried about by every wind of doctrine.” [Col. 0793B]

You are mistaken, good man—mistaken at the very entrance! Augustine is never alone. And if he was the first to say something about predestination, he did not say it alone, since so many subsequent Fathers have repeated Augustine’s words, a fact which the adversaries have not adequately noticed.

As for what Annatus adds concerning Coelestine’s words against the Semi-Pelagians—

> “They presume to oppose the most pious disputants, and although they do not hesitate to anathematize Pelagius and Coelestius, nevertheless they contradict our teachers, as though they had exceeded the necessary measure”—

it is asserted with complete incompetence that these words refer not to Augustine alone but also to Jerome. The Semi-Pelagians were speaking against Augustine alone, because he alone, they said, had taught that opinion concerning gratuitous predestination. For Prosper writes to Augustine:

> “They affirm that the things brought forward from the Apostle Paul’s letter to the Romans, for the manifestation of the divine grace that precedes the merits of the elect, have NEVER been understood by any ecclesiastical writer in the way they are understood NOW.”

Jerome, therefore, was not being censured by the Semi-Pelagians together with Augustine. Indeed, Jerome wrote so concerning grace against the Pelagians that to some he seemed to have held the opinion of the Semi-Pelagians. For in Book III of the *Dialogues against the Pelagians* he says:

> “Righteousness is preserved by labor, effort, diligence, and always above all by God’s mercy: it is ours to ask, his to grant what is asked; OURS TO BEGIN, his to bring to completion; OURS TO OFFER what we can, his to fulfill what we cannot.”

The Semi-Pelagians could take these words as supporting their own doctrine. Their position was, to use Prosper’s words in *Against the Collator*, chapter 8:

> “That good and salutary efforts cannot indeed make progress unless God assists them, but that they can nevertheless begin even if they are not inspired by God.”

And indeed Jansenius writes in that passage that Jerome agreed with the Semi-Pelagians; Vossius says that Jerome spoke too harshly; and even before both of them certain writers had expressed doubts about Jerome, as reported by Vasquez, part I, disputation 91, chapter 8.

The same Annatus attempts at length to defend Jerome in Book VII of his *Augustine Vindicated*, chapter 12. I agree with him, for Jerome plainly says that grace, once received, is preserved by God’s mercy. Nor are labor and effort to be understood in isolation—that is, without grace—as the same recent writer discusses at greater length. [Col. 0794A] The Semi-Pelagians, therefore, were not opposing Jerome, whom they could suspect of holding their own position.

Moreover, Coelestine says that the Semi-Pelagians were bent on scattering the memory of the brothers who had fallen asleep, and immediately after those words he praises Augustine, concluding that resistance must be made to the detractors. Augustine alone, therefore, is defended there. For if Jerome too was being attacked in their words together with Augustine, why does the pontiff offer praise concerning Augustine alone, while Jerome is wholly pushed into a corner?

Prosper, in fact, who had reported Augustine’s calumniators to Coelestine, referring in *Against the Collator*, chapter 42, to the decree of Coelestine which he himself had obtained, says:

> “Through this man, within Gaul, freedom of malicious speech has been taken away from those very men who criticize the writings of AUGUSTINE OF HOLY MEMORY.”

He writes that Augustine alone was criticized by the Massilians and praised by Coelestine, saying nothing about Jerome. Yet the recent writers make Jerome Augustine’s companion in the calumnies and injuries inflicted by the Semi-Pelagians—not to offer consolation, but so that only part of Coelestine’s encomium may devolve upon Augustine and the other part be reserved for Jerome.

Moreover, it will shortly become clear, when we speak of Felix IV, that Augustine was called “teachers” and “doctor” in the plural by the Apostolic See.

Saint Pope Gelasius is counted among the admirers of Saint Augustine, and Vasquez, part I, disputation 91, no. 75, not undeservedly calls him wholly Augustinian. Thus, in his letter to the bishops throughout Picenum, as we observed in Book II, chapter 17, of the *Pelagian History*, he writes:

> “A still greater crime is added, when, in the sight and presence of priests, the dying fly, as it is written, attempted to destroy and tear apart Jerome and Augustine of blessed memory, the shining lights of ecclesiastical teachers, thereby exterminating the oil of fragrance.”

Annatus adds his glosses here, Book I, chapter 8:

> “See: Jerome too is a light of teachers, just like Augustine, according to the testimony of the Roman pontiff.”

Who will deny this? Yet it matters greatly from whom the Church is more greatly enlightened against the darkness of the Pelagians, and from whom she receives more light—from Jerome or from Augustine.

At the gathering in Jerusalem against Pelagius, Orosius produced Augustine’s letter to Hilary; it was also produced shortly afterward at the Council of Diospolis. Concerning this matter the holy teacher writes in his book *On Original Sin*, chapter 10, reporting the words of the synod:

> “Since the holy bishop Augustine responded against his disciples in Sicily, writing to Hilary concerning the propositions set forth, and composing a book in which these matters are contained,” and so forth.

At that time Jerome had already published his letter to Ctesiphon against Pelagius, and he was himself present in Palestine, where the synod was being held. His very presence and the reputation of his holiness gave his name even greater authority. Nevertheless, Jerome’s letter was passed over, and Pelagius was examined according to the standard of Augustine’s letter.

The recent writers will object that John of Jerusalem was Jerome’s most bitter enemy. But at the Council of Diospolis the bishop of Jerusalem was not presiding; rather, it was Eulogius, metropolitan of Caesarea in Palestine. Thus, from the very beginning of those proceedings, it sufficiently appeared that Augustine alone had been divinely appointed above the others as the strongest and most vigorous leader in the Pelagian war, and that the synods of the Fathers had approved him as such.

But what is nobler than Jerome’s own testimony and example? When Orosius had brought to Asia, to Jerome, the earlier books published by Augustine against the Pelagians, the Father of Bethlehem admired the abundance of his doctrine, the excellence of his learning, the force of his arguments, and the work as a whole. He imposed silence upon himself and published it in writing before the whole world at the end of Book III of the *Dialogues*. Speaking of Augustine’s books against Pelagius, he says:

> “He is said to be forging other works specifically against your name, which have not yet come into our hands. Therefore I think this labor should be suspended, lest Horace’s words be applied to me: ‘Do not carry wood into the forest.’ For either we would say the same things unnecessarily, or, if we wished to say something new, the better things have been preempted by a MOST DISTINGUISHED INTELLECT.”

Jerome afterward observed this silence with such religious devotion that, when Annianus attacked his letter to Ctesiphon, he not only prepared no defense but urged Augustine by letter to refute that attack. We discussed this matter at greater length in Book I, chapter 19, of the *Pelagian History*.

That Jerome, I say, refused the contest, although once he had not even tolerated being lightly touched by his very dear Rufinus without retaliation; instead, he published apologies to repel each of the calumnies brought against him. Thus, when Jerome handed the torch to Augustine in this contest, the Church also received from Augustine alone the light by which she might illuminate the Catholic world.

From these facts it is also clear that Moraines’s statement in the preface addressed to the orthodox is empty:

> “What about Jerome? Will he too be Augustine’s disciple, or one of the lower angels?”

He was not Augustine’s disciple, but at the beginning of the contest he was his fellow soldier. Later, remaining quietly at home, he became an admirer of Augustine’s battles and victories, while the entire burden of the war fell upon Augustine.

Gelasius praises Jerome as much as Augustine because that heretical Seneca was attacking both with his slanderous tooth. Similarly, when Pope Coelestine specifically names Augustine alone as defending the Church against the efforts of the Semi-Pelagians, we understand that Augustine alone had been attacked by them—not Augustine together with Jerome, as Annatus imagines.

Furthermore, in that letter Gelasius presents the doctrine and teachings of Saint Augustine alone, including teachings that are by no means approved by the recent writers, so clearly that he truly must be called wholly Augustinian. We have already proved this brilliantly above.

Saint Pope Hormisdas succeeds these men. As we related in Book II, chapter 19, of the *Pelagian History*, when Bishop Possessor consulted him concerning the books of Faustus of Riez, Hormisdas replied that those books had by no means been received by the Church, and added:

> “Nevertheless, concerning free choice and the grace of God, what the Roman—that is, Catholic—Church follows and preserves can indeed be learned abundantly from various books of blessed Augustine, and especially from those addressed to Prosper and Hilary; nevertheless, explicit chapters are also contained in the ecclesiastical archives,” and so forth. [Col. 0796A]

By this commendation he declared Saint Augustine’s doctrine to be the doctrine of the Church. The recent writers, however, think that little weight is thereby added to Augustine’s authority, and they restrict Hormisdas’s testimony by perverse qualifications.

Annatus, Book VIII, chapter 6, says:

> “Since we are sent to the books *On the Good of Perseverance* and *On the Predestination of the Saints*, which were written to Prosper and Hilary, we must think only this: whatever Augustine intended throughout those books belongs to the Roman and Catholic faith.”

He adds that only two matters are intended there: that the beginning of faith and perseverance in good to the end are gifts of God. Hence he concludes on page 905:

> “Therefore, when the supreme pontiff sends us to these books to hear what the Roman—that is, Catholic—Church teaches concerning grace and free choice, he commands us to learn only this. Therefore, if anything else occurs in them while these matters are being confirmed by Augustine, and if those other things have no necessary connection with what is chiefly intended, it is not the pontiff’s mind that we adhere firmly to them, if nothing else compels us to do so, because it is not Augustine’s own mind either.”

These glosses are wholly malicious and topsy-turvy. For who does not know that Faustus’s books were written chiefly—or rather exclusively—against predestination before foreseen merits? That is their entire purpose: to refute Saint Augustine’s opinion. Hence Peter the Deacon, at the end of his book *On the Incarnation and Grace*, writes that he and his fellow monks anathematize:

> “the books of Faustus, bishop of Gaul, who advanced from the monastery of Lérins, books which there is no doubt were written against the doctrine of predestination.”

Therefore, when Hormisdas rejects Faustus’s work and, by contrast, urges that Saint Augustine’s books be read, he approves the doctrine of Saint Augustine concerning gratuitous predestination, which Annatus nevertheless casts aside as a matter of indifference.

The pontiff rejects Faustus’s books entitled *On Grace and Free Choice*; he approves what Augustine writes on that subject, especially in the works addressed to Prosper and Hilary. Accordingly, whatever theses concerning grace and free choice Augustine set forth against which Faustus opposed contrary propositions, Hormisdas teaches that those theses are maintained and defended by the Roman Church.

Certainly it reeks of the greatest ill will to reduce so extensive a testimony to only two statements. But the pontiff does not praise only those two books of Augustine; he refers to VARIOUS books of Augustine, especially those addressed to Prosper and Hilary. Therefore the other volumes of Augustine are also approved in that passage. Whatever Augustine teaches in them concerning grace and free choice, the Roman Church, according to Hormisdas, follows and preserves.

Annatus, however, as though the particle “especially” meant only a restrictive qualification, pretends that Hormisdas confirmed merely the two statements of the holy teacher which he chiefly establishes in the books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*. It is not so, Annatus—not so! Apart from what Augustine wrote in those two books, he also wrote in VARIOUS OTHER BOOKS on grace and free choice, and the whole of this teaching is approved by the Roman Church. [Col. 0797A]

Decampsius takes another route against Hormisdas’s testimony, in Book III of *On the Jansenian Heresy*, disputation 1, chapter 4. Since Hormisdas said that certain chapters concerning grace and free choice were contained in the ecclesiastical archives, Decampsius thinks that these were the statements found appended to Pope Coelestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul. He writes that only these statements, drawn from Augustine’s books, were approved by the Roman Church. His words are:

> “Hormisdas asserts that what the Church thinks concerning grace and free choice can be learned from the works of Saint Augustine, because these very chapters, which are contained in the ecclesiastical archives and which Coelestine inserted into his letter, are defended there with the greatest vigor. Who among us has ever denied this? We admit that Augustine’s works contain and vigorously defend those very things which were decreed by the Church against the Pelagians. But we deny that nothing else is found in his books; and Hormisdas supports us on this point when he calls those chapters collected by Coelestine the chapters in which it is explicitly stated that the deeper questions, which Augustine treats at greater length in his struggle against the Pelagians, were not approved by the Roman Church.”

But who unlocked the ecclesiastical archives for Decampsius, so that he could know with such confidence that Hormisdas meant those statements of Coelestine by the term “chapters”? How does he know that, from the whole of Saint Augustine’s doctrine, only Coelestine’s nine chapters were deposited in the ecclesiastical archives? We know that Saint Leo the Great, who occupied the pontifical see third after Coelestine, copied two complete chapters word for word from Saint Augustine’s book against the Pelagians in a letter to our metropolitan of Aquileia. Why should Hormisdas not also have referred to these?

We know that Saint Pope Gelasius wrote to Bishop Honorius against the Pelagians and mentioned certain chapters:

> “Concerning these matters,” he says, “if those whom your charity has sent wish to be instructed more fully, the following headings, together with their answers, will make them known.”

Why, then, did Hormisdas not mean these chapters indicated by Gelasius? Or are we to believe that Gelasius decreed nothing other than those matters published under Coelestine’s name? Who would believe such a claim made without evidence?

We know that the same Gelasius, in his letter to the bishops throughout Picenum, insisted upon three or four statements of Saint Augustine, as we showed above—statements criticized by the recent writers, who imagine that they slipped from Augustine in his frenzy against the Pelagians. It is therefore more credible that Gelasius also counted these among those headings than that he meant only Coelestine’s statements.

We know that Felix IV sent to the Fathers of Orange statements concerning divine grace extracted from Saint Augustine’s books against the Semi-Pelagians; these were arranged into twenty-five canons. Did the pontiff find all those assertions in the ecclesiastical archives? Or, having found only those nine selected by Coelestine, did he enrich the ecclesiastical archives with new riches from Augustine’s treasury? What do you say, new interpreters of the ancient constitutions of the Roman pontiffs? [Col. 0798A]

Since mention has arisen here of Felix IV’s chapters, we should recall from Book I, chapter 23, of the *Pelagian History* that the Roman pontiff, in order to settle by apostolic authority the disputes concerning the aids of divine grace that had disturbed Gaul for nearly a hundred years, selected twenty-five statements from Saint Augustine’s books and sent them to Saint Caesarius of Arles, for him and the other bishops of Gaul to sign.

Who, moreover, does not understand how much honor was thereby added to Augustine, when words that had previously been his own passed into the oracles of Roman pontiffs and synods? But here again the recent writers raise dust, so that the glory of the authority bestowed upon Augustine may be obscured.

Annatus cries out in chapter 6, page 903:

> “And Felix, whom the Baians also count among Augustine’s approvers, because he sent to the bishops of Gaul the canons of the Council of Orange, extracted from Augustine’s books and even composed in Augustine’s own words, showed by that extraction what it was necessary for everyone to accept from his entire doctrine—namely, what is expressed in those canons—while leaving readers free to form their own judgment concerning the other controversies that arise.”

Excellent and sound! Thus not only Coelestine’s nine statements were approved from Augustine’s books, as you repeat to the point of nausea, but many additional doctrines as well—twenty-five of them, indeed—so that it would be a sacrilege to oppose them.

But Annatus objects in the same place:

> “Therefore, by the force of this approval, no controversy ought to be raised against those who accept those selected chapters, even if they reject certain others.”

I do not wish to argue here whether the recent writers accept the Augustinian canons confirmed at Orange as they stand, without sometimes doing violence to them through forced interpretations—a practice for which they are rightly criticized by learned men. I shall deal with you more gently. However you explain the canons of Orange, as you please, we raise no question with you on that account. But that you reject other doctrines of Augustine we can in no way tolerate, and we prepare an accusation against you—not because you are contemptuous of an apostolic decree, but because you are contemptuous of its example.

Indeed, if the Apostolic See judged that all the disputes concerning divine grace which had arisen in Gaul should be settled by the doctrine of Augustine alone, it provided posterity with a notable example: whenever disputes concerning grace should again break out in the same matter, people should take refuge in the doctrine of that same holy bishop, hear judgment from Augustine’s books, and cling to Augustine alone. This is what Clement VIII accomplished in the old spirit and by a new example.

Therefore, since the adversaries openly declare that in many of the controversies concerning divine grace that have recently arisen they stand against Augustine, everyone can see that they oppose the judgment of Felix IV, make light of his example, and creep toward the truth by an entirely different path from Augustine’s.

Nevertheless, later men’s eyes were pained when they saw so much honor bestowed upon Augustinian doctrine by Felix IV and the Synod of Orange [Col. 0799A]. Therefore they attempt to bury it beneath the rubble of glosses, saying that the Church in her synods used Augustine’s opinions not out of necessity but on the strength of his authority, using him as a teacher, not as a disciple. This is Adam’s clever comment, chapter 9, p. 653. See how this answer strangles itself. The adversary intends to diminish the authority of the holy Doctor, yet increases it as much as possible. No one is surprised when he sees a disciple repeating his master’s words; but that a master should be willing to pronounce a judgment only by speaking through the mouth of a disciple is plainly extraordinary, and amounts to an exceptional elevation of the disciple. The synods and Roman pontiffs have always followed the opinions of the holy Fathers, so that they might propose for orthodox belief what had been handed down in the Church’s tradition.

This is gathered from the letter of Saint Leo to Leo Augustus, where, after adducing several testimonies of the holy Fathers—including many of Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo—he concludes: “We ought to follow these words; it is fitting for us to obey these doctrines.” At the Council of Chalcedon, session 1, after the creed of the Council of Nicaea had been recited, the Fathers said: “It seemed necessary to set forth the testimonies of the holy and catholic Fathers, which can satisfy us as to how they understood it and confidently proclaimed it, so that it may be clear that all who hold the right and undefiled faith both understand, interpret, and proclaim it in this way.” And in session 2, immediately after the beginning: “For the Fathers taught these things, and what they set forth is preserved in writing; we cannot say anything beyond them.” And in session 5: “Therefore, following the holy Fathers,” and so forth.

Pope Saint Agatho, in his letter to the emperor Constantine, which is preserved in the Sixth Synod, session 4, against the Monothelites, after producing the testimonies of the holy Fathers—where Augustine is praised as “the most discerning PREACHER OF THE TRUTH” and “the pre-eminent DOCTOR”—says: “Behold, most pious Lord and son, the doctrine of the Catholic and apostolic Church has been illumined by the testimonies of the holy Fathers like spiritual rays,” and so forth. There he also writes that the Monothelites must be condemned as not being followers of the holy Fathers. In session 10 all those testimonies of the Fathers were reread in the synod and compared with the books existing at Constantinople; and in session 8 the synod gave its assent to Agatho’s letter, declaring that it conformed to the doctrine of the holy Fathers. Hence George, bishop of Constantinople, said:

“Searching through the testimonies of the holy and approved Fathers preserved in the venerable patriarchal archives, I found that all the testimonies of the holy and approved Fathers contained in those same petitions were harmonious and in no respect at variance with the holy and approved Fathers. I agree with them, and thus I confess and believe.”

The others present subscribed to this statement. Countless testimonies could be brought forward to demonstrate that synods, compelled by necessity, professed to embrace and follow the doctrine of the holy Fathers.

But, you will say, you are speaking of Augustine alone, not of all the Fathers. The Church must necessarily follow all the Fathers when they teach the same thing with one accord in her synods, since she defines dogmas from the tradition of the Fathers; but she does not necessarily follow a private doctor such as Augustine. Yet this escape does not help you. For when you maintain that Pope Felix and the Fathers of Orange followed the opinion of Augustine alone by authority, not by necessity, I ask you: did they follow Augustine teaching against the other Fathers, or did they follow him while he shared the same opinion as the other Fathers?

If you say the first, they did not do so merely by authority. A private opinion of one man cannot be defined as a matter of faith if it is clear that all the Fathers handed down the contrary; yet, because of the supreme excellence of one holy Doctor, judgment may be suspended and neither opinion defined. This is what later writers affirm concerning Augustine’s private opinion about the simultaneous creation of all things. But if you choose the second, you now see that the opinion asserted by all the Fathers must necessarily be approved, if a correct judgment is to be given on the matter.

Moreover, when the Church is about to pronounce judgment on controversies of faith, she must necessarily define the position in which the truth lies, since she cannot in any way number falsehood among the dogmas of faith. Therefore, when Felix and the Fathers of Orange defined the opinions of Saint Augustine as Catholic, they followed them out of necessity, since they could not possibly follow the opposing errors of the Semi-Pelagians. Felix, indeed, could refrain from copying Augustine’s opinions word for word, as Prosper, Fulgentius, Prudentius, and other Doctors of the Augustinian school copied them; but he could not, by necessity, fail to transmit their meaning, since it was already certain that they were true before the council’s definition, and since the Church can define nothing except what is true.

With equal ease one may refute what they add: that the Synod of Orange employed Augustine’s opinions as a teacher, not as a disciple. They are certainly saying something remarkable when they claim that the Fathers of Orange, who lived an entire century after Augustine’s death, could have been Augustine’s teachers, by whom he could not even have been taught at all. A teacher, plainly, is one who teaches, and a disciple one who is taught; and if someone does not know this, it is strange that he should ever have been a disciple, or even could have been one. Who taught and who was taught—Augustine or the Synod of Orange—you can see for yourselves.

In former times Augustine was indeed a disciple of the Church, and he professed himself such when he wrote to Pope Boniface that he was sending his writings not so much to be learned as to be examined, and, if something perhaps displeased him, to be corrected: *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians to Boniface*, book 1, chapter 1. But since he obtained from God the grace of illumination for teaching, as Saint Fulgentius says, and alone shattered all the Pelagian contrivances, the Church bestowed such honor upon him that, through the apostolic see, he was consecrated as a teacher of that same Church.

Hence, in the letter so often repeated by later writers, Celestine calls Augustine “our teacher” as a mark of honor; Gelasius, in his letter to Honorius, calls him a teacher of the Church; and John II, as we shall soon say, writes of Augustine: “The Roman Church follows and preserves his doctrine according to the decrees of my predecessors.” Indeed, if the Roman Church follows Augustine’s doctrine, Augustine must be called a teacher of that same Church, just as we call those who follow the opinions of Saint Thomas or Scotus their disciples. Why should this seem remarkable? Did not that great Aquinas once sit among beginners in the schools, and afterward become the supreme master of the Scholastics?

When the aforementioned bishops said in the Councils of Chalcedon and Constantinople that they followed the holy Fathers, they professed themselves their disciples, submitting themselves to be instructed by their doctrines. Those Leos, Felixes, Athanasiuses, Hilarys, Augustines, Cyrils, Gregorys, and others whom they cite there were therefore teachers of the synods. Accordingly, since the Council of Orange followed Augustine alone, it had Augustine alone as its teacher.

Saint John II also deserves to be numbered among the encomiasts of Saint Augustine. In his third letter to the senators he says: “Saint Augustine, whose doctrine the Roman Church follows and preserves according to the decrees of my predecessors.” By these words the pontiff not only consecrated Saint Augustine’s doctrine, but also affirmed that it had been approved from ancient times by his predecessors.

But now listen to the interpretations of the later writers. Hear Decamps, cited work, book 3, disputation 1, chapter 4, no. 12:

“Since, then, this letter does not concern Saint Augustine’s doctrine against the Pelagians, nor does it name any of the books by which he attacked them, why do the Jansenists infer from it specifically that everything contained in Augustine’s works was approved by the apostolic see, so that to depart from them even slightly would be impious?”

Moraines adds, *Anti-Jansenian*, disputation 12, no. 50:

“What he adds from John II and Clement VIII is similar to what preceded, and proves nothing more. For they merely affirm that the Roman Church preserves and follows Augustine’s doctrine, bequeathed to her, as it were, as a legacy; yet she does not follow it in everything,” and so forth.

That is what they say. We know that Saint John’s letter is directed against the Nestorians, not the Pelagians; but we also know that the Nestorians arose from the Pelagians, that the two supported one another and were condemned together at Ephesus, and that Prosper inscribed the same epitaph of disgrace upon both heresies. Yet we reply that John there praised those works of the holy Doctor which possess no less authority than that bestowed by the apostolic see upon the books written against the Pelagians. For since Augustine surpassed all those who came after him by a long interval in the former works, while in the latter he surpassed even himself, if the Roman Church follows Augustine as a teacher where he was honored with lesser praise, she will adhere to him all the more reverently where he was received with the encomia of so many Roman prelates.

The Roman Church not only listens to Augustine when he teaches; she defends him when he is attacked. Thus, while she champions Augustine’s authority, the later writers who rise up against it will be wasting their oil and labor.

As for the decree of Clement VIII, by which he ordered all controversies concerning divine helps to be examined before the tribunal of Saint Augustine—a decree by which later writers were once pressed—they now evade it by the following evasions:

“For, they say, the objection sometimes made by some people—that Clement VIII, during the disputes concerning the helps, ordered Augustine’s opinion above all to be sought—is easily answered. He did not issue that command with the prejudice that it was impious to dissent from Augustine in any matter, while rejecting Celestine’s distinction between propositions which it was necessary to assert and those which it was not necessary to assert. Nor is it the same thing to wish disputants to investigate Augustine’s opinion and to wish them to follow it altogether in every respect.”

Again:

“Augustine’s opinion had to be investigated in order to determine whether the matters under dispute touched upon dogmas already established [Col. 0802B] or not, or whether they rather concerned indifferent questions. Moreover, since it is clear from the mind of Saint Bonaventure that Augustine sometimes intended less and said more, there was a reason for the supreme pontiff’s ordering that his opinion be investigated: namely, so that what it was clear he had intended might be retained, but not everything he was shown to have said.”

These are Annatus’s words, book 8, chapter 4, at the end. Until now no one has doubted that, in the sessions on the helps held before Clement VIII, Molina’s doctrine was called to the Augustinian doctrine’s exact standard.

Meanwhile, let them hear Paul Leonardus—truly a Scerlogus—in his *Apology for Middle Knowledge*, part 2, no. 39:

“Indeed,” he says, “in the disputations conducted at Rome before the holinesses of Clement VIII and Paul V, Saint Augustine’s mind was often and carefully questioned, because in this particular class of questions it was considered especially desirable that the best arguments should be brought forward under the support of so great a champion of divine grace. Thus, in the year 1602, the treatise was produced: ‘Who attributes greater powers to free will for good? Augustine or Molina?’ That article contains seven questions, in each of which Augustine’s mind is debated in relation to Molina’s, and so forth. From these matters it is clear that nearly the whole aim of the dispute concerned what Augustine thought.”

The matter could be dealt with briefly if I were permitted to recite the acts of those congregations, or the whole of Clement VIII’s address which preceded those disputations. But since this has been forbidden by a recent Roman decree, I omit the necessary defense, to the detriment of the cause I am defending. Indeed, I might perhaps say better things than others, since I have read all the manuscripts of Gregory Nugnius Coronel, a Portuguese Augustinian, who served as secretary of the congregations mentioned. I sacrifice this to a reverent silence.

Nevertheless, I shall repeat a fragment of the aforementioned address of Clement VIII, which Father Macedo inserted into his *Euchologium*, approved by the supreme congregation of the Holy Roman Inquisition, among the encomia of the pontiffs, which he recites under 28 August, p. 406:

“Although I must render an account of my actions to God alone, I shall nevertheless state at present the reasons why I have decided TO BIND this entire dispute TO THE STANDARD OF THE DOCTRINE OF SAINT AUGUSTINE concerning grace.

“The first is that, if, as Blessed Prosper says almost at the beginning of his book against the Collator, for twenty years the forces of the Catholic Church fought for grace against the Pelagians and finally conquered under Augustine’s leadership, then in this matter of counsel we must also RECOGNIZE AND FOLLOW THE SAME LEADER.

“The second is that this same saint appears to have omitted nothing that pertains to the present controversies, and so forth.

“The third and final reason is that, since many pontiffs and our predecessors were such vigorous defenders and champions of Saint Augustine’s doctrine that they wished it to remain in the Church as though by hereditary right, it is not right for me to allow it to be deprived of that inheritance.”

The most illustrious Lord Philip Viscount of Milan, bishop of Catacensis, showed me this address written in Clement’s own hand. He also left this attested in manuscript notes on chapter 4 of book 8 of *Augustine Vindicated*, a volume which is in my possession.

Here I cannot refrain from expressing indignation at Annatus, who pretends that in those disputes concerning the helps it was not his Molina, but our Augustine, who was subjected to examination. For he writes that those sessions were held “so that Augustine’s opinion might be investigated, namely, so that what it was clear he had intended might be retained, but not everything he was shown to have said.”

By this reasoning, the holy Doctor—whom the apostolic see declared judge of the matter then under dispute, and who was to pronounce judgment from his own books—is said by Annatus to have been subjected at that time to examination, with this judgment passed upon him: that what it was clear he had intended should be retained, but not everything he was shown to have said. And when Annatus says that Augustine sometimes spoke by excess, the conclusion is that Clement VIII’s judgment in those disputations was that such excess should not be retained.

But what is this other than making Augustine a defendant instead of a judge? Nor do I think Annatus thinks otherwise, for at the end of chapter 2, p. 864, he cries:

“Is Scholasticism to be buried so that Augustine alone may reign, or is Augustine to be read in the light of Scholasticism and measured by its standard?”

Neither alternative is our wish. We want Scholasticism to flourish, and we want it measured by Augustine’s standard, not the reverse, as you contend. Clement’s meaning is clear: he wished the Scholastic disputes concerning the helps to be measured “TO THE STANDARD OF THE DOCTRINE OF SAINT AUGUSTINE.” Everyone can see how well you agree with this when you measure Augustine’s doctrine by the standard of the Scholastics.

Indeed, the Master of the Sentences, who first reduced Scholasticism to a method, constructed it from the opinions of the Fathers, and especially of Augustine. Hence the Roman Church herself, among the prayers recited on Augustine’s feast day, says of him: “Those who afterward taught theological discipline by method and reason followed him above all.”

Therefore the Scholastics measured their own opinions by the standard of Augustine’s doctrine, and not a single word contrary to Augustine fell from the principal men of that ancient discipline. The later writers thought differently. One of them, Moraines, says in the preface to his *Anti-Jansenian*:

“Those who formerly demanded Augustine as judge in everything now consider themselves free even not to admit him as an honorary arbiter in other matters.”

Alas, what a dark day has mingled the lowest with the highest! Formerly Pope Clement appointed Augustine judge in the controversy concerning the helps; now the later writers, as they are not ashamed openly to confess, do not admit him even as an honorary arbiter. By charging him with excesses, contradictions, and errors, they not only publicly declare the holy Doctor a suspect judge but parade him as a defendant, so that no one can deny that they have imposed upon us the necessity of undertaking this lengthy defense.

And what else is this than violently dragging Augustine from the chair in which the apostolic see placed him, from which he expounded heavenly doctrines, and in which Catholics have until now listened to him with the highest reverence as a teacher of orthodox dogma? O powers above, gentle spirits . . .

But what the later writers might babble about the most recent encomium of Alexander VII, who, following in the footsteps of his predecessors, consecrated Saint Augustine’s doctrine, must now be explained. When Father Christian Lupus, the Augustinian and distinguished doctor of Louvain, was about to travel from Rome to Belgium, the aforementioned Alexander gave him a letter to deliver to the sacred theological faculty of Louvain. In it he testified to his paternal love for sons who had rendered good service, and encouraged them to uphold and defend the doctrine of Saint Augustine and his disciple Saint Thomas, which they had pursued with the highest praise, adding a new encomium for both holy Doctors.

“For the rest,” he says, “we do not doubt that, on account of your singular zeal for knowledge and piety, you will always embrace and defend against the enemies of orthodox religion the sound and uncorrupted doctrine required by so many declarations of the apostolic see and by the traditions of the holy Fathers. Nor do we doubt that you will always follow, as you assert, and earnestly revere the firm and most secure dogmas of the distinguished Doctors of the Church, Augustine and Thomas Aquinas.

“These most holy men, whose great names among all Catholics surpass every praise, do not need the commendation of a new proclamation,” and so forth.

“Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, under the Fisherman’s Ring, 7 August 1660; in the seventh year of our pontificate.”

After Lupus had left Rome and was passing through Pesaro, where at that time I was prefect of the theological school among our religious brethren, he told me what a treasure he was carrying with him to Belgium. When he reached Louvain and delivered the papal letter to the senate of theologians, it is astonishing how joyfully everyone, individually and collectively, received it. A theological suspension of lectures was proclaimed, a public service of thanksgiving was announced, and prayers were ordered for the safety of the most beneficent pontiff.

I present an extract from the edict published by the university’s dean; Father Gabriel of Saint Vincent, whom I shall soon praise, gives the complete text:

“[The faculty orders] that they attend the solemn Mass to be celebrated there by the same faculty for the long life, safety, and happy government of our most holy Lord Alexander VII, pope by divine providence, who, in addition to other proofs of his paternal benevolence toward the same academy, has deigned, by an apostolic rescript in the form of a brief, granted in response to its petition, to honor it by proclaiming Saint Augustine and Thomas Aquinas patrons and masters of the school of the faculty, as distinguished Doctors of the Catholic Church, and commending their dogmas as firm and most secure, and therefore always to be followed and earnestly revered. He adds that the great names of these most holy men, which among all Catholics surpass every praise, do not require the commendation of a new proclamation, and so forth.

“Given 6 November of the year 1660.”

These things brought as much joy to the most sincere disciples of Saint Augustine as they brought grief—not, I shall not say to envious men, but to those who for some time had not been well disposed toward Augustine. For some, as though driven into a frenzy, burst into these impious words: that the celebrated brief had been obtained by a diabolical machination.

The witness to this is Christian Lupus himself, in his *Apologetic Letter on Attrition and Contrition*, chapter 5, against accusation 11, p. 49, which he published at Louvain in 1667 and dedicated to me as a mark of honor, since he is exceedingly fond of me. Vincent Baronius identifies the person to whom such shameless words escaped, in part 4 of his *Opuscula*, book 1, section 2, article 5, § 1.

Another later writer says of Alexander’s celebrated encomium that the supreme pontiff never saw that private brief. He claims to have learned this from a man of his own religious community and, to lend greater credibility to his assertion, says: “I affirm this sincerely and swear it solemnly.” I do not wish to name this writer, because he has a powerful patron whose protection I too gladly enjoy. Nevertheless, the most learned Father Gabriel of Saint Vincent refuted him at length in his book *On Remedies for Ignorance*, disputation 14, doubt 9, no. 149, saying:

“Cardinal Nerlius, who at that time was secretary of briefs, told a very distinguished man that he himself had composed this brief on the commission of the said Alexander VII; that the pontiff had read it attentively; and that he had given the seal so that it might be sealed with it and sent to the University of Louvain. And this very distinguished man testified to the matter with his hand upon his breast.”

Father Gabriel committed these things to writing and soon afterward departed this life, leaving behind a profound longing for himself. He was an ornament of the Carmelite institute of stricter observance and was especially esteemed by Clement X, the excellent and greatest pontiff. He will live forever as one who deserved well of Augustine’s doctrine, to whose glorious name he dedicated a theological volume.

Let the later writers know that Alexander VII came from the most noble Chigi family, to which hereditary devotion to the name of Augustine has been perpetual, so that for more than three hundred years one member of the Chigi family has always wished to be called Augustine. I want no other witness for this statement than Alexander himself. In the very full senate of the cardinal Fathers and bishops, when discussing the canonization of Thomas of Villanova for the king of Spain (*From the Acts of the Canonization of Saint Thomas of Villanova*), after recounting the petitions of many princes and peoples, moved by their devotion to the Augustinian family, he added:

“Then indeed—we say it confidently—there was our devotion to the most holy Doctor of theology, the Lord Augustine, handed down, as it were, through our ancestors according to the flesh, and our particular veneration, dating from adolescence, for this pupil of his,” and so forth.

The hereditary devotion of so great a pontiff toward the most holy Doctor of theology was known to everyone. Hence, in that same assembly, Francis Albitius, the glory of the cardinal Fathers, a prince of outstanding learning and greater than any praise of ours, was asked for his opinion and said:

“Most blessed Father, the outcome of this arduous and most difficult matter has been prolonged, not without the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, so that by your holiness, which recognizes Augustine as patron and protector, the son of Augustine might be placed among the number of the saints.”

I had refuted at length several statements of that later writer, but, compelled by the authority of a great man, I omit them. For they are so absurd that it is better to consign them to silence than to spread them more widely by a lengthy refutation.

## CHAPTER VII

The approval by the apostolic see of Augustinian doctrine against the Pelagians defended against the wicked interpretations of later writers.

Up to this point we have vindicated the more distinguished testimonies of the Roman prelates concerning the excellence of Augustinian doctrine against the sinister opposition of later writers, affirming each of the pontiffs’ encomia of Augustine in its entirety. Now we must examine what those men object against the Church’s universal approval of Augustine.

I shall make the attempt with a light hand. I shall imitate the strategy of those who foment civil wars among enemies so that, after weakening them by domestic dissensions, they may afterward overcome them without difficulty. I shall set domestic witnesses against the Anti-Augustinians, and answer their threatening missiles with missiles. But I shall not oppose those witnesses to these novices as their equals; rather, they are far superior—men before whom the novices should not merely rise but fall completely silent: namely, Suárez and Vázquez. O, what great names of the schools! Therefore, in this contest I shall sit back while those two leaders descend into the battle on behalf of my Augustine against the recent adversaries.

Come, then: what do you think, Annatus, about the Church’s approval of Augustinian doctrine? If you have anything to say against it, state it freely.

“We object first,” he says, book 8, chapter 6, p. 902: “Either it was consecrated in such a way that Augustine was taken out of the number of noncanonical writers and transferred into the number of canonical writers, or it was not. If the first, then all Christianity is in error, since it has held the contrary not only since the time of the Scholastics but for twelve hundred years. If the second, then all that approval by the Church still leaves Augustine within the number of fallible writers, whom it is permissible to oppose without injury to anyone.”

But this objection had long ago been answered—not by some Baian, but by Suárez, a vigorous opponent of Baius, whose response they could surely have read at home. After Suárez, *Prolegomena* 6, *On Grace*, chapter 6, no. 15, had cited these words of Saint Prosper in praise of Augustine:

“But you, my most beloved and most venerable brother, if you truly desire to be instructed concerning these questions, as you ought to desire, devote your care to learning the disputations of Blessed Augustine himself, so that in confessing God’s grace you may attain the most purified and salutary understanding of evangelical and apostolic doctrine,”

he writes:

“Nevertheless, he does not say that Augustine wrote apostolically either because he was a canonical writer or because he possessed the infallible assistance of the Holy Spirit in writing, as the Apostles did. That would be foreign to Prosper’s meaning and to that of the whole Church. Rather, he says that Augustine wrote apostolically either because he drew his doctrine of grace chiefly from the Apostle Paul and confirmed it with his most powerful testimonies, or certainly because he wrote about grace so truly and faithfully that the apostolic see made Augustine’s doctrine, in matters pertaining to dogmas, its own and approved it.”

Annatus continues:

“We object secondly that those same supreme pontiffs who approved Augustine’s doctrine set aside what seemed necessary to them, while they did not wish either to reject or to assert other intervening questions. Celestine clearly indicated this, as we reported earlier,” p. 903.

Suárez, after reviewing Celestine’s restriction—which, as I shall say, he denies to have been Celestine’s—nevertheless adheres entirely to Augustine, writing:

“Nevertheless, even in these later questions concerning predestination, Augustine’s authority is greatest for the other reasons mentioned above, and therefore he will always be preferred by us to the others.”

But the adversary objects:

“We object thirdly that Augustine’s doctrine was approved together with that of the other holy Fathers. It follows that this approval applies to what Augustine shares with the other Fathers, not to what is proper to him, if there is anything of that kind.” Same place.

But Vázquez, protecting Augustine with a shield, received this weapon in *I–II*, disputation 190, chapter 6, no. 37:

“Although,” he says, “there were none among the Fathers mentioned whom the Scholastic Doctors could cite for this opinion concerning the necessity of grace for each individual good moral act, they would gladly place the support of their position in Augustine alone and in his school, and would rightly judge him sufficient for them, because he is the ONLY ONE who, when the necessity of grace is under discussion, shines among the others like the sun. We have an outstanding testimony and commendation of this doctrine in Celestine’s first letter to the bishops of Gaul.”

Celestine, moreover, praised Augustine alone. Read the same author, part 1, disputation 89, chapter 4, at the beginning.

But Annatus yields neither to Suárez nor to Vázquez. He again objects, p. 902:

“Gerson and Abulensis have already taught us what this approval means. It does not mean that we should understand Augustine to be free from all human defects, but only from the rarer and lesser ones, in the same way that the praises of the other saints are understood. And certainly, since the same hazard of judgment and affections applies to everyone, and Augustine fought against the Pelagians with such determination that he maintained that no one, however holy, has no need to say, ‘Forgive us our debts,’ because of the daily lapses of the will, I do not know what has entered the minds of the Baians, that the Augustinians wish to appear as though they were claiming that there are some who never err in judgment”—namely, Augustine.

But who does not know that Augustine, by a twofold act, lowering himself beneath the others, raised himself higher than all? That great teacher of the Church publicly disclosed both the errors of his affections and those of his judgment: the former in the books of the *Confessions*, the latter in the books of the *Reconsiderations*. This was an entirely singular example, since we see everyone else defending both their own statements and their actions against error.

Would that the adversaries would at some time adopt this opinion concerning their associates and the men of their own family. If they learn that one of these men has been attacked by some writer, they manufacture a thousand apologies, so that they may appear to be the only ones immune from error.

Thus Augustine underwent the same hazard of affection and judgment. Yet when he revisited his books against the Pelagians—book 2, chapters 33, 36, 37, 42, 50, 61, 62, 66, and 67—he corrected no opinion either concerning grace or concerning free will, but approved everything he had said, although in other treatises he had removed many of the theses he had asserted. Hence the holy Doctor nowhere acknowledged that he had fallen into error of judgment in combating the Pelagians. The adversaries, however, grievously err in judgment when they speak so humbly of Augustine.

Augustine perhaps foresaw future censors and, leaving correction to fall upon their shoulders, dealt less severely with himself in that examination, leaving to the later writers the glory of boasting that they had discovered stains in the books he published against the Pelagians—stains that had escaped Augustine’s keen eye and sponge.

What do you say, Annatus? That Augustine was subject to human defects, though rarer and lesser ones, and that he sometimes erred in judgment? The opinion of your Suárez was far different. In *Prolegomena* 6, *On Grace*, chapter 6, no. 17, he writes truly and worthily of Saint Augustine:

“Nothing made Augustine more worthy of admiration and reverence in the Church than his doctrine of grace. But if, in handing down and explaining it, he had at any time fallen into error, his authority would have been greatly weakened, and the Church would have followed his judgment in this doctrine with such confidence undeservedly. It is impious even to think this.”

Saint Prudentius of Troyes had excellently noted the same thing eight hundred years ago in his letter to Hincmar and Pardulus. But since I promised that, having formed something like a pact with Suárez and Vázquez, I would dismiss the assistance of others and fight the later writers for Augustine, I omit the most illustrious testimony of that bishop, to be recited elsewhere.

Annatus has still not been recalled from his unhappy contest by the voices of his own allies. Instead, he presses forward and thrusts upon us this inference:

“Therefore, if, while that testimony of Augustine stands, it is nevertheless permissible not to follow the individual thought of some other Father in these disputes, then, while that approval of the Church or of the supreme pontiffs stands, it will also be permissible not to adhere to every opinion of Augustine.”

But the most subtle of the later writers, Vázquez, had also anticipated and answered this objection. We gave his words from *I–II*, disputation 190, a little earlier; likewise, he says splendidly in part 1, disputation 89, no. 21:

“Although,” he says, “the authority of the other Fathers ought to carry great weight with everyone in every controversy, nevertheless, in this controversy now under discussion, AUGUSTINE ALONE WILL ALWAYS BE FOR ME AS MANY, not only because he stands out most among all who think rightly,” and so forth.

But what Annatus had prefaced in the same place, p. 909, is plainly false:

“From these things it is evident that the Church judged as much should be attributed to Augustine as Augustine himself judged should be attributed to the other Fathers.”

For although in his books against Julian he proved original sin more extensively from the holy Fathers, and likewise the necessity of grace in his book *On the Grace of Christ*, nevertheless, when the Massilians pressed him concerning predestination before foreseen merits, asserting that they did not wish to believe it unless he produced ancient testimonies on the subject, he replied in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 14:

“What need is there, then, for us to search through the little works of those who, before this heresy arose, had no need to engage with this difficult question, which they would undoubtedly have done if they had been compelled to answer such people?”

But in chapter 19 of *The Gift of Perseverance* he adduces Ambrose and Cyprian on his own behalf, from whom he gathers his own opinion not in express words but by necessary inference.

Therefore, in Augustine’s judgment, there is no need for us to search the works of those Fathers where gratuitous predestination is under discussion. Yet Hormisdas commended the books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*; the Synod of Sardica, composed of exiled bishops from Africa, referred us to them; and Clement VIII ordered Molina’s opinion concerning predestination to be examined according to the doctrine of the holy Doctor. Therefore, in that question Augustine did not attribute to the other Fathers as much as the Church attributed to him.

At last, in a final assault against the approval of Saint Augustine’s books, the same Annatus contends, p. 911: “All those approvals which the Neo-Augustinians invoke approve Augustine’s doctrine in general, but there is none that applies to all and each of his individual positions.” He serves up again the stale dish of the Semi-Pelagians. For when Saint Celestine had praised Saint Augustine’s books, they used to say that this commendation had been given only to Augustine’s books in general, and maintained that it had been bestowed on his earlier volumes but not on his later ones. Against them Saint Prosper writes admirably at the end of *Against the Collator*, chapter 42: “Let the slanderers recognize that they needlessly object that no special and distinct testimony was given to these books, whose standard is praised throughout all his volumes; for the apostolic see approves, together with what it already knows, what does not differ from it; and what it joins to its judgment in praise it does not separate.” Thus far he.

As a reserve force, Moraines leaps forward to support Annatus, already exhausted, though he attacks Augustine with a different kind of weapon. For, in order to diminish the splendor of the papal approval granted to Augustine, he does not indeed oppose it with the clouds of envious interpretations; rather, he sets before us more exalted praises bestowed by the apostolic see on other Fathers, in comparison with which those granted to Augustine may be judged far inferior. In this way, the sun, not by shadows but by an almost boundless light radiating in every direction, overwhelms the tiny brightness of a candle and nearly makes it disappear.

Moraines therefore raises his voice still higher in the preface *To the Orthodox*: “When has it ever been said of Augustine’s writings by some pontiff, in a law enacted concerning them, what Gelasius said about that wondrous letter of Leo the Great to Flavian—that if anyone did not accept it down to a single iota, he would be anathema?” But who does not see that those remarkable praises of Leo’s letter apply fully to Augustine? It is the settled opinion not only of the Latins but also of the Greeks that that celebrated letter of Leo to Flavian was composed by Saint Prosper, Augustine’s disciple. Let us hear Baronius in his notes on the *Martyrology*, under 25 June, where he says of Prosper: “Ado of Vienne and others relate that he was secretary to Saint Pope Leo; and it is said that he wrote that most famous letter of Saint Leo to Flavian on the Incarnation of the Word. This is attested not only by Gennadius, Honorius, and other Latins, but also by Marcellinus Comes in his *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Olybrius and Rusticus.”

This is that Prosper whom Annatus himself, book II, chapter 5, § 2, p. 179, calls “Augustine’s principal and immediate disciple, who appears to have carried his weapons and taken his place in defending the doctrine which he had received from him as though in trust.” Who, then, would deny that praises bestowed on the disciple redound to the master? Indeed, if Saint Gelasius said that Leo’s letter must be accepted down to the smallest iota, then that same pope did not reject even one iota of Augustine’s doctrine. Rather—as has often been thrown in the face of those modern writers—even those opinions of Augustine which seem false or harsh to them were inculcated by that pope of the Church who, according to Vasquez, was Augustinian in every respect.

Moraines again batters Augustinian authority with a double ram brought from Alexandria:

“Who has ever possessed Cyril of Alexandria’s authority in writing—not merely in a provincial or national synod, but in the general Council of Ephesus—so that he himself, on his own authority, could write the Anathemas, and to think or write against them would be virtually the same as resisting the faith? I seem to hear another saying: ‘What then? Will that great Athanasius also be one of the number of Augustine’s sons and disciples—he who is called, without exception, the Father of Fathers, the teacher of teachers, illuminating all the others like the first angel by his light?’”

Certainly, the great source of the troubles which the Council of Ephesus suffered from John, bishop of Antioch, Theodoret, and their fellow bishops, and from the emperor himself, Theodosius, was that the Eastern bishops refused to subscribe to the Anathemas established on the authority of a private individual, although they later abandoned that position.

But let us speak of Augustine. He was called the genius of the African councils because of his wisdom. He also incorporated into his commentaries the entire acts of the Council of Numidia and likewise of the Council of Carthage, although he had not attended the latter, according to the decree of the Fathers. Prosper writes of him at the end of his book *Against the Collator* that Pope Boniface, “although he was most learned, nevertheless requested the responses of the blessed bishop Augustine against the books of the Pelagians.”

Augustine’s opinions became the canons of the Council of Orange and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. On this subject I shall reproduce the words of the Jesuit Decamps: “Augustine,” he says, “was in a certain sense the Church’s precentor, when he went before the Roman pontiffs and councils with his voice in the judgment they pronounced concerning that most arrogant heresy. He was the Church’s tongue, when decrees were framed in his words, and when what had previously been Augustine’s utterances began to be oracles of the Holy Spirit. He was the leader and genius of the councils, when he supplied them with the reasons and arguments by which they overcame Pelagius and his accomplices,” and so forth.

If you believe the words of his colleague, you now see Augustine as Cyril’s equal. The emperor Theodosius certainly judged Augustine equal to Cyril, since he sent a *Sacra* to each of them—the imperial letters were called by this name. Indeed, the prince bestowed considerably greater honor on Augustine. For he wrote to Cyril as metropolitan, so that he might notify his suffragan bishops that a synod was to be convened; but when he had written to the primate of Africa, the bishop of Carthage, concerning the same matter, he nevertheless sent a private letter to Augustine, earnestly asking him to attend the synod. We discussed this matter in the first book of the *Pelagian History*, under the year 431.

Indeed, the testimony of ancient writers establishes that Cyril of Alexandria corresponded with Theodosius so that Saint Augustine might go to the Council of Ephesus. Cyril saw how great a help that illustrious leader, renowned throughout the world for the trophies he had raised in continuous battles against heretics, would be to him against the Nestorians.

We certainly do not make that great Athanasius, the opponent of Arius, Augustine’s disciple; rather, we assert that the war which Athanasius had launched against the Arians was at last successfully brought to an end by Augustine. John Rivius of Belgium, book IV *On the Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 8, § 6, states at length that Augustine alone overturned Arianism from its foundations, and that before him none of the Fathers had accomplished this so thoroughly. Indeed, Saint Augustine devoted himself expressly to combating the Arians both in his books and in sacred discourses. Possidius discusses this matter throughout chapter 17 of his *Life of Augustine*. Therefore, if the arguments and testimonies by which Augustine defeated the sect of Arius are taken into consideration, the holy doctor easily surpassed the earlier Fathers, in the judgment of all learned men.

Moraines presses the matter again: “What of Jerome? Will he too be Augustine’s disciple, or even inferior to the angels?” But we refuted this objection in the preceding chapter.

As for Moraines’ refusal to call Augustine “the teacher of teachers,” he openly contradicts the Fathers. Boniface wished to be taught by Augustine; Saint Celestine called Augustine “our teacher”; Saint Hormisdas referred the Easterners to Augustine; and, indeed, the Roman Church calls Augustine its teacher. Urban V states in his bull on the translation of Saint Thomas that Saint Thomas followed Augustine’s doctrine.

Regarding Scotus, the Spanish Franciscan Fathers say the following in a petition addressed to Peter a Campo, volume I of the *History of Augustine*, book III, chapter 30:

“He was so devoted to Augustinian doctrine that, in his theological commentaries alone, he produced Saint Augustine eight hundred and fifteen times as a witness to his assertions, earnestly striving above all other doctors to penetrate more deeply into Augustine’s mind,” and so forth.

Let Moraines therefore deny that Scotus, Saint Thomas, and so many pontiffs of the Roman Church were disciples and teachers of Saint Augustine, if he wishes Augustine not to be called the teacher of teachers.

I see, however, that Moraines cannot tolerate Augustine’s being called the teacher of teachers without qualification. Know, then, that Saint Augustine is the teacher of teachers in disputes concerning the helps of grace, but not of all teachers: not of those who preceded him—for he could not teach them—nor of those who came after him and refused to be taught by him, which was the hardened pride of the Semi-Pelagians and their unrestrained desire to defend an opinion once conceived. But the Fathers who preceded Augustine are not teachers whom one can compare with Augustine in the matter of grace. Augustine himself testifies in chapter 14 of *The Predestination of the Saints* that they had only briefly and incidentally touched upon what they thought about the grace of God in certain passages of their writings.

Anyone would be ridiculous who, setting aside Augustine’s books, wished to seek a solution to questions about grace from Hilary or Athanasius. Hence all those who illuminated the Church by writing about divine grace were disciples of Saint Augustine. He was the first of the holy Fathers—and specifically in the doctrine of grace—to establish a school of his own, to which Prosper, Fulgentius, Peter the Deacon, Eugyppius, Caesarius, Prudentius, and others gave their names. Thus Augustine may truly be called the teacher of teachers.

We shall never call Augustine the teacher of those later writers who disdain to be his disciples. They read Augustine not in order to have him as their guide, but in order—willingly or unwillingly—to make him a partisan of their own preconceived opinion, bringing against him even the machinery of countless violent interpretations.

Annatus devotes seven entire books to invoking Augustine; Moraines’ volume reproduces Augustine’s words a thousand times. Shall I call such men Augustine’s disciples and followers? They wish to appear to be Augustine’s disciples, but only deceptively; soon they return to their own nature.

Thus, when Moraines had recited praises of Augustine in the preface *To the Orthodox*, which he prefixed to his *Anti-Jansenist*, lest he should seem to yield to his adversary in this matter, he gradually turned the panegyric into a satire—a vigorous mutilator of Augustine’s glory, who at first seemed to be a not inelegant promoter of it. It is clear from what was said at the beginning of chapter 5 that Annatus followed the same path.

Who would not laugh at the man’s perverse plan? After he had disputed with the Jansenists before Augustine’s tribunal in seven books, and had boasted that Augustine had awarded him the whole case intact and entire, exclaiming at the threshold of book VIII that the Jansenists could hope for no support from Augustine, one might think that he would thank the judge, commend his favorable and friendly disposition toward him, and, in letters sent to his friends, pour out unrestrained praise of him. Yet we see Augustine treated most shamefully by him, with a long line of witnesses brought against him and assailed with a thousand insults—in a word, transformed from judge into defendant. O most grateful disciples of Saint Augustine!

Moreover, they cannot tolerate Augustine’s being said to have illuminated all the others by his light like the first angel. We know that Prosper once sang the following in chapter 2 of *Against the Ungrateful*:

> Augustine was he whom the grace of Christ,  
> watering him more abundantly,  
> gave as a light kindled from light to our age.

Saint Fulgentius, book II *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, chapter 18, writes:

“Let everyone who desires to attain eternal salvation read Augustine, humbly praying the Lord of mercy that, as he reads, he may receive the same spirit of understanding which Augustine received in order to write, and may obtain the same grace of illumination, so that he may learn what Augustine attained in order to teach.”

But why should we not hear Saint Thomas of Villanova, archbishop of Valencia, in sermon 1 *On Saint Augustine*?

“O most illustrious Father Augustine,” he says, “who irradiated the Church of Christ not only by the holiness of your life but also by the wondrous splendor of your wisdom—by a light of your own, a full light, a steadfast light! For if wisdom is light, who shines in the Church of God as Augustine does? All the stars shine from the sun; from Augustine all the doctors of wisdom who came after him receive their light. He himself, however, shines with a light of his own, which he received from no human being but from God alone, for without anyone handing it down and without any teacher he learned all the disciplines.”

Is Augustine not therefore, according to Thomas, like the first angel, through whom theologians assert that the light of understanding is passed on to the others, while he himself was enlightened by God alone?

Our angel of Hippo certainly illuminated Prosper, Fulgentius, Thomas, and the other orthodox Fathers with the rays of his doctrine. But the later writers who contend with Annatus that “something was lacking in Augustine’s light when he reconciled the efficacy of the divine decrees and helps with created freedom,” book VIII, chapter 4, p. 874; or who, as the same writer says elsewhere, *Disputation 3 on Middle Knowledge*, chapter 5, no. 113, “think they see a certain ray not emitted from Augustine’s sun”; and finally those who were not ashamed to write with Molina, part I, question 23, articles 4 and 5, disputation 1, member 6, “while, as it were under that mist, Saint Augustine did not attend to this, judging at first sight in accordance with his opinion concerning predestination,” and so forth—these later writers, I say, for whom the light of purer doctrine shines, do not receive the splendors of this first angel, with Augustine placed beneath a cloud; indeed, they almost despise them. It should therefore occasion no surprise that they are so distressed when so much light is attributed to Augustine that he could irradiate all the doctors who followed him and bring the earlier Fathers’ opinions concerning divine grace the light of a fuller and more solid doctrine.

But Annatus, gathering breath, again attacks Augustine. Imitating the deed of his colleague Moraines, he sets against the holy doctor a book of his own party, furnished by the apostolic see with a more explicit and more effective approval than any volume of Augustine.

The adversary’s words are:
