“Eighth, we object that all those approvals which the Neo-Augustinians invoke approve Augustine’s doctrine in general, but that there is none which applies to all and each of his individual positions. If there were any such approval, they will not deny, I think, that it would create a more explicit and more effective obligation to agree in every respect. What, then, will they do if there is found in the world another book whose every single content has been approved and promulgated by the authority of the apostolic see through a bull issued for the perpetual remembrance of the matter?”

Come now, reveal this little book which has surely fallen from heaven—unless you perhaps think it sacrilegious for sacred things to be made public so quickly.

“There is,” he says, “such a book in the world, and it is by a holy author.”

Now you arouse piety and religion, as you commend the author and declare him a saint. But Annatus continues to keep the reader in suspense:

“But who is it? Rather, I should say a little book, because it is small in bulk and contemptible in appearance, yet possesses very great virtue.”

Bring forth, then, quickly—very quickly—that little book whose apostolic approval creates “a more explicit and more effective obligation to agree in every respect” than all the great volumes of Augustine.

“But who, at last,” he adds, “and whose is it?”

Indeed, this is what we ask, this is what we beg: please do not torture our expectation for long. I invoke the holy name and power of the author of that little book.

“Let the Baianists,” he says, “contract their brows and glare fiercely; the pill must be swallowed.”

Do those whom you call Baianists need your medicine? We, for our part, already possess a stronger stomach, long accustomed to your insults against Augustine and to swallowing every kind of bitter pill. We do not need to be prepared with pills in order to hear about the author and the book without disgust or collapse.

Indeed, since you claim that the author of the book is a saint, we shall repeatedly beg you, with the utmost reverence, while kissing its pages sprinkled with sacred doctrines, to preserve this saintly author intact and unharmed as a defense of Augustine’s authority against the new censors—for it is the duty of saints, in turn, to protect their own.

But you say:

“It is the book of the *Spiritual Exercises* of Saint Ignatius, which Paul III, after having it rigorously examined, approved in such a way that he said that he approved, praised, and fortified with the protection of the present document, by the aforesaid authority, with certain knowledge, the aforesaid instructions and exercises, and all and each of the things contained in them.”

Thus he writes in book VIII, the final chapter, after keeping his readers in suspense for a long time, almost as if in jest. And on p. 912 he exclaims:

“I should like to know what those who invoke an approval less explicit and less clear—namely, Augustine’s—on behalf of their errors will answer to so eloquent and so explicit an approval.”

Far be it from us to detract in any way from the approval of Ignatius’s book. Indeed, your own writers testify how highly the Augustinians valued it in *The Image of the First Century*, book III, chapter 10. Speaking of the Exercises of the holy Father Ignatius, they write:

“Countless witnesses throughout the world testify that they have experienced them with no less delight than benefit. But one is sufficient in place of all: Augustine Caravajal, a theologian of the Augustinian order. After he had traveled through the West Indies, honorably discharged various offices in Spain, and, by order of the supreme pontiff, visited the monasteries of his order in Italy, he was finally sent by the same pontiff to Bologna as apostolic visitor to restore the monastery of Saint James to its ancient discipline. He undertook this task with no other means than these pious meditations of the Society. After exercising himself in them for a month, he candidly testified that, for as long as he had lived in religion, he had always desired some method by which he might proceed most correctly, and that he had found it only when he encountered these Exercises of Saint Ignatius. He drank them in with the greatest eagerness and took them into the deepest recesses of his heart, and valued them so highly that he openly said that something truly divine was contained in them,” and so forth.

This Caravajal was elected, from the Spanish assistants, bishop of Guamanga among the Peruvians. Herrera speaks of him in the *Augustinian Alphabet*.

Would that we could add still greater praise to the Ignatian writings! Yet we cannot easily tolerate Annatus’ claim that Augustinian doctrine has been confirmed by the apostolic see with an approval less clear and explicit than that granted to Ignatian doctrine.

I ask you: when did the doctrine of Saint Ignatius pass into the canons of the councils? The Council of Orange was composed from the very opinions of the holy doctor Augustine. When was that doctrine transcribed word for word into the letters of the Roman pontiffs? Leo the Great inserted two entire chapters from Augustine’s *Enchiridion* into his letter to the bishop of Aquileia, and that letter was indeed directed against the Pelagians. When were the orthodox referred by the apostolic see to Ignatius’s book for the attainment of the truth? Saint Hormisdas referred the leading men of the East, bishops and monks—in a word, the entire Catholic world—to Augustine’s books.

When did the pontiffs measure Catholic doctrine by Ignatius’s standard? Clement VIII ordered that disputes concerning the divine helps be settled according to Augustine’s mind.

When was Saint Ignatius’s little book received with such commendations from the Roman prelates, adorned with such praises from the holy Fathers, and honored with the applause of nearly every age? If these praises were gathered into a single book, it would already be ten times larger than the book of Saint Ignatius’s *Exercises*.

I certainly hear what the Roman Church judges concerning that book in the lessons of the Roman Breviary:

“A man,” it says, “entirely untrained in letters composed that admirable book of the *Exercises*, approved by the judgment of the apostolic see and for the benefit of all.”

It is indeed remarkable that this book was composed by a man entirely untrained in letters. But the deed of the modern writers is more remarkable still: on the testimony of the apostolic see, they attempt to set this man, entirely untrained in letters, in the field of wisdom, authority, and praise not merely as Augustine’s equal, but—as regards the more explicit and effective approval and obligation to agree with it—as his superior. They do this to Augustine, of whom the apostolic see judged that he possessed such immense learning that, in the words of Martin Vin in his sermon *On Saint Monica*, “scarcely anything in the sacred Scriptures can be understood without his guidance, and nothing can be explained without his interpretation.”

“Through him it came about that we do not envy the philosophers their wisdom, do not miss the eloquence of orators, do not seek the talents of scholars; finally, we do not need Aristotle’s acumen, Plato’s eloquence, Varro’s prudence, Socrates’ gravity, Pythagoras’ authority, Empedocles’ ingenuity, or the knowledge or virtue of any other class of men as an example or instruction. He conveys to us the oracles of the prophets; he conveys the voices of the apostles; he expresses the entire meaning of all the Scriptures; finally, he displays the minds and studies of all the Fathers and wise men in himself alone.”

Will you then, if it please heaven, set against this exceptional, distinguished, and supreme apostolic approval the approval of Ignatius’s little book, and oppose Ignatius to Augustine and Paul III to so many supreme pontiffs?

Annatus replies:

“I do not relate these things at all in order to oppose Ignatius to Augustine or Paul III to the earlier pontiffs—far be it from me!”

But his deeds do not accord with his words. For what, and how great, would Augustine have been if the Church had not approved him? He would now be counted with Cassian and Faustus. Therefore we must judge him to be exactly as worthy of approval as he was approved by the Church.

Accordingly, if Ignatius’s little book has been approved by the Church, and Augustine’s books have likewise been approved, but—as Annatus says—with an approval less explicit and less clear, and if, in your judgment, the Ignatian book creates a more effective obligation to agree in every respect than the Augustinian books, then you see that you either place Ignatius above Augustine or at least set him against Augustine as his equal.

But you quickly devise an explanation and offer this justification for your action. You say that you cited the approval of Ignatius’s book because:

“Since it is evident that this little book contains certain things opposed to the fundamental principles of the Baianists, I should like to know what those who invoke an approval less express or explicit on behalf of their errors will answer to so eloquent and so explicit an approval.”

For the Baianists we do not wish to prepare any answer, nor indeed can we. But we blame you for striking both Baianists and Augustine with the same blow, attacking Augustine through the flank of the Baianists.

Let there be in Ignatius’s book opinions that strangle their fundamental doctrines; they must see to that themselves. But we cannot approve your claim, in the same sentence, that Augustine’s approval by the apostolic see was less explicit and less clear.

Spare the Father, and send the Baianists into exile—not to Baiae, but to Gyara.

If we wished to follow Annatus’ example and return like for like, then, just as he rises against Saint Augustine—who wrote against the Pelagians—by corrupting the authority of the testimonies brought forward for that holy doctor through the interpretations, violent and distorted, which he imposes on the encomia of several Roman prelates, so could we with the same audacity bring back here what Abbot Constantine, Vincent Baronius—a well-known man—in part II of *Moral Theology*, disputation 3, section 1, article 2, § 2, and others have written about these same Exercises of Saint Ignatius. We could then repeat that cold excuse of Annatus, who insults Augustine on account of the censures of certain men:

“I merely report it; I do not approve it, if it gives cause for any justified offense,” book VIII, chapter 6, p. 864.

But far be it from me, while correcting the man’s error, to imitate him and become guilty of the very crime for which I charge this modern writer before the judges!

Let the adversaries be ashamed—let them be ashamed that, against our will, they drive us into this arena, where disputes over the authority of saints are conducted through utterly odious comparisons.

Know that the Augustinians accept, examine, and kiss the little book of Saint Ignatius as conforming to Augustinian doctrine. And lest anyone doubt this devotion of theirs, they profess it openly before the Catholic world in published commentaries.

Father Francis Macedo, a Portuguese Franciscan, the glory of the Seraphic order, most happily acquired this distinction. He is so devoted to Augustinian doctrine that, at the beginning of his *Isagoge*, in the opening of his *Cortina*, he entered the literary arena with this as his watchword:

“I am an Augustinian; I am the most Augustinian.”

In that learned volume in which he described the harmony of the praying Church and Augustine the writer, he also exhibited the harmony between the Exercises of Saint Ignatius, founder of the Society of Jesus, and the works of Saint Augustine, doctor of the Church—for he gave the work precisely this title. Its opening is as follows:

“I am accustomed to say—and I say it as one who has tested and understood the matter—that it is not easy to find among the saints another more like Augustine, both in the doctrine which comes from God and is called mystical, and in the manner of life which he established for himself and prescribed for others, than Ignatius.”

This most learned man proves the point at great length through twenty-eight chapters, comparing statements from both authors. There is therefore absolutely no reason to fear that anything will be taken away from Augustine by the more explicit and clearer approval of Ignatius’s little book, as you call it, or that Ignatius’s book will suffocate the Augustinian volumes, which are ennobled by the praises of so many Roman prelates and Fathers. Rather, since both the small book of Ignatius and Augustine’s extensive volumes teach the same doctrines concerning the helps of divine grace, they should be said to be fortified by precisely the same approval.

Augustine transfers both his doctrine and even its commendation into the Ignatian book, while Ignatius, having obtained a new approval from Paul III, confirms anew, by the more recent testimony of the same apostolic see, the ancient decrees of the pontiffs concerning Augustine’s books.

You, citizens of that blessed region of great souls, will remain concordant forever in the heavenly homeland, just as you are in your books; and the harmony of your doctrines will be recited in angelic songs, from which a sweeter concert will be heard. Send the same agreement in doctrine also into your children, and either preserve or make them mutually courteous toward one another. It is shameful that, amid such harmony among the Fathers, their children should contend over their authority through truly odious comparisons.

## CHAPTER VIII. The modern writers limit the authority of Saint Augustine on the basis of a letter of Saint Celestine, pope. They are refuted.

Saint Celestine, pope, Augustine’s friend through correspondence and afterward the defender of Augustine after his death against the Semi-Pelagians, used the most illustrious of all encomia in commending Augustinian doctrine. Hence the modern writers devote all their strength to cutting down and limiting it. And this is their ingenuity: from that same letter of Celestine—by which others are accustomed to raise Augustinian authority above the stars—they attempt to depress it.

They recite the final words of the letter, where Celestine says:

“As for the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions that arise, which those who resisted the heretics treated more extensively, just as we do not dare to despise them, so we do not find it necessary to establish them.”

They contend that by these words Celestine meant that, apart from the few opinions of Saint Augustine which had been received by ecclesiastical prelates and synods and which, as recited in the preceding chapters, he had confirmed by renewed approval, he did not wish the remaining opinions concerning divine grace which Augustine maintained in his published disputations against the Pelagians to be established as matters of faith. Nevertheless, out of respect for Augustine’s authority, they say that Celestine did not despise those opinions, but left them to the free assent or dissent of readers, without danger of reproach.

Annatus, indeed, in book VIII, chapter 1, when he was about to produce a numerous troop of witnesses against Augustine, gave Pope Celestine the position of leader, loudly proclaiming:

“The supreme pontiff Celestine I will lead the army, as is proper.”

Yet until now that same Celestine had held first place among the principal encomiasts of the holy doctor.

Moreover, these modern theologians boast that they have brought the limitation of this letter—which narrows Augustine’s authority—out of darkness and back before the eyes of the schools.

Let us hear Moraines in the preface *To the Orthodox*:

“How many people accepted Augustine’s authority without distinction who now, having heard the limitation which Celestine placed upon his approval, ask, whenever they hear something proposed from Augustine: ‘Is this one of those deeper questions which he judged it unnecessary to establish, and which he left in the uncertain freedom of opinion?’”

Annatus exults over those words of Celestine in book VIII, chapter 1, p. 858:

“We, with Celestine as our authority, distinguish between Augustine’s necessary and indifferent opinions, and we regard every light contrary to this light as darkness.”

Therefore, in this matter, we must engage the modern writers in close combat, as it were, with foot set against foot, on behalf of Augustinian doctrine. Others have held the modern writers’ attack in this field with less success, and they have consequently become more confident, singing to themselves of victory and triumph in this dispute concerning Augustine.

[Col. 0819A] First of all, the exceptional learning of the modern writers must be commended: they believe that they can draw a certain and invincible argument against Augustine from a matter that is altogether uncertain. For highly learned and wise men do not approve of attributing the words mentioned above to Celestine; rather, they insist that they must be assigned to some other student of Augustinian doctrine.

Celestine’s letter concludes with these words at the end of chapter 2: “May God keep you safe and sound, most beloved brothers.” Ten chapters are then appended, in which the errors of the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians are refuted from the decrees of Innocent, Zosimus, and the Council of Carthage. Moreover, the father of ecclesiastical history, Caesar Baronius, states that these ten chapters are not by Celestine, in the year 431, p. 603, where he says of that letter of Celestine: [Col. 0819B]

“Certain chapters against the Pelagian errors are joined to the letter—chapters formerly issued by the Apostolic See and by the African councils—which those ought to follow who, although they condemned Pelagius and Coelestius under the Catholic name, nevertheless attempted to defend their errors. Those chapters are thought to be by Prosper, who, as he seems to acknowledge, collected them from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs and from the African councils. The same author has the following at the end: ‘The deeper and more difficult parts of the questions that arise, which we shall discuss more fully,’ etc., as above.”

Before Baronius, Laurentius Surius, very renowned in sacred history, and other collectors of councils after him had already noted this very point. For in the Cologne edition of the Councils, published in 1551, the following is printed in the margin: [Col. 0819C]

“The eleven chapters that follow appear rather to have been inserted by someone else than to be by Pope Celestine himself.”

In the edition published under Sixtus V, this annotation is inserted after the second chapter:

“There seems to be no doubt that what follows is by Prosper, so closely do both its subject matter and its style resemble his writings.”

Gerardus Vossius, a man whom one might call a glutton for books, approves the same opinion by a twofold argument in book I of his *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 30. The first argument is that Celestine makes no mention in that letter of the chapters appended to it. He presents the other in these words:

“The other argument why it cannot be by Celestine is this: it repeatedly cites the letters of Innocent and Zosimus, yet nowhere calls one ‘this predecessor’ or the other ‘that predecessor,’ contrary to the custom of the Roman bishops—and Celestine himself does so in the letter, in these words: ‘Augustine was counted among the best teachers even before my predecessors.’ Certainly, these arguments carry such weight with me that I would not dare to attribute the work simply [ἁπλῶς, ‘without qualification’] to Celestine; but whose it is must be investigated further.”

Nor were there lacking theologians from the modern school who denied that those chapters were by Celestine. One example will suffice for a thousand: Francisco Suárez, *Prolegomena* 6 on Grace, chapter 1, no. 11, where he writes:

“From the manner of expression we understand that the writer of that section was not Celestine, nor any Roman pontiff, as is clear from those words.”

Because certain men who boast of the Catholic name, yet remain immersed—whether through perversity or ignorance—in the condemned opinions or depravity of heretics, presume to oppose the most pious disputants, and although they do not hesitate to anathematize Pelagius and Coelestius, nevertheless criticize our teachers as though they had exceeded what was necessary, claiming that they follow and approve only what the most sacred See of blessed Peter, through the ministry of its bishops, established and taught against the enemies of God’s grace, it was necessary to investigate carefully what the rulers of the Roman Church had judged concerning the heresy that had arisen in their time:

“These do not appear to be the words of a Roman bishop. He does not speak of the Roman See as his own, nor does he call its rulers his predecessors, as pontiffs customarily do. Yet he speaks with authority to issue a definition. Hence some believe that those chapters were collected by Prosper and appended to the letter. Baronius is not far from this opinion in the year 431, no. 185, and it is certainly plausible. This is indicated by the words: ‘They criticize our teachers as though they had exceeded what was necessary.’ For these words were spoken in Augustine’s favor, and they have more the scent of Prosper than of Celestine.”

Such is his statement.

Gabriel Vásquez saw these observations in Surius and, part I, disputation 91, no. 85, said that Surius had denied without foundation that those chapters were by Celestine, since Peter the Deacon had presented them as Celestine’s decrees. He could also have added Cresconius in his *Collection of Canons*. Yet Cresconius lived around the year 698, whereas Peter the Deacon flourished a full century after Celestine, as is clear from our *History of Pelagianism*. He therefore could have mistakenly attributed to Celestine chapters published by Prosper.

Hence Photius, a careful investigator and critic of ancient records, writes the following about the same Celestine in codex 53:

“He also wrote to the bishops of Gaul concerning the faith of blessed Augustine and against those who, inflated beyond measure by the license of heresy, were becoming insolent.”

These matters are contained in the first two chapters; nor does he mention in that letter any established doctrinal definitions. Jacobus Sirmondus likewise separated those chapters, appended to the aforementioned letter, from the letter itself by intervening lines in volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*, in order to show that they must be assigned wholly to a different author.

But let us proceed. Let us prove that those chapters were not written by Celestine—a proof that I shall certainly establish by the argument by which I myself was convinced. First, however, several points must be noted that clarify the judgment of such great writers: namely, that Prosper and Hilary, because of the Augustinian books attacked by the men of Massilia, and because they themselves were commonly denounced as heretics, went to Rome to Celestine. This is evident from Prosper’s chapter 40 *Against the Collator* and from chapter 1 of Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul.

Celestine sent a letter to the bishops of Gaul in which he highly commended Saint Augustine, forbidding that Augustine’s memory be shaken by the new efforts of the Massilians, and forbidding that Prosper and Hilary be accused of heresy. Yet he published nothing against those men by which their errors might be condemned. Hence the letter is entitled “For Prosper and Hilary.” But this is what we must demonstrate.

Saint Prosper, intending to prove against the *Collator* that the beginnings of good wills are generated by God’s inspiration, cites in chapter 10 the testimonies of Innocent, Zosimus, and the Council of Carthage—precisely the same testimonies that are found appended to Celestine’s letter—and concludes:

“Do you see your rules shattered by the solid strength of invincible decrees, and the crooked, ruinous joints in the structure of the faith collapsed, like the walls of Jericho, at the sound of the priests’ trumpets? For when the question between us and the Pelagians concerned the origin of holy wills and the beginnings of faith and charity, the contest was settled by no uncertain victory and no doubtful conclusion, so that we still need to discuss the peace of this most wicked compact of yours.”

But if those ten chapters had been by Celestine, why did Prosper not produce them as clearer, more effective, and entirely decisive for settling the dispute? Celestine expressly condemns Cassian’s opinion far more clearly than Innocent or Zosimus. Indeed, the Massilians interpreted the testimonies of these pontiffs and of Sacred Scripture in such a way that, according to Saint Augustine in chapter 2 of *On the Predestination of the Saints*, they were to be understood not of the beginning of faith but of its increase:

“But now I see that I must answer those who say that the divine testimonies we have brought to bear on this matter are valid only so that we may know that we have faith from ourselves, but that its increase is from God.”

This opinion of the Massilians is clearly condemned in chapter 12 of that letter, where we read:

“Strengthened, therefore, by these ecclesiastical rules and by teachings drawn from divine authority, and aided by the Lord, we have been so confirmed that we profess God to be the author of all good affections, all good works, all efforts, and all virtues by which one attends to the beginning of faith; and we do not doubt that all human merits are preceded by his grace, through which it comes about that we both begin to will and to do something good.”

Furthermore, the following is written in chapter 11:

“Besides the inviolable decrees of the most blessed Apostolic See, by which the most pious Fathers, after casting down the pestilential arrogance of novelty, taught that both the beginnings of good will, the growth of commendable efforts, and perseverance in them unto the end are to be referred to the grace of Christ,” etc.

The same is found in chapter 9:

“So that holy thought, pious counsel, and every movement of good will may be from God, because through him we can do something good, without whom we can do nothing.”

Can it really be believed that these oracles of Celestine, given at Prosper’s request and inserted into the letter sent to the bishops on his behalf, had so completely slipped from Prosper’s memory that he omitted them, even though they were especially necessary for repressing the insolence of the Massilians? Did he value so little the weapons forged and the arms prepared for himself that, when the Semi-Pelagians could have been utterly defeated by them, he refused to use them as though they were blunt—he who after Augustine is praised, and rightly so, by the moderns as the strongest and most skillful leader against the Massilians?

Vásquez writes that the letters in question were sent by Celestine to condemn the errors of the Massilians, part I, disputation 91, no. 83:

“In these passages, since Celestine refers all good works, efforts, and merits, at every time, in every cause and matter, to God as the author of grace, he plainly refutes the error of the Massilians.”

The moderns teach this so consistently that their most learned and wisest writer, Annatus, assuming the person of Celestine—which is sufficiently ridiculous—thunders against the Massilians in a higher and clearer voice:

“Since the policy and providence of the Roman See are directed solely toward ensuring that these MASSILIANS, FOR WHOSE SAKE WE ISSUE THESE DECREES, subtract absolutely nothing from divine grace, not even that awareness of illness and desire for medicine which they place before gratuitous and supernatural aid, the aforesaid rule or established judgment is sufficient to show that, just as whatever contradicts it ought not to be regarded as Catholic, so whatever does not contradict it ought not to be regarded as erroneous or alien to Catholic teaching.”

So writes the most elegant Paraphrast.

Here, however, I note in passing that whether this man begins speaking against his Baian opponents or against the Massilians, he always ends by speaking against Augustine. We saw this concerning the Baians in the preceding chapter. Here, after speaking in the person of Celestine, he immediately adds:

“From this it follows that if anything has been asserted or denied either by Augustine or by some other ecclesiastical writer that does not contradict those rules and judgments, it must be counted among indifferent matters [ἀδιάφορα, things indifferent], matters left to the free agreement or disagreement of Catholics.”

I am entirely convinced that, in those appended chapters, the capital errors of the Massilians—of which their other errors were, as it were, appendices—are openly condemned. Nor do I think that what Vásquez, Annatus, and others commonly observe on this point can reasonably be called into question.

There were two fundamental dogmas of the Semi-Pelagians: that faith begins from us, and that perseverance in the good unto the end is likewise from us, as Saint Augustine teaches in the final chapter of *On the Gift of Perseverance*:

“I believe that I have taught sufficiently—or rather, more than sufficiently—that the gifts of God include both beginning to believe in the Lord and remaining in the Lord unto the end.”

Both points are established in the letters attributed to Celestine. For in chapter 11 it is decreed, as I said, that “the beginnings of good will, the growth of commendable efforts, and perseverance in them unto the end are to be referred to the grace of Christ.” There it is proved at length that faith is not from us but is given by God; and in chapter 12 it is required that “we profess God to be the author of all good affections, all good works, all efforts, and all virtues by which one attends to the beginning of faith.” Thus far.

From these considerations we renew our argument. When Prosper had recited Celestine’s encomium in chapter 42 *Against the Collator*, he adds the envious interpretation of the Massilians, who repeatedly claimed that the earlier books of Saint Augustine had been praised by Celestine, but not the later ones—namely, *On Rebuke and Grace*, and the two sent to Prosper and Hilary, *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*.

Prosper immediately refutes this interpretation, both because Augustine always wrote the same thing in all his books, and because the same spirit and doctrine were always present in him, and because “the Apostolic See,” he says, “when it approves what does not differ from what it already knows, approves it together with what it already knows; and what it joins in judgment it does not separate in praise.”

But why does the Apostolic See’s approval of Saint Augustine’s books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance* come from so far away? Why did Prosper not produce Celestine’s letters, which he had obtained for himself and in which the doctrine of the holy doctor’s books on the beginning of faith and on perseverance is established by explicit definitions—those very letters, I say, which he had thrust into the face of Augustine’s slanderers in that same passage?

Annatus writes concerning Saint Augustine’s later books, book VIII, chapter 6:

“It is therefore evident that Augustine’s intention in these books is satisfied by one who acknowledges both that grace is necessary for the beginning of faith, and that it does not follow upon its merit but precedes it, and that perseverance is a gift of God.”

What more effective argument could have been brought forward to demonstrate that those later books had been approved by the Apostolic See than those letters of Celestine, in which the doctrine of the holy Father’s later books was asserted so expressly, so clearly, and so firmly?

When the Semi-Pelagians diminished Augustine’s authority, Prosper refuted them from Celestine’s letters, in which Augustine was highly praised. Why, then, when the same men attacked the doctrine of Saint Augustine, were they not silenced and convicted by those very same letters of Celestine? Prosper wrote against Cassian after Celestine, and he had Celestine’s letters at hand in that dispute. By this argument, therefore, those chapters are proved to have been inserted into Celestine’s letters.

I shall again state an argument that I have always preferred to the others. If those chapters were by Celestine and had proceeded from the Apostolic See, I do not see how Faustus of Riez, Vincent of Lérins, Hilary, bishop of Arles—if they persisted in their position—and other bishops of Gaul can be excused from heresy and counted among the saints with altars raised to them.

Faustus teaches in book II, chapters 6, 7, and 8, that faith is ours through the powers of nature. Hence in book I, chapter 7, he says:

“The time of grace, by which we were redeemed, did not await human merits; it did not seek works at all; God was content with the devotion of our faith alone.”

He adds:

“He expects faith from infants, and from the mature he also requires works together with faith, yet in such a way that he increases the affection of belief in those who are making progress.”

Let Vossius be read, book IV of the *History of Pelagianism*, part I, thesis 2. Likewise, in book II, chapter 10—and before him Vincent of Lérins in the *Commonitory*, chapter 37—they write that we can by our own powers ask, knock, and seek in order to obtain God’s grace. This was the opinion of the Semi-Pelagians according to Prosper’s letters to Augustine.

Moreover, after Faustus’s death, several bishops of Gaul also said that faith arose in us from ourselves, as is clear from the letter of Boniface II to Caesarius. These opinions are plainly condemned in those chapters in which faith and its beginning, holy thought, pious counsel, every good affection, and every good movement of the will are asserted to be from God, because through him we can do something good, without whom we can do nothing.

Indeed, if someone today were to assert the opinions of the Massilians, in the absence of the decrees of Orange or of other decrees of the Apostolic See, would he not be convicted of heresy from Celestine’s letters? They say, after all, that Celestine condemned the doctrines of the Massilians. What defense, then, shall we devise for Hilary, Faustus, Vincent, and the remaining bishops of Gaul, who before the Council of Orange stubbornly maintained the opinions of the Massilians?

Will they perhaps say that these men were entirely unaware of Celestine’s letters? But those letters had been sent not to bishops of Macedonia or Bithynia, but to the bishops of Gaul, at a time when Faustus was flourishing in the monastery of Lérins, of which he was appointed abbot a year later.

What is more, Vincent of Lérins himself produces these same letters in the *Commonitory Against Profane Innovations of Words* and praises them highly. With what face could Vincent have boasted that the letters favored him when they condemned his own opinions? He writes:

“But Saint Pope Celestine likewise, in the same manner and with the same judgment; for he says in the letter that he sent to the priests of Gaul,” etc.

Who among learned bishops could be thought not to have heard Celestine’s resounding words throughout Gaul, words also repeated by the mouths of Vincent and Prosper? Therefore those chapters were not issued by Celestine, lest we pronounce heretics those whom both holiness and learning have made renowned.

There remains, however, another question to be resolved: to whom should the chapters appended to Celestine’s letters be attributed?

In the *Book of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, which is listed among the works of Saint Augustine in volume III, eleven chapters are reproduced verbatim from Celestine’s letters beginning with chapter 22. But Saint Augustine is not the author of that volume, since chapters of the Council of Orange, celebrated in the year 529, are also inserted there. Nor could Gennadius have written them, for the reasons given in book II of the *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 16. Since Gennadius says that Cassian’s doctrines were wrongly attacked by Prosper as though they were Catholic, he could not have taught opinions that were entirely opposed to Cassian’s.

That compiler—whoever he may have been—is also inept. For in chapter 25 he says:

“The same teacher, in a letter given to the Council of Milevis, declares, saying,” etc.

Yet previously he had not cited Innocent, from whom those words are taken in the appended chapters—namely, chapter 7.

Furthermore, the final two chapters, 11 and 22, are found word for word in Saint John Chrysostom’s homily on Adam and Eve, volume II of the Basel edition. There too are placed at the end the words that have occasioned our present inquiry, namely: “The deeper and more difficult parts,” etc. In the same homily, in the section beginning “When, therefore, it is said that man is handed over to his desires,” forty verses are also inserted verbatim from book V of Saint Augustine’s *Against Julian*, chapter 3.

Therefore the author of that homily is not Chrysostom, but some Latin writer of feeble intellect, who could not speak in his own voice but merely compressed the opinions of others into a patchwork.

Baronius and Suárez consider it plausible, as some have written, that these chapters were arranged by Prosper. Vossius does not dare to affirm that they were prepared by Prosper alone; he assigns Hilary and other defenders of Augustine as companions to Prosper, since they speak in the plural. What can we conjecture in this matter?

Let us say, then, that those chapters were compiled by Prosper, and let us offer one or two conjectures.

The first is that chapter 8 contains the words of the letters of Zosimus and the African Fathers, which Prosper recites in precisely the same words and order in chapter 10 *Against the Collator*. In that passage he also places the same testimonies of Innocent that are found in the chapters commonly attributed to Celestine. Zosimus’s letters have perished, and their opening is found only in Prosper and in those chapters.

The second is that in chapter 9 *Against the Collator*, Prosper reproves the *Collator* for having said that Augustine had asserted certain things against the Pelagians more than was justified; there he also mocks the opponent’s moderation. But in chapter 3 of the so-called Celestinian material, the Massilians are reproved for daring to criticize Augustine as though he had exceeded what was necessary.

If these words had truly been spoken by Celestine, Prosper, while contending for Augustine against the *Collator*, certainly ought to have repeated them in that connection. What stronger argument could have been produced to silence the slanderer than so celebrated a testimony of the Apostolic See?

Thus the modern opinion that attributes those chapters without any hesitation to Celestine is even less convincing. When Prosper had obtained from Pope Celestine a diploma commending Augustine and approving his own faith, he returned to Gaul and taunted the same Semi-Pelagians. They, however, claimed that the praise had been given to Augustine’s earlier books, not to the later ones. To drive away every suspicion of error from themselves, they professed that they wished to defend only those doctrines concerning grace that had been established by the Apostolic See in its disputes against the Pelagians.

The burden therefore fell upon the Augustinians to demonstrate, from Innocent, Zosimus, and the African Council approved by the Roman See, that the opinions of the Massilians had been proscribed. Accordingly, when they composed those ten chapters, they prefixed to them Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul in order to give them the authority of a stronger source.

But when those writings fell into the hands of certain people, they adopted the view that the entire booklet had been published by Pope Celestine. Among the ancients, I see this opinion in Peter the Deacon, whom I have cited, and then in Cresconius. Four hundred years later, it was also held by the Church of Lyons in the book *On the Three Letters* and in other works published in the case of Gottschalk.

It must nevertheless be noted that Peter the Deacon and his Scythian companions were mistaken when, in the book *On the Incarnation and Grace*, chapter 8, they praised the words found at the beginning of chapter 8 of the so-called Celestinian material as though they were Innocent’s words to the Council of Milevis. It is therefore clear that they had not read Innocent’s letters but had come across these chapters attributed to Celestine, failing to distinguish the final words of chapter 7—which belong to Saint Innocent and were addressed to the people of Milevis—from the opening words of chapter 8, which belong to another author.

[Col. 0826A] From this it is clear that the moderns recklessly insult Augustinian authority on the basis of Celestine’s letters, attempting almost to bring Augustine into line. For it is not certain that the final appendix beginning “The deeper and more difficult parts,” etc., proceeded from the Apostolic See; the most distinguished writers deny that it did.

Which theologian, then, will they set against Suárez as his equal among their own writers, and which historian will they oppose to Baronius or to their own Sirmondus? Strongest arguments also confirm the same opinion, and I hope that many in the future will yield to them, unless the flattery of our own people deceives us.

What I shall say next will be stated for the benefit of the moderns, so that we may close every avenue by which they might mutilate Augustinian authority. Thus far the battle has been fought in a more distant field than they had imagined; now we approach their camp, ready to fight in the very arena into which they challenged us.

I shall therefore grant, as a favor, that those ten chapters were composed by Celestine, and I shall also concede that the appendix was added by him. Nevertheless, I shall show that nothing has thereby been taken away from Augustinian doctrine, dignity, or authority. Before carrying this out, however, we must investigate the mind and intention of the moderns and portray them, as it were, in their own colors.

The ancient Semi-Pelagians of Massilia, in order to conceal under some attractive pretext the hatred they had once conceived against Saint Augustine’s doctrine, condemned Pelagius and Coelestius and professed to embrace whatever the Apostolic See had established against them. In other matters, however, concerning which no decrees had been issued by the pontiffs, they said that they did not agree with Augustine, because in the doctrine he had handed down against the Pelagians he had exceeded what was necessary.

Hear Celestine’s words in chapter 3:

“Because certain men who boast of the Catholic name, yet remain immersed—whether through perversity or ignorance—in the condemned opinions of heretics, presume to oppose the most pious disputants, and although they do not hesitate to anathematize Pelagius and Coelestius, nevertheless criticize our teachers as though they had exceeded what was necessary, claiming that they follow and approve only what the most sacred See of blessed Peter, through the ministry of its bishops, established and taught against the enemies of God’s grace.”

But we propose to the moderns Saint Augustine’s opinion concerning gratuitous predestination to glory, and we ask them to accept it on the authority of its author. Moraines replies in disputation 9 of the *Anti-Jansenist*, no. 50, that if Augustine taught this opinion, it was not the affinity or connection—which does not exist—of this doctrine with the teaching established against the Pelagians that led him to it, but the heat of controversy.

They add that they are bound to defend only opinions approved by the Roman See:

“For although the opinion that entirely denies such a mode of predestination from merits ought to be preferred, nevertheless, in order for the opinion that affirms it also to be considered condemned, it must be examined how necessarily it is connected with the articles defined by Celestine. For if it is not, then, although Augustine inclines in the opposite direction, the determination of this question must still be left to the free choice of disputants.”

These are the words of Annatus, book VIII, chapter 1, p. 856.

Thus this modern judgment concerning Augustine differs in no degree from the old opinion of the Semi-Pelagians. Both admit the necessity of believing what the Apostolic See established against heretics concerning divine grace, but not what Saint Augustine asserted against them by going beyond what was necessary.

I shall nevertheless explain the difference between the two positions. When Saint Prosper opposed Celestine’s approval of Augustinian doctrine to the Massilians, they said that the praise had been given to Augustine’s earlier books, not to the later ones, in which both predestination without merits and faith as a gift of God are asserted.

The moderns, however, also accept Augustine’s later books and say that they are approved insofar as they teach that faith is a gift from God, but not insofar as they place predestination before foreseen merits. Thus the Massilians denied that Augustine’s final books had been praised by the Roman pontiffs at all, whereas the moderns concede that they were approved only in part.

It is certain that James Arminius brought Semi-Pelagianism back from the underworld among the Dutch—or, if it still survived anywhere, strengthened it. Hence Father Macedo writes in the prologue to his *Scrinium*:

“Are there enemies of grace today? Whoever wishes to know should examine whether there are enemies of Augustine today. When he finds the latter, let him think that he has found the former as well. But in Belgium there are enemies of Augustine, and there are also such in England, although far fewer: namely, the Arminians and the Remonstrants.”

Thus this new prince of the Dutch [Col. 0827C] Semi-Pelagians thought himself sufficiently armed and equipped against Augustine’s authority by that clause of Celestine. His friend, cited above, gives Arminius’s words in the *Arminian Antithesis*:

“So far is it from being the case,” says Arminius, “that even Augustine’s doctrine of predestination was received in those councils, that Celestine, bishop of Rome, who lived at that time, writing to the bishops of Gaul and condemning the doctrines of the Pelagians, concludes his letter at the end with these words: ‘The deeper and more difficult parts of the questions that arise, which we shall discuss more fully,’ etc.”

With these words of Celestine, Arminius stood as though he had raised a rampart against Augustine.

Hence Moraines’s words in the preface to the *Anti-Jansenist* are laughable:

“How many,” he says, “formerly accepted Augustine’s authority without distinction, but now, having heard the limitation that Celestine added to his approval, whenever they hear something proposed from Augustine, ask: Is this one of those deeper questions that he did not deem necessary to establish, but left to the uncertain freedom of opinion?”

As though the moderns themselves had noted those words of Celestine only in the recent Jansenist controversy, when not only Arminius, but also the Church of Lyons eighty years earlier, had recited them in chapter 12 of its work *On Maintaining the Truth of Sacred Scripture*.

Arminius, a reworker of the old Semi-Pelagianism, turned that clause of Celestine over and over; a chorus of his disciples repeated it, and the moderns sing along with them. One of them—a distinguished man at that—exclaims:

“Indeed, we have many things in common with the Arminians” (*Book I of the Jansenist Heresy*, chapter 3, no. 113).

Yet I seem to hear the moderns complaining that they are burdened only with hateful labels, not convicted of the falsity or error of their actual opinion. Come, then: let us leave these matters aside as offensive and approach the heart of the case.

The author of those chapters intends to explain against the Massilians what powers free will possesses for the good and how necessary grace is. This is clear from the end of the letter, where we read:

“Because we believe that, for confessing the grace of God, from whose work and favor nothing at all must be subtracted, whatever the Apostolic See has taught us according to the aforesaid rules is sufficient.”

Accordingly, the matters that Saint Augustine taught more extensively against Julian concerning original sin and the manner in which it is transmitted, concerning concupiscence, and concerning the remaining miseries that are punishments of original sin, are not defined in those letters of Celestine. There was no controversy between Augustine and the Massilians concerning these matters, nor did the Semi-Pelagians raise any question against Augustine on their account.

Therefore Celestine said: “We do not need to establish this”—meaning that he did not wish to issue canons concerning matters that did not pertain to the present controversy with the Massilians—not that he wished to leave to the free agreement or disagreement of disputants matters which the moderns foolishly interpret in that way.

From this it is clear that those who understand “the intervening questions” to mean certain matters taken from Augustine’s books are undertaking a vain labor. Annatus shows clearly and skillfully in book VIII, chapter 1, that these matters do not pertain to the issue.

But you will say: If what the holy doctor teaches so extensively against Julian concerning concupiscence was not approved by Celestine, then it is left to the free agreement or disagreement of readers.

We shall answer this in its proper place below. For the present, it must be known that Augustine, in book V *Against Julian*, chapter 12, proposed five questions concerning concupiscence—and in the third of these the moderns take their stand against Augustine, arguing with the same arguments Julian used—and that he said there:

“In these questions your impious novelty is suffocated by the Catholic truth handed down from ancient times.”

Here we may repeat what Cardinal Bellarmine said in another controversy, book II *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 11:

“For if Augustine’s opinion concerning predestination—or, if you prefer, concerning concupiscence—were false, the same Augustine could not be defended from the charge of immense rashness, since he not only contended so vehemently for a falsehood but also dared to pass it off as Catholic faith.”

The holy doctor would never have published opinions born from his own brain as Catholic doctrines. On this matter, repeat what was said in chapter 3, section 2.

The author writes at the end of chapter 3: “We make known the constitutions of the holy Fathers in a concise catalogue, so that anyone who is not excessively contentious may recognize that the whole connection of the disputations depends upon this brevity of the authorities set forth below.”

Here [Col. 0829A] great difficulties arise: how shall we be able to know this connection of the dogmas? The Moderns profess themselves teachers of this mystery and ridicule Augustine when he writes about that connection. We read in chapter 12 that infants do not receive baptism “until, through the exorcisms and exsufflations of the clergy, the unclean spirit has been driven away from them, so that then it may truly appear how ‘the prince of this world’ is cast out, etc.” We infer: therefore the devil can harm children infected with original sin by sensible punishment, since they are his slaves, whose prince he is. Annatus cries out, p. 858: “We deny the cruel consequence.”

But Saint Augustine asserted that connection quite consistently, *On the Unfinished Work against Julian*, book IV, chapter 200: “But if,” he says, “the child is not rescued from the power [Col. 0829B] of darkness and remains there, why do you wonder that he will be with the devil in eternal fire, since he is not permitted to enter the kingdom of God?”

Moraines replies, *Disputation 40 against the Anti-Jansenists*, no. 60, that Augustine said this, carried away by the heat of disputation. Here are the voices of the Semi-Pelagians: Augustine exceeded the necessary measure—voices condemned by Celestine. They accept Celestine’s letters insofar as this serves their cause, but insofar as they support Augustine’s position, they imitate them not at all. Thus Augustine erred, carried away by passion, when he asserted that connection which the Moderns maintain does not exist.

We oppose to them chapter 11: “Perseverance unto the end is to be referred to the grace of Christ”; for it is given gratuitously, as Augustine proves at length from the prayers, and as was defined in the Council of Orange, canon 10. [Col. 0829C] From this we infer that predestination to glory is likewise entirely gratuitous. For predestination, which separates the reprobate from the predestined, is founded upon, or connected with, the gift of final perseverance, added purely liberally to merits; therefore predestination depends upon God’s pure liberality.

Augustine saw and defended this connection; the Augustinian holy Fathers—Prosper, Fulgentius, Prudentius, Remigius, and others—likewise asserted it. But the Moderns deny this connection, although they accept Augustine’s teaching according to its connection with Celestine’s letters; yet, in accordance with their own opinions, they are neither reluctant nor ashamed to accept or reject that connection. In a word, Augustine’s books are to be examined according to the standard of Celestine’s letters, while Celestine’s letters are to be interpreted according to their own imagination.

Indeed, in order to prove that these chapters, which are connected with Celestine’s letter, were actually issued by the Apostolic See, they produce Peter the Deacon and the Church of Lyons, by whom those propositions are attributed to the praised pontiff. But we reply that those Fathers read that appendix to the letter and nevertheless established as Catholic dogma predestination without foreknowledge of merits. They will say that they do not abide by those Fathers’ milder judgment concerning Augustine’s doctrine. Very well: neither are we convinced by their testimony that those theses should be attributed to Celestine.

Since the subject of predestination has arisen, the modesty of the Moderns in examining [Col. 0830A] Saint Augustine’s teaching on purely gratuitous predestination comes to mind. For they say, with Molina, as a matter of respect, that it is harsh and unworthy of divine goodness, and that on its account the salvation of many has been endangered; with Mariana, that it is novel and that Augustine, by introducing it, leads people into despair; and with Lessius—and, shortly afterward, Petavius—that it is to be displaced by the contrary opinion.

Is this not precisely to despise Augustine’s teaching? And yet you assert that Celestine said of it that he did not dare to despise it.

That original sin is the principal and proximate cause of reprobation is Saint Augustine’s teaching; Adamus concedes this, p. 614 of his *Calvinus Destroyed*. On p. 667, chapter 10, part III, he writes: “I believe that I may now recoil in horror, because this [Col. 0830B] is the mother of Calvinist doctrine.” Could Augustine’s teaching have been received more contemptuously?

Annatus, book VIII, chapter 1, laughs at certain people who, in explaining those words of Celestine—“the deeper and more difficult parts of the intervening questions, which those who resisted heretics treated more extensively”—weave a catalogue of certain questions, and he rightly shows that they do not pertain to the subject; but we ask where Augustine treated that question of predestination more extensively against the Pelagians.

But we ask: where did Augustine discuss that question more extensively against the Pelagians? Certainly, in his letters to Paulinus and Sixtus he says little about it, so that he can scarcely be said to have treated it there at length. Yet in the books addressed to Prosper and Hilary he discusses it more extensively. But in that work the holy doctor was not resisting heretics: they were Catholic Semi-Pelagians, and the name designated a faction, not a heresy. Celestine, however, speaks of those questions which “those who resisted heretics” treated.

I know what you will answer: Celestine’s words are to be understood as meaning “those who resisted heretics” specifically, not reduplicatively. This is a scholastic interpretation. So that I may not be more contentious, I yield the point; nor does this last matter greatly to me. Let us move on to other things.

But let us deal with you most gently and humanely. Know that Saint Augustine’s authority is so secure that we can freely concede to you the entire case over which we have hitherto argued, without the dignity of Augustinian doctrine suffering any harm. Let Celestine have been the author of those ten chapters; let no Augustinian dogma have any connection with them—we grant everything, as you wish, as you please. [Col. 0830D]

Nevertheless, it does not follow that the principal dogmas of Saint Augustine should be numbered among indifferent matters, left to the free discretion of disputants. In those chapters it was decreed that the beginning of faith, pious counsel, probable endeavor, holy thought, and final perseverance are gifts of God. Let this glory be granted to Augustine: that his own theses, defended against the Massilians, were reported by Celestine as articles of faith.

I should like to ask the Moderns whether, after Celestine’s death, any other assertions of Augustine were established by the Apostolic See against heretics or others. Those who know that the twenty-five canons of Orange were taken from Saint Augustine’s books will certainly affirm it.

Celestine defined from Saint Augustine’s teaching whatever the Massilians called into doubt; and from the same opinions his successors likewise acted against the new efforts of the Pelagians. Saint Pope Gelasius approved, in his letter to the bishops throughout Picenum, Saint Augustine’s teaching concerning the transmission of original sin to offspring through concupiscence, exclusion from the kingdom of heaven, the miseries arising from original sin, the damnation of infants, the loss through sin of freedom for the good, and many other matters.

Leo the Great inserted two entire chapters of Augustinian doctrine into his letters. In them Augustine asserts that it may not improbably be said that even children are bound by the sins of their parents—not only by those of the first human beings, but also by those of their own parents—*Enchiridion*, chapter 46. Therefore, if that opinion of Augustine pleased the most holy and most learned pontiff Leo, who judged it merely “not improbable,” how shall we say that those opinions pleased the Apostolic See which Augustine defended with all his strength against the heretics as certain, as conformed to the sacred Scriptures, and finally as wholly orthodox?

Let Celestine therefore have established what all must hold against the Massilians. It does not follow that Augustinian doctrine is confined within very narrow bounds; it extends farther, and the Roman bishops proceed with it in unanimous agreement, always following Augustine with the greatest reverence when decreeing matters concerning the aids of divine grace.

Let the great cloud of dust which the Moderns have raised from these, as they suppose, chapters of Celestine against the most brilliant rays of the Augustinian sun at last settle; and, once the darkness of all false interpretations has been driven away, may the teaching of the holy prelate [Col. 0831C] illumine the whole Church.

## CHAPTER IX AND LAST

One hundred and thirty-five insults, taunts, and censures of the Moderns against Saint Augustine, refuted by that same holy doctor and by the holy Fathers.

[Note: [Col. 0831] In Migne, in Chapter IX, the sections headed “CENSORS” are printed in parallel with the sections headed “SAINT AUGUSTINE.”]

I can scarcely express my wonder that Augustine excelled with such great and fruitful genius that he not only trampled down and crushed, in a thousand volumes, those enemies with whom he fought most fiercely while alive, but also fortified the dogmas he asserted with such weapons of argument that he broke the efforts of all subsequent heretics and eluded the censures of every kind of person. No voice of either heresy or envy can be raised against him for which Augustine has not provided the fullest answer in his books.

Let the recent insults serve as an example—insults with which certain novice writers, by a rash undertaking, have tried to tear apart the venerable gray hairs of the great Father. Even if no one should draw his pen in Augustine’s defense, the words of that one man alone completely silence the mouths of all his slanderers.

I now undertake to demonstrate this by setting forth on one side the censures of the new writers and on the other Augustine’s replies. Whoever reads these attentively, with love and hatred kept far from the matter, will surely admit that Augustine spoke as though he had actually been disputing with these most recent men who emerged after twelve centuries.

It is nevertheless my decision to repel the insults inflicted upon Augustine while passing over their authors in silence. For when Augustine first undertook to attack the Pelagians, he pursued their errors without publishing their names. He gives this reason for his action in *Retractations*, book II, chapter 33: “In these books,” he says, “I still judged that their names should be kept silent, hoping that they could thus be corrected more easily.”

Following the footsteps of the great Father, the men of our own institution—Basilius Poncius, a Spaniard, and Charles Moreau, a Frenchman—refuted the injuries brought against Augustine while sparing the names of his adversaries. Following, therefore, this example familiar to our predecessors, I shall suppress the names of the Censors and refute their less honorable statements about Augustine from Augustine himself.

Those who supply antidotes deserve well of the human race, even if they do not expose the craftsmen of the poisons. We shall certainly provide a great example of patience, and a still greater example of modesty, so that from this we may at last hope that they will adopt gentler policies toward the distinguished teacher of the Church in the future.

But lest I bring the Censors into conflict with Augustine and then dismiss them while the case remains unresolved, I have decided to summon judges, by whom this most serious case—if ever there was one—may be examined.

Come, I beg you, Fathers of the ancient Church, invincible hands in war and renowned for so many triumphs over the Heterodox. Come, lights of the heavenly Senate and pillars of the Christian commonwealth, whose authority the Catholic world follows, whose wisdom all revere, and whose words each person venerates as the more secret oracles of the Godhead.

Sit as honorary judges of the Augustinian case. On one side you will hear the accusations of certain Moderns; on the other, Augustine’s defense. Whoever calls your integrity into suspicion will show that he is completely alien to the Orthodox faith.

And you, great Father, since no mortal can provide you with an advocate worthy of you, come forward as the supporter of your own case. Although you were once appointed judge by decree of the Apostolic See to pronounce judgment in controversies concerning the aids of divine grace, permit yourself for a little while—because of the importunity of certain persons, to speak most gently—to be brought before the tribunal of the Fathers as a defendant rather than a judge.

For I do not think you will take this badly, since when you were once accused by Julian of an unheard-of doctrine, you not only did not avoid the judgment of the Fathers, but even dragged your reluctant adversary to it by the scruff of his neck.

It will surely be pleasant to understand—or rather to see with one’s own eyes—the innumerable teachers of the Church add their white stones to Augustine’s side, commend his opinions, defend his authority, and strike the rashness of his adversaries with severe judgment.

But now, very quickly, the sacred Senate of the saints is present, and in great numbers, to examine the Augustinian case. The adversaries surge forward in a rounded column to accuse Augustine.

Meanwhile Saint Prosper, seated among the judges of the first bench, gives the accusers permission to speak:

“Behold, with the victory and peace of the Catholic faith preserved, and with reverence for the unbreakable decrees intact, we are prepared to hear the PATRONS [Col. 0833A] OF MORE CORRECT DOCTRINE and to recognize the lines of the most subtle discrimination, cut free from every error. Let what has arisen FROM NEW INTELLECTS be placed in the midst” (*Against the Collator*, at the beginning).

“So that an observer of even slight diligence may easily notice by what unjust reproaches the memory of THE CATHOLIC PREACHER is attacked, and into what sin fall those who, stirred up by another’s instigation, are readier to blame A WRITER OF THE MOST CELEBRATED NAME than to know him” (*Preface to the Reply to the Chapter of the Gauls*).

### SAINT AUGUSTINE
