For this is to say that a person despairs of his salvation precisely when he has learned to place his hope not in himself but in God, although the prophet cries out: ‘Cursed is everyone who places his hope in man’ (Jeremiah XVII, 5).” *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 17.

### SAINT PROSPER

“This purpose of God’s calling, by which the distinction between those to be chosen and those to be rejected is said to have been made either before the beginning of the world or at the very creation of the human race, etc., is said both to remove from the fallen the concern to rise again and to offer the saints an occasion for delay … Thus, if God’s decree precedes human wills, all diligence is removed and virtues are taken away, and under the name of predestination a certain fatal necessity is introduced.” He writes that the Semi-Pelagians think this way in his letter to Augustine.

## XI

### CENSORS

“Augustine and others have always judged it one of the most difficult tasks to discover a true explanation and method that would dispel every difficulty and render the human intellect entirely at peace concerning the coherence of free choice with divine grace, foreknowledge, and predestination.

“And although those heretics who have attempted to prejudice either divine grace or free choice have been effectively defeated from the sacred Scriptures and the principles of faith, I do not know whether a complete and sufficient explanation reconciling free choice with all three has been given, whether a path has been opened for heretics by which they might more easily return to the peace and unity of the Church, or whether the disputes that arose a thousand years ago among Catholic men have been settled as far as is proper.”

### SAINT AUGUSTINE

“But first it must be demonstrated, according to the authority of the sacred Scriptures, whether the matter of faith is really so. Then, if God wills and helps, perhaps we shall serve these talkative reasoners, more inflated than capable and therefore suffering from a more dangerous disease, in such a way that they may find something about which they cannot doubt.” *On the Trinity*, book I, chapter 2.

“Since human reasoning sometimes pleases you against the most evident authority, bring forward the rule of your own reasoning.” Sermon 14, *On the Words of the Apostle*.

### POPE SAINT INNOCENT

“We received with a most grateful spirit the letters of your holy fraternity, full of faith and strengthened by the entire vigor of Catholic religion, which you sent to us and to your councils through our brother and fellow bishop Julius. For their whole tenor and every point of their dispute consist in consideration of God’s daily grace and in the correction of those who think otherwise, so that it may remove every error from them and, by providing any suitable example of our law which they ought to follow, enable them to offer a worthy teacher.” In the letter to Saint Augustine, numbered 96 among the Augustinian letters.

## XII

### CENSORS

“Augustine’s other explanations of Paul’s passage—‘God wills all human beings to be saved’ (1 Timothy II)—apart from the explanation of Damascene and the common explanation of the Fathers, all appear at first sight to be foreign and contrived.”

### SAINT AUGUSTINE

“It is evident that those who resist this truth so plainly expressed do not understand at all in what sense it was said that God wills all human beings to be saved, since so many are not saved—not because they themselves do not will it, but because God does not will it. This is made clear without any obscurity in the case of infants.

“Rather, just as it was said, ‘All shall be made alive in Christ’ (1 Corinthians XV, 22), although so many are punished with eternal death—said because all who receive eternal life receive it only in Christ—so also what was said, ‘God wills all human beings to be saved,’ was said because all who are saved are saved only by his will. And if those apostolic words can be understood in some other way, it must nevertheless be in such a manner that they cannot contradict this most evident truth, in which we see that so many are not saved, even when human beings wish them to be saved, because God does not will it.” Letter 107 to Vitalis; likewise *Enchiridion*, chapter 103, and *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 14.

## XIII

### CENSORS

“Augustine was wrong to refuse to concede this will of God concerning the salvation of all, and he correctly explained that passage of Paul in none of the three ways.”

## XIV

### CENSORS

“When we were explaining his opinion, we mentioned three or four methods, drawn from Augustine, for explaining those words—‘God wills all human beings to be saved.’ These methods generally seem to me more suited to evasion than to truth and solidity.”

### THE CHURCH OF LYONS

“We too have previously mentioned the meaning of those words of the Apostle in which he says, ‘Who wills all human beings to be saved,’ and we said that they can be received faithfully, provided that the meaning of Blessed Augustine is also accepted—namely, the meaning which he diligently seeks according to the authority of another passage of divine Scripture and explains in many true ways.

“That meaning should not be condemned on account of this one; rather, because of the truthful and pious authority of the Fathers, obedience should faithfully be given to both meanings.” *On Three Letters*, chapter 26; the same is found in chapter 24.

“The explanations of the outstanding teacher Augustine concerning 1 Timothy II, 4—‘God wills all human beings to be saved’—are sound.” Saint Bonaventure, *Commentary on the Sentences*, book I, distinction 46, question 1, article 1.

## XV

### CENSORS

“Thus the objection which Augustine repeatedly raises ceases to apply, and it was this objection that caused him not to explain Paul’s testimony as referring universally to all human beings, but to take refuge in those three explanations. For he often objects that children in their mothers’ wombs sometimes die before baptism, although it depends neither on the children, nor on their parents, nor on the ministers—who most earnestly desire to help them and apply the remedy of baptism for their salvation—yet they cannot do so.”

### SAINT AUGUSTINE

“What do you say about those who die in the womb? What anguish!” Sermon 7, *On the Words of the Apostle*.

The same in Letter 105 to Sixtus:

“And why does the providence of God—for whom our hairs are numbered, without whose will not even a sparrow falls to the ground, who is not oppressed by fate, hindered by accidental events, or corrupted by any injustice—not provide for all the little children of his own children, so that they may be reborn to the heavenly inheritance, while it provides for some of the little children even of the impious?”

### SAINT FULGENTIUS

“For where, in the case of two little children, there are no merits in their actions and no different condition in their origin, it is clear to us that both were bound by the chains of original sin, but it is hidden from us why both were not absolved.

“Let us therefore know that it is inscrutable to us why God, leaving one behind, should freely rescue the other from that mass of perdition, etc.

“Someone may say: ‘Why did the Lord not bestow gratuitous mercy upon both, when one guilt bound both?’ To him we reply—without compromising the inscrutable depth of God’s judgments—that both were not either liberated or condemned because the Lord, who can neither will nor do evil, commanded that what was owed should be exacted from one with just severity, while he ordered that it be remitted to the other by gratuitous goodness.” *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, book I, chapter 13. Saint Prosper teaches the same in *Against the Ungrateful*, chapter 31.

## XVI

### CENSORS

“To call the cognitions of things in the Word and in their proper kind ‘a day,’ and by that method to multiply days by comparison with different objects, is to use words arbitrarily and contrary to everyone’s understanding and opinion. Nor does it possess any plausibility that Moses spoke with an uneducated people in a sense that scarcely anyone could devise and then persuade himself had been devised. Therefore to explain the Scriptures in that sense is plainly to weaken their authority and—if it is permissible to speak thus when opposing the opinion of that most holy and eminent doctor of the Church and of sacred theology, who has deserved so much from them—perhaps to expose it to ridicule before unbelievers. Augustine’s opinion is therefore deservedly rejected by the other Fathers and teachers in common.”

### SAINT AUGUSTINE

“Therefore, if anyone seeks in the enumeration of those days another opinion—not the one which, according to the measure of our ability, we have been able either to investigate or to suppose, but one that can be understood more properly and better in this creation of things, rather than figuratively in prophecy—let him seek and, with divine assistance, find it.

“For it may happen that I too shall perhaps find another interpretation more consonant with these words of divine Scripture. I do not confirm this interpretation in such a way as to maintain that another, which ought to be preferred, cannot be found.” *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book IV, chapter 28.

“With those, however, who do not deny that all those things which are true are true, honoring that holy Scripture which was issued through the holy Moses and establishing it with us at the summit of authority to be followed, yet contradicting us in some matter, I speak thus: ‘You, O God, be the judge between my confessions and their contradictions.’” *Confessions*, book XII, chapter 16.

### SAINT THOMAS

“Of these explanations, therefore, the first—namely, Augustine’s—is more subtle and better defends the Scriptures against the mockery of unbelievers. The second—namely, that of the other saints—is clearer and more consonant, insofar as the surface is concerned, with the words of the text.

“Because, however, neither of them disagrees with the truth of faith, and because the context of the text permits both meanings, neither explanation should be prejudged. Since we uphold both opinions, we must answer the arguments of both.” *Disputed Questions*, question 4, *On the Creation of Formless Matter*, article 2.

## XVII

### CENSORS

“We shall rashly assert that sufficient aid is denied to some, and we may ask Augustine and those who share his opinion how they became certain of this will of God.”

### SAINT AUGUSTINE
What shall I answer? You are about to hear Augustine, although you did not hear the Apostle saying: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9:20). Two little children were born; if you ask what was owed, both were holding the mass of perdition, etc. But the potter has power over the clay to make from the same mass one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (ibid., 21). Do you wish to argue with me? Rather, marvel with me and cry out with me: “O the depth of the riches” (Rom. 11:33). Sermon 11, *On the Words of the Apostle*.

**SAINT PROSPER**

At the very time when the preaching of the Gospel was being sent to all nations, certain places were forbidden to the apostles by him who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth—many, of course, being delayed and turned away there, and destined to die without the knowledge of the truth and without the consecration of regeneration because of the delay of the Gospel. Let Scripture, therefore, say what happened: “Having passed through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. When they had come to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them,” etc. In the letter to Rufinus. The same author teaches this in chapter 11 *Against the Ungrateful*:

> …Tell me where you prove that Christ’s grace  
>   
> Absolutely passes by no human being  
>   
> Of all who are born, to whom he does not wish  
>   
> To grant the kingdom and the blessed life? For not even in our own time  
>   
> Has the Gospel of Christ yet been certainly proclaimed  
>   
> In every land—not to mention that the beginnings of the gift  
>   
> Could not at once run their course throughout the whole world.

(See the synodical letter of the African Fathers, chapter 9.)

## XVIII.

**CRITICS**

I freely admit that the testimonies of Prosper and Fulgentius seem suspect to me, since they were the most diligent and exact disciples of Augustine.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

Now, when my most intimate associates, who do not share my opinion, have already been wounded, I, who do share it, am tortured as well. Book *On Two Souls*, chapter 14.

**SAINT PRUDENTIUS**

The holy bishop Fulgentius is a witness of this matter, and so forth. Certainly, if no other authority or argument were available to us, he alone could have sufficed for us in understanding this statement: his teaching and knowledge had gained such honor and affection in the Catholic Church that no one had ever doubted his writings, and no one had disparaged them, etc. The holy Prosper is also a witness, a man most learned and eloquent in every branch of literary knowledge, who vigorously and faithfully opposed the impudence of the Gauls and of others who followed them, both by books faithfully published and by the decree of the Roman pontiff obtained through his persistence. Accordingly, you are proved more impudent than the rest of those like you, since, after reading their venerable writings, you have dared to mutter something contrary to them. Book *On Predestination*, chapter 11.

## XIX.

**CRITICS**

Yet Augustine’s opinion, understood in this way, is no longer approved by scholastic theologians—and rightly so; for by it we are compelled to fall into the position of Pelagius.

**THE SAME AUTHOR ELSEWHERE**

Catherinus speaks rather immodestly against Augustine and makes a brazen attack upon Augustine’s opinion as understood in his own way. Again: Catherinus certainly fell most disgracefully into error in this respect: not understanding Augustine’s mind, he attacks and rejects him impudently.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

How can I hope that you will listen to what I say, when, being so close at hand, you yourself do not hear what you say, while you continually contradict yourself? Book II *Against Cresconius*, chapter 12, vol. VII.

## XX.

**CRITICS**

In this respect, the teaching of Blessed Augustine is not acceptable to me, etc.; but I believe that we must reason differently about the gifts that we lost in Adam.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

But if this assistance had been lacking to an angel or to a human being when they were first made—since that nature had not been made such that it could remain, if it wished, without divine assistance—they would certainly not have fallen through their own fault; for the assistance without which they could not remain would have been lacking. But now, for those to whom such assistance is lacking, this is already the punishment of sin. Book *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 11.

**SAINT INNOCENT, POPE**

For the first man, while possessing free choice, used his goods too heedlessly; falling, he was plunged into the depths of transgression and found no way by which he could rise from them thereafter. Deceived through his freedom forever, he would have lain crushed beneath this ruin, unless Christ’s coming, in accordance with his grace, had afterward raised him up, etc. In the letter to the Fathers of the Council of Carthage.

## XXI.

**CRITICS**

Augustine, overcome by arguments, introduced a new form of predestination: after the human fall, predestination was no longer fluid and uncertain in its outcome, as proceeding from free choice, but rather certain and fixed by grace.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

For we have learned that each of the heresies has introduced into the Church questions of its own, against which divine Scripture would be defended more diligently than it would have been if no such necessity had compelled us. What, then, compelled these passages of Scripture, in which predestination is commended, to be defended more fully and explicitly through our present labor, except that the Pelagians say that God’s grace is given according to our merits? Book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 20.

## XXXII.

**CRITICS**

Augustine was the first, so far as I know, among the ancients to discover, within the old course, a new path and to imprint new footprints.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

And therefore the faith of this predestination, which is now defended with new concern against the new heretics, has never been absent from the Church of Christ. Book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, at the end of chapter 23.

**SAINT FULGENTIUS**

Therefore, dearest brother, we have preferred for the present to insert in this little book these few passages from the books of Saint Augustine and from Prosper’s replies, so that all may know what they ought to think concerning the predestination of the saints and of the wicked, and at the same time so that it may appear that the tenor of our judgment agrees with the words of Blessed Augustine. Book I to Monimus, chapter 30.

## XXIII.

**CRITICS**

It must indeed be maintained that, although the opinion of Blessed Augustine, Blessed Fulgentius, and their followers concerning the hardening of Pharaoh may appear harsh and less conformable to divine benevolence, and therefore may not please us, nevertheless it is not to be struck down by a harsher judgment.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

For Scripture says to Pharaoh: “For this purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you,” etc. “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.” He does this in whom there is no unrighteousness. He therefore has mercy by a free gift, but he hardens by a most just merit. Letter 105 to Sixtus.

**THE CHURCH OF LYONS**

The blessed bishop and glorious confessor Fulgentius also wrote an outstanding book on this foreknowledge and predestination of judgment in both directions. Like his other admirable and venerable writings, it was always faithfully received by the Church and honorably numbered among ecclesiastical authors. Yet now, we do not know by what reasoning—or rather, by what faithlessness and contentiousness—it is rejected together with Blessed Augustine; and such great men of God are most unjustly insulted, despised as refuse and the vilest offscourings, and trampled underfoot by those who wish to appear Catholic. It is exceedingly astonishing—indeed horrifying—that they demand belief in their own inventions and absurdities after rejecting the most blessed Fathers and the most illustrious doctors of the Church. Book *On Three Letters*, chapter 8.

## XXIV.

**CRITICS**

Not everyone approves Augustine’s opinion concerning predestination; to many it appears dreadful and harsh.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

It is therefore the mark of excessive contentiousness to contradict predestination or to doubt concerning predestination. Book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, at the end of chapter 21.

**SAINT AMULO, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS**

But now let us hear Blessed Augustine, how he too, following the Apostle, the foremost preacher of predestination and grace, exhorts the faithful to devotion and perseverance in prayer, so that they may deserve to receive the reward of their calling. In a fragment of a letter to Hincmar.

## XXV.

**CRITICS**

When authority is at issue, let us love Augustine in such a way that we do not listen to those who strive to exalt him beyond what is fitting.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

So much was attributed to me that, whenever it was necessary to speak to the people in my presence, I was very rarely permitted to remain silent and listen to others. In the preface to the *Revisions*.

**HILARY OF ARLES**

Whatever you may wish or be able to do on behalf of the grace that we defend in you, the little with the great, we shall receive with the greatest gratitude, as though it had been decreed by us through the dearest and most revered authority. In a letter to Augustine. They are displeased that we resist what they asserted, after many conferences, against a man of the highest authority. Prosper, in a letter to Rufinus.

## XXVI.

**CRITICS**

What could those who were hostile to Faustus’s books press more vehemently than what Peter the Deacon and the others with him accuse them of in their letter—namely, that they were written against the doctrine of predestination? But what has this to do with Augustine? Faustus did not deny that he had written against the doctrine of predestination, but only against that doctrine which either asserts fate or denies free choice—both of which, they themselves admit, are not far removed from Augustine’s meaning.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

This is the manifest and certain predestination of the saints, which necessity compelled us afterward to defend more carefully and laboriously, when we were already disputing against the Pelagians, etc. Book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 20.

**FAUSTUS OF RIEZ**

If, then, one has been appointed to life and another to perdition, as they assert (Vasquez), as one of the saints said: “We are born not to be judged, but already judged” (Augustine, Book I *On Grace and Free Choice*, chapter 4). Part I, distinction 89, no. 6.

**BLESSED LUPUS, ABBOT OF FERRIÈRES**

When the most reverend Pope Gelasius, together with seventy highly learned bishops, determined which writers were or were not to be received, after approving Augustine and praising Jerome at length, he removed the aforesaid Faustus from authority in these words: “The little works of Faustus of Riez, a Gaul, are apocryphal.” Therefore, following the uncorrupted understanding of the sacred Scriptures and reverencing the dignity of the Apostolic See, what else can we say except: let Faustus be silent, and let Jerome and Augustine, who think similarly, speak with their companions—remembering, of course, that proverb: “Let the frogs fall silent while heaven thunders.” In the collection *On Three Questions*, question 3.

## XXVII.

**CRITICS**

For some time the question of predestination has begun to be debated in the schools on both sides, and Augustine’s authority has not been considered capable of deciding this controversy in favor of either side.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

This, then, is the predestination of the saints, which was made especially clear in the Holy of Holies. Who among those rightly understanding the utterances of truth can deny it? Book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 15.

## XXVIII.

**CRITICS**

Augustine embraced the opinion of a gratuitous election to glory and had many later supporters; nevertheless, neither his authority nor their agreement deterred certain theologians distinguished for piety and learning from following and defending the contrary position. Their example has carried such weight that, at the present time, the contrary view is commonly and indiscriminately employed in the schools; and, as it has begun, it appears gradually to have covered over the other and to be destined to prevail.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

This I know: no one has been able to argue against this predestination, which we defend according to the holy Scriptures, except by falling into error. Book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 19.

There is, I say, no more illustrious example of predestination than the Mediator himself. Whoever among the faithful wishes to understand it properly should attend to him and find himself in him. Ibid., chapter 24.

**SAINT PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP**

Although certain Gauls, as one of them says—“their counsels are always sudden”—did not condemn the predestination of the lost, they preferred, through a new collusion, to disparage the predestination of the saints. In response to their insane presumption, that same memorable Augustine, the outstanding teacher, replying orthodoxly at the request of Prosper and Hilary, composed two books with the greatest fullness and fidelity: one *On the Predestination of the Saints*, the other *On the Gift of Perseverance*. In them he discussed very little concerning those predestined to destruction, but much more, and most truthfully, concerning those predestined to glory. In the letter to Hincmar and Pardulus.

## XXIX.

**CRITICS**

Finally, not to prolong the matter, the Council of Trent seems to have undertaken, when it wished to confront the madness of the new heretics who were abusing Augustine’s teaching in defense of their error, to make that teaching Catholic by adding certain necessary qualifications.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

We have said many things, and perhaps long ago we were able to persuade them of what we wish; yet we still speak to such good minds as though they were dull, for whom even what is excessive is not enough. Book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 20, at the end.

**SAINT REMIGIUS WITH HIS CHURCH OF LYONS**

After first praising Saint Augustine magnificently, he says: Nothing should have been added to or taken away from the fullest and clearest definitions of the holy and orthodox Fathers concerning free choice, because they contain with the greatest fullness whatever is necessary for the Catholic faith; and if anything is removed from them, the integrity of the truth is violated. Book *On Holding Fast to the Truth of Sacred Scripture*, chapter 4, vol. IX of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

## XXX.

**CRITICS**

For Augustine’s doctrines are neither few nor contemptible—doctrines that are rejected either by the universal Church or by all or many theologians, and not merely by those of the lowest bench.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

Nor shall I be afraid to put forward my judgment, in which I shall prefer to be examined by the upright rather than fear being bitten by the perverse. For beautiful and most modest charity gladly receives the eye of a dove; but the tooth of a dog is either avoided by most cautious humility or blunted by most steadfast truth. I shall prefer to be criticized by anyone rather than praised either by one who is in error or by a flatterer. No critic is to be feared by one who loves the truth: for the critic is either an enemy or a friend. If an enemy insults, he must be endured; but if a friend is in error, he must be taught, and if he teaches, he must be heard, etc. Book II *On the Trinity*, preface.

## XXXI.

**CRITICS**

Numerous and far from trivial errors are circulated under the names of Augustine and the other Fathers whom the holy synod named and approved—errors that certainly are neither Catholic nor such as any ecumenical synod has wished to be accepted.

**SAINT PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP**

For if it had perceived anything in the teaching of Saint Augustine contrary to the orthodox faith, the venerable bishop of the Roman Church, Innocent, would never have accepted it together with the bishops of the whole world. Nor would he have honored that renowned man by the offices of his letters, publicly and privately; nor would his successor Zosimus have followed the same path; nor would Boniface, bishop of that same Apostolic See, have sent him the letters of the Pelagians that had been delivered to him, asking him to answer them; nor would he have received, with due approval and honor, his response published in four books. Celestine also, bishop of the aforesaid city, made known by the authority of his apostolic decrees what he thought concerning him and his teaching against the madness of the Gauls; those decrees are as follows, etc., where he recites the commendation bestowed on Saint Augustine. In the letter to Hincmar and Pardulus.

## XXXII.

**CRITICS**

Which councils or edicts of the Roman pontiffs have received Augustine’s opinion concerning predestination and reprobation, insofar as they concern eternal salvation, with the same degree of authority as his teachings concerning grace, so that they have passed into the dogmas of the faith?

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

And therefore the faith of this predestination, which is now defended with new concern against the new heretics, has never been absent from the Church of Christ. Book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 23.

**SAINT PROSPER**

Let the slanderers recognize that they are objecting in vain that these books—namely, the last books of Saint Augustine to Prosper and Hilary, in which he deals at length with predestination—have not received a special and distinct testimony, since the standard of these books is praised throughout all his volumes. For the Apostolic See approves what does not differ from what it already knows, and what it joins to its judgment it does not separate from its praise. *Against the Collator*, chapter 42.

## XXXIII.

**CRITICS**

By adding these words, the Fathers of Trent prudently moderated that rigid and excessively severe sense of Augustine, as some understood it—namely, the claim that no good work exists except one proceeding from the grace of Christ.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

God’s assistance is not of such a kind; Christ’s assistance is not of such a kind; the Holy Spirit’s assistance is not of such a kind. Again: If it is lacking, you will be able to do nothing good. You do act by free will when he does not assist you, but you act badly. Your will, which is called free, is capable of this; and by acting badly it becomes a punishable slave. Sermon 13, *On the Words of the Apostle*.

**THE HOLY AFRICAN FATHERS EXILED IN SARDINIA**

Before the abundance of grace, there is indeed free choice in a human being, but it is not good because it has not been enlightened. Therefore, unless grace is given, that choice is not good. For human free choice without the gift of grace is like an eye without light: the eye was made for seeing, but unless it receives light, it will not see. In the synodical letter, chapter 5, vol. VI of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, part I.

“No one has anything of his own except falsehood and sin” (Council of Orange, canon 22). This statement is copied from treatise 5 of the Holy Father on John.

## XXXIV.

**CRITICS**

The ridiculous worshipers of Saint Augustine say everywhere that he is the most faithful witness of antiquity, as Calvin puts it; the first oracle of the Church, the foremost of the Fathers, and the most subtle of all the doctors.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

But wherever you may be, wherever you may be able to read these things, I have placed you before those whom, in this dispute of ours, you have appointed as judges on my behalf—not as my friends and your enemies, inclined toward me by some favor, or turned away from you by some fault of yours and therefore hostile to you, etc. Book II *Against Julian*, chapter 10.

**SAINT JEROME AND OTHER FATHERS**

Jerome addresses Augustine in Letter 25 among the Augustinian letters as follows: “Well done for your courage! You are celebrated throughout the world; Catholics revere and honor you as the restorer of the ancient faith.”

Bishop Audax says in Letter 139: “I desired the treasure of wisdom, but I received less than I wished—although it should not be called less, but rather the gift that Augustine, the oracle of the law, the consecrator of righteousness, the restorer of spiritual glory, and dispenser of eternal salvation, bestowed.”

Sixtus IV, in the *Bullarium* concerning Augustine: “Augustine is foremost among the teachers of the undefiled Church and the most subtle investigator of the Gospel and sacred letters.”

## XXXV.

**CRITICS**

But fair-minded admirers teach that Saint Augustine never possessed such unrestricted authority in the Church that Catholics are obliged to submit blindly to all his opinions, or that those opinions cannot be challenged without rashness and error.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

But it is beyond doubt that you, being so cautious, so turbulent, and so novel, put forward nothing worthy of authority. Book *On the Usefulness of Believing*, chapter 14.

**SAINT JEROME**

For my part, I have resolved to love you, revere you, honor you, admire you, and defend your statements as though they were my own. Certainly, in the *Dialogue* that I recently published, I remembered your blessedness as was fitting. Letter 30 to Saint Augustine among the Augustinian letters.

But I do not wish your Holiness to suppose that I write these things as though I doubted what you have now published. Hilary, in a letter to Augustine.

## XXXVI.

We revere Saint Augustine as is fitting, but not like irrational beasts and without reason; with him we profess that we love him less than the truth.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

In this I plainly praise you: although you have never grasped the truth, you have at least preferred what you believed to be the truth to a human being. You did so rashly, because you thought you knew what you do not know; but freely, because, fearing no person, you chose to reveal what you think. Book IV *On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 1.

**SAINT ALYPIUS OF TAGASTE**

We have a guide—Augustine—who, with God now showing us the way, may lead us into the very secrets of truth. Book III of Augustine’s *Against the Academics*, at the end.

Rupert, Abbot, Book VII *On the Work of the Holy Spirit*, chapter 19: “This is Augustine, the pillar and foundation of truth.”

Prosper, in a letter to Rufinus: “The Spirit of truth filled Augustine most abundantly.”

## XXXVII.

**CRITICS**

We maintain that his weapons are not invincible in every respect, however illustrious they may be.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

Indeed, while you vauntingly brandish your weapons, which are empty and blunted. Book V *Against Julian*, chapter 9.

**SAINT PAULINUS**

And therefore, since by this Pentateuch of yours you have sufficiently armed me against the Manichaeans, if you have also prepared defenses against other enemies of the Catholic faith—for our enemy, who possesses a thousand arts of doing harm, must be defeated by as many weapons as he uses stratagems against us—I ask you not to refuse to bring out from your arsenal and entrust to me the weapons of righteousness. Letter 31, preserved by Saint Augustine.

For, among the many gifts of God with which the Spirit of truth filled him most abundantly, he also possessed this power of knowledge and wisdom arising from the love of God, so that he might combat not only this [heresy], still throbbing amid its mutilations, but also many earlier heresies with the invincible sword of the word. Saint Prosper to Rufinus.

John XXII says: “Augustine brought the truth of the Catholic faith into the light, brought it forth publicly, and established it upon firm and invincible arguments.”

## XXXVIII.

**CRITICS**

Nor was he so fortunate in selecting his judgments and the foundations by which he confirms them—as I shall demonstrate if this is enjoined upon me—that he leaves our minds the fullest freedom not to agree with his teaching, indeed to defend the opposite position; and he himself even casts doubt upon the certainty of the opinions that he teaches.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

This is indeed said; but you say: “Whoever reads and understands, if he is not a Pelagian, does not say this.” Book I of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 15, written to refute these words of Julian: “Therefore nothing there remains unrefuted of all Augustine’s arguments and propositions.”

Let him prove it, if he can, and I shall admit that I learned it from him. Book I *On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 14.

**SAINT PROSPER**

Thus he sings of Saint Augustine’s arguments against the Pelagians in chapter 3 of his poem *Against the Ungrateful*:

> Therefore, among all those who drove mad beasts  
>   
> From the holy flock, his zeal was greater;  
>   
> His work was greater, and more excellent, filling the whole world.  
>   
> Wherever the uncertain path proceeded through winding ways,  
>   
> Concealing itself, his approach forestalled it,  
>   
> So that, through a thousand paths of ambush,  
>   
> No entrance could be found.  
>   
> And while, shut out from without, the frenzy  
>   
> Of greedy wolves growled, and falsehood turned  
>   
> To every kind of trickery,  
>   
> So that it could not corrupt the minds of any sheep  
>   
> Or disturb uncertain hearts with crooked complaints,  
>   
> God caused rivers of books to flow through the whole world  
>   
> From this man’s mouth, from this man’s mouth—  
>   
> Rivers which the gentle and humble drink,  
>   
> And strive to send into the fields of their souls  
>   
> The streams of life-giving doctrine.

## XXXIX.

**CRITICS**

If Augustine says these things correctly, I can abandon him and join myself to all the doctors. But if he says them without reason, I can also abandon him on that very ground, because he asserts that I can do so while speaking without reason. Thus, however Augustine is understood, I am by no means compelled to become his slave and adore all his opinions.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

If it is shameful to believe anyone without reason, what are you expecting, what are you striving for, by asking me to believe someone without reason, so that I may more easily be led by your reasoning? Will your reason build anything solid upon a foundation of rashness? Book VI *On the Usefulness of Believing*, to Honoratus, chapter 14.

**SAINT BERNARD**

I am difficult to tear away from these two pillars—by Augustine and Ambrose I mean them—believe me; with them I acknowledge that I either err or think rightly. Letter 77 to Hugh.

## XL.

**CRITICS**

This is sufficient to extort from Augustine’s unrestrained worshipers the admission that it is permissible not always to follow Augustine’s opinions without incurring the stigma of error and rashness.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

I would not want anyone to embrace all my opinions in such a way as to follow me, except in those matters in which he has seen that I am not in error. Book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 21.

**SAINT ILDEFONSUS**

Let them hear Blessed Augustine, whom it is not permissible to contradict. Sermon 2, *On the Blessed Virgin*.

## XLI.

**CRITICS**

Many men distinguished for piety and learning—bishops, cardinals, and Augustine’s own friends, servants, supporters, brothers, and sons—have often left him.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

Would that you were not the ones who both speak and write your false testimony against the testimony of truth! Book II of the *Unfinished Work Against Julian*, chapter 79.

Will you therefore be able to escape the force of truth because, by slandering us, you bring forward partners in falsehood? Book V *Against Julian*, chapter 7.

**SAINT VINCENT FERRER**

I dare to say: All the doctors who came after Augustine are supported by his holy, pure, immaculate doctrine, of the purest gold, without the error of false opinions. Sermon *On Saint Augustine*.

## XLII.

**CRITICS**

It is unheard of in the Church—and Augustine himself detests it—that his irrelevant worshipers place him above the heads of all the other Fathers. Only madmen reason in this way: “One doctor asserted this; therefore it must be believed.”

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

Behold, it is not I alone, but so many and such great holy and learned doctors who answer you on my behalf, or with me, for the salvation of all of us—and of your own, if you are wise. Book I *Against Julian*, chapter 7.

**THE SAME AUTHOR**

Any doctor is satisfied in proving his statement if he can produce one authority of Augustine. Ibid.

## XLIII.

**CRITICS**

This obscurity of Augustine also appeared in his treatment of the mysteries of predestination and grace. For it introduced disagreements into the schools of theologians, divided doctors among themselves, and furnished an occasion for disturbances and controversies arising partly in Africa and partly in Gaul, both while he was alive and after his death.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

Concerning this most difficult question—that is, concerning will and grace—I did not need to argue at greater length in this letter also, since I had already given them another letter, as though they would return sooner. I also wrote a book to you; if, with the Lord’s help, you read it carefully and understand it keenly, I do not think that disagreements among you concerning this matter will continue any longer. Letter 47 to Valentinus.

**SAINT THOMAS OF VILLANOVA**

O greatest star, Father Augustine, how greatly you have illuminated God’s Church by the radiance of your wisdom! How greatly, by your presence, you have driven away the darkness of errors! For now, with you as author and teacher, everything is so clear that no one can err unless he deliberately wishes to be deluded. For, as it seems to me, in God’s Church there is a theological school, like a certain threshing floor, etc. First sermon *On Saint Augustine*.

## XLIV.

**CRITICS**

Indeed, this same obscurity of Augustine served as a shield for the predestinarian heresy, whose fierce and dreadful doctrines they founded upon the teaching of this Father.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

I certainly suppose that some slower minds will think that I meant what I did not mean, or did not mean what I did mean. Who does not know that their error ought not to be attributed to me if, while appearing to follow me and failing to understand me, they have strayed into some falsehood, since I am compelled to make my way through certain dense and obscure passages? For no one would rightly attribute to the sacred authorities of the divine books themselves such numerous and varied errors of heretics, even though all of them strive to defend their false and deceptive opinions from those same Scriptures. Book I *On the Trinity*, chapter 2.

**FACUNDUS, BISHOP OF HERMIANE**

Why should we be surprised at this? Augustine could not have spoken better than the prophets, apostles, and evangelists, whose words so many people attempt to use in defending their own errors after misunderstanding them in the same way and applying them improperly. Book *Against Mocianus*. Concerning Facundus of Hermiane, see Saint Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 19.

## XLV.

**CRITICS**

I may conclude that he did not wish to set forth clearly in his books the thoughts of his mind, or that he was not sufficiently clear in setting them forth to leave readers no opportunity for doubt concerning his true mind and intention.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

Those who still do not understand what I believe I have stated clearly in accordance with the nature of the questions should not slander me on account of the deficiency of my ability; rather, let them pray to God for the gift of understanding. Book III *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins Against Pelagius*, chapter 2.

**SAINT PRUDENTIUS, BISHOP**

O dreadful monster! O tongue that ought to be cut out! It does not fear to impute either ignorance or envy to such great doctors, so that those who undertook to reveal obscure matters may be thought to have entangled them in still more obscure statements, etc. On this matter, the books of the most blessed Father Augustine are witnesses to us. Book *On Predestination Against John Eriugena*, chapter 11.

## XLVI.

**CRITICS**

When Augustine was weighed down by the burden of some insuperable difficulty, he took refuge in those words of Scripture: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!”

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

They are guilty of excessive vanity and blindness if, even after considering these matters, they still do not deign to cry out with us: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” Letter 105 to Sixtus.

**POPE ADRIAN VI**

In all these matters we must cry out with Augustine: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” In *The Four Books of the Sentences*, question 1, on penance, in the solution of the third difficulty.

## XLVII.

**CRITICS**

The doctrine of Saint Augustine concerning the mysteries of grace, freedom, predestination, and the Eucharist is exceedingly difficult and obscure to understand.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

I am indeed understood completely, whether you wish it or not; but you wish that what I have said—something most true and firmly established—not be understood, because you mean to say nothing against it. Book IV of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 140. Read it again, and you will understand. Book III, chapter 191.

**CASSIODORUS**

That outstanding and most blessed doctor, Augustine himself, conqueror of heretics, defender of the faithful, and victor in famous struggles, is hidden in certain books by excessive difficulty; in others he is so perfectly clear that even little children find him acceptable. His open passages are sweet, while his obscure passages are enriched by great benefits. Chapter 22, *On Divine Reading*.

Where, because of the obscurity of the subjects and the subtlety of the arguments, we are less able to understand Augustine, let us either ask the Lord for understanding or humbly allow ourselves to be taught by those whom he has deigned to illuminate by his gift, and let us pray. The Church of Lyons, Book *On Holding Fast to the Truth of Sacred Scripture*, chapter 9.

## XLVIII.

**CRITICS**

New arguments are brought forward to prove that Saint Augustine’s doctrine concerning the mysteries of grace and predestination is obscure and difficult to understand.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

If you do not wish to understand, or if you pretend not to understand, do not obstruct those who wish and are able to understand. Book IV *Against Julian*, chapter 46.

**SAINT PROSPER**

In these statements of Augustine there is no obscurity, provided that, concerning the faith of predestination and grace—from which is the origin of all good things and the perseverance of merits—one holds what the truth contains. At the end of the reply to the excerpts of the Genoese from Saint Augustine’s books *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*.

## XLIX.

**CRITICS**

Finally, to conclude this chapter concerning the obscurity of Saint Augustine’s words by an irrefutable argument, and to demonstrate the difficulty of uncovering his true mind, etc.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**

You are not laboring to understand me, although you can do so very easily; rather, you are laboring to refute me, which you cannot do. Book III of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 141.

**SAINT ANTONINUS**

Like the shining sun, which is called the lord of the planets and the father of light, shining above all luminaries, pleasing to the eyes and looking upon everything—so Augustine illuminated the Church, the jewel of doctors and father of theologians, sweet in eloquence and making all subjects clear by penetrating them. Part II of the *History*, title 8.

And farther on: Rightly, therefore, just as the shining sun, so he shone in the temple of God with the splendor of most illustrious teaching.

Saint Prosper, in a letter to Augustine: “After reading this book of Your Blessedness, those who previously followed the holy and apostolic authority of your teaching have become much more intelligent and better instructed; while those who were hindered by the obscurity of their own conviction have withdrawn even more alienated than before.”

## L.

**CRITICS**

It must be observed that Saint Augustine himself confesses that he often remains uncertain concerning many questions of predestination and finds them filled with insuperable difficulties, and that he has never been able to give any answer with which he could rest, except a confession of his own ignorance and of the loftiness of God’s judgments.

**SAINT AUGUSTINE**
Are you asking for an explanation? I shall be awed by the profundity: “O depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” You reason; I marvel. You argue; I believe. I see the depth, but I do not reach the bottom. Later:

“He rested, because he found something to admire; let no one ask me for an explanation of hidden things. He says, ‘His judgments are unsearchable,’ and you have come to search them out? He says, ‘His ways are inscrutable,’ and you have come to investigate them? If you have come to search out what is unsearchable and to investigate what is inscrutable, believe me, you are already lost.” Sermon 20, *On the Words of the Apostle*.

### St. Fulgentius

Indeed, labor spent on a superfluous investigation is wasted where no possibility of discovery lends support, and culpable curiosity immediately falls into guilt when human frailty does not measure its own limits. Rather, in this deepest secret of the divine will, let us recognize that nothing accords with our salvation except that each of us should humbly say with David: “Your knowledge has become wonderful beyond me; it is established, and I cannot attain to it.” Let us also join to this the feeling of devout proclamation expressed by blessed Paul, who says: “O depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” Book I, *On the Truth of Predestination*. See Prosper, *To the Genuese*, doubts 4 and 7.

### LI.

#### Censors

Since Saint Augustine changed his opinion on this subject three times, this led us to believe that Saint Augustine, although he possessed an outstanding intellect, was not satisfied with his own reflections and, after exhausting so many efforts to penetrate the mystery of predestination, was compelled to confess his weakness.

#### St. Augustine

You certainly see what I then thought about faith and works, although I was laboring to commend the grace of God. I now see that these our brothers—that is, the Semi-Pelagians—hold that position, because, just as they did not take care to read my books, so they also did not take care to advance in them together with me. *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 4.

#### St. Prosper

Since, therefore, the conviction of those men cannot be understood as either just or reasonable—those who reduced the learning of this man, built up through so many stages of progress and refined through so many years of study, to the beginnings of his youth, so that what he had thought unskillfully at the beginning of his conversion might serve the heretics more than what the truth of his episcopal diligence had revealed benefited Catholics—the gravity of the devout teacher rightly censures those who, making use of this prejudice and lingering over matters long since renounced, refused to investigate all his meanings while advancing together with his learning. *Response to Doubt 3 of the Genuese Extracts*, at the end.

### LII.

#### Censors

Nor is it surprising that, with Augustine’s intellect wavering among so many opinions that appeared plausible to him, he is said to have changed his opinion three times.

#### St. Augustine

You say that I myself also altered my views and that at the beginning of my conversion I thought what you think. But you are mistaken—or you are deceiving yourself—either by slandering what I now say or by failing to understand, or rather by failing to read, what I said then. Book VI *Against Julian*, chapter 12.

#### The Same

Let this condition plainly remain, let it remain: that the novelty of these books be rejected if, in the same matter, the antiquity of the same man—that is, Augustine—disagrees with itself, and that whatever is found to be discordant with what he composed against the Pelagians be judged useless or inappropriate. At the end of the book *Against the Collator*.

### LIII.

#### Censors

Augustine very often confessed that the difficulties proposed either by himself or by his opponents in this matter exceeded his answers, and that his mind was troubled more by objections than satisfied by solutions.

#### St. Augustine

“I think that you see, Julian, that I have answered you on every point and refuted everything, and so on,” if you are not obstinate. Book VI *Against Julian*, chapter 26. Hence I think that in the two preceding books I answered you in such a way that no one would require anything further. At the beginning of Book V *Against the Same*.

#### The Same

“Nor is the power of the synods alone displayed there,

As though our people, unable to overcome them by reason,

Had pressed them by force; their arts were examined,

And the poison of the heretical mind exposed;

No argument was left at all

That learned faith could not dissolve.”

And later:

“Could the holy council proceed to any other end,

Aurelius being its leader and Augustine its intellect,

Augustine, whom the grace of Christ,

Watering him with a more abundant horn,

Gave as a light to our age?” *Against the Ungrateful*, chapter 2.

### LIV.

#### Censors

Augustine admits that his doctrine of predestination is such that it ought not to be preached to the masses or to people of slower understanding.

#### St. Augustine

When these and similar things are spoken either to a few Christians or to the multitude of the Church, why should we fear to preach the predestination of the saints and the true grace of God—that is, grace which is not given according to our merits—as Holy Scripture proclaims it? *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 22.

#### The Same

Augustine nevertheless proved abundantly, through a devout and steadfast doctrine, that the Church’s predestination ought to be preached—in it lies the preparation of grace; that grace ought to be preached—in it lies the effect of predestination; and that the foreknowledge of God ought to be preached, by which, before the eternal ages, he foreknew to whom he would bestow his gifts. Whoever opposes this preaching is a most obvious ally of Pelagian arrogance. At the end of the *Response to the Genuese Extracts*.

### LV.

#### Censors

I may add that, if I wished to gather together the various propositions of Saint Augustine concerning this subject, I would construct a kind of body from utterly diverse parts. In one place he asserts that our salvation was established by an absolute decree; elsewhere he nevertheless says that it depends upon our free will, and so forth.

#### St. Augustine

My statements, then, are not contradictory to one another, although you allow them to appear contradictory—either by failing to understand or by preventing others from understanding. Book V *Against Julian*, chapter 5.

#### The Same

Let the three books addressed to Marcellinus be read; let the letter to Saint Paulinus of Nola be reviewed; let the pages sent to the most blessed Xistus, then a presbyter of the Apostolic See but now its pontiff, be consulted again. Let the volumes separately published to Saint Pinianus, to Count Valerius, and to the servants of Christ, Timasius and Jacobus, be reread. Let the first six books *Against Julian*, one book addressed to Saint Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, *On the Palestinian Proceedings*, another addressed to the priests Paulus and Eutropius *Against the Questions of Pelagius and Coelestius*, and the four books addressed to Pope Boniface of blessed memory be examined. And so, throughout all these works and many others too numerous to list, the same spirit of doctrine and the same form of preaching preceded them. At the end of the book *Against the Collator*, chapter 41.

### LVI.

#### Censors

I conclude from this that, if I am not permitted to say that Saint Augustine contradicted himself in various passages of his books, at least I may believe that his doctrine is exceedingly intricate, since nothing can be found more intricate than that which appears to conflict with itself.

#### St. Augustine

This is why you think—or wish others to think—that my statements contradict one another, as though I disapproved what I had previously approved or embraced what I had previously rejected. Hear, then, my clear opinion, and understand—or, if you do not understand, at least do not obscure the serenity of the most sincere truth with the darkness of a clouded disputation. Book V *Against Julian*, chapter 9.

#### The Same

But, dearest and most revered brother, if you truly desire to be instructed concerning these questions, as it is fitting that you should desire, devote yourself to learning the disputations of blessed Augustine, so that, in confessing the grace of God, you may attain the purest and most salutary understanding of evangelical and apostolic doctrine. Letter to Rufinus, at the end.

### LVII.

#### Censors

Nevertheless, Augustine was never carried farther by the ardor of zeal than when he attacked the Pelagians. For while he intended to distance himself as far as possible from their manner of speaking and their errors, he fell into dangerous excesses. Hence certain theologians distinguished for doctrine and piety have said that he transgressed the boundaries of truth, was inflamed by excessive argumentative heat, or appeared to favor the heretics. These words would be insolent and shameless if they were not true.

#### St. Augustine

Whoever, with a Catholic mind, recoils from these wicked and condemnable dogmas in their threefold division should avoid the hiding places and ambushes of the fivefold division, and should be so cautious between the two that, while shunning Manichaeism, he does not incline toward Pelagianism, and while separating himself from the Pelagians, he does not join himself to the Manichaeans. Or, if he is already held by one side or the other, he should not protect himself from some opponents in such a way as to rush upon the others. Book IV *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 3.

#### St. Fulgentius

Blessed Augustine, clothed with power from on high, labored more abundantly than all those men—not he himself, but the grace of God with him, and so forth. For, possessing the mind of Christ, he distinguished both the functions and the merits of God’s grace and of human free will, always subjecting human things to divine things, and teaching truthfully that God bestows upon human beings, freely, both the gift of justification, the beginning of a good will, and the full effect of glorification. Book II *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, chapter 18.

### LVIII.

#### Censors

Augustine himself acknowledges in several passages of his works this impulse of his mind, by which—that is, in his disputations with the Pelagians and Manichaeans—he was so carried away that he inclined toward the error opposite to the one he intended to destroy.

#### St. Augustine

Two errors may be opposed to one another, but both are detestable because both are opposed to the truth. For if the Pelagians are to be loved because they hate the Manichaeans, then the Manichaeans must also be loved because they hate the Pelagians. But far be it from the Catholic mother to choose to love one side because of its hatred of the other, since, with God warning and helping, she ought to avoid both and desire to heal both! Book II *To Boniface*, chapter 2.

#### St. Prosper, or Pomerianus

Saint Augustine, bishop, was keen in intellect, gracious in speech, learned in secular literature, industrious in ecclesiastical labors, renowned in daily disputations, composed in all his actions, Catholic in the exposition of our faith, acute in resolving questions, CIRCUMSPECT in refuting heretics, and CAUTIOUS in explaining the canonical Scriptures. Book III *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 31.

### LIX.

#### Censors

It is certainly evident that Augustine sometimes spoke excessively in questions concerning grace and predestination, and that his words ought to be moderated. In order not to fall into the opposite error because of their harshness and severity, I ought to be permitted to seek some Catholic qualification to be added.

#### St. Augustine

Who would not fear or hate conclusions that lie, or that gradually insinuate themselves into assent to falsehood by diminishing or adding? Book II *On Order*, chapter 4.

Say what you are about to say, excellent corrector. Book III of the *Unfinished Work*, chapter 57.

#### Pope Sixtus III

What, finally, are the things that must be believed and said? Let no novelty be permitted beyond this, because nothing ought to be added to antiquity. Let the clear faith of our ancestors, and belief unmingled with any dregs, remain undisturbed. Letter to John of Antioch. (This is Sixtus, to whom Saint Augustine wrote his famous Letter 105 against the Pelagians.)

### LX.

#### Censors

Provided only that I do not fall into the errors of the Pelagians, whom Saint Augustine attacks, I may refrain from following the force of the expressions he uses to overthrow them.

#### St. Augustine

Thus we overcome and avoid both the Manichaeans and the Pelagians. Their respective errors are so different that the one which appears lesser is shown to be an ally of the one which appears greater. Book III *Against Julian*, *Unfinished Work*, chapter 178.

#### St. Prosper

Or has the stricter standard of the new censors so moderated itself that it asserts none of the things that have been cut away, while rejecting some of those that have been defended? *Against the Collator*, the Reprover of Saint Augustine, chapter 1.

### LXI.

#### Censors

Thus it comes about that I stand midway between Pelagius and Calvin. If, by moderating Augustine’s words, I were to descend too far, I would be a Pelagian; but if I wished to maintain their height, I would be a Calvinist. Therefore I hold the middle position with the Church.

#### St. Augustine

There is, then, no pit that I fear, as though I might return to the road to which you seem to wish to recall me. Nevertheless, tell me what that road is and explain your reasoning. Book III *Against Julian*, chapter 8.

#### The Same

But you are in complete agreement neither with the heretics nor with the Catholics. Later: “You have discovered some shapeless third position, unsuitable to either side, by which you would acquire neither the agreement of your enemies nor permanence in the understanding of our people.” Ibid., chapter 5.

### LXII.

#### Censors

The reason why we are not bound to follow Blessed Augustine in the question of the predestination of the saints to glory, in the manner of the operation of divine grace, and so forth, is this: the Pelagians never disputed those questions, and the doctrine of Saint Augustine is irrefragable only when he attacks their errors. Even if they had preached against opinions of that kind, the Church never on that account enrolled them among the heretics, nor could she have done so.

#### St. Augustine

This is the manifest and certain predestination of the saints, which necessity compelled us later to defend more carefully and laboriously, once we were already disputing against the Pelagians. For we have learned that each heresy introduced its own questions into the Church, against which divine Scripture was defended more diligently than it would have been if no such necessity had compelled us. *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 20.

#### The Same

Let the slanderers recognize that they object in vain that no special and distinct testimony has been offered to these books of Augustine, whose standard is praised throughout all his volumes. For the Apostolic See approves, together with things already known to it, whatever does not differ from them, and what it joins to its judgment it does not separate from its praise. Ibid., chapter 23.

### LXIII.

#### Censors

But if Augustine added that original sin is the sole cause of reprobation, and that it is the consideration by which God is moved to separate the predestined from the reprobate—which, Saint Augustine writes, is his opinion—I do not merely refuse to die in defense of this opinion; I believe that I am permitted to reject it with abhorrence, because it is the mother of that opinion which Calvin presses against the Church with such impiety and rage.

#### St. Augustine

For what did he love in Jacob before Jacob had done anything good, except the gratuitous gift of his mercy? And what did he hate in Esau before Esau had done anything evil, except original sin? Letter 105 to Sixtus, where he discusses this matter at greater length.

#### St. Thomas

God’s election, by which he chooses one and rejects another, is rational; yet it is not necessary that the reason for election be merit. Rather, in election the reason is divine goodness, while the reason for reprobation in human beings is original sin, as Augustine says. *Question 6 on Truth*, article 2, reply to objection 9.

### LXIV.

#### Censors

These, then, are the reasons why the books of that holy and learned teacher are covered with darkness and obscurity, as the most celebrated theologians have observed.

#### St. Augustine

Because they reprove your darkness, they do not appear bright to you; and whatever troubles you by its radiant light, you close your heart against, lest the night of error be driven away by it. Book III *Against Julian*, *Unfinished Work*, chapter 61.

#### Remigius of Auxerre

Blessed Augustine, the most subtle investigator of obscure matters, moving without stumbling among difficult things. And earlier: Other teachers are compared with stars, but Augustine with the sun; for just as the stars receive their light from the sun, so all teachers receive their light from Augustine. On the Second Epistle to the Corinthians.

### LXV.

#### Censors

When Saint Augustine appears to defend predestination to glory prior to the foreseen merits of human beings, he does not speak as an oracle; his opinion is not approved by the Church; nor do all theologians follow it. Indeed, those who revere him most greatly abandon him on this point.

#### St. Augustine

Let him, then, say that the Church once did not possess the truth of this predestination and grace, which is now defended with more diligent care against the new heretics. *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 23.

#### Synod of Byzacena

If anyone refuses to receive with the belief of his heart or to proclaim with the confession of his mouth the truth of this predestination—by which the Apostle testifies that we were predestined in Christ before the foundation of the world—and if, before the final day of his present life, he does not cast off the obstinacy of his impiety by which he rebels against the living and true God, it is evident that he does not belong to the number of those whom God freely chose and predestined in Christ before the foundation of the world to the kingdom. Epilogue to the book *On the Incarnation and Grace*, among the works of Saint Fulgentius.

### LXVI.

#### Censors

The most learned of mortals pour some water upon the fire of Saint Augustine’s words.

#### St. Augustine

“Rain upon my heart, Lord, your moderations, so that I may bear such men patiently.” Book XII of the *Confessions*, chapter 25.

#### St. Jerome

Concerning Augustine he writes to the same man: “You who have stood firm against the winds that blow, through the ardor of faith.” Letter 25, in Augustine; and Paulus Orosius, whom the Roman synod under Gelasius calls a most learned man, addresses Saint Augustine as follows: “I was compelled to publish hastily and to heap together in one place all the trees of destruction, with their roots and branches, and to offer them to your fiery spirit.” Preface to the *Memorandum*, volume VI, before the book *Against the Priscillianists*.

### LXVII.

#### Censors

For an impious mind hates even understanding itself, and so forth. Sermon 13 *On the Words of the Apostle*, against the Pelagians.

Book *Against John Erigena*, chapter 8. He flourished in the year 852.
