## C.

### Censors

I reply that the statement that blessed Augustine and other Fathers sometimes spoke excessively can be understood in two ways. First, knowingly and against their own mind, by asserting something alien to the truth; this is lying, that is, speaking against one’s mind. Second, unknowingly: they spoke as they thought, but through the heat of disputation and vehemence of spirit sometimes inclined toward the other extreme, both in understanding and in words. This is not lying, but being mistaken and saying what is false without lying. The cited authors affirm that this happened to Augustine and others, and so do many more.

### St. Augustine

“It is not so as you say, whoever you are who have said these things; it is not so. You are greatly mistaken, or you are planning to deceive.” *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book II, chapter 3. Julian had objected that Augustine, in wishing to withdraw farther from Pelagian teaching, was approaching the Manichaeans, “like beasts surrounded by wings so that they may be driven into nets, and because reason is lacking to them, they are thrust into certain destruction by an empty fear.” Augustine replied: “Recognize, then, your own name in your doctrine, and cease to cast upon Catholics, by whom you are refuted, both a doctrine and a name that belong to others. For truth rebukes both groups, the Manichaeans and you.” Ibid.

### St. Prosper

“You say that many, believing each of these points and asserting them more than is just, have become entangled in various errors contradictory to one another. Is it pleasing to you, then, to condemn Catholics together with heretics, the victors together with the vanquished, and to brand with the mark of error those who drove error from the Church?” *Against the Collator*, chapter 10. Hence that great theologian Gregory of Rimini, more than three hundred years ago the supreme governor of the Augustinian commonwealth, said: “By what authority do they say that Augustine here spoke not properly and truly, but excessively? Another person could similarly say that in other rules established by Augustine he spoke excessively, and that those rules are not to be held as they sound. But anyone who says this will undoubtedly fall into many errors, if he considers the matter carefully.” *Sentences*, Book II, distinction 33, question 3.

## CI.

### Censors

Augustine often clears himself in the books of the *Retractions*: formerly, when writing against the Manichaeans—who said that all good things came from the good God and all evil things from the evil god, as though by fate, rather than being done freely by human beings—he praised free choice in such a way that he appears to have forgotten grace; later, when Pelagius, the enemy of grace, arose, he exalted grace so highly that he seems to have depressed free choice.

### St. Augustine

Although in those books which were written not at all against them—namely, the Pelagians, since they did not yet exist—but against the Manichaeans, concerning free choice, we did not altogether remain silent about this grace of God which they seek to remove through abominable impiety: for we did say, etc. (After producing several testimonies on this subject, he concludes:) “See how long before the Pelagian heresy existed we argued as though we were already arguing against them.” *Retractions*, Book I, chapter 9.

### St. Prosper

Let those who are able to invent such absurdities see how they can free themselves from the disgrace of this falsehood, if those whose ears they abuse would devote even a little diligence to learning what that most excellent minister of grace—Augustine—discussed. Indeed, those who speak in this way ought themselves to anticipate all delay in this inquiry by producing and explaining the books, or by pointing out any passage which the holy man published that could, even by a doubtful interpretation, be exposed to such an explanation. Letter to Rufinus.

## CII.

### Censors

Is this not precisely what Molina concedes, and what his adversaries customarily exaggerate as having been arrogantly stated by him: that Augustine, when disputing against the Pelagians, did not provide or explain this reason for defending freedom?

### St. Augustine

Therefore, I think I answered you in such a way in the two preceding books that no one could require anything further. *Against the Pelagian Julian*, Book V, chapter 1.

### Pope St. Gelasius

If only they would study the books of our ancestors against them—namely, the Pelagians—and learn their replies! They would see in every respect that there is absolutely nothing which these men brought forward that was not crushed by those predecessors with magnificent truth. Thus the faithful, too, would appear to be instructed for the refutation of all their wickedness, so that nothing further would be sought. Letter to Bishop Honorius against the Pelagians.

## CIII.

### Censors

No infallibility was promised to any of the Fathers, and nearly all of them erred in some matters: Cyprian, for example, concerning the rebaptizing of heretics; Jerome, in rejecting some portion of Daniel; and, to speak more particularly of Augustine—

### St. Augustine

Bring against me what I have said, so that I may clear it up. *Against Julian*, Book IV, chapter 1. “For your tongue, as though it were that of a censor, does not frighten me.” Book III, chapter 21.

### St. Prosper

The doctrine which Bishop Augustine of holy memory asserted and committed to writing for many years against the Pelagians, enemies of Christ’s grace and destroyers of free choice, some people have thought fit to criticize, either because they did not understand it or because they did not wish it to be understood. They offered this as a kind of shortcut to knowledge for those who were guided by their judgment, publishing in brief chapter-headings what they boasted they had found condemnable in the books of that man. By such an artifice they both secured hatred for the man whom they attacked and, by frightening the reader, turned attention away from the things they had defamed. *Preface to the Reply to the Gallican Chapters*.

## CIV.

### Censors

He—that is, Augustine—held that the world was created in an instant (*On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book IV, from chapter 21 to the end of the book, and Book V, chapter 1 and following). This does not agree with what Moses wrote in Genesis, chapter 1, as the more exact theologians show, especially Suárez, Molina, and Martinon; and Catholic doctors commonly reject it.

### St. Augustine

“O God of the poor, whose bosom contains no contradiction, pour into my heart a spirit of forbearance, so that I may patiently endure such people. They do not say this to me because they are divine and have seen in the heart of your servant what they say; they say it because they are proud. They do not know Moses’ meaning, but love their own—not because it is true, but because it is theirs.” *Confessions*, Book XII, chapter 25.

### St. Thomas

But Augustine’s earlier opinion concerning the creation of the world in an instant is more reasonable and more effective in defending Sacred Scripture from the mockery of unbelievers. Augustine teaches in his commentary on Genesis, Book I, that this point must be carefully observed, so that Scripture may be expounded in a way that does not expose it to the mockery of unbelievers; and this opinion pleases me more. *Sentences*, Book II, distinction 12, question 1, article 2, at the end of the body of the article.

## CV.

### Censors

He also held that angels and demons were corporeal (*On the Psalms*, 85 and 145, and Letter 115), as in other places where he asserts or assumes that they possess certain more subtle bodies.

### St. Augustine

“Therefore, if they have no bodies, the spirits of demons—or rather, the demons who are spirits—will cling to corporeal fires, though incorporeal, to be tormented by them.” *City of God*, Book XXI, chapter 10.

### The Same

Augustine speaks here not by asserting the point, but by using the opinion of the Platonists, who held that there were certain aerial animals which they called demons. *Summa Theologiae*, Part I, question 51, article 1, reply to objection 1.

## CVI.

### Censors

He also doubted whether the sun and moon, and the other stars which we see with our eyes, are animate.

### St. Augustine

Things are said of the sun and moon as though they perceived, and therefore tolerated their foolish worshipers, although the words may there be understood as transferred from an animate being to an inanimate one, in the figure of speech called in Greek *metaphor*. *Retractions*, Book II, chapter 7.

### St. Thomas

Likewise, the doctors of the faith held different opinions on this matter. Origen held that the heavenly bodies were animate. Jerome also appears to have thought the same when explaining the passage in Ecclesiasticus, chapter 1: “Surveying all things,” etc. Basil and Damascene, however, assert that the heavenly bodies are not animate. Augustine left the matter in doubt, inclining toward neither side, as is evident from *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book II, and from the *Enchiridion*. *Summa Theologiae*, Part I, question 70, article 3.

## CVII.

### Censors

He also doubted the origin of souls: whether they are newly created—which is most certain—or propagated from Adam, as can be seen in Letter 29 to Jerome, Letter 157, and the book *On the Origin of the Soul*.

### St. Augustine

I would not be troubled if you reproved and rebuked my ignorance concerning the origin of souls; indeed, I would even give you great thanks, if you struck at it not only with harsh insults but also dispelled it with truthful words. *On the Origin of the Soul*, Book IV, chapter 3.

### St. Fulgentius

Seeing the depth of this question concerning the origin of the soul to be unfathomable to him, blessed Augustine wished to offer no defined judgment on the matter. He considered it wholly improper to affirm without hesitation something that another person could overthrow by a contrary answer. His discussion of the question shines forth as no less extensive than profound: in the tenth book of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, in the books *On the Origin of the Soul* addressed to Vincent Victor, in the first of the two books he wrote to St. Jerome, and also in three letters he composed to Bishop Optatus on this question. It is especially praiseworthy because it is governed by a fitting moderation. Whatever he saw needed to be investigated and examined by acumen of intellect, orderly reasoning, or the weight of authority, he investigated and examined with singular care; yet he withheld assent from either definition, lest he undertake the labor of so great a disputation in vain, only to have it emptied by a rash definition of either opinion. *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, Book III, chapter 18.

“How much better, then, that we refrain from contending over this question, in which we recognize that we labor in vain! Especially since, when we see that our holy predecessors did not define what we observe to have been left undefined by them, we ought to inquire with that much greater caution and restraint, the more clearly we see that those distinguished men did not reach its conclusion.” Chapter 20.

## CVIII.

### Censors

He also wrongly explains what the Apostle says in Romans 14:23: “Everything that is not from faith is sin,” as though the Apostle wished to say that all the works of unbelievers are sins and that no good work can be performed without true faith. Yet the passage concerns what is not done according to the judgment of conscience, which in good faith judges the act being performed to be lawful, as is clear from the text itself; and the common interpretation of the doctors contradicts Augustine. In several places, as we have noted elsewhere, he also seems to restrict his assertion to a good work useful for attaining eternal life, etc. Nevertheless, both interpretations are plainly foreign to the Apostle’s true meaning in the cited passage.

### St. Augustine

You accepted and explained the testimony which I quoted from the Apostle—“Everything that is not from faith is sin”—as you wished, and explained it not according to what it means but according to what you mean. The Apostle was speaking about foods; but after saying, “Whoever makes a distinction, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith,” he wished to establish by a general statement the kind of sin about which he was speaking, immediately adding: “For everything that is not from faith is sin.” *Against Julian*, Book IV, chapter 3. “For everything that is not from faith is sin, whether you wish it or not.” Later, ibid.

### Pope Boniface II

Those who, as you indicate, wish to attribute everything else to grace while placing faith first, we bind by their own profession, so that they are compelled all the more to ascribe faith itself to the gift of grace, apart from which no one can perform anything good according to God, as the blessed Apostle says: “Everything that is not from faith is sin.” Since this is so, either they will attribute no good to grace if they attempt to remove faith from it, or, if they say that something is good because of grace, then faith itself must necessarily be attributed to grace. Letter to St. Caesarius of Arles.

## CIX.

### Censors

All who have devoted themselves to reading him know that he was not always especially successful in investigating the literal meaning. From this, however, one must chiefly argue—and in this respect Jerome and Chrysostom must be preferred to him by far.

### St. Augustine

To those who do not say that all those things which are true are false, but honor and establish with us at the summit of authority to be followed that Sacred Scripture of yours which was issued through holy Moses, and yet contradict us in some matters, I speak thus: “Be you, O God, our arbiter between my confessions and their contradictions.” *Confessions*, Book XII, chapter 16.

### The Holy Fathers

Jerome says in Letter 30 to Augustine: “Certainly whatever could be said, and whatever could be drawn from the fountains of the Holy Scriptures by a lofty intellect, has been set forth and discussed by you.”

St. Prudentius, in his letter to Hincmar and Pardulus: “First of all, I admonish your sincerity concerning the doctrine of the most blessed Father Augustine, unquestionably the most learned of all in every respect, and in everything most harmonious with the authority of the Holy Scriptures: for no doctor has searched their hidden meanings more scrupulously, sought them out more diligently, found them more truly, stated them more truthfully, unraveled them more clearly, preserved them more faithfully, defended them more powerfully, or disseminated them more abundantly,” etc.

Remigius of Auxerre, on 2 Corinthians: “As the sun surpasses all the planets in brightness, so Augustine surpassed everyone in expounding the Sacred Scriptures.”

Hugh of Saint-Victor, sermon 25: “Hence, in this celebration of his feast, we sing of him that, full of the spirit of the prophets and apostles, he made accessible to us the mysteries they foretold; after them, he was the first in whom the grace of dispensing the word of God shone forth a second time,” etc.

## CX.

### Censors

He also speaks more harshly in several places concerning the reality of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, as we indicated above. For this reason the Calvinists falsely boast that he is altogether theirs; but the most eminent Cardinal Perronius, equal in learning and dignity, at the very beginning of his special book entitled *Refutation of Objections Drawn from St. Augustine against the Sacrament of the Holy Eucharist*, chapter 1, calls St. Augustine “the great pretended patron of the Sacramentarians.”

### St. Augustine

The law of Christ—that is, charity—plainly admonishes me and commands me with most gentle authority that, when people think I held something false in my books which I did not hold, and that same falsehood displeases one person but pleases another, I would rather be rebuked by the rebuker of falsehood than praised by its praiser. For although I am not rightly criticized by him, since I did not hold this view, the error itself is nevertheless rightly condemned by him. But the person who thinks I held what truth condemns does not rightly praise me, nor does he rightly praise the opinion which truth condemns. *On the Trinity*, Book I, chapter 3.

### Bishop Guitmundus

What will our shadow-dwellers reply here? Where, amid such great light, will our light-fleeing men find a shadow? Behold, Augustine’s most evident testimonies are recited: there is nothing scrupulous, nothing ambiguous in them. Let them explain these passages, or let them cease to bring Augustine against us. *On the Truth of the Eucharist*, Book III, against Berengarius, volume XI of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

## CXI.

### Censors

Likewise, in Book I of *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, chapter 20; in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 13; and in Book II of the *Unfinished Work against Julian*, chapter 29, he seems to teach that the sacrament of the Eucharist is no less necessary for the salvation of infants than baptism, and that the words in John 6:54 apply to them no less: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,” than do the words in John 3:6: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

### St. Augustine

See what you are to answer holy Innocent, who understands nothing else about this matter than those men do whose assembly I have introduced you into—if that accomplishes anything. He himself sits among them also, although later in time, prior in rank, etc. He finally determined that infants absolutely cannot have life unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man. Answer him—or rather, answer the Lord himself, whose testimony that bishop employed. *Against Julian*, Book I, chapter 4.

### Pope St. Innocent

As for what Your Fraternity says Pelagius and Celestius preach—that infants can be granted the rewards of eternal life even without the grace of baptism—it is utterly foolish. “Unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, they will not have life in themselves.” Those who defend their having this life without regeneration seem to me to wish to nullify baptism itself, since they preach that infants possess what, as is believed concerning them, can be conferred only through baptism. Letter to the Fathers of the Council of Milevis, cited by Augustine, Letter 93.

### Pope St. Gelasius

To cut off all the wickedness of the Pelagians through God’s providence, it was said not only, “Whoever has not been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” but likewise, “Whoever has not eaten the flesh of the Son of Man and drunk his blood will not have life in himself.” No one doubts that this was said of eternal life, since many who do not eat this sacrament nevertheless appear to possess present life. Letter to the bishops of Picenum.

## CXII.

### Censors

Thus, disputing against the Pelagians, he proves that infants cannot attain eternal life without receiving the Eucharist, and he distinguishes this reception from baptism, as though he wished infants necessarily to be actual and distinct participants in both sacraments—baptism and the Eucharist—in order to obtain eternal life. For this is how he speaks in that chapter 20 of Book I, *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*: “Let doubt, therefore, now be removed,” etc. These words are so clear that they scarcely permit the favorable interpretation by which most theologians try to excuse Augustine from error; for the error was identified and condemned under anathema by the Council of Trent.

### St. Augustine

Let us bring forward nothing of our own here; let us listen once more to the Apostle himself. Speaking, therefore, about this sacrament, he says: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body.” Understand and rejoice: unity, devotion, truth, charity—“we who are many are one bread, one body.” Recall, for bread is not made from one grain but from many. Therefore, when you were exorcized, you were, as it were, ground; when you were baptized, you were, as it were, sprinkled together; when you received the sanctification of the Spirit, you were, as it were, baked. Be what you see, and receive what you are, etc. Sermon to infants before the altar.

### St. Fulgentius
Blessed Augustine also delivered a very lucid sermon on this matter, well suited to the edification and instruction of the faithful. (After reciting the entire sermon, in which the words quoted immediately above occur:) “I judge, holy brother,” he says, “that our discussion has been established by the sermon of the outstanding teacher Augustine, and that there should be no uncertainty whatever that each of the faithful becomes a participant in the Lord’s body and blood when, in baptism, he is made a member of Christ’s body [Col. 0872A]; nor is he excluded from sharing in that bread and cup even if, before eating that bread and drinking from the cup, he departs from this world established in the unity of Christ’s body.” *Response to a Question concerning the Baptism of the Ethiopian.*

## COUNCIL OF TRENT

Nor is antiquity therefore to be condemned if it once maintained that practice in certain places—namely, giving the Eucharist to infants. For just as those most holy Fathers had a probable reason for their action according to the circumstances of that time, so it must certainly be believed without controversy that they did not do this from any necessity for salvation. Session 21, chapter 4.

## CXIII

### CENSORS

Furthermore, in Book II *Against Julian*, chapter 10, he teaches that lingering thoughts, or voluntary pleasures, concerning sexual matters are merely venial sin, provided that consent to the act, or an evil desire, or the danger of it, is absent. This doctrine has long since been rejected by all Catholics, and no one could advance it without scandal.

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“There is therefore one kind of writing that is thoroughly approved and, as it were, most pure: when good things have been written and are received in a good sense by the readers.” *On the Usefulness of Believing*, to Honoratus, chapter 5.

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“Thus it may be said that, in one man, if his thought willingly feeds itself solely on illicit pleasures from which it ought immediately to turn away, and if he does not resolve to commit evil deeds but merely retains them pleasantly in his memory, it is as though a woman could be condemned without a man: far be it from us to believe this! For this is one person, one man, and he will be condemned in his entirety unless, through the grace of the Mediator, those things are forgiven which, without the will to perform them but nevertheless with the will to delight the mind in them, are recognized as sins of thought alone.” *On the Trinity*, Book XII, chapter 12.

## CXIV

### CENSORS

Since the same hazard belongs to judgments and affections, and Augustine struggles so vigorously against the Pelagians that he establishes that no one, however holy, does not need to say, “Forgive us our debts,” because of daily lapses of the will, I do not know what entered the minds of the Baians, so that they wish to appear Augustinian while endeavoring with such great effort to persuade us that there are some—namely, Augustine—who never lapse in judgment.

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“For I ought not to deny that, just as in my own conduct, so also in my many little works there are many things that may rightly and without rashness be censured. If you were criticizing what belonged to another, I might perhaps show you there what sort of person I would wish you to be in matters where you were not wrong to criticize; and, as an older man to a younger and a superior to a subordinate, I might offer you an example of correction—one that would be all the more salutary because it was all the more humble. But you have criticized in me things which truth compels me not to correct through humility, but partly to confess and partly to defend.” *On the Origin of the Soul*, Book IV, chapter 1.

### B. JORDAN OF SAXONY

“Nevertheless, afterward he [Augustine] was purified both from errors of understanding and from corruption of affection through a hierarchical act.” Sermon 138.

Saint Thomas of Villanova says: “This profound humility of Augustine before God and men, together with his wisdom [Col. 0873A] and understanding, exalted him sublimely, because ‘God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble’ (James 4:6). Hence the prophet’s oracle may be understood of him: ‘The abyss uttered its voice, the height of its imagination’ (Habakkuk 3:70). The abyss, I say, of Augustine’s humility gave his voice of doctrine to the peoples, on account of the height of his imagination—that is, of his intellect—which God bestowed on him because of his humility.” Second Sermon on St. Augustine.

### CENSORS

“From these two columns—I mean Augustine and Ambrose—believe me, I am difficult to tear away. With these two, I admit that I either err or think rightly.” Letter 77 to Hugh of St. Victor.

“As regards the sufficiency of his statements, nothing is lacking in Augustine’s books that pertains to knowledge of the divine law. ### CENSORS

## CXVIII

[Col. 0874A]

### CENSORS

Augustine held that the world was created in an instant, which does not agree with what was written by Moses, and so forth.

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“Let no one now trouble me by saying, ‘Moses did not understand this as you say, but understood it as I say.’ For if he said to me, ‘How do you know that Moses understood what you say concerning these words of his?’ I ought to bear it calmly, and perhaps reply as I replied above, or somewhat more fully if I were more stubborn.

“But as for their insistence that Moses did not understand what I say but what they say, I do not want it, I do not like it. For even if it is so, such rashness is not knowledge but audacity; it was born not of vision but of conceit.” *Confessions*, Book XII, chapter 24; chapter 25.

“Restore my words, and your calumny will vanish.” *Against Julian*, Book IV, chapter 8.

## CXXIII

[Col. 0875B]

### CENSORS

We therefore ask the Baians how highly Augustine’s teaching should be regarded when he says that the authority of a noncanonical writer is fallible, and that this is the difference between such a writer and a canonical one: the former may at times be suspected without sin or injury to anyone. If they deny that this teaching is to be approved, they are mistaken and, by abandoning Augustine, transgress the limits they themselves first established. If they acknowledge that it is worthy of approval, then, since they cannot deny that Augustine belongs among the noncanonical writers, they must admit that his authority and opinion may at times appear doubtful without sin or injury to anyone. It would be absurd to say that what he says concerning the fallibility of a noncanonical writer is to be understood with Augustine himself excepted.

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“Certainly, in all my writings I desire not only a devout reader but also a free critic—especially in those matters where I wish the magnitude of the question itself had as many discoverers as it has contradictors. Nevertheless, just as I do not want my reader to be devoted to me, so I do not want my critic to be devoted to himself. Let the former love me no more than the Catholic faith, and let the latter love himself no more than the Catholic truth.

“To the former I say: Do not serve my writings as though they were canonical Scriptures; but, when you find in them what you did not believe, believe it without hesitation. In matters that you did not hold as certain, however, do not hold them firmly unless you have understood them to be certain. To the latter I say: Do not correct my writings according to your own opinion or contentiousness, but according to divine reading or unshaken reason.” *On the Trinity*, Book III, preface.

### ST. THOMAS OF VILLANOVA

“The final and most outstanding testimony of his intellect is this: Augustine so visibly contemplated the truth amid so great a fog, and so thoroughly elucidated it amid so great a forest of errors, that although he himself was the first to emerge in this matter, even today, after so long a time, the Church and the school of the faith hold and follow what Augustine decided.” First Sermon on St. Augustine, at the end.

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“I shall shatter your glassy sophistries and fragile arguments, by which you think yourself very clever and polished.” At the end of Book I *Against Julian*. “Laden, as it were, with the sharp darts of dialecticians, you enter the contest and brandish leaden daggers.” *Against Julian*, Book III, chapter 7.

### VENERABLE BEDE AND ST. PRUDENTIUS

“Julianus was a man as highly skilled in rhetoric as he was a fierce opponent of God’s grace after Pelagius, as his writings plainly show, in which he raged against Augustine, the most strenuous defender of that same grace.” Beginning of the preface to the *Song of Songs*.

Saint Prudentius says: “Since the Fathers, and especially the most blessed Augustine, have answered the Pelagians most suitably and most abundantly,” and so forth. Letter to Gelinonus, archbishop of Sens, before the book *On Predestination*.

## CXXV

### CENSORS

They wish to maintain that Julian’s side cannot be overcome by Augustine’s arguments [Col. 0876B].

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“I grasp and shatter, insofar as the Lord assists me, the essential points of your discourse, so that whoever reads both what is yours and what is ours may see the whole body lying defeated.” *Against Julian*, Book IV, chapter 9.

### ST. PROSPER

“Whatever you most powerfully defeated in the books against Julian concerning this question is proclaimed with the greatest insistence by these holy men.” Letter to St. Augustine.

## CXXVI

### CENSORS

If the Church’s triumph rested on Augustine’s later writings, the Church would have triumphed over the Pelagians unjustly [Col. 0876C].

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“I consider that, by God’s mercy, I have written with progress, though I did not begin from perfection.” *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 21.

### THE SAME

“Against this most resounding trumpet of praise”—for he is quoting Pope Celestine’s commendation of Saint Augustine—“against the dignity of this most sacred testimony, would anyone dare to utter the murmur of a malicious interpretation and cast a cloud of twisted ambiguity over a clear and most sincere judgment? That is, because the title of the books for which the matter was undertaken was not stated in the pope’s letter, should it therefore appear that those books were not approved, and that this praise of Saint Augustine was bestowed on account of the merits of his earlier writings?

“Let it plainly remain, let it remain as a condition, that the novelty of these books”—namely, those he had published later on the subject of grace [Col. 0876D]—“is to be rejected if the antiquity of the same man disagrees in the same matter, and that whatever is found to differ from what he composed against the Pelagians is to be judged useless or inappropriate.” *Against the Collator*, chapter 43.

## CXXVII

### CENSORS

Augustine was a teacher in the same way as any other modern teacher.

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“Whatever I understood concerning the art of speaking and disputing, whatever concerning the dimensions of figures, music, and numbers, without great difficulty and without anyone teaching me,” and so forth. “For I did not realize that even by diligent and gifted students those arts were understood only with the greatest difficulty, unless I attempted to explain those same things to them; and the one who followed me as I explained them without delay was outstanding in them.” *Confessions*, Book IV, chapter 16.

## CXXVIII

### CENSORS

Augustine’s gifts, whether natural or infused, were not of a higher order than those of other teachers, including the scholastics [Col. 0877A].

### ST. THOMAS OF VILLANOVA

“Augustine most justly claims this for himself. In this light of wisdom, Augustine surpasses all others after the apostles as the sun surpasses all the stars, and so forth. For in sharpness of understanding, clarity of intellect, vigor of disputation, abundance of invention, and subtlety of exposition, Augustine was a kind of marvel in nature. By God’s radiance he seemed to have transcended the limits of human understanding—a man, as someone said, almost divine in intellect and wisdom.” First Sermon on St. Augustine.

“For who excelled so greatly in intellect? Who possessed such eloquence? Who shone with such wisdom concerning human and divine things? Who enlightened the Church of God with so many and such great volumes? Who taught the ecclesiastical orders in such a manner? Someone says: ‘He lies who boasts that he has read all Augustine’s volumes; he was more capable of writing than we are of reading.’” Third Sermon on the same subject.

## CXXIX

### CENSORS

The Church must be vindicated from Augustine’s guardianship and tutelage.

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“Therefore I shall address you, true Bride of the true Christ, the Catholic Church; and I, whatever kind of son and servant of yours I may be, placed within you, shall distribute food to my fellow servants according to my ability.” *Against Faustus*, Book XV, chapter 13 [Col. 0877C].

### FACUNDUS OF HERMIANE

“Let these men dare, if they can, to call Augustine a heretic; let them dare, with anxious presumption, to condemn him. Then they will truly learn what are the piety and steadfastness of the Church of the Latins, which God established and strengthened through his teaching, when they have immediately been anathematized by everyone and cut off like rotten and diseased members.” *Against Mocianus*.

## CXXX

### CENSORS

Whether Augustine holds a view contrary to what we think is not a matter of great concern.

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“I care very little,” I said, “for the judgments of proud and ignorant men, who rush upon books to be read just as they rush upon people to be greeted.” *On Order*, Book I, chapter 11 [Col. 0877D].

### B. ALBERT THE GREAT AND ST. PAULINUS

“It must be said that he does, because Augustine states this openly, and it is impious to contradict him in matters touching faith and morals.” *Summa theologiae*, Part II, treatise 14, question 184, reply to question 3.

Saint Paulinus, in Letter 36 to Romanius, among the Augustinian letters, says: “If you listen to him, if you follow him”—to entice you again with Solomon’s words—“‘My son, you will receive a crown of graces for your crown.’” Later: “For you will truly be a pontiff and truly a consul, Licentius, if you cling inseparably to Augustine’s footsteps and to prophetic and apostolic disciplines, as blessed Elisha clung to Elijah and the young Timothy to the illustrious Apostle, accompanying them along the divine paths.” And so forth.

## CXXXI

[Col. 0878A]

### CENSORS

It is already evident from the published books what disturbances were stirred up by a single phrase, repeated with such great flattery: “The other Fathers are useful, but Augustine alone is necessary and sufficient for all theological subjects.” As though the Church of God had been reduced to such desolation that it had to derive the strength of its decisions not from the agreement of many Fathers but from the approval of one man.

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“So much was attributed to me that, whenever it was necessary to speak to the people in my presence, I was very rarely permitted to remain silent and listen to others.” *Retractions*, Prologue.

“Far be from me that arrogance which you charge me with, as though I had promised to conduct this case against you, one man for all.” At the end of *Against Julian*, Book II.

## CXXXII

[Col. 0878B]

### CENSORS

In the preceding section we saw the authors of a summary of his life—namely, Jansenius—report this celebrated statement of his as an apophthegm worthy of so great a man: “The other Fathers are useful, but Augustine is necessary; indeed, he alone is sufficient for every theological subject.” This proposition contains not only serious exaggeration but also a pernicious error.

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“I am one among many who, as we are able, refute your profane novelties, according to the measure of faith God has apportioned to each of us.” *Against Julian*, Book VI, chapter 8.

“Now then, lest the bellows of your stomach burst from the undigested crudity of your curses, vomit out against him, if you dare, your calumnious vanities and lying insanities,” and so forth. Thus speaks the distinguished teacher of the Churches. *Against the same man*, Book II, chapter 8.

### POPE MARTIN V

“Everyone who had any understanding of Christ, of faith, or of religion had Augustine on his lips, so that scarcely anything from the sacred writings could be understood except under his guidance, or explained except through his interpretation. Through his authority it has come about that we neither envy the philosophers their wisdom nor desire the eloquence of orators, nor require the intellects of scholars; finally, neither Aristotle’s acumen, nor Plato’s eloquence, nor Varro’s prudence, nor Socrates’ gravity, nor Pythagoras’ authority, nor Empedocles’ ingenuity, nor the knowledge or virtue of anyone of that kind need serve us as example or instruction.

“He conveys to us the oracles of the prophets and the voices of the apostles; he expresses the entire meaning of all the Scriptures; finally, he displays the intellects and labors of all the Fathers and wise men. If you seek truth, doctrine, and piety, who is more learned, more righteous, or, so to speak, holier than Augustine?” Sermon on the Translation of the Body of Saint Monica.

## CXXXIII

### CENSORS

There is no reason why we should be bound by the words of Saint Paul and Saint Augustine, who at times appear to attribute everything to God’s mere will, even without any consideration of our good works. These two great men must be regarded as two great seas: driven by the force of their intellect, they overflow toward one shore in such a way that they seem for a time to wish to leave the other shore dry. Yet just as the Ocean, after pouring itself more abundantly over one region, returns to the boundaries established for it by God, so such men, after attacking the rebellious opponents of the truth, return to a calm evenness suited to the edification of the faithful.

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“If, then, you wish not to prejudice Catholic disputants when we bring against you certain things which, as you think, they have poured forth too incautiously, what is this but saying that even in the sacred Scriptures those things which heretics appropriate for themselves have been poured forth too incautiously? What could be said more wickedly?” *Unfinished Work against Julian*, Book IV, chapter 112.

## CXXXIV

### CENSORS

The fervor of Saint Paul’s intellect was so intense that he was easily carried away into such expressions—namely, excessive ones. Thus, when he wishes to convey to Christians a sublime conception of baptismal grace and powerfully exhort them to preserve it, he seems to assert that those who have fallen into some crime cannot be restored to it again through repentance. When he exalts faith in the Letter to the Romans, he seems to furnish Calvin with weapons for establishing his heresy, and seems to assert that anyone can be saved by faith alone. But when he proclaims charity in the Letter to the Corinthians, he seems to overturn everything he had said concerning faith and to place all our hope in charity.

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“For if so-called dutiful lies are admitted into the sacred Scriptures, what authority will remain in them? What judgment will finally be pronounced concerning those Scriptures by whose weight the shamelessness of contentious falsehood may be crushed? As soon as you have produced it, if the person who resists thinks otherwise, he will say that what has been produced is a lie told by the writer for some honorable purpose.” Letter 9 to Jerome.

## CXXXV

### CENSORS

The lofty and fiery spirit of Paul is carried so vehemently in the direction toward which it inclines that it seems to move toward an extreme and deny the opposite extreme [Col. 0879C].

### ST. AUGUSTINE

“What authority of writings could be opened, what sacred book unfolded, what evidence of any Scripture brought forth to refute errors, if this statement is admitted and considered to have any weight?” *Against Faustus*, Book XI, chapter 2.

### ST. REMIGIUS

“Deeply shaken and distressed in mind, we saw that the most certain truth of Holy Scripture, and the venerable authority of the most blessed Fathers—especially that of Saint Augustine, received throughout the entire Catholic Church—were being attacked by a new effort and an exceedingly rash undertaking, and, insofar as it lay within their power, were being recklessly and insolently weakened.

“Therefore, moved and admonished by that charity through which all of us must be one in the one body of Christ, so that, as the Apostle says, ‘the members may be concerned for one another,’ and whether one member is honored all the members may rejoice together, or whether one member suffers all the members may suffer together (1 Corinthians 12:26), by this affection of charity, I say, it seemed good and fitting to us to write these things, whatever their worth, both as an admonition to ourselves and for the edification and confirmation of those who may wish to read them, in a concise and clear manner, insofar as the Lord deigns to inspire us.

“We affirm everything we have thought ought to be said in this work not on the basis of our own judgment or presumption, but by the venerable authority of the holy Fathers mentioned above. Far be it from us, or from those whom charity has compelled us to address these words, ever to depart from their footsteps and unity, lest, separated from them, we also be separated from the Lord himself, who says to them in particular: ‘Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me’ (Luke 10:16). He wished them to possess such great grace and glory in his Church that they might confidently say with the Apostle: ‘Therefore, whoever rejects these things rejects not man but God, who also gave his Holy Spirit in you’ (1 Thessalonians 4:8), and so forth.” *On Holding to the Truth of Scripture*, chapter 4.

### OUR HOLY FATHER AUGUSTINE

“Dearly beloved, when we hear false accusations from those whom we have offended by proclaiming the words of truth and refuting the empty talk of error, we have, as you know, abundant consolation. For if, in those matters with which they accuse me, the testimony of my conscience does not stand against me in the sight of God, toward whom no mortal eye is directed, I ought not merely not to grieve but also to rejoice and exult, because my reward is great in heaven. We must not consider how bitter what I hear is, but how false it is, and how truthful is the one for whose name I hear these things.” *Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book III.

“These things are certainly false, and therefore they do us no harm when you say them falsely and do not look to yourselves. But they harm you, because when you say these things falsely, they do not fall upon us; rather, because you consider them true, they fall back upon you.” *Against the same man*, Book II, chapter 33.

“For human reputation, there is an abundant supply of witnesses who know me; but before God there is only conscience. Although I keep it unafraid against your accusations, I do not dare to justify myself under the eyes of the Almighty. Rather, I await from him the overflowing bounty of mercy rather than the supreme scrutiny of judgment.” *Against Cresconius*, Book III, chapter 80.

“You say that, if I were oppressed by the authority of judges such as you yourself imagine, I would have nothing to do and nowhere to flee, since I could not find a way to meet your arguments. I would certainly have something to do; I would certainly have somewhere to flee. For I would appeal from Pelagian darkness to these clear Catholic lights, as I am doing even now. You, then, answer what you will do; say where you will flee.” *Against Julian*, Book II, final chapter.

“I did not fabricate in idle thought men who never existed, or no longer exist, or whose opinions concerning the matter we are debating are uncertain. Rather, I expressly named holy and illustrious bishops of God in the holy Church, trained not in Platonic, Aristotelian, Stoic, and other philosophies of that kind, whether Greek or Latin—although some of them were trained in these as well—but all trained in the sacred writings. I set out their opinions, insofar as seemed sufficient, without any ambiguity in the text.” *Ibid.*, chapter 10.

“If an episcopal synod were gathered from the whole world, it would be astonishing if so many such men could easily sit there, since these men did not exist at one time. But God himself distributes his faithful and exceptionally outstanding few stewards throughout different ages and across distances of time and place, as he wills and judges expedient. You see these men, gathered from different times and regions, from East and West—not into one place to which men would have to sail, but into a book that can sail to men.” *Against Julian*, Book II, chapter 10.

“They showed neither friendship toward us or toward you, nor hostility. What they found in the Church they retained; what they learned they taught; what they received from the Fathers they handed on to their children.

“WE HAD NOT YET BROUGHT ANYTHING WITH YOU BEFORE THESE JUDGES, AND OUR CASE WAS HEARD BEFORE THEM. WE HAD NOT YET CONTENDED WITH YOU, AND WHEN THEY PRONOUNCED JUDGMENT, WE WON.” *Ibid.*

“Christian peoples ought to prefer these men to your profane novelties and choose to adhere to them rather than to you.” *Ibid.*, chapter 9.

“Has not your entire cause been driven back, overthrown, crushed, and, as dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth, cast from the hearts of those whom you had begun to deceive, if they are willing to consider these things after laying aside their zeal for contention?” *Ibid.*, chapter 3.

“But we are more ready to endure every curse and insult with these men and with the Church of Christ, established upon the antiquity of this faith, than to be praised by the preaching of any Pelagian, however eloquent.” *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book II, chapter 29.

### ST. PROSPER OF AQUITAINE

“As I think has been sufficiently demonstrated, the REPROVERS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE both make empty objections, attack what is right, and defend what is wrong; and, waging internal war with the weapons of the defeated, rebel against divine and human constitutions.

“Nevertheless, so long as they have not yet been separated from fraternal fellowship, their intention should be tolerated rather than their correction despaired of, until the Lord, through the leaders of the Church and the legitimate ministers of his judgments, settles those matters which have been disturbed BY THE PRIDE OF A FEW AND THE IGNORANCE OF SOME.

“With God’s help, let it be our concern, through quiet and moderate patience, to return love for hatred, to avoid conflicts with foolish men, not to abandon the truth, and not to contend with falsehood.” In the peroration against the Collator.

[Col. 0882B]

### ST. ALIPIUS OF TAGASTE

“Therefore now, MY COMPANIONS, turn your expectation, by which you challenge me to answer, with more certain hope toward learning together with me. We have a guide—Augustine—who, with God now showing the way, may lead us into the very secrets of truth.” In Augustine, at the end of Book III *Against the Academics*.

According to the order in which their censures are reviewed in the *Augustinian Vindications*, chapter 9, printed at Padua in 1673 and at Brussels in 1675.

# THREE TREATISES

[Note: [Col. 0883] The title, written in French and without the author’s name, reads as follows: *Refutation of M. Bayle’s Criticisms of Saint Augustine, Containing Three Treatises: The first, A True Key to the Works of Saint Augustine against the Pelagians; the second, Examination of the Criticisms Scattered throughout M. Bayle’s Dictionary on Various Passages in the Writings of the Same Holy Doctor; the third, Dissertation Concerning the Nature of the Law of Moses*. Paris, 1732. We have included these three little works under one general title.]

WHICH THE REVEREND FATHER MERLIN PREPARED IN FRENCH IN DEFENSE OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

[Note: [Col. 0883] MERLIN (Carolus), of the Society of Jesus in the diocese of Amiens, died in Paris at the Collège Louis-le-Grand in 1747. He had taught the humanities and theology with great distinction. He earned the highest praise through: 1) a little work entitled *Historical and Dogmatic Treatise on the Words or Forms of the Seven Sacraments of the Church*; 2) several dissertations that, for the most part, enriched the *Tivoli Journal*. EDITOR.]

[Col. 0883]

# DEDICATORY LETTER

Sir,

You ask me how my refutation of M. Bayle’s *Historical and Critical Dictionary* is progressing, and you are curious to see a specimen of it. I hope you will find this one acceptable. It contains an interesting subject: I have made every effort to fill it with researches and discoveries likely to attract the attention of the learned world of today, which wants novelty in the new works presented to it. The proofs of my most unusual assertions have, if I am not mistaken, been carried as far as evidence and demonstration. But I lose sight of M. Bayle for too long, and you may judge that this piece ought to be published separately and included only in greatly abridged form in the universal refutation of the *Dictionary*—all the more since I have resolved to change the plan on which I have worked until now, in consequence of the advice you have been kind enough to give me.

You approve my having separated the sacred from the profane, and you believe it appropriate first to place before the public an examination of the criticisms scattered through M. Bayle’s *Dictionary* on matters concerning religion; but my intention of publishing the different parts of this first section one after another is not to your taste, and quarto volumes do not seem to you suitable for attacking folios. I accept your judgment. Indeed, someone who has purchased M. Bayle’s *Dictionary* may perhaps consider its refutation more substantial when it appears alongside the four volumes; he would think less of it if he could not place it symmetrically after them in his library. Today people love order and arrangement. For this reason, too, I have not been content with an external resemblance and proportion; I have thought it necessary to give my refutation the form of a dictionary, in which, following the alphabetical order of persons, I compose a text with remarks in M. Bayle’s manner. It will cost me little to divide what I had brought together. Besides, dictionaries are in fashion; grammar now has the honor of subjecting history, jurisprudence, medicine, philosophy, theology—in a word, the noblest sciences—to its method, reducing them to a, b, c. We must therefore be patient for a few years and wait until everything is ready for printing. I say everything, because the refutation of what does not concern the faith will appear at the same time from another hand. A highly skilled man, who undertook and began the same project before me, has been kind enough to leave the sacred portion to me and to devote himself exclusively to the profane.

But, so that you will not be surprised at the way I treat here what concerns Saint Augustine, I must explain what my original plan was. I intended first to publish a quarto volume with this title: *Examination of the Criticisms Scattered through M. Bayle’s Dictionary on the Saints of the Old and New Testament*. The following volume would have been entitled: *Examination of the Criticisms Scattered through M. Bayle’s Dictionary on the Holy Fathers and on the Councils*. In this second volume, which is already almost finished, the subjects are treated in the form of dialogues, letters, or speeches, which I always address to someone, in order to make the style livelier and more animated. What I am sending you is a piece of that second volume.

[Col. 0885]

# TREATISE ONE. A TRUE KEY TO THE WORKS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE AGAINST THE PELAGIANS

[Col. 0885A] After replying to all the reproaches M. Bayle directs against Tertullian, Origen, Arnobius, Lactantius, Saint Basil, and Saint Jerome, I introduce a person who had appealed to me to defend Saint Chrysostom, of whom people had spoken contemptuously in a company on the authority of M. Bayle’s criticisms. This man, pleased to see in the explanations he received from me the holy doctor’s complete vindication, then resumed the conversation and said to me:

I must confess it: those who pressed me on the subject of Saint Chrysostom do not greatly love this Father, whatever appearance they may put on; but they would be delighted if Saint Augustine were defended with equal solidity on every point on which M. Bayle mistreats him. “Not on every point,” I replied, “for you make me understand that they are entirely prejudiced in favor of Jansenism. They have read, I am sure, more than once and with extreme satisfaction these words of M. Bayle in the article on Saint Augustine (Remark E): ‘It is certain that the obligation resting on the Roman Church to respect Saint Augustine’s system throws it into an embarrassment that has much about it of the ridiculous’; and in the notes: ‘It is so evident to every person who examines matters without prejudice and with the necessary enlightenment that the doctrine of Saint Augustine and that of Jansenius, Bishop of Ypres, are one and the same doctrine, that one cannot see without indignation that the court of Rome has boasted of having condemned Jansenius while preserving for Saint Augustine all his authority and glory.’ And in the article on Jansenius (Remark H): ‘There are no sophisms of which the Molinists have not made use to show that Saint Augustine did not teach Jansenism.’

“Would your Jansenists be in the mood to listen patiently to sophisms of this sort? It is only on that condition that I shall undertake to satisfy them concerning the rest. I have at least as much zeal as they do for everything that concerns the glory of Saint Augustine; but in my view the greatest insult one can offer the holy doctor is to claim that the Church, committed to respecting his name, has anathematized his doctrine under the name of Jansenius. On that supposition, it is absolutely impossible to answer [Col. 0887A] the argument M. Bayle uses to prove that the Council of Trent, in condemning Calvin’s doctrine of free will, necessarily condemned Saint Augustine’s as well (Remark E). It is the same argument Catholics use to demonstrate that the Council of Trent, in condemning Calvin’s doctrine, necessarily condemned Jansenius’s. Here it is:

“‘There is no Calvinist who has denied, or could have denied, the concurrence of the human will and the freedom of our soul in the sense Saint Augustine gave to the words concurrence, cooperation, and freedom. There is no Calvinist who does not acknowledge free will and its use in conversion, if the term is understood according to Saint Augustine’s ideas. Those whom the Council of Trent condemned reject free will only insofar as it signifies freedom of indifference.’

“Let Jansenius’s name be substituted for Saint Augustine’s, and M. Bayle’s argument will be true and invincible.”

Indeed, as M. de Fénelon has very well demonstrated, [Col. 0887B] Calvin’s grace is no more intrinsically effective and necessitating than Jansenius’s. Calvin (*Institutes*, book II, chapter 3, no. 10) does not claim that the necessity of acting which results from and follows upon the motion of grace is an absolute and total necessity, but only a relative and partial one. Hence he approves and judges that he can adapt to his meaning the distinctions and terms commonly used in the schools: *Unde videmus non temere in scholis inventas fuisse distinctiones de necessitate secundum quid et absoluta: item consequentis et consequentiae* (*Institutes*, book II, chapter 16, no. 9)—“Thus we see that the distinctions between relative and absolute necessity, and likewise between the necessity of the consequent and of the consequence, were not devised in the schools without reason.”

He takes care to warn that the necessity he admits is not a necessity of constraint or violence, but a simple necessity compatible with the will’s inclination and tendency. “If freedom is opposed to coercion, I both admit and steadfastly assert that free will exists, and I regard as a heretic whoever thinks otherwise” (*On Free Will against Pighius*, book II). It must be acknowledged [Col. 0887C] that Luther sometimes calls the necessity of acting that he recognizes immutable; but he means only that a person has no power to overcome or change it: “We call it, for the moment, the necessity of immutability, because the will cannot change itself and turn elsewhere” (Luther, in *On the Bondage of the Will*).

As for Calvin, he teaches in countless places that the necessity of which he speaks is changeable: “I have said that interruptions of faith sometimes occur” (*Institutes*, book III, chapter 2, no. 24). According to him, the necessity imposed by the action of grace is caused by a victorious delight superior to that of concupiscence: *per eamdem gratiam impresso delectationis affectu* (“by the same grace, an affection of delight being impressed,” *Institutes*, book II, chapter 3, no. 14). He takes away from the will only the choice, or the act of choosing, which would presuppose the power to resist grace; but he assures us that grace forms in our heart the movement that we call choice or the act of choosing: *Ipsa est gratia quae in corde et electionem et voluntatem format*—“It is grace itself that forms both choice and will in the heart” (*Institutes*, book II, chapter 3, no. 13).

When [Col. 0887D] Luther and Calvin said that free will was like an inanimate thing, which had no action and was purely passive, they meant only the moral aspect of the action, whose entire merit was to be attributed to grace, which imposed the necessity of acting, and not to free will, which acted according to the impression of that necessity. For otherwise these heresiarchs, and Calvin above all, claimed that free will truly acted: *Non hic quaeritur agatne voluntas, quod extra dubium est, sed agatne ex se ipsa an pro modo divinae actionis*—“The question here is not whether the will acts, which is beyond doubt, but whether it acts from itself or according to the manner of divine action” (*On Free Will against Pighius*, book VI).

Finally, Calvin calls the necessity he establishes voluntary: *necessitas quodammodo voluntaria . . . voluntariae cujusdam servitutis*—“a necessity in some manner voluntary . . . of a certain voluntary servitude” (*Institutes*, book II, chapter 3, no. 5). Here, then, is a summary of Calvin’s doctrine, which was condemned by the Council of Trent; but it is also a very faithful extract of Jansenius’s doctrine. Therefore Jansenius’s doctrine was condemned by the Council of Trent.

Would you believe it? I have seen Jansenists so extreme that they were not greatly displeased with M. Bayle for failing to distinguish their master’s doctrine from Calvin’s, because he did them the favor of confusing both with Saint Augustine’s opinions. This critic flatters a large party and imitates its language when he boldly says, without the slightest proof: “It is certain”; “It is evident.”

Yet the contrary of what he asserts is easy to demonstrate, although it cannot be done in a few words. Several great men, such as M. de Fénelon and Father Dechamps, have already undertaken this task, and their writings have remained unanswered. It would be enough to read them to become convinced that M. Bayle was far from examining matters without prejudice and with the necessary enlightenment. The cause defended by these two illustrious writers is so good and so rich in invincible means of defense that, without borrowing almost anything from them or from all those who have printed works on this same subject, I believe myself capable of disabusing the persons of whom you spoke to me. You may assure them that my intention is not to draw them into a dispute, but simply to give them an account of the birth and progress of my anti-Jansenism; to tell them how a celebrated doctor whom I had consulted concerning the difference between Saint Augustine’s doctrine and Jansenius’s had found the secret of making me produce sophisms on the subject so seductive that I still take them for genuine demonstrations. He said only two or three words to me at intervals, very concise and almost enigmatic; and the understanding of these words directed my mind toward enchanting ideas that placed Jansenius at the antipodes of Saint Augustine. Our conversation soon came to an end, and early the following morning the same person [Col. 0888C] brought into my house a licentiate of the Sorbonne who had the face of a thoroughly honest man. He was one of those who had been mentioned the preceding day. He showed himself very eager to hear me. Therefore, after a brief preamble, I spoke as follows:

It has already been many years since a doctor promised to make this alleged chimera of the Molinists real before my eyes; to make palpable to me, to let me touch with my finger, what he called an incontestable truth that the malice of your party had obscured—namely, that there was as much distance between Saint Augustine’s true opinions and Jansenius’s system as between heaven and earth.

But let us not begin with an equivocation. It seems to me that there is one in the name “Molinist,” which M. Bayle and those of your party generally give to all true Catholics who respect the decisions of the Church. I remember a time when that name was applied only to theologians who had attached themselves to Molina’s particular opinions. But now, let a doctor refute Molina, follow a route and method different from his in explaining matters of predestination and grace: if he accepts the constitutions of the popes who, together with the episcopal body, have condemned Jansenism, he is a Molinist against his will. If a person in the world, whose circumstances have kept him away from disputes and controversies, simply believes his catechism, which teaches him that he must listen to the bishops united with the head of the Church, then he is already a Molinist without knowing what Molina is or in what singular manner he thought.

Nevertheless, the true Molinists protest against the excessive honor that the blind hatred of the heretics brings them. They frankly and ingenuously declare that the fame attached to their name—which people are willing to give to all prelates and all orthodox persons in the world—has traveled farther than their opinions; and that if the other Catholic schools happen to feel some jealousy because there is no lord or lady called a Thomist, Scotist, or Sorbonnist, while there are nevertheless quite a number called Molinists; if, in a word, these respectable schools take alarm and have reason to fear that, under cover of the name, Molinist doctrine will make too much progress, they are asked to consider that the Molinists properly so called are not responsible for this, and that it would be unjust to blame them for an advantage they never sought, which comes solely, shall I say, from the malice or imprudence of the common enemies of Catholicism. But let us return.

The person about whom I began speaking to you [Note: [Col. 0889A] Father Édouard de Vitri, who died in Rome on 30 October 1729.] was one of those broad and versatile minds who embrace every science and excel in all of them, as though they had devoted themselves exclusively to mastering each one individually. Wherever he happened to be, he was the general agent of the republic of letters; his house was the address office for scholars in every field, and they often stole his conversation from me. I paid him many fruitless visits. Whenever we were about to begin discussing matters of grace, a Titiana, a Probus [Note: [Col. 0890A] Rare medals.], a passage from Pliny or Lycophron [Note: [Col. 0890A] A very difficult Greek author to understand.], a new discovery in physics or astronomy, or a problem in geometry would be thrown across our path. I never left without being instructed in a hundred fine things, but precisely those I had not been curious to learn. At last the moment arrived when I forced him to fulfill his promise, and chance brought order to the things I drew from him.

# FIRST PART

Jansenius’s bad faith in citing Saint Augustine. The general principle of Jansenius’s heresy falsely attributed by him to Saint Augustine. The false key to Saint Augustine’s works supplied by Jansenius.

[Col. 0889]

[Col. 0889B] The several meetings I had with this learned man unintentionally prepared me to discover the true key to Saint Augustine’s works against the Pelagians. First I learned how dishonestly Jansenius cited this Father; next, how falsely Jansenius attributed the general principle of his heresy to the holy doctor; and finally I became convinced that the Bishop of Ypres supplied a false key to Saint Augustine’s works. For, weary of my doctor’s endless delays, I told him, with a freedom he willingly tolerated, that perhaps, despairing of being able to keep his word, he was trying to amuse me pleasantly and make me forget the question that occupied my heart by cultivating in me a taste for other branches of knowledge. He excused himself politely, asked me to take account of his occupations, and proposed an expedient: that I should read Saint Augustine under his direction.

## I. Jansenius’s Bad Faith in Citing Saint Augustine: Five Striking Proofs of This Bad Faith

[Col. 0889C]

“Begin,” he said, “by seeking out and transcribing every passage in which the holy doctor used these expressions: a victorious grace (*gratia victrix*), a victorious delight (*delectatio victrix*). This collection,” he added with a laugh, “will be of great use to you.”

“It seems to me,” I replied, “that you are trying to jest.”

“Not entirely,” he answered, recovering his seriousness, “and you will be delighted that you took the trouble.”

I therefore did not delay in consulting both the general index and the particular indexes of the edition of the Reverend Benedictine Fathers, in order to find the places where Saint Augustine might have joined these two words together, *gratia victrix*; and I did not see the slightest trace of them.

“What horrible negligence!” I exclaimed. “Is it bearable? What other expression of Saint Augustine deserved better to occupy its place here? What other should have escaped less easily the notice of one who took the trouble to compose all these indexes? The most learned men, I suppose, disdained such drudgery and entrusted it to some novice; they were greatly at fault.”

After grumbling at them thoroughly, I went through the indexes of the other editions, and none offered me anywhere these much-celebrated words, *gratia victrix*. From the indexes I passed to the concordances, and from the concordances I returned to the indexes. I had the patience to dig them out and inspect most of them, but with just as little success. Finally, I thought of consulting Jansenius’s book, of which I possessed the Louvain edition of 1640.

How pleased I was when, in the index to the third volume, entitled *On the Grace of Christ the Savior*, I noticed these words: “Various epithets of medicinal grace are collected from Augustine, etc. Augustine calls it most effective, etc.; likewise victorious, which no one can resist.” But then I became even more indignant against the Reverend Benedictine Fathers. “They have melted together,” I said, “in their general index, all the indexes and concordances of Saint Augustine’s works that have ever been made. Why did they not take advantage of this index of Jansenius’s to mark the citations from Saint Augustine that are about to be supplied here so abundantly? They would have spared me much boredom and distaste in moving and leafing through all these enormous folios.”

[Col. 0890C] I therefore searched with extraordinary eagerness for the four places indicated by Jansenius’s index: chapter 24 of book II; chapter 1 of book III; chapter 5 of book IV; and chapter 16 of book IX, at pages 200, 251, 410, and 954.

I was extremely surprised. I found many passages of Saint Augustine explained by Jansenius according to the heretical meaning he gives to the expression *gratia victrix*, but the expression itself was nowhere used. Yet it is the epithet “victorious” applied to grace, the expression “victorious grace,” that the index promises.

In chapter 24 of book II Jansenius writes as follows:

“Because of this effective manner of operating, Saint Augustine quite often gives the name ‘victorious’ to the medicinal grace of Jesus Christ. From this effective manner of operating it follows that Augustine not rarely calls the medicinal grace of Christ victorious, because by unconquered power it breaks through all opposing obstacles of the wills and affections” (Jansenius, book II, *On the Grace of Christ the Savior*, chapter 24, Louvain edition, 1640, p. 200).

He writes this, but he asks us to take his word for it: neither there nor anywhere else in his entire work does he cite a single passage of Saint Augustine in which grace is called victorious.

I soon concluded that this expression had been invented by Jansenius and that no one in the world had ever read it in Saint Augustine. For if anyone had read it in Saint Augustine, it would have been Jansenius rather than anyone else; and if Jansenius had read this expression in Saint Augustine, he would have repeated the passage in which he had read it a thousand times rather than fail to report this precious passage at least once.

I marvel at the boldness and success of so outstanding a lie. Its success has been such that everyone has been deceived by it. There is no one who does not naively believe that this way of speaking, *gratia victrix*, is very common in Saint Augustine. Far from suspecting that it is a lie, most learned people, even Catholics, would not need a quarter of an hour to prove a man a liar if he denied that this expression occurs in Saint Augustine’s writings. Since the birth of Jansenism—which alone brought this expression into vogue—so many voices have joined together to proclaim emphatically “Saint Augustine’s victorious grace” [Col. 0891B] that no one is more inclined to verify such an attribution with his own eyes than to go and see whether there is a city called Rome.

At last I recognized the considerate artifice of my doctor, who wanted me to feel the full difficulty and also taste the full pleasure of his discoveries. He deserves that I not steal the honor from him.

My reflections did not stop there. I judged that Jansenius had not foisted terms upon Saint Augustine with the intention of teaching Saint Augustine’s pure doctrine. I therefore carefully examined all the passages of the holy doctor that Jansenius associates with the expression he had invented, *gratia victrix*. I noticed several in which the grace of predestination is concerned—not one of those graces that we call actual, but one that is in a certain sense habitual, as I shall explain later. They are consequently misplaced and cited out of context.

As for all the others, Jansenius’s use of them rests on an assumption of meaning as crude and as obvious as his use of the expression itself. In the same chapter 24 of book II of *The Grace of the Savior*, and very often elsewhere, he says that Saint Augustine establishes victorious grace with respect to the human will and free will, so that, in the holy doctor’s thought, it is the will’s free choice that grace overcomes, over which it prevails, and which it triumphs over: *Quamobrem sexto, gratiam Dei Augustinus ita victricem statuit supra voluntatis arbitrium, etc.*—“For this reason, sixth, Augustine so establishes the grace of God as victorious over the will’s free choice, etc.” (Jansenius, volume III, p. 400).

Nothing is more contrary to the doctrine contained in the texts of Saint Augustine that he produces shortly beforehand and everywhere else.

The holy doctor truly recognizes in grace the action of conquering and overcoming—and, if Jansenius absolutely insists, of prevailing and triumphing—although Saint Augustine expresses himself in this way only in particular passages. But I [Col. 0891D] search in this Father’s passages for the enemy overcome and conquered by grace, and I find none other than concupiscence and temptations.

“What! Does he not teach that, along with concupiscence and temptations, the free choice of the human will is subdued and brought under the dominion of grace?”

No. This thought would have seemed ridiculous to Saint Augustine. For, according to him, grace is given to free will as a help that it uses to overcome the lure of sin: *Donat per Spiritum charitatem, cujus ope vincatur delectatio peccati*—“Through the Spirit he gives charity, by whose help the delight of sin may be conquered” (*Unfinished Work*, book I, no. 107).

According to him, grace gives our will exceedingly effective strength to conquer: *Ille facit ut faciamus, praebendo vires efficacissimas voluntati*—“He causes us to act by providing the will with exceedingly effective strength” (*On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 16, no. 32).

According to him, in this life the saints ask God for the power to fight and conquer through the grace of Jesus Christ: *Dari sibi pugnandi vincendique virtutem poscunt*—“They ask that the power to fight and to conquer be given to them” [Col. 0892A] (*On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 2, no. 29).

Besides these three passages cited by Jansenius, another presents itself, one that he did not know because it is drawn from a work first printed after Jansenius’s death. According to the holy doctor, God, through a hidden instinct, prepares and arouses human wills to accomplish with the utmost effectiveness what he wills.

“Is this to conquer wills, or is it not rather to help them conquer? *Cur ergo non confiteris . . . Deum occulto instinctu, ad id quod voluerit efficacissime implendum, praeparare atque excitare hominum voluntates*?”—“Why, then, do you not confess . . . that God, by a hidden instinct, prepares and arouses human wills to fulfill most effectively what he has willed?” (*Unfinished Work*, book III, no. 166).

Such is Saint Augustine’s doctrine. But to make free will an enemy or adversary overcome by grace; to assert that free will is conquered by the assistance given to it in order to conquer—this is an absurdity of which Saint Augustine was never capable, and which Jansenius could have borrowed only from Calvin.

The Jansenist licentiate, whose attentiveness in listening to me seemed extraordinary, prevented me from extending myself further on this subject and wished me to set out my investigations concerning the other expression, *delectatio victrix*. I did so, continuing my speech as follows.

I turned once more to the tables of the Reverend Benedictine Fathers, extremely embarrassed by all the evil I had said about them, and gladly doing justice to the able man who had compiled them. Yet nowhere did I still find the term “victorious delight.” But I judged this omission pardonable when I saw that the same term had escaped most makers of tables, and that, according to the unanimous testimony of the tables and concordances, Saint Augustine had used it only once in all his works.

It was then deliberately that I reserved Jansenius’s table for consultation last; I was no longer disposed to rely on what it might announce to me. Thus, returning to the word *gratia* (“grace”), I read the following words [Col. 0892C] and provisionally refuted them:

> “It consists essentially in heavenly sweetness and delight . . . hence it is repeatedly (*passim*) called by Augustine victorious delight.”

Only one place is indicated, namely chapter 6 of book IV of *The Grace of the Savior*, at page 410, and so forth. The title of the chapter is remarkable: “The name ‘victorious’ delight, drawn from and applied to the medicinal grace of Christ.” In the body of the chapter one reads:

> “Hence it follows that Augustine is accustomed to adorn this grace of Christ with an epithet especially proper and effective for this very purpose: for he very often (*plerumque*) calls it victorious delight.”

It immediately occurred to me that Jansenius had spent a fairly long time in Gascony, and that he might well have acquired there the habit of exaggeration, substituting the words *plerumque* (“very often”) and *passim* (“repeatedly,” “everywhere”) for the word *semel* (“once”); or else that he was cleverly presenting himself as Saint Augustine. For he endlessly repeats the terms “grace” and “victorious delight,” whereas from the genuine Saint Augustine he reports [Col. 0892D] only this one passage, cited by everyone:

> “Let us understand, insofar as it has been granted to us, and let us realize that the Lord God, being good, therefore sometimes does not grant his saints, in the performance of some righteous work, either certain knowledge or victorious delight, so that they may recognize that from him, not from themselves, comes the light by which their darkness is illuminated, and the sweetness by which their earth bears fruit” (*The Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book II, chapter 19, no. 32).

It is not that Jansenius fails to add a quantity of other passages in which Saint Augustine teaches that delight in righteousness leads us to overcome, and makes us overcome, the delight of sin. But it is the name “victorious delight”—the epithet “victorious” joined to the word “delight”—that Jansenius claims is found most often (*plerumque*), everywhere (*passim*), in Saint Augustine’s books. Moreover, one need not have read Saint Augustine’s works against the Pelagians thirty times to notice the distinction the holy Doctor makes between these two expressions: *delectatio victrix*, “a victorious delight,” and *delectatio vincens*, “a delight that secures the advantage in the struggle.”

On this occasion I undertook a study that greatly satisfied me, because it revealed plainly that Saint Augustine’s victorious delight was something entirely different from the medicinal grace of Jesus Christ, something entirely different from the efficacious grace of our present condition; and thus Jansenius had read in vain, through magnifying lenses, that one unique passage of the holy Doctor in which victorious delight is formally and expressly mentioned.

I had heard my doctor say that one of the best commentaries on Holy Scripture was a concordance of the Bible. The reason he gave was that a comparison of all the texts of one author, or of several authors who wrote in the same spirit, cannot be made with respect to a particular expression occurring in them without fixing and determining the meaning of that expression in places where it causes difficulty. For obscure or ambiguous passages always have some affinity with very clear passages in which that meaning is settled.
