I applied this rule to the interpretation of Saint Augustine, and by means of the concordances we possess of his works I brought together and compared all the passages in which he uses the terms “victory” or “victorious” concerning grace.

I first noticed the definition he gives in *On True Religion*: “Victory is the end of struggle”—*victoria est finis certandi* (*On True Religion*, chapter 53, no. 102). I then encountered several passages that place Jansenius very far from the truth, because Saint Augustine there uses this notion to exclude victorious grace from the present state of pilgrimage. He says:

> “There is a great difference between the grace that sustains and helps us in the struggle and that which makes us victorious, because it frees us from every enemy, whether inward or outward, and establishes us in eternal peace. The one is given to us to strengthen us in the laborious warfare of the present age; the other is reserved for us in the blessed rest of the age to come: *Aliter gratia CERTANTEM facit atque adjuvat, aliter VICTOREM sine hoste ullo vel externo vel interno in AETERNA PACE conservat.* This is the laborious warfare in the present age; that is the blessed rest in the future” (*Unfinished Work*, book II, no. 106).

“We fight,” he says farther on, “against the concupiscence of the flesh by the help of the Holy Spirit, until the time of victory, which will procure peace for us through deliverance from every enemy, whether inward or outward”:

> *Praelium contra concupiscentiam carnis usque ad VICTORIAE PACEM, quae nullum intrinsecus, nullum extrinsecus patietur inimicum*  
> “The battle against the concupiscence of the flesh continues until the peace of victory, which will suffer no enemy either within or without” (*ibid.*, no. 217).

And elsewhere he says:

> “Death will be swallowed up in victory, and when peace has been perfected there will no longer be anything to overcome” (*The Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book II, chapter 4, no. 3).

All this led me to conclude that, in the words “Victorious delight, which for Augustine is efficacious help, is relative,” Jansenius refers to himself alone (*The Grace of Christ*, volume III, chapter 2, no. 3), and that he is not speaking of Augustine of Hippo but of Augustine of Ypres. For in the doctrine of Augustine of Hippo, victorious delight is in no way relative: it is not called victorious when it overcomes another delight, but only when it has no opposing delight to overcome. It is the delight that grants the peace of victory, *victoriae pacem*, the peace of righteousness, *justitiae pacem* (*Unfinished Work*, book II, no. 106; and *The Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book II, chapter 19, no. 33), whether, after a long succession of struggles, it utterly destroys the enemy, or whether, having never been obliged to fight him, it holds him captive and disarmed.

“How strange!” exclaimed the licentiate. “You thus proscribe and banish grace and victorious delight from the present state? Do you realize what you are doing? Everyone will throw stones at you and overwhelm you. For to reduce all your reasoning to dust, it seems sufficient to observe that there are two kinds of victory over concupiscence: one lasting, which is the effect of the grace of perseverance and produces consummate or perfect righteousness; the other temporary, which is the effect of efficacious grace and produces begun or imperfect righteousness.”

“You truly frighten me,” I replied to the licentiate. “Nevertheless, I reassure myself with the conviction that fair-minded people will not attribute to me the rash intention of suppressing a manner of speaking now accepted by so many theologians who are as pious as they are learned, and whose faith is entirely pure. But is it not worth observing that before Jansenism it was not common and, I dare say, was not even known; that Jansenius introduced it with a bad purpose, in order to insinuate his error under cover of a fine expression; and finally that it is not Saint Augustine’s expression, although he might well have used it in the proper sense, distinguishing, as you do, two kinds of victory, one lasting and the other temporary, if he had not had an important reason for speaking otherwise, and for constantly attaching to the term ‘victory’ the cessation of every struggle, the end of every war, and the destruction of every enemy? The reason is that the Pelagians always took the word ‘victory’ in this sense and abused it to establish the Stoicism of their impeccability, which was one of their principal errors, as I shall demonstrate later.”

“That is strange,” replied the licentiate. “You admit that people today accept this expression in a Catholic sense to designate efficacious grace, which enables us to overcome a temptation; and you cannot deny that this Catholic sense is found in Saint Augustine. Consequently, this expression belongs to Saint Augustine, at least insofar as its orthodox meaning can apply to him.”

“We agree,” I replied.

The licentiate, completely disconcerted, then said to me: “You surprise me. It is against my expectation that you yield so readily. I had imagined that you had adopted a malicious tactic in order to suggest that Saint Augustine was not favorable to the Thomists’ intrinsically efficacious grace.”

“What idea are you attributing to me?” I exclaimed. “Do you not know that the Thomists’ doctrine is entirely independent of this expression, to say nothing more; that they did without it for a very long time; that throughout the entire course of the famous *de auxiliis* controversies they did not use it even once? This is a fact easily verified from the records reported in the two histories that have been made public for several years in support of the parties in that great lawsuit, as well as from the polemical writings published by the parties and their supporters during the controversy. And do not think me too bold if I assert that until the earliest beginnings of Jansenism one will find no Catholic author who called efficacious grace ‘victorious’ or ‘victorious delight.’

“But if the Thomists have recently adopted this same expression and adapted it to the highly orthodox meaning of their doctrine, are they alone in doing so? Even the Molinists do it. One does not understand the latter’s system if one believes them entirely at a loss to give, according to their ideas, a natural explanation of a term that is ambiguous once one decides to abandon the notion determined for it by Saint Augustine in the one place where he uses it, as well as his general definition of victory: ‘Victory is the end of struggle.’ To be brief, this is not a matter of a school dispute. My sole aim is to expose Jansenius’s bad faith. That is why you will permit me to resume the thread of my discourse.”

The licentiate interrupted me again, and I was delighted, seeing that he was taking it upon himself to defend Catholic theologians, whom the statement of my thoughts might, contrary to my intention, offend. “But does it not seem,” he added, “that you wish to bring some kind of charge against anyone who, following Saint Augustine, makes the efficacy of grace consist in victorious delight? You would not be too displeased, I think, if this opinion were branded heretical.”

“Must I be examined on that point?” I replied. “Provided that it is sincerely established that this delight is not necessitating, and that when one does not possess it the grace required for the genuine power to act is not lacking, I openly declare that those who embrace this opinion are very good Catholics. Nevertheless, they will permit me not to think as they do. I ask the Thomists for the same grace. And I continue.

“The victorious delight of the holy Doctor of grace is, first, the grace of the intuitive vision of God, which makes the saints enjoy perfect peace, complete peace [Note: [Col. 0895D] ‘Perfect peace.’ *The Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book II, chapter 4, no. 4. ‘Until full peace.’ *Confessions*, book X, chapter 30, no. 42; book XXII of *Against Faustus*, chapter 28.]; which makes them like the angels, whose entire happiness comes from God and whose whole occupation is the accomplishment of his holy will, without the experience of any temptation ever being able to trouble or distract them:

> *Ita particeps est legis aeternae, ut solus eam delectet Deus, cujus voluntati SINE ULLO EXPERIMENTO TENTATIONIS obtemperat.*  
> “He is so made a participant in the eternal law that God alone delights him, and he obeys God’s will WITHOUT ANY EXPERIENCE OF TEMPTATION.”

“The victorious delight of the holy Doctor of grace is, secondly, the grace of original righteousness, which in the first man before his sin subjected the flesh to the spirit without a struggle, and prevented him from feeling any movement of any passion whatsoever against his will:

> *Ut resistentem sibi carnem NULLO CERTAMINE pateretur, nec aliquid omnino ex aliqua cupiditate sentiret, quod nollet.*  
> “So that he would suffer no resistance from the flesh without any struggle, and would feel nothing at all arising from any desire that he did not wish to feel” (*Unfinished Work*, book VI, no. 14).

“This peace was not as perfect or complete as that of the blessed, because Adam’s grace was not victorious with regard to the outward enemy, by whom Adam could be attacked and tempted, as indeed he was, but only with regard to the inward enemy, whom this powerful grace rendered incapable both of attacking and of resisting. Thus, far from victorious delight being, in the language of the holy Doctor, the medicinal grace of Jesus Christ, it is not only the grace of eternal blessedness; it even belongs to the grace of the state of innocence, to the grace of health. Saint Augustine must therefore be turned upside down, if I may put it that way, in order to make him agree with Jansenius.

“The victorious delight of the holy Doctor of grace is, third, the ineffable miracle of the almighty Creator, by which, according to Saint Augustine, a man may be favored during this life and in our present condition; it consists in the complete extinction of the law of sin that dwells in our members and resists the law of the mind:

> *Nam nec grandibus hoc praestatur in baptismo, nisi forte miraculo omnipotentissimi Creatoris, ut lex peccati, quae inest in membris repugnans legi mentis, PRORSUS PENITUS EXSTINGUATUR et non sit.*  
> “For this is not granted even to adults in baptism, except perhaps by a miracle of the almighty Creator: that the law of sin, which is present in the members and resists the law of the mind, should be UTTERLY AND COMPLETELY EXTINGUISHED and no longer exist” (*The Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book II, chapter 39, no. 69).

“These words, which occur at the end of the first book of the work entitled *The Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, contain the precise definition of victorious delight—the victorious delight mentioned in the unique passage where this expression occurs, a passage taken from the second book of the same work.

“I sought to establish this for myself—that is, to demonstrate that the victorious delight which Saint Augustine says in that famous passage God sometimes refuses to the saints and to his most faithful servants is an extraordinary and miraculous favor that would deliver a person, in this life and in the present condition, from the rebellions of the flesh and from every temptation arising from concupiscence.

“To succeed, I used the same method from which I had benefited so much, and with the help of concordances I collected almost all the passages in which the holy Doctor teaches that God refuses grace to the saints. Having done this, I recognized: first, that in these passages the holy Doctor speaks only of the grace necessary for the perfection of righteousness; second, that by ‘perfection of righteousness’ the holy Doctor means the ability to serve God without any inward opposition to his holy law, without that resistance to the good and solicitation toward evil caused by the undeliberated and disordered movements of the sensual appetite; third, that the perfection of righteousness is the true victory and the proper effect of victorious delight—or, which is the same thing, that victorious delight is solely the grace necessary for the perfection of righteousness.

“Remember that the question is not what theology now understands by the words ‘grace’ or ‘victorious delight,’ but the notion Saint Augustine consistently attached to the terms ‘victory’ and ‘victorious’ when writing against the Pelagians.

“First, a testimony proving the first point presented itself to me in the same book and the same chapter, a few lines after the passage in question. It says that God delays giving his saints and faithful servants the delight sufficient to accomplish righteousness in every respect:

> *Idcirco etiam sanctos et fideles suos in aliquibus vitiis suis tardius sanat, ut in his eos minus quam IMPLENDAE EX OMNI PARTE justitiae delectet bonum.*  
> “For this reason he also heals his saints and faithful servants more slowly from certain of their vices, so that in these matters the good may delight them less than is required for righteousness to be fulfilled in every respect.”

“The words that follow are noteworthy:

> *Nec in eo ipso vult nos damnabiles esse, sed humiles.*  
> “Yet even in this he does not wish us to be liable to condemnation, but humble” (*The Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book II, chapter 19, no. 33).

“The third book of the same work supplied me with another passage, where we read that on various occasions God allows the righteous to lack the help necessary to fulfill righteousness perfectly:

> *Et in quibusdam etiam justos suos, quoniam adhuc extolli possunt, non adjuvat ad PERFICIENDAM justitiam.*  
> “And in certain matters he does not even help his righteous ones to PERFECT righteousness, because they can still become puffed up” (*The Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book III, chapter 13, no. 23).

“Turning to the examination of the second point, I thought I could see what the perfection of righteousness, and the perfect accomplishment of righteousness, meant at the end of the book entitled *On the Spirit and the Letter*, where Saint Augustine says that the righteous person lives by faith and is pleasing to God, although he has not yet, through an outstanding perfection of charity, absorbed and consumed all the movements of earthly desire:

> *Etsi nondum illa SUPEREMINENTISSIMA PERFECTIONE charitatis omnes terrenae libidinis motus ABSORBUERIT atque CONSUMPSERIT.*  
> “Although by that MOST EXALTED PERFECTION of charity he has not yet ABSORBED and CONSUMED all the movements of earthly desire” (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 36, no. 65).

“And in the fourth book against Julian, where he says that, in order to keep the saints humble, God does not extinguish concupiscence in their flesh, but obliges them to fight against it until human weakness has reached such a great perfection of health that it no longer fears either the corruption of impure desires [Col. 0897A] or the swelling of pride:

> *Sed quia in ista humana miseria pejor est hostis cavenda superbia, ideo nimirum non exstinguitur in carne continentium sanctorum ista concupiscentia, ut dum pugnatur adversus eam, periculorum suorum animus admoneatur, ne securus infletur; donec humana fragilitas ad tantam PERFECTIONEM perveniat SANITATIS, ut nulla putredo lasciviae, nullus tumor superbiae formidetur.*  
> “But because in this human misery pride is the worse enemy to be guarded against, this concupiscence is therefore not extinguished in the flesh of the continent saints, so that while the struggle against it continues, the mind may be reminded of its dangers and not become complacently inflated; until human frailty reaches such a PERFECTION OF HEALTH that no corruption of wantonness and no swelling of pride is feared” (*Against Julian*, book IV, chapter 2, no. 11).

“But I was not satisfied until I saw something more precise and decisive; so I went through the short book *On the Perfection of Righteousness*. At first it led me to think that Saint Augustine had developed this manner of speaking on the model of that used by Saint Paul when he complained of the importunate contradictions and inward warfare caused in him by the thorn of the flesh:

> *Velle adjacet mihi, PERFICERE autem non invenio* (Romans 7:18).  
> “The willing is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish it.”

“On this the holy Doctor comments:

> *Adjacet ei velle, sed perficere bonum non adjacet. Non, facere bonum non adjacet, sed PERFICERE . . . . Quod tunc erit, quando concupiscentia, quae habitat in membris ejus, NULLA ERIT.*  
> “The willing is present with him, but the accomplishment of the good is not present. Not the doing of good is absent, but its PERFECT accomplishment . . . . This will occur when the concupiscence that dwells in his members NO LONGER EXISTS” (*On the Perfection of Righteousness*, chapter 11, no. 28).

“Of a hundred other passages that I read, which give a similar notion of the perfection of righteousness, see these two as well:

> *Perfectio boni est, ut nec ipsa concupiscentia sit in homine, etc.*  
> “The perfection of the good is that concupiscence itself should not exist in a person, etc.” (*Retractations*, book I, chapter 15, no. 2).

> *Castigatione corporis frenatur concupiscentia, quae non frenari, sed OMNINO esse non debet, nec erit in illa PERFECTIONE justitiae, ubi nullum erit omnino peccatum.*  
> “By disciplining the body, concupiscence is restrained; but it ought not merely to be restrained—it ought NOT TO EXIST AT ALL, and it will not exist in that PERFECTION of righteousness where there will be absolutely no sin” (*On the Perfection of Righteousness*, chapter 8, no. 18).

“There, then, is the grace that God refuses to the saints: the complete extinction of concupiscence. Jansenius understands the passages in which Saint Augustine says that God refuses this grace to the saints as referring to the grace necessary for perseverance in righteousness. Is the trick not clever?

“It remained for me to demonstrate the third point: namely, that victorious delight, in Saint Augustine’s conception and sense, is precisely the grace necessary for the perfection of righteousness. This demonstration did not require a long search, for no sooner does Saint Augustine name victorious delight than he declares it to be a help toward perfectly accomplishing righteousness:

> *Nos quantum concessum est sapiamus, et intelligamus, si possumus, Dominum Deum justum ideo etiam sanctis suis alicujus operis justi non tribuere vel CERTAM SCIENTIAM vel VICTRICEM DELECTATIONEM, ut cognoscant non a se ipsis, sed ab illo sibi esse lucem qua illuminentur tenebrae eorum, et suavitatem qua det fructum terra eorum. Cum autem ab illo illud adjutorium deprecamur ad faciendam PERFICIENDAMQUE justitiam, quid aliud deprecamur, quam ut aperiat quod latebat, et suave fiat quod non delectabat.*  
> “Let us understand, insofar as it has been granted to us, and let us realize, if we can, that the just Lord God therefore does not grant even to his saints, in the performance of some righteous work, either CERTAIN KNOWLEDGE or VICTORIOUS DELIGHT, so that they may recognize that the light by which their darkness is illuminated, and the sweetness by which their earth bears fruit, come not from themselves but from him. And when we beseech him for that help in doing and PERFECTING righteousness, what else do we beseech him for than that he open what was hidden and make sweet what did not delight?” (*The Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book II, chapter 19, nos. 32–33).

“Moreover, Saint Augustine often designates concupiscence by the words ‘the difficulty of the good,’ and he habitually joins it to ignorance of the truth: *Ignorantia veri et difficultas recti*, ‘ignorance of the truth and difficulty in doing right.’ Here he joins certain knowledge to victorious delight, *certam scientiam et victricem delectationem* (*On Free Will*, book III, chapter 20, no. 55, and elsewhere; *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 11, no. 27; *Retractations*, book I, chapter 9, no. 6). These are consequently the opposites of the other two. And just as certain knowledge is the destruction of ignorance, victorious delight is the extinction of concupiscence.

“But, further, reading this entire book made me see more clearly than daylight that the words ‘Let us understand, insofar as it has been granted to us,’ and so forth, are the answer to this question: Why, although God could deliver us in this life through the grace of Jesus Christ from the wretched inclination that carries us toward evil, has he nevertheless not wished to do so? I shall develop this proof at greater length in due course, for my doctor made me investigate the matter of the perfection of righteousness much more deeply; he ordinarily called it ‘Jansenius’s stumbling block,’ or ‘the dividing wall between Jansenius and Saint Augustine.’”

The licentiate continued to listen to me with astonishing attention. I stopped to give him an opportunity to speak; but he was overcome with amazement, like a man suddenly transported into another world who can do nothing but occupy himself with the new objects that strike him, without yet being able to explain the thoughts and feelings they awaken in him. I therefore continued as follows.

When I went to see my doctor again to report on my work and offer him the happy harvest produced by the seed of two or three of his words, I found him disputing with several other doctors about God’s abandonment and the withdrawal of grace. But the question was nearly exhausted, and I benefited only from the verification of several glaring falsehoods of which Jansenius was found guilty. Here is the first.

[Col. 0898B] To establish that all grace is lacking to the hardened, he attributes these words to Saint Augustine:

> *Quasi non debeat Deo gratias agere, quia praecepta voluit, qui desertus omni lumine veritatis haec velle non POTEST.*  
> “As though he ought not to give thanks to God because he wished to obey the commandments—he who, abandoned by every light of truth, CANNOT will these things” (Jansenius, volume III, book III, chapter 10, page 301, citing Saint Augustine, *On the Perfection of Righteousness*, chapter 19, no. 41).

This would mean that Saint Augustine says that a person who cannot wish to observe the commandments because he is deprived of every light of truth must nevertheless give thanks to God, who has seen fit to subject him to the observance of the commandments despite his inability to wish to fulfill them. But Jansenius changes Saint Augustine’s text and corrupts its meaning in the most visible and outrageous manner. Saint Augustine wrote *haec velle non POSSET*, “could not will these things,” not *haec velle non POTEST*, “cannot will these things.” All editions and all manuscripts bear witness to this. Not only do the subject matter, the context, and the concordance of the discourse protest against the reading *haec velle non POTEST* and require the other reading, *haec velle non POSSET*, but they demonstrate with the utmost clarity that grace is not lacking to those under discussion here, and that the passage has nothing whatsoever to do with blinded or hardened sinners.

Caelestius, in order to show that a person possessed a power to fulfill God’s commandments independent of grace, had objected to Saint Augustine with this passage:

> *Si volueris mandata servare, conservabunt te* (Ecclesiasticus 15:16).  
> “If you will to observe the commandments, they will preserve you.”

The holy Doctor replies:

> *Videte tamen, obsecro, quale sit, ideo volenti et currenti misericordiam Dei non esse necessariam, quae illum etiam praevenit ut curreret . . . . quia dictum est, Si voles praecepta, servabunt te; quasi non debeat Deo agere gratias, quia praecepta voluit, qui desertus omni lumine veritatis haec velle non POSSET.*  
> “Consider, I beg you, what it would mean to say that God’s mercy is not necessary to one who wills and runs, when that mercy even goes before him so that he may run . . . . because it has been said, ‘If you will the commandments, they will preserve you’; as though he ought not to give thanks to God because he willed the commandments—he who, abandoned by every light of truth, could not will these things” (Saint Augustine, *ibid.*).

“One must be truly blinded,” said one of the doctors, “and truly hardened in the determination to make Saint Augustine speak the language of Calvin, to imagine that a sinner blinded and hardened by the withdrawal of grace is under discussion here—”

“And in order not to see,” said another, “that the words *quia praecepta voluit*, ‘because he willed the commandments,’ refer to the person himself. It follows that it would be contradictory to add afterward *haec velle non POTEST*, ‘he cannot will these things,’ for that would assert of the same person both that he willed to fulfill the commandments and that, without any change in his situation or state, he was unable to will to fulfill them.”

“It is evident,” said another, “that this person is supposed to have willed, through the help of grace, the fulfillment of the commandments, and that this is the help for which Saint Augustine says the person must thank God, because, if he had been deprived of it, he would not have willed to fulfill the commandments.”

“If only Jansenius,” I said, “had read all Saint Augustine’s works against the Pelagians properly once, instead of reading them so badly thirty times!”

[Col. 0899A] “I am tempted to believe,” replied my doctor, “that Jansenius read Saint Augustine in the manner of N***—and that, just as the latter read Saint Augustine only in Jansenius, so Jansenius read Saint Augustine only in Luther and Calvin. What is certain is that N*** copied this passage from Saint Augustine very faithfully from Jansenius; and although he says that his conscience protested when he was accused of Jansenism, having abandoned Saint Augustine’s reading, *haec velle non POSSET*, and having adopted Jansenius’s reading, *haec velle non POTEST*, there can no longer be any doubt which of the two was his master.”

The second falsehood verified in Jansenius was the following. To show that the righteous sometimes sin because God withdraws from them the help of his grace—*subinde substrahit auxilium suum . . . sinens eos cadere*, “he withdraws his help from them from time to time . . . allowing them to fall”—he adduces as proof the following words, taken from one of Saint Augustine’s sermons:

> *Bene ergo aliquando Deus differt adjutorium suum, ut probet hominem, ut exerceat hominem, ut ipse sibi innotescat, nam Deum nihil latet.*  
> “God therefore rightly sometimes delays his help, in order to test a person, to exercise a person, and so that the person may become known to himself, for nothing is hidden from God” (Jansenius, volume III, book III, chapter 13, page 336, citing Saint Augustine, *Sermon 2 in the Appendix*, now sermon 343, no. 8).

The doctor who searched for the sermon was surprised by the title, *On Susanna and Joseph*! “Would Saint Augustine prove the withdrawal of grace by the example of these saints?” he said. “Is Susanna or Joseph someone to whom God allowed a grievous fall by depriving them of the inward help of his grace? Why, whom else did God help more powerfully to resist temptation?”

As he searched the sermon for the passage cited by Jansenius, the doctor continually encountered passages completely contrary to Jansenius’s purpose:

> *Non deseruit ne moreretur, cui subvenit ne adulteraretur.*  
> “He did not abandon her so that she might perish; he helped her so that she would not commit adultery.”

And afterward:

> *Tentatori resistere docuit, pugnare docuit, laborare docuit, adjutorium implorare docuit.*  
> “He taught her to resist the tempter, taught her to fight, taught her to labor, taught her to implore help.”

And after that:

> *Si de femina tentata Scriptura talis est, numquid viros deseruit?*  
> “If this is what Scripture says about a woman who was tempted, did he ever abandon men?”

And again:

> *Nec ibi defuit Deus, quia ille non erat reus.*  
> “Nor was God absent there, because that man was not guilty.”

And further:

> *Adjuvat certantem, qui certamen indixit.*  
> “He who appointed the contest helps the contestant.”

And finally:

> *Deus quando exspectat certatores suos, adjuvat eos invocatus.*  
> “When God awaits his contestants, he helps them when called upon” (numbers 1, 4, 5, 8, 10).

“There is an error in the citation,” he said. “Jansenius has taken one sermon for another. But Providence has arranged for him to direct us to this one, in which his error is refuted fully and magnificently.”

The passage cited by Jansenius had escaped his notice, and he had to undertake a less hurried reading to find it. “Certainly,” he said, looking at my doctor, “your conjecture is correct: Jansenius read Saint Augustine as you said, in the manner of N***—or at least, when it is asserted that he read Saint Augustine’s works against the Pelagians more than thirty times and his other works more than ten times, with keen attention and careful application to noting and weighing all the thoughts and expressions of the holy Doctor, *attentione acri, et adnotatione diligenti* (*Synopsis of the Life of Jansenius*)—one must except this sermon. I maintain that he never read it with his own eyes.

“Could he have reflected on so many clear testimonies that overturn his doctrine, testimonies which my own rapid and hurried glance, moving almost involuntarily three lines at a time, has presented to me? Could he have considered Saint Augustine’s care and commitment to proving that God continually assists the righteous, and that his grace is always ready to preserve them from sin in a time of temptation, even though outwardly he seems to abandon them by allowing them to be oppressed by calumnies, treated as guilty, and condemned before human tribunals; and even though he delays giving them signs of his powerful protection by openly manifesting their virtue and innocence? In short, could he have recognized all this for himself and then resolved to disguise the outward abandonment in which God left Susanna [Col. 0900A] and Joseph as a total withdrawal of grace and spiritual desertion?”

“He may perhaps have flattered himself,” said another doctor, “that once the opinion of his great, assiduous, and profound reading of Saint Augustine was firmly established, everyone would believe that he had read enough Saint Augustine for the whole world, and that posterity would consist only of authors who would leave Augustine of Hippo in the dust and read only Augustine of Ypres.”

A third falsehood, as ridiculous as it was crude, was verified. “Would that you could persuade your wife,” Saint Augustine says to Count Boniface, “to live with you in continence, so that you might render to God without hindrance what you know you owe him! But if you cannot make such a proposal to this lady, at least preserve conjugal chastity, and pray to God, who will free you from the necessary bonds in which you are engaged, that what you cannot do now you may one day be able to do:

> *Atque utinam ei posses persuadere continentiam, ut sine impedimento redderes Deo quod te debere cognoscis! Sed si cum illa agere non potes, serva saltem pudicitiam conjugalem, et roga Deum, qui te de necessitatibus eruet, ut quod non potes modo, possis aliquando.*  
> “Would that you could persuade her to continence, so that you might render to God without hindrance what you know you owe him! But if you cannot deal with her in this way, at least preserve conjugal chastity, and pray to God, who will rescue you from the necessities in which you are bound, that what you cannot do now you may be able to do one day” (*Letter* 220, no. 12, formerly 70).

You understand. What Count Boniface cannot do now, and what Saint Augustine wishes him to be able to do one day, is not to observe the precept of conjugal chastity, but to follow the counsel of living in continence; and perhaps you are reading this passage of Saint Augustine for the first time. But Jansenius, who read it ten times, conceived—and undertook to make his readers conceive, on the authority of this testimony—that the grace of preserving conjugal chastity was lacking to Count Boniface. And this is one of Jansenius’s strongest proofs for showing that, according to Saint Augustine, observance of the precepts is sometimes impossible for the faithful, not only when they do not wish to observe them, but also [Col. 0900C] when they do: “He was speaking of those who are willing, when Augustine said to Boniface: ‘At least preserve conjugal chastity, and ask God that what YOU CANNOT NOW, YOU MAY BE ABLE TO DO SOMEDAY.’” He took care to omit the first part of the passage, and his editors took care to have the final words printed in capital letters.

Do not imagine that these are the only falsifications of Saint Augustine of which Jansenius is guilty; I have discovered many others. But I wanted to limit the proofs of his bad faith to five, so that the number would correspond to the five famous propositions that his supporters no longer see in his book since they were condemned. If there is a remedy for the fascination that troubles them, this is surely it. Try it, sir, I said to the licentiate: convince yourself with your own eyes of these five instances of the most shameless fraud, and the spell will be broken, your prejudice will cease, [Col. 0900D] and you will certainly see the five propositions in Jansenius’s book. I conclude that Jansenius wrote as someone himself thoroughly convinced that the text needed considerable assistance, so that Saint Augustine’s doctrine and his own might appear to be one and the same doctrine.

At that point a chronologist entered, and when I saw that he was going to turn the conversation toward history, I drew my doctor aside and gave him a very brief account of my work. I could not keep him away for long; he was eager to converse with the chronologist, and he invited me to listen. “Then let him speak,” I said, “about the history and chronology of Saint Augustine’s works, and of his struggles against the Pelagians and the other heretics; for Saint Augustine alone now occupies all my thoughts.”

I was fully satisfied, and the subject of the conversation [Col. 0901A] was the dates that the Reverend Benedictine Fathers have assigned to each of Saint Augustine’s works. I returned with abundant material on which to exercise myself. Here the licentiate raised several objections. They were not substantial; some troublesome people arrived and asked me to leave on business. I wanted to postpone the continuation of my narrative until another day. The licentiate preferred to wait for me, and occupied himself with verifying in Saint Augustine part of what I had told him. When I rejoined him, I resumed the thread of my discourse as follows.

## II. The General Principle of Jansenius’s Heresy Falsely Attributed by Him to Saint Augustine

I had read in the Dialogues of Monsieur de Fénelon, Archbishop of Cambrai, an irresistible argument drawn from the chronology of Saint Augustine’s works, demonstrating how falsely Jansenius claimed that his heretical system of the two delectations had been taught by the holy doctor in that [Col. 0901B] famous passage: “What gives us greater delight, according to that we must act” (*Quod amplius nos delectat, secundum id operemur necesse est*) (Saint Augustine, *Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians*, no. 49).

At the name of Monsieur de Fénelon, the licentiate began to smile. “I understand you,” I said to him. “He is an author without consequence; that is the title by which your party honors him. But surely you have not been initiated into the secret meaning of this language. It was introduced only after the publication of Monsieur de Fénelon’s two final works, one being his *Pastoral Instruction in the Form of Dialogues*, the other his *Mandate for the Reception of the Constitution Unigenitus*. Until then, the Jansenists had never ceased at least to pretend to defend themselves against the attacks of the learned and pious prelate, through pamphlets to which they gave the title and appearance of replies to his writings; but, in order to boast of having refuted them, even the colors and appearances were lacking. They had to resort to a piece of bluster: [Col. 0901C] it means nothing other than that, for them, the example of this great man’s submission and docility in listening to the Mother and Mistress Church is without consequence. For if the question concerns his works, and especially the two I have just named, they are full of consequences so well demonstrated, and so deeply humiliating to Jansenism, that the leaders’ entire concern is to snatch them from the hands of their followers and, by every possible means, prevent their reading—reading that is too dangerous to the interests of the faction. I appeal to the experience of all who have generally read these two works. If they were Catholics, they were confirmed in the common belief and in obedience to the Church; if they were Jansenists in good faith, they were convinced and changed; if Jansenism was merely a mask beneath which they concealed their irreligion, they grew pale, they trembled, they did violence to themselves before the world, so as to vent their spite and rage only in terms of contempt as ridiculous as they were pompous. [Col. 0901D]

“Let us return to Monsieur de Fénelon’s argument, which demonstrates that, whatever Saint Augustine’s meaning in the passage *Quod amplius nos delectat, secundum id operemur necesse est*, that meaning is necessarily very far removed from Jansenius’s meaning and from his heretical system of the two relatively victorious delectations, which he nevertheless bases chiefly on this passage. For Saint Augustine could not at the same time have been semi-Pelagian and Jansenist, and consequently he could not have laid the foundation of Jansenism in a work that he wrote while he was semi-Pelagian. Now, what is the most certain date of Saint Augustine’s semi-Pelagianism? The year 394, when he wrote his Commentary on Several Propositions of the Epistle to the Romans.

“He himself acknowledges the semi-Pelagianism of this Commentary in the first book of his *Retractions*, [Col. 0902A] chapter 23, and Jansenius assures us that it is a work thoroughly steeped in semi-Pelagianism: ‘His commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, sprinkled with semi-Pelagianism’ (*Ejus commentaria in Epistolam ad Romanos semi-pelagianismo respersa*) (Jansenius, volume I, Index, under ‘AUGUSTINUS’). How long did he continue to remain in this error? Until he wrote his books to Simplicianus; he himself testifies to this elsewhere: ‘Behold why I said above that I myself was particularly convicted by this apostolic testimony, when, concerning this matter, I thought otherwise from what God revealed to me in resolving this question, when, as I said, I was writing to Bishop Simplicianus’ (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 4, no. 8). This refers to the other passage: ‘When I was likewise in error, thinking that the faith by which we believe in God was not a gift of God, but came from us and was in us through us, and that by it we obtained God’s gifts’ (ibid., chapter 3, no. 7).

“Thus Saint Augustine’s semi-Pelagianism lasted for another three years after he had composed his Commentary on Several Propositions of the Epistle to the Romans—that is, from 394 until 397, shortly [Col. 0902B] after he became bishop; for the books to Simplicianus were the first work he produced during his episcopate: ‘Of the books that I composed as bishop, the first two are addressed to Simplicianus, bishop of the Church of Milan’ (*Retractions*, book II, chapter 1, no. 1). If, then, the Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, which contains this famous passage, *Quod amplius nos delectat*, and so forth, was composed during those three years, can there be any doubt that Saint Augustine was then semi-Pelagian?

“There is more. He composed the Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians immediately after his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans. He himself says so: ‘After this book I expounded the Epistle of the same apostle to the Galatians’ (*Retractions*, book I, chapter 24, no. 1); and according to the Reverend Benedictine Fathers, who in this are contradicted by no one, it was in the same year, namely 394, at the height of his semi-Pelagianism. And in all likelihood Saint Augustine’s tireless pen had no sooner finished one work than it began another: still soaked in the venom of the error that Jansenius accuses him of having poured in torrents over the Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, it immediately began to compose the Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians. [Col. 0902C]

“The force of this argument against Jansenius and his disciples is redoubled. When some passages from the books Saint Augustine wrote before his episcopate are presented to them in order to explain the holy doctor’s true sentiments concerning grace and free will, do they hesitate to reject all these testimonies? Not at all; they boldly declare that without exception they are infected with semi-Pelagianism. Guess what rule Jansenius gives for determining what semi-Pelagianism properly consists in. One must consult, he says without qualification, Saint Augustine’s writings from before his episcopate; and whatever he thought in all those writings about grace and free will, Jansenius wants the semi-Pelagians [Col. 0902D] to have thought in the same way:

‘But that the Massilians admitted that interior grace without which a rational creature can do absolutely no good, in order to believe, ask, and seek, can also be demonstrated from Augustine himself. For he admits on several occasions that before assuming the episcopate he was entirely involved in the same error as the Massilians . . . Certainly, we must consult the writings from before his episcopate, so that, if possible, by his own clear testimony we may know whether at that time he excluded all interior grace of God . . . from faith and prayer’ (Jansenius, vol. I, chapter 8, p. 475).

“Therefore this [Col. 0903A] principle, *Quod amplius nos delectat, secundum id operemur necesse est*, must necessarily be understood in a sense that the semi-Pelagians accepted, since it is taken from a work that Saint Augustine places among those he composed before his episcopate (*Retractions*, book I, chapter 24, no. 1). It is therefore as senseless as it is ridiculous to establish this principle as the foundation of the system of the prevenient, undeliberated, and relatively victorious delectations. For what does Jansenius make the heresy of the semi-Pelagians consist in? Is it not in this: that, concerning the beginning of faith and salvation, they acknowledged a grace that the human will could either obey or resist (Jansenius, Proposition 4)? Consequently, they were very far from believing that every prevenient and undeliberated delectation was irresistible. There is no delusion comparable to imagining that Saint Augustine is speaking of a prevenient and undeliberated delectation when, in a work in which he ought to have thought as the semi-Pelagians did, he says that we must act according to what pleases us more.

“That, in substance, is Monsieur de Fénelon’s argument—an author without consequence, as much as you please. But if Monsieur Bayle had read the *Pastoral Instruction in the Form of Dialogues*, which unfortunately appeared only after the death of that critic, he would have admitted that a Molinist has the talent to produce sophisms that closely resemble demonstrations. [Col. 0903B]

“Monsieur de Fénelon’s thought having led me to reflect on the dates of Saint Augustine’s various works, how many new arguments did I not find for showing that Saint Augustine had nothing less than Jansenist ideas in mind when he wrote his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians?

“In a work he produced a few years earlier (*On the Two Souls*, 391), while refuting the Manichaean system of two souls—one irresistibly determined to good, the other irresistibly determined to evil—he plainly destroys the system of the two delectations. What we say to the Jansenists, namely, that once freedom of indifference is removed we can no longer acknowledge any sin, Saint Augustine says to the Manichaeans:

‘Whatever those souls do, if they do it by nature and not by will—that is, [Col. 0903C] if they lack the soul’s free movement both to do and not to do; if, finally, they are granted no power to abstain from their action—we cannot hold them guilty of sin’ (chapter 12, no. 17).

“The Manichaeans admitted that good souls were sometimes compelled to sin by the mixture of evil, just as the Jansenists maintain that the just sin because earthly delectation sometimes gains the upper hand and becomes victorious, so that it drags them irresistibly and inevitably into sin. Saint Augustine replies: If the necessity is such that resistance is impossible, these souls do not sin. ‘But are they compelled by the commixture of evil? If they are compelled in such a way that there is no power to resist, they do not sin’ (ibid., no. 18). This is precisely the reply we make to the Jansenists: If you suppose that the inclination is insurmountable and that one must necessarily succumb to temptation, the just do not sin when they yield to it. [Col. 0903D]

“Furthermore, together with the holy doctor, we maintain that the deliberation by which we suspend our consent and incline it now toward good, now toward evil, is the mark of a free will that is master of its movements, able to turn toward this object or that one and to withdraw from either:

‘That in deliberating the assent changes now toward the evil side, now toward the good: why is this not rather a sign of one soul which, by that free will, can be carried here and there, and turned back from this side and that?’ (*On Free Will*, book I, chapter 13, no. 19).

“Finally, since Saint Augustine claims that the Manichaean error concerning freedom is overturned by the experience of repentance that follows sin, we maintain that this same inner sentiment undermines the foundation of Jansenism. Saint Augustine’s reasoning is that repentance clearly testifies that a person who repents of having done wrong was able to do right:

‘For that beneficial feeling of repentance testifies both that the repentant person did wrong and that he was able to do right’ (chapter 14, no. 22).

[Col. 0904A] “Now a person who followed the impulse of earthly delectation, by which he was inevitably anticipated and irresistibly determined to sin, could not have done right. Therefore, according to Saint Augustine, Jansenism is destroyed by the experience of repentance.

“The question now is whether Saint Augustine retained these anti-Jansenist ideas while writing his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians. I consulted the three books *On Free Will*. He had begun them at Rome before his priesthood, in the year 388; but he did not publish them until eight years later, shortly before his episcopate. My doctor maintained that Saint Augustine did not finish them until the year 396, and that this date was clearly indicated by two of his letters (*Epistle* 27, formerly 32, no. 4; *Epistle* 31, formerly 34, no. 7). The Reverend Benedictine Fathers believe that he finished them in 395. It makes little [Col. 0904B] difference for the present question, since either opinion makes it perfectly clear that during the year 394 he was putting the finishing touches to these three books at the same time as he was working on his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians—a work less substantial in every respect, which was merely a diversion compared with the former, which he polished at leisure and kept for a long time in order to publish it only in its perfected form.

“I did not need a very extensive or lengthy study to discover that the holy doctor seeks in these books to prove that man’s soul becomes the slave of passion only through the choice of its free will; that it possesses and exercises the power to restrain concupiscence; and that it enjoys the ability to repress the inclination that carries it toward goods inferior to itself.

[Col. 0904C] “To be convinced of this, one need only read the recapitulation Saint Augustine gives of the first two books at the beginning of the third, where he speaks to Evodius as follows:

‘Have we accomplished anything in our last two discussions?’

“Evodius replies: ‘Certainly.’

“Saint Augustine continues:

‘You remember, I believe, that in our first discussion it appeared sufficiently clear that the human mind becomes the slave of passion through its own will alone, since it cannot be forced into this disgrace either by a superior, because that would be unjust, or by an equal, for the same reason, or by an inferior, because that is impossible. It remains, therefore, that its own movement turns its will from the Creator toward the creature when it wishes to enjoy some illicit good. If this movement is counted as guilt—and who could doubt it without deserving ridicule?—then it is certainly not natural but voluntary. In this respect it resembles the movement by which a stone is carried downward: just as the latter movement belongs to the stone, so the former belongs to the soul and is proper to it. [Col. 0904D] Yet they differ in this, that the stone has no power to restrain the movement by which it is carried downward, whereas the soul does not move, if it does not wish to do so, in such a way as to abandon higher goods and choose lower ones.’

‘AUGUSTINE. Have we accomplished anything in the two preceding discussions?

‘EVODIUS. Certainly.

‘AUGUSTINE. I therefore believe that you remember that in the first discussion it was established clearly enough that the mind becomes the slave of lust through nothing except its own will. For it can be compelled to this disgrace neither by a superior, because that is unjust, nor by an equal, nor by an inferior, because that is impossible. It remains, therefore, that its own movement turns its will to enjoy from the Creator toward the creature. If this movement is counted as guilt—for anyone who doubts this deserves ridicule—it is certainly not natural but voluntary. In this respect it resembles the movement by which a stone is carried downward: just as that movement belongs to the stone, so this one belongs to the soul. Nevertheless, they differ in that the stone has no power to restrain the movement by which it is carried downward; whereas the mind, unless it wishes to do so, does not move in such a way as to abandon higher things and choose lower ones’ (*On Free Will*, book III, chapter 1, no. 2).” [Col. 0905A]

“In a word, Saint Augustine’s entire purpose in this work is to establish against the Manichaeans the doctrine of freedom according to its true conception, which is freedom of indifference. Someone once said: ‘If Jansenius’s three volumes of Augustine were placed in a retort, they would yield nothing but the five propositions.’ One may also say that if Saint Augustine’s three books *On Free Will* were placed in a retort, they would yield nothing but this syllogism, which reduces the system of the five propositions and the two delectations to nothing:

“Sin comes only from the domination of passion; but passion is dominant only through free will; therefore sin comes only from free will.

[Col. 0905B] “What could be more opposed to the meaning Jansenius gives to these words, *Quod amplius nos delectat, secundum id operemur necesse est*! If Saint Augustine had approved this Jansenist meaning at the same time as he was completing the books *On Free Will*, in which he attributes to the human soul the power to repress and restrain the movement that carries it toward the object of its pleasure, he would have fallen into the most shameful contradiction with himself. For the contradiction would have been between thoughts and opinions that he held simultaneously; consequently, he would no longer deserve credence. He would not merit the effort of investigating what he did or did not think, nor would anyone need to trouble himself to determine whether his authority was contrary or favorable.

“But since the supposition of such a contradiction in Saint Augustine’s mind is fanciful and ridiculous, if one nevertheless judged it extremely [Col. 0905C] difficult to reconcile what the holy doctor wrote in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians with what he wrote in his books *On Free Will*, could one hesitate for even a moment to explain—or even correct—what he wrote in that Commentary according to the meaning of what he wrote in his books *On Free Will*, which are a more substantial work, on which he labored longer and more carefully, and which he published later?

“Thus the Jansenists are reduced either to accepting the Catholic explanation that Monsieur de Fénelon gave of the words *Quod amplius nos delectat*, and so forth, or to dishonoring Saint Augustine in more than one way. They must establish that the holy doctor was semi-Pelagian until 394; that in that year he became a Jansenist while writing his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians; that in the same year he fell back into semi-Pelagianism while completing his books *On Free Will*; that in 397 he again became a Jansenist while composing his books to Simplicianus; and I shall show that, on this reckoning, he will once more have fallen back into semi-Pelagianism when writing the books against Faustus in 400. [Col. 0905D]

“For this purpose, from among a multitude of passages I shall choose only one, in which the holy doctor expressly asserts that man, in the state of restored nature, has the same power to refuse his consent to an illicit pleasure that he had before his fall:

‘Whether there is any rational creature that can be delighted by nothing illicit is a great question. But if there is such a creature, man was not made in that class, nor was that angelic nature which did not remain in the truth. Rather, rational beings were made in such a class that they possessed the possibility of restraining delectation from what is illicit; by failing to restrain it, they sinned. Great, therefore, is human nature, since it is restored through that same possibility, through which, if it had wished, it would not have fallen’ (*Against Faustus*, book XXII, chapter 28).

“Man, Saint Augustine says, had the possibility of abstaining from illicit things before his sin, and human nature is now restored by that same possibility. [Col. 0906A]

“There he is, semi-Pelagian for the third time, and twice a relapse; and what kind of semi-Pelagianism! Of the worst kind, one that differs in no respect from pure Pelagianism concerning grace, since it consists in recognizing no prevenient and undeliberated delectation that is irresistible—neither the heavenly, nor the earthly, nor that of grace, nor that of concupiscence. This is precisely the Catholic dogma that Jansenius treats as a Pelagian heresy (*The Augustinus*, vol. I, book VII, chapter 2, p. 400), in order to agree with Calvin, but not with Saint Augustine. For he could not accommodate the holy doctor to his own ideas without imposing upon him both the wrong kind and the wrong duration of his semi-Pelagianism.

[Col. 0906B] “I became convinced of this immediately, and for that purpose I began comparing Jansenius’s various censures of the works that came from Saint Augustine’s pen before his episcopate with the judgment Saint Augustine himself passed on them in the first book of his *Retractions*. What does Jansenius think of the three books *On Free Will*? They are no more free from semi-Pelagianism than the others. The holy doctor even slipped into them a Pelagian error concerning the possibility of the state of pure nature (*On the State of Pure Nature*, book III, chapter 19). Jansenius nevertheless adds that this was merely an imprudence, a blunder, a daydream that escaped Saint Augustine (Jansenius, vol. I, book VIII, chapter 8, p. 474). These are doubtless measured terms, and Jansenius seriously wishes to appear considerate toward this work. Why? Because Saint Augustine made too long and too exact an apology for it, and claimed to purge it of every affinity with Pelagianism. Jansenius and his disciples are not, at bottom, convinced that he succeeded, and they are not especially grateful to him [Col. 0906C] for failing humbly to recognize and acknowledge this imprudence, this blunder, this daydream.

“As for the book of the Eighty-Three Different Questions, and the books *On the Quantity of the Soul*, *On the Blessed Life*, and *On the Spirit and the Letter*, they are thoroughly steeped in semi-Pelagianism, just like the Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans:

‘His Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, sprinkled with semi-Pelagianism . . . Likewise, the book of the Eighty-Three Questions, together with the books *On the Quantity of the Soul*, *On the Blessed Life*, and *On the Spirit and the Letter*’ (Jansenius, vol. I, Index, under ‘AUGUSTINUS’).

“Thoroughly steeped in semi-Pelagianism—great God! And Saint Augustine, in the first book of his *Retractions*, does not retract or correct a single word concerning Pelagianism or semi-Pelagianism in all his books, except for the Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans. Even there, although the holy doctor acknowledges its semi-Pelagianism, he is far from regarding the book as thoroughly steeped in it. He would have judged the work worthy of the fire and would not have limited himself to reforming four sentences, all of which certainly are not semi-Pelagian. [Col. 0906D]

“You see: to reconcile Jansenius’s doctrine with Saint Augustine’s, one must add a supplement to this Father’s *Retractions* and, in composing it, follow the religious blueprint imagined by Jansenius. This supplement would be a thousand times more considerable, both in extent and in the importance of its subject, than the two books of the *Retractions*. All the propositions Saint Augustine advanced that do not fit the Jansenist system would there be branded as semi-Pelagian errors. Their number would be large, and they would not be a collection of trifles, as Jansenius regarded everything Saint Augustine corrected in his two books of the *Retractions*:

‘For he considered the things he later deleted in the books of the *Retractions* to be of little importance, and almost blemishes of words rather than of things’ (*Synopsis of the Life of Jansenius*).

[Col. 0907A] The licentiate could not help expressing his astonishment that the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, written by Saint Augustine against the Pelagians and during his episcopate, should be found in the list of works that Jansenius accuses of semi-Pelagianism. “And are you not astonished,” I said to him, “that the book of the Eighty-Three Different Questions is also among them? Does the holy doctor not testify that, although he had composed the different parts of this lengthy work at various times after his conversion, he was already bishop when he had these questions and answers, which had until then been scattered here and there among his friends, collected, put in order, and reduced to a single body? Thus this book must be counted among those that the holy doctor completed and published during his episcopate:

‘But since they had been scattered across many sheets . . . , I ordered, already being bishop, that they be collected and made into a single book’ (*Retractions*, book I, chapter 26, beginning).

“It is at least beyond doubt [Col. 0907B] that Saint Augustine reviewed these questions twice: once when publishing them at the beginning of his episcopate, and a second time when writing his *Retractions* at the end of his life; and he saw no trace of semi-Pelagianism in them.

“Jansenius, incomparably more clear-sighted, and who understood Saint Augustine better than Saint Augustine understood himself, perceives and seizes this heresy at Question 68 (no. 5), where, Jansenius says, Saint Augustine speaks of faith as he does in the passage of the Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans which, by his own admission, is semi-Pelagian. The truth is that the passage from the book of the Eighty-Three Different Questions is thoroughly Catholic. Here it is, as Jansenius cites it:

‘That those who had come could not come unless they were called, and that, once called, they should come—that is, believe—is within free will’ (Jansenius, vol. I, book VIII, chapter 8, p. 473).

“These words should not be compared with those in the Commentary on the Epistle [Col. 0907C] to the Romans:

‘Therefore, what we believe is ours, while what we do well is his, and so forth; it is ours to believe and to will, but it is his to grant believers and those who will the ability to do good, and so forth’ (Saint Augustine, *Exposition of Certain Propositions of the Epistle to the Romans*, nos. 60–61).

“They have far greater affinity and resemblance to this passage from *On the Spirit and the Letter*:

‘To consent to God’s calling, or to dissent from it, as I have said, belongs to one’s own will’ (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 34, no. 60).

“This passage, and another in which Saint Augustine teaches so clearly that God has a sincere will to save all human beings, drew from Jansenius, in the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, a censure of semi-Pelagianism, even though this book was written against the Pelagians and during Saint Augustine’s episcopate.

“On this occasion, and on many others, Jansenius employs an expedient that may serve as a method and rule for the author whom the party will commission to prepare the supplement to Saint [Col. 0907D] Augustine’s *Retractions*. The silence that the holy doctor maintains in his *Retractions* regarding so many instances of semi-Pelagianism that, in Jansenius’s eyes, swarm throughout his writings is certainly very inconvenient for Jansenius; but he disposes of the difficulty by establishing as a principle that we must persuade ourselves that the holy doctor revoked and condemned an opinion he had held whenever we clearly see that he later taught the contrary:

‘Did he not silently revoke the earlier opinion by neglecting it?’ (Jansenius, vol. I, book VIII, chapter 15, p. 513).

“This is not badly conceived, especially since he presents his own judgment as evidence concerning this alleged contradiction. But would one not have the right to answer Jansenius that this principle has no place when an author has left us books containing the revision and correction of all his works? For then, are not those more reasonable who maintain that we should admit no genuine contradictions except those that the author himself acknowledged—especially if he is assumed to be infinitely enlightened? [Col. 0908A]

“Let us return to the subject of your astonishment,” I said to the licentiate. “Is it not ridiculous that Saint Augustine’s semi-Pelagianism should begin or end whenever Jansenius finds convenient; that it should begin at his baptism, persist for several years of his episcopate, and still not have ended at the time of his first battles against the Pelagians? My doctor had said in the conversation I witnessed, concerning the dates of Saint Augustine’s works, that Jansenius and his disciples made the holy doctor semi-Pelagian against his will throughout the entire period preceding his episcopate. I verified his proposition in this way.

“Whatever Jansenius may claim, it is manifest that all semi-Pelagianism is reduced or related to a single point: namely, denying that the human will must necessarily be anticipated by God’s grace in order to begin to act beneficially for salvation. [Col. 0908B] And this is the only error in which Saint Augustine declares that he remained for some time before his episcopate. ‘For I did not think,’ he says, ‘that God’s grace preceded us in any other sense concerning faith than that the truth must be proclaimed to us so that we might be able to believe. But as for the consent we give to the truth proclaimed to us, I thought that it came from our own resources and was in us through our own powers’:

‘For I did not think that faith was preceded by the grace of God . . . except in the sense that we could not believe unless the proclamation of the truth came first; but I thought that, once the Gospel had been preached to us, our consenting to it was our own affair and came from ourselves’ (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 3, no. 7).

That being so, Saint Augustine was not a semi-Pelagian when he taught the doctrine opposed to the error of which he accuses himself in this passage. He was therefore not yet a semi-Pelagian in 389, since, in the first [Col. 0908C] book on Genesis, which he wrote that year against the Manichaeans, he says that Jesus Christ had produced faith in the hearts of believers, a faith that caused him admiration:

> “They praise our Lord in the Gospel for having marvelled at the faith of believers. But who had produced that very faith in them, if not the one who marvelled at it?”

(*Book I on Genesis against the Manichaeans*, ch. 8, no. 14).

He was therefore not yet a semi-Pelagian in 390, since, in the book *On True Religion*, which he composed that year, he generally maintains that every good is from God, in order to conclude that all salvation is from God. The beginning of salvation is included in the conclusion, just as in the premise:

> “All salvation, however, is from him from whom every good comes; and every good is from God; therefore all salvation is from God.”

He was therefore not yet a semi-Pelagian in 391, since, in the book *On Two Souls*, which he was composing at that time, he offers a prayer to God asking for the conversion of certain Manichaeans who had been his friends (*Book on Two Souls*, ch. 15, no. 24). [Col. 0908D] In his *Retractions*, Saint Augustine shows by this evidence that, while fighting against the Manichaeans, he recognized the necessity of prevenient grace even for the very beginning of conversion:

> “Thus, while praying, I already held by faith that not only are those who have been converted to God aided by his grace, so that they may advance and be perfected . . . but also that their conversion to God itself belongs to God’s grace. For I prayed for those who were exceedingly estranged from him, and I prayed that they might be converted to him.”

(*Book I of the Retractions*, ch. 15, no. 8).

He was therefore not yet a semi-Pelagian in 393, for it is probable that in that year, or shortly beforehand, he wrote the second book on Free Will, in which he asserts that the lesser goods, just as much as the greater ones, are from God; that every good thought comes only from God; and that a person cannot rise from his fall unless God extends and lends him his hand:

[Col. 0909A]

> “The abundance and greatness of God’s goodness has provided not only great goods, but also moderate and very small ones.”

(*Book II on Free Will*, ch. 19, no. 50).

And afterward:

> “But hold fast to unshaken piety, and let no good appear to you—whether in feeling, understanding, or thinking in any manner—that is not from God.”

And again:

> “But since a human being cannot rise of his own accord as he fell of his own accord, let us therefore hold fast in firm faith to the hand of God extended to us from above, that is, to our Lord Jesus Christ.”

(Ibid., ch. 20, no. 54).

[Col. 0909B] Saint Augustine uses these three passages in his *Retractions* to show that, long before the Pelagian heresy, he had taught that every good movement of free will is a gift from God. Therefore, after reporting several other testimonies from the third book, he concludes as follows:

> “Behold, before the Pelagian heresy had arisen, this is how we argued. For when all goods were said to be from God—that is, great, moderate, and very small goods—free will is certainly found among the moderate goods . . . But its good use is already a virtue, which is counted among the great goods . . . It follows, then, that the good use of free will is also from God.”

(*Book I of the Retractions*, ch. 9, no. 6).

The continuation of this study led me to seek out the book by the Reverend Father Le Porcq, of the Congregation of the Oratory, a learned theologian and zealous defender of the Catholic faith. I gladly adopted his view, namely, that Saint Augustine only began to incline toward semi-Pelagianism in 394, when he undertook to explain certain propositions from Saint Paul’s Epistle to the Romans and had reached this one: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” Indeed, this is the only place where Saint Augustine expressly acknowledges semi-Pelagianism; it is the only place that the priests of Marseille cited to support their error by Saint Augustine’s authority—unless one also counts a word from his Letter 49 to Deogratias (*Hilary’s Letter to Augustine*, no. 3).

I have seen Jansenists mock Father Le Porcq—for they are mockers. They sent this [Col. 0909C] good Father back to his primer because, they said, in these words of Saint Augustine he had taken a plural for a singular:

> “My error is sufficiently indicated by certain of my minor works, written before my episcopate, etc.”

(*Book on the Predestination of the Saints*, ch. 3, no. 7).

Apparently, according to the grammar of Port-Royal, it is a lesser fault to extend the meaning of terms than to restrict it.

Whatever the case may be, if Saint Augustine’s semi-Pelagianism is to be sought somewhere besides the *Commentary on Certain Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans*, it seems necessary to confine ourselves to examining the propositions that the holy doctor corrected in the books of his *Retractions*.

Respect for him, as well as reason, forbids us to think that, when revising his works, he failed to notice semi-Pelagianism wherever he had insinuated it, or that, having noticed it, he concealed it in order to reform only trivial matters: “stains of little importance, and almost more of words than of things” [Col. 0909D] (*Synopsis of the Life of Jansenius*). Now, if we rely on an examination of the propositions that the holy doctor corrects in his books of the *Retractions*, it is the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians* that must be counted alongside the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, and that verifies the plural in Saint Augustine’s words.

For in his *Retractions* the holy doctor judges that this proposition from the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians* requires correction:

> “The grace of God is that by which sins are forgiven us, so that we may be reconciled to God; peace, however, is that by which we are reconciled to God.”

(*Book I of the Retractions*, ch. 24, no. 2).

He judges this necessary in order to exclude the semi-Pelagian meaning, which attributed to God’s grace only the remission of sins, but not reconciliation. For in the semi-Pelagian system, since reconciliation is the fruit of nature’s desires and first efforts, it is not properly a grace in itself, but only insofar as it presupposes [Col. 0910A] the remission of sins merited by the blood of Jesus Christ. In this way semi-Pelagianism returned to Pelagianism, as Saint Augustine took care to observe elsewhere.

Thus we have reached the point from which we began, and we arrive at a new proof showing that Saint Augustine was a semi-Pelagian when he composed the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians* and that, consequently, he could not have given a Jansenist meaning to these words: “We must act according to that which delights us more.”

The licentiate then asked me whether I had anything to add to the manner in which Monsieur de Fénelon explained this passage, or to the proofs by which he supported his explanation. It seemed to me that he was not very familiar with that explanation and wished to know it.

“Saint Augustine,” I said, “as Monsieur de Fénelon demonstrates, is speaking of a habitual delight, whether infused or acquired through frequently repeated acts. We can cease to possess it by [Col. 0910B] changing it into another, entirely contrary delight; but it is necessarily the mainspring of our life and determines our conduct so long as we make no effort to suppress and extinguish it.

“This habitual delight is a love that dominates in our heart because we have freely surrendered our heart to it, or because we have caused it to arise through a succession of deliberate acts of complacency. It is compatible with the freedom that the schools call antecedent freedom, which applies to things said to be free in their causes but not in themselves. Therefore, the necessity of acting that it imposes is only moral and consequent—the same kind of necessity that arises from an inveterate habit. Such a habit can be completely overcome, though with great difficulty; yet, while it remains, it cannot fail to lead us to perform the same actions that produced it.

> ‘We must act according to that which delights us more.’

“The demonstration that Monsieur de Fénelon gives of this meaning, both from consideration of the text itself and from comparison with what precedes and follows, leaves nothing to be desired except the following [Col. 0910C] reflection, which serves greatly to confirm it.

“The principal heretics whom Saint Augustine was combating at that time were the Manichaeans. They abused certain passages of the Gospel in which the Savior declares that a good tree cannot bear bad fruit and that a bad tree cannot bear good fruit. They claimed that these words plainly signified and established their ridiculous doctrine of two coeternal natures, one being the nature of evil, which can never do any good, and the other the nature of good, which can never do any evil. From this they further concluded that there are two souls in every human being: one good, the principle of good actions, and the other evil, the principle of evil actions.

“Saint Augustine replied that these two trees designated [Col. 0910D] not the two natures or the two imaginary souls of the Manichaeans, but the differing dispositions of a single will, which exists in all human beings. For although it lies within each person’s power to make his will good or evil, nevertheless the will cannot act badly while it is good, nor act well while it is evil. This response of Saint Augustine is found in almost all the books he wrote against the Manichaeans. It is impossible to compare the various texts in which it occurs with the passage under discussion in the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians* without agreeing that the thought is the same.

“Here is one passage taken from the book against Adimantus, which Saint Augustine published in the same year, 394:

> ‘These two trees are most clearly set forth as representing two human beings, namely, the righteous and the unrighteous, because no one can do good unless he changes his will. That this lies within our power he teaches elsewhere, where he says: “Either make the tree good,” etc.’

(*Book against Adimantus*, ch. 26).

[Col. 0911A] “The holy doctor was then completely filled with this same thought; there is no work that he composed around that time in which he does not repeat it.

“In the same year, 394, he composed his work whose subject is our Lord’s Sermon on the Mount. There, after giving this same thought every possible turn and treatment, he concludes as follows:

> ‘What, then, are the fruits by which we recognize a bad tree? The Apostle says: “The works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication, impurity,” etc. And what are the fruits by which we recognize a good tree? The same Apostle immediately continues: “But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace,” etc.’

(*Book II on the Sermon on the Mount*, ch. 24, no. 81).

“The passage from chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Galatians cited here by Saint Augustine is the very one on the occasion of which, in his *Commentary on that Epistle*, he said: ‘We must act according to that which delights us more.’ Could one wish for more convincing proof that he intends the same thing in both texts?

[Col. 0911B] “Let Saint Augustine now be questioned: ‘What did you mean by these words, “That which delights us more”?’ He would reply: ‘Is it not clear that I meant the inward and habitual disposition by which we are a good or a bad tree?’ And what is this disposition? ‘It is,’ he would say, ‘the one we have formed voluntarily by surrendering our heart to the love of virtue or vice.’ And what did you mean by these words, ‘We must act according to that’? ‘Is there any doubt,’ he would exclaim, ‘that I intended to indicate the fruits necessarily borne by a good or bad tree while it remains such and makes no effort to change? And what are these fruits? Must one ask? They are the outward and perceptible works—the good or evil conduct—by which people’s character is revealed: “You will know them by their fruits.”’

[Col. 0911C] “Finally, we are compelled to recognize that the interpretation of these famous words is contained in the following words, which we read later in the *Commentary*:

> ‘It is certainly clear that we live according to that which we have pursued. But we will pursue what we have loved. Therefore, if two things stand opposed—a commandment and a carnal habit—and both are loved, we will pursue that which we have loved more.’

(Saint Augustine, *Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians*, no. 54).

“If Jansenius cannot show us an indeliberate delight in these words, ‘What we have loved, what we have pursued,’ how does he hope to make us see it in these other words, ‘That which delights us more’?

[Col. 0911D] “I was curious to see whether Saint Augustine had remained consistent in this manner of thinking and speaking that he had developed while disputing against the Manichaeans. I found that he had not forgotten it when writing against the Donatists:

> ‘The good person always has good works and life, and the evil person bad ones.’

(*Book III against the Letters of Petilian*, ch. 44, no. 53).

Nor had he reformed it when fighting against the Pelagians:

> ‘Works cannot be the works of an evil will when they are good, nor can they be the works of a good will when they are evil.’

(*Book I against Julian*, ch. 8, no. 38).

“I assured myself that he almost always took care to point out that he was speaking of a habit of delight or love freely acquired, from which a person had the power to strip himself:

> ‘We are therefore commanded to take away something from the weight of desire, so that it may be added to the weight of charity. For it lies within a person’s power to change his will for the better. Let him take delight in justice in such a way that he prefers it to all other delights belonging to the senses.’

(*Letter 157*, ch. 2, no. 9. See *Book I of the Retractions*, ch. 22, no. 4; and Sermon 159, *On the Words of the Apostle*, ch. 5).

“The conclusion of all this is as evident as it is natural. Jansenius’s abuse of a multitude of [Col. 0912A] texts, which he applies to his two prevenient, indeliberate, and relatively victorious delights, is genuine brigandage, since these texts rather designate two deliberate delights, two free loves of the human will, which the holy doctor opposed to the two natures and two souls of the Manichaeans. This doctrine, together with the manner of expressing it, remained with him thereafter from the controversies he had held with those heretics. Such is this language, so familiar to him:
