> ‘The mind is borne by love as though by a weight, wherever it is borne. Nor do bodies themselves seek anything through their weights more than souls do through their loves. Delight is, as it were, the soul’s weight. Delight therefore orders the soul.’

(*Letter 157*, ch. 2, no. 9; Letter 55 to Januarius, ch. 10, no. 18, formerly Letter 119; *Book VI on Music*, ch. 11, no. 29).

“The licentiate had the courtesy to oblige me to stop there, but he made me promise to finish that evening everything I had to say to him before turning to the important subject of the perfection of [Col. 0912B] justice. He returned at the appointed hour, and I addressed him as follows.

## III. Jansenius’s False Key to the Works of Saint Augustine

The victorious delight that Jansenius claims to be the medicinal grace of Jesus Christ proper to our condition is, according to him, the *quo* assistance of which Saint Augustine speaks in *Correction and Grace* (chs. 10–12). The holy doctor calls it this in opposition to the *sine quo non* assistance, which belonged to the condition of the first man before the fall.

I have always been firmly convinced that Jansenius learned from Luther and Calvin, and in no way from Saint Augustine, the application and use he makes of the distinction between these two kinds of assistance. Before consulting my doctor on the matter, I had already devoted myself, with some success, to refuting the absurdities that the false [Col. 0912C] interpreter of Saint Augustine expounds in an emphatic and presumptuous tone in his book *The Grace of the First Man and of the Angels*.

If we are to believe him, the holy doctor established in the distinction between these two kinds of assistance the true and immovable foundation that supports the entire body of Christian doctrine concerning the grace of the Savior:

> “He places a true and immovable foundation on which the whole doctrine concerning the grace of Christ the Savior rests; whoever does not understand it, and attempts to move it from its place, must fall into the confusion of countless delusions.”

(Jansenius, vol. II, *The Grace of the First Man and of the Angels*, ch. 17, pp. 169 ff.).

If we are to believe him, this distinction is the true and only key that opens the entrance to Saint Augustine’s writings, without which anyone who attempts to enter them will grope about like a blind man at [Col. 0912D] noon:

> “For this is the true key by which access to his writings must be opened; without it, anyone who attempts to enter them will grope like a blind man at midday.”

It is a thread that must always be held so as not to go astray and become lost in the labyrinth of the holy doctor’s works:

> “Whoever, having cast this foundation, follows that distinction as a thread in the labyrinth,” etc.

Finally, this distinction bears the same relation to Saint Augustine’s doctrine as definitions and axioms bear to a geometrical problem:

> “In geometry, if you are given the first principles, everything is given; here, if you embrace those two kinds of assistance,” etc.

Jansenius is here insulting the credulity of the human race.

When an author creates or expounds a system of doctrine, does he normally report only once what contains the foundation, the key, the thread, and the principle of that doctrine, without taking care to impress it upon his readers at every opportunity? [Col. 0913A] Jansenius himself may serve as an example. He established the false interpretation and manifest abuse of this passage from Saint Augustine as the foundation of his heretical system. Does he not speak of it almost everywhere? Does he not continually direct his reader back to consideration of the two kinds of assistance, *quo* and *sine quo non*, and to the manner in which he wants them to be understood? Did he not copy the sole passage in which Saint Augustine mentions these two kinds of assistance as many as 170 times? Father Deschamps counted them (*Deschamps, On the Heresy of Jansenius*, disputation 3, ch. 3, no. 1).

When an author creates or expounds a system of doctrine, does he normally refrain from disclosing what contains its foundation, key, thread, and principle until after he has given the public the entire body of the system? Is it a secret and a mystery that he communicates only accidentally, or that escapes him by chance? Does he not rather begin by explaining and developing it? And can one doubt that he ought to proceed deliberately in this way, since he writes in order [Col. 0913B] to make himself understood?

Does Jansenius follow another method? Immediately after his *History of the Pelagian Heresy* and his preliminary book, does he not place his book *The Grace of the First Man and of the Angels*, a considerable part of which he devotes to explaining the two kinds of assistance, *quo* and *sine quo non*? Does he wait until the end of the ten books *On the Grace of the Savior* to discuss these two kinds of assistance once again and at length, or does he not do so already in chapter 4 of Book II? It is clear that this should have been Saint Augustine’s procedure if he had intended to enclose in the distinction between these two kinds of assistance the foundation, key, thread, and principle of his entire doctrine.

Jansenius attempts to create an illusion regarding the first point. Wishing to indicate the difference between the grace proper to the state of innocence and the medicinal grace given to us through Jesus Christ, he says:

> “The former Augustine commonly calls the assistance *sine quo non*; the latter, the assistance *cum quo*.”

(*Index*, vol. III, under “GRACE”).

Without stopping to fault Jansenius for writing *adjutorium cum quo*—“assistance with which”—where Saint Augustine wrote *adjutorium quo*—“assistance by which”—or for giving these expressions a meaning entirely opposed to Saint Augustine’s thought and wording, I maintain that the holy doctor names the *quo* and *sine quo non* assistance in only one place, and that Jansenius’s falsehood on this point is a tacit admission of what the saint would have had to do if the foundation, key, thread, and principle of Jansenism and of Saint Augustine’s doctrine had been the same.

But when did Saint Augustine happen to speak for the first and only time of these two kinds of assistance? At the end of his life, after the complete defeat of the Pelagians, by a sort of accident, as he himself recounts:

[Col. 0913D]

> “I wrote to those same monks of Hadrumetum a second book, which I entitled *Correction and Grace*, when I was informed that one of them had said that no one ought to be corrected,” etc.

(*Book II of the Retractions*, final chapter).

Therefore, if the distinction between the *quo* and *sine quo non* assistance is the foundation, key, thread, and principle of Saint Augustine’s doctrine, then for more than twenty years this Father published writings while taking care at the same time to withhold their meaning from everyone. He wanted the foundation on which his entire doctrine rests to be known neither to Catholics nor to Pelagians, and he gave them good reason to believe that its foundation was ruined or doubtful. He concealed the key without which there can be no opening through which one may be admitted into the sanctuary of the sublime truths he teaches. People vainly flattered themselves that they had penetrated far into his system, while they were a hundred leagues from his thought. He begrudged his readers this fortunate thread of the distinction between the two kinds of assistance, for want of which they wandered [Col. 0914A] like *Andabatae*—blind gladiators—in the dark labyrinth of his works, unable to escape.

If the difficulties encountered in the holy doctor’s text are to be, in Jansenius’s forceful expression, frightful monsters and Minotaurs for anyone who has not grasped this thread—

> “Terrified as though confronted by monsters”

(Jansenius, vol. I, *The Grace of the First Man and of the Angels*, ch. 17, p. 170)—

did he mean that they were such only for the scholastics who lacked the intelligence to notice the thread presented to them by the book *Correction and Grace*, and not for those who, before the publication of *Correction and Grace*, could not have seen this thread anywhere?

Besides, how did Saint Augustine’s books serve at that time to convince the Pelagians? They were sealed letters for everyone. They offered the solution to a problem no less obscure than the problem itself, since the solution presupposed definitions and axioms that had yet to be supplied.

[Col. 0914B] If, unfortunately, Saint Augustine had died before writing *Correction and Grace*, or if there had never been any monks of Hadrumetum to give him the occasion to write that book, all the doctors down to our own time—and Jansenius himself—would have understood nothing at all in Saint Augustine’s works.

Thanks to this monk, who was concerned with practice, who wanted to benefit from Saint Augustine’s doctrine in order to give himself room and shake off the yoke of correction—or rather, thanks to his zealous confrères, who came to report him to Saint Augustine—Jansenius, taking advantage of the reflections of Luther and Calvin, discovered the foundation, key, thread, and principle of Saint Augustine’s doctrine. What a tale!

But what an amusing panegyrist Jansenius is! He never ceases to praise emphatically the solidity of Saint Augustine’s writings, yet he depicts him as an architect [Col. 0914C] who builds in the air and does not think of laying foundations for his building until after completing it. He enhances the value of the treasure that the holy doctor left to the Church in the monuments of his pen; and, if we are to believe him, Saint Augustine had securely enclosed this treasure, had kept and hidden its key throughout his life, and came very close to carrying it with him into the next world.

Jansenius exaggerates the sublimity, subtlety, and depth of Saint Augustine’s doctrine. According to him, it is a labyrinth from which one cannot escape without the fortunate thread of the distinction between the *quo* and *sine quo non* assistance. Jansenius would have Saint Augustine attach this thread not at the entrance of the labyrinth but at its opposite end, and make the thread so delicate that it remained invisible to every mind for twelve centuries, while being proportioned only to Jansenius’s Dutch eye!

Finally, Jansenius transforms Saint Augustine into an Archimedes, into a geometrical theologian—but one who overturns geometry, who begins at the end and ends at the beginning.

[Col. 0914D] From that moment I became firmly convinced that the distinction between the two kinds of assistance had no place in the holy doctor’s controversies with the Pelagians, nor in his system concerning the necessity or nature of what is properly called the medicinal grace of Jesus Christ.

I immediately recalled several passages that I had marked in the course of my reading and that clearly and absolutely refute the chimera Jansenius imagined when he decided to take Saint Augustine’s *quo* assistance for efficacious actual grace, which effects willing, and the *sine quo non* assistance for sufficient actual grace, which gives possibility. He then concluded that efficacious grace is so proper to our condition that it was in no way found in Adam’s condition, and that sufficient grace is so [Col. 0915A] proper to Adam’s condition that it is in no way found in ours.

I selected two of these passages that seem decisive to me. I have already cited the first:

> “But rational creatures were made in such a way that they possessed the possibility of restraining delight from what is unlawful. Great, therefore, is the human creature, since through that possibility he is restored—the same possibility by which, had he wished, he would not have fallen.”

(*Book XXII against Faustus*, ch. 28).

In what terms could Saint Augustine better express that the grace of possibility is not peculiar to Adam’s condition and also belongs to ours, than by saying here that a human being is raised from his fall by the same grace of possibility that would have prevented him from falling, had he wished?

The other passage could not have been known to Jansenius:

> “How will it be true that God made the human being upright? Was he upright without having a good will, but possessing only its possibility? Then he was also evil without having an evil will, but possessing only [Col. 0915B] its possibility; and his good will was from himself, and what is written would be false: ‘The will is prepared by the Lord,’ and, ‘God works in you to will.’”

(*Unfinished Work*, Book V, no. 57).

Are these words ambiguous as an indication that the grace of willing, or the grace that effects willing, is not peculiar to our condition and also belonged to Adam’s condition? By employing the authority of Saint Paul, who writes that God works willing in us—“God is the one who works in you to will” (Philippians 2:13)—the holy doctor proves against Julian that good will in Adam was a gift of God. Is this not a formal contradiction of Jansenius, who boldly asserts that this text of the Apostle must be understood of the *quo* assistance and designates a grace far more powerful and of an entirely different nature from that which belonged to Adam’s condition?

> “The Apostle calls for an assistance of a very different and much more powerful nature when he writes to the Philippians: ‘It is God who works in you to will and to accomplish.’”

(Vol. III, Book II, ch. 26, p. 209).

[Col. 0915C] The two testimonies of Saint Augustine that I have just reported ought to completely disconcert the Jansenists, especially the last. It pulverizes their imaginary foundation, breaks their false key, and severs their deceptive thread. There is no way to evade it. It is clear; it comes from a book written against the Pelagians several years after the publication of *Correction and Grace*, and near the end of Saint Augustine’s life.

I could not pursue my investigations any further without returning to my oracle. I never found him more difficult to approach. He was reasoning with geometers. Wanting at any cost to bring Saint Augustine into the discussion, I began by praising their method and complaining that Saint Augustine had not cultivated it sufficiently to define exactly the terms he used.

“Did he ever fail to do so?” my doctor abruptly replied.

“If he had always done so,” I answered, “I would not be so greatly troubled to know what he meant by the *quo* assistance and the *sine quo non* assistance.”

“Go,” he said, “and see whether he has asserted a single thing about the *quo* assistance that is not a necessary and immediate conclusion from this definition he gave:

[Col. 0915D]

> ‘It is the Savior’s mercy that attaches itself inseparably to the predestined, whether when they are converted, when they struggle, or when they attain the crown.’”

I asked no more and returned as quickly as possible to resume my study.

[Note: [Col. 0915D] Everything that will be said here about the *quo* assistance and the *sine quo non* assistance is merely the development and proof of what Father Annat said in a Latin work entitled *Augustinus a Baianis Vindicatus* (*Augustine Vindicated from the Baianists*), Book VII, ch. 6, section 8, toward the end. A Thomist author named Étienne Lorenzoni, a priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of Italy, advances something much more singular [Col. 0916D]. He maintains that Saint Augustine never even had the initial thought of distinguishing Adam’s grace from ours in the three famous chapters—10, 11, and 12—of *Correction and Grace*. His work is entitled *Dissertatio theologico-analytica, etc., seu de vera et falsa adjutoriorum distinctione* (*Theologico-Analytical Dissertation, etc., or On the True and False Distinction of the Assistances*). Padua, 1729.]

[Col. 0916A] At first it seemed to me supremely evident that Saint Augustine, when treating of the *quo* and *sine quo non* assistance, compares Adam only with the predestined. How did Jansenius fail to notice this?

> “What, then? Did Adam not have God’s grace? Indeed he did; he had great grace, but a different one. He was among the good . . . But the saints in this life, to whom the grace of deliverance belongs, are among the evil.”

(*Correction and Grace*, ch. 11, no. 29).

Did he read these words and those that follow thirty times without penetrating their meaning, which is so manifest?

> “To the first man, therefore, an assistance of perseverance was given—not one by which he would be made to persevere, but one without which he could not persevere by free will. But now the saints predestined to the kingdom of God are given no such assistance of perseverance.”

(Ibid., ch. 12, no. 34).

A little earlier the holy doctor had called Adam’s grace, which is under discussion here, “the power of perseverance” (*prima erat perseverantiae potestas*, “at first there was the power of perseverance”), and the grace of our condition, which he contrasts with Adam’s grace, “the blessedness of perseverance” (*novissima erit perseverantiae felicitas*, “last will be the blessedness of perseverance”) [Col. 0916B] (Ibid., no. 33).

Fearing that all these features might still be insufficient to make clear that he is speaking of a grace God grants only to the predestined, he adds the following warning:

> “I am speaking here of those who are predestined to the kingdom of God, whose number is so certain that no one is added to them and no one is taken away from them.”

(Ch. 13, no. 39).

Finally, it is beyond doubt that Saint Augustine, in order to explain his doctrine concerning the difference between the graces and helps in question, composed two books: one entitled *On the Predestination of the Saints*, the other entitled *On the Gift of Perseverance*. For his purpose in both was to answer the complaints made by the priests of Marseille against the distinction between the *quo* help and the *sine quo non* help; and he was prompted to compose them by these words from Hilary’s letter: “They are troubled that grace should be divided in this way: that which was given either then to the first man [Col. 0916C] or is now given to all, so that he received perseverance—not that by it he would persevere, etc.” (*Hilary’s Letter to Augustine*, no. 6). Now the grace that is the principal subject of these books, and consequently the *quo* help of the book *On Correction and Grace*, concerns only the predestined. The titles alone establish this, and the entire course of the works demonstrates it.

It is unquestionably true, on the basis of all these proofs, not only that Saint Augustine compares Adam exclusively with the predestined, but also that he compares the sole grace Adam received in order to persevere in righteousness with the sole grace granted to the predestined in order to persevere in righteousness. Thus, according to Saint Augustine, the efficacious grace given to the reprobate, whose fruit is a temporary justification, is not the *quo* help. Nor is the efficacious grace given to the predestined, which is not inseparably joined to that which leads to final perseverance—for example, the grace by which they are justified [Col. 0916D] before a fall—the *quo* help either.

What, then, was Jansenius thinking when he tells us that every efficacious grace which produces willing in us is the *quo* help? Did he secretly agree with Calvin concerning justification, and maintain that the reprobate have no efficacious grace properly so called—that is, no grace by which they are truly justified? If he embraces this opinion, then, like Calvin, he contradicts Saint Augustine, who recognizes in the reprobate a truly justifying grace:

> We must believe that some of the children of perdition, without having received the gift of persevering to the end, begin to live in the faith that works through love, and sometimes live faithfully and justly, and afterward fall; nor are they taken from this life before this happens to them. (*On Correction and Grace*, chapter 13, no. 40.)

And afterward:

> They receive the grace of God, but they are temporary, and they do not persevere; they abandon, and are abandoned. (*Ibid.*, no. 42.)

If Jansenius does not think, like Calvin, that the reprobate are incapable of receiving any grace properly so called—that is, grace that justifies them—then he contradicts Saint Augustine on a point where Calvin does not depart from the holy doctor’s thought: namely, that the *quo* help belongs exclusively to the predestined.

I turned to another consideration and found that Saint Augustine omitted nothing that might lead his readers to understand that the *quo* and *sine quo non* helps were habitual graces, not actual ones. Indeed, when speaking of one help or the other, he [Col. 0917B] avoids all the terms he customarily associates with actual grace and chooses those most suited to designate habitual grace. For example, he does not say that Adam or the saints correspond to and consent to this kind of grace; rather, he uses the expressions “to persevere,” “to remain,” “to continue,” “to stand” in this grace, “not to abandon it,” “to hold it,” and “to preserve it”: *in eo perseverare, manere, permanere, stare*; *illud non deserere, tenere*. This is how he expresses himself regarding the *quo* help:

> Who would dare say, “He will not remain”? Who would dare say, “Perhaps he will not remain”? (*On Correction and Grace*, chapter 12, no. 34.)

If he regarded this help as a passing action rather than as a habit and a state, with what propriety could he compare it, in the same passage, to blessedness?

> This help is both that by which something comes to be and that without which it does not come to be: for if blessedness is given to a human being, he immediately becomes blessed; and if it is never given, he will never be blessed. (*Ibid.*)

Jansenius should have made these reflections at least [Col. 0917C] the thirtieth time he read the book *On Correction and Grace*, and should not have presented the *quo* and *sine quo non* helps as actual graces. Calvin’s texts [Note: [Col. 0917D] *Institutes*, book II, chapter 3, no. 10; *Against Pighius*, book III, Amsterdam edition of 1667, p. 149; book VI, at the end, p. 177; *Antidote to the Council of Trent*, session 6, p. 240; *On the Eternal Predestination of God*, p. 600.], from which he partly plundered his doctrine concerning these two helps, warned him sufficiently to guard against such a mistake. Might it not have been somewhat deliberate? Was it not necessary to distinguish himself in some respect from Calvin in the eyes of the public, so that he could, with less scandal, agree with the heresiarch in corrupting the holy doctor’s meaning in everything else?

The licentiate then showed me how eager he was to see in Saint Augustine the definition of the *quo* help, which my doctor had taught me and which, he added, it was clear I had not lost sight of. I read him these words:

> Therefore the number of the saints predestined by the grace of God to God’s kingdom will be brought there intact by the perseverance granted to them unto the end; and there, already most perfectly blessed, they will be preserved forever without end, with the mercy of the Savior adhering to them—whether when they are converted, whether when they struggle, or whether when they are crowned. (*On Correction and Grace*, chapter 13, no. 40.)

The holy doctor, after describing at great length the nature and properties of the *quo* help, here gives an exact definition of it and declares that it is nothing other than a special and merciful providence, which contains and regulates the economy, sequence, and interconnection of the graces, whether interior or exterior, by means of which the predestined infallibly attain salvation.

It does not follow from this, as Calvin maintained, that righteousness or sanctifying grace is incapable of being lost in the predestined, but only that the grace of predestination, understood in the Catholic sense, cannot be lost. The holy doctor did not insinuate the slightest thing resembling the monstrous doctrine of the inalienable possession of righteousness and sanctifying grace that Calvin’s impiety guarantees to the predestined, and which he is not ashamed to unite with the state of crime when the predestined fall into it. Saint Augustine, on the contrary, teaches not only that the just can, by sinning, fall from the state of grace, but also that they sometimes sin mortally and, through mortal sin, lose grace and the friendship of God, as our controversialists have demonstrated through a multitude of testimonies.

Therefore, when he says that the Savior’s mercy adheres inseparably to the predestined, he uses the word *adhaerente* rather than *inhaerente*, in order to express merely an assistance, whether interior or exterior, by which God continually watches over the entire course of the saints’ lives—sometimes to prevent them from falling into [Col. 0918B] crime, sometimes to bring about their conversion and repentance before they leave this life. He himself declares this as follows:

> Therefore, whoever by this generosity of divine grace has been set apart from that original condemnation will undoubtedly be granted the opportunity to hear the Gospel; and when they hear it, they believe; and in the faith that works through love they persevere to the end; and if at any time they stray, they are corrected and reformed; and some of them, even if they are not corrected by human beings, return to the way they had abandoned; and some, having received grace at whatever age, are withdrawn from the dangers of this life. (*On Correction and Grace*, chapter 7, no. 13.)

Calvin erred by confusing the grace that justifies us with this special providence that never abandons the predestined, even during the time of their wanderings and disorders. Calvin and Jansenius erred by taking the *quo* help to be an interior grace from which the human will cannot withdraw and which it is incapable of overcoming, whereas it is a help of providence [Col. 0918C] and assistance that causes the will of a predestined person not to succumb to temptations, or to depart from righteousness only for a time, and not forever and until the end.

The principal foundation of the Calvinist and Jansenist doctrine is these words:

> Therefore help was given to the weakness of the human will, so that divine grace might act upon it in an undeclinable and insuperable manner; and therefore, although weak, it would nevertheless not fail, nor be overcome by any adversity . . . . . . For he left and permitted the very strong to do what they wished; but he preserved the weak, so that, by his granting it, they might most invincibly will what is good, and most invincibly refuse to abandon it. (*Ibid.*, chapter 12, no. 38.)

Saint Augustine does not say here, nor has he said anywhere, that grace inevitably and invincibly dominates the human will; and nothing is more false than these words, by which Jansenius assures us that Saint Augustine gives grace the name of that which dominates the human will:

> Augustine calls it . . . . . . that which dominates the human will in an insuperable and undeclinable manner. (*Index*, volume I, under the word “GRACE.”)

That is Calvin’s language, not Saint Augustine’s.

Indeed, grace gives the human will strength that makes it unshakable in righteousness and invincible against temptations; but it does not dominate the will by overcoming it, just as the will does not overcome grace. Our resistance to grace is the refusal of an offered help; our docility in following the impulses of grace is the acceptance of that help. But superiority and advantage exist only in the relationship and comparison between the human will, aided by grace, and those same passions and temptations.

[Col. 0919A] Such is Saint Augustine’s way of thinking [Note: [Col. 0919D] Saint Augustine teaches in a thousand places that God is almighty in inclining the human heart wherever he wills; but he calls the exercise of this omnipotence persuasion, never domination. [Col. 0920D] Nevertheless, one could, in a sound sense and with explanation, use the latter term; but one should at least not flatter oneself that one is speaking as Saint Augustine did.]. The ideas that represent grace and the human will as two adversaries and two enemies fighting one another, each prevailing over the other in turn, are anything but Augustinian ideas.

The meaning I am expounding is certainly the one conceived by the priests of Marseille when they read the relevant passage of *On Correction and Grace*, for Hilary reports their objection in this way:

> For if, they say, Adam was helped in such a way that he could both stand in righteousness and turn away from righteousness, whereas the saints are now helped in such a way that they cannot turn away, since they received the perseverance of willing, so that they cannot will otherwise. (*Hilary’s Letter to Augustine*, no. 6.)

According to Calvin and Jansenius, *indeclinabiliter* refers to grace, as though it expressed the fact that the will cannot resist it; according to the priests of Marseille, *indeclinabiliter* refers to righteousness and expresses the fact that the human will cannot depart from it when aided by grace.

[Col. 0919B] What am I saying? Saint Augustine’s text admits no ambiguity and clearly decides in favor of this meaning and explanation of *indeclinabiliter* and *invictissime*, and—if one persists in reading it so—of *insuperabiliter* as well. What do these words mean?

> And therefore, although weak, it would nevertheless not fail, nor be overcome by any adversity.

They mean nothing other than that the passage is not concerned with a grace whose action is to overcome and subdue the human will, but with an assistance of divine providence, whose merciful care governs the human will so securely that, despite its weakness and infirmity, it does not turn away from the path of salvation, and so invincibly that it proves superior to every adversity.

In short, it is not grace whose force Saint Augustine says is inevitable and insuperable for the human will; it is the human will that he says grace makes inseparable from the good and insuperable by evil. This must nevertheless not be understood as meaning that it is absolutely impossible for the human will to abandon the good and be overcome by temptation. For Saint Augustine explains himself and declares that he means an impossibility of supposition and fact, not a genuine necessity:

> Nevertheless, it would not fail, nor be overcome by any adversity.

His thought is not that it never happens, or cannot be supposed to happen, that the predestined should on some occasions fail and be overcome by temptation. He maintains only that they will not depart from righteousness and will not yield to the enemies of their salvation forever and irreversibly, because a special providence so directs their conduct that, although they sometimes leave the road leading to heaven, they never end their lives without having returned to the right path and recovered the righteousness and grace they had lost. I have already proved this truth; I add two passages to the one I have already cited:

> The faith of these people, which works through love, certainly either does not fail at all, or, if there are some whose faith does fail, it is restored before this life ends; and, once the iniquity that intervened has been removed, perseverance to the end is reckoned to them, etc. Without doubt it will not fail to the end, and consequently it will persevere to the end; nor will the end find it except remaining in this life. (*On Correction and Grace*, chapter 7, no. 16.)

“But,” the licentiate then said to me, “why do you appear to call into doubt whether *insuperabiliter* should be read in Saint Augustine’s text?”

“I do not call it into doubt,” I replied, “for I hold it certain that this reading is false and that *inseparabiliter* must be read instead.” [Col. 0920A] The entire sequence of the discourse rejects the one reading and requires the other. Pay attention to it. The holy doctor employs three adverbs in succession to express the nature of the grace of which he is speaking: *indeclinabiliter*, *insuperabiliter* or *inseparabiliter*, and *invictissime*. What would *invictissime* mean after *insuperabiliter*? The latter signifies the incapacity or impossibility of being overcome; the former signifies the act or fact of not being overcome. After assuring us that grace places the predestined in the incapacity or impossibility of being overcome, would Saint Augustine teach us, a few lines later, something very curious—namely, that grace gives them the advantage of not being overcome? Or, if this is the same thought repeated, would it not have been natural, or even necessary, for him to use the term *invincibiliter* rather than *invictissime*?

Suppose, on the contrary, that Saint Augustine wrote *inseparabiliter*. Nothing could be more exact or more consistent with the thoughts that filled him and that he inculcates throughout his work: namely, that the grace of predestination places the just in a kind of incapacity and impossibility of departing from the ways of righteousness, *ut declinare non possint*; and this because God’s mercy never abandons them and adheres inseparably to leading them, *adhaerente sibi misericordia Creatoris*. Hence it happens that their will, however weak it may be, is not overcome by any kind of misfortune or temptation: *quamvis infirma, non tamen deficeret, neque adversitate aliqua vinceretur*. The first text, *ut declinare non possint*, corresponds to the adverb *indeclinabiliter*; the second text, *adhaerente sibi misericordia Creatoris*, corresponds to *inseparabiliter*; the third text, *neque adversitate aliqua vinceretur*, corresponds to *invictissime*.

Here is another observation that should not be neglected. *Insuperabiliter* and *insuperabilis* are terms entirely foreign to Saint Augustine’s style; nowhere else, in the great number of writings he composed, did he use them, although the occasion presented itself a thousand times. Yet in other places he does use the words *inseparabiliter* and *inseparabilis* (*On the Nature and Grace*, chapter 51, no. 58; *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 8, no. 13).

None of this would be sufficient to establish a demonstration if, as the doctors of Louvain assert, *insuperabiliter* were found in all the manuscripts of *On Correction and Grace*. Did they imagine that in more than ten editions of Saint Augustine preceding theirs, *inseparabiliter* had been printed against the evidence of all the manuscripts?

Did Augustinus Dodo and Johannes Amerbach, who produced the first editions of Saint Augustine at Basel, in 1495 and 1506, have anything before their eyes other than manuscripts of *On Correction and Grace* that until then had never been put to press? And if this had been an error that escaped Amerbach twice, and that had again slipped into the Paris edition of 1515, would Erasmus, who reviewed the manuscripts collected by Augustinus Dodo and sought out new ones when he supervised the edition printed at Basel by Froben in 1528, not have corrected it?

Louis Miré and Jacques Hamer, whose tireless efforts in unearthing, examining, and deciphering ancient manuscripts are praised, in order—as they did—to produce at Basel in 1543 an edition more accurate than Erasmus’s, and the learned Franciscan Florent Bourgouin, who directed the Paris edition printed by Bonhomme in 1541—did they have financial motives for sparing *inseparabiliter*, motives such as might later have existed for showing it no mercy?

The same is true of those who supervised two other Paris editions, printed by Gaillard and by Chevallon.

Read the inscription of the first volume of the edition published at Venice in 1552:

> The first volume of all the works of the blessed Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, restored with the utmost care from ancient exemplars and cleansed of countless errors, with the readings of the ancient exemplars marked in the text and margin by their proper signs, so that so great a doctor of the Church might rightly be seen to have been reborn.

In this edition, where the various readings found in the ancient manuscripts are marked so exactly in the margin, *inseparabiliter* appears in the text, and the margin at this place contains no other reading.

Finally, Jean Coster and Martin Lipse produced a new edition at Basel in 1566; Jean Vlimmerius produced another at Basel in 1569, with a fidelity and [Col. 0921B] accuracy that earned them great praise. Their critical work was followed in the editions printed at Paris by Guillaume Merlin and Sébastien Nivelle in 1571, and *inseparabiliter* was retained.

This great number of editions, and consequently the manuscripts on which they were based, testify in favor of *inseparabiliter*. Calvin himself, who would have been more comfortable with *insuperabiliter* than with *inseparabiliter*, was forced to admit the latter.

Thus Henri Gravius, the one among the doctors of Louvain who was especially charged with reviewing and preparing Saint Augustine’s books against the Pelagians, was the first to proscribe the word *inseparabiliter* and substitute *insuperabiliter* for it. Perhaps he did not intend any subtlety by this; yet, like most of his colleagues, he was a disciple of Baius.

In any event, these gentlemen appealed to the authority of the manuscripts they possessed; [Col. 0921C] those formerly used by Martin Lipse and the other Flemish editors of Saint Augustine’s works had, I do not know how, disappeared. Thus, after the edition issued by the doctors of Louvain at Antwerp in 1577, people blindly deferred to their criticism, and the subsequent editions were merely reprints of theirs: at Venice in 1584, at Cologne in 1616, and at Paris in 1609, 1614, 1626, 1635, and 1652. This did not prevent Father Lenfant, a Dominican, from retaining the ancient reading *inseparabiliter* in his Augustinian *Concordances*, printed in 1656, any more than it prevented the scholar who had previously given us the separate edition of Saint Augustine’s works against the Pelagians in 1644.

But what do the Reverend Benedictine Fathers say about this? They keep silent. They content themselves with placing in the holy doctor’s text the reading favored by the doctor of Louvain, without making any comment on the matter, citing any manuscript, or mentioning the variant readings. I certainly do not intend to make a crime of this, since formerly the difference between these two words seemed no more significant to me than it does to them.

“It seems to me,” said the licentiate, “that you have taken considerable trouble over something that does not deserve it. Yet it has pleased me, because you have given the most exact enumeration I have seen of all the editions of Saint Augustine. That was apparently your whole purpose; for as regards this point of criticism, how important can it be? For my part, I think you will derive little or no advantage from it, even if you succeed in establishing *inseparabiliter* as the correct reading.”

“You are overlooking the matter,” I replied. “If *inseparabiliter* is the reading, it is demonstrated that the *quo* help is not a passing and actual grace, but a habitual grace inseparable from the predestined person even when he is in a state of mortal sin and gives himself over to the most frightful disorders. [Col. 0922A] It therefore sometimes happens that, for a fairly long period, this grace suspends its efficacy with regard to good works and is reduced to a providence that the Jansenists, who deny sufficient grace, must then regard as purely exterior. It follows that this is absolutely and without difficulty the grace of predestination, and that Jansenius can no longer make any use of the distinction between the *quo* and *sine quo non* helps to support his system. Do you think that this is of little importance?”

“It is getting late,” the licentiate then said to me, “but I will not leave you, if you please, until this matter is finished and you have clarified my ideas concerning the nature of the other help.”

I set about satisfying him and continued in this manner.

The Jansenists are delighted when they are granted that the *sine quo non* help is sufficient actual grace. Then, in a confident tone, they exclaim: “One need only read Saint Augustine. He describes the one and the other help in such a way that to refuse to admit that he attributes the *sine quo non* help exclusively to the state of innocence and the *quo* help exclusively to the state of repaired nature is to deny that it is daylight at high noon. For the holy doctor not only distinguishes the helps proper to the two states, but also explains why these helps must be different in the two states. It was fitting,” he says, “that Adam should receive a gentler and more gracious help, and that ours should be more efficacious and more powerful, because Adam was very strong and inwardly enjoyed perfect peace, whereas we are very weak and must endure temptations both very considerable and very numerous” (*On Correction and Grace*, chapter 11, no. 30). From this the Jansenists conclude that there are no sufficient graces in our state.

But those against whom they reason prove elsewhere, with complete clarity, that Saint Augustine recognized sufficient graces in our state; and they prove it [Col. 0922C] from the very book *On Correction and Grace*, in which the holy doctor assures us that even now one has the right to say to a person who does not persevere that, if he wished, he would persevere:

> For the excuse of those who say, “We did not receive hearing,” appears more just than that of those who say, “We did not receive perseverance”; for it can be said: “Human being, in that which you heard and retained, you would persevere if you wished; but it can in no way be said: ‘In that which you did not hear, you would believe if you wished.’” (*On Correction and Grace*, chapter 7, no. 11.)

To nullify this proof, the following commentary was devised: “If you wished,” that is, “if the same will remained,” as he says below, no. 17; or, “unless by an evil will you abandoned what you held.” This is as though the testimony I have just cited had to be given the illusory meaning that Saint Augustine rightly mocks in the following passage:

> Who does not know, he says, that Peter’s faith would have perished if the very will by which he was faithful had failed, and that it would have remained if that same will had remained? (*Ibid.*, chapter 8, no. 17.)

Saint Augustine attributes and concedes this proposition to his adversaries because of the excess of truth that makes it ridiculous; but he was not capable of seriously writing anything of the sort on his own authority.

Certainly, he did not repeat the words *perseveraret si vellet* so many times when speaking of Adam’s fall while intending a completely different meaning when, in the same work, he addressed the same words to a just person in our state who falls. Nor was he so foolish as to claim that this person was inexcusable for failing to preserve a will of which he was not master.

Nevertheless, there is a text that appears troublesome because it suggests that the power to persevere is given to the elect only together with the efficacious will to persevere:

> For their will is so kindled by the Holy Spirit that they can because they so will, and they will in this way because God works so that they will. (*Ibid.*, chapter 12, no. 38.)

But it is clear that Saint Augustine does not exclude a power antecedent to the will when he infers the power from the will. The holy doctor’s sole purpose is to show that the elect possess a special power, or, to put it that way, a power of favor, which proceeds from God’s gratuitous predestination.

It is therefore certain that Saint Augustine recognized sufficient graces in our state. I may perhaps have occasion to offer you an abundance of proofs of this that will astonish you.

For the moment, let us conclude not that the *sine quo non* help is found in our state, but that the *sine quo non* help is something entirely different from sufficient grace. The Jansenists are vexed that this position should be adopted; they are indignant and answer in an acerbically mocking tone: “What, then, is it? Is the *sine quo non* help in Saint Augustine some sort of unknown thing?” [Col. 0923B]

I have already said that it is not an actual grace but a habitual one; and I state without hesitation that, since Saint Augustine compares the *sine quo non* help that Adam had received from God in the state of innocence with the *quo* help that God grants to the predestined in our state, so that the comparison may be just, the *sine quo non* help must be the order of providence that God maintained with respect to Adam and the angels, before their sin, in the distribution of the means of salvation, just as the *quo* help is the order of providence that God now maintains toward the predestined.

Before sin, the order of divine providence, according to Saint Augustine’s thought, consisted solely in the generous distribution of supernatural gifts and actual graces that were necessary to avoid evil and do good; but neither the actions of human beings [Col. 0923C] nor those of angels were infallibly directed toward a happy end. Thus predestination to salvation and glory was in itself only conditional and became absolute only in dependence upon foreseen merits; consequently, the grace of predestination was left to free will, whose actions God did not govern through any special care or vigilance.

Now, according to the doctrine of the same Saint Augustine, God infallibly directs the predestined toward a happy end. Thus predestination to salvation and glory is absolute, independently of foreseen merits; consequently, the free will of the predestined is entrusted to the grace of predestination and governed by it. This does not mean, as Calvin and Jansenius maintain, that the use of free will contributes in no way to the work of salvation; rather, it means that the free actions of the predestined are directed by divine providence in such a way that they infallibly result in salvation. Before sin, no such direction existed, and everything came down to the wise and liberal distribution of graces.

I later heard my doctor say that every true Augustinian—and he openly professed to be one—could not avoid admitting this system. Nevertheless, he believed that Saint Thomas had departed from it, as had all those who used metaphysical arguments to support the view of an antecedent and absolute predestination to salvation and glory, because they held the same kind of predestination for both states, which is manifestly contrary to Saint Augustine’s doctrine.

Regarding those who embrace the view of conditional predestination for both states, he said that they would vainly flatter themselves that they had Saint Augustine on their side, and that they ought to be satisfied that Pope Innocent XII, in a brief addressed to the University of Louvain on 6 February 1694, had applied to the question of predestination to glory these words of Pope Saint Celestine:

> As for the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions that arise, which those who resisted the heretics treated at greater length, just as we do not dare to despise them, so we do not need to assert them. (Pope Saint Celestine, *Letter to the Gallican Bishops*, chapter 13.)

At these words the licentiate took his leave of me and promised to return as soon as possible.

## SECOND PART

The doctrine of the perfection of righteousness is the true key to Saint Augustine’s works against the Pelagians.

[Col. 0923]

[Col. 0923C] The licentiate, having returned several days later, assured me that the more he reflected on everything he had heard me say, the more his Jansenist ideas [Col. 0923D] dissipated; nevertheless, a considerable scruple remained, founded on the fact that an infinite number of passages in Saint Augustine express the doctrines of Jansenius in the most natural manner, whereas one must subject them to torture in order to reduce them to the meaning we call Catholic.

“You are wrong,” I replied, “to resort to a forced interpretation in order to explain these passages. But as for what you assert—that they naturally express the doctrines of Jansenius—my doctor used to say that they express them in the same way that, in the little poem of Proba Falconia and in certain other similar centos, the verses of Virgil or Homer very naturally express the circumstances of the Savior’s life and Passion, to which neither Virgil nor Homer ever gave any thought. Jansenius’s book should be regarded only as an artful cento, in which not only are Saint Augustine’s texts diverted from the meaning they have [Col. 0924C] in the holy doctor’s works, but they are even applied to entirely different subjects.”

What a paradox! exclaimed the licentiate. “It was [Col. 0924D] one for me as well as for you,” I replied, “before I had properly informed myself about what concerns the Pelagians’ doctrine of impeccance. My doctor urged me to study it without revealing too clearly where that study would lead me; and, fortunately, it led me to discover the true key to Augustine’s works against the Pelagians—a key that the heretics of recent centuries have tried to make disappear.”

## I. On Pelagian Impeccance

They have been seen above all to diminish the importance of this doctrine deliberately; and Father Quesnel, in his *Notes on Saint Leo*, reports an opinion already established through the efforts of his party when he writes that the Pelagian heresy, at its first origin, came down to two chief points: namely, the denial of original sin and of the necessity of grace for each individual act. [Col. 0925A] These two branches, he adds, produced several small offshoots, which are less significant questions—for example, whether a human being can be without sin in this life.

*Pelagiana haeresis duobus fere capitibus in suo ortu conclusa fuit, negatione scilicet peccati originalis et necessitatis gratiae ad singulos actus: sed geminus ille ramus alios subinde emisit ramusculos seu quaestiones minus graves, qualis est an homo possit esse sine peccato* (Quesnel, *ad S. Leon.*, vol. II, dissertation 3, no. 23).

This contradicts—or at least corrects—Saint Augustine, who everywhere counts three principal errors of Pelagianism:

“There are, as you know, three things that the Catholic Church especially defends against them: one is that the grace of God is not given according to our merits . . .; another is that, whatever one’s justice may be, no one in this corruptible body lives without some sins; the third is that a human being is born subject to the sin of the first man.”

[Note: [Col. 0925D] Saint Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 2, no. 4; and elsewhere, such as *To Boniface*, book III, chapter 8, no. 24, and book IV, chapter 7, no. 19, and chapter 12, no. 33; *Against Julian*, book III, chapter 1, no. 2; *On Heresies*, no. 88; Letter 176, no. 2; *The City of God*, book IV, chapter 9, no. 4, etc.]

I can show you a great many other similar passages in which Augustine places these three errors on the same level. He never limits himself to reporting only two of them; nowhere does he omit impeccance.

[Col. 0925B] Besides this, Quesnel contradicts history by asserting that the controversy over impeccance was not debated in the early period of Pelagianism. For in the year 412, when Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine had not yet written anything against the Pelagians, Paulinus, the accuser of Celestius, reproached that heresiarch, in the sixth article of the petition he presented against him at the Council of Carthage, with having taught that even before the coming of the Lord there had been people free from sin:

*Quod et ante adventum Domini homines fuerunt impeccabiles, id est sine peccato*—“that even before the coming of the Lord there were people who were impeccable, that is, without sin” (Marius Mercator, *Second Memorandum against the Pelagians*).

And Paul Orosius assures us that the same Council of Carthage condemned the proposition that “a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes”:

*Hominem posse esse sine peccato, et mandata Dei facile custodire si velit* (Paul Orosius, *Apology*, chapter 2).

This reasonably leads the Benedictine Fathers to judge that the proposition was removed from the sixth article of Paulinus’s petition, [Col. 0925C] of which it formed a part, as the corollary of the other proposition.

A third falsehood advanced by Quesnel is that the doctrine of impeccance was a consequence or offshoot of the more substantial Pelagian errors. On the contrary, it is the source and origin of all Pelagianism.

Can one doubt this when one sees Saint Jerome designate this heresy only by the doctrine of impeccance?

*Haeresis Pythagorae et Zenonis ἀπαθείας καὶ ἀναμαρτησίας coepit reviviscere*—“The heresy of Pythagoras and Zeno, of apatheia and sinlessness, has begun to revive” (Saint Jerome, preface to book IV on Jeremiah).

And can one doubt it when one sees him attack almost exclusively this one error in his three *Dialogues against the Pelagians*? One need only read these *Dialogues*, or at least one of the two analyses that the Benedictine Fathers have made public—one in their edition of Jerome’s works and the other in the preface to volume X of Augustine, no. 9—to be convinced that impeccance was the first and principal idea of Pelagianism formed by Saint Jerome. In more than one passage he represents this same doctrine of impeccance as having come directly [Col. 0925D] from pagan philosophy:

*Philosophi patriarchae haereticorum Ecclesiae puritatem perversa maculavere doctrina*—“The philosophers, patriarchs of the heretics, stained the purity of the Church with their perverse teaching” (Saint Jerome, letter to Ctesiphon).

It is well known to what imaginary moral perfection the sages of paganism boasted that they could attain, and that they attributed such natural powers to human reason that it was sufficient unto itself never to contradict itself and never to fail. Pelagius became fixated on their proud maxims, and his first error was that human beings possessed, in the very substance of their rational nature, the power to preserve themselves from all sin. From this he proceeded to deny the infirmity and weakness into which the human race had fallen after Adam’s fall, to deny original sin and the necessity of grace. [Col. 0926A] This, so to speak, is the genealogy of the Pelagian errors. This is why Saint Jerome regards impeccance as the root and principle from which they all arose.

Jansenius himself could not help bearing witness here to the truth. He expressly says that impeccance is the first doctrine by whose preaching Pelagius began to disturb the Church, and that the necessity of defending this first doctrine plunged him into the other errors. The reason he gives is that Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine, in their earliest writings against the Pelagians, attack impeccance as the principal doctrine of these heretics:

*Primum dogma, cujus praedicatione Pelagius turbare coepit Ecclesiam, tuendique necessitate in caeteros errores videtur esse praecipitatus, fuit illud de assequenda perfectione justitiae usque ad impeccantiam et apathiam. Hoc enim velut praecipuum [Col. 0926B] in primis suis lucubrationibus Hieronymus et Augustinus exagitant*—“The first doctrine by whose preaching Pelagius began to disturb the Church, and in the necessity of defending which he seems to have been precipitated into the other errors, was that concerning the attainment of perfection in justice, extending to impeccance and apatheia. For in their earliest writings Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine attack this as the principal doctrine” (Jansenius, vol. I, book VI, chapter 18, p. 377).

On this occasion, however, Jansenius (vol. I, book IV, chapter 19, p. 227) makes a petty and unfair objection to Saint Jerome, whom he accuses of having made no distinction between “not being able to sin,” *non posse peccare*, and “being able not to sin,” *posse non peccare*—as though the holy Doctor truly confused Jovinian’s error concerning the impeccability of the righteous with Pelagius’s error concerning impeccance, because he addresses the latter as follows:

*Joviniani secunda quaestio tui ingenii disciplina est, etc., cujus, o Pelagi, a te nunc haeresis suscitatur*—“The second question of Jovinian is the teaching of your mind, etc.; this is the heresy, O Pelagius, that you are now reviving” (Saint Jerome, letter to Ctesiphon and preface to the *Dialogue*, vol. IV, new edition, pp. 477, 484).

Whoever takes the trouble to compare the different manner in which Saint Jerome combats Jovinian’s impeccability in the second book of the work [Col. 0926C] he composed against that heretic, and Pelagius’s impeccance in the three books of his *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, will not find Jansenius’s criticism tolerable. The holy Doctor intended only to say that Pelagius’s error was contained within Jovinian’s, and that in this respect one was not distinguished from the other. His purpose was to show that these two heresies tended to destroy the same article of faith and therefore ought to be included under the same censure.

What is remarkable here is that Jansenius’s disciples, following their master’s example, make a similar quarrel with Catholic theologians. These theologians know perfectly well that Calvin’s and Jansenius’s heresies concerning the impossibility of God’s commandments are not one and the same error, yet they sometimes appear to make no distinction between them and do not hesitate to assert that the same decrees of the Church that anathematized Calvin’s opinion also proscribed Jansenius’s, on the grounds that one contains the other and that both conspire to ruin the same article of faith. For Jansenius and Calvin attack the same doctrine—that no one can merit or demerit without freedom—just as Pelagius and Jovinian attacked the same doctrine, namely, that through the sin of the first man the human race fell into infirmity and weakness. The parallel is exact: what Pelagius is to Jovinian, Jansenius is to Calvin.

I applied myself with renewed diligence to clarifying the nature of Pelagian impeccance, and I believed that I had portrayed it in its true and proper features by describing it in this way.

[Col. 0927A] The Pelagians persuaded themselves that it lay within human power not only to refuse consent to sin, but also to experience nothing disorderly within oneself; to feel no repugnance toward duty, no inward rebellion against the law; to remove even the slightest disturbance that weakens or confounds reason; to free oneself from every inward temptation and every inclination contrary to perfect justice; to keep all the actions, perceptions, and movements of one’s soul in order, so that the light of the mind would not be eclipsed for a single moment by the slightest cloud of error, and the heart would always move effortlessly toward the good; to rid oneself of every principle of cupidity and concupiscence, of every inclination toward evil, even involuntary; in short, to extinguish absolutely every seed of vice, every undeliberated feeling of concupiscence, which reason disapproves and which anticipates it.

“It is the apatheia of the Stoics,” says Saint Jerome; and [Col. 0927B] who does not know that the apatheia of the Stoics was the abolition and removal of every passion? These false sages boasted that they were the sovereign gods of the little world constituted by their own persons, and as much masters of the movements of their souls as Jupiter was thought to be master of the agitations aroused throughout the universe. The holy Doctor reproaches the Pelagians with a similar presumption:

“Can one imagine greater temerity than to claim for oneself, I do not say likeness to God, but equality with God, and to encompass in a brief statement all the poisons that the heretics have drawn as from their source from the teaching of the philosophers, especially that of Pythagoras and Zeno, the leader of the Stoics? For they assert that the passions—which in Greek are called *pathē*, and which we may call disturbances—can be uprooted from the mind, and that through meditation and continual practice of the virtues a person can, if he wishes, succeed in tearing out every last root and fiber [Col. 0927C] of vice:

*Quae enim potest alia major esse temeritas, quam Dei sibi non dicam similitudinem, sed aequalitatem vindicare, et brevi sententia omnium haereticorum venena complecti, quae de philosophorum, et maxime Pythagorae et Zenonis principis Stoicorum fonte manarint? Illi enim, quae Graece πάθη, nos perturbationes possumus dicere . . . . . asserunt extirpari posse de mentibus, et nullam fibram radicemque vitiorum in homine omnino residere meditatione et assidua exercitatione virtutum*” (Saint Jerome, letter to Ctesiphon, beginning).

Saint Augustine makes the same reproach to the Pelagians in innumerable places. After quoting a long passage from Saint Ambrose, in which it is shown that the lure of earthly desires often slips into our soul, and that an overflow of vanities, spreading through all its faculties, seizes and occupies it; that [Col. 0927D] it is difficult for a human being to defend himself against this troublesome necessity, and impossible to strip it away entirely and absolutely; that perfect dominion over our heart is not granted to us, and that thoughts which surprise us and, without our consent, engage us with a thousand objects cast confusion and disturbance into all our spiritual powers, he then addresses these words to Julian:

“If you do not suffer such misery, forgive us: we do not believe you on your own testimony. Rather, in these words of Saint Ambrose we recognize, as in a mirror, the infirmity common to all human beings; we recognize it, I say, provided that we are making some progress in virtue. If it sometimes happens that we are simple enough to believe your words and to say to you, ‘Pray for us, that God may grant us the grace to enjoy the same advantage as you and no longer be subject to the internal war waged against us by our passions,’ we find [Col. 0928A] you puffed up with such lofty wisdom that you dare answer us not only that you suffer none of these things, but also that it lies within everyone’s power to suffer none of them, and that there is no need to implore God’s assistance for this purpose:

*Haec si vos non patimini, ignoscite, non vobis credimus, sed in his potius sancti Ambrosii verbis quoddam speculum, et hoc si proficimus, communis humanae infirmitatis agnoscimus. Vobis autem si credamus et dicamus, Orate pro nobis, ut nec nos ista patiamur; ita vos invenimus elatos et alta sapientes, ut respondeatis nobis, non solum ista vos non pati, verum etiam in hominis esse potestate ne ista patiatur, nec esse causam cur ad hoc Dei poscatur adjutorium*” (Book II against Julian, chapter 8, no. 23).

And elsewhere, having opposed Pelagian impeccance with this passage from the Book of Wisdom, *Corpus enim quod corrumpitur aggravat animam, et terrena habitatio deprimit sensum multa cogitantem*—“For a corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wisdom 9:15)—he addresses Julian as follows:

“But you, as though already dwelling in heaven [Col. 0928B] immortally among the angels, mock words that express the infirmity and mortality of our condition:

*Sed tu tanquam in coelo jam inter angelos immortaliter habitans, verba infirmitatis et mortalitatis irrides*” (Book V against Julian, chapter 13, no. 40).

I could add many other testimonies from the two holy Doctors, and also cite Orosius, Pope Gelasius, Photius, and others.

The licentiate found it difficult to agree with me on this point. “Never in theology,” he said, “has anyone formed such an idea of Pelagian impeccance. Never has anyone attributed to the Pelagians the madness of claiming that a human being, as he is in this life and in our present condition, is completely master of his first movements.”

“I see it clearly,” I replied. “You require an irrefragable authority, and on this point you will doubtless assent to that of Jansenius, who not only admits the truth of what I am asserting, but proves it [Col. 0928C] by the very passages from Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine that I have cited, as well as by others.”

Yet I will not conceal from you that this author artfully insinuates, contrary to the evident testimonies of these holy Doctors, that one must distinguish apatheia from impeccance. His intention was not to say another word about the former throughout the remainder of his work, and to abuse passages from Saint Augustine concerning the sin contrary to apatheia and to the perfection of justice, by interpreting them as referring to the sin contrary to the action of justice. These two kinds of sin, which I shall soon discuss and which Saint Augustine precisely recognized and defined, destroy Jansenius’s distinction between apatheia and impeccance, a distinction he makes without warning his reader to take note of it.

In any event, it remains certain that Jansenius counts apatheia among the errors of the Pelagians, and the description he gives of it is entirely similar [Col. 0928D] to mine:

*Ex hac non peccandi facilitate ad asserendam ἀπαθείαν (Pelagiani) progrediuntur, quo nomine nihil aliud significatur, quam perturbationum quibus animus humanus inquietari solet seu passionum impassibilitas: nimirum ut non tantum fracto impetu regantur, sed etiam funditus exstirpentur, vel ita certe domentur rationis freno, ut nunquam homine commoveantur invito*—“From this facility of not sinning the Pelagians proceed to assert apatheia, by which term nothing other than freedom from the disturbances by which the human mind is usually disquieted, or freedom from passions, is signified: namely, that these disturbances should not merely be governed after their force has been broken, but should be uprooted entirely, or at least so subdued by the bridle of reason that they would never move a person against his will” (Jansenius, vol. I, book IV, chapter 19, beginning).

But because I need to rely on Saint Jerome’s thoughts and expressions on several important points, I hasten to establish fully this Father’s authority, whom Jansenius dares accuse of not having understood the Pelagians’ views very well:

*Minus accurate videtur divus Hieronymus in ipsis initiis nascentis haeresis sensum eorum latebrasque penetrasse*—“The holy Jerome seems to have penetrated less accurately into their meaning and hidden notions at the very beginning of the rising heresy” (Jansenius, ibid., p. 227).

Justus Lipsius accuses him of having erred in saying that the Pelagians had borrowed their doctrine of impeccance not only from the Stoics but also [Col. 0929A] from the Pythagoreans. Hence Jansenius does not seem to place much reliance on the testimony of the holy Doctor, fearing to assert that Pythagoras must be numbered among those pagan philosophers who taught the doctrine of impeccance:

*Quibus addit Pythagoram sanctus Hieronymus*—“To these Saint Jerome adds Pythagoras” (Jansenius, ibid.).

How could Saint Jerome have been mistaken concerning the Pythagoreans? In his letter to Ctesiphon, he complains that Rufinus of Aquileia attributed to Saint Sixtus, pope and martyr, the book of a certain Sixtus, a pagan philosopher of the Pythagorean sect; and he adds, addressing the Pelagians:

“He labeled the book of Sixtus, a Pythagorean, a man without Christ and a pagan, with the altered name of Sixtus the martyr and bishop of the Roman Church . . . . From this book you too appropriate numerous testimonies against the Church:

*Librum Xisti Pythagorici hominis absque Christo atque ethnici immutato nomine Xisti martyris et Romanae Ecclesiae episcopi praenotavit . . . . . . Unde et vos plurima contra Ecclesiam usurpatis testimonia*” (Letter to Ctesiphon, vol. IV, new edition, p. 476).

Would Saint Jerome have spoken in this way to the Pelagians if the fact had not been certain? [Col. 0929B]

It is even attested by Saint Augustine, who frankly admits that he had been deceived by Rufinus’s imposture. Believing that the book truly belonged to Saint Sixtus, and not to Sixtus the Pythagorean, he had tried to give a Catholic meaning to a passage that Pelagius had taken from it to confirm his heresy:

*Verba quaedam velut Xisti Romani episcopi et martyris Pelagius posuit, sic defendi, tanquam revera Xisti essent, id enim putaveram: sed postea legi Xisti philosophi esse, non Xisti Christiani*—“Pelagius put forward certain words as belonging to Sixtus, bishop and martyr of Rome, and I defended them as though they truly belonged to Sixtus, for that is what I had thought; but afterward I read that they belonged to Sixtus the philosopher, not to Sixtus the Christian” (Book II of the *Retractations*, chapter 42; *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 64, no. 77).

And what did this passage contain? It expressed, quite simply, the doctrine of impeccance:

*Quia libertatem arbitrii permisit hominibus Deus, ut pure et sine peccato viventes similes fiant Deo*—“Because God granted human beings freedom of choice, so that by living purely and without sin they might become like God” (Justus Lipsius, *Manual of Stoic Philosophy*, book III, discussion 7).

Pelagius and the Pelagians apparently knew better than Justus Lipsius where the source of their doctrine lay.

[Col. 0929C] How much weight, then, should be given to this critic’s arguments? According to him, among the disciples of Pythagoras there were some who rejected the doctrine of impeccance, or apatheia, and others who accepted it. But the latter, he adds, abandoned the principles of Pythagoras on this point in order to follow the teaching of Stilpo, Zeno’s master.

Yet did Pythagoras not teach that the human soul was a portion of the divine substance and entirely equal to God? “A particle of the divine breath,” says Horace, who, according to the unanimous testimony of his commentators, adopts here the system of the Pythagoreans. And is it not natural to conclude from this that, although ordinarily the soul, forgetting its heavenly origin, dishonored itself by some stain, nevertheless, by recalling the nobility of its being, it could make itself as pure and become as inaccessible to sin as God himself, and consequently place itself beyond every disturbance and every temptation?

[Col. 0929D] If it is therefore incontestable that the Pelagians drew this same consequence from this same Pythagorean principle, can one doubt that Justus Lipsius’s view is false? For, contrary to what he asserts, we must agree that those disciples of Pythagoras who rejected the doctrine of impeccance abandoned their master’s principles on this point, while those who accepted the doctrine—as the Pelagians did—adhered exactly to the principles of the Pythagorean sect.

Now Saint Augustine testifies that Pelagius reasoned as follows:

“If the soul cannot be without sin, then God himself is subject to sin, since a part of the divine substance—that is, the soul—is absolutely unable to guard itself from sin:

*Si anima non potest esse sine peccato, ergo et Deus subjacet peccato, cujus pars, hoc est anima, peccato obnoxia est*” (Saint Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 18, no. 42).

[Col. 0930A] And farther on, after reporting some words of Celestius, he adds that, according to the view of that heresiarch, our soul and God are one and the same, and that our soul is a part of the Divinity:

*Tanquam ejusdem naturae animam et Deum, et partem Dei animam esse dixerit*—“As though he had said that the soul and God are of the same nature, and that the soul is a part of God” (ibid., chapter 35, no. 65).

After all, Jansenius does not dispute this point, nor does he openly take Justus Lipsius’s side. It is principally with regard to the affinity between Origenism and Pelagianism that he attacks Saint Jerome. He nevertheless has no difficulty believing, on the authority of the holy Doctor, that Origen had insinuated the doctrine of impeccance into his writings:

*Et Origines ecclesiasticae veritati in Stromatibus suis miscere conatur*—“And Origen attempts in his *Stromata* to mingle it with ecclesiastical truth” (Saint Jerome, preface to the *Dialogue*, vol. IV, new edition, p. 484).

Indeed, for what purpose would Rufinus of Aquileia, by a flagrant piece of trickery, have substituted the name of Saint Sixtus, pope and martyr, for that of Sixtus the Pythagorean at the head of a work that later could furnish the Pelagians with weapons [Col. 0930B] for defending the doctrine of impeccance? Is it not known that Rufinus of Aquileia is famous in Church history chiefly for his attachment to Origen’s teaching, and that he tried every possible means to bring it into credit? The doctrine of impeccance was therefore an offshoot of Origenism:

*Origenis ramusculus est*—“It is a branch of Origen” (Letter to Ctesiphon, vol. IV, new edition, p. 477).

“But,” says Jansenius, “Saint Jerome went too far, and either through failing to understand the terms or through confusing two very different errors, attributed to Origen not only Pelagius’s impeccance, but also Jovinian’s impeccability, which is a doctrine directly opposed to all the points on which the system of Origenism rests and turns:

*Capitaliter ipsis cardinibus Origenicae doctrinae contrarium*—“Fundamentally contrary to the very pivotal principles of Origen’s doctrine” (Jansenius, vol. I, book IV, chapter 19, p. 227).

This is marvelous indeed: in the seventeenth century people understood better all the points on which the system of Origenism rests and turns [Col. 0930C] than they did at the beginning of the fifth century. The inner meaning of that ancient heresy was discovered by Jansenius; and Saint Jerome, despite having far more resources for penetrating it, failed to perceive it. Yet Jerome had read a far greater number of Origen’s writings than have survived to our own time, and he would have reason to complain that Jansenius was here prosecuting him without having the better part of the evidence in hand.

Enough nevertheless remains to show that this great man was not indulging in a vision, and that he had some passage of Origen’s works in mind when he said so affirmatively and precisely:

“But this is proper to Origen: that it is impossible for human nature, from the beginning to the end of life, not to sin; and again, that when someone turns toward better things, it is possible for him to attain such strength that he can no longer sin” (Saint Jerome, preface to the *Dialogue*, vol. IV, new edition, p. 489).

Let us nevertheless hear Jansenius, who wishes to argue against Saint Jerome:

[Col. 0930D] “Nothing is more certainly affirmed, more constantly established, or more frequently inculcated by Origen than the unlosable indifference of the will, by which a rational creature is always master of turning its free choice toward good or evil. On this sole principle he constructed the perpetual circulation that he admits between the state of the blessed and that of the damned, according to which demons are continually changed into angels and angels into demons” (Jansenius, ibid.).

How can this be reconciled with Jovinian’s impeccability?

If Jansenius had not been so hostile to freedom of indifference, he would not have slandered it in this way, for it is certainly quite innocent of Origen’s impious and chimerical circulation. There is no ambiguity here: it is false that Origen believed freedom of indifference to be unlosable with respect to [Col. 0931A] its use and exercise, which is all that impeccability requires. He even taught in several places that the blessed were impeccable; and the reason he gives, together with the reflections accompanying it, demonstrates that he believed one could attain a state of impeccability even in this life.

“What will prevent free choice from falling into sin in the age to come,” he says (*Commentary on Romans*, book V, on Romans 6, near the end), “the Apostle teaches us in these few words: ‘Charity never fails’ (1 Corinthians 13:8). He has no other reason for asserting that charity is above faith and hope than that charity alone grants the privilege of never being able to sin again. Once a human being has risen to such a degree of perfection that he loves God with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his strength, and his neighbor as himself, can sin have any place? . . . This is why Saint John says, among other things, of charity that whoever remains in it remains in God.

“It is therefore beyond dispute that charity, which is the greatest of all the virtues, will [Col. 0931B] preserve every creature from falling when God is all in all; for the Apostle had risen to this degree of perfection, and, having already become firmly established in it, he confidently said: ‘Who shall separate us from the charity of God, which is in Jesus Christ,’ and so forth? From this it is clearly shown that if none of the things the Apostle enumerates can separate us from the charity of God when we have risen to this summit of perfection, then, with even greater reason, free choice cannot separate us from it.”

I know that we possess only an inaccurate translation of this work of Origen, as appears from the genuine fragments that remain to us, and that it is falsely attributed to Saint Jerome; for Rufinus is its author, as Erasmus, Monsieur Huet, and all learned men agree. But certainly Rufinus, a zealous and learned Origenist, would not have attributed to his [Col. 0931C] master an error incompatible with the general system of Origenism.

We must therefore seek elsewhere for the principle that led Origen to imagine the circulation of the damned and the saved. This does not concern us at present; it is enough to note what misled Jansenius. Origen does indeed claim that the demons may one day convert and that the good angels may become perverted through the faculty of free choice, whose foundation has not been taken from them; but he does not claim that the use of this faculty for good and evil is restored to them before the time appointed for the reward of the one and the punishment of the other. I am surprised that Monsieur Huet did not think of this.

“That is excellent,” said the licentiate. “I understand that Jansenius might well have spared himself the criticism of Saint Jerome, but I am waiting with the utmost impatience to learn what connection the notion of Pelagian impeccance, which you have just explained and proved so well, can have with the promise [Col. 0931D] you made me of giving me the true key to Augustine’s works against the Pelagians.”

“You are now about to grasp that precious key,” I said. “For from the notion of impeccance that I have established, it follows evidently that, in the language of Saint Augustine and Saint Jerome, to be without sin means to be free not only from every formal sin, but also from every material sin; from every movement and every disordered feeling of concupiscence, even involuntary and undeliberated; from every inward temptation; from every inclination that carries us toward evil; and from every ignorance and every surprise that involves us in, and exposes us to, committing it. In combating Pelagian impeccance, they adopted its notion and understood it in its full extent.

“There is no difficulty about this; and through how many passages of Saint Augustine can I verify it!
