They are so numerous [Col. 0932A] and so explicit that, even if the distinctive features of Pelagian impeccance were otherwise unknown, one would recognize them readily from the manner in which Saint Augustine combats this error. I will refrain for now from reporting any of the passages in question; later I shall have occasion to produce enough of them to dispel the slightest doubt on this point.

“But before going farther, we must know precisely what censure Saint Augustine passed upon Pelagian impeccance, which, as I have remarked elsewhere, he called ‘the perfection of justice.’ To this end, let us reduce, with the holy Doctor, the Pelagian error on this matter to precise terms:

‘They believe that the human will can attain the perfection of justice without God’s assistance and by its own powers:

*Putant sine adjutorio Dei per se ipsam vim voluntatis humanae vel justitiam posse perficere*’” (Book on the Spirit and the Letter, chapter 2, no. 4).

[Col. 0932B] These words contain two propositions that must not be confused: first, that the human will could attain the perfection of justice in this life; second, that it could attain it by its own powers and without God’s assistance.

Saint Augustine condemned the second proposition as a horrible and detestable heresy. As for the first, he called it false and rash, although he did not think it appropriate to quibble with the Pelagians about it, provided that they confessed the necessity of God’s grace.

“You are too eager,” he says to Julian. “You want human beings to be capable of being perfected here below; would that in this you at least recognized the gift of God:

*Sed vos festinatis, hic vultis hominem perfici, atque utinam Dei dono*” (Book II against Julian, chapter 8, no. 23).

And elsewhere he declares that he is not overly concerned whether there has ever been, or is now, or might one day be, someone who has attained the perfection of justice:

*Neque illud nimis curo, utrum fuerint, vel sint, vel esse possint, qui perfectam, cui nihil addendum esset, habuerint, vel habeant, vel habituri sint charitatem: ipsa est enim verissima, plenissima, perfectissimaque justitia. Quoniam id quod voluntate hominis adjuta per gratiam Dei fieri posse confiteor et defendi, quando, vel ubi, vel in quo fiat, nimium certare non debeo*—“Nor am I greatly concerned whether there have been, or are, or can be, those who have had, or have, or will have, charity so perfect that nothing could be added to it; for this is the truest, fullest, and most perfect justice. Since I confess and maintain that this can be brought about by the human will aided by God’s grace, I ought not to contend excessively about when, where, or in whom it occurs” (Book on Nature and Grace, chapter 42, no. 49; ibid., chapter 68, no. 82; at the end of the book on the *Perfection of Justice*). [Col. 0932C]

He makes the same declaration in several places.

But nothing holds me back any longer, and I am going to fulfill your expectation. Since my studies had brought me to the point at which we now are, the desire to make what followed easier for me led me, for the last time, to visit my doctor. As soon as he saw me, he said:

“Well, [Col. 0932D] have you finally discovered which commandment, in Saint Augustine’s sense, is impossible for us? What kind of sin has become necessary for us since Adam’s fall and is attached to invincible ignorance and all its effects? What kind of freedom have we lost? What sort of grace is irresistible by its nature and ordinarily denied to us? The doctrine of Pelagian impeccance, properly understood, has doubtless acquainted you with all these questions and shown you their object as different in the writings of the Augustine of Ypres and those of the Augustine of Hippo as night is from day.”

I asked no more. A sudden light spread through my mind; and I delayed only as long as propriety required before returning as quickly as possible to examine these questions.

## II. Which Precepts, in Saint Augustine’s Sense, Are Impossible for Us

[Col. 0933A]

Having begun comparing all the passages in Saint Augustine where precepts are discussed, I came upon these words:

> “It is one thing to fulfill what is commanded, ‘You shall not covet’; and another, by a certain effort of abstinence, at least to do what is likewise written: ‘Do not follow your lusts’ [*Post concupiscentias tuas non eas*] . . . . [lacuna] To act, therefore, is to fight for justice in the true worship of God by an inward struggle against the inward evil of concupiscence; but to perfect it is to have no adversary at all” (Book *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 63, no. 72).

Here it is perfectly evident that by the expression “perfection of justice” Saint Augustine means a manner of acting entirely conformed to the order and peace that God had established in the faculties of our soul before the fall of the first man.

But what is most remarkable is that the holy Doctor distinguishes two precepts: one which obliges us to perform the act of justice (*facere justitiam*), and another which prescribes the perfection of justice (*perficere justitiam*). He declares that the perfection of justice consists in doing good without opposition and without struggle (*omnino adversarium non habere*), whereas the act of justice consists in doing good while fighting and resisting (*interna conflictatione pugnare*). In countless other places he teaches that, for the act of justice, it is enough to restrain the impulses of concupiscence, but that for the perfection of justice there must be a complete extinction of concupiscence. You will be satisfied with the following two passages.

In explaining these words of Saint Paul, which furnished him with the very expression “perfection of justice,” he makes this observation:

> “He does not say, ‘Doing is not at hand for me,’ but ‘Perfecting is not at hand for me’: for what is the perfection of good except the consumption and end of evil? And what is the consumption of evil except what the law says, ‘You shall not covet’? Not to covet at all is the perfection of good, which is the consumption of evil. This is what he meant: ‘It is not possible for me to perfect good,’ because he could not make himself cease to covet; he only managed to restrain concupiscence, not to consent to concupiscence, and not to place his members at concupiscence’s service. ‘To perfect good, therefore,’ he says, ‘is not possible for me; I cannot fulfill what was said, “You shall not covet.” What, then, is necessary in order that you may fulfill it? Do not follow your lusts’” (Treatise 41 on John, no. 12).

The other passage is shorter:

> “For the perfection of good is that concupiscence itself should not be in a man; his will does not consent to it when he lives well, yet he does not perfect good, because concupiscence still exists in him, and his will resists it” (Book I of the *Retractions*, ch. 15, no. 2).

Saint Augustine was led to distinguish these two precepts by the approach he chose to take in answering the Pelagians, who argued that impeccability and the perfection of justice were possible in this life, since they were commanded.

He therefore decided not to deny that there was a precept of the perfection of justice, and to acknowledge that two other precepts were contained within it: one affirmative, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind”; the other negative, “You shall not covet.” He maintained, therefore, that not only could neither of these precepts be fulfilled by the powers of nature alone, but also that they would never be fulfilled in this life even by the powers of grace—or, which amounts to the same thing, that in this life God refused the grace necessary to fulfill these two precepts. This is how he explains himself generally concerning the precept of the perfection of justice:

> “We are not asking whether it is a precept, which is perfectly clear; but whether this very thing, which is acknowledged to be a precept, can be fulfilled in this body of death, where the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do the things we wish” (Book *On the Perfection of Justice*, ch. 8, no. 17).

[Col. 0934A]

He proves the existence of this precept, in its affirmative aspect, by taking the words “with all your soul” in the full rigor and extent of their literal meaning, and he reasons as follows:

> “When there is still some carnal concupiscence, even if it is restrained by continence, God is not loved in every way and with the whole soul. For the flesh does not covet without the soul, although the flesh is said to covet, because the soul covets carnally. A man will then be just without any sin whatsoever, when there is no law at all in his members resisting the law of his mind, but when he loves God with his whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind; and this is the first and greatest commandment” (ibid., no. 19).

He likewise takes the other words, “You shall not covet,” in the full rigor and extent of their literal meaning, in order to prove the existence of the precept of the perfection of justice in its negative aspect, and he offers reasoning similar to the preceding argument:

[Col. 0934B]

> “He does much good who does what is written, ‘Do not follow your lusts’ (Ecclus. XVIII, 30); but he does not perfect it, because he does not fulfill what is written, ‘You shall not covet’ (Exod. XX, 17). It is for this purpose, therefore, that the law says, ‘You shall not covet,’ etc.” (Book X [as printed] *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 29, no. 32).

This doctrine of Saint Augustine, misunderstood and misapplied, led Luther and Calvin into an absurd and intolerable error: they asserted that the righteous formally sin even while performing the holiest actions, because it is impossible for them to observe these two general precepts: “You shall love God with all your soul”; “You shall not covet.” Yet the holy Doctor omitted nothing that could make his thought properly understood. He warned that although one cannot fulfill the precept of the perfection of justice in this life, one can nevertheless satisfy it in such a way as not to be considered to have violated it; that the nature of the precept of the perfection of justice is very different from that of the precept prescribing the act of justice; that the latter has one single object, whereas the former has two—namely, a mediate and remote object, which is the complete extinction of concupiscence, and a proximate and immediate object, which is the effort to diminish the reign of concupiscence.

With regard to the first object, which is mediate and remote, Saint Augustine expressly declares that one may fail to attain the perfection of justice without becoming guilty of any formal sin or fault:

> “For if such love of God as is owed to that full and perfect knowledge cannot yet exist, this must not already be counted as guilt” (Book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, ch. 36, no. 6);

and that, by leaving us unable to fulfill the precept of the perfection of justice, God does not intend to make us liable to condemnation, but humble:

> “Nor does He wish us to be condemnable on that account, but humble” (Book II *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, ch. 19, no. 33);

and that the sin precisely opposed to the perfection of justice is a misery, not a fault that our conscience can reproach us for:

> “Thus neither is he reproved in his own life—that is, in his faith—by his own heart, nor is he convicted of not being without sin” (Book *On the Perfection of Justice*, ch. 11, no. 28).

[Col. 0934D]

With regard to the second object, which is proximate and immediate, Saint Augustine maintains that man is obliged to strive and aspire toward the perfection of justice, and that, in order to deserve to attain it in the next life, God requires efforts from us in this one:

> “For this purpose, then, the law said, ‘You shall not covet’: so that, finding us lying in this sickness, we might seek the medicine of grace, and might learn from that precept both toward what we ought to strive in this mortality in order to be perfected, and toward what we may attain in that most blessed immortality. For unless it were destined to be perfected at some time, it would never have been commanded” (Book I *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 29, no. 32).

He says that this precept is intended to lead us to prayer and to animate our hope:

> “This first precept of justice, by which we are commanded to love God with our whole heart . . . we shall fulfill in that life, when we shall see face to face. But it is commanded to us even now so that we may be reminded what to seek by faith, toward what to direct our hope, and, forgetting what lies behind, toward what lies ahead we ought to stretch ourselves” (Book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, ch. 36, no. 64).

He says that this precept is intended to show us the goal toward which we must arrive:

> “Why, then, should this perfection not be commanded to man, although no one possesses it in this life? For one does not run rightly if one does not know where one must run; and how would one know, unless it were shown by precepts?” (Book *On the Perfection of Justice*, ch. 8, no. 19).

He says that it was necessary, through this precept, to arouse in us a hunger and thirst for justice, without which we could not deserve to be satisfied with it:

> “For no one will attain to the fullness of justice after leaving this life unless, while he is here, he has run toward it by hungering and thirsting . . . . [lacuna] This is now our justice, by which, hungering and thirsting, we run toward the perfection and fullness of justice, so that afterward we may be satisfied with it” (ibid., nos. 17–18).

In a word, the precept of the perfection of justice is, in Saint Augustine’s thought, more or less like the precept imposed upon us to work effectively for our salvation and actually to be saved. Its remote and mediate object is salvation; its proximate and immediate object is concern for salvation. The fulfillment of this kind of precept is impossible in the present life, if one speaks strictly, because the complete and final fulfillment of a precept includes the precept’s entire object and therefore its remote and mediate object.

I know that this comparison is not entirely exact; for Saint Augustine maintains that, in one sense, we transgress the precept of the perfection of justice by failing to fulfill it in this life, although this transgression is not criminal and is not imputed to us. But he means only that, in this respect, we have fallen from the blessedness of the state of innocence; that it is a defect of our condition and a misery that deserves to be called by the name of sin. This is sufficient for the refutation of Luther and Calvin.

But Jansenius, with far greater bad faith than either heresiarch, abused this doctrine of Saint Augustine. Everything that the holy Doctor said about the perfection of justice, Jansenius boldly applies to the act of justice. In order to show that there are precepts impossible for man with regard to the condition in which he finds himself and the present powers granted to him, he is not ashamed to cite the book *On the Perfection of Justice*, where:

> “Celestius,” he says, “employs all the subtlety of his mind and all his efforts to establish the possibility of the precepts; and his principal reason is that it would not be wise to command something impossible. Saint Augustine replies that one may very wisely command a man to walk straight, so that, when he realizes that he cannot do so, he may seek a remedy for his infirmity: ‘It is most wisely commanded that a man walk with straight feet, so that, when he has perceived that he cannot, he may seek medicine’” (vol. III, book III, ch. 13, p. 325; Book *On the Perfection of Justice*, ch. 3, no. 6).

The very title of the book and the words of Celestius show that the question here concerns the precept of impeccability:

> “It must again be asked whether it is a precept that man be without sin.”

Jansenius is not ashamed to repeat several times this other passage from the same place:

> “For when we see a lame man who can be healed, we rightly say, ‘This man ought to be without lameness’; and if he ought to be, he can. Yet when he wishes to do so, he cannot immediately; he can only do so once he has been healed by the application of treatment and medicine has assisted the will” (Saint Augustine, ibid.; Jansenius, ibid.).

He does this while attempting to convince his readers that precepts, as we ordinarily understand them, are sometimes impossible for the righteous, even though they presently have the will to fulfill them. He suggests that the healing in question is the actual grace of our condition, which is necessary for the practice of works of Christian piety. He conceals the fact that, a few lines lower, it becomes completely clear that the healing is one granted only in heaven, and that the charity in question is one that only the immediate vision of God can inspire:

> “Then justice will be complete when health is complete; then health will be complete when charity is complete; for the fullness of the law is charity; and charity will then be complete when we see Him as He is” (Saint Augustine, ibid.).

Jansenius is not ashamed . . . . [lacuna] It is worth warning you that, in the passage of Jansenius’s book that I am refuting, there is a fine rhetorical repetition that leads me to make a similar one. Jansenius, I say, is not ashamed to employ again this passage from the same place:

> “Faith cries out to God: Deliver me from my necessities, under which we are placed either unable to understand what we wish, or willing what we have understood but unable to fulfill it” (Jansenius, ibid., p. 326; Saint Augustine, ibid., ch. 4, no. 9).

Besides the general objection that applies to everything he has cited from a book dealing exclusively with the perfection of justice, one need only read a little farther to see that Saint Augustine is speaking of an impossibility from which we are not to be delivered until heaven. It consists in the fact that we are always enveloped in certain darknesses that conceal part of our duties from us, and that we do not have the strength to subject the entire extent of the powers of our soul to the law.

Jansenius is not ashamed to report almost none of the testimony from the great number of passages that he strings together in his fine rhetorical figure, although they concern the impossibility of the precept of the perfection of justice. This one is noteworthy:

> “There are also necessities that must be disapproved, when a man wishes to do right and cannot” (Jansenius, ibid., p. 327).

Jansenius stops there. What follows would have betrayed his imposture:

> “For from where come these words: ‘For I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I do not will’? And this: ‘To will is present with me, but to perfect I do not find’” (Saint Augustine, Book III *On Free Choice of the Will*, ch. 18, no. 51).

What precept was impossible for Saint Paul, whose words Saint Augustine cites? Was it not the precept of the perfection of justice? What, then, do this testimony and the others that Jansenius draws from the same passage prove?

The single word *perficere* is enough to deprive him of the following text, which he employs elsewhere:

> “But that the power to perfect good is not present belongs to the merit of original sin” (Book I *To Simplicianus*, question 1, no. 11).

Saint Augustine means that original sin is the cause of our inability to fulfill the precept of the perfection of justice, because, even after baptism, which wipes away original sin, concupiscence nevertheless remains, as material for struggle and testing.

[Col. 0936D]

“Since I am eager,” the licentiate then said, “to hear you on the other questions, I tremble lest you should begin stringing together all the passages of Saint Augustine that Jansenius employs here or elsewhere against the possibility of the precepts, and undertake to refute them one after another. We would never finish.”

“I will spare you that,” I replied, “for these passages either concern the perfection of justice or they do not. If they concern the perfection of justice, they no longer present any difficulty; if they do not, one need only weigh the words, or restore them to the text from which they were taken, in order to discover the evident abuse Jansenius makes of them. Thus I pass to the second question, namely:

## III. What Kind of Sin Has Become Necessary for Us Since the Fall of the First Man?

At the end of the book *On the Perfection of Justice*, Saint Augustine reports the opinion of certain Catholic doctors of his time. They maintained—not, like the Pelagians, that man in this life can master his first movements and the rebellions of the flesh, but—that the disordered and indeliberate desires of concupiscence, to which one gives no consent, ought not to be considered sins. Although the holy Doctor does not dare censure this opinion, he does not approve it, and he considers it false.

He therefore distinguishes two kinds of sin: one that, in the schools, we would call material, which is not a fault and which God does not impute; the other which, in our language, is a formal sin and a punishable fault:

> “Finally, if, excepting our one Head, the Savior of His body, it is asserted that there have been or are in this life some men who are just without sin—either because they never consent to its desires, or because what goes no further than this—that God does not impute it to a devout person—is to be regarded as no sin (although one person is blessed without sin in one way, and another is blessed in another way, because the Lord does not impute sin)—I do not think that we ought to resist too strongly. For I know that this has seemed so to certain persons, whose opinion on this matter I do not dare condemn, although I cannot defend it either” (Book *On the Perfection of Justice*, final chapter, §21, at the end, no. 44).

Saint Augustine here distinguishes two kinds of sin, just as he distinguished two kinds of precepts: one kind of sin consisting in consent to evil, and another kind consisting in the experience of evil. The former is contrary to the act of justice; the latter is contrary to the perfection of justice. The first kind of sin makes man guilty because it is opposed to a precept that we can fulfill in this life; the second makes man only miserable because it is opposed to a precept that we cannot fulfill in this life. The holy Doctor did not merely distinguish these two kinds of sin; he precisely defined them.

“Sin,” he says, “is a will to admit or retain what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain”:

> “*Peccatum est voluntas admittendi vel retinendi quod justitia vetat, et unde liberum est abstinere*” — “Sin is the will to admit or retain what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain” (Book *On Two Souls*, ch. 11, no. 15).

This is the definition of the sin opposed to the act of justice. He had used it against the Manichaeans, and he repeats and approves it in several places in his writings against the Pelagians (Book I *Unfinished Work against Julian*, nos. 44–47; Book II, no. 38; Book VI, nos. 17, 21).

As for the other kind of sin, which is opposed to the perfection of justice, he says that it consists in a defect of charity. There is sin, he says, when charity is not what it ought to be, or when it is less than it ought to be, whether one can avoid this defect by one’s will or cannot avoid it:

> “But sin exists when charity either is not what it ought to be or is less than it ought to be, whether this can be avoided by the will or cannot be avoided” (Book *On the Perfection of Justice*, ch. 6, no. 15).

[Col. 0937D]

It may seem surprising that, for the exclusion of every sin, Saint Augustine requires not merely charity, but a charity to which nothing could be added, *cui nihil addendum esset* (Book *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 42, no. 49). Did he not know that charity can increase without limit, and that among the blessed in heaven there are as many different degrees of charity as there are different degrees of holiness and glory?

But one must observe that, in his disputes with the Pelagians concerning impeccability, the holy Doctor measures charity only in relation to two of its effects. The first is to dispel the darkness that original sin has spread through our mind:

> “If such love of God as is owed to that full and perfect knowledge cannot yet exist” (Book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, ch. 36, no. 65).

The second is to extinguish the movements of our sensual appetite:

> “Finally, if in the righteous Abel the charity of God—by which alone whoever is righteous is truly righteous—still had something by which it could and ought to be increased, whatever was lacking was a defect; and there could be no lack until one reached that strength where the whole weakness of man would be absorbed” (Book *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 38, no. 45).

[Col. 0938A]

That is why, in heaven, where our darknesses will be entirely dispelled and concupiscence destroyed, nothing will oppose charity either in the mind or in the heart. Charity will possess the entire extent of the soul’s powers, and in this sense it will not be able to increase or be susceptible to more or less:

> “Love itself will be not only far above what we have here, but far above what we ask and understand; yet it will not on that account be able to be more than with the whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind. For nothing remains in us that could be added to the whole; because if something remained, it would not be the whole” (Book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, ch. 36, no. 64).

The defect of charity, so long as charity is not perfect—and as great as it can be in the sense I have just explained—is therefore the sin opposed to the perfection of justice. Every interior disorder, even when indeliberate and involuntary; every disordered feeling, although necessary and antecedent, is this same sin.

It is scarcely possible to open Saint Augustine’s books against the Pelagians without encountering the clearest proofs of this. “The question,” he says, “is not whether concupiscence should be restrained; it ought not to exist in any way, and it will not exist in that perfection of justice where there will be no sin whatsoever”:

> “Not to be restrained, but altogether not to exist, and it will not exist—concupiscence—in that perfection of justice where there will be no sin whatsoever” (Book *On the Perfection of Justice*, ch. 8, no. 18).

To show that Job was not exempt from sin, the final reason the holy Doctor gives is that Job could count among his sins the rebellions of the flesh that he experienced against his will:

> “It may also be that what he said, ‘And You have taken note if I have committed anything unwillingly,’ belongs to that statement in which it is said: ‘For I do not do what I will, but I do what I hate’” (Book II *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, ch. 10, no. 15).

Instead of giving you an enormous list of passages in the manner of Jansenius, I shall simply assert that Saint Augustine, in order to force the Pelagians to admit that no man in this life has been without sin, continually brings forward the example and words of Saint Paul. Paul complains of a sin dwelling in his flesh; deplores the tyranny of the law of his members, opposed to the law of his mind; and three times asks the Lord to deliver him from this domestic enemy, without being answered.

Saint Augustine repeats this argument endlessly in his earliest works against the Pelagians, in all his books against Julian, and in Sermons 151, 152, 154, 155, and 156 of the latest edition, which he delivered at Carthage when the controversy over impeccability was at its most heated. I have counted more than one hundred and fifty places where he repeats it, and I have by no means counted them all. He certainly believed that this was an unanswerable proof; but he was wrong to regard it as triumphant. On the contrary, it is the most pitiful proof if the sin opposed to Pelagian impeccability is not what I have described.

[Col. 0938D]

“‘I do not do the good that I will,’ Saint Paul says, ‘but I do the evil that I do not will’:

> “*Non quod volo bonum hoc ago, sed quod odi malum illud facio*” — “I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I hate” (Rom. VII, 15).

“Yet it is not I,” he adds, “who do the evil that I hate, but sin dwelling in me:

> “*Nunc autem jam non ego operor illud, sed quod habitat in me peccatum*” — “But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me.”

“‘My grace is sufficient for you,’ the Lord says to the Apostle, ‘for virtue is perfected in weakness’:

> “*Sufficit tibi gratia mea, nam virtus in infirmitate perficitur*” — “My grace is sufficient for you, for virtue is perfected in weakness” (II Cor. XII, 9).”

“Therefore,” Saint Augustine concludes, “no man in this life has been without sin.”

Should he not rather conclude: Therefore, despite the importunities and solicitations of the flesh, some person—for example, Saint Paul—has been without sin?

Thus the exclusion of formal sin is only one part of the dogma of Pelagian impeccability. The part that Saint Augustine most often and principally combats is the exclusion of material sin. The Pelagians refused to recognize this kind of sin; they maintained that nothing disordered within us could be necessary.

But what does Jansenius do? He explains, of the first article and of formal sin, what the holy Doctor says of the second article and of material sin. The authority and words of Saint Augustine of Hippo, teaching against the Pelagians the necessity of experiencing interior temptations that lead us to sin, are employed by Augustine of Ypres to teach, against the Church, the necessity of consenting to sin (Jansenius, vol. II, Book III *On the State of Fallen Nature*, ch. 9, p. 470, etc.). See the unfaithful and artful account he gives of the dispute between Saint Augustine and Julian concerning the definition of sin.

The true subject of this dispute is that Julian refused to confess that the disordered and indeliberate movements of the flesh were in any sense sins, unless he were shown that the definition of sin formerly given by Saint Augustine himself in his books against the Manichaeans applied to these movements. It is the definition I gave above, namely:

> “Sin is the will to admit or retain what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain: *Peccatum est voluntas admittendi vel retinendi quod justitia vetat, et unde liberum est abstinere*” (Saint Augustine, Book *On Two Souls*, ch. 11, no. 15).

Saint Augustine replies that the definition of which he was speaking, and on which Julian relied in vain, concerned the kind of sin into which the first man alone could fall when he was still innocent. At that time, since his flesh was perfectly subject to the spirit, it was free for him to abstain from everything he did and everything he felt when he violated the precept of justice. But in the present condition man is not free to abstain from the oppositions and repugnances that raise his sensual appetite against reason and the law:

> “For Adam, when he sinned, had absolutely nothing evil in himself by which he would be driven, unwilling, to do evil, and on account of which he might say, ‘I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I do not will.’ Thus, by sinning, he did what justice forbade and from which it is free to abstain. But now, for the one who says, ‘I do the evil that I do not will,’ it is not free to abstain from that” (Book I *Unfinished Work against Julian*, no. 47).

It is the disorder and rebellion of the senses from which Saint Augustine says that man is not now free to abstain—*abstinere inde*—that Jansenius supposes the holy Doctor means by formal sin, by consent to sin. First infidelity.

Saint Augustine adds that three things must be distinguished: sin, the punishment of sin, and that which is simultaneously sin and punishment of sin. He explains his thought by examples. The first kind, he says, is found without difficulty in Adam; for men perform many evil actions from which it is free for them to abstain, but no one ever enjoyed as much freedom as Adam:

> “If examples are sought of the three kinds, an example of the first kind is found in Adam without any difficulty in the question. For there are many things that men do from which it is free for them to abstain, but it was free for no one as it was for him” (ibid.).

It is easy to understand in what sense the holy Doctor had said that the definition concerned Adam:

> “It was Adam himself whom that definition of ours, which pleased you, had in view” (ibid.).

This does not mean that it concerned Adam alone, but that it alone applied to the sins of which Adam was capable in a state in which he experienced nothing disordered within himself. For, according to the holy Doctor, this definition also applies to the evil actions that men now perform and from which he assures us they can abstain. He therefore considers himself obliged to explain why he took his example from Adam rather than from other men for what he intended to define, and what is simply called sin.

But Jansenius absolutely insists that Saint Augustine’s definition applies exclusively to the sin by which Adam fell from the state of innocence. He is embarrassed by these words: “For there are many things that men do from which it is free for them to abstain.” How does he extricate himself? He places the freedom Saint Augustine attributes to men before every habit of sin and, following the ideas of his good friend Calvin, he does not distinguish this freedom from efficacious grace, which delivers men from the slavery of sin and prevents them from committing it:

> “namely, before the habit of sin had been contracted, and when they had already been freed from the slavery of sin by grace” (Jansenius, vol. II, Book III *On the State of Fallen Nature*, p. 472).

What does he mean by this, and what does he make Saint Augustine say? That men are free to abstain from sin when they abstain from it; whereas the holy Doctor says that men are free to abstain from sin when they commit it:

> “For there are many things that men do from which it is free for them to abstain.”

Second infidelity.

As for that which is simultaneously sin and punishment of sin, to which the definition given by Saint Augustine in his works against the Manichaeans does not apply, and from which man is not now free to abstain, Saint Augustine gives no other example than the two miseries that are effects of original sin: concupiscence and ignorance. He again returns to the words of Saint Paul, who complains of the tyranny exercised over his mind by the importunate sting of his flesh:

> “But an example of the third kind, in which sin itself and the punishment of sin can be understood, is found in the one who says: ‘I do the evil that I do not will,’ etc.” (ibid.).

Why did Saint Augustine not give as an example all the sins that men now commit! Nothing could have been more suitable to Jansenius’s argument. But a sin of Saint Paul is extremely inconvenient for him; he senses this, and skillfully diverts his reader’s attention from the person of the Apostle by means of this strange commentary:

> “Those who say, ‘I do not do what I will,’ that is, those whom concupiscence has so thoroughly subjugated that they do everything it compels them to do.”

And he presents this commentary as borrowed from Saint Augustine, who elsewhere understands the Apostle’s words in this way. The misfortune is that, in the passage cited by Jansenius—which belongs to a work composed long before the one whose text he is explaining—the holy Doctor rejects this interpretation as entirely false:

> “For I used to think that these things could not be said except of those whom the concupiscence of the flesh had so subjugated that they did whatever it compelled them to do; but to believe this of the Apostle is foolish . . . . But afterward I yielded to better and more discerning men—or rather, to truth itself, as must be confessed—so that I might see in those words of the Apostle the groaning of holy people struggling against carnal concupiscences” (Book VI *Against Julian*, ch. 23, no. 70).

Third infidelity.

Do not be afraid; I shall spare you the overwhelming discussion of the enormous number of passages that Jansenius accumulates to support this error—that man is now necessitated to sin. He does not cite a single passage whose subject in Augustine is not sin opposed to the perfection of justice, the material sin of undeliberated movements of concupiscence, or effects caused by invincible ignorance. Jansenius has deceived the world by making the true state of the question between Augustine and the Pelagians disappear. It must always be remembered that these heretics denied the existence of this material sin, maintaining, with Stoic pride, that nothing in man could be disordered [Col. 0941A] except through man’s free and personal fault; moreover, it is necessary to observe that Augustine, following the usage of his time and language, authorized by Scripture, not only had the right but could not refrain from calling by the name of sin every defect and misery that Adam’s transgression had introduced into the human will contrary to God’s established order and the perfection of its first condition.

It is not the holy doctor’s fault that, according to the usage and genius of modern languages, the word “sin” always awakens in our minds the idea of a fault. Augustine calls the way of thinking of Caelestius Pelagian because Caelestius continually said of material sin, contrary to the perfection of justice, what he could truly say only of formal sin, contrary to the action of justice; for this arch-heretic wanted there to be nothing blameworthy, disavowable, in need of reform or correction in the most rapid outbursts of the movements of concupiscence, [Col. 0941B] except insofar as we neglected to regulate and repress them—something he claimed was always within our power.

While I was speaking, the licentiate had Augustine’s works against the Pelagians in his hands, and he read the passages I had marked as I cited them. He then objected that, later in the text, he had noticed several propositions and expressions that could apply only to formal sin, and to what is called a fault, precisely in the places where I maintained that the holy doctor was speaking of material sin and a mere misery of the human will.

“That should not surprise you,” I replied, “and it will happen to you much more often when you read the passages concerning ignorance. This is a subject that I am eager to clarify thoroughly. To treat it fully, it seems to me that I must place in a new light the notion of sin that Augustine opposes to Pelagian impeccability [Col. 0941C]. The holy doctor conceives sin in general as a movement of the will that departs from justice; I would say that it separates the human will from justice, if habitual sin were in question. He divides sin into two kinds: one that turns the will away from the action of justice, and another that turns the will away from the perfection of justice—that is, from the justice in which our first father was created, to the inalienable possession of which we are destined in the future life, toward which we are obliged to strive, which we must continually approach by becoming more just from day to day and working constantly toward our perfection.

“Saint Jerome had the same ideas as Saint Augustine on this matter. Both taught that this sin—which, as I have said, would be called material in the schools—ought to be humbly acknowledged, blamed, and lamented as a misery, and that efforts ought to be made to free ourselves from it, at least in part [Col. 0941D] and as far as possible; but they were careful not to believe that this sin made us guilty before God or worthy of any punishment, as though it were a fault.

“The first error of the Pelagians, I repeat once more, was to assert that in this life man could make himself so perfect that he would completely fulfill the imaginary idea of the wise man that the pagan philosophers had fashioned. Now, in the battles that the holy Fathers waged against the Pelagians on this subject, it was for these heretics to show that man was capable of exercising such mastery over all the movements of his soul that he could purge all his actions of the slightest defect, so that nothing would ever escape him that was in the least contrary to the perfection of justice. But it was enough for the holy doctors who refuted the Pelagians to show that it was impossible for man not often to depart [Col. 0942A] from the most perfect justice, whether through free actions or through necessary actions—and this must be carefully noted. From this they concluded that the perfection of justice belonged properly to Adam’s state, from which we have fallen through original sin. It is therefore not surprising that in this controversy they confused formal sin and material sin: both served their purpose equally clearly, and material sin more effectively.

### IV. What kind of sin is attached to invincible ignorance, and all its effects

“The mixture of features relating to formal sin and material sin is customary and frequent in the writings of the holy doctors when ignorance is at issue, and here is the reason. The Pelagians were greatly embarrassed on this point; they did not know what position to take or what to hold, in order to establish their wavering doctrine upon a fixed point [Col. 0942B]. They had first maintained that the just man, to whom they attributed the power to guard himself from every sin, would have absolutely no ignorance of anything connected with the observance of the law. Saint Jerome states this as follows:

> ‘Hence you also assert that those who are without knowledge of the law cannot avoid sins’ (*Against the Letter of Ctesiphon*, vol. IV, p. 476).

And elsewhere:

> ‘You say that no one can be without sin except one who possesses knowledge of the law’ (*Dialogue* I, p. 500).

“The words that follow show that, according to the method of all heretics, Pelagius did not fail to flatter the ladies, and that he was very far from begrudging the female sex the right to aspire to perfect knowledge of the law. Saint Jerome therefore mocks him in these terms:

> ‘For how many Christians possess knowledge of the law, which in many teachers of the Church is found either rarely or only with difficulty? Yet you are so generous that you win favor among your Amazons, since in another place you have written that even women [Col. 0942C] ought to possess knowledge of the law’ (ibid.).

“However, once the Catholics had demonstrated that ignorance could sometimes be invincible, Pelagius’s disciples took the position of denying that, in such a case, one committed any sin by violating the law, in the sense in which both sides understood the word ‘sin’—which denoted a fault no more than it denoted a defect and misery incompatible with perfect justice. That is to say, the Pelagians refused to acknowledge that such an action, considered materially and in itself, was evil, blameworthy, and in need of reform, or that it required an excuse. On the contrary, they regarded it as good and so regular that the delicacy of the most perfect justice ought to accommodate itself to it; consequently, a man who, being well instructed in the law, observed it would be no better than another who violated it through ignorance. This is what we learn from Augustine, who speaks to Julian as follows:

> ‘Proceed to the rest. And weave together things more empty than emptiness itself . . . since you say that from this it ought to be understood that perfect ignorance must be called justice [Col. 0942D] . . . Why, then, do you not call them just, if perfect ignorance is to be named justice? For nothing is more perfect than ignorance; let it therefore be called nothing more just . . . Will you perhaps say that virtue is not justice? How, then, is the infant not yet full of virtue but capable of it, when he is full of ignorance, which you say is justice—unless you deny that virtue is justice?’ (*Against Julian* III, chap. 19, no. 36).

“The Pelagians went so far in their apology for ignorance, and were carried away by such a passion for justifying it, that they were commonly credited—as Saint Jerome implies—with believing that ignorance, inadvertence, and forgetfulness were not sins if one had fallen into them through mere negligence, and not through a wholly direct will that avoids and flees the light, blinding or distracting the mind out of hatred for the truth. This is why [Col. 0943A] the holy doctors, when disputing against these heretics, speak indiscriminately in the same terms of vincible and invincible ignorance. To this must be added the reason I have already suggested: the Pelagians were equally defeated if they were shown that man departed from perfect justice either by committing formal sin through vincible ignorance or by committing material sin through invincible ignorance.

“But on this point there was still some diversity in the Pelagians’ opinions, and it is true that, most often, Julian, Caelestius, and even Pelagius himself appear to acknowledge a true sin in vincible ignorance, whatever its form. Jansenius offers fairly good evidence of this, such as these words of Augustine to Julian:

> ‘See how rightly and gravely you rebuked those who neglected to learn what ought to be known’ (*Against Julian* VI, chap. 1, no. 2).

And this proposition of Caelestius, condemned at the Council of Diospolis [Col. 0943B]:

> ‘That forgetfulness and ignorance are not subject to sin, since they do not occur according to the will but according to necessity’ (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chap. 35, no. 65).

And above all this maxim of Pelagius:

> ‘Man ought to be constantly vigilant lest he be ignorant; therefore ignorance is blameworthy, because through his negligence a man does not know what, with due diligence, he ought to have known’ (*On Nature and Grace*, chap. 17, no. 19).

“Perhaps these heretics blamed only gross negligence. Whatever the case, Saint Jerome nevertheless adduces against them the punishment of Uzzah, who was struck dead (II Kings 6) for imprudently stretching out his hand toward the ark of the Lord:

> ‘David, the just man and prophet . . . when he sees ignorance punished by the Lord’s wrath, is terrified and saddened, and does not ask the Lord why he struck the ignorant man’ (*Dialogue* I, near the end, p. 508);

“the punishment of David, from whom a plague sent by God took 70,000 of his subjects because he had ordered their numbering (II Kings 24), in which he [Col. 0943C] did not think he was doing wrong:

> ‘When he ordered it to be done, he plainly did not know what he was saying; yet he himself reproached himself, and for this fault seventy thousand men were slain by the angel’s sword’ (Saint Jerome, ibid.);

“and Job’s sacrifices for the expiation of the sins that his children might have committed through ignorance (Job 1:5):

> ‘Hence Job also offers sacrifices for his sons, lest perhaps they had sinned in thought through ignorance’ (*Dialogue* I, p. 504).

“It is clear that these examples indicate vincible ignorance.

“Besides this, Augustine gives us occasion here to make an important observation: the Pelagians admitted a kind of invincible ignorance that was, in reality, vincible—namely, ignorance from which man could free himself with the help of grace, which he had neglected to implore.

> ‘He also treats of sins of ignorance, and says that man ought to be vigilant lest he be ignorant; therefore ignorance is blameworthy, because through his negligence a man does not know what, with due diligence [Col. 0943D], he ought to have known; yet he would rather discuss everything than pray and say, “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments.” For it is one thing not to have cared to know what negligence makes sinful—sins that even seemed to be expiated by certain sacrifices of the law; it is another to wish to understand and be unable, and to act against the law without understanding what it wishes to be done. Hence we are admonished by God to ask for wisdom, who gives generously to all—certainly to all who ask in the manner and measure in which so great a thing ought to be requested’ (*On Nature and Grace*, chap. 17, no. 19).

“After having thus explained to you the Pelagians’ views concerning ignorance, nothing is easier than to make you grasp the enormous contrast between Jansenius’s doctrine and that of Augustine and Jerome on the same subject.

“These two holy doctors maintain that ignorance itself is a sin, and not merely what one does against the law through ignorance. ‘Is there no evil in ignorance, and therefore nothing to be cleansed?’ asks Saint [Col. 0944A] Augustine (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* I, chap. 26, no. 66). ‘Must I now traverse the widest testimony of the Scriptures in order to teach that error and ignorance are sin?’ asks Jerome (*Dialogue* I, p. 504). Augustine almost everywhere offers children’s ignorance as an example of this sin; and Jerome, in order to demonstrate its reality through episodes from sacred history, goes so far as to appeal to Jacob’s ignorance, since he did not know what had become of his son Joseph; to Samuel’s ignorance, since he did not know which of Jesse’s sons God had destined to be king of his people; and to Ahijah of Shiloh’s ignorance, since he did not know that the queen of Israel, Jeroboam’s wife, was coming to him. It is true that Augustine speaks of a baptized man in these terms:

> ‘He is free from every sin, but not from every evil: *Omni peccato caret, et non omni malo*’ [He is free from every sin, but not from every evil] (*Against Julian* VI, chap. 16, no. 49).

“But he finds that his expression is not sufficiently precise, because it restricts the idea of sin to what [Col. 0944B] grounds the designation and quality of being guilty. He therefore corrects it in this way:

> ‘More clearly, this is said as follows: after baptism the believer is free from all guilt in respect of all evils, but he is not free from all evils: *Quod planius ita dicitur, omni reatu omnium malorum caret, non omnibus malis*’ [More plainly, he is free from the guilt of all evils, but not from all evils].

“Finally, ignorance places man in a condition opposed to the perfection of justice; from this it follows, according to the principles of Augustine and Jerome, that ignorance itself is a sin, just as its effects are.

“This is why Luther and Calvin, who taught Jansenius the secret of proclaiming a monstrous heresy under Augustine’s name by confusing the two kinds of sin—sin against the action of justice and sin against the perfection of justice—were better dialecticians than the Bishop of Ypres. They erred more consistently when, as the principle of their doctrine concerning invincible ignorance [Col. 0944C], they held that concupiscence and ignorance in themselves and by their nature deserve God’s hatred, are formal and properly so-called sins, and constitute in us the whole essence of original sin. From this the two arch-heretics conclude that original sin remains after baptism, since concupiscence and ignorance remain, and that the whole effect of baptism is to remove the external imputation of this sin—which through that sacrament is not erased but covered and buried, because God, in view of Jesus Christ, remits the penalty He would have the right to exact. They further conclude that all the effects of concupiscence and ignorance are so many new sins.

“Jansenius agrees with his teachers concerning the essence of original sin, which he likewise makes consist in concupiscence and ignorance; but he would not dare agree with them that baptism removes only its external imputation and certain outward appearances. He wants the virtue of this sacrament to cause concupiscence [Col. 0944D] and ignorance to cease making us hateful and guilty; that is, he wants original sin no longer to exist, while its nature remains (Jansenius, vol. II, book I, *On the State of Fallen Nature*, chap. 1, p. 186).

“Jansenius’s inconsistency does not end there. Although he admits that invincible ignorance is not a sin, and that it remains together with friendship with God in those who have received baptism, he nevertheless asserts at the same time that actions caused by invincible ignorance, when they are contrary to the natural law, are formal sins worthy of God’s hatred and eternal punishments. In other words, from an innocent principle, crime is a necessary effect. What is stranger is that he claims the same does not apply to concupiscence, whose first movements he teaches are as innocent as their principle (*On the State of Fallen Nature* II, chap. 6, p. 312). It is clear that in all this he contradicts Saint [Col. 0945A] Augustine more than he differs from Luther and Calvin.

“But it is not easy to decide whether he contradicts himself more than he contradicts his two predecessors. Is it not only pretense and equivocation that separate him from them and conceal from us a complete reconciliation and perfect agreement among all the modern predestinarians? Whatever the case, I have only just begun to explain to you the certain contrast that strangely divides Jansenius’s doctrine concerning ignorance from that of Augustine and Jerome.

“These holy doctors never thought of distinguishing between ignorance of a fact or of positive law, whether divine or human, and ignorance of natural law. They generally and without exception called every ignorance of duty, whatever its kind, a sin. Indeed, when they undertake to convince the Pelagians [Col. 0945B] from Scripture that both vincible and invincible ignorance are sin, they report almost no examples except those involving ignorance of fact or positive law. Such examples include a homicide committed accidentally, which the Mosaic law punishes with exile; Achan’s secret theft, for which God Himself holds the whole people responsible; and the transgression of an edict that had been entirely unknown, for which, when God is consulted, He reveals the author—even though he was a prince pleasing in His sight, whom He had just favored with a miraculous victory, and whom He exposes to punishment. Saint Jerome does not think he is straying when he seeks a hundred other similar examples, nor does he fear that anyone will reproach him for applying them incorrectly.

“But Jansenius appeals to Augustine as better informed about the Pelagian errors and more skilled in combating them; he will be condemned before Augustine’s tribunal. Has he not noticed that this saint himself uses similar examples and opposes to Caelestius’s heretical proposition concerning ignorance and forgetfulness the sacrifices offered under the ancient [Col. 0945C] law for the expiation of sins of ignorance?

> ‘Since under the law sacrifices are offered for ignorance as for sin’ (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chap. 18, no. 42).

“Is it Jansenius or Augustine who failed to reflect that all these sacrifices were prescribed only for ignorance of fact or of positive law?

“Luther and Calvin understood the holy doctor’s thought much better on this point. They did not hesitate to classify every kind of ignorance and all its effects equally as sin. They held to the generality of that condition without which Augustine judges it wrong to boast that one is without sin, namely, possessing a perfect knowledge of all things pertaining to justice:

> ‘If nothing of the things that pertain to justice were hidden from us’ (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, chap. 35, no. 63).

“This, properly speaking, had to be, and actually was, the doctrine of the Fathers who entered the lists against the Pelagians on this subject. Every ignorance that has some relation to duty is opposed to perfect justice; and [Col. 0945D] consequently ignorance of positive law and of facts that influence moral conduct is just as clearly contrary to it as ignorance of natural law. Both would equally have been banished from our minds if we had not fallen from the advantages and privileges of the state in which man was created.

“Jansenius vainly makes subtle distinctions to show that one, and not the other, is a consequence of original sin (Jansenius, vol. II, book II, *On the State of Fallen Nature*, chap. 6, p. 311). For certainly everything that deprives us of knowledge of rules of conduct—even arbitrary rules prescribed to us by legitimate authority; everything that conceals from us the circumstances from which arises a change in the situations to which reason requires our actions to conform; everything that causes inadvertence, forgetfulness, or prejudices whose effect is the violation of some positive law—is this anything other than the miseries whose unhappy source is Adam’s sin, and which very often [Col. 0946A] obstruct, and sometimes absolutely block, the passage of every kind of truth to us? Shall we call those deep darknesses that seize us from the moment we enter the world and keep us enveloped throughout a long childhood ignorance of natural law alone? Do the difficulty of learning, understanding, retaining, and recalling to memory what we have learned; the impossibility of dividing our attention among all the objects that demand it; the tyranny of the anticipatory movements of concupiscence, which deprive us of perfect control over our attention; the sudden vehemence of the passions; and an infinity of circumstances resulting from the weakness and corruption of nature—all these obstacles impede knowledge of facts relevant to duty and knowledge of positive laws any less than knowledge of natural law?

“Nevertheless,” says Jansenius, “it does not appear reasonable [Col. 0946B] to believe that in the state of innocence one would have been informed of every event that would take place in the world.” As though the issue here were every kind of accident and fact, rather than only those necessarily connected with obligations! Clearly, there would have been few such events if the first man had not sinned, because positive laws also would have been rarer. They could have been useful to innocent man only as a test of his obedience, whereas our needs have required that multitude of precepts which constitutes positive human and divine law. And where do these needs come from, if not from the scant resources that each person finds in his own reason, and from the little uprightness and strength that remain in his will since nature was weakened and corrupted by sin? This is why the wisdom of legislators had to become the common reason of society, and why, through the seal [Col. 0946C] of a respected authority, one person was given the power to will once what a great people would always be obliged to do. Thus the very necessity of positive laws comes from sin; how could invincible ignorance of these laws not be a consequence of it?

“Why, then,” Jansenius replies, “does Augustine teach in more than one place that ignorance of facts or of positive law excuses from sin?” He likewise teaches in several places that ignorance of natural law excuses from sin, as has been demonstrated so many times against Jansenius’s vain allegations. Thus the way to reconcile the holy doctor with himself is not to attend to the kind of ignorance, but rather to the kind of sin of which he is speaking. According to Augustine, every invincible ignorance excuses from the sin that is against the action of justice, and no ignorance, even invincible ignorance, excuses from the sin that is against the perfection of justice.

“That is the knot that Jansenius pretended not to see [Col. 0946D] and feared to touch.

“What! Because Luther and Calvin, Baius and Jansenius did not think fit to make this distinction, Augustine will therefore be an accomplice in their errors? This Father conformed himself to the ecclesiastical and theological language current in his time by calling sin not only a fault but also every noncriminal defect of the will that detracts from the nobility of our origin and from the perfection of the state of innocence to which the Pelagians wanted man to be able to aspire and attain in this life through the sole powers of nature. For certainly he did not create a private dictionary for himself, and such language was not his invention. Saint Jerome used it before him, and he revealed its meaning with the utmost clarity in the three books of his *Dialogue against the Pelagians*.

“Read the passage where Critobulus, a Pelagian, puts this question to Atticus, a Catholic:

> ‘Give me a [Col. 0947A] testimony from the New Testament where error, ignorance, and the impossibility of the commandment are held to be a crime: *Da mihi testimonium Novi Testamenti, ubi error et ignorantia et impossibilitas mandati teneatur in crimine*’ (*Dialogue* II, beginning, p. 510).

“Atticus replies:

> ‘I shall produce one that you certainly will not be able to contradict: *Unum proferam cui certe contradicere non poteris*’ (ibid.).

“And what is this unanswerable testimony? The words of Saint Paul, who complains of the unwelcome rebellions of concupiscence, to which he does not consent. The first movements, the undeliberated feelings of the carnal appetite, are full of darkness because they precede reason. This, according to Saint Jerome, is the error and invincible ignorance that is a sin.

> ‘For what I do, I do not understand’ (*Quod enim operor non cognosco*).

“Let us read the entire passage. The chosen vessel speaks plainly:

> ‘For I consent to the law of God according to the inward man. But I see another law in my members, fighting against the law [Col. 0947B] of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members.’

“And afterward:

> ‘Hear the Apostle preaching with the utmost clarity: “For what I do, I do not understand; for I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate. But if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good. Now, then, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me”’ (Saint Jerome, ibid.).

“Luther and Calvin are ridiculous and insulting toward the Apostle to imagine here a formal sin. Jansenius, I think, subscribes to this censure, and certainly deserves it by adopting their opinion concerning invincible ignorance, since Saint Jerome applies this example and these words of Saint Paul to the invincible ignorance being discussed against the Pelagians, and since this was the impossibility of the commandments of God that formed the principal subject of the controversy—*impossibilitas mandati*.

“But what testimonies from the Old Testament [Col. 0947C] had Atticus produced when Critobulus demanded that they be confirmed by a testimony from the New Testament? Consider them. Jacob mourns the death of his son Joseph, and for a long time rejects the consolation that his other sons strive to give him. This just man shows himself to be human by being ignorant of what had become of his just son Joseph:

> ‘Jacob mourns the death of his son Joseph and for a long time does not accept consolation . . . , and he proves himself human while the just man is ignorant of what has happened to his just son Joseph’ (*Dialogue* I, near the end, p. 505).

“Samuel goes to Bethlehem and stops at each of Jesse’s sons in turn, believing that each one is the man whom the Lord was seeking; he is mistaken regarding all of them, and regarding all of them he recognizes his error. From this the weakness of the human mind becomes evident:

> ‘Samuel . . . goes to Bethlehem, supposes each of Jesse’s sons in turn to be the one whom the Lord was seeking . . . he is mistaken concerning all, and concerning all he is corrected, so that the weakness of the human mind may be evident’ (ibid.).

“Ahijah, the prophet of Shiloh, did not know that Jeroboam’s wife was [Col. 0947D] coming to him:

> ‘Ahijah, the prophet of Shiloh, did not know that Jeroboam’s wife was coming to him’ (ibid.).

“Would Jansenius and his disciples not be ridiculous if they claimed that these were all formal sins worthy of punishment, committed by Jacob, Samuel, and Ahijah? Yet, according to Saint Jerome, this is the kind of sin caused by invincible ignorance and the subject of the controversy between Catholics and the Pelagians. We postponed the remaining questions until the following day.

### V. What kind of freedom we lost through Adam’s sin

“The licentiate came to my house very early, and began by speaking to me as follows:

“Nothing seems more obscure to me than Augustine’s view of the present state of our freedom. At one moment this Father wants us to have lost it; at another, to have preserved it; at another, to have had it weakened and diminished [Col. 0948A] by sin. For,” he added, intending to bring me immediately to the subject, “the explanation Jansenius gives for reconciling the different texts of the holy doctor on this matter will not please you, and you will not accept the commentary he has devised: We have lost the freedom that is exemption from necessity; we have preserved the freedom that is exemption from constraint; and, considering the two as parts of a single total freedom, one may say only that it has been weakened and diminished.”

“That is not all,” I replied. “Jansenius properly calls by the name of freedom the exemption from constraint that consists in the necessity of willing the good through the invincible determination caused, according to him, by efficacious grace; and he calls servitude the exemption from constraint that consists in the necessity of willing evil through the invincible determination caused, according to him, by concupiscence. Therefore he attributes to Augustine the view that the impossibility of doing evil when we do good is the freedom that the grace of Jesus Christ procures for us, and that the impossibility of doing good when we do evil is the servitude to which Adam’s sin has reduced us. But this system, horrible for the present state of the wayfarer, in which one must merit and demerit, is plainly imputed to the holy doctor. Here, on the contrary, is the outline of his doctrine on this point.

“Through the first man’s sin we fell from every right to supernatural good, which is true justice, and consequently we lost the possibility of attaining it. Jesus Christ came into the world and died to merit for us the restoration of this right and this possibility. But He willed that the possibility of supernatural good should be restored to us partly in this life and partly in the age to come. Thus, through His merits, we have recovered the possibility of supernatural good that suffices for the action of justice; or, which is the same thing, we now possess, through the help of the Savior’s grace, the freedom to choose good by resisting evil. But we have not recovered the possibility of supernatural good that is necessary for the perfection of justice; or, which is the same thing, we are deprived of the freedom Adam possessed to choose good without any inner contradiction. In a word, the freedom we have absolutely lost is the dominion of the will over our feelings; the freedom we have preserved is the dominion of the will over our consent; and this dominion over our consent, which is not accompanied—as it was in the state of innocence—by dominion over our feelings, is a weakened and diminished freedom.”

The mere correctness of the opposition between this doctrinal position and the Pelagian error concerning impeccability is sufficient to verify it; for it is certain that [Col. 0948D] the Pelagians taught two errors concerning freedom. The first was that man possessed a power of indifference and an exemption from simple necessity, not only with regard to every consent, but also with regard to every feeling. The second was that both powers were independent of the grace of the Redeemer, because man had not been deprived by sin either of the right to aspire to the supernatural good or of the possibility of attaining it. Nevertheless, let us enter into some detail of the proofs, and begin by setting out the texts of Saint Augustine that show what freedom we have lost through sin; for [Col. 0949A] you can well judge that I shall not stop there, and that I shall then show what freedom we have not lost.

Let us first examine these words of the holy Doctor:

> “Who among us says that, through the sin of the first man, free will perished from the human race? It is true that freedom perished through sin, but it was that freedom which existed in paradise: *Quis autem nostrum dicat quod primi hominis peccato perierit liberum arbitrium de humano genere? Libertas quidem periit per peccatum, sed illa quae in paradiso fuit*” (*Book I to Boniface*, chapter 2, no. 5).

Jansenius (*vol. II, book III, On the State of Fallen Nature*, chapter 5, p. 443) pays great attention to the words that follow, *Habendi plenam cum immortalitate justitiam* (“of possessing justice in its fullness together with immortality”). His purpose is not to point out that, according to Saint Augustine, the only freedom Adam possessed—that of possessing the fullness and perfection of justice—was taken from us by sin. Rather, it is to prevent anyone from understanding the passage in this way and noticing its opposition to what is read shortly beforehand:

> “By defending free will, they plunge it headlong, so that one trusts in it for the practice of justice rather than in the help of the Lord: *Liberum autem arbitrium defendendo praecipitant, ut de illo potius ad faciendam justitiam, quam de Domini adjutorio confidatur*.”

Saint Augustine makes it understood that grace and free will cooperate in the action of justice, although the Pelagians, who denied the necessity of grace, had [Col. 0949B] the presumption to rely upon free will rather than upon God’s help. When, therefore, he subsequently asserts that we have not lost free will, and yet that we have lost the freedom necessary for the perfection of justice, is it not clear that he means that we have not lost the freedom necessary for the action of justice?

Read this other passage:

> “Who does not know that man was created sound and innocent, and that he was established in possession of free will and of a free power to live justly? But the question now concerns the man whom robbers left half-dead on the road: *Quis enim eum nescit sanum et inculpabilem factum, et libero arbitrio atque ad juste vivendum potestate libera constitutum? Sed de illo agitur quem semivivum latrones in via reliquerunt*” (*On Nature and Grace*, chapter 43, no. 50).

As though he were saying, Jansenius continues: “The question now concerns [Col. 0949C] the man who, because of the deep wounds of ignorance and concupiscence that have weakened and cast him down, does not possess free will for living well.” But when Jansenius penetrated the words that immediately follow, did he not recognize that his interpretation was unfaithful, and that Saint Augustine was describing the loss of a free will sufficiently powerful to make us climb to the summit of justice?

> “Who, wounded and pierced by grievous injuries, cannot ascend to the summit of justice as he was able to descend from it: *Qui gravibus saucius confossusque vulneribus non ita potest ad justitiae culmen ascendere, sicut potuit inde descendere*.”

The passage I am about to cite is important.

> “You want,” Saint Augustine says to Julian, “man to be able to attain perfection here below; and would to God that you understood that he can attain it by a special gift of God, and not merely by the powers of free—or rather, enslaved—arbitrament of his own will: *Hic vultis hominem perfici, atque utinam Dei dono, et non libero vel potius servo propriae voluntatis arbitrio*” (*Book II Against Julian*, chapter 8, no. 23).

What are we to say of Jansenius’s boldness and confidence [Col. 0949D]? Not only does he apply to the freedom whose object is the action of justice a passage whose first proposition so clearly states that it must be understood of the freedom whose object is the perfection of justice; he also uses it to insinuate that Luther was wrongly censured for employing language borrowed from Saint Augustine.

If we believe Jansenius, the heresiarch learned from the holy Doctor of grace that, when speaking of the arbiter of our will, there was more reason to call it enslaved than free (Jansenius, vol. II, book III, *On the State of Fallen Nature*, chapter 5, toward the end, p. 445). He did not deign to consider—any more than Luther did—which arbiter of our will Saint Augustine had declared to be rather enslaved than free. This Father would certainly not have spoken or thought in this way of the arbiter of our will which he himself, in agreement with the Pelagians, readily acknowledged to be free with respect [Col. 0950A] to consents; and the single word *perfici* (“to be perfected”) clearly designates another arbiter of our will, which the Pelagians falsely claimed to be free with respect to first movements. The words immediately following make this so plain that it is impossible not to understand it:

> “You yourselves feel that you are far from that perfection; but there is deceit in your mouth, whether you say that you are sinners while wishing to be believed righteous, or whether you profess the perfection of justice, which you certainly feel is not in you: *A qua perfectione quidem longe vos esse sentitis: sed dolus est in ore vestro, sive peccatores vos esse dicatis, et justos credi velitis, sive profiteamini perfectionem justitiae, quam profecto in vobis non esse sentitis*” (Saint Augustine, ibid.).

Is it now tolerable to see Jansenius employ this passage of Saint Augustine in order to arrive at the conclusion that contradicts the holy Doctor’s thought?

> “Since Augustine most willingly used that word ‘enslaved’ to express the ruin of free will, whereby it is no longer free to live well—that is, to will and perform what is good—as it was before its fall: *Cum illud vocabulum (servi) Augustinus libentissime usurpaverit ad illam arbitrii stragem exprimendam, qua non est amplius liberum ut bene vivat, hoc est ut bonum velit et operetur, sicut ante ruinam suam fuit*” (Jansenius, ibid., p. 446).

Saint Augustine says: perfection—*perfici*, *perfectionem justitiae*; Jansenius [Col. 0950B] makes him say: action—*bene vivat, velit, operetur*. What a faithful interpreter! But then, falsification was the only worthy foundation for Luther’s apology.

The expression “great freedom,” which Saint Augustine employs elsewhere to specify the freedom we lost through Adam’s sin, is diverted in Jansenius’s commentary (ibid., p. 443), in the same way as the words of the preceding texts, to signify the freedom of indifference, which makes the soul mistress of its determination and choice in all its actions.

> “But now,” says the holy Doctor, “after that great freedom was lost through the deserving of sin, weakness remained, to be helped even by greater gifts: *Nunc vero, postea quam est illa magna peccati merito amissa libertas, etiam majoribus donis adjuvanda remansit infirmitas*” (*On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 12, no. 37).

But consult the description he gives of this same freedom a few lines earlier, and you will see that it consisted in the fact that man experienced no resistance from his sensual appetite:

> “Nothing arising from within him resisted him in the manner of concupiscence: *Nihil ex se ipso concupiscentialiter resistebat*.”

[Col. 0950C] Let us read in full this famous passage from the book *On the Perfection of Justice*, of which Jansenius makes a trophy (vol. II, book III, *On the State of Fallen Nature*, chapter 12, p. 483), and of which he deliberately inserts fragments everywhere to assist in misleading his readers concerning the meaning of the other passages:

> “It was through freedom of choice that man came to be with sin; but now punitive corruption has made necessity out of freedom. Hence faith cries out to God: ‘Deliver me from my necessities.’ Placed under them, we are either unable to understand what we want, or, having understood it, we want it but cannot accomplish it. For this very freedom is promised to believers by the Liberator. ‘If the Son,’ he says, ‘shall make you free, then you shall truly be free.’ For nature has been deprived of freedom, its will overcome by the fault into which it fell. Hence another Scripture says: ‘By whatever a person is overcome, to that he is enslaved.’ Therefore, just as a physician is not needed by those who are well but by the sick, so a liberator is not needed by the free but by the enslaved, so that thanksgiving for freedom may say to him: ‘You have saved my soul from necessities.’ [Col. 0950D]
>
> “For true freedom itself is health; it would not have perished if the good will had remained. But because the will sinned, the harsh necessity of possessing sin followed the sinning will, until the weakness is wholly healed and such freedom is received that, just as the will to live happily must remain in it, so there may also be a voluntary and happy necessity of living well and never sinning: *Respondetur per arbitrii libertatem factum, ut esset homo cum peccato, sed jam poenalis vitiositas ex libertate fecit necessitatem. Unde ad Deum fides clamat, De necessitatibus meis educ me. Sub quibus positi vel non possumus quod volumus intelligere, vel quod intellexerimus, volumus nec valemus implere. Nam et ipsa libertas credentibus a liberatore promittitur. Si vos, inquit, Filius liberaverit tunc vere liberi eritis. Victa enim vitio in quod cecidit voluntate, caruit libertate natura. Hinc alia Scriptura dicit: A quo enim quis devictus est, huic et servus addictus est. Sicut ergo non est opus sanis medicus, sed male habentibus, ita non est opus liberis liberator, sed servis, ut ei dicat gratulatio libertatis: Salvasti de necessitatibus animam meam. Ipsa enim sanitas est vera libertas, quae non periisset, si bona remansisset voluntas, quia vero peccavit voluntas, secuta est peccantem peccatum habendi dura necessitas, donec tota sanetur infirmitas, et accipiatur tanta libertas, in qua sicut necesse est permaneat beate vivendi voluntas, ita ut sit etiam bene vivendi et nunquam peccandi voluntaria felixque necessitas*” (*On the Perfection of Justice*, chapter 4, no. 9).

It is said that this passage of Saint Augustine made at least as many Jansenists as *subventum est infirmitati* (“help was given to weakness”), and *quod amplius nos delectat* (“what delights us more”), and so on—Jansenists by hearsay and without reflection, as most of them are.

The holy Doctor has gathered in this long passage all the characteristics of the freedom we lost through Adam’s sin. It is, first, a freedom whose contrary is a necessity under whose yoke one cannot do what one wants: *Volumus, nec valemus implere* (“We want, but cannot accomplish it”); a necessity not [Col. 0951A] of consenting to sin, but of having sin within oneself: *peccatum habendi dura necessitas* (“the harsh necessity of possessing sin”); a necessity that persists without interruption even [Col. 0951C] in the just, until the beatific vision of God has absorbed and healed all our weakness: *donec tota sanetur infirmitas* (“until the weakness is wholly healed”).
