This freedom, therefore, does not have as its contrary the Jansenist necessity, which reduces the soul’s power precisely to the measure of what it wants, which makes it consent to the act of sin, and which consists in the alternative of two necessities, one of which successively destroys the other. Rather, this freedom has as its contrary the necessity of which Saint Paul complained when he said:

> “I do not do the good that I want: *Non quod volo bonum hoc ago*; it is not I who perform evil, but sin dwelling in me: *Nunc autem jam non ego operor illud, sed quod habitat in me peccatum*; wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? *Infelix ego homo, quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?*”

These are precisely the three features with which Saint Augustine [Col. 0951B] depicted the necessity to which we are subjected through the loss of the freedom possessed by the first man, and they apply only to the necessity of experiencing the prevenient and undeliberated movements of concupiscence.

Moreover, this freedom was essentially the same in Adam as the freedom whose restoration is promised to the faithful:

> “For this very freedom is promised to believers by the Liberator: *Nam et ipsa libertas credentibus a liberatore promittitur*.”

It belonged properly to sound nature; it is not even distinguished from health—not merely from the health Adam enjoyed, but from that which the supreme Physician must procure for us, and which will make us say, while giving him eternal thanks:

> “You have delivered my soul from all necessities: *Salvam fecisti de necessitatibus animam meam*.”

“For true freedom itself is health: *Ipsa enim sanitas est vera libertas*.”

Finally, this freedom will not be restored to us until the blessed life:

> “Until the weakness is wholly healed and such freedom is received, in which, just as the will to live happily must remain, so also …: *Donec tota sanetur infirmitas, et accipiatur tanta libertas, in qua sicut necesse est permaneat* …”

Jansenius could not have thought—and in this he was quite right—that the freedom of indifference and exemption from simple necessity was the freedom whose restoration is promised to us, or that it was the grace of health received upon entering heaven. Should he not therefore have concluded that the freedom of indifference and exemption from simple necessity is not the freedom we lost through sin? He preferred instead to suppose a perpetual equivocation in Saint Augustine’s use of the word “freedom,” and to distinguish what the holy Doctor did not distinguish. For Jansenius plainly teaches everywhere that the freedom restored to us by Jesus Christ is something entirely different from the freedom whose loss was caused by Adam’s sin. Saint Augustine, on the contrary, is not content to have expressly stated more than once that there is no difference between them; he confirms it still further with these words:

> “For true freedom itself is health, which would not have perished if the good will had [Col. 0951D] remained: *Ipsa enim sanitas est vera libertas, quae non periisset, si bona permansisset voluntas*.”

We must therefore agree that Jansenius departs strangely from Saint Augustine in explaining this Father’s text, and that in this book, which treats of the perfection of justice, especially in this passage, the holy Doctor understands by the word “freedom” that which is contrary to the perfection of justice. For this alone—namely, the soul’s perfect dominion over all its inclinations and appetites—turns out to be a common possession of the inhabitants of both paradises, the earthly and the heavenly, with the difference, nevertheless, that I have noted between impeccance and impeccability.

In the earthly paradise one possessed the power to live well and never to sin, even materially; in the heavenly paradise this power is accompanied by a happy necessity:

> “So that there may be a voluntary and happy necessity of living well and never sinning: *Ita ut sit bene vivendi et nunquam peccandi voluntaria felixque necessitas*.”

The licentiate pointed out to me that, in several passages [Col. 0952A] cited by Jansenius, Saint Augustine attributes the loss of our freedom to every fall into mortal sin, and the recovery of our freedom to efficacious actual grace, which withdraws us from the state of mortal sin.

“Take care,” I replied, “for the freedom in question there is the power to perform meritorious actions. The state of mortal sin reduces you to the condition of slaves, who can gain nothing for themselves and are incapable of acquiring and possessing any good as their own. For in this unhappy state all our works are sterile and dead for us; and, like slaves, we may indeed merit punishments, but no rewards. Whereas, in the state of sanctifying grace, we amass immense riches for the future life: all our smallest actions increase the fund of our eternity and acquire for us a new degree of grace and glory.

“Efficacious actual grace delivers us from this slavery and restores to us the freedom of the children of God [Col. 0952B] by making us produce meritorious works of eternal life, once it has led us to justification. It is not surprising that Saint Augustine, when speaking on this subject, calls every action performed in the state of sin ‘sin.’ It is clear enough that, in this Father’s language, the term ‘sin’ is general and indeterminate, and must be assessed according to the circumstances in which it is employed. But Jansenius abuses it in order to assert that every sinner has lost the freedom to abstain from formal sin, and that in all his actions he is necessarily and truly guilty.

“This abuse is evident. Was it not natural that the holy Doctor should not spare the designation ‘sin’ for works that are sterile and useless for salvation, since he includes under this name everything contrary to the perfection of justice alone?

“The passage you have in mind is, I think, this one:

> ‘How does freedom remain in those who, in order to be freed [Col. 0952C] from the slavery to which they have been handed over by the conquering sin, need divine grace, unless they are themselves free—but free for justice? Hence the Apostle says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to justice”: *Quomodo manet libertas in eis qui, ut liberentur a servitute qua victori peccato addicti sunt, divina indigent gratia, nisi quia liberi sunt et ipsi, sed justitiae? Unde dicit Apostolus, Cum essetis servi peccati, liberi fuistis justitiae*’” (*Book I of the Unfinished Work*, no. 76).

“The explanation I have just given you is contained in the words that follow shortly afterward:

> ‘If you understand this, you will understand nothing other than that the free will worthy of praise is the will that has been freed by the grace of God: *Hoc si intelligatis, non aliud intelligetis esse arbitrium laudabiliter liberum, nisi quod fuerit Dei gratia liberatum*.’”

That is to say, the only praiseworthy use of free will consists in supernatural acts that dispose one toward justification and subsequently bring it to completion.

“I had another passage before my eyes,” the licentiate replied, “to which your explanation does not apply.” He gave it to me to read:

> “By using free will badly, man both destroyed himself and free will itself … When sin was committed through free will, free will was lost when sin prevailed: ‘By whatever a person is overcome, to that he is enslaved.’ This is certainly the judgment of the Apostle Peter; and since it is true, what freedom, I ask, can an enslaved person possess [Col. 0952D], unless when he takes pleasure in sinning? For he serves freely who willingly does the will of his master. Consequently, he is free for sinning who is the slave of sin. Hence he will not be free for doing justice unless, having been freed from sin, he begins to be a slave of justice. Before this begins to happen in a person, how can anyone boast of free will in a good work? *Libero arbitrio male utens homo, et se perdidit et ipsum . . . cum libero peccaretur arbitrio, victore peccato amissum est et liberum arbitrium: A quo enim quis devictus est, huic et servus addictus est. Petri certe apostoli est ista sententia, quae cum vera sit, qualis, quaeso, potest servi addicti esse libertas, nisi quando eum peccare delectat? Liberaliter enim servit qui domini sui voluntatem libenter facit. Ac per hoc ad peccandum liber est, qui peccati servus est. Unde ad juste faciendum liber non erit, nisi a peccato liberatus esse justitiae coeperit servus. Quod antequam fieri in homine incipiat, quomodo quisquam de libero arbitrio in bono glorietur opere, etc.*” (*Book I of the Enchiridion*, chapter 30).

“This text,” I said to him, “plainly concerns the freedom we lost through Adam’s sin. Saint Augustine therefore does not fail here to make it consist in the fact that man moves toward the good with all his heart and all his affection, without any repugnance or inner contradiction—much as the ungodly surrender themselves to their passions and to the pleasure they take in vice. This, the holy Doctor adds, is in them a kind of freedom for evil, opposed to the freedom we ought to have for the good. Such is the meaning of these words:

> ‘For he serves freely [Col. 0953A] who willingly does the will of his master: *Liberaliter enim servit, qui domini sui voluntatem libenter facit*.’”

Now observe Saint Augustine’s precision. Since efficacious actual grace only diminishes the reign of concupiscence within us and does not entirely destroy it; since it does not lead us to the perfection of justice, but merely brings us nearer to it by removing all contradiction to the good and all voluntary, though not involuntary, repugnance, the holy Doctor does not attribute to efficacious actual grace the full and complete restoration of the freedom we lost through Adam’s sin. He attributes to it only a deliverance and an incipient freedom. Nor is it without purpose that he expresses himself in this way:

> “And before this begins to happen: *Et quod antequam fieri incipiat*,”

to indicate that in this life we make the attempt rather than bear the yoke of justice.

These words of Saint Augustine remind me of a passage from Saint Fulgentius that demonstrates the truth and solidity of this observation. The disciple had admirably penetrated the deepest thoughts [Col. 0953B] of his master, and he declares in this way what sort of freedom was the subject of the controversy between Saint Augustine and the Pelagians:

> “This freedom, which does not arise from human free will but is granted by the gratuitous mercy of God, begins with good will, grows through the fruit of our sanctification, and receives its full effect only in eternal life: *Haec libertas quae non ex humano arbitrio nascitur, sed gratuita Dei miseratione confertur, a bona voluntate sumit exordium, et per fructum sanctificationis in vita aeterna plenum sortitur effectum*” (*On the Incarnation and Grace*, chapter 19, p. 308, edition of Sebastian Cramoisy).

There is, as we have seen, another kind of freedom that was not at all the subject of the controversy between Saint Augustine and the Pelagians. On this matter the holy Doctor had no dispute with these heretics except that they continually reproached him for not acknowledging it, while he, for his part, defended himself by openly confessing it and [Col. 0953C] treating their accusation as slander. It is the freedom necessary for doing evil and good:

> “We must therefore confess that we possess free will for doing both evil and good: *Liberum itaque arbitrium et ad malum et ad bonum faciendum confitendum est nos habere*” (*On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 1, no. 2),

and for leading either a bad or a good life:

> “Faith does not deny free will, whether toward an evil life or toward a good one: *Fides neque liberum arbitrium negat sive in vitam malam sive in bonam*”” (*Letter 215 to Valentine*, no. 4).

Consequently, it is the freedom as it must be understood when one regards it as a principle of merit and demerit, of the action of justice and of formal sin. Jansenius corrupted its notion in order to be able to say, with Saint Augustine, “We do not deny free will,” while nevertheless denying it with Calvin.

I have heard that a sultan gave the name of the wine he loved—and whose use the law of Muhammad forbids—to water, which he detested, so that he could say, along with the most religious Muslims, “I do not drink wine.” Jansenius’s artifice is much the same. According to him, Saint Augustine confessed only the freedom [Col. 0953D] that is exemption from compulsion. It follows that Calvin and Saint Augustine thought alike: one by denying free will, the other by confessing it, since Calvin protested more than once that he did not wish to quibble over words and was ready to confess free will if people agreed to accept this definition: freedom is exemption from compulsion, not from simple necessity (Calvin, *Institutes*, book II, chapter 2, no. 7; book II, *Against Pighius*).

Thus Mr. Bayle maintains that Saint Augustine’s doctrine and Calvin’s doctrine concerning freedom differ only in expression. “There is no Calvinist,” he says, “who does not acknowledge free will and its use in the conversion of the sinner, if the term is understood according to Saint Augustine’s ideas” (Mr. Bayle’s *Dictionary*, entry “AUGUSTINE,” remark E).

But what idea did the Pelagians have of freedom? They certainly understood it as exemption from [Col. 0954A] simple necessity. Jansenius asserts and proves this at length (vol. I, book II, chapter 2 and following). It is therefore exemption from simple necessity that Julian reproached Saint Augustine for denying and branding as a Celestian and Pelagian heresy:

> “If anyone says that there is free will in human beings, he is called a Celestian and a Pelagian: *Si quis liberum esse in hominibus arbitrium dixerit, Coelestianus et Pelagianus vocatur*” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book II, chapter 3, no. 8).

And consequently it is exemption from simple necessity that Saint Augustine, in answering Julian, confesses, and which he defends against the charge of Celestian and Pelagian heresy:

> “We do not deny free will … you are not for this reason Celestians and Pelagians: *Non liberum negamus arbitrium . . . non hinc estis Coelestiani et Pelagiani*” (ibid.).

Are we to suppose that, in this dispute, while using the same terms, Julian speaks of one thing and Saint Augustine of another?

The holy Doctor does indeed add that, since sin took from us the possibility of supernatural good, it is restored to us only through the grace [Col. 0954B] of Jesus Christ:

> “But if the Son shall make you free,” says the Truth, “then you shall truly be free: *Sed si vos Filius liberaverit, ait veritas, tunc vere liberi eritis*” (ibid.).

He rejects a freedom independent of grace, of which the Pelagians’ Stoic pride vainly boasted:

> “You begrudge this Liberator, while, as captives, you assign a vain freedom: *Hunc vos invidetis liberatorem, quibus captivis vanam tribuitis libertatem*” (ibid.).

But he does not destroy the idea of freedom that Julian had in mind. Thus, in removing the Pelagian error and transforming it into Catholic doctrine, he requires only that one not say that, in order to serve God properly, free will without God’s help is sufficient:

> “Therefore, it is not as you and others misleadingly say—that anyone who says there is free will in human beings is called a Celestian or a Pelagian—for the Catholic faith says this. But if anyone says that there is free will in human beings for rightly worshiping God without his help, that person is called a Pelagian and a Celestian: *Non itaque sicut te atque alios fallens loqueris, si quis liberum in hominibus arbitrium dixerit, Coelestianus aut Pelagianus vocatur: ista quippe catholica fides dicit. Sed si quis ad colendum recte Deum, sine ipsius adjutorio dicit esse in hominibus liberum arbitrium . . . ipse Pelagianus et Coelestianus vocatur*” (ibid.).

Saint Augustine expressly assures us here that the Catholic faith agrees with the Pelagians in saying that human beings have free will. His thought is certainly not that this agreement consists only in words and not in the reality, for faith does not have words as its object [Col. 0954C], but realities.

Besides, if a base and misleading equivocation is appropriate to a heretic seeking to disguise his error, is it not unworthy of a holy defender and Doctor of the Church, whose maxim is that to disguise the truth is to betray it? Saint Augustine is therefore very far from claiming that God’s help, which is necessary for free will to do good, annihilates what the Pelagians meant by the term “free will,” and consequently he is thinking of anything but a necessitating and irresistible assistance.

Let us read what follows:

> “Therefore, we say to both of you that there is free will in human beings; it is not for this reason that you are Celestians and Pelagians: *Liberum itaque in hominibus esse arbitrium . . . utrique dicimus, non hinc estis Coelestiani et Pelagiani*” (ibid.).

We say to both sides that human beings have free will; it is not on this account that you are Celestians and Pelagians.

Of what prevarication would Saint Augustine have been guilty in speaking in this way if he had not held the same notion of free will as the [Col. 0954D] Pelagians? For in that case the Pelagians’ notion of free will would have been heretical, and Saint Augustine could not have failed to point this out. What would one say of a Thomist who, speaking in the name of all those belonging to his school, addressed these words to the theologians of Geneva: “We both say that grace is efficacious of itself,” while neglecting to show the heretical character of the notion that Calvin’s sect attaches to grace being efficacious of itself?

There is more. The holy Doctor does not hesitate to assert that the dogma of free will is common to Catholics and Pelagians:

> “Why do you hold out the covering of a common dogma to deceive, so as to conceal your own crime? *Quid obtendis ad fallendum communis dogmatis tegmen, ut operias proprium crimen?*” (ibid.).

The common dogma is not merely the same language. A common dogma is the essential and complete idea, admitted and acknowledged on both sides as an article of faith. Otherwise it would be permissible to say that the dogma of the divinity of Jesus Christ [Col. 0955A] is common to Catholics and Socinians, since the Socinians have fashioned a definition of divinity according to their own model in order sometimes to be able to call Jesus Christ God.

I pass over a multitude of other highly convincing proofs customarily employed to show that Saint Augustine agreed with the Pelagians concerning the essence of free will required for meriting and demeriting in the state of fallen nature. I shall not stop to develop this very solid argument: the free will Saint Augustine confessed in disputing against the Pelagians is the same free will that he established with such force against the Manichaeans. For he confessed it in order to repel the foolish accusation of Manichaeism that the Pelagians continually brought against him on this point.

Moreover, he believed that one could push the defense of grace so far as to destroy free will:

> “Because some among you preach the grace of God in such a way as to deny that free will belongs to man: *Eo quod quidam in vobis sic gratiam Dei praedicent, ut negent hominis esse liberum arbitrium*” (*Letter 214 to Valentine*, no. 1).

Now the free will that the holy Doctor [Col. 0955B] established against the Manichaeans is exemption from simple necessity, and he could not have believed that an excessive defense of grace destroyed any other free will than that which consists in exemption from simple necessity. Nothing is more evident than these two propositions.

There has never been, and never will be, any heresy that destroys another kind of free will. The Jansenists have often been challenged to show that what they understand by the term “free will,” which remains to us after Adam’s fall, has ever been denied or could ever have been denied by anyone; and they have always turned a deaf ear to this challenge. Therefore, in disputing against the Pelagians, Saint Augustine confessed exemption from simple necessity.

For even greater conviction on this point, I urge you to read consecutively and compare with one another chapter 2 of the book *On Grace and Free Will*, which Saint Augustine composed toward the end of his disputes with the Pelagians, and chapter [Col. 0955C] 34 of book VI of *The Grace of the Savior*, in Jansenius’s *Augustine*. On the one hand, you will see the holy Doctor making an exquisite selection of testimonies from Sacred Scripture to prove the dogma that free will subsists in human nature after Adam’s fall, and doing so in such a way that one must either deliberately blind oneself or acknowledge that he plainly intends to prove—and in fact does prove—that exemption from simple necessity and freedom of indifference subsist.

On the other hand, you will see Jansenius objecting in general to these same passages, of which he reports only one; in reply, evading and weakening the force of the sacred text; turning to the essence of freedom in general; referring his reader to other places in his book; confusing the central point of the question; in short, extricating himself in the most ridiculous and miserable manner.

I hasten to resolve a few difficulties, in order to come as quickly as possible to the subject of grace. It is said that Saint Augustine reproached Pelagius for the following proposition:

> “Whatever is bound by natural necessity is deprived [Col. 0955D] of the arbitrariness of the will and of the power to deliberate: *Videamus quid inde contexat. Voluntatis enim arbitrio, inquit, ac deliberatione privatur, quidquid naturali necessitate constringitur*” (*On Nature and Grace*, chapter 46, no. 54).

In refuting this proposition, the holy Doctor seems to assert that the love of blessedness in us and the love of justice in God are free, although necessary:

> “And here there is some question. For it is exceedingly absurd to say that, because we cannot altogether refuse to wish to be blessed, through some good constraint of nature, what we wish to be blessed with does not belong to our will; nor do we dare say that God has not a will but a necessity for justice, because he cannot will to sin: *Et hic nonnulla quaestio est. Perquam enim absurdum est ut ideo dicamus non pertinere ad voluntatem nostram quod beati esse volumus, quia id omnino nolle non possumus, nescio qua et bona constrictione naturae; nec dicere audemus ideo Deum non voluntatem sed necessitatem habere justitiae, quia non potest velle peccare*” (ibid.).

Pay attention to these words: *et hic nonnulla quaestio est* (“and here there is some question”). Saint Augustine does not accuse Pelagius’s proposition of being manifestly false, but only [Col. 0956A] of being ambiguous and imprecise. He claims that it is too general, and that, when examined closely and rigorously, it will be found to be false. This was not mere quibbling. One needed only to understand the entire mystery of Pelagius’s heresy in order to let nothing pass that he might exploit.

That heresiarch insinuated that, whatever sort of necessity might be joined to the determinations of our will, free will was annihilated. His purpose was to conclude that, if our soul were not mistress of everything taking place within it, the necessity of feeling would entail the necessity of consent, and that the action of justice would be no more within our power than the perfection of justice.

Here, then, is the proper and true commentary on Saint Augustine’s reply. The necessary love of blessedness belongs to our free will in the sense that it is inseparable from the exercise of our free will; for whatever course our will takes, [Col. 0956B] it cannot determine itself to anything that is not in accord with the love of blessedness.

Similarly, the necessary love of justice belongs to God’s free will in the sense that it is inseparable from God’s free acts; for whatever God wills and does, he can will or do nothing that is not consistent with the love of justice. It is therefore false that every kind of necessity annihilates free will.

If Saint Augustine had thought, as Jansenius does, that our free will consisted solely in exemption from compulsion, he would not have said that Pelagius’s proposition required discussion—*et hic nonnulla quaestio est*—but would have condemned it absolutely and without hesitation.

This gives us the understanding of another passage in which Saint Augustine, comparing the power to live well according to God with the natural inclination that we have to be happy, says that we could lose the former, but could not be stripped of the latter; and he expresses himself in such a way that he appears to regard [Col. 0956C] the natural and necessary movement that makes us seek our happiness in everything as a kind of free will:

> “This is the free will immovably fixed in our minds—not the free will by which we wish to act well, for through human iniquity we could lose it, and through divine grace we can recover it, but the free will by which we wish to be blessed and do not wish to be wretched; neither can the wretched lose it, nor the blessed” (On the Unfinished Work, Book VI, no. 26).

Who does not see that what is here called free will is not the natural and necessary inclination that carries us toward the good in general, but the power to apply this inclination to various objects, chosen indifferently and freely, though always within the sphere of things suited to the love of blessedness?

Saint Augustine was very concerned that no one should say without explanation that necessity was opposed to freedom; the reason is easily understood: he had as much cause to be alarmed by this expression as we now have reason to be scandalized [Col. 0956D] when we hear it said that necessity does not injure freedom. He was engaged in combat with the Pelagians, who flattered human pride with the claim that man possessed complete and perfect dominion over all the inclinations and movements of his soul, and who sought to exclude from the determinations of the will every mixture of a necessary inclination or repugnance, so that these determinations might be deemed free. We, meanwhile, have to deal with the Jansenists, who nourish man’s laziness and cowardice by disputing his dominion generally and without exception over all his interior acts, and who maintain that even the determinations of the will, whether toward good or toward evil, are all necessary.

The holy Doctor was at the height of his struggles against the Pelagians when he wrote the books of *The City of God*. Thus this passage should not surprise us:

> “If necessity is defined as that according to which we say that something must be or must happen in such-and-such a way, I do not know why we should fear that it will take away the freedom of our will. For we do not place either God’s life or his foreknowledge under necessity if we say that God must live and must foreknow all things. Nor is his power diminished when it is said that he cannot die or be deceived” (*The City of God*, Book V, chapter 10).

This passage has appeared inexplicable to several Catholic theologians. I may be mistaken, but in my view its explanation is very simple and easy.

The holy Doctor’s thought is not that one can say that God’s life and foreknowledge are free acts, or that one can deny that they are necessary acts. He merely asserts that they are objects foreign to God’s freedom and that, consequently, although they are necessary, they are not necessary with a [Col. 0957B] necessity that harms God’s freedom. It follows that this necessity does not prevent God from being considered perfectly free with respect to the proper objects of his freedom. For in what sense does the holy Doctor then say that nothing is taken away from God’s power when it is said that he cannot die or be deceived? He surely means that the inability to die and to be deceived is not a true inability, because death and error are objects foreign to perfect power, such as God’s power is. Now, since he uses this comparison, it follows that, in his view, the necessity of living and of foreseeing everything is not a true necessity with respect to freedom, because God’s life and foreknowledge are objects foreign to God’s perfect freedom. He therefore intends nothing other than that necessity is not contrary to freedom when it does not remove from freedom its proper object.

Another comparison added by the holy Doctor [Col. 0957C] demonstrates this explanation:

> “Likewise, when we say, ‘It is necessary that, when we will, we will by free choice,’ we undoubtedly speak the truth; yet for that reason we do not subject free will to a necessity that takes away freedom” (*ibid.*).

That is: when we say that it is necessary for the free acts of our will to be produced by the faculty of free will, we certainly speak the truth, and yet we do not thereby subject free will to a necessity that removes freedom. Why? Because it is evidently an object foreign to freedom to make use of a faculty different from free will—for example, to use the understanding in order to produce free acts.

Thoughts and reflections of this kind would now be out of season and would be regarded as empty subtleties; but different times bring different concerns. When Saint Augustine thought and wrote in this way, there were heretics teaching that the necessity of the soul’s undeliberated feelings was sufficient to destroy free will, although such feelings are foreign to our freedom, whose exercise concerns only consent: the Pelagians were enemies of every necessity, while the Jansenists, who are attacking the Church today, are enemies of every freedom, even of the freedom they pretend to defend.

There remain only two passages of the holy Doctor on this subject that have seemed to me to merit a particular explanation. One of them (*Tractate 53 on John*, no. 9) would take us too far and has no connection with the perfection of justice; allow me to postpone speaking to you about it until you wish me to examine in your presence M. Bayle’s doctrine concerning moral good and evil. Here is the other.

Julian objected to Saint Augustine that free will could not subsist if man were necessitated, on the one hand, to the action of justice and, on the other, to sin:

> “It cannot stand in any other way than that the necessity of justice and of sin be removed from him.”

Saint Augustine answers him in these [Col. 0958A] terms:

> “If by necessity you mean that by which someone is oppressed against his will, there is no such necessity with respect to justice, because no one is just against his will; but the grace of God makes a willing person out of one who was unwilling. Yet if no one sinned against his will, it would not be written: ‘You have sealed up my sins in a bag and noted down whatever I committed unwillingly’” (*On the Unfinished Work*, Book III, no. 122).

I grant the Jansenists the option of understanding the word *invitus* either as simple necessity or as constraint properly so called. If they adopt the latter meaning, I conclude that the freedom required for demerit is not exemption from constraint, since Saint Augustine asserts that one can sin under constraint: “You noted whatever I committed unwillingly.” If they adhere to the former meaning, I conclude that the freedom required for merit is exemption from simple necessity, since Saint Augustine declares [Col. 0958B] that no one is just by necessity: “There is no necessity of justice by which someone is oppressed against his will.” Both conclusions are equally contrary to Jansenius’s system.

The truth is that the word *invitus* in this passage means a deliberate and consented-to repugnance, and Saint Augustine’s answer to Julian must be translated—or rather paraphrased—as follows:

If by necessity you call that which is accompanied by a repugnance that one acknowledges and approves, there is no such necessity with respect to justice, since one cannot freely recoil from justice when one embraces it, for no one is just against his will. And the grace that helps us overcome all our repugnances toward the good makes us do the good willingly. But with respect to sin, there is sometimes a necessity accompanied by a repugnance not merely acknowledged and approved, but one that reason itself brings forth and excites. For if no one sinned against his will, Job would not say that God had marked down what he had committed against his will. Saint Paul would not say: “I do the evil that I hate.” The subject, then, is sin as opposed to the perfection of justice, the freedom to attain that perfection, and the necessity that destroys this kind of freedom.

## VI. What grace is irresistible by its nature and is ordinarily denied to us

Since the licentiate seemed satisfied, I moved on to the subject of grace, and greatly surprised him by promising to show him in Saint Augustine a kind of grace endowed with almost all the qualities that Jansenius attributes to his own: essentially a delight, an actual and formal inspiration of charity, by itself and by its nature not merely effective but irresistible, and one that God refuses in time of need even to the most just. For, I said to him, Saint Augustine taught all this—not of the medicinal grace of Jesus Christ (and this is Jansenius’s deception), but of the grace of health, which is necessary to the perfection of justice. Thus you will constantly see Saint Augustine going in one direction and Jansenius in the other.

In the first ten chapters of Book IV of *The Grace of the Savior*, Jansenius gathered an infinite number of passages from Saint Augustine to prove that the essence of the medicinal grace of Jesus Christ must be a heavenly sweetness and delight. Most of them concern not prevenient grace, but cooperating and consented-to grace. It is therefore no small piece of ingenuity on his part to have waited until chapter 11 to declare that this delight had necessarily to be a vital and undeliberated act of love and desire, preceding the mind’s clear perception, the consent of the will, and the deliberate delight called the soul’s repose and joy. The reader does not think to go back over what he has just seen in order to look for this vital and undeliberated act in all the texts that have been cited. Nevertheless, it will be found in some of them, because prevenient grace very often is a delight; but unless the grace necessary to the perfection of justice is at issue, nothing indicates that this prevenient grace is essentially a delight.

Indeed, the holy Doctor took care not to think that the undeliberated movements of a godly sorrow, shame, or supernatural fear were not helps suited to restraining or repressing our disordered desires, or that the Holy Spirit did not inspire them on certain occasions. He would have departed from the doctrine of the Savior (Matthew 10:28) and of the Apostle (Philippians 2:12; 2 Corinthians 7:10); he would have contradicted himself. For he expressly taught that fear, shame, and sorrow were good and salutary movements (Saint Augustine, *Sermon* 214, now 348, and *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 5, no. 7). And when Jansenius reasons as follows—“We are carried toward evil by earthly delight alone; therefore we are carried toward good by heavenly delight alone” (Jansenius, vol. III, Book IV, chapter 3, p. 404)—Saint Augustine refutes this argument by asserting that people often sin without being preceded by any attraction of delight:

> “Has it not sufficiently appeared that even those sins are justly imputed which are committed not through the enticement of delight, but in order to avoid some trouble, pain, or death?” (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, Book II, chapter 10, no. 15).

But since the grace necessary to the perfection of justice must entirely extinguish concupiscence and establish perfect peace in the soul, since it is not a help that sustains us in combat and enables us to resist the enemy, but gives us complete victory and destroys every enemy, it consists essentially in delight: it is the victorious delight, as I have proved irresistibly.

Much the same is true with regard to charity. Can one doubt that Saint Augustine admitted prevenient graces that were not an actual and formal inspiration of divine love? Does he not say of fear not only that it is good and useful (*bonus est et utilis ille timor*), but also that it prepares a place for charity (*timor quasi praeparat locum charitati*); that it enters our heart first in order to introduce charity there (*opus est ergo ut intret timor primo, per quem veniat charitas*); that it is good to fear, because fear leads us to love (*time tamen ut ista formido custodiat te et perducat ad dilectionem*); and that there is a fear that makes the wicked abstain from sin and thereby renders them worthy to receive charity (*adhuc timor ille servilis est, custos quidem malorum, ut abstineant se a malis, et abstinendo digni sint ad se admittere charitatem*) (*On Psalm* 127, no. 7; *Tractate 9 on the First Epistle of John*, nos. 3–4; *Sermon 18 on the Words of the Apostle*, now 161, chapter 8, no. 8, and chapter 12, no. 12)?

Will it be said that, in the thought of the holy Doctor, this fear—which precedes charity, prepares a place for it, introduces it into our heart, leads us to charity, and makes us worthy to receive charity—is not supernatural fear inspired by the Holy Spirit? Will one make Saint Augustine a Pelagian by dint of wanting him to be a Jansenist?

Nevertheless, it is true that if one stops at the expression and confines oneself to the outer shell of the words, Saint Augustine will appear almost everywhere to confuse charity and the love of God with actual grace, which is necessary for every work useful to salvation. The grace whose necessity he requires Pelagius to recognize and acknowledge is a help for doing good, added to nature and doctrine through the inspiration of a most ardent and luminous charity. Thus men of great reputation have believed themselves entitled to take these words literally and have not [Col. 0960A] hesitated to declare that the definition of the grace of Jesus Christ is contained in this text:

> “A help for doing good, added to nature and doctrine through the inspiration of the most ardent and luminous charity” (*On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 35, no. 38).

But they themselves would not want their observation to be considered entirely sound; otherwise it would have to be said that, according to Saint Augustine’s doctrine, only the most ardent and luminous charity can count as the grace of Jesus Christ. Charity at a moderate degree of light and ardor—for example, Father Juenin’s attrition—would then be a Pelagian grace.

For my part, the first time I reflected on this passage, I thought I saw in it an exact description of the only grace necessary to the perfection of justice, of which the holy Doctor says elsewhere that it is a charity surpassing not only that which we have here below, but also that which we ask for and conceive:

> “That very love will be not only above what we have here, but above what we ask and understand.”

The words *bene agendi*, “for doing good,” subsequently made me doubt and left me in suspense, for they evidently indicate that the subject is grace necessary for action, and not for the perfection of justice. On the other hand, my respect for Saint Augustine did not allow me to think that he had inserted hyperbolic and exaggerated terms into a confession of faith that he prescribed to Pelagius. At last I noticed that the holy Doctor designated actual grace by the final term toward which the entire sequence of actual and effective graces leads us, by the entire and complete effect to which each particular grace contributes, and which the grace of the perfection of justice completes. This consists in the light of charity dispersing even the smallest shadow of the dense night in which sin has buried us, and in the fire of charity burning and consuming even the slightest fiber of the earthly and carnal affections whose unhappy seed sin is in our soul:

> “Of the most ardent and luminous charity.”

I conclude that, in all the places where the holy Doctor seems to make no distinction between charity and actual grace, he is being misrepresented when he is made to think that every actual grace is an actual and formal inspiration of charity. Accustomed to speak the language of Scripture, which calls the Church militant and visible that Jesus Christ established on earth the kingdom of heaven because it leads us to the kingdom of heaven, the holy Doctor calls every good movement that is a remote or proximate disposition toward charity “charity.” He uses the term in two roughly similar senses, just as he uses the term “sin.” As he sometimes takes the latter to mean a fault and sometimes a spiritual misery, so he uses the word “charity” both to signify an act of the third theological virtue and to express an act of any other supernatural virtue.

[Col. 0960D] A similar reason led him to this usage. He called “sin” everything that comes from sin and at the same time carries or disposes us toward sin. Likewise, he called “charity” everything inspired in us by eternal and substantial charity—that is, by the Holy Spirit—and which at the same time carries or disposes us, remotely or proximately, toward charity, through which the Holy Spirit establishes his dwelling in us. That is why good will, love or desire for the good, virtue, and charity are most often synonymous terms in his writings. He did not foresee the abuse that would be made of his language.

Moreover, in his controversies with the Pelagians, he almost always describes actual grace by the noblest effect and the principal end toward which it tends. One would think that he attributes to every actual grace the properties of true charity; and in fact he attributes them to it in a certain sense, with which the Jansenists are wrong not to be satisfied. The holy Doctor does not claim that these properties belong immediately and in itself to every actual grace, but only by reason of the grace that influences the act of charity and toward which the other graces prepare the will.

Certainly, when Saint Augustine confuses actual grace with charity, it is in a sense that can apply to the grace of supernatural fear, which precedes charity; it is in a sense that can apply to the grace of prayer, which, by Saint Augustine’s own admission, is a means of obtaining the charity of which one feels entirely deprived:

> “But when they do this, whether by not doing it at all or by not doing it out of charity, let them pray that they may receive what they do not yet possess” (*On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 2, no. 4).

There was considerable art in Saint Augustine’s procedure. For how could he better prove the necessity of an interior grace of the will for every work useful to salvation than by the effect of justification, toward which every grace disposes and which the grace of charity produces? [Col. 0961B] Jansenius was wrong to conclude from this that every actual grace was an actual and formal inspiration of charity.

Could one imagine that he had greater reason to claim that every grace is effective because the holy Doctor’s discourse most often has effective grace as its object—not only when he undertakes to emphasize the virtue and power of grace or to establish the necessity of cooperating grace, but also when he wishes to show that grace in general precedes our wills and that it alone gives us the complete and proximate power to do good?

He was compelled by the nature of the controversy in which he was engaged to proceed in this way. For what proofs could he have drawn from grace that is resisted and frustrated of its effect? It is at least beyond doubt that his best proofs had to be founded on the effects of grace that are marked out in the Holy Scriptures.

[Col. 0961C] Here Jansenius displays his doctrine concerning the distinction between grace in the two states, and makes a show of the discovery reserved to him alone of the key, foundation, and thread of Saint Augustine’s works. In short, he assigns the *quo* help to effective actual grace and the *sine quo non* help to sufficient actual grace; so that, having easily shown that the former belongs exclusively to our state and the latter exclusively to the state of innocence, it remains established that every grace in our state is effective and that sufficient grace is excluded from it.

But this great buttress of Jansenius’s system is, it seems to me, ruined from top to bottom. For it is clear as day that he has confused the habitual grace of predestination with effective actual grace, and moreover has confused both with the grace of impeccability and of the perfection of justice, which belongs to Adam’s state and to that of the blessed, and which Saint [Col. 0961D] Augustine calls victorious delight. This alone is essentially a grace of delight and charity; this alone is effective by itself and by its nature.

[Note: [Col. 0961D] I speak in my own fashion; the Thomists will permit me. Or, if one prefers, I understand “effective by itself and by its nature” in the Jansenists’ sense. [Col. 0962D]]

The most apparent testimony of Saint Augustine that has been produced to prove that the grace of our state which has its effect is effective by its nature and by itself is this:

> “When man’s will has been healed and helped, that very possibility comes to exist in the saints together with the effect” (*On Nature and Grace*, chapter 42, no. 49).

Others may quibble and dispute over the meaning of the words in this passage.

For my part, I freely admit it: here we truly have grace effective by itself and by its nature. Not only is the possibility not without the effect, but the possibility comes only with the effect. It is therefore impossible to conceive the possibility without conceiving the effect. What more could one want?

But Saint Augustine does not say that whenever the saints perform a good work, they act by the virtue of such grace. This possibility, which comes to the saints only with the effect, is the possibility of impeccability and of the perfection of justice. For what is Saint Augustine’s principal purpose in *On Nature and Grace*, from which this passage is taken? Is it not to refute a book of Pelagius in which that heresiarch treated at length the doctrine of impeccability and the perfection of justice? The holy Doctor declares this at the very beginning:

> “And consequently, if human nature, begotten from the flesh of that one transgressor, can suffice by itself to fulfill the law and PERFECT justice, it ought to be secure of its reward” (*On Nature and Grace*, chapter 2, no. 2).

The whole sequence up to the passage in question makes this sufficiently clear, especially these words:

> “For when we recall these things, we do not take away the freedom of the will, but proclaim the grace of God. For whom do these things benefit except one who wills—but wills humbly, not exalting himself on the strength of his will as though he alone were sufficient for the PERFECTION of justice?” (*ibid.*, chapter 32, no. 36).

In the very passage at issue, is not the subject the help necessary for the saints to possess a charity so perfect that nothing could be added to it? This is the same as enjoying the gift of impeccability and possessing the perfection of justice, as the saint expressly explains:

> “Those who have had, or have, or will have a perfect charity, to which nothing could be added—for this is the truest, fullest, and MOST PERFECT justice” (*ibid.*, chapter 42, no. 49).

This favor, he adds, is granted to the saints only when the charity of God is poured into their hearts by the Holy Spirit with all the fullness that a healthy nature, purified and empty of every earthly feeling, is capable of receiving:

> “When the charity of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, as fully as our healthy and purified nature can receive it” (*ibid.*).

Read a few pages farther, and you will see with the utmost clarity that the possibility at issue in the dispute between Saint Augustine and Pelagius is precisely the possibility of the perfection of justice—the possibility of being without concupiscence and of feeling nothing except according to one’s will and pleasure:

> “For this reason Pelagius attributes to God’s grace the possibility of not sinning, because God is the author of that nature in which he says the possibility of not sinning has been inseparably implanted. When he wills, therefore, he acts; because when he does not will, he does not act. For where there is an inseparable possibility, weakness of will—or rather, the will’s being subject to infirmity and its lack of perfection—cannot occur. If this is so, then where does the statement come from: ‘To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good is not present’?” (*On Nature and Grace*, chapter 51, no. 59).

The controversy therefore concerns the possibility that Saint Paul lacked when he said:

> “I do not do the good that I will; instead, I do the evil that I do not will. For to will the good is present in me, but to do the good perfectly is what I do not find” (Romans 7:15 and following).

And because the Apostle lacks this possibility, Saint Augustine concludes that it is not inseparably attached to human nature. It is therefore the possibility of not feeling the sting of the flesh, the possibility not of action but of the perfection of justice, that comes to the saints together with the effect.

I would depart from the purpose I have set myself if I stopped to show that the doctrine of grace effective by itself in the sense of several theologians—men praiseworthy for upholding it in a Catholic manner—has nothing in common with Saint Augustine’s principles. They admit a truly sufficient grace, and they teach that the human will has a real power to resist their grace effective by itself, or rather to prevent, by the force of a pure and free omission, the arrival of the predetermining help. One ought not to demand more from them.

According to Saint Augustine, there is no truly sufficient grace that gives the mere power of the perfection of justice, and the grace necessary to the perfection of justice is not only effective by itself and by its nature, but also irresistible. If the holy Doctor had used our terms, he would undoubtedly have reasoned as follows:

To be able to resist a grace effective by itself and by its nature is to be able to make a grace effective by itself and by its nature fail to have its effect; for to resist a grace and to make a grace fail to have its effect are precisely the same thing. Now the human will does not have the power to make a grace effective by itself and by its nature fail to have its effect. I prove it.

To be able to make a grace effective by itself and by its nature fail to have its effect is to be able to make a grace effective by itself and by its nature not be a grace effective by itself and by its nature; for to be effective by itself and by its nature means nothing other than to have its effect by itself and by its nature. Now the human will does not have the power to make a grace effective by itself and by its nature not be a grace effective by itself and by its nature. Therefore the human will does not have the power to make a grace effective by itself and by its nature fail to have its effect; therefore the human will does not have the power to resist a grace effective by itself and by its nature; therefore a grace effective by itself and by its nature is irresistible.

The licentiate then thought of becoming angry with me.

“Would you claim,” he said in an agitated manner and tone, “to turn the doctrine of grace effective by itself into heresy?”

“Gently,” I replied. “There is no malice in what I am saying. I am taking no notice whatsoever of the Thomistic school’s position; I have already warned you of that. They are peaceful and equitable opponents whom I honor. It is entirely unlikely that they would be offended by an argument that has no force against them and does not touch their doctrinal system. For I am making myself a Thomist for a moment, and I rightly treat this argument as a sophism if it is directed against physical predetermination and grace effective by itself as Alvarez and Lemos taught it.”

I deny that being able to resist grace effective by itself when one actually receives it, and being able to make grace effective by itself fail to have its effect, are precisely the same thing. But I maintain that being unable to resist grace effective by itself means having had, still having, and retaining a real power to prevent grace effective by itself from ever having been given; or, to express it another way, it means having had a perfectly sufficient grace preceding grace effective by itself, the abuse of which would have been an obstacle to grace effective by itself.

In short, the power to resist, as Alvarez expressly says (*On Helps*, Book IX, disputation 94, no. 4), bears upon the offer that God makes of grace effective by itself when he gives sufficient grace, and not upon grace effective by itself insofar as it is received in free will. This is how he explains the words of the Council of Sens:

> “Nor is the help of God who draws us such that it cannot be resisted” (Council of Sens, decree of faith, 15),

and these words of Saint Thomas:

> “God moves the human mind toward the good in such a way that it can nevertheless resist this motion” (Saint Thomas, *Quodlibet* 1, article 7, reply to objection 2).

Do you wish to be fully convinced of everything I have just explained concerning the way in which true Thomists demonstrate that grace effective by itself, understood in their sense, is not irresistible? Read attentively this passage of Alvarez:

> “It lies within the power of our will to impede itself so that it does not have that motion. Hence, if it does not perform the act that is commanded, this will be imputed to it as guilt, because through its own fault it impeded itself so that the effective help would not be given to it, which was necessary for it actually to perform the act of virtue that is commanded. It is as if God imposed on a man the command to fly and, on his part, offered him wings and the help necessary for flying, while the man, by his own freedom, replied: ‘Lord, I neither wish to receive wings nor to fly.’ He would rightly be considered guilty and a transgressor of the command, even if he could not fly without wings, because through his own fault he impeded himself so that God would not give them to him” (*On Helps*, Book III, disputation 18, no. 20).

Thus my argument ought to give the true Thomists more pleasure than pain, since it gives them an opportunity to demonstrate plainly the Catholic character of their position and serves as a touchstone by which to distinguish them from those who falsely adorn themselves with their name.

“Do you think they are very pleased,” added the licentiate, “to hear you assert that Saint Augustine never thought of their physical predetermination and their grace effective by itself?”

“They would be wrong to take offense that I should try to deprive them of the authority even of Saint Thomas, if I wished to raise here a school controversy that the different parties make it their duty to defend as best they can. But just as I would not object if, while combating the Jansenists, they incidentally expressed their distaste for middle knowledge, they will have the courtesy not to demand that I positively renounce theological principles that are permitted and that once had attractions for me. They would be far too astonished if I did so.”

Whatever the case may be, since one must not stir up a civil war [Col. 0964C] within Catholicism when it is a matter of arming ourselves against the enemies of the faith, I shall have the courtesy to modify my proposition as follows. The only grace effective in itself and by its nature that Saint Augustine evidently taught, and which one may conclude to be necessitating and irresistible, is that which is necessary for the perfection of justice—that is, the grace God gives only together with immortality, the grace of original justice that Adam received. An even more precious grace of this kind is the portion of the blessed in heaven; it consists in the complete extinction of concupiscence and is consequently independent of the cooperation of the will. Its total effect precedes both consent and the power to resist, since it consists in removing the involuntary impulses of inclination and feeling that arise within us before reason has deliberated. But Jansenius included the very act of consent within the irresistible necessity caused by the efficacy [Col. 0964D] of his victorious grace. His principal proof is this famous passage from Saint Augustine: *Quod amplius nos delectat secundum id operemur necesse est* (“We must act according to that which delights us more”) (*Exposition on Galatians*, no. 49). M. de Fénelon has taken this proof away from him, as we have seen. What breach would one make in Jansenius’s Augustine if one struck out all the passages where this text is improperly employed, as well as those in which the *quo* assistance is taken for actually efficacious grace, and those in which the action of justice is confused with the perfection of justice? Most of them belong to this last category.

Under cover of an equivocation that most readers are not in a position to detect, Jansenius commits enormous depredations upon Saint Augustine’s writings. I shall make this especially clear to you in the abuse of the testimonies by which he supports the error expressed at the end of the first proposition of the [Col. 0965A] five condemned by the Church, namely: that the grace of God, which makes the commandments possible, is sometimes lacking to the just when they are in need.

## VII. What Kind of Grace Is Ordinarily Refused to Us

Read these words from *On the Spirit and the Letter*:

> “Behold how, without example among human beings, perfect justice nevertheless is not impossible. It would come to pass if a will as great as suffices for so great a matter were applied. And it would be so great if nothing belonging to justice were hidden from us, and if these things so delighted the soul that this delight surpassed whatever other pleasure or pain might hinder it. That this is not so belongs not to impossibility but to the judgment of God. For who does not know that it is not within a human being’s power what he should know, nor does it follow that what has been recognized as desirable will be desired, unless it delights us as much as it ought to be loved? This, however, is the soul’s state of health.” (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, book I, chapter 35, no. 63)

Could Saint Augustine [Col. 0965B] have made it clearer that he is speaking here of the grace required to accomplish that perfect justice of which there is no example among human beings? It is a grace sufficient and proportionate to its effect only because it leaves nothing belonging to justice unknown, and fills the soul with a delight capable of absorbing and extinguishing every contrary feeling of pain and pleasure. It places within human power a measure of knowledge and attraction to pleasure equal to the love demanded by the supreme good. Finally, it is a grace proper to the state of health.

How indignant ought one to become when one reads in Jansenius that this perfect justice is nothing other than an ordinary work of justice—*perfecta justitia, id est opus justitiae* (“perfect justice, that is, a work of justice”) (vol. III, book III, chapter 13, p. 332)—so that he may persuade people that a judgment of God like that experienced by Saint Paul when the Lord refused to deliver him from the angel of Satan is a judgment by which God deprives the saints of the grace without which one cannot live well or observe the commandments whose transgression is punishable [Col. 0965C].

I shall pass over many other similar infidelities and other examples of bad faith whose exposition would take too long. Recall the citations from the letter to Count Boniface and from the homily on the history of Joseph and Susanna. Recall also the passage where Saint Augustine says that God does not always give the saints victorious delight. Jansenius repeats this a hundred times and more in order to make his readers conceive of the withdrawal of a grace necessary for preserving holiness. But what is meant is solely God’s refusal to remove from them the sting of the flesh, that angel of Satan who torments them, but whom they always have the power to overcome through the help of sufficient grace: *Sufficit tibi gratia mea* (“My grace is sufficient for you”; II Corinthians 12:9).

I now come to the conclusion Jansenius draws from the long list of testimonies he has assembled concerning the [Col. 0965D] refusal and withdrawal of grace. “From all this,” he says, “it follows that this sentence or axiom, ‘God commands nothing impossible,’ is true in no other sense than that the commandments can be fulfilled when God assists the human will by his all-powerful grace” (Jansenius, vol. III, book III, chapter 13, p. 337). To support this conclusion, he proves very well, by a passage from Saint Augustine, that the commandment of the perfection of justice is possible only in this sense:

> “By these and countless similar testimonies I cannot doubt either that God has commanded nothing impossible to human beings, or that nothing is impossible for God when he comes to our aid and assistance so that what he commands may be done. And therefore a human being can, if he wishes, be without sin, assisted by God.” (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book II, chapter 6, no. 7)

I have demonstrated that, in Saint Augustine’s sense, to be without sin is to be without concupiscence. This, then, is the possibility of God’s commandments [Col. 0966A] that the Jansenists admit—the possibility Saint Augustine admitted with respect to the commandment to be without concupiscence.

“Nothing more is lacking to my complete satisfaction,” said the licentiate, “than for you to remove the scruple that remains with me: that your way of explaining Saint Augustine is new.”

“It is,” I replied, “as ancient as Saint Augustine himself, since he alone is his own interpreter in everything you have seen. These are his definitions, his reasons, the purpose of his works, and the comparison of his various testimonies that I have brought into operation in order to make him understood. But there was scarcely any clarification to be made; I needed only to present his thoughts to you in a certain order and to direct your attention. Jansenius says that, without a miracle of almighty God, a person who reads Saint Augustine’s works only once cannot perceive their true meaning (vol. II, introductory book, chapter 28, p. 61). I maintain, on the contrary, that this Father did not write [Col. 0966B] an Apocalypse, and that, if it were not for the prodigious enchantment cast over minds by the self-assured tone of certain writers of recent centuries, people would have seen—as they saw before—that in him these three expressions are synonymous: *Esse sine peccato*, *Perficere bonum seu justitiam*, *Non omnino concupiscere* (“to be without sin,” “to perfect the good or justice,” “not to experience concupiscence at all”). For I am convinced that, until the birth of Lutheranism and Calvinism, Saint Augustine was very well understood.

Saint Thomas, for example, would certainly have expounded Saint Augustine’s doctrine of the perfection of justice as I have done. The manner in which he explains verse 18 of chapter 7 of the Epistle to the Romans leaves me no doubt:

> “But I do not find within my power how to perfect this good, namely, how to exclude concupiscence completely.”  
> (Saint Thomas, on chapter 7 of the Epistle to the Romans)

The author of the Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans attributed to Saint Remigius took this same meaning from Saint Augustine [Col. 0966C]:

> “But I do not find how to perfect it, since I cannot avoid concupiscence. Perfect good consists not only in perfecting, but also in not experiencing concupiscence.”

Before the holy Doctor, these words of Saint Paul—“But I do not find how to perfect it”—had been understood as referring to the extreme difficulty caused by the flesh in carrying out the good desires conceived by the spirit. Saint Augustine’s disciples could not notice and adopt the interpretation that pleased him without recognizing in it the true key to his works.

Primasius, bishop of Africa, who flourished approximately a hundred years after the holy Doctor’s death, holds a significant place among his disciples. Consider these words from his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans:

> “And this should be noted: he did not say, ‘I do not find how to do good,’ but ‘how to perfect it.’ For what is the perfection of good except the extinction of evil? The perfection of good is not to experience concupiscence. For what is easier for a human being placed under the law than to will the good and do evil? Now this is to perfect good: that a human being should not even experience concupiscence. Good is imperfect [Col. 0966D] when one experiences concupiscence, even if one does not consent to concupiscence for evil.”  
> (*On Romans* 7:18, vol. X of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyon edition, p. 157, col. 1A)

Do you think that Primasius, who speaks in this way, confused—as Jansenius did—the action and the perfection of justice, victorious delight and the medicinal grace of Jesus Christ (Jansenius, *On the Grace of Christ the Savior*, book III, chapter 13, p. 332)? Would Primasius have said, *Perfecta justitia, id est opus justitiae* (“perfect justice, that is, a work of justice”)?

To conclude, let us return to M. Bayle. He was pleased to suppose that the physical predetermination of the Thomists, the necessity of Saint Augustine, that of the Jansenists, and that of Calvin are essentially the same thing; and that the doctrine of the Council of Trent and of Saint Chrysostom concerning the nature of grace and free will is contrary to what Saint Augustine taught on both points. From this proceed the arguments, reflections, mockeries, and invectives that can be produced by an intelligent man [Col. 0967A] who has advanced improperly and has not examined matters without prejudice or with the necessary understanding. The licentiate left me with the firm intention of undertaking [Col. 0968A] a continuous reading of all Saint Augustine’s works and of working on a new *Augustinus* to oppose to that of Jansenius.

# THIRD PART. Examination of a Key to Saint Augustine’s Works against the Pelagians, Recently Found at Padua

[Col. 0967]

[Col. 0967A] I believe I shall please you by adding, following my conversations with the licentiate, a refutation of a work entitled *Dissertatio theologico-analytica de vero intellectu trium celeberrimorum [Col. 0967B] capitum, etc.*, that is: “Theological and Analytical Dissertation on the True Meaning of the Three Famous Chapters 10, 11, and 12 of Saint Augustine’s Book *On Rebuke and Grace*, or on the True and False Distinction between the Helps of Grace,” by Étienne Lorenzoni, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of Padua, quarto, 144 pages, not counting the dedicatory epistle, preface, and table of contents; Padua, 1729.

This little work is dedicated to Saint Philip Neri, founder of the Congregation of the Oratory of Italy. The author first pays homage to his holy patron for his progress in the doctrine of grace and in the understanding of Saint Augustine. This humble prayer of Saint Philip Neri—“What evil shall I not do, or what good shall I ever do, if you do not help me, O my Jesus!”—is for him incontestable proof that this great saint held grace to be effective in itself. For this reason Father Lorenzoni [Col. 0967C] next begs his holy founder to present him and his work to Pope Benedict XIII, and he dictates to the saint a harangue or compliment that he asks him to deliver to the sovereign pontiff, while he himself, prostrate at His Holiness’s feet, remains silent.

The preface, or rather the warning to the reader, is chiefly devoted to anticipating the various judgments that may be passed upon this work. “Perhaps,” says the author, “we shall be accused of not having arrived at the truth.” He responds with a passage from Saint Augustine, appropriating to himself words full of modesty and humility.

“If there are persons,” he adds, “who agree that we are speaking the truth but do not agree that what we say conforms to Saint Augustine, they will force us to exclaim with the same Father,” and so forth. He then describes another passage in which the holy Doctor asks God for the grace to bear gently and patiently the calumnies [Col. 0967D] of his adversaries, whom he reproaches for not having entered into his thought because they are proud and lovers not of speaking the truth but of their own particular opinion. This is entirely just, assuming that Father Lorenzoni is as certain of understanding Saint Augustine as Saint Augustine was of understanding himself.

He says nothing about those who will think that he has departed both from the truth and from Saint Augustine’s meaning. Since apparently this can happen only against his expectation, I declare, reluctantly, that I belong to the latter group.

Father Lorenzoni next explains why he did not treat his subject in the manner of the scholastics: he wished, he says, to warm hearts while enlightening minds, whereas the scholastic method, in his opinion, inspires too much conceit and malice.

Finally, he attributes the obscurity of his thoughts to the profundity of the mysteries [Col. 0968A] that he explains. As for obscurity of style, it is natural that an author should not notice it. Let us come to the body of the work.

[Col. 0968B] After a fairly brief exordium, in which the profession made by the author (no. 1 [Note: [Col. 0967] This number, and those that we shall place in parentheses in the following pages, designate the sections of Father Lorenzoni’s work.]) of loving truth, charity, unity, and peace is infinitely estimable, he sets out (no. 2) the state of the controversy among theologians who maintain that efficacious grace is so by itself and by its nature. For his intention is not to pronounce upon the theological disputes that the schools of Scotus and Molina, the defenders of moral predetermination and of middle knowledge, wage with the disciples of Bañez. He assumes that every advantage lies with the latter and that they alone possess the truth and the doctrine of Saint Augustine.

He therefore confines himself to settling the disagreement among the predeterminists themselves—that is, between the true and false disciples of Bañez: those who genuinely and without restriction enlist under the banner of the school called Thomistic, in order to uphold the necessity of grace effective in itself in every kind of state, and the auxiliary troops that have recently enlarged [Col. 0968C] this school in order to defend the necessity of grace effective in itself only in the state of corrupted nature.

“The question,” he says, “is to determine Saint Augustine’s view concerning the help of grace that Adam received, and how it differed from the help granted to human beings after their fall.” He understands this as actual grace, which is necessary for every good work that is performed, and he tells us that some locate the difference in the fact that, according to Saint Augustine, versatile grace sufficed for innocent humanity and for the angels to persevere in the good, but does not suffice after sin, which made grace effective in itself necessary. Others, by contrast, attribute to Saint Augustine the teaching that grace effective in itself was equally necessary in both states, and that consequently the entire difference consists in the fact that, in the state of corrupted nature, grace effective in itself is required for new reasons and produces effects particular and proper [Col. 0968D] to the needs of that state.

I shall not let Father Lorenzoni use the term “versatile grace,” whose first authors are suspect, which is not acknowledged by the Catholic opponents of physical predetermination, and which, if taken strictly, signifies something no Catholic has ever said—namely, that free will gives movement and action to grace.

Nor can I refrain from protesting again against the proposition that Father Lorenzoni attributes not only to the theologians of whom he speaks, as admitting versatile grace in the state of innocence, but also suggests must be acknowledged by all who deny that the holy angels were physically predetermined:

> “The will of the holy angels who made good use of grace was THE TRUE AND SOLE CAUSE of their perseverance and stability in the good.”

Does he believe that the will of a poor man who accepts a considerable sum offered to him [Col. 0969A] is the true and sole cause of his becoming rich? Yet there is even less right to say that the will of the holy angels, who consented to grace without the help of physical predetermination, was the true and sole cause of their perseverance and stability in the good, since the very strength of grace helped them to give that consent.

Moreover, Father Lorenzoni is too lenient toward those theologians who support versatile grace only for the state of innocence, since he does not call them Baianists. For, according to him, they agree—and must agree—that the merits of the angel and of innocent humanity are not gifts of God. Does he not know that the first of the propositions of Baius condemned by the sovereign pontiffs is this: “The merits of the angel and of the first human being should not be called grace”?

The author of the Dissertation then examines (no. 3) the basis of the arguments of the defenders of versatile grace—that is, the false Thomists who [Col. 0969B] exclude physical predetermination and grace effective in itself from the state of innocence. He finds (no. 4) that their principal support consists in the three famous chapters 10, 11, and 12 of the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, which they misunderstand, and which he undertakes to clarify (no. 5), taking Father Serry as his guide. Yet, in his opinion, Father Serry did not derive the full advantage he could have obtained from an admirable counterargument that these three chapters supplied against his opponents.

He therefore enters upon the path traced for him by this very illustrious and learned theologian and, with all due respect to both of them, goes astray with him from the very first step. For certainly the comparison Saint Augustine makes between the two states of humanity before and after [Col. 0969C] sin concerns neither the grace they deem it proper to call versatile, nor physical predetermination or grace effective in itself, nor, in short, the nature of any actual grace.

The *quo* help is the grace of predestination proper to our state: grace not only by which one is brought, sooner or later, and finally delivered irrevocably to the good, but in which one also perseveres, remains, stands firm and unchanging; grace that one does not abandon, but retains and preserves, and never loses. It is not a passing action of God upon us, but a habit and a state, and for that reason it is compared with blessedness. It is inseparably attached to the elect; it is unfailing; it is a mercy not inherent, as Calvin claimed, but adherent, as Saint Augustine expresses it. I have borrowed all these terms in order to describe the *quo* help. This help is consequently nothing other than a merciful and special providence that God employs to regulate the economy, succession, and interconnection of graces, both interior and exterior, by means [Col. 0969D] of which the predestined attain salvation.

The *sine quo non* help, being relative and opposed to the *quo* help, is certainly also something habitual. It can mean only the grace of predestination proper to the state of Adam and the angels, and an order of divine Providence over the angel and innocent humanity with respect to salvation, entirely different from that observed now.

Anyone who reads the three famous chapters of *On Rebuke and Grace* only to find proofs of a view or system already implanted in his mind grasps only whatever can favor his prejudices. He passes lightly over so many places where terms expressing habitual possession of these two kinds of grace occur. [Col. 0970A] Can these expressions apply to any actual grace?

> “For such was the help in which he would remain if he wished,” etc.;  
> “So that they might remain in God’s help if they wished,” etc.;  
> “So that divine grace might act in an unturning and inseparable manner,” etc.;  
> and elsewhere, “with the mercy of the Savior adhering to him,” etc.

If Father Lorenzoni had paid attention to this—a point that has nevertheless not escaped a great many ancient and modern theologians—he would not have applied (no. 6) to these three famous chapters what Jansenius says of all Saint Augustine’s works: that they are a labyrinth full of confusing turns. Still less would he have congratulated himself on having found the thread, rule, and principle needed to escape from it.

I said that a great many theologians, both ancient and modern, had clearly observed that by the two helps, *quo* and *sine quo non*, Saint Augustine meant habitual graces. At least a few must be cited. Without considering several who seem to recognize in them the habitual sanctifying graces [Col. 0970B] proper to the two states, I shall limit myself to a small number whose opinion comes closest to my own. I have already mentioned Father Annat; I shall first add Father Didaque Ruiz de Montoya, an eminent theologian, as learned and judicious as he is subtle, extensive, and deserving of being read in his entirety (*On Predestination*, disputation 50, *On Angels*, section 4). He is full of the doctrine of the holy Fathers, none of whom he understands better, and he justifies their thoughts by the soundest and most solid metaphysics. But I am being asked for theologians of another kind and another school.

The Reverend Father François Macedo, a Franciscan who was held in high regard by the queen of France, Anne of Austria, joins and applauds Father Annat’s opinion. This is how he speaks of it:

> “Annat clearly teaches that by this help are understood all antecedent helps connected with perseverance, so that the help of perseverance is not one single help but the collection of all those by which wills are anticipated. [Col. 0970C] I congratulate Annat on having grasped Augustine’s meaning.”  
> (Macedo, *The Scrinium of Saint Augustine*, book II, chapter 2)

“A fine authority!” someone will say. “This Franciscan was wholly devoted to the Jesuits; he was not ashamed to print these words: *Societatem Jesu amo* (‘I love the Society of Jesus’; p. 250).” Indeed, how could he have understood Saint Augustine while doing that? Well then, here is an Oratorian Father who proves—and these are his own words—that the *quo* help

> “is nothing other than the multitude, variety, cooperation, proportion, and harmony of several helps by which Providence guides and manages its elect with such gentleness, wisdom, and strength that they persevere to the end; or, if they fall, rise infallibly from their faults.”
