> [Note: [Col. 0969D] Reverend Father Thomassin, *Fourth Memoir on Grace*, chapter 20, p. 218.]

Franciscus Sylvius, who is known to have been attached for some time to the doctrine of Baius, held the same view and retained the reading *inseparabiliter*, without regard for the correction of the doctors of Louvain (Sylvius, *In the First Part of the Second Part*, question 109, article 10).

[Col. 0970D] I do not know what common opinion exists of M. du Hamel, of the Royal Academy of Sciences, concerning theology. For my part, I find in his treatises many reflections as beautiful and as just as his style is pure and polished. This author explains the three famous chapters of *On Rebuke and Grace* approximately according to the plan I have followed.

> “That *quo* help,” he says, “includes God’s effective purpose and intention, as well as the multitude of helps that arise from that purpose; it is not some motion that physically predetermines, nor some victorious delight, nor an actual grace that is singular, etc.”

And farther on:

> “Predestination, to which perseverance or the *quo* help is joined, is defined by that same Augustine as the preparation of benefits.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0970D] J.-B. du Hamel, *Theologia speculatrix et practica*, etc., treatise *On Grace*, book III, chapter 8, no. 4.]

[Col. 0971A] But these are only modern theologians, and I promised some ancient ones. They cannot fail me, since Suárez (*On the True Understanding of Efficacious Helps*, chapter 34) speaks of this way of understanding the two helps as not excessively recent. I pity this great man for not having employed the powers of his genius to overcome the difficulties that prevented him from embracing an opinion whose evidence is otherwise so striking.

The works of the illustrious Tapper have come into my hands. It is related that, in the public disputations of the University of Louvain, he consistently confounded Baius; [Note: [Col. 0971] See the *History of Baianism* published by Father Duchesne, book I, p. 22.] and that it was especially through learned explanations of the most difficult passages in Saint Augustine that he drove the young innovator to bay and made him feel that Tapper remained his master. What was Tapper’s triumphant answer to the passages Baius drew from the three famous chapters? We read it in his works, where he takes the *sine quo non* help to be the habitual power of persevering, [Col. 0971B] and the *quo* help to be a special direction and protection now added to that power because of the infirmity our nature contracted through sin.

> “The just, because of the infirmity of the flesh and the obscurity of the intellect, cannot use this faculty, owing to the various events of things and the impulses of temptations, without divine help directing and protecting them, as Saint Thomas declares in the *First Part of the Second Part*, question 109, articles 9 and 10, citing blessed Augustine in *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 11: that in the first state human beings received a gift by which they could persevere, but not one by which they would persevere.”  
> (Ruardus Tapperus, vol. I, article 7, *On Free Will*, Cologne edition, pp. 195–196)

Nothing distressed Baius more—he who displayed great contempt for Saint Thomas—than when Tapper undertook to find Saint Thomas’s true meaning of Saint Augustine’s texts. Here we see an example. If one consults the passage in the *First Part of the Second Part* cited by this grave doctor of the old school of Louvain, one will be surprised to see [Col. 0971C] that I am defending Saint Thomas’s opinion against a Thomist.

Father Lorenzoni will doubtless be mortified by this, and it is already a serious blow to his discovery. He prepares his readers to receive it favorably by examining the first part of chapter 10 of *On Rebuke and Grace*, where he promises to display it. At least this is a thread attached to the entrance of the labyrinth, and not at the other end, where Jansenius wants one to look for his.

“The question,” says Saint Augustine (*On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 10, no. 26), “is what one should think concerning the first human being with respect to final perseverance.” Adam was created free from every vice and in perfect rectitude. I would certainly not say: “If he did not receive the gift of perseverance that was necessary for him, how was he free from every vice?” For this question is easily answered by saying that he did not receive the gift of perseverance because he did not persevere in the [Col. 0971D] good itself that made him free from every vice.

Father Lorenzoni (no. 7) sees in these words, as clearly as in Saint Philip Neri’s prayer, the exclusion of versatile grace—that is, grace that is not physically predetermining. His reason is that, if Saint Augustine had admitted versatile grace for the state of innocence, he would have had an easier answer to give: Adam did not need the gift of perseverance, which he was not to receive from God but was to procure for himself. One sees that Father Lorenzoni is firmly convinced that there can be no giving unless the giver physically predetermines the recipient to accept the gift.

But let us come to the great difficulty contained in Saint Augustine’s text, which begins with these words: [Col. 0972A] *Sed illud magis quaerendum operosiusque tractandum est*, etc. Let us attend to the brief analysis of this passage presented to us by Father Lorenzoni. No one perseveres except the one who has received perseverance; Adam did not persevere; therefore he did not receive it. But how is the one who did not receive perseverance guilty of not having persevered? Or how can it be that the person did not receive perseverance when one cannot say that the reason he did not receive it was that, by the benefit of grace, he had not been separated from the mass of perdition, since at that time there was no mass of perdition? “Here,” Father Lorenzoni adds (no. 8), “is the difficulty set out in its full force.”

He then reasons as follows: The difficulty Saint Augustine proposes here is considerable, as these words show: *Operosius tractandum est ut respondeamus* (“It must be treated with greater labor in order that we may answer it”). But if the holy Doctor intends to establish a distinction between the helps of grace proper to sound nature and those proper to corrupted nature, so that [Col. 0972B] versatile grace belongs to sound nature and grace effective in itself belongs to corrupted nature, then there is not the slightest difficulty, says the theologian of Padua. Indeed, he continues (no. 9), with versatile grace perseverance is not a gift of God, and it is pointless to ask why a person sinned by not persevering, unless perseverance—which is a gift of God—is necessary in order to persevere.

This reasoning is defective in more than one respect. First, it assumes that Saint Augustine is speaking of an actual grace, whereas the contrary is demonstrated. Second, it assumes that the supporters of versatile grace for Adam’s state are the first to agree that, with this grace, perseverance was not a gift of God. This cannot be true, at least not of those with whom Father Lorenzoni implies that he publicly disputed at Padua, where no doubt Baianism is not publicly defended. Third, it assumes that physical predetermination [Col. 0972C] is essential to giving, and thus that among human beings, who cannot physically predetermine one another, there could be no true giving at all; they would therefore be greatly embarrassed to explain how the idea of giving ever occurred to them before they had heard of physical predetermination.

Besides, Father Lorenzoni, it seems to me, falls from one difficulty into another. The first is that Saint Augustine finds a difficulty where there is none. Our author strains every muscle to avoid this precipice. The second difficulty is that the holy Doctor should require investigation and labor to answer a difficulty while simply acknowledging that it is insoluble and can be met only by a confession of faith. Father Lorenzoni is about to be dashed against this obstacle.

How is the one who has not received perseverance guilty of not having persevered? This is the question and difficulty that Saint Augustine undertakes to resolve. The answer that Father Lorenzoni (No. 10) makes the holy doctor give is that one must believe, as an impenetrable mystery, that Adam was guilty of not having persevered, although he had not received the necessary gift of perseverance. If Saint Augustine had nothing else to teach us on this subject, he would plainly have overrated the effort he expended, and the words *Sed illud magis quaerendum operosiusque tractandum est* would suit him no better than they would a child who, asked why the three persons of the Trinity do not constitute three gods, had nothing to reply except that it is a truth of faith. For if these words indicate a difficulty that is not slight, they also mean that, by applying oneself to meditate upon and penetrate it, one hopes to clarify it. Should Saint Augustine have tormented his mind so greatly merely to leave an objection intact, and to establish a mystery within that objection by a humble confession of faith? “By a confession of faith the objection is not solved, but a mystery is established within the objection,” says Father Lorenzoni, without unfortunately having considered that it takes less effort to say “I do not know” than to explain what one does know.

[Col. 0972D]

But perhaps the theologian of Padua means that Saint Augustine made great efforts of genius to discover the mystery contained in this objection? That is contrary to all appearance and reason, since Saint Augustine immediately makes his confession of faith, and consequently this mystery was already known to him through tradition. I do not say through inspiration, for Father Lorenzoni, I think, shares the opinion of all the theologians in the world who recognize no new revelations concerning dogmas since the death of the apostles. If, nevertheless, he believes that knowledge of this mystery was given to Saint Augustine at the time and in the very moment when he was writing the beginning of chapter 10 of the book *On Correction and Grace*, then at least it cannot have cost the holy doctor much effort. Whatever the case, our author has forbidden himself so frivolous an escape as the claim that Saint Augustine devoted much labor and application to learning the truth that he professes.

[Col. 0973A]

Indeed, Father Lorenzoni presents this mystery as the true key not only to the three celebrated chapters—10, 11, and 12—of the book *On Correction and Grace*, but also to all Saint Augustine’s works against the Pelagians; and he foresaw that one might apply to his discovery the same mockery deserved by Jansenius’s discovery: namely, that if the disputes of the monastery of Hadrumetum had not induced Saint Augustine to write the book *On Correction and Grace*, the holy doctor would have carried the key to his works into the other world. For this reason Father Lorenzoni takes care to warn us that this mystery and this rule of faith, which is the key to Saint Augustine’s works against the Pelagians, present themselves everywhere to an attentive and watchful reader in the holy doctor’s other writings (*bene vigilanterque intuentibus undique occurrit*). Thus, what would all this long examination and painstaking inquiry, this arduous exertion of mind and intensified study, of which Saint Augustine boasts—*Magis quaerendum operosiusque tractandum*—amount to? To the answer that he has no answer to give, and to the discovery of a mystery that had already been discovered.

But let us show a solution where Father Lorenzoni sees none. What is the difficulty? It seems that Adam was not guilty of failing to persevere, since he did not receive the gift of perseverance, and it cannot be said that this gift was refused him because he had not been separated from the mass of corruption. Saint Augustine could not fully satisfy this difficulty in a few words, as he himself declares: *Magis quaerendum operosiusque tractandum*. He therefore contents himself first with establishing the principle of the answer, saying that God ordered the life of angels and human beings in such a way that he first showed what free will could do, and afterward what the gift of his grace could do: *Sic ordinasse angelorum hominumque vitam, ut in ea prius ostenderet quid eorum posset liberum arbitrium, deinde quid posset gratiae suae beneficium.*

[Col. 0973B]

In the first member of this passage there is no mention of the help of grace, and in the second there is no mention of the cooperation of free will. Nevertheless, both are implied. But why this double omission? Because in the first member the subject is a grace entrusted to free will, whereas in the second the subject is a grace to which free will is entrusted; consequently, in the first member free will must be considered particularly, and in the second, grace. The distinction between these two kinds of grace will be the answer to the question posed. The holy doctor does not yet explicitly make this distinction because, as I have said, he wishes here only to lay down the principle of his answer.

But judging from the way Saint Augustine subsequently speaks of these two kinds of grace, what are they? Versatile grace and grace efficacious in itself, or some other kinds of actual graces that one might imagine? Nothing of the sort. The first was a grace in which Adam would have remained had he wished to do so; the second is a grace now inseparably attached to the predestined. Thus, on both sides, it is habitual grace, and the latter is never found in any person, in any just person who is not predestined; both, therefore, are manifestly predestination-grace.

[Col. 0974A]

Thus the meaning of the text in which Father Lorenzoni recognizes a simple confession of faith, as it is explained and developed throughout the three chapters, is that in Adam’s state the grace of predestination did not govern the movements of free will, but limited itself to preceding it with the actual graces it needed; whereas in our state it infallibly directs to salvation everything free will does. Consequently, the predestination-grace proper to the restored nature contains an absolute right to the gift of actual perseverance, whereas the predestination-grace proper to innocent nature contained only a conditional right to that same gift. It follows further that the power of persevering appropriate to Adam was quite different from the power of persevering that now remains to the non-predestined just, who, in the holy doctor’s view, have no right to the special gift of actual perseverance because they have not been separated from the mass of corruption.

[Col. 0974B]

From this arises the answer to the question or difficulty proposed. It consists in recognizing that Adam sinned by failing to persevere, although he had not received the gift of perseverance, and that one cannot say that this gift was refused him because he had not been separated from the mass of corruption. How so? Because Adam had received a grace that contained a conditional right to the gift of actual perseverance, and by his fault he did not remain in that grace. That is the substance of the three celebrated chapters.

Nevertheless, the more closely I examine the mystery whose discovery gave Father Lorenzoni such pleasure (No. 11), the more I am convinced that he ought to find in it anything but a principle that suits his purposes. What kind of confession of faith does Saint Augustine make here? What object of faith does he present to us in these words?

*Quapropter saluberrime confitemur quod rectissime credimus Deum Dominumque rerum omnium, qui creavit omnia bona valde, et mala ex bonis exoritura esse praescivit, et scivit magis ad suam omnipotentissimam bonitatem pertinere etiam de malis benefacere, quam mala esse non sinere; sic ordinasse angelorum hominumque vitam, ut in ea prius ostenderet quid eorum posset liberum arbitrium, deinde quid posset gratiae suae beneficium justitiaeque judicium* (*On Correction and Grace*, book 1, chapter 10, no. 27).

“We therefore most beneficially confess what we most rightly believe: that God, the Lord of all things, who created all things very good, foresaw that evil would arise from good, and knew that it pertained more to his almighty goodness to bring good even out of evil than not to permit evil to exist, ordered the life of angels and human beings in such a way that in it he first showed what their free will could do, and afterward what the benefit of his grace and the judgment of his justice could do.”

There are three things to note in this text: the principal proposition, the incidental proposition, and the connection that the principal proposition may have with the incidental proposition.

Who doubts that the incidental proposition is a dogma of the Christian religion? Namely, that God created only good; that he foresaw the evil that would arise from this good; and that it belonged to his omnipotent goodness to prefer bringing good out of evil to preventing evil. If Father Lorenzoni thinks it appropriate to make the principal proposition an article of faith as well, I will not dispute that point with him; but I will point out that he must immediately renounce Thomism and agree that predestination to glory was consequent in the state of innocent humanity, and has been antecedent only since Adam’s fall. For Saint Augustine means nothing else when he says that God established such an order in the life of human beings and angels that he first showed what free will could do while directing their movements, and afterward what the gift of a grace directing the movements of free will could do.

[Col. 0975A]

This is awkward, all the more so because the belief that Saint Augustine here professes bears directly upon the principal proposition and upon the system of the two predestinations: *Saluberrime confitemur quod rectissime credimus Deum . . . sic ordinasse*, and so forth. However determined Father Lorenzoni may be not to depart from Saint Augustine, he would have some difficulty condemning Saint Thomas as erroneous, since Saint Thomas teaches antecedent predestination both before and after sin. Thus our author could extricate himself only by relaxing somewhat his claim that Saint Augustine presents his opinion as a dogma to be embraced by all Catholics. If only to preserve the honor of Saint Thomas and the entire Thomist school, he would say that the holy doctor of grace intended merely to indicate how firmly persuaded he was of the connection between his own opinion, expressed in the principal proposition, and the dogma contained in the incidental proposition; in short, that Saint Augustine had merely set forth his particular belief concerning the two kinds of predestination.

Perhaps I flatter myself in vain that I have demonstrated to Father Lorenzoni that by the words *quid possit gratiae suae beneficium*, Saint Augustine understands habitual predestination-grace, which in our state is wholly independent of merits, according to the holy doctor. But I have some confidence in our author’s frequent protestations that he is an enemy of prejudice and preconceived opinion. I have said enough to make him doubt; a new reading of the three celebrated chapters, which he will take the trouble to review attentively with regard to the characteristics of grace of which Saint Augustine speaks, will produce complete conviction. I shall now try to enter into the thought that occurred to Father Lorenzoni and uncover the weakness of his new interpretation.

[Col. 0975B]

To the question, “How did Adam sin by failing to persevere, since he did not receive the gift necessary for perseverance?” Saint Augustine responds with a confession of faith which, explained in the manner of the theologian of Padua, has as its object this mystery: that God wished to show, on the one hand, in the fall of the evil angels, in Adam’s sin, and in the impenitence of all those who until the end of the world will die in mortal sin, what free will deprived of grace efficacious in itself and of the precious gift of perseverance could do; and, on the other hand, in the fidelity of the good angels, in Adam’s penitence, and in the holy death of all those who until the end of the world will leave this life in the peace and friendship of the Lord, what grace efficacious in itself and the precious gift of perseverance could do. Thus everything Saint Augustine says here and will say afterward applies equally to angels and human beings, and equally to the two states of the human race. One must admit that this is novel and subtly imagined. But Father Lorenzoni himself clearly senses that so unusual a commentary, ingenious though it is, needs to be supported by some strong and solid proofs.

The first proof he employs is plainly worthless: namely, that if one does not accept his explanation, one must admit that Saint Augustine introduces the angels as though by machinery in order to join them to human beings in his answer, since the angels had no part in the question proposed. But that question concerns Adam alone, and the difficulty relates only to the state of innocence. Do the other human beings therefore enter the alleged answer by machinery as well as the angels? Father Lorenzoni would not have been surprised to find the angels placed here if he had noticed that the confession of faith does not serve as the answer, but merely lays down the principle from which the answer must arise. We shall soon see that the explicit mention of the angels, far from being useless, was necessary at this point.

[Col. 0975C]

Our author’s second reason (Nos. 13 and 14) has something dazzling about it: namely, that if Saint Augustine had wished to distinguish two kinds of help, one proper to innocent nature and the other to nature fallen into sin, he would not have confused the angels with human beings in general, but would have placed on one side the angels together with innocent humanity, and on the other fallen humanity; and he would have expressed himself as follows:

*Saluberrime confitemur quod rectissime credimus, Deum . . . sic ordinasse angelorum et primi hominis vitam, ut in ea prius ostenderet quid posset eorum liberum arbitrium, deinde in lapsis hominibus quid posset suae gratiae beneficium.*

“We most beneficially confess what we most rightly believe: that God ordered the life of the angels and the first human being in such a way that in it he first showed what their free will could do, and afterward, in fallen human beings, what the benefit of his grace could do.”

Saint Augustine was right to speak accurately. Had he failed to do so, people would have acquired the right to muddle what he said most clearly. And what would they not have dared, since the precision of his expressions does not save him from the forced attributions imposed upon his words? Let us suppose that the holy doctor had written *viam* instead of *vitam*, so that his text would have to be translated in this way: “God so ordered the state of the way in which he placed the angels and human beings that he first showed what free will could do, and afterward what the benefit of his grace could do.” Would the theologian of Padua’s quibble have any force? No, certainly not, for the angels’ way would be designated by the word *prius*, and could not be designated by the word *deinde*, because there were not two states of the way for the angels. By contrast, both words would designate the way of human beings, because there were two states of the way for human beings. Now I ask Father Lorenzoni whether, when reading Saint Augustine’s text, anyone would think of the blessed life of human beings and angels at the end, and whether it is not obvious that this text must be understood exclusively of the life of human beings and angels on the way? It is therefore the same as if the holy doctor had written *viam* instead of *vitam*. What more is needed?

Father Lorenzoni’s third reason is an argument *ad hominem* against the opponents whom he combats as being at least somewhat Baianist. “Is it tolerable,” he says, “to exclude the good angels from the benefit of grace?” He bases this on the false conviction that the *sine quo non* help is sufficient grace, which he distinguishes—how, I do not know—from purely natural grace. For I dare say that the way he speaks of it is not clear and precise enough to allow one to infer plainly that the state of pure nature is possible, and that the appointment of rational nature to a supernatural end is not owed to it as a consequence of the benefit of creation.

[Col. 0976A]

Whatever the case, our author’s argument reduces to this dilemma: Either the perseverance of the holy angels showed what the benefit of grace could do, or it showed what free will could do. If it showed what the benefit of grace could do, then the holy angels received the *quo* help, and not merely the *sine quo non* help, which is not suited to showing what the benefit of grace can do; consequently, the division between these two helps does not distinguish the two different states of rational creatures. If the perseverance of the holy angels served only to show what free will could do, then Adam’s fall and that of the evil angels did not serve to show the power of the same free will; for it is absurd that the perseverance of some and the fall of others should show precisely the same thing.

I am inclined to believe that this argument is strong on the supposition that the two helps are actual graces. Let the Baianists extricate themselves from it as best they can. Nevertheless, they—and Father Lorenzoni as well—ought to have understood better what this different power of free will and grace is which, according to Saint Augustine’s thought, God wished successively to show. It consists in this: free will, with a predestination-grace that was only conditional and that directed its movements, was capable of leading intelligent creatures to salvation, as the perseverance of the holy angels proves, but not infallibly, as the fall of Adam and the evil angels proves; whereas the grace of absolute predestination, governing the movements of free will, infallibly leads the saints of our state to salvation.

[Col. 0976B]

It is therefore not the perseverance of the holy angels alone, nor the fall of the evil angels and Adam alone, that shows the power of free will; it is both together. We now see why Saint Augustine needed to mention the angels.

I cannot conclude this article without indicating the distress caused me by these words of the theologian of Padua:

*Auxilium sine quo in statu naturae innocentis, et ratione finis supernaturalis, ad quem ordinabantur angeli et homines, tametsi esset donum Creatoris, dabatur nihilominus SECUNDUM DEBITUM, NON SECUNDUM GRATIAM; DEBEBATUR enim sive ordinationi naturae sive AEQUITATI DIVINAE JUSTITIAE, quae nullam intellectualem substantiam condere POTERAT SUIS ita nudatam muneribus, ut necessario et inevitabiliter corrueret.*

“The help without which, in the state of innocent nature and by reason of the supernatural end to which angels and human beings were ordained, although it was a gift of the Creator, was nevertheless given according to debt, not according to grace; for it was owed either to the ordering of nature or to the equity of divine justice, which could not create any intellectual substance so stripped of its gifts that it would necessarily and inevitably fall.”

I wish that a Baianist could not have been comfortable with the final sentence, and that it had instead been phrased as follows:

*quae intellectualem creaturam a se liberaliter ad statum supernaturalem elevatam non poterat suis ita nudare muneribus, ut necessario et inevitabiliter corrueret.*

“Which could not strip an intellectual creature, generously elevated by it to a supernatural state, of its gifts in such a way that it would necessarily and inevitably fall.”

I also have a scruple concerning the first sentence, which I shall state later. *Secundum debitum, non secundum gratiam* does not please me. Perhaps I am too suspicious and too delicate. I reproach myself for it, but I cannot keep myself from stating my thought candidly. It is certain that the ancient Thomists would never have spoken in this way. They all taught that sufficient help contained a real and genuine offer of efficacious help, and they would have feared asserting that the offer of efficacious help was not grace properly so called; for what is offered is not grace if the offer made of it is not grace.

[Col. 0976C]

The theologian of Padua (No. 16), before coming to his fourth reason, cannot entirely conceal the embarrassment caused him by the adverbs *prius* and *deinde*. Yet he does not appear to notice it, and in a rapid style he throws out, as though it were a thought that had escaped him in passing, the solution he has devised. Does he think to lessen the difficulty by seeming to regard it carelessly? “It is wrong,” he says, “to base a true distinction on the words *prius* and *deinde*, not to mention that they do not at all signify priority and posteriority in time, as is evident (*ut patet*), but only a succession of ideas, attention, and reflection. For,” he adds, “the perseverance of those who remain steadfast presents itself to the mind through comparison with those who fall, and the order of the two terms of this relation requires consideration of the fall to precede consideration of perseverance.”

In truth, this is too refined to have been discovered on the spot. I do not know whether Saint Augustine ever thought of it in his life. But let us suppose that he had somewhere used the adverbs *prius* and *deinde* to express, equally out of place, this stroke of profound logic: I am certain that a second reflection would have led him to erase them, all the more because Father Lorenzoni’s thought seems contrary to Saint Augustine’s metaphysics, according to which the idea of good precedes that of evil, and consequently the idea of perseverance precedes that of the fall. Is it really the natural succession of thoughts that is at issue here? Read the passage: it concerns an order that God, as sovereign master of all things, established in the life—in the state of the way—of angels and human beings: *Deum Dominumque rerum omnium . . . sic ordinasse angelorum hominumque vitam, ut in ea prius . . . et deinde*, and so forth.

[Col. 0977A]

But let us come to Father Lorenzoni’s strongest argument. It is anything but invincible, and our author most certainly has not meditated sufficiently on the passage so dear and precious to him when he calls absurd and extravagant the necessity of excluding the angels from the judgment of justice mentioned at the end of the passage. The holy doctor says that God wished to show—not after the life and state of the way, but in the life and state of the way—a judgment of justice. And in what life, in what state of the way could he have shown it? Was it with respect to the evil angels, who left the state of the way through the judgment that condemned them? Was it not rather with respect to non-predestined human beings, who, after Adam’s fall, without leaving the state of the way, are left in the mass of corruption by a judgment of justice, while the others are separated from it by the benefit of grace, in accordance with Saint Augustine’s doctrine?

These, then, are Father Lorenzoni’s proofs. Has he not well founded his principle, secured his rule, and verified his key? Let us examine the success with which he uses it. We are about to see (No. 17) a principle that contradicts the conclusions, a rule that fits nothing, a key that jams and strains every lock without opening any of them. The theologian of Padua foresaw this difficulty and remedied it with this fine axiom: The rule must not be made to fit what follows; rather, what follows must be made to fit the rule. Principles must not be clarified by conclusions; conclusions must be clarified by principles. He almost frightens us with the prospect of sacrilege if we dare dispute the meaning of his sacred canon, on the basis of what Saint Augustine added—perhaps, however, precisely to serve as its commentary. The ancient sages made fine observations about the senseless fury of a man who, making vain efforts to open his door, seized his key and bit it. But they failed to notice the injustice of this madman, who ought rather to have battered the lock. In those days no one had yet ordered all locks to be opened by keys, nor excused all keys from opening locks.

[Col. 0977B]

My view is that, in the remainder of chapter 10 of the book *On Correction and Grace*, Saint Augustine applies himself to developing this proposition: In the state of the angels and the first man, God entrusted the grace of predestination to free will in order to show what free will could do with the help of a providence that truly supplied it with actual graces for acting, but did not infallibly direct its movements. In my opinion, he begins to justify this by the example of the angels, some of whom, he says, withdrew from God by free will (*per liberum arbitrium a Domino Deo refugae facti sunt*, and so forth), while others, by that same free will, stood firm in the truth (*caeteri autem per ipsum liberum arbitrium in veritate steterunt*, and so forth). But Father Lorenzoni has the skill to insinuate his predetermining grace into the meaning he assigns to these latter words.

“Let us imagine,” he says (Nos. 18 and 19), “that Saint Augustine, instead of the term free will, had used the term life; the power of the benefit of grace would not be excluded.” Can the term free will be taken just as easily to mean life as the term life can be taken to mean the state of the way? And would Saint Augustine, who only a few lines earlier distinguishes free will from life, suddenly confuse free will with life at this point without informing his reader? On what basis? Who has ever heard of an author, a language, or, if I may say so, even a jargon in which these terms are synonymous on some occasions? And even if they were, what judicious writer, after representing two things separately, would immediately think of designating one by the same word he had used to express the other?

[Col. 0977C]

The following words are Father Lorenzoni’s great buttress:

*Refugientes ejus bonitatem, qua beati fuerunt, non potuerunt ejus effugere judicium, qua miserrimi effecti sunt.*

“By rejecting his goodness, through which they had been blessed, they could not escape his judgment, through which they were made most miserable.”

“There it is,” Father Lorenzoni exclaims, “the judgment of justice, which concerns angels as well as human beings! Why should the benefit of grace not concern them equally? Can the judgment of justice be common to both states without the benefit of grace being common to both?”

But if I wanted to make use of the right Father Lorenzoni’s example has given me, and assign to the word *judicium* whatever meaning I pleased; if I were tempted to make a compensation and restore to free will a place that the theologian of Padua has removed from it contrary to all right and reason, I would translate the final text as follows: “The evil angels, refusing God’s goodness, could not escape the fallibility of free will that they had received from God.” But no: *judicium* must mean judgment, and *liberum arbitrium* free will. One must only distinguish between the judgment exercised after life, after the state of the way, and that which, during life and during the state of the way, leaves a large part of humanity in the mass of corruption, according to Saint Augustine’s doctrine. It is this latter judgment alone that is meant in the text: *Deinde quid posset gratiae suae beneficium justitiaeque judicium?*

[Col. 0977D]

Saint Augustine continues, and what he had asserted concerning the angels in particular he now asserts concerning innocent humanity: namely, that the grace of predestination was entrusted to the power of free will. He says that if Adam had wished, he would have remained in the state of integrity and innocence in which he had been created, by the same free will whose proper use had saved the holy angels. To this Father Lorenzoni (Nos. 20 and 21) replies coldly that he adheres to his rule: his rule must not be made to fit what follows, but what follows must be made to fit his rule. This is the general and only solution to all the good difficulties he raises against himself. It returns at the proper time and at nearly equal intervals, like a kind of refrain, throughout the remainder of his dissertation.

Up to this point the holy doctor had not explicitly mentioned the grace of predestination proper to the state of the angels and that of the first man; he had merely represented their free will as entirely master of directing its own movements. Thus an inattentive reader might have imagined that the holy doctor excluded all grace from the state of Adam and the angels, although he intended to exclude only a habitual grace of absolute predestination that would govern and regulate the movements of free will so securely that eternal beatitude would be their infallible end. Therefore, to prevent or correct such a thought, he begins chapter 11 with these words: “What then? Did Adam not have grace? *Quid ergo, Adam non habuit Dei gratiam*” (Saint Augustine, book *On Correction and Grace*, chapter 11, no. 29).

[Col. 0978A]

Father Lorenzoni nevertheless flatters himself (Nos. 22 and 23) that his view is the only one on which the motive that led Saint Augustine to propose and resolve this objection can be explained. I am surprised that he neglects to insist on the fact that the holy doctor does not here join the angels to Adam, and does not say: “What then? Did Adam and the angels not have grace?” But it is clear that the difficulty that gave rise to all this discourse of Saint Augustine concerned Adam alone, and that for this reason the saint no longer speaks of the angels. In chapter 10 he had only intended to establish the principle of his answer to the difficulty stated at the beginning of that chapter. This principle consists in the fact that before sin God wished free will to direct the movements of human beings and angels, whereas in the saints of our state it is the grace of absolute predestination that directs their movements. In chapter 11 the holy doctor explains the nature both of the grace that governs the free will of the predestined of our state and of the grace that was governed by Adam’s free will.

Let us hear Father Lorenzoni. He will persuade us (No. 24) that Adam’s grace, which Saint Augustine calls great and which he declares to have been quite different from that granted to the predestined of our state, is not only the same grace that the demons had, but also the same grace resisted by all who sin, whatever their state. He will present it as a point decided by his sacred canon that the grace here compared and opposed to that grace is not proper to the predestined of our state, that the good angels received it, and that in substance it is no different in kind from the grace that obtains for a reprobate of our state a temporary holiness. He will add that this same grace was necessary to Adam to protect himself from his fall and to persevere effectively.

[Col. 0978B]

Let us nevertheless ask Saint Augustine what caused God to precede Adam with a kind of grace quite different from that which he now grants to the saints of our state. He will not think to answer us, in accordance with the principles of the theologian of Padua, that Adam did not persevere and consequently needed only a grace of possibility, without which he would not have been guilty of failing to persevere; whereas the saints of our state did persevere and consequently need the grace of action, without which one cannot suppose that they persevere. Rather, the holy doctor will answer us that the difference between the grace with which God preceded Adam and that with which he now precedes the predestined is founded, on the one hand, upon the strength of sound nature and Adam’s fortunate possession of everything capable of turning him away from sin and leading him to obedience; and, on the other hand, upon the weakness of nature corrupted by sin and the abundance of evils that expose the saints to a multitude of violent temptations.

*Ille in bonis erat, quae bonitate sui Conditoris acceperat . . . . sancti vero in hac vita ad quos pertinet liberationis haec gratia in malis sunt*, etc. (Saint Augustine, cited work).

“He was in possession of the good things that he had received through the goodness of his Creator . . . but the saints in this life, to whom this grace of deliverance pertains, are in evils,” and so forth.

How well he portrays by these expressions two different habitual graces of predestination! Because Adam was strong, a providence that confined itself to providing him with actual graces, and that did not absolutely and infallibly direct his actions, was sufficient for him; because the saints are weak, they need a more special providence, which does not merely provide them with actual graces, but absolutely and infallibly directs their actions—as a weak child needs a governess who keeps continual watch with an attentive eye over his gait, forestalls his falls, or lifts him up if he happens to fall, whereas in the vigor of adulthood one has no need of such assistance.

Let us return to Father Lorenzoni and put this question to him: Is it tolerable that Saint Augustine should allege that Adam was strong, giving as the sole reason the sufficiency of the gracious assistance he received, if that assistance was not sufficient for him to act effectively, if that assistance is the same as the sufficient assistance of our state, and if it is opposed to the efficacious assistance necessary for acting in every kind of state? Is it tolerable that Saint Augustine should allege that the saints of our state are weak, giving as the sole reason their need of another, more powerful kind of grace, if, supposing that they were not weak but very strong, this same kind of grace would still have been necessary for them, and if this same kind of grace was necessary for the angels, who were not weak but very strong? The reply of the theologian of Padua is too curious not to be postponed for a little while.

Beforehand, he wishes to point out to us (No. 25) that, in the book *On Correction and Grace*, Saint Augustine does not deign to call by the name of grace the assistance necessary for being able to act, when compared with that necessary for acting. But he must seek his proofs elsewhere than in this book. Adam had grace; he did not have the benefit of grace. Does this mean that the actual grace Adam had was not a benefit? No—much as Father Lorenzoni may dislike it—but it means that, in Adam’s state, perseverance would not have been the benefit of the grace of absolute predestination, although it would have been the benefit of actual grace.

Finally, the author of the *Dissertation* (No. 26), in order to prepare us to receive his answer with applause, presents himself as delighted by the alleged evidence of his explanations. He appeals to good faith, common sense, and the most rigorous criticism. Yet it is quite evident that the adversaries whom he attacks are wrong, and that he himself is not right; that he throws them into difficulty and remains there himself. For here, finally, is what he serves us.

To understand why Saint Augustine, on the one hand, alleges Adam’s strength and, on the other, the weakness of the saints of our state when speaking of the various forms of gracious assistance, one need only perceive that the holy doctor compares the grace now granted to the predestined not only with the grace Adam received, but also with that which he would have received had he persevered. “Whoever does not see this,” says Father Lorenzoni, “does not wish to see it”: *Quis non videat, nisi qui videre nolit?*

Let us therefore try not to be willfully blind, and let us understand with Father Lorenzoni that the holy doctor first says that Adam received a very great grace, but one different from that which he grants to the predestined of our state: *Quid ergo Adam non habuit Dei gratiam? Imo vero habuit magnam, sed disparem*—“What then, did Adam not have God’s grace? On the contrary, he had a great grace, but a different one.” And thereafter, let us not expect Saint Augustine to take the trouble to show why there is a difference between the grace Adam received and that which the predestined now receive. Let us instead suppose that he leaves aside for a long time the grace Adam received and that, without giving his readers the slightest warning, he spends nearly eighty lines showing why a grace Adam did not receive, but would have received had he persevered, would have been different from the grace now received by the predestined. For finally, when we least expect it, the holy doctor, without having distinguished the grace Adam did not receive from that which he did receive, will begin to explain what grounds the difference between the grace Adam received and that which the predestined now receive. I do not know how the following thought escaped Father Lorenzoni: namely, that after the words *imo vero habuit magnam*—“on the contrary, he had a great one”—everything that follows should be enclosed in a parenthesis of fairly considerable length, extending to the further words *istam gratiam non habuit primus homo, qua nunquam vellet esse malus*—“the first man did not have that grace by which he would never have wished to be evil.”

I shall pass over the arguments Father Lorenzoni makes afterward (Nos. 27–29). They are triumphant, but only on the supposition that it is impossible for both him and the adversaries he attacks to depart equally from Saint Augustine’s meaning. This is precisely what our author ought to have suspected when confronted with the difficulties that counterbalance his triumph.

He proposes the following difficulty (Nos. 30–31). Saint Augustine says:

> “Adam could therefore have remained, if he had wished, because God had given him assistance by which he could, and without which he could not, steadfastly retain the good that he wished to retain: *Posset ergo permanere, si vellet, quia dederat ei adjutorium per quod posset, et sine quo non posset bonum perseveranter tenere quod vellet*” (Saint Augustine, *On Correction and Grace*, chap. 11, no. 32).

The holy doctor adds:

> “But because he did not wish to remain, it was certainly his fault; whereas it would have been his merit if he had wished to remain, as the holy angels did, who, when the others fell through free choice, stood firm by that same free choice, and merited to receive the due reward of that steadfastness: *Sed quia noluit permanere, profecto ejus culpa fuit, cujus meritum fuisset, si permanere voluisset, sicut fecerunt angeli sancti, qui cadentibus aliis per liberum arbitrium, per idem liberum arbitrium steterunt ipsi, et hujus mansionis debitam mercedem recipere meruerunt*” (ibid.).

Saint Augustine therefore asserts that the holy angels persevered by the same free choice by which the evil angels and Adam fell. The word “by” obviously attributes perseverance to free choice just as it does the fall; and the word “same” can indicate nothing other than that, in both groups, free choice had been preceded by the same grace—that is, according to Father Lorenzoni’s adversaries, the same actual and versatile grace, and, according to me, the same habitual grace of predestination, which left the direction of their actions to free choice. How does Father Lorenzoni escape from this? He does not dare repeat what he said above: that the expression “by the same free choice” is equivalent to “in the same life” or “in the same state.” He contents himself with resorting to the convenient evasion he prepared for himself by establishing that his rule should not be adjusted to what follows, but that what follows should be adjusted to his rule. He may say what he likes; his forced adjustments condemn his rule, which is demonstrably false in itself.

The extreme partiality our author seems to show toward his Baianist adversaries leads him to find (No. 32) a difficulty equal to the preceding one in the words concerning Adam, *cujus meritum fuisset, si permanere voluisset*—“whose merit it would have been, had he wished to remain”—and in those concerning the angels, *cujus mansionis debitam mercedem recipere meruerunt*—“they merited to receive the due reward of that steadfastness.” “It is claimed,” he says, “that the terms *meritum* and *merces* evidently designate versatile grace. That is a mistake: they signify grace efficacious in itself, which would have been given to Adam on the supposition that he had persevered, and which was given to the holy angels who did persevere.”

But Saint Augustine intends these expressions only to convey the difference between the purely free choice Adam possessed and the choice liberated by the grace of Jesus Christ, which the predestined now possess. Such is the substance of Father Lorenzoni’s reply, which seems to concede to the Baianists that, according to Saint Augustine’s thought, good works would have been more properly merits, and heavenly glory more properly a reward, in the state of innocence than in the state of restored nature.

Yet the doctrine of the Church, in conformity with that of Saint Augustine, is that the good works of the state of innocence and those of our state are, in the same sense, properly called merits, and at the same time gifts of God. For the elevation of rational nature to divine adoption—the foundation of the Creator’s graces and of the good works of the state of innocence—is a gratuitous benefit distinct from the grace of creation, just as the restoration of human nature—the foundation of the Redeemer’s graces and of the good works of our state—is also distinct from it. The former was a pure act of liberality added to nature, just as the latter is a pure act of mercy.

This is supported by the condemnation of the first proposition of Baius and by canon 23 of the sixth session of the holy Council of Trent. There we see it decided that the good works of the state of innocence, which are acknowledged to have been properly merits, nevertheless remained gifts of God; and that the good works of our state, which are acknowledged to be gifts of God, nevertheless remain properly merits. Is the Church not more certain that it has correctly understood her tradition when pronouncing in this manner than heretics are certain that they have understood Saint Augustine’s meaning, which they presumptuously oppose to the teachings of the Bride of Jesus Christ? Examination of the two following passages will show how greatly they have deceived themselves.

The first passage that will detain us for some time with Father Lorenzoni (No. 33 and following) is this:

> “If this assistance had been lacking to either an angel or a man when they were first made, since their nature had not been made such that they could remain, if they wished, without divine assistance, they would certainly not have fallen through their own fault. For the assistance without which they could not remain would have been lacking. But now, for those who lack such assistance, it is already the punishment of sin; while for those to whom it is given, it is given according to grace, not according to debt; and it is given all the more abundantly through Jesus Christ our Lord to those to whom God has been pleased to give it, so that not only the assistance without which we cannot remain, even if we wish, may be present, but also assistance so great and of such a kind that we may wish to remain, and so forth” (Saint Augustine, as cited above).

One must concede to the Baianists that Saint Augustine, here contrasting the assistance *sine quo non*—“without which one cannot”—of the state of innocence with the assistance *quo*—“by which”—of our state, says of the latter that it is not owed but given by grace. But they must be disputed on two points.

First, the word *debitum*—“debt” or “what is owed”—does not signify something demanded by rational nature as a consequence of creation. It signifies only something demanded by the elevation of nature to the dignity of God’s adopted children, with which angel and man were honored from the moment of their creation.

Second, one must dispute with the Baianists whether this distinction between the two forms of assistance, established by Saint Augustine, applies to the actual grace proper to the two states. For, if we consider actual grace from the standpoint of Adam and the angels, who were unworthy of it only negatively, and from that of human beings in our state, who are positively unworthy of it because the former were created in innocence whereas the latter are born guilty, one may indeed say that the former were not as unworthy of actual grace as the latter. But one cannot say—even by way of comparison—that it was owed to them, without confusing nature with grace and at least introducing a proportion between them.

It is not under this aspect that actual grace should be considered when one maintains, in a proper sense, that it was owed to Adam and the angels. Such language is verified not by considering the recipients to whom grace is given, but by considering the idea of its author, from whom it comes. Grace is then regarded as a consequence and dependence of God’s liberality, by which he elevated nature to a supernatural state and, as a consequence of that elevation, required supernatural actions from Adam and the angels. That is, God owed actual grace not properly to Adam and the angels, but to the order established by his liberality, and to his justice, which did not permit him to require supernatural actions without a supernatural assistance that would make them possible.

Now, if the question is to compare the actual grace of our state with the actual grace of Adam and the angels, insofar as the latter was owed in the manner I have just explained, it is clear that we must not return to considering the recipients of grace. We must consider only the grace of our state as a consequence and dependence of God’s mercy, by which he restored nature through Jesus Christ and, as a consequence of that restoration, requires supernatural actions in our state.

That being so, I ask: Was God more indebted to the order that his liberality had established by pure grace than he is to the order that his mercy, also by pure grace, has restored? Does his justice permit him more readily to require supernatural actions from us without giving or offering us the actual grace that assists us in producing them as a consequence of the restoration of nature than that same justice permitted him to act in this way toward Adam and the angels as a consequence of the elevation of nature? The question is not whether we are more unworthy of God’s mercy than Adam was of his liberality, but whether the liberality shown to Adam constituted a stronger obligation to grant actual grace than the mercy shown to all human beings by virtue of Jesus Christ’s universal redemption; whether God was more bound by a decree of goodness that honored innocent man and angel with a gift to which their nature had no right to lay claim than he is bound by a decree of clemency that restores to fallen man, who has incurred his displeasure, the privilege of aspiring to that same gift.

Certainly, just as the distribution of actual graces necessary for the possibility of the supernatural actions that God requires before and after the fall of man was liberality and justice toward Adam, so it is mercy and justice toward us. But justice is the same on both sides, since this justice has as its object not what belongs to innocent or guilty man, but a covenant with Adam, a covenant with Jesus Christ, and promises to which God is no less faithful whether they were dictated by liberality or by mercy.

If the Baianists improperly cite Saint Augustine to prove, in their erroneous sense, that actual grace was owed to innocent man and angel, we shall cite Holy Scripture more appropriately to prove, in the Catholic sense, that actual grace is owed to all human beings insofar as they have been redeemed by the blood of Jesus Christ: *Quid est quod ultra debui facere vineae meae et non feci ei?*—“What more was there to do for my vineyard that I have not done for it?” (Isaiah 5:4).

What, then, is this grace of our state that Saint Augustine regards as not owed in any sense, when comparing it with another grace of Adam’s state? It is absolute predestination, which is a habitual grace, and the true assistance *quo*. For this grace is not contained within the generality of redemption; rather, it is a special application of the benefit of redemption to a small number of the elect.

What is this grace of Adam’s state that the holy doctor considers to have been owed, when comparing it with another grace of our state? It is conditional predestination, which the elevation of sound nature required, and the true assistance *sine quo non*. For this grace was contained in the elevation of nature, at a time when there was no mass of corruption in which God left some while drawing others out of it.

I am glad to point out in passing that Saint Augustine’s system of predestination is not as harsh as it appears at first glance. If one meditates upon it, weighs the saint’s expressions, and brings together all the passages in which he discusses it, one will find that this system is not incompatible with the true, universal, antecedent, and conditional will of God to save all human beings—a will that Saint Augustine acknowledged. For one does not understand the substance of Semipelagianism when one objects that the holy doctor appears in certain places to restrict this statement of the Apostle: “God wills all men to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4).

This same system of absolute predestination is not as different as people imagine from what was taught by all the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, who preceded Saint Augustine and who nevertheless admitted consequent predestination. I shall have occasion to develop all this in the examination I hope to undertake of the arguments by which M. Bayle tried to strengthen Manichaeism.

But let us not so quickly leave the passage of Saint Augustine under examination, for Father Lorenzoni makes use of it elsewhere in a manner that follows from his misunderstanding of it here. On the authority of these words, *Nunc autem quibus deest tale adjutorium jam poena peccati est*—“But now, for those who lack such assistance, it is already the punishment of sin”—he seriously tells us that no gracious assistance has been prepared for children who die without baptism, and he does not doubt that Saint Augustine’s authority makes his opinion respectable. “I would consider it a crime,” he says, “to depart in the slightest degree from this divine man.”

What! Without regard for the Apostle’s words, *Si unus pro omnibus mortuus est, ergo omnes mortui sunt*—“If one died for all, then all died” (2 Corinthians 5:14)? Saint Augustine himself uses this reasoning of Saint Paul to prove that all human beings without exception died in Adam, *nemine prorsus excepto*—“with absolutely no one excepted” (Saint Augustine, *The City of God*, book 20, chap. 6).

In particular, he maintains that all children are born with original sin, because one cannot deny that they are all included in the Apostle’s statement when he says that Jesus Christ died for all human beings: *A morte quae in peccato est, parvulos non ostendis immunes, quia et pro eis Christum mortuum negare non audes*—“You do not show infants to be exempt from the death that is in sin, since you do not dare deny that Christ died for them as well” (*Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 2, no. 174).

Indeed, the reasoning is null and frivolous unless the sacred author and the divine man assume as an incontestable truth that Jesus Christ died for all human beings and all children without exception, *nemine prorsus excepto*. Now, if one must consider it a crime to depart ever so slightly from the divine man, should one not at least have a scruple about departing so far from the sacred author as interpreted by the divine man?

Both teach us a mystery of mercy that confounds our reason, because we do not understand how, by virtue of the Savior’s death, God has provided for the salvation of all children who die without baptism. I adore it and believe it. But mysteries of justice, in which reason is no less confounded, are more to Father Lorenzoni’s taste; he likes to multiply them.

If, however, he based his opinion only on the authority of these words—*Nunc autem quibus deest tale adjutorium, jam poena peccati est*—it would be easy to make him abandon it. Let a Baianist maintain to him that these words must be understood of all human beings in our state who fall into sin, and that, according to Saint Augustine’s thought, the grace of possibility is lacking to all who violate the commandments. How will he defend himself?

Will it be by the following words, in which he thinks he sees the assistance *sine quo non* granted to some people in our state: *quibus autem datur, secundum gratiam datur, non secundum debitum*—“but for those to whom it is given, it is given according to grace, not according to debt”? He will be answered that he should look more closely and that it is evident that this latter passage concerns the assistance *sine quo non* joined to the assistance *quo*, and insofar as it is contained in the assistance *quo*. The continuation proves it:

> *Et tanto amplius datur per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum, quibus id Deo dare placuit, ut non solum adsit sine quo manere non possumus, verum etiam tantum ac tale sit ut velimus.*

“And it is given all the more abundantly through Jesus Christ our Lord to those to whom God has been pleased to give it, so that not only the assistance without which we cannot remain may be present, but also assistance so great and of such a kind that we may wish to remain.”

All those, says Saint Augustine, to whom God has now been pleased to give the assistance *sine quo non* receive it so abundantly and perfectly that they have not merely the assistance necessary to enable them to persevere, but assistance so great and of such a kind that they actually persevere. Could he have said more clearly that, in our state, the assistance *sine quo non* is not given without the assistance *quo*?

To confound the Baianist, one must point out to him that Saint Augustine attributes the assistance *quo* only to the predestined and describes it as a habit. Consequently, it is the habitual grace of absolute predestination, and not what is ordinarily meant by efficacious grace—which is a transitory action and is not denied to many of the reprobate.

The assistance *sine quo non* opposed to the assistance *quo* is the habitual grace of the proper predestination of Adam’s state, which was not absolute but conditional. Finally, the assistance *sine quo non* which, in our state, is inseparable from the assistance *quo* is the habitual grace of absolute predestination. It eminently contains conditional predestination, insofar as perseverance itself includes, and surpasses, the power to persevere that Adam possessed: namely, that perseverance in which one remains and which one does not abandon—a continuation and concatenation of actions, the last of which infallibly reaches the heavenly crown.

It follows that one cannot conclude from this testimony of the holy doctor that sufficient grace is lacking to anyone, but only that not everyone is predestined.

The other passage by which I promised to show that Saint Augustine advanced nothing that weakens the merits of the good works of our state in order to elevate those of the state of innocence is the following:

> *Nunc autem per peccatum perdito bono, merito in his qui liberantur factum est donum gratiae, quae merces meriti futura erat.*

“But now, the good having been lost through sin, what would have been the reward of merit has rightly become, in those who are delivered, a gift of grace.”

The only error—I mean a blunder, not a heresy or anything approaching one, God forbid!—the only error, I say, that led people to take the two forms of assistance, *quo* and *sine quo non*, for actual graces, had the power to persuade them that in this passage Saint Augustine, contrasting the good works of Adam’s state with those of ours, called the former merits and the latter gifts of grace.

But the holy doctor speaks only of one thing which, in the state of innocence, was a merit, and in the present state is a pure gift of grace: the privilege of being led to a happy end. For suppose that Adam had persevered, and compare him with a righteous person in our state who perseveres. All the good works of both would equally have been merits and gifts of God. But since Adam’s free choice directed his actions, being led to a happy end would have been a particular merit for him; whereas, since the habitual grace of absolute predestination directs the actions of the righteous person in our state, being led to a happy end is a pure gift of grace.

We have now arrived with our author (Nos. 36–37) at chapter 12 of *On Correction and Grace*, where Saint Augustine admirably represents the two kinds of predestination by comparing one to food and the other to blessedness (Saint Augustine, *On Correction and Grace*, chap. 12, no. 34).

Nevertheless, one must acknowledge that the comparison is neither complete nor perfect. The assistance *quo* causes one to persevere, and the assistance *sine quo non* gives one the power to persevere. But one cannot similarly say that blessedness makes one happy and that food gives one the power to be happy. Saint Augustine does not make such a proposition; rather, he expresses himself as follows:

> “Blessedness makes one happy, and food gives one the power not to die.”

“What an observation!” someone will say. “How childish!” Father Lorenzoni does not permit me to omit it. He seriously supposes that the holy doctor compares perseverance and the power to persevere with blessedness and the power to be happy. On this he bases a reasoning that he considers insurmountable: a man who has food is not actually happy without blessedness; therefore Adam, who had the assistance *sine quo non*, needed the assistance *quo* in order to persevere effectively.

Let it be judged whether the theologian of Padua has reason to admire the force of his logic and to exclaim in triumphant enthusiasm:

> “After so true, so solid, so certain a decision, where, I ask you, is versatile grace? Where is the much-vaunted distinction between the two forms of assistance? It has collapsed, been ruined, overturned, crushed, and thrown to the ground!”

For my part, I say: Where is Cicero’s *abiit, excessit, evasit, erupit*—“he has gone away, departed, escaped, burst forth”? It has been eclipsed, tarnished, and effaced.

Seriously speaking, our author ought to find more reasonable than he does the objection supplied against him by these words:

> *Major quippe libertas est necessaria adversus tot tantasque tentationes, quae in paradiso non fuerunt, dono perseverantiae munita atque firmata, ut cum omnibus terroribus, erroribus, amoribus suis vincatur hic mundus.*

“For a greater freedom is necessary against so many and such great temptations as did not exist in paradise; it must be fortified and strengthened by the gift of perseverance, so that this world, with all its terrors, errors, and desires, may be conquered” (Saint Augustine, ibid., no. 35).

I ask: Why is the assistance *quo* now necessary for the predestined? Saint Augustine answers: because they must conquer the terrors, errors, and desires by which they are continually assailed in this miserable life.

“Add,” says Father Lorenzoni, “that in order to act and to persevere effectively, the assistance *quo*, which is the grace of action, is necessary.”

I ask again: Why was the assistance *quo* not given to Adam? The holy doctor’s answer is that, in the earthly paradise, Adam was not exposed to the multitude of great and violent temptations that we experience.

“That is not the principal reason,” Father Lorenzoni replies. “Adam merely had the power to persevere; he did not in fact persevere, and consequently needed only the assistance *sine quo non*, which is the grace of possibility.”

But, I say to Father Lorenzoni, Saint Augustine has already repeated the same thing several times, and you are continually obliged to correct him. Show me at least that he declares once that, even if the saints were as strong as Adam, they would still need the assistance *quo*. But you will not succeed.

The holy doctor continues to speak in the same vein:

> *Ut ergo non acciperet hoc donum Dei, id est in bono perseverantiam, primus homo, sed perseverare vel non perseverare in ejus relinqueretur arbitrio, tales vires habebat ejus voluntas . . . . nunc vero posteaquam est illa magna peccati merito amissa libertas, etiam majoribus donis adjuvanda remansit infirmitas.*

“Thus, so that the first man would not receive this gift of God—that is, perseverance in the good—but that persevering or not persevering would be left to his choice, his will possessed such strength . . . . But now, after that great freedom was lost through the merit of sin, weakness remains, to be assisted by still greater gifts” (Saint Augustine, ibid., no. 37).

Who does not see in these words the resolution of the difficulty Saint Augustine posed for himself at the beginning of chapter 10? Adam was guilty for not persevering, although he had not received the special gift of habitual perseverance, which is the grace of absolute predestination. He did not need that grace because he was strong, whereas we need it because we are weak. For he had, moreover, received a great grace, namely conditional predestination, and a true power to persevere; entrusted to the direction of his free choice, this would have enabled him, had he wished, to merit actual perseverance.

Can I be mistaken in making this interpretation? Is it not clearly confirmed by the following passage?

> *Subventum est ergo infirmitati voluntatis humanae, ut divina gratia indeclinabiliter et inseparabiliter ageretur.*

“Thus assistance was given to the weakness of the human will, so that it might be acted upon by divine grace unfailingly and inseparably” (ibid., no. 38).

What do these words mean if they do not express the inevitable and inseparable attachment of a habitual grace to guide us, because we are too weak to guide ourselves? Does Saint Augustine stop there? No; he seems to have wished to force every Lorenzoni in the world to understand him better, despite their prejudices. He adds:

> *Fortissimo quippe dimisit atque permisit facere quod vellet; infirmis servavit ut ipso donante invictissime quod bonum est vellent; nec hoc deserere invictissime nollent.*

“To the very strong he left and permitted the doing of what they wished; for the weak he reserved this: that, by his own gift, they should most invincibly will what is good, and should most invincibly not will to abandon it” (ibid.).

This last passage must be considered attentively. *Fortissimo dimisit atque permisit facere quod vellet*—“To the very strong he left and permitted the doing of what they wished”: what other terms could the holy doctor have chosen to express more effectively a power which, on God’s part, possesses everything necessary to be brought into act?

*Infirmis servavit*, and so forth. What could be clearer in marking that the assistance *quo* was not necessary for Adam’s effective perseverance, but was reserved for the saints of our state precisely and solely because of their weakness?

In this connection, I may be permitted to relate a story that bears directly on the matter. It may, if one wishes, be taken as a parable intended to make clear the language Saint Augustine is supposed to use in the three famous chapters.

I knew a merchant from Calais who never stated the true reason for what people saw him do. He had two sons, and he had taken the younger one to England. His friends there asked him why he had not given the elder the satisfaction of accompanying him and making the same journey.

He replied that the elder was such a vigorous and robust boy that, if there had been a bridge from Calais to Dover, he would gladly have walked across it and would not have been inconvenienced in the least. But the younger was so delicate that, after half a league, he would have been unable to walk and would have remained on the bridge; besides, he could not tolerate any vehicle on land. “That is why,” he added, “I had this one board the vessel with me.”

This example may serve Father Lorenzoni, who ought to think that the assistance *quo* was necessary for Adam and for the saints of our state in order to persevere, just as the vessel was necessary for both brothers to cross from Calais to Dover; and that, just as the vessel would have been necessary for the younger brother even under the fanciful hypothesis of a bridge, so the assistance *quo* would still be necessary for us even on the supposition that the assistance *sine quo non* had been sufficient for Adam.

All that remains is to determine whether it is appropriate to make Saint Augustine speak in the manner of this merchant.

That is enough. It would be useless for me to linger over all the conclusions Father Lorenzoni draws from his explanation and his rule. But I cannot refrain, in closing, from doing him justice and declaring the impression his work has given me of his character.

I believe I see in it a piety and a religious foundation that are neither affected nor contrived; a search for truth and an uprightness that are likewise not put on for show; and a charity and love of peace of the same character. Quite unlike many authors whose devout and softened tone never imposed upon me, he portrays the good qualities of his heart in natural colors, wholly unborrowed.

As for his intellect, it is firm and consistent, sensitive to difficulty. Despite the partiality he displays toward his own inventions, one can feel that he is satisfied with them only provisionally and until something better is presented to him. His affirmative tone concerns only the adversaries he attacks, and he is entitled to be confident that he has destroyed their system.

In a word, the defects I have observed in his work belong to the principles by which he allowed himself to be prejudiced, and not to him at all:

[Col. 0989]

## SECOND TREATISE. EXAMINATION OF THE CRITICISMS SCATTERED THROUGH M. BAYLE’S DICTIONARY CONCERNING VARIOUS PASSAGES IN THE WRITINGS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE.

[Col. 0989] I waited in vain for several days for the licentiate, who had promised to return. I had time to write down both the entire comparison I had made in his presence between the doctrine of Saint Augustine and [Col. 0990] that of Jansenius, and the reflections that had occurred to me concerning the other reproaches with which M. Bayle charges the holy doctor.

First Part. Examination of the reproach that M. Bayle makes against Saint Augustine, of having lapsed into laxity in morals.

[Col. 0989]

I.

[Col. 0989A]

I began with the article on Acyndinus, a man of consular rank and governor of Syria, whose name found a place in M. Bayle’s Dictionary only to provide a pretext for a little anecdote of the sort that, in the author’s judgment, deserves to be reported.

A woman, in order to obtain the means of buying back her husband’s life, thought she ought to make use of the permission he gave her to yield to the desires of another man. Saint Augustine relates the incident; all the circumstances of his narration are carefully collected by M. Bayle and presented with the turn of phrase that this critic knows how to give to such matters. Yet one would think that he intended only to edify, and that he sought merely to avenge sound morality against the laxity into which Saint Augustine appears to him to have fallen on this occasion. Thus M. Bayle has not handed Saint Augustine over entirely to the Jansenists without also placing him at the head of the accommodating casuists. There they all are, united under the same leader; they have only to join hands.

According to our critic, “Saint Augustine does not dare decide whether this woman’s conduct is good or bad, and he inclines much more toward approving than condemning it—which is rather astonishing.”

It is utterly contrary to all likelihood that Saint Augustine should call into question whether adultery is permissible in order to preserve a husband’s life, he who decides without hesitation that lying is forbidden even if it were a matter of rescuing a father from death: *Nunquam pro cujusquam temporali vita mentiendum est*—“One must never lie for anyone’s temporal life.” It is manifestly incredible that the holy doctor should be indulgent toward sins against purity when they have become the sole means of preventing a man from perishing here below, he who does not wish modesty to be violated even to procure for one’s neighbor salvation itself and eternal life: *Cum veritas doceat nec propter hominem baptizandum facere quod est contrarium castitati* ( *On Lying*, chap. 6, no. 9)—“Since truth teaches that, even for the sake of baptizing a man, one must not do what is contrary to chastity”; that he should be less scrupulous about impurity than about lying, and should value a man’s life less than truth and more than purity, he [Col. 0990A] who is content not merely to prove that it is an absurd and criminal thing to corrupt one’s soul by lying so that another may enjoy bodily life, but who offers as his principal reason that, in everyone’s judgment, it is an infamous and criminal thing to surrender one’s body to impure acts for the sake of a similar act of charity: *Absurdum et nefarium est cur animam suam quisque mendacio corrumpat, ut alter vivat in corpore, cum si suum corpus propterea corrumpendum daret, omnium judicio nefariae turpitudinis damnaretur* ( *On Lying*, chap. 6, no. 15)—“It is absurd and wicked for anyone to corrupt his soul by lying so that another may live in the body, since, if he were to surrender his own body to corruption for that purpose, everyone would judge him guilty of abominable disgrace.”

But, someone will say to me, do you want us to blind ourselves so as not to see, in the two passages cited by M. Bayle, the scandalous doubt that this critic has so opportunely brought to light? It is irrelevant what Saint Augustine may have said or thought elsewhere.

The reasons M. Bayle alleges to show that this doubt is rather astonishing, and those by which I have just demonstrated that it is altogether too astonishing, are [Col. 0990B] strong enough, if necessary, to appeal from the printed text to the manuscripts; and, if the manuscripts agreed with it, to disavow them all—unless it could be verified that some of these manuscripts were written by Saint Augustine’s own hand. This means, at the very least, that however determined M. Bayle may have been not to spare Saint Augustine, the sound judgment, knowledge of religion, and moral rigor that must be recognized in this holy doctor ought to have induced our Aristarchus not to read too hastily the two passages he cites, and to make quite sure that he understood them before pronouncing judgment.
