Rivet, a Protestant theologian, had criticized Saint Augustine’s supposed doubt before Bayle (*Exercitation* 73 on Genesis); but he had maintained that this Father inclined more toward condemning than justifying the woman who prostituted her modesty in order to save her husband’s life. Bayle does not see what grounds Rivet has for this, and believes he decisively refutes him by the holy doctor’s text [Col. 0990C], which he has certainly understood even less than Rivet.

Saint Augustine asks whether the Apostle’s words, *Mulier non habet potestatem sui corporis, sed vir; similiter et vir non habet potestatem sui corporis, sed mulier* (1 Cor. 7:4)—“The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the man; likewise, the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman”—should be understood in such a way that a man may, with his wife’s permission, have intercourse with another woman who has no husband. He replies that they should not: *sed non est ita existimandum*—“but it must not be understood in this way”—lest it appear, he adds, that a woman too might have the right to use a similar liberty with her husband’s permission: *Ne hoc etiam femina viro permittente facere posse videatur* (Saint Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book I, chap. 16, no. 49, etc.). Rivet and Bayle have failed to understand what follows: *Quod omnium sensus excludit* (ibid.)—“which everyone’s natural feeling rules out.” Saint Augustine means that it is not contrary to natural law for a man to have intercourse with two women, just as it is contrary to natural law for a woman to have intercourse with two men; nevertheless, if the Apostle’s words were understood in such a way that a man could, with his wife’s permission, have intercourse with another woman, it would follow from those same words that a woman could also, with her husband’s permission, have intercourse [Col. 0991B] with another man—which is contrary to natural law. Consequently, the Apostle’s text restricts the husband to approaching only his wife, and the wife to approaching only her husband.

Saint Augustine then raises this objection: *Quanquam nonnullae causae possint existere, ubi et uxor mariti consensu, pro ipso marito hoc facere debere videatur, sicut et Antiochiae factum est, etc.* (Saint Augustine, ibid.)—“Although some circumstances might arise in which a wife might seem obliged, with her husband’s consent, to do this for the husband himself, as also happened at Antioch, etc.” Rivet and Bayle, for failing to penetrate the meaning of the words *Quod omnium sensus excludit*, believed that the holy doctor was proposing an exception to the evangelical law, which commands a man to look only to his wife and a woman only to her husband. In fact, he is speaking only of natural law, which he had invoked to support his interpretation of Saint Paul’s words; and he raises, in the form of a doubt or question, whether natural law—which requires a woman to concern herself with preserving her husband’s life—might not prevail over the law that forbids her, even with her husband’s permission, to yield to another man’s desires.

The question, therefore, is not whether the woman of Antioch acted rightly or wrongly, nor whether she sinned against the evangelical law. It is absurd to think so, and the continuation of the text does not permit us to believe that Saint Augustine presented this as a problem. The difficulty concerns solely the inner law revealed to everyone by natural feeling, *Quod omnium sensus excludit*—“which everyone’s natural feeling rules out.” Saint Augustine asks whether the voice that declares the Creator’s commands in the depths of every human heart ought to protest against this woman’s act. This is the point on which he says that he takes no position, and that he leaves each person to believe whatever he wishes: *Nihil hinc in aliquam partem disputo, licet cuique aestimare quod velit*—“I argue nothing here for either side; each person may judge as he wishes.” If the incident had been taken from the sacred history of the Old Testament, he would have considered himself obliged to decide: *Non enim de divinis auctoritatibus deprompta historia est*—“For this is not a history drawn from divine authorities.”

It is not even certain that the incident took place among Christians; for Saint Augustine does not say that this woman had been instructed by Scripture. It is M. Bayle alone who asserts this. The holy doctor simply says that she knew that her body was not under her own power, but under her husband’s.

Let us now examine the words by which it appears manifestly to M. Bayle that Saint Augustine inclines much more toward approving than condemning this woman’s act: *Sed tamen narrato hoc facto, non ita respuit hic sensus humanus quod in illa muliere viro jubente commissum est, quemadmodum antea, cum sine ullo exemplo res ipsa poneretur, horruimus.* Here is the translation: “Nevertheless, once this incident has been related in this way, judged by natural and human feeling, the act committed by this woman at her husband’s command does not revolt us as much as it did earlier, when we spoke of the matter in general and without setting it in this example.” Saint Augustine not only does not incline to approve this woman’s act; he does not even incline to believe that it is not contrary to natural law. He merely gives an opinion by comparison, saying that outside this example the matter is horrifying, whereas in this example it does not revolt us as much.

I am not yet finished. M. Bayle raises another passage from Saint Augustine. “Elsewhere,” he says, “this Father calls into question whether a woman’s chastity would lose its integrity if, for her husband’s life and at his command, she were to lie”—that is the term M. Bayle uses—“with another man: *Quanquam scrupulosius disputari possit, utrum illius mulieris pudicitia violaretur, etiamsi quisquam carni ejus commixtus foret, cum id in se fieri pro mariti vita nec illo nesciente sed jubente permitteret, nequaquam fidem deserens conjugalem, et potestatem non abnuens maritalem* (Book XX against Faustus, chap. 37)—“Although it may be debated more scrupulously whether that woman’s chastity would be violated, even if someone had intercourse with her body, since, for her husband’s life, she allowed this to be done to herself, not without his knowledge but at his command, in no way abandoning conjugal fidelity or rejecting marital authority.” Yet by that very passage, which M. Bayle believes provides such wonderful support for the censure he dares to direct against Saint Augustine, I clearly demonstrate the soundness and truth of the explanation I have used to justify the holy doctor.

The subject of his discourse here is not a woman in general, but Sarah, Abraham’s wife. Saint Augustine asks whether her chastity would have been violated if, in order to save her husband’s life and at his command, she had passed into the arms of Abimelech or Pharaoh—just as Abraham himself did not commit adultery when, submitting to Sarah’s will, he consented to father a child by Hagar, his slave: *Sicut ille adulter non fuit, quando uxoris obtemperans potestati, de ancilla prolem generare consensit* (Saint Augustine, ibid.)—“Just as he was not an adulterer when, obeying his wife’s authority, he consented to beget offspring by a slave-woman.” Saint Augustine resolves the question he had posed by saying that natural law forbids a woman to have several husbands, but does not forbid a man to have several wives; consequently, Abraham may have been permitted to have a concubine—that is, in the language of Scripture, a secondary wife—but Sarah could not have been permitted to take a second husband in addition to Abraham: *Sed propter vim principiorum, quia non ita duobus viris ad concumbendum femina una subditur, sicut duae feminae uno viro, multo verius et honestius illud accipimus, etc.* (Saint Augustine, ibid.)—“But because of the force of the principles involved, since one woman is not subjected to two men for intercourse in the same way that two women are subjected to one man, we accept that interpretation as much more true and honorable, etc.”

Is it not evident from the answer that the question concerned natural law? And from the subject of the question, that it is an act of infidelity to represent it as universal and applicable even to the time of the evangelical law? And finally, from Saint Augustine’s decision regarding Sarah, that this Father did not doubt whether the conduct of the woman of Antioch was good or bad, and that he did not hesitate to condemn it, far from inclining to justify it?

It would be rather amusing if M. Bayle made Saint Augustine apply strict morality to a virtuous woman of the Old Testament, and lax morality to a woman of the New Testament who does not appear to have possessed such pure virtue. The case is exactly the same: it concerns saving a husband’s life. What Sarah, in this situation, could not have done without committing a crime, according to Saint Augustine—would the woman of Antioch have committed innocently, according to that same Father?

II.

Under the article “Saint AUGUSTINE,” two noteworthy matters are found. The first is contained in these words: “If these gentlemen—Moreri and Du Pin—had not passed so lightly over Saint Augustine’s dissolute life, I could have dispensed entirely with this article. But, for the public’s greater instruction, it is good to make great men known on both sides.” I have recognized and verified this on every occasion: M. Bayle certainly makes the holy Fathers known on their unfavorable side; but he means that we, who are their children, must not pass lightly over, or draw a veil over, whatever may have dishonored their lives. He speaks in the same spirit that led him to provide us with the apology of Ham.

The second matter is M. Bayle’s presentation of the physician M. Petit’s interpretation of a passage in Saint Augustine’s *Confessions*, and of the way in which M. President Cousin refuted M. Petit. Here is the passage:

*Ebrietas longe est a me: misereberis ne appropinquet mihi. Crapula autem nonnunquam surrepit servo tuo; misereberis, ut longe fiat a me* (Saint Augustine, *Confessions*, book X, chap. 31)—“Drunkenness is far from me; have mercy that it may not come near me. But *crapula* sometimes steals upon your servant; have mercy that it may be far from me.”

“Drunkenness,” says M. Petit, “is the effect of intoxication; it is even its final stage. It is the headache that remains when sleep has dispersed the vapors of wine, and when a man who had become drunk regains consciousness and is no longer in the mental derangement that deprives him of sensation” (*Homer’s Nepenthes, or On Helen’s Drug*, chap. 15). This is confirmed by an impressive display of learning. How, then, could Saint Augustine truthfully say: “Drunkenness is far from me, but crapulence sometimes overtakes your servant”? M. Petit claims to remove the contradiction by supposing that Saint Augustine had a head strong enough to drink a great deal of wine without losing the use of reason, but not without suffering discomfort the following day. Yet it seems to me that the contradiction remains; or else M. Petit has failed to prove that the Latin word *crapula* always expresses the effect and final stage of drunkenness. From all the testimonies he cites, it follows that crapulence is never separable from drunkenness.

M. Bayle takes no trouble to make this observation. His aim is to please everyone, and here he did not wish to miss the opportunity of flattering good drinkers by associating [Col. 0994A] them with Saint Augustine. Let us turn to what he reports of M. Cousin’s response. This journalist, a friend of the supposed disciples of Saint Augustine and consequently zealous for the glory of their supposed master, is scandalized to the utmost by M. Petit’s strange paradox, who had the audacity to write that Saint Augustine sometimes made use of the strength he possessed to drink a great deal. M. Cousin demonstrates [Note: [Col. 0993C] *Journal des savants*, 27 June 1689], through very clear passages from both Saint Augustine and Possidius, that the holy doctor led a life not merely sober but austere; that he sought food only as he sought medicines; that he was always on guard against pleasure when satisfying the needs of nature; that he waged continual war against himself through fasting and abstinence; and that he therefore ought not to be suspected of having sometimes drunk to excess.

M. Bayle has nothing to say about this, but he does not show M. Cousin the same indulgence that he shows M. Petit. He allows the latter to contradict the authorities he cites by separating crapulence from drunkenness, while demanding of the former good evidence authorizing him to make the word *crapula* signify merely the pleasure of eating and drinking, which lies, as it were, in ambush along the passage of necessary nourishment required to appease hunger and thirst and maintain health. But what evidence is needed beyond Saint Augustine’s own text, which, in the place where it occurs, distinguishes what was then called *crapula* as much from excessive drinking as from drunkenness? I appeal to the good faith of everyone who will take the trouble to read it. And is it not enough for M. Cousin that the only authorities that can be set against his view are those that completely confuse crapulence with drunkenness, whereas Saint Augustine’s passage entirely distinguishes the two?

Second Part. Examination of M. Bayle’s boast: “I have vigorously challenged Saint Augustine.”

[Col. 0993]

[Col. 0993C]

Under the article “HAGAR,” after describing Saint Augustine as a fertile and imaginative mind, M. Bayle adds these words: “By Sarah’s conduct toward Hagar, he maintained that the true Church may inflict punishments upon the false Church, exile it, torment it, and so forth. He was driven back very forcefully in a few words, in the *Philosophical Commentary*, on the famous words: ‘Compel them to enter.’”

“He was vigorously challenged”—that is, I challenged him, for M. Bayle is the author of the *Philosophical Commentary*. Thus M. Bayle’s admirers will permit me to say on this subject: “I shall challenge M. Bayle in the examination that I intend one day to make of the principles, arguments, testimonies, and facts that he has ventured in favor of toleration.” This boast, “I shall challenge M. Bayle,” is not as great as the other, “I have vigorously challenged Saint Augustine.” There is as much difference between the two as there is between Saint Augustine and M. Bayle.

[Col. 0993D]

Father Adam contributes nothing to the discussion except to speak indignantly of Saint Augustine. M. Bayle and his guarantors reproach this Jesuit for having called the holy doctor a heated African, a fiery doctor, obscure in his writings, and inconsistent in his views on matters of grace. Let one read the *Philosophical Commentary*, and one will understand that if M. Bayle had it in for Father Adam, it may well have been because he had not supplied him with more insults against Saint Augustine—insults that he would have enjoyed inserting into his Dictionary. His politeness embarrasses his slander; he likes to place coarse expressions in other people’s mouths.

I yield to the impulse urging me to examine briefly this third part of M. Bayle’s *Philosophical Commentary*, in which, from beginning to end, he speaks in an elevated tone and with a triumphant air, as a man convinced that he is reducing to nothing all of Saint Augustine’s intelligence and judgment. He undertakes to refute what the holy doctor wrote in favor of the imperial laws that prescribed penalties against heretics.

It is unfortunate that, upon entering into the matter, he confuses the legitimate power possessed by Catholic princes to punish heresy as a crime, as well as the Church’s right to have recourse to temporal power in order to repress and destroy heresies, with the more or less appropriate use of this power and right according to differing circumstances. Saint Augustine [Col. 0994D] never doubted for a moment that this power and right existed—in vain does M. Bayle insinuate otherwise. Yet the same Saint Augustine had once believed that coercion was useless for the individual good of heretics and for bringing them back to the faith. From this it must not be concluded that the holy doctor ever denied that penalties could justly, and even ought to, be inflicted upon adherents of new sects if some other end were at issue than their conversion—for example, if it were necessary not only to prevent their revolts and violence, but also to halt the contagion of error and prevent the seduction of peoples.

I [Note: [Col. 0995] The following forty numbered sections correspond to those which divide the third part of the *Philosophical Commentary*.]

That being supposed, M. Bayle is wrong to assert, as he does, that Saint Augustine’s opening is the worst ever seen. For either this beginning is entirely reasonable, or it is even more absurd than M. Bayle represents it. Everything depends on whether one chooses to view Saint Augustine’s text in a natural or bizarre manner.

M. Bayle makes this Father say that, since the Donatists are as unruly as they are, one must have recourse to princes against heretics who are quiet and disturb no one. This is nonsensical. But according to the way M. Bayle chooses to understand Saint Augustine’s words, this Father carries extravagance much further: his thought would be that, since the Donatists are as unruly as they are, it will be beneficial for heretics who remain quiet and disturb no one that the authority of the secular arm be employed against them.

Fortunately for Saint Augustine, M. Bayle has misunderstood the relationship among the words of this holy doctor. He has not grasped—or has pretended not to grasp—their meaning. Here they are:

*Nunc me potius quietis esse avidum et petentem, quam cum me adolescentem, vivo adhuc Rogato, cui successisti apud Carthaginem, noveras; sed donatistae nimium inquieti sunt: quos per ordinatas a Deo potestates cohiberi atque corrigi non erit inutile* (Saint Augustine, Letter 93, formerly 48, to Vincent Rogatist, chap. 1, no. 1).

“Now I am more desirous of and devoted to peace and tranquility than when you knew me as a young man, while Rogatus was still alive, the man whom you succeeded at Carthage. But the Donatists are excessively troubled; and it will not be useless for them to be restrained and corrected by the powers ordained by God.”

Saint Augustine had formerly expressed to Vincent, a Donatist bishop of the Rogatist faction, how much he wished to see an end to the disturbances that Donatism’s schism had stirred up in the African Church. Long afterward, after the holy Father had consented to the course taken by the other Catholic bishops, who had obtained from the emperor Honorius severe edicts against [Col. 0995C] the Donatists, he received letters from Vincent that revealed the consternation into which the imperial laws had thrown all those involved in the schism. In these letters the Donatist reproached him for having abandoned his love of tranquility and peace.

The holy doctor replies that the consent he had given had in no way diminished his love of tranquility and peace, but that the Donatists were wrong to be troubled and alarmed, because the imperial laws aimed only at their usefulness and welfare.

Indeed, is this not how Saint Augustine’s text should be translated? “I am even more a lover of tranquility and peace than when you knew me as a young man at Carthage; but the Donatists are excessively anxious and alarmed, for I am convinced that it is not useless for them to be restrained and corrected by the powers established by God.”

Does M. Bayle consider this when he interprets the Donatists’ “anxiety” as referring to their former seditions and furies, the brigandage and acts of cruelty they had committed, rather than to the movements of fear and even despair caused among them by news of the edicts and the beginning of their execution? Is it reasonable to attribute to Saint Augustine the claim that the Donatists’ anxiety is the cause of the usefulness of the edicts, rather than that the usefulness of the edicts is what should bring their anxiety to an end?

If I were not dealing with an author of the first rank in literature, I would say that he was misled by the poor translation we have of Saint Augustine’s Letters. I call this translation poor without intending to deprive it of the reputation it enjoys, in the judgment of many, as the best written and most elegant translation we possess of this part of Saint Augustine’s works. But I would reproach M. Bayle for not consulting the Latin text, or for not understanding it better than M. Dubois—especially since the passage is so easy that one need not be M. Bayle to penetrate its meaning.

Who does not see at first glance that these Latin words—*Donatistae nimium inquieti sunt, quos per ordinatas a Deo potestates cohiberi atque coerceri mihi non videtur inutile*—“The Donatists are excessively troubled; I do not think it useless that they be restrained and checked by the powers ordained by God”—are very badly rendered in French by the following: “The Donatists being as troubled as they are, I nevertheless remain convinced that it is very appropriate to repress them by the authority of the powers established by God”? This is a mistranslation. If this turn of phrase pleased M. Dubois, he ought to have translated it as follows: “Since I nevertheless remain convinced that it is very advantageous for the Donatists to be repressed by the powers established by God, they appear to me excessively troubled.”

[Col. 0996B]

Where is M. Bayle’s criticism? Is it not his malice that prevents him from exercising it? And if so, upon whom does the blame fall for making himself suspected of bad faith, for speaking like a man who conceals the true state of the question, who seeks to mislead his readers, who wishes to win his case by trickery, and who for this purpose employs a deceptive and contrived preamble? Does it fall upon Saint Augustine or upon M. Bayle?

II.

The commentator sees—or pretends to see—in the holy doctor’s text two objects. One is odious, and of it he says that this Father turns his reader away: namely, that it is appropriate to have recourse to the secular arm in order to compel heretics to sign a new formulary. The other is entirely legitimate, and to it he claims that Saint Augustine directs his reader: namely, that it is good and praiseworthy to employ the sovereigns’ power to maintain the public peace, which rebellious, factious, and persecuting heretics disturb.

M. Bayle’s great scandal is that the proofs employed later by the holy doctor relate not to the second object, which is clearly stated, but to the first, which is expressed only in veiled terms. “Hence,” says M. Bayle, “the connection of Saint Augustine’s arguments is bad, there is no continuity in his discourse, and it consists only of words poorly linked and poorly arranged (*scopae dissolutae*—‘a scattered bundle of broom twigs’).”

But he maliciously invented the distinction between these two objects in order to make Saint Augustine ridiculous. The holy doctor is not speaking of the Donatists’ turbulent and seditious conduct, but of the terror that had struck them when the edicts issued against their sect were published.

Thus the truth—about which no one doubts—that it is the duty of princes to enact laws against heretics who disturb their neighbors is not found in Saint Augustine’s text. He is no more concerned to propose it than to prove it. As for the other proposition, M. Bayle obscures and disfigures it through a miserable equivocation borrowed from the inept translator of this Father’s letters. That translator does not say, either openly, covertly, or in any manner whatsoever: “It is appropriate”—that is, one has the right—to have recourse to the secular arm in order to compel heretics to sign a new formulary. He says only: “It is appropriate”—that is, it is beneficial, it is not useless—for heretics to be restrained and corrected by the authority of the powers established by God: *Quos per ordinatas a Deo potestates cohiberi atque corrigi mihi non videtur inutile*—“I do not think it useless for them to be restrained and corrected by the powers ordained by God.”

And the proof [Col. 0997A] of this proposition is not the Donatists’ anxiety, mentioned in the preceding sentence, but experience itself, attested in the words that follow:

*Nam de multorum jam correctione gaudemus, qui tam veraciter unitatem catholicam tenent atque defendunt, et a pristino errore se liberatos esse laetantes, ut eos cum magna gratulatione miremur* (Saint Augustine, cited passage).

“For we already rejoice at the correction of many who hold and defend Catholic unity with such sincerity, and who rejoice that they have been freed from their former error, that we admire them with great exultation.”

Was it not deliberately and deceptively that M. Bayle failed to place these words in their entirety at the head of his second article? Here is all he cites: “Thus we have the joy of seeing several whom this means has brought back to Catholic unity.”

Why does he omit the end of the passage, and all the expressions showing that the return of several Donatists was genuine and sincere, that these new converts had become zealous defenders of Catholic unity, and that they were delighted to have returned from their former error, so that everyone not only congratulated them but [Col. 0997B] could not admire them enough? Is it not because he fears that it would become apparent that Saint Augustine’s sole purpose is to prove how advantageous and salutary the coercion arising from the imperial laws is for heretics? This would completely undo the commentator’s criticism.

For if M. Bayle had not omitted the features I have just mentioned, he would have been ashamed to lecture Saint Augustine as a master of logic and prescribe how he ought to have reasoned—assuming that he had wished to express himself frankly and straightforwardly. It would have been far too evident that Saint Augustine’s syllogism, which M. Bayle has concealed and carefully hidden, is as follows:

The laws that have brought several people back to Catholic unity with complete sincerity are useful to the Donatists; now, the laws that command the Donatists to return to this unity under severe penalties have brought several of them back to it with complete sincerity; therefore, those laws are useful to the Donatists.

The professor of Rotterdam would have been obliged to suppress his lesson, or at most reserve it for his young pupils. For he must surely have taught them to reason better than Saint Augustine, offering them as models syllogisms such as the following, which he generously suggests to the holy doctor in order to have greater scope for beating him soundly:

The laws that bring several people back to Catholic unity are good; now, the laws that command the Donatists to return to this unity under severe penalties have brought several of them back to it; therefore, those laws are good.

Young pupils would not have noticed that Saint Augustine had no need to prove the absolute goodness of these laws, but only their relative goodness. The question was whether these laws were good and useful for the Donatists themselves, and whether charity could have moved the bishops to request them from the emperors.

Thank God! We have found continuity and connection in Saint Augustine’s arguments, uprightness and good faith in his discourse—but at the expense of M. Bayle’s uprightness and good faith, or of the much-vaunted penetration of his mind. It is not we, but his good friends the libertines, who should be distressed by this.

III.

Let us continue. Saint Augustine adds that the Donatists who had returned to unity with complete sincerity and from the bottom of their hearts would never have thought of changing and converting without the terror inspired by the secular powers, because the force of habit would never have allowed them to apply their minds to considering the truth. But this terror had been salutary for them, giving rise to an anxious reflection: namely, that perhaps they were not suffering for justice, etc.:

*Qui nescio qua vi consuetudinis, nullo modo mutari in melius cogitarent, nisi hoc terrore perculsi, sollicitam mentem ad considerationem veritatis intenderent, ne forte si non pro justitia, etc.* (Saint Augustine, ibid.).

“They, who through I know not what force of habit would never have thought of changing for the better, unless, struck by this terror, they had directed an anxious mind toward consideration of the truth, lest perhaps, if they were not suffering for justice, etc.”

It will easily be understood later why M. Bayle had reasons for not reporting Saint Augustine’s entire thought, and why, at the head of this article, he describes only the following words: “The force of habit was a chain that they would never have broken had they not been struck by the terror of the secular powers, and had this salutary terror not directed their minds toward consideration of the truth, etc.”

One can already understand what difficulty prevented M. Dubois from translating these words exactly: *nullo modo mutari in melius cogitarent, nisi hoc terrore perculsi*—“they would never have thought of changing for the better unless, struck by this terror.” And one can also see why M. Bayle’s criticism always shows respect for the weakening of Saint Augustine’s text in translation.

But what does the commentator reply to this passage? For my part, I confess that I would have thought it beyond all censure [Col. 0998B]: for what could one answer to it? Will one deny the fact of the sincere conversion of several Donatists, of which the holy doctor here does nothing more than explain the cause? One must therefore contradict this saint and treat him as a visionary when he speaks to us of zeal for Catholic unity and of the joy of being delivered from the error that he imagined himself to perceive in these new converts; one must reproach him with simplicity and imprudence for having admired what was merely hypocrisy, even if the signs of the Donatists’ return to unity had seemed to him no less unambiguous than the proofs Saint Paul gave of his renunciation of Judaism and his attachment to the Gospel.

On the other hand, assuming the fact to be true, what other cause will one assign for the Donatists’ change except the thought to which the terror of the secular powers led them: that perhaps they were not suffering for justice; that, afflicted by temporal hardships [Col. 0998C], they were vainly and fruitlessly suffering as victims of the perversity and presumption of certain individuals; and that afterward, before God, they might find nothing but the eternal punishments due to the ungodly: *ne forte si non pro justitia, sed pro perversitate et praesumptione hominum ipsas temporales molestias infructuosa et vana tolerantia paterentur, apud Deum postea non invenirent nisi debitas poenas impiorum*, etc. [“lest, if they were suffering these temporal troubles not for justice but for the perversity and presumption of men, through a fruitless and vain endurance, they should afterward find before God nothing but the punishments due to the ungodly”] (St. Augustine, ibid.).

What course does M. Bayle take? He contradicts Saint Augustine. Yet he does not appear to do so; for although he ordinarily shows himself determined not to spare the holy doctor, and treats him everywhere in the most unworthy manner, he does not have the audacity to contradict him openly concerning a fact of which the saint declares himself an eyewitness.

How, then, does he proceed? He refers us to the second part of his *Philosophical Commentary* (Part II, chapters 1–2), where he claims to have demonstrated [Col. 0998D] that rigorous measures can never awaken those who refuse to examine the truth, and that consequently they cannot produce any sincere conversion. Is it not highly amusing that M. Bayle genuinely employs the shameful artifice that he has just reproached Saint Augustine for using with such hauteur and contempt? When the commentator accused this Father of trickery and considered him convicted of proving something he did not dare to state because it was odious, were we to expect that he himself would prepare to impose upon us by a similar act of concealment? Would anyone have suspected that, rightly fearing to say that Saint Augustine had lied in reporting a fact of which he declares himself an eyewitness, the clever writer would point to proofs from which he expected no adequate answer, in order to have them used to infer the saint’s falsehood? Have we not [Col. 0999A] reason to return to M. Bayle one of the thrusts he directs against Saint Augustine’s good faith, and to say that, if the commentator had wished to speak frankly and straightforwardly, he would have reasoned as follows: “It is impossible for rigorous measures to produce genuine conversions; now Saint Augustine attests that he saw genuine conversions produced by rigorous measures; therefore Saint Augustine attests that he saw something impossible; therefore he is lying”?

I shall not enter now into the general thesis of this alleged impossibility. I shall merely remark in passing that M. Bayle has not even touched—and has actually avoided touching—the natural reason which, as Saint Augustine assures us, caused wisely applied vexation to become a useful counterweight to the Donatists’ prejudices and restored their wandering minds to the balance and condition in which they needed to be in order to choose the right side. It is the just fear that the experience of punishment caused them to conceive: that they were suffering not for justice, but [Col. 0999B] for the quarrel of certain perverse and presumptuous men, at the risk of still being punished by God eternally along with the ungodly.

If M. Bayle had clearly presented this reason, he would have been more hesitant to assert that persecution has as much effect against the orthodox as against those who are not orthodox—for “persecution against error” is a phrase as familiar to him as “persecution against the truth.” The commentator could not have avoided reducing his proposition to this: the fear of not suffering for justice arises just as readily in an orthodox person persecuted by a heretical prince as in a heretic punished by an orthodox prince; that is, the orthodox person has no stronger grounds for believing than the heretic, and God, who wishes people of every condition and state to be orthodox on pain of damnation, has not provided marks that are certain and proportionate to every [Col. 0999C] condition and state by which one might infallibly recognize on which side orthodox doctrine lies. But those who think in this way are rightly suspected of believing that God bears no greater witness to himself than to his Church. Let us return to Saint Augustine’s defense.

**IV.**

Does he need it with regard to these words, which are so reasonable?

“If a man saw his enemy, driven by a raging fever, about to throw himself headlong, would he not be returning evil for evil if he let him do it, rather than stopping and restraining him? Yet the frenzied man would regard this service of kindness and charity only as an insult and an effect of hatred; but if he recovered his health, he would clearly see that the more violence this supposed enemy had done him, the more he would be indebted to him. How many Circumcellions themselves do we now have who are zealous Catholics—and who declare that they detest their former life and the unhappy blindness that made them believe they were acting for the good of the Church, when in fact only their fury and recklessness inspired them? Yet they would never have returned to their senses if those same laws that displease you had not been employed to bind them like madmen” (St. Augustine, ibid., chapter 1, no. 2).

Thus far this is M. Dubois’s translation. I have taken care to distinguish what M. Bayle judged it appropriate to omit, doubtless for a reason other than brevity.

After placing this truncated text before his reader’s eyes, the commentator offers a carefully prepared preamble that ends by metamorphosing Saint Augustine into Aeolus and declaring that his discourse is nothing but wind. How does he attempt to substantiate this casual and burlesque verdict? By making every effort to confuse what is perfectly clear. One need only reread the holy doctor’s words attentively [Col. 1000A] to be convinced that M. Bayle introduces gibberish where there is only precision and clarity. Thus, if Saint Augustine’s discourse is nothing but wind, according to M. Bayle, M. Bayle’s censure, in the judgment of anyone who has eyes, is nothing but smoke dispersed by that wind. I shall demonstrate this.

Saint Augustine compares a heretic who is left in complete freedom to follow and profess his error with a sick man about to throw himself from a height in a fit of raging fever, because each is in a condition from which he will not return to his senses. He compares the imperial laws that forbid following and professing error under severe penalties with the chains and bonds used to prevent the frenzied man from throwing himself out of the window, because each means places the heretic and the frenzied man in a condition in which they can return to their senses. Finally, he compares the sincere conversion of the heretic, which would not have occurred without the rigor of the imperial laws, [Col. 1000B] with the frenzied man’s return to sanity, which would not have occurred if he had not been bound. This comparison, every part of which is found in Saint Augustine just as I have described it, casts an admirable light on what the holy doctor had said earlier and perfectly clarifies the question he is treating. If this is wind, it is of the kind that drives away clouds and makes the sky serene.

M. Bayle vainly strives to obscure the principal object of the comparison: his bad faith is visible, blatant, and, at the same time, inconceivable. He supposes that the heretic whom Saint Augustine here compares to a man who is chained in a frenzy converts only outwardly; that he does not follow the movements of his conscience; that he consents to nothing demanded of him; that he enters churches by force; that he receives communion by force, and so forth. He concludes that the comparison is pitiful and absurd [Col. 1000C], because one cannot preserve a man from hell and send him to paradise against his will, just as one saves a paralytic’s life against his will.

But does Saint Augustine not declare in sufficiently intelligible and precise terms that he is speaking of a multitude of Donatists whose conversion is manifest and in no way equivocal, *catholicos manifestos* [“manifest Catholics”]? Who openly condemn their former life and their wretched error, *damnantes suam pristinam vitam et miserabilem errorem* [“condemning their former life and wretched error”]. Who admit that it was right to trouble them, *fatentur nos sibi molestos esse debuisse* [“they confess that we ought to have troubled them”]. Does the holy doctor not make it sufficiently clear that the essential point of the comparison is the bodily recovery of the frenzied man who returns to his senses, *plane salute recuperata* [“with health plainly recovered”], and the spiritual recovery of the heretic who converts sincerely: *qui tamen ad hanc sanitatem non perducerentur?* [“yet they would not have been brought to this state of health”?]

I have said that M. Bayle did not believe the Donatists’ conversion to be sincere, and that in this respect he tacitly contradicted Saint Augustine. He goes much further: he contradicts the eyes of the whole world, which reads in Saint Augustine the proofs of the truth and sincerity of the Donatists’ conversion; he contradicts his own eyes, which saw in the passage under dispute what he removed from M. Dubois’s translation. He wants the holy doctor to have the same idea of the Donatists’ conversion as he does, and to say the exact opposite of what he expresses on this subject; otherwise M. Bayle could not possibly imagine any absurdity in the comparison of the heretic and the frenzied man. He may accuse this comparison as much as he pleases of presupposing what is false, but he cannot accuse it of lacking precision.

**V.**

Let us move on to a second comparison by Saint Augustine, which M. Bayle assures us is no better than the first. If it is even slightly better, it will be excellent, since we have established that the first [Col. 1001A] was very good. Saint Augustine places this objection in the mouth of the Donatist to whom he is writing:

“You will say that there are some over whom this achieves nothing; I grant it, but should medicine be abandoned because there are incurable patients?” (St. Augustine, ibid., no. 3).

To this the commentator replies with the air of superiority with which he ordinarily adorns himself: “If the Donatist proposed this objection as weakly as Saint Augustine represents it, he was a poor fellow. Why did he not point out to this Father the effect produced by the persecutions of the pagans in the time of Saint Cyprian, and so forth?”

M. Bayle, who draws this reinforcement for the Donatist’s objection from the treasury of his mind, so fertile in sophisms, does not present himself as a poor fellow. Yet if, whatever other merit one might possess, one were a poor fellow for advancing weak reasons, would one not be still more so for elevating arguments as poor in quality as the following into important difficulties?

“The fear of the edicts that pagan emperors issued against Christians [Col. 1001B] could lead only to apostasy; therefore the fear of the edicts that Christian emperors issued against heretics could lead only to hypocrisy.”

Is this other argument of M. Bayle’s any stronger?

“What served as poison against the truth cannot wisely be employed as a good medicine for error; therefore the fear of temporal punishments, which corrupted so many Christians, cannot wisely be employed to convert heretics.”

The physicians, I think, will not agree that what is poison for those who are healthy cannot wisely be employed as a good remedy for the sick. And from M. Bayle’s principle it would follow that in families one should not punish children who steal, because thieves train their children and embolden them to steal through fear of punishment.

[Col. 1001C] What am I saying? The commentator questions whether persecution is a medicine; he means to question whether there are medicinal punishments. I shall pass over several trifles on which he dwells in this connection and come to the principal reason that leads him to assert that the confiscation of property, imprisonment, exile, and the other punishments imposed by the imperial laws against the Donatists were not medicinal. It is, he says, that medicine must not be bad in itself and by its nature, but at least indifferent. Now such punishments, imposed against innocent people—as, in M. Bayle’s view, are all those who profess any heresy or impiety whatsoever—are not indifferent but bad in themselves and by their nature; they are injustices and crimes committed by sovereigns.

For, according to M. Bayle’s morality, the powers established by God offend him when they undertake to avenge injuries done to him. Laws enacted not only against the impious and even atheists [Col. 1001D] are no less criminal and tyrannical than if they had been enacted against a sect of philosophers who, believing everything the Church believes concerning faith and morals, held the particular opinion that the object of logic is not real beings but beings of reason. These are M. Bayle’s own words; as one can see, he placed the interests of religion on the same level as those that make disputants cry out in the schools of philosophy.

**VI.**

Let us not neglect the brief reflections he makes on the following words:

“If one were content merely to raise the rod over them and did not work to instruct them, our conduct would appear tyrannical; but likewise, if one were content to instruct them without pressing them through fear, they would not overcome a certain [Col. 1002A] torpor produced by habit” (St. Augustine, ibid.).

The commentator replies with two points:

1. Joining instruction to threat is indeed a lesser evil than threatening without instructing, but persecution prevents a proper examination.

2. When the heretic, after having sufficiently submitted himself to instruction, persists in his former convictions, one should not rigorously execute upon him what one has threatened him with.

From this let us understand two things:

1. M. Bayle does not agree with the prophet who says that vexation gives understanding (Isaiah 28:19).

2. He believes that whatever is merely against God is not a crime that the powers established by God have the right to punish.

Saint Augustine held different principles, which we shall readily justify in their proper place.

**VII.**

The commentator often reproaches this Father for employing the commonplaces of rhetoric. One might think one were hearing a great master and a profound writer [Col. 1002B] correcting a young beginner. At one moment he pleasantly says that Saint Augustine builds himself a palace whose inhabitants are great popular commonplaces; at another he exclaims: “Another commonplace and a small popular thought.”

This latter thrust is directed at the following passage:

“Not all who spare us are therefore our friends, nor are all who punish us our enemies. The wounds inflicted by a friend are better than the affected caresses of an enemy. The severity of those who love us is more beneficial to us than the gentleness of those who deceive us; and it is a greater charity to take bread away from a man, however hungry he may be, if, when he has food to eat, he neglects the duties of justice, than to give him bread and make it a bait to induce him to consent to iniquity” (St. Augustine, ibid., chapter 2, no. 4).

The holy doctor is merely paraphrasing this passage from Proverbs: *meliora sunt vulnera diligentis, quam fraudulenta oscula odientis* (Proverbs 27:6) [“the wounds of a lover are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates”]. And M. Bayle [Col. 1002C] is not displeased to teach us in passing that he regards the Book of Proverbs as a collection of small popular thoughts at which Saint Augustine should not have stopped.

The holy doctor applies the sacred author’s maxim to the punishments ordered against the Donatists by the imperial laws, and shows that these heretics are wrong to complain of them, because their rigor is beneficial and they are an effect of the love and charity shown toward them. What does M. Bayle find objectionable in this? He claims that there is no connection between the strong reprimands and censures mentioned by the author of Proverbs and the punishments inflicted by the laws. He never ceases repeating that these punishments, consisting in confiscation of property and acts of violence, are manifest injustices when ordered merely to punish crimes that injure religion—that is, crimes which are not crimes at all. For, according to M. Bayle, in the eyes of men there are no crimes [Col. 1002D] except actions prejudicial to the prosperity, strength, and tranquility of the republic, which ought not to concern itself in the least with matters touching the worship and honor of God.

Society owes nothing to God, and individuals must be left to examine, decide, and regulate their duties—not toward their neighbors, nor toward themselves, since their understanding is not sufficiently reliable to judge these matters correctly and error would have consequences—but their duties toward God. They are only too wise to know the proper bounds of these duties, and no danger is incurred by making a mistake.

This doctrine was not known in Saint Augustine’s time. Will anyone blame him so severely for not having followed it? It is a pity that M. Bayle arrived so late to popularize it: the libertines of past centuries would have applauded him just as much as those of our own day.

**VIII.**

[Col. 1003A]

Necessity alone makes me fall into certain repetitions; I believe I am excused from following M. Bayle through those that are wholly useless. For this reason I shall not pause to justify the opening words of this passage:

“To bind a frenzied man and awaken a lethargic one is to anger them, but it is to love them. God loves us with a more genuine love than anyone could show; nevertheless, he never ceases to join the salutary terrors of his threats to the sweetness of his instruction, and to mingle the bitterness of tribulations with the consolations he sends us. We see that he exercised the holiest and most devout patriarchs through famine” (St. Augustine, ibid.).

What I said a little earlier should, it seems to me, suffice to demonstrate that the comparison of a frenzied or lethargic person with a heretic is entirely apt. But concerning the persecutions that God inflicts upon his children, as M. Bayle chooses to express it [Col. 1003B], I shall show that they support everything Saint Augustine claims.

Here is the place to observe that one of M. Bayle’s great talents is the manner in which he prepares his readers to be taken by surprise. He takes extraordinary care to remove all suspicion of the trap he is setting, and his skill lies in ostentatiously blaming his adversaries and attributing to them the very deception and imposture he himself is contemplating. He accuses Saint Augustine of constantly throwing people off the scent, so that no one notices that M. Bayle himself is the one doing so everywhere, and especially here, where it is easiest to see.

The example of God’s exercising the most devout patriarchs through famine is so unsuitable for application to the justice of the imperial laws against heretics, and at the same time so well suited to make clear that these laws were solicited and enacted in a spirit of charity, that it was natural [Col. 1003C] to suspect M. Bayle of trying to impose upon us when he spoke as follows:

“The question is not so much whether one can love those whom one punishes—who doubts it?—as whether it is just to take a man’s property and freedom from him because he does not believe the same things in religion as his prince.”

For the example he cites presents an aspect of God’s goodness, not of his justice, toward the patriarchs; this aspect evidently concerns the charity exercised by princes, not their justice in punishing heretics.

This is precisely what M. Bayle does not want us to notice, still less to discover the sleight of hand he employs for this purpose. He therefore gets ahead of us: he is the first to charge Saint Augustine with an artful disguise. This removes the thought that the commentator alone is trying to make disappear the true state of the question Saint Augustine treats in his letter to Vincent, bishop of the Rogatist faction, which is here the object of M. Bayle’s censure.

The sleight of hand is [Col. 1003D] executed with great skill. Is it the act of an inept man to put the proposition serving as the holy doctor’s proof in place of the proposition that the holy doctor undertakes to prove? M. Bayle avoided saying: “The question is not whether the imperial laws were solicited and enacted in a spirit of charity.” How could he add: “Who doubts it?” Yet this is precisely the thesis Saint Augustine establishes. What malice there is in substituting for this proposition its proof—that one can love those whom one punishes! As though Saint Augustine were laboring uselessly to demonstrate something that is self-evident.

I know that the Donatists had two grievances against the imperial laws proscribing their schism, and that, in their view, both justice and charity were equally violated by them. But they did not dare to insist upon the first of these grievances except because, supposing their cause to be good, they judged that harming them [Col. 1004A] meant persecuting the true Church of Jesus Christ. M. Bayle does not consider this when he makes them speak in a manner resembling that of our tolerationists, attributing to them the claim that Christian princes had no right to punish the profession of heresy as a crime, and that bishops had no right to implore the assistance of the powers established by God in order to extirpate every kind of error.

Was there ever a sect more hostile to tolerationism than the sect and all the various factions of the Donatists? They had begun by submitting the judgment of ecclesiastical matters and religious disputes to the secular tribunals (St. Augustine, Letter 129, no. 4). More than once they had subjected to the coercive power of princes not only the cause of bishops but also the faith of the people. Unable to succeed in arming the legitimate sovereigns against the Catholic Church, they had turned to tyrants whose revolt and usurpation they supported on condition that they exterminate all those who [Col. 1004B] would not consent to be rebaptized (*Against the Letter of Parmenianus*, Book II, chapter 2). The intention of reuniting with the Catholic Church was among them a capital crime, which they had often punished with death. Having divided into several branches of schism and heresy, they waged internal war; and in one of the parties they had impersonated Catholics in order to oppress those belonging to the other party and subject them, through the authority of the magistrates, to the rigor of the edicts issued against all heretics (Letter 103, formerly 166, chapter 2, no. 3).

It is true that Saint Augustine reproaches the Donatists with all these excesses in order to convince them, by an argument *ad hominem*, that they were wrong to complain of the severity of the imperial laws being employed against them. But these complaints in no way attacked the justice or right of the emperors; they were based solely on the claim that charity and evangelical gentleness did not permit consciences to be violated by [Col. 1004C] such means.

For the Donatists confined themselves to pressing their second grievance: that charity was violated by the rigorous measures adopted to reunite them with the Church. Their brigandage and violence had often been brought against them, as had the cruelty and fury of their Circumcellions, who in several provinces had put everything to fire and blood in order to compel the people to adhere to their schism, embrace their errors, and submit to the practice of their rebaptism. The Catholic bishops opposed to this barbarous and bloody conduct the patience, gentleness, and charity of both the pastors and the children of the true Church.

But as soon as, at the urging of most of Africa’s orthodox prelates, the emperors published edicts condemning those who obstinately persisted in the schism and heresy of Donatus’s followers to various punishments, the Donatist bishops cried out. They reproached the Catholics for using [Col. 1004D] reprisals and asked them what had become of that patience, gentleness, and charity of which they made such a display. The answer to such an accusation is the subject of the letter to Vincent, bishop of the Rogatist faction; and it is solely from this perspective that the letter must be considered.

The question discussed in it is whether charity could have had any part in the decision to impose punishments upon the Donatists. Saint Augustine answers that it could, because these punishments might be useful to them; and he supports his view by the example of the sufferings with which God afflicts his children for their own good. What a remarkable thing! One is a wit, a great logician, and a subtle metaphysician, yet one has the perversity to see in this passage of Saint Augustine the model of reasoning as insane as the following:

“God exercised the most devout patriarchs through famine; therefore the king of France [Col. 1005A] has the right to strip of their property and reduce to bread and water all his subjects whom he pleases, in order to convert them and make them better!”

**IX.**

However just a punishment may be considered insofar as it is merited by the crime of heresy, it cannot be ordered in a spirit of charity, nor be an effect of charity, if it is not otherwise of a nature to secure the benefit of those who suffer it, and if the person whom one has the right to punish for having done wrong is not capable of profiting from it in order to do right.

This is the foundation of Vincent’s objection, which Saint Augustine resolves in these terms:

“You believe that no one should be compelled to do good; but have you not seen that the master of the household ordered his servants to compel those whom they encountered to enter the feast? Have you not seen with what violence Saul was forced by Jesus Christ to recognize and embrace [Col. 1005B] the truth? [lacuna] Do you not know that shepherds sometimes use the rod to make the sheep return to the fold? Do you not know that Sarah, according to the authority granted to her, subdued her maidservant’s rebellious spirit by harsh treatment? Yet she did not do this out of any hatred she had for Hagar, since she loved her so much that she wished Abraham to make her a mother, but in order to humble her pride. Now you are not unaware that, just as Sarah and her son Isaac represent the spiritual, Hagar and her son Ishmael represent the carnal. Nevertheless, although Scripture teaches us that Sarah made Hagar and Ishmael suffer greatly, Saint Paul did not fail to say that it was Ishmael who persecuted Isaac [lacuna] thereby giving those who have understanding to know that, although the Catholic Church strives to bring back the carnal through fear and temporal punishments, it is they who persecute her rather than she them” (St. Augustine, ibid., nos. 5–6).

[Col. 1005C] We shall discuss M. Bayle’s philosophy concerning these words—“Compel them to enter”—elsewhere. With regard to the violence that Jesus Christ inflicted upon Saint Paul, taking away his sight and throwing him to the ground, Saint Augustine mentions it to convince his adversary that violence is a kind of outward grace which, in its own manner and through the intervention of the inward grace that accompanies it, contributes to the change of hearts and disposes them to sincere conversion. From this the holy doctor claims to infer that it is often appropriate to compel the wicked to do good.

On this point, as on many others, M. Bayle has ideas that are truly singular. He cannot deny that God has placed several outward graces in human hands, so that people may obtain them for one another through charity; but he insists that these graces may legitimately be employed only when God has made human beings masters of inward grace. In truth, he speaks only of punishments [Col. 1005D]; but by a necessary consequence his proposition extends to all outward graces dependent upon human will. Thus not only may princes not punish bodies for the good of souls unless they have the power to bend hearts, but preachers themselves may not proclaim the word of God unless they possess the secret of making it understood and savored in the depths of the soul.

This gives the tolerationists ample room to maneuver. The sovereigns’ arm will be bound, and the preachers’ mouths will be closed for a long time. Here is another thought of M. Bayle’s, no less extraordinary. It is reserved to God to use punishments to bring the wicked back to themselves and onto the path of salvation, even though such punishments have very different effects, often hardening rather than converting them, and especially though they rarely change the opinions people hold concerning the [Col. 1006A] worship due to God. But human beings are not permitted to imitate the conduct of the sovereign Master in this respect, because they do not possess, as God does, the right to act without success. This must surely be understood of all the other outward graces whose administration is entrusted to human beings, and particularly of the preaching of God’s word. For why should human beings have the right to contribute to their neighbor’s hardening in one way rather than another? Let God, then, speak directly to human beings himself, as he did to Cain without result; according to M. Bayle’s reasoning, there is nothing to object to. But for human beings to presume to proclaim God’s word before being assured that it will be followed and practiced is, according to this writer’s principles, utterly senseless.

What alarm the commentator gives us! Kings, authorized by Saint Augustine to imitate God in his punishments, will consider themselves entitled—and often obliged—to set fire to their subjects’ grain, hay, [Col. 1006B] vineyards, and woods, and to send agents throughout their kingdoms to decimate children and send many fathers to the mines and galleys, in the belief that by this means their peoples will return to themselves and awaken from the lethargy of sin in which they are asleep.

Nevertheless, let us not be too frightened, and let us persuade ourselves that M. Bayle is going astray in order to cause us these panicked terrors. He has plainly lost his guiding star, which is the question at issue between St. Augustine and Vincent the Rogatist. The holy doctor’s sole purpose is to show that princes may have in view, and may set as their aim, the conversion of heretics when they condemn them to undergo penalties that are otherwise justly deserved by the crime of heresy; that is to say, princes, in performing an act of justice, practice charity. The holy doctor wishes them in this respect to conform to the conduct of [Col. 1006C] God, who afflicts his children so that they may amend.

Instead of this, M. Bayle imagines that he sees in St. Augustine’s text that the intention of converting heretics is by itself sufficient to make the penalties imposed upon them by princes just; that is to say, that princes perform an act of justice as soon as they perform an act of charity; and that St. Augustine, if we believe M. Bayle, proposes the conduct of God, who afflicts his children so that they may amend, as a model of justice, and not merely of the charity that princes exercise in punishing heretics.

Nothing could be farther from the holy doctor’s thought, who certainly did not need to await M. Bayle’s arrival in order to know the truth of this maxim: Before a penalty can be ordered as medicinal, it must be presumed just and well deserved according to the rules of the tribunal to which it belongs to impose it. If M. Bayle persists in maintaining that Catholic princes have no right to [Col. 1006D] banish from their states the open profession of errors opposed to the faith, and that, consequently, under their edicts the open profession of these errors ought not to be regarded as a crime in the civil jurisprudence of the states, that is not St. Augustine’s fault.

Let us therefore be reassured. The grain, the hay, the vineyards, and the woods are safe; the children will not be decimated, the fathers will not be sent to the mines or the galleys, and no one will be punished without knowing why or without having thoroughly deserved it.

As for the example of shepherds who sometimes drive sheep into the fold with a staff, it is, M. Bayle replies, fortunately ill-chosen; for the other party in the comparison would have to consist of creatures not endowed with freedom, whereas their conversion essentially and entirely depends upon consent. I shall remark in passing that M. Bayle [Col. 1007A] gives no thought to two things he taught elsewhere: first, that St. Augustine believed animals were not machines, but possessed a sensitive soul, whose movements were consequently voluntary; second, that St. Augustine did not recognize in man as he now is the freedom of indifference, nor any free will other than that which is reduced to the purely voluntary—and M. Bayle agrees on this point with Calvin and Jansenius.

Given this, I am surprised that the commentator did not confine himself here to censuring St. Augustine’s view concerning the soul of animals and to establishing the doctrine of automatism by means of this amusing argument, which I received from a person who thinks as he does: Either animals are pure machines and have no sensitive soul, or we must agree that they are free just as man is; for the movements of this soul are not constrained but voluntary; now, we must not agree that [Col. 1007B] animals are free just as man is; therefore animals are pure machines and have no sensitive soul.

That, at any rate, would be far preferable to imposing upon St. Augustine the claim—by making it appear that this Father compares the sheep returning to the fold with badly converted heretics who, against their will, attend the material churches of the Catholics. Is not Christ’s fold, according to St. Augustine, the sincere profession of the true faith, into which vexation often leads the most obstinate by making them fear that they may fail to suffer for righteousness? Far from being unaware that conversion essentially and entirely depends upon consent, did this Father omit anything that might make it understood that entering Christ’s fold was nothing other than this consent? But M. Bayle understands only what he wishes to understand; and whenever a lame comparison pleases him, it will limp with impunity; if it displeases him, a [Col. 1007C] slight disparity, which does not touch the substance of the comparison, will cause it to be treated as ridiculous and impertinent.

The same will be true of the figures of the Old Testament, and Sarah cannot be the type of the children of God, nor Hagar the type of the children of the world, in the manner understood by St. Augustine, because the children of God do not compel the children of the world to go and seek shelter in the deserts, as Sarah compelled Hagar to flee into a desert; although, moreover, suffering Hagar, who is inspired from heaven to submit to her mistress, represents perfectly well a heretic whom temporal penalties bring back to the true and sincere obedience that he owes to the Church.

Would one now like to see the basest and most unworthy dissimulation ever displayed? M. Bayle affects to spare St. Augustine for a rather astonishing mistake, as he calls it, but imputes it to him through an even more astonishing imposture. St. Augustine [Col. 1007D] writes that, when Sarah wished Hagar to become a mother in her place, the tender love she then bore her maidservant was strong enough to endure even when she mistreated her, in order to subdue her pride:

> *Et utique non eam, quam SUPERIUS beneficio suo matrem fecerat, crudeliter oderat, sed in ea superbiam salubriter edomabat.*

“And certainly she did not cruelly hate the woman whom she had previously made a mother through her own favor; rather, she was healthfully subduing pride in her.”

M. Bayle maliciously closes his eyes to the Latin text and confines himself to the wretched translation that confounds what St. Augustine precisely distinguishes—namely, the time when Sarah wished Hagar to become a mother in her place, and the time when Sarah mistreated Hagar in order to subdue her pride. M. Dubois renders the words *quam SUPERIUS beneficio suo matrem fecerat* in French as follows: “Since she loved her enough to wish Abraham to make her a mother.” He suppresses *superius* (“previously”); he changes the pluperfect *fecerat* (“had made”) into the present. And M. Bayle has the insolence to lay at St. Augustine’s door the false meaning and horrible anachronism resulting from this unfaithful translation. This is his discourse, which requires a patient reader:

“I say nothing of St. Augustine’s rather astonishing mistake, when, in order to prove his union of charity and persecution, he claims that Sarah treated Hagar very harshly at the very time when she loved her tenderly enough to wish her to share her husband’s bed. Scripture does not arrange these things in this way; it speaks to us of Sarah’s ill humor toward Hagar only after Hagar, seeing herself pregnant, became proud and despised the other.”

It was on this subject, nevertheless, that M. Bayle boasts in his *Dictionary* of having given St. Augustine a sound reprimand!

### X.

I was right to say that a comparison limped whenever it pleased M. Bayle; for he [Col. 1008A] asserts of the following passage, which is full of proofs grounded in examples, that these are “little arguments suitable for delivery before [Col. 1008B] a crowd of ignorant people incapable of seeing where a comparison limps.” But let us listen to St. Augustine:

“The good and the wicked often do and suffer the same things; and it is not by what they do, nor by what they suffer, that we must judge of their actions, but by the motive that makes them act or suffer. Pharaoh oppressed the people of God with crushing labors. Moses, for his part, punished the impiety of that same people with extremely severe penalties. The actions of the one and the other resemble each other, but their ends were very different: the one was a tyrant swollen with his power, and the other a father full of charity. Jezebel put the prophets to death, and Elijah the false prophets (St. Augustine, same work, no. 6); but what armed the hand of the one and the other is no less different than what brought death upon the former and the latter . . . . [lacuna] In the same book in which we see the Apostle St. Paul beaten by the Jews, we also see the Jew Sosthenes beaten by the Greeks for St. Paul: the one and the other are alike in the [Col. 1008C] outward appearance of the action, but they are very different in motive . . . .” (No. 7). “Paul is handed over to a jailer to have fetters put on his feet, and St. Paul himself hands the incestuous man of Corinth over to Satan, whose cruelty is far greater than that of the most barbarous jailers; but he hands this man over to Satan only so that, his flesh being mortified, his soul might be saved. . . .” (Same work.) “When that same St. Paul handed Philetus and Hymenaeus over to Satan, in order to teach them not to blaspheme, he was not seeking to return evil for evil, but judged that healing an evil was a good.” (Same work.)

In answering this text, M. Bayle continues to pursue the phantom he has fashioned for himself. He has in mind, and assumes, that St. Augustine is concerned to prove the justice of the laws enacted against heretics and the right to punish them; and he has no doubt that the holy doctor’s reasoning must be this: Moses, Elijah, and St. Paul proceeded by way of punishment to correct error and impiety, and their conduct was just and legitimate; therefore [Col. 1008D] Catholic princes may justly and legitimately proceed by way of punishment to correct error and impiety. But M. Bayle is a hundred leagues away from the point disputed between St. Augustine and Vincent the Rogatist. Here it is; it is necessary to drive it home.

The Catholics mistreated by the Donatists obtained from the Emperor Honorius rescripts condemning those who remained attached to Donat’s party to grievous penalties: is this not to use reprisals? Is it not to return evil for evil? Is it not to take revenge and repay the effects of hatred with others like them? This state of the question is presented so clearly every ten lines or so in St. Augustine’s letter to Vincent the Rogatist that to make it disappear and transform it in a commentary more sophistical than philosophical is to insult the world’s credulity.

[Col. 1009A] The passage we are examining does not achieve the aim of the controversy as M. Bayle has falsely imagined it; that is no marvel. But once it is conceived as I have just presented it, the passage is its evident and natural decision. The holy doctor says that the Church, being the true and legitimate mother, does not return evil for evil even when she causes a harsh and bitter treatment to be felt; rather, she brings the salutary good of correction by banishing as great an evil as sin—not from a desire to harm arising from hatred, but from a desire to bring healing arising from love:

> *Quidquid ergo facit vera et legitima mater, etiamsi asperum amarumque sentiatur, non malum pro malo reddit, sed bonum disciplinae, expellendo malum iniquitatis, apponit, non odio nocendi, sed dilectione sanandi* (St. Augustine, same work, no. 6).

“Whatever, therefore, the true and legitimate mother does, even if it is felt as harsh and bitter, she does not return evil for evil, but supplies the good of discipline, driving out the evil of iniquity—not from hatred of harming, but from love of healing.”

There follow the words I quoted above, which M. Bayle undertakes to refute in this article. It is evident that the Donatists who persecuted the Catholics are there [Col. 1009B] compared with Pharaoh, who oppressed and consumed the people of God with crushing labors; with Jezebel, who put the prophets to death; and with the Jews, who beat St. Paul. The Catholics who petitioned for or carried out the edicts enacted against the Donatists are compared with Moses, who punished the iniquity of the people of God with very severe penalties; with Elijah, who put the false prophets to death; and with St. Paul, who handed the incestuous man of Corinth over to the devil. Where does this leave M. Bayle now, with his observations that dismantle St. Augustine’s comparisons and arguments?

When I see him conclude from the holy doctor’s texts that the motive of charity changes the nature of every action, and that it would make an action good when it would otherwise be bad in itself; when I see him deduce from this the greatest horrors in moral matters, as though St. Augustine had established this dreadful principle, and at the same time express himself [Col. 1009C] as follows: “One discovers the illusion of the good St. Augustine,” I am tempted to say, not “One discovers the illusion of a presumptuous and poorly informed commentator,” but “One discovers the trickery of a dishonest writer.” For malice governs all M. Bayle’s deviations here, and his brilliant wit plainly destroys the reputation for probity and good faith that he enjoys.

### XI.

Will he succeed in making us perceive the strange things he pretends to discover in these words (St. Augustine, same work, no. 8)?

“If it were always a merit to be persecuted, Jesus Christ would have been content to say, ‘Blessed are those who suffer persecution,’ and would not have added, ‘for righteousness’ sake’ (Matt. 5:10). Likewise, if it were always an evil to persecute, David would not have said, ‘I persecuted those who secretly slander their neighbor’ (Ps. 101:5).”

“I can scarcely believe what I see,” exclaims M. Bayle. “What, then, if you please?” It is that St. Augustine [Col. 1009D] makes such poor use of passages from Scripture. Is this evil a monster in the passage before us? Yes and no, for it is a chimera, and M. Bayle’s enthusiasm ought to provoke laughter. He speaks like a disoriented man who has lost his way. Let us try to put him back on the right path.

The Donatists, protected by Julian the Apostate and subsequently supported by the tyrants Firmus and Gildo, who seized Africa during the reign of Honorius, had treated the Catholics very harshly. The Catholics were accustomed to console themselves with the thought that Holy Scripture often represents persecution as a good for those who suffer it and as an evil for those who cause it. When circumstances changed, and Honorius, having restored his affairs and exterminated the tyrants, caused severe edicts against the Donatists to be published and enforced, these sectarians wished to imitate the language of the Catholics; by giving them [Col. 1010A] the odious name of persecutors, they sought to appropriate the merit of persecuted people.

These circumstances must be considered, and this situation of the African Church must be kept in mind, in order properly to understand the passage in question. The Donatists (St. Augustine, *Epistle* 44, otherwise 163, chap. 4, no. 7) believed that they had as much reason as the Catholics had had to glory in being persecuted and to condemn their persecutors. This was tantamount to denying that the true merit of persecutions depended upon suffering them for righteousness, and that there could be good persecutors of any kind. In order to accommodate himself to the language of Scripture, St. Augustine here uses the word “persecutor” in a favorable sense, although elsewhere he condemns this usage. M. Bayle later takes him to task on this matter and accuses him of contradiction. That is of no consequence.

With regard to the passage now occupying us, the commentator’s principal objection is that the Psalmist is not speaking of religious persecution; [Col. 1010B] that St. Augustine therefore cites him improperly; and that this Father is intolerable for failing to distinguish religious persecution from other persecutions. Why should he have distinguished it, and why should he have scrupled to apply the Psalmist’s passage to every kind of persecution, since the Donatists generally, without specifying anything, took pride in being persecuted; since none of the various parties of this sect was tolerant, nor did any of them think of disputing with the Catholic princes the right to punish the profession of religious error as a crime; and since the Rogatists, who were the most moderate of Donat’s sectarians, after crying injustice on the mere supposition that the true communion of the Church of Jesus Christ was being proscribed in their persons, confined themselves to saying that, if they were in the wrong, charity was at least being violated?

### XII.

[Col. 1010C]

Nothing is more surprising than M. Bayle’s reflections on the words I am about to quote:

“The wicked have never ceased persecuting the good, nor the good the wicked; but the former act unjustly and with the intention of harming, whereas the latter act charitably and as much as the necessity of correction requires. . . . Just as impious men have put prophets to death, prophets have put impious men to death; just as Jews have been seen with whips in their hands against Jesus Christ, Jesus Christ has been seen with a whip in his hand against the Jews; men have handed the apostles over to secular powers, and the apostles have handed men over to infernal powers. What, then, must one pay attention to in all these examples, except which of the two acts for truth or for iniquity, to harm or to correct?” (St. Augustine, *Epistle* 93, otherwise 48, to Vincent the Rogatist, chap. 2, no. 8.)

This discourse continues the preceding text and thought.

[Col. 1010D] The sole thing that St. Augustine undertakes to develop and make clearly felt is that the Donatists were wrong to glory in the sufferings they brought upon themselves through their attachment to error, and to persuade themselves that the Catholics were moved to make them suffer by a spirit of vengeance and ill will—just as, shortly before, the Catholics had considered themselves fortunate to be mistreated for the cause of the Church and had attributed a perverse intention and cruel feelings to the Donatists who persecuted them. This is M. Bayle’s ridiculous and calumnious invention, which here makes St. Augustine appear to think that, provided one does things in favor of a true opinion and with the intention of correcting one’s neighbor, everything is permitted!
