And this because the commentator maliciously claims that St. Augustine is laboring to prove what the holy doctor merely presents as an uncontested point: namely, that every stubborn superstition [Col. 1011A] that rises against the true worship of God is a crime punishable even before the tribunal of men.

Does St. Augustine not suppose that the prophets, independently of the truth they preached and the good end they intended, were otherwise authorized by God to put the impious to death? Does he not suppose that Jesus Christ, independently of the zeal for the house of God that consumed him, was master of the Temple and had the right to drive out its profaners? Does he not suppose that the apostles, independently of their holiest aims, acted by virtue of the power of the keys entrusted to them when they handed sinners over to infernal powers? St. Augustine’s purpose, then, is not to show that teaching the truth, having the right intention, and setting out to correct and instruct are warrants for doing whatever one wishes. He is concerned only to confound the presumptuous consolation with which the Donatists flattered themselves, being justly punished by the emperor, by showing them [Col. 1011B] that one has no right to glory in persecutions or to condemn one’s persecutors when one does not possess truth or charity on one’s side. However evident this maxim may be, the Donatists contradicted it by their conduct.

M. Bayle is admirable: he cannot conceive that St. Augustine should inculcate upon blinded and obstinate men something clear, something no one doubts; yet he can conceive that the holy doctor should devote himself to persuading them of what is manifestly false, what everyone denies. But it is certainly M. Bayle alone who attributes to St. Augustine the detestable moral principle from which he delights in deducing horrible consequences in order to make this holy Father odious—like those unworthy officers of justice who, seizing an honest man’s papers, slip into them material with which to bring a case against him. The late M. de la Motte-Houdart made a remark worthy of him in the refutation he wrote of a critical judgment in which M. Bayle had treated him very badly. [Col. 1011C] After demonstrating that this censor had attacked him unjustly and in bad faith, he concluded with these words: “M. Bayle will blush in proportion to his probity.” I mention this phrase because it now comes back to my mind; it would fit just as well anywhere else as here.

### XIII.

A great cause for shame on the commentator’s part is that he has misunderstood almost every sentence of which the letter to Vincent the Rogatist is composed, and has not even properly entered into the meaning of what is clearest, as in these words:

“But, you say, nowhere in the Gospel or in the writings of the apostles do we find that they ever had recourse to the kings of the earth against the enemies of the Church. It is true. But this is because the prophecy, ‘Listen, kings of the earth; be instructed, you who judge the peoples, and serve the Lord with fear,’ had not been fulfilled” (St. Augustine, same work, chap. 3, no. 9).

[Col. 1011D] It is evident that the fulfillment of this prophecy is the conversion of rulers to Christianity, as a consequence of which, having become children of the Church, they are obliged to protect her. Thus St. Augustine’s thought is that, since the kings of the earth were not Christians, no secular power—whose sole prerogative it is to punish with temporal penalties crimes that injure religion—was favorable to Christianity. The holy doctor’s answer should be understood to mean not that force was lacking to the Christian commonwealth in the time of the apostles, but that it lacked the legitimate power to employ coercion by acting upon property and bodies. This passage of St. Augustine, then, is not remotely, nor even nearly, the same thing as what M. Bayle makes the canonists say: “If the first Christians did not take up arms against the pagans, it is because they were too weak.”

### XIV.

[Col. 1012A]

I shall be as brief as M. Bayle concerning what follows. Since it may happen that among those Christians who have allowed themselves to be seduced and led into error by wicked men there are sheep of Christ who, however strayed they may be, must sooner or later return to the fold, this is why the severity used toward them is tempered, and why all possible gentleness and moderation are maintained in the losses and banishments they are obliged to suffer in order to bring them to their senses (St. Augustine, same work, no. 10). This translation is not faithful, and it seems that M. Bayle gave M. Dubois the cue to render it in a manner that would serve to confound St. Augustine, as we shall see in the following article. For the moment it is enough to observe that M. Bayle has not found again the guiding star he lost. He continues to believe that St. Augustine is defending the imperial laws that proscribed the Donatist sect [Col. 1012B], in order to avert the charge of injustice, whereas the holy doctor merely intends to show that these laws are a paternal and benevolent punishment.

### XV.

Here is a passage in which the commentator’s deviations appear in their full light. St. Augustine continues as follows:

“There is no one among us, any more than among you Donatists, who does not approve the emperors’ laws against pagan sacrifices. Yet those laws impose much harsher penalties and put to death those who commit such impieties, whereas in the laws enacted against you, the aim was to draw you out of error rather than to punish your crime” (St. Augustine, same work).

M. Bayle here becomes entangled of his own free will. “It would be difficult to count,” he says, “all the errors of judgment that one discovers in these words.” Why did he not enumerate all the acts of bad faith that he had to imagine and [Col. 1012C] put into operation in order to serve as foundations for these alleged errors? He would have found an equal number of errors of judgment of which he himself, and not St. Augustine, is truly guilty.

1. M. Bayle evidently understood from this passage that it was not a disputed question between the Catholics and the Donatists, between St. Augustine and Vincent the Rogatist, whether powers established by God could justly forbid their subjects every form of worship rejected by the true religion and impose afflictive penalties upon those who resisted. It would be a very singular matter if the followers of Donat had granted the emperors the right to punish idolatry while disputing their right to punish heresy. In that case St. Augustine would have reasoned as follows: “One has the right to punish idolatry; therefore one has the right to punish heresy.” His attention would not have been confined to comparing the greater and lesser severity exercised against the two. This is demonstrative and obvious, yet M. Bayle, [Col. 1012D] who sees and feels it, nevertheless portrays St. Augustine as wholly occupied with piling proof upon proof in order to establish, in answering the Donatists, what they plainly had no intention of disputing with him. It is difficult to decide whether the commentator is more deficient in judgment or in good faith.

2. M. Bayle is troubled about what will become of this distinguishing mark of wicked persecutors given by St. Augustine (no. 8): that they seek the life, and pay no attention to what they cut away; and of this other distinguishing mark of good persecutors: that they seek only to heal and attack only the gangrene. He is, I say, troubled about what will become of these marks of distinction if good persecutors—the persecutors approved by St. Augustine and by the entire body of Christians—put the followers of paganism to death without remission. And I [Col. 1013A] am troubled about what will become of M. Bayle’s claim that St. Augustine adduces these distinguishing marks in order to persuade the Donatists of the justice of the persecution they suffer, since the persecutors approved by the Donatists themselves, just as by St. Augustine, put the followers of paganism to death without remission.

I am certain that the commentator could not give me as good an account of his claim as I am about to give him of the distinguishing marks that trouble him. Was this not a needless concern? Could M. Bayle have failed for a moment to understand that failing to proportion the punishment to the offense, condemning someone to death without any legitimate cause—and not simply condemning someone to death—is what is meant by seeking the life and paying no attention to what one cuts away? Those who seek only to heal, who attack only the gangrene without changing their intention or purpose, are often obliged to issue death sentences in order to prevent the contagion of bad example: [Col. 1013B] M. Bayle can easily understand this. St. Augustine would not lack judgment, and his distinction between wicked and good persecutors would be reasonable, even if he wished the death penalty sometimes to be ordered by good persecutors, provided that this Father, content to exterminate thieves and brigands, did not consent to let the impious live in peace and multiply with impunity. But why did the commentator not speak plainly? Why did he need to add bad faith to the insolent contempt he shows toward one of the Church’s greatest doctors, and to twist his thought in order to give himself the false appearance of possessing more sense than St. Augustine?

3. Another error of judgment that M. Bayle attributes to St. Augustine is founded upon the unfaithful translation M. Dubois gave us of the words that formed the subject of the preceding article:

> *Sed plane in eis qui sub nomine Christi errant, seducti a perversis, ne forte oves Christi sint errantes, et ad [Col. 1013C] gregem TALITER revocandae sint, temperata severitas et magis mansuetudo servatur, ut coercitione exsiliorum atque damnorum, admoneantur considerare quid quare patiantur.*

“But plainly, in the case of those who go astray under the name of Christ, led astray by wicked men—lest perhaps they should be Christ’s straying sheep and should have to be brought back to the fold in this manner (*taliter*)—severity is tempered and greater gentleness is maintained, so that, through the constraint of exiles and losses, they may be admonished to consider what they are suffering and why they are suffering it.”

According to St. Augustine, the reason why severity is tempered and all possible moderation is maintained toward heretics is not, as M. Dubois expresses it in his translation, that it may happen that among those Christians who have allowed themselves to be seduced there are predestined persons. Rather, it is that it may happen that there are predestined persons who must be brought back to the unity of the Catholic Church in this manner and by means of this tempered severity: *Et ad gregem TALITER revocandae sint*—“and must be brought back to the fold in this manner.” M. Dubois perhaps had some interest in not making St. Augustine say that predestined persons were to be converted through fear of punishments; just as M. Bayle, that learned man and famous critic, has some interest here in pretending not to understand Latin and not to be in a position to point out the enormous infidelities found [Col. 1013D] in M. Dubois’s translation.

Whatever the case, the meaning I have just explained is demonstrated not only by the word *taliter*, but also by the whole continuation of St. Augustine’s discourse. For let us suppose for a moment that M. Dubois’s translation is faithful and exact. M. Bayle, who adopts it, is too lenient when he merely saddles the holy doctor with this strange consequence: that there can be none among the pagans of those predestined souls, those sheep whom God has given to his Son and who will sooner or later take their place in the fold. It would follow further, as M. Bayle very properly infers, that ministers of the Gospel are and always have been exempt from laboring for the conversion of pagans. This is contradicted by all the monuments attesting that we are the descendants of pagans who believed the Gospel, and it is moreover contrary to a fact that St. Augustine himself [Col. 1014A] reports in this letter—namely, that the emperors’ laws against idolaters had converted a great many pagans and were still converting more every day.

That is saying too little, and M. Bayle graciously allows St. Augustine to escape one of the greatest absurdities, which is to reason as follows: “Gentlemen Donatists, the malice of those who seduced you is great; a false zeal for the glory and worship of God deceived you; your ignorance was indeed culpable, but it greatly lessens your crime; therefore there are predestined persons among you, but not among the pagans. Yet if you had not been seduced, if you had not been deceived, if your ignorance did not make you less culpable, there would be no more predestined persons among you than among the pagans.” This is how St. Augustine reasons, if M. Dubois and M. Bayle have correctly understood his thought. Shall we believe that the commentator was ashamed openly [Col. 1014B] to attribute to a holy Father this way of linking a consequence with its principle? No; a thousand examples would disabuse us of that notion. He does not blush to place such ravings incessantly at the expense of the most respectable figures; and, in order to acquire among the superficial minds of our libertines the reputation of being a powerful reasoner, he believes he must make Augustine, Chrysostom, and Basil speak the language of the madhouse.

But here it is too evident that Saint Augustine reasons correctly and speaks to the Donatists in this manner: “People deal with you quite differently from the way they deal with the pagans, because the light of the Gospel, having exposed the absurdity and folly of paganism with the utmost clarity, makes the idolaters of today more inexcusable than you, who, under the pretext of pity, have been deceived by wicked men, and of whom one may say, in a certain sense, what the Apostle said of the Jews: ‘I bear them witness that they have zeal for the law of God, but not according to knowledge; for, being ignorant of the righteousness that comes from God and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to the righteousness that comes from God’ [Col. 1014C] (Rom. 10:2–3). Therefore you ought to be corrected and restrained with every possible consideration and moderation, and the predestined who are among you ought to be brought back into the unity of the Catholic Church by means of measured severity, so that what is done to you may appear rather a warning to abandon error than the punishment of a crime.”

Saint Augustine’s Latin reads:

*De vobis autem corripiendis atque coercendis habita ratio est, qua potius admoneremini ab errore discedere, quam pro scelere puniremini. Potest enim fortasse de vobis dici quod Apostolus de Judaeis, Testimonium illis perhibeo, quia zelum Dei habent, sed non secundum scientiam, ignorantes enim Dei justitiam, et suam volentes constituere, justitiae Dei non sunt subjecti*.

“But in correcting and restraining you, account has been taken such that you might rather be admonished to depart from error than punished for a crime. For perhaps it may be said of you what the Apostle says of the Jews: ‘I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; for, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, they are not subject to God’s righteousness’” (Rom. 10:2–3; Saint Augustine, same work, no. 10).

[Col. 1014D]

**4.** M. Bayle flatly decides that Saint Augustine does not know what he is saying and that, consequently, he is a witness to be hissed off the stage whenever his authority is invoked concerning the coercion used to bring back those in error. It is clear that up to this point he has not supported his decision very well—a decision that is the object of the whole third part of his *Philosophical Commentary*. Nevertheless, it must be admitted that, for the moment, M. Bayle insults Saint Augustine in this way only conditionally: he merely supposes that M. Brueys, an excellent controversialist whom the commentator calls a poor man, is not deserving of all the public jeering because he cited Saint Augustine in favor of coercion in his response to the Protestants’ complaints.

[Col. 1015A]

It is worth observing that M. Bayle, according to the author of his *Life*, wrote in the style of Montaigne, and that in this style coarsenesses are refinements. But what puts M. Bayle in the mood to utter these pretty things? It is that he flatters himself that he has caught M. Brueys in manifest contradiction with Saint Augustine. “This Father,” he says, “approves violence both toward heretics and toward pagans; but toward the latter, even to the ultimate punishment, since they are farther removed from the Church, whereas for that very reason he wants heretics not to be mistreated to the point of being put to death. Sieur Brueys, on the contrary, maintains that the Church should employ only instruction toward pagans, and that she may punish heretics like rebellious children over whom she has rights and claims infinitely greater than over strangers and infidels; besides,” he adds, “pagans remain distant from the Church only because her dogmas are incomprehensible to them, whereas heretics are so out of aversion to her.”

[Col. 1015B]

Those worldly people who read M. Bayle for amusement—that is, superficially and without taking the trouble to examine in depth the matters he treats, which moreover are not within their practice or competence—such people, I say, may judge from this passage whether all their good sense and all their ability in financial affairs, jurisprudence, and a thousand other matters really qualify them to pronounce upon what they read and what appears clearest to them in the works of so artful a writer. Who would not say that the contradiction between M. Brueys and Saint Augustine is palpable? M. Brueys’s view is faithfully presented, and Saint Augustine’s words are reported exactly in this respect at the beginning of the article.

[Col. 1015C]

No one thinks to observe that M. Brueys speaks of idolaters and heretics without reference to any particular circumstance, considering simply the nature of their condition, which subjects those who have received baptism to the jurisdiction of the Church, but not the others; whereas Saint Augustine, on the contrary, is not speaking of idolaters and heretics in general, but of particular people who found themselves in a situation where the rule established by M. Brueys did not apply. Indeed, Saint Augustine is speaking of the Donatists, and he distinguishes among them those who had been deceived from their deceivers. The measured severity he wishes to be used concerns only the former. He is far from showing the same indulgence toward the latter. Moreover, the reason why he believes heretics who have been deceived should not be mistreated to the point of being put to death is their ignorance and the illusion of a false zeal, which lessens their guilt. By an artful piece of trickery, M. Bayle substitutes another reason for this one, without Saint Augustine’s acknowledgment and against his intention—namely, that pagans are farther from the Church and heretics less far from it. That reason would place all heretics on the same level, deceivers and deceived alike, and all idolaters as well, both those who had never heard of the Christian religion and those who knew it perfectly.

[Col. 1015D]

One ought to think more carefully when one undertakes to supply thoughts to Saint Augustine. The idolaters whom the holy doctor mentions were former subjects of the Roman Empire who, living among Christians, had always been surrounded by the light of the Gospel from the first use of their reason, yet had obstinately persisted in retaining the superstitious worship of idols, whose vanity had been demonstrated to them from every side and which it was much easier for them to recognize than for a Donatist to perceive his error. Finally, the death penalty decreed by the emperors against idolaters and approved by Saint Augustine was incurred neither by refusing to believe in Jesus Christ and prepare oneself for baptism, nor by the public profession of unbelief, but only by the external act of offering sacrifice to idols.

[Col. 1016A]

These reflections are necessary in order to discover by what infamous deception M. Bayle sets Saint Augustine against M. Brueys. They would cost too much effort for readers who seek only amusement and who, because they understand worldly affairs and the mechanisms of politics, or because they can understand at first glance a statement of accounts and a legal brief, presume that the same is true of works in which points of religion are debated. M. Bayle counted on their approval; and it seems that he also intended to impose just as easily upon that people of philosophers who call themselves such because they have read a few books of philosophy.

## XVI

The commentator declares that this matter does not concern him:

“As for urging the emperors to make laws against schismatics and heretics, or having them enforced once they have been made, you will remember the violence with which the other Donatists attacked the party of the Maximianists, etc.; and above all you will not forget that, in the petition by which they implored the authority of the emperor [Col. 1016B] Julian against us, they told that prince, whom they knew to be an apostate and an idolater, that he was concerned only with justice and that nothing else could influence him” (Saint Augustine, same work, chap. 4, no. 12).

This concerns M. Bayle so directly that, if one adds a few lines that follow shortly afterward, the third part of the *Philosophical Commentary* will evidently and indisputably appear to be a tissue of impostures. What is required for this? Only that, from reading this passage, it become as clear as daylight that the justice of the penalties imposed upon genuine heretics was an agreed point among the Donatists, and that it was not at all the issue in the dispute that arose between them and Saint Augustine concerning the imperial laws proscribing their sect. And in order for this to be as clear as daylight, is it not enough that Vincent the Rogatist wrote to Saint Augustine in these terms, or in terms equivalent to them?

“However just the laws you have obtained from the emperor [Col. 1016C] against us may seem to you, because you truly believe us to be heretics, did episcopal charity and gentleness allow you to ask the emperor for them?”

No sensible person who wished to be convinced that these were approximately the terms of Vincent the Rogatist’s letter to Saint Augustine would demand more evident proof than these words from Saint Augustine’s reply to Vincent the Rogatist, which follow the passage now under discussion:

“If nothing, however just, is to be asked of emperors, why did your authors ask Julian for what they believed to be just?”

There is no reason to fear that Saint Augustine’s meaning has been distorted in our favor in M. Dubois’s translation, as it has in favor of M. Bayle:

*Si nihil justum ab imperatore petendum est, cur a Juliano petitum est quod justum putatum est?*

[Col. 1016D]

These words give me occasion to cite a piece of logic to set beside the one M. Bayle employs: he readily adorns his discourse with the terms of the schools. In order to destroy the advantage Saint Augustine derives from the accusations brought against the Catholics by the Donatists before the emperors’ tribunal, the commentator says that this Father argues *a dicto simpliciter ad dictum secundum quid*—from what is said absolutely to what is said in a qualified sense. This reproach is based solely on the fact that M. Bayle himself argues *de falso supponente*—from a false supposition. In his view, the holy doctor confuses accusations for crimes with penalties inflicted for opinions.

This supposes, first, that Saint Augustine reproaches the Donatists only for bringing accusations concerning crimes, and not for harassing and tormenting their adversaries on account of opinions. M. Bayle flatters himself that his reader will forget Saint Augustine’s explicit mention of the excesses of cruelty to which the Donatists resorted both against the Maximianists and against the Rogatists, because they did not conform to their views in every respect:

[Col. 1017A]

“Those from whom you separated were exceedingly fierce, both against you, as far as we have been able to hear, and against the Maximianists; this we also prove by certain documents of the proceedings.”

*Illi quidem a quibus vos separastis, acerrimi fuerunt, et contra vos, quantum audire potuimus, et contra Maximianistas; quod gestorum etiam certis documentis probamus.*

This supposes, secondly, that the Donatists considered accusations for crimes just, but penalties inflicted for opinions in matters of faith unjust. That is the chimera upon which M. Bayle built the whole third part of his *Philosophical Commentary*, and which Saint Augustine destroys here with the utmost clarity. On this point the commentator charges the holy doctor only with a very transparent quibble; thereby he shows that he distrusts, in some measure, the success of his deception. The same is true when he pretends not to know whether he should be distressed or not at calling “little rhetorical artifices and sophistry” what Saint Augustine says: that, in giving Julian the praises they gave him, the Donatists either lied in an infamous manner or acknowledged that idolatry was a just thing.

[Col. 1017B]

M. Bayle notwithstanding, this is not a small matter, nor does it bear the slightest mark of quibbling. The name of Julian the Apostate had rightly become so odious to all Christians that they were not permitted to set aside his idolatry in order to tell him, in a public act, that he was concerned only with justice; just as English Catholics would not have been permitted to set aside Henry VIII’s schism in order to pay him a similar compliment. Charles II is ill chosen for comparison with Julian the Apostate. A prince who, through the misfortune of his birth, is an idolater or a heretic is a different case from a deserter of the faith.

[Col. 1017C]

Where does M. Bayle find his parallels? He compares the praise the Donatists gave Julian the Apostate with the praises Saint Gregory gave the emperor Phocas and Queen Brunhilda. On this subject, in his *Historical and Critical Dictionary*, he treated that holy and great pope very harshly, without thinking himself obliged to prove that the emperor Phocas and Queen Brunhilda were known to Saint Gregory to be as wicked as they were when he gave them those praises; yet he thinks it wrong for Saint Augustine to condemn the unworthy compliment with which the Donatists flattered an abominable apostate! But this critic’s maxim is to spare the saints nothing and excuse everything in the impious, to lower what is highest and raise what is lowest in the esteem of men. His system is to restore equality everywhere, and especially among religions. This is the end he pursues in the reflections he makes on the following words.

## XVII

[Col. 1017D]

“You see clearly now, I am sure, that one must not consider whether force is used, but what one is forced to do—that is, whether it is toward good or toward evil. This is not to say that anyone becomes good by force, but fear of what one does not wish to suffer makes one open one’s eyes to the truth” (Saint Augustine, same work, chap. 5).

Since M. Bayle always misconstrues Saint Augustine’s thought because he refuses to perceive the holy doctor’s true purpose, he makes him reason as follows:

“One does wrong in using force only when one forces those who were in the truth to pass into error. Now, we have not forced those who were in the truth to pass into error, for we, who are orthodox, have forced you, who are schismatics or heretics, to join our party; therefore we have done no wrong.”

M. Bayle remembers his logic well enough to say that this is the sophism called *petitio principii*—begging the question—but does not remember it well enough to see that here again he himself argues *de falso supponente*. In fact, Saint Augustine is not attempting to prove that it is not wrong or unjust to force heretics, but only that charity is not violated by doing so. Thus the sophism called *petitio principii* disappears: the Donatists’ objection was that, even supposing they truly were schismatics and heretics, they ought not to be forced, because, even if no injustice were committed, charity would at least be violated. Why does M. Bayle want to make them tolerant in spite of themselves?

[Col. 1018A]

Yet I do not doubt that, had he lived in their time, he would have won them over to toleration, however far removed they were from it. When the commentator speaks to schismatics and heretics, he proves to them without difficulty either that every sect has the right to use coercion or that none should have it. But if he addresses Catholics who are instructed in their catechism, they will laugh at his argument, which is founded on the supposed impossibility of the various parties convincing one another—as though God had given his true Church no other means of making herself unmistakably recognized than discussion of the substance of controversies!

[Col. 1018B]

The Calvinist doctrine of private judgment is the fixed point at which M. Bayle establishes his reader. From there he leads him to the equality and indifference of religions under the name of toleration; he brings him close to Pyrrhonism and leaves him within two steps of irreligion. But let us not stray from Saint Augustine, who continues as follows.

## XVIII

“We can produce not only individuals but entire cities which, formerly Donatist, are now Catholic and detest the diabolical crime of their former separation, and which would not be Catholic without those laws against which you protest” (Saint Augustine, same work).

[Col. 1018C]

M. Bayle finds this reasoning unworthy of refutation; he would be ashamed to display its weakness at length; Saint Augustine arouses his pity. The Catholics of France, who thought in the same way as Saint Augustine, had, he says, very limited vision, since they did not perceive that they were reasoning on the principle that everything whose outcomes are successful is just. From this it would follow that the religion of Muhammad and its opposite are just, and that a Roman Catholic would have to agree that the laws of Edward and Queen Elizabeth were as just as those of Queen Mary; thus, if utility is the sole rule of justice, the most diametrically opposed things are equally just.

Brilliant minds of M. Bayle’s stamp do not have limited vision, but sometimes they see beyond the object; and they are liable to such strange wanderings that they represent other people’s common sense in the colors of extravagance—provided, however, that they are brilliant minds and good people at the same time, and that malice has no part in their conduct.

[Col. 1018D]

The absurd consequences that M. Bayle draws in abundance, and very skillfully, from Saint Augustine’s words taken in the wrong sense have not caused him to doubt for a moment whether he had grasped the holy doctor’s thought correctly. They indicate in the commentator either extreme wickedness or an inconceivable intoxication of mind. Saint Augustine is setting forth the marvelous fruits obtained from enforcing the imperial laws that, under severe penalties, prohibited the Donatists from holding their private assemblies, solely in order to make them feel how beneficial those laws were to them and how wrong they were to complain that they had not been treated charitably. Should a sober and level-headed man see in this the extravagant principle that everything whose outcomes are successful is just?

[Col. 1019A]

M. Bayle pities the ingenuousness, as he calls it, with which Saint Augustine confessed that his colleagues had brought him back from his initial opinion by showing him the benefits of coercion. Can one read without indignation the temerity with which he asserts that Saint Augustine’s initial opinion was the same as his own—that is, that the holy doctor was initially tolerant, but that when the other African bishops pointed out to him the good effects produced by coercion and concluded that coercion was just, this Father could not withstand the force of reasoning worthy of a madhouse and, according to M. Bayle, so perfectly suited to Saint Augustine’s mind that it completely convinced him?

At the same time, the commentator continues to maintain that the only way to rid oneself of errors and come to know the truth in matters of faith and dogma is individual instruction and persuasion. Does he claim that God has given everyone a better mind than Saint Augustine?

## XIX

[Col. 1019B]

But M. Bayle is mistaken concerning this Father. Saint Augustine needed to be convinced by his colleagues only with regard to charity. He had difficulty reconciling its spirit and rules with the bishops’ intention of appealing to the emperor’s power and the severity of his rescripts in order to put an end to Donat’s schism. One of the reasons that contributed most to changing the holy doctor’s opinion was that he eventually understood that his supposed charity, which always led him to spare the persons of those in error, was contrary to the charity he owed to God and to Jesus Christ. What else does he express in these words?

“Was I to prevent the confiscation of what you call your property, while you proscribe Jesus Christ with impunity? Was I to prevent you from being deprived of the freedom to dispose of it by will according to Roman law, while by your slanderous accusations you trample underfoot the testament that God himself made in favor of our fathers, etc.?” (Saint Augustine, same work, chap. 5, no. 19).

[Col. 1019C]

I would forgive the commentator for calling these antitheses and pointed turns of phrase employed by Saint Augustine if he knew how to direct them toward their true purpose. But M. Bayle sees in this passage that it is just to confiscate the property of those who proscribe Jesus Christ, and that it is just to deprive those who trample underfoot God’s testament of the freedom to dispose of anything by will. By what enchantment does he see something other than what he reads?

“Was I to prevent the confiscation and removal, etc.” Does this mean: “It is just to confiscate and remove”? Is it not clear that Saint Augustine’s discourse presupposes, and in no way seeks to prove, the justice of the imperial laws that confiscated the Donatists’ property and deprived them of the power to dispose of it by will? Does the holy doctor not affirm solely that charity did not oblige him to prevent the promulgation of these laws?

[Col. 1019D]

It is therefore entirely useless for M. Bayle, in the third part of the *Philosophical Commentary*, to be tiresome to the point of death through the endless repetition of the false or misapplied principles upon which he had relied in the first two parts in order to dispute with the Church—or rather, with her protectors—the right to coerce heretics. For, as I have already said so many times, since the Donatists did not contest this right, Saint Augustine had no need to trouble himself with establishing it.

Someone will say to me: “How, then, would you have had the commentator proceed? He found Saint Augustine in his path. Was he not obliged somehow to respond to the authority of this Father, which was being invoked in favor of coercion? He had no means of drawing the weight of so respectable an authority to his side and making it incline in his favor, because that authority is evidently opposed to him. He therefore had to strive to destroy it by portraying the holy doctor’s thoughts in a form all the more hideous and contemptible because people are accustomed to hold his genius in higher and more magnificent esteem. What better course could he have taken than to reverse, but with art and subtlety, the meaning of Saint Augustine’s texts, and to turn the translator’s blunders against this Father, so as to have occasion to attribute to him a long series of arguments, each more impertinent than the last, and to make him responsible for a multitude of consequences as dreadful as they are ridiculous?”

[Col. 1020A]

Nevertheless, I believe he would have done better not to expose himself to being convicted of so many bold and glaring impostures. Why did he not content himself with this simple statement: “I, Pierre Bayle, hold that Saint Augustine is a fool”? He would have uttered only one foolishness, whereas he pours them out without number.

## XX

We have now reached a lengthy passage from which the commentator makes abundant material for triumph:

[Col. 1020B]

“If there are people who abuse those laws that the emperors have made against you and use them to exercise their private hatreds, instead of using them as an instrument of charity to draw you out of error, we disapprove their conduct and are deeply grieved by it. This is not because anyone can say that something belongs to him unless it belongs to him either by divine right, by which everything belongs to the just, or by the right established by human beings, which depends upon the temporal powers. Thus you cannot call your own what you could not claim as just persons and what, moreover, the emperors’ laws take away from you; and consequently you cannot be admitted to say, ‘This belongs to us, and we acquired it by our labor,’ since it is written that the just will profit from what the wicked have accumulated.

“Yet when, under cover of these laws . . . someone invades what you possess, we disapprove this conduct, and it causes us the greatest distress. In the same way, we condemn all those whom avarice rather than justice moves to take from you either the property of the poor or the places of your assemblies, although you possess neither of these except under the name of a church, and although only the true Church of Jesus Christ has a genuine right to such things” (Saint Augustine, same work, chap. 12, no. 50).

[Col. 1020C]

This passage appears to M. Bayle to contain paradoxes so mysterious, odious, and absurd that he believes himself obliged to number his reflections in order.

The first concerns the abuses to which enforcement of laws imposing penalties on heretics is liable. According to M. Bayle, to say that one disapproves these abuses is a vain excuse and a poor palliative remedy. Why? Because, he says, it is known that they are inevitable and extremely numerous. M. Bayle asserts this, but Saint Augustine, speaking of what was happening in his own time with regard to the Donatists, indicates that such abuses were so rare that he even doubts whether there were any. Since the commentator neglected to undertake the research that might authorize him to disparage the Roman administration and the efforts made by the governor of Africa to establish good order everywhere, why should we not abide by Saint Augustine’s testimony?

[Col. 1020D]

The second reflection is serious. “Is it not an abominable thing,” M. Bayle exclaims, “although veiled in a grand air of mystery, to say that everything belongs to the just by divine right?” He presses the consequences of this maxim, taken literally, as far as they can go. If Saint Augustine had nevertheless been a Nestorius, an Abelard, or a Calvin, he would have found favor in the eyes of our critic, who would have omitted nothing in order to imagine a favorable interpretation of these words or to show that they did not express Saint Augustine’s true thought.

[Col. 1021A]

I confess that I am as inclined to justify this saint as M. Bayle is inclined to defend the innovators and heresiarchs of every century; and it seems to me that a probable conjecture, one that cannot be decisively refuted, is sufficient to prevent our attributing to so great a doctor a ridiculous *galimatias*—a jumble of nonsense—and an abominable absurdity. I shall demand no more when it is a question of pronouncing upon the apology of an atheist or a libertine, several of which I shall encounter in M. Bayle’s *Dictionary*. Is this not perfectly reasonable?

There were four parties among the Donatists: the Claudianists, the Primianists, the Maximianists, and the Rogatists. Their particular error and folly consisted in believing themselves all just and free from sin. One need not look far for proof of this. Immediately before the passage that forms the subject of the present article, Saint Augustine reproaches Vincent for this vain presumption and makes fun of him on the matter in a very amusing way:

“Forgive me,” he says, “I am mistaken when I cite to you the example of baptism conferred by a drunkard. I had forgotten that I am dealing with a Rogatist, not with an ordinary Donatist. It may be that, since the number of your colleagues, and even of [Col. 1021B] your clerics, is as small as it is, there is not a single drunkard among them. Besides, your faith is Catholic, not because of the extent of your communion, but because of the observance of all the precepts as well as all the sacraments of Jesus Christ; consequently, faith will be found only in you. And even if it ought not to be found on earth, it will nevertheless be found in you, because you are no longer of the earth and no longer belong to the earth, but to heaven, where you already are in anticipation” (Saint Augustine, same work, chap. 11, no. 49).

[Col. 1021C]

It is therefore likely that this proposition—“Everything belongs to the just by divine right”—had been advanced by Vincent the Rogatist in his letter to Saint Augustine in order to prove that the emperor had no right to confiscate the property of members of his sect. Accordingly, since Saint Augustine always attacks his adversaries by the shortest route, after proving at considerable length that all the Donatists in general were outside the Church and specifically confounding the Rogatists in their claim to be all and the only just people, he puts this argument *ad hominem* to them:

“No one can say that something belongs to him unless it belongs to him either by divine right—by which, as you are pleased to maintain, everything belongs to the just—or by the right established by human beings. Now, your property does not belong to you by divine right, since you are not just, as I have just shown; nor does it belong to you by the right established by human beings, since it is taken away from you by the emperors’ laws. Therefore you cannot say that your property belongs to you.”

I am certain that M. Bayle has never said anything so plausible in favor of the heroes of irreligion. If someone in his place and under his name showed himself more difficult to satisfy when dealing with a holy Father, should he be listened to?

[Col. 1021D]

The third reflection consists in pointing out and making felt the manifest contradiction in which M. Bayle believes he has Saint Augustine trapped, a contradiction found in the alternative between divine right and the right established by human beings. For divine right, which gives everything to the just, destroys the right established by human beings without distinguishing between the just and sinners. But this contradiction no longer exists here; it exists only in the opinion of the Rogatists, who, consistently with their principles, ought to reject the right established by human beings.

The fourth reflection is employed to show that every law that does violence to even the most false conscience is unjust and tyrannical; and, according to M. Bayle, it is clear that it makes no difference whether that conscience is Huguenot, Socinian, deist, or atheist. But this had not occurred to the Donatists; there was no *Philosophical Commentary* to sharpen their minds on the subject. Does one want [Col. 1022A] Saint Augustine to have answered the objections of future advocates of toleration?

The fifth reflection concerns Saint Augustine’s application of a passage from Proverbs. M. Bayle can never admire it enough, because this Father confuses those who fall into religious error with those who commit crimes; because he transfers to what is called orthodoxy what is promised only to uprightness of heart and good conduct; and finally because he recognizes good morality only within orthodox society.

Let us bring the centuries together and set Saint Augustine opposite M. Bayle. Saint Augustine, for his part, is astonished that a supposedly Christian man should casually remove from the category of crimes everything that can be committed against God and religion; should boldly proclaim that God has given such equivocal signs for distinguishing the true religion that even the greatest uprightness of heart may fail to recognize it and reject it; and should finally claim to have an idea of sound morality when religion has no part in it.

[Col. 1022B]

The sixth reflection rests upon M. Dubois’s unfaithful translation of these words:

*Quisquis ex occasione hujus legis . . . res vestras proprias cupide appetit, displicet nobis.*

They should have been translated as follows:

“If, under cover of this law, anyone, out of greed, seeks the confiscation of your property, we disapprove this conduct, and it causes us the greatest distress.”

What displeases Saint Augustine is that the greed and covetousness of private individuals hasten the effect of a law which charity, by which it was dictated, requires to be enforced only as a last resort and with every possible consideration and moderation. Nothing could be better.

But M. Dubois translates it in this way:

“When, under cover of these laws . . . someone invades what you possess, we disapprove this conduct, etc.”

If the commentator had not confined himself exclusively to Saint Augustine’s text, distorted in this way by M. Dubois [Col. 1022C], he would have missed this playful and facetious stroke: “Admire Saint Augustine’s compassion: he approves with all his heart that the laws strip a Donatist of all his property, and he disapproves of the Catholics’ procedure in seizing that property.” This is amusing enough: blaming the executor while praising the one who orders the execution. Is this not a fine secret for finding something to admire and mock in Saint Augustine—to confuse him with his unfaithful translator, who generously attributes to him all the absurdity that surprises and provokes laughter?

Would anyone ever have suspected that a man who understood Latin would dare to prosecute Saint Augustine before the tribunal of the public solely on the authority of the French translation of his letters? And if anyone were capable of such a thing, would anyone ever have guessed that it would be M. Bayle, that learned and celebrated critic? I therefore have ample reason here to protest the nullity of the laughter and contempt that have been, are being, and will be directed against the Greek or Latin Fathers by M. Bayle’s readers, who do not know these languages, or who neglect to consult the originals [Col. 1022D].

In the seventh and final reflection, M. Bayle passes from jesting to ill temper. Let us quote his own words: “Finally, what he says” (Saint Augustine), “that the Donatists’ temples and the endowments they had established for the maintenance of their poor and sick belonged to the true Church, is so miserable that I shall not deign to refute it.” Apparently M. Bayle enjoys becoming angry as much as he enjoys joking, since the basis of his indignation is entirely his own. Does the commentator see in Saint Augustine’s text that the basilicas occupied by the Donatists had been built, and that the foundations they administered for the maintenance of the poor and sick had been established after their separation from the Catholic Church? If the matter were otherwise, was this not a restitution that they were being required to make of property they had taken from the Catholic Church [Col. 1023A]? And as for the new buildings, establishments, and acquisitions, were all these not attached to a district of which the Catholic Church alone had previously possessed legitimate possession and ownership? Who does not know that everything connected and annexed to an estate is rightly claimed by the master of that estate? Besides, Saint Augustine’s reasoning is as follows: Everything possessed under the name of the Church of Jesus Christ belongs to the true Church of Jesus Christ; now the Donatists’ temples and hospitals were possessed under the name of the Church of Jesus Christ; therefore the Donatists’ temples and hospitals belong to the true Church of Jesus Christ.

M. Bayle claims that it follows from this that the Turks’ mosques belong to Christians. He thereby informs us of something very curious: that the Turks’ mosques are possessed by them under the name of the Church of Jesus Christ. He will never find anything so amusing in Saint Augustine [Col. 1023B]. I reserve the rest for the general controversy into which M. Bayle will one day force me to enter.

## XXI

Let us finish with M. Bayle everything that concerns the letter to Vincent the Rogatist. What objection does he make to this final passage?

“But although you complain of these kinds of treatment, you have difficulty proving that they are inflicted upon you; and even if you proved it, we cannot always correct or punish those of whom you complain, and sometimes we are obliged to tolerate them” (Saint Augustine, ibid., no. 12).

Here M. Bayle overwhelms the French converters with insulting reproaches. Their pernicious maxims are, he says, always kneaded and steeped in bad faith, and we must take his word for it that they are outright scoundrels. Then he describes a fine passage from the historian Nicetas to show that Louis XIV was so absolute in his kingdom and so exactly obeyed that, if anyone had wished to prevent all the excesses committed against the Huguenots, this would have been done [Col. 1023C]. Is this not a fully complete refutation of Saint Augustine, leaving him covered with confusion?

## XXII

The first passage from the letter to Count Boniface that M. Bayle examines is this:

“When Nebuchadnezzar ordered that whoever blasphemed the God of the Hebrews should perish with his entire household, if there were some who, for having despised this law, suffered its penalty, could they have said, as these people do, that they were righteous, and could they have alleged as proof the persecution inflicted upon them by the king’s authority?” (Saint Augustine, *Epistle* 105, formerly 50, chapter 2, no. 8).

M. Bayle agrees with Saint Augustine’s censure of the Donatists’ reasoning, but at the same time he confines himself to condemning those who persecuted them. In short, the commentator would have spared himself the trouble of citing this passage if it had not given him an opportunity to speak of Nebuchadnezzar—no doubt in order to contradict Saint Augustine, who often says that this king of Babylon, insofar as he ordered the punishment of those who blasphemed the God of the Hebrews, was a type of the Christian emperors who chastised heretics [Col. 1023D].

M. Bayle points out a difference between Nebuchadnezzar’s edict and those issued against heretics. Does this prevent Nebuchadnezzar from being a type of the Christian emperors who issued edicts in favor of religion? Since when has perfect conformity between the thing signified and the type been necessary? One must have noticed that M. Bayle turns everything Saint Augustine says into an argument; that is more or less his method with respect to the other authors whom he censures.

He resembles, in some respect, a certain man who wanted to reason and to have others reason with him forever, and who, whenever a story was told, a description given, a sentiment expressed, a witty remark made, a compliment offered, or someone asked him about his health or wished him good morning or good evening, never failed to reply: “What does that prove? What do you conclude from it?” [Col. 1024A]

Moreover, M. Bayle returns here once again to his chimera, by which he imagines that Saint Augustine uses the example of Nebuchadnezzar as a reason justifying and establishing the right Christian princes possess to compel the Church to receive the obedience due to her. He is either mistaken or wishes to deceive.

In this very letter to Boniface, the question most often concerns showing that charity is not violated; there is never any question of showing that one does not sin against justice by imploring the aid of secular power to extirpate heresies. The holy Doctor everywhere takes the justice of the imperial laws for granted, and has no thought of proving it [Col. 1024B].

There are nevertheless several passages that might apparently favor M. Bayle’s claim. But if one examines them closely, the holy Doctor is not establishing the equity of coercion, or the right to coerce; he is asserting the duty and obligation, in certain circumstances, to use sovereign authority for coercion.

I am astonished that the commentator omitted a passage of this kind, which immediately precedes the one before us. Saint Augustine there declares that Christian princes must use their power to maintain the worship of God. For, he says, even in the time of the prophets, Holy Scripture condemns all the kings who did not proscribe or abolish the practices that superstition had introduced among God’s people against the law of God; conversely, it praises and exalts above all other kings those who proscribed and abolished these practices [Col. 1024C].

Why does M. Bayle not turn these words into an objection? Because he had no plausible answer to make to them. He had invoked the special and extraordinary calling that authorized Moses and Elijah to put to death those who sinned against religion; but that reason had no foundation with regard to the kings of Judah and Israel. According to M. Bayle’s principles, Moses’ and Elijah’s right should no more have been communicated to those princes than Saint Peter’s right to strike Ananias and Sapphira dead at his feet should have passed to all Christian princes.

It is wise to draw the curtain over what cannot be presented in a favorable light, and to expose repeatedly to view whatever one considers capable of making a favorable impression. That is why M. Bayle was careful not to omit the following passage.

## XXIII

“Was Hagar not persecuted by Sarah? Yet the one who persecuted was a saint, and the one who suffered persecution was wicked” (Saint Augustine, ibid., no. 9) [Col. 1024D].

The commentator may pretend as much as he likes to be weary of Saint Augustine’s repetitions: he complains of them only to conceal the fact that he delights in them, because they give him an opportunity to recall briefly to his reader’s mind what he believes he has produced most effectively against this Father’s sentiments and arguments. For in reality he is not unreasonable enough to find fault with the holy Doctor for repeating, while instructing Count Boniface, what he believed he had said well when refuting Vincent the Rogatist.

“Always the same illusion,” M. Bayle says impatiently: comparing the punishment inflicted for moral crimes with that imposed for religious opinions. Have the impious who have set themselves up as teachers of morality prevailed so far that actions offensive to religion—and in particular every form of false worship, both idolatrous worship and worship whose principle is heresy—are no longer moral crimes [Col. 1025A]? I know well that in Spinoza’s books religion is not counted among the moral virtues. But Saint Thomas, in the *Secunda Secundae*, question 81, article 5, proves that, since God is rather the end than the object or matter of religion, it follows that religion is not a theological virtue but a moral one: *Cum Deus religionis finis potius sit quam objectum vel materia, consequitur hinc religionem non theologicam, sed moralem virtutem esse*—“Since God is rather the end than the object or matter of religion, it follows from this that religion is not a theological but a moral virtue.”

And according to the doctrine of this Angel of the Schools, superstition is a crime against religion; every false worship is superstition; every worship directed by an error in faith is false worship. Therefore every worship directed by an error in faith is against religion—that is, against a moral virtue—and consequently is a moral crime.

Let us return to Saint Augustine. He is asked what possessed him to place all the blame on Hagar and to canonize Sarah’s conduct. It is true that the sacred historian in no way disapproves of the mistress and does blame the maidservant. But the Calvinist maxim of adding nothing to Scripture and adhering to the pure word of God may perhaps have been devised only to embarrass religion, not to restrain slander. At least the commentator pays it no heed when he feels like speaking ill of the ancient patriarchs. Weigh the testimonies: an angel from heaven spoke against Hagar; Calvin and M. Bayle have written against Sarah [Col. 1025B].

It is not irrelevant that the commentator includes in this section his reflections on what Saint Augustine says next (ibid., no. 10) about the case of Caecilianus. He reproaches the holy Doctor for confusing accusations brought against a prelate for his crimes or for defective ordination with the punishments inflicted upon him for his opinions. He is always playing the same note; let us answer him in the same tone. In the fifth century of the Church, people had not yet learned to distinguish from crime the public profession of attachment to, and conformity of life with, an error that dishonors God and religion. That happy discovery was reserved for the tolerants of our own day. And Saint Augustine ought to appear all the more excusable in their eyes because the Donatists were not free from this same prejudice.

But let us pay attention to these words that M. Bayle attributes to Saint Augustine: “They” (the Donatists) “persecuted Caecilianus, and they say that one is never persecuted justly.” With all due respect to the commentator, he misrepresents Saint Augustine. This Father does not attribute to the Donatists the claim that no one is ever persecuted justly. On the contrary, it is evident from the holy Doctor’s text that they did not say this, but sometimes spoke as though they held such an idea in their minds, because they had maintained, at the Conference of Carthage, that the mark of the true Church is to suffer persecution, not to inflict it: *Si autem putant quod nemo possit juste aliquem persequi, sicut in collatione dixerunt, illam esse veram Ecclesiam quae persecutionem patitur, non quae facit* (Saint Augustine, ibid.)—“But if they think that no one can justly persecute anyone, as they said at the Conference, that the true Church is the one that suffers persecution, not the one that inflicts it” [Col. 1025C].

This has been the language of all heretics whenever they were not the stronger party. They used it only to dazzle the people, and did not thereby intend to indicate that they fundamentally approved tolerance of every kind of error. The complaints of the Arians driven from the churches and exiled by the great Theodosius were not intended to request mercy for the Sabellians, nor were the Sabellians’ complaints intended to ask that the Arians be tolerated. The outcries of the Nestorians proscribed by Theodosius the Younger would not have entirely ceased if the Eutychians had been left in peace along with them. And while in this kingdom the Huguenots preached for freedom of conscience, they approved of Calvin’s having Servetus burned at Geneva [Col. 1026A]. The Donatists’ language must be interpreted in the same way. This enables us to understand the meaning of the words that follow.

## XXIV

“If good people never persecute anyone, and merely endure the persecution inflicted upon them, then it is not a saint or a good man who speaks in Psalm XVII, where it is said: ‘I will persecute my enemies, pursue them, overtake them, and give them no respite until I have defeated them’” (Saint Augustine, ibid., no. 11).

I grant M. Bayle that David is speaking here only of military exploits and of a victory won by God’s people over their enemies. I agree that Saint Augustine’s application is false, and that everyone must laugh and complain on seeing Scripture applied with so little judgment—provided, however, that the Donatists were genuinely tolerant. But if they regarded exile, imprisonment, and other punishments, when ordered or procured, as the mark and emblem of the bad party, and, when suffered, as the mark and emblem of the good party—as, for example, we see done today in order to win the favor of the multitude, which is hostile to violence and which compassion makes credulous regarding the injustice of those who inflict suffering and the innocence of those who suffer—then Saint Augustine could not have chosen or applied the passage of Scripture more aptly, and there is no one who will not laugh at the commentator’s criticism [Col. 1026B].

It is the generality of these marks and emblems—“Here are persecuted people; there are persecutors”—that imposes, and this generality is absurd: it represents every punishment and every war as hateful, and every indulgence and every peace as lovable. What could better expose its falsity and illusion than the example of David, who persecutes the enemies of God’s people [Col. 1026C]?

The description Saint Augustine next adds of the Donatists’ fury and of the brigandages they had committed against the Catholics makes their deceit evident. Afterward the saint continues:

“Since the Church had therefore been reduced to these extremities, how can one claim that we ought to endure everything rather than implore the assistance that God has provided for us through the Christian emperors? And how could we excuse ourselves before God for such negligence?” (Saint Augustine, ibid., chapter 4, no. 18) [Col. 1026D].

M. Bayle says that this is a repetition of the sophism *ignoratio elenchi*—“ignorance of the issue.” It is also a new opportunity he seizes to parade his logical terminology and to reinforce the confusion by which, from the beginning of the third part of his *Philosophical Commentary*, he has attempted to disguise the true state of the question between the Donatists and Saint Augustine. This Father means that the Donatists’ violence was the cause that determined the emperor Honorius to make them suffer the penalties they otherwise deserved for the crime of heresy, not that this violence was the sole reason they deserved punishment. Where, then, is the *ignoratio elenchi*? Is it M. Bayle or Saint Augustine who is so ineptly diverting the issue for learned readers?

What are we to make of the commentator’s surprise at not seeing the main roads and public squares filled with gibbets and pyres for the punishment of the Circumcellions, who had put the Catholic countryside to fire and sword, while seeing instead exiles, confiscations, and a thousand other punishments inflicted upon those Donatists who were honest people—that is, peaceful and tranquil [Col. 1027A]? Could the murderers and arsonists not have escaped and placed themselves beyond danger? Could they not have been punished separately, or obtained mercy through repentance and sincere conversion? Finally, does the exaggeration of the brigandages and cruelties committed by the Donatists—of which Saint Augustine is so improperly made suspect, and which are so unworthy of his character—have any foundation other than the commentator’s malignity?

## XXV

Yet he comes very close to approving this passage:

“The service that kings render to God as men is one thing, and the service they render to Him as kings is another. As men, they serve Him by living as true believers; but as kings, they serve Him only by establishing and firmly enforcing just laws whose purpose is to make people do good and prevent evil” (Saint Augustine, ibid., chapter 5, no. 19).

M. Bayle finds nothing to criticize in these words except that by “just laws” Saint Augustine means laws favorable to his own party, and by “good” he means whatever conforms to his ideas, just as by “evil” he means whatever contradicts them [Col. 1027B].

The holy Doctor would indeed be wrong if, in these two letters and in several other works, he did not demonstrate at length and with the utmost clarity that the Donatists were a party of rebels who had risen within the bosom of the Church; if he did not show more clearly than daylight both the falsity of their doctrines and the nullity of their defenses. Their cause was so miserable that M. Bayle has nowhere written in favor of their schism and heresy.

According to our critic, this is not enough, and Saint Augustine ought to have agreed upon a common principle for defining just laws. With whom? With the Donatists? No, but with the tolerants of our own day; otherwise he says nothing capable of enlightening the mind. But Saint Augustine did not believe that, in order to speak sensibly and clearly against the heretics of his century, he had to be a prophet and converse in the language of a future Bayle—an indefatigable poisoner of minds who, having set every imaginable snare for faith, prides himself on having reduced religion to a problem and insinuated a general Pyrrhonism regarding humanity’s relations with God, supplying the most ignorant and dull libertines with material for playing the reasoners and the learned [Col. 1027C].

## XXVI

Up to this point M. Bayle has attacked Saint Augustine with an air of hauteur and contempt that is unbearable. He somewhat tempers his presumptuous self-satisfaction and lowers his tone a little when confronted with these words:

“Would one not have to have lost one’s senses to say to princes: ‘Do not concern yourselves if the Church of the one you adore is attacked or revered in your kingdom’? What! They will take care to make people live according to the laws of honesty and modesty, without anyone daring to tell them that this is none of their concern, and yet one will dare to say that it is not for them to inquire whether, in their states, people follow the laws of the true religion or abandon themselves to impiety and sacrilege? For if, merely because God has given human beings free will, sacrilege must be permitted to them, why will adultery be punished? Is the soul that violates the fidelity it owes to its God less guilty than the woman who violates the fidelity she owes to her husband? And although people are punished less severely for sins committed through ignorance against religion, must religion therefore be left to be overthrown with impunity?” (Saint Augustine, ibid., chapter 5, no. 20) [Col. 1027D].

Saint Augustine’s entire discourse tends to prove the obligation, not merely the right, possessed by secular princes to use their authority to subject heretics to the yoke of obedience they owe the Church. Can this be doubted if one takes the trouble to set these words alongside those containing the objection to which Saint Augustine is responding here, expressed as follows:

“For what they say” (the Donatists), “who do not want JUST LAWS to be enacted against their impieties by the kings of the earth, is that the apostles did not ask such things of kings” (Saint Augustine, ibid., no. 19) [Col. 1028A].

Would Saint Augustine have expressed himself in this way if the Donatists had claimed that, even supposing they were wrong and genuine heretics, one could not call just the laws condemning their impieties? Instead of saying that they did not want their impieties repressed by just laws, would he not have made it clearly understood that they considered unjust every law prescribing penalties for any impiety whatsoever? That is M. Bayle’s view: he falsely charges the Donatists with supporting the same thesis, and this is the source of his perpetual error.

But what does he think of this passage? “This is highly specious,” he says, “and deserves to be answered precisely. Let us see how he proceeds.”

### 1

“I admit to Saint Augustine,” he continues, “that one would have to have lost one’s senses to object to princes’ concerning themselves with whether the Church of the God they worship is attacked or revered in their kingdom. But in what manner should they concern themselves with it? If their religion is attacked by arms, they should support it by arms; if it is attacked by books and sermons, they should support it by those same instruments.”

Indeed, Louis XIV would have achieved a fine masterpiece if, instead of revoking the Edict of Nantes, he had allowed Lutheranism and Calvinism—and not only those, but Socinianism, Mohammedanism, and atheism—to be freely taught throughout his kingdom in public writings and speeches, and had contented himself with having these various errors refuted by public writings and speeches. Would he not have been obliged to do something more—namely, to place all his subjects, male and female, in a position to be convinced and moved by sound reasons, rather than deceived and seduced by the sophisms, captious devices, and other illusions of discourse that the commentator knows all too well [Col. 1028C]? And consequently, should this prince not have had the water carriers, as well as people of quality, taught *ignoratio elenchi*, *petitio principii*, and what it means to argue *a dicto simpliciter ad dictum secundum quid*—“from an unqualified statement to a qualified one”? Should he not have made merchants and peasants, ladies and servants, more skilled in the art of reasoning than Saint Augustine, who, for lack of being a sufficiently good logician, falls into error at every step, as M. Bayle claims to show? Finally, would Louis XIV not have been charged with giving everyone intelligence, learning, and a sound taste for truth, so that each person might be capable of judging on which side truth lay?

For example, a thousand people, even among those who pride themselves most on being enlightened, may not have noticed that M. Bayle shows that sovereigns should not concern themselves at all with whether the Church of the God they worship is attacked or revered in their kingdom, at the very moment when he pretends to explain how they ought to concern themselves with it [Col. 1028D].

On reading the commentator’s words—“Princes must be content to have disputes clarified and, if possible, to convince those who err by sound reasons”—how many people will not have understood that he is mocking? Yet to say that princes must concern themselves with whether the Church of God is attacked or revered, and, in order to defend and cause the Church of God to be revered, to leave princes solely with the responsibility of having disputes clarified and convincing those who err by sound reasons, after having declared more than once that this means is impossible and chimerical—is this not mockery? That is precisely what M. Bayle does.

“The discussion of the substance of controversies,” he says, “would exhaust Methuselah’s life on the smallest article.” He therefore speaks against himself and pronounces his own condemnation when he admits that one would have to have lost one’s senses to object to princes’ concerning themselves with whether the Church of the God they worship is attacked or revered [Col. 1029A]. Not at all: for M. Bayle does not object to princes’ flattering themselves that they will live far longer than Methuselah. And a man who wraps his thought in such artifice has not lost his senses; rather, he abuses them so perniciously that one could wish he had never enjoyed the use of reason.

### 2

This objection—“Will a prince allow blasphemies, sacrileges, and impieties to be spewed forth freely and with impunity?”—does not embarrass M. Bayle. He decides that these matters must be defined by common principles; or rather, he wants the accusers and judges, in a trial brought for such crimes, to recognize as blasphemies, sacrileges, and impieties only what is such according to the accused person’s beliefs and principles [Col. 1029B].

The atheists will thank him heartily. Let them slander God and His saints at their leisure and commit the most enormous profanations: the commentator will compel the universe to agree that they are not merely not blasphemers, sacrilegious, or impious, but that it is manifestly contradictory to regard them as guilty of these crimes. They are his best friends. He has worked hard to bring them into honor, and he insinuates here that their good reputation ought unquestionably to be the universal dogma of all religions, including Christianity.

How could he fail on this occasion to assert that Saint Louis, when he ordered that all blasphemers have their tongues pierced, had committed a great injustice by not exempting those who declared themselves atheists?

M. Bayle proves what he has just said by applying for a second time a thought of M. Bossuet, Bishop of Meaux. From the Protestants’ supposition concerning the Church’s fallibility, Bossuet infers that Christianity would be the weakest of all societies in the world, the most exposed to irreconcilable divisions, and the most abandoned to innovators and factious people [Col. 1029C].

According to M. Bayle, one is compelled to admit a similar and even more horrible consequence if each sect within Christianity claims the right to define blasphemy, sacrilege, and impiety; for instead of tolerating one another peacefully, they will wage bloody war against one another. But with what appearance of reason would each Christian sect claim the right to define blasphemy, sacrilege, and impiety? From M. de Meaux’s evident thought, does it not follow just as evidently that the true Church must be infallible, and consequently that the Roman Church, which alone claims infallibility, is the true Church? It follows further that, since all the sects have issued from the Roman Church, which anathematized them all from their origin with infallible authority, that Church alone has the right to define blasphemy, sacrilege, and impiety [Col. 1029D].

I would have been curious to know M. Bayle’s true opinion concerning the punishment of the Waldensians and Anabaptists, who were condemned to the ultimate penalty for having incited peoples against magistrates and princes. Let no one tell me that his opinion on this point is in no way doubtful. For if, on the one hand, he favors prosecuting, with the full rigor of the laws, seditious heretics who cause disturbance and disorder in states, while on the other hand he claims that even the most erroneous and corrupt consciences must be shown respect for their false fear of displeasing God, it would seem that he would have authorized the Waldensians and Anabaptists to demand that not only blasphemy, sacrilege, and impiety be defined by common principles, but also sedition and revolt [Col. 1030A]. He would have obliged the accusers and judges to recognize as sedition and revolt only what was such according to the accused persons’ principles and beliefs.

Why should, in the conviction of a Calvinist or a Socinian, the false fear of displeasing God by worshiping the Eucharist or worshiping Jesus Christ be more respectable than the false fear of displeasing God by renouncing evangelical freedom in the conscience of a Waldensian or an Anabaptist? Why should the interest of God’s legitimate worship not prevail, while the interest of the peace and tranquility of states should prevail over the respect that is claimed to be due to a false fear of displeasing God?

### 3

“It is rightly,” says M. Bayle, “that princes should enforce the laws of honesty and modesty by penalties and punishments, because all their subjects acknowledge that these laws are just, and thus can violate them only maliciously, deliberately, and while believing that this displeases God, etc.”

“There,” he adds, “there is the great and fundamental reason that establishes the difference between civil actions and religious actions” [Col. 1030B].

This triumphant tone makes me suspicious. Have I understood M. Bayle’s thought correctly? Princes must enforce the laws of honesty and modesty only on the assumption that all their subjects regard these laws as just. Does what he says not amount to this? But should we not rather exclaim: “There, there is an infamous doctrine!” What! Princes should enforce the laws of honesty and modesty, provided none of their subjects is obstinately attached to the heresy of the Adamites and Picards, or persuaded that the laws of honesty and modesty are unjust by the arguments M. Bayle advances in favor of the Cynics—arguments by which he shamefully boasts of reducing human reason to impotence—provided, further, that those who, like M. Bayle, have erased from the code of natural law the chapter on duties toward God have not consequently removed from the chapter on duties toward oneself the article concerning honesty and modesty [Col. 1030C]?

I call all the readers of the *Historical and Critical Dictionary* to witness whether, in this matter, I am not a more faithful commentator on M. Bayle than he himself is on Saint Augustine.

### 4.

M. Bayle continues:

“The answer is now quite easy, by comparison with sacrilege and adultery. This is the précis of the answer: Nothing is found in the soul of a man accused of adultery to which one owes respect, and which prevents one from considering him guilty of a wicked action; whereas in the soul of a man accused of heresy one finds a motive worthy of respect—namely, fear of displeasing God—which prevents one from considering him guilty of sacrilege. Thus, if adultery had heresy as its principle, as among the Gnostics, Manichaeans, and Molinosists, it would no longer be a crime, and one could not punish it without injustice, because the accused would not admit that adultery is [Col. 1030D] a wicked action.”

M. Bayle leaves it to his readers formally to deduce this consequence, to which the abominable respect he demands for the false fear of displeasing God—formed by an erroneous and corrupted conscience—necessarily leads. Would heresy therefore have the privilege of making impurity and prostitution respectable? And from this, how eagerly all shameless persons would become heretics, in order to attract respect instead of the punishments they deserve.

### 5.

The comparison that Saint Augustine makes between a heretical soul and a woman who violates the fidelity she owes her husband greatly displeases M. Bayle; and on this subject he treats the holy Doctor very harshly. I cannot wonder at this enough, for this Father saw so clearly in what respect his comparison was defective that he forestalled the commentator’s criticism by acknowledging in the heretic a kind of ignorance that diminishes the crime [Col. 1031A] of his infidelity. It is not becoming for M. Bayle to make no mention of Saint Augustine’s observation, and to turn that observation into a reproach against the saint; but had he mentioned it, one would have understood that his censure was not sound.

For the commentator’s answer consists in making another comparison: that of a heretical soul with an honest woman who receives an impostor in place of her husband because the impostor resembles him. Saint Augustine would have said to M. Bayle:

“You are not satisfied with my comparison, nor am I with yours. Nevertheless, mine limps only a little, and I have warned you of this; but yours is manifestly false, and you do not notice it.
