To make you see this, let us reform both comparisons and settle on a third: that of a heretical soul with a woman who voluntarily allows herself to be deceived by an impostor’s resemblance to her husband, and fears nothing so much as looking too closely at him.”

[Col. 1031B] What separates M. Bayle from Saint Augustine on this point is that the former everywhere assumes equal uprightness and equal conviction of the goodness of their cause in heretics and Catholics alike, whereas Saint Augustine never imagined such a thing possible. Both are very far from the mark. In any event, the commentator complains here, quite improperly, that people like him are taken by the holy Doctor for fools. Certainly Saint Augustine never took heretics for fools except when he found them to be acting in good faith. Shall we not at least find evidence of M. Bayle’s sincerity and candor in his remark on the following text?

### XXVII.

“We agree that children who are guided by gentleness and love are much better than the others; but they are not the majority. There are incomparably more whom only fear can bring under control . . . . Thus we see in Scripture . . . . that the wicked servant is not brought back . . . . by words and admonitions, etc. (Prov. XXIX, 19), which assumes that something stronger must be employed. Elsewhere it states that blows must be used not only against wicked servants but also against disobedient children. It is true,” it says, “that the blows you give them make their bodies suffer, but you deliver their souls from death. And elsewhere: ‘He who spares the rod hates his son’ (Prov. XXV, 14; Saint Augustine, cited work, chap. 6, no. 21).”

The emphatic quotation of the poet’s words, *Pergis pugnantia secum frontibus adversis opponere*—“You continue to set things fighting against each other, head to head”—and the insipid pity over Saint Augustine’s unfortunate comparisons: these are affected flourishes that the commentator employs to conceal an egregious lack of good faith. They initially dazzle the reader and lead him to reflect only on the education of children, whose entire fruit is to learn to read and write and the first elements of the sciences, and to become polished and formed according to the world.

But permit me to speak in M. Bayle’s language. Does he take us for cranes, placing before our eyes a passage of Scripture to which he flatters himself we shall pay no attention? This passage, and consequently Saint Augustine, who cites it, concerns an education whose fruit is good living and salvation. The Holy Spirit declares that the blows a father gives his children deliver their souls from death, and Saint Augustine concludes that the blows with which a paternal hand strikes heretics are likewise very well suited to deliver their souls from death. I do not see in the sacred text that threats and punishments are necessary for disobedient children because their actions are needed precisely, while their opinions are of no use, and because it matters little whether their actions conform to their opinions, provided that the actions are performed, as M. Bayle maintains; rather, I see that the purpose of the threats and punishments mentioned by the Wise Man is to bring children to restrain themselves, so that they become disposed to adopt good dispositions, according to which they regulate their conduct and lead irreproachable lives.

One ought to have disputed with the Wise Man this fact—that punishment contributes in this way to the good morals of children and to the sanctification of their lives—and not have had the effrontery to conceal the manifest meaning of the text presented to us in order to say: “The conversion of heretics is not the same: *Pergis pugnantia secum frontibus adversis opponere*; Saint Augustine is unfortunate in his comparisons.”

### XXVIII.

Bad faith appears with somewhat greater skill in M. Bayle’s answer to the following words: [Col. 1032B] “Christ Himself used force against Saint Paul in order to compel him to believe. Let such people therefore no longer say, as they do: ‘It is free for each person to believe or not to believe’” (Saint Augustine, cited work, no. 22).

In the preceding article, M. Bayle straightforwardly reported and translated the passage from Proverbs that enabled us to expose his gross dissimulation; here he suppresses words of Saint Augustine that make palpable the shameful and base deception the commentator devised in order to repeat a censure of which he is proud and which I have already destroyed. I therefore suppose that he answers very effectively this argument: “Christ used force against Saint Paul in order to compel him to believe; therefore the emperor Honorius has the right to use force against the Donatists in order to compel them to believe.” But does Saint Augustine reason in this way?

One would think so if one considered only the words reported by M. Bayle. The holy Doctor appears to answer this objection of the Donatists: “It is free for each person to believe or not to believe.” But the Donatists added: “Against whom did Christ use force? Toward whom did He employ compulsion? *Cui Christus vim intulit? Quem coegit?*” Saint Augustine silences them by replying: “He used force against Saint Paul; He employed compulsion toward Saint Paul.”

The Donatists were neither as delicate nor as subtle as M. Bayle. They were ready to admit that, if Christ had forced anyone to believe, they would have no grounds for complaining that the emperor Honorius likewise forced them to do so. The question is not whether the Donatists were right or wrong to submit to the difficulties in which Saint Augustine entangles them with these words—“Christ forced Saint Paul.” I ask whether, in consequence of the Donatists’ question, Christ did force anyone. Can one imagine that these words, “Christ forced Saint Paul,” contain a sophism? What an honest man M. Bayle is! The most unworthy omission is the whole foundation on which he bases this insolent discourse: “Patience escapes truth when, after finding so many sophisms, one finds still more,” and so forth.

How astonishing! It is once again M. Dubois who is chiefly guilty of the omission of which I complain. Did the learned M. Bayle read Saint Augustine’s letters only in M. Dubois? What! When the commentator had shamelessly resolved to treat the holy Doctor, in refuting him, as the lowest of men, did he not once cast his eyes upon the Latin original? Did the translator and the commentator have a common interest in corrupting Saint Augustine’s text, the one out of affection and the other out of hatred? This, I confess, is an enigma to me, and, I think, to everyone.

### XXIX.

This objection or question of the Donatists—[Col. 1033A] “Against whom did Christ use force? Toward whom did He employ compulsion?”—was not intended to attack the right to compel, but the use of that right, which they claimed was contrary to the gentleness and evangelical charity. For the Donatists were recalling Saint Augustine to what Jesus Christ had done, insofar as the Savior is incontestably the model not of the rights that men may claim, but of the virtues they must practice. It is therefore not as easy as M. Bayle says to answer Saint Augustine’s question:

“Why should the Church not employ force to bring back into her bosom the children she has lost, since these unhappy children do not hesitate to employ it to destroy others?” (Saint Augustine, cited work, no. 23).

To this M. Bayle replies: “One must not sin by example.” True enough, but the conduct of the children of darkness in the evil they commit is itself proposed by Jesus Christ as an example of the conduct of the children of light in the good they must practice; and Saint Augustine’s thought is that the Church employs force out of charity to procure the salvation of heretics, just as heretics employ force out of hatred to destroy Catholics. This is not a mother who does something foolish in imitation of her daughter—one recognizes M. Bayle’s style and taste—but rather a mother who, after being mistreated by her daughter because of the care she took to restrain and discipline her, subsequently finds a means of punishing her in order to make her abandon her disorder and bring her back to her duty. Let us now judge which of the two is unfortunate in his comparisons, Saint Augustine or M. Bayle. Here is another comparison from the holy Doctor.

### XXX.

“If, for example, we saw two men in a house that we knew was about to collapse, and, however carefully we warned them of this, they [Col. 1033C] refused to believe us and obstinately persisted in remaining there, would it not be cruel not to remove them by force?” (Saint Augustine, cited work, chap. 8, no. 33).

“This,” says M. Bayle, “is the objection of the madman, slightly altered.” Let the texts in Saint Augustine be read, and it will be recognized that the alteration is considerable, and that the two comparisons have neither the same object nor the same purpose. After this, the commentator boasts that he has given the madman’s objection an insurmountable disparity; he declares that he is not afraid ever to see this objection recovered from its overthrow. I am too convinced of his intelligence to believe that he speaks sincerely. He has overthrown this objection—that is, he has made it disappear from the eyes of an inattentive reader, as the waves of the sea break against a rock and cover it. I demonstrated this above.

But it is important to examine what the objection or comparison now under discussion has in common with the other, and what is peculiar to it. [Col. 1033D] Under the pretext of abridging this passage, M. Bayle has maliciously altered it. First, he omitted this essential circumstance: after having forcibly removed the two men, one was certain of making them see the danger so clearly that, once they were outside the house, they would take good care not to reenter it: *Quibus imminentem eam ruinam postea demonstraremus, ut redire amplius sub ejus periculum non auderent*—“To whom we would afterward demonstrate the impending collapse, so that they would no longer dare to return under its danger.”

It is clear that these words, which represent and portray the heretic’s sincere conversion, cannot be suppressed without altering the meaning and force of the objection; and that, if M. Bayle had reported them, he could not have replied that compulsion and dragging people into the Church are a course of action undertaken at a total loss.

What a convenient way of creating insurmountable disparities: to cut away the part of the comparison that excludes every disparity! The comparison of the madman and this one agree in that, in both cases, good is done to unreasonable people against their will, though it is a solid good only because in the end they consent to it and accept it. The application of both comparisons is the heretic’s conversion, which begins with compulsion and is completed by a genuine disillusionment, an inward and sincere change. Is all this not clearly expressed in Saint Augustine?

One readily suspects that the comparison—or, better put, the parable—of the house about to collapse has something unusual about it. A reader of M. Bayle who is not superficial must wonder why two men rather than one are in danger of being crushed beneath the ruins of this house; and if he has the curiosity to consult the original text, he is surprised to see that this comparison is intended solely to show that Catholic bishops and emperors should not be held responsible for the deaths of certain furious Donatists who killed themselves at the first news of the edicts forbidding their assemblies, depriving them of possession of the churches they had seized, and prohibiting under severe penalties the public profession of their heresy.

The spirit of this sect was bloodthirsty and barbarous. Its leaders and most obstinate members spared neither the life of their neighbor, whether Catholic or one of their own party, nor their own lives. They made a sport of throwing themselves into precipices, waters, and flames. To these men Saint Augustine contrasts an innumerable multitude of peoples for whom the promulgation of the edicts was beneficial, whose sincere return to unity was beyond doubt because it was attested by extraordinary zeal and fervor in attending the sacred offices, an eager desire to hear the preaching of the Catholic bishops, a naive and palpable joy at having opened their eyes to the truth, signs of repentance and sorrow for having allowed themselves to be [Col. 1034C] deceived, a humble confession of their past excesses, and detestation and horror of the masters of falsehood who had imposed upon them.

These two kinds of Donatists are the two men in Saint Augustine’s parable. If one of them, he continues, said to us, “As soon as you undertake to pull us out of here, I shall kill myself,” while the other, although resisting like the first and refusing to leave the house, nevertheless preferred to be pulled out rather than kill himself, what course would we have to take? And so forth.

This is what M. Bayle wants us to take for an argument on which Saint Augustine bases the right to compel heretics! This is what he calls dragging people into the Church! He cuts away the part played by free consent in the deliverance from danger, both in the image and in the reality represented, in order to pretend that it is a course of action undertaken at a total loss. Unable to invalidate the factual proofs cited by the holy Doctor, which make the sincere conversion of a prodigious multitude of Donatists incontestable—the fear of the laws having brought them to their senses and led them back in good faith to unity—not only does he say nothing about them, but he gives the impression that Saint Augustine himself says nothing about them. In compensation, he condescends to give a kind of approval to the thought contained in the following passage.

### XXXI.

“As for what they say, that we covet their possessions and take them away from them, let them become Catholics, and we consent not only that they should possess what they call their possessions, but that they should share in ours. Passion blinds them so completely that they do not notice their contradiction. They reproach us, as something highly odious, for employing the authority of the laws to bring them forcibly back into our communion; would we do this, then, if we coveted their possessions?” (Saint Augustine, chap. 9, no. 35).

M. Bayle is willing to admit that this is expressed with great wit, provided nevertheless that he may believe it false. But what reason does he have for refusing to agree that the compulsion used against the Donatists, in execution of Honorius’s rescripts, was disinterested? It is that under Louis XIV, by virtue of the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, people sought to enrich themselves with the spoils of the Huguenots. Is the reasoning not conclusive? It is conclusive in the manner of so many others that make up the third part of the *Philosophical Commentary*, where M. Bayle, after presenting Saint Augustine’s text, sets it aside and declaims against the converters of France. They are impertinent; therefore Saint Augustine has no common sense. Huguenot ministers are more worthy of belief than the converters; therefore the complaints of the Donatists were more admissible than Saint Augustine’s testimony. Such is the analysis of our commentator’s reasoning. If one reduces it to syllogistic form more faithfully than he reduced Saint Augustine’s arguments, one will find that some are laughable in their absurdity, while others, founded on pure malice and deceit, ought to arouse indignation—for example, the argument concerning the following text.

### XXXII.

“It is not the Canaanites who will rise up on the day of judgment against the people of Israel, although Israel drove them from their country and took away the fruit of their labor; rather, it will be Naboth who will rise against Ahab, because Ahab took away the fruit of Naboth’s labor. And why the one and not the others? Because Naboth was just, whereas the Canaanites were impious” (Saint Augustine, cited work, chap. 9, no. 41).

This passage appears remarkable to M. Bayle; therefore, he says, he did not read it carelessly or in haste. “Here,” he adds, “the principle is clearly laid down that heretics who seize the possessions of Catholics do wrong, whereas Catholics who seize the possessions of heretics perform a good action.”

One need only read the five or six preceding lines to discover that this clearly stated principle is a pure invention of M. Bayle, who perceives nothing but impertinence in Saint Augustine, like a jaundiced man who sees yellow everywhere.

The holy Doctor wishes to persuade the Donatists that they would do far better to return to the Church in order to be justified than to remain outside the Church and slander it because, as punishment for their impiety, the emperor places it in possession of their spoils:

*Ideo si corpus Christi tollit spolia impiorum, et corpori Christi thesaurizantur divitiae impiorum, non debent impii foris remanere ut calumnientur, sed intrare potius ut justificentur*—“Therefore, if the body of Christ takes away the spoils of the impious, and the riches of the impious are stored up for the body of Christ, the impious ought not to remain outside in order to slander it, but should rather enter in order to be justified” (Saint Augustine, cited work, no. 40).

The reason Saint Augustine gives for proving this thesis is that Jesus Christ justifies only His mystical body, which is the Church: *Non autem justificat nisi corpus suum quod est Ecclesia*—“He justifies no one except His own body, which is the Church” (ibid.).

From this it follows that there are no just persons outside the Church, and consequently that the Donatists vainly flatter themselves that they belong to the number of those just persons who, on the day of judgment, will appear with their heads raised and with great confidence against those who oppressed them and took away the fruit of their labors (Wis. V, 1). All this in Saint Augustine determines the meaning of the words that are the subject of the present article. Justification, or holiness, which is found only in the Catholic Church, is not presented by Saint Augustine as a legitimate title for seizing the possessions of heretics, but only as a motive for returning to the bosom of the Catholic Church.

One need not be nearly as penetrating as M. Bayle to understand this; but without possessing all his wickedness, can one pretend that Saint Augustine here attaches the privilege of impeccability to the profession of orthodoxy? By what artful device does he insinuate this false accusation into the minds of his readers? It is plainly the effect of studied malice; and, carried away, if we are to believe him, by excessive zeal for the interests of truth and sound morality, he loses all self-control. Empty declamation! I guarantee that it was with the greatest composure that he conceived and wrote these words: “I no longer know where I am.” He maintains the appearance of plausibility; the affectation of astonishment and confusion continues, and it further seasons the remarks he makes on these other words, which he took from the letter to Emeritus.

### XXXIII.

“When temporal powers lay their hands heavily upon schismatics, it is because they regard their separation as an evil, according to the Apostle’s rule: ‘He who resists the powers resists the ordinance of God, and those who resist them bring condemnation upon themselves,’ etc. The whole question therefore comes down to seeing whether schism is not an evil, and whether you have not committed schism. For if this is so, it is not for a good but for an evil that you resist the powers . . . .” (Saint Augustine, Ep. 87, formerly 164, to Emeritus, no. 7).

“But,” you will say, “one ought not to persecute even wicked Christians.” Even if that were so, could one defend oneself by this against the powers established by God for the punishment of the wicked? Can we erase what Saint Paul says in the passage I have just cited? (ibid., no. 8).

M. Bayle cannot understand what Saint Augustine was thinking when he cited Scripture so badly; and I, who am about to demonstrate that Saint Augustine never cited it more appropriately, understand perfectly what M. Bayle is thinking when he ventures so many impostures against this saint: he is thinking of displaying the talent he believes he possesses for deceiving the public by his audacious frauds.

[Col. 1036C] Listen to him: Saint Augustine attributes to Saint Paul a falsehood that condemns all confessors and martyrs to rebellion against God and punishable wickedness. In all those passages from Saint Paul’s Epistles that Saint Augustine describes—“He who resists the power,” and so forth—the Apostle, says the commentator, excludes every case in which one is persuaded that God commands the opposite of what princes command. He would have said not simply “where one is persuaded,” but “where one is legitimately persuaded,” if he did not wholeheartedly favor Pyrrhonism in religion, if he were not the teacher of the impious of our day, who place paganism, Mohammedanism, and Christianity, the Catholic Church and all heresies, on the same level. Saint Augustine did not share his view; he was intimately convinced that finding what the Catholic Church teaches evidently credible, and knowing it, and finding what all other religions teach evidently false, and knowing them, are one and the same thing.

[Col. 1036D] But here I must take it upon myself to express astonishment after M. Bayle’s example and to say that I no longer know where I am—not because the commentator once again takes M. Dubois for Saint Augustine, which is no longer surprising, but because, if I may put it this way, he makes an appalling uproar about the matter. Here is what is at issue.

This Latin sentence of Saint Augustine—*Nam et terrenae potestates, cum schismaticos persequuntur, ea regula se defendunt, qua dicit Apostolus, Qui potestati resistit, etc.*—these words, I say, ought, it seems to me, to be rendered in French as follows:

“When temporal powers lay their hands heavily upon schismatics, they justify their conduct by this rule of the Apostle: ‘He who resists the powers,’ etc.”

M. Dubois substitutes for the meaning of the words *ea regula se defendunt* another meaning, namely, that the powers regard the schismatics’ separation [Col. 1037A] as an evil according to the rule established by Saint Paul, and so forth. On this basis M. Bayle triumphs. He puts into formal shape Saint Augustine’s supposed reasoning, and offers a retort in the person of an Arian bishop, who very effectively demonstrates by a similar argument the justice of the persecutions that Catholics suffered from the emperors Constantius and Valens. All the great display M. Bayle makes in order to drive the holy Doctor into a corner rests on words that belong solely to M. Dubois’s invention and are foreign to the holy Doctor’s text and meaning.

“To answer,” he says, “the Arian bishop’s syllogism, one will have to deny that, because an emperor regards something as an evil, he has the right to punish it.”

Indeed! Who doubts that Saint Augustine would readily deny a bad proposition falsely attributed to him by his translator? “But in denying this,” he adds, “one throws Saint Augustine into such disorder,” and so forth.

There is no need to throw the French Saint Augustine into disorder; he has been in disorder ever since he was composed. [Col. 1037B] As for the Latin, it will suffer no injury. “Saint Augustine must change his proposition,” he continues. There are many other things to change in the French Saint Augustine; but the proposition in question will not be changed in the Latin, for it was never there.

The commentator, after struggling against M. Dubois under the name of Saint Augustine, returns to the holy Doctor’s true thought—it was hardly worth attributing another thought to him—and reproaches him for assuming what is in question, namely, that the Donatists are truly schismatics. Had he not demonstrated this a thousand and a thousand times? After so many conferences and disputes, so many letters and substantial works in which the matter had been exhausted, what was lacking for their instruction and conviction?

But M. Bayle assures us that, if sufficiently strong proofs had been brought forward, they would willingly have reunited with the main body of the tree. He has no more reason to make himself their guarantor than to make himself the guarantor of all those who generally err on some article of faith—even of Mohammedans, idolaters, and atheists. Since experience shows that there are no erring persons who do not often stand firm against everything that can be said to disabuse them, here, according to M. Bayle, is the cause of God and of the Church of Jesus Christ deprived of sufficiently strong reasons to establish even the least of orthodox doctrines. On this principle, whenever, after a religious dispute—whatever its subject—each party persists in maintaining its own opinion, the commentator concludes that no one ought to be disturbed. Such is the critic and adversary of Saint Augustine.

His reputation as a great, profound, and brilliant intellect is universally established. He therefore has poor grace in so often pretending to have a difficult and obtuse understanding. “I understand nothing,” he says, “of what Saint Augustine says: that even if one ought not to persecute wicked Christians, one could not defend oneself by this against the powers established by God for the punishment of the wicked.”

In truth, in a few centuries it will be a great question whether the learned and famous M. Bayle is the author of the *Philosophical Commentary*. On the one hand, the proofs supplied by the author of his life and the editor of the collection of his various works will appear demonstrative; on the other hand, the reading of the *Philosophical Commentary* will persuade critics that its author did not know Latin. For, unable to understand Saint Augustine’s thought in the French translation of his letters, he would have been compelled to consult the Latin text—if he had been able to understand it for himself. At first sight his embarrassment would have ceased, and he would have corrected M. Dubois’s wretched translation.

Saint Augustine objects that Christians are not permitted to persecute the wicked, not that one must not persecute even wicked Christians, [Col. 1038A] as M. Dubois makes him say: *At enim et malos Christianos non licet persequi*—“But, one may object, it is not permitted to persecute wicked Christians.”

This is the common difficulty proposed in the schools, drawn from the precept forbidding one to return evil for evil, as though that precept were contrary to the public authority that punishes the wicked. Saint Augustine replies that one cannot defend oneself by this against the powers established by God for the punishment of the wicked, because the precept not to return evil for evil does not concern the conduct of princes and magistrates when they act as God’s ministers for the punishment of the wicked.

The critical spirit, which suffered so many eclipses in M. Bayle when he composed his *Philosophical Commentary*, seems to be attempting to reappear. He shares with us his discovery concerning the source from which M. Bossuet drew the question he put to one of his diocesan faithful: In what passage of Scripture are heretics and schismatics excepted from the number of those evildoers against whom Saint Paul himself armed princes? I would never have thought, however, that a man of M. Bossuet’s character, who had read so much Scripture, needed to learn elsewhere what is or is not found in it. Be that as it may, M. Bayle first claims that it was unnecessary to except heretics from the number of these evildoers—doubtless because, in his view, it is a truth known and acknowledged by everyone that evil committed directly, immediately, and exclusively against God ought to count for nothing in the eyes of the heads of civil society.

Moreover, the commentator produces a passage that he assures us is quite sufficient to answer Saint Augustine and M. Bossuet: “Do good to all, but especially to the household of faith” (Gal. VI, 10). Certainly M. Bayle is not speaking seriously; he cites this saying of Saint Paul only so as not to remain entirely without a reply. Is this not once again the difficulty drawn from the precept of charity toward one’s neighbor, in order to attack the power magistrates possess to punish evildoers? If this precept, insofar as it is addressed to private persons, commands them to do good to heretics, does it not also command them to do good to robbers and all other evildoers? If, insofar as it is addressed to princes and magistrates, it does not oblige them to spare robbers or all other evildoers, why would it oblige them to spare heretics?

### XXXIV.

Let us be approximately as brief on this point as M. Bayle: “Must one not have lost all shame to refuse to submit to what truth commands through the voice of the emperor” (St. Augustine, Epistle 105, formerly 166, to the Donatists, chap. 2, no. 7)?

[Col. 1038D]

All that M. Bayle has to say about this is that it can apply only to a man who is persuaded that the emperor is in fact issuing the commands of truth. But is it not enough that this man ought to be persuaded of it, and that he is not persuaded of it through his own fault? Does it take nothing more than obstinacy to place oneself beyond all prosecution and even all blame? What! One may shamelessly deny anything one wishes, and thereby avoid even the reproach of having lost all shame?

### XXXV.

I am still trying to find anything reasonable in the commentator’s replies. What censure does he apply to these words: “If it is the care we take to withdraw you from error and perdition that makes your hatred of us more ardent, blame God for it, who in Scripture addresses this threatening reproach to pastors: You have not brought back what had strayed, and you have not gone to seek what was lost” (Ezekiel 34:4; St. Augustine, ibid., chap. 4, no. 13)?

By this discourse Saint Augustine represents

[Col. 1039A]

to the Donatists that the bishops could not dispense with resorting to the authority of princes in order to bring back into the bosom of the Church—outside which there is no salvation—all those who obstinately persisted in remaining in schism; that, having this means in their hands of rescuing so many souls from error and the path of perdition, they would have made themselves guilty by failing to employ it; and that in this they had no other aim than to fulfill their duties and avoid incurring the just reproaches that God makes in the prophecy of Ezekiel against wicked pastors.

What! Because the prophet Ezekiel did not have the Donatists in view, and because he makes no mention of heresy or schism, are his words no more applicable to the present question than to the interests of the Great Mogul, and did Saint Augustine therefore quote them inappropriately? So claims M. Bayle, who on this occasion speaks of dragooning the avaricious and the lewd. Empty declamation, which will be refuted elsewhere.

### XXXVI.

[Col. 1039B]

Must I not be obliged at least once to concede that Saint Augustine has made some unsound argument pointed out by M. Bayle—for example, this one?

“If no one ought to be compelled, not even to do good, remember that the episcopate is a good thing, since the Apostle says so. Yet there are several whom people use force to oblige to accept it. They seize them, carry them away by force, and keep them confined until they have made them willing to accept that good” (St. Augustine, Epistle 173, formerly 204, no. 2).

M. Bayle calls this “an argument from the old days.” That is to say, in his view, since it is no longer customary to make men bishops against their will, one ought to abolish the practice of employing coercion to dispose heretics to become good Catholics.

But the four differences that prevent him from condemning coercion in the case of the episcopate,

[Col. 1039C]

far from establishing a disparity that would make coercion reprehensible in the case of professing the true faith, establish instead a disparity showing that the custom of compelling heretics is better than the other. Saint Augustine therefore concludes as follows:

“How much more fitting is it to tear you by force from a pernicious error to which one could not remain attached without being an enemy to oneself!”

Let us examine these four differences, and we shall see that each supplies an argument *a minori ad majus*—from the lesser to the greater—which strengthens Saint Augustine’s argument.

1. The man who was compelled to become a bishop was persuaded that the episcopate was an excellent thing, although it was not necessary for salvation; thus, no harm would have been done to him by not compelling him. But if the man who is compelled to become a Catholic is persuaded that the Catholic religion is evil, he is mistaken, because it is not only good but also necessary for salvation. Consequently,

[Col. 1039D]

one would wrong him by failing to attempt, with regard to him, a coercion capable of bringing him to a voluntary conviction of the truth and necessity of that religion.

2. The man who refused a bishopric did so only out of modesty. That is a great virtue, and he could be left in possession of it. But the man who refuses to enter the true Church does so out of malice or ignorance; both are vices from which, out of charity, he ought to be delivered.

3. Coercion was very well suited to removing the scruples of a man whose delicacy of conscience made him fear the episcopate. Is it not suited to dispelling prejudices, banishing passions, and making one perceive and hate the seduction that keeps people in heresy and schism?

4. If the man who had stiffened himself against accepting a bishopric had continued to refuse, he would not have been driven to extremes, and after a few entreaties

[Col. 1040A]

people would have ceased troubling him. Perhaps, too, he would have been treated as a rebel, and there was a right to punish him for his disobedience to the Church. With still greater reason, obstinacy in heresy and schism deserves harsh punishments.

### XXXVII.

I have taken care to repeat often and to insist that Saint Augustine’s arguments tend solely to justify the charity of the bishops who solicited the laws against the Donatists, and not to establish the right that the emperor had to enact those laws. I believe I have demonstrated this important point several times. Here is new proof:

“It is well known that, since it is only ill will that damns men, only good will can save them; but does the love we ought to have for them permit us to abandon them to their ill will? Is it not cruelty to leave them entirely free? And ought we not, as far as possible,

[Col. 1040B]

prevent men from doing evil and force them to do good?” (St. Augustine, ibid.)

The commentator replies that this can be achieved only through instruction and persuasion. Who doubts it? But is coercion not very often at least a remote cause of instruction and persuasion? “To force someone to do good,” he adds, “is contradictory.” But to force someone toward what disposes, prepares, and leads him to will and do good is surely not contradictory. There is no movement of the soul that, employed wisely, cannot contribute to a change of will. M. Bayle is too much a philosopher to have denied this except from the necessity of defending a bad cause.

### XXXVIII.

Saint Augustine continues in this way:

“If one must always abandon ill will to its natural freedom, why so many scourges and such perceptible goads to force the Israelites, despite their murmuring and their

[Col. 1040C]

obstinacy, to advance toward the Promised Land?” (St. Augustine, ibid., no. 3).

The holy doctor then recalls the examples of Saint Paul, who was thrown to the ground and blinded in order to be converted; of fathers, whom Scripture commands to employ blows to subdue the obstinacy of their children and force them into the right path; of pastors, who must run after stray sheep and seek them when they are lost; and so forth.

“I have refuted this so often,” says M. Bayle, “that I am tired of it.” Frankly, he has tired himself by doing nothing. He may distinguish between acts for which good will is required and those in which it need not have any part, so as to place among the latter what God required of the Israelites with respect to the conquest of the land of Canaan, and disparage Saint Augustine’s comparisons to the very end; he may impose upon persons who read Saint Augustine’s letters only in French, but not upon the others.

[Col. 1040D]

If M. Dubois, in translating the holy doctor’s text, suppressed essential words in order to curry favor with the Jansenists, was it appropriate to turn into a reproach against the holy doctor a mere courtesy toward people who claim to be the sole partisans of his glory? These people do not want fear to be able to turn the human will away from evil, nor do they want the Israelites ever to have abstained from doing evil.

Saint Augustine expressly affirms both points here:

“Why were the Israelites, refusing and murmuring, restrained from evil by such harsh scourges and compelled to the Promised Land?”

*Quare Israelitae recusantes et murmurantes tam duris flagellis a malo prohibebantur, et ad terram promissionis compellebantur?*

M. Dubois omits *a malo prohibebantur*—“were restrained from evil”—in his translation; and, as though these words had thereby been erased from all editions of Saint Augustine, the commentator boldly counts among the acts for which good will is not required what God demanded of the Israelites with respect to the conquest of the land of Canaan.

He takes advantage of the translator’s unfaithful omission, mistaking it for

[Col. 1041A]

the author’s silence; and, as though Saint Augustine’s Latin letters were closed books to him, he assumes that, by this Father’s own admission, the scourges with which God afflicted the Israelites in the desert had the sole purpose of making them march into battle, and not of making them worthy of victory by cutting short their murmuring and disobedience.

As for the alleged disciples of Saint Augustine, they must suffer the comparison repeated so many times by the holy doctor between the coercion used against heretics and the violence that Jesus Christ employed against Saint Paul just as impatiently as M. Bayle does. This comparison is obviously as absurd as M. Bayle finds it, if Saint Augustine does not mean that the coercion used against heretics is always accompanied by an interior grace of Jesus Christ that prepares the way for instruction and casts at least the remote seeds and foundations of conversion.

For this is Saint Augustine’s reasoning:

[Col. 1041B]

“It was an effect of Jesus Christ’s goodness to throw Saint Paul down and blind him in order to convert him; therefore, it is an effect of the emperors’ goodness to confiscate the possessions of heretics, exile them, and make them suffer other similar evils in order to convert them.”

The conclusion can be legitimate only on the assumption that the grace necessary for a change of heart, or for a disposition capable of bringing about that change, never fails to accompany the ill-treatment inflicted on heretics in order to reduce them to abandoning their errors.

Certainly, one would poorly establish this conclusion by saying: Grace is sometimes joined, and with regard to certain privileged souls, to the violence used against heretics, just as it was joined to the violence Jesus Christ employed against Saint Paul; therefore, if the violence inflicted on Saint Paul is an effect of Jesus Christ’s goodness,

[Col. 1041C]

the violence used against an entire sect of heretics, without excepting any of them, whether leaders or multitude, is an effect of the emperors’ charity.

Nevertheless, this is how Saint Augustine would reason under the Jansenist hypothesis.

One must not forget an egregious calumny by M. Bayle against Saint Augustine. He reproaches this Father for saying that tumult was necessary for Jesus Christ to accomplish Saint Paul’s conversion. This is truly a pure calumny, founded entirely on the words “it was necessary,” which belong to M. Dubois and not to Saint Augustine. The remainder of this article is refuted elsewhere or does not deserve an answer.

### XXXIX.

The words of Saint Augustine that M. Bayle reports

[Col. 1042A]

here concern the explanation of this saying from the Gospel: “Compel them to enter” (St. Augustine, ibid., no. 10). This is the subject of the first two parts of the *Philosophical Commentary*, to which M. Bayle refers us.

### XL.

“If one compares what charitable severity makes them suffer with the excesses to which their fury drives them, one will have no difficulty seeing who are the persecutors of them and of us. They would be persecutors even with regard to us in this matter; for whatever fathers and mothers may do to bring their children back to their duties . . . this can never be called persecution. On the contrary, from the moment children live badly, they are the ones who persecute their fathers and mothers, even when they would undertake no violence against them” (St. Augustine, Epistle 89, formerly 167, no. 2).

Of the three censures M. Bayle makes of this passage, the first is that the severity called charitable

[Col. 1042B]

by Saint Augustine ought not to have included the innocent with the guilty—that is, as M. Bayle understands it, the peaceful and tranquil heretic with the furious and bloodthirsty heretic.

The commentator should therefore have begun by destroying what the holy doctor says shortly beforehand concerning these peaceful and tranquil heretics: even if they had no other crime than schism and heresy, one would nevertheless be well-founded in punishing them for that alone:

“And this, indeed, I would say against those whom the mere darkness of heretical error enveloped; for that sacrilege they would deserve to pay the most fitting penalties, even though they dared to injure no one through any violent madness.”

*Et hoc quidem adversus eos dicerem, quos sola caligo haeretici erroris involveret, pro quo sacrilegio poenas dignissimas luerent, nec tamen ulla quemquam violenta insania laedere auderent.*

Another censure is that there are circumstances in which fathers and mothers deserve the title of persecutors; and, according to the commentator’s view, this is especially so when they trouble their children over religious matters.

But Saint Augustine is right not to share this view if the fathers and mothers follow the doctrine

[Col. 1042C]

of the Church while the children join the party of error. The question of the right to compel is the same in this case, whether in individual families or in a state. Saint Augustine therefore does not cite this example to demonstrate the justice of the penalties decreed by the emperors against the Donatists, but only to make clear that these are paternal punishments.

The third censure concerns the word “persecution” and the word “persecutor,” which Saint Augustine does not want to be taken in a favorable sense, although he himself departed from this rule more than once. I have observed that he did so only in places where it was necessary for him to conform to the expressions of Scripture on which he based his arguments.

From all this one may judge whether M. Bayle had reason to boast of having sharply pressed Saint Augustine.

## Third Part. Examination of M. Bayle’s Efforts to Destroy Saint Augustine’s Objection to the Pagans Concerning the Death of Lucretia

[Col. 1041]

[Col. 1041D]

In the article on **LUCRETIA**, M. Bayle, who takes pleasure in declaring victory for infidels, heretics, and all the enemies of religion who have been opposed by the holy Fathers, reports and praises an objection that Saint Augustine makes to the pagans concerning Lucretia’s death as one of the most reasonable objections, and he endeavors to show that it is unsound.

The holy doctor says that killing oneself is a crime, and he strengthens his argument by recalling the praises bestowed on Lucretia. He reasons *ad hominem* against the pagans and appeals to the laws of their courts.

[Col. 1042D]

Those laws would have obliged them to punish a man who had killed Lucretia:

“You would therefore be obliged,” he continues, “to punish her if she were accused before you of having killed herself. But if you reply that it is impossible to punish her, since she is not present, why do you adorn with so many praises the murderess of a virtuous person?”

This is how M. Bayle presents Saint Augustine’s objection. But let us examine the text:

“But what is this, that the woman who did not commit adultery is punished more severely? For the man was expelled from his fatherland together with his father; she was put to death with the supreme

[Col. 1043A]

punishment. If that is not unchastity, when she is violated against her will, then this is not justice, by which a chaste woman is punished.

“I appeal to you, Roman laws and judges. Surely, after crimes had been committed, you did not wish any criminal to be killed with impunity without a sentence. If, then, someone should bring this crime before your judgment and prove to you that a woman, not merely uncondemned but chaste and innocent, had been killed, would you not punish the one who had done this with fitting severity?

“This is what that Lucretia did—that Lucretia, that repeatedly praised Lucretia: she killed Lucretia, innocent, chaste, and violated. Pronounce your sentence. But if you cannot do so because the woman whom you could punish is not present, why do you praise with such lavish commendation the murderess of an innocent and chaste woman?”

*Sed quid est hoc quod in eam gravius vindicatur, quae adulterium non admisit? Nam ille patria cum patre pulsus est: haec summo est mactata supplicio. Si non est illa impudicitia, qua invita opprimitur, non est haec justitia, qua casta punitur. Vos appello, leges judicesque Romani. Nempe post perpetrata facinora, nec quemquam scelestum indemnatum impune voluistis occidi. Si ergo ad vestrum judicium quisquam deferret hoc crimen, vobisque probaretur, non solum indemnatam, verum etiam castam et innocentem interfectam esse mulierem, nonne eum qui id fecisset severitate congrua plecteretis? Hoc fecit illa Lucretia, illa, illa sic praedicata Lucretia innocentem, castam, vim perpessam Lucretiam insuper interemit. Proferte sententiam. Quod si propterea non potestis, quia non adstat quam punire possitis, cur interf ectricem innocentis et castae tanta praedicatione laudatis?*

(St. Augustine, Book I of *The City of God*, chap. 19.)

M. Bayle may not take offense, but he conceals the entire force of Saint Augustine’s reasoning, which is contained in this principle:

“You did not wish even a criminal to be killed with impunity

[Col. 1043B]

without being condemned in due form by judges entrusted with public authority.”

*Nec quemquam scelestum indemnatum impune voluistis occidi.*

That being established, let us see whether, as M. Bayle asserts, the Roman magistrates whom Saint Augustine addresses and asks to judge the question would easily have disabused him by showing him that the laws, which granted private individuals no authority over one another’s lives, did not deprive each person of the privilege of disposing of his own life.

What then, Saint Augustine would have replied, because your laws, being unable to punish those who killed themselves, did not expressly forbid suicide, you say that they do not deprive each person of the privilege of disposing of his own life? Is it not enough that they assume that no one has the privilege of disposing of his own life?

For why, I ask you, do you not want even a criminal to be killed with impunity

[Col. 1043C]

unless he has been condemned in due form by judges entrusted with public authority? Is it not because the life of each citizen belongs to the republic, and consequently it is for the republic alone to dispose of it and to decide whether it is expedient to cut off this member for the good of the whole body?

Every man who perishes is either a good citizen or a bad one. If he is a good citizen, his death is a loss to the republic, and whoever caused it is guilty—whether he himself or another. If he is a bad citizen, his death nevertheless concerns the republic; and whoever caused it, whether himself or another, has committed an assault upon the right that the republic possessed to judge whether this citizen was bad enough to be rid of, upon the right it possessed to correct him and afterward derive some benefit from him.

But the Roman magistrates whom M. Bayle makes speak reply:

“Do you ignore the admiration that has always been

[Col. 1043D]

felt for the Catos, the Brutuses, the Cassiuses, and so many other illustrious Romans who preferred death to a life that would have made them witnesses of the oppression of liberty, or exposed them to the discretion of their enemies or to a lingering condition,” and so forth?

This declamation is not capable of silencing Saint Augustine (Book I of *The City of God*, chap. 23); and I can make him answer in this manner:

“Instead of admiration, these ostentatious deaths deserve only shame and infamy. Have I not proved this sufficiently with regard to Cato’s death? They ought to be regarded as genuine acts of treachery by these false braves against their country, which alone possessed legitimate dominion over the days they cut short and which they were obliged to preserve for it, since it was not absolutely impossible that they might still have had an opportunity to serve it.

“If Varro, after the

[Col. 1044A]

battle of Cannae, had surrendered to Hannibal, or had killed himself, would Rome, which thanked him for not despairing of the republic, not have been equally betrayed? If the great Camillus had killed himself instead of going into exile, would he not have been guilty of the Gauls’ capture of the Capitol, which they would have seized without him?

“How many liberators has that furious wisdom perhaps taken from you which makes men murderers of themselves? If, instead of honoring it, you had attached to it more shame than to the most disordered life, and if fear of that shame had preserved for you only the courtesan Fulvia, who exposed Catiline’s conspiracy, would you not have had reason, by this example, to justify the infamy with which you would have covered Lucretia’s death?”

Here is the forceful objection that M. Bayle places in the mouth of the Roman magistrates, and which he considers capable of exhausting all Saint Augustine’s resources:

“The nation that you regard as the favorite people of the true God does not blame Saul, its first king, one of the bravest

[Col. 1044B]

princes of his age, for forestalling by suicide the distress of falling into the hands of his victorious enemy. His successor, one of your greatest prophets, nevertheless gave him very great praise. Do not the books of that same nation praise a brave man who imitated King Saul’s action? And after this you come and tell us: Anyone who had killed Lucretia would be punishable; therefore, she is punishable for having killed herself. Learn to reason better.”

M. Bayle here offends against probability; Roman urbanity would not have permitted those magistrates to say to Saint Augustine, “Learn to reason better.”

Whatever the case, this Father would have replied:

“And you, learn what the kingdom of God is. You give me the opportunity to teach it to you. There is a sovereign Lord, the first principle and final end of all things, creator of men and sole arbiter of their lives. They have received life

[Col. 1044C]

only from him; it exists only for him; it belongs and ought to be sacrificed only to him.

“Concerned for the rest and peace of every legitimate society, of which he is the Father, he has communicated to those who govern states a subordinate authority dependent upon his own, to which he has attached the right of the sword for the terror of the wicked. But no one ought to lay hands upon himself without the order or permission of this supreme Master, to whom every human life belongs.

“This truth was not unknown to the sages of Greece, nor to your own sages. Read their writings; they will teach you that it is a crime for a man to leave this world without the order of the God who caused him to be born, just as it is a crime for a soldier to leave his post without the order of the commander who placed him there:

‘Pythagoras forbids departing, without the order of the commander—that is, of God—from the garrison and station of life.’

*Vetatque Pythagoras injussu imperatoris, id est Dei, de praesidio et statione vitae decedere.*

(Cicero, *On Old Age*, no. 73.)

“Indeed, natural reason, which establishes the right of judges and magistrates over the lives of those

[Col. 1044D]

guilty of great crimes, dictates to all men that no one possesses the same right over his own life, because no one is his own master.

“Thus, although God may require or permit us to lend our ministry to the execution of the death sentence he has pronounced against us, it is evident that we must therefore be assured of his will by an extraordinary and unmistakable revelation.

“Say, if you dare, that Lucretia killed herself by the order and permission of your gods. I will attack the vanity of this claim by demonstrating the vanity of your gods, and you will see whether I have learned how to reason.”

For my part, I dare say that the brave Razias did not dispose of his own life; he merely obeyed the will of God, who inspired him to be the instrument of the sacrifice God demanded of him in circumstances when a great example of the horror deserved by idolatry and idolaters was necessary.

Thus he died while

[Col. 1045A]

bearing witness that God alone was master of human life:

“Calling upon the Lord of life and spirit.”

*Invocans dominatorem vitae et spiritus.*

(2 Maccabees 14:46.)

As for Saul, I do not need to resort to a similar inspiration, since the glory of his death is uncertain and greatly disputed. “His successor,” you say, “one of our greatest prophets, gave him very great praise after his death.” To make this proof solid, you should have added: “And he certainly knew that this prince had killed himself when he gave him that praise.”

But David had merely received the first news of Saul’s defeat and death from an Amalekite whom he had killed on the spot for boasting that, at the request of that unfortunate king, he had put him to death. David had therefore learned at most

[Col. 1045B]

that Saul had contributed to his own death by asking the Amalekite to bring it about.

On this basis I reason as follows: David could not have praised Saul for killing himself, but only for having himself killed by an Amalekite. Yet he did not praise him for that either. For either he believed the circumstance of Saul’s death—that Saul had asked an Amalekite to kill him—to be true, or he did not believe it to be true. If he did not believe it true, then he did not praise Saul for having himself killed by an Amalekite. If he believed it true, he did not approve it, since he punished the Amalekite with death.

Indeed, it is contradictory to judge Saul worthy of praise for having himself killed by an Amalekite while at the same time judging the Amalekite worthy of death for having killed Saul at his request and by his command.

M. Bayle, whom I am following step by step, here brings his prosopopoeia to an end. Let us imitate him and examine more simply his criticism of this dilemma of Saint Augustine:

“Thus this case is pressed from both sides, so that if the murder is attenuated, the adultery is confirmed; if the adultery is cleared, the murder is aggravated. There is no escape when it is said: If she was adulterous, why was she praised? If she was chaste, why was she killed?”

*Ita haec causa ex utroque latere coarctatur, ut si extenuatur homicidium, adulterium confirmetur; si purgatur adulterium, homicidium cumuletur: nec omnino invenitur exitus, ubi dicitur: Si adultera, cur laudata? si pudica, cur occisa?*

He claims that one cannot lessen this woman’s homicide without aggravating

[Col. 1045C]

her adultery, nor lessen her adultery without aggravating her homicide. Is he not right? He proved by his *ad hominem* argument that no one has the right to kill himself, and he adds that an innocent person has still less of that right than a guilty person; that if it were permissible to kill oneself, this dreadful privilege would suit criminals rather than virtuous persons.

This reminds me of an epigram I read somewhere:

[Col. 1046A]

> Must one ask so much why he hanged himself—  
> > This rogue, this thief so worthy of the gallows?  
> > Can one suppose that he was forbidden  
> > To perform an act of justice?

There is some truth in the wit of this thought, and it makes one feel the soundness of Saint Augustine’s reasoning. To show that this Father had not examined Lucretia’s case carefully enough, it is not sufficient to say that his argument proves too much; it must be shown somewhat better than by the comparison M. Bayle employs.

He supposes a very chaste woman who, in a roughly similar case, would not have killed herself but would have conceived such great grief that she contracted a fatal illness and eventually died. He claims that if we follow Saint Augustine’s dilemma, every praise bestowed upon her grief would be taken away from her chastity:

“If she was chaste, why did she die?”

*Si pudica, cur mortua?*

As though her grief proved that she was not chaste. He is not thinking clearly; he does not understand Saint Augustine’s

[Col. 1046B]

dilemma. He believes that the holy doctor reasons as follows:

“If Lucretia was chaste, she could not kill herself; or if she could kill herself, she was not chaste.”

The absurdity of this reasoning is indeed quite apparent from the comparison with the other woman, of whom one would have to say, following Saint Augustine’s dilemma:

“If she was chaste, she could not grieve; or if she could grieve, she was not chaste.”

But Saint Augustine reasons differently, and this is what he means:

“If Lucretia was chaste, she ought not to have killed herself; it was not reasonable for her to kill herself. Or if she ought to have killed herself, if it was reasonable for her to kill herself, she was not chaste.”

This dilemma no longer applies to the other woman, because Lucretia is assumed to have killed herself freely, whereas one must assume that the other woman’s grief was not entirely free in order for it to be evidence of her chastity.

For if it is assumed to have been free, M. Bayle will not be able to avoid approving this reasoning:

“If she was chaste, she

[Col. 1046C]

ought not to have grieved; it was not reasonable for her to grieve. Or if she ought to have grieved, if it was reasonable for her to grieve, she was not chaste.”

Would M. Bayle refuse his approval to reasoning founded on the moral principles that M. Descartes, for whom he has some esteem, establishes in his letters to Princess Elisabeth, where he teaches that one grieves reasonably only over an evil that has occurred through one’s own fault (Letters 4 and 6)?

## Fourth Part. Examination of the Passage That Gave M. Bayle Occasion to Say That Saint Augustine Was More Fortunate Than Wise

[Col. 1045]

[Col. 1045D]

In the article on **RORARIUS**, one of the places where M. Bayle reasons at length, and where most of his arguments are more dangerous than sound, he undertakes to show that M. Descartes’ opinion concerning the souls of animals is highly advantageous to the true faith, insofar as it yields, he says, theological benefits for several important principles that could not be maintained forcefully once one admitted that animals possess a sensitive soul.

He acknowledges that Saint Augustine held the latter view and admitted these principles; from this he concludes that, if the holy doctor did not suffer from these two things, which evidently cannot be reconciled, he was more fortunate than wise.

To demonstrate this contradiction within Saint Augustine himself, he borrows from Ambroise Victor [Note: [Col. 1045] Ambroise Victor is the assumed name of an Oratorian priest named André Martin.] and Father Malebranche a sample of the principles Saint Augustine upheld,

[Col. 1046D]

and which are incompatible with the possession of souls by animals:

1. What has never sinned cannot suffer evil.

2. The nobler cannot have the less noble as its legitimate end.

3. What is spiritual is immortal.

M. Bayle does not dwell on the third principle because, according to him, despite what Father Malebranche says, Saint Augustine believed that the soul of animals was corporeal. However, in order to refute Father Malebranche on this point, M. Bayle cites in the margin two works that are not by Saint Augustine: the book *On Knowledge of the True Life* and the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*.

It seems to me that he is nevertheless right; and if the matter were worth the effort, I believe one could easily prove, by unimpeachable testimonies, that the holy doctor believed the soul of animals to be corporeal. Thus it is M. Bayle

[Col. 1047A]

himself who is here more fortunate than wise.

As for Saint Augustine, is it certain that he admitted the first of the principles in question in the sense understood by Baïus, Jansenius, Ambroise Victor, Father Malebranche, and M. Bayle? We must not rely on their word, nor on their manner of interpreting Saint Augustine.

“What has never sinned cannot suffer eternal evil; what has never sinned cannot suffer the evil from which it has a right to be exempt.”

This is exactly true; this is Saint Augustine’s thought, and nothing more.

As proof of what I am asserting, is it not enough to point out that otherwise the holy doctor would have fallen into contradiction with himself—a contradiction so obvious that it would be astonishing not only that he himself failed to notice it at the first sight of a suffering animal in his presence, but especially that the Pelagians did not notice it and reproach him with it?

We are sufficiently trained in the schools to be satisfied with such an argument, which

[Col. 1047B]

, I admit, is not as novel as this cavalier remark: “Saint Augustine was more fortunate than wise.”

But did M. Bayle understand how, in this matter, Saint Augustine had been more fortunate than wise? Apparently not; he overlooked a contradiction still greater and more enormous, into which the holy doctor would have fallen if he had believed, without any modification or restriction, that what has never sinned cannot suffer evil. M. Bayle is content to address him as follows: “You reason badly when you say: Infants suffer evil and die; therefore they are guilty. For you assume a false principle, contradicted by the condition of animals—namely, that what has not sinned cannot suffer evil.” There was ample opportunity to rebuke the holy doctor much more forcefully by saying to him: Have you forgotten that you yourself proved that infants can suffer evil and die without being guilty? And that on this occasion you also showed that animals, although incapable of sinning, are nevertheless justly burdened with labor and subjected to every kind of suffering?

Indeed, when Saint Augustine undertakes to demonstrate to the Manichaeans the justice of the evils endured by infants, he assumes only principles that these heretics could not dispute. For this reason he makes no mention whatever of original sin, which they refused to admit; he does not suggest in the least that the miseries of childhood were the punishment for any sin. He reasons on the hypothesis of innocence, and believes that he is defending divine providence quite adequately against its inept slanderers, as he calls them, by saying that pains and death are transitory evils; that, for those who experience them in infancy, they will one day be as though they had never existed; and that, consequently, God was not obliged to spare them to infants, even if they could not benefit the children themselves, because they could serve to make better the parents and relatives who witnessed their sufferings:

“Why, then, should these things not occur, when, once they have passed away, they will be as though they had not occurred for those in whom they occurred, while those for whose sake they occurred will either become better, etc.” (*De libero arbitrio*, Book III, chap. 23, no. 68).

Moreover, he adds: “Who knows what reward God reserves for infants, whose sufferings soften the hardness of adults, exercise faith, or provide an occasion for the compassionate mercy of those advanced in years?”

*Quis autem novit quid parvulis, de quorum cruciatibus duritia majorum contunditur, aut exercetur fides, aut misericordia probatur . . . in secreto judiciorum suorum bonae compensationis reservet Deus* (ibid.).

He takes care to remind his reader that all this must be understood on the hypothesis of innocence:

“Although they had done nothing right, nevertheless they did not suffer these things as sinners” (ibid.).

[Col. 1048A] Saint Augustine does not stop there. He next defends divine providence even with regard to the pains and labors of animals:

“Although these slanderers—who are not diligent investigators of such questions but very loquacious disseminators of them—also commonly trouble the faith of the less learned concerning the pains and labors of animals, when they say: What evil have animals deserved that they should suffer such great hardships, or what good do they hope for, since they are exercised by such great hardships? But they say or think this because they judge of things most unjustly, etc.” (ibid., no. 69).

These words clearly contain a denial of the principle “What has never sinned cannot suffer evil,” and Saint Augustine recognizes its falsity by the very example of animals. Why, then, did M. Bayle need to take the trouble to make him perceive it, and to display his talent for reasoning in order to compel the holy doctor, by the force of consequence, to admit what he had expressly taught?

But how does Jansenius extricate himself from the difficulty? He is thoroughly embarrassed. To begin with, he passes over in silence the objection furnished by Saint Augustine’s view of the soul and sufferings of animals against the opinion attributed to him concerning the sufferings of infants, when this Father uses it to prove original sin. He imagined no plausible coloring with which to cloak a poor evasion that might serve to elude so great a difficulty. Descartes had not yet appeared. Otherwise Jansenius would not have hesitated to say that Saint Augustine believed in a material substantial form when disputing with the Manichaeans, and adhered to the machine theory when combating the Pelagians.

What he replies to the other objection is no more sound. He claims that, in attacking the Pelagians, the holy doctor corrected the imprudent words that had escaped him while refuting the Manichaeans: *Id quod incautius fuderat emendavit*—“He corrected what he had uttered too incautiously”; that he reproached himself for his blunder, *hallucinationem suam redarguit*—“he rebuked his own error”; that he emerged from the reverie into which he had fallen, *instar somnii fuit*—“it was like a dream” (Jansenius, vol. II, Book III, *De statu naturae purae*, chap. 19).

I catch M. Bayle in the act: he is a plagiarist. Here he pilfered Jansenius’s thought and turned it somewhat more agreeably by saying that Saint Augustine had been more fortunate than wise.

For the rest, try, if you can, to guess on what basis Jansenius asserted that the holy doctor had changed his position regarding the sufferings of infants, and that, after believing that they would suffer justly even if they were supposed to be without sin, he had adopted the contrary view. You would never manage it; I must tell you. Saint Augustine declares in one of his letters that the manner in which he had defended divine providence against the Manichaeans was insufficient to convince the Pelagians. The same objection had to be answered, an objection that both groups drew from the origin of the soul. It was not a serious difficulty on the Manichaeans’ side, because it was unnecessary to take a position on the origin of the soul; and since there was no question of proving original sin to them, the purpose of the controversy was to defend the justice and goodness of God, whether human beings were born innocent or brought into the world with some sin that their soul had contracted at birth or before it.

With the Pelagians, by contrast, it was necessary to determine the true state of affairs. It was not permissible to abstract from original sin; it was necessary to show that, at the moment of its creation, the soul is stained by a blemish that makes it deserving of passing through all the miseries now attached to human life. The transmission of this sin and blemish was extremely difficult to explain, and it had to be established in order to justify the miseries of infants. This is what Jansenius takes for a retraction, for a change of opinion:

“But when it comes to those punishments of infants, believe me, I am beset by great perplexities and quite unable to find an answer—not only concerning the punishments that await them after this life, to which they must necessarily be dragged if they depart from the body without the sacrament of Christian grace, but also concerning those very punishments that, while we suffer them in this life, lie before our eyes” (*Letter* 166 to Jerome, formerly 28, chap. 6, no. 16).

Admire Jansenius’s reasoning: Formerly, when disputing against the Manichaeans, Saint Augustine was not perplexed concerning the sufferings and miseries of childhood; now, when disputing against the Pelagians, he is perplexed; therefore he retracts and abandons as false the opinion he had defended.

Saint Augustine would have been very surprised by this reasoning, especially if he had seen Jansenius quote a second passage from the same letter, which serves as a commentary on the first and confirms the explanation I have just given:

“I did indeed say something in those books *On Free Will*, not about their natural capacities, but at least about the punishments that infants suffer in this life.” I shall explain what it means and why it is insufficient for me in the question we now have before us, and I shall insert in this letter the passage taken from the third book” (ibid., chap. 7, no. 17).

All the Jansenists, following their master’s example, read the words *In ista quam habemus in manibus quaestione*—“in the question that we now have before us”—as though they were written in a language unknown to them. Their eyes see words that mean: “What I said in the third book of *Free Will* is insufficient for the present question that I must address against the Pelagians”; but their minds see only this general proposition: “What I said in the third book is insufficient.” This is miraculous.

Jansenius places great emphasis on the following words:

“Now, however, I wish, if I can, to select one of them all by sound reasoning; and for that reason, examining more attentively, in what I have recalled from that book, my defense of this very matter with which we are now concerned, I do not find it strong and firm” (ibid., chap. 6, no. 19).

Saint Augustine says that he finally wishes to adhere to one of the four opinions he had proposed in the third book of *Free Will* concerning the origin of the soul; and that, for this purpose, when he attentively considered the manner in which he had defended divine justice on the hypothesis that souls were created at the moment when bodies were formed, he did not find the principal reason he had then employed to be sound. In what sense did he not find it sound? In relation to the present question, which had to be treated against the Pelagians by reasoning about the true state of affairs and presupposing original sin.

That reason was that God, in the secrecy of his judgments, reserves some reward for infants to compensate them for what they have suffered. This proof, as Saint Augustine observes, could properly apply only to children who died either as martyrs or after receiving baptism, but not to those unfortunate enough to perish without being regenerated in Jesus Christ:

“For the Church does not without reason commend even those infants who, when Herod was seeking to kill our Lord Jesus Christ, were killed and received into the honor of the martyrs” (ibid., no. 18; and Book III of *Free Will*, chap. 23, no. 67).

The holy doctor was therefore obliged to make this distinction and give this qualification when disputing with the Pelagians; he was not required to take it into account in his writings against the Manichaeans. What am I saying? He was not free to speak of original sin as an established dogma.

For Jansenius may try as he will to obscure the difference between these two controversies; it is evident to anyone familiar with both heresies that Saint Augustine was in a kind of impossibility of successfully attacking the Manichaeans by the authority of Scripture while assuming the present state of affairs, and that, to gain an advantage over them, he was most often forced to resort to pure reason and exercise it upon various hypotheses that he devised.

To refute the Pelagians, on the other hand, the holy doctor was obliged to remain with the present state of affairs, because the issue was to make them confess the dogma of original sin; and against them the proofs of Scripture, both Old and New Testament, had their full force. Saint Augustine himself makes this observation:

“This discussion must be held against the Manichaeans, who do not accept the holy Scriptures of the Old Testament, in which original sin is related, and who, with detestable impudence, contend that whatever is read about it in the apostolic writings was inserted by corrupters of Scripture, as though it had not been said by the apostles. Against the Pelagians, however, we must defend what both Scriptures commend, which they profess to accept” (*Retractions*, Book I, chap. 9, at the end).

Thus the holy doctor proved against the Pelagians that the sufferings of infants were just because they were the punishment of sin; and he proved against the Manichaeans that these same sufferings were just, whether or not they were the punishment of sin. And this doctrine, which he maintained against the Manichaeans, he not only never retracted but confirmed in his later works, in the sight of the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians, without fearing that they would accuse him of contradicting himself.

For who would dare deny that what he asserted concerning concupiscence and ignorance must equally be understood of the miseries attached to human childhood? “I believed,” he says, “that I ought to refute the Manichaeans in such a way that, whether these things were the punishment of original sin in infants—as the truth holds—or were not—as some who err suppose—they nevertheless could in no way serve to establish the error of the Manichaeans, which introduces a mixture of two natures, one good and the other evil” (ibid.).

Thus far I have heightened the alleged contradiction that led M. Bayle to say that Saint Augustine had been more fortunate than wise, while reserving the right to show that the holy doctor nowhere taught the principle “What has never sinned cannot suffer evil” in the sense given to it by Baïus, Jansenius, Ambrose Victor, Malebranche, and Bayle.

Before presenting the proofs on this point, let us see whether, as M. Bayle asserts, this is a principle of the utmost evidence, one that necessarily flows from the ideas we have of the justice and goodness of God. That would be most unfortunate for religion; for unless the proposition is modified and changed into something entirely different, belief in the Incarnation is overturned. With the utmost evidence, and on the basis of the ideas we have of the divine attributes, one would establish a monstrous heresy and necessarily arrive at one of two blasphemies: either the holy humanity of Jesus Christ, having been able to suffer evil, sinned; or, having never sinned, it could not suffer evil. Evidence of Servetus and Socinus, Marcionite or Photinian ideas—your deceptive clarity never shone in the mind of Saint Augustine.

Whoever believes that the spotless Lamb suffered for the sins of the world must admit a restriction that destroys the universality of the much-vaunted principle. Every Christian must confess that what has never sinned could suffer temporal evil out of charity and in order to benefit others, and that this suffering of an innocent person could have been ordained by God, since it is an article of faith that God commanded Jesus Christ to offer himself for us to torments and death.

Let us go further. Was it impossible that, in the state of innocence, human beings should know the value of patience and strength, humility, faith, and charity—the virtues that misery and suffering provide a special opportunity to practice, in a manner that heightens their excellence and increases their merit? If they had known this, could they not have wished to be afflicted with a temporal evil that would make them capable of such a heroic and God-pleasing perfection? What clear ideas contradict this wish or represent it as offensive to reason?

Now, this evil, which a person might legitimately seek out of charity toward himself and in order to acquire a good, could God not have the right to impose upon him? Could he not do so without injustice and as an effect of his goodness? What! The nobility of the end that a person would propose to himself in desiring to suffer would justify his attraction to suffering, yet it would not cleanse from injustice or cruelty God’s decree which, with the same end in view, compelled him to suffer?

I can here turn against Jansenius his own words. “No one,” he says (vol. II, Book III, *De statu naturae purae*, chap. 19), “who possesses common sense will find that a man is afflicted unjustly when, by taking an obol from him, one gives him a gold piece; or when, by lightly scratching him, one procures perfect health for him; or when, by causing him a small displeasure, one gives him great joy or great wisdom.” God, then, would afflict the innocent man without injustice by compelling him to pass through all the miseries of this life in order to bring him to the possession of an exceedingly great and excellent good.

“But,” someone will say, “infants would suffer without virtue and without merit, and those who died before the age of reason would derive no benefit from their sufferings; under a good and just God, these little innocents would be simply miserable.” There is the difficulty.

Saint Augustine resolved it. He maintains that a misery which passes away, and which the absence of understanding greatly diminishes, is not comparable with the benefit that comes from it to the whole human race. For the sight of the humiliating and painful condition of childhood reminds young people and adults of the lowliness of their origin and inspires in them sentiments of moderation and modesty. It teaches them not to become proud or to take advantage of their health, knowledge, wealth, power, or any of their talents (Saint Augustine, Book III of *Free Will*, chap. 23, no. 68).
