By what clear ideas can one demonstrate that God cannot, without derogating from his justice and goodness, will the temporal evil of some individuals when that evil would be the cause or occasion of the eternal good of many others?

I leave aside the arguments that Saint Augustine and the Catholic theologians employ to show that subjection to suffering and death belongs to the very constitution of human nature, and that the impassibility and immortality which innocent man would have enjoyed were a special and supernatural grace.

Here all the Jansenists and Malebranchists join their voices to that of M. Bayle and cry out: “So, then, all the proofs of original sin that Saint Augustine derives from the illnesses and death to which infants are subject have completely collapsed?”

Not at all. They remain and preserve an invincible force—not in isolation, but taken together with all that accompanies and follows from them, and referred to their principle: that the first man, at his creation, had received a right to impassibility and immortality. The holy doctor takes care to repeat, impress, and firmly establish this—not once or twice, but continually and on every occasion. I do not know whether he ever copied himself more frequently, using the same turns of phrase and the same terms in very long passages.

Thus, whenever he says that God would be neither good nor just if innocent man had been born subject to the miseries we experience in life, one must supply the following syllogism: It is contrary to the justice and goodness of God to deprive man of a privilege of which he had been placed in possession at his first origin; now, at his first origin, man had been placed in possession of the privilege of not suffering and not dying, etc.

In the system that Jansenius attributes to Saint Augustine, the justice and goodness of God would have been equally offended whether Adam, before his sin, had not been exempt from the evils we call natural, or whether his descendants, without sharing in his sin, inherited this sad condition from him.

Why, then, when reasoning against the Pelagians, who denied both points, does the holy doctor never say that God would have ceased to be just if the first man, upon emerging from his hands, had found himself assailed by a multitude of miseries like ours? Why, on the contrary, does he invariably set the justice and goodness of God against the Pelagian error, which, by assuming the original righteousness of Adam’s children, made them be born in a worse condition than that in which their father had been created? This observation is important and decisive.

Let Saint Augustine be asked: If our first parents, faithful to God, had not been expelled from the earthly paradise, and if human beings had multiplied in that dwelling, which through the merits of Adam and Eve had become the inheritance and homeland of all their descendants, would there not have been women there who experienced the discomforts of pregnancy, the pains and dangers of childbirth, and the misfortune of miscarriage? Would there not have been children who cried when coming into the world, who remained for a long time unable to speak, and who began to do so only by stammering; children for whom the advantage of being instructed and formed required so many years of repellent labor and harsh dependence?

Would there not have been men disfavored by nature, whose defects of mind and body made them objects of compassion to the most inhuman, of ridicule to the malicious, and of horror to the delicate? Would illnesses of every kind, which make animated corpses and living specters rather than human beings groan upon a bed of pain, have been unknown there? Would the various forms of death—of which the mildest is still terrifying, while some are so frightful and despairing—have been unknown? Would poverty and famine, which reduce an infinite number of people to such dreadful and extraordinary extremities, have been unknown? Would discord and war, which cause such deplorable devastation and disaster, have been unknown? Would all these evils have been unknown in the earthly paradise?

Saint Augustine replies [Note: [Col. 1051] Saint Augustine, *Opus imperfectum*, Book I, no. 67; Book III, no. [lacuna] 54; Book IV, no. 114; Book V, nos. 22–23; Book VI, nos. 5, 9, 16] that these questions are ridiculous and senseless. And on what does he base this? Is it on the claim that God cannot, without injustice and cruelty, permit innocent creatures to be subjected to such miseries? No. The holy doctor reserves that proof for when one assumes the innocence of the children born of Adam after his sin caused him to be banished from the earthly paradise. It has no force if one supposes that Adam, innocent and remaining in the earthly paradise, had children.

In the latter case Saint Augustine does not refer us to the ideas we have of the justice and goodness of God, but only to the idea that Holy Scripture gives us of the earthly paradise: Scripture calls it a paradise of delights (*paradisum voluptatis*).

The word “paradise” itself means a delightful garden. On this point Saint Augustine pleasantly says to the Pelagians: If one painted a paradise such as you portray it, no one would say that it was a paradise, even if he read that word inscribed above the painting. He would not say that the painter had made a mistake; rather, he would recognize him plainly as an eccentric who had wished to amuse himself and mock others. Yet none of those who know you would be surprised if your name were added to the title and the inscription read: “THE PARADISE OF THE PELAGIANS.”

“Certainly, if such a paradise were painted, no one would say that it was a paradise, not even if he read this name inscribed above it; nor would he say that the painter had erred, but would plainly recognize him as a mocker. Yet none of those who know you would be surprised if your name were added to the title and it were written: PARADISUS PELAGIANORUM” (Book III of *Opus imperfectum*, no. 154).

Another proof employed by the holy doctor is based on the expulsion from paradise, which was the punishment our first parents incurred immediately after their fall. From this he concludes that, if no one had sinned, evils would not have entered such a happy dwelling, since even after sin they could not enter it. Rather than introduce evils into the earthly paradise, God expelled its inhabitants at the moment when they deserved to be unhappy:

“Ambrose would answer that all these things, if no one had sinned, would in no way have occurred in a place of such great blessedness, where they could not exist even after sin, once those whose transgression brought about these evils had been expelled from it” (Book IV of *Opus imperfectum*, no. 114).

Finally, he draws a third proof from these words: *Viditque Deus cuncta quae fecerat, et erant valde bona* (Gen. 1:31)—“And God saw all the things he had made, and they were very good.” Now, says the holy doctor to Julian, why do you not notice that, of all the places in the world, the earthly paradise was undoubtedly the best that God had made? And yet, in that dwelling of such great blessedness and beauty, where we must believe that there could be no defect or bad quality in any tree, grass, fruit, grain, or animal, you do not hesitate to introduce, with respect to human beings, every defect of body and mind:

“Why do you not attend to the fact that, in the book where it is written that God made all things very good, paradise was planted as the best of all places? . . . And yet, in a place of such great blessedness and beauty, where we must believe that there could be no defect in any tree, grass, fruit, crop, or animal, you do not hesitate to introduce every defect of human bodies and minds” (Book VI of *Opus imperfectum*, no. 16).

Saint Augustine was very kind to scrutinize the expressions of Scripture in this way and embark on such arguments. He had a much shorter and more effective way of overturning the Pelagians’ paradise: he only had to say, “What has never sinned cannot suffer evil; this is a principle of the utmost evidence, necessarily flowing from the ideas we have of the justice and goodness of God.”

But did the holy doctor not speak in this manner somewhere—for example, in the passage before us, whose opening words were not printed in capitals without reason?

“*Justum enim erat ut imago Dei, nullo fuscata et obsoleta peccato, tali insereretur corpori, quamvis de terrena materie creato atque formato, ut ei de ligno vitae subministrata vivendi stabilitas permaneret*.”

“For it was just that the image of God, darkened and defaced by no sin, should be placed in such a body, although created and formed from earthly matter, so that the stability of life, supplied by the tree of life, might remain with it” (Book VI of *Opus imperfectum*, no. 39).

The capital letters initially frightened me. But since Saint Augustine was not the one who supplied them, I reassured myself and became thoroughly convinced that *justum erat* means “it was fitting.”

Indeed, Saint Augustine does not mean that immortality was owed to innocent man, but that the gift of immortality was granted to him with a certain propriety. It is in this sense that Virgil said, “*Justum pugnae tempus*”—“the fitting time for battle” (*Aeneid* X, verse 11), and Pliny the Elder: “*Justiore venia, justissimus casus*”—“with a more fitting pardon, a most fitting accident” (*Natural History*, Book III, no. 1; Book XXXVI, no. 10).

Read what follows, and you will see that Saint Augustine’s *justum erat*, far from being the conclusion of the principle “What has not sinned cannot suffer evil,” is proved by the example of Elijah and Enoch, who were transported to the earthly paradise so that they would not die:

“For I ask you: In what sort of body do you now suppose Elijah and Enoch to exist—in an animal or a spiritual body? Why are you unwilling to believe that Adam and Eve and their descendants, if they had violated God’s command through no transgression, although living in an animal body, would have lived as these men now live? For they were in the place to which these men were transported, and from which those were expelled so that they might die” (Saint Augustine, ibid.).

Here, then, is Saint Augustine’s thought: It was fitting that Adam and Eve, while innocent, should have the same privilege now enjoyed by Elijah and Enoch, and that they should not die, since they were in the same place to which those two saints were transported so as not to die. For why would God have refused the innocence of our first parents a grace that he granted to the holiness of these prophets—a grace that appears to have been attached to the dwelling from which the former were expelled because of their transgression, and into which the latter were received because of their faithfulness?

[Col. 1053]

## THIRD TREATISE

### Dissertation on the Nature of the Mosaic Law

[Col. 1053D] Sir,

The approval you give to my efforts to seek the true meaning of Saint Augustine pleases me so greatly that I cannot refuse to satisfy you by applying myself, as you wish, to clarifying the holy doctor’s precise and correct position concerning the nature of the Mosaic law. M. Bayle will therefore enjoy some respite until I have explained to you the difference found in this regard between the Augustine of Ypres and the Augustine of Hippo. For you will permit me, throughout this work, to address my thoughts and words to you, so that the ever-present desire to write things worthy of you may sustain and animate me.

I must first place before your eyes all the controversies that have ever been stirred up in the Church concerning the ancient law, following the order of time. “Why this digression?” you will ask. Because nothing has caused so much embarrassment and confusion in this matter as the diversity and contradiction of the errors that succeeded one another. The ancient sectarians supplied weapons to the more recent in their attacks on the Catholic faith; and, what deserves particular attention, the weapons that the Church had successfully employed to defeat the first were seized by the later ones and turned against the Church itself.

It is therefore appropriate that I distinguish four kinds of controversies concerning the law of Moses, and establish the state of the question between the apostles and the Jews, between the Fathers and the Manichaeans, between Saint Augustine and the Pelagians, and between the defenders of the faith of the Council of Trent and the heretics of our own day.

### Part One

## The State of the Question between the Apostles and the Jews

[Col. 1055] Take care, I beg you, to notice that the apostles spoke of the law of Moses while disputing both with Jews who believed in Jesus Christ and with unbelieving Jews. Certain people who confuse everything, even when they affect to speak more simply and clearly, will never make this observation, although it is nevertheless very important.

The Jews who had embraced Christianity began by entertaining the presumptuous notion that the Savior of the world had been granted only on account of the merits and distinction of their race, and that consequently the kingdom of heaven was open only to those of their nation; that the light of the Gospel was spreading throughout the universe to honor them, and grace to favor them, to the exclusion of all other peoples.

This is the error that the Apostle destroys when he teaches that the true children of Abraham are not born according to the flesh but according to the spirit (Rom. 9:7). Heaven had spoken, and the revelation that had brought the Gentiles into the path of faith and salvation nevertheless did not end the dispute.

The Jews who had become Christians obstinately maintained that, in order to become Christians, the Gentiles had to be proselytes of the law of Moses; that everyone was obliged to add circumcision to baptism and submit to all the observances and ceremonies prescribed by Judaism.

The Apostle rose up against this second error and showed forcefully that the faithful had been released from the yoke of the ancient law because that law was imperfect and henceforth useless.

The whole substance and body of Saint Paul’s teaching concerning the nature of the ancient law is contained in five of his Epistles. The principal question he addresses in the Epistle to the Romans is, according to Saint Augustine, whether the Gospel of Our Lord came to the Jews alone on account of the merit of their works, or whether, without any preceding merits of works, the justification of faith that is in Jesus Christ was offered to all nations: *Utrum Evangelium Domini nostri Judaeis solis venerit, an vero nullis operum meritis praecedentibus, omnibus gentibus venerit justificatio fidei, quae est in Christo Jesu* (“Whether the Gospel of our Lord came to the Jews alone, or whether, without any preceding merits of works, the justification of faith that is in Jesus Christ came to all nations”) (*In Expos. inchoata Epist. ad Rom.*, no. 2).

The Apostle uses two reasons to prove that the Jews did not receive the grace of the Gospel as a reward for the works of the law. The [Col. 1055D] first is that the law did not make them better, since they were content with the honor of having received it, without taking care to observe it. Therefore he rightly reproaches these transgressors in these words: “You, then, who teach others, do you not teach yourselves? You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal, and so forth?” *Qui ergo alium doces, te ipsum non doces? Qui praedicas non furandum, furaris, etc.* (“You, therefore, who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal?”) (Rom. II, 21). And afterward: “You who glory in the law dishonor God by transgressing the law. For, as it is written, the name of God is blasphemed [Col. 1056A] among the Gentiles because of you.” *Qui in lege gloriaris, per praevaricationem legis Deum inhonoras? Nomen enim Dei per vos blasphematur inter gentes, sicut scriptum est* (“You who glory in the law, do you dishonor God through transgression of the law? For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you, as it is written”) (ibid., 23, 24; Isa. LII, 5; Ezek. XXXVI, 20).

The second reason is that neither justification nor the [Col. 1056B] benefit of the faith and Gospel of Jesus Christ can be the wages of legal practices and observances; and Saint Paul proves this by the example of Abraham, whose justification was not the fruit of the works of the law, but of faith in God, which was counted to him as righteousness before circumcision was given to him. You see that, in this Epistle, the Apostle chiefly attacks the first error of the Jews who had acknowledged Jesus Christ as the Messiah. In the one addressed to the Ephesians, he announces to the Gentiles the consoling truth that he had upheld on their behalf: namely, that they were called to the Gospel and to the hope of eternal life just as the Jews were.

As for the second error, he devotes himself principally to combating it in the Epistle to the Galatians and in the Epistle to the Colossians. Both groups had passed from Judaism to the Christian religion. To the Galatians, who had resumed all the ancient practices of the religion of their fathers, he teaches that [Col. 1056C] Christianity has delivered them from the servitude of the Mosaic law; and, to make them willing to believe him rather than certain teachers who had spoken to them otherwise, he emphasizes the authority of his apostleship. The Colossians had too much attachment and deference toward those who had until then been the leaders and princes of their Synagogue; the Apostle had reason to fear that they would allow themselves to be persuaded that the rite and ceremonial of Judaism had to be added to faith in Jesus Christ. He tells them that Jesus Christ is the head of the Church, the head of all principalities and powers, with the right to command and to demand obedience to himself in preference to anyone else, and that consequently no account should henceforth be taken of any of the ordinances of the law.

Finally, the entire subject of the Epistle to the Hebrews is to show that Jesus Christ, by his dignity, is above Moses and the angels; that his priesthood was announced by the sacred Scriptures; and that it is more excellent [Col. 1056D] than that of Aaron. All this serves to conclude that the ancient sacrifices and the priesthood of Aaron were abolished by Jesus Christ, and that the priesthood of the Christian religion, the sacrifice of the cross, and the sacrifice of our altars succeeded them.

In most of these passages, Saint Paul instructs and disabuses the faithful Jews of their errors so thoroughly that, at the same time, he confounds the unbelief of the others, who rejected the Gospel and claimed not to need it in order to be righteous and attain salvation. It is not unimportant to observe which of these two kinds of Jews the Apostle chiefly has in view when [Col. 1057A] he teaches that neither righteousness nor salvation can come from the law.

This is the delicate point, I warn you. People mock us as wretched scholastics who feed ourselves on empty subtleties and imagine that we can satisfy the world with frivolous evasions and fanciful distinctions, when we maintain that the Apostle does not deny that, in the Old Testament, the assistance of grace was joined to the instruction of the law; rather, he had reasons for considering the law by itself, stripped of grace, although it was not in fact deprived of it. He had reason to make this qualification; for grace is the very substance of the evangelical law, and all the grace given in the Old Testament was an anticipated fruit of the new covenant, to which Jesus Christ, the author of grace, belonged wholly.

We are answered with disdain: “The Apostle was really thinking about these metaphysical qualifications! Was he speaking of things as they are in the mind of a contemplative person, or as they are in themselves?”

[Col. 1057B] Will our adversaries’ ill temper or bad faith patiently allow me, in turn, to ask them: What is Saint Paul’s purpose when he teaches that neither righteousness nor salvation can come from the law? Is it not to convince the enemies of the Gospel that the evangelical law is necessary and that it must absolutely be received? Whom, then, is he opposing, if not those unbelieving Jews who, not knowing the righteousness that comes from God and seeking to establish their own, are not subject to the righteousness that comes from God? *Ignorantes enim justitiam Dei et suam quaerentes statuere, justitiae Dei non sunt subjecti* (“For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to the righteousness of God”) (Rom. X, 3). Is Saint Paul not arguing against those who detested the law of Jesus Christ and maintained that the law of Moses was sufficient for them? Now, did these Jews not regard and uphold their religion independently of any relation to Jesus Christ? Did they not conceive it as deprived of all the advantages it [Col. 1057C] could derive from its affinity and connection with the Christian religion? And consequently, did they not force Saint Paul to reason within their hypothesis and to consider the ancient law as separated from the assistance of grace that the faith of the Messiah—faith that was a vow to embrace the Gospel—had truly attached to it?

For, in addition, Saint Paul joins his testimony to that of Moses to assure us that, in view of Jesus Christ, God granted grace to the faithful observers of the law. “The end of the law,” says the Apostle, “is Christ, so that those who believe may be justified.” Moses likewise wrote that the person who practices the righteousness commanded by the law will have life through it: *Finis legis Christus, ad justitiam omni credenti. Moyses enim scripsit, quoniam justitiam quae ex lege est qui fecerit homo, vivet in ea* (“The end of the law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes. For Moses wrote that the person who practices the righteousness that comes from the law will live by it”) (ibid., IV, 5; Lev. XVIII, 5).

It is not enough, in order to make clear the state of the question between the apostles and the Jews, to have distinguished the errors and truths that formed the subject of the controversy, or to have observed that two kinds of Jews opposed the apostles’ doctrine. The ambiguity of the word “law,” which is abused, must also be removed. Ambiguity is a great resource for all who defend a bad cause; it is counterfeit money that they use in place of the genuine money they lack.

The word “law” has three different meanings when applied to the Old and New Testaments. Sometimes it means the commandments and precepts that compose the positive divine law of the Old and New Testaments, insofar as they are precisely rules of morals and conduct possessing the power to guide and the force to oblige. In addition, the word is used to express the collection of things belonging to religion in either Testament, whether precepts or sacred ceremonies. Finally, the word “law” also denotes [Col. 1058A] a condition or society of human beings who, under the government of divine providence, strive by the same means God has given them toward a supernatural end; in this way it expresses the condition of the Jews or of Christians.

Saint Paul uses the word “law” in the first sense throughout chapter VII of the Epistle to the Romans, where he says that the written law became for many an occasion of more grievous sin, because an unhappy inclination leads a person to do what is forbidden. The law of the Gospel, understood in this way, contains grace no more than the law of Moses does.

Saint Paul uses the word “law” in the second sense when he says: “The preceding law was rejected because it was weak and useless; for the law brought nothing to perfection.” *Reprobatio fit praecedentis mandati propter infirmitatem et inutilitatem; nihil enim ad perfectum adducit lex* (“The preceding commandment is rejected because of weakness and uselessness; for the law brings nothing to perfection”) (Heb. VII, 18, 19). In this sense, the ancient law [Col. 1058B] is empty of graces, as Saint Paul indicates, whereas the new law has a great many exceedingly abundant sources of grace, namely, the sacraments instituted by Jesus Christ.

As for the third sense, Saint Paul indicates it whenever he contrasts Jews with Christians, and the condition of the worshipers of the true God formed by Moses with that of the faithful brought up in the school of Jesus Christ. The ancient law, considered in this way—that is, as the condition in which the people of God found themselves before the coming of the Savior—was in truth not only ennobled by faith in the future Messiah, but also sufficiently supplied and enriched with the graces needed by the people who composed that society to strive toward and attain a supernatural end. Nevertheless, in the contrast he draws, the Apostle makes the essential difference between Judaism and Christianity consist in the fact that the latter is the law of grace. I have already shown the reason for this, but this is the place to explain it.

[Col. 1058C] The obstinacy of unbelieving Jews in rejecting the Gospel and praising the excellence of the Old Testament to the exclusion of the New placed the Apostle under the necessity of reclaiming for the Christian religion all the spiritual advantages and benefits that the Jewish religion had possessed, as anticipated fruits from a source that belonged to the Christian religion. Now the person of Jesus Christ, his merits and satisfactions, and consequently all the assistance of grace that had been distributed to all human beings throughout all times through the price of Jesus Christ’s merits and satisfactions, properly belonged to the Christian religion. Saint Paul therefore had not only to set Jesus Christ against Moses and the angels who had dictated the law on Mount Sinai, and his priesthood against that of Aaron, as he does in the Epistle to the Hebrews; he was also obliged to attribute the new law exclusively to the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1058D] For although the Holy Spirit extended his saving operations, poured out his gifts, and bestowed the benefit of sanctification throughout all the ages of the human race, nevertheless, because he is the Spirit of Jesus Christ, he belongs to the New Testament; and this source of water springing up to eternal life had been given before all ages to the Church of Jesus Christ as its own. Therefore, when one concludes from Saint Paul’s doctrine that the new law not only teaches and commands what must be done, but also provides the assistance and strength necessary for acting, whereas the ancient law limited itself to teaching and commanding without lending any aid to human weakness, this means that the treasury from which graces are drawn is contained in the new law, and that, with regard to the ancient law, they are an external and borrowed good.

You will ask me what all Saint Paul’s arguments on this subject finally come down to. [Col. 1059A] They announce to the Jews that, if they refuse to yield to the call of Jesus Christ, they must no longer hope to share in the grace and justification they had previously been able to receive through an outpouring of the riches of the Gospel upon the ages that preceded it. They declare to them that God has resolved to relieve his people of the burdensome practices of the written law and to deprive of grace anyone who thereafter attaches himself to observing them, because through faith in Jesus Christ he has opened for everyone an easier and gentler way of salvation.

I have begun here to touch upon the first of the five advantages that, according to Saint Paul, raise the new law above the ancient law, and which he uses as so many powerful motives to persuade his nation to recognize a new lawgiver and to prefer Jesus Christ to Moses. “No one,” he says, “is justified before God by the law.” *In lege nemo justificabitur apud Deum* (“No one will be justified before God by the law”) (Gal. IV, 11). “If righteousness comes from the law, then Christ died [Col. 1059B] for nothing.” *Si ex lege justitia, ergo gratis Christus mortuus est* (“If righteousness comes from the law, then Christ died in vain”) (Gal. II, 21).

The second advantage that he recalls and emphasizes on every occasion is that the Old Testament was only a figure of the New, and that the latter presents us with the reality of the things of which the former gave only the shadow: *Umbram enim habens lex futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum* (“For the law, possessing a shadow of the good things to come, does not possess the very image of the things”) (Heb. XIX, 1).

The third consists in the fact that the law of Moses was wholly carnal and promised only earthly and temporal goods, whereas the law of Jesus Christ is wholly spiritual and proposes only heavenly and eternal rewards. “A more excellent hope,” Saint Paul says, “by which we draw near to God, has succeeded the first”: *Introductio vero melioris spei, per quam proximamus ad Deum* (“The introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God”) (Heb. VII, 19). But here too remember that the Apostle has regard only to what properly belonged to the ancient law, to what was distinctive of it, to what it drew from its own resources, and not to [Col. 1059C] what came to it from the expectation and faith of the Messiah, or to what it borrowed from the new law through its purpose of anticipating, like a dawn, that great and perfect light which, before it was born, was already communicating itself to the world. For it is indisputable, as we shall see below, that the hope of heavenly and eternal goods, no less than the assistance of grace, was not lacking to the Israelites. But it is enough that this hope and assistance were foreign to the nature of their religion when considered absolutely in itself and without any relation to the Christian religion, to prevent their entering into Saint Paul’s comparison of what is proper and special to the two Testaments.

The fourth advantage of the new law over the ancient is that the latter is a law of servitude, which, through fear of temporal punishments, irritated rather than restrained concupiscence, whereas the former is a law of liberty and love. In speaking of the law of Moses, Saint Paul pays particular attention to the threats it employs to turn people away from crime. He calls it a ministry of death, a ministry of condemnation [Col. 1059D] (II Cor. VII, 9). “All those,” he says, “who are subject to the works of the law are under a curse”: *Quicunque ex operibus legis sunt, sub maledicto sunt* (“All who are of the works of the law are under a curse”) (Gal. III, 10). The expression “to be under the law,” *esse sub lege*, which he often uses to signify subjection to the law of Moses, ordinarily gives us the idea of a vengeful and threatening law. Elsewhere he says that it gave birth only to slaves: *In servitutem generans* (“Generating servitude”) (Gal. IV, 24). But how does he speak to Jews who have become Christians? “You have not received the spirit of servitude, to return to fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption as children of God”: *Non enim accepistis spiritum servitutis in timore, sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum* (“For you have not received the spirit of servitude in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption as children”) (Rom. VIII, 15).

[Col. 1060A] Yet if one were to ask: Are there people bold enough to call truth what destroys Saint Paul’s doctrine? The answer should be: They are those who count this error among the truths: “Moses and the prophets, the priests and teachers of the law died without giving children to God, having made only slaves through fear.” For if, on the one hand, the Apostle, considering only the power that was in the law of Moses, says that it could make only slaves, on the other hand he assumes that a remedy given to all the Israelites to erase the stain of original sin made them heirs and children of the kingdom. Jesus Christ himself calls them this (Matt. VIII, 12). Therefore Saint Paul, joining the status of adopted children of God, which the Jews received from the Savior’s grace, with the condition of slaves to which the law reduced them, compares them to a ward under the direction of a guardian. “As long,” he says, “as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, although he is lord of all; but he is under [Col. 1060B] guardians and agents until the time appointed by his father. So we too, when we were children, lived as slaves under the elements of the world”: *Quanto tempore haeres parvulus est, nihil differt a servo, cum sit dominus omnium, sed sub tutoribus et actoribus est usque ad praefinitum tempus a patre. Ita et nos cum essemus parvuli, sub elementis mundi eramus servientes* (“As long as the heir is a minor, he differs in nothing from a slave, although he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and agents until the time fixed by his father. So we too, when we were children, were serving under the elements of the world”) (Gal. IV, 1–3).

But are you not indignant at another abuse made of Saint Paul’s doctrine on this point, when it is asserted: “A baptized person is still under the law like a Jew if he fulfills the law solely out of fear”? The objection concerns fear of hell; yet the Apostle has in view only the temporal punishments decreed by the divine law of the Old Testament. He is very far from thinking of eternal punishments in the next life when [Col. 1060C] he calls Judaism a law of fear, in opposition to Christianity, which is a law of love. On the contrary, he teaches us that fear of the punishments God will inflict in eternity is one of the graces of the Holy Spirit belonging to the new law, and that the ancient law enjoyed it only by communication and borrowing, since this fear had its figures in the history of the people of God, just as did the hope of heavenly happiness.

Indeed, after saying that most of the Hebrews who came out of Egyptian captivity displeased God and perished in the desert, he adds: “Now these things were figures for us, so that we might not desire evil things as they desired them”: *Haec autem in figura facta sunt nostri, ut non simus concupiscentes malorum* (“These things were done as a figure for us, so that we might not be desirers of evil things”) (I Cor. X, 6). Then he describes the terrible punishments those ungrateful people brought upon themselves, and he repeats the same conclusion: “Now all these things happened to them as figures, but they [Col. 1060D] were written to instruct us”: *Haec autem omnia in figura contingebant illis. Scripta sunt autem ad correptionem nostram* (“All these things happened to them as a figure. They were written for our correction”) (ibid., 11).

Will anyone nevertheless persist in maintaining that the reality, as well as the figure, of fear of eternal punishments properly belongs to the ancient law? Then let the reality, as well as the figure, of the expectation of eternal rewards be assigned to it at the same time. Neither one nor the other is possible; the division is settled. All the figures belong to the sphere of the ancient law, and all the things figured belong to the province of the new law. But is the latter therefore a law of fear as much as a law of love? “What an absurdity!” they exclaim. As though, in a law of love, it were necessary that everything should be love, rather than that everything should tend toward love! Now it is the very love God bears toward us, and his desire to be loved by us, that inspired and dictated the threats of an [Col. 1061A] eternity of punishments that the sacred authors of both Testaments deliver to us on his behalf. He has placed us between hell and himself, so that fear of our ruin might turn our heart toward him and oblige us to come and throw ourselves into his arms; and so that the love we bear ourselves might serve his tenderness toward us, first by inducing us to love him as our sole and supreme good, and then by leading us to consider closely how lovable he is, in order to raise us to the most perfect love.

Finally, the fifth advantage that makes the New Testament preferable to the Old is inward worship—the adoration in spirit and in truth that forms its soul and principal part. For outward forms, actions, and sensory ceremonies constituted the whole essence of Judaism. It was an inconvenient and oppressive religion because of the multitude of its practices, all of which were bodily and merely outward display. “Why,” Saint Peter says, “do you put God to the test by imposing upon the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” *Quid tentatis imponere jugum super cervices discipulorum, quod neque patres nostri neque nos portare potuimus* (“Why do you test God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?”) (Acts XV, 10). “This worship,” Saint Paul says, “was reduced to foods, drinks, various washings, and ordinances concerning the flesh”: *Solummodo in cibis, et in potibus, et variis baptismatibus et justitiis carnis* (“Only in foods, drinks, various baptisms, and ordinances of the flesh”) (Heb. IX, 6, 10), expressing the constraint [Col. 1062A] imposed by that crowd of observances which returned at every moment.

The same Saint Paul represents the law of Moses as a tutor who allows a young disciple no step or movement that his severe eye does not regulate and govern: *Lex paedagogus noster fuit* (“The law was our tutor”) (Gal. III, 24). Saint Augustine compares the temporal and sensory things that formed the proper and particular subject matter of this law to children’s toys, which one does not fail to take away from them when they grow up (St. Augustine, *Sermon* 302, chap. 1, no. 1, elsewhere numbered 3, *De Diversis*).

It is nevertheless certain that the law of Moses prescribed inward acts; but these precepts were too perfect to be attributed to the proper spirit of that law, and the Apostle was not to mention them in arguing against the Jews. For the entire controversy was precisely contained in these two questions: What account should be taken of the law of Moses when it is set against the law of the Messiah—that is, when the first is stripped of, and the second claims, all the [Col. 1062B] spiritual goods that come from the Messiah? What remains of the consideration in which the law of Moses was held solely because of the expectation of the Messiah, once the Messiah has arrived? The first question concerned unbelieving Jews who refused to embrace the Christian religion; the second concerned faithful Jews who wanted to mingle Judaism with Christianity.

## Second Part. STATE OF THE QUESTION BETWEEN THE FATHERS AND THE MANICHAEANS

[Col. 1061]

[Col. 1061C] Several of these latter adversaries did not submit to the authority of the apostles; and, persisting in bringing the Synagogue into the Church, they ended up separated from both. Cerinthus and Ebion placed themselves at their head. For this reason, the Fathers were obliged for some time to continue the same dispute concerning the Jewish ceremonies and to show their uselessness and vanity after the establishment of the Gospel.

But, on the other side, an entirely contrary error arose, which soon changed the controversy. Simon Magus, Menander, Saturninus, Basilides, and later Carpocrates, Cerdo, and Marcion conceived such horror for the law of Moses that they judged it unworthy to have a good and beneficent God as its author, and did not hesitate to say that it was the work of a malicious and destructive intelligence. This is one of the points of the impious doctrine transmitted to Mani through the writings of two less-known impostors, Scythianus and Terbinthus, whose pernicious inheritance he gathered up. The sect he formed was successfully opposed by several holy doctors, especially Saint Augustine, who turned to the advantage of the Church the misfortune of having attached himself in his youth to this heresy and professed it for nine full years.

You would not forgive me if I stopped here to set out and develop precisely the substance of the entire doctrine attributed particularly to the Manichaeans, merely because their zeal in promoting and perpetuating it distinguished them from their predecessors; nor if I elaborated upon the system of two principles, one good and the other evil, which, according to the fantasies of the Marcionites and Manichaeans, have existed from all eternity, share rule over the world, hate one another, and wage mutual war with alternating reversals and advantages. In your view, that would be entirely foreign to the subject now under discussion. But do you think it superfluous to observe that this capital error must not be confused with the one I have to discuss? Do you believe that I am not even obliged to warn you that the Manichaeans contradicted the Catholic faith not only by saying that the law of Moses had an evil principle, but also by maintaining that the law of Moses was evil in itself and by its very nature? If the observation is superfluous for you, it certainly will not be so for others.

In the reasoning used by the Manichaeans—“The Old Testament is evil; therefore it is not the good God but the evil god who authored it”—two different and independent heresies must be recognized: that of the two principles, and that which condemns the Old Testament as evil. By contrast, in the following reasoning—“The New Testament is good; therefore it is not the evil god but the good God who authored it”—there is only one heresy, namely that of the two principles.

[Col. 1062D] “There you have,” you will say, “what is called wasting one’s time and words. What reader needs to have pointed out to him what leaps to the eyes?” But do you not know that, with regard to such matters, a thousand people, otherwise very intelligent, have difficulty understanding and are resistant in judgment? How many do you know who persuade themselves that they do not think about freedom as the Manichaeans did because they do not claim that the necessity of acting which they admit comes from two souls—one good and one evil—given to each person by the good God and the evil god? Now, although in many respects these same people have no much more favorable idea of the law of Moses than the Manichaeans, will they not imagine themselves to hold an opinion very far removed from that of these heretics concerning the nature of the ancient law, while confessing that it was established by the true God?

Since the Manichaeans made an evil and malevolent god the author of the Old [Col. 1063A] Testament, they detested not only the religion of the Jews but also all the books that contained its ordering and monuments. They said that the Old Testament contradicted itself, that it contradicted the New Testament, and that it was blamed and condemned by the New Testament.

The objections of the first kind are not strong. They set against the law forbidding all work on the Sabbath the order Joshua received to have the Ark of the Covenant carried around the walls of Jericho on a Sabbath day; they set against the prohibition to make, possess, or preserve any statue or image of anything whatsoever the command given to Moses to construct and raise a bronze serpent, and the command to adorn the Ark with figures of two cherubim; and they set against the knowledge of all things that God claims for himself the apparent ignorance in the question he asked the first man after his sin: “Adam, where are you?” and in the question he asked Cain after the murder of Abel: [Col. 1063B] “Where is your brother?”

Tertullian and Saint Augustine [Note: [Col. 1063] Tertullian, book II *Against Marcion*, chapters 21, 22, 24, 25; Saint Augustine, book I *Against Adimantus*, chapter 22; *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, chapter 20.] take the trouble to resolve these difficulties and others like them, which were first proposed by the Marcionites and repeated by the Manichaeans. The work, these Fathers say, that is an act of religion or charity was not forbidden on the Sabbath. Statues and images that were not objects of idolatry were not proscribed, and a reproach was never intended as a mark of ignorance. The same heretics further objected in this connection that the God of the Hebrews had commanded the prophet Hosea to commit fornication, and that he had advised and authorized the theft committed by his people against the Egyptians, although he had forbidden both sins in his Decalogue. But, Saint Augustine says, why call fornication a marriage that brought it to an end? Why call theft what was a just wage? (Saint Augustine, book XXII *Against Faustus*, chapters 71 and 80.)

[Col. 1063C] As for the alleged contradictions that the Manichaeans believed they found between the Old and New Testaments, Saint Augustine reports most of them in his book against Adimantus, and reconciles them admirably. Moses says in Genesis that God himself created heaven, earth, and light (Gen. I, 1); and the Gospel says that the world was made through Jesus Christ (John I, 3). Saint Augustine replies that every Christian, on reading Genesis, recognizes in the Creator God a subsisting being in three persons, the second of whom is Our Lord Jesus Christ (Saint Augustine, *Against Adimantus*, chap. 1). Moses says in Genesis that God rested after the creation of the world (Gen. II, 2); and the Savior says in the Gospel: “My Father is continually at work” (John V, 17). Saint Augustine replies that this rest signifies only the end of creation and does not exclude the action by which God continually preserves and governs the world (Saint Augustine, *Against Adimantus*, chap. 2). Moses says that God made man in his image and likeness [Col. 1063D] (Gen. I, 26, 27); and the Savior says to the Jews: “You are children of the devil” (John VIII, 44). Saint Augustine replies that imitation gives children to those whom one takes as models, just as teaching gives children to the masters who instruct them (Saint Augustine, *Against Adimantus*, chap. 5, no. 1). None of this appears to the holy doctor to constitute a serious difficulty.

Allow me to dwell a little longer on the objections of the third kind. The purpose I have set myself requires it; they touch and concern it more directly, for I shall show later that the new doctrine concerning the law of Moses merges into Manichaeism and brings it back to life.

The Manichaeans prided themselves on demonstrating from the New Testament that the substance and purpose of the Old Testament [Col. 1064A] were evil. To justify their claim concerning its substance, the holy doctors used this testimony of Jesus Christ: “Truly I say to you: before heaven and earth pass away, everything contained in the law will be accomplished, without a single jot or tittle being omitted” (Matt. 5:18); and these two other statements of Saint Paul: “The law is holy, and the commandment is also holy, just, and good” (Rom. 7:12, 16). I agree that the law is good; indeed, what could the heretics criticize in the precepts called moral, or even in those that concerned merely civil regulation? One need only understand them in order to recognize their equity and wisdom.

The law of retaliation, and the laws that permitted divorce and usury with foreigners, are the only ones that the enemies of the Old Testament dared to censure. The first, they said, is expressly condemned by these words of Jesus Christ: “You have heard that it was said: An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. But I say to you not to resist, [Col. 1064B] if someone mistreats you” (Matt. 5:39). The second is rejected by these words: “But I say to you that whoever sends away his wife, unless it is for adultery, and marries another, himself commits adultery; and whoever marries the woman who has been sent away also commits adultery” (Matt. 19:9). Finally, the third law is blamed by this other Gospel passage: “Lend without hoping to receive anything in return.”

The Manichaeans were mistaken. Jesus Christ does not condemn the law of retaliation, but the false tradition of the scribes and Pharisees, who allowed private individuals to carry it out, although its execution ought to have been reserved to magistrates. For does the Gospel, which commands private individuals to forgive injuries, forbid magistrates to punish those who commit them? (Saint Augustine, *Against Adimantus*, chapter 8.) As for the law of divorce, the Savior himself defends it, saying: “It was because of the hardness of your hearts that Moses allowed you to send away your wives” (Matt. 19:8). From this one should conclude, [Col. 1064C] it seems to me, that such permission did not exempt those who used it from sin, but merely freed them from fear of temporal penalties, and that this law was purely political: for the sake of the public good, it left the punishment of divorce to the judgment of God alone. In the same sense Saint Thomas understood the law that permitted the Jews to practice usury with foreigners: “It was not granted to them as something lawful, but permitted in order to avoid a greater evil” (*Summa theologiae*, II–II, question 78, article 1, reply to objection 2). 

A learned man once objected to me that Beza and Piscator, both Protestants, were the only authorities supporting what I think concerning the law of divorce. But he was mistaken. Tertullian, Origen, Chromatius, Saint Jerome, the Venerable Bede, Euthymius, and Theophylact are cited by Maldonat in favor of the opinion I have adopted; and he admits that it is probable, although he embraces the contrary view. It is true that [Col. 1064D] this learned interpreter of Scripture seems afraid that he may not have understood the text of these Fathers correctly: “unless I am mistaken through misunderstanding.” But certainly he has grasped their meaning; and with this qualification he could have added Saint Chrysostom, who speaks more obscurely. And why should one not apply to the law of divorce what Saint Thomas says of the law of usury: “It was not granted to them as something lawful, but permitted in order to avoid a greater evil”? This appears to be the natural meaning of Jesus Christ’s words, “because of the hardness of your hearts.” I admit that polygamy was genuinely permitted among the Jews, but this means that a husband did not sin by having several wives, not that a woman had the right to marry several husbands.

As for the laws that were merely ceremonial, [Col. 1065A] if one considers the crude and unstable character, the hard, disobedient, and unyielding disposition of the people of Israel, together with the furious inclination that drove them toward idolatry—an inclination they had acquired in Egypt through long association with the most superstitious of all nations—one will be obliged to agree that, in order to turn the Israelites away from the worship of false gods, it was necessary not only to impress them with the greatness and majesty of their God through the pageantry and splendor of the solemnities and the entire external worship prescribed by the law, but also to bind them and continually bring them back to their God through the diversity and multitude of sacrifices, offerings, and expiations; to subject and captivate them through observances and ceremonies of every kind, so that religion would always remain present and perceptible to them.

To these considerations add the mutual relationship of the two Testaments, which required the Old Testament to express and prefigure in a thousand different ways the truths, mysteries, benefits, and perfection of the [Col. 1065B] New Testament. “Let no one find fault with the burdens of sacrifices, ritual works, and the laborious scruples of offerings, as though God had properly desired such things for himself . . . Rather, let him perceive that divine design whereby God wished to bind a people prone to idolatry and transgression by duties of this kind belonging to his own religion—duties by which the superstition of the age was practiced—in order to draw them away from it, commanding such things to be done for himself as though he desired them, lest they sin by making idols . . .” (Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book II, chapter 18). “But even in the ordinary dealings of human life and conduct, at home and abroad, down to the care of vessels, he distinguished everything in every way, so that these legal disciplines, meeting them everywhere, would prevent them from having a single moment free from the awareness of God . . . This law was promulgated not by the harshness of its author, but by the reason of supreme benevolence, subduing rather the people’s hardness and shaping their unformed faith through obedience by means of laborious observances—without touching upon the mysteries signified by the law, namely its spiritual and prophetic character, which is figurative throughout all its subject matter” (Idem, ibid., chapter 19).

Nevertheless, the Manichaeans said, does not the God of the [Col. 1065C] Hebrews himself admit that he gave his people commandments that are not good and judgments in which they would find no life? “And I gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments in which they will not live” (*Ezek.* 20:25). Surely this refers to the laws enacted and the civil or religious regulations established by Moses for the government of the Hebrew people! God is speaking of the just vengeance he exercised upon his unfaithful and transgressing people by delivering them into the power of their enemies and permitting the nations that had reduced them to servitude to treat them harshly and inhumanely, impose severe laws upon them, demand exorbitant tributes from them, and overwhelm them with burdens and misery, until life became unbearable for them. This is the true meaning of the prophet’s words. For in several preceding verses God says that the laws he had given his people were good and that observing them was a source of life: “Which, if a man does, he shall live in them.”

[Col. 1065D] Besides the passage from Ezekiel that I have just explained, another passage of Saint Paul is brought forward, namely: “For if that first covenant had been without fault, no place would have been sought for a second” (Heb. 8:7). This can be understood in two ways: either by taking the word *fault* not as a proper defect that would make the Old Covenant blameworthy, but as a lack of perfection that made it less worthy of esteem; or by referring the word not to the nature of the Old Covenant, but to those who received it, and to the Israelites with whom it was contracted.

Thus, according to the first interpretation, the meaning is that the evangelical law would not have been necessary if the law of Moses had not been imperfect. This interpretation is supported by the preceding text, where it is said that the New Covenant is more excellent and founded upon the promise of more excellent things: “He is the mediator of a better covenant, which has been established upon better promises” (Heb. 8:6). The other meaning is that the evangelical law would not have been necessary if the law of Moses had been faithfully observed and without any transgression. This is Saint Chrysostom’s interpretation (*Homily 14 on Hebrews*).

The authority of this Father does not prevent Cornelius a Lapide and our other interpreters from rejecting this interpretation as plainly false, because, regardless of the faithful observance or criminal transgression of the law, the shadow had to give way to the truth, and the state of servitude and insufficient sacrifices had to be succeeded by evangelical freedom and the precious victim of the New Testament.

Saint Chrysostom’s reasoning nevertheless presents a sufficiently serious difficulty to deserve an answer. This Father bases his explanation on the words, “For finding fault with them, he says.” He points out that the passage of Saint Paul in question refers to the passage from Jeremiah that is cited afterward, and that the Apostle indicates this relationship by warning that in this passage God does not blame the Old Testament, but the Jews who received it and did not observe it: “For he does not say, ‘finding fault with it,’ but ‘finding fault with them’” (Chrysostom, ibid.). Thus Saint Chrysostom believes that he has the right to explain Saint Paul’s words, “For if that first covenant had been without fault, no place would have been sought for a second,” by means of these other words from Jeremiah’s text, where God reproaches the Israelites for not remaining faithful to his covenant and declares that for this reason he had resolved to make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah: “I will complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah . . . because they did not remain in my covenant” (Jer. 31:31–32).

This persuades me that the two interpretations must be joined together, while modifying the second so that the word *fault* signifies both the imperfection of the Mosaic law and the fault of the Israelites [Col. 1066C] who did not observe it. That is, the Apostle’s meaning is that the law of Jesus Christ was necessary because of the imperfection and insufficiency of the Mosaic law, and that God had, in addition, another reason for abolishing the Old Testament and substituting the New: namely, the infidelity of the Israelites. It is clear that this second motive is only accessory, but it is nevertheless true, for Jeremiah asserts it. And can one doubt that Saint Paul recognizes this motive and takes it into account in the words, “For if that first covenant had been without fault, no place would have been sought for a second,” since he proves the truth contained in these very words by the passage from Jeremiah: “For finding fault with them,” and so forth? I observed that the second interpretation had to be modified by understanding that, if the Israelites had not despised and violated their law, the Gospel would not have been necessary for that particular reason, although it would have been necessary because of the imperfection and insufficiency of the ancient law.

The new heretics seem to agree with the Church on the preceding point. Yet they vainly flatter themselves that they can plausibly answer some of the difficulties I have just resolved; and they are wholly unable in general to justify the substance of the law of Moses, because they maintain with the Manichaeans that its purpose is evil. It is therefore important that I examine precisely what the Manichaeans taught concerning the establishment of a particular law and religion for the children of Jacob. The unanimous teaching of the Fathers is that God adopted this means to prevent faith in the future Savior—which he had promised to Adam and Eve immediately after their sin—from being completely extinguished among humanity.

He therefore wished to preserve and increase this faith by separating from the other nations and forming with particular care a chosen people who, through the voice of their prophets, would foretell the coming, [Col. 1067A] characteristics, actions, life, death, reign, and glory of Christ; who would prefigure and represent him through their religion, laws, princes, pontiffs, misfortunes, successes, condition, and circumstances, both in peace and in war; who would see him born in their midst and be the first to recognize him, and afterward announce him and show him to the rest of the world. It was not merely one or two persons, or a few individuals, Saint Augustine says; it was the entire nation, the whole kingdom, that was to be regarded as a great prophet announcing Christ and the Christian kingdom: “So that not merely this or that man, but the whole nation itself and the entire kingdom, might become a prophet of Christ and of the Christian kingdom. The kingdom itself was a great prophet” (Saint Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book XIII, chapters 4 and 15).

The Fathers contrasted this holy and beneficial purpose of the Old Testament with the purpose that the impiety of the Manichaeans attributed to the God of the Hebrews: namely, first to harm his own people, [Col. 1067B] and then, through his people, the other nations that did not worship him. In support of this, the heretics objected with these words of Isaiah: “I am the Lord who creates evil” (*Isa.* 45:7); and with these other words of the prophet Amos: “Is there evil in the city that the Lord has not made?” (*Amos* 3:6).

The Fathers replied by distinguishing between the evil of sin and the evil of punishment. The former came from the malice of the devil and from the abuse man made of his freedom; the latter was ordained by the one true God, who tested men through tribulations or employed just severity in punishing the idolatry of the nations and the infidelity of his people.

“What justice is this,” the Manichaeans added, “that makes children bear the punishment due to their fathers’ sins?” And this, they said, is God’s conduct throughout the entire Old Testament, of which he even boasts. “I am,” he says, “the Lord your God, strong and jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation: *Ego Dominus Deus tuus, fortis, zelotes, visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios in tertiam et quartam generationem*” (Exod. 20:5).

Nevertheless, Tertullian replies to the Marcionites, God declares through his prophet Ezekiel that the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son” (Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book II, chapter 15; Ezek. 18:20). Since neither the Marcionites nor the Manichaeans based an accusation of contradiction upon these words, they ought to have recognized in them an explanation capable of satisfying them. God includes children with their fathers in his vengeance only when he limits it to temporal punishments; and he has the right to encourage men to obey him by making them consider the happiness or misfortune of their descendants, whom they often love more than themselves.

[Col. 1067D] Whatever might be said, these heretics could not tolerate God’s severity, which is displayed throughout every part of the history of God’s people (Saint Augustine, *Against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets*, book I, chapter 16, no. 28). They could not contemplate without trembling and revolt that universal flood of waters which, by the death of almost all human beings, caused a universal flood of crimes to disappear from the earth; that rain of fire which so completely consumed two infamous cities that even the place where they had stood perished in a sense, becoming forever barren and uninhabitable; the miracles lavished upon the world, and nature astonished by the overthrow of its most inviolable laws, which completed the rejection of a hardened king; the earth melting beneath the feet of a band of rebellious and sacrilegious men and swallowing them alive into its depths; a multitude of serpents whose fiery breath and cruel bites turned the complaints [Col. 1068A] of an ungrateful people into mournful cries; and the fire from heaven, quick to compel respect for God in his ministers and to obey the voice of the prophets by falling upon the heads of the impious.

Tertullian might exhaust his eloquence in showing the necessary affinity between God’s justice and goodness, and in demonstrating that the punishment of crime was a genuine good (Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book II, chapter 11); Marcion nevertheless carried his impiety so far as to canonize Cain, Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, as well as all the criminals who had been the unfortunate victims of the wrath of the God of the Jews (Theodoret, *Against the Heresies*, book I, chapter 24). This heresiarch imagined greater gentleness and indulgence in the God of the Christians, deceived by the abuse he made of that passage in the Gospel where it is related that the apostles James and John, wishing to imitate the prophet Elijah by calling down fire from heaven upon the Samaritans who had refused Jesus Christ entry into their city, were told by the Savior: “You do not know of what spirit you are: *Nescitis cujus spiritus estis*” (Luke 9:55).

Marcion failed to consider the admirable designs of divine providence, which had prepared from afar the establishment of a perfect religion, in which one would live only by faith, hope only for rewards, and fear only future punishments belonging to another world. He did not understand that, in order to prevent the doubts that libertinism would produce, and to prevent the wicked from taking God’s long-suffering and patience in bearing with them as a sign that he did not exist or had no power over them, divine wisdom had caused another religion to precede it. Its entirely miraculous economy demonstrated that this universe is not governed by chance or by blind nature, but by a sovereign intelligence, by an all-powerful Creator whose word can be trusted when he promises blessings and threatens eternal evils. For a great people, still existing despite their rejection, testifies through the indisputable monuments of its history that, for several centuries, its temporal happiness or misery depended upon a continual succession of prodigies that could have been performed only by the arm that made nature and sustains it.

These were only pledges and signs of the blessings and evils proposed to us by the Christian faith. Thus one could say to the Marcionites and Manichaeans: God is more severe than you think; you are wrong to dwell upon shadows and figures in order to depict the rigors of his vengeance. Temporal evils are no more punishments worthy of God’s justice than earthly goods are a reward proportionate to his goodness and magnificence. If he has ceased to promise and guarantee to those who serve him the dew of heaven, the richness of the earth, and possession of the riches of this world, has he therefore forgotten his generosity toward the righteous? Likewise, if he no longer opens abysses beneath the feet of those who offend him, if he no longer hurls fires and thunderbolts upon their heads, if he no longer sends monsters to devour them, is he any less terrifying to all sinners? (Saint Augustine, *Against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets*, book I, chapter 16, no. 29.) Do you think that the inhabitants of Sodom and Gomorrah were treated more severely than so many immoral people who today seem to live and die in peace? Believe precisely the opposite. The fire of heaven did not consume those criminals so quickly that they did not see and feel its approach. Before closing off every avenue and penetrating everywhere, it gave them time to make some effort to escape. Those moments were moments of grace and mercy for them, of which they could have taken advantage. But now, when God is weary of enduring sinners, of two successive instants, one is the final instant of foolish joy and deceptive security in the state of sin, [Col. 1069A] and the other is the first instant of their eternal damnation (Saint Augustine, ibid.).

Let us not omit the great scandal of the followers of Marcion and Manes. “The God of the Old Testament,” they said, “is a God who delights in making men guilty, who blinds them, hardens them, and deceives them in order to lead them to destruction.” They cited several passages of the Scriptures of the Old Testament, which Calvin—who likes to clothe himself in the spoils of the Manichaeans—likewise abuses in order to make God the author of sin. For example, God is said to have hardened Pharaoh’s heart (Exod. 9:12) and to have inspired David with the intention of numbering all his subjects, which brought a terrible scourge upon him and upon his entire people (2 Sam. 24). In a prophetic vision, Micah saw the Lord sending a lying spirit to deceive Ahab (1 Kings 22:20).

There are many passages of approximately the same kind [Col. 1069B] even in the New Testament, as Saint Augustine observed while refuting the Manichaeans (Saint Augustine, *Against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets*, book I, chapter 16, no. 28). The rule of this holy doctor and of the other Fathers is that whenever Holy Scripture appears to attribute to God something that belongs only to the malice of the devil or of human beings, the sacred text must be understood as referring to a simple permission.

Is there no way to silence Calvin, who mocks this explanation by attributing it solely to the scholastics, and who takes it upon himself here to be scrupulous about accepting a meaning even slightly forced from the words of Scripture? Let us try. I say first that this interpretation is entirely consistent with the character of the sacred language, according to which one who has allowed something to happen, though he had the power to prevent it, is represented as having done it. The Chaldeans, at the devil’s instigation, had taken Job’s flocks, and God had merely permitted it; this is what Scripture explicitly declares. Yet Job says: “The Lord gave them to me, the Lord has taken them away” (Job 1:21). The author of Chronicles writes that it was a suggestion of the devil that led David to order the census of his subjects (1 Chron. 21:1); nevertheless, as we have just seen, the author of the history of the Kings writes that God urged him to undertake it.

I add that there is a very important reason why, in the sacred language, God is said to command, decree, and do everything that he merely permits: it is to make clear not only that nothing can happen without God’s foreseeing it and determining to allow it, but also that all the malice of angels and human beings, far from harming the least of his designs, becomes, through his infinite wisdom, a means that effectively contributes to their fulfillment. Thus all the sins and crimes committed against the divine will are directed by God toward a good end with such precision and such unfailing certainty that they would fit no better into the plan of his governance and serve no better the good he intends if he himself had decreed, commanded, and carried out all these sins and crimes for that purpose.

Listen, nevertheless, to Calvin, who says triumphantly: “If the blindness and madness of Ahab is a judgment of God, the chimera of a mere permission vanishes, because it would be ridiculous for a judge merely to permit, without also decreeing by a positive judgment what he wishes to be done and ordering its execution to his ministers: *Si Dei judicium est excaecatio et amentia Achab, nudae permissionis evanescit figmentum, quia ridiculum esset judicem tantum permittere, non etiam decernere quid fieri velit, et mandare exsecutionem ministris*” (Calvin, *Institutes*, book I, chapter 18).

[Col. 1070A] Saint Augustine did not find this so ridiculous; and the reason is that this Father did not confuse the supreme judge of the universe with human beings, who, not being masters of all events, cannot punish by mere permissions. According to the holy doctor, when one hears these words of Scripture, “I am the Lord who has deceived that prophet: *Ego Dominus decepi prophetam illum*,” or this text, “He hardens whom he wills: *Et quem vult indurat*,” one must consider the merits of the person whose hardening and deception God permitted: “When you hear, ‘I am the Lord; I have deceived him,’ and, ‘He hardens whom he wills,’ consider the merits of the one whom the Lord permitted to be hardened and deceived” (Saint Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 23, no. 45).

As for the following passage, on which the Manichaeans, like the Marcionites, also relied heavily—“The god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers: *Deus hujus saeculi excaecavit mentes infidelium*” (2 Cor. 4:4)—it is clear that Saint Paul is not speaking of the true God, but of the devil, to whom the pagan world attributed divine honors and whom it worshiped in idols [Note: [Col. 1069] Saint Irenaeus, book III, chapter 7, no. 1; book IV, chapter 29, no. 21; Saint Augustine, *Against Faustus*, chapter 2].

The Manichaeans were therefore foolish enough to believe that the same God who had armed the Jews to exterminate the peoples of the land of Canaan also caused the nations’ infidelity. They detested those bloody executions, the sackings of cities, the massacres of so many thousands of people, and the merciless wars that Moses and Joshua waged at God’s command in order to punish impieties of which God himself, according to the Manichaeans’ opinion, was the author.

Chapter 12 of the Book of Wisdom seems to have been written expressly to confound these heretics and those in our own day who have adopted part of their system. The author of this book intends to show that the Lord acts in all things with a spirit of goodness and gentleness; that for this reason he restrains his anger and pours it out little by little upon those who go astray, with the aim of correcting them; and that at the same time he warns them and speaks inwardly to them about the excesses they commit, so that, abandoning their wickedness, they may resolve to believe in him. What proof does he offer for this general and unrestricted assertion? He points to the way God dealt with the ancient inhabitants of the Holy Land, who had made themselves hateful and abominable in his sight through their enormous crimes, their magic and enchantments, their unjust and cruel sacrifices, and the murder of their own children, whom they slaughtered without pity, whose entrails they devoured and whose blood they drank. They were sacrilegious profaners of a land that particularly belonged to the Lord and that he had consecrated to himself. For when God resolved to avenge so many innocent and defenseless victims, who encountered the authors of their death in those from whom they had received life, and wished to destroy these criminals by the hands of the Hebrews, so as to place the Hebrews in possession of the land in the world most dear to him, the land that had been the place of pilgrimage of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, he nevertheless considered that the guilty were human beings whom he had created. Therefore he spared them to some extent; and, by showing them at close hand the formidable army of his people—which he held in their sight for forty years in the desert—he sent before it a terrible cloud of wasps, which infected the whole land of Canaan and gradually caused a large part of its inhabitants to perish. What was his purpose in this? It was not, the Sage continues, that God was unable to subject the impious to the righteous by force of arms, or to exterminate them all at once by sending wild beasts to devour them instead of insects, or even by speaking a single word; but he carried out his judgments upon them in stages, in order to give them the time and opportunity to repent, although he knew that they were a perverse nation, and that, having suckled error and crime with their mother’s milk, wickedness had become rooted in their hearts through the force of education, example, and habit, so that it had become natural to them. Consequently, he saw clearly that through their own fault they had placed themselves in a kind of inability ever to change and convert. For from the beginning, in the persons of their fathers Ham and Canaan, they were an accursed race, whose impiety they were to imitate.

You will not be among those who accuse me of weakening this passage by softening my commentary. It is evident that the Sage marks here only a great difficulty, not a real impossibility. Indeed, if the Canaanites could not change or convert, why does he say beforehand that God was giving them time and opportunity to repent: “You gave them room for repentance” (*Wisdom* 12:10)? Why, from the particular example of the Canaanites, does he conclude generally that God punishes sinners in this world in such a way as to give them time and means to repent: “You have taught your people by such deeds . . . that when judging, you give room for repentance in sins” (ibid., 19)? Why, finally, does he explicitly declare that God gave the Canaanites the power to change and renounce their wickedness: “You gave them time and opportunity by which they could be changed from their wickedness” (ibid., 20)? You will approve my reproducing here the entire text that I have paraphrased, so that my faithfulness in conveying its meaning may be judged.

“O how good and gentle is your Spirit, O Lord, in all things! Therefore you correct those who go astray little by little, and warn and address them concerning the sins they commit, so that, abandoning their wickedness, they may believe in you, O Lord. For you wished to destroy by the hands of our forefathers those ancient inhabitants of your holy land, whom you abhorred because they performed hateful deeds before you through sorceries and unjust sacrifices: merciless murderers of their own children, eaters of human entrails, devourers of blood in the midst of their sacrilegious rites, and parents who were the authors of helpless souls. You wished to destroy them so that the land of the children of God, which is dearest to you of all lands, might receive a worthy settlement. Yet you spared even them as human beings, and sent wasps before your army, so that they might gradually exterminate them. Not because you were powerless in battle to subject the impious to the righteous, or to exterminate them all at once by savage beasts or by a harsh word, but, judging them in stages, you gave them room for repentance, although you knew that their nation was wicked, that their malice was natural to them, and that their disposition could not be changed forever. For their seed was accursed from the beginning, and so forth” (*Wisdom* 12:1–11).

The constant obstinacy in evil that these barbarous and impious peoples opposed to God’s mercy finally exhausted his patience, and he delivered them over to the sword of the Israelites. This displeases the Manichaeans, says Saint Augustine (*Against Adimantus*, chapter 17, no. 4). These heretics considered it wrong that God should be just, or that he should have the right to entrust human beings with carrying out the judgments of his justice; and because the Acts of the Apostles relates that Ananias and Sapphira were struck dead at the word of Saint Peter, this was one of their reasons for rejecting that book.

Saint Augustine therefore applies himself to showing that vengeance is legitimate when it is authorized by God, especially when it concerns only the interests of God’s glory and worship, provided, however, that it is exercised without any feeling of hatred and through pure obedience to God’s commands. [Col. 1072A] “Now,” says the holy Doctor, “the Manichaeans will never prove that those among the Jews who were spiritual hated the nations whom divine justice commanded them to remove through their agency: *Unde isti convincent animos virorum spiritualium, qui in illo populo fuerunt, quod eos oderant qui per ipsos divina justitia jubebantur auferri*” (St. Augustine, ibid., no. 5).

The Manichaeans could here have raised against Saint Augustine a substantial objection, drawn from the feelings of hatred and vengeance, and from the horrible curses and imprecations scattered throughout the Psalms.
