It seems to me that one should answer that these sentiments are not properly personal, nor matters of choice for the one who expresses them—whether David himself, the people of Israel, or an individual Israelite is speaking in the Psalms; that this hatred and these curses are directed by the Holy Spirit against desperate sinners, whose attachment to impiety differed little from consummate reprobation; that these imprecations are acts of conformity to God’s will and an approval of the just judgments God has pronounced against enemies of his holy name, whom he foresaw would be irreconcilable; and finally, must we not agree that Christians are in a wholly similar disposition of heart and mind when they say to God: “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven”?

I cannot persuade myself that David, carried away by zeal against the wicked, directs his threats and deadly words against Saul, his father-in-law and his king, of whom he never spoke except with the deepest respect throughout the entire course of the unjust persecutions that this furious prince relentlessly inflicted upon him; I do not believe that he bears ill will toward his son Absalom, for whom his paternal tenderness increased when he was forced to expose that rebellious son to death; or toward Shimei, Doeg, Sheba, and Ahithophel, his subjects, whose crimes could not alter his goodness and gentleness. Would the sentiments he expressed in the Psalms contradict the character and conduct that sacred history attributes to him?

It seems to me more than probable that the enemies and persecutors whom David anathematizes are always idolaters, whose crimes the Hebrews were charged by God’s command to punish, or who, out of hatred for God, made war upon his people.

If it is difficult to explain Psalm 108 in this sense, must one therefore blaspheme with Grotius, who openly favors the Manichaeans’ cause and dares to say that the spirit prevailing in this psalm is not the spirit of the Gospel? Is it not more natural to acknowledge with the holy Fathers that everything in it is prophetic and merely announces the detestable end of the treacherous apostle who betrayed Jesus Christ, and of the Jews who crucified him? But will you find the thought that occurs to me sound?

[Col. 1072D] You know that it is an article of faith that the Israelites’ entry into the Promised Land is a figure of the reception of all the elect into heaven (Hebrews 4). Might this holy hatred of God’s people against the nations whom God had proscribed not be connected with that figure? Might it not have been intended to represent the entirely holy hatred and indignation that the Apocalypse and certain other sacred books attribute to the blessed, who throughout eternity will conform themselves to the sentiments of vengeance that they will see in God toward the unhappy victims of his wrath? In any case, it may also be legitimate, and it does not prevent the Mosaic Law from being in itself and by its nature the work of a good and benevolent God—which is the principal question debated on this subject between the Manichaeans and the holy Fathers.

## Part Three. THE STATE OF THE QUESTION BETWEEN SAINT AUGUSTINE AND THE PELAGIANS

[Col. 1073]

[Col. 1073A] Saint Augustine disputed with the Pelagians about the Mosaic Law, so to speak, only in passing and incidentally. The principal point concerning this matter that was debated between the holy Doctor and the enemies of grace concerned the law in general; the question was whether the law, whatever it might be, was sufficient for salvation without grace. For this reason Saint Augustine almost always uses the word “law” here not to designate the condition of the Jews or the practices and ceremonies instituted by Moses, but to signify the commandments and precepts that compose the positive law of the Old and New Testaments. Nevertheless, he sometimes brings back into view Saint Paul’s controversy with the Jews and argues specifically against the Pelagians for the weakness and uselessness of the old law, in order to establish the necessity of the Gospel and to infer from the necessity of the Gospel the necessity of grace.

[Col. 1073B] It will be of interest to you if I point out several things that the Apostle says exclusively about the old law, with the aim of convincing the Jews that they must absolutely receive the new law, and that Saint Augustine applies and extends to every kind of law, in order to demonstrate to the Pelagians our need for the assistance of grace.

In the Epistle to the Romans, Saint Paul teaches that, because of the inclination we have to do what is forbidden to us, the written law gave the Jews occasion to sin more grievously. “On the occasion of the commandment,” he says, “sin deceived me and through it put me to death: *Peccatum occasione accepta per mandatum seduxit me et per illud occidit*” (Romans 7:11). Saint Augustine explains this passage in a sermon that he delivered openly against the Manichaeans and, as the Reverend Benedictine Fathers have very rightly observed, tacitly against the Pelagians, whose heresy was not yet entirely public but was quietly spreading.

What example do you suppose the holy Doctor brings [Col. 1073C] to make the meaning of this passage understood and to make its truth evident? The law given to our first parents in the state of innocence. You will judge this better from his own words:

“Thus it happened at the beginning in paradise; then this statement was fulfilled: ‘Sin deceived me when it took occasion from the commandment.’ See the insinuating speech that the serpent addressed to the woman. He asked her what God had said; she replied: ‘God said to us: You may eat from every tree that is in paradise, but you shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. If you eat from it, you shall die.’ This is God’s commandment. But the serpent replied: ‘You shall certainly not die. For God knew that on the day you ate from it, your eyes would be opened and you would be like gods.’ Nothing, therefore, is truer than this statement: ‘Sin deceived me when it took occasion from the commandment, and through the commandment itself put me to death’: *Sic factum est primo in paradiso. Fefellit, inquit, me occasione accepta per mandatum. Vide serpentem mulieri susurrantem. Quaesivit ab ea quid dixerit Deus. Respondit illa, Dixit nobis Deus: Ex omni ligno quod est in paradiso edetis; de ligno autem boni et mali non edetis. Ex eo si ederitis, morte moriemini. Hoc est enim Dei mandatum. Contra serpens: Non, inquit, morte moriemini. Sciebat enim Deus quia qua die ederitis, aperientur oculi vestri, et eritis tanquam dii. Occasione ergo accepta peccatum per mandatum fefellit me et per illud occidit*” (St. Augustine, Sermon 4, *On the Words of the Apostle*, now 153, no. 11).

[Col. 1074A] Saint Augustine performs a marvelous feat here: he confounds five heresies at once—Manichaeism, Pelagianism, Lutheranism, Calvinism, and Jansenism. Here is the stroke he directs against Manichaeism, which the three modern heresies do not find agreeable:

“The enemy,” he continues, “used the sword you carried to kill you; he defeated you and put you to death by means of your own weapons. Receive the commandment; know that these are weapons given not to your enemy to kill you, but to you so that you may kill your enemy: *Gladio quem portabas te inimicus occidit; armis tuis te vicit, armis tuis te interemit. Recipe mandatum; scito esse arma, non quibus occidat te, sed quibus a te occidatur inimicus*” (St. Augustine, ibid.).

[Col. 1074B] But he adds—and this is the Pelagianism he now strikes down:

“Do not presume upon your strength. See little David advancing against Goliath; see the small boy attacking that giant. If he expects victory, it is in the name of the Lord. ‘You come against me,’ he says, ‘with shield and spear, but I come against you in the name of the almighty Lord.’ Thus, thus, and not otherwise—by no means otherwise—is the enemy brought down. Whoever presumes upon his own strength is himself brought down before the battle: *Sed noli praesumere de viribus tuis. Vide parvum David contra Goliam, vide parvum contra ingentem, sed in nomine Domini praesumentem. Tu venis ad me, inquit, cum clypeo et lancea, ego in nomine Domini omnipotentis. Sic, sic, aliter non, omnino aliter non, prosternitur inimicus. Qui praesumit de viribus suis antequam pugnet, ipse prosternitur*” (St. Augustine, ibid.).

Saint Augustine says against the Manichaeans that the commandment was given to us as a weapon that we are free to use in order to resist the enemy and overcome him. [Col. 1074C] Against the Pelagians he says that, nevertheless, we must not presume upon our strength, and he derives all this from the fall of our first parents. Am I not right to assert that, together with Manichaeism and Pelagianism, the holy Doctor destroys the three modern heresies that maintain that, since the fall of our first parents, the commandment has necessarily and inevitably wounded all who have transgressed it, and that the sinner’s presumption always implies a lack of grace?

You can well judge that it was not my reading of Jansenius that directed me to this passage of Saint Augustine. Jansenius did not think to cite it anywhere. He acted wisely, for the Bishop of Ypres maintains that when Saint Paul says that “on the occasion of the commandment sin deceives man and puts him to death,” this must be understood, following Saint Augustine’s interpretation, as occurring before grace. We, on the contrary, maintain that neither the Apostle nor the holy Doctor excludes the grace that makes the commandment possible, which we call sufficient grace, and that they merely abstract from it because they reason within the hypothesis of the Jews and Pelagians, who do not acknowledge the grace of Jesus Christ. [Col. 1074D] Now, in the passage I have just cited, Saint Augustine judges between Jansenius and us, and decides in our favor; for he uses the transgression of the commandment given to our first parents in the earthly paradise to demonstrate the truth of what Saint Paul says: that on the occasion of the commandment sin deceives man and puts him to death through the commandment itself. Saint Paul therefore does not speak, according to Saint Augustine, of an impossible commandment whose transgression excludes sufficient grace. Does one not know that Jansenius liberally grants our first parents this sufficient grace—of which he spoke so ill, which he has entirely discredited and ridiculed—by the gift he made them?

[Col. 1075A] Certainly, some people will think that Saint Augustine proves too much in this passage, and will judge that he did not possess the gift of prophecy; for if he had possessed it, would he not have been content with the defeat of the Manichaeans and Pelagians, who always regarded him as their mortal enemy? Would he have had the heart to unhorse in advance Luther, Calvin, Jansenius, and their disciples, who were to call themselves disciples of Saint Augustine and lend him their own ideas in order to clothe themselves in his glory?

The favorite passage of these false Augustinians—favored only because it seemed to them especially suitable for abuse—is the following, which I cannot translate until I have determined its exact meaning, since that meaning is disputed: “*Lex subintravit ut abundaret delictum*” (Romans 5:20). [Col. 1075B] It is clear that the Apostle means the Mosaic Law. Jansenius therefore uses this passage to show what end God intended when instituting the old law, and the meaning he gives Saint Paul’s words requires that they be translated as follows: “Now the law came in so that sin might abound” (Jansenius, vol. 3, book 1, chapters 9, 10, 11, pp. 40 ff.). If this is so, must we then also say that the law of the Gospel came in so that sin might abound? For Saint Augustine has more than once explained this text of the precepts that now bind Christians, and maintains that it is fulfilled either when people neglect what God commands, or when, presuming upon their own strength, they do not implore the help of grace and add pride to weakness: “*Lex subintravit ut abundaret delictum, sive cum homines negligunt quod Deus jubet, sive cum de suis viribus praesumentes adjutorium gratiae non implorant, et addunt infirmitati superbiam*” (Epistle 89 to Hilary, now 157, no. 16, and Book 1 *To Simplicianus*, no. 15).

[Col. 1075C] A Jansenist well instructed in his master’s principles will answer seriously that the Christians designated by Saint Augustine are really Jews, and that whenever one commits a mortal sin one is a Jew. For my part, I cannot believe this, and I prefer to follow all the Catholic interpreters by adhering to this other translation, which alone conforms to the Church’s doctrine: “Now the law came in, with the result that sin became more abundant.” Let Jansenius be as eager as he pleases to multiply the Jewish nation; he will never persuade me that reading Saint Augustine inspired him with so bizarre a taste.

Saint Paul often uses the expression “to be under the law,” and he always means the Mosaic Law. “You are not under the law but under grace,” he says to the Romans: *Non enim estis sub lege, sed sub gratia* (Romans 6:14)—that is, “You are not subject to the Mosaic Law, which, by threats of temporal punishments, irritates concupiscence; rather, you are under the yoke of the Gospel, which urges you to do good by promising eternal rewards.” This admits not the slightest difficulty if one compares all the passages in which this expression occurs. For should not these words—*Factus sum . . . . . iis qui sub lege sunt, quasi sub lege non essem, cum ipse non essem sub lege, ut eos qui sub lege erant lucrifacerem* (1 Corinthians 9:21)—be rendered in French as follows: “I made myself as one who was subject to the law among those who were subject to the law, as though I were subject to it, although I myself was not subject to it, in order to win those who were subject to the law”? And should not these other words—*Misit Deus Filium suum, factum ex muliere, factum sub lege, ut eos qui sub lege erant redimeret* (Galatians 4:4)—be expressed in our language as follows: “God sent his Son, born of a woman, born subject to the law, in order to redeem those who were subject to the law”? In short, “to be under the law,” in the Apostle’s language, means to be obliged—or to believe oneself obliged—to profess the Jewish religion.

But Saint Augustine appropriated this way of speaking in a quite different sense. According to this Father, to be under the law does not mean to be subject to the observances of the old law; it means the same thing as violating through one’s own fault a law of whatever kind. Consequently, to understand Saint Paul’s words to the Romans—*Non estis sub lege, sed sub gratia*—in the sense in which Saint Augustine chose to take them, one must explain them as follows: “You are not dominated by the law as by a judge who convicts and reproves criminals; rather, the grace of God, whose movements you faithfully follow, alone reigns within you.” The holy Doctor clearly sets out his thought in these terms:

“He who fulfills the law is not under the law but with the law; but he who is under the law is not helped by the law but burdened by it: *Qui legem implet, non est sub lege, sed cum lege: qui autem sub lege est, non juvatur, sed premitur a lege*” (Treatise 3 on John, no. 2).

And elsewhere:

“Those are said to be under the law over whom it exercises dominion; but it exercises dominion over those whom it punishes, and it punishes all transgressors: *Sub illa esse dicuntur quibus dominatur; eis autem dominatur quos punit; punit autem praevaricatores omnes*” (Book 1 *To Simplicianus*, Question 1, no. 15).

In any case, Saint Augustine cannot be blamed for using the Apostle’s words in a sense that does not exactly correspond to their natural meaning, because the ideas he substituted for those presented by the letter of the sacred text agree perfectly with the principles and spirit that Saint Paul spread throughout all his Epistles.

Saint Paul considers the Mosaic Law in itself and separates it from the advantages that the Gospel communicated to it through affinity and connection, in order to have an opportunity to set the two laws against each other. Such is Saint Augustine’s method. He considers the divine law, whatever it may be, in itself and separates it from grace, in order to have an opportunity to set law against grace.

He had the right, and was compelled, to make a distinction like that of the Apostle. For no law—not even the Christian law—when considered under the common notion of law and insofar as it is a collection of precepts, contains grace or gives strength to act.

If the Gospel is called the law of grace, it is evident that in this case the Gospel is not being considered precisely as a law, but rather as a condition and society of people who have the Son of God made man as their master and head. The holy Doctor therefore had the right to make such a distinction; but, beyond that, he was compelled to make it.

The Pelagians denied the necessity of grace, just as the Jews denied the necessity of the Gospel. The former maintained that the law in general was sufficient for salvation without grace, just as the latter maintained that the Mosaic Law was sufficient without the Gospel. Saint Augustine therefore had to reason within the Pelagian hypothesis in order to demonstrate its falsity, and to suppose the law stripped bare and deprived of the assistance of grace, although in fact it was not so, because the Pelagian hypothesis was false. He did this in order to show the insufficiency of the law considered in that manner and to conclude that grace was necessary—just as Saint Paul had to reason within the hypothesis of unbelieving Jews in order to demonstrate its falsity, and to suppose the Mosaic Law stripped bare and deprived of the anticipated fruits of salvation that it received from the Gospel, although in fact it was not so, because the hypothesis of the unbelieving Jews was false. He did this in order to show the insufficiency of the Mosaic Law considered in that manner and to conclude that the Gospel was necessary.

It is nevertheless true that, in the course of his argument—which has the law in general as its sole object—Saint Augustine sometimes imperceptibly begins to speak of the old law. This should not surprise us when we know that his principal method is to resort to examples that confirm what he has asserted with advantage and in the strongest and most vivid manner. If he must demonstrate the power of grace, its finest triumphs, and the heroic actions of the saints, in which it shines with the greatest magnificence, these immediately present themselves to him. If, on the contrary, the question is to prove the impotence of the law in general—which includes the law given to Adam, the law proclaimed by Moses to the Israelites, and even the precepts imposed upon Christians—his choice seizes upon the kind of law that is weakest and by its nature least capable of helping and sustaining the will: the law of Moses.

[Col. 1077B] At other times, the continuation of the dispute leads him into Saint Paul’s controversy with the Jews, since it resembles the controversy he was conducting against the Pelagians. Then he no longer appears to set grace and divine law in general against each other, but the evangelical law and the Mosaic Law, in imitation of Saint Paul, whom he unfailingly follows by reducing the Mosaic Law to the narrow limits of its particular substance and its own nature.

The reason for this conduct on the part of the holy Doctor is that the Pelagian error truly destroyed the distinction Saint Paul established between the old and the new law. For if human beings needed only the outward admonition of the law in order to possess the full power to make themselves good and righteous—which was the Pelagian claim—the evangelical law, even considered as a state, would provide no more assistance for salvation than the Mosaic Law. Both would equally provide a grace of knowledge and instruction, which alone Pelagius was willing to require and admit.

[Col. 1077C] That heresiarch endeavored to erase from the hearts of the faithful belief in the grace of God that Jesus Christ merited for the human race (St. Augustine, Epistle 106, now 186, no. 1). He said that before the law people were saved by the powers of nature, afterward by the assistance of the law, and finally through Jesus Christ—as though the blood of Jesus Christ had not been necessary for the people of the two earlier ages, that is, for those who lived before the law and during the time of the law (the same, Book 1 *To Boniface*, chapter 21, no. 39). He therefore fell back into the error of the Jews, who denied the necessity of the Gospel and of the redemption of Jesus Christ; he contradicted and destroyed what is written: “There is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). In all these passages, and in the works Saint Augustine published before anyone had heard of the Pelagians, he did not depart in the slightest from the natural meaning of Saint Paul’s text in the Epistle to the Romans.

[Col. 1077D] There were therefore two questions between Saint Augustine and the Pelagians. The first was whether the law, whatever it might be, could be useful for salvation without grace. The second was whether the Jews could be saved by the sole assistance of the Mosaic Law. The doctrine of impeccability and the perfection of righteousness entered deeply into both questions—or, more accurately, it produced a third question that it is important to develop.

[Col. 1078A] In almost all the passages where Saint Augustine examines the purpose of the law and the end God intended in giving it, the subject is the perfection of righteousness. That is, the holy Doctor is then refuting the Pelagian doctrine of impeccability, which consisted in maintaining that a person could live in this life free from every sin and without the assistance of grace. By the word “sin,” Pelagius and Saint Augustine agreed in understanding even every interior temptation and every disordered movement of the sensual appetite, what are called the first movements of concupiscence, as I demonstrated above.

What I assert here as something new is incontestable. In Letter 157 to Hilary; Letter 190 to Optatus; Sermons 26, 155, and 156; the explanations of Psalms 83, 102, and 118; the third treatise on Saint John; the book *On the Perfection of Righteousness*; the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*; Books 2 and 6 of the *Unfinished Work against Julian*; the book *On the Eighty-Three Questions*; the commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians; Book 1 *Against Faustus*; Book 2 *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*; and Book 1 of the *Acts with Felix* [Note: [Col. 1077D] Epistle 157, formerly 89, no. 2; Epistle 190, formerly 157, no. 7; Sermon 26, formerly 11, *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 8, no. 9; Sermon 155, formerly 6, *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 4, no. 4; Sermon 156, formerly 13, *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 2, no. 2; and Treatise 3 on John, no. 2. Book *On the Perfection of Righteousness*, chapter 5, no. 11. On Psalm 83, no. 10; on Psalm 102, no. 15; [Col. 1078D] on Psalm 118, Sermon 27, no. 2. Book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 6, no. 9. Book 2 of the *Unfinished Work*, no. 219; Book 6 of the *Unfinished Work*, no. 15. Book *On the Eighty-Three Questions*, Question 66, no. 1. Book 19 *Against Faustus*, chapter 7. Book 2 *Against the Adversary of the Law*, etc., chapter 7. Book 1 *On the Acts with Felix*, chapter 11.]: in all these works Saint Augustine speaks of the end God intended in giving the law, and there are many more of them than Jansenius cited. Now, almost everywhere—except perhaps when he is refuting the Manichaeans—the holy Doctor speaks of the law only while treating Pelagian impeccability or making an unmistakable allusion to it.

[Col. 1078B] Read chiefly the two letters to Hilary and Optatus, the three sermons, and the three commentaries on the Psalms, and nothing will seem more evident to you. But is it the condition of the Israelites—is it the whole of the Old Testament—that Saint Augustine investigates and determines with such care as the law’s end and purpose? Does he have in view the entire body of Jewish law and all its precepts, whether moral, ceremonial, or political? No. He reduces the law to this single phrase from the Decalogue: *Non concupisces*—“You shall not covet.” He mentions only this one precept, and it alone is his object when he determines the law’s purpose and end. The passages cited even by Jansenius do not permit us to doubt this, and I can assure you that Saint Augustine almost never fails to express it and place it before his reader. Thus this law, *Non concupisces*, “You shall not covet,” is the negative part of the precept of the perfection of righteousness, which, according to Saint Augustine, extends to forbidding even the feeling and interior temptation toward evil, what are called the first movements of concupiscence.

You may now be curious to know what rule Saint Augustine follows in precisely identifying the true purpose and exact end of the law “You shall not covet,” *Non concupisces*. Two difficulties guide him: one that he posed to the Pelagians, and another that the Pelagians posed to him.

[Col. 1078D] Since the holy Doctor maintained that not only was grace necessary for a person to remove concupiscence from the heart, but that the grace necessary to extinguish every form of concupiscence absolutely in the heart was ordinarily refused to a person in this life—or, which is the same thing, that the precept of the perfection of righteousness was impossible here below and would be fulfilled only in heaven—the Pelagians asked him: Why, then, did God promulgate this law? He could not simply answer, without further explanation: “God promulgated this law so that it might be observed and fulfilled”; he would have contradicted himself. Yet what prevented him from giving this answer: “God promulgated the law ‘You shall not covet,’ *Non concupisces*, so that, with the help of grace, one might obey it by never giving any consent to the disordered movements of concupiscence and by making every effort of which one was capable to suppress their outbursts and diminish their reign”?

The difficulty that the holy Doctor himself posed to the Pelagians did not permit him to take this course. For he said to them: If, as you claim, a person is able by the powers of nature alone to repress all the evil inclinations that concupiscence excites, why did God make a positive law forbidding every form of covetousness? Was the natural law not sufficient? Why was it necessary for him to engrave on stone tablets what he had written in the depths of hearts? Saint Augustine therefore reproached the Pelagians that, on their hypothesis, one could not explain why God had added the positive law to the natural law, which disapproves the disorder and rebellion of the senses, whereas in the Catholic system the reason that had moved God to do so was easy to discover.

[Col. 1079B] The statement of this reason was the true answer to the mutual question that he and the Pelagians were asking: Why did God institute the law? And this reason could have nothing in common with the natural law, since the point was to identify a usefulness of the positive law that would not be found in the natural law. Consequently, the reason was not obedience to and observance of the law, which applied equally to both laws. It was a proper purpose and particular end of the positive law, insofar as it differed from the natural law. Here it is.

God wanted to make human beings feel their need for grace, and for this purpose he made use of the positive law. Its more explicit and clearer proclamation, together with its threats, was naturally to irritate concupiscence, warn human beings of their weakness, and lead them to implore the help of their liberator; or, if that was not enough to humble them before God, their frequent and grievous falls were to finish subduing their pride.

In any case, in order not to interrupt the thread of this discussion, [Col. 1079C] which was necessary in order to place before you the true perspective from which Saint Augustine’s view of the law’s purpose and end must be considered, I refrained from supporting myself with any testimony. It is nevertheless appropriate to convince the most obstinate that I did not invent the plan I have just set out, but drew it from reading the writings of the holy Doctor.

“Why,” he says, “was the law given if nature was sufficient? And yet the law itself could not suffice, so infirm was nature itself. The law was given, but it was not such as could give life: *Quare autem dabatur lex, si sufficiebat natura? Et tamen nec lex sufficere potuit, ita infirma erat ipsa natura; data est lex, sed quae non posset vivificare*” (Sermon 26, formerly 11, *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 8, no. 9).

Here the law is opposed to nature. The subject is the positive law, insofar as it is added to the natural law, and Saint Augustine is seeking the proper purpose and particular end of this law when he continues:

[Col. 1079D] “Why, then, was the law given? ‘The law,’ says the Apostle, ‘was established because of transgressions,’ and in such a way that it would make you a transgressor. Why, ‘in such a way that it would make you a transgressor’? Because God knew your pride; he knew that you were saying: ‘Oh, if only there were someone to instruct me! Oh, if only there were someone to show me what to do!’ Here is the law saying to you: ‘You shall not covet.’ You came to know the law that forbids covetousness, and the covetousness that you did not know arose. It was within you, but you did not know it. You began trying to conquer this inner enemy, and what had been hidden became manifest. Proud man, through the law you have become a transgressor! Acknowledge and praise the grace of your God: *Quare ergo data est lex? Lex, inquit Apostolus, praevaricationis gratia posita est, ut te faceret praevaricatorem. Quare ut te faceret praevaticatorem? quia noverat Deus superbiam tuam; noverat quia dicebas: O si sit qui doceat! O si sit qui mihi ostendat! Ecce lex dicit tibi: Non concupisces. Surrexit concupiscentia, quam non noveras: inerat enim, sed nesciebatur. Coepisti conari vincere quod inerat, et apparuit quod latebat. Superbe, per legem factus es praevaricator! agnosce gratiam, et esto laudator*” (St. Augustine, ibid.).

The law about which Saint Augustine is disputing is here reduced, as everywhere else, to the positive divine precept, “You shall not covet”—*Non concupisces*—which, according to the same Saint Augustine, is the negative aspect of the precept of the perfection of righteousness. Consequently, throughout this sermon, when he contrasts law with grace, he means the grace that is necessary not only for action but also for the perfection of righteousness.

Those who persuade themselves that, in the thought of the holy doctor, transgression, or sin, is the purpose of the law will be disabused of their error, if they are willing, by reading the following passage, which certainly concerns the perfection of righteousness; for [Col. 1080B] Saint Augustine answers Hilary’s question: “Whether, then, you ask if anyone in this life can make such progress in the perfection of righteousness that he may live here the rest of his days without any sin whatsoever: *Si ergo quaeris utrum in hac vita quisquam ita in JUSTITIAE PERFECTIONE proficiat, ut hic sine ullo vivat omnino peccato*” (*Epist.* 152, formerly 89, chap. 1, no. 2).

And in the continuation of his answer he speaks as follows:

“The purpose of the law, for those who use it legitimately, is to be a help by which they may learn either how much of the gift of righteousness they have received, so that they may give thanks to God for it, or what they still lack of that precious gift, so that they may earnestly ask God to grant it to them. But as for those who listen to what the law says, ‘You shall not covet,’ in such a way that they persuade themselves that it is enough for them merely to have been instructed, and who do not believe or ask that, through the help of God’s grace, they are given the power to do what is commanded them, the purpose of the law for them is that it entered in order that sin might abound—something that was said concerning the Jews, and so forth: *Nam et ipsa lex in hoc adjutorium data est illis, qui ea legitime utuntur, ut per illam sciant, vel quid justitiae acceperint, unde gratias agant, vel quid adhuc eis desit, quod instanter petant; qui autem sic audiunt quod ait lex, Non concupisces, ut hoc quia didicerint sufficere sibi arbitrentur, nec adjutorio gratiae Dei ad faciendum sibi quod justum est dari sibi virtutem credant et petant, Ad hoc lex subintravit ut abundaret delictum, quod dictum est de Judaeis, etc.*” (Saint Augustine, cited above, no. 2).

This text proves that, according to the holy doctor’s opinion, the immediate and proximate purpose of the law, “You shall not covet”—*Non concupisces*—is the warning it gives us to prevent formal transgression and sin properly so called by humbly acknowledging our weakness, which this law makes us perceive, and whose recognition God intends to be for everyone an invitation to have recourse to grace. For who can doubt that God ever imposes a law without intending each person whom he subjects to it to use it legitimately? Therefore, when the holy doctor says, in the preceding passage and in many others, that the purpose of the law for the proud is the humiliation into which their shameful falls cast them, he is speaking of a remote and mediate purpose, which supplements the first. Indeed, he presupposes that the law has been violated by these proud people and, consequently, that an immediate and proximate purpose has been rendered ineffectual.

Would you not count as an unsound subtlety the reasoning that led me to assert that Saint Augustine did not think one should take the observance and fulfillment of the positive law, “You shall not covet”—*Non concupisces*—as the proper aim and particular purpose of that law? You might perhaps prefer me to maintain, with certain Catholic theologians of great renown, that the holy doctor leaves out the principal and direct purpose of the law through mere omission: namely, the obedience it demands; and that he regards this purpose as null because it did not produce its effect. He supposedly attaches himself to what actually happened all the more because he found there a felicitous means of demonstrating the necessity of grace.

The text I am about to cite decides in favor of my view.

“Man,” says Saint Augustine, “who was created just and upright, received a law in paradise so that he might be taught that obedience is either the sole or the principal virtue of a rational creature; but by violating that law he made himself evil. And because he could corrupt himself by himself but could not heal himself, the corrupted man also received a law afterward, at the time and in the place that divine wisdom judged appropriate—not one by which he could be corrected, but one by which he might feel that he was corrupt and that, even after receiving the law, he could not correct himself by himself: *In paradiso enim legem accepit homo, qui factus est rectus, ut rationabilis creaturae vel sola vel praecipua virtus esse obedientia doceretur. Sed ejusdem legis praevaricatione a se ipso factus est pravus. Et quoniam vitiari per se ipsum potuit, non sanari, etiam postea eo tempore et eo loco quando esse faciendum et ubi esse faciendum Dei sapientia judicavit, legem etiam pravus accepit, non per quam corrigi posset, sed per quam se pravum esse et nec accepta lege a se ipso corrigi posse sentiret, etc.*” (*Lib. VI Oper. Imp.*, no. 15).

Saint Augustine here contrasts the law given to Adam, forbidding him to eat the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, with the written law promulgated by Moses, which forbids coveting. He says that the proper and particular purpose of the law given to Adam was obedience; and he does not regard this purpose as null, although it did not produce its effect. Why, then, would he regard this same purpose as null in the law promulgated by Moses simply because it did not produce its effect? Moreover, does he not declare, by the contrast he establishes between the two laws, that obedience was not the proper and particular purpose of the Mosaic law, as it was of Adam’s law? And from where does he intend this difference to arise, if not from the fact that man, just and upright in his origin, needed only positive laws to test his obedience, and not laws to enlighten him concerning the duties of the natural law; whereas man, corrupted by sin, lacked not only strength but also understanding, and could not satisfy the natural law without a medicinal grace that would be denied him unless he asked for it, and that he would not have asked for had he not felt his weakness? This feeling, then, is the proper aim and particular purpose of the positive law, “You shall not covet”—*Non concupisces*—insofar as this law is distinguished from the natural law.

Besides this, it must be observed that Saint Augustine here, above all, understands obedience to the law as a full and complete fulfillment, which is what he customarily calls the perfection of righteousness. For certainly, in the text I have just quoted, he is treating of the freedom necessary for the perfection of righteousness; and he contrasts the two laws—that is, the one given to Adam and the one promulgated by Moses—in order to conclude against Julian that the Mosaic law does not prove that we possess, in our present condition, the freedom necessary for the perfection of righteousness. If it proved this, the holy doctor adds, that law would not concern the one who says: “I do not do the good that I wish, but, on the contrary, I do the evil that I do not wish.” *Non igitur lex quae in litteris per Moysen data est testimonium est liberae voluntatis; nam si ita esset, non ad eam pertineret ille qui dicit: Non quod volo facio bonum, sed quod odi malum hoc ago* (Saint Augustine, cited above). All this must shed considerable light on the controversy that follows.

## Fourth Part. THE STATE OF THE QUESTION BETWEEN THE DEFENDERS OF THE FAITH OF THE COUNCIL OF TRENT AND THE HERETICS OF OUR DAY

[Col. 1081]

[Col. 1081C] You will ask me whom I call the defenders of the faith of the Council of Trent. First listen to this text of the council:

“No one ought to use that rash expression, forbidden under anathema by the Fathers, namely, that the observance of God’s commandments is impossible for a justified person. For God does not command impossible things; but, by commanding, he admonishes you to do what you can and to ask for what you cannot, and he helps you so that you can. … God never abandons those who have once been justified by his grace, unless they first abandon him. … If anyone says that the observance of God’s commandments is impossible even for a justified person who is in the grace of God, let him be anathema: *Nemo temeraria illa et a Patribus sub anathemate prohibita voce uti debet, Dei praecepta homini justificato ad observandum esse impossibilia. Nam Deus impossibilia non jubet, sed jubendo monet et facere quod possis, et petere quod non possis, et adjuvat ut possis … Deus numque sua gratia semel justificatos non deserit, nisi ab eis prius deseratur …*” (Council of Trent, session 6, chap. 2). “If anyone says that God’s commandments are impossible to observe even for a justified person who is in a state of grace, let him be anathema” (*Si quis dixerit Dei praecepta homini etiam justificato et sub gratia constituto esse ad observandum impossibilia, anathema sit*; same session, canon 18).

Such is the faith of the Council of Trent.

[Col. 1082C] Those who speak or write in defense of this doctrine are the defenders of the faith of the Council of Trent. Such are all the truly Catholic authors and theologians whom Luther and Calvin called papists, and whom the followers of Jansenius call Molinists, even when they have nothing in common with Molina except their adherence to the faith of the Council of Trent, and even when they are purely Scotists or Thomists. True Molinists have no cause to complain of this; it does them honor.

Whatever the case, all the schools and academies that sincerely respect the holy Council of Trent have always agreed in combating the pernicious and impious dogma that God’s commandments are impossible. The new heretics have not been content to teach this in general; they claim to demonstrate it by the example of a great people chosen by God to be filled with temporal blessings and abandoned with respect to the matters of salvation. The issue concerns the impossibility of God’s commandments for justified persons; for, I think, it is not disputed that most of the Jews were justified from childhood by circumcision, or by some other ceremony instituted by God as a remedy for original sin.

Jansenius has treated this matter at much greater length than Luther and Calvin (*Luther, praefat. in Vetus Testam.* and *Comm. in Gal.* III; *Calvin, lib. II, Inst.*, chap. 7), and he seems to have carried the error farther than they did. I shall therefore concern myself exclusively with refuting him and shall follow him step by step; he is methodical. He first discusses the purpose God had in view when instituting the ancient law; then the rewards God promises to those who faithfully observe the ancient law; after that, the helps and graces that one might imagine God granted in order to make observance of the ancient law possible; and finally, the condition of the Synagogue. I shall examine these four points and shall conclude with a parallel between Manichaeism and Jansenism in relation to the ancient law.

## I. The Purpose God Had in View When Instituting the Ancient Law

In instituting the ancient law, God had four purposes in view, according to the doctrine of the Catholic Church: two ultimate and remote purposes, and two proximate and immediate purposes. The honor of Jesus Christ was the ultimate purpose God had in view for himself; I explained this above. Eternal salvation was the ultimate purpose God had in view for the Israelites; I shall treat of it in the following section. Observance of the law and the removal of sin was the proximate, principal, and direct purpose. Awareness of human beings’ need for grace was the proximate, subordinate, and indirect purpose; for since the law provoked concupiscence, this need was to be felt simply through the temptation to act against the law—and it must be noted that this temptation, in Saint Augustine’s language, is called a sin and a transgression because it is contrary to the law of impeccability and the perfection of righteousness. How much more, then, was the need for grace to be felt through the humiliation into which the Israelites were brought by the multitude of sins they committed through their own fault against the action and practice of righteousness, on the occasion of the law!

[Col. 1083C] This subordinate and indirect purpose therefore extended to the intention of drawing their own good from their sins. Since God foresaw the infidelity and transgression of his people, his wisdom resolved to turn their very wickedness to the advantage of those ungrateful people. It was up to them to benefit from this and to recognize and implore the grace of the Liberator. The effect and fruit of the law that I have just identified was therefore substituted, by God’s infinite mercy, for the observance of the law, which most of the Israelites neglected. Strictly speaking, however, it was not so much the purpose for which God instituted the law as the purpose for which, according to our way of conceiving things, he persisted in his resolve to institute it, notwithstanding his foreknowledge that the law would be violated and transgressed. This is the reason that moved him not to decree and will, but to permit, the excesses and disorders into which the Jews plunged; it was a resource that he reserved for them.

Saint Paul makes extensive mention of this in the Epistle to the Romans, where he shows that, because of our unfortunate inclination to do what is forbidden us, the written law became for many an occasion of more serious sin; and that, by a just permission of God, the Israelites, having abandoned his worship in order to embrace idolatry and having plunged into every kind of vice, were wrong to claim that they should be preferred to the Gentiles on account of the privilege of the law, which they had so badly observed. Nothing is better suited to demonstrate the necessity of grace than this second purpose, or second intention, of God in instituting the law. Saint Augustine therefore speaks of it everywhere and so frequently that he gave many people the same occasion for error that the law had given them for sinning; and this happened through no fault either of Saint Augustine or of the law. For allow me to apply, with the appropriate proportion, to Saint Augustine’s doctrine what Saint Paul says of the law: This doctrine is good, just, and holy. The abuse made of both comes solely from human presumption and pride. God permitted it so that the confusion of having been so grossly mistaken might lead the inventors of the new dogmas to recognize the necessity of a judge in controversies of faith, just as the shame of the sins into which the Jews fell ought to have led them to recognize the necessity of grace. A similar blindness in both groups obstructs the beneficial effect of God’s designs.

“When God gave the Mosaic law,” says Jansenius, “his intention was not that the Jews should live rightly by observing it, but that their pride should be subdued by the multitude of sins and transgressions that he knew would follow from a law that this people could not fulfill: *Consilium Dei reformando Judaeorum populo saluberrimum in danda lege fuit, non ut per gratiam sufficientem, quae adesset ipsis, eam observando recte viverent, quod eos nondum posse praesciebat, sed ut multitudine peccatorum et praevaricationum, quae per legem quam implere non poterant secutura sciebantur, eorum superbia frangeretur*” (Jansenius, vol. III, book I, chap. 11, p. 43).

But will I not be accused of translating him unfaithfully? There is no appearance of that. Jansenius says that God’s intention was not that the Jews should live rightly by observing the law through sufficient grace, and still less, no doubt, through efficacious grace. Thus he claims that God did not absolutely will that the Jews observe the law. He says that the Jews could not yet observe the law: this “yet” designates the whole period during which the law lasted; that is why he subsequently adds, quite simply, that the Jews could not observe the law. He says that this intention of God was highly salutary; I leave it to the reader to consider how. Finally, as usual, he attributes the whole matter to Saint Augustine.

What! Would Jansenius have us believe that Saint Augustine formally contradicted Scripture? God says to his people: “Observe all the things that I command you today”—*Observa cuncta quae hodie mando tibi* (Exod. 34:11). Moses says to this same people on God’s behalf: “Keep the commandments of the Lord your God”—*Custodite mandata Domini Dei vestri* (Deut. 4:2). “Learn them and put them into practice”—*Discite ea et opere complete* (ibid., 5:1). “Be careful to practice them”—*Cave diligenter ut facias* (ibid., 8:1). All the books of the law are full of similar expressions. Saint Augustine had read them, and this commentary is attributed to him: God said, “Observe, keep, practice,” without intending that his commandments be observed, kept, and practiced? Would Jansenius have us believe that Saint Augustine contradicted the doctrine and tradition of all the Fathers who preceded him?

Saint Justin, who lived close to the time of the apostles, spoke thus to the Jews:

“You understand that, because of the hardness of heart of your nation, God imposed upon you through the ministry of Moses such a great number of laws, so that the multitude of observances might keep God before your eyes in all your actions, and so that you might learn never to commit any injustice or impiety: *Propter duritiam cordis populi vestri cunctas hujusmodi sanctiones Deum per Moysen vobis tulisse intelligitis; ut per complura ista instituta in actione omni ob oculos vestros esset Deus, ac neque injuste facere neque impie agere acciperetis*” (Saint Justin, *Dial. cum Tryph.*, p. 205, no. 40, Commelin edition, 1593).

Saint Irenaeus, who lived not long afterward, says that the law given to slaves instructed the soul through external and corporeal things, and drew it, as by a chain, toward obedience to the precepts, so that man might learn to serve God: *Lex quippe servis posita per ea quae foris erant corporalia, animam erudiebat, velut per vinculum attrahens eam ad obedientiam praeceptorum, ut disceret homo servire Deo* (Saint Irenaeus, book IV, chap. 13, no. 2).

Saint John Chrysostom, who lived somewhat before Saint Augustine, asks what the purpose of the law was, and answers that it tended to make man righteous. That, he adds, was the purpose of the law; everything referred to it, everything was done for it: the solemnities, the precepts, the offerings, and everything else were intended to make man righteous: *Quid enim lex vult? hominem justum facere … Hic itaque legis quidem finis erat, atque huc respiciebant omnia, ad hoc omnia fiebant, sive solemnitates, sive mandata, sive oblationes, et si quae sunt reliqua, ut homo justus redderetur* (Saint Chrysostom, *Homily 17 on Romans*).

People would have Saint Augustine contradict these holy doctors, and so many others whom I could cite, who, having docilely instructed themselves within the bosom of the Catholic Church and enlightened it by their doctrine, deserved to be both its children and its Fathers. This is the praise Saint Augustine gives them (Saint Augustine, *Lib. IV Oper. Imp.*, no. 112). Would Jansenius have us believe that Saint Augustine contradicted common sense? Who has ever heard of a law enacted with the intention that it not be fulfilled? Is not a law the legislator’s own will concerning the matter governed by it?

Is this natural idea that we have of law not applied to the Mosaic law by the Holy Spirit? Among the sacred authors, are law and God’s will not the same thing? “He made known his ways to Moses, his will to the children of Israel,” says David: *Notas fecit vias suas Moysi, filiis Israel voluntates suas* (Ps. 102:7). “Teach me,” he says to the Lord, “to do your will”—that is, to fulfill your law: *Doce me facere voluntatem tuam* (Ps. 142:10). And yet people dare to assert that, according to Saint Augustine’s view, God did not intend that his law be fulfilled—that is, that God did not will what he willed.

[Col. 1085C] What does Jansenius take Saint Augustine for? Does he think that, because he has taken care to clothe his thought in the holy doctor’s expressions, we shall have less right to regard it as true delirium and the wandering of a mind devoted to error? Would Jansenius have us believe that Saint Augustine contradicted himself? The holy doctor not only recognizes that God’s law is not distinct from God’s will—*Voluntas Dei ipsa est lex Dei* (Sermon 3 on Psalm 36, no. 5)—but clearly condemns the contrary opinion, whose falsity and horror Jansenius has not feared to shelter beneath the respected name of this great saint.

The Pelagians had reproached the holy doctor for saying that the law of the Old Testament had not been given so that it might contribute to the justification of those who fulfilled it, but so that it might become the cause of a more serious sin: *Legem Veteris Testamenti nos aiunt dicere non ob hoc datam fuisse ut justificaret obedientes, sed ut gravioris fieret causa delicti* (Saint Augustine, *Book III to Boniface*, chap. 2, no. 2). Saint Augustine, however, treats this accusation as slander, and acknowledges that the law was given so that it might contribute to the justification of those who fulfilled it, provided that it be agreed that the obedience rendered to the law is an effect of grace. He accuses the Pelagians of failing to understand his view concerning the law:

“Clearly they do not understand what we say about the law. … Who would say that those who obey the law are not justified, when, unless they were justified, they could not be obedient? But we say that through the law it comes about that God’s will is heard, whereas through grace it comes about that the law is obeyed: *Prorsus non intelligunt quid de lege dicamus … Quis enim dicat non justificari eos qui sunt legi obedientes, quando nisi justificarentur non possent esse obedientes? Sed dicimus lege fieri ut Deus quid velit audiatur: gratia vero fieri ut legi obediatur*” (Saint Augustine, cited above).

I ask you to reread attentively the proposition that the Pelagians attributed to Saint Augustine, and to judge whether it is not the same proposition that Jansenius attributes to the holy doctor, and whether Jansenius does not take this proposition in the same sense in which the Pelagians took it. The bishop of Ypres is therefore here convicted [Col. 1086A] of having sought to verify the accusations that the Pelagians brought against Saint Augustine, and of presenting their slanders as the holy doctor’s genuine opinions.

Certainly Saint Augustine was far removed from that impious and absurd dogma which assigns to God’s legislative will, as its principal, direct, and immediate purpose, the abundance and multiplication of sin. This is the second part of Jansenius’s proposition, quoted above, which, in agreement with the Pelagians, he imputes to Saint Augustine. I say that this dogma is impious and absurd: does it not offend God’s wisdom no less than his holiness and infinite goodness?

I agree that nothing is more compatible with these three divine attributes than drawing good from evil, and making human beings’ disobedience and resistance to God’s will—which is contained and expressed in the precept—serve the execution of the noblest and most lovable designs. [Col. 1086B] But to choose sin, to propose it as the principal, direct, and immediate object, as a means and disposition preparing the way for grace; to positively will that human beings be wicked and criminal so that their wickedness and crimes may lead them to righteousness and holiness—is anything more opposed and injurious to all the divine attributes? Was Saint Augustine capable of accepting or approving such an idea, whose perversity is no less than its horror?

Jansenius nevertheless asserts with extreme boldness that this doctrine is very clearly established in Scripture, and that Saint Augustine disseminated it in an infinite number of passages of his writings, as being, on account of its importance, worthy of being strongly inculcated upon the Christian people (Jansenius, vol. III, book I, chap. 11, p. 43). One might think that Jansenius has attributed to Saint Augustine nothing here except something highly edifying. You have seen that the first part of his proposition is formally contrary to Scripture. And is the second not condemned by these words: “The ungodly are not necessary to him”—*Non enim necessarii sunt ei homines impii* (Ecclus. 15:12)? Will Jansenius say to the Wise Man: “You are mistaken; God needed your whole nation to be ungodly in order to make grace desired”?

Listen to him—and to his disciples—who first cite several texts of Saint Paul, only to overwhelm us afterward with a multitude of passages from Saint Augustine. Does not the Apostle affirm that the law was established because of transgressions—*Lex propter praevaricationes posita est* (Gal. 3:19)—and that Scripture confined everything under sin—*Conclusit Scriptura omnia sub peccato* (ibid., 22)? Does he not indicate clearly enough, in several places of his Epistle to the Romans, that the law was established because of sin? But why, when the Apostle simply says that the law was established because of transgressions, do they understand him to mean that the law was established in order to make people commit transgressions and then punish them? Why, when he says that Scripture confined everything under sin, do they understand him to mean that the written law has sin as its sole purpose, rather than that Holy Scripture has enclosed everyone—Jews and Gentiles alike—within the manifest conviction of sin, and has shown that all, without distinction or exception, were guilty?

The Jansenists flatter themselves that they possess the gift of understanding with respect to the writings of Saint Paul. Saint Paul, Saint Augustine, and truth are incontestably on their side; so they say—take their word for it—and be sure to call them Paulists, Augustinians, and the party of truth. Yet, even if I should appear ridiculous to them, I maintain that neither their master nor they have grasped the true meaning of the Epistle to the Romans as well as the holy Fathers did.

Saint John Chrysostom, explaining the words *Lex subintravit, ut abundaret delictum*—“The law entered in, so that transgression might abound”—takes care to warn that the particle *ut* does not here indicate causation but merely the outcome of events. For, he says:

“This word *ut* here does not state the cause but indicates the event. For the law was not enacted so that sin might abound, but was enacted so that it might diminish and remove sin. What happened, however, arose not from the nature of the law but from the laziness and negligence of those who received the law: *Hic haec vox UT non dicit causam sed rei eventum denotat. Neque enim lata lex est ut abundaret, sed lata ut minueret et tolleret peccatum; evenit autem non a legis natura, sed ab eorum ignavia et socordia qui legem accepere*” (Saint Chrysostom, Homily 10 on Romans 5:20).

Theodoret, in his exposition of these words—“What shall we say, then? Is the law sin? By no means. But I did not know sin except through the law”: *Quid ergo dicemus? lex peccatum est? Absit. Sed peccatum non cognovi, nisi per legem* (Rom. 7:7)—says:

“The Apostle showed that such a question was blasphemous when he used the negative expression, ‘By no means.’ Then he shows the usefulness of the law by adding, ‘But I did not know sin except through the law.’ He does not merely say, ‘The law is not a teacher of sin—far from it’; on the contrary, he says that the law is the accuser of sin: *Blasphemam hanc percontationem esse docuit, cum usus est voce negativa, Absit. Postea docet legis utilitatem, sed peccatum non cognovi nisi per legem. Non solum dicit: Lex non est peccati magistra, absit; sed e contrario peccati accusatrix*” (Theodoret on Romans 7:7).

When Saint John Chrysostom came to the words, “Taking occasion through the commandment, sin deceived me,” he said:

“If it is the law’s crime that sin began through the occasion it provided, the same thing will also be found in the New Testament: *Quod si crimen legis hoc est, quod peccatum per eam occasionem esse coeperit, idipsum etiam in Novo Testamento reperietur*” (Saint Chrysostom, Homily 12 on Romans, p. 156, Paris edition, 1633).

“Why are you surprised,” says Saint Ambrose, “if the law is death to some, since the Lord’s saving advent, through which we were redeemed, is also death: *Quid miraris, si lex quibusdam morti sit, cum morti sit et Domini salutaris adventus, per quem redempti sumus*” (Saint Ambrose, *Book I on Jacob and the Blessed Life*, no. 14)?

The Jansenists will not make much of these authorities. To accommodate them, one would have to reduce all sacred writers to Saint Paul, all interpreters of Saint Paul to Saint Augustine, and all interpreters of Saint Augustine to Jansenius together with Luther and Calvin. If one wishes, they will not quibble, provided that the interpretation of these heresiarchs is reported without naming them. Decorum requires it. The misfortune is that Saint Paul agrees with all the other sacred writers, Saint Augustine with all the other Fathers, and Jansenius has nothing in common with Saint Augustine except expressions wrested from their true meaning.

For on what basis does Jansenius attribute to Saint Augustine the teaching that the “highly salutary intention,” as he puts it, of reforming the Jewish people by giving them the law was not that they should live rightly by observing the law with the help of grace? On this basis: Saint Augustine says that it is impossible to extinguish concupiscence entirely in this life, and that consequently the law of the Decalogue, “You shall not covet”—*Non concupisces*—which was given to Moses on Mount Sinai, cannot be perfectly observed in this life, and was not even observed by Saint Paul, to whom God refused the grace of delivering him from the afflictions caused by the sting of the flesh; Saint Augustine distinguishes the positive law, “You shall not covet”—*Non concupisces*—from the natural law, of which it is the expression, and, wishing to assign it a proper and particular purpose, characterizes it by the awareness it arouses of the help man needs in order to fulfill [Col. 1088A] the natural law; and Saint Augustine, who never suspected that people would make him appear to think that a law is not a law—that is, that its principal and direct purpose is not its fulfillment, at least imperfectly—attached himself to subordinate and indirect purposes.

It cannot be too strongly emphasized that the holy doctor was obliged to proceed in this way when disputing either against the Manichaeans or against the Pelagians. Against the former, he had to justify God’s wisdom and goodness in having given a law, even though he foresaw that it would not be observed. Therefore, since God’s first intention—that the law should be obeyed—had produced its effect only in a small number of righteous people, Saint Augustine had to show that the law had been useful even to the great number who had neglected and violated it, insofar as it had made them humble themselves before God, recognize and confess their sins, and thus disposed them to have recourse to grace in order to obtain mercy. This is the natural explanation of the testimonies Jansenius cites from the Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians (no. 24) and from Saint Augustine’s writings against the Manichaeans (*Book XIX against Faustus*, chap. 7; *Book II against the Adversary of the Law*, chap. 7; *Book I on the Proceedings with Felix*, chap. 11).

Moreover, since the holy doctor had to demonstrate the insufficiency of the law without grace, the Pelagians reduced him to being able to do so only by relying on this subordinate purpose of the law, namely, to humble and confound man after his fall. This proved that the fall had been caused by the absence of grace, which an arrogant confidence in the powers of nature and in the sole light of the law had driven away. This is the true explanation of the passage Jansenius cited from *On the Spirit and the Letter* (ch. 6, no. 9). The purpose that God set for himself in instituting the law must now appear entirely clear to you; and you do not expect that the purpose he set before the [Col. 1088C] Israelites will present much greater difficulty.

## II. The purpose that God set before the Israelites in instituting the law

By the purpose that God set before the Israelites, I mean the reward he promised to faithful observers of the Mosaic law. Jansenius asserts that in the Old Testament nothing at all spiritual is promised, but only carnal things: *Nihil omnino spirituale in Veteri Testamento promittitur, sed sola carnalia* (“Absolutely nothing spiritual is promised in the Old Testament, but only carnal things”; Jans., vol. III, book III, ch. 6, p. 278). The Synagogue, he adds, considered as Synagogue, was nothing other than a throng of an earthly people and an assembly of carnal men, occupied solely with earthly and carnal goods, and worshiping one God solely in order to obtain them: *Synagoga, considerata ut Synagoga, non erat aliud quam terreni populi turba, hominumque carnalium congregatio solis terrenis et carnalibus incubantium, et propter illa sola colentium unum Deum* (“The Synagogue, considered as Synagogue, was nothing other than a crowd of an earthly people, an assembly of carnal men devoted exclusively to earthly and carnal things and worshiping one God for their sake alone”; Jans., ibid.).

[Col. 1088D] What does Jansenius mean? What! Was the hope of the kingdom of heaven not joined to faith in the future Messiah, which the Jews professed? Did God’s generosity toward this beloved people extend only to the advantages and pleasures that can be enjoyed in this lower world, and no farther than the course and term of the present life? When God dictated these words to Moses, to address them in his name to the whole people of Israel—“Keep my laws and judgments; whoever faithfully observes them shall have life through them”: *Custodite leges meas atque judicia, quae faciens homo vivet in eis* (“Keep my laws and judgments; the person who does them shall live by them”; Lev. XVIII, 5)—did he promise only the reward of temporal life? Saint Paul nevertheless understood this text as referring to justification, which includes the right to eternal life. “The end of the law,” he says, “is Christ, for the justification of everyone who believes. Moses likewise writes that the person who practices the righteousness commanded by the [Col. 1089A] law shall live by it: *Finis enim legis Christus, ad justitiam omni credenti. Moyses enim scripsit, quoniam justitiam quae ex lege est qui fecerit homo vivet in ea*” (“For Christ is the end of the law, for the justification of everyone who believes. For Moses wrote that the person who does the righteousness that comes from the law shall live by it”; Rom. X, 4–5).

Does that beautiful saying, “The just person lives by faith,” which the same Saint Paul so often employs, not testify that he borrowed it from the Old Testament—*Sicut scriptum est, justus autem ex fide vivit* (“As it is written: the just person lives by faith”; Rom. I, 17; Gal. III, 11; Heb. X, 38)? Let us consult the text cited by the Apostle: “This is what will happen: the unbeliever shall have no upright soul within him; but the just person shall live by faith”: *Ecce qui incredulus est, non erit recta anima ejus in semetipso; justus autem ex fide sua vivet* (“Behold, the unbeliever has no upright soul in himself; but the just person shall live by his faith”; Hab. II, 4). The Apostle and the prophet Habakkuk speak of a life that is the pledge, beginning, and foretaste of eternal life, and the prophet promises it to faithful Israelites—to all those who, in his time, were not among the unbelievers. Hear another prophet, who speaks [Col. 1089B] as follows: “Here is the book of God’s commandments, and the law that endures forever. All who hold fast to it shall attain life, but those who have abandoned it shall come to death”: *Hic liber mandatorum Dei, et lex quae est in aeternum; omnes qui tenent eam pervenient ad vitam; qui autem dereliquerunt eam, ad mortem* (“This is the book of God’s commandments, and the law that is forever; all who hold to it shall reach life, but those who have abandoned it, death”; Baruch IV, 1).

Compare this text with the question asked by a Jew who approached Jesus Christ and said to him: “Good Master, what good thing must I do to obtain eternal life? *Magister bone, quid boni faciam, ut habeam vitam aeternam?*” (“Good Master, what good must I do to have eternal life?”), and with the Savior’s reply: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments: *Si autem vis ad vitam ingredi, serva mandata*” (“If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments”; Matt. XIX, 16). You will agree that the prophet’s words and those of Jesus Christ have the same meaning.

Moreover, compare the Jew’s question with the discourse that the aged Tobit addressed to his son: “We are children of the saints, and we await [Col. 1089C] that life which God will give to those who never depart from their faith in him: *Filii sanctorum sumus, et vitam illam exspectamus quam daturus est Deus his qui fidem suam nunquam mutant ab eo*” (“We are children of the holy ones, and we await that life which God will give to those who never change their faith in him”; Tob. II, 18). You will dismiss Jansenius’s futile evasion, by which he claims that eternal life was promised and offered before Jesus Christ only to extraordinary men who did not belong to the Mosaic law. For is it not evident that the aged Tobit and the Jew who questioned the Savior expressed the common belief and hope of the nation?

The Wise Man says that the just shall live forever: *Justi autem in perpetuum vivent* (“But the just shall live forever”; Wis. V, 16). The second of the Maccabean children said at the moment of his death: “The King of the world, after the death we suffer in defense of his laws, will raise us up to eternal life: *Rex mundi defunctos nos pro suis legibus aeternae vitae resurrectione suscitabit*” (“The King of the world will raise us, who have died for his laws, to the resurrection of eternal life”; II Macc. XII, [Col. 1089D] 44). This was not a private opinion, but a public one. It served as the motive for the offerings that the elder Maccabee caused to be made for the dead; it was preserved by tradition in the soundest part of the Synagogue until the time of Jesus Christ, when the doctrine of the resurrection distinguished orthodox Jews, who were called Pharisees, from the heterodox, who were called Sadducees. Saint Paul, speaking of this doctrine, does not merely say, “I hope for what God promised to our fathers”: *In spe quae ad patres nostros repromissionis facta est a Deo* (“In the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers”; Acts XXVI, 6), but immediately adds: “and to which our twelve tribes hope to attain”: *In quam duodecim tribus nostrae nocte ac die sperant devenire* (“To which our twelve tribes hope to attain night and day”; ibid., 7). It is therefore an article of faith that God had promised the patriarchs of the Old Testament and all their posterity resurrection to eternal life as the reward for their good works. It is therefore also a matter of the law that the hope of attaining eternal life through [Col. 1090A] good works continued among the twelve tribes in Saint Paul’s time. And doubtless it had always continued and had never been entirely extinguished. What more can one ask? Will anyone set Saint Augustine against Scripture? Did he ever depart from it? And when Scripture favors us, will he oppose us?

This holy doctor teaches that before the law and during the time of the law people were justified by faith in the Mediator while living piously, although, he says, the law appeared to have carnal promises in the figures of spiritual things: *Quamvis in figuris rerum spiritualium habere videretur promissa carnalia* (“Although it seemed to have carnal promises in the figures of spiritual things”; *City of God*, book X, ch. 25). Elsewhere he repeats the same thought; consequently, he believed that in reality the law had spiritual promises, and that Israelites could stop at the appearance and be satisfied with the figure only through their own fault (*Questions on Numbers*, book IV, q. 33, no. 1).

But Jansenius will overwhelm us with passages from [Col. 1090B] Saint Augustine. And what do these passages prove? That the kingdom of heaven properly belonged to the New Testament, just as grace and its author did; that it was a good foreign to the state of the law, but nevertheless attached and secured to faithful observance of the law; that it was not the reward of purely legal works, but of the interior spirit by which grace animated them, which grace was itself an anticipated fruit of the Christian religion; finally, that this kingdom was promised and awaited together with the Messiah and as the Messiah; that it was to be opened and possessed outside the state of the old law and within that of the new law. Therefore the Fathers are right to say that the kingdom of heaven was preached only in the Gospel, and that one hears of the kingdom of heaven only in the Gospel, since it was not proclaimed that this kingdom was near until the coming of Jesus Christ (St. Jerome, *Dialogue 1 against the Pelagians*, pp. 50–51, Roman ed., 1576).

Jansenius, who had meditated so extensively on the errors of Pelagius, [Col. 1090C] did he not notice that this heresiarch, by denying original sin, also maintained that human nature had not lost through Adam’s transgression its right to the heavenly kingdom, and that consequently this right had not been restored to us through the Savior’s redemption? Did he not know that it was essential to Pelagianism to maintain that, together with original innocence, the sure pledge of the enjoyment of God and of an eternity of happiness had always been preserved among human beings, and was no more the exclusive property of the evangelical law than of the law of nature and the law of Moses? If this important point of the Pelagian system did not escape him, how did he fail to understand that Saint Augustine, wishing to contradict Pelagius, had no need to maintain that the kingdom of heaven was not promised to all true worshipers of the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but only that it was not promised to them by virtue of any covenant or law other than that of Jesus Christ?

[Col. 1090D] Would you like to see whether the holy doctor did not say more than was necessary? Consult the remarks he made on the acts of the Council of Diospolis. “Another article was read,” he says, “which Pelagius had written in his profession of faith: namely, that the kingdom of heaven had been promised in the Old Testament. Pelagius replied that this could be proved from the Scriptures, and that heretics denied it in order to discredit the Old Testament. After receiving this reply from Pelagius, the council said that this too was not contrary to ecclesiastical faith (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, ch. 5, no. 13).” What reflections does Saint Augustine make on this? He distinguishes two meanings of the Old Testament: the first signifies the law given to Moses on Mount Sinai; the second signifies the whole body of the sacred Scriptures, containing the books of the law and the prophets. In the first sense, he says, the Old Testament is a law of [Col. 1091A] servitude; how, then, could the kingdom of heaven, which belongs properly to freedom, belong to it? But the kingdom of heaven, he adds, could have been promised in the Old Testament if by that term one understands the books of the law and the prophets, just as in them one finds the promise of the New Testament, to which the kingdom of heaven belongs. The holy doctor then declares that those who lived under the Old Testament were also included in the promise of the New, with regard to the anticipatory benefits they could enjoy and the aids of grace that helped them become heirs of the New Testament: *Istam distinctionem, qui etiam illo tempore per Dei gratiam intelligentes, filii promissionis effecti sunt, Novi Testamenti haeredes in occulto Dei judicio deputati sunt* (“Those who, even at that time, understood this distinction through God’s grace became children of the promise and, by God’s hidden judgment, were reckoned heirs of the New Testament”; ibid., no. 4).

I do not yet examine whether the grace mentioned in this passage, according to the holy doctor’s teaching, was offered to all Israelites. It is enough for me to demonstrate that it is not contrary to the holy doctor’s purpose to claim that this grace was offered to everyone, and consequently to maintain that the kingdom of heaven was promised to all Israelites.

[Col. 1091B] Saint Augustine’s sole purpose in distinguishing two different meanings of the Old Testament is to destroy the equality that Pelagius placed between the Old and the New: *Novo fit injuria, si Veteri aequetur* (“The New is wronged if it is equated with the Old”). Now this equality is destroyed as soon as the kingdom of heaven is not promised to the Jews by virtue of the covenant God made with them on Mount Sinai through the ministry of Moses, although it was promised to them by virtue of the covenant God made with the human race on Calvary through the shedding of Jesus Christ’s blood—a blood whose efficacy, if I may put it this way, was retroactive and made itself felt in every age. This is what Saint Augustine’s distinction expresses.

For if the promise of another life is neither a [Col. 1091C] part nor an essential condition of the covenant God made with the Hebrew people on Mount Sinai, and if it is found only in those passages of the books of the law and the prophets where the affinity of the Old and New Testaments is indicated, is it not clear that the other life is not a good that comes from the law or belongs to the law? Saint Augustine could therefore say that the Old Testament promised only earthly felicity without excluding the Jews from the share that God gave them—or offered them in anticipation—of the promises of the Gospel: *Non invenitur promitti apertissime nisi terrena felicitas* (“Nothing is found to be promised openly except earthly happiness”; Saint Augustine, passage cited above).

How could Jansenius have imagined that Saint Augustine made such an exclusion? Let the bishop of Ypres and his disciples be asked whether it is wrong to love temporal goods for their own sake and to regard them as one’s final end. They will cry out that it is an insult to doubt for a moment that they consider this a very great crime. And understand, [Col. 1091D] if you can, that it is Jansenius himself and his disciples who think—and dare to make Saint Augustine think—that God offered the Hebrew people prosperity, riches, and the advantages of the present life so that they would love these goods for their own sake and regard them as their final end, and that God had no will or intention that the common run of Israelites should take these goods as images and figures meant to represent, make them desire, and make them hope for spiritual and eternal goods. Do the Jansenists think that a blasphemy ceases to be one when, in imitation of Calvin, they make Saint Augustine its accomplice and author? And is it not genuine blasphemy to hold this opinion, which requires one to deny that it is permissible to attach oneself to and aspire toward what God promises, in the manner in which he promises it, and to admit that God led the Israelites into crime by his promises?

[Col. 1092A] On the contrary, in the Catholic system, this nation could legitimately ask God and expect from him, as a temporal reward for its piety and as a sign of his benevolence and paternal care toward it, riches, power, success, the pleasures, and the repose of life. Their request and expectation were not only a testimony to their faith that God was the master and dispenser of these goods, but also rested on the fact that these goods were pledges of a more solid favor and of a generosity more worthy of God’s holiness and wisdom.

Nevertheless, let us examine a little more deeply, I beg you, the nature of the promises of temporal goods that God made to the Jews. They are set out chiefly in the twenty-eighth chapter of Deuteronomy. God undertakes to raise the people of Israel above all nations if they faithfully observe the law that had just been promulgated.
