He assures them of abundant [Col. 1092B] harvests, fertile flocks, profitable commerce, success in war, and superiority over all neighboring peoples. “If you walk in the way of my precepts,” he says elsewhere, “if you keep and practice my commandments, I will send you rain at the proper time; your land will produce grain in abundance, and your trees will be laden with fruit. The abundance of the harvest will be followed by that of the vintage, and the vintage by a season favorable and suitable for sowing, and so on. I will give you peace, and so on. The sword of your enemies shall not reach your borders; they will flee and be struck down before you,” and so forth (Lev. XXVI).

I see nothing here that is personal or addressed to each Israelite individually. These promises concern the entire commonwealth; they aim at the common welfare of the state, and not at anything that would distinguish one person from others or make his condition more agreeable than that of his fellow citizens. [Col. 1092C] For do you really believe, I beg you, that under these promises the field of a Jew who exactly fulfilled the duties of his religion was always more productive than the field of another Jew who lived impiously; that when land changed owners it became fertile or sterile according to the good or evil life of its possessor; that rain and fair weather came at the right time upon the estates of an honest man, while drought or floods devastated those of his wicked neighbor; that during an enemy incursion the ravages and plundering were miraculously directed and measured so that they fell upon the property of families in proportion to their greater or lesser guilt; that hypocrisy could not exist among the people of Israel; and that, by inspecting the lands, vineyards, and flocks belonging to each person, one could clearly know the state of his conscience? No, certainly not. Nor was it true for the first time in Jesus Christ’s day that God [Col. 1092D] “makes his sun rise on the good and the wicked and sends rain on the just and the unjust”: *Solem suum oriri facit super bonos et malos, et pluit super justos et injustos* (“He makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust”; Matt. V, 45). Tobit, Mordecai, and Ezekiel shared the hardships of captivity with those who had brought it upon themselves through their idolatry. And although Scripture mentions several just persons overwhelmed with temporal blessings, does it not also portray several impious people as prosperous? During the time of Israel’s greatest prosperity, was there no transgressor of the law who shared in the public happiness? And during the time of its greatest calamity, was there no good and faithful Israelite who suffered from the common misfortune?

These promises of temporal rewards therefore concerned only the body of the republic, not individuals. They concerned universal blessings [Col. 1093A] spread over the entire nation—common and public goods of which every Israelite, good or bad, was to partake, provided that the worship of God and observance of the law remained in force, that piety and religion were dominant, and that the majority—in a word, by their diligence and zeal—contributed to maintaining the good morals and practices that had been commanded. If this was so, what, then, was to be the reward of individuals who were obliged to serve God and fulfill all their duties, not only together with the multitude but despite the multitude, resisting the current of bad example in a time of corruption? Had God nothing to give them? One must either say so or admit that, in addition to the temporal goods promised to the nation, the hope of heaven and eternal life was offered to each Israelite.

Will Saint Augustine still be invoked here—he who is not content to affirm that God assigned [Col. 1093B] carnal and temporal rewards to the Jews, but adds that these goods alone were suited to the carnal and crude spirit of this people, and that spiritual and eternal goods were beyond its reach? *Notum esse jam debet carnali adhuc populo congruenter carnalia et temporalia praemia fuisse promissa* (“It ought now to be known that, for a people still carnal, carnal and temporal rewards were suitably promised”; *Against Adimantus*, ch. 18). That is to say, the Jews had to be led to reality through figures, and the nation had to be promised carnal and temporal goods so that individuals might aspire to spiritual and eternal goods. For God wished to prevent them, the holy doctor says, from perishing altogether: *ne penitus interirent* (“lest they perish completely”; *Tractates on John*, tract. 3, no. 19). Was it their temporal loss, rather than their eternal loss, that God wished to prevent, according to the holy doctor’s thought?

In any case, the question here is not what actually happened, but God’s design and intention. Let anyone therefore accumulate as many testimonies of Saint Augustine as he wishes [Col. 1093C] that state the fact—namely, that the Jews truly attached themselves only to carnal and temporal goods. He will have advanced no farther than if he claimed that God gave them idolatry as their end because they worshiped idols. The complete resolution of all this depends on the two following articles.

## III. The aids of grace that God granted under the law of Moses

After reading, at the beginning of chapter 11 of book I of *The Grace of the Savior* in Jansenius’s Augustine, these words: “The mystery of the divine plan is revealed, by which he gave the law, which produces nothing but transgression and wrath: *Aperitur mysterium divini consilii, quo legem tulit, quae non nisi praevaricationem et iram operatur*” (Jans., vol. III, book I, ch. 1, p. 43), I was not surprised to see that, in the title of chapter 7 of book III, Jansenius proposes to show that “the people who lived under the law had no sufficient grace to observe it or to fulfill any of its precepts: *Non affuisse hominibus sub lege viventibus gratiam sufficientem servandi legem vel ullum praeceptum ejus*” (ibid., p. 284).

But I was extremely surprised that he had entitled chapter 8 of the same book as follows: “The figurative and prophetic state of the Old Testament did not bring the Jews sufficient grace, but an impeding grace: *Status Veteris Testamenti figurativus et propheticus non afferebat Judaeis gratiam sufficientem, sed impedientem*” (p. 288). Let his disciples now come and tell us that grace is not needed in order to sin, for that is how they insult us when, from the existence of sin, we conclude the existence of sufficient grace—as though we assigned to this grace any other purpose than the power to refrain from sin. Here is their master admitting a grace [Col. 1094A] for the very act of sin, an effective grace of sin, which he calls “impeding.” What does he mean? Does he call “impeding grace” an impediment to grace? Have no doubt: by this means he subtly re-enters Calvin’s doctrine, which openly and formally makes God the author of sin. For perhaps you might think that Jansenius takes this impeding grace to be a grace of the devil. Not at all: he makes it proceed from the figurative and prophetic state in which God had placed the Jews, and consequently he wants it to be a pure grace of God.

This grace is not lacking among human beings today. Do not imagine that the figurative and prophetic state ceased after the coming of Jesus Christ, or that the world has been delivered from this unfortunate source of impeding graces. Jansenius places all sinners generally in a figurative and prophetic state. I have already warned you: under the new system every sinner is a Jew, and in the language of the party, “I have become a Jew” and “I have fallen into [Col. 1094B] mortal sin” mean the same thing. As for the term “impeding grace,” I do not know whether it has caught on; it does not appear in the public writings of the Jansenists. Nevertheless, I have no doubt that it is one of those subtle expressions whose explanation is reserved for those who show themselves worthy of initiation into their most secret mysteries.

One may say in two senses that grace was not found in the Old Testament. The first consists in teaching that the law of Moses did not, by itself or through its own power, give human beings the interior aids of grace necessary to observe it, and that it did not establish the Jews in a state to which the substance of these graces belonged. The second sense is to maintain that Jesus Christ, author of the New Testament, granted no share to those who lived under the law of Moses, or to the Jewish people, from the treasury of grace that he could even then pour out upon them as an anticipated fruit [Col. 1094C] of the merit of his death and passion. The first sense is the thought of Saint Paul and Saint Augustine; the second is the thought of Jansenius.

“All the heirs of the Old Testament,” he says, “were extremely far removed not only from invoking Jesus Christ and imploring the aid of his grace, but even from recognizing either him or it: *Effectum est ut quemadmodum ab ipso Christo, ita quoque ab ipsa gratia non solum invocanda, sed etiam agnoscenda longo intervallo omnes haeredes Veteris Testamenti distarent*” (“It came to pass that, just as all the heirs of the Old Testament were far removed from Christ himself, so they were also far removed from invoking and even recognizing grace”; Jans., vol. III, book III, ch. 8, p. 292). Such a grace, he says elsewhere, was diametrically opposed to the institution of the law and to God’s purpose: *Talis gratia lationi legis ac scopo Dei capitaliter repugnabat* (“Such a grace was fundamentally opposed to the giving of the law and to God’s purpose”; same book, ch. 15, p. 271). The reason he gives is that the Old Testament had not been established so that its promises and faithful observance would secure the Jews’ eternal salvation, or even serve as a proximate means [Col. 1094D] of attaining it: *Non ea de causa ut per hujusmodi Testamenti promissiones et observationem eorum salus aeterna in tuto collocaretur, vel etiam de propinquo curaretur* (“Not for the purpose that, through the promises of this Testament and their observance, their eternal salvation might be secured, or even provided for as a proximate matter”; ibid., p. 278).

I would hardly ask seriously whether Jansenius believed Scripture, but let us suppose for a moment that he did not. Could he have found a better way to turn it into ridicule? God reproaches the Israelites in these words: “How long will you refuse to observe my commandments and my law? *Usquequo non vultis custodire mandata mea et legem meam?*” (“How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my law?”; Exod. XVI, 28). Jansenius is their advocate and supplies them with this answer: “Until you yourself, Lord, wish us to observe them. But when you gave us commandments, your purpose was not that we should keep them; and our desire to keep them would be diametrically opposed, just as your grace is, [Col. 1095A] to the institution of the law and to the purpose you set for yourself in giving it to us.”

David blames his nation in this way: “They did not keep God’s Testament, and they did not wish to walk in the path he had marked out for them through his law: *Non custodierunt testamentum Dei, et in lege ejus noluerunt ambulare*” (“They did not keep God’s covenant, and they refused to walk in his law”; Ps. LXXVII, 10). Jansenius again suggests a convenient excuse for them: “We knew that this testament was not made to be kept; and if the path we followed is contrary to the law, it conforms to the law’s purpose. We did not desire what God did not desire. Why are we reproached and blamed, as though one supposed that we had grace, or as though one did not know that we do not have it, and that it is even contradictory that we should have it, ask for it, or know it?”

But God had removed every resource for justifying violators of the law and for Jansenius’s heresy through that famous passage of Isaiah: [Col. 1095B] “Men of Judah, be judges between me and my vineyard. What more ought I to have done for my vineyard than I have done? And will anyone accuse me of neglecting it because I expected it to produce good grapes, yet it produced only wild grapes: *Viri Juda, judicate inter me et vineam meam. Quid est quod ultra debui facere vineae meae, et non feci ei? An quod exspectavi ut faceret uvas, et fecit labruscas*?” (“Men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard. What more could I have done for my vineyard that I did not do? Why did I expect it to produce grapes, and did it produce wild grapes instead?”; Isa. V, 4). Here God acknowledges that he ought to have given the Jews the grace necessary for them, because he truly required and expected from them the fruit of good works, and he makes them judges themselves that he had not failed to give it to them.

Jansenius raises the difficulty drawn from this passage against his doctrine, and readily admits that it concerns grace, and that God not only acknowledges that he ought to have given it but even testifies that he did give it. You will doubtless conclude either that he yields to the truth or that he is greatly embarrassed; one or the other should be the case. But no: [Col. 1095C] he pities the poor judgment involved in making such an objection to him: “I am astonished,” he says, “at the judgment by which this passage is brought forward for this purpose: *Miror, quo judicio locus iste ad hoc propositum adducatur*” (vol. III, book III, ch. 17, p. 361).

We are quite foolish, we are, to persuade ourselves that this passage of Scripture concerns grace owed and given to the Jews to make possible the fulfillment of the law of Moses. What pitiable blindness! Jansenius thinks that God is speaking of the grace he ought to have given and did give to Adam to make possible the fulfillment of the commandment by which he had forbidden him to touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And what makes this seem evident to him? “Is it not clear,” he says, “that a grace that is owed can only be one appropriate to an innocent human being?” He brings us back, quite inappropriately, to his erroneous paradox concerning the nature of Adam’s grace. For since a thing can be owed in two ways—either absolutely and by virtue of a right properly so called, or as a consequence of a prior promise and free decision—is it not more evident that Isaiah’s passage should be explained as referring to a grace given to the Jews, rather than to Adam, than it is clear that the passage should be explained as referring to a grace owed absolutely and by virtue of a right properly so called?

Without pausing, then, [Col. 1095D] to destroy the error that led Jansenius to deny the gratuitous character of Adam’s grace, I shall demonstrate, as though it were necessary, that this passage has no connection with Adam, and that God had the Jews alone in view.

Will the explanation that God himself gives of his words not prevail over Jansenius’s commentary? Jansenius cites a very fine passage from Saint Augustine by which he proves that original sin can be reproached to human beings, and from this he [Col. 1096A] concludes that in Isaiah’s passage God reproaches the Jews with original sin. Thus, according to Jansenius, the vineyard is a figure of Adam, or of the human race in Adam, whom God had planted in the earthly paradise and who had received cultivation that was owed to him; and God, according to him, reproaches the Jews because he had expected this vineyard to produce good grapes, whereas it had produced only wild fruit. He could have made this reproach to all the nations of the world. God says, on the contrary: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and every man of the tribe of Judah is the shoot that he cultivated with delight; I expected judgment, and behold iniquity; justice, and behold a cry: *Vinea enim Domini exercituum domus Israel est, et vir Juda germen ejus delectabile; et exspectavi ut faceret judicium, et ecce iniquitas; et justitiam, et ecce clamor*” (“For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah his delightful plant; he expected justice, and behold iniquity; righteousness, and behold an outcry”; Isa. V, 7).

This text clearly relates to another passage in Jeremiah, [Col. 1096B] where God speaks to the Israelites as follows: “I planted you as a choice vine, composed entirely of genuine and sound shoots; how, then, have you degenerated in my hands into a wild vine: *Ego autem plantavi te vineam electam, omne semen verum; quomodo ergo conversa es mihi in pravum, vinea aliena*” (“I planted you as a choice vine, wholly genuine seed; how, then, have you turned before me into something corrupt, a foreign vine?”; Jer. II, 21)? In both passages, and everywhere else, it is the people of Israel who are represented under the figure of a vineyard planted by God’s hands in Palestine, not the human race in the earthly paradise. David says to the Lord: “You brought a vine out of Egypt, drove out the nations from that land, and planted it there: *Vineam de Aegypto transtulisti, ejecisti gentes et plantasti eam*” (“You transplanted a vine from Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it”; Ps. LXXIX, 9).

Finally, the very passage from Isaiah that we are discussing is employed by Jesus Christ in one of his parables, and applied exclusively to the Jews. “There was,” says the Savior, “a householder who planted a vineyard; after surrounding it with a hedge, he dug a winepress in it and built a tower there: *Homo erat paterfamilias qui plantavit vineam, et sepem circumdedit, et fodit in ea torcular, et aedificavit turrim* [“There was a householder who planted a vineyard, surrounded it with a hedge, dug a winepress in it, and built a tower”] (Matt. 21:33).” All these terms are borrowed from Isaiah, for the prophet begins as follows: “My beloved had a vineyard situated on a very fertile hill. After surrounding it with a hedge and removing its stones, he planted it with choice vines; he built a tower in its midst and dug a winepress in it: *Vinea facta est dilecto meo in cornu filio olei, et sepivit eam, et lapides elegit ex illa, et plantavit eam electam, et aedificavit turrim in medio ejus, et torcular exstruxit in ea* [“My beloved had a vineyard on a fertile hill; he hedged it, removed its stones, planted it with choice vines, built a tower in its midst, and constructed a winepress in it”] (Isa. 5:1).” The sole difference between Isaiah’s parable and that of Jesus Christ is that in Isaiah the vineyard represents the Jewish nation, whereas in the Gospel the vineyard represents the true Church that God had established within the Jewish nation, which itself is represented by the vine-dressers. But in both cases the cultivation of this vineyard is supposed to take place in Palestine, and not in the earthly paradise. You may perhaps think that I am dwelling on this too much; yet I have not done so at all.

I remember a Jansenist preacher who would sometimes introduce into his sermons God addressing Christians, and who, on such occasions, never failed to place in the Lord’s mouth a passage from Saint Augustine, with these words: “As my servant Saint Augustine says very well.”

I must accommodate myself to these gentlemen’s taste. They will not believe that Jansenius has been adequately refuted regarding his bad interpretation of Isaiah’s words unless I join the authority of Saint Augustine to that of God and Jesus Christ. “Lest anyone should suppose,” says the holy Doctor, “that he was speaking of a visible vineyard, he concluded in this way: ‘The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is his beloved young plant.’ Thus he was reproving that very vineyard from which he had expected grapes, but which produced thorns: *Ne quis putaret de vinea ista visibili dicere, sic conclusit: Vinea autem Domini Sabaoth domus Israel est, et homo Juda novelletum dilectum. Ergo ipsam vineam increpabat, quam exspectavit ut faceret uvam, fecit autem spinas* [“Lest anyone should think that he was speaking of this visible vineyard, he concluded thus: ‘The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is his beloved planting.’ He was therefore reproving that very vineyard, from which he expected grapes, but which produced thorns”] (Saint Augustine, on Psalm 35, no. 8).” If Saint Augustine had written this lest anyone should suppose that Isaiah’s text could be understood of Adam and of a vineyard planted in the earthly paradise, could he have fulfilled his purpose more effectively?

What shall I now say about that passage in the Acts of the Apostles where Saint Stephen attests that the Jews had always received sufficient grace? Yes, sufficient grace: making sport of the expression will not make the reality disappear from the sacred text, which states it plainly. For what is sufficient grace? It is a movement of the Holy Spirit that stirs us and offers us the assistance necessary for observing the law, and to which man resists. Now Saint Stephen reproached the Jews that their nation had always resisted this movement. “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you: *Dura cervice et incircumcisis cordibus et auribus, vos semper Spiritui sancto resistitis: sicut patres vestri, ita et vos* [“Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you”] (Acts 7:51).”

Jansenius made no mention of this passage; he relied on Calvin’s explanation, which his disciples would certainly not fail to consult. Here, then, is Calvin’s commentary: “Those who stubbornly reject the truths dictated by the Holy Spirit to the prophets are said to resist the Holy Spirit; for here the matter concerns not the secret revelations that God inspires inwardly in each person, but the outward ministry: *Resistere Spiritui dicuntur, qui eum in prophetis loquentem contumaciter rejiciunt. Neque enim de arcanis revelationibus hic agitur, quas Deus cuique intus inspirat, sed de externo ministerio* [“Those who obstinately reject him speaking in the prophets are said to resist the Spirit; for the question here is not of secret revelations which God inwardly inspires in each person, but of the external ministry”] (Calvin, Commentary on Acts, chapter 7).”

“But,” say our controversialists, writing against Calvin (Stapleton, vol. 3, *Antidoton Apostolicum* [“Apostolic Antidote”] on Acts, chapter 7), “is it not perfectly clear that Saint Stephen is speaking of the revelation and interior movement of the Holy Spirit, so that this needs no proof? Is it not the proper operation of the Holy Spirit to move us inwardly when the external preaching is heard? If the Holy Spirit does not touch the heart, does he effect anything in those who hear him? And if he effects nothing in them, can one say that they resist him or obey him? Therefore, someone who despises the speech of a prophet or preacher without experiencing any interior movement within himself does not resist the Holy Spirit; he resists the person whom he hears and the arguments that person advances. Neither that person nor those arguments is the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, if resisting the Holy Spirit is nothing other than resisting the external ministry and preaching, then one must also say that obeying the Holy Spirit is nothing other than obeying the external ministry and preaching. And would such an error accord with the hypothesis of Jansenius or Calvin? Finally, why does Saint Stephen call the Jews not only uncircumcised in ears but also uncircumcised in heart, if he intends to express merely their resistance to the words that struck their ears, and not the resistance they opposed to the grace that sought to insinuate itself into their hearts?”

Calvin and the Jansenists here abuse the language of Saint Augustine, who assumes almost everywhere that hearing with the heart, or in the heart, always means yielding and obeying grace. For although the holy Doctor ordinarily signifies by these words the touches of grace that are accepted and consented to, he nevertheless recognizes unconsidered movements of the heart that come from grace but are not admitted, as I shall show later.

Let us dwell only briefly on the authority of the other holy Fathers. I shall cite only two. Saint Cyril of Alexandria, explaining these words of Isaiah, “How has the faithful city become a prostitute: *Quomodo facta est meretrix civitas fidelis* (Isa. 1:21)?” says: “This city, which received so many opportunities for instruction, and indeed which abounded in spiritual aids, gradually gave itself over to defection and apostasy—formerly faithful and diligent in practicing works of justice: *Quae tot ad intelligendum occasiones accepit, imo vero quae spiritualibus adjumentis abundavit: in defectionem et apostasiam deflexit, olim fidelis et justitiae operatrix* [“She who received so many opportunities for understanding—indeed, who abounded in spiritual aids—declined into defection and apostasy, though formerly faithful and a doer of justice”] (Saint Cyril of Alexandria, *Commentary on Isaiah*, book 1, homily 1).”

This is how Saint Leo explains it: “God brought a remedy to the miseries of the human race—not as the result of a recently formed plan, nor through tardy compassion. Rather, from the beginning of the world he established one single and identical means of salvation. Thus the grace of God, by which the whole company of the saints who have ever existed has always been justified, did not begin but increased at the birth of Christ. And this mystery of great mercy, with which the whole world has been filled, was so powerful even in the figures that announced it that those who believed it when it was merely promised gained no less benefit from it than those who possessed it when it was finally bestowed: *Non enim novo consilio Deus rebus humanis nec sera miseratione consuluit; sed a constitutione unam eamdemque causam salutis instituit. Gratia autem Dei, qua semper est universitas justificata sanctorum, aucta est Christo nascente, non coepta. Et hoc magnae pietatis sacramentum, quo totus mundus impletus est, tam potens etiam in suis significationibus fuit, ut non minus adepti sint, qui illud credidere promissum, quam qui suscepere donatum* [“For God did not provide for human affairs by a new plan or by late compassion; from the foundation [of the world] he established one and the same cause of salvation. The grace of God, by which the whole company of saints has always been justified, was increased, not begun, at Christ’s birth. This sacrament of great mercy, with which the whole world has been filled, was so powerful even in its prefigurations that those who believed it promised gained no less than those who received it bestowed”] (Saint Leo, Sermon 5 on the Nativity).” How horrified Saint Leo would have been by the dogma of Jansenius, which treats the figurative and prophetic state as a grace that hinders—as an impediment to grace, and something worse!

But I am arguing against adversaries with whom I make no progress at all, while postponing a thorough examination of Saint Augustine’s view. Here is the sentence of their condemnation pronounced by this holy Doctor: “Who among the Catholics says what the Pelagians proclaim that we say—namely, that the Holy Spirit was not the helper of virtue in the Old Testament: *Quis enim catholicus dicat, quod nos dicere jactitant, Spiritum sanctum adjutorem virtutis in Veteri Testamento non fuisse* [“For what Catholic says what they boast that we say: that the Holy Spirit was not the helper of virtue in the Old Testament?”] (Saint Augustine, book 3, *To Boniface*, chapter 4, no. 6)?” It is the Jansenists who say this, and it is Saint Augustine himself who excludes them from the number of Catholics. It is Saint Augustine himself who recognizes sufficient grace in the Old Testament when he asserts that “the Jews, presuming upon themselves, rejected grace, and for that reason did not believe in Jesus Christ: *De se praesumentes gratiam repellebant, et propterea in Christum non credebant* [“Presuming upon themselves, they rejected grace and therefore did not believe in Christ”] (*On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 12, no. 24)”; and when he declares that, in addition to the grace of calling that was offered to Esau, God “would also have granted him the grace of willing and running, had he not become reprobate by despising the call: *Qui ei etiam velle et currere vocando praestaret, nisi vocatione contempta reprobus fieret* [“Who, by calling him, would also grant him to will and to run, unless, having despised the calling, he became reprobate”] (Book 1, *To Simplician*, question 2, no. 10).”

What more would you want to convince the most obstinate followers of Jansenius? Would you want Saint Augustine to have mentioned somewhat more often the sufficient grace granted to the Jews, so that the Jansenists could not evade the testimonies I have just cited by distinguishing between grace and external calling? But when Saint Augustine simply names grace and calling, does he not always mean inward grace and inward calling? Would he himself fall into the equivocation that he so strongly condemned in the Pelagians? What sense would there be in the two preceding passages if he were speaking of external grace and external calling? Would the Jews have believed in Jesus Christ if they had not rejected external grace? Would God have given Esau the grace of willing and running if he had not despised external calling? That is, would God have given the Jews and Esau inward grace if he had given it to them? The distinction is therefore miserable and untenable.

Nevertheless, there is no shortage of testimonies. And although on this occasion I resolve to follow Jansenius’s practice by setting out a long list of texts from Saint Augustine, you will see that I do not imitate him in setting out, as he ordinarily does, a long list of passages that prove nothing of what he claims. Will the reproach I make against him not be fully vindicated when I successfully employ the very passages he adduces against us, and show that the sufficient grace of the Jews is established precisely where he saw its proscription?

Before anything else, I must explain precisely one of the divisions of grace that Jansenius has taken pains to obscure. There is an imperfect, weak, initial, and remote grace; and there is another perfect, strong, complete, and proximate grace. The first is not limited to the unconsidered movements that, prior to any merit, the Holy Spirit causes in our understanding and will in order to awaken in us the beginning of a good will. This grace also includes the considered movements that follow, which cooperating grace helps us to form when we will the good that we are not yet able to do. The second grace is that which gives us sufficient strength to perform the good and fulfill the commandment.

“The grace of God,” says Saint Augustine, “is always good, and through it a man becomes of good will after having been of evil will: *Gratia vero Dei semper est bona et per hanc fit ut sit homo bonae voluntatis* [“But God’s grace is always good, and through it a man becomes of good will”] (Saint Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 15, no. 31).” This is the first grace, which I call imperfect, weak, initial, and remote. The holy Doctor continues and describes in this way the second grace, which I call perfect, strong, complete, and proximate: “Through it that good will, which has already begun to exist, is also increased and becomes so great that it can fulfill all the divine commandments that it wills, whenever it wills them, with great strength and perfection: *Per hanc fit ut ipsa bona voluntas, quae jam coepit esse, augeatur, et tam magna fiat, ut possit implere divina mandata quae voluerit, cum valde perfecteque voluerit* [“Through it that good will which has already begun is increased and becomes so great that it can fulfill the divine commandments it wills, whenever it wills them greatly and perfectly”] (Saint Augustine, same work).”

Initial grace draws from the man who faithfully responds to it the free acknowledgment of his own weakness, which the law demonstrates to him in two ways. First, when the law is promulgated: then knowledge of the sin forbidden by the law irritates concupiscence, and concupiscence harasses and tyrannizes reason, which finds itself too weak to resist it. The just as well as sinners experience this misery, which does not arise from any defect in the law but from the corruption of nature; and the Old Law has nothing distinctive in this respect, for the same effect belongs to the New Law. Second, the law demonstrates man’s weakness when he transgresses the law and consents to the disordered movements of concupiscence. Then the law is an occasion of death and sin, not in itself but through the fault of men.

It is now easy to prove that wherever Saint Augustine says that the law was given to convince man of his weakness and infirmity, he always presupposes an initial and remote grace that accompanies the law and is inseparable from it. For, according to Saint Augustine, either the law demonstrates man’s weakness through the irritation of concupiscence, which makes him feel what he lacks in order to fulfill the law; or that same law makes man feel his weakness through the transgression he commits, which humbles him and obliges him to recognize that he has relied too much on his own strength. In either case, the holy Doctor always presupposes that an initial and remote grace is inseparable from the law.

Why did the law come, so that sin might abound? “It was,” says the holy Doctor, “so that man, convicted and confounded by this means, might understand that he needed not merely a teacher to enlighten him, but God as helper—God who would direct his ways so that all iniquity might not dominate him, and who would heal him if he had recourse to divine mercy: *Ut eo modo convictus atque confusus videret non tantum doctorem sibi esse necessarium, sed adjutorem Deum, a quo ejus itinera dirigentur, ne dominetur ei omnis iniquitas, et confugiendo ad opem divinae misericordiae sanetur* [“So that, thus convicted and confounded, he might see that he needs not only a teacher but God as helper, by whom his paths will be directed, lest every iniquity rule him, and so that, by fleeing to the aid of divine mercy, he may be healed”] (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 6, no. 9, cited by Jansenius, vol. 3, book 1, chapter 11, p. 43).” God therefore intended—God willed—that man should understand his need for divine assistance; God intended—God willed—that man should have recourse to his divine mercy. What were the goal and effect of this intention and will of God, if not the grace that enabled man to understand his need and implore God’s mercy?

When, on Mount Sinai, God gave with such solemn display a law that he well knew would be violated, did he stop at the mere intention of crushing the Jews’ pride through the shame of their transgression? Did he not also set himself a further end, more glorious for him and more beneficial to them? Certainly, says Saint Augustine. For if he intended to humble his people through transgression, he intended that this humiliation would lead them to seek the grace of charity, which they could receive only in humiliation and without which they were utterly unable to fulfill the commandments of the law: “The law was therefore imposed upon a proud people so that, since it could not receive the grace of charity unless humbled, and since without this grace it could in no way fulfill the commandments of the law, it might be humbled by transgression and seek grace: *Superbienti ergo populo lex posita est, ut quoniam gratiam charitatis nisi humiliatus accipere non posset, et sine hac gratia nullo modo praecepta legis impleret, transgressione humiliaretur et quaereret gratiam* [“The law was therefore imposed on a proud people, so that, since it could not receive the grace of charity unless humbled and could in no way fulfill the commandments of the law without that grace, it might be humbled by transgression and seek grace”] (*Commentary on Galatians*, no. 24, cited by Jansenius, same work, p. 45).” By permitting sin, then, God was preparing his people to receive the grace of charity. He intended—he willed—that, in the state of sin, this people should seek grace. And certainly he did not intend—he did not will—that the Jews should seek the grace of charity through natural efforts and their own strength. Does it not follow that this intention and will of God preceded the Jews with an initial and remote grace that made it possible for them to seek a complete and proximate grace? But since God’s intention and will were that the Jews should seek the grace of charity, the figurative state of the Synagogue did not therefore contradict charity.

How did this reflection not occur to Jansenius? How did he fail to understand from the following words—which he cites just as accurately as the preceding ones—how, I ask, did he fail to understand that, according to Saint Augustine’s doctrine, the Son of God shed his blood to deliver the Jews, forgive their sins, reconcile them to God, and give them new life; and that, in order to procure all these spiritual benefits for transgressors of the law precisely during the time of the law, he had reserved for them, after their fall, an initial and remote grace that would oblige them to acknowledge their need for the Lord’s grace and mercy: “So that the mediator himself might deliver those who had already been compelled to confess that they needed the grace and mercy of the Lord; so that their sins might be forgiven them, and through him who shed his blood for them they might be reconciled to God in a new life: *Ut ipse mediator liberaret jam coactos confiteri, opus sibi esse gratiam et misericordiam Domini; ut sibi peccata dimitterentur, et in nova vita per eum, qui pro eis sanguinem fudit, reconciliarentur Deo* [“So that the mediator himself might deliver those already compelled to confess that they needed the grace and mercy of the Lord; so that their sins might be forgiven and, in a new life, they might be reconciled to God through him who shed his blood for them”] (Saint Augustine, same work).”

I read another passage from Saint Augustine in Jansenius, where it is said that the law made men transgressors so that, being humbled by this means, they might learn to belong to grace through faith, and so that they would no longer be subject to the law through guilt but joined to the law through righteousness: “It had also made them liable to transgression, so that, humbled by this means, they might learn to belong to grace through faith; so that they would no longer be subject to the law through guilt but joined to the law through righteousness: *Reos etiam praevaricationis effecerat, ut eo modo humiliati discerent, ad gratiam pertinere per fidem, ut jam non essent legi subditi per reatum, sed legi sociati per justitiam* [“It had also made them guilty of transgression, so that, thus humbled, they might learn through faith to belong to grace, and might no longer be subject to the law through guilt but joined to the law through righteousness”] (Book 19 against Faustus, chapter 7, cited by Jansenius, same work).” By denying that this purpose of the law was accompanied by any sufficient grace, Jansenius wants Saint Augustine’s words to be understood as follows: The law made them transgressors so that they might learn what they could not learn and become what they could not become. Is that not singular?

Let us pass to another passage. “The law,” says Saint Augustine, “was given to proud men who attributed everything to their own strength, so that, being unable to fulfill the law that had been given to them, they might be found transgressors, and, having become guilty under the law, might ask mercy from the author of the law: *Data est enim lex superbis hominibus et viribus suis totum tribuentibus, ut cum implere non possent legem datam, praevaricatores invenirentur, et facti rei sub lege, peterent misericordiam a legis conditore* [“For the law was given to proud men who attributed everything to their own powers, so that, unable to fulfill the law given, they might be found transgressors and, made guilty under the law, might ask mercy from the maker of the law”] (Book 2, *Proceedings with Felix*, chapter 11, cited by Jansenius).” That is, according to Jansenius, so that they might ask for mercy without being able to ask for it, or else so that they might pray without the grace of prayer. The former is absurd and the latter Pelagian. Consequently, this purpose of the law indicates a sufficient grace, at least for prayer—not a sufficient grace that is insufficient. The Jansenists have rightly mocked this, just as I have reason to mock an intention that would not be an intention, and a will that would not be a will, which Jansenius attributes to God when he claims that God permitted the Jews’ sins so that they might have recourse to grace and ask for mercy, without preceding them with any initial and remote grace.

I am speaking of truly sufficient grace and—will you believe it?—of grace that had an effect. Who says so? Saint Augustine. Where will one find such a testimony from the holy Doctor? Be astonished: Jansenius himself reports it immediately after the passage I have just discussed. Judge for yourself: “The manifestation of sin humbled the proud man; once humbled, the proud man became penitent; through repentance, mercy was obtained: *Apparens autem peccatum humiliavit superbum, humiliatus superbus factus est poenitens, de poenitentia impetrata est misericordia* [“But manifest sin humbled the proud man; humbled, the proud man became penitent; through penitence mercy was obtained”] (Saint Augustine, same work).” Complete and proximate grace came after initial and remote grace; efficacious grace after sufficient grace.

Let us continue. Elsewhere Saint Augustine says that God, in giving a law that he foresaw the Jews would not keep, “intended that their infirmity, which would not be healed but convicted by the law, should seek the remedy of grace: *Ut gratiae medicinam non sanata per legem, sed convicta infirmitas quaereret* [“So that infirmity, not healed by the law but convicted by it, might seek the medicine of grace”] (Letter 190, formerly 157, to Optatus, no. 7, cited by Jansenius, same work, p. 46).” God certainly did not intend that the Jews should confirm the opinion of the Semi-Pelagians by seeking grace without the assistance of another grace that preceded them. “The law,” Saint Augustine says elsewhere, “holds those who do not fulfill what is commanded guilty, so that, groaning under the weight of their sins and unable to fulfill what is commanded, it may eventually turn them toward the grace of the Liberator: *Non implentes jussa reos tenet, ut eos gementes et non valentes implere, quae jussa sunt, ad gratiam Liberatoris aliquando convertat* [“It holds guilty those who do not fulfill the commands, so that, groaning and unable to fulfill what is commanded, it may at last turn them to the grace of the Liberator”] (Book of 83 Questions, question 66, no. 1, cited by Jansenius, same work).” Notice these words: “So that the law may turn them toward grace.” The law alone? No; that would be Semi-Pelagian. Rather, the law joined with initial and remote grace.

All the passages I have examined thus far, in the order in which Jansenius set them out, express a sufficient grace which, being given to the Jews after their transgressions, disposed them to conversion. If one pays attention, most of them also show that such grace did not fail them before their fall, but that their pride and presumption most often rendered it useless. Without returning to any of the texts explained or indicated above, the passage now before us teaches that God’s established order “was for grace to come after the law, and to find man not only lying prostrate but also confessing and saying: ‘Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?’—so that the physician might come at the appropriate time: *Ut veniret gratia post legem, inveniret hominem, non solum jacentem, sed etiam confitentem et dicentem: Miser ego homo, quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus? ut opportune veniret medicus* [“So that grace might come after the law and find man not only lying prostrate but also confessing and saying, ‘Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?’ so that the physician might come at the fitting time”] (On Psalm 83, no. 10, cited by Jansenius, same work).”

I should very much like to ask the Jansenists which of the two—nature or grace—produces this sentiment and causes one to utter these words: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” If they answer that it is grace, I conclude from the preceding testimony that the law was accompanied by an initial and remote grace that prepared the way for a consummated and perfect grace. If they answer that it is nature, I conclude that they make Saint Augustine a Semi-Pelagian, since he declares that this sentiment and these words were a disposition for the coming of the divine physician. They will not deny that, in God, taking pity and showing mercy are the same thing as giving grace; at least, this is Saint Augustine’s constant language. Now, says the holy Doctor, precisely in commanding, the author of the law takes pity and shows mercy: “The law therefore commands; the giver of the law has mercy in that which the law commands: *Lex ergo jubet, dator legis miseretur in eo quod lex jubet* [“The law therefore commands; the giver of the law shows mercy in what the law commands”] (Treatise 3 on John, no. 2, cited by Jansenius, same work, p. 47).” The law is therefore never without some grace; it is inseparable from grace.

Indeed, throughout this chapter, in which Jansenius intended to establish and thoroughly support a principle from which he could then conclude that all grace of Jesus Christ was incompatible with the state of the Jews and of the Old Testament, he seems to have applied himself to assembling a multitude of passages from Saint Augustine most suited to destroying the consequences he expected to base upon that principle. Immediately after the preceding text, I read that those very people to whom the law was given implored the Liberator’s assistance after their fall: “Having become guilty under the law, they implored the assistance of the Liberator: *Facti rei sub lege imploraverunt Liberatoris auxilium* [“Made guilty under the law, they implored the Liberator’s aid”] (Saint Augustine, same work)”; and that the man bound under the law cries out to God before the physician comes: “He already cries out from his bondage: *Jam clamat de ligatura* [“He already cries out from his bondage”] (same work).” After this I see that the man who became a transgressor through the law is urged to recognize the necessity of grace: “Through the law you have become a transgressor; acknowledge grace: *Per legem factus es praevaricator, agnosce gratiam* [“Through the law you have become a transgressor; acknowledge grace”] (Sermon 26, formerly 11, *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 8, no. 9, cited by Jansenius, p. 47).” I then see not only that the purpose of the law was that the physician should be sought—“so that the physician might be sought: *ut medicus quaereretur* [‘so that the physician might be sought’]”—but that in fact the physician was sought—“the physician was sought: *quaesitus est medicus* [‘the physician was sought’]” (Sermon 156, formerly 13, *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 4, no. 4, cited by Jansenius, p. 48). These, says the saint elsewhere, repeating the same thought, are the hidden ways that God made known to Moses, through whom he gave the law: “These are the hidden ways that he made known to Moses, through whom he gave the law: *Istae sunt viae occultae, quas notas fecit Moysi, per quem legem dedit* [“These are the hidden ways which he made known to Moses, through whom he gave the law”] (Exposition on Psalm 102, no. 15, cited by Jansenius, p. 48).”

Readers of Saint Augustine who have not reflected sufficiently on his manner of thinking and speaking concerning the doctrine of the perfection of righteousness will imagine that this grace—which gives the awareness of the misery and sickness of sin, awakens the desire for healing, and causes one to implore and seek the physician’s assistance; which, according to Saint Augustine, is always offered together with the law; and which, as we see in the passages I have just cited, is sometimes merely sufficient and at other times efficacious—these readers, I say, will imagine that the holy Doctor assumes that this grace almost never arrives except after the fall into formal sin and the consent given to temptation, by which man has become properly guilty.

Jansenius supplies a testimony that seems expressly designed to disabuse them of this notion. “The author of the Psalms teaches,” says Saint Augustine, “that the law was given to convict sinners and dispose them to receive grace by invoking the divine physician. Thus was convicted the man whom the Apostle represents in his own person when he says: ‘Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?’ *Docet datam legem, ut convincerentur peccatores, et ad gratiam accipiendam medicum invocarent. Unde ille convictus est, quem in se transfigurat Apostolus dicens: Infelix ego homo, quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus* [“He teaches that the law was given so that sinners might be convicted and invoke the physician in order to receive grace. Thus was convicted the man whom the Apostle figures in himself, saying: ‘Unhappy man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?’”] (Jansenius, same work, p. 49).” Of what kind of sin does God’s grace, always joined to the law, here produce conviction? Of the unconsidered disorder of concupiscence; of the sin opposed to the perfection of righteousness; of material sin, from which even the greatest saints are not exempt. This testimony therefore demonstrates that the law is always accompanied by a grace that precedes the fall, and that the proud resist—a grace by which, Saint Augustine says, they can be humbled only through genuine and serious faults.

I believe you are weary of passages that all say almost the same thing. But you are no doubt astonished that Jansenius did not notice that all these texts attached a genuine grace to the law and assured it to those who received the law. Cease to be astonished: he noticed it very well; he clearly perceived it. For all these texts express God’s intention to make the men to whom he gave his law recognize the necessity of grace, to awaken desire for it in their hearts, and to engage them to seek that grace.

Jansenius understood that such an intention in God was a sincere will to give grace together with the law, and that it was a present and real offer of initial and remote grace. He reflected on the words of the holy Doctor, which signify that this intention of God often had its effect, and that the men who had received the law, immediately feeling their weakness or finally humbled by the shame of their sins, confessed their need for God’s assistance, implored it, and even obtained it: they were converted and justified. “The proud man, once humbled, became penitent; through repentance, mercy was obtained: *Humiliatus superbus factus est poenitens, de poenitentia impetrata est misericordia* [“Humbled, the proud man became penitent; through penitence mercy was obtained”] (Book 2, *Proceedings with Felix*, chapter 11, cited by Jansenius, same work, p. 46).”

I increase your astonishment rather than dispel it. You recall these words of Jansenius: “The heirs of the Old Testament were extremely far removed—not only from invoking Jesus Christ and imploring the assistance of his grace, but even from recognizing either one or the other: *Effectum est ut quemadmodum ab ipso Christo, ita quoque ab ipsa gratia non solum invocanda, sed etiam agnoscenda longo intervallo omnes haeredes Veteris Testamenti distarent* [“It came about that all the heirs of the Old Testament were far removed, not only from the grace that was to be invoked, but also from the grace that was to be recognized, just as they were from Christ himself”] (Jansenius, vol. 3, book 3, chapter 8, p. 292).” You see clearly that Jansenius regards as a grace the ability to recognize grace and invoke its assistance; your difficulty is to reconcile this with his own position. On the one hand, in order to exclude all grace from the Old Testament, he denies it every ability to recognize and implore the assistance of grace. On the other hand, he sets out a long list of passages from Saint Augustine proving that God, in giving the law to men through the ministry of Moses, intended them to recognize his grace and implore its assistance; that together with the law he gave them an initial and remote grace, which often had its effect and led them to a proximate and complete grace. Yet, in reality, Jansenius does not contradict himself.

You must be initiated into the secret mystery of his thoughts. This is what he attributes to the holy Doctor: The Jews received the law so that Christians might receive grace. The Jews made vain efforts to fulfill the law of Moses so that Christians might make fruitful efforts to fulfill the law of Jesus Christ. The law irritated the Jews’ concupiscence so that Christians might feel their own weakness and implore the assistance of grace, which the Jews had needed. The Jews were proud so that Christians might become humble. The Jews were sick so that Christians might be healed. The Jews fell so that Christians might rise again.

What extravagance! you will say. Does Saint Augustine not say of these same men that the law was given to them, that it aroused their concupiscence, that they felt their weakness before or after their fall, that they were humbled, that they implored the help of grace and the remedy for the illnesses of their souls, that they obtained this help and remedy, that they were healed, that they rose again from their falls, and that they obtained mercy? “He says this of the same men,” Jansenius will reply to you—that is, of the same human race—and what will you have to answer him? Does he not have an admirable reason for saying that God’s plan was most salutary for reforming the Jewish people—that is, the human race, of which the Jewish people formed a part—[Col. 1104C] although the reform did not take place in the Jewish people but only in the Christian people? *Consilium Dei reformando Judaeorum populo saluberrimum* (“God’s plan for reforming the Jewish people was most salutary”) (Jans., vol. III, book I, chapter 11, p. 43).

Jansenius believes that he is speaking the language of Saint Augustine; and the great art of this false interpreter of the holy doctor is to explain as referring to the condition of the Jews everything that the saint says about the law—for example, these words: “For the law commanded but did not accomplish, because where grace was absent, the flesh resisted with an unconquerable resistance”: *Lex enim jubebat et non implebat, quia caro, ubi non erat gratia, invictissime resistebat* (Saint Augustine, Sermon 55, formerly 6, *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 7, no. 7). Here and in a thousand other similar passages, the subject is the law’s own power, considered apart from grace; whereas here the question concerns the Jews who received the law. There is an extreme difference between these two propositions: “The law did not help,” and “Those who lived under the law were without help.” The first is Saint Augustine’s; the second is Jansenius’s, who gives us a frightful portrait of the Synagogue precisely as Synagogue. I shall explain this.

[Col. 1104D]

## IV. The condition of the Synagogue considered as such and precisely as Synagogue

Saint Augustine distinguishes two kinds of persons among the Hebrew people. Some were earthly and carnal Jews, who confined their outlook and desires to the temporal goods that God had promised them, and who did not perceive that eternal goods were represented and announced in those temporal goods. Others were the good Israelites, or spiritual Jews, who understood the mysteries represented in all the practices and ceremonies of their religion and who attached themselves to that understanding (Saint Augustine, book XV *Against Faustus*, chapter 2).

If we accept Jansenius and his disciples, [Col. 1105A] the latter kind of Jews—that is, the saints and all the devout men of the Old Testament—do not belong to the Old Testament. For one of the principal dogmas of the Jansenists is that there has never been but one single Church, namely, the Christian Church, which, they maintain, began with the world and has existed throughout all ages. “Nothing is so extensive,” they say, “as the Church of God, since all the elect and the righteous of every age compose it.” They have learned and retained the lesson of their master, who gives one of his chapters this title: “The condition of the Old Testament, as such, was not a condition of righteousness and salvation, but rather of sin and death: *Status Veteris Testamenti, ut talis, non erat justitiae et salutis, sed potius peccati et mortis*” (Jans., vol. III, book III, chapter 9, p. 294). Elsewhere he writes as follows: “The Synagogue, considered as Synagogue, was nothing other than a crowd of an earthly people and an assembly of carnal men occupied exclusively with earthly and carnal things [Col. 1105B] and worshiping the one God only for the sake of those things: *Synagoga, considerata ut Synagoga, non aliud erat quam terreni populi turba hominumque carnalium congregatio solis terrenis incubantium et propter illa colentium solum Deum*” (ibid., chapter 6, p. 276). This doctrine—which I dare call impious and horrible—is falsely attributed to Saint Augustine, and an attempt is made to support it by his authority through an equivocation of which I have already warned you.

Indeed, there are two ways of understanding the expression “to belong to the Old Testament” or “to be under the law.” The first is to adhere to the meaning of Saint Paul when he says: “I testify again to every man who is circumcised that he is bound to observe the whole law”: *Testificor autem rursus omni homini circumcidenti se, quoniam debitor est universae legis faciendae* (Galatians 5:3). According to this notion—which is the most natural and is that of Holy Scripture—to belong to the law and to be under the law means to have incurred [Col. 1105C] the obligation of keeping the law by virtue of the covenant and alliance that God made with the Israelites. All the children of Jacob, the holiest patriarchs, and the prophets belonged in this way to the law and were under the law. For if Saint Paul says of all of them and of himself: “Before faith came, we were under the law, shut up under its guard, awaiting the faith that was to be revealed”: *Prius autem quam veniret fides, sub lege custodiebamur conclusi in eam fidem quae revelanda erat* (Galatians 3:23), does he not elsewhere include all the Israelites, both good and bad, by declaring that “whatever the law says, it says to those who are under the law”: *Quoniam quaecunque lex loquitur, iis qui in lege sunt loquitur* (Romans 3:19)?

The second way of understanding the expression “to belong to the law” and “to be under the law” is to follow the meaning Saint Augustine gave it. He uses it to signify that one does not obey the law and violates it. [Col. 1105D]

“It seems to me,” he says, “that it is a great question what it means to be under the law, when the Apostle takes this expression in a bad sense and censures the thing it designates: *Magna mihi videtur quaestio quid sit esse sub lege, sic quemadmodum Apostolus culpat*” (Saint Augustine, *Letter to Jerome* 82, formerly 19, chapter 2, no. 20). He therefore recognizes another meaning of this term, according to which the Apostle takes it in a good sense and does not censure the thing designated. “For I do not think,” he continues, “that the Apostle is speaking there of circumcision, or of those sacrifices that were formerly performed by the fathers but are not performed by Christians now, or of other practices of this kind: *Neque enim hoc eum propter circumcisionem arbitror dicere, aut illa sacrificia, quae tunc facta a patribus, nunc a christianis non fiunt, et caetera hujusmodi*” (Saint Augustine, ibid.).

This notion, according to which “to belong to the law” and “to be under the law” is understood in a good sense, therefore signifies the obligation to fulfill the law of Moses—to be [Col. 1106A] circumcised, to offer sacrifices, and to observe all the ceremonies and observances prescribed by Leviticus.

Saint Augustine does not deny this notion; rather, he presupposes it. He then declares that the meaning he adopts concerns only the law’s command, “You shall not covet,” which Christians themselves must observe and which the preaching of the Gospel has brought into the clearest light: “But it is precisely what the law says, ‘You shall not covet,’ which we certainly confess that Christians must observe and which is proclaimed most fully in the light of the Gospel: *Sed hoc ipsum quod lex dicit, Non concupisces, quod fatemur certe christianos debere observare, atque evangelica maxime illustratione praedicari*” (ibid.).

It is not simply being under the law and belonging to the law, but being under the law and belonging to the law because of one’s fault and as a guilty person, that is the idea Saint Augustine forms—and, according to him, Saint Paul forms in certain passages. The holy doctor applies it to all people, Jews and Christians alike, whom the law’s command “You shall not covet” makes guilty because they do not fulfill it. Ignorant of the necessity of God’s grace, which they need [Col. 1106B] in order to obey the commandments, they abandon themselves to an arrogant presumption of their own strength: “These, therefore, he says are damnably under the law: the law makes them guilty because they do not fulfill it, while, by failing to understand the benefit of grace, they presume to perform God’s commandments as though by their own strength, with proud elation: *Hos ergo damnabiliter dicit esse sub lege; quos reos facit lex, non implentes legem, dum non intelligendo gratiae beneficium, ad facienda Dei praecepta quasi de suis viribus superba elatione praesumunt*” (ibid.).

But if there are two ways of belonging to the Old Testament and being under the law, there are also two ways of belonging to the New Testament and not being under the law. The first is the same as being freed from the yoke of the law of Moses with respect to its observances, because one is emancipated from them by baptism, in which one undertakes the obligation of submitting to the sole law of the New Testament—the law that Jesus Christ promulgated and the apostles proclaimed. The second way of belonging to the New Testament and not being under the law is to correspond to the grace of Jesus Christ, which has preceded human beings in every age in order [Col. 1106C] to help them observe faithfully and religiously the divine law, whatever that law may be, including the law of Moses itself.

It is only in this latter sense that, speaking the language of Saint Augustine, Moses and the other holy persons who lived before the Savior’s coming belonged to the Gospel and were not under the law. They were not under the law—that is, they did not violate it and did not incur the penalties decreed by it. The law did not hold them beneath it as guilty persons over whom it had the right to exercise its coercive and punitive power. They belonged to the Gospel—that is, grace, which preceded them and helped them in their actions, and the kingdom of heaven, which they merited by their good works, were the substance and proper possession of the Gospel. As participants in the blessings that the promised Messiah had been drawing upon the human race since the beginning of the world, they were made children of the promise and destined to possess the kingdom of heaven, which the author of the New Testament was to open [Col. 1106D] by his passion and death. In the hidden counsel of God, they were reckoned heirs of the New Testament: “They were made children of the promise; they were appointed heirs of the New Testament in the secret judgment of God: *Filii promissionis effecti sunt, Novi Testamenti haeredes in occulto Dei judicio deputati sunt*” (Saint Augustine, *On the Proceedings against Pelagius*, chapter 5, no. 14).

But did they therefore cease to belong to the Old Testament in the true, proper, exact, and rigorous sense? Did they belong to it only because they lived in the time of Moses? Did they not belong to it especially and principally because they were obliged to keep that law? Did their holiness not consist in walking, without reproach, in the way of all the commandments and laws that the Lord had imposed upon his people, as is said of Zechariah and Elizabeth (Luke 1:6)? Did it not consist not only in going to Jerusalem at all the times appointed by the law, to worship the Lord God of Israel in his temple, [Col. 1107A] but also in faithfully offering all the first fruits and tithes, and every three years distributing the whole tithe of their income to proselytes and foreigners, as is written of Tobit (Tobit 1:6)? Did it not consist in being ready to give their lives and endure the cruellest torments rather than violate the least of the legal ordinances, as did the holy elder Eleazar and the Maccabean youths (2 Maccabees 6–7)?

When Saint Augustine says that these saints were Christians in reality, and that they lacked only the name, what does he mean? “The same faith was in those who formerly were Christians not yet in name but in reality, and in those who are not only Christians but are also called Christians: *Eadem igitur fides et in illis qui nondum nomine, sed re ipsa fuerunt antea Christiani, et in istis qui non solum sunt, verum etiam vocantur*” (*Book III to Boniface*, chapter 4, no. 11). Does he mean that they placed no more value than we now do on circumcision, purifications, abstinences, the choice of foods, new moons, and the other Jewish solemnities? Does he mean that they were baptized and confirmed, that they confessed their sins to their [Col. 1107B] priests as we do, and that they sanctified Sunday instead of the Sabbath? That is false and absurd. He means only that the living water of grace, whose source is in Christianity, flowed over them and made them worthy of eternal life, whose price is in Christianity. That is why, Saint Paul says, all those people whose faith received such authentic testimony did not receive, during the time of the Old Testament, what had been promised. God, in his providence, had arranged something better for us, so that they might not reach the consummation of happiness and glory without us (Hebrews 11:39).

What an abuse it is to use this doctrine of Saint Augustine to disparage, without any respect for divine institution, a state and a society whose plan God had formed, whose organization he had regulated, and whose external government he had arranged, both with regard to religion and to civil order! The Synagogue, precisely as Synagogue, included all those who were obliged to practice [Col. 1107C] the law of Moses. It consisted not only of carnal Jews, who possessed only the outward forms and appearances of the worship and service of God, but also of true worshipers who, fulfilling exactly all the duties prescribed by the law, were inwardly animated by a spirit of piety approaching evangelical purity. For the Synagogue, precisely as Synagogue, must be considered independently of the holiness or impiety of the subjects who were found within it. It has reference only to the nature and quality of the covenant that God made with the Israelites. It seems to me that the proper definition is this: it was the multitude or community of the children of Israel insofar as they were bound to keep the laws and conditions of the covenant they had entered into with God through the ministry of Moses.

With all this established, I demonstrate that the Old Testament, as such, was not, as Jansenius asserts, a condition of sin and death, but rather a condition of life and salvation; [Col. 1107D] that the Synagogue, as Synagogue, was good in itself and by its nature, and that it was worthy of God. For the Old Testament, as such, and the Synagogue, as Synagogue, mean the Old Testament and the Synagogue as having God for their author, and insofar as the idea of that condition and that society conforms to the plan God had and the end he intended in instituting it. This is clear; otherwise one must say that God is not the author of the Old Testament, or one must admit that the Old Testament and the Synagogue cannot be considered according to their precise and formal idea without expressly regarding them as having God for their author and insofar as this idea conforms to the plan God had and the end he intended in instituting that condition.

Certainly, man as man is considered according to the essential relation he bears to his author, and [Col. 1108A] he is taken as a work entirely conformable to the plan God had and the end he intended in creating man. Can one maintain, then, that the Old Testament was a condition of sin and death? Can one deny that it was a condition of righteousness and salvation, and that the Synagogue was good and worthy of God, when one represents them as having God for their author and as a condition conforming to the plan God had and the end he intended in instituting it?

Will our adversaries, like the Manichaeans, deny that God is the author of the Old Testament? In any case, here is a passage from Saint Augustine that proves it: “God therefore made the Old Testament, because it pleased God, until the fullness of time, to veil the heavenly promises beneath the veil of earthly promises that seemed to be proposed as rewards, and to engrave upon tables of stone a wholly spiritual law in order to give it to a people greedy for earthly goods and therefore [Col. 1108B] hard of heart: *Vetus igitur Testamentum Deus condidit, quia Deo placuit usque ad plenitudinem temporis promissis terrenis tanquam in praemio constitutis promissa velare coelestia, et populo terrenis bonis inhianti, ac propterea aurum cor habenti, quamvis spiritalem, tamen in tabulis lapideis legem dare*” (Saint Augustine, *Book III to Boniface*, chapter 4, §10).

Moreover, did the Old Testament, as such, and the Synagogue, as Synagogue, not have Jesus Christ as their head? Were they not the Church of God? “Jesus Christ,” says Saint Ambrose, “was the head of the ancient Synagogue, which Moses founded and established: *Christus erat caput veteris Synagogae, quam Moyses fundavit et condidit*” (Saint Ambrose, *Exposition on Psalm 43*, no. 62). Saint Augustine calls it the assembly of the people of God, and he adds that “although one properly speaks [Col. 1108C] of the Synagogue of the Jews and the Church of the Christians, nevertheless we also find that the former is called the Church: *Quamvis enim proprie dicatur Synagoga Judaeorum, Ecclesia vero Christianorum . . . , tamen et illam dictam invenimus, Ecclesiam*” (Saint Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 77*, no. 3). The same argument returns: Is a society whose head is Jesus Christ and which is the Church of God a condition of sin and death? Is it not rather a condition of righteousness and salvation? Is it not essentially good, worthy of Jesus Christ, and worthy of God?

Turn through the Holy Scriptures and survey the works of the holy Fathers: how many testimonies will you not find in which the Hebrews, Israelites, and Jews, by reason of the nature and constitution of their commonwealth, are called a holy nation and the people of God! What titles for a condition of sin and death, for a society of men attached exclusively to the earth and, by profession and status, banishing thoughts of heaven!

It does Jansenius no good to accumulate countless texts from Saint Augustine proving that most Jews were sinful and carnal and [Col. 1108D] that they had neither faith nor hope concerning spiritual and eternal goods. It is contrary to all reason and impious for him and his followers to make the guilt and shame of the greater part of the nation fall upon the Synagogue, as Synagogue—which was the work of God—just as it would be unreasonable and impious to attribute to the Christian Church the vices and disorders that reign among Christians today.

There are theologians who reply, concerning some of Saint Augustine’s most difficult passages, that he exaggerated and spoke too harshly when, for example, he said that the common opinion of the Synagogue was that God gave it, as a magnificent reward, the riches and happiness of this world, and that he had nothing better with which he could reward those who loved and zealously [Col. 1109A] served him: “He thought that God considered this a great gift and had nothing better to give to those who loved and served him: *Putavit hoc pro magno dare Deum, nec habere melius quod dare posset diligentibus se et servientibus sibi*” (Saint Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 72*, no. 6). “Is it believable,” these theologians say, “that most Israelites were in so gross and absurd an error that it could not even be attributed to the pagans?”

Whatever the case may be, it remains entirely certain that the holy doctor is not considering the Synagogue here precisely as Synagogue, but rather as composed of men who were carnal through their own fault and who held opinions unworthy of God—opinions inspired by the perversity of their hearts, not by any defect in their law or religion. Jansenius therefore wrongly imputes a monstrous heresy to so great and learned a defender of the faith through the faithless commentary he gives on the holy doctor’s texts. Saint Augustine’s thought is as different from the meaning Jansenius assigns to it as day is from night.

To say that most Jews—even those who lacked [Col. 1109B] none of the outward forms of piety—were in such a frame of mind that they expected from God only earthly goods and worldly advantages is not, it seems to me, to say that the Synagogue, as Synagogue, and consequently as the work of God, was an assembly of carnal men. Nor is it to say that the particular purpose of the law of Moses was to promise everything that sustains and nourishes earthly greed as the reward of actions of which that greed is the principle.

Nor should one say with Jansenius (vol. III, book III, chapter 6, p. 280) that Saint Augustine manifestly conveys the same thing in these words: “For that Old Testament, having earthly promises, seems to urge that God not be worshiped gratuitously, but that he is loved because he gives something on earth: [Col. 1109C] *Illud enim Vetus Testamentum habens promissa terrena, hoc videtur suadere, ne gratis colatur Deus, sed quia aliquid dat in terra ideo diligitur*” (Saint Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 79*, no. 14). The word *videtur* (“seems”) warns us not to confuse the law with the abuse made of it, or the spirit of the law with the carnal understanding of the letter. “For the law,” says the holy doctor, “is spiritual; it does not compel men to understand it carnally. Rather, the fault lies with those who understand carnally even what they have received and who also hand down many things of their own, dissolving, as the Lord says, the commandment of God for the sake of their traditions: *Lex enim spiritualis est, nec carnaliter se cogit intelligi: sed illorum vitium est qui et illa quae acceperunt carnaliter sentiunt, et multa etiam sua tradiderunt, dissolventes, sicut Dominus dicit, mandatum Dei propter traditiones suas*” (*Exposition on Galatians*, no. 7).

I shall conclude this article by examining a passage of Saint Augustine on which Jansenius relies heavily: “He who submits to the law of God in order to receive earthly goods from him,” [Col. 1109D] says the holy doctor, “is an heir of the Old Testament: *Qui propter illa terrena suscipit legem Dei, ipse est haeres Veteris Testamenti*” (*On the Proceedings against Pelagius*, chapter 5, no. 14). “The whole hope of the Jews, all their charity toward God, and all the worship they offered him were therefore carnal and consequently vicious,” the innovators conclude; “and this did not arise from abuse but from the very nature of the Old Testament.”

If they took the trouble to clarify their ideas somewhat, they would see that there are three different ways of loving and serving God with a view to temporal rewards.

The first is to love and serve him with the resolution not to love or serve him if he refused temporal goods or took them away. This love is vicious and blameworthy. But far from being proper to the ancient law, it was expressly forbidden and condemned by that law, since the law commanded that God be loved above all things.

[Col. 1110A]

The second way of loving and serving God with a view to earthly rewards excludes the perverse disposition I have just described. It consists merely in abstracting from whatever feelings one might have and giving no thought at all to the state of mind and heart in which one would find oneself if those who love and serve God had no temporal rewards to expect from him. This love is imperfect because it is not sufficient for righteousness. Nevertheless, since it is not opposed to righteousness but rather prepares and leads toward it, it is not vicious: it turns one away from sin and inclines one to the observance of several commandments. The ancient law did not command this love; it merely provided an occasion for it by proposing temporal rewards.

The third way of loving and serving God from this motive is to ask and hope to receive from his generosity the goods and advantages of this world as an imperfect and transitory reward for human [Col. 1110B] piety, and as a simple sign of God’s benevolence—while loving and serving God for his own sake, preferring him without hesitation to all created goods. This places the soul in a disposition entirely like that of the holy man Job when he said: “God gave me these goods; God has taken them away; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). Now the law of Moses expressly commanded this disposition in the first words of the Decalogue: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength: *Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo et ex tota anima tua et ex tota fortitudine tua*” (Deuteronomy 6:5).

Do you hear the Jansenists saying that the precept of the love of God was given to the Jews so that Christians alone might observe it? Is this possible? Was the grace necessary to fulfill the precept of the love of God therefore also promised to the Jews so that Christians alone might obtain it? And the [Col. 1110C] Jews often asked God for this same grace so that he might grant it only to Christians?
