Do these words of Deuteronomy not contain a promise that God makes to the Hebrew people, to give them the grace necessary to fulfill the precept of the love of God? “The Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you may love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul: *Circumcidet Dominus Deus tuus cor tuum et cor seminis tui, ut diligas Dominum Deum tuum in toto corde tuo et in tota anima tua*” (Deuteronomy 30:6). Does a psalm—which can be shown to have been sung in the temple by the whole Hebrew people at least once each year, and which, like all the other psalms, was a form of prayer for the use of the Israelites—not begin as follows: “My God, who are my strength, I shall love you! *Diligam te, Domine, fortitudo mea*” (Psalm 17:1)?

[Col. 1110D]

They prayed, and we have obtained; they were promised, and we have received; they were commanded, and we have obeyed. For them, this prayer was a sin, this promise was a deception, and this precept was a trap: such is the Jansenist doctrine.

But why, then, does Saint Augustine call him who submits to the law of God with a view to receiving earthly goods an heir of the Old Testament? Because Saint Augustine’s custom is to understand the Old Testament according to what is proper to it and not shared with the New Testament. He could do this following the example of Saint Paul, and he had to do so because of the Pelagians, as I showed above. To keep my promise concerning the four controversies that I promised to develop for you, I have only to give you a parallel between Manichaeism and Jansenism with regard to the ancient law.

## V. Parallel between Manichaeism and Jansenism with regard to the ancient law

[Col. 1111A]

“The pivot,” as Jansenius expresses it, “around which the will of those who lived under the law of Moses turned was not faith working through a true love of God. Rather, as Saint Augustine taught more than once”—what an imposture!—“it was earthly greed, to which the law, by its very purpose, promised everything that sustains and nourishes it as the reward of the actions of which it is the principle: *Cardinem enim voluntatis rapiebat, non fide, quae per veram Dei dilectionem operatur, sed, ut non semel Augustinus docet, terrena cupiditas, cujus fomentum ac praemium lex illa ex professo promittebat*” (Jans., vol. III, chapter 6, at the end, p. 283).

And what are we to think of this earthly greed? Listen again to Jansenius: “To love God for carnal goods is not gratuitous love but mercenary love, and therefore impure, carnal, [Col. 1111B] and vicious: *Propter carnalia diligere Deum, non gratuitus, sed mercenarius amor est, ideoque impurus, carnalis, vitiosus*” (ibid., p. 279). Elsewhere, the subject and title of one of his chapters is this: “The affection of love cannot, without sin, rest upon a creature: *Affectus amoris non potest sine peccato haerere in creatura*” (Jans., vol. II, book II, *On the State of Fallen Nature*, chapter 12, p. 347).

Since, then, according to this doctrine of Jansenius, the law of Moses, by its very purpose, aroused and nourished earthly greed by presenting it with attractions and enticements and by offering it rewards; since, according to the same author’s principles, love of earthly or carnal things is vicious and impure; and since, in a word, affection for any created thing is a sin, it follows evidently that the law of Moses, by its very purpose, led toward sin. It follows further that the more a Jew was attached to his religion, the more careful he was to conform to the spirit and intention of his law, and the more ardently, in observing it, [Col. 1111C] he desired earthly and carnal things—and the more sins he committed.

Jansenius himself acknowledges and draws this conclusion. Fearing that it might escape his reader, he declares that “everything we have said about the carnal spirit of the children of the Old Testament is not to be understood of wicked Israelites, but rather of those who seemed to be the better sort: *Nec vero ista omnia, quae carnalibus istis animis filiorum Veteris Testamenti diximus, de improbis intelligenda sunt, sed potius de illis qui probiores esse viderentur*” (Jans., vol. III, book III, chapter 6, p. 279). Along with this, recall what Jansenius says about God’s purpose and design in establishing the law of Moses. It was, he asserts, the multiplication and abundance of sins that God intended as his goal in instituting it.

There is therefore not the slightest doubt that Manichaeans and Jansenists agree in thinking that the law of Moses is [Col. 1111D] evil in itself and by its nature, and that it was instituted with an evil design and evil intention. If they differ on one point—namely, that the Manichaeans would have an evil god, while the Jansenists have the good and true God, as the author of this law—the Jansenists’ cause is no better for that.

Will you demand proof of what I am asserting? First, does the agreement and concurrence of Jansenius and Manes in teaching that the law of Moses is evil in itself and by its nature not seem as clear as day? Can one give a more precise and less equivocal notion of a law evil in itself and by its nature than by saying that it is specifically and deliberately intended to nourish and reward a vicious greed? That the Old Testament, as such—that is, [Col. 1112A] in itself and by its nature—is a condition of sin and death? That the Synagogue, as Synagogue—that is, by its nature and institution—is an assembly of carnal men? Would Manes not have been highly pleased with this? Would any of the heresiarchs who despised or condemned the ancient law have asked for anything more? What did they find to criticize in it, if not that it commanded crime and nourished greed? Yet this is what Jansenius says; therefore, he teaches that the law of Moses is evil in itself and by its nature.

Secondly, do Jansenius and Manes not both agree that the law of Moses was established with an evil purpose and evil intention? For ask Jansenius whether God’s purpose in giving the law was not that sins should multiply and become abundant. Is it not for this reason that he maintains that grace was diametrically opposed to the institution of the law and to the end that God proposed to himself in establishing it? Invincible instigation to sin is diametrically opposed to grace; therefore the law of Moses is diametrically opposed to grace. Such is Jansenius’s reasoning (vol. III, book III, chapter 5, p. 271). He therefore believes, with Manes, that the author of the law directly and formally willed sin in making the law, and consequently that the law was made with an evil purpose and evil intention.

Thirdly, is it not more tolerable to say that an evil god is the author of sin and crime than to assert this of the good God? Is it not more insane to make the true and infinitely holy God work to extend and increase the reign of iniquity and corruption than to assign this task to the false and profane deities, who are none other than demons?

Yet Jansenius must not be condemned without hearing his means of defense and examining the terms that he sometimes used to lessen the horror of his opinions:

> “The law,” he says, “made sin more abundant, and it brought about wrath; but the manner in which this occurred places God beyond all reproach. For this happened accidentally with respect to God: *And the manner in which, upon the coming of the law, sin became abundant and man’s guilt was increased, places God outside all blame. For this happened accidentally on God’s part*” (Jansenius, vol. III, book I, chapter 10, p. 42).

“Moreover,” he adds, “the law in itself tends to restrain the impetuous outbursts of desire: *Therefore the coming of the law in itself tends to restrain the impulse of desire*; it is not in itself the fuel that enflames ardent passion, but rather a boundary that restrains it: *For the law in itself is not fuel but the limit of ardor*” (Jansenius, ibid.).

I confess that I cannot understand how what proceeds from the nature of the law, what is the law’s proper purpose, what befits the Synagogue as Synagogue and the Old Testament as such, and what conforms to the formal aim and purpose that God had in giving the law—how, I say, all this could have happened accidentally with respect to God and the law. I cannot understand how the law in itself could have tended toward one thing while its nature and proper purpose were to tend toward another. Or rather, I understand that Jansenius wished to throw dust in people’s eyes and that, so as not to frighten his readers too much, he occasionally scattered through his writings a few terms contradictory to his principles and to his entire doctrine. He was preparing some sort of resource against scandal and outcry.

Nevertheless, I have great difficulty convincing myself that Jansenius feared or respected his readers. For, wishing to say that the Old Testament was good insofar as it was a figure of the New, how does he express himself? It was nothing other, he boldly says, than a kind of great comedy that was being performed—not so much for its own sake as for the sake of what it represented, namely, the New Testament and the Church, which is the princess (Jansenius himself is speaking) and the heir of the New Testament. The actors were the Jews, a nation suited to play the part:

> “It is perfectly clear that that Testament was nothing other than a certain GREAT COMEDY, performed by that people as actors suited to the role, not so much for its own sake as for the sake of that for which it served as a prefiguration, namely, the New Testament and its princess and heir, the Church” (Jansenius, vol. III, book I, p. 282).

Can one speak of the Old Testament and of God its author with more insolent irreverence? Is this not to defy the piety of one’s readers and insult their understanding while pretending to spare them? And what does this unworthy comparison demonstrate except that God truly chose, intended, and procured crimes so that they might be images and figures of holy things?

Yet even paganism itself could not tolerate such an excess in the authors of its comedies; it did not forgive them for putting on stage obscenities whose allusion and moral were honorable.

For, as Maximus of Tyre very rightly says, to present an infamous thing as an allegory for something good and honorable, and to display what is harmful in order to suggest what is useful, is not fitting for one who wishes to do good, but rather for one who wishes to do harm, because in this procedure the benefit is obscure and hidden, while the damage is immediate and certain:

> “To place a good and honorable thing beneath an unworthy subject, and to display useful things through things that are harmful, is not the work of one who wishes to benefit—for the benefit there is hidden and obscure—but rather of one who desires to harm; for the harm is immediately apparent” (Maximus of Tyre, Oration 8, edition of Henri Estienne, p. 50, in Greek).

# FOUR SHORT WORKS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE, FIRST PUBLISHED BY FONTANI, PREFECT OF THE RICCARDIAN LIBRARY, IN THE COLLECTION ENTITLED: *New Delights of the Learned, or, Collections of Ancient Unpublished Works*

[Col. 1113]

## FIRST SHORT WORK, OR BOOK ON PRAYER (C, G, S)*

[Note: Entirely corrupt and not always accessible to understanding, although we have corrected it in many places. EDITOR.]

Evangelical precepts, dearly beloved brothers, are nothing other than divine instructions: foundations for building hope, supports for strengthening faith, nourishment for fostering the heart, guides for directing our journey, and safeguards for obtaining salvation. While instructing on earth the teachable minds of believers, they lead them to the heavenly kingdom.

The Lord willed that many things be spoken and heard through his prophets; but how much greater are the things spoken by the Son of God—by the Word of God, who was in his prophets and now bears witness with his own voice—not merely commanding that the way be prepared for the one who was to come, but himself coming, opening the way for us, and showing how we, who once wandered heedlessly in the darkness of death and were previously blind, might, illuminated by the light of his grace, keep to the way of life with the Lord himself as our guide.

Among his other salutary admonitions and divine precepts, by which he counseled his people for their salvation, he himself also gave the pattern of prayer; he himself taught and instructed us what we should pray for. He who made us live also taught us to pray, with that kindness by which he deigned to give and bestow all other things as well, so that when we speak to the Father in the prayer that the Son taught, we may more readily be heard.

He had already foretold that the hour would come when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit, and he fulfilled it when he promised it, so that we, who have received spirit and truth through his sanctification, may also worship truly and spiritually through his teaching. For what prayer could be more spiritual than that given to us by Christ, from whom the Holy Spirit was also sent to us? And what prayer could be more acceptable before the Father than that which was uttered by the Son, who is the truth, from his own mouth? Thus to pray in any other way than he taught is not merely ignorance but guilt, since he himself established and said: “You reject the commandment of God in order to establish your own tradition.”

Let us therefore pray, dearly beloved brothers, as God our teacher has taught. It is a friendly and familiar prayer of the Lord to ask with his own words; it is to cause Christ’s prayer to rise to his ears. When we pray, let the Father recognize the words of his Son. Let him who dwells within the heart also be present in the voice. Since we have him as our advocate with the Father, let us present, on behalf of our sins, the words of our advocate.

For since he says, “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you,” how much more effectively shall we obtain what we ask in Christ’s name if we ask in his own prayer? Let our speech and prayer, when we pray, contain discipline, quietness, and modesty. Let us remember that we stand in the sight of God. We must please the divine eyes both by the posture of our body and by the manner of our voice. Just as it is characteristic of the imprudent to make a din with shouting, so, on the contrary, it is fitting for the modest to pray with restrained petitions.

Finally, by his teaching the Lord commanded us to pray privately in secluded and hidden places, in our rooms. This accords especially with faith, so that we may know that God is present everywhere, hears and sees all things, and that the fullness of his majesty penetrates every hidden and concealed place, as it is written: “I am God who draws near, and not a God from afar. If a man is hidden in hidden places, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?” And again: “In every place the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the wicked.”

And when we gather together with our brothers and celebrate the divine sacrifices with God’s priest, we must remember modesty and discipline. We must not scatter our prayers indiscriminately in disordered voices, nor throw before God, with tumultuous loquacity, the petition that ought to be commended to him modestly, because God is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart. He need not be admonished by shouting, since he sees the thoughts, as the Lord confirms by saying: “Why are you thinking evil things in your hearts?” And elsewhere: “Let everyone know that I am the searcher of the kidneys and the heart.”

This is what Hannah, bearing and preserving a figure in the First Book of Kings, observes and fulfills. She prays to the Lord, not with a noisy petition, but silently and modestly amid the very recesses of her heart. She spoke in hidden prayer, but spoke with manifest faith—not with her voice but with her heart—for she knew that the Lord hears in this manner. She effectively obtained what she asked because she petitioned faithfully.

Holy Scripture declares this when it says: “She spoke in her heart, and her lips did not move.” We also read in the Psalm: “Speak within your hearts, and be pierced with remorse in your chambers.” Through Jeremiah, the Holy Spirit likewise suggests and teaches this, saying: “But the Lord must be worshiped in the understanding.”

When praying, dearly beloved brothers, let no one fail to know how the Publican prayed in the temple with the Pharisee. He did not impudently lift his eyes toward heaven or insolently raise his hands; rather, he beat his breast and, confessing the sins enclosed within him, implored the help of divine mercy. While the Pharisee pleased himself, the Publican, who prayed in this manner, deserved more to be sanctified. He did not place his hope of salvation in confidence in his own innocence, since no one is innocent; instead, he humbly confessed his sins and prayed. He who forgives the humble heard the one who prayed.

The Lord set this out and said in the Gospel:

> “Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a Publican. When the Pharisee had taken his stand, he prayed these things within himself: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of mankind—unjust, robbers, adulterers—or even like this Publican. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of everything I possess.’ But the Publican stood at a distance and would not even raise his eyes toward heaven; instead, he beat his breast, saying: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’ I tell you, this man went down to his house justified more than the other Pharisee, because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

Therefore we, dearest brothers, speaking [F. reading: learning] in accordance with the divine utterance, after we have learned how we ought to approach prayer, let us learn, as the Lord says, what we should pray for. He says:

> “Pray in this way: Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name; your kingdom come; your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth. Give us today our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen.”

Above all, the teacher of peace and master of unity did not wish prayer to be said individually and privately, as though the one who prays should pray only for himself. We must not say, “My Father,” nor, “Give me my bread today,” nor should each person ask that only his own debts be forgiven, or pray for himself alone not to be led into temptation and to be delivered from evil. For our prayer is public and common; and when we pray, we do not pray for one person but for the whole people, because we are all one people.

The God of peace and teacher of concord, who taught unity, also taught us to pray in this way. Thus he wished prayer to be made for all, just as he himself bore us all in one.

The three young men enclosed in the fiery furnace observed this law of prayer, agreeing in prayer and united in harmony of spirit. The faith of divine Scripture declares this; and, while teaching how such men prayed, it gives an example that we ought to imitate in our prayers, so that we may become like them.

“Then,” it says, “those three, as though with one mouth, were singing a hymn and blessing the Lord.” They spoke as though with one mouth, although Christ had not yet taught them to pray. For this reason their word was effective and obtained what they asked: their prayer was peaceful, simple, and spiritual, and therefore pleasing to God.

We likewise know how the apostles prayed with the disciples after the Lord’s ascension:

> “They were persevering with one accord in prayer, together with the women and Mary, who was the mother of Jesus, and his brothers.”

They persevered unanimously in prayer, expressing at once the persistence and the harmony of prayer, because God makes those who are united in one mind dwell in a house. He admits into the divine and eternal house only those among whom prayer is united.

I shall now briefly set forth what the mysteries of the Lord’s Prayer are, dearly beloved brothers, how many and how great they are—gathered together briefly in words but spiritually abundant in power—so that nothing whatsoever may be omitted that is not comprehended in our petitions and prayers through the concise teaching of heaven. Observe, then: “Pray in this way.”

> “Our Father, who are in heaven.”

The new man, reborn and restored to his God through his grace, says “Father” first of all, because he has already begun to be a son. “He came to his own,” it says, “and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him, he gave the power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name.” Whoever believes in his name and has become a child of God must begin here: he must give thanks and declare himself a child of God by naming the one in heaven as his Father.

He must also attest, in the very first words of his new birth, that he has renounced an earthly and fleshly father and has begun to know and possess as Father only the one who is in heaven, since it is written:

> “Those who say to their father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and who did not acknowledge their own sons—these have kept your words and observed your covenant.”

Likewise, in his Gospel the Lord commanded us not to call anyone on earth our father, since we have one Father, who is in heaven. And when a disciple had mentioned his father, he replied: “Let the dead bury their dead.” For he had called his father dead, whereas believers have one Father.

Nor must we merely observe and understand this, dearly beloved brothers, that we call our Father the one who is in heaven. We also join and add the words “Our Father,” that is, the Father of those who believe and who, having been sanctified through him and restored by the birth of spiritual grace, have begun to be sons.

This expression restrains and strikes the Jews, who not only faithlessly rejected Christ, announced to them through the prophets and first sent to them, but also cruelly killed him. They cannot call God Father, since the Lord confounds and rebukes them, saying:

> “You are born from your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him.”

And through the prophet Isaiah the Lord cries out indignantly:

> “I have begotten and exalted sons, but they rejected me. The ox knows its owner and the ass the manger of its lord; Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood. Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins, wicked seed, criminal sons! You have abandoned the Lord your God and provoked indignation, O seed of Israel [the transmitted reading is uncertain].”

As a reproach to these people, we Christians say “Our Father” first of all when we pray, because he has begun to be ours, while he has ceased to belong to the Jews who abandoned him.

Nor can a sinful people be sons. But to those who are granted forgiveness of sins, the name of sons is assigned, and to them eternity is promised, as the Lord himself says:

> “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin; but a slave does not remain in the house forever.”

How great is the Lord’s indulgence, and how abundant toward us is the richness of his condescension and goodness, that he has wished us to celebrate prayer in the presence of God, so that we call God Father and, just as Christ is the Son of God, so we too may be called sons. None of us would dare to assume this name unless he himself had permitted us to pray in this way.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, we must remember and know that when we call God Father, we ought to act as God’s sons, so that just as we take pleasure in God, he too may take pleasure in us. Let us live as God’s temples, so that it may be evident that God dwells within us. Let our conduct not be degenerate in relation to the spirit, so that, having begun to be spiritual and heavenly, we may think and act only in spiritual and heavenly ways.

For the Lord himself also said: “Those who glorify me, I will glorify; and whoever despises me will be despised.” The blessed apostle likewise explained in his Letter, saying:

> “You are not your own, for you were bought at a great price. Glorify, lift up, and bear God in your heart.”

After this we say:

> “Hallowed be your name.”

We do not ask that God be sanctified by our prayers, but we ask that his name be sanctified in us. For by whom is God sanctified, when he himself sanctifies? But because he said, “Be holy, for I am holy,” we ask and pray that we who were sanctified in baptism may persevere in what we have begun to be. We petition for this daily, since we need daily sanctification so that we who sin every day may cleanse our offenses through continual sanctification.

The Apostle proclaims what this sanctification is that will be conferred upon you by God’s gracious favor, saying:

> “Neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who pursue males, nor thieves, nor the fraudulent, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will inherit the kingdom of God. And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were justified, but you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.”

We pray that this sanctification may remain in us. And our Lord and judge threatens the one whom he has justified and healed that he must sin no more, lest something worse happen to him. We make this petition in continual prayers; by day and by night we ask that the life-giving grace received from God be preserved through his protection in prayer.

Then follows:

[Note: It might perhaps be better read and punctuated in this way: “This … we ask, so that the life … may be preserved.” The words *In oratione* (“In prayer”) should apparently be deleted, and *nobis* (“us”) inserted before *nomen* (“name”). EDITOR.]

> “Your kingdom come.”

We also ask that God’s kingdom be manifested to us, just as we ask that his name be sanctified in us. For when does God not reign? Or when did that which always was and will never cease to be begin with him?

We ask that our kingdom, promised to us by God and obtained through Christ’s blood and passion, come to us, so that we who previously served in the world may afterward reign with Christ as ruler, as he himself promises and says:

> “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

But, dearly beloved brothers, Christ himself can also be understood as the kingdom of God, since we desire his coming every day and wish that his arrival may be manifested to us quickly. For since he himself is the resurrection, because in him we rise again, so the kingdom of God may also be understood as being himself, because in him we shall reign.

We rightly ask for the kingdom of God—that is, the heavenly kingdom—because there is also an earthly kingdom. But whoever renounces the world is greater than its honors and kingdom; and therefore whoever declares himself devoted to God and Christ desires not earthly but heavenly kingdoms.

Continual prayer and petition are necessary lest we fall away from the heavenly kingdom, as the Jews fell away, although it had first been promised to them. The Lord demonstrated and proved this, saying:

> “Many will come from the east and the west and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

He shows that previously the Jews were children of the kingdom, when they also remained children of God. After the paternal name ceased in relation to them, the kingdom also ceased; and therefore we Christians, who in prayer call God Father and have begun to know him, pray that God’s kingdom may come to us.

We also add and say:

> “Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth.”

This does not mean that God should merely do what he wills, but that we may be able to do what he wills. For who can resist God and prevent him from doing whatever he wishes, whenever he wishes? But because the devil resists, preventing our mind and conduct from obeying God in all things, we pray and ask that God’s will be done in us.

For this to happen in us, God’s will is necessary—that is, his work and protection—because no one is strong by his own powers but is kept safe by God’s indulgence and mercy.

Finally, the Lord, showing the weakness of the humanity he bore, said:

> “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.”

And, giving his disciples an example so that they should do not their own will but God’s will, he added:

> “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.”

Elsewhere he says:

> “I have not come down from heaven to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”

If the Son obeyed in order to do the Father’s will, how much more ought a servant to obey in order to do the will of his Lord?

John likewise urges and instructs us in his Letter to do God’s will, saying:

> “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age. And the world passes away, and its desire; but whoever does the will of God remains forever, just as God remains forever.”

Therefore, if we wish to remain forever, we must do the will of God, who is eternal.

The will of God, which Christ both taught and fulfilled, consists in humility of conduct, steadfastness in faith, modesty in speech, justice in deeds, mercy in actions, and discipline in behavior: not knowing how to inflict injury, and being able to endure injury when it is inflicted; maintaining peace with one’s brothers; loving God with one’s whole heart; loving in him the fact that he is Father and fearing the fact that he is God; putting nothing at all before Christ, since he put nothing before us; clinging inseparably to his love; standing firmly and confidently beside his cross; when the struggle concerns his name and honor, displaying in speech the steadfastness by which we are strengthened, in examination the confidence with which we engage, and in death the patience by which we are crowned.

This is to wish to be Christ’s coheir; this is to follow God’s commandment; this is to do the Father’s will; this is to fulfill the Father’s will.

We ask that God’s will be done in heaven and on earth, because both pertain to the completion of our safety and salvation. Since we possess the body on earth and the spirit in heaven, we ourselves are both heaven and earth; and we pray that God’s will be done in both—in body and in spirit.

There is a struggle between flesh and spirit, and a daily conflict takes place between them as they oppose one another, so that we do not do what we wish: the spirit desires heavenly and divine things, while the flesh desires earthly and worldly things. Therefore we ask that, between these two, through God’s work and help, harmony may be brought about, so that God’s will may be done both in spirit and in flesh, and that the soul reborn through him may be preserved.

The apostle Paul openly and plainly declares this in his own words:

> “The flesh,” he says, “desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you may not do whatever you wish.”

The works of the flesh are manifest: adulteries, fornications, uncleanness, impurity, idolatries, sorceries, murders, hostilities, quarrels, jealousies, resentments, provocations, pretenses, dissensions, heresies, envy, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. Those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

But the fruit of the spirit is joy, love, peace, magnanimity, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control, and chastity. Therefore, in daily and continual prayers, we ask that God’s will be done in heaven and on earth with regard to us, because this is God’s will: that earthly things yield to heavenly things and spiritual things prevail over bodily things.

This may also be understood in the following way, dearly beloved brothers. Since the Lord commands and urges us both to love our enemies and to pray even for those who persecute us, let us also pray for those who are still earthly and have not yet begun to be heavenly, and ask that God’s will be done with regard to them, since Christ perfected humanity by preserving and restoring it.

For when the disciples are no longer called earthly by him but “the salt of the earth,” and the Apostle calls the first man one who is from the earth’s soil but the second one who is from heaven, it is fitting that we, who ought to be like God the Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust, should, in obedience to Christ’s teaching, pray and make our petition for the salvation of all.

Just as God’s will was done in heaven—in us through our faith—so that we might become heaven, may it also be done on earth, that is, in those who do not believe, so that they may become heavenly, being born of water and the Spirit. As our prayer proceeds, we ask for this and say:

“Give us this day our daily bread”—which can be understood both spiritually and in the plain sense. For we ask for what beneficially advances salvation. For Christ is the bread of life; and this bread does not belong to everyone, but is ours. Just as we say “Our Father,” because he is the Father of those who understand and believe, so we call it “our bread,” because Christ is ours: when we touch his body, he is bread.

We ask that this bread be given to us daily, lest we who are in Christ and receive the Eucharist daily as food for salvation, if some more serious offense intervenes, be cut off and, being forbidden to communicate, separated from the heavenly bread and from Christ’s body. He himself preaches and warns: “I am the bread of life who came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever; and the bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.” When, therefore, he says that anyone who eats his bread will live forever, it is plainly evident that those live who touch his body and receive the Eucharist in the reality of communion. Thus we must fear and pray lest, when someone is cut off and separated from Christ’s body, he remain cut off from salvation, since he himself threatens and says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.”

And therefore we ask that our bread—that is, Christ—be given to us daily, so that we who remain and live in Christ may not withdraw from his sanctification and body. [Col. 1120D]

It can also be understood in this way: we who renounce the world and, through faith in spiritual grace, have cast away its riches and splendors ask only for food and sustenance, since the Lord instructs us and says: “Whoever does not renounce all that belongs to him cannot be my disciple.” Whoever has begun to be a disciple of Christ must, in accordance with the will of his teacher, renounce everything and ask for his daily food, without extending the desires of his petition into the distant future; for the Lord again prescribes and warns: “Do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.”

Rightly, therefore, Christ’s disciple asks for sustenance for the day, since he is forbidden to worry about tomorrow. And it is contradictory and inconsistent that we should seek to live long in this world when we ask that the kingdom of God come swiftly. The blessed apostle likewise warns us, shaping and strengthening the firmness of our hope and faith. “We brought nothing,” he says, “into this world. It is certain that we can take nothing out of it. Therefore, having food and clothing, let us be content with these. But those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the desire for money is the root of all evils; by pursuing it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.”

He teaches that riches are not merely to be despised but are also dangerous to those who possess them: they are the root of evils that flatter, deceiving the human mind through hidden fraud. Thus he rebukes the foolish rich man who considers worldly wealth and boasts in the abundance of his exultant harvests, saying: “Fool, this very night your soul is demanded of you; and the things you have prepared—for whom will they be?” The fool rejoiced in his harvests on the night when he was about to die, and, though his life was already failing, he was thinking about an abundance of provisions.

But, on the other hand, the Lord teaches that the person who sells all his possessions and distributes them for the use of the poor, storing up treasure for himself in heaven, becomes perfect and complete. He says that such a person, enduring patiently, can follow him and imitate the glory of the Lord’s resurrection; freed and girded, he is entangled in no snares of household property, but, released and free, he himself accompanies to the Lord the resources he has sent on ahead.

So that each of us may prepare himself for this, he learns to pray in this way and, from the law of prayer, to recognize what prayer ought to be. [Col. 1121A] For daily food cannot be lacking to the righteous, since it is written: “The Lord will not kill the soul of the righteous by famine”; and again: “I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread.”

Again the Lord promises and says: “Do not worry, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘With what shall we be clothed?’ For the nations seek all these things. Your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”

To those who seek his kingdom and righteousness he promises that all things will be added. Since everything belongs to God, the person who possesses God will lack nothing, provided that he himself does not fail God. Thus, when Daniel was confined in the lions’ den by the king’s command, food was divinely provided for him, and the man of God was fed among the hungry beasts. Thus, too, Elijah, while fleeing and anxious [F. in solitude], was nourished during his persecution by ravens serving him and birds bringing him food. Oh, the detestable cruelty of human wickedness! Beasts feed him, birds feed him, but human beings plot and rage against him.

After this we also plead for our sins, saying: “And forgive us our sins, as we also forgive our debtors.”

First, the provision of food is requested, and then pardon for sin, so that the person who is nourished by God may live for God. Provision is made not only for the present and temporal life but also for eternal life, which can be attained if sins are forgiven. The Lord calls sins “debts,” as he says in his Gospel: “I forgave you all that debt because you entreated me.”

How necessarily, wisely, and beneficially we are reminded that we are sinners, since we are compelled to pray for our sins! While we ask forgiveness from God, the mind of our conscience is made to remember, lest anyone regard himself as innocent and, by exalting himself, perish all the more. A person is instructed and taught that he sins daily, since he is commanded to pray for his sins. Thus John also follows in his epistle, saying: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, the Lord is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.”

In that epistle he has embraced both groups, so that we ought to pray for our sins and obtain forgiveness when we pray. Therefore he calls the Lord faithful for the forgiveness of sins, because he keeps the promise of his faithfulness: he who taught us to pray concerning our debts and sins promised paternal mercy and added that forgiveness would follow. Indeed, he also added a law, binding us by a condition and pledge, so that we should ask for our debts to be forgiven in this way, knowing that what we ask for our sins cannot be obtained unless we ourselves have done the same toward our own sinners.

For this reason he says elsewhere: “In the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.” And because the fellow servant, after all his debt had been forgiven him, did not wish to forgive his fellow servant, he was bound in prison. Since he did not wish to show mercy to his fellow servant, he lost what had been forgiven him by the Lord. Christ also declared this more forcefully in his commands, with greater severity: “When you stand at prayer,” he says, “forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you your sins.” [Col. 1122D]

No excuse remains for you on the day of judgment, since you will be judged according to your own sentence, and what you have done, you yourself will suffer. God has commanded that we be peaceful, harmonious, and united in his household; and just as he made us through a second birth, so he wishes us to persevere as those who have been born, so that we who have begun to be children of God may remain in God’s peace. Since we have one Holy Spirit, let there also be one mind and one understanding.

For God does not receive the sacrifice of one who is at odds with others. Rather, he commands the peacemaker to withdraw from the altar and first be reconciled to his brother through peaceful prayers, so that God may be reconciled to him. Our peace and fraternal harmony are a greater sacrifice to God, and the people aided by the unity of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are more significant than sacrifices.

For in the sacrifices first offered by Cain and Abel, God did not look upon their gifts but upon their hearts, so that the one whose heart was pleasing might be pleasing in his gift. Abel, peaceful and righteous, sacrificing to the one God in innocence, taught the others also that, whenever they bring a gift to the altar, they should come with fear of God, with a pure heart, with the rule of righteousness, and with the peace of harmony.

Rightly, since he was such in God’s sacrifice, he himself afterward became a sacrifice to God, as the first of the martyrs, inaugurating with his blood the glorious passion of the Lord and displaying its beginnings—he who had possessed both the Lord’s righteousness and peace. Such people, in the end, are crowned by God; such people will judge with the Lord on the day of judgment.

But a person who is discordant and quarrelsome and has no peace with his brothers will not be able to escape the crime of dissension, even if he is killed for the Christian name, as the blessed apostle and sacred Scripture testify. For it is written: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer,” and a murderer neither reaches the kingdom of heaven nor lives with God. He cannot be with Christ who has preferred to imitate Cain and Judas rather than Christ. What an offense this is, which cannot be washed away even by a baptism of blood! What a crime this is, which martyrdom cannot expiate!

The Lord also necessarily warns us to say in prayer: “And do not allow us to be led into temptation.” Here it is shown in part that the adversary has no power against us unless God has first permitted it, so that all our fear and all our vigilance must necessarily be directed toward God in our prayers, since evil can do nothing unless power is granted to it.

Divine Scripture proves this when it says: “Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came against Jerusalem and attacked it, and the Lord delivered it into his hands.” Power is given to evil against us according to our sins, as it is written: “Who gave Jacob for plunder and Israel to those who despoiled him? Was it not God, because they sinned and were unwilling to walk in his ways or listen to his law? And he brought upon them the anger of his indignation.”

Again, when Solomon sinned and departed from the Lord’s commands and ways, it is written that “the Lord stirred up Satan against Solomon.” Power against us is given in two ways: either for punishment when we sin, or for glory when we are tested. Thus we see what happened to Job, when the Lord revealed it and said: “Behold, all that he has I give into your hands; but beware of touching him himself.”

And the Lord speaks in the Gospel at the time of his passion: “You would have no power against me unless it had been given to you from above.”

When we ask not to fall into temptation, we are reminded of our weakness and frailty. We pray in this way so that no one may insolently exalt himself, no one may assume anything proudly and arrogantly, and no one may claim the glory of confession or suffering as his own, since the Lord himself, teaching humility, said: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”

Thus, when a humble and submissive confession goes before us and everything that is asked with supplication, fear, and reverence for God is given over to God, it is granted through his own mercy.

After all these things, at the completion of the prayer comes that praise which gathers all our petitions and prayers into a brief conclusion. For at the end we have placed: “But deliver us from evil.” In this we embrace all adversities that the enemy contrives against us in this world. From them there can be faithful and firm protection if God delivers us, if he himself grants help to those who plead and implore him.

When we say, “Deliver us from evil,” nothing remains that ought still to be requested afterward, since we ask only for God’s protection against evil. Once this has been obtained, we stand secure and safe against everything that the devil and the world do. For what fear of the world has the person whose protector in the world is God?

What is surprising, dearest brothers, if such is the prayer that God taught—the God who, by his instruction, has condensed our entire petition into a short saving utterance? This had previously been foretold through the prophet Isaiah, when, filled with the Holy Spirit, he spoke of God’s majesty and mercy: “Completing and shortening,” he says, “he will make a shortened word in righteousness throughout the whole world.”

For when the Word of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, came to everyone, gathering the learned and the unlearned alike and issuing commands of salvation to every sex and age, he made a great abridgment of his commands, so that the memory of those learning the heavenly discipline would not be burdened but would quickly learn what was necessary for simple faith. Thus he taught what eternal life is, for in a great and divine brevity he embraced the mystery of life. And he showed that he intended to indicate eternal life when he said: “That they may know you, the only true God, and Christ whom you promised.”

Likewise, when he extracted the first and greatest commands from the Law and the Prophets, he said: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength.” This is the first commandment, and the second is like it: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” “On these two commandments,” he says, “the whole law and the prophets depend.”

And again: “Whatever good things you wish people to do for you, do the same for them; for this is the law and the prophets.”

The Lord taught us to pray not only by words but also by actions. He himself frequently prayed and pleaded, showing by the testimony of his example what we ought to do, as it is written: “He withdrew into the wilderness and prayed”; and again: “He went out onto the mountain to pray, and he spent the night in prayer to God.”

If he prayed who was without sin, how much more ought sinners to pray? And if he, keeping watch continually throughout the whole night, prayed with unceasing petitions, how much more ought we to keep watch at night, devoting ourselves to frequent prayer?

The Lord prayed and pleaded not for himself—for what could the innocent ask for himself? Rather, he prayed for our offenses, as he himself declares when he says to Peter: “Behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail.”

Afterward he pleads for everyone, saying: “I do not pray for these alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they too may be in us.”

Certainly great before God are Christ’s kindness and mercy toward our salvation: not content merely to redeem us with his blood, he also continued to plead for us.

Consider what the desire of his prayer was: that, just as the Father and Son are one, so we too might remain in one unity. From this also it can be understood how great is the offense of one who divides unity and peace, since the Lord prayed for this very thing, unwilling that his people should live among schismatics, knowing that discord does not enter the kingdom of God.

When we stand at prayer, dearest brothers, we must keep watch and devote ourselves to our prayers. Let every carnal and worldly thought depart, and let the mind think of nothing except what it is praying for.

For this reason the priest, after a preface before the prayer, prepares the minds of the brothers by saying: “Lift up your hearts,” so that, when the people respond, “We have them with the Lord,” they may be reminded that they ought to think of nothing else but God. [Col. 1125B]

Let the breast be closed against the adversary, and let it please God alone. During the time of prayer, let them not allow God’s enemy to approach them. For he frequently slips in and penetrates, subtly deceiving us, and turns our prayers away from God, so that we have one thing in our heart and another on our lips, when the Lord ought to be prayed to with sincere intention not by the sound of the voice but by the mind and understanding.

What sloth it is to be distracted and captured by foolish and profane thoughts while you plead with the Lord—as though there were something else you ought to think about more than what you are saying to God! How do you ask to be heard by God when you do not hear yourself? How do you wish the Lord to remember you when you yourself do not remember yourself?

This is wholly to fail to guard against the enemy. This is, when you pray to God, to offend God’s majesty through negligence. This is to keep watch with the eyes and sleep with the heart, whereas a Christian ought, even when sleeping with the eyes, to keep watch with the heart, as it is said in the person of the speaking Church in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake.”

Therefore the apostle carefully and cautiously warns us, saying: “Devote yourselves to prayer, keeping watch in it,” teaching and showing that those who pray can obtain what they ask from God when God sees them keeping watch in prayer.

But those who pray should not come before God with fruitless or empty prayers. A petition is ineffective when prayer to God is barren. Since every tree that does not produce fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire, surely speech that bears no fruit cannot win God’s favor, since it is fruitful in no action.

Therefore divine Scripture instructs us, saying: “Prayer is good with fasting and almsgiving.” For he who will repay the reward for works and almsgiving on the day of judgment is also today a gracious hearer of the person who comes to prayer with action.

Thus Cornelius the centurion, when he prayed, deserved to be heard; for he was giving many alms to the people and always praying to God. At the ninth hour an angel stood beside him as he prayed, bearing witness to his works and saying: “Cornelius, your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended as a memorial before the Lord.” Those prayers ascend quickly which the merits of our works carry before the Lord.

Thus the angel Raphael was also a witness to Tobiah, who always prayed and always acted, saying: “To reveal and confess the works of God is honorable. For when you prayed, I presented the memorial of your prayer in the evening before the presence of God’s glory; and likewise when you buried the dead. And because you did not hesitate to rise, leave your meal, go, and bury the dead, I was sent to test you. Again God sent me to heal you and Sarah, your daughter-in-law. I am Raphael, one of the seven righteous angels who stand before God and move about in the presence of God’s glory.”

Through Isaiah also the Lord admonishes and teaches similar things, testifying: “Release,” he says, “every bond of injustice; undo the constrictions of importunate neighbours [reading uncertain]; send the crushed away into rest; and destroy every injustice. Break your bread for the hungry; bring the needy without shelter into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise the members of your own household.”

“Then your timely light will break forth, and your garments will quickly arise; righteousness will go before you, and the glory of God will surround you. Then you will cry out, and the Lord will hear you; while you are still speaking, he will say: ‘Behold, I am here.’”

He promises that he will be present, hear, and protect those who loosen the bonds of injustice from their hearts and give alms to the members of God’s household according to his commands. When they hear what God has commanded to be done, they themselves also deserve to be heard by God.

The blessed apostle Paul, too, when aided by the brothers in the pressure of need, calls their works sacrifices: “I have been filled,” he says, “receiving from Epaphroditus what you sent, a fragrant odor, an acceptable sacrifice pleasing to God.” For when someone has compassion on the poor, he lends to God; and whoever gives to the least gives to God and spiritually offers a fragrant sacrifice to God.

In the celebration of prayers we find the three young men with Daniel, strong in faith and victorious in captivity, praying at the third, sixth, and ninth hours—clearly a mystery of the Trinity, which was to be revealed in the last times.

For the first hour, progressing to the third, also displays the completed number of the Trinity promised long ago; and again, proceeding through the fourth to the sixth, it declares another Trinity. When the ninth is completed from the seventh through three hours, the perfect Trinity is counted.

By anticipating these intervals of the hours, the worshipers of God served at appointed and lawful times for prayer. It was afterward made clear that these things had long been mysteries, since the righteous had previously prayed in this way.

For at the third hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples, fulfilling the grace of the Lord’s promise. Likewise, at the sixth hour Peter went up onto the upper roof and was instructed by both a sign and the voice of the Lord warning him to admit everyone to the grace of salvation, although he had previously doubted concerning the correction of the Gentiles.

And the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour, and at the ninth he washed away our sins. In order that he might redeem and give us life, his passion then completed his victory.

But for us, dearest brothers, besides the hours observed in ancient times, the intervals and mysteries of prayer have now increased. We must also pray in the morning, so that the Lord’s resurrection may be celebrated in morning prayer. The Holy Spirit indicated this long ago in a psalm, saying: “My King and my God, because I shall pray to you; in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I shall stand before you and contemplate you.” [Col. 1127A]

And again the Lord speaks through the prophet: “At dawn they will keep watch for me, saying, ‘Let us go and return to the Lord our God.’”

When the sun again withdraws and the day comes to an end, it is necessarily time to pray again. For our God is the sun and the true day. When the sun and day of this world withdraw, we pray and ask that the light come upon us anew; thus we ask again for Christ’s coming, which will grant the grace of eternal light.

That Christ is called the day the Holy Spirit declares in the psalm, saying: “This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes”; and again: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.”

That he has also been called the sun is attested by the prophet Malachi, who says: “But for you who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of righteousness will rise, while for others there is darkness.”

If in the sacred Scriptures Christ is the true sun and the true day, no hour is excluded for Christians from the duty of worshiping God frequently and continually. Since we are in Christ—that is, in the sun and in the true day—let us devote the whole day to prayers and pray so that, when the alternating cycles of the world and the law have run their course and night succeeds as the day dissolves, the darkness of night may bring no harm to those who pray, because for the children of light it is day even in the night. [Col. 1128A]

For when is there no light for one who has light in his heart? Or when is there no sun and day for one whose sun and day is Christ?

Since we have always been in Christ—that is, in the light—let us not cease from prayer even at night. Thus the widow Anna persevered without interruption, always praying and always keeping watch in order to please God, as it is written in the Gospel: “She did not depart from the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day.”

Those who have not been enlightened did not see this; the Jews, having been abandoned by the light, remained in darkness. But we, dearest brothers, who are always in the Lord’s light, who have been found worthy and have learned what we have begun to be through received grace, let us count night as day. Let us believe that we always walk in the light and not be hindered by the darkness from which we have escaped. Let there be no loss of prayer during the nighttime hours, no sluggish or ignorant neglect of our prayers.

Renewed spiritually and reborn through God’s indulgence, let us imitate what we shall be in the kingdom, when, without the interruption of night, we shall possess the everlasting day of the sun. Let us keep watch as though in the light, always praying and giving thanks to God; and therefore let us not cease here also to pray and give thanks.

[Col. 1127]

## SECOND OPUSCULUM, OR BOOK ON THE FOUR VIRTUES OF CHARITY. (C, G)

[Col. 1127C] The desire of your charity demands from us the duty of discourse; but there are so many things that terrify and restrain our mind that, if we wish to comply with your desire, doing so will not be without danger to us. For, intending to speak about charity, I shall not pass over in silence the good things that proceed from it and those that accompany it. But, constrained by the narrowness of time, where should I turn first except to the footsteps of charity itself, and beseech it to grant me the ability to say something worthy of it, so that I may both fulfill my ministry and satisfy your desire?

Among the other virtues of charity that the apostle Paul mentions, he says that charity does not envy, does not act improperly, is not provoked, and thinks no evil. Finally, he comprehends these four virtues of hers in a brief statement, saying: [Col. 1127D] “It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.” It is therefore fitting to speak to your holiness about these four virtues of holy charity; and first it is delightful to observe how the four hinges of the encompassing world have possessed the whole earth.

Let us therefore examine, if it pleases you, the examples of certain saints—those, namely, who were possessed by these virtues—and let us assign each virtue individually to each of them, so that we may understand that all are present in all, since everyone who piously bears something rightly believes, hopes for something [F. perhaps: “believes and hopes”], and whoever hopes endures, lest he fall without hope.

But now let us see who these people are, whose faith we may be able to attain insofar as we are helped from above. The virtue of holy charity that bears all things shone forth in holy Noah; that which believes all things, in holy Abraham; that which hopes all things, in our fathers, that is, in the people of Israel, from whom the Lord himself arose; and that which endures all things, in the very Head, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is true charity, which never fails.

Nor should your charity consider the other saints alien to these virtues. Know that they have been passed over in this discourse because of the brevity of time and the subject undertaken, while you must nevertheless know with complete certainty that all are in Christ and Christ in all.

But now let us see how holy Noah possessed the virtue of charity that bears all things. As soon as he had been warned, he fled to the wood and shut himself away in a narrow fortress after leaving behind the beauty of the fields. He endured the rumbling of the sky, the unleashed crashing of the waters [Col. 1128C] and the rainstorms; and after all this, he who had been accustomed to enjoy the fellowship of human beings became, in a certain sense, the companion of serpents and wild beasts. Nor was this man frightened that beasts were with him in the ark. Rather, there the wildness of the beasts recognized its order, because humanity had recognized itself; and they obeyed the man who commanded them, because they understood that the man obeyed the Lord above.

It was shown in Noah that Adam had lost what he possessed by despising the Lord’s command, and it was demonstrated that human beings can even rule over beasts if they submit themselves to obedience to the Creator. This holy man waits for and endures the end of the Flood, and the ark is not abandoned by the beasts before the Flood has ended. The good man endures the evil, and until the end, when even bodies are separated, remaining within, he is separated in heart, not in body.

If you are a soul that desires to possess the virtue of charity that bears all things, leave the world and flee to the wood of the cross. Do not fear the storms and whirlwinds of this Flood; you will not be submerged if you are carried by the wood. He who deigned to create knows how to steer. Only let the virtue of charity that bears all things not be absent from you; let no force tear you away from the solid fortress. Remain good and endure the wicked. For it is better, while placed within, to endure the wicked for the sake of the good than to go out and perish, abandoning both the good and the wicked.

If, then, beasts are with you—that is, if there are with you in the Church those who teach perversely, think falsely, or are heretics or schismatics, or even wicked Catholics themselves, seeking, like beasts, to devour souls—let them be endured until the end of the age, as until the end of the Flood. Let them roar, gnash their teeth, and attempt to shatter the ark itself. Do not be afraid. When the Flood has ended, the barren and thorny forest will carry them away, while the fertile earth will receive you.

After the end of the age, the impious will be carried away into the outer darkness; there will be “WEEPING AND GNASHING OF TEETH,” while the godly will be received into the land of the living. For holy Noah himself, after the end of the Flood, offered sacrifice to God—but from clean animals, not from unclean ones. Both clean and unclean animals were able to enter the ark together; but the wicked did not reach God’s sacrifice.

But let us now move on, so that we may examine the remaining matters. Let that holy man Abraham come forward and teach us by his own example to possess the virtue of charity that believes all things. He did not hesitate, at a single summons, to leave his homeland, his dwelling, his house, and his family. Everything was abandoned so that he might obey the Lord who commanded him. God said: “Go out from your kindred and from your house, and come into whatever land I shall show you.”

This holy man did not reflect within himself and say, “Where shall I go? To whom shall I entrust myself? Into what land shall I go?” But as soon as he heard, he rose, ran, hurried, and hastened. He did not see the promised land, but by believing he held it firmly. He walked on the straight path and did not turn his wandering footsteps elsewhere than where he ought, because the one who sent him to an unknown land—the very one, I say, who sent him—did not abandon him, nor did he deceive him.

A reward was given to the believer. He reached the land, expanded and multiplied; from poor he became rich, from obscure he became powerful. He was enriched with every good, and in him was fulfilled what the Lord promised his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “If anyone has left house or field or parents for the sake of my name, in this life he will receive a hundredfold, and in the age to come he will obtain eternal life.”

The reward of this faith was still heaped up, and a son was promised to an old man. The virtue of charity that believes all things was present in him. He heard, rejoiced, loved more greatly, and received a son from a barren wife whom barrenness and age had already deprived of hope of bearing. In that son he held most firmly the blessing promised to all nations.

But charity still tests him, commends him once he has been tested, and shows how he preferred nothing to God. The Lord called him from heaven, saying: “Abraham, Abraham.” And he, like an obedient servant, replied: “Behold, here I am.” And the Lord said: [Col. 1130A] “Take your son, that one whom you love, Isaac, and go into the high land, and offer him there as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that I shall tell you.”

Nor was the faithful servant disturbed or broken by this command. The virtue of charity that believes all things was present in him. He rose, went home, saddled the donkey, cut the wood, took the sword and fire, brought the boy with him, and proceeded to the place.

Now Isaac, becoming attentive, questioned his father, saying: “Father”—and he replied, “What is it, son?” And the son said: “Behold, here are the fire and the wood; where is the sheep that you are going to sacrifice as a burnt offering?” And the father answered: “God will provide himself a sheep for the sacrifice, my son.”

I see here a great and profound mystery: Abraham carried one thing in his heart and promised another to his son. Yet the son was not deceived by what he promised, nor had any weakness changed his heart from its purpose.

What more need be said? He continued on his way, saw the place from a distance, and, leaving his servants there, spoke these words to them: “Stay here with the donkey; I and the boy will go as far as that place, and when we have worshiped, we shall return to you.”

O holy Abraham, what is this that you say, when you have another thing to do with the boy? Are you deceiving either yourself or your servants? “No,” he says, “but the virtue of charity that believes, does, and speaks all things remains within me, in accordance with what I say and do prophetically.”

For I hear it speaking within my heart without any sound of voice, saying to me: “Although you lead the boy to be sacrificed with the full and perfect resolve of one who believes that he will rise again, your son will not be consumed in this sacrifice, because the resurrection has been reserved for the Son of God.”

The apostle James, rightly recalling this man’s faith, says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God.”

As we know, friendship is created by the union of minds. Hence a certain wise man of this world said: “To will and not to will the same things—that is at last a firm friendship.” Therefore, as we know, friendship is created by the union of minds. It is useful for us to learn how this holy man united his mind to God, so that he might be called God’s friend.

For just as God the Father did not spare his only Son, so Abraham, when God commanded that the son whom he had given him should be sacrificed, offered him with a devoted heart.

But let us see what follows; with the Lord’s help, we delight in giving you a full understanding of this history. After leaving the servants behind, the father came with his son to the place of sacrifice, built an altar, arranged the wood, [Col. 1130D] laid aside the signs of human paternal affection, put on the devoted steadfastness of a priest, and drew the sword to kill his son.

What do you think, brothers? We sense nothing human here; rather, we recognize everything as divine. But the son who shortly before had been asking for a sheep also perceived, in profound silence, what was happening to him, and he is found to have been patient, as though he were already the one who, like a sheep, was led to slaughter. And as a lamb before the one shearing it is without a voice, so he did not open his mouth.

O you also, holy Isaac, reveal to us the great secret of this silence. A little while ago you felt nothing being done to you and were asking your father for a ram; but now you are bound by the hands, placed upon the altar, in a certain manner hung upon the wood, and now you are silent?

“I am silent,” he says.

“Tell us, I beg you, so that we may know why.”

“You wish to know,” he says, “why I am silent now? Because I bear the figure of the one who lays down his life by his will, not by necessity.”

In this great and mystical sacrament of faith, holy Abraham was shown to have been tested, and the son was then delivered.

If you are a soul that desires to follow the footsteps of our father Abraham’s faith, go out from your land and your kindred. Leave your people and your father’s house—that is, faithfully renounce the devil, his pomp, and his angels—and follow the straight path that will lead you to the land where you may grow rich, rise high, and become Abraham’s companion.

But when you have done all this, if the virtue of charity that believes all things is in you, it will still test you and crown you once you have been tested; it will demand from you the sacrifice of your beloved.

What does it demand from you? What was said to Abraham: “Give me your only beloved.”

Wisdom says to you: “My son, give me your heart.” That is the only beloved. Why are you afraid to offer your heart? Offer to the Lord your God the sacrifice of a contrite heart, and say with the prophet: “You will not delight in burnt offerings. The sacrifice acceptable to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise.”

Fear nothing when such a sacrifice has been offered. It will be acceptable to you, and what you have offered will remain whole.

It is now pleasing to contemplate another virtue of charity that overcomes all things, which, as we know, we assigned above to the people of Israel and to our fathers. For its voice is heard in that prophetic verse: “In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you delivered them.”

They themselves were commanded to flee from Egypt, and a land flowing with milk and honey was promised to them. They crossed the Red Sea and came into the wilderness. The hope of charity led them, so that they might learn to love God freely.

The reward of faith was given to them; for he who deigns to make himself a debtor cannot fail to repay. After the wilderness, honey flowed from the rock; they ate the bread of heaven. They were not deprived of what they had hoped for and desired; they also received the promised land.

Let the soul arise that has been seized by the virtue of this charity. Let it flee from Egypt—that is, from desire for this world—and proceed to the Red Sea, namely, the baptism of Christ; it is called red because it has been cleansed by Christ’s blood.

Let enemies pursue you—namely, sins together with their author, the devil. Let them rage as they did from Egypt with their king Pharaoh; let them pursue those who flee. Why are you afraid? They will rage only as far as the water. You will enter, and they will enter after you; but when the water turns back, it will be their destruction and will bring you salvation. It will overwhelm them and wash you; it will condemn them and deliver you.

After this you will receive honey from the rock, with which you will satisfy your hunger and thirst. For the rock was Christ, and from his commands, as from springs of sweetness, you will be satisfied. You will also taste the bread, namely the one who says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.”

You will taste and see that the Lord is sweet. And if the virtue of charity that hopes all things rises high in you, you must pass through the wilderness—that is, you must use this world as though you did not use it, and recognize that you are a stranger in this life, if you desire to enter the promised land. This is the land of which the prophet sings and says: [Col. 1132A] “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

The final virtue of charity remains: it endures all things and never fails. We know that this virtue belongs to our Head himself, the Lord Jesus Christ, and therefore it is placed last, since Christ is the end of the law.

How much he himself endured for us, I think your charity cannot fail to know. Nevertheless, I shall say something about it—if, indeed, I can say anything worthy of so great a subject.

First, there is the fact that God became man; that the Word became flesh; that he did many good things and suffered evil; that he raised the dead and died; that with that singular patience he endured the devilish tempter and the betraying disciple; that he endured Judas himself as a thief before he endured him as a traitor; and that, before experiencing bonds, the cross, and death, he did not deny him the kiss of peace from his deceitful lips.

But how much did he endure in death itself? He endured the flames of hatred and the tongues that served an evil heart. The Jews cried out, “Crucify, crucify!” And, so that the Jews might remain guilty, the innocent Son of God was crucified by them.

He is led to the cross; he who is the palm of victory is struck on the face; he who came to break the thorns of our sins is crowned with thorns; he who frees the bound is tied; he who raises up the fallen is hung upon the wood; the fountain of life is given vinegar to drink; discipline is beaten; salvation is wounded; life dies; life is killed by death for a time, so that death might be killed by life forever.

What did the Jews gain from this death of Christ? They rejoiced as though victorious, and while they feared losing an earthly and perishable kingdom, they did not hesitate to kill the King of heaven and earth.

But they did not emerge victorious as they thought. For if they conquered, how did they lose the kingdom? How have they remained servants to this day?

This, indeed, was the reason Christ was killed by them. For, as the evangelist relates, the rulers of the Jews said among themselves: “You see,” they said, “that the whole world has gone after him. If we let him live, the Romans will come and take away from us both our place and our kingdom.” And they killed Christ, and lost both their place and their kingdom.

What did it profit you, O mad Jews, to commit so great a crime? Because you did not wish to serve Christ the Lord as was fitting, did you become anything other than wicked servants of Christ’s good servants? Through them he crushes your obstinacy; through them he scatters your plans; through them he brings your crimes upon your own heads.

But the Lord himself, whom you killed, wished you to be not servants but free when he said: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.” Yet you rejected God, the Lord, the King, and true freedom itself; indeed, wishing to deny him, you cried out: “We have no king but Caesar.”

But do not even glory in this, that you killed Christ. Rather, it is all over with you, and you do not know it. Hear the Lord himself speaking through the prophet: “I slept and began to sleep,” calling the death inflicted by you sleep.

For what kind of death could last three days—especially the death of one who says elsewhere through the same prophet: “Will one who sleeps not rise again?”

“I slept,” he says—“I who have the power to lay down my life. I slept, not because you raged, not because you went mad. I fulfilled what I willed; you remained in your crime.”

Who, brothers, demanded such great things from our God for our redemption and salvation, except charity, which never fails?

O charity, how great are your powers! You brought God down from heaven. O dear salvation, O holy and true charity, as great as you are on earth, so great will you be in heaven! What you can accomplish in this struggle of mortality, while you are still anxious, what will you be able to accomplish in that perfect peace, when you are secure?

Awake, then, every Christian soul. And if the virtue of charity that endures all things rises high in you, imitate the footsteps of your Lord. For Christ, the apostle Peter says, suffered for you, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps.

And if he descended for your sake from his heavenly seat to earthly things, then for your own sake flee earthly things and seek heavenly ones. If the world is sweet, Christ is sweeter; if the world is bitter, Christ endured all things for you.

The Savior himself has become your way. Rise and walk; you have somewhere to go. Do not grow sluggish. But perhaps you ask where you should go? You see the way and ask where this very way leads. To the truth and to life.

If you love truth, if you love life, and desire to come to truth and life, do not stray from the way.

“I see the way,” you say, “and I desire to walk it; but it is bitter. For the way that leads to life is narrow and constricted.”

Christ passed along it, and is it still rough? Old men passed along it; young men passed along it; girls passed along it. They have made smooth for you the way that you fear and dread.

Walk the way, therefore, securely. Walk—what do you fear on this way? Death? Do you fear death when you are running toward life? You are good; you are running well in this life. Death is a door for you, presenting you with life rather than taking life away.

Walk the way—or rather, let the one who became the way for you lead you through himself. For he himself is the way, the truth, and the life.

Say, then, O faithful and devout soul; say confidently, and cry out truthfully with the prophet: “Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth.” Then I shall reach you securely, if I do not abandon your grace to the end.

These things, dearly beloved brothers, which have been spoken to your holiness by the Lord of charity itself, should cling so firmly to your minds and hearts that this same charity may find in you the fruit of works, not merely leaves of praise.

[Col. 1133]

SECOND BOOKLET, OR HOMILY ON THE SECOND SUNDAY OF ADVENT. (C, G)
