[Col. 1133B] From the Gospel reading we are taught from which tribe Christ was to be born. That he would come from the stock of David according to the flesh was foretold in the Psalms in this way: “The Lord swore to David in truth, and he will not disappoint him: ‘From the fruit of your womb I shall place one upon your throne.’”

And again: “Once I have sworn by my holiness: if I lie to David, his seed shall remain forever, and his throne shall be like the sun before me, and like the full moon forever, and like a faithful witness in heaven.”

Likewise, in the Book of Chronicles: “And the word of the Lord came to Nathan the prophet, saying: ‘Go and say to my servant David: Thus says the Lord: I announce to you that the Lord will build a house for himself. And when your days are fulfilled, so that you go to your fathers, I shall raise up your seed after you, who will be among your sons, and I shall establish his kingdom. He himself will build me a house, and I shall make his throne firm forever. I shall be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me; and I shall not remove my mercy from him, as I removed it from the one who was before you. And I shall establish him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and my throne shall be most firmly established forever.’”

Anyone who thinks that all this was fulfilled in Solomon seems to be greatly mistaken. For how is it to be understood of Solomon that it was said: “After you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed after you, who will be among your sons, and I shall establish his kingdom”? Is it believed that this was prophesied concerning that Solomon? Certainly not. He began to reign while his father was still alive. But here it says: “When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed.” From this it is understood that another was promised and sent, one who would be proclaimed as raised up not before David’s death but after his death, who would build the house of the Lord—not from walls made by human hands, but from living and precious stones, that is, from saints and believers.

And let anyone attend to and observe that what follows—“His house shall be faithful, and his kingdom forever before me”—was not prophesied of Solomon. Solomon’s house was filled with foreign women who worshiped idols, and he himself, as king, was seduced by them into idolatry and cast down. Though he had been good at the beginning, he had an evil end.

Who, then, is this one whose house is faithful forever and who was promised to be raised up after David’s death? He is certainly the one of whom David himself, burning with zeal and crying out in the eighty-eighth Psalm, says: “But you have delayed your Christ.”

It is not Solomon, then, nor is it this David; rather, Christ has been deferred.

Behold, it has certainly become clear that the promises mentioned above were fulfilled not in Solomon but in Christ our Lord, who arose from David’s lineage. Concerning him the Lord himself says through Jeremiah: “Behold, days are coming, and I shall raise up for David a righteous Branch; he shall reign as king and shall be wise, and he shall execute judgment and justice upon the earth. In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely; and this is the name by which they shall call him: ‘The Lord our Righteousness.’”

And Isaiah, speaking of Christ, who was born from David’s seed according to the flesh, says in the continuation of his prophecy: “On that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples, the nations shall seek, and his resting place shall be glorious.”

The root of Jesse stands as a sign for the peoples because Christ impresses the sign of the cross upon their foreheads. “The nations shall seek him”—and it is already plainly seen that this has been fulfilled. His tomb is so glorious that, apart from the fact that we who have been redeemed by his death display his glory, the place itself, shining with miracles of its glory, draws the whole world to itself for this reason.

In the Hebrew text it reads: “And his rest shall be glorious”—certainly because, when his flesh died, it did not see corruption, in accordance with the statement of the Psalm: “His soul was not abandoned in Hades, nor was his Holy One permitted to see corruption.”

This is the one who was promised through Nathan from David’s seed, and who was also foretold through the prophet Isaiah in this way: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root.”

This rod from the root of Jesse is the virgin Mary, sprung from the root of David. She bore the flower, the Lord and Savior, concerning whom it also follows: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety. And the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.”

These many gifts of the Spirit are proclaimed concerning him because the Spirit does not dwell in him according to measure, as it does in us; rather, the whole fullness of divinity and of graces is present in him.

This is the one who does not judge according to the sight of the eyes or the hearing of the ears; rather, righteousness is the belt around his loins, and faith the girdle around his kidneys. In his Church the wolf dwells with the lamb—the one, certainly, who used to snatch prey from him but, when converted to him, dwells among the innocent.

In his fold the leopard lies down with the kid: the deceitful mixed together with sinners. There also the calf from the circumcision, the lion from the power of the world, and the sheep from the common people dwell together, because in the faith there is a common mingling of all.

The little child who guides them is certainly the one who humbled himself for us among the little ones. The ox and the lion will eat straw together, because rulers and subject peoples share a common teaching.

The infant delights at the breast over the serpent’s hole, while the nations that once used to preach poisons are converted and, like little children, take delight in hearing the faith of Christ. For the den of the basilisk is the hearts of unbelievers, in which that twisted serpent rested; the weaned child seized it there and led it away captive, so that in his holy mountain, which is the Church, it might do no harm.

Now, because prophetic speech bears witness concerning Christ, who was to be born from Moab, Isaiah himself also testifies: “For I shall place a lion over those who have fled from Moab and over the remnant of the land. Send forth, Lord, a lamb, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.”

From this nation of the Moabites came the immaculate Lamb who takes away the sin of the world and rules over the whole earth. The rock of the desert signifies Ruth, who, deprived by the death of her husband, bore Obed to Boaz; Obed begot Jesse, Jesse David, and from David’s line Christ was born.

By the mountain of the daughter of Zion he either means, historically, the city of Jerusalem itself, or, according to the tropological interpretation, the Church, established upon a watchtower—that is, upon the exalted height of the virtues.

[Col. 1135]

FOURTH BOOKLET, OR SERMON ON THE CIRCUMCISION OF THE LORD. (C, G)

[Col. 1135C] The mystery of the divine Incarnation and the outstanding sacrament of our remembrance are celebrated and honored by us in an annual observance so that the commemoration of so great a benefit bestowed upon us, unworthy as we are, may display it and remind us what we owe to such glory. Therefore, brothers, the more we have heard that the Lord Jesus Christ was mercifully humbled for our sake, the more let us acknowledge him as ineffably glorious. In him the Only-Begotten of God clearly displayed his unconquerable love toward us; for our sake, moved not by necessity but by goodness and pity, he assumed the humility of true flesh and true death.

For what good had we done, brothers, that so great a benefit should be granted us? What good merits of ours were there that the Only-Begotten of God should deign to become human, that the Most High should be sacrificed, [Col. 1135D] that the unfailing Bread of Angels should be suckled at a woman’s breasts, that the King of the ages should suffer insults, that eternal Life should most patiently deign to die?

Consider, then, human being, the condescension of such kindness, so that you may humbly render thanksgiving. Know that you return not honor but insult to divine grace if you begin to doubt the greatness of so great a benefit. Rather, let us believe without any hesitation that all those things we have heard about the Lord Savior’s humility and humanity are true. And therefore, brothers, let us give greater thanks: although we deserved punishment, we received grace; and by that grace it came about that, while death was owed to the lost, life was freely given to the unworthy.

The humility of the Most High Savior brought no injury to him but conferred great increase upon us; it did not cast down the Exalted One but raised up the fallen. For, in order that the Son of God might fully accomplish the work of our redemption, the Creator of all flesh not only deigned naturally to be born of the flesh of the Virgin, in the reality of flesh, and God, the Maker of humanity, to become true man from a human being; he also deigned to be wrapped in swaddling clothes in a most confined manger and carried in human hands.

[Col. 1136D] O glorious goodness of the most merciful God! O exalted humility of the Most High God! The immeasurable One who created a mother for himself was nourished as a little infant by his mother; as a small child he was carried by his parents into his own temple, while, as the great God, he was petitioned in that same temple by holy people; and he commanded a sacrifice to be offered for himself, although, sinless, he had come to be sacrificed for our sins.

[Col. 1137A] Consider, then, human being, what you owe your exalted Creator and your humbled Redeemer. Yet, beloved, the integrity of Christian faith has always held this principle: if we read or hear of anything done by Christ according to the canonical account of the Evangelists, we must first believe without hesitation that the history is true; then, within the historical truth, we must also seek its spiritual meaning.

For when the text of the divine history is believed to be true, Manichaeus is confounded in his severity. Since he does not believe the reality of flesh in Christ the Son of God, he attempts to charge the holy Scriptures, both Old and New, with falsehood. For when that wretched man curses the divine history of the Old Testament, in the New Testament he denies himself the remedy.

He does not wish to believe that human flesh was fashioned by God, or that circumcision of the flesh was commanded by our God to the holy fathers, or that in ancient times a sacrifice of animal flesh was offered to the living and true God, or that the Sabbath was observed by God’s command and will, or that a temple was built for the Lord at God’s command. Thus, because he does not distinguish the character of the times in the holy Scriptures, he rejects and despises the saving truth of the Lord’s Incarnation.

Therefore, so that Manichaeus may be defeated by the clearest reasoning—and, once defeated, may God grant that he be converted—let us defend the truth of the Old Testament from today’s Gospel reading, so that from this we may most plainly prove that the God of both the Old and the New Testaments is one.

Behold: as the holy Evangelist relates, we have learned that Christ the Son of God was truly born a human being, that Christ the Son of God was truly circumcised, and that a sacrifice of flesh was offered for Christ the Son of God according to the custom then established by divine institution. Both circumcision of the flesh and the rule of carnal sacrifices are known to have been instituted in the Old Testament.

Why, then, beloved, should it not most justly be believed that in the Old Testament humanity was fashioned by God’s hands, when in the New Testament the Only-Begotten Son of God himself became true man for us, so that humanity might not perish forever? Why should it not be believed that God also commanded circumcision of the flesh to be performed at the appropriate time as a sign of something, when the Son of God caused it to be performed in his own body? Why, moreover, should it not be believed that our God formerly commanded the Jewish people to offer typical sacrifices of flesh, when God himself, the Only-Begotten, born in time from the Jews, deigned in the flesh to sacrifice himself for our sins?

[Col. 1137D] Let Manichaeus, then, attend to the utterly clear and perfectly harmonious truth of both Testaments, and, converted, cast away his folly. Let him see in the Old Testament the signification of future things, and in the New the revelation of things past. Let him see Christ as the God of both Testaments: in the Old Testament promising what he was going to manifest, and in the New manifesting what he had promised—not false in his promise, nor deceitful in his gift, but everywhere good, everywhere just, everywhere holy, everywhere powerful, everywhere merciful.

In the Old Testament he is the all-powerful Creator of flesh and the human soul; in the New, the most merciful taker-up of that same flesh and soul—as though at first he were the maker of flesh and soul, and afterward the savior of flesh and soul. Let Manichaeus hear these things, compare them, acknowledge them, and believe; and, believing, return to the Catholic Church, in which he may find the benefit of true salvation.

Through the things the Lord did while established in the body, he not only deigned to demonstrate the harmony of both Testaments; he also wished beneficially to instruct Christian conduct, so that what we behold as having been done bodily in him for our salvation, we too might imitate spiritually.

Therefore Christ was born as a little child on earth, so that the Christian might learn humility. For this reason he was also subject to his fleshly parents, so that every Christian might always show honor to father and mother. Christ was wrapped in cheap garments so that the Christian might not be distinguished by costly clothing. Christ wished to appear poor on earth so that Christian rich people might learn not to love earthly wealth, but, by distributing alms to the poor, might be able to store their riches in heaven.

By the circumcision that the Son of God received in the flesh, he foreshadowed the circumcision of our heart in the spirit. This circumcision the legal word enjoins upon us, as Moses says: “Circumcise the foreskin of your heart, and be circumcised for the Lord your God.” The blessed apostle Paul agrees with this command, saying: “For the one who is a Jew outwardly is not a Jew, nor is circumcision outwardly in the flesh; rather, the one who is a Jew inwardly is a Jew, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; its praise is not from human beings but from God.”

[Col. 1138C] Accordingly, Christ had circumcision in his body so that the Christian might have it spiritually in his heart. For this reason he who could have no sin at all removed the foreskin of his flesh, so that we might cast away desires of wickedness.

Christ, therefore, was carried by hand to the temple so that the Christian might ascend into heaven through good works. Christ wished a sacrifice to be offered for him so that the Christian might offer himself at the Lord’s altar. Above all, let him hasten to offer himself to God by living well, and take care to present himself as a pure sacrifice before divine eyes. For in the sacrifice offered for Christ we recognize that a certain spiritual sacrifice is signified for us.

“A pair,” he says, “of turtledoves and two young pigeons.” In this kind of bird, beloved brothers, a great sacrament of the Catholic faith is commended to us: in the dove, love is recognized, and in the turtledove, chastity is found. The turtledove preserves undefiled fidelity to one mate, while the dove does not abandon the unity of its fellow inhabitants.

The Christian, therefore, truly becomes a spiritual turtledove if he preserves the true faith of the Trinity with firm belief and rejects the sense of heretical depravity as the defilement of fornication. He will then be a dove if he remains patiently to the end in the Catholic fellowship and stands with immovable firmness against the scandals of temptation, so that neither heretical fornication may corrupt the chastity of faith in his heart, nor bitter dissension destroy the unity of ecclesiastical love.

For this is the Catholic Church: it reserves its faith for the one God as for a lawful husband, and multiplies the gathering of many in love. In this turtledove and dove, beloved brothers, remain diligently; preserve this love among you all, so that neither an Arian may violate it, nor a Donatist trample it down, nor a Manichaean defile it. For these men, like evil hawks, wish to destroy the unity of the dove and desire to violate the chastity of the turtledove.

For the Manichaean does not believe that Christ had true flesh; the Arian diminishes the true divinity in him; the Donatist destroys the unity of the Catholic body. The Manichaean does not see the sacrament of the Redeemer; the Arian does not consider the greatness of the Savior; the Donatist, like a ravening wolf, does not hesitate to scatter the good shepherd’s flock.

These men, then, as I have said, like evil hawks wishing to kill the wretched who are greedy for vanity or ignorant of the truth, persecute the love of the dove and curse the chastity of the turtledove. Those whom they can, they either devour with their mouths or tear with their claws—that is, they corrupt them with arguments or torture them through persecution.

[Col. 1139B] Therefore, beloved brothers, guard Catholic truth in faith and preserve Catholic peace in love. For the one who preserves brotherly love and the true sacrament of the Catholic faith offers a sacrifice pleasing to God: there one God and one Trinity are worshiped; the Father is not greater than the Son, nor is the Son less than the Father according to divinity; the Son is proclaimed, and the substance of the Holy Spirit is not separated from them, for by nature he is one God with the Father and the Son.

For the power of the holy Trinity is one, since one natural substance remains in three persons. There is one power because there is one majesty; one dominion of the Creator because there is one condition of creation. Whatever the Father created, he fashioned through the Son and established in the Holy Spirit.

The Son was born from the Begetter; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the One who remains. Yet in being born the Son did not divide the Father, nor in proceeding did the Spirit diminish God. For the Son was not diminished by abiding with him as he was born, nor was the Holy Spirit separated by proceeding; rather, the blessed Trinity remains in itself, because unity remains there substantially. And since nothing created exists in the divinity of the Trinity, nothing there is separated.

[Col. 1140B] Hold these things faithfully, beloved brothers; remain constantly in them. Let this be your thought in the heart and this your confession in the mouth. Hold the faith you received in the name of the Trinity; preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace, so that spiritually you may always be turtledoves and doves in the house of God.

[Col. 1139]

FOUR SERMONS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE, NOW FIRST PUBLISHED BY THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS CARDINAL MAI.

(*Spicilegium Romanum*, vol. VIII.) (C, G, S)*

EDITOR’S NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING SERMONS

A long time ago I began collecting unpublished sermons of the ancient Fathers of the Church—Latin and Greek, and also written in Syriac and Arabic, though often derived from a Greek source. Accordingly, both in my collection of ancient writers, and in the classical authors, and also in this *Spicilegium*, I have published some items as occasion arose and, so to speak, for the sake of offering a taste; so now too I have been pleased to place four sermons of the great Augustine at the end of this volume. I sampled them five years ago from very ancient parchment manuscripts, sometimes not from a single copy but from several repeated exemplars. I believe them still to be unpublished, after the distinguished work of the Maurists and after the additions published at Vienna, Florence, Cassino, Rome, and Paris, which I have found reliable and examined.

The first, on Peter walking upon the sea at the Lord’s command, has testimony from that Possidius who lived with the blessed Augustine for nearly forty years and composed his life and a catalogue of his writings. For, among the blessed man’s sermons, he records this one under a title of the following kind: “On the Gospel reading in which Peter walked upon the sea at the Lord’s command.” Relying both on these words of Possidius and on the authority of a very ancient manuscript, I have absolutely no doubt that this is a genuine sermon of Augustine.

Possidius testifies that Augustine preached on the usefulness of fasting; that he did so many times is certain, as the years came around. One of these sermons appears in the Maurist edition, volume VI, page 613. This other one of ours should be accepted as another, which we place second, found in six ancient codices, and whose title is *How Much Fasting Is Worth*.

[Col. 1141] The third, *On the Wedding at Cana of Galilee*, has been preserved in a very ancient manuscript. Its first page, long since worn and fading, I restored as far as chemical aids allowed, and read with much labor and patience; yet not so completely that it is without several lacunae, which I scarcely think can ever be filled. I did compare this sermon with Augustine’s treatises eight and nine on John, where the same subject is developed; but in truth our sermon here is entirely different. Likewise, Bede, in his commentary on Paul’s First Epistle to Timothy, chapter IV—which, as we know, he pieced together from Augustine’s works—had before his eyes not our sermon but those works on John.

Nevertheless, anyone who has even a little familiarity with the style of blessed Augustine, especially in his sermons, will without doubt place the treatise we have in hand among the genuine works. Besides, who would not recognize as proceeding from Augustine’s mouth the things said at the very beginning against the Manichaeans?

Finally, the fourth sermon, entitled *On the Daily Mass*, likewise bears Augustine’s name in a very ancient exemplar. It appears to have been delivered while pagans and Jews were still living among Christians. Neither the subject, therefore, nor the period, nor, unless I am mistaken, the style itself prevents us from believing that it is the work of the author whose name the sermon bears in its title. For it is also established that Possidius did not include all of Augustine’s treatises in his catalogue.

As for the several gaps and the obscure or uncertain readings, especially in this sermon and the preceding one, let no one, I beg, be surprised: while preparing the edition I did not have the present opportunity to consult the original manuscript. I hope to remedy this inconvenience later.

For the present, this is all. Later I shall explain this matter and others more fully, and also thank those who have aided—or will aid—me by their favor in these labors and investigations.

SERMON ONE. On the Gospel in which Blessed Peter Endured a Storm at Sea in a Boat. Matthew 14:22 ff.

[Col. 1141A]

When a swallow trains its fledglings to fly, it lets them go for a little while in the air, yet remains nearby lest they fall in fear, since they are still weak at flying. So also our Savior Jesus Christ sent his disciples, like tender chicks from their quiet nests, onto the waves of the sea to test them.

But when the sea-storm began to disturb the wings of their devotion and the windy tempest to scatter them, he who commands the wind is powerful enough to follow the boat. He made himself a most powerful one-footed creature [Note: The lexicographers should note the word. It is so called because of its speed. Compare Du Cange, under *Monopedae*.], a singular chariot, making a roadway wondrous in its tracks—not adorned with marble but painted with waves, not with stones [Col. 1141B] but with feet.

He does not go far away who has piously gone ahead. They walked alone and not alone, to be tested, proved, and visited. He found an opportunity, like a clever burglar-breaker who stirs up a storm and does not love calm weather. As though the master were absent, he tests the disciples, inflates the winds, raises the sea, and does not see the governor who follows.

In the master’s absence, an *argutatum* [reading uncertain] shipwreck befalls the servants without cause [Note: The manuscript appeared to read *argutatum*. Understand it as “leaping up” or “surging”; [Col. 1142C] unless you prefer *agitatum* (“shaken”) or something else.], but the boat is held fast by piety. Meanwhile they stretch out their hands, pour forth tears, lower the sails; ropes and cables creak, so that Peter may be released and the devil bound.

When they cry out, they say, “Lord, are you our Savior? You sent us ahead and dismissed us. Behold the shipwrecked man: where are you, most powerful helmsman? Behold the storm: where is your mercy? Behold, the sea roars: where are you, Lamb of God, who [Col. 1141C] took away the sins of the world?”

Immediately the Lord arrives, smiling mercifully upon the tender chicks. He scatters the disturbing winds, comes in power, speaks kindly, and wisely restores his own. They see and are troubled, those who had been troubled because they did not see.

O indescribable things, my brothers! Everywhere there is fear—either because of danger or because of the miracle. But he removed their fear, because he calmed the storm. “Do not,” he says, [Col. 1142A] “be afraid; it is I.”

Great consolation comes to them through the interpretation of the Lord’s person. “Lord,” they cry, “we are safe if it is you; we are not afraid if it is you.”

And Peter says: “I can do what you are doing, if it is you. But prove to me truly that it is you, and command me to come upon the waters, if it is you. ‘Lord, to you I have spoken’: I did not presume without you. ‘If you command,’ I said; but if you help, then what I said will be done. If you do not help, do not command; but if you help, deign to command, and command me to come to you upon the waters.”

And the Lord replies: “Come to me, if you presume upon me.”

The Lord, joyful and kindly in countenance, favors and awaits his fisherman, his confessor, his bold disciple, his leader, his great companion, his first carbuncle and precious stone. He does not await him from far away but nearby, because of his mercy.

[Col. 1142B] The sea, then, steals Peter away as he trembles. The sea sensed faith failing in Peter and began to roar with a greater tongue of waves. What had been firm is loosened, because the foundation of faith had been loosened. As wax is melted by the heat of the sun, so the foundation was dissolved; and as wax melted by the sun becomes fluid, so the softened wave began to slacken.

Peter sensed the rock of the sea wavering [Note: The manuscript reads “flying about.”], already weak and flowing. With his footsteps sinking and his limbs trembling, he stretches out his hands, cries aloud, and says: “Help me, Lord, and have mercy on me. Without you I am always afraid. In the boat and upon the wave I presumed to come to you. Why am I being taken away from you? Help me; bring me back to the boat. Come aboard with me; I will come with you.”

The Lord of hosts who is with us, the God of Jacob our protector, lifted Peter up, strengthened him, made him walk without fear, restored the trembling disciples, restrained the storm, [Col. 1142C] and guided the little boat. May he calm his own bride, our mother, the Church; and amid this storm may we always have as our helmsman the one whom Peter had as his defender! Amen.

SERMON II. How Much Fasting Is Worth

Moses fasted in the wilderness for forty days and forty nights [Col. 1143A] so that he might deserve to receive the Lord’s law. Fasting obtained what a full belly despaired of obtaining.

Finally, beloved brothers, consider the difference between fasting and fullness, between an empty stomach and lungs heated by feasting. Moses, because he fasted, saw the Lord; but the people, because they ate and drank, fashioned idols.

Why should I speak of Moses and the Israelite multitude? Adam himself, the head of our race, remained in paradise as long as he did not eat; as soon as he ate, he was expelled from paradise. He who had been a virgin in God’s paradise, once expelled from paradise came to know his wife. For wantonness is always joined to fullness; the limbs of gluttony and lust lie close to each other, and according to the order of the limbs, the order of vices is chosen.

[Col. 1143B] Holy Elijah, whom the elements served, who had shut up heaven for three years and six months, at whose voice fire descended from above—when Jezebel wished to kill him and, exhausted, he lay beneath a shady tree in the wilderness, an angel was sent to him and ordered him to take a little bread and water. For he was about to travel through the desert to Mount Sinai in a forty-day fast.

Could the almighty Lord, who made heaven and earth and whose creature everything is, not have sent honey-wine or wine through an angel, or seasoned foods, or delicacies from the sea, or the delights of birds? But he knew that his prophet could not otherwise conquer the devil’s temptations unless he were trained by fasts.

Food expelled us, beloved brothers, from paradise; hunger may lead us back. That Daniel, who knew future things and was the clearest preacher of the Lord’s coming and the overthrow of Jerusalem, was called “a man of desires” because he did not eat the bread of desire or drink the drink of lust; for he desired Christ more than banquets.

John, the Lord’s forerunner, was nourished in the wilderness on locusts, not on the flesh of animals or the delicacies of birds. Certainly he could have procured for himself the delights of fish beside the streams of the Jordan; but since he was to preach repentance, he ought by his example to teach a doctrine of severity and fasting more than by his voice.

When a demon-possessed man was brought before the Lord, one whom the apostles had been unable to cleanse, they asked and heard: “This kind is expelled only by prayers and fasts.”

[Col. 1143D] See, brothers, how great is the power of fasts, since fasts can do what the apostles could not. Let old things be set aside; let each person consider and weigh for himself how great the difference in prayer is between an empty stomach and one that has been fed, between a flushed face and pale lips, between untainted saliva and lips loosened by drunken excess, between a mind oppressed by feasting and one kept watchful by the thinness of hunger.

I do not speak of doubled or multiplied fasts; I do not speak of weeks. Let us at least pass individual days without the luxury of food. Let baths, wines, and delicacies cease—not because we judge God’s creation deserving of condemnation, but so that we who have lived for ourselves throughout the year may at least be able to live for God for a few days, with the help of him who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

SERMON III. On the Gospel in which the Lord Made Wine from Water. John, chapter 2

Weddings at which Christ reclined both as giver of gifts and as guest: giver of gifts, that is, in their origin; guest, having become one of their kind, so that he who at the beginning of the new union had granted that a human being should be born from a human being might himself also deign to be born from a virgin. [lacuna]

Our ears have now been struck by the sound of the holy Gospel: “On the third day,” it says, “a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there; Jesus also was invited with [Col. 1144B] his disciples to the wedding.”

If the hidden and shameful depravity of the Manichaeans’ pleasure should inquire about weddings, it says, “God did not make them.” If, then, God did not make weddings, how did Christ sit as an invited guest at one with his disciples?

But now let us fan away the cloud of this obscure mystery. “On the third day,” it says, “a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee.” When, therefore, the day of the Trinity shone upon the world darkened by the obscuring of sins, Christ came to the wedding.

At that time the soul, which had already been rubbed raw through companionship with the mud, having been changed through the fornication of the enticing fruit into an adulterous husband, celebrates the wedding of a polluted fellowship. Hear Paul, again fearing the bonds of this evil union: “I fear,” he says, “that just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity and chastity that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

While, therefore, the devil and the soul were wantonly sporting in the apparatus of a single reclining place [Note: Perhaps for *stramentum*, “bedding” or “covering”?], Jesus was invited. [lacuna] while they had run out of the wine of lust.

But the mother of Christ—the woman who shrank from the pact of criminal intercourse [Note: Thus the manuscript: *facinus, facineris*, like *pignus, pigneris*.] and remained a virgin not only in body but also in mind—was present as an invited guest: present by the condition of her birth, not by participation in crime; by the universality of being born, not by fellowship in sin; she who would consent [lacuna] to Christ, not to the world’s pleasure.

This mother of Christ, therefore, moved by pity for the world’s long labor—she who knew that she had drawn from the vine of faith a great [lacuna] cluster—began to request wine from her own offspring. When she believed the angel, she then interceded for the world; then she began to plead the world’s cause, [Col. 1144D] when she did not tremble at the message: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

At once, propagated from the seed of the Holy Spirit in the virginal grove, the first vine blossomed. Shaded by heavenly coverings, it put forth branches [lacuna] and produced a hidden cluster. Salvation hung at the summit of faith, and the cluster swelled [lacuna]. Behold, afterward, from the womb of the mother, a bunch of divine offspring, animated [lacuna], was born.

Christ, the true cluster, contained within himself the wine of life [lacuna] the press of the cross had drawn near. His mother says: “They have no wine.”

O most wise virgin! You have only now deserved to produce your blossoming offspring, and already [lacuna] to press the cluster? Indeed, a shoot can only confront another shoot and resist its own branch.

But he who plucked punishment from the tree must await healing on the wood; and he who plucked the forbidden fruit from the tree must await [Note: *Expectare* appears for *spectare* (“look toward”) in other manuscripts as well. Unless it is preferable to write *expectare a cruce*, “await from the cross.”] the cross, so that where he had drawn [lacuna] dryness, there he might receive the drink of salvation.

“They have no wine,” he says. Attend, virgin, for a little while: let the Jew prepare the wood; let the nail descend into the cluster, and [lacuna] wine will be possible.

Why do you hurry to the winepress before the time, when Judas has not yet pressed his insolent heel upon the grape? For he is that Judas, destroyer of the sacred vintage, who, having agreed for thirty pieces of silver, sold the cluster of the divine offspring to the Jews [lacuna], and sold it to the impious [Note: Thus the manuscript.].

Concerning him it had already been sung in the Psalms: “For even the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has magnified his heel against me.”

A sure day will come, virgin, when your fruit will be pressed and a sword will pass through your own soul, when it is fulfilled concerning the hanging cluster that you had poured forth from the root [Note: The manuscript reads *botruo*. In this sermon, and elsewhere in Augustine, *botruus* and *botruum* occur occasionally, though not consistently.].

“They have no wine.” And Jesus: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” [lacuna]

Certainly it was not the hour of fate [Note: Augustine frequently wrote against the doctrine of fate.], but of desire; not imposed by necessity but bestowed by will [lacuna]; not the hour in which he would be compelled to die, but in which he would deign to die for the world.

“What is there between me and you, woman? Have you forgotten your mother? [lacuna] Do you discern your power? [lacuna; surviving fragment uncertain.] There is no communion between you and your mother? Or [lacuna; surviving fragments uncertain.] Do you designate yourself Creator? Or do you believe [lacuna; surviving fragments uncertain.]”

Here Christ exalted his divinity above his mother. He did not deny his mother, nor did he deny that he had been born from flesh; but he subjected his mother to his majesty. And therefore he says: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.”

In the miracle, divinity is proclaimed higher than the mother; in the hour, however, the sharing of death is intimated.

Meanwhile Christ intoxicates insipid draughts [Note: Observe the beautiful word.]. Tasteless water was poured into the jars, and intoxicated rivers were drawn out. What is this conversion so sudden? In water wine is born; in the wave flavor secretly arises. Sweetness sprouts in wines, and nowhere does a vine bear fruit; no grape is pressed, yet wines boil without a branch.

O great beauty of the miracle! The powers of the divine command are inserted, and fruit is born in water. What Christ did in the liquid is what he does at the appointed time in the vine.

For who else marries a root to rain? Who else, through the hidden fibers of its veins, knots together starry branches? Who else fattens swollen clusters, gemmed as though at their tips, except the one who brings forth and multiplies all things? Thus what is compressed in the seed is spread through the shoot, and what lies hidden in the grain grows wild in the leaf.

Meanwhile the Church, which had lain polluted at the world’s table with a foreign husband, is suddenly endowed by Christ with draughts. The wedding passes over to Christ. For the one who avoided her is the one who endowed her. Christ seized the banquet, and the Church changed husbands. Christ fed her, and the enemy was excluded. He mixed the drink of his blood and took her as his wife.

“I have betrothed you,” the apostle says, “to one man, to present a chaste virgin to Christ.”

Behold, she who was once fertile is now beautiful; once adulterous, now a married woman. She stands at God’s right hand in a golden garment, clothed in varied adornment, cleansed through water, made purple through blood, made radiant through the Lord’s resurrection, and adorned with the varied precious gems of grace [Note: Note the word again, unless it means “variegated.”].

And as Scripture says: “His eyes are bright with wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk.” Let us therefore drink his wine with his milk, if we wish to become beautiful in faith, to shine white in virtue, and to radiate in the adornment of the holy Church.

Receive another great mystery from a small one. At one time Judea also had no wine at its banquet, because it did not receive the gift of the sacred blood; and while it was married to the law, it found nothing at all to drink.

Christ came and changed the law into grace—the former puffing up, the latter helping. He poured the cup of blood into the law and made a banquet by dying.

The chief steward, that is, the Lord of the world, tasted the water made wine and said: “Every person first sets out the good wine, and when people have become drunk, the inferior; but you have kept the good wine until now.”

For the law too is holy, as a holy, just, and good commandment. But the law and the prophets prophesied until John; and therefore, when the Lord came, the Mosetic wines failed, and the wines of blood flowed forth. The former reached their end; the latter took their beginning.

Finally, this is the beginning of the signs that Jesus performed, when, having been killed, he fed the nations, and, having been wounded, made a banquet from the wine of his blood.

This cluster, which had sprung up in the promised land, or in the soil of virginity, a Jew once fixed upon a carrying-pole [Note: Numbers 13:24. Africans in particular used *palanga* or *phalanga* for a pole, according to Pliny as cited by Forcellini.] as a forewarning of the future cross, beneath which it would bend, not from which it would be refreshed.

For the Psalm had already spoken beforehand concerning them: “Let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and bend their back continually.”

Two men therefore carried the cluster, one in front and the other behind; the offspring of the budding branch hung between them. [Col. 1146D] The first signified the Jewish people; the second represented the people of the nations.

The Jew went ahead, certainly, but turned his back toward the cluster. The Gentile walked behind, but looked upon the cluster with the eyes of faith, because he believed in the one hanging there.

“They set their backs toward me,” the Lord says concerning the Jews, “and not their faces.” The first turned away; the second was nourished. The former labored beneath the burden of sin; the latter drank from heaven.

Thus the cluster was behind for the Jew, but before for the Gentile: for them at the end, for us at the beginning; it followed them to punishment, but invited us to food.

And so they were dried up and withered, while we ate, drank, and were refreshed, through Jesus Christ himself, who lives with the Father and with the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

SERMON IV. On the Daily Mass
The assembly of your blessedness, dearest brothers, fills us with immense joy. But because my breast trembles, bound by the chains of the body, I cannot express how much the splendor of your spirit delights me to hear. Nevertheless I begin, so that, as an earnest given by God, shining more brightly, and as a pledge of the most splendid light radiating, my sense may palpitate as I speak [Note: [Col. 1147D] This is how it appeared in the manuscript, which I presently have no opportunity to inspect again.]. I ask you to implant in your ears, [Col. 1147B] my brothers, the duties of a priest, through which he will not cease, by the compassion of mercy, to bring forth distress [Note: [Col. 1147D] That is, to create trouble through his zeal.], as the apostle Paul says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” But he said this to those who still held in their hearts the plantings of a newly begun faith and the first fruits of an as-yet-immature belief. Yet, by God’s favor, because the prerogative of faith grows old among you in such a way that it is also new [Note: This is an archaic spelling; compare below, *illut*, *aliut*.], it retains its newness in order to be old: for it is written thus: “Good wine grows old, and is drunk with sweetness.” Nevertheless, I could not conceal what had been cleansed for a long time [Note: [Col. 1148D] This is how it appeared in the manuscript.]. I did not wish to see what I would mourn; I did not wish to see what I would grieve. I cry out because I am a shepherd, not a hireling, who, on seeing the wolf, flees and abandons the sheep to perish. I cry out because I fear; I cry out because I grieve: for by crying out I both excuse myself, [Col. 1147C] and do not lose you. For if I remain silent, I neither excuse myself nor preserve you. God says through the prophet Isaiah: “Cry out,” he says, “in your strength, and do not spare; raise your voice like a trumpet, announce to my people their sins and to the house of Jacob their crimes.” For your devotion has grown so cold, my brothers, that I both perceive and fear this. What the Lord says—“Because iniquity abounds, the love of many grows cold”—I think is fulfilled in your devotion. For while you pursue sitting in your homes, you make the house of God deserted.

And hear how, through the prophet, divine indignation of this kind rebukes the minds of all. Hear, Christian, what you should fear; hear, reverent one, what you should avoid: “Because [Col. 1147D] his house is deserted, therefore heaven will withhold the rains, and the earth will not give its fruit, and I will bring the sword upon the works of human hands,” because God is not heard in the churches. Who, my brothers, attentive to this, would not tremble to his very vitals? Who, struck by such great threats, would not wither, when he hears the Lord indignant because you make his house deserted, “and the house of prayer is empty of a devout assembly”? The street is full of people, and the church is silent. Certainly, prudent man, you are not being told to gather at the house of God every hour. If at the morning offices [Col. 1148A] there is scarcely one hour, and on feast days scarcely two hours, behold how little your creator demands from you. And you do not wish to be blessed? You want heaven and earth, the sea, and all the elements to serve you at all times, and you do not wish to devote one hour or two hours to the Lord’s worship? Let your laziness, then, be corrected, so that the earth may not lose its offspring. The sword will be brought upon the works of their hands, because God is not heard in the churches.

Our laziness condemns us, my brothers. The Jew hurries to the synagogue in the morning; the pagan hastens and keeps vigil at the temple; yet the Christian neither keeps vigil nor hastens to the church. Great is the disgrace of Christians, who are urged to come to the house of God by the example and consideration of something worse, so that perhaps a Jew may be more observant in his sacrilege [Col. 1148B] than a Christian devoted in his religion. The pagan keeps watch, profane before idols, while the Christian neither keeps watch nor hastens to the church for whom Christ was crucified. Therefore God chastises the earth, so that a human being may receive discipline: so that the human being may be corrected, the earth may give [lacuna] to say. “You make my house deserted, and I will make your land deserted. You do not give me honor by coming to me, and I will cut off your labor; for,” he says, “whoever honors me, I will also honor.”

But perhaps you will say to me: “I am rich and abound in every resource; I lack nothing. What can I ask for?” Are you rich, then, from yourself? Or were you born with riches? Rather, the richer you are, the more you must hasten toward him whose riches they are, because he says: “The gold and silver are mine, [Col. 1148C] and I will give them to whomever I wish.” Do you possess anything that you did not receive? If, then, you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it? Certainly, if you received it, you possessed nothing, because naked you came forth from your mother’s womb into this world, covered with rags, exhausted by the utmost poverty, and already destined to die just as you were born. You have the blessed Job as a witness, saying: “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb; naked I must go into the earth.” You run to the house of the moneylender, you compose flattering words, and you do not run to the house of God, the generous giver without charge? What such great laziness is there among you, my brothers, that you do not keep watch at the house of God? I say to you, whoever you are, rustic idler: you are too lazy to come to the house of God, yet you are not too lazy to cultivate your land? And unless he gives you rain from above, you will not be able to break open the earth. [Col. 1148D] It will be able to provide you nothing of its own unless it receives it from above. For it is written: “It descends from above, from the Father of lights,” with whom there is no change or shadow caused by alteration. And it is likewise written in the Gospel: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.” Therefore, my brothers, you must keep watch for the church of God. This is what God expects: that you confess to him alone, and there is no delay in your being healed, since he seeks only your confession. Here ends.

[Col. 1149]

# THE FINAL CHAPTER OF THE *SOLILOQUIES* ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT AUGUSTINE, BROUGHT OUT OF DARKNESS BY J. TROMBELLI (C)

## JOHN CHRYSOSTOM TROMBELLI TO THE READER

[Col. 1149A] We know indeed that the book entitled Augustine’s *Soliloquies* was not composed by Augustine, bishop of Hippo and most distinguished Doctor of the Church; but we also know that it came from a praiseworthy writer. It will therefore, I think, be agreeable to the reader if we publish what we found appended to that little book [Col. 1150A] in a manuscript which the most noble and exceptionally gracious man Faustinus Avogadro, Count of Brescia, sent me as a gift from his select library. In many places, indeed repeatedly, that manuscript differs from the editions of the *Soliloquies*; but we have judged that only the final chapter of that book, which has not yet been published, should be brought forward. As for the value and authority of this addition, however, we leave the judgment to the reader. Here, then, is what we found after those words, “my gray hairs” [Note: [Col. 1149C] Compare our edition of the works of St. Augustine, vol. VI, cols. 863–898. EDITOR.].

## THE FINAL CHAPTER OF THE *SOLILOQUIES* BEGINS

[Col. 1149]

[Col. 1149B] May the merciful God lead you to his sublime things; bring him into your inmost being. For let this be certain for you: you love your sin excessively if, although perhaps you love him supremely, you do not yet love him uniquely—that is, if you seek or receive some other consolation. Consider, then, what it is that in your life you loved most ardently, desired with anxiety, that affected you more pleasantly and delighted, or could delight, you more deeply than everything else. Consider, then, whether you feel the same violence of affection and abundance of delight when you burn with desire for the supreme beloved, when you rest in his love. For there is no doubt that he does not yet possess the bosom of your affection if the goad of your inmost love penetrates your soul less deeply in divine affections, and stirs it less warmly, [Col. 1149C] than it once penetrated or could in some way stir it when drawn along by an affection for something else [Note: [Col. 1150C] Perhaps it should be read *tractu*, “by the drawing along.”]. You too are loved less by him if you are not yet called to those contemplative ecstasies, or have not yet deserved to follow him who calls you. “I no longer call you servants,” he says, “but my friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” [Note: [Col. 1150C] John 15:15.]. The sublimity, then, of divine revelations is a manifest indication that you love or are loved perfectly, if, in the desire for the highest things, you are carried away toward heavenly things and pass over into those anagogical endeavors through an alienation of mind. And whoever wishes to devote himself to this virtue of contemplation must learn to rest not only [Col. 1150B] from evil works but also from useless thoughts. What is needed is compunction and sighs rather than arguments; frequent groans rather than abundant reasonings; tears rather than propositions; prayer rather than reading; the grace of tears rather than literary knowledge; contemplation of heavenly things rather than occupation with earthly things.

O God, light of minds, drive away from me the night of folly, and grant me the day of wisdom. Bring forth truths and the sun of justice from the deepest recesses of your nature, which surpass all understanding, into the heaven of my spirit. Upon the earth of my heart extinguish the images of bodies and the phantasms of my varied thoughts. Create the offspring of your understandings in the womb of my mind. Pour out your Spirit upon [Col. 1150C] the waters of my weakness, so that, turned toward you and conformed to your Son, I may see you in yourself and all things beneath you. O you, purest truth, see yourself in me; understand yourself in me. Through myself I see nothing but vain, fleeting, and perishable things, nor do I see anything but false and bodily forms. Through myself I am nothing but death, a dark and shadowy abyss, and imperfection. In you I am what I am; in you I live what I live; in you I understand what I understand, because you are supreme understanding, supreme essence, supreme life: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a threefold unity, infinite and without end, one God forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1151]

# FOUR SERMONS ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT AUGUSTINE

[Note: [Col. 1151] Of these four sermons, the first two, composed on passages from St. Paul but lacking titles derived from their contents, were supplied by the most learned prefect of the library at Avranches, who, at our request, kindly transcribed them, with immense effort, from manuscript no. 2904, of the ninth or tenth century. At the beginning of this manuscript, in a hand which experts regard as Mabillon’s, is written: “That the readings on Paul’s epistles are Augustine’s.” The two later sermons were excerpted from another manuscript of the same library by M. Félix Ravaisson and inserted into a work entitled *Rapports sur les bibliothèques des départements de l’Ouest*. Paris, 1841. EDITOR.] (C, G, S)

## I.

[Col. 1151A]

“Brothers, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God,” etc. (Colossians 3:1).

Through his gracious clemency, let us faithfully venerate, dearest brothers, the honorable solemnity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and recall to mind his ineffable goodness. He not only assumed human flesh for the sake of our redemption, but also deigned to undergo various kinds of punishment for our salvation. And although, after the long sleep of our sluggishness and laziness, we have been awakened—not unwillingly, but willingly, summoned by the sweetness of holy and Christian religion—at the gathering for this most holy solemnity, let us rise gladly and devoutly, with all attentiveness, [Col. 1151B] according to what the Apostle says in the present reading: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth.”

It is as though he were saying: We, who were created in the image of the holy Trinity and baptized by a threefold immersion through invocation of that same holy Trinity, are renewed according to that same image. And we, who fell especially through a threefold sin into death—that is, through wicked thought, through the delight of the flesh, and through consent to evil works—having been raised three times from the font and having received remission of all sins through Christ’s grace [The source reads *precepta*, “enjoined”; its bracketed correction is *percepta*, “received”.], should rise to life, just as he rose on the third day. But if we desire to rise with Christ, let us first die to the world and to carnal desires, and let us put off the old person—that is, evil will, or wicked practice and the worst pleasures—[Col. 1151C] and let us put on kindness. Let us do good to our neighbors with complete devotion, and after love of the Lord let us place nothing before love of our neighbor, but let us love them as ourselves.

He continues: “Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth”—seeking only heavenly things, not earthly things; dying to the earth but living for the Lord; pursuing heavenly wisdom, not earthly wisdom. For it follows: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” When we have died to the world and to its resources and desires, our life is hidden with Christ in God, because we are sons of the Lord. Hence it follows: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him [Col. 1151D] in glory.” For it is not yet apparent what or what sort of people we shall be at the judgment; but when Christ appears to judge the living and the dead, then we too shall appear together with him [Col. 1152A], to rise in glory. For Christ is born, suffers, and rises for us and on our behalf, so that through him we may be reborn into life, suffer with him in tribulations, and rise with him through virtues.

Everything was restored through him on this night. On this night, as the firstfruits of those who sleep, he rose, so that afterward we might all rise. On this night, therefore, our captivity is released, the life lost in Adam is restored; on this night Adam, the first-formed man, a wanderer, returns to his homeland, paradise. From this night of the Lord’s resurrection onward, paradise is open to all; it is closed to no one except by that person’s own action, and opened to no one except by Christ. Therefore, with all attentiveness, let us beware lest, because of the works of the devil that drag us to destruction, we ourselves close to ourselves the open path of the heavenly kingdom; [Col. 1152B] rather, through works of justice and mercy, let us make the path to the kingdoms of heaven level for ourselves.

Let us therefore recall, in our humility, the humility of our Lord undertaken for us. Let us keep vigil humbly in this night; let us pray humbly to him who has illuminated this night for us with the glory of his name. To him we say: “My Lord, enlighten my darkness.” Let us ask him to grant light to our hearts, so that, just as our joyful eyes behold this splendor of lamps, so with an enlightened mind we may see the illustrious glory of this night. Let us entreat him to hear us keeping vigil at his solemnity—“that they sleep” [*quod dormiunt*, thus in the manuscripts; wording corrupt]—for our salvation.

Let us therefore keep vigil and pray; let us celebrate this vigil outwardly and inwardly. The Lord speaks to us in his readings; let us speak to the Lord in our prayers. If we obediently hear his words, the one whom we ask dwells within us. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## II.

“Brothers, purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, since you are unleavened,” etc. (1 Corinthians 5:7).

The resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, dearest brothers, strengthens our faith when it is believed as an event, and renews its memory when it is solemnly celebrated. Indeed, although Christ rose many years ago, we rightly say, when this solemnity is presented in its annual return: “Today the Lord has risen.” What was done once [Col. 1152D] so that we might be redeemed, therefore, we must observe every year with complete devotion. What was instituted once so that we might not forget it. For whoever desires to celebrate this day worthily must remember what the apostle Paul says in the present reading: “Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, since you are unleavened.” Every leaven of sin must therefore be excluded from our hearts, so that with a pure mind and an upright conscience we may become like unleavened loaves and thus rightly celebrate the Lord’s Passover.

But if we retain the leaven of sin and wickedness in our hearts, we do not deserve to celebrate the Lord’s Passover. Therefore the Apostle says: “Purge out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, since you are unleavened.” We are unleavened if we are strangers to every inscription [or: contamination] of sin. For, as Paul says, a little leaven corrupts the whole lump. Therefore we must purge and cast away from ourselves every leaven of sin, so that we may deserve to enjoy so great a solemnity of Passover. Since the Lord wished to make us participants in so great a Passover, let us pray that we may worthily receive its sacraments, so that [Col. 1153B] we may rightly obtain its blessing.

This is the day of the Lord’s resurrection and the beginning of our redemption; this, I say, is the day that the Lord has made. Let us rejoice and be glad in it. Let us all celebrate it with one voice, a joyful spirit, and a contrite heart; let us express spiritual joy in psalms and hymns, and, in memory of Christ’s passion and resurrection, joy in hope of the future life [Note: [Col. 1153D] The word “joy” appears to be redundant. EDITOR.].

Behold, on this day, when we hear “Alleluia,” our spirit in a certain way rejoices and is wholly suffused with gladness. For “alleluia” means “praise to the Lord on high.” It is fitting for us, therefore, with devoted minds, to sing praise to the Lord on high at all times, but especially on this day—that is, to strive to exalt the Lord our God in praise with voice [Col. 1153C] and heart, not only with the mouth but also through perfect works, so that through him we may deserve to be exalted in heavenly life. He lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, throughout immortal ages. Amen.

## III.

Rejoice, heaven, and be glad; earth. This day has shone upon you more brightly from the tomb than it has gleamed from the sun. Let hell rejoice too, because, when life descended into it, it was released from its wickedness. Let it be glad, because, when the Lord descended into its dwellings, it was visited. Let the human being Adam exult, because after long ages he saw an unknown light and, suffocated among the darkness of profound night, breathed again.

O beautiful light, which sprang forth from the shining summit of heaven and, after the streams of crimson, clothed those sitting [Col. 1153D] in darkness and the shadow of death with sudden brilliance. At once, then, the eternal night of the underworld shone resplendent when Christ descended. The groaning of those who mourned fell silent; the chains of the condemned fell. The stunned minds of the torturers were struck dumb with amazement; the entire impious workshop trembled when it suddenly saw Christ in its own dwellings.

“Who,” they say, “is this, so terrifying and flashing with snowy brilliance? Our Tartarus has never received such a one; the world has never vomited such a one into our cavern. We see a judge, not a suppliant; he has come to fight, not to succumb; to seize, not to remain. Where, do you think, had our gatekeepers been sleeping [Col. 1154A] when this conqueror was assaulting our barriers? If he were guilty, he would not be so bold. If some sins darkened him, he would never disperse our darkness with his own radiance. But if he is God, what is he doing in the tomb? If he is human, why does he release the captives? Has he perhaps made a pact with our ruler? Or has he perhaps attacked and defeated him too, and thus passed into our kingdoms? Certainly he was dead; certainly he was overcome. Our warrior was mocked in the world; he does not know what slaughter he has brought about in the underworld.

“O cross, deceiving your joys and bringing forth our losses! Through the wood we were enriched; through the wood we are overthrown. That power, always feared by all peoples, is perishing. No captive now trembles beneath our slaughter. Behold what must be mourned—and what mocks us. Nowhere are the ancient cries; nowhere do the wailings resound [Col. 1154B]. The murky cave has fallen silent. Do you think he will return without our destruction? No one has ever entered us alive. No one was ever so bold. No one so terrified the executioners. Never has a joyful light appeared in this chasm, blind with black darkness. Has the sun perhaps migrated from the world? Yet neither the heavens nor the stars are subject to us, and nevertheless hell shines.

“What are we to do? Where shall we turn? We cannot defend our bloody dwellings against this one or preserve the guardianship of our cavern. We have been entered to our misfortune. We cannot contain such great light; we cannot overpower one endowed with such great strength. We see our own necks being pressed, and now we fear our own destruction as well. Let us be content with the darkness of our night. Let us hide in our caves. Why are we exposed by the rays? Why are we disturbed by violence? Why [Col. 1154C] are we taken captive in our own dwellings?”

Then Christ directs his battle line against those cruel ministers of punishments themselves, and with the divine sword cuts down the implacable troops. The savage executioners are crushed beneath the torturer, and the more rabid they are, the more they waste away under the forced shrieks. The very caves of the iron bed are entered, and the strong are bound with eternal chains by one stronger than they. The Lord himself had promised this, saying: “No one enters the house of the strong man and plunders his goods unless he first binds the strong man; then he will plunder his goods.”

Then immediately the sad and grieving crowds and peoples, harassed by the squalor of the day, gather and throw themselves at the feet of our Redeemer. Behold, the apostolic words are proved true: “So that at the name of the Lord every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth.” At once, therefore, the captive souls, released from the [Col. 1154D] Tartarean prisons, rush forth and lament before the King of the ages in sorrowful supplication:

“You have come at last, O most merciful Jesus. Help us now and spare the exhausted. Now, Christ, extinguish the savage threats; release the pitiable groans. You redeemed the living by your cross; redeem the dead by your death. The world had perished with us under an equal stain. Every creature sighed for your coming. Our torments sighed for you. This hell always grew pale before you. While you are here, absolve the guilty; when you ascend, defend your own. You alone were able to crush the head of the dragon. You willed to break the bronze gates and iron bars. Let the door be opened, I beg, to those who pray [Col. 1155A]; let gentle light not be absent. And if you return to the body, let the underworld not be deprived of your majesty.”

After these prayers had been heard, after the laws had been established, and after the torturers had been plunged into a deep pit [Read: “of the chasm”?], our Judge today came forth from the underworld crowned with laurel. Nor was the white-robed procession absent; rather, the entire host of the blessed advanced joyfully with its prince. Let the triumphant one therefore return alive once more to the arena, so that the whole world may know that Christ has returned from the underworld. Let believers therefore glory; let every nation clap its hands, because our King has triumphed in the world. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, crucified and resurrected for us, forever and ever. Amen.

## IV. A sermon of the most illustrious doctor, Saint Augustine, dedicated to the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ

[Col. 1155B]

Hail, day to be celebrated in everlasting assemblies. At your rising, life rises again; at your radiance, light returns; and at your birthday, when the darkness of hell has been driven away, the sun of justice revives. God does not indeed die, nor is eternity measured by an end, nor is the light of majesty extinguished; but when death is sought from God, through a human being help is given to the human race.

After the triumphs of the cross, after the victorious standards, Christ, rejoicing, approaches the underworld to conquer death—he who had captured the author of death. O marvelous battle, brothers, and new aspect of recovered victory! Christ conquered by the wood through which the devil had earlier conquered; [Col. 1155C] and he who had struck down others was himself struck down by his own weapons. The punishment itself became for him what had previously been victory.

God therefore fought on behalf of the world, and, concealing his majesty for a little while in order to give the enemy confidence, pretended to possess a weak power. The cause of the world was being conducted through the wisdom of God. He was held as a prisoner, heard as a criminal, beaten and spat upon as ignoble and captive. Yet he concealed and restrained his own powers for this purpose, until, having died, he would conquer the one whom he was preparing to conquer. He restrained his power in order to fulfill all justice in the conflict and complete victory in rising again.

From there he came to the tree from which the laws of death had gone forth. But when he ascended the citadel of crime, there he subjected the enemy’s summit to the power of his own majesty. The one who had once been the mother and origin of punishments, knowing no guilt, received the just man, fastened him, and afflicted him. There is no guilt, yet punishment rages.

“O most cruel executioner of justice, you have lost the supports of your case! The cross itself protests against you; the workshop of death and wound rejects you. ‘I do not recognize as guilty the one whom I punish. These are not the fruits of my own stock; [uncertain: nothing here belongs to me]. You are mistaken, because you graft an alien offspring onto me. This one has nothing from me. Why does he hang upon me? I see the likeness of his appearance, but I do not recognize in him the native poison.’”

Then that strong one in battle, just upon the gibbet, innocent in another’s torture, crushed the horns of sin with clean hands. And when he fastened himself wholly to the wood, he blunted the sting of death and killed the sin that the tree had produced. Blood immediately poured from his side and washed away whatever crime had previously stained the world; and from the polluted little branches the shining cross radiated. Innocent blood ran through the deadly, punitive fibers of the wood, and the sacraments of salvation thereafter sprang forth from the very things that had supplied nourishment to death.

Yet the devil, still unaware, glories in having conquered. He sees the conquered one crucified; he sees him dead, and moreover struck; and, as though rejoicing over a rich slaughter, he is no longer concerned.

“Behold,” he says, “the one who used to present himself as the offspring of God, who had won faith for himself through miracles, who had cast my companions and partners out of human bodies and souls, and who moreover dared to challenge me in battle. He eagerly sought to snatch from my hands the world which from the beginning I hold captive by the law of combat and the right of victory. Now, if he is strong, let him conquer; now, if he prevails, let him rise; now, if he is God, let him come back to life.”

O devil, ignorant of your own end! This victory deceives you; your joys will be not joyful but sorrowful. You armed the tongues of the Jews against your own destruction; you destroyed yourself with those darts. What he suffered, indeed, he willed, and he acted for our benefit. For when you killed the just man, you lost the guilty whom you held. But endure for a little while; do not rejoice too arrogantly or unwisely. For behold, the underworld trembles at the living one whose death you were celebrating. Already he has shattered the ancient prisons; already he has plundered your spoils and afflicted the bloody ministers of your ferocity.

Is this what it means to conquer, or is it rather to transmit life to the dead? Set out the account here, most wicked one; let justice, the mistress, weigh the judgment. [Col. 1156C] From the beginning you put to death the world that you yourself had made guilty; a just vengeance followed the offense committed. But this man had been bound by neither his own guilt nor another’s. Why did you inflict death where you had found no crime? Why did you impose punishment where you could find no offense? Unjustly, then, you punished the just for the unjust; justly, you lost the unjust for whom you had killed the just.

Let the guilty party now change condition, because our cause has taken the better part. Freedom has arisen in slavery; captivity has come into dominion. The yoke of the ancient condition has been removed; now the mercy of compassion and grace reigns. For Christ, rising from the dead and from the tomb, has shone upon us today. Neither did his soul remain in hell, nor did his flesh remain in the tomb, as it is written: “For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption.”

Behold, now Christ rose at once, as soon as he willed it. Where is the death that the enemy inflicted? Great, brothers, is the sign of compassion: by dying in this way Christ gave life to the world, so that death itself could not hold him captive. Thus he completed our cause through merciful goodness and took nothing away from his own power, because, as soon as it pleased him, he came back to life—the God who lives and reigns throughout all ages. Amen.

[Col. 1157]

### MANUSCRIPT

[Col. 1157A]

Manuscript: The faith of our father Abraham is preeminent. See the variants in Maurin.

Same: And it is indeed so marvelous. See the same place.

Same: Because from such profound despair.

Same: Now an old man.

Same: Better with the edited text: “whose heart is upright.” See the variants in Maurin.

Same: To the devotion of the one who obeys.

Same: Better: “therefore he himself” [Col. 1157B] “to me.”

Same: He demands that he be killed.

Same: Better: “for already in what has been undertaken.”

Same: “How [*quam*] does God [act] by commanding?” Incorrect; but the edited text is also incorrect. It is evident that it should read *quia*, “because.”

Same: Of the old Law, of Holy Scripture.

Same: “Philip, having bread, give them something to eat”; and what follows.

Same: He expects to hear what he suffers.

Same: What, then, shall we say?

Same: If we act.

[Col. 1157C] Same: As in the variant in Maurin: “with different work, but with one art.”

Same: Such men, then.

Same: “Let Christ be understood”; other words are missing. See the variants in Maurin.

Same: Whatever has been written about Abraham.

Same: “Prophecy”; and “also” is missing.

Same: “But just as he was commanded to sacrifice his son, so he obeys God”—excellent.

Same: Finally, when he was already almost struck.

Same: Better: “and yet not without sacrifice.”

Same: “Without works of the law. How?” etc. All the rest that is read in the edited text is entirely absent, and in its place there is the following [Col. 1158A]:

“How? Pay attention, brothers. Someone believed; he received the sacraments of faith in bed and died. He lacked time for action. What shall we say? That he was not justified?”

Then other material taken from elsewhere follows, namely from Sermon IX, *On the Ten Strings*, concerning which see below.

In Cod. II the whole of section 21 differs, except for the final two sentences. It reads as follows:

“You see, therefore, my brothers, Christ’s mercy. Thanks be to God, because, while living, you hear these deadly dangers. Let no one deceive you: God hates these things; God avenges these things. Therefore he spares you, so that you may change; therefore God does not now avenge these things, so that you may turn to him. For he will avenge them later, if you do not turn. He does not avenge them now so that you may change your ways and be able to correct your conduct in his sight. There is complete security there, where you are neither subjected to nor commanded to endure or avoid anything of this sort. You do not break bread for the needy, because no one there hungers; you do not clothe the naked, because everyone is clothed in immortality; you do not receive the stranger, because all live in their own homeland; you do not visit the sick, because all are perpetually healthy; [Col. 1161A] you do not bury the dead, because there is perpetual life there; you do not reconcile yourself with the quarrelsome, because there is eternal peace there. Complete security is there,” etc. See Sermon XI, no. 1.

## SERMON CIV

It is read in Cod. Cass. CXI, fol. 112.

Edit. N. 4. “There are two lives: think about them more fully.”

[Col. 1165D] Cod. “There are two lives, which I have briefly described as best I could; now think about them more fully.”

At the end, after the final words “God gives the increase,” there follows:

“‘A certain woman from the crowd raised her voice and said to him: Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that you sucked’ (Luke XI, 27). Truly blessed is Mary, because, as though in the sanctuary of her womb, she bore the priest with a mystery. For everything that was to be in the age to come proceeded from her blessed womb. A priest and a victim proceeded from it: the God of resurrection, the priest of offering, and the victim of passion. We recognize all this in Christ: he is God insofar as he returned to the Father; he is high priest insofar as he offered himself as a victim for us.

“Therefore Mary’s womb is blessed—not merely a womb [Cod., ‘a blessed womb, not a womb’], but it was Christ’s temple. What is in heaven, moreover, except what must be reckoned above the heavens, where, as though in a more secret tabernacle, the mystery is divinely arranged? Mary’s blessed womb must plainly be reckoned above the heavens, because it sent the Creator, the Son of God, back to heaven. From there he came in order to suffer; from here he returned to be worshiped as king. From there he descended in humility; from here he ascended to the Father in glory.

“Plainly, the temple of the body is better than heaven: [Col. 1166B] when Christ is seated in heaven, he is fearsome there, but here he is gentle; there he avenges sins, here he forgives sins; there he exercises the authority of a judge, here he is honored through love among the brothers; and, so that we may be blessed, he is borne by those who hear the word of God and keep it (Luke XI, 28) . . .” [Note: [Col. 1165] Something seems to be missing here, unless one reads: “so that those who hear the word of God and keep it may be blessed.”]

“And therefore it is good to worship him when he invites us, so that we may not fear him when he judges.”
