## SERMON CXIV

It is read in Cod. Cassin. CX, fol. 205; likewise in Cod. Cassin. CV, fol. 131 or 136; and in four Laurentian manuscripts: plut. XVII, cod. XXXIX, fol. 179b; ibid., cod. XL, fol. 186b; ibid., cod. XLI, fol. 173; and ibid. [Col. 1168A] cod. XLII, fol. 202.

Here, as elsewhere, I had intended to record the variant readings; but although the thoughts agree, the wording differs so often and so greatly that I thought it shorter and more useful to publish the entire sermon, which you have here:

“At that time: Jesus, looking at his disciples, said to Simon Peter [Note: [Col. 1167D] The Gospel does not say that these words were spoken to Simon Peter]: ‘If your brother has sinned against you, go and correct him between you and him alone’ (Luke XVII, 3–4). And the rest.

### 1

In the holy Gospel, as it was just being read, we heard how the Lord Jesus admonishes us concerning the forgiveness of sins [Note: [Col. 1167D] Cod. CX has it this way; Cod. XXXIX has *Christus* (‘Christ’)]. From this, everyone is admonished [Note: [Col. 1167D] Cod. CX: ‘we are admonished’] by the Lord’s command. We, however, are ministers of the word of God and of the holy Gospel, which no one serves without glory [Note: [Col. 1167D] The manuscript incorrectly has *quem* (‘whom’)], and which no one despises without punishment.

“The Lord himself therefore says [Note: [Col. 1167D] Cod. CX adds ‘to us’ and then removes ‘us’], as we have all just heard: ‘If your brother,’ he says, ‘has sinned against you, correct him between you and him alone. And if he repents, forgive him—not only once, but seven times.’ This is the most certain principle. For over seven successive days, coming, going, and returning, the whole of time revolves. He who commanded that forgiveness be given seven times a day commanded that the sins of the whole of time be forgiven.

### 2

“If, then, you are someone [Note: [Col. 1167D] Cod. XXXIX incorrectly has *esse* (‘to be’)] who thinks of Christ and desires to receive what he promised, do not be lazy; do what he commanded. Do you know what he promised [Note: [Col. 1167D] Cod. CX incorrectly has *facere* (‘to do’)]? Eternal life. Do you know what he commanded [Note: [Col. 1168D] The manuscripts have *quod* incorrectly]? Give forgiveness to your brother [Note: [Col. 1168D] Some manuscripts incorrectly have *tunicam* (‘a tunic’)].

“He says to you: ‘O man, forgive your brother, so that I may give you everlasting pardon.’ The promise of the heavenly kingdom is known to all, I think; there our Creator promised that we shall be equal to his angels, so that without end we may live in that splendor [Col. 1168C] in the kingdom of heaven. You gladly accept this; why do you not wish to do what follows? You do not wish to receive from the Lord your God this command—that you grant forgiveness to your brother—if you do not wish to receive it [Note: [Col. 1168D] These words are absent from Cods. CX and XXXIX, but are found in CV and elsewhere]. You do well not to give it.

“What is this but not to grant it to one asking you to forgive your brother, when you desire to be forgiven by the Lord? Or, certainly, if you have nothing for which you need forgiveness, you do well not to forgive your brother. Even if you have no sin for which you need forgiveness, nevertheless forgive; for the Lord also always forgives, although he never knew sin. Every human being [Note: [Col. 1168D] Most manuscripts have *nam* (‘for’), but one reads *omnis* (‘every’)] is a sinner, even if he was born that very day.

### 3

“You will say: ‘God forgives well; but I am not God. I am a sinful human being.’ Thanks be to God, because you confess this. Recognize it, so that you too [Note: [Col. 1168D] *Tu* is absent from Cods. CV and CX] may be able to receive forgiveness.

“The blessed apostle Peter exhorts us in his Epistle, saying: ‘Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that you might follow in his footsteps’ (1 Peter II, 21). He certainly had no sin, yet he died for our sins and poured out his blood for our iniquities. He took upon himself for us the sin he did not commit, and freed us all from the debt of sin [Note: [Col. 1168D] The manuscripts have *peccato* (‘from sin’)].

[Col. 1169A] “He ought not to have died, but neither ought we to have lived, because we are sinners. Neither was death owed to him, nor life to us. He forgave what was owed to us, and took upon himself what was not owed to him.

“But since the matter concerns the forgiveness of sins, let us not take the long way around; let us imitate Christ the Lord. Hear the Apostle saying: ‘Forgive [Note: [Col. 1169D] Cods. XXXIX, CV, and CX: ‘Forgiving’] one another, just as God in Christ forgave you’ [Note: [Col. 1169D] So in Cods. CV and CX; Cod. XXXIX incorrectly has ‘us,’ here and above] (Ephesians IV, 32).

“These are the Apostle’s words, not ours: ‘Be imitators of God, as beloved children’ (Ephesians V, 1). Are you a son or a servant? Remember that servants too ought to be obedient, and that it is not fitting for sons to be degenerate. You are called a son; if you reject your father’s command, you will not obtain his inheritance.

### 4

“I would say this if you had no sin for which you wished to be forgiven. But now I say to you, O man, [Col. 1169B] if you are righteous, you are a human being [Note: The manuscripts incorrectly have ‘if nevertheless a human being’; we have corrected it from the printed editions]; if you are a layman, you are a human being; if you are a monk, you are a human being; if you are a cleric, you are a human being.

“Hear the voice of the apostle John saying this. See what sort of person he is whom [Note: Cods. CV and CX incorrectly have *quae* (‘which’)] I mean, so that you may hear the one who reclined upon the Lord’s breast, whom the Lord loved more than the others. Hear what he said: ‘If we say that we have no sin…’ He did not say, ‘If you say,’ but ‘If we say’; he included himself in the fault, so that he might arrive at forgiveness [Note: Cods. CV and CX incorrectly have ‘might be forgiven’]. He therefore says: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves [Note: Cod. CX: ‘we lead ourselves astray’], and the truth is not in us’ (1 John I, 8).

“Therefore we have sins; if we wish to obtain forgiveness, let us grant [Note: So in Cods. CV and CX; Cod. XXXIX incorrectly has ‘we ought to grant’] forgiveness to our brothers. Let us not retain enmity in our hearts, because retained enmity causes agitation.”

[Col. 1169C] **5.** I want you to be forgiving, because I know that you are always asking pardon. You ask that you be forgiven; you are commanded to forgive. You do not recognize what you say when you entreat the Lord. Come now and pray; where you pray [Note: [Col. 1169D] The manuscripts read *ut ores* (“that you may pray”).], there I convict you by your own words. Do you not say every day: “Our Father, who art in heaven”? For you cannot be counted among the sons if you do not say: “Our Father, who art in heaven.” Continue: “Hallowed be thy name.” Say further: “Thy kingdom come” [Note: [Col. 1170D] The same manuscript reads *veniat* (“let it come”).]. Continue further: “Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” See what you add: “Give us this day our daily bread.” Where are your riches? Look: you are begging. But that is another matter; let us pursue the matter with which we are concerned. Say further: “And forgive us our sins, as we also forgive those who are indebted to us” (Matthew 6:9–12).

I come to my words—and yours. You say: “Forgive us our debts and sins.” By what right? By what agreement? After reciting what written document? “As we also forgive those who are indebted to us.” A condition has been laid down; the law has been fixed. “Forgive us,” you say to the Lord, “as I forgive.” Therefore he will not forgive [Note: [Col. 1170D] Thus the manuscripts CV and CX; manuscript XXXIX, like the others, reads *dimittam* (“I shall forgive”).] if you do not forgive.

[Col. 1170A] If you want to be forgiven, forgive your brother who returns to you. The heavenly Jurist dictated this prayer; he does not deceive you [Note: [Col. 1170D] One manuscript has the erroneous reading *dictavit* (“he dictated”).] if you do what he taught you. Everyone who despises the Lord’s discipline loses his case and finds punishment. You yourself, when you pray, lie; you are convicted in the very prayer. For he does not need witnesses from you [Note: [Col. 1170D] The same manuscripts read *ad te* (“to you”).] in order for God to convict you. He who dictated these petitions is your advocate. If you deny, he is your witness; if you despise, he is your judge. Therefore say it, and do it. The words of this prayer cannot in any way be passed over. Or can we perhaps erase this verse from it?

Let us therefore say: “Forgive us our debts and sins,” and let us not say [Note: [Col. 1170D] Manuscript XXXIX erroneously reads *dicam* (“I shall say”).]: “As we also forgive those who are indebted to us.” Immediately the Lord says to us: “In the measure with which you measure, it shall be measured out to you” (Matthew 7:2).

[Col. 1170B] You must not erase this verse from your heart, lest you also be erased from the book of God. In this prayer you say, “Give”; you say [Note: [Col. 1170D] Thus manuscripts CV and CX; the word *dicis* (“you say”) is absent from manuscript XXXIX.], “Forgive,” so that you may receive what you do not possess—provided, however, that you forgive your brother. Hear the Savior himself saying elsewhere: “Give, and it shall be given to you; forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6:37–38). And, so as not to keep you longer, if we want the Lord to have mercy on us, let us have mercy on the needy; if we want our sins to be forgiven, let us also forgive the brother who sins.

## SERMON 118

This sermon is read in the Laurentian Library, Pluteus XII, manuscript XIV, folio 272 verso, and in the Venetian Library, manuscript LXIX, folio 47. The title is given as follows in the manuscripts: “Here begins a sermon of the same [Augustine] on the Nativity of the Lord.”—On what the Evangelist says, “In the beginning was the Word,” and on what is written in Genesis, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”: from this it is shown that he who [manuscript: “because”] was in the beginning was without a beginning [manuscript: “is”]; but that which was made in the beginning has a beginning because it did not exist, and came to be.

## SERMON 126

Numbers 2, 3, 4, and half of 5 of this sermon are read in the Laurentian Library, Pluteus XIII, manuscript VIII, folio 187 verso. This portion of the discourse is attached to Benedictine Sermon 380, as also occurs in other ancient manuscripts. See the Maurist notes on this sermon.

**Printed edition, Note 2.** How perverse they are, and how vicious through haste.

**Note 3.** The substance of those who hope.

[Col. 1170D] **Same place.** Unless from that which you do not see.

**Same place.** The inner inhabitant of the inner eyes.

[Col. 1171A] **Same place.** For when at some time you think of me; the Benedictines, whom you may consult, attempt to correct these words in the note.

**Same place.** Attend to the works and seek their maker.

**Same place.** The things that have been made are seen.

**Note 4.** But through constant familiarity they had become cheap.

**Same place.** Than that a human being should be born by dying, etc.

**Same place.** To fatten so many thousands with loaves.

**Same place.** To fill the lands with crops.

**Same place.** People saw that the water had been made wine and were astonished.

[Col. 1171B] **Same place.** Whence is the human being himself who marvels? Where was he? From where did he come forth?

**Same place.** He came, to whom it was said: “Renew the signs”; to whom it was said: “Work wonders,” etc.

**Same place.** What he does not will can be made equal.

**Same place.** The human being who was in the light.

**Note 5.** But how small.

**Same place.** He who called you did not abandon you.

**Same place.** Is creation itself evidence of the Creator?

**Same place.** Behold, he is born; behold, he comes forth from a woman.

[Col. 1170C] **Manuscript.** How perverse and blameworthy they are through vice.

**Same.** The substance of the things to be hoped for.

[Col. 1170D] **Same.** Unless from him whom you do not see.

**Same.** The inner inhabitant of the eyes.

[Col. 1171A] **Same.** For when you think excessively about something else.

**Same.** Attend to the work and seek its maker.

**Same.** The things that have been made are perceived intellectually.

**Same.** But through familiarity they have become cheap.

**Same.** Than that a human being, who did not exist, should be born by dying, etc.

**Same.** To satisfy so many thousands with loaves.

**Same.** To fill the land with crops.

**Same.** Those who saw the water made wine also saw it and were astonished.

[Col. 1171B] **Same.** Whence is he himself who marvels? Let him see from where he came forth.

**Same.** He came to this place, to whom it was said: “Work wonders,” etc.

**Same.** What he does not will can be made equal.

**Same.** The human being who was not in the light.

**Same.** But how small he would make it.

**Same.** He who called teaches.

**Same.** Are the indications of the Creator in creation itself?

**Same.** Behold, he is born; behold, he assumes a body; behold, he comes forth from a woman.

## SERMON 178

This sermon is found in Cassinese manuscript XI, folio 11, and from Note 7 onward in two Florentine manuscripts, namely Mugellian Library, manuscript XI, folio 31, and Fesulan Library, manuscript XI, folio 229 verso. This very beautiful sermon is written in the Florentine manuscripts in such a way that Augustine himself is cited in it, although it certainly must be attributed to him. From this it may be concluded that a sermon can sometimes legitimately be attributed to its author even though that author is cited within the work. This could sometimes have happened through the carelessness or ignorance of a copyist.

**Printed edition, Note 2.** He was deliberating where he should put it, not about the fields of any neighbor.

**Same place.** “What you are going to leave behind?” [Col. 1173B] Behold, he has been rebuked.

**Note 3.** For surely God is not going to give the kingdom of heaven to fools. But to whom, etc.

**Same place.** We seem to infer this; let us see it openly and clearly.

**Same place.** That he was merciless. For surely, etc.

**Note 5.** You are thinking of stripping a pagan [Col. 1173C] and clothing a Christian.

**Note 7.** Holy Scripture calls blessed the one who, after gold, etc.

**Same place.** “And did not do it.” But you say: “I have never denied another person’s property.” Perhaps no one entrusted anything to you; or perhaps someone did entrust something to you, but entrusted it before witnesses. Tell me, did you return it, etc.?

[Col. 1173D] **Same place.** After the one who entrusted it had died.

**Same place.** Because you did not pursue gold; because, etc.

**Same place.** If perhaps it was another person’s purse.

**Same place.** You hear the word of God.

**Same place.** You are moved with great joy.

**Same place.** Therefore I propose this. God says.

**Same place.** Which he gave to the former people.

**Same place.** Christ had not yet died; a discovery [of property] was to be returned as another’s. If anyone—

[Col. 1174A] **Same place.** Ought to return it.

**Note 8.** Because they are gifts of God?

**Same place.** I shall tell you what a very poor man did while we were staying at Milan—so poor that he was a *proscholus*.

**Same place.** But plainly a Christian, although that man was a pagan grammarian; better at the curtain than in the chair. So this poor man found a purse, unless the number deceives me, containing nearly two hundred solidi. Remembering the law, he announced, etc.

[Col. 1174B] **Same place.** And lest he be seeking someone else’s property, he sought it.

**Same place.** At least he asked that he might receive five or so.

**Same place.** An angry man.

**Same place.** He accepted what was offered; immediately, etc.

**Note 9.** What does this mean? If I have accomplished anything in your hearts, if the word of God has taken root in you, if it has found rest with you, do this, my brothers: do not think that you suffer loss if you do it; it is a great gain if you do what I say. “I lost twenty solidi; I lost two hundred, five hundred.” What did you lose? They had perished from your house: another person had lost them, not you. The earth, etc.

**Same place.** He put it down; he forgot it; it fell from him; you found it elsewhere. Whom did you find? A Christian. Whom did you find? One who heard the law, a Christian who heard the law. Whom did you find? You who, when you heard many things, praised them—you found it. Therefore, if you truly praised, return what you found. But if you did not return what you found, when you praised, you gave testimony against yourself. Be, etc.

**Same place.** For what you found and did not return, you stole.

**Same place.** You did as much as you could; because you could not do more, you therefore did no more.

**Same place.** He who denies another’s property, [Col. 1175A] if he can, also takes it.

**Same place.** Fear prevents it.

**Note 11.** But desire to see God.

**Same place.** Because it was said, beloved ones.

**Same place.** For if you love to see your God, if in this pilgrimage you sigh for him out of love, behold, your Lord God tests you, as if saying to you: “Behold, do what you wish,” etc.

[Col. 1175B] **Same place.** You loved gifts. If therefore my sermon—

**Same place.** Advocate by prayer, humility, and the sorrow of repentance.

[Col. 1175C] **Same place.** Fan this spark of good love within you.

**Same place.** [It] consumes hay.

[Col. 1173A] **Cassinese manuscript.** “He was thinking where to put it; to do violence to no one, not about, etc.”

**Same.** “What you are going to leave behind?” [Col. 1173B] Let what you will follow go ahead of you. Behold, he has been rebuked.

**Same.** For surely God is not going to give the kingdom of heaven to fools? The five virgins who are read of as shut out beyond the door prove this. But to whom, etc.

**Cassinese manuscript.** We seem to infer this; but we ought to consider it more attentively, so that we may see it more clearly.

**Same.** That he was merciless—not because he stole what belonged to others, but because he was unwilling to distribute from his own. For surely, etc.

**Same.** “And did not do it.” Brothers, let us question our consciences and see whether we despise greed so completely that we can be participants in this blessedness. Perhaps someone thinks within himself and says: “I commit neither theft nor violence; I practice no robbery; I have never denied another’s property.” Perhaps you did not deny it because no one wished to entrust anything to you; or, if someone entrusted it, he entrusted it before witnesses. Tell me, did you return it, etc.?

[Col. 1173D] **Same.** After the one who entrusted it had died.

**Same.** Because you did not go after gold; who, etc.

**Same.** Or if perhaps it was another person’s little purse.

**Same.** You gladly hear the word of God.

**Same.** You are admonished most extensively.

**Same.** Consider what I propose. God says.

**Same.** Which he gave to the former people.

**Same.** Consider, brothers, such a glorious example [Col. 1174C] and such a wondrous deed. I have accomplished something in your hearts if the word of God has found rest in your minds. Do this, my brothers. Do not think that you suffer loss if you return whatever has been found by you. Believe that it is a great gain if you do what I suggest. Perhaps someone came into your house and lost solidi. The earth, etc.

**Same.** He put it down; he forgot it, or it fell from him; you found it—you who heard in the law that a discovery must be returned. You who found it, you who praised when you heard the word of God, [Col. 1174D] return what you found. But if you do not return what you found, when you praised, you gave testimony against yourself. Be, etc. Both manuscripts read this way, except that the Fesulan manuscript has *quis invenisti* (“whom did you find?”) instead of *qui invenisti* (“you who found”), and the Mugellian manuscript has *non reddes* (“you will not return”) instead of *non reddideris* (“you have not returned”).

**Same.** For if you found it and did not return it, you stole it.

**Same.** You did as much as you could; because you did not find more, you therefore stole no more.

**Same.** He who denies another’s property, [Col. 1175A] if he could, would also take it. See the Maurist variants.

**Same.** But you fear evil. And the robber, etc.

**Same.** But may you desire to see God.

**Same.** What was said? Beloved ones.

**Same.** If you love to see your God, sigh for him with all your love in this pilgrimage; desire him. Behold, your God wishes to test you, so that it may become clear for what things you love him—whether for himself or for earthly things which he has granted you—and he says to you: “Do what you wish,” etc. The manuscripts add incorrectly: “Do [this] so that he may test you.”

**Same.** Here many things occur which are not read in the printed edition, as follows: “You loved freely. We have said this, brothers, because there are people so negligent and lukewarm, and, what is worse, even unbelieving, who say: ‘Would that God would grant me every good thing here in this world! I am not concerned with what he may wish to happen to me in the future.’ O unhappy soul! Even if God were to send you into punishment and merely not permit you to see his face, would it not have been better for you never to have been born? Since, however, it is impossible for one who has not deserved to see his face to escape eternal fire, why do you love the pleasure of the present world so much that you do not dread the burning of eternal fire?”

**Same.** Advocate by prayer of humility and the sorrow of repentance. [Col. 1175C] So reads the Leuven manuscript, and correctly. See the Maurist variants.

**Same.** Fan within you this spark of good love, of which the Lord said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?”

**Same.** It will consume the wood.

## SERMON 191

It is read in Cassinese manuscript XII, folio 5, with an opening which the Benedictines omitted from the text but added among the variants. We have considered it especially useful to report it here because in many places the manuscript differs.

The Only-Begotten Christ, the Son of God, the true sun of righteousness, [Col. 1176A] shone upon the earth in such a way that he did not abandon heaven: remaining there eternally and passing here temporally; establishing there an everlasting day and here enduring a human day; living there perpetually without the passage of hours and dying here temporally without the incursion of sin; remaining there as life without setting and here freeing our life from the danger of death; there setting the minds of the angels ablaze with the warmth of his majesty, here distinguishing the death of human beings by his life [Note: [Col. 1175D] The printed edition reads: “here distinguishing the life and conduct of human beings.”]. There the light is grasped [Note: [Col. 1175D] The same: “is received”] which no sinner [Note: [Col. 1175D] The same: “no sin”] extinguishes; here is born the human being who distinguishes all things by sin [Note: [Col. 1176D] The same: “sins”]. There, God with God; here, God and human being. There, light from light; here, that which enlightens every human being (John 1:13). There, by the Word he stretched out the heavens; here, he showed the way of reaching the heavens [Note: [Col. 1176D] The manuscript erroneously reads “he ascended”]. There, he established the mystery of his birth with the Father; here, he formed the members of his flesh in his mother. There, seated at the right hand [Col. 1176B] of the Father; here, lying in a manger. There, feeding the angels; here, as a little child on earth, hungering. There, remaining as unfailing bread for perfected powers; here, needing the nourishment of milk along with newborn infants. There, doing good things; here, suffering evil things. There, never dying; here, rising after death and granting eternal life to mortals. God became human so that the human being might become God. The Lord took the form of a servant so that the human being might be changed into the Lord [Note: [Col. 1176D] The manuscript erroneously reads “in the Lord”]. The inhabitant and creator of the heavens dwelt on earth so that the human being might migrate from earth to the heavens.

**Printed edition, Note 1.** Through whom we have received so many gifts. For this reason, etc.

**Note 3.** To present [oneself] to Christ. [Col. 1176C] Therefore the Church, etc.

**Note 4.** If you wish to have both.

**Same place.** And virginity should persevere.

[Col. 1176B] **Manuscript.** Through whom we have received so many gifts. But his humility is our exaltation, his cross is our victory, his gallows is our triumph, and his death is our life. For this reason, etc.

**Same.** To present [oneself] to Christ. [Col. 1176C] But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity and chastity that are in Christ. Therefore the Church, etc.

**Same.** If you wish to have one or the other.

**Same.** And virginity should persevere in Christ Jesus our Lord.

## SERMON 208

It is read in Cassinese manuscript XII, folio 88, where the following words occur at the beginning, absent from the printed editions:

“Several things have been read to us together, and neither the brevity of time nor the magnitude of our miseries permits us to speak about all of them. Nevertheless, it will be possible to gather a few little flowers from vast [manuscript: ‘pressing’] fields, and to take not as much as the field produces in abundance, but as much as is sufficient for the sense of smell; just as when someone approaches a spring, it is not necessary for him to draw as much as its rich vein has poured forth, but as much as may relieve his parched throat from thirst, lest an excess of the life-giving water, taken beyond what is proper, become the drinker’s destruction. And since it is a solemn season, etc.”

## SERMON 217

It is read in Cassinese manuscript XII, folio 93.

**Printed edition, Note 1.** The fountain indeed begot the fountain, but the begetting fountain and the begotten fountain; just as, etc.

[Col. 1177B] **Note 2.** You heard what he prayed for us—or rather, what he desired. He said: “Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be.” “I desire,” he says, “that where I am, they also may be with me.”

**Note 3.** Praise after the resurrection.

[Col. 1177A] **Manuscript.** The fountain indeed begot the fountain, but the begetting fountain and the begotten fountain are one fountain; just as, [Col. 1177B] etc.

**Same.** You heard what he prayed for us—or rather, what he said he desired: “Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be.” “I desire, Father; I do what you will; do what I desire.” What is this? “That where I am, they also may be with me.”

**Same.** Praise after the resurrection. Some Christians, brothers, thinking that they are observing the divine commandments more religiously, neglect the devotion of Lent, whose appointed season they now strive to fulfill, and falsely claim that they are observing Quinquagesima, although this is commanded neither by divine authority nor handed down by the authority of our predecessors. They do it solely through presumption of mind. And while they think they are acting more devoutly, they behave more superstitiously. The person who says he is observing Quinquagesima may perhaps scarcely be able to complete Lent.

It is indeed good to fast at all times, but it is better to fast Lent with Christ. For the Lord consecrated this Lent for us by his own fasting. I said “fasting,” not “fastings.” For the Lord’s fast was one [manuscript: “is”] fast: he took no food at all for forty continuous days and nights. Therefore, whatever Christian does not complete Lent, which is to be consecrated by fasting, will be held guilty of transgression and stubbornness, because by dining he himself annuls the law divinely given for his salvation. You annul the law when you do not keep the example of the Lord’s fast. What kind of Christian are you, when the Lord is fasting and you dine? What kind of Christian are you, when Christ is hungry and you refresh yourself [Manuscript: “you”]? He endures hunger for your salvation, while you fear fasting for your sins.

Let us abstain from the vices of the flesh so that we may be filled with eternal riches. For in that life our very occupation in the kingdom of God will be to see, love, and praise him. What will we be doing there? In this world some works belong to necessity, others to iniquity. What are the works of necessity? To sow, plow, cultivate, sail, grind, cook, weave, and whatever similar works belong to necessity; these are our good works of necessity [Manuscript: “is”]. You do not have the necessity of breaking bread for the hungry, but the person for whom you break bread has it. To receive a stranger, clothe the naked, redeem a captive, visit the sick, give counsel to one deliberating, free the oppressed—all these belong to almsgiving; they are works of necessity.

What are the works of iniquity? To steal, rob, become drunk, gamble, and exact interest. And who can enumerate all the acts of iniquity? In that kingdom there will be no works of necessity, because there will be no misery there; there will be no works of iniquity, because there will be no trouble there. Where there is no misery, there are no works of necessity; where there is no evil, there are no works of iniquity.

What will you do in order to eat, when no one is hungry? How will you perform those very works of almsgiving? For whom will you break bread where no one is in need? Whom will you visit as sick, where perpetual health endures? Whom will you bury as dead, where immortality never dies? The works of necessity perish; but if you perform works of iniquity here, you will not reach that place.

What will we do there? Tell me: will we sleep? Here people who have nothing to do sleep; there there is no sleep, because there is no failing. Therefore, if we will not perform works of necessity and will not sleep, what will we do? Let no one fear weariness; let no one think that weariness will exist there. Are you now weary of being healthy? Everything in this world becomes tiresome; health does not become tiresome. If health does not become tiresome, will immortality become tiresome?

What, then, will our activity be? “Amen” and “Alleluia.” Here we do one thing, there another—not, I say, day and night, but in a day without end. What do the heavenly powers now do? The Seraphim say without weariness: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Revelation 4:8). They say this without weariness.

Does the pulse of your vein grow tired now? As long as you live, your vein has a pulse. You do something, and by becoming tired you grow weary; then you rest and return to your work, while your vein does not grow tired. Just as your vein does not grow tired in preserving your life, so your tongue and your heart will not grow tired in praising God, in your immortality.

Hear testimony concerning your occupation. What is our occupation? This occupation is leisure [Note: [Col. 1177] See Saint Augustine, *Expositions on the Psalms* 110.1 and 147.3.]. What is the occupation of leisure? To praise God. Hear the statement concerning it: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house” (Psalm 83:5). The psalm says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house.” And as though we were asking, “From where are they blessed? Will they possess much gold?” Those who possess much gold are very miserable. “Blessed are those who dwell in your house.” From where are they blessed? This is their blessedness: “They will praise you forever and ever” (ibid.).

O peace without weariness! O tireless sweetness, Lord our God! Form us for yourself, reforming us so that we may see you, since when we have seen you, we shall not turn away from you. We shall love you and enjoy you, and without weariness we shall love you; our Lord Jesus Christ reigning, to whom are honor and glory through endless ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON 266

**Printed edition, Note 4.** Many believed in Samaria; those who believed were baptized. When the apostles heard this, they sent Peter and John to them, so that they might lay hands on those who had been baptized and, by laying hands upon them, obtain the Holy Spirit for them by invoking him. **Same.** The one who preached in Samaria, who baptized in Samaria, and to no one, etc.

**Same.** Let them read the text of the reading and see that the same Philip is named, the one who properly, etc.

**Same.** And that he should be summoned, and that whatever he commanded should be done. Then, however, etc.

Same. But God showed me; when did he show this? Where did he show it? “No one common,” etc.

[Col. 1180A] Same. For those who slandered or did not understand might have said to Peter: “You did wrong to give baptism to the uncircumcised.” Could one say to God: “You did wrong to give the Holy Spirit”?

## Sermons 280, 281, and 282

Sermon 281 is read for the most part in two manuscripts: one Cassinese manuscript, namely XII, fol. 1282, and another Florentine manuscript, Fesulan Library, cod. XX, fol. 262. In both, the title reads *On Saint Victoria*, or *On the Birthday of Saint Victoria*. Much is taken from Sermon 280, and much also from Sermon 282; much is not found in the printed edition. Here we have taken care to record the differences. It is not impossible that Saint Augustine adapted the notes he had written about Saints Perpetua and Felicity for the praise of Saint Victoria, especially since a certain sermon on Saint Victoria is cited in the Theodorician manuscript in these words: “Likewise, a sermon of the blessed Aurelius Augustine, bishop, on the birthday of Saint Victoria the virgin,” as may be seen in the notes to the works of Saint Augustine, Benedictine edition, vol. V.

## Sermon 280

**Printed edition.** Note 1. “And with a victorious step”; then two manuscripts add certain words proper to blessed Perpetua.

Same place. “The woman falling . . . ascending.”

Note 2. “Then with the beasts.”

[Col. 1180C] Same place. “Whose voices [are] against the flesh of the martyrs.”

Same place. “Now plainly there is no longer any.”

Note 4. “But it would have sufficed for exercise.”

Note 5. “Although it can now be compared with none of this world’s felicities or pleasures, a small part of the promise is at issue—or rather,” etc.

[Col. 1180D] Same place. “When their bodies had been restored.”

Note 6. “Because we are members of the body of him whose members they also are,” etc.

Same place. “And we embrace the same unity.” Thus it ends.

[Col. 1180B] **Manuscripts.** “And with a victorious step.” The additions proper to blessed Perpetua are absent up to the words: “Thus the head.”

Same. “Of the woman falling . . . of the woman ascending.”

**Manuscript XII.** “Then certainly [Col. 1180C] with the beasts.”

**Manuscripts.** “Whose voices in the flesh of the martyrs.”

Same. After these words they have nothing further; what is missing continues until these words in Note 4: “The martyrs of Christ for the name and justice of Christ,” and then, omitting two words, “they conquered both,” they continue: “not to die,” etc.

Same. After these words they omit much, continuing at the words: “What, when they have been dissolved,” etc.

Same. “Although it can now be compared with none of this world’s festivities or pleasures, a small portion of the promise is [being fulfilled], or rather,” etc.

The same is found in manuscript XX; manuscript XII has [Col. 1180D] “when in the body.”

**Manuscript XII.** “Because we are members of the body of him whose members they are also,” etc.

**Manuscripts.** “We embrace the same unity” (manuscript XII incorrectly has “humanity”). They then continue as follows:

“In this great contest, therefore, Saint Victoria was not held back by the weakness of her sex, nor enervated by feminine thought, nor softened by the world’s blandishments, nor terrified by its threats, nor overcome by its savagery. She fought bravely, conquering the flesh by the spirit, fear by hope, the devil by faith, and the world by love. With these weapons the army of our unconquered King is victorious; girded with these weapons, the soldiers of Christ, not preserving but slaughtering the members of their bodies, triumphed—not by killing, but by dying—and earned victory over the devil.”

## Sermon 281

[Col. 1181A]

**Printed edition.** Note 1. “The name of Perpetua and Felicity, holy servants of God.”

Same place. “Among women.” It should be read, “among women” [in the plural feminine].

Same place. “Feminine weakness did not fail.”

Note 2. “It delights a devout mind to contemplate such a spectacle as blessed Perpetua reported had been revealed to her concerning herself: that she had become a man and fought against the devil. In that contest she too was running toward the perfect man,” etc.

Same place. “Rightly, that ancient one.”

[Col. 1181B] Same place. “Through a woman he had deceived a man.”

Same place. “Through a man he attempted to overcome her.”

[Col. 1181A] **Manuscripts.** “The name of Saint Victoria, the servant of the Lord”; and so thereafter, with the name changed and used in the singular.

Same. “In the woman.”

Same. “The woman did not fail.”

Same. “It delights a devout mind to contemplate such a spectacle: blessed Victoria running in that contest toward the perfect man against the devil,” etc.

Same. “Rightly, that ancient one also.”

Same. “Through a woman he had conquered [Col. 1181B] the man.”

**Manuscript XII** adds after these words:

“Namely, through the cruel judge, to whom blessed Victoria yielded not even for a time; for he whom the virgin had borne was assisting her. And therefore, with the most prudent and steadfast strength of the inferior human being, she blunted all his snares and shattered his assaults.”

Manuscript XX, omitting the first sentence, has the final phrase, except that instead of the words “And therefore she,” it reads “But she.” Then both manuscripts take up a fragment of Sermon 280, Note 1, “And with a victorious step,” as may be seen above.

## Sermon 290

It is read in Cassinese manuscript XI, fol. 87. Its sole difference is that in Note 4, in place of the printed edition’s words:

“How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” And the angel: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Behold how,” etc.,

the manuscript has the better reading:

“How will this happen, while I do not know a man?” And the angel declared to the virgin: “Behold how,” etc.

Would that you were thinking of the apostles! You would see whether earthly happiness or eternal happiness had been promised to them. Listen to the Apostle, if his memory lives in you. For what is it? ‘For this momentary light affliction of ours is producing in us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, and beyond measure beyond measure, while we look not to the things that are seen but to those that are not seen; for the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal’ (2 Cor. 4:17–18).

“In Peter himself the flesh was temporal, and you do not want the stone of Rome to be temporal? The apostle Peter [Col. 1184D] reigns with the Lord; the body of the apostle Peter lies in a certain place. It is a memorial that arouses love for eternal things, not so that you may cling to the earth, but so that with the Apostle you may think of heaven. Tell me, if you are faithful: recall the memorials of the apostles, and also the memorial of the Lord your God, certainly now seated in heaven.

“Listen where the Apostle sends you: ‘If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things above, not on things on earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory’ (Col. 3:1–4).

“In one phrase you hear this: ‘Lift up your heart.’ Therefore you grieve and weep because wood and stones have fallen, and because those who were going to die have died? Give me someone dead who will live forever. Do you grieve because wood and stones have fallen, and because those who were going to die have died? If your heart is above, what has died there? What has fallen there? If your heart is above, ‘where your treasure is, there is your heart.’ Your flesh is below; and if your flesh is afraid, let your heart not be shaken.

“‘But,’ you say, ‘I did not want it.’ What did you not want? ‘I did not want Rome, so great, to suffer so much.’ We forgive you, because you did not want it. Do not be angry with God because he wanted it. You are a human being, and he is God. You say, ‘I do not want,’ where he says, ‘I want’? He does not condemn you because of your ‘I do not want’; and do you blaspheme his ‘I want’?

“But why did God will this? Why did God will this? For the present, obey the will of the Lord your God; once you have become his friend, you will know the counsel of your Lord God. What servant is so proud that, when his Lord orders something to be done, he says, ‘Why?’ The Lord keeps his counsel with himself. Obedience obeys; if the servant progresses, if he acts well, if he becomes a friend from a servant, as the Lord himself said, ‘I no longer call you servants, but friends’ (John 15:15), perhaps he will also learn the counsel of his Lord. For the present, before he knows the counsel, let him willingly bear the decision.

“I am still teaching patience, not yet wisdom; be patient. The Lord wills it. You ask why he wills it? I defer the pursuit of knowledge; I defer vigor. Prepare to obey; he wishes you to endure what he wills; endure what he wills,” etc.

Same. “I say to your Charity: our innards have been twisted by this. We confess to you that such diligence has not pleased us. I know that they acted out of zeal for God; I know, I do not doubt, that they acted out of zeal for God. But they must also consider the Apostle Paul, how he grieves even over those who have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Rom. 10:2).

“Behold, he has not been admitted today; tomorrow he will die. From whose hands will he be demanded? You will say: ‘But he is pretending.’ I answer: ‘But he is asking.’ I show that he is asking; you show that he is pretending. Christian, now I want you to teach me also. How do you know that he is pretending? ‘Because he fears for his property.’ We know that many feared for their property and therefore became Catholics; when they received freedom, some returned to those others, while others remained. As long as they did not enter, they feared for their property; and when they entered, they remained by learning.

“How do you know, then, lest this man who fears for his property be among those who were found to be pretending—especially now that so much light of truth and so much conviction of falsehood have come near? Why do you wish to judge the heart, human being? We sweated; we labored; truth was demonstrated as unconquered, so that it might be hostile to those who seek it? We labored so that truth might be shown and falsehood convicted. The Lord helped; it was done. Perhaps the one for whom it was done has been changed by some reflection. Why do you wish to judge the heart? I see one asking, and you accuse him of pretending? Christian, accept what you see; leave what you do not see to God.

“Briefly I say to your Charity: we heard from the Lord himself that the Lord’s sheep are to be fed, and we know that he says concerning the sheep through Ezekiel: ‘Let no sheep butt another sheep; let no sheep push another sheep; let the strong not crush the weak’ (Ezek. 34:1 ff.). Consider what the Apostle says: ‘Correct the disorderly, console the fainthearted, support the weak’ (1 Thess. 5:14). ‘Correct the disorderly’—let this be done; ‘console the fainthearted’—let this be done; ‘support the weak’—let this be done. ‘Be patient toward all’ (ibid.)—let this be done. ‘Let no one repay evil for evil to anyone’ (ibid., 5:16)—let this be done.

“He says so much. We pay attention only to ‘Correct the disorderly.’ Pay attention: ‘Correct the disorderly.’ Count them: ‘Console the fainthearted; support the weak; be patient toward all.’ See that no one repays evil for evil. You pay attention only to ‘Correct the disorderly.’ See that you yourself are not disorderly, lest—and what is worse—you wish to be disorderly and do not wish to be corrected.

“We ask you, through Christ; we implore you: do not destroy our labor. Do you think we ought to please ourselves because we have conquered falsehood? Victory always belongs to truth. What are we? Falsehood has been conquered; it was conquered long ago. But thanks be to God, because it has been openly conquered and made manifest to human beings. Worship has abounded; why is its fruit being hindered?

“From now on, brothers, let such things not be done. Let no one love the Church in such a way that he begrudges the Church’s gains. Two or three days ago, what I am speaking about happened, and a levite sounded it out to everyone: Donatists are not to be admitted when they come to the Church. Do you think nothing evil happened because this sounded out to everyone? I ask that this voice sound today, so that what sounded badly may be overwhelmed by what [Col. 1187C] has sounded well. Give your attention to this; this is what we have said, this is what we preach. Let them come; let them be admitted,” etc.

# SERMON CCCXVII

It is read in the Monte Cassino manuscript XI, folio 212, and likewise in the Monte Cassino manuscript XII, folio 127.

**Printed edition, no. 1:** “Crowned; those lands, etc.”

[Col. 1190B] **No. 2:** “Blindness was crucifying him, and the Crucified was making an eye-salve for them from his blood.”

**No. 4:** “‘No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house.’ The house is the world.”

**Same:** “And I to the world.”

**No. 5, at the end:** “He commended [him] to the Lord.”

[Col. 1190A] **Manuscripts:** “Crowned, he became first in martyrdom, although he appeared to be last in ecclesiastical rank. Those lands, etc.”

[Col. 1190B] **Manuscript XII:** “The blind were crucifying him, and after they had crucified him, Christ made an eye-salve for them from his blood.”

**Manuscripts:** “‘So let your light shine before men.’ Behold, Stephen’s light shines, so that all who are in the house may see. The house is the world.”

**Same:** “And I to the world. The remainder differs, but through the carelessness of the copyists it was not transcribed.”

**Manuscript XII:** After the words “he commended [him] to the Lord,” it adds the following:

> “Stephen therefore loved his enemies. For he who stood praying for himself knelt for them.[^c0122-1] Certainly he fulfilled what is written; he was a true imitator of the Lord’s passion and was approved as a perfect disciple of Christ, because he completed in his own passion what he had heard from his Master. For while the Lord hung on the cross, he said: ‘Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing’ (Luke 23:34). And blessed Stephen, when he was already almost overwhelmed by stones, said: ‘Lord Jesus, do not hold this sin against them’ (Acts 7:59). O apostolic man, already a teacher from being a disciple! For Christ’s first martyr ought to follow the teaching of his Master. He prays for the impious, he prays for blasphemers, for his own stoners. Since it was difficult for such people to be heard, weakness intervened so that charity might be strengthened. He forced the answer by kneeling. Do you suppose that he was not heard when he said, ‘Lord, do not hold this sin against them’? He was heard: many of them believed.
>
> “But I shall not send you far away. That Saul who stoned him with everyone’s hands, who kept the garments of those doing the stoning, was heard because Stephen prayed for him. Later he raged, after receiving letters against the Christians; he continued raging, thirsted for blood, and breathed out slaughter. And the Lord, who was hearing Stephen’s prayer for him, said: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ (Acts 9:4). The man whom you killed prayed for you, and I choose you to confess me and to die for me.
>
> “Let us therefore celebrate the birthday of holy Stephen with the veneration that is due. We have celebrated the Lord’s birthday; let us celebrate that of his servant also. We have frequently observed the Savior’s Nativity; let us frequently observe the martyr’s birthday also. For the incorrupt Virgin Mary gave birth to our Lord, and the holy Church brought glorious Stephen forward to the palms of martyrdom.”

[^c0122-1]: [Col. 1189D] See Sermon CCCXVI, no. 3.

# SERMON CCCLXXXI

[Col. 1194B]

It is read in the Monte Cassino manuscript CIX, folio 30. There, in the single section, instead of what has been printed from the words “the swelling of the proud would not be healed” through “with how great joy, therefore,” the following is found:

> “How easily and readily a rich man, if he were first called by Christ, would think and say: ‘In me wealth has been chosen; in the nobleman, high birth; in the senator, rank; in the king, power!’ How much better, then, and how much more orderly now. First he raised the needy from the earth and lifted the poor from the dungheap, to set him with the princes of his people, so that it might be evident that the gift of understanding and teaching belongs not only to God but also comes from God.”

# SERMON CCCLXXXII

[Col. 1194C]

It is read in the Monte Cassino manuscript XI, folio 214. There, in no. 3, instead of the words “He learned by reading, perfected by fulfilling. When he,” etc., it reads:

> “He learned by reading, fulfilled through love, because when he,” etc.

# FRAGMENT CONCERNING THE BIRTHDAY OF CHRIST

It is read under the name of Saint Augustine in manuscript XII, folio 31. I sought it in the work of the blessed Doctor but did not find it.

> “All the Scriptures that we have just heard, beloved, have announced to us public rejoicing and common joy. For the Psalmist says: ‘Rejoice in God our helper’ (Psalm 80:2). The Apostle, moreover: ‘Rejoice in the Lord always’ (Philippians 4:4). And the Evangelist says: ‘I announce to you a great joy’ (Luke 2:10). O blessed day, on which, according to the authority of the Scriptures, rejoicing and exulting, we celebrate the birthday of our Lord Jesus Christ with the Psalmist, honor it with the Evangelist, and celebrate it with the apostles and prophets. Great indeed is the exultation of the Christian people enacted today according to the example of the sacred Scriptures. Therefore our joy on this day is blessed, because a rejoicing people has done what it is commanded to do.
>
> “How holy the congregation of this Church would be if it always did what Christ commands! Therefore I beg you, brothers, always to do the Lord’s command, so that you may be able to rejoice in all things throughout eternity. For just as today we are joyful in this festival of the Lord’s birthday, so whoever does the will of his Lord in this world will always celebrate the Lord’s festival with the angels in heaven.”

[Col. 1195]

# EXPOSITION ON PSALM L

It is read in the Mugellan Library, manuscript XI, folio 40, and in the Fesulan Library, manuscript XI, folio 240.

**Printed edition, no. 1:** “From ‘the multitude,’ etc., to the end, this psalm demonstrates.”

[Col. 1197C] **No. 2:** “Captivated by the beauty of this woman, another man’s wife, etc.”

**Same:** “Nathan the prophet was sent to him, sent by the Lord.”

**No. 3:** “Therefore it is not an example for falling.”

**Same:** “If David, why not I too?”

**Same:** “You do not imitate his holiness; rather, you imitate his fall.”

**Same:** “But others, hearing this beneficially, measure their weakness by the fall of a strong man; and what he condemns, etc.” [Col. 1197D] See the Maurist variants.

**Same:** “Wishing to avoid it, they keep their eyes from a careless gaze; they do not fix them on beauty, etc.”

**Same:** “So that they do not wish to see the place from which they might fall. For they restrain, etc.”

**Same:** “They do not raise their unguarded eyes.”

**Same:** “Pay attention without fear.”

**Same:** “Are you stronger than David? He warns, etc.”

[Col. 1198A] **No. 4:** “David did not commit this sin, etc.”

**Same:** “The more wretched he appeared, the more intent he was upon God. Tribulation is something useful; the surgeon’s instrument is [more] useful than the devil’s temptation. He became, etc.” See the Maurist variants.

**Same:** “He was free from pressure.”

**Same:** “Therefore this example is effective.” [Col. 1198B]

**No. 5:** “But it happened; I may say this to those who have not committed it.”

**Same:** “But if someone who has already fallen hears this and holds some evil in his conscience, let him heed the words of this psalm: let him attend to the wound, etc.”

**Same:** “Let him not despair of the physician’s majesty.”

**Same:** “Therefore let no one say, ‘If I have already done some evil, I am condemned.’”

**Same:** “Let me enjoy this world in pleasure, wantonness, and wicked desire.”

**Same:** “Therefore this psalm, [Col. 1198C] just as it makes the cautious, etc.”

**Same:** “Hear the one who weeps and join your tears to his; hear the one who has been corrected and rejoice with him.”

**Same:** “For Nathan the prophet was sent to this man. Pay attention to the king’s humility. He did not reject the words of the one giving orders; he did not say, ‘Do you dare speak to me, the king?’ The exalted king listened to the prophet; let his humble people listen to Christ.”

**No. 6:** “Hear this, therefore, and say with him.”

[Col. 1198D] **Same:** “Come to the aid of my grievous wound according to your great medicine.”

**Same:** “This David could not say.”

**Same, and no. 7:** “But great mercy. More and more, etc.” through the words “For see whom you invoke.”

**Same:** “Let David answer; let those who have fallen answer; let them answer with David, so that they may merit mercy.”

[Col. 1199A] **No. 8:** “When the prophet was sent to me, and concerning the poor man’s ewe, etc.”

**Same:** “But he, angered, pronounces sentence.”

**Same:** “And the ewe is to be restored fourfold. Most severely and most justly. But the sin, etc.”

**Same:** “He made an instrument from his tongue. This he did, etc.”

[Col. 1196D] **Both manuscripts** differ completely and have the following opening, which in some respects approaches the printed text but in many respects departs from it:

> “Whenever, dearest brothers, you recognize that some of your sons are running, through empty persuasion and a destructive love, to spectacles that are either frenzied, bloody, or shameful, as though to some good work, you who, by God’s favor, now despise these entertainments—not only luxurious but also cruel—ought to correct them and pray to the Lord for them more abundantly, because you know that they are going after vanity and deceitful madnesses and neglecting that to which they have been called.
>
> “If by chance they become frightened for some reason in the very circus, they immediately make the sign [of the cross] and stand there carrying on their foreheads what they would depart from if they carried it in their hearts. For anyone who runs toward some evil deed, if he happens to stumble, makes the sign over his mouth, not knowing that he is thereby enclosing the demon rather than driving him out. He would then make the sign properly and drive the devil from his heart if he withdrew from that wicked work.
>
> “Therefore, again and again I beg you, dearest brothers, to pray for them with all your strength, so that they may deserve to receive understanding for condemning such things, the inclination to flee them, and mercy for forgiving them” (the manuscript incorrectly reads “for recognizing them”). “It will be appropriate” (the Fesulan manuscript thus; the Mugellan manuscript has *it was*) “because of the continual remorse of repentance, for us” (the Fesulan manuscript: “for you”) “to sing Psalm Fifty every day.
>
> “Let us also address those whom pleasurable spectacles frequently draw away from the Church’s assembly. I beg you, dearest ones, whenever you see them doing anything of this sort, correct them most severely in our place. Let our voice be present to them through your memory. Correct them by reproving” (the Fesulan manuscript: “reprove by correcting”), “comfort them by speaking to them, and provide an example by living well” (the printed edition has *well*; this word is absent from the manuscript). “He who was present to you will be present to them.
>
> “For the fountain of God’s mercy has not been cut off from you after you passed through these dangers. By the way you came, they will come; by the way you passed, they will pass. It is indeed troublesome and extremely dangerous, and certainly deadly, that, after being frequently warned by us, they sin not in ignorance but knowingly.
>
> “Yet the greatness of divine mercy clearly shows that we ought not to despair even of such people: it does not wish the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live. Finally, we recognize that this was most clearly fulfilled in blessed David, whose sin we mention with grief and trembling, etc.”

The remainder follows as it is read in the printed edition at the beginning of no. 2.

**Same:** “For blessed David, captivated by the beauty of another man’s wife, etc.”

**Same:** “Nathan the prophet was sent to him by the Lord.”

**Same:** “It was not an example for falling.” The Fesulan manuscript agrees with the printed text: “Therefore it was not.”

**Same:** “If David committed adultery, why should I not?”

**Same:** “Do not imitate his holiness, but his fall.”

**Same:** “But good men, sons of the Church, perfected in the love of Christ, hearing of the fall of so holy a man, [Col. 1197D] fear their own weakness, and what he condemns, etc.”

**Same:** “Wishing to avoid it, they keep their eyes away; they do not fix them on beauty, etc.”

**Same:** “So that they may not fall through carelessness, but rather fear seeing the place from which they might fall. Therefore they restrain, etc.”

**Mugellan manuscript:** “They do not easily raise their eyes”; the Fesulan manuscript agrees with the printed edition: “They do not raise their unguarded eyes.”

**Both manuscripts:** “You are paying attention without fear.”

**Same:** “Are you stronger than David? For I said that you cannot be stronger than David or wiser than Solomon. [Col. 1198A] If unguarded intimacy with women and harmful flatteries overcame men so holy, what do those people think about themselves who do not fear or blush to associate with strange women, to remain even in one house with them, or to participate frequently or always in their banquets? Of such people it can and must be said what the Apostle said of the pleasure-loving widow: ‘She is dead while she lives.’ He warns, etc.”

**Same:** “For David did not commit adultery and murder at the same time, etc.”

**Same:** “The more wretched he appeared, the more intent he was upon the Lord’s mercy. But when he became, etc.”

**Same:** “He was free from pressures.”

**Same:** “Therefore this example is effective.” [Col. 1198B]

**Same:** “Let those who have not committed this evil hear these things.”

**Same:** “But if someone who has already fallen hears this and, crushed by the great weight of his crime, has already begun to despair, let him attend to the wound, etc.”

**Same:** “Let him not despair of the physician’s power.”

**Same:** “Let no one say, ‘If I have already done some evil, I am condemned.’”

**Same:** “Let me enjoy the world in wanton pleasure and wicked desire.”

**Same:** “For our God, [Col. 1198C] just as he makes people cautious, etc.”

**Same:** “Hear the one who weeps and weep with him; hear the one who has been corrected and rejoice with him.”

**Same:** “For Nathan the prophet was sent to King David. But he did not consider the exalted position of his kingdom; humble and gentle, he did not reject the words of the one giving orders. He did not say to the prophet, ‘Since you are poor and humble, how did you dare speak to me, the king?’ The exalted king listened to the prophet; let the humble commoner listen to Christ.”

**Same:** “Hear this, therefore, whoever has committed a capital crime, and say with him.”

[Col. 1198D] **Same:** “Come to the aid of my grievous wound according to your great mercy.”

**Same:** “David could not say this.”

**Same:** “But great mercy. Say, therefore: ‘Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.’ But see whom you invoke. The rest is missing.”

**Same:** “Let David answer; let those who have fallen answer; let them answer with David, so that they may obtain mercy.” Thus the Fesulan manuscript; the Mugellan manuscript agrees with the printed edition.

[Col. 1199A] **Same:** “When the prophet was sent to me, who spoke of the poor man’s ewe, etc.”

**Same:** “He, angered, pronounces sentence.”

**Same:** “And the ewe is to be restored fourfold. He judged most severely and most justly. But the sin, etc.”

**Same:** “God made an instrument from his tongue.” Instead of the remainder, which is missing, the manuscript contains the following:

> “Therefore, dearest brothers, recognizing our iniquities, let us resist evil desires as much as we can. By fasts, vigils, prayers, and more generous almsgiving, let us redeem the evils we have committed; and with God’s help let us devote ourselves so diligently to good works that our desires may not be able to draw us back to our former sins. Rather, persevering in every good work, let us give thanks to the Lord with the prophet and say: ‘You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice an offering of praise.’”

# ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

**[Col. 1200D]**

## TREATISE I

It is read in the Laurentian Library, Plut. XXX sinist., fol. 60b, from no. 1 near the beginning to no. 11 near the middle.

**Editorial text, no. 2.** What is the justice which the hills receive?

Likewise: They would be illuminated by wisdom itself.

**No. 3.** When each person has pushed his boat out, he is released.

**No. 4.** For those unable to grasp the things that belong to God.

**No. 7.** But perhaps you will say this.

**[Col. 1201A]** Let him observe what sort of heart he raises, because he raises it to the Lord.

**No. 8.** Therefore did the Word of God both sound forth and come to completion? How, then, are all things, etc.

Likewise: It remains—this is in contrast to passing sounds.

**No. 9.** You see what I am leaving unsaid, lest I continue for a long time, etc.

**[Col. 1200D] Manuscript.** What is this justice which the hills receive?

And: They would be illuminated by wisdom itself.

And: When each person has pushed his boat out, he will be released.

And: For those unable to grasp the things that belong to the Spirit of God.

And: But perhaps you say this.

**[Col. 1201A]** Let him observe what sort of heart he raises, and to what he raises it; because he raises it to the Lord.

Therefore, if the Word of God both sounded forth and came to completion, how are all things, etc.

These things remain while the sounds pass away.

And you command me to be silent, lest I continue for a long time, etc.

## TREATISE IV

It is read in the Laurentian Library, Plut. XXX sinist., cod. 1, fol. 97, from no. 10 to the end.

**Editorial text, no. 10.** The sin of the world. Now pay attention.

Likewise: But who is innocent? [Col. 1201B] How innocent?

All from that stock.

He assumed flesh only.

**No. 11.** Since the man himself is full of sin.

**No. 12.** Let your charity pay a little attention.

**No. 14.** So that, because he received it from a servant—

Likewise: Who among us can be compared with Christ in any respect?

Likewise: Lest the baptism of John seem better.

**No. 16.** For if he did not know the one by whom he wished to be baptized—

**[Col. 1201C]** Likewise: If he recognized him once he had been baptized.

**[Col. 1201A] Manuscript.** The sins of the world. Therefore pay attention now. See the Maurist variant. Our manuscript always has “sins” instead of the “sin” found in the edition.

And: But who is innocent, [Col. 1201B] or how innocent?

And: All from that root.

And: He assumed flesh only.

And: Since that man is full of sin.

And: Let your charity pay attention now.

And: So that what he received from a servant—

And: Who among you can be exalted or compared with Christ in any respect?

And: Lest the baptism of John seem greater.

And: For if he did not know the one by whom he wished to be baptized—

**[Col. 1201C]** And: If he recognized the Lord once he had been baptized.

## TREATISE XII

It is read in the Mugellana Library, cod. XVI, fol. 57, from near the end of no. 11 to the end of the sermon.

**Editorial text, no. 11.** He exalted the serpent in the wilderness, and so forth.

Likewise: But he says this so that they may have eternal life.

**No. 12.** He came to heal the sick. He himself—

Likewise: What do you expect him to say except, “He is judged”? “He has already been judged,” he says.

Likewise: For the Lord knows those who are his; he knows, [Col. 1201D] etc.

Likewise: Why has he been judged? Because he did not believe.

**No. 13.** How did certain people do a good work, so that they might come?

Likewise: He heals those who had been bitten.

Likewise: If you too accuse, you are joined to God.

Likewise: You are not flattering yourself.

**No. 14.** It enters gradually through the bilge-pump.

Likewise: Lest sins overwhelm them [Col. 1202A] through groaning and fasting.

Likewise: In prosperous circumstances, let it not exalt him.

**[Col. 1201C] Manuscript.** He exalted the serpent in the desert, and so forth.

And: But these have eternal life.

And: He came to heal the sick. But he himself—

And: What do you expect him to say except, “Let him be judged”? He was about to add: “He has already been judged,” he says.

And: For the Lord knows those who are his, whom he predestined to eternal life; he knows, [Col. 1201D] etc.

And: Why has he been judged? Because he does not believe. See the Maurist variant.

And: How did certain people do a good work and come?

And: He was healing the sick who had been bitten.

And: If you too accuse, you are joined to God.

And: You are not flattering yourself. The older editions likewise have this. See the Maurist variant.

And: The waves enter gradually through the bilge-pump.

And: Lest sins overwhelm them [Col. 1202A] through groaning, repentance, and fasting.

And: In prosperous circumstances, let it not exalt you.

## TREATISE XXXIII

Its first two sections are read in five Florentine codices: the Laurentian Library, Plut. XVII, cod. XXVI, fol. 137; the same, cod. XL, fol. 228b; the Aedilian Library, cod. CXXXVIII, fol. 237; the same, cod. CXLII, fol. 185b; and finally the Library of Santa Croce, Plut. XXX sinist., fol. 138b.
