## TRACTATES L AND LI

A portion of the same work is read in the Aedilian Library, codex CXLII, folio 199 verso: an exposition of several verses of chapter XII of Saint John, which in many respects approaches Tractates L and LI of Saint Augustine, but in many respects departs from them. We therefore believe that it should be reproduced here in full, although it seems to contain nothing other than excerpts from Saint Augustine, arranged, nevertheless, in a pleasing order.

### HOMILY ON THE WORDS OF THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO JOHN

“Six days before Passover Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus had died, whom Jesus raised” (John XII, 1 ff.). And the rest.

### SYNOPSIS

I. Christ’s supper at the house of the resurrected Lazarus.  
II. Mary anoints Christ’s body with perfume.  
III. Judas’s complaint and Mary’s praise.  
IV. The Jewish leaders, distressed by Lazarus’s resurrection, want to kill him.  
V. Christ is honored with palm branches and the people’s acclamations.  
VI. What Jesus’ sitting upon the donkey signifies.  
VII. Christ’s words to the people.  
VIII. His glorification from heaven.  
IX. The prince of this world cast out.  
X. Christ, exalted, draws all things to himself.  
XI. We must walk in the light, not in darkness.

### I

He who made all things in six days, who created man on the sixth day, came in the sixth age to redeem him, and was going to die on the sixth day of the week, at the sixth hour. Six days before Passover he came to Bethany, so that the raising of Lazarus might be more firmly committed to everyone’s memory and the Jews, who were plotting the death of so great a raiser, might be confounded and left without excuse. He also asks from us the obedience of the young deer, which always obeyed the Father unto death, while by his presence he exalts Bethany, as though he were a lamb about to come to Jerusalem for sacrifice, so that we might have the true Passover.

They made him a supper there, and Martha served. Lazarus was one of those reclining at table with him (John XII, 2). Lazarus was present at the supper so that no one might think that it was a phantom who had risen from the dead. Although human beings may marvel at all the mighty works that the Son of God performed on earth [Col. 1212B] in order to reveal his majesty, and although they cannot adequately define them in words, nevertheless the miracle he performed concerning Lazarus surpasses every other: he commanded him to return to the upper world from the very inhabitant of hell itself (so the codex reads; perhaps “from the very habitation”), from that pallid seat, the Tartarean law having been destroyed, although he was death’s captive. And, to increase the miracle of divine power, while he reclined at the banquet, when the guests questioned him, Lazarus carefully narrated in order the sorrowful places of punishment and the lofty seats dark with profound night. Thus the underworld, long unknown, at last found its betrayer.

Mystically, the Lord’s supper takes place in the faith and devotion of the righteous. Martha serves, when each believer offers the Lord works of devotion. Lazarus—that is, those raised [Col. 1212C] from grave sins—feasts with those who remained in righteousness, rejoicing in the Lord’s presence.

### II

Mary therefore took an alabaster flask of costly perfume of pistic nard (the codex incorrectly has “spikenard”), and, breaking the alabaster flask, poured it over the head of Jesus as he reclined, anointed his feet, wiped them with her hair, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume (John XII, 3).

Alabaster is a kind of white marble streaked with various colors, which is usually hollowed out for perfume vessels and is said to preserve perfumes unspoiled. Nard is an aromatic shrub with, as they say, a heavy and thick root, but a short, black, and brittle one, smelling like cypress, with a small and dense leaf whose tips spread into spikes. Perfumers praise the spikes and leaves of nard. Hence Mark speaks of costly perfume of spikenard (Mark XIV, 3). For the perfume that Mary brought to the Lord had been made not only from the root of nard but also, so that it might be more costly, from its spikes and leaves.

Naturalists report that nard is chief among perfumes. There are indeed many varieties of it, but all are herbaceous (so the text reads) except the Indian variety, which is more precious. John, however, specifically wrote “a pound of perfume of pistic nard.” *Pistici* is named from a place and is interpreted as “faithful,” that is, not adulterated by any other mixture.

Mystically, Mary’s devotion signifies the faith of the Church, speaking in the Song of Songs: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song I, 11). Mary fulfilled these words both with her hands and spiritually fulfills them every day in her members: “But thanks be to God, who always manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place; for we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Cor. II, 14–15). The perfume is the exceedingly sweet grace of the Holy Spirit, sweetly fragrant when poured into the hearts of the faithful.

The pound of perfume of pistic nard is righteousness proceeding from pure faith. For *pistis* in Greek means “faith” in Latin, and the fragrant nard signifies the sweetly fragrant confession of faith. The alabaster of the perfume is the body of the faithful soul; the broken alabaster is carnal desire, which is broken upon the head, from which the whole body of the Church is joined together (Eph. IV, 16).

When, therefore, the Church proclaims the power of Christ’s divinity, she pours costly perfume over the head of him who reclines (the codex incorrectly has “pours deeply”). “Reclining” means humbling himself so that the Church’s faith might touch him [Col. 1213B]. In his majesty he was not understood; through the form of a servant he became visible. Whoever, therefore, honors the assumed humanity through the devout preaching of sacred Scripture pours perfume upon the Lord’s feet. He dyes the hair who, by a rational arrangement of words, drives all heresies far away from the Incarnation of the Word (the codex incorrectly has “the head’s hair”). For just as the nature of the body produces hair for its adornment in suitable moderation, so reason dictates an appropriate order of words for its own beauty.

“The house was filled with the fragrance”: that is, the world was filled with good repute.

### III

One of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, who was about to betray him, therefore said: “Why was this perfume not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” He said this not because he cared about the poor [Col. 1213C], but because he was a thief and, having the money box, carried what was put into it (John XII, 4–6).

Under the pretext of avarice he speaks a mystery of faith. For our faith is purchased, as it were, for three hundred denarii, through the ten senses, tripled through body, soul, and spirit. What is signified in ten tripled is signified in three hundred.

Let us therefore, taking upon ourselves, like Gideon, the number of the three hundred men, destroy the camps of the foreigners—the poor in spirit—with our little jars broken, together with trumpets and lamps; and, like Abraham with three hundred men, let us divide the spoils toward evening.

When Judas is called a thief, we are admonished to tolerate thieves and sacrilegious persons. Why did the Lord have a money box, unless because the Church was going to have a money box? Why did he admit a thief, unless so that the Church might tolerate thieves? Embezzlement is theft from the public treasury. Whoever steals something from the Church is compared with Judas the betrayer.

Concerning him alone, by synecdoche and in the plural number, they believe that what Mark says was spoken: “They grumbled against her.” “There were some who were indignant among themselves and said: Why has this waste of perfume been made?” (Mark XIV, 4–5). Some were indignant on behalf of the poor, perhaps persuaded by Judas’s words; Judas, however, was indignant on account of profit.

But Jesus, knowing this, said to them: “Why do you trouble the woman? She has performed a good work for me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you wish you can do good to them; but you will not always have me” (Matt. XXVI, 10–11; Mark XIV, 6–7).

He speaks to good and evil people about the presence of his body. For after he ascended into heaven he sits at the right hand of the Father, and according to the body he is not here (this does not seem to have been stated correctly); yet according to the presence of his majesty he is always here. If, however, you belong to the good, you always have Christ present through faith, through the sign, through the sacrament of baptism, and through the food and drink of the altar. Hence elsewhere he says to them: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

“By pouring this perfume upon my body, this woman has done it for my burial” (ibid. XXVI, 12). It is not a waste of perfume but a service for burial. The Lord’s patience does not accuse Judas of having spoken from avarice and not for the sake of the poor; rather, it commends Mary’s service.

What John says—“Leave her, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial” (John XII, 7)—is as though he were saying: “Let her do what she is doing, so that she may keep that deed in her heart until the day of my burial; then she will know that this service is an anticipation of my body’s burial.” Hence according to Mark it is said: “What she had”—that is, what she was able to do—“she did. She anticipated anointing my body for burial” (Mark XIV, 8), with “it must be understood that it is to be placed” being supplied (the codex incorrectly has “you should understand,” and likewise below). Thus he says: “Let her now prepare me for burial, according to the custom of the Jews, while she can; what she will then wish to do, she will not be able to do.”

“Amen I say to you, wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her” (ibid., 9); supply: “and what Judas spoke against her will be told to his disgrace.” She expended laudably what she had previously applied shamefully to herself as the fragrance of her flesh [Col. 1214C] (the codex incorrectly has “which she had applied shamefully”), while she was intent upon unlawful acts, before she became familiar with the Lord.

“In the whole world”: not so much this woman as the Church is preached. Consider his knowledge of future things: the Lord knew that, although he would suffer after a few days, his Gospel would be celebrated throughout the whole world. It should be noted that just as great a reputation as Mary acquired, Judas acquired just as great an infamy. But the Lord, rewarding what was good and worthy of praise, passed over in silence the future insults directed against the wicked man.

### IV

When Jesus was in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper (Mark XIV, 3), a great crowd of Jews learned that he was there, and they came not only because of Jesus but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead (John XII, 9). Curiosity, not love, brought them.

Simon had once been a leper, but at that time he was clean, because he had been healed by the Lord, while his former name still remained, just as Matthew is still called “the Publican,” although he had ceased to be a publican. Some understand Simon as signifying the faithful cleansed by the Lord from sins. For his name is interpreted as “obedient” or “clean.”

Through the sin of the first man, the earth became the house of Simon the leper. But the chief priests plotted to kill Lazarus, because many of the Jews were going away on his account and believing in Jesus (John XII, 10–11).

O foolish thought and blind savagery! If the one who could raise Lazarus could do so, would he not be able to raise the man who had been killed? When you inflicted death upon Lazarus, did you take power away from the Lord? But one thing seems to you to be a dead man and another a slain man. Behold, the Lord did both: he raised Lazarus, who was dead, and raised himself, who had been slain.

### V

On the next day the great crowd that had come to the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took palm branches and went out to meet him, crying: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel” (John XII, 12–13).

The palm branches are praises signifying the victory by which the Lord was going to overcome death by dying and triumph over the devil, the prince of death, by the trophy of the Cross.

The cry “Hosanna” is that of one entreating. So say some who know the Hebrew language: it indicates an emotion more than it signifies any particular thing, like the expressions that in Latin are called interjections. Thus, when grieving, we say “Alas!”; when delighted, “Ha!”; or when amazed, “O great thing!” At that point “O” signifies nothing except the emotion of the person expressing amazement. This should be believed to be the case because neither Greek nor Latin has been able to translate it, just as neither has translated the expression “who says to his brother, Raca” (Matt. V, 12). This too is said to be an interjection showing the emotion of one who is indignant.

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” This should rather be understood as “in the name of the Lord,” meaning in the name of God the Father, although it can also mean “in his own name,” since he himself is Lord. Hence it is written elsewhere: “The Lord rained from the Lord.” But his own words direct our understanding better: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me. Another will come in his own name; him you will receive” (John V, 43).

Christ is the teacher of humility: he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II, 8). He therefore does not lose his divinity when he teaches us humility. In the former he is equal to the Father; in the latter he is like us. By that in which he is equal to the Father, he created us to exist; by that in which he is like us, he redeemed us so that we would not perish.

The crowd sang these praises to him: “Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” What cross of mental anguish could the envy of the Jewish leaders endure when such a great multitude was proclaiming Christ its king?

But what did it mean for the Lord to be King of Israel? What great thing was it for the King of the ages to become king of human beings? Christ was not King of Israel in order to exact tribute, arm an army with iron, or visibly defeat enemies; he was King of Israel in order to rule minds, provide eternal care, and lead believers, those who hope and love, into the kingdom of heaven.

The Son of God, therefore, equal to the Father, the Word through whom all things were made, wished to be called King of Israel (the codex lacks *dici*, “to be called”). This is condescension, not promotion; a judgment of compassion, not an increase of power. For he who was called King of the Jews on earth is Lord of the angels in heaven.

### VI

Jesus found a young donkey and sat upon it (John XII, 14). This is stated briefly here, for how it happened is read at full length in the other evangelists. A prophetic testimony is applied to this event, so that it might become clear that the wicked Jewish leaders did not understand the one in whom the things they read were being fulfilled.

Jesus therefore found a young donkey and sat upon it, as it is written: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your king comes, sitting upon a donkey’s colt” (ibid., 15).

In that people, therefore, there was a daughter of Zion—that is, Jerusalem, which is Zion. In that people, I say, a rejected and blind people, there was nevertheless a daughter of Zion to whom it could be said: “Do not fear. Behold, your king comes upon a donkey’s colt.”

This daughter of Zion, to whom these things are divinely spoken, was among those sheep that heard the shepherd’s voice. She was among that multitude that praised the Lord who was coming with such devotion and escorted him in such a great procession. To her it was said: “Do not fear; recognize the one whom you praise, and do not tremble when he suffers, because that blood is poured out through which your offense is blotted out and life restored.”

But the colt of a donkey on which no one had sat—for this is what they found in the other evangelists—we understand as the people of the nations, who had not received the Lord’s law. The donkey, since both animals were brought to the Lord, signifies his people coming from the people of Israel: not entirely unbroken, but a people that recognized the Lord’s manger.

His disciples did not understand these things at first. But when Jesus was glorified—that is, when he displayed the power of his resurrection—they remembered that these things had been written about him (John XII, 16). Recalling, indeed, according to the utterances (*eloquia*) of Scripture what had been fulfilled before the Passion or in the Lord’s Passion, they found there also that, according to the prophetic utterances, he had sat upon the donkey’s colt.

### VII

The crowd that was with him therefore bore witness when he called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead. For this reason the crowd also came out to meet him, because they had heard that he had performed this sign.

The Pharisees therefore said among themselves: “You see that we accomplish nothing; behold, the whole world has gone after him” (ibid., 17–18). They prophesied, but without knowing it. Why should it be surprising if the world follows him through whom the world was made?

There were some Gentiles among those who had gone up to worship on the feast. These therefore approached Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying: “Lord, we wish to see Jesus.” Philip came and told Andrew . . . . . Andrew and Philip in turn told Jesus.

Jesus answered them, saying: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (John XII, 20–23). The Lord answered in this way to suggest that the fullness of believers would come after his Passion, when he had been glorified in heaven.

“Amen, amen I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (ibid., 25). He called himself the grain that was to be put to death through the unbelief of the Jews but multiplied through the faith of the nations. And because he specially compares himself to a grain of wheat, the Church’s custom arose of making the Lord’s body from this one grain alone.

“He who loves his soul will lose it, and he who hates his soul in this world preserves it for eternal life” (ibid.). He exhorts us to follow the footsteps of his Passion, as though he were saying: “If you desire to hold life in Christ, do not fear death for Christ. Do not love your soul in this life, lest you lose it in eternal life.”

A wonderful saying: how the love of a person for his own soul causes it to perish, while hatred prevents its perishing! If you have loved badly, then you have hated; if you have hated well, then you have loved. Blessed are those who hate in order to preserve, lest they lose by loving.

But take care not to wish to kill yourself in the meantime, as certain misguided people understand this verse. When the decisive moment comes, when it is proposed to you either that you do something against God’s commandment or that you die, then choose to die rather than to live, so that in this world you may hate your soul and preserve it for eternal life.

“If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John XII, 26). Hence Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps” (I Peter II, 21). “And where I am, there also will my servant be” [Col. 1217B] (John XII, 26). The reward for serving him is to be with him, without whom nothing is ever good and with whom nothing is ever evil.

Hence he adds more clearly: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him” (ibid.). With what honor, except that he may be with his Son—not equal in divinity, but joined to eternity?

When you hear, brothers, “There also will my servant be,” do not think only of good bishops and clerics. You too, according to your capacity, serve Christ by giving alms and preaching his teaching to those to whom you can. Every head of a household ought to exercise discipline over his own people by admonishing, teaching, correcting, and showing kindness.

### VIII

“Now my soul is troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour” (John XII, 27).

After foretelling the Passion and placing exhortation before it, as though he had given voice to his own strength, he implies the feeling of our weakness, which he truly assumed, but voluntarily and for our sake, so that we might not despair because of this weakness.

In this he also teaches what we ought to say and to whom we should flee if the soul is troubled. “What shall I say? Whom shall I invoke? Where shall I flee? In whom shall I hope?” In the Father who saves, whose will I place before my own, because for this reason I came to this hour: to suffer these things.

From this comes glorification both for me and for my members. This is what he says: “But for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name” (ibid., 27–28). “Save me from the hour of the Passion,” I ask, “but I do not refuse the Passion.” Therefore glorify me by raising me up, which is the glory of your name.

A voice therefore came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (ibid.). “I glorified it before I made the world”: that is, I begot him glorious, and I determined to glorify him in rational creatures.

Or in this way: “I glorified it when he was born from a virgin, worshiped by the Magi, recognized by the saints, revealed in the form of a dove, and transfigured on the mountain. I glorified it when he healed many, fed many from a few loaves, commanded the waves, and raised the dead. And I will glorify it again when he rises from the dead, ascends into heaven, and is recognized by all as judge, so that every knee may bow before him.”

The crowd standing by and hearing this said that thunder had occurred. Others said: “An angel has spoken to him.” Jesus answered and said: “This voice came not for my sake but for yours” (ibid., 30). He showed that the voice did not indicate to him something he already knew, but to those to whom it was necessary that it be indicated.

### IX

“Now is the judgment of the world; now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John XII, 31 ff.), and the rest.

Here “judgment” means the separation of the redeemed, not the condemnation by which he will condemn the wicked on the day of judgment. By “the prince of this world” he explains the judgment of which he spoke.

The devil had indeed been cast out from the righteous of former times, but what had then occurred among very few now occurred among a multitude through the preaching of the apostles.

It was fitting that Christ’s illumination should drive the prince of darkness out of the human being, because he had no right over him. For because, by malicious deception, he had alienated him from subjection to his Lord, he ought not thereby to have acquired any power over him; rather, if he had previously possessed any, he ought to have lost it. Whoever abuses a power granted to him deserves to lose the privilege.

Nor did God hand humanity over to him, nor could humanity hand itself over to him. For even if a servant flees from his own master, he cannot lawfully hand himself over to another.

Therefore, when the devil is said to have reigned as prince of this world from Adam until Christ’s Cross, this means that the children of Adam, oppressed by the heavy yoke of sin, readily consented to diabolical temptations. But the sacrifice of the Cross, pleasing to God the Father because of the love he poured into the human race, removed the slavery of sin, so that we might truly be free, because the Son set us free.

Hence the devil, envying humanity all the more and therefore deserving even greater punishment, nevertheless does not cease to tempt. But it is one thing to reign inwardly and another to attack outwardly. It is one thing to possess a captured city within, another to attack it with missiles hurled from a distance.

When the devil is called “the prince of this world,” he is not believed to be lord of heaven and earth. Rather, “the world” means the wicked people spread throughout the whole earth. We customarily call a house bad when wicked people are in it, and good when good people are in it. The world is also spoken of with reference to the good people spread throughout the world. Hence the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V, 19). The devil is cast out from these people.

### X

“And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.” He said this signifying by what death he was going to die (John XII, 32–33).

What are “all things” except those from which the devil is cast out? He did not say “all people,” but “all things,” because he did not refer this to the totality of human beings but to the integrities of creation: spirit, soul, and body—by which we understand, live, and are visible.

For he who said, “Not a hair of your head will perish,” draws all things after himself. Or, if “all things” means human beings, we can say that he draws all who are predestined to salvation. Or certainly he draws every kind of human being to himself as their head: in languages, ages, ranks of honor, varieties of intelligence, and professions of lawful arts.

“If I am lifted up,” that is, “when I am lifted up”; for he is not speaking doubtfully. He called the Passion upon the Cross an exaltation, and he looks back to what was said above, that the dead grain bears much fruit.

The crowd answered him: “We have heard from the law that the Christ remains forever. How then do you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?” (John XII, 34). They remembered what the Lord had said: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” For here he did not say, “If the Son of Man is lifted up,” but, “If I am lifted up.” They therefore thought that it was contradictory for Christ to remain forever and to be lifted up on the Cross.

### XI

Jesus therefore said to them: “There is still a little light among you. Walk while you have the light, so that the darkness of death may not seize you” (John XII, 35). Darkness exists if you believe Christ’s eternity in such a way that you deny the humility of his death.

Walk, therefore, from faith to faith, understanding everything: Christ both dying in order to redeem and living eternally in heaven in order to lead us there. “Walk,” he says, “while you have the light”—that is, advance in faith while I furnish you with the light of my words. Not to believe me will be the darkness of ignorance and eternal death.

“He who walks in darkness does not know where he is going” (the codex has “where he goes”). While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may be sons of light.

Jesus said these things, and he departed and hid himself from them (ibid., 35–36). He did not hide himself from those who had begun to believe, but from those who desired to kill him, consulting our weakness rather than detracting from his power.

In the same place: For Adam signified a great good before the great evil of transgression, lying and sleeping in a bodily form. And this second one, etc.

In the same place: As is the custom of the Jews to bury. This Joseph, a secret disciple of the Lord Jesus Christ, who was from the town of Arimathea, represented those who preserve chastity. For just as he deserved to carry the Lord’s body and place it in his own tomb, so those who possess chastity of body and soul deserve to receive Christ’s body and blood, according to the Apostle Paul: “Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat from the Lord’s bread and drink from the cup” (I Cor. XI, 28). For whoever receives one of these unworthily will be guilty of judgment.

And because it says: “Nicodemus also came, who had first come to Jesus by night, carrying a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds,” this should not be punctuated in that way, etc.

In the same place: But that he came afterward.

[Col. 1221A] In the same place: It is declared to nearly all the nations. Here Nicodemus represented the saints who were predestined: before baptism they were in ignorance, but they come to the Lord with a mixture of myrrh and aloes—that is, when they recognize themselves, they put their vices and desires to death, renounce the present age, deny themselves, and follow Christ.

And because the evangelist says that Nicodemus brought with him a hundred pounds and a mixture of myrrh and aloes—for the number one hundred is perfect, and the completeness of number is contained in it—he signified the perfect number of angels and human beings.

“Now there was a garden,” etc.

Id. Since it was the Parasceve, which the Jews call the “pure meal” and we Latins more commonly call the preparation [Col. 1221B], it was not permissible to do anything of that kind. For what else is understood by the garden than the Church of Christ? For the enclosed garden and sealed fountain (Song 4:12) is itself the Catholic Church. What, then, is signified by the tomb except the conscience of each person dwelling in the Church of God, where the body of Christ is laid? And because, as we said, it was called a new tomb [cod. “it is”] because no other dead person had been in it, so also the soul in which Christ dwells ought to be free from mortal sin, as from vices. The rest is missing.

## BOOK OF DIFFERENT QUESTIONS

Among the papers of D. Frangipane there is found a question said to supplement fol. 4 of volume VI of the Benedictine edition, but the location is not otherwise specified, and that vague reference does not seem correct. I have not been able to find this question among the works of Saint Augustine. It is as follows in Cassinese codex CLXII, fol. 20 verso.

### ON THE MAGICIANS OF PHARAOH

One ought not to be disturbed when miracles are sometimes performed by magical arts that resemble the miracles performed through the holy servants of God, just as it is written in Exodus that the magicians of Pharaoh performed certain things in a similar way [Col. 1225B] to Moses. We ought not, therefore, to be astonished at this, because everything that is done visibly is believed not absurdly to be capable of being done even through the lower powers of this air. But the difference is that, when the saints perform such things, the lower creature is commanded from the higher regions in the name of God, the Lord of all things. When evil people perform similar things by magical arts, they are delivered into the demons’ hands when their requests are granted by demons. For they are worthy to be deceived by such an answer, so that what they seem to obtain as a benefit becomes a punishment for them, when certain lower powers display miracles to them as though privately, in order to keep them subjected—though this occurs by permission of divine providence, so that such things are allotted to each according to the merits of their souls.

## FROM THE BOOK ON SUSANNA

[Col. 1225C] These excerpts are taken from the book on Susanna in Bede’s Commentary on Saint Augustine; nevertheless, after going through Augustine’s work, I did not find a book of this kind. I have therefore thought it proper to copy it here.

Why do the Hebrews reject the story of Susanna, saying that it is not contained in the volume of Daniel? We ought carefully to investigate the names *schini* and *prini*, which are interpreted in Latin as “holm oak” and “mastic tree,” to determine whether they exist among the Hebrews and what etymology they have, so that from *schini* one might say “cleaving,” and from *prini*, “cutting” or “sawing,” in their language. But if this is not found, we too will necessarily be compelled to agree with those who wish this passage to belong only to the Greek language, having only a Greek etymology and no Hebrew one [Col. 1225D]. But if someone should demonstrate an etymology in Hebrew for the cleaving and division of those two trees, then we shall also be able to accept this Scripture.

## QUESTION ON THE PROVIDENCE OF GOD

It is found under the name of Saint Augustine in codex CLXVIII, fol. 112 verso, and it is not unworthy of him, although it appears to be a mere fragment.

From this above all we should believe what piety proclaims: that a manifest judgment is to come. For now we see human prosperity and calamities shared indiscriminately by good and evil alike, as though without any judgment, whereas the justice of God—whose providence is so conspicuous in small matters—cannot possibly leave greater matters to drift about randomly without judgment. What is greater, not only in this human creature but also in the angelic creature, than that the evil should justly be punished with misery and the good should enjoy blessedness? What is now seemingly well for an evil person is a hidden punishment, a false happiness. But when things go badly for a good person [cod. “an evil person”], reward is not denied to piety; rather, the patience of piety is increased for greater rewards. Likewise, when at some time things go badly for an evil person even in this life, it is either correction or the affliction of sins; and when things go well for a good person, it is not the most certain joy of his heavenly homeland, but some kind of consolation in this dangerous pilgrimage.

If unbelieving impiety considered these and similar matters, it would not deny divine providence in governing and ordering human affairs. Nor would it persist in its own dark and deadly powers against the light and life of wisdom. Let the unbelieving person therefore attend to this: he cannot say that it was instituted by human beings, lest he deny that God gives order to human affairs—God who taught the little bee to arrange its honeycombs so wonderfully. Who, indeed, gave human beings the capacity to be offended by disorderly things and delighted by the order of things? Did they not find this in the nature of their own soul, which they themselves did not make?

For why, when order has not been discovered in human affairs, does he not believe that God governs human affairs, unless it is because he naturally knows how to prefer ordered things to disordered things [cod. “disordered things, and afterward ordered things”]? Does a human being therefore judge that arrangement rather than confusion is appropriate to divine works, while God has no ordered judgment concerning all human beings [Col. 1226C]—he who created the sense of order in each individual? Certainly, he has such a judgment. Piety does not doubt this, even though weakness does not comprehend it.

We praise the works of smiths, namely those that we are able to inspect; but we are astonished at the works of artisans, and unless they have been opened up and displayed, we marvel that they were able to accomplish what seems impossible. Why, then, do we rashly judge the judgments of God, and hasten to deny the order of divine work wherever we have not been able to see it, praising the providence of the Creator in the leaves of trees but not supposing it to exist in human affairs? Why do we not rather believe that the order of human affairs proceeds in an unfathomable and hidden way, an order which we are unable either to comprehend in its immensity or to observe in its concealment? Yet the manifest orders of things established by God, from which hidden orders are inferred [Col. 1226D], strike even the eyes of the impious.

## QUESTION ON HOW THE WISE PERSON USES THINGS

It is found in codex CLXVIII, fol. 113, under the name of Saint Augustine, in whose works one may see certain similar passages, *Questions on the Gospels*, Book II, no. 11.

Whoever uses passing things more sparingly than the customs of those with whom he lives require is either intemperate or superstitious. Whoever uses them in such a way as to exceed the limits of the customary practice of the good people among whom he lives either signifies something or is disgraceful. For in all such matters it is not the use of things but desire that is at fault. What, then, is appropriate to places, times, and persons must be carefully considered, lest we rashly condemn disgraceful conduct.

[Col. 1227A] It may happen that a wise person uses very costly food without any fault of desire or greed, while an unwise person burns with the flame of the foulest gluttony for the cheapest food. And it is better for a person to eat fish in the manner of the Lord than lentils in the manner of Esau, the grandson of Abraham, or herbs [the codex contains a word that cannot be read; we have conjecturally supplied “herbs”] in the manner of beasts. For most animals are not more temperate than we are merely because they are fed on cheaper foods. In all such matters, therefore, what we do is to be approved or condemned not from the nature of the things we use, but from the reason for using them [cod. “attend to”], and from the manner in which we desire them.

[Col. 1227B]

**Ibid.** For it was fitting, etc.

[Col. 1230A] **Cod.** Let us offer. The remainder is missing, and not inappropriately, up to the words: “Today, therefore,” etc.

**Ibid.** Who would make a son for God.

**Ibid.** And a woman poured him forth as a man on earth.

**Ibid.** In a mortal womb.

**Ibid.** Better, for the sake of the rhythm: “he received the emperor.”

**Ibid.** Christ is for us today.

**Ibid.** Defiled by no embrace. The chaste womb received the Holy Spirit; the innocent body brought him forth. Glorious virginity and splendid fruitfulness.

**Ibid.** The following differs in such a way that it seemed preferable to print it in full:

> “It was fitting that, at the Lord’s birth, chastity should rightly increase, and that integrity should not be violated by his coming—he who had come to heal what was corrupted. God is announced by angels, and the Lamb is shown to shepherds. No comforts arising from human solicitude were available to Mary in childbirth. Mary went forth relieved, the happier, and recognizes herself as a joyful mother, though she does not know herself as a wife. But as a woman who has borne a child, she marvels at the child’s origin; she rejoices that she has received the Holy Spirit; and she is not frightened because she has given birth unmarried, but, trusting in the one she has borne, she rejoices. Therefore we believe that great things are generated by great power. Rightly we venerate heavenly things at his coming, for we have learned that he came from heaven, and we have discovered that he was created through the power of God the Father and the Holy Spirit, so that divinity might be established within the womb of chastity. What virgin is so holy as this one through whom God deigns to come? What one so beautiful that she seeks God as her bridegroom? What one so strong that she can generate so great a power? What one so chaste that she is a virgin after childbirth? Did we not see, in the figure of Mary, the condition of the Church? She gives birth not to sorrow but to joy; she nourishes not with the breast of the body but with the milk of the teacher [cod. incorrectly “teachings”]. The first shepherds see the author of our light and the redeemer of all who believe. Wrapped in swaddling clothes, they marvel that he endures the loss of human association. These things had to be suffered at the birth [cod. “births”] by him who suffered to be born as a human being. All approve the angelic announcement; they proclaim an unbroken faith; they cry out to everyone that he is not merely what is seen, but that he is greater, since God was seen in a human being. This report runs everywhere through the peoples, and the faithful message of the birth penetrates the extended ears of all. Everyone speaks testimony to the truth, and what is proclaimed by pastoral eloquence [cod. “indulgence”] is not held to be doubtful. And the new miracle of the coming birth of our Lord Jesus Christ was first announced in the world to the shepherds [cod. “in the first places”]. For this reason, dearest ones, the Son of God deigned to assume a body of human frailty, so that God might conquer the devil from that same flesh which had been proud [Col. 1231A]. Your plans have therefore profited you nothing, enemy. Behold, we are free; behold, we remain secure in Christ. Your captivity brought us dominion. While you seek to destroy us, the Son of God has deigned to save us by his divinity; he defended us in such a way as to make us brothers, and loved us in such a way as to make us coheirs. Our Lord Christ lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”

There, in no. 2, in place of these words—“Therefore it is necessary that the one whom we see be of one substance with Christ,” etc.—the following is found: “Therefore it is necessary that the one whom we see be of one substance and one nature with Christ,” etc.

## SERMON CLXXXVI

It is read in Cassinese Codex XCIX, folio 229 verso, and likewise in Cassinese Codex CCCV, folio 102. After these words in no. 1—“Christ’s devout ascent”—the following is added: “Today we celebrate the sacrament of the Holy Spirit who visits us.” Then, after the further words “bestowing gifts of freedom upon servants,” the scribe adds several passages that are corrupt in Codex CCCV but clear in Codex XCIX. Their wording is as follows: “Well,” says he, “that friend of God, Tobias [Codex CCCV: Tobis; Codex XCIX: nobis], who was temporarily blinded, who, as though he did not possess light, nevertheless bestowed the light of righteousness, knew this when he said: ‘I was going,’ he says, ‘to the feast day of Pentecost, which is holy from the weeks.’ Likewise blessed Paul,” etc.

[Col. 1236A] ## SERMON CXCIX

It is read in Cassinese Codex CIX, folio 8 verso. There, in no. 3, in place of these words—“Here human speech is useless, brothers; the preacher’s discourse is silent, when,” etc.—it has: “Here human work is useless, brothers; speech is silent, the preacher’s preaching is mute, when,” etc.

## SERMON CCV

It is read in Cassinese Codex CIX, folio 8 verso. There, in no. 1, instead of “At the coming of the double festival,” it has: “The coming of the double festival.”

## SERMON CCXIX

It is read in Cassinese Codex XII, folio 39. There, in place of the words in no. 2—“A great miracle, a cruel spectacle”—the better reading is: “A great martyrdom, a cruel spectacle.”

[Col. 1236B] ## SERMON CCXXI

It is read in Cassinese Codex CXVII, folio 69.

**Edited text, no. 1.** “Therefore we magnify the martyrs, but especially those who, when Christ was born, confessed him at the very beginning—not by speaking, but by dying—and preceded the others into the eternal kingdoms. See,” etc.

The same. “Melchizedek. Properly they are placed beneath the altar,” etc.

[Col. 1236C] The same. “The first fruits of the martyrs for Christ.”

No. 4. “As it was said.”

The same. “They are honored among heavenly beings.”

Codex. “Therefore we magnify the martyrs, not because they endured severe punishments, but because they endured those punishments for the sake of righteousness. For we have seen many criminals suffer worse penalties. But these do them no good, because the cause justifies the martyrs, while conscience condemns the criminals. Therefore the blessed martyrs must be held in the highest and foremost place on account of faith. See,” etc.

The same. “Melchizedek. Properly the martyrs are placed beneath the altar, because Christ is placed upon the altar. Properly beneath the altar,” etc.

The same. “Who are the first fruits of the martyrs for Christ.”

The same. “As is fitting.”

The same. “They are honored among heavenly beings. Amen. The rest is missing.”

## SERMON CCXXVII

It is read in Cassinese Codex XII, folio 277.

## SERMON CCXXXI

It is read in Cassinese Codex CXXIII, folio 154, where there is much that is absent from the printed editions.

**Edited text, no. 1.** “He regenerates for salvation. This is,” etc.

No. 4. “Face to face. Then the blessed,” etc.

[Col. 1237A] The same. “Than the report that I heard. And truly,” etc.

The same. “It cannot be estimated. He will have,” etc.

[Col. 1236D] Codex. “He regenerates for salvation; through which Christ restores more by grace than nature begets, and he received the degenerate offspring of Adam the transgressor into the adoption of divine fatherhood, and made those disinherited from paradise co-heirs of heaven. This is,” etc.

The same. “Face to face. When, I say, each faithful and holy soul, in that age, full of the fruits of good works, has been presented before the divine sight, displaying in itself—or rather, itself as—an example for its God, bringing forth gifts worthy of heaven and powerful heavenly benefits, manifold gifts, jewels of mercy, pearls of righteousness, fragrances of various merits—that is, spices of compunction and sweet-smelling balsams of chastity—and bearing before it, as I said, exceedingly abundant gold, that is, imprinting within itself the complete and incomparable price of the merciful Redeemer, it takes up the voice of prophetic offering, to be inserted into the spiritual offerings of heart and body: ‘I will enter your house with burnt offerings.’ Then the blessed,” etc.

The same. “Than the report that I heard. O Lord, from your works [Codex: tribulations] I presumed to hope for great things, but I received greater things. The manifest sweetness that I behold surpasses the magnitude of my thought; the feeling of expectation exceeds understanding. And truly,” etc.

The same. “It cannot be estimated. A person will see his merits increase through the unsuspected generosity of rewards [Codex: decrease]. He will have,” etc.

## SERMON CCXLIX

That which will then be,” etc.

## SERMON CCLIII

It is read in Cassinese Codex XI, folio 2. There, in no. 1, in place of these almost unorthodox words—“Because he knows that we cannot return, we who fell through pride”—the following, more Catholic and more consistent with reason, is found: “Because he knows that we cannot return except through humility, we who fell through pride.”

## SERMON CCLXXVII

It is read in Cassinese Codex XII, folio 107, where it begins only with these words in no. 1: “The earth is the Lord’s,” etc.

**Edited text, no. 1.** “If you doubt, you have lost. Tithes,” etc.

[Col. 1238A] The same. “But if you do not have tithes from earthly produce, what the farmer has.”

The same. “Give back, because you deserved to be born. Thus, and the rest up to no. 2. Listen, then,” etc.

No. 2. “He does not demand a reward, but honor. He asks nothing of what is yours.”

The same. “And you think that you can deceive me: within your treasures and in your houses there will be plunder. You will give to an impious soldier,” etc.

The same. “And I will pour out my blessing upon you from above; and the fruits of your land will not be corrupted” [Col. 1238C].

No. 3. “Behold, the year is already finished; give back to the Lord the payment that brings forth fruit. Redeem yourself, man.”

The same. “You will lose both your life and its price. In vain you leave this to your wife, who perhaps will have another husband. In vain you leave this to your husband, woman, who perhaps desires to have another wife without delay.”

[Col. 1237D] Codex. “If you doubt, you have lost. Nevertheless, listen, unbeliever, while the Lord himself gives the account: ‘You shall offer,’ he says, ‘tithes of all your produce, and the Levite shall come, because he has neither a share nor a portion with you, and the resident alien, the orphan, and the widow; they shall eat and be satisfied, and the Lord your God shall bless you all the days of your life’ (Deuteronomy XIV, 28–29). Hear also the sacrament: ‘A libation is added to sacrifices.’ Tithes,” etc.

[Col. 1238A] The same. “But if you do not have tithes from all earthly produce, because you are not a farmer.”

The same. In place of these words it has the following: “Give back, because you deserved to be born.” To make you recognize that these things are true, the Lord thus previously instructs his priest, his agent: “‘You shall receive an offering from the children of Israel, which they shall give at their registration. They shall also give it for the redemption of their souls, and there will be no plague or disaster among them’ (Exodus XXX, 12). ‘This shall be the offering: everyone who comes from the twentieth year onward shall give an offering to God’ (ibid., 14). Behold, the lawful manner of offering. If you consider yourself, greedy old man [Codex: old men], you have scarcely ever lived for God. The same Lord also says: ‘Make atonement for your souls’ (Leviticus XVII, 11). And again to the priest: ‘Receive the money of the children of Israel, the offerings that they shall give for their atonement, and you shall give it for the work of the tabernacle of testimony’ [Col. 1238B], ‘so that it may be a memorial for the children of Israel and an atonement for their souls’ (Exodus XXX, 16). Listen, then,” etc.

The same. “He does not demand a reward, but honor; he is not nourished by offerings, but what we offer for salvation is the tax of our way [perhaps: of our tithe]. He asks nothing of what is yours.”

The same. “And you think that you can deceive me. The year has already been consumed, and you have brought my tithes into your treasures. Therefore, whoever you are, greedy man, who despises the divine commands, you will give to an impious soldier,” etc.

The same. “And I will pour out my blessing upon you from above until all good things abound for you; I will set them apart for your food, and I will not corrupt the fruit of your land.”

The same. “Behold, the year is completed, and another begins. Give back to the Lord the payment that brings forth fruit. Why do you pay Caesar? Caesar cannot make it rain. You, debtor, have nothing through Caesar with which to excuse yourself; in this way a share was also assigned to him, so that the tithe might not be denied to the Lord. For the Lord Christ says: ‘Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s’ (Matthew XXII, 21). Caesar is not a participant in God because he receives what is owed, nor is he named first; rather, Christ, mocking faithless people, preferred him [Codex: endured him] to religion. Redeem yourself, man.”

The same. “You will lose both your life and its price” [Codex incorrectly: “you have lost it”]. In vain you bequeath this to greedy heirs [Col. 1238D]; in vain to the wife you may perhaps marry; in vain you entrust these things to your husband, woman, who desires to take another wife [Codex incorrectly: “has begun to take”].

## SERMON CCCVI

It is read in Cassinese Codex XII, folio 117.

**Edited text, no. 1.** “Let us strive with all our strength to fulfill it.” Then no. 2 begins with these words: “And therefore,” and continues up to the middle of no. 4: “You, the shadows and mists of this age,” etc. [Col. 1239A] The codex contains the material presented here in their place.

No. 5. “Do I not return what I have received? I received earthly things; I shall return heavenly things; I shall give an eternal reward.”

The same. “I ask you, brothers” [Col. 1239C], “that these things be received in your hearts and thus benefit those who are pilgrims.”

[Col. 1238D] Codex. “Let us strive with all our strength to fulfill it. Dearest brothers, if we labor for our flesh, let us labor also for our souls. If we run for the sake of the flesh, we adorn the flesh and satisfy the flesh—which after a few years, or perhaps days, worms will devour in the tomb—how much more ought we not to despise our soul, which is presented to God and the angels in heaven? Let us consider, brothers, that when the flesh is satisfied with abundant delicacies and is excessively corrupted by plentiful wine [Codex incorrectly: wine], nourishment is provided for luxury and food is supplied and prepared for worms [Codex: of worms]. Again, I ask you, look at the tombs of the rich, and whenever you pass near them, consider and carefully observe: where are their riches? Where are their adornments? Where are their rings or earrings? Where are their precious diadems? Where is the honor of vanity? Where is the pleasure of luxury? Where are the spectacles, whether frenzied, bloody, or shameful? Surely all these things have passed away like a shadow. And if repentance has not come to their aid, only disgrace and crimes have remained forever. Consider carefully and look at the tombs of the proud, and recognize that nothing remains in them except ashes and the foul remains of worms. [Col. 1239B] Attend carefully to these things, therefore, man, and say to yourself—speak with yourself: ‘O wretched man! This person once also ran after desire. And this person, while he lived in the world, served lust; and behold, nothing remains of him except foul and horrible dust.’ If you wish to hear, O man, those very dry bones will be able to preach to you. The dust of another cries out to you from the tomb: ‘Why, unhappy one, do you run about so much for the desire of this world? Why do you submit your unhappy neck to pride or luxury? Why do you surrender yourself to serve the most cruel masters—that is, vices and crimes?’ The dead person cries out to you from the tomb: ‘You, the shadows and mists of this age,’ etc.”

The same. “Did I not return what I received? I received earthly things; I return heavenly things. I received things that pass away; I shall restore eternal things. I received what was mine; I return myself. I shall give an eternal reward.”

The same. “I ask you, brothers” [Col. 1239C], “that this admonition—or rather, this exhortation of ours—be received in your hearts and thus benefit those who are pilgrims.”

## Sermon on the Nativity of John the Baptist

(This is by Saint Fulgentius, in Combefis, vol. VII, folio 69, column 1.) [Patrologia, vol. LXV, col. 922.]

It is read in the Laurentian Library, Pluteus XIII, Manuscript VIII, folio 200 verso, where it differs in many respects from the printed editions.

Printed edition: “For the Church celebrates no day on which he assumed flesh; rather, it frequently observes the day on which, etc.”

Same place. “Saint John, filled with the Holy Spirit from the womb and in the womb, recognized him with joy and greeted him with the deepest reverence. Therefore a herald is sent, etc.”

Same place. “To proclaim the Savior.”

Same place. “And crooked things will be made straight, and rough things will become level roads.”

Same place. “All flesh will see the salvation of our God.”

Same place. “Humility is commanded to the mountains, and straightness and level ground are ordered for the higher roads and winding paths. A herald of faith is placed in human hearts, and human mortality is terrified. O [Col. 1248D] carnal weakness, what will you do at the coming of the most serene [possibly “most severe”] judge, when you begin to give an account of your deeds—yet now you do not wish to receive the preaching of so great a herald, who cries out and says: ‘Behold, the axe has already been placed at the root of the trees’; and: ‘Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire’? The sublimity of this herald at his birth appeared in the following way. While the mother was barren, the father had been appointed the most eloquent advocate for the people. But when the barren woman became fertile, the father was made mute and without a voice. During the time of his priesthood, when he entered the Holy of Holies on behalf of the people to offer incense to the Lord, behold, suddenly he saw Gabriel, that most intimate attendant of divine secrets, flying through the ether and standing in agitation among the altars. When he saw him with tranquil countenance, he encouraged the trembling man with this address: ‘Zechariah, do not fear; for your prayers have been heard,’ etc.”

Same place. “‘And my wife has advanced in her days.’ And the angel [said]: ‘Believe, Zechariah, the angel.’”

Same place. “To bring forth a son from the barren.”

[Col. 1249B] Same place. “I who stand before God.”

Same place. “To speak to you and announce these things to you.”

Same place. “In its proper time. O wondrous power! Zechariah does not believe that the barren woman will give birth at the Lord’s command, and by divine decree he deserved to receive the bond upon his tongue. The word is taken away from the father until the son is generated by the mother, etc.”

Same place. “He was astonished in the harp of the body, the instrument of the voice.”

Same place. “Zechariah denied the gift in his mind.”

[Col. 1249C] Same place. “He was wavering concerning the promised son, awaiting, etc.”

Same place. “Immediately he received fetters of silence in his mouth.”

Same place. “He signaled what he had bound by divine command. It is loosened, etc.”

Same place. “Thus the prophet is present in the light; from the maternal entrails a lamp is brought forth; there is uncertainty about the name; the father is asked what he should be called, and because he could not speak, he asks for tablets to receive. He wrote the name ‘John,’ [Col. 1249D] and immediately the knot of his voice was broken. And so that a name might be given to the Voice, the door of the voice, which had been closed, is opened. He begins, etc.”

Same place. “And the nativity of the son who had been made mute by unbelief granted the father the benefit of speech. The Voice, the Word, etc.”

Same place. “The Voice is born from a barren old man.”

[Col. 1254C] **ON PENANCE, THE SOUL’S FOOD, AND DIVINE SPEECH**

These fragments, which are read in codex CLXXIII, fol. 86, appear to be excerpts from various passages of Saint Augustine. Hence they are placed in the appendix.

### On Penance

I. Penance is present when and for the things for which we feel remorse, and when we are ashamed at their recollection or do not admit deeds similar to them.---

II. For as long as we are driven by delight in those things themselves or in things like them, let us recognize that we have not yet reached the end of repentance.---

III. But if harmful tickling and delight have been lulled to sleep by divine dew, let us not despair of being able to arrive there.---

IV. The sign of completed healing and repentance [Col. 1254D] is this: not only has no delight or tickling disturbed our mind, but not even the memory of past crimes.---

V. Yet this forgetting and obliteration of sins cannot rightly be obtained unless one first takes care to avoid and shun places, persons, and every occasion of sinning. For example, if someone grieves that he has been deceived through a harmful intimacy with some woman, he cannot proceed to satisfaction and the obliteration of his deception unless he has avoided their companionship.---

VI. This salutary forgetting is to be understood, in particular, of those sins which are punished by the Mosaic Law.---

VII. As for the lesser sins without which we cannot live, we must recall them daily through repentance before the eyes of our mind [Col. 1255A], saying: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12), etc.

### On the Soul’s Food

I. The soul’s food is contemplation of God. But it must be understood that, in order for the human mind to be nourished by divine contemplation, it must see itself with its own eye; that is, it must consider what and how great it is apart from the functions of the outward person.---

II. From there it should pass to contemplating the glory, ardor, and security of the blessed angels. For, aided by divine grace in these matters, the mind is able to expand itself more widely.---

II. From there it should pass to consideration of circumscribed light; that is, to consideration of the omnipotence of the Godhead. But in this consideration the mind must be disciplined, lest it imagine for itself any bodily likeness in [Col. 1255B] God. As long as it conceives some likeness, that is not God; but when it recognizes the substance of the Godhead as incomprehensible, ineffable, invisible, uncircumscribed, wholly present everywhere and excluded nowhere—this is God.

### On Divine Speech

I. God speaks in two ways: either through himself or through a subordinate creature. When through himself, the heart is taught without words, as in the passage: “The Spirit said to Philip,” etc. (Acts 8:29).---

II. But when through an angel, sometimes he speaks in words, as in: “I have glorified…” (John 12:28), etc.; sometimes through things without words, as when Ezekiel saw amber (Ezekiel 1:27); sometimes through words and things, as in the passage where the Lord, walking about, said to Adam: “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:8–9). Sometimes he speaks through an image shown to the eyes of the heart in imagination, as with Jacob’s ladder (Genesis 28:12); sometimes through an image shown bodily, as when Abraham saw three angels (Genesis 18:2); sometimes through a heavenly substance, as the voice from the cloud (Matthew 17:5); sometimes through an earthly substance, as through Balaam’s donkey (Numbers 22:28); sometimes through earthly and heavenly substances joined together.

The fire in the bush (Exodus 3:2) signified that the fiery Law would not consume the thorns of the Jews’ sins, or that the divine nature would assume the thorns of our mortality, while nevertheless that same humanity would neither be consumed nor changed. Sometimes he speaks through the hidden illumination of an angel, as in the passage: “The angel who spoke in me” (Zechariah 4:5), etc.

Human beings speak among themselves in ten ways [Col. 1256A]; in the same ways divine Scripture speaks of God. For we speak of substance, quality, quantity, relation, possession, position, place, time, action, and passion. And when we speak of God in these ways, sometimes we speak properly and sometimes relatively.

When we say that God is great, good, or acts, we speak properly. And this must be observed: for him, being and being great are not two different things, nor are being and being good different. God is good by the very fact that he is; by the very fact that he is, he is great.

He is spoken of relatively when we call him Father: he is related to the Son. Possession is spoken of metaphorically in God, as in: “The abyss as a garment” (Psalm 103:6), etc.; position, as in: “You who sit above the cherubim” (Psalm 79:2); place: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there” (Psalm 138:8), etc.; time, as in: “Your years shall not fail” [Col. 1256B] (Psalm 101:28); passion: “I have labored, bearing it” (Isaiah 1:14); and: “I repent of having made [—]” (Genesis 6:7).

In God’s nature, for whom being is always identical, change has no place, because nothing accidental exists in him. Creatures possess accidents, through which a change, whether great or of whatever kind, comes about. But in God, as it is written, there is no alteration (James 1:17), as Paul says: “There is not in him yes and no, but yes is in him” (2 Corinthians 1:19). And he says to Moses: “He who is has sent me to you” (Exodus 3:14).

## On the Books Against Heresies

These verses are present in codex CLXVIII, fol. 46, which contains various works, all attributed to Saint Augustine, as can be seen in his works. Yet I do not know how they can be ascribed to the holy Doctor. [Col. 1256C] This poem appears to have been written to be placed before two books dealing with heresies—perhaps the book *On Heresies* addressed to Quodvultdeus and the book *Against Five Heresies*.

If you wish to know how greatly lies corrupt  
and infect human life with evils,  
it is difficult to tell everything; nevertheless, let living zeal be present:  
from these twin books you will be able to learn it.

They deceive the wretched with various, pernicious [Note: A word seems to be missing, for example *dicta* (“sayings”) or something similar.] forms  
and promise that a new god can be made;  
or, by wicked art, they cast others somewhat lower down,  
so that they may lack their proper forms.

Here conceals wolfish rage beneath a sheep’s skin;  
there, with holy cunning, he covers a dog.

This one, excessively righteous, snarls with the ferocity of a lion  
[Codex: “snarling”];  
here one pretends to be holy, a deceitful little fox.

So that you may be able to avoid such great contagions of evil,  
read this book with devoted diligence.

For if by these men you have been crushed more wickedly,  
how disastrously you perish, image of the divine mind!

# AUGUSTINIAN VINDICATIONS

By de Noris. 571

Preface. Ibid.

**Chapter One.** The arguments by which some maintain that Saint Augustine’s doctrine of predestination and grace is difficult and obscure are refuted. The most holy judgment of Clement X, Supreme Pontiff, in favor of the holy Doctor. 575

**Chapter II.** Modern writers accuse the same doctrine of Saint Augustine of contradiction. They are refuted. 588

**Chapter III.** Modern writers accuse Saint Augustine’s doctrine against the Pelagians of excess. 593

§ I. What modern writers understand by “excess” is investigated. The testimonies of Saints Thomas and Bonaventure do not support them. Excess is wrongly charged against Augustine. 595

§ II. Whether Saint Augustine went too far when he wrote that concupiscence is contrary to reason and evil, and that the defect of human nature arose from original sin, but was not its natural good. 601

§ III. Whether Saint Augustine went too far in deriving the guilt of original sin from the countless miseries of human life. An eminent testimony of Thomas in favor of the Augustinian position. 616

§ IV. Whether Saint Augustine went too far when discussing the virtues of unbelievers. 620

§ V. Whether Saint Augustine, in asserting that infants are punished in hell with the mildest punishment of sensation, spoke excessively. 630

§ VI. Whether Augustine went too far when discussing the Old Law against the Pelagians. 670

§ VII. Whether Saint Augustine’s view of predestination to glory before any foreknowledge of merits was expressed excessively. 680

§ VIII. Whether Saint Augustine went too far in teaching that marital intercourse undertaken solely for pleasure is a venial sin. 682

**Chapter IV.** Modern writers wrongly attribute several errors to Saint Augustine. 685

§ I. Whether Saint Augustine erred in thinking that rational souls and angels are corporeal. 686

§ II. Whether the holy Doctor asserted that the sun and stars are living beings. 688

[Col. 1259] § III. Augustine is wrongly accused of error because he doubted the origin of the soul. It is shown that the holy Fathers remained with Augustine in that doubt for many centuries. 691

§ IV. Whether it was Saint Augustine’s view that baptized children cannot be saved without actually receiving the Eucharist. 701

§ V. That the holy Doctor did not err in explaining the Apostle’s statement, Romans 14:23: “Whatever is not from faith is sin.” The Catholic Church, the Roman pontiffs, and the Fathers approve Saint Augustine’s interpretation. 706

§ VI. Saint Augustine never held that lingering thoughts are merely venial sin, as modern writers falsely attribute to him. 712

§ VII. Whether Saint Augustine thought that baptism administered without intention is valid. 713

§ VIII. Whether Augustine said that the earth is not round and that there are no antipodes. 719

§ IX. Whether Saint Augustine’s view of the simultaneous creation of all things is erroneous. 720

§ X. That Saint Augustine did not err in asserting that original sin is the cause of reprobation. 723

§ XI. Whether Augustine erred in teaching that killing an attacker who intends death is unlawful. 735

§ XII. That Saint Augustine removed nothing concerning divine grace from the books written against the Pelagians when composing the books of the *Retractations*. 743

**Chapter V.** Modern writers produce the testimonies of thirty-five doctors—namely, pontiffs, cardinals, bishops, and others—against Saint Augustine; their reliability is examined. 745

§ I. The testimonies of Baronius and Sadolet are examined. The statements of Ludovicus Donius in favor of Sadolet and against Saint Augustine are refuted. 747

§ II. The statements of Saint Bonaventure and Cajetan are examined. 753

§ III. Cardinals Perron, Valerius, and Saint Charles Borromeo are cited less accurately than they should be against Saint Augustine. 754

§ IV. Those who slander Saint Augustine by claiming that he was sometimes too harsh toward free will are mistaken. 756

§ V. Those likewise are mistaken who say that Saint Augustine shifted toward Sabellius against Arius and toward Arius against Sabellius. 758

§ VI. The testimonies of those who accuse Saint Augustine of novelty are examined. 760

§ VII. The testimonies of Driedo, Taper, Medina, and Vallosillo produced against Saint Augustine are shown to have been falsified and not faithfully reported. 762

§ VIII. The testimonies of Viguier, Soto, Faber, and Horantius are discussed. 766

§ IX. The testimonies of John of Bologna, Arboreus, Aragon, Pennot, Estius, Vega, and Tostatus are examined. 768

§ X. The testimony of Dominic Bañez, exaggerated more strongly against Augustine, is examined. 773

§ XI. Saint Bernard is wrongly cited against Augustine by Annat. 782

§ XII. They set Saint Augustine against Augustine. 785

**Chapter VI.** The praises bestowed by the supreme pontiffs on Augustinian doctrine against the Pelagians are defended against the distorted interpretations of modern writers. 788

[Col. 1260] **Chapter VII.** The approval by the Apostolic See of Augustinian doctrine against the Pelagians is defended against the perverse interpretations of modern writers. 806

**Chapter VIII.** Modern writers limit the authority of Saint Augustine on the basis of a letter of Pope Saint Celestine. They are refuted. 818

**Chapter IX and Last.** One hundred and thirty-five insults, taunts, and censures directed by modern writers against Augustine are repelled by the same holy Doctor and by the holy Fathers. 531

# THREE TREATISES

Prepared in French by Merlin in defense of Saint Augustine. 883

Dedication letter. Ibid.

## FIRST TREATISE

Or, *The True Key to the Works of Saint Augustine*. 885

**First part.** Jansenius’s bad faith in citing Saint Augustine. The general principle of the Jansenist heresy falsely attributed by him to Saint Augustine. The false key to Saint Augustine’s works supplied by Jansenius. 889

**Second part.** The doctrine of the perfection of righteousness is the true key to Saint Augustine’s works against the Pelagians. 923

## SECOND TREATISE

Or, *Examination of Bayle’s Criticisms*. 989

**First part.** Examination of Bayle’s accusation that Saint Augustine gave way to laxity in morals. Ibid.

**Second part.** Examination of Bayle’s boast: “I have renewed my attack on Saint Augustine.” 993

**Third part.** Examination of Bayle’s efforts to destroy Saint Augustine’s objection to the pagans concerning the death of Lucretia. 1041

**Fourth part.** Examination of the passage that gave Bayle occasion to say that Saint Augustine was more fortunate than wise. 1045

## THIRD TREATISE

Or, *Dissertation on the Law of Moses*. 1053

**First part.** The state of the question between the apostles and the Jews. 1055

**Second part.** The state of the question between the apostles and the Manichaeans. 1061

**Third part.** The state of the question between Saint Augustine and the Pelagians. 1073

**Fourth part.** The state of the question between the defenders of the faith of the Council of Trent and the heretics of our own day. 1081
